shelves.title: Albumin & coronary calcium Deposit #7 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Does a lower serum albumin go with more coronary calcium and faster progression — and does LDL matter only when coronary calcium is present?
shelves.mesh: Serum Albumin · Coronary Artery Disease · Vascular Calcification · Atherosclerosis · Hypercholesterolemia · Disease Progression · Risk Factors · Longitudinal Studies
shelves.balance: Within the normal range, lower albumin goes with more coronary calcium and faster progression (Korea, Taiwan) — but the link is fragile: in the Taiwan cohort the coronary-calcium association disappeared once age was accounted for, and nothing on this shelf is randomized. The shelf’s strongest card is about LDL, not albumin: in 23,132 Danish patients, LDL predicted heart attacks and strokes only when coronary calcium was already present. Albumin here behaves as a marker travelling with age and inflammation — not a proven lever.

cards.headline: Djoussé 2003: Framingham — low albumin marked the patients who went on to heart attacks
cards.result: Djoussé L et al., Am J Cardiol 2003;91:485–488 (PMID 12586275). In the Framingham Offspring Study, 4,543 men and women free of myocardial infarction at baseline were followed a mean of 21.9 years; 221 men and 63 women developed myocardial infarction. Albumin was analyzed jointly with bilirubin (low = below the sex-specific 25th percentile for each). Read for its albumin arm — the reason this card sits on this shelf — low albumin (with high bilirubin) carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.15 (95% CI 0.82–1.61) in men: directionally higher risk, not statistically significant, and consistent with this shelf's working hypothesis that low albumin marks inflammation and the patients headed for events. The paper's own headline was the combination: low albumin with low bilirubin showed incidence of 118 vs 35 per 10,000 person-years and an adjusted HR of 2.18 (95% CI 1.47–3.23), with a reported synergy index of 1.7 (1.1–2.9) in men. That bilirubin synergy is recorded here as the paper's claim only: its mechanism is unclear, the interaction appeared in men and not women (P=0.015 vs P=0.72), and the developer holds it without endorsement. Observational throughout — background for a marker hypothesis, not evidence that raising albumin or bilirubin prevents infarction.

shelves.title: Chlorthalidone vs hydrochlorothiazide
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does chlorthalidone (long half-life, roughly 60 hours) give better cardiovascular, stroke, or mortality outcomes than hydrochlorothiazide (short half-life, roughly 6 hours) — and at what cost in potassium, sodium, and kidney effects?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension · Chlorthalidone · Hydrochlorothiazide · Diuretics · Sodium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Hypokalemia · Humans
shelves.balance: The head-to-head trial found no cardiovascular advantage for chlorthalidone over hydrochlorothiazide (HR 1.04, null) — but chlorthalidone lowers ambulatory and nighttime pressure more in small comparisons, and costs more potassium wherever it is measured head-to-head or matched (HR 1.38 in the trial, 1.70 in Ontario, 2.72 in LEGEND). The longer half-life buys pressure control, not proven outcome benefit — which is exactly what the developer’s individual-data paper is designed to test.

shelves.title: Potassium and blood pressure Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
shelves.question: Does potassium — as tablets, or as potassium-enriched salt — lower blood pressure, and does it prevent strokes, heart attacks, and death?
shelves.balance: Potassium lowers pressure modestly — about 4–5 mmHg systolic in meta-analyses, near 7 in untreated hypertension — but the one trial in high-normal pressure faded by 6 months, and the only hard-outcome win combined sodium cutting with potassium enrichment, so it doesn’t prove potassium tablets prevent strokes. The mechanism is plausible; the tablet benefit is pressure, not proven outcomes.

cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of oral potassium supplementation
cards.people: 23 trials, 1,213 participants
cards.result: Oral potassium lowered systolic blood pressure by 4.25 mmHg (95% CI −5.96 to −2.53; I²=41%) and diastolic blood pressure by 2.53 mmHg (95% CI −4.05 to −1.02; I²=65%)

shelves.title: Salt substitute and hyperkalemia (SSaSS)
shelves.question: Does potassium-enriched salt raise the risk of serious hyperkalemia?
shelves.balance: Checked in 20,995 people over 4.74 years and not found: serious hyperkalemia events 3.35 vs 3.30 per 1,000 person-years (RR 1.04), while the same trial cut stroke, major cardiovascular events, and death. A feared harm, looked for properly, that did not appear.

cards.headline: Neal 2021 (SSaSS): salt substitute — hyperkalemia checked and not found
cards.summary: Cluster-randomized trial, 20,995 adults in 600 villages — serious adverse events attributed to hyperkalemia 3.35 vs 3.30 per 1,000 person-years (rate ratio 1.04 ): the harm was looked for and not found.
cards.people: 20,995 adults from 600 rural Chinese villages
cards.result: Serious adverse events attributed to hyperkalemia 3.35 vs 3.30 per 1,000 person-years (rate ratio 1.04 , 95% CI 0.80–1.37) — the harm was looked for and not found; for context the same trial cut stroke (rate ratio 0.86 ), major cardiovascular events ( 0.87 ), and death ( 0.88 )
cards.watchOut: Open-label village-level trial in a high-risk rural Chinese population; people with known kidney disease or potassium-related risks were excluded
cards.source: Neal B, Wu Y, Feng X, et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:1067–1077, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2105675, PMID 34459569

shelves.title: Fish oil and atrial fibrillation: a dose-dependent harm?
shelves.question: Does taking fish oil (omega-3) raise the rate of atrial fibrillation in humans?
shelves.balance: High-dose omega-3 raises AF risk — about 25% relatively across the trials, roughly 1 extra case per 70–125 people treated at 4 g a day — and the risk climbs with dose: 4 g clearly, 1.8 g borderline, 840 mg no signal. The same 4 g of icosapent ethyl that cut heart events 25% in REDUCE-IT raised AF hospitalization from 2.1% to 3.1% — yet stroke was still lower overall. EVAPORATE, the 80-patient plaque trial, reported no AFib signal because it was far too small to see one.

cards.headline: 4 g of icosapent ethyl: heart events down 25%, AF up from 3.9% to 5.3%.
cards.summary: Primary composite 17.2% vs 22.0% (HR 0.75, 0.68–0.83, p<0.001) . AF: 5.3% vs 3.9% (p=0.003) ; AF/flutter requiring hospitalization 3.1% vs 2.1% (p=0.004) — 8,179 patients, median follow-up 4.9 years.
cards.people: 8,179 statin-treated patients with elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL) and established CVD or diabetes + ≥2 risk factors; median follow-up 4.9 years
cards.result: Primary composite (CV death, MI, stroke, revascularization, unstable angina) 17.2% vs 22.0% (HR 0.75, 0.68–0.83, p<0.001) . AF: 5.3% vs 3.9% (p=0.003) ; AF/flutter requiring hospitalization 3.1% vs 2.1% (p=0.004)
cards.watchOut: Despite more AFib, stroke was lower with icosapent ethyl (HR 0.72, 0.55–0.93). Placebo was mineral oil The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. N Engl J Med 2019;380:11–22. PMID 30415628
cards.search: reduce-it bhatt 2019 icosapent ethyl fish oil omega-3 atrial fibrillation af triglycerides cardiovascular events new england journal pmid 30415628

cards.headline: 4 g of mixed EPA/DHA: no heart benefit, new AF 2.2% vs 1.3%.
cards.summary: Primary composite HR 0.99 (0.90–1.09) — no benefit. New-onset AF 2.2% vs 1.3% (HR 1.69, 1.29–2.21, p<0.001) — 13,078 patients, median 42 months.
cards.people: 13,078 high-risk patients on statins, elevated TG, low HDL; median 42 months
cards.result: Primary composite HR 0.99 (0.90–1.09) — no benefit. New-onset AF 2.2% vs 1.3% (HR 1.69, 1.29–2.21, p<0.001) . Trial stopped early for futility and the AF signal
cards.watchOut: Corn-oil placebo; EPA+DHA mixture, not EPA alone The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. JAMA 2020;324(22):2268–2280. PMID 33190147

cards.headline: 1.8 g after a heart attack in older patients: AF 7.2% vs 4.0%, not quite significant.
cards.summary: Primary composite 21.4% vs 20.0% (HR 1.07, 0.82–1.41) — no benefit. New-onset AF 7.2% vs 4.0% (HR 1.84, 0.98–3.45, p=0.06) — 1,027 patients, mean age ~75, 2 years.
cards.people: 1,027 patients, mean age ~75, recent MI; 1.8 g/d EPA+DHA (930 mg EPA + 660 mg DHA) vs corn oil, 2 years
cards.result: Primary composite 21.4% vs 20.0% (HR 1.07, 0.82–1.41) — no benefit. New-onset AF 7.2% vs 4.0% (HR 1.84, 0.98–3.45, p=0.06) — a near-doubling that missed significance; AF was the key secondary endpoint
cards.watchOut: A 2023 secondary analysis counting brief (“micro”) AF episodes found 11.9% vs 6.5% (HR 1.90, 1.16–3.11, p=0.011), with the rise in serum EPA explaining 65% of the association The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: 840 mg a day: no AF signal — 3.7% vs 3.4%.
cards.summary: Incident AF 469 (3.7%) vs 431 (3.4%); HR 1.09 (0.96–1.24), p=0.19 — no significant difference. 7.2 vs 6.6 per 1,000 person-years — 25,119 people, median 5.3 years.

cards.result: Incident AF 469 (3.7%) vs 431 (3.4%); HR 1.09 (0.96–1.24), p=0.19 — no significant difference. 7.2 vs 6.6 per 1,000 person-years
cards.watchOut: AF was the primary outcome here — the only trial designed to test it — but the dose was the standard supplement dose, not the 4 g pharmaceutical dose The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: 81,210 patients, 7 trials: omega-3 raises AF 25%, and the risk climbs with dose.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (≥500 patients, ≥1 year follow-up)
cards.people: 81,210 patients, 7 trials, mean age 65, median follow-up 4.9 years; AF in 2,905 (3.6%)
cards.watchOut: AF was not the primary outcome in most included trials; ascertainment varied The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Gencer B et al. Circulation 2021;144:1981–1990. PMID 34612056

cards.headline: 35 trials, 114,592 people: the AF risk lives in high-risk patients on high doses.
cards.summary: Only high CVD risk + high dose (>1500 mg/d) showed a significant AF increase: pooled OR 1.43 (1.14–1.79) , absolute risk difference 0.8% (0.40–1.1%) . Other strata not significant.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (RCTs ≥500 mg/d EPA+DHA, ≥12 months, age ≥50)
cards.people: 35 RCTs, 37 datasets, 114,592 individuals
cards.result: Only high CVD risk + high dose (>1500 mg/d) showed a significant AF increase: pooled OR 1.43 (1.14–1.79) , absolute risk difference 0.8% (0.40–1.1%) . Other strata not significant: high-risk low-dose OR 1.07, low-risk low-dose 1.06, low-risk high-dose 1.03
cards.watchOut: Pooled published and investigator-provided unpublished AF data — the authors' stated method to reduce selective reporting; low-dose omega-3 did not raise AF risk even in high-risk patients The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Abuknesha NR et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2026. PMID 42517224

cards.headline: EVAPORATE's 80 patients: no AFib reported — and the developer has asked the author.
cards.summary: No AFib signal is reported in the published EVAPORATE results — 80 patients, 18 months. At 80 patients the trial could not detect one; the developer has written to the trial's author to ask whether any AFib occurred.
cards.people: 80 patients with coronary atherosclerosis (≥20% stenosis), on statins, TG 135–499 mg/dL; 18 months; icosapent ethyl 4 g/day vs mineral oil.
cards.result: No AFib signal is reported in the published EVAPORATE results (final Eur Heart J 2020; interim Cardiovasc Res 2021). At 80 patients over 18 months the trial could not detect one — at REDUCE-IT's rates roughly 2 events per arm would be expected. The developer has written to the trial's author to ask whether any AFib occurred.
cards.watchOut: The trial's headline plaque result — low-attenuation plaque −17% vs +109% on placebo — is not an AFib finding, and the placebo was mineral oil: the +109% progression may exceed natural history, so part of the apparent benefit may be the placebo arm getting worse rather than the drug arm getting better. This shelf is about AFib, not plaque. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Budoff MJ et al. Eur Heart J 2020;41:3925–3932. PMID 32860032; interim: Cardiovasc Res 2021. PMID 32609331
cards.search: evaporate budoff 2020 icosapent ethyl coronary plaque ccta atrial fibrillation afib context card european heart journal pmid 32860032 pmid 32609331

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure, across the ejection-fraction spectrum
shelves.question: Do SGLT2 inhibitors improve outcomes in established heart failure — reduced and preserved ejection fraction, with and without diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides · Hospitalization · Stroke Volume · Humans
shelves.balance: Three positive trials spanning reduced to preserved ejection fraction. The hospitalization benefit is uniform; the mortality benefit is clear in reduced-ejection-fraction disease and fades as ejection fraction rises.

cards.headline: Dapagliflozin reduced worsening heart failure and cardiovascular death in HFrEF — diabetic or not.
cards.summary: DAPA-HF — primary composite 16.3% vs 21.2% (HR 0.74); cardiovascular death 9.6% vs 11.5% (HR 0.82); effects similar with and without type 2 diabetes — 4,744 patients.
cards.people: 4,744 patients with NYHA class II–IV heart failure and ejection fraction ≤40%; median follow-up 18.2 months
cards.result: Primary composite (worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death) 16.3% vs 21.2% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.85); worsening heart failure HR 0.70; cardiovascular death 9.6% vs 11.5% (HR 0.82); death from any cause HR 0.83. Effects were similar with and without type 2 diabetes
cards.watchOut: A heart-failure trial, not a diabetes trial — about 58% of participants did not have diabetes at baseline
cards.source: McMurray JJV, et al.; DAPA-HF Trial Committees and Investigators. Dapagliflozin in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction. N Engl J Med. 2019;381:1995–2008. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1911303. PMID 31535829 · NCT03036124.

cards.headline: Empagliflozin cut heart-failure hospitalizations in HFrEF; the mortality difference was not significant.
cards.summary: EMPEROR-Reduced — primary composite 19.4% vs 24.7% (HR 0.75); total heart-failure hospitalizations HR 0.70; cardiovascular death HR 0.92, not significant — 3,730 patients.
cards.people: 3,730 patients with NYHA class II–IV heart failure and ejection fraction ≤40%; median follow-up 16 months
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death or hospitalization for worsening heart failure) 19.4% vs 24.7% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65–0.86); total heart-failure hospitalizations HR 0.70; cardiovascular death HR 0.92 (not significant); the annual eGFR decline was slower on empagliflozin (−0.55 vs −2.28 ml/min/1.73 m²/year)

shelves.title: Statins after ASCVD: the secondary-prevention trials
shelves.question: In patients with established ASCVD, does a statin — and driving LDL lower still — reduce deaths and further events?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Disease · Myocardial Infarction · Anticholesteremic Agents · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: Four trials, three decades, one direction: after ASCVD, statins cut deaths (4S, HPS), and driving LDL lower with high-intensity therapy cuts events further (TNT, PROVE-IT). This is the trial record under the Class 1, Level A recommendation for high-intensity statin in secondary prevention. (Panel position: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: The first statin trial to cut deaths: 8.2% vs 11.5% over 5.4 years.
cards.summary: 4S 1994 — all-cause mortality 8.2% vs 11.5% (RR 0.70 , P=0.0003); major coronary events RR 0.66 ; LDL −35% — 4,444 patients with prior MI or angina.
cards.people: 4,444 patients (35–70 y) with prior myocardial infarction or angina and serum cholesterol 5.5–8.0 mmol/L (212–309 mg/dL); simvastatin 20 mg titrated to 40 mg vs placebo; median follow-up 5.4 years
cards.result: Deaths 182 (8.2%) simvastatin vs 256 (11.5%) placebo — relative risk 0.70 (95% CI 0.58–0.85) , P=0.0003. Major coronary events RR 0.66 (0.59–0.75) ; LDL cholesterol fell 35%
cards.watchOut: Enrolled cholesterol was high by modern standards, and the comparison is a moderate statin dose against placebo, not against another statin
cards.source: Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study Group. Randomised trial of cholesterol lowering in 4444 patients with coronary heart disease: the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study (4S). Lancet. 1994;344(8934):1383–1389. PMID 7968073.

cards.headline: Simvastatin cut deaths and first major vascular events in 20,536 high-risk patients — at every starting LDL.
cards.summary: HPS 2002 — all-cause mortality 12.9% vs 14.7% (rate ratio 0.87 ); first major vascular event 19.8% vs 25.2% (rate ratio 0.76 ) — simvastatin 40 mg vs placebo, 5 years.
cards.people: 20,536 UK adults aged 40–80 with coronary disease, other occlusive arterial disease, or diabetes; simvastatin 40 mg daily vs placebo for 5 years
cards.result: All-cause mortality 12.9% vs 14.7% (rate ratio 0.87 ); first major vascular event 19.8% vs 25.2% (rate ratio 0.76 ). The proportional benefit was similar at every starting LDL, including LDL below 100 mg/dL

shelves.title: A statin for diabetes, risk score or not
shelves.question: Should adults 40–75 with diabetes take a statin even when their LDL and their calculated risk look unremarkable?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: In diabetes, the benefit does not wait for a high LDL or a high risk score: CARDS enrolled patients with unremarkable cholesterol and still cut first events by more than a third, HPS found the same proportional gain with or without prior disease, and the trialists’ pooled analysis shows the per-mmol benefit in diabetes equals everyone else’s. That record is why the statin in diabetes 40–75 is Class 1, Level A regardless of calculated risk. (Panel position: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: In type 2 diabetes with ordinary cholesterol, atorvastatin cut first events by 37% — and the trial stopped early.
cards.summary: CARDS 2004 — primary composite 5.8% vs 9.0% (HR 0.63 , 0.48–0.83); stroke HR 0.52 ; all-cause mortality HR 0.73, not significant — 2,838 patients with type 2 diabetes, no prior CVD.
cards.people: 2,838 patients aged 40–75 with type 2 diabetes, no documented prior CVD, LDL-cholesterol 4.14 mmol/L (160 mg/dL) or lower, and at least one additional risk factor (retinopathy, albuminuria, current smoking, or hypertension); atorvastatin 10 mg vs placebo; median follow-up 3.9 years
cards.result: Primary composite (acute coronary heart disease events, coronary revascularisation, stroke) 5.8% vs 9.0% — HR 0.63 (0.48–0.83) . Stroke HR 0.52 . All-cause mortality HR 0.73 (P=0.059) — not significant, stated plainly
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped about 2 years early for benefit, and its mortality difference did not reach significance
cards.source: Colhoun HM, Betteridge DJ, Durrington PN, et al; CARDS Investigators. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with atorvastatin in type 2 diabetes in the Collaborative Atorvastatin Diabetes Study (CARDS): multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2004;364(9435):685–696. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(04)16895-5. PMID 15325833.

cards.headline: Among 5,963 people with diabetes, simvastatin cut major coronary events from 12.6% to 9.4%.

cards.people: 5,963 UK adults aged 40–80 with diabetes — about half without prior occlusive arterial disease — within the Heart Protection Study; simvastatin 40 mg vs placebo over 5 years; average LDL difference 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL)

cards.headline: Pooled across 14 trials: each 1 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) of LDL lowering cut major vascular events 21% in diabetes.
cards.summary: CTT diabetes meta-analysis 2008 — per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction: major vascular events RR 0.79 , all-cause mortality RR 0.91 , vascular mortality RR 0.87 — 18,686 people with diabetes in 14 randomised trials.

shelves.title: Primary prevention at intermediate and high risk
shelves.question: In people without prior cardiovascular disease, who gains from a statin — and how much does the choice of population change the size of the win?
shelves.mesh: Hypercholesterolemia · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Disease · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Anticholesteremic Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Primary prevention works, and the size of the win tracks how the patients were chosen: −31% in high-LDL men (WOSCOPS), −36% in hypertensive patients with risk factors (ASCOT-LLA), −44% in an inflammation-selected trial stopped early (JUPITER), −24% in unselected intermediate risk (HOPE-3). The relative benefit is consistent; the absolute benefit is the baseline risk — which is why the recommendation is written around risk, not cholesterol alone. (Panel position: 2018 cholesterol / 2019 primary prevention guidelines, COR 1 LOE A at intermediate risk — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: In high-cholesterol men without prior MI, pravastatin cut nonfatal MI or CHD death by 31%.
cards.summary: WOSCOPS 1995 — nonfatal MI or CHD death 5.5% vs 7.9% (P<0.001); all-cause mortality 3.2% vs 4.1% (P=0.051, borderline) — 6,595 men aged 45–64, about 4.9 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 1995
cards.people: 6,595 men aged 45–64 with hypercholesterolaemia and no history of myocardial infarction; pravastatin 40 mg vs placebo; mean follow-up 4.9 years
cards.result: Nonfatal myocardial infarction or death from coronary heart disease 5.5% vs 7.9% (P<0.001) — a 31% relative reduction. All-cause mortality 3.2% vs 4.1% (P=0.051) — borderline, stated plainly
cards.watchOut: Men only, with markedly high cholesterol (mean total cholesterol 7.0 mmol/L (≈271 mg/dL)) — not today’s intermediate-risk population
cards.source: Shepherd J, Cobbe SM, Ford I, et al; West of Scotland Coronary Prevention Study Group. Prevention of coronary heart disease with pravastatin in men with hypercholesterolemia. N Engl J Med. 1995;333(20):1301–1307. PMID 7566020.

cards.headline: In hypertensive patients with average cholesterol, atorvastatin cut nonfatal MI and fatal CHD by 36%.
cards.summary: ASCOT-LLA 2003 — nonfatal MI or fatal CHD 1.9% vs 3.0% (100 vs 154 events; HR 0.64 , 0.50–0.83); stopped early at a median 3.3 years — 10,305 hypertensive patients with at least 3 risk factors.

cards.people: 10,305 hypertensive patients aged 40–79 with at least three additional cardiovascular risk factors and non-fasting total cholesterol 6.5 mmol/L (≈252 mg/dL) or less; atorvastatin 10 mg vs placebo; stopped early, median follow-up 3.3 years
cards.result: Nonfatal myocardial infarction or fatal CHD 1.9% vs 3.0% — 100 vs 154 events, HR 0.64 (0.50–0.83) , P=0.0005. Fatal and nonfatal stroke HR 0.73 . All-cause mortality HR 0.87 — not significant

shelves.title: Blocking the renin-angiotensin system in HFrEF: ACE inhibitor, ARB, ARNI
shelves.question: Does blocking the renin-angiotensin system — ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI — save lives in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Enalapril · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Neprilysin · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Each generation of renin-angiotensin blockade beat the last standard: enalapril cut deaths in the sickest patients (CONSENSUS) and then in ordinary HFrEF (SOLVD), candesartan covered the ACE-intolerant (CHARM-Alternative), and adding neprilysin inhibition beat enalapril itself by a fifth (PARADIGM-HF). Four trials, four decades, same pathway — which is why an ARNI, ACE inhibitor, or ARB is Class 1, Level A for every patient with HFrEF. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: In NYHA class IV heart failure, enalapril cut 6-month mortality from 44% to 26%.
cards.summary: CONSENSUS 1987 — mortality at 6 months 26% vs 44% ; at 1 year 36% vs 52% — 253 patients with severe (NYHA IV) heart failure, enalapril vs placebo.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 1987
cards.people: 253 patients with NYHA class IV heart failure (127 enalapril, 126 placebo), on conventional therapy including digoxin, diuretics and other vasodilators; follow-up averaged 188 days
cards.result: Mortality at 6 months 26% vs 44% — a 40% reduction (P=0.002); at 1 year 36% vs 52% — a 31% reduction (P=0.001). The entire mortality benefit was in deaths from progressive heart failure; no difference in sudden cardiac death
cards.watchOut: The sickest population ever randomised to this question — NYHA IV only; hypotension requiring withdrawal occurred in 7 enalapril patients and none on placebo
cards.source: The CONSENSUS Trial Study Group. Effects of enalapril on mortality in severe congestive heart failure. Results of the Cooperative North Scandinavian Enalapril Survival Study (CONSENSUS). N Engl J Med. 1987;316(23):1429–1435. DOI 10.1056/NEJM198706043162301. PMID 2883575.

cards.headline: In ordinary HFrEF, enalapril cut mortality from 39.7% to 35.2% over 41 months.
cards.summary: SOLVD Treatment 1991 — mortality 35.2% vs 39.7% (risk reduction 16% , P=0.0036); death or HF hospitalisation reduced 26% — 2,569 patients, EF ≤35%, mostly NYHA II–III.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 1991
cards.people: 2,569 patients with EF ≤0.35, about 90% in NYHA classes II–III; enalapril 2.5–20 mg daily vs placebo; follow-up averaged 41.4 months
cards.result: Deaths 452 (35.2%) enalapril vs 510 (39.7%) placebo — risk reduction 16% (95% CI 5–26), P=0.0036. Death or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure: 613 vs 736 — risk reduction 26% (P<0.0001). The largest mortality reduction was in deaths from progressive heart failure
cards.watchOut: Little apparent effect on deaths classified as due to arrhythmia without pump failure
cards.source: The SOLVD Investigators. Effect of enalapril on survival in patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fractions and congestive heart failure. N Engl J Med. 1991;325(5):293–302. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199108013250501. PMID 2057034.

cards.headline: For the ACE-intolerant, candesartan cut CV death or HF hospitalisation from 40.0% to 33.0%.
cards.summary: CHARM-Alternative 2003 — CV death or HF hospitalisation 33.0% vs 40.0% (unadjusted HR 0.77 ; covariate-adjusted HR 0.70 ) — 2,028 patients, EF ≤40%, intolerant to ACE inhibitors.

cards.headline: Sacubitril-valsartan beat enalapril itself: primary outcome 21.8% vs 26.5%.
cards.summary: PARADIGM-HF 2014 — primary (CV death or HF hospitalisation) 21.8% vs 26.5% (HR 0.80 ); CV death 13.3% vs 16.5% (HR 0.80 ); all-cause death 17.0% vs 19.8% (HR 0.84 ) — 8,442 patients; stopped early.

shelves.title: Beta-blockers in HFrEF: the drug class doctors feared
shelves.question: Do beta-blockers — once considered dangerous in heart failure — reduce mortality in HFrEF?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Carvedilol · Bisoprolol · Metoprolol · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Beta-blockers were once considered dangerous in heart failure; four randomized programs then showed the same ~35% mortality reduction, in mild disease and in the sickest patients, with three different molecules. When a feared drug class reproduces like that, it stops being controversial — bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate are Class 1, Level A. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Carvedilol cut mortality from 7.8% to 3.2% — a 65% reduction so large it was doubted.
cards.summary: US Carvedilol program 1996 — mortality 3.2% vs 7.8% , a 65% relative reduction; the program stopped early — 1,094 patients, EF ≤35%, across four linked protocols.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled program of four linked protocols, N Engl J Med 1996
cards.people: 1,094 patients with chronic heart failure and EF ≤0.35 (696 carvedilol, 398 placebo), stratified by exercise capacity, on background digoxin, diuretics and an ACE inhibitor; follow-up 6 months (12 months in the mild-heart-failure protocol)
cards.result: Mortality 3.2% carvedilol vs 7.8% placebo — a 65% relative reduction (95% CI 39–80); the combined risk of death or hospitalisation for cardiovascular reasons fell 38%. The program was stopped early
cards.watchOut: Small and short, with mortality observed across four symptom-focused protocols — a result so large it was initially doubted. The three trials that follow on this shelf are the confirmation
cards.source: Packer M, Bristow MR, Cohn JN, et al; U.S. Carvedilol Heart Failure Study Group. The effect of carvedilol on morbidity and mortality in patients with chronic heart failure. N Engl J Med. 1996;334(21):1349–1355. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199605233342101. PMID 8614419.

cards.headline: Bisoprolol cut all-cause mortality from 17.3% to 11.8% in NYHA III–IV heart failure.
cards.summary: CIBIS-II 1999 — all-cause mortality 11.8% vs 17.3% (HR 0.66 ); sudden death 3.6% vs 6.3% (HR 0.56 ) — 2,647 patients, EF ≤35%; stopped at the second interim analysis.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, Lancet 1999
cards.people: 2,647 patients in NYHA class III or IV with EF ≤35%, on standard therapy with diuretics and ACE inhibitors; bisoprolol titrated to a maximum of 10 mg daily vs placebo; mean follow-up 1.3 years
cards.result: All-cause mortality 156 (11.8%) bisoprolol vs 228 (17.3%) placebo — HR 0.66 (0.54–0.81) , P<0.0001. Sudden deaths 48 (3.6%) vs 83 (6.3%) — HR 0.56 (0.39–0.80) . Treatment effects were independent of the severity and cause of heart failure

cards.headline: In severe heart failure — EF under 25% — carvedilol cut the risk of death by 35%.

shelves.title: Mineralocorticoid antagonists: the third pillar, with a guardrail
shelves.question: Do mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — and what does the potassium guardrail cost?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Spironolactone · Eplerenone · Myocardial Infarction · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Three trials, three severity levels — post-MI, mild symptoms, severe disease — and the class cut deaths in all three, which is what Class 1, Level A means in practice. The guardrail is part of the evidence: every positive trial ran with potassium and renal monitoring and exclusions, and when real-world prescribing skipped the monitoring after RALES, hyperkalemia hospitalizations and deaths rose sharply (Juurlink 2004, observational — named in this note, not carded). The drug works; the surveillance is not optional. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: In severe heart failure, spironolactone cut mortality from 46% to 35%.
cards.summary: RALES 1999 — all-cause mortality 35% vs 46% (RR 0.70 , P<0.001); hospitalisation for worsening heart failure reduced 35% (RR 0.65 ) — 1,663 patients, NYHA III–IV, EF ≤35%; stopped early at a mean of 24 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 1999
cards.people: 1,663 patients with severe heart failure (NYHA class III–IV, EF ≤35%) receiving an ACE inhibitor, a loop diuretic and, in most cases, digoxin; spironolactone 25 mg daily vs placebo; patients with serum potassium >5.0 mmol/L or creatinine >2.5 mg/dL were excluded; the trial was stopped early, mean follow-up 24 months
cards.result: Deaths 284 (35%) spironolactone vs 386 (46%) placebo — RR 0.70 (0.60–0.82) , P<0.001, from reductions in both death from progressive heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Hospitalisation for worsening heart failure fell 35% (RR 0.65 ), and NYHA class improved on spironolactone while it worsened on placebo
cards.watchOut: Harm: gynecomastia or breast pain in 10% of men on spironolactone vs 1% on placebo. Serious hyperkalemia was rare in the trial ( 2% vs 1% , not significant) — but only under the trial’s potassium and renal exclusions and its monitoring

cards.people: 2,737 patients aged 55 or older with NYHA class II heart failure and EF ≤30% (or ≤35% with a QRS duration >130 ms), on recommended therapy including an ACE inhibitor or ARB and a beta-blocker; eplerenone up to 50 mg daily vs placebo; stopped early under prespecified rules, median follow-up 21 months
cards.result: Primary outcome (death from cardiovascular causes or hospitalisation for heart failure) 18.3% eplerenone vs 25.9% placebo — HR 0.63 (0.54–0.74) , P<0.001. Deaths 12.5% vs 15.5% — HR 0.76 (0.62–0.93) , P=0.008; hospitalisations for heart failure and for any cause were also reduced
cards.watchOut: Harm: serum potassium above 5.5 mmol/L in 11.8% on eplerenone vs 7.2% on placebo (P<0.001) — the guardrail again; patients with potassium >5.0 mmol/L or eGFR below 30 were excluded at entry

shelves.title: The ICD shelf: who actually benefits
shelves.question: Does a prophylactic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator reduce total mortality — and in whom?
shelves.balance: The ICD story is two true halves. In post-MI and mixed populations the device cut total mortality by roughly a quarter (MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT), earning Class 1, Level A. In modern nonischemic disease on contemporary therapy it halved sudden death and still did not significantly move total mortality (DANISH) — because the deaths it prevents are a smaller share of a better-treated total. The device works; the question the shelf leaves open is which patient, on today’s drugs, still has enough arrhythmic risk to gain. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: After MI with EF ≤30%, a prophylactic ICD cut mortality from 19.8% to 14.2%.
cards.summary: MADIT-II 2002 — mortality 14.2% vs 19.8% (HR 0.69 , P=0.016) — 1,232 patients with prior MI and EF ≤30%, no arrhythmia or electrophysiology-testing requirement; average follow-up 20 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2002
cards.people: 1,232 patients with a prior myocardial infarction and EF ≤0.30, randomly assigned in a 3:2 ratio to an implantable defibrillator (742) or conventional medical therapy (490); invasive electrophysiological testing for risk stratification was not required; average follow-up 20 months
cards.result: Mortality 14.2% in the defibrillator group vs 19.8% with conventional therapy — HR 0.69 (0.51–0.93) , P=0.016. The effect of defibrillator therapy on survival was similar in subgroup analyses by age, sex, ejection fraction, NYHA class and QRS interval
cards.watchOut: An implanted device, not a drug: procedural risk, inappropriate shocks and generator changes are the standing costs — and the trial predates contemporary drug therapy. The DANISH card below is the modern counterweight
cards.source: Moss AJ, Zareba W, Hall WJ, et al; Multicenter Automatic Defibrillator Implantation Trial II Investigators. Prophylactic implantation of a defibrillator in patients with myocardial infarction and reduced ejection fraction. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(12):877–883. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa013474. PMID 11907286.
cards.search: madit-ii moss 2002 nejm prophylactic implantation defibrillator myocardial infarction reduced ejection fraction icd pmid 11907286

cards.headline: An ICD cut mortality by 23% — while amiodarone, in the same trial, did nothing.
cards.summary: SCD-HeFT 2005 — deaths 22% ICD vs 29% placebo (HR 0.77 , P=0.007); amiodarone 28% (HR 1.06 — no benefit) — 2,521 patients, NYHA II–III, EF ≤35%; median follow-up 45.5 months.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2005
cards.people: 2,521 patients with NYHA class II (70%) or III heart failure and EF ≤35% — the cause ischemic in 52% and nonischemic in 48% — assigned to conventional therapy plus placebo (847), amiodarone (845), or a single-lead ICD (829); median follow-up 45.5 months
cards.result: Deaths: 182 (22%) ICD, 240 (28%) amiodarone, 244 (29%) placebo. ICD vs placebo HR 0.77 (97.5% CI 0.62–0.96) , P=0.007 — an absolute decrease in mortality of 7.2 percentage points after five years. Amiodarone vs placebo HR 1.06 (0.86–1.30) , P=0.53 — no benefit. Results did not vary by ischemic or nonischemic cause, but did vary by NYHA class
cards.watchOut: The amiodarone null is stated at full weight: the era’s standard antiarrhythmic drug did not save lives in this trial — the device did
cards.source: Bardy GH, Lee KL, Mark DB, et al; Sudden Cardiac Death in Heart Failure Trial (SCD-HeFT) Investigators. Amiodarone or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for congestive heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(3):225–237. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa043399. PMID 15659722.
cards.search: scd-heft bardy 2005 nejm amiodarone implantable cardioverter-defibrillator congestive heart failure sudden cardiac death pmid 15659722

cards.headline: In nonischemic heart failure on modern therapy, the ICD halved sudden death — and did not significantly cut total mortality.
cards.summary: DANISH 2016 — all-cause mortality 21.6% vs 23.4% (HR 0.87 , P=0.28 — not significant); sudden cardiac death 4.3% vs 8.2% (HR 0.50 ) — 1,116 patients, 58% with CRT in both groups; median follow-up 67.6 months.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2016
cards.people: 1,116 patients with symptomatic systolic heart failure not caused by coronary artery disease, EF ≤35%; ICD (556) vs usual clinical care (560); in both groups 58% of patients received CRT, and background therapy included beta-blockers, renin-angiotensin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid antagonists; median follow-up 67.6 months
cards.result: Death from any cause 120 (21.6%) in the ICD group vs 131 (23.4%) in the control group — HR 0.87 (0.68–1.12) , P=0.28, not significant. Sudden cardiac death 24 (4.3%) vs 46 (8.2%) — HR 0.50 (0.31–0.82) , P=0.005
cards.watchOut: Device infection occurred in 4.9% of the ICD group vs 3.6% of controls (P=0.29). A suggestion of greater benefit in younger patients was a subgroup finding, not the headline
cards.source: Køber L, Thune JJ, Nielsen JC, et al; DANISH Investigators. Defibrillator implantation in patients with nonischemic systolic heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(13):1221–1230. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1608029. PMID 27571011.

shelves.title: How low? The intensive blood pressure trials
shelves.question: How far should systolic pressure be pushed — and in whom does pushing it prevent events rather than just add harm?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension · Blood Pressure · Antihypertensive Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Stroke · Humans
shelves.balance: Five large trials, one arc: SPRINT said lower is better but excluded diabetes and stroke; ACCORD-BP then missed in diabetes and froze the field for a decade; STEP, ESPRIT, and BPROAD — 33,000 patients, including the diabetics and stroke survivors SPRINT left out — all landed the same way. Intensive systolic control prevents events across every population actually tested; the price is hypotension, syncope, and electrolytes, paid openly on every card. (Panel position: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline — attributed, for developer verification.) The J-curve pair, 2002 and 2018: pushing systolic down has a diastolic floor — both analyses put the risk nadir at a diastolic of 70–84 mmHg and warn below 70 in coronary patients.

cards.headline: Targeting systolic pressure below 120 cut major cardiovascular events by a quarter — and deaths by 27%.
cards.summary: SPRINT 2015 — primary composite 5.2% vs 6.8% (HR 0.75 ); all-cause mortality 3.3% vs 4.5% (HR 0.73 ) — 9,361 high-risk patients without diabetes or prior stroke; stopped early, median follow-up 3.26 years.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: 9,361 patients aged 50 or older with a systolic pressure of 130–180 mm Hg and increased cardiovascular risk, but without diabetes or prior stroke; intensive target <120 mm Hg (4,678) vs standard target <140 mm Hg (4,683); the trial was stopped early, at a median follow-up of 3.26 years
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (myocardial infarction, other acute coronary syndromes, stroke, heart failure, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 243 patients (5.2%) with intensive treatment vs 319 (6.8%) with standard treatment — HR 0.75 (0.64–0.89) . Death from any cause: 155 (3.3%) vs 210 (4.5%) — HR 0.73 (0.60–0.90) . Mean systolic pressure at 1 year was 121.4 vs 136.2 mm Hg
cards.watchOut: Serious adverse events were more frequent with intensive treatment: hypotension 2.4% vs 1.4% , syncope 2.3% vs 1.7% , electrolyte abnormalities 3.1% vs 2.3% , and acute kidney injury or failure 4.1% vs 2.5% . And the exclusions define the card: no diabetes, no prior stroke — the very populations the later trials on this shelf had to test
cards.source: The SPRINT Research Group. A randomized trial of intensive versus standard blood-pressure control. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(22):2103–2116. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1511939. PMID 26551272 · NCT01206062.
cards.search: sprint 2015 nejm intensive standard blood pressure control systolic 120 140 cardiovascular mortality hypotension syncope kidney pmid 26551272 age factors aged antihypertensive agents blood pressure cardiovascular diseases cause of death female goals humans hypertension male middle aged practice guidelines as topic risk factors nct01206062 i10 ba00

cards.headline: In diabetes, the same target below 120 missed: the primary outcome did not move.
cards.summary: ACCORD-BP 2010 — primary composite 1.87 vs 2.09 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.88 , 95% CI 0.73–1.06 — not significant ); stroke 0.32 vs 0.53 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.59 ); serious adverse events 3.3% vs 1.3% — 4,733 patients with type 2 diabetes.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2010
cards.people: 4,733 participants with type 2 diabetes at high risk for cardiovascular events, assigned to intensive therapy targeting systolic pressure <120 mm Hg (2,362) or standard therapy targeting <140 mm Hg (2,371); mean follow-up 4.7 years
cards.result: The annual rate of the primary composite (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) was 1.87% with intensive therapy vs 2.09% with standard therapy — HR 0.88 (0.73–1.06) , P=0.20, not significant. Stroke, a prespecified secondary outcome, was lower: 0.32 vs 0.53 per 100 patient-years — HR 0.59 (P=0.01). Death from any cause 1.28 vs 1.19 per year (HR 1.07), not significant. Mean systolic pressure after 1 year was 119.3 vs 133.5 mm Hg
cards.watchOut: The null is the finding, and it is shelved at full weight: serious adverse events attributed to antihypertensive treatment occurred in 77 of 2,362 (3.3%) on intensive therapy vs 30 of 2,371 (1.3%) on standard. Event rates ran lower than projected, limiting power — the caveat BPROAD, fourteen years later, was built to answer
cards.source: The ACCORD Study Group. Effects of intensive blood-pressure control in type 2 diabetes mellitus. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(17):1575–1585. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1001286. PMID 20228401 · NCT00000620.

cards.headline: SPRINT’s result, reproduced in 8,511 older Chinese patients: events 3.5% vs 4.6%.
cards.summary: STEP 2021 — primary composite 3.5% vs 4.6% (HR 0.74 ); hypotension 3.4% vs 2.6% — 8,511 patients aged 60–80, target 110–<130 vs 130–<150 mm Hg, median follow-up 3.34 years.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 8,511 Chinese patients aged 60–80 years with hypertension (mean age 66.2 years), assigned to intensive treatment (systolic target 110–<130 mm Hg) or standard treatment (130–<150 mm Hg); median follow-up 3.34 years
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (stroke, acute coronary syndrome, acute decompensated heart failure, coronary revascularization, atrial fibrillation, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 147 patients (3.5%) with intensive treatment vs 196 (4.6%) with standard treatment — HR 0.74 (0.60–0.92) . Stroke HR 0.67 and acute coronary syndrome HR 0.67
cards.watchOut: Hypotension was the one safety outcome that differed — 146 patients (3.4%) vs 113 (2.6%) , P=0.03; other safety outcomes and renal outcomes did not differ between the groups. Patients with previous stroke were excluded, and the population was Chinese — two limits the next trials on this shelf addressed
cards.source: Zhang W, Zhang S, Deng Y, et al; STEP Study Group. Trial of intensive blood-pressure control in older patients with hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(14):1268–1279. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2111437. PMID 34491661 · NCT03015311.

cards.headline: The trial that enrolled the people SPRINT left out — diabetes and previous stroke — and still won.
cards.summary: ESPRIT 2024 — primary outcome 9.7% vs 11.1% (HR 0.88 ); cardiovascular death HR 0.61 ; syncope 0.4% vs 0.1% — 11,255 high-risk Chinese patients, 39% with diabetes and 27% with previous stroke; achieved systolic pressure 119.1 vs 134.8 mm Hg.
cards.people: 11,255 participants at high cardiovascular risk enrolled from 116 hospitals or communities in China — 4,359 (39%) with diabetes and 3,022 (27%) with previous stroke ; intensive treatment (5,624) vs standard treatment (5,631); mean age 64.6 years; median follow-up 3.4 years
cards.result: The primary outcome (myocardial infarction, revascularisation, hospitalisation for heart failure, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 547 participants (9.7%) with intensive treatment vs 623 (11.1%) with standard treatment — HR 0.88 (0.78–0.99) , P=0.028. Cardiovascular death HR 0.61 ; death from any cause HR 0.79 . Mean systolic pressure through follow-up was 119.1 vs 134.8 mm Hg, and there was no heterogeneity of effect by diabetes status or history of stroke
cards.watchOut: Serious adverse events of syncope occurred more often with intensive treatment — 24 patients (0.4%) vs 8 (0.1%) , HR 3.00 — but there was no significant between-group difference in hypotension, electrolyte abnormality, injurious fall, or acute kidney injury
cards.source: Liu J, Li Y, Ge J, et al; ESPRIT Collaborative Group. Lowering systolic blood pressure to less than 120 mm Hg versus less than 140 mm Hg in patients with high cardiovascular risk with and without diabetes or previous stroke: an open-label, blinded-outcome, randomised trial. Lancet. 2024;404(10449):245–255. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01028-6. PMID 38945140 · NCT04030234.

cards.headline: BPROAD answered ACCORD: in 12,821 patients with diabetes, intensive control won.
cards.summary: BPROAD 2025 — primary outcome 393 vs 492 patients ( 1.65 vs 2.09 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.79 ) — 12,821 patients aged 50 or older with type 2 diabetes in China; median follow-up 4.2 years; symptomatic hypotension and hyperkalemia more frequent with intensive treatment.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 12,821 patients aged 50 or older with type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk, enrolled at 145 clinical sites in China; intensive treatment targeting systolic pressure <120 mm Hg vs standard treatment targeting <140 mm Hg; median follow-up 4.2 years
cards.result: The primary outcome (nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, treatment or hospitalization for heart failure, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 393 patients in the intensive-treatment group vs 492 in the standard-treatment group — 1.65 vs 2.09 events per 100 patient-years, HR 0.79 (0.69–0.90) , P<0.001. Stroke rates were 1.19 vs 1.50 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.79)
cards.watchOut: The incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups, but symptomatic hypotension and hyperkalemia occurred more frequently with intensive treatment. The trial was open-label and enrolled a single-country population — the same generalizability note carried by STEP and ESPRIT
cards.source: Bi Y, Li M, Liu Y, et al; BPROAD Research Group. Intensive blood-pressure control in patients with type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(12):1155–1167. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2412006. PMID 39555827 · NCT03808311.

cards.headline: The original J-curve: pooled patient by patient, mortality rose at low diastolic pressure — in treated and untreated patients alike.
cards.summary: INDANA 2002 — the diastolic pressure–mortality relationship was J-shaped in treated and untreated patients; risk nadirs at diastolic 84 mmHg in treated patients and 94 mmHg in controls (systolic nadirs 156 and 169 ) — individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 7 hypertension trials, 40,233 patients, 1,655 deaths.
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 7 hypertension trials — achieved-pressure analysis within trials, 2002, pre-SPRINT, Ann Intern Med 2002
cards.people: 40,233 patients pooled patient by patient from 7 hypertension trials, with 1,655 deaths; five of the seven trials enrolled elderly patients
cards.result: The diastolic pressure–mortality relationship was J-shaped in both treated and untreated patients. The risk nadirs — the pressures of lowest mortality — were diastolic 84 mmHg in treated patients and 94 mmHg in controls; the systolic nadirs were 156 and 169 mmHg . The rise in mortality at low pressure extended to non-cardiovascular deaths
cards.watchOut: Achieved pressure inside trials is not a randomized target — no patient was assigned to these pressures. The authors’ own conclusion: the J-curve mainly reflects poor health causing low blood pressure — reverse causality — not treatment harm. The analysis is from 2002, before SPRINT and the modern intensive-target trials on this shelf
cards.source: Boutitie F, et al.; INDANA Project. Ann Intern Med. 2002. PMID 11900496.

cards.headline: The J-curve, second generation: at a well-controlled systolic, a diastolic below 70 still cost heart attacks and heart-failure admissions.
cards.summary: Böhm 2018 — among 16,099 high-risk patients with achieved systolic 120 to <140 mmHg, lowest risk at diastolic 70 to <80; below 70: primary composite HR 1.29 (1.15–1.45) , myocardial infarction HR 1.54 (1.26–1.88) , heart-failure hospitalization HR 1.81 (1.47–2.24) , all-cause death HR 1.19 (1.04–1.35) — achieved-pressure analysis of ONTARGET and TRANSCEND.
cards.type: Achieved-pressure analysis of two randomised trials (ONTARGET and TRANSCEND), Eur Heart J 2018
cards.people: 16,099 high-risk patients from ONTARGET and TRANSCEND whose achieved systolic pressure was 120 to <140 mmHg
cards.result: The lowest risk sat at a diastolic of 70 to <80 mmHg. Below 70: primary composite HR 1.29 (95% CI 1.15–1.45) , myocardial infarction HR 1.54 (1.26–1.88) , heart-failure hospitalization HR 1.81 (1.47–2.24) , and all-cause death HR 1.19 (1.04–1.35) — with no signal for stroke or cardiovascular death. Diastolic ≥80 raised stroke and heart-failure risk; ≥90 raised myocardial infarction
cards.watchOut: Achieved pressure, not randomized targets — but the signal survived sensitivity analyses for reverse causality, which is why this card stands beside INDANA (Reference 6) rather than beneath it. The authors still label the analysis hypothesis-generating
cards.source: Böhm M, et al. Eur Heart J. 2018. PMID 29873709.

shelves.title: The foundation trials: treating hypertension at all, and with what first
shelves.question: Before asking how low to go — does treating blood pressure prevent events at all, does it still help past 80, and does the first drug chosen matter?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension · Antihypertensive Agents · Chlorthalidone · Nitrendipine · Indapamide · Cerebrovascular Disorders · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Before targets came foundations: SHEP and Syst-Eur proved treating systolic pressure in older adults prevents strokes, HYVET proved it saves lives past 80, and ALLHAT — 33,000 patients — proved the first drug matters less than starting, with the thiazide never beaten. Every modern target argument, including Shelf #93’s, stands on these four. (Panel position: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: The first proof: treating isolated systolic hypertension in older adults cut stroke by 36%.
cards.summary: SHEP 1991 — total stroke 5.2 vs 8.2 per 100 participants over 5 years (RR 0.64 ) — 4,736 patients aged 60 or older; chlorthalidone-based stepped care vs placebo; mean follow-up 4.5 years.
cards.people: 4,736 patients aged 60 or older with systolic pressure 160–219 mm Hg and diastolic below 90 mm Hg (2,365 active treatment, 2,371 placebo); step 1 was chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg/day, with atenolol added at step 2 if needed; mean age 72 years; mean follow-up 4.5 years
cards.result: The 5-year incidence of total stroke was 5.2 per 100 participants with active treatment vs 8.2 per 100 with placebo — RR 0.64 (0.50–0.82) , P=0.0003: a 36% reduction, an absolute benefit of 30 events per 1,000 participants over 5 years. Nonfatal myocardial infarction plus coronary death RR 0.73 ; major cardiovascular events RR 0.68 ; deaths from all causes RR 0.87 . Five-year average pressure was 143/68 vs 155/72 mm Hg
cards.watchOut: The trial was run when treating systolic hypertension in older adults was still doubted — the placebo arm is the point of the card. All-cause mortality (RR 0.87) did not reach significance, and the atenolol step means SHEP tested a stepped-care strategy, not chlorthalidone alone
cards.source: SHEP Cooperative Research Group. Prevention of stroke by antihypertensive drug treatment in older persons with isolated systolic hypertension: final results of the Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program (SHEP). JAMA. 1991;265(24):3255–3264. PMID 2046107.

cards.headline: Europe’s answer, with a calcium blocker first: stroke down 42%.
cards.summary: Syst-Eur 1997 — stroke 7.9 vs 13.7 per 1,000 patient-years ( −42% ); all cardiac endpoints −26% — 4,695 patients aged 60 or older; nitrendipine-based therapy vs placebo; stopped early, median follow-up 2 years.
cards.people: 4,695 patients aged 60 or older with sitting systolic pressure 160–219 mm Hg and diastolic below 95 mm Hg; nitrendipine 10–40 mg/day (2,398), with enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide added as needed, vs matching placebos (2,297); the trial was stopped early, at a median follow-up of 2 years
cards.result: Active treatment reduced total stroke from 13.7 to 7.9 endpoints per 1,000 patient-years — a 42% reduction (P=0.003); nonfatal stroke fell 44%. All fatal and nonfatal cardiac endpoints, including sudden death, fell 26% (P=0.03), and all cardiovascular endpoints fell 31% (P<0.001). Sitting pressure fell 23/7 mm Hg on active treatment vs 13/2 on placebo
cards.watchOut: Stopped early after a median of only 2 years, so the absolute gains are projections (treating 1,000 patients for 5 years might prevent 29 strokes). All-cause mortality was not significantly reduced (−14%, P=0.22) — the card carries that plainly

Randomised double-blind comparison of placebo and active treatment for older patients with isolated systolic hypertension. Lancet. 1997;350(9080):757–764. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(97)05381-6. PMID 9297994.

cards.headline: Past 80, treatment saved lives: deaths from any cause down 21%.
cards.summary: HYVET 2008 — death from any cause HR 0.79 ( −21% ); fatal or nonfatal stroke HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.49–1.01 — crosses 1); heart failure HR 0.36 ( −64% ) — 3,845 patients aged 80 or older; indapamide ± perindopril vs placebo; stopped early, median follow-up 1.8 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2008
cards.people: 3,845 patients aged 80 or older (mean age 83.6 years) with sustained systolic pressure of 160 mm Hg or more, enrolled in Europe, China, Australasia and Tunisia; indapamide (sustained release, 1.5 mg) (1,933) vs matching placebo (1,912), with perindopril 2 or 4 mg added if necessary for a target of 150/80 mm Hg; stopped early, median follow-up 1.8 years
cards.result: Active treatment was associated with a 21% reduction in death from any cause (HR 0.79 ; 95% CI 0.65–0.95, P=0.02), a 30% reduction in fatal or nonfatal stroke (HR 0.70 ; 95% CI 0.49–1.01, P=0.06), a 39% reduction in death from stroke, and a 64% reduction in heart failure (HR 0.36 ; 95% CI 0.22–0.58, P<0.001). At 2 years, sitting pressure was 15.0/6.1 mm Hg lower with active treatment
cards.watchOut: The primary end point’s confidence interval crosses 1 — stroke HR 0.70 (0.49–1.01), P=0.06, not conventionally significant — and the card states that honestly. The safety ledger ran the other way: fewer serious adverse events were reported with active treatment than with placebo ( 358 vs 448 ; P=0.001)
cards.source: Beckett NS, Peters R, Fletcher AE, et al; HYVET Study Group. Treatment of hypertension in patients 80 years of age or older. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(18):1887–1898. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0801369. PMID 18378519 · NCT00122811.

cards.headline: 33,357 patients, three first drugs: the thiazide was never beaten.
cards.summary: ALLHAT 2002 — primary coronary outcome identical (RR 0.98 amlodipine vs chlorthalidone; RR 0.99 lisinopril vs chlorthalidone); heart failure higher with amlodipine (RR 1.38 ) and lisinopril (RR 1.19 ); stroke higher with lisinopril (RR 1.15 ) — 33,357 high-risk patients aged 55 or older; mean follow-up 4.9 years.
cards.people: 33,357 patients aged 55 or older with hypertension and at least one other coronary risk factor, at 623 North American centers; chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg/day (15,255) vs amlodipine 2.5–10 mg/day (9,048) vs lisinopril 10–40 mg/day (9,054); mean follow-up 4.9 years
cards.result: The primary outcome (fatal coronary heart disease plus nonfatal myocardial infarction) did not differ: 6-year rates 11.5% with chlorthalidone, 11.3% with amlodipine (RR 0.98 ; 0.90–1.07) and 11.4% with lisinopril (RR 0.99 ; 0.91–1.08); all-cause mortality also did not differ. On secondary outcomes the diuretic pulled ahead: heart failure 10.2% vs 7.7% for amlodipine vs chlorthalidone (RR 1.38 ) and 8.7% vs 7.7% for lisinopril vs chlorthalidone (RR 1.19 ); stroke 6.3% vs 5.6% for lisinopril vs chlorthalidone (RR 1.15 )
cards.watchOut: Achieved pressure was not identical — 5-year systolic pressure ran 0.8 mm Hg higher on amlodipine and 2 mm Hg higher on lisinopril than on chlorthalidone, which may explain part of the secondary-outcome gaps. A fourth arm, doxazosin, had been stopped early for excess heart failure and is not part of this comparison
cards.source: The ALLHAT Officers and Coordinators for the ALLHAT Collaborative Research Group. Major outcomes in high-risk hypertensive patients randomized to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or calcium channel blocker vs diuretic: the Antihypertensive and Lipid-Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial (ALLHAT). JAMA. 2002;288(23):2981–2997. DOI 10.1001/jama.288.23.2981. PMID 12479763.

shelves.title: Salt substitution and sodium reduction: the outcome trials
shelves.question: Does changing the salt itself — swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched substitute, or eating less sodium for a few years — actually prevent strokes, cardiovascular events, and deaths, or does it only move the blood-pressure number? And what price, if any, does the added potassium carry?
shelves.balance: The salt shaker, trialed: SSaSS — 21,000 villagers — shows swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched substitute prevents strokes and saves lives, with no hyperkalemia price in a population screened for kidney risk; TOHP shows a few years of sodium reduction still paying off a decade later; DECIDE-Diet confirms the blood-pressure mechanism in institutional kitchens, and is labeled the surrogate of the three. Kinship: Shelf #25 covers potassium itself — this shelf covers the salt it replaces. (Panel positions: AHA and WHO sodium guidance — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: SSaSS: in 20,995 villagers, swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched substitute prevented strokes and deaths — with no hyperkalemia price.
cards.summary: SSaSS 2021 — stroke 29.14 vs 33.65 events per 1,000 person-years (rate ratio 0.86 ); major cardiovascular events rate ratio 0.87 ; death from any cause rate ratio 0.88 ; serious adverse events attributed to hyperkalemia not increased (rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.80–1.37) — 20,995 people in 600 villages in rural China, with a history of stroke or aged 60 or older with high blood pressure; mean follow-up 4.74 years.
cards.type: Open-label, cluster-randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 20,995 participants from 600 villages in rural China, randomised by village in a 1:1 ratio; mean age 65.4 years and 49.5% women; 72.6% had a history of stroke and 88.4% a history of hypertension; the intervention group used a salt substitute (75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride by mass) and the control group continued regular salt (100% sodium chloride); mean follow-up 4.74 years
cards.result: The rate of stroke was lower with the salt substitute than with regular salt ( 29.14 vs 33.65 events per 1,000 person-years ; rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.77–0.96 ; P=0.006), as were the rates of major adverse cardiovascular events ( 49.09 vs 56.29 per 1,000 person-years ; rate ratio 0.87, 0.80–0.94 ; P<0.001) and death from any cause ( 39.28 vs 44.61 per 1,000 person-years ; rate ratio 0.88, 0.82–0.95 ; P<0.001). The safety outcome: the rate of serious adverse events attributed to hyperkalemia was not significantly higher with the salt substitute ( 3.35 vs 3.30 per 1,000 person-years ; rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.80–1.37 ; P=0.76)
cards.watchOut: The trial was open-label, and the hyperkalemia finding rests on serious adverse events attributed to it clinically — serum potassium was not systematically measured in every participant. The safety result also travels with the trial’s screening: people at high risk of hyperkalemia, including serious kidney disease, were not the population tested. And this was rural China, where most salt is added in home cooking — precisely the setting where swapping the household salt can reach the whole diet
cards.source: Neal B, Wu Y, Feng X, et al. Effect of salt substitution on cardiovascular events and death. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(12):1067–1077. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2105675. PMID 34459569.
cards.search: ssass neal 2021 nejm salt substitute potassium chloride stroke cardiovascular events death hyperkalemia cluster randomized china villages pmid 34459569

cards.headline: TOHP: a few years of eating less sodium in the original trials was still paying off — 25% fewer cardiovascular events — 10–15 years later.
cards.summary: TOHP long-term follow-up 2007 — cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or cardiovascular death) 25% lower in the sodium-reduction groups (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.57–0.99 ) 10–15 years after randomisation — 3,126 adults aged 30–54 with prehypertension randomised in TOHP I and TOHP II.
cards.type: Observational long-term follow-up of two randomised trials, BMJ 2007
cards.people: Adults aged 30–54 years with prehypertension: 744 participants in TOHP I (1987–90, 10 clinic sites) and 2,382 in TOHP II (1990–5, nine sites) were randomised to a sodium-reduction intervention — comprehensive education and counselling on reducing intake — or control; long-term follow-up was conducted centrally by post and phone; vital status was obtained for all participants and follow-up information on morbidity from 2,415 (77%), with 200 reporting a cardiovascular event
cards.result: Net sodium reductions in the intervention groups during the trials were 44 mmol/24 h (TOHP I) and 33 mmol/24 h (TOHP II). At 10–15 years, the risk of a cardiovascular event was 25% lower among those in the sodium-reduction groups (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.57–0.99 ; P=0.04), adjusted for trial, clinic, age, race, and sex, and 30% lower after further adjustment for baseline sodium excretion and weight ( 0.70, 0.53–0.94 ), with similar results in each trial. Mortality was lower but not significantly: 67 participants died (relative risk 0.80, 0.51–1.26 ; P=0.34) — stated at its true weight
cards.watchOut: The follow-up is observational: randomised assignment ended with the trials, and what participants ate over the following decade was neither assigned nor fully measured — the randomisation is the anchor; the decade-long tail is follow-up. Morbidity data came from 77% of participants, the event count is modest (200), the confidence interval only just excludes 1 (0.57–0.99), and the mortality difference did not reach significance
cards.source: Cook NR, Cutler JA, Obarzanek E, et al. Long term effects of dietary sodium reduction on cardiovascular disease outcomes: observational follow-up of the trials of hypertension prevention (TOHP). BMJ. 2007;334(7599):885–888. DOI 10.1136/bmj.39147.604896.55. PMID 17449506.
cards.search: tohp cook 2007 bmj sodium reduction long term follow-up cardiovascular events trials of hypertension prevention prehypertension pmid 17449506

cards.headline: DECIDE-Salt: in 48 elderly-care facilities, salt substitute lowered systolic pressure by 7.1 mm Hg — the surrogate card of this shelf.
cards.summary: DECIDE-Salt 2023 — systolic blood pressure −7.1 mm Hg with salt substitute vs usual salt (95% CI −10.5 to −3.8), the trial’s primary outcome; cardiovascular events fewer as a secondary outcome (HR 0.60 ); total mortality unchanged (HR 0.84, CI crosses 1); progressive salt-supply restriction had no effect on any outcome — 48 residential elderly-care facilities in China, 1,612 residents aged 55 or older, over 2 years. This card’s primary outcome is blood pressure — a surrogate, not events; it is labeled so.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial, 2×2 factorial design, Nat Med 2023 — primary outcome blood pressure (surrogate)
cards.people: 48 residential elderly care facilities in China, cluster-randomised; 1,612 participants (1,230 men and 382 women) aged 55 years or older; facilities were assigned to provision of a salt substitute (62.5% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride) vs usual salt, and to a progressively restricted vs usual supply of salt or salt substitute, for 2 years
cards.result: Salt substitute compared with usual salt lowered systolic blood pressure by 7.1 mm Hg (95% CI −10.5 to −3.8) , meeting the primary outcome of the trial, and diastolic blood pressure by 1.9 mm Hg (−3.6 to −0.2) . As secondary outcomes, the substitute resulted in fewer cardiovascular events (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.38–0.96 ) but had no effect on total mortality (HR 0.84, 0.63–1.13 ). The second strategy failed cleanly: restricted supply compared with usual supply had no effect on systolic blood pressure or on any study outcome
cards.watchOut: The label, kept visible: this card is the surrogate of the shelf — its primary outcome is blood pressure, not events, and the event result (HR 0.60) is a secondary outcome from a trial powered for pressure. On safety, the substitute increased mean serum potassium and led to more frequent biochemical hyperkalemia, but was not associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Participants were 76% men, in institutional kitchens where the facility controls the salt — the setting where substitution is easiest to deliver and least like home cooking
cards.source: Yuan Y, Jin A, Neal B, et al. Salt substitution and salt-supply restriction for lowering blood pressure in elderly care facilities: a cluster-randomized trial. Nat Med. 2023;29(4):973–981. DOI 10.1038/s41591-023-02286-8. PMID 37055566.
cards.search: decide-salt decide-diet yuan 2023 nature medicine salt substitute salt-supply restriction elderly care facilities cluster randomized blood pressure surrogate pmid 37055566

shelves.title: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: from warfarin to the DOACs
shelves.question: In atrial fibrillation at elevated risk of stroke, does anticoagulation actually prevent strokes and emboli — and can the direct oral anticoagulants match or beat warfarin, the drug that proved the principle, without its monitoring burden and its bleeding price?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Anticoagulants · Warfarin · Stroke · Embolism · Hemorrhage · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Warfarin proved the principle (EAFT: events halved after cerebral ischemia), then four trials in five years replaced it: dabigatran superior on strokes, rivaroxaban noninferior in the highest-risk cohort, apixaban superior on strokes, bleeding, and death together, edoxaban noninferior with less bleeding — every one of them kinder to the brain than warfarin on hemorrhagic stroke. (Panel position: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: EAFT 1993: after a TIA or minor stroke with atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation cut the yearly event rate from 17% to 8% — aspirin did not.
cards.summary: EAFT 1993 — primary outcome (death from vascular disease, any stroke, myocardial infarction, or systemic embolism) 8% per year on anticoagulation vs 17% per year on placebo (HR 0.53 ); stroke alone fell from 12% to 4% per year (HR 0.34); aspirin showed no significant benefit (HR 0.83, CI crosses 1) — 1,007 patients with non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation and a recent TIA or minor ischaemic stroke; mean follow-up 2.3 years.
cards.type: Randomised trial (open anticoagulation; double-blind aspirin vs placebo), Lancet 1993
cards.people: 1,007 patients with non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation and a recent TIA or minor ischaemic stroke, from 108 centres in 13 countries. Group 1 (669 patients eligible for anticoagulation) was randomised to open anticoagulation (target INR 2.5–4.0) or double-blind aspirin 300 mg daily or placebo; group 2 (338 patients with contraindications to anticoagulation) was randomised to aspirin or placebo; mean follow-up 2.3 years
cards.result: The annual rate of outcome events was 8% in patients assigned to anticoagulants vs 17% in placebo-treated patients in group 1 (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.36–0.79 ). The risk of stroke alone was reduced from 12% to 4% per year (HR 0.34, 0.20–0.57 ). Among all patients assigned to aspirin (groups 1 and 2), the annual incidence of outcome events was 15%, against 19% on placebo (HR 0.83, 0.65–1.05 — not significant), and anticoagulation was significantly more effective than aspirin (HR 0.60, 0.41–0.87). In absolute terms, 90 vascular events — mainly strokes — are prevented if 1,000 patients are treated with anticoagulation for one year
cards.watchOut: The price, stated on the card: major bleeding events ran at 2.8% per year on anticoagulation vs 0.9% per year on aspirin — though no intracranial bleeds were identified in patients assigned to anticoagulation. The anticoagulation arm was open-label. And this is secondary prevention after cerebral ischaemia — the highest-risk setting in atrial fibrillation — so the absolute benefit is larger than primary-prevention trials would show
cards.source: EAFT (European Atrial Fibrillation Trial) Study Group. Secondary prevention in non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation after transient ischaemic attack or minor stroke. Lancet. 1993;342(8882):1255–1262. PMID 7901582.
cards.search: eaft european atrial fibrillation trial 1993 lancet warfarin anticoagulation secondary prevention tia minor stroke aspirin placebo non-rheumatic pmid 7901582 aged anticoagulants aspirin atrial fibrillation cerebrovascular disorders double-blind method female humans ischemic attack, transient male middle aged myocardial infarction recurrence survival analysis treatment outcome vascular diseases i48.91 bc81.3 rxcui 11289 warfarin

cards.headline: RE-LY: dabigatran 150 mg beat warfarin on strokes (RR 0.66) and cut hemorrhagic stroke by two-thirds — with no more major bleeding.
cards.summary: RE-LY 2009 — stroke or systemic embolism 1.11 vs 1.69% per year (RR 0.66 ) for dabigatran 150 mg twice daily vs warfarin; hemorrhagic stroke 0.12 vs 0.38% per year ; major bleeding 3.11 vs 3.36% per year — similar — 18,113 patients with atrial fibrillation and risk factors for stroke; median follow-up 2 years.
cards.type: Randomised, noninferiority trial with blinded dabigatran doses and open-label warfarin, N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 18,113 patients with atrial fibrillation and at least one additional risk factor for stroke, at 951 centres in 44 countries; mean CHADS 2 score 2.1; dabigatran 110 mg twice daily, dabigatran 150 mg twice daily, or warfarin dose-adjusted to an INR of 2.0–3.0; median follow-up 2.0 years
cards.result: Rates of the primary outcome (stroke or systemic embolism) were 1.69% per year in the warfarin group, 1.53% per year with dabigatran 110 mg (relative risk 0.91 — noninferior), and 1.11% per year with dabigatran 150 mg (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.53–0.82 ; P<0.001 for superiority). Hemorrhagic stroke: 0.38% per year on warfarin vs 0.12% on dabigatran 150 mg. Major bleeding: 3.36% per year on warfarin vs 3.11% on dabigatran 150 mg (similar) and 2.71% on dabigatran 110 mg (significantly less) — the 110 mg dose trades a little efficacy for less bleeding, and this card keeps both doses visible
cards.watchOut: Warfarin was given open-label while the two dabigatran doses were blinded — outcome adjudication was blinded, but the design is not the double-dummy of the later trials. Gastrointestinal bleeding was more frequent with dabigatran 150 mg than with warfarin, and dyspepsia was the commonest dabigatran complaint. The warfarin group spent about two-thirds of the time in the therapeutic INR range — good control, so the comparison is not against careless warfarin
cards.source: Connolly SJ, Ezekowitz MD, Yusuf S, et al; RE-LY Steering Committee and Investigators. Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(12):1139–1151. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0905561. PMID 19717844 · NCT00262600.

cards.headline: ROCKET-AF: rivaroxaban was noninferior to warfarin in the highest-risk AF cohort — intention-to-treat superiority was not shown, and the card says so.
cards.summary: ROCKET-AF 2011 — primary outcome (stroke or systemic embolism) on treatment 1.7 vs 2.2 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.79 ; noninferiority met); intention-to-treat 2.1 vs 2.4 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.88; P=0.12 for superiority — not significant ); intracranial hemorrhage 0.5% vs 0.7% (P=0.02) and fatal bleeding 0.2% vs 0.5% (P=0.003) favoured rivaroxaban — 14,264 patients, the highest-risk population of the four DOAC trials (mean CHADS 2 3.5).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2011
cards.people: 14,264 patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation at increased risk for stroke, at 1,178 sites in 45 countries; median age 73 years and about 40% women; mean CHADS 2 score 3.5, and 54.8% had a previous stroke, systemic embolism, or transient ischaemic attack — the highest-risk cohort of the DOAC trials. Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily (15 mg if creatinine clearance 30–49 mL/min) vs dose-adjusted warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0); median follow-up 707 days
cards.result: In the per-protocol, as-treated primary analysis, the primary end point occurred in 188 patients in the rivaroxaban group ( 1.7% per year ) and 241 in the warfarin group ( 2.2% per year ) — hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.66–0.96) , P<0.001 for noninferiority. In the intention-to-treat analysis the rates were 2.1% vs 2.4% per year (HR 0.88, 0.74–1.03 ; P=0.12 for superiority — not significant, stated at full weight). Major and nonmajor clinically relevant bleeding was similar (14.9% vs 14.5% per year), with significant reductions in intracranial hemorrhage ( 0.5% vs 0.7% , P=0.02) and fatal bleeding ( 0.2% vs 0.5% , P=0.003) in the rivaroxaban group
cards.watchOut: Three honest qualifications: the headline analysis is per-protocol by the trial’s prespecified design, and superiority was not demonstrated in either population; gastrointestinal bleeding occurred more often with rivaroxaban; and warfarin control was the weakest of the four DOAC trials — INR in range a mean of 55% of the time — in the cohort at highest risk. Noninferiority against imperfectly controlled warfarin is a slightly softer claim than the same word elsewhere on this shelf
cards.source: Patel MR, Mahaffey KW, Garg J, et al; ROCKET-AF Investigators. Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(10):883–891. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1009638. PMID 21830957 · NCT00403767.

cards.headline: ARISTOTLE: apixaban beat warfarin on strokes, on major bleeding, and on death — all three in the same trial.
cards.summary: ARISTOTLE 2011 — stroke or systemic embolism 1.27 vs 1.60% per year (HR 0.79 ); major bleeding 2.13 vs 3.09% per year (HR 0.69 ); death from any cause 3.52 vs 3.94% per year (HR 0.89 ); hemorrhagic stroke 0.24 vs 0.47% per year (HR 0.51) — 18,201 patients with atrial fibrillation and at least one additional stroke risk factor; median follow-up 1.8 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, designed for noninferiority with prespecified superiority tests, N Engl J Med 2011
cards.people: 18,201 patients with atrial fibrillation and at least one additional risk factor for stroke, at 1,034 centres in 39 countries; median age 70 years, mean CHADS 2 score 2.1; apixaban 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg twice daily in patients meeting dose-reduction criteria) vs warfarin dose-adjusted to an INR of 2.0–3.0; median follow-up 1.8 years
cards.result: The rate of the primary outcome was 1.27% per year in the apixaban group vs 1.60% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.66–0.95 ; P<0.001 for noninferiority, P=0.01 for superiority). Major bleeding: 2.13% vs 3.09% per year (HR 0.69, 0.60–0.80 ; P<0.001). Death from any cause: 3.52% vs 3.94% per year (HR 0.89, 0.80–0.99 ; P=0.047). Hemorrhagic stroke was halved ( 0.24 vs 0.47% per year ; HR 0.51) — apixaban is the only DOAC on this shelf superior on efficacy, bleeding, and mortality together
cards.watchOut: Kept at their true weight: the mortality difference only just reached significance (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.99; P=0.047) — real, but at the edge; and ischaemic stroke alone was not significantly reduced (0.97 vs 1.05% per year; HR 0.92) — the stroke advantage is driven substantially by the near-halving of hemorrhagic stroke. The warfarin group spent a median 66% of time in the therapeutic range — well-managed warfarin, fairly beaten
cards.source: Granger CB, Alexander JH, McMurray JJ, et al; ARISTOTLE Committees and Investigators. Apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(11):981–992. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1107039. PMID 21870978 · NCT00412984.
