cards.headline: ENGAGE AF: the largest AF trial ever run — edoxaban noninferior to warfarin, with a fifth less major bleeding.
cards.summary: ENGAGE AF–TIMI 48 2013 — primary outcome on treatment 1.18 vs 1.50% per year for high-dose edoxaban vs warfarin (HR 0.79 ; noninferior); by intention-to-treat HR 0.87 (97.5% CI 0.73–1.04; P=0.08 — a trend favouring edoxaban, not superiority ); major bleeding 2.75 vs 3.43% per year (HR 0.80 ); cardiovascular death 2.74 vs 3.17% per year (HR 0.86) — 21,105 patients, the largest atrial fibrillation trial; median follow-up 2.8 years, the longest of the four.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial, N Engl J Med 2013
cards.people: 21,105 patients with moderate-to-high-risk atrial fibrillation — the largest atrial fibrillation trial conducted; two once-daily edoxaban regimens (high-dose 60 mg, halved to 30 mg for reduced clearance, low body weight, or interacting drugs; and low-dose 30 mg) vs dose-adjusted warfarin; median follow-up 2.8 years; the warfarin group’s median time in the therapeutic range was 68.4% — the best warfarin control of the four DOAC trials
cards.result: During the treatment period, the annualized rate of the primary end point was 1.50% with warfarin vs 1.18% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.79, 97.5% CI 0.63–0.99 ; P<0.001 for noninferiority). In the intention-to-treat analysis there was a trend favouring high-dose edoxaban (HR 0.87, 0.73–1.04 ; P=0.08) — noninferior, not superior, and the card states both analyses. Major bleeding: 3.43% with warfarin vs 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (HR 0.80, 0.71–0.91 ; P<0.001); death from cardiovascular causes 3.17% vs 2.74% (HR 0.86, P=0.01)
cards.watchOut: This card covers the high-dose regimen, the one carried into practice. The trial’s second lesson sits in the low-dose arm: it bled least of all (major bleeding HR 0.47) but trended toward more ischaemic events (on-treatment HR 1.07; intention-to-treat HR 1.13) — dose intensity buys stroke protection at a bleeding price, and ENGAGE is the trial that maps the trade-off. Cross-trial comparisons on this shelf should also respect that ENGAGE’s warfarin was the best controlled (TTR 68.4%) and its follow-up the longest
cards.source: Giugliano RP, Ruff CT, Braunwald E, et al; ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 Investigators. Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(22):2093–2104. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1310907. PMID 24251359 · NCT00781391.

shelves.title: Rate versus rhythm: the strategy trials
shelves.question: In atrial fibrillation, is it better to restore and keep sinus rhythm, or simply to control the heart rate and let the rhythm be — and does the answer change if rhythm control starts early, if the rhythm is restored by ablation rather than drugs, or if the heart is failing?
shelves.balance: For twenty years the strategy question had one answer: AFFIRM and RACE said rhythm control buys nothing and costs hospitalizations. EAST-AFNET 4 reframed it — rhythm control delivered EARLY, within a year of diagnosis, cuts events by a fifth. Ablation’s own record is two-sided: CABANA’s intention-to-treat was null, CASTLE-AF’s failing-heart population won clearly. Timing and substrate, not the strategy label, decide. (Panel position: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: AFFIRM 2002: rhythm control bought no survival — five-year mortality 23.8% vs 21.3%, trending the wrong way, with more hospitalizations.
cards.summary: AFFIRM 2002 — deaths 356 in the rhythm-control group vs 310 in the rate-control group; five-year mortality 23.8% vs 21.3% (HR 1.15 , 95% CI 0.99–1.34; P=0.08 — not significant, and trending against rhythm control); hospitalizations and adverse drug effects, including torsades de pointes, were more frequent in the rhythm arm — 4,060 patients with atrial fibrillation aged 65 or older or with other risk factors for stroke or death; mean follow-up 3.5 years.
cards.type: Randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2002
cards.people: 4,060 patients with atrial fibrillation who were 65 years of age or older or had other risk factors for stroke or death (mean age 69.7 years; about 39% women). Rhythm control with antiarrhythmic drugs chosen by the treating physician, cardioversion as needed, vs rate control with beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, or digoxin; anticoagulation was encouraged in both arms; mean follow-up 3.5 years
cards.result: There were 356 deaths among patients assigned to rhythm control and 310 deaths among those assigned to rate control. Mortality at five years was 23.8% vs 21.3% (hazard ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.34 ; P=0.08) — no survival advantage to rhythm control, with the trend pointing the other way. The rhythm-control group had more hospitalizations and more adverse drug effects, including torsades de pointes
cards.watchOut: The trial compares strategies, not rhythms achieved: many rhythm-arm patients were not in sinus rhythm at any given visit, and some rate-arm patients were. In the rhythm arm, anticoagulation was sometimes stopped in patients judged to be in stable sinus rhythm — and several strokes followed; AFFIRM’s own lasting lesson is to continue anticoagulation whatever the strategy. The antiarrhythmic drugs of 2002 were also weaker and more toxic than today’s toolkit — which is why EAST-AFNET 4 (Reference 3) re-asked the question
cards.source: The Atrial Fibrillation Follow-up Investigation of Rhythm Management (AFFIRM) Investigators. A comparison of rate control and rhythm control in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(23):1825–1833. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa021328. PMID 12466506.

cards.headline: RACE 2002: after cardioversion for persistent AF, rate control was noninferior to rhythm control — 17.2% vs 22.6% on the composite.
cards.summary: RACE 2002 — the primary composite (death from cardiovascular causes, heart failure, thromboembolic complications, bleeding, pacemaker implantation, or severe adverse effects of antiarrhythmic drugs) occurred in 17.2% of the rate-control group vs 22.6% of the rhythm-control group over a mean of 2.3 years, meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion; at the end of follow-up only 39% of the rhythm group were in sinus rhythm, vs 10% of the rate group — 522 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation after a previous cardioversion.
cards.type: Randomised, noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2002
cards.people: 522 patients with recurrent persistent atrial fibrillation or flutter after a previous electrical cardioversion (256 assigned to rate control, 266 to rhythm control); rate control with oral rate-slowing drugs vs serial cardioversions with antiarrhythmic drug therapy; oral anticoagulation throughout; mean follow-up 2.3 years
cards.result: The primary end point occurred in 44 patients ( 17.2% ) in the rate-control group and 60 ( 22.6% ) in the rhythm-control group. The upper boundary of the 90% confidence interval for the absolute difference was 0.4 percentage points — well inside the prespecified noninferiority criterion of 10 points — so rate control was shown to be noninferior . At the end of follow-up, sinus rhythm was present in 39% of the rhythm-control group and 10% of the rate-control group; the individual components of the composite did not differ significantly between the groups
cards.watchOut: Small — 522 patients — and powered only against a wide noninferiority margin; subgroup analyses suggested women and patients with hypertension fared worse on rhythm control, but those are hypothesis-generating, not proof. Like AFFIRM, published in the same issue, RACE tested the antiarrhythmic drugs of its day; neither trial settles what early, modern rhythm control can do
cards.source: Van Gelder IC, Hagens VE, Bosker HA, et al; Rate Control versus Electrical Cardioversion for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation Study Group. A comparison of rate control and rhythm control in patients with recurrent persistent atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(23):1834–1840. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa021375. PMID 12466507.
cards.search: race van gelder rate control rhythm control recurrent persistent atrial fibrillation noninferior 2002 nejm pmid 12466507

cards.headline: EAST-AFNET 4 2020: rhythm control started within a year of diagnosis cut the composite by a fifth (HR 0.79) — the reversal of AFFIRM.
cards.summary: EAST-AFNET 4 2020 — the primary composite (death from cardiovascular causes, stroke, or hospitalization for worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome) occurred at 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 patient-years with early rhythm control vs usual care (HR 0.79 , 96% CI 0.66–0.94; P=0.005); the trial was stopped early for efficacy at a median follow-up of 5.1 years; serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy were more frequent with early rhythm control ( 4.9% vs 1.4% ) — 2,789 patients with atrial fibrillation diagnosed within the previous year, at 135 centers in 11 European countries.
cards.type: Randomised, open trial with blinded outcome assessment, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 2,789 patients with early atrial fibrillation — diagnosed no more than one year before enrollment (median, 36 days) — and cardiovascular risk conditions, at 135 centers in 11 European countries. Early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs and/or catheter ablation, with cardioversion of persistent AF) vs usual care; both groups received guideline-based anticoagulation and treatment of cardiovascular conditions; median follow-up 5.1 years, the trial having been stopped at the third interim analysis for efficacy
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 249 patients in the early-rhythm-control group ( 3.9 per 100 patient-years ) and 316 in the usual-care group ( 5.0 per 100 patient-years ) — hazard ratio 0.79 (96% CI 0.66–0.94; P=0.005) . The components — cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization for heart failure or acute coronary syndrome — each favored early rhythm control. There was no significant difference in nights spent in hospital. Serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy occurred in 4.9% of the early-rhythm-control group vs 1.4% of the usual-care group
cards.watchOut: Open-label by design, though outcomes were adjudicated blinded. Most rhythm control was delivered with antiarrhythmic drugs, not ablation — ablation was used in fewer than one in ten patients at the outset — so the result is not an ablation result; it is an early-treatment result, in a European population in which nearly everyone eligible received anticoagulation. Whether the active ingredient is the rhythm itself or the early, structured package of care around it, the trial cannot separate — and the higher rate of therapy-related serious adverse events is real
cards.source: Kirchhof P, Camm AJ, Goette A, et al; EAST-AFNET 4 Trial Investigators. Early rhythm-control therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(14):1305–1316. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2019422. PMID 32865375.
cards.search: east-afnet 4 kirchhof early rhythm control atrial fibrillation 2020 nejm stroke cardiovascular death ablation pmid 32865375

cards.headline: CABANA 2019: ablation vs drugs — the intention-to-treat primary was null (8.0% vs 9.2%; HR 0.86, CI crosses 1); quality of life favored ablation.
cards.summary: CABANA 2019 — the primary composite (death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, or cardiac arrest) occurred in 8.0% of the ablation group vs 9.2% of the drug-therapy group by intention-to-treat (HR 0.86 , 95% CI 0.65–1.15; P=.30 — NOT significant ); crossover was substantial — 27.5% of the drug group crossed over to ablation, and 9.2% of the ablation group never received it; AF recurrence was lower with ablation (HR 0.52) and quality-of-life scores favored ablation — 2,204 patients; median follow-up 48.5 months.
cards.people: 2,204 patients with new-onset or undertreated atrial fibrillation who were 65 years or older, or younger with at least one risk factor for stroke (median age 68 years; 63% men), at 126 centers in 10 countries. Catheter ablation with pulmonary vein isolation (1,108) vs drug therapy (1,096); of the ablation group 90.8% actually underwent ablation, and 27.5% of the drug group crossed over to ablation; median follow-up 48.5 months
cards.result: The primary end point occurred in 89 patients ( 8.0% ) in the ablation group and 101 ( 9.2% ) in the drug-therapy group — hazard ratio 0.86 (95% CI 0.65–1.15; P=.30) by intention-to-treat: not significant , and this card states the null at full weight. Secondary outcomes favored ablation: all-cause mortality 5.2% vs 6.1% (HR 0.85 — not significant), death or cardiovascular hospitalization 51.7% vs 58.1% (HR 0.83), and recurrence of atrial fibrillation 49.9% vs 69.5% (HR 0.52). Quality-of-life scores at 12 months favored ablation
cards.watchOut: Crossover dilutes the intention-to-treat comparison in both directions — more than a quarter of the drug group ultimately received ablation, and nearly one in ten assigned to ablation never had it — so treatment-received and per-protocol analyses, which favored ablation, are no longer protected by randomisation and cannot overturn the intention-to-treat null. Event rates were also lower than the trial projected, limiting power. Neither patients nor clinicians were blinded, which matters most for the quality-of-life findings — the domain where ablation looked best
cards.source: Packer DL, Mark DB, Robb RA, et al; CABANA Investigators. Effect of catheter ablation vs antiarrhythmic drug therapy on mortality, stroke, bleeding, and cardiac arrest among patients with atrial fibrillation: the CABANA randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2019;321(13):1261–1274. DOI 10.1001/jama.2019.0693. PMID 30874766.
cards.search: cabana packer catheter ablation antiarrhythmic drug therapy atrial fibrillation jama 2019 intention-to-treat crossover quality of life pmid 30874766

cards.headline: CASTLE-AF 2018: in AF with a failing heart, ablation cut death or HF hospitalization from 44.6% to 28.5% (HR 0.62) — in a small, selected population.
cards.summary: CASTLE-AF 2018 — the primary composite (death from any cause or hospitalization for worsening heart failure) occurred in 28.5% of the ablation group vs 44.6% of the medical-therapy group (HR 0.62 , 95% CI 0.43–0.87; P=0.007); all-cause mortality 13.4% vs 25.0% (HR 0.53) — 363 patients with atrial fibrillation and heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35% or less, every one carrying an ICD or CRT-D; median follow-up 37.8 months.
cards.type: Randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 363 patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation and heart failure — left ventricular ejection fraction 35% or less, NYHA class II, III, or IV — all with an implanted cardioverter–defibrillator or CRT-D, at 33 centers in 9 countries. Catheter ablation (179) vs medical therapy (184); median follow-up 37.8 months
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 51 patients ( 28.5% ) in the ablation group and 82 ( 44.6% ) in the medical-therapy group — hazard ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.43–0.87; P=0.007) . Death from any cause: 13.4% vs 25.0% (HR 0.53 , 0.32–0.86). Hospitalization for worsening heart failure: 20.7% vs 35.9% (HR 0.56). Death from cardiovascular causes: 11.2% vs 22.3% (HR 0.49). The burden of atrial fibrillation fell far more with ablation, and left ventricular ejection fraction improved more
cards.watchOut: Small and highly selected — stated plainly, as the brief for this card requires : 363 patients, screened from a much larger referred pool, younger than the typical HFrEF population (mean age about 64), treated at experienced ablation centers, and every participant carried a defibrillator, which guards against arrhythmic death in both arms. The trial was open-label, and its effect size is large precisely where the substrate gives ablation the most to fix — a ventricle whose failure the AF itself is helping to drive. It does not license extrapolating the same benefit to unselected AF populations (see CABANA, Card 4)
cards.source: Marrouche NF, Brachmann J, Andresen D, et al; CASTLE-AF Investigators. Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation with heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(5):417–427. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1707855. PMID 29385358.
cards.search: castle-af marrouche catheter ablation atrial fibrillation heart failure reduced ejection fraction nejm 2018 mortality hospitalization pmid 29385358

shelves.title: Peripheral artery disease: the antithrombotic trials
shelves.question: In peripheral artery disease, can antithrombotic therapy do better than a single antiplatelet drug — by blocking platelets harder, or by adding a small dose of anticoagulant alongside aspirin?
shelves.balance: PAD’s drug lesson comes in two parts: blocking platelets harder does nothing (EUCLID’s flat null), but blocking the clotting cascade a little — rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily on top of aspirin — prevents heart attacks, strokes, acute limb ischemia, and amputations in stable disease (COMPASS) and after revascularization (VOYAGER), at a bleeding price both cards state. Dual pathway, not dual platelet. (Panel position: ACC/AHA peripheral artery disease guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: COMPASS 2017: rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin cut events from 5.4% to 4.1% (HR 0.76) — major bleeding rose, fatal and intracranial bleeding did not.
cards.summary: COMPASS 2017 — the primary outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke, or myocardial infarction) occurred in 4.1% with rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin vs 5.4% with aspirin alone (HR 0.76 , 95% CI 0.66–0.86; P<0.001); major bleeding 3.1% vs 1.9% (HR 1.70), with no significant excess of fatal or intracranial bleeding; rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily alone did not beat aspirin; the trial was stopped early for efficacy at a mean of 23 months — 27,395 patients with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease, 7,470 of them with peripheral artery disease.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, stopped early for efficacy, N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 27,395 patients with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease — coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, or both — at 602 centers in 33 countries. Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily, rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily alone, or aspirin 100 mg alone; the peripheral artery disease cohort numbered 7,470 patients; the trial was stopped at the first interim analysis, at a mean follow-up of 23 months
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 379 patients ( 4.1% ) in the rivaroxaban-plus-aspirin group vs 496 ( 5.4% ) in the aspirin-alone group — hazard ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.66–0.86; P<0.001) . Rivaroxaban alone did not significantly beat aspirin (4.9% vs 5.4%; HR 0.90) — the win belongs to the combination. Major bleeding: 3.1% vs 1.9% (HR 1.70, 1.40–2.05), mostly gastrointestinal, with no significant excess of fatal bleeding, intracranial bleeding, or symptomatic bleeding into a critical organ; death from any cause was lower with the combination (3.4% vs 4.1%; HR 0.82). In the prespecified PAD analysis, the combination also reduced major adverse limb events by 46%, including acute limb ischemia, and major amputations fell
cards.watchOut: The bleeding price is real and is stated on this card, not footnoted: a 70% relative increase in major bleeding in exchange for the event reduction — the exchange rate each patient has to accept. The trial was stopped early for efficacy, which can flatter effect sizes, though the benefit was consistent across subgroups. Patients at high risk of bleeding were excluded, so the bleeding rates here are a floor, not a ceiling, for unselected practice
cards.source: Eikelboom JW, Connolly SJ, Bosch J, et al; COMPASS Investigators. Rivaroxaban with or without aspirin in stable cardiovascular disease. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(14):1319–1330. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1709118. PMID 28844192.
cards.search: compass eikelboom rivaroxaban aspirin stable cardiovascular disease peripheral artery disease nejm 2017 dual pathway major bleeding pmid 28844192

cards.headline: VOYAGER PAD 2020: after leg revascularization, the dual-pathway strategy cut limb and cardiovascular events (HR 0.85) — bleeding higher by one ruler, not by the other.
cards.summary: VOYAGER PAD 2020 — the primary outcome (acute limb ischemia, major amputation for vascular causes, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 15.5% with rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin vs 17.8% with aspirin alone — 3-year Kaplan–Meier estimates 17.3% vs 19.9% (HR 0.85 , 95% CI 0.76–0.96; P=0.009); TIMI major bleeding was not significantly higher (HR 1.43; P=0.07) while ISTH major bleeding was (HR 1.42; P=0.007) — 6,564 patients after lower-extremity revascularization; median follow-up 28 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 6,564 patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease after successful lower-extremity revascularization — surgical or endovascular — at 542 sites in 34 countries; median age 67 years. Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg (3,286) vs aspirin alone with placebo (3,278); clopidogrel was permitted for up to six months at the investigator’s discretion and was used in about half the patients, briefly; median follow-up 28 months
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 508 patients in the rivaroxaban group and 584 in the placebo group — 15.5% vs 17.8% of patients, corresponding to 3-year Kaplan–Meier estimates of 17.3% vs 19.9% — hazard ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.76–0.96; P=0.009) . Acute limb ischemia — the outcome these patients fear most — fell by about a third. On safety, this card states both rulers, as the brief requires: TIMI major bleeding occurred more often with rivaroxaban but the difference was not significant (HR 1.43, 0.97–2.10; P=0.07), whereas ISTH major bleeding was significantly higher (HR 1.42, 1.10–1.84; P=0.007). There was no excess of intracranial or fatal bleeding
cards.watchOut: The bleeding verdict depends on the definition applied — TIMI and ISTH count different events — and trials that report only one let the reader pick a conclusion; both are printed here for that reason. Benefit appeared early after the procedure and grew over time, so the patients with most to gain are those started promptly after revascularization. Background clopidogrel in half the cohort means some patients were briefly on three antithrombotic drugs
cards.source: Bonaca MP, Bauersachs RM, Anand SS, et al. Rivaroxaban in peripheral artery disease after revascularization. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(21):1994–2004. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2000052. PMID 32222135.
cards.search: voyager pad bonaca rivaroxaban peripheral artery disease revascularization nejm 2020 acute limb ischemia amputation bleeding timi isth pmid 32222135

cards.headline: EUCLID 2017: ticagrelor was not better than clopidogrel in symptomatic PAD — 10.8% vs 10.6%, a flat null.
cards.summary: EUCLID 2017 — the primary outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke) occurred in 10.8% on ticagrelor vs 10.6% on clopidogrel (HR 1.02 , 95% CI 0.92–1.13; P=0.65 — NO difference ); acute limb ischemia was 1.7% in both groups; TIMI major bleeding was 1.6% in both groups; dyspnea drove more discontinuations on ticagrelor (4.8% vs 0.8%) — 13,885 patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease; median follow-up 30 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial, N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 13,885 patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease — established by an ankle–brachial index of 0.80 or less (43% of patients) or by previous lower-limb revascularization (57%); mean ankle–brachial index 0.71 — at 811 sites in 28 countries. Ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily (6,930) vs clopidogrel 75 mg daily (6,955); median follow-up 30 months
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 751 patients ( 10.8% ) in the ticagrelor group and 740 ( 10.6% ) in the clopidogrel group — hazard ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.92–1.13; P=0.65) : ticagrelor was not superior , and the confidence interval excludes any large benefit. This null is stated at full weight. Acute limb ischemia occurred in 1.7% of patients in each group; ischemic stroke was somewhat less frequent with ticagrelor (1.9% vs 2.4%) — a secondary endpoint, not the question the trial asked. TIMI major bleeding: 1.6% in both groups (HR 1.10)
cards.watchOut: Ticagrelor’s burden was tolerability, not bleeding: dyspnea led 4.8% of ticagrelor patients to stop the drug, vs 0.8% on clopidogrel, and overall discontinuation for adverse events was higher. No subgroup — ABI-defined disease, prior revascularization, diabetes — showed a convincing benefit. The flat null in 13,885 patients is itself the information: within the platelet pathway, potency was not the constraint
cards.source: Hiatt WR, Fowkes FGR, Heizer G, et al; EUCLID Trial Steering Committee and Investigators. Ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in symptomatic peripheral artery disease. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(1):32–40. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1611688. PMID 27959717.
cards.search: euclid hiatt ticagrelor clopidogrel symptomatic peripheral artery disease nejm 2017 null dyspnea pmid 27959717

shelves.title: Stable coronary disease: open the artery, or not?
shelves.question: In stable coronary disease, does opening a narrowed artery with a stent prevent death or heart attack — or does it only relieve symptoms, and how much of that relief survives comparison with a placebo procedure?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Disease · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Angina, Stable · Coronary Angiography · Myocardial Ischemia · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Four trials discipline the catheter in stable disease: opening the artery does not prevent death or heart attack (COURAGE, ISCHEMIA), a sham procedure nearly matches it on exercise time in fully medicated patients (ORBITA) — and yet symptoms genuinely improve when PCI is tested against placebo in unmedicated patients (ORBITA-2). The synthesis the four support together: drugs carry the prognosis; the stent is a symptom treatment, chosen with open eyes. (Panel position: AHA/ACC chest pain guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: COURAGE 2007: adding PCI to optimal medical therapy did not reduce death or heart attack — 19.0% vs 18.5%.
cards.summary: COURAGE 2007 — the primary outcome (death from any cause or nonfatal myocardial infarction) occurred in 19.0% with PCI plus optimal medical therapy vs 18.5% with medical therapy alone (HR 1.05 , 95% CI 0.87–1.27; P=0.62 — NO difference ); angina relief came faster with PCI, but by five years 74% vs 72% were angina-free — 2,287 patients with stable coronary disease at 50 US and Canadian centers; median follow-up 4.6 years.
cards.type: Randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2007
cards.people: 2,287 patients with objective evidence of myocardial ischemia and significant coronary disease, with chronic stable angina or silent ischemia, at 50 centers in the United States and Canada. PCI plus intensive, guideline-directed medical and lifestyle therapy (1,149) vs the same optimal medical therapy alone (1,138); median follow-up 4.6 years
cards.result: Primary events occurred in 211 patients in the PCI group and 202 in the medical-therapy group; cumulative event rates were 19.0% vs 18.5% — hazard ratio 1.05 (95% CI 0.87–1.27; P=0.62) . The null is stated at full weight: no significant difference in death, in myocardial infarction (13.2% vs 12.3%), or in hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome. PCI did relieve angina faster, but the advantage narrowed over time — by five years 74% of the PCI group and 72% of the medical group were free of angina. About a third of the medical-therapy group eventually crossed over to revascularization, mostly for symptoms
cards.watchOut: Patients were enrolled after angiography, and those with left-main disease, severely reduced ejection fraction, or symptoms refractory to medical therapy were not the trial’s population — the null governs the stable middle, not every anatomy a catheter laboratory meets. Stents were bare-metal era; but ISCHEMIA (Reference 2) retested the question with contemporary stents and complete revascularization in view, and reached the same answer
cards.source: Boden WE, O’Rourke RA, Teo KK, et al; COURAGE Trial Research Group. Optimal medical therapy with or without PCI for stable coronary disease. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(15):1503–1516. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa070829. PMID 17387127 · NCT00007657.

cards.headline: ISCHEMIA 2020: an invasive start did not beat a conservative one in moderate-to-severe ischemia — deaths 145 vs 144.
cards.summary: ISCHEMIA 2020 — primary events (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for unstable angina, heart failure, or resuscitated cardiac arrest) numbered 318 in the invasive-strategy group vs 352 in the conservative group; estimated five-year event rates 16.4% vs 18.2% (difference −1.8 points, 95% CI −4.7 to 1.0 — not significant ); the curves crossed — more events early with the invasive strategy (5.3% vs 3.4% at six months, driven by procedural infarctions), fewer spontaneous infarctions later; deaths from any cause 145 vs 144 — 5,179 patients with moderate or severe ischemia; median follow-up 3.2 years.
cards.type: Randomised trial, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 5,179 patients with moderate or severe ischemia on stress testing and stable symptoms; significant left-main disease was excluded by blinded CT angiography before randomisation. Invasive strategy (2,588): angiography, then PCI or bypass surgery when feasible, plus guideline-directed therapy. Conservative strategy (2,591): the same therapy, with angiography reserved for symptoms or events; median follow-up 3.2 years
cards.result: Primary events occurred in 318 patients in the invasive group and 352 in the conservative group. The cumulative pattern crossed: at six months, 5.3% vs 3.4% (early excess in the invasive arm, driven by procedural myocardial infarctions); at five years, estimated rates of 16.4% vs 18.2% (difference −1.8 percentage points, 95% CI −4.7 to 1.0) — not significant, with spontaneous infarctions fewer in the invasive arm and procedural infarctions more, the two nearly balancing. Death from any cause: 145 vs 144 patients (HR 1.05). No mortality difference, in the largest stable-disease strategy trial ever run
cards.watchOut: About a quarter of the conservative group underwent revascularization during follow-up, mostly for worsening symptoms — the trial compares strategies of timing, not stent versus never. Left-main disease, recent acute coronary syndrome, advanced heart failure, and unacceptable angina were excluded, so the result does not reach those patients. The five-year figures are model-based estimates beyond the 3.2-year median follow-up. Symptoms and quality of life genuinely favored the invasive strategy in patients with frequent angina — Cards 3 and 4 price how much of symptom relief the stent itself delivers
cards.source: Maron DJ, Hochman JS, Reynolds HR, et al; ISCHEMIA Research Group. Initial invasive or conservative strategy for stable coronary disease. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(15):1395–1407. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1915922. PMID 32227755 · NCT01471522.

cards.headline: ORBITA 2018: against a sham procedure, PCI’s exercise-time advantage was 16.6 seconds — not significant (P=0.20).
cards.summary: ORBITA 2018 — after six weeks of intensive antianginal-medication optimization, exercise time increased by 28.4 seconds after PCI and 11.8 seconds after the placebo procedure — a between-group difference of 16.6 seconds (95% CI −8.9 to 42.0; P=0.200 — NOT significant ); PCI did objectively reduce ischemia on dobutamine stress echocardiography (P=0.0011); there were no deaths — 200 patients with severe single-vessel stenosis; endpoint at six weeks.
cards.people: 200 patients randomised (105 to PCI, 95 to placebo) with angina and severe single-vessel stenosis — mean area stenosis 84.4%, mean fractional flow reserve 0.69 — after a six-week phase of intensive antianginal medication optimization and symptom assessment; primary endpoint at six weeks after randomisation
cards.result: The increase in exercise time was 28.4 seconds in the PCI group and 11.8 seconds in the placebo group; the between-group difference was 16.6 seconds (95% CI −8.9 to 42.0; P=0.200) — the primary endpoint was not significant , and the null is stated at full weight. PCI did objectively reduce ischemia: the dobutamine stress echocardiography wall-motion score improved significantly more with PCI (P=0.0011). Differences in angina frequency, quality of life, and angina class were not significant; there were no deaths in either group
cards.watchOut: Small (200 patients), single-vessel disease only, and a six-week horizon: ORBITA was sized to detect a large symptomatic effect, and its confidence interval — up to a 42-second advantage — does not exclude a real, smaller one. Every patient arrived fully medicated, so ORBITA prices PCI added to pills; ORBITA-2 (Reference 4) re-asked the question with the pills stopped, and got a different answer. Both designs are the point
cards.source: Al-Lamee R, Thompson D, Dehbi HM, et al; ORBITA Investigators. Percutaneous coronary intervention in stable angina (ORBITA): a double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10114):31–40. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32714-9. PMID 29103656 · NCT02062593.
cards.search: orbita al-lamee pci stable angina placebo sham procedure lancet 2018 exercise time pmid 29103656 aged angina, stable coronary angiography coronary stenosis double-blind method exercise tolerance female humans male middle aged percutaneous coronary intervention treatment outcome united kingdom nct02062593 i25.1 ba52

cards.headline: ORBITA-2 2023: with antianginal pills stopped, PCI beat the sham clearly — angina score 2.9 vs 5.6 (OR 2.21) — yet about three in five PCI patients still had pain.
cards.summary: ORBITA-2 2023 — the mean angina symptom score at 12 weeks was 2.9 in the PCI group vs 5.6 in the placebo group (odds ratio 2.21 , 95% CI 1.41–3.47; P<0.001, for a better score with PCI); daily angina episodes and quality-of-life scores also favored PCI; nevertheless roughly 59% of PCI patients still reported chest pain — 301 patients with stable angina receiving little or no antianginal medication; follow-up 12 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled (sham-procedure) trial, N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 301 patients (151 PCI, 150 placebo) with stable angina and evidence of ischemia, mean age 64 years, 79% men; stenoses were severe (median fractional flow reserve 0.63). Antianginal medications were stopped before a two-week symptom-assessment phase, so the procedure was tested against the symptom burden patients actually present with; primary endpoint at 12 weeks
cards.result: The mean angina symptom score — a composite built from daily angina episodes, antianginal-medication use, and clinical events — was 2.9 in the PCI group vs 5.6 in the placebo group (odds ratio 2.21, 95% CI 1.41–3.47; P<0.001 ) for a better score with PCI. Daily angina episodes were fewer and disease-specific quality-of-life scores better with PCI; acute coronary syndrome events were few (4 vs 6). PCI relieves angina beyond the placebo effect when background medication is minimal — the complement of ORBITA, not its contradiction
cards.watchOut: A 12-week symptom endpoint: ORBITA-2 says nothing about death or heart attack, and no sham trial can. About 59% of PCI patients still reported some chest pain — a stent improves angina; it does not abolish it. The placebo group improved too, as placebo groups do; the trial’s contribution is to quantify PCI’s advantage over that improvement, in patients deliberately taken off their antianginal pills
cards.source: Rajkumar CA, Foley MJ, Ahmed-Jushuf F, et al; ORBITA-2 Investigators. A placebo-controlled trial of percutaneous coronary intervention for stable angina. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(25):2319–2330. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2310610. PMID 38015442 · NCT03742050.

shelves.title: Aspirin for primary prevention: the statin-era verdict
shelves.question: For a person who has never had a heart attack or stroke, does a daily aspirin still prevent more first events than the bleeding it causes — in diabetes, in healthy old age, and at moderate estimated risk?
shelves.mesh: Aspirin · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Hemorrhage · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Three trials, 47,000 people, one verdict: in the statin era, aspirin’s primary-prevention benefit shrank to the size of its bleeding harm — in diabetes the two nearly cancel (ASCEND), in healthy elders there is no benefit and a mortality signal nobody has explained (ASPREE), and at moderate risk there is nothing to weigh at all (ARRIVE). Secondary prevention is a different shelf and a different answer; this one is only about starting aspirin in people who have never had an event. (Panel positions: ACC/AHA primary prevention guideline and USPSTF — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: ASCEND 2018: in diabetes, aspirin prevented events (8.5% vs 9.6%) and caused bleeding (4.1% vs 3.2%) in nearly equal measure.
cards.summary: ASCEND 2018 — serious vascular events occurred in 658 patients ( 8.5% ) on aspirin vs 743 ( 9.6% ) on placebo (rate ratio 0.88 , 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01); major bleeding occurred in 314 ( 4.1% ) vs 245 ( 3.2% ) (rate ratio 1.29 , 1.09–1.52; P=0.003) — in absolute terms, about 11 vascular events prevented and about 9 major bleeds caused per 1,000 patients treated for 7.4 years; gastrointestinal cancer rates were identical (2.0% vs 2.0%) — 15,480 adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease; mean follow-up 7.4 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial (2×2 factorial, with omega-3 fatty acids as the second factor), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 15,480 adults, 40 years of age or older, with diabetes mellitus and no evident cardiovascular disease, recruited largely by mail-based methods in the United Kingdom. Aspirin 100 mg daily vs matching placebo; mean follow-up 7.4 years; adherence was high (about 70% still taking assigned treatment near the end)
cards.result: Serious vascular events — nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause excluding confirmed intracranial hemorrhage — occurred in 658 patients (8.5%) in the aspirin group vs 743 (9.6%) in the placebo group (rate ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01 ). Major bleeding occurred in 314 (4.1%) vs 245 (3.2%) (rate ratio 1.29, 1.09–1.52; P=0.003 ), most of the excess gastrointestinal or other extracranial. Aspirin therefore prevented about 11 serious vascular events per 1,000 patients over 7.4 years while causing about 9 major bleeds per 1,000 — benefit and harm nearly cancel. There was no significant difference in gastrointestinal cancer (2.0% vs 2.0%), disposing of the trial-era hope that aspirin would show a cancer dividend within this horizon
cards.watchOut: Participants were volunteers in a mail-recruited trial — more engaged and adherent than a general diabetes population — and the composite’s individual components (myocardial infarction, stroke) each trended favorable without individually reaching significance; the verdict belongs to the composite. Nothing on this card touches secondary prevention: after an established event, aspirin’s arithmetic is entirely different and is not this shelf’s question
cards.source: ASCEND Study Collaborative Group. Effects of aspirin for primary prevention in persons with diabetes mellitus. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(16):1529–1539. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1804988. PMID 30146931 · NCT00135226.

cards.headline: ASPREE 2018: in healthy elders, aspirin bought nothing — disability-free survival HR 1.01 — more major bleeding, and a mortality signal (HR 1.14) nobody has explained.
cards.summary: ASPREE 2018 — the primary endpoint (death, dementia, or persistent physical disability) occurred at 21.5 vs 21.2 per 1,000 person-years on aspirin vs placebo (HR 1.01 , 95% CI 0.92–1.11; P=0.79 — no benefit ); cardiovascular disease 10.7 vs 11.3 per 1,000 person-years (HR 0.95 — not significant); major hemorrhage 3.8% vs 2.8% (HR 1.38 ); all-cause mortality was higher on aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 per 1,000 person-years (HR 1.14 ) — driven by cancer-related deaths; the trial was stopped for futility — 19,114 healthy older adults; median follow-up 4.7 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, published as three companion papers, N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 19,114 community-dwelling older adults in Australia and the United States — 70 years of age or older (65 or older for Black and Hispanic participants in the United States) — free of cardiovascular disease, dementia, and physical disability at entry; median age 74 years; 56% women. Aspirin 100 mg daily vs placebo; median follow-up 4.7 years, the trial having been stopped after the monitoring board judged the primary endpoint futile
cards.result: The primary endpoint — the composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability — occurred at 21.5 per 1,000 person-years in the aspirin group vs 21.2 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.92–1.11; P=0.79 ): aspirin did not prolong disability-free survival. In the companion papers: cardiovascular disease occurred at 10.7 vs 11.3 per 1,000 person-years (HR 0.95, 0.83–1.08 — not significant), and major hemorrhage in 3.8% vs 2.8% (HR 1.38, 1.18–1.62; P<0.001 ). All-cause mortality was higher with aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 per 1,000 person-years (HR 1.14, 1.01–1.29 ) — driven by cancer-related death (3.1% vs 2.3%; HR 1.31, 1.10–1.56)
cards.watchOut: The mortality signal is carried on this card carefully, as the brief requires: it was unexpected and remains unexplained — a secondary finding, driven by cancer deaths in a population screened to be healthy, at odds with older trials’ late cancer-protection hypothesis, and not since settled. It is stated at full weight, but as a signal to interpret with caution, not as established aspirin carcinogenicity. Note the exact figures: the primary composite’s hazard ratio is 1.01; the often-quoted 0.95 belongs to the cardiovascular-disease endpoint, and it too was non-significant. Participants were unusually healthy elders; the verdict governs starting aspirin in healthy old age — not stopping it in patients with established disease

cards.headline: ARRIVE 2018: at “moderate” risk there was nothing to weigh — 4.29% vs 4.48% (HR 0.96), with twice the gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.summary: ARRIVE 2018 — the primary composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischemic attack) occurred in 269 patients ( 4.29% ) on aspirin vs 281 ( 4.48% ) on placebo (HR 0.96 , 95% CI 0.81–1.13; P=0.60 — NULL ); gastrointestinal bleeding doubled — 61 ( 0.97% ) vs 29 ( 0.46% ) (HR 2.11 ), predominantly mild; total deaths 2.55% vs 2.57% — 12,546 adults at moderate estimated cardiovascular risk in seven countries; median follow-up 60 months.
cards.people: 12,546 adults (6,270 assigned aspirin, 6,276 placebo) — men aged 55 years or older and women aged 60 years or older, with an average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of their risk-factor profile — in seven countries. Patients with diabetes or at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding were excluded. Enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg daily vs placebo; median follow-up 60 months
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 269 patients (4.29%) in the aspirin group and 281 (4.48%) in the placebo group — hazard ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.81–1.13; P=0.6038) : NULL , stated at full weight. Gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 61 patients (0.97%) vs 29 (0.46%) — HR 2.11 (1.36–3.28; P=0.0007) — predominantly mild events. Total mortality was identical (2.55% vs 2.57%; HR 0.99). The observed event rate was far lower than the “moderate risk” the design assumed — background statin and blood-pressure treatment had already shrunk the risk aspirin was meant to treat
cards.watchOut: The low event rate cuts both ways, and this card says so: ARRIVE cannot exclude a small benefit in a genuinely higher-risk population. But that limitation is itself the statin-era finding — populations once labeled moderate-risk now run low event rates on modern background therapy, while aspirin’s bleeding toll stays fixed, so the exchange rate keeps worsening. Adherence in a five-year prevention trial was imperfect, as in all such trials; the intention-to-treat result is the answer a prescribing clinician actually gets

shelves.title: Colchicine in coronary disease
shelves.question: Does low-dose colchicine prevent cardiovascular events in coronary disease — and how far do the guidelines follow the two trials?
shelves.mesh: Colchicine · Coronary Disease · Myocardial Infarction · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Intention to Treat Analysis · Proportional Hazards Models · Incidence · Humans
shelves.balance: Two blinded trials say low-dose colchicine prevents cardiovascular events after MI and in chronic coronary disease; Europe grades the recommendation weaker than the US, and a non-cardiovascular death signal in one trial is unexplained.

cards.headline: LoDoCo2 (Nidorf 2020): colchicine 0.5 mg daily cut the primary composite in chronic coronary disease.
cards.summary: Chronic coronary disease, colchicine 0.5 mg daily vs placebo — primary composite 6.8% vs 9.6% (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.57–0.83; P<0.001); non-cardiovascular death HR 1.51 (0.99–2.31).
cards.type: Randomized placebo-controlled trial (LoDoCo2), N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 5,522 patients with chronic coronary disease; median follow-up 28.6 months
cards.result: Primary composite 6.8% vs 9.6% (HR 0.69 , 95% CI 0.57–0.83; P<0.001)
cards.watchOut: Non-cardiovascular death was higher on colchicine — incidence 0.7 vs 0.5 per 100 person-years (HR 1.51, 0.99–2.31). It was not part of the primary composite, which counted cardiovascular death only — and the composite of cardiovascular death or spontaneous MI was significantly lower on colchicine. A signal, not a verdict.

shelves.title: The polypill: several proven medicines in one tablet
shelves.question: Cardiovascular prevention fails mostly at the pill bottle, not the prescription pad — what happens when the proven drugs are combined into a single tablet?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Drug Combinations · Aspirin · Atorvastatin · Hydrochlorothiazide · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Myocardial Infarction · Secondary Prevention · Humans
shelves.balance: Across three randomized trials on three continents, putting proven cardiovascular medicines into one tablet cut major events by roughly a quarter to a third — not because the drugs are new, but because people actually take one pill: adherence is the active ingredient. The evidence is strongest after a heart attack (SECURE) and in pragmatic primary prevention (PolyIran); in the blinded primary-prevention trial (TIPS-3), the polypill alone was borderline and needed aspirin added to reach significance.

cards.headline: SECURE: after a heart attack, one pill beat usual care (2022)
cards.result: Castellano JM et al., N Engl J Med 2022;387:967–977 (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2208275 · NCT02596126). 2,499 patients with a myocardial infarction within the previous 6 months (age 75 or older, or 65 or older with a risk factor; 57% had diabetes), randomized to a polypill — aspirin 100 mg, ramipril 2.5/5/10 mg, atorvastatin 20 or 40 mg — or to usual care, and followed a median of 3 years. The primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal type 1 MI, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or urgent revascularization) occurred in 9.5% on the polypill vs 12.7% on usual care (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.96; P=0.02); the key secondary composite occurred in 8.2% vs 11.7% (HR 0.70, 0.54–0.90), and cardiovascular death fell from 5.8% to 3.9% (HR 0.67). Self-reported adherence was higher on the polypill; adverse events were similar. Open-label and pragmatic — the trial tests a strategy, not a molecule — but it is the strategy real clinics can actually run.

cards.headline: TIPS-3: in primary prevention the pill alone was borderline — aspirin carried it over the line (2021)
cards.result: Yusuf S et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384:216–227 (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2028220 · NCT01646437). 5,713 people without cardiovascular disease at intermediate risk, in a 2×2 factorial trial of a polypill (simvastatin 40 mg, atenolol 100 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, ramipril 10 mg) and aspirin 75 mg, followed a mean of 4.6 years. The polypill alone lowered the primary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, resuscitated arrest, heart failure, or revascularization) from 5.5% to 4.4% — HR 0.79, with a confidence interval touching 1.00 (0.63–1.00), honestly borderline. Polypill plus aspirin: 4.1% vs 5.8% on double placebo (HR 0.69, 0.50–0.97). Aspirin alone: HR 0.86, not significant. The pill lowered LDL cholesterol by only ~19 mg/dL and systolic pressure by ~5.8 mm Hg — about half the expected effect — and hypotension or dizziness was more frequent (2.7% vs 1.1%); discontinuation climbed over the years, partly from drug-supply problems.

cards.headline: PolyIran: five years of one tablet in a whole population (2019)
cards.result: Roshandel G et al., Lancet 2019;394:672–683 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31791-X · NCT01271985). A pragmatic cluster-randomized trial of 6,838 adults aged 50–75 in rural Iran — 89% without prior cardiovascular disease — comparing a polypill (hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, and enalapril 5 mg, or valsartan 40 mg if cough developed) plus lifestyle advice against lifestyle advice alone, over 5 years. Major cardiovascular events: 5.9% with the polypill vs 8.8% without (adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.55–0.80; number needed to treat ≈ 35). Median adherence was 80.5%, and among high adherers the hazard ratio was 0.43. The effect was clearest in those with pre-existing disease (HR 0.61) and directionally similar without (HR 0.80, CI crossing 1). Adverse events were similar overall — intracranial hemorrhage 10 vs 11, upper gastrointestinal bleeding 13 vs 9.

cards.headline: Reading the three trials together
cards.result: Three randomized trials, three designs — open-label secondary prevention in Europe (SECURE), double-blind primary prevention across the global South (TIPS-3), and a pragmatic cluster trial in Iran (PolyIran) — land in the same place: hazard ratios of 0.66 to 0.79 for major cardiovascular events. None of the components is new or exotic; the trials test whether packaging proven drugs into one tablet gets them taken. The adherence gradient inside PolyIran (HR 0.43 in high adherers vs 0.66 overall) is the mechanism showing through. The limits are real: fixed doses cannot be titrated drug by drug, two of the three trials were open-label, and the one fully blinded trial needed aspirin added for its cleanest result. Judged as drug trials these are modest; judged as delivery trials — which is what they are — they are among the most consistent results in prevention.

shelves.title: Intravenous iron in heart failure: three trials, one direction, no clean win
shelves.question: Iron deficiency affects half of heart-failure patients. Does fixing it intravenously change outcomes — or only how patients feel?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Iron Deficiencies · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Ferric Compounds · Maltose · Hospitalization · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Humans
shelves.balance: Three large trials, one direction, no clean win: intravenous iron in iron-deficient heart failure makes people feel and function better — that part is proven — and probably keeps some out of hospital, but every outcomes trial has narrowly missed its primary endpoint and none has shown a mortality benefit. The guidelines recommend it for symptoms and quality of life; read the hospitalization claim as likely, not established, and the mortality claim as absent.

cards.headline: AFFIRM-AHF: the first near-miss — hospitalizations fell, the primary endpoint just missed (2020)
cards.result: Ponikowski P et al., Lancet 2020;396:1895–1904 (PMID 33197395 · NCT02937454). 1,132 iron-deficient patients hospitalized for acute heart failure (ejection fraction below 50%) were randomized to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose or placebo before discharge; 1,108 were in the primary analysis, followed 52 weeks. The primary endpoint — total heart-failure hospitalizations plus cardiovascular death — occurred at a rate ratio of 0.79 (95% CI 0.62–1.01; P=0.059): a whisker from significance. The hospitalizations component alone was significant (rate ratio 0.74, 0.58–0.94); cardiovascular death was not reduced. A prespecified sensitivity analysis counting only the pre-COVID-lockdown period gave 0.75 (0.59–0.96). The trial that launched a thousand infusions never actually met its primary endpoint.

cards.result: Kalra PR et al., Lancet 2022;400:2199–2209 (PMID 36347265 · NCT02642562). 1,137 patients with heart failure, reduced ejection fraction, and iron deficiency — mostly outpatients — received intravenous ferric derisomaltose or usual care in an open-label trial with blinded endpoint assessment, followed a median of 2.7 years. cards.headline: HEART-FID: the largest trial set a stricter bar — and did not clear it (2023)
cards.result: Mentz RJ et al., N Engl J Med 2023;389:975–986 (PMID 37632463 · NCT03037931). 3,065 ambulatory patients with heart failure (ejection fraction 40% or below) and iron deficiency received ferric carboxymaltose or placebo. The primary outcome was hierarchical — death at 12 months, then heart-failure hospitalizations, then change in 6-minute walk distance — and the trial prespecified an unusually strict significance threshold of 0.01. Result: win ratio 1.10 (99% CI 0.99–1.23), P=0.02 — better than placebo, but not by the standard the trial set for itself. Components: death 8.6% vs 10.3% at 12 months; 297 vs 332 hospitalizations; walk distance +8 m vs +4 m. The main secondary composite (cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization) was not significant (HR 0.93).

cards.headline: Reading the iron evidence together: symptoms proven, hospitalizations likely, mortality absent
cards.result: What is actually established: patients feel and function better. FAIR-HF (2009, 459 patients) improved patient global assessment, NYHA class, 6-minute walk distance, and quality of life; CONFIRM-HF (2015) confirmed the walk-distance benefit over 52 weeks. Oral iron does not do this (IRONOUT-HF was null — the gut will not absorb it in heart failure), which is why the evidence is intravenous-only. Patient-level meta-analyses pooling the outcomes trials find a consistent reduction in the composite of heart-failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death, driven by hospitalizations, with no effect on mortality. The 2023 ESC focused update grades intravenous iron Class I for symptom and quality-of-life improvement and IIa for reducing hospitalizations in iron-deficient patients with reduced or mildly reduced ejection fraction. The honest summary: a treatment for how patients feel, probably for keeping them out of hospital, and not — on current evidence — a treatment that extends life.

shelves.title: VTE prophylaxis: preventing clots, buying bleeding
shelves.question: Hospital clot prevention is universal and automatic — what do the big trials actually buy, and what do they charge?
shelves.mesh: Venous Thromboembolism · Venous Thrombosis · Pulmonary Embolism · Anticoagulants · Hemorrhage · Dalteparin · Enoxaparin · Rivaroxaban · Humans
shelves.balance: Prophylaxis prevents clots — that part is not in doubt. Everything after it is margins. In the ICU, the better-marketed drug tied on the clots the trial was powered for and won on pulmonary embolism and HIT only as secondary findings its own authors tell us to hold loosely. In medical patients, extending prophylaxis past the standard course prevented mostly silent clots and paid for them in bleeding, and the largest extension trial missed its primary endpoint outright. No prophylaxis trial has ever moved mortality. Give it to patients whose clot risk is real, stop it when the stay stops, and do not mistake an ultrasound endpoint for a life saved.

cards.headline: PROTECT: the primary was a tie; the headline came from the secondaries (2011)
cards.result: Cook D et al., N Engl J Med 2011;364:1305–1314 (PMID 21417952 · NCT00182143). In 67 ICUs, 3,764 critically ill patients were randomized to dalteparin 5,000 IU once daily or unfractionated heparin 5,000 IU twice daily, with twice-weekly leg ultrasounds. The primary outcome, proximal leg deep-vein thrombosis: 5.1% on dalteparin vs 5.8% on unfractionated heparin (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P=0.57) — a tie whose confidence interval excludes neither a 32% benefit nor a 23% harm. The findings that made the trial famous were secondary: pulmonary embolism 1.3% vs 2.3% (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30–0.88; P=0.01), and less heparin-induced thrombocytopenia in the per-protocol analysis (HR 0.27). Major bleeding (HR 1.00) and hospital death (HR 0.92) did not differ. The authors themselves supply the shelf's caution: nominally significant secondary outcomes in a trial that missed its primary deserve restraint — dalteparin may be the better ICU default, but PROTECT proved less than its reputation.

cards.headline: MAGELLAN: extending prophylaxis prevented clots and caused bleeding, in the same patients (2013)
cards.result: Cohen AT et al., N Engl J Med 2013;368:513–523 (PMID 23388003 · NCT00571649). 8,101 patients hospitalized with acute medical illness were randomized to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 35 days or enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 10 days followed by placebo. At day 10 the strategies tied on the primary outcome (asymptomatic proximal or symptomatic venous thromboembolism): 2.7% vs 2.7%, meeting noninferiority. By day 35 the extended drug had won on clots — 4.4% vs 5.7% (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.96; P=0.02) — and lost on bleeding at both horizons: clinically relevant bleeding 2.8% vs 1.2% at day 10 and 4.1% vs 1.7% at day 35 (P<0.001 for both), with mortality similar. MAGELLAN is the extended-prophylaxis trade in one trial: most of the clots prevented were ultrasound findings, most of the bleeding was clinically real, and the ledger has never balanced to a survival gain. Regulators noticed — rivaroxaban was not approved for this indication on these data.

cards.headline: MARINER: the biggest extension trial missed its primary endpoint (2018)
cards.result: Spyropoulos AC et al., N Engl J Med 2018;379:1118–1127 (PMID 30145946 · NCT02111564). 12,019 patients discharged after a hospitalization for medical illness — selected for elevated clot risk — were randomized to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 45 days or placebo. The primary outcome, symptomatic venous thromboembolism or death from venous thromboembolism: 0.83% on rivaroxaban vs 1.10% on placebo (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.52–1.09; P=0.14) — a favorable point estimate that did not reach significance, in the largest trial ever run on the question. Major bleeding was numerically higher (0.28% vs 0.15%; HR 1.88, CI spanning no effect), and a prespecified secondary outcome — symptomatic nonfatal venous thromboembolism — did fall (0.18% vs 0.42%; HR 0.44). Read plainly: after discharge, the events extension therapy exists to prevent are so uncommon that 12,000 high-risk patients could not prove the benefit, while the bleeding risk, though small, is always present.

cards.headline: Reading the prophylaxis trials together: an ultrasound literature with a bleeding bill
cards.result: Step back and the field's shape is consistent. Standard-duration prophylaxis in sick, immobile inpatients prevents venous thromboembolism — the control arms of these trials clot at rates no one would accept untreated — but the events are dominated by asymptomatic ultrasound-detected thrombi, the surrogate the trials are powered on. Comparisons between agents (PROTECT) resolve to ties on the primary and hints on the secondaries. Extensions in duration or into the post-discharge period (MAGELLAN, MARINER) shrink the surrogate further while adding measurable bleeding, and mortality — the outcome patients would vote for — has never significantly moved in any of them. Guidelines accordingly recommend prophylaxis during the acute stay for at-risk medical and ICU patients and recommend against routine extension. The evidence supports exactly that posture and no more: prophylaxis is a bounded, in-hospital intervention, not a subscription.

shelves.title: Stopping a statin: what happens next
shelves.mesh: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Withholding Treatment · Cardiovascular Diseases · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: across these cohorts, people who stop a statin fare worse than people who continue — death HR 1.92 and cardiovascular events HR 1.31 in the pooled review of 36 studies — but the underlying studies are observational and stoppers are often sicker, so read the numbers as association, not proof; the shelf’s one randomized trial is the exception, finding that stopping near the end of life probably made no difference in 60-day mortality; and delaying the start itself carried more events (HR 1.49).

shelves.title: Digoxin in heart failure: mortality neutral, fewer hospitalizations
shelves.mesh: Digoxin · Heart Failure · Cardiotonic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: in the only large randomized trial, digoxin at a median 0.25 mg a day did not change mortality (RR 0.99) and cut heart-failure hospitalizations (RR 0.72); two randomized withdrawal trials agree from the other direction — stopping it made heart failure worse within weeks. There is no randomized evidence of toxicity at these doses; the harm signal lives in one post-hoc analysis at serum levels of 1.2 ng/mL or more, so the practical lesson is to aim low (0.5–0.8 ng/mL), not to avoid the drug. The Beers 0.125 mg ceiling rests on that post-hoc signal and pharmacology; the developer’s evidence revision records the toxicity claim as unproven — Level B — with benefit the better-supported reading.

cards.headline: DIG (1997): digoxin did not change mortality — and cut heart-failure hospitalizations

cards.result: Mortality 34.8% with digoxin vs 35.1% with placebo (RR 0.99 , 95% CI 0.91–1.07; P=0.80) — no difference. Hospitalization for worsening heart failure 26.8% vs 34.7% (RR 0.72 , 95% CI 0.66–0.79; P<0.001)
cards.watchOut: Pre-beta-blocker/MRA era background therapy; the trial dose was double the 0.125 mg ceiling Beers later set

shelves.title: Renal denervation for hypertension: the sham reckoning
shelves.question: Does burning the nerves around the renal arteries lower blood pressure beyond a sham procedure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Denervation · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Radiography · Renal Artery · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Failure · Adult · Antihypertensive Agents · Australia · Austria · Bayes Theorem · Canada · Germany · Greece · Ireland · Japan · Kidney · Prospective Studies · Sympathectomy · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · United States
shelves.balance: The field's arc in two trials. After open-label results that looked dramatic, the first big sham-controlled trial found essentially nothing — a 2.4 mm Hg difference that wasn't significant — and the field reset. Six years later, a tighter trial in patients taking no medications found a real but modest effect: about 4 mm Hg on 24-hour ambulatory pressure. Both cards measure a surrogate: blood pressure, not strokes or deaths. No outcomes trial exists, and this shelf claims none.

cards.headline: HTN-3 2014: renal denervation beat sham by just 2.4 mm Hg (P=0.26) — the big blinded null that reset the field.
cards.summary: At 6 months, office systolic pressure fell 14.13 mm Hg on denervation vs 11.74 mm Hg on sham — a difference of −2.39 mm Hg (95% CI −6.89 to 2.12; P=0.26 for the superiority test), missing the primary endpoint. The 24-hour ambulatory difference was −1.96 mm Hg. No significant safety differences.
cards.people: 535 patients with resistant hypertension on maximally tolerated multi-drug regimens
cards.result: At 6 months, office systolic pressure fell 14.13 mm Hg on denervation vs 11.74 mm Hg on sham — a difference of −2.39 mm Hg (95% CI −6.89 to 2.12; P=0.26 for the superiority test), missing the primary endpoint. The 24-hour ambulatory difference was −1.96 mm Hg. No significant safety differences.
cards.watchOut: Both arms fell a lot — trial participation, adherence checks, and the sham itself lower pressure. The unblinded trials that built the hype had none of those controls, which is exactly why this one mattered.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al., N Engl J Med 2014 (PMID 24678939 · NCT01418261)

shelves.title: Beta-blockers after MI without heart failure: the ejection fraction decides
shelves.question: After a heart attack with normal pump function — in the era of stents and statins — do beta-blockers still help, and can long-term users stop?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Aged · Bisoprolol · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Metoprolol · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Secondary Prevention · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left · Ventricular Function, Left · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: At EF ≥50%, starting a beta-blocker after MI did nothing measurable over 3.5 years (REDUCE-AMI), while stopping one in stable long-term users failed to prove non-inferior (ABYSS). One band down, at EF 40–49%, the pooled patient-level data from four trials say treatment prevents events (HR 0.75). The old reflex survives — one ejection-fraction band below where it used to live.

cards.headline: REDUCE-AMI 2024: after MI with EF ≥50%, beta-blockers did not reduce death or new MI (7.9% vs 8.3%).
cards.summary: The primary outcome (death or new MI) occurred in 7.9% (199/2508) on beta-blockers vs 8.3% (208/2512) without (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.79–1.16; P=0.64). Death from any cause: 3.9% vs 4.1%; new MI: 4.5% vs 4.7%.
cards.people: 5,020 patients after myocardial infarction with ejection fraction ≥50%, median follow-up 3.5 years
cards.result: The primary outcome (death or new MI) occurred in 7.9% (199/2508) on beta-blockers vs 8.3% (208/2512) without (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.79–1.16; P=0.64). Death from any cause: 3.9% vs 4.1%; new MI: 4.5% vs 4.7%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and largely one country's registry population — but large, long, and hard-outcome. It retires the automatic prescription, not the drug: reduced EF remains a different, proven indication.

shelves.title: Exercise in heart failure: fitter, not longer-lived
shelves.question: Does structured exercise training change outcomes in heart failure — or only how patients feel and move?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ambulatory Care · Cardiac Rehabilitation · Chronic Disease · Echocardiography · Exercise · Exercise Test · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Frail Elderly · Global Health · Heart Failure · Heart Rate · Heart Ventricles · High-Intensity Interval Training · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Readmission · Physical Functional Performance · Prognosis · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function · Self Care · Stroke Volume · Survival Rate · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: Four exhibits, one shape. Training reliably makes heart-failure patients fitter and more functional — HF-ACTION's exercise-capacity gains, REHAB-HF's large SPPB jump in the frailest patients — and just as reliably fails to move death or hospitalization: HF-ACTION's unadjusted primary null, REHAB-HF's flat rehospitalization, SMARTEX's evaporating gains, and an 18-trial individual-patient pool with every hard-outcome estimate crossing 1. Prescribe exercise for what patients can do and how they feel. Don't promise it extends life — the trials haven't shown that.

cards.headline: HF-ACTION 2009: exercise training in 2,331 heart-failure patients — primary endpoint 65% vs 68%, HR 0.93, P=0.13 unadjusted. The field's biggest exercise trial missed.
cards.summary: Death or hospitalization occurred in 65% (759) of the exercise group vs 68% (796) of usual care (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84–1.02; P=0.13). Mortality alone: 16% vs 17% (HR 0.96; P=0.70). Adherence faded over the year (median 95 min/week at months 4–6, 74 by months 10–12); after adjustment for prognostic factors, the composite reached nominal significance.

Adherence faded over the year (median 95 min/week at months 4–6, 74 by months 10–12); after adjustment for prognostic factors, the composite reached nominal significance.
cards.watchOut: Read both ways honestly: the unadjusted primary analysis — the one that counts — was null, and the adjusted positive is the one that got quoted. Exercise capacity and quality of life did improve modestly. This is a “helps you live better, unproven to help you live longer” result.

shelves.title: Niacin added to treated cholesterol: AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE
shelves.question: In patients with established vascular disease whose LDL cholesterol is already treated with statin-based therapy, does adding niacin reduce major cardiovascular events?
shelves.balance: No. AIM-HIGH found no incremental clinical benefit from adding extended-release niacin to intensive statin therapy. HPS2-THRIVE likewise found no significant reduction in major vascular events with niacin-laropiprant and reported more serious adverse events. Together, the trials do not support adding niacin to well-treated LDL cholesterol to improve cardiovascular outcomes.

shelves.title: Closing a patent foramen ovale after cryptogenic stroke
shelves.question: After a cryptogenic stroke in a patient with a patent foramen ovale, does device closure beat medical therapy at preventing another stroke?
shelves.balance: In selected patients — younger, with a moderate-to-large shunt or an atrial septal aneurysm — the three 2017 NEJM trials all favored closure: RESPECT’s long-term follow-up HR 0.55, REDUCE 1.4% vs 5.4%, CLOSE zero strokes vs 14. The price is real: more atrial fibrillation after the device (up to 6.6%), procedural complications (about 6% in CLOSE), and venous clots in RESPECT. Absolute gains are small because recurrence on medical therapy is already low — this is a carefully-selected-patient treatment, not a close-every-PFO answer. The earlier 2013 RESPECT primary report, at a median 2.1 years, had been null; the benefit emerged with longer follow-up.

cards.headline: With 5.9 years of follow-up, closure halves recurrent stroke vs medical therapy
cards.summary: Recurrent ischemic stroke in 18 closure patients vs 28 on medical therapy — 0.58 vs 1.07 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.55; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.999; P=0.046).
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, open-label trial with blinded endpoint adjudication (extended follow-up)
cards.people: 980 patients, 18 to 60 years of age, with a patent foramen ovale and a cryptogenic ischemic stroke; median follow-up 5.9 years
cards.result: Recurrent ischemic stroke in 18 closure patients vs 28 on medical therapy — 0.58 vs 1.07 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.55; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.999; P=0.046). For strokes of undetermined cause, HR 0.38 (0.18 to 0.79). Venous thromboembolism was more common in the closure group.
cards.watchOut: The extended analysis was exploratory, treatment exposure was unequal (more dropout on medical therapy), and the original primary analysis at 2.1 years did not reach significance — the case rests on the long follow-up.
cards.source: Saver JL, Carroll JD, et al. (RESPECT). N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 28902590 · NCT00465270.

shelves.title: Colchicine for pericarditis: the recurrence is the disease
shelves.question: Does adding colchicine to standard anti-inflammatory treatment prevent pericarditis from coming back?
shelves.balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from the same Italian group — one in a first acute attack, one in patients with multiple recurrences — and both cut recurrence roughly in half, with numbers needed to treat of 4 and 5 and no serious-harm signal. The evidence is strong in effect and narrow in provenance: essentially one research group has run these trials, which is the honest caveat on the shelf. (Colchicine also lives on Shelf #120 for coronary disease — a different question, so no one-home conflict.)

cards.headline: Colchicine halves incessant or recurrent pericarditis after a first attack
cards.summary: The primary outcome — incessant or recurrent pericarditis — occurred in 16.7% vs 37.5% (relative risk reduction 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.72; NNT 4; P<0.001).
cards.people: 240 adults with a first episode of acute pericarditis (120 per group)
cards.result: Colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily (once daily if ≤70 kg) for 3 months, added to aspirin or ibuprofen. The primary outcome — incessant or recurrent pericarditis — occurred in 16.7% vs 37.5% (relative risk reduction 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.72; NNT 4; P<0.001). Symptoms persisting at 72 hours: 19.2% vs 40.0%; hospitalizations 5.0% vs 14.2%; remission at one week 85.0% vs 58.3%. Adverse effects and discontinuations were similar; no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One research group, four Italian centers — the result is large and clean, but independent replication is thin.
cards.source: Imazio M, et al. (ICAP). N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID: 23992557 · NCT00128453.

cards.summary: Recurrent pericarditis in 21.6% (26/120) vs 42.5% (51/120) — relative risk 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.65; P=0.0009; NNT 5).
cards.people: 240 adults with at least two prior recurrences of pericarditis (120 per group)
cards.result: Colchicine at the same weight-based dose for 6 months, added to conventional anti-inflammatory treatment. shelves.title: PCSK9 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes
shelves.question: In patients with established cardiovascular disease whose LDL cholesterol stays at or above 70 mg/dL on a statin, do PCSK9 inhibitor injections reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.balance: Two large double-blind trials, 46,488 patients: adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to a statin cut the combined rate of heart attack, stroke, and related events by about 15% — roughly 1.5 fewer events per 100 patients treated over 2–3 years — and lowered LDL by about 60%. Neither trial showed fewer cardiovascular deaths; the lower all-cause mortality in ODYSSEY OUTCOMES was a secondary endpoint. Injection-site reactions were the main excess harm.

Key secondary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke): 5.9% vs 7.4%, HR 0.80 (0.73–0.88), P<0.001. shelves.title: DASH diet and sodium reduction for blood pressure
shelves.question: Does the DASH eating pattern lower blood pressure, and does cutting sodium on top of it lower blood pressure further?
shelves.balance: The DASH eating pattern lowers blood pressure, and lowering sodium on top of it lowers it further — effects proven in controlled feeding trials. No trial has tested DASH itself against heart attacks or death; this shelf is about blood pressure, and says so. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for blood-pressure lowering (surrogate endpoint; no event claim).

shelves.title: PCSK9 inhibitors: long-term outcomes and the mortality signal
shelves.question: In patients already on a statin, does adding a PCSK9 inhibitor reduce cardiovascular events — and does it save lives?
shelves.mesh: PCSK9 Inhibitors · Proprotein Convertase 9 · Cholesterol, LDL · Cardiovascular Diseases · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large double-blind trials (46,488 patients) cut combined cardiovascular events by about 15% relative on top of a statin. On mortality the two trials split: FOURIER showed no reduction in cardiovascular death (HR 1.05); ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed fewer deaths from any cause (3.5% vs 4.1%) as a secondary endpoint. The open-label extension (Reference 3) is where a cardiovascular-death difference first appeared — with longer, earlier treatment. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

shelves.title: Ezetimibe added to a statin after acute coronary syndrome
shelves.question: After an acute coronary syndrome, does adding ezetimibe to a statin prevent cardiovascular events — and how big is the gain, honestly?
shelves.mesh: Ezetimibe · Simvastatin · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: IMPROVE-IT answers yes — with a small absolute gain: 32.7% vs 34.7% on the primary composite at 7 years, a 2.0-percentage-point absolute difference (HR 0.936, a 6.4% relative reduction) for adding ezetimibe 10 mg to simvastatin 40 mg. RACING (Reference 2) answers the practical follow-up: a moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe matched high-intensity statin alone, with more patients at LDL goal and fewer intolerance dropouts. EWTOPIA 75 (Reference 3) extends the evidence to primary prevention at age 75 and older, without a statin. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

cards.headline: IMPROVE-IT (Cannon 2015): ezetimibe added to simvastatin after ACS — 32.7% vs 34.7% at 7 years
cards.summary: Primary composite at 7 years 32.7% vs 34.7% (HR 0.936) — an absolute difference of 2.0 percentage points — 18,144 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (IMPROVE-IT), N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: 18,144 patients hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome within the preceding 10 days, with LDL 50–100 mg/dL on lipid-lowering therapy or 50–125 mg/dL without; simvastatin 40 mg + ezetimibe 10 mg vs simvastatin 40 mg + placebo; median follow-up 6 years.
cards.result: Time-weighted average LDL during the trial: 53.7 mg/dL on simvastatin–ezetimibe vs 69.5 mg/dL on simvastatin alone. Kaplan–Meier rate of the primary end point (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, coronary revascularization ≥30 days, or nonfatal stroke) at 7 years: 32.7% vs 34.7% — absolute risk difference 2.0 percentage points; HR 0.936 (0.89–0.99), P=0.016, a 6.4% relative reduction. Muscle, gallbladder, hepatic adverse effects and cancer were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real and small: about 2 fewer primary events per 100 patients treated for ~7 years, on a moderate-intensity statin (simvastatin 40 mg) that is no longer the usual post-ACS backbone.
cards.source: Cannon CP et al. Ezetimibe Added to Statin Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndromes. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID 26039521 · NCT00202878.

cards.headline: RACING (Kim 2022): moderate-intensity statin + ezetimibe matched high-intensity statin alone
cards.summary: Primary outcome at 3 years 9.1% vs 9.9% — noninferior; LDL <70 mg/dL in ~73–75% vs ~55–60% — 3,780 patients.
cards.people: 3,780 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at 26 centers in South Korea; rosuvastatin 10 mg + ezetimibe 10 mg (1,894) vs rosuvastatin 20 mg (1,886); 3-year follow-up.
cards.result: Primary end point (cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events, or nonfatal stroke) at 3 years: 9.1% on combination therapy vs 9.9% on high-intensity monotherapy (absolute difference −0.78%; 90% CI −2.39 to 0.83) — meeting the 2.0% noninferiority margin.
