shelves.title: Dual antiplatelet therapy after a stent: shorter vs longer
shelves.question: After a coronary stent, how long should two antiplatelet drugs continue — where does the bleeding cost overtake the ischemic gain?
shelves.mesh: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy · Drug-Eluting Stents · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Hemorrhage · Humans
shelves.balance: Duration is a trade, and the three trials price it from both ends. In high-bleeding-risk patients, stopping the second drug at 1 month cost nothing ischemic and cut bleeding (MASTER DAPT). Dropping aspirin instead — ticagrelor alone after 3 months — halved major bleeding with identical ischemic outcomes (TWILIGHT). Extending both drugs to 30 months prevented stent thrombosis and MI but raised bleeding, with a borderline excess of deaths (2.0% vs 1.5%) that has never been fully explained (DAPT Study). Shorter wins for high bleeding risk; longer buys ischemic protection only in patients who tolerate the first year cleanly. Developer's verdict: LIKELY.

cards.headline: MASTER DAPT (Valgimigli 2021): in high bleeding risk, 1 month of DAPT was enough — and bled less
cards.summary: Net adverse clinical events 7.5% vs 7.7% (noninferior); major or clinically relevant bleeding 6.5% vs 9.4% — 4,579 patients at high bleeding risk.
cards.type: Open-label RCT (MASTER DAPT), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 4,579 patients at high bleeding risk randomized 1 month after stent implantation (4,434 in the per-protocol population); abbreviated therapy (stop DAPT immediately) vs standard therapy (continue ≥2 additional months); outcomes at 335 days.
cards.result: Net adverse clinical events (death, MI, stroke, or major bleeding): 7.5% abbreviated vs 7.7% standard (difference −0.23 points; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Major adverse cardiac or cerebral events: 6.1% vs 5.9% (noninferior). Major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding: 6.5% vs 9.4% (difference −2.82 points; P<0.001 for superiority).
cards.watchOut: A high-bleeding-risk population by design, and a single stent platform — the result licenses short DAPT where bleeding risk dominates, not everywhere.

shelves.title: CABG vs PCI in diabetes and multivessel disease
shelves.question: In a patient with diabetes and multivessel coronary disease, does bypass surgery beat stenting — and does either beat medicines alone?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Bypass · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Coronary Artery Disease · Humans
shelves.balance: FREEDOM is the head-to-head answer: at 5 years the composite of death, MI, or stroke was 18.7% with CABG vs 26.6% with PCI — fewer deaths (10.9% vs 16.3% at five years, P=0.049) and far fewer MIs with surgery, paid for with more strokes (5.2% vs 2.4%). BARI-2D adds the humbler lesson that prompt revascularization of either kind did not beat intensive medical therapy overall in stable disease; the CABG stratum was the exception. SYNTAX's diabetes subgroup points the same way in complex disease, driven by repeat revascularization. Developer's verdict: LIKELY — and flagged: the balance line rests in part on FREEDOM's mortality difference (P=0.049).

cards.headline: FREEDOM (Farkouh 2012): CABG beat PCI in diabetes — death/MI/stroke 18.7% vs 26.6% at 5 years, more strokes
cards.summary: Primary outcome at 5 years 18.7% CABG vs 26.6% PCI (P=0.005); death from any cause 10.9% vs 16.3% (P=0.049); stroke 5.2% vs 2.4% — 1,900 patients, mean age 63.1 years, 29% women.
cards.people: 1,900 patients with diabetes and multivessel coronary artery disease at 140 international centers; mean age 63.1±9.1 years, 29% women, 83% with three-vessel disease; PCI with drug-eluting stents vs CABG, all on guideline medical therapy; minimum 2 years, median follow-up among survivors 3.8 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome (death from any cause, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke) at 5 years: 18.7% in the CABG group vs 26.6% in the PCI group (P=0.005). The CABG benefit was driven by lower rates of myocardial infarction (P<0.001) and death from any cause ( 10.9% vs 16.3% at 5 years; P=0.049). Stroke went the other way: 5.2% with CABG vs 2.4% with PCI (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: First-generation drug-eluting stents and 2005–2010 surgical practice; the mortality component of the composite was the weakest leg (P=0.049). The stroke excess with CABG is part of the trade, not a footnote.
cards.source: Farkouh ME et al. Strategies for Multivessel Revascularization in Patients with Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID 23121323 · NCT00086450.

cards.headline: BARI-2D (2009): prompt revascularization did not beat medical therapy overall — except in the CABG stratum
cards.summary: Survival at 5 years 88.3% revascularization vs 87.8% medical therapy (P=0.97); in the CABG stratum, major cardiovascular events 22.4% vs 30.5% (P=0.01) — 2,368 patients.
cards.type: RCT with 2×2 factorial design (BARI-2D), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 2,368 patients with type 2 diabetes and heart disease; prompt revascularization + intensive medical therapy vs intensive medical therapy alone, and insulin-sensitization vs insulin-provision glycemic strategy; the PCI-vs-CABG stratum was chosen before randomization as the more appropriate procedure; 5-year follow-up.
cards.result: Survival at 5 years did not differ: 88.3% revascularization vs 87.8% medical therapy (P=0.97), and 88.2% vs 87.9% for insulin sensitization vs provision (P=0.89). Freedom from major cardiovascular events: 77.2% vs 75.9% (P=0.70). In the PCI stratum there was no difference; in the CABG stratum, major cardiovascular events were lower with revascularization ( 22.4% vs 30.5% , P=0.01; interaction P=0.002). Severe hypoglycemia was more frequent with insulin provision (9.2% vs 5.9%).
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial, not a CABG-vs-PCI head-to-head: the CABG-stratum finding compares CABG + medicines vs medicines alone in patients pre-selected as surgical candidates — it supports FREEDOM's direction but does not substitute for it.
cards.source: BARI 2D Study Group. A Randomized Trial of Therapies for Type 2 Diabetes and Coronary Artery Disease. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID 19502645 · NCT00006305.

cards.headline: SYNTAX diabetes subgroup (Banning 2010): at 1 year, death/stroke/MI equal — repeat revascularization 20.3% vs 6.4%
cards.summary: In diabetic patients: death, stroke or MI 10.1% (PCI) vs 10.3% (CABG) at 1 year; repeat revascularization 20.3% vs 6.4% — 452 patients with diabetes within SYNTAX.
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of an RCT (SYNTAX), J Am Coll Cardiol 2010
cards.people: 452 patients with medically treated diabetes among 1,800 randomized in SYNTAX (left main and/or three-vessel disease); paclitaxel-eluting stents (PES) vs CABG; 1-year outcomes.
cards.result: At 1 year, the composite of death, stroke, or MI in diabetic patients was 10.1% with PES vs 10.3% with CABG (P=0.96); overall major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events were higher with PES, driven by repeat revascularization: 20.3% vs 6.4% (P<0.001). shelves.title: TAVR vs surgical aortic valve replacement, by surgical risk
shelves.question: For severe aortic stenosis, when does a transcatheter valve (TAVR) match or beat surgical replacement — and what is not yet known?
shelves.mesh: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation · Humans
shelves.balance: Across every surgical-risk stratum tested, TAVR was at least noninferior to surgery on death and stroke: high risk (PARTNER 1), intermediate risk (PARTNER 2), and low risk with either a balloon-expandable valve (PARTNER 3 — the 1-year composite actually favored TAVR) or a self-expanding valve (Evolut Low Risk). TAVR's consistent prices are paravalvular leak and, with the self-expanding valve, pacemakers (17.4% vs 6.1%); surgery's are bleeding, kidney injury, and new atrial fibrillation. The honest limit: these primary reports run 1–2 years. Valve durability over the 10–20 years a younger low-risk patient needs is not in this evidence. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

cards.headline: PARTNER 1 (Smith 2011, high risk): death at 1 year 24.2% vs 26.8% — noninferior, different periprocedural prices
cards.summary: Death from any cause at 1 year 24.2% TAVR vs 26.8% surgery (noninferior); major vascular complications 11.0% vs 3.2%; major bleeding 9.3% vs 19.5% — 699 high-risk patients.
cards.type: RCT (PARTNER 1, Cohort A), N Engl J Med 2011
cards.people: 699 high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis at 25 centers; TAVR with a balloon-expandable bovine pericardial valve (transfemoral or transapical) vs surgical replacement; primary end point death from any cause at 1 year.
cards.result: Death at 30 days: 3.4% TAVR vs 6.5% surgery (P=0.07); at 1 year 24.2% vs 26.8% (P=0.44; P=0.001 for noninferiority against a 7.5-point margin). Major stroke at 1 year: 5.1% vs 2.4% (P=0.07). Major vascular complications were more frequent with TAVR (11.0% vs 3.2%, P<0.001); major bleeding (9.3% vs 19.5%) and new-onset atrial fibrillation (8.6% vs 16.0%) were more frequent after surgery.
cards.watchOut: First-generation device and transapical access in a quarter of patients; the stroke numbers numerically favored surgery at both time points without reaching significance.
cards.source: Smith CR et al. Transcatheter versus Surgical Aortic-Valve Replacement in High-Risk Patients. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID 21639811 · NCT00530894.

cards.headline: PARTNER 2 (Leon 2016, intermediate risk): death or disabling stroke at 2 years 19.3% vs 21.1% — noninferior
cards.summary: Death or disabling stroke at 2 years 19.3% TAVR vs 21.1% surgery (HR 0.89; noninferior) — 2,032 intermediate-risk patients.
cards.people: 2,032 intermediate-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis at 57 centers; TAVR vs surgical replacement; 76.3% in the transfemoral-access cohort, 23.7% transthoracic; primary end point death from any cause or disabling stroke at 2 years.
cards.result: Death or disabling stroke at 2 years: 19.3% TAVR vs 21.1% surgery (HR 0.89, 0.73–1.09; P=0.001 for noninferiority, P=0.25 for superiority). In the transfemoral cohort the rates favored TAVR (HR 0.79); in the transthoracic cohort they were similar. cards.watchOut: Noninferiority, not superiority, overall — and the transthoracic-access subgroup did not share the transfemoral subgroup's favorable trend.

cards.headline: PARTNER 3 (Mack 2019, low risk): the 1-year composite favored TAVR — 8.5% vs 15.1%
cards.summary: Death, stroke, or rehospitalization at 1 year 8.5% TAVR vs 15.1% surgery (HR 0.54; superiority P=0.001) — 1,000 low-risk patients, mean age 73 years.
cards.people: 1,000 patients with severe aortic stenosis and low surgical risk at 71 centers; mean age 73 years, mean STS risk score 1.9%; transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve vs surgery; primary end point (death, stroke, or rehospitalization) at 1 year, as-treated population.
cards.result: The primary composite at 1 year was 8.5% with TAVR vs 15.1% with surgery (absolute difference −6.6 points; HR 0.54, 0.37–0.79; P<0.001 for noninferiority, P=0.001 for superiority). cards.headline: Evolut Low Risk (Forrest 2019): self-expanding TAVR noninferior at 24 months — pacemakers 17.4% vs 6.1%
cards.summary: Death or disabling stroke at 24 months 5.3% TAVR vs 6.7% surgery (noninferior); pacemaker implantation 17.4% vs 6.1%; moderate/severe aortic regurgitation 3.5% vs 0.5% — 1,468 low-risk patients, mean age 74 years.
cards.type: RCT, Bayesian noninferiority analysis (Evolut Low Risk), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 1,468 patients with severe aortic stenosis and low surgical risk randomized (procedure attempted in 1,403); mean age 74 years; TAVR with a self-expanding supraannular bioprosthesis vs surgical replacement; primary end point death or disabling stroke at 24 months.

shelves.title: Complete vs culprit-only revascularization in STEMI
shelves.question: In STEMI with multivessel disease, should the non-culprit lesions be opened too — or only the artery that caused the infarct?
shelves.mesh: ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Myocardial Revascularization · Humans
shelves.balance: COMPLETE, the large trial, gives the hard-outcome answer: the composite of cardiovascular death or MI was 7.8% with complete revascularization vs 10.5% with culprit-only PCI over a median 3 years (HR 0.74, a 26% relative reduction) — but the gain was fewer heart attacks, not fewer deaths: cardiovascular death itself was unchanged, and with ischemia-driven revascularization added the gap widened (8.9% vs 16.7%, HR 0.51) on far fewer repeat procedures. No mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf. The two smaller earlier trials pointed the same way on their composites (CvLPRIT 10.0% vs 21.2%; DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI 13% vs 22%) but were driven by repeat revascularization and showed no death or MI difference on their own. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

cards.headline: COMPLETE (Mehta 2019): complete revascularization cut CV death or MI — 7.8% vs 10.5%
cards.summary: Cardiovascular death or MI 7.8% vs 10.5% (HR 0.74); with ischemia-driven revascularization added, 8.9% vs 16.7% (HR 0.51) — 4,041 patients, median follow-up 3 years.
cards.people: 4,041 patients with STEMI and multivessel coronary artery disease after successful culprit-lesion PCI; complete revascularization (during or after the index hospitalization, per pre-randomization intent) vs no further revascularization; median follow-up 3 years.
cards.result: First coprimary outcome (cardiovascular death or MI): 158 of 2,016 ( 7.8% ) on complete revascularization vs 213 of 2,025 ( 10.5% ) on culprit-only PCI (HR 0.74, 0.60–0.91; P=0.004 — a 26% relative reduction). Second coprimary outcome (adding ischemia-driven revascularization): 8.9% vs 16.7% (HR 0.51). Benefit was consistent whether nonculprit PCI was intended during or after the index hospitalization.
cards.watchOut: Nonculprit lesions were treated on angiographic severity (with FFR reserved for intermediate lesions) — the trial licenses treating significant-looking lesions, not every lesion.
cards.source: Mehta SR et al. Complete Revascularization with Multivessel PCI for Myocardial Infarction. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID 31475795 · NCT01740479.

cards.headline: CvLPRIT (Gershlick 2015): complete revascularization during the index admission — composite 10.0% vs 21.2%
cards.summary: Primary composite at 12 months 10.0% vs 21.2% (HR 0.45); no significant reduction in death or MI alone — 296 patients.
cards.type: Open-label RCT (CvLPRIT), J Am Coll Cardiol 2015

shelves.title: Bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients
shelves.question: In patients who cannot or will not take a statin, does bempedoic acid prevent cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Bempedoic Acid · Dicarboxylic Acids · Fatty Acids · Cardiovascular Diseases · Humans
shelves.balance: One outcomes trial, honestly sized: in 13,970 statin-intolerant patients, bempedoic acid cut the primary composite from 13.3% to 11.7% (HR 0.87 — a 13% relative reduction; absolute difference 1.6 percentage points over a median 40.6 months), with fewer MIs and fewer revascularizations — and no effect on stroke or on death from any cause. Gout (3.1% vs 2.1%) and gallstones (2.2% vs 1.2%) were the price. Card 2 is the supporting LDL/safety trial in statin-treated patients. A single outcomes trial cannot carry a Level A verdict. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

cards.headline: CLEAR Outcomes (Nissen 2023): bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients — 11.7% vs 13.3%
cards.summary: Primary composite 11.7% vs 13.3% (HR 0.87); MI HR 0.77; no effect on stroke or death — 13,970 statin-intolerant patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (CLEAR Outcomes), N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 13,970 statin-intolerant patients with, or at high risk for, cardiovascular disease; bempedoic acid 180 mg daily (6,992) vs placebo (6,978); mean baseline LDL 139.0 mg/dL in both groups; median follow-up 40.6 months.
cards.result: LDL fell by an additional 29.2 mg/dL vs placebo at 6 months (difference in percent reduction 21.1 points). Primary end point (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or coronary revascularization): 819 patients ( 11.7% ) vs 927 ( 13.3% ) — HR 0.87 (0.79–0.96), P=0.004, a 13% relative reduction and a 1.6-percentage-point absolute difference. MI: 3.7% vs 4.8% (HR 0.77); coronary revascularization: 6.2% vs 7.6% (HR 0.81). No significant effect on fatal or nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death, or death from any cause. Gout 3.1% vs 2.1%; cholelithiasis 2.2% vs 1.2%; small rises in creatinine, uric acid, and hepatic enzymes were more frequent.
cards.watchOut: 'Statin-intolerant' here means unable or unwilling to take statins owing to unacceptable adverse effects — a definition that includes unwillingness. This remains the only cardiovascular-outcomes trial of the drug.
cards.source: Nissen SE et al. Bempedoic Acid and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Statin-Intolerant Patients. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 36876740 · NCT02993406.

shelves.title: Which P2Y12 inhibitor after PCI: ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel
shelves.question: After PCI for an acute coronary syndrome, which P2Y12 inhibitor — ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel — prevents the most events, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists · Ticagrelor · Prasugrel Hydrochloride · Clopidogrel · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Humans
shelves.balance: Each potent agent beat clopidogrel in its own trial: ticagrelor in PLATO (9.8% vs 11.7%, with vascular death 4.0% vs 5.1% and all-cause death 4.5% vs 5.9% — a mortality finding flagged below) and prasugrel in TRITON-TIMI 38 (9.9% vs 12.1%), prasugrel paying with more major and fatal bleeding. Head-to-head, ISAR-REACT 5 favored prasugrel over ticagrelor (6.9% vs 9.3%) with similar major bleeding — in an open-label trial. Stronger platelet blockade prevents more ischemic events than clopidogrel; between the two potent agents the only direct trial favors prasugrel. Developer's verdict: LIKELY.

cards.headline: PLATO (Wallentin 2009): ticagrelor beat clopidogrel — 9.8% vs 11.7%, vascular death 4.0% vs 5.1%
cards.summary: Primary composite 9.8% vs 11.7% (HR 0.84); death from any cause 4.5% vs 5.9%; overall major bleeding 11.6% vs 11.2% — 18,624 patients with ACS.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (PLATO), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 18,624 patients admitted with an acute coronary syndrome; ticagrelor (180 mg load, 90 mg twice daily) vs clopidogrel (300–600 mg load, 75 mg daily); outcomes at 12 months.
cards.result: Primary end point (death from vascular causes, MI, or stroke) at 12 months: 9.8% ticagrelor vs 11.7% clopidogrel (HR 0.84, 0.77–0.92). MI: 5.8% vs 6.9%; death from vascular causes: 4.0% vs 5.1% ; death from any cause: 4.5% vs 5.9%. Stroke alone did not differ (1.5% vs 1.3%). Overall major bleeding did not differ (11.6% vs 11.2%), but non-CABG major bleeding was higher on ticagrelor (4.5% vs 3.8%), including more fatal intracranial bleeding.
cards.watchOut: Flagged for the developer: PLATO's balance includes a mortality difference (vascular and all-cause) favoring ticagrelor — unusual among P2Y12 trials and not reproduced head-to-head in ISAR-REACT 5 (Reference 3). Dyspnea and ventricular pauses were also more frequent on ticagrelor in the full report.
cards.source: Wallentin L et al. Ticagrelor versus Clopidogrel in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndromes. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID 19717846 · NCT00391872.

cards.headline: TRITON-TIMI 38 (Wiviott 2007): prasugrel beat clopidogrel — 9.9% vs 12.1%, fatal bleeding 0.4% vs 0.1%
cards.summary: Primary composite 9.9% vs 12.1% (HR 0.81); stent thrombosis 1.1% vs 2.4%; major bleeding 2.4% vs 1.8%; fatal bleeding 0.4% vs 0.1% — 13,608 patients with ACS and planned PCI.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (TRITON-TIMI 38), N Engl J Med 2007
cards.people: 13,608 patients with moderate-to-high-risk acute coronary syndromes and scheduled PCI; prasugrel (60 mg load, 10 mg daily) vs clopidogrel (300 mg load, 75 mg daily) for 6–15 months.
cards.result: Primary efficacy end point: 9.9% prasugrel vs 12.1% clopidogrel (HR 0.81, 0.73–0.90). MI: 7.4% vs 9.7%; urgent target-vessel revascularization: 2.5% vs 3.7%; stent thrombosis: 1.1% vs 2.4%. Major bleeding rose with prasugrel (2.4% vs 1.8%; HR 1.32), as did life-threatening bleeding (1.4% vs 0.9%) and fatal bleeding ( 0.4% vs 0.1% ). Overall mortality did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Prasugrel's bleeding price fell hardest on patients with prior stroke/TIA, the elderly, and the low-weight — the subgroups in whom the drug is now avoided or dose-reduced; those exclusions postdate this trial.
cards.source: Wiviott SD et al. Prasugrel versus Clopidogrel in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndromes. N Engl J Med. 2007. PMID 17982182 · NCT00097591.

cards.headline: ISAR-REACT 5 (Schüpke 2019): head-to-head, prasugrel beat ticagrelor — 6.9% vs 9.3%
cards.summary: Death, MI, or stroke at 1 year 6.9% prasugrel vs 9.3% ticagrelor (HR 1.36 for ticagrelor); major bleeding 4.8% vs 5.4% — 4,018 patients.
cards.type: Open-label RCT (ISAR-REACT 5), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 4,018 patients with acute coronary syndromes (with or without ST elevation) and planned invasive evaluation, randomized to ticagrelor or prasugrel; primary end point death, MI, or stroke at 1 year.
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 137 of 2,006 patients ( 6.9% ) on prasugrel vs 184 of 2,012 ( 9.3% ) on ticagrelor (HR 1.36, 1.09–1.70; P=0.006). cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the strategies differed in loading timing as well as drug (prasugrel loading was deferred until angiography in non-STEMI) — it compares two treatment strategies built around the two drugs, not the molecules in isolation.

shelves.title: Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation
shelves.question: Does catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation improve hard outcomes — death, stroke, hospitalization — or mainly symptoms and rhythm?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Heart Failure · Humans
shelves.balance: The two landmark trials answer differently because they enrolled different hearts. In CABANA's broad symptomatic-AF population, ablation did not significantly reduce the primary composite in the intention-to-treat analysis (8.0% vs 9.2%; HR 0.86, P=0.30) — while clearly reducing AF recurrence and death-or-cardiovascular-hospitalization. In CASTLE-AF's failing hearts (LVEF ≤35%), ablation cut death or heart-failure hospitalization from 44.6% to 28.5%, with all-cause death 13.4% vs 25.0% — a mortality finding from one small, open-label trial, flagged below. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CABANA (Packer 2019): ablation vs drug therapy — the intention-to-treat primary composite was not significant

cards.people: 2,204 symptomatic patients with AF at 126 centers in 10 countries (median age 68 years; 37.2% women; 42.9% paroxysmal, 57.1% persistent AF), aged ≥65 years or <65 with ≥1 stroke risk factor; catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation ± additional procedures; 1,108) vs drug therapy with rhythm and/or rate control (1,096); median follow-up 48.5 months.

All-cause mortality: 5.2% vs 6.1% (HR 0.85; P=0.38). Death or cardiovascular hospitalization: 51.7% vs 58.1% (HR 0.83; P=0.001). AF recurrence: 49.9% vs 69.5% (HR 0.52).

Crossover blurs the intention-to-treat answer: 27.5% of the drug-therapy group ultimately received ablation, and 9.2% assigned to ablation never had it.

shelves.title: Left atrial appendage closure vs anticoagulation
shelves.question: In non-valvular atrial fibrillation, does closing the left atrial appendage prevent stroke as well as long-term anticoagulation — and at what procedural price?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Atrial Appendage · Warfarin · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Stroke · Humans
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, one consistent answer on efficacy and one consistent price. Against warfarin, Watchman closure was noninferior for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in PROTECT-AF and PREVAIL — with more early safety events, mostly periprocedural. Against a modern DOAC, PRAGUE-17 again met noninferiority for its broad net-benefit composite (sHR 0.84; P=0.004 for noninferiority) in high-risk patients, with major device complications in 4.5%. None of the three shows closure prevents strokes better than anticoagulation; the case for the device is avoiding lifelong blood thinners in selected patients, bought with an upfront procedural risk. The honest label is: LIKELY — for noninferiority, not superiority.

cards.headline: PROTECT-AF (Holmes 2009): LAA closure noninferior to warfarin — efficacy 3.0 vs 4.9 events per 100 patient-years, safety events higher
cards.summary: Primary efficacy rate 3.0 vs 4.9 per 100 patient-years (RR 0.62, 95% CrI 0.35–1.25; probability of noninferiority >99.9%); primary safety events 7.4 vs 4.4 per 100 patient-years (RR 1.69) — 707 patients.
cards.people: 707 patients with non-valvular AF and at least one of: previous stroke or TIA, congestive heart failure, diabetes, hypertension, or age 75 or older (mean age 72 years; 30% women, per the trial's registry record); LAA closure with the Watchman device (463) vs warfarin (244), 2:1 randomization; 1,065 patient-years of follow-up.
cards.result: Primary efficacy events: 3.0 per 100 patient-years with closure vs 4.9 per 100 patient-years with warfarin (rate ratio 0.62, 95% credible interval 0.35–1.25) — the probability of noninferiority exceeded 99.9%. Primary safety events (major bleeding, pericardial effusion, device embolization) were more frequent with closure: 7.4 vs 4.4 per 100 patient-years (RR 1.69, 1.01–3.19), mainly periprocedural complications.
cards.watchOut: Bayesian credible intervals and a generous two-fold non-inferiority margin, with an early-generation device on its learning curve — the safety penalty was concentrated around the implant procedure. Event rates are per patient-year, not simple percentages.
cards.source: Holmes DR et al. Percutaneous closure of the left atrial appendage versus warfarin therapy for prevention of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation: a randomised non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID 19683639 · NCT00129545.

cards.type: Randomized trial (PREVAIL), J Am Coll Cardiol 2014
cards.people: 407 patients with non-valvular AF (mean age 74 years; 30% women, per the trial's registry record); Watchman closure (269) vs chronic warfarin (138), 2:1 randomization; coprimary endpoints assessed at 18 months.
cards.result: First coprimary efficacy endpoint (stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/unexplained death): rate 0.064 in the device group vs 0.063 in the control group (rate ratio 1.07, 95% credible interval 0.57–1.89) — the prespecified noninferiority criterion was NOT achieved, because the upper credible bound crossed 1.75. The second coprimary endpoint (stroke or systemic embolism more than 7 days after randomization) did achieve noninferiority (0.0253 vs 0.0200). Early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, meeting the prespecified safety goal; on a broader definition, adverse events remained lower than in PROTECT-AF (4.2% vs 8.7%; P=0.004), and pericardial effusions requiring surgery fell from 1.6% to 0.4%.
cards.watchOut: A trial often summarized as positive that formally missed its first noninferiority endpoint — event rates were low and numerically similar, but with 407 patients the credible interval was too wide to prove the prespecified claim. Read it as supportive of the device, not definitive.

shelves.title: Early rhythm control in atrial fibrillation
shelves.question: Does starting rhythm control early — within a year of an atrial fibrillation diagnosis — prevent cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization, where the older strategy trials found nothing?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Dronedarone · Catheter Ablation · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: The old verdict — rhythm control buys nothing — came from trials that started late, in established AF, with older drugs. EAST-AFNET 4 asked the timing question and got a different answer: early rhythm control cut the cardiovascular composite (3.9 vs 5.0 events per 100 person-years; HR 0.79, a 21% relative reduction), at the cost of more therapy-related serious adverse events (4.9% vs 1.4%). ATHENA, the dronedarone outcomes trial, points the same way on its hospitalization-or-death composite (31.9% vs 39.4%; HR 0.76), though dronedarone did not significantly reduce death from any cause, and the drug later proved harmful in permanent AF and advanced heart failure — populations ATHENA did not enroll. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: EAST-AFNET 4 (Kirchhof 2020): rhythm control started within a year of diagnosis cut the cardiovascular composite — 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years
cards.summary: Primary composite 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years (HR 0.79, 96% CI 0.66–0.94; P=0.005); nights in hospital no different; therapy-related serious adverse events 4.9% vs 1.4% — 2,789 patients. Re-card; home Shelf #101 .
cards.type: Open-label RCT with blinded outcome assessment (EAST-AFNET 4), N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 2,789 patients with early AF (diagnosed no more than 1 year before enrollment; median time since diagnosis 36 days) and cardiovascular conditions, at 135 centers in 11 European countries; early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or AF ablation) vs usual care, in which rhythm control was limited to managing AF-related symptoms; trial stopped for efficacy at the third interim analysis after a median of 5.1 years of follow-up per patient.
cards.result: A first-primary-outcome event occurred in 249 patients assigned to early rhythm control (3.9 per 100 person-years) vs 316 assigned to usual care (5.0 per 100 person-years) — HR 0.79 (96% CI 0.66–0.94; P=0.005), a 21% relative reduction. Nights spent in hospital per year did not differ (5.8 ± 21.9 vs 5.1 ± 15.5 days; P=0.23), and symptoms and left ventricular function at 2 years did not differ significantly. Serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy occurred in 4.9% of the early-rhythm-control group vs 1.4% of the usual-care group.
cards.watchOut: Re-card with a different question: the home card on Shelf #101 asks the general rate-versus-rhythm strategy question; this card isolates timing — early versus symptom-triggered — as the intervention. Open-label, and stopped early at an interim analysis, which tends to flatter the effect; most rhythm control was antiarrhythmic drug therapy, not ablation, so this is an early-treatment result, not an ablation result.
cards.source: Kirchhof P et al. Early Rhythm-Control Therapy in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID 32865375 · NCT01288352 · ISRCTN04708680.

cards.headline: ATHENA (Hohnloser 2009): dronedarone cut cardiovascular hospitalization or death — 31.9% vs 39.4%
cards.summary: Primary outcome 31.9% vs 39.4% (HR 0.76; P<0.001); death from any cause 5.0% vs 6.0% (HR 0.84; P=0.18 — not significant); cardiovascular death 2.7% vs 3.9% (HR 0.71) — 4,628 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (ATHENA), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 4,628 patients with AF and additional risk factors for death (mean age 71.6 years; 47% women, per the trial's registry record); dronedarone (2,301) vs placebo (2,327) on top of usual care; mean follow-up 21 ± 5 months; the study drug was stopped prematurely in about 30% of each group, mostly for adverse events.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 734 patients (31.9%) on dronedarone vs 917 (39.4%) on placebo — HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.69–0.84; P<0.001), a 24% relative reduction. Death from any cause: 116 (5.0%) vs 139 (6.0%) — HR 0.84 (0.66–1.08; P=0.18), not significant. Death from cardiovascular causes: 63 (2.7%) vs 90 (3.9%) — HR 0.71 (0.51–0.98; P=0.03), largely from fewer arrhythmic deaths. Bradycardia, QT-interval prolongation, nausea, diarrhea, rash, and increased serum creatinine were all more common on dronedarone; thyroid and pulmonary adverse events were not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: The win is hospitalization, not proven survival — all-cause mortality did not reach significance. And ATHENA enrolled the safer slice of AF: dronedarone is contraindicated in permanent AF and in advanced or recently decompensated heart failure, where later trials found harm; do not generalize this card beyond its population.
cards.source: Hohnloser SH et al. Effect of dronedarone on cardiovascular events in atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID 19213680 · NCT00174785.

shelves.title: Cardiac resynchronization therapy in HFrEF
shelves.question: In heart failure with a wide QRS complex, does resynchronizing the ventricles keep people alive and out of hospital — and how far down the symptom scale does the benefit reach?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Heart Failure · Defibrillators, Implantable · Pacemaker, Artificial · Humans
shelves.balance: The most consistent device story in heart failure. In severe symptoms, CRT cut the composite of death or major hospitalization by about a third in CARE-HF (39% vs 55%; HR 0.63) — with death itself down from 30% to 20% — and COMPANION's CRT-defibrillator arm reduced mortality by a 36% relative margin. The benefit follows the QRS down the symptom scale but changes character: RAFT (NYHA class II–III) reduced both death or heart-failure hospitalization (33.2% vs 40.3%; HR 0.75) and death alone (HR 0.75), while MADIT-CRT (NYHA I–II) prevented heart-failure events (17.2% vs 25.3%; HR 0.66) with no mortality difference at all. The price is procedural — RAFT saw roughly twice as many 30-day device adverse events with CRT. The honest label is: LIKELY.

cards.headline: CARE-HF (Cleland 2005): resynchronization cut death or cardiovascular hospitalization — 39% vs 55%
cards.summary: Primary endpoint 39% vs 55% (HR 0.63); death from any cause 20% vs 30% (HR 0.64) — 813 patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure and cardiac dyssynchrony.
cards.type: Open-label RCT (CARE-HF), N Engl J Med 2005
cards.people: 813 patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure, left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and cardiac dyssynchrony, on standard pharmacologic therapy; medical therapy plus cardiac resynchronization vs medical therapy alone; mean follow-up 29.4 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was reached by 159 patients in the resynchronization group vs 224 in the medical-therapy group ( 39% vs 55% ; HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.51–0.77; P<0.001). Deaths: 82 vs 120 ( 20% vs 30% ; HR 0.64, 0.48–0.85; P<0.002) — a 36% relative reduction in mortality. Resynchronization also reduced interventricular mechanical delay and end-systolic volume, increased ejection fraction, and improved symptoms and quality of life (P<0.01 for all comparisons).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, as device trials must be, with a hospitalization-heavy composite — but the mortality component stands on its own here. Conducted before contemporary quadruple drug therapy, so today's absolute benefit stacks on better background treatment. A pre-registration-era trial: no registry ID exists in its record.
cards.source: Cleland JGF et al. The effect of cardiac resynchronization on morbidity and mortality in heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID 15753115.

cards.headline: COMPANION (Bristow 2004): CRT with a defibrillator cut death by a 36% relative margin; pacing alone missed significance
cards.summary: Death or hospitalization HR 0.81 (CRT-pacemaker) and 0.80 (CRT-defibrillator); risk of death reduced 24% relative (P=0.059) and 36% relative (P=0.003) respectively — 1,520 patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure.
cards.type: Open-label RCT (COMPANION), N Engl J Med 2004
cards.people: 1,520 patients with NYHA class III or IV heart failure due to ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy and QRS at least 120 ms, randomized 1:2:2 to optimal pharmacologic therapy (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, spironolactone) alone, therapy plus CRT-pacemaker, or therapy plus CRT-pacemaker-defibrillator.
cards.result: Against drug therapy alone, CRT-pacemaker reduced the primary composite (time to death from or hospitalization for any cause) with HR 0.81 (P=0.014), and CRT-defibrillator with HR 0.80 (P=0.01). The combined endpoint of death from or hospitalization for heart failure fell by 34% relative in the pacemaker group (P<0.002) and 40% relative in the pacemaker-defibrillator group (P<0.001). Death from any cause: reduced by 24% relative with CRT-pacemaker (P=0.059 — not significant) and by 36% relative with CRT-defibrillator (P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: The trial reports its headline effects as relative reductions (the abstract gives no absolute event rates), so this card quotes them as relative, per the library's rule. The mortality claim that survived significance testing belongs to the defibrillator combination, not to resynchronization pacing alone. A pre-registration-era trial: no registry ID exists in its record.
cards.source: Bristow MR et al. Cardiac-resynchronization therapy with or without an implantable defibrillator in advanced chronic heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2004. PMID 15152059.

cards.headline: RAFT (Tang 2010): adding CRT to an ICD in NYHA class II–III cut death or heart-failure hospitalization — 33.2% vs 40.3%
cards.summary: Primary outcome 33.2% vs 40.3% (HR 0.75); death 20.8% vs 26.1% (HR 0.75); heart-failure hospitalization 19.5% vs 26.1% (HR 0.68); more device adverse events at 30 days (124 vs 58 patients) — 1,798 patients.
cards.people: 1,798 patients with NYHA class II or III heart failure, LVEF 30% or less, and an intrinsic QRS of 120 ms or more (or paced QRS of 200 ms or more); ICD plus CRT (894) vs ICD alone (904), both with optimal medical therapy; mean follow-up 40 months.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 297 of 894 patients (33.2%) in the ICD-CRT group vs 364 of 904 (40.3%) in the ICD group — HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.64–0.87; P<0.001). Deaths: 186 vs 236 (20.8% vs 26.1% computed from the reported counts; HR 0.75, 0.62–0.91; P=0.003). Hospitalization for heart failure: 174 vs 236 patients (19.5% vs 26.1%; HR 0.68, 0.56–0.83; P<0.001). At 30 days after implantation, adverse events had occurred in 124 ICD-CRT patients vs 58 ICD patients (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The control arm already carried a defibrillator, so RAFT isolates the resynchronization increment — and prices it: the early procedural harm is part of the trade. Percentages for death and heart-failure hospitalization are computed from the event counts in the trial report.
cards.source: Tang AS et al. Cardiac-resynchronization therapy for mild-to-moderate heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID 21073365 · NCT00251251.

cards.headline: MADIT-CRT (Moss 2009): in NYHA class I–II, CRT-D prevented heart-failure events (17.2% vs 25.3%) but not death
cards.summary: Primary endpoint 17.2% vs 25.3% (HR 0.66), driven by a 41% relative reduction in heart-failure events, concentrated at QRS 150 ms or more; no difference in mortality (about 3% per year in both groups) — 1,820 patients.
cards.people: 1,820 patients with ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 30% or less, QRS 130 ms or more, and NYHA class I or II symptoms, enrolled over 4.5 years; CRT-ICD (1,089) vs ICD alone (731), 3:2 randomization; average follow-up 2.4 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (death or a nonfatal heart-failure event) occurred in 187 of 1,089 patients (17.2%) in the CRT-ICD group vs 185 of 731 (25.3%) in the ICD-only group — HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.52–0.84; P=0.001). The superiority was driven by a 41% relative reduction in heart-failure events and was evident primarily in the prespecified subgroup with QRS 150 ms or more. There was no significant difference in the risk of death — about 3% per year in each group. CRT reduced left ventricular volumes and improved ejection fraction.
cards.watchOut: Heart-failure events were diagnosed by physicians who knew the treatment assignments (a blinded committee adjudicated them) — a softer endpoint than death, in the mildest population on this shelf. The honest headline at this end of the symptom scale: CRT prevents decompensations, not deaths.

shelves.title: Ivabradine in HFrEF
shelves.question: Does slowing the sinus rate with ivabradine, on top of standard therapy, improve outcomes in heart failure — or only in the trial built around a high heart rate?
shelves.mesh: Ivabradine · Benzazepines · Heart Failure · Heart Rate · Coronary Disease · Humans
shelves.balance: One trial says yes, inside its chosen boundaries; the other says no, outside them. SHIFT enrolled exactly the physiology the drug targets — sinus rhythm, resting heart rate 70 or above, LVEF 35% or less, a heart-failure hospitalization within the previous year — and ivabradine cut the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization (24% vs 29%; HR 0.82), driven by hospitalizations (16% vs 21%), not by a demonstrated survival effect. BEAUTIFUL, in stable coronary disease with left-ventricular dysfunction but mostly no heart-failure syndrome, was flat on its primary composite (HR 1.00), including in its heart-rate-70-and-above subgroup. The claim that survives both trials: fewer heart-failure hospitalizations for SHIFT-shaped patients. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SHIFT (Swedberg 2010): ivabradine cut cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization — 24% vs 29%
cards.summary: Primary composite 24% vs 29% (HR 0.82; P<0.0001); hospital admission for worsening heart failure 16% vs 21% (HR 0.74); deaths due to heart failure 3% vs 5% (HR 0.74); symptomatic bradycardia 5% vs 1% — 6,558 patients.
cards.people: 6,558 patients with symptomatic heart failure, LVEF 35% or lower, sinus rhythm with heart rate at least 70 bpm, and a heart-failure admission within the previous year, on stable background treatment including a beta-blocker if tolerated; ivabradine titrated to a maximum of 7.5 mg twice daily (3,268) vs placebo (3,290); median follow-up 22.9 months.
cards.result: A primary-endpoint event occurred in 793 of 3,241 analyzed patients (24%) on ivabradine vs 937 of 3,264 (29%) on placebo — HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.75–0.90; P<0.0001), an 18% relative reduction. The effect was driven mainly by hospital admissions for worsening heart failure (514 [16%] vs 672 [21%]; HR 0.74, 0.66–0.83; P<0.0001) and deaths due to heart failure (113 [3%] vs 151 [5%]; HR 0.74, 0.58–0.94; P=0.014). Fewer serious adverse events occurred on ivabradine; symptomatic bradycardia was more common (150 patients [5%] vs 32 [1%]; P<0.0001), as were phosphenes (3% vs 1%).
cards.watchOut: A composite win carried by hospitalization; this card claims no all-cause mortality benefit, because the trial does not establish one. The entry ticket matters: benefit was shown only in sinus rhythm at heart rates of 70 or above despite background therapy — ivabradine is not a general heart-failure drug, and it does nothing for patients in atrial fibrillation.
cards.source: Swedberg K et al. Ivabradine and outcomes in chronic heart failure (SHIFT): a randomised placebo-controlled study. Lancet. 2010. PMID 20801500 · ISRCTN70429960.
cards.search: shift (swedberg 2010): ivabradine cut cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization — 24% vs 29% in patients with symptomatic heart failure and lvef of 35% or lower, in sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 70 beats per minute or higher and a hospital admission for heart failure within the previous year, does ivabradine reduce the composite of cardiovascular death or hospital admission for worsening heart failure? double-blind rct (shift), lancet 2010 6,558 patients with symptomatic heart failure, lvef 35% or lower, sinus rhythm with heart rate at least 70 bpm, and a heart-failure admission within the previous year, on stable background treatment including a beta-blocker if tolerated; ivabradine titrated to a maximum of 7.5 mg twice daily (3,268) vs placebo (3,290); median follow-up 22.9 months. a primary-endpoint event occurred in 793 of 3,241 analyzed patients (24%) on ivabradine

cards.headline: BEAUTIFUL (Fox 2008): ivabradine in stable coronary disease with LV dysfunction — the primary composite was flat (HR 1.00)
cards.summary: Primary composite HR 1.00 (0.91–1.10; P=0.94); in the prespecified heart-rate 70-or-above subgroup the composite remained nonsignificant (HR 0.91), though admission for myocardial infarction (HR 0.64) and coronary revascularization (HR 0.70) fell — 10,917 patients.
cards.people: 10,917 patients with coronary artery disease and LVEF under 40%, enrolled at 781 centers in 33 countries (mean age 65 years; 17% women, per the trial's registry record); ivabradine 5 mg with the intention of increasing to 7.5 mg twice daily (5,479) vs matched placebo (5,438), in addition to appropriate cardiovascular medication (87% were receiving beta-blockers); median follow-up 19 months.
cards.result: Mean baseline heart rate was 71.6 bpm; ivabradine reduced heart rate by 6 bpm at 12 months, corrected for placebo. The primary composite endpoint was unchanged: HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.91–1.10; P=0.94). Serious adverse events were similar (22.5% vs 22.8%). In the prespecified subgroup with heart rate 70 bpm or higher, ivabradine still did not affect the primary composite (HR 0.91, 0.81–1.04; P=0.17), cardiovascular death, or heart-failure admission — but it reduced secondary endpoints: admission for fatal and nonfatal myocardial infarction (HR 0.64, 0.49–0.84; P=0.001) and coronary revascularization (HR 0.70, 0.52–0.93; P=0.016).
cards.watchOut: The null that disciplines SHIFT: same drug, same rate-lowering, different population — no heart-failure syndrome and no recent decompensation — and no outcome benefit. The coronary subgroup findings are secondary endpoints inside an overall null trial. A later outcomes trial of ivabradine in stable coronary disease without clinical heart failure (SIGNIFY) likewise found no benefit; it is not carded here because it enrolled no heart-failure patients.
cards.source: Fox K et al. Ivabradine for patients with stable coronary artery disease and left-ventricular systolic dysfunction (BEAUTIFUL): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2008. PMID 18757088 · NCT00143507.

shelves.title: ARNI in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
shelves.question: After sacubitril-valsartan's win in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, does neprilysin inhibition also help when the ejection fraction is preserved?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure · Stroke Volume · Aminobutyrates · Valsartan · Neprilysin · Humans
shelves.balance: The preserved-ejection-fraction sequel never matched the reduced-ejection-fraction original (carded on Shelf #87 ). PARAGON-HF, the 4,822-patient outcomes trial, missed its primary endpoint — total heart-failure hospitalizations and death from cardiovascular causes, rate ratio 0.87 with P=0.06 — and cardiovascular death itself was flat (8.5% vs 8.9%). The two companion trials explain how the field got there: PARAMOUNT and PARALLAX both lowered NT-proBNP significantly more than their comparators, and PARALLAX found no accompanying gain in walking distance, quality of life, or NYHA class. A surrogate that moves while outcomes do not is the whole lesson of this shelf. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit unproven.

cards.headline: PARAGON-HF (Solomon 2019): sacubitril-valsartan missed its primary endpoint in HFpEF — rate ratio 0.87, P=0.06
cards.summary: Primary events 894 in 526 patients vs 1,009 in 557 (rate ratio 0.87, 0.75–1.01; P=0.06); death from cardiovascular causes 8.5% vs 8.9% (HR 0.95); more hypotension and angioedema, less hyperkalemia — 4,822 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (PARAGON-HF), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 4,822 patients with NYHA class II–IV heart failure, LVEF 45% or higher, elevated natriuretic peptide levels, and structural heart disease (51.7% women, per the trial's registry record; more than four in five aged 65 or older); sacubitril-valsartan (target dose 97 mg sacubitril with 103 mg valsartan twice daily) vs valsartan (target 160 mg twice daily).
cards.result: There were 894 primary events in 526 patients in the sacubitril-valsartan group vs 1,009 events in 557 patients in the valsartan group — rate ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.75–1.01; P=0.06), not significant. Death from cardiovascular causes: 8.5% vs 8.9% (HR 0.95, 0.79–1.16). Total hospitalizations for heart failure: 690 vs 797 (rate ratio 0.85, 0.72–1.00). NYHA class improved in 15.0% vs 12.6% (OR 1.45), renal function worsened less often (1.4% vs 2.7%; HR 0.50), and the KCCQ clinical summary score improved by 1.0 point more. Hypotension and angioedema were more frequent on sacubitril-valsartan; hyperkalemia was less frequent.
cards.watchOut: P=0.06 is a missed endpoint, not a win to round up. The suggestion of heterogeneity — possible benefit at lower ejection fractions and in women — comes from prespecified subgroups and is hypothesis-generating only. The comparator was valsartan, an active drug, so this trial cannot say what the ARNI does against no renin-angiotensin blockade at all.
cards.source: Solomon SD et al. Angiotensin-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID 31475794 · NCT01920711.

cards.headline: PARAMOUNT (Solomon 2012): the phase 2 signal — NT-proBNP fell further on LCZ696 than on valsartan
cards.summary: NT-proBNP at 12 weeks: ratio LCZ696/valsartan 0.77 (0.64–0.92; P=0.005); serious adverse events 15% vs 20% — 301 patients treated for 36 weeks.

cards.headline: PARALLAX (Pieske 2021): NT-proBNP fell, walking distance and quality of life did not improve
cards.summary: NT-proBNP adjusted geometric mean ratio 0.84 vs comparator (P<0.001) at 12 weeks; 6-minute walk distance change +9.7 m vs +12.2 m at 24 weeks (P=0.42); KCCQ and NYHA class no different; hypotension 14.1% vs 5.5% — 2,572 patients.
cards.people: 2,572 patients with heart failure, LVEF over 40%, elevated NT-proBNP, structural heart disease, and reduced quality of life, enrolled at 396 centers in 32 countries (mean age 72.6 years; 1,301 women, 50.7%); sacubitril-valsartan (1,286) vs an individualized comparator — enalapril, valsartan, or placebo, stratified by prior renin-angiotensin-system inhibitor use (1,286); follow-up 24 weeks.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, NT-proBNP fell significantly more on sacubitril-valsartan (adjusted geometric mean ratio to baseline 0.82) than on the comparator (0.98) — adjusted ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.80–0.88; P<0.001). At 24 weeks there was no significant difference in 6-minute walk distance (median change +9.7 m vs +12.2 m; adjusted mean difference −2.5 m, −8.5 to 3.5; P=0.42), in KCCQ clinical summary score change (12.3 vs 11.8; difference 0.52), or in NYHA class improvement (23.6% vs 24.0%; adjusted OR 0.98). The most frequent adverse events on sacubitril-valsartan vs comparator were hypotension (14.1% vs 5.5%), albuminuria (12.3% vs 7.6%), and hyperkalemia (11.6% vs 10.9%).
cards.watchOut: The cleanest surrogate-versus-function split in the HFpEF literature: the peptide obeyed the drug; the patient did not walk further. Twenty-four weeks is short, and the mixed comparator blurs the contrast — but nothing here rescues the outcome claim PARAGON-HF could not make.

shelves.title: Bedtime vs morning dosing of blood-pressure medicines
shelves.question: Should antihypertensive medicines be taken at bedtime rather than in the morning — and what should a patient actually do with the answer?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension · Antihypertensive Agents · Chronotherapy · Circadian Rhythm · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Humans
shelves.balance: One large independent trial says the clock does not matter; one research group's trials say it matters implausibly much. TIME randomized 21,104 UK patients to evening vs morning dosing of their usual medicines and found no difference in vascular death or hospitalization for nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke (3.4% vs 3.7%; HR 0.95; P=0.53). The Hygia trial reported a 45% relative reduction in its cardiovascular composite with bedtime dosing (adjusted HR 0.55) — an effect size that timing alone cannot plausibly deliver, from a paper that has drawn sustained methodological criticism and an expression of concern from its journal. The teaching point of this shelf is adherence, not timing: blood-pressure medicines protect when they are taken, so take them at the time of day they will actually be taken, every day. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for any bedtime advantage; TIME's null is the reliable anchor.

cards.headline: TIME (Mackenzie 2022): evening vs morning dosing — no difference in cardiovascular outcomes (3.4% vs 3.7%)
cards.summary: Primary endpoint 3.4% (evening) vs 3.7% (morning) — HR 0.95 (0.83–1.10; P=0.53) over a median 5.2 years; no safety concerns identified — 21,104 patients.
cards.type: Pragmatic, prospective, open-label RCT with blinded endpoint adjudication (TIME), Lancet 2022
cards.people: 21,104 UK adults (aged 18 or older) with hypertension and taking at least one antihypertensive medication (mean age 65.1 years; 57.5% men); randomized to take all usual antihypertensive medications in the evening, 20:00–00:00 (10,503), or in the morning, 06:00–10:00 (10,601); median follow-up 5.2 years.
cards.result: A primary endpoint event occurred in 362 participants (3.4%) assigned to evening treatment (0.69 events per 100 patient-years) vs 390 (3.7%) assigned to morning treatment (0.72 per 100 patient-years) — unadjusted HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.83–1.10; P=0.53). No safety concerns were identified. The investigators' conclusion: patients can be advised to take their regular antihypertensive medications at a convenient time that minimises undesirable effects.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and decentralized — 5.0% of the evening group vs 3.0% of the morning group withdrew from all follow-up, and dosing time was self-reported. But at 21,104 patients it dwarfs every other trial of the question, and its confidence interval (upper bound 1.10) excludes the large benefits claimed elsewhere. This is the card to act on.
cards.source: Mackenzie IS et al. Cardiovascular outcomes in adults with hypertension with evening versus morning dosing of usual antihypertensives in the UK (TIME study): a prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint clinical trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID 36240838 · ISRCTN18157641.

cards.headline: Hygia (Hermida 2020): a claimed 45% relative risk reduction from bedtime dosing — reported here as contested
cards.summary: As reported: primary composite adjusted HR 0.55 (0.50–0.61), with every component also significant — a claim later flagged by an expression of concern in the journal; 19,084 patients.
cards.type: Multicentre prospective endpoint trial (Hygia Chronotherapy Trial), Eur Heart J 2020 — contested
cards.people: 19,084 hypertensive patients in the Spanish primary-care setting (10,614 men and 8,470 women; mean age 60.5 ± 13.7 years); assigned 1:1 to ingest at least one medication at bedtime (9,552) or all medications upon awakening (9,532), with 48-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring at inclusion and at least annually; median follow-up 6.3 years.
cards.result: As reported by the investigators: during follow-up, 1,752 participants experienced the primary cardiovascular outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, heart failure, or stroke). The adjusted hazard ratio for the primary outcome was 0.55 (95% CI 0.50–0.61; P<0.001) for bedtime vs upon-awakening treatment — a claimed 45% relative reduction — with each component also reported as significant: cardiovascular death HR 0.44 (0.34–0.56), myocardial infarction 0.66 (0.52–0.84), coronary revascularization 0.60 (0.47–0.75), heart failure 0.58 (0.49–0.70), and stroke 0.51 (0.41–0.63).
cards.watchOut: Carded as a contested claim, not as evidence to act on. The claimed effect is far larger than the achieved blood-pressure differences can explain; randomization and endpoint procedures drew extensive published criticism; and the European Heart Journal published an expression of concern about this trial. Hygia and the same group's earlier MAPEC study are one group's work, not two independent confirmations. TIME (Reference 1) — larger, independently run, blinded-endpoint — found no effect at all: when one group's results are this much better than everyone else's, the burden of proof sits with the outlier.
cards.source: Hermida RC et al. Bedtime hypertension treatment improves cardiovascular risk reduction: the Hygia Chronotherapy Trial. Eur Heart J. 2020. PMID 31641769 · NCT00741585.

shelves.title: The fourth drug for resistant hypertension
shelves.question: When blood pressure stays high on three medicines, which fourth drug actually works best?
shelves.mesh: Hypertension · Spironolactone · Bisoprolol · Doxazosin · Clonidine · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Humans
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials, one answer: spironolactone. PATHWAY-2's crossover design — every patient tried every option — showed spironolactone lowered home systolic pressure by 8.70 mmHg against placebo, beat the average of bisoprolol and doxazosin by a further 4.26 mmHg, and beat each drug individually; its advantage was many-fold greater at low plasma renin, the fingerprint of the sodium retention the trial was designed to detect. ReHOT, testing spironolactone against clonidine head-to-head, found identical control rates (about 21% in both arms) but greater 24-hour pressure reductions with spironolactone and a simpler once-daily regimen. The honest label is: LIKELY.

cards.headline: PATHWAY-2 (Williams 2015): spironolactone beat placebo, bisoprolol, and doxazosin as the fourth drug
cards.summary: Reduction in home systolic BP with spironolactone: −8.70 mmHg vs placebo; −4.26 mmHg beyond the bisoprolol/doxazosin average; −4.03 vs doxazosin and −4.48 vs bisoprolol (all P<0.0001) — 335 patients in a crossover design.
cards.people: 335 patients aged 18–79 with resistant hypertension, from 12 secondary and two primary care sites in the UK (mean age 61.4 years; 31% women, per the paper's Table 1); each patient rotated in randomized order through 12 weeks of each of spironolactone 25–50 mg, bisoprolol 5–10 mg, doxazosin modified-release 4–8 mg, and placebo, added to baseline drugs, with doses doubled after 6 weeks of each cycle; 230 patients completed all treatment cycles.
cards.result: Spironolactone's average reduction in home systolic blood pressure was superior to placebo (−8.70 mm Hg, 95% CI −9.72 to −7.69; P<0.0001), superior to the mean of the other two active treatments (−4.26 mm Hg, −5.13 to −3.38; P<0.0001), and superior to each drug individually: vs doxazosin −4.03 (−5.04 to −3.02) and vs bisoprolol −4.48 (−5.50 to −3.46), both P<0.0001. Spironolactone was the most effective treatment throughout the distribution of baseline plasma renin, but its margin of superiority was many-fold greater at lower renin levels. All treatments were well tolerated; in 6 of 285 patients who received spironolactone, serum potassium exceeded 6.0 mmol/L on one occasion.
cards.watchOut: A blood-pressure endpoint over 12-week cycles — not an outcomes trial. For the fourth-drug decision, though, pressure is the question at hand, and the crossover design makes every patient their own control, which is why one 335-patient trial carries this much weight. Doses were forced upward at 6 weeks in each cycle, which ordinary prescribing often fails to do.
cards.source: Williams B et al. Spironolactone versus placebo, bisoprolol, and doxazosin to determine the optimal treatment for drug-resistant hypertension (PATHWAY-2): a randomised, double-blind, crossover trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID 26414968 · NCT02369081.

cards.headline: ReHOT (Krieger 2018): spironolactone vs clonidine as the fourth drug — equal control rates, greater pressure falls with spironolactone
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (control on both office and ambulatory measurement): 20.8% with clonidine vs 20.5% with spironolactone (RR 1.01; P=1.00); spironolactone produced greater decreases in 24-hour systolic and diastolic pressure — 187 patients with true resistant hypertension.
cards.people: 187 patients with true resistant hypertension in Brazil (of 1,597 patients recruited, 11.7% met the criteria), randomized to 12 weeks of additional spironolactone 12.5–50 mg once daily (95) or clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg twice daily (92).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — blood-pressure control on both office (<140/90 mm Hg) and 24-hour ambulatory (<130/80 mm Hg) measurement — was reached by 20.5% of the spironolactone group and 20.8% of the clonidine group (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.55–1.88; P=1.00): clonidine was not superior. Office control (33.3% vs 29.3%) and ambulatory control (44% vs 46.2%) were also similar. Spironolactone, however, produced a greater decrease in 24-hour systolic and diastolic pressure and in daytime diastolic ambulatory pressure. The investigators concluded spironolactone is preferable as fourth-drug therapy, given easier dosing and the greater secondary-endpoint reductions.
cards.watchOut: The sobering number is the control rate itself: about 21% in both arms — four drugs in, four of five patients still uncontrolled. A small trial (187 patients), so the similarity claim is weaker than PATHWAY-2's head-to-head win; but nothing here contradicts spironolactone as the default fourth drug.

shelves.title: Lipid lowering in kidney disease: SHARP vs the dialysis nulls
shelves.question: Does lowering LDL cholesterol prevent cardiovascular events in chronic kidney disease — and does the answer change once a patient is on dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Renal Dialysis · Simvastatin · Ezetimibe · Atorvastatin · Rosuvastatin Calcium · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: The kidney is where the LDL story splits in two. SHARP — 9,270 patients with chronic kidney disease, a third of them already on dialysis — found simvastatin plus ezetimibe cut major atherosclerotic events (11.3% vs 13.4%; rate ratio 0.83, a 17% relative reduction), and its prespecified analyses found no good evidence that the proportional effect differed between dialysis and non-dialysis patients. But the two trials confined to established dialysis populations both returned null primary endpoints: 4D, atorvastatin in diabetic hemodialysis patients (relative risk 0.92; P=0.37), and AURORA, rosuvastatin in hemodialysis (HR 0.96; P=0.59) — despite LDL falls of 42–43% in each. Why the broad-CKD trial benefited where the dialysis-only trials did not is genuinely unsettled: a different event mix on dialysis (more sudden death, heart failure, and infection; less plaque rupture), treatment started too late, and subgroup power all play a part. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SHARP (Baigent 2011): simvastatin plus ezetimibe cut major atherosclerotic events in CKD — 11.3% vs 13.4%
cards.summary: Major atherosclerotic events 11.3% vs 13.4% (rate ratio 0.83, 0.74–0.94; P=0.0021); nonfatal MI or coronary death 4.6% vs 5.0% (not significant); non-hemorrhagic stroke 2.8% vs 3.8%; arterial revascularization 6.1% vs 7.6% — 9,270 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (SHARP — Study of Heart and Renal Protection), Lancet 2011
cards.people: 9,270 patients with chronic kidney disease (3,023 on dialysis and 6,247 not) and no history of myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization (mean age 62 years; 37% women, per the trial's registry record); simvastatin 20 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg daily (4,650) vs matching placebo (4,620); median follow-up 4.9 years.
cards.result: Treatment produced an average LDL cholesterol difference of 0.85 mmol/L (≈33 mg/dL). Major atherosclerotic events (nonfatal myocardial infarction or coronary death, non-hemorrhagic stroke, or any arterial revascularization) occurred in 526 patients (11.3%) on simvastatin plus ezetimibe vs 619 (13.4%) on placebo — rate ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.74–0.94; P=0.0021), a 17% relative reduction and a 2.1-percentage-point absolute difference. Non-hemorrhagic stroke: 131 (2.8%) vs 174 (3.8%) — RR 0.75 (P=0.01). Arterial revascularization: 284 (6.1%) vs 352 (7.6%) — RR 0.79 (P=0.0036). Nonfatal MI or coronary death: 213 (4.6%) vs 230 (5.0%) — RR 0.92 (P=0.37), not significant. There was no excess of myopathy (0.2% vs 0.1%), hepatitis, gallstones, or cancer (9.4% vs 9.5%), and no significant excess of non-vascular death (14.4% vs 13.2%; P=0.13).
cards.watchOut: The composite leans on revascularization and stroke; its hardest component, MI or coronary death, was not significant on its own. SHARP found no good evidence that the proportional benefit differed in patients on dialysis — but it was not powered to prove benefit within the dialysis subgroup alone, which is precisely where 4D and AURORA (Cards 2 and 3) found none.
cards.source: Baigent C et al. The effects of lowering LDL cholesterol with simvastatin plus ezetimibe in patients with chronic kidney disease (Study of Heart and Renal Protection): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2011. PMID 21663949 · NCT00125593 · ISRCTN54137607.

cards.headline: 4D (Wanner 2005): atorvastatin in diabetic hemodialysis — LDL down 42%, primary endpoint null
cards.summary: Primary composite relative risk 0.92 (0.77–1.10; P=0.37); death from all causes RR 0.93 (P=0.33); fatal stroke RR 2.03 (1.05–3.93; P=0.04); all cardiac events combined RR 0.82 (P=0.03, nominally significant) — 1,255 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (4D — Deutsche Diabetes Dialyse Studie), N Engl J Med 2005
cards.people: 1,255 patients with type 2 diabetes receiving maintenance hemodialysis, in a multicenter German trial; atorvastatin 20 mg per day vs matching placebo; median follow-up 4 years.
cards.result: After 4 weeks, median LDL cholesterol had fallen 42% on atorvastatin vs 1.3% on placebo. During follow-up, 469 patients (37%) reached the primary endpoint — 226 assigned to atorvastatin and 243 to placebo (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.77–1.10; P=0.37). Atorvastatin had no significant effect on the individual components of the primary endpoint, except fatal stroke, whose relative risk was 2.03 (1.05–3.93; P=0.04). All cardiac events combined were reduced (RR 0.82, 0.68–0.99; P=0.03, nominally significant); all cerebrovascular events combined (RR 1.12; P=0.49) and total mortality (RR 0.93, 0.79–1.08; P=0.33) were not.
cards.watchOut: One nominally significant harm (fatal stroke) and one nominally significant benefit (cardiac events) inside an overall null are exactly what secondary-endpoint multiplicity produces; neither should be quoted without the other. The durable finding is the null: in established diabetic dialysis patients, a large LDL fall did not move the composite. A pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID appears in its PubMed record.

cards.headline: AURORA (Fellström 2009): rosuvastatin in hemodialysis — LDL down 43%, events unchanged (HR 0.96)
cards.summary: Primary endpoint 9.2 vs 9.5 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.96, 0.84–1.11; P=0.59); death from all causes 13.5 vs 14.0 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.96; P=0.51) — 2,776 patients aged 50–80 on hemodialysis.
cards.type: Double-blind RCT (AURORA), N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 2,776 patients, 50 to 80 years of age, undergoing maintenance hemodialysis in an international multicenter trial (mean age 64 years; 38% women, per the trial's registry record); rosuvastatin 10 mg daily vs placebo; median follow-up 3.8 years.
cards.result: By 3 months, mean LDL cholesterol had fallen 43% on rosuvastatin, from a mean baseline of 100 mg/dL. The primary endpoint was reached by 396 patients in the rosuvastatin group and 408 in the placebo group (9.2 vs 9.5 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.84–1.11; P=0.59). Rosuvastatin had no effect on the individual components of the primary endpoint, and no significant effect on all-cause mortality (13.5 vs 14.0 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.96, 0.86–1.07; P=0.51). Event rates here are per patient-year, not percentages.
cards.watchOut: Together with 4D (Reference 2), AURORA defines the dialysis null: in patients already established on long-term dialysis — whose deaths are dominated by sudden death, heart failure, and infection rather than plaque rupture — starting a statin did not reproduce the benefit SHARP found across the broader CKD spectrum. Neither null proves statins useless in kidney disease; both say where the proof runs out.

shelves.title: Claudication: supervised exercise vs stenting
shelves.question: For intermittent claudication, what works better — supervised exercise, opening the narrowed artery with a stent, or the two combined?
shelves.mesh: Intermittent Claudication · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Exercise Therapy · Stents · Walking · Humans
shelves.balance: Exercise is the treatment to beat. CLEVER randomized aortoiliac claudication three ways, and at 6 months supervised exercise produced the largest gain in peak walking time (+5.8 minutes, vs +3.7 for stenting and +1.2 for medical care alone) — although patients reported better disease-specific quality of life with a stent. ERASE then showed the ceiling sits higher when the two are combined: endovascular revascularization plus supervised exercise beat exercise alone by 282 m of maximum walking distance at one year, with better disease-specific quality of life. Neither trial was powered for limb or cardiovascular events; these are walking and quality-of-life verdicts, and both depend on exercise programs patients actually attend. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CLEVER (Murphy 2012): supervised exercise beat stenting on the treadmill — +5.8 vs +3.7 minutes of peak walking time
cards.summary: Change in peak walking time at 6 months: +5.8 min (supervised exercise) vs +3.7 min (stent) vs +1.2 min (optimal medical care alone); disease-specific quality of life improved more with stenting on most scales — 111 patients with aortoiliac disease.
cards.people: 111 patients with aortoiliac peripheral artery disease and claudication (mean age 64 years; 38% women — computed from the paper's Table 1), randomly assigned to optimal medical care alone, medical care plus supervised exercise, or medical care plus stent revascularization.
cards.result: At 6 months, the change in peak walking time on a graded treadmill test — the primary endpoint — was greatest for supervised exercise, intermediate for stenting, and least for medical care alone: mean change +5.8 ± 4.6 vs +3.7 ± 4.9 vs +1.2 ± 2.6 minutes (P<0.001 for exercise vs medical care; P=0.02 for stent vs medical care; P=0.04 for exercise vs stent). Disease-specific quality of life (Walking Impairment Questionnaire and Peripheral Artery Questionnaire) also improved with both active treatments vs medical care, but for most scales the improvement was greater with stenting than with exercise. Free-living step activity increased more with stenting, without reaching statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: A split verdict in 111 patients over 6 months: the objective treadmill crown goes to exercise, the patient's own rating to the stent — and a supervised program only works for patients who can attend one. Aortoiliac disease only; femoropopliteal claudication may not behave the same. ERASE (Reference 2) is the larger test of combining the two.
cards.source: Murphy TP et al. Supervised exercise versus primary stenting for claudication resulting from aortoiliac peripheral artery disease: six-month outcomes from the claudication: exercise versus endoluminal revascularization (CLEVER) study. Circulation. 2012. PMID 22090168 · NCT00132743.

cards.headline: ERASE (Fakhry 2015): revascularization plus supervised exercise beat exercise alone — 282 m more maximum walking distance at 1 year
cards.summary: Improvement in maximum walking distance: 1,237 m (combination) vs 955 m (exercise only) — mean between-group difference 282 m (99% CI 60–505); pain-free walking distance difference 408 m; VascuQol difference 0.62 — 212 patients.
cards.people: 212 patients with intermittent claudication at 10 sites in the Netherlands, allocated to endovascular revascularization (with selective stenting) plus supervised exercise (106) or supervised exercise only (106), followed for 12 months and analyzed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Maximum walking distance improved from 264 m to 1,501 m (an improvement of 1,237 m) in the combination group vs from 285 m to 1,240 m (955 m) with exercise only — a mean between-group difference of 282 m (99% CI 60–505). Pain-free walking distance improved by 1,120 m vs 712 m (difference 408 m, 99% CI 195–622). Disease-specific quality of life (VascuQol) improved more with combination therapy (difference 0.62, 99% CI 0.20–1.03), as did the SF-36 physical functioning score (difference 9.8, 1.4–18.2); the other SF-36 domains examined did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: An open trial with a treadmill endpoint — expectation can walk a long way — and the comparison is combination vs exercise, not vs stenting alone. ERASE says adding a procedure to exercise improves walking; CLEVER (Reference 1) says exercise alone out-walks a stent alone. Both can be true, and together they put exercise at the center of claudication care either way.
cards.source: Fakhry F et al. Endovascular Revascularization and Supervised Exercise for Peripheral Artery Disease and Intermittent Claudication: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID 26547465 · NTR2249.

shelves.title: Catheter-directed thrombolysis for deep-vein thrombosis
shelves.question: After an acute proximal deep-vein thrombosis, does dissolving the clot through a catheter prevent the post-thrombotic syndrome — or mainly add bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Venous Thrombosis · Thrombolytic Therapy · Postthrombotic Syndrome · Catheterization, Peripheral · Tissue Plasminogen Activator · Humans
shelves.balance: The biggest trial says no, and the smaller trial that said yes explains why the question was worth asking. ATTRACT (692 patients with proximal DVT) found pharmacomechanical catheter-directed thrombolysis did not reduce the post-thrombotic syndrome at all (47% vs 48%; risk ratio 0.96) while causing more major bleeding (1.7% vs 0.3%) — though moderate-to-severe post-thrombotic syndrome was less frequent (18% vs 24%) and severity scores were lower. CaVenT, confined to iliofemoral DVT, had found fewer cases of post-thrombotic syndrome with additional catheter-directed thrombolysis (41.1% vs 55.6%; absolute reduction 14.4 percentage points, NNT 7), at the price of 20 bleeding complications. Read together: no routine role for thrombolysis to prevent the syndrome; the residual case is the selected patient with iliofemoral clot, severe symptoms, and low bleeding risk, where CaVenT's signal and ATTRACT's severity signal overlap. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: ATTRACT (Vedantham 2017): pharmacomechanical thrombolysis did not prevent post-thrombotic syndrome — 47% vs 48% — and bled more
cards.summary: Post-thrombotic syndrome 47% vs 48% (risk ratio 0.96; P=0.56); moderate-to-severe syndrome 18% vs 24% (risk ratio 0.73; P=0.04); major bleeding within 10 days 1.7% vs 0.3% (P=0.049); recurrent VTE 12% vs 8% (P=0.09) — 692 patients.
cards.people: 692 patients with acute proximal deep-vein thrombosis (median age 53 years; 38% women, per the trial's registry record); anticoagulation alone (control) vs anticoagulation plus pharmacomechanical thrombolysis — catheter- or device-mediated intrathrombus delivery of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator with thrombus aspiration or maceration, with or without stenting.
cards.result: Between 6 and 24 months, the post-thrombotic syndrome developed in 47% of the pharmacomechanical-thrombolysis group vs 48% of the control group (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.82–1.11; P=0.56) — no significant difference. Moderate-to-severe post-thrombotic syndrome occurred in 18% vs 24% (risk ratio 0.73, 0.54–0.98; P=0.04), and Villalta severity scores were lower with thrombolysis at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months, but improvement in quality of life did not differ significantly. Major bleeding within 10 days: 1.7% vs 0.3% (P=0.049). Recurrent venous thromboembolism over 24 months: 12% vs 8% (P=0.09).
cards.watchOut: The headline null with a severity signal inside it. Any residual benefit would live in the iliofemoral subgroup — the CaVenT population (Reference 2) — but rescuing a null trial by subgroup is a hypothesis, not a verdict. What ATTRACT rules out is routine lysis for unselected proximal DVT, and it prices the attempt in major bleeding.
cards.source: Vedantham S et al. Pharmacomechanical Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis for Deep-Vein Thrombosis. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID 29211671 · NCT00790335.

cards.headline: CaVenT (Enden 2012): additional catheter-directed thrombolysis cut post-thrombotic syndrome in iliofemoral DVT — 41.1% vs 55.6%
cards.summary: Post-thrombotic syndrome at 24 months 41.1% vs 55.6% (absolute risk reduction 14.4 percentage points; NNT 7, 95% CI 4–502); iliofemoral patency at 6 months 65.9% vs 47.4%; 20 bleeding complications related to thrombolysis, 3 of them major — 209 patients.
cards.people: 209 patients aged 18–75 years with a first-time iliofemoral DVT, included within 21 days of symptom onset at 20 hospitals in the southeastern Norwegian health region; additional catheter-directed thrombolysis (101) vs conventional treatment alone (108); 24-month clinical data available for 189 patients (90%).
cards.result: At 24 months, 37 patients (41.1%, 95% CI 31.5–51.4) allocated to additional thrombolysis had the post-thrombotic syndrome vs 55 (55.6%, 45.7–65.0) on conventional treatment (P=0.047) — an absolute risk reduction of 14.4 percentage points (0.2–27.9), corresponding to a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 4–502). Iliofemoral patency after 6 months: 58 patients (65.9%) on thrombolysis vs 45 (47.4%) on conventional treatment (P=0.012). Twenty bleeding complications were related to thrombolysis, including 3 major and 5 clinically relevant bleeds.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a partly clinical endpoint (Villalta scoring), a P value of 0.047, and an NNT whose confidence interval runs from 4 to 502 — a fragile, single-region result confined to iliofemoral clots. ATTRACT's larger and broader test (Reference 1) is why this result did not make lysis routine; its population is also why the question is not closed for iliofemoral disease.
cards.source: Enden T et al. Long-term outcome after additional catheter-directed thrombolysis versus standard treatment for acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis (the CaVenT study): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2012. PMID 22172244 · NCT00251771.
