shelves.title: Thrombolysis for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism: collapse prevented, paid for in bleeding
shelves.question: In normotensive patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism — right-ventricular dysfunction plus myocardial injury — does thrombolysis with tenecteplase prevent death or hemodynamic collapse, and what does it cost in major bleeding and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Embolism · Tenecteplase · Fibrinolytic Agents · Heparin · Hemorrhage · Stroke · Humans
shelves.balance: PEITHO is a trade, stated in one breath: tenecteplase halved the composite of death or hemodynamic collapse (2.6% vs 5.6%; odds ratio 0.44) — a benefit carried almost entirely by preventing collapse, since death itself did not differ (1.2% vs 1.8% at 7 days; 2.4% vs 3.2% at 30 days) — and paid for it with major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and hemorrhagic stroke in 2.0% of treated patients vs 0.2% on placebo. For roughly every 30 patients treated, one collapse is prevented and one serious bleed is caused. Whether that trade is worth making, and in which patient, is a bedside judgment — the shelf’s job is to print both sides at full size. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: PEITHO: death or collapse 2.6% vs 5.6% (OR 0.44) — bought with major bleeding 6.3% vs 1.2% and hemorrhagic stroke 2.0% vs 0.2%
cards.summary: Primary outcome (death or hemodynamic decompensation within 7 days): 2.6% on tenecteplase vs 5.6% on placebo (odds ratio 0.44 , 95% CI 0.23 to 0.87; P=0.02). Death alone did not differ: 1.2% vs 1.8% at 7 days, 2.4% vs 3.2% at 30 days. The harms, on the same card: major extracranial bleeding 6.3% vs 1.2% (P<0.001); stroke 2.4% vs 0.2% , hemorrhagic in 10 of the 12 tenecteplase strokes ( 2.0% vs 0.2% ) — 1,005 patients.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind trial (PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2014. Re-card: this study’s home is Shelf #237, where it is carded among the catheter treatments for the same condition; it is re-carded here for the thrombolysis question and counted once, at its home shelf
cards.people: 1,005 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis (506 tenecteplase, 499 placebo), normotensive with right-ventricular dysfunction and myocardial injury. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Death or hemodynamic decompensation occurred in 13 of 506 patients (2.6%) in the tenecteplase group vs 28 of 499 (5.6%) in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.87; P=0.02). Between randomization and day 7, 6 patients (1.2%) on tenecteplase and 9 (1.8%) on placebo died (P=0.42); by day 30, deaths numbered 12 (2.4%) vs 16 (3.2%) (P=0.42). Major extracranial bleeding occurred in 32 patients (6.3%) vs 6 (1.2%) (P<0.001). Stroke occurred in 12 patients (2.4%) on tenecteplase — hemorrhagic in 10 (2.0% of the group) — vs 1 patient (0.2%) on placebo, whose stroke was also hemorrhagic (P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: Read the composite honestly: its win is preventing hemodynamic collapse in patients who would otherwise deteriorate and need rescue therapy — it is not a mortality benefit, and at 30 days the death rates are statistically indistinguishable. The bleeding price is not a footnote: a 2.0% risk of hemorrhagic stroke is roughly one in fifty treated patients. This is also the shelf’s only card — no second thrombolysis trial of this size exists to confirm or soften the trade.

shelves.title: PFO closure after cryptogenic stroke: fewer second strokes in the young, high-risk-anatomy patient — bought with atrial fibrillation and a device
shelves.question: After a cryptogenic stroke in a patient with a patent foramen ovale, does device closure beat medical therapy at preventing another stroke?
shelves.mesh: Foramen Ovale, Patent · Septal Occluder Device · Stroke · Secondary Prevention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Humans
shelves.balance: In selected patients — younger, with a moderate-to-large shunt or an atrial septal aneurysm — the three 2017 trials all favoured closure: CLOSE found zero strokes in 238 closure patients vs 14 of 235 on antiplatelets; REDUCE found 1.4% vs 5.4%; RESPECT’s long-term follow-up gave a hazard ratio of 0.55 (relative), with absolute rates of 0.58 vs 1.07 events per 100 patient-years. The selection card (Kent 2021) sharpens the fence: pooled across all six trials, benefit concentrated in PASCAL-’probable’ patients (HR 0.10) and vanished in ’unlikely’ ones (HR 1.14), while device atrial fibrillation rose most in the group that gained least. The price is real throughout: atrial fibrillation after the device in 4.6–6.6%, procedural complications in about 6% in CLOSE, and more venous thromboembolism in RESPECT. Absolute gains are small because recurrence on medical therapy is already low — a carefully-selected-patient treatment, not a close-every-PFO answer, and no mortality benefit is claimed. Cards 1–3 are re-cards homed on Shelf #189; each is counted once, at its home shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CLOSE (Mas 2017): in high-risk PFO anatomy, zero strokes with closure vs 14 on antiplatelets (re-card; home: Shelf #189)
cards.summary: Stroke over a mean of 5.3 years: 0 of 238 patients with PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy vs 14 of 235 on antiplatelet therapy alone (hazard ratio 0.03; 95% CI 0–0.26; P<0.001) — 663 patients aged 16–60 whose PFO came with an atrial septal aneurysm or a large shunt.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, open-label trial (CLOSE), New England Journal of Medicine 2017. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #189, asked here for this slate’s PFO question; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 663 patients aged 16–60 with a recent stroke attributed to PFO with an associated atrial septal aneurysm or large interatrial shunt, randomized among closure plus antiplatelet therapy, antiplatelet therapy alone, and oral anticoagulation; mean follow-up 5.3 years. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: No stroke occurred in the closure group vs 14 in the antiplatelet-only group (HR 0.03). Procedural complications from closure occurred in 14 patients (5.9%). Atrial fibrillation was more frequent after closure (4.6% vs 0.9%; P=0.02). Serious adverse events overall did not differ (P=0.56). The anticoagulation-vs-antiplatelet comparison was small and inconclusive (stroke in 3 of 187 vs 7 of 174).
cards.watchOut: The cleanest result of the three trials — and the narrowest population: CLOSE deliberately enrolled only the highest-risk anatomy. A zero-event arm also means the confidence interval, not the point estimate, is the honest summary (HR 0.03, CI up to 0.26). The 5-year absolute reduction is about 4.9 points (number needed to treat roughly 20), and the price list — procedural complications in 1 in 17, new atrial fibrillation in about 1 in 22 — is part of the result, not a footnote.

cards.headline: REDUCE (Søndergaard 2017): closure plus antiplatelet beat antiplatelet alone — stroke 1.4% vs 5.4%; atrial fibrillation 6.6% (re-card; home: Shelf #189)
cards.summary: Clinical ischaemic stroke over a median of 3.2 years: 6 of 441 patients (1.4%) with closure plus antiplatelet therapy vs 12 of 223 (5.4%) on antiplatelet therapy alone (hazard ratio 0.23; 95% CI 0.09–0.62; P=0.002) — 664 patients, 81% with moderate or large shunts.

cards.people: 664 patients with PFO and cryptogenic stroke (mean age 45.2 years), randomized 2:1 to closure plus antiplatelet therapy or antiplatelet therapy alone; 81% had moderate or large interatrial shunts; brain imaging at baseline and 24 months; median follow-up 3.2 years. cards.result: Clinical ischaemic stroke: 1.4% vs 5.4% (HR 0.23). New brain infarction (clinical or silent, on imaging): 5.7% vs 11.3% (relative risk 0.51, relative; P=0.04), though silent infarction alone did not differ (P=0.97). The atrial fibrillation excess was mostly early and peri-procedural, but it is the mechanism by which a stroke-prevention device can cause the disease it prevents, and it is printed here for that reason.

cards.headline: RESPECT long-term (Saver 2017): with 5.9 years of follow-up, closure’s hazard ratio was 0.55 — rates 0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 patient-years (re-card; home: Shelf #189)
cards.summary: Recurrent ischaemic stroke over a median of 5.9 years: 18 patients on closure vs 28 on medical therapy — 0.58 vs 1.07 events per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.31–0.999; P=0.046) — 980 patients aged 18–60. The hazard ratio is a relative measure; the absolute rates are printed beside it.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, open-label trial with blinded endpoint adjudication, extended follow-up (RESPECT), New England Journal of Medicine 2017. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #189; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 980 patients aged 18–60 (mean age 45.9 years) with PFO and cryptogenic ischaemic stroke, at 69 sites; medical therapy was aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, or aspirin plus extended-release dipyridamole; median follow-up 5.9 years. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: Recurrent ischaemic stroke occurred in 18 closure patients vs 28 on medical therapy (0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 patient-years; HR 0.55; P=0.046). For strokes of undetermined cause the hazard ratio was 0.38 (95% CI 0.18–0.79). Venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism and deep-vein thrombosis) was more common in the closure group.
cards.watchOut: The honest history matters: RESPECT’s original primary analysis at a median 2.1 years was null, and this extended analysis is labelled exploratory by its authors, with unequal treatment exposure (3,141 vs 2,669 patient-years) from higher dropout on medical therapy. The case for closure rests on the totality — this long follow-up plus CLOSE and REDUCE — not on RESPECT alone. No mortality or disability benefit has been shown on this shelf; the claim is recurrent stroke only.
cards.source: Saver JL et al. Long-Term Outcomes of Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Medical Therapy after Stroke. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID 28902590 · NCT00465270. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1610057

cards.headline: The selection card (Kent 2021, SCOPE pooled analysis): benefit concentrated where the PFO plausibly caused the stroke — PASCAL ’probable’ HR 0.10, ’unlikely’ HR 1.14
cards.summary: Across all 6 closure trials (3,740 patients, median follow-up 57 months): adjusted hazard ratio for recurrent stroke 0.41 with closure overall (annualized stroke 0.47% vs 1.09%). By PASCAL causal-likelihood class: unlikely — HR 1.14 (no benefit); possible — HR 0.38; probable — HR 0.10 (interaction P=0.003). Two-year absolute reductions: −0.7%, 2.1%, and 2.1% respectively.
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient-data analysis of 6 randomized trials (SCOPE Consortium), JAMA 2021
cards.people: 3,740 participants aged 18–60 with PFO-associated stroke from all six randomized closure trials worldwide (conducted 2000–2017), classified by the RoPE score and the PASCAL system (RoPE plus high-risk PFO features: atrial septal aneurysm or large shunt). (The pooled record does not print a combined sex mix.)
cards.result: Stroke occurred in 121 patients over a median 57 months. The treatment effect interacted significantly with causal likelihood: patients classified PASCAL-probable (younger, few vascular risk factors, high-risk anatomy) gained most (HR 0.10; 95% CI 0.03–0.35), PASCAL-possible patients gained (HR 0.38), and PASCAL-unlikely patients gained nothing (HR 1.14; 95% CI 0.53–2.46). Device-associated atrial fibrillation beyond day 45 rose most in exactly the group that gained least: absolute increases of 4.41% (unlikely), 1.53% (possible), and 0.65% (probable).
cards.watchOut: This is the fence, quantified: the trials did not show that ’PFOs should be closed’ — they showed closure helps when the stroke was probably the PFO’s fault, and exposes the unlikely group to device atrial fibrillation with no offsetting gain. Two corollaries ride on every referral: prolonged rhythm monitoring to exclude occult atrial fibrillation before closure is considered, and the trials compare closure against antiplatelet therapy — closure vs anticoagulation remains unsettled (CLOSE’s anticoagulation arm was inconclusive). Trials are silent over age 60. A pooled analysis — no registry number applies.
cards.source: Kent DM et al. Heterogeneity of Treatment Effects in an Analysis of Pooled Individual Patient Data From Randomized Trials of Device Closure of Patent Foramen Ovale After Stroke. JAMA. 2021. PMID 34905030. DOI 10.1001/jama.2021.20956 (Pooled analysis — no registry number.)

shelves.title: Perioperative beta-blockade (POISE): starting metoprolol around surgery prevented heart attacks and caused deaths and strokes — continue chronic therapy, never start it on the day
shelves.question: Should a beta-blocker be started around noncardiac surgery to protect the heart — and what does the largest trial say about the trade?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Metoprolol · Perioperative Care · Cardiovascular Diseases · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke · Hypotension
shelves.balance: POISE is the cleanest benefit-harm trade in perioperative medicine, and both sides are printed on one card, as the ruling requires: starting extended-release metoprolol in 8,351 patients cut the primary composite (HR 0.84, relative) and myocardial infarction (HR 0.73, relative) — and increased death (HR 1.33, relative) and stroke (HR 2.17, relative). Per 1,000 patients treated: about 15 fewer MIs, bought with about 8 extra deaths and 5 extra strokes. The trials that had made perioperative beta-blockade look safe — the DECREASE family — were discredited for research misconduct and fabricated data; the meta-analysis of only the secure trials (Reference 2) finds starting beta-blockade raises 30-day mortality by 27% in relative terms. The guideline rule that survived (Reference 3): continue a chronic beta-blocker through surgery (Class 1); do not start one on the day of surgery (Class 3, Harm). Tier C — developer-ruled, harm-inclusive. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: POISE (Devereaux 2008): MI prevented (HR 0.73, relative) AND death and stroke caused (HR 1.33 and 2.17, relative) — the whole trade on one card
cards.summary: 8,351 patients with or at risk of atherosclerotic disease undergoing noncardiac surgery, extended-release metoprolol started 2–4 hours before surgery vs placebo: primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal cardiac arrest) 5.8% vs 6.9% (HR 0.84, relative; P=0.04); MI 4.2% vs 5.7% (HR 0.73, relative; P=0.002). The other side: death 3.1% vs 2.3% (HR 1.33 , relative; P=0.03); stroke 1.0% vs 0.5% (HR 2.17 , relative; P=0.005); clinically important hypotension 15.0% vs 9.7% and bradycardia 6.6% vs 2.4% (full-report figures).
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (POISE), Lancet 2008 — 190 hospitals, 23 countries
cards.people: 8,351 patients (4,174 metoprolol, 4,177 placebo) with, or at risk of, atherosclerotic disease undergoing noncardiac surgery; 99.8% completed 30-day follow-up. Registry verified against the record's own databank entry.
cards.result: Fewer metoprolol patients reached the primary endpoint (244 [5.8%] vs 290 [6.9%]; HR 0.84 [0.70–0.99]; P=0.0399) and fewer had myocardial infarction (176 [4.2%] vs 239 [5.7%]; HR 0.73 [0.60–0.89]; P=0.0017) — both relative effects, with the absolute rates printed beside them. But more metoprolol patients died (129 [3.1%] vs 97 [2.3%]; HR 1.33 [1.03–1.74]; P=0.0317) and more had stroke (41 [1.0%] vs 19 [0.5%]; HR 2.17 [1.26–3.74]; P=0.0053). The per-1,000-patients ledger, computed from the trial's own rates: ~11 fewer primary-composite events and ~15 fewer MIs per 1,000, against ~8 more deaths and ~5 more strokes per 1,000. The full report adds the mechanism: clinically significant hypotension (15.0% vs 9.7%; HR 1.55) and bradycardia (6.6% vs 2.4%; HR 2.74) were substantially more common on metoprolol — the hypotension pathway is how an MI-preventing drug killed and stroked people.
cards.watchOut: The trialists' own sentence is the card's: patients are unlikely to accept these risks. Do not let the composite (HR 0.84, 'significant') be quoted alone — its components point in opposite directions, and the harmful components (death, stroke) outweigh the prevented ones (mostly nonfatal MI) in any patient-weighted accounting. This was a start-it-now, high-dose, long-acting regimen in beta-blocker-naive patients; it says nothing against continuing a chronic beta-blocker, which is Card 3's separate rule.
cards.source: Devereaux PJ et al.; POISE Study Group. Effects of extended-release metoprolol succinate in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery (POISE trial): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2008;371:1839–1847. PMID 18479744 · NCT00182039 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(08)60601-7

cards.headline: The DECREASE problem (Bouri 2014): the trials behind 'start a beta-blocker' were discredited — pooling only the secure trials, starting raised mortality 27% (relative)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis restricted to secure randomized trials of initiating perioperative beta-blockade (9 trials, 10,529 patients): initiation caused a 27% relative increase in 30-day all-cause mortality (P=0.04), reduced nonfatal MI (RR 0.73, relative), and increased stroke (RR 1.73, relative) and hypotension (RR 1.51, relative) — a POISE-shaped result. The DECREASE family of trials, previously the bedrock for initiation, 'are no longer secure' after the Erasmus misconduct investigation and substantially contradict the secure-trial pool (P=0.05 for divergence).
cards.type: Meta-analysis of secure randomized controlled trials, Heart 2014
cards.people: 9 secure trials totalling 10,529 patients (291 deaths), with the DECREASE family analysed separately rather than pooled.
cards.result: Initiation of a course of beta-blockers before surgery increased 30-day all-cause mortality by 27% in relative terms (P=0.04). Nonfatal myocardial infarction was reduced (RR 0.73; P=0.001), while stroke (RR 1.73; P=0.05) and hypotension (RR 1.51; P<0.00001) increased. The DECREASE studies substantially contradicted the secure-trial meta-analysis on mortality (P=0.05 for divergence). The authors' conclusion, printed as theirs: guideline bodies should retract recommendations based on the DECREASE data; this should not be read as an argument against continuing chronic beta-blockade, which the initiation trials do not test.
cards.watchOut: Why this card exists: the DECREASE trials (Poldermans group, Erasmus MC) were found to rest on misconduct including fabricated data, and were retracted/discredited — yet their conclusions lived on in guidelines and in secondary citations for years. An agent citing DECREASE as support for starting perioperative beta-blockade is citing discredited work; this card is the shelf's tripwire against that. The secure-trial pool is dominated by POISE (Reference 1), so the two cards are not independent — the point here is the exclusion, and what it does to the answer.
cards.source: Bouri S, Shun-Shin MJ, Cole GD, et al. Meta-analysis of secure randomised controlled trials of β-blockade to prevent perioperative death in non-cardiac surgery. Heart. 2014;100:456–464. PMID 23904357. DOI 10.1136/heartjnl-2013-304262

cards.headline: The surviving guideline rule (2024 AHA/ACC perioperative guideline): continue chronic beta-blockers (Class 1) — do not initiate on the day of surgery (Class 3, Harm)
cards.summary: The 2024 multisociety perioperative guideline — the document that supersedes the 2014 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline — keeps the two rules POISE and the DECREASE collapse produced: patients on chronic beta-blocker therapy should continue it perioperatively, and beta-blockers should not be started on the day of surgery . Continuation and initiation are opposite recommendations for the same drug class, and quoting either without the other misstates the guideline.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (2024 AHA/ACC/ACS/ASNC/HRS/SCA/SCCT/SCMR/SVM perioperative guideline), Journal of the American College of Cardiology 2024
cards.people: Adults undergoing noncardiac surgery — the guideline's population. The recommendation text summarized on this card is the guideline's beta-blocker position as carried in its pharmacological-therapy recommendations; class assignments (1 for continuation, 3 Harm for day-of-surgery initiation) follow the guideline's published recommendation table.
cards.result: The 2024 guideline provides updated recommendations for perioperative cardiovascular evaluation and management, explicitly superseding the 2014 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline, with evidence-based management strategies including pharmacological therapies. Its beta-blocker position: continuation of chronic beta-blocker therapy through the perioperative period is recommended; initiation — in particular starting a beta-blocker on the day of surgery, the POISE regimen's defining feature — is not recommended and is classified as potentially harmful. Where initiation is contemplated in selected high-risk patients, the guideline frames it as starting well before surgery with titration — never as a day-of-surgery bolus strategy.
cards.watchOut: A guideline card, labeled as such — the evidence cards are Cards 1–2; this card exists so agents quote the operational rule correctly, with both halves attached. Guideline class language summarizes a committee's weighing of POISE, the secure-trial pool, and continuation data (largely observational); it is not itself a trial result.
cards.source: Thompson A et al. 2024 AHA/ACC/ACS/ASNC/HRS/SCA/SCCT/SCMR/SVM Guideline for Perioperative Cardiovascular Management for Noncardiac Surgery. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024. PMID 39320289. DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.06.013 (companion Circulation report: PMID 39316661)

shelves.title: POISE-2: perioperative aspirin did not prevent death or MI but caused bleeding; clonidine did not prevent events but caused hypotension and cardiac arrests
shelves.question: Around noncardiac surgery, do aspirin or clonidine prevent death and heart attack — the two cheap-drug hopes POISE left standing?
shelves.mesh: Aspirin · Clonidine · Perioperative Care · Myocardial Infarction · Hypotension · Postoperative Hemorrhage · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors
shelves.balance: One factorial trial of 10,010 patients answered both questions, and both answers are no-with-harm. Aspirin: primary outcome (death or nonfatal MI) HR 0.99 — a null — while major bleeding rose (HR 1.23, relative; 4.6% vs 3.8%). The eye-catching exception, a prior-PCI subgroup with HR 0.50, is carded as what it is: a hypothesis-grade subgroup finding inside a null trial, not a license. Clonidine: primary HR 1.08 — null leaning harmful — with clinically important hypotension in 47.6% vs 37.1% (HR 1.32, relative) and nonfatal cardiac arrest tripled in relative terms (HR 3.20; 0.3% vs 0.1%). The POISE programme's combined lesson with Shelf #352: around surgery, starting cardiovascular drugs on spec does not protect the heart — it destabilizes the circulation. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: POISE-2 aspirin (Devereaux 2014): death or MI 7.0% vs 7.1% (HR 0.99 — null); major bleeding 4.6% vs 3.8% (HR 1.23, relative)
cards.summary: 10,010 patients at risk for vascular complications undergoing noncardiac surgery (2×2 factorial with clonidine), aspirin vs placebo: primary outcome of death or nonfatal MI at 30 days in 7.0% vs 7.1% (HR 0.99 [0.86–1.15]; P=0.92) — null, in both the aspirin-initiation and aspirin-continuation strata. Major bleeding: 4.6% vs 3.8% (HR 1.23, relative; P=0.04). A later prior-PCI subgroup report suggested benefit (HR ≈0.50); it is a subgroup of a null trial and is printed on this card as hypothesis-grade only.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with 2×2 factorial design (POISE-2, aspirin comparison), New England Journal of Medicine 2014
cards.people: 10,010 patients at 135 centers in 23 countries preparing for noncardiac surgery and at risk for vascular complications; 5,628 in the aspirin-initiation stratum (not previously taking aspirin) and 4,382 in the continuation stratum. Aspirin 200 mg before surgery, then 100 mg daily (30 days initiation stratum; 7 days continuation stratum, then usual regimen resumed).
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 351 of 4,998 patients (7.0%) in the aspirin group and 355 of 5,012 (7.1%) in the placebo group (HR 0.99 [0.86–1.15]; P=0.92). Major bleeding was more common with aspirin (230 patients [4.6%] vs 188 [3.8%]; HR 1.23 [1.01–1.49]; P=0.04 — a relative effect; absolute excess 0.8 points, roughly 8 extra major bleeds per 1,000). Primary and secondary results were similar across the initiation and continuation strata — continuing aspirin through surgery did not show benefit either, within this trial's design (continuation-stratum patients resumed their usual aspirin after 7 days).
cards.watchOut: The prior-PCI subgroup (patients with a previous percutaneous coronary intervention) later reported a primary-outcome HR of about 0.50 favoring aspirin — printed here because agents will meet it in the wild, and fenced: it is a small subgroup inside a null trial, hypothesis-generating, and it does not repeal the overall null or the bleeding excess. Patients with recent coronary stents, for whom aspirin interruption carries stent-thrombosis risk, are a separate management question this trial was not designed to answer.
cards.source: Devereaux PJ et al.; POISE-2 Investigators. Aspirin in patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. N Engl J Med. 2014;370:1494–1503. PMID 24679062 · NCT01082874 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1401105

cards.headline: POISE-2 clonidine (Devereaux 2014): death or MI HR 1.08 (null) — with hypotension HR 1.32 and nonfatal cardiac arrest HR 3.20 (both relative)
cards.summary: Same 10,010-patient factorial trial, clonidine 0.2 mg/day vs placebo from just before surgery to 72 hours after: primary outcome (death or nonfatal MI) 367 vs 339 events (HR 1.08 [0.93–1.26]; P=0.29) — null. Clinically important hypotension: 47.6% vs 37.1% (HR 1.32, relative; P<0.001). Nonfatal cardiac arrest: 0.3% vs 0.1% (HR 3.20 , relative; P=0.02). MI itself was numerically higher on clonidine (6.6% vs 5.9%; HR 1.11, not significant).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with 2×2 factorial design (POISE-2, clonidine comparison), New England Journal of Medicine 2014
cards.people: 10,010 patients with, or at risk for, atherosclerotic disease undergoing noncardiac surgery at 135 centers in 23 countries; clonidine 0.2 mg/day (oral tablet plus transdermal delivery per protocol) vs placebo, started just before surgery and continued until 72 hours after.
cards.result: Clonidine did not reduce the primary outcome (367 vs 339 events; HR 1.08 [0.93–1.26]; P=0.29). Myocardial infarction occurred in 329 patients (6.6%) on clonidine and 295 (5.9%) on placebo (HR 1.11 [0.95–1.30]; P=0.18). Significantly more clonidine patients had clinically important hypotension (2,385 [47.6%] vs 1,854 [37.1%]; HR 1.32 [1.24–1.40]; P<0.001), and clonidine was associated with an increased rate of nonfatal cardiac arrest (16 patients [0.3%] vs 5 [0.1%]; HR 3.20 [1.17–8.73]; P=0.02). All hazard ratios are relative effects; the absolute rates travel with them on this card.
cards.watchOut: The clonidine hypothesis was sympathetic blunting without hemodynamic instability; the trial delivered the instability without the protection — the same failure shape as POISE's metoprolol (Shelf #352), through the same hypotension pathway. Cardiac-arrest counts are small (16 vs 5), so HR 3.20 is a wide-interval relative figure; the hypotension result, on thousands of events, is not fragile. Neither POISE-2 drug earned a perioperative start.
cards.source: Devereaux PJ et al.; POISE-2 Investigators. Clonidine in patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. N Engl J Med. 2014;370:1503–1513. PMID 24679061 · NCT01082874 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1401106

shelves.title: Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes — the five-trial family: benefit proven for the composite, with the hierarchy breaks and the retinopathy harm kept on the cards
shelves.question: Across its five cardiovascular-outcome trials, what has semaglutide actually proven — and which of its headline numbers are supportive only, or not shown at all?
shelves.mesh: Semaglutide · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Cardiovascular Diseases · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Myocardial Infarction · Diabetic Retinopathy
shelves.balance: One-home discipline governs this shelf: SUSTAIN-6 is counted on Shelf #71 and SOUL on Shelf #72 — their cards here are labeled re-cards; FLOW's kidney primary is counted on Shelf #75 and appears here only as a pointer to its MACE strand; SELECT and PIONEER-6 are carded here for the first time. Read as a family: the composite verdict is consistent — SELECT HR 0.80, SUSTAIN-6 HR 0.74, SOUL HR 0.86, FLOW's MACE strand HR 0.82, and the pooled T2D estimate HR 0.83, all relative effects with absolute rates on the cards. Read with the discipline the ruling requires: in SELECT, cardiovascular death (HR 0.85, P=0.07) was NOT significant, the testing hierarchy broke there, and everything below it — the heart-failure composite (0.82) and all-cause death (0.81) — prints as SUPPORTIVE ONLY, never as proven benefit. In PIONEER-6, superiority was NOT shown (HR 0.79 [0.57–1.11]); its striking death ratios (0.49, 0.51) rest on 15-vs-30 and 23-vs-45 events and are not mortality evidence. In SOUL, the confirmatory kidney secondary was NOT significant. And SUSTAIN-6 carries the family's harm on its face: retinopathy complications HR 1.76. Tirzepatide's cardiovascular trials are a different molecule and are excluded — they live on Shelf #282. Tier C — developer-ruled. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SELECT (Lincoff 2023): MACE 6.5% vs 8.0%, HR 0.80 (relative) — cardiovascular death HR 0.85, P=0.07, NOT significant; everything below the break is SUPPORTIVE ONLY
cards.summary: 17,604 patients ≥45 with established cardiovascular disease and BMI ≥27, WITHOUT diabetes, weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg vs placebo, mean follow-up 39.8 months: primary MACE 6.5% vs 8.0% (HR 0.80 [0.72–0.90], relative; P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 1.5 points. Nonfatal MI HR 0.72. Cardiovascular death: HR 0.85, P=0.07 — NOT significant. The prespecified hierarchy stopped there: the heart-failure composite (HR 0.82) and all-cause death (HR 0.81) are supportive only . Adverse events leading to discontinuation: 16.6% vs 8.2% . The FDA extended the label to cardiovascular risk reduction in March 2024.
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, event-driven superiority trial (SELECT), New England Journal of Medicine 2023
cards.people: 17,604 patients (8,803 semaglutide, 8,801 placebo) aged ≥45 with preexisting cardiovascular disease and BMI ≥27 and no history of diabetes; mean exposure 34.2 months, mean follow-up 39.8 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: A primary endpoint event occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients (6.5%) on semaglutide vs 701 of 8,801 (8.0%) on placebo (HR 0.80 [0.72–0.90]; P<0.001). Component and secondary results, with their evidentiary rank printed as the trial's hierarchy assigns it: nonfatal MI HR 0.72; cardiovascular death HR 0.85 [0.71–1.01], P=0.07 — not significant, and the point at which the prespecified testing hierarchy stopped, so the heart-failure composite outcome (HR 0.82) and death from any cause (HR 0.81) that follow it in the sequence are supportive, hypothesis-level findings, NOT proven benefits, and must not be quoted as established effects. Adverse events leading to permanent discontinuation occurred in 1,461 patients (16.6%) vs 718 (8.2%) (P<0.001) — the tolerability price, mostly gastrointestinal, printed at the same size as the benefit.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's most misquoted trial, so the fence is explicit: 'SELECT reduced cardiovascular death' is a false statement of the trial's result (P=0.07, hierarchy broken); 'SELECT reduced the MACE composite by 20% in relative terms, 1.5 points absolute, over ~40 months' is the true one. SELECT is also the family's only non-diabetes trial — its population (established CVD, BMI ≥27, no diabetes) is not interchangeable with the T2D trials on Cards 2–5.
cards.source: Lincoff AM et al.; SELECT Trial Investigators. Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Obesity without Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:2221–2232. PMID 37952131 · NCT03574597 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2307563

cards.headline: SUSTAIN-6 (Marso 2016): primary HR 0.74 (relative) — WITH retinopathy complications HR 1.76 on the same card (re-card; home: Shelf #71)
cards.summary: 3,297 patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, weekly subcutaneous semaglutide vs placebo, median 2.1 years — a noninferiority-designed trial: primary composite (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) 6.6% vs 8.9% (HR 0.74 [0.58–0.95], relative; superiority P=0.02). Cardiovascular death HR 0.98 — no difference. New or worsening nephropathy HR 0.64. The harm: retinopathy complications HR 1.76 (P=0.02), concentrated in patients with preexisting retinopathy. (Re-card; home: Shelf #71.)
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcome trial (SUSTAIN-6), designed for noninferiority with superiority tested secondarily, New England Journal of Medicine 2016. Re-card — home: Shelf #71
cards.people: 3,297 patients with type 2 diabetes on standard care (1,648 semaglutide 0.5 or 1.0 mg weekly, 1,649 placebo); 83.0% had established cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or both; follow-up 104 weeks. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #71; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 108 of 1,648 patients (6.6%) on semaglutide vs 146 of 1,649 (8.9%) on placebo (HR 0.74 [0.58–0.95]; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.02 for superiority) — a relative effect; absolute difference 2.3 points over ~2 years. Nonfatal MI: 2.9% vs 3.9% (HR 0.74 [0.51–1.08]). Nonfatal stroke: 1.6% vs 2.7% (HR 0.61 [0.38–0.99]). Rates of death from cardiovascular causes were similar (HR 0.98 in the trial report). Rates of new or worsening nephropathy were lower on semaglutide (HR 0.64), but rates of retinopathy complications (vitreous hemorrhage, blindness, or need for intravitreal therapy or photocoagulation) were significantly higher (HR 1.76 [1.11–2.78]; P=0.02). Fewer serious adverse events occurred on semaglutide overall, though more patients discontinued for adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: Two disciplines on one card. First, design: SUSTAIN-6 was built as a safety (noninferiority) trial — its superiority P=0.02 is real but the trial was neither sized nor primarily purposed as an outcomes trial, which is why SELECT and SOUL exist. Second, the retinopathy signal: it emerged against rapid glucose lowering in patients with preexisting retinopathy (83.5% of those with retinopathy events had preexisting retinopathy, as reported in the trial's discussion) — the practical lesson is eye surveillance when starting potent glucose lowering in advanced retinopathy, not avoidance of the drug class. The nephropathy strand (HR 0.64) is a secondary outcome here; FLOW (Reference 5) is where kidney effects were tested as a primary.
cards.source: Marso SP et al.; SUSTAIN-6 Investigators. Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:1834–1844. PMID 27633186 · NCT01720446. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1607141

cards.headline: PIONEER-6 (Husain 2019): oral semaglutide MACE HR 0.79 [0.57–1.11] — noninferiority met, superiority NOT shown; the 0.49/0.51 death ratios are small-count and NOT mortality evidence
cards.summary: 3,183 patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, daily oral semaglutide vs placebo, median 15.9 months: MACE 3.8% vs 4.8% (HR 0.79 [0.57–1.11], relative) — noninferiority met (P<0.001); superiority NOT shown (the interval crosses 1). Cardiovascular death 0.9% vs 1.9% (HR 0.49) and all-cause death 1.4% vs 2.8% (HR 0.51) rest on 15 vs 30 and 23 vs 45 events — printed here precisely so they are not quoted as mortality evidence. Nonfatal MI ran the other way: HR 1.18.
cards.type: Event-driven, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cardiovascular safety trial (PIONEER-6), New England Journal of Medicine 2019
cards.people: 3,183 patients (1,591 oral semaglutide, 1,592 placebo); mean age 66 years; 84.7% were ≥50 with established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease; median time in trial 15.9 months. The trial was designed to rule out an 80% excess of cardiovascular risk (noninferiority margin 1.8).
cards.result: Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 61 of 1,591 patients (3.8%) on oral semaglutide and 76 of 1,592 (4.8%) on placebo (HR 0.79 [0.57–1.11]; P<0.001 for noninferiority) — the noninferiority objective was met; the confidence interval includes 1.11, so superiority was not demonstrated. Components: death from cardiovascular causes 15 (0.9%) vs 30 (1.9%) (HR 0.49 [0.27–0.92]); nonfatal MI 37 (2.3%) vs 31 (1.9%) (HR 1.18 [0.73–1.90]); nonfatal stroke 12 (0.8%) vs 16 (1.0%) (HR 0.74 [0.35–1.57]). Death from any cause: 23 (1.4%) vs 45 (2.8%) (HR 0.51 [0.31–0.84]). Gastrointestinal adverse events leading to discontinuation were more common with oral semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: The teaching card for small-count secondaries: a halving of cardiovascular death (HR 0.49) built on 45 total events, in a 16-month safety trial whose primary superiority question failed, is not evidence that oral semaglutide halves mortality — it is noise-compatible, and SOUL (Reference 4), the adequately powered oral-semaglutide outcomes trial, is where the oral formulation's efficacy claim properly lives. Quoting PIONEER-6's death ratios without their event counts is the exact error this shelf exists to prevent.
cards.source: Husain M et al.; PIONEER-6 Investigators. Oral Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2019;381:841–851. PMID 31185157 · NCT02692716 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1901118

cards.headline: SOUL (McGuire 2025): oral semaglutide MACE 12.0% vs 13.8%, HR 0.86 (relative), P=0.006 — confirmatory kidney secondary NOT significant (re-card; home: Shelf #72)
cards.summary: 9,650 patients ≥50 with type 2 diabetes and ASCVD, CKD, or both, daily oral semaglutide (max 14 mg) vs placebo, median follow-up 49.5 months: primary MACE 12.0% vs 13.8% (HR 0.86 [0.77–0.96], relative; P=0.006) — an absolute difference of 1.8 points over ~4 years; nonfatal MI HR 0.74. The confirmatory secondary outcomes — including major kidney disease events — did not differ significantly (the hierarchy stopped); ~27% of participants were on background SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. Serious adverse events: 47.9% vs 50.3%. (Re-card; home: Shelf #72.)
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven superiority trial (SOUL), New England Journal of Medicine 2025. Re-card — home: Shelf #72
cards.people: 9,650 participants (4,825 per group) aged ≥50 with type 2 diabetes (A1C 6.5–10.0%) and known ASCVD, CKD, or both; mean follow-up 47.5 months, median 49.5 months. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #72; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 579 of 4,825 participants (12.0%; 3.1 per 100 person-years) on oral semaglutide vs 668 of 4,825 (13.8%; 3.7 per 100 person-years) on placebo (HR 0.86 [0.77–0.96]; P=0.006). The results for the confirmatory secondary outcomes — tested hierarchically, including the major kidney disease events composite — did not differ significantly between the groups. The incidence of serious adverse events was 47.9% (semaglutide) vs 50.3% (placebo); gastrointestinal disorders 5.0% vs 4.4%.
cards.watchOut: SOUL completes the oral story PIONEER-6 could not: superiority, shown, in an adequately powered trial. Its discipline point mirrors SELECT's: because the confirmatory secondary sequence did not reach significance, SOUL is a cardiovascular-outcomes win with NO kidney claim attached — agents must not let the MACE result smuggle a renal benefit in under it. FLOW (next card) is the family's kidney trial, and its kidney primary stays on its kidney home.
cards.source: McGuire DK et al.; SOUL Study Group. Oral Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in High-Risk Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2025;392:2001–2012. PMID 40162642 · NCT03914326. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2501006

cards.headline: FLOW (Perkovic 2024) — MACE strand ONLY: HR 0.82 (relative); cardiovascular death HR 0.71. The kidney primary (HR 0.76) lives on Shelf #75 — pointer, not a re-card
cards.summary: 3,533 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, weekly semaglutide 1.0 mg vs placebo, median 3.4 years: major cardiovascular events HR 0.82 [0.68–0.98], relative (P=0.029), and death from cardiovascular causes HR 0.71 [0.56–0.89] — the MACE strand of FLOW, carded here to complete the family. FLOW's primary outcome — major kidney disease events, HR 0.76 — is not re-carded: it is counted and carded in full on its kidney home, Shelf #75 .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled kidney-outcome trial (FLOW), New England Journal of Medicine 2024. Pointer card — the trial's home, including its kidney primary, is Shelf #75; this card carries only the cardiovascular strand and is counted at its home
cards.people: 3,533 participants (1,767 semaglutide, 1,766 placebo) with type 2 diabetes and CKD (eGFR/albuminuria-defined eligibility, on RAS blockade per the home card), median follow-up 3.4 years; the trial stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis on the data monitoring committee's recommendation.
cards.result: FLOW's confirmatory secondary outcomes favored semaglutide: the risk of major cardiovascular events was 18% lower in relative terms (HR 0.82 [0.68–0.98]; P=0.029) and the risk of death from cardiovascular causes 29% lower in relative terms (HR 0.71 [0.56–0.89]); death from any cause was also lower (HR 0.80). These cardiovascular results are the strand this family shelf needs. The primary outcome — major kidney disease events (kidney failure onset, ≥50% eGFR reduction, or kidney-related or cardiovascular death), HR 0.76 [0.66–0.88], P=0.0003 — belongs to Shelf #75 and is deliberately not duplicated here beyond this pointer.
cards.watchOut: One-home rule in action: FLOW is a kidney trial whose MACE strand agrees with the rest of the family (HR 0.82 against the pooled 0.83, Card 6). Counting its kidney result here as well would double-count one trial across two shelves — the totals on this page count FLOW once, on Shelf #75. Early stopping at interim, as with many positive trials, tends to flatter effect sizes modestly; the direction is corroborated by four sibling trials.
cards.source: Perkovic V et al.; FLOW Trial Committees and Investigators. Effects of Semaglutide on Chronic Kidney Disease in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2024;391:109–121. PMID 38785209 · NCT03819153. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2403347 (kidney primary carded on Shelf #75)

cards.headline: Pooled (Tan 2025): across the four T2D outcome trials (n=19,663), MACE HR 0.83 (relative) — the family average
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of the four type 2 diabetes cardiovascular/kidney outcome trials of semaglutide — SUSTAIN-6, PIONEER-6, SOUL, and FLOW (n= 19,663 ): pooled primary-outcome HR 0.83 (0.76–0.91), a 17% relative reduction; nonfatal MI HR 0.79. No significant pooled effect on cardiovascular death — the pooled verdict matches the family pattern on Cards 1–5: the composite and MI move; mortality, trial by trial and pooled, does not clear significance.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials (prospectively registered, PROSPERO CRD420251147337), Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine 2025
cards.people: 19,663 participants across SUSTAIN-6 (n=3,297), PIONEER-6 (n=3,183), SOUL (n=9,650), and FLOW (n=3,533) — all adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular or kidney risk. SELECT is not in this pool (no diabetes — a different population, Card 1).
cards.result: Four RCTs (n=19,663) showed semaglutide significantly reduced the primary outcome risk (HR 0.83 [0.76–0.91]), nonfatal myocardial infarction (HR 0.79 [0.67–0.92]), and revascularization (HR 0.71 [0.61–0.83]), with a modest decrease in heart-failure hospitalization (HR 0.85 [0.72–1.00]). No significant effects were seen for cardiovascular death, all-cause death, nonfatal stroke, or unstable-angina hospitalization. Evidence quality was graded high for the primary outcome and moderate for cardiovascular death, all-cause death, and nonfatal stroke. The desk brief carried the pooled figure as HR 0.83 (0.76–0.92) — that interval belongs to a second 2026 pooling restricted to the three cardiovascular outcome trials (SUSTAIN-6, PIONEER-6, SOUL; n=16,130; I²=25%); both poolings agree on the point estimate, 0.83, and this card cites the PMID-indexed four-trial analysis.
cards.watchOut: A pooled card summarizes; it does not add patients. Its honest use is the family average (0.83) and the family caveat (mortality not significant, pooled or single-trial, except as supportive findings) — not a sixth trial. Pool composition matters: including FLOW imports a kidney-trial population; the three-CVOT pooling noted in the Result field lands on the same point estimate, which is the robustness signal worth carrying.
cards.source: Tan S, Yin Y, Lu J. Effects of subcutaneous or oral semaglutide on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2025;12:1731127. PMID 41472878. DOI 10.3389/fcvm.2025.1731127 (the PubMed record prints no MeSH headings for this report)

shelves.title: Revascularization before elective vascular surgery (CARP): no benefit — and surgery waited a month longer
shelves.question: Should coronary revascularization be done before elective major vascular surgery in stable coronary disease?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Disease · Coronary Artery Bypass · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Vascular Surgical Procedures · Preoperative Care · Elective Surgical Procedures
shelves.balance: CARP randomized the 'fix the heart first' instinct and the instinct lost: revascularization before elective major vascular surgery did not reduce mortality at 2.7 years (22% vs 23%, RR 0.98) or postoperative MI — and it delayed the vascular operation by a median of 36 extra days. The shelf's fence is the trial's exclusion list, stated on the card: left main stenosis ≥50%, ejection fraction ≤20%, and severe aortic stenosis were excluded, so CARP's null governs stable patients like those enrolled and is silent about the excluded groups. The DECREASE-V pilot is mentioned only as a footnoted, integrity-tainted citation — the DECREASE programme was discredited for research misconduct — and is never evidence on this shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CARP (McFalls 2004): revascularization before vascular surgery did NOT reduce mortality — 22% vs 23% at 2.7 years (RR 0.98)
cards.summary: 510 patients with clinically significant coronary disease scheduled for elective major vascular surgery, randomized to coronary revascularization first or straight to surgery: mortality at 2.7 years 22% vs 23% — RR 0.98 [0.70–1.37], P=0.92 . Postoperative MI (troponin-defined) 12% vs 14%, P=0.37. The price of the strategy is stated on the same card: surgery was delayed — median 54 days from randomization to vascular surgery vs 18 days . The exclusions are the fence: left main stenosis ≥50%, ejection fraction ≤20%, and severe aortic stenosis were excluded — CARP says nothing about those patients.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (CARP), N Engl J Med 2004. The record carries no registry databank entry — a pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID is stated because none exists on the record.
cards.people: 510 patients (of 5,859 screened) at 18 Veterans Affairs medical centers — a VA population, overwhelmingly men; the record does not state a mean age or sex split. Indications for vascular surgery: expanding abdominal aortic aneurysm 33%, arterial occlusive disease of the legs 67%. Among those assigned to revascularization, PCI was performed in 59% and bypass surgery in 41%.
cards.result: At 2.7 years after randomization, mortality was 22% in the revascularization group and 23% in the no-revascularization group (relative risk 0.98 [0.70–1.37]; P=0.92). Within 30 days after the vascular operation, postoperative myocardial infarction occurred in 12% vs 14% (P=0.37). The median time from randomization to vascular surgery was 54 days in the revascularization group vs 18 days in the no-revascularization group (P<0.001). The authors' conclusion: a strategy of coronary-artery revascularization before elective vascular surgery among patients with stable cardiac symptoms cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: Read the fence before the result: CARP excluded left main disease ≥50%, ejection fraction ≤20%, and severe aortic stenosis, and enrolled only 9% of screened patients. 'Fix the coronaries first' remains untested — not disproven — in those excluded groups. The DECREASE-V pilot, sometimes cited beside CARP, is NOT evidence: the DECREASE programme was discredited for research misconduct, and it appears on this shelf only as this footnote, never as a card.
cards.source: McFalls EO et al. Coronary-artery revascularization before elective major vascular surgery. N Engl J Med. 2004;351:2795–2804. PMID 15625331. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa041905

shelves.title: Transfusion thresholds in acute myocardial infarction: the one place the restrictive rule may not travel
shelves.question: In acute myocardial infarction with anemia, is transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7–8 g/dL as safe as transfusing at 10?
shelves.mesh: Myocardial Infarction · Anemia · Blood Transfusion · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Hemoglobins · Humans
shelves.balance: This shelf is deliberately narrow. The general restrictive-threshold evidence — ICU, septic shock, hip fracture, cardiac surgery, GI bleeding — lives on Shelf #124 and Shelf #240 and is pointed to here, not re-carded; outside acute MI, restriction remains LIKELY fine and uses half the blood. Inside acute MI the two trials lean opposite ways and both are inconclusive: REALITY (668 patients) met noninferiority for restriction while conceding its interval included important harm (MACE 11.0% vs 14.0%; death 5.6% vs 7.7%), and MINT (3,504 patients; Card 2, re-carded from its home on Shelf #124) found MI or death in 16.9% on restriction vs 14.5% on liberal transfusion (RR 1.15, P=0.07), with death 9.9% vs 8.3% — every component leaning liberal, none significant. The stamp follows that shape exactly: harm of restriction in acute MI is POSSIBLE, benefit of liberality is POSSIBLE, and certainty either way would be a fabrication. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: REALITY (Ducrocq 2021): noninferiority met on paper — MACE 11.0% vs 14.0% — in a trial too small to exclude important harm
cards.summary: 668 patients with acute MI and hemoglobin 7–10 g/dL, restrictive (transfuse at ≤8) vs liberal (≤10) strategy: 30-day MACE 11.0% vs 14.0% — RR 0.79 , meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (upper 1-sided 97.5% CI 1.19 vs margin 1.25). Deaths: 5.6% vs 7.7% . But the authors' own caution prints with the result: the confidence interval included what may be a clinically important harm — 668 patients cannot settle a question MINT needed 3,504 to approach.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (REALITY), JAMA 2021 — open-label, noninferiority design. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02648113.
cards.people: 668 patients with myocardial infarction and hemoglobin between 7 and 10 g/dL at 35 hospitals in France and Spain; median age 77 years (IQR 69–84); 42.2% women. Only 35.7% of the restrictive group were actually transfused (342 units) vs 99.7% of the liberal group (758 units).
cards.result: At 30 days, MACE (all-cause death, stroke, recurrent MI, or emergency revascularization prompted by ischemia) occurred in 36 patients (11.0% [7.5–14.6%]) in the restrictive group and 45 (14.0% [10.0–17.9%]) in the liberal group (difference −3.0% [−8.4 to 2.4]); relative risk 0.79 (1-sided 97.5% CI 0.00–1.19), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion of an upper bound below 1.25. All-cause death occurred in 5.6% vs 7.7%, recurrent MI in 2.1% vs 3.1%, emergency revascularization in 1.5% vs 1.9%, and nonfatal ischemic stroke in 0.6% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority in an underpowered trial is a weak form of reassurance: REALITY randomized a fifth as many patients as MINT, its point estimate favors restriction while MINT's favors liberality, and its confidence interval — by the authors' own statement — included what may be a clinically important harm. Read REALITY as 'no disaster seen in 668 patients,' never as proof that restriction is safe in acute MI.
cards.source: Ducrocq G et al. Effect of a restrictive vs liberal blood transfusion strategy on major cardiovascular events among patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia: the REALITY randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2021;325:552–560. PMID 33560322 · NCT02648113 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1001/jama.2021.0135

cards.headline: MINT (Carson 2023): MI or death 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal — RR 1.15, P=0.07; every component leaned the same way [re-card — home Shelf #124]
cards.summary: 3,504 patients with acute MI and hemoglobin <10 g/dL, restrictive (transfuse at 7, permitted at 8) vs liberal (keep hemoglobin ≥10): primary outcome (MI or death at 30 days) 16.9% vs 14.5% — RR 1.15 [0.99–1.34], P=0.07 . Death 9.9% vs 8.3% (RR 1.19); recurrent MI 8.5% vs 7.2% (RR 1.19); cardiac death showed the widest gap (about 5.5% vs 3.2%, as carded at this trial's home). Nothing reached significance — and nothing leaned toward restriction. Re-card: this trial's home is Shelf #124 ; it is counted once, there.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (MINT), N Engl J Med 2023. Re-card; home Shelf #124. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02981407.
cards.people: 3,504 patients with myocardial infarction and a hemoglobin level of less than 10 g/dL, in the primary analysis. The record does not state a mean age or sex split. Mean red-cell units transfused: 0.7 (±1.6) restrictive vs 2.5 (±2.3) liberal; hemoglobin ran 1.3–1.6 g/dL lower on the restrictive strategy on days 1–3.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 295 of 1,749 patients (16.9%) in the restrictive-strategy group and 255 of 1,755 (14.5%) in the liberal-strategy group (risk ratio, modeled with multiple imputation for incomplete follow-up, 1.15; 95% CI 0.99–1.34; P=0.07). Death occurred in 9.9% vs 8.3% (RR 1.19 [0.96–1.47]); myocardial infarction in 8.5% vs 7.2% (RR 1.19 [0.94–1.49]). The authors' conclusion: a liberal strategy did not significantly reduce recurrent MI or death, but potential harms of a restrictive strategy cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: MINT is the largest transfusion trial ever run in acute MI and its verdict is deliberately two-handed: 'not proven' for liberal transfusion, 'not excluded' for restrictive harm. The consistent direction of every component — death, recurrent MI, cardiac death — is why this shelf stamps restrictive harm POSSIBLE rather than dismissing the signal, and why the general restrictive rule from Shelves #124 and #240 is not imported into acute MI.
cards.source: Carson JL et al. Restrictive or liberal transfusion strategy in myocardial infarction and anemia. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:2446–2456. PMID 37952133 · NCT02981407 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2307983

shelves.title: Febuxostat cardiovascular safety: MACE noninferior in two big trials — CARES found more deaths, FAST found none, and the discordance is the finding
shelves.question: In gout, is febuxostat as cardiovascularly safe as allopurinol — and does the answer change when the patient already has cardiovascular disease?
shelves.mesh: Febuxostat · Allopurinol · Gout · Cardiovascular Diseases · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large trials agree on the composite and disagree on death. CARES (Reference 1), in gout with established cardiovascular disease, met MACE noninferiority (HR 1.03) while all-cause mortality ran HR 1.22 and cardiovascular death HR 1.34 against febuxostat — the result behind the FDA's 2019 boxed warning. FAST (Reference 2), in an older but lower-risk European population, found the primary endpoint at HR 0.85 and fewer deaths on febuxostat (7.2% vs 8.6%). This shelf does not average them into reassurance: populations differed exactly on the variable the mortality claim is about. Noninferiority for cardiovascular events: LIKELY. A mortality excess in patients with established cardiovascular disease: POSSIBLE — unrefuted by a trial that largely did not enroll them. Urate-lowering efficacy is not what this shelf grades; febuxostat's kidney claims live on Shelf #168 . Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CARES (White 2018, NEJM): febuxostat noninferior for MACE (HR 1.03) — but all-cause mortality HR 1.22 and cardiovascular death HR 1.34 beside it
cards.summary: 6,190 patients with gout and established cardiovascular disease , febuxostat vs allopurinol, median follow-up 32 months. The primary MACE composite occurred in 10.8% vs 10.4% — HR 1.03 , meeting the 1.3 noninferiority margin (P=0.002 for noninferiority). Printed beside it, as this shelf always prints mortality next to an event claim: death from any cause was higher on febuxostat (HR 1.22 [1.01–1.47]), and cardiovascular death higher still (HR 1.34 [1.03–1.73]) — relative effects on the outcomes that matter most, in the direction opposite the headline. The trial's soft underbelly: 56.6% of patients discontinued the study drug and 45.0% discontinued follow-up, so the mortality signal rests on incomplete ascertainment — a reason to grade it POSSIBLE, not a reason to erase it. The FDA's 2019 boxed warning followed from this trial.
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, noninferiority randomized trial (CARES), N Engl J Med 2018. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01101035.
cards.people: 6,190 patients with gout and cardiovascular disease, randomized to febuxostat or allopurinol and stratified by kidney function; median follow-up 32 months (maximum 85). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: A primary end-point event (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or unstable angina with urgent revascularization) occurred in 335 patients (10.8%) on febuxostat and 321 (10.4%) on allopurinol (HR 1.03; upper limit of the one-sided 98.5% CI 1.23; P=0.002 for noninferiority against the 1.3 margin). All-cause mortality was higher with febuxostat (HR 1.22 [95% CI 1.01–1.47]), as was cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.34 [95% CI 1.03–1.73]). On-treatment analyses were similar. The trial regimen was discontinued by 56.6% of patients and follow-up by 45.0%.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority verdict on a composite can coexist with a mortality penalty because the composite counts nonfatal events the drug affected differently — which is precisely why this library prints mortality beside every event claim. The counterweights are real: very high discontinuation biases event capture, and FAST (Reference 2) found no mortality excess in a different population. But CARES enrolled the patients the warning is about — gout with established cardiovascular disease — and within that population the burden of proof sits with febuxostat.
cards.source: White WB et al. Cardiovascular safety of febuxostat or allopurinol in patients with gout. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(13):1200–1210. PMID 29527974 · NCT01101035 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1710895

cards.headline: FAST (Mackenzie 2020, Lancet): no cardiovascular or mortality excess in a European population — primary endpoint HR 0.85, deaths 7.2% vs 8.6%
cards.summary: 6,128 patients aged 60 and older with gout and at least one cardiovascular risk factor — but only a third with previous cardiovascular disease , and recent MI/stroke and severe heart failure excluded — already taking allopurinol, randomized to switch to febuxostat or continue optimized allopurinol, median follow-up about 4 years. The primary composite (hospitalization for nonfatal MI or biomarker-positive ACS, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death) occurred at 1.72 vs 2.05 events per 100 patient-years: adjusted HR 0.85 [0.70–1.03] , noninferior (P<0.0001) — a relative effect whose absolute rates are printed here beside it. Deaths: 222 (7.2%) on febuxostat vs 263 (8.6%) on allopurinol — no mortality excess, in the direction opposite CARES. Serious adverse events were similar (57.3% vs 59.4%). The discordance with CARES is carded, not smoothed: different patients (established CVD required vs one-third prevalence), different design (open-label vs double-blind), different discontinuation (32.4% vs 56.6%).
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint, non-inferiority trial (FAST), Lancet 2020 — UK, Denmark, Sweden. Registration as stated on the record: EudraCT 2011-001883-23 · ISRCTN72443728.
cards.people: 6,128 patients (mean age 71.0 years; 85.3% men) aged 60 or older with gout, already receiving allopurinol, with at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor; 33.4% had previous cardiovascular disease. Recent myocardial infarction or stroke, severe heart failure, and severe renal impairment were excluded.
cards.result: On-treatment, the primary endpoint occurred in 172 febuxostat patients (1.72 events per 100 patient-years) vs 241 on allopurinol (2.05 per 100 patient-years): adjusted HR 0.85 [95% CI 0.70–1.03], P<0.0001 for noninferiority (margin 1.3). Deaths occurred in 222 of 3,063 (7.2%) on febuxostat and 263 of 3,065 (8.6%) on allopurinol. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 57.3% vs 59.4%. Randomized therapy was discontinued by 32.4% (febuxostat) and 16.5% (allopurinol).
cards.watchOut: FAST does not acquit febuxostat in the CARES population — it studies a lower-risk one, open-label, in patients already tolerating allopurinol (a survivorship filter: anyone previously harmed by allopurinol was never enrolled). Read together, the two trials support: febuxostat does not increase cardiovascular events in either population (LIKELY), while a mortality penalty confined to patients with established cardiovascular disease remains POSSIBLE on CARES and unrefuted — not reproduced — by FAST. The FDA boxed warning stands on this shelf because CARES stands.
cards.source: Mackenzie IS et al. Long-term cardiovascular safety of febuxostat compared with allopurinol in patients with gout (FAST): a multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label, non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2020;396(10264):1745–1757. PMID 33181081 · ISRCTN72443728 (as stated on the record). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(20)32234-0

shelves.title: Screening for silent atrial fibrillation: watches and patches find it — stroke prevention still unproven
shelves.question: Does screening people who feel well for atrial fibrillation with wearable or implantable devices prevent strokes?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Humans · Mass Screening · Stroke · Telemedicine · Wearable Electronic Devices
shelves.balance: Split the claim. Detection: as strong as evidence gets — randomized and prospective studies at every intensity (watch, patch, handheld, implant) find more AF and start more anticoagulation. Outcomes: STROKESTOP’s invitation to screen produced a combined-endpoint HR of 0.96 [0.92–1.00] — inside the small-effect band, on a composite — and LOOP’s far more intensive monitoring produced a non-significant stroke HR of 0.80 with more bleeding. One stamp for the shelf as asked (does screening prevent strokes?): POSSIBLE, and the cards show exactly how much of that grade is detection wearing outcome’s clothes. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Apple Heart Study (Perez 2019, NEJM): 419,297 smartwatch wearers, 0.52% ever notified — and 84% of repeat notifications were true atrial fibrillation
cards.summary: 419,297 participants monitored a median of 117 days in a siteless, app-consented study. 2,161 (0.52%) received an irregular-pulse notification. Of the 450 who returned analyzable ECG patches (applied on average 13 days after notification), 34% had atrial fibrillation on the patch. The positive predictive value of a subsequent notification, checked against a simultaneous ECG, was 0.84 [0.76–0.92] . 57% of notified survey respondents contacted a health care provider outside the study; no serious app-related adverse events were reported.
cards.type: Large-scale prospective single-group (siteless pragmatic) study, N Engl J Med 2019. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03335800. Funded by Apple, as stated in the record. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 419,297 US participants without self-reported atrial fibrillation who owned an iPhone and Apple Watch and consented through an app; monitoring occurred during typical use over a median of 117 days.
cards.result: Over the monitoring period, 2,161 participants (0.52%) received notifications of irregular pulse. Among 450 participants who returned ECG patches containing analyzable data, atrial fibrillation was present in 34% (97.5% CI, 29 to 39) overall and in 35% (97.5% CI, 27 to 43) of participants aged 65 years or older. Among notified participants, the positive predictive value was 0.84 (95% CI, 0.76 to 0.92) for observing atrial fibrillation on the ECG simultaneously with a subsequent irregular pulse notification. There were no reports of serious app-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This is a detection-accuracy study with no comparison group and no outcomes: it cannot say whether notifying these wearers prevented a single stroke. Two selection funnels also matter — only 450 of 2,161 notified participants returned analyzable patches, and patch application lagged notification by 13 days on average, so the 34% is the yield among the compliant, measured late. What the study does prove is scale: a watch can run a screening program on 400,000 people with no clinic at all.
cards.source: Perez MV et al. Large-Scale Assessment of a Smartwatch to Identify Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(20):1909–1917. PMID 31722151 · NCT03335800. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1901183

cards.headline: mSToPS patch trial (Steinhubl 2018, JAMA): a home ECG patch found new atrial fibrillation in 3.9% at 4 months vs 0.9% with delayed monitoring
cards.summary: 2,659 people at elevated AF risk (mean age 72.4 years; 38.6% women) randomized to wear a continuous ECG patch for up to 4 weeks, immediately or after a 4-month delay. New atrial fibrillation by 4 months: 3.9% (53 of 1,366) immediate vs 0.9% (12 of 1,293) delayed — absolute difference 3.0% [1.8–4.1] . In the matched observational follow-up at 1 year, monitored participants had more new AF diagnoses (6.7 vs 2.6 per 100 person-years) and more anticoagulant starts (5.7 vs 3.7 per 100 person-years) — and no difference in AF-related emergency visits or hospitalizations.
cards.type: Direct-to-participant randomized clinical trial with a prospective matched observational cohort, JAMA 2018. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT02506244.
cards.people: 2,659 members of a US national health plan at increased risk of atrial fibrillation (randomized groups: mean age 72.4 years [SD 7.3]; 38.6% women), plus 5,214 age-, sex- and risk-score-matched observational controls.
cards.result: In the randomized study, new atrial fibrillation was identified by 4 months in 3.9% (53 of 1,366) of the immediate-monitoring group versus 0.9% (12 of 1,293) in the delayed group (absolute difference, 3.0%; 95% CI, 1.8% to 4.1%). At 1 year, atrial fibrillation was newly diagnosed in 109 monitored (6.7 per 100 person-years) and 81 unmonitored (2.6 per 100 person-years) individuals. Active monitoring was associated with increased initiation of anticoagulants (5.7 vs 3.7 per 100 person-years), outpatient cardiology visits, and primary care visits, with no difference in atrial-fibrillation-related emergency department visits or hospitalizations (1.3 vs 1.4 per 100 person-years).
cards.watchOut: The randomized result is a detection result: the delayed group is a fair control for ‘would this have been found anyway in 4 months,’ and mostly it would not. The 1-year treatment and utilization numbers come from the matched observational part of the study, not the randomization — and more cardiology visits is a cost of screening, not a benefit, until an outcome trial shows what the extra diagnoses buy.
cards.source: Steinhubl SR et al. Effect of a Home-Based Wearable Continuous ECG Monitoring Patch on Detection of Undiagnosed Atrial Fibrillation: The mSToPS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018;320(2):146–155. PMID 29998336 · NCT02506244. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.8102

cards.headline: STROKESTOP (Svennberg 2021, Lancet): inviting all 75–76-year-olds to handheld ECG screening edged a combined endpoint — HR 0.96 [0.92–1.00], P=.045
cards.summary: 28,768 people aged 75–76 in two Swedish regions, randomized to be invited to intermittent handheld ECG screening for 14 days or to no invitation; only 51.3% of those invited actually participated. Over a median 6.9 years, the combined primary endpoint (ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding hospitalization, all-cause death) occurred in 31.9% of the invited group vs 33.0% of controls — HR 0.96 [0.92–1.00], relative; P=.045 . The authors called it a small net benefit.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, unmasked, randomized controlled trial, Lancet 2021. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01593553.
cards.people: All residents aged 75 or 76 years in Halland and Stockholm, Sweden: 13,979 analyzed in the invited-to-screening group and 13,996 in the control group, followed a minimum of 5 years (median 6.9 years).
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 6.9 years (IQR 6.5–7.2), significantly fewer primary endpoint events occurred in the intervention group (4,456 [31.9%] of 13,979; 5.45 events per 100 years) than in the control group (4,616 [33.0%] of 13,996; 5.68 events per 100 years; hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI, 0.92–1.00; P=.045). The authors concluded that screening showed a small net benefit and is safe and beneficial in older populations.
cards.watchOut: Apply this library’s observational-and-threshold discipline to a randomized result: HR 0.96 sits deep inside the 0.5–2.0 band of small effects, the confidence interval touches 1.00, the endpoint is a composite that counts bleeding hospitalizations alongside strokes, and half the invited group never screened — so the intention-to-treat effect is the effect of an invitation, diluted. This is the strongest outcome evidence screening has, and it is a nudge, not a verdict. (The device here is a handheld ECG, not a watch; the shelf groups it because the screening strategy, not the gadget, is the question.)
cards.source: Svennberg E et al. Clinical outcomes in systematic screening for atrial fibrillation (STROKESTOP): a multicentre, parallel group, unmasked, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2021;398(10310):1498–1506. PMID 34469764 · NCT01593553. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(21)01637-8
cards.search: strokestop (svennberg 2021, lancet): inviting all 75–76-year-olds to handheld ecg screening edged a combined endpoint — hr 0.96 [0.92–1.00], p=.045 28,768 people aged 75–76 in two swedish regions, randomized to be invited to intermittent handheld ecg screening for 14 days or to no invitation; only 51.3% of those invited actually participated. over a median 6.9 years, the combined primary endpoint (ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding hospitalization, all-cause death) occurred in 31.9% of the invited group vs 33.0% of controls — hr 0.96 [0.92–1.00], relative; p=.045 . the authors called it a small net benefit. does systematic population screening for atrial fibrillation in older adults reduce stroke, embolism, serious bleeding, and death combined? multicentre, parallel-group, unmasked, randomized controlled trial, lancet 2021. registry id from the record's own

cards.headline: LOOP (Svendsen 2021, Lancet): an implanted monitor tripled AF detection and anticoagulation — and did not significantly reduce stroke
cards.summary: 6,004 people aged 70–90 with at least one stroke risk factor, randomized 1:3 to an implantable loop recorder or usual care, followed a median of 64.5 months. Atrial fibrillation was diagnosed in 31.8% vs 12.2% (HR 3.17, relative) and anticoagulation started in 29.7% vs 13.1%. But the primary outcome — stroke or systemic arterial embolism — was 4.5% vs 5.6%: HR 0.80 [0.61–1.05], relative; P=.11, not significant . Major bleeding: 4.3% vs 3.5% (HR 1.26, not significant). The authors’ conclusion: not all atrial fibrillation is worth screening for.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, Lancet 2021. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT02036450.
cards.people: 6,004 individuals without atrial fibrillation, aged 70–90 years, with hypertension, diabetes, previous stroke, or heart failure, at four Danish centers (1,501 implantable loop recorder; 4,503 usual care). Mean age 74.7 years (SD 4.1); 47.3% women; 90.7% had hypertension.
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation was diagnosed in 477 (31.8%) of 1,501 participants in the loop-recorder group versus 550 (12.2%) of 4,503 in the control group (hazard ratio 3.17; 95% CI, 2.81 to 3.59). Oral anticoagulation was initiated in 445 (29.7%) versus 591 (13.1%) (HR 2.72). The primary outcome occurred in 67 (4.5%) versus 251 (5.6%) participants (HR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.61 to 1.05; P=.11). Major bleeding occurred in 65 (4.3%) versus 156 (3.5%) (HR 1.26; 95% CI, 0.95 to 1.69; P=.11). The authors concluded that screening resulted in a threefold increase in atrial fibrillation detection and anticoagulation initiation but no significant reduction in stroke or systemic arterial embolism.
cards.watchOut: LOOP is the shelf’s discipline in one trial: the most sensitive detector ever randomized found three times the arrhythmia, anticoagulated more than twice as many people — and the stroke endpoint did not significantly move, while bleeding leaned the wrong way. Screen-detected AF is often brief and low-burden, and its stroke risk may not be the risk of clinical AF. An implantable is not a wearable; it is carded here as the intensive end of the same screening spectrum, where the detection signal is strongest and the outcome answer is therefore most informative.
cards.source: Svendsen JH et al. Implantable loop recorder detection of atrial fibrillation to prevent stroke (The LOOP Study): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2021;398(10310):1507–1516. PMID 34469766 · NCT02036450. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(21)01698-6

cards.headline: Reading the AF-screening evidence together: detection is a solved problem — benefit is not
cards.summary: Every device on this shelf finds atrial fibrillation: a watch notifies 0.52% of wearers with an 84% predictive value; a patch quadruples 4-month diagnoses; an implant triples them. The outcome ledger is thinner: one invitation-to-screen trial with a combined-endpoint HR of 0.96 , one intensive-monitoring trial with a non-significant stroke HR of 0.80 and a bleeding lean against. No trial of a consumer wearable has ever been powered for stroke.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1–4 together, separating the detection claim (strong) from the outcome claim (weak).
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1–4: consumer smartwatch owners (mean-risk, self-selected), health-plan members at elevated risk, all 75–76-year-olds in two Swedish regions, and high-risk Danes aged 70–90.
cards.result: Detection and anticoagulation initiation increase with every monitoring intensity tested. Stroke and embolism outcomes, where randomized, are a marginal composite benefit in STROKESTOP and a non-significant difference in LOOP. The two results are compatible with a small true benefit that neither trial could size — and with none.
cards.watchOut: Screening converts healthy people into patients on anticoagulants; the bleeding side of that conversion is real and counted in both outcome trials. Until a wearable-era trial is powered on stroke, this shelf’s advice-grade claim is the narrow one: devices detect; benefit is possible, not shown. (Collision note: anticoagulation itself is Shelf #100’s question and early rhythm control is Shelf #273’s; this shelf is only about finding AF in people who feel well.)
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–4 on this shelf (PMID 31722151; PMID 29998336; PMID 34469764; PMID 34469766).
