shelves.title: Polygenic risk scores: real prediction, tiny increment, no outcome evidence
shelves.question: Do polygenic risk scores improve prediction or prevention enough to belong in clinical care?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Disease · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genome-Wide Association Study · Humans · Multifactorial Inheritance · Polymorphism, Single Nucleotide · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: The three cards tell one story at three altitudes. The scores genuinely stratify: 8% of people carry a polygenic coronary risk above threefold (Reference 1). Added to the clinical equations already in use, that stratification buys almost nothing: a C-statistic gain of 0.02 and net reclassification of 4% (Reference 2). And the single randomized trial of actually using a score changed a process — more statins started, LDL 9.4 mg/dL lower at 6 months, n=203 — not an outcome (Reference 3). No trial shows a polygenic score preventing a heart attack, a stroke, or a death, and the scores transport poorly beyond the ancestries they were built in. MAYBE (weak evidence), as briefed. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Genome-wide scores find monogenic-sized risk in ordinary genomes (Khera 2018, Nature Genetics): 8.0% of people carry >3-fold polygenic risk for coronary disease
cards.summary: Using genome-wide polygenic scores for five common diseases, the authors identified the share of the population at more than threefold increased risk : 8.0% for coronary artery disease , 6.1% for atrial fibrillation, 3.5% for type 2 diabetes, 3.2% for inflammatory bowel disease, and 1.5% for breast cancer. For coronary disease, that high-risk share is 20-fold more common than carriers of the rare single-gene mutations conferring comparable risk — the paper’s argument for bringing polygenic prediction into clinical care.
cards.type: Genomic prediction study (development and validation in population biobank data), Nature Genetics 2018. No registry ID — a genomic prediction study; none on the record. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Population-scale genomic and health-record data (UK Biobank and validation cohorts) used to derive and validate genome-wide polygenic scores for coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and breast cancer.
cards.result: The genome-wide polygenic score approach identified 8.0%, 6.1%, 3.5%, 3.2%, and 1.5% of the population at greater than threefold increased risk for coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and breast cancer, respectively. For coronary artery disease, this prevalence is 20-fold higher than the carrier frequency of rare monogenic mutations conferring comparable risk.
cards.watchOut: A >3-fold relative risk sounds like a diagnosis; it is a rank in a distribution. Threefold a small absolute risk can remain small, the scores were derived and validated mainly in European-ancestry data (they transport poorly across ancestries), and identifying risk is not the same as reducing it — Cards 2 and 3 test exactly those next steps and find much less.
cards.source: Khera AV et al. Genome-wide polygenic scores for common diseases identify individuals with risk equivalent to monogenic mutations. Nat Genet. 2018;50(9):1219–1224. PMID 30104762. DOI 10.1038/s41588-018-0183-z

cards.headline: Adding the score to standard prediction (Elliott 2020, JAMA): C-statistic 0.76 → 0.78 — a statistically significant, clinically modest improvement
cards.summary: 352,660 UK Biobank participants , 6,272 incident coronary events over a median 8 years. Discrimination for incident coronary artery disease: polygenic score alone C=0.61 ; pooled cohort equations alone C=0.76 ; both combined C=0.78 — an improvement of 0.02 [0.01–0.03]. At a 7.5% risk threshold, adding the score reclassified a net 4.0% of individuals appropriately. The authors’ verdict: a statistically significant, yet modest, improvement — further investigation warranted before clinical implementation.
cards.type: Observational predictive-accuracy study (UK Biobank), JAMA 2020. No registry ID — an observational cohort study; none on the record.
cards.people: 352,660 UK Biobank participants (mean age 55.9 years; 205,297 women [58.2%]) without the case-control enrichment used for score tuning, followed to 2017 with 6,272 incident coronary artery disease events.
cards.result: Discrimination for incident coronary artery disease was C statistic 0.61 (95% CI, 0.60 to 0.62) for the polygenic risk score, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.77) for pooled cohort equations, and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.77 to 0.79) for both combined; the change from adding the score was 0.02 (95% CI, 0.01 to 0.03). Using a 7.5% risk threshold, addition of the polygenic risk score resulted in a net reclassification improvement of 4.4% for cases and −0.4% for noncases (overall 4.0%; 95% CI, 3.1% to 4.9%). The authors concluded that the addition was associated with a statistically significant, yet modest, improvement in predictive accuracy.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf’s reality check on Card 1: alone, the score predicts worse than the free clinical equations doctors already use (0.61 vs 0.76), and on top of them it adds two hundredths of a C-statistic. Statistical significance at n=352,660 is not clinical significance — a distinction this library exists to keep visible.
cards.source: Elliott J et al. Predictive Accuracy of a Polygenic Risk Score-Enhanced Prediction Model vs a Clinical Risk Score for Coronary Artery Disease. JAMA. 2020;323(7):636–645. PMID 32068818. DOI 10.1001/jama.2019.22241

cards.headline: The one randomized test of using a score (MI-GENES, Kullo 2016, Circulation): disclosing genetic risk lowered LDL by 9.4 mg/dL — via more statins, in 203 people
cards.summary: 203 adults at intermediate coronary risk, not on statins , randomized to receive their 10-year risk from a conventional score alone, or the conventional score plus a genetic risk score, disclosed with a genetic counselor and shared decision-making. At 6 months, LDL cholesterol was lower in the genetic-score group: 96.5 vs 105.9 mg/dL (P=.04) — driven by statin initiation ( 39% vs 22% , P<.01), concentrated in those told their genetic risk was high. Diet and physical activity did not differ between groups.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (MI-GENES), Circulation 2016. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01936675.
cards.people: 203 participants aged 45–65 years at intermediate risk for coronary heart disease and not taking statins (mean age 59.4 years [SD 5]; 48% men; mean 10-year risk 8.5% [SD 4.1%]): 100 received conventional-score risk disclosure, 103 conventional plus genetic score disclosure.
cards.result: At 6 months, the group whose risk estimate incorporated the genetic risk score had a lower LDL cholesterol than the conventional group (96.5 [SD 32.7] versus 105.9 [SD 33.3] mg/dL; P=.04). Participants with high genetic risk scores had lower LDL levels (92.3 [SD 32.9] mg/dL) than conventional-group participants (P=.02), but not participants with low genetic scores (100.9 [SD 32.2] mg/dL; P=.18). Statins were initiated more often in the genetic-score group (39% versus 22%, P<.01). No significant differences in dietary fat intake or physical activity were noted.
cards.watchOut: A process victory, honestly bounded: one small trial, a surrogate endpoint (LDL at 6 months), an effect that runs entirely through prescribing a drug the conventional score already indicated for many of these patients, and no event outcomes. It shows a score can move a clinic visit; it does not show a score should be in the visit. This is the only randomized card the shelf has, and it is why the grade is MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than nothing at all.
cards.source: Kullo IJ et al. Incorporating a Genetic Risk Score Into Coronary Heart Disease Risk Estimates: Effect on Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Levels (the MI-GENES Clinical Trial). Circulation. 2016;133(12):1181–1188. PMID 26915630 · NCT01936675. DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.115.020109

shelves.title: Influenza vaccine after a heart attack: one double-blind trial, fewer deaths — a Tier C claim
shelves.question: Does influenza vaccination given early after a myocardial infarction reduce death and further cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Humans · Influenza Vaccines · Myocardial Infarction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One trial carries this shelf: IAMI randomised 2,571 patients in hospital after myocardial infarction to influenza vaccine or saline placebo and found the 12-month composite of death, infarction or stent thrombosis lower on vaccine (5.3% vs 7.2%; HR 0.72 [0.52–0.99]), with all-cause death lower as well (2.9% vs 4.9%; HR 0.59 [0.39–0.89]). The fences are on the card: the trial stopped early in the COVID-19 pandemic, the composite interval ends at 0.99, and the mortality difference rests on small counts. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: IAMI (Fröbert 2021, Circulation): flu vaccine in hospital after a heart attack — composite down (HR 0.72), deaths down (HR 0.59)
cards.summary: 2,571 participants randomised at 30 centres in 8 countries to in-hospital inactivated influenza vaccine or saline placebo, 99.7% shortly after myocardial infarction. The trial was halted early (the COVID-19 pandemic) before its target sample size. At 12 months the primary composite (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or stent thrombosis) occurred in 5.3% on vaccine vs 7.2% on placebo — HR 0.72 [0.52–0.99], P=0.040 . All-cause death: 2.9% vs 4.9% — HR 0.59 [0.39–0.89], P=0.010 ; cardiovascular death HR 0.59 [0.39–0.90]; myocardial infarction HR 0.86 [0.50–1.46], not significant.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial, Circulation 2021. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT02831608.
cards.people: 2,571 participants randomised (1,290 vaccine; 1,281 placebo) at 30 centres across 8 countries, 99.7% after myocardial infarction and 0.3% with high-risk stable coronary disease; 2,532 received study treatment and form the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over the 12-month follow-up, the primary outcome occurred in 67 participants (5.3%) assigned influenza vaccine and 91 participants (7.2%) assigned placebo (hazard ratio, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.52–0.99]; P=0.040). Rates of all-cause death were 2.9% and 4.9% (hazard ratio, 0.59 [95% CI, 0.39–0.89]; P=0.010), rates of cardiovascular death were 2.7% and 4.5% (hazard ratio, 0.59 [95% CI, 0.39–0.90]; P=0.014), and rates of myocardial infarction were 2.0% and 2.4% (hazard ratio, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.50–1.46]; P=0.57) in the influenza vaccine and placebo groups, respectively.
cards.watchOut: One trial, stopped early, with a primary confidence interval ending at 0.99 — and a mortality difference (two percentage points absolute) doing most of the composite’s work while the recurrent-infarction component did not significantly move. Early stopping for an external reason (a pandemic, not an interim peek) is less biasing than stopping for benefit, but the trial is smaller than designed and the estimate is fragile in a way a second trial would settle. The mortality claim is exactly why this shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Fröbert O et al. Influenza vaccination after myocardial infarction: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial. Circulation. 2021;144(18):1476–1484. PMID 34459211 · NCT02831608. DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.121.057042

cards.headline: Reading IAMI alone: a plausible, cheap, one-trial claim — mortality resting on 158 events
cards.summary: The whole shelf is one trial and 158 primary events. Its strengths are real: double-blind, placebo-controlled, hard endpoints, an intervention that costs almost nothing and is already recommended to this population for influenza’s own sake. Its weakness is arithmetic: a single trial, truncated by a pandemic, whose composite confidence interval reaches 0.99 and whose mortality component — the claim that matters most — is a secondary endpoint with 2.9% vs 4.9% built on small counts. Under this library’s rules a mortality claim of this shape is Tier C and grades no higher than POSSIBLE until a second randomised trial reports; the shelf names no in-flight replication, because none is on the record it cards.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card states why this shelf is Tier C and what would change its grade.
cards.people: The population of Card 1: 2,571 patients randomised in hospital after myocardial infarction (or with high-risk stable coronary disease) across 8 countries.
cards.result: IAMI establishes that in-hospital influenza vaccination after myocardial infarction was followed by fewer deaths and composite events at 12 months in one double-blind trial. It does not establish the effect’s size precisely (the primary interval spans a 1% to a 48% relative reduction), nor whether the benefit is influenza prevention, an off-target vascular effect, or chance amplified by early stopping.
cards.watchOut: Cite IAMI for what it is — the best randomised evidence that vaccinating after a heart attack helps, from exactly one trial — and not as settled proof that it saves lives. The intervention’s low cost and existing recommendation for influenza prevention mean the clinical bet and the evidence claim are different things; this shelf grades the evidence claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Card 1 on this shelf (PMID 34459211; NCT02831608).

shelves.title: Exercise dose for blood pressure: isometric training network meta-analysis
shelves.question: In adults, how do exercise modes — especially isometric training — compare for lowering resting blood pressure, and what dose maintains the benefit?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Exercise · Hypertension · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY: All major exercise modes lowered resting blood pressure in large meta-analyses, with isometric training ranked first — systolic/diastolic falls of -8.24/-4.00 mm Hg in pairwise analysis — and a small randomised trial in unmedicated hypertension found -11.2 mm Hg (handgrip) and -12.9 mm Hg (wall squat) systolic falls versus -0.4 mm Hg in controls. Effects are on a surrogate outcome (resting blood pressure), not on cardiovascular events, and the isometric estimate rests on far fewer trials than the aerobic estimate. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Isometric training ranked first of five exercise modes for lowering resting blood pressure
cards.summary: Across 270 randomised trials and 15,827 participants , every exercise mode lowered resting blood pressure and isometric exercise ranked first : systolic/diastolic −8.24/−4.00 mm Hg , ahead of combined training (−6.04/−2.54), dynamic resistance (−4.55/−3.04), aerobic (−4.49/−2.53) and HIIT (−4.08/−2.50). Isometric wall squat was the most effective submode for systolic pressure.
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Pooled sample of 15,827 participants across 270 randomised controlled trials; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Pairwise reductions in resting systolic/diastolic blood pressure: isometric exercise training -8.24/-4.00 mm Hg (p<0.001), combined training -6.04/-2.54 mm Hg (p<0.001), dynamic resistance training -4.55/-3.04 mm Hg (p<0.001), aerobic exercise training -4.49/-2.53 mm Hg (p<0.001) and high-intensity interval training -4.08/-2.50 mm Hg (p<0.001). In the network meta-analysis, isometric exercise training ranked first for systolic blood pressure (SUCRA 98.3%), followed by combined training (75.7%), dynamic resistance training (46.1%), aerobic exercise training (40.5%) and high-intensity interval training (39.4%); isometric wall squat was the most effective submode for reducing systolic blood pressure (90.4%) and running for diastolic blood pressure (91.3%).
cards.watchOut: Ranking is by SUCRA in a network meta-analysis of mostly indirect comparisons; blood pressure is a surrogate outcome and no cardiovascular-event outcomes are reported in the abstract.
cards.source: Edwards JJ et al. Exercise training and resting blood pressure: a large-scale pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med. 2023 Oct;57(20):1317-1326. PMID: 37491419. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — this is a systematic review/network meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Earlier meta-analysis also found the largest systolic fall with isometric resistance training
cards.summary: The earlier pairwise meta-analysis (77 trials in hypertension) found the same ordering: systolic pressure fell −10.9 mm Hg with isometric resistance training, versus −3.5 for endurance and −1.8 for dynamic resistance — the isometric advantage is not an artefact of the network method.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 5,223 participants (3,401 exercise and 1,822 control) in 93 trials of healthy adults aged 18 years or older; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure was reduced after endurance training (-3.5 mm Hg, confidence limits -4.6 to -2.3), dynamic resistance training (-1.8 mm Hg, -3.7 to -0.011) and isometric resistance training (-10.9 mm Hg, -14.5 to -7.4), but not after combined training. Diastolic blood pressure fell after endurance (-2.5 mm Hg, -3.2 to -1.7), dynamic resistance (-3.2 mm Hg, -4.5 to -2.0), isometric resistance (-6.2 mm Hg, -10.3 to -2.0) and combined training (-2.2 mm Hg, -3.9 to -0.48). After endurance training, reductions were greater in 26 study groups of hypertensive subjects (-8.3/-5.2 mm Hg) than in 50 groups of prehypertensive subjects (-2.1/-1.7 mm Hg) and 29 groups with normal blood pressure (-0.75/-1.1 mm Hg).
cards.watchOut: Only 5 isometric resistance groups were included, so the large isometric estimate is imprecise; trials lasted at least 4 weeks and were published up to February 2012.
cards.source: Cornelissen VA, Smart NA. Exercise training for blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Am Heart Assoc. 2013 Feb 1;2(1):e004473. PMID: 23525435. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review/meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Three isometric sessions a week lowered systolic pressure, and one session a week maintained it
cards.summary: A direct randomised trial of isometric training: after 12 weeks of three sessions a week, systolic pressure fell −11.2 mm Hg (handgrip) and −12.9 mm Hg (wall squat) versus −0.4 in controls; one session a week then maintained the gain for 12 more weeks. Diastolic changes were not significant.
cards.people: 77 unmedicated hypertensive adults (systolic blood pressure 130 mmHg or higher): handgrip n=28, squat n=27, controls n=22; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 12 weeks of three sessions per week (phase 1), mean systolic blood pressure reductions were -11.2 mmHg in the handgrip group and -12.9 mmHg in the squat group versus -0.4 mmHg in controls, but changes in diastolic blood pressure were not significant. During 12 further weeks of one session per week (phase 2) there were no significant within-group changes, and systolic blood pressure was 3.8 mmHg lower in the wall squat than the handgrip group. The authors report the time investment to achieve and retain the reductions as 42 and 12 min respectively.
cards.watchOut: Small, single trial in unmedicated hypertensive adults in a workplace setting; diastolic blood pressure did not change significantly and no clinical events were reported.
cards.source: Cohen DD et al. Reductions in systolic blood pressure achieved by hypertensives with three isometric training sessions per week are maintained with a single session per week. J Clin Hypertens (Greenwich). 2023 Apr;25(4):380-387. PMID: 36965163. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in the record's databank.

cards.headline: Synthesis: exercise lowers resting blood pressure; isometric training looks largest, on the thinnest trial base
cards.summary: Both meta-analyses and the maintenance trial agree: exercise lowers resting blood pressure, and isometric training shows the largest point estimates — on the thinnest trial base of the five modes, which is why the ranking is claimed and the exact dose is not.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 270 randomised trials (15,827 participants) in the network meta-analysis, 93 trials (5,223 participants) in the earlier meta-analysis, and one 77-person randomised trial in unmedicated hypertension.
cards.result: Across both meta-analyses every major mode lowered resting blood pressure, and isometric training gave the largest point estimates (-8.24/-4.00 mm Hg in the 2023 network meta-analysis and -10.9 mm Hg systolic in the 2013 meta-analysis), while the direct randomised maintenance trial found -11.2 mmHg (handgrip) and -12.9 mmHg (wall squat) systolic falls versus -0.4 mmHg in controls. This shelf is stamped LIKELY: the direction is consistent, but the headline isometric advantage comes from indirect ranking and few isometric trials, and all outcomes are blood pressure, not events.
cards.watchOut: Do not present the isometric ranking as proven superiority over aerobic exercise; it is a network ranking, and hypertensive subgroups showed larger falls than normotensive groups, so baseline pressure drives much of the apparent dose effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Edwards JJ et al. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(20):1317-1326. PMID: 37491419; Cornelissen VA, Smart NA. J Am Heart Assoc. 2013;2(1):e004473. PMID: 23525435; Cohen DD et al. J Clin Hypertens. 2023;25(4):380-387. PMID: 36965163. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: HIIT vs moderate continuous training: cardiometabolic outcomes
shelves.question: How does high-intensity interval training compare with moderate-intensity continuous training for cardiometabolic outcomes such as fitness, body composition, blood pressure and glucose regulation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Humans · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Education and Training · Physical Endurance · Physical Fitness · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: High-intensity interval training and moderate continuous training produce similar, modest cardiometabolic gains. Interval training gave a small extra fitness gain in one meta-analysis (1.2 mL/kg/min versus endurance training) and similar fat-mass and waist reductions to continuous training in overweight adults while requiring about 40% less training time, but the evidence is meta-analyses of small, short trials with surrogate outcomes only — no trial shows an event benefit, so this shelf is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Interval training improved VO2max slightly more than endurance training in healthy adults
cards.summary: Versus no-exercise controls, endurance training improved VO2max by 4.9 mL/kg/min and interval training by 5.5 ; head-to-head, interval training’s edge was small ( +1.2 mL/kg/min , possibly trivial) — a fitness edge, not a rout.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials
cards.people: 723 participants in 28 studies of healthy adults aged 18-45 years, mean (SD) age 25.1 (5) years and initial fitness 40.8 (7.9) mL/kg/min; the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Versus no-exercise controls, endurance training improved maximal oxygen consumption by 4.9 mL/kg/min (95% confidence limits plus/minus 1.4) and high-intensity interval training by 5.5 mL/kg/min (plus/minus 1.2). cards.headline: HIIT and continuous training reduced fat mass and waist size similarly — HIIT in about 40% less time
cards.summary: HIIT and moderate continuous training reduced fat mass and waist circumference similarly , with no significant difference on any body-composition measure — but interval training took about 40% less time .
cards.people: 13 studies in overweight or obese participants aged 18-45 years; studies averaged 10 weeks at 3 sessions per week. The abstract does not state total participant number or sex mix.
cards.result: Both high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training elicited significant (p<0.05) reductions in whole-body fat mass and waist circumference, with no significant differences between them for any body composition measure, but interval training required approximately 40% less training time commitment (a relative time saving; no absolute body-composition values are given in the abstract). Running training showed large effects on whole-body fat mass for both interval (standardized mean difference -0.82) and continuous training (-0.85), while cycling training did not induce fat loss.
cards.watchOut: Only 13 short studies (average 10 weeks); body-composition improvements occurred without accompanying body-weight changes, and the modality (running versus cycling) appeared to matter as much as intensity.

cards.headline: HIIT improved fitness and some risk factors in overweight/obese adults, but not insulin or lipids
cards.summary: In overweight and obese adults, short-term interval training improved VO2max (SMD 0.74), diastolic pressure (−0.52) and fasting glucose (−0.35); it did not significantly improve insulin or lipids in this analysis.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention studies
cards.people: 65 intervention studies in adults, analysed separately in overweight/obese and normal-weight populations; the abstract does not state total participant number, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In overweight/obese populations, short-term interval training (under 12 weeks) improved maximal oxygen uptake (standardised mean difference 0.74, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.12; p<0.001), diastolic blood pressure (-0.52, 95% CI -0.89 to -0.16; p<0.01) and fasting glucose (-0.35, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.09; p<0.01). Interval training demonstrated no effect on insulin, lipid profile, C reactive protein or interleukin 6 in overweight/obese populations.
cards.watchOut: Effects are standardised mean differences from mostly small intervention studies, not head-to-head event outcomes; several prespecified cardiometabolic markers (insulin, lipids, inflammatory markers) showed no effect.

cards.headline: For glucose regulation, HIIT beat control and continuous training on insulin resistance in a 50-study meta-analysis
cards.summary: Across 50 studies, interval training reduced insulin resistance versus control (SMD −0.49 ) and versus continuous training (−0.35), and lowered HbA1c by 0.19% versus control — the one outcome domain where HIIT edged ahead.
cards.people: 50 studies of adult participants, excluding dual interventions and type 1 diabetes; the abstract does not state total participant number, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Insulin resistance fell following interval training compared with both control (standardized mean difference -0.49, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.12, P=0.009) and continuous training (standardized mean difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.02, P=0.036). Compared with control, hemoglobin A1c decreased by 0.19% (95% CI, -0.36 to -0.03, P=0.021) and body weight decreased by 1.3 kg (95% CI, -1.9 to -0.7, P<0.001). Participants at risk of or with type 2 diabetes had reductions in fasting glucose of -0.92 mmol/L (≈-17 mg/dL) (95% CI, -1.22 to -0.62, P<0.001) versus control. There were no statistically significant differences between groups in other outcomes overall.
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves call for larger randomised trials of longer duration to confirm these results; the hemoglobin A1c difference (0.19%) is small and most included trials were short.

cards.headline: Synthesis: HIIT is a time-efficient equal of continuous training, not a proven superior
cards.summary: The pattern is equivalence with a small fitness edge and a large time saving: HIIT is a time-efficient equal of continuous training, not a proven superior — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: meta-analyses covering 28, 13, 65 and 50 studies respectively, in healthy, overweight/obese and diabetes-risk adults.
cards.result: The consistent pattern is equivalence with a small fitness edge: interval training improved maximal oxygen consumption by 1.2 mL/kg/min more than endurance training, matched continuous training on fat mass and waist circumference with approximately 40% less training time, and lowered insulin resistance versus continuous training (standardized mean difference -0.35). No included synthesis reports cardiovascular events or mortality. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: All outcomes are surrogates from short, small trials pooled in meta-analyses; larger and longer randomised trials are still needed, as the glucose-regulation meta-analysis itself states.

shelves.title: Cardiac rehab after MI: mortality evidence
shelves.question: Does exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction / coronary heart disease reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Disease · Exercise · Humans · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — Tier C (mortality claim; developer's personal ruling required). Pooled older trials show a relative reduction in cardiovascular mortality, but the largest single modern-era trial of rehabilitation as actually delivered (RAMIT) was null for mortality, and the 2021 Cochrane update's short-term estimates for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality both cross 1.0, with cardiovascular mortality benefit appearing only at medium/long-term follow-up in fewer trials. Hospital admission and quality-of-life benefits are separate claims; the mortality claim itself is POSSIBLE, not established, and all-cause mortality is not shown. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: Anderson/Cochrane 2016: cardiovascular mortality lower in pooled trials, total mortality not reduced
cards.summary: Anderson/Cochrane 2016 (63 trials, 14,486 patients): exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation lowered cardiovascular mortality, relative risk 0.74 [0.64–0.86], and hospital admissions (0.82) — both relative, with no absolute rates in the abstract; all-cause mortality and reinfarction did not significantly differ.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane, JACC version)
cards.people: 63 studies, 14,486 participants after MI, revascularisation, angina or angiographic CHD; median follow-up 12 months; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: Cardiovascular mortality: relative risk ratio 0.74 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.86) — a relative measure; the abstract reports no absolute cardiovascular mortality rates, so no absolute difference can be paired with it here. Hospital admissions: relative risk ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.96), also relative with no absolute rates in the abstract. There was no significant effect on total mortality, myocardial infarction, or revascularisation (no figures given for those in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: Pooled mostly small, older trials from an era before modern post-MI therapy; a pooled relative cardiovascular mortality benefit alongside a null total-mortality result is exactly the pattern that requires the RAMIT card beside it.
cards.source: Anderson L et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2016;67(1):1-12. PMID: 26764059. Registry: none in the PubMed record for this review.

cards.headline: RAMIT: comprehensive cardiac rehab as delivered in England and Wales did not reduce mortality
cards.summary: RAMIT (1,813 patients, England and Wales): comprehensive rehabilitation as delivered did not reduce all-cause mortality at 2 years (relative risk 0.98 [0.74–1.30]) or at 7–9 years (0.99), nor cardiac events or well-being — the strongest single counterweight to the pooled estimate.
cards.people: 1,813 patients referred after acute MI in representative hospitals in England and Wales (entry 1997-2000), randomised to comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation vs usual care without referral; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 2 years: relative risk ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.30); at 7-9 years 0.99 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.15) — relative measures; the abstract reports no absolute mortality rates to pair with them. No significant differences in cardiac events, seven of eight SF-36 quality-of-life domains, or psychological well-being; rehabilitation patients reported slightly less physical activity.
cards.watchOut: Tests rehabilitation as practised in the UK at that time, not an idealised high-dose programme; usual care has also changed since 2000. It remains the honest counterweight to pooled older-trial meta-analyses.
cards.source: West RR et al (RAMIT). Heart. 2012;98(8):637-644. PMID: 22194152. Registry: none in the PubMed record (trial entry 1997-2000, pre-registration era).

cards.watchOut: Overall trial reporting was poor and women remain heavily under-represented; the long-term cardiovascular mortality estimates rest on few trials (5 and 8) and sit beside null all-cause mortality at every time point.

shelves.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work and endocarditis: no-trial guideline
shelves.question: In people at risk of infective endocarditis, does antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures prevent endocarditis, serious illness or death compared with no prophylaxis — and what evidence, in the complete absence of randomized trials, supports current guideline recommendations?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Cohort Studies · Dentistry · Endocarditis · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Medicare · United States
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — No randomized trial of dental antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis has ever been done, in any era: the Cochrane review found no RCTs, controlled trials or cohort studies, only one small case-control study with no significant effect. Guidelines still recommend prophylaxis for the highest-risk patients, resting on observational data — a US study linking invasive dental work to subsequent endocarditis in high-risk people and linking prophylaxis to lower incidence, against an English time-series in which endocarditis rose after prophylaxis was stopped, which cannot prove causation. Tier C: developer ruling — a guideline-only topic resting on observational data for a serious-outcome prevention claim. Proposed grade: MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022: no RCT exists — one case-control study, no significant effect, very low certainty
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022: no randomised trials, controlled trials or cohort studies exist — in this update or any previous version. The single case-control study found no significant effect of penicillin prophylaxis, very low certainty. The evidence base for a worldwide practice is, at trial level, empty.
cards.people: The only included study was a case-control study of 48 people who had contracted bacterial endocarditis after a medical or dental procedure with an indication for prophylaxis, matched to controls who had not; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: No randomised controlled trials, controlled clinical trials or cohort studies were found for inclusion, in this update or any previous version. The single case-control study found no significant effect of penicillin prophylaxis on the incidence of endocarditis, and reported no data on mortality, serious illness, harms or costs. The reviewers rated the certainty of the evidence very low and concluded there is no clear evidence whether prophylaxis is effective or ineffective.
cards.watchOut: Absence of trial evidence is not evidence of absence of effect — endocarditis is rare, so a definitive trial would need to be very large; the review's harms-versus-benefit question could not be answered at all.
cards.source: Rutherford SJ et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022 May 10. PMID 35536541. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: AHA 2021: prophylaxis kept for the highest-risk only — and the statement itself calls for RCTs
cards.summary: AHA 2021: prophylaxis survives only for the four highest-risk categories (the 2007 scale-back, reaffirmed), and the statement itself calls for randomised trials — a guideline holding a line it acknowledges is unproven.
cards.people: No study participants — a guideline writing group statement for cardiac patients undergoing invasive dental procedures; age and sex not applicable.
cards.result: The 2007 AHA guidelines had already scaled prophylaxis back to only 4 categories of patients judged at highest risk of adverse outcome. Reviewing the interval evidence in 2021, the AHA found good general awareness but variable compliance, and no convincing evidence that viridans group streptococcal endocarditis frequency, morbidity or mortality had increased since 2007; it recommended no changes, emphasised oral health and dental access for all, and stated plainly that randomized controlled studies of whether prophylaxis works are needed.
cards.watchOut: This is a consensus guideline card, not evidence of efficacy — it documents what experts recommend and what they concede is unproven; it must not be cited as proof prophylaxis prevents endocarditis.
cards.source: Wilson WR et al. J Am Dent Assoc. 2021 Nov (AHA Scientific Statement). PMID 34711348. Registry ID: none — guideline statement, not a trial; no registry ID in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: England after NICE stopped prophylaxis: prescribing collapsed and endocarditis incidence rose above trend
cards.summary: England’s natural experiment (interrupted time series): after NICE ended routine prophylaxis in 2008, prescriptions fell from 10,900 to 2,236 a month , and endocarditis incidence then rose above the projected trend by 0.11 cases per 10 million people per month — ecological, and the shelf’s most-discussed signal.
cards.people: Whole-population English data: antibiotic prophylaxis prescriptions 2004–2013 and hospital episodes with a primary diagnosis of infective endocarditis 2000–2013; individual age and sex not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: After the March 2008 NICE guidance ending routine prophylaxis, prescriptions fell from a mean of 10,900 per month to 2,236 per month (p < 0.0001). From March 2008, endocarditis cases rose above the projected historical trend by 0.11 cases per 10 million people per month (95% CI 0.05 to 0.16; p < 0.0001) — an absolute rate — reaching 35 more cases per month by March 2013 than the previous trend predicted, in both high-risk and lower-risk individuals.
cards.watchOut: The authors state their data do not establish a causal association: this is an ecological time trend with no individual-level link between who lost prophylaxis and who developed endocarditis, and coding or ascertainment changes cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Dayer MJ et al. Lancet. 2015 Mar 28. PMID 25467569. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — observational study, not a registered trial.

cards.headline: US claims study: dental work preceded endocarditis in high-risk patients, and prophylaxis was linked to less of it
cards.summary: US claims (case-crossover/cohort): in high-risk patients, endocarditis was temporally associated with an invasive dental procedure in the prior 4 weeks (relative odds 2.00 ), most strongly extractions (11.08) and oral surgery (50.77) — relative odds, confounded by indication, and printed as relative.
cards.people: 7,951,972 US subjects with employer-provided Commercial or Medicare Supplemental coverage; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: In high-risk individuals, endocarditis was temporally associated with an invasive dental procedure in the preceding 4 weeks (relative odds OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.59 to 2.52), most strongly for extractions (relative OR 11.08, 95% CI 7.34 to 16.74) and oral surgery (relative OR 50.77, 95% CI 20.79 to 123.98). Antibiotic prophylaxis was associated with lower endocarditis incidence after invasive procedures (relative OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.85); the cohort analysis gave relative ORs of 0.13 (extractions) and 0.09 (oral surgery) with prophylaxis. No absolute event rates are reported in the abstract, so no absolute benefit can be stated.
cards.watchOut: Observational insurance-claims data: people given prophylaxis differ from those who are not (confounding by indication and by clinician judgement), and relative odds for a rare outcome cannot be turned into an absolute benefit or a number-needed-to-treat from this abstract.
cards.source: Thornhill MH et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2022 Sep 13. PMID 35987887. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — observational study, not a registered trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a guideline recommendation with no trial underneath it — say so plainly
cards.summary: Plainly: no trial underlies this practice. Guideline consensus plus observational signals pointing both ways — MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C, the developer rules.
cards.people: No new participants — synthesis of the four verified cards above.
cards.result: Stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence). Plainly: no RCT of antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work for endocarditis exists, and none was found in the 2024–2026 sweep. Current practice — prophylaxis for the highest-risk categories only — rests on guideline consensus plus observational signals that point the same way but cannot prove causation or size an absolute benefit.

shelves.title: Czechoslovakia’s shelf: the WHO clofibrate trial — fewer heart attacks, more deaths (Prague centre, 1978)
shelves.question: Does lowering cholesterol with clofibrate prevent ischaemic heart disease — and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol · Clinical Trials as Topic · Clofibrate · Coronary Disease · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Hypercholesterolemia · Male
shelves.balance: The balance must carry both halves, because the trial did: clofibrate lowered cholesterol ~9% and cut major ischaemic heart disease by 20% relative (5.9 vs 7.4 per 1,000/year), driven by non-fatal infarction — and raised all-cause mortality during treatment (162 vs 127 deaths; 4.9 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years), an excess that vanished when exposure stopped. POSSIBLE grades the pair of claims together: the event benefit is real and randomised; so is the mortality signal, unexplained then and now. The Prague centre (IKEM) enrolled roughly a third of the 15,745 men — Czechoslovakia is this shelf’s country of evidence, flying its own flag by the developer’s ruling. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: WHO co-operative clofibrate trial (1978, British Heart Journal): heart attacks down a fifth — deaths up. The Prague centre was one of three, run from IKEM in what was then Czechoslovakia
cards.summary: 15,745 men aged 30–59 with high cholesterol, in three centres — Edinburgh, Budapest, and Prague (then Czechoslovakia; the Prague centre ran from IKEM, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine) — randomised double-blind to clofibrate 1.6 g/day or placebo (two control groups: high-cholesterol and low-cholesterol), treated a mean of 5.3 years. Cholesterol fell about 9% . Major ischaemic heart disease incidence: 20% lower on clofibrate, relative (5.9 vs 7.4 per 1,000/year, P<0.05) , driven by non-fatal myocardial infarction ( 25% lower, relative ); fatal infarction was unchanged. All-cause mortality was higher on clofibrate during treatment: 162 vs 127 deaths (4.9 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years) . (The 1978 PubMed record carries no abstract; these figures are from the report itself, PMC-verified.)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled primary-prevention trial, British Heart Journal 1978. Pre-registration-era trial (begun 1965): the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 15,745 men aged 30–59 years with elevated cholesterol and no prior ischaemic heart disease, enrolled at three European centres: Edinburgh (Scotland), Budapest (Hungary), and Prague (Czechoslovakia, centre based at IKEM). Roughly a third of the trial’s participants were enrolled in Prague.
cards.result: Clofibrate lowered mean serum cholesterol by about 9%. The incidence of major ischaemic heart disease was 20% lower in the clofibrate group than in the high-cholesterol control group (5.9 vs 7.4 per 1,000 men per year; P<0.05), an effect concentrated in non-fatal myocardial infarction, reduced by about 25% (relative); fatal myocardial infarction did not fall (36 vs 34 events). Against that benefit, all-cause mortality during the treatment period was significantly higher in the clofibrate group (162 vs 127 deaths; 4.9 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years). The excess deaths were spread across causes rather than concentrated in one diagnosis, and the investigators could not explain them.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions belong on the face of this card. First, the mortality excess was never explained and could still be chance multiplied across many causes of death — the trial was not powered for all-cause mortality as a primary question. Second, the country attribution: Prague was a full centre enrolling roughly a third of the men, not a token site — Czechoslovakia is carded as a country of evidence on that basis, under the developer’s ruling that the defunct country flies its own flag (modern Czechia is separately covered elsewhere in the library).

cards.headline: Final follow-up (1984, The Lancet): when the drug stopped, the extra deaths stopped — the excess was confined to the treatment period
cards.summary: The trial’s extended mortality follow-up (Lancet 1984) asked the obvious question: did the men randomised to clofibrate keep dying faster after the trial ended? They did not. The excess all-cause mortality observed during the treatment period did not persist during the post-treatment follow-up years — mortality in the two groups converged once exposure ceased. A harm that arrives with a drug and leaves with it is a different evidentiary object from a chance imbalance: the pattern strengthened the case that the excess was drug-related, without ever identifying a mechanism. Clofibrate’s later history closed the story: gallstones and other toxicities accumulated in its record, the drug was withdrawn in many markets (2002 in the US), and its chemical descendants — the modern fibrates — inherited its event benefit only in narrower forms.
cards.type: Extended follow-up report of the WHO co-operative trial, The Lancet 1984 (Lancet. 1984;2(8407):600–604). No registry ID — pre-registration era.
cards.people: The surviving participants of the 1978 trial cohort (Reference 1): 15,745 men randomised at Edinburgh, Budapest, and Prague, followed beyond the end of the treatment period.
cards.result: During the treatment period, all-cause mortality had been higher in the clofibrate group (162 vs 127 deaths). In the post-treatment follow-up reported in 1984, that excess did not continue: the mortality difference was confined to the years of exposure. The committee’s reports never assigned the excess to a single cause; the spread across causes, and its disappearance off-treatment, are the two facts the record supports.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up after a trial ends is observational in everything but the original randomisation: men who survived treatment are a selected group in both arms, and post-trial care was uncontrolled. The confinement of the excess to the exposure window is suggestive, not proof — but it is exactly the pattern a real drug harm produces, and exactly the pattern this library asks for before treating a mortality signal as more than noise.

cards.headline: Reading the clofibrate trial whole: the first modern lesson that a risk factor improved is not a patient helped
cards.summary: The two halves, side by side: a 9% cholesterol reduction; major ischaemic events 20% lower, relative (1.5 fewer events per 1,000 men per year) — and 1.1 more deaths per 1,000 men per year from all causes while taking the drug. Both halves were true at once, in the same randomised men. The trial became the founding cautionary tale of lipid medicine: a surrogate can move, events can even fall, and the patient can still be worse off — which is why this library grades mortality beside every benefit claim, and why the developer chose this shelf for the country that no longer exists: it is the balance-line discipline’s own origin story.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states the shelf’s fence.
cards.people: The population of Cards 1 and 2: 15,745 middle-aged European men with high cholesterol and no prior heart disease, randomised 1965 onward at Edinburgh, Budapest, and Prague (Czechoslovakia).
cards.result: The trial establishes that clofibrate lowered cholesterol and non-fatal infarction, and that it raised all-cause mortality during exposure by an amount exceeding its event benefit (162 vs 127 deaths against roughly 1.5 major events prevented per 1,000 per year). It does not establish the mechanism of the harm, and it does not convict the modern fibrate class as a whole — later fibrates are different molecules with their own trials, carded elsewhere in this library on their own evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not let either half of this trial be quoted alone: ‘cholesterol lowering worked in 1978’ omits the graves; ‘the cholesterol hypothesis killed people’ omits the prevented infarctions and misreads a drug toxicity as a refutation of lipid lowering — statins’ later trials settled that question on their own data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 361054; Lancet 1984 final follow-up).

shelves.title: The fibrates after clofibrate: lipids improved, outcomes mostly didn’t
shelves.question: Do fibrates reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Bezafibrate · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Disease · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Fenofibrate · Gemfibrozil · Humans · Hypertriglyceridemia · Hypolipidemic Agents · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: Every fibrate trial moved the lipids it aimed at; the events followed only twice. Gemfibrozil, in the pre-statin era, cut coronary events by 34% relative in primary prevention (Helsinki, 4,081 men) and by 22% relative in secondary prevention (VA-HIT, 2,531 men) — with total mortality unchanged in both. Then the class’s modern record is a run of well-run nulls: bezafibrate’s primary endpoint missed, its benefit confined to a post hoc high-triglyceride subgroup (BIP); fenofibrate’s primary missed in 9,795 people with diabetes (FIELD, HR 0.89 [0.75–1.05]) and again when added to a statin (ACCORD-Lipid, HR 0.92 [0.79–1.08]); and pemafibrate — the most potent agent, tested in exactly the high-triglyceride, low-HDL phenotype the subgroups had pointed to — lowered triglycerides 26% and produced a hazard ratio of 1.03 (PROMINENT). Ciprofibrate has no outcome trial at all: unknown, not disproven. Split stamp: POSSIBLE for gemfibrozil’s pre-statin event benefit; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the statin-era fibrates. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Helsinki Heart Study (Frick 1987, NEJM): gemfibrozil cut coronary events by 34% (relative) in primary prevention — total deaths unchanged
cards.summary: 4,081 asymptomatic men aged 40–55 with dyslipidemia (non-HDL cholesterol ≥200 mg/dL), randomised double-blind to gemfibrozil 600 mg twice daily or placebo for five years. Cumulative cardiac end points at five years: 27.3 per 1,000 on gemfibrozil vs 41.4 per 1,000 on placebo — a 34.0% relative reduction [95% CI 8.2–52.6], P<0.02 (about 14 events per 1,000 over five years, absolute). Gemfibrozil raised HDL cholesterol and lowered total, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. There was no difference in the total death rate, and no difference in cancer rates.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled primary-prevention trial, N Engl J Med 1987. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 4,081 asymptomatic middle-aged men (aged 40–55 years) with primary dyslipidemia (non-HDL cholesterol ≥200 mg/dL on two pretreatment measurements), Finland — 2,051 assigned gemfibrozil, 2,030 placebo. All participants were men; the record does not print a mean age.
cards.result: The cumulative rate of cardiac end points at five years was 27.3 per 1,000 in the gemfibrozil group and 41.4 per 1,000 in the placebo group — a reduction of 34.0 percent in the incidence of coronary heart disease (95 percent confidence interval, 8.2 to 52.6; P less than 0.02). The decline became evident in the second year and continued throughout the study. There was no difference between the groups in the total death rate, nor did the treatment influence the cancer rates.
cards.watchOut: A pre-statin-era trial in men only, and its benefit is an event benefit, not a survival benefit: coronary events fell by a third while total mortality did not move. That pattern — events down, deaths flat — is the fibrate class’s signature, and it recurs on every card of this shelf. It also predates background statin therapy entirely; what gemfibrozil adds on top of a statin is a different question, answered (for fenofibrate) on Card 5.
cards.source: Frick MH et al. Helsinki Heart Study: primary-prevention trial with gemfibrozil in middle-aged men with dyslipidemia. N Engl J Med. 1987;317(20):1237–1245. PMID 3313041. DOI 10.1056/NEJM198711123172001

cards.headline: VA-HIT (Rubins 1999, NEJM): gemfibrozil in men with coronary disease and low HDL — events down 22% (relative), deaths from all causes unchanged
cards.summary: 2,531 men with coronary heart disease, HDL cholesterol ≤40 mg/dL and LDL ≤140 mg/dL, randomised double-blind to gemfibrozil 1,200 mg/day or placebo; median follow-up 5.1 years. Primary outcome (nonfatal myocardial infarction or coronary death): 219 of 1,264 (17.3%) on gemfibrozil vs 275 of 1,267 (21.7%) on placebo — a 22% relative reduction [95% CI 7–35], P=0.006 , 4.4 percentage points absolute. The combined outcome including stroke fell 24% relative (P<0.001). At one year HDL was 6% higher and triglycerides 31% lower on gemfibrozil; LDL cholesterol did not differ . No significant difference in death from any cause, or in cancer.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled secondary-prevention trial (Veterans Affairs HDL Intervention Trial), N Engl J Med 1999. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 2,531 men with coronary heart disease whose primary lipid abnormality was a low HDL cholesterol level (HDL ≤40 mg/dL; LDL ≤140 mg/dL), at US Veterans Affairs medical centres. All participants were men; the record’s abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: A primary event occurred in 275 of the 1,267 patients assigned to placebo (21.7 percent) and in 219 of the 1,264 patients assigned to gemfibrozil (17.3 percent). The overall reduction in the risk of an event was 4.4 percentage points, and the reduction in relative risk was 22 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 7 to 35 percent; P=0.006). There was a 24 percent reduction in the combined outcome of death from coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke (P<0.001). There were no significant differences in the rates of coronary revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina, death from any cause, and cancer.
cards.watchOut: The class’s strongest card — and still fenced. The population is men in a veterans’ system with a specific phenotype (established coronary disease, low HDL, LDL already ≤140), and the benefit arrived without any LDL lowering, which is the best evidence the fibrate mechanism — triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and HDL — can matter. But all-cause mortality again did not differ, and the trial says nothing about women or about patients already on a statin.
cards.source: Rubins HB et al.; Veterans Affairs High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Intervention Trial Study Group. Gemfibrozil for the secondary prevention of coronary heart disease in men with low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. N Engl J Med. 1999;341(6):410–418. PMID 10438259. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199908053410604

cards.headline: BIP (Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention, 2000, Circulation): the primary endpoint missed — the benefit lived in a post hoc triglyceride subgroup
cards.summary: 3,090 patients with a previous myocardial infarction or stable angina, randomised double-blind to bezafibrate 400 mg/day or placebo, followed a mean of 6.2 years. Bezafibrate raised HDL cholesterol by 18% and reduced triglycerides by 21%. The primary end point (fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction or sudden death) occurred in 13.6% on bezafibrate vs 15.0% on placebo (P=0.26) — not significant; the reduction in cumulative probability was 7.3% (P=0.24). In a post hoc subgroup with baseline triglycerides ≥200 mg/dL, the reduction in the cumulative probability of the primary end point was 39.5% (P=0.02) . Total and noncardiac mortality were similar; adverse events and cancer were equally distributed.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled secondary-prevention trial, Circulation 2000. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 3,090 patients with a previous myocardial infarction or stable angina, total cholesterol 180–250 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol ≤45 mg/dL, triglycerides ≤300 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol ≤180 mg/dL, Israel. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or a sex breakdown.
cards.result: The frequency of the primary end point was 13.6% on bezafibrate versus 15.0% on placebo (P=0.26). After 6.2 years, the reduction in the cumulative probability of the primary end point was 7.3% (P=0.24). In a post hoc analysis in the subgroup with high baseline triglycerides (≥200 mg/dL), the reduction in the cumulative probability of the primary end point by bezafibrate was 39.5% (P=0.02). The authors concluded that the reduction in the primary end point in patients with high baseline triglycerides requires further confirmation.
cards.watchOut: This card is the hinge of the whole shelf. The trial’s headline is a null; its legacy is a post hoc subgroup — exactly the kind of finding this library treats as a hypothesis, not a result. The hypothesis was respectable (it matches the class’s mechanism and VA-HIT’s phenotype), and the field spent the next two decades testing it properly: FIELD and ACCORD-Lipid enrolled broader diabetic populations, and PROMINENT (Reference 6) enrolled precisely the high-triglyceride, low-HDL phenotype. The subgroup’s fate is on those cards.

cards.headline: FIELD (Keech 2005, The Lancet): fenofibrate in 9,795 people with diabetes — the primary coronary outcome missed (HR 0.89, P=0.16)
cards.summary: 9,795 people aged 50–75 with type 2 diabetes , not on a statin at entry, randomised to micronised fenofibrate 200 mg daily or placebo for five years. Primary outcome (coronary death or non-fatal myocardial infarction): 5.2% on fenofibrate vs 5.9% on placebo — HR 0.89 [0.75–1.05], P=0.16 , not significant. Inside the composite the two halves pulled apart: non-fatal myocardial infarction fell (HR 0.76 [0.62–0.94], P=0.010) while coronary heart disease mortality leaned the other way (HR 1.19 [0.90–1.57], P=0.22). Total cardiovascular events were lower (12.5% vs 13.9%; HR 0.89 [0.80–0.99], P=0.035), driven by non-fatal infarction and revascularisation. Total mortality: 7.3% vs 6.6% (P=0.18). Harms: pancreatitis 0.8% vs 0.5% (P=0.031) and pulmonary embolism 1.1% vs 0.7% (P=0.022); microvascular benefits included less laser treatment for retinopathy (3.6% vs 5.2%, P=0.0003).
cards.type: Multinational randomised controlled trial, Lancet 2005. Registry ID from the record’s own text: ISRCTN64783481.
cards.people: 9,795 participants aged 50–75 years with type 2 diabetes mellitus, not taking statin therapy at study entry (2,131 with previous cardiovascular disease, 7,664 without), in Australia, New Zealand, and Finland. The record’s abstract does not print a sex breakdown.
cards.result: 5.9% (n=288) of patients on placebo and 5.2% (n=256) of those on fenofibrate had a coronary event (relative reduction of 11%; hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.75–1.05; p=0.16). This finding corresponds to a significant 24% reduction in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.76, 0.62–0.94; p=0.010) and a non-significant increase in coronary heart disease mortality (1.19, 0.90–1.57; p=0.22). Total cardiovascular disease events were significantly reduced from 13.9% to 12.5% (0.89, 0.80–0.99; p=0.035). Total mortality was 6.6% in the placebo group and 7.3% in the fenofibrate group (p=0.18). Fenofibrate was associated with less albuminuria progression and less retinopathy needing laser treatment, and with a slight increase in pancreatitis and pulmonary embolism.
cards.watchOut: One asymmetry belongs on the face of this card: during the trial, more placebo patients than fenofibrate patients started other lipid therapy, predominantly statins (17% vs 8%) — a drop-in imbalance that biases the comparison against fenofibrate, and the authors say it might have masked a moderately larger benefit. That caveat is real, and it still does not rescue the primary endpoint: the trial as run, in the population as enrolled, missed — and its coronary mortality component leaned toward harm. FIELD is a null with an asterisk, not a positive in disguise.

PMID 16310551 · ISRCTN64783481. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(05)67667-2

cards.headline: ACCORD-Lipid (2010, NEJM): fenofibrate added to a statin in diabetes — no benefit overall (HR 0.92, P=0.32)
cards.summary: 5,518 patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, all on open-label simvastatin, randomised double-blind to fenofibrate or placebo; mean follow-up 4.7 years. Primary outcome (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death): annual rate 2.2% on fenofibrate vs 2.4% on placebo — HR 0.92 [0.79–1.08], P=0.32 . Annual death rates 1.5% vs 1.6% (HR 0.91 [0.75–1.10], P=0.33). No secondary outcome differed significantly. Two prespecified subgroup interactions were flagged: by sex (benefit for men, possible harm for women; P=0.01 for interaction) and by lipid subgroup (possible benefit in patients with both high triglycerides and low HDL; P=0.057 for interaction).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the lipid arm of the ACCORD programme), N Engl J Med 2010. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT00000620.
cards.people: 5,518 patients with type 2 diabetes who were at high risk for cardiovascular disease, treated with open-label simvastatin, in the United States and Canada. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or a sex breakdown — though its subgroup analysis by sex is carded in the Result.
cards.result: The annual rate of the primary outcome was 2.2% in the fenofibrate group and 2.4% in the placebo group (hazard ratio in the fenofibrate group, 0.92; 95% confidence interval, 0.79 to 1.08; P=0.32). There were also no significant differences between the two study groups with respect to any secondary outcome. Prespecified subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity in treatment effect according to sex, with a benefit for men and possible harm for women (P=0.01 for interaction), and a possible interaction according to lipid subgroup, with a possible benefit for patients with both a high baseline triglyceride level and a low baseline level of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P=0.057 for interaction). The authors concluded that the results do not support the routine use of combination therapy with fenofibrate and simvastatin to reduce cardiovascular risk in the majority of high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes.
cards.watchOut: This is the exact question the modern clinic asks — a fibrate on top of a statin — and the answer is no for the average patient. The two interactions are printed because they are prespecified, and fenced because they are interactions: the lipid-subgroup signal (P=0.057) did not meet significance and was later tested head-on by PROMINENT (Reference 6); the sex interaction (P=0.01), with possible harm in women, is a standing caution against assuming the class is uniformly benign, not a proven sex-specific effect. Note the registry number is the ACCORD programme’s umbrella number; the lipid, blood-pressure and glycaemia randomisations are separate trials with separate reports, each carded at its own home.

cards.headline: PROMINENT (Das Pradhan 2022, NEJM): pemafibrate lowered triglycerides by 26% in the exact target phenotype — events identical (HR 1.03)
cards.summary: 10,497 patients with type 2 diabetes , triglycerides 200–499 mg/dL and HDL ≤40 mg/dL, on guideline-directed lipid therapy; 66.9% with previous cardiovascular disease. Randomised double-blind to pemafibrate 0.2 mg twice daily or placebo; median follow-up 3.4 years. At four months pemafibrate had lowered triglycerides by 26.2% , VLDL cholesterol by 25.8%, remnant cholesterol by 25.6% and apolipoprotein C-III by 27.6% relative to placebo. Primary end point (nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, coronary revascularisation, or cardiovascular death): 572 events on pemafibrate vs 560 on placebo — HR 1.03 [0.91–1.15] , with no effect modification in any prespecified subgroup. Pemafibrate was associated with more adverse renal events and venous thromboembolism, and less nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
cards.type: Multinational, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2022. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT03071692.
cards.people: 10,497 patients with type 2 diabetes, mild-to-moderate hypertriglyceridemia (triglycerides 200–499 mg/dL) and HDL cholesterol ≤40 mg/dL, with LDL cholesterol ≤100 mg/dL on guideline-directed therapy or statin intolerance — the high-triglyceride, low-HDL phenotype the BIP subgroup had pointed to. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or a sex breakdown.
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 572 patients in the pemafibrate group and in 560 of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.03; 95% confidence interval, 0.91 to 1.15), with no apparent effect modification in any prespecified subgroup. The overall incidence of serious adverse events did not differ significantly between the groups, but pemafibrate was associated with a higher incidence of adverse renal events and venous thromboembolism and a lower incidence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. The authors concluded that the incidence of cardiovascular events was not lower among those who received pemafibrate than among those who received placebo, although pemafibrate lowered triglyceride, VLDL cholesterol, remnant cholesterol, and apolipoprotein C-III levels.
cards.watchOut: This is the cleanest test the hypothesis ever got: a potent, selective agent, the precise phenotype (high triglycerides, low HDL, diabetes, statin-treated), 10,497 patients — and a point estimate of 1.03, on the harm side of 1.0, excluding any benefit larger than about 9% relative. After PROMINENT, ‘the right subgroup just hasn’t been tried’ stops being an available defence for triglyceride lowering as such: the subgroup was tried, at scale, and the events did not follow the lipids.

cards.headline: Reading the fibrate trials together: two pre-statin wins for one drug, then thirty years of well-run nulls
cards.summary: The arc, honestly: gemfibrozil, twice, before statins existed — coronary events down 34% relative in primary prevention (Helsinki) and 22% relative in secondary prevention (VA-HIT), with total mortality unmoved both times. Then the class’s modern record: bezafibrate’s primary missed (BIP), fenofibrate’s primary missed alone (FIELD) and added to a statin (ACCORD-Lipid), and pemafibrate — the most potent triglyceride-lowering fibrate, in the exact phenotype — dead level (PROMINENT, HR 1.03). Every trial moved the lipids it aimed at. The events followed only in the two pre-statin gemfibrozil trials. One class member stands outside the arc entirely: ciprofibrate, in wide use in Europe and Latin America, has no large hard-outcome randomised trial at all — its outcome effects are unknown, which is a different thing from disproven, and a different thing from shown.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1–6 together and states the shelf’s split grade and its fence.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1–6: Finnish and US men with dyslipidemia or coronary disease (gemfibrozil, 1987–1999); Israeli coronary patients (bezafibrate); and three large diabetic populations across four continents (fenofibrate and pemafibrate, 2005–2022).
cards.result: What the record establishes: (1) fibrates reliably improve triglycerides and HDL cholesterol; (2) gemfibrozil reduced coronary events in two double-blind trials conducted before statin background therapy, without reducing total mortality; (3) in the statin era, no fibrate trial has shown a cardiovascular event benefit — not fenofibrate alone or added to simvastatin in diabetes, and not pemafibrate in the enriched high-triglyceride phenotype; (4) the recurring high-triglyceride/low-HDL subgroup signal (BIP post hoc; ACCORD-Lipid interaction) was tested prospectively by PROMINENT and not confirmed. What it does not establish: any fibrate benefit on top of modern therapy, any mortality benefit for any fibrate, and anything at all about ciprofibrate’s outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Quote the split, not a blend: ‘fibrates don’t work’ erases two genuine randomised wins and the low-HDL phenotype they were won in; ‘fibrates prevent heart attacks’ imports 1987 into a statin-era clinic where three large trials say otherwise. The shelf’s neighbour states the class’s opening warning: Shelf #525 (the WHO clofibrate trial) is where a fibrate first cut events and raised mortality in the same men — the modern drugs are safer than clofibrate, and this shelf is the record of what they bought.

shelves.title: Dietary nitrate (beetroot) for blood pressure
shelves.question: Does dietary inorganic nitrate lower blood pressure in hypertensive patients?
shelves.mesh: Beta vulgaris · Beverages · Biotransformation · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Combined Modality Therapy · Dietary Supplements
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: one phase-2 randomised trial in the target population (Kapil 2015, 68 hypertensive patients) found sustained 4-week reductions with daily beetroot juice versus nitrate-free juice on all three measurement methods — clinic -7.7/-2.4 mm Hg, 24-hour ambulatory -7.7/-5.2 mm Hg and home -8.1/-3.8 mm Hg — and meta-analyses of many very small, short cross-over trials find systolic falls of about -4 mm Hg. The ceiling is POSSIBLE: Kapil is a single small phase-2 trial, the pooled trials enrolled 7-65 participants each for days to weeks, and the medium-term meta-analysis found the effect significant in clinic measurements but not on 24-hour ambulatory or home monitoring. No trial measures cardiovascular events.

cards.headline: Kapil 2015: four weeks of dietary nitrate lowered clinic, ambulatory and home blood pressure in hypertension
cards.summary: Kapil 2015: four weeks of dietary nitrate lowered pressure on every measure — clinic −7.7/2.4 , ambulatory −7.7/5.2 , home −8.1/3.8 mm Hg .
cards.people: 68 patients with hypertension aged 18 to 85 years (34 drug-naive and 34 treated), randomised to dietary nitrate or placebo as 250 mL beetroot juice daily for 4 weeks, after a 2-week run-in and followed by a 2-week washout; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean reduction in clinic blood pressure was 7.7/2.4 mm Hg (95% CI 3.6-11.8 / 0.0-4.9; P<0.001 and P=0.050), 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure fell by 7.7/5.2 mm Hg (4.1-11.2 / 2.7-7.7; P<0.001 for both) and home blood pressure by 8.1/3.8 mm Hg (3.8-12.4 / 0.7-6.9; P<0.001 and P<0.01), with no evidence of tachyphylaxis over the 4 weeks. Endothelial function improved by about 20% (P<0.001) and arterial stiffness fell by 0.59 m/s (0.24-0.93; P<0.01), with no change on placebo; the intervention was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A single phase-2 trial of 68 patients over 4 weeks — the authors present it as the first evidence of durable lowering in this population, and it has not been followed by a larger confirmatory trial in the records carded here. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Kapil V et al. Dietary nitrate provides sustained blood pressure lowering in hypertensive patients: a randomized, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Hypertension. 2015;65(2):320-7. PMID: 25421976. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01405898, from the record's databank.

cards.headline: Siervo 2013: across 16 tiny cross-over trials, systolic pressure fell 4.4 mm Hg; diastolic did not reach significance
cards.summary: Siervo 2013 (16 tiny cross-over trials): systolic −4.4 mm Hg ; diastolic −1.1, not significant (P=0.06).
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 16 cross-over trials totalling 254 participants, with 7-30 participants per study and interventions lasting from 2 hours to 15 days, conducted 2006-2012; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix, and the trials were largely in healthy adults rather than hypertensive patients.
cards.result: Inorganic nitrate and beetroot juice consumption were associated with a greater change in systolic blood pressure (-4.4 mm Hg; 95% CI -5.9 to -2.8; P<0.001) than in diastolic blood pressure (-1.1 mm Hg; -2.2 to 0.1; P=0.06), and meta-regression showed an association between daily nitrate dose and systolic change (P<0.05). The authors state the findings need testing in long-term trials and in individuals at greater cardiovascular risk.
cards.watchOut: Acute and very short studies in mostly healthy volunteers — this card supports a real short-term physiological effect, not sustained treatment of hypertension. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Ashor 2017: medium-term, the effect was significant for clinic pressure only — not ambulatory or home.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 13 trials totalling 325 participants, with 7 to 65 participants per study and durations of 1 to 6 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.

shelves.title: Anticoagulation for device-detected subclinical atrial fibrillation: one positive trial, one stopped trial
shelves.question: In patients whose devices detect brief subclinical AF, does anticoagulation prevent stroke enough to justify the bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/complications/diagnosis · Embolism/drug therapy/etiology · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Stroke/etiology/prevention & control · Electrodes, Implanted
shelves.balance: Proposed stamp — SPLIT, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): ARTESiA POSSIBLE / NOAH-AFNET 6 MAYBE (weak evidence). The two trials point in different directions. Apixaban versus aspirin (ARTESiA) lowered stroke or systemic embolism from 1.24% to 0.78% per patient-year (hazard ratio 0.63) while raising major bleeding from 0.94% to 1.71% per patient-year (hazard ratio 1.80). Edoxaban versus placebo (NOAH-AFNET 6) did not significantly reduce its composite of cardiovascular death, stroke or systemic embolism (3.2% vs 4.0% per patient-year; hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08) and increased the composite of death or major bleeding (hazard ratio 1.31); that trial was stopped early. Both hazard ratios for benefit sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on their own, so the absolute rates printed on the cards carry the argument. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: NOAH-AFNET 6: edoxaban did not significantly cut cardiovascular death, stroke or embolism — and the safety composite rose
cards.summary: NOAH-AFNET 6: efficacy composite 3.2% vs 4.0% per patient-year on edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.81 [0.60 to 1.08]) — not significant , in a trial stopped early; the safety composite rose.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (double-blind, double-dummy, event-driven; stopped early)
cards.people: 2,536 patients aged 65 years or older with device-detected atrial high-rate episodes lasting at least 6 minutes plus at least one additional stroke risk factor; mean age 78 years, 37.4% women; median AHRE duration 2.8 hours.
cards.result: Primary efficacy outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke or systemic embolism): 83 patients (3.2% per patient-year) on edoxaban vs 101 (4.0% per patient-year) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.08; P=0.15), not significant. Stroke incidence was approximately 1% per patient-year in both groups. Safety outcome (death from any cause or major bleeding): 149 patients (5.9% per patient-year) on edoxaban vs 114 (4.5% per patient-year) on placebo — hazard ratio 1.31 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.67; P=0.03). ECG-diagnosed atrial fibrillation developed in 18.2% of patients during the trial.
cards.watchOut: The trial was terminated early at a median follow-up of 21 months for safety concerns and an informal futility assessment, although planned enrollment was complete; the benefit hazard ratio of 0.81 lies inside the 0.5–2.0 band and its interval crosses 1.0, so it is not solid evidence of benefit in either direction.

cards.headline: ARTESiA: apixaban lowered stroke or systemic embolism versus aspirin — 0.78% vs 1.24% per year — and raised major bleeding
cards.summary: ARTESiA: stroke or systemic embolism 0.78% vs 1.24% per year on apixaban (hazard ratio 0.63 ) — bought with major bleeding 1.71% vs 0.94% (hazard ratio 1.80 ).
cards.people: 4,012 patients with device-detected subclinical atrial fibrillation lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours; mean age 76.8 years (SD 7.6), 36.1% women; mean CHA2DS2-VASc score 3.9 (SD 1.1). Mean follow-up 3.5 years (SD 1.8).

cards.summary: Two large trials, two different answers: benefit ratios inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so the absolute rates carry the argument — Tier C split, proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 2,536 patients in NOAH-AFNET 6 (edoxaban vs placebo) and 4,012 in ARTESiA (apixaban vs aspirin), all with device-detected brief atrial episodes and no clinical AF at entry.
cards.result: ARTESiA shows a statistically significant relative reduction in stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio 0.63) bought with a near-doubling of major bleeding (hazard ratio 1.80); NOAH-AFNET 6, stopped early, shows no significant efficacy benefit (hazard ratio 0.81, CI crossing 1.0) and a significant increase in death or major bleeding (hazard ratio 1.31).
