shelves.title: Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for secondary mitral regurgitation: COAPT vs MITRA-FR, the discordant pair
shelves.question: Does TEER (MitraClip) on top of medical therapy improve outcomes in heart failure with secondary mitral regurgitation?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Heart Failure/etiology/mortality/surgery · Heart Valve Prosthesis/adverse effects · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/adverse effects · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). The discordance is the finding and is not averaged away. In COAPT-selected patients, TEER plus medical therapy cut heart-failure hospitalisation (35.8% vs 67.9% per patient-year at 2 years) and all-cause mortality beside it (29.1% vs 46.1% at 2 years; 57.3% vs 67.2% at 5 years). In MITRA-FR, the same device strategy changed nothing at 1 year: death or unplanned heart-failure hospitalisation 54.6% vs 51.3%, with all-cause mortality 24.3% vs 22.4%. RESHAPE-HF2 (2024), in a broader moderate-to-severe population, again lowered hospitalisation-based composites but its abstract reports no all-cause mortality figure. Benefit appears real in COAPT-like anatomy and unproven as a class claim. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: COAPT: TEER halved heart-failure hospitalisation and lowered all-cause mortality at 2 years — benefit sustained at 5 years
cards.summary: COAPT: HF hospitalisation 35.8% vs 67.9% per patient-year (hazard ratio 0.53 ), with all-cause mortality beside it — 29.1% vs 46.1% at 2 years; at 5 years mortality 57.3% vs 67.2% .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (COAPT; primary report with its 5-year follow-up folded in — one study, counts once)
cards.people: 614 patients with heart failure and moderate-to-severe or severe secondary mitral regurgitation who remained symptomatic despite maximal guideline-directed medical therapy, at 78 US and Canadian sites (302 device, 312 control). The abstracts do not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 24 months: annualised rate of all hospitalisations for heart failure 35.8% per patient-year in the device group vs 67.9% in the control group (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.70; P<0.001) — printed with all-cause mortality beside it, as required: death from any cause within 24 months occurred in 29.1% of the device group vs 46.1% of the control group (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.82; P<0.001). Freedom from device-related complications at 12 months was 96.6%. At 5 years (same trial): annualised heart-failure hospitalisation 33.1% vs 57.2% per year (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.68), all-cause mortality 57.3% vs 67.2% (hazard ratio 0.72; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.89), death or heart-failure hospitalisation 73.6% vs 91.5% (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.64).
cards.watchOut: COAPT enrolled a selected phenotype — severe regurgitation (larger effective regurgitant orifice) with less dilated ventricles than MITRA-FR — and required maximally tolerated medical therapy before randomisation; its result does not automatically extend to all secondary mitral regurgitation. Five-year device-specific safety events occurred in 4 of 293 treated patients (1.4%), all within 30 days.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COAPT (614 patients, severe regurgitation on maximal therapy), MITRA-FR (304 patients, lower severity threshold, more dilated ventricles) and RESHAPE-HF2 (505 patients, moderate-to-severe).

shelves.title: Left main coronary disease: PCI vs bypass surgery — EXCEL vs NOBLE, discordant composites, convergent mortality
shelves.question: For left main disease, is PCI with modern stents an acceptable alternative to CABG?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Bypass/adverse effects · Coronary Artery Disease/mortality/surgery/therapy · Drug-Eluting Stents · Everolimus/administration & dosage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary
shelves.balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). EXCEL and NOBLE are carded two-handed and not averaged away. EXCEL met noninferiority at 3 years for death, stroke or MI (15.4% PCI vs 14.7% CABG), but at 5 years all-cause death was higher with PCI (13.0% vs 9.9%) even though the composite did not differ significantly (22.0% vs 19.2%). NOBLE's wider composite (MACCE, including repeat revascularisation and non-procedural MI) favoured CABG at 5 years (29% vs 19%; hazard ratio 1.48) while all-cause mortality did not differ (12% vs 9%; hazard ratio 1.07) — and at 10 years mortality was 23% with PCI vs 25% with CABG (hazard ratio 0.93). Repeat revascularisation is consistently more frequent after PCI in both trials. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: EXCEL: PCI noninferior at 3 years for death, stroke or MI — but at 5 years all-cause death was 13.0% with PCI vs 9.9% with CABG
cards.summary: EXCEL: primary outcome at 3 years 15.4% vs 14.7% (noninferior) — but at 5 years all-cause death was 13.0% (PCI) vs 9.9% (CABG) .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (EXCEL; primary 3-year report with its 5-year report folded in — one study, counts once)
cards.people: 1,905 patients with left main coronary artery disease of low or intermediate anatomical complexity (site-assessed SYNTAX score 32 or lower): 948 PCI with everolimus-eluting stents, 957 CABG. The abstracts do not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 3 years, the primary end point (death from any cause, stroke or myocardial infarction) occurred in 15.4% of the PCI group vs 14.7% of the CABG group (difference 0.7 percentage points; upper 97.5% confidence limit 4.0 points; P=0.02 for noninferiority; hazard ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.26). Death, stroke, MI or ischaemia-driven revascularisation at 3 years: 23.1% vs 19.1%. At 5 years (same trial): primary outcome 22.0% PCI vs 19.2% CABG (difference 2.8 percentage points; 95% CI -0.9 to 6.5; P=0.13), with death from any cause in 13.0% vs 9.9% (difference 3.1 percentage points; 95% CI 0.2 to 6.1); definite cardiovascular death 5.0% vs 4.5% and MI 10.6% vs 9.1% did not differ significantly; ischaemia-driven revascularisation 16.9% vs 10.0%.
cards.watchOut: The 5-year all-cause mortality gap (driven by non-cardiovascular deaths, since cardiovascular death did not differ) sits uneasily beside the 3-year noninferiority verdict — both are printed, neither is hidden. EXCEL applies only to low/intermediate anatomical complexity; high-SYNTAX left main disease was not randomised here.

cards.headline: NOBLE: MACCE favoured CABG at 5 years (29% vs 19%) while mortality did not differ — and at 10 years mortality was 23% PCI vs 25% CABG
cards.summary: NOBLE: MACCE 29% vs 19% favoured CABG (hazard ratio 1.48 ); mortality did not differ at 5 years (12% vs 9%) or 10 years (23% vs 25%); repeat revascularisation consistently followed PCI.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (NOBLE; primary report with its 10-year final report folded in — one study, counts once)
cards.people: 1,201 patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease at 36 northern-European centres (598 PCI, 603 CABG; 592 per group in the intention-to-treat analysis). In the 10-year report: mean age 66.2 years in both groups; 256 of 1,184 participants (22%) were female. The primary report's abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Primary report (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimates): MACCE — all-cause mortality, non-procedural MI, any repeat revascularisation or stroke — 29% for PCI (121 events) vs 19% for CABG (81 events); hazard ratio 1.48 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.96), exceeding the noninferiority limit (p=0.0066 for CABG superiority). Components at 5 years, PCI vs CABG: all-cause mortality 12% vs 9% (hazard ratio 1.07; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.72; p=0.77); non-procedural MI 7% vs 2% (hazard ratio 2.88; 95% CI 1.40 to 5.90; p=0.0040); any revascularisation 16% vs 10% (hazard ratio 1.50; 95% CI 1.04 to 2.17; p=0.032); stroke 5% vs 2% (hazard ratio 2.25; 95% CI 0.93 to 5.48; p=0.073). At 10 years (same trial): all-cause mortality 23% (136 of 592) with PCI vs 25% (145 of 592) with CABG — hazard ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.18; p=0.56), with no significant mortality difference by SYNTAX score.
cards.watchOut: NOBLE's composite counts repeat revascularisation and excludes procedural MI, while EXCEL's composite does the opposite — much of the famous EXCEL/NOBLE discordance is endpoint construction, stated here rather than averaged away. The mortality hazard ratios (1.07 at 5 years, 0.93 at 10 years) sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band with intervals crossing 1.0: mortality equivalence is 'no difference shown', not proof of sameness.

shelves.title: Mavacamten for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: better exercise capacity, fewer septal-reduction candidates
shelves.question: Does the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten improve symptoms and gradients in obstructive HCM, and spare septal-reduction therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Benzylamines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Calcium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Cardiac Myosins/antagonists & inhibitors · Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic/drug therapy/physiopathology · Cardiovascular Agents/therapeutic use · Exercise Tolerance/physiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials point the same way on symptoms, gradients and function. In EXPLORER-HCM, 37% of mavacamten patients vs 17% on placebo met the primary exercise-capacity/NYHA composite (difference +19.4 percentage points), with a -36 mm Hg greater fall in post-exercise outflow gradient. In VALOR-HCM, among patients already referred for septal-reduction therapy, only 17.9% on mavacamten vs 76.8% on placebo still met guideline criteria or proceeded to the procedure at 16 weeks. All outcomes are symptoms, gradients, exercise capacity and procedure eligibility — no mortality or event outcome is claimed or was shown.

cards.headline: EXPLORER-HCM: mavacamten met the exercise-capacity and symptom composite in 37% vs 17% on placebo
cards.summary: EXPLORER-HCM: the exercise/symptom composite was met by 37% vs 17% on placebo (difference +19.4 points ).
cards.people: 251 adults with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, left ventricular outflow tract gradient 50 mm Hg or greater and NYHA class II–III symptoms, at 68 centres in 13 countries (123 mavacamten, 128 placebo), treated for 30 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Primary end point (1.5 mL/kg/min or greater rise in peak oxygen consumption with at least one NYHA class reduction, or 3.0 mL/kg/min or greater rise without NYHA worsening): 45 of 123 patients (37%) on mavacamten vs 22 of 128 (17%) on placebo — difference +19.4 percentage points (95% CI 8.7 to 30.1; p=0.0005). Versus placebo, mavacamten gave a greater reduction in post-exercise LVOT gradient (-36 mm Hg; 95% CI -43.2 to -28.1; p<0.0001), a greater rise in peak oxygen consumption (+1.4 mL/kg/min; 0.6 to 2.1; p=0.0006) and better symptom scores (KCCQ clinical summary +9.1 points; 5.5 to 12.7). At least one NYHA class improved in 80 of 123 vs 40 of 128 patients. Safety and tolerability were similar to placebo; one patient in the placebo group died suddenly.
cards.watchOut: A 30-week trial with symptom, gradient and exercise endpoints — no mortality, heart-failure or arrhythmia outcome is reported, and none is claimed on this shelf. The sudden death occurred on placebo and is printed for completeness, not as a treatment effect.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: Two concordant blinded trials for symptoms, gradients and procedure eligibility — no outcome-trial claims; LIKELY for those claims only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 251 symptomatic obstructive-HCM patients in EXPLORER-HCM and 112 septal-reduction candidates in VALOR-HCM.
cards.result: Two concordant double-blind trials: mavacamten improves exercise capacity, NYHA class, health-status scores and outflow gradients, and sharply reduces short-term eligibility for septal-reduction therapy. Proposed stamp LIKELY — for those symptom, gradient and eligibility claims only. No trial here reports mortality or major-event outcomes, so this shelf makes no such claim.

shelves.title: Endovascular (EVAR) vs open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm: early gain, late loss, no durable survival winner
shelves.question: For patients fit for either, does EVAR beat open repair on early and late survival?
shelves.mesh: Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal/mortality/surgery · Blood Vessel Prosthesis · Endovascular Procedures/methods/mortality · Survival Rate/trends · Angioplasty/mortality · Disease-Free Survival · Elective Surgical Procedures/mortality
shelves.balance: Proposed stamp LIKELY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). The pattern is consistent across three trials and is time-dependent, so it is stated as a pattern, not a single winner. EVAR wins early: aneurysm-related mortality was lower in the first months (EVAR trial 1 adjusted hazard ratio 0.47 for aneurysm-related death at 0–6 months; DREAM's 2-year aneurysm-related death 2.1% EVAR vs 5.7% open, a perioperative-period effect). The advantage then disappears (DREAM at 6 years: survival 68.9% EVAR vs 69.9% open) and in EVAR trial 1 reverses after 8 years (total mortality adjusted hazard ratio 1.25; aneurysm-related mortality 5.82, driven by secondary sac rupture). The US OVER trial found no significant survival difference at any epoch over up to 14 years (deaths 68.0% EVAR vs 70.0% open; hazard ratio 0.96). EVAR consistently requires more secondary procedures. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: EVAR trial 1 at 15 years: early survival benefit, then late reversal — aneurysm-related mortality hazard ratio 5.82 beyond 8 years
cards.summary: EVAR trial 1 at 15 years: mortality 9.3 vs 8.9 deaths per 100 person-years (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11) — early benefit, then late reversal (aneurysm mortality hazard ratio 5.82 beyond 8 years).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (UK EVAR trial 1; 15-year follow-up report)
cards.people: 1,252 patients aged 60 years or older with aneurysms of at least 5.5 cm in diameter, judged suitable and fit for either repair, at 37 UK centres (626 EVAR, 626 open repair), enrolled 1999–2004 and followed for a mean of 12.7 years. The abstract does not state mean age beyond the 60-plus eligibility or sex mix.
cards.result: Over follow-up, mortality was 9.3 deaths per 100 person-years in the EVAR group vs 8.9 in the open-repair group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.27; p=0.14). At 0–6 months the EVAR group had lower mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.37 to 1.02 for total mortality; 0.47; 0.23 to 0.93 for aneurysm-related mortality; p=0.031), but beyond 8 years open repair had significantly lower mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.25; 95% CI 1.00 to 1.56; p=0.048 for total mortality; 5.82; 1.64 to 20.65; p=0.0064 for aneurysm-related mortality). The late aneurysm-related excess in the EVAR group was mainly secondary aneurysm sac rupture (13 deaths [7%] in EVAR vs 2 [1%] in open repair); increased cancer mortality was also observed in the EVAR group.
cards.watchOut: First-generation devices and 1999–2004 practice: absolute rates may not transfer to modern grafts, but the late-rupture mechanism is the reason lifelong EVAR surveillance exists. The beyond-8-years aneurysm hazard ratio of 5.82 rests on few events (13 vs 2 deaths) with a wide interval — printed with its base, not as a precise risk.
cards.source: Patel R et al. Endovascular versus open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in 15-years' follow-up of the UK endovascular aneurysm repair trial 1 (EVAR trial 1): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10058):2366-2374. PMID: 27743617. Registry ID: ISRCTN55703451 (record databank).

cards.headline: DREAM: the perioperative advantage was gone by 2 years and survival was identical at 6 years — with more reinterventions after EVAR
cards.summary: DREAM: survival 89.6% vs 89.7% at 2 years and 69.9% vs 68.9% at 6 years — identical, with more secondary interventions after EVAR.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (DREAM; 2-year report with its 6-year long-term report folded in — one study, counts once)
cards.people: 351 patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm of at least 5 cm in diameter considered suitable for both techniques (178 open repair, 173 endovascular repair). The abstracts do not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 2 years: cumulative survival 89.6% for open repair vs 89.7% for endovascular repair (difference -0.1 percentage points; 95% CI -6.8 to 6.7). Aneurysm-related death: 5.7% open vs 2.1% endovascular (difference 3.7 percentage points; 95% CI -0.5 to 7.9) — an advantage the authors attribute entirely to the perioperative period, with no significant difference in subsequent aneurysm-related mortality. At 6 years (same trial): cumulative survival 69.9% open vs 68.9% endovascular (difference 1.0 percentage point; 95% CI -8.8 to 10.8; P=0.97), while freedom from secondary interventions was 81.9% open vs 70.4% endovascular (difference 11.5 percentage points; 95% CI 2.0 to 21.0; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: The 2-year aneurysm-related mortality difference has an interval crossing zero and reflects operative deaths, not late protection. The primary 2005 record carries no registry ID in its databank fields (pre-registration era); the long-term report of the same trial carries NCT00421330 — each is stated on its own record, not merged.

cards.headline: OVER: over up to 14 years, overall survival did not differ significantly in any epoch — 68.0% died after EVAR vs 70.0% after open repair
cards.summary: OVER (up to 14 years): deaths 68.0% vs 70.0% (hazard ratio 0.96) — no significant difference in any epoch.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (OVER, US Veterans Affairs)
cards.people: 881 patients with asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms, all candidates for either procedure (444 endovascular repair, 437 open repair), followed for up to 14 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Primary outcome, all-cause mortality: 302 patients (68.0%) in the endovascular group and 306 (70.0%) in the open-repair group died (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.82 to 1.13). Survival appeared higher with endovascular repair in the first 4 years, higher with open repair from year 4 through year 8, and higher again with endovascular repair after 8 years (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.18) — none of these trends was significant. Aneurysm-related deaths: 12 (2.7%) endovascular vs 16 (3.7%) open (difference -1.0 percentage points; 95% CI -3.3 to 1.4), mostly perioperative. Aneurysm rupture occurred in 7 patients (1.6%) in the endovascular group. More patients in the endovascular group underwent secondary procedures.
cards.watchOut: OVER's neutral long-term result conflicts with EVAR trial 1's late reversal — the authors themselves note the inconsistency with the two European trials, and this shelf prints both rather than choosing. A veteran population limits generalisation, and the abstract gives no sex mix, so none is stated.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: EVAR's survival advantage is early and perioperative only, paid for in reinterventions — Tier C, proposed LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EVAR trial 1 (1,252 patients), DREAM (351 patients) and OVER (881 patients) — 2,484 patients fit for either repair.
cards.result: All three trials agree that EVAR's survival advantage is early and perioperative, and none shows a durable long-term survival advantage for EVAR. They disagree on the late phase: EVAR trial 1 finds significantly worse late survival after EVAR, DREAM finds identical 6-year survival, and OVER finds no significant difference over up to 14 years. Proposed stamp LIKELY (for the shared early-gain/no-durable-advantage pattern), pending the developer's personal verdict. Aneurysm screening is a different question, owned by proposed shelf #530 — not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Any survival claim from this shelf must name its epoch: 'EVAR saves lives' is true of the perioperative window in these trials and false as an unqualified long-term claim. EVAR's higher secondary-procedure burden appears in every trial and belongs beside any survival statement.
cards.source: Synthesis of Patel R et al. PMID: 27743617; Blankensteijn JD et al. PMID: 15944424; De Bruin JL et al. PMID: 20484396; Lederle FA et al. PMID: 31141634. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ultrafiltration for acute decompensated heart failure: more fluid off in UNLOAD, worse kidneys in CARRESS-HF
shelves.question: Does ultrafiltration relieve congestion better than intravenous diuretics in acute heart failure with cardiorenal syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Diuretics/administration & dosage · Heart Failure/therapy · Hemofiltration · Infusions, Intravenous · Ultrafiltration · Algorithms · Cardio-Renal Syndrome/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The three trials disagree by population, and none shows an outcome benefit that survives its own caveats. In broad decompensated heart failure (UNLOAD, 200 patients), ultrafiltration removed more weight and fluid than intravenous diuretics at 48 hours (5.0 vs 3.1 kg) and was followed by fewer 90-day heart-failure rehospitalisations (18% vs 32% of patients) — with deaths printed beside it, 9 vs 11, no difference. In the cardiorenal population the shelf question names (CARRESS-HF, 188 patients), ultrafiltration was worse: creatinine rose (+0.23 vs -0.04 mg/dL), weight loss was the same, and serious adverse events were more frequent (72% vs 57%). The third trial, AVOID-HF, was stopped by its sponsor at 224 of 810 planned patients and is inconclusive. Fluid removal is achievable; routine outcome benefit is unproven, and in cardiorenal syndrome the tested strategy harmed renal function.

cards.headline: UNLOAD: ultrafiltration removed more weight and fluid than IV diuretics, with fewer 90-day heart-failure rehospitalisations
cards.summary: UNLOAD: ultrafiltration removed more — weight −5.0 vs −3.1 kg , fluid 4.6 vs 3.3 L — with fewer 90-day HF rehospitalisations.
cards.people: 200 patients hospitalised for heart failure with at least two signs of hypervolaemia (mean age 63 years [SD 15], 69% men, 71% with ejection fraction 40% or lower), randomised to ultrafiltration or intravenous diuretics.
cards.result: At 48 hours, weight loss was 5.0 kg (SD 3.1) with ultrafiltration vs 3.1 kg (SD 3.5) with diuretics (p=0.001) and net fluid loss 4.6 vs 3.3 litres (p=0.001); dyspnoea scores were similar and there were no serum creatinine differences between groups. At 90 days, fewer ultrafiltration patients were rehospitalised for heart failure (16 of 89 [18%] vs 28 of 87 [32%]; p=0.037), with fewer rehospitalisations and rehospitalisation days per patient and fewer unscheduled visits (14 of 65 [21%] vs 29 of 66 [44%]; p=0.009). Deaths are printed beside the rehospitalisation result, as required: 9 deaths in the ultrafiltration group and 11 in the diuretics group.
cards.watchOut: A 200-patient, unblinded trial whose 90-day resource-use endpoints were secondary, with denominators shrinking by outcome (89/87 for rehospitalisation, 65/66 for visits). The mortality counts are far too small to support any survival claim in either direction, and none is made.
cards.source: Costanzo MR et al. Ultrafiltration versus intravenous diuretics for patients hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2007;49(6):675-683. PMID: 17291932. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00124137 (record databank).

cards.headline: CARRESS-HF: in cardiorenal syndrome, stepped drug therapy beat ultrafiltration — creatinine rose and adverse events were more frequent
cards.summary: CARRESS-HF: in cardiorenal syndrome, stepped drug therapy beat ultrafiltration (creatinine +0.23 vs −0.04 mg/dL; P=0.003 for the primary end point).
cards.people: 188 patients with acute decompensated heart failure, worsened renal function and persistent congestion (94 stepped pharmacologic therapy, 94 ultrafiltration), followed for 60 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Ultrafiltration was inferior on the bivariate primary end point of change in serum creatinine and body weight at 96 hours (P=0.003), driven by creatinine: mean change +0.23 mg/dL (SD 0.70) with ultrafiltration vs -0.04 mg/dL (SD 0.53) with pharmacologic therapy (P=0.003). Weight loss at 96 hours did not differ (loss of 5.7 kg [SD 3.9] vs 5.5 kg [SD 5.1]; P=0.58). A higher percentage of ultrafiltration patients had a serious adverse event (72% vs 57%; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: This is the population the shelf question names — acute heart failure with cardiorenal syndrome — and here the device strategy was the harmful one. The result is about the tested fixed-rate ultrafiltration strategy versus a stepped drug algorithm, not about fluid removal in principle.
cards.source: Bart BA et al. Ultrafiltration in decompensated heart failure with cardiorenal syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2012;367(24):2296-2304. PMID: 23131078. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00608491 (record databank).

cards.headline: AVOID-HF: the largest ultrafiltration trial was stopped by its sponsor at 224 of 810 planned patients — inconclusive
cards.summary: AVOID-HF, the largest trial: stopped by its sponsor at 224 of 810 planned patients — inconclusive.
cards.people: 224 hospitalised heart-failure patients randomised (110 adjustable ultrafiltration, 114 adjustable intravenous loop diuretics) of 810 planned, before the sponsor terminated the trial early. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Estimated days to first heart-failure event within 90 days were 62 with ultrafiltration vs 34 with diuretics (p=0.106), not significant. At 30 days the ultrafiltration group had fewer heart-failure and cardiovascular events (rates not stated in the abstract, so none are printed here). Renal function changes were similar; 90-day mortality was similar (figures not stated in the abstract). More ultrafiltration patients experienced an adverse effect of special interest (p=0.018) and a serious study product-related adverse event (p=0.026).
cards.watchOut: A trial stopped unilaterally by its sponsor at 27.5% of planned enrollment cannot settle the question; its non-significant trend is hypothesis-generating only and is carded as documentation of an unfinished test, not as evidence of benefit.
cards.source: Costanzo MR et al. Aquapheresis Versus Intravenous Diuretics and Hospitalizations for Heart Failure. JACC Heart Fail. 2016;4(2):95-105. PMID: 26519995. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: Fluid removal is reliable; outcome benefit is unshown and the cardiorenal trial went the other way — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: UNLOAD (200 patients, broad decompensated heart failure), CARRESS-HF (188 patients, cardiorenal syndrome) and AVOID-HF (224 of 810 planned, stopped early).
cards.result: Ultrafiltration reliably removes fluid — in UNLOAD more than standard diuretics, in CARRESS-HF the same amount as stepped drug therapy but at a renal cost. No trial shows a mortality benefit, and in the cardiorenal population the question names, ultrafiltration was inferior. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) for any outcome benefit; the honest summary is 'works as a fluid-removal method, unproven as an outcome therapy, harmful as tested in cardiorenal syndrome'.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite UNLOAD's rehospitalisation result without its mortality counts (9 vs 11 deaths) or without CARRESS-HF beside it — population determines the answer on this shelf, and chronic heart-failure drug shelves do not cover this acute decongestion question.

shelves.title: Treatment of varicose veins: laser vs surgery vs foam — laser and surgery ahead on disease-specific quality of life at 5 years
shelves.question: For primary varicose veins, how do endovenous laser ablation, surgery and ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy compare on symptoms, quality of life and recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Intention to Treat Analysis · Laser Therapy/adverse effects · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Postoperative Complications · Saphenous Vein/surgery · Sclerotherapy/adverse effects/methods · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large three-way randomised trial (CLASS, 798 participants) with its 5-year follow-up answers the comparison directly. At 6 months, generic quality of life did not differ between treatments; disease-specific quality of life was slightly worse after foam than after surgery, and similar after laser and surgery; procedural complications were least frequent after laser (1% vs 7% surgery, 6% foam), while successful ablation of the saphenous trunks was less common after foam. At 5 years, disease-specific quality of life was better after laser or surgery than after foam (adjusted differences -2.86 and -2.60 points on the Aberdeen questionnaire), and cost-effectiveness modelling favoured laser (77.2% of iterations at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold).

cards.headline: CLASS at 6 months: quality of life broadly similar — foam slightly worse disease-specific scores, laser fewest procedural complications
cards.summary: CLASS at 6 months: quality of life broadly similar across laser, foam and surgery — foam slightly worse on disease-specific scores, laser fewest procedural complications.
cards.people: 798 participants with primary varicose veins at 11 UK centres, randomised to ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy, endovenous laser ablation or surgery. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, after adjustment, mean disease-specific quality of life was slightly worse after foam than after surgery (P=0.006) and similar in the laser and surgery groups; generic quality-of-life measures did not differ significantly between surgery and either foam or laser. Procedural complications: foam 6%, surgery 7%, laser 1% (laser vs surgery P<0.001). Serious adverse events were approximately 3% in all groups. Clinical success measures were similar among groups, but successful ablation of the main saphenous trunks was less common in the foam group than in the surgery group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Quality of life, not recurrence or reoperation, was the primary outcome at 6 months, and the abstract reports no recurrence rates — none are printed here. Patients and treating teams could not be blinded to a procedure comparison.
cards.source: Brittenden J et al. A randomized trial comparing treatments for varicose veins. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(13):1218-1227. PMID: 25251616. Registry ID: ISRCTN51995477 (record databank).

cards.headline: CLASS cost-effectiveness: at 6 months foam and laser both cost less than surgery; modelled over 5 years laser was favoured
cards.summary: CLASS cost-effectiveness: at 6 months foam cost £655 less and laser £160 less than surgery; modelled over 5 years, laser was favoured .
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis alongside a randomised trial (CLASS)
cards.people: Participants of the CLASS trial (798 participants with primary varicose veins); costs and utilities collected alongside the trial, with a Markov model extrapolating recurrence over a 5-year horizon.
cards.result: Compared with surgery at 6 months, foam reduced mean health-service costs by £655 and laser by £160 (savings rising to £902 and £392 when theatre overhead costs were included). Foam produced 0.005 fewer quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) than surgery; laser produced 0.011 additional QALYs. Extrapolated to 5 years, laser cost £3,640 per QALY gained compared with foam, and compared with surgery laser both saved costs (£206–439) and gained QALYs (0.078). At a willingness-to-pay ceiling of £20,000 per QALY, laser had the highest probability (78.7%) of being cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: The 5-year figures are model extrapolations built partly on recurrence rates from outside the trial, in UK NHS costs — they rank the three options for that system and era and are not clinical outcome data. This record's databank fields carry no registry ID; the trial's registration appears on the main CLASS report (previous card), not here.
cards.source: Tassie E et al. Cost-effectiveness of ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy, endovenous laser ablation or surgery as treatment for primary varicose veins from the randomized CLASS trial. Br J Surg. 2014;101(12):1532-1540. PMID: 25274220. Registry ID: none in this record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CLASS at 5 years: disease-specific quality of life better after laser or surgery than after foam
cards.summary: CLASS at 5 years: disease-specific quality of life better after laser ( −2.86 ) and surgery ( −2.60 ) than after foam.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial follow-up (CLASS 5-year report — same trial as cards 1–2, counts once)
cards.people: The same 798 CLASS participants with primary varicose veins; quality-of-life questionnaires were completed by 595 (75%) at 5 years.
cards.result: At 5 years, adjusted Aberdeen Varicose Vein Questionnaire scores (0–100, lower is better) were lower after laser ablation than after foam (adjusted difference -2.86; 95% CI -4.49 to -1.22; P<0.001) and after surgery than after foam (-2.60; 95% CI -3.99 to -1.22; P<0.001). Generic quality-of-life measures did not differ among the groups. In the cost-effectiveness model at a £20,000 ($28,433) per QALY threshold, 77.2% of iterations favoured laser ablation; in a two-way foam-vs-surgery comparison, 54.5% favoured surgery.
cards.watchOut: A quarter of participants did not return 5-year questionnaires, so the quality-of-life comparison rests on responders. shelves.title: Tafamidis for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy: one pivotal trial — mortality 29.5% vs 42.9% at 30 months
shelves.question: Does tafamidis reduce death and cardiovascular hospitalisation in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Amyloid Neuropathies, Familial/complications/drug therapy · Benzoxazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cardiomyopathies/complications/drug therapy · Disease Progression · Heart Failure/etiology/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane) — capped at POSSIBLE because the shelf rests on a single pivotal trial. In ATTR-ACT (441 patients, 30 months), all-cause mortality was 29.5% (78 of 264) on tafamidis vs 42.9% (76 of 177) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.96) — an absolute difference of 13.4 percentage points — printed beside the cardiovascular-hospitalisation result, as required: 0.48 vs 0.70 hospitalisations per year (relative risk ratio 0.68, a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). Decline in 6-minute walk distance and quality-of-life score was also slower on tafamidis. The long-term extension, in which placebo patients crossed to tafamidis, found better survival in those treated from the start (deaths 44.9% vs 62.7%; hazard ratio 0.59) — supportive, but no longer a placebo-controlled comparison. No second placebo-controlled trial exists. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: ATTR-ACT: tafamidis lowered all-cause mortality (29.5% vs 42.9%) and cardiovascular hospitalisations over 30 months
cards.summary: ATTR-ACT: all-cause mortality 29.5% vs 42.9% (hazard ratio 0.70 ) and fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations (0.48 vs 0.70 per year) on tafamidis.
cards.people: 441 patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (264 tafamidis 80 mg or 20 mg pooled, 177 placebo), treated for 30 months in a multicentre international trial. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the hierarchical primary analysis, all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalisation rates were lower on tafamidis than placebo (P<0.001). All-cause mortality: 78 of 264 (29.5%) on tafamidis vs 76 of 177 (42.9%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.96) — printed beside the hospitalisation result: cardiovascular-related hospitalisations 0.48 per year on tafamidis vs 0.70 per year on placebo (relative risk ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.81, a relative measure). At month 30, tafamidis was also associated with a lower rate of decline in 6-minute walk distance and in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score (both P<0.001; the abstract gives no absolute values, so none are printed). Adverse-event incidence and types were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A single pivotal trial — the shelf's certainty ceiling. The mortality hazard ratio of 0.70 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so the claim rests on the randomised design, the absolute difference (13.4 percentage points over 30 months) and the concordant hospitalisation and functional results, not on the ratio alone. The two tafamidis doses were pooled in the primary analysis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: One pivotal trial carries a mortality claim, with no second placebo-controlled trial — Tier C, proposed POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATTR-ACT (441 patients randomised for 30 months) and its long-term extension (353 of the original patients followed to a median of about 58 months).
cards.result: One placebo-controlled trial shows lower all-cause mortality (29.5% vs 42.9%) and fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations (0.48 vs 0.70 per year) with tafamidis, and the extension is consistent with benefit from starting earlier rather than later. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict — the single-trial cap applies even though the trial is large, blinded and positive on mortality. No second randomised trial of tafamidis exists to raise it.
cards.watchOut: Do not print the hospitalisation relative risk ratio (0.68) without the absolute rates and the mortality figures beside it. Other transthyretin-directed drugs (for example the silencer vutrisiran, HELIOS-B) answer a different shelf's question and are not evidence for or against tafamidis here.

shelves.title: Dietary sodium restriction in chronic heart failure: SODIUM-HF — a large trial, a null result
shelves.question: Does restricting dietary sodium to under 100 mmol/day improve outcomes in chronic heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Canada · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Sodium · Sodium, Dietary
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single-trial cap, for the null): In SODIUM-HF (806 patients), a dietary intervention targeting under 100 mmol of sodium per day did not reduce the composite of cardiovascular hospital admission, cardiovascular emergency-department visit or all-cause death at 12 months (15% low-sodium vs 17% usual care; hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.26; p=0.53), and all-cause death — printed beside the composite, as required — was numerically higher in the low-sodium group (6% vs 4%; hazard ratio 1.38; 95% CI 0.73 to 2.60; p=0.32), not significantly. Achieved intake separation was modest: median sodium fell to 1,658 mg/day in the intervention group vs 2,073 mg/day on usual care. One large trial, honestly null on its own terms; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because a single trial carries the shelf.

cards.headline: SODIUM-HF: targeting under 100 mmol/day of sodium did not reduce cardiovascular admissions, emergency visits or death at 12 months
cards.summary: SODIUM-HF: achieved sodium fell (2,286 → 1,658 mg/day vs 2,119 → 2,073) — and the primary composite did not fall (hazard ratio 0.89 [0.63 to 1.26]).
cards.people: 806 ambulatory patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class 2–3) on optimally tolerated guideline-directed therapy, at 26 sites in six countries (397 low-sodium diet, 409 usual care). Median age 67 years (IQR 58–74); 268 (33%) women and 538 (66%) men, as printed in the record.
cards.result: Median sodium intake fell from 2,286 mg/day at baseline to 1,658 mg/day at 12 months in the low-sodium group, vs 2,119 to 2,073 mg/day in usual care. Primary outcome (cardiovascular hospital admission, cardiovascular emergency-department visit or all-cause death within 12 months): 60 of 397 (15%) low-sodium vs 70 of 409 (17%) usual care (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.26; p=0.53). Components: all-cause death 22 (6%) vs 17 (4%) (hazard ratio 1.38; 0.73 to 2.60; p=0.32); cardiovascular hospitalisation 40 (10%) vs 51 (12%) (hazard ratio 0.82; 0.54 to 1.24; p=0.36); cardiovascular emergency visits 17 (4%) vs 15 (4%) (hazard ratio 1.21; 0.60 to 2.41; p=0.60). No safety events related to the study treatment were reported in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label dietary trial: the achieved contrast (about 400 mg/day between groups at 12 months) was smaller than the under-100-mmol target implies, because usual-care intake also fell and adherence waned — the trial tests the intervention as delivered, not a metabolic-ward sodium clamp. The hazard ratios all sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band with intervals crossing 1.0: a null, with no hidden benefit or harm signal claimed.
cards.source: Ezekowitz JA et al. Reduction of dietary sodium to less than 100 mmol in heart failure (SODIUM-HF): an international, open-label, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet. 2022;399(10333):1391-1400. PMID: 35381194. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02012179 (record databank).

cards.summary: A genuinely thin shelf — one large trial, stated plainly; POSSIBLE, capped by the single-trial base.

shelves.title: Allopurinol in ischaemic heart disease without gout: ALL-HEART — 5,721 patients, no cardiovascular benefit
shelves.question: Does allopurinol improve cardiovascular outcomes in patients with ischaemic heart disease who do not have gout?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/therapeutic use · Coronary Artery Disease/drug therapy · Gout/drug therapy · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy · Myocardial Ischemia/drug therapy · Stroke/drug therapy · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single-trial cap, for the null): In ALL-HEART (5,721 patients aged 60 or older with ischaemic heart disease and no gout history, mean follow-up 4.8 years), allopurinol titrated to 600 mg daily did not improve the primary composite of non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke or cardiovascular death (11.0% allopurinol vs 11.3% usual care; hazard ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.89 to 1.21; p=0.65), and all-cause mortality — printed beside it — was 10.1% vs 10.6% (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.20; p=0.77). The trial is null, so no benefit claim arises and the shelf is not Tier C. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because one trial, however large, carries the shelf alone.

cards.headline: ALL-HEART: allopurinol 600 mg daily did not reduce MI, stroke or cardiovascular death in ischaemic heart disease without gout
cards.summary: ALL-HEART (5,721 patients): primary outcome 11.0% vs 11.3% on allopurinol 600 mg (hazard ratio 1.04 [0.89 to 1.21]) — no reduction in MI, stroke or cardiovascular death.
cards.people: 5,721 patients aged 60 years or older with ischaemic heart disease but no history of gout, recruited from 424 UK primary-care practices (2,853 allopurinol, 2,868 usual care), in the modified intention-to-treat population. Mean age 72.0 years (SD 6.8); 4,321 (75.5%) male; 5,676 (99.2%) white, as printed in the record. Mean follow-up 4.8 years (SD 1.5).
cards.result: Primary outcome (non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke or cardiovascular death): 314 participants (11.0%) in the allopurinol group (2.47 events per 100 patient-years) vs 325 (11.3%) in the usual-care group (2.37 per 100 patient-years) — hazard ratio 1.04 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.21; p=0.65). All-cause death: 288 (10.1%) on allopurinol vs 303 (10.6%) on usual care (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.20; p=0.77). The authors conclude there was no difference in the primary outcome between the randomised groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (with blinded endpoint assessment) and a modified intention-to-treat population that excluded 216 patients randomised in error — stated on the card rather than hidden. The hazard ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band with intervals crossing 1.0: a clean null in this population, which says nothing about allopurinol for gout itself.

shelves.title: Hydroxyurea in sickle cell disease: adults and infants
shelves.question: Does hydroxyurea reduce painful crises in adults with sickle cell anaemia (MSH) — and is it safe and spleen-protective in infants (BABY HUG)?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Sickle Cell/drug therapy,physiopathology · Hydroxyurea/therapeutic use · Pain/prevention & control · Acute Chest Syndrome/etiology,prevention & control · Anemia, Sickle Cell/complications,drug therapy,metabolism,pathology,physiopathology · Antisickling Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: a mortality signal in long-term MSH follow-up was flagged at topic stage; neither carded abstract reports mortality, and no mortality figure is printed on this shelf). Two randomised trials, in different populations, agree that hydroxyurea cuts sickle pain: in adults with three or more crises a year (MSH, 299 patients) the median crisis rate fell from 4.5 to 2.5 per year, and in infants aged 9–18 months (BABY HUG, 193 randomised) pain events numbered 177 on hydroxycarbamide versus 375 on placebo. BABY HUG's primary organ endpoints were null — no significant difference in splenic function (p=0.21) or glomerular filtration rate (p=0.84) — so the spleen-protection half of the question is not answered yes; the infant claim carded is fewer pain and dactylitis events with only mild-to-moderate neutropenia over 2 years.

cards.headline: MSH 1995: hydroxyurea cut the median painful-crisis rate from 4.5 to 2.5 per year in adults with frequent crises
cards.summary: MSH 1995: hydroxyurea cut the median painful-crisis rate from 4.5 to 2.5 per year in adults with frequent crises.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, stopped early after a mean follow-up of 21 months
cards.people: 299 adults (148 men and 151 women) with sickle cell anaemia and a history of three or more painful crises per year, at 21 clinics; 152 assigned to hydroxyurea and 147 to placebo. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The median annual crisis rate was 2.5 crises per year on hydroxyurea versus 4.5 on placebo (P<0.001). Median time to the first crisis was 3.0 versus 1.5 months (P=0.01) and to the second crisis 8.8 versus 4.6 months (P<0.001). Fewer hydroxyurea patients had chest syndrome (25 vs 51, P<0.001) or underwent transfusion (48 vs 73, P=0.001). Hydroxyurea doses at study end ranged from 0 to 35 mg/kg/day, and no important adverse effects were reported; the authors state that long-term safety was uncertain.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early, and the benefit takes several months to appear; the abstract reports no mortality outcome — the long-term mortality signal flagged for this shelf lives in follow-up reports that are not carded here.
cards.source: Charache S et al. Effect of hydroxyurea on the frequency of painful crises in sickle cell anemia. Investigators of the Multicenter Study of Hydroxyurea in Sickle Cell Anemia. N Engl J Med. 1995;332(20):1317-1322. PMID: 7715639. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: BABY HUG 2011: hydroxycarbamide cut pain and dactylitis in infants, but did not significantly improve spleen or kidney function
cards.summary: BABY HUG 2011: hydroxycarbamide cut pain and dactylitis in infants, but did not significantly improve spleen or kidney function (primary endpoints null).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (2 years)

shelves.title: Preventing stroke in sickle cell disease: transfusion, and switching to hydroxyurea
shelves.question: In children with abnormal transcranial Doppler, does chronic transfusion prevent first stroke (STOP) — and can hydroxyurea replace transfusion for maintenance (TWiTCH)?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Sickle Cell/complications,diagnostic imaging,physiopathology,therapy · Blood Flow Velocity · Blood Transfusion · Cerebral Hemorrhage/epidemiology,etiology · Cerebral Infarction/epidemiology,etiology · Cerebrovascular Circulation · Cerebrovascular Disorders/etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: stroke-prevention claim). STOP (130 children with transcranial Doppler velocities ≥200 cm/s) was stopped early after 11 stroke events on standard care versus 1 on transfusion — a 92% relative difference in stroke risk, with absolute rates of 11 of 67 versus 1 of 63 over the trial period. TWiTCH then showed that, after at least a year of transfusions and in children without severe vasculopathy, switching to hydroxycarbamide kept 24-month Doppler velocities non-inferior to continued transfusion (138 vs 143 cm/s), with no strokes identified among 29 adjudicated neurological events. The carded claim is: transfusion prevents first stroke in high-velocity children; hydroxyurea is a maintenance alternative once velocities are controlled — not a first-line substitute tested from diagnosis.

cards.summary: STOP 1998: transfusion cut first-stroke events from 11 of 67 children to 1 of 63 — a 92% relative difference in risk. (Tier C — stroke-prevention claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stopped early because of the stroke difference
cards.people: 130 children with sickle cell anaemia, no history of stroke, and two transcranial Doppler studies showing time-averaged mean velocity ≥200 cm/s in the internal carotid or middle cerebral artery; mean age 8.3 (SD 3.3) years; 63 assigned to transfusion (target haemoglobin S below 30%) and 67 to standard care. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: There were 10 cerebral infarctions and 1 intracerebral haematoma in the standard-care group versus 1 infarction in the transfusion group — a 92% difference in the risk of stroke (P<0.001), a relative measure far beyond the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute event counts of 11 of 67 versus 1 of 63. Ten patients dropped out of the transfusion group and two crossed over from standard care. The result led to early termination of the trial.
cards.watchOut: A small trial stopped early, in a screened high-risk subgroup only (velocity ≥200 cm/s on two studies); it does not address children with normal velocities, and indefinite transfusion carries the iron and alloimmunisation burdens the abstract does not quantify.

cards.headline: TWiTCH 2016: hydroxycarbamide was non-inferior to continued transfusion for maintaining Doppler velocities over 24 months
cards.summary: TWiTCH 2016: hydroxycarbamide was non-inferior to continued transfusion for maintaining Doppler velocities over 24 months.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Doppler readings centrally masked)
cards.people: 121 children aged 4–16 years with sickle cell anaemia and abnormal Doppler velocities (≥200 cm/s) but no severe vasculopathy, who had received chronic transfusions, at 26 US and Canadian centres; 61 continued standard transfusions and 60 switched to hydroxycarbamide (starting 20 mg/kg/day, escalated to maximum tolerated dose). The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Final model-based 24-month Doppler velocities were 143 cm/s (95% CI 140–146) on transfusions and 138 cm/s (135–142) on hydroxycarbamide — difference 4.54 cm/s (0.10–8.98) against a 15 cm/s non-inferiority margin; non-inferiority p=8.82×10⁻¹⁶, with post-hoc superiority p=0.023. The sponsor terminated the study at the first scheduled interim analysis once non-inferiority was shown. Of 29 new neurological events adjudicated centrally, no strokes were identified in either group.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a Doppler velocity surrogate, not stroke itself, and entrants were pre-treated with transfusions and free of severe vasculopathy — TWiTCH licenses a switch in that setting, not starting hydroxyurea instead of transfusion in a newly identified high-velocity child.

cards.summary: Transfuse first for high Doppler velocities; hydroxyurea can then maintain — LIKELY, Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: STOP (130 children, transfusion vs standard care) and TWiTCH (121 children, switch to hydroxycarbamide vs continued transfusion).
cards.result: The sequence the two trials support is sequential, not interchangeable: STOP's 11-versus-1 stroke split establishes transfusion as first-stroke prevention in children with velocities ≥200 cm/s, and TWiTCH's non-inferior 24-month velocities (138 vs 143 cm/s, no strokes among adjudicated events) establish hydroxycarbamide as a maintenance switch after transfusion control in children without severe vasculopathy. cards.watchOut: Neither trial tests hydroxyurea as the initial response to a first abnormal Doppler; presenting TWiTCH that way overstates it.

shelves.title: Emicizumab prophylaxis in haemophilia A
shelves.question: Does emicizumab prophylaxis reduce bleeding versus no prophylaxis or prior factor therapy — in patients with and without inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Bispecific/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Blood Coagulation Factors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor VIII/immunology,therapeutic use · Factor VIIa/therapeutic use · Hemophilia A/drug therapy,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 trials, one in each population, show very large reductions in treated bleeding versus no prophylaxis. With inhibitors (HAVEN 1, 109 males aged ≥12): annualised bleeding rate 2.9 versus 23.3 events — 87% lower — with 63% of emicizumab patients having zero bleeds versus 6% without prophylaxis. Without inhibitors (HAVEN 3, 152 participants): annualised rates of 1.5 (weekly) and 1.3 (every 2 weeks) versus 38.2 events with no prophylaxis — 96–97% lower — and an intraindividual 68% lower rate than prior factor VIII prophylaxis. The claim carded is bleeding reduction; neither trial was powered for joint outcomes or mortality.

cards.headline: HAVEN 1 2017: emicizumab cut the annualised bleeding rate by 87% versus no prophylaxis in haemophilia A with inhibitors
cards.summary: HAVEN 1 2017: emicizumab cut the annualised bleeding rate by 87% relative vs no prophylaxis in haemophilia A with inhibitors (2.9 vs 23.3 events).
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, open-label randomised trial (prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis)
cards.people: 109 male participants aged 12 years or older with haemophilia A with factor VIII inhibitors; those previously on episodic bypassing-agent treatment were randomised 2:1 to emicizumab prophylaxis (group A, 35) or no prophylaxis (group B, 18); a further group C (which included 24 participants from a non-interventional study) had previously received bypassing-agent prophylaxis. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The annualised bleeding rate was 2.9 events (95% CI 1.7 to 5.0) with emicizumab versus 23.3 events (12.3 to 43.9) without prophylaxis — a significant difference of 87% in favour of emicizumab (P<0.001), a relative measure beyond the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute rates as stated. Zero bleeding events occurred in 22 of 35 group A participants (63%) versus 1 of 18 (6%) in group B. In group C, emicizumab's bleeding rate was 79% lower than the same patients' previous bypassing-agent prophylaxis (P<0.001). Injection-site reactions occurred in 15% of emicizumab participants; thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis were each reported in 2 participants who had received multiple infusions of activated prothrombin complex concentrate for breakthrough bleeding. No antidrug antibodies were detected.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a small no-prophylaxis control group (18 patients), and the thrombotic events cluster in patients also receiving repeated activated prothrombin complex concentrate — the interaction, not emicizumab alone, is the safety signal to carry forward.
cards.source: Oldenburg J et al. Emicizumab Prophylaxis in Hemophilia A with Inhibitors. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(9):809-818. PMID: 28691557. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02622321, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: HAVEN 3 2018: weekly or fortnightly emicizumab cut treated bleeding by 96–97% versus no prophylaxis without inhibitors
cards.summary: HAVEN 3 2018: weekly or fortnightly emicizumab cut treated bleeding by 96–97% relative vs no prophylaxis without inhibitors (1.5 and 1.3 vs 38.2 events).
cards.people: 152 participants aged 12 years or older with haemophilia A without factor VIII inhibitors, previously on episodic factor VIII, randomised 2:2:1 to emicizumab 1.5 mg/kg weekly (group A), 3.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks (group B), or no prophylaxis (group C); group D comprised patients previously on factor VIII prophylaxis. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Annualised treated bleeding rates were 1.5 events (95% CI 0.9 to 2.5) weekly and 1.3 events (0.8 to 2.3) every 2 weeks versus 38.2 events (22.9 to 63.8) with no prophylaxis — 96% and 97% lower respectively (P<0.001 for both), relative measures with the absolute rates as stated. No treated bleeding events occurred in 56% (group A) and 60% (group B) versus 0% in group C. In the intraindividual comparison (48 participants), emicizumab's annualised rate was 68% lower than prior factor VIII prophylaxis (P<0.001). shelves.title: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists for immune thrombocytopenia
shelves.question: Do romiplostim and eltrombopag raise and sustain platelet counts and reduce bleeding in chronic ITP versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Carrier Proteins/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Platelet Count · Purpura, Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic/blood,drug therapy,immunology · Receptors, Fc/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two placebo-controlled phase 3 programmes agree. Romiplostim (Kuter 2008, two parallel trials, 125 patients) produced a durable platelet response in 16 of 42 splenectomised patients versus 0 of 21 on placebo, and 25 of 41 non-splenectomised versus 1 of 21. Eltrombopag (RAISE, 197 patients) achieved a platelet response at least once in 79% versus 28%, with odds ratio 8.2 for response across 6 months, less rescue treatment (18% vs 40%) and more patients reducing concomitant therapy (59% vs 32%). The carded claim is platelet response and reduced rescue/concomitant treatment; bleeding outcomes were secondary and are stated as such.

cards.headline: Kuter 2008: romiplostim produced durable platelet responses in 38% of splenectomised and 61% of non-splenectomised ITP patients, versus 0–5% on placebo
cards.summary: Kuter 2008: romiplostim produced durable platelet responses in 38% of splenectomised and 61% of non-splenectomised ITP patients, vs 0–5% on placebo.
cards.type: Two parallel double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials (24 weeks)
cards.people: 125 patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura and platelet counts ≤30×10⁹/L: 63 splenectomised (42 romiplostim, 21 placebo) and 62 non-splenectomised (41 romiplostim, 21 placebo); weekly subcutaneous injections with dose adjusted to hold platelets at 50–200×10⁹/L. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: A durable platelet response (≥50×10⁹/L during at least 6 of the last 8 weeks) was achieved by 16 of 42 splenectomised patients on romiplostim versus 0 of 21 on placebo (difference 38%, 95% CI 23.4–52.8; p=0.0013), and by 25 of 41 non-splenectomised versus 1 of 21 (difference 56%, 38.7–73.7; p<0.0001). Overall response rates were 79% (splenectomised) and 88% (non-splenectomised) on romiplostim versus 0% and 14% on placebo (p<0.0001). Among responders assessed, 87% (20 of 23) on romiplostim reduced or discontinued concurrent ITP therapy versus 38% (6 of 16) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a platelet-count surrogate sustained over the last 8 of 24 weeks, in a per-protocol analysis; the trials were not powered to show reduced major bleeding or mortality.

cards.headline: RAISE 2011: eltrombopag tripled the response rate over 6 months (79% vs 28%) and halved rescue-treatment use
cards.summary: RAISE 2011: eltrombopag tripled the response rate over 6 months ( 79% vs 28% ) and halved rescue-treatment use.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (6 months)
cards.people: 197 adults with previously treated immune thrombocytopenia of more than 6 months' duration and baseline platelet counts below 30,000 per μL, randomised 2:1 to eltrombopag 50 mg daily (135) or placebo (62) on top of local standard care. Concomitant ITP treatment was reduced by 59% of eltrombopag patients versus 32% on placebo (p=0.016), and rescue treatment was needed by 18% versus 40% (p=0.001). Thromboembolic events occurred in 3 eltrombopag patients (2%) versus none on placebo, and mild alanine aminotransferase increases in 7% versus 3%.
cards.watchOut: Response is again a platelet-count outcome; the thromboembolic and liver-enzyme signals, though small in absolute terms, are the class cautions and come from a 6-month horizon.

shelves.title: Intravenous iron for iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy
shelves.question: Does intravenous ferric carboxymaltose correct anaemia faster and more completely than oral iron in pregnant women with iron deficiency?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/blood,drug therapy · Ferric Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Ferrous Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Infant, Newborn · Maltose/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — faster, more complete correction (FER-ASAP) · POSSIBLE — no difference in anaemia prevalence at 36 weeks (IVON). The two trials differ in population and timing and their headline results pull apart. FER-ASAP (252 women, haemoglobin entry at 16–33 weeks) found more women corrected to Hb ≥11.0 g/dL with ferric carboxymaltose than oral ferrous sulfate (84% vs 70%; odds ratio 2.06) and corrected faster (median 3.4 vs 4.3 weeks). IVON (1,056 Nigerian women with Hb <10 g/dL at 20–32 weeks) found no significant difference in anaemia at 36 weeks (58% vs 61%; risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.85–1.06) or preterm birth, though iron deficiency itself was reduced more by intravenous iron. Both trials are open-label and single per half, so each half is capped at POSSIBLE. Intravenous iron in kidney disease is Shelf #294 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: FER-ASAP 2017: ferric carboxymaltose corrected anaemia in 84% versus 70% on oral iron, and corrected it faster
cards.summary: FER-ASAP 2017: ferric carboxymaltose corrected anaemia in 84% vs 70% on oral iron, and corrected it faster.
cards.type: International, open-label, randomised controlled trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 252 pregnant women (gestational weeks 16–33) with iron-deficiency anaemia, randomised 1:1 to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (1000–1500 mg iron) or oral ferrous sulfate (200 mg iron/day). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Haemoglobin improved at comparable rates in both groups, but significantly more women achieved anaemia correction (Hb ≥11.0 g/dL) with ferric carboxymaltose than oral iron: 84% versus 70% (odds ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.07–3.97; P=0.031) — a relative measure at the edge of the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute rates as stated — and correction came sooner (median 3.4 vs 4.3 weeks). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 11% (ferric carboxymaltose) and 15% (oral iron); gastrointestinal disorders were reported by 16 women on oral iron versus 3 on intravenous iron. Newborn characteristics were similar across treatments.

shelves.title: Lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes: luspatercept and lenalidomide
shelves.question: Does luspatercept free patients with ring-sideroblast MDS from transfusions (MEDALIST) — and does lenalidomide do the same in del(5q) disease?
shelves.mesh: Activin Receptors, Type II/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anemia, Sideroblastic/drug therapy,therapy · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Hematinics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hemoglobins/analysis · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Infusions, Subcutaneous
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, in two biologically distinct lower-risk MDS populations, both show large transfusion-independence gains. Luspatercept in ring-sideroblast disease (MEDALIST, 229 transfusion-dependent patients): transfusion independence for ≥8 weeks in 38% versus 13% on placebo, and for ≥12 weeks (weeks 1–48) in 33% versus 12%. Lenalidomide in del(5q) disease (MDS-004, 205 patients): transfusion independence for ≥26 weeks in 56.1% (10 mg) and 42.6% (5 mg) versus 5.9% on placebo. The claim carded is transfusion independence in the named subtypes only — neither trial's question was survival, and no survival claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: MEDALIST 2020: luspatercept freed 38% of ring-sideroblast MDS patients from transfusions for at least 8 weeks, versus 13% on placebo
cards.summary: MEDALIST 2020: luspatercept freed 38% of ring-sideroblast MDS patients from transfusions for at least 8 weeks, vs 13% on placebo.
cards.people: 229 patients with very-low, low, or intermediate-risk MDS (Revised IPSS) with ring sideroblasts, receiving regular red-cell transfusions and refractory to, intolerant of, or unlikely to respond to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents; 153 assigned to luspatercept (1.0–1.75 mg/kg subcutaneously every 3 weeks) and 76 to placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Transfusion independence for 8 weeks or longer during weeks 1–24 occurred in 38% on luspatercept versus 13% on placebo (P<0.001). The key secondary endpoint, independence for 12 weeks or longer, was met by 28% versus 8% over weeks 1–24 and 33% versus 12% over weeks 1–48 (P<0.001 for both). The most common luspatercept adverse events were fatigue, diarrhoea, asthenia, nausea and dizziness, decreasing in incidence over time.
cards.watchOut: The population is restricted to ring-sideroblast MDS after erythropoiesis-stimulating-agent failure; results do not extend to other MDS subtypes, and the endpoint is transfusion independence, not leukaemia progression or survival.

cards.summary: MDS-004 2011: lenalidomide freed 56% (10 mg) and 43% (5 mg) of del(5q) patients from transfusions for at least 26 weeks, vs 6% on placebo.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (crossover to lenalidomide allowed after 16 weeks)
cards.people: 205 red-cell transfusion-dependent patients with IPSS Low- or Intermediate-1-risk MDS with del(5q); 69 received lenalidomide 10 mg/day on days 1–21, 69 received 5 mg/day on days 1–28 of 28-day cycles, and 67 received placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.

shelves.title: Lenalidomide maintenance after autologous transplant in myeloma
shelves.question: Does lenalidomide maintenance after stem-cell transplantation prolong progression-free and overall survival — at what second-malignancy price?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Disease-Free Survival · Lenalidomide · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Neoplasms, Second Primary/epidemiology · Stem Cell Transplantation
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — longer time to progression · POSSIBLE — survival benefit — both PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: survival claim). Two placebo-controlled trials agree on progression: CALGB 100104 (460 patients) found median time to progression of 46 versus 27 months, and IFM 2005-02 (614 patients) found median progression-free survival of 41 versus 23 months (hazard ratio 0.50, a relative measure at the solidity threshold). They disagree on survival at the reported horizons: CALGB found fewer deaths on lenalidomide (15% vs 23%, P=0.03), while IFM found overall survival similar at 4 years (more than 70% alive in both groups). Both trials found more second primary cancers on lenalidomide (CALGB 8% vs 3%; IFM 3.1 vs 1.2 per 100 patient-years, P=0.002) and more grade 3–4 haematologic toxicity.

cards.headline: CALGB 100104 2012: lenalidomide maintenance stretched median time to progression to 46 versus 27 months, with fewer deaths (15% vs 23%)
cards.summary: CALGB 100104 2012: lenalidomide maintenance stretched median time to progression to 46 vs 27 months , with fewer deaths (15% vs 23%). (Tier C — survival claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (unblinded in 2009 after a planned interim analysis; placebo patients without progression could cross over)
cards.people: 460 patients younger than 71 years with stable disease or a marginal, partial, or complete response 100 days after autologous stem-cell transplantation for multiple myeloma; 231 assigned to lenalidomide (starting dose 10 mg/day) and 229 to placebo, continued until progression. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: At a median follow-up of 34 months, 37% of lenalidomide patients (86 of 231) versus 58% on placebo (132 of 229) had progressed or died; median time to progression was 46 versus 27 months (P<0.001). Deaths numbered 35 (15%) on lenalidomide versus 53 (23%) on placebo (P=0.03). Second primary cancers occurred in 18 lenalidomide patients (8%) versus 6 (3%) on placebo, and grade 3–4 haematologic and grade 3 non-haematologic adverse events were more frequent with lenalidomide (P<0.001 for both). Of 128 placebo patients without progression at unblinding, 86 crossed over to lenalidomide.
cards.watchOut: Early unblinding and crossover (86 of 128 eligible placebo patients) blur the survival comparison after 2009; the survival difference is carded as reported, and the second-cancer excess is part of the same result, not a footnote.
cards.source: McCarthy PL et al. Lenalidomide after stem-cell transplantation for multiple myeloma. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(19):1770-1781. PMID: 22571201. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00114101, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: IFM 2005-02 2012: lenalidomide maintenance stretched median progression-free survival to 41 versus 23 months (hazard ratio 0.50), with no survival difference at 4 years
cards.summary: IFM 2005-02 2012: lenalidomide maintenance stretched median progression-free survival to 41 vs 23 months (hazard ratio 0.50, relative), with no survival difference at 4 years.
cards.people: 614 patients younger than 65 years with non-progressive disease after first-line autologous transplantation, assigned to lenalidomide maintenance (10 mg/day for 3 months, then 15 mg if tolerated) or placebo until relapse. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 41 months on lenalidomide versus 23 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.50; P<0.001) — a relative measure at the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid, with the median times as the absolute anchor. Second primary cancers occurred at 3.1 per 100 patient-years on lenalidomide versus 1.2 on placebo (P=0.002). cards.headline: Synthesis: progression delayed in both trials; survival verdict split; second cancers are the price — Tier C proposed
cards.summary: Progression delayed in both trials (LIKELY); survival verdict split (POSSIBLE); second cancers are the price — Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CALGB 100104 (460 patients) and IFM 2005-02 (614 patients).

shelves.title: First-line therapy for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: targeted agents vs chemoimmunotherapy
shelves.question: Does ibrutinib beat chlorambucil in older untreated CLL (RESONATE-2) — and does fixed-duration venetoclax–obinutuzumab beat chlorambucil–obinutuzumab (CLL14)?
shelves.mesh: Adenine/analogs & derivatives · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chlorambucil/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Disease-Free Survival · Fatigue/chemically induced · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy,mortality
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — progression-free survival · POSSIBLE — survival benefit — both PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate at topic stage: survival/PFS claims in a cancer shelf; ruled Tier C at build under the brief's mortality-claim rule). Both trials beat their chlorambucil-based controls on progression by wide margins: RESONATE-2 (269 patients aged ≥65) found a hazard ratio of 0.16 for progression or death with ibrutinib, and CLL14 (432 patients with coexisting conditions) found a hazard ratio of 0.35 for venetoclax–obinutuzumab, with 24-month progression-free survival of 88.2% versus 64.1%. On survival they diverge: RESONATE-2 reported 24-month survival of 98% versus 85% (hazard ratio 0.16), while CLL14's all-cause mortality was 9.3% on venetoclax–obinutuzumab versus 7.9% on the control at a median 28.1 months — no survival advantage. Both controls are chlorambucil regimens, a weak comparator by current standards, which is why the survival half stays POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RESONATE-2 2015: ibrutinib beat chlorambucil on progression (hazard ratio 0.16) and 24-month survival (98% vs 85%) in older untreated CLL
cards.summary: RESONATE-2 2015: ibrutinib beat chlorambucil on progression (hazard ratio 0.16, relative) and 24-month survival (98% vs 85%) in older untreated CLL. (Tier C — survival claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 269 previously untreated patients aged 65 years or older with CLL or small lymphocytic lymphoma (median age 73 years), randomised to continuous ibrutinib or chlorambucil; median follow-up 18.4 months. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly longer with ibrutinib (median not reached vs 18.9 months), with a risk of progression or death 84% lower in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.16; P<0.001) — a relative measure well beyond the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Estimated 24-month overall survival was 98% with ibrutinib versus 85% with chlorambucil (hazard ratio for death 0.16; P=0.001). The overall response rate was 86% versus 35% (P<0.001). Among ibrutinib patients, diarrhoea, fatigue, cough and nausea each occurred in at least 20%; four patients had grade 3 haemorrhage and one grade 4. At reporting, 87% of the ibrutinib group remained on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, against chlorambucil alone — the weakest standard comparator — with only 18.4 months' median follow-up at this report; the survival hazard ratio of 0.16 rests on few deaths and is exactly the kind of early extreme estimate that attenuates.

cards.result: Progression-free survival favoured venetoclax–obinutuzumab: 30 versus 77 primary-endpoint events (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.23–0.53; P<0.001) — a relative measure beyond the 0.5–2.0 caution band — with 24-month progression-free survival of 88.2% (83.7–92.6) versus 64.1% (57.4–70.8). The benefit held in TP53-deleted/mutated and IGHV-unmutated subgroups. All-cause mortality was 9.3% with venetoclax–obinutuzumab versus 7.9% with chlorambucil–obinutuzumab. Grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 52.8% versus 48.1%, and grade 3–4 infections in 17.5% versus 15.0%.
cards.watchOut: The comparator shares obinutuzumab with the experimental arm, isolating venetoclax-versus-chlorambucil; mortality at this horizon numerically favoured the control, so any survival claim for the regimen is unsupported by this record.
cards.source: Fischer K et al. Venetoclax and Obinutuzumab in Patients with CLL and Coexisting Conditions. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(23):2225-2236. PMID: 31166681. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02242942, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: targeted first-line regimens clearly delay progression; survival benefit unproven as a class — Tier C proposed
cards.summary: Targeted first-line regimens clearly delay progression (LIKELY); survival benefit unproven as a class (POSSIBLE) — Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RESONATE-2 (269 patients, ibrutinib vs chlorambucil) and CLL14 (432 patients, venetoclax–obinutuzumab vs chlorambucil–obinutuzumab).
cards.result: Progression: hazard ratios of 0.16 and 0.35 against chlorambucil-based controls — LIKELY. Survival: one trial reports a large early advantage (98% vs 85% at 24 months) and the other none (mortality 9.3% vs 7.9%) — POSSIBLE at best, and regimen-specific rather than a class property. The regimens also differ in kind: continuous ibrutinib until progression versus fixed-duration venetoclax–obinutuzumab, a distinction the progression figures alone do not settle.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate head-to-head targeted-agent comparisons; beating chlorambucil is a low bar, and this shelf does not rank ibrutinib against venetoclax-based therapy.
