shelves.title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: polatuzumab with R-CHP (POLARIX) and the R-CHOP benchmark
shelves.question: Does replacing vincristine with polatuzumab vedotin in first-line R-CHOP improve progression-free survival in DLBCL?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cyclophosphamide/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Doxorubicin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Immunoconjugates/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse/drug therapy,mortality · Prednisone/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C at build: the benchmark card carries the survival claim that established R-CHOP). POLARIX (879 patients with intermediate- or high-risk disease) found 2-year progression-free survival of 76.7% with pola-R-CHP versus 70.2% with R-CHOP (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.95; P=0.02) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own — with no survival difference (88.7% vs 88.6% at 2 years; hazard ratio 0.94). A single trial with a modest relative effect caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The benchmark card (Coiffier 2002, 399 patients aged 60–80) is why R-CHOP is the control: adding rituximab to CHOP raised complete responses (76% vs 63%) and reduced the relative risk of death (risk ratio 0.64, 0.45–0.89).

cards.headline: POLARIX 2022: pola-R-CHP improved 2-year progression-free survival (76.7% vs 70.2%; hazard ratio 0.73) with no survival difference
cards.summary: POLARIX 2022: pola-R-CHP improved 2-year progression-free survival ( 76.7% vs 70.2% ; hazard ratio 0.73, relative) with no survival difference.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled international phase 3 trial
cards.people: 879 patients aged 18–80 years with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL; 440 assigned to pola-R-CHP (polatuzumab vedotin replacing vincristine) and 439 to R-CHOP, each for six cycles plus two cycles of rituximab alone; median follow-up 28.2 months. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Two-year progression-free survival was 76.7% (95% CI 72.7–80.8) with pola-R-CHP versus 70.2% (65.8–74.6) with R-CHOP (stratified hazard ratio for progression, relapse, or death 0.73, 0.57–0.95; P=0.02) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute 2-year rates as stated (a 6.5-percentage-point difference). Overall survival at 2 years did not differ: 88.7% (85.7–91.6) versus 88.6% (85.6–91.6) (hazard ratio for death 0.94, 0.65–1.37; P=0.75). The safety profile was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A single trial whose relative effect (0.73) sits in the band this library treats as not solid on its own, in intermediate/high-risk disease only; the survival comparison is null at 2 years and later readouts are not carded here.

cards.headline: Coiffier 2002: adding rituximab to CHOP raised complete responses (76% vs 63%) and reduced the relative risk of death (risk ratio 0.64)
cards.summary: Coiffier 2002: adding rituximab to CHOP raised complete responses (76% vs 63%) and reduced the relative risk of death (risk ratio 0.64, relative). (Tier C — the benchmark card carries a mortality-benefit claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 399 previously untreated patients aged 60–80 years with DLBCL; 202 received eight cycles of CHOP plus rituximab on day 1 of each cycle and 197 received CHOP alone; median follow-up 2 years. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The complete-response rate was 76% with CHOP plus rituximab versus 63% with CHOP alone (P=0.005). Event-free and overall survival were significantly longer with rituximab (P<0.001 and P=0.007); the addition of rituximab reduced the relative risk of treatment failure (risk ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77) and of death (risk ratio 0.64, 0.45–0.89) — relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, carried by the concordant response and survival results of the trial itself. Clinically relevant toxicity was not significantly greater with rituximab.
cards.watchOut: An elderly-only (60–80 years), pre-registration-era trial against CHOP without rituximab — it benchmarks the R in R-CHOP; it is not evidence about any modern modification, and its survival claim is why this shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Coiffier B et al. CHOP chemotherapy plus rituximab compared with CHOP alone in elderly patients with diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(4):235-242. PMID: 11807147. cards.summary: Pola-R-CHP delays progression modestly over a proven benchmark; no survival gain shown — POSSIBLE, Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: POLARIX (879 patients, pola-R-CHP vs R-CHOP) and Coiffier 2002 (399 patients, R-CHOP vs CHOP).
cards.result: The benchmark matters: R-CHOP earned its place with better responses and survival than CHOP (Coiffier). cards.watchOut: Do not present POLARIX as a survival advance; on its own record it is a progression result only.

shelves.title: Platelet transfusion strategy in haematologic malignancy: prophylaxis and dose
shelves.question: Does a no-prophylaxis (therapeutic-only) platelet strategy increase bleeding versus prophylaxis (TOPPS) — and does platelet dose matter (PLADO)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Hematologic Neoplasms/complications,therapy · Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Intention to Treat Analysis · Platelet Count · Platelet Transfusion · Stem Cell Transplantation
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials settle the two halves. TOPPS (600 patients) tested dropping prophylaxis and failed to show non-inferiority: WHO grade 2–4 bleeding occurred in 50% without prophylaxis versus 43% with it (adjusted difference 8.4 percentage points, 90% CI 1.7–15.2; P=0.06 for non-inferiority), with more bleeding days and shorter time to first bleed without prophylaxis — although a prespecified subgroup undergoing autologous transplantation showed similar rates. PLADO (1,272 transfused patients) found bleeding of grade 2 or higher in 71%, 69% and 70% at low, medium and high doses respectively — dose, across a fourfold range, did not change bleeding; the low dose simply used fewer platelets per patient (median 9.25×10¹¹) at the cost of more transfusion episodes (median 5 vs 3). Red-cell transfusion thresholds are Shelf #124 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: TOPPS 2013: dropping platelet prophylaxis increased grade 2–4 bleeding (50% vs 43%) and failed its non-inferiority test
cards.summary: TOPPS 2013: dropping platelet prophylaxis increased grade 2–4 bleeding ( 50% vs 43% ) and failed its non-inferiority test.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, non-inferiority trial (14 centres, UK and Australia)
cards.people: 600 patients aged 16 years or older receiving chemotherapy or stem-cell transplantation for haematologic cancers, with or expected to develop thrombocytopenia; 301 assigned to no prophylaxis and 299 to prophylactic transfusion when morning platelet counts fell below 10×10⁹/L, randomised 2006–2011. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Bleeding of WHO grade 2, 3, or 4 up to 30 days occurred in 151 of 300 patients (50%) without prophylaxis versus 128 of 298 (43%) with prophylaxis (adjusted difference 8.4 percentage points, 90% CI 1.7–15.2; P=0.06 for non-inferiority — non-inferiority not shown). Patients without prophylaxis had more days with bleeding and a shorter time to the first bleeding episode; platelet use was markedly reduced. A prespecified subgroup analysis found similar bleeding rates in the two groups among patients undergoing autologous stem-cell transplantation. A significant number of patients bled despite prophylaxis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a bleeding endpoint assessed clinically; the autologous-transplant subgroup similarity is a subgroup finding, and 43% bleeding even with prophylaxis bounds what prophylaxis can achieve.
cards.source: Stanworth SJ et al. A no-prophylaxis platelet-transfusion strategy for hematologic cancers. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(19):1771-1780. PMID: 23656642. Registry ID: ISRCTN: ISRCTN08758735, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PLADO 2010: platelet dose did not change bleeding (71% vs 69% vs 70% across low, medium and high doses)
cards.summary: PLADO 2010: platelet dose did not change bleeding (71% vs 69% vs 70% across low, medium and high doses).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (dose comparison, prophylactic transfusion at counts ≤10,000 per cubic millimetre)
cards.people: 1,272 hospitalised patients undergoing stem-cell transplantation or chemotherapy for haematologic cancers or solid tumours who received at least one prophylactic platelet transfusion, assigned to low dose (1.1×10¹¹), medium dose (2.2×10¹¹), or high dose (4.4×10¹¹) platelets per square metre of body-surface area. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Bleeding of grade 2 or higher occurred in 71% (low dose), 69% (medium) and 70% (high) — differences not significant — and higher grades of bleeding and other adverse events were similar across groups. The median total platelets transfused per patient was lower at low dose (9.25×10¹¹) than medium (11.25×10¹¹) or high (19.63×10¹¹) (P=0.002 low vs medium; P<0.001 high vs low and high vs medium), but the median number of transfusions was higher at low dose (5 vs 3 and 3; P<0.001). Bleeding occurred on 25% of study days with morning counts ≤5,000 per cubic millimetre versus 17% of days with counts of 6,000–80,000 (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A dose trial within a prophylaxis policy — it cannot answer whether to transfuse at all (that is TOPPS), and its population mixes transplant, haematologic-cancer and solid-tumour patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: keep prophylaxis at the 10×10⁹/L trigger; dose within the tested range does not change bleeding — LIKELY
cards.summary: Keep prophylaxis at the 10×10⁹/L trigger; dose within the tested range does not change bleeding — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TOPPS (600 patients, prophylaxis vs none) and PLADO (1,272 patients, three doses).
cards.result: TOPPS answers the strategy question — abandoning prophylaxis costs bleeding (50% vs 43% grade 2–4, non-inferiority not shown) — and PLADO answers the dose question: across 1.1 to 4.4×10¹¹ platelets per square metre, bleeding is unchanged (69–71%), so the low dose conserves platelets per patient while requiring more episodes. Together they support prophylaxis at the standard trigger with dose chosen on supply and logistics, not on expected bleeding.
cards.watchOut: The autologous-transplant subgroup in TOPPS, where rates looked similar without prophylaxis, is the live uncertainty — it is a subgroup, and this shelf does not card a no-prophylaxis policy for that group.

shelves.title: Subcutaneous vs transvenous ICD: trading lead complications for shocks?
shelves.question: In patients who need a defibrillator but not pacing, does a fully subcutaneous ICD match a transvenous ICD on complications and inappropriate shocks (PRAETORIAN, ATLAS)?
shelves.mesh: Arrhythmias, Cardiac/therapy · Cardiomyopathies/therapy · Death, Sudden, Cardiac/epidemiology,prevention & control · Defibrillators, Implantable/adverse effects · Electrodes, Implanted/adverse effects · Equipment Failure · Heart Diseases/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the trade-off, not a winner): Two randomised trials and their individual-patient-data pooling agree on the shape of the exchange. The subcutaneous ICD avoids the vein and the lead: perioperative lead-related complications were 0.4% vs 4.8% in ATLAS, and device-related complications ran lower in PRAETORIAN (hazard ratio 0.69). In return it shocks inappropriately more often — the pooled first-inappropriate-shock rate was 2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.61, a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on its own, though here it is pooled randomised data, not an observational claim). PRAETORIAN's composite of complications plus inappropriate shocks was noninferior (hazard ratio 0.99). Who benefits from a prophylactic ICD at all is Shelf #90; this shelf is only about which box, once one is chosen.

cards.headline: PRAETORIAN 2020: subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to transvenous ICD on complications plus inappropriate shocks — hazard ratio 0.99
cards.summary: PRAETORIAN 2020: subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to transvenous ICD on complications plus inappropriate shocks — hazard ratio 0.99.
cards.people: 849 patients with an indication for an ICD but no indication for pacing, randomised to subcutaneous ICD (426) or transvenous ICD (423); median follow-up 49.1 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: A primary end-point event (device-related complications or inappropriate shocks) occurred in 68 patients in each group (48-month Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence 15.1% vs 15.7%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.39; P=0.01 for noninferiority, P=0.95 for superiority). Device-related complications occurred in 31 vs 44 patients (hazard ratio 0.69, 0.44 to 1.09) and inappropriate shocks in 41 vs 29 (hazard ratio 1.43, 0.89 to 2.30). Death occurred in 83 vs 68 patients (hazard ratio 1.23, 0.89 to 1.70) and appropriate shocks in 83 vs 57 (hazard ratio 1.52, 1.08 to 2.12) — secondary figures, printed because this shelf's trade-off cannot be read without them.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on a composite that mixes the two opposing harms can hide the trade-off inside it; the component figures above are the shelf's real content. Device trials cannot be blinded.
cards.source: Knops RE et al. Subcutaneous or Transvenous Defibrillator Therapy. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(6):526-536. PMID: 32757521. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01296022, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ATLAS 2022: lead-related perioperative complications 0.4% with subcutaneous vs 4.8% with transvenous ICD
cards.summary: ATLAS 2022: lead-related perioperative complications 0.4% with subcutaneous vs 4.8% with transvenous ICD.
cards.people: 544 eligible patients with a primary or secondary prevention ICD indication who were younger than 60 years, had a cardiogenetic phenotype, or had prespecified risk factors for lead complications; 503 randomised to subcutaneous ICD (251) or transvenous ICD (252); mean age 49.0 years (SD 11.5); 141 of the 544 eligible patients were female; mean follow-up 2.5 years (SD 1.1).
cards.result: Perioperative major lead-related complications occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) with a subcutaneous ICD and 12 patients (4.8%) with a transvenous ICD (difference −4.4 percentage points, 95% CI −6.9 to −1.9; P=0.001). There was a trend to more inappropriate shocks with the subcutaneous device (hazard ratio 2.37, 0.98 to 5.77 — a relative figure) and no increase in failed appropriate shocks (hazard ratio 0.61, 0.15 to 2.57). Implant-site pain was higher with the subcutaneous device on the day of implant (4.2 vs 2.9 on a 10-point scale; P<0.001) and at 1 month (1.3 vs 0.9; P=0.035).
cards.watchOut: A younger, lead-risk-enriched population (mean age 49) — the lead-complication advantage may be smaller in older, lower-risk recipients; the trial states it is as yet underpowered for clinical shock outcomes, with extended follow-up ongoing.

cards.headline: IPD meta-analysis 2026: first inappropriate shock was more frequent with subcutaneous ICDs — 2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years
cards.summary: IPD meta-analysis 2026: first inappropriate shock was more frequent with subcutaneous ICDs — 2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years.
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Pooled modified intention-to-treat population of PRAETORIAN and ATLAS: 1,342 patients randomised to subcutaneous or transvenous ICD; median age 58 years, 21.8% women, 77.7% primary-prevention indications; median follow-up 3.5 years.
cards.result: A first inappropriate shock occurred more frequently with subcutaneous ICDs (2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years; hazard ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.45; P=0.03 — a relative figure). By cause, subcutaneous devices had a higher hazard of inappropriate shock from cardiac oversensing (hazard ratio 15.07, 3.60 to 63.15) and electromagnetic interference or myopotentials (hazard ratio 8.19, 1.88 to 35.64), but a lower hazard from atrial arrhythmia (hazard ratio 0.37, 0.19 to 0.71). cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PRAETORIAN (849 patients), ATLAS (503 randomised) and their individual-patient-data pooling (1,342 patients).
cards.result: No trial shows one device better overall: PRAETORIAN's composite was a dead heat (68 events in each arm), ATLAS shows the lead-complication gap at its widest in young, lead-risk patients (0.4% vs 4.8%), and the pooling shows the inappropriate-shock gap (2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years). A patient with decades of lead life ahead, difficult venous access or infection risk buys the subcutaneous trade gladly; a patient in whom an inappropriate shock would be especially harmful, or who may later need pacing or resynchronisation the subcutaneous box cannot give, may not. shelves.title: Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator after myocardial infarction (VEST)
shelves.question: In patients with a low ejection fraction early after MI, does wearing a defibrillator vest until reassessment reduce arrhythmic death?
shelves.mesh: Death, Sudden, Cardiac/etiology,prevention & control · Defibrillators/adverse effects · Myocardial Infarction/complications,mortality,therapy · Stroke Volume · Tachycardia, Ventricular/mortality,prevention & control · Wearable Electronic Devices/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on arrhythmic death) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: arrhythmic-mortality claim): The single large trial, VEST (2,302 patients), found the wearable defibrillator did not significantly reduce its primary outcome of arrhythmic death at 90 days (1.6% vs 2.4%; relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.21; P=0.18 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, with absolute rates beside it). All-cause death was lower in the device group (3.1% vs 4.9%; relative risk 0.64) but at an uncorrected P=0.04 on a secondary outcome, in a trial whose primary outcome was null — that is hypothesis-grade, not a mortality claim this shelf will make. A very large single null trial can carry LIKELY for the null; the stamp is proposed, Tier C, pending the developer's verdict.

cards.headline: VEST 2018: the vest did not significantly reduce arrhythmic death at 90 days — 1.6% vs 2.4%, relative risk 0.67 (CI crosses 1)
cards.summary: VEST 2018: the vest did not significantly reduce arrhythmic death at 90 days — 1.6% vs 2.4% , relative risk 0.67 (CI crosses 1); all-cause death 3.1% vs 4.9% printed beside it. (Tier C — mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (2:1 allocation, unblinded device)
cards.people: 2,302 patients with acute myocardial infarction and an ejection fraction of 35% or less, randomised to a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator plus guideline-directed therapy (1,524) or guideline-directed therapy alone (778). Device-group participants wore the device a median of 18.0 hours per day (interquartile range 3.8 to 22.7). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Arrhythmic death (the primary outcome: sudden death or death from ventricular tachyarrhythmia at 90 days) occurred in 1.6% of the device group and 2.4% of controls (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.21; P=0.18). Death from any cause occurred in 3.1% vs 4.9% (relative risk 0.64, 0.43 to 0.98; uncorrected P=0.04) and nonarrhythmic death in 1.4% vs 2.2% (relative risk 0.63, 0.33 to 1.19; uncorrected P=0.15). Of the 48 device-group participants who died, 12 were wearing the device at the time of death. In the device group, 20 participants (1.3%) received an appropriate shock and 9 (0.6%) an inappropriate shock.
cards.watchOut: The all-cause mortality difference is a secondary outcome with an uncorrected P value in a trial that missed its primary outcome — and a vest cannot explain fewer nonarrhythmic deaths, which is exactly why it should not be read as proof the device saves lives overall. Wear time varied widely (interquartile range 3.8–22.7 hours/day).

shelves.title: Ablation as first-line treatment for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
shelves.question: In symptomatic paroxysmal AF, does first-line cryoballoon ablation prevent recurrence better than starting with antiarrhythmic drugs (EARLY-AF, STOP AF First)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy,prevention & control,surgery · Atrial Flutter · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects · Cryosurgery · Heart Rate · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials of first-line cryoballoon ablation in drug-naïve symptomatic paroxysmal AF agree. EARLY-AF (303 patients, continuous implantable monitoring) found recurrence of any atrial tachyarrhythmia in 42.9% with ablation vs 67.8% with drugs at 1 year (hazard ratio 0.48 — a relative figure at the edge of this library's 0.5 solidity threshold, with the absolute rates beside it). STOP AF First (203 patients) found 12-month treatment success of 74.6% vs 45.0% (P<0.001). Serious adverse events were uncommon and similar in both. The claim is recurrence and symptoms only: whether ablation improves hard outcomes in established AF is Shelf #271, and early rhythm control as a strategy is Shelf #273 — neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: EARLY-AF 2021: first-line cryoablation halved recurrence vs drugs — 42.9% vs 67.8% at 1 year, hazard ratio 0.48
cards.summary: EARLY-AF 2021: first-line cryoablation halved recurrence vs drugs — 42.9% vs 67.8% at 1 year, hazard ratio 0.48, relative. (The topic file had swapped the EARLY-AF / STOP AF First PMIDs; the cards follow the records.)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with implantable continuous rhythm monitoring in all patients
cards.people: 303 patients with symptomatic, paroxysmal, previously untreated atrial fibrillation, randomised to cryoballoon catheter ablation (154) or antiarrhythmic drug therapy (149) as initial rhythm control; follow-up 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Recurrence of any atrial tachyarrhythmia between days 91 and 365 occurred in 66 of 154 ablation patients (42.9%) and 101 of 149 drug patients (67.8%) (hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; P<0.001 — a relative figure). Symptomatic recurrence occurred in 11.0% vs 26.2% (hazard ratio 0.39, 0.22 to 0.68). The median percentage of time in atrial fibrillation was 0% (interquartile range 0 to 0.08) with ablation and 0.13% (0 to 1.60) with drugs. Serious adverse events occurred in 5 ablation patients (3.2%) and 6 drug patients (4.0%).
cards.watchOut: One year of follow-up in relatively young, drug-naïve paroxysmal disease, with recurrence detected by implanted monitors patients in ordinary care do not have; the endpoint is rhythm, not stroke, hospitalisation or death.

cards.headline: STOP AF First 2021: first-line cryoballoon treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0% with drugs at 12 months
cards.summary: STOP AF First 2021: first-line cryoballoon treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0% with drugs at 12 months.
cards.people: 203 participants aged 18 to 80 years with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation not previously treated with rhythm-control therapy, who underwent randomisation and received treatment: cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation (104) or antiarrhythmic drugs, class I or III (99); monitoring included scheduled ECGs, weekly patient-activated telephone monitoring and 24-hour ambulatory monitoring.
cards.result: Initial procedural success was achieved in 97% of the ablation group. The Kaplan–Meier estimate of treatment success at 12 months (freedom from initial failure or atrial arrhythmia recurrence after a 90-day blanking period) was 74.6% (95% CI 65.0 to 82.0) with ablation and 45.0% (34.6 to 54.7) with drugs (P<0.001 by log-rank test). cards.headline: Synthesis: first-line cryoablation beats starting with drugs on recurrence — LIKELY, for rhythm outcomes only
cards.summary: First-line cryoablation beats starting with drugs on recurrence — LIKELY, for rhythm outcomes only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EARLY-AF (303 patients, continuous monitoring) and STOP AF First (203 patients, intermittent monitoring).
cards.result: Two trials, two monitoring intensities, one direction: first-line cryoballoon ablation kept roughly 25–30 percentage points more patients free of recurrence at one year than starting with antiarrhythmic drugs (42.9% vs 67.8% recurrence in EARLY-AF; 74.6% vs 45.0% treatment success in STOP AF First), with serious adverse events in the 2–4% range in both arms of both trials. That earns LIKELY for the rhythm claim in drug-naïve paroxysmal AF. It says nothing about ablation after drugs have failed, about radiofrequency ablation as first line, or about hard outcomes — Shelf #271 (ablation and hard outcomes in established AF) and Shelf #273 (early rhythm-control strategy) hold those questions and are pointed to, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled symptomatic paroxysmal patients willing to have a procedure; asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic patients were not the population tested.

shelves.title: Catheter ablation for ventricular tachycardia in ischaemic cardiomyopathy
shelves.question: In patients with prior MI, an ICD, and recurrent VT, does catheter ablation beat escalating antiarrhythmic drugs — and does ablating after the first shock beat waiting (VANISH, PARTITA)?
shelves.mesh: Amiodarone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cardiomyopathies/complications,mortality · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects · Defibrillators, Implantable · Disease-Free Survival · Myocardial Infarction/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both anchors' composites include death): VANISH (259 patients) found ablation lowered a composite of death, VT storm or appropriate ICD shock vs escalating antiarrhythmic drugs (59.1% vs 68.5%; hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.98 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, not solid on its own) with no significant mortality difference on its own. PARTITA found ablating immediately after the first ICD shock markedly lowered a composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (4% vs 42%; hazard ratio 0.11) — but in only 47 randomised patients, in a trial stopped early at interim analysis, the exact setting in which effects inflate. Direction is consistent, proof is not yet strong: POSSIBLE, and Tier C because death sits inside both composites; heart-failure figures are printed with mortality beside them on every card, per this library's rule.

cards.headline: VANISH 2016: ablation beat escalating drugs on death, VT storm or ICD shock — 59.1% vs 68.5%, hazard ratio 0.72; mortality itself did not differ
cards.summary: VANISH 2016: ablation beat escalating drugs on death, VT storm or ICD shock — 59.1% vs 68.5%, hazard ratio 0.72, relative; mortality itself did not differ (printed on the card). (Tier C — death inside the composite; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 259 patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and an ICD who had ventricular tachycardia despite antiarrhythmic drug therapy, randomised to catheter ablation with continuation of baseline drugs (132) or escalated drug therapy (127: amiodarone started, dose increased, or mexiletine added); mean follow-up 27.9 months (SD 17.1). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (death, three or more VT episodes within 24 hours [VT storm], or appropriate ICD shock) occurred in 59.1% of the ablation group and 68.5% of the escalated-therapy group (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.98; P=0.04 — a relative figure). There was no significant between-group difference in mortality. Harms split by arm: two cardiac perforations and three major bleeds with ablation; two deaths from pulmonary toxicity and one from hepatic dysfunction with escalated drugs.
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven by arrhythmia events, not survival — mortality did not differ, and the hazard ratio of 0.72 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid evidence on its own. Unblinded procedural trial, as all such trials are.

cards.headline: PARTITA 2022: ablation right after the first ICD shock — composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation 4% vs 42%, but only 47 patients randomised
cards.summary: PARTITA 2022: ablation right after the first ICD shock — composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation 4% vs 42%, but only 47 patients randomised.
cards.type: Two-phase prospective multicentre randomised trial (Bayesian adaptive design, stopped early at interim analysis)
cards.people: 517 patients with ischaemic or non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy and an ICD were enrolled in an observational phase until a first appropriate shock; 56 received a shock over a median 2.4 years, 47 reconsented and were randomised to immediate ablation (23, within 2 months of the shock) or standard therapy (24). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: After a median of about 24 months, the primary endpoint (death from any cause or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure) occurred in 1 of 23 ablation patients (4%) and 10 of 24 controls (42%) (hazard ratio 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.85; P=0.034 — a relative figure). Deaths: none in the ablation group vs 8 (33%) in controls (P=0.004); worsening-heart-failure hospitalisation 1 (4%) vs 4 (17%) (P=0.159) — the heart-failure figure printed with its mortality beside it, as this library requires. ICD shocks were less frequent with ablation (9% vs 42%; P=0.039). Amiodarone was not allowed except for documented atrial tachyarrhythmias.
cards.watchOut: Forty-seven randomised patients and a trial stopped at its first interim analysis for crossing a Bayesian superiority criterion: effects estimated at early stops are systematically too large. The mortality split (0 vs 8) is the kind of number that regresses hard in any replication — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE and Tier C, not more.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ablation helps arrhythmia outcomes; the survival question is open — POSSIBLE, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: Ablation helps arrhythmia outcomes; the survival question is open — POSSIBLE, proposed (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VANISH (259 patients, VT despite drugs) and PARTITA (47 randomised after a first shock, from 517 enrolled).
cards.result: The two trials test different moments — ablation instead of escalating drugs once VT breaks through (VANISH: composite 59.1% vs 68.5%, mortality not significantly different) and ablation immediately at the first shock (PARTITA: composite 4% vs 42%, deaths 0 vs 8, in 47 patients). Together they support ablation as the better arrhythmia strategy and raise, but do not settle, a survival benefit. Until a larger trial confirms PARTITA's mortality split, the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf sits in the Tier C slow lane for the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote PARTITA's 0 vs 8 deaths without its denominator (47 randomised) and its early stop in the same sentence.

shelves.title: Cardiac resynchronization in narrow QRS: the EchoCRT harm
shelves.question: In heart failure with a narrow QRS but echocardiographic dyssynchrony, does CRT help — or harm (EchoCRT)?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm / no benefit) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality harm signal): EchoCRT (809 randomised patients with QRS <130 ms and echocardiographic dyssynchrony) was stopped for futility and found no reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalisation with CRT switched on (28.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 1.20) and more deaths (11.1% vs 6.4%; hazard ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.93 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, printed with its absolute rates). A large trial stopped early with a null primary and a mortality signal in the wrong direction carries LIKELY for 'do not do this'. This is the mirror image of Shelf #274, where CRT in wide-QRS heart failure is carded; the wide-QRS trials are not re-carded here. Heart-failure figures are printed with mortality beside them throughout.

cards.people: 809 patients at 115 centres with NYHA class III or IV heart failure, left ventricular ejection fraction 35% or less, QRS duration less than 130 ms, and echocardiographic evidence of left ventricular dyssynchrony, randomised to CRT-on (404) or CRT-off (405); mean follow-up 19.4 months at study closure. cards.result: The primary outcome (death from any cause or first hospitalisation for worsening heart failure) occurred in 116 of 404 CRT patients and 102 of 405 controls (28.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.57; P=0.15) — printed with its mortality beside it: deaths were 45 vs 26 (11.1% vs 6.4%; hazard ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.93; P=0.02 — a relative figure). cards.watchOut: The mortality excess is a secondary outcome in a trial stopped for futility — but with a null primary leaning the wrong way (hazard ratio 1.20) there is no reading of this trial in which narrow-QRS CRT helps. shelves.title: Transcatheter tricuspid repair for severe tricuspid regurgitation (TRILUMINATE)
shelves.question: In severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation, does edge-to-edge repair improve quality of life versus medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Catheterization/adverse effects,methods · Heart Failure/etiology · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/adverse effects,methods · Tricuspid Valve Insufficiency/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single pivotal trial, TRILUMINATE Pivotal (350 patients), found percutaneous tricuspid edge-to-edge repair beat medical therapy on a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.48) — but the win was carried by quality of life: the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score rose 12.3 points with repair vs 0.6 with control (P<0.001), while death or tricuspid surgery and heart-failure hospitalisation did not differ between groups (the heart-failure figure printed with mortality beside it, per this library's rule — neither is carded as a benefit). Repair did reduce regurgitation severity (87.0% vs 4.8% at no more than moderate at 30 days) and was safe (98.3% free of major adverse events at 30 days). One trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the claim carded is quality of life, nothing harder. Mitral repair for secondary MR is Shelf #550 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: TRILUMINATE Pivotal 2023: tricuspid repair improved quality of life (KCCQ +12.3 vs +0.6 points) but death/surgery and heart-failure hospitalisation did not differ
cards.summary: TRILUMINATE Pivotal 2023: tricuspid repair improved quality of life (KCCQ +12.3 vs +0.6 points) but death/surgery and heart-failure hospitalisation did not differ (printed together on the card).
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (open-label device vs medical therapy)
cards.people: 350 patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation at 65 centres in the United States, Canada and Europe, randomised 1:1 to transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (175) or medical therapy (175); mean age 78 years; 54.9% women; primary end point assessed at 1 year.
cards.result: The hierarchical primary end point (death from any cause or tricuspid-valve surgery; hospitalisation for heart failure; or an improvement of at least 15 points in KCCQ score) favoured repair (win ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.13; P=0.02). The incidence of death or tricuspid-valve surgery and the rate of hospitalisation for heart failure did not appear to differ between the groups — the heart-failure component printed with mortality beside it, neither showing a difference. KCCQ score changed by a mean of 12.3 (SD 1.8) points with repair vs 0.6 (1.8) with control (P<0.001). At 30 days, 87.0% of repair patients vs 4.8% of controls had tricuspid regurgitation of no greater than moderate severity (P<0.001), and 98.3% of patients who underwent the procedure were free from major adverse events at 30 days.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded trial whose composite win is a quality-of-life win: patients who know they received a device report feeling better, and there was no sham control. No mortality or hospitalisation benefit was shown at 1 year, and the abstract reports those components qualitatively ('did not appear to differ'), so no rates are invented here.
cards.source: Sorajja P et al. Transcatheter Repair for Patients with Tricuspid Regurgitation. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(20):1833-1842. PMID: 36876753. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03904147, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: repair makes severe tricuspid regurgitation smaller and patients feel better — POSSIBLE, quality of life only
cards.summary: Repair makes severe tricuspid regurgitation smaller and patients feel better — POSSIBLE, quality of life only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: TRILUMINATE Pivotal (350 patients, 1 year).
cards.result: One trial: a real mechanical effect (87.0% vs 4.8% reduced to moderate-or-less regurgitation), a real quality-of-life effect (KCCQ +12.3 vs +0.6), and no shown difference in death, valve surgery or heart-failure hospitalisation. The stamp is POSSIBLE because a single pivotal trial is the whole evidence base and its hardest endpoints were neutral. Any future claim that tricuspid repair prolongs life or keeps patients out of hospital will need a trial powered to show it.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise to asymptomatic or moderate tricuspid regurgitation, or to surgical-risk populations unlike this elderly (mean age 78) symptomatic cohort.

shelves.title: Mitral repair vs replacement surgery for primary (degenerative) mitral regurgitation (EVEREST II)
shelves.question: For severe degenerative mitral regurgitation, how does percutaneous edge-to-edge repair compare with surgery on effectiveness and safety?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure/epidemiology · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/methods · Intention to Treat Analysis · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Mitral Valve/surgery · Mitral Valve Insufficiency/classification,mortality,surgery,therapy · Postoperative Complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised comparison, EVEREST II (279 patients), found percutaneous clip repair less effective than surgery at 12 months on its efficacy composite (freedom from death, surgery for valve dysfunction, or grade 3+/4+ regurgitation: 55% vs 73%; P=0.007) — the gap driven by more patients needing surgery after the clip (20% vs 2%), with death identical (6% in each group; mortality printed beside every figure here per this library's rule) — but much safer at 30 days (major adverse events 15% vs 48%). Both groups improved in ventricular size, functional class and quality of life. One trial, from the first-generation device era, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Transcatheter repair for SECONDARY (functional) MR is Shelf #550 (COAPT/MITRA-FR) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: EVEREST II 2011: the clip was less effective than surgery at 12 months (55% vs 73% free of the efficacy composite) but safer at 30 days (major adverse events 15% vs 48%); death was 6% in both groups
cards.summary: EVEREST II 2011: the clip was less effective than surgery at 12 months (55% vs 73% free of the efficacy composite; death 6% in each group) but safer at 30 days.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (2:1 allocation, percutaneous repair vs conventional surgery)
cards.people: 279 patients with moderately severe or severe (grade 3+ or 4+) mitral regurgitation, randomised 2:1 to percutaneous edge-to-edge clip repair or conventional surgery (repair or replacement). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 12 months the primary efficacy end point (freedom from death, from surgery for mitral-valve dysfunction, and from grade 3+ or 4+ mitral regurgitation) was reached by 55% of the percutaneous group and 73% of the surgery group (P=0.007). Components: death 6% in each group; surgery for valve dysfunction 20% vs 2%; grade 3+ or 4+ regurgitation 21% vs 20%. Major adverse events within 30 days occurred in 15% of the percutaneous group and 48% of the surgery group (P<0.001). At 12 months both groups had improved left ventricular size, NYHA functional class and quality-of-life measures versus baseline.
cards.watchOut: A 2011 first-generation-device trial in patients eligible for surgery: later devices, operator experience and imaging have moved on, and the result does not answer the clip question in patients surgery cannot take — that population's evidence (secondary MR) is Shelf #550.
cards.source: Feldman T et al. Percutaneous Repair or Surgery for Mitral Regurgitation. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(15):1395-1406. PMID: 21463154. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00209274, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery fixes degenerative MR more durably; the clip trades durability for safety — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Surgery fixes degenerative MR more durably; the clip trades durability for safety — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: EVEREST II (279 surgical candidates with grade 3+/4+ mitral regurgitation).
cards.result: Read component by component, the trial is unusually clear: same deaths (6% vs 6%), same residual severe regurgitation (21% vs 20%), but one in five clip patients came to surgery within a year vs one in fifty surgical patients — while the surgical group's early major-adverse-event rate was three times the clip's (48% vs 15%). For a good surgical candidate with degenerative disease, surgery remained the more definitive fix; the clip's case rests on safety and on patients unlike those enrolled. A single trial keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: The 48% surgical major-adverse-event rate includes transfusion-era events of its time; do not carry that exact figure into a modern consent conversation without contemporary local rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feldman T et al. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(15):1395-1406. PMID: 21463154. Registry ID as on the card above.

shelves.title: Antithrombotic therapy after TAVR: when anticoagulation harmed (GALILEO, ATLANTIS)
shelves.question: After transcatheter aortic valve replacement, does routine anticoagulation (rivaroxaban, apixaban) beat antiplatelet-based standard care — or cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Aspirin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Clopidogrel/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heart Valve Prosthesis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (routine anticoagulation does not help, and rivaroxaban harmed) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: GALILEO carries a mortality harm claim): GALILEO (1,644 patients without an anticoagulation indication) was stopped early for safety: rivaroxaban 10 mg produced more death or thromboembolic events than an antiplatelet strategy (9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.35) and more deaths (5.8 vs 3.4 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.69 — relative figures, absolute rates beside them). ATLANTIS (1,500 patients) found apixaban not superior to standard care on its primary composite (18.4% vs 20.1%; hazard ratio 0.92), with less obstructive valve thrombosis but a signal of higher non-cardiovascular mortality in the no-indication stratum. Two trials, no benefit, one clear harm: LIKELY, proposed in the Tier C lane. TAVR versus surgery is Shelf #266 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: GALILEO 2020: rivaroxaban after TAVR caused more death or thromboembolism (9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years) and more deaths (5.8 vs 3.4) — trial stopped early for safety
cards.summary: GALILEO 2020: rivaroxaban after TAVR caused more death or thromboembolism (9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years) and more deaths (5.8 vs 3.4) — trial stopped. (Tier C — harm; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, terminated prematurely by the data and safety monitoring board because of safety concerns
cards.people: 1,644 patients without an established indication for oral anticoagulation after successful TAVR, randomised to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (with aspirin for the first 3 months) or aspirin (with clopidogrel for the first 3 months); median follow-up 17 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Death or a first thromboembolic event occurred in 105 rivaroxaban patients and 78 antiplatelet patients (incidence 9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.81; P=0.04 — a relative figure). Major, disabling or life-threatening bleeding occurred in 46 vs 31 patients (4.3 vs 2.8 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.50, 0.95 to 2.37; P=0.08). Deaths numbered 64 vs 38 (5.8 vs 3.4 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.69, 1.13 to 2.53).
cards.watchOut: The rivaroxaban dose was 10 mg — below the full anticoagulant dose — so the trial condemns this strategy at this dose after TAVR, not anticoagulation for patients who have their own indication (atrial fibrillation, thrombus), who were excluded.
cards.source: Dangas GD et al. A Controlled Trial of Rivaroxaban after Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(2):120-129. PMID: 31733180. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02556203, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ATLANTIS 2022: apixaban was not superior to standard care after TAVI (18.4% vs 20.1%; hazard ratio 0.92) — less valve thrombosis, a non-cardiovascular mortality signal in the no-indication stratum
cards.summary: ATLANTIS 2022: apixaban was not superior to standard care after TAVI (18.4% vs 20.1%; hazard ratio 0.92) — less valve thrombosis, a non-cardiovascular death signal noted on the card.
cards.type: International, randomised, open-label superiority trial, stratified by anticoagulation indication
cards.people: 1,500 patients after successful TAVI, randomised to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (749; 2.5 mg if impaired renal function or concomitant antiplatelet therapy) or standard of care (751): vitamin K antagonist if an anticoagulation indication existed (stratum 1, n=451) or antiplatelet therapy if not (stratum 2, n=1,049); follow-up 1 year. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (death, myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, systemic embolism, intracardiac or bioprosthesis thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, and life-threatening, disabling or major bleeding) occurred in 138 apixaban patients (18.4%) and 151 standard-care patients (20.1%) (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.16 — a relative figure), with no interaction by stratum (P=0.57). The primary safety end point (major, disabling or life-threatening bleeding) was similar (hazard ratio 1.02, 0.72 to 1.44). In stratum 2, obstructive valve thrombosis was lower with apixaban (hazard ratio 0.19, 0.08 to 0.46) while a signal of higher non-cardiovascular mortality was observed with apixaban — reported qualitatively in the abstract, so no invented rate is printed here.
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial against a two-stratum standard of care: 'not superior overall' mixes patients with and without an anticoagulation indication, and the valve-thrombosis win is an imaging endpoint that did not translate into a better primary outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: after TAVR, anticoagulate for an indication, not by routine — LIKELY, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: After TAVR, anticoagulate for an indication, not by routine — LIKELY, proposed (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: GALILEO (1,644 patients, no anticoagulation indication) and ATLANTIS (1,500 patients, stratified by indication).
cards.result: Two different anticoagulants, two designs, one conclusion: routine anticoagulation after TAVR bought no protection. Rivaroxaban actively harmed (death or thromboembolism 9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years; deaths 5.8 vs 3.4); apixaban was neutral overall (hazard ratio 0.92) with an imaging win on valve thrombosis that never surfaced in clinical outcomes. Antiplatelet-based care remains the default for patients without their own indication for anticoagulation. The stamp is LIKELY and the shelf is Tier C — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict — because its load-bearing claim is a mortality harm.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here touches patients with atrial fibrillation or another standing indication for anticoagulation after TAVR; ATLANTIS's stratum 1 comparison (apixaban vs vitamin K antagonist) showed no difference and is a separate, narrower question.

shelves.title: Stent-grafting for uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (INSTEAD-XL)
shelves.question: In stable, uncomplicated type B dissection, does pre-emptive thoracic endovascular repair plus medical therapy beat medical therapy alone over five years?
shelves.mesh: Aortic Dissection/mortality,pathology,surgery · Aorta, Thoracic/pathology · Aortic Aneurysm, Thoracic/mortality,pathology,surgery · Blood Vessel Prosthesis Implantation/methods · Disease Progression · Proportional Hazards Models · Stents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: aorta-related mortality claim at 5 years): INSTEAD-XL's 5-year analysis of 140 randomised patients found aorta-specific mortality lower with stent-grafting plus medical therapy than with medical therapy alone (6.9% vs 19.3%; P=0.04), with all-cause mortality not significantly different (11.1% vs 19.3%; P=0.13) — mortality figures always printed in pairs on this shelf. But the long-term analysis rests on landmark analyses of a small trial, and the second randomised trial, ADSORB (61 patients), showed only a 1-year remodelling benefit with no deaths in either arm at 30 days and one death by 1 year in the stent group. Two small trials, one surrogate and one fragile long-term signal: POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only. Aneurysm repair (EVAR) is Shelf #553, a different disease, and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: INSTEAD-XL 2013: at 5 years, aorta-specific mortality was 6.9% with stent-graft plus medical therapy vs 19.3% with medical therapy alone; all-cause mortality 11.1% vs 19.3% (not significant)
cards.summary: INSTEAD-XL 2013: at 5 years, aorta-specific mortality was 6.9% with stent-graft plus medical therapy vs 19.3% with medical therapy alone; all-cause mortality 11.1% vs 19.3% — the two printed together. (Tier C — mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Long-term (5-year) analysis of a randomised trial, with landmark analyses of years 2–5
cards.people: 140 patients with stable type B aortic dissection previously randomised to optimal medical treatment plus thoracic endovascular repair (72) or optimal medical treatment alone (68); analyses intention-to-treat. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 5 years the risk of aorta-specific mortality was 6.9% with stent-grafting vs 19.3% with medical therapy alone (P=0.04); all-cause mortality was 11.1% vs 19.3% (P=0.13) — the two mortality figures printed together, as this library requires. Disease progression was 27.0% vs 46.1% (P=0.04). Landmark analysis of years 2–5 suggested benefit on all end points (for example all-cause mortality 0% vs 16.9%, P=0.0003, and aorta-specific mortality 0% vs 16.9%, P=0.0005, in that window). Improved survival and less progression were associated with stent-graft-induced false-lumen thrombosis, present in 90.6% of cases.
cards.watchOut: A 140-patient trial whose late benefit emerges in landmark (survivor-window) analyses: patients had to survive the early period to enter the window in which the benefit appears, and the headline all-cause mortality difference is not significant. This is a signal to weigh in selected anatomy, not proof for all uncomplicated dissections.
cards.source: Nienaber CA et al. Endovascular Repair of Type B Aortic Dissection: Long-Term Results of the Randomized Investigation of Stent Grafts in Aortic Dissection Trial. cards.headline: ADSORB 2014: stent-grafting remodelled the aorta at 1 year (incomplete false-lumen thrombosis 43% vs 97%) but the trial was far too small for mortality — one death, in the stent group
cards.summary: ADSORB 2014: stent-grafting remodelled the aorta at 1 year (incomplete false-lumen thrombosis 43% vs 97%) but the trial was far too small for mortality.
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (best medical treatment vs best medical treatment plus stent graft)
cards.people: 61 patients with acute uncomplicated type B aortic dissection of less than 14 days' history (80% DeBakey type IIIB), randomised to medical treatment alone (31) or medical treatment plus a Gore TAG stent graft (30); mean age 63 years in both groups; rupture, impending rupture and malperfusion were exclusions.
cards.result: The primary end point (incomplete or no false-lumen thrombosis, aortic dilatation, or aortic rupture at 1 year) favoured the stent group (P<0.001 for the overall end point): incomplete false-lumen thrombosis was found in 13 of the stent group (43%) vs 30 of the medical group (97%) (P<0.001), the false lumen shrank with the stent and grew without it, and the true lumen increased only in the stent group. In the first 30 days there were no deaths in either group; three medical-group patients crossed over to stent-grafting for disease progression within a week. By 1 year, one death had occurred — in the stent-graft group — alongside two further medical-group failures (one malperfusion, one aneurysm formation).
cards.watchOut: A 61-patient, 1-year remodelling trial: every clinical figure in it is a handful of events, and its only death fell in the stent arm. It supports the mechanism (false-lumen thrombosis and remodelling) behind INSTEAD-XL's late signal; it cannot support a survival claim of its own — mortality is printed beside its remodelling figures for exactly that reason.
cards.source: Brunkwall J et al. Endovascular Repair of Acute Uncomplicated Aortic Type B Dissection Promotes Aortic Remodelling: 1 Year Results of the ADSORB Trial. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg. 2014;48(3):285-291. PMID: 24962744. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00742274, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Ablate-and-pace for permanent atrial fibrillation (APAF-CRT, PABA-CHF)
shelves.question: In permanent AF with heart failure, does AV-junction ablation plus resynchronization (or pulmonary-vein isolation) beat pharmacological rate control?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation/therapy · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Research Design · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/physiopathology,surgery,therapy · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Catheter Ablation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: APAF-CRT carries a mortality claim): APAF-CRT (133 patients with severely symptomatic permanent AF, narrow QRS and a recent heart-failure hospitalisation) was stopped early for efficacy: all-cause mortality was 11% with ablation plus CRT vs 29% with pharmacological rate control (hazard ratio 0.26; estimated 2-year death rates 5% vs 21%), and the composite of mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation was 29% vs 51% (hazard ratio 0.40) — heart-failure figures printed with mortality beside them throughout, per this library's rule. The effect is large but the trial is small and stopped early, the classic inflation setting. PABA-CHF (81 patients) answers the neighbouring question — pulmonary-vein isolation beat AV-node ablation with biventricular pacing on function and quality of life at 6 months — and is carded as that comparator, not as a second test of ablate-and-pace vs drugs. Rate-vs-rhythm drug strategy is Shelf #101 and CRT in HFrEF generally is Shelf #274; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: APAF-CRT 2021: ablation plus CRT cut mortality vs drug rate control — 11% vs 29%, hazard ratio 0.26; mortality-or-heart-failure-hospitalisation 29% vs 51% — in 133 patients, stopped early
cards.summary: APAF-CRT 2021: ablation plus CRT cut mortality vs drug rate control — 11% vs 29% , hazard ratio 0.26, relative; mortality-or-heart-failure-hospitalisation 29% vs 47% printed beside it. (Tier C — mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: International, open-label randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment, stopped for efficacy at interim analysis
cards.people: 133 patients with severely symptomatic permanent AF of more than 6 months, narrow QRS (110 ms or less), and at least one heart-failure hospitalisation in the previous year, randomised to AV-junction ablation plus CRT or pharmacological rate control; mean age 73 years (SD 10); 62 patients (47%) were women; median follow-up 29 months.
cards.result: The primary end point, all-cause mortality, occurred in 7 patients (11%) in the ablation-plus-CRT arm and 20 (29%) in the drug arm (hazard ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.65; P=0.004 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it; estimated death rates 5% vs 21% at 2 years and 14% vs 41% at 4 years). The secondary composite of all-cause mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation was also lower with ablation plus CRT: 18 patients (29%) vs 36 (51%) (hazard ratio 0.40, 0.22 to 0.73; P=0.002) — printed with its mortality component, never alone. The mortality benefit was similar in patients with ejection fraction 35% or less and in those above 35%.
cards.watchOut: One hundred and thirty-three patients, stopped early for efficacy: the hazard ratio of 0.26 is exactly the species of estimate that shrinks on replication, and the population was narrow — severely symptomatic, recently hospitalised, narrow QRS. Open-label treatment (outcomes were blinded).
cards.source: Brignole M et al. AV Junction Ablation and Cardiac Resynchronization for Patients With Permanent Atrial Fibrillation and Narrow QRS: The APAF-CRT Mortality Trial. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(46):4731-4739. PMID: 34453840. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02137187, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PABA-CHF 2008: pulmonary-vein isolation beat AV-node ablation with biventricular pacing on the functional composite at 6 months in AF with heart failure
cards.summary: PABA-CHF 2008: pulmonary-vein isolation beat AV-node ablation with biventricular pacing on the functional composite at 6 months in AF with heart failure.
cards.people: 81 patients with symptomatic, drug-resistant atrial fibrillation, ejection fraction 40% or less, and NYHA class II or III heart failure, randomised to pulmonary-vein isolation (41) or AV-node ablation with biventricular pacing (40); no patient was lost to follow-up at 6 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The composite primary end point favoured pulmonary-vein isolation on all three components at 6 months: Minnesota Living with Heart Failure questionnaire score 60 vs 82 (lower is better; P<0.001), 6-minute walk distance 340 m vs 297 m (P<0.001), and ejection fraction 35% vs 28% (P<0.001). In the isolation group, 88% of patients receiving antiarrhythmic drugs and 71% of those not receiving them were free of atrial fibrillation at 6 months. Harms: pulmonary-vein stenosis in two patients, pericardial effusion in one and pulmonary oedema in another with isolation; lead dislodgment in one patient and pneumothorax in another with AV-node ablation and pacing.
cards.watchOut: A 6-month functional-endpoint trial with no mortality or hospitalisation outcome: it ranks two procedures against each other, it does not test either against drugs, and it must not be cited as survival evidence for ablate-and-pace.
cards.source: Khan MN et al. Pulmonary-Vein Isolation for Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Heart Failure. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(17):1778-1785. PMID: 18946063. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00599976, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a striking mortality signal from one small stopped-early trial — POSSIBLE, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: A striking mortality signal from one small stopped-early trial — POSSIBLE, proposed (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: APAF-CRT (133 patients, mortality primary, median 29 months) and PABA-CHF (81 patients, functional endpoints, 6 months).
cards.result: The shelf's two trials answer different questions and must not be pooled into false confidence. Against drugs, ablate-and-pace has exactly one mortality trial, and it is small and stopped early (deaths 11% vs 29%). Against pulmonary-vein isolation, ablate-and-pace lost on function in PABA-CHF — a reminder that 'ablate-and-pace beats drugs' and 'ablate-and-pace is the best procedure' are different claims, and only the first, weaker-supported one is this shelf's. POSSIBLE, Tier C, stamp proposed pending the developer's personal verdict on the mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: APAF-CRT's narrow-QRS, recently-hospitalised, severely symptomatic population is not 'permanent AF with heart failure' in general; extrapolating its hazard ratio to stable outpatients would repeat the early-stop error at the bedside.

shelves.title: Aldosterone synthase inhibition for hypertension: baxdrostat and lorundrostat
shelves.question: Do aldosterone synthase inhibitors lower blood pressure in uncontrolled/resistant hypertension beyond standard care (BrigHTN, Target-HTN)?
shelves.mesh: Aldosterone/blood,metabolism · Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cytochrome P-450 CYP11B2/antagonists & inhibitors · Hypertension/drug therapy,etiology · Aldosterone · Cytochrome P-450 CYP11B2
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for baxdrostat — a phase 2 dose-ranging trial (BrigHTN: systolic change −20.3 mm Hg at 2 mg vs −9.4 on placebo; placebo-corrected −11.0 mm Hg) now confirmed by a phase 3 trial (BaxHTN, 794 treated: placebo-corrected −9.8 mm Hg at 2 mg and −8.7 at 1 mg at 12 weeks). POSSIBLE for lorundrostat on the carded evidence — one phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Target-HTN: placebo-corrected −9.6 mm Hg at 50 mg daily) — with its two 2025 phase 3 trials (Launch-HTN and Advance-HTN) fenced in the synthesis rather than carded. Blood-pressure endpoints only: no outcome trial exists for this class, and none is claimed. The fourth-drug question for resistant hypertension (spironolactone / PATHWAY-2) stays home on Shelf #278 and is fenced on the synthesis card.

cards.headline: BrigHTN 2023: baxdrostat lowered systolic blood pressure dose-dependently in treatment-resistant hypertension — placebo-corrected −11.0 mm Hg at 2 mg
cards.summary: BrigHTN 2023: baxdrostat lowered systolic blood pressure dose-dependently in treatment-resistant hypertension — placebo-corrected −11.0 mm Hg at 2 mg.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 dose-ranging trial
cards.people: Patients with treatment-resistant hypertension (blood pressure at least 130/80 mm Hg on stable doses of at least three antihypertensive agents including a diuretic) randomised to baxdrostat 0.5 mg, 1 mg or 2 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks; 248 patients completed the trial. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Dose-dependent changes in systolic blood pressure were −20.3 mm Hg (2 mg), −17.5 mm Hg (1 mg), −12.1 mm Hg (0.5 mg) and −9.4 mm Hg (placebo). The difference versus placebo was −11.0 mm Hg (95% confidence interval −16.4 to −5.5; P<0.001) for the 2-mg dose and −8.1 mm Hg (−13.5 to −2.8; P=0.003) for the 1-mg dose. No deaths occurred during the trial, no serious adverse events were attributed to baxdrostat, and there were no instances of adrenocortical insufficiency; potassium rose to at least 6.0 mmol per liter in 2 patients on baxdrostat and did not recur after withdrawal and reinitiation.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, 12 weeks, blood pressure only — and a notably large placebo fall (−9.4 mm Hg) that is part of the comparison; potassium elevation is the class effect to watch.
cards.source: Freeman MW et al. Phase 2 Trial of Baxdrostat for Treatment-Resistant Hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(5):395-405. PMID: 36342143. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04519658, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Target-HTN 2023: lorundrostat lowered office systolic blood pressure — placebo-corrected −9.6 mm Hg at 50 mg daily in the suppressed-renin cohort
cards.summary: Target-HTN 2023: lorundrostat lowered office systolic blood pressure — placebo-corrected −9.6 mm Hg at 50 mg daily in the suppressed-renin cohort.
cards.people: 200 adults with uncontrolled hypertension taking at least two antihypertensive medications, randomised between July 2021 and June 2022: an initial cohort of 163 participants with suppressed plasma renin activity (at most 1.0 ng/mL/h) and elevated aldosterone, plus 37 participants with higher renin activity, across placebo and five lorundrostat dose regimens. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 8 weeks in the suppressed-renin cohort, changes in office systolic blood pressure were −14.1 mm Hg (100 mg daily), −13.2 mm Hg (50 mg daily), −6.9 mm Hg (12.5 mg daily) and −4.1 mm Hg (placebo); twice-daily doses gave −10.1 mm Hg (25 mg) and −13.8 mm Hg (12.5 mg). The least-squares mean difference versus placebo was −9.6 mm Hg (90% confidence interval −15.8 to −3.4; P=0.01) for 50 mg daily and −7.8 mm Hg (−14.1 to −1.5; P=0.04) for 100 mg daily. In participants without suppressed renin, 100 mg daily lowered systolic pressure by 11.4 mm Hg, similar to the same dose in the suppressed cohort. Six participants had serum potassium above 6.0 mmol/L, correcting with dose reduction or discontinuation; no cortisol insufficiency occurred.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 dose-finding with a renin-stratified design and 8-week endpoints: it selected doses for phase 3 rather than settling the drug's place in therapy.
cards.source: Laffin LJ et al. Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition With Lorundrostat for Uncontrolled Hypertension: The Target-HTN Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;330(12):1140-1150. PMID: 37690061. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05001945, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: BaxHTN 2025: phase 3 confirmation — baxdrostat lowered seated systolic pressure by a placebo-corrected 9.8 mm Hg (2 mg) and 8.7 mm Hg (1 mg) at 12 weeks
cards.summary: BaxHTN 2025 (found by the currency sweep and carded): phase 3 confirmation — baxdrostat lowered seated systolic pressure by a placebo-corrected 9.8 mm Hg (2 mg) at 12 weeks; lorundrostat's phase 3s are fenced by name.
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 796 patients underwent randomisation and 794 received baxdrostat 1 mg (264), baxdrostat 2 mg (266) or placebo (264) once daily for 12 weeks, added to background therapy: adults with seated systolic pressure 140 to under 170 mm Hg despite two antihypertensive medications (uncontrolled) or at least three including a diuretic (resistant), after a 2-week placebo run-in. The placebo-corrected differences were −8.7 mm Hg (−11.5 to −5.8) for 1 mg and −9.8 mm Hg (−12.6 to −7.0) for 2 mg (P<0.001 for both). cards.headline: Synthesis: a new class with concordant blood-pressure effects — baxdrostat confirmed at phase 3, lorundrostat's phase 3s fenced
cards.summary: A new class with concordant blood-pressure effects — LIKELY for baxdrostat, POSSIBLE for lorundrostat.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BrigHTN (248 completers, phase 2), Target-HTN (200 participants, phase 2) and BaxHTN (794 treated, phase 3).
cards.result: Placebo-corrected systolic reductions cluster around 8–11 mm Hg across both drugs and all phases carded: baxdrostat −11.0 mm Hg (2 mg, phase 2) and −9.8 / −8.7 mm Hg (2 mg / 1 mg, phase 3); lorundrostat −9.6 mm Hg (50 mg, phase 2). Lorundrostat's two 2025 phase 3 trials — Launch-HTN (JAMA 2025) and Advance-HTN (N Engl J Med 2025) — exist and are fenced here by name; no figures from them are printed, because they are not carded on this shelf, and lorundrostat's stamp stays at the phase 2 level until they are. shelves.title: Natriuretic-peptide-guided heart-failure therapy
shelves.question: Does titrating heart-failure therapy to an NT-proBNP target beat usual care on outcomes (GUIDE-IT; TIME-CHF in older patients)?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/blood · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Heart Failure/blood,drug therapy,physiopathology,therapy · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials, one in high-risk US/Canadian patients with reduced ejection fraction and one in older European patients, both found natriuretic-peptide-guided titration no better than good usual or symptom-guided care on their primary outcomes. GUIDE-IT was stopped for futility at 894 of 1,100 planned patients (primary composite of first heart-failure hospitalisation or cardiovascular mortality 37% vs 37%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.79-1.22; cardiovascular mortality itself 12% vs 13% — reported as a null component of the composite, not as a benefit claim). TIME-CHF (499 patients aged 60 or older) found survival free of all-cause hospitalisation in 41% vs 40% (HR 0.91, 0.72-1.14). Two concordant nulls of this size earn LIKELY the null under the library's large-null rule. Heart-failure hospitalisation figures are paired with mortality wherever they appear on this shelf, per the developer's rule.

cards.headline: Felker 2017 (GUIDE-IT): NT-proBNP-guided therapy was stopped for futility — primary outcome 37% vs 37% (adjusted HR 0.98)
cards.summary: Felker 2017 (GUIDE-IT): NT-proBNP-guided therapy was stopped for futility — primary outcome 37% vs 37% (HF hospitalisation or cardiovascular mortality; adjusted hazard ratio 0.98, relative).
cards.type: Randomized multicenter clinical trial (stopped early for futility)
cards.people: 894 patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 40% or less), elevated natriuretic peptide levels within the prior 30 days, and a history of a prior HF event, at 45 clinical sites in the United States and Canada, randomized to an NT-proBNP-guided strategy (446) or usual care (448), of 1,100 planned; median age 63 years; 286 (32%) women, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The primary end point (time to first HF hospitalization or cardiovascular mortality) occurred in 164 patients (37%) in the biomarker-guided group and 164 patients (37%) in the usual care group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.79-1.22; P=.88). Cardiovascular mortality was 12% (n=53) in the biomarker-guided group and 13% (n=57) in the usual care group (HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.65-1.37; P=.75). None of the secondary end points, nor the decreases in NT-proBNP levels achieved, differed significantly between groups. The data and safety monitoring board recommended stopping the study for futility when 894 of the planned 1,100 patients had been enrolled, with follow-up for a median of 15 months.
cards.watchOut: Usual care in GUIDE-IT was itself guideline-directed titration at heart-failure centres — the trial shows peptide targets add nothing on top of good care, not that titration in general is useless.

cards.headline: Pfisterer 2009 (TIME-CHF): in patients aged 60 or older, BNP-guided therapy did not improve survival free of all-cause hospitalisation (41% vs 40%)
cards.summary: Pfisterer 2009 (TIME-CHF): in patients aged 60 or older, BNP-guided therapy did not improve survival free of all-cause hospitalisation (41% vs 40%).
cards.people: 499 patients aged 60 years or older with systolic heart failure (ejection fraction 45% or less), NYHA class II or greater, prior hospitalization for heart failure within 1 year, and N-terminal BNP level of 2 or more times the upper limit of normal, at 15 outpatient centers in Switzerland and Germany, followed for 18 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Heart failure therapy guided by N-terminal BNP and symptom-guided therapy resulted in similar rates of survival free of all-cause hospitalizations (41% vs 40%, respectively; hazard ratio 0.91 [95% CI 0.72-1.14]; P=.39), and quality-of-life metrics improved similarly in both strategies over 18 months. Survival free of hospitalization for heart failure, a secondary end point, was higher in the BNP-guided group (72% vs 62%; HR 0.68 [95% CI 0.50-0.92]; P=.01) — printed here beside the trial's primary null, not as a standalone hospitalisation claim. Heart failure therapy guided by N-terminal BNP improved outcomes in patients aged 60 to 75 years but not in those aged 75 years or older (P<.02 for interaction).
cards.watchOut: The positive findings are a secondary endpoint and an age subgroup under a null primary outcome — hypothesis-grade, and the age interaction cuts against using peptide guidance in the oldest patients.

shelves.title: Ruxolitinib for myelofibrosis: COMFORT-I and COMFORT-II
shelves.question: Does ruxolitinib shrink spleens and relieve symptoms in myelofibrosis versus placebo (COMFORT-I) and versus best available therapy (COMFORT-II)?
shelves.mesh: Cell Transformation, Neoplastic · Intention to Treat Analysis · Janus Kinase 1/antagonists & inhibitors · Janus Kinase 2/antagonists & inhibitors · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/mortality · Nitriles
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for spleen and symptom benefit — the shelf's question; no standalone survival claim is stamped): Two randomised trials agree closely: a ≥35% spleen-volume reduction in 41.9% vs 0.7% against placebo at 24 weeks (COMFORT-I) and in 28% vs 0% against best available therapy at 48 weeks (COMFORT-II), with ≥50% symptom-score improvement in 45.9% vs 5.3% in COMFORT-I. Anaemia and thrombocytopenia are the consistent costs. COMFORT-I's abstract also reports fewer deaths on ruxolitinib (13 vs 24; hazard ratio 0.50) as a secondary outcome — it is reported on its card as the trial reported it, but this shelf stamps the spleen/symptom benefit only, and COMFORT-II explicitly states an influence on overall survival had not been shown.

cards.headline: COMFORT-I 2012: spleen-volume response 41.9% vs 0.7% on placebo, symptom response 45.9% vs 5.3% at 24 weeks
cards.summary: COMFORT-I (2012): ruxolitinib spleen-volume response 41.9% vs 0.7% on placebo; symptom response 45.9% vs 5.3% at 24 weeks.
cards.people: 309 patients with intermediate-2 or high-risk myelofibrosis, randomised to twice-daily oral ruxolitinib (155) or placebo (154). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥35% reduction in spleen volume at 24 weeks by MRI) was reached in 41.9% of the ruxolitinib group vs 0.7% of the placebo group (P<0.001); among responders, 67.0% maintained the response for 48 weeks or more. Improvement of ≥50% in total symptom score at 24 weeks: 45.9% vs 5.3% (P<0.001). Thirteen deaths occurred in the ruxolitinib group vs 24 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.98; P=0.04) — a secondary outcome, reported here without a survival claim being stamped on this shelf. Discontinuation for adverse events: 11.0% vs 10.6%. Anaemia and thrombocytopenia were the most common adverse events on ruxolitinib but rarely led to discontinuation (one patient each); two patients in the ruxolitinib group had transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.
cards.watchOut: The survival difference rests on 37 deaths in a trial powered for spleen response, with crossover-era follow-up — it is hypothesis-grade, which is why the shelf stamps spleen/symptoms and not survival; the cytopenias are early-treatment effects needing dose management.
cards.source: Verstovsek S et al. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ruxolitinib for myelofibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(9):799-807. PMID: 22375971. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00952289, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: COMFORT-II 2012: spleen-volume response 28% vs 0% against best available therapy at 48 weeks, with durable responses
cards.summary: COMFORT-II (2012): spleen-volume response 28% vs 0% against best available therapy at 48 weeks, with durable responses.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, controlled trial (vs best available therapy)
cards.people: 219 patients with intermediate-2 or high-risk primary myelofibrosis, post-polycythaemia-vera myelofibrosis or post-essential-thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis, assigned to oral ruxolitinib or best available therapy. The abstract does not state the arm sizes, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 48, 28% of the ruxolitinib group had a ≥35% reduction in spleen volume vs 0% with best available therapy (P<0.001); at week 24 the figures were 32% and 0% (P<0.001). Mean palpable spleen length fell by 56% with ruxolitinib and rose by 4% with best available therapy at 48 weeks. The median duration of response was not reached, with 80% of responders still responding at a median follow-up of 12 months. Quality-of-life and symptom measures improved with ruxolitinib. Grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia and anaemia were the most common haematologic abnormalities in either group, managed by dose reduction, interruption or transfusion; one patient in each group discontinued for thrombocytopenia and none for anaemia. Two cases of acute myeloid leukaemia were reported with best available therapy. The authors state an influence on overall survival had not yet been shown.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against a heterogeneous 'best available therapy' comparator, so symptom and quality-of-life outcomes are expectation-sensitive; the imaging-measured spleen endpoint is the robust part, and it agrees with the blinded COMFORT-I.
