shelves.title: Polycythaemia vera after hydroxycarbamide: ruxolitinib and ropeginterferon
shelves.question: In polycythaemia vera inadequately controlled by hydroxycarbamide, does ruxolitinib control haematocrit and spleen versus standard therapy (RESPONSE) — and is ropeginterferon non-inferior to standard therapy from diagnosis (PROUD-PV)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Blood Cell Count · Hydroxyurea/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Janus Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Nitriles · Organ Size/drug effects
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — ruxolitinib after hydroxycarbamide · POSSIBLE — ropeginterferon over the long term: RESPONSE (222 patients, open-label) found the composite of haematocrit control plus ≥35% spleen reduction in 21% on ruxolitinib vs 1% on standard therapy, with haematocrit control alone in 60% vs 20%. PROUD-PV/CONTINUATION-PV (257 randomised) missed non-inferiority at 12 months on its composite endpoint (21% vs 28%) but showed higher responses by 36 months (complete haematological response with improved disease burden 53% vs 38%). Two different drugs, populations and time-shapes — one stamp for each.

cards.headline: RESPONSE 2015: ruxolitinib beat standard therapy on the haematocrit-plus-spleen composite, 21% vs 1%; haematocrit control 60% vs 20%
cards.summary: RESPONSE (2015): ruxolitinib beat standard therapy on the haematocrit-plus-spleen composite, 21% vs 1% ; haematocrit control 60% vs 20%.
cards.people: 222 phlebotomy-dependent patients with polycythaemia vera and splenomegaly who had an inadequate response to, or unacceptable side effects from, hydroxyurea, randomised 1:1 to ruxolitinib (110) or standard therapy (112). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (haematocrit control through week 32 plus ≥35% spleen-volume reduction at week 32) was achieved in 21% on ruxolitinib vs 1% on standard therapy (P<0.001). Haematocrit control alone: 60% vs 20%; ≥35% spleen reduction alone: 38% vs 1%. Complete haematologic remission: 24% vs 9% (P=0.003); ≥50% reduction in total symptom score at week 32: 49% vs 5%. Grade 3–4 anaemia occurred in 2% vs 0% and grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia in 5% vs 4%; herpes zoster was reported in 6% vs 0% (all grade 1–2). Thromboembolic events occurred in one patient on ruxolitinib and six on standard therapy.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in a splenomegaly-selected, hydroxyurea-failing population — the composite is driven partly by the spleen criterion, so the 60% vs 20% haematocrit-control figure is the cleaner read for patients without spleen enlargement.
cards.source: Vannucchi AM et al. Ruxolitinib versus standard therapy for the treatment of polycythemia vera. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(5):426-435. PMID: 25629741. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01243944, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PROUD-PV/CONTINUATION-PV 2020: ropeginterferon missed non-inferiority at 12 months (21% vs 28%) but led by 36 months (53% vs 38% on the disease-burden composite)
cards.summary: PROUD-PV/CONTINUATION-PV (2020): ropeginterferon missed non-inferiority at 12 months ( 21% vs 28% ) but led by 36 months (53% vs 38%).
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, controlled, open-label, non-inferiority trial with extension study
cards.people: 257 patients aged 18 or older with early-stage polycythaemia vera (no prior cytoreduction, or under 3 years of hydroxyurea), at 48 European clinics, randomised 1:1 to ropeginterferon alfa-2b subcutaneously every 2 weeks (127 treated) or hydroxyurea/standard therapy (127 treated); 171 rolled over into the CONTINUATION-PV extension. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In PROUD-PV, the composite primary endpoint (complete haematological response with normal spleen size at 12 months) was met by 26 (21%) of 122 on ropeginterferon vs 34 (28%) of 123 on standard therapy — non-inferiority was not shown. In CONTINUATION-PV at 36 months, complete haematological response with improved disease burden was met by 50 (53%) of 95 vs 28 (38%) of 74 (p=0.044), and complete haematological response without the spleen criterion by 67 (71%) of 95 vs 38 (51%) of 74 (p=0.012); at 12 months the same measure had been 53 (43%) of 123 vs 57 (46%) of 125 (p=0.63). The commonest grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were raised γ-glutamyltransferase (6%) and raised alanine aminotransferase (3%) on ropeginterferon, and leucopenia (5%) and thrombocytopenia (4%) on standard therapy; treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 2% vs 4%, and one treatment-related death (acute leukaemia) occurred in the standard-therapy group.
cards.watchOut: A negative primary endpoint followed by positive 36-month extension analyses — the long-term advantage is real on the printed figures but comes from an opt-in extension population (171 of 257), so attrition and selection temper it; the 12-month miss belongs on the card, not under it.
cards.source: Gisslinger H et al. Lancet Haematol. 2020;7(3):e196-e208. PMID: 32014125. shelves.title: First-line therapy for chronic-phase CML: imatinib's benchmark and dasatinib's challenge (IRIS, DASISION)
shelves.question: Did imatinib beat interferon plus cytarabine in newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML (IRIS) — and does dasatinib beat imatinib on early molecular response (DASISION)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Benzamides · Cytarabine/administration & dosage · Disease Progression · Imatinib Mesylate · Interferon-alpha/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (on cytogenetic and molecular response — surrogate endpoints, stated as such): IRIS (1,106 patients) established imatinib over interferon plus low-dose cytarabine with a major cytogenetic response at 18 months of 87.1% vs 34.7% and freedom from progression to accelerated phase or blast crisis of 96.7% vs 91.5%. DASISION (519 patients) then showed dasatinib ahead of imatinib on confirmed complete cytogenetic response by 12 months (77% vs 66%) and major molecular response (46% vs 28%). Two large concordant trials on response endpoints support LIKELY; neither card claims a survival difference, because neither abstract reports one.

cards.headline: IRIS 2003: imatinib dwarfed interferon-plus-cytarabine — major cytogenetic response 87.1% vs 34.7% at 18 months
cards.summary: IRIS (2003): imatinib dwarfed interferon-plus-cytarabine — major cytogenetic response 87.1% vs 34.7% at 18 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (open-label, crossover allowed on failure/intolerance)
cards.people: 1,106 patients with newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia, randomised to imatinib (553) or interferon alfa plus low-dose cytarabine (553); median follow-up 19 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Estimated major cytogenetic response at 18 months: 87.1% (95% CI 84.1 to 90.0) with imatinib vs 34.7% (29.3 to 40.0) with interferon plus cytarabine (P<0.001). Estimated complete cytogenetic response: 76.2% (72.5 to 79.9) vs 14.5% (10.5 to 18.5) (P<0.001). Estimated freedom from progression to accelerated-phase or blast-crisis CML at 18 months: 96.7% vs 91.5% (P<0.001). Imatinib was better tolerated than the combination therapy.
cards.watchOut: An early (median 19-month) report with crossover allowed — later IRIS follow-up exists outside this anchor record, and the endpoints are cytogenetic responses, powerful surrogates in CML but surrogates nonetheless; no survival figures appear in this abstract.
cards.source: O'Brien SG et al. Imatinib compared with interferon and low-dose cytarabine for newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia. N Engl J Med. 2003;348(11):994-1004. PMID: 12637609. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: DASISION 2010: dasatinib beat imatinib on confirmed complete cytogenetic response (77% vs 66%) and major molecular response (46% vs 28%) at 12 months
cards.summary: DASISION (2010): dasatinib beat imatinib on confirmed complete cytogenetic response ( 77% vs 66% ) and major molecular response (46% vs 28%) at 12 months.
cards.people: 519 patients with newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML, randomised to dasatinib 100 mg once daily (259) or imatinib 400 mg once daily (260); minimum follow-up 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Confirmed complete cytogenetic response by 12 months: 77% with dasatinib vs 66% with imatinib (P=0.007); complete cytogenetic response on at least one assessment: 83% vs 72% (P=0.001). Major molecular response: 46% vs 28% (P<0.0001), achieved in a shorter time with dasatinib (P<0.0001). Progression to accelerated or blastic phase occurred in 5 patients on dasatinib (1.9%) and 9 on imatinib (3.5%). The safety profiles of the two treatments were similar.
cards.watchOut: Deeper, faster responses are not the same as longer life: the progression counts (5 vs 9) are small and not significant on the printed figures, and the abstract's own claim is the conditional one — that early complete cytogenetic response has been associated with better long-term progression-free survival.
cards.source: Kantarjian H et al. Dasatinib versus imatinib in newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(24):2260-2270. PMID: 20525995. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00481247, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: imatinib set the benchmark; dasatinib answers faster and deeper — and asciminib is the next challenger, fenced
cards.summary: Imatinib set the benchmark; dasatinib answers faster and deeper — and asciminib is the next challenger, fenced — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: IRIS (1,106 patients) and DASISION (519 patients).
cards.result: The two trials form the spine of first-line chronic-phase CML: imatinib's 87.1% vs 34.7% major cytogenetic response displaced interferon-based therapy, and dasatinib's 46% vs 28% major molecular response at 12 months showed a second-generation inhibitor could deepen the same benchmark. The currency sweep surfaced the ASC4FIRST programme (asciminib vs investigator-selected tyrosine kinase inhibitors in newly diagnosed CML) — a genuine newer first-line challenge, fenced here rather than carded, because this shelf's question is the imatinib benchmark and the dasatinib comparison. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is drafted at #676 — a different disease.
cards.watchOut: Response depth drives modern CML management (including treatment-free-remission attempts), but this shelf's stamps attach to response endpoints only; survival equivalence among modern first-line TKIs is a separate question these abstracts do not answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Brien SG et al. N Engl J Med. 2003;348(11):994-1004. PMID: 12637609; Kantarjian H et al. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(24):2260-2270. PMID: 20525995. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Venetoclax combinations for older or unfit acute myeloid leukaemia (VIALE-A, VIALE-C)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed AML patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy, does adding venetoclax to azacitidine (VIALE-A) or to low-dose cytarabine (VIALE-C) improve survival and remission versus the backbone alone?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Azacitidine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bridged Bicyclo Compounds, Heterocyclic/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy,mortality · Leukopenia/chemically induced
shelves.balance: Tier C — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (overall-survival claim): Split: LIKELY — venetoclax plus azacitidine · POSSIBLE — venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine. VIALE-A (431 patients, double-blind) found median overall survival of 14.7 vs 9.6 months (hazard ratio for death 0.66, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.85) and composite complete remission of 66.4% vs 28.3% — the hazard ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so the stamp rests on a large blinded trial with a significant survival primary plus a doubled remission rate, and is PROPOSED pending the developer's verdict on the mortality claim. VIALE-C (211 patients) missed its planned primary survival analysis (hazard ratio 0.75, 0.52 to 1.07; P=.11), reaching significance only in an unplanned analysis with 6 more months of follow-up (hazard ratio 0.70, 0.50 to 0.98) — POSSIBLE. Febrile neutropenia was more frequent on the combinations in both trials.

cards.headline: VIALE-A 2020: venetoclax plus azacitidine extended median survival to 14.7 vs 9.6 months (hazard ratio for death 0.66) — Tier C survival claim
cards.summary: VIALE-A (2020): venetoclax plus azacitidine extended median survival to 14.7 vs 9.6 months (hazard ratio for death 0.66) — Tier C survival claim.
cards.people: 431 previously untreated patients with confirmed AML ineligible for standard induction therapy (because of coexisting conditions, age 75 or older, or both); 286 assigned to azacitidine plus venetoclax and 145 to azacitidine plus placebo; median age 76 years in both groups (range 49 to 91); median follow-up 20.5 months. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 14.7 months with azacitidine–venetoclax vs 9.6 months with azacitidine alone (hazard ratio for death 0.66, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.85; P<0.001 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band; the absolute medians are printed beside it). Complete remission: 36.7% vs 17.9% (P<0.001); composite complete remission (complete remission or complete remission with incomplete haematological recovery): 66.4% vs 28.3% (P<0.001). Grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia occurred in 45% vs 38%, neutropenia in 42% vs 28%, and febrile neutropenia in 42% vs 19%; infections of any grade in 85% vs 67%, and serious adverse events in 83% vs 73%. Nausea of any grade occurred in 44% vs 35%.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: this card carries an overall-survival claim and is proposed only, pending the developer's personal verdict. The population is specifically patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy — the result does not transfer to fit patients, for whom intensive and venetoclax-containing induction trials are a separate, active question.
cards.source: DiNardo CD et al. Azacitidine and Venetoclax in Previously Untreated Acute Myeloid Leukemia. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(7):617-629. PMID: 32786187. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02993523, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: VIALE-C 2020: venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine missed its planned survival primary (hazard ratio 0.75, P=.11); remission rates clearly higher (48% vs 13%)
cards.summary: VIALE-C (2020): venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine missed its planned survival primary (hazard ratio 0.75, P=.11); remission rates were clearly higher.
cards.people: 211 adults (median age 76 years, range 36–93; 38% had secondary AML and 20% had received prior hypomethylating-agent treatment) with newly diagnosed AML ineligible for intensive chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 to venetoclax (143) or placebo (68), each plus low-dose cytarabine on days 1–10 of 28-day cycles. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The planned primary analysis showed a 25% relative reduction in the risk of death with venetoclax plus low-dose cytarabine (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.07; P=.11 — not statistically significant), with median overall survival of 7.2 vs 4.1 months. An unplanned analysis with an additional 6 months of follow-up showed median survival of 8.4 months for the venetoclax arm (hazard ratio 0.70, 0.50 to 0.98; P=.04). Complete remission plus complete remission with incomplete blood-count recovery: 48% vs 13%. Key grade ≥3 adverse events (venetoclax vs control) were febrile neutropenia (32% vs 29%), neutropenia (47% vs 16%) and thrombocytopenia (45% vs 37%).
cards.watchOut: Tier C context and a two-handed read: the trial's own planned primary analysis was negative, and significance arrived only in an unplanned later analysis — quote the P=.11 primary whenever the 0.70 figure is quoted. Survival claims on this shelf are proposed pending the developer's verdict.
cards.source: Wei AH et al. Venetoclax plus LDAC for newly diagnosed AML ineligible for intensive chemotherapy: a phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trial. Blood. 2020;135(24):2137-2145. PMID: 32219442. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03069352, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the azacitidine combination is the proven backbone change; the cytarabine combination is the weaker sibling — Tier C, proposed
cards.summary: The azacitidine combination is the proven backbone change; the cytarabine combination is the weaker sibling — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VIALE-A (431 patients, azacitidine backbone) and VIALE-C (211 patients, low-dose cytarabine backbone).
cards.result: One programme, two strengths of evidence: a significant survival primary with doubled composite remission for venetoclax–azacitidine (14.7 vs 9.6 months; 66.4% vs 28.3%), and a missed planned primary with a later unplanned significance for venetoclax–LDAC (median 7.2 vs 4.1 months at the primary analysis; remission 48% vs 13%). cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two backbones into a single 'venetoclax works' claim — the LDAC trial's own primary analysis forbids it, and the azacitidine result does not rescue it.

shelves.title: Daratumumab first-line in transplant-ineligible myeloma: MAIA and ALCYONE
shelves.question: Does adding daratumumab to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (MAIA) or to bortezomib–melphalan–prednisone (ALCYONE) improve progression-free survival in newly diagnosed myeloma patients ineligible for transplant?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Lenalidomide/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy · Neutropenia/chemically induced · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for progression-free survival — the trials' primary endpoint; no standalone survival claim is stamped): Two large randomised trials of adding daratumumab to two different backbones agree: MAIA (737 patients) found disease progression or death in 26.4% vs 38.8% at a median 28 months (hazard ratio 0.56), and ALCYONE (706 patients) found 18-month progression-free survival of 71.6% vs 50.2% (hazard ratio 0.50). Both hazard ratios are relative figures at or near the 0.5 boundary, printed with their absolute rates; response depth (complete response and MRD negativity) moved the same way in both. Neutropenia and pneumonia/infections are the consistent costs.

cards.headline: MAIA 2019: adding daratumumab cut progression or death to 26.4% vs 38.8% (hazard ratio 0.56); 30-month progression-free survival 70.6% vs 55.6%
cards.summary: MAIA (2019): adding daratumumab cut progression or death to 26.4% vs 38.8% (hazard ratio 0.56); 30-month progression-free survival 70.6% vs 55.6%.
cards.people: 737 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for autologous stem-cell transplantation, randomised to daratumumab plus lenalidomide–dexamethasone (368) or lenalidomide–dexamethasone alone (369), treated until progression or unacceptable side effects; median follow-up 28.0 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Disease progression or death occurred in 97 of 368 patients (26.4%) in the daratumumab group and 143 of 369 (38.8%) in the control group; the estimated proportion alive without progression at 30 months was 70.6% (95% CI 65.0 to 75.4) vs 55.6% (49.5 to 61.3) (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.56, 0.43 to 0.73; P<0.001 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Complete response or better: 47.6% vs 24.9% (P<0.001); minimal-residual-disease negativity (threshold 1 tumour cell per 10^5 white cells): 24.2% vs 7.3% (P<0.001). The most common grade 3–4 adverse events were neutropenia (50.0% vs 35.3%), anaemia (11.8% vs 19.7%), lymphopenia (15.1% vs 10.7%) and pneumonia (13.7% vs 7.9%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the endpoint is progression-free survival — a composite in which deaths are counted, but this anchor report makes no overall-survival claim and neither does this shelf; a MAIA final survival analysis appeared in the currency sweep and is a follow-up record of this same trial, fenced in the synthesis.
cards.source: Facon T et al. Daratumumab plus Lenalidomide and Dexamethasone for Untreated Myeloma. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(22):2104-2115. PMID: 31141632. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02252172, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ALCYONE 2018: daratumumab plus VMP gave 18-month progression-free survival of 71.6% vs 50.2% (hazard ratio 0.50)
cards.summary: ALCYONE (2018): daratumumab plus VMP gave 18-month progression-free survival of 71.6% vs 50.2% (hazard ratio 0.50).
cards.people: 706 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for stem-cell transplantation, randomised to nine cycles of bortezomib–melphalan–prednisone alone or with daratumumab (continued until progression); this report is a prespecified interim analysis at a median follow-up of 16.5 months. The abstract does not state the arm sizes, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The 18-month progression-free survival rate was 71.6% (95% CI 65.5 to 76.8) in the daratumumab group vs 50.2% (43.2 to 56.7) in the control group (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.50, 0.38 to 0.65; P<0.001 — a relative figure at the 0.5 boundary, absolute rates beside it). Overall response: 90.9% vs 73.9% (P<0.001); complete response or better: 42.6% vs 24.4% (P<0.001); MRD negativity: 22.3% vs 6.2% (P<0.001). Grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 39.9% vs 38.7%, thrombocytopenia in 34.4% vs 37.6%, and anaemia in 15.9% vs 19.8%; grade 3–4 infections in 23.1% vs 14.7%, with discontinuation for infection in 0.9% vs 1.4%; daratumumab infusion-related reactions occurred in 27.7%.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis at 16.5 months on a melphalan-based backbone that has since been displaced in many health systems — the drug's contribution replicates in MAIA on a modern backbone, which is what carries the class reading.
cards.source: Mateos MV et al. Daratumumab plus Bortezomib, Melphalan, and Prednisone for Untreated Myeloma. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(6):518-528. PMID: 29231133. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02195479, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: daratumumab deepens and prolongs first-line control on two different backbones — LIKELY for progression-free survival
cards.summary: Daratumumab deepens and prolongs first-line control on two different backbones — LIKELY for progression-free survival.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MAIA (737 patients, lenalidomide backbone) and ALCYONE (706 patients, VMP backbone), both in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma.
cards.result: Hazard ratios of 0.56 and 0.50 for progression or death, complete-response rates roughly doubling (47.6% vs 24.9%; 42.6% vs 24.4%) and MRD negativity tripling in both trials make the pattern backbone-independent. A MAIA final survival analysis (2026, in the currency sweep) is a follow-up record of the MAIA trial carded here — it is fenced, not re-carded, and any survival reading belongs to the developer's Tier C process, not to this shelf's stamp. Lenalidomide maintenance after transplant is drafted at #675 — a different phase and population.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free-survival stamps do not settle sequencing questions (daratumumab now vs at relapse) or overall survival; both remain outside what these two anchor reports claim.

shelves.title: Beyond eculizumab in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria: pegcetacoplan and iptacopan
shelves.question: Does proximal complement inhibition beat eculizumab on haemoglobin in PNH — pegcetacoplan in patients already on eculizumab (PEGASUS), and oral iptacopan in patients with residual anaemia (APPLY-PNH)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Complement C3/antagonists & inhibitors · Complement C5/antagonists & inhibitors · Complement Inactivating Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Drug Therapy, Combination · Erythrocyte Transfusion
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — pegcetacoplan superior to eculizumab on haemoglobin · POSSIBLE — iptacopan: PEGASUS (80 patients, randomised, open-label) found pegcetacoplan superior to eculizumab on the change in haemoglobin at week 16 (adjusted mean difference 3.84 g/dL), with transfusion independence in 85% vs 15%. The iptacopan paper pairs one randomised trial (APPLY-PNH: 51 of 60 on iptacopan vs 0 of 35 continuing anti-C5 therapy reached the ≥2 g/dL haemoglobin-rise endpoint) with a single-arm trial in complement-inhibitor-naïve patients (APPOINT-PNH: 31 of 33) — a dramatic randomised contrast but a programme half of which is uncontrolled, in a rare disease with small numbers; POSSIBLE for iptacopan, LIKELY for pegcetacoplan's head-to-head superiority.

cards.headline: PEGASUS 2021: pegcetacoplan beat eculizumab on haemoglobin by an adjusted 3.84 g/dL at week 16; transfusion-free 85% vs 15%
cards.summary: PEGASUS (2021): pegcetacoplan beat eculizumab on haemoglobin by an adjusted 3.84 g/dL at week 16; transfusion-free 85% vs 15%.
cards.people: 80 adults with PNH and haemoglobin below 10.5 g/dL despite eculizumab therapy; after a 4-week run-in in which all patients received pegcetacoplan plus eculizumab, patients were randomised to subcutaneous pegcetacoplan monotherapy (41) or intravenous eculizumab (39); primary endpoint at week 16. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Pegcetacoplan was superior to eculizumab for the mean change in haemoglobin from baseline to week 16 (adjusted least-squares mean difference 3.84 g/dL; P<0.001). Thirty-five patients (85%) on pegcetacoplan vs 6 (15%) on eculizumab no longer required transfusions. Non-inferiority was shown for the change in absolute reticulocyte count but not for the change in lactate dehydrogenase. Fatigue scores (FACIT-Fatigue) improved from baseline in the pegcetacoplan group. The most common adverse events on pegcetacoplan vs eculizumab were injection-site reactions (37% vs 3%), diarrhoea (22% vs 3%), breakthrough haemolysis (10% vs 23%), headache (7% vs 23%) and fatigue (5% vs 15%). There were no cases of meningitis in either group.
cards.watchOut: Only 80 patients with a 16-week primary endpoint in a rare disease, open-label, after a run-in that pre-exposed everyone to pegcetacoplan — the effect size is large, but durability and rare-harm questions sit outside this trial.
cards.source: Hillmen P et al. Pegcetacoplan versus Eculizumab in Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(11):1028-1037. PMID: 33730455. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03500549, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: APPLY-PNH 2024: switching to iptacopan, 51 of 60 reached a ≥2 g/dL haemoglobin rise vs 0 of 35 staying on anti-C5 therapy
cards.summary: APPLY-PNH (2024): switching to iptacopan, 51 of 60 patients reached a ≥2 g/dL haemoglobin rise vs 0 of 35 staying on anti-C5 therapy.
cards.type: Two phase 3 trials in one paper: one randomised switch trial (APPLY-PNH) and one single-group trial (APPOINT-PNH)
cards.people: Patients with PNH and haemoglobin below 10 g/dL over a 24-week treatment period: in APPLY-PNH, anti-C5-treated patients were randomised to switch to oral iptacopan (62 received it; 60 in the endpoint counts) or continue anti-C5 therapy (35); in APPOINT-PNH, 33 patients who had not received complement inhibitors and had LDH over 1.5 times the upper limit of normal received iptacopan in a single-group trial. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In APPLY-PNH, 51 of the 60 patients who received iptacopan had a haemoglobin increase of at least 2 g/dL from baseline and 42 reached at least 12 g/dL, each without red-cell transfusion; none of the 35 anti-C5-treated patients attained the endpoint levels. In APPOINT-PNH, 31 of 33 patients had a haemoglobin increase of at least 2 g/dL without transfusion. In APPLY-PNH, 59 of 62 iptacopan patients and 14 of 35 anti-C5 patients did not require or receive transfusion; in APPOINT-PNH no patient required or received transfusion. Iptacopan also reduced fatigue and reticulocyte and bilirubin levels, with mean LDH below 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. Headache was the most frequent adverse event with iptacopan.
cards.watchOut: Half the paper (APPOINT-PNH) has no control group at all, follow-up is 24 weeks, and the randomised half is open-label — the 51-vs-0 contrast is striking but the programme is small, as rare-disease programmes are; the final 48-week report in the currency sweep is a follow-up of these same trials.

shelves.title: Caplacizumab for acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TITAN, HERCULES)
shelves.question: Does adding the von-Willebrand-factor inhibitor caplacizumab to plasma exchange and immunosuppression speed platelet recovery and cut exacerbations in acquired TTP?
shelves.mesh: ADAM Proteins/metabolism · ADAMTS13 Protein · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Purpura, Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic/drug therapy,metabolism · Recurrence · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A phase 2 trial (TITAN, 75 patients) and a double-blind phase 3 trial (HERCULES, 145 patients) agree: caplacizumab shortened the time to platelet-count normalisation (39% reduction in median time in TITAN; median 2.69 vs 2.88 days and 1.55 times the likelihood of normalisation in HERCULES), cut exacerbations in TITAN (3 vs 11 patients) and, in HERCULES, reduced the composite of TTP-related death, recurrence or thromboembolism during treatment by a relative 74% (12% vs 49%) and recurrence at any time by a relative 67% (12% vs 38%). Mucocutaneous bleeding is the consistent cost (65% vs 48% in HERCULES). The shelf stamps faster recovery and fewer recurrences; deaths were few (all in the placebo arms during treatment) and no standalone mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: TITAN 2016: caplacizumab cut the median time to platelet response by 39% and exacerbations from 11 patients to 3
cards.summary: TITAN (2016): caplacizumab cut the median time to platelet response by 39% and exacerbations from 11 patients to 3.
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, controlled study (single-blind era design, placebo-controlled during plasma exchange)
cards.people: 75 patients with acquired TTP, randomised to subcutaneous caplacizumab 10 mg daily (36) or placebo (39) during plasma exchange and for 30 days afterwards; the primary endpoint was the time to confirmed normalisation of the platelet count. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The time to a response was significantly reduced with caplacizumab vs placebo (39% reduction in median time; P=0.005 — a relative figure). Three patients in the caplacizumab group had an exacerbation, vs 11 in the placebo group. Eight patients in the caplacizumab group relapsed in the first month after stopping the study drug, of whom 7 had ADAMTS13 activity still below 10%, suggesting unresolved autoimmune activity. Bleeding-related adverse events (mostly mild to moderate) were more common with caplacizumab (54% of patients vs 38%); other adverse-event frequencies were similar. Two patients in the placebo group died, vs none in the caplacizumab group.
cards.watchOut: A 75-patient phase 2 study, and its relapse-after-stopping signal (8 patients, mostly with unresolved ADAMTS13 deficiency) is the mechanistic warning that caplacizumab bridges but does not treat the underlying autoimmunity — immunosuppression still does that work.
cards.source: Peyvandi F et al. Caplacizumab for Acquired Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(6):511-522. PMID: 26863353. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01151423, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: HERCULES 2019: caplacizumab cut the death/recurrence/thromboembolism composite to 12% vs 49% (a relative 74% lower) and recurrence to 12% vs 38%
cards.summary: HERCULES (2019): caplacizumab cut the death/recurrence/thromboembolism composite to 12% vs 49% and recurrence to 12% vs 38%.
cards.people: 145 patients with acquired TTP, randomised to caplacizumab (10 mg intravenous loading bolus, then 10 mg daily subcutaneously) or placebo during plasma exchange and for 30 days thereafter; the primary outcome was the time to platelet-count normalisation with discontinuation of daily plasma exchange within 5 days. The abstract does not state the arm sizes, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to platelet normalisation: 2.69 days (95% CI 1.89 to 2.83) with caplacizumab vs 2.88 days (2.68 to 3.56) with placebo (P=0.01); patients on caplacizumab were 1.55 times as likely to have platelet normalisation as those on placebo (a relative figure). The composite of TTP-related death, TTP recurrence or a thromboembolic event during the treatment period occurred in 12% vs 49% (74% lower with caplacizumab; P<0.001 — relative, absolute rates beside it), and TTP recurrence at any time in 12% vs 38% (67% lower; P<0.001). Refractory disease developed in no caplacizumab patients and three placebo patients; caplacizumab patients needed less plasma exchange and had shorter hospitalisation. The most common adverse event was mucocutaneous bleeding (65% vs 48%). During the treatment period three placebo patients died; one caplacizumab patient died of cerebral ischaemia after the treatment period ended.
cards.watchOut: The headline composite is dominated by recurrence, not death — quote the components (deaths: 3 vs 0 during treatment) with it, and note the median time-to-normalisation difference is small in days (2.69 vs 2.88) even though the normalisation likelihood and recurrence outcomes clearly favour caplacizumab.

cards.headline: Synthesis: caplacizumab buys platelet protection while immunosuppression catches up — LIKELY, with bleeding as the tariff
cards.summary: Caplacizumab buys platelet protection while immunosuppression catches up — LIKELY, with bleeding as the tariff.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TITAN (75 patients) and HERCULES (145 patients), both on a plasma-exchange backbone.
cards.result: Faster platelet recovery in both trials, fewer exacerbations (3 vs 11) in TITAN and a recurrence-inclusive composite of 12% vs 49% in HERCULES, consistently bought with more mucocutaneous bleeding (65% vs 48%). shelves.title: Newer disease-modifying drugs for sickle cell disease: voxelotor and crizanlizumab — and their reversals
shelves.question: Does voxelotor raise haemoglobin and reduce haemolysis in sickle cell disease (HOPE) — and did crizanlizumab reduce pain crises (SUSTAIN), given its confirmatory-trial failure and withdrawal that the shelf must carry?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Sickle Cell/blood,drug therapy · Antisickling Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzaldehydes/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Biomarkers/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hemoglobin, Sickle/drug effects,metabolism
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — voxelotor haemoglobin response (surrogate; drug later withdrawn) · MAYBE (weak evidence) — crizanlizumab for pain crises: HOPE (274 participants) found a haemoglobin response in 51% on voxelotor 1500 mg vs 7% on placebo, with reduced haemolysis markers — a surrogate-endpoint benefit, and voxelotor was later withdrawn from the market after post-approval safety findings, which this shelf carries on its face. Crizanlizumab's phase 2 SUSTAIN trial (198 patients) found a 45.3% relative lower annual crisis rate at the high dose, but the phase 3 STAND trial (252 patients, carded here from the currency sweep) found no significant difference from placebo (rate ratios 1.08 and 0.89) — a positive phase 2 followed by a null confirmatory phase 3 and withdrawal is the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: HOPE 2019: voxelotor 1500 mg produced a haemoglobin response in 51% vs 7% on placebo at week 24
cards.summary: HOPE (2019): voxelotor 1500 mg produced a haemoglobin response in 51% vs 7% on placebo at week 24.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 274 participants with sickle cell disease (most with sickle cell anaemia — homozygous haemoglobin S or haemoglobin Sβ0-thalassaemia; about two thirds receiving hydroxyurea at baseline), randomised 1:1:1 to once-daily oral voxelotor 1500 mg, voxelotor 900 mg, or placebo; the primary endpoint was a haemoglobin response (rise of more than 1.0 g/dL from baseline) at week 24. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A haemoglobin response occurred in 51% (95% CI 41 to 61) of the 1500-mg voxelotor group vs 7% (1 to 12) of the placebo group. Anaemia worsened between baseline and week 24 in fewer participants in each voxelotor group than on placebo, and at week 24 the 1500-mg group had significantly greater reductions in indirect bilirubin and reticulocyte percentage than the placebo group. Adverse events of grade 3 or worse occurred in 26% (1500 mg), 23% (900 mg) and 26% (placebo); most adverse events were judged not related to the trial drug or placebo.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is haemoglobin and haemolysis markers, not pain crises, organ damage or survival — and voxelotor was subsequently withdrawn from the market worldwide after post-approval trial safety findings, so this card is a record of a surrogate benefit that did not survive confirmatory scrutiny, not a current treatment recommendation.
cards.source: Vichinsky E et al. A Phase 3 Randomized Trial of Voxelotor in Sickle Cell Disease. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(6):509-519. PMID: 31199090. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03036813, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SUSTAIN 2017: high-dose crizanlizumab lowered the annual crisis rate by a relative 45.3% (median 1.63 vs 2.98 crises per year)
cards.summary: SUSTAIN (2017): high-dose crizanlizumab lowered the annual crisis rate by a relative 45.3% (median 1.63 vs 2.98 crises per year).
cards.people: 198 patients with sickle cell disease at 60 sites, randomised to low-dose crizanlizumab (2.5 mg/kg), high-dose crizanlizumab (5.0 mg/kg) or placebo, given intravenously 14 times over 52 weeks; patients receiving concomitant hydroxyurea and those not receiving it were both included. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median annual rate of sickle-cell-related pain crises was 1.63 with high-dose crizanlizumab vs 2.98 with placebo (a 45.3% lower rate; P=0.01 — a relative figure, medians beside it). Median time to first crisis was 4.07 vs 1.38 months (P=0.001) and to second crisis 10.32 vs 5.09 months (P=0.02). The median annual rate of uncomplicated crises was 1.08 vs 2.91 (a 62.9% lower rate; P=0.02). Adverse events occurring in at least 10% of an active-treatment group and at least twice the placebo frequency were arthralgia, diarrhoea, pruritus, vomiting and chest pain.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 result that the phase 3 STAND trial (next card) failed to confirm — SUSTAIN must never be quoted on this shelf without STAND beside it; that reversal, and the drug's subsequent withdrawal, is why the crizanlizumab stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: STAND 2025: the phase 3 confirmatory trial found no benefit — annualised crisis-rate ratios 1.08 (5 mg/kg) and 0.89 (7.5 mg/kg) vs placebo
cards.summary: STAND (2025): the phase 3 confirmatory trial found no benefit — annualised crisis-rate ratios 1.08 (5 mg/kg) and 0.89 (7.5 mg/kg) vs placebo.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (found in the 2026 currency sweep)
cards.people: 252 patients with sickle cell disease aged 12 years and older at 65 sites in 21 countries, randomised 1:1:1 to crizanlizumab 5.0 mg/kg, crizanlizumab 7.5 mg/kg or placebo, in addition to standard of care, for 1 year; the primary endpoint was the annualised rate of vaso-occlusive crises leading to a health-care visit in the first year. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Adjusted annualised crisis rates were 2.49 (95% CI 1.90 to 3.26) in the 5.0 mg/kg group, 2.04 (1.56 to 2.65) in the 7.5 mg/kg group and 2.30 (1.75 to 3.01) on placebo; rate ratios vs placebo were 1.08 (0.76 to 1.55) for 5.0 mg/kg and 0.89 (0.62 to 1.27) for 7.5 mg/kg (both p>0.999 — relative figures inside the 0.5–2.0 band, and null). Adverse-event incidence was similar across groups; grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 47 (56%) of 84 patients on 5.0 mg/kg, 32 (39%) of 83 on 7.5 mg/kg and 27 (32%) of 85 on placebo. The authors note the COVID-19 pandemic, varied global patterns of health-care use and crisis management, and the drug's commercial availability as possible influences on the result.
cards.watchOut: STAND is the confirmatory trial and it is null at both doses — any residual case for crizanlizumab must argue against its own phase 3, and the drug was withdrawn following this failure; this card is the shelf's centre of gravity for the crizanlizumab half.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two celebrated approvals, two post-approval reversals — this shelf is the cautionary tale, honestly stamped
cards.summary: Two celebrated approvals, two post-approval reversals — this shelf is the cautionary tale, honestly stamped — Split: POSSIBLE (voxelotor surrogate) · MAYBE (weak evidence) (crizanlizumab).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HOPE (274 participants), SUSTAIN (198 patients) and STAND (252 patients).
cards.result: Voxelotor delivered a large surrogate response (haemoglobin response 51% vs 7%) and crizanlizumab a large relative phase 2 crisis reduction (45.3%), yet neither programme survived post-approval scrutiny: voxelotor was withdrawn after later safety findings, and crizanlizumab's own phase 3 found rate ratios of 1.08 and 0.89 against placebo before its withdrawal. The currency sweep also surfaced mitapivat's RISE UP phase 3 and the HOPE Kids 2 voxelotor-in-children trial — next-generation or pre-withdrawal questions, fenced here. Hydroxyurea (drafted #669) and transfusion programmes (#670) remain the established sickle-cell backbone and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not use this shelf to imply either drug is currently available or endorsed; its value is the pattern — surrogate or phase 2 success is a promissory note, and confirmatory trials are where it is redeemed or defaulted.

shelves.title: Eltrombopag added to immunosuppression in severe aplastic anaemia (RACE)
shelves.question: Does adding eltrombopag to horse antithymocyte globulin plus ciclosporin improve haematologic response in treatment-naïve severe aplastic anaemia — the randomised RACE trial, on the earlier NIH cohort-randomised experience?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Aplastic/drug therapy,genetics,therapy · Antilymphocyte Serum/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Benzoates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cyclosporine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hydrazines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Immunosuppression Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial plus one prospective cohort programme with a historical comparison — labelled as such, not double-Level-A. RACE (197 patients, open-label) found complete response at 3 months in 22% with eltrombopag added vs 10% without (odds ratio 3.2), and overall response at 6 months in 68% vs 41%, with faster time to first response (median 3.0 vs 8.8 months). The NIH Townsley programme (92 consecutive patients) found complete response at 6 months of 58% in its best-timing cohort vs 10% in its historical cohort. A single RCT, however consistent with the cohort experience, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RACE 2022: adding eltrombopag doubled complete response at 3 months (22% vs 10%; odds ratio 3.2) and raised overall response at 6 months to 68% vs 41%
cards.summary: RACE (2022): adding eltrombopag doubled complete response at 3 months ( 22% vs 10% ; odds ratio 3.2) and raised overall response at 6 months to 68% vs 41%.
cards.type: Prospective, investigator-led, open-label, multicentre, randomised, phase 3 trial
cards.people: 197 previously untreated patients with severe aplastic anaemia, assigned to horse antithymocyte globulin plus cyclosporine alone (Group A, 101) or the same immunosuppression plus eltrombopag (Group B, 96); the primary endpoint was haematological complete response at 3 months; median follow-up 24 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Complete response at 3 months: 10% in Group A vs 22% in Group B (odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.3 to 7.8; P=0.01 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Overall response (complete or partial) at 6 months: 41% vs 68%. Median time to first response: 8.8 months vs 3.0 months. The incidence of severe adverse events was similar in the two groups. With a median follow-up of 24 months, a karyotypic abnormality classified as myelodysplastic syndrome developed in 1 patient in Group A and 2 in Group B; event-free survival was 34% and 46% respectively. Somatic mutations were detected at baseline in 29% (Group A) and 31% (Group B), rising to 66% and 55% at 6 months, without affecting haematological response or 2-year outcome.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with response (not survival) endpoints, and only 197 patients with a rare disease — the mutation and clonal-evolution numbers (myelodysplasia in 1 vs 2 patients) are far too small to settle the long-term safety question they gesture at; a long-term RACE outcomes report appeared in the currency sweep as a follow-up of this same trial.

cards.headline: Townsley 2017 (NIH): eltrombopag from day 1 gave a 58% complete response at 6 months, against 10% in the programme's historical cohort
cards.summary: NIH cohort (2017): eltrombopag from day 1 gave a 58% complete response at 6 months, against 10% in the programme's historical cohort.
cards.type: Prospective phase 1–2 cohort programme with historical-cohort comparison (not a randomised trial)
cards.people: 92 consecutive, previously untreated patients with severe aplastic anaemia enrolled in three sequential cohorts differing in eltrombopag timing and duration (cohort 1: from day 14 for 6 months; cohort 2: from day 14 for 3 months; cohort 3: from day 1 for 6 months), each receiving standard immunosuppression plus eltrombopag; median follow-up 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Complete haematological response at 6 months: 33% in cohort 1, 26% in cohort 2 and 58% in cohort 3; overall response rates were 80%, 87% and 94% respectively. In the combined cohorts, complete and overall response rates were higher than in the programme's historical cohort (complete response 10%; overall response 66%). At a median follow-up of 2 years the survival rate was 97%, with one death from a non-haematological cause. Rates of relapse and clonal evolution were similar to the programme's historical experience; severe rashes in two patients led to early eltrombopag discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Labelled plainly: the comparison is against a historical cohort, not a randomised control — era effects in supportive care and selection can inflate such contrasts, which is why RACE (previous card), not this programme, carries the shelf's randomised weight.

shelves.title: Reversing anticoagulants: andexanet for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding, and idarucizumab for dabigatran
shelves.question: Does andexanet alfa achieve haemostasis in factor-Xa-inhibitor intracerebral haemorrhage versus usual care (ANNEXA-I) — and does idarucizumab fully reverse dabigatran in bleeding or urgent surgery (RE-VERSE AD)?
shelves.mesh: Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cerebral Hemorrhage/drug therapy,chemically induced · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Factor Xa/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Hematoma/chemically induced,drug therapy · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy,complications · Acute Disease
shelves.balance: Tier C — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (thrombotic-harm signal, including ischaemic stroke): Split: POSSIBLE — andexanet haemostatic efficacy with a thrombotic-harm signal · POSSIBLE — idarucizumab reversal (single-arm evidence). ANNEXA-I (530 patients, randomised) found haemostatic efficacy in 67.0% on andexanet vs 53.1% on usual care (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points), but thrombotic events in 10.3% vs 5.6% — including ischaemic stroke in 6.5% vs 1.5% — with no appreciable difference in modified Rankin score or death within 30 days; that harm signal is why this shelf is Tier C. RE-VERSE AD (503 patients) is a single-arm cohort: idarucizumab reversed dabigatran by a median maximum of 100% on clotting assays, with thrombotic events in 6.3–7.4% and mortality of about 19% at 90 days in a very sick population — reversal of a laboratory effect is well shown; comparative clinical benefit is not testable from this design, hence POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ANNEXA-I 2024: andexanet improved haemostatic efficacy (67.0% vs 53.1%) but raised thrombotic events (10.3% vs 5.6%), including ischaemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%) — Tier C harm signal
cards.summary: ANNEXA-I (2024): andexanet improved haemostatic efficacy ( 67.0% vs 53.1% ) but raised thrombotic events (10.3% vs 5.6%), including ischaemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (open-label with blinded endpoint adjudication design, vs usual care)
cards.people: 530 patients who had taken a factor Xa inhibitor within 15 hours before an acute intracerebral haemorrhage, randomised 1:1 to andexanet (263) or usual care (267); efficacy was assessed in an interim analysis of 452 patients and safety in all 530. Atrial fibrillation was the most common indication for factor Xa inhibitors, and 85.5% of the usual-care group received prothrombin complex concentrate. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Haemostatic efficacy (haematoma expansion of 35% or less at 12 hours, NIH Stroke Scale increase of under 7 points at 12 hours, and no rescue therapy between 3 and 12 hours) was achieved in 150 of 224 patients (67.0%) on andexanet vs 121 of 228 (53.1%) on usual care (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points, 95% CI 4.6 to 22.2; P=0.003). The median reduction in anti-factor Xa activity to the 1–2-hour nadir was 94.5% vs 26.9% (P<0.001). Thrombotic events occurred in 27 of 263 patients (10.3%) on andexanet vs 15 of 267 (5.6%) on usual care (difference 4.6 percentage points, 0.1 to 9.2; P=0.048); ischaemic stroke occurred in 17 patients (6.5%) vs 4 (1.5%). There were no appreciable differences between the groups in the modified Rankin scale score or in death within 30 days.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: the trade at the heart of this card — better haematoma control against more thrombosis, with no functional-outcome or mortality advantage at 30 days — is exactly a developer-verdict question. The comparator was mostly prothrombin complex concentrate (85.5%), so this is not a trial against no treatment.

cards.headline: RE-VERSE AD 2017: idarucizumab reversed dabigatran by a median maximum of 100%; median time to bleeding cessation 2.5 hours in assessable patients
cards.summary: RE-VERSE AD (2017): idarucizumab reversed dabigatran by a median maximum of 100% ; median time to bleeding cessation 2.5 hours in assessable patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, open-label, single-arm cohort study (no control group)
cards.people: 503 patients given 5 g of intravenous idarucizumab: group A (301) with uncontrolled dabigatran-associated bleeding, and group B (202) about to undergo an urgent procedure; the primary endpoint was the maximum percentage reversal of dabigatran's anticoagulant effect within 4 hours, by diluted thrombin time or ecarin clotting time. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median maximum percentage reversal was 100% (95% CI 100 to 100) on either assay. In group A, 137 patients (45.5%) presented with gastrointestinal bleeding and 98 (32.6%) with intracranial haemorrhage; among patients who could be assessed, the median time to cessation of bleeding was 2.5 hours. In group B, the median time to initiation of the intended procedure was 1.6 hours, and periprocedural haemostasis was assessed as normal in 93.4%, mildly abnormal in 5.1% and moderately abnormal in 1.5%. At 90 days, thrombotic events had occurred in 6.3% of group A and 7.4% of group B, and mortality was 18.8% and 18.9% respectively. There were no serious adverse safety signals.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm by design (a placebo-controlled reversal trial in exsanguinating patients was not feasible) — the 100% figure is reversal of a clotting assay, and the ~19% mortality reflects the underlying emergencies, not a drug effect in either direction; clinical outcomes have no comparator and cannot be stamped beyond POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Off-pump versus on-pump coronary-artery bypass grafting
shelves.question: Does avoiding cardiopulmonary bypass in CABG improve early outcomes or graft patency versus conventional on-pump surgery (ROOBY, CORONARY)?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Bypass/mortality · Coronary Artery Bypass, Off-Pump/mortality · Coronary Disease/surgery · Graft Occlusion, Vascular/epidemiology · Health Resources/statistics & numerical data · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Memory Disorders/diagnosis,epidemiology
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — no 30-day advantage for off-pump · POSSIBLE — worse 1-year composite and graft patency in ROOBY. CORONARY (4752 patients) found the 30-day composite of death, stroke, myocardial infarction or dialysis-requiring renal failure at 9.8% off-pump versus 10.3% on-pump (hazard ratio 0.95, relative, non-significant), with less transfusion, reoperation for bleeding, acute kidney injury and respiratory complications off-pump, but more early repeat revascularisation (0.7% vs 0.2%). ROOBY (2203 patients) found no 30-day difference (7.0% vs 5.6%; P=0.19) but a worse 1-year composite off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04), fewer completed grafts (17.8% vs 11.1% incomplete) and lower graft patency (82.6% vs 87.8%). Mortality was a component of both composites and neither trial claims a mortality benefit, so the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Shroyer 2009 (ROOBY): no 30-day difference (7.0% vs 5.6%), but the 1-year composite was worse off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%) and graft patency lower (82.6% vs 87.8%)
cards.summary: ROOBY (2009): no 30-day difference (7.0% vs 5.6%), but the 1-year composite was worse off-pump ( 9.9% vs 7.4% ) and graft patency lower (82.6% off-pump).
cards.people: 2203 patients scheduled for urgent or elective CABG, randomised to off-pump or on-pump procedures; follow-up angiography in 1371 patients covering 4093 grafts. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The 30-day composite of death or complications was 7.0% off-pump versus 5.6% on-pump (P=0.19) — no significant difference. The 1-year composite of death, repeat revascularisation or nonfatal myocardial infarction was higher off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04). Fewer grafts than planned were completed in 17.8% versus 11.1% (P<0.001), and overall graft patency was lower off-pump (82.6% vs 87.8%; P<0.01). There were no differences in neuropsychological outcomes or short-term use of major resources.
cards.watchOut: A VA population operated on in an era of variable off-pump experience; the 1-year signal is a composite driven in part by revascularisation, not a mortality result — and the card does not present it as one.
cards.source: Shroyer AL et al. On-pump versus off-pump coronary-artery bypass surgery. The New England journal of medicine. 2009;361(19):1827-37. PMID: 19890125. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00032630, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: CORONARY (2012): the 30-day composite was 9.8% off-pump vs 10.3% on-pump (hazard ratio 0.95, non-significant), with less transfusion and kidney injury.
cards.people: 4752 patients in whom CABG was planned, at 79 centres in 19 countries, randomised to off-pump or on-pump CABG. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the composite of death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction or new renal failure requiring dialysis at 30 days (9.8% vs 10.3%; hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.14; P=0.59) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates — nor in any individual component. Off-pump surgery reduced transfusion (50.7% vs 63.3%; relative risk 0.80), reoperation for perioperative bleeding (1.4% vs 2.4%; relative risk 0.61), acute kidney injury (28.0% vs 32.1%; relative risk 0.87) and respiratory complications (5.9% vs 7.5%; relative risk 0.79), all relative measures, but increased early repeat revascularisation (0.7% vs 0.2%; hazard ratio 4.01).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-day outcomes only in this report; the process gains (transfusion, kidney injury) are real but none of the composite's hard components moved, and the early-revascularisation hazard ratio of 4.01 rests on very small absolute rates (0.7% vs 0.2%).

shelves.title: Vericiguat after a worsening heart-failure event (VICTORIA), and in stable HFrEF (VICTOR)
shelves.question: In HFrEF patients recently worsened (hospitalised or given IV diuretics), does vericiguat reduce cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation — and does it help patients who have not recently worsened?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Chronic Disease · Heart Failure/drug therapy,physiopathology · Heterocyclic Compounds, 2-Ring/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Hypotension/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the composites include cardiovascular death): After a worsening event, VICTORIA (5,050 patients) found the composite of cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation in 35.5% on vericiguat vs 38.5% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.98) — a modest relative effect inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own, with cardiovascular death itself not significantly reduced (16.4% vs 17.5%; HR 0.93, 0.81 to 1.06). In patients WITHOUT recent worsening, VICTOR (6,105 patients) missed its primary composite (18.0% vs 19.1%; HR 0.93, 0.83 to 1.04; p=0.22); its lower cardiovascular-death rate (9.6% vs 11.3%) is nominal only, because the primary endpoint failed. The dose-finding SOCRATES-REDUCED trial did not significantly lower NT-proBNP at 12 weeks. Benefit, if real, is confined to the post-worsening setting and is modest.

cards.headline: VICTORIA 2020: vericiguat lowered the composite of cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation after a worsening event — 35.5% vs 38.5%, hazard ratio 0.90
cards.summary: VICTORIA 2020: vericiguat cut the composite of cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation after a worsening event ( 35.5% vs 38.5% ; HR 0.90).
cards.people: 5,050 patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–IV) and ejection fraction below 45% who had recently been hospitalised or received intravenous diuretic therapy, assigned to vericiguat (target 10 mg daily; 2,526) or placebo (2,524) on top of guideline-based therapy, followed for a median of 10.8 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (death from cardiovascular causes or first hospitalisation for heart failure) occurred in 897 of 2,526 patients (35.5%) on vericiguat and 972 of 2,524 (38.5%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.98; P=0.02 — a relative measure). Hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 27.4% vs 29.6% (HR 0.90, 0.81 to 1.00), and death from cardiovascular causes in 16.4% vs 17.5% (HR 0.93, 0.81 to 1.06) — the mortality component was not significantly reduced, and per this library's rule the heart-failure figures are printed with mortality beside them. The composite of death from any cause or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 37.9% vs 40.9% (HR 0.90, 0.83 to 0.98). Symptomatic hypotension (9.1% vs 7.9%) and syncope (4.0% vs 3.5%) were numerically more common on vericiguat, neither significantly.
cards.watchOut: The headline hazard ratio of 0.90 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence on its own: the absolute gain is about 3 percentage points over ~11 months in a very high-risk population, and it is driven by hospitalisations, not by a proven mortality reduction.

cards.headline: SOCRATES-REDUCED 2015: vericiguat did not significantly lower NT-proBNP at 12 weeks; an exploratory dose-response pointed to the 10 mg dose
cards.summary: SOCRATES-REDUCED 2015: no significant NT-proBNP fall at 12 weeks; an exploratory dose-response pointed to the 10 mg dose.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding phase 2 trial
cards.people: 456 patients with worsening chronic heart failure and LVEF below 45% (within 4 weeks of a worsening event), randomised to placebo (92) or one of four daily vericiguat target doses (1.25, 2.5, 5 or 10 mg; 91 each) for 12 weeks, across Europe, North America and Asia. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in log-transformed NT-proBNP from baseline to week 12 — was not significantly different between the pooled three highest vericiguat doses and placebo (difference of means −0.122; 90% CI −0.32 to 0.07; ratio of geometric means 0.885, 90% CI 0.73 to 1.08; P=.15). An exploratory secondary analysis suggested a dose-response relationship, with higher doses associated with greater NT-proBNP reductions (P<.02). Any adverse event occurred in 77.2% on placebo and 71.4% on 10 mg vericiguat.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate-endpoint dose-finding trial whose prespecified primary analysis was null: it justified testing 10 mg in phase 3, it is not evidence of clinical benefit, and it is counted as programme background, not as a second positive trial.
cards.source: Gheorghiade M et al. cards.summary: VICTOR 2025: in stable HFrEF without recent worsening, vericiguat missed its primary composite ( 18.0% vs 19.1% ; HR 0.93, p=0.22).

shelves.title: Cardiac myosin activation with omecamtiv mecarbil (GALACTIC-HF, METEORIC-HF)
shelves.question: Does omecamtiv mecarbil reduce heart-failure events or cardiovascular death in HFrEF — and does it improve exercise capacity or symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Myosins/drug effects,metabolism · Cardiotonic Agents/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Heart Failure, Systolic/drug therapy,metabolism,physiopathology · Myocardial Contraction/drug effects · Stroke Volume · Urea/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,pharmacology,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; GALACTIC-HF's composite includes cardiovascular death): GALACTIC-HF (8,256 patients) found the composite of a first heart-failure event or cardiovascular death in 37.0% on omecamtiv mecarbil vs 39.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.99) — a small relative effect inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band — while cardiovascular death itself was identical (19.6% vs 19.4%; HR 1.01) and symptom scores did not improve. METEORIC-HF then found no improvement in exercise capacity (peak VO2 difference −0.45 mL/kg/min, favouring placebo numerically). This is a drug that moved a composite modestly without moving mortality, symptoms or exercise capacity.

cards.headline: GALACTIC-HF 2021: omecamtiv mecarbil lowered the composite of heart-failure events or cardiovascular death — 37.0% vs 39.1%, hazard ratio 0.92 — with cardiovascular death unchanged (19.6% vs 19.4%)
cards.summary: GALACTIC-HF 2021: omecamtiv mecarbil lowered the composite of heart-failure events or cardiovascular death slightly ( 37.0% vs 39.1% ; HR 0.92).
cards.people: 8,256 inpatients and outpatients with symptomatic chronic heart failure and ejection fraction of 35% or less, assigned to omecamtiv mecarbil (25, 37.5 or 50 mg twice daily by plasma level; 4,120) or placebo (4,112) in addition to standard therapy, followed for a median of 21.8 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (first heart-failure event — hospitalisation or urgent visit — or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 1,523 of 4,120 patients (37.0%) on omecamtiv mecarbil and 1,607 of 4,112 (39.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.99; P=0.03 — a relative measure). Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 808 patients (19.6%) and 798 (19.4%), respectively (HR 1.01, 0.92 to 1.11) — no mortality benefit, printed beside the heart-failure composite per this library's rule. There was no significant difference in the change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score. Median NT-proBNP change at week 24 was 10% lower on omecamtiv mecarbil; median cardiac troponin I was 4 ng/L higher. Cardiac ischaemic and ventricular arrhythmia event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: The entire composite gain comes from heart-failure events, the effect size (HR 0.92) sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own, and the troponin rise, though small, runs against the drug's 'no extra oxygen demand' rationale.

cards.headline: METEORIC-HF 2022: omecamtiv mecarbil did not improve exercise capacity — peak VO2 changed by −0.24 vs +0.21 mL/kg/min on placebo
cards.summary: METEORIC-HF 2022: no exercise-capacity benefit — peak VO2 changed by −0.24 vs +0.21 mL/kg/min.
cards.people: 276 patients with chronic HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%), NYHA class II–III, NT-proBNP ≥200 pg/mL and baseline peak VO2 ≤75% of predicted, randomised 2:1 to omecamtiv mecarbil (185) or placebo (91) for 20 weeks at 63 sites in North America and Europe; median age 64 years (IQR 55–70); 15% women; 90% completed the trial.
cards.result: Mean change in peak VO2 from baseline to week 20 did not differ significantly between groups (−0.24 mL/kg/min on omecamtiv mecarbil vs +0.21 on placebo; least-squares mean difference −0.45 mL/kg/min, 95% CI −1.02 to 0.13; P=.13). Total workload, ventilatory efficiency and accelerometer-measured daily activity were the secondary endpoints and the authors conclude the findings do not support omecamtiv mecarbil for improving exercise capacity. cards.watchOut: A small, short functional trial — but it tested exactly the outcome patients feel, and the point estimate favoured placebo; combined with GALACTIC-HF's flat symptom score, the 'better contraction' mechanism did not translate into patients doing or feeling more.

shelves.title: Finerenone in heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (FINEARTS-HF)
shelves.question: In HFmrEF/HFpEF, does finerenone reduce the composite of cardiovascular death and total worsening heart-failure events?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the composite includes cardiovascular death): FINEARTS-HF is a single large trial (6,001 patients): the primary composite of total worsening heart-failure events and cardiovascular death occurred at a rate ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.95) versus placebo, driven by worsening heart-failure events (rate ratio 0.82), while cardiovascular death itself was 8.1% vs 8.7% (hazard ratio 0.93, 0.78 to 1.11) — not significant. shelves.title: Fixed-dose isosorbide dinitrate plus hydralazine in Black patients with HFrEF (A-HeFT)
shelves.question: In self-identified Black patients with advanced HFrEF already on standard therapy, does adding fixed-dose isosorbide dinitrate–hydralazine reduce mortality?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; mortality claim): A-HeFT (1,050 Black patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure) was stopped early because mortality was lower on isosorbide dinitrate–hydralazine than placebo (6.2% vs 10.2%; hazard ratio for death 0.57) — a large relative effect, from a single trial, in one self-identified population, stopped early (which inflates effects). The predecessor V-HeFT programme points the same way for the combination (V-HeFT I: two-year mortality 25.6% vs 34.3% on placebo, an era before ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers) but V-HeFT II found enalapril superior to the combination for mortality (18% vs 25% at two years). One population-specific pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: A-HeFT 2004: adding fixed-dose isosorbide dinitrate–hydralazine lowered mortality in Black patients with advanced heart failure — 6.2% vs 10.2% — and the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: A-HeFT 2004: fixed-dose isosorbide dinitrate–hydralazine lowered mortality in Black patients with advanced heart failure ( 6.2% vs 10.2% ) — the trial stopped early.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, terminated early for benefit
cards.people: 1,050 self-identified Black patients with NYHA class III or IV heart failure and dilated ventricles, assigned to fixed-dose isosorbide dinitrate plus hydralazine or placebo in addition to standard therapy (including neurohormonal blockers). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The trial was terminated early owing to significantly higher mortality on placebo: death from any cause occurred in 6.2% on the combination vs 10.2% on placebo (P=0.02), a 43% relative reduction in the rate of death (hazard ratio 0.57; P=0.01). First hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 16.4% vs 22.4% (a 33% relative reduction; P=0.001) — printed beside the mortality figure per this library's rule. The primary composite score was also better on the combination (−0.1±1.9 vs −0.5±2.0; P=0.01), as was quality-of-life change (−5.6±20.6 vs −2.7±21.2; P=0.02; lower is better).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, stopped early — early stops exaggerate effects — in a self-identified racial subgroup selected because earlier trials hinted at a favourable response; it does not establish the combination's effect in other populations, and no confirmatory trial exists.

cards.headline: V-HeFT I 1986: hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate lowered two-year mortality versus placebo (25.6% vs 34.3%); prazosin did not
cards.summary: V-HeFT I 1986: the combination lowered two-year mortality versus placebo ( 25.6% vs 34.3% ); prazosin did not.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Veterans Administration cooperative trial
cards.people: 642 men with chronic congestive heart failure and reduced exercise tolerance, all taking digoxin and a diuretic, assigned to additional placebo, prazosin (20 mg/day) or hydralazine (300 mg/day) plus isosorbide dinitrate (160 mg/day); follow-up averaged 2.3 years (range 0.5–5.7).

cards.summary: V-HeFT II 1991: enalapril beat the combination on mortality ( 18% vs 25% at two years).
cards.people: 804 men with chronic heart failure receiving digoxin and diuretic therapy, assigned to enalapril 20 mg daily or hydralazine 300 mg plus isosorbide dinitrate 160 mg daily (the V-HeFT I regimen); followed for two years and beyond.
cards.result: Mortality at two years was significantly lower on enalapril (18%) than on hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate (25%) (P=0.016; a 28.0% relative reduction), with overall mortality tending lower (P=0.08); the enalapril advantage came from fewer sudden deaths. shelves.title: Spironolactone for HFpEF: TOPCAT's regional split, and Aldo-DHF
shelves.question: Does spironolactone reduce cardiovascular death, aborted arrest or heart-failure hospitalisation in HFpEF — and how much of the answer depends on where patients were enrolled?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Heart Failure/drug therapy,mortality,physiopathology · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Spironolactone/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split stamp — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; TOPCAT's composite includes cardiovascular death): MAYBE (weak evidence) for event reduction — TOPCAT (3,445 patients) missed its primary composite (18.6% vs 20.4%; hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.04; P=0.14); only the heart-failure-hospitalisation component fell (12.0% vs 14.2%; HR 0.83), neither total deaths nor all hospitalisations fell, and the trial is shadowed by its Americas-vs-Russia/Georgia enrolment split (canrenone levels later suggested many Russia/Georgia participants may not have taken or received active drug — a conduct problem the abstract cannot show). POSSIBLE for a physiological effect — Aldo-DHF (422 patients) improved diastolic function (E/e′ difference −1.5) but not peak VO2, symptoms or quality of life, and slightly shortened 6-minute walk distance. Hyperkalaemia doubled in TOPCAT (18.7% vs 9.1%).

cards.headline: TOPCAT 2014: spironolactone did not significantly reduce the primary composite in HFpEF — 18.6% vs 20.4% (P=0.14) — though heart-failure hospitalisation fell (12.0% vs 14.2%)
cards.summary: TOPCAT 2014: spironolactone did not significantly reduce the primary composite in HFpEF ( 18.6% vs 20.4% , P=0.14).
cards.people: 3,445 patients with symptomatic heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% or more, assigned to spironolactone (15–45 mg daily; 1,722) or placebo (1,723); mean follow-up 3.3 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (death from cardiovascular causes, aborted cardiac arrest, or hospitalisation for management of heart failure) occurred in 320 of 1,722 patients (18.6%) on spironolactone and 351 of 1,723 (20.4%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.04; P=0.14) — not significant. Of its components, only hospitalisation for heart failure was significantly lower (206 patients [12.0%] vs 245 [14.2%]; HR 0.83, 0.69 to 0.99; P=0.04 — a relative measure, printed beside the null mortality-containing composite per this library's rule). Neither total deaths nor hospitalisations for any reason were significantly reduced. Hyperkalaemia occurred in 18.7% vs 9.1%, serum creatinine rose more on spironolactone, but serious adverse events, creatinine ≥3.0 mg/dL and dialysis did not differ significantly with monitoring.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the trial as designed; it cannot show the regional problem that dominates TOPCAT's interpretation — event rates and apparent response differed sharply between the Americas and Russia/Georgia, and later drug-level testing suggested substantial non-exposure in the Russia/Georgia cohort. A null primary with a positive component is hypothesis-generating, not proof.
cards.source: Pitt B et al. Spironolactone for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(15):1383-92. PMID: 24716680. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00094302, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Aldo-DHF 2013: spironolactone improved diastolic function (E/e′ −1.5) but not exercise capacity, symptoms or quality of life in HFpEF
cards.summary: Aldo-DHF 2013: diastolic function improved (E/e′ −1.5) but exercise capacity, symptoms and quality of life did not.
cards.people: 422 ambulatory patients with HFpEF (mean age 67 [SD 8] years; 52% female), NYHA class II–III, LVEF ≥50% with diastolic dysfunction, at 10 sites in Germany and Austria, assigned to spironolactone 25 mg daily (213) or placebo (209) for 12 months.
cards.result: Of the co-primary endpoints, diastolic function improved: E/e′ fell from 12.7 (SD 3.6) to 12.1 (SD 3.7) on spironolactone and rose from 12.8 (SD 4.4) to 13.6 (SD 4.3) on placebo (adjusted mean difference −1.5, 95% CI −2.0 to −0.9; P<.001); peak VO2 did not change differently (+0.1 mL/min/kg, −0.6 to +0.8; P=.81). Left ventricular mass index fell (difference −6 g/m²; P=.009) and NT-proBNP improved (geometric mean ratio 0.86; P=.03), but symptoms and quality of life did not improve, 6-minute walk distance slightly worsened (−15 m; P=.03), potassium rose (+0.2 mmol/L) and eGFR fell (−5 mL/min/1.73 m²), without affecting hospitalisations.
cards.watchOut: A 12-month surrogate-endpoint trial: the echocardiographic improvement is real but every patient-centred endpoint was flat or worse — it explains a possible mechanism for TOPCAT's hospitalisation component without rescuing its null primary.
cards.source: Edelmann F et al. Effect of spironolactone on diastolic function and exercise capacity in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: the Aldo-DHF randomized controlled trial.
