shelves.title: Tolvaptan in hospitalised worsening heart failure (EVEREST)
shelves.question: Does tolvaptan improve dyspnoea, weight and hyponatraemia short-term in hospitalised worsening heart failure — without improving long-term mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Benzazepines/therapeutic use · Blood Urea Nitrogen · Body Weight/drug effects · Cardiovascular Agents/therapeutic use · Creatinine/blood
shelves.balance: Split stamp — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; mortality was a co-primary outcome): LIKELY the long-term null — EVEREST (4,133 hospitalised patients) found all-cause mortality of 25.9% on tolvaptan vs 26.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.11) and the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation at 42.0% vs 40.2% (HR 1.04) over a median 9.9 months: a large, precise null. POSSIBLE for short-term decongestion — the twin EVEREST clinical-status trials found better day-1 dyspnoea relief, greater weight loss and improved oedema within days, and sodium rose in hyponatraemic patients; those are days-long symptom effects in one programme, not outcome benefits. Tolvaptan's other homes (hyponatraemia, ADPKD) are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: EVEREST Outcome Trial 2007: tolvaptan had no effect on long-term mortality (25.9% vs 26.3%) or on cardiovascular death/heart-failure hospitalisation (42.0% vs 40.2%)
cards.summary: EVEREST Outcome 2007: tolvaptan had no effect on long-term mortality ( 25.9% vs 26.3% ) or the cardiovascular death/heart-failure composite.
cards.type: Event-driven, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled outcome trial
cards.people: 4,133 patients hospitalised with worsening heart failure at 359 sites in North and South America and Europe, assigned within 48 hours of admission to oral tolvaptan 30 mg daily (2,072) or placebo (2,061) for a minimum of 60 days on top of standard therapy; median follow-up 9.9 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: All-cause mortality (a dual primary endpoint) occurred in 537 patients (25.9%) on tolvaptan and 543 (26.3%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.11; P=.68), with non-inferiority formally met (upper confidence limit within the 1.25 margin). The composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 42.0% vs 40.2% (HR 1.04, 0.95 to 1.14; P=.55) — the heart-failure figures printed beside the mortality null, per this library's rule. Secondary endpoints of cardiovascular mortality and worsening heart failure also did not differ. Tolvaptan improved day-1 dyspnoea, day-1 body weight and day-7 oedema, raised sodium in hyponatraemic patients, and caused more thirst and dry mouth; major adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: One programme, one (large) trial: the mortality null is precise enough to carry LIKELY as a null, but the trial tested 30 mg started in hospital for worsening failure — it does not speak to tolvaptan's licensed hyponatraemia or ADPKD uses, which live on other shelves.
cards.source: Konstam MA et al. Effects of oral tolvaptan in patients hospitalized for worsening heart failure: the EVEREST Outcome Trial. JAMA. 2007;297(12):1319-31. PMID: 17384437. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00071331, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: EVEREST Clinical Status Trials 2007: tolvaptan improved dyspnoea at day 1 and weight loss over the first week in two identical inpatient trials
cards.summary: EVEREST Clinical Status 2007: dyspnoea improved at day 1 and weight loss was greater over the first week.
cards.type: Two identical prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Trials A and B) nested in the EVEREST programme
cards.people: 2,048 patients (Trial A) and 2,085 patients (Trial B) hospitalised with heart failure and congestion at 359 sites, randomised within 48 hours of admission to tolvaptan 30 mg daily or placebo in addition to standard therapy including diuretics. cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (global clinical status plus body weight at day 7 or discharge) favoured tolvaptan in both trials (mean [SD] 1.06 [0.43] vs 0.99 [0.44] in Trial A and 1.07 [0.42] vs 0.97 [0.43] in Trial B; both P<.001), driven by weight: day-1 loss 1.71 vs 0.99 kg (A) and 1.82 vs 0.95 kg (B), and day-7/discharge loss 3.35 vs 2.73 kg (A) and 3.77 vs 2.79 kg (B) (all P<.001). shelves.title: Implantable pulmonary-artery pressure monitoring to guide heart-failure care (CHAMPION, GUIDE-HF)
shelves.question: Does management guided by an implanted pulmonary-artery pressure sensor (CardioMEMS) reduce heart-failure hospitalisations and death?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory/instrumentation · Cardiac Catheterization/instrumentation · Electrodes, Implanted · Equipment Design · Equipment Failure Analysis · Heart Failure/diagnosis,physiopathology · Hemodynamics/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; GUIDE-HF's composite includes all-cause mortality): CHAMPION (550 patients, NYHA class III with a prior admission) found fewer heart-failure hospitalisations with pressure-guided care at 6 months (83 vs 120 events; hazard ratio 0.70) and over full follow-up (HR 0.64). GUIDE-HF (1,000 implanted patients, NYHA II–IV) then missed its primary composite of all-cause mortality and total heart-failure events overall (0.563 vs 0.640 events per patient-year; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05; p=0.16); only its prespecified pre-COVID-19 analysis was positive (HR 0.81, CI reaching 1.00; p=0.049), the difference vanishing during the pandemic as control-group event rates fell. Neither trial shows a mortality reduction. One strongly positive smaller trial and one larger null-overall trial give POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CHAMPION 2011: pressure-guided management cut heart-failure hospitalisations — 83 vs 120 events at 6 months (hazard ratio 0.70)
cards.summary: CHAMPION 2011: pressure-guided management cut heart-failure hospitalisations ( 83 vs 120 events at 6 months; HR 0.70).
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial (patients masked; device/management strategy, unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 550 patients with NYHA class III heart failure, irrespective of ejection fraction, and a previous heart-failure hospital admission, at 64 US centres, all implanted with the wireless pulmonary-artery haemodynamic monitor and assigned to pressure-guided management (270) or standard care (280), for at least 6 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months there were 83 heart-failure-related hospitalisations in the treatment group vs 120 in the control group (rates 0.31 vs 0.44; hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.84; p<0.0001 — a relative measure). Over the entire follow-up (mean 15 months [SD 7]) the reduction was 39% in relative terms (153 vs 253 hospitalisations; HR 0.64, 0.55 to 0.75; p<0.0001). Freedom from device- or system-related complications was 98.6% (prespecified criterion 80%) and freedom from pressure-sensor failure 100%. The trial's endpoint was hospitalisation; no mortality figure is reported in the abstract, and no mortality claim is made on this shelf from CHAMPION — mortality for this strategy is addressed by GUIDE-HF, carded below.
cards.watchOut: A single-blind strategy trial in which the treating team knew the pressures: performance and co-intervention bias can inflate hospitalisation effects, and the population was narrow (NYHA III with a prior admission, US centres).

cards.summary: GUIDE-HF 2021: no overall reduction in the composite of mortality and total heart-failure events (HR 0.88; p=0.16).
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blind randomised controlled trial (patients masked; management strategy unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 1,000 successfully implanted patients (of 1,022 enrolled) with heart failure of any ejection fraction, NYHA class II–IV, and either a recent heart-failure hospitalisation or elevated natriuretic peptides, at 118 centres in the USA and Canada, assigned to haemodynamic-guided management (497) or usual care (503); follow-up completed January 2021, spanning the COVID-19 pandemic.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (all-cause mortality plus total heart-failure events at 12 months) occurred at 0.563 events per patient-year in the guided group (253 events) vs 0.640 (289 events) in controls (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05; p=0.16) — not significant; the abstract gives no separate mortality rate, and no mortality benefit is claimed. In the prespecified pre-COVID-19 impact analysis the primary endpoint favoured guided management (0.553 vs 0.682 per patient-year; HR 0.81, 0.66 to 1.00; p=0.049), driven by heart-failure events (HR 0.76, 0.61 to 0.95); during COVID-19 the difference disappeared (HR 1.11, 0.80 to 1.55) as control-group event rates fell 21%. Freedom from device/system complications was 99%.
cards.watchOut: The positive reading rests on a prespecified pandemic sensitivity analysis whose confidence interval touches 1.00, in a trial whose overall primary analysis is null — it rescues the hypothesis for the CHAMPION-like population, it does not confirm benefit across NYHA II–IV.
cards.source: Lindenfeld J et al. Haemodynamic-guided management of heart failure (GUIDE-HF): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2021;398(10304):991-1001. PMID: 34461042. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03387813, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Acute heart-failure vasodilators that failed: nesiritide (ASCEND-HF) and serelaxin (RELAX-AHF-2)
shelves.question: Do intravenous vasodilator or recombinant-peptide therapies for acute decompensated heart failure improve dyspnoea or outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Dyspnea/drug therapy,etiology · Heart Failure/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Hypotension/chemically induced · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kidney Diseases/etiology · Natriuretic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; serelaxin's programme began with a mortality signal and RELAX-AHF-2's primary endpoint was cardiovascular death): Two large double-blind trials are concordantly null on hard outcomes. ASCEND-HF (7,141 patients): nesiritide did not meet its prespecified dyspnoea significance criteria and did not change 30-day death or heart-failure rehospitalisation (9.4% vs 10.1%). RELAX-AHF-2 (6,545 patients): serelaxin did not reduce cardiovascular death at 180 days (8.7% vs 8.9%; hazard ratio 0.98) or worsening heart failure at day 5 (6.9% vs 7.7%), refuting its smaller predecessor's mortality signal. Two very large concordant nulls carry LIKELY for the null, per this library's rule.

cards.headline: ASCEND-HF 2011: nesiritide's dyspnoea effect missed its prespecified significance bar, and 30-day death or heart-failure rehospitalisation was unchanged (9.4% vs 10.1%)
cards.summary: ASCEND-HF 2011: nesiritide's dyspnoea effect missed its prespecified significance bar, and 30-day death or heart-failure rehospitalisation was unchanged.
cards.people: 7,141 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure, assigned to nesiritide or placebo for 24–168 hours in addition to standard care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Dyspnoea was more often markedly or moderately improved on nesiritide at 6 hours (44.5% vs 42.1%; P=0.03) and 24 hours (68.2% vs 66.1%; P=0.007), but the prespecified significance level (P≤0.005 for both, or P≤0.0025 for either) was not met. The composite of rehospitalisation for heart failure or death from any cause within 30 days occurred in 9.4% vs 10.1% (absolute difference −0.7 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 0.7; P=0.31); death from any cause at 30 days was 3.6% vs 4.0% (−0.4 points, −1.3 to 0.5) — printed beside the heart-failure figure per this library's rule. Worsening renal function (>25% eGFR fall) was 31.4% vs 29.5% (odds ratio 1.09, 0.98 to 1.21). Hypotension was more common on nesiritide. The authors conclude nesiritide cannot be recommended for routine use in the broad acute heart-failure population.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of one drug — the null is large and precise for nesiritide as used here (broad population, background standard care); it does not test every vasodilator, which is why this shelf pairs it with the serelaxin trial rather than generalising from it alone.

cards.headline: RELAX-AHF-2 2019: serelaxin did not reduce cardiovascular death at 180 days (8.7% vs 8.9%) or worsening heart failure at 5 days (6.9% vs 7.7%)
cards.summary: RELAX-AHF-2 2019: serelaxin did not reduce cardiovascular death at 180 days ( 8.7% vs 8.9% ) or worsening heart failure at 5 days.
cards.people: 6,545 patients hospitalised for acute heart failure with dyspnoea, congestion on chest radiography, raised natriuretic peptides, mild-to-moderate renal insufficiency and systolic blood pressure ≥125 mm Hg, assigned within 16 hours of presentation to a 48-hour infusion of serelaxin 30 μg/kg/day (3,274) or placebo (3,271) in addition to standard care.
cards.result: Death from cardiovascular causes at 180 days (a primary endpoint) occurred in 285 of 3,274 patients (8.7%) on serelaxin and 290 of 3,271 (8.9%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.15; P=0.77). Worsening heart failure at day 5 (the other primary endpoint) occurred in 6.9% vs 7.7% (HR 0.89, 0.75 to 1.07; P=0.19). There were no significant differences in all-cause death at 180 days, the composite of cardiovascular death or rehospitalisation for heart or renal failure, or length of stay. Adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: The large trial refuted the mortality signal of its own smaller predecessor (RELAX-AHF) — the classic small-trial-to-large-trial reversal; the shelf's claim is the large trial's null, not a class verdict on every relaxin-pathway agent at every dose.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large, concordant nulls on hard outcomes — LIKELY the null, Tier C
cards.summary: Two large, concordant nulls on hard outcomes — LIKELY the null, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ASCEND-HF (7,141 patients, nesiritide) and RELAX-AHF-2 (6,545 patients, serelaxin).
cards.result: Together these trials close the question they tested: in broad acute heart-failure populations, adding these intravenous vasodilator/peptide therapies to standard care did not reduce death (30-day all-cause 3.6% vs 4.0% for nesiritide; 180-day cardiovascular 8.7% vs 8.9% for serelaxin) or heart-failure rehospitalisation/worsening, and nesiritide's dyspnoea effect did not reach its own prespecified bar. Two very large concordant nulls justify LIKELY for the null — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C), because the serelaxin programme's history is a mortality claim that failed to replicate.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the earlier small RELAX-AHF mortality signal without RELAX-AHF-2 beside it; that is the reversal this shelf exists to record.

shelves.title: Sotagliflozin in diabetes with recent worsening heart failure (SOLOIST-WHF)
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes patients recently hospitalised for worsening heart failure, does the dual SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisations or urgent visits?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/chemically induced · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology,mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications,drug therapy · Glycosides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heart Failure/complications,drug therapy · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Hypotension/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the composite includes cardiovascular death): SOLOIST-WHF is a single trial (1,222 patients) stopped early because the sponsor lost funding: the total-events primary endpoint (cardiovascular deaths plus heart-failure hospitalisations and urgent visits) ran at 51.0 vs 76.3 events per 100 patient-years on sotagliflozin vs placebo (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.85), while cardiovascular death alone (10.6 vs 12.5 per 100 patient-years; HR 0.84, 0.58 to 1.22) and all-cause death (HR 0.82) were not significantly reduced. A post hoc analysis of patients dosed before discharge found larger early effects (90-day HR 0.54) — post hoc, and so labelled. One early-stopped trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Diarrhoea (6.1% vs 3.4%) and severe hypoglycaemia (1.5% vs 0.3%) were more common on sotagliflozin.

cards.headline: SOLOIST-WHF 2021: sotagliflozin lowered total cardiovascular deaths and heart-failure hospitalisations/urgent visits — 51.0 vs 76.3 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.67) — in a trial stopped early for loss of funding
cards.summary: SOLOIST-WHF 2021: sotagliflozin lowered total cardiovascular deaths and heart-failure hospitalisations/urgent visits ( 51.0 vs 76.3 events per 100 patient-years ).
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, ended early (sponsor funding lost)
cards.people: 1,222 patients with type 2 diabetes recently hospitalised for worsening heart failure, assigned to sotagliflozin (608) or placebo (614), first dose given before discharge in 48.8% and at a median of 2 days after discharge in the rest; median follow-up 9.0 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (total number of deaths from cardiovascular causes and hospitalisations and urgent visits for heart failure, first and subsequent events) occurred 600 times in total — 245 events on sotagliflozin and 355 on placebo — at rates of 51.0 vs 76.3 per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.85; P<0.001 — a relative measure). Death from cardiovascular causes ran at 10.6 vs 12.5 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.84, 0.58 to 1.22) and death from any cause at 13.5 vs 16.3 (HR 0.82, 0.59 to 1.14) — neither significant, and printed beside the heart-failure event figures per this library's rule. Diarrhoea was more common on sotagliflozin (6.1% vs 3.4%), as was severe hypoglycaemia (1.5% vs 0.3%); hypotension (6.0% vs 4.6%) and acute kidney injury (4.1% vs 4.4%) were similar.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, stopped early for funding (not for benefit), with 1,222 patients and 9 months of follow-up: early termination truncates the evidence even when it does not bias it, and the significant result is a total-events composite whose mortality component is neutral.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Recent Worsening Heart Failure. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(2):117-128. PMID: 33200892. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03521934, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SOLOIST-WHF post hoc 2023: in patients dosed before discharge, sotagliflozin cut the 90-day composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure events (HR 0.54) — a post hoc subgroup analysis
cards.summary: Post hoc 2023: dosing before discharge cut the 90-day composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure events (HR 0.54 ) — labelled post hoc on the card.
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised, double-blind trial (SOLOIST-WHF)
cards.people: 596 of SOLOIST-WHF's 1,222 randomised patients who received study drug on or before their discharge date from the index worsening-heart-failure hospitalisation.
cards.result: Sotagliflozin reduced the main endpoint (cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation/urgent visit) at 90 days after discharge (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.82; P=0.004) and at 30 days (HR 0.49, 0.27 to 0.91; P=0.023), and all-cause mortality at 90 days (HR 0.39, 0.17 to 0.88; P=0.024) — all relative measures from a post hoc subgroup; the abstract reports no absolute event rates for this subset. Effects were consistent across the subgroups examined. Diarrhoea and volume-related events were slightly more frequent on sotagliflozin.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and subset-restricted: it can support 'start before discharge' as a hypothesis aligned with the main trial, but its 90-day mortality hazard ratio (0.39) comes from few events in 596 patients and must never be quoted as the trial's mortality result — the trial's own cardiovascular-death estimate was HR 0.84 and non-significant.

shelves.title: Levosimendan versus dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure (SURVIVE)
shelves.question: Does the calcium sensitiser levosimendan improve survival versus dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure with low output?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Cardiotonic Agents/therapeutic use · Dobutamine/therapeutic use · Heart Failure/blood,drug therapy,mortality · Hydrazones/therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood
shelves.balance: Split stamp — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; all-cause mortality at 180 days was SURVIVE's primary outcome): LIKELY the null on survival — SURVIVE (1,327 patients needing inotropic support) found 180-day all-cause mortality of 26% on levosimendan vs 28% on dobutamine (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.13; P=.40), with no secondary clinical outcome significantly different despite greater BNP falls. MAYBE (weak evidence) for the older signal — LIDO (203 patients) met its haemodynamic primary endpoint (28% vs 15% achieving the response definition) and reported lower 180-day mortality (26% vs 38%; HR 0.57) as a secondary finding in a small trial; SURVIVE, six times larger and powered on mortality, did not reproduce it.

cards.headline: SURVIVE 2007: levosimendan did not reduce 180-day all-cause mortality versus dobutamine — 26% vs 28% (HR 0.91; P=.40)
cards.summary: SURVIVE 2007: levosimendan did not reduce 180-day all-cause mortality versus dobutamine ( 26% vs 28% ; HR 0.91).
cards.people: 1,327 patients hospitalised with acute decompensated heart failure who required inotropic support, at 75 centres in 9 countries, assigned to intravenous levosimendan (664) or dobutamine (663) between March 2003 and December 2004. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 180 days (the primary outcome) occurred in 173 patients (26%) on levosimendan and 185 (28%) on dobutamine (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.13; P=.40). No secondary endpoint differed significantly (31-day mortality, days alive and out of hospital, global assessment, dyspnoea at 24 hours, cardiovascular mortality at 180 days), although B-type natriuretic peptide fell more with levosimendan through 5 days (P<.001). Cardiac failure events were more frequent on dobutamine; atrial fibrillation, hypokalaemia and headache were more frequent on levosimendan.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial with no placebo arm: it shows levosimendan is not superior to dobutamine for survival, not whether either drug beats no inotrope — and its BNP advantage is a surrogate that its own mortality result contradicts as a benefit signal.

cards.headline: LIDO 2002: levosimendan beat dobutamine on its haemodynamic endpoint (28% vs 15%) and reported lower 180-day mortality (26% vs 38%) — in 203 patients
cards.summary: LIDO 2002: better haemodynamics (28% vs 15%) and lower reported 180-day mortality (26% vs 38%) — in only 203 patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group trial
cards.people: 203 patients with severe low-output heart failure under continuous haemodynamic monitoring, assigned to levosimendan (103; loading dose then 24-hour infusion) or dobutamine (100; 24-hour infusion). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary haemodynamic endpoint (≥30% rise in cardiac output with ≥25% fall in pulmonary-capillary wedge pressure at 24 hours) was achieved by 29 patients (28%) on levosimendan and 15 (15%) on dobutamine (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.3; p=0.022 — as reported). At 180 days, 27 levosimendan patients (26%) had died vs 38 (38%) on dobutamine (hazard ratio 0.57, 0.34 to 0.95; p=0.029 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Small, haemodynamics-first, with mortality a secondary endpoint and few deaths (65 in total): exactly the profile whose survival signals large trials exist to test — and SURVIVE (card above), powered on mortality, found HR 0.91. LIDO's mortality figure is therefore stamped MAYBE (weak evidence) wherever it appears on this shelf.

shelves.title: Torsemide versus furosemide after a heart-failure hospitalisation (TRANSFORM-HF)
shelves.question: In patients discharged after a heart-failure hospitalisation, does torsemide reduce all-cause mortality versus furosemide — or is the choice of loop diuretic a distinction without an outcome difference?
shelves.mesh: Furosemide/therapeutic use · Torsemide/therapeutic use · Patient Discharge · Sodium Potassium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Hospitalization
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality was the primary outcome). TRANSFORM-HF (2,859 patients discharged after a heart-failure hospitalisation, open-label pragmatic) found death in 26.1% on torsemide versus 26.2% on furosemide (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.18) over a median 17.4 months, and no significant difference in death or hospitalisation at 12 months. A very large single trial that is null may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); the caveats are real — open-label design, crossover, nonadherence and loss to follow-up all bias toward the null and are stated on the card.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM-HF (Mentz 2023): torsemide did not reduce all-cause mortality versus furosemide — 26.1% versus 26.2% (HR 1.02)
cards.summary: TRANSFORM-HF 2023: torsemide did not reduce all-cause mortality vs furosemide ( 26.1% vs 26.2% ; hazard ratio 1.02).
cards.people: 2,859 participants hospitalised with heart failure (regardless of ejection fraction) at 60 US hospitals, randomised to a torsemide strategy (1,431) or furosemide strategy (1,428) with investigator-selected dosage; median age 65 years (IQR 56–75), 36.9% women, 33.9% Black; median follow-up 17.4 months.
cards.result: Death occurred in 373 of 1,431 patients (26.1%) in the torsemide group and 374 of 1,428 (26.2%) in the furosemide group (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.18) — no significant difference in the primary outcome of all-cause mortality. Over 12 months, all-cause mortality or all-cause hospitalisation occurred in 677 patients (47.3%) versus 704 (49.3%) (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.02), and total hospitalisations numbered 940 versus 987 (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.07). Results were similar across prespecified subgroups, including by ejection fraction. A total of 113 patients (3.7% torsemide, 4.2% furosemide) withdrew consent before completion.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic: crossover, nonadherence and loss to follow-up all dilute any true difference toward the null, as the authors state. The trial tests a discharge diuretic strategy with investigator-chosen doses, not a fixed-dose pharmacological comparison.
cards.source: Mentz RJ et al. Effect of Torsemide vs Furosemide After Discharge on All-Cause Mortality in Patients Hospitalized With Heart Failure: The TRANSFORM-HF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;329(3):214-223. PMID: 36648467. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03296813, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Acetazolamide added to loop diuretics in acute decompensated heart failure (ADVOR)
shelves.question: In acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload, does intravenous acetazolamide added to standard loop diuretics increase successful decongestion within three days?
shelves.mesh: Acetazolamide/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Acute Disease · Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors/adverse effects · Diuretics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/analysis · Sodium
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single large double-blind trial (ADVOR, 519 patients), adding intravenous acetazolamide to standardised loop diuretics raised successful decongestion within 3 days from 30.5% to 42.2% (risk ratio 1.46, relative), with higher urine output and natriuresis. The composite of death or heart-failure rehospitalisation at 3 months did not differ (29.7% versus 27.8%; hazard ratio 1.07) — the HF figures are printed beside that mortality-inclusive composite on the card, and no event benefit is claimed. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ADVOR (Mullens 2022): acetazolamide raised successful decongestion at 3 days — 42.2% versus 30.5% (relative risk ratio 1.46)
cards.summary: ADVOR 2022: acetazolamide raised successful decongestion at 3 days ( 42.2% vs 30.5% ; relative risk ratio 1.46 — an absolute gain of about 12 points).
cards.people: 519 patients with acute decompensated heart failure, clinical signs of volume overload (oedema, pleural effusion or ascites) and NT-proBNP above 1000 pg/mL or BNP above 250 pg/mL, randomised to intravenous acetazolamide 500 mg once daily (256 analysed) or placebo (259 analysed) added to standardised intravenous loop diuretics at twice the oral maintenance dose; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Successful decongestion (absence of signs of volume overload within 3 days, without escalation of decongestive therapy) occurred in 108 of 256 patients (42.2%) in the acetazolamide group and 79 of 259 (30.5%) in the placebo group (risk ratio 1.46, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.82; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). Death from any cause or rehospitalisation for heart failure during 3 months occurred in 76 of 256 (29.7%) versus 72 of 259 (27.8%) (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.48) — no difference. Acetazolamide was associated with higher cumulative urine output and natriuresis. Worsening kidney function, hypokalaemia, hypotension and adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The proven gain is faster decongestion, a process outcome: the trial was not powered for, and did not show, any difference in death or rehospitalisation. Single pivotal trial to date.
cards.source: Mullens W et al. Acetazolamide in Acute Decompensated Heart Failure with Volume Overload. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(13):1185-1195. PMID: 36027559. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03505788, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Hydrochlorothiazide added to furosemide in acute heart failure (CLOROTIC)
shelves.question: In acute heart failure, does adding hydrochlorothiazide to intravenous furosemide improve diuretic response — weight loss and dyspnoea — versus furosemide alone, and at what renal and electrolyte cost?
shelves.mesh: Furosemide/therapeutic use · Sodium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Hypokalemia/chemically induced,complications · Heart Failure · Diuretics/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Hydrochlorothiazide/therapeutic use · Dyspnea
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single double-blind trial (CLOROTIC, 230 patients), adding hydrochlorothiazide to intravenous furosemide produced more weight loss at 72 hours (2.3 versus 1.5 kg) and greater diuresis, but no difference in patient-reported dyspnoea, and more impaired renal function (46.5 versus 17.2, as printed in the abstract). Mortality and rehospitalisations did not differ — the HF-adjacent outcome figures are printed with that null on the card. One trial, a weight-loss (not symptom or outcome) benefit, and a renal cost: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CLOROTIC (Trullàs 2023): adding hydrochlorothiazide increased weight loss at 72 hours but not dyspnoea relief, with more renal impairment
cards.summary: CLOROTIC 2023: adding hydrochlorothiazide increased weight loss at 72 hours (2.3 vs 1.5 kg) but not dyspnoea relief, with more renal impairment.
cards.people: 230 patients with acute heart failure randomised to hydrochlorothiazide or placebo added to an intravenous furosemide regimen; 48 women; age 83 years as stated in the abstract (the abstract does not specify mean or median).
cards.result: Patients assigned to hydrochlorothiazide lost more weight at 72 hours than those assigned to placebo (2.3 versus 1.5 kg; adjusted estimated difference 1.14, P=0.002), with similar results at 96 hours, greater 24-hour diuresis (1775 versus 1400 mL; P=0.05) and greater weight loss per 40 mg of furosemide (P=0.001). There was no significant difference in patient-reported dyspnoea (area under the visual-analogue-scale curve 960 versus 720; P=0.497). Impaired renal function occurred more frequently with hydrochlorothiazide (46.5 versus 17.2, as printed in the abstract; P=0.001), while hypokalaemia rates were similar. There were no differences in mortality or rehospitalisations at 30 and 90 days.
cards.watchOut: A diuretic-response trial in an elderly population (age 83 years as stated): weight and urine volume improved, breathlessness and outcomes did not, and kidneys paid part of the price. Single pivotal trial to date.
cards.source: Trullàs JC et al. Combining loop with thiazide diuretics for decompensated heart failure: the CLOROTIC trial. Eur Heart J. 2023;44(5):411-421. PMID: 36423214. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01647932 and EudraCT 2013-001852-36, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: How to give furosemide in acute heart failure: dose and route (DOSE)
shelves.question: In acute decompensated heart failure, does a high-dose versus low-dose furosemide strategy — or bolus versus continuous infusion — change symptom relief, kidney function, or outcomes (the DOSE trial's 2×2 factorial)?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Area Under Curve · Creatinine/blood · Diuretics/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Dyspnea/etiology · Furosemide/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single pivotal trial (DOSE, 308 patients, 2×2 factorial, double-blind) found no significant difference in patients' global symptom assessment or in change in creatinine between bolus and continuous infusion, or between high-dose (2.5× the oral dose) and low-dose strategies; the high-dose strategy gave greater diuresis and some more favourable secondary measures at the price of transient worsening kidney function. Small, short (72-hour) and symptom-focused: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: DOSE (Felker 2011): neither bolus-versus-infusion nor high-versus-low dose changed symptoms or creatinine significantly at 72 hours
cards.summary: DOSE 2011: neither bolus-vs-infusion nor high-vs-low dose changed symptoms or creatinine significantly at 72 hours.
cards.people: 308 patients with acute decompensated heart failure assigned to intravenous furosemide by bolus every 12 hours or continuous infusion, and at a low dose (equivalent to the previous oral dose) or high dose (2.5 times the previous oral dose), with specified dose adjustments allowed after 48 hours; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For bolus versus continuous infusion there was no significant difference in patients' global assessment of symptoms (mean area under the curve 4236 versus 4373; P=0.47) or in mean change in creatinine (0.05 versus 0.07 mg/dL; P=0.45). For high-dose versus low-dose there was a non-significant trend toward greater symptom improvement with high dose (mean AUC 4430 versus 4171; P=0.06) and no significant difference in creatinine change (0.08 versus 0.04 mg/dL; P=0.21). The high-dose strategy was associated with greater diuresis and more favourable outcomes in some secondary measures but also with transient worsening of renal function.
cards.watchOut: 308 patients and 72-hour coprimary outcomes: DOSE settles the route question pragmatically but cannot speak to mortality or rehospitalisation, and its high-dose symptom trend (P=0.06) is a trend, not a finding.
cards.source: Felker GM et al. Diuretic strategies in patients with acute decompensated heart failure. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(9):797-805. PMID: 21366472. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00577135, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Natriuresis-guided diuretic therapy in acute heart failure (PUSH-AHF)
shelves.question: In acute heart failure, does a urinary-sodium (natriuresis)-guided diuretic algorithm improve natriuresis and decongestion — and change death or heart-failure rehospitalisation — versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Diuretics/therapeutic use · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Natriuresis · Sodium/urine · Sodium Potassium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pragmatic open-label trial (PUSH-AHF, 310 patients), natriuresis-guided therapy met its first dual primary end point — 24-hour urinary sodium excretion 409 versus 345 mmol (P=0.0061) — but not its second: death or heart-failure rehospitalisation at 180 days occurred in 31% versus 31% (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.38), the HF event figures printed beside the mortality-inclusive composite as required. The event composite was secondary in interpretation and null, and no benefit claim is made from it, so this shelf is not Tier C. A guidance strategy that moves a urine number but not outcomes, in one trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PUSH-AHF (ter Maaten 2023): natriuresis guidance raised 24-hour sodium excretion (409 vs 345 mmol) but death or HF rehospitalisation was identical (31% vs 31%)
cards.summary: PUSH-AHF 2023: natriuresis guidance raised 24-hour sodium excretion (409 vs 345 mmol) but death or heart-failure rehospitalisation was 31% in both arms.
cards.people: 310 patients (45% female) with acute heart failure requiring intravenous loop diuretics, randomly assigned to natriuresis-guided therapy (spot urinary sodium checked at set timepoints, with treatment intensification if below 70 mmol/L) or standard of care; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The first dual primary end point was met: 24-hour urinary sodium excretion was 409 ± 178 mmol in the natriuresis-guided arm versus 345 ± 202 mmol with standard care (P=0.0061). The second dual primary end point was not: the combined end point of time to all-cause mortality or first heart-failure rehospitalisation at 180 days occurred in 46 patients (31%) in the natriuresis-guided arm and 50 (31%) in the standard-care arm (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.38; P=0.6980).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and modest-sized, with a biomarker first end point: PUSH-AHF proves the algorithm changes urine sodium, and its own event composite says that change did not translate into fewer deaths or rehospitalisations within 180 days.
cards.source: ter Maaten JM et al. Natriuresis-guided diuretic therapy in acute heart failure: a pragmatic randomized trial. Nat Med. 2023;29(10):2625-2632. PMID: 37640861. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04606927, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Aprocitentan for resistant hypertension (PRECISION)
shelves.question: In resistant hypertension confirmed on standardised triple background therapy, does the dual endothelin antagonist aprocitentan lower office and ambulatory blood pressure through its randomised withdrawal phase (PRECISION) — and at what fluid-retention price?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects · Hypertension/drug therapy · Pyrimidines · Sulfonamides · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A phase 3 trial with a built-in randomised withdrawal (PRECISION, 730 patients on standardised triple therapy: office systolic pressure −3.8 and −3.7 mm Hg versus placebo at 4 weeks for the 12.5 mg and 25 mg doses, with pressure rising again by 5.8 mm Hg when treatment was withdrawn) plus an earlier dose-finding trial (Verweij 2020, 490 patients: placebo-corrected office systolic/diastolic decreases of 7.05/4.93, 9.90/6.99 and 7.58/4.95 mm Hg at 10, 25 and 50 mg) establish that the endothelin pathway lowers blood pressure when finally targeted — modestly in resistant hypertension, at a fluid-retention price (oedema or fluid retention in 9% and 18% on drug versus 2% on placebo in PRECISION's blinded part). LIKELY for the blood-pressure claim; there is no outcomes trial, and no event claim is made.

cards.headline: PRECISION (Schlaich 2022): aprocitentan lowered office systolic pressure by about 4 mm Hg versus placebo in resistant hypertension — and withdrawal raised it back
cards.summary: PRECISION (2022): aprocitentan lowered office systolic pressure by about 4 mm Hg versus placebo in resistant hypertension — and withdrawal confirmed the effect.
cards.type: Multicentre, blinded, randomised, parallel-group, phase 3 trial with a randomised withdrawal part
cards.people: 730 patients with sitting systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg or higher despite standardised background therapy of three antihypertensive drugs including a diuretic, at centres in Europe, North America, Asia and Australia, randomised 1:1:1 to aprocitentan 12.5 mg, aprocitentan 25 mg or placebo for the 4-week double-blind part, then all on aprocitentan 25 mg for 32 weeks, then re-randomised to aprocitentan 25 mg or placebo for a 12-week double-blind withdrawal part; 704 (96%) completed part 1. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 4 weeks, least-square mean office systolic change was −15.3 (SE 0.9) mm Hg on aprocitentan 12.5 mg, −15.2 (0.9) on 25 mg and −11.5 (0.9) on placebo — differences versus placebo of −3.8 (97.5% CI −6.8 to −0.8; p=0.0042) and −3.7 (−6.7 to −0.8; p=0.0046) mm Hg; the 24-hour ambulatory systolic differences were −4.2 mm Hg (95% CI −6.2 to −2.1) and −5.9 (−7.9 to −3.8). After 4 weeks of withdrawal, office systolic pressure rose significantly on placebo versus continued aprocitentan (5.8 mm Hg, 95% CI 3.7 to 7.9; p<0.0001). The most frequent adverse event was mild-to-moderate oedema or fluid retention — 9%, 18% and 2% on 12.5 mg, 25 mg and placebo during the blinded part — leading to discontinuation in seven aprocitentan patients; 11 treatment-emergent deaths occurred during the trial, none of which were regarded by the investigators to be related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group's own −11.5 mm Hg fall (standardised background therapy and trial effect) is most of the observed drop: aprocitentan's added effect is the −3.8 mm Hg difference, and the fluid-retention signal is dose-related and class-typical for endothelin blockade.
cards.source: Schlaich MP et al. Dual endothelin antagonist aprocitentan for resistant hypertension (PRECISION): a multicentre, blinded, randomised, parallel-group, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2022;400(10367):1927-1937. PMID: 36356632. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03541174, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Zilebesiran, the twice-yearly RNA-interference antihypertensive: KARDIA-1 and KARDIA-2
shelves.question: Does a single subcutaneous dose of zilebesiran (RNA interference against hepatic angiotensinogen) lower ambulatory blood pressure for up to six months — alone in mild-to-moderate hypertension (KARDIA-1) and added to a standard first-line drug in inadequately controlled hypertension (KARDIA-2)?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects,administration & dosage · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Angiotensinogen/pharmacology,therapeutic use · RNA · RNA Interference · Hypertension/drug therapy · Hypotension/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two phase 2 randomised, double-blind trials — KARDIA-1 (394 patients, monotherapy after washout: least-squares mean differences versus placebo in 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure at 3 months of −14.1 to −16.7 mm Hg across regimens) and KARDIA-2 (663 randomised patients, add-on to indapamide, amlodipine or olmesartan: differences of −12.1, −9.7 and −4.5 mm Hg by background-drug cohort) — show that silencing hepatic angiotensinogen lowers pressure for months after a single injection. The stamp is POSSIBLE: both trials are phase 2 with a 3-month primary end point, the placebo group's pressure rose 6.8 mm Hg in KARDIA-1 (inflating the between-group difference), hyperkalaemia, hypotension and acute kidney failure were all numerically commoner on zilebesiran in KARDIA-2, and no trial yet tests repeated dosing over years or any clinical outcome.

cards.headline: KARDIA-1 (Bakris 2024): a single zilebesiran injection lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by 14–17 mm Hg versus placebo at 3 months
cards.summary: KARDIA-1 (2024): a single zilebesiran injection lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by 14–17 mm Hg versus placebo at 3 months.
cards.people: 394 adults with mild-to-moderate hypertension (daytime mean ambulatory systolic pressure 135–160 mm Hg after antihypertensive washout) at 78 sites in 4 countries, randomised to zilebesiran (150, 300 or 600 mg once every 6 months, or 300 mg once every 3 months) or placebo (once every 3 months) for 6 months; 377 comprised the full analysis set (302 zilebesiran, 75 placebo), mean age 57 (SD 11) years, 167 (44.3%) women, 93 (24.7%) Black patients.
cards.result: At 3 months, 24-hour mean ambulatory systolic changes were −7.3 mm Hg (150 mg every 6 months), −10.0 mm Hg (300 mg every 3 or 6 months) and −8.9 mm Hg (600 mg every 6 months), versus +6.8 mm Hg with placebo; least-squares mean differences versus placebo were −14.1 mm Hg (95% CI −19.2 to −9.0), −16.7 (−21.2 to −12.3) and −15.7 (−20.8 to −10.6) (all P<.001). Over 6 months, adverse events occurred in 60.9% on zilebesiran versus 50.7% on placebo and serious adverse events in 3.6% versus 6.7%; nonserious drug-related events (mainly injection-site reactions and mild hyperkalaemia) occurred in 16.9% versus 8.0%.
cards.watchOut: The washout design means the placebo group's pressure rose 6.8 mm Hg off treatment: roughly half the headline between-group difference is the placebo rise, not the drug's fall. Three months is the primary horizon of a drug intended to be given for decades.
cards.source: Bakris GL et al. RNA Interference With Zilebesiran for Mild to Moderate Hypertension: The KARDIA-1 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024;331(9):740-749. PMID: 38363577. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04936035, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: KARDIA-2 (Desai 2025): added to a first-line drug, single-dose zilebesiran 600 mg lowered ambulatory systolic pressure by −12.1 (indapamide), −9.7 (amlodipine) and −4.5 (olmesartan) mm Hg versus placebo
cards.summary: KARDIA-2 (2025): added to a first-line drug, single-dose zilebesiran 600 mg lowered ambulatory systolic pressure by −12.1 mm Hg (indapamide cohort) versus placebo.
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled add-on trial in three background-drug cohorts
cards.people: 663 patients with uncontrolled hypertension (130 of 1,491 run-in patients on indapamide, 240 on amlodipine, 293 on olmesartan after at least 4 weeks of open-label run-in on that drug) at 150 sites in 8 countries, randomised 1:1 within cohorts to a single subcutaneous dose of zilebesiran 600 mg (332) or matching placebo (331). cards.result: The least-squares mean difference versus placebo in change in 24-hour mean ambulatory systolic pressure at 3 months was −12.1 mm Hg (95% CI −16.5 to −7.6; P<.001) in the indapamide cohort, −9.7 (−12.9 to −6.6; P<.001) in the amlodipine cohort and −4.5 (−8.2 to −0.8; P=.02) in the olmesartan cohort. cards.headline: Synthesis: twice-yearly angiotensinogen silencing is pharmacologically real — the open questions are duration, kidneys and outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: twice-yearly angiotensinogen silencing is pharmacologically real — the open questions are duration, kidneys and outcomes — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: KARDIA-1 (394 randomised patients, monotherapy) and KARDIA-2 (663 randomised patients, add-on therapy).
cards.result: Both trials show the same drug doing the same thing in the two settings that matter — replacing pills after washout (−14.1 to −16.7 mm Hg versus placebo at 3 months) and adding to a standard first-line drug (−4.5 to −12.1 mm Hg, smallest on an ARB background). What the shelf cannot yet say is whether the effect survives repeated dosing, what years of angiotensinogen suppression do to potassium and kidney function (the adverse-event pattern to watch), or whether any of this prevents events. The pill and device hypertension shelves are different questions and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: An injectable that cannot be switched off for months cuts both ways: the adherence advantage is the point of the drug, and the same irreversibility governs its hypotension and pregnancy-safety questions.

shelves.title: Sotatercept for pulmonary arterial hypertension: PULSAR and STELLAR
shelves.question: Does the activin-signalling inhibitor sotatercept, added to background PAH therapy, improve exercise capacity and pulmonary vascular resistance (PULSAR, phase 2) and six-minute walk distance with a favourable clinical-worsening composite (STELLAR, phase 3)?
shelves.mesh: Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Injections, Subcutaneous · Least-Squares Analysis · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension/blood,drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf carries death-containing composites, so it was ruled Tier C at build by the mortality-in-composite test). Three randomised, double-blind trials: PULSAR (phase 2, 106 adults: pulmonary vascular resistance −239.5 dyn·sec·cm-5 versus placebo at the target dose), STELLAR (phase 3, 323 adults: 6-minute walk difference 40.8 m at 24 weeks, with time to death or clinical worsening among its significantly improved secondary end points — its abstract prints no figure for that end point, and none is printed here), and ZENITH (phase 3, 172 high-risk patients, stopped early: the composite of death, transplant or hospitalisation occurred in 17.4% versus 54.7%, relative hazard ratio 0.24, with death itself in 8.1% versus 15.1%). The exercise-capacity and haemodynamic claims earn LIKELY; the event claims are printed with their components and remain PROPOSED at the Tier C gate. The haematologic and bleeding-adjacent prices (thrombocytopenia, raised haemoglobin, epistaxis, telangiectasia) recur across the programme.

cards.headline: PULSAR (Humbert 2021): sotatercept reduced pulmonary vascular resistance by −239.5 dyn·sec·cm-5 versus placebo at the 0.7 mg/kg dose in PAH (phase 2)
cards.summary: PULSAR (2021): sotatercept reduced pulmonary vascular resistance by −239.5 dyn·sec·cm⁻⁵ versus placebo at 0.7 mg/kg in PAH.
cards.people: 106 adults receiving background therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension, in a 24-week multicentre trial, randomly assigned to subcutaneous sotatercept 0.3 mg/kg every 3 weeks, 0.7 mg/kg every 3 weeks, or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference versus placebo in change in pulmonary vascular resistance at week 24 (primary end point) was −145.8 dyn·sec·cm-5 (95% CI −241.0 to −50.6; P=0.003) for the 0.3-mg group and −239.5 (−329.3 to −149.7; P<0.001) for the 0.7-mg group. The least-squares mean differences in 6-minute walk distance were 29.4 m (95% CI 3.8 to 55.0) and 21.4 m (−2.8 to 45.7) respectively, and sotatercept was associated with a decrease in NT-proBNP. cards.headline: STELLAR (Hoeper 2023): sotatercept improved 6-minute walk distance by 40.8 m versus placebo at 24 weeks in PAH (phase 3)
cards.summary: STELLAR (2023): sotatercept improved 6-minute walk distance by 40.8 m versus placebo at 24 weeks (phase 3).
cards.people: 323 adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO functional class II or III) receiving stable background therapy, randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous sotatercept (starting dose 0.3 mg/kg, target 0.7 mg/kg; 163 patients) or placebo (160) every 3 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The median change in 6-minute walk distance at week 24 was 34.4 m (95% CI 33.0 to 35.5) on sotatercept and 1.0 m (−0.3 to 3.5) on placebo (Hodges-Lehmann difference 40.8 m, 95% CI 27.5 to 54.1; P<0.001). Adverse events commoner with sotatercept included epistaxis, dizziness, telangiectasia, increased haemoglobin, thrombocytopenia and increased blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks in 323 patients on top of background therapy: the trial proves exercise capacity and haemodynamics, and its worsening composite — significant per the abstract, unquantified in it — awaits the developer's personal verdict before any harder claim is printed (Tier C).

cards.headline: ZENITH (Humbert 2025): in high-risk PAH, sotatercept cut the composite of death, transplant or hospitalisation to 17.4% versus 54.7% (relative HR 0.24); death itself 8.1% versus 15.1%
cards.summary: ZENITH (2025): in high-risk PAH, sotatercept cut the composite of death, transplant or hospitalisation to 17.4% vs 54.7% (relative effect large; stopped early — flagged on the card).
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis
cards.people: 172 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO functional class III or IV) at high 1-year risk of death (REVEAL Lite 2 score of 9 or more) receiving the maximum tolerated dose of background therapy, randomised to add-on sotatercept (starting dose 0.3 mg/kg, escalated to a target of 0.7 mg/kg; 86) or placebo (86) every 3 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At least one primary end-point event — death from any cause, lung transplantation, or hospitalisation (24 hours or more) for worsening PAH — occurred in 15 patients (17.4%) in the sotatercept group and 47 (54.7%) in the placebo group (relative hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.43; P<0.001). The components, printed beside the composite: death from any cause in 7 patients (8.1%) versus 13 (15.1%); lung transplantation in 1 (1.2%) versus 6 (7.0%); and hospitalisation for worsening PAH in 8 (9.3%) versus 43 (50.0%). The most common adverse events with sotatercept were epistaxis and telangiectasia.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for efficacy in 172 patients: trials stopped at an interim peak tend to overstate effects, and the composite is driven by hospitalisation (8 vs 43 events) far more than by death (7 vs 13). shelves.title: Inclisiran, the twice-yearly PCSK9 siRNA: ORION-10, ORION-11 and ORION-9
shelves.question: Does inclisiran — small interfering RNA against PCSK9, dosed twice a year after loading — lower LDL cholesterol by about half versus placebo in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and risk equivalents (ORION-10/11) and in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (ORION-9), with the cardiovascular OUTCOMES trial still pending?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials across two reports — ORION-10 (1,561 patients with ASCVD: LDL cholesterol −52.3% placebo-corrected at day 510) and ORION-11 (1,617 patients with ASCVD or risk equivalents: −49.9%), and ORION-9 in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (482 patients: between-group difference −47.9 percentage points) — agree that twice-yearly inclisiran lowers LDL cholesterol by about half, sustained between doses (time-adjusted reductions of 53.8%, 49.2% and −44.3 percentage points), with injection-site reactions the only clearly excess adverse event. Two reports and three trials earn LIKELY — for the LDL claim only, stated on the shelf face: the cardiovascular OUTCOMES trial is still pending, and no event claim is made or implied.

shelves.title: Lipoprotein(a) lowering with RNA therapies: pelacarsen and olpasiran phase 2
shelves.question: Do hepatocyte-targeted RNA therapies lower lipoprotein(a) by 80–98% — the antisense oligonucleotide pelacarsen in its phase 2 dose-ranging trial, and the siRNA olpasiran in OCEAN(a)-DOSE — with both programmes' cardiovascular OUTCOMES trials still running and no event claim yet earned?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/blood,drug therapy · Cholesterol/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Hypolipidemic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Least-Squares Analysis · Lipoprotein(a)/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two phase 2 randomised, double-blind dose-ranging trials of two different hepatocyte-targeted RNA molecules agree that lipoprotein(a) can be lowered by magnitudes no previous drug approached — pelacarsen (Tsimikas 2020, 286 patients with cardiovascular disease: mean decreases of 35% to 80% across dosing regimens versus 6% on placebo) and olpasiran (OCEAN(a)-DOSE, 281 patients: placebo-adjusted mean changes of −70.5% to −101.1% at 36 weeks). The stamp is POSSIBLE, and the shelf face carries the limit in plain words: lipoprotein(a) is a surrogate, both trials are phase 2, and both programmes' cardiovascular OUTCOMES trials are still running — no event claim has been earned by any Lp(a)-lowering drug, and none is made here.

cards.headline: Tsimikas 2020: pelacarsen lowered lipoprotein(a) dose-dependently — mean decreases of 35% to 80% versus 6% on placebo (phase 2)
cards.summary: Tsimikas (2020): pelacarsen lowered lipoprotein(a) dose-dependently — mean decreases of 35% to 80% vs 6% on placebo (phase 2).
cards.people: 286 patients with established cardiovascular disease and screening lipoprotein(a) levels of at least 60 mg/dL (150 nmol/L), randomised to the hepatocyte-directed antisense oligonucleotide APO(a)-LRx (pelacarsen; 20, 40 or 60 mg every 4 weeks, 20 mg every 2 weeks, or 20 mg every week) or saline placebo subcutaneously for 6 to 12 months; median baseline lipoprotein(a) levels across the six groups ranged from 204.5 to 246.6 nmol/L. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean percent decreases in lipoprotein(a) at the primary end point (month 6 of exposure) were 35% at 20 mg every 4 weeks, 56% at 40 mg every 4 weeks, 58% at 20 mg every 2 weeks, 72% at 60 mg every 4 weeks and 80% at 20 mg every week, versus 6% with placebo (P values for the comparisons ranged from 0.003 to <0.001). There were no significant differences between any dose and placebo in platelet counts, liver or renal measures, or influenza-like symptoms; the most common adverse events were injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: Five small dose groups and a biomarker end point: the trial ranks regimens for the outcomes trial, and the weekly regimen with the largest effect is not the regimen an outcomes programme would choose.
cards.source: Tsimikas S et al. Lipoprotein(a) Reduction in Persons with Cardiovascular Disease. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(3):244-255. PMID: 31893580. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03070782, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: OCEAN(a)-DOSE (O'Donoghue 2022): olpasiran lowered lipoprotein(a) by placebo-adjusted −97.4% to −101.1% at the 75 mg and 225 mg doses (phase 2)
cards.summary: OCEAN(a)-DOSE (2022): olpasiran lowered lipoprotein(a) by placebo-adjusted −97.4% to −101.1% at the 75 mg and 225 mg doses (phase 2).
cards.people: 281 patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) concentration above 150 nmol/L, randomised to olpasiran (10 mg every 12 weeks, 75 mg every 12 weeks, 225 mg every 12 weeks, or 225 mg every 24 weeks) or matching placebo subcutaneously; median baseline lipoprotein(a) was 260.3 nmol/L and median LDL cholesterol 67.5 mg/dL; at baseline 88% were taking a statin, 52% ezetimibe and 23% a PCSK9 inhibitor. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 36 weeks, lipoprotein(a) had increased by a mean of 3.6% on placebo, while olpasiran produced placebo-adjusted mean percent changes of −70.5% (10 mg), −97.4% (75 mg every 12 weeks), −101.1% (225 mg every 12 weeks) and −100.5% (225 mg every 24 weeks) (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The overall incidence of adverse events was similar across groups; the most common olpasiran-related events were injection-site reactions, primarily pain. The authors state that longer and larger trials will be necessary to determine the effect on cardiovascular disease.
cards.watchOut: Percent changes beyond −100% are an artefact of placebo adjustment against a rising placebo group, not a biological claim: read them as 'near-complete suppression relative to placebo', and remember the end point is the biomarker itself.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the lipoprotein(a) barrier is pharmacologically broken — whether breaking it prevents events is the unanswered question
cards.summary: Synthesis: the lipoprotein(a) barrier is pharmacologically broken — whether breaking it prevents events is the unanswered question — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Tsimikas 2020 (286 patients, pelacarsen) and OCEAN(a)-DOSE (281 patients, olpasiran).
cards.result: Two molecules, two RNA chemistries, one consistent finding: hepatic apo(a) silencing lowers lipoprotein(a) by 80–98% at the effective doses, far beyond the ~20–25% seen with PCSK9 antibodies. The rest of the lipid library — statins, ezetimibe, the PCSK9 antibodies (Shelves #191, #262) and bempedoic acid — does not touch this particle and is not re-carded here. The shelf's stamp stays at POSSIBLE because everything so far is a phase 2 surrogate result; the outcomes trials named in the trials' own conclusions are the evidence that would move it. Two further molecules are fenced here as class context, not carded: lepodisiran, a long-duration siRNA (phase 2, PMID 40162643), and muvalaplin, an oral small molecule (PMID 39556768) — each lowers lipoprotein(a) in its own early trial, neither has an outcomes trial, and neither displaces the two carded anchors.
cards.watchOut: Genetic evidence that Lp(a) causes disease is strong, but the library's rule applies: a causal risk factor plus a drug that moves it is not yet a proven event reduction — niacin moved lipids for decades without one.

Adverse events of moderate severity judged related to study drug or placebo occurred in 4 patients in the 80-mg group.

shelves.title: Evinacumab for homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (ELIPSE HoFH)
shelves.question: In homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia — including patients with little or no LDL-receptor function, in whom statins and PCSK9 antibodies barely work — does the ANGPTL3 antibody evinacumab lower LDL cholesterol versus placebo (ELIPSE HoFH)?
shelves.mesh: Angiopoietin-Like Protein 3 · Angiopoietin-like Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Homozygote · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/blood,drug therapy,genetics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial — ELIPSE HoFH (65 patients: between-group LDL difference of −49.0 percentage points at 24 weeks, including in patients with null-null LDL-receptor variants, in whom receptor-dependent drugs barely work) — plus a large open-label, single-arm long-term study (116 patients: mean LDL reduction of 43.6% by week 24, sustained over a median 104.3 weeks of treatment) support the claim that ANGPTL3 blockade lowers LDL cholesterol independently of the LDL receptor. The stamp is POSSIBLE under the library's single-pivotal-trial ceiling, stated with its rare-disease context on the shelf face: homozygous FH is ultra-rare, a second blinded trial is unlikely ever to be run, and the uncontrolled extension supports durability and safety rather than efficacy. No event claim is made.

cards.headline: ELIPSE HoFH (Raal 2020): evinacumab lowered LDL cholesterol by a between-group −49.0 percentage points at 24 weeks — including in null-null patients
cards.summary: ELIPSE HoFH (2020): evinacumab lowered LDL cholesterol by a between-group −49.0 percentage points at 24 weeks — including in null-null patients.
cards.people: 65 patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia receiving stable, maximal lipid-lowering therapy (mean baseline LDL cholesterol 255.1 mg/dL), randomised 2:1 to intravenous evinacumab 15 mg/kg every 4 weeks or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, LDL cholesterol changed by −47.1% in the evinacumab group versus +1.9% on placebo (between-group least-squares mean difference −49.0 percentage points, 95% CI −65.0 to −33.1; P<0.001), an absolute difference of −132.1 mg/dL (95% CI −175.3 to −88.9; P<0.001). The reduction held in patients with null-null variants (−43.4% vs +16.2%) and in those with non-null variants (−49.1% vs −3.8%) — the receptor-independence that defines the drug. Adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-five patients is the whole randomised evidence base; the null-null subgroup result, while mechanistically decisive, rests on a fraction of those 65.
cards.source: Raal FJ et al. Evinacumab for Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(8):711-720. PMID: 32813947. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03399786, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Gaudet 2024: in the open-label long-term study, evinacumab's LDL reduction (43.6% by week 24) was sustained over a median 104 weeks in 116 patients
cards.summary: Gaudet (2024): in the open-label long-term study, the LDL reduction (43.6% by week 24) was sustained over a median 104 weeks.
cards.people: 116 patients aged 12 years or older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (102 adults, 14 adolescents; 57 [49.1%] female), evinacumab-naïve or continuing from earlier trials, treated with intravenous evinacumab 15 mg/kg every 4 weeks plus stable lipid-lowering therapy for a median (range) of 104.3 (28.3–196.3) weeks.
cards.result: From baseline to week 24, evinacumab decreased mean LDL cholesterol by 43.6% (mean [SD] 3.4 [3.2] mmol/L (≈132 mg/dL)); reductions were 41.7% in adults and 55.4% in adolescents, and the authors report efficacy and safety were sustained over the long term. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 93 (80.2%) patients and serious events in 27 (23.3%); two patients (1.7%) died, neither death considered related to evinacumab, and three (2.6%) discontinued for adverse events, none considered related.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and uncontrolled, mixing naïve and continuing patients: it can show the effect does not vanish and the drug is tolerated, and it cannot re-prove efficacy — the efficacy claim rests on ELIPSE alone.
cards.source: Gaudet D et al. Evinacumab in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: long-term safety and efficacy. Eur Heart J. 2024;45(27):2422-2434. PMID: 38856678. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record's abstract names the pivotal trial (NCT03399786) and the study itself as a phase 3 open-label trial; its own registration number does not appear in the fetched record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the receptor-independent LDL drug — one rigorous small trial, one long uncontrolled shadow
cards.summary: Synthesis: the receptor-independent LDL drug — one rigorous small trial, one long uncontrolled shadow — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ELIPSE HoFH (65 randomised patients) and Gaudet 2024 (116 patients, open-label).
cards.result: The evidence pattern is the classic ultra-rare-disease shape: a single small blinded trial with a large, mechanistically coherent effect (−49.0 percentage points, holding in null-null patients where statins and PCSK9 antibodies have almost nothing to work with), followed by a much larger uncontrolled study showing the effect persists (43.6% at week 24, median exposure over two years). The heterozygous-FH material on the lipid shelves concerns receptor-dependent drugs in a different population and is not re-carded here. POSSIBLE is the stamp the single-trial rule assigns; the shelf face says why the rule, not the evidence, is what binds.
cards.watchOut: LDL lowering in HoFH is a surrogate for the premature cardiovascular disease that defines the condition: no trial of evinacumab measures events, and in a population this small, none feasibly can.

shelves.title: Riociguat for pulmonary hypertension: PATENT-1 (PAH) and CHEST-1 (inoperable CTEPH)
shelves.question: Does the soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator riociguat improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PATENT-1) — and in inoperable or persistent chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CHEST-1), the first drug ever to win that indication?
shelves.mesh: Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Hypertension, Pulmonary/drug therapy,physiopathology · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials published in the same journal issue — PATENT-1 (443 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension: 6-minute walk distance least-squares difference of 36 m at 12 weeks) and CHEST-1 (261 patients with inoperable or persistent CTEPH: difference of 46 m at 16 weeks, with pulmonary vascular resistance differing by −246 dyn·sec·cm-5) — agree that riociguat improves exercise capacity and haemodynamics in both diseases, with concordant NT-proBNP, functional-class and time-to-clinical-worsening improvements. Two concordant blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the exercise-capacity claim. The end points are walk distance and haemodynamics over 12–16 weeks, not survival, and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: PATENT-1 (Ghofrani 2013): riociguat improved 6-minute walk distance by a least-squares difference of 36 m at 12 weeks in PAH
cards.summary: PATENT-1 (2013): riociguat improved 6-minute walk distance by a least-squares difference of 36 m at 12 weeks in PAH.
cards.people: 443 patients with symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension, randomised to placebo, riociguat individually titrated to a maximum of 2.5 mg three times daily, or riociguat capped at 1.5 mg three times daily (exploratory group, analysed descriptively); patients could be treatment-naïve or receiving endothelin-receptor antagonists or non-intravenous prostanoids. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: By week 12, 6-minute walk distance had increased by a mean of 30 m in the 2.5 mg-maximum group and decreased by 6 m on placebo (least-squares mean difference 36 m, 95% CI 20 to 52; P<0.001), with improvement both in treatment-naïve patients and in those on background therapy. There were significant improvements in pulmonary vascular resistance (P<0.001), NT-proBNP (P<0.001), WHO functional class (P=0.003), time to clinical worsening (P=0.005) and Borg dyspnoea score (P=0.002). The most common serious adverse event was syncope — 4% on placebo and 1% in the 2.5 mg-maximum group.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and a walk-distance primary end point: the trial's worsening result is a secondary P value without an effect figure in the abstract, and none is printed on this card.
cards.source: Ghofrani HA et al. Riociguat for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(4):330-340. PMID: 23883378. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00810693 (PATENT-1) and NCT00863681 (PATENT-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CHEST-1 (Ghofrani 2013): riociguat improved 6-minute walk distance by a least-squares difference of 46 m at 16 weeks in inoperable CTEPH
cards.summary: CHEST-1 (2013): riociguat improved 6-minute walk distance by a least-squares difference of 46 m at 16 weeks in inoperable CTEPH.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 261 patients with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or persistent or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after pulmonary endarterectomy, randomly assigned to placebo or riociguat individually titrated. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: By week 16, 6-minute walk distance had increased by a mean of 39 m on riociguat and decreased by 6 m on placebo (least-squares mean difference 46 m, 95% CI 25 to 67; P<0.001). Pulmonary vascular resistance decreased by 226 dyn·sec·cm-5 on riociguat and increased by 23 on placebo (difference −246, 95% CI −303 to −190; P<0.001), with significant improvements in NT-proBNP (P<0.001) and WHO functional class (P=0.003). The most common serious adverse events were right ventricular failure (3% in each group) and syncope (2% riociguat, 3% placebo).
cards.watchOut: Inoperable CTEPH is the population: patients operable for endarterectomy were not the trial's question, and riociguat's trial result should never be read as a reason to defer a surgical opinion.
cards.source: Ghofrani HA et al. Riociguat for the treatment of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(4):319-329. PMID: 23883377. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00855465 (CHEST-1) and NCT00910429 (CHEST-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one drug, two pulmonary-hypertension diseases, the same walk-distance answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: one drug, two pulmonary-hypertension diseases, the same walk-distance answer — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PATENT-1 (443 patients with PAH) and CHEST-1 (261 patients with CTEPH).
cards.result: Riociguat's pair of trials is unusually symmetrical: walk-distance differences of 36 m and 46 m, haemodynamic improvement in both, and the first drug approval in inoperable CTEPH as the programme's historical marker. Vericiguat is a different sGC stimulator tested in heart failure, not pulmonary hypertension (draft Shelf #970), and the endothelin/prostacyclin PAH shelf is #814; neither is re-carded here. Both trials predate the modern combination-therapy era in PAH, which is an era caveat on the shelf face, not a flaw in the trials.
cards.watchOut: Riociguat is contraindicated with nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors and carries an embryo-foetal toxicity warning: the walk-distance benefit belongs to a carefully selected, monitored population.

shelves.title: Inhaled treprostinil for pulmonary hypertension due to interstitial lung disease (INCREASE)
shelves.question: In pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease — a group with no approved therapy at the time — does inhaled treprostinil improve six-minute walk distance versus placebo (INCREASE), and at what cough and discontinuation cost?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Epoprostenol/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Hypertension, Pulmonary/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Least-Squares Analysis · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial — INCREASE (326 patients: least-squares difference in 6-minute walk distance of 31.12 m at 16 weeks, NT-proBNP treatment ratio 0.58, and clinical worsening in 22.7% versus 33.1%, relative hazard ratio 0.61) — plus its open-label extension (242 patients: walk distance and NT-proBNP broadly maintained to week 52–64, with adverse events leading to discontinuation in 22.3%) support inhaled treprostinil as the first therapy shown to help in pulmonary hypertension due to interstitial lung disease. The stamp is POSSIBLE under the single-pivotal-trial ceiling: 16 weeks of controlled evidence, an extension without a control group, and a worsening composite whose relative ratio of 0.61 sits inside the library's 0.5–2.0 band where ratios alone are not treated as solid evidence. The clinical-worsening end point is reported as INCREASE reported it; no mortality claim is made (Tier C: no, per the topic ruling — the shelf's claim is exercise capacity).

cards.headline: INCREASE (Waxman 2021): inhaled treprostinil improved 6-minute walk distance by 31.12 m versus placebo at 16 weeks in PH due to interstitial lung disease
cards.summary: INCREASE (2021): inhaled treprostinil improved 6-minute walk distance by 31.12 m versus placebo at 16 weeks in PH due to interstitial lung disease.
cards.people: 326 patients with interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension documented by right heart catheterisation, randomised 1:1 to inhaled treprostinil (up to 12 breaths, 72 µg total, four times daily by ultrasonic pulsed-delivery nebuliser; 163) or placebo (163) for 16 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At week 16, the least-squares mean difference in change in peak 6-minute walk distance was 31.12 m (95% CI 16.85 to 45.39; P<0.001) in favour of treprostinil. NT-proBNP fell 15% from baseline on treprostinil and rose 46% on placebo (treatment ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.72; P<0.001). Clinical worsening occurred in 37 patients (22.7%) on treprostinil versus 54 (33.1%) on placebo (relative hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.92; P=0.04) — printed as relative, with its absolute rates beside it. The most frequent adverse events were cough, headache, dyspnoea, dizziness, nausea, fatigue and diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks, one trial, and a cough signal intrinsic to inhaled prostacyclin delivery that can unblind patients in practice; the worsening composite's ratio (0.61) is in the band the library treats as insufficient on its own.
cards.source: Waxman A et al. Inhaled Treprostinil in Pulmonary Hypertension Due to Interstitial Lung Disease. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(4):325-334. PMID: 33440084. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02630316, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: INCREASE OLE (Waxman 2023): in the open-label extension, walk distance and NT-proBNP were broadly maintained to a year — and 22.3% stopped the drug for adverse events
cards.summary: INCREASE OLE (2023): in the open-label extension, walk distance and NT-proBNP were broadly maintained to a year — and 22.3% stopped treatment.
cards.people: 242 of 258 eligible INCREASE participants enrolled in the open-label extension and received inhaled treprostinil; at extension baseline the median age was 70 years, mean 6-minute walk distance 274.2 m, and 52.1% were male.
cards.result: For the overall population, mean 6-minute walk distance at week 52 was 279.1 m, and the mean change from the randomised trial's baseline was 3.5 m (22.1 m for the prior treprostinil arm and −19.5 m for the prior placebo arm); median NT-proBNP decreased from 389 pg/mL at trial baseline to 359 pg/mL at week 64. Patients who had received treprostinil rather than placebo in the randomised trial had a 31% lower relative risk of exacerbation of underlying lung disease in the extension (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; p=0.03). Adverse events leading to drug discontinuation occurred in 54 (22.3%) patients.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and survivorship-shaped: the patients in the extension are those who tolerated and stayed on the drug, so its stability figures describe continuers, not the randomised population.
