cards.headline: Synthesis: a first foothold in group 3 pulmonary hypertension — real at 16 weeks, unproven beyond it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a first foothold in group 3 pulmonary hypertension — real at 16 weeks, unproven beyond it — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: INCREASE (326 randomised patients) and its open-label extension (242 patients).
cards.result: INCREASE remains the only positive randomised trial in pulmonary hypertension due to interstitial lung disease: a 31.12 m walk advantage, a biomarker moving the right way (NT-proBNP ratio 0.58), and fewer clinical-worsening events (22.7% vs 33.1%). Pulmonary ARTERIAL hypertension (group 1) is a different population with its own therapies, home on Shelf #814, and is not re-carded here. The single-trial ceiling and the 22.3% extension discontinuation rate hold the stamp at POSSIBLE until a second controlled trial exists. The TETON phase 3 trials of inhaled treprostinil in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (PMIDs 42149993 and 41812190, titles verified in this shelf's currency sweep) are fenced here by name: IPF without the PH-ILD population definition is a neighbouring question, not this shelf's.
cards.watchOut: Four-times-daily nebulised therapy is a heavy regimen in breathless patients: trial adherence under protocol support should not be assumed to transfer to ordinary practice.

shelves.title: A community package for cardiovascular risk: HOPE-4
shelves.question: Does a community-based comprehensive intervention — non-physician health workers with tablet-based decision support, free combination medicines, and a treatment supporter — reduce cardiovascular risk and improve blood-pressure control in hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control · Colombia · Community Participation/methods · Hypertension/complications,drug therapy,prevention & control,therapy · Malaysia · Risk Reduction Behavior
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In one open cluster-randomised trial (30 communities in Colombia and Malaysia; 1,371 people with new or poorly controlled hypertension), the HOPE-4 package cut the Framingham 10-year risk estimate by 4.78 percentage points more than usual care, lowered systolic pressure by an additional 11.45 mm Hg, and doubled blood-pressure control (69% vs 30%) at 12 months. These are risk-score and blood-pressure outcomes — no cardiovascular event claim is made — and a single open cluster trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Community health workers for hypertension control in the COBRA-BPS programme live on Shelf #880 and the polypill as a product on Shelf #121; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: HOPE-4 (Schwalm 2019): risk score fell 4.78 points more, systolic pressure 11.45 mm Hg more, control 69% versus 30% at 12 months
cards.summary: HOPE-4 (2019): risk score fell 4.78 points more, systolic pressure 11.45 mm Hg more, control 69% vs 30% at 12 months.
cards.type: Open, community-based, cluster-randomised controlled trial (30 communities in Colombia and Malaysia)
cards.people: 1,371 individuals with new or poorly controlled hypertension from 30 communities (14 intervention, 644 people; 16 control, 727), followed 12 months with data on 97% of living participants (1,299). Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The Framingham Risk Score 10-year cardiovascular risk estimate fell by 11.17% in the intervention group versus 6.40% in controls (difference in change −4.78%, 95% CI −7.11 to −2.44; p<0.0001). Systolic blood pressure fell 11.45 mm Hg more (95% CI −14.94 to −7.97) and LDL cholesterol 0.41 mmol/L (≈16 mg/dL) more (−0.60 to −0.23) with the intervention (both p<0.0001). Blood-pressure control (<140 mm Hg) was 69% versus 30% (p<0.0001). There were no safety concerns. The intervention combined non-physician health workers using tablet-based algorithms and counselling, free antihypertensive and statin medicines supervised by physicians, and a family or friend treatment supporter.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial, and its primary endpoint is a risk SCORE — a modelled surrogate — not events; the package's components cannot be separated, and free medicines inside the package may be its active ingredient as much as its community structure.

shelves.title: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy after tafamidis: acoramidis (ATTRibute-CM) and vutrisiran (HELIOS-B)
shelves.question: In transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, do acoramidis, a near-complete transthyretin stabiliser, and vutrisiran, an RNA-interference silencer of transthyretin production, improve outcomes beyond placebo?
shelves.mesh: Functional Status · Hospitalization · Amyloidosis/drug therapy,pathology · Heart · Cardiomyopathies/drug therapy,pathology · Prealbumin/drug effects,therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Agents/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both composites carry mortality and cardiovascular-event claims). Two pivotal phase 3 trials of two different mechanisms in the same disease each beat placebo: acoramidis on a hierarchical composite of death, cardiovascular hospitalisation, NT-proBNP and walk distance (win ratio 1.8), and vutrisiran on death and recurrent cardiovascular events (relative hazard ratio 0.72, absolute 38.3% vs 48.3% with at least one primary event). This is a two-mechanism shelf, not two trials of one drug; tafamidis itself is home on Shelf #556 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: ATTRibute-CM 2024: acoramidis beat placebo on the hierarchical composite of death, cardiovascular hospitalisation, NT-proBNP and 6-minute walk (win ratio 1.8)
cards.summary: ATTRibute-CM (2024): acoramidis beat placebo on the hierarchical composite of death, cardiovascular hospitalisation, NT-proBNP and 6-minute walk ( win ratio 1.8 relative).
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (30 months)
cards.people: 632 patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy randomised 2:1 to acoramidis 800 mg twice daily or placebo; efficacy assessed in patients with eGFR at least 30 ml/min/1.73 m2. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary hierarchical analysis favoured acoramidis (P<0.001); win ratio 1.8 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.2), with 63.7% of pairwise comparisons favouring acoramidis and 35.9% favouring placebo. Death from any cause and cardiovascular-related hospitalisation together contributed 58% of all pairwise comparisons. Overall adverse events were similar (98.1% vs 97.6%); serious adverse events were reported in 54.6% on acoramidis and 64.9% on placebo. The abstract reports the composite as a win ratio and gives no separate absolute death or hospitalisation rates, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A hierarchical win-ratio composite is not an absolute mortality figure: the mortality and hospitalisation components cannot be separated from the abstract, and the shelf does not claim a stand-alone survival benefit from this trial.

cards.headline: HELIOS-B 2025: vutrisiran lowered death and recurrent cardiovascular events (relative hazard ratio 0.72; 38.3% vs 48.3% had at least one primary event)
cards.summary: HELIOS-B (2025): vutrisiran lowered death and recurrent cardiovascular events (HR 0.72 relative; 38.3% vs 48.3% had at least one event).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (up to 36 months)
cards.people: 655 patients with transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous vutrisiran 25 mg or placebo every 12 weeks (326 vs 329). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite of death from any cause and recurrent cardiovascular events was lower with vutrisiran: hazard ratio 0.72 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.93; P=0.01) in the overall population — a relative measure — and 0.67 (0.49 to 0.93) in the monotherapy population not receiving tafamidis at baseline. At least one primary event occurred in 125 of 326 vutrisiran patients (38.3%) and 159 of 329 placebo patients (48.3%). Death from any cause through 42 months: hazard ratio 0.65 (0.46 to 0.90). Decline in 6-minute walk distance was less with vutrisiran (least-squares mean difference 26.5 m, 13.4 to 39.6) and in KCCQ-OS score (5.8 points, 2.4 to 9.2). Serious adverse events occurred in 62% vs 67%.
cards.watchOut: The hazard ratios 0.72 and 0.65 are relative measures sitting inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on their own; they are printed with the absolute event proportions beside them. About a third of patients were on background tafamidis, so this is not purely a silencer-versus-nothing test in the overall population.

shelves.title: Pulsed field ablation versus thermal ablation for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (ADVENT)
shelves.question: Does pulsed field ablation match conventional thermal (radiofrequency or cryoballoon) ablation on one-year freedom from atrial arrhythmia in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and with what safety profile?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation/classification,surgery · Bayes Theorem · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects,methods · Pulmonary Veins/surgery · Recurrence · Tachycardia/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (ADVENT, 607 patients) found pulsed field ablation noninferior to thermal ablation for both its one-year efficacy composite (73.3% vs 71.3% free of events) and its serious device/procedure safety endpoint (2.1% vs 1.5%). A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The wider pulsed-field literature is dominated by single-arm pivotal studies and registries, which is stated on the shelf face; the confirmatory randomised report sought at build could not be pinned to a verified record, so the shelf rests on ADVENT alone (see summary). No mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: ADVENT 2023: pulsed field ablation was noninferior to thermal ablation at 1 year — efficacy composite met in 73.3% vs 71.3%, safety events 2.1% vs 1.5%
cards.summary: ADVENT (2023): pulsed field ablation was noninferior to thermal ablation at 1 year — efficacy composite met in 73.3% vs 71.3% .
cards.people: 607 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal atrial fibrillation assigned to pulsed field ablation (305) or conventional radiofrequency or cryoballoon ablation (302). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 1 year the primary efficacy endpoint (freedom from initial procedural failure, documented atrial tachyarrhythmia after a 3-month blanking period, antiarrhythmic drug use, cardioversion, or repeat ablation) was met in an estimated 73.3% with pulsed field ablation and 71.3% with thermal ablation (difference 2.0 percentage points; 95% Bayesian credible interval -5.2 to 9.2; posterior probability of noninferiority >0.999). Primary safety endpoint events (acute and chronic device- and procedure-related serious adverse events) occurred in an estimated 2.1% vs 1.5% (difference 0.6 points, -1.5 to 2.8; noninferiority probability >0.999).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on a composite dominated by arrhythmia recurrence and repeat procedures is not superiority, and 1 year is short for ablation durability; the trial's 4-year report is a follow-up of this same trial, not a second trial.
cards.source: Reddy VY et al. Pulsed Field or Conventional Thermal Ablation for Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2023;389(18):1660-1671. PMID: 37634148. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04612244, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Cerebral embolic protection in TAVR: PROTECTED TAVR and BHF PROTECT-TAVI
shelves.question: Does a cerebral embolic protection device deployed during transcatheter aortic-valve replacement reduce periprocedural stroke?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/etiology · Aortic Valve/surgery · Aortic Valve Stenosis/surgery · Delirium/etiology · Embolic Protection Devices · Intracranial Embolism/etiology,prevention & control · Ischemic Attack, Transient/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: stroke is the primary outcome of both trials). Two large randomised trials of the same device question were concordantly non-positive on their primary stroke endpoints: PROTECTED TAVR (3,000 patients; stroke 2.3% vs 2.9%, P=0.30) and the much larger BHF PROTECT-TAVI (7,635 patients; stroke 2.1% vs 2.2%, P=0.94). The one disabling-stroke secondary signal in PROTECTED TAVR (0.5% vs 1.3%) was not reproduced in BHF PROTECT-TAVI (1.2% vs 1.4%) and is labelled secondary wherever it appears.

cards.headline: PROTECTED TAVR 2022: cerebral embolic protection did not significantly reduce periprocedural stroke (2.3% vs 2.9%, P=0.30); disabling stroke, a secondary outcome, was 0.5% vs 1.3%
cards.summary: PROTECTED TAVR (2022): cerebral embolic protection did not significantly reduce periprocedural stroke ( 2.3% vs 2.9% ; P=0.30).
cards.people: 3,000 patients with aortic stenosis across North America, Europe and Australia randomised 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR with cerebral embolic protection (1,501) or without (1,499); the device was successfully deployed in 94.4% of attempts. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Stroke within 72 hours or before discharge: 2.3% with protection vs 2.9% control (difference -0.6 percentage points; 95% CI -1.7 to 0.5; P=0.30) — not significant. Disabling stroke (secondary) occurred in 0.5% vs 1.3%. Death was 0.5% vs 0.3% (printed beside the stroke figures, per the library's pairing rule); stroke/TIA/delirium 3.1% vs 3.7%; acute kidney injury 0.5% vs 0.5%. One patient (0.1%) had a vascular complication at the protection-device access site. The authors note the confidence interval does not rule out a benefit.
cards.watchOut: The disabling-stroke difference is a secondary outcome in a trial whose primary endpoint missed; it is hypothesis-generating, and the larger BHF trial below did not reproduce it.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised trial (RATE-AF, 160 patients) found no difference in its primary outcome — patient-reported quality of life at 6 months (SF-36 physical component 31.9 vs 29.7, P=0.28) — while most later secondary outcomes favoured digoxin (symptom class, NT-proBNP, fewer adverse events). One small open-label trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the trial was not powered for clinical events and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: RATE-AF 2020: digoxin and bisoprolol tied on quality of life at 6 months (SF-36 PCS 31.9 vs 29.7, P=0.28); digoxin ahead on symptoms, NT-proBNP and adverse events by 12 months
cards.summary: RATE-AF (2020): digoxin and bisoprolol tied on quality of life at 6 months (SF-36 PCS 31.9 vs 29.7; P=0.28); digoxin ahead on symptoms and NT-proBNP.
cards.people: 160 patients aged 60 years or older with permanent atrial fibrillation and dyspnoea of NYHA class II or higher, recruited in England; mean age 76 (SD 8) years, 74 (46%) women, mean baseline heart rate 100/min; digoxin (n=80, mean dose 161 µg/day) or bisoprolol (n=80, mean dose 3.2 mg/day); 145 (91%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Primary outcome — normalised SF-36 physical component summary at 6 months: 31.9 (SD 11.7) with digoxin vs 29.7 (11.4) with bisoprolol (adjusted mean difference 1.4; 95% CI -1.1 to 3.8; P=0.28), not significant. Resting heart rate at 6 months was similar (76.9 vs 74.8/min). The modified EHRA symptom class differed: 53% on digoxin vs 9% on bisoprolol reported a 2-class improvement (adjusted odds ratio 10.3, 4.0 to 26.6 — a relative measure). At 12 months, 8 of 20 outcomes significantly favoured digoxin, including median NT-proBNP 960 vs 1250 pg/mL (ratio of geometric means 0.77, 0.64 to 0.92; P=0.005). At least one adverse event occurred in 20 patients (25%) on digoxin vs 51 (64%) on bisoprolol (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with a patient-reported primary outcome, 160 patients, and many secondary endpoints without the trial being powered for any of them: the digoxin-favouring secondaries are signals, not proof. No mortality or hospitalisation comparison is possible at this size.
cards.source: Kotecha D et al. Effect of Digoxin vs Bisoprolol for Heart Rate Control in Atrial Fibrillation on Patient-Reported Quality of Life: The RATE-AF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(24):2497-2508. PMID: 33351042. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02391337, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the old drug ties on the primary and looks gentler in one small trial — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: RATE-AF (160 older patients with permanent AF and heart-failure symptoms).
cards.result: For rate control in permanent AF, RATE-AF supports basing the digoxin-versus-beta-blocker choice on symptoms, tolerability and NT-proBNP rather than on any proven quality-of-life advantage: the primary score tied (31.9 vs 29.7), adverse events were fewer with digoxin (25% vs 64% of patients), and symptom class improved more. cards.watchOut: RATE-AF used low digoxin doses (mean 161 µg/day) in a monitored trial; it is not evidence about digoxin safety at higher doses or without monitoring.

shelves.title: Occluding the left atrial appendage during other cardiac surgery (LAAOS III)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing cardiac surgery for another reason, does concomitant surgical occlusion of the left atrial appendage reduce ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism, in a population most of whom stayed on anticoagulation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Atrial Appendage/surgery · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy,surgery · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Combined Modality Therapy · Embolism/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is stroke prevention). One very large randomised trial (LAAOS III, 4,770 patients, mean follow-up 3.8 years) found stroke or systemic embolism in 4.8% with occlusion vs 7.0% without (relative hazard ratio 0.67), on top of usual care in which 76.8% were still anticoagulated at 3 years. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A substudy carded below shows the benefit was consistent whether or not patients received oral anticoagulation — the same trial, counted once.

cards.headline: LAAOS III 2021: appendage occlusion during cardiac surgery cut stroke or systemic embolism — 4.8% vs 7.0% (relative hazard ratio 0.67)
cards.summary: LAAOS III (2021): appendage occlusion during cardiac surgery cut stroke or systemic embolism — 4.8% vs 7.0% (HR 0.67 relative).
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (participants, staff and physicians other than surgeons blinded to assignment)
cards.people: 4,770 participants with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2 scheduled for cardiac surgery for another indication (primary analysis population 2,379 occlusion vs 2,391 no occlusion); mean age 71 years, mean CHA2DS2-VASc score 4.2; mean follow-up 3.8 years; 76.8% continued oral anticoagulation at 3 years.
cards.result: Ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 114 participants (4.8%) in the occlusion group and 168 (7.0%) in the no-occlusion group (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.85; P=0.001) — the hazard ratio is a relative measure; the absolute rates are 4.8% vs 7.0% over a mean 3.8 years. The incidence of perioperative bleeding, heart failure, or death did not differ significantly between the groups (the abstract gives no separate mortality rates, so none are printed). 92.1% received the assigned procedure.
cards.watchOut: The operation was added to surgery already happening, in patients mostly kept on anticoagulation: the trial does not support appendage occlusion as a substitute for anticoagulation, nor a stand-alone operation to get it.
cards.source: Whitlock RP et al. Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion during Cardiac Surgery to Prevent Stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2021;384(22):2081-2091. PMID: 33999547. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01561651, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: LAAOS III substudy 2023: the occlusion benefit was consistent in patients on and off oral anticoagulation (hazard ratios 0.70, 0.63 and 0.76 by anticoagulant-use pattern)
cards.summary: LAAOS III substudy (2023): the occlusion benefit was consistent on and off oral anticoagulation (HRs 0.70, 0.63 and 0.61); a 2026 LAAOS III report from the currency sweep is fenced in the synthesis.
cards.type: Prespecified-style substudy report of the LAAOS III randomised trial (same trial, counted once as evidence)
cards.people: The LAAOS III population (4,770 participants): 2,887 (60.5%) received oral anticoagulants at all follow-up visits, 1,401 (29.4%) at some visits, and 472 (9.9%) never; at discharge 63.5% were on a vitamin K antagonist and 18.5% on a direct oral anticoagulant, with no difference between arms.
cards.result: The effect of appendage occlusion on ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism was consistent across anticoagulant-use groups after discharge: hazard ratios 0.70 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.96) in those always on anticoagulation, 0.63 (0.43 to 0.94) in those on it at some visits, and 0.76 (0.32 to 1.79) in those never on it — all relative measures. A time-dependent-covariate model likewise showed similar stroke/embolism reduction whether patients were receiving anticoagulants or not.
cards.watchOut: Anticoagulant use after randomisation was not itself randomised: the never-anticoagulated group is small (472 patients) and its confidence interval (0.32 to 1.79) is wide, so this substudy supports consistency, not a licence to stop anticoagulation after occlusion.

cards.summary: Synthesis: sewing the appendage shut during surgery already happening prevents strokes on top of anticoagulation — POSSIBLE (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: LAAOS III (4,770 patients) and its anticoagulation-use substudy (same trial).
cards.result: In patients with AF already undergoing cardiac surgery, concomitant appendage occlusion reduced stroke or systemic embolism from 7.0% to 4.8% over a mean 3.8 years (relative hazard ratio 0.67), with no significant excess of perioperative bleeding, heart failure or death, and with benefit consistent across anticoagulation patterns. shelves.title: Semaglutide for obesity-related HFpEF: STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM
shelves.question: Does once-weekly semaglutide improve symptoms, physical limitations and weight in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, in patients without diabetes and in patients with type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Glucagon-Like Peptides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Heart Failure/complications,drug therapy,physiopathology · Obesity/complications · Stroke Volume · Semaglutide · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy,etiology · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: cardiovascular death sits inside the trials' confirmatory hierarchical composites). Two parallel phase 3 trials in the two glycaemic populations agree: semaglutide improved KCCQ clinical summary score by 7.8 points (no diabetes) and 7.3 points (type 2 diabetes) over placebo at 52 weeks, with weight differences of -10.7 and -6.4 percentage points. The shelf's claims are symptoms, function and weight — the trials were not powered for mortality or heart-failure events, and none is claimed. SGLT2 inhibitors' HFpEF home is Shelf #70; no sequencing claim against them is made.

cards.headline: STEP-HFpEF 2023: semaglutide improved symptoms (KCCQ-CSS +7.8 points over placebo) and weight (-10.7 percentage points) in HFpEF with obesity, without diabetes
cards.summary: STEP-HFpEF (2023): semaglutide improved symptoms (KCCQ-CSS +7.8 points over placebo) and weight (−10.7 percentage points) in HFpEF with obesity.
cards.people: 529 patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and BMI of 30 or higher, without diabetes, randomised to once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Dual primary endpoints: mean change in KCCQ clinical summary score 16.6 points with semaglutide vs 8.7 with placebo (estimated difference 7.8 points; 95% CI 4.8 to 10.9; P<0.001), and mean percentage change in body weight -13.3% vs -2.6% (difference -10.7 points, -11.9 to -9.4; P<0.001). The 6-minute walk distance changed by 21.5 m vs 1.2 m (difference 20.3 m, 8.6 to 32.1). The hierarchical composite (including death and heart-failure events) produced more wins for semaglutide (win ratio 1.72, 1.37 to 2.15); CRP fell by -43.5% vs -7.3% (treatment ratio 0.61). Serious adverse events were reported in 35 participants (13.3%) on semaglutide and 71 (26.7%) on placebo. The components of the hierarchical composite are not reported separately in the abstract, so no mortality or heart-failure-event rates are printed.
cards.watchOut: A 529-patient, 52-week symptom-and-weight trial: the win-ratio composite mixes death and HF events with symptom change and cannot be read as an events benefit.
cards.source: Kosiborod MN et al. Semaglutide in Patients with Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Obesity. The New England journal of medicine. 2023;389(12):1069-1084. PMID: 37622681. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04788511, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: STEP-HFpEF DM (2024): in HFpEF with obesity and type 2 diabetes, KCCQ-CSS improved by 7.3 points and weight by −6.4 percentage points.

shelves.title: iFR- versus FFR-guided PCI: DEFINE-FLAIR and iFR-SWEDEHEART
shelves.question: Can the instantaneous wave-free ratio, measured at rest without adenosine, guide revascularisation decisions as safely as fractional flow reserve, on death, myocardial infarction or unplanned revascularisation at one year?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/diagnostic imaging,physiopathology · Angina Pectoris/diagnostic imaging,physiopathology · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Stenosis/diagnostic imaging,physiopathology,therapy · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both composites include death and myocardial infarction). Two large noninferiority trials published side by side in 2017 agree: iFR-guided revascularisation was noninferior to FFR-guided revascularisation for the 1-year composite of death, MI or unplanned revascularisation (6.8% vs 7.0% in DEFINE-FLAIR; 6.7% vs 6.1% in iFR-SWEDEHEART), with fewer procedural symptoms and shorter procedure time without adenosine. The claim is noninferiority of the measurement, not superiority of either strategy.

cards.headline: DEFINE-FLAIR 2017: iFR-guided PCI was noninferior to FFR-guided PCI — major adverse cardiac events 6.8% vs 7.0% at 1 year
cards.summary: DEFINE-FLAIR (2017): iFR-guided PCI was noninferior to FFR-guided PCI — major adverse cardiac events 6.8% vs 7.0% at 1 year.
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial (noninferiority margin 3.4 percentage points)
cards.people: 2,492 patients with coronary artery disease randomised 1:1 to iFR-guided or FFR-guided revascularisation; primary-endpoint data in 1,148 (iFR) and 1,182 (FFR) patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (death from any cause, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 78 of 1,148 patients (6.8%) in the iFR group and 83 of 1,182 (7.0%) in the FFR group (risk difference -0.2 percentage points; 95% CI -2.3 to 1.8; P<0.001 for noninferiority; hazard ratio 0.95, 0.68 to 1.33 — a relative measure). No component, including death from any cause, differed significantly. Adverse procedural symptoms and signs were far fewer with iFR (39 patients [3.1%] vs 385 [30.8%], P<0.001) and median procedural time was shorter (40.5 vs 45.0 minutes).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority within a 3.4-point margin at 1 year is a statement about the guidance index, not about whether physiology-guided PCI itself beats angiography — that strategy question lives elsewhere in the library.
cards.source: Davies JE et al. Use of the Instantaneous Wave-free Ratio or Fractional Flow Reserve in PCI. The New England journal of medicine. 2017;376(19):1824-1834. PMID: 28317458. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02053038, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: iFR-SWEDEHEART (2017): registry-based randomised trial confirms noninferiority — events 6.7% vs 6.1% at 12 months.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label, registry-based noninferiority trial (margin 3.2 percentage points)
cards.people: 2,037 participants with stable angina or acute coronary syndrome and an indication for physiologically guided assessment, enrolled through the Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry; primary-endpoint data in 1,012 (iFR) and 1,007 (FFR) patients. Rates of myocardial infarction, target-lesion revascularisation, restenosis and stent thrombosis did not differ significantly; chest discomfort during the procedure was reported more often with FFR (adenosine).

shelves.title: Intravascular-imaging-guided PCI: ULTIMATE, OCTOBER and ILUMIEN IV
shelves.question: Does guiding stent implantation with intravascular imaging (IVUS or OCT) beat angiography alone on clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease/diagnostic imaging,surgery · Drug-Eluting Stents · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods · Radiography, Interventional · Ultrasonography, Interventional · Coronary Angiography/adverse effects,methods
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — benefit in ULTIMATE and OCTOBER · POSSIBLE — the treatment made no difference in ILUMIEN IV — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composites include cardiac death and myocardial infarction). Three large trials split two-to-one: IVUS guidance reduced target-vessel failure in all-comers in ULTIMATE (2.9% vs 5.4%; relative hazard ratio 0.53), and OCT guidance reduced major adverse cardiac events in complex bifurcation lesions in OCTOBER (10.1% vs 14.1%; relative hazard ratio 0.70), but the largest trial, ILUMIEN IV, improved stent expansion yet missed its clinical endpoint (target-vessel failure 7.4% vs 8.2%, P=0.45). The discordance is the shelf: lesion selection and optimisation criteria, not the imaging catheter alone, appear to decide the benefit.

cards.headline: ULTIMATE 2018: IVUS-guided stent implantation reduced target-vessel failure at 12 months — 2.9% vs 5.4% (relative hazard ratio 0.530)
cards.summary: ULTIMATE (2018): IVUS-guided stenting reduced target-vessel failure at 12 months — 2.9% vs 5.4% (HR 0.53 relative).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (all-comers requiring drug-eluting stents)
cards.people: 1,448 all-comer patients requiring drug-eluting stent implantation, randomised 1:1 to IVUS guidance or angiography guidance. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Target-vessel failure at 12 months (cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 21 patients (2.9%) with IVUS guidance and 39 (5.4%) with angiography guidance (hazard ratio 0.530; 95% CI 0.312 to 0.901; p=0.019) — a relative measure; absolute rates 2.9% vs 5.4%. Within the IVUS group, target-vessel failure was 1.6% when all IVUS-defined optimal criteria were met vs 4.4% when they were not (hazard ratio 0.349). The component rates (cardiac death, target-vessel MI) are not reported separately in the abstract, so none are printed separately.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) all-comer trial from an earlier stent era, and the benefit concentrated in patients achieving all optimal IVUS criteria — guidance plus achieved optimisation, not guidance alone.
cards.source: Zhang J et al. Intravascular Ultrasound Versus Angiography-Guided Drug-Eluting Stent Implantation: The ULTIMATE Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2018;72(24):3126-3137. PMID: 30261237. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02215915, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: OCTOBER 2023: OCT guidance in complex bifurcation lesions reduced major adverse cardiac events at 2 years — 10.1% vs 14.1% (relative hazard ratio 0.70)
cards.summary: OCTOBER (2023): OCT guidance in complex bifurcation lesions reduced major adverse cardiac events at 2 years — 10.1% vs 14.1% .
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, open-label trial (38 European centres)
cards.people: 1,201 patients with a clinical indication for PCI and a complex bifurcation lesion, randomised to OCT-guided PCI (600) or angiography-guided PCI (601); 18.5% and 19.3% respectively had left-main bifurcation lesions. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At a median follow-up of 2 years, a primary-endpoint event (death from a cardiac cause, target-lesion myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation) occurred in 59 patients (10.1%) with OCT guidance and 83 (14.1%) with angiography guidance (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.98; P=0.035) — a relative measure; absolute rates 10.1% vs 14.1%. Procedure-related complications occurred in 41 patients (6.8%) vs 34 (5.7%). The cardiac-death and MI components are not reported separately in the abstract, so none are printed separately.
cards.watchOut: A lesion-specific trial (complex bifurcations, a fifth of them left main): its positive result does not generalise to routine PCI in simple lesions, which is the population where ILUMIEN IV was null.

cards.headline: ILUMIEN IV 2023: OCT guidance enlarged stent area but did not reduce target-vessel failure (7.4% vs 8.2%, P=0.45) in the largest imaging trial
cards.summary: ILUMIEN IV (2023): OCT guidance enlarged stent area but did not reduce target-vessel failure ( 7.4% vs 8.2% ; P=0.45) in the largest imaging trial.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, single-blind trial (80 sites, 18 countries)
cards.people: 2,487 patients with medication-treated diabetes or complex coronary lesions, randomised to OCT-guided PCI (1,233) or angiography-guided PCI (1,254). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Minimum stent area after PCI was larger with OCT guidance (5.72±2.04 mm2 vs 5.36±1.87 mm2; mean difference 0.36 mm2; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.51; P<0.001), but target-vessel failure within 2 years (death from cardiac causes, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 88 vs 99 patients (Kaplan-Meier estimates 7.4% and 8.2%; hazard ratio 0.90, 0.67 to 1.19; P=0.45) — no significant difference. Stent thrombosis within 2 years occurred in 6 patients (0.5%) vs 17 (1.4%). OCT-related adverse events occurred in 1 vs 2 patients.
cards.watchOut: The surrogate moved (stent area) and the clinical endpoint did not: ILUMIEN IV is the standing warning against equating better-looking stents with better outcomes at this event rate and follow-up.

cards.headline: Synthesis: imaging helps where lesions are complex or criteria are met; the largest trial is null — split POSSIBLE, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: imaging helps where lesions are complex or criteria are met; the largest trial is null — split POSSIBLE / POSSIBLE (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ULTIMATE (1,448 patients, IVUS, all-comers), OCTOBER (1,201 patients, OCT, bifurcations) and ILUMIEN IV (2,487 patients, OCT, diabetes/complex lesions).
cards.result: Two of three large trials found fewer composite events with imaging guidance (absolute 2.9% vs 5.4% and 10.1% vs 14.1%), and the largest found none (7.4% vs 8.2%) despite measurably larger stent areas. Read together: intravascular imaging is a tool whose payoff depends on lesion complexity and on acting to defined optimisation criteria — it is not a blanket mandate for every PCI. No earlier imaging shelf exists in the library; this shelf is the home for all three trials.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the three hazard ratios into a single claim: the populations and the achieved-optimisation rates differ, and the split stamp is the honest summary.

shelves.title: Inferior vena cava filters added to anticoagulation: PREPIC and PREPIC2
shelves.question: Does adding an inferior vena cava filter to anticoagulation prevent pulmonary embolism in patients with proximal deep-vein thrombosis or severe pulmonary embolism?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Enoxaparin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hemorrhage/etiology · Heparin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pulmonary Embolism/etiology,mortality,prevention & control · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference for routine use): In PREPIC, a permanent filter cut pulmonary embolism at day 12 (1.1% vs 4.8%) but raised recurrent deep-vein thrombosis at 2 years (20.8% vs 11.6%) with no mortality difference; in PREPIC2, a retrievable filter added to anticoagulation in severe PE changed nothing (recurrent PE 3.0% vs 1.5% at 3 months, not significant). Mortality was null in both trials and no survival benefit is claimed, so the topic is not Tier C. The shelf's answer: filters are not a routine adjunct for patients who can be anticoagulated.

cards.headline: PREPIC 1998: a permanent vena cava filter cut early PE (1.1% vs 4.8% at day 12) but increased recurrent DVT by 2 years (20.8% vs 11.6%), with no mortality difference
cards.summary: PREPIC (1998): a permanent filter cut early PE ( 1.1% vs 4.8% at day 12) but increased recurrent DVT by 2 years (20.8% vs 11.6%).
cards.type: Randomised trial with two-by-two factorial design (filter vs no filter; low-molecular-weight vs unfractionated heparin)
cards.people: 400 patients with proximal deep-vein thrombosis at risk for pulmonary embolism, randomised to a vena caval filter (200) or no filter (200), and to enoxaparin (195) or unfractionated heparin (205). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At day 12, symptomatic or asymptomatic pulmonary embolism had occurred in 2 patients (1.1%) assigned to filters vs 9 (4.8%) assigned to no filter (odds ratio 0.22; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.90 — a relative measure). At 2 years, recurrent deep-vein thrombosis had occurred in 37 filter patients (20.8%) vs 21 (11.6%) without (odds ratio 1.87, 1.10 to 3.20 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's edge). There were no significant differences in mortality or other outcomes. The heparin comparison likewise showed no significant difference in early PE (1.6% vs 4.2%; odds ratio 0.38, 0.10 to 1.38).
cards.watchOut: A 1998 permanent-filter trial from the early low-molecular-weight-heparin era: its early-PE endpoint included asymptomatic events, and the filter's harm (more DVT) accrued over the full 2 years while its benefit was front-loaded into 12 days.
cards.source: Decousus H et al. A clinical trial of vena caval filters in the prevention of pulmonary embolism in patients with proximal deep-vein thrombosis. Prévention du Risque d'Embolie Pulmonaire par Interruption Cave Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1998;338(7):409-15. PMID: 9459643. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (1998).

cards.headline: PREPIC2 2015: a retrievable filter added to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent PE in severe PE/DVT (3.0% vs 1.5% at 3 months, P=0.50)
cards.summary: PREPIC2 (2015): a retrievable filter added to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent PE in severe PE/DVT ( 3.0% vs 1.5% at 3 months).
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial with 6-month follow-up
cards.people: 399 hospitalised patients with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism associated with lower-limb vein thrombosis and at least one severity criterion, at 17 French centres; retrievable filter plus anticoagulation (n=200) or anticoagulation alone (n=199); the filter was successfully inserted in 193 and retrieved as planned in 153 of 164 attempts. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: By 3 months, symptomatic recurrent pulmonary embolism had occurred in 6 patients (3.0%; all fatal) in the filter group and 3 (1.5%; 2 fatal) in the control group (relative risk with filter 2.00; 95% CI 0.51 to 7.89; P=0.50) — a relative measure with absolute rates beside it, pointing the wrong way and not significant. Results were similar at 6 months, and no difference was seen in recurrent DVT, major bleeding, or death at 3 and 6 months (figures not separated in the abstract). Filter thrombosis occurred in 3 patients.
cards.watchOut: The trial tests retrievable filters in patients who could all receive full anticoagulation; it says nothing about the classic filter indication — PE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation — where no randomised trial exists.
cards.source: Mismetti P et al. Effect of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter plus anticoagulation vs anticoagulation alone on risk of recurrent pulmonary embolism: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(16):1627-35. PMID: 25919526. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00457158, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: early mechanical protection, later venous harm, no survival gain — LIKELY the null for routine use
cards.summary: Synthesis: early mechanical protection, later venous harm, no survival gain — LIKELY the null for routine use.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PREPIC (400 patients, permanent filter) and PREPIC2 (399 patients, retrievable filter).
cards.result: Seventeen years apart, the two randomised tests agree on the bottom line: in patients who can be anticoagulated, a vena cava filter does not improve net outcomes — PREPIC traded fewer early emboli (1.1% vs 4.8% at day 12) for more recurrent DVT (20.8% vs 11.6% at 2 years) with identical mortality, and PREPIC2 found no benefit at all (recurrent PE 3.0% vs 1.5%). Treatment of established PE is home on Shelves #237/#307; this shelf is the prevention-device question only.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled anticoagulable patients; the shelf must not be cited against filter use when anticoagulation is impossible.

shelves.title: Bilateral versus single internal-thoracic-artery grafting at 10 years (ART)
shelves.question: Does bilateral internal-thoracic-artery grafting beat a single mammary graft on death, myocardial infarction or stroke at ten years after coronary bypass surgery?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Bypass/methods · Coronary Artery Disease/mortality,surgery · Intention to Treat Analysis · Mammary Arteries/transplantation · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology · Stroke/epidemiology · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the outcomes are death, MI and stroke). The Arterial Revascularization Trial randomised 3,102 patients and followed them for 10 years: death from any cause was 20.3% with bilateral grafting vs 21.2% with single grafting (relative hazard ratio 0.96; P=0.62), and the composite of death, MI or stroke was 24.9% vs 27.3% (hazard ratio 0.90, CI including 1). A single very large null trial may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's rule — stated here as the reasoning. Crossover (13.9% of the bilateral group received a single graft) and radial-artery use in the single group (21.8%) cloud the contrast and are flagged on the card.

cards.headline: ART 2019 (10 years): bilateral mammary grafting did not reduce death (20.3% vs 21.2%, P=0.62) or the composite of death, MI or stroke (24.9% vs 27.3%)
cards.summary: ART (2019, 10 years): bilateral mammary grafting did not reduce death ( 20.3% vs 21.2% ; P=0.62) or the composite of death, MI or stroke.
cards.people: 3,102 patients scheduled for coronary-artery bypass grafting, randomised to bilateral internal-thoracic-artery grafting (1,548) or single internal-thoracic-artery grafting (1,554); additional arterial or vein grafts as indicated. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. Vital status was unknown for 2.3% at 10 years.
cards.result: Death from any cause at 10 years: 315 deaths (20.3%) in the bilateral group vs 329 (21.2%) in the single group (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.82 to 1.12; P=0.62) — a relative measure with absolute rates beside it. The composite of death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 385 patients (24.9%) vs 425 (27.3%) (hazard ratio 0.90, 0.79 to 1.03). In the bilateral group, 13.9% of patients in fact received only a single internal-thoracic-artery graft; in the single group, 21.8% also received a radial-artery graft.
cards.watchOut: The intention-to-treat contrast was diluted both ways — crossover away from bilateral grafting and radial-artery grafts (a second arterial graft by another route) in the control arm — so ART answers the strategy as practised, not the pure biological question; its 5-year report is the same trial, not a second anchor.
cards.source: Taggart DP et al. Bilateral versus Single Internal-Thoracic-Artery Grafts at 10 Years. The New England journal of medicine. 2019;380(5):437-446. PMID: 30699314. Registry ID: ISRCTN46552265, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Age of transfused red blood cells (ABLE and the storage-age trials)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, does transfusion of fresh (short-storage) red cells reduce 90-day mortality versus standard-issue (older) red cells?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Erythrocyte Transfusion/adverse effects · Blood Preservation · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, 90-day mortality primary outcome in both trials): Two large randomised, blinded trials agree. ABLE (2,430 critically ill adults; mean storage 6.1 days fresh versus 22.0 days standard-issue) found 90-day mortality of 37.0% versus 35.3% (absolute difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 5.5; hazard ratio 1.1 relative, 0.9 to 1.2). TRANSFUSE (4,919 patients analysed; mean storage 11.8 versus 22.4 days) found 90-day mortality of 24.8% versus 24.1% (absolute difference 0.7 points, −1.7 to 3.1; P=0.57). Fresh blood does not save lives in the ICU; the storage-age question is settled at this scale, and the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome is mortality (Tier C).

cards.headline: ABLE 2015: fresh red cells did not reduce 90-day mortality in critically ill adults (37.0% vs 35.3%)
cards.summary: ABLE 2015: fresh red cells did not reduce 90-day mortality in critically ill adults (37.0% vs 35.3%)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, blinded trial (64 centres, Canada and Europe)
cards.people: 2,430 critically ill adults randomised between March 2009 and May 2014 to red cells stored for less than 8 days (1,211) or standard-issue red cells — the oldest compatible units available (1,219). Mean storage was 6.1 (SD 4.9) days in the fresh group versus 22.0 (SD 8.4) days in the standard group. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 90 days, 448 patients (37.0%) in the fresh-blood group and 430 patients (35.3%) in the standard-blood group had died (absolute risk difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 5.5). In the survival analysis, the hazard ratio for death with fresh blood was 1.1 relative (95% CI 0.9 to 1.2; P=0.38). There were no significant between-group differences in any secondary outcome (major illnesses; duration of respiratory, haemodynamic or renal support; hospital stay; transfusion reactions) or in subgroup analyses.

shelves.title: Prothrombin complex concentrate versus plasma for warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage (INCH)
shelves.question: In patients with vitamin-K-antagonist-related intracerebral haemorrhage, does 4-factor PCC normalise INR faster and limit haematoma expansion versus fresh frozen plasma?
shelves.mesh: Intracranial Hemorrhages/chemically induced · Blood Coagulation Factors/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Plasma · International Normalized Ratio · Vitamin K/antagonists & inhibitors · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised test (INCH, 50 patients treated) found 4-factor PCC normalised the INR far faster than fresh frozen plasma — INR of 1.2 or lower within 3 hours in 67% on PCC versus 9% on plasma (adjusted odds ratio 30.6 relative, 95% CI 4.7 to 197.9; P=0.0003) — and the trial was stopped early after a safety analysis because of harm signals in the plasma arm: 8 of 23 plasma patients (35%) died, five of them from haematoma expansion within 48 hours, versus 5 of 27 (19%) on PCC, none from haematoma expansion. A small, stopped-early, open-label trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the primary claim is reversal speed and haematoma behaviour, so the shelf is not Tier C, with the mortality figures printed on the card.

cards.headline: INCH 2016: PCC normalised INR within 3 hours in 67% versus 9% on plasma; the trial stopped early over plasma-arm haematoma expansion and deaths
cards.summary: INCH 2016: PCC normalised INR within 3 hours in 67% versus 9% on plasma; the trial stopped early over plasma-arm haematoma expansion and deaths
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial — terminated early after a safety analysis
cards.people: 54 adults (aged at least 18 years) with vitamin-K-antagonist-related intracranial haemorrhage presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset with an INR of at least 2.0, randomised to 20 mL/kg intravenous fresh frozen plasma (26) or 30 IU/kg intravenous 4-factor PCC (28) within 1 hour of the initial CT; 50 received study drug (23 plasma, 27 PCC) between August 2009 and January 2015. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Two (9%) of 23 patients in the plasma group versus 18 (67%) of 27 in the PCC group reached the primary endpoint of INR 1.2 or lower within 3 hours of treatment initiation (adjusted odds ratio 30.6 relative, 95% CI 4.7 to 197.9; P=0.0003). Thirteen patients died: eight (35%) of 23 in the plasma group (five from haematoma expansion, all within 48 hours of symptom onset) and five (19%) of 27 in the PCC group (none from haematoma expansion; the first occurred on day 5). Three thromboembolic events occurred within 3 days (one plasma, two PCC) and six after day 12 (one and five). Forty-three serious adverse events occurred in 26 patients; six were judged plasma-related (four haematoma expansions, one anaphylactic reaction, one ischaemic stroke) and two PCC-related (ischaemic stroke and pulmonary embolism).
cards.watchOut: Fifty treated patients and early termination: the odds ratio's confidence interval (4.7 to 197.9) is very wide, the trial was open-label (endpoints observer-masked), and it was stopped for safety concerns in the plasma arm — which strengthens the direction of the finding but leaves its size imprecise.
cards.source: Steiner T et al. Fresh frozen plasma versus prothrombin complex concentrate in patients with intracranial haemorrhage related to vitamin K antagonists (INCH): a randomised trial. Lancet Neurol. 2016. PMID: 27302126. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00928915, from the record's databank fields (the report also names EudraCT 2008-005653-37). cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: INCH 2016 (54 randomised; 50 treated with vitamin-K-antagonist-related intracerebral haemorrhage).
cards.result: INCH is a small trial with a lopsided result: reversal within 3 hours in two-thirds on PCC versus under one-tenth on plasma, and all five early haematoma-expansion deaths in the plasma arm. Reversal of other anticoagulants and of antiplatelet effects (desmopressin, Shelf #1292) are different questions and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Desmopressin for intracerebral haemorrhage on antiplatelet drugs (DASH)
shelves.question: In patients with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage taking antiplatelet drugs, does desmopressin improve functional outcome?
shelves.mesh: Cerebral Hemorrhage/drug therapy,chemically induced · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin/adverse effects · Feasibility Studies · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death-or-dependency outcome): DASH is explicitly a phase 2 feasibility trial, not an efficacy trial: 54 patients were randomised (27 desmopressin, 27 placebo) of 1,380 screened, and recruitment itself was the primary outcome. The outcome figures are hypothesis-generating only — death or dependency at day 90 (modified Rankin Scale score above 4) in 22% on desmopressin versus 37% on placebo, with serious adverse events in 44% versus 48% — in a sample far too small to support any efficacy reading. The honest stamp for whether desmopressin improves outcome is MAYBE (weak evidence): feasibility was shown, benefit was not tested at scale, and a definitive trial is what the record calls for.

cards.headline: DASH 2023: a 54-patient feasibility trial — desmopressin could be given, but efficacy was not established (death or dependency 22% vs 37%)
cards.summary: DASH 2023: a 54-patient feasibility trial — desmopressin could be given, but efficacy was not established (death or dependency 22% vs 37%)
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre feasibility trial (ten UK acute stroke centres)
cards.people: 54 adults (mean age 76.4 years [SD 11.3]; 36 [67%] male; 50 [93%] White) with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, symptom onset within 24 hours of randomisation, and taking an antiplatelet drug, recruited between April 2019 and March 2022 from 1,380 screened patients; 27 received a single intravenous dose of desmopressin 20 μg and 27 matching placebo. The main reason eligible patients were not recruited was arrival out of hours (74 [61%] of 122 not recruited).
cards.result: The primary outcome was feasibility: 176 (13%) of 1,380 screened patients were potentially eligible, 57 (32%) were approached, and 54 (31%) consented and were randomised; 53 (98%) received all their allocated treatment and none were lost to follow-up. Death or dependency on others for daily activities at day 90 (modified Rankin Scale score above 4) occurred in six (22%) of 27 participants in the desmopressin group and ten (37%) of 27 in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred in 12 (44%) on desmopressin and 13 (48%) on placebo; the most common adverse events were expansion of the haemorrhagic stroke (four [15%] on desmopressin and six [22%] on placebo).
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial by design: with 27 patients per arm, the 22% versus 37% outcome contrast is compatible with a wide range of true effects, and quoting it as evidence of benefit would repeat the classic small-trial error. This is the card the MAYBE (weak evidence) label exists for.
cards.source: Desborough MJR et al. shelves.title: Intraoperative cell salvage
shelves.question: In patients having surgery with expected blood loss, does intraoperative cell salvage reduce allogeneic transfusion versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Blood Transfusion, Autologous/economics · Coronary Artery Bypass, Off-Pump/economics · Hemoglobins/analysis · Intraoperative Period · Humans · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The carded randomised test is small and single-specialty: 61 patients having off-pump coronary bypass were randomised to washed salvaged-blood autotransfusion or homologous blood only; the salvage group had a higher 24-hour haemoglobin (11.9 vs 10.5 g/dL; P=0.0007) and a lower frequency of homologous blood product use (5 of 30 versus 11 of 31) that did not reach significance (P=0.095), with no derangement of clotting measures, no excess bleeding or adverse events, and no significant cost difference. The direction favours salvage for transfusion sparing, but the carded evidence is one 61-patient trial with a transfusion-exposure surrogate, so the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf says so.

cards.headline: Murphy 2005: cell salvage after off-pump bypass raised 24-hour haemoglobin and modestly reduced donor-blood use (5/30 vs 11/31; P=0.095)
cards.summary: Murphy 2005: cell salvage after off-pump bypass raised 24-hour haemoglobin and modestly reduced donor-blood use (5/30 vs 11/31; P=0.095)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single specialty: first-time off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting)
cards.people: 61 patients undergoing off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting, prospectively randomised to autotransfusion of washed salvaged red cells (30) or control — homologous blood only, given by unit protocols (31). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Patients in the autotransfusion group had a significantly higher 24-hour postoperative haemoglobin concentration (11.9 g/dL [SD 1.41]) than controls (10.5 g/dL [SD 1.37]) (mean difference 1.02 g/dL, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.60; P=0.0007), and a 20% reduction in the frequency of homologous blood product use (5 of 30 versus 11 of 31; P=0.095). Autotransfusion was not associated with derangement of thromboelastograph values or laboratory clotting measures (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen), increased postoperative bleeding, fluid requirements, or adverse clinical events. Total operation, hospitalisation and management costs per patient did not differ significantly (median difference USD 1015.90, 95% CI −2260 to 206; P=0.11).
cards.watchOut: Sixty-one patients in one operation type: the transfusion-sparing endpoint is a surrogate (exposure to donor blood, not a clinical outcome), the headline use difference was not statistically significant, and extrapolation to other operations or to unwashed salvage systems is beyond this record.
cards.source: Murphy GJ et al. Safety, efficacy, and cost of intraoperative cell salvage and autotransfusion after off-pump coronary artery bypass surgery: a randomized trial. J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2005. PMID: 15999036. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Granulocyte transfusion for neutropenic infection (RING)
shelves.question: In neutropenic patients with bacterial or fungal infection, do transfused granulocytes from G-CSF/dexamethasone-stimulated donors improve infection response and survival?
shelves.mesh: Neutropenia/complications,therapy · Leukocyte Transfusion/methods · Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor/pharmacology · Infections/complications,drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The definitive randomised test (RING, 114 patients randomised) found no overall effect: the composite of survival plus microbial response at 42 days succeeded in 42% with granulocyte transfusion versus 43% with standard antimicrobial therapy alone (P>0.99), and 49% versus 41% among patients who received their assigned treatments (P=0.64), with no difference in any infection-type subgroup. But RING enrolled only half its planned sample, so its power to detect a true benefit was low, and a post hoc analysis hinted that patients receiving higher granulocyte doses (at least 0.6×10^9 per kilogram per transfusion) fared better. An underpowered null caps at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): no demonstrated benefit, with the dose question honestly left open.

cards.headline: RING 2015: granulocyte transfusion did not improve the survival-plus-response composite (42% vs 43%), in a trial that enrolled half its planned sample
cards.summary: RING 2015: granulocyte transfusion did not improve the survival-plus-response composite (42% vs 43%), in a trial that enrolled half its planned sample
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (microbial response adjudicated by a blinded panel)
cards.people: 114 patients with neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count below 500/μL) and proven, probable or presumed bacterial or fungal infection, randomised to standard antimicrobial therapy alone (58) or standard therapy plus daily granulocyte transfusions from donors stimulated with G-CSF and dexamethasone (56); transfused patients received a median of 5 transfusions at a mean dose of 54.9×10^9 granulocytes. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Overall success rates (survival plus microbial response at 42 days after randomisation) were 42% for the granulocyte group and 43% for the control group (P>0.99), and 49% and 41% respectively among subjects who received their assigned treatments (P=0.64). Success rates did not differ within any infection type. In a post hoc analysis, subjects who received an average dose per transfusion of at least 0.6×10^9 granulocytes per kilogram tended to have better outcomes than those receiving a lower dose. The authors conclude there was no overall effect on the primary outcome, but because enrolment was half that planned, power to detect a true beneficial effect was low.
cards.watchOut: The post hoc dose signal is exactly that — post hoc, in an under-enrolled trial; it justifies a future adequate-dose trial, not a benefit claim. Equally, the null does not prove high-dose granulocytes are useless: the trial never delivered its planned test.
cards.source: Price TH et al. Efficacy of transfusion with granulocytes from G-CSF/dexamethasone-treated donors in neutropenic patients with infection. Blood. 2015. PMID: 26333778. cards.summary: Synthesis: no demonstrated benefit at the doses delivered; the adequate-dose question was never fully tested — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: RING 2015 (114 neutropenic patients with infection).
cards.result: After 20 years of availability without conclusive evidence, RING remains the randomised reference point: at a median of 5 transfusions, granulocyte transfusion added nothing measurable to standard antimicrobial therapy on survival plus microbial response (42% vs 43%). The stamp is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than LIKELY because the trial's own caveat — half the planned enrolment — is part of the record.

shelves.title: Erythropoietin in critically ill and trauma patients
shelves.question: In critically ill patients, does epoetin alfa reduce transfusion or mortality versus placebo — and does any mortality benefit concentrate in trauma patients?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Erythropoietin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Epoetin Alfa · Erythrocyte Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Thrombosis/chemically induced · Wounds and Injuries/blood,drug therapy,mortality · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — transfusion sparing in critical illness overall · POSSIBLE — a mortality benefit confined to trauma patients — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality claim): In the 1,460-patient trial (Corwin 2007), epoetin alfa did NOT reduce transfusion (relative risk 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.06) and overall mortality was not significantly lower (day-29 adjusted hazard ratio 0.79 relative, 0.56 to 1.10) — while thrombotic events increased (hazard ratio 1.41 relative, 1.06 to 1.86). The trauma signal is a prespecified subgroup finding repeated across the programme: day-29 mortality hazard ratio 0.37 relative (0.19 to 0.72) in Corwin's trauma patients, and the pooled trauma-cohort analysis of the two large trials (EPO-2 and EPO-3) found day-29 mortality of 4.1% versus 8.9% and 3.5% versus 6.7% (hazard ratios 0.46 and 0.51 relative). A subgroup-replicated mortality signal without an overall effect is POSSIBLE, not more — the trauma analysis authors themselves call for a definitive trauma trial.

cards.headline: Corwin 2007: epoetin alfa did not reduce transfusion in 1,460 critically ill patients, increased thrombotic events — but the trauma subgroup's mortality was lower
cards.summary: Corwin 2007: epoetin alfa did not reduce transfusion in 1,460 critically ill patients, increased thrombotic events — but the trauma subgroup's mortality was lower
cards.people: 1,460 medical, surgical or trauma patients enrolled 48 to 96 hours after ICU admission, receiving weekly epoetin alfa 40,000 U or placebo for a maximum of 3 weeks, followed for 140 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Epoetin alfa did not decrease the percentage of patients receiving a red-cell transfusion (relative risk 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.06) or the mean number of units transfused (4.5 [SD 4.6] versus 4.3 [SD 4.8]; P=0.42), although haemoglobin at day 29 rose more with epoetin (1.6 [SD 2.0] versus 1.2 [SD 1.8] g/dL; P<0.001). Mortality tended to be lower at day 29 (adjusted hazard ratio 0.79 relative, 0.56 to 1.10), an effect also seen in prespecified analyses of patients with trauma (adjusted hazard ratio 0.37 relative, 0.19 to 0.72), and a similar pattern held at day 140 (overall 0.86 relative, 0.65 to 1.13; trauma 0.40 relative, 0.23 to 0.69). Epoetin alfa significantly increased thrombotic events (hazard ratio 1.41 relative, 1.06 to 1.86).
cards.watchOut: The trauma mortality finding is a subgroup of a trial whose primary endpoint (transfusion) was null and whose overall mortality difference was not significant — and the same drug increased thrombotic events overall. Both facts belong on the face of any trauma claim.

cards.summary: Napolitano 2008: across both large trials, trauma patients on epoetin alfa had roughly half the day-29 mortality (pooled trauma-cohort analysis)
cards.type: Pooled trauma-cohort analysis of two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (EPO-2 and EPO-3) — EPO-3 is the trial on the card above, counted once
cards.people: The trauma cohorts of two similarly designed randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trials — EPO-2 (1,302 critically ill patients) and EPO-3 (1,460 patients, the Corwin trial carded above) — receiving 40,000 U epoetin alfa or placebo weekly (4 doses in EPO-2, 3 in EPO-3) from ICU day 3. The abstract does not state the trauma-cohort sizes, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality was consistently reduced by approximately 50% (relative) in both trauma cohorts at day 29: EPO-2 mortality 4.1% on epoetin alfa versus 8.9% on placebo (unadjusted hazard ratio 0.46 relative, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.89) and EPO-3 mortality 3.5% versus 6.7% (hazard ratio 0.51 relative, 0.27 to 0.98). Adjusted hazard ratios were similar (EPO-2 0.50 relative, 0.26 to 0.97; EPO-3 0.38 relative, 0.19 to 0.74), and the EPO-3 day-140 adjusted hazard ratio was 0.39 relative (0.21 to 0.72). Clinically relevant thrombovascular events were numerically higher on epoetin in EPO-3 (16.4% vs 12.5%; relative risk 1.3 relative, 0.93 to 1.85) but not in EPO-2 (11.1% vs 13.3%; relative risk 0.84 relative, 0.56 to 1.28). The authors conclude that a definitive study in trauma subjects is warranted.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of subgroups: the trauma cohorts were prespecified strata of trials designed and powered for transfusion outcomes in the whole ICU population, not for trauma mortality. Replication across two trials strengthens it beyond a single subgroup fishing trip — to POSSIBLE, not beyond.

shelves.title: Leukocyte depletion of transfused blood
shelves.question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, does leukocyte-depleted transfusion reduce postoperative complications and mortality versus standard transfusion?
shelves.mesh: Blood Transfusion/methods · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Filtration · Postoperative Complications/mortality · Bacterial Infections/mortality · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality claim): One randomised trial (van de Watering 1998, 914 cardiac-surgery patients in three arms) found 60-day postoperative mortality of 7.8% with buffy-coat-reduced (non-filtered) packed cells versus 3.6% with fresh-filtered and 3.3% with stored-filtered leukocyte-depleted units (P=0.015), while infection rates (23.0% versus 16.9% and 17.9%) did not differ significantly (P=0.13) and hospital and ICU stay were unchanged. A single 1998 three-arm trial, with the mortality difference only partly explained by infections and later leukoreduction literature mixed, supports POSSIBLE — not more — and the mortality claim makes it Tier C.

cards.headline: van de Watering 1998: leukocyte-depleted transfusion halved 60-day postoperative mortality in cardiac surgery (3.6% and 3.3% vs 7.8%)
cards.summary: van de Watering 1998: leukocyte-depleted transfusion halved 60-day postoperative mortality in cardiac surgery (3.6% and 3.3% vs 7.8%)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (three arms: non-filtered, fresh-filtered, stored-filtered)
cards.people: 914 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery, randomised to receive, when transfusion was indicated, packed cells without buffy coat (306), fresh-filtered leukocyte-depleted units (305), or stored-filtered leukocyte-depleted units (303). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The average hospital stay was 10.7 days, of which 3.2 days were in intensive care, without significant differences between groups. Infections occurred in 23.0% of patients in the non-filtered arm versus 16.9% (fresh-filtered) and 17.9% (stored-filtered) (P=0.13). Within 60 days, 45 patients had died: 24 (7.8%) in the non-filtered arm versus 11 (3.6%) and 10 (3.3%) in the leukocyte-depleted arms (P=0.015). The authors conclude that leukocyte depletion by filtration significantly reduced postoperative mortality, especially in patients requiring more than three transfusions, an effect only partially explained by the higher infection incidence in the non-filtered arm.
cards.watchOut: A single 1998 trial from the pre-universal-leukoreduction era: the comparator (buffy-coat-reduced but unfiltered cells) is no longer standard in many systems, the infection endpoint that might explain the mortality gap was itself not significant, and the effect concentrated in heavily transfused patients.
cards.source: van de Watering LM et al. Beneficial effects of leukocyte depletion of transfused blood on postoperative complications in patients undergoing cardiac surgery: a randomized clinical trial. Circulation. 1998. PMID: 9494026. shelves.title: Pathogen-reduced platelets (SPRINT and successors)
shelves.question: In patients receiving platelet transfusions for thrombocytopenia, do pathogen-reduced (amotosalen/UVA) platelets prevent bleeding as effectively as conventional platelets?
shelves.mesh: Platelet Transfusion/adverse effects · Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Thrombocytopenia/therapy · Furocoumarins/pharmacology · Photochemistry · Humans · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pivotal randomised trial (SPRINT, 645 thrombocytopenic patients) met its non-inferiority test on the bleeding endpoint: WHO grade 2 bleeding occurred in 58.5% on amotosalen/UVA pathogen-inactivated platelets versus 57.5% on conventional platelets, and grade 3 or 4 bleeding in 4.1% versus 6.1% (non-inferiority P=0.001), with fewer transfusion reactions (3.0% vs 4.4%; P=0.02). The price was platelet quality: 1-hour corrected count increments were lower (11.1 versus 16.0 ×10^3), the interval to the next transfusion shorter (1.9 versus 2.4 days), and more platelet transfusions were needed (8.4 versus 6.2). Bleeding-grade endpoints are surrogates for the outcomes that matter most, and a single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SPRINT 2004: pathogen-inactivated platelets were non-inferior for grade 2 bleeding (58.5% vs 57.5%) — but increments were lower and more transfusions were needed
cards.summary: SPRINT 2004: pathogen-inactivated platelets were non-inferior for grade 2 bleeding (58.5% vs 57.5%) — but increments were lower and more transfusions were needed
cards.type: Randomised transfusion trial (pathogen-inactivated versus conventional platelets)
cards.people: 645 patients with thrombocytopenia (318 photochemically treated, 327 control) randomly assigned to receive pathogen-inactivated (amotosalen HCl plus UVA) or conventional platelets for up to 28 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, the incidence of WHO grade 2 bleeding during platelet support, was 58.5% with treated platelets versus 57.5% with control platelets, and grade 3 or 4 bleeding occurred in 4.1% versus 6.1% (both equivalent between groups; P=0.001 by non-inferiority). The mean 1-hour posttransfusion corrected count increment was lower with treated platelets (11.1 versus 16.0 ×10^3), as were the average days to next platelet transfusion (1.9 versus 2.4) and the number of platelet transfusions was higher (8.4 versus 6.2) (all P<0.001). Transfusion reactions were fewer following treated platelets (3.0% versus 4.4%; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority was shown for a bleeding-grade surrogate in patients receiving prophylactic support; the trial simultaneously showed the treated platelets performed worse on every platelet-quality measure (increment, interval, number of transfusions) — 'as effective at preventing grade 2 bleeding, at the cost of more product' is the accurate summary.

shelves.title: Cold-stored platelets for surgical bleeding (CHIPS)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery at risk of bleeding, are cold-stored platelets non-inferior to room-temperature platelets for postoperative bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Platelet Transfusion/adverse effects,methods · Blood Preservation/methods · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,mortality · Cold Temperature · Postoperative Hemorrhage/therapy · Humans · Adult · Child · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 3 trial (CHIPS, 989 patients analysed — children and adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at 27 sites) found cold-stored platelets (stored up to 21 days) non-inferior to room-temperature platelets (up to 7 days) on the primary haemostatic efficacy score, with a posterior probability of non-inferiority above 99.9% for every cold-storage duration tested (pooled mean difference 0.09 points on a 1–5 scale where higher means more bleeding, 95% credible interval −0.06 to 0.23, against a 1-point margin) and no significant difference in 24-hour chest-tube output. A single — albeit large and adaptive — trial on a haemostatic-score surrogate, in a mixed paediatric-adult population, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CHIPS 2026: cold-stored platelets were non-inferior to room-temperature platelets for haemostatic efficacy in cardiac surgery (probability of non-inferiority >99.9%)
cards.summary: CHIPS 2026: cold-stored platelets were non-inferior to room-temperature platelets for haemostatic efficacy in cardiac surgery (probability of non-inferiority >99.9%)
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, partially blinded, adaptive, non-inferiority, storage duration-ranging trial
cards.people: 1,000 patients who underwent platelet transfusion during cardiac surgery with planned cardiopulmonary bypass at 27 sites in the US and Australia (December 2021 to March 2025), of whom 989 were included in the primary analysis (650 cold-stored, 339 room-temperature, randomised 2:1). The cohort included paediatric and adult patients: mean age 42.1 years (SD 30.1); 67.8% were male. Cold-stored platelets were stored for a maximum of 21 days, room-temperature platelets for a maximum of 7 days.
cards.result: Cold-stored platelets were non-inferior to room-temperature platelets for the primary outcome (a haemostatic efficacy score from 1 to 5, higher values indicating greater bleeding), with a probability of greater than 99.9% for all cold-storage durations against the 1-point non-inferiority margin. Pooled across storage durations, the mean difference from room-temperature platelets was 0.09 (95% credible interval −0.06 to 0.23). Median 24-hour chest-tube output did not differ significantly (8.9 mL/kg [IQR 5.2–15.4] cold-stored versus 8.4 mL/kg [5.5–15.9] room-temperature; difference in medians 0.4, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.5). In a post hoc pooled analysis, mean haemostatic efficacy scores were 3.08 (SD 1.15) cold-stored versus 2.99 (SD 1.10) room-temperature.
cards.watchOut: The population spans infants to older adults (mean age 42.1 with SD 30.1) and the primary endpoint is a 5-point haemostatic efficacy score, not mortality or reoperation; the partially blinded adaptive design and the very wide 1-point margin on a 5-point scale are part of the record. The finding licenses cold storage up to 21 days for this indication — it does not address prophylactic transfusion in thrombocytopenia (Shelf #1297).
cards.source: Spinella PC et al. Cold and Room-Temperature Platelets in Cardiac Surgery: The CHIPS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 42606886.
