shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality within the outcome composite): The single large trial (HEMOTION, 742 patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury and anaemia) found an unfavourable 6-month neurological outcome in 68.4% on the liberal strategy (transfuse at haemoglobin 10 g/dL or below) versus 73.5% on the restrictive strategy (7 g/dL or below) — an adjusted absolute difference of 5.4 percentage points favouring liberal (restrictive versus liberal, 95% CI −2.9 to 13.7) that did not reach significance — and no association between strategy and mortality. A single trial whose confidence interval still includes a meaningful liberal benefit caps the null at POSSIBLE. (Anchor note: the topic draft left the primary report to be pinned at build; it is pinned here as Turgeon et al., NEJM 2024, PMID 38869931 — the draft's sub-study record, PMID 41774107, is not the primary report and is not carded.)

cards.headline: HEMOTION 2024: a liberal transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce unfavourable 6-month neurological outcome in TBI (68.4% vs 73.5%)
cards.summary: HEMOTION 2024: a liberal transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce unfavourable 6-month neurological outcome in TBI (68.4% vs 73.5%)
cards.type: Randomised trial of transfusion strategy (liberal versus restrictive threshold) in critically ill patients with TBI
cards.people: 742 adults with moderate or severe traumatic brain injury and anaemia, randomly assigned to a liberal transfusion strategy (transfusions initiated at a haemoglobin level of 10 g/dL or below; 371) or a restrictive strategy (7 g/dL or below; 371); the primary-outcome analysis included 722 patients. Median ICU haemoglobin was 10.8 g/dL in the liberal group and 8.8 g/dL in the restrictive group. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: An unfavourable outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended, by sliding dichotomy based on baseline prognosis) at 6 months occurred in 249 of 364 patients (68.4%) in the liberal-strategy group and 263 of 358 (73.5%) in the restrictive-strategy group (adjusted absolute difference, restrictive versus liberal, 5.4 percentage points; 95% CI −2.9 to 13.7). Among survivors, a liberal strategy was associated with higher scores on some but not all scales of functional independence and quality of life. No association was observed between transfusion strategy and mortality or depression. Venous thromboembolic events occurred in 8.4% of patients in each group; acute respiratory distress syndrome occurred in 3.3% (liberal) and 0.8% (restrictive).
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours the liberal strategy by 5.4 points and the confidence interval runs from a 2.9-point advantage for restrictive to a 13.7-point advantage for liberal — this is an imprecise null, not proof the strategies are equal; the ARDS imbalance (3.3% vs 0.8%) is also part of the record.
cards.source: Turgeon AF et al. Liberal or Restrictive Transfusion Strategy in Patients with Traumatic Brain Injury. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38869931. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03260478, from the record's databank fields. cards.result: HEMOTION answers the brain-injury version of the threshold question separately from the general-ICU and myocardial-infarction threshold shelves (#124 and #368, not re-carded here): transfusing at 10 g/dL rather than 7 g/dL did not significantly improve 6-month neurological outcome (68.4% vs 73.5% unfavourable) and did not change mortality. shelves.title: Radial versus femoral access for coronary angiography and intervention in ACS (RIVAL and MATRIX)
shelves.question: In patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing angiography with possible PCI, does radial access, compared with femoral access, reduce the composite of death, MI, stroke, and non-CABG major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Catheterization, Peripheral · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Bypass · Female · Femoral Artery · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Reperfusion · Radial Artery · Stents
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death, MI and stroke): Two large randomised trials point the same way on net clinical events but not identically. RIVAL (7,021 ACS patients) found no difference in its primary composite of death, MI, stroke or non-CABG major bleeding at 30 days (3.7% radial vs 4.0% femoral; HR 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.17; P=0.50), with death/MI/stroke identical (3.2% vs 3.2%) and major bleeding itself not significantly different (0.7% vs 0.9%) — the clear RIVAL gains were local vascular complications (large haematoma 42 vs 106 patients; pseudoaneurysm needing closure 7 vs 23). MATRIX (8,404 ACS patients) met its net adverse clinical events co-primary outcome (9.8% vs 11.7%; rate ratio 0.83 relative, 0.73 to 0.96; P=0.0092), driven by BARC major bleeding (1.6% vs 2.3%) and all-cause mortality (1.6% vs 2.2%; rate ratio 0.72 relative, 0.53 to 0.99) — while its MACE co-primary (8.8% vs 10.3%; P=0.0307) did NOT reach significance at the prespecified split alpha of 0.025. Two large trials with a consistent bleeding and net-event advantage, one mortality component significant in one trial, support LIKELY for the net-benefit claim; the topic draft's framing of RIVAL as showing a mortality signal is corrected on the card — RIVAL's death/MI/stroke rates were identical, and its significant interactions were for the primary composite in STEMI and in high-radial-volume centres.

cards.headline: RIVAL 2011: no difference in death, MI, stroke or major bleeding (3.7% vs 4.0%), but far fewer access-site vascular complications with radial access
cards.summary: RIVAL 2011: no difference in death, MI, stroke or major bleeding (3.7% vs 4.0%), but far fewer access-site vascular complications with radial access
cards.type: Randomised, parallel-group, multicentre trial (158 hospitals, 32 countries)
cards.people: 7,021 patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing coronary angiography with possible intervention, randomly assigned to radial (3,507) or femoral (3,514) access between June 2006 and November 2010; patients and investigators were not masked, with a masked central committee adjudicating the primary outcome. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (death, MI, stroke, or non-CABG-related major bleeding at 30 days) occurred in 128 of 3,507 (3.7%) radial versus 139 of 3,514 (4.0%) femoral patients (HR 0.92 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.72 to 1.17; P=0.50). Death, MI or stroke occurred in 3.2% versus 3.2% (HR 0.98 relative, 0.76 to 1.28). Non-CABG major bleeding was 0.7% versus 0.9% (HR 0.73 relative, 0.43 to 1.23; P=0.23 — not significant). Large haematoma occurred in 42 versus 106 patients (HR 0.40 relative, 0.28 to 0.57; P<0.0001) and pseudoaneurysm needing closure in 7 versus 23 (HR 0.30 relative, 0.13 to 0.71). Of six prespecified subgroups, the primary outcome showed significant interactions favouring radial in the highest-tertile radial-volume centres (HR 0.49 relative) and in STEMI patients (HR 0.60 relative).
cards.watchOut: The topic draft described a RIVAL 'mortality signal' — the record shows death/MI/stroke exactly equal (3.2% vs 3.2%); the STEMI and high-volume-centre findings are subgroup interactions on the composite, not a mortality result. The trial's own conclusion is equivalence on events with fewer local vascular complications.
cards.source: Jolly SS et al. Radial versus femoral access for coronary angiography and intervention in patients with acute coronary syndromes (RIVAL): a randomised, parallel group, multicentre trial. Lancet (London, England). 2011. PMID: 21470671. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01014273, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: MATRIX 2015: net adverse clinical events lower with radial access (9.8% vs 11.7%), driven by major bleeding and mortality; the MACE co-primary missed its prespecified alpha
cards.summary: MATRIX 2015: net adverse clinical events lower with radial access (9.8% vs 11.7%), driven by major bleeding and mortality; the MACE co-primary missed its prespecified alpha
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, superiority trial (outcome assessors masked)
cards.people: 8,404 patients with acute coronary syndrome, with or without ST-segment elevation, about to undergo coronary angiography and PCI, randomly allocated to radial (4,197) or femoral (4,207) access. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 30 days, major adverse cardiovascular events (death, MI, or stroke) occurred in 369 (8.8%) radial versus 429 (10.3%) femoral patients (rate ratio 0.85 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.74 to 0.99; P=0.0307), which was non-significant at the prespecified two-sided alpha of 0.025 for the co-primary outcomes. Net adverse clinical events (MACE or BARC major bleeding unrelated to CABG) occurred in 410 (9.8%) versus 486 (11.7%) (rate ratio 0.83 relative, 0.73 to 0.96; P=0.0092). The difference was driven by BARC major bleeding (1.6% vs 2.3%; rate ratio 0.67 relative, 0.49 to 0.92) and all-cause mortality (1.6% vs 2.2%; rate ratio 0.72 relative, 0.53 to 0.99; P=0.045).
cards.watchOut: The authors' interpretation claims a mortality reduction; the mortality figure is a component of the co-primary outcomes, and the MACE co-primary itself did not cross the prespecified 0.025 threshold (P=0.0307) — the card prints both facts so the claim is not read as stronger than the design supports.

cards.headline: Synthesis: radial access wins on net clinical events and access complications across two large trials — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: radial access wins on net clinical events and access complications across two large trials — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RIVAL 2011 (7,021 ACS patients) and MATRIX 2015 (8,404 ACS patients).
cards.result: Across 15,425 randomised ACS patients, radial access consistently reduced access-site vascular complications and major bleeding, and reduced net adverse clinical events in the trial powered for that composite; a standalone mortality advantage rests on one component analysis in MATRIX and was absent in RIVAL. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the composites embed death, MI and stroke (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate contemporary femoral practice refinements (ultrasound guidance, micropuncture); the access-complication gap may be narrower today, and neither trial was masked for the operator.

shelves.title: Bivalirudin versus heparin monotherapy in myocardial infarction treated with PCI (VALIDATE-SWEDEHEART)
shelves.question: In patients with STEMI or NSTEMI undergoing PCI, does bivalirudin, compared with heparin monotherapy, reduce the composite of death, MI, and major bleeding at 180 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Hemorrhage · Heparin · Hirudins · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Peptide Fragments · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists · Recombinant Proteins
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death and MI): In the largest and most contemporary test — VALIDATE-SWEDEHEART (6,006 patients with STEMI or NSTEMI undergoing PCI with potent P2Y12 inhibitors, predominantly radial access, no planned glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors) — the composite of death, MI or major bleeding at 180 days occurred in 12.3% on bivalirudin versus 12.8% on heparin (HR 0.96 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.10; P=0.54), with no component differing: death 2.9% vs 2.8%, MI 2.0% vs 2.4%, major bleeding 8.6% vs 8.6%. A single very large trial with a tight interval around no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for modern practice as tested. The earlier contested literature (HEAT-PPCI favouring heparin; the MATRIX bivalirudin comparison) was run under different background therapy and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded; the MATRIX access trial is carded on Shelf #1530.

cards.headline: VALIDATE-SWEDEHEART 2017: bivalirudin did not lower death, MI or major bleeding versus heparin alone (12.3% vs 12.8% at 180 days)
cards.summary: VALIDATE-SWEDEHEART 2017: bivalirudin did not lower death, MI or major bleeding versus heparin alone (12.3% vs 12.8% at 180 days)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, registry-based, open-label clinical trial (Sweden)
cards.people: 6,006 patients with STEMI (3,005) or NSTEMI (3,001) undergoing PCI and receiving a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor, prasugrel, or cangrelor) without planned glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, randomly assigned to bivalirudin or heparin during PCI, performed predominantly via radial access. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 180 days, a primary end-point event (death from any cause, MI, or major bleeding) had occurred in 369 of 3,004 (12.3%) bivalirudin patients versus 383 of 3,002 (12.8%) heparin patients (HR 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.83 to 1.10; P=0.54), consistent between STEMI and NSTEMI and across major subgroups. MI occurred in 2.0% versus 2.4% (HR 0.84 relative), major bleeding in 8.6% and 8.6% (HR 1.00 relative), definite stent thrombosis in 0.4% versus 0.7% (HR 0.54 relative; P=0.09), and death in 2.9% versus 2.8% (HR 1.05 relative; P=0.76).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and registry-based, and set in near-universal radial access with potent P2Y12 cover — the null answers the modern-practice question; it does not rewind the earlier femoral-era, GP IIb/IIIa-era trials in which bivalirudin showed bleeding advantages.
cards.source: Erlinge D et al. Bivalirudin versus Heparin Monotherapy in Myocardial Infarction. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28844201. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02311231; EudraCT 2012-005260-10, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Routine manual thrombus aspiration in STEMI (TASTE and TOTAL)
shelves.question: In patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI, does routine manual thrombus aspiration before PCI, compared with PCI alone, reduce cardiovascular death and related hard outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Coronary Thrombosis · Electrocardiography · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Suction · Thrombectomy · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality and stroke outcomes): Two large randomised trials agree there is no benefit. TASTE (7,244 STEMI patients) found 30-day all-cause mortality of 2.8% with thrombus aspiration versus 3.0% with PCI alone (HR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.22; P=0.63). TOTAL (10,732 randomised; 10,064 in the 1-year analysis) found its primary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure) identical at 1 year (8% vs 8%; HR 1.00 relative, 0.87 to 1.15), cardiovascular death 4% vs 4%, and a significant excess of stroke with aspiration (1.2% vs 0.7%; HR 1.66 relative, 1.10 to 2.51; P=0.015). Two large concordant nulls with a harm signal on stroke carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The carded TOTAL report is the trial's 1-year follow-up; its abstract states the 180-day primary outcome was likewise null.

cards.headline: TASTE 2013: routine thrombus aspiration did not reduce 30-day mortality in STEMI (2.8% vs 3.0%)
cards.summary: TASTE 2013: routine thrombus aspiration did not reduce 30-day mortality in STEMI (2.8% vs 3.0%)
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised, controlled, open-label, registry-based trial (Sweden)
cards.people: 7,244 patients with STEMI undergoing PCI, enrolled through the national Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry, randomly assigned to manual thrombus aspiration followed by PCI (3,621) or PCI only (3,623), with end points evaluated through national registries and no patients lost to follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause at 30 days occurred in 103 of 3,621 (2.8%) patients in the thrombus-aspiration group versus 110 of 3,623 (3.0%) in the PCI-only group (HR 0.94 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.72 to 1.22; P=0.63). Hospitalisation for recurrent MI was 0.5% versus 0.9% (HR 0.61 relative; P=0.09) and stent thrombosis 0.2% versus 0.5% (HR 0.47 relative; P=0.06); there was no significant difference in stroke or neurological complications at discharge (P=0.87), and results were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including thrombus burden and pre-PCI flow.
cards.watchOut: Registry-based and open-label with a 30-day horizon: TASTE alone leaves the longer term open — which is why the TOTAL 1-year card sits beside it.
cards.source: Fröbert O et al. Thrombus aspiration during ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23991656. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01093404, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: TOTAL 1-year follow-up 2016: no benefit on the cardiovascular composite (8% vs 8%) and more strokes with aspiration (1.2% vs 0.7%)
cards.summary: TOTAL 1-year follow-up 2016: no benefit on the cardiovascular composite (8% vs 8%) and more strokes with aspiration (1.2% vs 0.7%)
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, investigator-initiated trial — 1-year follow-up report of the TOTAL trial (87 hospitals, 20 countries)
cards.people: 10,732 patients with STEMI enrolled within 12 hours of symptom onset and randomly assigned to routine manual thrombectomy with PCI (5,372) or PCI alone (5,360); after exclusions of patients who did not undergo index PCI, the 1-year analysis population was 10,064 (5,035 thrombectomy; 5,029 PCI alone). Participants and investigators were not masked. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (cardiovascular death, MI, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure) at 1 year occurred in 395 of 5,035 (8%) thrombectomy patients versus 394 of 5,029 (8%) PCI-alone patients (HR 1.00 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.87 to 1.15; P=0.99). Cardiovascular death occurred in 179 (4%) versus 192 (4%) (HR 0.93 relative; P=0.48). The key safety outcome, stroke within 1 year, occurred in 60 (1.2%) thrombectomy patients versus 36 (0.7%) (HR 1.66 relative, 1.10 to 2.51; P=0.015). The report's background states the trial had shown no difference at 180 days in the same primary outcome, despite improvements in the surrogate outcomes of ST-segment resolution and distal embolisation.
cards.watchOut: This card is the trial's 1-year follow-up report, carded as such; the 180-day primary result it recaps was also null. The stroke excess is a safety outcome, not the primary end point — but it is significant, directionally consistent with catheter manipulation, and is the reason routine aspiration lost its recommendation.
cards.source: Jolly SS et al. Outcomes after thrombus aspiration for ST elevation myocardial infarction: 1-year follow-up of the prospective randomised TOTAL trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. shelves.title: Culprit-lesion-only versus multivessel PCI in cardiogenic shock with multivessel disease (CULPRIT-SHOCK)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI, multivessel disease, and cardiogenic shock, does culprit-lesion-only PCI (with optional staged revascularisation), compared with immediate multivessel PCI, reduce the composite of death and severe renal failure at 30 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Renal Insufficiency · Renal Replacement Therapy · Risk · Shock, Cardiogenic · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite is death-driven): One large definitive trial (CULPRIT-SHOCK, 706 patients with acute MI, multivessel disease and cardiogenic shock) found the 30-day composite of death or severe renal failure requiring renal-replacement therapy lower with culprit-lesion-only PCI (45.9% vs 55.4%; RR 0.83 relative, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.96; P=0.01), with death itself lower (RR 0.84 relative, 0.72 to 0.98; P=0.03) and renal-replacement therapy directionally lower (RR 0.71 relative, 0.49 to 1.03). A single trial, however practice-changing, caps at POSSIBLE on this library's scale. The topic draft printed absolute mortality rates (43.3% vs 51.6%) that do not appear in the record's abstract; the card prints the abstract's own figures only.

cards.headline: CULPRIT-SHOCK 2017: culprit-only PCI lowered the 30-day composite of death or dialysis (45.9% vs 55.4%) in MI with cardiogenic shock
cards.summary: CULPRIT-SHOCK 2017: culprit-only PCI lowered the 30-day composite of death or dialysis (45.9% vs 55.4%) in MI with cardiogenic shock
cards.people: 706 patients with multivessel disease, acute MI and cardiogenic shock randomly assigned to culprit-lesion-only PCI with the option of staged revascularisation of nonculprit lesions, or immediate multivessel PCI; the primary analysis included 344 and 341 patients per group. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 30 days, the composite primary end point of death or severe renal failure leading to renal-replacement therapy occurred in 158 of 344 (45.9%) patients in the culprit-lesion-only group versus 189 of 341 (55.4%) in the multivessel PCI group (RR 0.83 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.71 to 0.96; P=0.01) — an absolute difference of 9.5 percentage points. The relative risk of death was 0.84 (0.72 to 0.98; P=0.03) and of renal-replacement therapy 0.71 (0.49 to 1.03; P=0.07). Time to haemodynamic stabilisation, catecholamine measures, troponin T and creatine kinase levels, and rates of bleeding and stroke did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports death as a relative risk without the group mortality percentages; the absolute mortality rates quoted in the topic draft (43.3% vs 51.6%) come from beyond the abstract and are not carded. The result is a 30-day result; later crossover to staged revascularisation is part of the culprit-only strategy, not a contamination of it.

shelves.title: Intra-aortic balloon pump in MI complicated by cardiogenic shock (IABP-SHOCK II)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI and cardiogenic shock undergoing early revascularisation, does intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, compared with no balloon pump, reduce 30-day all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Coronary Artery Bypass · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Intra-Aortic Balloon Pumping · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Prospective Studies · Shock, Cardiogenic · Stents · Survival Rate · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): IABP-SHOCK II (600 patients with MI and cardiogenic shock, all planned for early revascularisation) found 30-day all-cause mortality of 39.7% with intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation versus 41.3% without (RR 0.96 relative, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.17; P=0.69), with no differences in haemodynamic stabilisation, ICU stay, lactate, catecholamine dose or renal function, and no safety penalty or benefit. The companion programme trial CRISP-AMI — a different population (anterior STEMI WITHOUT shock) and a surrogate primary outcome (MRI infarct size) — was likewise null (infarct size 42.1% vs 37.5% of LV mass). The mortality null in shock rests on IABP-SHOCK II; CRISP-AMI is carded as programme support and labelled by its own population. The topic draft's claim of 'none at 6-year follow-up' refers to a later report not pinned at build and is fenced in the synthesis.

cards.headline: IABP-SHOCK II 2012: balloon pump did not reduce 30-day mortality in MI with cardiogenic shock (39.7% vs 41.3%)
cards.summary: IABP-SHOCK II 2012: balloon pump did not reduce 30-day mortality in MI with cardiogenic shock (39.7% vs 41.3%)
cards.people: 600 patients with cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI, randomly assigned to intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation (301) or no counterpulsation (299); all were expected to undergo early revascularisation (PCI or bypass surgery) and best available medical therapy; 300 and 298 patients were analysed for the primary end point. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 30 days, 119 of 300 patients (39.7%) in the IABP group and 123 of 298 (41.3%) in the control group had died (RR 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.79 to 1.17; P=0.69). There were no significant differences in secondary end points or process measures (time to haemodynamic stabilisation, ICU length of stay, serum lactate, catecholamine dose and duration, renal function), nor in major bleeding (3.3% vs 4.4%), peripheral ischaemic complications (4.3% vs 3.4%), sepsis (15.7% vs 20.5%), or stroke (0.7% vs 1.7%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the confidence interval (0.79 to 1.17, relative) cannot exclude a modest benefit — but the point estimate sits on the null and every process measure agrees, which is why the field read this trial as closing the routine-use question.

cards.headline: CRISP-AMI 2011: balloon pump before PCI did not reduce infarct size in anterior STEMI without shock (42.1% vs 37.5% of LV mass)
cards.summary: CRISP-AMI 2011: balloon pump before PCI did not reduce infarct size in anterior STEMI without shock (42.1% vs 37.5% of LV mass)
cards.type: Open, multicentre, randomised controlled trial (30 sites, 9 countries)
cards.people: 337 patients with acute anterior STEMI WITHOUT cardiogenic shock, enrolled June 2009 to February 2011, randomly assigned to intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation initiated before primary PCI and continued at least 12 hours, versus primary PCI alone. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean infarct size by cardiac MRI at 3 to 5 days was 42.1% (95% CI 38.7 to 45.6) of LV mass with IABC plus PCI versus 37.5% (34.3 to 40.8) with PCI alone (difference 4.6 percentage points, −0.2 to 9.4; P=0.06) — numerically larger, not smaller, with the pump. At 30 days there were no significant differences in major vascular complications (4.3% vs 1.1%; P=0.09) or major bleeding/transfusion (3.1% vs 1.7%). By 6 months, 3 patients (1.9%) in the IABC group and 9 (5.2%) in the PCI-alone group had died (P=0.12).
cards.watchOut: A different question from the shelf's: no shock, a surrogate primary outcome, and a 6-month mortality count of 3 versus 9 patients that is far too small to read as a signal. The card supports the programme-level null; it does not bear on shock mortality. The record also notes the device strategy this trial's rationale rested on — infarct-size reduction seen in animal models — did not translate.

shelves.title: Early routine VA-ECMO in infarct-related cardiogenic shock (ECLS-SHOCK and ECMO-CS)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI and cardiogenic shock planned for revascularisation, does early extracorporeal life support (VA-ECMO), compared with usual care without routine ECLS, reduce 30-day all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation · Myocardial Infarction · Retrospective Studies · Risk · Shock, Cardiogenic · Treatment Outcome · Myocardial Revascularization
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcome): Two randomised trials of early routine VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock are concordantly null on mortality. ECLS-SHOCK (420 patients with acute MI and shock planned for early revascularisation) found 30-day all-cause mortality of 47.8% with early ECLS versus 49.0% without (RR 0.98 relative, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.19; P=0.81), with more moderate/severe bleeding (23.4% vs 9.6%; RR 2.44 relative) and more peripheral vascular complications (11.0% vs 3.8%). ECMO-CS (117 patients analysed, severe or rapidly deteriorating cardiogenic shock of mixed cause) found its composite primary end point not significantly different (63.8% vs 71.2%; HR 0.72 relative, 0.46 to 1.12) and 30-day mortality 50.0% versus 47.5%, with 39% of the conservative group crossing over to downstream VA-ECMO. Routine early VA-ECMO, as tested, does not reduce mortality and adds bleeding: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: ECLS-SHOCK 2023: early VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality in infarct shock (47.8% vs 49.0%) and doubled major bleeding
cards.summary: ECLS-SHOCK 2023: early VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality in infarct shock (47.8% vs 49.0%) and doubled major bleeding
cards.people: 420 patients with acute MI complicated by cardiogenic shock for whom early revascularisation was planned, randomly assigned to early ECLS plus usual medical treatment or usual treatment alone; 417 were included in the final analyses (209 ECLS; 208 control). cards.result: At 30 days, death from any cause occurred in 100 of 209 (47.8%) patients in the ECLS group and 102 of 208 (49.0%) in the control group (RR 0.98 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.80 to 1.19; P=0.81). Median duration of mechanical ventilation was 7 days with ECLS versus 5 days without. Moderate or severe bleeding occurred in 23.4% versus 9.6% (RR 2.44 relative, 1.50 to 3.95) and peripheral vascular complications warranting intervention in 11.0% versus 3.8% (RR 2.86 relative, 1.31 to 6.25).
cards.watchOut: The interval (0.80 to 1.19, relative) cannot exclude a moderate benefit, but the point estimate is the null and the harms are significant and mechanistically expected; this is the definitive infarct-shock trial the smaller ECMO-CS card complements.

cards.headline: ECMO-CS 2023: immediate VA-ECMO did not improve the 30-day composite versus a conservative strategy allowing downstream ECMO (63.8% vs 71.2%; mortality 50.0% vs 47.5%)
cards.summary: ECMO-CS 2023: immediate VA-ECMO did not improve the 30-day composite versus a conservative strategy allowing downstream ECMO (63.8% vs 71.2%; mortality 50.0% vs 47.5%)
cards.people: 122 patients with rapidly deteriorating or severe cardiogenic shock randomly assigned to immediate VA-ECMO or no immediate VA-ECMO; 117 were analysed (58 immediate; 59 conservative), and VA-ECMO was used downstream in 23 (39%) of the conservative group. Shock causes were mixed, not restricted to acute MI. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The composite primary end point (death from any cause, resuscitated circulatory arrest, or implementation of another mechanical circulatory support device at 30 days) occurred in 37 (63.8%) immediate-ECMO patients versus 42 (71.2%) conservative patients (HR 0.72 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.46 to 1.12; P=0.21). Thirty-day all-cause mortality was 50.0% versus 47.5% (risk difference 2.5 points, −15.6 to 20.7). Resuscitated cardiac arrest (10.3% vs 13.6%), serious adverse events (60.3% vs 61.0%), sepsis, pneumonia, stroke, leg ischaemia and bleeding did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Small, with a composite that counts starting another device as an event and 39% crossover to ECMO in the control arm — ECMO-CS tests immediate-versus-selective timing more than ECMO-versus-none, and its population is broader than infarct shock. It corroborates ECLS-SHOCK; it cannot substitute for it.

shelves.title: Microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) in STEMI-related cardiogenic shock (DanGer Shock)
shelves.question: In patients with STEMI and cardiogenic shock, does a microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) plus standard care, compared with standard care alone, reduce all-cause mortality at 180 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Heart-Assist Devices · Incidence · Shock, Cardiogenic · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction · Treatment Outcome · Assisted Circulation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality benefit claim): DanGer Shock (360 randomised; 355 analysed) is the first randomised trial of a mechanical support device to show a mortality benefit in infarct shock: death from any cause at 180 days occurred in 45.8% with the microaxial flow pump versus 58.5% with standard care (HR 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; P=0.04) — an absolute difference of 12.7 percentage points. The price was substantial: the composite safety end point (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, or worsening aortic regurgitation) occurred in 24.0% versus 6.2% (RR 4.74 relative), and renal-replacement therapy in 41.9% versus 26.7%. One trial of 355 analysed patients, with a P value of 0.04 and heavy harms, earns POSSIBLE — a real but fragile and costly benefit claim after the null device trials on Shelves #1534 and #1535.

cards.headline: DanGer Shock 2024: Impella CP lowered 180-day mortality in STEMI shock (45.8% vs 58.5%; HR 0.74) but quadrupled the composite of severe device-related harms
cards.summary: DanGer Shock 2024: Impella CP lowered 180-day mortality in STEMI shock (45.8% vs 58.5%; HR 0.74) but quadrupled the composite of severe device-related harms
cards.people: 360 patients with STEMI and cardiogenic shock underwent randomisation to a microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) plus standard care or standard care alone; 355 were included in the final analysis (179 pump; 176 standard care). The median age was 67 years, and 79.2% were men.
cards.result: Death from any cause at 180 days occurred in 82 of 179 (45.8%) patients in the pump group and 103 of 176 (58.5%) in the standard-care group (HR 0.74 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; P=0.04). A composite safety end-point event (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, or worsening aortic regurgitation) occurred in 43 patients (24.0%) versus 11 (6.2%) (RR 4.74 relative, 2.36 to 9.55). Renal-replacement therapy was administered to 75 (41.9%) pump patients versus 47 (26.7%) (RR 1.98 relative, 1.27 to 3.09).

shelves.title: FFR-guided complete revascularisation in STEMI with multivessel disease (DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI and Compare-Acute)
shelves.question: In patients with STEMI and multivessel disease after successful culprit PCI, does FFR-guided complete revascularisation, compared with culprit-lesion-only treatment, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Coronary Stenosis · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Myocardial Revascularization · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Postoperative Complications · Reoperation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death and MI): Two randomised trials of FFR-guided complete revascularisation after culprit PCI in STEMI both reduced their composites — DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI (627 patients: 13% vs 22%; HR 0.56 relative, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.83; P=0.004) and Compare-Acute (885 patients: 8 vs 21 events per 100 patients at 12 months; HR 0.35 relative, 0.22 to 0.55) — and in both the benefit was driven by fewer repeat revascularisations, with no significant difference in death or MI (Compare-Acute: death 1.4% vs 1.7%; MI 2.4% vs 4.7%, HR 0.50 relative, CI crossing 1). A revascularisation-driven composite earns POSSIBLE, not more. Build correction: the topic draft anchored this shelf on FAME (Tonino 2009, PMID 19144937), but FAME enrolled stable multivessel disease and tested FFR-guided lesion selection against angiography-guided PCI — it does not test this shelf's question and is fenced, not carded. The DANAMI-3 programme design paper (PMID 25965708) is likewise fenced; the carded report is the PRIMULTI primary publication. Angiography-guided complete revascularisation (COMPLETE) is a separate strategy and is not folded in.

cards.headline: DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI 2015: FFR-guided complete revascularisation cut the composite (13% vs 22%) — driven by repeat revascularisation, with no difference in death or reinfarction
cards.summary: DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI 2015: FFR-guided complete revascularisation cut the composite (13% vs 22%) — driven by repeat revascularisation, with no difference in death or reinfarction
cards.type: Open-label, randomised controlled trial (two university hospitals, Denmark)
cards.people: 627 patients with STEMI and one or more clinically significant stenoses beyond the infarct-related artery, enrolled March 2011 to February 2014 after successful PCI of the infarct-related artery, randomly allocated to no further invasive treatment (313) or complete FFR-guided revascularisation before discharge (314); median follow-up 27 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point (all-cause mortality, non-fatal reinfarction, or ischaemia-driven revascularisation of non-infarct-related lesions) occurred in 40 (13%) patients with complete revascularisation versus 68 (22%) with culprit-only treatment (HR 0.56 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.38 to 0.83; P=0.004). The authors state the effect was driven by significantly fewer repeat revascularisations, because all-cause mortality and non-fatal reinfarction did not differ between groups (the abstract does not print the component event rates, and none are supplied here).
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial whose winning component — ischaemia-driven revascularisation — is a clinician-mediated decision in an unblinded comparison; the hard components were null. The complete-revascularisation procedures were done before discharge, not necessarily during the index procedure, so the trial does not settle timing.

shelves.title: Early versus delayed invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS (TIMACS and VERDICT)
shelves.question: In patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes, does an early invasive strategy (angiography within 24 hours), compared with a delayed strategy (after 36 hours), reduce the composite of death, MI, and stroke at 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Angina Pectoris · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Bypass · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Risk · Stroke · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) overall / POSSIBLE benefit in highest-risk patients — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death, MI and stroke): TIMACS (3,031 NSTE-ACS patients; angiography at a median of 14 vs 50 hours) found no significant difference in death, MI or stroke at 6 months (9.6% early vs 11.3% delayed; HR 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.06; P=0.15), while its secondary composite including refractory ischaemia favoured early intervention (9.5% vs 12.9%; HR 0.72 relative) and a prespecified analysis showed benefit confined to the highest-risk third (HR 0.65 relative, 0.48 to 0.89; P=0.01 for heterogeneity). VERDICT (2,147 patients; angiography at 4.7 vs 61.6 hours; median follow-up 4.3 years) was likewise null overall (27.5% vs 29.5%; HR 0.92 relative, 0.78 to 1.08) with a significant interaction favouring very early treatment at GRACE score >140 (HR 0.81 relative, 0.67 to 1.01; interaction P=0.023). Two trials, the same shape: no overall benefit, a high-risk subgroup signal in both. Note VERDICT's primary composite differs from the shelf question's — it adds admissions for refractory ischaemia and heart failure and does not include stroke — disclosed on its card.

cards.headline: TIMACS 2009: early angiography did not significantly reduce death, MI or stroke at 6 months (9.6% vs 11.3%) — benefit confined to the highest-risk third
cards.summary: TIMACS 2009: early angiography did not significantly reduce death, MI or stroke at 6 months (9.6% vs 11.3%) — benefit confined to the highest-risk third
cards.people: 3,031 patients with acute coronary syndromes without ST-segment elevation, randomly assigned to routine early intervention (coronary angiography within 24 hours; performed in 97.6%, median 14 hours) or delayed intervention (angiography at 36 hours or later; performed in 95.7%, median 50 hours). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months the primary outcome (death, MI, or stroke) occurred in 9.6% of the early group versus 11.3% of the delayed group (HR 0.85 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.68 to 1.06; P=0.15). The prespecified secondary outcome of death, MI or refractory ischaemia occurred in 9.5% versus 12.9% (HR 0.72 relative, 0.58 to 0.89; P=0.003 — a 28% relative reduction). Prespecified analyses showed early intervention improved the primary outcome in the third of patients at highest risk (HR 0.65 relative, 0.48 to 0.89) but not in the two thirds at low-to-intermediate risk (HR 1.12 relative, 0.81 to 1.56; P=0.01 for heterogeneity).
cards.watchOut: The headline secondary outcome is won partly on refractory ischaemia — a softer component — and the high-risk finding, though prespecified, is a subgroup of a null trial; VERDICT's concordant interaction (next card) is what lifts it above a lone subgroup claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: timing within 1–3 days does not move hard outcomes overall; the highest-risk patients may gain — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: timing within 1–3 days does not move hard outcomes overall; the highest-risk patients may gain — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TIMACS 2009 (3,031 NSTE-ACS patients) and VERDICT 2018 (2,147 NSTE-ACS patients).
cards.result: Across both trials, moving angiography from ~50–62 hours to ~5–14 hours did not significantly reduce the primary composites in all-comers, and in both trials the only favourable signal sat in the highest-risk stratum with a significant interaction. shelves.title: Deferred stenting after initial reperfusion in STEMI (DANAMI-3-DEFER)
shelves.question: In patients with STEMI and restored flow after initial intervention, does deferred stent implantation (48 hours later), compared with conventional immediate stenting, improve clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Calcium Channel Blockers · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death and MI): DANAMI-3-DEFER (1,215 STEMI patients with stabilised flow in the infarct artery) found its primary composite — all-cause mortality, heart-failure admission, recurrent infarction, or unplanned target-vessel revascularisation over a median 42 months — in 17% with deferred stenting versus 18% with conventional immediate stenting (HR 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.29; P=0.92), with no difference in procedure-related complications (4% vs 5%). A completed trial with the point estimate dead on the null carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine deferral. The smaller earlier trials named in the topic draft (DEFER-STEMI, INNOVATION) tested microvascular surrogates and are fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

cards.headline: DANAMI-3-DEFER 2016: deferring the stent by 48 hours did not improve outcomes in STEMI (17% vs 18%; HR 0.99)
cards.summary: DANAMI-3-DEFER 2016: deferring the stent by 48 hours did not improve outcomes in STEMI (17% vs 18%; HR 0.99)
cards.type: Open-label, randomised controlled trial (four primary PCI centres, Denmark)
cards.people: 1,215 patients with STEMI (symptoms 12 hours or less) randomly assigned to standard primary PCI with immediate stent implantation (612) or deferred stent implantation 48 hours after the index procedure if stabilised flow could be obtained in the infarct-related artery (603); median follow-up 42 months; patients, investigators and treating clinicians were not masked. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Events comprising the primary end point (all-cause mortality, hospital admission for heart failure, recurrent infarction, or any unplanned revascularisation of the target vessel) occurred in 105 (17%) deferred-stent patients versus 109 (18%) standard-PCI patients (HR 0.99 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.76 to 1.29; P=0.92). Procedure-related MI, bleeding requiring transfusion or surgery, contrast-induced nephropathy, or stroke occurred in 27 (4%) deferred versus 28 (5%) conventional patients, with no significant differences.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the interval (0.76 to 1.29, relative) still admits a moderate effect either way — the LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) stamp leans on the point estimate of 0.99 and the completeness of follow-up, not on the interval alone. shelves.title: Antithrombotic strategy after PCI in atrial fibrillation (AUGUSTUS)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who have had an ACS or PCI and are taking a P2Y12 inhibitor, does apixaban (versus warfarin) and aspirin versus placebo change bleeding and ischaemic outcomes — i.e., is dual therapy without aspirin safer than triple therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Atrial Fibrillation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists · Pyrazoles · Pyridones · Vitamin K
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ischaemic outcomes include death, MI and stroke): AUGUSTUS (4,614 patients with AF and recent ACS or PCI, all on a P2Y12 inhibitor, 2×2 factorial, 6 months) answered both halves of the question. Apixaban caused less major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding than a vitamin K antagonist (10.5% vs 14.7%; HR 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.81) and less death or hospitalisation (23.5% vs 27.4%; HR 0.83 relative). Aspirin caused much more bleeding than placebo (16.1% vs 9.0%; HR 1.89 relative, 1.59 to 2.24) with no difference in death/hospitalisation or ischaemic events. Dual therapy with apixaban plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, without aspirin, is the trial's supported regimen — LIKELY, concordant with the wider four-trial programme fenced in the synthesis. This shelf is the post-PCI combination question, distinct from Shelf #719 (apixaban vs warfarin for AF generally).

cards.headline: AUGUSTUS 2019: apixaban bled less than warfarin (10.5% vs 14.7%) and aspirin bled far more than placebo (16.1% vs 9.0%) with no ischaemic gain
cards.summary: AUGUSTUS 2019: apixaban bled less than warfarin (10.5% vs 14.7%) and aspirin bled far more than placebo (16.1% vs 9.0%) with no ischaemic gain
cards.type: International randomised trial with a two-by-two factorial design (33 countries)
cards.people: 4,614 patients with atrial fibrillation who had an acute coronary syndrome or had undergone PCI and were planning to take a P2Y12 inhibitor, randomly assigned to apixaban or a vitamin K antagonist and, independently, to aspirin or matching placebo for 6 months; there were no significant interactions between the two randomisation factors. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding occurred in 10.5% of patients receiving apixaban versus 14.7% receiving a vitamin K antagonist (HR 0.69 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.58 to 0.81; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority), and in 16.1% receiving aspirin versus 9.0% receiving placebo (HR 1.89 relative, 1.59 to 2.24; P<0.001). Death or hospitalisation was lower with apixaban than with a vitamin K antagonist (23.5% vs 27.4%; HR 0.83 relative, 0.74 to 0.93; P=0.002) and similar between aspirin and placebo; ischaemic events were similar in both comparisons (the abstract does not print the ischaemic event rates, and none are supplied here).
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for bleeding, not for ischaemic events: 'no significant difference' in ischaemic outcomes is not proof of equivalence, and the aspirin comparison's ischaemic reassurance inherits that limit. Six months is the whole of the randomised window.
cards.source: Lopes RD et al. Antithrombotic Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndrome or PCI in Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30883055. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02415400, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: drop the aspirin, prefer apixaban — the factorial answer is LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: drop the aspirin, prefer apixaban — the factorial answer is LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: AUGUSTUS 2019 (4,614 patients with AF after ACS or PCI).
cards.result: Both randomisations point the same clinical direction: the bleeding burden of post-PCI antithrombotic therapy is bought mainly by aspirin and by warfarin, and removing them cost nothing measurable in ischaemic events over 6 months. The companion trials of the programme (WOEST, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI, ENTRUST-AF PCI) converge on dual therapy and are fenced here by name rather than carded; AUGUSTUS is the only one that isolated aspirin's contribution with a placebo. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Patients at very high stent-thrombosis risk were a small minority of such trials; the no-aspirin conclusion is a population average over 6 months, not a rule for every anatomy.

shelves.title: Clopidogrel versus aspirin as long-term monotherapy after PCI (HOST-EXAM)
shelves.question: In patients who have completed 6–18 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI without events, does clopidogrel monotherapy, compared with aspirin monotherapy, reduce the composite of death, MI, stroke, readmission for ACS, and major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin · Clopidogrel · Coronary Artery Disease · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Prospective Studies · Republic of Korea
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death, MI and stroke): HOST-EXAM (5,438 patients randomised in South Korea after 6–18 event-free months of dual antiplatelet therapy following drug-eluting stent PCI) found the composite of all-cause death, nonfatal MI, stroke, readmission for ACS, and BARC type ≥3 bleeding lower on clopidogrel monotherapy than aspirin monotherapy at 24 months (5.7% vs 7.7%; HR 0.73 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.0035). A single trial — open-label, single-country, in event-free survivors of the DAPT period — caps at POSSIBLE; the topic draft's 'borderline THIN' flag is answered by the stamp rather than a thin label, since the trial is large and its end point clinical. The record's abstract prints only the composite, so no claim is made here about which components drove it.

cards.headline: HOST-EXAM 2021: clopidogrel monotherapy beat aspirin monotherapy on the net composite after PCI (5.7% vs 7.7%; HR 0.73)
cards.summary: HOST-EXAM 2021: clopidogrel monotherapy beat aspirin monotherapy on the net composite after PCI (5.7% vs 7.7%; HR 0.73)
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre trial (37 sites, South Korea)
cards.people: 5,530 patients enrolled who had maintained dual antiplatelet therapy without clinical events for 6–18 months after PCI with drug-eluting stents; 5,438 were randomly assigned to clopidogrel 75 mg daily (2,710) or aspirin 100 mg daily (2,728) for 24 months, with primary-endpoint ascertainment completed in 5,338 (98.2%). Patients with any ischaemic or major bleeding complication during DAPT were excluded. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: During 24-month follow-up, the primary outcome (composite of all-cause death, nonfatal MI, stroke, readmission due to acute coronary syndrome, and BARC bleeding type 3 or greater) occurred in 152 (5.7%) clopidogrel patients versus 207 (7.7%) aspirin patients (HR 0.73 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.0035) — an absolute difference of 2.0 percentage points. The abstract reports the composite only; component event rates are not printed in the record and are not supplied here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country (South Korea — where CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, which blunt clopidogrel, are commoner than in European populations, making the direction of any transportability bias non-obvious), and restricted to patients who had already completed DAPT without events. The authors' abstract conclusion claims reductions in both thrombotic and bleeding outcomes; the record's abstract prints no component rates to verify that split, so this card claims the composite only.
cards.source: Koo BK et al. shelves.title: Gastroprotection with a PPI during dual antiplatelet therapy (COGENT)
shelves.question: In patients taking clopidogrel plus aspirin who are at risk of gastrointestinal complications, does adding omeprazole, compared with clopidogrel plus aspirin alone, reduce gastrointestinal events without increasing cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin · Cardiovascular Diseases · Clopidogrel · Coronary Artery Disease · Drug Interactions · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Omeprazole · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Ticlopidine
shelves.balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for gastrointestinal protection / MAYBE (weak evidence) for cardiovascular safety — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: cardiovascular events — death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal MI, revascularisation, or stroke — were a primary end point of this trial, so the shelf carries an event claim): COGENT (3,873 randomised; 3,761 analysed; terminated prematurely when the sponsor lost financing, against ~5,000 planned) found gastrointestinal events at 180 days markedly lower with omeprazole (1.1% vs 2.9%; HR 0.34 relative, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.63) and overt upper GI bleeding lower still (HR 0.13 relative). The cardiovascular end point did not differ (4.9% vs 5.7%; HR 0.99 relative, 0.68 to 1.44) — but the authors themselves state the results 'do not rule out a clinically meaningful difference in cardiovascular events', and with only 109 cardiovascular events in a stopped-early trial, they cannot. Hence the split: GI protection POSSIBLE (one trial, stopped early, but a large effect on its primary end point); cardiovascular safety only MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: COGENT 2010: omeprazole cut GI events on DAPT (1.1% vs 2.9%; HR 0.34); cardiovascular events did not differ (4.9% vs 5.7%) in a trial stopped early
cards.summary: COGENT 2010: omeprazole cut GI events on DAPT (1.1% vs 2.9%; HR 0.34); cardiovascular events did not differ (4.9% vs 5.7%) in a trial stopped early
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial (fixed-dose clopidogrel/omeprazole combination vs clopidogrel, both with aspirin) — terminated prematurely
cards.people: 3,873 patients with an indication for dual antiplatelet therapy randomly assigned to clopidogrel combined with omeprazole or with placebo, in addition to aspirin; 3,761 were included in analyses, against a planned enrolment of about 5,000. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 180 days, the primary gastrointestinal end point (overt or occult bleeding, symptomatic gastroduodenal ulcers or erosions, obstruction, or perforation) occurred in 1.1% with omeprazole versus 2.9% with placebo (HR 0.34 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.18 to 0.63; P<0.001), with overt upper GI bleeding also reduced (HR 0.13 relative, 0.03 to 0.56). The primary cardiovascular end point (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal MI, revascularisation, or stroke) occurred in 109 patients overall: 4.9% with omeprazole versus 5.7% with placebo (HR 0.99 relative, 0.68 to 1.44; P=0.96), with no significant heterogeneity in high-risk subgroups. Serious adverse events did not differ significantly; diarrhoea was increased with omeprazole. The trial was terminated prematurely when the sponsor lost financing.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion contains the shelf's central caveat verbatim in substance: no apparent cardiovascular interaction, but the data do not rule out a clinically meaningful difference. Early termination for a financing failure (not for efficacy or futility) truncates both end points; the GI win and the CV uncertainty are both products of the same shortened trial.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Clopidogrel with or without omeprazole in coronary artery disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20925534. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00557921, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Platelet-function-guided escalation of antiplatelet therapy after PCI (GRAVITAS and ARCTIC)
shelves.question: In patients with high on-treatment platelet reactivity after PCI, does high-dose clopidogrel guided by platelet-function testing, compared with standard-dose clopidogrel, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stent thrombosis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Cardiovascular Diseases · Clopidogrel · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Platelet Activation · Platelet Aggregation · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Platelet Function Tests · Prospective Studies · Risk · Thrombosis · Ticlopidine
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include cardiovascular death and MI): Two randomised trials of test-guided antiplatelet adjustment are concordantly null. GRAVITAS (2,214 patients with high on-treatment platelet reactivity after drug-eluting stent PCI) found doubling clopidogrel (150 mg daily) produced an identical primary event rate to standard dosing (2.3% vs 2.3% at 6 months; HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.76) despite a real pharmacodynamic effect (persistently high reactivity at 30 days 40% vs 62%). ARCTIC (2,440 patients scheduled for coronary stenting) found a monitoring-and-adjustment strategy no better than conventional care — primary composite 34.6% vs 31.1% at 1 year (HR 1.13 relative, 0.98 to 1.29), numerically worse. The biomarker predicts events; acting on it does not prevent them: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The wider programme (ANTARCTIC, TAILOR-PCI) is fenced in the synthesis.

cards.headline: GRAVITAS 2011: high-dose clopidogrel in patients with high platelet reactivity changed the test result but not the outcomes (2.3% vs 2.3%)
cards.summary: GRAVITAS 2011: high-dose clopidogrel in patients with high platelet reactivity changed the test result but not the outcomes (2.3% vs 2.3%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-control trial (83 centres, North America)
cards.people: 2,214 patients with high on-treatment platelet reactivity 12 to 24 hours after PCI with drug-eluting stents, randomly assigned to high-dose clopidogrel (600 mg initial dose, then 150 mg daily; 1,109) or standard-dose clopidogrel (75 mg daily; 1,105) for 6 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, the primary end point (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal MI, or stent thrombosis) occurred in 25 of 1,109 (2.3%) high-dose patients and 25 of 1,105 (2.3%) standard-dose patients (HR 1.01 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.58 to 1.76; P=0.97). Severe or moderate (GUSTO) bleeding was not increased (1.4% vs 2.3%; HR 0.59 relative; P=0.10). Pharmacodynamically the strategy worked: high-dose clopidogrel gave a 22-percentage-point absolute reduction in persistently high on-treatment reactivity at 30 days (40% vs 62%; P<0.001) — without any clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: The event rate was low (2.3%) and the interval (0.58 to 1.76, relative) wide, so GRAVITAS alone cannot exclude a modest effect; ARCTIC's concordant null in a broader strategy is what firms the shelf up. The trial also answers only the dose-doubling response, not switching to a stronger P2Y12 inhibitor.
cards.source: Price MJ et al. Standard- vs high-dose clopidogrel based on platelet function testing after percutaneous coronary intervention: the GRAVITAS randomized trial. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21406646. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00645918, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ARCTIC 2012: a platelet-monitoring and drug-adjustment strategy did not improve outcomes after stenting (34.6% vs 31.1%)
cards.summary: ARCTIC 2012: a platelet-monitoring and drug-adjustment strategy did not improve outcomes after stenting (34.6% vs 31.1%)
cards.people: 2,440 patients scheduled for coronary stenting randomly assigned to platelet-function monitoring with drug adjustment in poor responders, or to a conventional strategy without monitoring; in the monitoring group, high platelet reactivity on clopidogrel (34.5% of patients) or aspirin (7.6%) triggered additional clopidogrel, prasugrel or aspirin boluses plus glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors periprocedurally, with later outpatient re-testing. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point (death, MI, stent thrombosis, stroke, or urgent revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 34.6% of the monitoring group versus 31.1% of the conventional group (HR 1.13 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.98 to 1.29; P=0.10). The main secondary end point (stent thrombosis or any urgent revascularisation) occurred in 4.9% versus 4.6% (HR 1.06 relative; P=0.77), and major bleeding did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The primary composite is dominated by urgent revascularisation and periprocedural events in an elective-stenting population (hence the 31–35% rates) — a different event mix from GRAVITAS's post-PCI high-reactivity population; the two trials nonetheless agree that acting on the assay does not improve outcomes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: measuring platelet reactivity and acting on it does not prevent events — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: measuring platelet reactivity and acting on it does not prevent events — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: GRAVITAS 2011 (2,214 patients with high on-treatment reactivity) and ARCTIC 2012 (2,440 stenting patients).
cards.result: The guided-escalation idea failed in both its forms — fixed dose-doubling for assay-positive patients, and a full monitor-and-adjust strategy — while the assay itself demonstrably changed (GRAVITAS pharmacodynamics). Later programme trials (ANTARCTIC in the elderly; TAILOR-PCI, genotype- rather than function-guided) are fenced here by name; the function-guided question is answered by the two carded trials. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: A null for guided ESCALATION is not a null for platelet testing's prognostic value, nor for unguided use of more potent P2Y12 inhibitors after ACS, which has its own trial evidence elsewhere.

shelves.title: Vorapaxar for secondary prevention after MI (TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 and TRACER)
shelves.question: In patients with prior MI or peripheral artery disease on standard antiplatelet therapy, does adding the PAR-1 antagonist vorapaxar, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brain Ischemia · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lactones · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Pyridines · Retreatment · Risk · Secondary Prevention · Stroke
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY benefit-with-harm in stable secondary prevention / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, with harm) in ACS — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, benefit and harm both on death/MI/stroke territory): TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 (26,449 patients with prior MI, ischaemic stroke, or PAD) found vorapaxar reduced cardiovascular death, MI or stroke at 3 years (9.3% vs 10.5%; HR 0.87 relative, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.94) — an absolute reduction of 1.2 points — while increasing moderate or severe bleeding (4.2% vs 2.5%; HR 1.66 relative) and intracranial haemorrhage (1.0% vs 0.5%); the data and safety monitoring board stopped treatment in the prior-stroke subgroup for ICH risk. TRACER (12,944 patients with NSTE-ACS, follow-up terminated early after a safety review) found no significant reduction in its primary composite (2-year rates 18.5% vs 19.9%; HR 0.92 relative, 0.85 to 1.01; P=0.07) with more major bleeding (7.2% vs 5.2%) and a threefold ICH excess (1.1% vs 0.2%; HR 3.39 relative). The shelf question names prior MI or PAD; the trial's stroke-history stratum is disclosed on the card, since its early discontinuation is part of the record.

cards.headline: TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 2012: vorapaxar reduced cardiovascular death, MI or stroke (9.3% vs 10.5%) but raised major bleeding (4.2% vs 2.5%) and intracranial haemorrhage (1.0% vs 0.5%)
cards.summary: TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 2012: vorapaxar reduced cardiovascular death, MI or stroke (9.3% vs 10.5%) but raised major bleeding (4.2% vs 2.5%) and intracranial haemorrhage (1.0% vs 0.5%)
cards.people: 26,449 patients with a history of myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, or peripheral arterial disease, randomly assigned to vorapaxar 2.5 mg daily or matching placebo on standard therapy, followed for a median of 30 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 3 years, the primary end point (death from cardiovascular causes, MI, or stroke) occurred in 1,028 patients (9.3%) on vorapaxar versus 1,176 (10.5%) on placebo (HR 0.87 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.80 to 0.94; P<0.001). The wider composite including recurrent ischaemia leading to revascularisation occurred in 11.2% versus 12.4% (HR 0.88 relative). Moderate or severe bleeding occurred in 4.2% versus 2.5% (HR 1.66 relative, 1.43 to 1.93; P<0.001), and intracranial haemorrhage in 1.0% versus 0.5% (P<0.001). After 2 years, the data and safety monitoring board recommended discontinuing study treatment in patients with a history of stroke because of the intracranial haemorrhage risk.
cards.watchOut: Benefit and harm are the same size order: roughly 12 fewer primary events and 17 more moderate/severe bleeds (including 5 more intracranial haemorrhages) per 1,000 treated over 3 years. The trial's qualifying populations included prior stroke — excluded from the drug's eventual use — and the headline composite pools the MI, stroke and PAD strata.

cards.headline: TRACER 2012: in acute coronary syndromes vorapaxar did not significantly reduce the primary composite (18.5% vs 19.9%) and tripled intracranial haemorrhage (1.1% vs 0.2%)
cards.summary: TRACER 2012: in acute coronary syndromes vorapaxar did not significantly reduce the primary composite (18.5% vs 19.9%) and tripled intracranial haemorrhage (1.1% vs 0.2%)
cards.type: Multinational, double-blind, randomised trial — follow-up terminated early after a safety review
cards.people: 12,944 patients with acute coronary syndromes without ST-segment elevation, randomly assigned to vorapaxar or placebo added to standard therapy; median follow-up 502 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point (death from cardiovascular causes, MI, stroke, recurrent ischaemia with rehospitalisation, or urgent coronary revascularisation) occurred in 1,031 of 6,473 vorapaxar patients versus 1,102 of 6,471 placebo patients (Kaplan-Meier 2-year rates 18.5% vs 19.9%; HR 0.92 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.85 to 1.01; P=0.07). The harder composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke occurred in 14.7% versus 16.4% (HR 0.89 relative, 0.81 to 0.98; P=0.02 — a secondary reading). Moderate and severe bleeding occurred in 7.2% versus 5.2% (HR 1.35 relative, 1.16 to 1.58) and intracranial haemorrhage in 1.1% versus 0.2% (HR 3.39 relative, 1.78 to 6.45).
cards.watchOut: Early termination after a safety review truncates the efficacy read; the significant hard-composite result (P=0.02) is not the primary end point and should not be quoted as the trial's verdict. In the acute setting — where patients are also loaded with dual antiplatelet therapy — the bleeding price was paid immediately.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real secondary-prevention benefit bought with bleeding, and a failed ACS trial — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real secondary-prevention benefit bought with bleeding, and a failed ACS trial — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 2012 (26,449 patients with stable atherosclerosis) and TRACER 2012 (12,944 patients with NSTE-ACS).
cards.result: Vorapaxar is the library's clearest benefit-harm equipoise case: in stable patients it prevents about as many ischaemic events as the serious bleeds it causes, with the intracranial-haemorrhage excess — and the prior-stroke discontinuation — deciding most real-world assessments; in acute coronary syndromes it did not significantly prevent events at all and bled more. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial supports vorapaxar in patients with prior stroke — the subgroup stopped for harm — and any summary quoting only the 0.87 hazard ratio without the 1.0% intracranial haemorrhage rate misrepresents the record.

shelves.title: Fondaparinux versus enoxaparin in acute coronary syndromes (OASIS-5 and OASIS-6)
shelves.question: In patients with non-ST-elevation ACS, does fondaparinux, compared with enoxaparin, achieve similar protection against death, MI, and refractory ischaemia with less major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina, Unstable/drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Anticoagulants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Enoxaparin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Fondaparinux · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Polysaccharides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Recurrence · Stroke · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death and MI): OASIS-5 (20,078 patients with ACS) found fondaparinux noninferior to enoxaparin on death, MI or refractory ischaemia at 9 days (5.8% vs 5.7%; HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13) with less than half the major bleeding (2.2% vs 4.1%; HR 0.52 relative; P<0.001) and significantly fewer deaths at 30 days (295 vs 352 patients; P=0.02) and 180 days (574 vs 638; P=0.05). The companion OASIS-6 trial — a different question, STEMI patients randomised against placebo/UFH usual care — found death or reinfarction reduced (9.7% vs 11.2% at 30 days; HR 0.86 relative), with the explicit exception of patients undergoing primary PCI, in whom there was no benefit. Equal ischaemic protection with half the bleeding in the head-to-head trial earns LIKELY.

cards.headline: OASIS-5 2006: fondaparinux matched enoxaparin on ischaemic events (5.8% vs 5.7%) with half the major bleeding (2.2% vs 4.1%) and fewer deaths
cards.summary: OASIS-5 2006: fondaparinux matched enoxaparin on ischaemic events (5.8% vs 5.7%) with half the major bleeding (2.2% vs 4.1%) and fewer deaths
cards.people: 20,078 patients with acute coronary syndromes randomly assigned to fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for a mean of six days, followed for up to six months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (death, MI, or refractory ischaemia at nine days) occurred in 579 fondaparinux patients (5.8%) versus 573 enoxaparin patients (5.7%) (HR 1.01 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13), satisfying the prespecified noninferiority criteria. Major bleeding at nine days occurred in 217 (2.2%) versus 412 (4.1%) (HR 0.52 relative; P<0.001), and the composite of the primary outcome plus major bleeding favoured fondaparinux (7.3% vs 9.0%; HR 0.81 relative). Deaths were fewer with fondaparinux at 30 days (295 vs 352 patients; P=0.02) and at 180 days (574 vs 638; P=0.05); the combined ischaemic outcome showed nonsignificant trends favouring fondaparinux at 30 days and at study end.
cards.watchOut: The authors' conclusion claims fondaparinux 'improves long term mortality' — the mortality difference is a secondary outcome of a trial whose primary ischaemic end point was a noninferiority tie, and the P values (0.02, 0.05) are unadjusted for the multiple looks; the card prints the counts so the claim can be weighed, and the bleeding advantage — the trial's robust finding — is the shelf's load-bearing result.
cards.source: Yusuf S et al. Comparison of fondaparinux and enoxaparin in acute coronary syndromes. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16537663. cards.headline: OASIS-6 2006: in STEMI, fondaparinux reduced death or reinfarction versus usual care (9.7% vs 11.2%) — except in primary PCI, where there was no benefit
cards.summary: OASIS-6 2006: in STEMI, fondaparinux reduced death or reinfarction versus usual care (9.7% vs 11.2%) — except in primary PCI, where there was no benefit
cards.people: 12,092 patients with acute ST-segment elevation MI randomly assigned to fondaparinux 2.5 mg once daily or control (placebo where unfractionated heparin was not indicated, or unfractionated heparin for up to 48 hours then placebo) for up to 8 days, enrolled September 2003 to January 2006. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death or reinfarction at 30 days occurred in 585 of 6,036 (9.7%) fondaparinux patients versus 677 of 6,056 (11.2%) controls (HR 0.86 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 0.96; P=0.008), an absolute reduction of 1.5 percentage points, with benefits present at 9 days and at study end and mortality significantly reduced throughout. There was, however, no benefit in patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention; benefits were observed in those receiving thrombolytic therapy (HR 0.79 relative) and those receiving no reperfusion therapy (HR 0.80 relative). Severe bleeds tended to be fewer with fondaparinux (61 vs 79; P=0.13), with significantly fewer cardiac tamponades (28 vs 48; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A different comparison from this shelf's question: control was placebo or short-course UFH, not enoxaparin, and the population was STEMI, not NSTE-ACS. Its negative primary-PCI stratum is the clinically vital caveat — fondaparinux's wins sit with lytic-treated and non-reperfused patients.

cards.summary: Synthesis: same ischaemic protection, half the bleeding in the head-to-head trial — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OASIS-5 2006 (20,078 ACS patients) and OASIS-6 2006 (12,092 STEMI patients).
cards.result: The OASIS programme established fondaparinux as the safer default anticoagulant for ACS managed without immediate primary PCI: noninferior ischaemic protection, a 1.9-point absolute reduction in major bleeding, and concordant mortality findings in both trials. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate routine radial access and contemporary DAPT; absolute bleeding rates have fallen since, but the relative comparison is the evidence and it is one-directional.

shelves.title: Bridging anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation patients interrupting warfarin for a procedure (BRIDGE and PERIOP2)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who need to interrupt warfarin for an elective procedure, does forgoing bridging anticoagulation, compared with low-molecular-weight heparin bridging, prevent arterial thromboembolism as well while causing less bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Double-Blind Method · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Hemorrhage · Heparin, Low-Molecular-Weight · Humans · Male · Perioperative Period · Postoperative Complications · Thromboembolism · Warfarin
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the thromboembolism outcomes include stroke): BRIDGE (1,884 patients with AF interrupting warfarin for an elective procedure, double-blind) found forgoing bridging noninferior for arterial thromboembolism (0.4% no-bridging vs 0.3% bridging; risk difference 0.1 points, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.8) and superior for major bleeding (1.3% vs 3.2%; RR 0.41 relative, 0.20 to 0.78). PERIOP2 (1,471 patients with AF or mechanical heart valves) tested the postoperative half of bridging and likewise found no thromboembolism benefit (1.0% dalteparin vs 1.2% placebo) and no significant bleeding difference (1.3% vs 2.0%). Two double-blind trials agree there is nothing to buy with bridging in these populations: LIKELY.

cards.headline: BRIDGE 2015: skipping bridging was noninferior for thromboembolism (0.4% vs 0.3%) and halved major bleeding (1.3% vs 3.2%)
cards.summary: BRIDGE 2015: skipping bridging was noninferior for thromboembolism (0.4% vs 0.3%) and halved major bleeding (1.3% vs 3.2%)
cards.people: 1,884 patients with atrial fibrillation whose warfarin was interrupted for an elective operation or invasive procedure, randomly assigned after interruption to bridging with low-molecular-weight heparin (dalteparin 100 IU/kg twice daily; 934) or matching placebo (950), from 3 days before until 24 hours before the procedure and for 5 to 10 days after; warfarin was stopped 5 days before and resumed within 24 hours after; follow-up 30 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Arterial thromboembolism (stroke, systemic embolism, or transient ischaemic attack) occurred in 0.4% of the no-bridging group and 0.3% of the bridging group (risk difference 0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.8; P=0.01 for noninferiority). Major bleeding occurred in 1.3% versus 3.2% (RR 0.41 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.20 to 0.78; P=0.005 for superiority).
cards.watchOut: Event rates were very low (0.3–0.4%), so the noninferiority statement is about absolute differences under 1 point in a mostly moderate-risk AF population; patients with mechanical valves and the highest-risk features were not BRIDGE's population — PERIOP2 (next card) covers mechanical valves for the postoperative question only.
