cards.headline: PERIOP2 2021: postoperative dalteparin bridging did not prevent major thromboembolism in AF or mechanical-valve patients (1.0% vs 1.2%)
cards.summary: PERIOP2 2021: postoperative dalteparin bridging did not prevent major thromboembolism in AF or mechanical-valve patients (1.0% vs 1.2%)
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, randomised controlled trial (10 thrombosis research sites, Canada and India)
cards.people: 1,471 patients aged 18 or older with atrial fibrillation or mechanical heart valves who required temporary interruption of warfarin for a procedure, randomly assigned AFTER the procedure to dalteparin bridging (821) or placebo (650); outcomes assessed within 90 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Major thromboembolism (stroke, TIA, proximal DVT, pulmonary embolism, MI, peripheral embolism, or vascular death) within 90 days occurred in 1.0% (8 events in 820 patients) on dalteparin versus 1.2% (8 events in 650) on placebo (P=0.64; risk difference −0.3 points, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.8). Major bleeding occurred in 1.3% (11 of 820) versus 2.0% (13 of 650) (P=0.32). Results were consistent for the atrial fibrillation and mechanical heart valve groups.
cards.watchOut: PERIOP2 randomised only the postoperative limb of bridging (pre-procedure management was not its randomised question) and accrued few events (8 per arm) over a 2007–2016 enrolment; it corroborates BRIDGE's direction rather than independently settling the question, and its bleeding rates run opposite to BRIDGE's without significance.

shelves.question: In patients on warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator surgery, does continuing the anticoagulant, compared with interruption (with heparin bridging for warfarin), reduce clinically significant device-pocket haematoma?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY that continued warfarin beats heparin bridging / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for continued versus interrupted DOAC: The two programme trials answer different halves of peri-device anticoagulation. BRUISE CONTROL-1 (681 patients analysed, annual thromboembolic risk ≥5%) found clinically significant device-pocket haematoma in 3.5% with continued warfarin versus 16.0% with heparin bridging (RR 0.19 relative, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.36) — the trial was stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis because the difference was so large. BRUISE CONTROL-2 (662 patients with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 on a DOAC) found haematoma rates identical with continued versus interrupted DOAC (2.1% vs 2.1%; P=0.97), with complications uncommon (one stroke and one symptomatic pericardial effusion in each arm). Not Tier C: the claim is pocket haematoma, not death/MI/stroke.

cards.headline: BRUISE CONTROL-1 2013: operating on continued warfarin cut pocket haematoma five-fold versus heparin bridging (3.5% vs 16.0%)
cards.summary: BRUISE CONTROL-1 2013: operating on continued warfarin cut pocket haematoma five-fold versus heparin bridging (3.5% vs 16.0%)
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial — terminated early on data and safety monitoring board recommendation after the second prespecified interim analysis
cards.people: Patients with an annual risk of thromboembolic events of 5% or more undergoing pacemaker or ICD surgery, randomly assigned to continued warfarin or bridging therapy with heparin; 343 (continued warfarin) and 338 (bridging) patients were analysed for the primary outcome. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinically significant device-pocket haematoma (necessitating prolonged hospitalisation, interruption of anticoagulation, or further surgery) occurred in 12 of 343 (3.5%) patients in the continued-warfarin group versus 54 of 338 (16.0%) in the heparin-bridging group (RR 0.19 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.10 to 0.36; P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 12.5 percentage points. Major surgical and thromboembolic complications were rare and did not differ significantly: one cardiac tamponade and one MI in the bridging group, one stroke and one TIA in the continued-warfarin group.
cards.watchOut: Early termination at an interim analysis can exaggerate effect sizes, but a 12.5-point absolute gap with an interval of 0.10 to 0.36 (relative) leaves the direction in no doubt; this is the trial that rewrote device-surgery guidance toward continuing warfarin.
cards.source: Birnie DH et al. Pacemaker or defibrillator surgery without interruption of anticoagulation. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23659733. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00800137, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: BRUISE CONTROL-2 2018: continuing a DOAC through device surgery gave the same haematoma rate as interrupting it (2.1% vs 2.1%)
cards.summary: BRUISE CONTROL-2 2018: continuing a DOAC through device surgery gave the same haematoma rate as interrupting it (2.1% vs 2.1%)
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial (primary outcome blindly evaluated)
cards.people: 662 patients with atrial fibrillation and CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more undergoing device surgery, randomly assigned to continued (328) or interrupted (334) direct oral anticoagulant (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, or apixaban); median time between pre- and post-operative DOAC doses was 12 hours in the continued arm and 72 hours in the interrupted arm. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinically significant device-pocket haematoma (resulting in re-operation, interruption of anticoagulation, or prolonged hospital stay) occurred in 7 of 328 (2.1%; 95% CI 0.9 to 4.3) patients in the continued arm and 7 of 334 (2.1%; 0.9 to 4.3) in the interrupted arm (P=0.97). Complications were uncommon and included one stroke and one symptomatic pericardial effusion in each arm. The authors conclude either strategy might be reasonable in patients similar to those enrolled.
cards.watchOut: The record's databank fields carry no registry ID for this trial (a DOI only) — stated here rather than filled from elsewhere. With 7 events per arm, the trial excludes large differences but not small ones; it does not test bridging for DOACs, which neither arm used.
cards.source: Birnie DH et al. Continued vs. interrupted direct oral anticoagulants at the time of device surgery, in patients with moderate to high risk of arterial thrombo-embolic events (BRUISE CONTROL-2). European heart journal. 2018. PMID: 30462279. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: never bridge warfarin for device surgery; for DOACs, continuing or briefly interrupting are equivalent — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: never bridge warfarin for device surgery; for DOACs, continuing or briefly interrupting are equivalent — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BRUISE CONTROL-1 2013 (681 patients analysed, warfarin) and BRUISE CONTROL-2 2018 (662 patients, DOACs).
cards.result: The programme's combined message is that peri-device bleeding is driven by heparin exposure, not by the oral anticoagulant: continued warfarin beat bridging by 12.5 absolute points, and continued DOAC matched interrupted DOAC exactly. BRUISE CONTROL-1's PMID, unpinned in the topic draft, was pinned and verified at build (PMID 23659733).
cards.watchOut: Both trials concern elective pacemaker/ICD procedures; extraction and lead-revision surgery carry higher bleeding risk and were not this programme's population.

shelves.title: Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in high-risk triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (TRAPS)
shelves.question: In patients with high-risk (triple-positive) antiphospholipid syndrome, is rivaroxaban, compared with warfarin, noninferior for preventing thromboembolic events, major bleeding, and vascular death?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticoagulants · Antiphospholipid Syndrome · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Humans · Italy · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Rivaroxaban · Thromboembolism · Treatment Outcome · Warfarin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, thromboembolism and vascular death outcomes): TRAPS was a small open-label noninferiority trial (120 triple-positive APS patients, Italy) terminated prematurely because of excess events on rivaroxaban: the composite of thromboembolic events, major bleeding and vascular death occurred in 11 of 59 (19%) rivaroxaban patients versus 2 of 61 (3%) on warfarin over a mean follow-up of 569 days; thromboembolic events were 7 (12%) versus 0 — four ischaemic strokes and three MIs, all arterial, all on rivaroxaban — and major bleeding 4 (7%) versus 2 (3%); no deaths occurred. The two-year post-closure follow-up (115 patients) again found more events in the handful who stayed on DOACs, but that report is no longer a randomised comparison (patients were advised to switch to warfarin; only six remained on a DOAC) and is carded as supportive follow-up, not as a second trial. One small stopped trial earns POSSIBLE (harm) — directionally stark, numerically fragile. Build note: the primary Blood 2018 report, unpinnable by search in the topic-drafting pass, was pinned by title at build (PMID 30002145) and is the anchor card; the follow-up report pinned in the draft is the second card.

cards.headline: TRAPS primary report 2018: rivaroxaban caused excess arterial events in triple-positive APS (composite 19% vs 3%) and the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: TRAPS primary report 2018: rivaroxaban caused excess arterial events in triple-positive APS (composite 19% vs 3%) and the trial was stopped early
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre noninferiority trial with blinded end-point adjudication (Italy) — terminated prematurely
cards.people: 120 patients with thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome who were triple positive for lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies of the same isotype, randomly assigned to rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily (15 mg if kidney function required; 59 patients) or warfarin (INR target 2.5; 61 patients); mean follow-up 569 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The trial was terminated prematurely after enrolment of 120 patients because of an excess of events in the rivaroxaban arm. Outcome events (thromboembolic events, major bleeding, or vascular death) occurred in 11 (19%) rivaroxaban patients versus 2 (3%) warfarin patients. Thromboembolic events occurred in 7 (12%) on rivaroxaban — 4 ischaemic strokes and 3 myocardial infarctions — versus none on warfarin. Major bleeding occurred in 4 (7%) versus 2 (3%). No death was reported. The authors conclude rivaroxaban showed no benefit and excess risk in this high-risk population.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (with blinded adjudication), small, and stopped early — early-stopped harm trials can overstate effects, and 13 total events is a thin base; but the events were concentrated exactly where APS biology predicts failure (arterial thrombosis), which is why guidelines moved against DOACs in triple-positive APS on this evidence.
cards.source: Pengo V et al. Rivaroxaban vs warfarin in high-risk patients with antiphospholipid syndrome. Blood. 2018. PMID: 30002145. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02157272, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: TRAPS two-year post-closure follow-up: events remained concentrated in patients who stayed on DOACs — a non-randomised follow-up, carded as support only
cards.summary: TRAPS two-year post-closure follow-up: events remained concentrated in patients who stayed on DOACs — a non-randomised follow-up, carded as support only
cards.type: Two-year follow-up report of the TRAPS trial cohort after trial closure (14 centres, Italy)
cards.people: Of the 120 randomised patients, 115 were available for follow-up from January 2018 to January 2020; after the trial's premature closure, patients on rivaroxaban were advised to switch to warfarin — 109 were on warfarin during follow-up and only 6 remained on direct oral anticoagulants. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Outcome events occurred in 2 of 6 (33.3%) patients who remained on DOACs (one on dabigatran, one on rivaroxaban; both thromboembolic) versus 6 of 109 (5.7%) patients on warfarin (HR 6.9 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.4 to 34.5; P=0.018); for thromboembolic events the hazard ratio was 13.3 relative (2.2 to 79.9). The topic draft dated this report 2020; the record is the Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2021.
cards.watchOut: This is NOT a randomised comparison: treatment after closure was by advice and choice, the DOAC group is six patients, and two events among six cannot carry a hazard ratio of 6.9 with any stability. It is carded because the topic draft pinned it as the anchor — its correct role is supportive follow-up beside the primary report (previous card), and the shelf's stamp rests on the primary report alone.
cards.source: Pengo V et al. Trial of Rivaroxaban in AntiPhospholipid Syndrome (TRAPS): Two-year outcomes after the study closure. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2021. PMID: 33128325. cards.headline: Synthesis: in triple-positive APS, warfarin stands and rivaroxaban harmed — POSSIBLE (harm)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in triple-positive APS, warfarin stands and rivaroxaban harmed — POSSIBLE (harm)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TRAPS primary report 2018 (120 triple-positive APS patients) and its two-year post-closure follow-up 2021 (115 patients).
cards.result: The randomised evidence, though small and stopped early, is one-directional: every thromboembolic event in the trial occurred on rivaroxaban, and they were arterial (stroke, MI) — the events APS patients most fear. A second smaller RCT (Ordi-Ros 2019) and the stopped ASTRO-APS apixaban trial point the same way in the literature but were not pinned at build and are fenced here by name. The answer is scoped to triple-positive, high-risk APS; it does not speak to lower-risk or venous-only APS phenotypes. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise to all antiphospholipid syndrome: single- or double-positive patients and purely venous disease were not TRAPS's population, and DOAC evidence there is thinner rather than negative.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pengo V et al. Blood. 2018. PMID: 30002145; Pengo V et al. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2021. PMID: 33128325. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Prasugrel pretreatment before angiography in NSTE-ACS (ACCOAST)
shelves.question: In patients with non-ST-elevation ACS scheduled for angiography, does prasugrel pretreatment before the anatomy is known, compared with prasugrel given only after angiography confirms PCI, reduce ischaemic events without increasing bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Bypass · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Piperazines · Prasugrel Hydrochloride · Premedication · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists · Thiophenes
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with bleeding harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death, MI and stroke): ACCOAST (4,033 troponin-positive NSTE-ACS patients scheduled for angiography within 2 to 48 hours) found prasugrel pretreatment (30 mg before angiography) did not reduce its primary efficacy composite through day 7 versus deferred dosing (HR 1.02 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.25; P=0.81) — including among the 69% who proceeded to PCI — while significantly increasing TIMI major bleeding (HR 1.90 relative, 1.19 to 3.02; P=0.006), with non-CABG major bleeding increased threefold and life-threatening bleeding sixfold (relative factors as printed in the record). One large trial with a dead-null efficacy result and a significant harm result carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with harm). The record's abstract does not print the absolute primary event rates, and none are supplied here.

cards.headline: ACCOAST 2013: prasugrel pretreatment did not reduce ischaemic events (HR 1.02) and increased TIMI major bleeding (HR 1.90)
cards.summary: ACCOAST 2013: prasugrel pretreatment did not reduce ischaemic events (HR 1.02) and increased TIMI major bleeding (HR 1.90)
cards.people: 4,033 patients with NSTE acute coronary syndromes and a positive troponin level scheduled to undergo coronary angiography within 2 to 48 hours, randomly assigned to prasugrel 30 mg before angiography (with a further 30 mg at PCI if indicated) or placebo before angiography (with 60 mg prasugrel at PCI if indicated); 69% of patients underwent PCI. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy end point (death from cardiovascular causes, MI, stroke, urgent revascularisation, or glycoprotein IIb/IIIa bailout through day 7) did not differ between groups (HR with pretreatment 1.02 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.84 to 1.25; P=0.81; the abstract does not print the absolute event rates). The key safety end point — all TIMI major bleeding through day 7 — was increased with pretreatment (HR 1.90 relative, 1.19 to 3.02; P=0.006); TIMI major bleeding and life-threatening bleeding not related to CABG were increased by factors of 3 and 6 respectively. Pretreatment did not reduce the primary outcome among patients undergoing PCI but increased their TIMI major bleeding; all results were confirmed at 30 days and in prespecified subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The harm extends to patients who never received a stent — the group pretreatment exposes without any possible benefit — which is the practice-changing core of the trial. Pretreatment here means a split 30 mg + 30 mg regimen; the trial does not test pretreating with other P2Y12 inhibitors, though its logic shaped class-wide guidance.
cards.source: Montalescot G et al. Pretreatment with prasugrel in non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndromes. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23991622. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01015287, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Chlorthalidone versus placebo for hypertension in advanced CKD (CLICK)
shelves.question: In patients with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and poorly controlled hypertension, does chlorthalidone, compared with placebo on top of existing therapy, lower 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albuminuria · Blood Pressure · Chlorthalidone · Creatinine · Diuretics · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Severity of Illness Index · Sodium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: CLICK (160 patients with stage 4 CKD — mean eGFR 23.2 ml/min/1.73 m² — and poorly controlled hypertension on a mean of 3.4 antihypertensive drugs) found chlorthalidone (12.5 mg titrated to 50 mg) lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP by 11.0 mm Hg versus 0.5 mm Hg on placebo at 12 weeks (between-group difference −10.5 mm Hg, 95% CI −14.6 to −6.4; P<0.001), with the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio falling 50 percentage points more than placebo. Harms were the class's own: hypokalaemia, reversible creatinine increases, hyperglycaemia, dizziness and hyperuricaemia all occurred more frequently with chlorthalidone (the abstract does not print their rates). One small, single, 12-week trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point caps at POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is blood pressure. Distinct from Shelf #1052 (CLOROTIC — HCTZ add-on in acute heart failure).

cards.headline: CLICK 2021: chlorthalidone lowered 24-hour systolic BP by 10.5 mm Hg more than placebo at 12 weeks in stage 4 CKD
cards.summary: CLICK 2021: chlorthalidone lowered 24-hour systolic BP by 10.5 mm Hg more than placebo at 12 weeks in stage 4 CKD
cards.people: 160 patients with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and poorly controlled hypertension confirmed by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, randomly assigned to chlorthalidone (initial dose 12.5 mg daily, titrated every 4 weeks to a maximum of 50 mg) or placebo, stratified by prior loop-diuretic use; 121 (76%) had diabetes mellitus, 96 (60%) were receiving loop diuretics, mean eGFR was 23.2 ml/min/1.73 m², and the mean number of antihypertensive medications was 3.4. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Baseline mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP was 142.6 mm Hg (chlorthalidone) and 140.1 mm Hg (placebo). The adjusted change at 12 weeks was −11.0 mm Hg (95% CI −13.9 to −8.1) with chlorthalidone and −0.5 mm Hg (−3.5 to 2.5) with placebo — a between-group difference of −10.5 mm Hg (−14.6 to −6.4; P<0.001). The percent change in urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio was lower with chlorthalidone by 50 percentage points (37 to 60). Hypokalaemia, reversible increases in serum creatinine, hyperglycaemia, dizziness, and hyperuricaemia occurred more frequently in the chlorthalidone group (rates not printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and 160 patients: the trial overturns the old teaching that thiazides stop working below eGFR 30, but says nothing about cardiovascular events, kidney progression, or durability — and the reversible creatinine rises it reports are exactly the signal that needs longer follow-up to interpret.
cards.source: Agarwal R et al. Chlorthalidone for Hypertension in Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34739197. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02841280, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: thiazides do work in advanced CKD — a large BP effect in one small short trial — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: thiazides do work in advanced CKD — a large BP effect in one small short trial — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: CLICK 2021 (160 patients with stage 4 CKD and uncontrolled hypertension).
cards.result: CLICK's −10.5 mm Hg ambulatory difference is a big effect for an add-on drug in patients already on 3.4 agents, and its albuminuria signal points the same way; its limits are size, duration, and a surrogate end point. No second RCT in advanced CKD exists.

shelves.title: Quadruple single-pill combination as initial therapy for hypertension (QUARTET)
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension starting or on monotherapy, does initial treatment with a single pill containing quarter-doses of four antihypertensive classes, compared with standard-dose monotherapy, achieve better blood-pressure control?
shelves.mesh: Amlodipine · Antihypertensive Agents · Australia · Bisoprolol · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Indapamide · Irbesartan · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: QUARTET (591 Australian adults with hypertension, untreated or on monotherapy; mean age 59 years, 60% men) found starting treatment with a quarter-dose quadpill (irbesartan 37.5 mg, amlodipine 1.25 mg, indapamide 0.625 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg) beat starting with standard-dose irbesartan monotherapy: unattended office systolic BP lower by 6.9 mm Hg (95% CI 4.9 to 8.9) and control (<140/90) in 76% versus 58% at 12 weeks (RR 1.30 relative, 1.15 to 1.47), with the advantage maintained at 52 weeks in the continuation subgroup (−7.7 mm Hg; control 81% vs 62%) and far fewer add-on medications needed (15% vs 40% by 12 weeks). Serious adverse events up to 12 weeks were 7 (3%) on quadpill versus 3 (1%) on control, with no difference in withdrawals for adverse events. One double-blind trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is BP control.

cards.headline: QUARTET 2021: starting with a quarter-dose quadpill controlled BP in 76% versus 58% on monotherapy, sustained to 12 months
cards.summary: QUARTET 2021: starting with a quarter-dose quadpill controlled BP in 76% versus 58% on monotherapy, sustained to 12 months
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, parallel-group, active-controlled randomised trial (Australia)
cards.people: 591 adults (≥18 years) with hypertension who were untreated or receiving monotherapy, randomly assigned to initial quadpill treatment (300) or indistinguishable monotherapy control (irbesartan 150 mg; 291), with additional medications added in both groups if BP was not at target (starting with amlodipine 5 mg); mean age 59 years (SD 12), 356 (60%) male, baseline mean unattended office BP 141/85 mm Hg. A subgroup of 417 continued the randomised allocation to 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, systolic BP was lower by 6.9 mm Hg (95% CI 4.9 to 8.9; P<0.0001) and BP control rates were 76% versus 58% (RR 1.30 — a relative measure — 1.15 to 1.47; P<0.0001); additional BP medications had been started in 15% of the quadpill group versus 40% of controls. At 52 weeks (continuation subgroup), unattended systolic BP remained lower by 7.7 mm Hg (5.2 to 10.3) and control rates were 81% versus 62% (RR 1.32 relative). There was no difference in adverse-event-related withdrawals at 12 weeks (4.0% vs 2.4%; P=0.27); up to 12 weeks there were seven (3%) serious adverse events in the intervention group and three (1%) in the control group.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a strategy (start with monotherapy, titrate up) rather than a placebo, and treating clinicians could add drugs — by design; the 12-month figures come from the 417-patient continuation subgroup, not all 591 randomised. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID; the trial's registration (ACTRN12616001144404) is stated in its abstract and is printed on this card as such.
cards.source: Chow CK et al. shelves.title: Low-dose triple-pill combination versus usual care for hypertension (TRIUMPH)
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate hypertension needing treatment, does a fixed low-dose triple combination pill, compared with usual care, increase the proportion reaching target blood pressure?

cards.headline: TRIUMPH 2018: a low-dose triple pill got 70% to target BP versus 55% on usual care at 6 months
cards.summary: TRIUMPH 2018: a low-dose triple pill got 70% to target BP versus 55% on usual care at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, pragmatic clinical trial (11 urban hospital clinics, Sri Lanka)
cards.people: 700 adults with hypertension requiring initiation or escalation of therapy (mean age 56 years; 58% women; 29% with diabetes; mean baseline BP 154/90 mm Hg), randomly assigned to a once-daily fixed-dose triple combination pill (349) or usual care (351); 675 (96%) completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary outcome (target systolic/diastolic BP — <140/90 mm Hg, or <130/80 with diabetes or CKD — at 6 months) was achieved by 70% on the triple pill versus 55% on usual care (risk difference 12.7 percentage points, 95% CI 3.2 to 22.0; P<0.001). Mean BP at 6 months was 125/76 versus 134/81 mm Hg (adjusted differences over follow-up: systolic −9.8 mm Hg, diastolic −5.0 mm Hg; P<0.001 for both). Adverse events were reported in 38.1% versus 34.8% (most commonly musculoskeletal pain and dizziness/presyncope/syncope), with no significant difference in withdrawal of BP therapy for adverse events (6.6% vs 6.8%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label against 'usual care' — a comparator whose intensity varies with clinician behaviour when the alternative is visible — and single-country (Sri Lanka); the effect is a strategy effect (one pill, three drugs, no titration visits) as much as a pharmacological one.

cards.summary: CREOLE 2019: amlodipine-based pairs lowered 24-hour systolic BP ~3 mm Hg more than perindopril plus HCTZ in Black African patients
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind, three-group trial (six countries in sub-Saharan Africa)
cards.people: 728 Black patients with uncontrolled hypertension (≥140/90 mm Hg untreated or on one drug), randomly assigned to amlodipine 5 mg plus HCTZ 12.5 mg, amlodipine 5 mg plus perindopril 4 mg, or perindopril 4 mg plus HCTZ 12.5 mg daily for 2 months, with doses then doubled for 4 months; mean age 51 years, 63% women; 621 patients had 24-hour ambulatory monitoring at baseline and 6 months.

shelves.title: Community-based intensive BP management by non-physician providers in rural populations (CRHCP)
shelves.question: In rural adults with hypertension, does a village-doctor-led multifaceted intervention (protocol-based treatment, coaching, monitoring), compared with usual care, reduce cardiovascular events and death?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cardiovascular Diseases · Blood Pressure · Antihypertensive Agents · Public Health · Hypertension · Hypotension · Stroke · Myocardial Infarction · Heart Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events and death are the primary outcomes of the effectiveness report): The China Rural Hypertension Control Project randomised 326 villages (33,995 hypertensive adults aged ≥40). Its 36-month effectiveness report found the primary composite (MI, stroke, heart failure hospitalisation, or cardiovascular death) lower with the village-doctor-led intervention (1.62% vs 2.40% per year; HR 0.67 relative, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.73), with every component and all-cause death also reduced (all-cause death HR 0.85 relative, 0.76 to 0.95), at the cost of more hypotension (1.75% vs 0.89%). The trial's earlier primary report showed the mechanism: BP <130/80 at 18 months in 57.0% versus 19.9%, with systolic BP 14.5 mm Hg lower. Both cards are reports of ONE cluster trial (counted once): a single-country, open-label, cluster-randomised delivery-model trial caps at POSSIBLE. Build correction: the topic draft attributed the event outcomes to the 2022 anchor record; that record (PMID 35500594) reports the 18-month BP outcomes only — the events live in the trial's 2023 effectiveness report (PMID 36871573), pinned at build and carded here.

cards.headline: CRHCP effectiveness report 2023: village-doctor-led intensive BP control reduced cardiovascular events and death over 36 months (HR 0.67)
cards.summary: CRHCP effectiveness report 2023: village-doctor-led intensive BP control reduced cardiovascular events and death over 36 months (HR 0.67)
cards.type: Open-label, blinded-endpoint, cluster-randomised trial (326 villages, rural China) — 36-month effectiveness report of the CRHCP trial
cards.people: 33,995 individuals aged at least 40 years with hypertension, recruited from 163 intervention and 163 usual-care villages between May and November 2018. In the intervention group, trained non-physician community health-care providers initiated and titrated antihypertensive medications to a target of <130/80 mm Hg under primary-care physician supervision, and delivered discounted or free medications and health coaching. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over 36 months, the net group difference in systolic BP reduction was −23.1 mm Hg (95% CI −24.4 to −21.9) and in diastolic reduction −9.9 mm Hg. The primary outcome (MI, stroke, heart failure requiring hospitalisation, or cardiovascular disease death) occurred in 1.62% per year in the intervention group versus 2.40% per year in usual care (HR 0.67 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.61 to 0.73; P<0.0001). Secondary outcomes were also reduced: MI (HR 0.77 relative, 0.60 to 0.98), stroke (HR 0.66 relative, 0.60 to 0.73), heart failure (HR 0.58 relative, 0.42 to 0.81), cardiovascular death (HR 0.70 relative, 0.58 to 0.83), and all-cause death (HR 0.85 relative, 0.76 to 0.95; P=0.0037). Hypotension was more frequent with the intervention (1.75% vs 0.89%; P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: One cluster trial in one country's rural health system, open-label (with blinded end-point assessment), where the intervention bundled free/discounted drugs, coaching and protocolised titration — the event reduction cannot be apportioned among components, and the delivery model may not travel to systems without village doctors. The 36-month systolic difference printed here (−23.1 mm Hg net reduction difference) is larger than the 18-month between-group difference in the companion report; both are the trial's own figures at their own timepoints.
cards.source: He J et al. Effectiveness of a non-physician community health-care provider-led intensive blood pressure intervention versus usual care on cardiovascular disease (CRHCP): an open-label, blinded-endpoint, cluster-randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2023. PMID: 36871573. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03527719, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Self-monitoring of blood pressure in pregnancy with hypertension (BUMP 1 and BUMP 2)
shelves.question: In pregnant individuals with chronic or gestational hypertension, does self-monitoring of blood pressure (with telemonitoring in BUMP 2), compared with usual clinic-based monitoring, improve blood-pressure control or detect pre-eclampsia sooner?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Chronic Disease · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Hypertension, Pregnancy-Induced · Pre-Eclampsia · Pregnancy · Self-Testing · Telemedicine
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The BUMP programme's two randomised trials (one programme, one registry number, two populations and two questions) are both null on their primary outcomes. BUMP 2 (850 pregnant individuals with chronic or gestational hypertension) found self-monitoring with telemonitoring did not improve clinic systolic BP before birth in either cohort (chronic: 133.8 vs 133.6 mm Hg, adjusted difference 0.03 mm Hg; gestational: 137.6 vs 137.2 mm Hg, difference −0.03 mm Hg). BUMP 1 (2,441 pregnant individuals at higher risk of pre-eclampsia, without diagnosed hypertension at entry) found self-monitoring did not detect hypertension sooner (time to clinic-recorded hypertension 104.3 vs 106.2 days; difference −1.6 days, 95% CI −8.1 to 4.9). Build correction: the topic draft describes BUMP 1 as the gestational-hypertension trial — it is not; BUMP 2 itself contains both the chronic and gestational cohorts, and BUMP 1 answers the detection question in higher-risk pregnancy. Not Tier C: process/BP outcomes, no drug-initiation claim (self-monitoring only).

cards.headline: BUMP 2 2022: self-monitoring did not improve clinic blood pressure in chronic (133.8 vs 133.6 mm Hg) or gestational (137.6 vs 137.2 mm Hg) hypertension
cards.summary: BUMP 2 2022: self-monitoring did not improve clinic blood pressure in chronic (133.8 vs 133.6 mm Hg) or gestational (137.6 vs 137.2 mm Hg) hypertension
cards.type: Unblinded, randomised clinical trial (15 hospital maternity units, England)
cards.people: 850 pregnant individuals randomised: 454 with chronic hypertension (mean age 36 years; mean gestation at entry 20 weeks) and 396 with gestational hypertension (mean age 34 years; mean gestation at entry 33 weeks), assigned to BP self-monitoring with a validated monitor and secure telemonitoring in addition to usual care (430) or usual care alone (420); primary outcome data were available for 97.8% and 95.2% of the two cohorts.
cards.result: The primary outcome was the difference in mean systolic BP recorded by health-care professionals between randomisation and birth. In the chronic hypertension cohort there was no significant difference (133.8 mm Hg self-monitoring vs 133.6 mm Hg usual care; adjusted mean difference 0.03 mm Hg, 95% CI −1.73 to 1.79). In the gestational hypertension cohort there was likewise no significant difference (137.6 vs 137.2 mm Hg; adjusted difference −0.03 mm Hg, −2.29 to 2.24). Serious adverse events numbered 8 in the self-monitoring group and 3 in the usual care group.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the outcome is clinic-measured BP — self-monitoring could change home readings, visit patterns or anxiety without moving this end point; the trial answers the clinic-BP question it asked. Eight versus three serious adverse events is a small-number contrast the abstract does not analyse further.

shelves.title: Endothelin-receptor antagonism with darusentan in resistant hypertension (DORADO)
shelves.question: In patients with resistant hypertension on at least three drugs including a diuretic, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist darusentan, compared with placebo, lower blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analysis of Variance · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Diastole · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Edema · Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylpropionates · Pyrimidines · Receptor, Endothelin A · Systole · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of darusentan in resistant hypertension agree on blood-pressure lowering. DORADO (379 patients on at least three drugs including a diuretic at full or maximally tolerated doses) found clinic systolic/diastolic reductions at 14 weeks of 17/10, 18/10 and 18/11 mm Hg at 50, 100 and 300 mg versus 9/5 mm Hg on placebo (P<0.0001 for all dose effects), with oedema or fluid retention in 27% on darusentan versus 14% on placebo. The earlier forced-titration dose-ranging trial (Black 2007, 115 patients) likewise found dose-dependent reductions, largest at 300 mg (−11.5/−6.3 mm Hg at week 10 as printed). The stamp is LIKELY for the BP-lowering claim only: the end points are blood pressure (surrogate), the harm is fluid retention, and the programme was abandoned before marketing — no outcome claim is made. Distinct from Shelf #743 (the aprocitentan/baxdrostat era). Not Tier C.

cards.headline: DORADO 2009: darusentan lowered clinic BP by a further ~9/5 mm Hg beyond placebo in resistant hypertension, with fluid retention in 27%
cards.summary: DORADO 2009: darusentan lowered clinic BP by a further ~9/5 mm Hg beyond placebo in resistant hypertension, with fluid retention in 27%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (117 sites, North and South America, Europe, New Zealand, Australia)
cards.people: 379 patients with systolic BP of 140 mm Hg or more (130 if diabetic or with chronic kidney disease) despite at least three BP-lowering drugs including a diuretic at full or maximum tolerated doses, randomly assigned to 14 weeks of placebo (132) or darusentan 50 mg (81), 100 mg (81) or 300 mg (85) once daily; all participants were analysed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean reductions in clinic systolic/diastolic BP were 9/5 mm Hg (SD 14/8) with placebo, 17/10 mm Hg (15/9) with darusentan 50 mg, 18/10 mm Hg (16/9) with 100 mg, and 18/11 mm Hg (18/10) with 300 mg (P<0.0001 for all effects). The main adverse effects were related to fluid accumulation: oedema or fluid retention occurred in 67 (27%) patients given darusentan versus 19 (14%) given placebo. One patient in the placebo group died (sudden cardiac death), and five patients in the three darusentan dose groups combined had cardiac-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A flat dose-response above 50 mg with a fluid-retention price that rises with exposure is the profile that ended this programme; the trial's 14 weeks cannot speak to heart-failure risk from chronic fluid retention, the harm that matters for an endothelin antagonist (the class's known liability).
cards.source: Weber MA et al. cards.headline: Black 2007: dose-ranging trial found dose-dependent BP reductions with darusentan, largest at 300 mg (−11.5/−6.3 mm Hg at week 10)
cards.summary: Black 2007: dose-ranging trial found dose-dependent BP reductions with darusentan, largest at 300 mg (−11.5/−6.3 mm Hg at week 10)
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled forced dose-titration study
cards.people: 115 patients with resistant hypertension receiving at least three antihypertensive medications including a diuretic at full doses, randomised 2:1 to escalating darusentan doses (10, 50, 100, 150, then 300 mg) or matching placebo once daily for 10 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Darusentan decreased mean systolic and diastolic BP in a dose-dependent fashion compared with placebo; the largest reductions were observed at week 10 at the 300-mg dose (systolic −11.5 ± 3.1 mm Hg [P=0.015]; diastolic −6.3 ± 2.0 mm Hg [P=0.002]) — the abstract prints these as the dose's reductions without separating within-group change from placebo-adjusted difference, and they are carded as printed. Darusentan also decreased mean 24-hour, daytime and night-time ambulatory BP. Mild-to-moderate oedema and headache were the most common adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A forced-titration phase 2 design: every darusentan patient passed through all doses, so the week-10 figure belongs to the titration schedule as much as to the 300-mg dose; the record's databank fields carry no registry ID (a DOI only).

shelves.title: Midodrine for prevention of recurrent vasovagal syncope
shelves.question: In patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope, does midodrine, compared with placebo, reduce the recurrence of syncope?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Midodrine · Syncope, Vasovagal · Vasoconstrictor Agents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (Sheldon 2021, 133 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope — median 6 episodes in the prior year, median age 32 years, 73% female) found fewer patients on midodrine had at least one syncope episode over 12 months (42% [28 of 66] vs 61% [41 of 67]; RR 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; P=0.035), an absolute reduction of 19 percentage points (number needed to treat 5.3), with time to first syncope also longer (HR 0.59 relative, 0.37 to 0.96) and adverse effects similar between groups. A single small trial in young, healthy, high-burden patients caps at POSSIBLE, matching the authors' own stated limitations. Not Tier C: syncope recurrence, not a mortality/event claim. (This is a blood-pressure-regulation disorder shelf, adjacent to the hypertension slate.)

cards.headline: Sheldon 2021: midodrine reduced one-year syncope recurrence in recurrent vasovagal syncope (42% vs 61%; NNT 5.3)
cards.summary: Sheldon 2021: midodrine reduced one-year syncope recurrence in recurrent vasovagal syncope (42% vs 61%; NNT 5.3)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial (25 university hospitals in Canada, the United States, Mexico, and the United Kingdom)
cards.people: 133 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope and no serious comorbid conditions, randomly assigned 1:1 to midodrine (66) or placebo (67) and followed for 12 months; participants had had a median of 6 syncope episodes in the prior year, median age was 32 years, and 73% were female.
cards.result: Fewer patients receiving midodrine had at least 1 syncope episode during follow-up (28 of 66 [42%] vs 41 of 67 [61%]): relative risk 0.69 (a relative measure; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; P=0.035), an absolute risk reduction of 19 percentage points (CI 2 to 36) and a number needed to treat of 5.3 (CI 2.8 to 47.6). Time to first syncope was longer with midodrine (HR 0.59 relative, 0.37 to 0.96; P=0.035). Adverse effects were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own limitations, printed in the record: small study size, young and healthy patients, relatively short observation, and a high proportion of patients from one centre. The interval on the number needed to treat (2.8 to 47.6) shows how wide the plausible benefit range is.
cards.source: Sheldon R et al. Midodrine for the Prevention of Vasovagal Syncope : A Randomized Clinical Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2021. PMID: 34339231. shelves.title: Droxidopa for symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
shelves.question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, or autonomic failure, does droxidopa, compared with placebo, improve orthostatic symptoms and standing blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Autonomic Agents · Autonomic Nervous System Diseases · Blood Pressure · Dizziness · Double-Blind Method · Droxidopa · Female · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple System Atrophy · Nervous System Diseases · Parkinson Disease · Posture · Pure Autonomic Failure · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The droxidopa programme is two short, responder-enriched phase 3 trials with mixed primary results. Kaufmann 2014 (162 responders randomised after open-label titration) found droxidopa improved the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire composite over a 7-day double-blind phase (between-group improvement 0.90 units; P=0.003) and raised standing systolic BP more (11.2 vs 3.9 mm Hg; P<0.001) — with supine systolic BP also higher (7.6 vs 0.8 mm Hg) and supine systolic >180 mm Hg in 4.9% versus 2.5%. The randomised-withdrawal trial (Biaggioni 2015, 101 responders) FAILED its primary end point (worsening of dizziness/lightheadedness 1.3 vs 1.9 units favouring continued droxidopa; P=0.509 — not significant), with significance only in secondary and post hoc composite analyses. Build correction: the topic draft describes the Biaggioni trial as 'positive on falls/symptoms' — the record shows a missed primary end point and no falls outcome. One positive 7-day trial and one primary-null withdrawal trial, both enriched for responders, earn POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: symptom claim.

cards.headline: Kaufmann 2014: in open-label responders, droxidopa improved orthostatic symptoms over 7 blinded days (OHQ composite +0.90 units) and raised standing systolic BP
cards.summary: Kaufmann 2014: in open-label responders, droxidopa improved orthostatic symptoms over 7 blinded days (OHQ composite +0.90 units) and raised standing systolic BP
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial with open-label titration and responder enrichment
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension due to Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure, or nondiabetic autonomic neuropathy underwent open-label droxidopa dose optimisation (100–600 mg three times daily); responders then had a 7-day washout and a 7-day double-blind trial of droxidopa versus placebo, with 162 patients in the randomised analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Improvement in mean Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire (OHQ) composite score favoured droxidopa over placebo by 0.90 units (P=0.003); the symptom subscore favoured droxidopa by 0.73 units (P=0.010, maximum change in dizziness/lightheadedness) and the symptom-impact subscore by 1.06 units (P=0.003, maximum change for 'standing a long time'). Mean standing systolic BP increased by 11.2 versus 3.9 mm Hg (P<0.001) and mean supine systolic BP by 7.6 versus 0.8 mm Hg (P<0.001); supine systolic BP >180 mm Hg was observed in 4.9% of droxidopa versus 2.5% of placebo recipients. Adverse events in ≥3% of droxidopa recipients were headache (7.4%) and dizziness (3.7%); no patient discontinued double-blind treatment for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Seven days of blinded treatment in patients pre-selected for responding to the drug: the design maximises the chance of a positive result and cannot speak to durability, falls, or non-responders. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID (a DOI only). The supine hypertension signal (BP >180 in 4.9%) is the class's standing caution.
cards.source: Kaufmann H et al. Droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: a randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Neurology. 2014. PMID: 24944260. cards.headline: Biaggioni 2015: the randomised-withdrawal trial missed its primary end point (P=0.509) — secondary scores favoured droxidopa
cards.summary: Biaggioni 2015: the randomised-withdrawal trial missed its primary end point (P=0.509) — secondary scores favoured droxidopa
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure, or nondiabetic autonomic neuropathy) underwent open-label droxidopa titration; responders received a further 7 days of open-label treatment, then were randomised to continue droxidopa or withdraw to placebo for 14 days; the primary-outcome population was 101 patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — mean worsening of the OHQ dizziness/lightheadedness score from randomisation to end of study — was 1.3 ± 2.8 units with droxidopa versus 1.9 ± 3.2 with placebo (P=0.509 — not significant). Four of the other five OHQ symptom scores and all four symptom-impact scores favoured droxidopa, with statistical significance for activities requiring standing a short time (P=0.033) and standing a long time (P=0.028); a post hoc analysis of a predefined composite of all symptoms favoured droxidopa (P=0.013). Standing systolic BP did not differ significantly (P=0.680). Droxidopa was well tolerated. The authors state the study failed to meet its primary efficacy end point and that additional trials are needed.

Cited beside Kaufmann 2014, it tempers rather than confirms.

shelves.title: Spironolactone versus clonidine as fourth-line therapy for resistant hypertension (ReHOT)
shelves.question: In patients with true resistant hypertension on a three-drug regimen including a diuretic, does spironolactone, compared with clonidine, achieve better 24-hour blood-pressure control as the fourth drug?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Clonidine · Drug Monitoring · Drug Resistance · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Spironolactone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference for clonidine superiority): ReHOT (187 patients with true resistant hypertension — uncontrolled on office and ambulatory measurement despite three drugs including a diuretic for 12 weeks, adherence checked by pill counting; Brazil) found the primary end point (combined office <140/90 and 24-hour ambulatory <130/80 control after 12 weeks as fourth drug) nearly identical: 20.8% on spironolactone versus 20.5% on clonidine (RR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.88; P=1.00). Secondary readings were also similar for control (office 33.3% vs 29.3%; ambulatory 44% vs 46.2%), though spironolactone produced greater decreases in 24-hour systolic and diastolic BP (magnitudes not printed in the abstract). The dominant finding is that only about one in five truly resistant patients reached combined control on either drug. One small single-country trial: POSSIBLE. Build note: the topic draft's 'n=159' misreads the record — 1,597 patients were recruited, of whom 187 met the resistant-hypertension criteria and were randomised. Not Tier C: BP-control claim. PATHWAY-2 (spironolactone vs alternatives including placebo) is a different comparison, housed in the main hypertension shelves.

cards.headline: ReHOT 2018: as fourth drug, spironolactone and clonidine controlled BP equally often (20.8% vs 20.5%) — and both usually failed
cards.summary: ReHOT 2018: as fourth drug, spironolactone and clonidine controlled BP equally often (20.8% vs 20.5%) — and both usually failed
cards.people: Of 1,597 patients recruited, 187 (11.7%) fulfilled true resistant-hypertension criteria (no office and no ambulatory BP control despite 3 drugs including a diuretic for 12 weeks; adherence checked by pill counting) and were randomised to an additional 12 weeks of spironolactone 12.5–50 mg daily (95) or clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg twice daily (92). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point (BP control by both office [<140/90 mm Hg] and 24-hour ambulatory [<130/80 mm Hg] criteria) was achieved by 20.8% on spironolactone versus 20.5% on clonidine (RR 1.01 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.55 to 1.88; P=1.00). Secondary end points: office control 33.3% versus 29.3% and ambulatory control 44% versus 46.2% (spironolactone versus clonidine respectively), while spironolactone promoted greater decreases in 24-hour systolic and diastolic BP and daytime diastolic ambulatory BP (the abstract does not print the magnitudes). Per-protocol analysis (≥80% adherence) showed similar primary results. The authors conclude clonidine was not superior, overall control was low (~21%), and spironolactone is preferable as fourth drug given easier dosing and greater secondary-endpoint BP decreases.
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed to test whether clonidine could beat the incumbent fourth drug; 'not superior' with an interval of 0.55 to 1.88 (relative) in 187 patients is not proof of exact equivalence. The screening funnel (1,597 recruited → 187 truly resistant) is itself a finding: most apparent resistance was pseudo-resistance.
cards.source: Krieger EM et al. Spironolactone Versus Clonidine as a Fourth-Drug Therapy for Resistant Hypertension: The ReHOT Randomized Study (Resistant Hypertension Optimal Treatment). Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2018. PMID: 29463627. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01643434, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the two fourth-line candidates tie on control; spironolactone edges the BP falls — POSSIBLE (the null for clonidine superiority)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the two fourth-line candidates tie on control; spironolactone edges the BP falls — POSSIBLE (the null for clonidine superiority)

cards.result: ReHOT is the only head-to-head of the two classic fourth-line choices, and its answer is a tie on the outcome that matters (combined office + ambulatory control, ~21% either way), with spironolactone ahead on continuous BP decreases and dosing convenience. The low absolute control rate is the shelf's most useful number for counselling: four of five truly resistant patients remain uncontrolled on a fourth drug.

shelves.title: Icosapent ethyl for cardiovascular risk reduction in statin-treated patients with raised triglycerides (REDUCE-IT)
shelves.question: In statin-treated patients with established cardiovascular disease or diabetes plus risk factors and triglycerides 135–499 mg/dL, does icosapent ethyl 4 g daily, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eicosapentaenoic Acid · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Hypertriglyceridemia · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke benefit claim): REDUCE-IT (8,179 statin-treated patients, 70.7% secondary prevention, median follow-up 4.9 years) found icosapent ethyl 4 g daily cut the primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, unstable angina) from 22.0% to 17.2% (HR 0.75 relative), the key secondary composite from 14.8% to 11.2% (HR 0.74 relative), and cardiovascular death from 5.2% to 4.3% (HR 0.80 relative), offset by more hospitalisations for atrial fibrillation or flutter (3.1% vs 2.1%) and a small, non-significant excess of serious bleeding (2.7% vs 2.1%). The one discordant note is the comparator trial of a different agent: STRENGTH's mixed EPA/DHA carboxylic acids were null against corn oil (HR 0.99), and REDUCE-IT's placebo was mineral oil, which critics argue may have raised LDL cholesterol and inflammatory markers in the control group and inflated the relative benefit — that controversy is unresolved and sits on the card. One large positive trial of this agent, with no second outcomes trial, carries LIKELY rather than a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: REDUCE-IT 2019: icosapent ethyl cut the primary ischemic composite from 22.0% to 17.2% over a median 4.9 years
cards.summary: REDUCE-IT 2019: icosapent ethyl cut the primary ischemic composite from 22.0% to 17.2% over a median 4.9 years
cards.people: 8,179 patients with established cardiovascular disease or diabetes plus other risk factors, on statin therapy, with fasting triglycerides 135–499 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol 41–100 mg/dL; 70.7% were enrolled for secondary prevention. They were randomly assigned to icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily (4 g/day) or placebo (mineral oil) and followed for a median of 4.9 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary end-point event (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, or unstable angina) occurred in 17.2% on icosapent ethyl versus 22.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.75 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.83; P<0.001). The key secondary end point (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke) occurred in 11.2% versus 14.8% (HR 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.83; P<0.001), and cardiovascular death in 4.3% versus 5.2% (HR 0.80 relative, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.98; P=0.03). Hospitalisation for atrial fibrillation or flutter was more frequent on icosapent ethyl (3.1% vs 2.1%, P=0.004); serious bleeding events occurred in 2.7% versus 2.1% (P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: The placebo was mineral oil. Whether mineral oil raised LDL cholesterol and inflammatory markers in the control group — and so inflated the apparent relative benefit — remains contested and is not settled by this record. There is no second outcomes trial of icosapent ethyl itself, and the atrial-fibrillation signal is a real harm to weigh.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30415628. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01492361, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: STRENGTH 2020 (a different agent): mixed EPA/DHA carboxylic acids were null against corn oil — HR 0.99
cards.summary: STRENGTH 2020 (a different agent): mixed EPA/DHA carboxylic acids were null against corn oil — HR 0.99
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a different agent (fenced comparator, carded for contrast)
cards.people: 13,078 statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk with hypertriglyceridaemia and low HDL cholesterol, randomly assigned to omega-3 carboxylic acids (mixed EPA/DHA) 4 g/day or corn oil; mean age 62.5 years, 35% women, 70% with diabetes. This trial does NOT test icosapent ethyl; it is carded because it is the class's discordant outcomes trial.
cards.result: The trial was halted early for futility. The primary end point (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for unstable angina) occurred in 12.0% on omega-3 carboxylic acids versus 12.2% on corn oil (hazard ratio 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.09; P=0.84). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with omega-3 CA (24.7% vs 14.7%).
cards.watchOut: A null result for a mixed EPA/DHA formulation does not refute a benefit of purified EPA — but it removes any class-effect presumption, and it is part of why the mineral-oil-placebo question in REDUCE-IT matters: the two trials used different placebos (corn oil versus mineral oil) as well as different agents.

shelves.title: Pemafibrate for cardiovascular risk reduction in diabetes with hypertriglyceridaemia (PROMINENT)
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, triglycerides 200–499 mg/dL, and low HDL on statins, does pemafibrate, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Apolipoprotein C-III · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol · Cholesterol, LDL · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Heart Disease Risk Factors · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Hyperlipidemias · Hypertriglyceridemia · Risk Factors · Triglycerides · Hypolipidemic Agents · PPAR alpha · Cholesterol, HDL · Benzoxazoles · Butyrates
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events claim): PROMINENT (10,497 patients with type 2 diabetes, hypertriglyceridaemia and low HDL, median follow-up 3.4 years) lowered triglycerides by 26.2% relative to placebo, along with VLDL cholesterol, remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein C-III — and changed cardiovascular outcomes not at all: 572 primary events on pemafibrate versus 560 on placebo (HR 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.15), with no subgroup signal. Pemafibrate was associated with more adverse renal events and more venous thromboembolism, and less nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. A single very large, well-powered null on the exact question, with the lipid hypothesis cleanly falsified (the drug did lower triglycerides), carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in the statin era, triglyceride lowering by this mechanism does not buy events. It complements Shelf #528 (fibrates).

cards.headline: PROMINENT 2022: pemafibrate lowered triglycerides 26% and cardiovascular events not at all — HR 1.03
cards.summary: PROMINENT 2022: pemafibrate lowered triglycerides 26% and cardiovascular events not at all — HR 1.03
cards.people: 10,497 patients with type 2 diabetes, fasting triglycerides 200–499 mg/dL (median 271), HDL cholesterol ≤40 mg/dL (median 33) and LDL cholesterol ≤100 mg/dL (median 78), on guideline-directed therapy; 66.9% had previous cardiovascular disease. They received pemafibrate 0.2 mg twice daily or placebo over a median follow-up of 3.4 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 4 months, versus placebo, pemafibrate changed lipid levels by −26.2% for triglycerides, −25.8% for VLDL cholesterol, −25.6% for remnant cholesterol, −27.6% for apolipoprotein C-III and +4.8% for apolipoprotein B (all relative differences). The primary end point (nonfatal MI, ischemic stroke, coronary revascularisation, or cardiovascular death) occurred in 572 patients on pemafibrate and 560 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.15), with no effect modification in any prespecified subgroup. The abstract prints event counts rather than per-group percentages, and does not print the per-group denominators, so percentages cannot be stated from this record. Overall serious adverse events did not differ, but adverse renal events and venous thromboembolism were more frequent with pemafibrate, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease less frequent.
cards.watchOut: This is the cleanest possible falsification design: the surrogate moved exactly as intended and the outcome did not follow. Any shelf claiming event reduction from triglyceride lowering in statin-treated diabetes must answer this trial.
cards.source: Das Pradhan A et al. Triglyceride Lowering with Pemafibrate to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 36342113. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03071692, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: CETP inhibition with anacetrapib in atherosclerotic vascular disease (REVEAL)
shelves.question: In patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease on intensive atorvastatin, does anacetrapib, compared with placebo, reduce major coronary events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticholesteremic Agents · Atherosclerosis · Cholesterol · Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins · Coronary Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Oxazolidinones
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, coronary events benefit claim): REVEAL (30,449 patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease on intensive atorvastatin, median follow-up 4.1 years) found anacetrapib 100 mg daily reduced major coronary events from 11.8% to 10.8% (rate ratio 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97; P=0.004) — a real but modest 1.0-percentage-point absolute benefit over about four years, with no difference in death or cancer. Anacetrapib raised HDL cholesterol by 43 mg/dL and lowered non-HDL cholesterol by 17 mg/dL at the trial midpoint; the benefit is generally attributed to the non-HDL/LDL lowering, not the HDL rise. The drug was never marketed — it accumulates in adipose tissue — so the shelf is a class-evidence shelf: it shows CETP inhibition can reduce events modestly, against a class history in which torcetrapib harmed and dalcetrapib and evacetrapib were null (named here without figures; those trials are fenced, not carded). One very large positive trial carries LIKELY.

cards.headline: REVEAL 2017: anacetrapib reduced major coronary events from 11.8% to 10.8% over a median 4.1 years
cards.summary: REVEAL 2017: anacetrapib reduced major coronary events from 11.8% to 10.8% over a median 4.1 years
cards.people: 30,449 adults with atherosclerotic vascular disease receiving intensive atorvastatin (mean LDL cholesterol 61 mg/dL, non-HDL 92 mg/dL, HDL 40 mg/dL at baseline), randomly assigned to anacetrapib 100 mg daily (15,225) or placebo (15,224) for a median follow-up of 4.1 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (first major coronary event: coronary death, myocardial infarction, or coronary revascularisation) occurred in 1,640 of 15,225 patients (10.8%) on anacetrapib versus 1,803 of 15,224 (11.8%) on placebo (rate ratio 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97; P=0.004), with a similar relative difference across prespecified subgroups. At the trial midpoint, HDL cholesterol was 43 mg/dL higher (a relative difference of 104%) and non-HDL cholesterol 17 mg/dL lower (a relative difference of −18%) with anacetrapib. There were no significant differences in the risk of death, cancer, or other serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Anacetrapib is not available clinically: its developer stopped development because the drug accumulates in adipose tissue with a very long tail. The shelf's value is mechanistic — event reduction tracked non-HDL lowering, consistent with the LDL principle — not a prescribing recommendation.

cards.result: REVEAL is the only CETP-inhibitor outcomes trial to show benefit, and the benefit is small in absolute terms (1.0 percentage point over ~4 years) despite a doubling of HDL — supporting the interpretation that non-HDL/LDL lowering, not HDL raising, drives event reduction. shelves.title: Pitavastatin for cardiovascular prevention in people with HIV (REPRIEVE)
shelves.question: In people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at low-to-moderate traditional cardiovascular risk, does pitavastatin, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Middle Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · HIV Infections · Myocardial Infarction · Quinolines · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events benefit claim): REPRIEVE (7,769 people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at low-to-moderate traditional risk, median age 50) was stopped early for efficacy after a median follow-up of 5.1 years, with major adverse cardiovascular events at 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin 4 mg versus placebo (HR 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002). The offsets: muscle-related symptoms in 2.3% versus 1.4%, and new diabetes in 5.3% versus 4.0%. Two cautions temper the stamp: trials stopped early tend to overestimate benefit, and the absolute event rates were low (about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years difference), so the absolute gain in this risk stratum is small even if the relative effect is real. One large trial, stopped early, in a population no other outcomes trial covers: LIKELY.

cards.headline: REPRIEVE 2023: pitavastatin cut MACE from 7.32 to 4.81 per 1,000 person-years in people with HIV — trial stopped early
cards.summary: REPRIEVE 2023: pitavastatin cut MACE from 7.32 to 4.81 per 1,000 person-years in people with HIV — trial stopped early
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (phase 3), stopped early for efficacy
cards.people: 7,769 participants with HIV infection at low-to-moderate risk of cardiovascular disease, all receiving antiretroviral therapy, randomly assigned to pitavastatin calcium 4 mg daily or placebo. Median age was 50 years (IQR 45–55) and median CD4 count 621 cells/mm³; HIV RNA was below quantification in 87.5% of those with data. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The trial was stopped early for efficacy after a median follow-up of 5.1 years. A major adverse cardiovascular event (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, hospitalisation for unstable angina, stroke, transient ischemic attack, peripheral arterial ischemia, revascularisation, or death from an undetermined cause) occurred at 4.81 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002). Muscle-related symptoms occurred in 2.3% versus 1.4%, and diabetes mellitus in 5.3% versus 4.0%.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping inflates effect estimates on average, and this composite is broad (it includes revascularisation and death from undetermined cause). The relative reduction is large; the absolute difference — about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years — is the number to carry into a prescribing conversation, alongside the diabetes excess.

cards.headline: Synthesis: statins prevent events in HIV at low traditional risk — a large relative effect, a small absolute one — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: statins prevent events in HIV at low traditional risk — a large relative effect, a small absolute one — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: REPRIEVE 2023 (7,769 people with HIV).
cards.result: REPRIEVE extends the statin evidence to a population guidelines previously left in a grey zone: people with HIV whose traditional risk scores look low but whose inflammation-driven risk is higher. The direction is concordant with the whole statin literature; the magnitude (HR 0.65 relative) should be read with the early-stopping discount.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers primary prevention in HIV specifically; it does not displace the general-population statin shelves, and it tested pitavastatin — chosen for its antiretroviral interaction profile — not statins as an interchangeable class in this population.

shelves.title: Pravastatin in older adults at risk of vascular disease (PROSPER)
shelves.question: In adults aged 70–82 with a history of, or risk factors for, vascular disease, does pravastatin 40 mg, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of coronary death, nonfatal MI, and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cholesterol, LDL · Coronary Artery Disease · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Male · Pravastatin · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, coronary death/MI/stroke claim): PROSPER (5,804 men and women aged 70–82 with vascular disease or risk factors, mean follow-up 3.2 years) found pravastatin 40 mg reduced the primary composite (coronary death, nonfatal MI, fatal or nonfatal stroke) with 408 events versus 473 on placebo (HR 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97; P=0.014), driven by coronary events (HR 0.81 relative); coronary mortality fell 24% in relative terms (P=0.043). Stroke was unaffected (HR 1.03 relative). The debated signal: new cancer diagnoses were more frequent on pravastatin (HR 1.25 relative, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.51; P=0.020) — the record itself notes that pooling with all other pravastatin and statin trials showed no overall increase, and no outcomes trial since has reproduced a statin–cancer effect. The abstract prints event counts and hazard ratios rather than percentages, and the card follows the record. LIKELY for coronary prevention in this age band; the stroke and cancer lines are stated as printed.

cards.headline: PROSPER 2002: pravastatin cut the coronary composite in 70–82-year-olds (408 vs 473 events, HR 0.85) — stroke unaffected, cancer signal debated
cards.summary: PROSPER 2002: pravastatin cut the coronary composite in 70–82-year-olds (408 vs 473 events, HR 0.85) — stroke unaffected, cancer signal debated
cards.people: 5,804 men (2,804) and women (3,000) aged 70–82 years with a history of, or risk factors for, vascular disease (baseline cholesterol 4.0–9.0 mmol/L (≈155–348 mg/dL)), randomly assigned to pravastatin 40 mg daily (2,891) or placebo (2,913) and followed for a mean of 3.2 years.
cards.result: Pravastatin lowered LDL cholesterol by 34% in relative terms. The primary endpoint (coronary death, nonfatal MI, and fatal or nonfatal stroke) occurred in 408 patients on pravastatin versus 473 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97; P=0.014); the abstract prints counts and hazard ratios rather than percentages. Coronary heart disease death and nonfatal MI were reduced (HR 0.81 relative, 0.69 to 0.94; P=0.006) and mortality from coronary disease fell by 24% in relative terms (P=0.043). Stroke risk was unaffected (HR 1.03 relative, 0.81 to 1.31; P=0.8); the hazard ratio for transient ischemic attack was 0.75 (0.55 to 1.00; P=0.051). New cancer diagnoses were more frequent on pravastatin (HR 1.25 relative, 1.04 to 1.51; P=0.020), though the record notes that incorporating this finding into a meta-analysis of all pravastatin and all statin trials showed no overall increase in risk. Pravastatin had no significant effect on cognitive function or disability.
cards.watchOut: The cancer finding is a single-trial subgroup-of-safety signal that the wider statin evidence does not support — it is carded because the record prints it, and the record's own pooling caveat is carded with it. The stroke null within a positive composite is the other line not to lose: the benefit here is coronary.
cards.source: Shepherd J et al. Pravastatin in elderly individuals at risk of vascular disease (PROSPER): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2002. PMID: 12457784. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (a 2002 trial, predating routine registration). shelves.title: Ezetimibe for primary prevention in adults aged 75 and older (EWTOPIA 75)
shelves.question: In adults aged 75 or older with raised LDL and no history of coronary disease, does ezetimibe, compared with dietary counselling alone, prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atherosclerosis · Ezetimibe · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypolipidemic Agents · Incidence · Japan · Primary Prevention · Prospective Studies · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events benefit claim): EWTOPIA 75 (3,796 Japanese patients aged ≥75 with raised LDL and no coronary history, open-label with blinded end-point evaluation, median follow-up 4.1 years) found ezetimibe reduced the primary composite (sudden cardiac death, MI, coronary revascularisation, or stroke) with a hazard ratio of 0.66 relative (95% CI 0.50 to 0.86; P=0.002), and the composite of cardiac events at HR 0.60 relative — note the topic draft assigned the 0.66 figure to the cardiac composite; the record assigns 0.66 to the primary composite and 0.60 to cardiac events, and the card follows the record. There was no difference in stroke, all-cause mortality, or adverse events. The discounts are substantial: open-label treatment, premature termination, and 385 randomised patients (about 10%) excluded from the primary analysis over consent and protocol issues, with high discontinuation — the authors themselves say the magnitude should be interpreted with caution. A single open-label trial with those caveats caps at POSSIBLE. Cross-reference: the staged Shelf #263 carries an EWTOPIA note; this shelf is the trial's home and the pointer should be reconciled at insert.

cards.headline: EWTOPIA 75 2019: ezetimibe reduced the primary cardiovascular composite in over-75s (HR 0.66) in an open-label Japanese trial
cards.summary: EWTOPIA 75 2019: ezetimibe reduced the primary cardiovascular composite in over-75s (HR 0.66) in an open-label Japanese trial
cards.people: 3,796 patients aged 75 or older with elevated LDL cholesterol and no history of coronary artery disease, enrolled at 363 institutions in Japan and randomly assigned (1,898 each) to ezetimibe 10 mg daily or usual care; all received dietary counselling. Median follow-up was 4.1 years. After exclusion of 182 ezetimibe and 203 control patients for lack of appropriate informed consent and other protocol violations, 1,716 (90.4%) and 1,695 (89.3%) were included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Ezetimibe reduced the primary outcome — a composite of sudden cardiac death, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularisation, or stroke — with a hazard ratio of 0.66 relative (95% CI 0.50 to 0.86; P=0.002); the abstract prints hazard ratios rather than event percentages. The composite of cardiac events (HR 0.60 relative, 0.37 to 0.98; P=0.039) and coronary revascularisation (HR 0.38 relative, 0.18 to 0.79; P=0.007) were also lower with ezetimibe, but there was no difference in stroke, all-cause mortality, or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with a revascularisation component in the composite is exactly the design most vulnerable to ascertainment and decision bias, and the trial was terminated prematurely with about 10% of randomised patients excluded from the primary analysis. The authors' own conclusion carries the caution: 'the magnitude of benefit observed should be interpreted with caution.'

cards.summary: Synthesis: a positive but open-label, single-country trial in the over-75s — POSSIBLE
