shelves.title: ApoA1 infusion (CSL112) after acute myocardial infarction (AEGIS-II)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI, multivessel coronary disease, and additional risk factors, do four weekly infusions of the apoA1 preparation CSL112, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Apolipoprotein A-I · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Artery Disease · Double-Blind Method · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lipoproteins, HDL · Myocardial Infarction · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Stroke · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): AEGIS-II (18,219 patients with acute MI, multivessel disease and additional risk factors) gave four weekly infusions of CSL112 6 g or placebo, first dose within 5 days, and found no significant difference in the primary composite (MI, stroke, or cardiovascular death) at 90 days — 4.8% versus 5.2% (HR 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.24) — nor at 180 days (HR 0.91 relative) or 365 days (HR 0.93 relative). The confidence interval at 90 days excludes a relative benefit larger than about 19%, and the trial is by far the largest test of the cholesterol-efflux hypothesis: raising efflux capacity pharmacologically after MI does not translate into fewer events. More hypersensitivity events were reported with CSL112; other adverse events were similar. One very large definitive null: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: AEGIS-II 2024: CSL112 infusions after MI did not reduce events at 90 days — 4.8% vs 5.2%, HR 0.93
cards.summary: AEGIS-II 2024: CSL112 infusions after MI did not reduce events at 90 days — 4.8% vs 5.2%, HR 0.93
cards.people: 18,219 patients with acute myocardial infarction, multivessel coronary artery disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors, randomly assigned to four weekly infusions of CSL112 6 g (9,112) or matching placebo (9,107), the first within 5 days of first medical contact. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary end point (myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) at 90 days: 439 patients (4.8%) on CSL112 versus 472 (5.2%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.24). The null persisted at 180 days (6.9% vs 7.6%; HR 0.91 relative, 0.81 to 1.01) and at 365 days (9.8% vs 10.5%; HR 0.93 relative, 0.85 to 1.02). Adverse events overall were similar; more hypersensitivity events were reported in the CSL112 group.
cards.watchOut: CSL112 did what it was designed to do mechanistically — increase cholesterol-efflux capacity — so the null is informative about the pathway, not about dosing. As with PROMINENT, a surrogate that moves without the outcome following is the finding.

shelves.title: Lp-PLA2 inhibition with darapladib in stable coronary disease and after ACS (STABILITY; SOLID-TIMI 52)
shelves.question: In patients with stable chronic coronary heart disease on guideline therapy — and, in the companion trial, after an acute coronary syndrome — does the Lp-PLA2 inhibitor darapladib, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Benzaldehydes · Coronary Artery Disease · Coronary Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Oximes · Phospholipase A2 Inhibitors · Stroke · Treatment Failure · Biphenyl Compounds · Diethylamines · Pyrimidinones · Sulfides
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): two large outcomes trials of darapladib 160 mg, in complementary populations, both missed. STABILITY (15,828 patients with stable coronary disease, median follow-up 3.7 years): primary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke) 9.7% versus 10.4% (HR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03; P=0.20), with no difference in any component or in all-cause mortality; secondary coronary composites were nominally lower (major coronary events HR 0.90 relative, P=0.045) — secondary findings under a null primary, carded as such. SOLID-TIMI 52 (13,026 patients within 30 days of an ACS, median follow-up 2.5 years): primary coronary composite HR 1.00 relative (P=0.93), cardiovascular death/MI/stroke identical at 15.0% versus 15.0%, all-cause mortality HR 0.94 relative — null across the board, with more odour-related complaints (11.5% vs 2.5%) and diarrhoea (10.6% vs 5.6%). Two concordant large nulls (a DOUBLE-A pair): LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for Lp-PLA2 inhibition as an event-prevention strategy.

cards.headline: STABILITY 2014: darapladib did not reduce cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke in stable coronary disease — 9.7% vs 10.4%, HR 0.94

shelves.title: Lomitapide (MTP inhibition) in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia
shelves.question: In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on standard lipid-lowering therapy, does the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein inhibitor lomitapide, compared with baseline on continued standard therapy, lower LDL cholesterol, and at what hepatic cost?
shelves.mesh: Benzimidazoles · Carrier Proteins · Cholesterol, LDL · Female · Homozygote · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: the entire clinical evidence for lomitapide in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia is one single-arm, open-label phase 3 study of 29 patients, with no comparator group: LDL cholesterol fell 50% in relative terms from baseline (8.7 to 4.3 mmol/L (≈337 to 166 mg/dL)) at 26 weeks and remained 38% lower at 78 weeks, on a median dose of 40 mg/day. The hepatic cost is real: gastrointestinal symptoms were the most common adverse event, and 4 patients had aminotransferase levels above five times the upper limit of normal (resolving with dose reduction or interruption; no one discontinued permanently for liver abnormalities). A within-patient change of this size in a disease this severe is unlikely to be artefact, but with no control group, 29 patients, and a surrogate end point, the record earns no more than MAYBE (weak evidence). Not Tier C: the claim is LDL lowering; there are no outcomes data. Flagged for the developer: this is a two-trial-gate exception candidate — no randomised trial exists or is likely in this ultra-rare disease — as with other rare-disease shelves.

cards.headline: Cuchel 2013: lomitapide lowered LDL by 50% at 26 weeks in 29 patients with homozygous FH — single-arm, with liver-enzyme rises
cards.summary: Cuchel 2013: lomitapide lowered LDL by 50% at 26 weeks in 29 patients with homozygous FH — single-arm, with liver-enzyme rises
cards.people: 29 men and women aged 18 or older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, recruited at 11 centres in four countries (USA, Canada, South Africa, Italy), continued on their existing lipid-lowering therapy; lomitapide was escalated from 5 mg to a maximum of 60 mg daily (median dose 40 mg). 23 of 29 completed both the 26-week efficacy phase and the full 78 weeks. The abstract does not state the sex breakdown or mean age.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell by 50% in relative terms (95% CI −62 to −39) from baseline (mean 8.7 mmol/L (≈337 mg/dL)) to week 26 (4.3 mmol/L (≈166 mg/dL); P<0.0001), remained 44% lower at week 56 and 38% lower at week 78; eight patients reached LDL below 2.6 mmol/L (≈101 mg/dL) at 26 weeks. Gastrointestinal symptoms were the most common adverse event. Four patients had aminotransferase levels more than five times the upper limit of normal, resolving after dose reduction or temporary interruption; no patient permanently discontinued because of liver abnormalities. There is no control group: every figure is a change from the patient's own baseline.
cards.watchOut: Without randomisation or a comparator, regression to the mean, adherence effects and background-therapy changes cannot be separated from drug effect — the design is a necessity in an ultra-rare disease, not a choice, but it caps what the shelf can claim. Hepatic fat accumulation is the class concern the abstract flags through its enzyme data; long-term registry data exist but are not randomised and are not carded.
cards.source: Cuchel M et al. Efficacy and safety of a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein inhibitor in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: a single-arm, open-label, phase 3 study. Lancet (London, England). 2013. PMID: 23122768. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: CETP inhibition with obicetrapib for LDL lowering in high-risk patients (BROADWAY; BROOKLYN)
shelves.question: In patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease whose LDL remains raised on maximally tolerated therapy, does obicetrapib, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Anticholesteremic Agents · Atherosclerosis · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins · Cholesterol, HDL · Cholesterol, LDL · Double-Blind Method · Heart Disease Risk Factors · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for LDL lowering only): two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials. BROADWAY (2,530 patients with HeFH or ASCVD on maximally tolerated therapy) found obicetrapib 10 mg lowered LDL cholesterol by 29.9% while placebo rose 2.7% — a between-group difference of −32.6 percentage points at day 84 (P<0.001). BROOKLYN (354 patients with HeFH) found a placebo-adjusted LDL change of −36.3% at day 84, with placebo-adjusted reductions in apolipoprotein B (−24.4%), non-HDL cholesterol (−34.5%) and lipoprotein(a) (−45.9%). Adverse events appeared similar to placebo in BROADWAY and the drug was reported well tolerated in BROOKLYN. Not Tier C, deliberately: this shelf claims LDL lowering only. A pooled cardiovascular-events analysis of the phase 3 programme (2025) exists but is hypothesis-generating and is fenced, not carded; the dedicated cardiovascular-outcomes trial (PREVAIL) is still in flight and is named on the closing card — any events language must wait for it. Contrast Shelf #1562 (REVEAL): anacetrapib showed that a CETP inhibitor can reduce events modestly, which raises — but does not answer — the outcomes question for this agent.

cards.headline: BROADWAY 2025: obicetrapib lowered LDL by 32.6 percentage points more than placebo at day 84

cards.result: The least-squares mean percent change in LDL cholesterol from baseline to day 84 was −29.9% (95% CI −32.1 to −27.8) on obicetrapib versus +2.7% (−0.4 to 5.8) on placebo — a between-group difference of −32.6 percentage points (95% CI −35.8 to −29.5; P<0.001). shelves.title: Darbepoetin alfa for anaemia in systolic heart failure (RED-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with systolic heart failure and mild-to-moderate anaemia, does darbepoetin alfa titrated to haemoglobin 13 g/dL, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death and hospitalisation for worsening heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anemia · Darbepoetin alfa · Double-Blind Method · Erythropoietin · Female · Heart Failure, Systolic · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Shock, Septic · Stroke · Thromboembolism · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death claim): RED-HF (2,278 patients with systolic heart failure and haemoglobin 9.0–12.0 g/dL) titrated darbepoetin alfa to a haemoglobin target of 13 g/dL and found the primary composite (death from any cause or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure) in 50.7% on darbepoetin versus 49.5% on placebo (HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13; P=0.87) — no benefit in any secondary outcome or prespecified subgroup. The topic draft's figures (49.6% vs 50.1%) are not the proportions this record prints (50.7% vs 49.5%); the card follows the record. Harm ran the other way: thromboembolic adverse events in 13.5% versus 10.0% (P=0.01), with fatal or nonfatal stroke numerically higher (3.7% vs 2.7%, P=0.23). Correcting anaemia with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in heart failure does not improve outcomes and adds thromboembolic risk: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with harm. Distinct from the intravenous-iron shelves — different mechanism, different claim.

shelves.title: Patiromer to enable RAAS-inhibitor therapy in HFrEF with hyperkalaemia risk (DIAMOND; PEARL-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with HFrEF and current or previous hyperkalaemia on RAAS inhibitors, does patiromer, compared with placebo after a run-in, maintain potassium control and allow continued guideline-directed RAAS-inhibitor dosing?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hyperkalemia · Heart Failure · Stroke Volume · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Renin-Angiotensin System · Potassium · Polymers
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: DIAMOND randomised 878 patients with HFrEF and current or previous RAAS-inhibitor-related hyperkalaemia — but only after a patiromer run-in in which 84.6% achieved the specified target RAAS-inhibitor doses, so the randomised population is enriched for people who tolerate the strategy. Over a median 27 weeks, patiromer's adjusted mean potassium change was 0.10 mmol/L lower than placebo's, with fewer hyperkalaemia episodes above 5.5 mmol/L (HR 0.63 relative), fewer MRA dose reductions (HR 0.62 relative), and fewer total hyperkalaemia events (77.7 vs 118.2 per 100 person-years). The predecessor trial PEARL-HF (105 patients, 4 weeks) points the same way: potassium 0.45 mEq/L lower, hyperkalaemia 7.3% versus 24.5%, and more patients titrated to spironolactone 50 mg (91% vs 74%). The claim is enablement — a potassium and dosing outcome, not an events outcome — and no trial shows the strategy improves death or hospitalisation. Run-in enrichment, a surrogate primary end point, and modest effect sizes cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: no mortality or events claim is made.

cards.headline: DIAMOND 2022: patiromer kept potassium lower and MRA doses up after a run-in — K+ difference −0.10 mmol/L
cards.summary: DIAMOND 2022: patiromer kept potassium lower and MRA doses up after a run-in — K+ difference −0.10 mmol/L
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial after an open run-in
cards.people: 1,642 patients with HFrEF and current or a history of RAAS-inhibitor-related hyperkalaemia were screened; 1,195 entered a run-in with patiromer and RAAS-inhibitor optimisation, in which 878 (84.6% of those assessed) achieved the specified target doses (≥50% of recommended ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI dose and 50 mg of spironolactone or eplerenone) and were randomised — 439 to continued patiromer and 439 to placebo — with a median follow-up of 27 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The adjusted mean change in serum potassium was +0.03 mmol/L on patiromer versus +0.13 mmol/L on placebo — a between-group difference of −0.10 mmol/L (the 95% CI is printed in the record as −0.13 to 0.07, which as printed is asymmetric around the estimate; the card reproduces it as printed and flags it rather than repairing it; P<0.001). Hyperkalaemia above 5.5 mmol/L (HR 0.63 relative, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.87; P=0.006), reduction of MRA dose (HR 0.62 relative, 0.45 to 0.87; P=0.006), and total hyperkalaemia events per 100 person-years (77.7 vs 118.2; HR 0.66 relative, 0.53 to 0.81; P<0.001) were all lower with patiromer; total RAAS-inhibitor use score favoured patiromer (win ratio 1.25, P=0.048). Adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: The randomised comparison begins only after non-responders and non-tolerators have been filtered out by the run-in — the effect applies to patients who have already demonstrated they can reach target doses on patiromer, not to all comers with hyperkalaemia. The end point is potassium control and dose maintenance, not clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: PEARL-HF 2011: the predecessor binder trial — potassium 0.45 mEq/L lower, hyperkalaemia 7.3% vs 24.5% over 4 weeks
cards.summary: PEARL-HF 2011: the predecessor binder trial — potassium 0.45 mEq/L lower, hyperkalaemia 7.3% vs 24.5% over 4 weeks
cards.people: 105 patients with chronic heart failure and a history of hyperkalaemia that had forced discontinuation of a RAAS inhibitor or beta-blocker, or chronic kidney disease with eGFR below 60 mL/min, randomised to the potassium binder RLY5016 (patiromer) 30 g/day (55) or placebo (49) for 4 weeks, with spironolactone started at 25 mg/day and increased to 50 mg/day on day 15 if potassium allowed.
cards.result: Serum potassium at the end of treatment was lower with RLY5016 by 0.45 mEq/L versus placebo (P<0.001). Hyperkalaemia (potassium above 5.5 mEq/L) occurred in 7.3% on RLY5016 versus 24.5% on placebo (P=0.015), and 91% versus 74% were titrated to spironolactone 50 mg/day (P=0.019). Adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal and mild or moderate; hypokalaemia occurred in 6% on RLY5016 versus 0% on placebo (P=0.094).
cards.watchOut: Four weeks and 105 patients: PEARL-HF establishes the pharmacology of the enablement strategy, nothing more. Its consistency with DIAMOND is reassuring but the two trials share the same surrogate logic.

shelves.title: Sacubitril–valsartan versus ramipril after acute myocardial infarction (PARADISE-MI)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI complicated by left-ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary congestion, or both, does sacubitril–valsartan, compared with ramipril, reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aminobutyrates · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Biphenyl Compounds · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Hypotension · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Proportional Hazards Models · Ramipril · Stroke Volume · Valsartan · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death and heart-failure events claim): the PARADISE-MI primary report (NEJM 2021; 5,661 patients with MI complicated by reduced ejection fraction, pulmonary congestion, or both; median follow-up 22 months) found the primary outcome — cardiovascular death or incident heart failure — in 11.9% on sacubitril–valsartan versus 13.2% on ramipril (HR 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.04; P=0.17): not significant, with cardiovascular death (5.9% vs 6.7%; HR 0.87 relative) and all-cause death (7.5% vs 8.5%; HR 0.88 relative) also non-significant — per the developer's rule, the heart-failure figures are printed with mortality beside them. Build note: the topic draft anchored this shelf on the trial's win-ratio analysis because the primary report could not be pinned in the drafting pass; the primary report has now been pinned (PMID 34758252) and leads the shelf. The win-ratio paper is carded second, with its status disclosed: it is a post-hoc analysis (Berwanger et al., European Journal of Heart Failure 2022 — the draft said European Heart Journal and Pfeffer as first author; the record says otherwise), it reaches significance (win ratio 1.17) only when investigator-identified events without committee confirmation are included, and its own committee-confirmed sensitivity analysis is null (win ratio 1.11, 0.96 to 1.30; P=0.16). A post-hoc re-analysis cannot overturn the primary report of the same trial: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for superiority over ramipril post-MI.

cards.headline: PARADISE-MI primary report 2021: sacubitril–valsartan was not superior to ramipril after MI — 11.9% vs 13.2%, HR 0.90, P=0.17
cards.summary: PARADISE-MI primary report 2021: sacubitril–valsartan was not superior to ramipril after MI — 11.9% vs 13.2%, HR 0.90, P=0.17
cards.people: 5,661 patients with myocardial infarction complicated by a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, pulmonary congestion, or both, randomly assigned to sacubitril–valsartan (97/103 mg twice daily; 2,830) or ramipril (5 mg twice daily; 2,831) on top of recommended therapy, over a median follow-up of 22 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (death from cardiovascular causes or incident heart failure — outpatient symptomatic heart failure or heart-failure hospitalisation — whichever first) occurred in 338 patients (11.9%) on sacubitril–valsartan versus 373 (13.2%) on ramipril (hazard ratio 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.04; P=0.17). Cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 10.9% versus 11.8% (HR 0.91 relative, 0.78 to 1.07); cardiovascular death in 5.9% versus 6.7% (HR 0.87 relative, 0.71 to 1.08); and death from any cause in 7.5% versus 8.5% (HR 0.88 relative, 0.73 to 1.05) — none significant. Treatment was discontinued for an adverse event in 12.6% versus 13.4%.
cards.watchOut: This is the trial's primary report and the shelf's governing record: a well-powered active-comparator trial that missed. The chronic-HFrEF benefit of sacubitril–valsartan (housed in the main HF shelves) does not transfer automatically to the post-MI setting, where the comparator is a proven ACE inhibitor rather than enalapril-era standard care.

cards.summary: PARADISE-MI win-ratio analysis 2022 (second report of the same trial): post-hoc win ratio 1.17 — but null on committee-confirmed events
cards.type: Post-hoc secondary analysis of the same randomised trial (not a second trial)
cards.people: The same 5,661 PARADISE-MI patients (2,830 sacubitril–valsartan; 2,831 ramipril), re-analysed by an unmatched win-ratio method over a hierarchical composite (cardiovascular death, then first heart-failure hospitalisation, then first outpatient symptomatic heart failure).
cards.result: Counting both committee-confirmed events and investigator-identified events that did not meet study definitions, the sacubitril–valsartan group recorded more wins than losses (win ratio 1.17 relative, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.33; P=0.015). This record's databank fields carry no registry ID; the trial is NCT02924727 as on the primary-report card.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc analysis that turns positive only by admitting non-adjudicated events is hypothesis-generating, and its authors' conclusion of superiority outruns the trial's own primary analysis. It is carded so the shelf shows both reports of the trial — and which one governs.

shelves.title: Eplerenone in left-ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction (EPHESUS)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI complicated by left-ventricular systolic dysfunction and heart failure (or diabetes), does adding eplerenone to standard therapy, compared with placebo, reduce all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Double-Blind Method · Eplerenone · Female · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Myocardial Infarction · Potassium · Spironolactone · Survival Analysis · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality benefit claim): EPHESUS (6,632 patients with MI complicated by left-ventricular dysfunction and heart failure, or diabetes; mean follow-up 16 months) found 478 deaths on eplerenone versus 554 on placebo (relative risk 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.96; P=0.008), with cardiovascular death (RR 0.83 relative), sudden cardiac death (RR 0.79 relative), and the co-primary composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for cardiovascular events (RR 0.87 relative) all reduced — the record prints death counts and relative risks rather than mortality percentages, and the card follows the record (the topic draft's 14.4% vs 16.7% come from the full text's denominators). cards.headline: EPHESUS 2003: eplerenone after complicated MI cut all-cause mortality — 478 vs 554 deaths, RR 0.85
cards.summary: EPHESUS 2003: eplerenone after complicated MI cut all-cause mortality — 478 vs 554 deaths, RR 0.85
cards.people: 6,632 patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure (diabetes sufficed in place of heart-failure signs), randomly assigned to eplerenone 25 mg daily titrated to a maximum of 50 mg (3,319) or placebo (3,313) in addition to optimal medical therapy, followed until 1,012 deaths had occurred (mean follow-up 16 months). cards.result: There were 478 deaths in the eplerenone group and 554 in the placebo group (relative risk 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.96; P=0.008); the abstract prints counts and relative risks rather than mortality percentages. Cardiovascular deaths numbered 407 versus 483 (RR 0.83 relative, 0.72 to 0.94; P=0.005), sudden cardiac death was reduced (RR 0.79 relative, 0.64 to 0.97; P=0.03), and the other primary end point — cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for cardiovascular events, including heart failure — was reduced (RR 0.87 relative, 0.79 to 0.95; P=0.002). Serious hyperkalaemia occurred in 5.5% on eplerenone versus 3.9% on placebo (P=0.002); hypokalaemia occurred in 8.4% versus 13.1% (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The benefit comes with a monitoring obligation: a 1.6-percentage-point absolute excess of serious hyperkalaemia in a post-MI population often also on ACE inhibitors. shelves.title: Empagliflozin in patients hospitalised with acute heart failure (EMPULSE)
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised for acute heart failure, does empagliflozin started once stabilised, compared with placebo, improve the hierarchical composite of death, heart-failure events, and symptoms at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Benzhydryl Compounds · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Glucosides · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the hierarchical composite includes death): EMPULSE (530 patients hospitalised with acute de novo or decompensated chronic heart failure, randomised a median of 3 days after admission once stable, treated for 90 days) met its primary end point: clinical benefit — a hierarchical composite of death from any cause, heart-failure events, and a ≥5-point difference in KCCQ symptom-score change — by a stratified win ratio of 1.36 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.68; P=0.0054), consistent across ejection fraction and diabetes status, with fewer serious adverse events on empagliflozin (32.3% vs 43.6%). The restraint: 530 patients and 90 days, a win ratio whose component numbers (deaths and heart-failure events separately) the abstract does not print — so neither the mortality nor the hospitalisation contribution can be quantified from this record — and a composite in which symptom scores do much of the work. A positive, well-conducted but small and short trial with an opaque composite: POSSIBLE. Distinct from Shelf #70 (SGLT2 inhibitors in chronic established HF) and from Shelf #978 (sotagliflozin in worsening HF).

cards.headline: EMPULSE 2022: empagliflozin started in hospital improved the 90-day hierarchical outcome — win ratio 1.36
cards.summary: EMPULSE 2022: empagliflozin started in hospital improved the 90-day hierarchical outcome — win ratio 1.36
cards.people: 530 patients with a primary diagnosis of acute de novo or decompensated chronic heart failure, regardless of ejection fraction, randomly assigned in hospital once clinically stable (median 3 days from admission) to empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo for up to 90 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: More patients on empagliflozin had clinical benefit — the hierarchical composite of death from any cause, number and timing of heart-failure events, or a ≥5-point difference in change in KCCQ Total Symptom Score at 90 days — than on placebo (stratified win ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.68; P=0.0054). Benefit was seen in de novo and decompensated chronic heart failure alike, and regardless of ejection fraction or diabetes. The abstract does not print the death or heart-failure-event components separately, so their individual contributions cannot be stated from this record. Serious adverse events were reported in 32.3% on empagliflozin versus 43.6% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A win ratio of 1.36 over 90 days in 530 patients is a genuine but modest evidentiary base — and because the composite mixes deaths, events, and symptoms without printed components, the shelf cannot say how much of the win is survival and how much is symptoms. Read it as 'start in hospital, benefit by 90 days', not as a mortality result.

cards.result: EMPULSE supports starting empagliflozin during an acute heart-failure admission once the patient is stable, across ejection fractions. shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibition after acute myocardial infarction at risk of heart failure (EMPACT-MI; DAPA-MI)
shelves.question: In patients with acute MI and newly reduced ejection fraction or congestion, plus an additional risk factor, does empagliflozin — and, in the companion trial, dapagliflozin in patients without diabetes or prior heart failure — compared with placebo, reduce first heart-failure hospitalisation or death?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Benzhydryl Compounds · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Glucosides · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Myocardial Infarction · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Heart Disease Risk Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death/heart-failure-hospitalisation claims): on the hard outcomes, both post-MI SGLT2 trials are null. EMPACT-MI (6,522 patients at risk of heart failure after acute MI, median follow-up 17.9 months): the primary composite of first heart-failure hospitalisation or all-cause death occurred in 8.2% on empagliflozin versus 9.1% on placebo (HR 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21); first heart-failure hospitalisation alone was lower (3.6% vs 4.7%; HR 0.77 relative, 0.60 to 0.98) while death was not (5.2% vs 5.5%; HR 0.96 relative) — the hospitalisation and mortality figures are printed together here, as they must be. DAPA-MI (4,017 post-MI patients without diabetes or prior heart failure): the cardiovascular death/heart-failure-hospitalisation composite occurred in 2.5% versus 2.6% (HR 0.95 relative, 0.64 to 1.40) — null, in a low-event population. The other half of the split: DAPA-MI's primary hierarchical win-ratio outcome was positive (1.34, 1.20 to 1.50), driven by its cardiometabolic components (new diabetes, weight, functional class) — after the analysis method was changed mid-trial because event accrual was low, a change the card discloses. So: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for preventing death or heart-failure hospitalisation after MI; POSSIBLE for a cardiometabolic composite benefit whose event core is null. Neither trial supports starting an SGLT2 inhibitor after MI to prevent heart-failure events on current evidence.

cards.headline: EMPACT-MI 2024: empagliflozin after MI missed its primary composite — 8.2% vs 9.1%, HR 0.90, P=0.21
cards.summary: EMPACT-MI 2024: empagliflozin after MI missed its primary composite — 8.2% vs 9.1%, HR 0.90, P=0.21
cards.people: 6,522 patients hospitalised for acute myocardial infarction and at risk for heart failure (newly reduced ejection fraction or congestion, plus an additional risk factor), randomly assigned within 14 days to empagliflozin 10 mg daily (3,260) or placebo (3,262) on standard care, over a median follow-up of 17.9 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A first hospitalisation for heart failure or death from any cause occurred in 267 patients (8.2%) on empagliflozin versus 298 (9.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21). For the components: first heart-failure hospitalisation in 118 (3.6%) versus 153 (4.7%) (HR 0.77 relative, 0.60 to 0.98), and death from any cause in 169 (5.2%) versus 178 (5.5%) (HR 0.96 relative, 0.78 to 1.19). Adverse events were consistent with the known profile of empagliflozin and similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The nominally lower heart-failure-hospitalisation component sits inside a null primary composite with a null mortality component; under the developer's rule no heart-failure claim is made from this trial without the mortality figure beside it — both are printed here.

cards.headline: DAPA-MI 2024: dapagliflozin's win ratio was positive on cardiometabolic outcomes — its death/HF-hospitalisation composite was null (2.5% vs 2.6%)
cards.summary: DAPA-MI 2024: dapagliflozin's win ratio was positive on cardiometabolic outcomes — its death/HF-hospitalisation composite was null (2.5% vs 2.6%)
cards.people: 4,017 patients with acute myocardial infarction and impaired left ventricular systolic function, without prior diabetes or chronic heart failure, randomly assigned to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily (2,019) or placebo (1,998) for about a year. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary hierarchical composite (death, heart-failure hospitalisation, nonfatal MI, atrial fibrillation/flutter, new type 2 diabetes, NYHA class at last visit, and ≥5% weight loss at last visit) favoured dapagliflozin (win ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.50; P<0.001) — driven, by the record's own statement, mainly by the added cardiometabolic outcomes. The composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 50 of 2,019 (2.5%) on dapagliflozin versus 52 of 1,998 (2.6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.95 relative, 0.64 to 1.40). Other cardiovascular event rates were low and not significantly different. No safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: The win-ratio outcome was adopted in a change of analysis during the trial because of low event accrual — disclosed on this card because it conditions how the positive primary should be read: the trial's event composite, the outcome this shelf's question asks about, was null. Registry-based design and a population deliberately excluding diabetes and prior heart failure further limit reach.

cards.headline: Synthesis: post-MI SGLT2 inhibition does not prevent death or HF hospitalisation on current evidence — split verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: post-MI SGLT2 inhibition does not prevent death or HF hospitalisation on current evidence — split verdict
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EMPACT-MI 2024 (6,522 patients) and DAPA-MI 2024 (4,017 patients).

shelves.title: Fully magnetically levitated centrifugal LVAD (HeartMate 3) in advanced heart failure (MOMENTUM 3)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced heart failure eligible for a durable LVAD, does the fully magnetically levitated centrifugal-flow pump, compared with the axial-flow pump, improve survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation for pump malfunction?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Heart Failure · Heart-Assist Devices · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Prosthesis Design · Prosthesis Failure · Reoperation · Stroke
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival and stroke claims): MOMENTUM 3's final report (1,028 patients with advanced heart failure, randomised irrespective of bridge-to-transplant or destination-therapy intent) found the centrifugal-flow HeartMate 3 superior on the primary composite — alive at 2 years free of disabling stroke or reoperation to replace or remove a malfunctioning device — in 76.9% versus 64.8% on the axial-flow HeartMate II (P<0.001 for superiority), driven above all by pump replacement (2.3% vs 11.3%; RR 0.21 relative): the magnetically levitated rotor nearly abolishes pump thrombosis. The 5-year extended-phase follow-up of the same trial (an observational, per-protocol analysis of patients still on support at 2 years — carded as a follow-up report, not a second trial) found the composite at 54.0% versus 29.7% (HR 0.55 relative) and overall survival 58.4% versus 43.7% (HR 0.72 relative; P=0.003). One trial programme, randomised once against the incumbent device: the device comparison carries LIKELY; the 5-year survival figures carry the observational-extension caveat on their card. The topic draft pinned the trial's 2018 interim report (first 366 patients); the final report leads this shelf and the interim report is fenced as superseded.

cards.headline: MOMENTUM 3 final report 2019: HeartMate 3 beat axial-flow on survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation — 76.9% vs 64.8% at 2 years
cards.summary: MOMENTUM 3 final report 2019: HeartMate 3 beat axial-flow on survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation — 76.9% vs 64.8% at 2 years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (final report; noninferiority and superiority design)
cards.people: 1,028 patients with advanced heart failure randomly assigned to the fully magnetically levitated centrifugal-flow pump (516) or the mechanical-bearing axial-flow pump (512), irrespective of the intended goal of support. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 2 years, 397 patients (76.9%) in the centrifugal-flow group versus 332 (64.8%) in the axial-flow group remained alive and free of disabling stroke or reoperation to replace or remove a malfunctioning device (P<0.001 for superiority). The record prints a relative risk of 0.84 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.91) alongside these proportions — as printed, that ratio runs with the risk of failing the composite, opposite to the direction of the percentages; the card prints both exactly as they appear and flags the point rather than repairing it. Pump replacement was less common with the centrifugal pump (12 patients [2.3%] vs 57 [11.3%]; RR 0.21 relative, 0.11 to 0.38; P<0.001), and events per patient-year for stroke of any severity, major bleeding, and gastrointestinal haemorrhage were lower (rates not printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: An earlier interim report of this trial (NEJM 2018, PMID 29526139; first 366 patients, 79.5% vs 60.2%) is superseded by this final report and is not counted as separate evidence. The comparator is a device no longer implanted in most programmes, so the shelf's modern relevance is the pump-thrombosis lesson, not a live device choice in most centres.
cards.source: Mehra MR et al. A Fully Magnetically Levitated Left Ventricular Assist Device — Final Report. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30883052. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02224755, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: MOMENTUM 3 five-year extended phase 2022 (follow-up of the same trial): survival 58.4% vs 43.7% — observational, per-protocol
cards.summary: MOMENTUM 3 five-year extended phase 2022 (follow-up of the same trial): survival 58.4% vs 43.7% — observational, per-protocol
cards.type: Extended-phase observational follow-up of the same randomised trial (not a second randomisation)
cards.people: Of the 1,020 patients in the trial's per-protocol population, 536 were still receiving LVAD support at 2 years; 477 (295 enrolled plus 182 providing limited data) contributed to the 5-year analysis. Median age in this follow-up set was 62 years and 18% were women.
cards.result: The 5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate of survival to transplant, recovery, or LVAD support free of debilitating stroke or reoperation was 54.0% with the centrifugal-flow pump versus 29.7% with the axial-flow pump (hazard ratio 0.55 relative, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.67; P<0.001). Overall Kaplan-Meier survival was 58.4% versus 43.7% (HR 0.72 relative, 0.58 to 0.89; P=0.003). Serious adverse events of stroke, bleeding, and pump thrombosis were less frequent in the centrifugal-flow group.
cards.watchOut: This analysis conditions on still receiving LVAD support at 2 years and is per-protocol and observational — it extends the randomised finding in time but cannot carry the same causal weight, and survivorship selection runs in both arms. It is carded as the same trial's follow-up, never as independent confirmation.

cards.summary: Synthesis: magnetic levitation wins the device comparison — LIKELY; five-year survival gap is follow-up evidence, not a second trial

shelves.title: Withdrawal of heart-failure therapy in recovered dilated cardiomyopathy (TRED-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with dilated cardiomyopathy whose ejection fraction, volumes, and biomarkers have normalised on therapy, does phased withdrawal of heart-failure treatment, compared with continuation, lead to relapse of cardiomyopathy?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers · Cardiomyopathy, Dilated · Cardiovascular Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Pilot Projects · Prognosis · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Left · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: TRED-HF (51 patients whose dilated cardiomyopathy had apparently recovered — asymptomatic, ejection fraction improved from below 40% to 50% or more, normalised volumes, NT-pro-BNP below 250 ng/L) randomised patients to phased treatment withdrawal or continuation. Within 6 months, 11 of 25 (44%) in the withdrawal group met the prespecified relapse definition versus none continuing treatment (Kaplan-Meier estimate 45.7%; P=0.0001); when the continuation group then withdrew, 9 more relapsed (36.0%). No deaths occurred; three serious adverse events (non-cardiac admissions) were reported in the withdrawal group. The effect is dramatic and the relapse definition is objective-leaning (imaging, biomarker, or clinical criteria), but this is a single, small, open-label pilot with a 6-month horizon — POSSIBLE, and enough to ground the counselling message: recovered dilated cardiomyopathy is usually remission on treatment, not cure. Not Tier C: the claim is relapse of ventricular dysfunction; no mortality claim is made (there were no deaths).

cards.headline: TRED-HF 2019: withdrawing therapy in 'recovered' DCM caused relapse in 44% within 6 months — versus none who continued
cards.summary: TRED-HF 2019: withdrawing therapy in 'recovered' DCM caused relapse in 44% within 6 months — versus none who continued
cards.people: 51 patients with previous dilated cardiomyopathy who were asymptomatic with left ventricular ejection fraction improved from below 40% to 50% or greater, normalised left ventricular end-diastolic volume, and NT-pro-BNP below 250 ng/L, randomly assigned to phased withdrawal of heart-failure treatment (25) or continuation (26), assessed at a single centre in the UK. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over the first 6 months, 11 patients (44%) assigned to withdrawal met the primary endpoint of relapse — a fall in ejection fraction of more than 10% to below 50%, a rise in ventricular volume of more than 10% beyond the normal range, a two-fold rise in NT-pro-BNP to above 400 ng/L, or clinical heart failure — versus none assigned to continue (Kaplan-Meier estimate of event rate 45.7%, 95% CI 28.5 to 67.2; P=0.0001). After 6 months, 25 of the 26 continuation patients attempted withdrawal by the same method and 9 met the relapse endpoint over the following 6 months (Kaplan-Meier estimate 36.0%). No deaths were reported in either group; three serious adverse events were reported in the withdrawal group (admissions for non-cardiac chest pain, sepsis, and an elective procedure). Treatments were re-established at relapse.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 51 patients, open-label, 6 months, single-centre assessment. The relapse definition is mostly objective, which blunts the open-label concern, but the trial cannot identify who the minority who tolerate withdrawal are — its own conclusion is that treatment should continue until such predictors exist.
cards.source: Halliday BP et al. Withdrawal of pharmacological treatment for heart failure in patients with recovered dilated cardiomyopathy (TRED-HF): an open-label, pilot, randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 30429050. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02859311, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: 'recovered' DCM usually relapses off treatment — POSSIBLE from one small pilot with a stark result
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: TRED-HF 2019 (51 patients).
cards.result: The crossover phase strengthens the inference: relapse followed withdrawal in both randomised orderings, at similar rates (44% and 36%), and in no patient who kept taking treatment. shelves.title: Aficamten for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (SEQUOIA-HCM)
shelves.question: In patients with symptomatic obstructive HCM on background therapy, does the cardiac myosin inhibitor aficamten, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity and symptoms over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Benzylamines · Cardiac Myosins · Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance · Oxygen Consumption · Uracil · Valsalva Maneuver · Ventricular Outflow Obstruction · Cardiovascular Agents · Myocardial Contraction · Administration, Oral
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: SEQUOIA-HCM (282 patients with symptomatic obstructive HCM; mean age 59.1 years; 59.2% men; mean resting gradient 55.1 mm Hg) found aficamten improved the primary end point — change in peak oxygen uptake at 24 weeks — by 1.8 versus 0.0 mL/kg/min (least-squares mean difference 1.7, 95% CI 1.0 to 2.4; P<0.001), with all 10 prespecified secondary end points (symptoms by KCCQ, NYHA class, post-Valsalva gradient, septal-reduction-therapy eligibility, workload) also significantly improved, and adverse events similar to placebo. The restraints are the class's usual ones: 24 weeks, 282 patients, and surrogate/functional end points — no outcome data on death, arrhythmia, or progression, and long-term safety is still accruing. One positive pivotal trial on functional end points: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: an exercise-capacity and symptom claim. The class's first agent, mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM), is housed on its own shelf under the one-home rule and is not duplicated here.

cards.headline: SEQUOIA-HCM 2024: aficamten raised peak oxygen uptake by 1.7 mL/kg/min more than placebo at 24 weeks, with all 10 secondary end points positive
cards.summary: SEQUOIA-HCM 2024: aficamten raised peak oxygen uptake by 1.7 mL/kg/min more than placebo at 24 weeks, with all 10 secondary end points positive
cards.people: 282 adults with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on background therapy, randomly assigned to aficamten (starting dose 5 mg, maximum 20 mg, titrated by echocardiography; 142) or placebo (140) for 24 weeks. Mean age was 59.1 years, 59.2% were men, mean resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient was 55.1 mm Hg, and mean ejection fraction 74.8%.
cards.result: At 24 weeks the mean change in peak oxygen uptake was +1.8 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3) on aficamten versus 0.0 (−0.5 to 0.5) on placebo (least-squares mean difference 1.7, 1.0 to 2.4; P<0.001). All 10 prespecified secondary end points — KCCQ clinical summary score, NYHA class improvement, post-Valsalva gradient change and abolition, duration of eligibility for septal reduction therapy, and total workload, at weeks 12 and 24 as prespecified — were significantly improved with aficamten. The incidence of adverse events appeared similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Every end point here is functional or symptomatic over 24 weeks. Whether myosin inhibition changes the disease's hard outcomes — sudden death, heart failure progression, atrial fibrillation — is not answered by this trial, and ejection-fraction surveillance is intrinsic to the class's safe use.

shelves.title: Influenza vaccination to reduce vascular events in heart failure (IVVE)
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure in low- and middle-income settings, does annual influenza vaccination, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and heart-failure hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Adolescent · Adult · Male · Influenza Vaccines · Influenza, Human · Canada · Heart Failure · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke · Pneumonia · Kenya
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): IVVE (5,129 heart-failure patients in ten countries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, vaccinated annually for up to 3 years) missed both co-primary outcomes over the full observation period: the first-event composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) at 14.8% versus 16.0% (HR 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.30), and the recurrent-events composite including heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 0.92 relative, 0.84 to 1.02; P=0.12); all-cause death, cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and heart-failure hospitalisation individually did not differ. The other half of the split: pneumonia was clearly reduced (HR 0.58 relative; P=0.0006), all-cause hospitalisation modestly so (HR 0.84 relative; P=0.013), and in the prespecified analysis restricted to periods of peak influenza circulation, the first co-primary outcome and all-cause and cardiovascular death were significantly lower with vaccination. The authors' interpretation — that a clinical benefit is likely — leans on that period-restricted analysis; this shelf presents the full-period null first and the peak-season result as the secondary, prespecified-but-conditional finding it is. Split verdict: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for year-round event prevention; POSSIBLE for benefit concentrated in influenza season. Adjacent and distinct: IAMI (vaccination after MI) is housed with the vaccine shelves (#442–#451 family).

cards.headline: IVVE 2022: influenza vaccine missed both co-primary vascular composites in heart failure (HR 0.93 and 0.92) but cut pneumonia (HR 0.58)
cards.summary: IVVE 2022: influenza vaccine missed both co-primary vascular composites in heart failure (HR 0.93 and 0.92) but cut pneumonia (HR 0.58)
cards.people: 5,129 participants aged 18 or older with heart failure (NYHA class II–IV) at 30 centres in ten countries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, randomly assigned (2,560 vaccine; 2,569 placebo) to annual intramuscular inactivated influenza vaccine or saline placebo for up to 3 years; 52.1% were women. People vaccinated in 2 of the previous 3 years were excluded.
cards.result: The first co-primary outcome (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke, first event) occurred in 380 of 2,560 (14.8%) on vaccine versus 410 of 2,569 (16.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.30). The second co-primary (the same events plus heart-failure hospitalisation, recurrent events) occurred in 754 (29.5%) versus 819 (31.9%) (HR 0.92 relative, 0.84 to 1.02; P=0.12). Among secondary outcomes, all-cause hospitalisation (HR 0.84 relative, 0.74 to 0.97; P=0.013) and pneumonia (HR 0.58 relative, 0.42 to 0.80; P=0.0006) were significantly reduced, while all-cause death, cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and heart-failure hospitalisation were not. In the prespecified analysis limited to periods of peak influenza circulation, the first co-primary outcome and the secondary outcomes of all-cause death, cardiovascular death, and pneumonia were significantly lower in the vaccine group.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own interpretation emphasises the peak-circulation analysis; readers should notice the structure — both co-primaries over the full period were null, and the positive reading depends on restricting the window to influenza season. That restriction is biologically sensible (a vaccine can only prevent influenza-triggered events while influenza circulates) and was prespecified, but it is still the weaker evidentiary leg, and it is stamped as such.

shelves.title: Apixaban for treatment and extended treatment of acute venous thromboembolism (AMPLIFY; AMPLIFY-EXT)
shelves.question: In patients with acute symptomatic proximal DVT or pulmonary embolism, is oral apixaban (without initial parenteral therapy), compared with enoxaparin followed by warfarin, noninferior for recurrent VTE and superior for major bleeding — and, after 6–12 months of anticoagulation, does extended apixaban beat placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Double-Blind Method · Enoxaparin · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles · Pyridones · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thromboembolism · Warfarin
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: AMPLIFY's primary efficacy outcome is recurrent symptomatic VTE or death related to VTE, a mortality-bearing composite, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; no mortality claim is made or supported by the record). AMPLIFY (5,395 patients with acute VTE): apixaban alone was noninferior to enoxaparin-then-warfarin for recurrent VTE or VTE-related death (2.3% vs 2.7%; RR 0.84 relative) and clearly safer — major bleeding 0.6% versus 1.8% (RR 0.31 relative) and major plus clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding 4.3% versus 9.7% (RR 0.44 relative). AMPLIFY-EXT (2,486 patients in equipoise after 6–12 months of anticoagulation) then showed both apixaban doses (2.5 mg and 5 mg twice daily) cut recurrence from 8.8% on placebo to 1.7%, without increasing major bleeding (0.2% and 0.1% vs 0.5%), with all-cause death numerically lower (0.8% and 0.5% vs 1.7% — printed here beside the recurrence figures, and not a powered mortality finding). Two large, concordant, double-blind trials (a DOUBLE-A pair): LIKELY.

cards.headline: AMPLIFY 2013: apixaban alone was noninferior to enoxaparin–warfarin for recurrent VTE (2.3% vs 2.7%) with a third of the major bleeding (0.6% vs 1.8%)
cards.summary: AMPLIFY 2013: apixaban alone was noninferior to enoxaparin–warfarin for recurrent VTE (2.3% vs 2.7%) with a third of the major bleeding (0.6% vs 1.8%)
cards.people: 5,395 patients with acute symptomatic venous thromboembolism (proximal DVT or pulmonary embolism), randomly assigned to apixaban (10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily for 6 months) or conventional therapy (subcutaneous enoxaparin followed by warfarin). The efficacy population numbered 2,609 (apixaban) and 2,635 (conventional). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (recurrent symptomatic VTE or death related to VTE) occurred in 59 of 2,609 patients (2.3%) on apixaban versus 71 of 2,635 (2.7%) on conventional therapy (relative risk 0.84 relative, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.18), meeting prespecified noninferiority for both relative risk and risk difference. Major bleeding occurred in 0.6% on apixaban versus 1.8% on conventional therapy (RR 0.31 relative, 0.17 to 0.55; P<0.001 for superiority), and the composite of major plus clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding in 4.3% versus 9.7% (RR 0.44 relative, 0.36 to 0.55; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on efficacy with superiority on safety is the strongest combination an anticoagulant trial can show — but the 6-month horizon and the selected trial population (fewer cancers, less extensive PE than real-world caseloads) bound its reach. Fixed dosing without monitoring is the practical point, not a licence to skip renal and interaction checks.

shelves.title: Rivaroxaban versus aspirin for extended secondary prevention after VTE (EINSTEIN CHOICE)
shelves.question: In patients who have completed 6–12 months of anticoagulation for VTE and in whom there is equipoise about continuing, does rivaroxaban 20 mg or 10 mg daily, compared with aspirin, prevent recurrent VTE without excess major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aspirin · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Rivaroxaban · Secondary Prevention · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here for the same reason as Shelf #1580: the primary outcome is symptomatic recurrent fatal or nonfatal VTE, a mortality-bearing composite; no mortality claim is made or supported). EINSTEIN CHOICE (3,396 patients in equipoise after 6–12 months of anticoagulation, treated for up to 12 months) found recurrent VTE in 1.5% on rivaroxaban 20 mg (HR 0.34 relative) and 1.2% on rivaroxaban 10 mg (HR 0.26 relative) versus 4.4% on aspirin — relative reductions of two-thirds to three-quarters — with major bleeding statistically indistinguishable (0.5%, 0.4%, and 0.3% respectively) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding modestly higher on rivaroxaban (2.7%, 2.0%, 1.8%). Aspirin is therefore not an adequate substitute for continued anticoagulation in this population, and the 10 mg dose performed as well as 20 mg. One large trial, consistent with AMPLIFY-EXT across the class (Shelf #1580): LIKELY.

cards.headline: EINSTEIN CHOICE 2017: rivaroxaban 20 mg and 10 mg both beat aspirin for extended VTE prevention (1.5% and 1.2% vs 4.4%)
cards.summary: EINSTEIN CHOICE 2017: rivaroxaban 20 mg and 10 mg both beat aspirin for extended VTE prevention (1.5% and 1.2% vs 4.4%)
cards.people: 3,396 patients with venous thromboembolism who had completed 6–12 months of anticoagulation and were in equipoise regarding continued anticoagulation, randomly assigned to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (1,107 in the intention-to-treat analysis), rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (1,127), or aspirin 100 mg daily (1,131) for up to 12 months (median treatment duration 351 days). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (symptomatic recurrent fatal or nonfatal VTE) occurred in 17 of 1,107 patients (1.5%) on rivaroxaban 20 mg and 13 of 1,127 (1.2%) on rivaroxaban 10 mg, versus 50 of 1,131 (4.4%) on aspirin (hazard ratio for 20 mg vs aspirin 0.34 relative, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.59; for 10 mg vs aspirin 0.26 relative, 0.14 to 0.47; P<0.001 for both). Major bleeding occurred in 0.5% (20 mg), 0.4% (10 mg) and 0.3% (aspirin); clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding in 2.7%, 2.0% and 1.8% respectively. Overall adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: The comparator lesson cuts both ways: aspirin lost badly on efficacy, so this trial should not be cited as showing aspirin 'works' for extended prophylaxis. And the equipoise entry criterion matters — these were patients for whom stopping was a genuine option, not the highest-risk recurrence group.

shelves.title: Aspirin versus rivaroxaban for extended prophylaxis after hip or knee arthroplasty (EPCAT II)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty who have received 5 days of rivaroxaban, is switching to aspirin, compared with continuing rivaroxaban, noninferior for preventing symptomatic VTE and as safe for major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee · Aspirin · Double-Blind Method · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Postoperative Complications · Risk Factors · Rivaroxaban · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: LIKELY: EPCAT II (3,424 arthroplasty patients, all given rivaroxaban 10 mg for the first 5 postoperative days, then randomised) found symptomatic VTE in 0.64% after switching to aspirin 81 mg versus 0.70% on continued rivaroxaban (difference 0.06 percentage points; P<0.001 for noninferiority), over an additional 9 days (knee) or 30 days (hip) of prophylaxis with 90-day follow-up. Major bleeding was 0.47% on aspirin versus 0.29% on rivaroxaban (P=0.42), and clinically important bleeding 1.29% versus 0.99% — no significant differences, with point estimates marginally favouring rivaroxaban on safety even as efficacy was identical. One large, well-conducted trial with a clear-cut result: after a 5-day rivaroxaban lead-in, aspirin is an equally effective, cheaper completion strategy. LIKELY. Not Tier C: symptomatic VTE and bleeding claims only.

cards.headline: EPCAT II 2018: after 5 days of rivaroxaban, switching to aspirin was noninferior for VTE prophylaxis after arthroplasty (0.64% vs 0.70%)
cards.summary: EPCAT II 2018: after 5 days of rivaroxaban, switching to aspirin was noninferior for VTE prophylaxis after arthroplasty (0.64% vs 0.70%)
cards.people: 3,424 patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty (1,804) or total knee arthroplasty (1,620), all of whom received rivaroxaban 10 mg daily until postoperative day 5 and were then randomly assigned to switch to aspirin 81 mg daily (1,707) or continue rivaroxaban (1,717) for a further 9 days (knee) or 30 days (hip), with 90 days of follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age; the record's MeSH terms do not include a female descriptor.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism occurred in 11 of 1,707 patients (0.64%) in the aspirin group and 12 of 1,717 (0.70%) in the rivaroxaban group (difference 0.06 percentage points, 95% CI −0.55 to 0.66; P<0.001 for noninferiority, P=0.84 for superiority). Major bleeding complications occurred in 8 patients (0.47%) on aspirin and 5 (0.29%) on rivaroxaban (difference 0.18 points, −0.65 to 0.29; P=0.42), and clinically important bleeding in 22 (1.29%) versus 17 (0.99%) (P=0.43).
cards.watchOut: Every patient received 5 days of rivaroxaban first — the trial licenses a switch strategy, not aspirin from day zero, and its predecessor (EPCAT I, hip arthroplasty with a dalteparin comparator) is context, not carded. Event rates under 1% mean the absolute stakes of the choice are small either way.

shelves.title: Fondaparinux for superficial-vein thrombosis of the legs (CALISTO)
shelves.question: In patients with acute symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis of the lower limbs at least 5 cm long, does fondaparinux 2.5 mg for 45 days, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death, symptomatic VTE, and extension or recurrence of superficial thrombosis?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Anticoagulants · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fondaparinux · Hemorrhage · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Polysaccharides · Pulmonary Embolism · Recurrence · Risk · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: the primary composite leads with death from any cause among its components, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; deaths were identical at 0.1% in both groups and no mortality claim is made). CALISTO (3,002 patients with acute symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis at least 5 cm long, without concomitant DVT or PE) found 45 days of fondaparinux 2.5 mg cut the primary composite (death, symptomatic PE or DVT, extension to the saphenofemoral junction, or recurrence) from 5.9% to 0.9% at day 47 — an 85% relative risk reduction as printed in the record — with PE or DVT specifically at 0.2% versus 1.3% (88 patients needed to treat to prevent one), death identical (0.1% both groups), and major bleeding in one patient per group. One large trial with a big effect on a clinically meaningful composite and a clean safety record: LIKELY, with the caveat that most prevented events were extension and recurrence of superficial thrombosis rather than embolism.

cards.headline: CALISTO 2010: fondaparinux for 45 days cut the superficial-thrombosis composite from 5.9% to 0.9% — with no excess bleeding
cards.summary: CALISTO 2010: fondaparinux for 45 days cut the superficial-thrombosis composite from 5.9% to 0.9% — with no excess bleeding
cards.people: 3,002 patients with acute, symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis of the legs at least 5 cm long, without concomitant deep-vein thrombosis or symptomatic pulmonary embolism, randomly assigned to fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously once daily (1,502) or placebo (1,500) for 45 days, with follow-up to day 77. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (death from any cause, symptomatic pulmonary embolism, symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis, symptomatic extension to the saphenofemoral junction, or symptomatic recurrence of superficial-vein thrombosis, at day 47) occurred in 13 of 1,502 patients (0.9%) on fondaparinux versus 88 of 1,500 (5.9%) on placebo (relative risk reduction 85% relative, 95% CI 74 to 92; P<0.001 — the record prints the relative risk reduction; the corresponding risk ratio is not printed). Every component except death was significantly reduced; death occurred in 0.1% in both groups. Pulmonary embolism or deep-vein thrombosis occurred in 0.2% versus 1.3% (85% lower in relative terms), with 88 patients needing treatment to prevent one such event. Major bleeding occurred in one patient in each group; serious adverse events occurred in 0.7% versus 1.1%. Similar reductions held at day 77.
cards.watchOut: The composite is dominated by extension and recurrence of superficial thrombosis — uncomfortable and treatment-changing, but not embolism; the hard-event yield is the 1.1-percentage-point absolute reduction in PE/DVT. Cost and 45 days of injections for a mostly self-limited condition remain the legitimate counter-arguments.

shelves.title: Graduated compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome (SOX)
shelves.question: In patients with a first proximal DVT, do graduated compression stockings worn for two years, compared with placebo (sham) stockings, prevent post-thrombotic syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Canada · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Postthrombotic Syndrome · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Stockings, Compression · Treatment Outcome · United States · Venous Thrombosis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): SOX (806 patients with a first symptomatic proximal DVT in Canada and the USA) is the trial that reversed a decades-old practice by finally using a sham control: post-thrombotic syndrome by Ginsberg's criteria occurred in 14.2% with active graduated compression stockings versus 12.7% with placebo stockings worn for 2 years (HR 1.13 relative, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.76; P=0.58) — a point estimate on the harm side of null — and the prespecified per-protocol analysis of frequent wearers was the same. The older positive trials (Brandjes, Prandoni) were small, single-centre and open-label without sham stockings, which is why this blinded trial governs the shelf. One well-designed trial against weak contrary evidence: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome. Not Tier C: a symptom-syndrome claim only.

cards.headline: SOX 2014: sham-controlled trial found compression stockings did NOT prevent post-thrombotic syndrome — 14.2% vs 12.7%, HR 1.13
cards.summary: SOX 2014: sham-controlled trial found compression stockings did NOT prevent post-thrombotic syndrome — 14.2% vs 12.7%, HR 1.13
cards.people: 806 patients with a first symptomatic proximal deep-vein thrombosis at centres in Canada and the USA, randomly assigned to active graduated compression stockings (410) or placebo stockings (396) for 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The cumulative incidence of post-thrombotic syndrome (diagnosed at 6 months or later by Ginsberg's criteria — leg pain and swelling of at least a month's duration) was 14.2% in the active-stocking group versus 12.7% in the placebo group (hazard ratio adjusted for centre 1.13 relative, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.76; P=0.58). A prespecified per-protocol analysis of patients who reported frequent use of their allocated stockings gave similar results.
cards.watchOut: The trial's importance is methodological: it is the first sham-controlled test of a practice that open-label trials had entrenched. The result addresses prevention of the syndrome after a first proximal DVT — it does not speak to stockings for symptom relief in established post-thrombotic syndrome, a different question.

shelves.title: Large-bore mechanical thrombectomy versus catheter-directed thrombolysis for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PEERLESS)
shelves.question: In patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, does large-bore mechanical thrombectomy, compared with catheter-directed thrombolysis, improve the hierarchical composite of death, intracranial haemorrhage, major bleeding, clinical deterioration, and ICU use?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Pulmonary Embolism · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Thrombolytic Therapy · Aged · Prospective Studies · Thrombectomy · Treatment Outcome · Risk Factors · Length of Stay · Fibrinolytic Agents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death and intracranial haemorrhage): PEERLESS (550 patients with intermediate-risk PE, right-ventricular dilatation and additional risk factors) met its primary end point for large-bore mechanical thrombectomy over catheter-directed thrombolysis (win ratio 5.01, 95% CI 3.68 to 6.97; P<0.001) — but the win is carried by the softest components: post-procedural ICU admission (41.6% vs 98.6%) and ICU stay over 24 hours (19.3% vs 64.5%), in a comparison where the thrombolysis pathway conventionally mandates ICU care, plus less clinical deterioration or bailout (1.8% vs 5.4%; P=0.04). On the hard components there was no difference: the secondary win ratio excluding ICU use was 1.34 (0.78 to 2.35; P=0.30), and 30-day mortality was 0.4% versus 0.8% (P=0.62) — mortality is printed here beside the composite, as it must be. Hospital stay was shorter (4.5 vs 5.3 nights) and readmissions fewer (3.2% vs 7.9%). A first-of-kind, open-label device trial whose headline number overstates its hard-outcome content: POSSIBLE for the procedural-strategy claim, with the composition of the win stated plainly. The follow-on trial against anticoagulation alone (PEERLESS II) is in flight and is named on the closing card.

cards.headline: PEERLESS 2025: thrombectomy beat thrombolysis on the hierarchical composite (win ratio 5.01) — driven by ICU use, not by death or bleeding
cards.summary: PEERLESS 2025: thrombectomy beat thrombolysis on the hierarchical composite (win ratio 5.01) — driven by ICU use, not by death or bleeding
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, controlled trial (device versus catheter-directed therapy)
cards.people: 550 patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism with right-ventricular dilatation and additional clinical risk factors, randomly assigned 1:1 to large-bore mechanical thrombectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary hierarchical end point (all-cause mortality; intracranial haemorrhage; major bleeding; clinical deterioration and/or escalation to bailout; post-procedural ICU admission and length of stay — assessed at the sooner of discharge or 7 days) favoured thrombectomy (win ratio 5.01, 95% CI 3.68 to 6.97; P<0.001). Clinical deterioration and/or bailout occurred in 1.8% versus 5.4% (P=0.04); post-procedural ICU admissions were 41.6% versus 98.6% and ICU stays over 24 hours 19.3% versus 64.5% (both P<0.001). There were no significant differences in mortality, intracranial haemorrhage, or major bleeding, and the secondary win ratio restricted to the first four components was 1.34 (0.78 to 2.35; P=0.30). At 24 hours, respiratory rate, dyspnoea scores, NYHA class and right-ventricular dysfunction all favoured thrombectomy, with similar RV/LV ratio reduction. Total hospital stay was 4.5 versus 5.3 nights (P=0.002), all-cause readmission 3.2% versus 7.9% (P=0.03), and 30-day mortality 0.4% versus 0.8% (P=0.62).
cards.watchOut: Read the win ratio's recipe before quoting it: when one strategy's standard care requires ICU admission and the other's does not, ICU use inside the primary composite nearly guarantees the result. The trial's hard-outcome comparison — death, intracranial haemorrhage, major bleeding — is the secondary win ratio of 1.34, and it is null. Open-label design compounds the caution for the deterioration/bailout component.
cards.source: Jaber WA et al. Large-Bore Mechanical Thrombectomy Versus Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis in the Management of Intermediate-Risk Pulmonary Embolism: Primary Results of the PEERLESS Randomized Controlled Trial. Circulation. 2025. PMID: 39470698. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05111613, from the record's databank fields. cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: PEERLESS 2025 (550 patients with intermediate-risk PE).
cards.result: PEERLESS establishes that a thrombectomy-first strategy gets patients out of ICU and hospital faster with less early deterioration than catheter-directed thrombolysis, at no measured hard-outcome advantage or penalty in 550 patients. That is a real but narrower claim than 'win ratio 5.01' suggests. The comparison that would change practice most — thrombectomy versus anticoagulation alone — is being tested in PEERLESS II, which is in flight and named here so this shelf is re-swept when it reports.
cards.watchOut: Neither arm of PEERLESS is anticoagulation alone: the shelf cannot say whether either intervention beats heparin for intermediate-risk PE. That question stays open until PEERLESS II and its contemporaries report.

shelves.title: Cilostazol for intermittent claudication
shelves.question: In patients with intermittent claudication from peripheral artery disease, does cilostazol, compared with placebo, increase maximal walking distance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cilostazol · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Female · Humans · Intermittent Claudication · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Risk Factors · Survival Analysis · Tetrazoles · Treatment Outcome · United States · Vasodilator Agents · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: the pivotal trial (Beebe et al., 1999; 516 patients with moderately severe stable claudication, 24 weeks) found cilostazol 100 mg twice daily produced a 51% geometric-mean improvement in maximal walking distance and 50 mg a 38% improvement (both P<0.001 versus placebo; the record does not print the placebo group's geometric-mean change, so no placebo-adjusted percentage is stated), with maximal distance rising in absolute terms from 129.7 m to 258.8 m on the 100 mg dose, corroborated by pain-free distance, quality-of-life and global assessments. Headache, diarrhoea, dizziness and palpitations were the common adverse effects; withdrawals for adverse events were 14.5% overall, evenly spread; there was no difference in cardiovascular morbidity or all-cause mortality. Two corrections to the topic draft: the anchor's first author is Beebe HG (Dawson DL is second author), and the draft's '~25% over placebo' figure is not what this record prints — the card follows the record. The pentoxifylline-comparator trial in the programme (Dawson 2000) could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced, not carded. Old, smallish trials, a surrogate end point, and an agent contraindicated in heart failure: POSSIBLE for a modest walking-distance benefit. Not Tier C: no events claim (the mortality line is a safety observation, printed as such).

cards.headline: Beebe 1999: cilostazol 100 mg twice daily improved maximal walking distance by 51% (geometric mean) over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Beebe 1999: cilostazol 100 mg twice daily improved maximal walking distance by 51% (geometric mean) over 24 weeks
cards.people: 516 men and women aged 40 or older with moderately severe chronic stable symptomatic intermittent claudication (663 screened) at 37 US outpatient vascular clinics, randomly assigned to cilostazol 100 mg twice daily, cilostazol 50 mg twice daily, or placebo for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex breakdown.
cards.result: Superiority over placebo was evident from week 4. At 24 weeks, maximal walking distance improved by a geometric mean of 51% on cilostazol 100 mg and 38% on 50 mg (both P<0.001 versus placebo; the placebo group's geometric-mean change is not printed in the abstract). In arithmetic terms, mean maximal distance rose from 129.7 m at baseline to 258.8 m at week 24 on the 100 mg dose, and from 131.5 m to 198.8 m on the 50 mg dose. Pain-free walking distance improved by geometric means of 59% and 48% respectively. Subjective quality-of-life and global assessments corroborated the treadmill results. Headache, abnormal stools or diarrhoea, dizziness, and palpitations were the most common potentially drug-related adverse events and were self-limited; 75 patients (14.5%) withdrew for adverse events, evenly across groups, and there were no between-group differences in combined cardiovascular morbidity or all-cause mortality.
cards.watchOut: A 1999 trial with geometric-mean percentage reporting and no printed placebo change: the honest summary is 'walking distance clearly improves, by an amount that is hard to state precisely from this record'. Cilostazol is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity — a population overlap with claudication that prescribers must actively check.
cards.source: Beebe HG et al. A new pharmacological treatment for intermittent claudication: results of a randomized, multicenter trial. Archives of internal medicine. 1999. PMID: 10510990. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (a 1999 trial, predating routine registration).
