shelves.title: Renal-artery stenting versus medical therapy for atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis (CORAL; ASTRAL)
shelves.question: In patients with atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis and hypertension or chronic kidney disease, does renal-artery stenting plus medical therapy, compared with medical therapy alone, reduce cardiovascular and renal events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amlodipine · Angioplasty, Balloon · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers · Anticholesteremic Agents · Antihypertensive Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Combined Modality Therapy · Drug Combinations · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heptanoic Acids · Humans · Hypertension · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrroles · Renal Artery · Renal Artery Obstruction · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Stents · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes cardiovascular/renal death, MI, and stroke): two large trials agree. CORAL (947 patients with renal-artery stenosis and hypertension on two or more drugs or CKD; median follow-up 43 months) found the composite of cardiovascular or renal death, MI, stroke, heart-failure hospitalisation, progressive renal insufficiency, or dialysis in 35.1% with stenting versus 35.8% without (HR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.17; P=0.58), no component differences, and no all-cause-mortality difference — only a 2.3 mm Hg systolic advantage. ASTRAL (806 patients, unblinded; median follow-up 34 months) found no worthwhile difference in renal-function trajectory (P=0.06), renal events (HR 0.97 relative), major cardiovascular events (HR 0.94 relative), or death (HR 0.90 relative), while revascularisation itself caused serious complications in 23 patients, including 2 deaths and 3 amputations. Two concordant large nulls (a DOUBLE-A pair) with procedural harm on the record: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine stenting in atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis.

cards.headline: CORAL 2014: renal-artery stenting did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events — 35.1% vs 35.8%, HR 0.94
cards.summary: CORAL 2014: renal-artery stenting did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events — 35.1% vs 35.8%, HR 0.94
cards.people: 947 participants with atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis and either systolic hypertension on two or more antihypertensive drugs or chronic kidney disease, randomly assigned to medical therapy plus renal-artery stenting or medical therapy alone, followed for a median of 43 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite end point (death from cardiovascular or renal causes, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospitalisation for congestive heart failure, progressive renal insufficiency, or need for renal-replacement therapy) occurred in 35.1% with stenting versus 35.8% with medical therapy alone (hazard ratio 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.17; P=0.58). No individual component, and not all-cause mortality, differed significantly. Systolic blood pressure was modestly lower with stenting (−2.3 mm Hg, 95% CI −4.4 to −0.2; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: CORAL excluded some phenotypes clinicians most want to stent (flash pulmonary oedema, rapidly declining function with bilateral disease) — its null governs the broad atherosclerotic population randomised, and those rescue indications remain untested rather than disproven.
cards.source: Cooper CJ et al. Stenting and medical therapy for atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24245566. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00081731, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ASTRAL 2009: revascularisation likewise showed no renal or event benefit — and caused 23 serious complications, including 2 deaths
cards.summary: ASTRAL 2009: revascularisation likewise showed no renal or event benefit — and caused 23 serious complications, including 2 deaths
cards.people: 806 patients with atherosclerotic renovascular disease randomly assigned to revascularisation plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone, followed for a median of 34 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — renal function measured by the slope of the reciprocal of serum creatinine — differed by 0.06 ×10⁻³ L/µmol per year in favour of revascularisation (95% CI −0.002 to 0.13; P=0.06), and mean serum creatinine was 1.6 µmol/L (≈0.02 mg/dL) lower with revascularisation (CI spanning zero). There were no significant differences in renal events (hazard ratio 0.97 relative, 0.67 to 1.40; P=0.88), major cardiovascular events (HR 0.94 relative, 0.75 to 1.19; P=0.61), or death (HR 0.90 relative, 0.69 to 1.18; P=0.46); diastolic pressure fell less in the revascularisation group. Serious complications of revascularisation occurred in 23 patients, including 2 deaths and 3 amputations of toes or limbs.
cards.watchOut: ASTRAL was unblinded and enrolled many patients whose clinicians were uncertain — including some with mild disease — which biases toward null; CORAL's tighter design reaching the same answer is what makes the pair decisive.
cards.source: Wheatley K et al. (ASTRAL Investigators). Revascularization versus medical therapy for renal-artery stenosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2009. PMID: 19907042. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN59586944, from the record's databank fields (no ClinicalTrials.gov ID in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: routine renal-artery stenting does not prevent events — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with procedural harm documented
cards.summary: Synthesis: routine renal-artery stenting does not prevent events — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with procedural harm documented
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CORAL 2014 (947 patients) and ASTRAL 2009 (806 patients).
cards.result: Across 1,753 randomised patients, opening an atherosclerotic renal artery did not reduce death, cardiovascular events, or renal failure, and the procedure itself killed and maimed a small number in ASTRAL. Medical therapy is the default this evidence supports.
cards.watchOut: Both trials under-enrolled the flash-pulmonary-oedema and rapid-decline phenotypes; the shelf's null is for the populations randomised, and those niches remain a matter of judgement, not evidence.

shelves.title: Doxycycline to slow growth of small abdominal aortic aneurysms (N-TA3CT)
shelves.question: In patients with small (3.5–5.0 cm) infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms, does doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two years, compared with placebo, slow aneurysm growth?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Aorta, Abdominal · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal · Doxycycline · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Size · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): N-TA3CT (261 patients aged 50 or older with small infrarenal aneurysms — 3.5–5.0 cm in men, 3.5–4.5 cm in women; mean age 71.0 years; 14% women) found no effect of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily on aneurysm growth over 2 years: the primary rank-based analysis was null (one-sided P=0.71), and the directly measured change in maximum transverse diameter was identical — 0.36 cm in both groups (difference 0.0 cm, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.07; two-sided P=0.93). Aneurysm repair occurred in 10% versus 7% and death in 2% versus 3% (both embedded in the rank outcome and printed here for completeness). No patient withdrew for adverse effects; joint pain was common in both groups (65% vs 63%). The topic draft's growth figures (≈0.36 vs 0.31 cm/year) do not match the record, which prints 0.36 cm versus 0.36 cm total over 2 years — the card follows the record. One definitive trial with a precisely estimated zero: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Not Tier C: an aneurysm-growth claim.

cards.headline: N-TA3CT 2020: doxycycline did not slow small aneurysm growth — diameter grew 0.36 cm in both groups over 2 years
cards.summary: N-TA3CT 2020: doxycycline did not slow small aneurysm growth — diameter grew 0.36 cm in both groups over 2 years
cards.people: 261 patients aged 50 or older with small infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms (3.5–5.0 cm in men, 3.5–4.5 cm in women) at 22 US centres, randomly assigned to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (133) or placebo (128) for 2 years; the analysis set numbered 129 and 125 after 7 patients had no follow-up CT. Mean age was 71.0 years and 35 patients (14%) were women.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a rank-based 'normal score' combining measured change in maximum transverse diameter with aneurysm repair and death — did not differ between groups (mean change in normal scores 0.0262 vs −0.0258; one-sided P=0.71). The measured change in maximum transverse diameter at 2 years was 0.36 cm (95% CI 0.31 to 0.40) on doxycycline versus 0.36 cm (0.30 to 0.41) on placebo (difference 0.0 cm, −0.07 to 0.07; two-sided P=0.93), from a mean baseline diameter of 4.3 cm in both groups. Aneurysm repair occurred in 13 patients (10%) versus 9 (7%), and death in 3 (2%) versus 4 (3%). No patient withdrew because of adverse effects; joint pain occurred in 65% versus 63%.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval on diameter change (−0.07 to +0.07 cm over 2 years) excludes any growth effect worth having — this is an informative null, not an underpowered one. Smaller earlier doxycycline trials were likewise null or worse and are not needed to stamp it.
cards.source: Baxter BT et al. Effect of Doxycycline on Aneurysm Growth Among Patients With Small Infrarenal Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 32453369. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01756833, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Endovascular repair versus no intervention in patients unfit for open AAA repair (EVAR-2)
shelves.question: In patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm of at least 5.5 cm who are physically ineligible for open repair, does endovascular aneurysm repair, compared with no intervention, reduce all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal · Blood Vessel Prosthesis Implantation · Female · Humans · Male · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Stents · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, all-cause mortality claim): EVAR-2 (338 patients aged 60 or older with aneurysms of at least 5.5 cm judged unfit for open repair, at 31 UK hospitals) found no survival benefit from endovascular repair: all-cause mortality did not differ (HR 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.69; P=0.25 — the point estimate runs against EVAR), aneurysm-related mortality did not differ in this report, overall mortality reached 64% by 4 years, and EVAR carried a 9% 30-day operative mortality in this frail group plus substantially higher costs (£13,632 vs £4,983 per patient over 4 years) with no quality-of-life gain. Crossover was substantial (47 patients assigned no intervention underwent repair; adherence 80%), which biases toward null — one reason the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. The topic draft's 'fewer aneurysm-related deaths later' belongs to the trial's long-term follow-up report, not this record, whose abstract reports no difference in aneurysm-related mortality; it is fenced here. EVAR-1 and OVER address fit patients and are separate questions.

cards.headline: EVAR-2 2005: in patients unfit for open repair, EVAR did not improve survival over no intervention (HR 1.21) and cost far more
cards.summary: EVAR-2 2005: in patients unfit for open repair, EVAR did not improve survival over no intervention (HR 1.21) and cost far more
cards.people: 338 patients aged 60 years or older with abdominal aortic aneurysms of at least 5.5 cm diameter who were physically ineligible for open repair, at 31 UK hospitals, randomly assigned to endovascular aneurysm repair (166) or no intervention (172). In all, 197 patients underwent aneurysm repair — including 47 assigned to no intervention — and 80% adhered to protocol. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, all-cause mortality, did not differ between groups (hazard ratio 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.69; P=0.25), and there was no difference in aneurysm-related mortality: 142 patients died during follow-up, 42 of aneurysm-related causes, with overall mortality of 64% after 4 years. The 30-day operative mortality in the EVAR group was 9% (13 of 150), and the no-intervention group had an aneurysm rupture rate of 9.0 per 100 person-years. Mean hospital costs over 4 years were £13,632 per patient with EVAR versus £4,983 with no intervention (difference £8,649), with no difference in health-related quality-of-life scores.
cards.watchOut: One in five patients crossed over, diluting the comparison toward null — the honest reading is 'no benefit shown, in a frail population with heavy competing mortality', not proof that no subgroup benefits. The trial's later long-term follow-up is a separate report and is not carded here; this record's aneurysm-mortality line is 'no difference'.
cards.source: EVAR trial participants. Endovascular aneurysm repair and outcome in patients unfit for open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm (EVAR trial 2): randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2005. PMID: 15978926. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (a 2005 trial). The record carries no individual author list; the paper is group-authored. cards.summary: Synthesis: fixing the aneurysm did not extend life in patients too unfit for open surgery — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

cards.result: In a population where two-thirds are dead within 4 years whatever is done, aneurysm exclusion did not convert into survival — competing mortality dominates, and the procedure's own 9% upfront mortality in this group is part of the arithmetic. shelves.title: Bosentan to prevent new digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis (RAPIDS-1 and RAPIDS-2)
shelves.question: In patients with systemic sclerosis and a history of digital ulcers, does bosentan, compared with placebo, reduce the number of new digital ulcers over 16–24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bosentan · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Female · Fingers · Hand Dermatoses · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Scleroderma, Systemic · Skin Ulcer · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from the same programme point the same way on the same surrogate-style count endpoint: RAPIDS-1 (122 patients, 16 weeks) found 48% fewer new ulcers on bosentan (mean 1.4 vs 2.7; P=0.0083), and RAPIDS-2 (188 patients, 24 weeks) found a 30% reduction (mean 1.9 vs 2.7 new ulcers; P=0.04) — both figures are relative reductions in ulcer counts, and neither trial showed any benefit on healing of existing ulcers, pain, or disability. The effect is consistent but rests on ulcer counts in a single sponsor programme in a restricted population, with the class's known hepatic signal (aminotransferase elevations in RAPIDS-2; transaminases >3× the upper limit of normal in RAPIDS-1) and no patient-centred outcome gain. Two concordant RCTs on a count endpoint with null secondary clinical outcomes: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RAPIDS-2 2011: bosentan cut new digital ulcers by 30% relative (mean 1.9 vs 2.7 over 24 weeks) but did not speed healing of existing ulcers
cards.summary: RAPIDS-2 2011: bosentan cut new digital ulcers by 30% relative (mean 1.9 vs 2.7 over 24 weeks) but did not speed healing of existing ulcers
cards.people: 188 patients with systemic sclerosis and at least one active digital ulcer ('cardinal ulcer') at 41 centres in Europe and North America, randomised to bosentan (62.5 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, then 125 mg twice daily for 20 weeks; n=98) or placebo (n=90). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over 24 weeks, bosentan was associated with a 30% relative reduction in the number of new digital ulcers compared with placebo (mean ± SE: 1.9±0.2 vs 2.7±0.3; P=0.04), with a greater effect in patients entering with more ulcers. There was no difference between treatments in healing of the cardinal ulcer, or in the secondary endpoints of pain and disability. Peripheral oedema and elevated aminotransferases were associated with bosentan treatment.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is confined to preventing new ulcers; healing, pain, and disability were all unchanged, so this is not a treatment for established ulcers. The hepatic signal is a class effect that requires monitoring, and the trial population (patients with an active ulcer at entry) is narrower than systemic sclerosis at large.
cards.source: Matucci-Cerinic M et al. Bosentan treatment of digital ulcers related to systemic sclerosis: results from the RAPIDS-2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2011. PMID: 20805294. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (stated as absent, not supplied). cards.headline: RAPIDS-1 2004: bosentan reduced new ulcers by 48% relative (1.4 vs 2.7 over 16 weeks), with transaminase elevations >3× normal
cards.summary: RAPIDS-1 2004: bosentan reduced new ulcers by 48% relative (1.4 vs 2.7 over 16 weeks), with transaminase elevations >3× normal
cards.people: 122 patients with systemic sclerosis at 17 centres in Europe and North America, randomised to bosentan or placebo for 16 weeks; the primary outcome was the number of new digital ulcers during the study period. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Patients receiving bosentan had a 48% relative reduction in the mean number of new ulcers (1.4 vs 2.7 new ulcers; P=0.0083). In the subgroup with digital ulcers at entry, the mean number of new ulcers fell from 3.6 to 1.8 (P=0.0075). Hand function improved significantly on bosentan, but there was no difference in healing of existing ulcers. Serum transaminase levels were elevated to >3-fold the upper limit of normal in bosentan-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: The hand-function gain seen here was not reproduced as a pain or disability benefit in RAPIDS-2, so it should not be carried forward as established. Both trials come from one development programme; there is no independent replication.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bosentan prevents new scleroderma digital ulcers in two concordant trials, without healing existing ones — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: bosentan prevents new scleroderma digital ulcers in two concordant trials, without healing existing ones — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RAPIDS-2 2011 (188 patients, 24 weeks) and RAPIDS-1 2004 (122 patients, 16 weeks).
cards.result: A single-programme pair of double-blind trials with the same directional result on new-ulcer counts (30% and 48% relative reductions) and the same null result on healing, pain, and disability. The claim the record supports is narrow: fewer new ulcers in patients with systemic sclerosis who already ulcerate, bought at the price of hepatic monitoring.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate routine trial-registration databank fields, and neither record carries a registry ID; none has been invented. Ulcer count is a surrogate for the outcomes patients feel — tissue loss and amputation were not endpoints in either trial.

shelves.title: Dabigatran versus warfarin for cerebral venous thrombosis (RE-SPECT CVT), with the SECRET rivaroxaban feasibility trial
shelves.question: In patients with cerebral venous thrombosis stabilised after initial parenteral anticoagulation, is dabigatran, compared with dose-adjusted warfarin, similarly safe and effective over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Antithrombins · Dabigatran · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Humans · Intracranial Thrombosis · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis · Warfarin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: the second carded trial, SECRET, has a primary safety composite that includes mortality at 180 days, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; no mortality claim is made or supported — the only primary-outcome event in SECRET was a haemorrhage, and RE-SPECT CVT recorded no deaths as an endpoint). RE-SPECT CVT (120 patients, exploratory, open-label with blinded adjudication) found no recurrent VTE in either arm over 24 weeks, one major bleed on dabigatran (intestinal, 1.7%) versus two on warfarin (both intracranial, 3.3%) — reassuring but far too small to establish efficacy, with zero events in both arms. SECRET (55 patients, rivaroxaban vs standard care) was a feasibility trial: its single primary safety event, and all its bleeding and recurrence events, fell in the rivaroxaban arm, at rates the authors describe as low overall. Two small trials, no efficacy events between them, directionally reassuring safety: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RE-SPECT CVT 2019: no recurrent VTE in either arm; major bleeding 1.7% on dabigatran vs 3.3% on warfarin in 120 patients
cards.summary: RE-SPECT CVT 2019: no recurrent VTE in either arm; major bleeding 1.7% on dabigatran vs 3.3% on warfarin in 120 patients
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial with blinded endpoint adjudication (PROBE), exploratory
cards.people: 120 adults with acute cerebral venous thrombosis, stable after 5–15 days of parenteral heparin, at 51 sites in 9 countries, randomised to dabigatran 150 mg twice daily (n=60) or dose-adjusted warfarin (n=60) for 24 weeks. Mean (SD) age 45.2 (13.8) years; 66 (55.0%) were women. Patients with CVT from CNS infection or major trauma were excluded; intracranial haemorrhage from the index CVT was allowed.
cards.result: No recurrent venous thromboembolism was observed in either group. One major bleeding event (intestinal; 1.7%, 95% CI 0.0–8.9) occurred in the dabigatran group and two (both intracranial; 3.3%, 95% CI 0.4–11.5) in the warfarin group; one additional warfarin patient had a clinically relevant non-major bleed. Recanalisation occurred in 60.0% on dabigatran and 67.3% on warfarin. The authors conclude both drugs may be safe and effective, in a trial explicitly designed as exploratory.
cards.watchOut: Zero events in both arms means the trial cannot distinguish the drugs on efficacy — it bounds only very large harms. The warfarin bleeds were intracranial and the dabigatran bleed was intestinal, a pattern worth noting but based on three events in total.
cards.source: Ferro JM et al. Safety and Efficacy of Dabigatran Etexilate vs Dose-Adjusted Warfarin in Patients With Cerebral Venous Thrombosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA neurology. 2019. cards.headline: SECRET 2023: 55-patient rivaroxaban feasibility trial — the single primary safety event and all bleeding/recurrence events fell in the rivaroxaban arm
cards.summary: SECRET 2023: 55-patient rivaroxaban feasibility trial — the single primary safety event and all bleeding/recurrence events fell in the rivaroxaban arm
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint phase II feasibility trial
cards.people: 55 adults within 14 days of a new symptomatic cerebral venous thrombosis at 12 Canadian centres, randomised to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily or standard-of-care anticoagulation (warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin) for 180 days. Median age 48.0 years (IQR 38.5–73.2); 66% were female.
cards.result: The primary safety outcome was a composite of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, major extracranial haemorrhage, or mortality at 180 days. There was 1 primary event (a symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage), 2 clinically relevant non-major bleeding events, and 1 recurrent CVT by day 180 — all in the rivaroxaban group. All participants in both arms had at least partial recanalisation by day 180. Recruitment reached 21.3 participants/year, with 57% of eligible candidates consenting.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial answers 'can a definitive trial be run?', not 'which drug is better?' — with 55 patients and four total events, the clustering of events in the rivaroxaban arm is a signal to note, not a verdict. Tier C note: its primary composite includes mortality, which is why this shelf is before the developer; no death is reported as an outcome event in the abstract, and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Synthesis: DOACs after cerebral venous thrombosis look safe in two small trials that between them recorded almost no events — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: DOACs after cerebral venous thrombosis look safe in two small trials that between them recorded almost no events — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RE-SPECT CVT 2019 (dabigatran vs warfarin, 120 patients) and SECRET 2023 (rivaroxaban feasibility, 55 patients).
cards.result: The randomised evidence in cerebral venous thrombosis totals 175 patients. RE-SPECT CVT found no recurrent VTE on either drug and numerically fewer major bleeds on dabigatran; SECRET showed a definitive trial is feasible and recorded its few events in the rivaroxaban arm. Nothing here establishes efficacy equivalence; everything here is consistent with DOACs being a reasonable option after stabilisation.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: SECRET's primary safety composite includes mortality (component event-free in the event — the one primary event was a haemorrhage). The verdict requested is on the shelf as built, which makes no mortality claim.

shelves.title: D-dimer-guided duration of anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE (PROLONG; DULCIS)
shelves.question: In patients who have completed anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE, does a D-dimer-guided strategy (stopping if normal, resuming if abnormal), compared with stopping in everyone, reduce recurrent VTE without excess bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Acenocoumarol · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants · Antiphospholipid Syndrome · Antithrombins · Drug Administration Schedule · Fibrin Fibrinogen Degradation Products · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Humans · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism · Recurrence · Survival Analysis · Ultrasonography · Venous Thrombosis · Vitamin K · Warfarin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. PROLONG (2006) randomised only the patients whose D-dimer was abnormal one month after stopping anticoagulation: recurrence was 15.0% in those who stayed off treatment versus 2.9% in those who resumed (adjusted HR 4.26 for stopping); patients with a normal D-dimer, who were not randomised, recurred at 6.2%. The DULCIS management study (2014) then applied serial D-dimer testing in practice: patients who stopped on persistently negative D-dimers recurred at 3.0% per patient-year, versus 0.7% per patient-year in those who resumed and 8.8% per patient-year in the self-selected group who refused to resume, at a cost of major bleeding of 2.3% per patient-year in those who resumed. The randomised core is a single trial of a single assay strategy, and the confirmatory study's key comparison is not randomised: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PROLONG 2006: with an abnormal D-dimer after stopping, recurrence was 15.0% off anticoagulation vs 2.9% on it (adjusted HR 4.26)
cards.summary: PROLONG 2006: with an abnormal D-dimer after stopping, recurrence was 15.0% off anticoagulation vs 2.9% on it (adjusted HR 4.26)
cards.type: Randomised trial nested in a D-dimer-stratified cohort
cards.people: 608 patients with a first unprovoked proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism who had received a vitamin K antagonist for at least 3 months; D-dimer was tested 1 month after discontinuation. The assay was abnormal in 223 (36.7%): 120 patients stopped anticoagulation and 103 resumed it by randomisation. The 385 patients with a normal D-dimer did not resume and were not randomised. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The composite outcome (recurrent VTE and major bleeding) occurred in 18 of 120 patients who stopped (15.0%) versus 3 of 103 who resumed (2.9%) — adjusted hazard ratio 4.26 (95% CI 1.23 to 14.6; P=0.02) over an average follow-up of 1.4 years. Thromboembolism recurred in 24 of 385 patients (6.2%) with a normal D-dimer. Among those who stopped, an abnormal versus normal D-dimer carried an adjusted hazard ratio for recurrence of 2.27 (95% CI 1.15 to 4.46; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Only the abnormal-D-dimer group was randomised, so the often-quoted comparison is narrower than the shelf question. The 'normal D-dimer' group's 6.2% recurrence is not negligible — the authors themselves state the optimal course for that group was not established. Results are assay- and threshold-specific.
cards.source: Palareti G et al. D-dimer testing to determine the duration of anticoagulation therapy. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 17065639. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00264277, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: DULCIS 2014: serial D-dimer management study — stopping on negative D-dimers recurred at 3.0%/year; resuming cost 2.3%/year major bleeding
cards.summary: DULCIS 2014: serial D-dimer management study — stopping on negative D-dimers recurred at 3.0%/year; resuming cost 2.3%/year major bleeding
cards.people: 1,010 outpatients with a first VTE (unprovoked or associated with weak risk factors) after at least 3 months of anticoagulation (12 months if residual thrombosis), managed with serial D-dimer measurements using commercial assays with predefined age- and sex-specific cutoffs, followed for up to 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Anticoagulation was stopped in 528 patients (52.3%) with persistently negative D-dimers, who then had 25 recurrences (3.0% per patient-year; 95% CI 2.0–4.4). Of the remaining 482 patients, 373 resumed anticoagulation and 109 refused; recurrence developed in 4 of those who resumed (0.7% per patient-year) and 15 of those who refused (8.8% per patient-year), with a printed hazard ratio of 2.92 (95% CI 1.87–9.72; P=0.0006). Major bleeding occurred in 14 patients (2.3% per patient-year; 95% CI 1.3–3.9) who resumed anticoagulation.
cards.watchOut: The resumed-versus-refused contrast is self-selected, not randomised — patients who refused resumption differ from those who accepted it, so the 0.7% vs 8.8% gap overstates what randomisation would show. The printed confidence interval for the hazard ratio (1.87–9.72 around 2.92) is asymmetric as printed in the record; it is reproduced as printed, not repaired.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a positive D-dimer after stopping identifies patients who benefit from resuming; the strategy's randomised base is one trial — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a positive D-dimer after stopping identifies patients who benefit from resuming; the strategy's randomised base is one trial — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PROLONG 2006 (608 patients tested; 223 randomised) and DULCIS 2014 (1,010 patients managed by serial D-dimer).
cards.result: Both studies agree on the shape of the answer: D-dimer status after a first unprovoked VTE stratifies recurrence risk strongly enough that resuming anticoagulation in the abnormal group prevents most recurrences, while a persistently negative D-dimer identifies a group whose recurrence rate (3.0–6.2%) some clinicians and patients will accept. The price of resuming is major bleeding at about 2.3% per patient-year.
cards.watchOut: The two studies used different testing schedules and cutoffs (single test at one month versus serial testing with age/sex-specific cutoffs), so the shelf supports the strategy, not a single protocol. Neither study was powered for mortality, and none is claimed.

shelves.title: Anticoagulation for symptomatic calf deep-vein thrombosis (CACTUS)
shelves.question: In low-risk outpatients with a first symptomatic calf (distal) deep-vein thrombosis, does therapeutic-dose nadroparin for six weeks, compared with placebo, reduce proximal extension or pulmonary embolism without excess bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Canada · Double-Blind Method · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Exanthema · Female · France · Hemorrhage · Humans · Leg · Male · Middle Aged · Nadroparin · Pulmonary Embolism · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Stockings, Compression · Switzerland · Thrombocytopenia · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography · Veins · Venous Thrombosis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). CACTUS is the only randomised trial of anticoagulation for isolated calf DVT, and it was stopped early — at 259 of a planned ~520 patients, because of slow recruitment and expiry of the study drug. The composite of proximal extension, contralateral proximal DVT, and symptomatic pulmonary embolism occurred in 3% on nadroparin versus 5% on placebo (risk difference −2.1%, 95% CI −7.8 to 3.5; P=0.54), while bleeding occurred in 4% versus 0% (risk difference 4.1%, 95% CI 0.4 to 9.2; P=0.0255). A single, underpowered, stopped-early trial whose point estimate mildly favours treatment on efficacy and clearly disfavours it on bleeding: the null on net benefit is POSSIBLE, not proven.

cards.headline: CACTUS 2016: nadroparin did not reduce proximal extension or PE (3% vs 5%, P=0.54) and increased bleeding (4% vs 0%)
cards.summary: CACTUS 2016: nadroparin did not reduce proximal extension or PE (3% vs 5%, P=0.54) and increased bleeding (4% vs 0%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, terminated early
cards.people: 259 low-risk outpatients (no active cancer, no previous VTE) with a first acute symptomatic calf deep-vein thrombosis at 23 centres in Canada, France, and Switzerland, randomised to nadroparin 171 IU/kg subcutaneously once daily or saline placebo for 6 weeks; the intention-to-treat population was 122 (nadroparin) and 130 (placebo). All patients received compression stockings and were followed for 90 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (extension of calf DVT to proximal veins, contralateral proximal DVT, or symptomatic pulmonary embolism at day 42) occurred in 4 patients (3%) on nadroparin and 7 (5%) on placebo (risk difference −2.1%, 95% CI −7.8 to 3.5; P=0.54). Bleeding occurred in 5 patients (4%) on nadroparin and none on placebo (risk difference 4.1%, 95% CI 0.4 to 9.2; P=0.0255). One nadroparin patient died of metastatic pancreatic cancer and one developed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type 2.
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled only half its prespecified sample before termination, so its confidence interval (−7.8 to +3.5 points) cannot exclude a clinically useful benefit; 'not superior' here means 'not shown superior in a stopped trial'. The enrolled population was deliberately low-risk, so the result does not govern calf DVT with cancer, prior VTE, or extensive thrombosis.
cards.source: Righini M et al. Anticoagulant therapy for symptomatic calf deep vein thrombosis (CACTUS): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Haematology. 2016. PMID: 27836513. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00421538, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one stopped-early trial found no net benefit from anticoagulating low-risk calf DVT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one stopped-early trial found no net benefit from anticoagulating low-risk calf DVT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: CACTUS 2016 (259 patients randomised; 252 in the intention-to-treat analysis).
cards.result: CACTUS stands alone: no second randomised trial exists. Its efficacy estimate is compatible with anything from a 7.8-point benefit to a 3.5-point harm, and its bleeding estimate is a clear harm. On this record, systematic anticoagulation of low-risk symptomatic calf DVT is not supported, and ultrasound surveillance is the evidence-consistent default the trial's authors point to.
cards.watchOut: A single small null trial is the weakest form of 'the null' — the stamp is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), not LIKELY, precisely because the trial stopped at half its planned size.

shelves.title: Drug-coated balloon for dysfunctional dialysis arteriovenous fistulas (IN.PACT AV; Lutonix AV)
shelves.question: In patients with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas for haemodialysis, does a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon, compared with standard balloon angioplasty, improve target-lesion primary patency at six months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon · Arteriovenous Shunt, Surgical · Cardiovascular Agents · Coated Materials, Biocompatible · Constriction, Pathologic · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Paclitaxel · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis · Single-Blind Method · Upper Extremity · Vascular Access Devices · Vascular Patency
shelves.balance: LIKELY. IN.PACT AV (330 patients) showed target-lesion primary patency at 6 months of 82.2% with the drug-coated balloon versus 59.5% with standard angioplasty (difference 22.8 percentage points; P<0.001), with the 30-day access-circuit safety endpoint noninferior. The second randomised trial, Lutonix AV (285 patients), points the same way in its final 2-year report: target-lesion primary patency favoured the coated balloon at 9 months (58% vs 46%; P=0.02) and 12 months (44% vs 36%; P=0.04), attenuating by 18–24 months, with mortality not different between groups. Two concordant RCTs on a patency endpoint: LIKELY for patency — a surrogate; neither trial was designed or powered for mortality, and none is claimed. (The topic draft's named second trial, a Passeo-18 Lux fistula RCT, could not be verified as a randomised trial — see the synthesis card.)

cards.headline: IN.PACT AV 2020: drug-coated balloon kept 6-month target-lesion patency at 82.2% vs 59.5% for standard angioplasty (P<0.001)
cards.summary: IN.PACT AV 2020: drug-coated balloon kept 6-month target-lesion patency at 82.2% vs 59.5% for standard angioplasty (P<0.001)
cards.people: 330 participants at 29 international sites with new or restenotic lesions in native upper-extremity arteriovenous fistulas, randomised after successful high-pressure angioplasty to a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon (n=170) or a standard balloon (n=160). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Target-lesion primary patency at 6 months (freedom from clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation or access-circuit thrombosis) was 82.2% (125 of 152) with the drug-coated balloon versus 59.5% (88 of 148) with the standard balloon (difference 22.8 percentage points; 95% CI 12.8 to 32.8; P<0.001). The primary safety endpoint (serious adverse events involving the arteriovenous access circuit within 30 days) was noninferior: 4.2% (7 of 166) versus 4.4% (7 of 158) (P=0.002 for noninferiority).
cards.watchOut: Patency at 6 months is a surrogate: the trial does not show fewer cannulation failures, fewer missed dialysis sessions, or longer fistula survival, and randomisation happened only after successful pre-dilatation, which selects lesions that already respond to a plain balloon.
cards.source: Lookstein RA et al. Drug-Coated Balloons for Dysfunctional Dialysis Arteriovenous Fistulas. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32813949. cards.headline: Lutonix AV (2-year report, 2020): patency advantage at 9–12 months (44% vs 36% at 12 months) attenuating by 24 months; mortality not different
cards.summary: Lutonix AV (2-year report, 2020): patency advantage at 9–12 months (44% vs 36% at 12 months) attenuating by 24 months; mortality not different
cards.people: 285 subjects with dysfunctional arm arteriovenous fistulas at 23 US sites, randomised 1:1 to a paclitaxel-coated balloon or an uncoated balloon after successful ultra-high-pressure vessel preparation; 96 of 141 (coated) and 111 of 144 (control) subjects completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Target-lesion primary patency for coated versus control balloons was 58% vs 46% at 9 months (P=0.02), 44% vs 36% at 12 months (P=0.04), 34% vs 28% at 18 months (P=0.06), and 27% vs 24% at 24 months (P=0.09). Mean time to a patency event was longer with the coated balloon (322 vs 207 days; P<0.0001). The noninferiority safety target was met at all intervals, and mortality did not differ between groups (P=0.27; the abstract prints no mortality rates).
cards.watchOut: This card is the trial's final 2-year report; its abstract does not print the 6-month primary-endpoint rates, so none are carded here. Attrition was substantial (about a third of the coated-balloon arm did not complete), and the patency gap narrows to non-significance by 18–24 months.

shelves.question: In patients with symptomatic femoropopliteal peripheral artery disease, does a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon, compared with standard percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, improve 12-month primary patency?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: LEVANT 2's primary safety endpoint is a composite built from freedom from perioperative death from any cause and freedom from limb-related death at 12 months, so a carded primary endpoint embeds death; no mortality claim is made or supported — IN.PACT SFA reported no device- or procedure-related deaths, and LEVANT 2 found no difference in death). On patency the two pivotal trials agree: IN.PACT SFA (331 patients) found 12-month primary patency of 82.2% versus 52.4% (P<0.001) with clinically driven reintervention of 2.4% versus 20.6%; LEVANT 2 (476 patients) found 65.2% versus 52.6% (P=0.02). Two large concordant RCTs on a surrogate endpoint: LIKELY for patency. The late-mortality signal that once prompted regulatory scrutiny of paclitaxel devices is a safety watch-out, addressed on the cards; it is not what this shelf claims.

shelves.title: Bypass surgery versus endovascular therapy for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (BEST-CLI; BASIL-2)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia suitable for both strategies, does surgical bypass, compared with endovascular therapy, reduce the composite of major adverse limb events and death — and does the answer depend on having a good single-segment saphenous vein?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia · Endovascular Procedures · Limb Salvage · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Surgical Procedures · Saphenous Vein
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both primary outcomes embed death). The two trials pull in opposite directions in different anatomies. BEST-CLI (1,830 patients): in cohort 1 — patients with an adequate single-segment great saphenous vein — surgery beat endovascular therapy on the composite of major adverse limb events or death (42.6% vs 57.4%; HR 0.68); in cohort 2 (alternative conduit needed) there was no significant difference (42.8% vs 47.7%; HR 0.79). BASIL-2 (345 patients, infrapopliteal disease with or without more proximal work): a vein-bypass-first strategy was worse on amputation-free survival (major amputation or death 63% vs 53%; adjusted HR 1.35), driven mainly by more deaths in the bypass group (53% vs 45%; adjusted HR 1.37). The honest synthesis is anatomical: vein-available, largely infrainguinal disease favours surgery in BEST-CLI; infrapopliteal disease favours endovascular-first in BASIL-2. Neither verdict can be generalised over the other: SPLIT, both sides POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: BEST-CLI 2022: with a good saphenous vein, surgery cut major limb events or death (42.6% vs 57.4%; HR 0.68); without one, no difference
cards.summary: BEST-CLI 2022: with a good saphenous vein, surgery cut major limb events or death (42.6% vs 57.4%; HR 0.68); without one, no difference
cards.type: Randomised trial in two parallel cohorts
cards.people: 1,830 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and infrainguinal peripheral artery disease at international centres, enrolled in two parallel cohorts: cohort 1 (1,420 patients) had a single segment of great saphenous vein suitable for bypass; cohort 2 (393 patients) required an alternative conduit. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In cohort 1, after a median follow-up of 2.7 years, a primary-outcome event (major adverse limb event — above-ankle amputation or a major limb reintervention — or death from any cause) occurred in 302 of 709 surgical patients (42.6%) versus 408 of 711 endovascular patients (57.4%) (hazard ratio 0.68 relative; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.79; P<0.001). In cohort 2, after a median 1.6 years, events occurred in 83 of 194 (42.8%) versus 95 of 199 (47.7%) (HR 0.79 relative; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.06; P=0.12). Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups in both cohorts.
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven substantially by major reintervention, a softer component than amputation or death, and the trial's endovascular arm reflects the techniques of its enrolment era. Cohort 2's confidence interval is wide; 'no significant difference' there is not equivalence.

cards.headline: BASIL-2 2023: in infrapopliteal disease, bypass-first was worse — amputation or death 63% vs 53% (adjusted HR 1.35), driven by deaths
cards.summary: BASIL-2 2023: in infrapopliteal disease, bypass-first was worse — amputation or death 63% vs 53% (adjusted HR 1.35), driven by deaths
cards.people: 345 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia requiring an infrapopliteal, with or without an additional more proximal infra-inguinal, revascularisation procedure, at 41 units in the UK, Sweden, and Denmark; 172 were assigned vein bypass first and 173 best endovascular treatment first. Median age 72.5 years (IQR 62.7–79.3); 65 (19%) were women.
cards.result: Major amputation or death occurred in 108 of 172 patients (63%) in the vein bypass group and 92 of 173 (53%) in the best endovascular group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.35 relative; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.80; P=0.037) over a minimum 2 years of follow-up. Deaths were 91 of 172 (53%) versus 77 of 173 (45%) (adjusted HR 1.37 relative; 95% CI 1.00 to 1.87); cardiovascular and respiratory events were the most common causes of death in both groups. Most bypasses used great saphenous vein; most endovascular interventions were plain balloon angioplasty with selective stenting.
cards.watchOut: BASIL-2's population is anatomically distinct from BEST-CLI's (infrapopliteal target, older, high competing mortality), and its result is driven by deaths rather than amputations — a pattern that may reflect case mix and the burden of open surgery in frail patients rather than limb strategy alone. The two trials are a genuine tension, presented here unresolved.

shelves.title: Sulodexide for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE (SURVET)
shelves.question: In patients who have completed oral anticoagulation for a first unprovoked deep-vein thrombosis, does sulodexide, compared with placebo, reduce recurrent venous thromboembolism without increasing bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycosaminoglycans · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. SURVET is a single double-blind trial of 615 patients: recurrent VTE occurred in 15 of 307 on sulodexide versus 30 of 308 on placebo over 2 years (hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.27–0.92; P=0.02), with no major bleeding in either arm and two clinically relevant bleeds in each. (The topic draft's 'HR ≈0.35' does not match the record; the record's figure of 0.49 is carded, and a sensitivity analysis assigning losses to follow-up as failures gives a risk ratio of 0.54.) A halving of recurrence with no bleeding penalty is an attractive result, but it rests on one trial of 45 total events from one research tradition, for an agent unavailable in several major markets, with no replication: POSSIBLE.

cards.summary: SURVET 2015: recurrent VTE 15 of 307 on sulodexide vs 30 of 308 on placebo (HR 0.49 relative); no major bleeding in either arm
cards.people: 615 patients with a first-ever unprovoked venous thromboembolism who had completed 3–12 months of oral anticoagulation, randomised to sulodexide 500 lipasemic units twice daily (n=307) or placebo (n=308) for 2 years, in addition to elastic stockings. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism recurred in 15 of 307 patients on sulodexide and 30 of 308 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.27–0.92; P=0.02). An analysis assigning patients lost to follow-up as failures yielded a risk ratio of 0.54 relative (95% CI 0.35–0.85; P=0.009). No major bleeding episodes occurred; two patients in each group had a clinically relevant bleeding episode, and adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty-five recurrence events in total carry this result — the confidence interval runs from a 73% to an 8% relative reduction. The correction on this card matters: summaries of SURVET sometimes quote a hazard ratio near 0.35; the trial record prints 0.49. Sulodexide is not marketed in several major countries, which bounds the shelf's practical reach.

shelves.title: Naftidrofuryl for intermittent claudication (Cochrane individual-patient-data meta-analysis)
shelves.question: In patients with intermittent claudication, does naftidrofuryl oxalate, compared with placebo, improve pain-free and maximal walking distance?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Humans · Intermittent Claudication · Nafronyl · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vasodilator Agents · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. FORMAT EXCEPTION, flagged for the developer as the topic draft itself requests: this shelf's anchor is a systematic review, not a trial, because no single naftidrofuryl trial is cardable on its own — the randomised programme is a set of old, small, heterogeneously reported trials whose usable evidence exists only as an individual-patient-data (IPD) meta-analysis. That analysis (Cochrane, updated 2012; 7 trials, 1,266 patients; main analysis 1,083) found the ratio of relative improvement in pain-free walking distance was 1.37 (95% CI 1.27 to 1.49; P<0.001) for naftidrofuryl versus placebo, with an absolute responder-rate difference of 22.3% (responder = ≥50% improvement in walking distance) and an NNT of 4.5. The topic draft pinned the 2008 version of this review; the record shows it was updated in 2012, and the updated version is the carded one. A pooled, moderately sized benefit on a walking-distance surrogate from old small trials, available only at review level: POSSIBLE.

cards.people: Seven randomised trials of oral naftidrofuryl versus placebo in people with intermittent claudication, totalling 1,266 patients; one study (n=183) contributed only to the sensitivity analysis, leaving 1,083 patients in the main analysis. cards.result: The ratio of the relative improvement in pain-free walking distance (naftidrofuryl compared with placebo) was 1.37 (95% CI 1.27 to 1.49; P<0.001), adjusted for baseline walking distance. The absolute difference in responder rate (proportion improving walking distance by at least 50%) was 22.3% (95% CI 17.1% to 27.6%), giving a number needed to treat of 4.5 (95% CI 3.6 to 5.8) over about six months of treatment. The authors call the effect statistically significant and clinically meaningful, although moderate.
cards.watchOut: This is a review card, not a trial card: the constituent trials are old and small, the endpoint is treadmill walking distance rather than symptoms in daily life or hard outcomes, and the analysis depends on the manufacturer's individual patient data being made available. The topic draft pinned the 2008 version of this review (PMID 18425872); the record marks that version as updated by this 2012 version, which is what is carded.
cards.source: De Backer TL et al. Naftidrofuryl for intermittent claudication. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235580 (an update of the 2008 version, PMID: 18425872). shelves.title: Off-pump versus on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (CORONARY, ROOBY, GOPCABE)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing CABG, does off-pump surgery, compared with on-pump surgery, reduce the composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and renal failure requiring dialysis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Transfusion · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Artery Bypass, Off-Pump · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Postoperative Complications · Renal Insufficiency · Reoperation · Single-Blind Method · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death, myocardial infarction, and stroke). Three large randomised trials, in three different populations, found no reduction in the death/MI/stroke/dialysis composite with off-pump CABG. CORONARY (4,752 patients): 9.8% versus 10.3% at 30 days (HR 0.95; P=0.59) and 23.1% versus 23.6% at five years. ROOBY (2,203 US veterans): no 30-day difference, a worse 1-year composite off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04) and lower graft patency (82.6% vs 87.8%). GOPCABE (2,539 patients aged 75 or older): 7.8% versus 8.2% at 30 days and 13.1% versus 14.0% at 12 months. Off-pump surgery buys fewer transfusions, less acute kidney injury, and fewer respiratory complications, at the price of more early repeat revascularisation; it does not buy fewer deaths, infarctions, or strokes: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: CORONARY 2012: no difference in death, MI, stroke, or dialysis at 30 days (9.8% off-pump vs 10.3% on-pump; P=0.59)
cards.summary: CORONARY 2012: no difference in death, MI, stroke, or dialysis at 30 days (9.8% off-pump vs 10.3% on-pump; P=0.59)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (30-day primary report of the CORONARY trial)
cards.people: 4,752 patients in whom CABG was planned, at 79 centres in 19 countries, randomised to off-pump or on-pump CABG. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The first coprimary outcome (death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or new renal failure requiring dialysis at 30 days) did not differ: 9.8% off-pump versus 10.3% on-pump (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.14; P=0.59), nor did any individual component. Off-pump CABG reduced blood-product transfusion (50.7% vs 63.3%; relative risk 0.80), reoperation for perioperative bleeding (1.4% vs 2.4%), acute kidney injury (28.0% vs 32.1%), and respiratory complications (5.9% vs 7.5%), but increased early repeat revascularisation (0.7% vs 0.2%; hazard ratio 4.01; P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: The benefits of off-pump surgery are real but sit in secondary, softer outcomes; the hard composite the trial was powered on did not move. The five-year report of the same trial is the next card — the same patients, counted once.

cards.headline: ROOBY 2009: no 30-day benefit, and a worse 1-year composite with off-pump surgery (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04) with poorer graft patency
cards.summary: ROOBY 2009: no 30-day benefit, and a worse 1-year composite with off-pump surgery (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04) with poorer graft patency
cards.people: 2,203 patients scheduled for urgent or elective CABG in the US Veterans Affairs system, randomised to on-pump or off-pump procedures; 1,371 patients underwent follow-up angiography. The abstract does not state mean age; the VA population is predominantly male, but the abstract does not print the sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: The 30-day composite of death or complications did not differ (7.0% off-pump vs 5.6% on-pump; P=0.19). The 1-year composite of death, repeat revascularisation, or nonfatal myocardial infarction was higher with off-pump surgery (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04). Fewer grafts than planned were completed off-pump (17.8% vs 11.1%; P<0.001), and overall graft patency at one year was lower off-pump (82.6% vs 87.8%; P<0.01). Neuropsychological outcomes and short-term resource use did not differ.
cards.watchOut: ROOBY is the discordant trial of the three: its surgeons' off-pump experience was limited by modern standards, a criticism the authors acknowledged; but its patency finding is objective angiographic data and points the same way as CORONARY's early-revascularisation signal.

cards.summary: GOPCABE 2013: in patients 75 and older, no difference at 30 days (7.8% vs 8.2%) or 12 months (13.1% vs 14.0%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (GOPCABE trial, elderly patients)
cards.people: 2,539 patients aged 75 years or older scheduled for elective first-time CABG in Germany, randomised to off-pump or on-pump surgery; 177 patients crossed over between strategies. The abstract does not state the sex mix.

cards.headline: Synthesis: off-pump CABG does not reduce death, MI, stroke, or dialysis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: off-pump CABG does not reduce death, MI, stroke, or dialysis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CORONARY 2012 with its five-year report (4,752 patients, one trial), ROOBY 2009 (2,203 patients), and GOPCABE 2013 (2,539 patients) — 9,494 randomised patients in three trials.
cards.result: Across general, veteran, and elderly populations, off-pump CABG never reduced the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and renal failure requiring dialysis. What it reliably reduces is transfusion, acute kidney injury short of dialysis, and respiratory complications; what it costs is completeness and durability of revascularisation. The choice between techniques is a trade of perioperative soft outcomes against graft quality, not a route to fewer hard events.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: no mortality claim is made for either technique; component event rates are printed on every card. CORONARY's two reports are one trial and are counted once, as the gate requires.

shelves.title: Radial artery versus saphenous vein and right internal thoracic artery as the second bypass conduit (RAPCO)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing CABG, does using the radial artery as the second conduit, compared with saphenous vein (older patients) or the right internal thoracic artery (younger patients), improve long-term patency and clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Coronary Artery Bypass · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Male · Mammary Arteries · Middle Aged · Mortality · Radial Artery · Survival Rate · Vascular Patency
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: long-term mortality is reported on the shelf). The RAPCO programme (one centre, two randomised comparisons, 619 patients) found better 10-year graft patency for the radial artery than for the free right internal thoracic artery (89% vs 80%; hazard ratio for graft failure 0.45 relative) and than for saphenous vein (85% vs 71%; HR 0.40 relative, with a confidence interval touching 1.00). Ten-year survival estimates favoured the radial artery over the right internal thoracic artery (90.9% vs 83.7%; HR for mortality 0.53 relative) but not significantly over saphenous vein (72.6% vs 65.2%; HR 0.76, CI 0.47 to 1.22) — and mortality was a nonpowered coprimary end point in a single-centre programme, so those survival figures are hypothesis-generating, not a mortality claim. The drafting note for this shelf said clinical event rates did not differ significantly; the record prints a nominally significant survival difference against the right internal thoracic artery, and the card follows the record. Patency is a surrogate; the clinical-outcome question stays open: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RAPCO 2020: radial-artery patency at 10 years beat both free right internal thoracic artery (89% vs 80%) and saphenous vein (85% vs 71%); survival analyses were nonpowered
cards.summary: RAPCO 2020: radial-artery patency at 10 years beat both free right internal thoracic artery (89% vs 80%) and saphenous vein (85% vs 71%); survival analyses were nonpowered
cards.type: Randomised controlled trials (two parallel randomised comparisons within one single-centre programme)
cards.people: RAPCO-RITA: 394 patients younger than 70 years (or younger than 60 with diabetes) randomised to radial artery or free right internal thoracic artery on the second most important coronary target. RAPCO-SV: 225 patients aged 70 or older (or 60 or older with diabetes) randomised to radial artery or saphenous vein. Single-centre programme (Melbourne, Australia). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix beyond the age-band eligibility.
cards.result: In the radial-versus-RITA comparison, estimated 10-year patency was 89% for radial artery versus 80% for free RITA (hazard ratio for graft failure 0.45 relative; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.88); the 10-year patient survival estimate was 90.9% versus 83.7% (hazard ratio for mortality 0.53 relative; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.95). In the radial-versus-vein comparison, estimated 10-year patency was 85% versus 71% (hazard ratio for graft failure 0.40 relative; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.00), and 10-year survival was 72.6% versus 65.2% (hazard ratio for mortality 0.76 relative; 95% CI 0.47 to 1.22). The primary outcome was 10-year graft failure; long-term mortality was a nonpowered coprimary end point.
cards.watchOut: Three cautions. First, this is one centre's programme with 619 patients — surgical expertise effects cannot be separated from conduit effects. Second, the survival difference against RITA comes from a nonpowered end point and should not be read as a mortality claim. Third, the vein comparison's patency confidence interval touches 1.00. The drafting note's statement that clinical event rates did not differ significantly understates the printed RITA survival result; the record governs, and both are disclosed here.
cards.source: Buxton BF et al. Long-Term Results of the RAPCO Trials. Circulation. 2020. PMID: 33017209. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00475488, from the record's databank fields. cards.result: The radial artery outlasts both alternative second conduits on angiographic patency at ten years. Whether that patency advantage converts into fewer deaths or infarctions is not established by this programme: the one nominally significant survival result rests on a nonpowered end point in a single centre. The patient-level pooled analysis of six conduit trials by the RADIAL collaboration (Gaudino et al., JAMA 2020, PMID 32662861) reports fewer events with radial grafts, but it is a pooled analysis — a different evidentiary tier — and is fenced here, not carded: it is named so the developer can find it, and no figures are taken from it.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: the mortality figures are printed beside the patency figures on the trial card, labelled nonpowered; no mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf. A multicentre trial powered on clinical events remains the missing evidence.

shelves.title: Perioperative corticosteroids for cardiac surgery (DECS dexamethasone; SIRS methylprednisolone)
shelves.question: In adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, does a prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone 1 mg/kg in DECS; methylprednisolone in SIRS), compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal or respiratory failure, and infection within 30 days?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Cardiopulmonary Bypass · Dexamethasone · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Intraoperative Period · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Postoperative Complications · Renal Insufficiency · Respiratory Insufficiency · Stroke · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composites include death, myocardial infarction, and stroke). Two large double-blind trials, testing two different steroids, both failed. DECS (4,494 patients, single 1 mg/kg dexamethasone dose): primary composite 7.0% versus 8.5% (relative risk 0.83; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; P=0.07). SIRS (7,507 high-risk patients, methylprednisolone 250 mg twice): 30-day mortality 4% versus 5% (RR 0.87; P=0.19) and death-or-major-morbidity 24% versus 24% (RR 1.03; P=0.52). Suppressing the bypass inflammatory response with a prophylactic steroid bolus does not prevent major adverse events: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), a two-trial class answer in 12,001 patients.

cards.headline: DECS 2012: high-dose dexamethasone did not reduce major adverse events (7.0% vs 8.5%; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; P=0.07)
cards.summary: DECS 2012: high-dose dexamethasone did not reduce major adverse events (7.0% vs 8.5%; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; P=0.07)
cards.people: 4,494 patients aged 18 or older undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at 8 centres in the Netherlands; 2,239 received a single intraoperative dose of dexamethasone 1 mg/kg and 2,255 placebo; 4,482 were evaluable for the primary outcome. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, or respiratory failure within 30 days) occurred in 157 patients (7.0%) on dexamethasone and 191 (8.5%) on placebo (relative risk 0.83; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; absolute risk reduction −1.5%; P=0.07) — not significant. Dexamethasone was associated with fewer postoperative infections, shorter mechanical ventilation, and shorter ICU and hospital stays, and with higher postoperative glucose levels.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate leans toward dexamethasone without reaching significance, and the secondary benefits (infection, ventilation time) are the kind of findings that keep a practice alive after its primary question has failed; the companion SIRS trial, on the next card, tested the same idea at even larger scale and found nothing.

cards.result: The inflammatory-response rationale for steroid prophylaxis at bypass is biologically coherent and empirically empty at trial scale: neither drug reduced death or the major-morbidity composite. shelves.title: Perioperative levosimendan in cardiac surgery with low ejection fraction (LEVO-CTS, LICORN, CHEETAH)
shelves.question: In patients with reduced ejection fraction undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, or who need haemodynamic support after cardiac surgery, does levosimendan, compared with placebo, reduce death and major postoperative complications?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiac Output, Low · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Cardiotonic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart-Assist Devices · Humans · Hydrazones · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Myocardial Infarction · Perioperative Period · Postoperative Complications · Pyridazines · Renal Replacement Therapy · Simendan · Stroke Volume · Treatment Failure · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composites include death and myocardial infarction, and one trial's primary outcome is mortality itself). Three randomised trials tested levosimendan around cardiac surgery and all three failed. LEVO-CTS (882 patients, EF 35% or less, prophylactic infusion): the four-component primary composite occurred in 24.5% versus 24.5% (adjusted OR 1.00; P=0.98). LICORN (336 patients, EF 40% or less, preoperative infusion): the low-cardiac-output-syndrome composite occurred in 52% versus 61% (adjusted difference −7%; P=0.15). CHEETAH (506 patients needing haemodynamic support after surgery): 30-day mortality 12.9% versus 12.8%, and the trial was stopped for futility. Small-trial meta-analyses had suggested a survival benefit; the three adequately sized trials refute it: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.people: 882 patients with left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were randomised; 849 received levosimendan (0.2 µg/kg/min for 1 hour, then 0.1 µg/kg/min for 23 hours, started before surgery) or placebo and formed the modified intention-to-treat population. cards.result: The four-component primary end point (death through day 30, renal-replacement therapy through day 30, perioperative myocardial infarction through day 5, or mechanical cardiac assist device through day 5) occurred in 105 of 428 patients (24.5%) on levosimendan and 103 of 421 (24.5%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 1.00; 99% CI 0.66 to 1.54; P=0.98). The two-component end point (death or assist device) occurred in 13.1% versus 11.4% (adjusted OR 1.18; P=0.45). Adverse-event rates did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of exactly 1.00 on the primary composite in the largest prophylaxis trial leaves little room for a dosing or timing rescue of the hypothesis; the two companion trials tested the neighbouring questions and agree.

cards.headline: LICORN 2017: preoperative levosimendan did not significantly reduce low cardiac output syndrome (52% vs 61%; adjusted difference −7%, 95% CI −17 to 3; P=0.15)
cards.summary: LICORN 2017: preoperative levosimendan did not significantly reduce low cardiac output syndrome (52% vs 61%; adjusted difference −7%, 95% CI −17 to 3; P=0.15)
cards.people: 336 patients with left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less scheduled for isolated or combined CABG with cardiopulmonary bypass, at 13 French centres (mean age 68 years; 16% women); 167 received a 24-hour levosimendan infusion (0.1 µg/kg/min) begun after anaesthetic induction and 168 placebo; 333 completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary composite — reflecting low cardiac output syndrome: catecholamine infusion still needed 48 hours after drug initiation, mechanical assist device need or failure to wean, or renal-replacement therapy at any time — occurred in 87 patients (52%) on levosimendan and 101 (61%) on placebo (absolute difference adjusted for centre, −7%; 95% CI −17% to 3%; P=0.15). No predefined subgroup (EF under 30%, surgery type, beta-blocker, balloon pump, or catecholamine use) showed an interaction. Hypotension (57% vs 48%) and atrial fibrillation (50% vs 40%) were numerically more frequent on levosimendan.
cards.watchOut: LICORN is the smallest of the three trials and its confidence interval cannot exclude a modest benefit on its syndrome composite; it is carded as consistent with, not proof of, the class null — the weight of the shelf rests on LEVO-CTS and CHEETAH.

cards.headline: CHEETAH 2017: levosimendan for haemodynamic support after cardiac surgery — 30-day mortality 12.9% vs 12.8%; stopped for futility
cards.summary: CHEETAH 2017: levosimendan for haemodynamic support after cardiac surgery — 30-day mortality 12.9% vs 12.8%; stopped for futility
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, stopped early for futility
cards.people: 506 patients in whom perioperative haemodynamic support was indicated after cardiac surgery by prespecified criteria; 248 received levosimendan (continuous infusion 0.025 to 0.2 µg/kg/min for up to 48 hours or ICU discharge) plus standard care and 258 placebo plus standard care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome, 30-day mortality, occurred in 32 patients (12.9%) on levosimendan and 33 (12.8%) on placebo (absolute risk difference 0.1 percentage points; 95% CI −5.7 to 5.9; P=0.97). Durations of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and hospital stay did not differ significantly, nor did rates of hypotension or cardiac arrhythmias. The trial was stopped for futility after 506 patients were enrolled.
cards.watchOut: CHEETAH is the treatment (rather than prophylaxis) trial of the three, and its primary outcome is mortality itself: dead even. A futility stop on a mortality primary is the clearest of the three verdicts.

shelves.title: Posterior left pericardiotomy to prevent atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery (PALACS)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery, does posterior left pericardiotomy (draining the pericardium into the left pleural space), compared with no pericardiotomy, reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · New York City · Pericardial Effusion · Pericardiectomy · Postoperative Complications · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single-centre, single-trial result awaiting multicentre confirmation. In PALACS (420 patients undergoing elective coronary, aortic-valve, or ascending-aorta surgery at one centre), postoperative atrial fibrillation occurred in 17% (37 of 212) with posterior left pericardiotomy versus 32% (66 of 208) without (adjusted odds ratio 0.44 relative; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.70; P=0.0005), and pericardial effusion was also less frequent (12% vs 21%; relative risk 0.58). No intervention-related complications were seen, and 30-day deaths were 2 versus 1. The effect is large and mechanistically direct, but one centre's surgeons and one trial are all the evidence there is: POSSIBLE. Note for the developer: the drafting figures for this shelf (11.9% vs 25.9%, OR 0.40) do not match the trial record; the record's figures (17% vs 32%, adjusted OR 0.44) are what is carded.

cards.headline: PALACS 2021: posterior left pericardiotomy halved postoperative atrial fibrillation (17% vs 32%; adjusted OR 0.44; P=0.0005) in a single-centre trial
cards.summary: PALACS 2021: posterior left pericardiotomy halved postoperative atrial fibrillation (17% vs 32%; adjusted OR 0.44; P=0.0005) in a single-centre trial
cards.type: Adaptive, single-centre, single-blind, randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 420 adults undergoing elective surgery on the coronary arteries, aortic valve, or ascending aorta (or a combination) at one centre (Weill Cornell Medicine, New York), with no history of atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmia; 212 were assigned to posterior left pericardiotomy and 208 to no intervention. Median age 61.0 years; 102 patients (24%) were women. Three patients assigned to pericardiotomy did not receive it; follow-up data were complete.
cards.result: Postoperative atrial fibrillation during the in-hospital stay occurred in 37 of 212 patients (17%) in the pericardiotomy group versus 66 of 208 (32%) in the control group (odds ratio adjusted for the stratification variable 0.44 relative; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.70; P=0.0005). Postoperative pericardial effusion was less frequent with pericardiotomy (26 of 209 [12%] vs 45 of 211 [21%]; relative risk 0.58; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.91). Major adverse events occurred in 6 patients (3%) versus 4 (2%), deaths within 30 days after discharge were 2 (1%) versus 1 (under 1%), and no pericardiotomy-related complications were seen.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own numbers differ from the figures in this shelf's drafting note (which gave 11.9% vs 25.9% and OR 0.40); the record's intention-to-treat figures are carded, and the discrepancy is disclosed in the balance. Single-centre surgical-technique trials are prone to expertise and enthusiasm effects, and the adaptive design adds a further reason to want independent replication before the stamp rises.

shelves.title: Mitral-valve repair versus replacement for severe ischaemic mitral regurgitation (CTSN)
shelves.question: In patients with severe ischaemic mitral regurgitation, does mitral-valve repair, compared with chordal-sparing replacement, improve left-ventricular reverse remodelling, survival, and valve durability?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mitral Valve · Mitral Valve Annuloplasty · Mitral Valve Insufficiency · Myocardial Ischemia · Postoperative Complications · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is reported throughout). LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for remodelling and survival: in the CTSN trial (251 patients), left-ventricular end-systolic volume index at 12 months and at 2 years did not differ between repair and replacement, and neither did mortality (14.3% vs 17.6% at 1 year, HR 0.79, P=0.45; 19.0% vs 23.2% at 2 years, HR 0.79, P=0.39). LIKELY for the durability advantage of replacement: recurrent moderate or severe regurgitation was far more common after repair — 32.6% versus 2.3% at 1 year and 58.8% versus 3.8% over 2 years (both P<0.001) — and by 2 years the repair group had more heart-failure-related serious adverse events and cardiovascular readmissions. Repair and replacement remodel the ventricle and keep patients alive at the same rate; replacement corrects the valve far more durably. The smaller RIME trial asked a different question (repair plus CABG versus CABG alone) and is fenced, not carded.

cards.headline: CTSN 2014 (1-year report): no difference in remodelling or death (14.3% vs 17.6%); recurrent regurgitation far more common after repair (32.6% vs 2.3%)
cards.summary: CTSN 2014 (1-year report): no difference in remodelling or death (14.3% vs 17.6%); recurrent regurgitation far more common after repair (32.6% vs 2.3%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (1-year primary report of the CTSN severe ischaemic MR trial)
cards.people: 251 patients with severe ischaemic mitral regurgitation randomised to mitral-valve repair or chordal-sparing replacement. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary end point, left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVI) at 12 months, was 54.6 ml/m² in the repair group and 60.7 ml/m² in the replacement group among survivors (mean change from baseline −6.6 and −6.8 ml/m²); after adjustment for death there was no significant difference (P=0.18). Death occurred in 14.3% (repair) versus 17.6% (replacement) (hazard ratio 0.79 relative; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.47; P=0.45). Moderate or severe recurrent mitral regurgitation at 12 months was much more frequent after repair (32.6% vs 2.3%; P<0.001). Composite major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events, functional status, and quality of life did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered on a remodelling surrogate, not on survival; the mortality confidence interval (0.42 to 1.47) is wide. The two-year report of the same trial is the next card — same patients, counted once.
