cards.headline: CTSN 2016 (2-year report): remodelling and survival still equal; regurgitation recurred in 58.8% after repair versus 3.8% after replacement
cards.summary: CTSN 2016 (2-year report): remodelling and survival still equal; regurgitation recurred in 58.8% after repair versus 3.8% after replacement
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (two-year report of the same CTSN trial, PMID 24245543 — one trial, two reports)
cards.people: The same 251 CTSN patients, followed for 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Two-year LVESVI was 52.6 ml/m² (repair) versus 60.6 ml/m² (replacement) among survivors, with no significant between-group difference on the rank-based assessment incorporating deaths (P=0.19). Two-year mortality was 19.0% versus 23.2% (hazard ratio 0.79 relative; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.35; P=0.39). Recurrence of moderate or severe mitral regurgitation over 2 years was 58.8% after repair versus 3.8% after replacement (P<0.001). Overall serious adverse events and readmissions did not differ significantly, but the repair group had more heart-failure-related serious adverse events (P=0.05) and cardiovascular readmissions (P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: By two years, more than half of repaired valves had leaked again at moderate-or-worse grade — the durability gap is the trial's most robust finding, and it began to convert into heart-failure events within the follow-up window.

shelves.title: Concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty at mitral surgery for degenerative regurgitation (CTSN)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing mitral-valve surgery for degenerative regurgitation who have moderate tricuspid regurgitation or annular dilatation, does concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty, compared with mitral surgery alone, reduce progression of tricuspid regurgitation and reoperation at two years, and at what cost in permanent pacemakers?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiac Valve Annuloplasty · Dilatation, Pathologic · Disease Progression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Mitral Valve · Mitral Valve Insufficiency · Pacemaker, Artificial · Postoperative Complications · Quality of Life · Reoperation · Survival Analysis · Tricuspid Valve · Tricuspid Valve Insufficiency
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite includes death). One definitive trial (CTSN, 401 patients): the two-year composite of death, tricuspid reoperation, or tricuspid-regurgitation progression was lower with concomitant annuloplasty (3.9% vs 10.2%; relative risk 0.37 relative), driven almost entirely by less progression to severe regurgitation (0.6% vs 6.1%). Two-year mortality did not differ significantly (3.2% vs 4.5%; RR 0.69, CI 0.25 to 1.88) — no mortality claim is made or supported. The price was permanent pacemaker implantation: 14.1% versus 2.5% (rate ratio 5.75 relative) — roughly one extra pacemaker for every nine concomitant repairs. Whether preventing an echocardiographic progression endpoint converts into long-term clinical benefit is unproven; the trial's own authors say only longer follow-up can tell. A real benefit on a surrogate-heavy composite, bought with a real harm: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CTSN 2022: concomitant tricuspid repair cut the 2-year composite (3.9% vs 10.2%) but multiplied pacemakers (14.1% vs 2.5%)
cards.summary: CTSN 2022: concomitant tricuspid repair cut the 2-year composite (3.9% vs 10.2%) but multiplied pacemakers (14.1% vs 2.5%)
cards.people: 401 patients undergoing mitral-valve surgery for degenerative mitral regurgitation, with moderate tricuspid regurgitation or less-than-moderate regurgitation with annular dilatation, randomised to mitral surgery with or without tricuspid annuloplasty. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary two-year composite (reoperation for tricuspid regurgitation, progression of tricuspid regurgitation by two grades or presence of severe regurgitation, or death) occurred in 3.9% of the surgery-plus-annuloplasty group versus 10.2% of the surgery-alone group (relative risk 0.37 relative; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.86; P=0.02), driven by progression of tricuspid regurgitation (0.6% vs 6.1%; RR 0.09). Two-year mortality was 3.2% versus 4.5% (relative risk 0.69; 95% CI 0.25 to 1.88) — not significantly different. Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events, functional status, and quality of life were similar at 2 years. Permanent pacemaker implantation was markedly higher with annuloplasty: 14.1% versus 2.5% (rate ratio 5.75 relative; 95% CI 2.27 to 14.60).
cards.watchOut: Read the composite honestly: its engine is an echocardiographic progression grade, not death or reoperation, while the harm — a lifelong pacemaker in one of seven patients — is entirely concrete. The authors' conclusion itself flags that long-term clinical benefit is undetermined; the card follows the record, not the headline.

shelves.title: Early surgery versus conventional treatment for infective endocarditis with large vegetations (EASE)
shelves.question: In patients with left-sided infective endocarditis, severe valve dysfunction, and vegetations larger than 10 mm, does early valve surgery (within 48 hours), compared with conventional treatment, reduce the composite of in-hospital death and embolic events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Embolism · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Prospective Studies · Secondary Prevention · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death). One small trial (EASE, 76 patients at one Korean centre, all at low predicted surgical risk): the primary composite of in-hospital death and embolic events within 6 weeks occurred in 1 patient (3%) with early surgery versus 9 (23%) with conventional treatment (hazard ratio 0.10 relative; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.82; P=0.03), driven almost entirely by embolism — there were no embolic events after early surgery. Six-month all-cause mortality did not differ significantly (3% vs 5%; HR 0.51, CI 0.05 to 5.66) — no mortality claim is made or supported. Two structural caveats cap the stamp: 77% of the conventional group underwent surgery anyway during the same admission, so the trial tests timing more than surgery itself; and the population was young and low-risk, unlike the older, comorbid endocarditis population in most Western series. A strong embolism signal in a narrow population: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: EASE 2012: early surgery cut the death-or-embolism composite (3% vs 23%; HR 0.10) in 76 selected patients; mortality alone did not differ
cards.summary: EASE 2012: early surgery cut the death-or-embolism composite (3% vs 23%; HR 0.10) in 76 selected patients; mortality alone did not differ
cards.people: 76 patients with left-sided infective endocarditis, severe valve disease, and large vegetations (over 10 mm), at a single centre in South Korea, randomised to early surgery (37 patients) or conventional treatment (39). All early-surgery patients were operated within 48 hours of randomisation; 30 patients (77%) in the conventional group also underwent surgery during the initial hospitalisation (27) or follow-up (3). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix; the enrolled population was selected for low surgical risk.
cards.result: The primary end point (in-hospital death or embolic events within 6 weeks) occurred in 1 patient (3%) in the early-surgery group versus 9 (23%) in the conventional-treatment group (hazard ratio 0.10 relative; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.82; P=0.03). All-cause mortality at 6 months was 3% versus 5% (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.05 to 5.66; P=0.59) — not significantly different. The 6-month composite of death, embolic events, or recurrence of endocarditis was 3% versus 28% (hazard ratio 0.08; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The composite's drama comes from embolism, and the comparison is blurred by design: three quarters of the 'conventional' group had the same operation a little later. The trial shows that in operable patients with large vegetations, waiting invites emboli; it does not show that early surgery saves lives, and its patients were younger and fitter than typical endocarditis cohorts.
cards.source: Kang DH et al. Early surgery versus conventional treatment for infective endocarditis. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22738096. shelves.title: Partial oral versus intravenous antibiotic therapy for left-sided endocarditis (POET)
shelves.question: In stabilised patients with left-sided infective endocarditis who have completed at least 10 days of intravenous therapy, is switching to oral antibiotics noninferior to continuing intravenous therapy for the composite of mortality, unplanned surgery, embolism, and relapse?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bacteremia · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes all-cause mortality). One trial (POET, 400 stabilised Danish patients with streptococcal, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococcal left-sided endocarditis, after at least 10 days of intravenous therapy): the primary composite (all-cause mortality, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapse of bacteraemia, to 6 months after treatment completion) occurred in 9.0% after oral switch versus 12.1% with continued intravenous therapy (between-group difference 3.1 percentage points; 95% CI −3.4 to 9.6; P=0.40), meeting the trial's noninferiority criteria. The abstract does not print the mortality component separately, so no mortality claim is made or supported either way. The result applies to patients who have already stabilised on intravenous therapy — not to initial treatment — and to the four organism groups studied: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: POET 2019: switching stabilised endocarditis patients to oral antibiotics was noninferior (composite 9.0% vs 12.1%)
cards.summary: POET 2019: switching stabilised endocarditis patients to oral antibiotics was noninferior (composite 9.0% vs 12.1%)
cards.people: 400 adults in stable condition with left-sided endocarditis caused by streptococcus, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococci, all treated intravenously for at least 10 days, randomised to continue intravenous treatment (199 patients) or switch to oral treatment (201), in Denmark. After randomisation, treatment was completed after a median of 19 days (intravenous) and 17 days (oral); patients in the oral group were discharged to outpatient treatment where feasible. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (all-cause mortality, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapse of bacteraemia with the primary pathogen, from randomisation until 6 months after antibiotic treatment was completed) occurred in 18 patients (9.0%) in the oral group and 24 (12.1%) in the intravenous group (between-group difference, 3.1 percentage points; 95% CI −3.4 to 9.6; P=0.40), which met the trial's prespecified noninferiority criteria.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority here was declared on a confidence interval whose favourable end approaches a 10-point absolute margin — the trial excludes a large penalty for oral switch, not a small one. Eligibility required clinical stability after at least 10 days of intravenous therapy, and four organism groups only; the abstract does not break out mortality separately, so the card does not either.
cards.source: Iversen K et al. Partial Oral versus Intravenous Antibiotic Treatment of Endocarditis. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30152252. shelves.title: Early valve intervention for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (EARLY TAVR; EVOLVED)
shelves.question: In patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, does early transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (EARLY TAVR), or fibrosis-guided early valve intervention (EVOLVED), compared with clinical surveillance or guideline-directed management, reduce the composite of death, stroke, and unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Aortic Valve · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Asymptomatic Diseases · Cardiovascular Diseases · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Hospitalization · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Postoperative Complications · Severity of Illness Index · Stroke · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement · Watchful Waiting · Follow-Up Studies · Prospective Studies · Incidence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both composites include death; EARLY TAVR's includes stroke). EARLY TAVR (901 patients, transfemoral TAVR versus surveillance): the composite of death, stroke, or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation occurred in 26.8% versus 45.3% (hazard ratio 0.50 relative; P<0.001) over a median 3.8 years — but the components show what drove it: death 8.4% versus 9.2% and stroke 4.2% versus 6.7% did not differ significantly, while unplanned hospitalisation did (20.9% vs 41.7%); 87.0% of the surveillance group crossed over to valve replacement during follow-up, so the trial compares early with eventually — POSSIBLE for the composite, with no death or stroke claim made or supported. EVOLVED (224 patients selected for myocardial fibrosis, early surgical or transcatheter intervention versus guideline-directed care): the primary composite of all-cause death or unplanned aortic-stenosis hospitalisation was neutral (18% vs 23%; HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=0.44), in a trial that enrolled 224 of a planned 356 patients; deaths were 14% versus 13%. The divergence is real and is stated, not averaged away: an unselected echocardiographic population with a hospitalisation endpoint benefited; a smaller fibrosis-selected trial did not show it.

cards.headline: EARLY TAVR 2025: early TAVR halved the composite (26.8% vs 45.3%; HR 0.50) — driven by hospitalisation, not death (8.4% vs 9.2%) or stroke (4.2% vs 6.7%)
cards.summary: EARLY TAVR 2025: early TAVR halved the composite (26.8% vs 45.3%; HR 0.50) — driven by hospitalisation, not death (8.4% vs 9.2%) or stroke (4.2% vs 6.7%)
cards.people: 901 patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis and preserved ejection fraction at 75 centres in the US and Canada, randomised to early transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve (455) or clinical surveillance (446). Mean age 75.8 years; mean STS predicted risk of mortality 1.8%; 83.6% were at low surgical risk. The abstract does not state the sex mix. Median follow-up was 3.8 years, during which 87.0% of the surveillance group underwent aortic-valve replacement.
cards.result: A primary end-point event (death, stroke, or unplanned hospitalisation for cardiovascular causes) occurred in 122 patients (26.8%) on early TAVR versus 202 (45.3%) on surveillance (hazard ratio 0.50 relative; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.63; P<0.001). The components: death 8.4% versus 9.2%; stroke 4.2% versus 6.7%; unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation 20.9% versus 41.7%. Procedure-related adverse events did not differ apparently between the TAVR group and surveillance patients who later underwent valve replacement.
cards.watchOut: The headline hazard ratio of 0.50 is a hospitalisation story: with 87% of the surveillance arm eventually receiving a valve, 'clinical surveillance' meant planned-later intervention plus the unplanned admissions that symptoms bring. Death and stroke — the components a patient would weight most — were not significantly different, and the balance line says so.
cards.source: Généreux P et al. Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement for Asymptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39466903. cards.headline: EVOLVED 2025: fibrosis-guided early intervention was neutral on its primary outcome (18% vs 23%; HR 0.79; P=0.44) in an under-enrolled trial
cards.summary: EVOLVED 2025: fibrosis-guided early intervention was neutral on its primary outcome (18% vs 23%; HR 0.79; P=0.44) in an under-enrolled trial
cards.people: 224 asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis and myocardial fibrosis on cardiac MRI, at 24 centres in the UK and Australia (mean age 73 years; 63 women [28%]); 113 were assigned to early valve intervention (transcatheter or surgical) and 111 to guideline-directed conservative management. The trial enrolled 224 of a planned 356 patients.
cards.result: The primary composite (all-cause death or unplanned aortic-stenosis-related hospitalisation) occurred in 20 of 113 patients (18%) with early intervention versus 25 of 111 (23%) with conservative management (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=0.44) — not significant. All-cause death was 14% versus 13% (HR 1.22), while unplanned aortic-stenosis hospitalisation was 6% versus 17% (HR 0.37; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.88). Seven of nine prespecified secondary outcomes showed no significant difference; early intervention did reduce NYHA class II–IV symptoms at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: EVOLVED differs from EARLY TAVR in population (fibrosis-selected), intervention (mixed surgical and transcatheter), and size — it stopped short of its planned sample, so its confidence interval (0.44 to 1.43) cannot exclude the kind of benefit EARLY TAVR found on hospitalisation. 'Neutral and underpowered' is the honest label, not 'disproof'.
cards.source: Loganath K et al. Early Intervention in Patients With Asymptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis and Myocardial Fibrosis: The EVOLVED Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 39466640. cards.result: Both trials agree on the component that matters most and find nothing: no significant difference in death in either. They diverge on composites built largely from hospitalisation — strongly positive in the large unselected trial, neutral in the small fibrosis-selected one. Treating asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis early is, on current evidence, a way to convert unplanned admissions into planned procedures; whether it extends life is untested at adequate power. shelves.title: Pitavastatin to prevent cardiovascular disease in HIV (REPRIEVE)
shelves.question: In people with HIV at low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk on antiretroviral therapy, does pitavastatin 4 mg daily reduce major adverse cardiovascular events versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Middle Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · HIV Infections · Myocardial Infarction · Quinolines · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C), because the primary outcome is a cardiovascular-event composite. In REPRIEVE (7,769 people with HIV at low-to-moderate predicted risk), the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was 4.81 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin versus 7.32 on placebo (HR 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002) over a median 5.1 years — an absolute difference of about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years. The trial was stopped early for efficacy, which can exaggerate effect sizes, and it is a single trial. Muscle-related symptoms (2.3% versus 1.4%) and incident diabetes (5.3% versus 4.0%) were more frequent on pitavastatin. Correction printed on the card: the topic file gives the pitavastatin rate as 5.10 per 1,000 person-years; the record prints 4.81.

cards.headline: REPRIEVE: major cardiovascular events 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin (HR 0.65 relative)
cards.summary: REPRIEVE: major cardiovascular events 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin (HR 0.65 relative)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (stopped early for efficacy)
cards.people: 7,769 participants with HIV infection at low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk on antiretroviral therapy; median age 50 years (IQR 45–55), median CD4 count 621 cells/mm³, HIV RNA below quantification in 87.5% of those with available data. The abstract does not print the sex split.
cards.result: The trial was stopped early for efficacy after a median follow-up of 5.1 years. Major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, hospitalisation for unstable angina, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, peripheral arterial ischaemia, revascularisation, or death from an undetermined cause) occurred at 4.81 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin versus 7.32 on placebo (HR 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002) — an absolute difference of about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years. Muscle-related symptoms occurred in 2.3% versus 1.4%, and diabetes mellitus in 5.3% versus 4.0%.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, stopped early — early stopping tends to inflate relative effects, and the absolute benefit is small because the population was chosen for low-to-moderate baseline risk. The topic file's figure of 5.10 events per 1,000 person-years does not match the record, which prints 4.81; the record governs.

shelves.title: Fostamatinib for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (FIT-1 & FIT-2)
shelves.question: In adults with persistent or chronic ITP and an insufficient response to prior therapy, does fostamatinib achieve stable platelet responses versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aminopyridines · Blood Platelets/drug effects · Chronic Disease · Humans · Morpholines · Oxazines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Platelet Count · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic/drug therapy · Pyridines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrimidines · Splenectomy · Syk Kinase/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two parallel phase III randomised trials (FIT-1 and FIT-2), reported together in a single publication and carded as what they are: two trials in one report, with the pooled denominators the report itself uses. A correction to the topic file: stable response was 18% on fostamatinib versus 2% on placebo (P=.0003), not 0% as filed. Responses were achieved in a heavily pretreated population (median ITP duration 8.5 years; baseline median platelet count 16,000/µL; many had failed splenectomy, thrombopoietin agents and/or rituximab). The 'overall response' figure (43% versus 14%) was defined retrospectively in the report and is flagged as such on the card; the prespecified stable-response endpoint carries the stamp. Costs: diarrhoea (31% versus 15%), hypertension (28% versus 13%), nausea and transaminase rises. The trials' registry IDs do not appear in the record's databank fields and are stated as absent rather than supplied from elsewhere.

cards.headline: FIT-1 & FIT-2 (reported together): stable platelet response in 18% on fostamatinib versus 2% on placebo (P=.0003)
cards.summary: FIT-1 & FIT-2 (reported together): stable platelet response in 18% on fostamatinib versus 2% on placebo (P=.0003)
cards.type: Two parallel phase III, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported in one publication (24 weeks; 2:1 randomisation; dose increase to 150 mg twice daily in nonresponders after week 4)
cards.people: 150 adults with persistent or chronic immune thrombocytopenia across the two trials (101 fostamatinib starting at 100 mg twice daily, 49 placebo). Baseline median platelet count was 16,000/µL and median ITP duration 8.5 years; patients had failed prior therapies including, in many cases, splenectomy, thrombopoietic agents and/or rituximab. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — stable response (platelets ≥50,000/µL at at least 4 of 6 biweekly visits during weeks 14–24 without rescue therapy) — occurred in 18% on fostamatinib versus 2% on placebo (P=.0003). Overall response (at least one count ≥50,000/µL within 12 weeks; the report states this definition was retrospective) occurred in 43% versus 14% (P=.0006). Median time to response was 15 days on the 100 mg dose, and 83% of responders responded within 8 weeks. Common adverse events: diarrhoea 31% versus 15%, hypertension 28% versus 13%, nausea 19% versus 8%, dizziness 11% versus 8% and ALT increase 11% versus 0%, mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The pooled reporting means per-trial (FIT-1 versus FIT-2) results cannot be separated from this record — the two trials are counted as two, but only their combined figures can be quoted. The retrospective definition of 'overall response' should always be flagged when the 43% figure is used; the prespecified stable-response figure is 18%.
cards.source: Bussel J et al. Fostamatinib for the treatment of adult persistent and chronic immune thrombocytopenia: results of two phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled trials. Am J Hematol. 2018. PMID: 29696684. Registry IDs: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Luspatercept in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (BELIEVE)
shelves.question: In adults with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, does luspatercept reduce red-cell transfusion burden versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activin Receptors, Type II/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Erythrocyte Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Female · Ferritins/blood · Hematinics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Splenectomy · Young Adult · beta-Thalassemia/drug therapy/genetics/surgery/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one phase III trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, reported in its primary paper and a long-term final report (one trial, counted once). The topic file anchored the shelf on the final-results paper and described sustained benefit 'versus placebo over long-term follow-up'; the record is more precise — placebo-controlled comparison ends at unblinding, and the final report explicitly performs no comparative analyses after week 96 because of crossover. The randomised result stands on the primary report: a ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction with ≥2 fewer units during weeks 13–24 in 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo (P<0.001), with 70.5% versus 29.5% achieving ≥33% reduction over any 12-week interval. Long-term follow-up shows the effect is durable on treatment (77% achieved a ≥33% reduction over some 12-week interval across follow-up) with no treatment-related deaths. If the developer rejects the single-trial exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

cards.headline: BELIEVE (primary report): ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction in 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo during weeks 13–24 (P<0.001)
cards.summary: BELIEVE (primary report): ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction in 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo during weeks 13–24 (P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase III, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (2:1; luspatercept 1.00–1.25 mg/kg every 3 weeks plus best supportive care)
cards.people: 336 adults with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia were randomised (224 luspatercept, 112 placebo); treatment was given for a median of approximately 64 weeks in both groups. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split (the long-term report below gives median age 30 and 58% women).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — reduction in transfusion burden of at least 33% from baseline during weeks 13–24 plus at least 2 fewer red-cell units — was met by 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo (P<0.001). Over any 12-week interval, ≥33% reduction occurred in 70.5% versus 29.5%, and ≥50% reduction in 40.2% versus 6.3%. Serum ferritin at week 48 favoured luspatercept (least-squares mean difference −348 µg/L, 95% CI −517 to −179). Transient bone pain, arthralgia, dizziness, hypertension and hyperuricaemia were more common on luspatercept; few adverse events led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint's response fraction (about one in five) is much lower than the 'any 12-week interval' figure (about seven in ten) — quoting the latter without the former overstates the drug. Transfusion burden is a treatment-burden endpoint; the trial does not report mortality or organ-outcome benefits, and none are claimed here.
cards.source: Cappellini MD et al. A phase 3 trial of luspatercept in patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (BELIEVE). N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 32212518. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02604433 and EudraCT 2015-003224-31, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: BELIEVE final results (long-term report of the same trial): burden reductions sustained to week 192; no comparative analysis after week 96
cards.summary: BELIEVE final results (long-term report of the same trial): burden reductions sustained to week 192; no comparative analysis after week 96
cards.type: Long-term follow-up / final-results report of the BELIEVE randomised trial — same trial as the card above, counted once
cards.people: The same 336 randomised patients (median age 30 years, IQR 23–40; 58% female), followed for a median 163.1 weeks; after unblinding, placebo patients could cross over to open-label luspatercept (315 patients received luspatercept in total, including 92 crossovers).
cards.result: Because treatment duration diverged after unblinding, no comparative analyses between the original groups were performed after week 96. In the luspatercept group, transfusion burden stayed reduced through week 192 (mean decreases of 6.2 units during weeks 97–144 and 6.4 units during weeks 145–192); a ≥33% reduction over any 12-week interval was seen in 173 patients (77%) and over any 24-week interval in 116 (52%), with a median response duration of 586 days. Among all luspatercept-exposed patients, grade ≥3 events included anaemia (3%), increased liver iron concentration (2%) and bone pain (2%); serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 23%; no treatment-related deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Everything after week 96 is single-arm experience: durability on drug, not continued proof against placebo. The 77% figure spans up to four years of opportunities to qualify as a responder and must not be compared with the primary endpoint's 21.4% as if like-for-like.

shelves.title: Mitapivat in pyruvate kinase deficiency (ACTIVATE)
shelves.question: In adults with pyruvate kinase deficiency who are not regularly transfused, does mitapivat raise haemoglobin versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anemia, Hemolytic, Congenital Nonspherocytic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Hemoglobins/analysis/drug effects · Hemolysis/drug effects · Humans · Piperazines/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Pyruvate Kinase/deficiency · Pyruvate Metabolism, Inborn Errors/drug therapy · Quinolines/pharmacology/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one phase III randomised trial in a rare disease, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. In ACTIVATE (n=80, patients not regularly transfused), a sustained haemoglobin response (rise ≥1.5 g/dL at two or more of the week 16/20/24 assessments) occurred in 16 of 40 patients (40%) on mitapivat versus none of 40 on placebo (adjusted difference 39.3 percentage points, 95% CI 24.1–54.6; two-sided P<0.001), with all secondary endpoints favouring mitapivat; the abstract asserts the average haemoglobin change favoured mitapivat without printing its size, and none is supplied here. A correction to the topic file's 'DOUBLE-A' label: the companion ACTIVATE-T study is an open-label, SINGLE-ARM trial in regularly transfused patients — a different population and no control group — so it cannot serve as this shelf's second randomised trial; it is fenced in the synthesis card, not carded as evidence. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent on mitapivat (25% versus 13%). If the developer rejects the rare-disease exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

cards.headline: ACTIVATE: haemoglobin response in 40% on mitapivat versus 0% on placebo (adjusted difference 39.3 points; P<0.001)
cards.summary: ACTIVATE: haemoglobin response in 40% on mitapivat versus 0% on placebo (adjusted difference 39.3 points; P<0.001)
cards.type: Global phase III, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks; mitapivat 5 mg twice daily with escalation to 20 or 50 mg twice daily)
cards.people: 80 adults with pyruvate kinase deficiency who were not receiving regular red-cell transfusions (40 mitapivat, 40 placebo). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a haemoglobin increase of at least 1.5 g/dL sustained at two or more scheduled assessments at weeks 16, 20 and 24 — was met by 16 of 40 patients (40%) on mitapivat versus none of 40 on placebo (adjusted difference 39.3 percentage points, 95% CI 24.1–54.6; two-sided P<0.001). Every secondary endpoint (average haemoglobin change, haemolysis and haematopoiesis markers, and two disease-specific patient-reported outcomes) favoured mitapivat; the abstract does not print the average haemoglobin change figure, and none is supplied here. Nausea occurred in 18% on mitapivat versus 23% on placebo and headache in 15% versus 33%; adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 10 patients (25%) versus 5 (13%). No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: A 40%-versus-zero result in 80 patients is striking but rests on a responder definition (sustained ≥1.5 g/dL) chosen by the programme; the unprinted mean haemoglobin change is the figure a sceptic would ask for first, and it cannot be quoted from this record. Twenty-four weeks is the horizon; durability and bone-health effects of long-term pyruvate-kinase activation are outside it.
cards.source: Al-Samkari H et al. Mitapivat versus placebo for pyruvate kinase deficiency (ACTIVATE). N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 35417638. shelves.title: Ravulizumab versus eculizumab in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (Studies 301 and 302)
shelves.question: In adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, is the long-acting C5 inhibitor ravulizumab (every 8 weeks) non-inferior to eculizumab (every 2 weeks) — in patients new to complement inhibition, and in patients already stable on eculizumab?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Complement Inactivating Agents/therapeutic use · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm/drug effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemoglobinuria, Paroxysmal/drug therapy/immunology/pathology · Hemolysis/drug effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Salvage Therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two parallel phase 3 randomised trials, one in complement-inhibitor-naive patients (Study 301) and one in patients stable on eculizumab (Study 302), each found ravulizumab non-inferior to eculizumab on every prespecified endpoint, with a similar safety profile; the practical gain is dosing every 8 weeks instead of every 2. Both trials were open-label (the infusion schedules cannot be blinded) and both were non-inferiority designs against an active standard, not placebo tests of efficacy. Scope boundary: this shelf is the terminal-C5 head-to-head; proximal complement inhibition (pegcetacoplan and its class) is a different question, homed on Shelf #845. PROPOSED: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Study 301: ravulizumab non-inferior to eculizumab on both co-primary endpoints in complement-inhibitor-naive PNH
cards.summary: Study 301: ravulizumab non-inferior to eculizumab on both co-primary endpoints in complement-inhibitor-naive PNH
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label non-inferiority trial (183 days; 1:1 randomisation)
cards.people: 246 adults with PNH who had never received a complement inhibitor, with lactate dehydrogenase at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal and at least one PNH symptom. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Ravulizumab was non-inferior to eculizumab for both co-primary endpoints (P for non-inferiority <.0001 for all endpoints): transfusion avoidance 73.6% versus 66.1% (difference 6.8 percentage points, 95% CI -4.66 to 18.14) and LDH normalisation 53.6% versus 49.4% (odds ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.77). Key secondary endpoints also met non-inferiority: LDH reduction -76.8% versus -76.0%, breakthrough haemolysis 4.0% versus 10.7% (difference -6.7 points, 95% CI -14.21 to 0.18), stabilised haemoglobin 68.0% versus 64.5%, and FACIT-Fatigue change 7.07 versus 6.40 points. No meningococcal infections occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: patients and clinicians knew the assignment, though the endpoints are laboratory-based. Non-inferiority against eculizumab shows the two drugs perform alike; it is not a placebo-controlled demonstration that either works, and the trial was not powered for rare harms such as meningococcal infection (none occurred, in a vaccinated-era programme).

cards.headline: Study 302: switching stable patients from eculizumab to ravulizumab was non-inferior to continuing eculizumab
cards.summary: Study 302: switching stable patients from eculizumab to ravulizumab was non-inferior to continuing eculizumab
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label non-inferiority trial (183 days; 1:1 randomisation)
cards.people: 195 adults with PNH who had been clinically stable on labelled-dose eculizumab (900 mg every 2 weeks) for more than 6 months; 97 were assigned to switch to ravulizumab and 98 to continue eculizumab; 191 completed 183 days. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Ravulizumab was non-inferior to continued eculizumab on the primary endpoint, percentage change in LDH from baseline to day 183 (difference 9.21%, 95% CI -0.42 to 18.84; P=.058 for superiority), and on all key secondary endpoints (P for non-inferiority <.0006): breakthrough haemolysis (difference 5.1 points, 95% CI -8.89 to 18.99), FACIT-Fatigue change (difference 1.47, 95% CI -0.21 to 3.15), transfusion avoidance (difference 5.5, 95% CI -4.27 to 15.68) and stabilised haemoglobin (difference 1.4, 95% CI -10.41 to 13.31). Headache was the most frequent adverse event (26.8% on ravulizumab versus 17.3% on eculizumab). No meningococcal infections and no discontinuations due to adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The enrolled population was selected for stability on eculizumab, so the result licenses switching stable patients; it says nothing about patients doing badly on eculizumab. Percentages for the secondary endpoints are printed in the record only as between-group differences, not as arm-level rates, and are carded that way.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ravulizumab matches eculizumab in both PNH populations, at one quarter of the infusion burden — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: ravulizumab matches eculizumab in both PNH populations, at one quarter of the infusion burden — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Study 301 (Lee 2019), 246 complement-inhibitor-naive adults, and Study 302 (Kulasekararaj 2019), 195 adults stable on eculizumab.
cards.result: Across two randomised non-inferiority trials covering the two clinical situations — starting C5 inhibition and switching from the incumbent drug — ravulizumab given every 8 weeks performed indistinguishably from eculizumab every 2 weeks on transfusion avoidance, LDH control, breakthrough haemolysis and fatigue, with similar tolerability. shelves.title: Abelacimab versus rivaroxaban in atrial fibrillation (AZALEA-TIMI 71)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, does the factor XI inhibitor abelacimab reduce major or clinically relevant bleeding versus rivaroxaban?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Atrial Fibrillation/blood/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Factor Xa Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Factor XI/analysis/antagonists & inhibitors · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/diagnosis/epidemiology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Rivaroxaban/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Stroke/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Incidence · Severity of Illness Index · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the trial was stopped early because bleeding on monthly abelacimab injections was far lower than on rivaroxaban (hazard ratios 0.38 and 0.31 for the two doses). Two cautions define this shelf. First, the primary endpoint is bleeding, a safety outcome: the record reports no stroke or systemic-embolism efficacy results, and no claim that abelacimab prevents stroke as effectively as rivaroxaban can be made or supported from this record. Second, early stopping for a larger-than-expected benefit tends to inflate the estimated effect. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): an anticoagulant comparison in atrial fibrillation, where any benefit claim is framed against stroke-prevention therapy. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial, stopped early; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: AZALEA-TIMI 71: bleeding rates were roughly two-thirds lower on abelacimab than on rivaroxaban; the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: AZALEA-TIMI 71: bleeding rates were roughly two-thirds lower on abelacimab than on rivaroxaban; the trial was stopped early
cards.type: Randomised trial (1:1:1) with blinded abelacimab injections (150 mg or 90 mg subcutaneously once monthly) against open-label oral rivaroxaban 20 mg daily
cards.people: 1287 patients with atrial fibrillation at moderate-to-high risk of stroke; median age 74 years, 44% women.
cards.result: Free factor XI levels fell by a median of 99% (150 mg dose) and 97% (90 mg dose) at 3 months. The primary endpoint, major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, occurred at 3.2 events per 100 person-years on 150 mg abelacimab and 2.6 per 100 person-years on 90 mg, versus 8.4 per 100 person-years on rivaroxaban (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.60, for 150 mg; hazard ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.51, for 90 mg; P<0.001 for both — relative measures, printed beside the absolute event rates above). The independent data monitoring committee recommended stopping the trial early because the reduction in bleeding was greater than anticipated. The incidence and severity of adverse events appeared similar across the three groups.
cards.watchOut: This is a bleeding-safety result, not a stroke-prevention result: the record prints no efficacy outcomes, so whether abelacimab prevents stroke as well as rivaroxaban is unknown from this trial. Effects estimated at an early stop for benefit are usually optimistic. Rivaroxaban was open-label while abelacimab was blinded.
cards.source: Ruff CT et al. Abelacimab versus Rivaroxaban in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39842011. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04755283, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Treating microalbuminuria to prevent cardiovascular events (PREVEND IT)
shelves.question: In people with microalbuminuria but no hypertension or hypercholesterolaemia, does fosinopril (or pravastatin) prevent cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Albuminuria · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cohort Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fosinopril · Hospitalization · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Incidence · Life Tables · Male · Middle Aged · Pravastatin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PREVEND IT is the cautionary tale for treating a screening marker: a 2×2 factorial trial that randomised 864 microalbuminuric people drawn from a city-wide screening programme (28,256 urine samples screened to find them) to fosinopril 20 mg or placebo, and pravastatin 40 mg or placebo, for four years. Fosinopril did exactly what the surrogate promised — urinary albumin excretion fell 26% (P<0.001) — but the clinical endpoint did not follow: the composite of cardiovascular mortality and hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, end-stage renal disease, or vascular intervention occurred in 45 patients overall (5.2%), with a hazard ratio for fosinopril of 0.60 whose confidence interval crosses 1.0 (95% CI 0.33–1.10; P=0.098) — not significant. Pravastatin showed even less (HR 0.87, CI 0.49–1.57; P=0.649). With only 45 events the trial was underpowered for the question it asked, and two decades on it remains essentially the only randomised test of treating isolated microalbuminuria. The topic draft's wording that fosinopril 'reduced the composite' overstates a non-significant trend; this shelf corrects it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C (cardiovascular mortality in the composite — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: PREVEND IT 2004: fosinopril cut albuminuria 26% but did NOT significantly reduce cardiovascular events (HR 0.60, CI 0.33–1.10; P=0.098); pravastatin HR 0.87 (CI 0.49–1.57)
cards.summary: PREVEND IT 2004: fosinopril cut albuminuria 26% but did NOT significantly reduce cardiovascular events (HR 0.60, CI 0.33–1.10; P=0.098); pravastatin HR 0.87 (CI 0.49–1.57)
cards.people: 864 subjects with microalbuminuria (urinary albumin excretion 15–300 mg/24 h), persistent on retesting, without hypertension or hypercholesterolaemia, identified by screening 28,256 inhabitants of Groningen, the Netherlands aged 28–75 (the PREVEND cohort). Subjects were randomised double-blind to fosinopril 20 mg daily or placebo, and independently to pravastatin 40 mg daily or placebo, and followed for a mean of 46 months. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular mortality or hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, stroke, or end-stage renal disease.
cards.result: Only 45 subjects (5.2%) reached the primary endpoint over nearly four years. Fosinopril reduced urinary albumin excretion by 26% relative to placebo (P<0.001) and slightly lowered blood pressure, but the primary endpoint hazard ratio was 0.60 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.33–1.10 (P=0.098) — the interval includes no effect, so the result is not statistically significant. Pravastatin lowered cholesterol but its endpoint hazard ratio was 0.87 (95% CI 0.49–1.57; P=0.649). The authors concluded the primary endpoint rate was unexpectedly low and further studies were needed — studies that, for this exact population, have not settled the question.
cards.watchOut: The gap between the surrogate (albuminuria −26%, highly significant) and the outcome (HR 0.60, not significant) is the shelf's lesson: marker response is not outcome benefit. The trial cannot exclude a real benefit — its interval spans a 40% relative reduction to a 10% increase — which is why the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a no-difference stamp. This population (normotensive, normocholesterolaemic, isolated microalbuminuria) is also narrower than the albuminuric diabetes and hypertension populations where ACE inhibition has outcome evidence; do not generalise in either direction. No registry ID exists for this 2004 trial.
cards.source: Asselbergs FW et al. Effects of fosinopril and pravastatin on cardiovascular events in subjects with microalbuminuria. Circulation. 2004. PMID: 15492322. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial. shelves.title: Levothyroxine after myocardial infarction with subclinical hypothyroidism (ThyrAMI): no ejection-fraction benefit in a small trial
shelves.question: In patients with acute myocardial infarction and subclinical hypothyroidism, does levothyroxine titrated to TSH 0.4–2.5 mU/L improve left ventricular ejection fraction at 52 weeks compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Thyroxine/pharmacology · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects
shelves.balance: A plausible idea, tested once, in a trial too small to settle it. In ThyrAMI (95 patients with acute myocardial infarction and subclinical hypothyroidism, 6 UK hospitals), levothyroxine starting at 25 μg and titrated to a TSH of 0.4–2.5 mU/L for 52 weeks did not improve left ventricular ejection fraction versus placebo: LVEF rose from 51.3% to 53.8% on levothyroxine and from 54.0% to 56.1% on placebo (adjusted difference +0.76%, 95% CI −0.93% to 2.46%; p=0.37). None of the six secondary outcomes — ventricular volumes, infarct size, vascular measures, or patient-reported outcomes — differed, and cardiovascular adverse events were similar (33.3% vs 36.7%). The authors call the study preliminary. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a null result, but from a single 95-patient trial whose confidence interval still allows a small LVEF benefit; it argues against routine treatment, it does not prove none can exist.

cards.headline: ThyrAMI (Jabbar 2020): LVEF improved equally with levothyroxine and placebo after MI (adjusted difference +0.76%, p=0.37)
cards.summary: ThyrAMI (Jabbar 2020): LVEF improved equally with levothyroxine and placebo after MI (adjusted difference +0.76%, p=0.37)
cards.people: 95 patients with acute myocardial infarction (ST-elevation and non-ST-elevation) and subclinical hypothyroidism at 6 UK hospitals — mean age 63.5 years, 76.6% men, median TSH 5.7 mU/L — randomised to levothyroxine (n=46) starting at 25 μg daily, titrated to TSH 0.4–2.5 mU/L, or identical placebo (n=49) for 52 weeks. Primary outcome: LVEF at 52 weeks by MRI; primary outcome data were available for 85 patients (89.5%).
cards.result: Mean LVEF at baseline and 52 weeks was 51.3% and 53.8% in the levothyroxine group versus 54.0% and 56.1% in the placebo group (adjusted difference 0.76%, 95% CI −0.93% to 2.46%; P=.37). None of the 6 secondary outcomes showed a significant difference between groups. Cardiovascular adverse events occurred in 15 patients (33.3%) on levothyroxine and 18 (36.7%) on placebo. The authors conclude the findings do not support treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism in patients with acute myocardial infarction.
cards.watchOut: Explicitly preliminary: 95 patients, baseline LVEF already near-normal (~51–54%), and subclinical disease was mild (median TSH 5.7 mU/L). A trial this size cannot detect modest effects on LVEF, let alone on death or reinfarction, which were not endpoints. The null applies to this mild-SCH post-MI population, not to overt hypothyroidism, which should be treated on its own merits.

shelves.title: Coronary disease: treating to an LDL target of 50–70 mg/dL matched fixed high-intensity statin (LODESTAR)
shelves.question: In patients with coronary artery disease, does treating to an LDL cholesterol target of 50–70 mg/dL with titrated statin therapy prevent major cardiovascular events as well as a fixed high-intensity statin strategy?
shelves.mesh: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Cholesterol, LDL · Coronary Artery Disease · Humans
shelves.balance: One large strategy trial, and the two strategies landed in the same place — partly because they produced nearly identical LDL levels. In LODESTAR, 4,400 patients with coronary artery disease in South Korea were randomised to treat-to-target (LDL 50–70 mg/dL, titrated) or fixed high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 20 mg or atorvastatin 40 mg). Mean LDL over 3 years was 69.1 versus 68.4 mg/dL. The 3-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or coronary revascularisation occurred in 8.1% versus 8.7% (absolute difference −0.6 percentage points; upper boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 1.1 points; P<.001 for non-inferiority, against a 3.0-point margin). In the target arm, 43% ended on moderate-intensity dosing — the practical dividend is dose flexibility, not better outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY — non-inferiority of treat-to-target is established by this trial (Tier C: the composite includes death, MI and stroke).

cards.headline: LODESTAR 2023: primary composite 8.1% (treat-to-target) vs 8.7% (high-intensity); non-inferiority met
cards.summary: LODESTAR 2023: primary composite 8.1% (treat-to-target) vs 8.7% (high-intensity); non-inferiority met
cards.people: 4,400 patients with coronary artery disease at 12 centres in South Korea (enrolled 2016–2019; mean age 65.1 years; 27.9% women); 4,341 (98.7%) completed the trial. Treat-to-target group (n=2,200): statin titrated to LDL-C 50–70 mg/dL. High-intensity group (n=2,200): rosuvastatin 20 mg or atorvastatin 40 mg. Primary endpoint: 3-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or coronary revascularisation; non-inferiority margin 3.0 percentage points.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 177 patients (8.1%) in the treat-to-target group and 190 (8.7%) in the high-intensity group (absolute difference −0.6 percentage points; upper boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI, 1.1 percentage points; P<.001 for non-inferiority). Mean LDL-C over 3 years was 69.1 (SD 17.8) mg/dL versus 68.4 (SD 20.1) mg/dL (P=.21). In the treat-to-target group, moderate-intensity dosing was used in 43% and high-intensity in 54%.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority is not superiority, and the near-identical achieved LDL levels explain the near-identical outcomes: the trial compares management strategies, not LDL levels. A single-country (South Korea), open-label trial; the 3.0-point margin is generous relative to an 8–9% event rate.
cards.source: Hong SJ et al. Treat-to-Target or High-Intensity Statin in Patients With Coronary Artery Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 36877807. shelves.title: Torcetrapib raised HDL by 72% — and increased deaths and cardiovascular events (ILLUMINATE)
shelves.question: In high-risk patients, does adding torcetrapib to atorvastatin — raising HDL cholesterol substantially — reduce cardiovascular events, or cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins · Anticholesteremic Agents · Atorvastatin · Cardiovascular Diseases · Humans
shelves.balance: The canonical warning against treating a surrogate. In ILLUMINATE, 15,067 high-risk patients were randomised to torcetrapib plus atorvastatin or atorvastatin alone. At 12 months the torcetrapib group had HDL cholesterol up 72.1% and LDL cholesterol down 24.9% in relative terms — and systolic blood pressure up 5.4 mm Hg, with lower potassium and higher sodium, bicarbonate and aldosterone, an off-target pattern. Cardiovascular events were increased (hazard ratio 1.25 — a 25% relative increase; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.44; P=0.001) and death from any cause was increased (HR 1.58 — a 58% relative increase; 95% CI 1.14 to 2.19; P=0.006); the trial was terminated prematurely. The authors could not rule out an adverse effect of CETP inhibition itself, but the blood-pressure and aldosterone signals point at this molecule. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — for torcetrapib specifically (Tier C: a mortality claim).

cards.headline: ILLUMINATE 2007: stopped early — cardiovascular events HR 1.25 relative, all-cause death HR 1.58 relative, despite HDL +72%
cards.summary: ILLUMINATE 2007: stopped early — cardiovascular events HR 1.25 relative, all-cause death HR 1.58 relative, despite HDL +72%
cards.people: 15,067 patients at high cardiovascular risk, randomised double-blind to torcetrapib plus atorvastatin or atorvastatin alone. Primary outcome: time to first major cardiovascular event (death from coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalisation for unstable angina). The trial was terminated prematurely because of increased death and cardiac events on torcetrapib.
cards.result: At 12 months, torcetrapib produced a 72.1% relative increase in HDL cholesterol and a 24.9% relative decrease in LDL cholesterol versus baseline (P<0.001 for both), plus a 5.4 mm Hg increase in systolic blood pressure and decreases in potassium with increases in sodium, bicarbonate and aldosterone (P<0.001 for all). Risk of cardiovascular events was increased (hazard ratio 1.25; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.44; P=0.001) and death from any cause was increased (HR 1.58; 95% CI 1.14 to 2.19; P=0.006) — both hazard ratios are relative effects; the abstract does not print the groups' absolute event rates. Post hoc analyses showed higher death risk in torcetrapib patients whose potassium fell or bicarbonate rose more than the median.
cards.watchOut: This is a verdict on torcetrapib, not on every CETP inhibitor: the off-target blood-pressure/aldosterone pattern is molecule-specific, and later CETP inhibitors were designed and tested separately (see the anacetrapib pack, Shelf #1562). Early termination can exaggerate harm estimates, but a mortality signal of this size in 15,067 patients is not a chance artefact to explain away.
cards.source: Barter PJ et al. Effects of torcetrapib in patients at high risk for coronary events. N Engl J Med. 2007. PMID: 17984165. Registry ID: NCT00134264, from the record. shelves.title: Heart failure: rosuvastatin did not reduce death or major events in two large trials (CORONA and GISSI-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does rosuvastatin reduce mortality and major cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Heart Failure · Mortality · Humans
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A: two large, independent, placebo-controlled trials of the same drug in heart failure, and both are null on the outcomes that matter. In CORONA (5,011 older patients with ischaemic systolic heart failure), rosuvastatin 10 mg did not reduce the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.02; P=0.12) or all-cause mortality (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.05; P=0.31). In GISSI-HF (4,574 patients with heart failure of any cause), rosuvastatin did not reduce death (29% vs 28%; adjusted HR 1.00; 95.5% CI 0.898 to 1.122; p=0.943) or death-or-cardiovascular-admission (adjusted HR 1.01; 99% CI 0.908 to 1.112). CORONA did show fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations on rosuvastatin (a prespecified secondary count of hospitalisations) — but hospitalisation benefit without a mortality or primary-endpoint benefit is exactly the pattern this library does not oversell, and GISSI-HF's admission composite was null. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C: a mortality question).

cards.headline: CORONA 2007: primary composite HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.83–1.02); death HR 0.95 — rosuvastatin null in ischaemic systolic HF
cards.summary: CORONA 2007: primary composite HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.83–1.02); death HR 0.95 — rosuvastatin null in ischaemic systolic HF
cards.people: 5,011 patients aged 60 or older with New York Heart Association class II–IV ischaemic systolic heart failure, randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg daily or placebo; median follow-up 32.8 months. Primary outcome: composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 692 patients on rosuvastatin and 732 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.02; P=0.12). Deaths from any cause: 728 versus 759 (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.05; P=0.31). LDL cholesterol fell by 45.0% relative and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein by 37.1% relative on rosuvastatin versus placebo (P<0.001 for both); there were fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations in the rosuvastatin group (2,193 vs 2,564 hospitalisations; P<0.001), a prespecified secondary outcome counted as hospitalisations, not patients.
cards.watchOut: The hospitalisation signal (a count of hospitalisations, secondary) sits beside null mortality and a null primary endpoint — this library pairs them and does not let the admission number stand alone. The population is established ischaemic systolic failure; the trial does not address starting a statin for a separate indication.

cards.people: 4,574 patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–IV, any cause and any ejection fraction) at 357 Italian centres, randomly assigned to rosuvastatin 10 mg daily (n=2,285) or placebo (n=2,289); median follow-up 3.9 years. shelves.title: Fish oil (n-3 PUFA) after a heart attack: benefit in 1999, none on modern therapy (GISSI-Prevenzione, OMEGA, Alpha Omega)
shelves.question: In patients after myocardial infarction, does n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation (about 1 g daily) reduce death and major cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Fatty Acids, Omega-3 · Fish Oils · Myocardial Infarction · Secondary Prevention · Humans
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A with an era split — this is the honest way to read three large trials. GISSI-Prevenzione (1999; 11,324 patients soon after myocardial infarction, in an era before routine statins and modern antiplatelet therapy) found n-3 PUFA 1 g daily lowered the composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke by a relative 10% (two-way analysis; 95% CI 1 to 18) to 15% (four-way), driven by fewer deaths. A decade later, on guideline-directed therapy, both OMEGA (3,851 patients; sudden cardiac death 1.5% vs 1.5%) and Alpha Omega (4,837 patients; EPA-DHA hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.17 for major cardiovascular events) found nothing. The 1999 result may have been real for its era — an untreated-baseline effect that modern therapy now covers — but for a patient on today's post-MI treatment, the randomised evidence says fish oil capsules add nothing measurable. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit in the pre-modern-therapy era / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on modern therapy (Tier C: a mortality claim).

cards.headline: GISSI-Prevenzione 1999: n-3 PUFA cut the primary endpoint by a relative 10–15%, driven by fewer deaths
cards.summary: GISSI-Prevenzione 1999: n-3 PUFA cut the primary endpoint by a relative 10–15%, driven by fewer deaths
cards.people: 11,324 patients surviving a recent (within 3 months) myocardial infarction, randomly assigned in a factorial design to n-3 PUFA 1 g daily (n=2,836), vitamin E 300 mg daily (n=2,830), both (n=2,830), or neither (n=2,828), followed 3.5 years. Primary combined endpoint: death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and stroke.
cards.result: n-3 PUFA significantly lowered the risk of the primary endpoint (relative-risk decrease 10% [95% CI 1–18] by two-way analysis; 15% [2–26] by four-way analysis) — relative effects; the abstract does not print the groups' absolute event rates for this endpoint. The benefit was attributable to decreased risk of death (14% [3–24] two-way; 20% [6–33] four-way) and cardiovascular death (17% [3–29]; 30% [13–44]). Vitamin E had no benefit, and combined treatment behaved like n-3 PUFA alone.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, no placebo, and conducted in 1993–95 Italy — before statins, dual antiplatelet therapy and early revascularisation were standard after myocardial infarction. Its population-level diet context also differs from today's supplement users. Vitamin E is carded only as the trial's other factor; this shelf makes no vitamin E claim either way.

Lancet. 1999. PMID: 10465168. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: OMEGA 2010: on guideline therapy, sudden death 1.5% vs 1.5% — nothing added
cards.summary: OMEGA 2010: on guideline therapy, sudden death 1.5% vs 1.5% — nothing added
cards.people: 3,851 patients randomised double-blind 3 to 14 days after acute myocardial infarction at 104 German centres, to omega-3 fatty acid ethyl esters 1 g daily or placebo for 1 year, both on top of guideline-directed therapy. Primary end point: sudden cardiac death.
cards.result: Sudden cardiac death occurred in 1.5% of patients in both groups (P=0.84; odds ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.56 to 1.60). Total mortality was 4.6% versus 3.7% (P=0.18; OR 1.25; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.72). Major adverse cerebrovascular and cardiovascular events occurred in 10.4% versus 8.8% (P=0.1), and revascularisation in 27.6% versus 29.1% (P=0.34). The authors concluded 1 year of omega-3 treatment did not reduce sudden cardiac death or other outcomes.
cards.watchOut: One year of treatment and a low sudden-death rate on modern therapy (1.5%) limit power for rare endpoints — but the point estimates give no hint of benefit in any outcome, including a numerically higher total mortality on omega-3.

cards.headline: Alpha Omega 2010: EPA-DHA HR 1.01 for major cardiovascular events — null at food-level doses in margarine
cards.summary: Alpha Omega 2010: EPA-DHA HR 1.01 for major cardiovascular events — null at food-level doses in margarine
cards.people: 4,837 patients aged 60 to 80 years (78% men) who had had a myocardial infarction and were receiving state-of-the-art therapy, randomised double-blind to margarines supplying EPA-DHA (target extra 400 mg/day), alpha-linolenic acid (target 2 g/day), both, or placebo, for 40 months. Primary end point: rate of major cardiovascular events.
cards.result: 671 patients (13.9%) had a major cardiovascular event during follow-up. Neither EPA-DHA (hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.17; P=0.93) nor alpha-linolenic acid (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.05; P=0.20) reduced the primary end point. Achieved intakes were modest (226 mg EPA plus 150 mg DHA daily in the EPA-DHA groups).
cards.watchOut: The dose delivered (~376 mg/day EPA+DHA in food) is well below GISSI-Prevenzione's 1 g capsule — so Alpha Omega alone does not refute the 1 g dose; OMEGA, which used 1 g of ethyl esters, is the trial that does. A prespecified subgroup signal for alpha-linolenic acid in women (HR 0.73; P=0.07) is hypothesis-generating only and is not carded as a finding.
cards.source: Kromhout D et al. n-3 fatty acids and cardiovascular events after myocardial infarction (Alpha Omega). N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20929341. Registry ID: NCT00127452, from the record.

shelves.title: After acute coronary syndrome, adding ezetimibe to pitavastatin and driving LDL below 70 did not significantly cut events (HIJ-PROPER)
shelves.question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and dyslipidaemia, does pitavastatin plus ezetimibe targeting LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL reduce cardiovascular events versus pitavastatin alone targeting below 100 mg/dL?
shelves.mesh: Ezetimibe · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — one open-label Japanese trial, underpowered beside the ezetimibe outcome trials in broader populations, and formally negative. In HIJ-PROPER, 1,734 patients with acute coronary syndrome and dyslipidaemia were randomised to pitavastatin plus ezetimibe targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL or pitavastatin alone targeting below 100 mg/dL; achieved LDL was 65.1 versus 84.6 mg/dL. The primary composite (death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, unstable angina or ischaemia-driven revascularisation) occurred in 32.8% versus 36.9% (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04; P=0.152) — a point estimate favouring combination therapy whose confidence interval includes both a 24% relative benefit and a small harm, so the trial settles nothing by itself. A prespecified subgroup with high sitosterol (cholesterol-absorption markers) showed HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.91), a hypothesis about who benefits from absorption blockade, not a trial-level result. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: the composite includes death, MI and stroke).

cards.headline: HIJ-PROPER 2017: primary endpoint 32.8% vs 36.9% (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.76–1.04; P=0.152) — not significant
cards.summary: HIJ-PROPER 2017: primary endpoint 32.8% vs 36.9% (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.76–1.04; P=0.152) — not significant
cards.people: Prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) trial in 1,734 patients with acute coronary syndrome and dyslipidaemia at 19 Japanese hospitals. Intervention: pitavastatin plus ezetimibe, targeted LDL-C below 70 mg/dL. Control: pitavastatin alone, targeted below 100 mg/dL. Primary endpoint: composite of all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, unstable angina, or ischaemia-driven revascularisation.
cards.result: Mean follow-up LDL-C was 65.1 mg/dL in the pitavastatin-plus-ezetimibe group and 84.6 mg/dL in the pitavastatin-monotherapy group. The primary endpoint occurred in 283 of 864 patients (32.8%) versus 316 of 857 (36.9%) (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04; P=0.152). In the prespecified subgroup with sitosterol at or above 2.2 µg/mL (high cholesterol absorption), the hazard ratio was 0.71 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.91). Trial registration number in the record: UMIN000002742.
cards.watchOut: THIN: single trial, open-label treatment, and an event rate so high (33–37%) because the composite counts unstable angina and revascularisation. The sitosterol subgroup is a biomarker hypothesis — it should not be quoted as proof that combination therapy works in absorbers without a dedicated trial.
cards.source: Hagiwara N et al. shelves.title: Hypertension: pravastatin versus usual care did not reduce mortality in ALLHAT's lipid trial
shelves.question: In older hypertensive patients with moderately elevated LDL cholesterol, does open-label pravastatin 40 mg reduce all-cause mortality and coronary events versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Pravastatin · Anticholesteremic Agents · Hypertension · Mortality · Humans
shelves.balance: A very large pragmatic trial with a null result — and a built-in explanation. In the ALLHAT lipid-lowering trial, 10,355 hypertensive patients aged 55 or older with LDL cholesterol 120–189 mg/dL were randomised to pravastatin 40 mg or usual care and followed a mean of 4.8 years. All-cause mortality was essentially identical (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=.88; 6-year rates 14.9% vs 15.3%), and coronary heart disease events were not significantly reduced (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.04; P=.16; 6-year rates 9.3% vs 10.4%). The catch is contrast: by year 4, about a third of the usual-care group had started lipid-lowering drugs themselves, so total cholesterol fell 17% relative on pravastatin versus 8% on usual care — a much smaller lipid gap than in blinded placebo trials. The trial shows that offering pravastatin into a usual-care system that adopts statins anyway changes outcomes little; it does not overturn the blinded-trial evidence that statins lower events versus no statin. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for pravastatin versus usual care as delivered (Tier C: a mortality question).

cards.headline: ALLHAT-LLT 2002: mortality RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.89–1.11); CHD events RR 0.91 (0.79–1.04) — both null
cards.summary: ALLHAT-LLT 2002: mortality RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.89–1.11); CHD events RR 0.91 (0.79–1.04) — both null
cards.people: 10,355 ambulatory persons aged 55 years or older with hypertension and at least one additional coronary risk factor, with LDL cholesterol 120–189 mg/dL (100–129 mg/dL if known coronary disease) and triglycerides below 350 mg/dL, randomised nonblind at 513 North American centres to pravastatin 40 mg/day (n=5,170) or usual care (n=5,185); mean follow-up 4.8 years. Main outcomes: all-cause mortality and the composite of fatal coronary heart disease or nonfatal myocardial infarction.
cards.result: All-cause mortality did not differ (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=.88; 6-year mortality rates 14.9% pravastatin vs 15.3% usual care). Coronary heart disease events: RR 0.91 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.04; P=.16; 6-year rates 9.3% vs 10.4%). Total cholesterol fell 17% relative on pravastatin versus 8% on usual care at year 4 (LDL cholesterol, in a random sample, −28% vs −11%); 32% of usual-care participants with coronary disease and 29% without had started lipid-lowering drugs by year 4. Findings were similar across subgroups, including patients with diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is usual care, not placebo: with nearly a third of controls on statins by year 4, this trial estimates the effect of a prescribing strategy in a statin-adopting system, not the pharmacological effect of pravastatin. Quoting it as 'statins don't work in hypertension' misreads the design; quoting the blinded trials alone and ignoring it misreads real-world delivery.

shelves.title: Familial chylomicronaemia: volanesorsen cut triglycerides sharply but lowered platelets (APPROACH)
shelves.question: In familial chylomicronaemia syndrome, does volanesorsen (an apolipoprotein C-III antisense oligonucleotide) lower triglycerides versus placebo, and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Oligonucleotides · Apolipoprotein C-III · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type I · Triglycerides · Thrombocytopenia · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — one small phase 3 trial in a rare disease, with a dramatic surrogate benefit and a real harm, so this shelf splits. In APPROACH, 66 patients with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome received volanesorsen (named specifically because, as of the trial era, it was not FDA-approved; it is an apolipoprotein C-III antisense oligonucleotide) or placebo for 52 weeks. At 3 months, triglycerides had fallen 77% relative on volanesorsen (mean decrease 1,712 mg/dL) versus an 18% relative increase on placebo; 77% of volanesorsen patients reached triglycerides below 750 mg/dL versus 10% on placebo. Against that: injection-site reactions in 20 of 33 treated patients versus none on placebo, and platelet counts below 100,000 per microlitre in 15 of 33 versus none — including two patients below 25,000; no patient fell below 50,000 after enhanced platelet monitoring began. The trial reports the triglyceride endpoint, not a demonstrated reduction in pancreatitis. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for triglyceride lowering (a surrogate, from one 66-patient trial) / LIKELY (harm) for thrombocytopenia and injection-site reactions.

cards.headline: APPROACH 2019: triglycerides −77% relative vs +18% at 3 months; platelets <100,000 in 15 of 33 vs 0
cards.summary: APPROACH 2019: triglycerides −77% relative vs +18% at 3 months; platelets <100,000 in 15 of 33 vs 0
cards.people: 66 patients with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome in a phase 3 double-blind randomised trial of volanesorsen versus placebo over 52 weeks. Primary end point: percentage change in fasting triglyceride level from baseline to 3 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, patients on volanesorsen had a 77% relative decrease in triglycerides (mean decrease 1,712 mg/dL; 95% CI 1,330 to 2,094) versus an 18% relative increase on placebo (mean increase 92.0 mg/dL; 95% CI −301 to 486) (P<0.001). Apolipoprotein C-III fell 84% relative (mean −25.7 mg/dL) versus a 6.1% relative rise on placebo. 77% of volanesorsen patients versus 10% on placebo had triglycerides below 750 mg/dL at 3 months. The most common adverse events were injection-site reactions (20 of 33 volanesorsen patients; none on placebo). Platelet counts fell below 100,000/µL in 15 of 33 versus none on placebo; two patients fell below 25,000/µL, and no patient fell below 50,000/µL after enhanced monitoring was implemented.
cards.watchOut: THIN: 66 patients, and the proven endpoint is a blood level, not pancreatitis or survival — do not let the size of the triglyceride fall smuggle in a clinical-outcome claim. The platelet harm is dose-limiting and drove the monitoring requirements; volanesorsen is not FDA-approved (it was authorised in the EU as Waylivra), which is why the product is named here under the library's clarification exception. Distinct from Shelf #1105, which covers olezarsen, a different apoC-III agent.
cards.source: Witztum JL et al. Volanesorsen and Triglyceride Levels in Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome (APPROACH). N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 31390500. Registry ID: NCT02211209, from the record.
