shelves.title: Heart failure: fat-soluble (lipophilic) statins — atorvastatin and pitavastatin — as a contrast to the water-soluble rosuvastatin trials
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure, do fat-soluble (lipophilic) statins such as atorvastatin or pitavastatin improve clinical outcomes, in contrast to the water-soluble (hydrophilic) rosuvastatin that was null in CORONA and GISSI-HF?
shelves.mesh: Atorvastatin · C-Reactive Protein · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Failure · Heart Ventricles · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Inflammation Mediators · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Aged · Chronic Disease · Japan · Quinolines
shelves.balance: This shelf exists as the contrast to Shelf #2232, where two large trials of rosuvastatin — a water-soluble (hydrophilic) statin — found no benefit in heart failure. The hypothesis behind it (argued in an editorial by this library's developer at the time) is that the null belonged to the molecule's solubility class: a fat-soluble (lipophilic) statin, which penetrates cell membranes including myocardium, might behave differently. The direct randomised evidence for fat-soluble statins in heart failure is much thinner than the rosuvastatin evidence, and it does not confirm the hypothesis on clinical outcomes. PEARL randomised 574 Japanese patients with chronic heart failure to pitavastatin (lipophilic) or control: the primary composite of cardiac death or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure did not differ (adjusted HR 0.922; 95% CI 0.632 to 1.345; P=0.672). There was a significant interaction with ejection fraction (P=0.004): in patients with LVEF at least 30%, the composite was lower on pitavastatin (adjusted HR 0.525; 95% CI 0.308 to 0.896; P=0.018), while below 30% the point estimate ran the other way (adjusted HR 1.582; 95% CI 0.890 to 2.813) — a subgroup pattern, not an overall benefit. The one placebo-controlled atorvastatin trial (Sola 2006, 108 patients with non-ischaemic heart failure and LVEF at most 35%) improved ejection fraction (0.33 to 0.37 on atorvastatin while placebo declined; P=0.01), reduced ventricular dimensions, and lowered inflammatory markers over 12 months — surrogate and imaging endpoints only, with no power for death or hospitalisation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the fat-soluble hypothesis remains biologically coherent and was exactly what PEARL set out to test (its abstract opens by contrasting lipophilic pitavastatin with the negative hydrophilic rosuvastatin trials), but on hard outcomes the lipophilic evidence is one null-primary trial with a subgroup signal plus one small surrogate-endpoint trial. Nothing here overturns #2232; it records that the contrast was tested and not confirmed. Tier C: heart-failure mortality and hospitalisation claims, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

cards.headline: PEARL 2013: pitavastatin (lipophilic) did not reduce cardiac death or HF hospitalisation overall (adjusted HR 0.922); benefit only in the LVEF ≥30% subgroup
cards.summary: PEARL 2013: pitavastatin (lipophilic) did not reduce cardiac death or HF hospitalisation overall (adjusted HR 0.922); benefit only in the LVEF ≥30% subgroup
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (PEARL; lipophilic statin vs control)
cards.people: 574 Japanese patients with chronic heart failure, randomly assigned to pitavastatin (n=288) or control (n=286). Primary outcome: composite of cardiac death and hospitalisation for worsening heart failure. The trial was explicitly designed against the background of the negative hydrophilic (rosuvastatin) trials.
cards.result: No significant difference in the primary outcome: adjusted hazard ratio 0.922 (95% CI 0.632 to 1.345; P=0.672). There was a strongly significant interaction with left ventricular ejection fraction (P=0.004): with LVEF at least 30%, the primary outcome was significantly reduced on pitavastatin (adjusted HR 0.525; 95% CI 0.308 to 0.896; P=0.018); with LVEF below 30%, no benefit (adjusted HR 1.582; 95% CI 0.890 to 2.813; P=0.118).
cards.watchOut: The overall trial is null; the LVEF ≥30% result is a subgroup of a null trial — hypothesis-generating, not a demonstrated benefit — and the below-30% point estimate runs toward harm. Control was not placebo in the abstract's description, and the population is Japanese chronic HF patients; no mortality claim can be printed from this trial.

cards.headline: Sola 2006: atorvastatin improved ejection fraction and inflammatory markers in non-ischaemic heart failure — surrogate endpoints only
cards.summary: Sola 2006: atorvastatin improved ejection fraction and inflammatory markers in non-ischaemic heart failure — surrogate endpoints only
cards.people: 108 patients with non-ischaemic heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction at most 35%, randomised double-blind to atorvastatin 20 mg/day or placebo for 12 months. Outcomes: echocardiographic LVEF and ventricular dimensions, and serum markers of inflammation and oxidation.
cards.result: LVEF increased from 0.33 ± 0.05 to 0.37 ± 0.04 on atorvastatin (P=0.01), while placebo patients' ejection fraction declined. LV end-diastolic diameter fell from 57.1 ± 5.9 mm to 53.4 ± 5.1 mm (P=0.007) and end-systolic diameter from 42.4 ± 3.8 mm to 39.1 ± 3.8 mm (P=0.02) on atorvastatin, while dimensions increased on placebo. Erythrocyte superoxide dismutase activity increased, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and tumour necrosis factor-alpha receptor II fell significantly on atorvastatin.
cards.watchOut: A pilot-scale trial (n=108) measuring imaging and blood markers, not death or hospitalisation. Improved ejection fraction on a statin in non-ischaemic HF is a mechanism signal; CORONA and GISSI-HF (Shelf #2232) show that favourable marker movement with a statin in HF does not by itself produce outcome benefit. Pre-registration-era trial: no registry ID exists, legitimately.
cards.source: Sola S et al. Atorvastatin improves left ventricular systolic function and serum markers of inflammation in nonischemic heart failure. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2006. PMID: 16412856. shelves.title: Frail elderly patients stable on a vitamin K antagonist: switching to a DOAC caused more bleeding (FRAIL-AF)
shelves.question: In frail patients aged 75 or older with atrial fibrillation already stable on a vitamin K antagonist, does switching to a direct oral anticoagulant reduce bleeding compared with continuing the VKA?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Frail Elderly · Frailty · Thromboembolism · Vitamin K · Administration, Oral · Stroke
shelves.balance: A large pragmatic trial whose result ran against its hypothesis. FRAIL-AF randomised 1,330 frail patients (age 75 or older, Groningen Frailty Indicator score at least 3; mean age 83) with atrial fibrillation who were managed on a vitamin K antagonist, to switch to a non-vitamin-K oral anticoagulant (NOAC/DOAC) or to continue INR-guided VKA treatment, followed for 12 months. The primary outcome — major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding — occurred more often after switching: 101 events in the switch arm versus 62 in the continuation arm, hazard ratio 1.69 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.32), and the trial was stopped early for futility. Thromboembolic events were not reduced (HR 1.26; 95% CI 0.60 to 2.61). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in frail elderly patients already stable on a VKA, switching to a DOAC increases bleeding without a thromboembolism advantage. This is a verdict about switching stable patients, not about starting anticoagulation: in the untreated very elderly, low-dose edoxaban helped (ELDERCARE-AF, drafted topic #2244) — the pair is the balance.

cards.headline: FRAIL-AF 2024: switching frail elderly patients from VKA to a NOAC raised major or clinically relevant bleeding (HR 1.69 relative); thromboembolism unchanged
cards.summary: FRAIL-AF 2024: switching frail elderly patients from VKA to a NOAC raised major or clinically relevant bleeding (HR 1.69 relative); thromboembolism unchanged
cards.people: 1,330 frail older patients with AF on INR-guided VKA therapy (mean age 83; median Groningen Frailty Indicator 4), randomised to switch to a NOAC (662 analysed) or continue VKA (661); patients with GFR below 30 or valvular AF were excluded. Primary outcome: major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding over 12 months, with death as a competing risk.
cards.result: After 163 primary-outcome events (101 switch vs 62 continue), the trial was stopped for futility at a prespecified analysis. The hazard ratio for bleeding was 1.69 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.32) — a 69% relative increase with switching. The hazard ratio for thromboembolic events was 1.26 (95% CI 0.60 to 2.61) — no advantage to switching.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable for INR-guided therapy) with adjudicated endpoints. The population is frail patients already tolerating a VKA — the result does not argue against starting a DOAC in a patient newly needing anticoagulation, and it sits opposite ELDERCARE-AF's untreated population by design.

shelves.title: Where dronedarone harms: permanent AF with risk factors, and severe heart failure (PALLAS + ANDROMEDA)
shelves.question: In permanent atrial fibrillation with cardiovascular risk factors, and in recently decompensated severe heart failure, does dronedarone reduce events — or increase death and hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amiodarone · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Dronedarone · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Stroke · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A harm: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, in two different populations, both stopped early because dronedarone hurt people. In PALLAS (permanent AF in patients 65 or older with risk factors for major vascular events; 3,236 enrolled), dronedarone roughly doubled the first coprimary outcome of stroke, myocardial infarction, systemic embolism or cardiovascular death (43 vs 19 events; hazard ratio 2.29 — a 129% relative increase; 95% CI 1.34 to 3.94; P=0.002), doubled cardiovascular death (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.00 to 4.49), more than doubled stroke (HR 2.32), and increased heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 1.81). In ANDROMEDA (627 patients hospitalised with symptomatic heart failure and severe LV systolic dysfunction), dronedarone doubled early mortality — 8.1% versus 3.8% died over a median of 2 months (HR 2.13; 95% CI 1.07 to 4.25; P=0.03) — the excess predominantly from worsening heart failure. The positive sibling trial (ATHENA, non-permanent AF) is carded elsewhere in this library; this shelf is the harm boundary. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C: mortality claims, developer's personal-approval territory.

cards.headline: PALLAS 2011: in permanent AF, dronedarone doubled stroke/MI/embolism/cardiovascular death (HR 2.29 relative) — stopped for safety
cards.summary: PALLAS 2011: in permanent AF, dronedarone doubled stroke/MI/embolism/cardiovascular death (HR 2.29 relative) — stopped for safety
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, stopped early (PALLAS)
cards.people: Patients at least 65 years old with at least a 6-month history of permanent AF and risk factors for major vascular events, assigned to dronedarone or placebo; 3,236 enrolled before the study was stopped for safety reasons. Coprimary outcomes: stroke, myocardial infarction, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular death; and unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation or death.
cards.result: The first coprimary outcome occurred in 43 patients on dronedarone versus 19 on placebo (hazard ratio 2.29; 95% CI 1.34 to 3.94; P=0.002). Cardiovascular death: 21 vs 10 (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.00 to 4.49; P=0.046), including arrhythmia death 13 vs 4 (HR 3.26). Stroke: 23 vs 10 (HR 2.32; 95% CI 1.11 to 4.88; P=0.02). Hospitalisation for heart failure: 43 vs 24 (HR 1.81; 95% CI 1.10 to 2.99; P=0.02). The authors' conclusion: dronedarone should not be used in such patients.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports event counts rather than full group denominators for each outcome; the hazard ratios are relative effects. Early termination can exaggerate effect sizes, but the direction is corroborated by ANDROMEDA in a second population.

cards.headline: ANDROMEDA 2008: in severe recently decompensated heart failure, dronedarone doubled early mortality (8.1% vs 3.8%)
cards.summary: ANDROMEDA 2008: in severe recently decompensated heart failure, dronedarone doubled early mortality (8.1% vs 3.8%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, stopped early (ANDROMEDA)
cards.people: 627 patients hospitalised with symptomatic heart failure and severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (310 dronedarone 400 mg twice daily, 317 placebo), of a planned 1,000; the trial was prematurely terminated for safety at the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation. Primary endpoint: death from any cause or hospitalisation for heart failure. Median follow-up 2 months.

shelves.title: Adding vein-of-Marshall ethanol infusion to ablation for persistent AF: a modest gain in freedom from AF (VENUS)
shelves.question: In persistent atrial fibrillation, does vein-of-Marshall ethanol infusion plus catheter ablation improve freedom from AF or atrial tachycardia versus ablation alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Combined Modality Therapy · Ethanol · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Single-Blind Method · Tachycardia · Treatment Outcome · Vena Cava, Superior
shelves.balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a real but modest gain. VENUS randomised 350 patients with persistent AF referred for first ablation (343 analysed) to catheter ablation alone or ablation plus retrograde ethanol infusion into the vein of Marshall. Freedom from AF or atrial tachycardia after a single procedure, off antiarrhythmic drugs, at both 6 and 12 months was 49.2% with the ethanol addition versus 38.0% with ablation alone — an absolute difference of 11.2 percentage points (95% CI 0.8 to 21.7; P=.04). Ethanol delivery succeeded in 155 of 185 assigned patients; AF burden and perimitral block success also favoured the combined approach, and adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a single trial, a borderline P value on the primary outcome, and success still under half — promising adjunct, not a new standard on this evidence alone.

cards.headline: VENUS 2020: freedom from AF/AT at 6 and 12 months 49.2% with vein-of-Marshall ethanol plus ablation vs 38.0% ablation alone
cards.summary: VENUS 2020: freedom from AF/AT at 6 and 12 months 49.2% with vein-of-Marshall ethanol plus ablation vs 38.0% ablation alone
cards.people: 350 patients with persistent AF referred for first ablation at 12 US centres (343 randomised and analysed; mean age 66.5 years; 261 men), assigned to catheter ablation alone (n=158) or ablation plus vein-of-Marshall ethanol infusion (n=185), with blinded outcome assessment. Primary outcome: freedom from AF or atrial tachycardia longer than 30 seconds after a single procedure, without antiarrhythmic drugs, at both 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 49.2% (91/185) with ethanol plus ablation versus 38.0% (60/158) with ablation alone (difference 11.2 percentage points; 95% CI 0.8 to 21.7; P=.04). Secondary outcomes favouring the combined approach included zero AF burden (78.3% vs 67.9%; P=.01), freedom from AF after multiple procedures (65.2% vs 53.8%; P=.04), and perimitral block (80.6% vs 51.3%; P<.001); 9 of 12 secondary outcomes did not differ. Ethanol was successfully delivered in 155 of 185 patients. Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Single trial with a primary-outcome P value of .04 and a 15% technical failure rate for ethanol delivery built into the design; follow-up is 12 months. The absolute gain (~11 points) leaves most patients in both arms with recurrence or on further procedures.
cards.source: Valderrábano M et al. Effect of Catheter Ablation With Vein of Marshall Ethanol Infusion vs Catheter Ablation Alone on Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: The VENUS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33107945. shelves.title: After successful AF ablation, rivaroxaban versus aspirin: event rates too low to separate (OCEAN)
shelves.question: In patients free of recurrence at least a year after successful AF ablation and at moderate stroke risk, is rivaroxaban superior to aspirin for preventing stroke, systemic embolism, or covert embolic stroke on MRI?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Aspirin · Atrial Fibrillation · Brain · Catheter Ablation · Embolism · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Fibrinolytic Agents · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Rivaroxaban · Stroke · Treatment Outcome · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: THIN on events, whatever its size. OCEAN randomised 1,284 patients who had undergone successful catheter ablation at least a year earlier and had a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 1, to rivaroxaban 15 mg daily or aspirin, followed for 3 years with MRI after enrolment and at 3 years. The primary composite — stroke, systemic embolism, or new covert embolic stroke (a new infarct at least 15 mm on MRI) — occurred in just 5 patients on rivaroxaban (0.31 events per 100 patient-years) versus 9 on aspirin (0.66 per 100 patient-years): relative risk 0.56, but with a 95% confidence interval of 0.19 to 1.65 (P=0.28) — the data are compatible with rivaroxaban being much better, no better, or somewhat worse. Fatal or major bleeding was numerically more frequent with rivaroxaban (1.6% vs 0.6%; HR 2.51; 95% CI 0.79 to 7.95). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): what the trial actually establishes is that event rates after successful ablation are very low; it does not establish that stopping anticoagulation is safe, nor that continuing it helps. Tier C: a stroke claim, so the developer reviews it personally.

cards.headline: OCEAN 2026: primary composite 5 events on rivaroxaban vs 9 on aspirin over 3 years (RR 0.56 relative; 95% CI 0.19 to 1.65) — too few events to judge
cards.summary: OCEAN 2026: primary composite 5 events on rivaroxaban vs 9 on aspirin over 3 years (RR 0.56 relative; 95% CI 0.19 to 1.65) — too few events to judge
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment (OCEAN)
cards.people: 1,284 patients at least 1 year after successful catheter ablation for AF, with CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 or more (2 or more for women or when vascular disease was the risk factor); 641 assigned rivaroxaban 15 mg daily, 643 aspirin 70–120 mg daily; followed 3 years with head MRI at enrolment and 3 years. Primary outcome: composite of stroke, systemic embolism, or new covert embolic stroke (at least one new infarct of 15 mm or more on MRI) at 3 years.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 5 patients (0.31 per 100 patient-years) on rivaroxaban and 9 (0.66 per 100 patient-years) on aspirin (relative risk 0.56; 95% CI 0.19 to 1.65; absolute difference at 3 years −0.6 percentage points; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.5; P=0.28). New cerebral infarcts smaller than 15 mm: 3.9% vs 4.4% (RR 0.89; 95% CI 0.51 to 1.55). Fatal or major bleeding: 10 patients (1.6%) on rivaroxaban versus 4 (0.6%) on aspirin (HR 2.51; 95% CI 0.79 to 7.95).
cards.watchOut: Only 14 primary events in 1,284 patients — the trial is a demonstration of low absolute risk after successful ablation, not a verdict for either drug. Covert MRI infarcts dominate what events there were. Open-label drug assignment with blinded outcome assessment.
cards.source: Verma A et al. Antithrombotic Therapy after Successful Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID: 41211931. Registry ID: NCT02168829, from the record. shelves.title: After AF ablation, left atrial appendage closure matched anticoagulation on events with less bleeding (OPTION)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing AF ablation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, is left atrial appendage closure with Watchman FLX noninferior to continued oral anticoagulation for death, stroke or systemic embolism, with less bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Anticoagulants · Atrial Appendage · Atrial Fibrillation · Embolism · Hemorrhage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Left Atrial Appendage Closure · Septal Occluder Device · Stroke · Postoperative Hemorrhage · Treatment Outcome · Follow-Up Studies · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: A large randomised trial that met both of its tests. OPTION randomised 1,600 patients with AF undergoing catheter ablation and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score (at least 2 in men, at least 3 in women; mean 3.5) to left atrial appendage closure or continued oral anticoagulation. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint — non-procedure-related major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding — occurred in 8.5% with closure versus 18.1% with anticoagulation (P<0.001 for superiority): an absolute reduction of about 10 percentage points. The primary efficacy composite of death from any cause, stroke, or systemic embolism was 5.3% versus 5.8% (P<0.001 for noninferiority), and major bleeding including procedure-related bleeding was also noninferior (3.9% vs 5.0%). Device- or procedure-related complications occurred in 23 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY: closure after ablation is noninferior for events and clearly gentler on bleeding — in patients already undergoing ablation. Distinct from Shelf #272 (occlusion versus anticoagulation outside the ablation setting).

cards.headline: OPTION 2025: bleeding 8.5% with appendage closure vs 18.1% on anticoagulation (superior); death/stroke/embolism 5.3% vs 5.8% (noninferior)
cards.summary: OPTION 2025: bleeding 8.5% with appendage closure vs 18.1% on anticoagulation (superior); death/stroke/embolism 5.3% vs 5.8% (noninferior)
cards.people: 1,600 patients with AF and elevated CHA2DS2-VASc scores undergoing catheter ablation, randomised 1:1 to left atrial appendage closure (803; Watchman FLX) or oral anticoagulation (797). Mean age 69.6 years; 34.1% women; mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.5. Endpoints at 36 months: primary safety (non-procedure-related major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, superiority), primary efficacy (death from any cause, stroke, or systemic embolism, noninferiority), secondary (major bleeding including procedure-related, noninferiority).
cards.result: Primary safety endpoint: 65 patients (8.5%) in the closure group versus 137 (18.1%) in the anticoagulation group (P<0.001 for superiority). Primary efficacy endpoint: 41 patients (5.3%) versus 44 (5.8%) (P<0.001 for noninferiority). Secondary endpoint: 3.9% versus 5.0% (P<0.001 for noninferiority). Complications related to the device or procedure occurred in 23 patients.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not superiority on events — the win is bleeding, and it is bought with an implant procedure and its early complications. The population is patients already undergoing ablation; the shelf does not extend to patients who would need a standalone procedure solely for closure.
cards.source: Wazni OM et al. Left Atrial Appendage Closure after Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 39555822. Registry ID: NCT03795298, from the record. shelves.title: Severe tricuspid regurgitation: transcatheter valve replacement beat medical therapy on a hierarchical composite, driven by symptoms (TRISCEND II)
shelves.question: In symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation, does transfemoral tricuspid valve replacement (EVOQUE) improve the hierarchical composite of survival, heart-failure events, and patient-reported health status versus medical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Cardiac Catheterization · Heart Failure · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation · Hospitalization · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Tricuspid Valve · Tricuspid Valve Insufficiency · Prospective Studies · Postoperative Hemorrhage · Heart-Assist Devices · Heart Transplantation · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: One randomised trial, a positive composite whose weight sits in how patients feel, not in whether they live or stay out of hospital. TRISCEND II randomised 400 patients with severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation 2:1 to transcatheter tricuspid-valve replacement plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone. The hierarchical primary outcome (death, RVAD or transplant, postindex tricuspid intervention, heart-failure hospitalisation, then KCCQ improvement of at least 10 points, NYHA class, and 6-minute walk) favoured replacement with a win ratio of 2.02 (95% CI 1.56 to 2.62; P<0.001). But the pair comparisons show where the wins came from: quality-of-life improvement (23.1% vs 6.0% of pairs) and NYHA class (10.2% vs 0.8%), while heart-failure hospitalisation pairs slightly favoured control (9.7% vs 10.0%) and the death comparison was close (14.8% vs 12.5%). The costs were real: severe bleeding 15.4% versus 5.3% (P=0.003) and new permanent pacemakers 17.4% versus 2.3% (P<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: the composite embeds death, so the developer reviews it personally) — symptoms and quality of life improve, at a procedural price, with no demonstrated survival or hospitalisation benefit at one year.

cards.headline: TRISCEND II 2025: win ratio 2.02 for replacement — driven by KCCQ and NYHA wins; severe bleeding 15.4% vs 5.3%, new pacemakers 17.4% vs 2.3%
cards.summary: TRISCEND II 2025: win ratio 2.02 for replacement — driven by KCCQ and NYHA wins; severe bleeding 15.4% vs 5.3%, new pacemakers 17.4% vs 2.3%
cards.people: 400 patients with severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation at international centres, randomised 2:1 to transcatheter tricuspid-valve replacement plus medical therapy (267) or medical therapy alone (133). Primary outcome: hierarchical composite of death from any cause, RVAD implantation or heart transplantation, postindex tricuspid-valve intervention, heart-failure hospitalisation, KCCQ overall-summary improvement of at least 10 points, NYHA improvement of at least one class, and 6-minute-walk improvement of at least 30 m, analysed by win ratio at 1 year.
cards.result: Win ratio 2.02 (95% CI 1.56 to 2.62; P<0.001) favouring replacement. Pair wins by component: death 14.8% vs 12.5%; postindex tricuspid intervention 3.2% vs 0.6%; KCCQ-OS improvement 23.1% vs 6.0%; NYHA improvement 10.2% vs 0.8%; 6-minute-walk improvement 1.1% vs 0.9%; heart-failure hospitalisation pairs favoured control, 9.7% vs 10.0%. Severe bleeding occurred in 15.4% of the replacement group versus 5.3% of controls (P=0.003); new permanent pacemakers in 17.4% versus 2.3% (P<0.001). The authors conclude superiority for the composite, driven primarily by symptoms and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A hierarchical composite can be won on its softest rungs: here the symptom rungs dominate and the hospitalisation rung went the other way. One-year horizon; open-label (unavoidable for a device), so patient-reported outcomes carry expectation effects. The pacemaker rate (about 1 in 6) is a permanent consequence to weigh against symptom relief.
cards.source: Hahn RT et al. Transcatheter Valve Replacement in Severe Tricuspid Regurgitation. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 39475399. Registry ID: NCT04482062, from the record. shelves.title: Severe mitral annular calcification: transcatheter mitral replacement met its performance goal in a single-arm study (SUMMIT-MAC)
shelves.question: In patients with severe mitral disease and severe annular calcification at high surgical risk, what are the outcomes of Tendyne transcatheter mitral valve replacement against prespecified performance goals?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement · Calcinosis · Mitral Valve · Mitral Valve Insufficiency · Aged · Male · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Aged, 80 and over · Mitral Valve Stenosis
shelves.balance: THIN by construction — a single-arm pivotal study with no comparator, carded as an explicit exception to the two-trial gate and labelled as such on its face. SUMMIT-MAC treated 103 patients (mean age 78; 55% women) with severe mitral annular calcification and significant mitral disease (regurgitation in nearly all) at high surgical risk with the Tendyne transcatheter mitral valve. Technical success was 94.2% and 30-day mortality 6.8%. The prespecified primary endpoint — freedom from all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months — was 60.4%, against a performance goal of 43% (P=0.0002), so the goal was met. Symptoms improved markedly among survivors assessed (NYHA class I/II from 30.6% at baseline to 87.5% at 12 months; KCCQ overall summary up 18.7 points on average). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the study shows the procedure can be done in this anatomy with outcomes better than a prespecified floor; without a control group it cannot show the valve caused the difference, and 12-month freedom from death or HF hospitalisation of 60.4% also states how sick this population is.

cards.headline: SUMMIT-MAC 2026: technical success 94.2%, 30-day mortality 6.8%; freedom from death/HF hospitalisation 60.4% at 12 months vs a 43% performance goal

cards.people: 103 symptomatic patients with mitral disease due to severe mitral annular calcification at high surgical risk (mean age 78.0 years; 55% female; mitral regurgitation grade 2+ or worse in 97%), treated with the Tendyne transcatheter mitral valve system. Echocardiography core-lab assessed; adverse events adjudicated by an independent committee. Primary endpoint: freedom from all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months, tested against a prespecified performance goal.
cards.result: Technical success 94.2%; 30-day mortality 6.8%. The primary endpoint was met: freedom from all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation was 60.4% at 12 months (performance goal 43%; P=0.0002). NYHA class I/II rose from 30.6% at baseline to 87.5% at 12 months in paired assessments (P<0.0001), and mean KCCQ overall summary rose 18.7 points (SD 24.4; P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: No control group: a performance goal is a floor set in advance, not a comparison with surgery or medical therapy, and symptom scores in survivors are subject to survivorship and expectation effects. This shelf is a labelled exception to the library's two-trial gate — it documents feasibility and a benchmark, and must not be cited as comparative effectiveness.

shelves.title: Degenerative mitral regurgitation: PASCAL edge-to-edge repair noninferior to MitraClip at one year (CLASP IID)
shelves.question: In prohibitive-surgical-risk degenerative mitral regurgitation, is the PASCAL edge-to-edge repair system noninferior to MitraClip for major adverse events and mitral regurgitation reduction at one year?
shelves.balance: THIN — a single randomised device-comparison trial, and a clean one. CLASP IID randomised 300 prohibitive-risk patients with significant symptomatic degenerative mitral regurgitation 2:1 to the PASCAL system or MitraClip. Noninferiority held on both primary endpoints in the full cohort: 30-day major adverse events 4.6% versus 5.4% (rate difference −0.8 points, upper 95% confidence bound 4.6%), and mitral regurgitation of 2+ or less at 6 months in 97.9% versus 95.7% (difference 2.2 points, lower bound −2.5%). At one year, MR 2+ or less was 95.8% versus 93.8% and MR 1+ or less 77.1% versus 71.3%; differences in survival, freedom from heart-failure hospitalisation, and major adverse events were not significant, and functional and quality-of-life gains were sustained in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: PASCAL is a noninferior alternative device — an equivalence result from one trial at one year, in prohibitive-risk patients only. (Desk note: this record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID in the PubMed record — checked at the desk pass, never invented.)

cards.headline: CLASP IID 2023: PASCAL noninferior to MitraClip — 30-day major adverse events 4.6% vs 5.4%; MR ≤2+ at 6 months 97.9% vs 95.7%
cards.summary: CLASP IID 2023: PASCAL noninferior to MitraClip — 30-day major adverse events 4.6% vs 5.4%; MR ≤2+ at 6 months 97.9% vs 95.7%
cards.people: 300 prohibitive-surgical-risk patients with 3+/4+ degenerative mitral regurgitation, randomised 2:1 to PASCAL (n=204) or MitraClip (n=96). Primary endpoints: 30-day composite major adverse events (safety) and MR ≤2+ at 6 months (effectiveness), tested for noninferiority in the full cohort; one-year outcomes include MR ≤2+ and ≤1+, survival, heart-failure hospitalisation, function and quality of life.
cards.result: Noninferiority persisted for both primary endpoints in the full cohort: 30-day major adverse events 4.6% (PASCAL) vs 5.4% (MitraClip), difference −0.8 points (95% upper bound 4.6%); 6-month MR ≤2+ 97.9% vs 95.7%, difference 2.2 points (95% lower bound −2.5%). At 1 year: MR ≤2+ 95.8% vs 93.8% (difference 2.1; lower bound −4.1%); MR ≤1+ 77.1% vs 71.3% (difference 5.8; lower bound −5.3%). Differences in survival, freedom from heart-failure hospitalisation and major adverse events at 1 year were nonsignificant; functional class and quality of life improved significantly and were sustained in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A device-versus-device noninferiority result — it does not compare either device with surgery or medical therapy, and one year is short for durability of repair. Prohibitive-risk degenerative MR only; functional MR is a different question.
cards.source: Zahr F et al. One-Year Outcomes From the CLASP IID Randomized Trial for Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation. JACC Cardiovasc Interv. 2023. PMID: 37962288. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. MeSH: none assigned on the PubMed record.

shelves.title: After TAVR, dapagliflozin reduced death or worsening heart failure (DapaTAVI)
shelves.question: In older patients after successful TAVR who have heart failure plus diabetes, kidney disease, or reduced ejection fraction, does dapagliflozin reduce all-cause death or worsening heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement · Follow-Up Studies · Drug Administration Schedule · Spain · Incidence · Reproductive Tract Infections · Hypotension · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: An OUTSTANDING-SINGLE candidate by this library's rule: one randomised trial with a hard-endpoint composite in a population the big SGLT2 trials excluded. DapaTAVI randomised 1,257 older patients with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI — all with a history of heart failure plus renal insufficiency, diabetes, or LV systolic dysfunction — to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or standard care alone after TAVI; 1,222 were analysed. At one year the primary composite of death from any cause or worsening heart failure (hospitalisation or urgent visit) occurred in 15.0% on dapagliflozin versus 20.1% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.72 — a 28% relative reduction; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95; P=0.02). The components: death 7.8% versus 8.9% (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.28 — not significant on its own) and worsening heart failure 9.4% versus 14.4% (subhazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88), so the composite win is carried by heart-failure events. Genital infection and hypotension were significantly more common on dapagliflozin. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a mortality-embedding composite — the developer's personal approval, sought here). Single trial, open-label, one country (Spain); the stamp reflects a large, well-sized effect on a hard composite, and the shelf says 'one trial' on its face.

cards.people: Older patients with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI in Spain, all with a history of heart failure plus at least one of renal insufficiency, diabetes, or left ventricular systolic dysfunction; 620 assigned dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and 637 standard care alone after TAVI; 1,222 included in the primary analysis. Primary outcome: composite of death from any cause or worsening heart failure (hospitalisation or urgent visit) at 1 year.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 91 patients (15.0%) on dapagliflozin and 124 (20.1%) on standard care (hazard ratio 0.72; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95; P=0.02). Death from any cause: 47 (7.8%) versus 55 (8.9%) (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.28). Worsening heart failure: 9.4% versus 14.4% (subhazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88). Genital infection and hypotension were significantly more common in the dapagliflozin group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-country; the mortality component alone is not significant, so do not print a survival claim — the claim is the composite, carried by worsening-heart-failure events. The population is post-TAVI patients already at high heart-failure risk, not all TAVI patients.

shelves.title: Aortic stenosis: intensive lipid lowering did not slow the valve (SEAS + SALTIRE)
shelves.question: In aortic stenosis, does intensive lipid lowering slow valve progression or reduce valve-related events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticholesteremic Agents · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Azetidines · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, LDL · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ezetimibe · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Neoplasms · Simvastatin · Treatment Outcome · Atorvastatin · Calcinosis · Echocardiography, Doppler
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A null on the valve: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, two different regimens, the same answer. SEAS randomised 1,873 patients with mild-to-moderate asymptomatic aortic stenosis to simvastatin 40 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg or placebo for a median of 52.2 months: the primary composite (cardiovascular death, valve replacement, MI, unstable-angina hospitalisation, heart failure, bypass surgery, PCI, non-haemorrhagic stroke) occurred in 35.3% versus 38.2% (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.12; P=0.59), and valve replacement itself was identical (28.3% vs 29.9%; HR 1.00). SALTIRE randomised 155 patients with calcific aortic stenosis to atorvastatin 80 mg or placebo: despite LDL falling to 63 versus 130 mg/dL, aortic-jet velocity progressed identically (0.199 vs 0.203 m/s per year; P=0.95) and valve calcium progressed identically (22.3% vs 21.7% per year; P=0.93). SEAS did show fewer ischaemic cardiovascular events on treatment (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.97) — an atherosclerosis effect, not a valve effect — and a cancer excess (105 vs 70 cases; P=0.01) that later pooled analyses of the statin-ezetimibe programme did not confirm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for valve progression and valve events (Tier C: the composite embeds cardiovascular death). Lipid lowering treats these patients' arteries; it does not treat their valve.

cards.headline: SEAS 2008: simvastatin + ezetimibe — primary composite HR 0.96 relative, valve replacement HR 1.00; fewer ischaemic events, a cancer signal not later confirmed
cards.summary: SEAS 2008: simvastatin + ezetimibe — primary composite HR 0.96 relative, valve replacement HR 1.00; fewer ischaemic events, a cancer signal not later confirmed
cards.people: 1,873 patients with mild-to-moderate asymptomatic aortic stenosis randomised to simvastatin 40 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg or placebo daily; median follow-up 52.2 months. Primary outcome: composite of major cardiovascular events including cardiovascular death, aortic-valve replacement, nonfatal MI, hospitalisation for unstable angina, heart failure, bypass grafting, PCI, and non-haemorrhagic stroke. Secondary outcomes: aortic-valve events and ischaemic cardiovascular events.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 333 patients (35.3%) on simvastatin-ezetimibe and 355 (38.2%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.12; P=0.59). Aortic-valve replacement: 267 (28.3%) versus 278 (29.9%) (HR 1.00; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.18; P=0.97). Ischaemic cardiovascular events were fewer on treatment (148 vs 187 patients; HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.97; P=0.02), mainly fewer bypass operations. Cancer occurred more frequently on treatment (105 vs 70; P=0.01) — a signal later pooled analyses did not confirm.
cards.watchOut: The ischaemic-event reduction is the drug class doing its known job on coronary atherosclerosis; it does not rescue the valve hypothesis, and the trial's own conclusion separates the two. The cancer imbalance is reported here because the abstract reports it; it was not confirmed in later pooled data and should not be quoted without that context.

cards.headline: SALTIRE 2005: atorvastatin 80 mg halved LDL but jet velocity and valve calcium progressed exactly as on placebo
cards.summary: SALTIRE 2005: atorvastatin 80 mg halved LDL but jet velocity and valve calcium progressed exactly as on placebo
cards.people: 155 patients with calcific aortic stenosis randomised to atorvastatin 80 mg daily (77) or matched placebo (78); median follow-up 25 months. Primary endpoints: change in aortic-jet velocity (Doppler echocardiography) and aortic-valve calcium score (helical CT).
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell to 63 ± 23 mg/dL on atorvastatin versus 130 ± 30 mg/dL on placebo (P<0.001). Aortic-jet velocity increased 0.199 ± 0.210 m/s per year on atorvastatin and 0.203 ± 0.208 on placebo (P=0.95; adjusted mean difference 0.002; 95% CI −0.066 to 0.070). Valvular calcification progressed 22.3 ± 21.0% per year versus 21.7 ± 19.8% (P=0.93). The authors concluded intensive lipid lowering does not halt progression or induce regression, while noting the trial could not exclude a small effect or an effect on clinical endpoints — the gap SEAS then closed.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=155) and a progression-endpoint trial; read as the mechanistic half of the pair, with SEAS supplying the clinical events. Pre-registration-era trial: no registry ID exists, legitimately.
cards.source: Cowell SJ et al. A randomized trial of intensive lipid-lowering therapy in calcific aortic stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID: 15944423. Registry ID: none (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis: early surgery won on a composite in AVATAR; imaging-selected early intervention was null in EVOLVED
shelves.question: In truly asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis with normal ejection fraction and negative exercise test, does early surgical AVR reduce death, MI, stroke, or heart-failure hospitalisation versus conservative care — and does selecting patients by myocardial fibrosis change the answer?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Fibrosis · Myocardium · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement · Conservative Treatment · Asymptomatic Diseases
shelves.balance: Two small randomised trials of early intervention in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis that do not agree, because they asked different questions. AVATAR randomised 157 patients with severe AS, normal LV function and a mandatory negative exercise test to early surgical AVR or conservative care: the primary composite (all-cause death, MI, stroke, or unplanned HF hospitalisation) occurred in 13 patients on early surgery versus 26 on conservative care (hazard ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.90; P=0.02), with operative mortality 1.4% among the 92.3% who underwent surgery; no secondary endpoint, including mortality alone, differed significantly at this size. EVOLVED randomised 224 asymptomatic patients selected for myocardial fibrosis on cardiac MRI (of 356 planned — the trial under-enrolled) to early valve intervention or guideline-directed conservative care: the primary composite (death or unplanned AS-related hospitalisation) was 18% versus 23% (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=.44), death was 14% versus 13%, while AS-related hospitalisation (6% vs 17%; HR 0.37) and 12-month symptoms favoured early intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): early surgery plausibly reduces the composite in carefully tested asymptomatic patients (AVATAR), but the effect rests on 39 events in one small trial, and fibrosis-based selection did not reproduce it (EVOLVED). How patients are chosen matters more than the blanket question suggests.

cards.headline: AVATAR 2022: primary composite 13 events with early surgery vs 26 with conservative care (HR 0.46 relative); mortality alone not significantly different
cards.summary: AVATAR 2022: primary composite 13 events with early surgery vs 26 with conservative care (HR 0.46 relative); mortality alone not significantly different
cards.people: 157 patients with asymptomatic severe AS (valve area at most 1 cm² with jet velocity above 4 m/s or mean gradient at least 40 mm Hg), normal LV function, and mandatory negative exercise testing, at 9 centres in 7 European countries; 78 randomised to early surgical AVR, 79 to conservative guideline care. Primary composite: all-cause death, acute MI, stroke, or unplanned hospitalisation for heart failure. Median follow-up 32 months; event-driven design (minimum 35 events).
cards.result: 39 primary events in total: 13 in the early-surgery group and 26 in the conservative group (hazard ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.90; P=0.02). In the early-surgery group 72 patients (92.3%) underwent SAVR with operative mortality 1.4%. No secondary endpoint — including all-cause mortality, first HF hospitalisation, major bleeding, or thromboembolic complications — differed significantly, though trends were consistent with the primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: 39 events in 157 patients: the composite result is real but fragile, and this trial cannot support a mortality claim. The population is tightly defined (proven asymptomatic by exercise testing, normal EF) — do not generalise to patients who simply have not reported symptoms.
cards.source: Banovic M et al. Aortic Valve Replacement Versus Conservative Treatment in Asymptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis: The AVATAR Trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 34779220. Registry ID: NCT02436655, from the record. cards.headline: EVOLVED 2025: in fibrosis-selected asymptomatic severe AS, early intervention did not reduce death or AS hospitalisation (HR 0.79 relative; P=.44)
cards.summary: EVOLVED 2025: in fibrosis-selected asymptomatic severe AS, early intervention did not reduce death or AS hospitalisation (HR 0.79 relative; P=.44)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with masked endpoints (EVOLVED)
cards.people: 224 asymptomatic patients with severe AS and myocardial fibrosis on cardiac MRI at 24 centres in the UK and Australia (mean age 73; 28% women; mean peak velocity 4.3 m/s), of 356 planned, randomised to early valve intervention (surgical or transcatheter; 113) or guideline-directed conservative management (111). Primary outcome: composite of all-cause death or unplanned AS-related hospitalisation.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 20 of 113 (18%) with early intervention and 25 of 111 (23%) with conservative management (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=.44). All-cause death: 16 (14%) versus 14 (13%) (HR 1.22; 95% CI 0.59 to 2.51). Unplanned AS hospitalisation: 7 (6%) versus 19 (17%) (HR 0.37; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.88). NYHA class II–IV symptoms at 12 months were less frequent with early intervention (19.7% vs 37.9%; odds ratio 0.37; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.70). Seven of 9 secondary endpoints showed no significant difference; the authors note the wide confidence interval and the need for further research.
cards.watchOut: Under-enrolled (224 of 356 planned), so the null is also imprecise; the fibrosis-selection hypothesis is neither confirmed nor fully excluded. Read with AVATAR: exercise-test-proven asymptomatic patients benefited on a composite; MRI-fibrosis selection did not show an event benefit — symptoms and AS hospitalisations still favoured intervening.
cards.source: Loganath K et al. Early Intervention in Patients With Asymptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis and Myocardial Fibrosis: The EVOLVED Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 39466640. shelves.title: AF with a bioprosthetic mitral valve: rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin (RIVER)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and a bioprosthetic mitral valve, is rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin for death, major cardiovascular events, or major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Bioprosthesis · Cardiovascular Diseases · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mitral Valve · Rivaroxaban · Single-Blind Method · Stroke · Warfarin
shelves.balance: THIN in setting (one trial, one country, open-label warfarin management) but large and internally consistent. RIVER randomised 1,005 patients with AF and a bioprosthetic mitral valve at 49 Brazilian sites to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily or dose-adjusted warfarin (INR 2.0–3.0). The primary outcome — death, major cardiovascular events (stroke, TIA, systemic embolism, valve thrombosis, HF hospitalisation), or major bleeding at 12 months — occurred at a mean of 347.5 days on rivaroxaban versus 340.1 days on warfarin (restricted mean survival time difference 7.4 days; 95% CI −1.4 to 16.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). The components leaned toward rivaroxaban: cardiovascular death or thromboembolic events 3.4% versus 5.1% (HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.20), stroke 0.6% versus 2.4% (HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.88), major bleeding 1.4% versus 2.6% (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.21 to 1.35). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: the composite embeds death and stroke): rivaroxaban is a legitimate alternative to warfarin in this specific valve population — bioprosthetic mitral valves only; mechanical valves are the opposite story (Shelf #2257).

cards.headline: RIVER 2020: rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin (mean time to primary event 347.5 vs 340.1 days); stroke 0.6% vs 2.4%
cards.summary: RIVER 2020: rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin (mean time to primary event 347.5 vs 340.1 days); stroke 0.6% vs 2.4%
cards.people: 1,005 patients with AF and a bioprosthetic mitral valve at 49 sites in Brazil, randomised to rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily or dose-adjusted warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.0). Primary outcome: composite of death, major cardiovascular events (stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic embolism, valve thrombosis, or hospitalisation for heart failure), or major bleeding at 12 months, analysed as mean time to event (restricted mean survival time).
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred at a mean of 347.5 days in the rivaroxaban group and 340.1 days in the warfarin group (difference 7.4 days; 95% CI −1.4 to 16.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Death from cardiovascular causes or thromboembolic events: 17 patients (3.4%) versus 26 (5.1%) (hazard ratio 0.65; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.20). Stroke: 0.6% versus 2.4% (HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.88). Major bleeding: 7 patients (1.4%) versus 13 (2.6%) (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.21 to 1.35). Other serious adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (Brazil), open-label, 12-month horizon; noninferiority on a time-to-event composite is not superiority. The population is bioprosthetic mitral valves — the result must never be extended to mechanical valves, where dabigatran caused harm (Shelf #2257) and warfarin remains required.
cards.source: Guimarães HP et al. Rivaroxaban in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and a Bioprosthetic Mitral Valve. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 33196155. Registry ID: NCT02303795, from the record. shelves.title: Mechanical heart valves: dabigatran caused more clots and more bleeding than warfarin (RE-ALIGN)
shelves.question: In patients with mechanical aortic or mitral valves, does dabigatran prevent valve thrombosis and embolism as safely as warfarin?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Benzimidazoles · Dabigatran · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Thromboembolism · Warfarin · beta-Alanine
shelves.balance: A definitive harm result from a trial stopped early. RE-ALIGN was a phase 2 dose-validation study randomising patients with mechanical aortic or mitral valves — either within a week of surgery or at least 3 months after — 2:1 to dabigatran (dose by kidney function, adjusted to a trough level of at least 50 ng/mL) or warfarin. After 252 patients the trial was terminated prematurely because of excess thromboembolic AND bleeding events on dabigatran: ischaemic or unspecified stroke occurred in 9 patients (5%) on dabigatran versus none on warfarin, and major bleeding in 7 (4%) versus 2 (2%) — all of it pericardial. Nearly a third of dabigatran patients (32%) needed dose adjustment or discontinuation. Direct thrombin inhibition fails where valve-surface thrombin generation dominates, and no dosing strategy in the trial fixed it. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) (Tier C): mechanical valves mean warfarin; this is the trial that settled it.

cards.headline: RE-ALIGN 2013: stroke 5% on dabigatran vs 0% on warfarin; major bleeding 4% vs 2% — stopped early for harm
cards.summary: RE-ALIGN 2013: stroke 5% on dabigatran vs 0% on warfarin; major bleeding 4% vs 2% — stopped early for harm
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised dose-validation trial, terminated early (RE-ALIGN)
cards.people: 252 patients with mechanical aortic or mitral prostheses (two populations: valve replacement within the past 7 days, or at least 3 months earlier), randomised 2:1 to dabigatran (initial dose 150, 220, or 300 mg twice daily by kidney function, adjusted to a trough plasma level of at least 50 ng/mL) or warfarin (INR 2 to 3 or 2.5 to 3.5 by thromboembolic risk). Primary endpoint: trough dabigatran level (dose validation). The trial was terminated prematurely after 252 enrolments because of excess thromboembolic and bleeding events on dabigatran.
cards.result: In the as-treated analysis, dose adjustment or discontinuation of dabigatran was required in 52 of 162 patients (32%). Ischaemic or unspecified stroke occurred in 9 patients (5%) in the dabigatran group and in no patients in the warfarin group. Major bleeding occurred in 7 patients (4%) versus 2 (2%); all major bleeds were pericardial. The authors' conclusion: dabigatran in mechanical valves showed no benefit and an excess risk.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial with a pharmacokinetic primary endpoint — but the clinical harm is unambiguous and bidirectional (more clots and more bleeding), so the small size does not soften the verdict. The two population strata (early post-operative and remote) were both represented in the harm.
cards.source: Eikelboom JW et al. Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves. N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID: 23991661. Registry IDs: NCT01452347 and NCT01505881, from the record. shelves.title: Amulet or Watchman for left atrial appendage occlusion: noninferior, with better sealing (Amulet IDE)
shelves.question: In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation at stroke risk, is the dual-seal Amulet occluder noninferior to Watchman for occlusion success, safety, and stroke prevention?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Septal Occluder Device · Stroke
shelves.balance: A large device-versus-device trial with a split practical answer: the same protection, a better seal, a rockier procedure. Amulet IDE randomised 1,878 patients with nonvalvular AF at increased stroke risk to the Amulet dual-seal occluder or Watchman. Amulet was noninferior on the primary safety composite (14.5% vs 14.7% at 12 months) and on effectiveness — ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism 2.8% versus 2.8% at 18 months — and the composite of stroke, systemic embolism or cardiovascular/unexplained death was 5.6% versus 7.7% (noninferior). Complete occlusion at 45 days was higher with Amulet (98.9% vs 96.8% with residual jet at most 5 mm; P=0.003 for superiority). The trade: procedure-related complications were higher with Amulet (4.5% vs 2.5%), mainly more pericardial effusions and device embolisations, falling with operator experience; major bleeding and death were similar. PROPOSED LIKELY: device choice can rest on anatomy and operator experience; neither device prevents stroke better at 18 months. (Desk note: this record's MeSH is sparse as published — copied verbatim, not supplemented.)

cards.headline: Amulet IDE 2021: safety 14.5% vs 14.7% and stroke/embolism 2.8% vs 2.8% (noninferior); occlusion 98.9% vs 96.8% (superior); procedure complications 4.5% vs 2.5%
cards.summary: Amulet IDE 2021: safety 14.5% vs 14.7% and stroke/embolism 2.8% vs 2.8% (noninferior); occlusion 98.9% vs 96.8% (superior); procedure complications 4.5% vs 2.5%
cards.people: 1,878 patients with nonvalvular AF at increased stroke risk, randomised 1:1 to percutaneous implantation of the Amplatzer Amulet occluder or the Watchman device. Primary endpoints: safety (procedure-related complications, all-cause death, or major bleeding at 12 months), effectiveness (ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism at 18 months), and LAA occlusion rate at 45 days.
cards.result: Primary safety: 14.5% (Amulet) versus 14.7% (Watchman) (difference −0.14 points; 95% CI −3.42 to 3.13; P<0.001 for noninferiority); major bleeding 10.6% versus 10.0% and all-cause death 3.9% versus 5.1% within that composite. Procedure-related complications were higher with Amulet (4.5% vs 2.5%), largely pericardial effusion and device embolisation. Primary effectiveness: 2.8% versus 2.8% (difference 0.00; 95% CI −1.55 to 1.55; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Stroke/systemic embolism/cardiovascular-or-unexplained death: 5.6% versus 7.7% (noninferior). Major bleeding at 18 months: 11.6% versus 12.3% (P=0.32 for superiority). LAA occlusion at 45 days: 98.9% versus 96.8% (difference 2.03 points; P=0.003 for superiority).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority between two devices — neither is compared here with anticoagulation or with no treatment (see Shelves #272 and #2249 for those settings). The early-complication excess with Amulet fell with operator experience, so centre volume is part of the result.
cards.source: Lakkireddy D et al. Amplatzer Amulet Left Atrial Appendage Occluder Versus Watchman Device for Stroke Prophylaxis (Amulet IDE): A Randomized, Controlled Trial. Circulation. 2021. shelves.title: Rheumatic mitral stenosis: balloon valvotomy matched closed surgical commissurotomy over long follow-up — in one very small trial
shelves.question: In rheumatic mitral stenosis, does percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy give better long-term event-free survival than closed mitral commissurotomy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Echocardiography · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mitral Valve · Mitral Valve Stenosis · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — a genuinely randomised comparison, but only 40 patients, from the era before trial registration, and its abstract reports comparability rather than the superiority sometimes claimed for it. Rifaie and colleagues randomised 40 consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (valve area under 1.5 cm²) to percutaneous mitral valvotomy by the double-balloon technique (20) or closed surgical commissurotomy (20), with echocardiographic follow-up yearly for up to 15 years (mean follow-up 99 ± 12 months). Immediate results did not differ: final valve area 1.8 cm² in both groups and similar mean gradients. Restenosis occurred in 5 of 19 followed patients after valvotomy (26.3%) versus 5 of 18 after commissurotomy (27.8%), and restenosis-free survival curves did not differ. The authors' conclusion is that balloon valvotomy achieves comparable results to closed commissurotomy in the short and long term. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): randomised long-term data this old and this small can support 'no large difference was seen' — nothing stronger, in either direction.

cards.headline: Rifaie 2009: 40 patients — valve area, gradients, restenosis (26.3% vs 27.8%) and restenosis-free survival all comparable between balloon valvotomy and closed commissurotomy
cards.summary: Rifaie 2009: 40 patients — valve area, gradients, restenosis (26.3% vs 27.8%) and restenosis-free survival all comparable between balloon valvotomy and closed commissurotomy
cards.type: Prospective randomised study with long-term follow-up
cards.people: 40 consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis (mitral valve area under 1.5 cm²) randomised to percutaneous mitral valvotomy (double-balloon technique; n=20) or closed surgical commissurotomy (n=20). Full echocardiographic assessment before, after, at 1 and 6 months, then yearly for up to 15 years; mean follow-up 99 ± 12 months. Three patients dropped out (1 valvotomy, 2 commissurotomy).
cards.result: Immediate echocardiographic results did not differ significantly: final mitral valve area 1.8 ± 0.3 cm² (valvotomy) versus 1.8 ± 0.4 cm² (commissurotomy), mean diastolic gradient 7 ± 4 versus 6.6 ± 4 mmHg (both p>0.05). Mitral restenosis occurred in 5 patients (26.3%) versus 5 (27.8%) (p>0.05); Kaplan-Meier restenosis-free survival showed no difference between the groups. The authors conclude percutaneous valvotomy achieves comparable results to closed commissurotomy in the short and long term.
cards.watchOut: Very small (37 patients followed), single-centre, pre-registration era, and closed commissurotomy is itself now largely of historical and low-resource-setting interest. The shelf records comparability as the abstract states it; summaries claiming balloon superiority overstate this record.

shelves.title: Stable chest pain: adding coronary CT angiography to standard care cut coronary death and MI at five years (SCOT-HEART)
shelves.question: In patients with suspected stable angina, does CTCA-guided management reduce coronary heart disease death or nonfatal myocardial infarction at five years versus standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chest Pain · Computed Tomography Angiography · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Disease · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Risk
shelves.balance: A large open-label strategy trial with a hard-outcome win, achieved without more procedures at five years. SCOT-HEART randomised 4,146 patients with stable chest pain referred to cardiology clinics to standard care plus coronary CT angiography or standard care alone, followed a median of 4.8 years. Death from coronary heart disease or nonfatal MI occurred in 2.3% with CTA versus 3.9% without (hazard ratio 0.59 — a 41% relative reduction; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.84; P=0.004). Invasive angiography and revascularisation were more frequent early in the CTA group but identical overall at 5 years (angiography HR 1.00; revascularisation HR 1.07). The plausible mechanism is on the face of the trial: more preventive therapies were started in the CTA group (odds ratio 1.40) — a clearer diagnosis led to better-targeted prevention. There were no significant differences in cardiovascular, noncardiovascular, or all-cause death individually. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: an MI/mortality composite — the developer's personal approval territory). Pairs with PROMISE (Shelf #2261) as designed: positive in a UK secondary-care population, neutral in a lower-risk US one.

cards.headline: SCOT-HEART 2018: coronary death or nonfatal MI 2.3% with CTA vs 3.9% without (HR 0.59 relative); 5-year angiography and revascularisation rates the same
cards.summary: SCOT-HEART 2018: coronary death or nonfatal MI 2.3% with CTA vs 3.9% without (HR 0.59 relative); 5-year angiography and revascularisation rates the same
cards.people: 4,146 patients with stable chest pain referred to a cardiology clinic, randomised to standard care plus coronary CTA (2,073) or standard care alone (2,073); follow-up 3 to 7 years (median 4.8 years; 20,254 patient-years). Primary endpoint: death from coronary heart disease or nonfatal myocardial infarction at 5 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 48 patients (2.3%) in the CTA group and 81 (3.9%) in the standard-care group (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.84; P=0.004). Invasive coronary angiography at 5 years: 491 versus 502 patients (HR 1.00; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.13); coronary revascularisation: 279 versus 267 (HR 1.07; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.27) — after higher early rates in the CTA group. More preventive therapies (odds ratio 1.40; 95% CI 1.19 to 1.65) and more antianginal therapies (OR 1.27) were initiated with CTA. No significant differences in cardiovascular death, noncardiovascular death, or all-cause death individually.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: the benefit plausibly flows from treatment changes the scan triggered, not the scan itself — which is the point of a strategy trial, but it means the result depends on clinicians acting on findings. The population is UK secondary-care referrals; compare PROMISE (Shelf #2261) before generalising to lower-risk populations.
cards.source: SCOT-HEART Investigators. Coronary CT Angiography and 5-Year Risk of Myocardial Infarction. N Engl J Med. 2018. PMID: 30145934. Registry ID: NCT01149590, from the record. randomised open-label strategy trial (scot-heart) 4,146 patients with stable chest pain referred to a cardiology clinic, randomised to standard care plus coronary cta (2,073) or standard care alone (2,073); follow-up 3 to 7 years (median 4.8 years; 20,254 patient-years). primary endpoint: death from coronary heart disease or nonfatal myocardial infarction at 5 years. the primary endpoint occurred in 48 patients (2.3%) in the cta group and 81 (3.9%) in the standard-care group (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% ci 0.41 to 0.84; p=0.004). invasive coronary angiography at 5 years: 491 versus 502 patients (hr 1.00; 95% ci 0.88 to 1.13); coronary revascularisation: 279 versus 267 (hr 1.07; 95% ci 0.91 to 1.27) — after higher early rates in the cta group. more preventive therapies (odds ratio 1.40; 95% ci 1.19 to 1.65) and more antianginal therapies (or 1.27) were initiated with cta. no significant differences in cardiovascular death, noncardiovascular death, or all-cause death individually. open-label: the benefit plausibly flows from treatment changes the scan triggered, not the scan itself — which is the point of a strategy trial, but it means the result depends on clinicians acting on findings. the population is uk secondary-care referrals; compare promise (shelf #2261) before generalising to lower-risk populations. scot-heart investigators. coronary ct angiography and 5-year risk of myocardial infarction. n engl j med. 2018. pmid: 30145934. registry id: nct01149590, from the record. mesh: adult · aged · chest pain · computed tomography angiography · coronary angiography · coronary disease · female · follow-up studies · humans · incidence · male · middle aged · myocardial infarction · percutaneous coronary intervention · risk

shelves.title: Suspected coronary disease: anatomic (CTA) versus functional first testing — no outcome difference (PROMISE)
shelves.question: In symptomatic patients with suspected coronary artery disease, does an initial coronary CT angiography strategy improve outcomes versus initial functional testing (stress ECG, echo, or nuclear)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina, Unstable · Cardiac Catheterization · Chest Pain · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Echocardiography, Stress · Electrocardiography · Exercise Test · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Myocardial Infarction · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: The necessary counterweight to SCOT-HEART, and the pair is the balance. PROMISE randomised 10,003 symptomatic patients with suspected CAD (mean age 60.8; 52.7% women; mean pretest likelihood of obstructive CAD 53.3%) to initial anatomical testing with coronary CTA or initial functional testing. Over a median of 25 months the primary composite (death, MI, hospitalisation for unstable angina, or major procedural complication) occurred in 3.3% with CTA versus 3.0% with functional testing (adjusted hazard ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.29; P=0.75). CTA led to more catheterisation within 90 days (12.2% vs 8.1%) but fewer catheterisations showing no obstructive disease (3.4% vs 4.3%; P=0.02); median radiation exposure per patient was lower with CTA, though overall exposure was higher because a third of the functional group had none. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the testing strategy — made no difference to outcomes) (Tier C). Read with Shelf #2260: in a UK secondary-care population with five years of follow-up, adding CTA to standard care prevented infarctions; in this broader, lower-event-rate US population over two years, choosing CTA first did not.

cards.headline: PROMISE 2015: primary composite 3.3% (CTA) vs 3.0% (functional) — adjusted HR 1.04 relative; more early catheterisation with CTA, fewer negative catheterisations
cards.summary: PROMISE 2015: primary composite 3.3% (CTA) vs 3.0% (functional) — adjusted HR 1.04 relative; more early catheterisation with CTA, fewer negative catheterisations
cards.people: 10,003 symptomatic patients with suspected CAD requiring noninvasive testing, randomised to initial coronary CTA (4,996) or functional testing (5,007: exercise ECG, nuclear stress, or stress echocardiography). Mean age 60.8 years; 52.7% women; 87.7% had chest pain or exertional dyspnoea; mean pretest likelihood of obstructive CAD 53.3%. Primary endpoint: death, myocardial infarction, hospitalisation for unstable angina, or major procedural complication; median follow-up 25 months.
cards.result: A primary-endpoint event occurred in 164 of 4,996 patients in the CTA group (3.3%) and 151 of 5,007 (3.0%) in the functional-testing group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.29; P=0.75). Catheterisation showing no obstructive CAD was less frequent with CTA (3.4% vs 4.3%; P=0.02), but more CTA patients underwent catheterisation within 90 days (12.2% vs 8.1%). Median cumulative radiation exposure was 10.0 mSv (CTA) versus 11.3 mSv (functional), though 32.6% of the functional group had no exposure, making mean exposure higher with CTA (12.0 vs 10.1 mSv; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A strategy comparison, not a test-accuracy study: outcomes were identical even though the pathways differed. Event rates were low and follow-up (25 months) shorter than SCOT-HEART's five years — the two trials' results differ, and this shelf states both rather than averaging them away.
cards.source: Douglas PS et al. Outcomes of anatomical versus functional testing for coronary artery disease. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25773919. Registry ID: NCT01174550, from the record. shelves.title: Referred for invasive angiography: a CT-first strategy matched catheterisation on events with far fewer procedural complications (DISCHARGE)
shelves.question: In patients with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability referred for invasive angiography, does a CT-first strategy match catheterisation on major adverse cardiovascular events with fewer procedural complications?
shelves.mesh: Angina Pectoris · Chest Pain · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Male · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: A pragmatic trial in the exact population where the question bites: patients already referred for the catheter lab. DISCHARGE randomised 3,561 patients with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD at 26 European centres to initial CT or initial invasive coronary angiography. Over 3.5 years, major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) occurred in 2.1% with CT versus 3.0% with invasive angiography (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.07; P=0.10) — similar, and numerically lower with CT. Major procedure-related complications were fourfold lower with the CT-first strategy (0.5% vs 1.9%; HR 0.26; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.55). Angina in the final follow-up weeks did not differ significantly (8.8% vs 7.5%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): CT first is at least as safe on events and clearly gentler in this referred population. (Desk note: the record's MeSH is brief as published — copied verbatim.)

cards.headline: DISCHARGE 2022: MACE 2.1% (CT) vs 3.0% (invasive) over 3.5 years; major procedure complications 0.5% vs 1.9% (HR 0.26 relative)
cards.summary: DISCHARGE 2022: MACE 2.1% (CT) vs 3.0% (invasive) over 3.5 years; major procedure complications 0.5% vs 1.9% (HR 0.26 relative)
cards.people: 3,561 patients with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD referred for invasive coronary angiography at 26 European centres, randomised to CT or invasive angiography as the initial strategy (56.2% women); follow-up complete in 3,523 (98.9%). Primary outcome: major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) over 3.5 years. Key secondaries: procedure-related complications and angina.
cards.result: Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 38 of 1,808 patients (2.1%) in the CT group and 52 of 1,753 (3.0%) in the invasive group (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.07; P=0.10). Major procedure-related complications occurred in 9 patients (0.5%) versus 33 (1.9%) (HR 0.26; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.55). Angina during the final 4 weeks of follow-up: 8.8% versus 7.5% (odds ratio 1.17; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.48). The authors conclude event risk was similar and procedural complications lower with initial CT.
cards.watchOut: The MACE confidence interval (0.46 to 1.07) includes a small excess with CT — 'similar' is the trial's own word, and this shelf does not upgrade it to 'better'. The population had already been referred for angiography; results do not speak to unselected chest pain.

shelves.title: FFRCT-guided care in stable chest pain: no cost saving and no outcome difference, fewer invasive angiograms (FORECAST)
shelves.question: In stable chest pain, does a CT angiography plus selective FFRCT strategy reduce total cardiac costs or improve outcomes versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Angina, Stable · Computed Tomography Angiography · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Coronary Stenosis · Coronary Vessels · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Humans · Predictive Value of Tests · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: THIN — one trial, recruited through the COVID period, with a null primary endpoint whose confidence interval still spans meaningful savings and meaningful extra cost. FORECAST randomised 1,400 patients with stable chest pain at 11 UK centres to CTCA with selective FFRCT or standard clinical care pathways. Total cardiac costs at 9 months were £114 higher (8%) in the FFRCT group — not significant (95% CI −£112 to +£337; P=0.10). Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events did not differ (10.2% vs 10.6%), and angina and quality of life improved similarly in both groups. The strategy did reshape downstream testing: invasive coronary angiography fell (19% vs 25%; P=0.01). In the experimental group 96% had initial CTCA and 38% of those underwent FFRCT. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): FFRCT-guided care demonstrably reduces invasive angiography; whether it saves money or changes outcomes is unproven on this trial. (Registry ID: none printed in the fetched record — flagged, not invented.)

cards.headline: FORECAST 2021: costs +£114 (+8%) with FFRCT strategy, not significant; events 10.2% vs 10.6%; invasive angiography reduced 19% vs 25%
cards.summary: FORECAST 2021: costs +£114 (+8%) with FFRCT strategy, not significant; events 10.2% vs 10.6%; invasive angiography reduced 19% vs 25%
cards.people: 1,400 patients with stable chest pain at 11 UK centres, randomised to initial CTCA with selective FFRCT (experimental) or standard clinical care pathways. Primary endpoint: total cardiac costs at 9 months. Secondaries: angina status, quality of life, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events, and invasive coronary angiography use.
cards.result: Mean total cardiac costs were higher by £114 (+8%) in the experimental group (95% CI −£112 to +£337; P=0.10) — not significant. Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events: 10.2% versus 10.6% (no significant difference); angina and quality of life improved to a similar degree in both groups. Invasive angiography was significantly reduced in the experimental group (19% vs 25%; P=0.01). Most patients had initial CTCA (63% of the standard group vs 96% of the experimental group); 254 experimental patients (38% of those scanned) underwent FFRCT.
cards.watchOut: The cost confidence interval includes both an 8% saving and a 23% increase — the trial does not settle the economics. Recruitment was curtailed by COVID-19, and standard care itself used CTCA in most patients, narrowing the contrast between strategies.
