shelves.title: Suspected acute coronary syndrome: early CT coronary angiography did not improve one-year outcomes (RAPID-CTCA)
shelves.question: In intermediate-risk suspected acute coronary syndrome presenting to emergency care, does early CT coronary angiography reduce death or subsequent type 1 myocardial infarction, or shorten stay?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Acute Disease · Aged · Chest Pain · Computed Tomography Angiography · Early Diagnosis · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Heart Disease Risk Factors · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Assessment · Standard of Care · Time Factors
shelves.balance: A large, well-run negative trial of a plausible idea. RAPID-CTCA randomised 1,748 adults with suspected or provisionally diagnosed ACS at intermediate risk (prior coronary disease, raised troponin, or abnormal ECG; mean GRACE score 115) at 37 UK hospitals to early CTCA plus standard care or standard care alone; scans happened a median of 4.2 hours after randomisation. The primary endpoint — all-cause death or subsequent type 1 or 4b MI at one year — occurred in 5.8% with early CTCA versus 6.1% with standard care (adjusted hazard ratio 0.91; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.35; P=0.65). There were no overall differences in revascularisation, ACS drug treatment, or later preventive therapy. Early CTCA did reduce invasive coronary angiography (54.0% vs 60.8%; adjusted HR 0.81; P=0.001) but slightly lengthened hospital stay (median increase 0.21 days). The authors conclude the findings do not support routine early CTCA in intermediate-risk acute chest pain. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the early-scan strategy — made no difference to outcomes) (Tier C).

cards.headline: RAPID-CTCA 2021: death or type 1/4b MI at 1 year 5.8% (early CTCA) vs 6.1% (standard care) — adjusted HR 0.91 relative; fewer invasive angiograms, slightly longer stay
cards.summary: RAPID-CTCA 2021: death or type 1/4b MI at 1 year 5.8% (early CTCA) vs 6.1% (standard care) — adjusted HR 0.91 relative; fewer invasive angiograms, slightly longer stay
cards.people: 1,748 adults with suspected or provisional ACS and at least one of prior coronary heart disease, raised troponin, or abnormal ECG, at 37 UK hospitals (mean age 62; 64% men; mean GRACE score 115); 877 randomised to early CTCA plus standard care, 871 to standard care only. Median time from randomisation to CTCA 4.2 hours. Primary endpoint: all-cause death or subsequent type 1 or 4b myocardial infarction at one year.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 51 participants (5.8%) in the CTCA group and 53 (6.1%) in the standard-care group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.91; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.35; P=0.65). Invasive coronary angiography was performed in 474 (54.0%) versus 530 (60.8%) (adjusted HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.72 to 0.92; P=0.001). There were no overall differences in coronary revascularisation, drug treatment for ACS, or subsequent preventive treatments. Early CTCA was associated with a slightly longer hospital stay (median increase 0.21 days; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.40; from a median of 2.0 to 2.2 days).
cards.watchOut: Intermediate-risk patients only — the trial does not address low-risk ED chest pain pathways or high-risk presentations. Reduced invasive angiography without changed treatment or outcomes is a resource pattern, not a patient benefit, and the stay went the wrong way.

shelves.title: Catheter ablation versus drug therapy in AF: no hard-endpoint win overall (CABANA), a large one in heart failure (CASTLE-AF)
shelves.question: Does catheter ablation reduce death, stroke, bleeding, or cardiac arrest versus drug therapy in symptomatic AF overall — and in AF with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Female · Heart Arrest · Hemorrhage · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke · Heart Failure · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: The pair is the balance: the same intervention, a null result in the broad population and a large benefit in the sickest subgroup. CABANA randomised 2,204 symptomatic AF patients (median age 68; ≥65, or younger with stroke risk factors) to ablation or drug therapy (rhythm and/or rate control): over a median 48.5 months the primary composite (death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, cardiac arrest) was 8.0% versus 9.2% (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.15; P=.30) and mortality 5.2% versus 6.1% (HR 0.85, not significant), while death or cardiovascular hospitalisation (51.7% vs 58.1%; HR 0.83; P=.001) and AF recurrence (49.9% vs 69.5%; HR 0.52) clearly favoured ablation; 27.5% of the drug group crossed over to ablation, diluting the intention-to-treat contrast. CASTLE-AF randomised 363 patients with AF, EF at most 35%, NYHA class II–IV and an implanted defibrillator, who had failed, not tolerated, or declined antiarrhythmic drugs: the composite of death or worsening-HF hospitalisation was 28.5% with ablation versus 44.6% with medical therapy (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.87; P=0.007), and death alone was 13.4% versus 25.0% (HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86; P=0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): ablation's hard-endpoint case is strong in HFrEF and unproven in the general symptomatic population — population, not procedure, is the difference.

cards.headline: CABANA 2019: primary composite 8.0% (ablation) vs 9.2% (drugs), HR 0.86 relative, not significant; recurrence halved; 27.5% crossover
cards.summary: CABANA 2019: primary composite 8.0% (ablation) vs 9.2% (drugs), HR 0.86 relative, not significant; recurrence halved; 27.5% crossover
cards.people: 2,204 symptomatic AF patients at 126 centres in 10 countries (median age 68; 37.2% women; 42.9% paroxysmal), randomised to catheter ablation (1,108; pulmonary vein isolation plus discretionary additional lesions) or drug therapy (1,096; guideline rhythm and/or rate control). Primary endpoint: composite of death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, or cardiac arrest. Median follow-up 48.5 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 89 patients (8.0%) in the ablation group versus 101 (9.2%) in the drug group (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.15; P=.30). All-cause mortality: 5.2% versus 6.1% (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.21; P=.38). Death or cardiovascular hospitalisation: 51.7% versus 58.1% (HR 0.83; 95% CI 0.74 to 0.93; P=.001). AF recurrence: 49.9% versus 69.5% (HR 0.52; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.60; P<.001). Of the ablation group, 90.8% underwent the procedure; 301 drug-group patients (27.5%) ultimately received ablation. The authors note lower-than-expected event rates and crossovers affected the estimated treatment effect.
cards.watchOut: The intention-to-treat null coexists with a 27.5% crossover and event rates below plan — per-protocol analyses favoured ablation but cannot carry a causal stamp. Do not quote CABANA as 'ablation does not help': recurrence and hospitalisation clearly improved. Do not quote it as a mortality trial win either.
cards.source: Packer DL et al. cards.summary: CASTLE-AF 2018: death or HF hospitalisation 28.5% (ablation) vs 44.6% (medical) — HR 0.62 relative; death 13.4% vs 25.0%
cards.people: 363 patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF unresponsive to, intolerant of, or unwilling to take antiarrhythmic drugs, with NYHA class II–IV heart failure, LVEF at most 35%, and an implanted defibrillator; randomised to catheter ablation (179) or medical therapy (rate or rhythm control; 184), all on guideline heart-failure therapy. Primary endpoint: composite of death from any cause or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure. Median follow-up 37.8 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 51 patients (28.5%) in the ablation group versus 82 (44.6%) in the medical group (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.87; P=0.007). Death from any cause: 24 (13.4%) versus 46 (25.0%) (HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86; P=0.01). Hospitalisation for worsening heart failure: 37 (20.7%) versus 66 (35.9%) (HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.83; P=0.004). Cardiovascular death: 20 (11.2%) versus 41 (22.3%) (HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.29 to 0.84; P=0.009).
cards.watchOut: Small (363 patients) and open-label, in a highly selected HFrEF population with defibrillators — the effect size is large enough that selection alone is an unlikely full explanation, but replication in this exact population remains thin. shelves.title: Cryoballoon versus contact-force radiofrequency ablation: identical rhythm outcomes under continuous monitoring (CIRCA-DOSE)
shelves.question: In drug-refractory paroxysmal AF, do cryoballoon (4-minute or 2-minute freezes) and contact-force radiofrequency ablation differ in one-year arrhythmia recurrence measured by an implanted loop recorder?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Cryosurgery · Female · Fluoroscopy · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A three-way randomised comparison with the most honest rhythm ascertainment in the ablation literature — every patient carried an implantable loop recorder — and a flat result. CIRCA-DOSE randomised 346 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to contact-force radiofrequency (115), 4-minute cryoballoon (115), or 2-minute cryoballoon (116) ablation. One-year freedom from any atrial tachyarrhythmia (days 91–365) was 53.9%, 52.2%, and 51.7% respectively (P=0.87); freedom from symptomatic arrhythmia was 79.1%, 78.2%, and 73.3% (P=0.26); AF burden fell by a median of about 99% in all three groups (P=0.36). Serious adverse events did not differ significantly (2.6%, 5.3%, 6.0%; P=0.24). Radiofrequency took longer but used less fluoroscopy. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the energy source and freeze duration — made no difference): operator and anatomy, not energy, should drive the choice; and the 53% freedom figure under continuous monitoring is the honest benchmark against which intermittently monitored trials' higher success rates should be read.

cards.headline: CIRCA-DOSE 2019: 1-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia 53.9% (RF) vs 52.2% (Cryo-4) vs 51.7% (Cryo-2), P=0.87; AF burden down ~99% in all arms
cards.summary: CIRCA-DOSE 2019: 1-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia 53.9% (RF) vs 52.2% (Cryo-4) vs 51.7% (Cryo-2), P=0.87; AF burden down ~99% in all arms
cards.people: 346 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF at multiple centres, randomised to contact force-guided radiofrequency ablation (n=115), 4-minute cryoballoon ablation (n=115), or 2-minute cryoballoon ablation (n=116). All patients received an implantable loop recorder. Primary outcome: time to first documented recurrence of symptomatic or asymptomatic atrial tachyarrhythmia between days 91 and 365, or repeat ablation at any time. Follow-up 12 months.
cards.result: One-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia: 53.9% (CF-RF), 52.2% (Cryo-4), 51.7% (Cryo-2) (P=0.87). Freedom from symptomatic atrial tachyarrhythmia: 79.1%, 78.2%, 73.3% (P=0.26). Median AF-burden reduction from baseline: 99.3%, 99.9%, 98.4% (P=0.36). Serious adverse events: 3 patients (2.6%), 6 (5.3%), 7 (6.0%) (P=0.24). The radiofrequency group had significantly longer procedure duration but significantly shorter fluoroscopy exposure (P<0.001 versus cryoballoon groups).
cards.watchOut: Continuous monitoring detects recurrences that symptom-driven follow-up misses — cross-trial comparisons of 'success rates' without matching the monitoring method are meaningless. Paroxysmal, drug-refractory AF only.

shelves.title: Surgical ablation added to mitral valve surgery: far more sinus rhythm, no mortality or stroke difference in the randomised trials, more pacemakers
shelves.question: In patients with AF undergoing mitral valve surgery, does concomitant surgical ablation improve sinus rhythm, mortality, stroke, and pacemaker rates in randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation · Mitral Valve · Treatment Outcome · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Catheter Ablation · Stroke · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation
shelves.balance: THIN for hard outcomes, strong for rhythm: a randomised-trials-only meta-analysis separates what surgical ablation proves from what it merely suggests. Pooling 13 randomised trials (1,089 patients) of concomitant surgical ablation during mitral valve replacement or repair, sinus rhythm was far more frequent with ablation at discharge (odds ratio 9.62; 95% CI 4.87 to 19.02), 6 months (OR 7.21), and 1 year (OR 8.41; 95% CI 5.14 to 13.77). But all-cause mortality did not differ, stroke and thromboembolic events did not differ, and permanent pacemaker implantation was more likely with ablation (OR 1.87; 95% CI 1.11 to 3.17). A larger 2025 meta-analysis including observational studies (38 studies; 24 analysed for mortality, 41,678 patients) did find lower long-term mortality (HR 0.78) and stroke (HR 0.60) with ablation — while stating in its own abstract that the survival benefits were predominantly observed in the observational studies, which is exactly why this shelf rests on the randomised pool. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rhythm benefit is real and large; hard-outcome benefit is unproven in randomised data; the pacemaker cost is real.

cards.headline: Surgical ablation at mitral surgery (13 RCTs, 1,089 patients): sinus rhythm at 1 year OR 8.41 relative odds; mortality and stroke not different; pacemakers OR 1.87
cards.summary: Surgical ablation at mitral surgery (13 RCTs, 1,089 patients): sinus rhythm at 1 year OR 8.41 relative odds; mortality and stroke not different; pacemakers OR 1.87
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 13 randomised trials (search to August 2022) comparing mitral valve surgery alone with mitral valve surgery plus concomitant surgical ablation for AF, 1,089 patients in total. Primary outcome: sinus rhythm at 12 months. Secondaries: sinus rhythm at discharge and 6 months, all-cause mortality, permanent pacemaker implantation, stroke and thromboembolic events. Random-effects meta-analysis, odds ratios.
cards.result: Sinus rhythm was significantly more frequent with ablation at discharge (odds ratio 9.62; 95% CI 4.87 to 19.02; I²=55%), at 6 months (OR 7.21; 95% CI 4.30 to 12.11; I²=34%), and at 1 year (OR 8.41; 95% CI 5.14 to 13.77; I²=48%). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups, and neither did stroke and thromboembolic events. Permanent pacemaker implantation was more likely with ablation (OR 1.87; 95% CI 1.11 to 3.17; I²=0%). The authors note excellent short-term rhythm outcomes, a slightly higher pacemaker rate, and the need for longer follow-up to know whether sinus rhythm is maintained.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios overstate relative risks when outcomes are common — sinus rhythm is common, so read OR 8.41 as 'much more often', not '8.4 times the probability'. Follow-up in the pooled trials is short (12 months for the primary outcome); durability and late hard outcomes are open.

cards.summary: Larger mixed-design pool (38 studies): mortality HR 0.78 and stroke HR 0.60 favour ablation — but the authors state the survival benefit was predominantly observational
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis including observational studies
cards.people: 38 studies of concomitant surgical AF ablation versus no ablation during cardiac surgery; 9 randomised trials and 15 observational studies (41,678 patients) contributed adjusted outcomes to the mortality analysis, weighted median follow-up 62 months. Primary outcome: long-term all-cause mortality. Only adjusted outcomes were used from observational studies.
cards.result: Surgical ablation was associated with lower long-term mortality (hazard ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.84), stroke (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.76), and heart-failure rehospitalisation (HR 0.92; 95% CI 0.87 to 0.96), more freedom from AF (relative risk 1.93), and more permanent pacemaker implantation (HR 1.35; 95% CI 1.03 to 1.77); major bleeding did not differ. The authors state the survival benefits were predominantly observed in observational studies and that further randomised trials are necessary to confirm them.
cards.watchOut: Carded so the shelf does not hide the favourable signal — and does not promote it either. Patients selected for ablation in observational cohorts differ from those not selected in ways adjustment only partly removes; the randomised pool above is the governing evidence.

shelves.title: Early rhythm control works: EAST-AFNET 4 for outcomes, EARLY-AF for first-line ablation
shelves.question: In recently diagnosed AF, does early rhythm control — drugs or ablation — reduce cardiovascular outcomes versus usual care, and is first-line cryoablation better than first-line drugs at preventing recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiovascular Diseases · Catheter Ablation · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Incidence · Length of Stay · Male · Risk · Secondary Prevention · Single-Blind Method · Ventricular Function, Left · Cryosurgery · Recurrence · Monitoring, Physiologic · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A support for acting early, from two directions. EAST-AFNET 4 randomised 2,789 patients with early AF (diagnosed within a year; median 36 days) and cardiovascular conditions to early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or ablation) or usual care, and was stopped for efficacy after a median 5.1 years: the first primary outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome) occurred at 3.9 versus 5.0 per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.79; 96% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.005), with no significant difference in nights in hospital or in the primary safety composite — though serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy were more frequent with early rhythm control (4.9% vs 1.4%). EARLY-AF randomised 303 patients with symptomatic paroxysmal AF, untreated, to first-line cryoballoon ablation or antiarrhythmic drugs, with implantable monitors in everyone: recurrence of atrial tachyarrhythmia at 1 year was 42.9% with ablation versus 67.8% with drugs (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; P<0.001), symptomatic recurrence 11.0% versus 26.2% (HR 0.39), and serious adverse events were similar (3.2% vs 4.0%). A second first-line cryoballoon trial (STOP AF First) points the same way (treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: EAST's composite embeds cardiovascular death).

cards.headline: EAST-AFNET 4 2020: first primary outcome 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years (HR 0.79 relative; P=0.005); safety composite not different
cards.summary: EAST-AFNET 4 2020: first primary outcome 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years (HR 0.79 relative; P=0.005); safety composite not different
cards.type: Randomised open trial with blinded outcome assessment, stopped for efficacy (EAST-AFNET 4)
cards.people: 2,789 patients with early AF (diagnosed at most 1 year before enrolment; median 36 days since diagnosis) and cardiovascular conditions at 135 centres, randomised to early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or AF ablation) or usual care (rhythm control reserved for symptoms). First primary outcome: composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation with worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome. Second primary: nights in hospital per year. Stopped for efficacy at the third interim analysis; median follow-up 5.1 years.
cards.result: A first-primary-outcome event occurred in 249 patients assigned to early rhythm control (3.9 per 100 person-years) and 316 assigned to usual care (5.0 per 100 person-years) (hazard ratio 0.79; 96% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.005). Nights in hospital did not differ significantly (5.8 vs 5.1 days per year; P=0.23). The primary safety outcome (death, stroke, or serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy) did not differ significantly in overall percentage; serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy occurred in 4.9% of the early-rhythm-control group versus 1.4% of usual care. Symptoms and LV function at 2 years did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with blinded outcome assessment; the early-rhythm group received more of everything (drugs, ablations, follow-up), so the strategy — not one component — is what was tested. Stopped early for efficacy, which tends to flatter the point estimate modestly.
cards.source: Kirchhof P et al. Early Rhythm-Control Therapy in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 32865375. cards.headline: EARLY-AF 2021: first-line cryoablation — recurrence 42.9% vs 67.8% on drugs (HR 0.48 relative); symptomatic recurrence 11.0% vs 26.2%
cards.summary: EARLY-AF 2021: first-line cryoablation — recurrence 42.9% vs 67.8% on drugs (HR 0.48 relative); symptomatic recurrence 11.0% vs 26.2%
cards.people: 303 patients with symptomatic, paroxysmal, previously untreated AF, randomised to cryoballoon catheter ablation (154) or antiarrhythmic drug therapy for initial rhythm control (149). All received an implantable cardiac monitor. Primary endpoint: first recurrence of any atrial tachyarrhythmia between days 91 and 365. Follow-up 12 months.
cards.result: Recurrence occurred in 66 of 154 patients (42.9%) assigned to ablation and 101 of 149 (67.8%) assigned to drug therapy (hazard ratio 0.48; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; P<0.001). Symptomatic atrial tachyarrhythmia recurred in 11.0% versus 26.2% (HR 0.39; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.68). Median time in AF was 0% (IQR 0 to 0.08) with ablation versus 0.13% (IQR 0 to 1.60) with drugs. Serious adverse events occurred in 5 patients (3.2%) with ablation and 6 (4.0%) with drug therapy.
cards.watchOut: A rhythm endpoint at 1 year in paroxysmal AF — it establishes ablation as a legitimate first move for rhythm control, not as an outcome-modifying therapy; the outcome evidence is EAST's. Continuous monitoring in both arms makes the recurrence figures honest.
cards.source: Andrade JG et al. Cryoablation or Drug Therapy for Initial Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33197159. Registry ID: NCT02825979, from the record. cards.headline: STOP AF First 2021: first-line cryoballoon treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0% on drugs at 12 months
cards.summary: STOP AF First 2021: first-line cryoballoon treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0% on drugs at 12 months
cards.people: 203 patients aged 18 to 80 with symptomatic paroxysmal AF and no previous rhythm-control therapy, randomised and treated with cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation (104) or class I/III antiarrhythmic drugs (99). Monitoring: ECG at 1, 3, 6, 12 months, weekly patient-activated telephone monitoring, and 24-hour ambulatory monitoring at 6 and 12 months. Primary efficacy endpoint: treatment success (freedom from initial failure or recurrence after a 90-day blanking period).
cards.result: Initial procedural success was 97% in the ablation group. The Kaplan-Meier estimate of treatment success at 12 months was 74.6% (95% CI 65.0 to 82.0) in the ablation group and 45.0% (95% CI 34.6 to 54.7) in the drug-therapy group (P<0.001). Two primary safety endpoint events occurred in the ablation group (Kaplan-Meier estimate 1.9%; 95% CI 0.5 to 7.5).
cards.watchOut: Intermittent (not continuous) monitoring, so its success rates read higher than EARLY-AF's for similar biology — compare within trials, not across. Included as the second first-line cryoballoon trial pointing the same way.
cards.source: Wazni OM et al. Cryoballoon Ablation as Initial Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33197158. Registry ID: NCT03118518, from the record. shelves.title: Persistent AF: adding MRI-guided fibrosis ablation to pulmonary vein isolation did not reduce recurrence — and caused strokes (DECAAF II)
shelves.question: In persistent AF, does ablating MRI-detected left atrial fibrosis in addition to pulmonary vein isolation reduce atrial arrhythmia recurrence versus isolation alone?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Female · Fibrosis · Heart Atria · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Veins · Recurrence · Surgery, Computer-Assisted · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A well-powered negative trial with a harm signal — the combination that should change practice. DECAAF II randomised 843 patients with persistent AF at 44 centres in 10 countries to pulmonary vein isolation plus MRI-guided fibrosis ablation (421) or isolation alone (422); 815 contributed to efficacy analyses. Atrial arrhythmia recurrence after the 90-day blanking period did not differ: 43.0% versus 46.1% (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17; P=.63). The safety composite (stroke, pulmonary vein stenosis, bleeding, heart failure, or death within 30 days) occurred in 9 patients (2.2%) in the fibrosis-guided group versus none with isolation alone (P=.001) — including 6 ischaemic strokes (1.5%) versus none, and 2 deaths in the fibrosis-guided group, the first possibly procedure-related. The authors' conclusion: findings do not support MRI-guided fibrosis ablation for persistent AF. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on efficacy, with the early safety excess stated on the shelf's face — more ablation was worse, not merely useless.

cards.headline: DECAAF II 2022: recurrence 43.0% (fibrosis-guided + PVI) vs 46.1% (PVI alone), HR 0.95 relative; safety events 2.2% vs 0%, with 6 strokes vs none
cards.summary: DECAAF II 2022: recurrence 43.0% (fibrosis-guided + PVI) vs 46.1% (PVI alone), HR 0.95 relative; safety events 2.2% vs 0%, with 6 strokes vs none
cards.people: 843 patients with persistent AF (symptomatic or asymptomatic) undergoing ablation at 44 academic and nonacademic centres in 10 countries, randomised to PVI plus MRI-guided atrial fibrosis ablation (421) or PVI alone (422). Delayed-enhancement MRI before ablation in both groups and at 3 months for scar assessment. Primary endpoint: time to first atrial arrhythmia recurrence after a 90-day blanking period. Primary safety composite: stroke, PV stenosis, bleeding, heart failure, or death within 30 days. 815 patients (96.9%) contributed to efficacy analyses.
cards.result: Atrial arrhythmia recurrence: 175 patients (43.0%) in the fibrosis-guided plus PVI group versus 188 (46.1%) with PVI alone (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17; P=.63) — no significant difference. The safety composite occurred in 9 patients (2.2%) versus 0 (P=.001). Six patients (1.5%) in the fibrosis-guided group had an ischaemic stroke versus none in the PVI-only group. Two deaths occurred in the fibrosis-guided group, the first possibly related to the procedure.
cards.watchOut: The harm is early procedural harm concentrated in the more extensive lesion set — the result argues against empirical extra ablation beyond vein isolation in persistent AF, not against ablation itself. Fibrosis burden still predicts recurrence; predicting is not the same as being a useful target.
cards.source: Marrouche NF et al. shelves.title: Device-detected subclinical AF: apixaban beat aspirin for stroke (ARTESiA); edoxaban did not beat placebo (NOAH-AFNET 6)
shelves.question: In patients with device-detected subclinical AF or atrial high-rate episodes (6 minutes to 24 hours) and stroke risk factors, does anticoagulation reduce stroke and systemic embolism enough to justify its bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Atrial Fibrillation · Embolism · Hemorrhage · Stroke · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Electrodes, Implanted · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A trials that point in the same direction with different comparators — and the comparator is the lesson. ARTESiA randomised 4,012 patients with device-detected subclinical AF lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours (mean age 76.8; mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.9) double-blind to apixaban or aspirin 81 mg: stroke or systemic embolism occurred at 0.78% per patient-year on apixaban versus 1.24% on aspirin (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88; P=0.007), while major bleeding was higher on apixaban (1.71% vs 0.94% per patient-year; HR 1.80; 95% CI 1.26 to 2.57; P=0.001), with fatal bleeding numerically lower on apixaban (5 vs 8 patients). NOAH-AFNET 6 randomised 2,536 patients aged 65 or older with atrial high-rate episodes of at least 6 minutes plus a stroke risk factor to edoxaban or placebo, and was terminated early (median follow-up 21 months) for safety concerns and informal futility: the efficacy composite (cardiovascular death, stroke, systemic embolism) was 3.2% versus 4.0% per patient-year (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08; P=0.15), stroke itself ran at about 1% per patient-year in both groups, and the safety composite (death or major bleeding) was higher on edoxaban (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67; P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): against aspirin there is a real relative stroke reduction bought with more major bleeding; against placebo the event rates are so low that no benefit could be shown — the absolute gains are small either way, and the decision is genuinely individual. A study-level meta-analysis of the two trials exists (PMID 37952187) and is consistent with this reading.

cards.headline: ARTESiA 2024: stroke/systemic embolism 0.78%/yr on apixaban vs 1.24%/yr on aspirin (HR 0.63 relative); major bleeding 1.71% vs 0.94%/yr (HR 1.80)
cards.summary: ARTESiA 2024: stroke/systemic embolism 0.78%/yr on apixaban vs 1.24%/yr on aspirin (HR 0.63 relative); major bleeding 1.71% vs 0.94%/yr (HR 1.80)
cards.people: 4,012 patients with subclinical AF lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours detected by implanted devices (mean age 76.8 years; mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.9; 36.1% women), randomised to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg where indicated) or aspirin 81 mg daily; trial drug stopped and anticoagulation started if episodes exceeded 24 hours or clinical AF developed. Primary efficacy: stroke or systemic embolism (intention-to-treat). Primary safety: major bleeding (on-treatment). Mean follow-up 3.5 years.
cards.result: Stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 55 patients in the apixaban group (0.78% per patient-year) and 86 in the aspirin group (1.24% per patient-year) (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88; P=0.007). Major bleeding (on-treatment): 1.71% per patient-year on apixaban versus 0.94% on aspirin (HR 1.80; 95% CI 1.26 to 2.57; P=0.001). Fatal bleeding occurred in 5 patients on apixaban and 8 on aspirin.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is aspirin, itself an antithrombotic — the absolute stroke rates (about 1% per year) are the clinically decisive numbers, and the bleeding excess is of the same order as the stroke benefit. Episodes longer than 24 hours were treated as clinical AF and left the comparison.
cards.source: Healey JS et al. Apixaban for Stroke Prevention in Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 37952132. Registry ID: NCT01938248, from the record. cards.headline: NOAH-AFNET 6 2023: edoxaban vs placebo — efficacy composite HR 0.81 relative, not significant; death/major bleeding HR 1.31; stopped early
cards.summary: NOAH-AFNET 6 2023: edoxaban vs placebo — efficacy composite HR 0.81 relative, not significant; death/major bleeding HR 1.31; stopped early
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy trial, terminated early (NOAH-AFNET 6)
cards.people: 2,536 patients aged 65 or older with device-detected atrial high-rate episodes lasting at least 6 minutes and at least one additional stroke risk factor (mean age 78; 37.4% women; median AHRE duration 2.8 hours), randomised 1:1 to edoxaban or placebo. Primary efficacy: composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism. Safety: composite of death from any cause or major bleeding. Event-driven; terminated early at a median follow-up of 21 months because of safety concerns and an independent informal futility assessment, after planned enrolment completed.
cards.result: A primary efficacy event occurred in 83 patients (3.2% per patient-year) on edoxaban and 101 (4.0% per patient-year) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08; P=0.15). Stroke incidence was approximately 1% per patient-year in both groups. The safety outcome occurred in 149 patients (5.9% per patient-year) on edoxaban versus 114 (4.5% per patient-year) on placebo (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67; P=0.03). ECG-diagnosed AF developed in 18.2% of patients overall (8.7% per patient-year).
cards.watchOut: Early termination limits precision, and placebo is not aspirin — NOAH's null and ARTESiA's positive result are compatible once comparators and absolute rates are compared. AHRE populations are device patients, not the general population with brief palpitations.
cards.source: Kirchhof P et al. Anticoagulation with Edoxaban in Patients with Atrial High-Rate Episodes. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37622677. shelves.title: Pulsed field ablation versus thermal ablation for paroxysmal AF: noninferior at one year (ADVENT)
shelves.question: In drug-refractory paroxysmal AF, is pulsed field ablation noninferior to conventional thermal ablation (radiofrequency or cryoballoon) for effectiveness and safety at one year?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation · Bayes Theorem · Catheter Ablation · Pulmonary Veins · Recurrence · Single-Blind Method · Tachycardia · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a clean noninferiority result, at one year. ADVENT randomised 607 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to pulsed field ablation (305) or conventional thermal ablation (302; radiofrequency or cryoballoon). The primary efficacy endpoint — freedom from initial procedural failure, documented atrial tachyarrhythmia after a 3-month blanking period, antiarrhythmic drug use, cardioversion, or repeat ablation — was met in an estimated 73.3% with pulsed field versus 71.3% with thermal (difference 2.0 points; 95% Bayesian credible interval −5.2 to 9.2; posterior probability of noninferiority >0.999). Primary safety events were 2.1% versus 1.5% (difference 0.6 points; credible interval −1.5 to 2.8; noninferiority >0.999). PROPOSED LIKELY: pulsed field ablation is a noninferior alternative energy at one year in paroxysmal AF, from a single trial using Bayesian noninferiority analysis; claims of superiority — for safety rarities like oesophageal or phrenic injury, or for durability — are not established by this trial, whose event counts for such harms are far too small. (Desk note: the trial's sample size appears as 607 randomised in the record; some summaries cite 687 enrolled — the record governs.)

cards.headline: ADVENT 2023: efficacy success 73.3% (pulsed field) vs 71.3% (thermal); safety events 2.1% vs 1.5% — noninferior on both
cards.summary: ADVENT 2023: efficacy success 73.3% (pulsed field) vs 71.3% (thermal); safety events 2.1% vs 1.5% — noninferior on both
cards.people: 607 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF randomised 1:1 to pulsed field ablation (305) or conventional thermal ablation (radiofrequency or cryoballoon; 302). Primary efficacy endpoint: freedom from a composite of initial procedural failure, documented atrial tachyarrhythmia after a 3-month blanking period, antiarrhythmic drug use, cardioversion, or repeat ablation at 1 year. Primary safety endpoint: acute and chronic device- and procedure-related serious adverse events. Bayesian noninferiority analysis.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint was met (no events) in 204 patients who underwent pulsed field ablation (estimated probability 73.3%) and 194 who underwent thermal ablation (71.3%) — between-group difference 2.0 percentage points (95% Bayesian credible interval −5.2 to 9.2; posterior probability of noninferiority >0.999). Primary safety endpoint events occurred in 6 patients (estimated incidence 2.1%) versus 4 (1.5%) (difference 0.6 points; 95% Bayesian credible interval −1.5 to 2.8; posterior probability of noninferiority >0.999). The authors conclude pulsed field ablation was noninferior to conventional thermal ablation on both endpoints at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority within prespecified margins is not equivalence and not superiority; the rare-harm advantages claimed for pulsed field energy (oesophageal fistula, pulmonary vein stenosis, phrenic palsy) occur too infrequently for a 607-patient trial to settle. One year is short for durability comparisons.
cards.source: Reddy VY et al. Pulsed Field or Conventional Thermal Ablation for Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37634148. Registry ID: NCT04612244, from the record. shelves.title: At cardiac surgery, occluding the left atrial appendage cut stroke or systemic embolism — on top of anticoagulation (LAAOS III)
shelves.question: In patients with AF and elevated stroke risk undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication, does concomitant surgical left atrial appendage occlusion reduce ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism versus no occlusion, when most patients continue anticoagulation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Appendage · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Combined Modality Therapy · Embolism · Female · Humans · Intraoperative Complications · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Risk · Severity of Illness Index · Stroke
shelves.balance: A large, well-blinded surgical trial with a clear hard-outcome win — and an important framing: the benefit came on top of anticoagulation, not instead of it. LAAOS III randomised 4,811 patients with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2 who were undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication to appendage occlusion or no occlusion (4,770 in the primary analysis; mean age 71; mean score 4.2); surgeons aside, everyone was blinded. Over a mean 3.8 years, ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 4.8% with occlusion versus 7.0% without (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.85; P=0.001). At 3 years, 76.8% of participants were still receiving oral anticoagulation. Perioperative bleeding, heart failure, and death did not differ significantly. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a stroke-embedding composite reviewed personally). The shelf must not be read as permission to stop anticoagulation after surgical occlusion — most of the trial's benefit accrued in patients who stayed on it.

cards.headline: LAAOS III 2021: stroke or systemic embolism 4.8% (occlusion) vs 7.0% (no occlusion) — HR 0.67 relative; three quarters still anticoagulated at 3 years
cards.summary: LAAOS III 2021: stroke or systemic embolism 4.8% (occlusion) vs 7.0% (no occlusion) — HR 0.67 relative; three quarters still anticoagulated at 3 years
cards.people: 4,811 participants with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2 scheduled for cardiac surgery for another indication, randomised to undergo or not undergo left atrial appendage occlusion during surgery (primary analysis: 2,379 occlusion, 2,391 no occlusion; mean age 71; mean CHA2DS2-VASc 4.2). All were expected to receive usual care including oral anticoagulation. Participants, research personnel, and primary care physicians (other than surgeons) were blinded to assignment. Primary outcome: ischaemic stroke (including TIA with positive neuroimaging) or systemic embolism. Mean follow-up 3.8 years.
cards.result: 92.1% of participants received the assigned procedure; at 3 years, 76.8% continued to receive oral anticoagulation. Stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 114 participants (4.8%) in the occlusion group and 168 (7.0%) in the no-occlusion group (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.85; P=0.001). The incidence of perioperative bleeding, heart failure, or death did not differ significantly between the groups.
cards.watchOut: An add-on result: occlusion plus usual care (mostly continued anticoagulation) versus usual care. It does not test occlusion as a substitute for anticoagulation — that question belongs to the percutaneous-occlusion shelves in different settings (#2249, #2258, #272). The population is patients already undergoing cardiac surgery.

shelves.title: Adding surgical ventricular reconstruction to bypass surgery shrank the ventricle but changed nothing that matters (STICH Hypothesis 2)
shelves.question: In ischaemic cardiomyopathy with dominant anterior left ventricular dysfunction, does adding surgical ventricular reconstruction to CABG reduce death or cardiac hospitalisation versus CABG alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Disease · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure · Heart Ventricles · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Patient Selection · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: A clean anatomical-success/clinical-null trial: the operation did exactly what it was designed to do to the ventricle and none of what it was meant to do for the patient. STICH Hypothesis 2 randomised 1,000 patients with EF at most 35%, coronary disease amenable to CABG, and dominant anterior LV dysfunction amenable to reconstruction, to CABG alone (499) or CABG plus surgical ventricular reconstruction (501); median follow-up 48 months. Reconstruction reduced end-systolic volume index by 19% versus 6% with CABG alone — the anatomical goal achieved. But the primary outcome (death from any cause or hospitalisation for cardiac causes) occurred in 59% with CABG alone and 58% with the combined approach (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.17; P=0.90), and cardiac symptoms and exercise tolerance improved to a similar degree in both groups. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C). A smaller ventricle is not the same thing as a better outcome — the shelf is the library's standing example of that distinction.

cards.headline: STICH 2009: death or cardiac hospitalisation 59% (CABG alone) vs 58% (CABG + reconstruction) — HR 0.99 relative — despite end-systolic volume falling 19% vs 6%
cards.summary: STICH 2009: death or cardiac hospitalisation 59% (CABG alone) vs 58% (CABG + reconstruction) — HR 0.99 relative — despite end-systolic volume falling 19% vs 6%
cards.people: 1,000 patients with LVEF at most 35%, coronary artery disease amenable to CABG, and dominant anterior left ventricular dysfunction amenable to surgical ventricular reconstruction, randomised between September 2002 and January 2006 to CABG alone (499) or CABG with surgical ventricular reconstruction (501). Primary outcome: composite of death from any cause and hospitalisation for cardiac causes. Median follow-up 48 months.
cards.result: Surgical ventricular reconstruction reduced the end-systolic volume index by 19%, versus a 6% reduction with CABG alone. Cardiac symptoms and exercise tolerance improved from baseline to a similar degree in both groups. The primary outcome occurred in 292 patients (59%) assigned to CABG alone and 289 (58%) assigned to CABG plus reconstruction (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.17; P=0.90). The authors conclude the anatomical change was not associated with greater symptom improvement or with a reduction in death or cardiac hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Selected anatomy (dominant anterior dysfunction deemed reconstructable) and the surgical era (2002–2006 enrolment) bound the result; it does not address reconstruction for discrete aneurysm with thrombus or rupture mechanics, which are different indications. The null is precise enough (CI 0.84 to 1.17) to exclude a large benefit in this population.

shelves.title: Advanced heart failure: sacubitril/valsartan showed no advantage over valsartan alone (LIFE)
shelves.question: In advanced HFrEF with recent NYHA class IV symptoms, does sacubitril/valsartan reduce NT-proBNP and improve clinical outcomes versus valsartan alone?
shelves.mesh: Aminobutyrates · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Biomarkers · Biphenyl Compounds · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Stroke Volume · Valsartan
shelves.balance: The PARADIGM-HF result does not extend to the sickest patients, and LIFE is the trial that drew that boundary. LIFE randomised patients with advanced HFrEF and recent NYHA class IV symptoms to sacubitril/valsartan (target 200 mg twice daily — the trial-size dose designation) or valsartan alone (target 160 mg twice daily) on top of recommended therapy; 335 patients entered the analysis after a run-in that itself excluded 72 eligible patients (18%) who could not tolerate even 100 mg/day of sacubitril/valsartan, and 29% of those assigned to it discontinued during the 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — the area under the curve for NT-proBNP ratio to baseline through 24 weeks — did not differ: estimated ratio of change 0.95 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.08; P=.45). Nor did the clinical composite of days alive, out of hospital, and free from heart-failure events improve. Non-life-threatening hyperkalaemia was more frequent on sacubitril/valsartan (17% vs 9%; P=.04). The trial was stopped early (March 2020) because of COVID-19 risk, which limits its size — but nothing in it trends toward the benefit seen in less advanced disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C: the clinical composite embeds survival) in this advanced population; the shelf governs advanced/NYHA IV disease only and does not touch the PARADIGM-HF population.

cards.headline: LIFE 2022: NT-proBNP AUC ratio 0.95 (P=.45) for sacubitril/valsartan vs valsartan in advanced HFrEF; clinical composite also not improved; hyperkalaemia 17% vs 9%
cards.summary: LIFE 2022: NT-proBNP AUC ratio 0.95 (P=.45) for sacubitril/valsartan vs valsartan in advanced HFrEF; clinical composite also not improved; hyperkalaemia 17% vs 9%
cards.people: Patients with advanced heart failure, reduced ejection fraction, and recent NYHA class IV symptoms; 335 included in the analysis (73% men; mean age 59.4 years), randomised to sacubitril/valsartan (target dose 200 mg twice daily; n=167) or valsartan (target 160 mg twice daily; n=168) in addition to recommended therapy. Primary endpoint: area under the curve for the NT-proBNP ratio to baseline through 24 weeks. The trial began March 2017 and was stopped early on March 23, 2020 owing to COVID-19 risk. A short run-in preceded randomisation: 72 eligible patients (18%) could not tolerate sacubitril/valsartan 100 mg/day and were not randomised; 49 patients (29%) discontinued sacubitril/valsartan during the trial.
cards.result: Median NT-proBNP AUC was 1.19 (IQR 0.91 to 1.64) in the valsartan arm and 1.08 (IQR 0.75 to 1.60) in the sacubitril/valsartan arm; the estimated ratio of change was 0.95 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.08; P=.45) — no significant difference. Sacubitril/valsartan did not improve the clinical composite of days alive, out of hospital, and free from heart-failure events. Non-life-threatening hyperkalaemia was more frequent with sacubitril/valsartan (28 patients [17%] vs 15 [9%]; P=.04); no other safety concerns were observed. The authors conclude there was no statistically significant difference in NT-proBNP reduction in chronic advanced HFrEF.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker primary endpoint in a trial stopped early — the shelf's no-difference stamp rests on the biomarker and the clinical composite agreeing, plus the tolerability facts (nearly 1 in 5 could not tolerate the run-in), which are themselves the practical finding in class IV disease. Do not generalise to NYHA II–III, where the evidence base is different.
cards.source: Mann DL et al. Effect of Treatment With Sacubitril/Valsartan in Patients With Advanced Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2022. PMID: 34730769. Registry ID: NCT02816736, from the record. shelves.title: Suspected angina: imaging-guided care (CMR or perfusion scintigraphy) cut unnecessary angiography fourfold versus guideline-directed care (CE-MARC 2)
shelves.question: In suspected coronary heart disease, does care guided by cardiovascular magnetic resonance or myocardial perfusion scintigraphy reduce unnecessary invasive angiography versus NICE-guideline-directed care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina Pectoris · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Coronary Stenosis · Coronary Vessels · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Perfusion Imaging · Patient Care · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Unnecessary Procedures
shelves.balance: A pragmatic three-arm strategy trial whose endpoint is the angiograms that should not have happened. CE-MARC 2 randomised 1,202 symptomatic patients with suspected coronary disease (pretest likelihood 10–90%; mean 49.5%) at 6 UK hospitals to NICE-guideline-directed care (240), CMR-guided care (481), or perfusion-scintigraphy-guided care (481). Protocol-defined unnecessary angiography within 12 months (angiography showing no significant disease by FFR or quantitative criteria) occurred in 28.8% under guideline care versus 7.5% with CMR guidance and 7.1% with scintigraphy guidance — adjusted odds ratio 0.21 for CMR versus guidelines (95% CI 0.12 to 0.34; P<.001), with no significant difference between CMR and scintigraphy (OR 1.27; P=.32). Positive angiography rates were similar (12.1%, 9.8%, 8.7%), and major adverse cardiovascular events did not differ (1.7% guideline, 2.5% CMR, 2.5% scintigraphy) — this is a pathway-efficiency result, not an outcome result. PROPOSED LIKELY: gatekeeping the cath lab with imaging works; which of the two imaging tests is a local-resources question.

cards.headline: CE-MARC 2 2016: unnecessary angiography 28.8% (guideline care) vs 7.5% (CMR) vs 7.1% (MPS); MACE did not differ
cards.summary: CE-MARC 2 2016: unnecessary angiography 28.8% (guideline care) vs 7.5% (CMR) vs 7.1% (MPS); MACE did not differ
cards.people: 1,202 symptomatic patients with suspected CHD and pretest likelihood 10–90% at 6 UK hospitals, randomised 240:481:481 to NICE-guideline-directed management, CMR-guided care, or myocardial perfusion scintigraphy (MPS)-guided care. Primary endpoint: protocol-defined unnecessary coronary angiography within 12 months (FFR above 0.8, or no stenosis of at least 70% in one view or 50% in two views in any vessel at least 2.5 mm). Secondaries: positive angiography, MACE, procedural complications.
cards.result: Invasive angiography was performed in 102 patients (42.5%) in the NICE group, 85 (17.7%) in the CMR group, and 78 (16.2%) in the MPS group. Unnecessary angiography occurred in 69 patients (28.8%), 36 (7.5%), and 34 (7.1%) respectively; adjusted odds ratio for CMR versus NICE guidelines 0.21 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.34; P<.001) and for CMR versus MPS 1.27 (95% CI 0.79 to 2.03; P=.32). Positive angiography: 12.1% (NICE), 9.8% (CMR), 8.7% (MPS). MACE at 12 months or more: 1.7%, 2.5%, 2.5% (adjusted HR CMR vs NICE 1.37; 95% CI 0.52 to 3.57; CMR vs MPS 0.95; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.95) — no significant differences.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a process measure defined by the protocol; event rates were low and the trial was not powered for outcomes. The comparator is UK NICE-guideline care as practised in 2012–2016 — the size of the win depends on how angiography-happy the local default pathway is.
cards.source: Greenwood JP et al. Effect of Care Guided by Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance, Myocardial Perfusion Scintigraphy, or NICE Guidelines on Subsequent Unnecessary Angiography Rates: The CE-MARC 2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27570866. Registry ID: NCT01664858, from the record. shelves.title: Stable angina: a perfusion-CMR strategy matched an FFR strategy on events with fewer revascularisations (MR-INFORM)
shelves.question: In stable angina with risk factors, does management guided by stress-perfusion CMR match FFR-guided invasive management on major adverse cardiac events, with less revascularisation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Angina, Stable · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Angiography · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: A strategy noninferiority trial that met its margin with room to spare. MR-INFORM randomised 918 patients with typical angina plus at least two risk factors or a positive exercise test to a perfusion-CMR strategy (revascularise if ischaemia in at least 6% of myocardium) or an invasive FFR strategy (revascularise if FFR at most 0.8). The primary outcome (death, nonfatal MI, or target-vessel revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 3.6% with the CMR strategy versus 3.7% with FFR (risk difference −0.2 points; 95% CI −2.7 to 2.4; noninferiority margin 6 points — met). Fewer CMR-strategy patients met criteria for revascularisation (40.5% vs 45.9%) and fewer actually underwent index revascularisation (35.7% vs 45.0%; P=0.005). Freedom from angina at 12 months did not differ significantly (49.2% vs 43.8%; P=0.21). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: the composite embeds death and MI): a noninvasive-first strategy is a legitimate equal in stable angina — with fewer procedures. Note Shelf #2263 (FORECAST): adding FFRCT on top of CTCA did not show the same economy — different strategy, different answer.

cards.headline: MR-INFORM 2019: primary outcome 3.6% (CMR strategy) vs 3.7% (FFR strategy) — noninferior; index revascularisation 35.7% vs 45.0%
cards.summary: MR-INFORM 2019: primary outcome 3.6% (CMR strategy) vs 3.7% (FFR strategy) — noninferior; index revascularisation 35.7% vs 45.0%
cards.people: 918 patients with typical angina and either at least two cardiovascular risk factors or a positive exercise treadmill test, randomised to a cardiovascular-MRI perfusion strategy (454; revascularisation recommended for ischaemia in at least 6% of the myocardium) or an invasive angiography plus FFR strategy (464; revascularisation for FFR at most 0.8). Primary outcome: death, nonfatal MI, or target-vessel revascularisation within 1 year; noninferiority margin 6 percentage points (risk difference). 421 and 430 patients contributed to the primary-outcome analysis.
cards.result: Revascularisation was recommended in 184 of 454 patients (40.5%) in the MRI group and 213 of 464 (45.9%) in the FFR group (P=0.11); index revascularisation was performed in 162 (35.7%) versus 209 (45.0%) (P=0.005). The primary outcome occurred in 15 of 421 patients (3.6%) versus 16 of 430 (3.7%) (risk difference −0.2 percentage points; 95% CI −2.7 to 2.4), meeting the noninferiority threshold. Freedom from angina at 12 months: 49.2% versus 43.8% (P=0.21).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, one-year horizon, and 'noninferior within 6 points' on a 3.6% event rate is a wide relative margin — the observed difference was near zero, which is stronger than the margin alone implies. Stable angina with risk factors only; not an acute-presentation strategy.
cards.source: Nagel E et al. Magnetic Resonance Perfusion or Fractional Flow Reserve in Coronary Disease. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 31216398. Registry ID: NCT01236807, from the record. shelves.title: After STEMI: FFR guidance of complete revascularisation showed no advantage over angiography guidance (FLOWER-MI)
shelves.question: In STEMI with multivessel disease undergoing complete revascularisation, does FFR guidance beat angiography guidance on death, MI, or urgent revascularisation at one year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Confidence Intervals · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Stenosis · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Revascularization · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Proportional Hazards Models · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction · Single-Blind Method · Stents
shelves.balance: THIN on conclusion despite a thousand patients — the trial's own authors decline to interpret it definitively, and this shelf follows them. FLOWER-MI randomised 1,171 patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, after successful culprit PCI, to complete revascularisation guided by FFR or by angiography alone (1,163 analysed). The primary outcome (death, nonfatal MI, or unplanned hospitalisation leading to urgent revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 5.5% with FFR guidance versus 4.2% with angiography guidance (hazard ratio 1.32; 95% CI 0.78 to 2.23; P=0.31). Components: death 1.5% versus 1.7%; nonfatal MI 3.1% versus 1.7%; urgent revascularisation 2.6% versus 1.9%. FFR guidance used fewer nonculprit stents (1.01 vs 1.50 per patient). The point estimate leans against FFR guidance, the interval spans meaningful effects in both directions, and the authors state the findings do not allow a conclusive interpretation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C): no advantage was shown for adding FFR in this setting; harm is not established either. Distinct from Shelf #267 (complete versus culprit-only revascularisation — a settled benefit); this shelf is about guidance within complete revascularisation.

cards.headline: FLOWER-MI 2021: primary outcome 5.5% (FFR-guided) vs 4.2% (angiography-guided) — HR 1.32 relative, P=0.31, authors call interpretation inconclusive
cards.summary: FLOWER-MI 2021: primary outcome 5.5% (FFR-guided) vs 4.2% (angiography-guided) — HR 1.32 relative, P=0.31, authors call interpretation inconclusive
cards.people: 1,171 patients with STEMI and multivessel disease who had undergone successful PCI of the infarct-related artery, randomised to complete revascularisation guided by FFR (586 analysed) or by angiography (577 analysed). Primary outcome: composite of death from any cause, nonfatal MI, or unplanned hospitalisation leading to urgent revascularisation at 1 year.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 32 of 586 patients (5.5%) in the FFR-guided group and 24 of 577 (4.2%) in the angiography-guided group (hazard ratio 1.32; 95% CI 0.78 to 2.23; P=0.31). Death: 9 patients (1.5%) versus 10 (1.7%). Nonfatal MI: 18 (3.1%) versus 10 (1.7%). Unplanned hospitalisation leading to urgent revascularisation: 15 (2.6%) versus 11 (1.9%). The mean number of stents placed for nonculprit lesions was 1.01 ± 0.99 with FFR guidance versus 1.50 ± 0.86 with angiography guidance. The authors conclude FFR guidance had no significant benefit, and that the wide confidence intervals do not allow a conclusive interpretation.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert 'not significant' into 'FFR guidance is harmful' — the interval includes a 22% relative benefit. Equally, do not cite the fewer-stents finding as an outcome win; it is a resource pattern attached to a neutral-to-negative event trend.

shelves.title: Angina with non-obstructive arteries: stratified therapy guided by invasive coronary function testing improved angina (CorMicA)
shelves.question: In ischaemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries (INOCA), does disclosing invasive coronary function test results and stratifying therapy (vasospasm, microvascular angina, noncardiac) improve angina and quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Male · Microvascular Angina · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: THIN — one small trial, but randomised with a blinded control and a patient-reported primary endpoint that matters in a population medicine usually sends home unexplained. CorMicA enrolled 391 patients with angina referred for angiography; 206 (53.7%) had obstructive disease, and the 151 without obstruction were randomised to an interventional diagnostic procedure (guidewire coronary flow reserve, microcirculatory resistance, FFR, then acetylcholine vasoreactivity testing) with results disclosed and therapy stratified, or to a sham procedure with standard care. At 6 months the Seattle Angina Questionnaire summary score improved by a mean of 11.7 points more with stratified therapy (95% CI 5.0 to 18.4; p=0.001), with quality of life also better (EQ-5D index +0.10; p=0.024; visual analogue score +14.5; p<0.001). Major adverse cardiac events did not differ (2.6% in both groups). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: knowing the mechanism — vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, or neither — and treating accordingly makes these patients feel better; event effects are unknown at this size.

cards.headline: CorMicA 2018: Seattle Angina Questionnaire improved 11.7 points more with stratified therapy at 6 months; events identical (2.6% both groups)
cards.summary: CorMicA 2018: Seattle Angina Questionnaire improved 11.7 points more with stratified therapy at 6 months; events identical (2.6% both groups)
cards.people: 391 patients with angina undergoing invasive coronary angiography; 151 without angiographically obstructive CAD were randomised 1:1 to stratified medical therapy guided by an interventional diagnostic procedure (76) or standard care with a sham procedure (75). The procedure measured coronary flow reserve, index of microcirculatory resistance, and FFR, followed by acetylcholine vasoreactivity testing; results were disclosed only in the intervention group and therapy stratified by endotype. Primary endpoint: mean difference in Seattle Angina Questionnaire summary score at 6 months.
cards.result: The intervention improved the Seattle Angina Questionnaire summary score by a mean of 11.7 units at 6 months (95% CI 5.0 to 18.4; p=0.001). Quality of life improved (EQ-5D index +0.10 units; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; p=0.024; visual analogue score +14.5 units; 95% CI 7.8 to 21.3; p<0.001). Major adverse cardiac events at 6 months did not differ (2.6% control vs 2.6% intervention; p=1.00). The authors conclude stratified medical therapy linked to the diagnostic procedure is routinely feasible and improves angina in patients with no obstructive CAD.
cards.watchOut: A symptom endpoint in 151 patients at 6 months; the disclosure itself (being believed, receiving a named diagnosis) is part of the intervention and cannot be separated from the drug changes. No power for events — do not cite for prognosis.
cards.source: Ford TJ et al. Stratified Medical Therapy Using Invasive Coronary Function Testing in Angina: The CorMicA Trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2018. PMID: 30266608. shelves.title: Before cardioversion for AF: a TEE-guided strategy matched conventional anticoagulation-first on embolic events, with less bleeding and cardioversion a month sooner (ACUTE)
shelves.question: In AF of more than 48 hours, does a transoesophageal-echo-guided strategy (cardiovert if no thrombus, with short anticoagulation) match the conventional three-weeks-of-anticoagulation-first strategy on embolic events and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Echocardiography, Transesophageal · Electric Countershock · Embolism · Female · Heart Atria · Heart Diseases · Hemorrhage · Heparin · Humans · Ischemic Attack, Transient · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Prospective Studies · Stroke · Thromboembolism · Thrombosis · Warfarin
shelves.balance: THIN — a single trial, but a large one for its question, and its answer has aged well. ACUTE randomised 1,222 patients with AF of more than two days' duration awaiting elective cardioversion to a TEE-guided strategy (anticoagulate, image, cardiovert promptly if no thrombus) or conventional care (warfarin for three weeks first). The primary composite (stroke, TIA, or peripheral embolism within 8 weeks) did not differ significantly: 5 events (0.8%) with TEE guidance versus 3 (0.5%) conventionally (P=0.50) — absolute rates tiny in both arms, and the trial cannot exclude a small difference in either direction. Haemorrhagic events were significantly fewer with the TEE strategy (2.9% vs 5.5%; P=0.03), cardioversion came a month sooner (mean 3.0 vs 30.6 days; P<0.001), and sinus rhythm was restored more often (71.1% vs 65.2%; P=0.03); death, maintenance of sinus rhythm, and functional status did not differ at 8 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: TEE guidance is a clinically effective alternative when cardioversion should not wait — warfarin-era logistics, but the comparison (image now versus anticoagulate blindly for weeks) is unchanged by direct-acting agents.

cards.headline: ACUTE 2001: embolic events 0.8% (TEE-guided) vs 0.5% (conventional), P=0.50; haemorrhage 2.9% vs 5.5% (P=0.03); cardioversion at 3.0 vs 30.6 days
cards.summary: ACUTE 2001: embolic events 0.8% (TEE-guided) vs 0.5% (conventional), P=0.50; haemorrhage 2.9% vs 5.5% (P=0.03); cardioversion at 3.0 vs 30.6 days
cards.people: 1,222 patients with AF of more than two days' duration scheduled for elective electrical cardioversion at multiple centres, randomised to management guided by transoesophageal echocardiography (619) or conventional treatment (603; warfarin for three weeks before cardioversion). Primary endpoint: composite of cerebrovascular accident, TIA, and peripheral embolism within 8 weeks. Secondaries: functional status, restoration and maintenance of sinus rhythm, haemorrhage, death.
cards.result: Embolic events: 5 among 619 patients (0.8%) in the TEE group versus 3 among 603 (0.5%) in the conventional group (P=0.50) — no significant difference. Haemorrhagic events were significantly lower with TEE guidance (18 events [2.9%] vs 33 [5.5%]; P=0.03). Time to cardioversion was much shorter (mean 3.0 ± 5.6 vs 30.6 ± 10.6 days; P<0.001) and successful restoration of sinus rhythm more frequent (440 patients [71.1%] vs 393 [65.2%]; P=0.03). At 8 weeks there were no significant differences in death, maintenance of sinus rhythm, or functional status.
cards.watchOut: Only 8 embolic events in 1,222 patients — the embolic comparison is compatible with equivalence but cannot prove it to a narrow margin. Pre-registration era: no registry ID exists, legitimately. The trial predates DOACs; the strategy logic transfers, the exact bleeding rates may not.
cards.source: Klein AL et al. Use of transesophageal echocardiography to guide cardioversion in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2001. PMID: 11346805. Registry ID: none (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Cardiac rehabilitation by phone matches the rehab centre for exercise capacity — at a third of the delivery cost (REMOTE-CR + Telerehab III)
shelves.question: After a cardiac event, does remotely monitored home-based telerehabilitation match centre-based rehabilitation for exercise capacity, risk factors, and durability of benefit?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Disease · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Internet · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand · Quality of Life · Rehabilitation Centers · Telemedicine · Treatment Outcome · Cardiac Rehabilitation · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Telerehabilitation · Follow-Up Studies · Surveys and Questionnaires · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: DOUBLE-A for the delivery question. REMOTE-CR randomised 162 adults with coronary heart disease to 12 weeks of real-time smartphone-monitored telerehabilitation or centre-based rehabilitation: peak oxygen uptake was comparable and telerehabilitation was noninferior (adjusted mean difference +0.51 mL/kg/min; 95% CI −0.97 to 1.98; prespecified inferiority margin −1.25). Telerehabilitation participants were less sedentary at 24 weeks; waist and hip measures slightly favoured the centre group at 12 weeks; no other differences were detected. Costs clearly favoured telerehabilitation: programme delivery NZD 1,130 versus 3,466 per participant (about £573 vs £1,758) and medication costs were lower; hospital-utilisation costs did not differ significantly. Telerehab III's two-year follow-up (126 patients) found the telerehabilitation group's exercise capacity had declined after the programme ended (peak VO2 24 to 22 mL/kg/min) yet remained better than the no-telerehabilitation group (P=0.032), with quality-of-life gains and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of −€3,993 per QALY — better outcomes at lower cost. PROPOSED LIKELY: the centre is a delivery vehicle, not the active ingredient; monitored home rehabilitation reaches the same capacity for less money, with partial decay once supervision stops.

cards.headline: REMOTE-CR 2019: VO2max noninferior for telerehab (difference +0.51 mL/kg/min); delivery cost about a third of centre-based
cards.summary: REMOTE-CR 2019: VO2max noninferior for telerehab (difference +0.51 mL/kg/min); delivery cost about a third of centre-based
cards.people: 162 adults with coronary heart disease randomised to 12 weeks of REMOTE-CR telerehabilitation (individualised exercise prescription, real-time monitoring and coaching, behavioural strategies via a bespoke platform) or centre-based exercise rehabilitation. Primary outcome: maximal oxygen uptake at 12 weeks, noninferiority margin −1.25 mL/kg/min. Secondaries at 12/24 weeks: risk factors, adherence, motivation, quality of life, programme, hospital, and medication costs.
cards.result: VO2max was comparable at 12 weeks and REMOTE-CR was noninferior (adjusted mean difference +0.51 mL/kg/min; 95% CI −0.97 to 1.98; P=0.48). Telerehabilitation participants were less sedentary at 24 weeks (adjusted difference −61.5 min/day; 95% CI −117.8 to −5.3; P=0.03); centre-based participants had smaller waist (P=0.04) and hip (P=0.04) circumferences at 12 weeks; no other between-group differences. Per-capita programme delivery cost NZD 1,130 (about £573) versus NZD 3,466 (£1,758); medication costs NZD 331 versus 605 (P=0.02); hospital service utilisation costs not significantly different (P=0.20).
cards.watchOut: Small and single-country (New Zealand); the population had smartphones and the platform was bespoke — reach gains presume the technology works for the patients who currently miss rehab, who are often the least connected. Registry ID not printed in the fetched record; ISRCTN registration exists for the sister trial below.

cards.headline: Telerehab III follow-up 2017: two years after the programme, the telerehab group still had better exercise capacity (P=0.032) and the strategy was cost-saving (−€3,993/QALY)
cards.summary: Telerehab III follow-up 2017: two years after the programme, the telerehab group still had better exercise capacity (P=0.032) and the strategy was cost-saving (−€3,993/QALY)
cards.people: 126 cardiac patients who had completed the multicentre randomised Telerehab III trial (a 6-month telerehabilitation programme added to conventional rehabilitation) and entered its follow-up study, evaluated 2 years after the intervention ended. Primary endpoint: peak aerobic capacity (VO2 peak). Secondaries: self-reported physical activity, HeartQoL quality of life, and cost-effectiveness (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio).
cards.result: Peak VO2 declined within the tele-intervention group after the programme ended (24 ± 8 at end of intervention to 22 ± 6 mL/min/kg two years later; P≤0.001), but the group remained better than the no-tele-intervention group overall (P=0.032). The incremental cost was −€878 per patient and the differential gain 0.22 QALYs, giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of −€3,993 per QALY (cost-saving). The authors note partial decay of benefits once tele-supervision ends and call for behaviour-change techniques that persist.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of trial completers (126 of the original randomised cohort) — durability estimates carry attrition. The decay finding is the honest core: benefits fade when monitoring stops, in both delivery models' literature.
cards.source: Frederix I et al. Cardiac telerehabilitation: A novel cost-efficient care delivery strategy that can induce long-term health benefits. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2017. PMID: 28925749. shelves.title: HFpEF exercise training: interval and continuous training both nudged peak VO2 at 3 months — below the meaningful threshold, gone by 12 (OptimEx-Clin)
shelves.question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do high-intensity interval training or moderate continuous training beat guideline activity advice on peak oxygen consumption — and does intensity matter?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Evidence-Based Medicine · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Heart Failure · High-Intensity Interval Training · Humans · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: THIN — one well-run three-arm trial whose honest headline is how small the differences are. OptimEx-Clin randomised 180 sedentary patients with chronic stable HFpEF at 5 European sites to high-intensity interval training (3 sessions/week), moderate continuous training (5 sessions/week), or one-time guideline activity advice, for 12 months (3 months supervised, then telemonitored home training). At 3 months, peak VO2 rose 1.1 mL/kg/min with interval training and 1.6 with continuous training against a 0.6 fall with advice (differences 1.5 [95% CI 0.4 to 2.7] and 2.0 [0.9 to 3.1]) — but neither difference met the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 2.5 mL/kg/min, interval versus continuous did not differ (−0.4; 95% CI −1.4 to 0.6), and no comparison was significant at 12 months. Diastolic function and natriuretic peptides did not change. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: supervised training of either intensity gives a modest early capacity gain over advice alone; intensity does not matter; without continued structure the gain does not persist. Distinct from Shelf #171 (exercise in HFrEF).

cards.headline: OptimEx-Clin 2021: 3-month peak VO2 differences vs advice +1.5 (HIIT) and +2.0 (MCT) mL/kg/min — both below the 2.5 threshold; nothing significant at 12 months
cards.summary: OptimEx-Clin 2021: 3-month peak VO2 differences vs advice +1.5 (HIIT) and +2.0 (MCT) mL/kg/min — both below the 2.5 threshold; nothing significant at 12 months
cards.people: 180 sedentary patients with chronic stable HFpEF (mean age 70; 67% women) at 5 sites in Germany, Belgium, and Norway, randomised 1:1:1 (60 per group) to high-intensity interval training, moderate continuous training, or guideline control (one-time physical-activity advice). Intervention 12 months: 3 months in clinic, then 9 months telemedically supervised home exercise. Primary endpoint: change in peak VO2 at 3 months; minimal clinically important difference prespecified as 2.5 mL/kg/min. 166 patients (92%) were evaluated at 3 months and 154 (86%) at 12 months.
cards.result: Change in peak VO2 at 3 months: +1.1 mL/kg/min (interval) versus −0.6 (control), difference 1.5 (95% CI 0.4 to 2.7); +1.6 (continuous) versus −0.6 (control), difference 2.0 (95% CI 0.9 to 3.1); interval versus continuous difference −0.4 (95% CI −1.4 to 0.6). Neither training group met the prespecified minimal clinically important difference against control, and no comparisons were statistically significant after 12 months. Diastolic function and natriuretic peptides did not change significantly. Acute coronary syndrome occurred in 4 interval (7%), 3 continuous (5%), and 5 control (8%) patients. The authors conclude the findings do not support either training mode over guideline-based activity advice.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own conclusion is cooler than this shelf's POSSIBLE — the stamp credits the consistent direction and precision of the 3-month differences while the balance prints the failed threshold and the 12-month null. If a stricter stamp is wanted, MAYBE (weak evidence) is defensible; the numbers do not change.

shelves.title: After AF ablation: comprehensive rehabilitation improved physical capacity, not mental health (CopenHeartRFA)
shelves.question: In patients treated with ablation for AF, does a comprehensive rehabilitation programme (exercise plus psychoeducation) improve physical capacity and mental health versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare · Aged · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Rehabilitation · Catheter Ablation · Denmark · Exercise Test · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Humans · Male · Mental Health · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption · Patient Education as Topic · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — one trial, a clear physical result and a clean mental-health null. CopenHeartRFA randomised 210 patients treated with catheter ablation for AF (mean age 59; 74% men; 72% paroxysmal) to 12 weeks of exercise training plus four psychoeducational consultations, or usual care. Peak VO2 at 4 months was higher with rehabilitation (24.3 vs 20.7 mL/kg/min; main effect P=0.003; time-by-intervention interaction P=0.020). Self-rated mental health (SF-36) did not differ (53.8 vs 51.9 points; P=.20). Serious adverse events were 2 versus 1 (including one death unrelated to rehabilitation in each group pattern) — no significant difference (P=.56); non-serious adverse events were reported more often with rehabilitation (16 vs 7 patients; P=.047). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rehabilitation after ablation buys fitness, not measurable mental-health improvement, in this population — a narrower claim than rehabilitation advocates usually make, and the trial's own.

cards.people: 210 patients treated with catheter ablation for AF (mean age 59 years; 74% men; 72% paroxysmal AF), randomised 1:1 (stratified by AF type and sex) to comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation (12 weeks of physical exercise plus four psycho-educational consultations, plus usual care) or usual care alone. Primary outcome: peak VO2. Secondary: self-rated mental health (Short Form-36).
cards.result: Peak VO2 at 4 months was 24.3 mL/kg/min in the rehabilitation group versus 20.7 with usual care (P=0.003 for the main effect; P=0.020 for the time-by-intervention interaction). SF-36 mental health did not differ significantly (53.8 vs 51.9 points; P=.20). Two serious adverse events occurred in the rehabilitation group (AF during exercise; a death unrelated to rehabilitation) versus one in usual care (death unrelated to intervention) (P=.56). Non-serious adverse events: 16 patients versus 7 (P=.047).
