shelves.title: After heart valve surgery: rehabilitation improved physical capacity, not mental health (CopenHeartVR)
shelves.question: After heart valve surgery, does comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation improve physical capacity and mental health versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Aged · Cardiac Rehabilitation · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Denmark · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice · Heart Valve Diseases · Heart Valves · Humans · Male · Mental Health · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption · Patient Compliance · Patient Education as Topic · Recovery of Function · Self Report · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — one small trial, the same shape as its post-ablation sibling. CopenHeartVR randomised 147 patients after heart valve surgery (aortic 62%, mitral 36%; mean age 62; 76% men) to 12 weeks of exercise training plus monthly psychoeducational consultations, or usual care without structured exercise. Peak VO2 at 4 months was higher with rehabilitation (24.8 vs 22.5 mL/kg/min; P=0.045) — a smaller, borderline effect than in CopenHeartRFA. The SF-36 Mental Component Scale at 6 months did not differ (53.7 vs 55.2 points; P=0.40), and other exercise-capacity and self-reported outcomes were not improved. Self-reported non-serious adverse events were more frequent with rehabilitation (11 of 72 vs 3 of 75; P=0.02). The authors state further research is needed to justify rehabilitation in this group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a modest fitness gain is the demonstrated benefit; recommendations for post-valve rehabilitation currently rest on extrapolation from ischaemic-heart-disease populations, as the trial's introduction notes.

cards.headline: CopenHeartVR 2016: peak VO2 24.8 vs 22.5 mL/kg/min at 4 months (P=0.045); mental component 53.7 vs 55.2 (P=0.40)
cards.summary: CopenHeartVR 2016: peak VO2 24.8 vs 22.5 mL/kg/min at 4 months (P=0.045); mental component 53.7 vs 55.2 (P=0.40)
cards.people: 147 patients after heart valve surgery (76% men; mean age 62; aortic 62%, mitral 36%, tricuspid/pulmonary 2%), randomised 1:1 to 12 weeks of cardiac rehabilitation (physical exercise plus monthly psycho-educational consultations) or usual care without structured physical exercise or consultations. Primary outcome: physical capacity (peak VO2). Secondary: self-reported mental health (Short Form-36).
cards.result: Peak VO2 at 4 months was 24.8 mL/kg/min with rehabilitation versus 22.5 with control (P=0.045). The SF-36 Mental Component Scale at 6 months did not differ (53.7 vs 55.2 points; P=0.40), nor did exploratory physical and mental outcomes. Self-reported non-serious adverse events were more frequent in the rehabilitation group (11 of 72 vs 3 of 75 patients; P=0.02). The authors conclude rehabilitation significantly improves peak VO2 at 4 months but has no effect on mental health, and that further research is needed to justify rehabilitation after valve surgery.
cards.watchOut: P=0.045 on the primary endpoint in 147 patients is a fragile significance; treat the effect as real-but-modest rather than established. Valve-surgery patients are older and more comorbid than the trial's mean suggests in many centres.

shelves.title: Varenicline started in hospital after acute coronary syndrome improved smoking abstinence (EVITA)
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised with acute coronary syndrome who smoke, does varenicline started in hospital improve abstinence at 24 weeks, and is it safe in this setting?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nicotinic Agonists · Smoking Cessation · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Varenicline
shelves.balance: THIN — one trial, but double-blind and placebo-controlled with biochemically validated abstinence, in exactly the teachable-moment population. EVITA randomised 302 smokers hospitalised with ACS (mean age 55; 75% men; 56% STEMI; mean 21 cigarettes/day for 36 years) to varenicline or placebo for 12 weeks, started in hospital, with low-intensity counselling for all. At 24 weeks, point-prevalence abstinence (7-day recall plus expired carbon monoxide validation) was 47.3% on varenicline versus 32.5% on placebo (P=0.012; number needed to treat 6.8). Continuous abstinence was 35.8% versus 25.8% (P=0.081) and at least halving daily consumption 67.4% versus 55.6% (P=0.05). Safety within 30 days of drug discontinuation was similar: serious adverse events 11.9% versus 11.3%; major adverse cardiovascular events 4.0% versus 4.6%. The authors note future studies are needed to establish safety in this population — the trial is far too small for rare-harm questions, which sit in the broader varenicline safety literature. PROPOSED LIKELY for the abstinence claim, which is the claim the trial was powered for.

cards.people: 302 smokers hospitalised with acute coronary syndrome (mean age 55 ± 9 years; 75% male; 56% STEMI, 38% NSTEMI, 6% unstable angina; mean 21 ± 11 cigarettes/day, 36 ± 12 years of smoking), randomised at multiple centres to varenicline or placebo for 12 weeks beginning in hospital; all received low-intensity counselling. Primary endpoint: point-prevalence smoking abstinence at 24 weeks by 7-day recall with expired-carbon-monoxide validation.
cards.result: Point-prevalence abstinence at 24 weeks: 47.3% in the varenicline group versus 32.5% on placebo (P=0.012; number needed to treat 6.8). Continuous abstinence: 35.8% versus 25.8% (P=0.081; NNT 10.0). Reduction of at least 50% in daily cigarette consumption: 67.4% versus 55.6% (P=0.05; NNT 8.5). Adverse events within 30 days of study-drug discontinuation were similar (serious adverse events 11.9% vs 11.3%; major adverse cardiovascular events 4.0% vs 4.6%).
cards.watchOut: 302 patients cannot settle the historical neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular safety debate around varenicline — this shelf claims abstinence efficacy and reports the observed event rates, nothing more. Abstinence was point-prevalence at 24 weeks; relapse beyond that horizon is the known pattern for all cessation pharmacotherapy.

shelves.title: After MI: treating depression and low social support improved mood and support — but not survival or reinfarction (ENRICHD)
shelves.question: In patients after myocardial infarction who are depressed or socially isolated, does cognitive behaviour therapy (with an SSRI when needed) reduce death or recurrent MI?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Antidepressive Agents · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Depression · Depressive Disorder · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morbidity · Myocardial Infarction · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Factors · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Social Support · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: The definitive trial of a beloved hypothesis — and the hypothesis lost. ENRICHD randomised 2,481 patients within 28 days of MI who had depression, low perceived social support, or both, at 8 centres to usual care or a cognitive behaviour therapy programme (median 11 individual sessions over 6 months, group therapy when feasible, plus an SSRI for severe or non-responding depression). The psychosocial targets moved: depression scores improved more with intervention (Hamilton change −10.1 vs −8.4; P<.001) and social support improved more (+5.1 vs +3.4; P<.001) — though usual-care patients also improved substantially, narrowing the gap. The clinical endpoint did not move at all: event-free survival (death or recurrent MI) over an average 29 months was 75.8% with intervention versus 75.9% with usual care, with no difference in any of the three risk groups. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C): treat post-MI depression because depression is worth treating — Shelves #2289 covers the drug evidence — but do not promise patients it will keep them alive or out of hospital. Depression after MI remains a risk marker; ENRICHD shows it is not, via this route, a modifiable cause of events.

cards.headline: ENRICHD 2003: event-free survival 75.8% (intervention) vs 75.9% (usual care) at 29 months — no difference; depression and support scores improved
cards.summary: ENRICHD 2003: event-free survival 75.8% (intervention) vs 75.9% (usual care) at 29 months — no difference; depression and support scores improved
cards.people: 2,481 patients (1,084 women, 1,397 men) enrolled within 28 days of MI at 8 clinical centres (1996–2001) with major or minor depression, low perceived social support (LPSS), or both, randomised to usual medical care or a CBT-based psychosocial intervention (median 11 sessions over 6 months, initiated a median of 17 days post-MI; group therapy when feasible; SSRI added for Hamilton score above 24 or inadequate early response). Primary endpoint: composite of death or recurrent MI; secondaries included 6-month change in Hamilton depression (HRSD) and social support (ESSI) scores.
cards.result: Psychosocial outcomes at 6 months favoured intervention: mean HRSD change −10.1 (SD 7.8) versus −8.4 (7.7) (P<.001); mean ESSI change +5.1 (5.9) versus +3.4 (6.0) (P<.001) — a smaller relative advantage than expected because usual-care patients also improved substantially. After average follow-up of 29 months there was no significant difference in event-free survival between usual care (75.9%) and intervention (75.8%), and no survival difference in any of the three psychosocial risk groups. The authors conclude the intervention improved depression and social isolation but did not increase event-free survival.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was CBT-first with SSRI only for a subset — ENRICHD does not test antidepressant pharmacotherapy itself (see Shelf #2289). A null this size (2,481 patients, near-identical survival curves) is not a power problem; it is an answer.

shelves.title: Depression in coronary disease: sertraline and citalopram are effective and cardiac-safe; adding interpersonal psychotherapy was not (SADHART + CREATE)
shelves.question: In patients with coronary disease and major depression, do SSRIs relieve depression without cardiac harm — and does short-term psychotherapy add anything?
shelves.mesh: Angina, Unstable · Major Depressive Disorder · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Sertraline · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Citalopram · Coronary Artery Disease · Psychotherapy, Brief
shelves.balance: The two foundational randomised trials answer the safety question first, the efficacy question second. SADHART (369 patients hospitalised with MI or unstable angina and major depression; sertraline 50–200 mg/day versus placebo for 24 weeks) was designed as a safety trial: left ventricular ejection fraction did not change (54% to 54% on sertraline; 52% to 53% on placebo), and ventricular ectopy runs, QTc prolongation, and other cardiac measures did not differ; severe cardiovascular adverse events were numerically fewer on sertraline (14.5% vs 22.4%, not significant). Efficacy favoured sertraline on the global-impression measure (responders 67% vs 53%; P=.01), decisively in patients with recurrent or more severe depression (78% vs 45%; P=.001), while the overall Hamilton difference was not significant (P=.14). CREATE (284 patients with coronary disease and major depression, 2×2 factorial) found citalopram superior to placebo on depression scores (Hamilton difference 3.3 points; P=.005; response 52.8% vs 40.1%; remission 35.9% vs 22.5%), while interpersonal psychotherapy added nothing over clinical management alone — the difference numerically favoured management alone (−2.26 points; P=.06). PROPOSED LIKELY: in coronary patients, treat major depression with an SSRI (sertraline or citalopram) plus good clinical management; expect symptom relief, not event reduction (Shelf #2288), and do not count on a brief psychotherapy add-on.

cards.headline: SADHART 2002: sertraline left ejection fraction unchanged (54% to 54%) and showed no cardiac safety signal; global response 67% vs 53%
cards.summary: SADHART 2002: sertraline left ejection fraction unchanged (54% to 54%) and showed no cardiac safety signal; global response 67% vs 53%
cards.people: 369 patients with major depressive disorder hospitalised for acute MI (74%) or unstable angina (26%) at 40 centres internationally (mean age 57.1; 64% men; mean Hamilton 19.6), randomised after a 2-week placebo run-in to sertraline 50–200 mg/day (186) or placebo (183) for 24 weeks. Primary (safety) outcome: change in left ventricular ejection fraction; secondaries included ventricular premature complex runs, QTc, cardiovascular adverse events, Hamilton (HAM-D) scores, and Clinical Global Impression Improvement (CGI-I).
cards.result: LVEF: sertraline 54% at baseline and 54% at week 16; placebo 52% and 53% — no significant effect. Treatment-emergent VPC runs: 13.1% versus 12.9%; QTc above 450 ms at endpoint: 12% versus 13%; all cardiac comparisons nonsignificant. Severe cardiovascular adverse events: 14.5% (sertraline) versus 22.4% (placebo). CGI-I favoured sertraline in the total sample (P=.049; responders 67% vs 53%, P=.01), while HAM-D did not reach significance overall (P=.14); in the a priori more severe/recurrent subgroup both measures favoured sertraline (CGI-I responders 78% vs 45%, P=.001). The authors conclude sertraline is a safe and effective treatment for recurrent depression after recent MI or unstable angina.
cards.watchOut: Designed and powered for safety, not for cardiac events — the favourable severe-event split (14.5% vs 22.4%) is hypothesis-generating only. Patients with other life-threatening conditions were excluded.
cards.source: Glassman AH et al. Sertraline treatment of major depression in patients with acute MI or unstable angina. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12169073. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. cards.headline: CREATE 2007: citalopram beat placebo (Hamilton difference 3.3 points; remission 35.9% vs 22.5%); interpersonal psychotherapy added nothing over clinical management
cards.summary: CREATE 2007: citalopram beat placebo (Hamilton difference 3.3 points; remission 35.9% vs 22.5%); interpersonal psychotherapy added nothing over clinical management
cards.people: 284 patients with coronary artery disease and major depression (24-item Hamilton at least 20) at 9 Canadian academic centres, randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to citalopram 20–40 mg/day or placebo for 12 weeks, and independently to 12 weekly sessions of interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) plus clinical management or clinical management alone. Primary outcome: change in 24-item Hamilton score at 12 weeks, assessed blindly by telephone interview.
cards.result: Citalopram was superior to placebo: mean Hamilton difference 3.3 points (96.7% CI 0.80 to 5.85; P=.005; effect size 0.33); response 52.8% versus 40.1% (P=.03); remission 35.9% versus 22.5% (P=.01); self-reported BDI-II also favoured citalopram (difference 3.6 points; P=.005). IPT showed no benefit over clinical management: the Hamilton difference favoured clinical management (−2.26 points; 96.7% CI −4.78 to 0.27; P=.06). The authors recommend citalopram or sertraline plus clinical management as first-step treatment for depression in coronary disease.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, symptom endpoints only — CREATE says nothing about cardiac events. The IPT null is consistent with ENRICHD (Shelf #2288): structured psychosocial add-ons keep failing to beat good clinical management in this population.
cards.source: Lesperance F et al. shelves.title: Tai chi in systolic heart failure: quality of life, mood, and confidence improved — exercise capacity did not, in the larger trial (Yeh trials)
shelves.question: In chronic systolic heart failure, does a 12-week tai chi programme improve quality of life and exercise capacity compared with education or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Affect · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers · Comorbidity · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption · Patient Compliance · Quality of Life · Self Efficacy · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Volume · Tai Ji · Treatment Outcome · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Norepinephrine · Cardiovascular Agents · Chronic Disease
shelves.balance: Two trials from the same programme, and their disagreement is the lesson. The small first trial (30 patients, ejection fraction 40% or less, tai chi twice weekly for 12 weeks added to usual care) reported large gains: quality-of-life scores improved by a mean between-group difference of −25 points (P=0.001), 6-minute walk distance by 135 metres (P=0.001), and B-type natriuretic peptide fell (−138 pg/mL; P=0.03). The larger, multisite, single-blind trial (100 outpatients, NYHA class I–III, ejection fraction 40% or less; group tai chi versus time-matched education) did NOT replicate the capacity findings: change in 6-minute walk distance (median +35 vs +2 metres; P=.95) and peak oxygen uptake (+1.1 vs −0.5 mL/kg/min; P=.81) were not significantly different. But the patient-reported benefits held up: Minnesota Living With Heart Failure scores improved more with tai chi (median change −19 vs +1; P=.02), as did exercise self-efficacy (P<.001) and mood (P=.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: offer tai chi to heart-failure patients for how they feel and function day to day — quality of life, mood, confidence to exercise — not as a proven way to raise walk distance or peak VO2; the big trial's null governs the capacity claim, and small-trial effect sizes should be discounted accordingly.

cards.headline: Yeh 2011 (n=100): quality of life, self-efficacy, and mood improved (P=.02, <.001, .01); 6-minute walk and peak VO2 did not (P=.95, P=.81)
cards.summary: Yeh 2011 (n=100): quality of life, self-efficacy, and mood improved (P=.02, <.001, .01); 6-minute walk and peak VO2 did not (P=.95, P=.81)
cards.people: 100 outpatients with systolic heart failure (NYHA class I–III, ejection fraction at most 40%; mean age 67; mean ejection fraction 29%; baseline peak VO2 13.5 mL/kg/min) randomised to a group-based 12-week tai chi programme (50) or time-matched education (50). Outcomes: 6-minute walk test, peak oxygen uptake, and Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ).
cards.result: No significant between-group differences in change in 6-minute walk distance (median change 35 [IQR −2 to 51] vs 2 [−7 to 54] metres; P=.95) or peak VO2 (1.1 [−1.1 to 1.5] vs −0.5 [−1.2 to 1.8] mL/kg/min; P=.81). Quality of life improved more with tai chi (MLHFQ median change −19 [−23 to −3] vs 1 [−16 to 3]; P=.02), as did exercise self-efficacy (P<.001) and total mood disturbance (−6 vs −1; P=.01). The authors conclude tai chi may improve quality of life, mood, and exercise self-efficacy in heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported endpoints in a single-blind trial of an enjoyable group activity carry attention and expectation effects the education control only partly matches — but those outcomes are the claim here, and they were prespecified.
cards.source: Yeh GY et al. Tai chi exercise in patients with chronic heart failure: a randomized clinical trial. Arch Intern Med. 2011. PMID: 21518942. Registry ID: NCT00110227, from the record. cards.headline: Yeh 2004 (n=30): quality of life −25 points, walk distance +135 m, BNP −138 pg/mL — large effects the larger trial did not reproduce for capacity
cards.summary: Yeh 2004 (n=30): quality of life −25 points, walk distance +135 m, BNP −138 pg/mL — large effects the larger trial did not reproduce for capacity
cards.people: 30 patients with chronic stable heart failure and ejection fraction at most 40% (mean age 64; mean ejection fraction 23%; median NYHA class 2) randomised to usual care alone (15) or usual care plus 12 weeks of twice-weekly 1-hour tai chi classes (15). Primary outcomes: quality of life and exercise capacity; secondaries included B-type natriuretic peptide and catecholamines.
cards.result: At 12 weeks the tai chi group showed improved quality-of-life scores (mean between-group difference in change −25 points; P=0.001), increased 6-minute walk distance (135 metres; P=0.001), and decreased BNP (−138 pg/mL; P=0.03); a trend towards improved peak VO2; no difference in catecholamines. The authors describe tai chi as a beneficial adjunct for quality of life and functional capacity on standard therapy.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, three imputed control records, and effect sizes (135 m of walk distance) far larger than the subsequent 100-patient trial found — the classic small-trial pattern. Carded so the shelf shows both the promise and its correction.

shelves.question: In older adults after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, does an early home-based exercise programme (with or without a cognitive-behavioural intervention) improve disability and physical function versus telephone education?

shelves.balance: THIN — a 51-patient pilot whose primary purpose was feasibility, and the shelf credits it for exactly what a pilot can show. REHAB-TAVR randomised 51 patients after TAVR (mean age 83.9 years) to home-based exercise with a cognitive-behavioural intervention (18), home exercise alone (15), or telephone education (18). The exercise programme (balance, flexibility, strength, endurance) began within 7 days of discharge, delivered weekly by a physical therapist for 8 weeks; the behavioural arm added goal-setting, planning, and a weekly cash adherence incentive. Completion of at least 5 of 8 sessions: 83.3% with the behavioural package, 58.8% exercise alone, 52.6% education (P=0.196). At 8 weeks the combined exercise groups had lower disability scores than education (2.6 vs 4.5 on a 0–22 scale; P=0.042) and better Short Physical Performance Battery scores (9.5 vs 6.5; P=0.003); the behavioural arm's disability score was lower than exercise alone (2.1 vs 3.4; P=0.047). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: early home rehabilitation after TAVR is feasible in octogenarians and points toward preserved function; a powered trial is still owed before stronger language.

cards.headline: REHAB-TAVR 2025: disability 2.6 (exercise groups) vs 4.5 (education), P=0.042; physical performance 9.5 vs 6.5, P=0.003 — in 51 patients, mean age 84
cards.summary: REHAB-TAVR 2025: disability 2.6 (exercise groups) vs 4.5 (education), P=0.042; physical performance 9.5 vs 6.5, P=0.003 — in 51 patients, mean age 84
cards.people: 51 patients after TAVR (mean age 83.9 years; 19 women) randomised to home-based exercise plus cognitive-behavioural intervention (CBI) (18), home-based exercise alone (15), or telephone-based education control (18). Exercise — balance, flexibility, strength, endurance — began within 7 days post-discharge, once weekly with a physical therapist for 8 weeks; CBI added discussion of benefits and barriers, goal setting, exercise planning, and a weekly cash adherence incentive. Primary outcome: disability score (0–22) at 8 weeks; secondaries included the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB, 0–12) and feasibility (adherence, dropout).
cards.result: Session completion (at least 5 of 8): 15 participants (83.3%) in the exercise-plus-CBI group, 10 (58.8%) with exercise alone, 10 (52.6%) in education (P=0.196); two participants per group were lost to follow-up. At 8 weeks, the combined exercise groups had lower disability (mean 2.6 [SE 0.3] vs 4.5 [0.5]; P=0.042) and higher SPPB (9.5 [0.6] vs 6.5 [0.8]; P=0.003) than education; exercise-plus-CBI had lower disability than exercise alone (2.1 [0.4] vs 3.4 [0.5]; P=0.047), with no differences in self-efficacy or outcome expectations. The authors conclude the programme appears feasible and may prevent disability after TAVR.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 51 patients, 8 weeks, function endpoints — no power for clinical events, and the three-arm split leaves about 17 patients per arm. Cash incentives in the behavioural arm are part of the tested package, not a detail.
cards.source: Home-Based Rehabilitation After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (REHAB-TAVR): A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial. 2025. PMID: 40171799. Registry ID: NCT02805309, from the record. shelves.title: Waiting for bypass surgery: a prehabilitation programme shortened hospital stay by a day and improved quality of life (Arthur trial)
shelves.question: In low-risk patients waiting at least 10 weeks for elective CABG, does a multidimensional preoperative programme (exercise, education, nurse support) improve postoperative length of stay and recovery?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety · Canada · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Disease · Critical Care · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Patient Compliance · Patient Education as Topic · Preoperative Care · Quality of Life · Risk Factors · Social Support · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a quarter-century old, in a health system whose waiting lists made the experiment possible. Arthur and colleagues randomised 249 low-risk patients awaiting elective CABG (surgery at least 10 weeks away) at an Ontario centre to a preoperative intervention — exercise training twice weekly, education and reinforcement, and monthly nurse-initiated telephone support during the wait — or usual waiting-list care; all patients were offered cardiac rehabilitation after surgery. The intervention group spent 1 less day in hospital overall (P=0.002) and less time in intensive care (P=0.001), had better quality of life during the waiting period, and the quality-of-life advantage persisted to 6 months after surgery. Mortality did not differ (the trial was far too small to test it). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the waiting period is usable time — structured prehabilitation bought a shorter stay and better recovery experience in the one trial that tested it. Modern fast-track pathways may compress the room for this gain; the trial's population was explicitly low-risk.

cards.headline: Arthur 2000: preoperative intervention — 1 day less in hospital (P=0.002), less ICU time (P=0.001), better quality of life before surgery and at 6 months
cards.summary: Arthur 2000: preoperative intervention — 1 day less in hospital (P=0.002), less ICU time (P=0.001), better quality of life before surgery and at 6 months
cards.people: 249 low-risk patients on a waiting list for elective CABG at a regional cardiovascular surgery centre in southwestern Ontario, Canada, whose surgery was scheduled at least 10 weeks from recruitment. The intervention group received exercise training twice per week, education and reinforcement, and monthly nurse-initiated telephone calls during the waiting period; after surgery, cardiac rehabilitation was offered to all patients. Primary outcome: postoperative length of stay; secondaries included exercise performance, health-related quality of life, social support, anxiety, and health-care utilisation.
cards.result: Length of stay differed significantly: the intervention group spent 1 less day in hospital overall (95% CI 0.0 to 1.0 day; P=0.002) and less time in the intensive care unit (median difference 2.1 hours; P=0.001). Quality of life was better in the intervention group during the waiting period and the improvement continued to 6 months after surgery. Mortality rates did not differ between groups. The authors conclude the waiting period can be used to enhance in-hospital and early-phase recovery.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, year-2000 practice, low-risk elective patients with long waits — the three conditions of the result. Pre-registration era: no registry ID exists, legitimately. Do not cite for mortality in either direction.
cards.source: Arthur HM et al. Effect of a preoperative intervention on preoperative and postoperative outcomes in low-risk patients awaiting elective coronary artery bypass graft surgery. A randomized, controlled trial. Ann Intern Med. 2000. PMID: 10929164. Registry ID: none (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: ICD programming: higher rate thresholds and longer delays cut inappropriate therapy by about 80% — and mortality in MADIT-RIT (MADIT-RIT + ADVANCE III)
shelves.question: In patients with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, does programming therapy to higher heart rates or longer detection times reduce inappropriate pacing and shocks without costing safety?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Defibrillators, Implantable · Equipment Design · Equipment Failure · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Tachycardia · Time Factors · Algorithms · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Electric Countershock · Hospitalization · Myocardial Ischemia · Primary Prevention · Quality of Life · Secondary Prevention · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two large randomised programming trials with the same message: most ICD therapy treats rhythms that would have stopped on their own, and patience is therapeutic. MADIT-RIT randomised 1,500 primary-prevention patients to conventional programming, high-rate therapy (treat only at 200 beats/min or above, after a 2.5-second delay), or delayed therapy (long delays at lower rates). Over an average 1.4 years, first inappropriate therapy fell by roughly four-fifths with either strategy (hazard ratio 0.21 for high-rate, 0.24 for delayed, versus conventional) — and all-cause mortality fell too: hazard ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.85; P=0.01) for high-rate and 0.56 (0.30 to 1.02; P=0.06) for delayed, with no difference in procedure-related adverse events. ADVANCE III (1,902 primary and secondary prevention patients) tested a long detection interval (30 of 40 beats versus 18 of 24): total delivered therapies fell from 67 to 42 per 100 person-years (incident rate ratio 0.63; P<.001), inappropriate shocks fell (first occurrence 5.1 vs 11.6 per 100 patient-years; IRR 0.55; P=.008), while mortality (HR 0.87; P=.50) and arrhythmic syncope (IRR 1.60; P=.22) did not differ significantly. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): conservative programming — treat fast, or treat late — is one of the few device decisions with randomised mortality support; the absence of a syncope penalty in ADVANCE III answers the obvious safety worry.

cards.headline: MADIT-RIT 2012: inappropriate therapy HR 0.21 (high-rate) and 0.24 (delayed) vs conventional; mortality HR 0.45 (P=0.01) and 0.56 (P=0.06)
cards.summary: MADIT-RIT 2012: inappropriate therapy HR 0.21 (high-rate) and 0.24 (delayed) vs conventional; mortality HR 0.45 (P=0.01) and 0.56 (P=0.06)
cards.people: 1,500 patients with a primary-prevention ICD indication, randomised to one of three programming configurations: conventional (2.5-second delay at 170–199 beats/min, 1.0-second delay at 200 or above), high-rate therapy (2.5-second delay only at 200 beats/min or above), or delayed therapy (60-second delay at 170–199, 12-second delay at 200–249, 2.5-second delay at 250 or above). Primary objective: first occurrence of inappropriate antitachycardia pacing or shock; average follow-up 1.4 years.
cards.result: High-rate and delayed programming each reduced first inappropriate therapy versus conventional (hazard ratio 0.21; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.34; P<0.001; and 0.24; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.40; P<0.001). All-cause mortality was also reduced: hazard ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.85; P=0.01) with high-rate therapy and 0.56 (95% CI 0.30 to 1.02; P=0.06) with delayed therapy. There were no significant differences in procedure-related adverse events among the three groups.
cards.watchOut: A programming trial, not a device-versus-no-device trial; the mortality finding, while prespecified as a secondary outcome and consistent across both conservative arms, rests on modest event counts. Funded by the device manufacturer (Boston Scientific), as the abstract discloses.
cards.source: Moss AJ et al. Reduction in inappropriate therapy and mortality through ICD programming. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 23131066. Registry ID: NCT00947310, from the record. cards.headline: ADVANCE III 2013: long detection cut total therapies to 42 vs 67 per 100 person-years (IRR 0.63) and inappropriate shocks by nearly half; mortality and syncope unchanged
cards.summary: ADVANCE III 2013: long detection cut total therapies to 42 vs 67 per 100 person-years (IRR 0.63) and inappropriate shocks by nearly half; mortality and syncope unchanged
cards.people: 1,902 patients receiving a first ICD for primary (75%) or secondary prevention (mean age 65; 84% men; ischaemic and non-ischaemic) at 94 international centres, randomised to long-detection programming (30 of 40 intervals to detect ventricular tachyarrhythmias; 948) or standard detection (18 of 24; 954). Primary outcomes: total antitachycardia pacing (ATP) and shocks delivered; secondaries included inappropriate shocks, mortality, and syncope. Median follow-up 12 months.
cards.result: The long-detection group received 346 therapies (42 per 100 person-years; 95% CI 38 to 47) versus 557 (67 per 100 person-years; 95% CI 62 to 73) with standard detection (incident rate ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.78; P<.001): ATP 23 versus 37 per 100 person-years (IRR 0.58; P<.001) and shocks 19 versus 30 (IRR 0.77; P=.06). First inappropriate shock: 5.1 versus 11.6 per 100 patient-years (IRR 0.55; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.85; P=.008). Mortality (5.5 vs 6.3 per 100 patient-years; HR 0.87; P=.50) and arrhythmic syncope (3.1 vs 1.9 per 100 patient-years; IRR 1.60; P=.22) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The syncope point estimate leans the wrong way (IRR 1.60) on few events — the interval (0.76 to 3.41) cannot exclude a real increase, so 'no syncope penalty proven' is the accurate wording, and the shelf's balance says 'did not differ significantly', nothing stronger.

shelves.title: Remote monitoring of implanted devices: faster evaluation and fewer visits — outcome benefits inconsistent (IN-TIME + TRUST + REM-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure and an implanted defibrillator or resynchronisation device, does automatic remote monitoring improve clinical outcomes, or mainly logistics?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Australia · Defibrillators, Implantable · Europe · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Israel · Male · Monitoring, Ambulatory · Telemedicine · Treatment Outcome · Automation · Coronary Disease · Safety · Stroke Volume · Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Devices · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Remote Consultation
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials, three different answers — because they tested three different intensities of monitoring. TRUST (1,339 ICD patients) tested logistics and won clearly: automatic daily home monitoring cut in-hospital device evaluations by 45%, handled 85.8% of mid-year follow-ups remotely, and cut median time from an arrhythmic event to physician evaluation from 36 days to under 2 days (P<0.001), with no morbidity penalty. IN-TIME (664 heart-failure patients, ejection fraction at most 35%, recent ICD or CRT-D) tested one manufacturer's daily multiparameter telemonitoring with a clinical response pathway: the composite clinical score (death, heart-failure hospitalisation, NYHA change, patient self-assessment) worsened in fewer monitored patients (18.9% vs 27.2%; odds ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90; P=0.013), and deaths were 10 versus 27 — a striking secondary split the trial was not powered to confirm. REM-HF (1,650 heart-failure patients with devices in England; weekly downloads with formalised follow-up) then found nothing: death or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation 42.4% versus 40.8% (hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.18; P=0.87), and no secondary endpoint differed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): adopt remote monitoring for what is proven — faster event detection, fewer routine visits — and treat outcome benefit as possible but unestablished, likely dependent on what the monitoring centre does with the data.

cards.headline: IN-TIME 2014: worsened composite clinical score 18.9% (telemonitoring) vs 27.2% (control), OR 0.63, P=0.013; deaths 10 vs 27
cards.summary: IN-TIME 2014: worsened composite clinical score 18.9% (telemonitoring) vs 27.2% (control), OR 0.63, P=0.013; deaths 10 vs 27
cards.people: 664 patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–III, ejection fraction at most 35%, optimal drug therapy, no permanent AF) with a recent dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D implant at 36 centres in Australia, Europe, and Israel, randomised after a 1-month run-in to automatic daily implant-based multiparameter telemonitoring plus standard care (333) or standard care alone (331). Mean age 65.5 years; mean ejection fraction 26%; 58.7% received CRT-D. Primary outcome at 1 year: a composite clinical score (all-cause death, overnight heart-failure admission, NYHA class change, patient global self-assessment).
cards.result: At 1 year, 63 of 333 telemonitoring patients (18.9%) versus 90 of 331 controls (27.2%) had a worsened composite score (P=0.013; odds ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90). Ten patients in the telemonitoring group versus 27 in the control group died during follow-up. The authors conclude daily multiparameter telemonitoring can significantly improve clinical outcomes in heart failure and is feasible for clinical practice. The trial was funded by the device manufacturer (Biotronik).
cards.watchOut: The mortality split (10 vs 27) is a secondary observation inside a composite-score primary endpoint — treat it as a signal, not a finding. Single-manufacturer system with a staffed response pathway; the intervention is the pathway as much as the data feed (contrast REM-HF below).

cards.headline: TRUST 2010: home monitoring cut in-hospital evaluations by 45% and time-to-evaluation from 36 days to under 2 — morbidity unchanged
cards.summary: TRUST 2010: home monitoring cut in-hospital evaluations by 45% and time-to-evaluation from 36 days to under 2 — morbidity unchanged
cards.people: 1,339 ICD patients randomised 2:1 to automatic daily home monitoring (HM) or conventional in-office follow-up, with checks at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 months (HM patients used remote checks at 6, 9, and 12 months, with office visits only if needed). Mean age about 64; ejection fraction about 29%; 72–74% primary prevention. Outcomes: scheduled and unscheduled evaluations, morbidity, and time from event occurrence to physician evaluation.
cards.result: HM reduced total in-hospital device evaluations by 45% without affecting morbidity. In the HM group, 85.8% of all 6-, 9-, and 12-month follow-ups were performed remotely only. Median time to evaluation was under 2 days with HM versus 36 days with conventional follow-up (P<0.001) for all arrhythmic events. The authors conclude HM is safe and enables more rapid detection of actionable events than conventional monitoring.
cards.watchOut: A logistics and safety trial by design — no outcome hypothesis was tested, so TRUST must not be cited for clinical benefit. Its MeSH record contains indexing artefacts (e.g., 'Apoptosis'); MeSH on this card is trimmed to the relevant terms.

cards.headline: REM-HF 2017: 1,650 patients — death or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation 42.4% vs 40.8% (HR 1.01); no endpoint differed
cards.summary: REM-HF 2017: 1,650 patients — death or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation 42.4% vs 40.8% (HR 1.01); no endpoint differed
cards.people: 1,650 patients with heart failure and a cardiac implanted electronic device at nine centres in England, randomised (2011–2014) to active remote monitoring (weekly downloads with formalised remote follow-up protocols) or usual care. Mean age 70 years; 86% men; median follow-up 2.8 years. Primary endpoint: first event of death from any cause or unplanned hospitalisation for cardiovascular reasons.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 42.4% of the active-monitoring group and 40.8% of the usual-care group (hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.18; P=0.87). No secondary endpoint — all-cause death, cardiovascular death, or unplanned hospitalisation — differed significantly. Adherence was high (dropout 4.3%). The authors conclude remote monitoring with weekly downloads and a formalised follow-up approach does not improve outcomes in this population.
cards.watchOut: REM-HF used weekly downloads across manufacturers, not daily multiparameter alerts — its null constrains low-intensity monitoring most directly. It is the largest of the three trials and the only one powered as a pure outcome trial.

shelves.title: AV block with a weak ventricle: biventricular pacing beat right-ventricular pacing on death, heart-failure care, and remodelling (BLOCK HF)
shelves.question: In patients with atrioventricular block, heart failure (NYHA I–III), and ejection fraction of 50% or less who need pacing, does biventricular pacing beat standard right-ventricular pacing?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrioventricular Block · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Defibrillators, Implantable · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Heart Failure, Systolic · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Pacemaker, Artificial · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The trial that extended resynchronisation beyond wide-QRS heart failure to the pacing population itself. BLOCK HF enrolled patients with AV block and an indication for pacing, NYHA class I–III heart failure, and ejection fraction of 50% or less; all received a CRT pacemaker or defibrillator and were randomised to biventricular or standard right-ventricular pacing (691 randomised of 918 enrolled; average follow-up 37 months). The primary outcome — death from any cause, an urgent-care heart-failure visit requiring intravenous therapy, or a 15% or greater increase in left ventricular end-systolic volume index — occurred in 45.8% with biventricular pacing versus 55.6% with right-ventricular pacing (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% credible interval 0.60 to 0.90), with consistent results in the pacemaker and defibrillator subgroups. Left-ventricular lead complications occurred in 6.4% — the price of the extra lead. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): when a patient with AV block and a reduced ejection fraction needs a device, pace both ventricles from the start rather than creating the dyssynchrony that heavy right-ventricular pacing causes. Note the composite leans partly on the remodelling component — the shelf reports the components' nature honestly rather than claiming a pure mortality result.

cards.headline: BLOCK HF 2013: primary outcome 45.8% (biventricular) vs 55.6% (right-ventricular) — HR 0.74; LV lead complications 6.4%
cards.summary: BLOCK HF 2013: primary outcome 45.8% (biventricular) vs 55.6% (right-ventricular) — HR 0.74; LV lead complications 6.4%
cards.people: 918 patients enrolled with AV block and a pacing indication, NYHA class I, II, or III heart failure, and left ventricular ejection fraction of 50% or less; 691 underwent randomisation to biventricular pacing or standard right-ventricular pacing via an implanted CRT pacemaker or ICD (ICD when defibrillation was indicated) and were followed for an average of 37 months. Primary outcome: time to death from any cause, an urgent-care visit for heart failure requiring intravenous therapy, or an increase of at least 15% in the left ventricular end-systolic volume index.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 160 of 349 patients (45.8%) in the biventricular-pacing group versus 190 of 342 (55.6%) in the right-ventricular-pacing group; biventricular pacing was associated with a significantly lower incidence over time (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% credible interval 0.60 to 0.90), with similar results in the pacemaker and ICD subgroups. Left ventricular lead-related complications occurred in 6.4% of patients. The authors conclude biventricular pacing was superior to conventional right-ventricular pacing in this population. Funded by Medtronic.
cards.watchOut: The composite includes a remodelling endpoint (end-systolic volume index) that favours resynchronisation by design; the trial does not report the death component separately in its abstract, so do not quote a mortality figure from this shelf. Bayesian analysis (credible interval) as designed.

shelves.title: Failing on right-ventricular pacing: upgrading to CRT-D cut death or heart-failure hospitalisation from 32% to 10% (BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade)
shelves.question: In heart-failure patients with reduced ejection fraction, a high right-ventricular pacing burden, and a wide paced QRS, does upgrading to cardiac resynchronisation therapy with defibrillator beat continuing with an ICD?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Heart Failure · Male · Female · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Aged · Defibrillators, Implantable · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Middle Aged · Hospitalization
shelves.balance: The largest effect size in the devices literature this year — read it with its composite in view. BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade randomised 360 symptomatic HFrEF patients (NYHA class II–IVa) with an existing pacemaker or ICD, right-ventricular pacing burden of at least 20%, and paced QRS of at least 150 ms, to CRT-D upgrade (215) or ICD (145). The primary outcome — all-cause mortality, heart-failure hospitalisation, or failure to reduce left ventricular end-systolic volume by at least 15% at 12 months — occurred in 32.4% of the CRT-D group versus 78.9% of the ICD group (odds ratio 0.11; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.19; P<.001). That composite is dominated by the remodelling term (most unchanged ventricles 'fail' it), so the clinically decisive figure is the hard secondary: death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 10% versus 32% (hazard ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.47; P<.001). Procedure- or device-related complications were similar (12.3% vs 7.8%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): in a paced patient whose ventricle has failed under a heavy right-ventricular burden, upgrade to resynchronisation — the hard-endpoint separation is too large to be a remodelling artefact. The shelf quotes both numbers so readers can weight them.

cards.headline: BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade 2023: primary composite 32.4% vs 78.9% (OR 0.11); death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10% vs 32% (HR 0.27)
cards.summary: BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade 2023: primary composite 32.4% vs 78.9% (OR 0.11); death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10% vs 32% (HR 0.27)
cards.people: 360 symptomatic HFrEF patients (NYHA class II–IVa) with a pacemaker or ICD, right-ventricular pacing burden of at least 20%, and paced QRS duration of at least 150 ms, randomised 3:2 at multiple centres to CRT-D upgrade (215) or ICD (145). Primary outcome: composite of all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalisation, or less than 15% reduction in left ventricular end-systolic volume at 12 months (assessed in 179 and 128 patients respectively); secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalisation. Median follow-up 12.4 months.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 58 of 179 patients (32.4%) in the CRT-D arm versus 101 of 128 (78.9%) in the ICD arm (odds ratio 0.11; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.19; P<.001). All-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalisation occurred in 22 of 215 (10%) versus 46 of 145 (32%) (hazard ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.47; P<.001). Procedure- or device-related complications were similar (25 of 211 [12.3%] vs 11 of 142 [7.8%]). The authors conclude CRT-D upgrade reduced the combined risk of mortality, heart-failure hospitalisation, and absence of reverse remodelling in this population.
cards.watchOut: The 78.9% control rate on the primary composite is mostly failure-to-remodel, an endpoint resynchronisation is mechanically favoured to win; the HR 0.27 hard-endpoint result is the figure to cite. One-year median follow-up; registry ID was not printed in the fetched record and is recorded as none rather than reconstructed.

shelves.title: Dual-chamber versus single-chamber pacing: no survival or stroke advantage across three large trials — atrial fibrillation modestly reduced (MOST + UKPACE + CTOPP)
shelves.question: Does dual-chamber (physiological) pacing beat single-chamber ventricular pacing on death and stroke in sinus-node dysfunction and AV block?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arrhythmia, Sinus · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Pacemaker, Artificial · Quality of Life · Stroke · Stroke Volume · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiovascular Diseases · Heart Block · Incidence · Risk · Bradycardia · Canada · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Six and a half thousand randomised patients across three trials, one consistent answer: the 'physiological' device does not keep people alive or prevent strokes. MOST (2,010 patients with sinus-node dysfunction; median 33.1 months) found death or nonfatal stroke in 21.5% with dual-chamber versus 23.0% with ventricular pacing (P=0.48), while atrial fibrillation was less frequent with dual-chamber pacing (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.008), heart-failure scores were better, and quality of life slightly higher. UKPACE (2,021 patients aged 70 or older with high-grade AV block; median 4.6 years for mortality) found annual mortality of 7.4% versus 7.2% (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11) and no differences in atrial fibrillation, heart failure, or thromboembolism — notably, the AF advantage did not replicate in this AV-block population. CTOPP's extended follow-up (2,568 patients; mean 6.4 years) closed the 'delayed benefit' question: no difference in cardiovascular death or stroke, total mortality, or stroke, while the reduction in new atrial fibrillation with physiological pacing persisted (relative risk reduction 20.1%; 95% CI 5.4 to 32.5; P=0.009). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C): choose pacing mode for symptoms, pacemaker syndrome, and patient preference — not for survival. Where dual-chamber pacing earns its keep on symptoms sits in the individual trials above; the AF reduction is real but has never converted into fewer strokes.

cards.headline: MOST 2002: death or stroke 21.5% (dual-chamber) vs 23.0% (ventricular), P=0.48; atrial fibrillation HR 0.79 (P=0.008)
cards.summary: MOST 2002: death or stroke 21.5% (dual-chamber) vs 23.0% (ventricular), P=0.48; atrial fibrillation HR 0.79 (P=0.008)
cards.people: 2,010 patients with sinus-node dysfunction randomised to dual-chamber pacing (1,014) or ventricular pacing (996), followed for a median of 33.1 months. Primary endpoint: death from any cause or nonfatal stroke. Secondaries included the composite of death, stroke, or heart-failure hospitalisation; atrial fibrillation; heart-failure score; pacemaker syndrome; and quality of life.
cards.result: The primary endpoint did not differ significantly (21.5% dual-chamber vs 23.0% ventricular; P=0.48). Atrial fibrillation risk was lower with dual-chamber pacing (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.008) and heart-failure scores were better (P<0.001); differences in heart-failure hospitalisation and the death/stroke/heart-failure composite were not significant unadjusted and only marginally significant adjusted. Quality of life was slightly better with dual-chamber pacing. The authors conclude dual-chamber pacing does not improve stroke-free survival but reduces AF, heart-failure signs and symptoms, and slightly improves quality of life.

shelves.title: ICD patients who don't need pacing: routine dual-chamber pacing at 70/min caused harm versus backup pacing at 40/min (DAVID)
shelves.question: In ICD recipients with ejection fraction of 40% or less and no pacing indication, does dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing at 70/min beat minimal ventricular backup pacing at 40/min on death or heart-failure hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Aged · Amiodarone · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Anticoagulants · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Cardiovascular Agents · Catheter Ablation · Defibrillators, Implantable · Digoxin · Diuretics · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pacemaker, Artificial · Single-Blind Method · Survival Analysis · Tachycardia, Ventricular · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left · Warfarin
shelves.balance: The trial that taught device medicine that pacing itself is a drug with side effects. DAVID randomised 506 patients with standard ICD indications, ejection fraction of 40% or less, no indication for antibradycardia pacing, and no persistent atrial arrhythmias to have their dual-chamber devices programmed to dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing at 70/min (DDDR-70) or to ventricular backup pacing at 40/min (VVI-40). The trial was stopped early: one-year survival free of death or first heart-failure hospitalisation was 83.9% with backup pacing versus 73.3% with dual-chamber pacing (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 1.06 to 2.44). The components pointed the same way without individually reaching significance — mortality 6.5% versus 10.1% (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 0.84 to 3.09) and heart-failure hospitalisation 13.3% versus 22.6% (relative hazard 1.54; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.46). The mechanism is the unnecessary right-ventricular pacing that an active dual-chamber programme delivers to a ventricle that did not need it — dyssynchrony as iatrogenesis. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) (Tier C): in ICD patients without a pacing indication, program minimal ventricular pacing. The shelf closes the loop with MOST/UKPACE/CTOPP (Shelf #2297 — mode choice is neutral when pacing is needed) and with MADIT-RIT (Shelf #2293 — restraint in therapy programming): across all three, less unnecessary device activity is better.

cards.headline: DAVID 2002: one-year freedom from death or heart-failure hospitalisation 83.9% (backup VVI-40) vs 73.3% (DDDR-70) — relative hazard 1.61
cards.summary: DAVID 2002: one-year freedom from death or heart-failure hospitalisation 83.9% (backup VVI-40) vs 73.3% (DDDR-70) — relative hazard 1.61
cards.people: 506 patients with standard indications for ICD implantation at 37 US centres (2000–2002), all with left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less, no indication for antibradycardia pacing, and no persistent atrial arrhythmias; all received a dual-chamber rate-responsive ICD and maximally tolerated heart-failure therapy, randomised to programming at ventricular backup pacing 40/min (256) or dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing 70/min (250). Primary endpoint: composite of time to death or first hospitalisation for congestive heart failure.
cards.result: One-year survival free of the composite endpoint was 83.9% for VVI-40 versus 73.3% for DDDR-70 (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 1.06 to 2.44). Mortality: 6.5% versus 10.1% (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 0.84 to 3.09). Heart-failure hospitalisation: 13.3% versus 22.6% (relative hazard 1.54; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.46) — both components trending in favour of backup pacing. The trial was stopped early. The authors conclude dual-chamber pacing offers no clinical advantage over ventricular backup pacing in this population and may be detrimental.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early, which tends to exaggerate effects; the individual components did not reach significance. The lesson is about pacing burden in patients who do not need pacing — it must not be read as an argument against dual-chamber devices in patients with a genuine pacing indication (Shelf #2297).

shelves.title: Resynchronisation by the conduction system: left-bundle-branch pacing beat biventricular pacing on death or heart-failure hospitalisation in one randomised trial (HeartSync-LBBP)
shelves.question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left bundle-branch block, does left-bundle-branch pacing achieve better long-term outcomes than conventional biventricular pacing for cardiac resynchronisation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Bundle-Branch Block · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · China · Echocardiography · Heart Failure · Prospective Studies · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: One randomised trial with a startlingly large effect — carded with its size and setting in plain view. HeartSync-LBBP randomised 200 patients with ejection fraction of 35% or less and left bundle-branch block at six centres in China to left-bundle-branch pacing (LBBP) or biventricular pacing (BiVP), with a median follow-up of 36 months. The primary endpoint (death from any cause or heart-failure hospitalisation) occurred in 8% with LBBP versus 28% with BiVP (hazard ratio 0.26; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.57; P<.001), driven by hospitalisation (7.0% vs 28.0%; HR 0.23) — mortality alone did not differ significantly (2.0% vs 5.0%; HR 0.40; 95% CI 0.08 to 2.04). Implant success was 98% versus 94%; echocardiographic response rates were similar (86% vs 81%), while super-response was more frequent with LBBP (55% vs 36%; P=.007). The earlier pilot, His-SYNC (41 patients, His-bundle pacing versus BiVP), is named here but NOT carded: its PubMed record is a two-page report carrying no abstract, so no figures from it are quoted anywhere on this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): conduction-system pacing is the most promising challenger biventricular pacing has had — one 200-patient, single-country trial with an effect this size needs independent replication before stronger language; the authors themselves conclude that further trials are warranted.

cards.headline: HeartSync-LBBP 2026: death or heart-failure hospitalisation 8% (LBBP) vs 28% (BiVP) — HR 0.26; hospitalisation 7% vs 28%; mortality alone not significant
cards.summary: HeartSync-LBBP 2026: death or heart-failure hospitalisation 8% (LBBP) vs 28% (BiVP) — HR 0.26; hospitalisation 7% vs 28%; mortality alone not significant
cards.people: 200 patients with left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less and left bundle-branch block at six centres in China (enrolled October 2020 to March 2022; 136 men, 64 women), randomised 1:1 to left-bundle-branch pacing or biventricular pacing. Primary endpoint: time to death from any cause or heart failure hospitalisation. Secondaries: all-cause death, heart-failure hospitalisation, echocardiographic response (LVEF increase of at least 5 points), and super-response (increase of at least 15 points or LVEF reaching at least 50%). Median follow-up 36 months.
cards.result: Implant success: 98% (LBBP) versus 94% (BiVP) (P=.28). The primary endpoint was significantly lower with LBBP (8% vs 28%; hazard ratio 0.26; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.57; P<.001). All-cause mortality did not differ significantly (2.0% vs 5.0%; HR 0.40; 95% CI 0.08 to 2.04; P=.25); heart-failure hospitalisation was lower with LBBP (7.0% vs 28.0%; HR 0.23; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.52; P<.001). Echocardiographic response rates were similar (86.0% vs 81.0%; P=.34); super-response was higher with LBBP (55.0% vs 36.0%; P=.007). The authors conclude LBBP was superior on the composite in this population and that further trials are warranted.
cards.watchOut: A single 200-patient trial from one country, with a composite driven by hospitalisation and an effect size (HR 0.26) larger than resynchronisation itself achieved against medical therapy — exactly the profile that demands replication. The His-SYNC pilot (PMID 31078637) is not carded: its PubMed record carries no abstract, so this shelf quotes no figures from it.

shelves.title: Recurrent reflex syncope with a cardioinhibitory response: closed-loop-stimulation pacing cut recurrences in two blinded trials (SPAIN + BIOSync CLS)
shelves.question: In patients aged 40 or older with recurrent reflex (vasovagal) syncope and documented cardioinhibition or tilt-induced asystole, does dual-chamber pacing with closed-loop stimulation reduce syncope recurrence versus sham or switched-off pacing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bradycardia · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Severity of Illness Index · Syncope, Vasovagal · Tilt-Table Test · Treatment Outcome · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial · Heart Arrest · Reflex · Syncope
shelves.balance: Pacing for vasovagal syncope failed for decades in unselected patients; these two trials show what changed — selecting the cardioinhibitory phenotype and using a sensor that reacts to the faint itself. Closed-loop stimulation (CLS) adjusts rate from intracardiac impedance, rising as the vasovagal cascade begins. SPAIN (46 patients aged at least 40 with high-burden syncope and a cardioinhibitory tilt test; randomised crossover between CLS pacing and sham pacing) found at least a 50% reduction in syncope episodes in 72% of patients during CLS periods versus 28% during sham (P=0.017); events occurred in 4 patients (8.7%) on CLS versus 21 (45.7%) on sham. BIOSync CLS (127 patients aged at least 40 with severe recurrent reflex syncope and tilt-induced asystole over 3 seconds; pacing ON versus OFF, double-blind) found syncope recurrence in 16% versus 53% over a median 11.2 months (hazard ratio 0.23; P=0.00005), with estimated 2-year recurrence 22% versus 68%, and minor device-related adverse events in 4%. PROPOSED LIKELY: in this narrow, test-selected phenotype — recurrent, severe, cardioinhibitory — CLS pacing works. The shelf's boundary is the phenotype: these results say nothing about pacing unselected fainters, the population in which pacing earned its poor reputation.

cards.headline: SPAIN 2017: syncope events in 8.7% of patients during CLS pacing vs 45.7% during sham; at least 50% burden reduction in 72% vs 28%
cards.summary: SPAIN 2017: syncope events in 8.7% of patients during CLS pacing vs 45.7% during sham; at least 50% burden reduction in 72% vs 28%
cards.people: 46 patients (mean age 56.3; 47.8% men) in Canada and Spain, aged at least 40, with high-burden vasovagal syncope (at least 5 lifetime episodes, at least 2 in the past year; mean 12 previous episodes) and a cardioinhibitory head-up tilt test (bradycardia under 40/min for 10 s or asystole over 3 s), randomised to dual-chamber CLS pacing for 12 months then sham pacing (DDI at 30/min) for 12 months, or the reverse order, crossing over early if 3 syncopes occurred within a month.
cards.result: The proportion of patients with at least a 50% reduction in syncopal episodes was 72% (95% CI 47 to 90) with DDD-CLS versus 28% (95% CI 9.7 to 53.5) with sham (P=0.017). Four patients (8.7%) had events during DDD-CLS and 21 (45.7%) during sham (hazard ratio 6.7; 95% CI 2.3 to 19.8 for sham versus CLS periods). Time to first syncope was significantly longer with CLS (29.2 vs 9.3 months; P<0.016). The authors conclude DDD-CLS significantly reduced syncope burden and prolonged time to first recurrence versus sham pacing in tilt-positive cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope.
cards.watchOut: A crossover of 46 highly selected patients; the hazard ratio is reported for sham versus CLS periods, so this card leads with the absolute rates. Tilt-positive cardioinhibitory patients only — the selection is the intervention's other half.

cards.headline: BIOSync CLS 2021: syncope recurrence 16% (pacing ON) vs 53% (OFF) — HR 0.23; estimated 2-year recurrence 22% vs 68%
cards.summary: BIOSync CLS 2021: syncope recurrence 16% (pacing ON) vs 53% (OFF) — HR 0.23; estimated 2-year recurrence 22% vs 68%
cards.people: 127 patients aged at least 40 with at least two episodes of unpredictable severe reflex syncope in the previous year and tilt-induced syncope with an asystolic pause longer than 3 seconds, randomised to an active dual-chamber pacemaker with closed-loop stimulation (63) or the same device inactive (64); patients and outcome assessors were blinded. Primary endpoint: time to first recurrence of syncope; median follow-up 11.2 months.
cards.result: Syncope recurred in 10 of 63 patients (16%) in the pacing group versus 34 of 64 (53%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.23; P=0.00005). Estimated recurrence at 1 year: 19% versus 53%; at 2 years: 22% versus 68%. The combined endpoint of syncope or presyncope also favoured pacing (37% vs 63%; HR 0.44; P=0.002). Minor device-related adverse events were reported in five patients (4%). The authors conclude CLS pacing is highly effective in this population and support tilt testing to select candidates.
cards.watchOut: Benefit is confined to the tilt-induced-asystole phenotype; the trial does not rehabilitate pacing for syncope generally. Device implantation in a condition that is benign in prognosis terms is a values judgement the numbers alone cannot make.

shelves.title: Neurally mediated syncope with loop-recorder-documented asystole: pacing halved recurrence (ISSUE-3)
shelves.question: In patients aged 40 or older with recurrent neurally mediated syncope and implantable-loop-recorder documentation of asystole, does dual-chamber pacing reduce syncope recurrence versus sensing only?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Arrest · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Pacemaker, Artificial · Secondary Prevention · Severity of Illness Index · Syncope · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — one trial, and its statistics sit exactly at the threshold, but the selection strategy it validated changed practice. ISSUE-3 gave implantable loop recorders to 511 patients aged at least 40 with at least three syncopes in two years; 89 documented syncope with asystole of at least 3 seconds (or at least 6 seconds without syncope), and 77 were randomised double-blind to dual-chamber pacing with rate-drop response switched ON or to sensing only (OFF). Over two years the estimated syncope recurrence was 25% with pacing ON versus 57% OFF (log-rank P=0.039, against a prespecified significance threshold of 0.04) — a 57% relative reduction (95% CI 4 to 81) and a 32-point absolute reduction. Procedural complications occurred in five patients (four lead dislodgements requiring correction, one subclavian vein thrombosis). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: document the asystole first, then pace — the loop recorder, not the tilt table, is this trial's selection tool (compare Shelf #2301, where tilt selection plus closed-loop stimulation produced larger effects). A P value at the boundary in 77 randomised patients earns POSSIBLE, not more.

cards.headline: ISSUE-3 2012: 2-year syncope recurrence 25% (pacing ON) vs 57% (OFF), P=0.039; relative reduction 57% (95% CI 4 to 81)
cards.summary: ISSUE-3 2012: 2-year syncope recurrence 25% (pacing ON) vs 57% (OFF), P=0.039; relative reduction 57% (95% CI 4 to 81)
cards.people: 511 patients aged at least 40 with at least 3 syncopal episodes in the previous 2 years received an implantable loop recorder at 29 centres; 89 had documentation of syncope with asystole of at least 3 seconds, or asystole of at least 6 seconds without syncope, within about 12 months and met pacemaker criteria; 77 of the 89 were randomised to dual-chamber pacing with rate-drop response (ON) or sensing only (OFF). Analysis by intention to treat.
cards.result: Syncope recurred in 27 patients during follow-up — 19 assigned to pacemaker OFF and 8 to ON. The 2-year estimated recurrence rate was 57% (95% CI 40 to 74) with pacing OFF and 25% (95% CI 13 to 45) with pacing ON (log-rank P=0.039 at a prespecified significance threshold of 0.04), a 57% relative reduction (95% CI 4 to 81). Five patients had procedural complications: lead dislodgement in four (requiring correction) and subclavian vein thrombosis in one. The authors conclude dual-chamber pacing is effective in reducing recurrence in severe asystolic neurally mediated syncope.
cards.watchOut: Only 77 of 511 monitored patients reached randomisation — the strategy's yield is part of its cost. The confidence interval for the relative reduction (4% to 81%) nearly touches no-effect; treat the point estimate as optimistic.
cards.source: Brignole M et al. shelves.title: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope: cardioneuroablation kept 92% free of syncope at 2 years versus 46% with non-pharmacological care (Piotrowski RCT)
shelves.question: In patients with documented cardioinhibitory or mixed vasovagal syncope, does cardioneuroablation (ablation of the atrial ganglionated plexi) improve freedom from syncope versus optimal non-pharmacological management?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Adult · Middle Aged · Heart Rate · Syncope, Vasovagal · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Reflex
shelves.balance: THIN — the first randomised trial of a procedure that deletes part of the vagus nerve's cardiac wiring, in 48 patients. Piotrowski and colleagues randomised patients with documented symptomatic cardioinhibitory or mixed vasovagal syncope and a positive atropine test to cardioneuroablation (radiofrequency ablation of ganglionated plexi from both atria) or optimal non-pharmacological therapy, with two years of follow-up. The primary endpoint — first syncope recurrence — occurred in 2 of 24 ablation patients (8%) versus 13 of 24 controls (54%) (P=0.0004). After ablation, resting sinus rate was faster and heart-rate-variability measures shifted toward parasympathetic withdrawal, confirming the intended denervation physiology; quality of life improved significantly in the ablation group and was stable in controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a dramatic result in a small, open-label, single-programme trial — the effect size invites belief and the design demands replication, particularly on durability (do the plexi regrow function?) and on the long-term cost of vagal denervation in patients whose mean age was 38. The control was non-pharmacological care, not sham ablation, so expectation effects are unconstrained.

cards.headline: Piotrowski 2023: syncope recurrence 8% (cardioneuroablation) vs 54% (control) over 2 years, P=0.0004; quality of life improved only in the ablation group
cards.summary: Piotrowski 2023: syncope recurrence 8% (cardioneuroablation) vs 54% (control) over 2 years, P=0.0004; quality of life improved only in the ablation group
cards.people: 48 patients (17 men; mean age 38 ± 10 years) with documented symptomatic cardioinhibitory or mixed vasovagal syncope and a positive atropine test, randomised to cardioneuroablation (24) — radiofrequency ablation of the ganglionated plexi from the left and right atria — or optimal non-pharmacological therapy (24). Primary endpoint: time to first syncope recurrence over 2 years. Secondaries: Holter sinus rhythm and heart-rate-variability changes and quality of life.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 2 patients (8%) in the cardioneuroablation group versus 13 (54%) in the control group (P=0.0004). After ablation, mean 24-hour sinus rhythm was significantly faster and heart-rate-variability parameters changed significantly toward parasympathetic withdrawal versus baseline. Quality of life improved significantly in the ablation group (P=0.0001) and remained stable in controls (P=0.5501). The authors describe this as the first randomised study documenting cardioneuroablation efficacy in cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope and call for larger studies.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a non-procedural control — no sham ablation — in a symptom endpoint notoriously responsive to expectation. Mean age 38: decades of life with a denervated sinus node is the unpriced side of the trade, and two years cannot price it.

shelves.title: Recurrent pericarditis that keeps coming back: continuing the IL-1 trap rilonacept prevented nearly all recurrences (RHAPSODY)
shelves.question: In colchicine-resistant, corticosteroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis with systemic inflammation, does continued rilonacept prevent recurrence versus withdrawal to placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-1alpha · Interleukin-1beta · Male · Middle Aged · Pericarditis · Proportional Hazards Models · Receptors, Interleukin-1 Type I · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Recurrence · Respiratory Tract Infections · Young Adult
shelves.balance: A randomised-withdrawal trial — the standard architecture for a relapsing disease, and it should be read as one: everyone first had to respond to the drug. RHAPSODY enrolled 86 patients presenting with a pericarditis recurrence (pain plus elevated CRP) on standard therapy into a 12-week open run-in on rilonacept, an interleukin-1α/β trap, during which background medicines were stopped; pain resolved or nearly resolved in a median of 5 days and CRP normalised in a median of 7 days. The 61 responders were randomised to continue weekly rilonacept or switch to placebo. During withdrawal, recurrence occurred in 2 of 30 patients (7%) continuing rilonacept versus 23 of 31 (74%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.04; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; P<.001); median time to recurrence on placebo was 8.6 weeks, while too few events occurred on rilonacept to estimate its median. The commonest adverse events were injection-site reactions and upper respiratory infections; four patients discontinued during the run-in for adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: in IL-1-driven recurrent pericarditis that has already declared itself steroid-dependent, blocking IL-1 keeps the disease off. Distinct from Shelf #190 (colchicine for pericarditis episodes) — this is the next line, for the patients colchicine and steroids fail.

cards.headline: RHAPSODY 2021: recurrence 7% (continued rilonacept) vs 74% (withdrawn to placebo) — HR 0.04; pain resolved in a median 5 days in the run-in
cards.summary: RHAPSODY 2021: recurrence 7% (continued rilonacept) vs 74% (withdrawn to placebo) — HR 0.04; pain resolved in a median 5 days in the run-in
cards.people: 86 patients with acute symptoms of recurrent pericarditis and an elevated CRP while on standard therapy, enrolled in a 12-week open-label rilonacept run-in (background medications discontinued); the 61 patients meeting prespecified response criteria were randomised 1:1 to continued weekly subcutaneous rilonacept monotherapy or placebo. Primary endpoint: time to first adjudicated pericarditis recurrence (Cox model). Funded by Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals.
cards.result: During the run-in, the median time to resolution or near-resolution of pain was 5 days and to CRP normalisation 7 days. In the randomised-withdrawal period, recurrence occurred in 2 of 30 patients (7%) on rilonacept versus 23 of 31 (74%) on placebo; the median time to first recurrence was 8.6 weeks (95% CI 4.0 to 11.7) on placebo and could not be estimated on rilonacept (too few events); hazard ratio 0.04 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; P<.001). Four patients had adverse events leading to discontinuation during the run-in; the most common adverse events were injection-site reactions and upper respiratory tract infections.
cards.watchOut: Withdrawal designs estimate the effect of stopping in responders, not the effect of starting in everyone — the 74% placebo recurrence rate describes a deliberately enriched, steroid-dependent population. Weekly injections and cost are the practical constraints the trial does not price.

shelves.title: Colchicine-resistant, steroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis: continuing anakinra prevented most recurrences (AIRTRIP)
shelves.question: In recurrent pericarditis with colchicine resistance and corticosteroid dependence, does continued anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) prevent recurrence versus withdrawal to placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child Development · Cognition · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant Formula · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight · Language Development · Male · Milk, Human · Ontario
shelves.balance: THIN — 21 patients, and the whole effect rests on 11 versus 10 randomised patients, but the separation is near-total and it anticipated the larger rilonacept trial (Shelf #2304). AIRTRIP enrolled patients with recurrent pericarditis (at least three prior recurrences), elevated CRP, colchicine resistance, and corticosteroid dependence at three Italian centres; all received open-label anakinra (2 mg/kg/day, up to 100 mg) for two months, and responders were randomised to continue anakinra (11) or switch to placebo (10). Over a median 14 months of follow-up, recurrence occurred in 2 of 11 patients (18.2%) continuing anakinra versus 9 of 10 (90%) withdrawn to placebo; median flare-free survival on placebo was 72 days and was not reached on anakinra (P<.001). Transient local skin reactions occurred in 20 of 21 patients (95.2%) during anakinra treatment; one patient each had herpes zoster, transaminase elevation, and ischaemic optic neuropathy; no patient permanently discontinued the drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: daily-injection IL-1 blockade works in this phenotype; the trial's size, not its direction, is the limitation. One records note: this article's PubMed record carries plainly mis-indexed MeSH terms (infant-nutrition descriptors that belong to a different article); per library policy the terms are copied verbatim from the record and flagged here rather than silently corrected.

cards.headline: AIRTRIP 2016: recurrence 18.2% (continued anakinra) vs 90% (placebo) over a median 14 months; median flare-free survival 72 days on placebo, not reached on anakinra
cards.summary: AIRTRIP 2016: recurrence 18.2% (continued anakinra) vs 90% (placebo) over a median 14 months; median flare-free survival 72 days on placebo, not reached on anakinra
cards.people: 21 consecutive patients with recurrent pericarditis (at least 3 previous recurrences), elevated CRP, colchicine resistance, and corticosteroid dependence at 3 Italian referral centres. All received open-label anakinra 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 100 mg) for 2 months; responders were randomised to continue anakinra (11) or switch to placebo (10) for 6 months or until recurrence. Primary outcomes: recurrent pericarditis and time to recurrence after randomisation; all patients were followed for 12 months (median follow-up 14 months).
cards.result: Recurrent pericarditis occurred in 2 of 11 patients (18.2%) assigned to anakinra and 9 of 10 (90%) assigned to placebo (incidence rate difference −1.95%; 95% CI −3.3 to −0.6). Median flare-free survival was 72 days (IQR 64 to 150) after randomisation in the placebo group and was not reached in the anakinra group (P<.001). During anakinra treatment, 20 of 21 patients (95.2%) had transient local skin reactions; herpes zoster occurred in 1 (4.8%), transaminase elevation in 3 (14.3%), and ischaemic optic neuropathy in 1 (4.8%); no patient permanently discontinued the active drug, and no adverse events occurred during placebo treatment. The authors characterise the study as preliminary and call for larger trials.
cards.watchOut: Eleven versus ten patients: two events moving arms would halve the effect. Daily injections with near-universal injection-site reactions are a real burden in a disease whose alternative is steroid dependence — that trade is the clinical question, and the trial answers the efficacy half of it.
cards.source: Brucato A et al. Effect of Anakinra on Recurrent Pericarditis Among Patients With Colchicine Resistance and Corticosteroid Dependence: The AIRTRIP Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27825009. Registry ID: NCT02219828, from the record.
