shelves.title: Idiopathic recurrent pericarditis: goflikicept prevented every recurrence in a small withdrawal trial
shelves.question: In idiopathic recurrent pericarditis, does the interleukin-1 inhibitor goflikicept maintain remission versus withdrawal to placebo after an open-label response?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Chest Pain · Chronic Disease · Odds Ratio · Pericardial Effusion · Pericarditis · Rare Diseases
shelves.balance: THIN — the third IL-1 agent to clear the same bar, in the smallest and most geographically concentrated trial of the three. This phase II/III study at two centres enrolled 22 patients with idiopathic recurrent pericarditis into an open-label goflikicept run-in; CRP, chest pain, and pericardial effusion all improved from baseline, and the 20 responders were randomised to continue goflikicept or switch to placebo for a 24-week withdrawal period. Recurrence occurred in 9 of 10 patients on placebo and in none on goflikicept (P<0.001). A total of 122 adverse events were reported in 21 of 22 patients (95.5%) — a high count that reflects event-by-event reporting in a small cohort; there were no deaths and no new safety signals identified. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: directionally identical to rilonacept (Shelf #2304) and anakinra (Shelf #2305) — IL-1 blockade as a class holds remission in this disease — but goflikicept's own evidence base is 20 randomised patients from two centres in one region, and availability outside its home market is limited; the shelf claims class concordance, not a standalone verdict.

cards.headline: Goflikicept 2023: recurrence 0 of 10 (continued drug) vs 9 of 10 (placebo) within 24 weeks of randomisation, P<0.001
cards.summary: Goflikicept 2023: recurrence 0 of 10 (continued drug) vs 9 of 10 (placebo) within 24 weeks of randomisation, P<0.001
cards.people: 22 patients with idiopathic recurrent pericarditis (with and without recurrence at enrolment) at 2 centres, treated open-label with goflikicept (RPH-104, an interleukin-1 inhibitor) in a run-in period; the 20 patients with clinical response were randomised 1:1 to continue goflikicept or switch to placebo. Primary endpoint: time to first pericarditis recurrence during the withdrawal period.
cards.result: During the run-in, CRP fell and chest pain and pericardial effusion were reduced compared with baseline. In the withdrawal period, recurrence occurred in 9 of 10 patients in the placebo group and in no patient in the goflikicept group within 24 weeks after randomisation (P<0.001). A total of 122 adverse events were reported in 21 patients (95.5%); there were no deaths and no new safety signals. The authors conclude goflikicept prevented recurrences and maintained remission with a favourable risk-benefit ratio.
cards.watchOut: Twenty randomised patients, two centres, one country, sponsor-developed agent with limited availability elsewhere. Zero events in the treatment arm means the confidence interval around the benefit is wide even when the P value is small.
cards.source: Myachikova VY et al. Treatment of Idiopathic Recurrent Pericarditis With Goflikicept: Phase II/III Study Results. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2023. PMID: 37380301. shelves.title: After cardiac surgery: colchicine prevents the post-pericardiotomy syndrome in two trials — but not postoperative AF (COPPS + COPPS-2)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, does perioperative colchicine prevent the post-pericardiotomy syndrome, postoperative atrial fibrillation, and effusions?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiac Tamponade · Colchicine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pericarditis · Postpericardiotomy Syndrome · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome · Tubulin Modulators · Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Gastrointestinal Diseases · Pericardial Effusion · Perioperative Care · Pleural Effusion · Postoperative Complications
shelves.balance: Two multicentre double-blind trials from the same Italian programme, concordant on the syndrome and honestly split on the rhythm. COPPS (360 patients; colchicine started on postoperative day 3 for one month) cut the post-pericardiotomy syndrome at 12 months from 21.1% to 8.9% (P=0.002; number needed to treat 8) and reduced the composite of disease-related hospitalisation, tamponade, constriction, and relapses (0.6% vs 5.0%; P=0.024), with similar side-effect rates (8.9% vs 5.0%; P=0.212). COPPS-2 (360 patients; colchicine started 48–72 hours before surgery and continued one month) again cut the syndrome (19.4% vs 29.4%; absolute difference 10.0%; NNT 10) — but on intention-to-treat it did NOT significantly reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation (33.9% vs 41.7%; absolute difference 7.8%, CI crossing zero) or pericardial/pleural effusions (57.2% vs 58.9%), though a prespecified on-treatment analysis did show less AF (27.0% vs 41.2%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with colchicine in COPPS-2 (20.0% vs 11.7%; number needed to harm 12), with similar discontinuation rates and no serious adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: a month of colchicine around cardiac surgery prevents roughly one post-pericardiotomy syndrome per ten patients treated; do not prescribe it for the AF — the larger perioperative trial's primary analysis says no.

cards.headline: COPPS 2010: post-pericardiotomy syndrome 8.9% (colchicine) vs 21.1% (placebo) at 12 months — P=0.002, NNT 8
cards.summary: COPPS 2010: post-pericardiotomy syndrome 8.9% (colchicine) vs 21.1% (placebo) at 12 months — P=0.002, NNT 8
cards.people: 360 cardiac-surgery patients (mean age 65.7; 66% men) at multiple centres, randomised on the third postoperative day to colchicine (180; 1.0 mg twice daily on day one, then 0.5 mg twice daily for one month at 70 kg or above, halved below 70 kg or if intolerant) or placebo (180). Primary endpoint: incidence of post-pericardiotomy syndrome at 12 months. Secondary: composite of disease-related hospitalisation, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, and relapses.
cards.result: Colchicine significantly reduced post-pericardiotomy syndrome at 12 months (8.9% vs 21.1%; P=0.002; number needed to treat 8) and the secondary composite (0.6% vs 5.0%; P=0.024). Side effects, mainly gastrointestinal intolerance, were similar (8.9% vs 5.0%; P=0.212). The authors conclude colchicine is safe and efficacious for primary prevention of the syndrome and its complications after cardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: Postoperative-day-3 start — COPPS does not test pre-operative loading; that was COPPS-2's design, with a less comfortable adverse-event profile.
cards.source: Imazio M et al. COlchicine for the Prevention of the Post-pericardiotomy Syndrome (COPPS): a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Eur Heart J. 2010. PMID: 20805112. Registry ID: NCT00128427, from the record. cards.headline: COPPS-2 2014: syndrome 19.4% vs 29.4% (NNT 10); postoperative AF NOT significantly reduced (33.9% vs 41.7%); gastrointestinal events 20.0% vs 11.7% (NNH 12)
cards.summary: COPPS-2 2014: syndrome 19.4% vs 29.4% (NNT 10); postoperative AF NOT significantly reduced (33.9% vs 41.7%); gastrointestinal events 20.0% vs 11.7% (NNH 12)
cards.people: 360 consecutive cardiac-surgery candidates (mean age 67.5; 69% men; 36% valvular surgery) at 11 Italian centres, randomised to colchicine (180; 0.5 mg twice daily at 70 kg or above, once daily below) or placebo (180), started 48–72 hours before surgery and continued for one month afterwards. Primary endpoint: post-pericardiotomy syndrome within 3 months; secondaries: postoperative AF and pericardial or pleural effusion.
cards.result: Post-pericardiotomy syndrome occurred in 35 patients (19.4%) on colchicine versus 53 (29.4%) on placebo (absolute difference 10.0%; 95% CI 1.1 to 18.7; NNT 10). Postoperative AF did not differ significantly on intention-to-treat (33.9% vs 41.7%; absolute difference 7.8%; 95% CI −2.2 to 17.6), nor did effusions (57.2% vs 58.9%); a prespecified on-treatment analysis did show less AF with colchicine (27.0% vs 41.2%; absolute difference 14.2%). Adverse events were more frequent with colchicine (20.0% vs 11.7%; absolute difference 8.3%; NNH 12), mainly gastrointestinal; discontinuation rates were similar and no serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: The on-treatment AF signal is the kind of secondary-analysis result that misleads when quoted alone — the trial's own conclusion is that colchicine did not reduce postoperative AF. Quote both numbers or neither.
cards.source: Imazio M et al. Colchicine for prevention of postpericardiotomy syndrome and postoperative atrial fibrillation: the COPPS-2 randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25172965. Registry ID: NCT01552187, from the record. shelves.title: Tuberculous pericarditis: steroids and immunotherapy did not move the composite of death, tamponade, or constriction — constriction fell, cancers rose (IMPI)
shelves.question: In tuberculous pericarditis, mostly in people with HIV, does adjunctive prednisolone or Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy reduce death, cardiac tamponade, or constrictive pericarditis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiac Tamponade · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Glucocorticoids · HIV Infections · Humans · Immunotherapy · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Mycobacterium · Pericardiocentesis · Pericarditis, Constrictive · Pericarditis, Tuberculous · Prednisolone · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: A 1,400-patient factorial trial that answered a decades-old practice question with a split verdict — and the split is the shelf. IMPI randomised adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis (two-thirds with HIV infection) to prednisolone or placebo for six weeks and, independently, to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy or placebo, on top of antituberculosis therapy. The primary composite (death, cardiac tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis) did not differ for either intervention: 23.8% versus 24.5% for prednisolone (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) and 25.0% versus 24.3% for immunotherapy (HR 1.03; P=0.81). Inside the composite, prednisolone did reduce constriction (4.4% vs 7.8%; HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; HR 0.79; P=0.04). Against that, both interventions increased cancer incidence (prednisolone 1.8% vs 0.6%, HR 3.27; immunotherapy 1.8% vs 0.5%, HR 3.69), owing mainly to HIV-associated cancers. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C) on the question as posed: neither adjunct improves the composite outcome that matters most. The constriction finding keeps a narrower, judgement-level case for steroids alive in selected patients — and the cancer signal, in an HIV-prevalent population, is the price that has to be weighed against it; the shelf presents both rather than resolving that bedside trade.

cards.headline: IMPI 2014: primary composite 23.8% vs 24.5% (prednisolone, HR 0.95) and 25.0% vs 24.3% (immunotherapy, HR 1.03); constriction 4.4% vs 7.8% (HR 0.56); cancer 1.8% vs 0.6% and 1.8% vs 0.5%

cards.people: 1,400 adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis, randomised in a 2-by-2 factorial design to prednisolone or placebo for 6 weeks and to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy (five injections over 3 months) or placebo, in addition to antituberculosis therapy. Two-thirds of participants had concomitant HIV infection. Primary efficacy outcome: composite of death, cardiac tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary outcome for prednisolone versus placebo (23.8% vs 24.5%; hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) or for M. indicus pranii versus placebo (25.0% vs 24.3%; HR 1.03; 95% CI 0.82 to 1.29; P=0.81). Prednisolone significantly reduced constrictive pericarditis (4.4% vs 7.8%; HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.99; P=0.04). Both prednisolone (1.8% vs 0.6%; HR 3.27; 95% CI 1.07 to 10.03; P=0.03) and immunotherapy (1.8% vs 0.5%; HR 3.69; 95% CI 1.03 to 13.24; P=0.03) significantly increased cancer incidence, mainly HIV-associated cancers.
cards.watchOut: The population — largely sub-Saharan African, two-thirds HIV-positive, in the era studied — bounds transportability to low-HIV settings, where the cancer calculus may differ. The composite null and the constriction benefit are both real; which one governs an individual prescription is a clinical judgement this shelf deliberately does not make.
cards.source: Mayosi BM et al. Prednisolone and Mycobacterium indicus pranii in tuberculous pericarditis. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25178809. Registry ID: NCT00810849, from the record. shelves.title: Exudative pericarditis: intrapericardial urokinase prevented constriction in one randomised study — the wider literature is case reports
shelves.question: In large exudative (especially tuberculous or purulent) pericardial effusion, does intrapericardial fibrinolysis prevent constrictive pericarditis and drainage failure versus drainage alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericardiocentesis · Pericarditis · Pericarditis, Constrictive · Thrombolytic Therapy · Urokinase-Type Plasminogen Activator · Fibrinolysis · Pericardial Effusion · Pericardium · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Streptokinase · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One randomised study with a large effect, surrounded by a literature of anecdotes — the shelf holds both facts at once. Cui and colleagues randomised 94 patients with infectious exudative pericarditis (60 tuberculous, 34 purulent; disease course under one month) to pericardiocentesis and drainage with or without intrapericardial urokinase irrigation (200,000–600,000 units). Over a mean follow-up of about 57 months, constriction developed in 9 of 47 patients (19.1%) with urokinase versus 27 of 47 (57.4%) with drainage alone (Cox relative hazard coefficient 0.185; P<0.0001); pericardial thickness fell from 3.1 to 1.6 mm in the urokinase group and was unchanged in controls; intrapericardial bleeding occurred in 6 of 47 patients with non-bloody effusion, with no systemic bleeding, no severe puncture complications, and no cardiac deaths. The systematic review alongside it is the cold water: across the whole published literature, Wiyeh and colleagues found 29 reports totalling just 109 patients — 17 case reports, 11 case series, and that single randomised trial — all at high risk of bias, with non-fatal procedure complications in 19.2% and, in the reviewers' words, very low certainty of efficacy and safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C — the trial's endpoint is a serious structural outcome and the shelf is graded for its evidence structure, not its topic): lysing the fibrin while the effusion is drained is biologically coherent and the one trial is strongly positive; a literature this thin cannot carry more.

cards.headline: Cui 2005: constriction 19.1% (urokinase + drainage) vs 57.4% (drainage alone) over ~57 months — relative hazard coefficient 0.185, P<0.0001
cards.summary: Cui 2005: constriction 19.1% (urokinase + drainage) vs 57.4% (drainage alone) over ~57 months — relative hazard coefficient 0.185, P<0.0001
cards.people: 94 consecutive patients (ages 9–66; 44 men, 50 women) with infectious exudative pericarditis recruited 1993–2002 — 34 purulent and 60 tuberculous, all with disease courses under one month — randomly assigned to intrapericardial urokinase irrigation (200,000–600,000 U; mean 320,000 U) plus conventional treatment including pericardiocentesis and drainage, or conventional treatment alone. Follow-up 8–120 months (mean 56.8) by telephone survey and echocardiography.
cards.result: Urokinase promoted complete drainage and significantly reduced pericardial thickness (3.1 ± 1.6 mm to 1.6 ± 1.0 mm, P<0.001) versus no change in controls (3.4 ± 1.6 to 3.2 ± 1.8 mm, P>0.05), and alleviated adhesion. Intrapericardial bleeding related to fibrinolysis occurred in 6 of 47 patients with non-blood effusion; there was no systemic bleeding and no severe puncture-related complication. During follow-up there were no cardiac deaths, and pericardial constriction occurred in 9 of 47 patients (19.1%) in the urokinase group versus 27 of 47 (57.4%) in controls; Cox analysis gave a relative hazard coefficient of 0.185 (P<0.0001). The authors conclude early intrapericardial urokinase with pericardiocentesis appears safe and effective in preventing constriction in infectious exudative pericarditis.
cards.watchOut: One centre, one country, one agent (urokinase), recruited over a decade ending in 2002; the abstract does not describe blinding or allocation concealment. A hazard reduction this large from a study this small should be read as an upper bound.
cards.source: Cui HB et al. Prevention of pericardial constriction by transcatheter intrapericardial fibrinolysis with urokinase. Chin Med Sci J. 2005. PMID: 15844302. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. cards.headline: Wiyeh 2018: the entire literature is 29 reports and 109 patients, all high risk of bias — certainty rated very low
cards.summary: Wiyeh 2018: the entire literature is 29 reports and 109 patients, all high risk of bias — certainty rated very low
cards.people: Systematic review of published and unpublished studies of intrapericardial fibrinolysis for pericardial effusion: 29 studies totalling 109 patients (17 case reports, 11 case series, 1 randomised trial). Commonest causes were Staphylococcus aureus (23 cases) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (19 cases); commonest agents streptokinase (15 studies) and urokinase (5).
cards.result: Intrapericardial fibrinolysis prevented complications in 94 of 109 patients (86.2%) in the assembled reports; non-fatal procedure-related complications were reported in 21 patients (19.2%); no patient died following the procedure. The reviewers conclude there is very low certainty of the efficacy and safety of intrapericardial fibrinolysis in preventing complications of pericardial effusion, and that high-quality randomised trials are required.
cards.watchOut: This is why the shelf is POSSIBLE and not higher: the randomised result and the literature's overall fragility are both on the record, and the review's verdict governs the confidence, not the trial's P value.
cards.source: Wiyeh AB et al. A systematic review of the efficacy and safety of intrapericardial fibrinolysis in patients with pericardial effusion. Int J Cardiol. 2018. PMID: 29107356. shelves.title: Malignant pericardial effusion: prolonged catheter drainage matched surgical window on recurrence, with far fewer complications (retrospective)
shelves.question: In malignant pericardial effusion with tamponade, does percutaneous prolonged drainage match surgical pericardiotomy for recurrence, complications, and diagnostic yield?
shelves.mesh: Biopsy · Diagnosis, Differential · Drainage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericardial Effusion · Pericardiectomy · Pleural Neoplasms · Prognosis · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: THIN — a single retrospective comparison, and the shelf says so up front; but it is the direct head-to-head for a decision made weekly on oncology wards, and its three answers are clean. Patel and colleagues reviewed 88 patients presenting with tamponade associated with malignancy: 43 treated with pericardiocentesis and extended catheter drainage, 45 with surgical pericardiotomy. Recurrence did not differ (12% with drainage versus 13% with surgery; P=0.78), and neither did diagnostic yield (44% versus 53%; P=0.39) — the surgical biopsy added no significant diagnostic value beyond the cytology available from the tap. Complications did differ, substantially: 2% overall with prolonged drainage versus 20% with surgery (P=0.007), with serious complications in none of the drainage patients versus 9% of the surgical group. Survival in this population is driven by the underlying malignancy, not by the drainage route — which is precisely why the less invasive route's equal efficacy matters. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: retrospective treatment selection (sicker patients may have been routed either way) caps the stamp; within that limit, prolonged drainage is the defensible default and surgery the exception for specific indications.

cards.headline: Patel 2013: recurrence 12% (prolonged drainage) vs 13% (surgical pericardiotomy); complications 2% vs 20% (P=0.007); diagnostic yield 44% vs 53% (not significant)
cards.summary: Patel 2013: recurrence 12% (prolonged drainage) vs 13% (surgical pericardiotomy); complications 2% vs 20% (P=0.007); diagnostic yield 44% vs 53% (not significant)
cards.people: 88 patients presenting with pericardial tamponade associated with a malignancy, treated with pericardiocentesis with extended (prolonged) drainage (43) or surgical pericardiotomy (45). Outcomes: effusion recurrence, diagnostic yield, and complications.
cards.result: The recurrence rate did not differ significantly between prolonged catheter drainage and surgical pericardiotomy (12% vs 13%; P=0.78), nor did diagnostic yield (44% vs 53%; P=0.39). The overall complication rate was significantly lower with prolonged drainage (2% vs 20%; P=0.007), and there were no serious complications in the drainage group versus 9% in the surgical group. The authors conclude that surgical pericardiotomy with biopsy does not add significant diagnostic value beyond pericardiocentesis cytology, does not improve clinical outcomes over pericardiocentesis with prolonged drainage, and carries a higher complication rate.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: which patients were sent to theatre was a clinical decision, so residual confounding runs in an unknown direction. One centre's era and technique; percutaneous practice (and imaging guidance) has continued to improve since.

shelves.title: Constrictive pericarditis: survival after pericardiectomy is set by the cause — idiopathic best, post-radiation worst (Bertog cohort)
shelves.question: In chronic constrictive pericarditis, how do survival after pericardiectomy and its predictors differ by aetiology — idiopathic, post-surgical, or post-radiation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericardiectomy · Pericarditis, Constrictive · Proportional Hazards Models · Radiotherapy · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Virus Diseases
shelves.balance: No randomised trial of pericardiectomy exists or will — this 163-patient surgical cohort is the evidence, presented as prognosis rather than as a treatment comparison. Bertog and colleagues followed 163 patients who underwent pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis over 24 years at a single surgical centre (perioperative mortality 6%; 61 deaths over a median 6.9 years of follow-up among survivors). Cause-specific seven-year survival diverged sharply: idiopathic constriction fared best (88%; 95% CI 76 to 94), post-surgical constriction next (66%; 95% CI 52 to 78), and post-radiation constriction worst by far (27%; 95% CI 9 to 58). In bootstrap-validated proportional-hazards analyses, predictors of poor overall survival were prior radiation, worse renal function, higher pulmonary artery systolic pressure, abnormal left ventricular systolic function, lower serum sodium, and older age; pericardial calcification had no impact on survival. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C — mortality is the outcome throughout): the numbers to bring to the consent conversation are these aetiology-stratified ones, and the relatively good survival after idiopathic pericardiectomy is itself an argument that the operation, in that subgroup, is safe and durable. The shelf makes no claim that surgery beats medical management in any subgroup — no such comparison exists in the record.

cards.headline: Bertog 2004: 7-year survival after pericardiectomy — idiopathic 88%, post-surgical 66%, post-radiation 27%; perioperative mortality 6%
cards.summary: Bertog 2004: 7-year survival after pericardiectomy — idiopathic 88%, post-surgical 66%, post-radiation 27%; perioperative mortality 6%
cards.people: 163 patients who underwent pericardiectomy for surgically confirmed constrictive pericarditis at a single centre over 24 years. Aetiology: idiopathic in 75 (46%), prior cardiac surgery in 60 (37%), radiation in 15 (9%), miscellaneous in 13 (8%). Vital status from the Social Security Death Index; median follow-up among survivors 6.9 years (range 0.8–24.5), with 61 deaths.
cards.result: Perioperative mortality was 6%. Seven-year Kaplan-Meier survival was 88% (95% CI 76 to 94) for idiopathic constriction, 66% (95% CI 52 to 78) after prior cardiac surgery, and 27% (95% CI 9 to 58) after radiation. In bootstrap-validated proportional hazards analyses, predictors of poor overall survival were prior radiation, worse renal function, higher pulmonary artery systolic pressure, abnormal left ventricular systolic function, lower serum sodium level, and older age. Pericardial calcification had no impact on survival. The authors conclude long-term survival after pericardiectomy is related to underlying aetiology, LV systolic function, renal function, serum sodium, and pulmonary artery pressure.
cards.watchOut: A surgical series can only describe people who reached the operating table — it is silent on patients declined for surgery, whose outcomes define the other half of the decision. The radiation subgroup is 15 patients; its confidence interval (9% to 58%) is correspondingly wide.

shelves.title: Autoreactive pericardial effusion: intrapericardial triamcinolone prevented most recurrences in an uncontrolled series — at the lower dose, with less Cushing syndrome
shelves.question: In autoreactive (non-infectious, non-malignant) pericardial effusion, does intrapericardial triamcinolone achieve remission while sparing systemic corticosteroid toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Evaluation · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericardial Effusion · Pericardium · Recurrence · Safety · Time · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone
shelves.balance: Hypothesis-grade evidence, stamped as such. Maisch and colleagues worked up 260 consecutive patients with pericarditis/myopericarditis by pericardiocentesis, pericardioscopy, and epicardial biopsy with viral PCR and immunohistochemistry; 84 classified as autoreactive received intrapericardial triamcinolone — 54 at 600 mg/m² over 24 hours and 30 at 300 mg/m² (dose cohorts, not a randomised comparison). Symptomatic improvement with no effusion recurrence was seen in 92.6% (high dose) versus 86.7% (low dose) at 3 months and 86.0% versus 82.1% at one year (no significant difference between doses). There were no treatment-related acute complications; transient iatrogenic Cushing syndrome developed in 29.6% of the high-dose group versus 13.3% of the low-dose group (P<0.05) — the systemic spill was reduced, not abolished. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): there is no untreated or systemically treated control group, so the recurrence rates cannot be credited to the drug against the disease's natural history; what the series genuinely supports is feasibility, the lower dose's equal performance, and a smaller — real, but partial — steroid-sparing effect. The diagnostic pathway it depends on (pericardioscopy and epicardial biopsy for every effusion) is itself a specialised-centre undertaking.

cards.headline: Maisch 2002: recurrence-free at 1 year in 86.0% (600 mg/m²) vs 82.1% (300 mg/m²); transient Cushing syndrome 29.6% vs 13.3% (P<0.05); no acute complications
cards.summary: Maisch 2002: recurrence-free at 1 year in 86.0% (600 mg/m²) vs 82.1% (300 mg/m²); transient Cushing syndrome 29.6% vs 13.3% (P<0.05); no acute complications
cards.type: Prospective uncontrolled series with two dose cohorts
cards.people: 260 consecutive patients with pericarditis/myopericarditis underwent pericardiocentesis, pericardioscopy, and epicardial biopsy with pericardial fluid and tissue analysis (PCR for cardiotropic viruses and bacteria; immunohistochemistry and immunocytochemistry). The 84 patients classified as autoreactive pericarditis received intrapericardial triamcinolone: group 1, 54 patients at 600 mg/m² per 24 h; group 2, 30 patients at 300 mg/m² per 24 h.
cards.result: Intrapericardial triamcinolone produced symptomatic improvement and prevented effusion recurrence in 92.6% versus 86.7% of patients at 3 months and 86.0% versus 82.1% at 1 year in groups 1 and 2 respectively (P>0.05). There were no treatment-related acute complications. During follow-up, transient iatrogenic Cushing syndrome developed in 29.6% of group 1 versus 13.3% of group 2 (P<0.05). The authors conclude the 300 mg/m² regimen prevented recurrence of symptoms and effusion relapse as effectively as the 600 mg/m² regimen, with significantly fewer side effects.
cards.watchOut: No control group of any kind — neither untreated nor systemically treated — so efficacy against natural history is unestablished; the dose comparison was not randomised. 'The way to avoid side effects of systemic corticosteroid therapy' (the paper's subtitle) overstates it: one in eight low-dose patients still developed Cushing syndrome.
cards.source: Maisch B et al. Intrapericardial treatment of autoreactive pericardial effusion with triamcinolone; the way to avoid side effects of systemic corticosteroid therapy. Eur Heart J. 2002. PMID: 12242070. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.title: Acute pericarditis: CRP is up in three of four patients, settles within four weeks — and a still-high CRP at week 1 flags recurrence risk (Imazio cohort)
shelves.question: In a first episode of acute pericarditis, how often is C-reactive protein elevated, how fast does it normalise on treatment, and does persistent elevation identify patients at risk of recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · C-Reactive Protein · Chest Pain · Cohort Studies · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericarditis · Prognosis · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: A prognostic cohort, carded as prognosis — it describes the disease's inflammatory signature and the company recurrence keeps. Imazio and colleagues followed 200 consecutive patients with viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis at two Italian referral centres, measuring high-sensitivity CRP at presentation and weekly until normalisation. CRP was elevated in 156 of 200 patients (78%) at presentation; among the 44 without elevation, the recognised explanations were very early assessment (34%) and anti-inflammatory therapy already started (50%) — so a normal CRP does not exclude the diagnosis. On treatment, CRP normalised in 60% by week 1, 85% by week 2, 95% by week 3, and 100% by week 4. In multivariable analysis, three features independently predicted recurrence: incomplete response to empirical anti-inflammatory therapy at week 1 (hazard ratio 2.98; 95% CI 1.80 to 4.94), corticosteroid therapy (HR 2.80; 95% CI 1.59 to 4.95), and elevated hs-CRP still present at week 1 (HR 2.36; 95% CI 1.32 to 4.21). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: this is the observational basis for CRP-guided treatment duration — a strategy that has itself never been randomised, and the shelf says so; the steroid association, in particular, is the familiar confounding-by-severity pattern (steroids go to the worst cases) and should not be quoted as proof that steroids cause recurrences.

cards.headline: Imazio 2011: hs-CRP elevated in 78% at presentation, normalised in all by week 4; week-1 CRP elevation (HR 2.36), incomplete week-1 response (HR 2.98) and steroid therapy (HR 2.80) predicted recurrence
cards.summary: Imazio 2011: hs-CRP elevated in 78% at presentation, normalised in all by week 4; week-1 CRP elevation (HR 2.36), incomplete week-1 response (HR 2.98) and steroid therapy (HR 2.80) predicted recurrence
cards.people: 200 consecutive patients with viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis (mean age 53; 103 men) at 2 Italian referral centres (2005–2007). High-sensitivity CRP was measured at presentation and weekly until normalisation; predictors of recurrence were assessed by multivariable analysis.
cards.result: Hs-CRP was elevated in 156 of 200 cases (78%) at presentation; causes of a negative hs-CRP were early assessment (15 of 44; 34%) and previous anti-inflammatory therapy (22 of 44; 50%). Normalisation was achieved in 120 of 200 (60%) at week 1, 170 (85%) at week 2, 190 (95%) at week 3, and all cases at week 4. Independent risk factors for recurrence were incomplete response to empirical anti-inflammatory therapy at week 1 (hazard ratio 2.98; 95% CI 1.80 to 4.94; P<0.001), corticosteroid therapy (HR 2.80; 95% CI 1.59 to 4.95; P<0.001), and elevated hs-CRP at week 1 (HR 2.36; 95% CI 1.32 to 4.21; P=0.004). The authors conclude hs-CRP is elevated in about three of four cases, identifies patients at higher risk of recurrence, and could be used to monitor activity and select therapy length.
cards.watchOut: Associations from a single prospective cohort; corticosteroid use here marks severity, not necessarily causation. CRP-guided treatment duration is an inference from this cohort, not a tested strategy.
cards.source: Imazio M et al. Prevalence of C-reactive protein elevation and time course of normalization in acute pericarditis: implications for the diagnosis, therapy, and prognosis of pericarditis. Circulation. 2011. PMID: 21357824. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.title: Eisenmenger syndrome: bosentan improved walk distance and haemodynamics without worsening oxygen saturation (BREATHE-5)
shelves.question: In Eisenmenger syndrome (WHO functional class III), does bosentan improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics without worsening systemic oxygen saturation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents · Bosentan · Double-Blind Method · Eisenmenger Complex · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THIN — 54 patients and surrogate endpoints, but it was the first placebo-controlled trial in this disease and it answered the safety fear that had kept the drug class away. BREATHE-5 randomised patients with WHO class III Eisenmenger syndrome 2:1 to bosentan (37) or placebo (17) for 16 weeks, with haemodynamics by right- and left-heart catheterisation. The primary safety endpoint cleared: the placebo-corrected effect on systemic pulse oximetry was +1.0% (95% CI −0.7 to 2.8) — bosentan did not worsen oxygen saturation by shunting more blood right-to-left. The primary efficacy endpoint also moved: pulmonary vascular resistance index fell by 472 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ versus placebo (P=0.0383), mean pulmonary artery pressure fell by 5.5 mm Hg (P=0.0363), and 6-minute walk distance rose by 53.1 m (P=0.0079). Four patients discontinued for adverse events (2 on bosentan, 5%; 2 on placebo, 12%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a small, short, surrogate-endpoint trial whose lasting contribution is permission — endothelin blockade does not desaturate Eisenmenger patients. Its class sibling's larger failure sits on the next shelf (MAESTRO, #2315), and the pair should be read together.

cards.headline: BREATHE-5 2006: walk distance +53.1 m vs placebo (P=0.0079); PVR index −472 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ (P=0.0383); oxygen saturation unchanged (+1.0%, CI −0.7 to 2.8)
cards.summary: BREATHE-5 2006: walk distance +53.1 m vs placebo (P=0.0079); PVR index −472 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ (P=0.0383); oxygen saturation unchanged (+1.0%, CI −0.7 to 2.8)
cards.people: 54 patients with World Health Organization functional class III Eisenmenger syndrome, randomised 2:1 to bosentan (37) or placebo (17) for 16 weeks in a multicentre trial. Primary safety endpoint: systemic pulse oximetry; primary efficacy endpoint: pulmonary vascular resistance index, both with catheterisation. Secondaries: 6-minute walk distance, further haemodynamics, functional class, and safety.
cards.result: The placebo-corrected effect on systemic pulse oximetry was 1.0% (95% confidence interval −0.7 to 2.8), demonstrating bosentan did not worsen oxygen saturation. Versus placebo, bosentan reduced pulmonary vascular resistance index (−472.0 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵; P=0.0383) and mean pulmonary arterial pressure (−5.5 mm Hg; P=0.0363), and increased exercise capacity (6-minute walk +53.1 m; P=0.0079). Four patients discontinued for adverse events — 2 (5%) on bosentan and 2 (12%) on placebo. The authors conclude that in this first placebo-controlled trial in Eisenmenger syndrome, bosentan was well tolerated and improved exercise capacity and haemodynamics without compromising peripheral oxygen saturation.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks, 54 patients, no clinical-event endpoints — the trial licenses use, it does not measure benefit on outcomes patients feel over years. The walk-distance gain (~53 m) sits just above the usual threshold of clinical noticeability and rests on 17 placebo patients.
cards.source: Galiè N et al. Bosentan therapy in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome: a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study (BREATHE-5). Circulation. 2006. PMID: 16801459. shelves.title: Eisenmenger syndrome: macitentan did not improve walk distance in the larger phase 3 trial (MAESTRO)
shelves.question: In Eisenmenger syndrome (WHO functional class II–III), does macitentan improve 6-minute walk distance versus placebo over 16 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents · Biomarkers · Child · Double-Blind Method · Down Syndrome · Eisenmenger Complex · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Pulmonary Artery · Pyrimidines · Recovery of Function · Sulfonamides · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Walk Test · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The larger, better-powered test of the endothelin hypothesis in Eisenmenger syndrome — and the primary endpoint missed cleanly, in the wrong direction by a whisker. MAESTRO randomised 226 patients aged at least 12 in WHO class II–III (60% in class II; 27% already on a PDE5 inhibitor; complex defects and Down syndrome eligible) to macitentan 10 mg daily (114) or placebo (112) for 16 weeks. Walk distance improved by 18.3 m on macitentan and 19.7 m on placebo (least-squares mean difference −4.7 m; 95% confidence limits −22.8 to 13.5; P=0.612); functional class improved in fewer macitentan patients (8.8% vs 14.3%; odds ratio 0.53). Two secondary signals favoured the drug — NT-proBNP fell relative to placebo (geometric-mean ratio 0.80; 95% CL 0.68 to 0.94) and, in the 39-patient haemodynamic substudy, pulmonary vascular resistance index fell (ratio 0.87; 95% CL 0.73 to 1.03) — biomarkers moving while the patient-centred endpoint did not. A haemoglobin fall of at least 2 g/dL occurred in 36.0% on macitentan versus 8.9% on placebo; headache was commoner (11.4% vs 4.5%); one patient died, in the macitentan group. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) on the primary question as posed. Placed beside BREATHE-5 (Shelf #2314) by design: small positive predecessor, larger null successor — the standard correction pattern of this literature, and a standing warning about class-level inference from pilot trials.

cards.headline: MAESTRO 2019: walk change +18.3 m (macitentan) vs +19.7 m (placebo) — difference −4.7 m, P=0.612; NT-proBNP fell (ratio 0.80); haemoglobin dropped ≥2 g/dL in 36.0% vs 8.9%
cards.summary: MAESTRO 2019: walk change +18.3 m (macitentan) vs +19.7 m (placebo) — difference −4.7 m, P=0.612; NT-proBNP fell (ratio 0.80); haemoglobin dropped ≥2 g/dL in 36.0% vs 8.9%
cards.people: 226 patients with Eisenmenger syndrome aged at least 12 years in WHO functional class II–III (60% class II at baseline; 27% receiving PDE5 inhibitors; complex cardiac defects and Down syndrome eligible), randomised 1:1 to macitentan 10 mg once daily (114) or placebo (112) for 16 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in 6-minute walk distance. Secondaries included functional class; exploratory endpoints included NT-proBNP and, in a substudy, pulmonary vascular resistance index.
cards.result: At week 16, mean walk distance changed by 18.3 m on macitentan and 19.7 m on placebo (least-squares mean difference −4.7 m; 95% confidence limits −22.8 to 13.5; P=0.612). Functional class improved in 8.8% versus 14.3% (odds ratio 0.53; 95% CL 0.23 to 1.24). NT-proBNP decreased with macitentan versus placebo (ratio of geometric means 0.80; 95% CL 0.68 to 0.94), and in the haemodynamic substudy (39 patients) pulmonary vascular resistance index decreased (ratio 0.87; 95% CL 0.73 to 1.03). Commonest adverse events: headache (11.4% vs 4.5%) and upper respiratory infection (9.6% vs 6.3%); a haemoglobin decrease of at least 2 g/dL occurred in 36.0% versus 8.9%. Five patients discontinued prematurely (3 macitentan, 2 placebo) and one patient died (macitentan group). The authors conclude macitentan did not show superiority over placebo on exercise capacity in Eisenmenger syndrome.

shelves.title: Fontan circulation: udenafil missed its peak-exercise primary endpoint but improved submaximal exercise measures (FUEL)
shelves.question: In adolescents with Fontan physiology, does the PDE5 inhibitor udenafil improve peak oxygen consumption and submaximal exercise performance versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Exercise · Female · Fontan Procedure · Heart Diseases · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Oxygen Consumption · Phosphodiesterase 5 Inhibitors · Placebo Effect · Pyrimidines · Sulfonamides · Thrombosis · Treatment Outcome · Benzenesulfonamides
shelves.balance: A genuinely split result, and the shelf keeps it split. FUEL randomised 400 adolescents with Fontan physiology (mean age 15.5) at 30 centres to udenafil 87.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 26 weeks. The primary outcome — change in peak oxygen consumption — missed: peak VO2 rose 44 ± 245 mL/min (2.8%) on udenafil and fell 3.7 ± 228 mL/min (−0.2%) on placebo (P=0.071). At the ventilatory anaerobic threshold, however, three prespecified exercise measures all improved significantly with udenafil: oxygen consumption (+33 ± 185 [3.2%] vs −9 ± 193 [−0.9%] mL/min; P=0.012), ventilatory equivalents for carbon dioxide (−0.8 vs −0.06; P=0.014), and work rate (+3.8 vs +0.34 W; P=0.021). There was no difference in myocardial performance index, reactive hyperaemia index, or BNP. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the honest summary is that submaximal exercise — the intensity at which Fontan patients actually live their days — improved, while the maximal-effort primary did not reach significance; whether the submaximal gains are worth a twice-daily drug in an adolescent is a judgement the trial informs but cannot settle. The shelf resists both available spins: it is not a positive trial, and it is not a nothing-happened trial.

cards.headline: FUEL 2020: peak VO2 change +44 vs −3.7 mL/min (P=0.071 — primary missed); at the anaerobic threshold, VO2 +33 vs −9 mL/min (P=0.012) and work rate +3.8 vs +0.34 W (P=0.021)
cards.summary: FUEL 2020: peak VO2 change +44 vs −3.7 mL/min (P=0.071 — primary missed); at the anaerobic threshold, VO2 +33 vs −9 mL/min (P=0.012) and work rate +3.8 vs +0.34 W (P=0.021)
cards.people: 400 participants with Fontan physiology randomised 1:1 to udenafil 87.5 mg twice daily or placebo at 30 centres in North America and Korea (2017–2019). Mean age 15.5 ± 2 years; 60% male; 81% white. Primary outcome: between-group difference in change in peak oxygen consumption at 26 weeks. Secondaries: submaximal exercise at the ventilatory anaerobic threshold, myocardial performance index, log reactive hyperaemia index, and BNP. All 400 were included in the primary analysis with imputation for 21 with missing endpoints.
cards.result: Peak oxygen consumption increased by 44 ± 245 mL/min (2.8%) in the udenafil group and declined by 3.7 ± 228 mL/min (−0.2%) in the placebo group (P=0.071) — the primary outcome was not significantly improved. At the ventilatory anaerobic threshold, udenafil improved oxygen consumption (+33 ± 185 [3.2%] vs −9 ± 193 [−0.9%] mL/min; P=0.012), ventilatory equivalents of carbon dioxide (−0.8 vs −0.06; P=0.014), and work rate (+3.8 vs +0.34 W; P=0.021). There was no difference in change of myocardial performance index, log reactive hyperaemia index, or serum BNP. The authors conclude udenafil was not associated with improved peak exercise oxygen consumption but was associated with improvements in multiple measures of exercise performance at the ventilatory anaerobic threshold.
cards.watchOut: Secondary endpoints after a missed primary are hypothesis-strengthening, not confirmatory — the P values here are nominal across several submaximal measures. The peak-VO2 standard deviations (±245 mL/min against a 48 mL/min separation) show how noisy maximal testing is in this population.
cards.source: Goldberg DJ et al. Results of the FUEL Trial. Circulation. 2020. PMID: 31736357. Registry ID: NCT02741115, from the record. shelves.title: Fontan circulation: bosentan improved peak oxygen uptake and functional class over 14 weeks (TEMPO)
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults after the Fontan operation, does bosentan improve peak oxygen uptake, exercise time, and functional class versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Bosentan · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Fontan Procedure · Hemodynamics · Humans · Infant · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Placebos · Postoperative Complications · Receptor, Endothelin A · Statistics, Nonparametric · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: THIN — small and short, but randomised, double-blind, and positive on its primary where its larger macitentan successor (RUBATO, Shelf #2318) was not. TEMPO randomised 75 adolescents and adults after Fontan palliation 1:1 to bosentan or placebo for 14 weeks; 69 (92%) completed. Peak oxygen consumption rose 2.0 mL/kg/min (28.7 to 30.7) on bosentan versus 0.6 (28.4 to 29.0) on placebo (P=0.02); exercise test time rose 0.48 versus 0.08 minutes (P=0.04); nine bosentan patients improved one functional class and no placebo patient did (P=0.0085). Side effects were mild and equally frequent in both groups; no serious adverse effects occurred and no patient's liver enzymes exceeded three times the upper limit — notable for a bosentan trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a 14-week, 75-patient trial can show that exercise capacity moves; it cannot show durability, and the Fontan literature's pattern (promising small trial, null large trial — BREATHE-5 into MAESTRO, this trial into RUBATO) is itself part of the evidence. The shelf is deliberately shelved adjacent to RUBATO so the pair is read together.

cards.people: 75 adolescents and adults after the Fontan operation, randomised 1:1 to bosentan or placebo for 14 weeks. Assessments: cardiopulmonary exercise testing, functional class, blood samples, and quality-of-life questionnaires at baseline and end of treatment. Sixty-nine patients (92%) completed the study.
cards.result: Peak oxygen consumption increased 2.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (28.7 to 30.7) in the bosentan group versus 0.6 (28.4 to 29.0) in the placebo group (P=0.02). Exercise test time increased 0.48 minutes (6.79 to 7.27) versus 0.08 minutes (6.94 to 7.02) (P=0.04). Nine bosentan-treated patients improved one functional class; none improved on placebo (P=0.0085). Side effects were mild and occurred equally in both groups; no serious adverse effects were seen and no patients had liver enzyme levels above three times the upper limit of normal. The authors conclude bosentan improves exercise capacity, exercise time, and functional class in Fontan patients without serious adverse events or hepatotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen weeks is a demonstration, not a treatment course; and the trial predates the larger null RUBATO trial of macitentan in the same physiology (Shelf #2318). Functional-class improvement of 9 versus 0 rests on very small numbers.

shelves.title: Fontan circulation: macitentan did not improve exercise capacity over 52 weeks in the phase 3 trial (RUBATO)
shelves.question: In Fontan-palliated adolescents and adults (NYHA class II–III), does macitentan improve peak oxygen consumption versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Fontan Procedure · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Pyrimidines · Adolescent · Child · Treatment Outcome · Sulfonamides · Heart Defects, Congenital · Adult · Prospective Studies · Young Adult · Oxygen Consumption · Time Factors · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Endothelin A Receptor Antagonists
shelves.balance: The definitive-sized endothelin trial in Fontan physiology, and it closed the question its pilot literature had opened. RUBATO randomised 137 Fontan-palliated patients aged at least 12 (NYHA class II–III, total cavopulmonary connection more than a year earlier, no signs of Fontan failure) to macitentan 10 mg (68) or placebo (69); 92.7% completed 52 weeks of double-blind treatment. The primary endpoint — change in peak oxygen consumption at week 16 — was not met: −0.16 ± 2.86 mL/kg/min on macitentan versus −0.67 ± 2.66 on placebo (treatment difference estimate 0.62; 99% CI −0.62 to 1.85; P=.19), and no treatment effect appeared in either secondary endpoint (peak VO2 change over 52 weeks; accelerometer-measured daily activity at week 16). Macitentan was generally well tolerated — headache, nasopharyngitis, and pyrexia were the commonest events in the double-blind phase — and the open-label extension was discontinued early precisely because the double-blind trial had missed. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): in stable Fontan patients without failure, macitentan does not improve exercise capacity. Beside TEMPO's small positive bosentan result (Shelf #2317), this completes the slate's repeated lesson — in congenital-heart physiology, the bigger trial is the one to believe.

cards.headline: RUBATO 2025: week-16 peak VO2 change −0.16 vs −0.67 mL/kg/min (difference 0.62; 99% CI −0.62 to 1.85; P=.19); no secondary endpoint met; extension stopped early
cards.summary: RUBATO 2025: week-16 peak VO2 change −0.16 vs −0.67 mL/kg/min (difference 0.62; 99% CI −0.62 to 1.85; P=.19); no secondary endpoint met; extension stopped early
cards.people: 137 Fontan-palliated patients aged at least 12 years with NYHA functional class II or III, more than one year after total cavopulmonary connection and without signs of Fontan failure or clinical deterioration, randomised to macitentan 10 mg (68) or placebo (69) in a multicentre 52-week double-blind study (RUBATO-DB), followed by an open-label extension (RUBATO-OL). Primary endpoint: change in peak oxygen consumption from baseline to week 16. Secondaries: peak VO2 change over 52 weeks and accelerometer-measured daily physical activity at week 16. 92.7% completed double-blind treatment.
cards.result: At week 16, mean change in peak oxygen consumption was −0.16 ± 2.86 mL/kg/min with macitentan versus −0.67 ± 2.66 with placebo (median unbiased treatment difference estimate 0.62 mL/kg/min; 99% repeated CI −0.62 to 1.85; P=.19) — the primary endpoint was not met. No treatment effect was observed in either secondary endpoint. The most common adverse events with macitentan were headache, nasopharyngitis, and pyrexia; across both study phases, COVID-19, headache, and fatigue were most common. The open-label extension was prematurely discontinued because the double-blind trial met neither its primary nor secondary endpoints. The authors conclude macitentan did not improve exercise capacity versus placebo in Fontan palliation and was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The population was stable Fontan patients explicitly without failure — the null does not address macitentan in deteriorating Fontan physiology, where no randomised data exist. The point estimate (both groups declined slightly) also documents the natural history: exercise capacity erodes even in 'stable' Fontan patients.
cards.source: Clift P et al. Efficacy and safety of macitentan in Fontan-palliated patients: 52-week randomized, placebo-controlled RUBATO Phase 3 trial and open-label extension. J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2025. PMID: 39216715. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.question: In children and young adults after the Fontan operation, does oral sildenafil improve exercise performance?

shelves.balance: The mechanistic hope in Fontan physiology is that lowering pulmonary vascular resistance improves cardiac filling, and this small crossover trial (STEP) is the cleanest test of sildenafil against it. Twenty-eight children and young adults after Fontan were randomised to sildenafil 20 mg three times daily or placebo for 6 weeks, washed out for 6 weeks, then crossed over, with exercise testing at the start and end of each phase. Peak oxygen consumption did not change on sildenafil. What did improve was ventilatory efficiency: respiratory rate and minute ventilation at peak exercise fell significantly, and at the anaerobic threshold the ventilatory equivalents of carbon dioxide fell significantly. A suggestion of improved oxygen consumption at the anaerobic threshold was confined to two subgroups — single left or mixed ventricular morphology, and baseline BNP at least 100 pg/mL. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: sildenafil measurably improves ventilatory efficiency during peak and submaximal exercise after Fontan, but the headline exercise measure — peak oxygen uptake — did not move, and the trial is 28 patients. Read beside FUEL (Shelf #2316, udenafil: peak VO2 also missed) and RUBATO (Shelf #2318), the Fontan pharmacotherapy pattern is consistent: submaximal signals recur, peak capacity does not.

cards.headline: STEP 2011: no change in peak oxygen consumption; ventilatory equivalents of CO2 at the anaerobic threshold significantly improved; subgroup-only suggestion of better submaximal oxygen uptake
cards.summary: STEP 2011: no change in peak oxygen consumption; ventilatory equivalents of CO2 at the anaerobic threshold significantly improved; subgroup-only suggestion of better submaximal oxygen uptake
cards.people: 28 children and young adults with single-ventricle physiology after the Fontan operation, in a double-blind crossover trial of sildenafil 20 mg three times daily versus placebo, 6 weeks per phase separated by a 6-week washout, with exercise stress testing at the start and finish of each phase.
cards.result: After sildenafil, subjects had a significantly decreased respiratory rate and decreased minute ventilation at peak exercise, and at the anaerobic threshold significantly decreased ventilatory equivalents of carbon dioxide. There was no change in oxygen consumption during peak exercise. A suggestion of improved oxygen consumption at the anaerobic threshold was limited to the subgroup with single left or mixed ventricular morphology and to the subgroup with baseline serum brain natriuretic peptide at least 100 pg/mL. The authors conclude sildenafil significantly improved ventilatory efficiency during peak and submaximal exercise and may be an important agent for improving exercise performance after Fontan.
cards.watchOut: A 28-patient crossover with surrogate exercise endpoints: the subgroup findings (morphology, BNP) are hypothesis-generating only, and no clinical outcome was measured. The null on peak VO2 is the result to carry away alongside the ventilatory signal.
cards.source: Goldberg DJ et al. shelves.title: Fontan thromboprophylaxis in children: rivaroxaban looked comparable to aspirin in the descriptive UNIVERSE study
shelves.question: In children after the Fontan procedure, is weight-adjusted rivaroxaban an acceptable alternative to aspirin for thromboprophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Child · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Hemorrhage · Humans · Rivaroxaban · Stroke · Thrombosis · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: UNIVERSE is the only randomised evidence for an everyday Fontan question, and it was designed to describe, not to prove. In part B, 100 children post-Fontan were randomised 2:1 to open-label body-weight-adjusted liquid rivaroxaban or aspirin for 12 months (112 enrolled overall including the 12-patient pharmacokinetic part A). Thrombotic events were few in both arms: one pulmonary embolism on rivaroxaban (2% overall event rate) versus one ischaemic stroke and two venous thromboses on aspirin (9% overall event rate) — fewer on rivaroxaban, not statistically significant. Bleeding: one major bleed on rivaroxaban (epistaxis requiring transfusion); clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding 6% on rivaroxaban versus 9% on aspirin; trivial bleeding 33% versus 35%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rivaroxaban's safety profile looked similar to aspirin's and no efficacy signal ran against it, but with event counts of 1 versus 3 the study cannot establish equivalence — it establishes that the question is answerable and that neither arm misbehaved in a year of use.

cards.headline: UNIVERSE 2021: thrombotic events 2% on rivaroxaban vs 9% on aspirin (1 vs 3 patients; NS); one major bleed on rivaroxaban; nonmajor bleeding 6% vs 9%
cards.summary: UNIVERSE 2021: thrombotic events 2% on rivaroxaban vs 9% on aspirin (1 vs 3 patients; NS); one major bleed on rivaroxaban; nonmajor bleeding 6% vs 9%
cards.type: Randomised open-label multicentre study (UNIVERSE, parts A and B)
cards.people: 112 children post-Fontan enrolled across 35 sites in 10 countries. Part A (12 participants) established the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic dosing of a body-weight-adjusted liquid rivaroxaban regimen. Part B randomised 100 participants 2:1 to open-label rivaroxaban versus aspirin (ASA) over 12 months.
cards.result: In part B, one participant on rivaroxaban had a pulmonary embolism (2% overall thrombotic event rate); on aspirin, one participant had an ischaemic stroke and two had venous thrombosis (9% overall event rate) — fewer events on rivaroxaban, albeit not statistically significant. For safety: major bleeding occurred in one rivaroxaban participant (epistaxis requiring transfusion); clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding occurred in 6% on rivaroxaban versus 9% on aspirin; trivial bleeding in 33% versus 35%. The authors conclude rivaroxaban had a similar safety profile to aspirin with numerically fewer thrombotic events.
cards.watchOut: Descriptive by design — no power calculation for efficacy, open-label, and single-digit event counts. The 2% vs 9% contrast is three patients versus one and must not be quoted as a treatment effect. This remains the only randomised data for post-Fontan thromboprophylaxis in children.
cards.source: McCrindle BW et al. Thromboprophylaxis for Children Post-Fontan Procedure: Insights From the UNIVERSE Study. J Am Heart Assoc. 2021. PMID: 34558312. Registry ID: NCT02846532. shelves.title: Systemic right ventricle: valsartan did not preserve ventricular function over 3 years in the van der Bom trial
shelves.question: In adults with a systemic right ventricle, does valsartan preserve right ventricular ejection fraction versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Defects, Congenital · Heart Ventricles · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Multidetector Computed Tomography · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pilot Projects · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Tetrazoles · Transposition of Great Vessels · Valine · Valsartan · Ventricular Dysfunction, Right
shelves.balance: The systemic right ventricle — after atrial switch for transposition, or in congenitally corrected transposition — fails late, and whether renin–angiotensin blockade slows that failure was extrapolated for years from left-ventricular practice. The van der Bom trial is the direct test: 88 adults with a systemic right ventricle randomised double-blind to valsartan 160 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 years, with ejection fraction measured by cardiac magnetic resonance (or CT where MRI was contraindicated). The primary endpoint was null: the treatment effect on systemic RV ejection fraction was 1.3% (95% CI −1.3 to 3.9; P=0.34), and there was no significant effect on maximum exercise capacity, quality of life, or the frequency of significant clinical events; no serious adverse effects occurred in either group. The one asymmetry ran the other way from harm: right ventricular end-diastolic volume and mass rose more on placebo (by 15 mL and 8 g more) — remodelling markers favouring valsartan without a functional dividend. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): three years of valsartan does not preserve systemic RV function in this population, and the confidence interval excludes a large ejection-fraction benefit.

cards.headline: van der Bom 2013: RV ejection fraction treatment effect 1.3% (95% CI −1.3 to 3.9; P=0.34); no effect on exercise capacity, quality of life, or clinical events over 3 years
cards.summary: van der Bom 2013: RV ejection fraction treatment effect 1.3% (95% CI −1.3 to 3.9; P=0.34); no effect on exercise capacity, quality of life, or clinical events over 3 years
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled pilot trial (van der Bom)
cards.people: 88 adults with a systemic right ventricle due to congenitally or surgically corrected transposition of the great arteries, randomised to valsartan 160 mg twice daily (44) or placebo (44) for 3 years. Primary endpoint: change in right ventricular ejection fraction by cardiovascular magnetic resonance or multidetector CT. Secondary endpoints: RV volumes and mass, peak oxygen uptake, quality of life. Intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: There was no significant effect of 3-year valsartan therapy on systemic right ventricular ejection fraction (treatment effect 1.3%; 95% CI −1.3% to 3.9%; P=0.34), maximum exercise capacity, or quality of life, and valsartan was associated with a similar frequency of significant clinical events as placebo. Right ventricular end-diastolic volume increased more in the placebo group than the valsartan group (difference 15 mL; 95% CI 3 to 28; P<0.01), as did RV mass (8 g; 95% CI 2 to 14; P=0.01). No serious adverse effects occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Pilot-sized (88 patients) and powered on a surrogate; a modest functional benefit inside the confidence interval cannot be excluded, and the volume/mass signal keeps a remodelling hypothesis alive without supporting treatment. The trial enrolled stable outpatients — it does not address valsartan started after systemic RV failure is established.
cards.source: van der Bom T et al. Effect of valsartan on systemic right ventricular function: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial. Circulation. 2013. PMID: 23247302. shelves.title: Systemic right ventricular dysfunction: dapagliflozin was followed by better walk distance and function in a small uncontrolled study (DAPA-SRV)
shelves.question: In symptomatic patients with systemic right ventricular dysfunction, is starting dapagliflozin safe, and what happens to functional status and ventricular measures?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Glucosides · Ventricular Dysfunction, Right · Adult · Prospective Studies · Benzhydryl Compounds · Aged · Quality of Life · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Right · Stroke Volume · Young Adult · Heart Failure · Walk Test · Exercise Tolerance
shelves.balance: Read this shelf for what the study is, because the gap between its design and its promise is the whole story. DAPA-SRV is NOT a randomised trial: it is a prospective, observational, single-centre before-and-after study of 32 symptomatic patients (NYHA class at least 2) with systemic right ventricular dysfunction — 62% transposition with atrial switch, 38% congenitally corrected transposition — assessed before and 3 and 6 months after dapagliflozin was started, on background therapy including sacubitril/valsartan. At 6 months, 6-minute walk distance had improved (585 m versus 558 m at baseline; P=0.04), as had quality of life (KCCQ-12 score 91.5 versus 80.5; P<0.001) and systemic RV function (fractional area change 33% versus 28%; P=0.02; global longitudinal strain −13.1% versus −11.2%; P=0.04), and no significant side effects were observed. Every one of those numbers comes from an uncontrolled comparison in which expectation, regression to the mean, and co-interventions all push the same direction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): dapagliflozin appeared safe and well tolerated in 32 systemic-RV patients and the within-patient changes are encouraging — this is a reason to run the randomised trial the authors themselves call for, not a reason to treat the benefit as shown.

cards.headline: DAPA-SRV 2025: in 32 patients, 6-minute walk 558→585 m (P=0.04), KCCQ-12 80.5→91.5 (P<0.001), RV fractional area change 28%→33% (P=0.02) at 6 months; no significant side effects
cards.summary: DAPA-SRV 2025: in 32 patients, 6-minute walk 558→585 m (P=0.04), KCCQ-12 80.5→91.5 (P<0.001), RV fractional area change 28%→33% (P=0.02) at 6 months; no significant side effects
cards.type: Prospective observational single-centre before-and-after study (DAPA-SRV) — not randomised
cards.people: 32 symptomatic patients (NYHA functional class at least 2) with systemic right ventricular dysfunction despite medical treatment, enrolled at a single centre from February 2023 to February 2024; mean age 48 years (range 19–79), 62% men; 12 (38%) with congenitally corrected transposition and 20 (62%) with transposition after atrial switch. Assessments at baseline and 3 and 6 months after dapagliflozin introduction. Primary endpoint: 6-minute walk distance. There was no control group.
cards.result: At 6 months, 6-minute walk distance significantly improved (585 m versus 558 m; P=0.04). Quality of life (KCCQ-12: 91.5 versus 80.5; P<0.001) and systemic RV function (fractional area change 33% versus 28%, P=0.02; global longitudinal strain −13.1% versus −11.2%, P=0.04) also improved. No significant side effects were observed. The authors conclude this is the first study demonstrating functional benefits and safety of dapagliflozin in symptomatic systemic RV dysfunction on sacubitril/valsartan, and that larger randomized trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled pre–post design: walk distance and quality-of-life scores are exactly the measures most inflated by expectation and repeated testing, and there is no comparator arm to absorb them. The drafting slate described this study as a randomised evaluation — the record says observational, and the shelf is stamped accordingly.
cards.source: Albertini M et al. Safety and Efficacy of Dapagliflozin in Patients With Systemic Right Ventricular Dysfunction: DAPA-SRV Trial. J Am Heart Assoc. 2025. PMID: 40439149. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.title: Fontan circulation: resistance training raised cardiac output and exercise capacity in an 11-patient controlled study (Cordina)
shelves.question: In adults with a Fontan circulation, does lower-limb resistance training improve cardiac output, exercise capacity, and tolerance of positive airway pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiac Output · Exercise · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Fontan Procedure · Heart Defects, Congenital · Humans · Male · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Resistance Training
shelves.balance: The Fontan circulation has no subpulmonary ventricle, so cardiac filling leans on the respiratory bellows and the peripheral muscle pump — which makes this the rare exercise study with a direct haemodynamic hypothesis. Cordina and colleagues studied 11 adults with Fontan-type circulation; 6 underwent 20 weeks of high-intensity resistance training and the rest were non-exercising controls, with cardiac magnetic resonance flow measurement and exercise testing. In the trained state, muscle strength rose 43% (P=0.002), total muscle mass rose 1.94 kg (P=0.003), and peak oxygen uptake rose 183 mL/min (P=0.02). The detraining phase is what makes the physiology persuasive: after 12 months detrained, peak VO2 fell (2.72 versus 2.18 L/min; P<0.001), stroke volume fell at rest (by 11 mL; P=0.01) and during moderate exercise (by 16 mL; P=0.04), inspiratory-dependent inferior vena cava return during exercise rose 40% (P=0.02), and cardiac output on continuous positive airway pressure was lower than in the trained state (77 versus 101 mL/s; P=0.03). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the within-person training–detraining pattern fits the muscle-pump mechanism beautifully, but this is 11 patients, six of them trained, in a non-randomised comparison — a mechanism demonstrated, not a therapy established.

cards.summary: Cordina 2013: strength +43% (P=0.002), peak VO2 +183 mL/min (P=0.02) after 20 weeks of resistance training; detraining reversed stroke volume, VO2, and CPAP cardiac output
cards.type: Small controlled training study with detraining follow-up (Cordina)
cards.people: 11 adults with Fontan-type circulation (mean age 32 years); 6 underwent 20 weeks of high-intensity resistance training and the remainder were non-exercising controls. Cardiac magnetic resonance with real-time flow at rest, during exercise, and on continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) was performed in 4 trainers in the trained state and again after 12 months of detraining; cardiopulmonary exercise testing before and after training.
cards.result: In the trained state, muscle strength increased by 43% (P=0.002), total muscle mass by 1.94 kg (P=0.003), and peak VO2 by 183 mL/min (P=0.02). After detraining, calf muscle mass and peak workload fell significantly (P<0.03 for both), as did peak VO2 (2.72 vs 2.18 L/min; P<0.001) and oxygen pulse (16% lower; P=0.005). Stroke volume on MRI decreased after detraining at rest (by 11 mL; P=0.01) and during moderate-intensity exercise (by 16 mL; P=0.04); inspiratory-dependent IVC blood return during exercise was 40% higher (P=0.02). On CPAP, cardiac output was lower in the detrained state (101 vs 77 mL/s; P=0.03). The authors conclude resistance training improves muscle mass and strength and is associated with improved cardiac filling, stroke volume, exercise capacity, and cardiac output on CPAP.
cards.watchOut: Six trained patients and a non-randomised control group — selection and motivation effects are unconstrained, and the detraining comparisons involve only 4 patients. Treat as mechanistic proof of concept for the muscle-pump hypothesis, not as a prescription-grade effect size.

shelves.title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: dexrazoxane roughly halved cardiac events in two blinded trials (Swain)
shelves.question: In patients receiving doxorubicin-based chemotherapy, does dexrazoxane reduce cardiac events without compromising antitumour effect?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibiotics, Antineoplastic · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Cardiovascular Agents · Cyclophosphamide · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Doxorubicin · Female · Fluorouracil · Heart Failure · Humans · Prospective Studies · Razoxane · Risk Factors · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Dexrazoxane is the one cardioprotectant whose evidence predates the imaging-surrogate era: two multicentre double-blind trials (088001 and 088006) randomised 534 women with advanced breast cancer receiving fluorouracil, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide to dexrazoxane (10:1 ratio to doxorubicin) or placebo, with serial MUGA monitoring and a cardiac-event endpoint of predefined ejection-fraction change or clinical heart failure. Placebo patients carried markedly higher cardiac-event hazard: hazard ratio for placebo versus dexrazoxane 2.63 (95% CI 1.61 to 4.27; P<.001) in 088001 and 2.00 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.96; P=.038) in 088006 — i.e., dexrazoxane cut the cardiac-event hazard by roughly 60% and 50% relative, respectively. The honest complication is antitumour effect: objective response rate was lower with dexrazoxane in 088001 (46.8% versus 60.5%, a 14-point difference; P=.019) but not in 088006 (53.7% versus 49.3%), and time to progression and survival did not differ significantly in either study. Toxicity traded mildly: lower granulocyte and platelet nadirs and more injection pain on dexrazoxane, no difference in fever, infection, or haemorrhage. PROPOSED LIKELY: dexrazoxane genuinely prevents doxorubicin cardiac events — the first agent shown to do so — while the single-study response-rate dip is why its use settled into high-cumulative-dose and metastatic settings rather than routine adjuvant care.

cards.headline: Swain 1997 (two trials): cardiac-event hazard ratio, placebo vs dexrazoxane, 2.63 (P<.001) and 2.00 (P=.038); survival and time to progression not significantly different
cards.summary: Swain 1997 (two trials): cardiac-event hazard ratio, placebo vs dexrazoxane, 2.63 (P<.001) and 2.00 (P=.038); survival and time to progression not significantly different
cards.type: Two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Swain 088001 + 088006)
cards.people: 534 patients with advanced breast cancer randomised in two multicentre, double-blind studies (088001 and 088006, 1988–1991) to fluorouracil, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide (FAC) with dexrazoxane (dexrazoxane-to-doxorubicin ratio 10:1) or placebo every 3 weeks, monitored with serial MUGA scans. A cardiac event was a predefined ejection-fraction change or congestive heart failure.
cards.result: The hazard ratio of placebo to dexrazoxane for a cardiac event was 2.63 (95% CI 1.61 to 4.27; P<.001) for 088001 and 2.00 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.96; P=.038) for 088006 — a roughly 60% and 50% relative reduction in the cardiac-event hazard with dexrazoxane. Objective response rates for 088001 were 46.8% on dexrazoxane and 60.5% on placebo (difference 14%; 95% CI −25% to −2%; P=.019), and for 088006 were 53.7% and 49.3% (P=.63). Time to progression and survival were not significantly different between arms in either study. Dexrazoxane arms had lower granulocyte and platelet counts at nadir (P=.009 and P=.004) and more pain on injection (P=.001), with no difference in fever, infection, or haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: The population is metastatic breast cancer on FAC in 1988–1991 — anthracycline doses, monitoring, and alternatives have all moved on, and the 088001 response-rate finding is a real (if unreplicated) shadow. The historical paediatric secondary-malignancy debate around dexrazoxane is outside this record and should not be silently imported into either direction.

shelves.title: Anthracycline therapy in breast cancer: candesartan slightly attenuated LVEF decline, metoprolol did not (PRADA)
shelves.question: In early breast cancer receiving anthracycline-based adjuvant therapy, do candesartan or metoprolol prevent decline in left ventricular ejection fraction?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Anthracyclines · Antineoplastic Agents · Benzimidazoles · Biphenyl Compounds · Breast Neoplasms · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Metoprolol · Middle Aged · Tetrazoles · Trastuzumab · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PRADA asked whether the two cheapest neurohormonal drugs could blunt the ejection-fraction decline of adjuvant breast-cancer therapy, and it answered differently for each. In a 2×2 factorial double-blind trial, 130 women with early breast cancer receiving anthracycline-containing regimens (with or without trastuzumab and radiation) were randomised to candesartan, metoprolol, both, or matching placebos, with LVEF measured by cardiac magnetic resonance (a 5-point change was prespecified as clinically important). The overall LVEF decline was 2.6 percentage points (95% CI 1.5 to 3.8) in the placebo group versus 0.8 points (95% CI −0.4 to 1.9) in the candesartan group — a between-group difference significant at P=0.026, but a fraction of the trial's own 5-point importance threshold. Metoprolol had no observed effect on LVEF decline, and there was no interaction between the two treatments (P=0.530). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: candesartan softens the early LVEF drift of anthracycline therapy by roughly 2 points on average — a real pharmacological signal on a surrogate, at a magnitude whose clinical meaning (events, later dysfunction) this trial could not show.

cards.headline: PRADA 2016: LVEF decline 0.8 points on candesartan vs 2.6 on placebo (P=0.026 for difference); metoprolol without effect
cards.summary: PRADA 2016: LVEF decline 0.8 points on candesartan vs 2.6 on placebo (P=0.026 for difference); metoprolol without effect
cards.people: 130 adult women with early breast cancer and no serious comorbidity, randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to candesartan cilexetil, metoprolol succinate, or matching placebos alongside adjuvant anthracycline-containing therapy with or without trastuzumab and radiation. Primary outcome: change in LVEF by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; a 5-point change was a priori considered clinically important.
cards.result: There was no interaction between candesartan and metoprolol (P=0.530). The overall decline in LVEF was 2.6 (95% CI 1.5, 3.8) percentage points in the placebo group and 0.8 (95% CI −0.4, 1.9) in the candesartan group in the intention-to-treat analysis (P=0.026 for the between-group difference). No effect of metoprolol on the overall decline in LVEF was observed. The authors conclude that concomitant candesartan provides protection against early decline in global left ventricular function during adjuvant anthracycline-containing therapy.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, 130 patients, imaging surrogate — and the candesartan effect (~1.8 points) is well under the 5-point difference the investigators themselves called clinically important. A statistically real, clinically small effect; no event outcomes.
