shelves.title: Intensive chemotherapy for blood cancers: enalapril plus carvedilol preserved LVEF and cut death or heart failure in a small trial (OVERCOME)
shelves.question: In patients with haematological malignancies receiving intensive anthracycline chemotherapy, does combined enalapril plus carvedilol prevent LV systolic dysfunction and the composite of death or heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antineoplastic Agents · Carbazoles · Carvedilol · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Echocardiography, Doppler · Enalapril · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hematologic Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Propanolamines · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: OVERCOME is the most clinically suggestive of the small cardioprotection trials — and the one whose control arm should make a careful reader pause. Ninety patients with haematological malignancies receiving intensive anthracycline chemotherapy (36 with acute leukaemia, 54 undergoing autologous stem-cell transplantation) and no baseline LV dysfunction were randomised to enalapril plus carvedilol or to control. At 6 months, LVEF was unchanged in the intervention group and fell significantly in controls — an absolute difference of −3.1% by echocardiography (P=0.035) and −3.4% by cardiac magnetic resonance (P=0.09). The clinical composite ran the same way: death or heart failure occurred in 6.7% on intervention versus 22.2% on control (P=0.036), and death, heart failure, or a final LVEF under 45% in 6.7% versus 24.4% (P=0.02). Those are large absolute differences from a 90-patient single-centre trial in which the untreated arm fared strikingly badly — contemporary anthracycline cohorts (see ICOS-ONE, Shelf #2328) usually show far less damage. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, and flagged Tier C because the composite embeds death: the direction is coherent and the LVEF preservation is real within the trial; the size of the clinical benefit is the part not to swallow whole.

cards.headline: OVERCOME 2013: death or heart failure 6.7% vs 22.2% (P=0.036); LVEF preserved on enalapril + carvedilol (−3.1% absolute difference by echo, P=0.035)
cards.summary: OVERCOME 2013: death or heart failure 6.7% vs 22.2% (P=0.036); LVEF preserved on enalapril + carvedilol (−3.1% absolute difference by echo, P=0.035)
cards.people: 90 patients with recently diagnosed acute leukaemia (36) or malignant haematological disease undergoing autologous stem-cell transplantation (54), without LV systolic dysfunction, randomised to enalapril plus carvedilol (45) or control (45). Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance before and 6 months after randomisation. Primary efficacy endpoint: absolute change in LVEF.
cards.result: At 6 months, LVEF did not change in the intervention group but significantly decreased in controls, an absolute difference of −3.1% by echocardiography (P=0.035) and −3.4% by CMR (P=0.09). The difference was larger in acute leukaemia (−6.38%; 95% CI −11.9 to −0.9) than in transplant patients (−1.0%; 95% CI −4.5 to 2.5). The intervention group had a lower incidence of the combined event of death or heart failure (6.7% vs 22%, P=0.036) and of death, heart failure, or final LVEF <45% (6.7% vs 24.4%, P=0.02). The authors conclude the combination may prevent LV systolic dysfunction during intensive chemotherapy and that larger studies should confirm clinical relevance.
cards.watchOut: Ninety patients, one centre, and a control arm with a 22% death-or-heart-failure rate at 6 months — far above comparable cohorts. The treatment effect is probably real in direction and overstated in size; the composite includes death, which is why this shelf is flagged Tier C for the developer's adjudication.

shelves.title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: carvedilol did not prevent LVEF decline in the largest beta-blocker trial (CECCY)
shelves.question: In HER2-negative breast cancer receiving anthracyclines, does carvedilol prevent LVEF decline?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Antineoplastic Agents · Breast Neoplasms · Cardiotoxicity · Carvedilol · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: CECCY is the largest beta-blocker prevention trial in this literature, and its primary answer is no. Two hundred patients with HER2-negative breast cancer and normal LVEF receiving anthracyclines (240 mg/m²) were randomised double-blind to carvedilol or placebo until chemotherapy completion. The primary endpoint — a reduction in LVEF of at least 10% at 6 months — occurred in 14.5% on carvedilol and 13.5% on placebo (P=1.0), and there were no differences in change in LVEF or in B-type natriuretic peptide between groups. Two secondary measures favoured carvedilol: troponin I levels over time were significantly lower (P=0.003), and the incidence of diastolic dysfunction was lower (P=0.039). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) on the question the trial was powered for: carvedilol does not prevent early LVEF-defined cardiotoxicity at contemporary anthracycline doses. The troponin and diastolic signals are the familiar secondary-endpoint residue — worth a hypothesis, not a prescription — and they sit beside PRADA's null metoprolol arm (Shelf #2325) as the beta-blocker half of the cardioprotection story.

cards.people: 200 patients with HER2-negative breast cancer and normal LVEF referred for anthracycline chemotherapy (240 mg/m²), randomised double-blind to carvedilol or placebo until chemotherapy completion. Primary endpoint: prevention of a ≥10% reduction in LVEF at 6 months. Secondary outcomes: troponin I, B-type natriuretic peptide, diastolic dysfunction.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 14 patients (14.5%) in the carvedilol group and 13 patients (13.5%) in the placebo group (P=1.0). No differences in changes of LVEF or B-type natriuretic peptide were noted between groups. Troponin I levels over time were significantly lower in the carvedilol group (P=0.003), and a lower incidence of diastolic dysfunction was noted (P=0.039). Cardiotoxicity incidence overall was 13.5% to 14.5%. The authors conclude carvedilol had no impact on the incidence of early-onset LVEF reduction, while reducing troponin levels and diastolic dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: The null is on an imaging-defined endpoint at 6 months with a moderate anthracycline dose — it does not exclude benefit at higher cumulative doses or on late dysfunction. Secondary troponin/diastolic findings are multiplicity-exposed and should not be promoted over the primary result.

shelves.title: Anthracycline cardioprotection strategy: troponin-triggered enalapril matched universal enalapril in a low-event trial (ICOS-ONE)
shelves.question: In patients receiving anthracyclines, is enalapril given only when troponin rises as good as enalapril given to everyone from the start at preventing cardiotoxicity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Anthracyclines · Antineoplastic Agents · Cardiotoxicity · Enalapril · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Troponin C · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: ICOS-ONE compared two philosophies of enalapril prevention — give it to everyone before chemotherapy, or give it only to patients whose troponin rises — and the trial's real finding is how little cardiotoxicity there was to prevent. In this multicentre open-label trial, 273 patients receiving anthracyclines (76% breast cancer; median cumulative epirubicin 360 mg/m², doxorubicin 240 mg/m²; low cardiovascular risk) were randomised to universal pre-chemotherapy enalapril ('prevention') or troponin-triggered enalapril. The primary outcome, incidence of troponin elevation, was 23% in the prevention arm and 26% in the troponin-triggered arm (P=0.50). Cardiotoxicity — a 10-point LVEF reduction to below 50% — developed in just 3 patients (1.1%): two on prevention, one on triggered treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference): the strategies did not differ on the troponin endpoint, and with three outcome events in 273 patients the trial cannot rank them on the endpoint patients care about. The authors' own reading — that in low-risk patients at these cumulative doses a troponin-triggered strategy may be the more convenient way to capture enalapril's benefit — is a reasonable inference and an unproven one.

cards.headline: ICOS-ONE 2018: troponin elevation 23% (prevention) vs 26% (troponin-triggered), P=0.50; cardiotoxicity in 3 of 273 patients (1.1%)
cards.summary: ICOS-ONE 2018: troponin elevation 23% (prevention) vs 26% (troponin-triggered), P=0.50; cardiotoxicity in 3 of 273 patients (1.1%)
cards.people: 273 patients receiving anthracycline-containing chemotherapy in 21 Italian hospitals (88% women, mean age 51; 76% breast cancer; 3% hypertension, 4% diabetes), randomised open-label to enalapril started before chemotherapy in all patients ('prevention') or enalapril started only on troponin increase ('troponin-triggered'). Troponin assayed on 2,596 samples across cycles and visits; echocardiograms at baseline and 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Primary outcome: incidence of troponin elevation above threshold.
cards.result: The incidence of troponin elevation was 23% in the prevention group and 26% in the troponin-triggered group (P=0.50). Three patients (1.1%) — two in the prevention and one in the troponin-triggered group — developed cardiotoxicity, defined as a 10-point reduction in LVEF to a value below 50%. Median cumulative doses were 360 mg/m² for epirubicin and 240 mg/m² for doxorubicin. The authors conclude that low cumulative anthracycline doses in low-cardiovascular-risk adults raise troponins without differences between the two enalapril strategies, and that a troponin-triggered strategy may be more convenient if enalapril's preventive benefit is assumed.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the population's event rate (1.1% cardiotoxicity) is far below the cohorts that motivated troponin-guided therapy — the trial compares strategies in a setting where little prevention was needed, so its null does not travel to high-dose or high-risk patients.

shelves.title: Anthracycline therapy in lymphoma: atorvastatin cut EF-defined cardiac dysfunction from 22% to 9% (STOP-CA)
shelves.question: In patients with lymphoma receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy, does atorvastatin 40 mg prevent significant LVEF decline?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Anthracyclines · Antibiotics, Antineoplastic · Atorvastatin · Double-Blind Method · Heart Failure · Retrospective Studies · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Cardiovascular Agents · Lymphoma · Heart Diseases · Follow-Up Studies · Male · Adult · Aged
shelves.balance: STOP-CA is the cleanest positive prevention trial in the cardio-oncology slate — with the discipline that its endpoint is an ejection-fraction definition, not heart failure. Three hundred patients with lymphoma receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy at nine US and Canadian centres were randomised double-blind to atorvastatin 40 mg daily or placebo for 12 months. The primary endpoint — an absolute LVEF decline of at least 10 points to a final value below 55% — occurred in 9% (13/150) on atorvastatin versus 22% (33/150) on placebo (P=.002): an absolute difference of 13 points, about a 59% relative reduction (the odds of the endpoint were roughly 3 times higher on placebo; odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.4 to 6.4). The secondary endpoint (decline of at least 5 points to below 55%) also favoured atorvastatin (13% versus 29%; P=.001). Clinical heart failure, printed here as the charter requires beside any dysfunction claim, did not differ: 13 adjudicated events (4%) over 24 months, 3% on atorvastatin versus 6% on placebo (P=.26). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: one well-executed blinded trial shows atorvastatin substantially reduces EF-defined cardiac dysfunction during lymphoma chemotherapy; whether that converts into fewer heart-failure events is untested at this size and horizon.

cards.headline: STOP-CA 2023: primary endpoint (LVEF decline ≥10 points to <55%) 9% atorvastatin vs 22% placebo (P=.002); heart failure events 3% vs 6% (P=.26)
cards.summary: STOP-CA 2023: primary endpoint (LVEF decline ≥10 points to <55%) 9% atorvastatin vs 22% placebo (P=.002); heart failure events 3% vs 6% (P=.26)
cards.people: 300 patients with lymphoma scheduled for anthracycline-based chemotherapy at 9 academic centres in the US and Canada, randomised to atorvastatin 40 mg/day (150) or placebo (150) for 12 months; mean age 50 years, 47% women; 286 (95%) completed the trial; study-drug adherence 91%. Primary outcome: proportion with an absolute LVEF decline of ≥10% from before chemotherapy to a final value <55% over 12 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 9% (13/150) on atorvastatin and 22% (33/150) on placebo (P=.002) — an absolute reduction of 13 percentage points, roughly 59% relative; the odds of the endpoint were almost 3 times greater on placebo (odds ratio 2.9; 95% CI 1.4 to 6.4). The secondary endpoint (≥5% decline to <55%) occurred in 13% versus 29% (P=.001). There were 13 adjudicated heart failure events (4%) over 24 months, with no difference between groups (3% atorvastatin, 6% placebo; P=.26). Serious related adverse events were few and similar. The authors conclude atorvastatin reduced the incidence of cardiac dysfunction in lymphoma patients receiving anthracyclines.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate primary endpoint, single trial, lymphoma only — anthracycline regimens and baseline risk differ in breast cancer and sarcoma populations. Note the record's own MeSH includes 'Retrospective Studies' — copied verbatim; the study itself is a randomised trial. The heart-failure neutrality at 24 months is part of the claim, not a footnote.

shelves.title: Cardiotoxicity surveillance: strain-guided cardioprotection halved cardiotoxicity-criteria events but not overall EF decline (SUCCOUR)
shelves.question: In patients at risk of anthracycline cardiotoxicity, does starting cardioprotection on a global-longitudinal-strain trigger beat waiting for an ejection-fraction trigger?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anthracyclines · Cardiotoxicity · Echocardiography · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Prospective Studies · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SUCCOUR tested a surveillance philosophy: act on the sensitive early signal (global longitudinal strain) or wait for the established one (ejection fraction)? Three hundred thirty-one anthracycline-treated patients with another heart-failure risk factor were randomised internationally to start cardioprotective therapy on a relative GLS reduction of at least 12% or on an absolute LVEF reduction over 10%. At 1 year, the primary outcome — change in LVEF across the whole arms — was not significantly different between strategies. Beneath that null, the strain-guided arm used more cardioprotective therapy and fewer of its patients met the trial's cardiotoxicity (CTRCD) criteria: 5.8% versus 13.7% (P=0.02); 1-year EF was 57±6% versus 55±7% (P=0.05). Among patients who actually received cardioprotection, the EF-guided group's LVEF fell further by follow-up (9.1±10.9% versus 2.9±7.4%; P=0.03) — consistent with treatment starting later in the EF pathway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: strain-guided surveillance plausibly catches injury earlier and halves the proportion crossing the cardiotoxicity definition, but the whole-population EF trajectory — the outcome least gamed by definitions — did not significantly separate, so the strategy's net clinical value remains an open question rather than a settled upgrade.

cards.headline: SUCCOUR 2021: primary outcome (change in LVEF) not significantly different; cardiotoxicity criteria met by 5.8% (GLS-guided) vs 13.7% (EF-guided), P=0.02
cards.summary: SUCCOUR 2021: primary outcome (change in LVEF) not significantly different; cardiotoxicity criteria met by 5.8% (GLS-guided) vs 13.7% (EF-guided), P=0.02
cards.people: 331 patients receiving anthracyclines with at least one additional heart-failure risk factor (94% women in the analysed cohort; most had breast cancer; baseline LVEF 59±6%, GLS −20.6±2.4%), randomised to cardioprotective-therapy initiation guided by ≥12% relative GLS reduction (166) or >10% absolute LVEF reduction (165), followed for 1 year; 307 patients in the main follow-up analysis.
cards.result: At 1 year, the primary outcome of change in LVEF was not significantly different between the two arms. Significantly more cardioprotective therapy was used in the GLS-guided arm, and fewer GLS-guided patients met cancer-therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) criteria (5.8% vs 13.7%; P=0.02); 1-year EF was 57±6% versus 55±7% (P=0.05). Among patients who received cardioprotective therapy, those in the EF-guided arm had a larger LVEF reduction at follow-up (9.1±10.9% vs 2.9±7.4%; P=0.03). Two patients died and 22 withdrew or were lost. The authors conclude the results support GLS in surveillance for CTRCD.
cards.watchOut: The favourable endpoint (CTRCD criteria) is partly a definitional product of the surveillance strategy itself — strain triggers treatment before the EF criterion can be met — while the definition-free primary (overall LVEF change) was null. Single consortium trial; longer-term EF follow-up has been reported to narrow the gap, which is why the stamp stays POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity: neither perindopril nor bisoprolol prevented LV remodelling in a small three-arm trial (MANTICORE)
shelves.question: In HER2-positive early breast cancer receiving trastuzumab, do perindopril or bisoprolol prevent LV remodelling or LVEF decline?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-1 Receptor Antagonists · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bisoprolol · Breast Neoplasms · Cardiotoxicity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Middle Aged · Perindopril · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Stroke Volume · Trastuzumab · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: MANTICORE is the trastuzumab counterpart to the anthracycline prevention trials, and it splits the same way they do: remodelling no, ejection fraction maybe. Ninety-four patients with HER2-positive early breast cancer receiving adjuvant trastuzumab were randomised double-blind to perindopril, bisoprolol, or placebo for the duration of therapy, with cardiac magnetic resonance at baseline and after cycle 17. The primary outcome — trastuzumab-mediated left ventricular remodelling, measured as indexed LV end-diastolic volume — was not prevented by either drug: LVEDV index rose +7±14 mL/m² on perindopril, +8±9 on bisoprolol, and +4±11 on placebo (P=.36). In secondary analyses, the LVEF decline was attenuated in the bisoprolol group (−1±5%) relative to perindopril (−3±4%) and placebo (−5±5%) (P=.001), and both drugs independently predicted maintained LVEF on multivariable analysis. Both drugs were well tolerated with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference on the primary endpoint): with under 100 patients split three ways and a null primary, the LVEF attenuation is a secondary signal — interesting beside PRADA's candesartan result (Shelf #2325), not a stand-alone reason to pre-treat.

cards.headline: MANTICORE 2017: primary remodelling endpoint not prevented (LVEDV index P=.36); LVEF decline attenuated with bisoprolol (−1%) vs perindopril (−3%) vs placebo (−5%), P=.001
cards.summary: MANTICORE 2017: primary remodelling endpoint not prevented (LVEDV index P=.36); LVEF decline attenuated with bisoprolol (−1%) vs perindopril (−3%) vs placebo (−5%), P=.001
cards.people: 94 patients with HER2-positive early breast cancer receiving adjuvant trastuzumab, randomised double-blind to perindopril (33), bisoprolol (31), or placebo (30) for the duration of trastuzumab therapy. Cardiac magnetic resonance at baseline and post-cycle 17 measured indexed LV end-diastolic volume (primary remodelling outcome) and LVEF.
cards.result: Indexed LV end-diastolic volume increased in all groups — perindopril +7±14 mL/m², bisoprolol +8±9 mL/m², placebo +4±11 mL/m² (P=.36) — so neither drug prevented the primary remodelling outcome. In secondary analyses, trastuzumab-mediated decline in LVEF was attenuated in bisoprolol-treated patients (−1±5%) relative to perindopril (−3±4%) and placebo (−5±5%) (P=.001); perindopril and bisoprolol were independent predictors of maintained LVEF on multivariable analysis. Study drugs were well tolerated with no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-four patients across three arms and a null primary: the LVEF contrast everyone cites is a secondary analysis. Trastuzumab dysfunction also frequently recovers spontaneously, which caps what prevention can add — a confounder the trial's short horizon cannot resolve.
cards.source: Pituskin E et al. Multidisciplinary Approach to Novel Therapies in Cardio-Oncology Research (MANTICORE 101-Breast): A Randomized Trial for the Prevention of Trastuzumab-Associated Cardiotoxicity. J Clin Oncol. 2017. PMID: 27893331. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.title: Metastatic breast cancer: liposomal doxorubicin cut cardiotoxicity by about two-thirds relative at comparable efficacy (O'Brien)
shelves.question: In first-line metastatic breast cancer, do liposomal doxorubicin formulations reduce cardiotoxicity while preserving efficacy compared with conventional doxorubicin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibiotics, Antineoplastic · Breast Neoplasms · Doxorubicin · Female · Heart Diseases · Humans · Liposomes · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols · Prognosis · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Instead of protecting the heart from doxorubicin, liposomal formulations keep the drug away from it — and the randomised evidence says the trade works on the heart without costing antitumour effect. The anchor is O'Brien's phase III trial: 509 women with metastatic breast cancer and normal cardiac function randomised to pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (Caelyx/Doxil, 50 mg/m² every 4 weeks) or conventional doxorubicin (60 mg/m² every 3 weeks). Efficacy was comparable (progression-free survival 6.9 versus 7.8 months; hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.22; overall survival 21 versus 22 months), while the risk of cardiotoxicity was significantly higher on conventional doxorubicin (hazard ratio 3.16; 95% CI 1.58 to 6.31; P<0.001) — i.e., the liposomal formulation cut the cardiotoxicity hazard by roughly two-thirds relative. Toxicity moved rather than vanished: less alopecia, nausea, vomiting, and neutropenia with the liposomal drug; more palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (48% versus 2%), stomatitis, and mucositis. The supporting citation (Batist) is a retrospective pooled analysis of prior-adjuvant-doxorubicin patients from two earlier phase III trials of the non-pegylated liposomal formulation — cardiac events 22% versus 39% favouring liposomal — and is graded as supportive, not co-equal, evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY: a formulation change with randomised proof of less cardiotoxicity at comparable efficacy.

cards.headline: O'Brien 2004: cardiotoxicity hazard ratio 3.16 for conventional vs pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (P<0.001); progression-free survival comparable (HR 1.00); survival 21 vs 22 months
cards.summary: O'Brien 2004: cardiotoxicity hazard ratio 3.16 for conventional vs pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (P<0.001); progression-free survival comparable (HR 1.00); survival 21 vs 22 months
cards.type: Phase III randomised trial (O'Brien — pegylated liposomal vs conventional doxorubicin)
cards.people: 509 women with metastatic breast cancer and normal cardiac function, randomised to pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 50 mg/m² every 4 weeks or conventional doxorubicin 60 mg/m² every 3 weeks as first-line therapy. Cardiac events were based on LVEF reductions as a function of cumulative anthracycline dose.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was comparable (6.9 versus 7.8 months; hazard ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.82 to 1.22), and overall survival was similar (21 and 22 months; HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.19). The overall risk of cardiotoxicity was significantly higher with conventional doxorubicin than with the pegylated liposomal formulation (HR 3.16; 95% CI 1.58 to 6.31; P<0.001). Alopecia (66% vs 20%), nausea (53% vs 37%), vomiting (31% vs 19%), and neutropenia (10% vs 4%) were more frequent with conventional doxorubicin; palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (48% vs 2%), stomatitis (22% vs 15%), and mucositis (23% vs 13%) were more frequent with the liposomal formulation.
cards.watchOut: Cardiotoxicity was tracked as LVEF-based events against cumulative dose rather than clinical heart failure alone, and the comparison is against 3-weekly bolus doxorubicin in metastatic disease — the absolute gain in an adjuvant, lower-dose setting is smaller. The two formulations (pegylated here, non-pegylated below) are distinct products; the shelf claim is at class level for liposomal delivery.

cards.headline: Batist 2006 (retrospective pooled subgroup): cardiac events 22% liposomal vs 39% conventional (P=0.001) in prior-adjuvant-doxorubicin patients; response 31% vs 11%
cards.summary: Batist 2006 (retrospective pooled subgroup): cardiac events 22% liposomal vs 39% conventional (P=0.001) in prior-adjuvant-doxorubicin patients; response 31% vs 11%
cards.type: Retrospective pooled subgroup analysis of two phase III trials (Batist — non-pegylated liposomal doxorubicin)
cards.people: Retrospective analysis of 68 patients with metastatic breast cancer who had received prior adjuvant doxorubicin, pooled from two prospective phase III trials of non-pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (Myocet, with cyclophosphamide or single-agent) versus conventional doxorubicin regimens; 32 received liposomal-containing and 36 conventional regimens for metastatic disease.
cards.result: Cardiac events occurred in 22% of liposomal-treated patients (one congestive heart failure) versus 39% of conventionally treated patients (three heart failures) (log-rank P=0.001); median lifetime dose at cardiotoxicity onset was 780 mg/m² versus 580 mg/m² (HR 4.8; P=0.001). Overall response rates were 31% versus 11% (P=0.04; odds ratio 4.0). Median time to progression was 4.5 versus 3.4 months (P=0.66) and median survival 16 versus 15 months (P=0.71).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and subgroup-defined (68 of 521 pooled patients): the response-rate advantage in particular should be read as hypothesis-grade. This card supports the O'Brien randomised result; it does not independently establish the claim, and the drafting slate's description of it as a head-to-head randomised comparison was corrected against the record.

shelves.title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: spironolactone preserved LVEF in a small trial with an unusually steep control-arm fall (Akpek)
shelves.question: In breast-cancer patients receiving anthracyclines, does spironolactone prevent LVEF decline?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anthracyclines · Antibiotics, Antineoplastic · Breast Neoplasms · Cardiomyopathies · Double-Blind Method · Doxorubicin · Echocardiography · Epirubicin · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Spironolactone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Akpek's trial is the mineralocorticoid chapter of the cardioprotection story, and it carries the largest ejection-fraction contrast in the whole slate — which is precisely why it should be read slowly. Eighty-three women with breast cancer were randomised to spironolactone 25 mg daily or control alongside anthracycline chemotherapy. LVEF was essentially preserved on spironolactone (67.0±6.1% to 65.7±7.4%; P=0.094 for the within-group change) while the control group's LVEF fell from 67.7±6.3% to 53.6±6.8% (P<0.001), with the between-group interaction significant at P<0.001; diastolic function grade was likewise protected on spironolactone and deteriorated in controls. A 14-point mean LVEF collapse in an untreated anthracycline arm is far outside what CECCY, PRADA, or ICOS-ONE saw in their control groups at comparable eras and doses — either this population was unusually vulnerable or something in the single-centre conduct amplified the contrast. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the direction matches the rest of the neurohormonal literature and the drug was well tolerated, but an effect size this large from 83 patients in one centre is a finding to replicate, not to bank.

cards.headline: Akpek 2015: LVEF 67.0→65.7% on spironolactone vs 67.7→53.6% in controls (interaction P<0.001); diastolic grade protected
cards.summary: Akpek 2015: LVEF 67.0→65.7% on spironolactone vs 67.7→53.6% in controls (interaction P<0.001); diastolic grade protected
cards.people: 83 women diagnosed with breast cancer receiving anthracycline-group chemotherapy, randomised to spironolactone 25 mg/day (43; mean age 50±11 years) or control (40; mean age 51±10 years). Ejection fraction and diastolic function assessed by echocardiography.
cards.result: LVEF decreased from 67.0±6.1 to 65.7±7.4 (P=0.094) in the spironolactone group and from 67.7±6.3 to 53.6±6.8 in the control group (P<0.001); the between-group interaction for LVEF decrease was significantly lower with spironolactone (P<0.001). The diastolic functional grade was protected in the spironolactone group (P=0.096) and deteriorated in the control group (P<0.001). The authors conclude spironolactone used simultaneously with anthracycline chemotherapy protects systolic and diastolic function.
cards.watchOut: The control arm's ~14-point mean LVEF fall is implausibly large beside every neighbouring trial's control arm — treat the magnitude as unreliable even if the direction is believed. The drafting slate also attributed troponin and natriuretic-peptide blunting to this paper; the fetched record's abstract does not report those endpoints, so they are not claimed here.
cards.source: Akpek M et al. Protective effects of spironolactone against anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy. Eur J Heart Fail. 2015. PMID: 25410653. Registry ID: NCT02053974. shelves.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: sildenafil improved walk distance by 45–50 m at every dose in SUPER-1
shelves.question: In symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension, does sildenafil improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: 3',5'-Cyclic-GMP Phosphodiesterases · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors · Piperazines · Purines · Sildenafil Citrate · Sulfones · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: SUPER-1 is the pivotal trial that opened the PDE5 era in pulmonary arterial hypertension, and its most instructive feature is the flat dose-response. Two hundred seventy-eight patients with symptomatic PAH (idiopathic, connective-tissue-disease-associated, or after repaired congenital shunts) were randomised double-blind to placebo or sildenafil 20, 40, or 80 mg three times daily for 12 weeks. Six-minute walk distance rose in every sildenafil arm, with mean placebo-corrected effects of 45 m (+13.0%), 46 m (+13.3%), and 50 m (+14.7%) for 20, 40, and 80 mg respectively — all P<0.001, and all essentially the same, which is why 20 mg three times daily became the licensed dose. All doses reduced mean pulmonary artery pressure and improved WHO functional class; the incidence of clinical worsening did not differ significantly, and the trial was not powered for mortality (stated on its face). Among 222 patients completing one year of sildenafil monotherapy in the extension, the walk improvement from baseline was 51 m. Side effects were the class's familiar flushing, dyspepsia, and diarrhoea. PROPOSED LIKELY: sildenafil improves exercise capacity, functional class, and haemodynamics in PAH — a surrogate-primary claim, and the shelf claims nothing further.

cards.headline: SUPER-1 2005: placebo-corrected 6-minute walk +45 m (20 mg), +46 m (40 mg), +50 m (80 mg), all P<0.001; clinical worsening not significantly different
cards.summary: SUPER-1 2005: placebo-corrected 6-minute walk +45 m (20 mg), +46 m (40 mg), +50 m (80 mg), all P<0.001; clinical worsening not significantly different
cards.people: 278 patients with symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, associated with connective tissue disease, or with repaired congenital systemic-to-pulmonary shunts), randomised double-blind to placebo or sildenafil 20, 40, or 80 mg orally three times daily for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in 6-minute walk distance at week 12. The study was not powered to assess mortality.
cards.result: The distance walked in 6 minutes increased from baseline in all sildenafil groups; mean placebo-corrected treatment effects were 45 m (+13.0%), 46 m (+13.3%), and 50 m (+14.7%) for the 20, 40, and 80 mg doses respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). All sildenafil doses reduced mean pulmonary artery pressure (P=0.04, P=0.01, P<0.001) and improved WHO functional class (P=0.003, P<0.001, P<0.001). The incidence of clinical worsening did not differ significantly between sildenafil and placebo. Side effects included flushing, dyspepsia, and diarrhoea. Among 222 patients completing one year of sildenafil monotherapy, the improvement in 6-minute walk from baseline was 51 m.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate primary endpoint over 12 weeks; no mortality claim is possible from this trial, and the shelf makes none. The fourfold dose range producing a five-metre spread is the durable lesson: more sildenafil was not more benefit.
cards.source: Galiè N et al. Sildenafil citrate therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID: 16291984. Registry ID: none in the fetched record. shelves.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: only the 40 mg tadalafil dose met its walk-distance endpoint in PHIRST
shelves.question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension, does once-daily tadalafil improve exercise capacity and delay clinical worsening?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bosentan · Carbolines · Double-Blind Method · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors · Quality of Life · Sulfonamides · Tadalafil · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PHIRST gave the PDE5 class its once-daily member and a dose-finding lesson in the opposite direction from SUPER-1: here, only the top dose cleared the bar. Four hundred five PAH patients — treatment-naïve or on background bosentan — were randomised double-blind to placebo or tadalafil 2.5, 10, 20, or 40 mg once daily for 16 weeks. Six-minute walk rose dose-dependently, but only 40 mg met the prespecified significance level (P<0.01): the mean placebo-corrected effect was 33 m (95% CI 15 to 50), larger in bosentan-naïve patients (44 m; 95% CI 20 to 69) than in those on background bosentan (23 m; 95% CI −2 to 48). Tadalafil 40 mg also improved time to clinical worsening (P=0.041) and reduced the incidence of clinical worsening by 68% relative (P=0.038) — a relative figure; the fetched record does not report the absolute worsening rates — and improved health-related quality of life, while WHO functional class change was not statistically significant. Headache, myalgia, and flushing were the common treatment-related adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: tadalafil 40 mg daily improves exercise capacity in PAH and delays clinical worsening over 16 weeks; the lower doses are licensed-dose archaeology, not options.

cards.headline: PHIRST 2009: only tadalafil 40 mg met significance for 6-minute walk (+33 m placebo-corrected; 95% CI 15 to 50); clinical worsening incidence reduced 68% relative (P=0.038)
cards.summary: PHIRST 2009: only tadalafil 40 mg met significance for 6-minute walk (+33 m placebo-corrected; 95% CI 15 to 50); clinical worsening incidence reduced 68% relative (P=0.038)
cards.people: 405 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic or associated), either treatment-naïve or on background bosentan therapy, randomised double-blind to placebo or tadalafil 2.5, 10, 20, or 40 mg orally once daily for 16 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in 6-minute walk distance at week 16.
cards.result: Tadalafil increased 6-minute walk distance dose-dependently; only the 40 mg dose met the prespecified level of statistical significance (P<0.01), with a mean placebo-corrected treatment effect of 33 m (95% CI 15 to 50) — 44 m (95% CI 20 to 69) in bosentan-naïve patients versus 23 m (95% CI −2 to 48) on background bosentan. Tadalafil 40 mg improved time to clinical worsening (P=0.041), the incidence of clinical worsening (68% relative risk reduction; P=0.038; absolute rates not reported in the fetched record), and health-related quality of life. WHO functional class changes were not statistically significant. The most common treatment-related adverse events were headache, myalgia, and flushing.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks, surrogate primary; the background-bosentan subgroup's walk effect (23 m; CI crossing zero) foreshadows the add-on attenuation seen across this class. The 68% figure is a relative reduction in a low-frequency endpoint and is labelled as such on the face.

shelves.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: ambrisentan improved walk distance in both ARIES trials, with no liver-enzyme signal
shelves.question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension, does ambrisentan improve exercise capacity, and what is its hepatic safety profile?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Administration, Oral · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Exercise · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Phenylpropionates · Placebos · Pyridazines · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The ARIES programme answered two questions at once: whether the endothelin pathway's walk benefit survived a second drug, and whether an endothelin antagonist could escape the class's hepatic shadow. ARIES-1 (202 patients; ambrisentan 5 or 10 mg) and ARIES-2 (192 patients; 2.5 or 5 mg) were concurrent 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled trials in PAH. Walk distance improved at every dose: placebo-corrected effects of 31 m (P=0.008) and 51 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-1, and 32 m (P=0.022) and 59 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-2, with improvements in subsets of the secondary measures (time to clinical worsening in ARIES-2, functional class in ARIES-1, dyspnoea score and BNP in both). On safety, the distinguishing result: no patient treated with ambrisentan developed aminotransferase concentrations above 3 times the upper limit of normal — against the background of bosentan-era liver monitoring, that was a genuine product-level difference. In the extension, 280 patients completing 48 weeks of ambrisentan monotherapy held a 39 m improvement from baseline. PROPOSED LIKELY: ambrisentan improves exercise capacity in PAH with a hepatic profile cleaner than its class predecessor — two concordant trials, surrogate primary endpoints, no mortality claim attempted or made.

cards.headline: ARIES 2008: walk distance +31 to +59 m placebo-corrected across both trials and all doses; zero ambrisentan patients with aminotransferases >3× ULN
cards.summary: ARIES 2008: walk distance +31 to +59 m placebo-corrected across both trials and all doses; zero ambrisentan patients with aminotransferases >3× ULN
cards.type: Two concurrent randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (ARIES-1 + ARIES-2)
cards.people: ARIES-1 randomised 202 and ARIES-2 randomised 192 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension to placebo or ambrisentan once daily for 12 weeks (ARIES-1: 5 or 10 mg; ARIES-2: 2.5 or 5 mg), with a long-term extension study. Primary endpoint for each study: change in 6-minute walk distance from baseline to week 12.
cards.result: The 6-minute walk distance increased in all ambrisentan groups: mean placebo-corrected treatment effects were 31 m (P=0.008) and 51 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-1 for 5 and 10 mg, and 32 m (P=0.022) and 59 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-2 for 2.5 and 5 mg. Improvements were observed in time to clinical worsening (ARIES-2), WHO functional class (ARIES-1), Short Form-36 score (ARIES-2), Borg dyspnoea score (both studies), and B-type natriuretic peptide (both studies), with statistical significance more variable across endpoints. No patient treated with ambrisentan developed aminotransferase concentrations >3 times the upper limit of normal. In 280 patients completing 48 weeks of ambrisentan monotherapy, the improvement in 6-minute walk from baseline was 39 m.
cards.watchOut: Twelve-week surrogate primaries; secondary-endpoint significance was patchy between the twin trials, and the clean liver result is a 12-week observation — later real-world hepatic experience with the class is outside this record. No outcome (worsening/mortality) claim is made on walk data alone.

shelves.title: Early pulmonary arterial hypertension: bosentan improved pulmonary vascular resistance but missed its walk-distance coprimary (EARLY)
shelves.question: In WHO functional class II pulmonary arterial hypertension, does bosentan improve haemodynamics and exercise capacity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antihypertensive Agents · Bosentan · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Male · Middle Aged · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Resistance · Walking
shelves.balance: EARLY asked whether PAH treatment should start while patients are still mildly symptomatic — WHO functional class II — and its two coprimary endpoints split the answer down the middle. One hundred eighty-five class II patients with walk distance below 80% of predicted (or under 500 m with a Borg dyspnoea index of at least 2) were randomised double-blind to bosentan or placebo for 6 months. The haemodynamic coprimary was met decisively: pulmonary vascular resistance at month 6 was 83.2% of baseline on bosentan versus 107.5% on placebo (treatment effect −22.6%; 95% CI −33.5 to −10.0; P<0.0001). The walk coprimary was not: 6-minute walk rose 11.2 m on bosentan and fell 7.9 m on placebo, a treatment effect of 19.1 m (95% CI 3.6 to 41.8) that did not reach significance (P=0.0758). Serious adverse events occurred in 13% on bosentan and 9% on placebo — syncope the commonest on bosentan, right ventricular failure on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: bosentan clearly moves pulmonary haemodynamics in early PAH and probably slows the walk decline, but the trial's own functional coprimary missed, so 'treat early' rests on physiology and trajectory, not on a demonstrated symptomatic win at 6 months. Distinct from BREATHE-5 (Shelf #2314, Eisenmenger syndrome) — this is the early-disease question.

cards.headline: EARLY 2008: PVR coprimary met (treatment effect −22.6%; P<0.0001); 6-minute walk coprimary missed (treatment effect 19.1 m; P=0.0758)
cards.summary: EARLY 2008: PVR coprimary met (treatment effect −22.6%; P<0.0001); 6-minute walk coprimary missed (treatment effect 19.1 m; P=0.0758)
cards.people: 185 patients aged at least 12 years with WHO functional class II pulmonary arterial hypertension and 6-minute walk distance under 80% of predicted (or under 500 m with Borg dyspnoea index at least 2), randomised to bosentan (93) or placebo (92) for a 6-month double-blind period. Coprimary endpoints: pulmonary vascular resistance at month 6 as a percentage of baseline, and change in 6-minute walk distance.
cards.result: At month 6, geometric mean pulmonary vascular resistance was 83.2% (95% CI 73.8 to 93.7) of baseline in the bosentan group and 107.5% (95% CI 97.6 to 118.4) in the placebo group (treatment effect −22.6%; 95% CI −33.5 to −10.0; P<0.0001). Mean 6-minute walk distance increased 11.2 m (−4.6 to 27.0) on bosentan and decreased 7.9 m (−24.3 to 8.5) on placebo, a treatment effect of 19.1 m (95% CI 3.6 to 41.8; P=0.0758) — not significant. Serious adverse events were reported in 12 (13%) bosentan patients and 8 (9%) placebo patients; the most common were syncope (bosentan) and right ventricular failure (placebo).
cards.watchOut: A split coprimary is a split verdict — the shelf stamps the haemodynamic success and the functional miss together. The drafting slate credited this trial with a time-to-clinical-worsening hazard ratio; the fetched record's abstract reports only the two coprimary endpoints, so no such figure is claimed here.

shelves.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: adding oral treprostinil to monotherapy reduced clinical worsening (FREEDOM-EV)
shelves.question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension on a single background oral therapy, does adding oral treprostinil reduce clinical worsening?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Double-Blind Method · Epoprostenol · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension · Young Adult
shelves.balance: FREEDOM-EV is the PAH slate's event-driven trial — the one that asked whether a prostacyclin-pathway drug added to a single background oral therapy changes clinical course, not just walk distance. Six hundred ninety patients with PAH who had recently begun one approved oral monotherapy were randomised double-blind to oral treprostinil extended-release three times daily or placebo, in an event-driven design whose primary endpoint was time to first adjudicated clinical worsening (death, hospitalisation for worsening PAH, initiation of inhaled or parenteral prostacyclin, disease progression, or unsatisfactory long-term response). Clinical worsening occurred in 26% on oral treprostinil versus 36% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; P=0.028) — a 10-percentage-point absolute reduction, about 26% relative. Functional class, Borg dyspnoea score, and NT-proBNP all favoured treprostinil from week 24 onward. The fetched record does not report mortality separately from the worsening composite, so no mortality claim is made here — the composite embeds death, which is why this shelf is Tier C. The price was tolerability: headache, diarrhoea, flushing, nausea, and vomiting were the commonest adverse events — the prostacyclin class burden that the earlier add-on trial (FREEDOM-C, against dual background therapy) could not get past. PROPOSED LIKELY: adding oral treprostinil to monotherapy genuinely delays clinical worsening; the absolute gain over the trial's horizon is about one worsening event avoided per ten patients treated.

cards.headline: FREEDOM-EV 2020: clinical worsening 26% vs 36% (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; P=0.028); functional class, dyspnoea, and NT-proBNP favoured treprostinil
cards.summary: FREEDOM-EV 2020: clinical worsening 26% vs 36% (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; P=0.028); functional class, dyspnoea, and NT-proBNP favoured treprostinil
cards.people: 690 participants with pulmonary arterial hypertension on approved oral monotherapy for more than 30 days before randomisation, with baseline 6-minute walk distance at least 150 m, randomised 1:1 double-blind to oral treprostinil extended-release tablets three times daily or placebo. Event-driven design; primary endpoint: time to first adjudicated clinical worsening event — death, hospitalisation due to worsening PAH, initiation of inhaled or parenteral prostacyclin, disease progression, or unsatisfactory long-term clinical response.
cards.result: Clinical worsening occurred in 26% of the oral treprostinil group compared with 36% of placebo participants (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; P=0.028) — a 10-point absolute reduction, about 26% relative. Functional class, Borg dyspnoea score, and NT-proBNP all favoured oral treprostinil at week 24 and beyond. A noninvasive risk analysis showed the treprostinil group achieved a lower risk profile from weeks 12 to 60 despite higher baseline mortality risk. The most common adverse events on oral treprostinil were headache, diarrhoea, flushing, nausea, and vomiting. Mortality was not reported separately from the worsening composite in the fetched record.
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven by its softer components (progression, unsatisfactory response, hospitalisation) alongside death, and the record gives no stand-alone mortality result — do not upgrade the claim. Benefit accrued in patients on exactly one background agent; the sibling FREEDOM-C trial against dual background therapy failed on tolerability, which bounds how far the add-on logic extends.

shelves.title: Coffee and the heart (CRAVE): no significant rise in atrial ectopy — more ventricular ectopy, about 1,000 extra steps, 36 minutes less sleep
shelves.question: In ambulatory adults, does drinking caffeinated coffee on randomly assigned days change atrial or ventricular ectopy, daily steps, sleep, or glucose compared with avoiding caffeine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Atrial Premature Complexes/chemically induced, etiology · Caffeine/adverse effects, pharmacology · Coffee/adverse effects · Glucose · Prospective Studies · Drinking · Cross-Over Studies · Blood Glucose/analysis · Walking · Sleep Duration/drug effects · Accelerometry · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Mobile Applications · Text Messaging · Ventricular Premature Complexes/chemically induced, etiology
shelves.balance: Patients ask whether coffee is bad for palpitations, and CRAVE is the rare trial that randomised the beverage itself: 100 ambulatory adults wore a continuous ECG patch, an accelerometer and a glucose monitor for 14 days, receiving daily text instructions to drink caffeinated coffee or avoid caffeine. On coffee days, premature atrial contractions — the primary outcome — averaged 58 versus 53 per day (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.98–1.20; p=0.10): no significant difference, and no signal for sustained arrhythmia. Premature ventricular contractions were higher on coffee days (154 vs 102 per day; rate ratio 1.51, 1.18–1.94). Coffee days also brought about 1,058 more steps and 36 fewer minutes of sleep; glucose was unchanged. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the atrial-ectopy question patients actually ask about; the ventricular-ectopy increase is a count of extra beats, not a clinical-event finding, and rides in the balance rather than the stamp. THIN: one trial, surrogate counts.

cards.result: Premature atrial contractions: 58 vs 53 per day (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.98–1.20; p=0.10). Premature ventricular contractions: 154 vs 102 per day (rate ratio 1.51, 1.18–1.94). Steps: 10,646 vs 9,665 (mean difference 1,058; 441–1,675). Sleep: 397 vs 432 minutes (mean difference 36 fewer minutes; 25–47). Glucose: 95 vs 96 mg/dL (no difference).

shelves.title: Alcohol abstinence in atrial fibrillation: recurrence 53% vs 73% over six months in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In regular drinkers (10 or more standard drinks per week) with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation, does abstaining from alcohol reduce AF recurrence and AF burden compared with continuing usual drinking?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alcohol Abstinence · Alcohol Drinking/adverse effects · Atrial Fibrillation/etiology, prevention & control · Australia · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: Alcohol is the modifiable exposure patients with atrial fibrillation most often ask about, and one open-label randomised trial has tested abstinence itself. In 140 Australian patients drinking at least 10 standard drinks a week (abstinence group cut from 16.8 to 2.1 drinks/week; controls from 16.4 to 13.2), AF recurred over 6 months in 53% of the abstinence group versus 73% of controls — an absolute difference of 20 percentage points — with a hazard ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84) for time to recurrence and a lower AF burden (0.5% vs 1.2% of time in AF). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial, open-label, in mostly male volunteers willing to attempt abstinence — the developer rules personally.

cards.headline: Abstinence cut AF recurrence from 73% to 53% over 6 months (HR 0.55 for time to recurrence); AF burden halved
cards.summary: Abstinence cut AF recurrence from 73% to 53% over 6 months (HR 0.55 for time to recurrence); AF burden halved
cards.type: Multicentre prospective open-label randomised controlled trial (Voskoboinik 2020)
cards.people: 140 adults (85% men, mean age 62) consuming ≥10 standard drinks/week with paroxysmal or persistent AF in sinus rhythm at baseline, at six Australian hospitals, randomised to abstinence or usual drinking, with a 2-week blanking period before endpoint counting.
cards.result: Alcohol intake fell from 16.8±7.7 to 2.1±3.7 drinks/week with abstinence versus 16.4±6.9 to 13.2±6.5 with control drinking. AF recurred in 37/70 (53%) vs 51/70 (73%); HR for recurrence 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84; p=0.005). AF burden: median 0.5% vs 1.2% of time in AF (p=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Open-label (abstinence cannot be blinded), self-selected volunteers, 85% men, and an Australian standard-drink definition (~12 g alcohol); the control group also cut down by a fifth, which if anything shrinks the contrast. No mortality or stroke endpoints — Tier C on the single-trial rule.
cards.source: Voskoboinik A et al.. Alcohol Abstinence in Drinkers with Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 31893513. Registry ID: ACTRN12616000256471 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, as recorded in the record). shelves.title: Blood thinners after TAVI when anticoagulation is needed: edoxaban matched warfarin on the composite but bled more; adding clopidogrel only added bleeding
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who need oral anticoagulation after successful TAVI, does edoxaban match a vitamin K antagonist — and does adding clopidogrel to anticoagulation help or harm?
shelves.mesh: 4-Hydroxycoumarins/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Mortality · Phenindione/analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Pyridines/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Thiazoles/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Thromboembolism/prevention & control · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement/adverse effects · Vitamin K/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: This shelf covers patients who already have an indication for anticoagulation after TAVI — a different question from Shelf #717 (routine anticoagulation in patients without an indication, where anticoagulation harmed). Two trials draw the map. ENVISAGE-TAVI AF (1,426 patients, mean age 82) found edoxaban noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist on the composite of death, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, valve thrombosis or major bleeding (17.3 vs 16.5 per 100 person-years; HR 1.05) — but major bleeding was significantly higher on edoxaban (9.7 vs 7.0 per 100 person-years; HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03–1.91), driven by gastrointestinal bleeding. POPular TAVI cohort B (313 patients) tested the add-on question: three months of clopidogrel on top of anticoagulation raised all bleeding from 21.7% to 34.6% over a year, while the ischaemic composite was noninferior without it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — the harms are the actionable findings: extra antiplatelet therapy adds bleeding without shown benefit, and edoxaban's convenience costs gastrointestinal bleeds. Tier C: harm shelf.

cards.headline: ENVISAGE-TAVI AF: composite noninferior on edoxaban (HR 1.05) but major bleeding higher (9.7 vs 7.0 per 100 person-years; HR 1.40)
cards.summary: ENVISAGE-TAVI AF: composite noninferior on edoxaban (HR 1.05) but major bleeding higher (9.7 vs 7.0 per 100 person-years; HR 1.40)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, open-label, adjudicator-masked noninferiority trial (Van Mieghem 2021, ENVISAGE-TAVI AF)
cards.people: 1,426 patients (mean age 82.1 years; 47.5% women) with prevalent or incident atrial fibrillation as the indication for oral anticoagulation after successful TAVR, randomised open-label to edoxaban or a vitamin K antagonist with blinded adjudication.
cards.result: Primary efficacy composite: 17.3 vs 16.5 events per 100 person-years (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.85–1.31; p=0.01 for noninferiority against a 1.38 margin). Major bleeding: 9.7 vs 7.0 per 100 person-years (HR 1.40, 1.03–1.91), the difference mainly gastrointestinal. Death or stroke: 10.0 vs 11.7 per 100 person-years (HR 0.85, 0.66–1.11).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority was declared against a wide (1.38) margin, and the efficacy composite embeds major bleeding, which blurs the benefit–harm read; the clean signals are the bleeding excess and the neutral death/stroke rates.
cards.source: Van Mieghem NM et al.. Edoxaban versus Vitamin K Antagonist for Atrial Fibrillation after TAVR. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34449183. Registry ID: NCT02943785. cards.headline: POPular TAVI cohort B: adding clopidogrel to anticoagulation raised bleeding (34.6% vs 21.7%); ischaemic composite noninferior without it
cards.summary: POPular TAVI cohort B: adding clopidogrel to anticoagulation raised bleeding (34.6% vs 21.7%); ischaemic composite noninferior without it
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Nijenhuis 2020, POPular TAVI cohort B)
cards.people: 313 patients undergoing TAVI who were receiving oral anticoagulation for appropriate indications, randomised before TAVI to no clopidogrel or to clopidogrel for 3 months; primary outcomes all bleeding and non-procedure-related bleeding over 12 months.
cards.result: All bleeding: 21.7% on anticoagulation alone vs 34.6% with added clopidogrel (risk ratio 0.63 for OAC alone, 95% CI 0.43–0.90; p=0.01); non-procedure-related bleeding 21.7% vs 34.0% (risk ratio 0.64). The ischaemic secondary composite (cardiovascular death, ischaemic stroke, MI) occurred in 13.4% vs 17.3% — noninferior without clopidogrel. Most bleeding was at the access site and in the first month, and mostly minor.
cards.watchOut: Modest size (313), so the ischaemic noninferiority carries wide intervals; patients with a recent coronary stent mandating dual therapy were not the population this answers for.
cards.source: Nijenhuis VJ et al.. Anticoagulation with or without Clopidogrel after Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Implantation. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32223116. shelves.title: Plant sterol and stanol spreads for cholesterol: two blinded trials show real LDL lowering — with no trial of heart attacks or strokes
shelves.question: In adults with normal or mildly raised cholesterol, do margarines enriched with plant sterols or stanols (about 2 g/day) lower LDL cholesterol compared with ordinary margarine?

shelves.balance: Plant sterols and stanols are sold in margarines and drinks on the claim that they lower cholesterol, and unusually for a supermarket health claim, the randomised evidence is real. In the Finnish trial (153 adults with mildly raised cholesterol, 12 months), margarine carrying sitostanol ester lowered LDL cholesterol by 14.1% while the control margarine lowered it by 1.1%. In a second double-blind trial (100 adults), margarines enriched with soy sterol esters or sitostanol esters lowered total and LDL cholesterol by 8–13% (0.37–0.44 mmol/L (≈14–17 mg/dL)), with no effect on HDL. The honest limits: these are cholesterol numbers, not heart attacks — no trial of a sterol spread has ever been powered for clinical events — the effect needs roughly 2 g of sterols a day eaten as part of a fat spread, and sterols also lower blood levels of some fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent LDL lowering in two blinded trials; an add-on to, not a substitute for, proven lipid therapy.

cards.headline: Sitostanol-ester margarine lowered LDL cholesterol 14.1% over 12 months versus 1.1% on control margarine
cards.summary: Sitostanol-ester margarine lowered LDL cholesterol 14.1% over 12 months versus 1.1% on control margarine
cards.people: 153 adults with mild hypercholesterolaemia randomised double-blind to margarine containing sitostanol ester or a control margarine for 12 months, with cholesterol absorption markers measured alongside lipids.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell 14.1% in the sitostanol-ester group versus 1.1% in the control group over the year; cholesterol absorption fell as expected (serum campesterol, a plant-sterol absorption marker, fell by about a third). No major safety signal was reported.
cards.watchOut: A lipid endpoint, not clinical events: the trial says nothing about heart attacks or strokes. The product was a sitostanol-ester margarine used daily; the publication describes the preparation by its sterol content and does not rest the claim on a retail brand.
cards.source: Miettinen TA et al.. Reduction of serum cholesterol with sitostanol-ester margarine in a mildly hypercholesterolemic population. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7566021. cards.headline: Sterol- and stanol-ester margarines lowered total and LDL cholesterol 8–13% (0.37–0.44 mmol/L (≈14–17 mg/dL))
cards.summary: Sterol- and stanol-ester margarines lowered total and LDL cholesterol 8–13% (0.37–0.44 mmol/L (≈14–17 mg/dL))
cards.people: 100 adults with normal or mildly raised cholesterol (95 completed) in a double-blind randomised comparison of plant sterol-ester (from soybean oil) and sitostanol-ester margarines against a control margarine.
cards.result: Total and LDL cholesterol fell 8–13% (0.37–0.44 mmol/L (≈14–17 mg/dL)) on both enriched margarines relative to control; HDL cholesterol did not change. Plasma carotenoid levels fell modestly on the enriched spreads, as expected when cholesterol absorption is blocked.
cards.watchOut: Short treatment periods and a surrogate endpoint; the result supports an LDL-lowering claim for the tested ester margarines, not an event-reduction claim, and sterol products vary in dose per serving. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Aged garlic extract vs coronary calcium: slower progression in four small trials — one of them independent — but calcium is a surrogate and no trial counted heart attacks
shelves.question: In adults with subclinical coronary atherosclerosis, does aged garlic extract slow the progression of coronary artery calcium (CAC) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Arteriosclerosis/diagnostic imaging, *drug therapy · Calcinosis/diagnostic imaging, drug therapy · Coronary Artery Disease/*drug therapy · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · *Garlic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/*therapeutic use · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome · *Vascular Calcification/drug therapy, therapy
shelves.balance: Four small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — each 1 year long, with 19 to 104 participants — have tested aged garlic extract (AGE) against placebo on coronary artery calcium progression, and all four found slower progression on treatment. In the Harbor-UCLA pilot (Budoff 2004), patients on statins gained a mean of 7.5% in calcium score on AGE versus 22.2% on placebo (relative percentage changes, P=0.046). In firefighters (Zeb 2012), CAC rose 32 versus 58 Agatston units on a combined AGE + coenzyme Q10 capsule. The one independent trial — Lund, Sweden (Wlosinska 2020), testing AGE alone as Kyolic Reserve 2,400 mg/day — found the adjusted odds of the lowest CAC progression were 2.95 times higher on AGE (95% CI 1.05–8.27). A 2023 systematic review of 49 calcification trials found AGE (6 trials) the one intervention that consistently attenuated calcification. Read the confounds on the face of the cards: two of the four trials tested combinations (AGE + B vitamins/folate/L-arginine in Budoff 2009; AGE + CoQ10 in Zeb 2012) from which garlic's own contribution cannot be separated; three of the four trials come from a single centre (Harbor-UCLA); and the manufacturer, Wakunaga, funded or supplied product for trials on both sides of the Atlantic. Above all: no trial measured heart attacks or deaths — CAC progression is a surrogate endpoint, and these trials were neither large enough nor long enough to test outcomes. For the separate question of AGE and blood pressure, see Shelf #2482. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent direction of effect across four randomised trials, one of them independent and testing AGE alone, backed by a systematic review — held at POSSIBLE by the surrogate endpoint, small samples, single-centre predominance, combination confounding, and manufacturer involvement.

cards.headline: Budoff 2004 pilot: on statins, coronary calcium rose 7.5% on aged garlic extract versus 22.2% on placebo over 1 year (P=0.046)
cards.summary: Budoff 2004 pilot: on statins, coronary calcium rose 7.5% on aged garlic extract versus 22.2% on placebo over 1 year (P=0.046)
cards.people: 23 patients receiving statin therapy enrolled at Harbor-UCLA in a placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised pilot study; 19 completed the protocol (9 on AGE, 10 on placebo). Coronary calcium was measured by electron beam tomography at baseline and 1 year, and blood S-allylcysteine was measured as a compliance marker.
cards.result: Mean change in calcium score (volumetric method) over 1 year was +7.5 ± 9.4% (a relative percentage change) on aged garlic extract 4 ml daily versus +22.2 ± 18.5% on placebo (P = 0.046). There were no significant differences in cholesterol parameters or C-reactive protein between the groups. Registry ID: none in the record (2004, pre-registration era).
cards.watchOut: A pilot in size as well as name — 19 completers — and the headline figures are relative percentage changes in a volumetric calcium score, not events. The publication does not name the brand of AGE used or a funder; the group's later trials used Wakunaga's Kyolic preparations.
cards.source: Budoff MJ et al.. Inhibiting progression of coronary calcification using Aged Garlic Extract in patients receiving statin therapy: a preliminary study. Preventive Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15475033. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Budoff 2009: AGE combined with B vitamins, folic acid and L-arginine slowed CAC progression — garlic cannot be separated from the combination
cards.summary: Budoff 2009: AGE combined with B vitamins, folic acid and L-arginine slowed CAC progression — garlic cannot be separated from the combination
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a combination supplement (Budoff 2009)
cards.people: 65 intermediate-risk patients (mean age 60 ± 9 years, 79% male) at Harbor-UCLA, randomised double-blind to a daily capsule of aged garlic extract (250 mg) plus vitamin B12 (100 µg), folic acid (300 µg), vitamin B6 (12.5 mg) and L-arginine (100 mg), or placebo, for 1 year (trial conducted 2005–2007). All underwent coronary artery calcium scanning at baseline and 12 months.
cards.result: CAC progression — pre-defined as an increase in CAC score of >15% per year — was significantly lower in the AGE-with-supplements group than the placebo group after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors (p<0.05); the abstract reports no absolute calcium-score changes. Vascular reactivity (temperature rebound) was also significantly higher on treatment. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The tested capsule is a five-ingredient combination, and folate/B-vitamin therapy has its own vascular effects — this trial cannot attribute any of the benefit to garlic. It is carded because the systematic reviews count it among the aged-garlic-extract trials; its confound must not be missed. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Budoff MJ et al.. Aged garlic extract supplemented with B vitamins, folic acid and L-arginine retards the progression of subclinical atherosclerosis: a randomized clinical trial. Preventive Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19573556. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zeb 2012: AGE + coenzyme Q10 (Kyolic 110) — calcium rose 32 Agatston units on treatment versus 58 on placebo in 65 firefighters (P=0.01)
cards.summary: Zeb 2012: AGE + coenzyme Q10 (Kyolic 110) — calcium rose 32 Agatston units on treatment versus 58 on placebo in 65 firefighters (P=0.01)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a combination supplement (Zeb 2012)
cards.people: 65 intermediate-risk firefighters (mean age 55 ± 6 years) at Harbor-UCLA, randomised double-blind to a daily capsule of aged garlic extract 1,200 mg plus coenzyme Q10 120 mg — the combined Kyolic 110 preparation (Wakunaga) — or placebo, for 1 year, with CAC scanning and C-reactive protein at baseline and 12 months.
cards.result: Mean CAC progression at 1 year was 32 ± 6 Agatston units on AGE+CoQ10 versus 58 ± 8 on placebo (P = 0.01). CRP changed by −0.12 versus +0.91 mg/L (P<0.05). After adjustment for age, sex, conventional risk factors and statin therapy, AGE+CoQ10 was associated with 3.99-fold odds (95% CI 1.3–12.2, P = 0.01) of lack of CAC progression. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: A combination product again — coenzyme Q10 cannot be separated from the garlic — in a selected occupational cohort. The paper discloses that the trial was supported by a grant from Wakunaga of America, the manufacturer, to Dr Budoff.
cards.source: Zeb I et al.. Aged garlic extract and coenzyme Q10 have favorable effect on inflammatory markers and coronary atherosclerosis progression: A randomized clinical trial. Journal of Cardiovascular Disease Research. 2012. PMID: 22923934. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Wlosinska 2020 (independent, Lund, Sweden): AGE alone (Kyolic Reserve, 2,400 mg/day) — odds of the lowest CAC progression 2.95 times higher than on placebo
cards.summary: Wlosinska 2020 (independent, Lund, Sweden): AGE alone (Kyolic Reserve, 2,400 mg/day) — odds of the lowest CAC progression 2.95 times higher than on placebo
cards.people: 104 patients with a Framingham risk score ≥10 at Lund University Hospital, Sweden, randomised double-blind to aged garlic extract 2,400 mg daily (Kyolic Reserve formula, Wakunaga of America — two 600 mg capsules twice daily) or placebo for 1 year; 93 were analysed (46 AGE, 47 placebo). This is the only CAC trial from outside the Harbor-UCLA group, and it tests AGE on its own rather than in a combination.
cards.result: Every patient's calcium score increased over the year, but progression was lower on AGE: the adjusted odds of belonging to the lowest-progression half were 2.95 times higher on AGE than on placebo (adjusted OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.05–8.27, p=0.040). Systolic blood pressure fell from 148 (SD 19) to 140 (SD 15) mmHg within the AGE group (p=0.027). No side effects were reported in either group. Registry ID: NCT03860350 (verified in the record; retrospectively registered).
cards.watchOut: Independence has a limit: the paper reports a Wakunaga research grant to the senior author and that Wakunaga supplied the AGE and placebo capsules free of charge (stating the company had no role in design, analysis or writing); the trial registration was retrospective. The headline odds ratio comes from a median-split analysis, not a difference in mean calcium change.
cards.source: Wlosinska M et al.. The effect of aged garlic extract on the atherosclerotic process - a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies. 2020. PMID: 32349742. Registry ID: NCT03860350. cards.headline: Systematic review 2023: across 49 calcification trials, aged garlic extract (6 trials) was the intervention that consistently attenuated calcification
cards.summary: Systematic review 2023: across 49 calcification trials, aged garlic extract (6 trials) was the intervention that consistently attenuated calcification
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Murali 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review of 49 randomised controlled trials (9,901 participants; median 104 participants and 12 months' duration per trial) of interventions to attenuate cardiovascular calcification progression in people without chronic kidney disease, with Cochrane risk-of-bias and GRADE assessments.
cards.result: Trials involving aged garlic extract (n=6 studies) consistently showed attenuation of cardiovascular calcification, whereas statins (n=14), other lipid-lowering agents, hormone replacement, vitamin K, lifestyle measures and omega-3 fatty acids consistently did not. The authors conclude that aged garlic extract 'appears most promising, but evaluable studies were small and of short duration'; GRADE certainty was moderate for a majority of analyses and overall risk of bias was moderate. Registry ID: none (systematic review).
cards.watchOut: The review's six AGE trials substantially overlap the small Harbor-UCLA programme carded above — it is a map of the same small evidence base, not six independent confirmations. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Murali S et al.. Interventions to Attenuate Cardiovascular Calcification Progression: A Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2023. PMID: 38014685. Registry ID: none (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: slower calcium progression in every trial — POSSIBLE on a surrogate endpoint, with no outcome data
cards.summary: Synthesis: slower calcium progression in every trial — POSSIBLE on a surrogate endpoint, with no outcome data
cards.people: Four randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of aged garlic extract preparations with coronary calcium endpoints (19–104 participants each, all 1 year), plus a 2023 systematic review of cardiovascular calcification trials.
cards.result: The direction of effect is consistent: AGE alone (Wlosinska 2020, independent of the Harbor-UCLA group) and AGE-containing combinations (Budoff 2004, 2009; Zeb 2012) all slowed CAC progression versus placebo, and the 2023 systematic review found aged garlic extract the most promising of all interventions tested against calcification. But no trial measured myocardial infarction or death, the samples are small, two of the four trials tested combinations from which garlic cannot be isolated, and three of the four came from one centre. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: For aged garlic extract and blood pressure — a different question, with its own trials — see Shelf #2482. Nothing here shows that slowing a calcium score with garlic prevents a single heart attack; that trial has never been run.

Journal of Cardiovascular Disease Research. 2012 (PMID: 22923934); Wlosinska M et al. BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies. 2020 (PMID: 32349742); Murali S et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2023 (PMID: 38014685). shelves.title: Horse chestnut seed extract for chronic venous insufficiency
shelves.question: Does oral horse chestnut seed extract reduce the leg swelling and symptoms of chronic venous insufficiency?
shelves.mesh: Bandages · Edema · Humans · Leg · Plant Extracts · Treatment Outcome · Venous Insufficiency · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Escin · Exercise Test
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a 240-patient trial found the extract equivalent to compression stockings and superior to placebo for leg oedema, a small double-blind trial agrees, and the Cochrane review finds consistent short-term benefit for leg pain and volume; old, small trials and sign-based outcomes keep it at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Horse chestnut extract reduced leg oedema as much as compression stockings over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Horse chestnut extract reduced leg oedema as much as compression stockings over 12 weeks
cards.people: 240 patients with chronic venous insufficiency; dried extract (50 mg aescin twice daily) vs class II compression stockings vs placebo for 12 weeks
cards.result: Lower-leg volume of the worse limb fell by 43.8 mL on the extract and 46.7 mL on compression, and rose by 9.8 mL on placebo. Both active treatments beat placebo (extract P = 0.005; compression P = 0.002) and were shown equivalent to each other (P = 0.001). No serious treatment-related events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Only partially blinded — stockings cannot be disguised — and the outcome is leg volume, a sign, rather than symptoms, ulcers or thrombosis. The record names no brand of extract.
cards.source: Diehm C et al.. Comparison of leg compression stocking and oral horse-chestnut seed extract therapy in patients with chronic venous insufficiency. Lancet. 1996. PMID: 8569363. cards.headline: In a small double-blind trial, the extract reduced venous oedema versus placebo
cards.summary: In a small double-blind trial, the extract reduced venous oedema versus placebo
cards.people: 40 patients with venous oedema from chronic deep-vein incompetence; extract vs placebo, double-blind
cards.result: The oedema-reducing effect of horse chestnut seed extract over placebo was statistically significant on water-displacement measurement (hydroplethysmography), including after oedema provocation; leg-circumference and venous-pressure measurements pointed the same way. The abstract reports no effect size. The preparation was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and no numbers in the abstract — supportive, not load-bearing.

cards.headline: Cochrane review: the extract improves leg pain and swelling in the short term versus placebo
cards.summary: Cochrane review: the extract improves leg pain and swelling in the short term versus placebo
cards.people: Randomised trials of oral horse chestnut seed extract mono-preparations vs placebo or reference therapy for chronic venous insufficiency
cards.result: Leg pain was assessed in seven placebo-controlled trials — six found significant reductions on the extract (one trial: weighted mean difference 42.4 mm on a 100 mm pain scale, 95% CI 34.9–49.9). Leg volume in six trials (502 participants) fell by a weighted mean 32.1 mL (95% CI 13.5–50.7) versus placebo. One trial suggested equivalence with compression stockings. Adverse events were usually mild and infrequent.
cards.watchOut: The reviewers themselves call for larger, definitive trials to confirm efficacy; most included trials are small and old.
cards.source: Pittler MH et al.. Horse chestnut seed extract for chronic venous insufficiency. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012. PMID: 23152216. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: Standardised horse chestnut seed extract (50 mg aescin twice daily) shrinks venous leg swelling about as much as compression stockings over 12 weeks and eases leg pain versus placebo. It is a short-term symptom treatment — nothing here shows it prevents ulcers or thrombosis, and compression remains the standard it was compared against.
cards.watchOut: Trials predate modern reporting standards, and extract standardisation varies between products; the trial records name no brands.
