shelves.title: Hibiscus (sour) tea for high blood pressure
shelves.question: Does drinking hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa, sour) tea lower blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Electrolytes · Female · Hibiscus · Humans · Hypertension · Lisinopril · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three randomised trials all point downward, but only McKay 2010 is placebo-controlled (net systolic effect about −6 mmHg, P = 0.030; diastolic not significant). The larger effects come from an active-comparator trial with no placebo group and a trial with a 16 mmHg baseline imbalance between its groups. A modest systolic effect is plausible; its size is uncertain.

cards.headline: A standardised hibiscus extract lowered blood pressure by 17/12 mmHg in 4 weeks — less than lisinopril did
cards.summary: A standardised hibiscus extract lowered blood pressure by 17/12 mmHg in 4 weeks — less than lisinopril did
cards.people: 171 analysed patients with stage I–II hypertension (193 enrolled); standardised Hibiscus sabdariffa extract (250 mg total anthocyanins daily) vs lisinopril 10 mg for 4 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Blood pressure on the extract fell from 146.5/97.8 to 129.9/86.0 mmHg — absolute reductions of 17.1 systolic and 12.0 diastolic (P < 0.05) — and 65.12% of patients reached the diastolic effectiveness criterion. Reductions and effectiveness were significantly lower than with lisinopril. Plasma ACE activity fell on the extract; tolerability and safety measures were 100%.
cards.watchOut: No placebo group — part of any fall in a trial like this is the trial effect itself (regression to the mean, measurement habituation). The record names the standardised extract (HsHMP) but no brand.
cards.source: Herrera-Arellano A et al.. Clinical effects produced by a standardized herbal medicinal product of Hibiscus sabdariffa on patients with hypertension. A randomized, double-blind, lisinopril-controlled clinical trial. Planta Med. 2007. PMID: 17315307. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sour tea drinkers' systolic pressure fell 22 mmHg in a month — but the two groups started 16 mmHg apart
cards.summary: Sour tea drinkers' systolic pressure fell 22 mmHg in a month — but the two groups started 16 mmHg apart
cards.people: 60 patients with type 2 diabetes and mild hypertension, taking no blood-pressure medicines; sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa) vs black tea infusions twice daily for one month, double-blind
cards.result: Systolic pressure in the sour-tea group fell from 134.4 ± 11.8 to 112.7 ± 5.7 mmHg (P < 0.001), while in the black-tea group it rose from 118.6 ± 14.9 to 127.3 ± 8.7 mmHg (P = 0.002). Diastolic pressure did not change significantly in either group; pulse pressure fell in the sour-tea group (52.2 to 34.5 mmHg).
cards.watchOut: The groups were badly imbalanced at baseline (systolic 134.4 vs 118.6 mmHg) — with randomisation this uneven the comparison is unreliable, and black tea is not an inert control.
cards.source: Mozaffari-Khosravi H et al.. The effects of sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa) on hypertension in patients with type II diabetes. J Hum Hypertens. 2009. PMID: 18685605. cards.headline: Three servings of hibiscus tea a day lowered systolic pressure about 6 mmHg more than a placebo drink
cards.summary: Three servings of hibiscus tea a day lowered systolic pressure about 6 mmHg more than a placebo drink
cards.people: 65 prehypertensive or mildly hypertensive adults aged 30–70, taking no blood-pressure medication; three 240-mL servings of brewed hibiscus tea daily or a placebo beverage for 6 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Systolic pressure fell by 7.2 ± 11.4 mmHg on hibiscus vs 1.3 ± 10.0 mmHg on placebo (P = 0.030) — a net effect of about 6 mmHg. Diastolic pressure fell by 3.1 vs 0.5 mmHg, not a significant difference (P = 0.160). Participants with higher starting systolic pressures responded most.
cards.watchOut: The cleanest trial here shows the smallest effect — about 6 mmHg net on systolic pressure and nothing proven on diastolic.

cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: Hibiscus preparations probably lower systolic blood pressure modestly — around 6 mmHg net in the one placebo-controlled trial. cards.watchOut: Preparations differ between trials (brewed tea, standardised extract, infusions), and no trial ran longer than six weeks.

shelves.title: Artichoke leaf extract for high cholesterol
shelves.question: Does artichoke leaf extract lower cholesterol?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking · Anthropometry · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cholesterol · Double-Blind Method · Enzymes · Female · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemias · Liver Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two double-blind trials both favoured the extract on total cholesterol (the between-group difference significant in each), but the stricter trial's effect was small (total cholesterol −4.2% vs +1.9% on placebo) and its LDL result was null, and no trial measured cardiovascular events.

cards.headline: Artichoke dry extract cut total cholesterol by 18.5% in six weeks — but placebo also fell 8.6%
cards.summary: Artichoke dry extract cut total cholesterol by 18.5% in six weeks — but placebo also fell 8.6%
cards.people: 143 adults with initial total cholesterol above 7.3 mmol/L (280 mg/dL); artichoke dry extract CY450, 1,800 mg/day, or placebo for 6 weeks; multicentre, double-blind
cards.result: Total cholesterol fell 18.5% in the extract group vs 8.6% on placebo, and LDL cholesterol fell 22.9% vs 6.3% (both P = 0.0001); the LDL/HDL ratio fell 20.2% vs 7.2%. No drug-related adverse events occurred. The tested product was the extract CY450, sold under the tradename Valverde Artischocke (per the record).
cards.watchOut: Percentage falls from a very high starting cholesterol over just six weeks, with a large placebo-group fall (8.6%) suggesting diet change and regression to the mean did much of the work; the between-group gap is the real signal.
cards.source: Englisch W et al.. Efficacy of Artichoke dry extract in patients with hyperlipoproteinemia. Arzneimittelforschung. 2000. PMID: 10758778. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: In a stricter, longer trial the effect was modest: total cholesterol −4.2% vs +1.9% on placebo — and LDL did not differ
cards.summary: In a stricter, longer trial the effect was modest: total cholesterol −4.2% vs +1.9% on placebo — and LDL did not differ
cards.people: 75 otherwise healthy adults with total cholesterol 6.0–8.0 mmol/L (≈232–310 mg/dL) (of 131 screened); standardised artichoke leaf extract 1,280 mg/day or matched placebo for 12 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Total cholesterol fell by an average of 4.2% on the extract (7.16 to 6.86 mmol/L (≈277 to 265 mg/dL)) and rose 1.9% on placebo (6.90 to 7.03 mmol/L (≈267 to 272 mg/dL)) — a statistically significant between-group difference (P = 0.025). No significant between-group differences were seen for LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol or triglycerides. General well-being improved in both groups (11% vs 9%).
cards.watchOut: The LDL difference — the lipid outcome that matters most — was not significant in this, the better-controlled of the two trials. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Bundy R et al.. shelves.title: Gene therapy for sickle cell disease: exa-cel freed 97% of evaluable patients from severe crises for at least a year; lovo-cel resolved severe events in all 25 evaluable patients
shelves.question: In severe sickle cell disease, does one-time gene therapy — CRISPR-edited exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) or lentiviral lovotibeglogene autotemcel (lovo-cel) — eliminate vaso-occlusive crises?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · *Anemia, Sickle Cell/complications/genetics/therapy · Antigens, CD34 · Busulfan/therapeutic use · CRISPR-Cas Systems · *Fetal Hemoglobin/biosynthesis/genetics · Gene Editing · *Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Hematopoietic Stem Cells · Repressor Proteins · Transplantation Conditioning · Cell- and Tissue-Based Therapy/methods · Myeloablative Agonists/therapeutic use · Europe · North America
shelves.balance: In the two pivotal single-arm studies, yes — for at least the first one to three years. In the phase 3 CLIMB SCD-121 study of the CRISPR-edited therapy exa-cel (Frangoul 2024), 44 patients aged 12–35 with at least two severe vaso-occlusive crises a year received the one-time treatment after busulfan myeloablation; of the 30 with enough follow-up to judge, 29 (97%) stayed free of severe crises for at least 12 consecutive months and all 30 stayed out of hospital for crises. The lentiviral therapy lovo-cel (Kanter 2022, HGB-206) reached the same place by a different route: all 25 evaluable patients had complete resolution of severe vaso-occlusive events, against a median of 3.5 events a year before treatment, with haemoglobin rising from 8.5 to at least 11 g/dL. The founding report (Frangoul 2021) is the first two patients ever treated this way — one with sickle cell disease, one with thalassaemia. What tempers the stamp: no randomised or controlled comparison exists for either product; median follow-up is 19.3 and 17.3 months in the pivotal cohorts; every patient first undergoes myeloablative busulfan conditioning with its own infertility and malignancy risks; and durability beyond about four years, and lifetime surveillance for late effects, are still unknown. The drug-therapy shelves are separate homes: hydroxyurea is #669, transfusion for stroke prevention #670, and voxelotor/crizanlizumab and their withdrawals #847. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): near-complete elimination of the disease's defining events in two independent single-arm programmes — short of LIKELY only because nothing here is controlled and the follow-up is short against a lifetime disease. Tier C: one-time irreversible therapy on single-arm evidence, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Frangoul 2024: exa-cel in severe sickle cell disease — 29 of 30 evaluable patients (97%) free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 months, all 30 free of hospitalisation for crises
cards.summary: Frangoul 2024: exa-cel in severe sickle cell disease — 29 of 30 evaluable patients (97%) free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 months, all 30 free of hospitalisation for crises
cards.people: 44 patients aged 12 to 35 years with sickle cell disease and at least two severe vaso-occlusive crises in each of the 2 years before screening. Their own CD34+ stem cells were edited ex vivo with CRISPR-Cas9 at the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate fetal haemoglobin, and returned after pharmacokinetically dose-adjusted busulfan myeloablation. Median follow-up 19.3 months (range 0.8 to 48.1).
cards.result: Neutrophils and platelets engrafted in every patient. Of the 30 patients with sufficient follow-up, 29 (97%; 95% CI 83 to 100) were free from severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 consecutive months and all 30 (100%; 95% CI 88 to 100) were free from inpatient hospitalisation for severe crises (P < 0.001 for both against a null hypothesis of 50% response). The safety profile was generally consistent with busulfan myeloablation and autologous transplantation. No cancers occurred.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 97% is compared against a statistical null (50%), not against hydroxyurea, transfusion programmes or allogeneic transplant, and 14 of the 44 treated patients had too little follow-up to count toward the endpoint. A therapy whose price of admission is myeloablation cannot be judged on crisis counts alone — infertility and second-malignancy risks ride along, and the record's follow-up cannot yet weigh them.
cards.source: Frangoul H et al. Exagamglogene Autotemcel for Severe Sickle Cell Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38661449. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03745287, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Kanter 2022: lovo-cel (LentiGlobin) resolved severe vaso-occlusive events in all 25 evaluable patients; haemoglobin rose from 8.5 to 11 g/dL or more
cards.summary: Kanter 2022: lovo-cel (LentiGlobin) resolved severe vaso-occlusive events in all 25 evaluable patients; haemoglobin rose from 8.5 to 11 g/dL or more
cards.type: Phase 1–2 study, pivotal Group C cohort (HGB-206) (Kanter 2022)
cards.people: 35 patients with sickle cell disease in the pivotal Group C received LentiGlobin (lovotibeglogene autotemcel): autologous stem cells transduced with the BB305 lentiviral vector encoding a modified β-globin (HbAT87Q). Group C required at least four severe vaso-occlusive events in the 24 months before enrolment. Median follow-up 17.3 months (range 3.7 to 37.6). This is an unprespecified interim analysis.
cards.result: Engraftment occurred in all 35 patients. Median total haemoglobin rose from 8.5 g/dL at baseline to 11 g/dL or more from month 6 through month 36; the engineered haemoglobin made up at least 40% of total haemoglobin across a mean 85% of red cells, and haemolysis markers fell. Among the 25 evaluable patients, all had resolution of severe vaso-occlusive events, compared with a median of 3.5 events per year (range 2.0 to 13.5) in the 24 months before enrolment. Three patients had a nonserious adverse event judged related or possibly related to the product, resolving within a week. No cases of haematologic cancer were observed during up to 37.6 months of follow-up.
cards.watchOut: An unprespecified interim analysis of a single-arm study whose treatment process had already been revised twice (Groups A and B used earlier versions), so the 35 patients are the optimised-process cohort, not everyone ever treated. Lentiviral insertion carries a theoretical oncogenesis risk that 37.6 months cannot exclude; the abstract's reassurance is cohort- and window-specific.
cards.source: Kanter J et al. Biologic and Clinical Efficacy of LentiGlobin for Sickle Cell Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 34898139. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02140554, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Frangoul 2021: the first two patients — one with sickle cell disease, one with thalassaemia — stayed free of crises and transfusions for over a year after CRISPR editing
cards.summary: Frangoul 2021: the first two patients — one with sickle cell disease, one with thalassaemia — stayed free of crises and transfusions for over a year after CRISPR editing
cards.type: First-in-human report of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, 2 patients (Frangoul 2021)
cards.people: Two patients — one with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia and one with sickle cell disease — received autologous CD34+ cells edited with CRISPR-Cas9 at the BCL11A erythroid enhancer (the exa-cel approach), after myeloablation. Laboratory work in donor cells showed about 80% of alleles at the target locus modified, with no evidence of off-target editing.
cards.result: More than a year after infusion, both patients had high levels of allelic editing in bone marrow and blood, increases in fetal haemoglobin distributed across red cells, transfusion independence (the thalassaemia patient), and elimination of vaso-occlusive episodes (the patient with sickle cell disease).
cards.watchOut: Two patients, reported because they were first: this card is the proof of concept the two phase 3 programmes grew from, and it carries no statistical weight of its own. It is homed on this shelf because its sickle-cell patient opened the CLIMB SCD-121 programme; the thalassaemia patient's disease is followed up at scale on shelf #2554.
cards.source: Frangoul H et al. CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing for Sickle Cell Disease and β-Thalassemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33283989. cards.headline: Synthesis: two different one-time gene therapies abolished severe crises in nearly every evaluable patient — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two different one-time gene therapies abolished severe crises in nearly every evaluable patient — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Two phase 3/1–2 single-arm programmes (44 patients treated with exa-cel, 35 with lovo-cel in its pivotal cohort) and the 2-patient first-in-human report that preceded both.
cards.result: Freedom from severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 months in 29 of 30 evaluable exa-cel patients (97%) and complete resolution of severe events in all 25 evaluable lovo-cel patients, with haemoglobin normalised or near-normalised in both programmes. The two technologies — CRISPR editing of a fetal-haemoglobin switch, and lentiviral addition of an anti-sickling β-globin — converge on the same clinical result, which strengthens belief that the effect is real rather than a single product's artefact. What no card here can speak to: comparison with allogeneic transplantation (the established cure), fertility after busulfan, cost and access, and durability past roughly four years.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf is a proportion in an uncontrolled cohort, judged against each patient's own pre-treatment history — exactly the design that flatters interventions in a disease whose crisis frequency varies naturally. The size and consistency of the effect (near-total abolition, not a percentage shaved off) is why the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) rather than MAYBE; the absence of controls and the short follow-up are why it is not LIKELY.
cards.source: Synthesis of Frangoul H et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38661449); Kanter J et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34898139); Frangoul H et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33283989).

shelves.title: Gene therapy for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia: transfusion independence in 91% with exa-cel and 89–91% with beti-cel, including the severe β0/β0 genotypes
shelves.question: In transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia, does one-time gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel, exa-cel, or betibeglogene autotemcel, beti-cel) free patients from regular transfusions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Antigens, CD34 · *beta-Thalassemia/therapy/genetics · Blood Transfusion · Busulfan/therapeutic use · CRISPR-Cas Systems · *Fetal Hemoglobin/biosynthesis/genetics · *Gene Editing/methods · *Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation/methods · Hematopoietic Stem Cells · Repressor Proteins/genetics · Transplantation Conditioning · Transplantation, Autologous · Myeloablative Agonists/therapeutic use · North America · Europe
shelves.balance: In three phase 3 single-arm studies, about nine in ten patients stopped transfusing altogether. The CRISPR-edited therapy exa-cel (Locatelli 2024, CLIMB THAL-111) produced transfusion independence — a weighted average haemoglobin of at least 9 g/dL with no red-cell transfusion for at least 12 consecutive months — in 32 of 35 evaluable patients (91%), with mean haemoglobin 13.1 g/dL during independence. The lentiviral therapy beti-cel reached 20 of 22 evaluable patients (91%) in genotypes with some residual β-globin production (Locatelli 2022, HGB-207) and 16 of 18 (89%) in the severe β0/β0-type genotypes that make no β-globin at all (Kwiatkowski 2024, HGB-212), the latter with the longest follow-up here (median 47.9 months). No deaths and no cancers were reported in any of the three studies. The caveats mirror the sickle-cell shelf (#2553): no controlled comparison, busulfan myeloablation as the price of admission, evaluable-patient denominators smaller than the treated numbers, and durability proven only to about four years so far. The two-patient first-in-human CRISPR report (Frangoul 2021), which included the first thalassaemia patient treated, is homed on #2553. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: one-time irreversible therapy on single-arm evidence, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Locatelli 2024: exa-cel in transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia — transfusion independence in 32 of 35 evaluable patients (91%), mean haemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
cards.summary: Locatelli 2024: exa-cel in transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia — transfusion independence in 32 of 35 evaluable patients (91%), mean haemoglobin 13.1 g/dL
cards.type: Phase 3 single-group open-label study (CLIMB THAL-111), prespecified interim analysis (Locatelli 2024)
cards.people: 52 patients aged 12 to 35 years with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (β0/β0, β0/β0-like, or non-β0/β0-like genotypes) received exa-cel: their own CRISPR-Cas9-edited CD34+ cells (BCL11A enhancer), after pharmacokinetically dose-adjusted busulfan myeloablation. Median follow-up 20.4 months (range 2.1 to 48.1).
cards.result: Neutrophils and platelets engrafted in every patient. Among the 35 patients with sufficient follow-up, transfusion independence occurred in 32 (91%; 95% CI 77 to 98; P < 0.001 against a null hypothesis of 50%). During independence the mean total haemoglobin was 13.1 g/dL and mean fetal haemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, distributed across at least 94% of red cells. The safety profile was generally consistent with busulfan myeloablation and autologous transplantation. No deaths or cancers occurred.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis in which only 35 of the 52 treated patients had yet reached the 12-month landmark — the 91% is a proportion of the evaluable, and late failures or late toxicities in the remainder are not yet visible. As on the sickle shelf, the comparison is a statistical null, not allogeneic transplant or continued transfusion.
cards.source: Locatelli F et al. Exagamglogene Autotemcel for Transfusion-Dependent β-Thalassemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38657265. cards.headline: Locatelli 2022: beti-cel in non-β0/β0 thalassaemia — transfusion independence in 20 of 22 evaluable patients (91%), including 6 of 7 children under 12
cards.summary: Locatelli 2022: beti-cel in non-β0/β0 thalassaemia — transfusion independence in 20 of 22 evaluable patients (91%), including 6 of 7 children under 12
cards.people: 23 patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia and a non-β0/β0 genotype (some residual β-globin production) received beti-cel: autologous CD34+ cells transduced with the BB305 lentiviral vector encoding a modified β-globin (βA-T87Q), after pharmacokinetically adjusted busulfan myeloablation. Median follow-up 29.5 months (range 13.0 to 48.2).
cards.result: Transfusion independence (weighted average haemoglobin at least 9 g/dL without transfusion for at least 12 months) occurred in 20 of 22 evaluable patients (91%), including 6 of 7 patients younger than 12. Average haemoglobin during independence was 11.7 g/dL (range 9.5 to 12.8). Four patients had adverse events judged related or possibly related to beti-cel, all nonserious except one case of thrombocytopenia. No cases of cancer were observed.
cards.watchOut: The non-β0/β0 population is the easier half of the disease — these patients make some β-globin of their own, so the engineered contribution has less ground to cover. The severe genotypes are the next card. A lentiviral product also carries the insertion-site caveat that follow-up of this length cannot retire.
cards.source: Locatelli F et al. Betibeglogene Autotemcel Gene Therapy for Non-β0/β0 Genotype β-Thalassemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 34891223. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02906202, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Kwiatkowski 2024: beti-cel in severe-genotype thalassaemia (β0/β0 and related) — 16 of 18 patients (89%) reached and maintained transfusion independence, median follow-up 47.9 months
cards.summary: Kwiatkowski 2024: beti-cel in severe-genotype thalassaemia (β0/β0 and related) — 16 of 18 patients (89%) reached and maintained transfusion independence, median follow-up 47.9 months
cards.type: Phase 3 non-randomised multicentre single-arm open-label trial (HGB-212) (Kwiatkowski 2024)
cards.people: 18 patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia of severe genotype (12 with β0/β0; the rest β0/β+IVS-I-110 or β+IVS-I-110/β+IVS-I-110) and a heavy transfusion history (at least 100 mL/kg per year or at least 8 transfusions a year) received beti-cel after busulfan myeloablative conditioning, at eight centres in six countries; 13 of the 18 were under 18. All enrolled in the 13-year long-term follow-up study; median follow-up 47.9 months (range 23.8 to 59.0).
cards.result: All 18 patients were evaluable, and 16 (89%) reached and maintained transfusion independence to last follow-up (estimated effect size 89.9%; 95% CI 65.3 to 98.6). All patients had at least one adverse event after infusion; there were no serious adverse events considered related to beti-cel and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three studies (18 patients) but the most informative denominator — every treated patient counted — and the longest follow-up. It is published in The Lancet (the record's journal field) as a phase 3 report; the confidence interval (65–99%) honestly reflects how few patients stand behind the 89%.
cards.source: Kwiatkowski JL et al. Betibeglogene autotemcel gene therapy in patients with transfusion-dependent, severe genotype β-thalassaemia (HGB-212): a non-randomised, multicentre, single-arm, open-label, single-dose, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. 2024. PMID: 39527960. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03207009 (HGB-212), from the record's databank fields; the long-term follow-up study is NCT02633943 (LTF-303). cards.headline: Synthesis: two gene-therapy platforms, three phase 3 studies, one result — about 9 in 10 patients transfusion-free — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two gene-therapy platforms, three phase 3 studies, one result — about 9 in 10 patients transfusion-free — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Three phase 3 single-arm studies: exa-cel in mixed genotypes (52 treated, 35 evaluable), beti-cel in non-β0/β0 genotypes (23 treated, 22 evaluable) and beti-cel in severe β0/β0-type genotypes (18 treated, all evaluable).
cards.result: Transfusion independence of at least 12 months in 91%, 91% and 89% of evaluable patients respectively, with haemoglobin during independence averaging 11.7–13.1 g/dL — achieved in young children as well as adults, and in the genotypes that produce no β-globin at all. Because one platform edits a fetal-haemoglobin switch and the other adds a working β-globin gene, the agreement between them argues the benefit belongs to restored haemoglobin production, not to one manufacturer's process. The first thalassaemia patient ever treated with the editing approach sits inside the two-patient report homed on shelf #2553.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm throughout: transfusion independence is a hard, countable endpoint (unlike symptom scores), which is why this shelf reads stronger than most uncontrolled evidence — but patients were selected for fitness to survive myeloablation, iron-overload damage already done is not undone by stopping transfusions, and 15-year follow-up studies exist precisely because nobody yet knows the lifetime ledger.
cards.source: Synthesis of Locatelli F et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38657265); Locatelli F et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34891223); Kwiatkowski JL et al. The Lancet. 2024 (PMID: 39527960).

shelves.title: Gene therapy for haemophilia: bleeding rates fell 64–84% (relative) against each cohort's own prophylaxis baseline in three phase 3 studies — liver enzyme rises were the tax
shelves.question: In severe haemophilia A and moderate-to-severe haemophilia B, does a single gene-therapy infusion replace regular factor prophylaxis and cut bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Dependovirus · Factor VIII/therapeutic use · *Genetic Therapy/methods · *Genetic Vectors · *Hemophilia A/complications/therapy · *Hemorrhage/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · HIV Seronegativity · Infusions, Intravenous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Gene Therapy Agents
shelves.balance: One infusion of an AAV vector carrying the factor gene cut bleeding substantially in all three phase 3 programmes — each compared against the patients' own prophylaxis lead-in period, not against a randomised control. For severe haemophilia A, valoctocogene roxaparvovec (Ozelo 2022, GENEr8-1, 134 men) raised factor VIII activity by a mean of 41.9 IU/dL at one year and reduced treated bleeding by 83.8% relative and factor concentrate use by 98.6% relative in the rollover cohort. For haemophilia B, etranacogene dezaparvovec (Pipe 2023, HOPE-B, 54 men) cut the annualised bleeding rate from 4.19 to 1.51 (rate ratio 0.36 — a 64% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed here), and fidanacogene elaparvovec (Cuker 2024, BENEGENE-2, 45 men) cut it from 4.42 to 1.28 (a 71% relative reduction). The price is hepatic: alanine aminotransferase rose in 85.8% of valoctocogene recipients, and 62% of fidanacogene recipients needed glucocorticoids for enzyme rises or falling factor levels — the immune response against the vector capsid is the therapy's running battle, and it is why factor VIII expression after valoctocogene is known to wane over the years after infusion (the carded record reports the first year). Pre-existing anti-AAV antibodies excluded most screened men from BENEGENE-2 (59.5% of those ineligible). No inhibitors and no thrombosis in any of the three studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: single-arm evidence with durability unresolved, taken to the developer personally. Emicizumab prophylaxis — the non-gene-therapy comparator most patients now use — is on shelves #671 and #1414.

cards.headline: Ozelo 2022: valoctocogene in severe haemophilia A — factor VIII up a mean 41.9 IU/dL at one year; treated bleeding down 83.8% relative, concentrate use down 98.6% relative
cards.summary: Ozelo 2022: valoctocogene in severe haemophilia A — factor VIII up a mean 41.9 IU/dL at one year; treated bleeding down 83.8% relative, concentrate use down 98.6% relative
cards.people: 134 men with severe haemophilia A (factor VIII at most 1 IU/dL), previously on factor VIII prophylaxis, without pre-existing anti-AAV5 antibodies or a history of factor VIII inhibitors, received one infusion of valoctocogene roxaparvovec (AAV5 carrying a factor VIII cDNA) at 6×10^13 vector genomes per kilogram.
cards.result: At weeks 49–52, mean factor VIII activity had risen by 41.9 IU/dL (95% CI 34.1 to 49.7; median change 22.9). Among the 112 participants rolled over from a prospective non-interventional study, mean annualised factor VIII concentrate use and treated bleeding after week 4 fell by 98.6% and 83.8% respectively relative to their prophylaxis baseline (P < 0.001 for both — relative reductions; the abstract does not print the absolute bleeding rates behind them). All participants had at least one adverse event and 16.4% had serious adverse events. Alanine aminotransferase elevations occurred in 85.8% and were managed with immunosuppressants. No factor VIII inhibitors and no thrombosis occurred.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative reductions against the patients' own baseline in an unblinded study — bleeding is partly a reported outcome, and people who have just received a one-time 'curative' infusion may report and treat bleeds differently. The record covers about one year; the known waning of factor VIII expression in later years is outside this abstract, so the shelf claims the first-year result only.
cards.source: Ozelo MC et al. Valoctocogene Roxaparvovec Gene Therapy for Hemophilia A. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35294811. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03370913, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pipe 2023: etranacogene in haemophilia B — annualised bleeding rate 4.19 on prophylaxis fell to 1.51 (rate ratio 0.36); factor IX up about 35 points and stable to 18 months
cards.summary: Pipe 2023: etranacogene in haemophilia B — annualised bleeding rate 4.19 on prophylaxis fell to 1.51 (rate ratio 0.36); factor IX up about 35 points and stable to 18 months
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label study with prospective prophylaxis lead-in (HOPE-B) (Pipe 2023)
cards.people: 54 men with haemophilia B (factor IX activity at most 2% of normal) received one infusion of etranacogene dezaparvovec (AAV5 expressing the high-activity Padua factor IX variant) after at least 6 months of factor IX prophylaxis as their own lead-in control; pre-existing AAV5 neutralising antibodies were not an exclusion. The primary endpoint was the annualised bleeding rate in months 7–18 after treatment versus the lead-in.
cards.result: The annualised bleeding rate fell from 4.19 (95% CI 3.22 to 5.45) during lead-in to 1.51 (0.81 to 2.82) after treatment — a rate ratio of 0.36 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.64; P < 0.001), meeting both noninferiority (margin 1.8) and superiority; that is a 64% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed alongside. Factor IX activity rose by a least-squares mean of 36.2 percentage points at 6 months and 34.3 points at 18 months, and factor IX concentrate use fell by a mean of 248,825 IU per year per participant. Benefits and safety were seen in participants with pre-dose AAV5 antibody titres under 700. No treatment-related serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The strongest-designed of the three cards — a prospective lead-in, a pre-set noninferiority margin, and factor IX expression holding at 18 months — but still a before–after comparison in 54 men, and the antibody-titre ceiling (under 700) quietly defines who the result applies to.
cards.source: Pipe SW et al. Gene Therapy with Etranacogene Dezaparvovec for Hemophilia B. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36812434. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03569891, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Cuker 2024: fidanacogene in haemophilia B — bleeding rate 4.42 fell to 1.28 (71% relative reduction); 62% needed steroids for liver-enzyme rises or falling factor IX
cards.summary: Cuker 2024: fidanacogene in haemophilia B — bleeding rate 4.42 fell to 1.28 (71% relative reduction); 62% needed steroids for liver-enzyme rises or falling factor IX
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label study with prophylaxis lead-in (BENEGENE-2) (Cuker 2024)
cards.people: 45 men aged 18–65 with haemophilia B (factor IX at most 2%) received one infusion of fidanacogene elaparvovec (AAV vector carrying the Padua high-activity factor IX variant) after at least 6 months of prophylactic factor IX. Of 316 men screened into the lead-in study, 204 (64.6%) were ineligible — 188 of them (59.5% of those ineligible) because of anti-AAV neutralising antibodies.
cards.result: The annualised rate of all bleeding episodes fell from 4.42 (95% CI 1.80 to 7.05) in the lead-in to 1.28 (0.57 to 1.98) from week 12 to month 15 — a treatment difference of −3.15 episodes (P = 0.008), a 71% relative reduction with absolute rates alongside — meeting noninferiority and superiority against prophylaxis. Mean factor IX activity at 15 months was 26.9% (range 1.9 to 119.0). Twenty-eight participants (62%) received glucocorticoids for raised aminotransferases or falling factor IX, starting between days 11 and 123. No infusion-related serious adverse events, thrombosis, factor IX inhibitors or malignancies were observed.
cards.watchOut: The screening funnel is part of the result: nearly two-thirds of volunteers could not be treated, most because of pre-existing vector antibodies, so this is a therapy for a pre-selected minority of men with haemophilia B. The wide range of achieved factor IX (1.9% to 119%) means 'average 26.9%' conceals both near-nonresponders and supranormal expressors.
cards.source: Cuker A et al. Gene Therapy with Fidanacogene Elaparvovec in Adults with Hemophilia B. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39321362. cards.headline: Synthesis: three AAV gene therapies, three before–after victories over prophylaxis — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three AAV gene therapies, three before–after victories over prophylaxis — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Three phase 3 single-arm studies with prospective prophylaxis lead-ins: valoctocogene for severe haemophilia A (134 men) and etranacogene and fidanacogene for haemophilia B (54 and 45 men).
cards.result: Bleeding fell by 83.8% relative (treated bleeds, valoctocogene), to a rate ratio of 0.36 (etranacogene; 4.19 to 1.51 bleeds a year), and by 71% relative (fidanacogene; 4.42 to 1.28 a year), with factor levels rising into the mild-haemophilia or near-normal range and concentrate use collapsing. No inhibitors, no thrombosis, no treatment-related deaths in any programme. Set against that: liver-enzyme rises in most recipients, glucocorticoid courses in up to 62%, antibody exclusions that bar many patients, factor VIII expression that wanes after valoctocogene beyond the year this record covers, and no randomised comparison against modern prophylaxis (including emicizumab, shelves #671 and #1414) anywhere.
cards.watchOut: A before–after design in a disease whose bleeding is episodic and partly self-reported will flatter any intervention; what rescues these cards from MAYBE is the objective factor-level rise moving with the bleeding fall, in three independent programmes. What keeps them from LIKELY is durability — a 'one-time' therapy is only one-time if expression lasts.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ozelo MC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35294811); Pipe SW et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36812434); Cuker A et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39321362).

shelves.title: INVICTUS: in rheumatic heart disease with atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban was worse than a vitamin K antagonist — more cardiovascular events and more deaths, with no bleeding advantage
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation due to rheumatic heart disease, is rivaroxaban as good as a vitamin K antagonist at preventing stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction and death?
shelves.mesh: *Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy/etiology · Echocardiography · *Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Rheumatic Heart Disease/complications/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging · *Rivaroxaban/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Stroke/etiology/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin K/antagonists & inhibitors · Warfarin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: The direct-oral-anticoagulant trials that changed practice excluded rheumatic heart disease, and INVICTUS shows why that exclusion mattered. In 4,531 analysed patients with atrial fibrillation and echocardiographically documented rheumatic heart disease (Connolly 2022, PMID: 36036525), the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction or death occurred in 560 patients on rivaroxaban versus 446 on a dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonist; restricted mean survival time was 1599 versus 1675 days (difference −76 days, 95% CI −121 to −31, P<0.001), and the mortality component alone favoured the vitamin K antagonist by 72 days of restricted mean survival. Major bleeding did not differ significantly — rivaroxaban bought its worse efficacy with no safety gain. Permanent discontinuation of trial medication was more common on rivaroxaban at every visit, a real-world weakness of a fixed-dose drug in this population. The result does not touch ordinary non-valvular atrial fibrillation, where the DOAC evidence stands on its own trials; it closes the door on extrapolating that evidence to rheumatic mitral disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm — rivaroxaban inferior) (Tier C: a mortality-bearing cardiovascular-outcome shelf resting on one trial).

cards.headline: Connolly 2022 (INVICTUS): 560 primary events on rivaroxaban versus 446 on a vitamin K antagonist; survival time 76 days shorter on rivaroxaban; major bleeding not different
cards.summary: Connolly 2022 (INVICTUS): 560 primary events on rivaroxaban versus 446 on a vitamin K antagonist; survival time 76 days shorter on rivaroxaban; major bleeding not different
cards.people: 4,565 patients enrolled and 4,531 included in the final analysis, with atrial fibrillation and echocardiographically documented rheumatic heart disease, plus at least one of: CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2, mitral-valve area ≤2 cm², left atrial spontaneous echo contrast, or left atrial thrombus. Mean age 50.5 years; 72.3% women. Standard-dose rivaroxaban versus dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonist; the trial tested rivaroxaban for noninferiority.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 560 patients in the rivaroxaban group and 446 in the vitamin K antagonist group had a primary-outcome event (stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or death from vascular or unknown causes). The restricted mean survival time was 1599 days on rivaroxaban versus 1675 days on the vitamin K antagonist (difference −76 days; 95% CI −121 to −31; P<0.001). Death alone: restricted mean survival time 1608 versus 1680 days (difference −72 days; 95% CI −117 to −28). There was no significant between-group difference in major bleeding. Permanent discontinuation of trial medication was more common with rivaroxaban at all visits.
cards.watchOut: The survival curves were nonproportional, which is why the trial reports restricted mean survival time rather than a single hazard ratio — quoting a hazard ratio for this trial misstates it. This is a younger, mostly female, largely low- and middle-income-country population with rheumatic mitral disease; it says nothing about DOACs in the non-valvular atrial fibrillation of older adults, where separate trials govern.
cards.source: Connolly SJ et al. Rivaroxaban in Rheumatic Heart Disease-Associated Atrial Fibrillation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36036525. Registry ID: NCT02832544. cards.headline: Synthesis: vitamin K antagonists remain the standard in rheumatic atrial fibrillation — LIKELY (harm from rivaroxaban)
cards.summary: Synthesis: vitamin K antagonists remain the standard in rheumatic atrial fibrillation — LIKELY (harm from rivaroxaban)
cards.people: One randomised trial of 4,531 patients with rheumatic heart disease-associated atrial fibrillation — the only large trial of a factor Xa inhibitor in this population.
cards.result: Rivaroxaban versus vitamin K antagonist: 560 versus 446 primary composite events; 76 fewer days of restricted mean survival time (95% CI −121 to −31) and 72 fewer days for death alone; major bleeding not significantly different; more permanent drug discontinuation on rivaroxaban. A drug class validated in non-valvular atrial fibrillation failed — on efficacy, including mortality — in the rheumatic population its trials had excluded.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one drug: the shelf condemns rivaroxaban in rheumatic atrial fibrillation, and by extension warns against class extrapolation, but apixaban, dabigatran and edoxaban have not been trialled here and are 'untested', not 'proven harmful'. Warfarin's win also depended on trial-grade INR management; where INR control is poor in practice, the margin could narrow — the trial does not measure that setting.
cards.source: Synthesis of Connolly SJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36036525).

shelves.title: GOAL: four-weekly benzathine penicillin injections for two years cut echocardiographic progression of latent rheumatic heart disease from 8.2% to 0.8%
shelves.question: In children and adolescents found by echocardiographic screening to have latent rheumatic heart disease, does secondary antibiotic prophylaxis with four-weekly benzathine penicillin G prevent progression of the valve lesions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · *Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Child · Child, Preschool · Disease Progression · Echocardiography · Female · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Intention to Treat Analysis · Latent Infection/drug therapy · Male · Mass Screening · Penicillin G Benzathine/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Rheumatic Heart Disease/diagnostic imaging/*drug therapy · Uganda
shelves.balance: Echocardiographic screening finds rheumatic heart disease years before symptoms, but until GOAL nobody had shown that treating the screen-detected, latent stage changes anything. In the GOAL trial (Beaton 2022, PMID: 34767321), Ugandan children and adolescents aged 5–17 with latent rheumatic heart disease were randomised to benzathine penicillin G injections every 4 weeks for 2 years or to no prophylaxis; at 2 years, echocardiographic progression had occurred in 3 participants (0.8%) on prophylaxis versus 33 (8.2%) without (risk difference −7.5 percentage points, 95% CI −10.2 to −4.7; P<0.001) — roughly 13 children treated for two years to prevent one progression. Harms were small: two serious adverse events attributable to prophylaxis, including one mild anaphylactic reaction (under 0.1% of all doses given). The caveats are structural, not statistical: the outcome is echocardiographic progression, not clinical heart failure or death; the trial sits in one high-burden country; and the screening funnel was enormous — 102,200 children screened to find 926 eligible — which is why the authors themselves say further research is needed before population-level screening can be recommended. Treating latent disease once found is supported; building the screening programme to find it is a separate, unproven step. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: single-trial benefit on an imaging outcome).

cards.headline: Beaton 2022 (GOAL): progression of latent rheumatic heart disease at 2 years in 0.8% with penicillin prophylaxis versus 8.2% without (risk difference −7.5 percentage points, P<0.001)
cards.summary: Beaton 2022 (GOAL): progression of latent rheumatic heart disease at 2 years in 0.8% with penicillin prophylaxis versus 8.2% without (risk difference −7.5 percentage points, P<0.001)
cards.people: Ugandan children and adolescents 5 to 17 years of age with latent (screen-detected, asymptomatic) rheumatic heart disease, randomised to penicillin G benzathine injections every 4 weeks for 2 years or no prophylaxis. Of 102,200 children screened by echocardiography, 926 received a definitive diagnosis and were eligible; 916 were randomised, 818 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, and 799 (97.7%) completed the trial. Echocardiographic change was adjudicated by a panel blinded to group assignment.
cards.result: Echocardiographic progression at 2 years occurred in 3 participants (0.8%) in the prophylaxis group versus 33 (8.2%) in the control group (risk difference −7.5 percentage points; 95% CI −10.2 to −4.7; P<0.001) — an absolute reduction of about 7.5 progressions per 100 children treated for 2 years. Two participants in the prophylaxis group had serious adverse events attributable to prophylaxis, including one episode of mild anaphylaxis (representing <0.1% of all administered doses).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is progression on echocardiography over 2 years — a validated disease-stage measure, but not symptoms, heart failure, surgery or death, and the event count is small (3 versus 33), so the estimate rests on few events. The trial also cannot answer its own precondition: whether screening 110 children to find one treatable case is a programme worth building is an implementation and cost question the authors explicitly leave open.
cards.source: Beaton A et al. Secondary Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Latent Rheumatic Heart Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 34767321. Registry ID: NCT03346525. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis works on the lesions screening finds — POSSIBLE, with the screening programme itself still unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis works on the lesions screening finds — POSSIBLE, with the screening programme itself still unproven
cards.people: One randomised trial: 818 children and adolescents with latent rheumatic heart disease analysed, drawn from 102,200 screened in Uganda.
cards.result: Four-weekly benzathine penicillin G for 2 years reduced echocardiographic progression from 8.2% to 0.8% (absolute difference −7.5 percentage points; number needed to treat ≈13 over 2 years), with serious prophylaxis-attributable events in 2 children and anaphylaxis in under 0.1% of doses. Benefit is established for the treatment step only; the value of the population screening that feeds it is not established by this trial.
cards.watchOut: A single trial in a single high-burden setting, on an imaging outcome, with 36 total progression events: the direction is unlikely to be wrong, but the size of the clinical (as opposed to echocardiographic) dividend — heart failure or deaths prevented over a childhood — remains unmeasured, and adherence to 26 injections over 2 years outside a trial is its own problem.
cards.source: Synthesis of Beaton A et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34767321).

shelves.title: Treating the soil, not just the rhythm: sustained weight loss, aggressive risk-factor management and exercise each reduced atrial fibrillation — but only one of the three tests was randomised
shelves.question: In people with atrial fibrillation, does structured management of weight and cardiovascular risk factors — sustained weight loss, exercise, blood pressure, lipids, glycaemia, alcohol and sleep apnoea — reduce atrial fibrillation burden and recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation/*complications · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Goals · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/*complications/*therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Time · Time Factors · *Weight Loss
shelves.balance: Three Adelaide programmes make the same point at three levels of rigour. LEGACY (Pathak 2015, PMID: 25792361) followed 355 patients with atrial fibrillation and BMI ≥27 who had been offered goal-directed weight management: those who lost ≥10% of body weight had a 6-fold greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival than those who lost less (95% CI 3.4 to 10.3, a relative measure), while weight fluctuation over 5% doubled recurrence risk — but patients chose their own effort, so motivation is entangled with the weight loss itself. ARREST-AF (Pathak 2014, PMID: 25456757) applied aggressive risk-factor management after ablation in patients who opted in: arrhythmia-free survival was markedly better than in matched controls (multivariate hazard ratio 4.8, 95% CI 2.04 to 11.4, relative), with only 16% of the managed group still using antiarrhythmic drugs after multiple procedures versus 42.4% of controls. The one randomised test is of exercise rather than weight: ACTIVE-AF (Elliott 2023, PMID: 36752479) randomised 120 patients to a 6-month supervised-plus-home exercise programme and found freedom from AF at 12 months in 40% versus 20% (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78), with less severe symptoms — without any between-group difference in weight or blood pressure. Nothing here shows a mortality benefit, and none of it replaces anticoagulation or rate/rhythm therapy; it says the substrate responds to treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: the weight and risk-factor claims rest on self-selected cohorts; the single randomised trial is small).

cards.headline: Pathak 2015 (LEGACY): patients who lost ≥10% of body weight had a 6-fold greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival; weight fluctuation over 5% doubled the risk of recurrence
cards.summary: Pathak 2015 (LEGACY): patients who lost ≥10% of body weight had a 6-fold greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival; weight fluctuation over 5% doubled the risk of recurrence
cards.people: Prospective cohort: of 1,415 consecutive patients with atrial fibrillation, 825 had BMI ≥27 kg/m² and were offered weight management; after exclusions, 355 were analysed in three groups by weight lost — group 1 ≥10% (n with the largest loss), group 2 3–9%, group 3 <3% — with yearly follow-up of weight trend and fluctuation, AF severity scores and 7-day ambulatory monitoring.
cards.result: AF burden and symptom severity decreased more in group 1 than in groups 2 and 3 (p<0.001 for all), and arrhythmia-free survival, with and without rhythm-control strategies, was greatest in group 1 (p<0.001 for both). In multivariate analyses, weight loss ≥10% was associated with a 6-fold (95% CI 3.4 to 10.3; p<0.001) greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival compared with the other two groups (a relative measure from an observational cohort). Weight fluctuation >5% partially offset the benefit, with a 2-fold (95% CI 1.0 to 4.3; p=0.02) increased risk of arrhythmia recurrence.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: patients sorted themselves by how much weight they actually lost, so the 6-fold figure bundles the effect of weight loss with everything that makes sustained loss possible — adherence, resources, fewer comorbid barriers. It is a dose-response association in a selected clinic cohort, and 'arrhythmia-free survival' here includes patients managed with drugs and ablation, not weight loss alone.
cards.source: Pathak RK et al. Long-Term Effect of Goal-Directed Weight Management in an Atrial Fibrillation Cohort: A Long-Term Follow-Up Study (LEGACY). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015. PMID: 25792361. Registry ID: ACTRN12614001123639. cards.headline: Pathak 2014 (ARREST-AF): after ablation, patients who took up aggressive risk-factor management had markedly better arrhythmia-free survival (hazard ratio 4.8) and far fewer still needed antiarrhythmic drugs (16% vs 42.4%)
cards.summary: Pathak 2014 (ARREST-AF): after ablation, patients who took up aggressive risk-factor management had markedly better arrhythmia-free survival (hazard ratio 4.8) and far fewer still needed antiarrhythmic drugs (16% vs 42.4%)
cards.type: Prospective cohort study with self-selected intervention (Pathak 2014, ARREST-AF)
cards.people: Cohort study of 281 consecutive patients undergoing atrial fibrillation ablation; 149 with BMI ≥27 kg/m² and at least one cardiac risk factor were offered risk-factor management (RFM) per AHA/ACC guidelines — weight, blood pressure, lipids, glycaemia, smoking, alcohol and sleep apnoea. The 61 who opted for RFM were compared with 88 controls, assessed every 3–6 months with clinic review and 7-day Holter monitoring; baseline characteristics, procedure numbers and follow-up did not differ.
cards.result: RFM produced greater reductions in weight (p=0.002) and blood pressure (p=0.006) and better glycaemic control (p=0.001) and lipid profiles (p=0.01). AF frequency, duration, symptoms and severity decreased more in the RFM group (all p<0.001). Single-procedure drug-unassisted arrhythmia-free survival was greater in RFM patients (p<0.001), as was multiple-procedure arrhythmia-free survival; after multiple procedures, 16% of the RFM group versus 42.4% of controls were using antiarrhythmic drugs (p=0.004). On multivariate analysis, RFM was an independent predictor of arrhythmia-free survival (hazard ratio 4.8; 95% CI 2.04 to 11.4; p<0.001 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Patients opted in — 61 of 149 eligible chose the programme — so the comparison is between the motivated and the rest, in a single expert centre whose ablation outcomes may not travel. The hazard ratio of 4.8 is the kind of effect size observational self-selection produces and randomised trials rarely confirm; treat it as an upper bound, not an expectation.
cards.source: Pathak RK et al. Aggressive risk factor reduction study for atrial fibrillation and implications for the outcome of ablation: the ARREST-AF cohort study. cards.headline: Elliott 2023 (ACTIVE-AF): the randomised test — a 6-month exercise programme doubled freedom from AF at 12 months (40% vs 20%; hazard ratio 0.50) and reduced symptom severity
cards.summary: Elliott 2023 (ACTIVE-AF): the randomised test — a 6-month exercise programme doubled freedom from AF at 12 months (40% vs 20%; hazard ratio 0.50) and reduced symptom severity
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 120 patients with paroxysmal or persistent symptomatic atrial fibrillation, assigned 1:1 to a 6-month exercise intervention (supervised plus home aerobic exercise) or usual care. Co-primary outcomes: AF recurrence off antiarrhythmic drugs and without ablation, and symptom severity on a validated questionnaire, followed to 12 months.
cards.result: By 12 months, freedom from AF was achieved in 24 of 60 patients (40%) in the exercise group versus 12 of 60 (20%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78). AF symptom severity was lower with exercise at 6 months (mean difference −2.3; 95% CI −4.3 to −0.2; P=0.033) and at 12 months (−2.3; −4.5 to −0.1; P=0.041); peak oxygen consumption increased at both time points. There were no between-group differences in cardiac structure or function, body mass index, or blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=120), unblinded by necessity, and the benefit arrived without weight loss or blood-pressure change — so it supports exercise itself, not the whole risk-factor package, and says nothing about stroke or mortality. Recurrence was assessed off antiarrhythmic drugs and without ablation, a cleaner but narrower endpoint than everyday practice.
cards.source: Elliott AD et al. An Exercise and Physical Activity Program in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation: The ACTIVE-AF Randomized Controlled Trial. JACC: Clinical Electrophysiology. 2023. cards.headline: Synthesis: risk-factor treatment reduces AF burden across three designs, with the randomised evidence thinnest where the claims are largest — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: risk-factor treatment reduces AF burden across three designs, with the randomised evidence thinnest where the claims are largest — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Two self-selected Adelaide cohorts (355 patients in LEGACY; 149 ablation patients in ARREST-AF) and one randomised trial of exercise (120 patients, ACTIVE-AF).
cards.result: Sustained ≥10% weight loss: 6-fold relative greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival (observational). Aggressive risk-factor management after ablation: hazard ratio 4.8 for arrhythmia-free survival, antiarrhythmic-drug use 16% versus 42.4% (observational). Exercise, randomised: freedom from AF at 12 months 40% versus 20% (HR 0.50). All three point the same way on burden and symptoms; none measures stroke, hospitalisation or death, and the two largest effects come from the two weakest designs.
cards.watchOut: The cohorts come from one research group and one clinic population, and their effect sizes should be expected to shrink under randomisation — ACTIVE-AF's halving of recurrence is the realistic scale. Risk-factor management is an addition to, never a substitute for, stroke prevention: nothing on this shelf licenses stopping anticoagulation in a patient whose AF quiets down.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pathak RK et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015 (PMID: 25792361); Pathak RK et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014 (PMID: 25456757); Elliott AD et al. JACC: Clinical Electrophysiology. 2023 (PMID: 36752479).

shelves.title: Etripamil nasal spray: the first trial missed its 5-hour primary endpoint, but the repeat-dose RAPID trial converted 64% versus 31% within 30 minutes — a self-treatment for PSVT that works in minutes, with a stuffy nose as the price
shelves.question: In adults with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, does self-administered etripamil nasal spray convert an acute episode to sinus rhythm faster than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adolescent · Adult · *Tachycardia, Supraventricular/drug therapy · *Tachycardia, Paroxysmal/drug therapy · Benzoates/therapeutic use · *Tachycardia, Ventricular · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: Etripamil is a fast-acting L-type calcium-channel blocker given as a nasal spray, designed — in the trials' own framing — as an investigational self-treatment for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) outside a medical setting. The programme's two randomised parts tell a before-and-after story about endpoints. NODE-301 part 1 (Stambler 2022, PMID: 36441560) tested a single 70 mg dose against placebo with a 5-hour primary endpoint and missed it: hazard ratio for time to conversion 1.086 (95% CI 0.726 to 1.623, P=0.12) across 156 adjudicated events — although conversions in the first 30 minutes already favoured etripamil (53.7% vs 34.7%, HR 1.87, P=0.02). RAPID (Stambler 2023, PMID: 37331368), part 2 of the same study programme and registry number, added a symptom-prompted repeat dose at 10 minutes and a 30-minute primary endpoint, and hit it clearly: conversion by 30 minutes in 64% on etripamil versus 31% on placebo (HR 2.62, 95% CI 1.66 to 4.15, p<0.0001), median time to conversion 17.2 versus 53.5 minutes. The open-label extension (Ip 2023, PMID: 37753718) found a consistent 60.2% conversion within 30 minutes across 188 self-treated episodes, with repeat episodes in the same patient tending to respond the same way. Adverse effects are dominated by the nose: discomfort in about a quarter, congestion and rhinorrhoea in about a tenth, transient and mild-to-moderate, with no serious drug-related events reported in RAPID. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one positive randomised trial for the regimen that works, from a single development programme).

cards.headline: Stambler 2022 (NODE-301 part 1): the single-dose trial missed its primary endpoint — time-to-conversion over 5 hours, hazard ratio 1.086 (P=0.12) — despite a clear separation by 30 minutes (53.7% vs 34.7%)
cards.summary: Stambler 2022 (NODE-301 part 1): the single-dose trial missed its primary endpoint — time-to-conversion over 5 hours, hazard ratio 1.086 (P=0.12) — despite a clear separation by 30 minutes (53.7% vs 34.7%)
cards.people: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of self-administered etripamil 70 mg nasal spray in adults with symptomatic sustained PSVT. After a medically supervised test dose in sinus rhythm, patients were randomised 2:1 to etripamil or placebo; on symptoms they applied a cardiac monitor, attempted a vagal manoeuvre, and if symptoms persisted self-administered the blinded spray. The efficacy population was 156 positively adjudicated PSVT events (107 etripamil, 49 placebo), reviewed by an independent adjudication committee from continuous ECG recordings.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — time to conversion to sinus rhythm during the 5-hour observation period — was not met: hazard ratio 1.086 (95% CI 0.726 to 1.623; P=0.12). In predefined sensitivity analyses, etripamil's effect appeared at 3, 5, 10, 20 and 30 minutes (P<0.05); at 30 minutes, 53.7% of etripamil-treated episodes had converted versus 34.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.87; 95% CI 1.09 to 3.22; P=0.02). Etripamil was well tolerated; adverse events were mainly transient nasal discomfort (19.6%) and congestion (8.0%).
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint is a missed primary endpoint: the 5-hour window let placebo episodes convert spontaneously and washed out the early drug effect, and the favourable 30-minute numbers are sensitivity analyses, however prespecified. This card is the discipline of the shelf — the programme only became convincing when the trial was redesigned around the drug's actual speed (RAPID, next card).

cards.headline: Stambler 2023 (RAPID): with a repeat dose allowed at 10 minutes, conversion within 30 minutes was 64% on etripamil versus 31% on placebo (hazard ratio 2.62, p<0.0001); median time to conversion 17.2 versus 53.5 minutes
cards.summary: Stambler 2023 (RAPID): with a repeat dose allowed at 10 minutes, conversion within 30 minutes was 64% on etripamil versus 31% on placebo (hazard ratio 2.62, p<0.0001); median time to conversion 17.2 versus 53.5 minutes
cards.people: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled event-driven trial at 160 sites in North America and Europe, conducted as part 2 of the NODE-301 study. Adults with ECG-documented PSVT and sustained symptomatic episodes (≥20 minutes) received two test doses of etripamil 70 mg in sinus rhythm; tolerators (692 randomised) self-administered etripamil or placebo at symptom onset, with an optional repeat dose if symptoms persisted beyond 10 minutes. The primary analysis covers 184 patients (99 etripamil, 85 placebo) who treated an adjudicated atrioventricular-nodal-dependent episode.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier conversion rates by 30 minutes were 64% (63/99) with etripamil versus 31% (26/85) with placebo (hazard ratio 2.62; 95% CI 1.66 to 4.15; p<0.0001). Median time to conversion was 17.2 minutes (95% CI 13.4 to 26.5) with etripamil versus 53.5 minutes (38.7 to 87.3) with placebo. Adverse events were more frequent on etripamil (68 patients versus 12 on placebo reported treatment-emergent events), were mostly at the administration site, mild or moderate, and transient: nasal discomfort 23%, nasal congestion 13%, rhinorrhoea 9%. No serious etripamil-related adverse events or deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: Only 184 of 692 randomised patients contribute to the primary analysis — the rest never had a confirmed AV-nodal-dependent episode during follow-up — and every participant had first tolerated supervised test doses, so the trial population is pre-screened for tolerability. The evidence covers AV-nodal-dependent PSVT only; other supraventricular tachycardias were adjudicated out.

cards.headline: Ip 2023 (NODE-302): in open-label long-term use, 60.2% of 188 self-treated episodes converted within 30 minutes (median 15.5 minutes), and patients tended to respond consistently from episode to episode
cards.summary: Ip 2023 (NODE-302): in open-label long-term use, 60.2% of 188 self-treated episodes converted within 30 minutes (median 15.5 minutes), and patients tended to respond consistently from episode to episode
cards.people: Open-label extension study: 169 patients enrolled from the NODE-301 programme, of whom 105 self-administered etripamil at least once for perceived PSVT over a median follow-up of 232 days. Episodes were monitored with a self-applied cardiac monitoring system for 5 hours after dosing; 188 episodes in 92 patients were positively adjudicated as AV-nodal-dependent PSVT.
cards.result: The probability of conversion to sinus rhythm within 30 minutes of etripamil was 60.2% (Kaplan–Meier), with a median time to conversion of 15.5 minutes. Among 40 patients who self-treated two episodes, responses were significantly consistent: 21 converted on both episodes and 9 on neither (χ²=8.09; P=0.0045). Forty-five of 105 patients (42.9%) had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event — generally transient and mild-to-moderate, including nasal congestion (14.3%), nasal discomfort (14.3%) and rhinorrhoea (12.4%). No serious cardiac safety events were observed within 24 hours of etripamil.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled: the 60.2% figure includes spontaneous conversions that placebo would also have caught (31% by 30 minutes in RAPID), so it confirms durability and consistency of use, not efficacy. Patients are programme veterans who had already tolerated the drug — first-use tolerability in an unselected population is less well characterised.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a repeat-dose self-administered spray converts about two-thirds of AV-nodal-dependent PSVT episodes within 30 minutes, roughly double placebo — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a repeat-dose self-administered spray converts about two-thirds of AV-nodal-dependent PSVT episodes within 30 minutes, roughly double placebo — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One development programme: NODE-301 part 1 (156 adjudicated events, single dose, primary endpoint missed), RAPID (184 treated patients, repeat-dose regimen, primary endpoint met), and the NODE-302 open-label extension (188 episodes).
cards.result: Conversion within 30 minutes: 53.7% versus 34.7% (single dose, sensitivity analysis), 64% versus 31% (repeat-dose regimen, primary endpoint, HR 2.62), and 60.2% in open-label repeated use, with median conversion times of 15–17 minutes against 53.5 minutes on placebo. Harms are local and transient — nasal discomfort in about a quarter of treated patients — with no serious drug-related adverse events in the randomised programme. In the trial records the drug is investigational; the shelf reports the trial evidence, not a prescribing recommendation.
cards.watchOut: A single sponsor's programme (Milestone Pharmaceuticals funded RAPID), a single positive randomised trial for the regimen in use, and a study population pre-screened by test doses and restricted to AV-nodal-dependent episodes. What the trials do not show: fewer emergency-department visits or ablations over years, safety in patients who self-treat without any prior supervised exposure, or performance against the 'pill-in-the-pocket' verapamil/diltiazem strategy many patients already use.

shelves.title: REACH-HF: a facilitated home-based rehabilitation programme improved quality of life in heart failure — tested against usual care, not against centre-based rehab
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure, does home-based cardiac rehabilitation work as well as centre-based programmes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiac Rehabilitation/economics · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · Health Care Costs · Heart Failure/diagnosis/economics/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Home Care Services/economics · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Self Care/economics · Stroke Volume · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: The honest starting point is that the head-to-head question — home-based versus centre-based rehabilitation in heart failure — has never been randomised. What has been tested is a specific facilitated home programme, REACH-HF (Rehabilitation EnAblement in CHronic Heart Failure), against usual care, in a health system where usual care for most heart-failure patients meant no rehabilitation at all. In the main trial (Dalal 2019, PMID: 30304644), 216 patients with HFrEF (mean ejection fraction 34%) gained a clinically meaningful improvement in disease-specific quality of life at 12 months — Minnesota Living with Heart Failure score 5.7 points better than usual care (95% CI −10.6 to −0.7) — with no significant difference in clinical events, in a trial far too small to judge them. A 50-patient pilot extended the same programme to HFpEF with a favourable but imprecise signal (Lang 2018, PMID: 29632081), and UK modelling put the programme at £1,720 per quality-adjusted life-year (Taylor 2019, PMID: 30884975). So home-based rehabilitation is a reasonable, cheap way to deliver a benefit that exercise-based rehabilitation itself carries (homed at shelf #171); whether it matches a good centre-based programme patient-for-patient is unknown, and centre-based telerehabilitation after cardiac events is a separate question (shelf #2283), as is rehabilitation after myocardial infarction (shelf #458). Tier C: the shelf rests on a single trial programme, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: REACH-HF (Dalal 2019): home-based facilitated rehabilitation beat usual care on quality of life by 5.7 points at 12 months in 216 patients with HFrEF — clinical events unchanged
cards.summary: REACH-HF (Dalal 2019): home-based facilitated rehabilitation beat usual care on quality of life by 5.7 points at 12 months in 216 patients with HFrEF — clinical events unchanged
cards.people: 216 adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (mean left ventricular ejection fraction 34%, mean age 70 years, 78% men) in a multicentre UK randomised trial, allocated to the REACH-HF home-based facilitated self-care and rehabilitation programme plus usual care, or usual care alone. Primary outcome: disease-specific health-related quality of life (Minnesota Living with Heart Failure questionnaire, MLHFQ) at 12 months; 185 participants (86%) provided primary-outcome data.
cards.result: At 12 months the MLHFQ score favoured REACH-HF by −5.7 points (95% CI −10.6 to −0.7, p = 0.025) — a difference the investigators describe as clinically meaningful. Patient self-care also improved (p < 0.001), but there was no significant difference in other secondary outcomes, including clinical events. The mean cost of delivering the intervention was £418 per participant.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was usual care — in a setting where most heart-failure patients receive no rehabilitation — so this trial cannot say whether home-based delivery matches centre-based delivery, only that a structured home programme beats the nothing most patients get. It was powered for a questionnaire score, not for hospitalisation or death, and the confidence interval (−10.6 to −0.7) reaches close to a trivial effect.
cards.source: Dalal HM et al. The effects and costs of home-based rehabilitation for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: The REACH-HF multicentre randomized controlled trial. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 30304644. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lang 2018: the same home programme in HFpEF — a 50-patient feasibility pilot with a favourable but very imprecise quality-of-life signal (−11.5 points, CI −22.8 to 0.3)
cards.summary: Lang 2018: the same home programme in HFpEF — a 50-patient feasibility pilot with a favourable but very imprecise quality-of-life signal (−11.5 points, CI −22.8 to 0.3)
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial (REACH-HF HFpEF pilot, Lang 2018)
cards.people: 50 symptomatic patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45%, mean age 73.9 years, 54% female) and 21 caregivers in Tayside, Scotland, randomised to the REACH-HF home-based programme plus usual care or usual care alone, with outcomes at 3 and 6 months assessed by blinded assessors. This was a feasibility study, not powered for effectiveness.
cards.result: Retention (90%) and intervention uptake (92%) were excellent. At 6 months, the between-group difference in MLHFQ total score was −11.5 points in favour of the intervention (95% CI −22.8 to 0.3) — a point estimate larger than in the HFrEF trial but with a confidence interval including no effect. Eleven patients (4 intervention, 7 control) had a hospital admission over 6 months, 4 of them (all control) heart-failure-related.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot: its job was to show the programme could be delivered and studied in HFpEF, and the effectiveness numbers are hypothesis-generating only — the confidence interval spans from a large benefit to none. It should never be quoted as evidence that home rehabilitation works in HFpEF; it is evidence that a definitive trial is worth running.
cards.source: Lang CC et al. A randomised controlled trial of a facilitated home-based rehabilitation intervention in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): the REACH-HFpEF Pilot Study. BMJ Open. 2018. PMID: 29632081. Registry ID: ISRCTN78539530 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Taylor 2019: modelled cost-effectiveness of REACH-HF — £1,720 per QALY gained versus usual care, with a 78% probability of being cost-effective at a £20,000 threshold
cards.summary: Taylor 2019: modelled cost-effectiveness of REACH-HF — £1,720 per QALY gained versus usual care, with a 78% probability of being cost-effective at a £20,000 threshold
cards.people: A Markov cost-utility model over a patient lifetime horizon, integrating the REACH-HF trial results with a systematic review and meta-analysis of rehabilitation trials, UK mortality and hospital-admission estimates, and UK costs at 2015/2016 prices, from a UK National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective.
cards.result: Adding REACH-HF to usual care gained a mean 0.23 quality-adjusted life-years per patient at a mean added cost of £400, giving £1,720 per QALY gained; probabilistic sensitivity analysis gave a 78% probability that REACH-HF is cost-effective versus usual care at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold. Results were similar for home-based cardiac rehabilitation generally versus usual care, and robust in sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: A model, not a measurement: the QALY gain is extrapolated over a lifetime from a 12-month questionnaire difference in one 216-patient trial, so the attractive ratio inherits all of that trial's uncertainty. It speaks to UK costs and thresholds and to the comparison against usual care — not to value for money against a centre-based programme.
cards.source: Taylor RS et al. The cost effectiveness of REACH-HF and home-based cardiac rehabilitation compared with the usual medical care for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: A decision model-based analysis. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 30884975. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a home programme that beats usual care on quality of life — POSSIBLE — while the home-versus-centre comparison remains untested in heart failure
cards.summary: Synthesis: a home programme that beats usual care on quality of life — POSSIBLE — while the home-versus-centre comparison remains untested in heart failure
cards.people: One multicentre RCT of a named home-based programme in HFrEF (n = 216), one feasibility pilot in HFpEF (n = 50), and one UK cost-effectiveness model built on them.
cards.result: Quality of life: MLHFQ −5.7 points (95% CI −10.6 to −0.7) at 12 months versus usual care. Clinical events: no significant difference (trial not powered for them).
