shelves.title: THEMIS: ticagrelor added to aspirin cut ischaemic events by a tenth relative and doubled major bleeding — the net gain sat in patients with a previous stent
shelves.question: In patients with stable coronary disease and type 2 diabetes, does adding ticagrelor to aspirin reduce cardiovascular events, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Coronary Artery Disease/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/epidemiology/mortality · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology/prevention & control · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Stroke/epidemiology/prevention & control · Ticagrelor/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: THEMIS randomised 19,220 patients aged 50 or over with stable coronary disease and type 2 diabetes — none with previous myocardial infarction or stroke — to ticagrelor plus aspirin or aspirin alone (Steg 2019, PMID: 31475798). Over a median 39.9 months the primary ischaemic composite fell from 8.5% to 7.7% (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.99): a 10% relative reduction worth 0.8 percentage points absolute. The price was TIMI major bleeding more than doubled in relative terms, 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32) — 1.2 percentage points absolute, more harm events added than ischaemic events removed — plus more intracranial haemorrhage (0.7% versus 0.5%). The trial's own irreversible-harm composite (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, fatal bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage) was statistically unchanged: 10.1% versus 10.8% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.02). The prespecified THEMIS-PCI analysis (Bhatt 2019, PMID: 31484629) locates the favourable trade: in the 11,154 patients with previous PCI, the composite fell 8.6% to 7.3% (HR 0.85) and net clinical benefit was positive (9.3% versus 11.0%, HR 0.85), while in patients without previous PCI it was not (interaction p = 0.012). A third of patients stopped ticagrelor early (34.5% versus 25.4%), which blunts any real-world gain further. Tier C: one trial and its own subgroup analysis, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: THEMIS (Steg 2019): 19,220 patients — ischaemic events 7.7% versus 8.5% (HR 0.90), TIMI major bleeding 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32), irreversible-harm composite unchanged
cards.summary: THEMIS (Steg 2019): 19,220 patients — ischaemic events 7.7% versus 8.5% (HR 0.90), TIMI major bleeding 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32), irreversible-harm composite unchanged
cards.people: 19,220 patients aged 50 or older with stable coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus, excluding anyone with previous myocardial infarction or stroke, randomised double-blind to ticagrelor plus aspirin or placebo plus aspirin. Median follow-up 39.9 months. Primary efficacy outcome: composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke; primary safety outcome: TIMI major bleeding.
cards.result: Primary efficacy outcome: 7.7% on ticagrelor versus 8.5% on placebo (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.99, p = 0.04) — a 10% relative reduction, 0.8 percentage points absolute. TIMI major bleeding: 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32, 95% CI 1.82 to 2.94, p < 0.001) — 1.2 percentage points absolute more. Intracranial haemorrhage: 0.7% versus 0.5% (HR 1.71). Fatal bleeding did not differ significantly (0.2% versus 0.1%). The exploratory composite of irreversible harm (death from any cause, myocardial infarction, stroke, fatal bleeding, or intracranial haemorrhage) was similar: 10.1% versus 10.8% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.02). Permanent discontinuation was commoner on ticagrelor: 34.5% versus 25.4%.
cards.watchOut: The headline '10% relative reduction' is 0.8 percentage points absolute over more than three years, bought with 1.2 percentage points more major bleeding — in a population chosen to be at low bleeding risk and free of prior infarction or stroke. The result does not transfer to post-infarction patients (a different question, homed with the post-MI antiplatelet shelves) or to anyone at high bleeding risk.
cards.source: Steg PG et al. Ticagrelor in Patients with Stable Coronary Disease and Diabetes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31475798. Registry ID: NCT01991795. cards.headline: THEMIS-PCI (Bhatt 2019): in the 11,154 with previous PCI, events fell 8.6% to 7.3% and net clinical benefit was positive (HR 0.85) — absent in patients without previous PCI (interaction p = 0.012)
cards.summary: THEMIS-PCI (Bhatt 2019): in the 11,154 with previous PCI, events fell 8.6% to 7.3% and net clinical benefit was positive (HR 0.85) — absent in patients without previous PCI (interaction p = 0.012)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (THEMIS-PCI, Bhatt 2019)
cards.people: The prespecified subgroup of THEMIS patients with a history of previous percutaneous coronary intervention: 11,154 patients (58% of the trial), median follow-up 3.3 years, analysed in the intention-to-treat population with the same primary efficacy composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke).
cards.result: Primary efficacy outcome: 7.3% (404/5558) on ticagrelor versus 8.6% (480/5596) on placebo (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97, p = 0.013); no such effect in patients without previous PCI (interaction p = 0.16 for efficacy). TIMI major bleeding: 2.0% versus 1.1% (HR 2.03). Net clinical benefit favoured ticagrelor in the previous-PCI group — 9.3% versus 11.0% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.95, p = 0.005) — but not in patients without previous PCI (interaction p = 0.012). Cardiovascular death alone did not differ (3.1% versus 3.3%).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup, however prespecified: the overall trial's irreversible-harm endpoint was null, and slicing by previous PCI is exactly the kind of analysis that can manufacture a winner. The interaction test for net benefit (p = 0.012) supports the split, but the claim remains 'consider it in selected post-PCI patients at low bleeding risk', not a general licence for dual therapy in stable diabetes.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Ticagrelor in patients with diabetes and stable coronary artery disease with a history of previous percutaneous coronary intervention (THEMIS-PCI): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31484629. Registry ID: none in the record (subgroup analysis of THEMIS, NCT01991795). cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — a real but small ischaemic gain, paid for in bleeding; net benefit only where a stent already marks high ischaemic risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — a real but small ischaemic gain, paid for in bleeding; net benefit only where a stent already marks high ischaemic risk
cards.people: One randomised trial of 19,220 patients with stable coronary disease and type 2 diabetes without prior infarction or stroke, plus its prespecified previous-PCI subgroup analysis (n = 11,154).
cards.result: Overall: ischaemic composite 7.7% versus 8.5% (HR 0.90); major bleeding 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32); irreversible harm 10.1% versus 10.8% (HR 0.93, not significant). Previous PCI: composite 7.3% versus 8.6% (HR 0.85); net clinical benefit HR 0.85 with a significant interaction against the no-PCI group.
cards.watchOut: Both cards come from a single industry-funded trial programme (AstraZeneca), and a third of the ticagrelor group stopped treatment — tolerability (dyspnoea, bleeding, twice-daily dosing) is part of the real-world answer. Nothing here applies to the first year after stenting or after an acute coronary syndrome, where dual therapy is a separate, settled question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steg PG et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31475798); Bhatt DL et al. Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 31484629).

shelves.title: Anticoagulation in sinus-rhythm heart failure: warfarin halved ischaemic stroke in relative terms and doubled major bleeding — three trials found no net winner
shelves.question: In patients with HFrEF in sinus rhythm, does warfarin anticoagulation prevent stroke without unacceptable bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aspirin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Brain Ischemia/prevention & control · Cerebral Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/epidemiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Risk · Stroke/epidemiology/prevention & control · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Warfarin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials have asked whether anticoagulating heart-failure patients who are in sinus rhythm pays. WARCEF (Homma 2012, PMID: 22551105), the definitive warfarin-versus-aspirin test in 2,305 patients with reduced ejection fraction, found no difference in its primary composite of ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage or death: 7.47 versus 7.93 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.10). Inside that null, warfarin did exactly what anticoagulation promises and threatens: ischaemic stroke fell from 1.36 to 0.72 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.52 — a 48% relative reduction) while major haemorrhage rose from 0.87 to 1.78 per 100 patient-years. The earlier WATCH trial (Massie 2009, PMID: 19289640), stopped early at 1,587 of a planned 4,500 patients, found the same pattern — no difference between warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel on death, infarction or stroke, with fewer nonfatal strokes on warfarin. COMMANDER HF (Zannad 2018, PMID: 30146935) then tested the modern version of the idea — low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily in 5,022 patients with worsening heart failure and coronary disease — and its primary composite of death, infarction or stroke was likewise unchanged (25.0% versus 26.2%, HR 0.94). The answer to the question as posed is therefore no: strokes are prevented, but not 'without unacceptable bleeding', and no trial shows a net outcome gain. This shelf does not cover atrial fibrillation, where anticoagulation is a different and settled question.

cards.headline: WARCEF (Homma 2012): warfarin versus aspirin in 2,305 patients — primary composite unchanged (HR 0.93); ischaemic stroke halved in relative terms (HR 0.52), major haemorrhage doubled
cards.summary: WARCEF (Homma 2012): warfarin versus aspirin in 2,305 patients — primary composite unchanged (HR 0.93); ischaemic stroke halved in relative terms (HR 0.52), major haemorrhage doubled
cards.people: 2,305 patients in sinus rhythm with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, randomised double-blind to warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.5) or aspirin 325 mg daily, followed for up to 6 years (mean 3.5 years). Primary outcome: time to first event in a composite of ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, or death from any cause.
cards.result: Primary outcome rates: 7.47 events per 100 patient-years on warfarin versus 7.93 on aspirin (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.10, p = 0.40) — no significant difference. Ischaemic stroke: 0.72 versus 1.36 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.82, p = 0.005) — a 48% relative reduction, worth about 0.6 events per 100 patient-years absolute. Major haemorrhage: 1.78 versus 0.87 per 100 patient-years (p < 0.001) — about 0.9 events per 100 patient-years absolute more. Intracerebral/intracranial haemorrhage rates did not differ significantly (0.27 versus 0.22 per 100 patient-years).
cards.watchOut: The stroke-versus-bleeding trade is finely balanced and patient-specific: the trial's own conclusion was that the choice should be individualised. A time-varying analysis hinted warfarin might pull ahead after the fourth year (p = 0.046), a marginal, secondary finding that should not be quoted as a late benefit. Aspirin 325 mg — a full dose — was the comparator, which stacks the bleeding comparison in warfarin's favour relative to modern low-dose practice, and warfarin still bled more.
cards.source: Homma S et al. Warfarin and aspirin in patients with heart failure and sinus rhythm. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22551105. Registry ID: NCT00041938. cards.headline: WATCH (Massie 2009): warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel statistically indistinguishable on death, infarction or stroke (HR 0.98 warfarin versus aspirin) in a trial stopped at a third of its planned size
cards.summary: WATCH (Massie 2009): warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel statistically indistinguishable on death, infarction or stroke (HR 0.98 warfarin versus aspirin) in a trial stopped at a third of its planned size
cards.type: Randomised trial, open-label warfarin with blinded antiplatelet comparison (WATCH, Massie 2009)
cards.people: 1,587 men and women with symptomatic chronic heart failure for at least 3 months, in sinus rhythm, with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%, randomised to open-label warfarin (target INR 2.5 to 3.0) or double-blind aspirin 162 mg daily or clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The trial enrolled 1,587 of a planned 4,500 patients before stopping early.
cards.result: Primary composite (death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke): warfarin versus aspirin HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.12, p = 0.77); clopidogrel versus aspirin HR 1.08 (0.83 to 1.40); warfarin versus clopidogrel HR 0.89 (0.68 to 1.16) — no significant differences, and mortality data supported none of the hypotheses. Warfarin was associated with fewer nonfatal strokes than either antiplatelet. Hospitalisation for worsening heart failure was commoner on aspirin (22.2%) than on warfarin (16.5%, p = 0.02).
cards.watchOut: Severely underpowered by early termination — it randomised about a third of its target — so its null is weaker evidence than WARCEF's. The heart-failure hospitalisation difference favouring warfarin over aspirin is a secondary endpoint in an open-label comparison and is hypothesis-generating at most.
cards.source: Massie BM et al. Randomized trial of warfarin, aspirin, and clopidogrel in patients with chronic heart failure: the Warfarin and Antiplatelet Therapy in Chronic Heart Failure (WATCH) trial. Circulation. 2009. PMID: 19289640. Registry ID: NCT00007683. cards.headline: COMMANDER HF (Zannad 2018): low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily in 5,022 patients with worsening heart failure — death, infarction or stroke unchanged (25.0% versus 26.2%, HR 0.94)
cards.summary: COMMANDER HF (Zannad 2018): low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily in 5,022 patients with worsening heart failure — death, infarction or stroke unchanged (25.0% versus 26.2%, HR 0.94)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (COMMANDER HF, Zannad 2018)
cards.people: 5,022 patients with chronic heart failure, left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%, coronary artery disease and raised natriuretic peptides, without atrial fibrillation, randomised double-blind to rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily or placebo on top of standard care after an episode of worsening heart failure. Median follow-up 21.1 months. Primary efficacy outcome: composite of death from any cause, myocardial infarction, or stroke; principal safety outcome: fatal bleeding or bleeding into a critical space.
cards.result: Primary endpoint: 25.0% (626/2507) on rivaroxaban versus 26.2% (658/2515) on placebo (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05, p = 0.27). All-cause mortality: 21.8% versus 22.1% (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.10). The principal safety outcome occurred in 18 patients on rivaroxaban and 23 on placebo (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.49) — at this low dose, the feared excess of catastrophic bleeding did not materialise, but neither did any benefit.
cards.watchOut: COMMANDER HF tested a vascular dose (2.5 mg twice daily), not full anticoagulation — so it does not directly answer the warfarin question; it answers whether the thrombin hypothesis in heart failure pays at a dose chosen to be safe. It did not. Full-dose anticoagulation in this population is WARCEF's question, and its answer was a trade, not a win.
cards.source: Zannad F et al. Rivaroxaban in Patients with Heart Failure, Sinus Rhythm, and Coronary Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30146935. Registry ID: NCT01877915. cards.headline: Synthesis: LIKELY no net benefit — anticoagulation in sinus-rhythm HFrEF trades ischaemic strokes for major bleeds, and the composite outcomes never move
cards.summary: Synthesis: LIKELY no net benefit — anticoagulation in sinus-rhythm HFrEF trades ischaemic strokes for major bleeds, and the composite outcomes never move
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 8,914 patients with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure in sinus rhythm: WARCEF (n = 2,305, warfarin versus aspirin), WATCH (n = 1,587, warfarin versus aspirin versus clopidogrel), and COMMANDER HF (n = 5,022, low-dose rivaroxaban versus placebo).
cards.result: Primary composites: HR 0.93 (WARCEF), 0.98 (WATCH, warfarin versus aspirin), 0.94 (COMMANDER HF) — all non-significant. Warfarin's components in WARCEF: ischaemic stroke 0.72 versus 1.36 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.52); major haemorrhage 1.78 versus 0.87 per 100 patient-years. Mortality: unchanged in every trial.
cards.watchOut: Sinus rhythm only. The moment atrial fibrillation, a mechanical valve, or a left-ventricular thrombus enters the picture, anticoagulation has its own established indications and this shelf must not be quoted against them. Individual patients at very high stroke risk and low bleeding risk remain a judgement call, as WARCEF's authors themselves concluded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Homma S et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22551105); Massie BM et al. Circulation. 2009 (PMID: 19289640); Zannad F et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30146935).

shelves.title: Physical counterpressure manoeuvres: leg-crossing and muscle-tensing cut recurrence from about a half to about a third in the one randomised trial — free, safe, and impossible to blind
shelves.question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, do physical counterpressure manoeuvres prevent syncope?
shelves.mesh: Actuarial Analysis · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Arm/physiology · Hand/physiology · Hemodynamics · Humans · Leg/physiology · Middle Aged · Motor Activity/physiology · Pressure · Survival Analysis · Syncope, Vasovagal/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Physical counterpressure manoeuvres — crossing the legs and tensing the muscles, tensing the arms, handgrip, squatting — are the one syncope treatment that costs nothing and can do no direct harm. The evidence is a single randomised trial, the PC-Trial (van Dijk 2006, PMID: 17045903): 223 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope and recognisable warning symptoms were randomised to conventional advice alone or conventional advice plus manoeuvre training; over a mean 14 months, syncope recurred in 31.6% of the trained group versus 50.9% of controls — a 39% relative risk reduction (95% CI 11% to 53%), about 19 percentage points absolute — with no adverse events. A prospective Dutch cohort of 100 frequent fainters given the full non-pharmacological package (fluids, salt, exercise and manoeuvres) points the same way, though without a control group: median recurrences fell from 3 in the prior year to 0, yet 49% still fainted at least once (Romme 2010, PMID: 20047924). Two cautions keep this at POSSIBLE: the manoeuvres cannot be blinded, and a 2024 meta-analysis of syncope trials found unblinded trials systematically report larger benefits than blinded ones (Kaza 2024, PMID: 38890128, carded at shelf #2615); and the treatment only exists for patients who get a prodrome long enough to use it. Drug and device options for the same condition are homed separately — midodrine at shelf #1557, fludrocortisone at shelf #2615, pacing and cardioneuroablation at shelves #2301–#2303. Tier C: a single unblinded randomised trial plus uncontrolled data, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: PC-Trial (van Dijk 2006): training in counterpressure manoeuvres cut syncope recurrence to 31.6% versus 50.9% on conventional therapy alone — a 39% relative risk reduction
cards.summary: PC-Trial (van Dijk 2006): training in counterpressure manoeuvres cut syncope recurrence to 31.6% versus 50.9% on conventional therapy alone — a 39% relative risk reduction
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, open (PC-Trial, van Dijk 2006)
cards.people: 223 patients (mean age 38.6 years) with recurrent vasovagal syncope and recognisable prodromal symptoms, in a multicentre prospective randomised trial: 117 to standardised conventional therapy alone, 106 to conventional therapy plus training in physical counterpressure manoeuvres (leg crossing with muscle tensing, arm tensing, handgrip). Mean follow-up 14 months. The trial was necessarily open — patients know whether they are tensing their muscles.
cards.result: Syncopal recurrence during follow-up: 31.6% in the manoeuvre group versus 50.9% in the control group (p = 0.005) — about 19 percentage points absolute fewer patients fainting. The median yearly syncope burden was significantly lower with manoeuvres (p = 0.004), recurrence-free survival was better (log-rank p = 0.018), and the authors report a relative risk reduction of 39% (95% CI 11% to 53%). No adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Unblindable and unblinded: patients who have been taught a technique, and believe in it, may report — and genuinely experience — fewer faints through expectation and through the accompanying lifestyle advice. The 39% relative figure should be read as an upper bound. The trial also only enrolled patients with a recognisable prodrome; it says nothing for syncope that arrives without warning, where injury risk is highest.

multicentre randomised controlled trial, open (pc-trial, van dijk 2006) 223 patients (mean age 38.6 years) with recurrent vasovagal syncope and recognisable prodromal symptoms, in a multicentre prospective randomised trial: 117 to standardised conventional therapy alone, 106 to conventional therapy plus training in physical counterpressure manoeuvres (leg crossing with muscle tensing, arm tensing, handgrip). mean follow-up 14 months. the trial was necessarily open — patients know whether they are tensing their muscles. syncopal recurrence during follow-up: 31.6% in the manoeuvre group versus 50.9% in the control group (p = 0.005) — about 19 percentage points absolute fewer patients fainting. the median yearly syncope burden was significantly lower with manoeuvres (p = 0.004), recurrence-free survival was better (log-rank p = 0.018), and the authors report a relative risk reduction of 39% (95% ci 11% to 53%). no adverse events were reported. unblindable and unblinded: patients who have been taught a technique, and believe in it, may report — and genuinely experience — fewer faints through expectation and through the accompanying lifestyle advice. the 39% relative figure should be read as an upper bound. the trial also only enrolled patients with a recognisable prodrome; it says nothing for syncope that arrives without warning, where injury risk is highest. van dijk n et al. effectiveness of physical counterpressure maneuvers in preventing vasovagal syncope: the physical counterpressure manoeuvres trial (pc-trial). journal of the american college of cardiology. 2006. pmid: 17045903. registry id: isrctn45146526. mesh: actuarial analysis · adolescent · adult · aged · arm/physiology · hand/physiology · hemodynamics · humans · leg/physiology · middle aged · motor activity/physiology · pressure · survival analysis · syncope, vasovagal/prevention & control · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Romme 2010: in 100 frequent fainters given the full non-drug package, median yearly recurrences fell from 3 to 0 — but 49% still fainted at least once, and there was no control group
cards.summary: Romme 2010: in 100 frequent fainters given the full non-drug package, median yearly recurrences fell from 3 to 0 — but 49% still fainted at least once, and there was no control group
cards.people: 100 patients with at least 3 episodes of vasovagal syncope in the previous 2 years, openly given non-pharmacological treatment — adequate fluid and salt intake, regular exercise, and physical counterpressure manoeuvres — and followed prospectively for recurrence and quality of life in a Dutch syncope unit.
cards.result: The median number of syncopal recurrences was lower in the first year of treatment than in the last year before it (median 0 versus 3, p < 0.001), but 49% of patients experienced at least one recurrence. A higher syncope burden before inclusion predicted recurrence. Disease-specific quality of life improved over time, most in patients whose syncope burden fell most.
cards.watchOut: Before-and-after comparisons in syncope flatter every treatment: patients enrol at the peak of their symptoms, and vasovagal syncope naturally remits, so some of the fall from 3 to 0 would have happened untreated (regression to the mean). This study supports feasibility and safety of the package; the randomised PC-Trial is the effectiveness evidence.

cards.people: One randomised trial (n = 223) of counterpressure training added to conventional advice, and one prospective uncontrolled cohort (n = 100) of the combined non-pharmacological package.
cards.result: Randomised: recurrence 31.6% versus 50.9% over ~14 months (relative risk reduction 39%, 95% CI 11% to 53%); no adverse events. Uncontrolled: median recurrences 0 versus 3 per year, 49% with at least one recurrence. Effect on injuries, driving outcomes, or quality of life in randomised data: not established.

shelves.title: POST 2: fludrocortisone missed its primary endpoint (p = 0.069) — a possible benefit only after the dose settled, and blinded-trial syntheses call it neutral
shelves.question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, does fludrocortisone prevent recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fludrocortisone/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Syncope, Vasovagal/prevention & control · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POST 2 (Sheldon 2016, PMID: 27364043) is the only adequately designed test: 210 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope (median 15 lifetime spells) randomised double-blind to fludrocortisone, titrated to the highest tolerated dose between 0.05 and 0.2 mg daily, or placebo for a year. It missed its prespecified target — the primary analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.69 for first recurrence (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069), short of both significance and the 40% relative reduction the trial was built to detect. The supportive findings are all secondary or post hoc: a multivariable model (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.94) and an analysis restricted to the period after a 2-week dose-stabilisation phase (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.89). Against even that charitable reading, the 2024 meta-analysis of syncope trials (Kaza 2024, PMID: 38890128) found that under blinded conditions fludrocortisone was neutral — the favourable syncope literature for several treatments shrinks or vanishes when blinding is enforced. The honest summary is MAYBE: a small benefit is not excluded, the point estimates lean favourable, but the one good trial did not prove it. Non-drug treatment is homed at shelf #2614 and midodrine at shelf #1557. Tier C: a single trial that missed its primary endpoint, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: POST 2 (Sheldon 2016): fludrocortisone's primary analysis missed — HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069); benefit appeared only in adjusted and post-stabilisation analyses (HR 0.51)
cards.summary: POST 2 (Sheldon 2016): fludrocortisone's primary analysis missed — HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069); benefit appeared only in adjusted and post-stabilisation analyses (HR 0.51)
cards.people: 210 patients (71% female, median age 30 years) with more than 2 lifetime syncopal spells (median 15 spells over a median 9 years) and a Calgary Syncope Symptom Score above −3, randomised double-blind in the multicentre POST 2 trial to fludrocortisone at the highest tolerated dose from 0.05 mg to 0.2 mg daily, or matching placebo, over a 1-year treatment period. Main outcome: first recurrence of syncope; 96 patients had at least one recurrence and only 14 were lost to follow-up before recurring.
cards.result: Primary analysis: hazard ratio for syncope recurrence 0.69 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069) — a marginally non-significant result that did not meet the prespecified objective of at least a 40% relative risk reduction. In a multivariable model the effect was significant (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.94, p = 0.024), and when the analysis was restricted to outcomes after 2 weeks of dose stabilisation it was larger (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.89, p = 0.019).
cards.watchOut: A trial that misses its primary endpoint does not become positive because secondary analyses are significant — the stabilisation-phase analysis in particular was constructed after the data were in, and it discards exactly the early period when a preventive drug should already work. Fludrocortisone also carries mineralocorticoid baggage (fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalaemia) that a borderline syncope benefit must outweigh; the abstract reports the efficacy analyses, and prescribers should check tolerability in the full text.
cards.source: Sheldon R et al. Fludrocortisone for the Prevention of Vasovagal Syncope: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2016. PMID: 27364043. cards.headline: Kaza 2024 meta-analysis: across 47 syncope trials, blinded studies were neutral for fludrocortisone — while unblinded trials flattered almost every treatment
cards.summary: Kaza 2024 meta-analysis: across 47 syncope trials, blinded studies were neutral for fludrocortisone — while unblinded trials flattered almost every treatment
cards.people: A systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of all randomised trials of pharmacological, device-based or supportive interventions for neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope, 1950 to April 2023: 47 eligible trials randomising 3,518 patients, with the primary endpoint of spontaneously recurring syncope, analysed separately by whether the trial was blinded.
cards.result: In blinded trials, fludrocortisone (like beta-blockers and conventional dual-chamber pacing) was neutral for syncope recurrence; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.63), midodrine (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.94) and closed-loop-stimulation pacing (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35) were favourable. Unblinded trials reported significant benefits for nearly every category and consistently larger effects than blinded trials — direct evidence that open designs overestimate syncope treatments.
cards.watchOut: The fludrocortisone stratum of this meta-analysis rests heavily on POST 2 itself, so it is not independent confirmation — its real contribution is the blinding comparison across the whole syncope literature, which is the reason to distrust the more enthusiastic unblinded results elsewhere (including, in part, the counterpressure trial at shelf #2614).
cards.source: Kaza N et al. Therapeutic options for neurocardiogenic syncope: a meta-analysis of randomised trials with and without blinding. Open Heart. 2024. PMID: 38890128. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42022330148 (review registration, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) — point estimates lean fludrocortisone's way, but the single rigorous trial missed its endpoint and the blinded synthesis is neutral
cards.summary: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) — point estimates lean fludrocortisone's way, but the single rigorous trial missed its endpoint and the blinded synthesis is neutral
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial (POST 2, n = 210) and one meta-analysis of 47 syncope trials (3,518 patients) analysing fludrocortisone under blinded conditions.
cards.result: POST 2 primary: HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069) — not significant; post-stabilisation analysis HR 0.51 (0.28 to 0.89). Blinded-trial meta-analysis: neutral for fludrocortisone. Roughly 46% of POST 2 patients (96/210) fainted again within the year whichever arm they were in.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE is not a prescription: for a young fainter with frequent recurrences, a trial of fludrocortisone is a defensible shared decision, but it should be sold to the patient as unproven, with blood pressure and potassium kept in view — and it should not displace the free, safe first-line measures at shelf #2614.

shelves.title: Beta-blockers in HFmrEF: in the individual-patient pooling, deaths at ejection fraction 40–49% ran 7.2% versus 12.4% — on only 575 patients, with the interval touching no effect
shelves.question: In heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction, do beta-blockers reduce death and hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Atrial Fibrillation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stroke Volume/physiology
shelves.balance: No trial has ever randomised 'HFmrEF' as an entry criterion — the category (ejection fraction 40–49%) was named after the trials were done. The best evidence is the Beta-Blockers in Heart Failure Collaborative Group's individual-patient meta-analysis of 11 double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Cleland 2018, PMID: 29040525). Among 14,262 patients in sinus rhythm, the mortality benefit of beta-blockers was consistent across ejection-fraction strata below 50%. In the 40–49% stratum itself — only 575 patients — all-cause death occurred in 7.2% on beta-blockers versus 12.4% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.03): a large point estimate whose interval just touches no effect, while cardiovascular death was significantly lower (4.5% versus 9.2%, adjusted HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.97). Two qualifiers matter. First, rhythm: in the 3,050 patients in atrial fibrillation, beta-blockers raised ejection fraction but did not improve prognosis at any level below 50% — this shelf's answer is a sinus-rhythm answer. Second, the hospitalisation half of the question is not reported for the 40–49% stratum in this analysis. SENIORS (Flather 2005, PMID: 15642700) is consistent background: nebivolol in 2,128 patients aged 70 or over across a broad ejection-fraction range reduced death or cardiovascular admission (31.1% versus 35.3%, HR 0.86) with no interaction by ejection fraction — but only 35% of its patients had an ejection fraction above 35%, so it supports a class effect in older patients rather than proving the HFmrEF case. The HFrEF mortality evidence itself is homed at shelf #88.

cards.headline: Cleland 2018 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 11 trials): at ejection fraction 40–49%, death 7.2% versus 12.4% (adjusted HR 0.59, CI 0.34–1.03); cardiovascular death significantly lower (HR 0.48)
cards.summary: Cleland 2018 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 11 trials): at ejection fraction 40–49%, death 7.2% versus 12.4% (adjusted HR 0.59, CI 0.34–1.03); cardiovascular death significantly lower (HR 0.48)
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (Beta-Blockers in Heart Failure Collaborative Group, Cleland 2018)
cards.people: Individual patient data from 11 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled beta-blocker trials in heart failure: 14,262 patients in sinus rhythm (median ejection fraction 27%), of whom 575 had a baseline ejection fraction of 40–49% and 244 an ejection fraction of 50% or more; plus 3,050 patients in atrial fibrillation analysed separately. Primary outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular death over a median 1.3 years of follow-up, by intention to treat.
cards.result: In sinus rhythm, beta-blockers reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortality consistently across ejection-fraction strata except the small subgroup at 50% or above. For ejection fraction 40–49%: all-cause death 21/292 (7.2%) on beta-blockers versus 35/283 (12.4%) on placebo — an absolute difference of about 5 percentage points — adjusted HR 0.59 (95% CI 0.34 to 1.03); cardiovascular death 13/292 (4.5%) versus 26/283 (9.2%), adjusted HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.97). Ejection fraction rose on beta-blockers over about a year in every sinus-rhythm stratum below 50%. In atrial fibrillation, ejection fraction improved but prognosis did not, at any baseline level below 50%.
cards.watchOut: The HFmrEF stratum is a subgroup of a pooling — 575 patients and 56 deaths — so the estimate is fragile: the all-cause mortality interval (0.34 to 1.03) cannot exclude no effect, and the patients were enrolled in HFrEF-era trials, not recruited as HFmrEF. The finding also does not extend to atrial fibrillation, where the same analysis found no prognostic benefit — rate-control prescribing there rests on different reasoning.
cards.source: Cleland JGF et al. Beta-blockers for heart failure with reduced, mid-range, and preserved ejection fraction: an individual patient-level analysis of double-blind randomized trials. European Heart Journal. 2018. PMID: 29040525. Registry ID: none in the record (the analysis was registered as PROSPERO CRD42014010012). cards.headline: SENIORS (Flather 2005): nebivolol cut death or cardiovascular admission in patients over 70 (31.1% versus 35.3%, HR 0.86) with no variation by ejection fraction — but only a minority had preserved-range function
cards.summary: SENIORS (Flather 2005): nebivolol cut death or cardiovascular admission in patients over 70 (31.1% versus 35.3%, HR 0.86) with no variation by ejection fraction — but only a minority had preserved-range function
cards.people: 2,128 patients aged 70 years or older (mean age 76) with a history of heart failure — a heart-failure hospital admission within the previous year or a known ejection fraction of 35% or less — randomised to nebivolol (titrated 1.25 mg to 10 mg daily) or placebo. Mean ejection fraction was 36%, with 35% of patients above 35%; mean follow-up 21 months. Primary outcome: composite of all-cause mortality or cardiovascular hospital admission.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 31.1% (332/1067) on nebivolol versus 35.3% (375/1061) on placebo (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.99, p = 0.039) — a 14% relative reduction, about 4 percentage points absolute. All-cause death alone did not reach significance: 15.8% versus 18.1% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.08, p = 0.21). There was no significant influence of age, gender, or ejection fraction on the treatment effect.
cards.watchOut: SENIORS is an elderly-heart-failure trial, not an HFmrEF trial: its mean ejection fraction was 36% and most participants would today be classified HFrEF. 'No interaction by ejection fraction' in a trial with few high-ejection-fraction patients is weak evidence about the 40–49% band specifically — it is consistency, not proof. Nebivolol is also a single agent with vasodilating properties; generalising to the whole class leans on the meta-analysis, not on this trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE — the direction is consistent and the cardiovascular-death endpoint is significant, but the HFmrEF numbers rest on 575 pooled patients in sinus rhythm
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE — the direction is consistent and the cardiovascular-death endpoint is significant, but the HFmrEF numbers rest on 575 pooled patients in sinus rhythm
cards.people: An individual-patient meta-analysis of 11 placebo-controlled trials (14,262 patients in sinus rhythm; 575 in the ejection-fraction 40–49% stratum) and one large trial of nebivolol in elderly heart failure across ejection fractions (n = 2,128).
cards.result: HFmrEF stratum, sinus rhythm: all-cause death 7.2% versus 12.4% (adjusted HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.03); cardiovascular death 4.5% versus 9.2% (adjusted HR 0.48, 0.24 to 0.97). Atrial fibrillation: no prognostic benefit. Hospitalisation in the 40–49% stratum: not reported in the analysis. SENIORS: composite reduced (HR 0.86) without ejection-fraction interaction.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers for sinus rhythm. A patient with HFmrEF and atrial fibrillation should not be promised a mortality benefit from a beta-blocker on this evidence — and a patient whose ejection fraction has recovered into the 40s on treatment is a different question again (withdrawing therapy), not covered here.

shelves.title: COSIRA: the coronary sinus Reducer doubled the chance of a two-class angina improvement over a sham procedure (35% versus 15%) — in 104 patients, with no gain in exercise time
shelves.question: In refractory angina, does a coronary sinus reducer improve symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angina Pectoris/classification/therapy · Cardiac Catheterization · Cardiac Catheters · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Sinus/diagnostic imaging · Equipment Design · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Revascularization/instrumentation · Patient Acuity · Quality of Life · Surgical Mesh
shelves.balance: The coronary sinus Reducer (Neovasc) is a balloon-expandable, hourglass-shaped implant that narrows the coronary sinus, intended to redistribute blood toward ischaemic myocardium in patients with refractory angina who have no revascularisation option. Its evidence turns on one small sham-controlled trial, COSIRA (Verheye 2015, PMID: 25651246): 104 patients with class III–IV angina and myocardial ischaemia, not candidates for revascularisation, were randomised to the device or a sham procedure. At 6 months, 35% of the device group versus 15% of the sham group had improved by at least two angina classes (p = 0.02), and 71% versus 42% by at least one class (p = 0.003); quality-of-life scores also favoured the device (Seattle Angina Questionnaire improvement 17.6 versus 7.6 points). But the objective measures did not move — no significant difference in exercise time or in dobutamine-echocardiography wall-motion index — and a sham arm in which 42% of patients improve by a class or more is a standing warning about expectation effects in angina. The wider literature pooled by Hochstadt (2022, PMID: 34968714) — 9 prospective studies, 846 patients, all but one uncontrolled — reports 76% improving by at least one class with 98% procedural success and 3% non-major complications; consistent with COSIRA, but uncontrolled series cannot separate device effect from placebo effect and natural history. Tier C: a single small trial for a symptom endpoint, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: COSIRA (Verheye 2015): improvement of at least two angina classes in 35% versus 15% with sham (p = 0.02); at least one class in 71% versus 42% — but exercise time and wall motion did not improve
cards.summary: COSIRA (Verheye 2015): improvement of at least two angina classes in 35% versus 15% with sham (p = 0.02); at least one class in 71% versus 42% — but exercise time and wall motion did not improve
cards.people: 104 patients with Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III or IV angina and myocardial ischaemia who were not candidates for revascularisation, randomised to implantation of the coronary-sinus reducing device (the Reducer, Neovasc) or to a sham procedure. Primary endpoint: proportion improving by at least two CCS angina classes at 6 months. The trial was funded by Neovasc, the device manufacturer.
cards.result: Improvement of at least two CCS classes at 6 months: 35% (18/52) with the device versus 15% (8/52) with sham (p = 0.02) — about 20 percentage points absolute. Improvement of at least one class: 71% (37/52) versus 42% (22/52, p = 0.003). Seattle Angina Questionnaire quality-of-life improvement: 17.6 versus 7.6 points on a 100-point scale (p = 0.03). There were no significant between-group differences in exercise time or in dobutamine-echocardiography wall-motion index. At 6 months the device group had had 1 myocardial infarction; the sham group 1 death and 3 myocardial infarctions (numbers far too small to interpret).
cards.watchOut: A 104-patient, manufacturer-funded trial with a subjective primary endpoint and a strikingly responsive sham arm (42% improved at least one class): the between-group difference is real by design, but its size should be discounted for expectation effects, and the failure of exercise time and wall motion to improve means the mechanism's objective footprint is unproven. Nothing here speaks to mortality, infarction, or durability beyond 6 months.
cards.source: Verheye S et al. Efficacy of a device to narrow the coronary sinus in refractory angina. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25651246. Registry ID: NCT01205893. cards.headline: Hochstadt 2022 meta-analysis: across 9 prospective studies and 846 patients, 76% improved by at least one angina class and 40% by two — nearly all of it uncontrolled
cards.summary: Hochstadt 2022 meta-analysis: across 9 prospective studies and 846 patients, 76% improved by at least one angina class and 40% by two — nearly all of it uncontrolled
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies (Hochstadt 2022)
cards.people: A meta-analysis of prospective studies of coronary sinus narrowing for refractory angina published to June 2021: 9 studies including 846 patients — the single randomised sham-controlled trial (COSIRA) plus multiple uncontrolled prospective series. Outcomes: proportions improving by at least one or at least two Canadian Cardiovascular Society angina classes, procedural success, complications, Seattle Angina Questionnaire scores and 6-minute walk distance.
cards.result: Improvement of at least one CCS class: 76% of patients (95% CI 73% to 80%). Improvement of at least two classes: 40% (95% CI 35% to 46%). Procedural success 98%, with no major and 3% non-major periprocedural complications. Seattle Angina Questionnaire scores and 6-minute walk distance improved significantly after implantation in the pooled before-and-after data.
cards.watchOut: Proportions from uncontrolled series are not treatment effects: COSIRA's sham arm improved by at least one class in 42% of patients, so a pooled 76% improvement rate in uncontrolled data is compatible with a much smaller true device effect plus placebo response, regression to the mean, and publication selection. Use this card for procedural safety and consistency, not for efficacy.
cards.source: Hochstadt A et al. Effectiveness of Coronary Sinus Reducer for Treatment of Refractory Angina: A Meta-analysis. The Canadian Journal of Cardiology. 2022. PMID: 34968714. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE — a genuine sham-controlled symptom benefit in a small trial, of uncertain size, with objective endpoints unmoved
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE — a genuine sham-controlled symptom benefit in a small trial, of uncertain size, with objective endpoints unmoved
cards.people: One randomised sham-controlled trial (n = 104) and one meta-analysis of 9 prospective studies (846 patients, predominantly uncontrolled).
cards.result: Sham-controlled: at least two angina classes better in 35% versus 15%; at least one class in 71% versus 42%; quality of life better by about 10 points more on a 100-point scale; exercise time and wall-motion index not significantly different. Uncontrolled pooled: 76% improve at least one class; procedural success 98%; non-major complications 3%.
cards.watchOut: For 'no-option' patients the relevant comparison is often device versus continued medical therapy and time; this evidence supports offering the device within that conversation, with the size of the benefit honestly hedged. It does not support use in patients who still have revascularisation or drug options untried.

shelves.title: SIGNIFY: ivabradine slowed the heart and changed nothing — 19,102 patients, a null primary endpoint, and more events in patients with limiting angina
shelves.question: In patients with stable coronary artery disease and resting heart rate at least 70, does ivabradine reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Angina, Stable/drug therapy · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Benzazepines/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · Coronary Artery Disease/drug therapy/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Heart Failure · Heart Rate/drug effects · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Ivabradine · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Risk
shelves.balance: SIGNIFY (Fox 2014, PMID: 25176136) tested the pure heart-rate hypothesis in stable coronary disease: 19,102 patients without clinical heart failure and with a resting heart rate of at least 70 beats per minute received ivabradine (up to 10 mg twice daily, titrated to a heart rate of 55–60) or placebo on top of standard therapy. The drug did its pharmacological job — at 3 months heart rate averaged 60.7 versus 70.6 beats per minute — and it changed no outcomes. After a median 27.8 months, the primary composite of cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 6.8% on ivabradine versus 6.4% on placebo (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.20, p = 0.20), with neither component significantly different. Worse, among the 12,049 patients with activity-limiting angina — the subgroup with the most symptomatic reason to take the drug — ivabradine was associated with an increase in the primary endpoint (p = 0.02 for interaction). Bradycardia was common: 18.0% versus 2.3%. The contrast with heart failure is the point of the cross-reference: in HFrEF, ivabradine reduced heart-failure hospitalisation in SHIFT (homed at shelf #275) — a different population, a different substrate, and no licence to extrapolate the benefit to stable coronary disease without heart failure. Tier C: a single (very large) trial shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: SIGNIFY (Fox 2014): 19,102 patients — primary endpoint 6.8% versus 6.4% (HR 1.08, p = 0.20) despite heart rate falling by 10 beats per minute; bradycardia 18.0% versus 2.3%
cards.summary: SIGNIFY (Fox 2014): 19,102 patients — primary endpoint 6.8% versus 6.4% (HR 1.08, p = 0.20) despite heart rate falling by 10 beats per minute; bradycardia 18.0% versus 2.3%
cards.people: 19,102 patients with stable coronary artery disease without clinical heart failure and a heart rate of 70 beats per minute or more, including 12,049 with activity-limiting angina (Canadian Cardiovascular Society class II or higher), randomised double-blind to ivabradine (dose up to 10 mg twice daily, adjusted to a target heart rate of 55 to 60) or placebo, added to standard background therapy. Primary endpoint: composite of death from cardiovascular causes or nonfatal myocardial infarction. Median follow-up 27.8 months. Funded by Servier.
cards.result: Heart rate at 3 months: 60.7 ± 9.0 beats per minute on ivabradine versus 70.6 ± 10.1 on placebo. Primary endpoint: 6.8% versus 6.4% (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.20, p = 0.20) — no significant difference, with the point estimate favouring placebo; neither cardiovascular death nor nonfatal myocardial infarction differed significantly on its own. Among patients with activity-limiting angina, ivabradine was associated with an increase in the primary endpoint, an effect not seen in patients without limiting angina (p = 0.02 for interaction). Bradycardia: 18.0% versus 2.3% (p < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup interaction (p = 0.02) is not proof of harm in angina patients, but it removes any temptation to prescribe for symptom relief on outcome grounds in exactly that group — and ivabradine for angina symptoms is a separate, symptomatic claim that this outcomes trial does not support either. The doses used (up to 10 mg twice daily) exceeded the currently licensed maximum, which may have contributed to the bradycardia burden; even read charitably, there is no dose at which this trial shows benefit.
cards.source: Fox K et al. Ivabradine in stable coronary artery disease without clinical heart failure. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25176136. Registry ID: ISRCTN61576291. shelves.title: Statin loading before PCI: small trials cut biomarker-defined injury; the one large clinical-outcome trial, SECURE-PCI, found nothing
shelves.question: In patients undergoing PCI, does high-dose statin loading (or reloading) beforehand reduce periprocedural myocardial infarction and later events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina Pectoris/etiology/therapy · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary/adverse effects · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Atorvastatin · Biomarkers · Coronary Stenosis/complications/therapy · Creatine Kinase/blood · Creatine Kinase, MB Form · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heptanoic Acids/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Isoenzymes/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/blood/etiology/prevention & control · Myocardial Reperfusion Injury/blood/complications/prevention & control · Myoglobin/blood · Premedication · Prospective Studies · Pyrroles/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Stents · Treatment Outcome · Troponin I/blood
shelves.balance: The statin-loading literature is a study in what endpoints do to conclusions. The ARMYDA programme randomised small numbers of patients to atorvastatin pretreatment and measured myocardial injury with cardiac biomarkers. In the original trial (Pasceri 2004, PMID: 15277322), 153 statin-naïve patients with stable angina given atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 7 days before elective intervention had less biomarker injury on every measure, and periprocedural myocardial infarction by creatine-kinase-MB criteria in 5% versus 18% on placebo. ARMYDA-RECAPTURE (Di Sciascio 2009, PMID: 19643320) extended the idea to reloading patients already on chronic statins (383 patients): the 30-day composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction or unplanned revascularisation fell from 9.4% to 3.7% (p = 0.037), driven by periprocedural infarction. Then SECURE-PCI (Berwanger 2018, PMID: 29525821) tested loading properly: 4,191 patients with acute coronary syndrome and planned invasive management received two 80 mg atorvastatin loads or placebo, and 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events were 6.2% versus 7.1% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.11, p = 0.27) — no significant difference, in a trial where only 64.7% of patients actually proceeded to PCI. The reconciliation is that loading probably does blunt the small enzyme leaks that follow stenting — a surrogate whose link to prognosis is contested — while no trial shows it prevents death, spontaneous infarction, or other events patients feel. Nearly all these patients should be on a high-intensity statin anyway; the shelf answers only the narrower question of whether the extra pre-procedure load itself earns its keep.

cards.headline: ARMYDA (Pasceri 2004): atorvastatin 40 mg for 7 days before elective PCI in 153 statin-naïve patients — periprocedural infarction by CK-MB 5% versus 18%, biomarker injury lower on every measure
cards.summary: ARMYDA (Pasceri 2004): atorvastatin 40 mg for 7 days before elective PCI in 153 statin-naïve patients — periprocedural infarction by CK-MB 5% versus 18%, biomarker injury lower on every measure
cards.people: 153 patients with chronic stable angina and no previous statin treatment, scheduled for elective coronary intervention, randomised double-blind to atorvastatin 40 mg daily (n = 76) or placebo (n = 77) for 7 days before the procedure. Creatine kinase-MB, troponin I and myoglobin were measured at baseline and at 8 and 24 hours after intervention.
cards.result: Marker elevation above the upper limit of normal: creatine kinase-MB 12% on atorvastatin versus 35% on placebo (p = 0.001); troponin I 20% versus 48% (p = 0.0004); myoglobin 22% versus 51% (p = 0.0005). Myocardial infarction by creatine-kinase-MB determination: 5% versus 18% (p = 0.025). Peak post-procedural levels of all three markers were significantly lower in the statin group.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker trial of 153 patients from the pre-high-sensitivity-troponin era: its 'infarctions' are enzyme leaks defined by CK-MB thresholds, most of which patients never feel, and the trial could not and did not address death or later events. It establishes a biological effect on procedural injury markers, not a clinical dividend.
cards.source: Pasceri V et al. Randomized trial of atorvastatin for reduction of myocardial damage during coronary intervention: results from the ARMYDA (Atorvastatin for Reduction of Myocardial Damage during Angioplasty) study. Circulation. 2004. PMID: 15277322. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: ARMYDA-RECAPTURE (Di Sciascio 2009): reloading patients already on statins cut 30-day events from 9.4% to 3.7% (p = 0.037) — again driven by periprocedural infarction
cards.summary: ARMYDA-RECAPTURE (Di Sciascio 2009): reloading patients already on statins cut 30-day events from 9.4% to 3.7% (p = 0.037) — again driven by periprocedural infarction
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ARMYDA-RECAPTURE, Di Sciascio 2009)
cards.people: 383 patients (mean age 66 years) with stable angina (53%) or non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes (47%), all on chronic statin therapy and undergoing PCI, randomised double-blind to an atorvastatin reload (80 mg 12 hours before intervention plus a further 40 mg pre-procedure, n = 192) or placebo (n = 191); everyone received long-term atorvastatin 40 mg daily afterwards. Primary endpoint: 30-day incidence of major adverse cardiac events (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or unplanned revascularisation).
cards.result: Primary endpoint: 3.7% with reload versus 9.4% with placebo (p = 0.037) — a relative reduction of about 60%, 5.7 percentage points absolute — driven mostly by reduced periprocedural myocardial infarction. Post-procedural CK-MB elevation above normal: 13% versus 24% (p = 0.017); troponin-I elevation 37% versus 49% (p = 0.021). On multivariable analysis the reload predicted fewer 30-day events (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.80), with the largest effect in the acute-coronary-syndrome subgroup (82% relative risk reduction, p = 0.027).
cards.watchOut: Still small (383 patients, 25 primary events in total) and still an endpoint built substantially from periprocedural enzyme-defined infarctions — the event type most sensitive to the intervention and least clearly tied to prognosis. A composite difference resting on roughly 11 events should be read as fragile, and the trial predates contemporary antiplatelet and statin background therapy.
cards.source: Di Sciascio G et al. Efficacy of atorvastatin reload in patients on chronic statin therapy undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention: results of the ARMYDA-RECAPTURE (Atorvastatin for Reduction of Myocardial Damage During Angioplasty) randomized trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2009. PMID: 19643320. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SECURE-PCI (Berwanger 2018): 4,191 patients with acute coronary syndrome — two 80 mg atorvastatin loads did not reduce 30-day major events (6.2% versus 7.1%, HR 0.88, p = 0.27)
cards.summary: SECURE-PCI (Berwanger 2018): 4,191 patients with acute coronary syndrome — two 80 mg atorvastatin loads did not reduce 30-day major events (6.2% versus 7.1%, HR 0.88, p = 0.27)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SECURE-PCI, Berwanger 2018)
cards.people: 4,191 patients with acute coronary syndrome evaluated by angiography with a plan to proceed to PCI if anatomically feasible, at 53 sites in Brazil, randomised double-blind to two loading doses of atorvastatin 80 mg (before and 24 hours after the planned procedure, n = 2087) or matching placebo (n = 2104); all patients then received atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 30 days. In the event, 64.7% underwent PCI, 8% bypass surgery, and 27.3% medical management alone. Primary outcome: 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, unplanned revascularisation).
cards.result: At 30 days, MACE occurred in 6.2% on atorvastatin loading versus 7.1% on placebo — an absolute difference of 0.85 percentage points (95% CI −0.70 to 2.41) in loading's favour, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.11, p = 0.27), not statistically significant. No hepatic failure was reported; rhabdomyolysis occurred in 3 patients, all in the placebo group. The authors conclude the findings do not support routine loading doses in unselected ACS patients planned for invasive management.
cards.watchOut: SECURE-PCI's dilution is the honest caveat in the other direction: over a third of randomised patients never had PCI (surgery or medical therapy instead), so the trial tests a loading policy for ACS presentations more than loading in confirmed PCI patients. Even so, it is an order of magnitude larger than the positive trials and it is the only one powered for events patients experience — its null is the weight-bearing result for practice.
cards.source: Berwanger O et al. Effect of Loading Dose of Atorvastatin Prior to Planned Percutaneous Coronary Intervention on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Acute Coronary Syndrome: The SECURE-PCI Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29525821. Registry ID: NCT01448642. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — biomarker injury falls in small trials; clinical events do not fall in the large one
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — biomarker injury falls in small trials; clinical events do not fall in the large one
cards.people: Three double-blind randomised trials spanning the loading question: statin-naïve elective PCI (n = 153), reloading on chronic statins (n = 383), and loading in acute coronary syndrome at scale (n = 4,191).
cards.result: Biomarker-defined periprocedural infarction: 5% versus 18% (ARMYDA, CK-MB criteria); 30-day composite driven by periprocedural infarction 3.7% versus 9.4% (ARMYDA-RECAPTURE). Clinical events at scale: 30-day MACE 6.2% versus 7.1% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.11) — not significant (SECURE-PCI). No trial shows an effect on mortality.
cards.watchOut: Loading is cheap and safe, so many operators will keep doing it — but this shelf should not be quoted as outcome evidence for that habit. The question it answers is narrow: extra pre-procedure doses, on top of the high-intensity statin these patients should receive regardless, have no demonstrated effect on events that matter to patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pasceri V et al. Circulation. 2004 (PMID: 15277322); Di Sciascio G et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2009 (PMID: 19643320); Berwanger O et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29525821).

shelves.title: AFIRE: rivaroxaban alone was noninferior for efficacy and superior for bleeding — the combination arm's excess deaths stopped the trial early
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary disease more than a year after stenting, is rivaroxaban alone as safe and effective as rivaroxaban plus an antiplatelet drug?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Disease/complications/therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Proportional Hazards Models · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Rivaroxaban/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: AFIRE (Yasuda 2019, PMID: 31475793) randomised 2,236 Japanese patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary disease — PCI or bypass surgery more than a year earlier, or angiographic disease not requiring revascularisation — to rivaroxaban alone or rivaroxaban plus a single antiplatelet agent. The trial was stopped early because mortality was higher in the combination group. Rivaroxaban monotherapy was noninferior for the primary efficacy composite (stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring revascularisation, or death from any cause): 4.14% versus 5.75% per patient-year (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95, against a noninferiority margin of 1.46) — the point estimate favours dropping the antiplatelet, though a noninferiority design should not be read as proving superiority. On safety it was superior outright: major bleeding by ISTH criteria 1.62% versus 2.76% per patient-year (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.89, p = 0.01). The answer to the question is therefore yes on both halves — as effective, and safer — within the limits of a single open-label trial stopped early in one country's population. Tier C: a single trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: AFIRE (Yasuda 2019): rivaroxaban alone — efficacy 4.14% versus 5.75% per patient-year (HR 0.72, noninferior); major bleeding 1.62% versus 2.76% (HR 0.59, superior); trial stopped early for excess deaths on combination therapy
cards.summary: AFIRE (Yasuda 2019): rivaroxaban alone — efficacy 4.14% versus 5.75% per patient-year (HR 0.72, noninferior); major bleeding 1.62% versus 2.76% (HR 0.59, superior); trial stopped early for excess deaths on combination therapy
cards.type: Multicentre randomised open-label noninferiority trial (AFIRE, Yasuda 2019)
cards.people: 2,236 patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease in Japan — previous PCI or coronary-artery bypass grafting more than 1 year earlier, or angiographically confirmed coronary disease not requiring revascularisation — randomised in an open-label multicentre trial to rivaroxaban monotherapy or rivaroxaban plus a single antiplatelet agent. Primary efficacy endpoint: composite of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring revascularisation, or death from any cause (noninferiority margin 1.46). Primary safety endpoint: ISTH major bleeding (superiority analysis).
cards.result: The trial was stopped early because of increased mortality in the combination-therapy group. Primary efficacy endpoint: 4.14% per patient-year on monotherapy versus 5.75% on combination therapy (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95, p < 0.001 for noninferiority). Primary safety endpoint: 1.62% versus 2.76% per patient-year (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.89, p = 0.01 for superiority) — about 1.1 percentage points fewer major bleeds per patient-year on monotherapy, a 41% relative reduction.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, and stopped early: early stopping for a mortality signal in the comparator arm can exaggerate the apparent benefit of the winning strategy, and the efficacy claim is formally noninferiority, not superiority, despite the favourable point estimate. The population is specifically patients whose coronary disease is stable and remote — nothing here licenses dropping antiplatelets in the first year after stenting or after an acute coronary syndrome, where the balance is different and separately homed.
cards.source: Yasuda S et al. Antithrombotic Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation with Stable Coronary Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31475793. shelves.title: Pyridostigmine in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: standing diastolic fall cut from 34 to about 28 mm Hg with no rise in supine pressure — a modest, physiologically tidy effect
shelves.question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does pyridostigmine raise standing blood pressure without worsening supine hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Arteries/innervation/physiopathology · Autonomic Nervous System Diseases/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Baroreflex/drug effects/physiology · Cholinergic Fibers/drug effects/metabolism · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Ganglia, Autonomic/drug effects/metabolism/physiopathology · Ganglia, Sympathetic/drug effects/metabolism/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Midodrine/adverse effects · Neural Pathways/drug effects/metabolism/physiopathology · Norepinephrine/metabolism · Pyridostigmine Bromide/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Regional Blood Flow/drug effects/physiology · Shy-Drager Syndrome/drug therapy/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstriction/drug effects/physiology · Vasoconstrictor Agents/adverse effects
shelves.balance: Yes on the blood-pressure mechanics, modestly. The rationale is elegant: pyridostigmine amplifies sympathetic ganglionic transmission, which is quiet lying down and active standing — so it should lift standing pressure without the supine hypertension that limits midodrine. The double-blind 4-way crossover trial (Singer 2006, PMID: 16476804; 58 patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, single 60 mg doses) found exactly that pattern: supine systolic and diastolic pressures did not differ from placebo (P = .36 and .85), while the fall in standing diastolic pressure was significantly blunted — 27.6 mm Hg on pyridostigmine versus 34.0 mm Hg on placebo (P = .04), and 27.2 mm Hg when 5 mg midodrine was added (P = .002) — and standing-pressure improvement tracked symptom improvement. The longer randomised evidence is weaker in design: Byun 2017 (PMID: 28794253; 87 patients, open-label, 3 months) found orthostatic drops improved in all three arms (midodrine, pyridostigmine, both) and symptoms improved least on pyridostigmine alone; the authors grade their own study Class IV. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — one small single-dose crossover trial plus open-label follow-up; the standing-pressure claim is supported, the symptom claim only partly. Droxidopa and the midodrine/fludrocortisone comparisons are homed at #931 and #1558.

cards.headline: Singer 2006: a single 60 mg dose of pyridostigmine cut the standing diastolic fall from 34.0 to 27.6 mm Hg (P = .04) — with supine blood pressure statistically indistinguishable from placebo
cards.summary: Singer 2006: a single 60 mg dose of pyridostigmine cut the standing diastolic fall from 34.0 to 27.6 mm Hg (P = .04) — with supine blood pressure statistically indistinguishable from placebo
cards.people: Double-blind, randomised, 4-way crossover study in 58 patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. On successive days each patient received, in random order: placebo; pyridostigmine bromide 60 mg; pyridostigmine 60 mg + midodrine 2.5 mg; and pyridostigmine 60 mg + midodrine 5 mg. Supine and standing blood pressure and heart rate were measured before treatment and hourly for 6 hours. Primary endpoint: the fall in standing diastolic blood pressure.
cards.result: Supine blood pressure did not differ significantly between treatments (systolic P = .36; diastolic P = .85). The fall in standing diastolic pressure was significantly reduced overall (P = .02): pyridostigmine alone, a fall of 27.6 mm Hg versus 34.0 mm Hg on placebo (P = .04); pyridostigmine + midodrine 5 mg, 27.2 versus 34.0 mm Hg (P = .002). Improvement in standing blood pressure significantly regressed with improvement in orthostatic symptoms. The authors conclude pyridostigmine improves standing blood pressure without worsening supine hypertension, with the greatest effect on diastolic pressure, consistent with increased total peripheral resistance.
cards.watchOut: Single doses, one day per arm, a physiological primary endpoint: this trial proves the mechanism behaves as designed for a few hours — it does not prove that daily pyridostigmine prevents falls, fractures or syncope over months, outcomes no trial here measured. The absolute gain, about 6–7 mm Hg of diastolic fall, is modest next to midodrine's pressor effect.
cards.source: Singer W et al. Pyridostigmine treatment trial in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Arch Neurol. 2006. PMID: 16476804. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Byun 2017: over 3 months, orthostatic drops improved on pyridostigmine, midodrine, or both — but symptoms improved least on pyridostigmine alone; the authors grade the study Class IV
cards.summary: Byun 2017: over 3 months, orthostatic drops improved on pyridostigmine, midodrine, or both — but symptoms improved least on pyridostigmine alone; the authors grade the study Class IV
cards.people: Randomised, open-label trial of 87 patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension allocated to midodrine only, pyridostigmine only, or the combination, followed at 1 and 3 months. Primary outcome: improvement in the orthostatic blood-pressure drop at 3 months; secondary outcomes included the 1-month drop and a questionnaire score of orthostatic symptoms.
cards.result: Orthostatic systolic and diastolic drops improved significantly at 3 months in all three treatment groups, and orthostatic symptoms were significantly ameliorated during treatment — with symptom severity ordered midodrine only < combination < pyridostigmine only (midodrine best). Mild-to-moderate adverse events were reported by 11.5% of patients. The authors classify the study as Class IV evidence that single or combined treatment is safe and has similar effects on the orthostatic drop up to 3 months.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo arm: 'all groups improved' in a fluctuating condition measured by effort-dependent standing tests is weak evidence of efficacy, and the authors' own Class IV grading says so. Its useful contributions are the 3-month safety picture and the symptom ranking, which tempers enthusiasm for pyridostigmine as monotherapy.
cards.source: Byun JI et al. Efficacy of single or combined midodrine and pyridostigmine in orthostatic hypotension. Neurology. 2017. PMID: 28794253. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308124, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the physiology delivers — standing pressure rises, supine pressure does not — but the effect is small, the symptom benefit is the weakest of the pressor options, and falls have never been an endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: the physiology delivers — standing pressure rises, supine pressure does not — but the effect is small, the symptom benefit is the weakest of the pressor options, and falls have never been an endpoint
cards.people: One double-blind single-dose crossover trial (58 patients) and one open-label 3-month randomised trial (87 patients) in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
cards.result: Standing diastolic fall: 27.6 vs 34.0 mm Hg (pyridostigmine vs placebo, single dose); supine pressure unchanged (P = .36/.85). Over 3 months all pressor strategies improved measured drops; symptoms ranked midodrine best and pyridostigmine alone worst of the three. Pyridostigmine's niche on this evidence is the patient whose supine hypertension forbids more midodrine — as an adjunct with a mechanism that switches off lying down — not as first-line monotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled for, or reported, falls, syncope recurrence or fractures — the outcomes patients care about. Gastrointestinal cholinergic effects (the dose-limiting problem in practice) appear in these reports only inside an 11.5% mild-to-moderate adverse-event figure in the open-label trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singer W et al. Arch Neurol. 2006 (PMID: 16476804); Byun JI et al. Neurology. 2017 (PMID: 28794253).
