shelves.title: Fludrocortisone vs midodrine in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: never compared for benefit in any trial — and on the one head-to-head safety study, fludrocortisone users were hospitalised more
shelves.question: In neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does fludrocortisone help as much as midodrine?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Agonists/adverse effects* · Aged · Blood Pressure/drug effects* · Databases, Factual · Female · Fludrocortisone/adverse effects* · Heart Failure/diagnosis, epidemiology, physiopathology, therapy · Hospitalization* · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic/diagnosis, drug therapy*, epidemiology, physiopathology · Incidence · Logistic Models · Male · Medicaid · Middle Aged · Midodrine/adverse effects* · Multivariate Analysis · Prevalence · Propensity Score · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Tennessee/epidemiology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United States · Vasoconstrictor Agents/adverse effects*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the honest headline is an absence: no trial has ever randomised fludrocortisone against midodrine for efficacy in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and the one attempt to build that trial (Mossop H et al., PMID: 41217271, the CONFORM-OH pilot) recruited 13 patients in ten months and was judged not feasible in its current design. What direct comparative evidence exists is about safety, and it favours midodrine: in a Tennessee Medicaid cohort of 1,324 fludrocortisone initiators and 797 midodrine initiators (Grijalva CG et al., PMID: 29025750), all-cause hospitalisation rates were higher with fludrocortisone (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.40), the gap widened in patients with prior heart failure (1.42, 1.07 to 1.90), and heart-failure hospitalisations specifically did not differ significantly (1.33, 0.79 to 2.56) — despite midodrine users carrying more cardiovascular disease at baseline. Uncontrolled before-and-after ambulatory monitoring series (de Lange FJ et al., PMID: 39718670) report both drugs raise 24-hour pressures and reduce systolic drops, fludrocortisone perhaps more so, but with no control group and a mostly syncope population that is hypothesis, not comparison. Each drug's placebo-controlled evidence is homed separately — midodrine at shelf #2498, droxidopa at shelves #931 and #1558, pyridostigmine at shelf #2691 — and fludrocortisone's own randomised data are in vasovagal syncope (shelf #2615), not neurogenic hypotension. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): 'helps as much' is unknown for benefit and doubtful on hospitalisations; the choice between them today rests on mechanism, comorbidity (especially heart failure), and habit, not on comparative trials.

cards.headline: Grijalva 2017: the only head-to-head study — 2,121 new users in Tennessee Medicaid; fludrocortisone carried a 20% higher adjusted rate of all-cause hospitalisation than midodrine, and 42% higher in patients with heart failure
cards.summary: Grijalva 2017: the only head-to-head study — 2,121 new users in Tennessee Medicaid; fludrocortisone carried a 20% higher adjusted rate of all-cause hospitalisation than midodrine, and 42% higher in patients with heart failure
cards.people: 1,324 adults initiating fludrocortisone and 797 initiating midodrine for orthostatic hypotension in Tennessee Medicaid (1995–2009), compared in a retrospective cohort with propensity and regression adjustment. Midodrine users had a higher prevalence of cardiovascular conditions at baseline. The study compared safety — hospitalisations — not symptom relief or blood-pressure efficacy, and the population had orthostatic hypotension of mixed cause rather than confirmed neurogenic disease.
cards.result: All-cause hospitalisation rates were 1,489 per 1,000 person-years on fludrocortisone versus 1,330 on midodrine (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.40). Heart-failure hospitalisation rates were 76 versus 84 per 1,000 person-years (adjusted ratio 1.33, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.56 — not significant). Among patients with a history of congestive heart failure, all-cause hospitalisation was 2,448 versus 1,820 per 1,000 person-years (adjusted ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.90) and heart-failure exacerbation hospitalisation 297 versus 263 (adjusted ratio 1.48, 95% CI 0.69 to 3.16). The authors conclude fludrocortisone users had higher hospitalisation rates than midodrine users, especially with heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Observational prescribing data: doctors chose the drug, and the choice tracks the patient — fludrocortisone is often given to younger, volume-depleted patients and midodrine to sicker cardiac ones (as the baseline imbalance here shows), and adjustment cannot fully undo that. Hospitalisation is also a downstream, multi-cause outcome; the study cannot say fludrocortisone caused the excess, only that its users were hospitalised more after adjustment. And it is silent on the question patients ask first — which drug makes them feel less dizzy.
cards.source: Grijalva CG et al. Fludrocortisone Is Associated With a Higher Risk of All-Cause Hospitalizations Compared With Midodrine in Patients With Orthostatic Hypotension. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2017. PMID: 29025750. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CONFORM-OH pilot (Mossop 2025): the trial that was supposed to answer this question recruited 13 patients in 10 months and was declared not feasible — the efficacy comparison does not exist because it could not be run
cards.summary: CONFORM-OH pilot (Mossop 2025): the trial that was supposed to answer this question recruited 13 patients in 10 months and was declared not feasible — the efficacy comparison does not exist because it could not be run
cards.type: Pilot randomised trial and feasibility study (CONFORM-OH, Mossop 2025)
cards.people: A UK pilot of a pragmatic, open-label, three-arm randomised trial (non-drug therapy alone vs plus fludrocortisone 50–400 micrograms daily vs plus midodrine 5–30 mg daily) in adults with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, run across falls/syncope, movement-disorder, geriatrics and cardiology clinics; 282 patients were screened over ten months.
cards.result: Only 13 participants were recruited, from 4 of 9 open sites. Current or recent use of one of the study drugs accounted for 120 of the exclusions (52%) — most candidates were already taking one of the two drugs, which is itself a measure of how entrenched untested prescribing is. Ten of 13 participants (77%) remained at the six-month primary endpoint and outcome completion was high, but the investigators conclude the trial was not feasible in its current design and that novel designs are needed to answer the question. No efficacy comparison between fludrocortisone and midodrine is reported, because there were never enough patients to make one.
cards.watchOut: A pilot that failed on recruitment is evidence about research feasibility and about prescribing culture, not about the drugs — it must never be quoted as showing the drugs are equal or ineffective. Its population was symptomatic orthostatic hypotension broadly, not neurogenic disease specifically. COVID-era staffing redeployment contributed to the recruitment failure, so 'infeasible' is partly a verdict on 2020–2022 research conditions.
cards.source: Mossop H et al. Control, Fludrocortisone or Midodrine for the treatment of Orthostatic Hypotension: CONFORM-OH pilot RCT and economic evaluation. Health Technology Assessment. 2025. PMID: 41217271. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: de Lange 2025: uncontrolled ambulatory monitoring in 53 hypotensive patients — both drugs raised 24-hour systolic pressure and cut systolic drops, fludrocortisone numerically more; the authors themselves ask for randomised studies
cards.summary: de Lange 2025: uncontrolled ambulatory monitoring in 53 hypotensive patients — both drugs raised 24-hour systolic pressure and cut systolic drops, fludrocortisone numerically more; the authors themselves ask for randomised studies
cards.type: Uncontrolled before-and-after ambulatory blood pressure study (de Lange 2025)
cards.people: 53 patients (mean age 41, 37 women) with recurrent syncope and/or symptoms due to hypotension and documented daytime systolic drops on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, treated in practice with fludrocortisone (32 patients, 0.05–0.2 mg daily), midodrine (14 patients, 2.5–10 mg two or three times daily), or both (7 patients), with a second ambulatory recording within six months.
cards.result: On fludrocortisone, 24-hour systolic pressure rose from 107.1 to 116.3 mmHg (p = 0.0001), daily drops below 90 mmHg fell by 73% and below 100 mmHg by 41%. On midodrine, 24-hour systolic pressure rose from 112.7 to 115.0 mmHg (p = 0.12), drops below 90 fell by 52% and below 100 by 34%. On both drugs, pressure rose from 110.1 to 114.0 mmHg. The authors conclude both drugs increased 24-hour pressure and reduced drops, fludrocortisone seemingly more effectively, and that randomised studies are needed to confirm the observation.
cards.watchOut: There is no control group, no randomisation, and no blinding: before-and-after pressure changes absorb regression to the mean, dose titration, and every other treatment change, and the groups were chosen by clinicians, not chance. The population — mean age 41, mostly syncope and low-pressure phenotypes — is far from the older neurogenic orthostatic hypotension population of this shelf's question. Treat the fludrocortisone-leaning numbers as a hypothesis about potency, nothing more.
cards.source: de Lange FJ et al. Haemodynamic effects of fludrocortisone and midodrine in patients with symptoms due to hypotension. Clinical Autonomic Research. 2025. PMID: 39718670. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: benefit — never compared; harm — one large cohort leans against fludrocortisone; feasibility — the definitive trial has been attempted and failed
cards.summary: Synthesis: benefit — never compared; harm — one large cohort leans against fludrocortisone; feasibility — the definitive trial has been attempted and failed
cards.people: One retrospective safety cohort (2,121 initiators), one failed pilot RCT (13 recruited), and one uncontrolled monitoring series (53 patients) — the entire direct comparative record for the two oldest drugs in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
cards.result: Efficacy (standing pressure, symptoms, falls): no randomised or controlled head-to-head data exist. Safety: all-cause hospitalisation adjusted rate ratio 1.20 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.40) for fludrocortisone versus midodrine, 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90) in prior heart failure; heart-failure hospitalisation not significantly different. Ambulatory pressures: both drugs raise them in uncontrolled data. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the comparison the clinic makes every week is one the evidence base has never made.
cards.watchOut: This shelf must not be read as 'midodrine is better' — it shows the efficacy question is unanswered and the safety question has exactly one observational answer, vulnerable to confounding by indication. For what each drug does against placebo, use the drug shelves: midodrine #2498, droxidopa #931 and #1558, pyridostigmine #2691; fludrocortisone's randomised evidence in vasovagal syncope is at #2615 and does not transfer automatically to neurogenic disease. Tier C is set because the comparative claim rests on observational data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grijalva CG et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2017 (PMID: 29025750); Mossop H et al. Health Technology Assessment. 2025 (PMID: 41217271); de Lange FJ et al. Clinical Autonomic Research. 2025 (PMID: 39718670).

shelves.title: STRONG-HF: pushing heart-failure drugs to full dose within two weeks of discharge, with four close visits, cut death or readmission by a third in relative terms
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with acute heart failure, does a high-intensity strategy of rapid up-titration of guideline-directed medical therapy with close follow-up, compared with usual care, reduce death or heart-failure readmission?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Stroke Volume · Quality of Life* · Ventricular Function, Left · Heart Failure* · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large multinational randomised trial (1,078 patients) tested the whole strategy, not a single drug: rapid up-titration to full recommended doses within 2 weeks of discharge plus four close follow-up visits over 2 months, against usual local care. By day 90 the strategy plainly worked as a delivery system — full-dose renin-angiotensin blockers in 55% versus 2%, beta-blockers 49% versus 4%, mineralocorticoid antagonists 84% versus 46% — and the clinical endpoint followed: heart-failure readmission or all-cause death by day 180 in 15.2% versus 23.3% (adjusted risk difference 8.1%, risk ratio 0.66, a 34% relative reduction). The cautions are real: the trial was open-label, stopped early on the data monitoring board's advice (which can exaggerate effects), the primary endpoint was amended mid-trial with down-weighting, and adverse events were more frequent with high-intensity care (41% versus 29% by 90 days) although serious (16% versus 17%) and fatal (5% versus 6%) events were not. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): rapid up-titration with close follow-up after an acute heart-failure admission reduces death or readmission, provided the monitoring visits that make it safe are actually delivered.

cards.headline: Mebazaa 2022 (STRONG-HF): rapid up-titration plus close follow-up cut 180-day heart-failure readmission or death to 15.2% versus 23.3% (risk ratio 0.66)
cards.summary: Mebazaa 2022 (STRONG-HF): rapid up-titration plus close follow-up cut 180-day heart-failure readmission or death to 15.2% versus 23.3% (risk ratio 0.66)
cards.people: 1,078 adults (mean age 63 years, 39% women) admitted to hospital with acute heart failure at 87 hospitals in 14 countries who were not on full doses of guideline-directed therapy, randomised before discharge to high-intensity care or usual care, stratified by ejection fraction (≤40% versus >40%).
cards.result: High-intensity care meant up-titration to 100% of recommended doses within 2 weeks and four scheduled outpatient visits over 2 months with clinical, laboratory and NT-proBNP monitoring. By day 90, full-dose up-titration was achieved far more often (renin-angiotensin blockers 55% versus 2%; beta-blockers 49% versus 4%; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists 84% versus 46%), and blood pressure, pulse, NYHA class, bodyweight and NT-proBNP all fell more. The primary endpoint — heart-failure readmission or all-cause death to day 180 — occurred in 74 of 506 (15.2%, down-weighted adjusted estimate) versus 109 of 502 (23.3%): adjusted risk difference 8.1% (95% CI 2.9 to 13.2), p=0.0021, risk ratio 0.66 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.86), a 34% relative reduction. Adverse events by 90 days were more common with high-intensity care (41% versus 29%), but serious adverse events (16% versus 17%) and fatal adverse events (5% versus 6%) were similar.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, stopped early for greater-than-expected benefit, and the primary endpoint was amended during the trial with earlier patients down-weighted — all three features tend to flatter the estimate. The intervention is also inseparable from its safety net of four early visits with laboratory and NT-proBNP checks; rapid up-titration without that monitoring is not what was tested.
cards.source: Mebazaa A et al. Safety, tolerability and efficacy of up-titration of guideline-directed medical therapies for acute heart failure (STRONG-HF): a multinational, open-label, randomised, trial. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 36356631. Registry ID: NCT03412201. cards.headline: Synthesis: a single large trial, a large relative effect, and a strategy that only works if the follow-up visits happen
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single large trial, a large relative effect, and a strategy that only works if the follow-up visits happen
cards.people: One multinational randomised trial of 1,078 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure (STRONG-HF) — the entire randomised record for protocolised rapid up-titration after discharge.
cards.result: Death or heart-failure readmission at 180 days: 15.2% versus 23.3% (risk ratio 0.66, a 34% relative reduction; absolute difference 8.1%). Dose achievement at 90 days separated dramatically (for example beta-blockers at full dose 49% versus 4%). Harms: more overall adverse events (41% versus 29%), no excess of serious or fatal events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No systematic review or second trial of this exact strategy was found in-session, so the shelf rests on one trial — hence LIKELY rather than a stronger claim, and Tier C is set. Early stopping is the main reason to expect the true effect to be somewhat smaller than 0.66.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mebazaa A et al. Lancet (London, England). 2022 (PMID: 36356631).

shelves.title: Digitoxin in modern HFrEF (DIGIT-HF): the death-or-admission composite fell (HR 0.82), but death alone did not — a single-trial, borderline result
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on modern therapy, does digitoxin, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Cardiotonic Agents*/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Digitoxin*/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure*/diagnosis · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Stroke Volume*/physiology · Disease Progression · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — digitoxin is not digoxin: it is a different cardiac glycoside, and this shelf asks what it does on top of modern guideline-directed therapy. DIGIT-HF (1,212 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population, median follow-up 36 months) found the composite of death from any cause or first hospital admission for worsening heart failure in 39.5% on digitoxin versus 44.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.98, p=0.03) — an 18% relative reduction. Neither component alone was significant: death 27.2% versus 29.5% (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.07) and first worsening-heart-failure admission 28.1% versus 30.4% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.05). Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on digitoxin (4.7% versus 2.8% of patients with at least one). It is a single trial with a borderline composite and no proven mortality benefit on its own. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): digitoxin modestly reduces the combined risk of death or worsening-heart-failure admission in HFrEF on modern therapy; a mortality benefit is not established.

cards.headline: Bavendiek 2025 (DIGIT-HF): digitoxin lowered the composite of death or worsening-heart-failure admission — 39.5% versus 44.1%, HR 0.82 — but neither death nor admission alone was significant
cards.summary: Bavendiek 2025 (DIGIT-HF): digitoxin lowered the composite of death or worsening-heart-failure admission — 39.5% versus 44.1%, HR 0.82 — but neither death nor admission alone was significant
cards.people: 1,240 patients randomised (1,212 in the modified intention-to-treat population: 613 digitoxin, 599 placebo) with chronic heart failure, ejection fraction ≤40% with NYHA class III or IV, or ejection fraction ≤30% with NYHA class II, treated on top of guideline-directed medical therapy; median follow-up 36 months. Digitoxin started at 0.07 mg once daily.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (death from any cause or hospital admission for worsening heart failure, whichever first) occurred in 242 patients (39.5%) on digitoxin versus 264 (44.1%) on placebo: hazard ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.98), p=0.03 — an 18% relative reduction, absolute difference 4.6 percentage points. Death from any cause: 167 (27.2%) versus 177 (29.5%), HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.07). First hospital admission for worsening heart failure: 172 (28.1%) versus 182 (30.4%), HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.05). At least one serious adverse event occurred in 29 patients (4.7%) on digitoxin versus 17 (2.8%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The composite is significant while both of its components are not, and the upper confidence limit (0.98) sits close to no effect — this is a borderline single-trial result, not a settled one. Digitoxin results should not be read across to digoxin, which has its own shelf (#136, the DIG trial) in a pre-modern-therapy era.
cards.source: Bavendiek U et al. Digitoxin in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40879434. shelves.title: Fluid restriction in chronic heart failure (FRESH-UP): liberal drinking missed its quality-of-life endpoint, restriction bought nothing but thirst — four trials, no outcome benefit
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does liberal fluid intake, compared with fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day, improve quality of life without increasing death or hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Heart Failure*/therapy · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Aged · Chronic Disease · Thirst/physiology · Drinking* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day is widely advised in chronic heart failure, but the randomised record does not show it helps. In FRESH-UP (504 outpatients), advice for liberal fluid intake versus restriction gave a Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall score at 3 months of 74.0 versus 72.2 — an adjusted difference of 2.17 points (95% CI −0.06 to 4.39, p=0.06) favouring liberal intake that did not meet the primary outcome — while thirst distress was higher in the restriction group and safety events did not differ. A 2026 systematic review of all four randomised trials (682 patients) found no trial showed a difference in mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation, contradictory quality-of-life results, and more thirst distress with restriction; only one trial was at low risk of bias. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): liberal intake has not been shown to improve quality of life, but routine restriction has no demonstrated outcome benefit either and costs patients thirst — the honest reading is that the case for routine restriction is unproven, not that liberal intake is proven better.

cards.headline: Herrmann 2025 (FRESH-UP): liberal fluid intake versus 1.5 L/day restriction — quality-of-life difference 2.17 points (p=0.06, primary outcome not met), more thirst distress with restriction, no safety difference
cards.summary: Herrmann 2025 (FRESH-UP): liberal fluid intake versus 1.5 L/day restriction — quality-of-life difference 2.17 points (p=0.06, primary outcome not met), more thirst distress with restriction, no safety difference
cards.people: 504 outpatients with chronic heart failure (67.3% men) randomised in a multicentre open-label trial to advice for liberal fluid intake or advice for fluid restriction to a maximum of 1,500 ml per day; primary outcome was health status at 3 months (KCCQ Overall Summary Score).
cards.result: KCCQ-OSS at 3 months was 74.0 in the liberal group versus 72.2 in the restriction group; the baseline-adjusted mean difference was 2.17 (95% CI −0.06 to 4.39, p=0.06), so the primary outcome was not met. Thirst distress was higher in the fluid-restriction group, and no differences were observed in safety events between the groups. The authors conclude the findings question the benefit of fluid restriction in chronic heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Open-label advice (patients knew their allocation, and the primary outcome is a self-reported score), only 3 months of follow-up, and a confidence interval that runs from essentially no difference to a modest benefit for liberal intake — the trial excludes neither. It was not powered for death or hospitalisation.
cards.source: Herrmann JJ et al. Liberal fluid intake versus fluid restriction in chronic heart failure: a randomized clinical trial. Nature medicine. 2025. PMID: 40159556. Registry ID: NCT04551729. cards.headline: Herrmann 2026 (systematic review): four trials, 682 patients — no mortality or hospitalisation difference anywhere, no clear quality-of-life benefit for restriction, more thirst distress
cards.summary: Herrmann 2026 (systematic review): four trials, 682 patients — no mortality or hospitalisation difference anywhere, no clear quality-of-life benefit for restriction, more thirst distress
cards.people: Four randomised trials (682 patients in total; individual trials 46 to 504 patients) of fluid restriction versus liberal/unrestricted intake, less strict restriction or usual care in adults with heart failure who were inpatients, recently discharged or stable outpatients; literature searched to 1 May 2025. No meta-analysis was performed because of heterogeneity.
cards.result: None of the four trials found a significant difference in mortality or heart-failure hospitalisations. Quality-of-life results were contradictory, with no clear benefit for fluid restriction, but restriction resulted in more thirst distress. No significant differences were seen in NYHA class or (NT-pro)BNP. Only one study had a low risk of bias. The reviewers conclude the current evidence does not support the routine use of fluid restriction in heart failure.
cards.watchOut: The review's senior evidence is the same group's FRESH-UP trial, which supplies 504 of the 682 patients — the review largely restates one trial plus three small older ones, most at high risk of bias. Absence of a mortality signal in 682 patients is not proof of safety for unrestricted intake in decompensated patients, a population these trials barely cover.

cards.summary: Synthesis: restriction is an unproven habit with a real thirst cost; liberal intake is unproven as a benefit
cards.people: Four randomised trials, 682 patients (systematic review 2026), dominated by one 504-patient open-label trial (FRESH-UP 2025).
cards.result: Quality of life: adjusted difference 2.17 KCCQ points favouring liberal intake (95% CI −0.06 to 4.39) in FRESH-UP; contradictory across the four trials. Mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation: no significant difference in any trial. Thirst distress: consistently worse with restriction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as showing liberal intake is safe in acute decompensation — the trials enrolled chronic, mostly stable patients. What the evidence undermines is routine restriction in stable chronic heart failure, a narrower and still useful claim. Tier C is set because the whole record is four small trials, one at low risk of bias.
cards.source: Synthesis of Herrmann JJ et al. Nature medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40159556); Herrmann JJ et al. Heart (British Cardiac Society). 2026 (PMID: 41529956).

shelves.title: Vitamin D in heart failure (VINDICATE): ejection fraction rose 6 points, walking distance did not move — a surrogate benefit with no outcomes trial behind it
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure and vitamin D deficiency, does high-dose vitamin D supplementation improve cardiac function and exercise capacity?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calcifediol/blood · Calcitriol/blood · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Echocardiography · Female · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Heart Ventricles/diagnostic imaging · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Cine · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Systole/drug effects · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/complications · Ventricular Remodeling/drug effects · Vitamins/administration & dosage · Walk Test
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — VINDICATE randomised 229 patients with chronic heart failure from left ventricular systolic dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency to 4,000 IU (100 µg) vitamin D3 daily or placebo for a year. The primary endpoint was negative: 6-minute walk distance did not improve. The secondary imaging endpoints moved — ejection fraction rose by 6.07% more than placebo (95% CI 3.20 to 8.95, p<0.0001), with reversal of remodelling (left ventricular end-diastolic diameter −2.49 mm; end-systolic diameter −2.09 mm). A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,215 patients) likewise found an ejection-fraction gain of 3.30% (95% CI 0.95 to 5.65). But ejection fraction is a surrogate: no trial here shows fewer deaths or hospitalisations, and the one patient-centred measure in the anchor trial — walking distance — was null. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): high-dose vitamin D improves the echocardiogram in deficient heart-failure patients; whether that translates into outcomes patients feel is untested.

cards.headline: Witte 2016 (VINDICATE): vitamin D3 4,000 IU daily for a year — walk distance unchanged, but ejection fraction up 6.07% versus placebo and remodelling reversed
cards.summary: Witte 2016 (VINDICATE): vitamin D3 4,000 IU daily for a year — walk distance unchanged, but ejection fraction up 6.07% versus placebo and remodelling reversed
cards.people: 229 patients (179 men) with chronic heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency (25(OH) vitamin D <50 nmol/l [<20 ng/ml]), allocated to vitamin D3 4,000 IU (100 µg) daily or matching non-calcium-based placebo for 1 year, on contemporary optimal medical therapy.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, change in 6-minute walk distance at 12 months, did not improve. Cardiac function did: left ventricular ejection fraction improved by +6.07% versus placebo (95% CI 3.20 to 8.95, p<0.0001), and left ventricular remodelling reversed (end-diastolic diameter −2.49 mm, 95% CI −4.09 to −0.90, p=0.002; end-systolic diameter −2.09 mm, 95% CI −4.11 to −0.06, p=0.043). Renal function and serum calcium were monitored every 3 months as safety measures.
cards.watchOut: A positive secondary surrogate alongside a negative primary functional endpoint is the classic pattern that demands an outcomes trial before belief. The trial enrolled only vitamin-D-deficient patients, so nothing here speaks to supplementing replete patients.
cards.source: Witte KK et al. Effects of Vitamin D on Cardiac Function in Patients With Chronic HF: The VINDICATE Study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2016. PMID: 27058906. Registry ID: NCT01619891. cards.headline: Naghedi 2021 (meta-analysis): 13 trials, 1,215 patients — vitamin D raised ejection fraction by 3.30% on average
cards.summary: Naghedi 2021 (meta-analysis): 13 trials, 1,215 patients — vitamin D raised ejection fraction by 3.30% on average
cards.people: Thirteen randomised clinical trials (1,215 patients with heart failure, published 2005–2019) of vitamin D supplementation versus placebo or no treatment, pooled for the ejection-fraction outcome; literature searched to 1 January 2020.
cards.result: Vitamin D significantly enhanced left ventricular ejection fraction by 3.304% (95% CI 0.954 to 5.654, p=0.006). The review reports the ejection-fraction outcome only; it does not pool mortality or hospitalisation. The authors' own conclusion — that vitamin D should be prescribed to all patients with heart failure pending better trials — goes beyond what a surrogate-only pooled result can carry.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen small trials pooled on a surrogate endpoint, with no pooled clinical outcomes — small-study effects and publication bias inflate exactly this kind of result. The pooled gain (3.3%) is also smaller than the anchor trial's (6.07%), which is what regression to the mean looks like.
cards.source: Naghedi A et al. Effect of vitamin D supplements on left ventricular ejection fraction in patients with heart failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Revista portuguesa de cardiologia. 2021. PMID: 34274087. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: the pump looks better on imaging; the patient walks no further, and outcomes are unmeasured
cards.people: One 229-patient trial in vitamin-D-deficient HFrEF (VINDICATE) plus a 13-trial, 1,215-patient meta-analysis — all evidence on surrogate or functional endpoints.
cards.result: Ejection fraction: +6.07% versus placebo in VINDICATE; +3.30% pooled. Six-minute walk distance: no improvement (VINDICATE primary endpoint). Mortality and hospitalisation: not reported as improved in either record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Correcting deficiency has other justifications (bone health), and this shelf judges only the cardiac claim. Tier C is set because every positive number here is an imaging surrogate from small trials.

shelves.title: Allopurinol for hyperuricaemic heart failure (EXACT-HF): uric acid fell 4 points, every clinical measure stayed flat — the oxidative-stress hypothesis failed its direct test
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and hyperuricaemia, does allopurinol, compared with placebo, improve clinical status, quality of life and left ventricular function?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Allopurinol/adverse effects · Biomarkers/blood · Diuretics/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Gout/drug therapy · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use · Heart Failure/blood · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Hyperuricemia/complications · Male · Middle Aged · Oxidative Stress · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography · Xanthine Oxidase/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the mechanistic story was attractive: xanthine oxidase generates oxidative stress, and hyperuricaemia tracks with worse heart failure. EXACT-HF tested it directly in 253 patients with symptomatic heart failure, ejection fraction ≤40% and uric acid ≥9.5 mg/dL, randomised to allopurinol (target 600 mg daily) or placebo for 24 weeks. Allopurinol lowered uric acid as intended (treatment difference −4.2 mg/dL at 12 weeks and −3.5 mg/dL at 24 weeks) and changed nothing else: the primary clinical-status composite was identical (worsened 45% versus 46%; improved 13% versus 19%, p=0.68), with no difference in quality-of-life scores, 6-minute walk distance or ejection fraction, and more rash (10% versus 2%). A 2020 meta-analysis of 11 studies went further, associating allopurinol with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.24) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.42) — but with high heterogeneity (I²=73%) and a mix of study designs, that harm signal is hypothesis-raising, not proof. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): allopurinol does not improve clinical status, function or ejection fraction in hyperuricaemic HFrEF; treat gout if present, not the heart failure.

cards.headline: Givertz 2015 (EXACT-HF): allopurinol lowered uric acid by 3.5–4.2 mg/dL and improved nothing — clinical status, quality of life, walk distance and ejection fraction all null at 24 weeks
cards.summary: Givertz 2015 (EXACT-HF): allopurinol lowered uric acid by 3.5–4.2 mg/dL and improved nothing — clinical status, quality of life, walk distance and ejection fraction all null at 24 weeks
cards.people: 253 patients with symptomatic heart failure, left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40% and serum uric acid ≥9.5 mg/dL, randomised double-blind to allopurinol (target dose 600 mg daily) or placebo for 24 weeks in a multicentre trial.
cards.result: Uric acid fell significantly more with allopurinol (treatment difference −4.2 mg/dL [−4.9 to −3.5] at 12 weeks and −3.5 mg/dL [−4.2 to −2.7] at 24 weeks, both p<0.0001). The primary composite of survival, worsening heart failure and patient global assessment showed no difference at 24 weeks (worsened 45% versus 46%, unchanged 42% versus 34%, improved 13% versus 19%; p=0.68). There was no significant difference in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores, 6-minute walk distances, or left ventricular ejection fraction at 12 or 24 weeks. Rash was more frequent with allopurinol (10% versus 2%, p=0.01); serious adverse events did not differ (20% versus 15%, p=0.36).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks and 253 patients cannot exclude a small long-term outcome effect — but with every intermediate measure flat despite a large uric-acid fall, the burden of proof has shifted to anyone proposing a bigger trial. The population was selected for marked hyperuricaemia (≥9.5 mg/dL); results need not extend to milder elevations.
cards.source: Givertz MM et al. Effects of Xanthine Oxidase Inhibition in Hyperuricemic Heart Failure Patients: The Xanthine Oxidase Inhibition for Hyperuricemic Heart Failure Patients (EXACT-HF) Study. Circulation. 2015. PMID: 25986447. Registry ID: NCT00987415. cards.headline: Kanbay 2020 (meta-analysis): 11 studies — allopurinol in heart failure associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.24) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.42), with high heterogeneity
cards.summary: Kanbay 2020 (meta-analysis): 11 studies — allopurinol in heart failure associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.24) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.42), with high heterogeneity
cards.people: Eleven clinical studies of uric-acid-lowering agents (allopurinol, febuxostat, oxypurinol) in patients with heart failure, pooled for all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, cardiovascular events and cardiovascular hospitalisation.
cards.result: Allopurinol treatment was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.49, p=.02) and increased cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.81, p=.005), with a non-significant trend to more cardiovascular hospitalisation (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.53, p=.12). Heterogeneity was high (χ²=37.3, I²=73%, p<.001). The authors conclude uric-acid-lowering treatments increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in this analysis.
cards.watchOut: This pools 'clinical studies', not only randomised trials, so confounding by indication — sicker patients with gout and kidney disease are the ones prescribed allopurinol — can manufacture exactly this harm pattern, and I² of 73% says the studies do not agree with each other. Read it as a reason for caution, not as proof allopurinol kills heart-failure patients; the randomised anchor (EXACT-HF) showed no mortality signal, only futility.
cards.source: Kanbay M et al. Effect of Uric Acid-Lowering Agents on Cardiovascular Outcome in Patients With Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Studies. Angiology. 2020. PMID: 32000517. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the target was hit, the disease was not — and the observational literature adds an unresolved harm question
cards.summary: Synthesis: the target was hit, the disease was not — and the observational literature adds an unresolved harm question
cards.people: One 253-patient randomised trial (EXACT-HF) plus an 11-study meta-analysis mixing designs (Kanbay 2020).
cards.result: Randomised: uric acid −3.5 to −4.2 mg/dL; clinical status, quality of life, walk distance, ejection fraction all unchanged; rash 10% versus 2%. Pooled observational-inclusive data: all-cause mortality HR 1.24 and cardiovascular mortality HR 1.42 with allopurinol, heterogeneity I²=73%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for any heart-failure benefit — none was shown.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against allopurinol for gout in a heart-failure patient — that indication stands on its own evidence (and allopurinol's ischaemic-heart-disease record sits at shelf #558). Tier C is set because the randomised base is one small, short trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Givertz MM et al. Circulation. 2015 (PMID: 25986447); Kanbay M et al. Angiology. 2020 (PMID: 32000517).

shelves.title: Sildenafil and nitrates in HFpEF (RELAX, NEAT-HFpEF): no gain in exercise capacity — and patients on the nitrate actually did less each day
shelves.question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do sildenafil or long-acting isosorbide mononitrate improve exercise capacity and daily activity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Tolerance* · Female · Health Status · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outpatients · Oxygen Consumption · Phosphodiesterase 5 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Piperazines/therapeutic use · Purines/therapeutic use · Sildenafil Citrate · Stroke Volume · Sulfones/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two well-run trials from the same network tested the two classic vasodilator ideas in HFpEF, and both failed. RELAX (216 outpatients, ejection fraction ≥50%) gave sildenafil for 24 weeks: peak oxygen consumption changed identically in both arms (median −0.20 ml/kg/min each, p=0.90), the clinical-status rank score was no different (94.2 versus 95.8, p=0.85), 6-minute walk distance was no different, and serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on sildenafil (22% versus 16%). NEAT-HFpEF (110 patients, crossover) gave isosorbide mononitrate up to 120 mg daily and patients were, if anything, less active on the drug: daily accelerometer units trended lower (−381, p=0.06) at the top dose and were significantly lower across all doses (−439, p=0.02), with fewer hours of activity per day (−0.30, p=0.02) and no gain in walk distance, quality of life or NT-proBNP. An earlier meta-analysis had found sildenafil improved peak VO2 in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure but not in HFpEF — consistent with RELAX. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): neither sildenafil nor long-acting nitrate improves exercise capacity or daily activity in HFpEF, and nitrates may reduce activity; 'weak' reflects the modest trial sizes, not any positive signal.

cards.headline: Redfield 2013 (RELAX): sildenafil for 24 weeks in HFpEF — peak oxygen consumption identical (−0.20 versus −0.20 ml/kg/min, p=0.90), clinical status and walk distance no different
cards.summary: Redfield 2013 (RELAX): sildenafil for 24 weeks in HFpEF — peak oxygen consumption identical (−0.20 versus −0.20 ml/kg/min, p=0.90), clinical status and walk distance no different
cards.people: 216 stable outpatients with heart failure and ejection fraction ≥50%, elevated natriuretic peptide or invasively measured filling pressures, and reduced exercise capacity, at 26 North American centres (median age 69 years, 48% women); sildenafil 20 mg three times daily for 12 weeks then 60 mg three times daily for 12 weeks (n=113) versus placebo (n=103).
cards.result: At 24 weeks the median change in peak oxygen consumption was −0.20 ml/kg/min in both groups (p=0.90); the intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis gave a mean between-group difference of 0.01 ml/kg/min (95% CI −0.60 to 0.61). The clinical-status rank score did not differ (94.2 sildenafil versus 95.8 placebo, p=0.85), nor did change in 6-minute walk distance (median 5.0 m versus 15.0 m, p=0.92). Adverse events occurred in 80% on sildenafil versus 76% on placebo; serious adverse events in 22% versus 16%.
cards.watchOut: A clean null in a well-phenotyped HFpEF population — elevated filling pressures were required, so this is not a misdiagnosis artefact. The trial does not address sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension or erectile dysfunction, which have their own shelves.
cards.source: Redfield MM et al. Effect of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibition on exercise capacity and clinical status in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a randomized clinical trial. cards.headline: Redfield 2015 (NEAT-HFpEF): isosorbide mononitrate made HFpEF patients less active — daily activity significantly lower across all doses (−439 units, p=0.02), no walk, quality-of-life or NT-proBNP gain
cards.summary: Redfield 2015 (NEAT-HFpEF): isosorbide mononitrate made HFpEF patients less active — daily activity significantly lower across all doses (−439 units, p=0.02), no walk, quality-of-life or NT-proBNP gain
cards.people: 110 patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction in a multicentre double-blind crossover study: 6 weeks of dose-escalating isosorbide mononitrate (30 mg to 60 mg to 120 mg once daily) and 6 weeks of placebo, in random order, with activity measured by patient-worn accelerometers.
cards.result: At the 120-mg dose, daily activity trended lower on isosorbide mononitrate than placebo (−381 accelerometer units, 95% CI −780 to 17, p=0.06) and hours of activity per day were significantly lower (−0.30 hours, 95% CI −0.55 to −0.05, p=0.02). Across all dose regimens activity was significantly lower on the nitrate (−439 units, 95% CI −792 to −86, p=0.02), and activity fell progressively as the nitrate dose rose. There were no significant differences in 6-minute walk distance, quality-of-life scores or NT-proBNP levels.
cards.watchOut: Accelerometer-measured daily activity is a real-world endpoint patients care about, and the dose-response gradient (less activity at higher doses) strengthens the reading that this is a drug effect, not noise. Nitrates remain indicated for angina; this shelf judges only the HFpEF activity indication.

cards.headline: Zhuang 2014 (meta-analysis): sildenafil improved peak VO2 in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure but not in HFpEF — the split RELAX confirmed
cards.summary: Zhuang 2014 (meta-analysis): sildenafil improved peak VO2 in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure but not in HFpEF — the split RELAX confirmed
cards.people: Nine randomised trials enrolling 612 patients with heart failure comparing sildenafil with placebo, analysed separately by ejection-fraction phenotype.
cards.result: Sildenafil improved peak VO2 in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (mean difference 3.25, 95% CI 2.07 to 4.42, p<0.00001) but not in HFpEF. Across heart-failure patients it also improved VO2 at anaerobic threshold (MD 3.47), VE/VCO2 slope (MD −7.06) and ejection fraction (MD 5.43), with no significant difference in adverse events (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.65) and no quality-of-life difference.
cards.watchOut: The HFrEF signal comes from small, short trials and has never been tied to outcomes; the HFpEF null is the part corroborated by the largest, best trial (RELAX). Pooling across phenotypes would have hidden the split — phenotype is the whole story here.

shelves.title: Patisiran for cardiac amyloidosis (APOLLO-B): patients walked 15 metres further and felt slightly better at a year — the death and hospitalisation composites did not move
shelves.question: In patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, does patisiran, compared with placebo, slow decline in functional capacity and quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cardiomyopathies*/drug therapy · Prealbumin*/genetics · RNA, Small Interfering*/therapeutic use · Amyloidosis, Familial/complications · Liver/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Amyloidosis*/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — APOLLO-B randomised 360 patients with hereditary (variant) or wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis to patisiran 0.3 mg/kg or placebo every 3 weeks for 12 months. The primary endpoint was met, modestly: the decline in 6-minute walk distance was smaller on patisiran (median difference 14.69 m, 95% CI 0.69 to 28.69, p=0.02), and quality of life moved in opposite directions in the two arms (KCCQ-OS least-squares mean difference 3.7 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 7.2, p=0.04). The harder composites did not follow: significant benefit was not observed for the composite of death, cardiovascular events and walk-distance change, and the record reports no significant result for the death/hospitalisation composite either. Infusion-related reactions, arthralgia and muscle spasms were more common on patisiran. A 2020 systematic review, written before APOLLO-B, could only call patisiran 'promising' from a polyneuropathy-trial subgroup — APOLLO-B is the first direct cardiomyopathy test, and it shows preserved function, not saved lives. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patisiran slows functional and quality-of-life decline over 12 months in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis; an effect on death or hospitalisation is not established.

cards.headline: Maurer 2023 (APOLLO-B): patisiran preserved walk distance (median difference 14.69 m, p=0.02) and quality of life (+3.7 KCCQ points, p=0.04) at 12 months — the death/event composites were not significant
cards.summary: Maurer 2023 (APOLLO-B): patisiran preserved walk distance (median difference 14.69 m, p=0.02) and quality of life (+3.7 KCCQ points, p=0.04) at 12 months — the death/event composites were not significant
cards.people: 360 patients with hereditary (variant) or wild-type transthyretin (ATTR) cardiac amyloidosis randomised 1:1 to patisiran 0.3 mg per kilogram (181 patients) or placebo (179 patients) once every 3 weeks for 12 months, in a phase 3 double-blind trial with hierarchical testing of one primary and three secondary endpoints.
cards.result: At month 12 the decline in 6-minute walk distance was lower with patisiran (Hodges-Lehmann median difference 14.69 m, 95% CI 0.69 to 28.69, p=0.02). The KCCQ-OS score rose on patisiran and fell on placebo (least-squares mean difference 3.7 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 7.2, p=0.04). Significant benefit was not observed for the second secondary endpoint (composite of death from any cause, cardiovascular events, and change in walk distance). Infusion-related reactions, arthralgia and muscle spasms occurred more often with patisiran than placebo.
cards.watchOut: Both significant endpoints are functional/quality-of-life measures with confidence intervals whose lower bounds sit near zero (0.69 m; 0.2 points), over only 12 months, in a disease whose stakes are death and hospitalisation — neither shown to improve. Patisiran for polyneuropathy (APOLLO) is a different population, shelved at #1411.

cards.headline: Marques 2020 (systematic review): before APOLLO-B, patisiran's cardiac evidence was a subgroup analysis only — 'promising results… to be confirmed in RCTs'
cards.summary: Marques 2020 (systematic review): before APOLLO-B, patisiran's cardiac evidence was a subgroup analysis only — 'promising results… to be confirmed in RCTs'
cards.people: A systematic literature review (search to 29 November 2019) of specific therapies for transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis: 24 publications covering 4 randomised trials and 16 non-randomised studies in variant or wild-type disease.
cards.result: Tafamidis significantly improved all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations and slowed worsening in walk test, KCCQ-OS and NT-proBNP. Patisiran showed promising results only in a subgroup analysis of patients with variant transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, which the reviewers said had to be confirmed in randomised trials. Inotersen showed conflicting cardiac-imaging results, and evidence for diflunisal, green-tea extract and doxycycline combinations was limited to small non-comparative studies.
cards.watchOut: This review predates APOLLO-B and cannot confirm or refute it; it is carded to show how thin the patisiran cardiac evidence was before 2023, and to mark that another agent in the same review carried the mortality data. Cross-drug comparisons from a narrative review are not head-to-head evidence.
cards.source: Marques N et al. Specific Therapy for Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Systematic Literature Review and Evidence-Based Recommendations. shelves.title: Bromocriptine for peripartum cardiomyopathy: hearts recovered impressively — in a trial where every woman received the drug, so its share of the credit is unknowable
shelves.question: In women with peripartum cardiomyopathy, does adding bromocriptine to standard heart-failure therapy improve recovery of left ventricular function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bromocriptine/administration & dosage · Cardiomyopathies/drug therapy · Cardiotonic Agents/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Cardiovascular/drug therapy · Puerperal Disorders/drug therapy · Recovery of Function/physiology · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the biology is coherent (a cleaved prolactin fragment is thought to drive peripartum cardiomyopathy, and bromocriptine blocks prolactin release), and recovery rates in the one randomised study look high — but that study had no placebo arm. Hilfiker-Kleiner 2017 randomised 63 women with peripartum cardiomyopathy and ejection fraction ≤35% to 1 week versus 8 weeks of bromocriptine, both on top of standard heart-failure therapy: ejection fraction rose from 28% to 49% (+21 points) and from 27% to 51% (+24 points) respectively (p=0.381 for the difference), full recovery (ejection fraction ≥50%) occurred in 52% versus 68%, heart-failure hospitalisations were 9.7% versus 6.5%, and no patient died, needed a transplant or an assist device. Without an untreated comparator, how much of that recovery is bromocriptine and how much is the well-known spontaneous recovery of peripartum cardiomyopathy cannot be separated from this trial. A 2023 meta-analysis (10 studies, only 3 randomised) found higher follow-up ejection fraction with bromocriptine (pooled mean differences 12.56 and 14.25 points in cohort and trial analyses) and higher odds of left ventricular recovery (OR 3.55), but no difference in all-cause mortality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): bromocriptine may aid recovery of ventricular function in peripartum cardiomyopathy; the randomised record cannot prove it, because everyone in the trial received it.

cards.headline: Hilfiker-Kleiner 2017: 1 week versus 8 weeks of bromocriptine in peripartum cardiomyopathy — ejection fraction rose ~21–24 points in both arms, full recovery 52% versus 68%, no deaths; there was no placebo group
cards.summary: Hilfiker-Kleiner 2017: 1 week versus 8 weeks of bromocriptine in peripartum cardiomyopathy — ejection fraction rose ~21–24 points in both arms, full recovery 52% versus 68%, no deaths; there was no placebo group
cards.people: 63 women with peripartum cardiomyopathy and left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35% in a multicentre randomised study, assigned to short-term bromocriptine (2.5 mg for 7 days) or long-term bromocriptine (5 mg for 2 weeks, then 2.5 mg for 6 weeks), each added to standard heart-failure therapy; primary endpoint was change in ejection fraction at 6 months by magnetic resonance imaging.
cards.result: Ejection fraction increased from 28±10% to 49±12% (delta +21±11%) in the 1-week group and from 27±10% to 51±10% (delta +24±11%) in the 8-week group (p=0.381 for the between-group difference). Full recovery (ejection fraction ≥50%) occurred in 52% (1-week) versus 68% (8-week). Heart-failure hospitalisations were 9.7% versus 6.5% (p=0.651). No patient needed heart transplantation or a left ventricular assist device, and none died. Bromocriptine was well tolerated. The authors note recovery rates were high compared with other peripartum-cardiomyopathy cohorts not treated with bromocriptine.
cards.watchOut: This is a dose-duration comparison, not a test of bromocriptine versus none — the design cannot estimate the drug's effect, only whether longer treatment beats shorter. The favourable comparison with untreated historical cohorts is exactly the kind of evidence that flatters treatments for conditions with high spontaneous recovery.
cards.source: Hilfiker-Kleiner D et al. Bromocriptine for the treatment of peripartum cardiomyopathy: a multicentre randomized study. European heart journal. 2017. PMID: 28934837. randomised controlled trial, duration comparison (hilfiker-kleiner 2017) 63 women with peripartum cardiomyopathy and left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35% in a multicentre randomised study, assigned to short-term bromocriptine (2.5 mg for 7 days) or long-term bromocriptine (5 mg for 2 weeks, then 2.5 mg for 6 weeks), each added to standard heart-failure therapy; primary endpoint was change in ejection fraction at 6 months by magnetic resonance imaging. ejection fraction increased from 28±10% to 49±12% (delta +21±11%) in the 1-week group and from 27±10% to 51±10% (delta +24±11%) in the 8-week group (p=0.381 for the between-group difference). full recovery (ejection fraction ≥50%) occurred in 52% (1-week) versus 68% (8-week). heart-failure hospitalisations were 9.7% versus 6.5% (p=0.651). no patient needed heart transplantation or a left ventricular assist device, and none died. bromocriptine was well tolerated. the authors note recovery rates were high compared with other peripartum-cardiomyopathy cohorts not treated with bromocriptine. this is a dose-duration comparison, not a test of bromocriptine versus none — the design cannot estimate the drug's effect, only whether longer treatment beats shorter. the favourable comparison with untreated historical cohorts is exactly the kind of evidence that flatters treatments for conditions with high spontaneous recovery. hilfiker-kleiner d et al. bromocriptine for the treatment of peripartum cardiomyopathy: a multicentre randomized study. european heart journal. 2017. pmid: 28934837. registry id: nct00998556. mesh: adult · bromocriptine/administration & dosage · cardiomyopathies/drug therapy · cardiotonic agents/administration & dosage · drug administration schedule · female · humans · pregnancy · pregnancy complications, cardiovascular/drug therapy · puerperal disorders/drug therapy · recovery of function/physiology · treatment outcome · ventricular dysfunction, left/drug therapy

cards.headline: Kumar 2023 (meta-analysis): bromocriptine plus standard therapy — higher follow-up ejection fraction and odds of recovery (OR 3.55), no mortality difference
cards.summary: Kumar 2023 (meta-analysis): bromocriptine plus standard therapy — higher follow-up ejection fraction and odds of recovery (OR 3.55), no mortality difference
cards.people: Ten studies (3 randomised trials, 2 retrospective and 5 prospective cohorts) of prolactin inhibition, chiefly bromocriptine plus standard guideline-directed therapy versus standard therapy alone, in peripartum cardiomyopathy; literature to March 2022.
cards.result: The bromocriptine group had higher ejection fraction at follow-up (pooled mean difference 12.56, 95% CI 5.84 to 19.28, I²=0%, from two cohorts; and 14.25, 95% CI 0.61 to 27.89, I²=88%, from two randomised trials) and higher odds of left ventricular recovery (pooled OR 3.55, 95% CI 1.39 to 9.1, I²=62%). There was no difference in all-cause mortality between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies are cohorts, the randomised pooling rests on two trials with I² of 88%, and treated-versus-untreated cohort comparisons in peripartum cardiomyopathy are confounded by era and by who gets offered the drug. The mortality null is the most trustworthy number in the card.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. Prolactin Inhibition in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Current problems in cardiology. 2023. PMID: 36261102. cards.headline: Synthesis: recovery looks better with bromocriptine everywhere it is looked for — and nowhere is it compared fairly with no bromocriptine in a large trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: recovery looks better with bromocriptine everywhere it is looked for — and nowhere is it compared fairly with no bromocriptine in a large trial
cards.people: One 63-patient randomised duration comparison (no untreated arm) plus a 10-study meta-analysis dominated by cohorts.
cards.result: Ejection-fraction recovery: +21 to +24 points within treated arms; pooled advantage 12.56–14.25 points versus standard therapy in the meta-analysis; recovery odds ratio 3.55. Mortality: no deaths in the anchor trial's 63 patients; no mortality difference in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: A placebo-controlled trial in a condition affecting young mothers is ethically and practically hard, which is why the evidence looks like this — but difficulty does not upgrade the evidence. Tier C is set. Bromocriptine also stops lactation, a consequence families weigh alongside any cardiac benefit; that trade-off belongs in the clinical conversation, not in this stamp.

shelves.title: Immune therapy for myocarditis splits by phenotype: TIMIC's virus-negative chronic patients improved on steroids — unselected myocarditis (Mason) and immune globulin (IMAC) did not
shelves.question: In biopsy-proven virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy or lymphocytic myocarditis, does immunosuppressive therapy (prednisone with azathioprine or ciclosporin) or intravenous immune globulin improve left ventricular function and survival compared with conventional therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Myocarditis/drug therapy · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/etiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by which myocarditis. In chronic, biopsy-proven, virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy unresponsive to conventional therapy, TIMIC (85 patients, double-blind) found prednisone plus azathioprine improved ejection fraction and shrank ventricular dimensions and volumes over 6 months, while no placebo patient improved and placebo ejection fraction significantly worsened; 12% of treated patients did not respond, and no major adverse reactions were registered. In unselected biopsy-proven myocarditis, the Myocarditis Treatment Trial (111 patients) found no difference: ejection fraction rose 0.10 with immunosuppression versus 0.07 with conventional therapy alone, survival did not differ (p=0.96), and mortality was 20% at 1 year and 56% at 4.3 years in the whole cohort. And intravenous immune globulin in recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy or myocarditis (IMAC, 62 patients) was a flat null — ejection fraction rose 0.14–0.16 in both arms alike. A 30-year meta-analysis (Cheng 2021) lands in the same place: a non-significant mortality trend in prospective studies (12.5% versus 18.2%; OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.64), a significant survival association only in retrospective studies (HR 0.82), and a conclusion that tailored immunosuppression may be considered depending on disease phase and type. PROPOSED SPLIT: immunosuppression helps the selected virus-negative chronic inflammatory phenotype (TIMIC); it does not help unselected myocarditis, and immune globulin does not help recent-onset disease.

cards.headline: Frustaci 2009 (TIMIC): in virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy, prednisone plus azathioprine improved ejection fraction — no placebo patient improved, and placebo ejection fraction worsened
cards.summary: Frustaci 2009 (TIMIC): in virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy, prednisone plus azathioprine improved ejection fraction — no placebo patient improved, and placebo ejection fraction worsened
cards.people: 85 patients with biopsy-proven myocarditis and chronic (>6 months) heart failure unresponsive to conventional therapy, with no evidence of myocardial viral genomes, randomised double-blind to prednisone (1 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then 0.33 mg/kg/day for 5 months) plus azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day for 6 months) (43 patients) or placebo (42 patients), each added to conventional heart-failure therapy; primary outcome was 6-month improvement in left ventricular function.
cards.result: The immunosuppression group showed a significant improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction and a significant decrease in left ventricular dimensions and volumes compared with baseline. None of the placebo patients showed improvement in ejection fraction, which significantly worsened compared with baseline. No major adverse reaction was registered as a result of immunosuppression. Lack of response in 12% of treated cases suggested unscreened viruses or inflammation mechanisms not susceptible to immunosuppression. (The record's abstract reports the direction and significance of the ejection-fraction changes without pooled point values.)
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-style, 85-patient trial in a tightly selected phenotype — virus-negative on biopsy, chronic, conventional-therapy-resistant. Its result licenses treatment of that phenotype, not of myocarditis generally, and virus testing of biopsy tissue is what makes the selection possible.
cards.source: Frustaci A et al. Randomized study on the efficacy of immunosuppressive therapy in patients with virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy: the TIMIC study. cards.headline: Mason 1995 (Myocarditis Treatment Trial): immunosuppression in unselected myocarditis — ejection fraction gain 0.10 versus 0.07 (no difference), survival no different (p=0.96), mortality 20% at 1 year
cards.summary: Mason 1995 (Myocarditis Treatment Trial): immunosuppression in unselected myocarditis — ejection fraction gain 0.10 versus 0.07 (no difference), survival no different (p=0.96), mortality 20% at 1 year
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Mason 1995, Myocarditis Treatment Trial)
cards.people: 111 patients with a histopathological diagnosis of myocarditis and left ventricular ejection fraction <0.45, randomised to conventional therapy alone or conventional therapy plus 24 weeks of immunosuppression (prednisone with either ciclosporin or azathioprine); primary outcome was change in ejection fraction at 28 weeks.
cards.result: Overall ejection fraction improved from 0.25±0.01 at baseline to 0.34±0.02 at 28 weeks (p<0.001). The mean change did not differ significantly between groups: a gain of 0.10 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.12) with immunosuppression versus 0.07 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.12) with conventional therapy. There was no significant difference in survival between the groups (p=0.96). Mortality for the entire cohort was 20% at 1 year and 56% at 4.3 years. Higher baseline ejection fraction, less intensive conventional therapy and shorter disease duration — not treatment assignment — predicted ejection fraction at week 28.
cards.watchOut: Patients were selected by biopsy histology, not by viral-genome status — by TIMIC's logic, virus-positive patients (in whom suppressing immunity could plausibly harm) are mixed into both arms, diluting any benefit in the virus-negative subset. The two trials are reconcilable once the populations are distinguished, which is the point of this shelf's SPLIT stamp.
cards.source: Mason JW et al. A clinical trial of immunosuppressive therapy for myocarditis. The Myocarditis Treatment Trial Investigators. The New England journal of medicine. 1995. PMID: 7596370. cards.headline: McNamara 2001 (IMAC): intravenous immune globulin in recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy/myocarditis — ejection fraction rose identically in both arms (+0.14 to +0.16); transplant-free survival 92% at 1 year
cards.summary: McNamara 2001 (IMAC): intravenous immune globulin in recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy/myocarditis — ejection fraction rose identically in both arms (+0.14 to +0.16); transplant-free survival 92% at 1 year
cards.people: 62 adults (37 men, 25 women; mean age 43 years) with recent-onset (≤6 months of symptoms) idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and ejection fraction ≤0.40, randomised to intravenous immune globulin 2 g/kg or placebo; all underwent endomyocardial biopsy before randomisation, which showed cellular inflammation in 16%.
cards.result: Ejection fraction improved overall from 0.25±0.08 to 0.41±0.17 at 6 months and 0.42±0.14 at 12 months (both p<0.001 versus baseline) — identically in both arms (6 months: IVIG +0.14±0.12, placebo +0.14±0.14; 12 months: IVIG +0.16±0.12, placebo +0.15±0.16). At 1 year, 56% of patients had gained ≥0.10 in ejection fraction and 36% had normalised it (≥0.50). Transplant-free survival was 92% at 1 year and 88% at 2 years. The authors conclude IVIG does not augment the improvement in ejection fraction, and that short-term prognosis in recent-onset disease is favourable regardless.
cards.watchOut: Only 16% had biopsy inflammation, so this is largely a trial of recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy, not proven myocarditis — and its real lesson is how often recent-onset disease recovers on its own, which inflates every uncontrolled myocarditis series ever published.
cards.source: McNamara DM et al. Controlled trial of intravenous immune globulin in recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy. Circulation. 2001. PMID: 11342473. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cheng 2021 (30-year meta-analysis): prospective studies show only a non-significant mortality trend for immunosuppression (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.64); the significant survival signal is retrospective only
cards.summary: Cheng 2021 (30-year meta-analysis): prospective studies show only a non-significant mortality trend for immunosuppression (OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.64); the significant survival signal is retrospective only
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of immunosuppression/immunomodulation in myocarditis covering 1987 to November 2019: 37 analysable studies (8 randomised, 26 retrospective, 2 prospective, 1 case-control) plus case reports and series, from 5,452 records screened.
cards.result: In prospective studies, mortality tended to be lower with immunosuppression (12.5% versus 18.2%; OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.64 — not significant), and the pooled ejection-fraction increase tended to be higher (95% CI for the difference 7.26, −2.29 to 16.81 — not significant). In retrospective studies, survival significantly favoured immunosuppression (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.96). The authors conclude tailored immunosuppression may be considered depending on the phase of disease and the underlying autoimmune or immune-mediated form.
cards.watchOut: When the randomised/prospective pooling is null and only the retrospective pooling is positive, the standard reading is confounding, not confirmation. The review's value here is its conclusion — tailoring by phase and type — which matches the TIMIC-versus-Mason split rather than averaging it away.
cards.source: Cheng CY et al. Efficacy of immunosuppressive therapy in myocarditis: A 30-year systematic review and meta analysis. Autoimmunity reviews. 2021. PMID: 33197576. cards.headline: Synthesis: phenotype decides — virus-negative chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy responds; unselected myocarditis and recent-onset disease do not need immune therapy to recover, or do not respond
cards.summary: Synthesis: phenotype decides — virus-negative chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy responds; unselected myocarditis and recent-onset disease do not need immune therapy to recover, or do not respond
cards.people: Three randomised trials (85 + 111 + 62 patients) spanning the three phenotypes, plus a 37-study, 30-year meta-analysis.
cards.result: Virus-negative chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy: ejection fraction improved on prednisone/azathioprine, worsened on placebo (TIMIC). Unselected biopsy myocarditis: ejection-fraction gain 0.10 versus 0.07, survival p=0.96 (Mason). Recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy/myocarditis: IVIG identical to placebo, with 92% transplant-free survival at 1 year on conventional care (IMAC). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: TIMIC's abstract reports no pooled ejection-fraction point values, so this shelf cannot quantify its benefit — only its direction and the placebo arm's deterioration. Tier C is not set (miner flag: no): three direct randomised trials plus a meta-analysis answer the question, albeit for different sub-questions, which is precisely why the stamp is SPLIT rather than a single grade.

shelves.title: Drugs after Takotsubo syndrome: the biggest registry links ACE inhibitors and statins to lower mortality — and finds nothing for the beta-blockers everyone prescribes
shelves.question: In patients with Takotsubo syndrome, are beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs or statins associated with lower long-term mortality?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy*/drug therapy · Male · Registries* · Sweden/epidemiology · Aged · Coronary Angiography* · Survival Rate/trends · Follow-Up Studies · Retrospective Studies · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no randomised trial of any drug in Takotsubo syndrome; everything known comes from registries, and this shelf's anchor is the SWEDEHEART analysis of 1,724 Takotsubo patients (mean age 66, 77% women) identified among 228,263 angiography patients from 2009–2016. Mortality was 2.5% at 30 days and 16.6% at 6 years. In adjusted registry analyses, ACE inhibitors (HR 0.60, p=0.025) and statins (HR 0.62, p=0.040) were associated with lower long-term mortality, and heparins with lower 30-day mortality (HR 0.63, p=0.01), while beta-blockers — the drug most reflexively prescribed — showed no statistical correlation with mortality, nor did ARBs, oral anticoagulants, aspirin or P2Y12 inhibitors. Intravenous inotropes (HR 9.92) and diuretics (HR 3.22) were associated with higher 30-day mortality, which almost certainly marks sicker patients rather than drug harm. Every one of these associations is vulnerable to confounding by indication: clinicians give ACE inhibitors and statins to patients they expect to live. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ACE inhibitors and statins are associated with lower long-term mortality after Takotsubo; beta-blockers, despite their intuitive appeal, have no mortality association in the largest registry — all of it observational and none of it a basis for certainty.

cards.headline: Petursson 2024 (SWEDEHEART): 1,724 Takotsubo patients — ACE inhibitors (HR 0.60) and statins (HR 0.62) associated with lower long-term mortality; beta-blockers, aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors not associated at all
cards.summary: Petursson 2024 (SWEDEHEART): 1,724 Takotsubo patients — ACE inhibitors (HR 0.60) and statins (HR 0.62) associated with lower long-term mortality; beta-blockers, aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors not associated at all
cards.people: 1,724 patients with Takotsubo syndrome (mean age 66±14 years, 77% women) identified in the SWEDEHEART registry among 228,263 patients undergoing coronary angiography in Sweden between 2009 and 2016; 49.4% presented as non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome and 25.9% as ST-elevation MI; 79.1% had non-obstructive coronary disease. Median follow-up was 877 days.
cards.result: All-cause mortality was 2.5% at 30 days and 16.6% at 6 years (Kaplan-Meier). ACE inhibitors were associated with decreased long-term mortality (HR 0.60, p=0.025) and statins likewise (HR 0.62, p=0.040). Unfractionated and low-molecular-weight heparins were associated with reduced 30-day mortality (HR 0.63, p=0.01). Angiotensin receptor blockers, oral anticoagulants, P2Y12 antagonists, aspirin and beta-blockers did not statistically correlate with mortality. Intravenous inotropes (HR 9.92, p<0.001) and intravenous diuretics (HR 3.22, p=0.001) were associated with increased 30-day mortality. Most patients received beta-blockers (77.8% oral, 8.3% intravenous), aspirin (66.7%) or P2Y12 inhibitors (43.6%).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective registry associations, with treatment chosen by clinicians — the inotrope hazard ratio of 9.92 is the tell: it measures how sick the recipients were, not what the drug did, and the same machinery generated the flattering ACE-inhibitor and statin numbers. The record reports hazard ratios with p-values but no confidence intervals in its abstract, limiting precision judgements.
cards.source: Petursson P et al. Effects of pharmacological interventions on mortality in patients with Takotsubo syndrome: a report from the SWEDEHEART registry. ESC heart failure. 2024. PMID: 38454651. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a whole drug cupboard prescribed on instinct, one large registry, and no randomised evidence for any of it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a whole drug cupboard prescribed on instinct, one large registry, and no randomised evidence for any of it
cards.people: One national registry cohort of 1,724 Takotsubo patients (SWEDEHEART) — the largest pharmacological-outcome dataset located for this question.
cards.result: Long-term mortality associations: ACE inhibitors HR 0.60, statins HR 0.62 (both nominally significant); beta-blockers, ARBs, aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, oral anticoagulants — no association. Thirty-day mortality: heparins HR 0.63; inotropes and diuretics associated with higher mortality (confounded by severity). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: A beta-blocker meta-analysis in Takotsubo was located in-session (PMID: 37544139) but its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so no numbers from it could be verified or carded — this shelf therefore rests on the registry alone. Tier C is set: observational evidence only, and a randomised trial in Takotsubo remains the missing piece.
cards.source: Synthesis of Petursson P et al. ESC heart failure. 2024 (PMID: 38454651).
