shelves.title: Vigorous exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LIVE-HCM): 1,660 patients, event rates identical between vigorous exercisers and the rest — the blanket ban loses its evidence
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is vigorous exercise associated with a higher risk of death or ventricular arrhythmia than moderate or no exercise?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Cohort Studies · Prospective Studies · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/complications · Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic* · Heart Arrest*/complications · Exercise
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for decades, vigorous exercise was simply forbidden in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on the theory that exertion triggers lethal arrhythmia. LIVE-HCM is the first large prospective test of that assumption: 1,660 participants aged 8–60 with HCM (or genotype-positive/phenotype-negative) at 42 high-volume centres, classified by self-reported activity as sedentary (15%), moderate (43%) or vigorous (42%, of whom 37% competed). Over the study period, 77 participants (4.6%) reached the composite of death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, arrhythmic syncope or appropriate ICD shock — 4.7% of the vigorous group versus 4.6% of the non-vigorous group, event rates 15.9 versus 15.3 per 1,000 person-years, adjusted hazard ratio 1.01, with the upper one-sided 95% confidence bound (1.48) just inside the prespecified noninferiority boundary of 1.5. That is reassurance with edges: it is observational (people who choose vigorous exercise differ from those who do not), participants were cared for at expert centres, and the confidence bound cannot exclude a moderate increase in risk. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in expert-centre HCM populations, vigorous exercise was not associated with higher rates of death or life-threatening arrhythmia than moderate exercise or sedentary life — enough to inform a shared decision, not enough to declare exertion proven safe for every patient.

cards.headline: Lampert 2023 (LIVE-HCM): 1,660 patients — vigorous exercisers had the same event rate as everyone else (4.7% versus 4.6%; adjusted HR 1.01), meeting the prespecified noninferiority boundary
cards.summary: Lampert 2023 (LIVE-HCM): 1,660 patients — vigorous exercisers had the same event rate as everyone else (4.7% versus 4.6%; adjusted HR 1.01), meeting the prespecified noninferiority boundary
cards.people: 1,660 participants (mean age 39 years, 60% men) aged 8–60 years with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or genotype-positive/phenotype-negative status, enrolled 2015–2019 at 42 high-volume HCM centres in the US and internationally (self-enrolment also possible), without conditions precluding exercise; activity was self-reported as sedentary (252, 15%), moderate (709, 43%) or vigorous (699, 42%, including 259 competitive athletes). Events were adjudicated blinded to exercise category.
cards.result: Seventy-seven participants (4.6%) reached the primary composite endpoint (death, resuscitated sudden cardiac arrest, arrhythmic syncope, or appropriate ICD shock): 33 of the vigorous group (4.7%) versus 44 of the non-vigorous group (4.6%), at rates of 15.9 versus 15.3 per 1,000 person-years. In multivariable Cox analysis, vigorous exercise was not associated with a higher event rate (adjusted HR 1.01), and the upper 95% one-sided confidence level of 1.48 fell below the prespecified noninferiority boundary of 1.5. The authors conclude that, in patients treated at experienced centres, vigorous exercise was not associated with a higher rate of death or life-threatening arrhythmias.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority in an observational cohort is not randomisation: vigorous exercisers self-selected, were likely lower-risk in ways adjustment cannot fully capture, and the 1.48 upper bound sits a hair under the 1.5 boundary — the data remain compatible with a meaningful increase in risk. Participants were managed at expert HCM centres, which is part of the intervention whether or not it appears in the methods.
cards.source: Lampert R et al. Vigorous Exercise in Patients With Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy. JAMA cardiology. 2023. PMID: 37195701. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the blanket ban on vigorous exercise in HCM is not supported by the best prospective data — and 'not supported' is as far as observational data go
cards.summary: Synthesis: the blanket ban on vigorous exercise in HCM is not supported by the best prospective data — and 'not supported' is as far as observational data go
cards.people: One prospective multicentre cohort of 1,660 adolescents and adults with HCM or genotype-positive/phenotype-negative status (LIVE-HCM) — the direct evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Composite of death, resuscitated arrest, arrhythmic syncope or appropriate ICD shock: 4.7% (vigorous) versus 4.6% (non-vigorous); adjusted HR 1.01; upper confidence bound 1.48 against a 1.5 noninferiority margin. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of exercise in HCM exists or is likely, and no usable systematic review was verified in-session, so this single cohort carries the shelf. Tier C is set. The result supports individualised, expert-guided decisions — it does not clear high-risk subgroups (prior arrest, severe hypertrophy, unexplained syncope) whom clinicians may still advise differently.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lampert R et al. JAMA cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 37195701).

shelves.title: Myectomy versus alcohol septal ablation: identical long-term survival in 8,453 patients — ablation trades a safer procedure day for a one-in-nine chance of needing it done again
shelves.question: In symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, how do septal myectomy and alcohol septal ablation compare on long-term mortality and reintervention?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques/methods · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/methods · Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic/therapy · Cause of Death/trends · Ethanol/pharmacology · Heart Ventricles/surgery · Humans · Survival Rate/trends · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — there is no randomised comparison of septal myectomy and alcohol septal ablation for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; the evidence is a meta-analysis of 45 observational cohorts (Osman 2019: 22 ablation cohorts, 4,213 patients, mean follow-up 6.6 years; 23 myectomy cohorts, 4,240 patients, 6.8 years), and it splits by time horizon. Around the procedure, myectomy cost more: periprocedural mortality 2% versus 1.2% (p=0.009) and stroke 1.5% versus 0.8% (p=0.013), while ablation cost more pacemakers (10% versus 5%, p<0.001). Over the long term the survival lines converge — all-cause mortality 1.1% versus 1.5% per person-year (p=0.21), cardiovascular mortality 0.5% versus 0.4% (p=0.53), sudden death 0.3% in both (p=0.43) — but ablation patients needed repeat septal-reduction procedures far more often (11% versus 1.5%, p<0.001). PROPOSED SPLIT: long-term mortality is indistinguishable between the two procedures in observational data; the choice trades myectomy's higher upfront risk against ablation's higher pacemaker and reintervention rates — a trade shaped by age, anatomy and centre expertise, none of which a cohort meta-analysis can randomise away.

cards.headline: Osman 2019 (meta-analysis of 45 cohorts, 8,453 patients): long-term mortality identical after ablation and myectomy — but ablation meant more pacemakers (10% versus 5%) and far more reintervention (11% versus 1.5%), myectomy more periprocedural death and stroke
cards.summary: Osman 2019 (meta-analysis of 45 cohorts, 8,453 patients): long-term mortality identical after ablation and myectomy — but ablation meant more pacemakers (10% versus 5%) and far more reintervention (11% versus 1.5%), myectomy more periprocedural death and stroke
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 45 observational cohorts (Osman 2019)
cards.people: Twenty-two alcohol septal ablation cohorts (4,213 patients, follow-up 6.6 years) and 23 surgical myectomy cohorts (4,240 patients, follow-up 6.8 years) reporting long-term (>3-year) outcomes in symptomatic hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: Periprocedurally, myectomy carried higher mortality (2% versus 1.2%, p=0.009) and stroke (1.5% versus 0.8%, p=0.013), while ablation carried a higher pacemaker-implantation rate (10% versus 5%, p<0.001). During long-term follow-up there was no difference in all-cause mortality (ablation 1.5% versus myectomy 1.1% per person-year, p=0.21), cardiovascular mortality (0.4% versus 0.5%, p=0.53) or sudden cardiac death (0.3% versus 0.3%, p=0.43). Repeat septal-reduction intervention was much more common after ablation (11% versus 1.5%, p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Every included study is a cohort, and the two procedures are not offered to the same patients — ablation skews older and less surgically fit, myectomy younger with more complex anatomy — so even the 'identical' long-term mortality may reflect selection as much as equivalence. Era effects matter too: cohorts span decades of evolving technique at centres of very different volume.
cards.source: Osman M et al. Alcohol septal ablation vs myectomy for symptomatic hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical cardiology. 2019. PMID: 30421437. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Lenient versus strict rate control in permanent AF (RACE II): a resting rate under 110 did everything under 80 did — with a tenth of the clinic visits
shelves.question: In patients with permanent atrial fibrillation, does lenient rate control (resting heart rate <110/min) match strict rate control on death, hospitalisation and symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/complications · Calcium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Confidence Intervals · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Rate* · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strict rate control in permanent atrial fibrillation was guideline doctrine without outcome evidence behind it; RACE II tested it head-to-head. In 614 patients with permanent AF, a lenient target (resting heart rate <110/min) was compared with a strict target (resting <80/min and <110/min during moderate exercise) over 2–3 years. The primary composite — cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation, stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding and life-threatening arrhythmic events — occurred in an estimated 12.9% with lenient control versus 14.9% with strict control (absolute difference −2.0 percentage points, 90% CI −7.6 to 3.5), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (p<0.001 for noninferiority), with similar frequencies for every component. Lenient control was also far easier to live with: 97.7% of lenient patients met their target versus 67.0% of strict patients, with a median of 0 versus 2 extra visits (75 versus 684 total visits), and symptoms and adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lenient rate control matches strict control on outcomes in permanent AF while demanding fewer drugs, fewer visits and less titration — the benefit is equivalence with less burden, from a single moderately sized trial.

cards.headline: Van Gelder 2010 (RACE II): lenient rate control (<110/min) was noninferior to strict (<80/min) in permanent AF — primary outcome 12.9% versus 14.9% at 3 years, targets met by 97.7% versus 67.0%
cards.summary: Van Gelder 2010 (RACE II): lenient rate control (<110/min) was noninferior to strict (<80/min) in permanent AF — primary outcome 12.9% versus 14.9% at 3 years, targets met by 97.7% versus 67.0%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Van Gelder 2010, RACE II)
cards.people: 614 patients with permanent atrial fibrillation randomised to lenient rate control (resting heart rate <110 beats per minute) or strict rate control (resting <80 beats per minute and <110 beats per minute during moderate exercise), followed for at least 2 and up to 3 years.
cards.result: The estimated cumulative incidence of the primary outcome (composite of death from cardiovascular causes, hospitalisation for heart failure, stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding, and life-threatening arrhythmic events) at 3 years was 12.9% in the lenient group and 14.9% in the strict group — an absolute difference of −2.0 percentage points (90% CI −7.6 to 3.5), p<0.001 for the prespecified noninferiority margin. The frequencies of the individual components were similar in the two groups, as were symptoms and adverse events. More lenient-group patients met their heart-rate targets (304 [97.7%] versus 203 [67.0%], p<0.001), with far fewer total visits (75 [median 0] versus 684 [median 2], p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority in 614 patients over 2–3 years does not exclude small long-term differences, and the population had permanent AF — the result does not set targets for paroxysmal AF, for AF with decompensated heart failure, or for patients whose symptoms demand tighter control. A third of strict-group patients never reached the strict target, which is itself part of the pragmatic comparison.

cards.search: van gelder 2010 (race ii): lenient rate control (<110/min) was noninferior to strict (<80/min) in permanent af — primary outcome 12.9% versus 14.9% at 3 years, targets met by 97.7% versus 67.0% van gelder 2010 (race ii): lenient rate control (<110/min) was noninferior to strict (<80/min) in permanent af — primary outcome 12.9% versus 14.9% at 3 years, targets met by 97.7% versus 67.0% in patients with permanent atrial fibrillation, does lenient rate control (resting heart rate <110/min) match strict rate control on death, hospitalisation and symptoms? randomised controlled trial (van gelder 2010, race ii) 614 patients with permanent atrial fibrillation randomised to lenient rate control (resting heart rate <110 beats per minute) or strict rate control (resting <80 beats per minute and <110 beats per minute during moderate exercise), followed for at least 2 and up to 3 years. the estimated cumulative incidence of the primary outcome (composite of death from cardiovascular causes, hospitalisation for heart failure, stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding, and life-threatening arrhythmic events) at 3 years was 12.9% in the lenient group and 14.9% in the strict group — an absolute difference of −2.0 percentage points (90% ci −7.6 to 3.5), p<0.001 for the prespecified noninferiority margin. the frequencies of the individual components were similar in the two groups, as were symptoms and adverse events. more lenient-group patients met their heart-rate targets (304 [97.7%] versus 203 [67.0%], p<0.001), with far fewer total visits (75 [median 0] versus 684 [median 2], p<0.001). noninferiority in 614 patients over 2–3 years does not exclude small long-term differences, and the population had permanent af — the result does not set targets for paroxysmal af, for af with decompensated heart failure, or for patients whose symptoms demand tighter control. a third of strict-group patients never reached the strict target, which is itself part of the pragmatic comparison. van gelder ic et al. lenient versus strict rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation. the new england journal of medicine. 2010. pmid: 20231232. registry id: nct00392613. mesh: adrenergic beta-antagonists/therapeutic use · aged · anti-arrhythmia agents/therapeutic use · atrial fibrillation/complications · calcium channel blockers/therapeutic use · confidence intervals · female · follow-up studies · heart rate* · humans · kaplan-meier estimate · male · middle aged

shelves.title: Ablation in end-stage heart failure with AF: one small trial stopped early found death, LVAD or urgent transplant in 8% versus 30% — a huge signal that still needs a second trial
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and end-stage heart failure eligible for transplantation or assist devices, does catheter ablation, compared with medical therapy, reduce death or urgent transplantation/LVAD?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation*/complications, surgery · Catheter Ablation*/adverse effects, methods · Germany · Heart Failure*/complications, surgery · Heart Transplantation · Heart-Assist Devices · Referral and Consultation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a single-centre, open-label German trial of 194 patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation and end-stage heart failure referred for transplant evaluation, catheter ablation plus guideline-directed medical therapy produced a strikingly lower rate of the composite of death, left ventricular assist device implantation, or urgent transplantation than medical therapy alone (8% versus 30%; HR 0.24 relative, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.52), and death alone was lower too (6% versus 20%; HR 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.72). The cautions are structural, not numerical: the trial was stopped early for efficacy after only 97 patients per arm, which tends to inflate effect sizes; it was unblinded; ablation was actually performed in only 84% of the ablation arm while 16% of the control arm crossed over to ablation; and procedure-related complications occurred in 3 ablation patients versus 1 control patient. An effect this large from one small stopped-early trial is a strong signal that needs a confirmatory multicentre trial before it can be called established. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ablation probably helps this very specific end-stage population, but the size of the benefit is almost certainly overstated by the design that found it.

cards.headline: CASTLE-HTx 2023: ablation plus medical therapy cut the composite of death, LVAD or urgent transplant to 8% versus 30% (HR 0.24 relative) — and death alone to 6% versus 20%
cards.summary: CASTLE-HTx 2023: ablation plus medical therapy cut the composite of death, LVAD or urgent transplant to 8% versus 30% (HR 0.24 relative) — and death alone to 6% versus 20%
cards.people: 194 patients (97 per arm) with symptomatic atrial fibrillation and end-stage heart failure referred for heart transplantation evaluation at a single German centre; single-centre, open-label randomised trial comparing catheter ablation plus guideline-directed medical therapy with medical therapy alone; median follow-up 18.0 months (IQR 14.6 to 22.6).
cards.result: The primary composite end point (death from any cause, implantation of a left ventricular assist device, or urgent heart transplantation) occurred in 8 patients (8%) in the ablation group and 29 patients (30%) in the medical-therapy group (hazard ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.52; P<0.001) — a 76% relative reduction, 22 percentage points absolute. Death from any cause occurred in 6 patients (6%) versus 19 patients (20%) (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.72). Catheter ablation was performed in 81 of 97 patients (84%) in the ablation group and in 16 of 97 patients (16%) in the medical-therapy group. Procedure-related complications occurred in 3 patients in the ablation group and 1 patient in the medical-therapy group. The trial was stopped for efficacy by the data and safety monitoring board 1 year after randomisation was completed.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, open-label trial stopped early for efficacy with 194 patients is exactly the design that produces the largest, least reproducible effects in cardiology. The 16% crossover to ablation in the control arm and the 16% of the ablation arm never ablated blur the contrast, and transplant/LVAD decisions in an unblinded trial can be influenced by knowing the treatment arm. This population — transplant-referred, end-stage — is not general heart failure with AF, and the result should not be quoted for it.
cards.source: Sohns C et al. Catheter Ablation in End-Stage Heart Failure with Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 37634135. Registry ID: NCT04649801. cards.people: The entire randomised record for this exact question is CASTLE-HTx: 194 transplant-referred patients with end-stage heart failure and symptomatic atrial fibrillation, one German centre, median follow-up 18 months.
cards.result: Composite of death, LVAD implantation or urgent transplantation: 8% with ablation plus medical therapy versus 30% with medical therapy alone (HR 0.24 relative, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.52). Mortality: 6% versus 20% (HR 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.72). Procedure-related complications: 3 versus 1 patients. No second trial in this end-stage, transplant-eligible population was found. cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with the general AF-ablation-in-heart-failure evidence (housed elsewhere): CASTLE-HTx patients were sick enough to be referred for transplantation, and both the potential gain and the procedural risk are different there. shelves.title: Treating the causes underneath persistent AF: RACE 3's bundled upstream therapy kept 75% in sinus rhythm at a year versus 63% — one trial, a borderline P value, and no way to credit a single component
shelves.question: In patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, does targeted treatment of underlying risk factors and upstream therapy, added to rhythm control, improve sinus-rhythm maintenance compared with conventional management?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy, etiology, therapy · Counseling · Diet, Healthy · Exercise Therapy · Female · Heart Failure/complications, drug therapy, therapy · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Risk Reduction Behavior
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — RACE 3 randomised 245 patients with early persistent atrial fibrillation and mild-to-moderate heart failure to a bundled targeted-therapy programme (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, statin, ACE inhibitor/ARB optimisation, and cardiac rehabilitation with exercise, dietary counselling) on top of rhythm control, or to conventional management. At 1 year, sinus rhythm on 7-day Holter was present in 75% of the targeted group versus 63% of controls (odds ratio 1.765, lower limit of the 95% CI 1.021; P=0.042) — a real but borderline result, 12 percentage points absolute, from a single trial whose intervention was a bundle: the contrast was driven mainly by MRA use (85% versus 4%) and statin use (93% versus 48%), since ACE inhibitor/ARB use did not differ, so no single component can be credited. The endpoint is rhythm on a monitor at one year, not stroke, hospitalisation, or death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): treating underlying conditions alongside rhythm control probably helps maintain sinus rhythm, but one 245-patient trial with a P value of 0.042 cannot say which part of the bundle does the work.

cards.headline: RACE 3 2018: targeted risk-factor therapy kept 75% in sinus rhythm at 1 year versus 63% with conventional care (OR 1.765, P=0.042)
cards.summary: RACE 3 2018: targeted risk-factor therapy kept 75% in sinus rhythm at 1 year versus 63% with conventional care (OR 1.765, P=0.042)
cards.people: 245 patients with early persistent atrial fibrillation and mild-to-moderate heart failure, randomised to targeted therapy of underlying conditions (119) or conventional therapy (126); both groups received causal treatment of AF and heart failure plus rhythm-control therapy; the primary endpoint was sinus rhythm at 1 year during 7 days of Holter monitoring.
cards.result: Sinus rhythm at 1 year was present in 89 patients (75%) in the targeted group versus 79 patients (63%) in the conventional group (odds ratio 1.765, lower limit of 95% confidence interval 1.021; P=0.042) — 12 percentage points absolute. The treatment contrast was achieved mainly through mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (101 patients [85%] versus 5 [4%]; P<0.001) and statins (111 [93%] versus 61 [48%]; P<0.001); ACE inhibitor/ARB use was not different between groups. Cardiac rehabilitation was completed by 109 patients (92%) in the intervention group. Underlying conditions were more successfully treated in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: A bundle trial cannot attribute its effect: because ACE inhibitor/ARB use ended up identical in both arms, the tested contrast was effectively 'add an MRA, add a statin, add rehabilitation' — and the headline P value (0.042, with the confidence interval's lower limit at 1.021) is fragile to a handful of patients changing category. The outcome is an electrocardiographic state at one year, not a clinical event.
cards.source: Rienstra M et al. Targeted therapy of underlying conditions improves sinus rhythm maintenance in patients with persistent atrial fibrillation: results of the RACE 3 trial. European heart journal. 2018. PMID: 29401239. Registry ID: NCT00877643. shelves.title: Procainamide versus amiodarone for stable wide-complex tachycardia: the one randomised trial favours procainamide on safety (9% vs 41% major events) and speed (67% vs 38% terminated)
shelves.question: In patients with tolerated sustained monomorphic wide-QRS tachycardia, does intravenous procainamide terminate the arrhythmia more safely than intravenous amiodarone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amiodarone/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Cardiomyopathies/complications · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Procainamide/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Tachycardia, Ventricular/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PROCAMIO is the only randomised head-to-head trial of intravenous procainamide versus intravenous amiodarone for tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia, and it favoured procainamide on both of its main measures: major predefined cardiac adverse events within 40 minutes occurred in 9% of procainamide patients versus 41% of amiodarone patients (odds ratio 0.1; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.6; P=0.006), and the tachycardia terminated within 40 minutes in 67% versus 38% (OR 3.3; 95% CI 1.2 to 9.3; P=0.026). Over the following 24 hours adverse events were 18% versus 31% (OR 0.49; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.61; P=0.24), not significantly different. The restraint is size and design: 74 patients were enrolled, only 62 could be analysed, the trial was open-label, and the population was the selected minority whose tachycardia is haemodynamically tolerated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for the stable patient in front of you, procainamide looks both safer and faster than amiodarone — on the strength of one small open-label trial.

cards.headline: PROCAMIO 2017: major cardiac adverse events 9% with procainamide versus 41% with amiodarone (OR 0.1), and termination within 40 minutes 67% versus 38%
cards.summary: PROCAMIO 2017: major cardiac adverse events 9% with procainamide versus 41% with amiodarone (OR 0.1), and termination within 40 minutes 67% versus 38%
cards.people: Patients with sustained monomorphic well-tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia (probably ventricular) at multiple centres; 74 patients included, 62 analysed (procainamide 33, amiodarone 29); open-label randomisation to intravenous procainamide (10 mg/kg over 20 min) or amiodarone (5 mg/kg over 20 min); primary endpoint was major predefined cardiac adverse events within 40 minutes of starting the infusion.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 3 of 33 procainamide patients (9%) and 12 of 29 amiodarone patients (41%) (odds ratio 0.1; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.6; P=0.006). Tachycardia terminated within 40 minutes in 22 procainamide patients (67%) and 11 amiodarone patients (38%) (OR 3.3; 95% CI 1.2 to 9.3; P=0.026). In the following 24 hours, adverse events occurred in 18% of procainamide and 31% of amiodarone patients (OR 0.49; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.61; P=0.24). Among 49 patients with structural heart disease, the primary endpoint was less common with procainamide (3 patients [11%] versus 10 [43%]; OR 0.17; 95% CI 0.04 to 0.73; P=0.017).
cards.watchOut: Twelve of 74 enrolled patients (16%) could not be analysed, the trial was open-label with an endpoint (major cardiac adverse events within 40 minutes) that includes clinician-judged deterioration, and the amiodarone dose and infusion rate (5 mg/kg over 20 minutes) are only one of the regimens in use. A 62-patient trial can rank these two drugs for a stable patient; it cannot set policy for unstable tachycardia, where neither drug is the treatment — electricity is.
cards.source: Ortiz M et al. Randomized comparison of intravenous procainamide vs. intravenous amiodarone for the acute treatment of tolerated wide QRS tachycardia: the PROCAMIO study. shelves.title: Pill-in-the-pocket for paroxysmal AF: 94% of episodes ended at home in patients pre-tested in hospital — effective for the selected, never randomised
shelves.question: In patients with infrequent, well-tolerated paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, does self-administered "pill-in-the-pocket" flecainide or propafenone safely terminate episodes and reduce emergency visits?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Ambulatory Care · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/complications, drug therapy · Feasibility Studies · Female · Flecainide/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/complications, physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Propafenone/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Self Administration · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the evidence for pill-in-the-pocket is a single prospective cohort, not a randomised trial. Alboni and colleagues first proved the approach in hospital in 268 patients with recent-onset, haemodynamically tolerated AF and mild or no heart disease, then sent the 210 patients (79% of those screened in) in whom it had worked and caused no problems home to self-treat: over a mean 15 months, 165 patients had 618 episodes, treatment succeeded in 94% of treated episodes, symptoms resolved in a mean 113 minutes, adverse effects occurred in 7% of patients (including one case of atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rate), and monthly emergency visits and hospitalisations fell significantly compared with the prior year (P<0.001 for both). The 2010 Health Technology Assessment systematic review found the strategy slightly less effective than continuous antiarrhythmic therapy or in-hospital treatment but also less costly, with the balance turning on age. The catch is in the funnel: 22% of patients were excluded before self-treatment even began because in-hospital treatment failed or caused side effects — the 94% success rate belongs to a pre-selected group in whom the drug was already known to work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in carefully selected, pre-tested patients this is a workable, visit-sparing strategy; it has never been randomised against the alternatives.

cards.headline: Alboni 2004: in pre-tested patients, self-administered flecainide or propafenone terminated 94% of treated AF episodes, with adverse effects in 7% and far fewer emergency visits
cards.summary: Alboni 2004: in pre-tested patients, self-administered flecainide or propafenone terminated 94% of treated AF episodes, with adverse effects in 7% and far fewer emergency visits
cards.people: 268 patients with mild or no heart disease presenting to emergency departments with recent-onset, haemodynamically well-tolerated atrial fibrillation, given a single oral loading dose of flecainide or propafenone in hospital; the 210 patients (mean age 59±11 years) in whom treatment succeeded without side effects were then trained to self-administer at home and followed for a mean of 15±5 months. Prospective cohort study, not randomised.
cards.result: 58 patients (22%) were excluded after the in-hospital phase because of treatment failure or side effects. During follow-up, 165 patients (79%) had a total of 618 arrhythmia episodes; 569 episodes (92%) were treated, beginning 36±93 minutes after symptom onset. Treatment was successful in 534 episodes (94%), with time to resolution of symptoms 113±84 minutes. Among the 165 patients with recurrences, the drug was effective during all episodes in 139 patients (84%). Adverse effects were reported during one or more episodes by 12 patients (7%), including atrial flutter at a rapid ventricular rate in 1 patient and noncardiac side effects in 11. Monthly emergency-room visits and hospitalisations were significantly lower during follow-up than during the year before the target episode (P<0.001 for both comparisons).
cards.watchOut: There is no control group: the fall in emergency visits is a before-and-after comparison in patients who had just had an index visit (regression to the mean and changed behaviour after enrolment both predict fewer visits). And the safety denominator matters — the 22% who failed or reacted to the drug in hospital were removed before the 'safe' home phase began, so 94% success and 7% adverse effects describe survivors of a screening step, not all comers with paroxysmal AF.
cards.source: Alboni P et al. Outpatient treatment of recent-onset atrial fibrillation with the "pill-in-the-pocket" approach. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 15575054. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Saborido 2010 (HTA systematic review): pill-in-the-pocket was slightly less effective than continuous therapy or in-hospital treatment, but cheaper — cost-effectiveness turned on age
cards.summary: Saborido 2010 (HTA systematic review): pill-in-the-pocket was slightly less effective than continuous therapy or in-hospital treatment, but cheaper — cost-effectiveness turned on age
cards.type: Systematic review and cost-effectiveness evaluation (Saborido 2010, HTA)
cards.people: UK Health Technology Assessment systematic review and economic model of the pill-in-the-pocket strategy for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, compared with episodic in-hospital treatment and with continuous antiarrhythmic drug therapy; 201 randomised trials were identified in the wider paroxysmal-AF literature, of which 12 were relevant to the decision problem and used to inform the model.
cards.result: The model results indicate that the pill-in-the-pocket strategy is slightly less effective than the other two strategies but also less costly, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £45,916 per quality-adjusted life-year when compared with continuous antiarrhythmic drugs and £12,424 per QALY when compared with in-hospital treatment. One-way sensitivity analyses did not substantially change the relative cost-effectiveness except in relation to patient age, where pill-in-the-pocket dominated continuous therapy in men over 65. The review's clinical-effectiveness base for the strategy itself rested on the same small, selected literature as the Alboni cohort.
cards.watchOut: A cost-effectiveness model is only as good as its inputs, and here the inputs for the strategy's effectiveness come from uncontrolled cohort data; the QALY figures should be read as 'plausibly good value in the right patient', not as measured outcomes. The review also predates contemporary ablation and wearable-rhythm-monitoring practice.
cards.source: Saborido CM et al. Systematic review and cost-effectiveness evaluation of 'pill-in-the-pocket' strategy for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation compared to episodic in-hospital treatment or continuous antiarrhythmic drug therapy. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2010. PMID: 20569652. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a workable strategy for the pre-tested few — 94% of episodes terminated at home, 7% adverse effects, and no randomised comparison behind any of it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a workable strategy for the pre-tested few — 94% of episodes terminated at home, 7% adverse effects, and no randomised comparison behind any of it
cards.people: One prospective cohort (268 screened in hospital, 210 self-treating at home, 618 episodes) and one HTA systematic review with economic modelling — the entire evidence base for pill-in-the-pocket flecainide or propafenone.
cards.result: Episode success 94% in patients pre-selected for in-hospital success; adverse effects in 7% of patients, including one rapid atrial flutter; emergency visits and hospitalisations significantly lower than the patients' own prior year (P<0.001, uncontrolled). Economic modelling: slightly less effective but less costly than continuous therapy or in-hospital treatment. Mortality and stroke: not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), confined to selected, pre-tested patients with infrequent tolerated episodes.
cards.watchOut: Selection is the intervention here as much as the drug: patients with structural heart disease, conduction disease, frequent episodes or a failed in-hospital test were excluded, and the shelf must not be read as endorsing self-treatment for unselected paroxysmal AF. Tier C is set because there is no randomised trial of the strategy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Alboni P et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15575054); Saborido CM et al. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2010 (PMID: 20569652).

shelves.title: Ivabradine for hyperadrenergic POTS: heart rate down and quality of life up in a 22-patient crossover trial — promising, tiny, and one month long
shelves.question: In patients with hyperadrenergic postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, does ivabradine, compared with placebo, reduce heart rate and improve quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiovascular Agents/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Ivabradine/therapeutic use · Male · Norepinephrine/blood · Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome/drug therapy · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial is the whole randomised record: 22 patients with hyperadrenergic postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (plasma norepinephrine >600 pg/ml with an abnormal tilt test; mean age 33.9 years, 95.5% women) each spent a month on ivabradine and a month on placebo. Heart rate was significantly lower on ivabradine (P<0.001), and patients reported significant improvements in quality of life on the RAND 36-Item Health Survey for physical functioning (P=0.008) and social functioning (P=0.021); standing norepinephrine showed a strong trend to reduction (P=0.056), and no significant side effects such as bradycardia or hypotension occurred. The 2023 systematic review of drug therapy in POTS found the same pattern across the whole field — midodrine, ivabradine, bisoprolol and others showed positive signals in studies of only 10–50 patients, most underpowered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ivabradine probably lowers heart rate and improves how these patients feel, but 22 patients treated for a month each cannot establish durability, and the result applies to the hyperadrenergic subtype that was enrolled, not to all POTS.

cards.headline: Taub 2021: in 22 patients with hyperadrenergic POTS, a month of ivabradine significantly reduced heart rate (P<0.001) and improved physical and social functioning scores
cards.summary: Taub 2021: in 22 patients with hyperadrenergic POTS, a month of ivabradine significantly reduced heart rate (P<0.001) and improved physical and social functioning scores
cards.people: 22 patients with hyperadrenergic postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome as the predominant subtype (plasma norepinephrine >600 pg/ml and abnormal tilt-table test; average age 33.9±11.7 years, 95.5% women) who completed a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial: 1 month of ivabradine and 1 month of placebo in random order, with heart rate, quality of life and plasma norepinephrine measured at baseline and at the end of each treatment month.
cards.result: There was a significant reduction in heart rate between placebo and ivabradine (P<0.001). Patients reported significant improvements in quality of life with ivabradine on the RAND 36-Item Health Survey 1.0 for physical functioning (P=0.008) and social functioning (P=0.021). There was a strong trend toward reduction of norepinephrine levels upon standing with ivabradine (P=0.056). Patients did not experience any significant side effects, such as bradycardia or hypotension, with ivabradine. The abstract reports P values without the underlying heart-rate or quality-of-life point values.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two completers, one month per period, and a record that reports significance levels without effect sizes: the trial shows direction, not magnitude. Crossover designs in a fluctuating symptom condition are also vulnerable to period effects, and a hyperadrenergic-only entry criterion (norepinephrine >600 pg/ml) means the result says nothing about neuropathic or hypovolaemic POTS.
cards.source: Taub PR et al. Randomized Trial of Ivabradine in Patients With Hyperadrenergic Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2021. PMID: 33602468. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vasavada 2023 systematic review: every POTS drug literature is the same shape — positive signals in studies of 10–50 patients, most underpowered
cards.summary: Vasavada 2023 systematic review: every POTS drug literature is the same shape — positive signals in studies of 10–50 patients, most underpowered
cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA) of pharmacological treatment studies in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome published before 8 April 2023: of 421 potential articles assessed, 17 met the inclusion criteria, covering midodrine, ivabradine, bisoprolol, fludrocortisone, droxidopa, desmopressin, propranolol, modafinil, methylphenidate and melatonin.
cards.result: Pharmacological treatment options for POTS were effective in reducing symptoms in the included studies, but most studies were underpowered and several were terminated for various reasons. The studied drugs showed positive impact but with low sample sizes in the range of 10–50 subjects. The reviewers concluded that the treatment options effectively improve symptoms of POTS and increase orthostatic tolerance, but that more evidence is needed because most studies had low sample sizes. The record carries no MeSH terms and reports no pooled effect estimate for ivabradine specifically.
cards.watchOut: This is a narrative systematic review without meta-analysis, in a journal of modest editorial weight, and its 'effective' language is stronger than its own data description (small, underpowered, sometimes terminated studies) supports. It is carded as a map of the field's weakness, not as independent confirmation of ivabradine.

shelves.title: Which beta-blocker for long QT? The registries agree the class works and the drugs differ — nadolol covers LQT1 and LQT2, metoprolol reaches significance in neither
shelves.question: In patients with congenital long QT syndrome, do beta-blockers differ — in particular nadolol versus metoprolol, atenolol or propranolol — in preventing syncope, cardiac arrest and death?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Atenolol/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Death, Sudden, Cardiac/prevention & control · Female · Genotype · Heart Arrest/prevention & control · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Long QT Syndrome/drug therapy · Male · Metoprolol/therapeutic use · Multivariate Analysis · Nadolol/therapeutic use · Proportional Hazards Models · Propranolol/therapeutic use · Registries · Regression Analysis · Risk Factors · Syncope/prevention & control · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by genotype and by drug. All of this evidence is observational — there has never been a randomised trial of beta-blockers in long QT syndrome — but the registry data are large and consistent that beta-blockade as a class reduces first cardiac events. In the Rochester registry analysis of 1,530 patients, hazard ratios for a first cardiac event versus no beta-blocker were 0.71 for atenolol, 0.70 for metoprolol, 0.65 for propranolol and 0.51 for nadolol. The split appears by genotype: in LQT1 the four drugs looked similar, but in LQT2 nadolol was the only drug with a significant risk reduction (HR 0.40 relative, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.98). The 2017 meta-analysis of 10 studies and 9,727 patients agrees: nadolol significantly reduced risk in both LQT1 (HR 0.47 relative) and LQT2 (HR 0.27 relative), atenolol and propranolol reduced risk only in LQT1, and metoprolol showed no significant reduction in either genotype; in LQT3 the data were insufficient. A second split: among patients who had already had an event on a beta-blocker, propranolol was the least effective drug for preventing recurrence. PROPOSED SPLIT: beta-blockers work, but they are not interchangeable — nadolol has the broadest support across LQT1 and LQT2, and metoprolol the weakest.

cards.headline: Abu-Zeitone 2014 (Rochester registry, 1,530 patients): all four beta-blockers cut first events, but in LQT2 only nadolol was significant (HR 0.40 relative) — and propranolol was weakest after a breakthrough event
cards.summary: Abu-Zeitone 2014 (Rochester registry, 1,530 patients): all four beta-blockers cut first events, but in LQT2 only nadolol was significant (HR 0.40 relative) — and propranolol was weakest after a breakthrough event
cards.people: 1,530 patients from the Rochester, New York long QT syndrome registry prescribed atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol or nadolol; time-dependent Cox regression comparing each drug with being off beta-blockers for first cardiac events (syncope, aborted cardiac arrest, sudden cardiac death), including genotype-positive LQT1 and LQT2 subgroups. Observational registry analysis, not randomised.
cards.result: Relative to being off beta-blockers, hazard ratios for first cardiac events were 0.71 (95% CI 0.50 to 1.01) for atenolol, 0.70 (0.43 to 1.15) for metoprolol, 0.65 (0.46 to 0.90) for propranolol and 0.51 (0.35 to 0.74) for nadolol. In LQT1, risk reduction for first cardiac events was similar among the four beta-blockers; in LQT2, nadolol provided the only significant risk reduction (hazard ratio 0.40 relative; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.98). Among patients who had a prior cardiac event while taking beta-blockers, efficacy for recurrent events differed by drug (P=0.004), and propranolol was the least effective compared with the other beta-blockers.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs through every number here: clinicians choose drugs for reasons (age, symptoms, era, genotype knowledge) that themselves predict events, and 'off beta-blocker' periods are not a randomised control. The individual-drug confidence intervals for atenolol and metoprolol cross 1.0, so the cleanest reading is a class effect with a nadolol advantage in LQT2 — not four separately proven drugs.
cards.source: Abu-Zeitone A et al. Efficacy of different beta-blockers in the treatment of long QT syndrome. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 25257637. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ahn 2017 meta-analysis (10 studies, 9,727 patients): nadolol reduced risk in both LQT1 (HR 0.47 relative) and LQT2 (HR 0.27 relative); metoprolol in neither
cards.summary: Ahn 2017 meta-analysis (10 studies, 9,727 patients): nadolol reduced risk in both LQT1 (HR 0.47 relative) and LQT2 (HR 0.27 relative); metoprolol in neither
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 10 studies (7 registry-based cohort studies and 3 interrupted time-series studies) involving 9,727 patients with congenital long QT syndrome treated with atenolol, nadolol, propranolol or metoprolol; outcomes were cardiac events (syncope, aborted cardiac arrest or sudden cardiac death) and serious cardiac events (aborted cardiac arrest or sudden cardiac death).
cards.result: Beta-blocker use was associated with significant reduction of all cardiac events (hazard ratio 0.49 relative, P<0.001 in cohort studies; relative risk 0.39, P<0.001 in interrupted time-series studies) and of serious cardiac events (HR 0.47 relative, P<0.001 in cohort studies). In both LQT1 and LQT2, risk was reduced with beta-blocker therapy in cohort studies (HR 0.59 relative in LQT1; HR 0.39 relative in LQT2) and in time-series studies (RR 0.29 relative in LQT1; RR 0.48 relative in LQT2). Among the drugs, nadolol showed significant risk reduction in both LQT1 and LQT2 (HR 0.47 and 0.27 relative, respectively), whereas atenolol and propranolol decreased risk only in LQT1 (HR 0.36 and 0.46 relative, respectively); metoprolol showed no significant reduction in either genotype. In LQT3, beta-blocker therapy was not as effective as in LQT1 or LQT2, but the data were insufficient for a conclusion.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of registries pools the same confounding as its parts, and several included cohorts overlap in source populations with the Rochester registry carded above — the two cards are not fully independent evidence. LQT3, where sodium-channel biology makes beta-blockade least plausible, remains genuinely unanswered.
cards.source: Ahn J et al. Effectiveness of beta-blockers depending on the genotype of congenital long-QT syndrome: A meta-analysis. PloS one. 2017. PMID: 29059199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a class effect everyone agrees on, a drug ranking only registries can offer — nadolol first across genotypes, metoprolol last, propranolol weakest after breakthrough events
cards.summary: Synthesis: a class effect everyone agrees on, a drug ranking only registries can offer — nadolol first across genotypes, metoprolol last, propranolol weakest after breakthrough events
cards.people: Observational evidence only: a 1,530-patient registry analysis comparing the four drugs head-to-head, and a 10-study meta-analysis of 9,727 patients by genotype. No randomised trial of beta-blockers in congenital long QT syndrome exists.
cards.result: First cardiac events versus no beta-blocker: nadolol HR 0.51 relative, propranolol 0.65, metoprolol 0.70, atenolol 0.71 (registry). By genotype (meta-analysis): nadolol significant in LQT1 (HR 0.47 relative) and LQT2 (HR 0.27 relative); atenolol and propranolol significant only in LQT1; metoprolol significant in neither; LQT3 inconclusive. Recurrent events on therapy: propranolol least effective (P=0.004 for drug differences). Mortality is inside the composite (sudden cardiac death is a component) but is not reported as a standalone drug-by-drug figure in either record. PROPOSED SPLIT — by genotype and by drug.
cards.watchOut: Because none of this is randomised, the ranking could partly reflect prescribing habits across four decades of registry practice rather than pharmacology alone; it is nonetheless the best comparative evidence that exists and is unlikely ever to be replaced by a trial. Tier C is set because the evidence is entirely observational.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abu-Zeitone A et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014 (PMID: 25257637); Ahn J et al. PloS one. 2017 (PMID: 29059199).

shelves.title: Flecainide added to beta-blockade in CPVT: exercise arrhythmias nearly abolished in a 14-patient crossover trial — suppression proven, survival inferred
shelves.question: In patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, does adding flecainide to beta-blockade reduce exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmias?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Death, Sudden, Cardiac/prevention & control · Defibrillators, Implantable · Drug Therapy, Combination · Exercise* · Exercise Test · Female · Flecainide/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Single-Blind Method · Tachycardia, Ventricular/drug therapy, physiopathology · Young Adult · Polymorphic Catecholaminergic Ventricular Tachycardia
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is a single small crossover trial: 14 patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and an implantable defibrillator (median age 16 years), all on maximally tolerated beta-blockade, received flecainide and placebo for 3 months each. The median exercise-test ventricular arrhythmia score (0 = no ectopy to 4 = nonsustained ventricular tachycardia) fell to 0 on flecainide versus 2.5 on placebo (P<0.01), with complete suppression of exercise-induced arrhythmia in 11 of 13 completers (85%), and no difference in overall or serious adverse events. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (7 retrospective cohorts plus this 1 trial; 333 patients, 152 treated with flecainide) points the same way: combination flecainide plus beta-blocker beat beta-blocker alone for arrhythmic events (relative risk 0.29; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.69) and symptomatic events (RR 0.36 relative; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.62). What neither source can show is the outcome that matters most — no deaths were reported among flecainide-treated patients in the meta-analysis, but the samples are far too small and the follow-up too short to prove a survival effect; the proven endpoint is suppression of exercise-provoked arrhythmia, a close surrogate in this disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding flecainide to beta-blockade very likely suppresses CPVT arrhythmias; whether it saves lives is inferred, not shown.

cards.headline: Kannankeril 2017: adding flecainide to beta-blockade cut the median exercise arrhythmia score to 0 versus 2.5 on placebo (P<0.01), with complete suppression in 85%
cards.summary: Kannankeril 2017: adding flecainide to beta-blockade cut the median exercise arrhythmia score to 0 versus 2.5 on placebo (P<0.01), with complete suppression in 85%
cards.people: 14 patients (7 male, 7 female; median age 16 years, IQR 15.0–22.5) with a clinical diagnosis of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, at 10 US sites; single-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial — maximally tolerated beta-blocker throughout, with 3 months of oral flecainide (dosed to therapeutic trough levels) and 3 months of placebo in random order separated by a 1-week washout; 13 patients completed the study; the endpoint was the worst ventricular arrhythmia on exercise testing, scored 0 (no ectopy) to 4 (nonsustained ventricular tachycardia).
cards.result: The median baseline exercise test score was 3.0 (range 0–4), with no difference between baseline and placebo (median 2.5; range 0–4). The median ventricular arrhythmia score during exercise was significantly reduced by flecainide (0 [range 0–2] versus 2.5 [range 0–4] for placebo; P<0.01), with complete suppression observed in 11 of 13 patients (85%). Overall and serious adverse events did not differ between the flecainide and placebo arms.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen completers and a surrogate endpoint: exercise-test ectopy is mechanistically central in CPVT, but the trial cannot speak to syncope, cardiac arrest or death, and a midtrial protocol change (noted in the record) plus single-blind design add fragility. Every participant also had a defibrillator, which is not universal in CPVT.
cards.source: Kannankeril PJ et al. Efficacy of Flecainide in the Treatment of Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28492868. Registry ID: NCT01117454. cards.headline: Wang 2019 meta-analysis (8 studies, 333 patients): flecainide plus beta-blocker beat beta-blocker alone for arrhythmic events (RR 0.29 relative) and symptomatic events (RR 0.36 relative)
cards.summary: Wang 2019 meta-analysis (8 studies, 333 patients): flecainide plus beta-blocker beat beta-blocker alone for arrhythmic events (RR 0.29 relative) and symptomatic events (RR 0.36 relative)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 retrospective cohort studies and 1 randomised trial in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, totalling 333 patients, of whom 152 were treated with flecainide (as monotherapy or combined with beta-blockers).
cards.result: Combination therapy with flecainide and beta-blockers was superior to beta-blocker monotherapy in reducing the risk of arrhythmic events (relative risk 0.29; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.69; P=0.005) and symptomatic events (RR 0.36 relative; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.62; P=0.0003), peak heart rate (mean difference −16.81; 95% CI −28.21 to −5.41; P=0.004) and exercise-induced arrhythmia scores (mean difference −1.87; 95% CI −2.71 to 1.04 as printed in the record; P<0.0001). Flecainide monotherapy was superior to standard therapy for arrhythmic events (RR 0.46 relative; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.56; P<0.00001). Flecainide did not increase the risk of all side effects compared with beta-blockers alone (RR 0.76 relative; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.40; P=0.38). No deaths were reported among patients treated with flecainide.
cards.watchOut: Seven of the eight studies are retrospective cohorts, where flecainide is typically added after beta-blocker failure — a design that can flatter or penalise the drug depending on how events before the switch are counted. 'No deaths reported' in 152 treated patients is reassurance about reporting, not a mortality result.
cards.source: Wang G et al. Safety and efficacy of flecainide for patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31441899. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: arrhythmia suppression is consistent across the one trial and the pooled cohorts; survival benefit remains an inference from a surrogate
cards.summary: Synthesis: arrhythmia suppression is consistent across the one trial and the pooled cohorts; survival benefit remains an inference from a surrogate
cards.people: One randomised crossover trial (14 randomised, 13 completers, all with defibrillators, median age 16) plus a meta-analysis of 8 studies and 333 patients, in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on background beta-blockade.
cards.result: Exercise arrhythmia score: median 0 on flecainide versus 2.5 on placebo (P<0.01); complete suppression in 85% of completers. Pooled clinical events: arrhythmic events RR 0.29 relative and symptomatic events RR 0.36 relative for flecainide plus beta-blocker versus beta-blocker alone. Adverse events: no excess in either source. Deaths: none reported among flecainide-treated patients in the pooled record — too few patients to estimate a mortality effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The exercise-score confidence interval in the meta-analysis record is printed as −2.71 to 1.04 alongside P<0.0001, which is internally inconsistent — the point estimate and direction are used here, the interval should not be quoted. Tier C is set because the only randomised trial enrolled 14 patients.

shelves.title: Stent everything today or stage it? Immediate completion won both big trials' composites — and the pooled record flags more early cardiac deaths with doing it all at once
shelves.question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease, does immediate complete revascularisation at the index procedure match staged complete revascularisation on death, myocardial infarction and unplanned revascularisation?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Aged · Female · Coronary Artery Disease* · Acute Coronary Syndrome*/surgery, etiology · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention*/methods · Prospective Studies · Myocardial Infarction*/etiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two large trials and the pooled record pull in different directions on different outcomes. In BIOVASC (1,525 patients with STEMI or non-ST acute coronary syndrome), immediate complete revascularisation was non-inferior to staged on the 1-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation or cerebrovascular events (7.6% versus 9.4%; HR 0.78 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.11), with fewer infarctions (1.9% versus 4.5%; HR 0.41 relative) but numerically more deaths (1.9% versus 1.2%; HR 1.56 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.61). In MULTISTARS AMI (840 haemodynamically stable STEMI patients), immediate multivessel PCI clearly won its composite (8.5% versus 16.3%; risk ratio 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.72), driven by fewer infarctions and revascularisations, with death, stroke and heart-failure hospitalisation similar. Against that, the updated meta-analysis of 9 trials and 4,213 STEMI patients found short-term all-cause mortality of 2.0% after immediate versus 1.2% after staged complete revascularisation (risk ratio 1.66 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.78; P=0.053) and significantly increased short-term cardiac death (RR 2.19 relative, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.44), concluding that the pooled data currently favour staging for most patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: on composite endpoints immediate completion is at least as good and prevents early infarctions and repeat procedures; on the pooled early-mortality signal, staging looks safer — the honest answer depends on which outcome you weight.

cards.headline: BIOVASC 2023: immediate complete revascularisation non-inferior at 1 year (7.6% vs 9.4%), with fewer MIs (1.9% vs 4.5%) but numerically more deaths (1.9% vs 1.2%)
cards.summary: BIOVASC 2023: immediate complete revascularisation non-inferior at 1 year (7.6% vs 9.4%), with fewer MIs (1.9% vs 4.5%) but numerically more deaths (1.9% vs 1.2%)
cards.people: 1,525 patients aged 18–85 presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction or non-ST-segment acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease (two or more arteries ≥2.5 mm with ≥70% stenosis or positive physiology) with an identifiable culprit lesion, at 29 hospitals in Belgium, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain; open-label non-inferiority trial of immediate complete revascularisation (764) versus staged completion within 6 weeks (761).
cards.result: The primary outcome (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, any unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation, or cerebrovascular events at 1 year) occurred in 57 patients (7.6%) in the immediate group and 71 (9.4%) in the staged group (hazard ratio 0.78 relative; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.11; P for non-inferiority = 0.0011, against a margin of 1.39). All-cause death did not differ (14 patients [1.9%] versus 9 [1.2%]; HR 1.56 relative; 95% CI 0.68 to 3.61; P=0.30). Myocardial infarction occurred in 14 patients (1.9%) versus 34 (4.5%) (HR 0.41 relative; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.76; P=0.0045). Unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation was also less frequent with immediate treatment (31 patients [4.2%] versus 50 [6.7%]; HR 0.61 relative; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.95; P=0.030).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on a composite can hide opposite movements in its parts — here infarction and revascularisation favoured immediate treatment while death numerically favoured staging, and the trial was not powered to resolve the death difference (HR 1.56 relative with a confidence interval reaching 3.61). The staged window was up to 6 weeks, longer than in MULTISTARS AMI.
cards.source: Diletti R et al. cards.headline: MULTISTARS AMI 2023: immediate multivessel PCI halved the 1-year composite (8.5% vs 16.3%; RR 0.52 relative), with death, stroke and heart-failure admission similar
cards.summary: MULTISTARS AMI 2023: immediate multivessel PCI halved the 1-year composite (8.5% vs 16.3%; RR 0.52 relative), with death, stroke and heart-failure admission similar
cards.people: 840 haemodynamically stable patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel coronary artery disease at 37 European sites; open-label non-inferiority trial of immediate multivessel PCI (418) versus culprit-only PCI followed by staged multivessel PCI within 19–45 days (422); primary endpoint was death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation or heart-failure hospitalisation at 1 year (Kaplan-Meier estimates).
cards.result: A primary end-point event occurred in 35 patients (8.5%) in the immediate group versus 68 (16.3%) in the staged group (risk ratio 0.52 relative; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.72; P<0.001 for non-inferiority and P<0.001 for superiority). Nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 8 patients (2.0%) versus 22 (5.3%), and unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation in 17 (4.1%) versus 39 (9.3%). The risk of death from any cause, the risk of stroke, and the risk of hospitalisation for heart failure appeared similar in the two groups. Serious adverse events occurred in 104 patients in the immediate group and 145 in the staged group.
cards.watchOut: Much of the staged group's disadvantage accrues before the staged procedure happens — events in the 19–45 day waiting window count against staging, which is partly the question being asked and partly a design feature. Only haemodynamically stable STEMI patients were enrolled, so nothing here applies to shock or instability.

cards.headline: Elbahloul 2026 meta-analysis (9 trials, 4,213 patients): short-term cardiac death was higher after immediate completion (RR 2.19 relative) — pooled data favour staging for most patients
cards.summary: Elbahloul 2026 meta-analysis (9 trials, 4,213 patients): short-term cardiac death was higher after immediate completion (RR 2.19 relative) — pooled data favour staging for most patients
cards.people: Updated meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (4,213 patients) comparing immediate versus staged complete revascularisation in ST-elevation myocardial infarction with multivessel disease; primary endpoints were short-term and long-term all-cause mortality, reported as risk ratios (short-term) and incidence rate ratios (long-term).
cards.result: Short-term all-cause mortality occurred in 2.0% of patients after immediate complete revascularisation versus 1.2% after staged (risk ratio 1.66 relative; 95% CI 0.99 to 2.78; P=0.053; I²=0%). Short-term cardiac death was increased after immediate treatment (RR 2.19 relative; 95% CI 1.08 to 4.44; P=0.03; I²=0%). At a median 1-year follow-up, all-cause mortality was 4.7% versus 3.5% (incidence rate ratio 1.40 relative; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.03; P=0.07). No significant differences were found for myocardial infarction, repeat revascularisation, stent thrombosis, stroke, major bleeding or the composite of major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events. The authors conclude that an immediate strategy may increase short-term cardiac death and that the results currently favour a staged strategy for most patients.
cards.watchOut: The mortality signal rests on small absolute numbers (2.0% versus 1.2% short-term) pooled across trials with different staged windows and different composite definitions, and the all-cause mortality comparisons themselves did not reach significance (P=0.053 and P=0.07). It is a caution flag against the two big trials' composites, not a refutation of them — which is exactly why this shelf is a split.
cards.source: Elbahloul MA et al. Timing of Complete Revascularization in Patients With STEMI and Multivessel Disease: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. Circulation. cards.headline: Synthesis: immediate completion wins the composites and the waiting-window events; the pooled early-death signal is the one finding that points the other way
cards.summary: Synthesis: immediate completion wins the composites and the waiting-window events; the pooled early-death signal is the one finding that points the other way
cards.people: Two large randomised trials (BIOVASC 1,525 mixed acute coronary syndrome; MULTISTARS AMI 840 stable STEMI) plus an updated meta-analysis of 9 trials and 4,213 STEMI patients, all comparing immediate with staged complete revascularisation of multivessel disease.
cards.result: Composites at 1 year: 7.6% versus 9.4% (BIOVASC, non-inferior) and 8.5% versus 16.3% (MULTISTARS AMI, RR 0.52 relative). Myocardial infarction consistently favoured immediate treatment (1.9% vs 4.5%; 2.0% vs 5.3%). Mortality: no significant difference within either large trial, but pooled short-term cardiac death was higher with immediate treatment (RR 2.19 relative, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.44) and pooled 1-year all-cause mortality leaned the same way (4.7% vs 3.5%, not significant). PROPOSED SPLIT — by outcome: composites and infarctions favour immediate; the pooled early-mortality signal favours staged.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers only the timing question — whether to complete revascularisation at all is housed with the complete-versus-culprit-only shelves. Populations differ across the three cards (mixed ACS versus stable STEMI only), and no card includes cardiogenic shock. Tier C is not set: two large randomised trials plus a 9-trial meta-analysis are a substantial base, even though they disagree.
cards.source: Synthesis of Diletti R et al. Lancet (London, England). 2023 (PMID: 36889333); Stähli BE et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37634190); Elbahloul MA et al. Circulation. Cardiovascular interventions. 2026 (PMID: 42059073).

shelves.title: FFR-guided PCI versus bypass in three-vessel disease: FAME 3's answer was no — 10.6% versus 6.9% for death, MI, stroke or repeat revascularisation at one year
shelves.question: In patients with three-vessel coronary disease without left main involvement, does FFR-guided PCI match coronary artery bypass grafting on death, myocardial infarction or stroke at one year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Coronary Artery Bypass*/adverse effects · Coronary Stenosis/mortality, surgery · Female · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial* · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Operative Time · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects, methods · Reoperation · Stents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — FAME 3 asked the strongest version of the PCI question: in 1,500 patients with three-vessel disease (left main excluded), PCI guided by fractional flow reserve with current-generation stents was compared with CABG in a non-inferiority design, and it failed. The 1-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or repeat revascularisation occurred in 10.6% with PCI versus 6.9% with CABG (hazard ratio 1.5 relative; 95% CI 1.1 to 2.2; P=0.35 for non-inferiority, against a prespecified margin of 1.65 for the upper confidence bound) — that is 3.7 percentage points more events in absolute terms with PCI. The harder composite of death, infarction or stroke was 7.3% versus 5.2% (HR 1.4 relative; 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1). Surgery paid its usual upfront price: major bleeding, arrhythmia and acute kidney injury were all more frequent in the CABG group, and PCI patients received a mean of 3.7 stents. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — for PCI as the strategy: even with physiology guidance and modern stents, PCI did not match bypass surgery at one year in three-vessel disease; the harm framing applies to choosing PCI expecting equivalence, not to PCI where surgery is not an option.

cards.headline: FAME 3 2022: FFR-guided PCI was NOT non-inferior to CABG — 1-year death, MI, stroke or repeat revascularisation 10.6% versus 6.9% (HR 1.5 relative)
cards.summary: FAME 3 2022: FFR-guided PCI was NOT non-inferior to CABG — 1-year death, MI, stroke or repeat revascularisation 10.6% versus 6.9% (HR 1.5 relative)
cards.people: 1,500 patients with three-vessel coronary artery disease (no left main involvement) randomised at 48 centres to CABG or to FFR-guided PCI with current-generation zotarolimus-eluting stents; multicentre international non-inferiority trial with a prespecified non-inferiority upper boundary of 1.65 for the 95% confidence interval of the hazard ratio; primary endpoint was a major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event within 1 year.
cards.result: The 1-year incidence of the composite primary endpoint was 10.6% with FFR-guided PCI and 6.9% with CABG (hazard ratio 1.5 relative; 95% CI 1.1 to 2.2), which was not consistent with non-inferiority of FFR-guided PCI (P=0.35 for non-inferiority). The incidence of death, myocardial infarction or stroke was 7.3% in the PCI group and 5.2% in the CABG group (HR 1.4 relative; 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1). Patients assigned to PCI received a mean of 3.7±1.9 stents; those assigned to CABG received 3.4±1.0 distal anastomoses. Major bleeding, arrhythmia and acute kidney injury were more frequent in the CABG group than in the PCI group.
cards.watchOut: One year is early in a CABG-versus-PCI comparison — surgical benefit in earlier trials grew with time, and repeat revascularisation (the softest component) is where PCI typically loses most. Conversely, patients or anatomy unsuitable for either strategy were not randomised, and diabetes and lesion-complexity subgroups matter clinically even though the record's abstract does not report them.
cards.source: Fearon WF et al. Fractional Flow Reserve-Guided PCI as Compared with Coronary Bypass Surgery. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 34735046. Registry ID: NCT02100722. cards.headline: Synthesis: the best-case PCI strategy — physiology-guided, modern stents — still lost to bypass at one year in three-vessel disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the best-case PCI strategy — physiology-guided, modern stents — still lost to bypass at one year in three-vessel disease
cards.people: The randomised record for this exact question is FAME 3 alone: 1,500 patients with three-vessel disease without left main involvement, FFR-guided PCI versus CABG, 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: Primary composite: 10.6% PCI versus 6.9% CABG (HR 1.5 relative, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.2; non-inferiority not met). Death, MI or stroke: 7.3% versus 5.2% (HR 1.4 relative, 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1). Early hazards (major bleeding, arrhythmia, acute kidney injury) were higher with CABG. Mortality alone was not separately reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for FFR-guided PCI relative to CABG in this population.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge with the left-main PCI-versus-CABG shelf — FAME 3 deliberately excluded left main disease, and the two populations have different evidence and different answers. Tier C is set per the assignment flag: one trial, one year of follow-up, for a decision whose consequences run for decades.

shelves.title: Cangrelor at PCI: fewer clots and stent thromboses in the first 48 hours (4.7% vs 5.9%), no more severe bleeding — and no mortality claim anywhere in the record
shelves.question: In patients undergoing PCI who are not pre-treated with oral P2Y12 inhibitors, does intravenous cangrelor, compared with clopidogrel, reduce periprocedural ischaemic events without excess severe bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine Monophosphate/adverse effects, analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary*/adverse effects · Clopidogrel · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hemorrhage/etiology · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/mortality, therapy · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Stents/adverse effects · Thrombosis/mortality, prevention & control · Ticlopidine/adverse effects, analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in CHAMPION PHOENIX (11,145 patients undergoing urgent or elective PCI who had not been pre-treated), intravenous cangrelor reduced the 48-hour composite of death, myocardial infarction, ischaemia-driven revascularisation or stent thrombosis from 5.9% with clopidogrel loading to 4.7% (adjusted odds ratio 0.78 relative; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; P=0.005) — a 22% relative reduction, 1.2 percentage points absolute — and stent thrombosis from 1.4% to 0.8% (OR 0.62 relative; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90). Severe bleeding at 48 hours was 0.16% versus 0.11% (OR 1.50 relative; 95% CI 0.53 to 4.22; P=0.44), not significantly different, though transient dyspnoea was more common with cangrelor (1.2% versus 0.3%). The prespecified patient-level pooled analysis of all three CHAMPION trials (24,910 patients, comparators clopidogrel or placebo) found the same shape: primary outcome 3.8% versus 4.7% (OR 0.81 relative; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.91), stent thrombosis 0.5% versus 0.8% (OR 0.59 relative), no difference in severe or life-threatening bleeding (0.2% in both groups), but more mild bleeding (16.8% versus 13.0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cangrelor prevents early periprocedural ischaemic events, mostly periprocedural infarction and stent thrombosis, at the cost of more minor bleeding; neither record shows a mortality difference.

cards.headline: CHAMPION PHOENIX 2013: cangrelor cut 48-hour death, MI, revascularisation or stent thrombosis to 4.7% versus 5.9% with clopidogrel (OR 0.78 relative), severe bleeding unchanged
cards.summary: CHAMPION PHOENIX 2013: cangrelor cut 48-hour death, MI, revascularisation or stent thrombosis to 4.7% versus 5.9% with clopidogrel (OR 0.78 relative), severe bleeding unchanged
cards.people: 11,145 patients undergoing urgent or elective PCI receiving guideline-recommended therapy, randomised double-blind to a bolus and infusion of intravenous cangrelor or to a loading dose of clopidogrel (600 mg or 300 mg); primary efficacy endpoint was the composite of death, myocardial infarction, ischaemia-driven revascularisation or stent thrombosis at 48 hours; primary safety endpoint was severe bleeding at 48 hours.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint occurred in 4.7% of the cangrelor group and 5.9% of the clopidogrel group (adjusted odds ratio 0.78 relative; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; P=0.005) — a 22% relative reduction, 1.2 percentage points absolute. Stent thrombosis developed in 0.8% versus 1.4% (OR 0.62 relative; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90; P=0.01). The primary safety endpoint (severe bleeding) was 0.16% versus 0.11% (OR 1.50 relative; 95% CI 0.53 to 4.22; P=0.44). Adverse events related to treatment were low in both groups, though transient dyspnoea occurred more frequently with cangrelor (1.2% versus 0.3%). The benefit was consistent across prespecified subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint window is 48 hours and the composite is dominated by periprocedural myocardial infarction, whose definition in PCI trials is contested; the comparator was clopidogrel loading given at the time of PCI, not the more potent oral agents or pre-treatment strategies used in much contemporary practice. A 48-hour ischaemic gain with no demonstrated mortality effect is a procedural tool, not a prognostic therapy.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Effect of platelet inhibition with cangrelor during PCI on ischemic events. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23473369. Registry ID: NCT01156571.
