cards.headline: Steg 2013 pooled patient-level analysis (3 CHAMPION trials, 24,910 patients): primary outcome 3.8% versus 4.7% (OR 0.81 relative), stent thrombosis nearly halved, severe bleeding identical
cards.summary: Steg 2013 pooled patient-level analysis (3 CHAMPION trials, 24,910 patients): primary outcome 3.8% versus 4.7% (OR 0.81 relative), stent thrombosis nearly halved, severe bleeding identical
cards.people: Prespecified pooled analysis of patient-level data from the three double-blind CHAMPION trials (CHAMPION-PCI, CHAMPION-PLATFORM and CHAMPION-PHOENIX) comparing cangrelor with control (clopidogrel or placebo) in 24,910 patients undergoing PCI for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (11.6%), non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes (57.4%) or stable coronary disease (31.0%); efficacy assessed in the modified intention-to-treat population at 48 hours.
cards.result: Cangrelor reduced the odds of the primary outcome (death, myocardial infarction, ischaemia-driven revascularisation or stent thrombosis at 48 hours) by 19% relative (3.8% versus 4.7%; odds ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.91; P=0.0007), and stent thrombosis by 41% relative (0.5% versus 0.8%; OR 0.59; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.80; P=0.0008). The triple composite of death, myocardial infarction or ischaemia-driven revascularisation was also reduced by 19% relative (3.6% versus 4.4%; OR 0.81; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.92). Benefits were maintained at 30 days. There was no difference in the primary safety outcome of non-CABG-related GUSTO severe or life-threatening bleeding (0.2% in both groups), GUSTO moderate bleeding (0.6% versus 0.4%) or transfusion (0.7% versus 0.6%), but cangrelor increased GUSTO mild bleeding (16.8% versus 13.0%; P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Two of the three pooled trials used placebo or clopidogrel strategies that were stopped or designed differently from PHOENIX, and pooling them mixes comparators; the consistent direction is reassuring, but the pooled estimate should not be read as a fourth trial. Mild bleeding at 16.8% is common enough to matter for patient experience even when severe bleeding is unchanged.
cards.source: Steg PG et al. Effect of cangrelor on periprocedural outcomes in percutaneous coronary interventions: a pooled analysis of patient-level data. Lancet (London, England). 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent early ischaemic benefit across 36,000 randomised patients, bought with minor bleeding, with mortality untouched in every record
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent early ischaemic benefit across 36,000 randomised patients, bought with minor bleeding, with mortality untouched in every record
cards.people: CHAMPION PHOENIX (11,145 patients, cangrelor versus clopidogrel loading at PCI) plus the prespecified pooled analysis of all three CHAMPION trials (24,910 patients, versus clopidogrel or placebo), in patients not pre-treated with oral P2Y12 inhibitors.
cards.result: 48-hour primary composite: 4.7% versus 5.9% (PHOENIX, OR 0.78 relative) and 3.8% versus 4.7% (pooled, OR 0.81 relative). Stent thrombosis: 0.8% versus 1.4% and 0.5% versus 0.8% respectively. Severe bleeding: no significant difference in either record (0.16% vs 0.11%; 0.2% vs 0.2%); mild bleeding increased in the pooled analysis (16.8% vs 13.0%). Mortality: no difference reported in either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The pooled analysis includes CHAMPION PHOENIX, so the two cards overlap rather than independently replicate. Tier C is set per the assignment flag, reflecting the 48-hour surrogate-heavy endpoint and a clopidogrel-era comparator rather than any inconsistency in the results.

shelves.title: IV metoprolol before the artery opens: smaller infarcts in early anterior STEMI, nothing at all in the larger all-comer trial — a split verdict by phenotype
shelves.question: In patients with anterior STEMI undergoing primary PCI, does early intravenous metoprolol before reperfusion reduce infarct size and improve left ventricular function?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Biomarkers · Cardiotonic Agents/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Creatine Kinase, MB Form/blood · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Heart Failure/prevention & control · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Metoprolol/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy, pathology, physiopathology, surgery · Myocardium/pathology · Necrosis · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention* · Premedication* · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Thrombolytic Therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by trial and by population. METOCARD-CNIC (270 patients with anterior STEMI, Killip class II or less, treated within 6 hours) found that intravenous metoprolol before reperfusion reduced infarct size on magnetic resonance imaging at 5–7 days (25.6±15.3 g versus 32.0±22.2 g; adjusted difference −6.52 g; 95% CI −11.39 to −1.78; P=0.012) and modestly raised ejection fraction (adjusted difference 2.67%; 95% CI 0.09 to 5.21; P=0.045), with no excess of the 24-hour composite of death, malignant arrhythmia, shock, heart block or reinfarction (7.1% versus 12.3%; P=0.21). EARLY-BAMI — larger (683 patients), double-blind and placebo-controlled, in an unselected STEMI population — found nothing: infarct size by magnetic resonance at 30 days was 15.3±11.0% of the left ventricle on metoprolol versus 14.9±11.5% on placebo (P=0.616), enzyme release and ejection fraction were the same, though malignant arrhythmias were fewer (3.6% versus 6.9%; P=0.050). The 2022 meta-analysis of 8 trials pools its way back to a positive average (infarcted myocardium lower by a mean 3.84 g at 6 months; ejection fraction higher by 3.57 points), but pooling cannot erase the fact that the one large blinded trial in a general STEMI population was neutral. PROPOSED SPLIT: a benefit is plausible in early-presenting anterior STEMI without heart failure — the METOCARD phenotype — and unproven for STEMI at large.

cards.headline: METOCARD-CNIC 2013: early IV metoprolol shrank infarct size in anterior STEMI (25.6 vs 32.0 g; adjusted difference −6.52 g, P=0.012) and raised ejection fraction
cards.summary: METOCARD-CNIC 2013: early IV metoprolol shrank infarct size in anterior STEMI (25.6 vs 32.0 g; adjusted difference −6.52 g, P=0.012) and raised ejection fraction
cards.people: 270 patients with Killip class II or less anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention within 6 hours of symptom onset, randomised to intravenous metoprolol before reperfusion (131) or control (139); all patients without contraindications received oral metoprolol within 24 hours; the primary endpoint was infarct size on magnetic resonance imaging at 5–7 days, performed in 220 patients (81%). Single-blind trial.
cards.result: Mean infarct size by magnetic resonance imaging was smaller after intravenous metoprolol (25.6±15.3 g versus 32.0±22.2 g; adjusted difference −6.52; 95% CI −11.39 to −1.78; P=0.012). In patients with pre-PCI TIMI grade 0–1 flow, the adjusted difference was −8.13 (95% CI −13.10 to −3.16; P=0.0024). Infarct size estimated by peak and area-under-the-curve creatine kinase release was significantly reduced in all study populations. Left ventricular ejection fraction was higher with intravenous metoprolol (adjusted difference 2.67%; 95% CI 0.09 to 5.21; P=0.045). The composite of death, malignant ventricular arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock, atrioventricular block and reinfarction at 24 hours was 7.1% versus 12.3% (P=0.21).
cards.watchOut: A single-blind trial with imaging in only 81% of patients, restricted to anterior infarcts presenting early with Killip class II or less — precisely the phenotype with the most salvageable myocardium and the least beta-blocker risk. The ejection-fraction confidence interval (0.09 to 5.21) only just excludes zero, and no clinical-outcome benefit was shown.
cards.source: Ibanez B et al. Effect of early metoprolol on infarct size in ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention: the Effect of Metoprolol in Cardioprotection During an Acute Myocardial Infarction (METOCARD-CNIC) trial. cards.headline: EARLY-BAMI 2016: the larger double-blind placebo-controlled trial found no infarct-size benefit at all (15.3% vs 14.9% of the left ventricle, P=0.616)
cards.summary: EARLY-BAMI 2016: the larger double-blind placebo-controlled trial found no infarct-size benefit at all (15.3% vs 14.9% of the left ventricle, P=0.616)
cards.people: 683 patients (mean age 62±12 years, 75% male) with ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting within 12 hours, Killip class I–II without atrioventricular block, randomised 1:1 to intravenous metoprolol (two 5-mg boluses; 336 patients) or matched placebo (346) before primary PCI, in the Netherlands and Spain; infarct size was assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance at 30 days in 342 patients. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, international multicentre trial.
cards.result: Infarct size (percent of left ventricle) by magnetic resonance did not differ between metoprolol (15.3±11.0%) and placebo (14.9±11.5%; P=0.616). Peak and area-under-the-curve creatine kinase did not differ between groups. Left ventricular ejection fraction by magnetic resonance was 51.0±10.9% with metoprolol and 51.6±10.8% with placebo (P=0.68). Malignant arrhythmias occurred in 3.6% of the metoprolol group versus 6.9% with placebo (P=0.050). Adverse events — symptomatic bradycardia, symptomatic hypotension and cardiogenic shock — did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only about half the randomised patients had the magnetic-resonance primary endpoint measured, and the enrolled population (any STEMI location, up to 12 hours) dilutes the anterior, early phenotype in which METOCARD-CNIC was positive — so EARLY-BAMI refutes a general claim more cleanly than it refutes the narrow one. The arrhythmia difference sits exactly at P=0.050.
cards.source: Roolvink V et al. Early Intravenous Beta-Blockers in Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Before Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention. cards.headline: Motawea 2022 meta-analysis (8 trials): pooled infarct size was lower and ejection fraction higher with early metoprolol — an average its largest blinded trial does not share
cards.summary: Motawea 2022 meta-analysis (8 trials): pooled infarct size was lower and ejection fraction higher with early metoprolol — an average its largest blinded trial does not share
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of early intravenous metoprolol in ST-elevation myocardial infarction before PCI, with infarct size measured by cardiac magnetic resonance and left ventricular ejection fraction; 18 studies were included in the systematic review and 8 clinical trials in the meta-analysis.
cards.result: At 6 months, metoprolol was associated with increased left ventricular ejection fraction compared with controls (mean difference 3.57; 95% CI 2.22 to 4.92; P<0.00001) and decreased infarcted myocardium in grams (mean difference −3.84; 95% CI −5.75 to −1.93; P<0.0001). At 1 week, metoprolol was likewise associated with increased ejection fraction (mean difference 2.98; 95% CI 1.26 to 4.69; P=0.0007) and decreased infarcted myocardium in percent (mean difference −3.21; 95% CI −5.24 to −1.18; P=0.002). All endpoints are imaging surrogates; no pooled mortality or heart-failure result is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Pooling many small, variably blinded imaging trials can manufacture a precise average that the single large double-blind trial contradicts; the meta-analysis also mixes measurement times (1 week, 6 months) and infarct-size units. It is carded because it is the pooled record, and its tension with EARLY-BAMI is the reason this shelf carries a split stamp.
cards.source: Motawea KR et al. Effect of early metoprolol before PCI in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction on infarct size and left ventricular ejection fraction. systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 rcts (motawea 2022) systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of early intravenous metoprolol in st-elevation myocardial infarction before pci, with infarct size measured by cardiac magnetic resonance and left ventricular ejection fraction; 18 studies were included in the systematic review and 8 clinical trials in the meta-analysis. at 6 months, metoprolol was associated with increased left ventricular ejection fraction compared with controls (mean difference 3.57; 95% ci 2.22 to 4.92; p<0.00001) and decreased infarcted myocardium in grams (mean difference −3.84; 95% ci −5.75 to −1.93; p<0.0001). at 1 week, metoprolol was likewise associated with increased ejection fraction (mean difference 2.98; 95% ci 1.26 to 4.69; p=0.0007) and decreased infarcted myocardium in percent (mean difference −3.21; 95% ci −5.24 to −1.18; p=0.002). all endpoints are imaging surrogates; no pooled mortality or heart-failure result is reported in the record. pooling many small, variably blinded imaging trials can manufacture a precise average that the single large double-blind trial contradicts; the meta-analysis also mixes measurement times (1 week, 6 months) and infarct-size units. it is carded because it is the pooled record, and its tension with early-bami is the reason this shelf carries a split stamp. motawea kr et al. effect of early metoprolol before pci in st-segment elevation myocardial infarction on infarct size and left ventricular ejection fraction. a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials. clinical cardiology. 2022. pmid: 36040709. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · metoprolol/therapeutic use · myocardial infarction*/drug therapy · percutaneous coronary intervention*/adverse effects · st elevation myocardial infarction*/drug therapy, therapy · stroke volume · ventricular function, left

cards.headline: Synthesis: positive in early anterior STEMI, neutral in all-comer STEMI, positive again only when small trials are pooled — the phenotype is the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: positive in early anterior STEMI, neutral in all-comer STEMI, positive again only when small trials are pooled — the phenotype is the answer
cards.people: Two randomised trials (METOCARD-CNIC, 270 anterior STEMI patients; EARLY-BAMI, 683 unselected STEMI patients) plus an 8-trial meta-analysis, all testing intravenous metoprolol before primary PCI with imaging endpoints.
cards.result: Infarct size: reduced in METOCARD-CNIC (adjusted difference −6.52 g; P=0.012); unchanged in EARLY-BAMI (15.3% vs 14.9% of left ventricle; P=0.616); reduced in the pooled analysis (mean difference −3.84 g at 6 months). Ejection fraction: +2.67 points (METOCARD-CNIC), no difference (EARLY-BAMI), +3.57 points pooled at 6 months. Safety: no excess bradycardia, hypotension or shock in EARLY-BAMI; 24-hour clinical composite not significantly different in METOCARD-CNIC. Mortality: not demonstrated in any card. PROPOSED SPLIT — by population: early anterior STEMI versus STEMI in general.
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint on this shelf is an imaging surrogate; no trial here was powered for death or heart failure, so even the positive reading is 'smaller scars in a selected phenotype', not 'better outcomes'. Tier C is not set: the base is two randomised trials and a meta-analysis, but their disagreement is the finding.

shelves.title: Remote ischaemic conditioning in STEMI: the cuff cycles were safe and the 5,401-patient answer was no — 9.4% versus 8.6% for cardiac death or heart-failure admission
shelves.question: In patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing PCI, does remote ischaemic conditioning reduce cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Death, Sudden, Cardiac/prevention & control · Female · Heart Failure/etiology · Hospitalization · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Ischemic Preconditioning, Myocardial/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/complications, surgery, therapy · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention* · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit not shown) — remote ischaemic conditioning is the cleanest negative on this shelf's run of shelves. In CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI, 5,401 patients with suspected STEMI eligible for primary PCI were randomised to four cycles of arm-cuff inflation/deflation before PCI or standard treatment; in the intention-to-treat population (5,115 patients), cardiac death or hospitalisation for heart failure at 12 months occurred in 9.4% of the conditioning group versus 8.6% of controls (hazard ratio 1.10 relative; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.32) — the point estimate favours the control arm. No important unexpected adverse events were observed; the intervention is safe, it simply does not work on clinical outcomes. The updated meta-analysis (12 trials, 8,239 patients, 816 major adverse events) explains the history: earlier meta-analyses were positive, but once the three newest trials including CONDI-2 (5,712 patients) are added, the pooled effect on composite clinical endpoints is null (odds ratio 0.77 relative; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; P=0.105), and the pooled result only becomes significant if CONDI-2 itself is removed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit not shown): a biologically elegant idea that reduced infarct size in small studies and then failed, definitively, at clinical-outcome scale.

cards.headline: CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI 2019: cardiac death or heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months was 9.4% with remote conditioning versus 8.6% control (HR 1.10 relative) — a clear null in 5,401 patients
cards.summary: CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI 2019: cardiac death or heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months was 9.4% with remote conditioning versus 8.6% control (HR 1.10 relative) — a clear null in 5,401 patients
cards.people: 5,401 patients (age >18 years) with suspected ST-elevation myocardial infarction eligible for primary PCI at 33 centres in the UK, Denmark, Spain and Serbia, randomised to remote ischaemic conditioning (2,700; four cycles of 5-minute arm-cuff inflation and 5-minute deflation before PCI) or standard treatment including a sham procedure at UK sites (2,701); single-blind trial with masked outcome assessment; intention-to-treat population 5,115 patients (2,546 conditioning, 2,569 control).
cards.result: At 12 months, the Kaplan-Meier-estimated frequency of cardiac death or hospitalisation for heart failure (the primary endpoint) was 239 patients (9.4%) in the remote conditioning group and 220 (8.6%) in the control group (hazard ratio 1.10 relative; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.32). No important unexpected adverse events or side effects of remote ischaemic conditioning were observed. The authors conclude that remote ischaemic conditioning does not improve clinical outcomes at 12 months in patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI.
cards.watchOut: This is a well-powered null, not an underpowered shrug: the confidence interval (0.91 to 1.32) excludes any large benefit and the point estimate leans the wrong way. Earlier small positive infarct-size studies do not rescue the clinical claim — they are the reason the large trial was done.
cards.source: Hausenloy DJ et al. cards.headline: Borracci 2021 updated meta-analysis (12 trials, 8,239 patients): no significant effect on clinical outcomes (OR 0.77 relative, P=0.105) — significance returns only if CONDI-2 is removed
cards.summary: Borracci 2021 updated meta-analysis (12 trials, 8,239 patients): no significant effect on clinical outcomes (OR 0.77 relative, P=0.105) — significance returns only if CONDI-2 is removed
cards.people: Updated meta-analysis of randomised trials of any form of remote ischaemic conditioning in ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention, including three new trials (5,712 patients) published after earlier positive meta-analyses; 12 trials, 8,239 patients, 816 major adverse cardiovascular events, follow-up 1–45 months.
cards.result: The random-effects model showed no significant effect of remote ischaemic conditioning on composite clinical endpoints (odds ratio 0.77 relative; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; P=0.105; heterogeneity Q=18.8, P=0.065, I²=41.5%). Sensitivity analysis demonstrated that only the exclusion of the CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI trial modified the significance of the global effect (OR 0.66 relative; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93), favouring the intervention. The authors conclude that remote conditioning added no significant benefit for clinical outcomes assessed between 6 and 45 months, in direct contrast to previously published meta-analyses.
cards.watchOut: A pooled result whose significance depends entirely on deleting its largest, most rigorous trial is not evidence of benefit — it is a measurement of small-study effects. The meta-analysis is carded because it documents exactly how the field's earlier positive consensus dissolved.
cards.source: Borracci RA et al. Acta cardiologica. 2021. PMID: 32619160. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: small-study infarct-size promise, large-trial clinical null — remote conditioning in STEMI is a closed question at outcome scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: small-study infarct-size promise, large-trial clinical null — remote conditioning in STEMI is a closed question at outcome scale
cards.people: One large international randomised trial (5,401 randomised, 5,115 analysed) plus an updated meta-analysis of 12 trials and 8,239 patients, in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI.
cards.result: Primary clinical outcome (cardiac death or heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months): 9.4% conditioning versus 8.6% control (HR 1.10 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.32). Pooled composite clinical endpoints: OR 0.77 relative (95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; P=0.105), significant only on exclusion of the largest trial. Safety: no important adverse effects — the intervention is harmless and ineffective on outcomes. Mortality is inside the primary endpoint and shows no benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit not shown).
cards.watchOut: Remote conditioning for stroke is a separate shelf with a separate record and should not borrow this verdict in either direction. Tier C is set per the assignment flag despite the definitive trial, because the stamp records an absence of benefit rather than a graded positive claim.

shelves.title: Anakinra after STEMI: the inflammatory surge was cut by two-thirds and new heart failure was rarer — in a 99-patient trial whose clinical endpoints were secondary
shelves.question: In patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction, does interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra blunt the acute inflammatory response and prevent new heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Heart Failure/epidemiology · Hospitalization · Humans · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction/complications, drug therapy, mortality · Stroke Volume · Survival Rate · Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome/blood, epidemiology, prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — VCU-ART3 randomised just 99 patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction to two weeks of anakinra once daily (33), anakinra twice daily (31) or placebo (35), and its primary endpoint was inflammatory, not clinical: the hsCRP area under the curve over 14 days was far lower on anakinra (median 67 versus 214 mg·day/L; P<0.001), with no difference between the two doses. The clinical signals are secondary and fragile at this size, but they point the right way: death or new-onset heart failure occurred in 9.4% on anakinra versus 25.7% on placebo (P=0.046), and death or heart-failure hospitalisation in 0% versus 11.4% (P=0.011), while left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction at 12 months did not differ (end-systolic volume change P=0.21; ejection fraction change P=0.61). The 2023 meta-analysis of NLRP3/IL-1/IL-6 pathway inhibition in STEMI (9 trials, 1,211 patients) supports the heart-failure signal for anakinra specifically (new-onset or worsening heart failure relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.77) alongside a clear CRP reduction, at the cost of more injection-site reactions — in VCU-ART3, 22% versus 3% (P=0.016), with serious infection no different (14% versus 14%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the anti-inflammatory effect is certain and the heart-failure signal is consistent, but 99 patients cannot carry a clinical-outcome claim; a powered outcomes trial is still owed.

cards.headline: VCU-ART3 2020: anakinra cut the 14-day hsCRP area under the curve from 214 to 67 mg·day/L (P<0.001), and death or new heart failure was 9.4% versus 25.7% (P=0.046) — in 99 patients
cards.summary: VCU-ART3 2020: anakinra cut the 14-day hsCRP area under the curve from 214 to 67 mg·day/L (P<0.001), and death or new heart failure was 9.4% versus 25.7% (P=0.046) — in 99 patients
cards.people: 99 patients with ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction in a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 2 weeks of treatment: anakinra once daily (33), anakinra twice daily (31) or placebo (35); the primary endpoint was the area under the curve for high-sensitivity C-reactive protein over the first 14 days; left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction were reassessed at 12 months.
cards.result: The hsCRP area under the curve was significantly lower with anakinra than placebo (median 67 [IQR 39–120] versus 214 [IQR 131–394] mg·day/L; P<0.001), without significant differences between the anakinra arms. No significant differences were found in interval changes in left ventricular end-systolic volume (median 1.4 [IQR −9.8 to 9.8] versus −3.9 [IQR −15.4 to 1.4] mL; P=0.21) or ejection fraction (median 3.9% [IQR −1.6% to 10.2%] versus 2.7% [IQR −1.8% to 9.3%]; P=0.61) at 12 months. The incidence of death or new-onset heart failure was significantly lower with anakinra (9.4% versus 25.7%; P=0.046), as was death and hospitalisation for heart failure (0% versus 11.4%; P=0.011), without difference between the anakinra arms. Serious infection did not differ (14% versus 14%; P=0.98); injection-site reactions were more frequent with anakinra (22% versus 3%; P=0.016).
cards.watchOut: With 99 patients, the heart-failure composites rest on a handful of events (the 0% versus 11.4% comparison is roughly zero events against four), they were not the primary endpoint, and the two P values (0.046, 0.011) are unadjusted for the trial's multiple secondary looks. The neutral remodelling result at 12 months also cuts against a large structural benefit.

cards.headline: He 2023 meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,211 patients): anakinra reduced new or worsening heart failure after STEMI (RR 0.32 relative) and CRP, with more injection-site reactions
cards.summary: He 2023 meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,211 patients): anakinra reduced new or worsening heart failure after STEMI (RR 0.32 relative) and CRP, with more injection-site reactions
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (1,211 patients) of inhibiting the NLRP3/IL-1β/IL-6 pathway (including colchicine and anakinra) given within 7 days of symptom onset in ST-elevation myocardial infarction, following PRISMA guidelines; efficacy outcomes included all-cause and cardiovascular death, recurrent infarction, new-onset or worsening heart failure and stroke; safety outcomes included serious infection, gastrointestinal events and injection-site reactions.
cards.result: Anakinra was associated with reduced risk of new-onset or worsening heart failure (relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.77; I²=0.0%) and decreased C-reactive protein levels (standardised mean difference −1.34; 95% CI −2.04 to −0.65; I²=0.0%). Colchicine, the other main agent pooled, reduced recurrent myocardial infarction (RR 0.28 relative; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.74). Colchicine and anakinra increased gastrointestinal adverse events (RR 4.43 relative; 95% CI 2.75 to 7.13) and injection-site reactions (RR 4.52 relative, confidence interval incompletely printed in the record) respectively. The record reports no significant pooled mortality result for anakinra.
cards.watchOut: The anakinra heart-failure estimate pools the same small VCU-ART programme that supplies the anchor card, so it is corroboration of direction rather than independent replication, and pooling across different pathway drugs (colchicine is not interleukin-1 blockade) means only the anakinra-specific estimates belong on this shelf.

95% ci 0.13 to 0.77; i²=0.0%) and decreased c-reactive protein levels (standardised mean difference −1.34; 95% ci −2.04 to −0.65; i²=0.0%). colchicine, the other main agent pooled, reduced recurrent myocardial infarction (rr 0.28 relative; 95% ci 0.10 to 0.74). colchicine and anakinra increased gastrointestinal adverse events (rr 4.43 relative; 95% ci 2.75 to 7.13) and injection-site reactions (rr 4.52 relative, confidence interval incompletely printed in the record) respectively. the record reports no significant pooled mortality result for anakinra. the anakinra heart-failure estimate pools the same small vcu-art programme that supplies the anchor card, so it is corroboration of direction rather than independent replication, and pooling across different pathway drugs (colchicine is not interleukin-1 blockade) means only the anakinra-specific estimates belong on this shelf. he f et al. efficacy and safety of inhibiting the nlrp3/il-1β/il-6 pathway in patients with st-elevation myocardial infarction: a meta-analysis. european journal of clinical investigation. 2023. pmid: 37427709. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · st elevation myocardial infarction*/drug therapy, mortality · interleukin-1beta*/antagonists & inhibitors · nlr family, pyrin domain-containing 3 protein*/antagonists & inhibitors · interleukin-6* · interleukin 1 receptor antagonist protein*/therapeutic use · randomized controlled trials as topic · heart failure/epidemiology · stroke/epidemiology · signal transduction/drug effects · recurrence

cards.headline: Synthesis: inflammation is unquestionably blunted and the heart-failure signal repeats — in a combined evidence base still only in the hundreds of patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: inflammation is unquestionably blunted and the heart-failure signal repeats — in a combined evidence base still only in the hundreds of patients
cards.people: One 99-patient randomised trial of 2 weeks of anakinra after STEMI (VCU-ART3) plus a 9-trial, 1,211-patient meta-analysis of early NLRP3/IL-1/IL-6 pathway inhibition in STEMI.
cards.result: Inflammation: hsCRP area under the curve 67 versus 214 mg·day/L (P<0.001); pooled CRP standardised mean difference −1.34. Heart failure: death or new-onset heart failure 9.4% versus 25.7% (P=0.046) in VCU-ART3; pooled new/worsening heart failure RR 0.32 relative (95% CI 0.13 to 0.77). Mortality: inside the composites above; no standalone mortality benefit is reported in either record. Remodelling: no difference in ventricular volumes or ejection fraction at 12 months. Harms: injection-site reactions 22% versus 3%; serious infection unchanged (14% versus 14%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers the acute post-STEMI window only; chronic secondary-prevention anti-inflammatory therapy (canakinumab, low-dose methotrexate, colchicine programmes) is housed on its own shelves and answers a different question. Tier C is set because the anchor trial enrolled 99 patients and its clinical endpoints were secondary.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abbate A et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2020 (PMID: 32122219); He F et al. European journal of clinical investigation. 2023 (PMID: 37427709).

shelves.title: Opening a chronic total occlusion: one trial found better angina scores, the other found no health-status gain at all — and neither found fewer deaths, infarctions or strokes
shelves.question: In patients with a chronic total coronary occlusion and angina or ischaemia, does PCI plus optimal medical therapy improve symptoms and quality of life compared with optimal medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Asia/epidemiology · Chronic Disease · Coronary Occlusion/diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy* · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention*/adverse effects/instrumentation/mortality · Quality of Life · Risk Factors · Stroke/epidemiology · Tachycardia, Ventricular/epidemiology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the two randomised trials point in different directions on the very outcome this question asks about. EuroCTO (Werner GS et al., PMID: 29722796; 396 patients) found PCI improved Seattle Angina Questionnaire angina-frequency scores by 5.23 points (95% CI 1.75 to 8.71) and quality of life by 6.62 points (1.78 to 11.46) at 12 months, with complete freedom from angina in 71.6% versus 57.8%. DECISION-CTO (Lee SW et al., PMID: 30813758; 834 randomised, median follow-up 4.0 years) found significant health-status improvement in both strategies with no between-group difference sustained through 36 months, and no difference in the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or any revascularisation (22.3% versus 22.4%; HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.37). A meta-analysis of randomised and propensity-matched studies (Iannaccone M et al., PMID: 30549199; 3,971 patients) likewise found no difference in major adverse cardiac events, repeat PCI or infarction; its lower cardiovascular death signal (OR 0.52) was driven by the propensity-matched observational studies, not the trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a symptom-driven, case-by-case decision after optimal medical therapy — not a prognostic intervention, and not a guaranteed symptomatic one.

cards.headline: DECISION-CTO 2019: no difference in death, infarction, stroke or revascularisation (22.3% vs 22.4%) and no health-status advantage for CTO-PCI over 36 months
cards.summary: DECISION-CTO 2019: no difference in death, infarction, stroke or revascularisation (22.3% vs 22.4%) and no health-status advantage for CTO-PCI over 36 months
cards.people: 834 patients with a de novo chronic total occlusion eligible for PCI, randomised at multiple centres to a CTO-PCI strategy (n=417) or a no-CTO-PCI strategy (n=398 as reported), with PCI of non-CTO lesions allowed in both groups; 19.6% of the no-PCI group crossed over to staged CTO-PCI within 3 days. The trial stopped early for slow recruitment, before its planned 1,284 enrolments.
cards.result: CTO-PCI success was 90.6%. Over a median follow-up of 4.0 years the primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or any revascularisation occurred in 22.3% with CTO-PCI versus 22.4% without (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.37; P=0.86). Disease-specific health status improved significantly in both groups with no between-group difference, sustained through 36 months. Serious nonfatal procedural complications occurred in 3 patients (1 stroke, 1 cardiac tamponade, 1 recurrent ventricular tachyarrhythmia from intracoronary thrombus).
cards.watchOut: Early stopping and a 19.6% crossover within 3 days both dilute any true difference, and about half of each group had PCI to non-CTO lesions, so this is a test of adding CTO-PCI on top of otherwise similar care — not of PCI versus tablets in isolation. The authors themselves flag low power for clinical endpoints.
cards.source: Lee SW et al. Randomized Trial Evaluating Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for the Treatment of Chronic Total Occlusion. Circulation. 2019. PMID: 30813758. Registry ID: NCT01078051. cards.headline: EuroCTO 2018: PCI improved angina frequency (+5.23 points) and quality of life (+6.62 points) at 12 months, with freedom from angina 71.6% vs 57.8%
cards.summary: EuroCTO 2018: PCI improved angina frequency (+5.23 points) and quality of life (+6.62 points) at 12 months, with freedom from angina 71.6% vs 57.8%
cards.people: 396 patients with at least one chronic total occlusion and stable angina, randomised 2:1 to PCI or optimal medical therapy alone; 52% had multivessel disease, with all significant non-occlusive lesions treated before randomisation. Failed procedures were 13.4% in the PCI group and crossovers 7.3% in the medical group.
cards.result: At 12 months the Seattle Angina Questionnaire angina-frequency subscale improved more with PCI than medical therapy (difference 5.23, 95% CI 1.75 to 8.71; P=0.003) and quality of life likewise (6.62, 95% CI 1.78 to 11.46; P=0.007), meeting the prespecified significance level of 0.01 for the primary endpoint; physical limitation also improved (P=0.02). Complete freedom from angina was more frequent with PCI (71.6% versus 57.8%; P=0.008). There was no periprocedural death or myocardial infarction, and major adverse cardiac events at 12 months were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a patient-reported primary endpoint — the design most vulnerable to expectation effects after a successful procedure — and a 12-month horizon that cannot speak to durability or events. Its symptom result directly contradicts DECISION-CTO's null health-status finding; the difference in comparators (non-CTO lesions treated in both EuroCTO arms before randomisation) may explain part of the gap.
cards.source: Werner GS et al. A randomized multicentre trial to compare revascularization with optimal medical therapy for the treatment of chronic total coronary occlusions. European Heart Journal. 2018. PMID: 29722796. Registry ID: NCT01760083. cards.headline: Iannaccone 2019 meta-analysis: 3,971 patients — no difference in major events, infarction or repeat PCI; the cardiovascular-death signal came from propensity-matched studies, not trials
cards.summary: Iannaccone 2019 meta-analysis: 3,971 patients — no difference in major events, infarction or repeat PCI; the cardiovascular-death signal came from propensity-matched studies, not trials
cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis, 8 studies (4 RCTs, 4 propensity-matched)
cards.people: Eight studies (4 randomised trials and 4 propensity-score-matched observational studies) comparing CTO-PCI (2,050 patients) with optimal medical therapy (1,921 patients), mean follow-up 3 years.
cards.result: No significant differences were found for overall major adverse cardiac events (cardiovascular death, acute coronary syndrome or repeat PCI), repeat PCI, or acute myocardial infarction. Cardiovascular death favoured CTO-PCI (OR 0.52; P<0.01), but the authors state this was driven by the propensity-matched studies. Their conclusion: CTO-PCI was associated with a similar major-event rate to medical therapy, and may be associated with reduced cardiovascular death mainly due to the propensity-study effect.
cards.watchOut: Half the evidence base is observational with propensity adjustment — exactly the design in which patients selected for a difficult, expensive procedure differ from those managed medically in ways matching cannot fully remove. The cardiovascular-death signal should be read as hypothesis-generating; the randomised subset shows no event benefit.
cards.source: Iannaccone M et al. Optimal medical therapy vs. coronary revascularization for patients presenting with chronic total occlusion: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and propensity score adjusted studies. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. 2019. PMID: 30549199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no event benefit in any randomised data; a symptom benefit in one of two trials — the honest offer is 'possibly less angina', not 'longer life'
cards.summary: Synthesis: no event benefit in any randomised data; a symptom benefit in one of two trials — the honest offer is 'possibly less angina', not 'longer life'
cards.people: Two randomised trials (834 and 396 patients) plus a meta-analysis of 3,971 patients across randomised and propensity-matched studies.
cards.result: Clinical events: DECISION-CTO primary composite 22.3% versus 22.4% (HR 1.03); meta-analysis null for major events, infarction and repeat PCI, with a cardiovascular-death signal confined to observational studies. Symptoms: EuroCTO positive on angina frequency (+5.23 points) and quality of life (+6.62) at 12 months; DECISION-CTO null on health status through 36 months. Harms: CTO-PCI success ~91%, with rare serious complications (3 patients in DECISION-CTO). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled selected, PCI-eligible patients at experienced centres; results do not transfer to occlusions with no viable distal vessel, minimal symptoms, or anatomy where success is unlikely. Tier C is not set: two genuine randomised trials exist — the weakness is their disagreement and DECISION-CTO's early stop, not absence of trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lee SW et al. Circulation. 2019 (PMID: 30813758); Werner GS et al. European Heart Journal. 2018 (PMID: 29722796); Iannaccone M et al. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. 2019 (PMID: 30549199).

shelves.title: DK crush for true left main bifurcation lesions: target-lesion failure halved at one year in one 482-patient trial (5.0% vs 10.7%) — a technique result from expert centres
shelves.question: In patients with complex left main distal bifurcation lesions, does a planned double-kissing crush two-stent strategy beat provisional stenting on target-lesion failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiography · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary/methods · Coronary Artery Disease/surgery* · Coronary Restenosis/surgery · Coronary Stenosis/surgery · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/surgery · Myocardial Revascularization · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods* · Stents* · Thrombosis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DKCRUSH-V (Chen SL et al., PMID: 29096915) randomised 482 patients with true distal left main bifurcation lesions (Medina 1,1,1 or 0,1,1) at 26 centres and found one-year target-lesion failure in 5.0% with planned double-kissing (DK) crush versus 10.7% with provisional stenting (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.85) — a relative reduction of about half, or 5.7 fewer events per 100 patients in absolute terms. The difference was carried by target-vessel myocardial infarction (0.4% versus 2.9%) and definite or probable stent thrombosis (0.4% versus 3.3%); cardiac death did not differ, and target-lesion revascularisation only tended to differ (3.8% versus 7.9%, P=0.06). A Bayesian meta-analysis of the three randomised trials of DK crush versus provisional stenting in bifurcation lesions (Kumar A et al., PMID: 38537883; 916 patients, not left-main-specific) is directionally consistent, with an absolute risk difference for target-lesion revascularisation centred at −0.05 (95% credible interval −0.08 to −0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real advantage for a planned two-stent strategy in this specific anatomy, resting substantially on one trial performed by operators expert in the technique.

cards.headline: DKCRUSH-V 2017: target-lesion failure 5.0% with DK crush vs 10.7% with provisional stenting at 1 year (HR 0.42)
cards.summary: DKCRUSH-V 2017: target-lesion failure 5.0% with DK crush vs 10.7% with provisional stenting at 1 year (HR 0.42)
cards.people: 482 patients from 26 centres in 5 countries with true distal left main bifurcation lesions (Medina 1,1,1 or 0,1,1) undergoing PCI for unprotected left main disease, randomised to provisional stenting (n=242) or planned DK crush two-stent technique (n=240). Primary endpoint: one-year composite of cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction or clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation.
cards.result: Target-lesion failure occurred in 12 patients (5.0%) with DK crush versus 26 (10.7%) with provisional stenting (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.85; P=0.02). Target-vessel myocardial infarction was 0.4% versus 2.9% (P=0.03) and definite or probable stent thrombosis 0.4% versus 3.3% (P=0.02). Clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation (3.8% versus 7.9%; P=0.06) and angiographic restenosis in the left main complex (7.1% versus 14.6%; P=0.10) tended to be less frequent with DK crush. There was no significant difference in cardiac death.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and DK crush is one of the most technically demanding stent techniques — the result was achieved by operators who helped develop it, in selected true-bifurcation anatomy. Event counts are small (12 versus 26 primary events), cardiac death did not differ, and the composite is carried by infarction and stent-thrombosis definitions sensitive to periprocedural events.
cards.source: Chen SL et al. Double Kissing Crush Versus Provisional Stenting for Left Main Distal Bifurcation Lesions: DKCRUSH-V Randomized Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 29096915. Registry ID: ChiCTR-TRC-11001213. cards.headline: Kumar 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis: 3 trials, 916 patients — target-lesion revascularisation absolute difference centred at −5 points with DK crush; cardiac death and infarction differences small and uncertain
cards.summary: Kumar 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis: 3 trials, 916 patients — target-lesion revascularisation absolute difference centred at −5 points with DK crush; cardiac death and infarction differences small and uncertain
cards.people: Three randomised trials (916 patients) comparing DK crush with provisional stenting for coronary bifurcation lesions (all bifurcation sites, not only left main), published to January 2023, pooled with Bayesian methods to estimate absolute risk differences.
cards.result: The absolute risk difference (DK crush minus provisional) was centred at −0.01 for cardiac death (95% credible interval −0.04 to 0.02), −0.03 for myocardial infarction (−0.9 to 0.03 as printed in the record), 0.00 for stent thrombosis (−0.04 to 0.03), and −0.05 for target-lesion revascularisation (−0.08 to −0.03, with 99.97% probability the difference was below zero). The authors conclude DK crush showed a lower probability of cardiac death, infarction and revascularisation, with minimal probability of a stent-thrombosis difference.
cards.watchOut: Only three trials and 916 patients, mixing left-main and non-left-main bifurcations, so it supports the direction of DKCRUSH-V rather than independently proving the left-main claim. Credible intervals for death and infarction comfortably include no difference; the firmest pooled signal is on revascularisation, the softest component.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. A Bayesian meta-analysis of double kissing (DK) crush or provisional stenting for coronary artery bifurcation lesions. Indian Heart Journal. 2024. PMID: 38537883. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one dedicated left-main trial plus a consistent small meta-analysis — planned DK crush wins on lesion-level outcomes, with no mortality difference shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: one dedicated left-main trial plus a consistent small meta-analysis — planned DK crush wins on lesion-level outcomes, with no mortality difference shown
cards.people: DKCRUSH-V (482 patients with true distal left main bifurcation lesions) and a Bayesian meta-analysis of 3 bifurcation trials (916 patients).
cards.result: Target-lesion failure at 1 year: 5.0% versus 10.7% (HR 0.42) in the left-main trial. Components: target-vessel infarction 0.4% versus 2.9%, stent thrombosis 0.4% versus 3.3%, revascularisation 3.8% versus 7.9% (P=0.06), cardiac death no significant difference. Pooled absolute differences favour DK crush most clearly for revascularisation (−0.05). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf compares stent techniques within PCI; it does not revisit PCI versus bypass surgery for left main disease (that question lives on the left-main PCI-versus-CABG shelf). The benefit is plausible only where the anatomy is a true bifurcation and the operator is practised in DK crush — a provisional strategy remains the default the trial's control arm represents. Tier C is set because the left-main evidence is essentially one trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chen SL et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017 (PMID: 29096915); Kumar A et al. Indian Heart Journal. 2024 (PMID: 38537883).

shelves.title: Ultrasound for femoral access: first-pass success jumped (86.6% vs 70.0%) but bleeding and major vascular complications did not significantly fall in the 621-patient UNIVERSAL trial
shelves.question: In patients undergoing coronary procedures via femoral access, does routine ultrasound guidance reduce vascular access complications compared with fluoroscopic landmark guidance?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Femoral Artery* · Prospective Studies · Radial Artery* · Coronary Angiography/methods · Fluoroscopy/adverse effects · Hemorrhage/epidemiology/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — UNIVERSAL (Jolly SS et al., PMID: 36116089) randomised 621 patients having coronary angiography or intervention with planned femoral access to ultrasound guidance or fluoroscopic landmarking alone. The primary composite of BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding or major vascular complications at 30 days occurred in 12.9% versus 16.1% (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.20; P=0.25) — a point estimate favouring ultrasound that the trial could not distinguish from no effect; bleeding (10.0% versus 10.7%) and major vascular complications (6.4% versus 9.4%) were each likewise non-significant. What ultrasound clearly did was mechanical: first-pass success 86.6% versus 70.0%, fewer puncture attempts, and far fewer accidental venipunctures (3.1% versus 11.7%). An earlier meta-analysis of five smaller trials (Rashid MK et al., PMID: 31257213; 1,553 patients) found fewer vascular complications with ultrasound (1.9% versus 4.3%; OR 0.44), but the effect was driven by local haematomas and disappeared for other complications and for major bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the outcomes patients feel — major bleeding and vascular injury — with a genuine, separate gain in puncture efficiency.

cards.headline: UNIVERSAL 2022: primary outcome 12.9% vs 16.1% (OR 0.77, P=0.25) — no significant reduction in bleeding or major vascular complications, despite much better first-pass success
cards.summary: UNIVERSAL 2022: primary outcome 12.9% vs 16.1% (OR 0.77, P=0.25) — no significant reduction in bleeding or major vascular complications, despite much better first-pass success
cards.people: 621 patients at 2 Canadian centres randomised to ultrasound-guided versus non-ultrasound-guided femoral arterial access for coronary angiography or intervention (mean age 71 years; 25.4% women); patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction were excluded. Ultrasound was added on a background of fluoroscopic landmarking in both groups.
cards.result: The primary composite (BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding or major vascular complications within 30 days) occurred in 40 of 311 patients (12.9%) with ultrasound versus 50 of 310 (16.1%) without (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.20; P=0.25). BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding was 10.0% versus 10.7% (OR 0.93; P=0.78) and major vascular complications 6.4% versus 9.4% (OR 0.67; P=0.18). Ultrasound improved first-pass success (86.6% versus 70.0%; OR 2.76; P<0.001), reduced puncture attempts (mean 1.2 versus 1.4) and venipuncture (3.1% versus 11.7%; OR 0.24; P<0.001), with similar time to access. All prespecified subgroups were consistent with the overall finding.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.49 to 1.20) cannot exclude a clinically worthwhile reduction — 621 patients is small for access complications, and the authors note larger trials may be required. The control was fluoroscopic landmarking by experienced operators, not blind puncture; results may differ where landmark technique is less practised.
cards.source: Jolly SS et al. Routine Ultrasonography Guidance for Femoral Vascular Access for Cardiac Procedures: The UNIVERSAL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiology. 2022. PMID: 36116089. Registry ID: NCT03537118. cards.headline: Rashid 2019 meta-analysis: vascular complications 1.9% vs 4.3% (OR 0.44) across 5 small trials — but driven by haematomas; major bleeding not significantly reduced
cards.summary: Rashid 2019 meta-analysis: vascular complications 1.9% vs 4.3% (OR 0.44) across 5 small trials — but driven by haematomas; major bleeding not significantly reduced
cards.people: Five randomised trials (1,553 patients) of ultrasound versus control guidance for femoral artery catheterisation in adults, searched to April 2018 — all before UNIVERSAL — with blinded outcome assessment in two trials.
cards.result: Ultrasound was associated with fewer vascular-access-related complications (1.9% versus 4.3%; OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.81; P<0.01), primarily driven by fewer local haematomas: excluding haematomas, the association was no longer significant (0.6% versus 1.7%; OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.07; P=0.07). Major bleeding (0.3% versus 1.3%; OR 0.28; P=0.08) and minor bleeding (1.4% versus 2.8%; OR 0.50; P=0.07) were not significantly reduced. The authors conclude larger trials are needed for major bleeding and non-haematoma complications.
cards.watchOut: Small, older trials with heterogeneous complication definitions; the headline benefit is mostly fewer haematomas — a real but minor harm — and this synthesis predates UNIVERSAL, whose larger, null result now dominates the evidence for major outcomes.
cards.source: Rashid MK et al. Ultrasound Guidance in Femoral Artery Catheterization: A Systematic Review and a Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Invasive Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 31257213. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ultrasound makes femoral puncture cleaner and quicker, but a reduction in major bleeding or vascular injury remains unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: ultrasound makes femoral puncture cleaner and quicker, but a reduction in major bleeding or vascular injury remains unproven
cards.people: UNIVERSAL (621 patients, 2022) plus five earlier randomised trials pooled in 2019 (1,553 patients).
cards.result: Major outcomes: UNIVERSAL primary composite 12.9% versus 16.1% (OR 0.77, non-significant); major bleeding non-significant in both the trial-era synthesis and UNIVERSAL. Process outcomes: first-pass success 86.6% versus 70.0%, venipuncture 3.1% versus 11.7%, fewer attempts. Minor outcomes: fewer local haematomas in the pre-UNIVERSAL meta-analysis (complications 1.9% versus 4.3% including haematomas). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for major bleeding/vascular complications.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about guiding femoral access, not about femoral versus radial access (that comparison lives on its own shelf). A null on complications is not an argument against using ultrasound where it is already routine — the efficiency gains are real — only against claiming a proven major-safety benefit. Tier C is set because the total randomised evidence remains small for the outcomes that matter.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jolly SS et al. JAMA Cardiology. 2022 (PMID: 36116089); Rashid MK et al. Journal of Invasive Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 31257213).

shelves.title: Ranolazine after incomplete revascularisation: the 2,651-patient RIVER-PCI trial found no reduction in ischaemia-driven revascularisation or hospitalisation (26% vs 28%)
shelves.question: In patients with angina and incomplete revascularisation after PCI, does ranolazine improve angina frequency and quality of life compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina Pectoris/therapy* · Coronary Artery Disease/therapy · Coronary Stenosis/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Ischemic Attack, Transient/epidemiology · Male · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology · Myocardial Ischemia/epidemiology/therapy · Myocardial Revascularization/statistics & numerical data · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention* · Ranolazine/therapeutic use* · Sodium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use* · Stroke/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — RIVER-PCI (Weisz G et al., PMID: 26474810) is a large, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 2,651 patients with chronic angina and incomplete revascularisation after PCI were randomised to ranolazine 1000 mg twice daily or placebo, and over a median 643 days the composite of ischaemia-driven revascularisation or ischaemia-driven hospitalisation occurred in 26% versus 28% (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10; P=0.48), with neither component differing significantly. More patients stopped ranolazine for adverse events (14% versus 11%; P=0.04). That null needs one careful boundary: RIVER-PCI tested a prognostic endpoint in a post-PCI population. In the different population of symptomatic chronic stable coronary disease, a meta-analysis of six trials (Savarese G et al., PMID: 24063912; 9,223 patients) found ranolazine reduced weekly angina frequency and nitroglycerin consumption and prolonged exercise duration and time to ischaemia — symptom effects, with no substantial blood-pressure or heart-rate change. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): after incomplete revascularisation, ranolazine should not be prescribed expecting fewer procedures or admissions; any role is symptomatic, on evidence drawn from a different population.

cards.headline: RIVER-PCI 2016: primary endpoint 26% on ranolazine vs 28% on placebo (HR 0.95, P=0.48) — no benefit, and more discontinuations for adverse events
cards.summary: RIVER-PCI 2016: primary endpoint 26% on ranolazine vs 28% on placebo (HR 0.95, P=0.48) — no benefit, and more discontinuations for adverse events
cards.people: 2,651 patients (aged 18 or over) with a history of chronic angina and incomplete revascularisation after PCI — at least one remaining lesion of 50% or more in a vessel 2 mm or larger — randomised at 245 centres in 15 countries to ranolazine 1000 mg twice daily (n=1,332) or placebo (n=1,319); 2,604 patients formed the full analysis set. Median follow-up 643 days.
cards.result: The primary composite of ischaemia-driven revascularisation or ischaemia-driven hospitalisation without revascularisation occurred in 345 patients (26%) on ranolazine versus 364 (28%) on placebo (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10; P=0.48). Neither component differed significantly between groups. Study-drug discontinuation because of an adverse event was more common on ranolazine (189 patients, 14%, versus 137, 11%; P=0.04). The authors conclude ranolazine did not reduce the composite rate in this population.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint was prognostic (procedures and admissions), not angina frequency or quality of life as the shelf question's wording invites — the trial does not directly test whether these particular patients felt better, only that their event course was unchanged. Incomplete revascularisation was angiographically defined and common; results apply to that high-risk post-PCI group, not to stable angina generally.
cards.source: Weisz G et al. Ranolazine in patients with incomplete revascularisation after percutaneous coronary intervention (RIVER-PCI): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 26474810. Registry ID: NCT01442038. cards.headline: Savarese 2013 meta-analysis: in chronic stable coronary disease (a different population), ranolazine reduced weekly angina and nitroglycerin use and prolonged exercise time across 6 trials and 9,223 patients
cards.summary: Savarese 2013 meta-analysis: in chronic stable coronary disease (a different population), ranolazine reduced weekly angina and nitroglycerin use and prolonged exercise time across 6 trials and 9,223 patients
cards.people: Six randomised trials enrolling 9,223 symptomatic patients with chronic stable coronary artery disease, testing ranolazine added to conventional therapy versus control, with exercise, angina-frequency, nitroglycerin-consumption and haemodynamic endpoints. The record reports directions of effect rather than pooled numeric estimates for most endpoints.
cards.result: At trough and peak levels, ranolazine significantly improved exercise duration, time to onset of angina and time to 1-mm ST-segment depression, and significantly reduced weekly angina frequency and weekly sublingual nitroglycerin consumption compared with control. It did not significantly reduce supine systolic or diastolic blood pressure or heart rate (with a modest reduction in standing systolic pressure), and sensitivity analyses showed results were not influenced by concomitant background therapy.
cards.watchOut: Different question, different patients: chronic stable angina trials with short-term symptom and exercise endpoints — not post-PCI incomplete revascularisation, and not procedures, admissions or events. It explains why ranolazine has a symptomatic reputation while RIVER-PCI is null; it cannot rescue a prognostic claim in the RIVER-PCI population. The abstract reports significance without pooled magnitudes, so no effect size is claimed here.
cards.source: Savarese G et al. Effects of ranolazine in symptomatic patients with stable coronary artery disease. A systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Cardiology. 2013. PMID: 24063912. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a symptom drug tested on a prognostic endpoint — no fewer procedures or admissions after incomplete revascularisation; symptom benefit is evidenced only in stable angina populations
cards.summary: Synthesis: a symptom drug tested on a prognostic endpoint — no fewer procedures or admissions after incomplete revascularisation; symptom benefit is evidenced only in stable angina populations
cards.people: RIVER-PCI (2,651 post-PCI patients with incomplete revascularisation) and a six-trial meta-analysis in chronic stable coronary disease (9,223 patients).
cards.result: Prognostic endpoint (RIVER-PCI): 26% versus 28% (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10) over a median 643 days; adverse-event discontinuation 14% versus 11%. Symptom endpoints (stable-angina meta-analysis): significant improvements in angina frequency, nitroglycerin use, exercise duration and time to ischaemia, magnitudes not pooled in the record. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the post-PCI prognostic question.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as 'ranolazine does not relieve angina' — RIVER-PCI did not measure that as its primary question, and the stable-angina trials say otherwise. Equally, do not quote the stable-angina data to justify ranolazine for prognosis after PCI. Tier C is set because the direct evidence for the shelf's symptom wording in this exact population is indirect.

shelves.title: Enhanced external counterpulsation for refractory angina: one small sham-controlled trial, a longer time to exercise ischaemia, no clear gain in exercise duration — and more adverse events
shelves.question: In patients with refractory angina ineligible for revascularisation, does enhanced external counterpulsation improve exercise-induced ischaemia and angina compared with a sham procedure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angina Pectoris/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology/therapy* · Coronary Angiography · Counterpulsation/methods* · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance/physiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology/therapy · Prospective Studies · Safety · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire sham-controlled randomised record in angina is MUST-EECP (Arora RR et al., PMID: 10362181): 139 outpatients with angina, documented coronary disease and a positive exercise test received 35 hours of active or inactive counterpulsation over four to seven weeks. Time to 1-mm ST-segment depression increased significantly with active treatment (P=0.01), and more active-treatment patients reported fewer angina episodes (P<0.05); but exercise duration — the outcome patients experience as stamina — increased in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P>0.3), and nitroglycerin use did not differ significantly between groups (P>0.7). The Health Technology Assessment systematic review (McKenna C et al., PMID: 19409154; five studies) put the ischaemia-time gain at a mean 41 seconds (95% CI 9.10 to 73.90), found no significant difference in exercise duration, self-reported angina episodes or daily nitroglycerin use, noted more withdrawals and adverse events with EECP (RR 2.13, 95% CI 1.35 to 3.38), and concluded the single trial does not provide firm evidence of clinical effectiveness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a non-invasive option with a plausible small physiological effect, unproven patient-important benefit, and a 35-hour time burden.

cards.headline: MUST-EECP 1999: time to exercise ischaemia improved (P=0.01) but exercise duration did not differ between groups (P>0.3) in 139 patients
cards.summary: MUST-EECP 1999: time to exercise ischaemia improved (P=0.01) but exercise duration did not differ between groups (P>0.3) in 139 patients
cards.people: 139 outpatients at seven university hospitals with angina, documented coronary artery disease and a positive exercise treadmill test, randomised to 35 hours of active counterpulsation or inactive (sham) counterpulsation over a four- to seven-week period, in a prospective, blinded, controlled design.
cards.result: Exercise duration increased in both groups, with no significant between-group difference (P>0.3). Time to 1-mm or greater ST-segment depression increased significantly from baseline in the active group compared with the inactive group (P=0.01). More active-treatment patients saw a decrease, and fewer an increase, in angina episodes compared with inactive treatment (P<0.05). Nitroglycerin usage decreased in the active group but not the inactive group, without a significant between-group difference (P>0.7). The authors conclude EECP reduces angina and extends time to exercise-induced ischaemia, and was relatively well tolerated and free of limiting side effects in most patients.
cards.watchOut: Small, old, and short: 139 patients, outcomes at the end of a 4–7-week course, no long-term follow-up, and the abstract reports P values without the underlying magnitudes for most endpoints. The positive results are a surrogate (time to ST depression) and a directional angina count; the most patient-important measure, exercise duration, was null between groups.
cards.source: Arora RR et al. The multicenter study of enhanced external counterpulsation (MUST-EECP): effect of EECP on exercise-induced myocardial ischemia and anginal episodes. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 1999. PMID: 10362181. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McKenna 2009 HTA systematic review: ischaemia time +41 seconds, no significant gain in exercise duration, angina episodes or nitroglycerin use — and adverse events more than doubled (RR 2.13)
cards.summary: McKenna 2009 HTA systematic review: ischaemia time +41 seconds, no significant gain in exercise duration, angina episodes or nitroglycerin use — and adverse events more than doubled (RR 2.13)
cards.type: Systematic review and economic analysis (HTA), 5 studies
cards.people: A systematic review of five studies of EECP for refractory stable angina and heart failure (searches November 2007 to March 2008), anchored on MUST-EECP for angina, with three non-randomised comparisons and the PEECH heart-failure trial also reviewed, plus an economic model.
cards.result: In MUST-EECP, time to 1-mm ST depression improved with EECP versus sham (mean difference 41 seconds, 95% CI 9.10 to 73.90), but there was no statistically significant difference in change in exercise duration, self-reported angina episodes or daily nitroglycerin use, and the clinical significance of the limited benefits was unclear. There were more withdrawals due to adverse events with EECP and a greater proportion of patients with adverse events (RR 2.13, 95% CI 1.35 to 3.38). The non-randomised studies carried a high risk of selection bias. The reviewers conclude that results from the single randomised trial do not provide firm evidence of the clinical effectiveness of EECP in refractory stable angina or heart failure, and that high-quality studies are required.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2009 and its searches end in 2008; it is carded because no larger sham-controlled trial has superseded MUST-EECP in this record set, not because it is recent. Its reading of the angina-episode outcome (no significant difference) is more conservative than the trial abstract's directional P<0.05 — both are shown, and the discrepancy is itself a reason for the weak stamp.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a 41-second gain in time to ischaemia, null exercise duration, uncertain angina benefit, and a doubling of adverse events — evidence too thin for a firm recommendation
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 41-second gain in time to ischaemia, null exercise duration, uncertain angina benefit, and a doubling of adverse events — evidence too thin for a firm recommendation
cards.people: One sham-controlled randomised trial (139 patients) and an HTA systematic review of five studies.
cards.result: Time to exercise-induced ischaemia: improved (mean difference 41 seconds, 95% CI 9.10 to 73.90). Exercise duration: no significant between-group difference in trial or review. Angina episodes and nitroglycerin use: directionally favourable in the trial report, non-significant in the HTA synthesis. Adverse events: RR 2.13 (95% CI 1.35 to 3.38), with more withdrawals on EECP. Long-term outcomes: no data. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The population here is stable angina with a positive exercise test; 'refractory, ineligible for revascularisation' patients — the group most often offered EECP — are sicker and even less directly studied. The coronary-sinus Reducer for refractory angina is a different intervention, homed on its own shelf. Tier C is set: one small trial from 1999 is the whole sham-controlled base.

shelves.title: Milrinone versus dobutamine in cardiogenic shock: the blinded DOREMI trial found no difference — composite 49% vs 54%, in-hospital death 37% vs 43%
shelves.question: In patients with cardiogenic shock, does milrinone differ from dobutamine on death or the composite of resuscitated arrest, transplantation/mechanical support, myocardial infarction, stroke or renal replacement?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Agonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Cardiotonic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Comorbidity · Dobutamine/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Milrinone/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Phosphodiesterase 3 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Shock, Cardiogenic/drug therapy*/mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — DOREMI (Mathew R et al., PMID: 34347952) is a double-blind randomised trial of 192 patients with cardiogenic shock, 96 per group. The primary composite — in-hospital death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, cardiac transplantation or mechanical circulatory support, nonfatal myocardial infarction, transient ischaemic attack or stroke, or initiation of renal replacement therapy — occurred in 49% on milrinone versus 54% on dobutamine (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.19; P=0.47). In-hospital death, which this shelf reports separately as heart-failure and shock questions require, was 37% versus 43% (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.21), and resuscitated arrest, mechanical support and renal replacement each likewise did not differ significantly. A meta-analysis dominated by observational data (Biswas S et al., PMID: 35545181) leans the other way — lower mortality with milrinone in acute heart failure overall (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.97, event rates 9.4% versus 9.8%) — but in the cardiogenic-shock subgroup the difference was only a non-significant trend, and its bridge-to-transplant subgroup trended toward dobutamine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on randomised evidence the choice between these two inotropes in shock is not a survival decision; it is made on haemodynamics, rhythm, renal function and familiarity.

cards.headline: DOREMI 2021: primary composite 49% milrinone vs 54% dobutamine (RR 0.90, P=0.47); in-hospital death 37% vs 43% — no significant difference on any component
cards.summary: DOREMI 2021: primary composite 49% milrinone vs 54% dobutamine (RR 0.90, P=0.47); in-hospital death 37% vs 43% — no significant difference on any component
cards.people: 192 patients with cardiogenic shock randomised double-blind to milrinone (n=96) or dobutamine (n=96). The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital death from any cause, resuscitated cardiac arrest, receipt of cardiac transplant or mechanical circulatory support, nonfatal myocardial infarction, transient ischaemic attack or stroke diagnosed by a neurologist, or initiation of renal replacement therapy.
cards.result: A primary outcome event occurred in 47 participants (49%) on milrinone and 52 (54%) on dobutamine (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.19; P=0.47). Secondary outcomes did not differ significantly: in-hospital death 37% versus 43% (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.21), resuscitated cardiac arrest 7% versus 9% (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.29 to 2.07), receipt of mechanical circulatory support 12% versus 15% (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.71), and initiation of renal replacement therapy 22% versus 17% (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.67).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 192 patients: the confidence interval for the composite (0.69 to 1.19) cannot exclude a meaningful benefit for either drug, so this is 'no difference shown', not equivalence proven. Shock aetiology and severity were mixed, and dosing was clinician-managed after randomisation.
cards.source: Mathew R et al. Milrinone as Compared with Dobutamine in the Treatment of Cardiogenic Shock. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34347952. Registry ID: NCT03207165. cards.headline: Biswas 2023 meta-analysis: mostly observational data lean to milrinone in acute heart failure (mortality RR 0.87), but only a non-significant trend in cardiogenic shock — and a trend to dobutamine as bridge to transplant
cards.summary: Biswas 2023 meta-analysis: mostly observational data lean to milrinone in acute heart failure (mortality RR 0.87), but only a non-significant trend in cardiogenic shock — and a trend to dobutamine as bridge to transplant
cards.people: Ten studies comparing milrinone with dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure, with subgroups for heart failure with cardiogenic shock, bridge to transplantation and destination therapy; the record reports 4,918 patients in the milrinone group and 15,188 in the dobutamine group, with only one randomised trial among the ten studies.
cards.result: Milrinone was associated with lower mortality in acute heart failure overall (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.97; P<0.05; I²=0%), with event rates of 9.4% versus 9.8% (number needed to treat 250 as reported). In heart failure with cardiogenic shock there was a non-significant trend toward improved mortality with milrinone; in bridge-to-transplant patients, a non-significant trend toward improved mortality with dobutamine. There was no difference between strategies for acute kidney injury, renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, arrhythmias, symptomatic hypotension or hospital length of stay in the overall population.
cards.watchOut: Nine of ten studies are not randomised — inotrope choice in practice tracks renal function, blood pressure and rhythm, so confounding by indication is built in, and the pooled mortality advantage (0.4 percentage points absolute) is far smaller than the biases that could produce it. The record itself contains internal inconsistencies (a subgroup confidence interval that does not contain its point estimate, and a total patient count that does not match its own arm counts), so only its clearly reported figures are carded here. Where it conflicts with DOREMI, the blinded trial governs.
