shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DACAB (Zhao Q et al., PMID: 29710164) randomised 500 patients having elective bypass surgery with saphenous vein grafting to ticagrelor plus aspirin, ticagrelor alone, or aspirin alone, started within 24 hours. One-year graft patency (FitzGibbon grade A) was 88.7% (432 of 487 grafts) with the combination versus 76.5% (371 of 485) with aspirin alone — an absolute difference of 12.2 percentage points (95% CI 5.2 to 19.2; P<0.001) — while ticagrelor alone (82.8%) did not differ significantly from aspirin alone (difference 6.3 points, 95% CI −1.1 to 13.7; P=0.10). The bleeding price in this trial was small in count and imprecise: five major bleeding episodes in a year (three on the combination, two on ticagrelor alone, none reported on aspirin alone). A network meta-analysis of ten post-CABG antiplatelet trials (Hasan SU et al., PMID: 39087882; 2,139 patients) is consistent, ranking aspirin plus ticagrelor lowest for saphenous vein graft occlusion (mean absolute risk 0.144) without a significantly higher major-bleeding signal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the patency benefit is randomised and coherent, but patency is an imaging outcome, the trial was open-label, and neither source can yet show fewer infarctions or deaths — or exclude a real bleeding cost at scale.

cards.headline: DACAB 2018: graft patency 88.7% with ticagrelor + aspirin vs 76.5% with aspirin alone (difference 12.2 points, P<0.001); ticagrelor alone not significantly better
cards.summary: DACAB 2018: graft patency 88.7% with ticagrelor + aspirin vs 76.5% with aspirin alone (difference 12.2 points, P<0.001); ticagrelor alone not significantly better
cards.people: 500 patients aged 18 to 80 undergoing elective CABG with saphenous vein grafting at six tertiary hospitals in China, randomised within 24 hours after surgery to ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily (n=168), ticagrelor alone (n=166), or aspirin alone (n=166), in an open-label design with blinded outcome adjudication; 461 patients (92.2%) completed the trial. Mean age 63.6 years; 18.2% women.
cards.result: Saphenous vein graft patency at one year was 88.7% (432 of 487 grafts) with ticagrelor plus aspirin, 82.8% (404 of 488) with ticagrelor alone, and 76.5% (371 of 485) with aspirin alone. The combination versus aspirin difference was 12.2% (95% CI 5.2% to 19.2%; P<0.001); ticagrelor alone versus aspirin was 6.3% (95% CI −1.1% to 13.7%; P=0.10). Five major bleeding episodes occurred during one year of follow-up (three with ticagrelor plus aspirin; two with ticagrelor alone).
cards.watchOut: Patency is counted per graft, not per patient, and is an imaging surrogate — the trial was not powered for myocardial infarction, death or repeat revascularisation. Open-label treatment (with blinded adjudication), an elective Chinese population, and only five major bleeds in total mean the harm side of the ledger is the least certain part of this shelf.
cards.source: Zhao Q et al. Effect of Ticagrelor Plus Aspirin, Ticagrelor Alone, or Aspirin Alone on Saphenous Vein Graft Patency 1 Year After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29710164. Registry ID: NCT02201771. cards.headline: Hasan 2025 network meta-analysis: across 10 trials and 2,139 patients, aspirin + ticagrelor ranked lowest for vein graft occlusion, with no significantly higher major bleeding
cards.summary: Hasan 2025 network meta-analysis: across 10 trials and 2,139 patients, aspirin + ticagrelor ranked lowest for vein graft occlusion, with no significantly higher major bleeding
cards.people: Ten randomised trials (2,139 patients) of post-CABG antiplatelet strategies — aspirin alone, ticagrelor alone, aspirin plus ticagrelor, and aspirin plus clopidogrel — searched to August 2022 and pooled in a Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis with Cochrane RoB-2 quality assessment.
cards.result: For preventing saphenous vein graft occlusion, aspirin plus ticagrelor showed the lowest mean absolute risk (0.144 ± 0.068), with trends toward lower postoperative myocardial infarction (mean absolute risk 0.040 ± 0.053) and all-cause mortality (0.018 ± 0.029). For internal mammary artery patency, aspirin plus clopidogrel ranked lowest (0.092 ± 0.053). For major bleeding, ticagrelor alone and aspirin plus ticagrelor showed similar mean absolute risks (0.049 ± 0.075 and 0.049 ± 0.045). The authors conclude aspirin plus ticagrelor can be the ideal therapy for patients undergoing CABG with saphenous vein grafts, decreasing occlusion without a significantly higher major-bleeding risk.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean heavily on DACAB for the ticagrelor combination, so this is corroboration of structure rather than independent replication; the reported figures are modelled absolute risks with wide standard deviations, and 'no significantly higher bleeding' across 2,139 patients still leaves room for a clinically important bleeding increase.
cards.source: Hasan SU et al. Comparative effectiveness of antiplatelet therapies for saphenous venous graft occlusion and cardiovascular outcomes: a network meta-analysis. Minerva Cardiology and Angiology. 2025. PMID: 39087882. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a clear one-year patency advantage for the combination, an unproven clinical-outcome advantage, and a bleeding cost measured in single digits
cards.summary: Synthesis: a clear one-year patency advantage for the combination, an unproven clinical-outcome advantage, and a bleeding cost measured in single digits
cards.people: DACAB (500 randomised patients, ~1,460 grafts assessed) and a ten-trial network meta-analysis (2,139 patients).
cards.result: Patency: 88.7% versus 76.5% (absolute difference 12.2 points, 95% CI 5.2 to 19.2) for ticagrelor plus aspirin versus aspirin alone; ticagrelor alone intermediate and non-significant. Network ranking: aspirin plus ticagrelor lowest for graft occlusion. Bleeding: five major episodes in DACAB (three on the combination); no significant excess in the network analysis. Death and infarction: no demonstrated difference in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Patients who need anticoagulation, urgent surgery, or concomitant valve surgery were excluded from DACAB — do not extend the patency claim to them. A patent graft at one year is not the same as a prevented infarction; a clinical-outcomes trial is the missing piece. Tier C is set because one trial carries the combination's evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhao Q et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29710164); Hasan SU et al. Minerva Cardiology and Angiology. 2025 (PMID: 39087882).

shelves.title: After TAVR, aspirin alone beat aspirin plus clopidogrel on bleeding (15.1% vs 26.6%) with no ischaemic penalty at one year — POPular TAVI cohort A
shelves.question: In patients without an indication for anticoagulation after successful TAVR, does aspirin alone, compared with aspirin plus clopidogrel, reduce bleeding without increasing ischaemic events?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aspirin/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology/mortality · Clopidogrel/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced*/epidemiology · Humans · Incidence · Male · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Postoperative Period · Thrombosis/epidemiology/prevention & control* · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement*
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — POPular TAVI cohort A (Brouwer J et al., PMID: 32865376) randomised 665 patients undergoing transcatheter aortic-valve implantation who had no indication for long-term anticoagulation to aspirin alone or aspirin plus clopidogrel for three months. At one year, all bleeding occurred in 15.1% on aspirin alone versus 26.6% on dual therapy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77; P=0.001) — about 12 fewer bleeding events per 100 patients — and non-procedure-related bleeding in 15.1% versus 24.9% (risk ratio 0.61). The composite of cardiovascular death, non-procedure-related bleeding, stroke or infarction favoured aspirin alone (23.0% versus 31.1%; risk ratio 0.74; P=0.04 for superiority), while the purely ischaemic composite was essentially identical (9.7% versus 9.9%; risk ratio 0.98), meeting non-inferiority. A meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Lin X et al., PMID: 33570686; four studies, 1,086 patients) agrees: by 6 to 12 months dual therapy increased bleeding (relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.24) with no difference in mortality, stroke or infarction. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in patients without an anticoagulation indication, adding clopidogrel after TAVR buys bleeding and no measurable ischaemic protection.

cards.headline: POPular TAVI cohort A 2020: bleeding 15.1% on aspirin alone vs 26.6% on aspirin + clopidogrel (RR 0.57); ischaemic composite identical (9.7% vs 9.9%)
cards.summary: POPular TAVI cohort A 2020: bleeding 15.1% on aspirin alone vs 26.6% on aspirin + clopidogrel (RR 0.57); ischaemic composite identical (9.7% vs 9.9%)
cards.people: 665 patients undergoing TAVI without an indication for long-term anticoagulation, randomised to aspirin alone (n=331) or aspirin plus clopidogrel for 3 months (n=334). Primary outcomes were all bleeding and non-procedure-related bleeding over 12 months; secondary composites were tested sequentially for non-inferiority (margin 7.5 percentage points) and superiority. During the trial, 13.3% of the aspirin-alone group and 9.6% of the dual group received oral anticoagulation.
cards.result: Bleeding occurred in 50 patients (15.1%) on aspirin alone versus 89 (26.6%) on dual therapy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77; P=0.001); non-procedure-related bleeding in 50 (15.1%) versus 83 (24.9%) (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.83; P=0.005). Secondary composite 1 (cardiovascular death, non-procedure-related bleeding, stroke or myocardial infarction) occurred in 76 (23.0%) versus 104 (31.1%) (difference −8.2 points; risk ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95; P=0.04 for superiority). Secondary composite 2 (cardiovascular death, ischaemic stroke or myocardial infarction) occurred in 32 (9.7%) versus 33 (9.9%) (difference −0.2 points; risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.55), meeting non-inferiority (P=0.004).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment, and the non-inferiority margin for the ischaemic composite was a generous 7.5 percentage points — non-inferiority here excludes a large penalty, not any penalty. Patients who developed an anticoagulation indication during follow-up (about one in eight in the aspirin arm) leave the question this shelf answers; cohort B, in anticoagulated patients, is a different population and is not carded here.
cards.source: Brouwer J et al. Aspirin with or without Clopidogrel after Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Implantation. New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32865376. Registry ID: NCT02247128. cards.headline: Lin 2022 meta-analysis: 4 trials, 1,086 patients — dual therapy increased bleeding by 6–12 months (RR 1.67) with no difference in death, stroke or infarction
cards.summary: Lin 2022 meta-analysis: 4 trials, 1,086 patients — dual therapy increased bleeding by 6–12 months (RR 1.67) with no difference in death, stroke or infarction
cards.people: Four randomised trials (1,086 patients; 541 aspirin alone, 545 dual antiplatelet therapy) comparing aspirin plus clopidogrel with aspirin alone after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, searched to October 2020.
cards.result: At 30 days there was no statistically significant difference between aspirin alone and dual therapy in bleeding (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.39), all-cause mortality (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.52 to 2.84), stroke (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.24 to 2.79) or myocardial infarction (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.45 to 35.22). At 6 to 12 months, dual therapy increased bleeding compared with aspirin alone (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.24; P<0.001), with no significant difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.48), stroke (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.92) or myocardial infarction (RR 1.65, 95% CI 0.52 to 5.26). The authors conclude aspirin alone decreases bleeding without higher mortality, stroke or infarction.
cards.watchOut: POPular TAVI is the largest of the four trials, so the meta-analysis substantially restates it rather than independently replicating it; the component trials are small, with wide intervals on infarction and stroke. The 30-day null on bleeding, against the clear 6–12-month excess, is a reminder that the harm of dual therapy accrues over the months it is continued.
cards.source: Lin X et al. Aspirin Alone Versus Dual Antiplatelet Therapy after Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cardiovascular Drugs and Therapy. 2022. PMID: 33570686. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: less bleeding, same ischaemic outcomes — single aspirin is the supported default after TAVR when there is no anticoagulation indication
cards.summary: Synthesis: less bleeding, same ischaemic outcomes — single aspirin is the supported default after TAVR when there is no anticoagulation indication
cards.people: POPular TAVI cohort A (665 randomised patients) and a four-trial meta-analysis (1,086 patients).
cards.result: Bleeding at 1 year: 15.1% versus 26.6% (risk ratio 0.57) in the trial; pooled relative risk 1.67 for dual versus single therapy at 6–12 months. Ischaemic composite (cardiovascular death, ischaemic stroke, infarction): 9.7% versus 9.9% (risk ratio 0.98), non-inferior. Mortality and stroke: no significant differences in the pooled analysis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers only patients without an indication for oral anticoagulation; anticoagulated TAVR patients (the POPular TAVI cohort B question) and the anticoagulation-harm trials (GALILEO/ATLANTIS) live on their own shelves. Tier C is set per the build slate, though the direction of evidence — one adequately sized randomised trial plus a consistent meta-analysis — is firmer than most single-trial shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brouwer J et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32865376); Lin X et al. Cardiovascular Drugs and Therapy. 2022 (PMID: 33570686).

shelves.title: TAVR for moderate aortic stenosis in heart failure: TAVR UNLOAD missed its primary endpoint (win ratio 1.31, P=0.14) but improved quality of life at one year
shelves.question: In patients with systolic heart failure and moderate aortic stenosis, does TAVR, compared with medical therapy and surveillance, reduce death or heart-failure hospitalisation?

shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — TAVR UNLOAD (Van Mieghem NM et al., PMID: 39480381) randomised just 178 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on guideline-directed therapy and moderate aortic stenosis to transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or to clinical surveillance with valve replacement on progression to severe stenosis. Over a median 23 months the primary hierarchical endpoint — all-cause death, then disabling stroke, then disease-related hospitalisations and heart-failure equivalents, then change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score — was not significantly better with TAVR (win ratio 1.31, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14). The trial's structure blurs its own contrast: 38 of 89 surveillance patients (43%) underwent TAVR at a median of 12 months, 35 of them after progressing to severe stenosis, so the comparison became early versus deferred TAVR for nearly half the control group. The one clearly positive component was quality of life at one year (KCCQ improvement 12.8 versus 3.2 points; P=0.018), and the authors describe pre-emptive TAVR as safe. No systematic review of this intervention question exists in the record set searched, so the shelf rests on this single small trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): feeling better sooner is plausible; living longer or staying out of hospital is unproven, and surveillance with prompt treatment at severe stenosis remains a defensible strategy.

cards.headline: TAVR UNLOAD 2025: primary hierarchical endpoint not met (win ratio 1.31, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14); KCCQ quality of life improved more with TAVR at 1 year (+12.8 vs +3.2 points)
cards.summary: TAVR UNLOAD 2025: primary hierarchical endpoint not met (win ratio 1.31, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14); KCCQ quality of life improved more with TAVR at 1 year (+12.8 vs +3.2 points)
cards.people: 178 patients with HFrEF on guideline-directed medical therapy and moderate aortic stenosis, suitable for transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve, randomised 1:1 to TAVR (n=89) or clinical aortic stenosis surveillance with valve replacement on progression to severe AS (n=89), at international centres from 2017 to 2022. Mean age 77 years; 20.8% women; 55.6% in NYHA class III or IV. Median follow-up 23 months.
cards.result: TAVR was associated with wins in 47.6% of pairs versus 36.6% for surveillance, giving a win ratio of 1.31 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14) for the hierarchical composite of all-cause death, disabling stroke, disease-related hospitalisations and heart-failure equivalents, and KCCQ change. At one year, KCCQ Overall Summary Score improved more with TAVR (12.8 ± 21.9 points) than surveillance (3.2 ± 22.8 points; P=0.018). In the surveillance group, 38 patients (43%) underwent TAVR at a median of 12 months after randomisation, of whom 35 had progressed to severe AS. The authors conclude TAVR was not superior for the primary endpoint, was safe, and may provide clinically meaningful quality-of-life benefits.
cards.watchOut: The record reports the hierarchical composite and the quality-of-life component but not separate death or hospitalisation rates, so no mortality claim can be extracted from it — the shelf question's death/hospitalisation framing is answered only through the composite, which was null. With 178 patients and 43% crossover to TAVR in the control arm, the trial was never positioned to detect a mortality difference; an open-label design also leaves the subjective KCCQ component open to expectation effects.
cards.source: Van Mieghem NM et al. Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients With Systolic Heart Failure and Moderate Aortic Stenosis: TAVR UNLOAD. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2025. PMID: 39480381. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial, a null primary endpoint, heavy crossover, and a single positive quality-of-life component — the case for pre-emptive TAVR in moderate AS remains unmade
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial, a null primary endpoint, heavy crossover, and a single positive quality-of-life component — the case for pre-emptive TAVR in moderate AS remains unmade
cards.people: TAVR UNLOAD only: 178 randomised patients with HFrEF and moderate aortic stenosis, median follow-up 23 months. No eligible systematic review or meta-analysis of TAVR for moderate AS was found in-session.
cards.result: Primary hierarchical composite (death, disabling stroke, hospitalisation/heart-failure equivalents, KCCQ change): win ratio 1.31 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14) — not significant. Quality of life at 1 year: +12.8 versus +3.2 KCCQ points (P=0.018). Crossover: 43% of the surveillance group received TAVR at a median 12 months. Separate mortality and hospitalisation rates: not reported in the record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Severe aortic stenosis TAVR evidence (homed on the severe-AS shelves) must not be imported here: moderate stenosis imposes a smaller afterload burden, which is precisely why the trial was worth doing and why its null matters. A larger trial with less crossover could still change this verdict, particularly on quality of life. Tier C is set: single small trial, no synthesis available.

shelves.title: A dedicated transcatheter valve for pure aortic regurgitation: ALIGN-AR met its safety and one-year mortality performance goals — in a single-arm study of 180 high-risk patients
shelves.question: In patients at high surgical risk with severe symptomatic native aortic regurgitation, can dedicated transcatheter aortic valve implantation achieve acceptable one-year outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Aortic Valve/diagnostic imaging/surgery · Aortic Valve Insufficiency*/etiology/surgery · Aortic Valve Stenosis*/surgery · Heart Valve Prosthesis* · Prospective Studies · Prosthesis Design · Risk Factors · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement*/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ALIGN-AR (Vahl TP et al., PMID: 38552656) is a prospective single-arm study of the Trilogy transcatheter heart valve (JenaValve Technology, Irvine, CA, USA) — the specific tested product, named here because transcatheter valves for pure regurgitation are device-specific and not interchangeable — in 180 patients with symptomatic moderate-to-severe or severe native aortic regurgitation at high risk for surgical complications. Technical success was 95%. The 30-day composite safety endpoint occurred in 27% of patients, meeting non-inferiority against a prespecified performance goal of 40.5% (P<0.0001), and one-year all-cause mortality was 7.8%, meeting non-inferiority against a 25% goal (P<0.0001). The price on the face of the record: new pacemaker implantation in 24% of patients, with four deaths (2%) and four strokes (2% disabling, 2% non-disabling as counts of two each) by 30 days. A systematic review of transcatheter treatment for aortic regurgitation (Liu R et al., PMID: 38749505; 31 studies, 1,851 patients) found new-generation dedicated ('on-label') devices achieved 97.8% device success and 2.6% 30-day mortality, better than off-label devices on success, pacemaker, paravalvular leak and mortality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): performance goals are a low bar set against historical surgical-era expectations, there is no concurrent control group, and durability beyond one year is unknown.

cards.headline: ALIGN-AR 2024: 30-day safety endpoint 27% vs a 40.5% performance goal, and 1-year mortality 7.8% vs a 25% goal — both met; pacemaker implantation 24%
cards.summary: ALIGN-AR 2024: 30-day safety endpoint 27% vs a 40.5% performance goal, and 1-year mortality 7.8% vs a 25% goal — both met; pacemaker implantation 24%
cards.people: 180 patients (of 346 screened) with symptomatic moderate-to-severe or severe native aortic regurgitation, deemed high risk for mortality or complications after surgical aortic valve replacement by heart team and independent screening, treated with transfemoral implantation of the Trilogy transcatheter heart valve (JenaValve Technology) at 20 US sites. Mean age 75.5 years; 47% women.
cards.result: Technical success was achieved in 171 patients (95%). At 30 days there were four deaths (2%), two disabling strokes (1%) and two non-disabling strokes (1%). The primary safety endpoint (Valve Academic Research Consortium-2 composite) occurred in 48 patients (27%, 97.5% CI 19.2 to 34.0), meeting non-inferiority against the 40.5% performance goal (P<0.0001); new pacemaker implantation occurred in 36 patients (24%). The primary efficacy endpoint was met, with one-year all-cause mortality in 14 patients (7.8%, 97.5% CI 3.3 to 12.3) against a 25% performance goal (P<0.0001). The authors report promising short-term clinical and haemodynamic outcomes and signs of left ventricular remodelling, with long-term follow-up necessary.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: 'non-inferiority' here means beating a prespecified performance goal, not matching a randomised comparator — and a 25% one-year mortality goal is generous. Nearly half of screened patients (48%) were excluded, so the results describe a selected anatomical subset. One in four patients needed a new pacemaker, the highest price on this card, and follow-up beyond one year was still ongoing at publication.
cards.source: Vahl TP et al. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation in patients with high-risk symptomatic native aortic regurgitation (ALIGN-AR): a prospective, multicentre, single-arm study. Lancet. 2024. PMID: 38552656. Registry ID: NCT04415047. cards.headline: Liu 2024 meta-analysis: 31 studies, 1,851 patients — dedicated on-label devices beat off-label devices on success (97.8% vs 89.9%), 30-day mortality (2.6% vs 5.1%) and pacemaker rate (6.9% vs 18.4%)
cards.summary: Liu 2024 meta-analysis: 31 studies, 1,851 patients — dedicated on-label devices beat off-label devices on success (97.8% vs 89.9%), 30-day mortality (2.6% vs 5.1%) and pacemaker rate (6.9% vs 18.4%)
cards.people: Thirty-one studies including 1,851 patients treated with new-generation transcatheter devices for severe aortic regurgitation, searched to April 2023; 1,067 patients (57.6%) received 'on-label' dedicated devices (JenaValve and J-Valve) and the remainder off-label devices designed for stenosis.
cards.result: For new-generation devices overall, 30-day device success was 94.5%, all-cause mortality 4.2%, permanent pacemaker implantation 8.8%, and greater-than-mild paravalvular leak 1.2%. On-label devices performed significantly better than off-label devices on device success (97.8% versus 89.9%; P<0.001), 30-day mortality (2.6% versus 5.1%; P=0.006), pacemaker implantation (6.9% versus 18.4%; P<0.001) and greater-than-mild paravalvular leak (0.9% versus 3.8%; P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: The underlying studies are single-arm series, so these are pooled proportions and between-study comparisons, not randomised contrasts — centres using dedicated devices may differ systematically from centres improvising with stenosis devices. ALIGN-AR's own pacemaker rate (24%) sits far above this pooled on-label average (6.9%), a reminder that pooled single-arm rates hide wide between-study variation.
cards.source: Liu R et al. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement for aortic regurgitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. ESC Heart Failure. 2024. PMID: 38749505. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a dedicated valve can be implanted successfully in selected high-risk regurgitation patients with acceptable early outcomes — comparative and long-term evidence does not yet exist
cards.summary: Synthesis: a dedicated valve can be implanted successfully in selected high-risk regurgitation patients with acceptable early outcomes — comparative and long-term evidence does not yet exist
cards.people: ALIGN-AR (180 patients, single-arm, dedicated Trilogy valve) and a 31-study meta-analysis of new-generation devices (1,851 patients).
cards.result: Technical/device success: 95% in ALIGN-AR; 94.5% pooled (97.8% on-label). Thirty-day mortality: four deaths (2%) in ALIGN-AR; 4.2% pooled (2.6% on-label). One-year mortality: 7.8% in ALIGN-AR against a 25% performance goal. Pacemaker: 24% in ALIGN-AR; 8.8% pooled. Randomised or concurrent-control evidence: none. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Surgery remains the only recommended intervention for native aortic regurgitation in the ALIGN-AR record itself; this shelf answers 'can it be done acceptably in high-risk patients', not 'should it replace surgery'. Device naming follows the tested-product rule: results belong to the Trilogy/JenaValve device and other dedicated devices as studied, and should not be transferred to stenosis valves used off-label. Tier C is set: single-arm evidence only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vahl TP et al. Lancet. 2024 (PMID: 38552656); Liu R et al. ESC Heart Failure. 2024 (PMID: 38749505).

shelves.title: Lower INR for the On-X mechanical aortic valve: major bleeding roughly halved (1.48% vs 3.26% per patient-year) with no significant rise in thromboembolism in PROACT's interim report
shelves.question: In patients with an On-X mechanical aortic valve, does reduced-intensity warfarin (lower INR target) plus aspirin match standard anticoagulation on thromboembolism and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/administration & dosage* · Aortic Valve/surgery* · Aspirin/administration & dosage* · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis/adverse effects* · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Thromboembolism/etiology*/prevention & control* · United States · United States Food and Drug Administration · Warfarin/administration & dosage*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PROACT (Puskas J et al., PMID: 24512654) randomised 375 patients three months after mechanical aortic valve replacement with the On-X bileaflet valve — the specific tested valve, named because the result is valve-specific — and higher-risk features for thromboembolism, to a test INR target of 1.5–2.0 or the standard 2.0–3.0, all on aspirin 81 mg daily with home INR monitoring. Over an average 3.82 years, major bleeding was significantly lower in the test group (1.48% versus 3.26% per patient-year; P=0.047), as was minor bleeding (1.32% versus 3.41%; P=0.021), while stroke, transient ischaemic attack, total neurological events and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. A systematic review of lower versus higher INR targets across left-sided mechanical valves (Pandey AK et al., PMID: 34622377; nine randomised trials) points the same way: thromboembolism 2.4% versus 2.3% (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.60) and total bleeding 21.9% versus 40.9% (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.78), though the reviewers downgraded the evidence for bias and imprecision. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the bleeding gain is consistent across both sources; the reassurance on thromboembolism is 'no significant increase in an interim, modest-sized trial', not proof of equality, and it belongs to this valve, this aspirin co-therapy and home-monitored patients.

cards.headline: PROACT 2014 (interim): major bleeding 1.48% vs 3.26% per patient-year (P=0.047) and minor bleeding 1.32% vs 3.41% at INR 1.5–2.0, with stroke, TIA and mortality similar
cards.summary: PROACT 2014 (interim): major bleeding 1.48% vs 3.26% per patient-year (P=0.047) and minor bleeding 1.32% vs 3.41% at INR 1.5–2.0, with stroke, TIA and mortality similar
cards.type: Randomised trial, interim report (PROACT, aortic limb)
cards.people: 375 patients at 33 US centres randomised three months after mechanical aortic valve replacement with the On-X bileaflet prosthesis, all with elevated risk factors for thromboembolism, to lower-dose warfarin (test INR 1.5–2.0, n=185) or standard warfarin (control INR 2.0–3.0, n=190), with INR adjusted by home monitoring and all patients receiving aspirin 81 mg daily. Mean age 55.2 years; 79% men; mean achieved INR 1.89 in the test group versus 2.50 in controls. Follow-up averaged 3.82 years (675.2 versus 755.7 patient-years).
cards.result: The test group experienced significantly lower major bleeding (1.48% versus 3.26% per patient-year; P=0.047) and minor bleeding (1.32% versus 3.41% per patient-year; P=0.021). The incidence of stroke, transient ischaemic attack, total neurological events and all-cause mortality was similar between the two groups. The authors conclude INR can be safely maintained between 1.5 and 2.0 after aortic valve replacement with this approved bileaflet mechanical prosthesis, with low-dose aspirin, resulting in significantly lower bleeding without a significant increase in thromboembolism.
cards.watchOut: An interim report of one limb of a larger trial, in 375 patients: 'similar' thromboembolism rates in a study this size cannot exclude a meaningful absolute increase in valve thrombosis or stroke, the outcomes patients fear most. The result is bound to the On-X valve, concomitant aspirin, and home INR monitoring — it does not license lower targets for other mechanical valves, mitral prostheses, or unmonitored patients. The record carries no registry identifier.
cards.source: Puskas J et al. Reduced anticoagulation after mechanical aortic valve replacement: interim results from the prospective randomized on-X valve anticoagulation clinical trial randomized Food and Drug Administration investigational device exemption trial. Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2014. PMID: 24512654. Registry ID: none in the record. p=0.047) and minor bleeding (1.32% versus 3.41% per patient-year; p=0.021). the incidence of stroke, transient ischaemic attack, total neurological events and all-cause mortality was similar between the two groups. the authors conclude inr can be safely maintained between 1.5 and 2.0 after aortic valve replacement with this approved bileaflet mechanical prosthesis, with low-dose aspirin, resulting in significantly lower bleeding without a significant increase in thromboembolism. an interim report of one limb of a larger trial, in 375 patients: 'similar' thromboembolism rates in a study this size cannot exclude a meaningful absolute increase in valve thrombosis or stroke, the outcomes patients fear most. the result is bound to the on-x valve, concomitant aspirin, and home inr monitoring — it does not license lower targets for other mechanical valves, mitral prostheses, or unmonitored patients. the record carries no registry identifier. puskas j et al. reduced anticoagulation after mechanical aortic valve replacement: interim results from the prospective randomized on-x valve anticoagulation clinical trial randomized food and drug administration investigational device exemption trial. journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery. 2014. pmid: 24512654. registry id: none in the record. mesh: anticoagulants/administration & dosage* · aortic valve/surgery* · aspirin/administration & dosage* · female · heart valve prosthesis/adverse effects* · heart valve prosthesis implantation* · humans · male · middle aged · prospective studies · thromboembolism/etiology*/prevention & control* · united states · united states food and drug administration · warfarin/administration & dosage*

cards.headline: Pandey 2022 meta-analysis: 9 RCTs — thromboembolism essentially identical (2.4% vs 2.3%) and total bleeding much lower (21.9% vs 40.9%, RR 0.46) with lower INR targets
cards.summary: Pandey 2022 meta-analysis: 9 RCTs — thromboembolism essentially identical (2.4% vs 2.3%) and total bleeding much lower (21.9% vs 40.9%, RR 0.46) with lower INR targets
cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis, 9 RCTs + 17 observational studies
cards.people: Nine randomised trials of lower versus higher INR targets in left-sided mechanical heart valve patients (six Western trials, n=5,496; three East Asian trials, n=209), plus 17 observational studies, with low and high targets as defined by the individual studies.
cards.result: In the randomised trials, lower compared with higher targets were associated with similar rates of thromboembolism (2.4% versus 2.3%; relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.60; I²=0%) and lower rates of total bleeding (21.9% versus 40.9%; relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.78; I²=88%) and major bleeding. Effects were consistent in the observational data, with no statistical heterogeneity by region in the trial data. The reviewers downgraded the quality of evidence due to serious risk of bias and imprecision, rating the thromboembolism evidence low quality and the bleeding evidence moderate quality.
cards.watchOut: 'Lower' and 'higher' targets varied by study, valves and positions are mixed (not On-X aortic only), and heterogeneity for total bleeding was high (I²=88%). The thromboembolism confidence interval (0.82 to 1.60) still allows a substantial relative increase — consistency of direction is not precision about the harm that matters most.
cards.source: Pandey AK et al. Efficacy and safety of low intensity vitamin K antagonists in Western and East-Asian patients with left-sided mechanical heart valves. cards.headline: Synthesis: bleeding falls by about half when INR targets are lowered; thromboembolism shows no significant rise — but the reassurance rests on interim and downgraded evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: bleeding falls by about half when INR targets are lowered; thromboembolism shows no significant rise — but the reassurance rests on interim and downgraded evidence
cards.people: PROACT aortic limb (375 patients with the On-X valve, mean 3.82 years) and a nine-trial meta-analysis across left-sided mechanical valves (5,705 randomised patients).
cards.result: Bleeding: major 1.48% versus 3.26% per patient-year in PROACT; total bleeding relative risk 0.46 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.78) pooled. Thromboembolism: similar rates in PROACT; pooled 2.4% versus 2.3% (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.60). Mortality: similar in PROACT. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Direct oral anticoagulants in mechanical valves are a separate, settled-harm question (RE-ALIGN, homed elsewhere) — nothing here softens that. Lower-INR management as tested requires the aspirin co-therapy and monitoring intensity of the trial; stripping those away while keeping the lower target is an untested strategy. Tier C is set: the valve-specific evidence is a single interim trial report.
cards.source: Synthesis of Puskas J et al. Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2014 (PMID: 24512654); Pandey AK et al. Journal of Thrombosis and Thrombolysis. 2022 (PMID: 34622377).

shelves.title: The Ross operation versus homograft root replacement: 10-year survival 97% vs 83% in the one randomised trial — a striking result from a single centre and 216 analysed patients
shelves.question: In adults needing aortic root replacement, does the Ross pulmonary autograft give better long-term survival and valve durability than a homograft root replacement?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aortic Valve/transplantation* · Aortic Valve Insufficiency/mortality/surgery* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Pulmonary Valve/transplantation* · Reoperation · Survival Rate · Transplantation, Autologous · Transplantation, Homologous · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is one single-centre UK trial (El-Hamamsy I et al., PMID: 20684981): 228 adults under 69 needing aortic valve surgery were randomised to Ross pulmonary autograft or homograft aortic root replacement, with 108 per group analysed. At ten years, four autograft patients had died versus 15 homograft patients — actuarial survival 97% versus 83%, with a hazard ratio for death in the homograft group of 4.61 (95% CI 1.71 to 16.03; P=0.0060) — and autograft survival matched an age- and sex-matched British population (96%). Perioperative death was one versus three patients. A network meta-analysis of randomised and propensity-matched studies (Yokoyama Y et al., PMID: 36565200; 4,812 patients) extends the comparison beyond homografts: all-cause mortality was lower after Ross than after mechanical replacement (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.97) or bioprosthetic replacement (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.59), with less major bleeding and stroke than mechanical replacement — at the cost of more reintervention than mechanical valves, though less than bioprostheses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent across both sources, but the head-to-head trial is small, single-centre and surgeon-specific, its comparator (homograft root) is now uncommon, and 19 deaths in total carry the survival claim.

cards.headline: El-Hamamsy 2010: 10-year survival 97% with autograft vs 83% with homograft (HR for death 4.61 with homograft); deaths 4 vs 15
cards.summary: El-Hamamsy 2010: 10-year survival 97% with autograft vs 83% with homograft (HR for death 4.61 with homograft); deaths 4 vs 15
cards.type: Randomised trial (Ross vs homograft root replacement)
cards.people: 228 patients under 69 years requiring aortic valve surgery at one UK centre, randomised to autograft (Ross) or homograft aortic root replacement; 12 patients under 18 were excluded, leaving 108 in each group who received their assigned surgery and were analysed. Treatment was not masked. Primary endpoint: survival at 10 years.
cards.result: Perioperative death occurred in one patient (<1%) in the autograft group versus three (3%) in the homograft group (P=0.621). At 10 years, four patients had died in the autograft group versus 15 in the homograft group; actuarial survival was 97% (SD 2) versus 83% (SD 4), with a hazard ratio for death in the homograft group of 4.61 (95% CI 1.71 to 16.03; P=0.0060). Survival in the autograft group was similar to that of an age- and sex-matched British population (96%). The authors conclude a living valve substitute in the aortic position significantly improves long-term outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, unmasked, and 216 analysed patients with 19 deaths — the hazard ratio's interval (1.71 to 16.03) shows how much uncertainty a striking point estimate can carry. The comparator is homograft root replacement, not the mechanical or bioprosthetic valves most patients are actually offered, and the record reports survival without the reintervention detail the durability question needs; the network meta-analysis card supplies the wider comparison.
cards.source: El-Hamamsy I et al. Long-term outcomes after autograft versus homograft aortic root replacement in adults with aortic valve disease: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20684981. Registry ID: ISRCTN03530985. cards.headline: Yokoyama 2023 network meta-analysis: mortality lower after Ross than mechanical (HR 0.58) or bioprosthetic (HR 0.32) replacement across 4,812 patients; reintervention higher than mechanical, lower than bioprosthetic
cards.summary: Yokoyama 2023 network meta-analysis: mortality lower after Ross than mechanical (HR 0.58) or bioprosthetic (HR 0.32) replacement across 4,812 patients; reintervention higher than mechanical, lower than bioprosthetic
cards.type: Systematic review / network meta-analysis, 2 RCTs + 8 propensity-matched studies
cards.people: Two randomised trials and eight propensity score-matched studies in patients aged 16 or over undergoing the Ross procedure (n=1,991), mechanical aortic valve replacement (n=2,019) or bioprosthetic replacement (n=802), searched to March 2022.
cards.result: All-cause mortality was significantly lower with the Ross procedure than with mechanical replacement (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.97; P=0.035) and bioprosthetic replacement (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.59; P<0.001). Reintervention was lower after Ross and mechanical replacement than after bioprosthetic replacement, but higher after Ross than after mechanical replacement. Major bleeding was lower after Ross than mechanical replacement; long-term stroke was lower after Ross than either comparator; endocarditis was lower after Ross than bioprosthetic replacement. The authors conclude the Ross procedure shows improved long-term outcomes over conventional options.
cards.watchOut: Eight of ten studies are propensity-matched observational comparisons: patients offered the Ross operation are typically younger, fitter and operated on at expert centres, and matching cannot remove all of that selection. The network's Ross-versus-mechanical mortality advantage is therefore supportive of, not independent from, the trial evidence — and it averages across eras and techniques of a demanding operation.
cards.source: Yokoyama Y et al. Ross Procedure Versus Mechanical Versus Bioprosthetic Aortic Valve Replacement: A Network Meta-Analysis. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2023. PMID: 36565200. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: better survival than homograft in the trial and than conventional prostheses in the network — balanced against more reintervention than a mechanical valve and single-centre origins
cards.summary: Synthesis: better survival than homograft in the trial and than conventional prostheses in the network — balanced against more reintervention than a mechanical valve and single-centre origins
cards.people: One randomised trial (216 analysed patients, 10-year follow-up) and a network meta-analysis of 4,812 patients across Ross, mechanical and bioprosthetic replacement.
cards.result: Survival: 97% versus 83% at 10 years against homograft (deaths 4 versus 15); pooled mortality HR 0.58 versus mechanical and 0.32 versus bioprosthetic replacement. Durability trade-off (network): reintervention higher after Ross than mechanical, lower than bioprosthetic; major bleeding and stroke lower after Ross than mechanical. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The Ross operation creates two-valve disease from one-valve disease — the pulmonary autograft and the right-sided replacement can both need later intervention — and outcomes are strongly surgeon- and centre-dependent. Nothing here applies to older patients or to centres without a Ross programme. Tier C is set: one small randomised trial anchors the entire comparison.
cards.source: Synthesis of El-Hamamsy I et al. Lancet. 2010 (PMID: 20684981); Yokoyama Y et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2023 (PMID: 36565200).

shelves.title: Self-expanding transcatheter pulmonary valve (Harmony): 98% had acceptable valve function at a median 13 months in a 243-patient registry — but one in five needed treatment for ventricular arrhythmia
shelves.question: In children and young adults with right-ventricular outflow tract dysfunction after repaired congenital heart disease, does transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement with a self-expanding valve achieve durable valve function without surgery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · Pulmonary Valve*/surgery · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation*/adverse effects · Heart Valve Prosthesis* · Cardiac Catheterization/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Pulmonary Valve Insufficiency*/surgery/etiology · Registries · Prosthesis Design · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the evidence for the self-expanding Harmony transcatheter pulmonary valve (Medtronic) — the specific tested device, named because transcatheter pulmonary valves are device-specific — is a multicentre US registry (Goldstein BH et al., PMID: 38569760): 243 patients with native or surgically repaired right-ventricular outflow tract pulmonary regurgitation, median age 31 years, 71% with tetralogy of Fallot. Acute technical success was achieved in all but one case, hospital stay was one day in 86%, and at a median follow-up of 13 months 98% of patients had acceptable haemodynamic function, with estimated freedom from the composite of haemodynamic dysfunction or outflow-tract reintervention of 99% at one year and 96% at two years, and freedom from valve-related endocarditis of 98% at one year. The counterweights are on the same card: procedural serious adverse events in 4%, ventricular arrhythmia prompting treatment in 19%, and five deaths during follow-up (one COVID-19, two unknown causes, two bloodstream infection). A systematic review comparing transcatheter with surgical pulmonary valve replacement generally (Chongmelaxme B et al., PMID: 40392782; 28 studies, 16,150 patients, all observational) found lower mortality with the transcatheter route (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.95 — a 36% relative reduction as reported, with absolute rates not given in the record) but three-fold higher odds of infective endocarditis (OR 3.10, 95% CI 2.22 to 4.33). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): short-term function is excellent in selected anatomy, but there is no randomised or controlled evidence for this device, and 'durable' beyond two years is exactly what a 13-month median follow-up cannot show.

cards.headline: Goldstein 2024 Harmony registry: technical success in all but 1 of 243 patients; 98% acceptable valve function at median 13 months; freedom from dysfunction/reintervention 99% at 1 year, 96% at 2 years
cards.summary: Goldstein 2024 Harmony registry: technical success in all but 1 of 243 patients; 98% acceptable valve function at median 13 months; freedom from dysfunction/reintervention 99% at 1 year, 96% at 2 years
cards.people: 243 consecutive patients with native right-ventricular outflow tract pulmonary regurgitation undergoing transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement with the self-expanding Harmony valve (Medtronic) at 11 US centres to April 2022. Median age 31 years (IQR 19–45); cardiac diagnoses were tetralogy of Fallot (71%), valvular pulmonary stenosis (21%) and other (8%). Primary outcome: composite of haemodynamic dysfunction (more-than-mild regurgitation or mean outflow gradient over 30 mm Hg) and outflow-tract reintervention.
cards.result: Acute technical success was achieved in all but one case. Procedural serious adverse events occurred in 4% of cases, with no device embolisation or death; hospital length of stay was one day in 86% of patients. Ventricular arrhythmia prompting treatment occurred in 19% of cases. At a median follow-up of 13 months (IQR 8–19), 98% of patients had acceptable haemodynamic function; estimated freedom from the composite clinical outcome was 99% at one year and 96% at two years, and freedom from valve-related endocarditis was 98% at one year. Five patients died (COVID-19, one; unknown causes, two; bloodstream infection, two).
cards.watchOut: A registry without a comparator: it can show the device works in patients selected for it, not that it beats surgery or another valve. Median age 31 means the 'children and young adults' of the question are mostly adults in this data; median follow-up of 13 months cannot answer durability, and the 19% treated ventricular arrhythmia rate — in a population already prone to arrhythmia after tetralogy repair — needs longer surveillance, not dismissal.
cards.source: Goldstein BH et al. Early Outcomes From a Multicenter Transcatheter Self-Expanding Pulmonary Valve Replacement Registry. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2024. cards.headline: Chongmelaxme 2025 meta-analysis: transcatheter vs surgical pulmonary valve replacement — mortality OR 0.64 favouring transcatheter, but infective endocarditis OR 3.10 against it (28 observational studies, 16,150 patients)
cards.summary: Chongmelaxme 2025 meta-analysis: transcatheter vs surgical pulmonary valve replacement — mortality OR 0.64 favouring transcatheter, but infective endocarditis OR 3.10 against it (28 observational studies, 16,150 patients)
cards.people: Twenty-eight studies (16,150 patients) comparing transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement with surgical pulmonary valve replacement in patients with pulmonary valve or right-ventricular outflow tract dysfunction, searched to March 2024; all comparative evidence observational, pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: Compared with surgical replacement, transcatheter replacement was associated with lower mortality over follow-up (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.95 — described by the authors as a 36% relative reduction in risk; absolute rates are not reported in the record) but three-fold greater odds of infective endocarditis over follow-up (OR 3.10, 95% CI 2.22 to 4.33). No significant differences were observed for 30-day mortality, early pulmonary regurgitation, early endocarditis or early re-intervention, or for regurgitation and re-intervention during follow-up. Results varied by geographical region, publication-year cut-off and country income status. All groups showed improved heart function and relevant post-procedural complications.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trials exist for this comparison, and patients routed to catheter versus surgical replacement differ in anatomy, prior operations and frailty in ways observational pooling cannot undo — the mortality advantage may be selection wearing a treatment's clothes. The endocarditis signal, by contrast, is large, directionally consistent with the Harmony registry's own infection-related deaths, and applies across transcatheter devices, not only the self-expanding one.
cards.source: Chongmelaxme B et al. Comparative effects of transcatheter versus surgical pulmonary valve replacement: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLOS ONE. 2025. PMID: 40392782. cards.headline: Synthesis: excellent short-term valve function without surgery in selected patients; the open questions are endocarditis, arrhythmia and durability past two years
cards.summary: Synthesis: excellent short-term valve function without surgery in selected patients; the open questions are endocarditis, arrhythmia and durability past two years
cards.people: The Harmony self-expanding valve registry (243 patients, median follow-up 13 months) and a 28-study observational meta-analysis of transcatheter versus surgical pulmonary valve replacement (16,150 patients).
cards.result: Valve function: 98% acceptable at median 13 months; freedom from dysfunction or reintervention 99% at one year, 96% at two years (registry). Comparative outcomes (observational): mortality OR 0.64 favouring transcatheter; endocarditis OR 3.10 against transcatheter; no difference in 30-day mortality or re-intervention. Harms in the registry: serious procedural events 4%, treated ventricular arrhythmia 19%, five deaths. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Device results are not a class effect: the Harmony self-expanding valve treats native or patched outflow tracts that balloon-expandable valves often cannot, so registry success reflects both device and anatomy selection. For a child, the relevant horizon is decades and multiple lifetime interventions — a frame no study here reaches. Tier C is set: single-arm registry plus observational comparisons only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Goldstein BH et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 38569760); Chongmelaxme B et al. PLOS ONE. 2025 (PMID: 40392782).

shelves.title: A statin straight after a heart transplant: one small 1995 trial found less severe rejection, less graft vasculopathy and better one-year survival — and pooled data since point the same way
shelves.question: In heart transplant recipients, does pravastatin started soon after transplantation reduce rejection with haemodynamic compromise, cardiac allograft vasculopathy and death?
shelves.mesh: Cholesterol/blood · Coronary Disease/etiology/prevention & control* · Coronary Vessels/diagnostic imaging · Cytotoxicity, Immunologic/drug effects · Female · Graft Rejection/prevention & control* · Heart Transplantation/adverse effects*/immunology/mortality · Humans · Hypercholesterolemia/blood/etiology/prevention & control* · Incidence · Killer Cells, Natural/drug effects/immunology · Male · Middle Aged · Pravastatin/therapeutic use* · Prospective Studies · Survival Rate · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised anchor is a single, small, unblinded 1995 trial of 97 patients, but its results were large and internally consistent: pravastatin started early after cardiac transplantation cut rejection with haemodynamic compromise (3 vs 14 patients), improved one-year survival (94% vs 78%), and reduced angiographic/autopsy vasculopathy (3 vs 10 patients), alongside the expected cholesterol fall (193 vs 248 mg/dL). A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies and 4,627 recipients (Mardani-Nafchi H et al., PMID: 38840403) points the same way for the outcomes that matter — lower odds of mortality (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.75) and of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (OR 0.71, 0.53 to 0.96) among statin users — while its rejection result was null overall (OR 0.69, 0.41 to 1.15) and positive only in the randomised subgroup (OR 0.42, 0.21 to 0.82), and most of its weight is observational, with a possible publication-bias signal on Egger's test. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early statin therapy after heart transplantation probably reduces vasculopathy and death, but the randomised base is one small pre-modern-immunosuppression trial, so the size of the effect in contemporary recipients is not pinned down.

cards.headline: Kobashigawa 1995: pravastatin after heart transplant — rejection with haemodynamic compromise 3 vs 14 patients, one-year survival 94% vs 78%, vasculopathy 3 vs 10
cards.summary: Kobashigawa 1995: pravastatin after heart transplant — rejection with haemodynamic compromise 3 vs 14 patients, one-year survival 94% vs 78%, vasculopathy 3 vs 10
cards.people: 97 consecutive patients randomised early after cardiac transplantation to pravastatin (47 patients) or no HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (50 patients), followed for 12 months, with angiography/autopsy assessment of transplant coronary vasculopathy and an intracoronary ultrasound substudy.
cards.result: At 12 months the pravastatin group had lower mean cholesterol (193 ± 36 vs 248 ± 49 mg/dL, P < 0.001), less frequent cardiac rejection accompanied by haemodynamic compromise (3 vs 14 patients, P = 0.005), better survival (94% vs 78%, P = 0.025), and a lower incidence of coronary vasculopathy in the transplant by angiography and at autopsy (3 vs 10 patients, P = 0.049). There was no difference in mild or moderate rejection episodes. In the ultrasound subgroup, maximal intimal thickness progressed less with pravastatin (0.11 ± 0.09 mm vs 0.23 ± 0.16 mm, P = 0.002), as did the intimal index (0.05 ± 0.03 vs 0.10 ± 0.10, P = 0.031); natural-killer-cell cytotoxicity was lower in the pravastatin group (9.8% vs 22.2% specific lysis, P = 0.014).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, unblinded trial of 97 patients from 1995, run before modern immunosuppression (no routine tacrolimus/mycophenolate era practice) and before statins became near-universal after transplant — the absolute gains (a 16-percentage-point survival difference) are implausibly large to carry forward unchanged, and no second randomised trial of this size on clinical outcomes has tested the question since. It establishes direction, not a contemporary effect size.
cards.source: Kobashigawa JA et al. Effect of pravastatin on outcomes after cardiac transplantation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7637722. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mardani-Nafchi 2024 (meta-analysis, 17 studies, 4,627 recipients): statin use after heart transplant associated with lower mortality (OR 0.49) and vasculopathy (OR 0.71); rejection null overall, positive only in RCTs
cards.summary: Mardani-Nafchi 2024 (meta-analysis, 17 studies, 4,627 recipients): statin use after heart transplant associated with lower mortality (OR 0.49) and vasculopathy (OR 0.71); rejection null overall, positive only in RCTs
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies (4,627 heart transplant recipients, studies conducted 1995–2021) comparing postoperative statin users with non-users for mortality, rejection, and cardiac allograft vasculopathy.
cards.result: Compared with non-users, the odds of mortality were lower among statin users (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.75, p < 0.001), as were the odds of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.96, p = 0.027). The odds of rejection were not significantly different overall (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.15, p = 0.152), but rejection odds were lower with statins in the randomised-trial subgroup (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.82, p = 0.012) and not in case-control studies (OR 0.87, 0.49 to 1.52, p = 0.615). No publication bias was observed with Begg's test, but Egger's test showed possible bias.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies are observational: recipients who take statins differ from those who do not (survivor and adherence effects), so the halving of mortality odds almost certainly overstates any causal effect. The analysis is best read as confirming that the randomised signal was never contradicted at scale, not as an independent precise estimate.
cards.source: Mardani-Nafchi H et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Statin Therapy on Heart Transplantation. Reviews on Recent Clinical Trials. 2024. PMID: 38840403. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Heart Transplantation*/adverse effects · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors*/therapeutic use · Graft Rejection*/prevention & control

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small randomised trial with large benefits, backed by a mostly observational meta-analysis pointing the same way on death and vasculopathy
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small randomised trial with large benefits, backed by a mostly observational meta-analysis pointing the same way on death and vasculopathy
cards.people: One randomised trial (97 recipients, 1995) and a 17-study meta-analysis (4,627 recipients) of statin therapy started after heart transplantation.
cards.result: Randomised: rejection with haemodynamic compromise 3 vs 14 patients, one-year survival 94% vs 78%, vasculopathy 3 vs 10 patients, cholesterol 193 vs 248 mg/dL. Pooled: mortality OR 0.49 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.75), vasculopathy OR 0.71 (0.53 to 0.96), rejection OR 0.69 (0.41 to 1.15) overall but OR 0.42 (0.21 to 0.82) in randomised studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here compares one statin or dose with another, and nothing addresses recipients already years post-transplant — the evidence is specifically about starting a statin early after transplantation. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single small 1995 trial and the supporting pooled evidence is largely observational.

shelves.title: Swapping the kidney-toxic immune drug out after a heart transplant: kidneys, graft vessels and CMV all did better on everolimus — rejection did worse
shelves.question: In de novo heart transplant recipients, does everolimus initiation with early calcineurin-inhibitor withdrawal preserve renal function without increasing treated rejection compared with standard calcineurin therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Adult · Aged · Calcineurin Inhibitors/administration & dosage* · Cyclosporine/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Everolimus · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection · Heart Failure/surgery · Heart Transplantation* · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage* · Male · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Sirolimus/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives* · TOR Serine-Threonine Kinases/metabolism · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the trade is explicit in the one randomised trial. In SCHEDULE (Andreassen AK et al., PMID: 25041227), 115 de novo heart transplant recipients assigned to everolimus with ciclosporin withdrawal at 7–11 weeks had markedly better measured GFR at 12 months (79.8 vs 61.5 mL/min/1.73 m²), less progression of intimal thickening, a lower incidence of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (50.0% vs 64.6%), and far fewer cytomegalovirus infections (5.4% vs 30.5%) than standard ciclosporin — but biopsy-proven acute rejection after the withdrawal window was more frequent with everolimus. A network meta-analysis of 15 maintenance-immunosuppression studies (Ueyama H et al., PMID: 32424550) generalises the pattern without resolving it: no mortality difference between regimens, less vasculopathy with calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR inhibitor, the lowest rejection rates in calcineurin-containing regimens, and better renal function and fewer CMV infections when the mTOR inhibitor replaced the calcineurin inhibitor. PROPOSED SPLIT: early calcineurin withdrawal on everolimus buys kidney function, vasculopathy and CMV advantages at the price of more treated rejection — a regimen choice to individualise, not a uniform upgrade.

cards.headline: Andreassen 2014 (SCHEDULE): everolimus with early ciclosporin withdrawal — GFR 79.8 vs 61.5 mL/min/1.73 m² and vasculopathy 50.0% vs 64.6% at 12 months, but more rejection after withdrawal
cards.summary: Andreassen 2014 (SCHEDULE): everolimus with early ciclosporin withdrawal — GFR 79.8 vs 61.5 mL/min/1.73 m² and vasculopathy 50.0% vs 64.6% at 12 months, but more rejection after withdrawal
cards.people: 115 de novo heart transplant recipients randomised within 5 days of transplantation to low-exposure everolimus (3–6 ng/mL) with reduced-exposure ciclosporin (n = 56) — ciclosporin withdrawn at 7–11 weeks and everolimus exposure raised (6–10 ng/mL) — or standard-exposure ciclosporin (n = 59); both groups received mycophenolate mofetil and corticosteroids. Primary endpoint was measured GFR at 12 months.
cards.result: Measured GFR at 12 months was significantly higher with everolimus than with ciclosporin (mean ± SD 79.8 ± 17.7 vs 61.5 ± 19.6 mL/min/1.73 m²; p < 0.001). On coronary intravascular ultrasound, the mean increase in maximal intimal thickness was smaller with everolimus (0.03 mm [95% CI 0.01 to 0.05] vs 0.08 mm [0.05 to 0.12], p = 0.03) and the incidence of cardiac allograft vasculopathy was lower (50.0% vs 64.6%, p = 0.003). Biopsy-proven acute rejection after weeks 7–11 was more frequent with everolimus (p = 0.03). Left ventricular function was not inferior with everolimus. Cytomegalovirus infection was less common with everolimus (5.4% vs 30.5%, p < 0.001); bacterial infection incidence was similar.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and small (115 patients, 12 months): the GFR gap is large and objective, but the trial cannot speak to graft survival or mortality, and the excess rejection clustered exactly where the design predicted risk — after ciclosporin was withdrawn. The comparison is also against ciclosporin, not tacrolimus, the calcineurin inhibitor most contemporary programmes use.
cards.source: Andreassen AK et al. Everolimus initiation and early calcineurin inhibitor withdrawal in heart transplant recipients: a randomized trial. American Journal of Transplantation. 2014. PMID: 25041227. Registry ID: NCT01266148. cards.headline: Ueyama 2022 (network meta-analysis, 15 studies): no mortality difference between regimens; calcineurin + mTOR inhibitor lowest for vasculopathy, mTOR-based calcineurin-free best for kidneys and CMV, worst for rejection
cards.summary: Ueyama 2022 (network meta-analysis, 15 studies): no mortality difference between regimens; calcineurin + mTOR inhibitor lowest for vasculopathy, mTOR-based calcineurin-free best for kidneys and CMV, worst for rejection
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 15 studies of maintenance immunosuppression after heart transplantation comparing mTOR antagonist plus antimetabolite, calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR antagonist, and calcineurin inhibitor plus antimetabolite (8 studies using everolimus and 7 sirolimus as the mTOR antagonist). Outcomes were all-cause mortality, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, acute rejection, CMV infection, and change in eGFR.
cards.result: There was no statistical difference in all-cause mortality among the three regimens. Vasculopathy rates were significantly lower with calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR antagonist (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.92). Acute rejection rates were significantly lower with calcineurin inhibitor plus antimetabolite (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.56) and with calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR antagonist (OR 0.16, 0.07 to 0.33) than with mTOR antagonist plus antimetabolite. CMV infections were significantly lower with mTOR antagonist plus antimetabolite (OR 0.13, 0.03 to 0.46) and with calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR antagonist (OR 0.27, 0.20 to 0.38) than with calcineurin inhibitor plus antimetabolite. The calcineurin-free mTOR regimen led to higher eGFR than calcineurin inhibitor plus antimetabolite (9.06 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI 3.15 to 14.97), though heterogeneity for the renal outcome was significant.
cards.watchOut: Network comparisons lean heavily on indirect evidence across eras and co-therapies, and the renal-function pooling was significantly heterogeneous. The analysis ranks regimens outcome by outcome — it does not identify a single best regimen, because the regimen that wins on kidneys and CMV loses on rejection.
cards.source: Ueyama H et al. Maintenance immunosuppression in heart transplantation: insights from network meta-analysis of various immunosuppression regimens. Heart Failure Reviews. 2022. PMID: 32424550. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: kidney function, vasculopathy and CMV favour everolimus-based calcineurin withdrawal; rejection control favours keeping a calcineurin inhibitor — mortality is a wash
cards.summary: Synthesis: kidney function, vasculopathy and CMV favour everolimus-based calcineurin withdrawal; rejection control favours keeping a calcineurin inhibitor — mortality is a wash
cards.people: One randomised trial of everolimus initiation with early ciclosporin withdrawal (115 de novo recipients) and a 15-study network meta-analysis of maintenance immunosuppression after heart transplantation.
cards.result: Renal function: measured GFR 79.8 vs 61.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 12 months in SCHEDULE; pooled eGFR advantage ~9 mL/min/1.73 m² for calcineurin-free mTOR therapy. Vasculopathy: 50.0% vs 64.6% in SCHEDULE; OR 0.53 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.92) for calcineurin + mTOR in the network. CMV: 5.4% vs 30.5% in SCHEDULE. Rejection: more frequent after ciclosporin withdrawal in SCHEDULE (p = 0.03), and highest with the calcineurin-free regimen in the network. Mortality: no difference between regimens. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit on renal function, vasculopathy and CMV; harm on rejection.
cards.watchOut: Neither source answers the question for recipients whose kidneys are already severely impaired, for tacrolimus-based programmes, or beyond the first few years — and 'more rejection' in SCHEDULE was biopsy-proven acute rejection in a monitored trial setting, which may not translate one-for-one to rejection rates in routine practice. Tier C is set because the head-to-head randomised base for this exact strategy is one open-label trial of 115 patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andreassen AK et al. American Journal of Transplantation. 2014 (PMID: 25041227); Ueyama H et al. Heart Failure Reviews. 2022 (PMID: 32424550).

shelves.title: Hearts from donors after circulatory death: six-month survival matched brain-death donors in the randomised trial — pooled curves raise a question about years two to four
shelves.question: In patients awaiting heart transplantation, do hearts donated after circulatory death give non-inferior recipient survival compared with hearts donated after brain death?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Brain Death* · Graft Survival · Heart Transplantation* · Organ Preservation · Tissue and Organ Procurement* · Tissue Donors · Death · Patient Safety
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the time horizon. The one randomised trial (Schroder JN et al., PMID: 37285526) met its noninferiority endpoint clearly: risk-adjusted 6-month survival was 94% with hearts donated after circulatory death (DCD), reanimated and assessed on extracorporeal nonischemic perfusion, versus 90% with standard brain-death (DBD) hearts on cold storage — though the noninferiority margin was a generous 20 percentage points, follow-up was short, and graft-related serious adverse events at 30 days were similar. The pooled observational record is less settled: a 2025 meta-analysis reconstructing time-to-event data from six studies and 3,240 recipients (Al-Tawil M et al., PMID: 40121872) found no overall survival difference (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.25), but the proportional-hazards assumption was violated, and landmark analyses suggested lower survival in DCD recipients from two years (HR 1.67) and four years (HR 2.78), on data that thin out beyond six years. PROPOSED SPLIT: early survival after DCD heart transplantation is non-inferior in randomised evidence; a possible late survival disadvantage in observational pooling is unresolved and is the number to watch.

cards.headline: Schroder 2023: DCD hearts non-inferior at 6 months — risk-adjusted survival 94% vs 90% for brain-death hearts, against a 20-percentage-point margin
cards.summary: Schroder 2023: DCD hearts non-inferior at 6 months — risk-adjusted survival 94% vs 90% for brain-death hearts, against a 20-percentage-point margin
cards.people: Randomised noninferiority trial in adult heart-transplant candidates assigned 3:1 to receive a heart donated after circulatory death (reanimated and assessed with extracorporeal nonischemic perfusion) if available first, or only a brain-death donor heart preserved with traditional cold storage. 180 patients underwent transplantation (90 received a DCD heart, 90 a DBD heart); the as-treated primary analysis included 166 recipients (80 DCD, 86 DBD).
cards.result: Risk-adjusted 6-month survival in the as-treated population was 94% (95% CI 88 to 99) among recipients of a circulatory-death donor heart versus 90% (95% CI 84 to 97) among recipients of a brain-death donor heart (least-squares mean difference −3 percentage points; 90% CI −10 to 3; P < 0.001 for noninferiority, margin 20 percentage points). There were no substantial between-group differences in the mean per-patient number of serious adverse events associated with the heart graft at 30 days after transplantation.
cards.watchOut: Six months is early for a transplant question, the 20-percentage-point noninferiority margin is wide, and the as-treated analysis (166 of 180 transplanted patients) — not the randomised assignment — carries the primary result. The DCD hearts were also a selected, perfusion-assessed subset: hearts that failed reanimation assessment never reached a recipient, which is part of the technology's safety, but means the trial tests a procurement system, not DCD hearts in the raw.
cards.source: Schroder JN et al. Transplantation Outcomes with Donor Hearts after Circulatory Death. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37285526. Registry ID: NCT03831048. cards.headline: Al-Tawil 2025 (meta-analysis, 6 studies, 3,240 recipients): overall survival identical (HR 1.01), but landmark analyses show DCD survival falling behind at 2 years (HR 1.67) and 4 years (HR 2.78)
cards.summary: Al-Tawil 2025 (meta-analysis, 6 studies, 3,240 recipients): overall survival identical (HR 1.01), but landmark analyses show DCD survival falling behind at 2 years (HR 1.67) and 4 years (HR 2.78)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of reconstructed individual time-to-event data from six studies (3,240 patients: 2,242 brain-death donor and 998 circulatory-death donor heart transplant recipients) reporting Kaplan-Meier survival comparisons, with searches to August 2024.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in overall survival between DCD and DBD recipients (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.25, P = 0.91). However, the proportional-hazards assumption was violated, making the single hazard ratio inconclusive; a time-varying flexible parametric model showed significantly declining survival in DCD recipients three years after surgery, and landmark analyses suggested the same trend at the two-year landmark (HR 1.67, p = 0.021) and the four-year mark (HR 2.78, p = 0.002). Data beyond six years were limited, and evidence comparing direct procurement with normothermic regional perfusion was scarce, with no significant survival differences observed between those methods.
cards.watchOut: Reconstructed curves from published Kaplan-Meier plots, dominated by observational series in which DCD and DBD recipients differ (era, centre experience, donor selection) — the late landmark hazard ratios rest on shrinking numbers at risk and could reflect early-programme learning curves as easily as graft biology. It is a signal demanding follow-up, not a verdict.
cards.source: Al-Tawil M et al. Survival after heart transplants from circulatory-dead versus brain-dead donors: Meta-analysis of reconstructed time-to-event data. Transplantation Reviews. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: randomised evidence says early survival is non-inferior; pooled observational curves hint the DCD advantage may not hold past two to three years
cards.summary: Synthesis: randomised evidence says early survival is non-inferior; pooled observational curves hint the DCD advantage may not hold past two to three years
cards.people: One randomised noninferiority trial (180 transplanted patients, 6-month endpoint) and a six-study reconstructed time-to-event meta-analysis (3,240 recipients) comparing circulatory-death with brain-death donor hearts.
cards.result: At 6 months: risk-adjusted survival 94% (DCD) vs 90% (DBD), noninferiority P < 0.001 against a 20-point margin; 30-day graft serious adverse events similar. Pooled overall: HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.25) with violated proportional hazards; landmark HRs against DCD of 1.67 at two years and 2.78 at four years, on thinning data. PROPOSED SPLIT — early non-inferiority established, long-term equivalence not yet.
cards.watchOut: The two sources are not in direct conflict — they look at different horizons with different designs — and neither can separate the effect of the donor pathway from the effect of the perfusion technology used to assess DCD hearts. Tier C is set because long-term randomised data do not exist and the late signal comes from reconstructed observational curves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schroder JN et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37285526); Al-Tawil M et al. Transplantation Reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40121872).
