shelves.title: Balloon angioplasty versus riociguat for inoperable CTEPH: the balloon lowered lung-artery resistance far more — and caused serious adverse events in 42% versus 9%
shelves.question: In patients with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, does balloon pulmonary angioplasty improve haemodynamics and exercise capacity compared with riociguat?
shelves.mesh: Angioplasty/adverse effects · Angioplasty, Balloon*/adverse effects · Chronic Disease · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary*/drug therapy/etiology · Pulmonary Embolism*/complications/drug therapy · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) won the haemodynamic contest and lost the safety contest in the only head-to-head randomised trial. In RACE (Jaïs X et al., PMID: 35926542), 105 treatment-naive patients with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) randomised to BPA or riociguat had, at 26 weeks, a fall in pulmonary vascular resistance to 39.9% of baseline with BPA versus 66.7% with riociguat (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.69) — but treatment-related serious adverse events in 42% versus 9%, driven by lung injury in 35% of the BPA group, with no treatment-related deaths. The trial's own follow-up softens the either/or framing: by week 52, after symptomatic patients crossed to add-on therapy, resistance reductions were similar (ratio 0.91, 0.79 to 1.04), and BPA after riociguat pretreatment caused fewer serious adverse events (14% vs 42%). A meta-analysis of BPA series (Guo Q et al., PMID: 37295014) confirms the direction of the haemodynamic and walking-distance gains without a randomised comparator. PROPOSED SPLIT: BPA lowers pulmonary vascular resistance more than riociguat at six months, at a substantially higher serious-adverse-event cost; the evidence points toward sequencing the two rather than choosing one.

cards.headline: Jaïs 2022 (RACE): BPA cut pulmonary vascular resistance to 39.9% of baseline vs 66.7% on riociguat at 26 weeks — but serious adverse events 42% vs 9%
cards.summary: Jaïs 2022 (RACE): BPA cut pulmonary vascular resistance to 39.9% of baseline vs 66.7% on riociguat at 26 weeks — but serious adverse events 42% vs 9%
cards.people: 105 treatment-naive patients aged 18–80 with newly diagnosed, inoperable CTEPH and pulmonary vascular resistance above 320 dyn·s/cm⁵, randomised at 23 French expert centres to balloon pulmonary angioplasty (n = 52) or riociguat (n = 53); primary endpoint was change in pulmonary vascular resistance at week 26. Patients completing the trial entered a 26-week ancillary follow-up in which symptomatic patients with resistance still above threshold received add-on therapy (riociguat after BPA, or BPA after riociguat).
cards.result: At week 26, geometric mean pulmonary vascular resistance had fallen to 39.9% (95% CI 36.2 to 44.0) of baseline in the BPA group and 66.7% (60.5 to 73.5) in the riociguat group (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.69; p < 0.0001). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 22 (42%) of 52 BPA patients and 5 (9%) of 53 riociguat patients; the most frequent were lung injury with BPA (18 patients, 35%) and severe hypotension with syncope with riociguat (2 patients, 4%). There were no treatment-related deaths. At week 52, resistance reduction was similar between first-line strategies (ratio of geometric means 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.04), and BPA-related serious adverse events were less frequent in patients pretreated with riociguat (5 of 36, 14%) than in first-line BPA patients (22 of 52, 42%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 105 patients, and a haemodynamic primary endpoint — the trial was not powered for death or clinical worsening, and the week-52 comparison is an observational follow-up of crossovers, not a randomised sequence comparison. BPA results also come from expert French centres; lung-injury rates during a programme's learning curve elsewhere may differ in either direction.
cards.source: Jaïs X et al. Balloon pulmonary angioplasty versus riociguat for the treatment of inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (RACE): a multicentre, phase 3, open-label, randomised controlled trial and ancillary follow-up study. cards.headline: Guo 2023 (meta-analysis, 7 studies): BPA lowered pulmonary vascular resistance (MD −4.70 Wood units) and mean pulmonary pressure, and added ~44 m to six-minute walk distance
cards.summary: Guo 2023 (meta-analysis, 7 studies): BPA lowered pulmonary vascular resistance (MD −4.70 Wood units) and mean pulmonary pressure, and added ~44 m to six-minute walk distance
cards.people: Meta-analysis of seven studies of balloon pulmonary angioplasty in patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, pooling haemodynamics, six-minute walk distance, NT-proBNP, and WHO functional class before and after BPA.
cards.result: BPA was associated with a significant reduction in pulmonary arterial pressure (mean difference −9.80, P < .00001) and in pulmonary vascular resistance (mean difference −4.70, 95% CI −7.17 to −2.22, P = .0002), an improvement in six-minute walk distance (mean difference 43.86 m, 95% CI 26.19 to 61.53, P < .00001), and improvement in WHO functional class distribution. NT-proBNP change was not significant (mean difference −3.46, 95% CI −10.63 to 3.71, p = 0.34).
cards.watchOut: These are before–after pools from uncontrolled series: regression to the mean, background drug therapy, and operator selection all inflate apparent benefit, and the record itself prints an internally inconsistent confidence interval for the pressure outcome. It corroborates that BPA moves haemodynamics and walking distance; the randomised comparison with riociguat is RACE, above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: BPA is the stronger haemodynamic intervention and the riskier one; the trial's crossover phase suggests riociguat-first sequencing may capture much of both benefits
cards.summary: Synthesis: BPA is the stronger haemodynamic intervention and the riskier one; the trial's crossover phase suggests riociguat-first sequencing may capture much of both benefits
cards.people: One randomised head-to-head trial (105 patients, RACE) with a 26-week crossover follow-up, plus a seven-study before–after meta-analysis of BPA in CTEPH.
cards.result: Pulmonary vascular resistance at 26 weeks: 39.9% of baseline (BPA) vs 66.7% (riociguat), ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.69). Treatment-related serious adverse events: 42% vs 9%; no treatment-related deaths. At 52 weeks after add-on crossover: resistance ratio 0.91 (0.79 to 1.04); BPA serious adverse events 14% when pretreated with riociguat vs 42% first-line. Uncontrolled pooling: walk distance +43.86 m, resistance −4.70 Wood units. PROPOSED SPLIT — greater efficacy, greater procedural harm.
cards.watchOut: No trial here compares either strategy against pulmonary endarterectomy (the operable-CTEPH standard) or reports mortality — 'inoperable' was a centre judgement, and operability calls vary. Tier C is set because the comparative evidence is a single open-label trial of 105 patients with a surrogate primary endpoint.

shelves.title: A medium-dose statin plus ezetimibe matched a high-dose statin on three-year heart outcomes — with more patients at LDL goal and half the intolerance dropouts
shelves.question: In patients at high cardiovascular risk, does moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe match high-intensity statin monotherapy for cardiovascular outcomes, with fewer intolerance-related discontinuations?
shelves.mesh: Anticholesteremic Agents*/adverse effects · Atherosclerosis*/drug therapy · Cardiovascular Diseases*/drug therapy · Cholesterol, LDL · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ezetimibe/adverse effects · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors*/adverse effects · Rosuvastatin Calcium · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the strategy question was tested head-on in one large open-label noninferiority trial. In RACING (Kim BK et al., PMID: 35863366), 3,780 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg or rosuvastatin 20 mg alone had near-identical three-year rates of the composite of cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events, or non-fatal stroke (9.1% vs 9.9%; absolute difference −0.78%, 90% CI −2.39 to 0.83, inside the 2.0% noninferiority margin), while the combination put more patients below an LDL cholesterol of 70 mg/dL at every year checked (73% vs 55% at one year) and halved intolerance-related discontinuation or dose reduction (4.8% vs 8.2%). A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials and 5,412 participants (Yasmin F et al., PMID: 40492183) supports the lipid half of the claim — greater LDL reduction with low/moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe (mean difference −6.59 mg/dL) — but found no significant difference in major adverse cardiovascular events, so the outcomes equivalence rests on RACING alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combination therapy is a legitimate equal-outcomes, better-tolerated alternative to high-intensity statin monotherapy, proven in one Korean trial population rather than across many.

cards.headline: Kim 2022 (RACING): moderate statin + ezetimibe non-inferior to high-intensity statin — 3-year primary endpoint 9.1% vs 9.9%, LDL <70 mg/dL in 73% vs 55% at 1 year, intolerance discontinuation 4.8% vs 8.2%
cards.summary: Kim 2022 (RACING): moderate statin + ezetimibe non-inferior to high-intensity statin — 3-year primary endpoint 9.1% vs 9.9%, LDL <70 mg/dL in 73% vs 55% at 1 year, intolerance discontinuation 4.8% vs 8.2%
cards.people: 3,780 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at 26 clinical centres in South Korea, randomised open-label (1:1) to moderate-intensity statin with ezetimibe (rosuvastatin 10 mg + ezetimibe 10 mg; n = 1,894) or high-intensity statin monotherapy (rosuvastatin 20 mg; n = 1,886). Primary endpoint was the 3-year composite of cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events, or non-fatal stroke, with a noninferiority margin of 2.0%.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 172 patients (9.1%) in the combination group and 186 (9.9%) in the monotherapy group (absolute difference −0.78%; 90% CI −2.39 to 0.83), meeting noninferiority. LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL was observed at 1, 2, and 3 years in 73%, 75%, and 72% of the combination group versus 55%, 60%, and 58% of the monotherapy group (all p < 0.0001). Discontinuation or dose reduction of study drug because of intolerance occurred in 88 patients (4.8%) versus 150 (8.2%) (p < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country (South Korea), and a noninferiority design: it shows the combination is not worse by more than the prespecified 2% margin, not that it is superior, and event adjudication in an unblinded trial of a strategy patients can feel (side effects) deserves the caution the intolerance endpoint itself invites. It also compares one specific pairing — rosuvastatin 10 mg + ezetimibe against rosuvastatin 20 mg — not every statin at every dose.
cards.source: Kim BK et al. cards.headline: Yasmin 2025 (meta-analysis, 20 RCTs, 5,412 participants): low/moderate statin + ezetimibe lowered LDL more than high-intensity statin alone (MD −6.59 mg/dL); no significant difference in MACE
cards.summary: Yasmin 2025 (meta-analysis, 20 RCTs, 5,412 participants): low/moderate statin + ezetimibe lowered LDL more than high-intensity statin alone (MD −6.59 mg/dL); no significant difference in MACE
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 randomised controlled trials (5,412 participants) comparing low- or moderate-intensity statin combined with ezetimibe against high-intensity statin monotherapy, with lipid changes, inflammatory markers, safety enzymes, and major adverse cardiovascular events as outcomes; searches to May 2023.
cards.result: Low/moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe produced a significantly greater reduction in LDL cholesterol than high-intensity statin monotherapy (mean difference −6.59 mg/dL, 95% CI −10.95 to −2.24; p = 0.003; I² = 84%). No significant differences were observed for total cholesterol, triglycerides, or HDL cholesterol. High-sensitivity CRP was significantly higher with combination therapy (mean difference 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.64; p = 0.04; I² = 0%), creatine phosphokinase levels increased significantly more with monotherapy, and there was no significant difference in major adverse cardiovascular events between strategies.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled trials are short lipid-endpoint studies (hence the very high heterogeneity, I² = 84%, on the LDL result), so the meta-analysis cannot independently confirm the clinical-outcomes equivalence — for events, RACING carries nearly all the weight. The small hs-CRP difference favouring monotherapy is of uncertain meaning and is printed here so the card is not read as one-directional.
cards.source: Yasmin F et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal three-year outcomes in the one outcomes trial, better LDL target attainment and tolerability with the combination, and pooled lipid data agreeing on the LDL advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal three-year outcomes in the one outcomes trial, better LDL target attainment and tolerability with the combination, and pooled lipid data agreeing on the LDL advantage
cards.people: One open-label noninferiority outcomes trial (3,780 patients with ASCVD) and a 20-trial meta-analysis (5,412 participants) of the same strategy comparison.
cards.result: Outcomes: 3-year composite 9.1% (combination) vs 9.9% (high-intensity alone), difference −0.78% (90% CI −2.39 to 0.83), noninferior; pooled MACE not significantly different. LDL: target <70 mg/dL reached by 73% vs 55% at one year in RACING; pooled LDL reduction greater by 6.59 mg/dL with the combination. Tolerability: intolerance-related discontinuation or dose reduction 4.8% vs 8.2% in RACING. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not sameness: the confidence interval allows the combination to be up to ~0.8 percentage points worse on the three-year composite in the trial's own (90%) terms, and no trial has tested the strategy in primary prevention or with non-rosuvastatin pairings at outcome level. Tier C is set because one open-label trial carries the clinical-outcome claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kim BK et al. The Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35863366); Yasmin F et al. Journal of Lipid and Atherosclerosis. 2025 (PMID: 40492183).

shelves.title: Zodasiran silences ANGPTL3 and triglycerides fell by up to 63% in a 204-patient phase 2 trial — a lipid result only, with heart outcomes entirely untested
shelves.question: In adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia, does zodasiran (RNA interference against ANGPTL3) lower triglycerides and other atherogenic lipids compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Angiopoietin-Like Protein 3*/antagonists & inhibitors/genetics/metabolism · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Hyperlipidemias*/blood/drug therapy/metabolism · Injections, Subcutaneous · Liver/metabolism · RNAi Therapeutics*/adverse effects/methods · Treatment Outcome · Triglycerides*/blood · RNA, Small Interfering*/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — zodasiran, a small interfering RNA against ANGPTL3, does exactly what its mechanism promises to blood lipids, and nothing yet to clinical events. In the phase 2b ARCHES-2 trial (Rosenson RS et al., PMID: 38809174), 204 adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia had dose-dependent placebo-adjusted triglyceride falls of 51, 57, and 63 percentage points at 50, 100, and 200 mg at week 24, with parallel falls in non-HDL cholesterol (up to 36 percentage points), apolipoprotein B (up to 22), and LDL cholesterol (up to 20), and a transient rise in glycated haemoglobin at the highest dose in patients with pre-existing diabetes as the one flagged safety signal. A 2026 meta-analysis of target-specific RNA lipid therapies (Widjaja JS et al., PMID: 42863556; 16 trials, 5,604 participants) found adverse-event rates comparable with placebo across the class but states plainly that long-term clinical outcome data are lacking. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a potent, durable lipid-lowering signal from a single 204-patient, 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial — whether silencing ANGPTL3 this way prevents cardiovascular events is untested.

cards.headline: Rosenson 2024 (ARCHES-2): zodasiran cut triglycerides by 51–63 percentage points vs placebo at week 24, dose-dependently; non-HDL down up to 36 points, LDL up to 20
cards.summary: Rosenson 2024 (ARCHES-2): zodasiran cut triglycerides by 51–63 percentage points vs placebo at week 24, dose-dependently; non-HDL down up to 36 points, LDL up to 20
cards.people: 204 adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia (fasting triglycerides 150–499 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol ≥70 mg/dL or non-HDL cholesterol ≥100 mg/dL), randomised 3:1 in a double-blind dose-ranging phase 2b trial to subcutaneous zodasiran (50, 100, or 200 mg) or placebo on day 1 and week 12, followed through week 36. Primary endpoint was percent change in triglyceride level from baseline to week 24.
cards.result: At week 24, ANGPTL3 levels fell dose-dependently versus placebo (difference in change −54 percentage points with 50 mg, −70 with 100 mg, −74 with 200 mg), as did triglyceride levels (−51, −57, and −63 percentage points respectively; P < 0.001 for all comparisons). Other placebo-adjusted differences: non-HDL cholesterol −29, −29, and −36 percentage points; apolipoprotein B −19, −15, and −22 percentage points; LDL cholesterol −16, −14, and −20 percentage points. A transient elevation in glycated haemoglobin was observed in patients with pre-existing diabetes who received the highest dose.
cards.watchOut: Two injections and 24 weeks in 204 patients: this is a pharmacology demonstration, not an outcomes trial. Percent changes in triglycerides are relative changes in a biomarker with no absolute event rates beside them, because there were no clinical events to report — and the glycaemic signal at the top dose, though transient, is exactly the kind of thing only larger, longer exposure can settle.
cards.source: Rosenson RS et al. Zodasiran, an RNAi Therapeutic Targeting ANGPTL3, for Mixed Hyperlipidemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38809174. Registry ID: NCT04832971. cards.headline: Widjaja 2026 (meta-analysis, 16 RCTs, 5,604 participants): RNA lipid therapies lower lipids target-specifically, with adverse events comparable to placebo — and no long-term outcome data
cards.summary: Widjaja 2026 (meta-analysis, 16 RCTs, 5,604 participants): RNA lipid therapies lower lipids target-specifically, with adverse events comparable to placebo — and no long-term outcome data
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised controlled trials (5,604 participants) of RNA-based lipid-lowering therapies — inclisiran (PCSK9), olezarsen and plozasiran (APOC3), and zodasiran (ANGPTL3) — versus placebo in hyperlipidaemia or hypertriglyceridaemia, with pooled analyses stratified by molecular target.
cards.result: PCSK9-targeting therapy produced the greatest reductions in LDL cholesterol (mean difference −53.01%, 95% CI −57.56 to −48.45), apolipoprotein B (−39.59%, −43.33 to −35.85), and non-HDL cholesterol (−44.62%, −47.73 to −41.51), whereas APOC3-targeting therapies produced the greatest triglyceride reduction (−52.26%, −56.50 to −48.02). Total adverse events, serious adverse events, and adverse events leading to discontinuation were comparable between RNA-based therapies and placebo. The authors note that differences in individual adverse outcomes and the limited availability of long-term clinical outcome data require further investigation.
cards.watchOut: The pooled numbers quoted are for the PCSK9 and APOC3 target strata, not an ANGPTL3-specific pooled estimate — the record does not print one — so this card supports class-level safety and the target-specific pattern of lipid effects, while the zodasiran-specific efficacy numbers remain ARCHES-2's own. Pooling across four different drugs and populations is context, not confirmation.
cards.source: Widjaja JS et al. Effectiveness and safety of target-specific RNA-based lipid-lowering therapies: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. European Journal of Pharmacology. 2026. PMID: 42863556. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, dose-ordered triglyceride and non-HDL effect from one small phase 2 trial; the class looks safe short-term; no cardiovascular outcome has been tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, dose-ordered triglyceride and non-HDL effect from one small phase 2 trial; the class looks safe short-term; no cardiovascular outcome has been tested
cards.people: One phase 2b randomised trial of zodasiran in mixed hyperlipidaemia (204 patients, 24-week primary endpoint) and a 16-trial meta-analysis of RNA-based lipid therapies including zodasiran (5,604 participants).
cards.result: Triglycerides: −51 to −63 percentage points versus placebo across zodasiran doses at week 24. Non-HDL cholesterol: −29 to −36 points; apolipoprotein B: −15 to −22 points; LDL cholesterol: −14 to −20 points. Safety: transient glycated-haemoglobin rise at 200 mg in patients with diabetes in ARCHES-2; class-wide adverse events comparable with placebo in pooled data. Cardiovascular events and mortality: not assessed in either source. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not borrow the ANGPTL3 antibody evidence (evinacumab in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, shelved separately) for this drug: different molecule, delivery, population, and indication. Tier C is set because the entire zodasiran-specific base is one 204-patient surrogate-endpoint trial.

shelves.title: A daily pill that inhibits PCSK9: enlicitide cut LDL by 58% versus placebo in familial hypercholesterolaemia — cholesterol proven, heart outcomes not yet
shelves.question: In adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does the oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide lower LDL cholesterol compared with placebo on top of standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Anticholesteremic Agents*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Apolipoproteins B/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Double-Blind Method · Heterozygote · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II*/drug therapy/blood/genetics · Lipoprotein(a)/blood · PCSK9 Inhibitors*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Proprotein Convertase 9/metabolism · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — enlicitide is the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor to complete a phase 3 trial, and the LDL effect is large and durable over a year. In CORALreef HeFH (Ballantyne CM et al., PMID: 41206969), 303 adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia already on statins (81.5% high-intensity; 64.4% also on ezetimibe; mean baseline LDL 119.0 mg/dL) randomised to enlicitide 20 mg daily or placebo had a week-24 LDL change of −58.2% versus +2.6% (between-group difference −59.4 percentage points, 95% CI −65.6 to −53.2), sustained at week 52 (−55.3% vs +8.7%; difference −61.5 points), with parallel falls in non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, and lipoprotein(a), and adverse-event, serious-adverse-event, and discontinuation rates similar to placebo. A 2026 dose-stratified meta-analysis of oral PCSK9 inhibitors (Marchetta M et al., PMID: 42765777; 4 trials, 949 participants, moderate GRADE certainty) confirms substantial atherogenic-lipoprotein reductions without a short-term safety signal — while stating that no cardiovascular outcome benefit or equivalence to injectable PCSK9 antibodies is established. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): proven, injectable-class-sized LDL lowering from a pill in HeFH; the outcomes trial that would make this LIKELY has not reported.

cards.headline: Ballantyne 2026 (CORALreef HeFH): oral enlicitide lowered LDL by 58.2% vs a 2.6% rise on placebo at week 24 (difference −59.4 points), sustained at week 52
cards.summary: Ballantyne 2026 (CORALreef HeFH): oral enlicitide lowered LDL by 58.2% vs a 2.6% rise on placebo at week 24 (difference −59.4 points), sustained at week 52
cards.people: 303 adults (mean age 52.4 years, 51% women) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on lipid-lowering therapy (all on statins, 81.5% high-intensity; 64.4% on ezetimibe), with LDL ≥55 mg/dL plus a history of major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or LDL ≥70 mg/dL without one; mean baseline LDL 119.0 mg/dL. Randomised 2:1 at 59 sites in 17 countries to enlicitide 20 mg once daily (n = 202) or placebo (n = 101) for 52 weeks; 96.7% completed the trial. Primary outcome was mean percent change in LDL cholesterol at week 24.
cards.result: Mean percent change in LDL cholesterol at week 24 was −58.2% with enlicitide versus +2.6% with placebo (between-group difference −59.4%, 95% CI −65.6 to −53.2; P < .001), and at week 52 was −55.3% versus +8.7% (difference −61.5%, 95% CI −69.4 to −53.7; P < .001). At week 24, non-HDL cholesterol changed by −52.3% versus +2.1% (difference −53.0%, −58.5 to −47.4), apolipoprotein B by −48.2% versus +1.8% (difference −49.1%, −54.0 to −44.3), and lipoprotein(a) median change was −24.7% versus −1.6% (difference −27.5%, −34.3 to −20.6) — all P < .001. The incidence of adverse events, serious adverse events, and discontinuation due to adverse events was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: An LDL surrogate endpoint in 303 patients: the trial proves the pill lowers cholesterol in HeFH on top of statins, not that it prevents the heart attacks that make HeFH dangerous, and 52 weeks in 202 exposed patients cannot exclude uncommon or late harms. Percent LDL changes are relative changes in a biomarker; absolute LDL levels achieved depend on each patient's starting value (mean baseline here 119.0 mg/dL despite statins).

cards.headline: Marchetta 2026 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 949 participants): oral PCSK9 inhibitors significantly reduced LDL, ApoB, non-HDL and Lp(a) at both dose strata, with no detected short-term safety increase; GRADE certainty moderate
cards.summary: Marchetta 2026 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 949 participants): oral PCSK9 inhibitors significantly reduced LDL, ApoB, non-HDL and Lp(a) at both dose strata, with no detected short-term safety increase; GRADE certainty moderate
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised placebo-controlled trials (949 participants) of oral PCSK9 inhibitors reporting lipid or safety outcomes, searching PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL to November 2025, with efficacy analysed separately for the lowest and highest evaluated dose strata and GRADE certainty assessment.
cards.result: Both dose strata significantly reduced LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, non-HDL cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a), with larger pooled reductions generally observed in the highest evaluated stratum. Short-term safety analyses did not detect statistically significant increases in overall adverse events, serious adverse events, or selected individual adverse events in either stratum, and sensitivity analyses excluding the HeFH trial yielded consistent estimates. Certainty of evidence for all primary efficacy outcomes was moderate. The authors conclude the findings demonstrate pharmacodynamic lipid-lowering efficacy but do not establish a class-wide dose-response relationship, cardiovascular outcome benefit, or clinical equivalence to outcome-proven PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials of investigational agents, pooled by dose stratum rather than by drug, with the HeFH trial contributing a large share of participants — the sensitivity analysis excluding it is reassuring for direction, but the class evidence remains early and entirely surrogate-based, as the authors themselves state.
cards.source: Marchetta M et al. Dose-stratified lipid-lowering efficacy and safety of oral PCSK9 inhibitors: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42765777. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Blocking interleukin-6 in kidney patients: ziltivekimab lowered CRP by up to 92% in a 264-patient phase 2 trial — inflammation suppressed, events untested
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease, elevated interleukin-6 and high atherosclerotic risk, does ziltivekimab lower inflammatory biomarkers (hsCRP, fibrinogen, Lp(a)) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage* · Atherosclerosis · Biomarkers/blood · C-Reactive Protein/drug effects* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inflammation/complications/drug therapy · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-6 Inhibitors* · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/drug therapy* · Thrombosis/complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — RESCUE (Ridker PM et al., PMID: 34015342) is a clean phase 2 biomarker trial and nothing more. In 264 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease and high-sensitivity CRP of at least 2 mg/L, monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab — a monoclonal antibody against the interleukin-6 ligand — reduced median hsCRP at 12 weeks by 77%, 88%, and 92% at 7.5, 15, and 30 mg versus 4% on placebo (pairwise differences −66.2, −77.7, and −87.8 percentage points, all p < 0.0001), with stable effects over 24 weeks and dose-dependent reductions in fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, secretory phospholipase A2, and lipoprotein(a). It was well tolerated, with no serious injection-site reactions and no sustained grade 3 or 4 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia, and it did not affect the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio. No cardiovascular event was an endpoint, no on-question systematic review pooling clinical outcomes exists yet, and the authors' own conclusion is that a large outcomes trial is the next step. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): profound, dose-ordered suppression of inflammatory biomarkers in exactly the high-risk CKD population of interest — with event prevention entirely unproven.

cards.headline: Ridker 2021 (RESCUE): ziltivekimab cut hsCRP by 77–92% across doses vs 4% on placebo at 12 weeks in CKD patients with raised CRP
cards.summary: Ridker 2021 (RESCUE): ziltivekimab cut hsCRP by 77–92% across doses vs 4% on placebo at 12 weeks in CKD patients with raised CRP
cards.people: 264 participants (66 per group) aged 18 or older with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease and high-sensitivity CRP of at least 2 mg/L, randomised double-blind at 40 US sites to subcutaneous placebo or ziltivekimab 7.5 mg, 15 mg, or 30 mg every 4 weeks for up to 24 weeks. Primary outcome was percent change in hsCRP at 12 weeks; additional biomarker and safety data were collected over 24 weeks.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, median hsCRP was reduced by 77% (7.5 mg), 88% (15 mg), and 92% (30 mg) versus 4% with placebo; median pairwise differences in percent change versus placebo were −66.2% (7.5 mg), −77.7% (15 mg), and −87.8% (30 mg), all p < 0.0001. Effects were stable over the 24-week treatment period. Dose-dependent reductions were also observed for fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, secretory phospholipase A2, and lipoprotein(a). Ziltivekimab was well tolerated, did not affect the total cholesterol to HDL cholesterol ratio, and there were no serious injection-site reactions or sustained grade 3 or 4 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia.
cards.watchOut: Biomarkers are not events: hsCRP is a marker of the inflammatory pathway, and the history of this field (shelved at the IL-1 shelves) is that suppressing a marker and preventing myocardial infarction are separable claims. The trial ran 24 weeks in 264 patients — far too small and short to detect either clinical benefit or uncommon harms of chronic immune-pathway suppression, such as serious infection.
cards.source: Ridker PM et al. IL-6 inhibition with ziltivekimab in patients at high atherosclerotic risk (RESCUE): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. The Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34015342. Registry ID: NCT03926117. shelves.title: Asundexian versus apixaban in atrial fibrillation: the trial was stopped early — strokes nearly quadrupled (1.3% vs 0.4%) even though major bleeding fell (0.2% vs 0.7%)
shelves.question: In patients with atrial fibrillation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, does the factor XIa inhibitor asundexian, compared with apixaban, prevent stroke or systemic embolism without excess bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Administration, Oral · Anticoagulants*/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Atrial Fibrillation*/drug therapy/complications · Double-Blind Method · Embolism*/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Factor Xa Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Hemorrhage*/chemically induced/epidemiology · Hydrocarbons, Fluorinated · Intention to Treat Analysis · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pyridones/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Stroke*/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Benzamides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Triazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — this is a stopped-for-inferiority trial, and the numbers are not close. In OCEANIC-AF (Piccini JP et al., PMID: 39225267), 14,810 high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation randomised to asundexian 50 mg daily or standard-dose apixaban were followed until the independent data monitoring committee stopped the trial prematurely: stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 1.3% on asundexian versus 0.4% on apixaban (HR 3.79, 95% CI 2.46 to 5.83) — nearly four times the hazard, an absolute excess of about 0.9 percentage points over the truncated follow-up. The hoped-for safety advantage was real but smaller in absolute terms: major bleeding 0.2% versus 0.7% (HR 0.32, 0.18 to 0.55). A 2026 meta-analysis of factor XI/XIa inhibitors versus direct oral anticoagulants in atrial fibrillation (de Alcântara JPTL et al., PMID: 41734570) shows the same class pattern — major bleeding roughly a third (OR 0.30) but ischaemic stroke roughly tripled (OR 3.20, 1.85 to 5.55) — so this is not one trial's accident. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): at the dose tested, asundexian traded away stroke prevention that apixaban demonstrably provides; less bleeding does not compensate for strokes not prevented.

cards.headline: Piccini 2025 (OCEANIC-AF): asundexian stopped early for inferiority — stroke or systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4% on apixaban (HR 3.79); major bleeding 0.2% vs 0.7% (HR 0.32)
cards.summary: Piccini 2025 (OCEANIC-AF): asundexian stopped early for inferiority — stroke or systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4% on apixaban (HR 3.79); major bleeding 0.2% vs 0.7% (HR 0.32)
cards.people: 14,810 patients with atrial fibrillation at high risk of stroke (mean age 73.9 years, 35.2% women, mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 4.3; 18.6% with chronic kidney disease, 18.2% with previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack), randomised double-blind 1:1 internationally to asundexian 50 mg once daily or standard-dose apixaban. Primary efficacy objective was noninferiority for prevention of stroke or systemic embolism; primary safety objective was superiority for major bleeding. The trial was stopped prematurely on the recommendation of the independent data monitoring committee.
cards.result: Stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 98 patients (1.3%) assigned to asundexian and 26 (0.4%) assigned to apixaban (hazard ratio 3.79, 95% CI 2.46 to 5.83). Major bleeding occurred in 17 patients (0.2%) on asundexian and 53 (0.7%) on apixaban (hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.55). The incidence of any adverse event appeared similar in the two groups. The authors conclude that asundexian at 50 mg daily was associated with a higher incidence of stroke or systemic embolism than apixaban in the period before the trial was stopped, with fewer major bleeding events.
cards.watchOut: Event counts accrued over a truncated follow-up, so the percentages are not annualised rates — but the hazard ratio of 3.79 with a confidence interval entirely above 2.4 leaves no room for a 'not enough time' reading: the drug at this dose under-anticoagulated. The result condemns asundexian 50 mg for stroke prevention in AF; it does not by itself settle whether a different dose or a different factor XI agent could do better — the meta-analysis card is the place for that class question.
cards.source: Piccini JP et al. Asundexian versus Apixaban in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39225267. Registry ID: NCT05643573. cards.headline: de Alcântara 2026 (meta-analysis of FXI/XIa inhibitors vs DOACs in AF): major bleeding OR 0.30, but ischaemic stroke OR 3.20 — the class pattern matches OCEANIC-AF
cards.summary: de Alcântara 2026 (meta-analysis of FXI/XIa inhibitors vs DOACs in AF): major bleeding OR 0.30, but ischaemic stroke OR 3.20 — the class pattern matches OCEANIC-AF
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 RCTs (de Alcântara 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing factor XI/XIa inhibitors with direct oral anticoagulants in adults with atrial fibrillation (four trials — OCEANIC-AF, AZALEA-TIMI 71, PACIFIC-AF, and the LIBREXIA-AF design protocol — 16,852 patients in qualitative synthesis; three trials contributing to quantitative pooling; searches to February 2025). Primary outcome was ISTH major bleeding.
cards.result: Compared with DOACs, factor XI/XIa inhibitors were associated with significantly less ISTH major bleeding (0.40% vs 1.32%; OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.43; P < 0.001; I² = 0%) and less clinically relevant non-major bleeding (1.53% vs 3.94%; OR 0.38, 0.30 to 0.47; P < 0.001). However, they were associated with a significantly increased risk of ischaemic stroke (1.12% vs 0.35%; OR 3.20, 95% CI 1.85 to 5.55; P = 0.004; I² = 0%). A modest reduction in all-cause mortality was observed (1.37% vs 1.68%; OR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95; P = 0.021). The authors conclude the unfavourable stroke profile raises concerns about net clinical benefit for the currently evaluated agents.
cards.watchOut: The pooled stroke signal is dominated by OCEANIC-AF's size, and one included item (LIBREXIA-AF) contributed design only, not events — so the meta-analysis largely re-states the anchor trial with class framing. Its mortality finding (OR 0.81) sits awkwardly beside the stroke excess and should not be quoted without it; short, partly truncated follow-up makes mortality the least stable number on the card.
cards.source: de Alcântara JPTL et al. Factor XI inhibitors versus direct oral anticoagulants for the prevention of thromboembolic events and safety in patients with atrial fibrillation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Heart & Lung. 2026. PMID: 41734570. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: factor XIa inhibition at the tested dose prevents bleeding by under-anticoagulating — stroke or embolism nearly quadrupled versus apixaban while major bleeding fell by two-thirds
cards.summary: Synthesis: factor XIa inhibition at the tested dose prevents bleeding by under-anticoagulating — stroke or embolism nearly quadrupled versus apixaban while major bleeding fell by two-thirds
cards.people: One phase 3 head-to-head trial stopped early for inferiority (14,810 patients) and a four-trial class meta-analysis (16,852 patients in qualitative synthesis) of factor XI/XIa inhibitors versus direct oral anticoagulants in atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Efficacy: stroke or systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4% (HR 3.79, 95% CI 2.46 to 5.83) for asundexian vs apixaban; pooled ischaemic stroke OR 3.20 (1.85 to 5.55) for the class. Safety: major bleeding 0.2% vs 0.7% (HR 0.32, 0.18 to 0.55); pooled ISTH major bleeding OR 0.30 (0.20 to 0.43). Mortality: pooled all-cause OR 0.81 (0.69 to 0.95), on short follow-up. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) for asundexian 50 mg as AF stroke prevention.
cards.watchOut: Keep the abelacimab evidence (shelved separately from AZALEA-TIMI 71) distinct: that agent was compared on bleeding endpoints in a trial not powered for stroke efficacy, whereas OCEANIC-AF is the one trial that measured the efficacy price directly — and it was decisive. Tier C is set because the class is still evolving and other agents/doses remain in trials, even though the asundexian result itself is firm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Piccini JP et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39225267); de Alcântara JPTL et al. Heart & Lung. 2026 (PMID: 41734570).

shelves.title: Intensive statin, ACE inhibitor and aspirin for women with chest pain but open arteries: WARRIOR found no event reduction — 221 events versus 200 on usual care
shelves.question: In women with ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, does intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor/ARB and aspirin), compared with usual care, reduce angina burden and cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Prospective Studies · Middle Aged · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors*/therapeutic use · Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors*/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · United States/epidemiology · Coronary Artery Disease*/drug therapy/mortality/diagnosis/complications · Treatment Outcome · Quality of Life · Time Factors · Risk Factors · Coronary Angiography · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists*/therapeutic use · Aspirin*/therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Agents*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — WARRIOR is the largest randomised trial of empiric intensive therapy in women with ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, and it found no benefit — but it also failed to recruit as planned and the population arrived already well treated. In WARRIOR (Pepine CJ et al., PMID: 41932694), 2,476 women (mean age 64) with suspected ischaemia referred for coronary angiography randomised to intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, and aspirin) versus usual care had no difference in the primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, or hospitalisation for angina or heart failure at 2.5 years (221 vs 200 events; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.37, p = 0.20), with hospitalisations for angina dominating the endpoint and no secondary outcome favouring intensive therapy. The authors note the trial was underpowered relative to plan, baseline blood pressure and LDL were already well controlled, and baseline use of statins and ACE inhibitors/ARBs was already high in usual care — a contamination problem a sensitivity analysis (estimated HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.352 to 1.558, p = 0.43) could not resolve. No on-question systematic review of intensive therapy for INOCA was found on a verified search. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intensive empiric therapy did not reduce events in WARRIOR, and the trial's own limitations mean that is a negative trial, not proof of no effect.

cards.headline: Pepine 2026 (WARRIOR): intensive statin + ACE inhibitor/ARB + aspirin did not reduce events in women with INOCA — 221 vs 200 events at 2.5 years (HR 1.13)
cards.summary: Pepine 2026 (WARRIOR): intensive statin + ACE inhibitor/ARB + aspirin did not reduce events in women with INOCA — 221 vs 200 events at 2.5 years (HR 1.13)
cards.people: 2,476 women (mean age 64 years) with suspected ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries referred for coronary angiography at 71 US sites, randomised to intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, and aspirin) versus usual care, in a randomised, prospective, blinded-outcomes trial. Primary outcome was the composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke/transient ischaemic attack, or hospitalisation for angina or heart failure.
cards.result: At 2.5 years, 421 events had occurred (221 in the intensive-therapy group, 200 in usual care), with no difference in the primary outcome (HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.37, for intensive therapy vs usual care; p = 0.20) or in secondary outcomes. Hospitalisations for angina were the dominant contributor to the composite. A sensitivity analysis allowing for contamination gave an estimated HR of 0.74 (95% CI 0.352 to 1.558, p = 0.43). The authors note recruitment was lower than planned, the population was older than expected, and baseline blood pressure and LDL cholesterol were well controlled with relatively high rates of statin and ACE inhibitor/ARB use already in usual care.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial that cannot quite carry its own weight: recruitment fell short, the absolute event rate was driven by angina hospitalisations rather than death or myocardial infarction, and the usual-care arm was already receiving much of the intervention (statins and ACE inhibitors/ARBs at baseline), which blunts the contrast. The contamination-adjusted hazard ratio of 0.74 with a confidence interval from 0.35 to 1.56 is compatible with almost anything. Note also that the trial tested empiric intensive therapy in all comers — it does not answer whether therapy stratified by an underlying mechanism (microvascular dysfunction, vasospasm) helps, which is the CorMicA question shelved separately.
cards.source: Pepine CJ et al. Women's IschemiA TRial to Reduce Events In Non-ObstRuctive CAD (WARRIOR): a randomised controlled trial. Open Heart. 2026. PMID: 41932694. Registry ID: NCT03417388. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large randomised trial, no benefit found, and the trial's own design weaknesses leave the question open rather than settled
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large randomised trial, no benefit found, and the trial's own design weaknesses leave the question open rather than settled
cards.people: One randomised trial of intensive medical therapy in women with suspected ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries (2,476 women, 2.5 years). No on-question systematic review or meta-analysis was found on a verified search — the shelf therefore carries the anchor and this synthesis only.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 221 events (intensive therapy) vs 200 (usual care); HR 1.13 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.37), p = 0.20. Secondary outcomes: no difference, including quality of life and win ratio. Contamination sensitivity analysis: HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.352 to 1.558), p = 0.43. Death, myocardial infarction, stroke: no separate benefit shown; angina hospitalisations dominated the composite. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote WARRIOR as showing that statins, ACE inhibitors, or aspirin individually fail in INOCA — it tested a bundled empiric regimen against a usual care that already included those drugs for many women. Tier C is set because the base is a single underpowered trial whose negative result is itself undercut by contamination.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pepine CJ et al. Open Heart. 2026 (PMID: 41932694).

shelves.title: After a spontaneous coronary tear: beta-blockers were linked to far fewer recurrences, while two blood thinners fared worse than one — all from observational data
shelves.question: In patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection managed conservatively, are beta-blockers and single versus dual antiplatelet therapy associated with lower recurrence and major adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use* · British Columbia/epidemiology · Coronary Angiography/methods* · Coronary Vessel Anomalies/complications/diagnosis*/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology/etiology* · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods* · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Survival Rate/trends · Time Factors · Vascular Diseases/complications/congenital*/diagnosis/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — every number on this shelf is observational, and the two sources agree on one association and disagree in spirit on the other. In a prospective cohort of 327 patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Saw J et al., PMID: 28838364), followed for a median 3.1 years, overall major adverse cardiac events occurred in 19.9% (death 1.2%, recurrent myocardial infarction 16.8%, recurrent SCAD 10.4%); in multivariable modelling only hypertension raised recurrence risk (HR 2.46) and beta-blocker use lowered it (HR 0.36, p = 0.004) — consistent with a 2022 meta-analysis of 14 studies and 4,206 patients (Chi G et al., PMID: 35866498), in which beta-blocker use was associated with a lower risk of recurrence (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77) while hypertension (RR 1.49) and fibromuscular dysplasia (RR 2.02) raised it. The antiplatelet question points the other way: in the DISCO registry's 199 conservatively managed patients (Cerrato E et al., PMID: 34338759), dual antiplatelet therapy had a higher 12-month MACE rate than single antiplatelet therapy (18.9% vs 6.0%; HR 2.62, 95% CI 1.22 to 5.61), driven by early non-fatal myocardial infarction or unplanned revascularisation, and DAPT was independently associated with MACE (OR 4.54) — but treatment was chosen by clinicians, so sicker or more complex dissections may have been given two drugs. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): beta-blockers look protective against recurrence in all observational sources; dual antiplatelets look worse, on data that cannot separate drug effect from confounding by indication.

cards.headline: Saw 2017: in 327 SCAD patients followed 3.1 years, beta-blocker use was the only factor that lowered recurrence (HR 0.36); hypertension raised it (HR 2.46)
cards.summary: Saw 2017: in 327 SCAD patients followed 3.1 years, beta-blocker use was the only factor that lowered recurrence (HR 0.36); hypertension raised it (HR 2.46)
cards.people: 327 patients with non-atherosclerotic spontaneous coronary artery dissection prospectively followed at Vancouver General Hospital (average age 52.5 years, 90.5% women; all presented with myocardial infarction, 25.7% STEMI; fibromuscular dysplasia present in 62.7%). 83.1% were initially treated medically; most were taking aspirin and beta-blocker therapy at discharge and follow-up. Median follow-up 3.1 years.
cards.result: Median hospital stay was 3.0 days and the overall major adverse event rate was 7.3% in hospital. At median 3.1-year follow-up the overall major adverse cardiac event rate was 19.9% (death 1.2%; recurrent myocardial infarction 16.8%; stroke/transient ischaemic attack 1.2%; revascularisation 5.8%). Recurrent SCAD occurred in 10.4% of patients. In multivariate modelling, only hypertension increased recurrent SCAD risk (hazard ratio 2.46, p = 0.011) and beta-blocker use diminished it (hazard ratio 0.36, p = 0.004) — a 64% relative reduction in recurrence hazard.
cards.watchOut: One centre, observational, and beta-blocker use was not randomised — patients prescribed a beta-blocker may differ in dissection severity, ejection fraction, or blood pressure from those not prescribed one, and the analysis cannot prove that starting the drug causes the lower recurrence. The recurrence rate (10.4% over 3.1 years) is nonetheless the best long-term figure on the shelf, and death was rare (1.2%).
cards.source: Saw J et al. Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection: Clinical Outcomes and Risk of Recurrence. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28838364. Registry ID: none in the record. recurrent myocardial infarction 16.8%; stroke/transient ischaemic attack 1.2%; revascularisation 5.8%). recurrent scad occurred in 10.4% of patients. in multivariate modelling, only hypertension increased recurrent scad risk (hazard ratio 2.46, p = 0.011) and beta-blocker use diminished it (hazard ratio 0.36, p = 0.004) — a 64% relative reduction in recurrence hazard. one centre, observational, and beta-blocker use was not randomised — patients prescribed a beta-blocker may differ in dissection severity, ejection fraction, or blood pressure from those not prescribed one, and the analysis cannot prove that starting the drug causes the lower recurrence. the recurrence rate (10.4% over 3.1 years) is nonetheless the best long-term figure on the shelf, and death was rare (1.2%). saw j et al. spontaneous coronary artery dissection: clinical outcomes and risk of recurrence. journal of the american college of cardiology. 2017. pmid: 28838364. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adrenergic beta-antagonists/therapeutic use* · british columbia/epidemiology · coronary angiography/methods* · coronary vessel anomalies/complications/diagnosis*/therapy · female · follow-up studies · humans · incidence · male · middle aged · myocardial infarction/epidemiology/etiology* · percutaneous coronary intervention/methods* · prognosis · prospective studies · recurrence · risk factors · survival rate/trends · time factors · vascular diseases/complications/congenital*/diagnosis/therapy

cards.headline: Cerrato 2021 (DISCO): in conservatively managed SCAD, dual antiplatelet therapy had more 12-month MACE than single (18.9% vs 6.0%; HR 2.62), driven by early MI or unplanned PCI
cards.summary: Cerrato 2021 (DISCO): in conservatively managed SCAD, dual antiplatelet therapy had more 12-month MACE than single (18.9% vs 6.0%; HR 2.62), driven by early MI or unplanned PCI
cards.people: 199 patients with SCAD managed with initial conservative treatment from the multicentre international DISCO registry (89% female, mean age 52.3 years; 92% presented with acute coronary syndrome). 67 patients (33.7%) received single antiplatelet therapy and 132 (66.3%) dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel in 62.9% of DAPT patients or ticagrelor in 36.4%). Primary endpoint was 12-month MACE: all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or any unplanned percutaneous coronary intervention.
cards.result: Overall 12-month MACE rate was 14.6%. Patients treated with dual antiplatelet therapy had a significantly higher MACE rate than those with single antiplatelet therapy (18.9% vs 6.0%; HR 2.62, 95% CI 1.22 to 5.61; P = 0.013), driven by an early excess of non-fatal myocardial infarction or unplanned PCI. In multivariable regression, type 2a SCAD (OR 3.69, 95% CI 1.41 to 9.61; P = 0.007) and the DAPT regimen (OR 4.54, 95% CI 1.31 to 14.28; P = 0.016) were independently associated with a higher risk of 12-month MACE.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication is the whole question here: clinicians chose DAPT for patients they judged higher risk, and although the regression adjusted for measured factors, dissection anatomy and lesion severity are exactly the unmeasured variables that drive both the prescription and the event. The early timing of the excess (non-fatal MI or unplanned PCI) is consistent with a drug effect, but it is also consistent with treating more dangerous dissections. No randomised comparison of SAPT versus DAPT in SCAD exists.
cards.source: Cerrato E et al. Antiplatelet therapy in patients with conservatively managed spontaneous coronary artery dissection from the multicentre DISCO registry. European Heart Journal. 2021. PMID: 34338759. Registry ID: NCT04415762. cards.headline: Chi 2022 (meta-analysis, 14 studies, 4,206 patients): beta-blocker use associated with half the recurrence risk (RR 0.51); hypertension (RR 1.49) and fibromuscular dysplasia (RR 2.02) raised it
cards.summary: Chi 2022 (meta-analysis, 14 studies, 4,206 patients): beta-blocker use associated with half the recurrence risk (RR 0.51); hypertension (RR 1.49) and fibromuscular dysplasia (RR 2.02) raised it
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies representing 4,206 patients with angiographically confirmed spontaneous coronary artery dissection, estimating pooled relative risks for recurrence by pregnancy, ventricular arrhythmia at presentation, hypertension, migraine, fibromuscular dysplasia, extracoronary vascular abnormalities, recent emotional or physical stress, and use of thienopyridine, beta-blocker, or statin.
cards.result: Hypertension (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.12; P = 0.0247) and fibromuscular dysplasia (RR 2.02, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.94; P = 0.0404) were associated with a greater risk of SCAD recurrence. Use of beta-blocker (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; P = 0.0013) was associated with a lower risk of recurrence. Pregnancy, ventricular arrhythmia at presentation, migraine, extracoronary vascular abnormalities, recent emotional or physical stress, and use of thienopyridine or statin were not significantly associated with recurrent SCAD (P > 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Fourteen observational studies pooled: the beta-blocker RR of 0.51 is the same association as Saw's HR of 0.36, not independent confirmation from a different kind of evidence — Saw's cohort is one of the studies inside it. Thienopyridine use (the DAPT question in another form) showed no significant association here, which sits uneasily beside DISCO's DAPT excess and underlines that the antiplatelet question is unresolved rather than settled against DAPT.
cards.source: Chi G et al. Factors associated with recurrent spontaneous coronary artery dissection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Coronary Artery Disease. 2022. PMID: 35866498. cards.headline: Synthesis: recurrence is common after SCAD (10.4% at 3.1 years); beta-blockers are consistently associated with less recurrence, dual antiplatelets with more early events — both from observational data
cards.summary: Synthesis: recurrence is common after SCAD (10.4% at 3.1 years); beta-blockers are consistently associated with less recurrence, dual antiplatelets with more early events — both from observational data
cards.people: One prospective cohort (327 patients), one multicentre registry analysis of conservatively managed SCAD (199 patients), and a 14-study meta-analysis (4,206 patients).
cards.result: Recurrence: 10.4% over 3.1 years; MACE 19.9% (death 1.2%). Beta-blockers: HR 0.36 (Saw) and pooled RR 0.51 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.77) for recurrence; hypertension HR 2.46 / RR 1.49 and fibromuscular dysplasia RR 2.02 increased risk. Dual vs single antiplatelet: 12-month MACE 18.9% vs 6.0% (HR 2.62, 1.22 to 5.61), OR 4.54 in multivariable analysis; thienopyridine use not significant in pooled analysis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of any medical therapy after SCAD has reported — the shelf is a record of associations in a young, mostly female population whose dissections mostly heal with conservative care (83.1% managed medically in Saw's cohort). Tier C is set because the base is entirely observational.
cards.source: Synthesis of Saw J et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017 (PMID: 28838364); Cerrato E et al. European Heart Journal. 2021 (PMID: 34338759); Chi G et al. Coronary Artery Disease. 2022 (PMID: 35866498).

shelves.title: Fish oil in chronic heart failure: one very large trial found a small survival edge — 27% vs 29% died over about four years — that a later pooled analysis did not confirm
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation (1 g daily), compared with placebo, reduce death and hospital admission for cardiovascular reasons?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/classification/drug therapy/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Italy · Male · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the GISSI-HF trial (Tavazzi L et al., PMID: 18757090) randomised 6,975 patients with chronic heart failure to n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1 g daily or placebo and followed them for a median 3.9 years: death from any cause occurred in 27% on n-3 PUFA versus 29% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.91, 95.5% CI 0.833 to 0.998; p = 0.041) — a 9% relative reduction in the hazard of death, 2 percentage points in absolute terms, with 56 patients treated for 3.9 years to avoid one death — and death or admission for cardiovascular reasons occurred in 57% versus 59% (adjusted HR 0.92, 99% CI 0.849 to 0.999; p = 0.009). Gastrointestinal adverse effects were the commonest reaction and were equal (3% vs 3%). A 2024 meta-analysis of the randomised record (Dwiputra B et al., PMID: 38826182; 5 studies) found no significant association with cardiovascular mortality (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05) or heart-failure hospitalisation (OR 0.94, 0.88 to 1.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but small effect in one very large, well-run trial, with a confidence limit that only just excludes no effect and a pooled estimate that does not confirm it — and the trial predates modern heart-failure therapy, so the margin available on top of today's treatment is unknown.

cards.headline: Tavazzi 2008 (GISSI-HF): in 6,975 patients with chronic heart failure, n-3 PUFA 1 g daily lowered death from 29% to 27% over a median 3.9 years (adjusted HR 0.91) — a small, borderline-significant benefit
cards.summary: Tavazzi 2008 (GISSI-HF): in 6,975 patients with chronic heart failure, n-3 PUFA 1 g daily lowered death from 29% to 27% over a median 3.9 years (adjusted HR 0.91) — a small, borderline-significant benefit
cards.people: 6,975 patients with chronic symptomatic heart failure (New York Heart Association class II–IV, of any cause and any left ventricular ejection fraction) at 326 cardiology and 31 internal medicine centres in Italy, randomised to n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1 g daily (n = 3,494) or placebo (n = 3,481) on top of usual care, followed for a median of 3.9 years (IQR 3.0–4.5). Primary endpoints were time to death and time to death or admission to hospital for cardiovascular reasons; analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: Death from any cause: 955 patients (27%) on n-3 PUFA versus 1,014 (29%) on placebo — adjusted hazard ratio 0.91 (95.5% CI 0.833 to 0.998; p = 0.041), a 9% relative reduction in the hazard of death alongside a 2-percentage-point absolute difference. Death or admission for cardiovascular reasons: 1,981 (57%) versus 2,053 (59%) — adjusted HR 0.92 (99% CI 0.849 to 0.999; p = 0.009). In absolute terms, 56 patients needed treatment for a median 3.9 years to avoid one death, and 44 to avoid one death or cardiovascular admission. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent adverse reaction in both groups (3% vs 3%).
cards.watchOut: The mortality confidence interval only just excludes no effect (upper limit 0.998), so the result is statistically fragile despite the trial's size, and the absolute gain is small. The trial also ran in a treatment era before sacubitril/valsartan and SGLT2 inhibitors became standard heart-failure therapy; whether any n-3 PUFA margin survives on top of modern therapy is untested. This shelf asks the heart-failure question only — the separate rosuvastatin arm of GISSI-HF and the post-myocardial-infarction fish-oil trials live on other shelves.
cards.source: Tavazzi L et al. Effect of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids in patients with chronic heart failure (the GISSI-HF trial): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2008. PMID: 18757090. Registry ID: NCT00336336. cards.headline: Dwiputra 2024 (meta-analysis, 5 studies): omega-3 supplementation showed no significant association with cardiovascular mortality (OR 0.94) or heart-failure hospitalisation (OR 0.94) in heart failure
cards.summary: Dwiputra 2024 (meta-analysis, 5 studies): omega-3 supplementation showed no significant association with cardiovascular mortality (OR 0.94) or heart-failure hospitalisation (OR 0.94) in heart failure
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Dwiputra 2024)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 5 studies of omega-3 supplementation in patients with heart failure, identified from MEDLINE, Embase and Cochrane databases (clinical trials and preprints of relevant articles), pooling cardiovascular mortality and hospitalisation due to heart failure.
cards.result: Omega-3 supplementation was not significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05; p = 0.16) nor with hospitalisation due to heart failure (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.02; p = 0.13). The authors conclude that omega-3 supplementation has no beneficial effect in patients with heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Only 5 studies were pooled, and GISSI-HF supplies most of the patients, so this is not independent evidence against the trial so much as a re-expression of the same record with different endpoints (cardiovascular rather than all-cause mortality) and an odds-ratio analysis that dilutes a borderline time-to-event result. Its null is nonetheless the honest pooled summary: no analysis of the full randomised record shows a clear heart-failure outcome benefit. The record carries no MeSH list, so none is quoted.
cards.source: Dwiputra B et al. The Effect of Omega-3 Supplementation on Heart Failure Outcome: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Lipid and Atherosclerosis. 2024. PMID: 38826182. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a 2-percentage-point mortality difference in one huge trial, a null pooled estimate — a small possible benefit that modern therapy may have shrunk further
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 2-percentage-point mortality difference in one huge trial, a null pooled estimate — a small possible benefit that modern therapy may have shrunk further
cards.people: One randomised trial of 6,975 patients with chronic heart failure (GISSI-HF) and a 5-study meta-analysis of omega-3 supplementation in heart failure — effectively the whole randomised outcome record for this question.
cards.result: Death: 27% vs 29% over a median 3.9 years (adjusted HR 0.91, 95.5% CI 0.833 to 0.998) in GISSI-HF; number needed to treat 56 to avoid one death. Death or cardiovascular admission: 57% vs 59% (adjusted HR 0.92). Pooled across 5 studies: cardiovascular mortality OR 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05) and heart-failure hospitalisation OR 0.94 (0.88 to 1.02), both non-significant. Harm: gastrointestinal effects equal at 3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not carry this shelf's small heart-failure signal over to the post-infarction fish-oil question (a different population, answered on its own shelf) or to high-dose prescription omega-3 preparations tested for triglycerides and post-infarction events — different doses, different products, different trials. The GISSI-HF preparation was a simple 1 g daily supplement, and the result has never been re-tested against contemporary heart-failure treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tavazzi L et al. Lancet. 2008 (PMID: 18757090); Dwiputra B et al. Journal of Lipid and Atherosclerosis. 2024 (PMID: 38826182).

shelves.title: Distal radial access for coronary procedures: pooled trials show far fewer blocked radial arteries, but the largest trial — with meticulous conventional technique — found occlusion under 1% in both arms, with more crossovers from the distal site
shelves.question: In patients undergoing coronary angiography or intervention, does distal radial access, compared with conventional transradial access, reduce forearm radial artery occlusion without increasing crossover or access complications?
shelves.mesh: Arterial Occlusive Diseases* · Catheterization, Peripheral*/adverse effects/methods · Coronary Angiography/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention*/adverse effects/methods · Radial Artery/diagnostic imaging · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the largest trial and the pooled record point in different directions on the primary question. In DISCO RADIAL (Aminian A et al., PMID: 35595673), 1,307 patients were randomised to distal or conventional radial access with systematic best practice to prevent occlusion: forearm radial artery occlusion at discharge was 0.31% with distal versus 0.91% with conventional access (P = 0.29) — no significant difference — while crossover was higher with distal access (7.4% vs 3.5%; P = 0.002), radial spasm was more frequent (5.4% vs 2.7%; P = 0.015), and haemostasis was shorter (median 153 vs 180 minutes; P < 0.001), with no difference in bleeding or vascular complications. An updated meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials and 8,205 patients (Mufarrih SH et al., PMID: 38432336) found occlusion risk much lower with distal access (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.46) — a 69% relative reduction — and haemostasis about 51 minutes shorter, but crossover more than doubled (RR 2.39, 1.71 to 3.32), with longer access time, more pain and more multiple puncture attempts. PROPOSED SPLIT: distal access plausibly protects the forearm radial artery where conventional occlusion rates are not already driven below 1% by patent-haemostasis technique, and it shortens haemostasis — at the cost of a harder, more often abandoned puncture.

cards.headline: Aminian 2022 (DISCO RADIAL): forearm radial occlusion did not differ between distal and conventional access (0.31% vs 0.91%; P = 0.29) when best-practice prevention was used — but crossover doubled with distal access (7.4% vs 3.5%)
cards.summary: Aminian 2022 (DISCO RADIAL): forearm radial occlusion did not differ between distal and conventional access (0.31% vs 0.91%; P = 0.29) when best-practice prevention was used — but crossover doubled with distal access (7.4% vs 3.5%)
cards.people: 1,307 patients with an indication for a percutaneous coronary procedure using a 6-F Slender sheath, randomised internationally at multiple centres to distal radial access (n = 650) or conventional transradial access (n = 657), with systematic implementation of best practices to reduce radial artery occlusion; patent haemostasis was achieved in 94.4% of conventional-access patients. The primary endpoint was forearm radial artery occlusion assessed by vascular ultrasound at discharge.
cards.result: Forearm radial artery occlusion did not differ between groups: 0.31% with distal access versus 0.91% with conventional access (P = 0.29). Crossover rates were higher with distal access (7.4% vs 3.5%; P = 0.002), median haemostasis time was shorter with distal access (153 vs 180 minutes; P < 0.001), and radial artery spasm occurred more often with distal access (5.4% vs 2.7%; P = 0.015). Overall bleeding events and vascular complications did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: This was a superiority trial that did not show superiority: with rigorous patent haemostasis, the conventional-access occlusion rate was already under 1%, leaving almost no room for distal access to improve on it. The result does not rule out a distal advantage in laboratories where conventional occlusion rates run higher, and occlusion was assessed at discharge, not in the long term. Operator experience with the newer distal technique also matters — crossover and spasm partly measure a learning curve.

cards.headline: Mufarrih 2024 (meta-analysis, 18 RCTs, 8,205 patients): distal access cut radial artery occlusion risk by 69% relative (RR 0.31) and shortened haemostasis by about 51 minutes — but crossover more than doubled (RR 2.39)
cards.summary: Mufarrih 2024 (meta-analysis, 18 RCTs, 8,205 patients): distal access cut radial artery occlusion risk by 69% relative (RR 0.31) and shortened haemostasis by about 51 minutes — but crossover more than doubled (RR 2.39)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mufarrih 2024)
cards.people: Updated meta-analysis of 18 randomised controlled trials (published 2017 to October 2023) comparing distal transradial access (n = 4,096) with proximal (conventional) transradial access (n = 4,109) for coronary angiography and/or intervention, pooling radial artery occlusion and access-site complications using a random-effects model.
cards.result: Radial artery occlusion risk was significantly lower with distal access (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.46; p ≤ 0.001) — a 69% relative reduction — and time to haemostasis was shorter (mean difference −51.18 minutes, 95% CI −70.62 to −31.73; p < 0.001). Against that, crossover rates were higher with distal access (RR 2.39, 1.71 to 3.32; p < 0.001), as were access time (mean difference +0.93 minutes, 0.50 to 1.37), procedural pain (mean difference 0.46, 0.13 to 0.79) and multiple puncture attempts (RR 2.13, 1.10 to 4.11).
cards.watchOut: The pooled occlusion advantage comes mostly from smaller trials in which conventional-access occlusion rates were far higher than the 0.91% achieved in DISCO RADIAL — a relative reduction of 69% applied to a sub-1% baseline is a fraction of a percentage point in absolute terms. Occlusion definitions and ultrasound timing also varied across trials, and the meta-analysis cannot separate the access site itself from the haemostasis technique that accompanied it in each trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the artery-protection case for distal access depends on how good conventional technique already is — the trade is a harder puncture for a possibly preserved forearm artery and faster haemostasis
cards.summary: Synthesis: the artery-protection case for distal access depends on how good conventional technique already is — the trade is a harder puncture for a possibly preserved forearm artery and faster haemostasis
cards.people: One international randomised trial of 1,307 patients (DISCO RADIAL) and a meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials with 8,205 patients comparing distal with conventional transradial access for coronary procedures.
cards.result: Forearm radial occlusion: 0.31% vs 0.91% (P = 0.29) in the largest trial with best-practice haemostasis; pooled RR 0.31 (0.21 to 0.46) across 18 trials. Haemostasis: about 27 minutes shorter (median) in DISCO RADIAL and about 51 minutes shorter (mean difference) pooled. Costs of distal access: crossover 7.4% vs 3.5% in DISCO RADIAL, pooled RR 2.39; spasm 5.4% vs 2.7%; more multiple puncture attempts (RR 2.13) and slightly more pain. Bleeding and vascular complications: no difference. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Neither source answers the question patients feel most — long-term hand function — and neither was powered for the downstream benefit that motivates the technique (keeping the forearm radial artery available for future procedures or bypass grafting), which is inferred from occlusion rates rather than measured. Where a laboratory's conventional occlusion rate is already under 1%, DISCO RADIAL is the best guide and it found nothing to gain on occlusion; where rates are higher, the pooled estimate is the better guide.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aminian A et al. JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2022 (PMID: 35595673); Mufarrih SH et al. The American Journal of Cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 38432336).

shelves.title: Epinephrine vs norepinephrine in shock after a heart attack: the same blood pressure and cardiac index, but refractory shock in 37% vs 7% stopped the only head-to-head trial early
shelves.question: In patients with cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction, does epinephrine, compared with norepinephrine, improve haemodynamics without increasing refractory shock?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Epinephrine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Female · France/epidemiology · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Shock, Cardiogenic/drug therapy/etiology/mortality · Vasoconstrictor Agents/pharmacology/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for epinephrine. The only randomised head-to-head trial, OptimaCC (Levy B et al., PMID: 29976291), randomised 57 patients with cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction to epinephrine or norepinephrine, double-blind: cardiac index evolution from baseline to 72 hours was similar between groups (p = 0.43), but refractory shock occurred in 37% of the epinephrine group (10 of 27) versus 7% of the norepinephrine group (2 of 30; p = 0.008), which led to early termination of the study; heart rate rose with epinephrine while remaining unchanged with norepinephrine (p < 0.0001), and cardiac double product and lactic acidosis were likewise unfavourable to epinephrine. The wider evidence base offers no counterweight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies and 2,478 patients with infarction-related cardiogenic shock (Karami M et al., PMID: 32629772) found no routinely used vasopressor or inotrope associated with a mortality difference, on evidence graded low quality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): epinephrine buys no haemodynamic advantage over norepinephrine in this setting and carries a substantially higher risk of refractory shock, so norepinephrine is the safer default vasopressor after infarction — on the strength of one small trial stopped early, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is that single small trial.

cards.headline: Levy 2018 (OptimaCC): epinephrine and norepinephrine raised cardiac index equally in shock after myocardial infarction, but refractory shock struck 37% on epinephrine vs 7% on norepinephrine (p = 0.008) and the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: Levy 2018 (OptimaCC): epinephrine and norepinephrine raised cardiac index equally in shock after myocardial infarction, but refractory shock struck 37% on epinephrine vs 7% on norepinephrine (p = 0.008) and the trial was stopped early
cards.people: 57 patients with cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction, randomised in a prospective, double-blind, multicentre French study to epinephrine (n = 27) or norepinephrine (n = 30). The primary efficacy outcome was cardiac index evolution; the primary safety outcome was refractory shock, defined as cardiogenic shock with sustained hypotension, end-organ hypoperfusion and hyperlactataemia, and high inotrope and vasopressor doses.
cards.result: For the primary efficacy endpoint, cardiac index evolution was similar between the two groups (p = 0.43) from baseline to hour 72. For the main safety endpoint, refractory shock occurred in 10 of 27 patients (37%) on epinephrine versus 2 of 30 (7%) on norepinephrine (p = 0.008), and this higher incidence led to early termination of the study. Heart rate increased significantly with epinephrine from hour 2 to hour 24 while remaining unchanged with norepinephrine (p < 0.0001); cardiac double product (p = 0.0002) and lactic acidosis from hour 2 to hour 24 (p < 0.0001) were also unfavourable to epinephrine.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-seven patients is a very small base for a practice question, and trials stopped early for harm tend to overstate the effect that stopped them — the true excess of refractory shock is probably smaller than 37% vs 7%, though the direction is supported by the coherent metabolic pattern (faster heart rate, higher double product, worse lactic acidosis). The trial measured haemodynamics and refractory shock, not mortality, and it says nothing about epinephrine's separate role in cardiac arrest, which is a different question.
cards.source: Levy B et al. Epinephrine Versus Norepinephrine for Cardiogenic Shock After Acute Myocardial Infarction. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2018. PMID: 29976291.
