cards.headline: Karami 2020 (systematic review, 19 studies, 2,478 patients): no routinely used vasopressor or inotrope was associated with lower mortality in infarction-related cardiogenic shock — the evidence was graded low quality
cards.summary: Karami 2020 (systematic review, 19 studies, 2,478 patients): no routinely used vasopressor or inotrope was associated with lower mortality in infarction-related cardiogenic shock — the evidence was graded low quality
cards.people: Systematic review of 19 studies (6 randomised trials) comprising 2,478 patients with acute myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock, comparing mortality in patients treated with a vasopressor or inotrope (adrenaline, noradrenaline, vasopressin, milrinone, levosimendan, dobutamine or dopamine) against control groups not exposed to that agent; case reports and post-cardiac-surgery-only studies were excluded.
cards.result: Treatment with adrenaline, noradrenaline, vasopressin, milrinone, levosimendan, dobutamine or dopamine was not associated with a difference in mortality between therapy and control groups. A trend toward better outcome was found for levosimendan compared with control (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.00). The overall quality of evidence was graded low, and the authors conclude there is insufficient evidence that routinely used vasopressors and inotropes reduce mortality in this setting, emphasising the need for randomised trials with appropriate endpoints.
cards.watchOut: This review mostly compares each agent against not receiving that agent — largely in observational data where the sickest patients get the most drugs — rather than comparing epinephrine directly with norepinephrine, so its mortality null does not contradict OptimaCC's refractory-shock finding; it shows instead that no agent in this class has proven a survival benefit to set against epinephrine's safety signal. The record carries no MeSH list, so none is quoted.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no haemodynamic gain from epinephrine, a clear safety signal against it, and no proven mortality benefit for any vasopressor in infarction-related shock — norepinephrine is the default on a thin record
cards.summary: Synthesis: no haemodynamic gain from epinephrine, a clear safety signal against it, and no proven mortality benefit for any vasopressor in infarction-related shock — norepinephrine is the default on a thin record
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial of 57 patients directly comparing epinephrine with norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction (OptimaCC), set in a systematic review of 19 studies and 2,478 patients covering all routinely used vasopressors and inotropes in the same condition.
cards.result: Haemodynamics: cardiac index evolution identical (p = 0.43). Safety: refractory shock 37% (10/27) vs 7% (2/30; p = 0.008); heart rate, cardiac double product and lactic acidosis all unfavourable to epinephrine. Mortality: no vasopressor or inotrope associated with a mortality difference in the pooled record (levosimendan trend RR 0.69, 0.47 to 1.00); evidence quality low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for epinephrine.
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf is about vasopressor choice after infarction — it does not cover inotrope choice in shock (milrinone vs dobutamine is a separate shelf question), mechanical support, or epinephrine in cardiac arrest resuscitation, where the evidence and the trade-offs are different. A larger confirmatory trial of epinephrine vs norepinephrine is unlikely to be run after an early stop for harm, so this 57-patient trial may remain the direct record; treat its effect size as an upper bound, its direction as the signal. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Levy B et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2018 (PMID: 29976291); Karami M et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32629772).

shelves.title: Testosterone in chronic heart failure: an early meta-analysis found better walking capacity, a later, larger one did not — and neither showed fewer deaths or hospital admissions
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does testosterone supplementation, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity, cardiac function, quality of life, or clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chronic Disease · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects/physiology · Heart Failure/drug therapy/epidemiology/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods/statistics & numerical data · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Testosterone/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two meta-analyses of the same small trial record disagree. The earlier one (Toma M et al., PMID: 22511747; 4 trials, 198 patients) found testosterone therapy significantly improved exercise capacity versus placebo: 6-minute walk distance by 54.0 m (95% CI 43.0 to 65.0), incremental shuttle walk by 46.7 m (12.6 to 80.9) and peak oxygen consumption by 2.70 mL/kg per min, a pooled net effect of 0.52 SD (0.10 to 0.94), with no significant adverse cardiovascular events noted. The later, larger one (Tao J et al., PMID: 32231640; 8 randomised trials, 170 patients on testosterone and 162 controls) found no significant improvement in exercise capacity overall (standardised mean difference 0.36; p = 0.07), none in peak VO2, functional class or quality of life, no effect on ejection fraction or B-type natriuretic peptide, and no difference in the composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (RR 1.02; p = 0.96) — with benefit appearing only in the subgroup whose end-of-treatment testosterone reached at least 25 nmol/L (SMD 1.12; p = 0.02), and systolic blood pressure rising by 5.68 mmHg on treatment (p < 0.001). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a few hundred patients in short, small trials, conflicting pooled answers on a surrogate outcome, and no evidence at all on the outcomes that matter.

cards.headline: Tao 2020 (meta-analysis, 8 RCTs, 332 patients): testosterone did not significantly improve exercise capacity, peak VO2, functional class or quality of life in chronic heart failure — and did not change death or hospitalisation (RR 1.02)
cards.summary: Tao 2020 (meta-analysis, 8 RCTs, 332 patients): testosterone did not significantly improve exercise capacity, peak VO2, functional class or quality of life in chronic heart failure — and did not change death or hospitalisation (RR 1.02)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Tao 2020)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials of testosterone supplementation in chronic heart failure, including 170 patients in the testosterone groups and 162 in the control groups, evaluating chronic effects on exercise capacity and cardiac function; sensitivity analyses were limited to male patients and subgroups were split by baseline and end-of-treatment total testosterone.
cards.result: Testosterone supplementation was not associated with improved exercise capacity overall (walking test: standardised mean difference 0.36; p = 0.07), and results were similar in men only (SMD 0.21; p = 0.15) and in subgroups by baseline testosterone. Patients whose end-of-treatment total testosterone reached at least 25 nmol/L did show improved exercise capacity (SMD 1.12; p = 0.02), unlike those below that level (SMD 0.24; p = 0.12). Peak VO2 (weighted mean difference 0.85; p = 0.43), New York Heart Association class (−0.08; p = 0.16) and quality of life on the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure questionnaire (−6.03; p = 0.12) were not significantly affected; nor were left ventricular ejection fraction (−1.52%; p = 0.37), B-type natriuretic peptide (SMD −0.19; p = 0.23) or the composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (RR 1.02; p = 0.96). Systolic blood pressure rose on testosterone (weighted mean difference +5.68 mmHg; p < 0.001); diastolic pressure and heart rate did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: Eight small trials and 332 patients cannot detect clinical-outcome effects, so the RR of 1.02 for death or hospitalisation is an absence of evidence as much as evidence of absence. The one positive finding rests on a subgroup defined by a post-treatment measurement (achieved testosterone level), which breaks the randomised comparison — patients who absorb or adhere to treatment differ from those who do not. The systolic pressure rise of about 6 mmHg is a real, if modest, counter-signal in a heart-failure population.
cards.source: Tao J et al. Testosterone Supplementation in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Frontiers in Endocrinology. 2020. PMID: 32231640. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Toma 2012 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 198 patients): testosterone improved exercise capacity on every measure — 6-minute walk by 54 m, shuttle walk by 46.7 m, peak VO2 by 2.70 mL/kg per min
cards.summary: Toma 2012 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 198 patients): testosterone improved exercise capacity on every measure — 6-minute walk by 54 m, shuttle walk by 46.7 m, peak VO2 by 2.70 mL/kg per min
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Toma 2012)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 4 randomised controlled trials (n = 198; 84% men; mean age 67 years) of testosterone therapy versus placebo in stable chronic heart failure, with exercise capacity assessed by the 6-minute walk test (2 trials), the incremental shuttle walk test (2 trials) or peak oxygen consumption (2 trials) after up to 52 weeks of treatment.
cards.result: Testosterone therapy was associated with a significant improvement in exercise capacity compared with placebo: the mean increase between groups was 54.0 m on the 6-minute walk test (95% CI 43.0 to 65.0), 46.7 m on the incremental shuttle walk test (12.6 to 80.9) and 2.70 mL/kg per min in peak oxygen consumption (2.68 to 2.72), a pooled net effect of 0.52 standard deviations (0.10 to 0.94). No significant adverse cardiovascular events were noted. The authors conclude testosterone appears promising for functional capacity in heart failure but that adequately powered trials are required for quality of life, clinical events and safety.
cards.watchOut: Four trials and 198 patients, with each exercise measure resting on only 2 trials — small-study effects are the likeliest explanation for why this earlier pool looks so much better than the later 8-trial pool that contains it. The peak VO2 confidence interval printed in the record (2.68 to 2.72) is implausibly narrow for 2 small trials and should be read as a reporting artefact, not precision. No trial measured mortality or hospitalisation with any power.
cards.source: Toma M et al. Testosterone supplementation in heart failure: a meta-analysis. Circulation: Heart Failure. 2012. PMID: 22511747. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: at most a few hundred patients, two pooled answers that conflict, a blood-pressure rise, and no outcome data — testosterone for heart-failure stamina remains unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: at most a few hundred patients, two pooled answers that conflict, a blood-pressure rise, and no outcome data — testosterone for heart-failure stamina remains unproven
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials of testosterone supplementation in chronic heart failure: 4 trials with 198 patients (Toma 2012) and 8 trials with 332 patients (Tao 2020), the later pool including the earlier trials.
cards.result: Exercise capacity: improved on all measures in the 4-trial pool (6-minute walk +54.0 m; pooled effect 0.52 SD, 0.10 to 0.94) but not significant in the 8-trial pool (SMD 0.36; p = 0.07), except in the subgroup achieving testosterone at least 25 nmol/L (SMD 1.12; p = 0.02). Cardiac function and symptoms: no significant effect on ejection fraction, B-type natriuretic peptide, functional class or quality of life. Clinical outcomes: death or heart-failure hospitalisation RR 1.02 (p = 0.96). Harm signal: systolic blood pressure +5.68 mmHg (p < 0.001). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about testosterone given to improve function in established heart failure — it does not address testosterone replacement for confirmed hypogonadism on its own indications, nor testosterone's cardiovascular safety in the general older male population, which larger trials outside heart failure have examined separately. Until a trial in heart failure is powered for clinical events, any use here is an individual experiment in exercise capacity, not an evidence-based treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tao J et al. Frontiers in Endocrinology. 2020 (PMID: 32231640); Toma M et al. Circulation: Heart Failure. 2012 (PMID: 22511747).

shelves.title: Sutimlimab in cold agglutinin disease: 73% met the composite response versus 15% on placebo in CADENZA — haemolysis halted within weeks, in 42 randomised patients
shelves.question: In adults with cold agglutinin disease, does sutimlimab reduce haemolysis and raise haemoglobin compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Hemolytic, Autoimmune*/blood/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized*/therapeutic use · Bilirubin/blood · Double-Blind Method · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a small randomised trial, backed by a single-arm study in a sicker population. In CADENZA (Röth A et al., PMID: 35687757), 42 patients without a transfusion in the prior six months met the composite endpoint — haemoglobin rise of at least 1.5 g/dL at assessment, no transfusion, no prohibited therapy — in 73% on sutimlimab versus 15% on placebo (odds ratio 15.9, 95% CI 2.9 to 88.0). In CARDINAL (Röth A et al., PMID: 33826820), 24 recently transfused patients on open-label sutimlimab gained a least-squares mean of 2.6 g/dL of haemoglobin, 54% met their composite endpoint, and 71% needed no transfusion from week 5 to 26. Bilirubin normalised within one to three weeks in both studies, tracking near-complete classical-pathway inhibition, and fatigue improved. The price in these short trials was mostly nuisance-grade — headache, hypertension, rhinitis, Raynaud phenomenon and acrocyanosis were commoner on drug — with three CADENZA discontinuations for adverse events and no meningococcal infections; the numbers are far too small to exclude rare complement-blockade harms, and neither trial ran beyond 26 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sutimlimab clearly switches off haemolysis in cold agglutinin disease while it is given; durability, long-term safety and any effect beyond blood counts and fatigue are unproven. Tier C is set for the small, single-programme evidence base.

cards.headline: Röth 2022 (CADENZA): composite response 73% (16/22) on sutimlimab versus 15% (3/20) on placebo — odds ratio 15.9, bilirubin normalised by week 1
cards.summary: Röth 2022 (CADENZA): composite response 73% (16/22) on sutimlimab versus 15% (3/20) on placebo — odds ratio 15.9, bilirubin normalised by week 1
cards.people: 42 adults with cold agglutinin disease, screening haemoglobin ≤10 g/dL, elevated bilirubin and at least one disease symptom, with no transfusion in the six months before enrolment, randomised to sutimlimab (n=22) or placebo (n=20) on days 0 and 7 then every two weeks for 26 weeks.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (haemoglobin increase ≥1.5 g/dL at the mean of weeks 23, 25 and 26, no transfusion, and no prohibited therapy during weeks 5–26) was met by 16 patients (73%) on sutimlimab and 3 (15%) on placebo — odds ratio 15.9 (95% CI 2.9 to 88.0), p<0.001, with the absolute rates printed alongside (73% versus 15%). Mean haemoglobin and FACIT-Fatigue scores improved significantly only on sutimlimab, and mean bilirubin normalised by week 1 alongside near-complete classical complement pathway inhibition (2.3% mean activity at week 1). At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 96% on sutimlimab and 100% on placebo; headache, hypertension, rhinitis, Raynaud phenomenon and acrocyanosis were more frequent on sutimlimab, and three sutimlimab patients discontinued for adverse events versus none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Forty-two patients and 26 weeks: the confidence interval on the odds ratio runs from 2.9 to 88, rare harms of complement blockade cannot be assessed, and the composite leans on a haemoglobin threshold rather than on survival or organ outcomes. The effect size is nonetheless large, rapid and mechanistically coherent.
cards.source: Röth A et al. Sutimlimab in patients with cold agglutinin disease: results of the randomized placebo-controlled phase 3 CADENZA trial. Blood. 2022. PMID: 35687757. Registry ID: NCT03347422. cards.headline: Röth 2021 (CARDINAL): in recently transfused patients, haemoglobin rose a mean 2.6 g/dL, 54% met the composite endpoint, and 71% stayed transfusion-free from week 5
cards.summary: Röth 2021 (CARDINAL): in recently transfused patients, haemoglobin rose a mean 2.6 g/dL, 54% met the composite endpoint, and 71% stayed transfusion-free from week 5
cards.people: 24 adults with cold agglutinin disease and a recent history of transfusion, treated with intravenous sutimlimab for 26 weeks in a multicentre open-label single-group study. The composite primary endpoint was haemoglobin normalisation to ≥12 g/dL or a rise of ≥2 g/dL from baseline, without transfusion or prohibited medication.
cards.result: Thirteen patients (54%) met the composite endpoint. The least-squares mean haemoglobin increase was 2.6 g/dL at assessment (weeks 23, 25, 26); mean haemoglobin stayed above 11 g/dL from week 3, mean bilirubin normalised by week 3, and 17 patients (71%) received no transfusion from week 5 through week 26. Fatigue fell meaningfully by week 1 and stayed down. At least one adverse event occurred in 22 patients (92%); seven (29%) had a serious adverse event, none judged related to sutimlimab; no meningococcal infections occurred.
cards.watchOut: No control group: in a fluctuating disease, some improvement would be expected from regression to the mean and from the transfusions that enrolled these patients. CARDINAL's value is showing the drug works in the sickest, transfusion-dependent end of the disease — the size of the effect against no treatment comes from CADENZA.
cards.source: Röth A et al. Sutimlimab in Cold Agglutinin Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33826820. Registry ID: NCT03347396. cards.headline: Synthesis: haemolysis switched off in weeks in both studies — response rates 73% against placebo and 54% in transfusion-dependent patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: haemolysis switched off in weeks in both studies — response rates 73% against placebo and 54% in transfusion-dependent patients
cards.people: One 42-patient randomised placebo-controlled trial (CADENZA) and one 24-patient single-arm study in recently transfused patients (CARDINAL), each 26 weeks — the controlled record for sutimlimab in cold agglutinin disease.
cards.result: Haemoglobin: composite response 73% versus 15% on placebo (odds ratio 15.9); mean rise 2.6 g/dL in the single-arm study. Haemolysis markers: bilirubin normalised by week 1–3. Transfusion: 71% transfusion-free from week 5 in CARDINAL. Fatigue: improved in both. Harms: mostly cold- and infusion-type symptoms; three discontinuations in CADENZA; no meningococcal infections seen — in 66 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Cold agglutinin disease is rare and these are the only trials; there is no randomised evidence beyond 26 weeks, no comparison with rituximab-based therapy, and no data on what happens between doses or after stopping. The grade reflects a big, fast, mechanistically direct effect in very few patients. Tier C is set.
cards.source: Synthesis of Röth A et al. Blood. 2022 (PMID: 35687757); Röth A et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33826820).

shelves.title: Crovalimab in untreated PNH: haemolysis control 79.3% versus 79.0% on eculizumab — non-inferior in the single phase 3 trial, with monthly self-administered injections as the practical gain
shelves.question: In adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria not previously treated with a complement C5 inhibitor, is crovalimab non-inferior to eculizumab for haemolysis control and transfusion avoidance?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hemoglobinuria, Paroxysmal*/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized*/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Complement Inactivating Agents*/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Hemolysis/drug effects · Complement C5/antagonists & inhibitors · Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferiority to the standard C5 inhibitor, demonstrated once. In COMMODORE 2 (Röth A et al., PMID: 38884175), 204 C5-inhibitor-naive patients were randomised 2:1 to crovalimab or eculizumab for a 24-week primary period. Haemolysis control (LDH ≤1.5× the upper limit of normal) was achieved by 79.3% on crovalimab and 79.0% on eculizumab (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.8), and transfusion avoidance by 65.7% versus 68.1% (weighted difference −2.8 percentage points, 95% CI −15.7 to 11.1) — both meeting non-inferiority, neither suggesting superiority. Breakthrough haemolysis (10.4% versus 14.5%), haemoglobin stabilisation (63.4% versus 60.9%) and fatigue improvement were likewise similar, safety profiles were similar, and no meningococcal infections occurred. The genuine advantage is practical, and it is in the record: crovalimab is a low-volume subcutaneous self-administration every four weeks, and most patients who switched from eculizumab after the primary period preferred it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): crovalimab matches eculizumab on the measured outcomes in a single open-label trial, with convenience — not efficacy — as the reason to choose it. Tier C is set for the single-trial base. Ravulizumab is compared with eculizumab at shelf #1804 and the proximal inhibitors at shelf #845.

cards.headline: Röth 2024 (COMMODORE 2): haemolysis control 79.3% versus 79.0% (odds ratio 1.0); transfusion avoidance 65.7% versus 68.1% — non-inferior on both co-primary endpoints
cards.summary: Röth 2024 (COMMODORE 2): haemolysis control 79.3% versus 79.0% (odds ratio 1.0); transfusion avoidance 65.7% versus 68.1% — non-inferior on both co-primary endpoints
cards.people: 204 patients with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and LDH at least twice the upper limit of normal, none previously treated with a C5 inhibitor, randomised 2:1 to crovalimab (n=135) — a C5 inhibitor given as low-volume subcutaneous self-administration every 4 weeks — or eculizumab (n=69), in a global open-label multicentre trial with a 24-week primary treatment period.
cards.result: Co-primary endpoints: haemolysis control (central LDH ≤1.5× ULN) in 79.3% on crovalimab versus 79.0% on eculizumab (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.8), and transfusion avoidance in 65.7% versus 68.1% (weighted difference −2.8, 95% CI −15.7 to 11.1) — non-inferiority met for both. Secondary endpoints: breakthrough haemolysis 10.4% versus 14.5% (weighted difference −3.9, −14.8 to 5.3); haemoglobin stabilisation 63.4% versus 60.9% (difference 2.2, −11.4 to 16.3); FACIT-Fatigue improved meaningfully in both arms. Terminal complement activity inhibition was generally maintained on crovalimab, safety profiles were similar with no meningococcal infections, and most patients who switched from eculizumab to crovalimab after the primary period preferred crovalimab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 24 weeks, and a non-inferiority design: the confidence interval for transfusion avoidance (−15.7 to +11.1 points) is wide enough to hide a clinically real disadvantage, and 'non-inferior' is a statement about a pre-set margin, not proof of equality. Long-term and rare-harm data (including meningococcal risk under lifelong C5 blockade) cannot come from 204 patients over six months.
cards.source: Röth A et al. Phase 3 randomized COMMODORE 2 trial: Crovalimab versus eculizumab in patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria naive to complement inhibition. transfusion avoidance 65.7% versus 68.1% — non-inferior on both co-primary endpoints in adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria not previously treated with a complement c5 inhibitor, is crovalimab non-inferior to eculizumab for haemolysis control and transfusion avoidance? randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial (röth 2024, commodore 2) 204 patients with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and ldh at least twice the upper limit of normal, none previously treated with a c5 inhibitor, randomised 2:1 to crovalimab (n=135) — a c5 inhibitor given as low-volume subcutaneous self-administration every 4 weeks — or eculizumab (n=69), in a global open-label multicentre trial with a 24-week primary treatment period. co-primary endpoints: haemolysis control (central ldh ≤1.5× uln) in 79.3% on crovalimab versus 79.0% on eculizumab (odds ratio 1.0, 95% ci 0.6 to 1.8), and transfusion avoidance in 65.7% versus 68.1% (weighted difference −2.8, 95% ci −15.7 to 11.1) — non-inferiority met for both. secondary endpoints: breakthrough haemolysis 10.4% versus 14.5% (weighted difference −3.9, −14.8 to 5.3); haemoglobin stabilisation 63.4% versus 60.9% (difference 2.2, −11.4 to 16.3); facit-fatigue improved meaningfully in both arms. terminal complement activity inhibition was generally maintained on crovalimab, safety profiles were similar with no meningococcal infections, and most patients who switched from eculizumab to crovalimab after the primary period preferred crovalimab. open-label, 24 weeks, and a non-inferiority design: the confidence interval for transfusion avoidance (−15.7 to +11.1 points) is wide enough to hide a clinically real disadvantage, and 'non-inferior' is a statement about a pre-set margin, not proof of equality. long-term and rare-harm data (including meningococcal risk under lifelong c5 blockade) cannot come from 204 patients over six months. röth a et al. phase 3 randomized commodore 2 trial: crovalimab versus eculizumab in patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria naive to complement inhibition. american journal of hematology. 2024. pmid: 38884175. registry id: nct04434092. mesh: humans · hemoglobinuria, paroxysmal*/drug therapy · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized*/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · male · female · middle aged · adult · complement inactivating agents*/therapeutic use/adverse effects · hemolysis/drug effects · complement c5/antagonists & inhibitors · aged

shelves.title: Cutting down drinking lowers blood pressure only in heavier drinkers: about 5.5/4.0 mm Hg in those drinking six or more drinks a day who halved their intake, and nothing measurable at two drinks a day or fewer
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension who drink alcohol regularly, does reducing alcohol intake lower blood pressure compared with continuing usual drinking?
shelves.mesh: Alcohol Drinking/prevention & control · Blood Pressure · Humans · Hypertension/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with a threshold. Two meta-analyses of randomised trials, 15 years apart, agree that cutting alcohol lowers blood pressure in a dose-dependent way. Roerecke 2017 (36 trials, 2,865 participants) found no significant blood-pressure reduction in people drinking two or fewer drinks per day, but a mean reduction of −5.50 mm Hg systolic (95% CI −6.70 to −4.30) and −3.97 mm Hg diastolic (−4.70 to −3.25) in participants drinking six or more drinks per day who reduced intake by about 50%. Xin 2001 (15 trials, 2,234 participants) found an overall reduction of −3.31 mm Hg systolic (−4.10 to −2.52) and −2.04 mm Hg diastolic (−2.58 to −1.49), with a dose–response between the percentage of alcohol reduction and the blood-pressure fall, and larger effects at higher baseline blood pressure. The benefit is real but belongs to heavier drinkers; at low intake there is nothing to gain on blood pressure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alcohol reduction lowers blood pressure dose-dependently in people drinking more than two drinks a day, with the largest falls in the heaviest drinkers.

cards.headline: Roerecke 2017: no blood-pressure gain from cutting down at ≤2 drinks a day; −5.50/−3.97 mm Hg in those drinking ≥6 drinks a day who cut by about half
cards.summary: Roerecke 2017: no blood-pressure gain from cutting down at ≤2 drinks a day; −5.50/−3.97 mm Hg in those drinking ≥6 drinks a day who cut by about half
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Roerecke 2017)
cards.people: 36 trials with 2,865 participants (2,464 men and 401 women) testing a quantifiable change in alcohol consumption lasting at least 7 days, with blood pressure measured before and after.
cards.result: In people who drank two or fewer drinks per day, alcohol reduction was not associated with a significant blood-pressure reduction. In people drinking more than two drinks per day, reduction was associated with progressively larger falls; the strongest effect was in participants drinking six or more drinks per day who reduced intake by about 50%: systolic −5.50 mm Hg (95% CI −6.70 to −4.30) and diastolic −3.97 mm Hg (−4.70 to −3.25).
cards.watchOut: Most participants were men, trial durations were short, and the analysis pools many different reduction strategies; the threshold at two drinks a day is a stratified finding, not a tested cut-off in a single trial.
cards.source: Roerecke M et al. The effect of a reduction in alcohol consumption on blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. Public health. 2017. PMID: 29253389. cards.headline: Xin 2001: overall −3.31/−2.04 mm Hg from alcohol reduction, with a dose–response and larger effects at higher starting blood pressure
cards.summary: Xin 2001: overall −3.31/−2.04 mm Hg from alcohol reduction, with a dose–response and larger effects at higher starting blood pressure
cards.people: 15 randomised controlled trials with a total of 2,234 participants, published before June 1999, in which alcohol reduction was the only intervention difference between groups.
cards.result: Alcohol reduction was associated with a significant fall in mean systolic blood pressure of −3.31 mm Hg (95% CI −4.10 to −2.52) and diastolic of −2.04 mm Hg (−2.58 to −1.49). A dose–response relationship was observed between the mean percentage of alcohol reduction and the mean blood-pressure reduction, and effects were enhanced in those with higher baseline blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: An older, smaller evidence base than Roerecke 2017 and analysed with a fixed-effects model; it does not stratify cleanly by baseline intake, so its overall average mixes light drinkers (little to gain) with heavy drinkers (most to gain).
cards.source: Xin X et al. Effects of alcohol reduction on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2001. PMID: 11711507. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one dose–response — the blood-pressure benefit of drinking less belongs to heavier drinkers
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one dose–response — the blood-pressure benefit of drinking less belongs to heavier drinkers
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised alcohol-reduction trials (Xin 2001: 15 trials, 2,234 participants; Roerecke 2017: 36 trials, 2,865 participants).
cards.result: Overall pooled falls are modest (−3.31/−2.04 mm Hg, Xin 2001) because they average across intake levels; stratified, there is no significant effect at ≤2 drinks per day and the largest fall (−5.50/−3.97 mm Hg) in people drinking ≥6 drinks per day who halved their intake (Roerecke 2017). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither meta-analysis tests hard outcomes, and adherence to reduced drinking outside trials is the practical limit; the claim here is blood pressure only, in heavier drinkers only.

shelves.title: Device-guided slow breathing: the small pooled blood-pressure fall vanishes when manufacturer-linked trials are removed, and the 2022 meta-analysis finds no significant effect at all
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does device-guided slow breathing lower office and ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care or a control device?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antihypertensive Agents/pharmacology · Blood Pressure/physiology · Breathing Exercises · Equipment and Supplies · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Hypertension/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Rate · Systole · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — once the manufacturer's own trials are set aside. Mahtani 2012 pooled eight trials of the RESPeRATE device (InterCure Ltd) in 494 adults and found systolic pressure lower by 3.67 mm Hg (95% CI −5.99 to −1.39) and diastolic by 2.51 mm Hg (−4.15 to −0.87) — but five of the eight trials were sponsored by or involved the manufacturer, and excluding them left no overall effect. The independent 2022 meta-analysis (de Freitas Gonçalves et al.) likewise found device-guided slow breathing did not significantly reduce systolic (mean difference −2.13 mm Hg, 95% CI −12.71 to 8.44) or diastolic pressure (−0.90, −3.97 to 2.11) versus usual care, with high heterogeneity. The honest reading is that any effect is small, short-term (maximum trial duration 9 weeks in Mahtani), and unproven independently. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): device-guided slow breathing has not been shown to lower blood pressure in trials independent of the device manufacturer.

cards.headline: Mahtani 2012: −3.67/−2.51 mm Hg pooled — but no effect at all after excluding the five manufacturer-linked trials of eight
cards.summary: Mahtani 2012: −3.67/−2.51 mm Hg pooled — but no effect at all after excluding the five manufacturer-linked trials of eight
cards.people: Eight trials of the RESPeRATE device (InterCure Ltd, Lod, Israel) comprising 494 adult patients with hypertension; maximum trial duration 9 weeks.
cards.result: Device-guided breathing reduced systolic blood pressure by 3.67 mm Hg (95% CI −5.99 to −1.39; P=0.002) and diastolic by 2.51 mm Hg (−4.15 to −0.87; P=0.003), with no overall effect on heart rate or quality of life. However, sensitivity analysis excluding the five trials sponsored by or involving the manufacturer revealed no overall effect on blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: The positive pooled result is inseparable from manufacturer involvement, follow-up was at most 9 weeks, and the review's own conclusion is that longer-term independent trials are required — none had appeared by the 2022 update.
cards.source: Mahtani KR et al. Device-guided breathing exercises in the control of human blood pressure: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of hypertension. 2012. PMID: 22495126. cards.headline: de Freitas Gonçalves 2022: device-guided slow breathing did not significantly reduce systolic (−2.13 mm Hg, CI crossing zero widely) or diastolic pressure versus usual care
cards.summary: de Freitas Gonçalves 2022: device-guided slow breathing did not significantly reduce systolic (−2.13 mm Hg, CI crossing zero widely) or diastolic pressure versus usual care
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (de Freitas Gonçalves 2022)
cards.people: Twenty-two studies involving 17,214 participants were included in the quantitative analysis overall; the device-guided slow-breathing comparisons against usual care rested on 288 individuals for blood-pressure values and 443 for blood-pressure variations.
cards.result: Device-guided slow breathing did not significantly reduce systolic blood pressure (mean difference −2.13 mm Hg, 95% CI −12.71 to 8.44; I²=93%) or diastolic blood pressure (mean difference −0.90, 95% CI −3.97 to 2.11; I²=63%) compared with usual care, and blood-pressure variation analyses were likewise non-significant.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was high to substantial throughout, and the device-guided subset is far smaller than the headline 17,214 participants (most of whom were in non-device comparisons) — the null is a genuine absence of demonstrated effect, not proof of an exact zero.
cards.source: de Freitas Gonçalves KS et al. Device and nondevice-guided slow breathing to reduce blood pressure in hypertensive patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Health science reports. 2022. PMID: 35601033. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Spironolactone lowers blood pressure more than eplerenone in primary aldosteronism — diastolic 12.5 versus 5.6 mm Hg in the one blinded trial — but causes far more breast side effects; a small unrandomised series found the two similar
shelves.question: In primary aldosteronism, is spironolactone more effective than eplerenone at controlling blood pressure, and how do their side effects compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Eplerenone · Female · Humans · Hyperaldosteronism/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Quality of Life · Spironolactone/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — spironolactone wins on blood pressure, eplerenone wins on sex-hormone side effects. In the one double-blind randomised head-to-head trial (Parthasarathy 2011), titrated spironolactone (75–225 mg daily) lowered seated diastolic pressure by 12.5 mm Hg versus 5.6 mm Hg on eplerenone (100–300 mg daily) over 16 weeks — a difference of −6.9 mm Hg (95% CI −10.6 to −3.3; P<0.001), so eplerenone failed its non-inferiority test. The price was hormonal: male gynaecomastia in 21.2% on spironolactone versus 4.5% on eplerenone (P=0.033) and female mastodynia in 21.1% versus 0.0% (P=0.026). A small unrandomised Japanese comparison (Karashima 2016, 54 patients treated for 12 months) found the two decreased blood pressure and raised potassium to similar degrees — a weaker design that does not overturn the blinded trial. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose spironolactone for maximum blood-pressure effect, eplerenone when anti-androgen side effects bite — accepting less pressure reduction.

cards.headline: Parthasarathy 2011: diastolic fall 12.5 mm Hg on spironolactone versus 5.6 mm Hg on eplerenone (difference −6.9, P<0.001) — gynaecomastia 21.2% versus 4.5%
cards.summary: Parthasarathy 2011: diastolic fall 12.5 mm Hg on spironolactone versus 5.6 mm Hg on eplerenone (difference −6.9, P<0.001) — gynaecomastia 21.2% versus 4.5%
cards.people: Patients with hypertension and biochemical criteria for primary aldosteronism (seated diastolic 90 to <120 mm Hg, systolic <200 mm Hg), randomised 1:1 after a placebo run-in to 16 weeks of spironolactone 75–225 mg once daily or eplerenone 100–300 mg once daily, titrated to effect.
cards.result: The change from baseline in seated diastolic blood pressure was −12.5 ± 1.3 mm Hg on spironolactone versus −5.6 ± 1.3 mm Hg on eplerenone (difference −6.9 mm Hg, 95% CI −10.6 to −3.3; P<0.001); eplerenone was not non-inferior. Overall adverse-event incidence did not differ significantly, but male gynaecomastia occurred in 21.2% on spironolactone versus 4.5% on eplerenone (P=0.033) and female mastodynia in 21.1% versus 0.0% (P=0.026).
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks only, diastolic pressure as the primary endpoint, and doses were titrated to effect rather than fixed — the comparison is of the two drugs as used, not milligram-for-milligram potency.

cards.headline: Karashima 2016: in 54 unrandomised patients treated for 12 months, eplerenone and spironolactone decreased blood pressure and raised potassium to similar degrees
cards.summary: Karashima 2016: in 54 unrandomised patients treated for 12 months, eplerenone and spironolactone decreased blood pressure and raised potassium to similar degrees
cards.people: 54 patients with primary aldosteronism treated with eplerenone 25–100 mg daily (n=27) or spironolactone 12.5–100 mg daily (n=27) for 12 months, with metabolic and renal measures and CT-quantified adipose tissue.
cards.result: Eplerenone and spironolactone decreased blood pressure and increased serum potassium levels to similar degrees, and plasma aldosterone and renin activity did not differ between groups. Neither drug changed insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) or serum lipids; both significantly decreased urinary albumin excretion and visceral adipose tissue (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Treatment was not randomised — the candidate list described this anchor as a randomised comparison, but the record shows patients simply treated with one of the two drugs, so confounding by choice of drug is uncontrolled; its 'similar' finding carries far less weight than the blinded trial.
cards.source: Karashima S et al. Comparison of eplerenone and spironolactone for the treatment of primary aldosteronism. Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension. 2016. PMID: 26606875. cards.headline: Synthesis: one blinded trial says spironolactone is stronger and harsher; one unrandomised series says they look alike — the blinded trial governs
cards.summary: Synthesis: one blinded trial says spironolactone is stronger and harsher; one unrandomised series says they look alike — the blinded trial governs
cards.people: One randomised double-blind head-to-head trial (Parthasarathy 2011, 16 weeks) and one non-randomised 12-month comparison (Karashima 2016, 54 patients) in primary aldosteronism.
cards.result: Blood pressure: diastolic −12.5 versus −5.6 mm Hg favouring spironolactone in the blinded trial; similar falls in the unrandomised series. Side effects: gynaecomastia 21.2% versus 4.5% and mastodynia 21.1% versus 0.0%, both favouring eplerenone (Parthasarathy 2011). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the split rests on a single blinded trial plus observational data, so it goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: Neither study reports cardiovascular or kidney outcomes; the choice is a blood-pressure-versus-tolerability trade, and eplerenone's twice-the-milligrams dosing in the trial reflects its lower potency per milligram.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parthasarathy HK et al. Journal of hypertension. 2011 (PMID: 21451421); Karashima S et al. Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension. 2016 (PMID: 26606875).

shelves.title: TONE: in older hypertensive patients, cutting sodium or losing weight each cut the risk of needing medication again by about 30% in relative terms — combined, the hazard ratio was 0.47 — with no excess of cardiovascular events
shelves.question: In older adults with hypertension, does combining sodium reduction with weight loss lower blood pressure and reduce the need for antihypertensive medication compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Algorithms · Analysis of Variance · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypertension/complications/diet therapy/drug therapy · Likelihood Functions · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/complications · Proportional Hazards Models · Sodium, Dietary/administration & dosage · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Survival Analysis · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large randomised trial. In TONE (Whelton 1998), 975 men and women aged 60–80 whose blood pressure was controlled on a single drug attempted medication withdrawal after 3 months of intervention. The combined endpoint (high blood pressure at follow-up, restarting medication, or a cardiovascular event) was less frequent with reduced sodium intake (relative hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.59–0.81; P<0.001) and, in the 585 obese participants, with weight loss (0.70, 0.57–0.87; P<0.001). Among obese participants versus usual care, hazard ratios were 0.60 for sodium reduction alone, 0.64 for weight loss alone, and 0.47 (0.35–0.64; P<0.001) for the two combined — relative effects; the trial reports hazards, not absolute event rates, in its record. Cardiovascular events were similar across all six groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sodium reduction, and weight loss in obese patients, genuinely delay the return of hypertension after drug withdrawal in older adults; the combination is best.

cards.headline: TONE (Whelton 1998): hazard ratio 0.69 for sodium reduction and 0.70 for weight loss on recurrent hypertension or restarting drugs; 0.47 for both combined in obese participants
cards.summary: TONE (Whelton 1998): hazard ratio 0.69 for sodium reduction and 0.70 for weight loss on recurrent hypertension or restarting drugs; 0.47 for both combined in obese participants
cards.people: 975 men and women aged 60–80 years at four US academic centres, with systolic pressure <145 mm Hg and diastolic <85 mm Hg on a single antihypertensive drug; the 585 obese participants were randomised to reduced sodium intake, weight loss, both, or usual care, and the 390 non-obese to reduced sodium or usual care; drug withdrawal was attempted after 3 months; follow-up 15–36 months (median 29).
cards.result: The combined outcome (diagnosis of high blood pressure, treatment with antihypertensive medication, or a cardiovascular event) was less frequent among those assigned to reduced sodium intake (relative hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.59–0.81; P<0.001) and, in obese participants, to weight loss (0.70, 0.57–0.87; P<0.001). Versus usual care in obese participants: 0.60 (0.45–0.80) for sodium alone, 0.64 (0.49–0.85) for weight loss alone, and 0.47 (0.35–0.64) for both combined. The frequency of cardiovascular events was similar in each of the six treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is mostly restarting medication — a treatment decision, not a hard outcome — and participants were selected volunteers whose pressure was already controlled on one drug; the record reports relative hazards without the absolute event rates a reader would want alongside.
cards.source: Whelton PK et al. Sodium reduction and weight loss in the treatment of hypertension in older persons: a randomized controlled trial of nonpharmacologic interventions in the elderly (TONE). TONE Collaborative Research Group. JAMA. 1998. PMID: 9515998. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial, a process endpoint — sodium and weight loss buy time off medication in older patients, not proven event reduction
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial, a process endpoint — sodium and weight loss buy time off medication in older patients, not proven event reduction
cards.people: One randomised trial (TONE, 975 older hypertensive patients, median follow-up 29 months) testing sodium reduction and weight loss against usual care around a drug-withdrawal attempt.
cards.result: Relative hazard ratios for recurrent hypertension/restarting treatment: 0.69 (sodium), 0.70 (weight loss, obese), 0.47 (both combined, obese); cardiovascular events similar across groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf, so it goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: No second randomised trial in this exact older, drug-withdrawal population was carded; general sodium and weight-loss evidence in younger populations is a different shelf's question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whelton PK et al. JAMA. 1998 (PMID: 9515998).

shelves.title: POTS: low-dose propranolol (20 mg) acutely slows the standing heart rate and eases symptoms — a higher 80 mg dose slows the heart more but helps symptoms less; midodrine helped only the neuropathic subtype in one small adolescent crossover trial
shelves.question: In postural tachycardia syndrome, do low-dose propranolol or midodrine improve standing heart rate and orthostatic symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage · Adult · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Heart Rate/drug effects · Humans · Male · Placebos · Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome/drug therapy · Propranolol/administration & dosage · Sympathetic Nervous System/drug effects · Tachycardia/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — acute, low-dose, and subtype-specific. Raj 2009 randomised 54 patients with POTS in a crossover design to single doses: propranolol 20 mg lowered supine and standing heart rates versus placebo (both P<0.001) and improved symptom burden at 2 hours more than placebo (median −4.5 versus 0 arbitrary units; P=0.044), while 80 mg lowered standing heart rate further yet improved symptoms less than 20 mg (−2 versus −6 units; P=0.041) — less is more. Arnold 2013 found a single 20 mg dose raised peak oxygen consumption in POTS (27.6 ± 1.0 versus 24.5 ± 0.7 mL/min/kg on placebo; P=0.024). For midodrine, Ross 2014 (20 patients aged 12–20, double-blind crossover) found haemodynamic improvement in neuropathic POTS but a placebo-like pattern in hyperadrenergic POTS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose propranolol acutely improves tachycardia and symptoms in POTS; chronic-dosing and hard-outcome evidence does not exist in this record.

cards.headline: Raj 2009: propranolol 20 mg beat placebo on standing heart rate and symptoms (P=0.044); 80 mg slowed the heart more but improved symptoms less (P=0.041)
cards.summary: Raj 2009: propranolol 20 mg beat placebo on standing heart rate and symptoms (P=0.044); 80 mg slowed the heart more but improved symptoms less (P=0.041)
cards.people: 54 patients with POTS in protocol 1 (acute randomised crossover of oral propranolol 20 mg versus placebo on separate mornings, with seated and standing measures for up to 10 minutes before and hourly after dosing) and 18 patients in protocol 2 (80 mg versus 20 mg).
cards.result: Supine (P<0.001) and standing (P<0.001) heart rates were significantly lower after propranolol 20 mg than placebo, and symptom-burden improvement at 2 hours was greater with propranolol (median −4.5 versus 0 arbitrary units; P=0.044). In protocol 2 the 80 mg dose produced a greater decrease in standing heart rate and orthostatic tachycardia (both P<0.001) but less symptom improvement at 2 hours than 20 mg (−2 versus −6 arbitrary units; P=0.041).
cards.watchOut: Single-dose, same-day physiology — this trial says nothing about weeks or months of treatment, and the symptom scale is an arbitrary-unit burden score, not a validated quality-of-life instrument.
cards.source: Raj SR et al. Propranolol decreases tachycardia and improves symptoms in the postural tachycardia syndrome: less is more. Circulation. 2009. PMID: 19687359. cards.headline: Arnold 2013: a single 20 mg propranolol dose raised peak oxygen consumption in POTS (27.6 versus 24.5 mL/min/kg; P=0.024) — 80 mg propranolol and 100 mg metoprolol did not
cards.summary: Arnold 2013: a single 20 mg propranolol dose raised peak oxygen consumption in POTS (27.6 versus 24.5 mL/min/kg; P=0.024) — 80 mg propranolol and 100 mg metoprolol did not
cards.people: 11 patients with POTS and 7 healthy subjects comparing placebo versus a single low dose of propranolol 20 mg on maximal exercise capacity (semirecumbent bicycle to maximal effort), with a separate POTS cohort tested on propranolol 80 mg and metoprolol 100 mg.
cards.result: Low-dose propranolol improved peak oxygen consumption in POTS (24.5 ± 0.7 on placebo versus 27.6 ± 1.0 mL/min/kg on propranolol; P=0.024) but not in healthy subjects, alongside attenuated peak heart rate (142 ± 8 versus 165 ± 4 bpm; P=0.005) and improved stroke volume (81 ± 4 versus 67 ± 3 mL; P=0.013). Neither high-dose propranolol nor metoprolol improved peak oxygen consumption in the separate cohort despite similar heart-rate lowering.
cards.watchOut: Eleven patients and a single dose — Class II evidence by the authors' own grading; the metoprolol comparison was in a separate cohort, not a randomised head-to-head.
cards.source: Arnold AC et al. Low-dose propranolol and exercise capacity in postural tachycardia syndrome: a randomized study. Neurology. 2013. PMID: 23616163. cards.headline: Ross 2014: midodrine improved postural tachycardia in neuropathic POTS (12 patients) but not hyperadrenergic POTS (8), where placebo looked the same
cards.summary: Ross 2014: midodrine improved postural tachycardia in neuropathic POTS (12 patients) but not hyperadrenergic POTS (8), where placebo looked the same
cards.people: 20 patients with POTS aged 12–20 years (12 neuropathic, 8 hyperadrenergic; 15 female), receiving 2 weeks of midodrine (titrated 2.5 to 10 mg three times daily) or placebo, a 7-day washout, then the crossover treatment, with supine and 35° head-up-tilt haemodynamics.
cards.result: In neuropathic POTS, midodrine decreased supine and upright heart rate, calf blood flow, and calf venous capacitance while increasing mean arterial pressure and calf vascular resistance versus placebo. In hyperadrenergic POTS, placebo and midodrine both decreased upright heart rate, and the midodrine-specific vascular effects were not seen — the authors conclude midodrine is probably effective for neuropathic but not hyperadrenergic POTS.
cards.watchOut: Adolescents and young adults only, 20 patients, haemodynamic endpoints over 2 weeks — symptom benefit is inferred from physiology, and the subtype split was the hypothesis being tested in very small numbers.
cards.source: Ross AJ et al. A double-blind placebo-controlled cross-over study of the vascular effects of midodrine in neuropathic compared with hyperadrenergic postural tachycardia syndrome. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 2014. PMID: 23978222. cards.headline: Synthesis: acute low-dose propranolol works on the day; midodrine's signal is confined to neuropathic POTS; nothing here tests chronic treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: acute low-dose propranolol works on the day; midodrine's signal is confined to neuropathic POTS; nothing here tests chronic treatment
cards.people: Three small randomised crossover studies in POTS (Raj 2009, 54 patients; Arnold 2013, 11 patients; Ross 2014, 20 patients aged 12–20).
cards.result: Propranolol 20 mg: standing heart rate and symptoms better than placebo (Raj 2009; symptom P=0.044), peak oxygen consumption 27.6 versus 24.5 mL/min/kg (Arnold 2013). Higher doses slowed heart rate more and symptoms less. Midodrine: haemodynamic benefit in neuropathic POTS only (Ross 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: small, acute, single-centre crossover evidence, so the shelf goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: All three studies come from specialist autonomic centres and two share an investigator group; patients with undifferentiated POTS in general practice may not reproduce these responses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raj SR et al. Circulation. 2009 (PMID: 19687359); Arnold AC et al. Neurology. 2013 (PMID: 23616163); Ross AJ et al. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 2014 (PMID: 23978222).

shelves.title: Sacubitril/valsartan lowers blood pressure a few mm Hg more than an ARB alone: central systolic −3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan at 12 weeks in older patients, and sitting systolic −2.3 to −3.5 mm Hg at 8 weeks in Asian patients
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does sacubitril/valsartan lower blood pressure more than an angiotensin receptor blocker alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aminobutyrates/administration & dosage · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/administration & dosage · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage · Biphenyl Compounds · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy/physiopathology · Imidazoles/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Systole · Tetrazoles/administration & dosage · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Valsartan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small extra fall in blood pressure. In PARAMETER (Williams 2017), 454 older patients (mean age 67.7 years, mean seated systolic 158.6 mm Hg) randomised to sacubitril/valsartan or olmesartan showed a greater fall in central aortic systolic pressure at 12 weeks with sacubitril/valsartan (−3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan; P=0.010), with 24-hour ambulatory systolic lower by 4.1 mm Hg (P<0.001); by 52 weeks pressures were similar, though fewer sacubitril/valsartan patients needed add-on therapy (32% versus 47%; P<0.002). In Huo 2019 (1,438 Asian patients), sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg beat olmesartan 20 mg on sitting systolic pressure at 8 weeks by −2.33 mm Hg (95% CI −4.00 to −0.66) and the 400 mg dose by −3.52 mm Hg (−5.19 to −1.84). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sacubitril/valsartan lowers blood pressure modestly more than olmesartan alone in hypertension — a few mm Hg, with no hypertension outcome trial behind it.

cards.headline: PARAMETER (Williams 2017): central aortic systolic −3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan at 12 weeks (P=0.010); by 52 weeks pressures equal but add-on therapy needed by 32% versus 47%
cards.summary: PARAMETER (Williams 2017): central aortic systolic −3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan at 12 weeks (P=0.010); by 52 weeks pressures equal but add-on therapy needed by 32% versus 47%
cards.people: 454 patients aged ≥60 years with systolic hypertension and pulse pressure >60 mm Hg (mean age 67.7 years, mean seated systolic 158.6 mm Hg, mean pulse pressure 69.7 mm Hg), randomised to once-daily sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg or olmesartan 20 mg, force-titrated to double doses at 4 weeks, primary assessment at 12 weeks, with add-on amlodipine then hydrochlorothiazide permitted to 52 weeks.
cards.result: At week 12 sacubitril/valsartan reduced central aortic systolic pressure more than olmesartan by −3.7 mm Hg (P=0.010), central aortic pulse pressure by −2.4 mm Hg (P<0.012), and mean 24-hour ambulatory brachial and central systolic pressures by −4.1 and −3.6 mm Hg (both P<0.001), with differences pronounced during sleep. After 52 weeks blood-pressure parameters were similar, but more patients required add-on therapy on olmesartan (47%) than sacubitril/valsartan (32%; P<0.002). Both treatments were equally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is central aortic pressure — a surrogate for the brachial pressures clinicians act on — and the 52-week convergence under add-on therapy means the durable advantage is fewer extra drugs, not lower final pressure.
cards.source: Williams B et al. Effects of Sacubitril/Valsartan Versus Olmesartan on Central Hemodynamics in the Elderly With Systolic Hypertension: The PARAMETER Study. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2017. PMID: 28093466. cards.headline: Huo 2019: sitting systolic −2.33 mm Hg (200 mg) and −3.52 mm Hg (400 mg) versus olmesartan at 8 weeks in 1,438 Asian patients
cards.summary: Huo 2019: sitting systolic −2.33 mm Hg (200 mg) and −3.52 mm Hg (400 mg) versus olmesartan at 8 weeks in 1,438 Asian patients
cards.people: 1,438 Asian patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension (mean age 57.7 years) randomised to sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg (n=479), sacubitril/valsartan 400 mg (n=473), or olmesartan 20 mg (n=486) once daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg gave a significantly greater reduction in mean sitting systolic pressure than olmesartan at week 8 (between-treatment difference −2.33 mm Hg, 95% CI −4.00 to −0.66; P<0.05 for non-inferiority and superiority), as did 400 mg (−3.52 mm Hg, −5.19 to −1.84; P<0.001 for superiority). Greater reductions were also seen in the Chinese subpopulation, in patients ≥65 years, and in isolated systolic hypertension, and both doses gave greater reductions in night-time ambulatory pressure.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks, one ethnic population, and a fixed olmesartan 20 mg comparator (not titrated) — the margin over a fully titrated ARB regimen is likely smaller.
cards.source: Huo Y et al. Efficacy and safety of sacubitril/valsartan compared with olmesartan in Asian patients with essential hypertension: A randomized, double-blind, 8-week study. Journal of clinical hypertension (Greenwich, Conn.). 2019. PMID: 30536595. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one message — a few extra mm Hg over olmesartan, no hypertension outcomes data
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one message — a few extra mm Hg over olmesartan, no hypertension outcomes data
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials of sacubitril/valsartan versus olmesartan in hypertension (PARAMETER, 454 older patients; Huo 2019, 1,438 Asian patients).
cards.result: Advantage for sacubitril/valsartan: −3.7 mm Hg central systolic at 12 weeks (PARAMETER) and −2.33 to −3.52 mm Hg sitting systolic at 8 weeks (Huo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for stroke, myocardial infarction, or death in hypertension, and sacubitril/valsartan's hypertension role remains off the back of its heart-failure indication in most health systems; cost and angioedema precautions are not addressed by these records.

shelves.title: Meditation lowers blood pressure modestly in randomised trials: Transcendental Meditation pooled at −4.7/−3.2 mm Hg, and −10.7/−6.4 mm Hg versus an education control in the one older trial in African American patients
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, do meditation and mindfulness-based stress-reduction programmes lower office and ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Pressure/physiology · Female · Humans · Hypertension/physiopathology/psychology/therapy · Male · Meditation · Middle Aged · Quality Assurance, Health Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest falls, from trials of uneven quality. Anderson 2008 meta-analysed nine randomised controlled trials of Transcendental Meditation versus control and found systolic pressure lower by 4.7 mm Hg (95% CI −7.4 to −1.9) and diastolic by 3.2 mm Hg (−5.4 to −1.3), with similar reductions in hypertensive subgroups and in the three high-quality studies. The largest single trial in the pool's tradition, Schneider 1995, randomised 127 older African American patients (aged 55–85) with mild hypertension: Transcendental Meditation reduced systolic pressure by 10.7 mm Hg (P<0.0003) and diastolic by 6.4 mm Hg (P<0.00005) versus a lifestyle-education control over 3 months, beating progressive muscle relaxation as well. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meditation — best evidenced for the Transcendental Meditation technique — lowers clinic blood pressure by roughly 3–5 mm Hg in pooled randomised evidence; ambulatory-pressure and outcome data are thin.

cards.headline: Anderson 2008: nine randomised trials pooled — systolic −4.7 mm Hg (95% CI −7.4 to −1.9) and diastolic −3.2 mm Hg (−5.4 to −1.3) with Transcendental Meditation
cards.summary: Anderson 2008: nine randomised trials pooled — systolic −4.7 mm Hg (95% CI −7.4 to −1.9) and diastolic −3.2 mm Hg (−5.4 to −1.3) with Transcendental Meditation
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials comparing blood-pressure responses to the Transcendental Meditation technique with a control group, identified through PubMed and Cochrane searches to December 2006; study-quality scores ranged from 7 to 16 on a 20-point scale (three high quality, three acceptable).
cards.result: The random-effects meta-analysis found Transcendental Meditation, compared with control, was associated with a change in systolic blood pressure of −4.7 mm Hg (95% CI −7.4 to −1.9) and diastolic of −3.2 mm Hg (−5.4 to −1.3). Subgroup analyses of hypertensive groups and of high-quality studies showed similar reductions.
cards.watchOut: Only three of nine trials were high quality, most were small and short, and the evidence is for one branded technique (Transcendental Meditation) — mindfulness-based programmes as a class are extrapolated, not directly pooled, here.
cards.source: Anderson JW et al. Blood pressure response to transcendental meditation: a meta-analysis. American journal of hypertension. 2008. PMID: 18311126. cards.headline: Schneider 1995: Transcendental Meditation −10.7/−6.4 mm Hg versus education control at 3 months (P<0.0003 and P<0.00005) in 127 older African American patients
cards.summary: Schneider 1995: Transcendental Meditation −10.7/−6.4 mm Hg versus education control at 3 months (P<0.0003 and P<0.00005) in 127 older African American patients
cards.people: 127 African American men and women aged 55–85 years with mild hypertension (diastolic 90–109 mm Hg, systolic ≤189 mm Hg) at an inner-city primary-care health centre, randomised to Transcendental Meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, or a lifestyle-modification education control, with 3 months of follow-up and blinded blood-pressure observers; 16 did not complete follow-up measurements.
cards.result: Adjusted for baseline differences and compared with control, Transcendental Meditation reduced systolic pressure by 10.7 mm Hg (P<0.0003) and diastolic by 6.4 mm Hg (P<0.00005); progressive muscle relaxation lowered systolic by 4.7 mm Hg (P=0.0054) and diastolic by 3.3 mm Hg (P<0.02), and the Transcendental Meditation reductions were significantly greater than relaxation for both systolic (P=0.02) and diastolic (P=0.03) pressure.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1995 trial with an education control that cannot blind participants to a meditation intervention, and effect sizes larger than the pooled estimate — expectancy effects in unblindable behavioural trials are the standing caveat.
cards.source: Schneider RH et al. A randomised controlled trial of stress reduction for hypertension in older African Americans. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 1995. PMID: 7591024. shelves.title: POST: metoprolol did not prevent vasovagal syncope — 208 patients with a median of 9 lifetime spells, recurrences no different from placebo over a year, in any age group
shelves.question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, does metoprolol prevent syncope recurrence compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Age Factors · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Metoprolol/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Placebos · Recurrence · Syncope, Vasovagal/drug therapy/prevention & control · Tilt-Table Test · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive placebo-controlled trial was flatly negative. In POST (Sheldon 2006), 208 patients (mean age 42 ± 18 years) with more than two syncopal spells and a positive tilt test — a median of 9 spells over a median of 11 years — were randomised to metoprolol or placebo at highest-tolerated doses of 25–200 mg daily for 1 year. Seventy-five patients had at least one recurrence, and the likelihood of recurrent syncope was not significantly different between groups; neither age (<42 versus ≥42 years) nor needing isoproterenol for a positive tilt test predicted benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): metoprolol does not prevent recurrent vasovagal syncope in tilt-positive patients.

cards.headline: POST (Sheldon 2006): 75 of 208 patients fainted again within a year — no significant difference between metoprolol and placebo, and no age or tilt-test subgroup benefited
cards.summary: POST (Sheldon 2006): 75 of 208 patients fainted again within a year — no significant difference between metoprolol and placebo, and no age or tilt-test subgroup benefited
cards.people: 208 patients (mean age 42 ± 18 years) with >2 syncopal spells and a positive tilt test (median 9 spells over a median 11 years), randomised to metoprolol (n=108) or placebo (n=100) at highest-tolerated doses from 25 to 200 mg daily for 1 year, stratified by age <42 and ≥42 years.
cards.result: A total of 75 patients had ≥1 recurrence of syncope. The likelihood of recurrent syncope was not significantly different between the metoprolol and placebo groups, and neither the patient's age nor the need for isoproterenol to produce a positive tilt test predicted significant benefit from metoprolol. The authors conclude metoprolol was not effective in preventing vasovagal syncope in this population.
cards.watchOut: The record does not print the per-group recurrence counts, so no absolute rates can be quoted from it; enrolment required a positive tilt test, so the null formally applies to tilt-positive recurrent syncope.
cards.source: Sheldon R et al. Prevention of Syncope Trial (POST): a randomized, placebo-controlled study of metoprolol in the prevention of vasovagal syncope. Circulation. 2006. PMID: 16505178. cards.headline: Synthesis: one adequately designed trial, no signal anywhere — beta-blockade with metoprolol is not syncope prevention
cards.summary: Synthesis: one adequately designed trial, no signal anywhere — beta-blockade with metoprolol is not syncope prevention
cards.people: One multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (POST, 208 patients with recurrent tilt-positive vasovagal syncope, 1 year).
cards.result: 75 patients had ≥1 recurrence; likelihood of recurrence not significantly different on metoprolol versus placebo, with no prespecified subgroup (age, isoproterenol requirement) showing benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf, so it goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: Other beta-blockers and tilt-negative patients were not tested here; the shelf answers the metoprolol question as asked, in the population POST enrolled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sheldon R et al. Circulation. 2006 (PMID: 16505178).

shelves.title: Growth hormone in chronic heart failure: pooled small trials show ejection fraction up about 3–5 points and better exercise capacity — and a 2025 meta-analysis claims fewer death/worsening events (relative risk 0.59), a hard-endpoint claim built on small trials that no large trial has tested
shelves.question: In chronic heart failure, does growth hormone supplementation improve exercise capacity, cardiac function, or clinical outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Growth Hormone/therapeutic use · Heart/drug effects/physiopathology · Heart Failure/drug therapy/physiopathology · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/analysis · Stroke Volume · Vascular Resistance/drug effects · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for function and symptoms, on small-trial evidence. Le Corvoisier 2007 pooled 12 trials and found growth hormone improved left ventricular ejection fraction by 5.10% (weighted mean difference), maximal oxygen uptake by 2.48 mL/kg/min, exercise duration by 103.7 seconds, and NYHA class by −0.97, alongside thicker walls and smaller cavity dimensions. The updated Theodorakis 2025 meta-analysis of 17 randomised placebo-controlled studies found ejection fraction +3.34% (95% CI 1.09–5.59; P=0.0037), peak oxygen consumption +2.84 mL/kg/min (1.32–4.36; P=0.0002), NYHA class −0.44, and a composite of death, worsening heart failure, or ventricular tachycardia reduced with a relative risk of 0.59 (0.39–0.90; P=0.013) — a relative effect from small trials, with no large event-driven trial behind it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the hard-endpoint claim rests on pooled small trials and goes to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Le Corvoisier 2007: ejection fraction +5.10%, maximal oxygen uptake +2.48 mL/kg/min, NYHA class −0.97 across 12 small trials
cards.summary: Le Corvoisier 2007: ejection fraction +5.10%, maximal oxygen uptake +2.48 mL/kg/min, NYHA class −0.97 across 12 small trials
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials and open studies (Le Corvoisier 2007)
cards.people: Twelve trials of sustained growth hormone treatment in chronic heart failure identified across three databases; the component trials involved small numbers of patients.
cards.result: Growth hormone significantly improved morphological parameters (interventricular septum +0.55 mm, posterior wall +1.01 mm, left ventricular end-diastolic diameter −2.02 mm, end-systolic diameter −5.30 mm), haemodynamics (ejection fraction +5.10%, systemic vascular resistance changed, end-systolic wall stress −38.9 dynes/cm²), and function (NYHA class −0.97, exercise duration +103.7 seconds, maximal oxygen uptake +2.48 mL/kg/min). Effects correlated with the IGF-I response.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes randomised trials with open studies, every component trial was small, and the authors themselves state the results must be confirmed by a large randomised placebo-controlled trial — which has still not been done.
cards.source: Le Corvoisier P et al. Cardiac effects of growth hormone treatment in chronic heart failure: A meta-analysis. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2007. PMID: 17062772. cards.headline: Theodorakis 2025: ejection fraction +3.34%, peak oxygen uptake +2.84 mL/kg/min — and a composite of death, worsening heart failure, or ventricular tachycardia at relative risk 0.59 (0.39–0.90)
cards.summary: Theodorakis 2025: ejection fraction +3.34%, peak oxygen uptake +2.84 mL/kg/min — and a composite of death, worsening heart failure, or ventricular tachycardia at relative risk 0.59 (0.39–0.90)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials (Theodorakis 2025)
cards.people: Seventeen randomised placebo-controlled studies of growth hormone therapy in adult heart-failure patients, selected from 1,184 records; random-effects models were used because of heterogeneity.
cards.result: Growth hormone improved left ventricular ejection fraction (+3.34%; 95% CI 1.09–5.59; P=0.0037), peak oxygen consumption (+2.84 mL/kg/min; 1.32–4.36; P=0.0002), and NYHA class (−0.44; −0.08 to −0.81; P=0.023), and reduced the composite of death, worsening heart failure, or ventricular tachycardia by a relative risk of 0.59 (0.39–0.90; P=0.013). Subgroup analyses suggested greater benefit in ischaemic cardiomyopathy, baseline ejection fraction ≥30%, and longer treatment.
cards.watchOut: The composite is a relative effect pooled from small short trials — exactly the setting where pooled hard-endpoint signals evaporate in a large trial; the authors call for event-driven trials to validate it.
cards.source: Theodorakis N et al. GH Therapy in Chronic Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2025. PMID: 39566897. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent functional gains across two decades of small trials; the clinical-outcome claim remains a hypothesis
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent functional gains across two decades of small trials; the clinical-outcome claim remains a hypothesis
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of growth hormone in chronic heart failure (Le Corvoisier 2007: 12 trials including open studies; Theodorakis 2025: 17 randomised placebo-controlled studies).
cards.result: Ejection fraction +5.10% (2007) and +3.34% (2025); peak oxygen uptake +2.48 and +2.84 mL/kg/min; NYHA class improved in both. Composite death/worsening heart failure/ventricular tachycardia relative risk 0.59 in the 2025 pool only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the hard-endpoint claim.
cards.watchOut: Growth hormone is not a licensed heart-failure treatment; dosing, duration, and safety (fluid retention, glucose) vary across the small trials and are not standardised in either record.

shelves.title: Thiamine for heart failure: the one positive trial was 30 patients selected for furosemide-induced deficiency; pooling all seven randomised trials (274 patients) shows no significant effect on ejection fraction, walk distance, or symptoms
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure, does thiamine supplementation improve ejection fraction and symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Diuresis/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Echocardiography · Erythrocytes/metabolism · Female · Furosemide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Heart Failure/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/physiopathology · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Thiamine/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Thiamine Deficiency/chemically induced/drug therapy/physiopathology · Thiamine Pyrophosphate/metabolism · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — except for correcting deficiency itself. Shimon 1995 randomised 30 patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure on furosemide ≥80 mg/day: after intravenous thiamine, ejection fraction rose from 0.28 ± 0.11 to 0.32 ± 0.09 (P<0.05) and diuresis increased, in patients selected for biochemical thiamine deficiency. But He 2024 pooled all seven randomised double-blind trials (274 patients) and found no significant effect of thiamine versus placebo on ejection fraction (weighted mean difference 1.653%, 95% CI −1.098 to 4.405; P=0.239), 6-minute walk (16.526 m, −36.582 to 69.634; P=0.542), NT-proBNP, or NYHA class — while confirming thiamine does correct thiamine deficiency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine thiamine supplementation does not improve cardiac function or symptoms in heart failure; treating documented deficiency is a different, narrower claim.

cards.headline: Shimon 1995: in 30 furosemide-treated patients with biochemical deficiency, thiamine raised ejection fraction from 0.28 to 0.32 (P<0.05) and increased diuresis
cards.summary: Shimon 1995: in 30 furosemide-treated patients with biochemical deficiency, thiamine raised ejection fraction from 0.28 to 0.32 (P<0.05) and increased diuresis
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial with open extension (Shimon 1995)
cards.people: 30 patients with moderate-to-severe congestive heart failure receiving furosemide ≥80 mg/day for at least 3 months, randomised to 1 week of double-blind inpatient intravenous thiamine 200 mg/day or placebo (n=15 each), after which all 30 received oral thiamine 200 mg/day for 6 weeks; thiamine status was measured by the erythrocyte thiamine-pyrophosphate effect (TPPE).
cards.result: With intravenous placebo, TPPE, diuresis, and ejection fraction were unchanged. After intravenous thiamine, TPPE fell (11.7% ± 6.5% to 5.4% ± 3.2%; P<0.01), ejection fraction increased (0.28 ± 0.11 to 0.32 ± 0.09; P<0.05), diuresis rose (1,731 ± 800 to 2,389 ± 752 mL/day; P<0.02), and sodium excretion increased (84 ± 52 to 116 ± 83 mEq/day; P<0.05). In the 27 patients completing 7 weeks, ejection fraction rose from 0.27 ± 0.10 to 0.33 ± 0.11 (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients selected precisely because long-term high-dose furosemide had made them thiamine-deficient — a repletion study in deficiency, not a test of thiamine for heart failure in general; most of the follow-up was open-label, with everyone on thiamine.
cards.source: Shimon I et al. Improved left ventricular function after thiamine supplementation in patients with congestive heart failure receiving long-term furosemide therapy. The American journal of medicine. 1995. PMID: 7733128.
