cards.headline: He 2024: pooling seven randomised trials, thiamine versus placebo — ejection fraction +1.653% (95% CI −1.098 to 4.405; P=0.239), walk test and NYHA class likewise non-significant
cards.summary: He 2024: pooling seven randomised trials, thiamine versus placebo — ejection fraction +1.653% (95% CI −1.098 to 4.405; P=0.239), walk test and NYHA class likewise non-significant
cards.people: Seven randomised double-blind controlled trials (five parallel, two crossover) involving a total of 274 patients with chronic heart failure, searched to May 2023.
cards.result: Thiamine showed no significant effect versus placebo on left ventricular ejection fraction (weighted mean difference 1.653%, 95% CI −1.098 to 4.405; P=0.239; I²=61.8%), left ventricular end-diastolic volume (−6.831 mL; P=0.493), 6-minute walk test (16.526 m; −36.582 to 69.634; P=0.542), NT-proBNP (258.150 pg/mL; P=0.306), or NYHA class (−0.223; P=0.434). It did effectively improve thiamine-deficiency status.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and heterogeneous (I² up to 87.1% for NYHA class), so the null is 'no demonstrated effect in 274 randomised patients', not proof of an exact zero in deficient subgroups.
cards.source: He S et al. Role of Thiamine Supplementation in the Treatment of Chronic Heart Failure: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Clinical cardiology. 2024. PMID: 38940395. cards.summary: Synthesis: repletion helps the deficient few in one tiny trial; supplementation for heart failure itself shows nothing in the pooled record
cards.people: One 30-patient randomised trial in furosemide-induced thiamine deficiency (Shimon 1995) and one meta-analysis of seven randomised trials in chronic heart failure overall (He 2024, 274 patients).
cards.result: Shimon 1995: ejection fraction 0.28 to 0.32 on thiamine in deficient patients. shelves.title: Repeated levosimendan infusions in advanced heart failure: LION-HEART (69 patients) cut NT-proBNP and heart-failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.25), but LevoRep (120 patients) missed its functional primary endpoint — a split verdict from two small trials
shelves.question: In advanced heart failure with recurrent decompensation, do repeated intermittent levosimendan infusions reduce hospitalisation and death compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiotonic Agents/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/blood/drug therapy/physiopathology · Heart Ventricles/physiopathology · Humans · Injections, Intravenous/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Outpatients · Peptide Fragments/blood · Protein Precursors · Retrospective Studies · Simendan/administration & dosage · Stroke Volume/physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the biomarker and hospitalisation signals point one way, the functional endpoint the other, and death is unanswered. LION-HEART (Comín-Colet 2018) randomised 69 outpatients with advanced heart failure to levosimendan 0.2 µg/kg/min for 6 hours every 2 weeks for 12 weeks or placebo: NT-proBNP exposure was significantly lower on levosimendan (area under the curve 344 × 10³ versus 535 × 10³ pg·day/mL; P=0.003) and heart-failure hospitalisation was reduced (hazard ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.11–0.56; P=0.001) — a relative effect in 69 patients. LevoRep (Altenberger 2014, 120 patients) found its primary endpoint — combined ≥20% improvement in 6-minute walk and ≥15% improvement in quality-of-life score — in 19% on levosimendan versus 15.8% on placebo (odds ratio 1.25, 0.44–3.59; P=0.810). Neither trial was powered for death. PROPOSED SPLIT: promising hospitalisation signal, unproven function, unknown mortality — an adequately powered event-driven trial is still owed.

cards.headline: LION-HEART (Comín-Colet 2018): NT-proBNP area under the curve 344 versus 535 ×10³ pg·day/mL (P=0.003) and heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.25 (0.11–0.56) — in 69 patients
cards.summary: LION-HEART (Comín-Colet 2018): NT-proBNP area under the curve 344 versus 535 ×10³ pg·day/mL (P=0.003) and heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.25 (0.11–0.56) — in 69 patients
cards.people: 69 outpatients with advanced chronic heart failure at 12 centres, randomised 2:1 to levosimendan or placebo as a 6-hour intravenous infusion (0.2 µg/kg/min without bolus) every 2 weeks for 12 weeks.
cards.result: The NT-proBNP area under the curve over the treatment period was significantly lower with levosimendan (344 × 10³ [95% CI 283 × 10³–404 × 10³] versus 535 × 10³ [443 × 10³–626 × 10³] pg·day/mL; P=0.003). Heart-failure hospitalisation was reduced (hazard ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.11–0.56; P=0.001), patients on levosimendan were less likely to have a clinically significant decline in health-related quality of life (P=0.022), and adverse-event rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A pilot study of 69 patients whose primary endpoint is a biomarker; the hospitalisation hazard ratio is a relative effect on very few events, and the authors state efficacy and safety should be confirmed in larger trials.
cards.source: Comín-Colet J et al. Efficacy and safety of intermittent intravenous outpatient administration of levosimendan in patients with advanced heart failure: the LION-HEART multicentre randomised trial. European journal of heart failure. 2018. PMID: 29405611. cards.headline: LevoRep (Altenberger 2014): primary functional endpoint in 19% on levosimendan versus 15.8% on placebo (odds ratio 1.25; P=0.810) — cardiac deaths 1 versus 4, acute heart failure 9 versus 14, on small numbers
cards.summary: LevoRep (Altenberger 2014): primary functional endpoint in 19% on levosimendan versus 15.8% on placebo (odds ratio 1.25; P=0.810) — cardiac deaths 1 versus 4, acute heart failure 9 versus 14, on small numbers
cards.people: 120 outpatients with advanced heart failure (ejection fraction ≤35%, NYHA class III or IV) at 11 centres in Austria, Greece, and Germany, receiving levosimendan 0.2 µg/kg/min or placebo for 6 hours at 2-week intervals over 6 weeks plus standard care, followed to 24 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥20% improvement in 6-minute walk test plus ≥15% increase in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score at 24 weeks) was reached by 19% on levosimendan versus 15.8% on placebo (odds ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.44–3.59; P=0.810). Cardiac death (four versus one), heart transplants (two versus one), and acute heart failure (14 versus nine) were more frequent with placebo than levosimendan, and side-effect incidence was comparable.
cards.watchOut: The event counts favouring levosimendan are single digits in a trial powered for a functional composite it missed; reading them as outcome evidence would repeat the LION-HEART over-read in the opposite trial.
cards.source: Altenberger J et al. Efficacy and safety of the pulsed infusions of levosimendan in outpatients with advanced heart failure (LevoRep) study: a multicentre randomized trial. shelves.title: Hypertonic saline with high-dose furosemide: SMAC-HF reported readmissions 18.5% versus 34.2% and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% — huge effects from one research group's single-blind programme, pooled at relative risk 0.55 for death, that independent replication has not confirmed
shelves.question: In acute decompensated heart failure, does adding hypertonic saline to high-dose furosemide improve diuresis, kidney function, and outcomes compared with furosemide alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Diuresis · Female · Furosemide/administration & dosage · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Readmission · Saline Solution, Hypertonic/therapeutic use · Sodium/blood/chemistry · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the strongest caveat on this shelf: the effects are implausibly large and trace mainly to one group. In SMAC-HF (Paterna 2011), 1,771 patients with NYHA class III heart failure were single-blind randomised to furosemide 250 mg plus hypertonic saline 150 mL twice daily with a moderate sodium diet, or furosemide alone with a low-sodium diet: hospital stay was 3.5 ± 1 versus 5.5 ± 1 days (P<0.0001), and over 57 ± 15 months readmissions were 18.5% versus 34.2% (P<0.0001) and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% (P<0.0001). Liu 2021 pooled 11 randomised trials (2,987 patients) and found hypertonic saline plus furosemide associated with lower all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.67) and fewer heart-failure readmissions (relative risk 0.50, 0.33–0.76), with greater diuresis (mean difference 583.87 mL/day) — relative effects, with certainty graded only low to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a mortality claim dominated by one investigator group's trials goes to the developer personally.

cards.headline: SMAC-HF (Paterna 2011): stay 3.5 versus 5.5 days; readmissions 18.5% versus 34.2% and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% over about 57 months — in a single-blind trial where the diets also differed
cards.summary: SMAC-HF (Paterna 2011): stay 3.5 versus 5.5 days; readmissions 18.5% versus 34.2% and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% over about 57 months — in a single-blind trial where the diets also differed
cards.people: 1,771 patients (881 hypertonic saline group, 890 without) with uncompensated NYHA class III heart failure, ejection fraction <40%, creatinine <2.5 mg/dL, randomised to intravenous furosemide 250 mg plus hypertonic saline 150 mL twice daily with moderate sodium restriction (120 mmol/day), or furosemide 250 mg bolus twice daily without saline with a low-sodium diet (80 mmol/day); fluid intake 1,000 mL/day in both; follow-up 57 ± 15 months.
cards.result: The hypertonic saline group had increased diuresis and serum sodium, shorter hospitalisation (3.5 ± 1 versus 5.5 ± 1 days; P<0.0001), and during follow-up lower readmissions (18.5% versus 34.2%; P<0.0001) and mortality (12.9% versus 23.8%; P<0.0001). The no-saline group showed a significant increase in blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, single research group, and the comparison bundles three differences at once — saline, and a more liberal sodium diet in the saline arm during and after hospital — so the long-term benefit cannot be attributed to saline alone; effects of this size from a diuretic adjunct have no independent replication.
cards.source: Paterna S et al. Short-term effects of hypertonic saline solution in acute heart failure and long-term effects of a moderate sodium restriction in patients with compensated heart failure with New York Heart Association class III (Class C) (SMAC-HF Study). The American journal of the medical sciences. 2011. PMID: 21701268. cards.headline: Liu 2021: 11 trials pooled — mortality relative risk 0.55 (0.46–0.67), readmissions 0.50, diuresis +583.87 mL/day, stay −3.28 days; certainty only low to moderate
cards.summary: Liu 2021: 11 trials pooled — mortality relative risk 0.55 (0.46–0.67), readmissions 0.50, diuresis +583.87 mL/day, stay −3.28 days; certainty only low to moderate
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Liu 2021)
cards.people: Eleven randomised controlled trials comprising 2,987 patients with acute decompensated heart failure comparing simultaneous hypertonic saline plus intravenous furosemide with furosemide alone, searched to March 2020.
cards.result: Hypertonic saline plus furosemide was associated with lower all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.67; I²=12%) and heart-failure readmissions (relative risk 0.50, 0.33–0.76; I²=61%), shorter stay (mean difference −3.28 days; I²=93%), increased daily diuresis (583.87 mL; I²=76%), greater weight loss (−1.76 kg), and lower serum creatinine (−0.46 mg/dL). GRADE certainty ranged from low to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 2,987 patients are dominated by the Paterna group's 1,771-patient trial, so the meta-analysis largely re-states SMAC-HF rather than independently confirming it; heterogeneity for stay and diuresis was very high (I² 76–95%).
cards.source: Liu C et al. Simultaneous Use of Hypertonic Saline and IV Furosemide for Fluid Overload: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Critical care medicine. 2021. PMID: 34166286. shelves.title: ATHENA-HF: high-dose spironolactone (100 mg) in acute heart failure changed nothing — NT-proBNP, congestion, dyspnoea, urine output, weight, and 30-day death or hospitalisation all no different from usual care at 96 hours
shelves.question: In acute heart failure, does high-dose spironolactone improve decongestion and dyspnoea compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Failure/blood/drug therapy/physiopathology · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Mortality · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Spironolactone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a clean null in a properly blinded trial. ATHENA-HF (Butler 2017) randomised 360 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure (median ejection fraction 34%, median NT-proBNP 4,601 pg/mL in the high-dose group and 3,753 pg/mL in usual care) to spironolactone 100 mg daily or usual care (placebo or 25 mg) for 96 hours. The primary endpoint, change in log NT-proBNP, did not differ (−0.55 [95% CI −0.92 to −0.18] versus −0.49 [−0.98 to −0.14]; P=0.57), and neither did the congestion score, dyspnoea, net urine output, weight change, or day-30 all-cause mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation; potassium and kidney function changed similarly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): 96 hours of high-dose spironolactone is well tolerated in acute heart failure but does not decongest faster than usual care.

cards.headline: ATHENA-HF (Butler 2017): log NT-proBNP change −0.55 versus −0.49 (P=0.57); every secondary endpoint and day-30 death/hospitalisation also no different
cards.summary: ATHENA-HF (Butler 2017): log NT-proBNP change −0.55 versus −0.49 (P=0.57); every secondary endpoint and day-30 death/hospitalisation also no different
cards.people: 360 patients at 22 US acute-care hospitals with acute heart failure, previously on no or low-dose (12.5 or 25 mg) spironolactone, with NT-proBNP ≥1,000 pg/mL or BNP ≥250 pg/mL regardless of ejection fraction (median age 65 years, 36% women, median ejection fraction 34%), randomised to high-dose spironolactone 100 mg or placebo/25 mg usual care daily for 96 hours.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in log NT-proBNP reduction (−0.55 [95% CI −0.92 to −0.18] with high-dose spironolactone versus −0.49 [−0.98 to −0.14] with usual care; P=0.57). No secondary endpoint (clinical congestion score, dyspnoea assessment, net urine output, net weight change) and neither day-30 all-cause mortality nor heart-failure hospitalisation differed between groups; changes in serum potassium and estimated glomerular filtration rate at 24, 48, 72, and 96 hours were similar.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-six hours is a short exposure and NT-proBNP is a surrogate primary endpoint — but the clinical secondary endpoints pointed the same way, so a longer course would be a new hypothesis, not a rescue of this one. This trial does not touch spironolactone's proven chronic HFrEF role at standard doses.
cards.source: Butler J et al. Efficacy and Safety of Spironolactone in Acute Heart Failure: The ATHENA-HF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28700781. Registry ID: NCT02235077. shelves.title: DICTATE-AHF: early dapagliflozin in acute heart failure missed its primary diuretic-efficiency endpoint (odds ratio 0.65; P=0.06) — patients lost the same weight on less loop diuretic (560 versus 800 mg), with no safety penalty
shelves.question: In acute heart failure, does early dapagliflozin improve diuretic efficiency and decongestion compared with usual care alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Sodium Potassium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Acute Disease · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Diuretics · Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoint the trial chose, with a diuretic-sparing signal underneath. DICTATE-AHF (Cox 2024) randomised 240 patients within 24 hours of presentation with hypervolaemic acute heart failure, open-label, to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or structured usual care with protocolised diuretic titration to day 5 or discharge. Diuretic efficiency (cumulative weight change per cumulative loop diuretic dose) did not differ significantly (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.41–1.02; P=0.06). Dapagliflozin patients achieved equivalent weight loss on lower loop diuretic doses (560 mg [Q1–Q3 260–1,150] versus 800 mg [380–1,715]; P=0.006) with fewer intravenous diuretic up-titrations, better 24-hour natriuresis (P=0.03) and urine output (P=0.005), and no increase in diabetic, renal, or cardiovascular safety events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for diuretic efficiency as defined; the shelf records the diuretic-sparing findings without upgrading them past the missed primary endpoint.

cards.headline: DICTATE-AHF (Cox 2024): diuretic efficiency odds ratio 0.65 (0.41–1.02; P=0.06) — primary endpoint missed; loop diuretic dose 560 versus 800 mg (P=0.006) for the same weight loss
cards.summary: DICTATE-AHF (Cox 2024): diuretic efficiency odds ratio 0.65 (0.41–1.02; P=0.06) — primary endpoint missed; loop diuretic dose 560 versus 800 mg (P=0.006) for the same weight loss
cards.people: 240 patients randomised within 24 hours of hospital presentation for hypervolaemic acute heart failure to dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily or structured usual care with protocolised diuretic titration, until day 5 or hospital discharge; secondary and safety outcomes were adjudicated by a blinded committee.
cards.result: For the primary outcome of diuretic efficiency there was no difference between dapagliflozin and usual care (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.41–1.02; P=0.06). Dapagliflozin was associated with reduced loop diuretic doses (560 mg [Q1–Q3: 260–1,150 mg] versus 800 mg [380–1,715 mg]; P=0.006), fewer intravenous diuretic up-titrations (P≤0.05), improved median 24-hour natriuresis (P=0.03) and urine output (P=0.005), and no increase in diabetic, renal, or cardiovascular safety events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with a weight-per-dose efficiency metric is vulnerable to clinician behaviour (the usual-care arm's titration was protocolised, the dapagliflozin arm's diuretic decisions were not blinded); the trial was not powered for death or hospitalisation, and dapagliflozin's chronic heart-failure outcome benefits are a separate shelf's evidence.
cards.source: Cox ZL et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dapagliflozin in Patients With Acute Heart Failure. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2024. PMID: 38569758. Registry ID: NCT04298229. shelves.title: TRUE-AHF: ularitide lowered blood pressure and NT-proBNP but not cardiovascular death — 21.7% versus 21.0% (hazard ratio 1.03) over a median 15 months in 2,157 patients with acute heart failure
shelves.question: In acute heart failure, does the natriuretic peptide ularitide improve dyspnoea, cardiovascular death, or heart-failure hospitalisation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atrial Natriuretic Factor/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Diuretics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality · Humans · Hypotension/chemically induced · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/adverse effects/blood/therapeutic use · Troponin T/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large, definitive null. TRUE-AHF (Packer 2017) randomised 2,157 patients with acute heart failure, a median of 6 hours after initial evaluation, to a 48-hour infusion of ularitide 15 ng/kg/min or placebo on top of standard therapy. Cardiovascular death occurred in 236 patients on ularitide and 225 on placebo (21.7% versus 21.0%; hazard ratio 1.03, 96% CI 0.85–1.25; P=0.75) over a median follow-up of 15 months, and the hierarchical composite of the initial 48-hour clinical course also did not differ significantly. Ularitide did lower systolic blood pressure and NT-proBNP more than placebo, but cardiac troponin T changes did not differ — the physiological effects never became clinical benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): early ularitide infusion does not improve the clinical course or reduce cardiovascular mortality in acute heart failure.

cards.headline: TRUE-AHF (Packer 2017): cardiovascular death 236 versus 225 patients (21.7% versus 21.0%; hazard ratio 1.03; P=0.75); early clinical-course composite also not significantly different
cards.summary: TRUE-AHF (Packer 2017): cardiovascular death 236 versus 225 patients (21.7% versus 21.0%; hazard ratio 1.03; P=0.75); early clinical-course composite also not significantly different
cards.people: 2,157 patients with acute heart failure randomised to continuous intravenous ularitide 15 ng per kilogram per minute or matching placebo for 48 hours in addition to accepted therapy, started a median of 6 hours after initial clinical evaluation; median follow-up 15 months.
cards.result: Death from cardiovascular causes occurred in 236 patients in the ularitide group and 225 in the placebo group (21.7% versus 21.0%; hazard ratio 1.03, 96% CI 0.85–1.25; P=0.75). There was no significant between-group difference in the hierarchical composite endpoint evaluating the initial 48-hour clinical course. Ularitide produced greater reductions in systolic blood pressure and NT-proBNP, but changes in cardiac troponin T during infusion did not differ in the 55% of patients with paired data.
cards.watchOut: The dyspnoea-specific results sit inside the hierarchical composite rather than as a standalone figure in the record; the shelf therefore answers the dyspnoea part of the question through that composite, which was not significantly different.
cards.source: Packer M et al. Effect of Ularitide on Cardiovascular Mortality in Acute Heart Failure. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28402745. Registry ID: NCT01661634. shelves.title: Baroreflex activation therapy in HFrEF: quality of life, walk distance, and NT-proBNP improved durably — but the long-term primary endpoint of cardiovascular death and heart-failure morbidity was neutral (rate ratio 0.94) in BeAT-HF
shelves.question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does baroreflex activation therapy improve symptoms, exercise capacity, and heart-failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Baroreflex/physiology · Electric Stimulation Therapy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume/physiology · Ventricular Function, Left/physiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — symptoms and function improve and stay improved; hard outcomes do not. In BeAT-HF's FDA-intended-use cohort (Zile 2020; 245 patients with HFrEF, ejection fraction ≤35%, no CRT indication), baroreflex activation therapy plus medical management beat medical management alone at 6 months on quality of life (Δ −14.1 points, 95% CI −19 to −9; P<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (Δ +60 m, 40–80; P<0.001), and NT-proBNP (Δ −25%, −38% to −9%; P=0.004), with a 97% freedom rate from major adverse neurological/cardiovascular events. But the long-term report (Zile 2024; median follow-up 3.6 years per patient, 332 primary events) found the primary endpoint of cardiovascular mortality and heart-failure morbidity not significantly different (rate ratio 0.94, 0.57–1.57; P=0.82), while the symptom gains remained durable. PROPOSED SPLIT: an implanted symptom treatment with neutral hard outcomes — hospitalisation benefit, part of the candidate question, was not shown.

cards.headline: BeAT-HF (Zile 2020): at 6 months quality of life −14.1 points, walk distance +60 m, NT-proBNP −25% versus control in the 245-patient intended-use cohort; event-free safety rate 97%
cards.summary: BeAT-HF (Zile 2020): at 6 months quality of life −14.1 points, walk distance +60 m, NT-proBNP −25% versus control in the 245-patient intended-use cohort; event-free safety rate 97%
cards.people: 408 patients with HFrEF randomised 1:1 to baroreflex activation therapy plus optimal medical management or medical management alone (NYHA class III, or class II with recent class III history; ejection fraction ≤35%; stable management ≥4 weeks; no class I CRT indication); cohort D, the FDA-approved intended-use population (adding NT-proBNP <1,600 pg/mL), comprised 245 patients (120 therapy, 125 control) followed for 6 months.
cards.result: In cohort D, quality-of-life score decreased more with therapy (Δ −14.1; 95% CI −19 to −9; P<0.001), 6-minute walk distance increased (Δ +60 m; 40–80; P<0.001), NT-proBNP decreased (Δ −25%; −38% to −9%; P=0.004), and the major adverse neurological or cardiovascular system or procedure-related event-free rate was 97% (93% to 100%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: An unblinded device trial with a non-implanted control — quality of life and walk distance are exactly the endpoints most open to expectation effects, and the headline cohort is a regulator-defined subset of the 408 randomised.
cards.source: Zile MR et al. Baroreflex Activation Therapy in Patients With Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2020. PMID: 32616150. cards.headline: BeAT-HF long-term (Zile 2024): primary endpoint rate ratio 0.94 (0.57–1.57; P=0.82) over a median 3.6 years — symptom improvements durable, hard outcomes neutral
cards.summary: BeAT-HF long-term (Zile 2024): primary endpoint rate ratio 0.94 (0.57–1.57; P=0.82) over a median 3.6 years — symptom improvements durable, hard outcomes neutral
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, long-term follow-up (Zile 2024, BeAT-HF)
cards.people: Patients with NYHA class III heart failure, ejection fraction ≤35%, previous heart-failure hospitalisation or NT-proBNP >400 pg/mL, no class I CRT indication, and NT-proBNP <1,600 pg/mL, randomised to baroreflex activation therapy plus optimal medical management or medical management alone; 323 patients had 332 primary events, with median follow-up 3.6 years per patient.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (cardiovascular mortality and heart-failure morbidity) did not differ significantly (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.57–1.57; P=0.82), nor did its components. The system- and procedure-related major adverse event-free rate remained 97%. Symptom improvement (quality of life, 6-minute walk distance, NYHA class; all nominal P<0.001) was durable; the win ratio (1.26, 1.02–1.58) and freedom from death, LVAD, or transplant (hazard ratio 0.66, 0.43–1.01) favoured therapy but did not reach significance for the latter.
cards.watchOut: The long-term analysis population and event structure differ from the 6-month regulatory cohort, and the trial remained unblinded throughout — durable symptom gains in an open device trial still carry that asterisk.
cards.source: Zile MR et al. Baroreflex activation therapy in patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction: Long-term outcomes. European journal of heart failure. 2024. PMID: 38606555. shelves.title: Cardiac contractility modulation in narrow-QRS HFrEF: the confirmatory trial grew from a post-hoc subgroup of a negative parent trial — peak oxygen uptake +0.84 mL/kg/min and better quality of life at 24 weeks, unblinded, with a Bayesian analysis borrowing from that subgroup
shelves.question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and a narrow QRS, does cardiac contractility modulation improve exercise capacity and quality of life compared with sham or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial/adverse effects/standards · Cohort Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Contraction/physiology · Prospective Studies · Retrospective Studies · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real functional gains, fragile provenance. The parent FIX-HF-5 trial (428 patients, ejection fraction ≤35%) missed its primary endpoint overall; its subgroup analysis (Abraham 2011) found that patients with NYHA class III symptoms and ejection fraction ≥25% (206 patients) responded: peak oxygen uptake rose by 0.34 ± 3.11 versus −0.97 ± 2.31 mL/kg/min on medical therapy alone (P=0.001), with ≥1-class NYHA improvement in 44% versus 23% (P=0.002). The confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial (Abraham 2018) randomised 160 such patients (ejection fraction 25–45%, QRS <130 ms), unblinded, and met its primary endpoint: peak oxygen uptake difference 0.84 mL/kg/min (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.123–1.552), with better quality of life (P<0.001), NYHA class (P<0.001), and 6-minute walk (P=0.02), and a composite of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation of 2.9% versus 10.8% (P=0.048). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for exercise capacity and quality of life in this narrow subgroup — no sham control exists in either trial.

cards.headline: FIX-HF-5 subgroup (Abraham 2011): parent trial negative overall; in NYHA III with ejection fraction ≥25%, peak oxygen uptake +0.34 versus −0.97 mL/kg/min (P=0.001) and NYHA improvement 44% versus 23%
cards.summary: FIX-HF-5 subgroup (Abraham 2011): parent trial negative overall; in NYHA III with ejection fraction ≥25%, peak oxygen uptake +0.34 versus −0.97 mL/kg/min (P=0.001) and NYHA improvement 44% versus 23%
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a randomised controlled trial (Abraham 2011, FIX-HF-5)
cards.people: 428 patients with NYHA class III/IV heart failure, ejection fraction ≤35%, and narrow QRS, randomised to optimal medical treatment plus cardiac contractility modulation (n=215) or medical treatment alone (n=213); the responsive subgroup (NYHA class III and ejection fraction ≥25%) comprised 206 patients (109 device, 97 control).
cards.result: The parent trial found no significant effect on ventilatory anaerobic threshold, its primary endpoint. In the subgroup, ventilatory anaerobic threshold increased by 0.10 ± 2.36 on device versus −0.54 ± 1.83 mL/kg/min on control (P=0.03) and peak oxygen uptake by 0.34 ± 3.11 versus −0.97 ± 2.31 (P=0.001) at 24 weeks; 44% of device versus 23% of control patients improved ≥1 NYHA class (P=0.002) and 59% versus 42% achieved a ≥10-point quality-of-life improvement (P=0.01), with similar findings at 50 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective, hypothesis-generating subgroup of a negative trial — the authors say so themselves; it defined the population the confirmatory trial then tested, which is legitimate, but the effect sizes inherit the subgroup's optimism.
cards.source: Abraham WT et al. Subgroup analysis of a randomized controlled trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of cardiac contractility modulation in advanced heart failure. subgroup analysis of a randomised controlled trial (abraham 2011, fix-hf-5) 428 patients with nyha class iii/iv heart failure, ejection fraction ≤35%, and narrow qrs, randomised to optimal medical treatment plus cardiac contractility modulation (n=215) or medical treatment alone (n=213); the responsive subgroup (nyha class iii and ejection fraction ≥25%) comprised 206 patients (109 device, 97 control). the parent trial found no significant effect on ventilatory anaerobic threshold, its primary endpoint. in the subgroup, ventilatory anaerobic threshold increased by 0.10 ± 2.36 on device versus −0.54 ± 1.83 ml/kg/min on control (p=0.03) and peak oxygen uptake by 0.34 ± 3.11 versus −0.97 ± 2.31 (p=0.001) at 24 weeks; 44% of device versus 23% of control patients improved ≥1 nyha class (p=0.002) and 59% versus 42% achieved a ≥10-point quality-of-life improvement (p=0.01), with similar findings at 50 weeks. a retrospective, hypothesis-generating subgroup of a negative trial — the authors say so themselves; it defined the population the confirmatory trial then tested, which is legitimate, but the effect sizes inherit the subgroup's optimism. abraham wt et al. subgroup analysis of a randomized controlled trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of cardiac contractility modulation in advanced heart failure. journal of cardiac failure. 2011. pmid: 21872139. mesh: aged · cardiac pacing, artificial/adverse effects/standards · cohort studies · female · follow-up studies · heart failure/physiopathology/therapy · humans · male · middle aged · myocardial contraction/physiology · prospective studies · retrospective studies · surveys and questionnaires · treatment outcome

cards.headline: FIX-HF-5C (Abraham 2018): peak oxygen uptake difference 0.84 mL/kg/min (credible interval 0.123–1.552); cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation 2.9% versus 10.8% (P=0.048) at 24 weeks
cards.summary: FIX-HF-5C (Abraham 2018): peak oxygen uptake difference 0.84 mL/kg/min (credible interval 0.123–1.552); cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation 2.9% versus 10.8% (P=0.048) at 24 weeks
cards.people: 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and ejection fraction ≥25% and ≤45%, randomised to continued medical therapy (control, n=86) or cardiac contractility modulation (treatment, n=74) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: The difference in peak oxygen uptake between groups was 0.84 (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.123–1.552) mL/kg/min, satisfying the primary endpoint; quality of life (P<0.001), NYHA class (P<0.001), and 6-minute walk (P=0.02) were all better with the device. There were 7 device-related events (lower bound 80% of patients event-free, meeting the safety endpoint), and the composite of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation was 2.9% versus 10.8% (P=0.048).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded (no sham implant), 24 weeks, and the primary analysis borrowed 30% of its information from the FIX-HF-5 subgroup by Bayesian design — the hospitalisation composite rests on a handful of events and should not be read as outcome evidence.
cards.source: Abraham WT et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Safety and Efficacy of Cardiac Contractility Modulation. JACC. Heart failure. 2018. PMID: 29754812. shelves.title: ACE inhibitors and ARBs in HFpEF: three large trials, three missed primary endpoints — candesartan 22% versus 24% (P=0.118), irbesartan hazard ratio 0.95 (P=0.35), perindopril 100 versus 107 events (P=0.545); only hospitalisation hints survive
shelves.question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers improve death or hospitalisation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Benzimidazoles/therapeutic use · Biphenyl Compounds · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Placebos · Stroke Volume/physiology · Tetrazoles/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Left/physiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three concordant large placebo-controlled trials. CHARM-Preserved (Yusuf 2003; 3,023 patients, ejection fraction >40%) found the primary outcome of cardiovascular death or heart-failure admission in 333 (22%) on candesartan versus 366 (24%) on placebo (unadjusted hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.77–1.03; P=0.118), with cardiovascular death identical (170 versus 170) though first heart-failure admissions were fewer (230 versus 279; P=0.017). I-PRESERVE (Massie 2008; 4,128 patients, ejection fraction ≥45%) found the primary outcome at 100.4 versus 105.4 per 1,000 patient-years on irbesartan versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.95, 0.86–1.05; P=0.35) and death rates of 52.6 versus 52.3 per 1,000 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.00). PEP-CHF (Cleland 2006; 850 patients aged ≥70) found the primary endpoint in 100 patients on perindopril versus 107 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.919, 0.700–1.208; P=0.545). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): renin–angiotensin blockade does not improve death or the primary composites in HFpEF.

cards.headline: CHARM-Preserved (Yusuf 2003): primary outcome 333 (22%) on candesartan versus 366 (24%) on placebo (P=0.118); cardiovascular death 170 versus 170; first heart-failure admissions 230 versus 279 (P=0.017)
cards.summary: CHARM-Preserved (Yusuf 2003): primary outcome 333 (22%) on candesartan versus 366 (24%) on placebo (P=0.118); cardiovascular death 170 versus 170; first heart-failure admissions 230 versus 279 (P=0.017)
cards.people: 3,023 patients with NYHA class II–IV chronic heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction >40%, randomised to candesartan (n=1,514, target 32 mg daily) or placebo (n=1,509); median follow-up 36.6 months.
cards.result: The primary outcome (cardiovascular death or admission for heart failure) occurred in 333 (22%) on candesartan versus 366 (24%) on placebo (unadjusted hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.77–1.03; P=0.118; covariate-adjusted 0.86, 0.74–1.0; P=0.051). Cardiovascular death did not differ (170 versus 170), but fewer candesartan patients were admitted for heart failure once (230 versus 279; P=0.017) or multiple times.
cards.watchOut: The adjusted analysis (P=0.051) and the admission finding will be quoted as 'nearly positive' — the trial's own unadjusted primary analysis is the governing result, and death was exactly equal.
cards.source: Yusuf S et al. Effects of candesartan in patients with chronic heart failure and preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction: the CHARM-Preserved Trial. Lancet (London, England). 2003. PMID: 13678871. cards.headline: I-PRESERVE (Massie 2008): primary outcome 100.4 versus 105.4 per 1,000 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.95; P=0.35); death 52.6 versus 52.3 (hazard ratio 1.00) on irbesartan versus placebo
cards.summary: I-PRESERVE (Massie 2008): primary outcome 100.4 versus 105.4 per 1,000 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.95; P=0.35); death 52.6 versus 52.3 (hazard ratio 1.00) on irbesartan versus placebo
cards.people: 4,128 patients aged ≥60 years with NYHA class II–IV heart failure and ejection fraction ≥45%, randomised to irbesartan 300 mg or placebo daily; mean follow-up 49.5 months.
cards.result: The primary composite (death from any cause or cardiovascular hospitalisation) occurred in 742 patients on irbesartan and 763 on placebo (100.4 versus 105.4 per 1,000 patient-years; hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.86–1.05; P=0.35). Death rates were 52.6 versus 52.3 per 1,000 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.00, 0.88–1.14; P=0.98), cardiovascular hospitalisation 70.6 versus 74.3 (hazard ratio 0.95; P=0.44), and no prespecified outcome differed significantly.
cards.watchOut: The largest and longest of the three trials and the most completely null — it closes the door on the argument that CHARM-Preserved was merely underpowered for an ARB effect.
cards.source: Massie BM et al. Irbesartan in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 19001508. Registry ID: NCT00095238. cards.headline: PEP-CHF (Cleland 2006): primary endpoint in 100 patients on perindopril versus 107 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.919; P=0.545) — an underpowered ACE-inhibitor trial with heavy crossover to open-label treatment
cards.summary: PEP-CHF (Cleland 2006): primary endpoint in 100 patients on perindopril versus 107 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.919; P=0.545) — an underpowered ACE-inhibitor trial with heavy crossover to open-label treatment
cards.people: 850 patients aged ≥70 years (mean 76, 55% women) with heart failure on diuretics and echocardiographic diastolic dysfunction, randomised to perindopril 4 mg/day or placebo; median follow-up 2.1 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (all-cause mortality or unplanned heart-failure hospitalisation) occurred in 100 patients on perindopril versus 107 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.919, 95% CI 0.700–1.208; P=0.545). By 1 year there were reductions in the primary outcome (hazard ratio 0.692, 0.474–1.010; P=0.055) and heart-failure hospitalisation (0.628, 0.408–0.966; P=0.033), with improved functional class and walk distance on perindopril.
cards.watchOut: Lower-than-expected enrolment and event rates cut power for the primary endpoint to 35%, and 28% (perindopril) and 26% (placebo) withdrew after 1 year, many starting open-label ACE inhibitors — the 1-year signals are hypothesis-grade, the overall result null.
cards.source: Cleland JG et al. The perindopril in elderly people with chronic heart failure (PEP-CHF) study. European heart journal. 2006. PMID: 16963472. cards.people: Three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials in HFpEF (CHARM-Preserved, candesartan, 3,023 patients; I-PRESERVE, irbesartan, 4,128; PEP-CHF, perindopril, 850).
cards.result: Primary composites: hazard ratios 0.89 (P=0.118), 0.95 (P=0.35), and 0.919 (P=0.545). Death: identical in CHARM-Preserved (170 versus 170) and I-PRESERVE (hazard ratio 1.00). shelves.title: Obese older HFpEF: diet and exercise each raised peak oxygen consumption (by 1.3 and 1.2 mL/kg/min), and together the gains added up (2.5) — quality of life, oddly, did not significantly improve in the SECRET trial
shelves.question: In older obese patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, does combining caloric restriction with aerobic exercise improve exercise capacity more than either alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Body Composition · Body Mass Index · Caloric Restriction/adverse effects · Combined Modality Therapy · Exercise/physiology · Exercise Tolerance/physiology · Female · Heart Failure/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/physiopathology/therapy · Oxygen Consumption/physiology · Patient Compliance · Physical Conditioning, Human/adverse effects/methods/physiology · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Volume/physiology · Surveys and Questionnaires · Weight Loss/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for exercise capacity, in one centre's programme of two trials. In SECRET (Kitzman 2016), 100 obese older patients with stable HFpEF (mean age 67 years, body mass index 39.3) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to 20 weeks of caloric restriction, aerobic exercise, both, or attention control. By main-effects analysis, peak oxygen consumption rose with exercise (+1.2 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.7–1.7; P<0.001) and with diet (+1.3, 0.8–1.8; P<0.001), and the combination was additive (joint effect 2.5 mL/kg/min); weight fell 7% on diet, 3% on exercise, and 10% on both. Neither intervention significantly changed the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure quality-of-life score. Brubaker 2023 then showed adding resistance training to diet plus aerobic exercise (88 patients) improved leg strength and muscle quality without further raising peak oxygen consumption. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combined caloric restriction and aerobic exercise additively improve exercise capacity in obese older HFpEF.

cards.headline: SECRET (Kitzman 2016): peak oxygen consumption +1.2 mL/kg/min with exercise and +1.3 with diet (both P<0.001), joint effect 2.5 combined; weight −10% on both; quality of life not significantly changed
cards.summary: SECRET (Kitzman 2016): peak oxygen consumption +1.2 mL/kg/min with exercise and +1.3 with diet (both P<0.001), joint effect 2.5 combined; weight −10% on both; quality of life not significantly changed
cards.people: 100 older obese patients with chronic stable HFpEF (mean age 67 years, body mass index 39.3) at one urban academic centre, randomised to 20 weeks of exercise (n=26), diet (n=24), exercise plus diet (n=25), or attention control (n=25); 92 completed; exercise attendance 84% and diet adherence 99%.
cards.result: By main-effects analysis, peak oxygen consumption increased significantly with exercise (1.2 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.7–1.7; P<0.001) and diet (1.3, 0.8–1.8; P<0.001), and the combination was additive (joint effect 2.5 mL/kg/min). Neither intervention significantly changed the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure total score (exercise −1 unit, −8 to 5; P=0.70; diet −6 units, −12 to 1; P=0.08). Body weight fell by 7% (diet), 3% (exercise), 10% (both), and 1% (control); there were no study-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 100 selected volunteers with a surrogate primary endpoint (peak oxygen consumption) at 20 weeks — no hospitalisation or mortality data, and the quality-of-life null sits awkwardly beside the exercise gains.
cards.source: Kitzman DW et al. Effect of Caloric Restriction or Aerobic Exercise Training on Peak Oxygen Consumption and Quality of Life in Obese Older Patients With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. randomised 2×2 factorial trial (kitzman 2016, secret) 100 older obese patients with chronic stable hfpef (mean age 67 years, body mass index 39.3) at one urban academic centre, randomised to 20 weeks of exercise (n=26), diet (n=24), exercise plus diet (n=25), or attention control (n=25); 92 completed; exercise attendance 84% and diet adherence 99%. by main-effects analysis, peak oxygen consumption increased significantly with exercise (1.2 ml/kg/min, 95% ci 0.7–1.7; p<0.001) and diet (1.3, 0.8–1.8; p<0.001), and the combination was additive (joint effect 2.5 ml/kg/min). neither intervention significantly changed the minnesota living with heart failure total score (exercise −1 unit, −8 to 5; p=0.70; diet −6 units, −12 to 1; p=0.08). body weight fell by 7% (diet), 3% (exercise), 10% (both), and 1% (control); there were no study-related serious adverse events. a single-centre trial of 100 selected volunteers with a surrogate primary endpoint (peak oxygen consumption) at 20 weeks — no hospitalisation or mortality data, and the quality-of-life null sits awkwardly beside the exercise gains. kitzman dw et al. effect of caloric restriction or aerobic exercise training on peak oxygen consumption and quality of life in obese older patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a randomized clinical trial. jama. 2016. pmid: 26746456. registry id: nct00959660. mesh: aged · body composition · body mass index · caloric restriction/adverse effects · combined modality therapy · exercise/physiology · exercise tolerance/physiology · female · heart failure/physiopathology/therapy · humans · male · middle aged · obesity/physiopathology/therapy · oxygen consumption/physiology · patient compliance · physical conditioning, human/adverse effects/methods/physiology · quality of life · single-blind method · stroke volume/physiology · surveys and questionnaires · weight loss/physiology

cards.headline: Brubaker 2023: adding resistance training to diet plus aerobic exercise improved leg strength (+4.9 versus −1.1 Nm; P=0.05) but did not further raise peak oxygen consumption or spare muscle
cards.summary: Brubaker 2023: adding resistance training to diet plus aerobic exercise improved leg strength (+4.9 versus −1.1 Nm; P=0.05) but did not further raise peak oxygen consumption or spare muscle
cards.people: 88 patients with chronic HFpEF and body mass index ≥28 kg/m² randomised to 20 weeks of resistance training plus caloric restriction plus aerobic exercise, or caloric restriction plus aerobic exercise alone; 77 completed the trial.
cards.result: Weight loss did not differ significantly between groups (−8 kg [95% CI −9 to −7] versus −9 kg [−11 to −8]; P=0.21), nor did loss of body fat or skeletal muscle. Resistance training produced greater increases in leg muscle strength (4.9 [0.7 to 9.0] versus −1.1 [−5.5 to 3.2] Nm; P=0.05) and leg muscle quality (0.07 versus 0.02 Nm/cm²; P=0.04). Both groups improved peak oxygen consumption and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores significantly, with no significant between-group differences; there were no study-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers the 'add resistance training?' follow-on, not the diet-plus-exercise question directly — its value here is confirming, in a second randomised cohort from the same programme, that diet plus aerobic exercise again produced large within-group exercise-capacity gains.
cards.source: Brubaker PH et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: diet and exercise are additive for exercise capacity in obese HFpEF — the programme's two trials agree on capacity, and neither shows an outcome benefit

cards.result: Peak oxygen consumption: +1.2 (exercise) and +1.3 (diet) mL/kg/min main effects, 2.5 joint (SECRET). Added resistance training: better leg strength, no extra peak oxygen consumption (Brubaker 2023). Quality of life: not significantly improved in SECRET. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Non-invasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: breathing and acidosis improve within an hour and intubation falls in pooled trials — but the largest trial (3CPO, 1,069 patients) found 7-day mortality identical at 9.5% versus 9.8%
shelves.question: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, does non-invasive ventilation reduce intubation and mortality compared with standard oxygen therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Disease Progression · Female · Heart Diseases/complications · Humans · Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation/methods · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Edema/etiology/mortality/therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — intubation and early physiology favour ventilation; mortality depends on which evidence you trust. In 3CPO (Gray 2008), 1,069 patients (mean age 77.7 years) randomised to standard oxygen, CPAP, or non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation showed no difference in 7-day mortality (9.8% on oxygen versus 9.5% on non-invasive ventilation; P=0.87) and no difference between CPAP and NIPPV in death or intubation (11.7% versus 11.1%; P=0.81) — though dyspnoea, heart rate, acidosis, and hypercapnia all improved faster at 1 hour on ventilation. The Cochrane review (Berbenetz 2019; 24 studies, 2,664 participants) pooled a mortality benefit (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.51–0.82; low-quality evidence; number needed to treat 17) and a clearer intubation reduction (risk ratio 0.49, 0.38–0.62; moderate-quality evidence; NNT 13) — relative effects driven by smaller, older trials that 3CPO outweighs. PROPOSED SPLIT: use non-invasive ventilation to relieve distress and avoid intubation; a mortality benefit is claimed by the pooled small trials and contradicted by the one large trial.

cards.headline: 3CPO (Gray 2008): 7-day mortality 9.5% on non-invasive ventilation versus 9.8% on oxygen (P=0.87); death-or-intubation 11.7% CPAP versus 11.1% NIPPV (P=0.81); dyspnoea and acidosis improved faster at 1 hour
cards.summary: 3CPO (Gray 2008): 7-day mortality 9.5% on non-invasive ventilation versus 9.8% on oxygen (P=0.87); death-or-intubation 11.7% CPAP versus 11.1% NIPPV (P=0.81); dyspnoea and acidosis improved faster at 1 hour
cards.people: 1,069 patients with severe acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (mean age 77.7 ± 9.7 years, 56.9% female) in a multicentre open prospective randomised trial, assigned to standard oxygen therapy (n=367), CPAP 5–15 cm of water (n=346), or NIPPV (n=356).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in 7-day mortality between standard oxygen (9.8%) and non-invasive ventilation (9.5%; P=0.87), and no significant difference in death or intubation within 7 days between CPAP (11.7%) and NIPPV (11.1%; P=0.81). Versus oxygen, ventilation gave greater mean improvement at 1 hour in dyspnoea (treatment difference 0.7 on a 1–10 visual-analogue scale; P=0.008), heart rate (4 beats/min; P=0.004), acidosis (pH 0.03; P<0.001), and hypercapnia (0.7 kPa; P<0.001). There were no treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and conducted in UK emergency departments with high early-treatment intensity in all arms; intubation rates were low overall, which compresses any absolute intubation benefit in modern practice.
cards.source: Gray A et al. Noninvasive ventilation in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18614781. Registry ID: ISRCTN07448447. cards.headline: Cochrane (Berbenetz 2019): hospital mortality relative risk 0.65 (0.51–0.82) and intubation 0.49 (0.38–0.62) across 24 studies — graded low- and moderate-quality evidence respectively
cards.summary: Cochrane (Berbenetz 2019): hospital mortality relative risk 0.65 (0.51–0.82) and intubation 0.49 (0.38–0.62) across 24 studies — graded low- and moderate-quality evidence respectively
cards.people: 24 randomised studies with 2,664 participants with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema not requiring immediate mechanical ventilation, treated in emergency-department or intensive-care settings, comparing non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation (CPAP or bilevel) plus standard medical care with standard care alone.
cards.result: Compared with standard medical care, non-invasive ventilation may reduce hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.51–0.82; 2,484 participants, 21 studies; I²=6%; low-quality evidence; number needed to treat for benefit 17, range 12–32) and probably reduces endotracheal intubation (risk ratio 0.49, 0.38–0.62; 2,449 participants, 20 studies; I²=0%; moderate-quality evidence; NNT 13, range 11–18). Acute myocardial infarction incidence probably did not differ (risk ratio 1.03, 0.91–1.16).
cards.watchOut: The mortality pool is dominated numerically by small older trials — 3CPO alone contributes 1,069 of the 2,664 participants and found no mortality effect, so the pooled relative risk and the largest trial cannot both be taken at face value; the review itself grades the mortality evidence low quality.
cards.source: Berbenetz N et al. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP or bilevel NPPV) for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019. PMID: 30950507. cards.headline: Synthesis: ventilation for distress and intubation-sparing is supported; the mortality claim is a small-trial pool against a large-trial null
cards.summary: Synthesis: ventilation for distress and intubation-sparing is supported; the mortality claim is a small-trial pool against a large-trial null
cards.people: One large randomised trial (3CPO, 1,069 patients) and one Cochrane meta-analysis (24 studies, 2,664 participants, including 3CPO).
cards.result: Mortality: 9.5% versus 9.8% at 7 days in 3CPO; pooled hospital-mortality relative risk 0.65 in Cochrane. Intubation: pooled relative risk 0.49 (Cochrane); death-or-intubation did not differ between CPAP and NIPPV in 3CPO. Early dyspnoea/acidosis improvement: shown in 3CPO. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: a mortality benefit claim contradicted by the largest trial goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: Neither source separates CPAP from bilevel ventilation with a convincing difference — 3CPO compared them directly and found none — so the shelf does not recommend one mode over the other.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gray A et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18614781); Berbenetz N et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019 (PMID: 30950507).

shelves.title: Multidisciplinary heart-failure programmes cut hospitalisations — and, when a specialist team follows patients, death too (relative risk 0.75): telephone-only programmes cut heart-failure admissions but not mortality in two concordant McAlister reviews
shelves.question: In chronic heart failure, do multidisciplinary disease-management programmes reduce hospitalisation and death compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Disease Management · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for programmes built around a specialist multidisciplinary team. McAlister 2001 pooled 11 randomised trials (2,067 patients): disease-management programmes reduced hospitalisations (risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79–0.96) but not all-cause mortality (0.94, 0.75–1.19), were cost-saving in 7 of 8 trials reporting costs, and worked when follow-up was by a specialised multidisciplinary team (hospitalisation risk ratio 0.77, 0.68–0.86; n=1,366) but not when they were telephone-only with primary-care coordination (1.15, 0.96–1.37; n=646). McAlister 2004, across 29 trials (5,039 patients), found specialised multidisciplinary follow-up also reduced mortality (risk ratio 0.75, 0.59–0.96), heart-failure hospitalisations (0.74, 0.63–0.87), and all-cause hospitalisations (0.81, 0.71–0.92), with cost-saving in 15 of 18 trials reporting costs — all relative effects. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): multidisciplinary team follow-up reduces hospitalisation in heart failure, with a mortality reduction in the larger review; programme design decides the result.

cards.headline: McAlister 2001: hospitalisations risk ratio 0.87 (0.79–0.96), mortality 0.94 (0.75–1.19) — benefit concentrated in multidisciplinary-team follow-up (0.77), absent in telephone-only programmes (1.15)
cards.summary: McAlister 2001: hospitalisations risk ratio 0.87 (0.79–0.96), mortality 0.94 (0.75–1.19) — benefit concentrated in multidisciplinary-team follow-up (0.77), absent in telephone-only programmes (1.15)
cards.people: 11 randomised trials involving 2,067 patients with heart failure, identified from Medline, Embase, Cinahl, and Cochrane sources to 1999, with summary risk ratios calculated under random- and fixed-effects models.
cards.result: Disease-management programmes reduced hospitalisations (risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79–0.96) but not all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.94, 0.75–1.19), were cost-saving in 7 of the 8 trials reporting costs, and improved prescribing. Specialised follow-up by a multidisciplinary team substantially reduced hospitalisation (risk ratio 0.77, 0.68–0.86; n=1,366), whereas telephone-contact programmes with primary-care coordination found no benefit (risk ratio 1.15, 0.96–1.37; n=646).
cards.watchOut: Trials ran in the 1990s, before modern quadruple heart-failure therapy — the incremental value of a programme on top of today's drug background is inferred, not measured, in this record.
cards.source: McAlister FA et al. A systematic review of randomized trials of disease management programs in heart failure. The American journal of medicine. 2001. PMID: 11286953. cards.headline: McAlister 2004: specialist-team strategies — mortality risk ratio 0.75 (0.59–0.96), heart-failure hospitalisations 0.74, all-cause hospitalisations 0.81 across 29 trials
cards.summary: McAlister 2004: specialist-team strategies — mortality risk ratio 0.75 (0.59–0.96), heart-failure hospitalisations 0.74, all-cause hospitalisations 0.81 across 29 trials
cards.people: 29 randomised trials with 5,039 patients with heart failure, grouped a priori into homogeneous intervention types suitable for pooling: specialised multidisciplinary team follow-up (clinic or non-clinic), patient self-care enhancement, and telephone contact with primary-care referral advice.
cards.result: Strategies with follow-up by a specialised multidisciplinary team reduced mortality (risk ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.96), heart-failure hospitalisations (0.74, 0.63–0.87), and all-cause hospitalisations (0.81, 0.71–0.92). Self-care programmes reduced heart-failure (0.66, 0.52–0.83) and all-cause hospitalisations (0.73, 0.57–0.93) without a mortality effect (1.14, 0.67–1.94); telephone strategies reduced heart-failure hospitalisations (0.75, 0.57–0.99) only. In 15 of 18 trials evaluating cost, multidisciplinary strategies were cost-saving.
cards.watchOut: Programmes were too heterogeneous to pool as one intervention (the review pooled only within strategy types), and all effects are relative risks without the absolute admission rates of the underlying trials in this record.
cards.source: McAlister FA et al. Multidisciplinary strategies for the management of heart failure patients at high risk for admission: a systematic review of randomized trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: team-based follow-up is the active ingredient — hospitalisation falls in both reviews, mortality falls where teams follow patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: team-based follow-up is the active ingredient — hospitalisation falls in both reviews, mortality falls where teams follow patients
cards.people: Two systematic reviews of randomised heart-failure disease-management trials by the same group (McAlister 2001: 11 trials, 2,067 patients; McAlister 2004: 29 trials, 5,039 patients).
cards.result: Hospitalisations: risk ratio 0.87 overall (2001) and 0.74 for heart-failure admissions with team follow-up (2004). Mortality: 0.94 overall (2001) but 0.75 (0.59–0.96) for specialised multidisciplinary follow-up (2004). Telephone-only programmes: no hospitalisation benefit in 2001. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: the mortality benefit claim goes to the developer personally under the standing rule.

shelves.title: Rolofylline in acute heart failure with kidney dysfunction: the 2,033-patient PROTECT trial was neutral on symptoms, kidneys and 60-day outcomes — the pilot's promise did not survive phase 3
shelves.question: In acute heart failure with renal dysfunction, does the adenosine A1 antagonist rolofylline improve dyspnoea and kidney outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adenosine A1 Receptor Antagonists · Aged · Diuretics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Failure/drug therapy/mortality · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Odds Ratio · Patient Readmission · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk · Treatment Failure · Xanthines/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial is neutral on every outcome the drug was designed to move. In PROTECT (Massie BM et al., PMID: 20925544), 2,033 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure and impaired renal function were randomised 2:1 to intravenous rolofylline 30 mg daily for up to 3 days or placebo: the primary clinical composite (treatment success, failure, or no change) did not differ (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.09; P=0.35), persistent renal impairment developed in 15.0% on rolofylline versus 13.7% on placebo (P=0.44), and death or cardiovascular/renal readmission by 60 days occurred in 30.7% versus 31.9% (P=0.86). The earlier 301-patient pilot (Cotter G et al., PMID: 18926433) had shown the trends that justified phase 3 — better dyspnoea, stable creatinine, and a trend to fewer 60-day events at the 30 mg dose (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.04) — none of which the large trial confirmed. The one clear harm signal was seizures, which occurred only in rolofylline patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adenosine A1 blockade with rolofylline does not improve dyspnoea, kidney function, or 60-day outcomes in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction.

cards.headline: PROTECT (Massie 2010): primary composite odds ratio 0.92 (0.78–1.09); persistent renal impairment 15.0% vs 13.7%; 60-day death or readmission 30.7% vs 31.9%
cards.summary: PROTECT (Massie 2010): primary composite odds ratio 0.92 (0.78–1.09); persistent renal impairment 15.0% vs 13.7%; 60-day death or readmission 30.7% vs 31.9%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Massie 2010, PROTECT)
cards.people: 2,033 patients hospitalised for acute heart failure with impaired renal function (estimated creatinine clearance 20–80 mL/min in the programme), randomised within 24 hours of presentation in a 2:1 ratio to intravenous rolofylline 30 mg daily for up to 3 days or placebo, on top of usual care including loop diuretics.
cards.result: Rolofylline did not improve the primary end point of treatment success, failure, or no change in clinical condition (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.09; P=0.35). Persistent renal impairment developed in 15.0% of the rolofylline group and 13.7% of the placebo group (P=0.44). By 60 days, death or readmission for cardiovascular or renal causes had occurred in 30.7% and 31.9% respectively (P=0.86). Adverse-event rates were similar overall, except that seizures — a known potential effect of A1-receptor antagonists — occurred only in patients receiving rolofylline.
cards.watchOut: The primary end point is an ordinal composite that folds survival, heart-failure status and renal change into one judgement, so a small effect in one component could hide — but the renal and 60-day clinical endpoints, reported separately, are equally flat, which is why the null is credible rather than an artefact of the composite.
cards.source: Massie BM et al. Rolofylline, an adenosine A1-receptor antagonist, in acute heart failure. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20925544. cards.headline: PROTECT pilot (Cotter 2008): dose-related protection of creatinine and a 60-day trend at 30 mg (HR 0.55, 0.28–1.04) in 301 patients — the signal phase 3 was built on
cards.summary: PROTECT pilot (Cotter 2008): dose-related protection of creatinine and a 60-day trend at 30 mg (HR 0.55, 0.28–1.04) in 301 patients — the signal phase 3 was built on
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled dose-finding pilot trial (Cotter 2008, PROTECT pilot)
cards.people: 301 patients hospitalised for acute heart failure with estimated creatinine clearance 20–80 mL/min and elevated natriuretic peptides, enrolled within 24 hours and randomised to placebo or rolofylline 10, 20 or 30 mg as 4-hour infusions for 3 days, in addition to intravenous loop diuretics.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, rolofylline produced trends toward more patients with marked or moderately improved dyspnoea and fewer with worsening heart failure or renal function. Serum creatinine rose on placebo and stayed stable or fell on rolofylline; by day 14 the between-group difference in creatinine change grew with dose (r = -0.12, P = .030). The 30 mg dose — the one taken into phase 3 — was associated with a trend toward reduced 60-day mortality or cardiovascular/renal readmission (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.04).
cards.watchOut: A pilot explicitly not powered around any hypothesis, with post hoc analyses for the endpoints later chosen for phase 3: its trends are exactly the kind of signal that regresses away in a definitive trial, as happened here. It is carded as the honest origin of the hypothesis, not as independent confirmation.
cards.source: Cotter G et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: a textbook pilot-to-phase-3 evaporation — dyspnoea, kidney protection and 60-day outcomes all neutral at scale, seizures the only separation
cards.people: One 301-patient dose-finding pilot and one 2,033-patient double-blind phase 3 trial of intravenous rolofylline 30 mg for up to 3 days in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction (PROTECT programme).
cards.result: Phase 3: primary composite OR 0.92 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.09); persistent renal impairment 15.0% vs 13.7%; 60-day death or cardiovascular/renal readmission 30.7% vs 31.9%. shelves.title: SERCA2a gene therapy for heart failure: a 39-patient phase 2 trial met its success criteria — the 250-patient CUPID 2 trial then found nothing (recurrent events HR 0.93)
shelves.question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does SERCA2a gene therapy delivered by intracoronary infusion improve outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calcium/metabolism · Dependovirus/genetics · Double-Blind Method · Female · Genetic Therapy/methods · Genetic Vectors · Heart Failure/metabolism/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Calcium-Transporting ATPases/genetics · Treatment Outcome · Up-Regulation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by trial size and rigour. The phase 2 CUPID trial (Jessup M et al., PMID: 21709064) randomised just 39 patients with advanced heart failure to intracoronary AAV1/SERCA2a or placebo and met its prespecified success criteria at group, individual and outcome level at 6 months, with a hazard ratio of 0.12 (P=0.003) for time to clinical events at 12 months and cardiovascular hospitalisation duration of 0.4 versus 4.5 days. The phase 2b CUPID 2 trial (Greenberg B et al., PMID: 26803443) then randomised 250 patients at 67 centres to a single intracoronary infusion of AAV1/SERCA2a or placebo and found no improvement in time to recurrent heart-failure events (104 vs 128 events; hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.65; p=0.81), with deaths in 21% on gene therapy versus 16% on placebo. No safety signals were noted in CUPID 2. PROPOSED SPLIT: the small phase 2 result was positive on its own terms; the adequately sized confirmatory trial was neutral, and the therapy as tested does not improve the clinical course of heart failure.

cards.headline: CUPID phase 2 (Jessup 2011): prespecified success criteria met at 6 and 12 months in 39 patients; time to clinical events HR 0.12 (P=0.003)
cards.summary: CUPID phase 2 (Jessup 2011): prespecified success criteria met at 6 and 12 months in 39 patients; time to clinical events HR 0.12 (P=0.003)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Jessup 2011, CUPID)
cards.people: 39 patients with advanced heart failure randomised to a single intracoronary infusion of AAV1/SERCA2a (low, mid or high dose) or placebo, assessed over 12 months on symptoms, functional status, NT-proBNP, ventricular function/remodelling and clinical outcomes.
cards.result: The high-dose group versus placebo met the prespecified success criteria (group-level, individual-level and outcome analyses) at 6 months, confirmed at 12 months, with improvement or stabilisation in NYHA class, Minnesota Living With Heart Failure score, 6-minute walk, peak oxygen consumption, NT-proBNP and left ventricular end-systolic volume. Time to clinical events was significantly longer and cardiovascular events fewer at 12 months (hazard ratio 0.12; P=0.003), and mean duration of cardiovascular hospitalisations was 0.4 versus 4.5 days (P=0.05). No untoward safety findings.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine patients split across three dose groups: the headline hazard ratio of 0.12 rests on a handful of events, and the success criteria were a bespoke composite engineered so that success by chance alone had a probability of 2.7% — a design that can certify a signal far weaker than it looks. This is precisely the profile that demands a confirmatory trial before belief.
cards.source: Jessup M et al. Calcium Upregulation by Percutaneous Administration of Gene Therapy in Cardiac Disease (CUPID): a phase 2 trial of intracoronary gene therapy of sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase in patients with advanced heart failure. cards.headline: CUPID 2 (Greenberg 2016): recurrent heart-failure events 104 vs 128, HR 0.93 (0.53–1.65), p=0.81 — deaths 21% vs 16% — in 250 patients
cards.summary: CUPID 2 (Greenberg 2016): recurrent heart-failure events 104 vs 128, HR 0.93 (0.53–1.65), p=0.81 — deaths 21% vs 16% — in 250 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (Greenberg 2016, CUPID 2)
cards.people: 250 high-risk ambulatory patients with NYHA class II–IV heart failure and ejection fraction ≤0.35 (ischaemic or non-ischaemic) at 67 centres in the USA, Europe and Israel, randomised 1:1 to a single intracoronary infusion of 1×10¹³ DNase-resistant particles of AAV1/SERCA2a or placebo; 243 in the modified intention-to-treat population, median follow-up 17.5 months.
cards.result: AAV1/SERCA2a did not improve time to recurrent events (hospital admission for heart failure or ambulatory treatment for worsening heart failure): 104 versus 128 events, hazard ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.65; p=0.81). Deaths occurred in 25 (21%) patients on gene therapy and 20 (16%) on placebo, 22 and 18 of them cardiovascular. No safety signals were noted.
cards.watchOut: CUPID 2 tested one dose in one delivery; a neutral result does not exclude benefit from higher transduction efficiency or a different vector — but as a test of the therapy actually developed, in the largest gene-transfer study in heart failure at the time, it is definitive. The mortality counts (21% vs 16%) lean the wrong way without reaching significance.

cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 said go, phase 2b said no — the recurrent-event endpoint at real scale is the result that stands
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of single-infusion intracoronary AAV1/SERCA2a in advanced heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: CUPID (n=39) and CUPID 2 (n=250).
cards.result: CUPID: prespecified composite success at 6–12 months; clinical-event hazard ratio 0.12. CUPID 2: recurrent-event hazard ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.65); deaths 21% vs 16%; no safety signals. PROPOSED SPLIT, with the weight on CUPID 2.

shelves.title: Cell therapy for advanced heart failure: both large sham-controlled trials missed their primary endpoints — DREAM-HF's heart-attack and stroke signal is exploratory only
shelves.question: In advanced heart failure, do mesenchymal or cardiopoietic cell therapies improve death and hospitalisation compared with control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Heart Failure · C-Reactive Protein · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke · Inflammation · Cell- and Tissue-Based Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoints these trials were built to answer. In DREAM-HF (Perin EC et al., PMID: 36858705), 565 patients with high-risk heart failure with reduced ejection fraction were randomised to a single transendocardial administration of mesenchymal precursor cells or sham control: the primary endpoint of recurrent decompensated heart-failure or resuscitated ventricular-arrhythmia events was similar between groups (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.69; P = 0.41), as were terminal cardiac events and the hierarchical secondary endpoints. In CHART-1 (Bartunek J et al., PMID: 28025189), 315 patients with ischaemic heart failure were randomised to cardiopoietic cells or sham: the 39-week hierarchical composite primary endpoint was neutral (Mann-Whitney estimator 0.54, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.61; P = 0.27). The counterweight sits inside DREAM-HF: mesenchymal precursor cells reduced myocardial infarction or stroke by a relative 58% (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.76) in the analysis population — but the trial's own conclusion is that the primary and secondary endpoints were negative and these are prespecified and post hoc exploratory signals, strongest in patients with inflammation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): neither cell therapy improved its primary heart-failure endpoint; the anti-inflammatory event signal is a hypothesis for another trial, not a result.

cards.headline: DREAM-HF (Perin 2023): primary endpoint HR 1.17 (0.81–1.69), P = 0.41 in 565 patients — MI or stroke HR 0.42 in exploratory analyses
cards.summary: DREAM-HF (Perin 2023): primary endpoint HR 1.17 (0.81–1.69), P = 0.41 in 565 patients — MI or stroke HR 0.42 in exploratory analyses
cards.people: 565 intention-to-treat patients with high-risk heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on guideline-directed therapy, randomised to a single transendocardial administration of allogeneic mesenchymal precursor cells or a sham-control procedure; echocardiography at baseline and 12 months, with baseline high-sensitivity C-reactive protein measured.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (time to recurrent events from decompensated heart failure or successfully resuscitated symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias) was similar between groups (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.69; P = 0.41), as were terminal cardiac events and hierarchical secondary endpoints. Ejection fraction rose more with cells by 12 months, especially in patients with inflammation. In the analysis population (n = 537), cells reduced myocardial infarction or stroke (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.76 — a 58% relative reduction) and 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events by a relative 28% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.03), with larger effects in patients with baseline hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L (HR 0.25 and 0.62 respectively). The authors state the primary and secondary endpoints were negative and these are prespecified and post hoc exploratory signals.
cards.watchOut: A neutral primary endpoint with a nominally strong exploratory signal is the classic configuration for a false dawn: the MI/stroke analysis was not the trial's powered question, the inflammation subgroup is defined by a biomarker cut-off, and no absolute event rates for the exploratory outcomes appear in the record. The signal justifies a new trial; it does not rehabilitate this one.
cards.source: Perin EC et al. Randomized Trial of Targeted Transendocardial Mesenchymal Precursor Cell Therapy in Patients With Heart Failure. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023. PMID: 36858705. MeSH: Humans · Heart Failure · C-Reactive Protein · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Function, Left · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke · Inflammation · Cell- and Tissue-Based Therapy
