cards.headline: CHART-1 (Bartunek 2017): hierarchical composite at 39 weeks neutral (estimator 0.54, 0.47–0.61; P = 0.27); a large-ventricle subgroup leaned positive
cards.summary: CHART-1 (Bartunek 2017): hierarchical composite at 39 weeks neutral (estimator 0.54, 0.47–0.61; P = 0.27); a large-ventricle subgroup leaned positive
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic ischaemic heart failure on guideline-directed therapy at 39 hospitals: 484 screened, 348 underwent bone-marrow harvest and mesenchymal stem-cell expansion, and 315 achieving >24 million cells were randomised to cardiopoietic cells delivered endomyocardially with a retention-enhanced catheter (n = 157) or sham (n = 158); 271 were treated as randomised.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint — a Finkelstein-Schoenfeld hierarchical composite of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure score, 6-minute walk distance, left ventricular end-systolic volume and ejection fraction at 39 weeks — was neutral (Mann-Whitney estimator 0.54, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.61, where >0.5 favours cells; P = 0.27). Exploratory analysis suggested benefit in patients with baseline left ventricular end-diastolic volume 200–370 mL (estimator 0.61, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.70; P = 0.015). Serious adverse events did not differ; aborted or sudden cardiac death occurred in 1 (0.9%) cell patient and 9 (5.4%) sham patients.
cards.watchOut: Only patients whose marrow yielded enough expanded cells could be randomised, and only 271 of 315 randomised patients were treated as assigned — the tested population is pre-selected for manufacturability. The end-diastolic-volume subgroup is exploratory and defined post hoc around the observed data.
cards.source: Bartunek J et al. Cardiopoietic cell therapy for advanced ischaemic heart failure: results at 39 weeks of the prospective, randomized, double blind, sham-controlled CHART-1 clinical trial. European heart journal. 2017. PMID: 28025189. cards.headline: Synthesis: two different cell products, two sham-controlled trials, two neutral primaries — the field's positive signals all live in exploratory analyses
cards.summary: Synthesis: two different cell products, two sham-controlled trials, two neutral primaries — the field's positive signals all live in exploratory analyses
cards.people: DREAM-HF (565 patients, allogeneic mesenchymal precursor cells, transendocardial) and CHART-1 (315 randomised, autologous cardiopoietic cells, endomyocardial) in advanced heart failure on guideline therapy.
cards.result: Primary endpoints: DREAM-HF recurrent-event HR 1.17 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.69); CHART-1 composite estimator 0.54 (0.47 to 0.61), P = 0.27. Exploratory signals: DREAM-HF myocardial infarction or stroke HR 0.42; CHART-1 large-ventricle subgroup estimator 0.61. Safety: no excess of serious adverse events in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the primary questions.
cards.watchOut: The products, cell sources and delivery routes differ, so this is a class-level read across two programmes, not a pooled estimate. A future trial enriched for inflammation (the DREAM-HF signal) would be a new question and would need its own shelf. Tier C is not set: two large concordant sham-controlled trials carry the null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Perin EC et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 36858705), Bartunek J et al. European heart journal. 2017 (PMID: 28025189).

shelves.title: Interatrial shunt for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: it lowered exercise wedge pressure in a 44-patient phase 2 trial — then the 626-patient sham-controlled trial found no fewer heart-failure events and no better health status
shelves.question: In heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction and raised left atrial pressure, does an interatrial shunt device improve symptoms and outcomes compared with sham?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiac Catheterization/instrumentation · Flavins · Heart Atria/surgery · Heart Failure/physiopathology · Humans · Luciferases · Male · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the mechanism works and the clinical benefit does not follow. In the phase 2 REDUCE LAP-HF I trial (Feldman T et al., PMID: 29142012), 44 patients with ejection fraction ≥40% and exercise wedge pressure ≥25 mm Hg were randomised to the Corvia interatrial shunt device or sham: at 1 month the device produced a greater reduction in exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (P=0.028 across exercise stages; peak wedge fell 3.5 ± 6.4 versus 0.5 ± 5.0 mm Hg, P=0.14). In the phase 3 REDUCE LAP-HF II trial (Shah SJ et al., PMID: 35120593), 626 patients were randomised to the device or sham: the hierarchical primary endpoint was exactly neutral (win ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.2; p=0.85), no component differed, and the composite safety endpoint occurred in 38% on the device versus 31% on sham (p=0.11). Prespecified subgroups with high exercise pulmonary artery pressure, large right atria, and men fared worse on heart-failure events with the device. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real haemodynamic effect in phase 2; no reduction in heart-failure events or improvement in health status in the definitive sham-controlled trial.

cards.headline: REDUCE LAP-HF I (Feldman 2018): exercise wedge pressure fell more with the shunt at 1 month (P=0.028 across stages) in 44 randomised patients
cards.summary: REDUCE LAP-HF I (Feldman 2018): exercise wedge pressure fell more with the shunt at 1 month (P=0.028 across stages) in 44 randomised patients
cards.type: Randomised sham-controlled phase 2 trial (Feldman 2018, REDUCE LAP-HF I)
cards.people: 44 patients (mean age 70 ± 9 years, 50% women) with NYHA class III or ambulatory class IV heart failure, ejection fraction ≥40%, exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≥25 mm Hg and a wedge-to-right-atrial gradient ≥5 mm Hg, randomised 1:1 to the Corvia interatrial shunt device or a sham procedure (venous access and intracardiac echo, no device); patients and follow-up assessors blinded.
cards.result: At 1 month, the shunt produced a greater reduction in exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure than sham across all exercise stages (P=0.028); peak wedge pressure fell by 3.5 ± 6.4 mm Hg with the device versus 0.5 ± 5.0 mm Hg with sham (P=0.14). There were no peri-procedural or 1-month major adverse cardiac, cerebrovascular or renal events in the device group and one event (worsening renal function) in the control group.
cards.watchOut: Forty-four patients and a 1-month haemodynamic endpoint: this trial could only ever show the device does what it is engineered to do. The peak-pressure comparison itself was not significant (P=0.14); the positive P value comes from the repeated-measures model across exercise stages.
cards.source: Feldman T et al. Transcatheter Interatrial Shunt Device for the Treatment of Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction (REDUCE LAP-HF I [Reduce Elevated Left Atrial Pressure in Patients With Heart Failure]): A Phase 2, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Trial. Circulation. 2018. PMID: 29142012. Registry ID: NCT02600234. cards.headline: REDUCE LAP-HF II (Shah 2022): primary composite win ratio 1.0 (0.8–1.2), p=0.85; safety events 38% vs 31% — in 626 patients
cards.summary: REDUCE LAP-HF II (Shah 2022): primary composite win ratio 1.0 (0.8–1.2), p=0.85; safety events 38% vs 31% — in 626 patients
cards.type: Randomised blinded sham-controlled trial (Shah 2022, REDUCE LAP-HF II)
cards.people: 626 patients aged ≥40 years with symptomatic heart failure, ejection fraction ≥40% and exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≥25 mm Hg exceeding right atrial pressure by ≥5 mm Hg, at 89 centres, randomised 1:1 to the Corvia atrial shunt device (n = 314) or sham procedure (n = 312); patients and outcome assessors masked.
cards.result: There was no difference in the hierarchical primary endpoint — cardiovascular death or non-fatal ischaemic stroke at 12 months, total heart-failure events to 24 months, and change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score at 12 months (win ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.2; p=0.85) — nor in any individual component. The composite safety endpoint occurred in 116 (38%) device patients versus 97 (31%) sham patients (p=0.11). Prespecified subgroups showed worse heart-failure-event outcomes with the device at high exercise pulmonary artery systolic pressure (>70 mm Hg at 20 W), larger right atrial volume index (≥29.7 mL/m²), and in men.
cards.watchOut: The neutral average conceals prespecified harm-leaning subgroups — patients with latent pulmonary vascular disease may be hurt by a left-to-right shunt — so the result is not 'the device does nothing' but 'no benefit overall, possible harm where pulmonary pressures run high'. Enrolment required an invasive exercise-haemodynamic phenotype that routine practice rarely measures.
cards.source: Shah SJ et al. Atrial shunt device for heart failure with preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction (REDUCE LAP-HF II): a randomised, multicentre, blinded, sham-controlled trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35120593. Registry ID: NCT03088033. cards.headline: Synthesis: a clean mechanistic win that did not convert — wedge pressure down, events and symptoms unchanged at scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: a clean mechanistic win that did not convert — wedge pressure down, events and symptoms unchanged at scale
cards.people: Two randomised sham-controlled trials of the Corvia interatrial shunt device in heart failure with ejection fraction ≥40% and raised exercise wedge pressure: phase 2 (n = 44, 1-month haemodynamics) and phase 3 (n = 626, events and health status to 24 months).
cards.result: Phase 2: greater exercise wedge-pressure reduction with the device (P=0.028 across stages). Phase 3: primary composite win ratio 1.0 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.2); safety composite 38% vs 31%. PROPOSED SPLIT — surrogate positive, clinical outcomes neutral, with harm-leaning subgroups on the face of the phase 3 card.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from one device programme with one sponsor; no independent replication exists. Tier C is not set: the clinical null rests on a large blinded sham-controlled trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shah SJ et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35120593), Feldman T et al. Circulation. 2018 (PMID: 29142012).

shelves.title: Vagus nerve stimulation for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: no reduction in death or heart-failure events (INOVATE-HF HR 1.14) and no reverse remodelling (NECTAR-HF) — quality of life improved in both trials, only one of them sham-controlled
shelves.question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does vagus nerve stimulation improve symptoms, remodelling, or outcomes compared with control?
shelves.mesh: Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Conduction System/physiopathology · Heart Failure/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Stroke Volume · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vagus Nerve/physiopathology · Vagus Nerve Stimulation/methods · Ventricular Function, Left/physiology · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: SPLIT — patients felt better; hearts and event rates did not change. In INOVATE-HF (Gold MR et al., PMID: 27058909), 707 patients with NYHA class III heart failure and ejection fraction ≤40% were randomised 3:2 to vagus nerve stimulation or continued medical therapy: the primary composite of death or first worsening-heart-failure event occurred in 30.3% versus 25.8% (hazard ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.53; p = 0.37), while quality of life, NYHA class and 6-minute walk distance favoured stimulation (p < 0.05) and left ventricular end-systolic volume index did not differ (p = 0.49). In the sham-controlled NECTAR-HF trial (Zannad F et al., PMID: 25176942), 96 implanted patients were randomised 2:1 to stimulation on or off: the primary remodelling endpoint, change in left ventricular end-systolic diameter at 6 months, was -0.04 ± 0.25 cm on therapy versus -0.08 ± 0.32 cm on control (P = 0.60), every other echo, exercise and biomarker endpoint was neutral, and quality-of-life measures again improved significantly. PROPOSED SPLIT: no effect on death, heart-failure events or remodelling in either trial; a consistent improvement in symptoms and quality of life, proven against sham only in the small trial.

cards.headline: INOVATE-HF (Gold 2016): death or worsening heart failure 30.3% vs 25.8% (HR 1.14, 0.86–1.53) — quality of life, NYHA class and walk distance favoured stimulation
cards.summary: INOVATE-HF (Gold 2016): death or worsening heart failure 30.3% vs 25.8% (HR 1.14, 0.86–1.53) — quality of life, NYHA class and walk distance favoured stimulation
cards.people: 707 patients with chronic NYHA class III heart failure and ejection fraction ≤40% at 85 centres, randomised 3:2 to implantation of a vagus nerve stimulation device (active, n = 436) or continued medical therapy without implantation (control, n = 271), followed for a mean of 16 months.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (death from any cause or first worsening-heart-failure event) occurred in 132 of 436 stimulation patients versus 70 of 271 controls (30.3% vs 25.8%; hazard ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.53; p = 0.37). Estimated annual mortality was 9.3% versus 7.1% (p = 0.19). Quality of life, NYHA functional class and 6-minute walking distance were favourably affected by stimulation (p < 0.05), but left ventricular end-systolic volume index was not different (p = 0.49).
cards.watchOut: The control group had no device and no sham, so the symptom and quality-of-life gains — the trial's only positive findings — were measured unblinded in patients who knew they had an active implant. The event point estimate leans against stimulation, though the confidence interval is wide.
cards.source: Gold MR et al. Vagus Nerve Stimulation for the Treatment of Heart Failure: The INOVATE-HF Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2016. PMID: 27058909. cards.headline: NECTAR-HF (Zannad 2015): end-systolic diameter change -0.04 vs -0.08 cm (P = 0.60) — remodelling neutral against sham, quality of life improved
cards.summary: NECTAR-HF (Zannad 2015): end-systolic diameter change -0.04 vs -0.08 cm (P = 0.60) — remodelling neutral against sham, quality of life improved
cards.people: 96 patients with symptomatic heart failure and severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction despite guideline-recommended therapy, all implanted with a vagal stimulation system and randomised 2:1 to stimulation ON (therapy) or OFF (control) for 6 months; 87 had paired primary-endpoint data.
cards.result: Change in left ventricular end-systolic diameter at 6 months was -0.04 ± 0.25 cm on therapy versus -0.08 ± 0.32 cm on control (P = 0.60). End-diastolic dimension and volume, end-systolic volume, ejection fraction, peak VO₂ and NT-proBNP all failed to show superiority. Quality of life improved significantly on therapy: Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (P = 0.049), NYHA class (P = 0.032) and SF-36 Physical Component (P = 0.016).
cards.watchOut: Ninety-six patients and 6 months is a remodelling study, not an outcomes trial — it cannot exclude a small structural effect, and its quality-of-life P values (0.049, 0.032) sit at the edge of significance across several measures. Its value is that the symptom benefit survived a sham control, which INOVATE-HF's did not have to.

shelves.title: Pulmonary-artery-catheter-guided care in severe heart failure: ESCAPE found the same days alive out of hospital (133 vs 135) and more in-hospital adverse events — and a 13-trial meta-analysis found no mortality benefit in any setting
shelves.question: In hospitalised acute heart failure, does management guided by a pulmonary artery catheter improve death or hospitalisation compared with clinical assessment alone?
shelves.mesh: Catheterization, Swan-Ganz/adverse effects · Female · Heart Failure/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Hospital Mortality · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Wedge Pressure · Risk · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large trial and the pooled randomised literature agree. In ESCAPE (Binanay C et al., PMID: 16204662), 433 patients hospitalised with severe symptomatic recurrent heart failure were randomised to therapy guided by clinical assessment plus a pulmonary artery catheter or by clinical assessment alone: days alive out of hospital in 6 months were 133 versus 135 (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21; P = .99), mortality was 10% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.03; P = .35), and in-hospital adverse events were more common with the catheter (21.9% vs 11.5%; P = .04). The accompanying meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials and 5,051 critically ill patients (Shah MR et al., PMID: 16204666) found a combined mortality odds ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.20; P = .59) and no difference in hospital days, with catheter-guided care associated with more inotrope (OR 1.58) and vasodilator (OR 2.35) use. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): catheter numbers change what doctors prescribe, not whether patients live or how long they stay in hospital.

cards.headline: ESCAPE (Binanay 2005): days alive out of hospital 133 vs 135 (HR 1.00); mortality 10% vs 9%; in-hospital adverse events 21.9% vs 11.5%
cards.summary: ESCAPE (Binanay 2005): days alive out of hospital 133 vs 135 (HR 1.00); mortality 10% vs 9%; in-hospital adverse events 21.9% vs 11.5%
cards.people: 433 patients at 26 sites hospitalised with severe symptomatic and recurrent heart failure (mean ejection fraction 19%, systolic blood pressure 106 mm Hg, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL), randomised to therapy guided by clinical assessment plus pulmonary artery catheter (targets: wedge pressure 15 mm Hg, right atrial pressure 8 mm Hg) or clinical assessment alone; inotrope use explicitly discouraged in both groups; primary endpoint days alive out of hospital over 6 months.
cards.result: The pulmonary artery catheter did not affect the primary endpoint (133 vs 135 days alive out of hospital; hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21; P = .99), mortality (43 [10%] vs 38 [9%] patients; odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.03; P = .35), or days hospitalised (8.7 vs 8.3; HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.27; P = .67). In-hospital adverse events were more common in the catheter group (47 [21.9%] vs 25 [11.5%]; P = .04), with no catheter-related deaths and no difference in in-hospital plus 30-day mortality (4.7% vs 5.0%). Symptoms, jugular venous pressure and oedema improved substantially in both groups.
cards.watchOut: ESCAPE tested catheter guidance in expert heart-failure centres with inotropes discouraged — a fair test of the catheter as an information tool, but not of catheter use in shock or diagnostic uncertainty, which the trial did not enrol. The adverse-event excess is the anticipated procedural burden, not a mortality signal.
cards.source: Binanay C et al. Evaluation study of congestive heart failure and pulmonary artery catheterization effectiveness: the ESCAPE trial. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 16204662. cards.headline: Shah 2005 meta-analysis: 13 randomised trials, 5,051 patients — mortality OR 1.04 (0.90–1.20); more inotropes (OR 1.58) and vasodilators (OR 2.35) with the catheter
cards.summary: Shah 2005 meta-analysis: 13 randomised trials, 5,051 patients — mortality OR 1.04 (0.90–1.20); more inotropes (OR 1.58) and vasodilators (OR 2.35) with the catheter
cards.people: 13 randomised trials (1985–2005, including ESCAPE) totalling 5,051 critically ill patients — surgical, intensive-care, advanced heart failure, and ARDS/sepsis populations — randomised to pulmonary artery catheter or no catheter, with death and hospital/ICU days as outcomes.
cards.result: The combined odds ratio for mortality was 1.04 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.20; P = .59). Mean hospital days differed by 0.11 days (95% CI -0.51 to 0.74; P = .73). Catheter use was associated with higher use of inotropes (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.19 to 2.12; P = .002) and intravenous vasodilators (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.75 to 3.15; P<.001). The authors conclude that across almost 20 years of trials no strategy pairing catheter information with effective treatment has improved survival.
cards.watchOut: Pooling spans very different populations and haemodynamic protocols, so the pooled null is a statement about the catheter as generally used, not about every niche. It includes ESCAPE itself, so it is not fully independent of the first card — it is carded because it extends the answer beyond heart failure to all randomised settings.

shelves.title: Disopyramide for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy still obstructed on a beta-blocker: outflow gradients roughly halved and symptoms improved in two large cohorts — but no randomised trial has ever tested it
shelves.question: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, does disopyramide reduce the outflow gradient and symptoms in patients still obstructed on a beta-blocker?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Disopyramide/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Echocardiography · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Contraction/drug effects · Safety · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — consistent before-and-after improvement in the only evidence there is: uncontrolled cohorts. In the four-centre study (Sherrid MV et al., PMID: 15837258), 118 patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy treated with disopyramide (mean dose 432 ± 181 mg/day, 97% also on beta-blockers) for a mean of 3.1 years saw resting outflow gradient fall from 75 ± 33 to 40 ± 32 mm Hg (p < 0.0001) and NYHA class from 2.3 ± 0.7 to 1.7 ± 0.6 (p < 0.0001); 66% were managed without myectomy, alcohol ablation or pacing, and annual cardiac mortality was 1.4% versus 2.6% per year in 373 untreated obstructed patients (p = 0.07). In the later single-centre series (Sherrid MV et al., PMID: 23704138), disopyramide was added in 221 of 299 patients still symptomatic after beta-blockade or verapamil, and pharmacological control of symptoms was achieved in 141 (64%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): disopyramide probably lowers gradient and symptoms in patients who remain obstructed on first-line therapy, on cohort evidence only — there is no randomised, placebo-controlled, or blinded evidence at all.

cards.headline: Sherrid 2005 (four centres): gradient 75 ± 33 → 40 ± 32 mm Hg and NYHA 2.3 → 1.7 on disopyramide; 66% avoided invasive intervention over ~3 years
cards.summary: Sherrid 2005 (four centres): gradient 75 ± 33 → 40 ± 32 mm Hg and NYHA 2.3 → 1.7 on disopyramide; 66% avoided invasive intervention over ~3 years
cards.people: 118 patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy treated with disopyramide at 4 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy centres, followed for 3.1 ± 2.6 years on a mean dose of 432 ± 181 mg/day, 97% also receiving beta-blockers; mortality compared with 373 obstructed patients not treated with disopyramide.
cards.result: Resting outflow gradient fell from 75 ± 33 to 40 ± 32 mm Hg (p < 0.0001) and mean NYHA class from 2.3 ± 0.7 to 1.7 ± 0.6 (p < 0.0001). Seventy-eight patients (66%) remained on disopyramide without needing surgical myectomy, alcohol ablation or pacing; 40 (34%) required major invasive intervention for inadequate control or vagolytic side effects. All-cause cardiac mortality was 1.4%/year on disopyramide versus 2.6%/year in untreated obstructed patients (p = 0.07), and sudden death 1.0%/year versus 1.8%/year (p = 0.08).
cards.watchOut: No control group for the gradient and symptom outcomes: patients start disopyramide when symptoms peak, so regression to the mean and the accompanying beta-blockade are folded into the improvement. The mortality comparison is between non-randomised groups assembled differently, and its ratios sit in the range this library does not let observational data carry — it is reported here as the record states it, not as evidence of a survival effect.

cards.headline: Sherrid 2013: of 299 patients failing beta-blocker or verapamil, 221 had disopyramide added and 141 (64%) achieved pharmacological control of symptoms
cards.summary: Sherrid 2013: of 299 patients failing beta-blocker or verapamil, 221 had disopyramide added and 141 (64%) achieved pharmacological control of symptoms
cards.people: 299 of 737 prospectively registered hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients who required further therapy for obstruction after beta-blockade or verapamil (rest gradient 61 ± 45, provoked gradient 115 ± 49 mm Hg), followed for 4.8 years under a stepped programme of added disopyramide and, when needed, surgical relief of obstruction.
cards.result: Disopyramide was added in 221 (74%) patients and pharmacological control of symptoms was achieved in 141 (64%). Overall, 138 (46%) patients ultimately had surgical relief of obstruction (91% myectomy) and 6 (2%) alcohol septal ablation. Across the whole stepped programme, resting gradients in the 299 patients fell from 61 ± 44 to 10 ± 25 mm Hg and NYHA class from 2.7 ± 0.7 to 1.8 ± 0.5 (both P<0.0001); 10-year Kaplan-Meier survival was 88%, with one sudden death (0.06%/year).
cards.watchOut: The gradient and NYHA figures for the 299 are for the whole stepped strategy including myectomy in nearly half — they must not be read as disopyramide's own effect. The disopyramide-specific number is the 64% pharmacological-control rate, itself uncontrolled and judged by the treating team.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a physiologically coherent, consistently observed gradient effect — held at MAYBE because nobody has ever randomised it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a physiologically coherent, consistently observed gradient effect — held at MAYBE because nobody has ever randomised it
cards.people: Two cohorts from the same investigative group (118 patients across 4 centres; 221 disopyramide-treated patients within a 299-patient stepped-care registry) with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy symptomatic despite beta-blockade or verapamil.
cards.result: Gradient: 75 ± 33 → 40 ± 32 mm Hg (cohort 1). Pharmacological control without invasive intervention: 66% (cohort 1) and 64% of those given the drug (cohort 2). cards.watchOut: Both cohorts come from one group of specialist centres, so there is no independent replication, and publication of a negative cohort would be unlikely. Tier C is set: the shelf rests entirely on observational, uncontrolled evidence for a benefit claim.

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the drug does exactly what it is meant to do to the parasite, and it does not change the disease. In the BENEFIT trial (Morillo CA et al., PMID: 26323937), 2,854 patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy were randomised to benznidazole or placebo for up to 80 days and followed for a mean of 5.4 years: the primary composite (death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, device insertion, transplantation, new heart failure, stroke or thromboembolism) occurred in 27.5% on benznidazole versus 29.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.31). Parasite detection told the opposite story: conversion to negative PCR was 66.2% versus 33.5% at the end of treatment, 55.4% versus 35.3% at 2 years and 46.7% versus 33.1% at 5 years or more (P<0.001 for all comparisons), though the size of the PCR effect varied sharply by region and did not correspond to clinical effects. PROPOSED SPLIT: trypanocidal therapy clears parasites from blood without significantly reducing cardiac clinical deterioration in established cardiomyopathy — by the time the heart is damaged, the damage, not the parasite load in blood, drives events.

cards.headline: BENEFIT (Morillo 2015): primary cardiac composite 27.5% vs 29.1% (HR 0.93, 0.81–1.07) over 5.4 years — PCR conversion 66.2% vs 33.5% at end of treatment
cards.summary: BENEFIT (Morillo 2015): primary cardiac composite 27.5% vs 29.1% (HR 0.93, 0.81–1.07) over 5.4 years — PCR conversion 66.2% vs 33.5% at end of treatment
cards.people: 2,854 patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy at centres in Latin America, randomised to benznidazole or placebo for up to 80 days and followed for a mean of 5.4 years; a baseline PCR assay for Trypanosoma cruzi was performed in 1,896 patients, of whom 60.5% were PCR-positive.
cards.result: The primary outcome (first of death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, pacemaker or defibrillator insertion, cardiac transplantation, new heart failure, stroke, or other thromboembolic event) occurred in 394 patients (27.5%) on benznidazole and 414 (29.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.31). PCR conversion to negative was 66.2% versus 33.5% at the end of treatment, 55.4% versus 35.3% at 2 years, and 46.7% versus 33.1% at 5 years or more (P<0.001 for all). The PCR effect varied by region (odds ratio at 2 years 3.03 in Brazil, 1.33 in Colombia and El Salvador, 2.63 in Argentina and Bolivia; P<0.001 for interaction) and did not correspond to effects on clinical outcome (P=0.16 for interaction).
cards.watchOut: This is a trial of established cardiomyopathy — it says nothing about treating indeterminate or early Chagas disease, where parasite clearance might still prevent the cardiomyopathy from forming. PCR conversion is a blood test, not tissue parasite eradication, and the regional heterogeneity in conversion is unexplained.
cards.source: Morillo CA et al. Randomized Trial of Benznidazole for Chronic Chagas' Cardiomyopathy. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26323937. Registry ID: NCT00123916. cards.people: The BENEFIT trial alone: 2,854 patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy, benznidazole versus placebo for up to 80 days, mean follow-up 5.4 years.

shelves.title: Amiodarone, sotalol or propafenone to keep atrial fibrillation away: amiodarone holds sinus rhythm longest in two randomised trials (median 487 vs 74 days against sotalol in SAFE-T) — and is stopped for side effects most often
shelves.question: In atrial fibrillation needing rhythm control, how do amiodarone, sotalol, and propafenone compare at keeping patients in sinus rhythm?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amiodarone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/complications/drug therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Myocardial Ischemia/complications · Quality of Life · Secondary Prevention · Sotalol/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — amiodarone is the most effective of the three at maintaining sinus rhythm, in two concordant randomised trials, and the least tolerable. In SAFE-T (Singh BN et al., PMID: 15872201), 665 anticoagulated patients with persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised double-blind to amiodarone, sotalol or placebo: median time to recurrence was 487 days on amiodarone versus 74 days on sotalol and 6 days on placebo (intention-to-treat), with spontaneous conversion in 27.1%, 24.2% and 0.8% respectively — though in patients with ischaemic heart disease amiodarone and sotalol did not differ significantly (569 vs 428 days; P=0.53). In the three-arm Kochiadakis trial (Kochiadakis GE et al., PMID: 11139949), 214 patients with recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation had recurrence in 25 of 75 on amiodarone, 51 of 75 on sotalol and 24 of 64 on propafenone, while adverse effects forcing discontinuation struck 14 on amiodarone, 5 on sotalol and 1 on propafenone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for keeping sinus rhythm, amiodarone first, propafenone a close and better-tolerated second, sotalol last — an efficacy ranking bought with amiodarone's side-effect burden.

cards.headline: SAFE-T (Singh 2005): median time to recurrence 487 days on amiodarone vs 74 on sotalol vs 6 on placebo — but no amiodarone advantage in ischaemic heart disease (569 vs 428 days, P=0.53)
cards.summary: SAFE-T (Singh 2005): median time to recurrence 487 days on amiodarone vs 74 on sotalol vs 6 on placebo — but no amiodarone advantage in ischaemic heart disease (569 vs 428 days, P=0.53)
cards.people: 665 anticoagulated patients with persistent atrial fibrillation randomised to amiodarone (267), sotalol (261) or placebo (137), monitored by weekly transtelephonic recordings for 1 to 4.5 years; primary endpoint time to recurrence of atrial fibrillation from day 28.
cards.result: Spontaneous conversion occurred in 27.1% on amiodarone, 24.2% on sotalol and 0.8% on placebo; direct-current cardioversion failed in 27.7%, 26.5% and 32.1%. Median times to recurrence (intention-to-treat) were 487 days (amiodarone), 74 days (sotalol) and 6 days (placebo); amiodarone was superior to sotalol and to placebo (both P<0.001), and sotalol superior to placebo (P<0.001). In ischaemic heart disease, median time to recurrence was 569 days on amiodarone versus 428 days on sotalol (P=0.53). Major adverse events did not differ significantly among the three groups, and sustained sinus rhythm was associated with better quality of life and exercise capacity.
cards.watchOut: SAFE-T has no propafenone arm — the three-way comparison this question asks for is completed by the second card, not by this trial. The population was predominantly male veterans with persistent AF, and the ischaemic subgroup null is a reminder that the headline ranking is an average, not a law.
cards.source: Singh BN et al. Amiodarone versus sotalol for atrial fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 15872201. cards.headline: Kochiadakis 2000: recurrence in 25/75 on amiodarone, 51/75 on sotalol, 24/64 on propafenone — discontinuation for side effects in 14, 5 and 1 patients
cards.summary: Kochiadakis 2000: recurrence in 25/75 on amiodarone, 51/75 on sotalol, 24/64 on propafenone — discontinuation for side effects in 14, 5 and 1 patients
cards.people: 214 consecutive patients (mean age 64 ± 8 years, 106 men) with recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation, randomised after restoration of sinus rhythm to amiodarone 200 mg/day (n = 75), propafenone 450 mg/day (n = 64) or sotalol 320 ± 20 mg/day (n = 75), with follow-up at 1, 2, 4 and 6 months and 3-monthly thereafter.
cards.result: Recurrent atrial fibrillation occurred in 25 of 75 patients on amiodarone, 51 of 75 on sotalol and 24 of 64 on propafenone. Adverse effects in sinus rhythm necessitating discontinuation occurred in 14 patients on amiodarone, 5 on sotalol and 1 on propafenone. The amiodarone–propafenone difference was not significant when recurrence and discontinuation were combined, but amiodarone was more effective than propafenone for recurrence alone (P < 0.05). The authors conclude amiodarone and propafenone were both superior to sotalol for maintaining sinus rhythm, with amiodarone tending to superiority but limited by side effects.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre open trial of 214 patients from 2000, without placebo or blinding, using doses (notably sotalol 320 mg/day) that do not map exactly onto current practice. It is carded because it is the direct three-way randomised comparison; its weight is corroborative, and SAFE-T carries the shelf.
cards.source: Kochiadakis GE et al. Amiodarone, sotalol, or propafenone in atrial fibrillation: which is preferred to maintain normal sinus rhythm? Pacing and clinical electrophysiology : PACE. 2000. PMID: 11139949. cards.headline: Synthesis: the ranking is stable across both trials — amiodarone most effective, sotalol least, propafenone between on efficacy and best tolerated of the effective two
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ranking is stable across both trials — amiodarone most effective, sotalol least, propafenone between on efficacy and best tolerated of the effective two
cards.people: SAFE-T (665 patients, double-blind, persistent AF, amiodarone vs sotalol vs placebo) and Kochiadakis 2000 (214 patients, open, recurrent symptomatic AF, all three drugs).
cards.result: Recurrence: SAFE-T median 487 vs 74 days (amiodarone vs sotalol); Kochiadakis 33% (25/75) amiodarone, 68% (51/75) sotalol, 38% (24/64) propafenone. Tolerability: discontinuation for adverse effects highest on amiodarone (14/75) in Kochiadakis; major adverse events not significantly different in SAFE-T. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for amiodarone as the most effective maintenance drug of the three.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measures death, stroke or hospitalisation — this is a rhythm-maintenance ranking only, from the pre-ablation era, and neither trial's population resembles a modern post-ablation clinic. The Canadian CTAF trial, the other large three-way comparison, is not carded here because it is already carded on live shelf #137; the coordinator may wish to note the cross-reference. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singh BN et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2005 (PMID: 15872201), Kochiadakis GE et al. Pacing and clinical electrophysiology : PACE. 2000 (PMID: 11139949).

shelves.title: Restarting anticoagulation after a brain haemorrhage in atrial fibrillation: two small trials and their pooled analysis — ischaemic events clearly fewer (HR 0.27), haemorrhagic events possibly more, the net still unresolved
shelves.question: In atrial fibrillation after a spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, does restarting oral anticoagulation reduce ischaemic stroke enough to outweigh recurrent bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation/complications/drug therapy · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the trade-off is real in both directions and neither small trial could settle it. In SoSTART (SoSTART Collaboration, PMID: 34487722), 203 survivors of spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage with atrial fibrillation were randomised to start or avoid oral anticoagulation: recurrent intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 8% versus 4% (adjusted HR 2.42, 95% CI 0.72 to 8.09), non-inferiority of starting was not shown (p=0.152), and 22% versus 11% died. In APACHE-AF (Schreuder FHBM et al., PMID: 34687635), 101 patients were randomised to apixaban or no anticoagulation after anticoagulant-associated intracerebral haemorrhage: non-fatal stroke or vascular death occurred in 26% versus 24% (adjusted HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.31; p=0.90). Pooling all four eligible trials (412 participants) in the COCROACH individual-participant meta-analysis (Al-Shahi Salman R et al., PMID: 37839434), starting anticoagulation gave a pooled HR of 0.68 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.10) for any stroke or cardiovascular death, 0.27 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.56) for ischaemic major cardiovascular events, and 1.80 (95% CI 0.77 to 4.21) for haemorrhagic major events. PROPOSED SPLIT: restarting prevents ischaemic events convincingly and may cause haemorrhagic ones; whether the net favours restarting awaits the adequately powered trials still running.

cards.headline: SoSTART (2021): recurrent intracranial haemorrhage 8% starting vs 4% avoiding anticoagulation (adjusted HR 2.42, 0.72–8.09) — non-inferiority not shown; deaths 22% vs 11%
cards.summary: SoSTART (2021): recurrent intracranial haemorrhage 8% starting vs 4% avoiding anticoagulation (adjusted HR 2.42, 0.72–8.09) — non-inferiority not shown; deaths 22% vs 11%
cards.type: Randomised open-label pilot-phase non-inferiority trial (SoSTART Collaboration 2021, SoSTART)
cards.people: 203 adults in 67 UK hospitals who had survived at least 24 hours after symptomatic spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage, had atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2, randomised a median of 115 days after the haemorrhage to start (n = 101, direct oral anticoagulant or vitamin K antagonist) or avoid (n = 102, antiplatelet or no antithrombotic) long-term oral anticoagulation; median follow-up 1.2 years.
cards.result: Starting was not non-inferior to avoiding: recurrent symptomatic spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 8 (8%) of the start group versus 4 (4%) of the avoid group (adjusted HR 2.42, 95% CI 0.72 to 8.09; p=0.152 for non-inferiority). Serious adverse events occurred in 17% versus 15%, and 22 (22%) versus 11 (11%) patients died. Event rates were lower than expected, and the authors call for adequately powered trials, noting weak signals that starting might reduce major vascular events overall.
cards.watchOut: A pilot-phase trial that recruited 203 of a planned 190 but with far fewer haemorrhages than the power calculation assumed — every estimate is fragile, including the doubled mortality count, which the trial was not designed to explain. Open-label treatment with masked adjudication.
cards.source: SoSTART Collaboration. cards.headline: APACHE-AF (Schreuder 2021): non-fatal stroke or vascular death 26% on apixaban vs 24% avoiding anticoagulation (adjusted HR 1.05, 0.48–2.31) in 101 patients
cards.summary: APACHE-AF (Schreuder 2021): non-fatal stroke or vascular death 26% on apixaban vs 24% avoiding anticoagulation (adjusted HR 1.05, 0.48–2.31) in 101 patients
cards.people: 101 patients (median age 78 years) at 16 Dutch hospitals who survived an intracerebral haemorrhage while taking anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 and modified Rankin score ≤4, randomised a median of 46 days after the haemorrhage to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (or reduced dose) or to avoid anticoagulation (51% of the avoid group took antiplatelet therapy); median follow-up 1.9 years.
cards.result: Non-fatal stroke or vascular death occurred in 13 (26%) patients on apixaban (annual rate 12.6%) and 12 (24%) avoiding anticoagulation (11.9%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.31; p=0.90). Serious adverse events not counted as outcomes occurred in 58% and 57%. The authors emphasise the high subsequent event rate in both strategies and the need for larger trials.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial designed to estimate event rates for planning, not to compare strategies — its confidence interval (0.48 to 2.31) is compatible with substantial benefit and substantial harm. The avoid group was half-treated with antiplatelets, so the contrast is apixaban versus mostly-antiplatelet care, not versus nothing.
cards.source: Schreuder FHBM et al. randomised open-label phase 2 trial (schreuder 2021, apache-af) 101 patients (median age 78 years) at 16 dutch hospitals who survived an intracerebral haemorrhage while taking anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, with cha2ds2-vasc ≥2 and modified rankin score ≤4, randomised a median of 46 days after the haemorrhage to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (or reduced dose) or to avoid anticoagulation (51% of the avoid group took antiplatelet therapy); median follow-up 1.9 years. non-fatal stroke or vascular death occurred in 13 (26%) patients on apixaban (annual rate 12.6%) and 12 (24%) avoiding anticoagulation (11.9%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.05, 95% ci 0.48 to 2.31; p=0.90). serious adverse events not counted as outcomes occurred in 58% and 57%. the authors emphasise the high subsequent event rate in both strategies and the need for larger trials. a phase 2 trial designed to estimate event rates for planning, not to compare strategies — its confidence interval (0.48 to 2.31) is compatible with substantial benefit and substantial harm. the avoid group was half-treated with antiplatelets, so the contrast is apixaban versus mostly-antiplatelet care, not versus nothing. schreuder fhbm et al. apixaban versus no anticoagulation after anticoagulation-associated intracerebral haemorrhage in patients with atrial fibrillation in the netherlands (apache-af): a randomised, open-label, phase 2 trial. the lancet. neurology. 2021. pmid: 34687635. registry id: nct02565693. mesh: apache · aged · anticoagulants/adverse effects · atrial fibrillation/complications/drug therapy · cerebral hemorrhage/chemically induced/drug therapy · female · humans · male · netherlands/epidemiology · prospective studies · pyrazoles · pyridones · stroke/drug therapy/prevention & control · treatment outcome

cards.headline: COCROACH (Al-Shahi Salman 2023): pooled HR 0.68 (0.42–1.10) for stroke or cardiovascular death; ischaemic events HR 0.27 (0.13–0.56); haemorrhagic events HR 1.80 (0.77–4.21) — 412 participants, 4 trials
cards.summary: COCROACH (Al-Shahi Salman 2023): pooled HR 0.68 (0.42–1.10) for stroke or cardiovascular death; ischaemic events HR 0.27 (0.13–0.56); haemorrhagic events HR 1.80 (0.77–4.21) — 412 participants, 4 trials
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised trials (Al-Shahi Salman 2023, COCROACH)
cards.people: 412 participants with atrial fibrillation and spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage from 4 randomised trials (SoSTART, APACHE-AF, NASPAF-ICH, and the intracranial-haemorrhage subgroup of ELDERCARE-AF); 75% aged 75 or older; the intervention was a direct oral anticoagulant in 99% of those assigned to start, and the comparator was antiplatelet monotherapy in 33% of those assigned to avoid.
cards.result: Any stroke or cardiovascular death occurred in 29 (14%) of 212 starting versus 43 (22%) of 200 avoiding oral anticoagulation (pooled HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.10; I²=0%). Ischaemic major cardiovascular events were reduced (9 [4%] vs 38 [19%]; pooled HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.56). Haemorrhagic major events were not significantly increased (15 [7%] vs 9 [5%]; pooled HR 1.80, 95% CI 0.77 to 4.21), nor were death from any cause (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.11) or death or dependence at 1 year (odds ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.79).
cards.watchOut: Four hundred and twelve participants is the entire world's randomised evidence on this question, and two of the four trials contribute only 30 and 80 participants; the ischaemic benefit is driven by few events, and trials completing in 2028 may move every estimate. The pooled population mixes lobar and deep haemorrhages, whose recurrence risks differ greatly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: restart and you trade clots for bleeds at rates nobody has yet measured precisely — the honest answer is 'unresolved, leaning protective against ischaemia'
cards.summary: Synthesis: restart and you trade clots for bleeds at rates nobody has yet measured precisely — the honest answer is 'unresolved, leaning protective against ischaemia'
cards.people: Two pilot/phase 2 randomised trials (203 and 101 patients) and the individual-participant meta-analysis of all four eligible trials (412 participants) of starting versus avoiding oral anticoagulation after intracranial haemorrhage in atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Recurrent haemorrhage: 8% vs 4% (SoSTART). Stroke or vascular death: 26% vs 24% (APACHE-AF). Pooled: stroke/cardiovascular death HR 0.68 (0.42 to 1.10); ischaemic events HR 0.27 (0.13 to 0.56); haemorrhagic events HR 1.80 (0.77 to 4.21). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — small trials and a possible cardiovascular benefit claim are exactly what the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Every patient here survived their haemorrhage and was judged eligible for a trial of restarting — the highest-risk patients (large lobar bleeds, cerebral amyloid angiopathy) are under-represented, so the haemorrhage rates shown are a floor, not a ceiling, for unselected practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of SoSTART Collaboration et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2021 (PMID: 34487722), Schreuder FHBM et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2021 (PMID: 34687635), Al-Shahi Salman R et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2023 (PMID: 37839434).

shelves.title: Standardised perioperative DOAC interruption without bridging (PAUSE): major bleeding 0.90–1.85% and arterial thromboembolism 0.16–0.60% at 30 days in 3,007 patients — a large prospective cohort, not a randomised trial
shelves.question: In patients on a direct oral anticoagulant who need an elective procedure, does a standardised interruption protocol without bridging keep bleeding and thromboembolism acceptably low?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a simple rule, applied prospectively to 3,007 patients, produced low event rates. In the PAUSE cohort (Douketis JD et al., PMID: 31380891), patients with atrial fibrillation on apixaban, dabigatran or rivaroxaban stopped their drug 1 day before a low-bleeding-risk procedure and 2 days before a high-bleeding-risk procedure, resuming 1 day or 2–3 days afterwards, with no heparin bridging and no coagulation testing: 30-day major bleeding was 1.35% in the apixaban cohort, 0.90% in the dabigatran cohort and 1.85% in the rivaroxaban cohort, and arterial thromboembolism was 0.16%, 0.60% and 0.37% respectively; in high-bleeding-risk procedures major bleeding reached 2.96% (apixaban) and 2.95% (rivaroxaban). The randomised PAUSE-2 pilot (Douketis JD et al., PMID: 40086754) found preoperative residual drug levels nearly identical under PAUSE-based and ASRA-based management (<30 ng/mL in 94.4% vs 95.6% of tested patients). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the standardised interruption protocol is associated with acceptably low bleeding and thromboembolism, on prospective-cohort evidence — no trial has randomised patients against bridging or against unstructured care.

cards.headline: PAUSE (Douketis 2019): 30-day major bleeding 1.35% (apixaban), 0.90% (dabigatran), 1.85% (rivaroxaban); thromboembolism 0.16%, 0.60%, 0.37% — 3,007 patients, no bridging, no testing
cards.summary: PAUSE (Douketis 2019): 30-day major bleeding 1.35% (apixaban), 0.90% (dabigatran), 1.85% (rivaroxaban); thromboembolism 0.16%, 0.60%, 0.37% — 3,007 patients, no bridging, no testing
cards.people: 3,007 patients with atrial fibrillation (mean age 72.5 years, 66.1% men) on long-term apixaban (1,257), dabigatran (668) or rivaroxaban (1,082) at 23 centres in Canada, the USA and Europe, scheduled for elective surgery or a procedure, managed by one standardised interruption protocol (omit 1 day before low-risk and 2 days before high-risk procedures; resume 1 day or 2–3 days after); 33.5% had a high-bleeding-risk procedure; follow-up 30 days.
cards.result: Thirty-day major bleeding: 1.35% (95% CI 0% to 2.00%) apixaban, 0.90% (0% to 1.73%) dabigatran, 1.85% (0% to 2.65%) rivaroxaban. Arterial thromboembolism: 0.16% (0% to 0.48%), 0.60% (0% to 1.33%) and 0.37% (0% to 0.82%) respectively. In high-bleeding-risk procedures, major bleeding was 2.96% in the apixaban cohort and 2.95% in the rivaroxaban cohort. Most patients had undetectable or minimal residual anticoagulant levels (<50 ng/mL) at the time of the procedure.
cards.watchOut: There is no comparison group: 'acceptably low' is a judgement against historical bridging-era rates, not a measured contrast, and clinicians could exclude patients they judged unsuitable for the protocol. The confidence intervals as printed in the record have lower bounds of 0%, reflecting the small event counts — the upper bounds (up to ~2.7% for bleeding, ~4.8% in high-risk procedures) are the honest planning numbers.
cards.source: Douketis JD et al. Perioperative Management of Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Receiving a Direct Oral Anticoagulant. JAMA internal medicine. 2019. PMID: 31380891. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: PAUSE-2 pilot (Douketis 2025): residual DOAC levels <30 ng/mL in 94.4% (PAUSE-based) vs 95.6% (ASRA-based) of 141 tested patients — a feasibility trial, not an outcomes trial
cards.summary: PAUSE-2 pilot (Douketis 2025): residual DOAC levels <30 ng/mL in 94.4% (PAUSE-based) vs 95.6% (ASRA-based) of 141 tested patients — a feasibility trial, not an outcomes trial
cards.people: 159 patients with atrial fibrillation on apixaban (86), dabigatran (12) or rivaroxaban (61) needing elective high-bleeding-risk surgery and/or neuraxial anaesthesia, randomised to ASRA-based or PAUSE-based perioperative management; 141 had preoperative drug-level testing.
cards.result: Median residual DOAC level was 20 ng/mL (IQR 19–24) in the PAUSE group and 19 ng/mL (19–24) in the ASRA group. Residual levels were <30 ng/mL in 94.4% versus 95.6%, 30–50 ng/mL in 2.8% versus 1.4%, and >50 ng/mL in 2.8% versus 2.9%. The authors conclude recruitment is feasible and levels are similar under both approaches, providing the foundation for a larger trial.
cards.watchOut: A proof-of-concept pilot whose endpoints are drug levels and feasibility — it randomised 159 patients and reports no bleeding or thromboembolism comparison. It is carded to show where the randomised evidence actually stands: not yet at outcomes.
cards.source: Douketis JD et al. Perioperative management of direct oral anticoagulants in patients having a high-bleed-risk surgery or neuraxial procedure: the Perioperative Anticoagulant Use for Surgery Evaluation (PAUSE)-2 pilot randomized trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: the protocol's safety case rests on one large careful cohort — low absolute rates, honestly labelled as association, not proof
cards.summary: Synthesis: the protocol's safety case rests on one large careful cohort — low absolute rates, honestly labelled as association, not proof
cards.people: The PAUSE prospective cohort (3,007 patients with atrial fibrillation on three direct oral anticoagulants) and the PAUSE-2 randomised pilot (159 patients, drug-level endpoints).
cards.result: Cohort 30-day rates: major bleeding 0.90–1.85% by drug (2.95–2.96% in high-bleeding-risk procedures); arterial thromboembolism 0.16–0.60%. Pilot: residual levels <30 ng/mL in ~95% under either management approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — the evidence is observational, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: The cohort is atrial-fibrillation patients having elective procedures; emergency surgery, and patients whose indication is venous thromboembolism or a mechanical valve (for whom these drugs are not used), are outside the evidence. Event rates in the first days after resumption depend on surgical haemostasis, which no protocol controls.
cards.source: Synthesis of Douketis JD et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31380891), Douketis JD et al. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2025 (PMID: 40086754).

shelves.title: Direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin around cardioversion: three randomised trials, stroke and bleeding rates at or under 1% on both sides — each DOAC strategy matched the vitamin-K-antagonist strategy
shelves.question: Before cardioversion for atrial fibrillation, do direct oral anticoagulants match warfarin for stroke, embolism, and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Atrial Fibrillation/therapy · Electric Countershock/methods · Factor Xa Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Rivaroxaban · Stroke/prevention & control · Thiophenes/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Thromboembolism/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin K/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three dedicated randomised trials, one per drug, all telling the same story of very low event rates on both strategies. In X-VeRT (Cappato R et al., PMID: 25182247), 1,504 patients were randomised to rivaroxaban or dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists around early or delayed cardioversion: the primary efficacy composite occurred in 0.51% versus 1.02% (risk ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.73) and major bleeding in 0.6% versus 0.8%. In ENSURE-AF (Goette A et al., PMID: 27590218), 2,199 patients were randomised to edoxaban or enoxaparin-warfarin: the efficacy composite occurred in under 1% versus 1% (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.43) and major plus clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 1% versus 1% (OR 1.48, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.55). In EMANATE (Ezekowitz MD et al., PMID: 29659797), 1,500 patients had 0 strokes on apixaban versus 6 on heparin/VKA, with major bleeding in 3 versus 6 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): DOACs are a safe, effective alternative to warfarin around cardioversion — the trials establish comparability at low event rates, not superiority, and none was powered for the rare events that matter most.

cards.headline: X-VeRT (Cappato 2014): efficacy composite 0.51% on rivaroxaban vs 1.02% on VKA (RR 0.50, 0.15–1.73); major bleeding 0.6% vs 0.8%; faster cardioversion
cards.summary: X-VeRT (Cappato 2014): efficacy composite 0.51% on rivaroxaban vs 1.02% on VKA (RR 0.50, 0.15–1.73); major bleeding 0.6% vs 0.8%; faster cardioversion
cards.people: 1,504 patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing elective cardioversion, randomised 2:1 to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if creatinine clearance 30–49 mL/min; n = 978 analysed) or dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists (n = 492), with investigator-chosen early (1–5 days) or delayed (3–8 weeks) cardioversion strategy.
cards.result: The primary efficacy outcome (stroke, transient ischaemic attack, peripheral embolism, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death) occurred in 5 patients (0.51%, two strokes) on rivaroxaban versus 5 (1.02%, two strokes) on VKA (risk ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.73). Major bleeding occurred in 6 (0.6%) versus 4 (0.8%) patients (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.21 to 2.67). Time to cardioversion was significantly shorter with rivaroxaban (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Ten efficacy events in total: the confidence interval runs from an 85% relative reduction to a 73% relative increase, so X-VeRT establishes feasibility and rough comparability, not equivalence in any strict sense. The first randomised trial of its kind, with event rates lower than its planners expected.
cards.source: Cappato R et al. Rivaroxaban vs. vitamin K antagonists for cardioversion in atrial fibrillation. European heart journal. 2014. PMID: 25182247. Registry ID: NCT01674647. cards.headline: ENSURE-AF (Goette 2016): efficacy composite <1% on edoxaban vs 1% on enoxaparin-warfarin (OR 0.46, 0.12–1.43); bleeding 1% vs 1% — the largest cardioversion trial
cards.summary: ENSURE-AF (Goette 2016): efficacy composite <1% on edoxaban vs 1% on enoxaparin-warfarin (OR 0.46, 0.12–1.43); bleeding 1% vs 1% — the largest cardioversion trial
cards.people: 2,199 patients undergoing electrical cardioversion of non-valvular atrial fibrillation at 239 sites in 19 countries, randomised to edoxaban 60 mg daily (30 mg with dose-reduction criteria; n = 1,095) or enoxaparin-warfarin (n = 1,104; mean time in therapeutic range 70.8%), stratified by transoesophageal-echo guidance; follow-up 28 days on drug plus 30 days for safety.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint (stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death) occurred in 5 (<1%) patients on edoxaban versus 11 (1%) on enoxaparin-warfarin (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.43). The primary safety endpoint (major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding) occurred in 16 (1%) of 1,067 versus 11 (1%) of 1,082 patients (OR 1.48, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.55). Results were independent of the echo-guided strategy and prior anticoagulation status.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (blinded endpoints), and the bleeding point estimate leans against edoxaban while the efficacy estimate leans for it — both on 16 and 27 events respectively. Warfarin control here was good (70.8% time in range), so the comparison is against warfarin done well.
cards.source: Goette A et al. Edoxaban versus enoxaparin-warfarin in patients undergoing cardioversion of atrial fibrillation (ENSURE-AF): a randomised, open-label, phase 3b trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27590218. Registry ID: NCT02072434. cards.headline: EMANATE (Ezekowitz 2018): strokes 0/753 on apixaban vs 6/747 on heparin/VKA; major bleeding 3 vs 6 — in patients with ≤48 hours of prior anticoagulation
cards.summary: EMANATE (Ezekowitz 2018): strokes 0/753 on apixaban vs 6/747 on heparin/VKA; major bleeding 3 vs 6 — in patients with ≤48 hours of prior anticoagulation
cards.people: 1,500 patients with atrial fibrillation and 48 hours or less of anticoagulation before randomisation, scheduled for cardioversion, randomised to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg with dose-reduction criteria; a 10 mg loading dose permitted to expedite cardioversion) or heparin/vitamin K antagonist; 1,038 active and 300 spontaneous cardioversions, imaging in 855 patients.
cards.result: Strokes occurred in 0 of 753 patients on apixaban versus 6 of 747 on heparin/VKA (relative risk 0; 95% CI 0 to 0.64; nominal P = 0.015), with no systemic emboli in either group and 2 versus 1 deaths. Major bleeding occurred in 3 of 735 versus 6 of 721 patients (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.07) and clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 11 versus 13. All 61 patients found to have intracardiac thrombi on imaging completed the study without outcome events.
cards.watchOut: Zero events in one arm makes the relative risk look dramatic on six events in the other; the trial's own framing is that rates were low with both strategies. EMANATE also enrolled a lower-risk group (minimal prior anticoagulation, many spontaneous cardioversions), so its rates do not transfer directly to long-standing persistent AF.
cards.source: Ezekowitz MD et al. Apixaban compared to heparin/vitamin K antagonist in patients with atrial fibrillation scheduled for cardioversion: the EMANATE trial. European heart journal. 2018. PMID: 29659797. Registry ID: NCT02100228. cards.headline: Synthesis: three drugs, three trials, one answer — comparability at very low event rates, with speed and convenience as the real gains
cards.summary: Synthesis: three drugs, three trials, one answer — comparability at very low event rates, with speed and convenience as the real gains
cards.people: X-VeRT (rivaroxaban, n = 1,504), ENSURE-AF (edoxaban, n = 2,199) and EMANATE (apixaban, n = 1,500) — randomised comparisons of a direct oral anticoagulant against heparin/vitamin-K-antagonist strategies around elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Efficacy composites: 0.51% vs 1.02% (rivaroxaban); <1% vs 1% (edoxaban); strokes 0 vs 6 patients (apixaban). Major bleeding: 0.6% vs 0.8%; 1% vs 1% (major plus clinically relevant non-major); 3 vs 6 patients. No trial showed a significant difference on its primary comparisons except EMANATE's nominal stroke P value on six events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — 'benefit' here means a matched, simpler alternative, not better outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Dabigatran has no dedicated randomised cardioversion trial in this set (its evidence is a substudy of its main trial, not carded here). All three trials were underpowered for stroke individually; the case rests on consistency across 5,203 patients. Tier C is not set: three concordant randomised trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cappato R et al. European heart journal. 2014 (PMID: 25182247), Goette A et al. Lancet. 2016 (PMID: 27590218), Ezekowitz MD et al. European heart journal. 2018 (PMID: 29659797).

shelves.title: Colchicine after atrial fibrillation ablation: three months of it halved early recurrence in one trial (16% vs 33.5%) — ten days of it did nothing for recurrence in a larger later trial, though pericarditis chest pain fell from 15% to 4%
shelves.question: After catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation, does colchicine reduce early arrhythmia recurrence and pericarditis compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · C-Reactive Protein/biosynthesis · Colchicine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Interleukin-6/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Placebos · Pulmonary Veins/pathology · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome · Tubulin Modulators/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by regimen, era and population. In the 2012 trial (Deftereos S et al., PMID: 23040570), 161 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation undergoing pulmonary vein isolation were randomised to colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months, without antiarrhythmic drugs: recurrence within 3 months occurred in 16% (13/81) on colchicine versus 33.5% (27/80) on placebo (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.80), alongside larger falls in C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, at the cost of diarrhoea in 8.6% versus 1.3%. In the 2024 trial (Benz AP et al., PMID: 38126206), 199 patients were randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or placebo for just 10 days starting before ablation: atrial arrhythmia recurrence was 31% versus 32% at 2 weeks (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.61) and 14% versus 15% at 3 months (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.02), but post-ablation chest pain consistent with pericarditis fell from 15% to 4% (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.77; P=0.02) while diarrhoea rose from 7% to 26% (HR 4.74). PROPOSED SPLIT: a 3-month course after isolation of paroxysmal AF reduced early recurrence in one small trial; a 10-day course in a broader modern population did not — its demonstrable benefit is less pericarditis pain.

cards.headline: Deftereos 2012: recurrence at 3 months 16% (13/81) on colchicine vs 33.5% (27/80) on placebo (OR 0.38, 0.18–0.80); diarrhoea 8.6% vs 1.3%
cards.summary: Deftereos 2012: recurrence at 3 months 16% (13/81) on colchicine vs 33.5% (27/80) on placebo (OR 0.38, 0.18–0.80); diarrhoea 8.6% vs 1.3%
cards.people: 161 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation undergoing radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation, randomised to colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months, without antiarrhythmic drug treatment; inflammatory markers measured on days 1 and 4; follow-up 3 months.
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation recurred in 13 (16%) of 81 patients on colchicine versus 27 (33.5%) of 80 on placebo (odds ratio 0.38, 95% confidence interval 0.18 to 0.80). Colchicine produced larger reductions in C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 between days 1 and 4 (median CRP change -1.18 vs -0.46 mg/l; p < 0.01 for both markers). Diarrhoea was reported in 7 patients (8.6%) on colchicine versus 1 (1.3%) on placebo (p = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 161 patients from the early ablation era, in paroxysmal AF only and with no antiarrhythmic drugs — a cleaner, more inflamed substrate than a modern mixed ablation list. The 3-month recurrence window is the blanking period, during which recurrences are common and often transient; the trial does not show a durable rhythm benefit.
cards.source: Deftereos S et al. Colchicine for prevention of early atrial fibrillation recurrence after pulmonary vein isolation: a randomized controlled study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012. PMID: 23040570. cards.headline: Benz 2024: recurrence 31% vs 32% at 2 weeks and 14% vs 15% at 3 months on 10 days of colchicine — pericarditis pain 4% vs 15% (HR 0.26); diarrhoea 26% vs 7%
cards.summary: Benz 2024: recurrence 31% vs 32% at 2 weeks and 14% vs 15% at 3 months on 10 days of colchicine — pericarditis pain 4% vs 15% (HR 0.26); diarrhoea 26% vs 7%
cards.people: 199 patients (median age 61 years, 22% women, 70% first procedure) undergoing radiofrequency (79%) or cryoballoon (21%) ablation for atrial fibrillation, randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or placebo for 10 days beginning within 4 hours before ablation; antiarrhythmic drugs prescribed at discharge in 75%; rhythm assessed by two 14-day Holters (immediately and at 3 months).
cards.result: Colchicine did not prevent atrial arrhythmia recurrence at 2 weeks (31% vs 32%; hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.61; P=0.92) or at 3 months (14% vs 15%; HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.02; P=0.89), and did not reduce the 1.3-year composite of emergency visit, cardiovascular hospitalisation, cardioversion or repeat ablation (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.99). Post-ablation chest pain consistent with pericarditis was reduced (4% vs 15%; HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.77; P=0.02) and diarrhoea increased (26% vs 7%; HR 4.74, 95% CI 1.95 to 11.53; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The 10-day course is the key difference from the 2012 trial — this study cannot refute a 3-month regimen, only its own. Three quarters of patients also received antiarrhythmic drugs, which compress any anti-inflammatory effect on recurrence. Recurrence at 3 months (14–15%) was far lower than in 2012, reflecting modern ablation and monitoring differences.
cards.source: Benz AP et al. Colchicine to Prevent Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence After Catheter Ablation: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Circulation. Arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2024. PMID: 38126206. cards.headline: Synthesis: duration is the live hypothesis — the anti-inflammatory effect on pericarditis is consistent; the effect on recurrence depends on a regimen only one small trial has tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: duration is the live hypothesis — the anti-inflammatory effect on pericarditis is consistent; the effect on recurrence depends on a regimen only one small trial has tested
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials of colchicine after atrial fibrillation ablation: 3 months of 0.5 mg twice daily in paroxysmal AF without antiarrhythmics (n = 161, 2012) versus 10 days of 0.6 mg twice daily in a mixed population mostly on antiarrhythmics (n = 199, 2024).
cards.result: Recurrence: 16% vs 33.5% (OR 0.38) with 3 months; HR 0.98 at 2 weeks and 0.95 at 3 months with 10 days. Pericarditis pain: 4% vs 15% (HR 0.26) in 2024. Diarrhoea: increased in both trials (8.6% vs 1.3%; 26% vs 7%). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised duration itself, so the 'longer is better' reading is an inference across trials that differ in era, AF type, ablation technology and co-therapy — it is flagged here as the open question, not a conclusion. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials, presented split.
cards.source: Synthesis of Deftereos S et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012 (PMID: 23040570), Benz AP et al. Circulation. Arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2024 (PMID: 38126206).

shelves.title: Ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation with unexplained cardiomyopathy: ejection fraction rose 18 points versus 4 with rate control in a 68-patient trial — a large effect on a surrogate endpoint, in a small, carefully selected group
shelves.question: In persistent atrial fibrillation with reduced ejection fraction and suspected tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, does catheter ablation improve ejection fraction compared with medical rate control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation/diagnostic imaging/epidemiology/therapy · Catheter Ablation/methods/trends · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory/methods/trends · Female · Gadolinium/administration & dosage · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Cine/methods/trends · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/diagnostic imaging/epidemiology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect is large, mechanistically coherent, and rests on very few patients. In CAMERA-MRI (Prabhu S et al., PMID: 28855115), 68 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation and idiopathic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction ≤45%) were randomised to catheter ablation or continued medical rate control: at 6 months, ejection fraction had improved by 18 ± 13% with ablation versus 4.4 ± 13% with rate control (p < 0.0001), and normalised (≥50%) in 58% versus 9% (p = 0.0002), with post-ablation AF burden of 1.6 ± 5.0%; patients without ventricular fibrosis on MRI improved most. The earlier meta-analysis of ablation versus rate control in persistent AF with heart failure (Zhu M et al., PMID: 27472728) pooled just 3 randomised trials and 143 patients, finding an ejection-fraction advantage of 6.22% (95% CI 0.7 to 11.74; P = 0.03) and better peak oxygen consumption and NYHA class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in AF with unexplained cardiomyopathy, restoring sinus rhythm by ablation recovers ventricular function far more than rate control — on surrogate endpoints, in small selected trials, with no mortality or hospitalisation data.

cards.headline: CAMERA-MRI (Prabhu 2017): ejection fraction +18 ± 13% with ablation vs +4.4 ± 13% with rate control at 6 months (p < 0.0001); normalisation 58% vs 9%
cards.summary: CAMERA-MRI (Prabhu 2017): ejection fraction +18 ± 13% with ablation vs +4.4 ± 13% with rate control at 6 months (p < 0.0001); normalisation 58% vs 9%
cards.people: 68 patients (33 per arm after 2 dropouts, from 301 screened) with persistent atrial fibrillation and idiopathic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction ≤45%, no other cause found), rate control optimised first, cardiac MRI before randomisation to catheter ablation (pulmonary vein plus posterior wall isolation) or ongoing medical rate control; AF burden by implanted loop recorder; primary endpoint change in ejection fraction on repeat MRI at 6 months.
cards.result: Absolute ejection fraction improved by 18 ± 13% in the ablation group versus 4.4 ± 13% in the rate-control group (p < 0.0001) and normalised (≥50%) in 58% versus 9% (p = 0.0002). Mean AF burden after ablation was 1.6 ± 5.0% at 6 months. In ablated patients, absence of late gadolinium enhancement (fibrosis) predicted greater ejection-fraction improvement (10.7% greater; p = 0.0069) and normalisation (73% vs 29%; p = 0.0093).
cards.watchOut: Sixty-eight patients, a 6-month imaging endpoint, and a population screened down from 301 to find unexplained cardiomyopathy — the 18-point gain describes the reversible, tachycardia-mediated end of the AF–heart-failure spectrum, not AF with scarred ventricles, where the fibrosis subgroup already shows the effect shrinking. Single-blind, no sham procedure, no clinical-event endpoints.
cards.source: Prabhu S et al. Catheter Ablation Versus Medical Rate Control in Atrial Fibrillation and Systolic Dysfunction: The CAMERA-MRI Study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28855115. Registry ID: ACTRN12613000880741. cards.headline: Zhu 2016 meta-analysis: 3 randomised trials, 143 patients — ejection fraction +6.22% (0.7 to 11.74) with ablation over rate control; peak VO₂ and NYHA also better
cards.summary: Zhu 2016 meta-analysis: 3 randomised trials, 143 patients — ejection fraction +6.22% (0.7 to 11.74) with ablation over rate control; peak VO₂ and NYHA also better
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Zhu 2016)
cards.people: 3 randomised controlled trials totalling 143 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, heart failure and left ventricular systolic dysfunction, comparing catheter ablation with medical rate control; endpoints included ejection fraction, NYHA class, BNP, peak oxygen consumption, 6-minute walk and quality of life.
cards.result: Catheter ablation improved ejection fraction more than rate control (mean difference 6.22%, 95% CI 0.7 to 11.74; P = 0.03), improved peak oxygen consumption (mean difference 2.81 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.78 to 4.85; P = 0.007), reduced NYHA class (mean difference 0.9, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.21; P < 0.001) and improved Minnesota Living with Heart Failure scores (mean difference -11.05, 95% CI -19.45 to -2.66; P = 0.01). BNP, 6-minute walk and SF-36 differences favoured ablation without reaching significance.
cards.watchOut: Three small trials and 143 patients in total, all pre-dating CAMERA-MRI — the pooled ejection-fraction confidence interval (0.7 to 11.74) barely excludes no effect. It corroborates direction, not size, and shares the same surrogate-endpoint limitation as the trial it supports.
cards.source: Zhu M et al. Catheter ablation versus medical rate control for persistent atrial fibrillation in patients with heart failure: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27472728. cards.headline: Synthesis: where the cardiomyopathy is the arrhythmia, removing the arrhythmia recovers the ventricle — proven for ejection fraction, unproven for events
cards.summary: Synthesis: where the cardiomyopathy is the arrhythmia, removing the arrhythmia recovers the ventricle — proven for ejection fraction, unproven for events
cards.people: CAMERA-MRI (68 patients with persistent AF and idiopathic cardiomyopathy) plus a meta-analysis of 3 earlier randomised trials (143 patients with persistent AF and heart failure) of catheter ablation versus medical rate control.
cards.result: Ejection fraction: +18 ± 13% vs +4.4 ± 13% (CAMERA-MRI); pooled +6.22% (meta-analysis). Normalisation of ejection fraction: 58% vs 9% (CAMERA-MRI). No mortality, hospitalisation or stroke data in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — a single small trial carries the headline effect on a surrogate endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Patients whose ventricular dysfunction has another cause, or extensive fibrosis, are outside the proven benefit; generalising the 18-point figure to all AF with low ejection fraction would overstate the evidence severalfold. Larger trials in broader AF–heart-failure populations ask a related but different question and are not carded here.
