shelves.title: Hybrid surgical–catheter ablation for long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation: freedom from arrhythmia 68–72% versus 39–50% with catheter ablation alone in two randomised trials, without more major complications
shelves.question: In long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation, does hybrid surgical–catheter ablation improve freedom from arrhythmia compared with catheter ablation alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/diagnosis/physiopathology/surgery · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects/methods · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Veins/physiopathology/surgery · Recurrence · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · United States
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent randomised trials agree, with large absolute differences. In CONVERGE (DeLurgio DB et al., PMID: 33185144), 153 patients with persistent or long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised 2:1 to the hybrid convergent procedure or catheter ablation: primary effectiveness (freedom from AF/flutter/tachycardia without new or increased previously failed antiarrhythmic drugs) at 12 months was 67.7% versus 50.0% (P=0.036), and 53.5% versus 32.0% off antiarrhythmic drugs (P=0.0128); major adverse events occurred in 2.9% within 7 days and 4.9% between days 8 and 30, with no deaths, perforations or atrioesophageal fistulas. In CEASE-AF (Doll N et al., PMID: 37425372), 154 patients were randomised 2:1 to hybrid or catheter ablation: freedom from arrhythmia off class I/III drugs at 12 months was 71.6% versus 39.2% — an absolute benefit increase of 32.4% (95% CI 14.3% to 48.0%; p < 0.001) — with major complications in 7.8% versus 5.8% (p = 0.75). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for symptomatic drug-refractory persistent and long-standing persistent AF, hybrid ablation keeps substantially more patients arrhythmia-free at one year than catheter ablation alone, at similar major-complication rates in trial centres.

cards.headline: CONVERGE (DeLurgio 2020): freedom from arrhythmia 67.7% with hybrid convergent vs 50.0% with catheter ablation (P=0.036); 53.5% vs 32.0% off antiarrhythmic drugs
cards.summary: CONVERGE (DeLurgio 2020): freedom from arrhythmia 67.7% with hybrid convergent vs 50.0% with catheter ablation (P=0.036); 53.5% vs 32.0% off antiarrhythmic drugs
cards.people: 153 patients with symptomatic persistent or long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation (42% long-standing persistent; left atrium up to 6 cm, no limit on AF duration) randomised 2:1 to hybrid convergent epicardial–endocardial ablation (n = 102) or endocardial catheter ablation alone; 149 evaluable at 12 months; primary effectiveness freedom from AF/atrial flutter/atrial tachycardia absent new or increased dosage of previously failed or intolerant class I/III antiarrhythmic drugs.
cards.result: Primary effectiveness was achieved in 67.7% (67/99) of hybrid patients versus 50.0% (25/50) of catheter-ablation patients (P=0.036), and in 53.5% (53/99) versus 32.0% (16/50) off antiarrhythmic drugs (P=0.0128). At 18 months, ≥90% AF-burden reduction on 7-day Holter occurred in 74.0% (53/72) versus 55% (23/42). Primary safety events occurred in 2.9% (3/102) within 7 days and 4.9% (5/102) between 8 and 30 days; there were no deaths, cardiac perforations or atrioesophageal fistulas, and all but one safety event resolved.
cards.watchOut: Sponsor-run, unblinded procedural trial with effectiveness definitions that credit being on previously failed drugs — the off-drug figures (53.5% vs 32.0%) are the stricter read. Eighteen-month burden data come from the subset with Holter recordings (72 and 42 patients), not the full randomised cohort.
cards.source: DeLurgio DB et al. Hybrid Convergent Procedure for the Treatment of Persistent and Long-Standing Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: Results of CONVERGE Clinical Trial. Circulation. Arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2020. PMID: 33185144. Registry ID: NCT01984346. cards.headline: CEASE-AF (Doll 2023): freedom from arrhythmia off class I/III drugs 71.6% hybrid vs 39.2% catheter ablation (absolute increase 32.4%, 14.3–48.0; p < 0.001); major complications 7.8% vs 5.8%
cards.summary: CEASE-AF (Doll 2023): freedom from arrhythmia off class I/III drugs 71.6% hybrid vs 39.2% catheter ablation (absolute increase 32.4%, 14.3–48.0; p < 0.001); major complications 7.8% vs 5.8%
cards.people: 154 patients (75% men, mean age 60.7 years, mean left atrial diameter 4.7 cm; 81% persistent, the rest long-standing persistent AF; symptomatic and drug-refractory, left atrium >4.0 cm) at 9 hospitals in five European countries, randomised 2:1 to hybrid ablation (thoracoscopic epicardial isolation of pulmonary veins and posterior wall plus left atrial appendage exclusion, with endocardial touch-up at 91–180 days) or catheter ablation (endocardial isolation, repeat permitted at 91–180 days); primary effectiveness in the modified intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Primary effectiveness (freedom from AF/atrial flutter/atrial tachycardia >30 seconds through 12 months, absent class I/III antiarrhythmic drugs except at previously failed doses) was 71.6% (68/95) with hybrid versus 39.2% (20/51) with catheter ablation — an absolute benefit increase of 32.4% (95% CI 14.3% to 48.0%; p < 0.001). Major complications through 30 days after index and second-stage/repeat procedures were 7.8% (8/102) versus 5.8% (3/52) (p = 0.75).
cards.watchOut: The hybrid arm bundles appendage exclusion and a planned second-stage procedure, so the comparison is of strategies, not of a single lesion set; rhythm monitoring was core-lab masked but patients and operators were not blinded. Results come from experienced European hybrid programmes and a selected, mostly male, drug-refractory population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the hardest AF population gets its clearest procedural win — roughly one in three extra patients arrhythmia-free at a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: the hardest AF population gets its clearest procedural win — roughly one in three extra patients arrhythmia-free at a year
cards.people: CONVERGE (153 patients, USA/UK) and CEASE-AF (154 patients, five European countries) — randomised comparisons of hybrid epicardial–endocardial ablation versus catheter ablation alone in persistent and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Freedom from arrhythmia at 12 months: 67.7% vs 50.0% (CONVERGE primary definition) and 71.6% vs 39.2% off class I/III drugs (CEASE-AF). shelves.title: Adding linear lesions or fractionated-signal ablation to pulmonary vein isolation in persistent atrial fibrillation: STAR AF II found no fewer recurrences (freedom 59% with isolation alone vs 49% and 46% with more ablation) — only longer procedures
shelves.question: In persistent atrial fibrillation, does adding linear lesions or ablation of complex fractionated signals to pulmonary vein isolation improve freedom from arrhythmia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation/surgery · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects/methods · Disease-Free Survival · Electrocardiography · Female · Heart Atria/surgery · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mitral Valve/surgery · Operative Time · Proportional Hazards Models · Pulmonary Veins · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial and the pooled literature point the same way. In STAR AF II (Verma A et al., PMID: 25946280), 589 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised to pulmonary vein isolation alone (n = 67), isolation plus ablation of complex fractionated electrograms (n = 263), or isolation plus linear ablation (n = 259): after 18 months, freedom from recurrent atrial fibrillation was 59% with isolation alone versus 49% and 46% with the adjunctive strategies (P=0.15), with no differences in secondary endpoints, and procedure time was significantly shorter with isolation alone (P<0.001). The meta-analysis of adjunctive strategies (Scott PA et al., PMID: 26559915) pooled 10 studies and 1,821 patients: adding fractionated-electrogram ablation (risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.16; P = 0.32) or linear ablation (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.09; P = 0.10) did not significantly improve arrhythmia-free survival, while increasing procedure and fluoroscopy times. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in persistent AF, more ablation is not better ablation — pulmonary vein isolation alone remains the benchmark these strategies failed to beat.

cards.headline: STAR AF II (Verma 2015): freedom from AF at 18 months 59% (isolation alone) vs 49% (plus fractionated-electrogram ablation) vs 46% (plus linear ablation), P=0.15 — in 589 patients
cards.summary: STAR AF II (Verma 2015): freedom from AF at 18 months 59% (isolation alone) vs 49% (plus fractionated-electrogram ablation) vs 46% (plus linear ablation), P=0.15 — in 589 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Verma 2015, STAR AF II)
cards.people: 589 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation randomised 1:4:4 to pulmonary vein isolation alone (67), isolation plus ablation of electrograms showing complex fractionated activity (263), or isolation plus additional linear ablation across the left atrial roof and mitral isthmus (259); follow-up 18 months; primary endpoint freedom from documented AF recurrence >30 seconds after a single procedure.
cards.result: After 18 months, 59% of patients assigned to isolation alone were free from recurrent atrial fibrillation, versus 49% with added fractionated-electrogram ablation and 46% with added linear ablation (P=0.15). There were no significant differences in secondary endpoints, including freedom from AF after two procedures and freedom from any atrial arrhythmia. Procedure time was significantly shorter for isolation alone (P<0.001). Complications included tamponade (3 patients), stroke or transient ischaemic attack (3) and atrioesophageal fistula (1).
cards.watchOut: The isolation-alone arm was deliberately small (67 patients, a 1:4:4 design powered around the adjunctive arms), so its 59% carries a wide interval — but the direction is consistent: both larger, more-ablated arms did numerically worse, which is the opposite of what underpowering alone would be expected to hide.
cards.source: Verma A et al. Approaches to catheter ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 25946280. Registry ID: NCT01203748. cards.headline: Scott 2016 meta-analysis: 10 studies, 1,821 patients — fractionated-electrogram ablation RR 0.86 (0.64–1.16); linear ablation RR 0.64 (0.37–1.09); both with longer procedures
cards.summary: Scott 2016 meta-analysis: 10 studies, 1,821 patients — fractionated-electrogram ablation RR 0.86 (0.64–1.16); linear ablation RR 0.64 (0.37–1.09); both with longer procedures
cards.people: 10 studies (6 of fractionated-electrogram ablation, 3 of linear ablation, 1 of both) totalling 1,821 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, comparing pulmonary vein isolation plus an adjunctive substrate strategy against isolation-based strategies alone; randomised and non-randomised studies included.
cards.result: Compared with isolation alone, adding complex fractionated electrogram ablation did not significantly improve arrhythmia-free survival (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.16; P = 0.32), nor did adding left atrial linear ablation (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.09; P = 0.10). Adjunctive fractionated-electrogram ablation significantly increased procedure and fluoroscopy times, with non-significant increases for linear ablation.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes randomised and non-randomised studies and predates full assimilation of STAR AF II-era technique; the linear-ablation point estimate (0.64) is imprecise enough to hide a real effect in either direction. It is carded as concordance for the trial, not as independent proof.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the field tested 'more is better' properly, and more lost — isolation alone is shorter, simpler and at least as effective
cards.summary: Synthesis: the field tested 'more is better' properly, and more lost — isolation alone is shorter, simpler and at least as effective
cards.people: STAR AF II (589 randomised patients, three ablation strategies, 18 months) and a 10-study meta-analysis of adjunctive substrate ablation in persistent atrial fibrillation (1,821 patients).
cards.result: STAR AF II freedom from AF: 59% vs 49% vs 46% (P=0.15). Meta-analysis: RR 0.86 (fractionated electrograms) and 0.64 (linear), neither significant; procedure and fluoroscopy times increased with adjunctive ablation. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This verdict covers the two adjunctive strategies as delivered in that era; it does not condemn every form of substrate modification (for example, imaging-guided or posterior-wall approaches tested since), which would need their own shelves. Tier C is not set: a large definitive trial plus a concordant meta-analysis.

shelves.title: Fish oil around cardiac surgery: the 1,516-patient OPERA trial found postoperative atrial fibrillation in 30.0% on fish oil versus 30.7% on placebo — while a pooled analysis of 19 smaller trials still claims a modest reduction
shelves.question: After cardiac surgery, does fish oil (omega-3) supplementation prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation/etiology/prevention & control · Cardiovascular Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Female · Fish Oils/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Risk · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the best trial says no; the average of all trials says a little. In OPERA (Mozaffarian D et al., PMID: 23128104), 1,516 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery in three countries were randomised double-blind to fish oil (preoperative loading of 10 g over 3–5 days, then 2 g/day) or placebo: postoperative atrial fibrillation occurred in 30.0% versus 30.7% (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20; P = .74), with no difference in any secondary endpoint and no excess bleeding. The updated systematic review and meta-analysis (Langlois PL et al., PMID: 27293143) pooled 19 randomised trials and 4,335 cardiac-surgery patients: omega-3 reduced postoperative atrial fibrillation (odds ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.90; P = 0.004) and hospital stay (weighted mean difference -1.37 days) but not ICU stay, ventilation duration or mortality — with, in the authors' own words, considerable clinical and statistical heterogeneity weakening the findings. PROPOSED SPLIT: the largest, broadest, best-blinded trial is flatly null; the pooled estimate leans positive on the strength of smaller trials, the pattern that most often means the true effect is small or absent.

cards.headline: OPERA (Mozaffarian 2012): postoperative AF in 227 patients (30.0%) on fish oil vs 233 (30.7%) on placebo (OR 0.96, 0.77–1.20; P = .74)
cards.summary: OPERA (Mozaffarian 2012): postoperative AF in 227 patients (30.0%) on fish oil vs 233 (30.7%) on placebo (OR 0.96, 0.77–1.20; P = .74)
cards.people: 1,516 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery at 28 centres in the USA, Italy and Argentina (mean age 64 years, 72.2% men, 51.8% planned valve surgery), randomised to fish oil (1 g capsules with ≥840 mg omega-3 as ethyl esters; loading 10 g over 3–5 days or 8 g over 2 days, then 2 g/day to discharge or day 10) or placebo; primary endpoint postoperative AF lasting >30 seconds.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 227 (30.0%) patients on fish oil and 233 (30.7%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20; P = .74). No secondary endpoint differed: sustained, symptomatic or treated AF (29.6% vs 30.5%), AF excluding flutter, time to first AF, episodes per patient, hospital utilisation, major cardiovascular events, 30-day mortality or bleeding. Supplementation was well tolerated with no increase in serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: OPERA's dosing (a few days of loading) tests perioperative supplementation as actually deliverable; it cannot exclude an effect of months of prior intake. But with 460 events it is by far the most precise single estimate on this question, and its confidence interval excludes the pooled benefit claimed by the meta-analysis card below.
cards.source: Mozaffarian D et al. Fish oil and postoperative atrial fibrillation: the Omega-3 Fatty Acids for Prevention of Post-operative Atrial Fibrillation (OPERA) randomized trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23128104. Registry ID: NCT00970489. cards.headline: Langlois 2017 meta-analysis: 19 trials, 4,335 patients — postoperative AF OR 0.78 (0.68–0.90); hospital stay -1.37 days; no effect on ICU stay, ventilation or mortality
cards.summary: Langlois 2017 meta-analysis: 19 trials, 4,335 patients — postoperative AF OR 0.78 (0.68–0.90); hospital stay -1.37 days; no effect on ICU stay, ventilation or mortality
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Langlois 2017)
cards.people: 19 randomised controlled trials totalling 4,335 adult patients undergoing open-heart surgery, testing perioperative omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (oral/enteral or parenteral) against control; primary outcome ICU length of stay; secondary outcomes included hospital stay, postoperative atrial fibrillation, mortality and ventilation duration.
cards.result: Omega-3 did not reduce ICU length of stay (weighted mean difference -2.95, 95% CI -10.28 to 4.39; P = 0.43) but reduced hospital stay (WMD -1.37, 95% CI -2.41 to -0.33; P = 0.010) and postoperative atrial fibrillation (odds ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.90; P = 0.004). No effects were found on mortality or ventilation duration. Subgroup analyses suggested larger AF reductions with extracorporeal circulation and with oral/enteral administration. The authors state that considerable clinical and statistical heterogeneity weakens the findings.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate includes OPERA itself plus many small trials with varied doses, routes and AF definitions — exactly the mixture in which small-study effects flourish. Its hospital-stay result (a significant -1.37 days alongside a null ICU result with an interval spanning -10 to +4) shows how unstable the pooling is.
cards.source: Langlois PL et al. Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids in cardiac surgery patients: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2017. PMID: 27293143. shelves.title: Amiodarone prophylaxis after cardiac surgery: atrial tachyarrhythmias in 16.1% versus 29.5% in the PAPABEAR trial, and roughly halved odds across 14 trials — with no difference in mortality or serious complications
shelves.question: After cardiac surgery, does prophylactic amiodarone prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation and shorten hospital stay compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Amiodarone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/etiology/prevention & control · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Coronary Artery Bypass/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/adverse effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Preoperative Care · Survival Analysis · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large double-blind trial and the pooled literature agree on fewer arrhythmias, and neither shows a mortality price. In PAPABEAR (Mitchell LB et al., PMID: 16380589), 601 patients listed for bypass and/or valve surgery were randomised to oral amiodarone 10 mg/kg daily or placebo from 6 days before to 6 days after surgery: atrial tachyarrhythmias lasting ≥5 minutes and prompting therapy occurred in 16.1% (48/299) versus 29.5% (89/302) (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.69; P<.001), consistently across age, surgery type and beta-blocker subgroups, with postoperative sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmias in 0.3% versus 2.6% (P = .04), more dose reductions on amiodarone (11.4% vs 5.3%; P = .008), and no differences in serious complications, in-hospital mortality, 6-month readmission or 1-year mortality. The dose-and-timing meta-analysis (Buckley MS et al., PMID: 17316148) pooled 14 trials and 2,864 patients: odds ratios for postoperative AF were 0.58 (low dose), 0.45 (medium) and 0.44 (high), with no significant difference between preoperative (OR 0.50) and postoperative (OR 0.48) initiation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a short perioperative amiodarone course roughly halves postoperative atrial tachyarrhythmias; it has not been shown to shorten stay or save lives, and the question's hospital-stay limb remains unanswered by these records.

cards.headline: PAPABEAR (Mitchell 2005): atrial tachyarrhythmias 16.1% (48/299) on amiodarone vs 29.5% (89/302) on placebo (HR 0.52, 0.34–0.69; P<.001); ventricular tachyarrhythmias 0.3% vs 2.6%
cards.summary: PAPABEAR (Mitchell 2005): atrial tachyarrhythmias 16.1% (48/299) on amiodarone vs 29.5% (89/302) on placebo (HR 0.52, 0.34–0.69; P<.001); ventricular tachyarrhythmias 0.3% vs 2.6%
cards.people: 601 patients listed for non-emergency coronary bypass and/or valve replacement or repair at one tertiary centre, randomised to oral amiodarone 10 mg/kg daily or placebo for 13 days (6 days before through 6 days after surgery), stratified by age, surgery type and preoperative beta-blocker use; primary endpoint atrial tachyarrhythmias lasting ≥5 minutes that prompted therapy by postoperative day 6; follow-up 1 year.
cards.result: Atrial tachyarrhythmias occurred in 48/299 (16.1%) on amiodarone versus 89/302 (29.5%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.69; P<.001), with consistent effects in younger (11.2% vs 21.1%) and older (21.7% vs 41.2%) patients, bypass-only (11.3% vs 23.6%) and valve surgery (23.8% vs 44.1%), and with (15.3% vs 25.0%) or without (16.3% vs 35.8%) preoperative beta-blockers. Sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmias occurred in 1/299 (0.3%) versus 8/302 (2.6%) (P = .04). Dose reductions were more common on amiodarone (11.4% vs 5.3%; P = .008). There were no differences in serious postoperative complications, in-hospital mortality, readmission within 6 months, or 1-year mortality.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial from 1999–2003 whose endpoint is arrhythmias that prompted therapy — clinician-triggered, though under double-blind conditions. The record reports no hospital-length-of-stay result, so the candidate question's stay limb is answered only by silence: prophylaxis prevents arrhythmias, and any stay benefit is inference, not data.
cards.source: Mitchell LB et al. cards.headline: Buckley 2007 meta-analysis: 14 trials, 2,864 patients — odds of postoperative AF 0.58 (low dose), 0.45 (medium), 0.44 (high); starting after surgery as good as before (OR 0.48 vs 0.50)
cards.summary: Buckley 2007 meta-analysis: 14 trials, 2,864 patients — odds of postoperative AF 0.58 (low dose), 0.45 (medium), 0.44 (high); starting after surgery as good as before (OR 0.48 vs 0.50)
cards.people: 14 randomised controlled trials (of 23 identified, 1966–2005) totalling 2,864 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, comparing amiodarone prophylaxis (by total dose: low <3,000 mg, medium 3,000–5,000 mg, high >5,000 mg; and by initiation before versus after surgery) with placebo for postoperative atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Amiodarone significantly reduced postoperative atrial fibrillation overall (p<0.001). Odds ratios by dose were 0.58 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.77) for low, 0.45 (0.30 to 0.69) for medium and 0.44 (0.33 to 0.58) for high total dose, without significant differences between dose groups (p=0.238), though the authors suggest doses of 3,000 mg or more may be more effective. Odds ratios for preoperative (0.50, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.63) and postoperative (0.48, 0.37 to 0.63) initiation did not differ (p=0.862).
cards.watchOut: The pool includes PAPABEAR-era small trials with varying AF definitions and surveillance intensity, and it predates modern fast-track surgical care, in which baseline AF rates and beta-blocker use differ. The dose-response pattern is a between-trial comparison, not a randomised dose comparison — the confidence intervals of the three dose groups overlap almost completely.

shelves.title: Intravenous magnesium added to standard treatment for rapid atrial fibrillation: rate control achieved more often in two meta-analyses (63% vs 40% in the largest pool), conversion to sinus rhythm modestly more often — flushing the main side effect
shelves.question: In acute atrial fibrillation in the emergency department, does intravenous magnesium added to standard therapy improve rate control or conversion compared with standard therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Humans · Magnesium · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two independent meta-analyses of small randomised trials agree. The 2021 analysis (Ramesh T et al., PMID: 34162502) pooled 6 randomised trials and 745 patients receiving intravenous magnesium plus standard care versus standard care alone for rapid atrial fibrillation: rate control was achieved in 63% versus 40% (odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.80 to 3.45) and conversion to sinus rhythm in 21% versus 14% (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.84), with flushing in 9% versus 0.4% (OR 19.79, 95% CI 4.30 to 91.21); lower doses (≤5 g) performed better for rhythm control than higher doses in subgroup analysis. The 2023 analysis (Enayati A et al., PMID: 37186322) pooled 9 trials and 1,048 non-postoperative patients: rate control OR 1.87 (95% CI 1.13 to 3.11; p = .02) and rhythm control OR 1.45 (95% CI 1.04 to 2.03; p = .03), with no significant difference in side effects as reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): as an adjunct — not a substitute — intravenous magnesium improves the odds of rate control by roughly twofold and conversion modestly, on pooled small-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Ramesh 2021: 6 trials, 745 patients — rate control 63% vs 40% (OR 2.49, 1.80–3.45); conversion 21% vs 14% (OR 1.75); flushing 9% vs 0.4%
cards.summary: Ramesh 2021: 6 trials, 745 patients — rate control 63% vs 40% (OR 2.49, 1.80–3.45); conversion 21% vs 14% (OR 1.75); flushing 9% vs 0.4%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ramesh 2021)
cards.people: 6 randomised controlled trials totalling 745 patients with rapid atrial fibrillation (non-postoperative), comparing intravenous magnesium given in addition to standard care against placebo/standard care alone; outcomes were study-defined rate control and conversion to sinus rhythm.
cards.result: Magnesium plus standard care was superior for rate control (63% vs 40%; odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.80 to 3.45) and for conversion to sinus rhythm (21% vs 14%; OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.84). Flushing was more frequent with magnesium (9% vs 0.4%; OR 19.79, 95% CI 4.30 to 91.21). In subgroup analysis, lower-dose magnesium (≤5 g) was superior for rhythm control (24% vs 13%; OR 2.10, 95% CI 1.22 to 3.61) while higher doses (>5 g) were not (16% vs 13%; OR 1.23, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.32).
cards.watchOut: Six small trials with differing standard-care backbones (digoxin, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers in varying mixes) and differing rate-control definitions; the flushing odds ratio of 19.79 rests on a 0.4% control rate and is correspondingly unstable. The dose subgroup finding is a between-trial comparison and should be read as hypothesis, not instruction.

cards.summary: Enayati 2023: 9 trials, 1,048 patients — rate control OR 1.87 (1.13–3.11); rhythm control OR 1.45 (1.04–2.03); side effects not significantly different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Enayati 2023)
cards.people: 9 randomised controlled trials totalling 1,048 patients with non-postoperative atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response, comparing intravenous magnesium plus standard pharmacotherapy against placebo plus standard pharmacotherapy; primary endpoints study-defined rate control and reversion to sinus rhythm.
cards.result: Intravenous magnesium in addition to standard care increased successful rate control (odds ratio 1.87, 95% confidence interval 1.13 to 3.11; p = .02) and rhythm control (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.03; p = .03). cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses overlap in their included trials, so this is corroboration of a pooled estimate rather than two independent bodies of evidence; both inherit the small size and variable quality of the underlying emergency-department trials, none of which was large enough to answer the question alone.

shelves.title: Diltiazem versus metoprolol for acute atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate: randomised trials favour diltiazem for reaching rate control (OR 4.75) — observational studies show no difference, and hypotension looks similar
shelves.question: In acute atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, does intravenous diltiazem control heart rate faster and more reliably than intravenous metoprolol?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Atrial Flutter/drug therapy · Diltiazem/therapeutic use · Hypotension · Metoprolol/therapeutic use · Observational Studies as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer changes with the study design. The largest meta-analysis (Bolton A et al., PMID: 37856044) pooled 16 studies — 7 randomised and 9 observational — of intravenous diltiazem versus metoprolol for atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response: in randomised trials, diltiazem was more effective for rate control (odds ratio 4.75, 95% CI 2.50 to 9.04; I² = 14%), but in observational studies there was no significant difference (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.80; I² = 55%), and observational data showed no difference in hypotension (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.45). The earlier emergency-medicine systematic review (Martindale JL et al., PMID: 25564459) found only two randomised double-blind trials (n = 92) and a combined relative risk of acute rate control of 1.8 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.6) favouring diltiazem. PROPOSED SPLIT: on randomised evidence diltiazem reaches rate control more reliably; the observational record, which reflects sicker and more hypotension-prone real-world selections, cannot confirm it — and neither body of evidence shows a hypotension penalty for either drug.

cards.headline: Bolton 2024: rate control in randomised trials OR 4.75 (2.50–9.04) for diltiazem — in observational studies OR 1.26 (0.89–1.80); hypotension OR 1.12 (observational)
cards.summary: Bolton 2024: rate control in randomised trials OR 4.75 (2.50–9.04) for diltiazem — in observational studies OR 1.26 (0.89–1.80); hypotension OR 1.12 (observational)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised and observational studies (Bolton 2024)
cards.people: 16 studies (7 randomised, 9 observational) directly comparing intravenous diltiazem with intravenous metoprolol for atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response in hospital settings, excluding cardiac-surgery and ablation patients; primary outcome rate control (heart rate <110 bpm and/or ≥20% fall from baseline); secondary outcome hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg).
cards.result: In randomised trials, diltiazem was more effective than metoprolol for rate control (odds ratio 4.75, 95% CI 2.50 to 9.04; I² = 14%). In observational studies, there was no significant difference (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.80; I² = 55%). In observational studies, odds of hypotension did not differ between the drugs (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.45; I² = 18%). The authors note the randomised advantage was not reproduced observationally.
cards.watchOut: The randomised estimate pools small emergency-department trials in patients stable enough to be randomised — clinicians' real-world habit of steering hypotension-prone or heart-failure patients to one drug is exactly what the observational half captures and randomisation removes. Neither half reports patient-important outcomes (symptoms, admission, length of stay) in this record; the contest is over a heart-rate number at early time points.

cards.people: Systematic search of PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Registry for studies comparing calcium-channel blockers with beta-blockers for acute rate control of atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in the emergency department; two randomised double-blind trials (n = 92 in total) comparing intravenous diltiazem with intravenous metoprolol met the criteria with sufficient data.
cards.result: The combined relative risk of acute rate control with diltiazem versus metoprolol was 1.8 (95% confidence interval 1.2 to 2.6). The authors conclude that, on the paucity of available evidence, diltiazem may be more effective than metoprolol for rapid rate control, and that high-quality randomised studies are needed.
cards.watchOut: A 2015 review whose entire randomised base is 92 patients: it is carded to show how thin the direct randomised evidence was — and largely remains — beneath a comparison made thousands of times a day. Its two trials are contained within the later meta-analysis's randomised pool, so the cards corroborate rather than independently replicate.

shelves.title: Aspirin 81 mg versus 325 mg in established cardiovascular disease: 15,076 patients, no difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke hospitalisation (7.28% vs 7.51%) and none in major bleeding — in a trial where 41.6% of the high-dose group switched down
shelves.question: In established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, is aspirin 81 mg daily as effective and as safe as 325 mg daily?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Atherosclerosis/drug therapy · Cardiovascular Diseases/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology/prevention & control · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Secondary Prevention · Stroke/epidemiology/prevention & control · Drug Monitoring
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one very large pragmatic trial, flat on both effectiveness and safety. In ADAPTABLE (Jones WS et al., PMID: 33999548), 15,076 patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were randomised open-label to aspirin 81 mg or 325 mg daily and followed for a median of 26.2 months: death, hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, or hospitalisation for stroke occurred in 590 patients (estimated 7.28%) on 81 mg versus 569 (7.51%) on 325 mg (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.14), and hospitalisation for major bleeding in 53 (0.63%) versus 44 (0.60%) (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.77). The trial's own caveat is adherence to the assigned strategy: 41.6% of the 325 mg group switched dose (versus 7.1% of the 81 mg group), and median exposure to the assigned dose was 434 versus 650 days — and 96.0% of patients with prior-use data were already taking aspirin before randomisation, 85.3% of them 81 mg. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in established cardiovascular disease there is no demonstrated advantage — in events prevented or bleeding caused — to 325 mg over 81 mg, and patients vote for the lower dose with their feet.

cards.summary: ADAPTABLE (Jones 2021): primary outcome 7.28% on 81 mg vs 7.51% on 325 mg (HR 1.02, 0.91–1.14); major bleeding hospitalisation 0.63% vs 0.60% (HR 1.18, 0.79–1.77)
cards.people: 15,076 patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease randomised to a strategy of aspirin 81 mg or 325 mg daily, followed for a median of 26.2 months (IQR 19.0 to 34.9); before randomisation, 96.0% of those with available data were already taking aspirin, 85.3% of them at 81 mg daily; outcomes ascertained through health-system and claims data in a patient-centred pragmatic design.
cards.result: Death from any cause, hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, or hospitalisation for stroke occurred in 590 patients (estimated percentage 7.28%) in the 81-mg group and 569 (7.51%) in the 325-mg group (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.14). Hospitalisation for major bleeding occurred in 53 (0.63%) versus 44 (0.60%) patients (hazard ratio 1.18, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.77). Patients assigned to 325 mg switched dose far more often (41.6% vs 7.1%) and had fewer median days of exposure to the assigned dose (434 days, IQR 139 to 737, vs 650 days, IQR 415 to 922).
cards.watchOut: The trial compares strategies as actually lived, not doses as pharmacologically taken: with two-fifths of the high-dose arm switching (mostly down to 81 mg), a true dose effect would be diluted toward the null — the honest reading is 'no advantage was demonstrated for a 325 mg strategy', which is also the clinically operative question. Open-label, with outcomes from routine data rather than adjudication.

shelves.title: Omega-3 carboxylic acids in STRENGTH: 12.0% versus 12.2% major cardiovascular events — no difference in 13,078 high-risk patients, the trial stopped early for futility, and gut side effects nearly doubled
shelves.question: In statin-treated patients with raised triglycerides, do omega-3 carboxylic acids reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control* · Cholesterol/blood · Corn Oil/therapeutic use* · Docosahexaenoic Acids/administration & dosage* · Double-Blind Method · Eicosapentaenoic Acid/administration & dosage* · Female · Heart Disease Risk Factors · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Hypertriglyceridemia/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Triglycerides/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one very large double-blind trial answers this formulation's question directly. In STRENGTH (Nicholls SJ et al., PMID: 33190147), 13,078 statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk with hypertriglyceridemia and low HDL cholesterol were randomised to omega-3 carboxylic acids (a carboxylic acid formulation of EPA and DHA) 4 g/d or corn oil. The primary composite — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, or unstable angina requiring hospitalisation — occurred in 785 patients (12.0%) on omega-3 CA versus 795 (12.2%) on corn oil (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09; P = .84). The trial was halted prematurely, after 1,384 patients had experienced a primary end point event of a planned 1,600 events, on an interim analysis indicating a low probability of clinical benefit. The only clear difference was harm-side and modest: gastrointestinal adverse events in 24.7% on omega-3 CA versus 14.7% on corn oil. This is a statement about the EPA+DHA carboxylic-acid formulation, not about icosapent ethyl, a different agent tested in a different trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in statin-treated high-risk patients with raised triglycerides, omega-3 carboxylic acids did not reduce major adverse cardiovascular events versus corn oil, and the record does not support using this formulation for that purpose.

cards.headline: Nicholls 2020 (STRENGTH): primary events 12.0% on omega-3 CA versus 12.2% on corn oil (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09; P = .84) — halted for futility, gastrointestinal events 24.7% versus 14.7%
cards.summary: Nicholls 2020 (STRENGTH): primary events 12.0% on omega-3 CA versus 12.2% on corn oil (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09; P = .84) — halted for futility, gastrointestinal events 24.7% versus 14.7%
cards.people: 13,078 statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk with hypertriglyceridemia and low HDL cholesterol, randomised at 675 academic and community hospitals in 22 countries (enrollment October 30, 2014 to June 14, 2017) to 4 g/d of omega-3 CA — a carboxylic acid formulation of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) — (n = 6,539) or corn oil, intended to serve as an inert comparator (n = 6,539), in addition to usual background therapies including statins. Mean age 62.5 years, 35% women, 70% with diabetes; median LDL cholesterol 75.0 mg/dL, median triglycerides 240 mg/dL, median HDL cholesterol 36 mg/dL, median high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 2.1 mg/L.
cards.result: The primary end point — a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, or unstable angina requiring hospitalisation — occurred in 785 patients (12.0%) treated with omega-3 CA versus 795 (12.2%) treated with corn oil (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09; P = .84), the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effect. When 1,384 patients had experienced a primary end point event (of a planned 1,600 events), the trial was prematurely halted (study termination January 8, 2020) based on an interim analysis that indicated a low probability of clinical benefit of omega-3 CA versus the corn oil comparator; 12,633 patients (96.6%) completed the trial with ascertainment of primary end point status. A greater rate of gastrointestinal adverse events was observed in the omega-3 CA group (24.7%) compared with corn oil-treated patients (14.7%). The authors' conclusion: among statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk, adding omega-3 CA to usual background therapies resulted in no significant difference in the composite outcome, and the findings do not support use of this omega-3 fatty acid formulation to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was corn oil, intended as inert, not a pharmacologically blank placebo — the candidate question's 'placebo' is the trial's corn-oil control. The result is formulation-specific: STRENGTH tested an EPA+DHA carboxylic-acid mixture at 4 g/d, and its null cannot be read across to icosapent ethyl (EPA only), which was tested separately. Early stopping for futility means the trial never reached its planned 1,600 events, but with 1,384 events accrued and a hazard ratio of 0.99 with a confidence interval of 0.90–1.09, the record excludes any large benefit of this formulation in this population.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. Effect of High-Dose Omega-3 Fatty Acids vs Corn Oil on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk: The STRENGTH Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33190147. Registry ID: NCT02104817. shelves.title: Dalcetrapib after acute coronary syndrome: HDL up 31–40%, events unchanged (8.0% vs 8.3%) — a 15,871-patient trial stopped for futility
shelves.question: In patients after acute coronary syndrome with raised HDL cholesterol, does the CETP inhibitor dalcetrapib reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/drug therapy · Aged · Amides · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Apolipoproteins/blood · Biomarkers/blood · Blood Pressure/drug effects · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Esters · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk · Secondary Prevention · Sulfhydryl Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Triglycerides/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — dalcetrapib did exactly what it was designed to do to the blood test and nothing to outcomes. In dal-OUTCOMES (Schwartz GG et al., PMID: 23126252), 15,871 patients after an acute coronary syndrome received dalcetrapib 600 mg daily or placebo on top of best evidence-based care; HDL cholesterol rose 31–40% with dalcetrapib versus 4–11% with placebo, with minimal effect on LDL cholesterol. Over a median 31 months the primary composite (coronary death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, unstable angina, or resuscitated cardiac arrest) occurred in 8.0% on dalcetrapib and 8.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.93–1.16; p=0.52), and the trial was stopped for futility at a prespecified interim analysis. Total mortality did not differ, while median C-reactive protein was 0.2 mg/L higher and mean systolic blood pressure 0.6 mm Hg higher on dalcetrapib (p<0.001 for both). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): a very large, well-powered trial shows raising HDL with dalcetrapib after acute coronary syndrome does not reduce cardiovascular events.

cards.headline: Schwartz 2012 (dal-OUTCOMES): primary events 8.0% on dalcetrapib vs 8.3% on placebo (HR 1.04) — trial terminated for futility
cards.summary: Schwartz 2012 (dal-OUTCOMES): primary events 8.0% on dalcetrapib vs 8.3% on placebo (HR 1.04) — trial terminated for futility
cards.people: 15,871 patients who had had a recent acute coronary syndrome (mean HDL cholesterol 42 mg/dL, mean LDL cholesterol 76 mg/dL at randomisation), assigned to dalcetrapib 600 mg daily or placebo in addition to best available evidence-based care; median follow-up 31 months.
cards.result: HDL cholesterol increased from baseline by 31–40% in the dalcetrapib group versus 4–11% in the placebo group; dalcetrapib had a minimal effect on LDL cholesterol. The primary end point (death from coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, unstable angina, or cardiac arrest with resuscitation) occurred in 8.0% on dalcetrapib and 8.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.93–1.16; p=0.52), with no significant effect on any component or on total mortality. The independent data and safety monitoring board recommended termination for futility at an interim analysis including 1,135 primary events (71% of projected). Median C-reactive protein was 0.2 mg/L higher and mean systolic blood pressure 0.6 mm Hg higher with dalcetrapib (p<0.001 for both).
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), and it was stopped early — but at 71% of projected events with a hazard ratio of 1.04 and narrow confidence intervals, a clinically useful benefit is effectively excluded. The small rises in blood pressure and C-reactive protein lean the wrong way and echo the class's earlier harm signal with torcetrapib.
cards.source: Schwartz GG et al. Effects of dalcetrapib in patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 23126252. Registry ID: NCT00658515. shelves.question: In patients with atherosclerotic disease, does the CETP inhibitor evacetrapib reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzodiazepines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood · Cardiovascular Diseases/blood/drug therapy/prevention & control · Cholesterol Ester Transfer Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Diabetes Mellitus/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intracranial Arteriosclerosis/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/drug therapy · Peripheral Vascular Diseases/drug therapy · Risk · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the strongest lipid changes in the CETP class bought no events at all. In ACCELERATE (Lincoff AM et al., PMID: 28514624), 12,092 patients with high-risk vascular disease received evacetrapib 130 mg daily or placebo on top of standard therapy. At 3 months LDL cholesterol had fallen 31.1% on evacetrapib versus a 6.0% rise on placebo, and HDL cholesterol had risen 133.2% versus 1.6%. Yet after a median 26 months a primary end-point event (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for unstable angina) occurred in 12.9% on evacetrapib and 12.8% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.91–1.11; p=0.91), and the trial was terminated early for lack of efficacy after 1,363 of 1,670 planned events. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): evacetrapib's favourable effects on lipid biomarkers did not reduce cardiovascular events.

cards.summary: Lincoff 2017 (ACCELERATE): primary events 12.9% evacetrapib vs 12.8% placebo (HR 1.01; p=0.91) — stopped early for lack of efficacy
cards.people: 12,092 patients with high-risk vascular disease (acute coronary syndrome within the previous 30–365 days, cerebrovascular atherosclerotic disease, peripheral arterial disease, or diabetes with coronary artery disease), assigned to evacetrapib 130 mg daily or matching placebo in addition to standard medical therapy; median follow-up 26 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, mean LDL cholesterol fell 31.1% with evacetrapib versus a 6.0% increase with placebo, and mean HDL cholesterol rose 133.2% versus 1.6%. A primary end-point event (death from cardiovascular causes, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for unstable angina) occurred in 12.9% of the evacetrapib group and 12.8% of the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.91–1.11; p=0.91). cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C). It was stopped before all planned events accrued, but the point estimate sits exactly on unity with tight intervals. shelves.title: Intravenous magnesium in acute myocardial infarction: a 24% relative mortality reduction in LIMIT-2, nothing at all in MAGIC's 6,213 high-risk patients — the early promise did not survive bigger trials
shelves.question: In acute myocardial infarction, does intravenous magnesium reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/drug therapy · Coronary Care Units · Female · Heart Failure/drug therapy · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/mortality
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by trial size and era. The early evidence was strongly positive: an overview of seven small randomised trials (Teo KK et al., PMID: 1838289; 1,301 patients) found short-term mortality of 3.8% on magnesium versus 8.2% on control, and LIMIT-2 (Woods KL et al., PMID: 1351547; 2,316 patients) found 28-day mortality of 7.8% on intravenous magnesium versus 10.3% on saline — a 24% relative reduction (95% CI 1–43%; p=0.04) — with left ventricular failure in the coronary care unit reduced by 25% relative. But the largest dedicated trial, MAGIC (PMID: 12401244; 6,213 high-risk patients with ST-elevation infarction), found 30-day mortality of 15.3% on magnesium versus 15.2% on placebo (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.9–1.2; p=0.96), with no benefit in any prespecified subgroup. The 58,050-patient ISIS-4 factorial trial — carded on shelf #3334 for its captopril question — also tested intravenous magnesium and is named here without figures. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit in the small early trials and LIMIT-2, none in MAGIC's high-risk reperfusion-era population; routine intravenous magnesium in acute myocardial infarction is not supported by the largest evidence.

cards.headline: Teo 1991 (overview of 7 small trials, 1,301 patients): mortality 3.8% on magnesium vs 8.2% on control — a 55% reduction in the odds of death
cards.summary: Teo 1991 (overview of 7 small trials, 1,301 patients): mortality 3.8% on magnesium vs 8.2% on control — a 55% reduction in the odds of death
cards.people: Seven randomised trials totalling 1,301 patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction in coronary care units, allocated to intravenous magnesium or otherwise similar treatment without magnesium; short-term (mostly in-hospital) follow-up.
cards.result: Considering the seven trials collectively there were 25 deaths (3.8%) among 657 patients allocated magnesium and 53 (8.2%) among 644 allocated control, representing a 55% reduction in the odds of death (p<0.001), with 95% confidence intervals from about one-third to about two-thirds. Serious ventricular arrhythmias occurred in 70 of 648 patients on magnesium versus 109 of 641 controls, though definitions varied between trials.
cards.watchOut: Seven small trials and 78 deaths in total: exactly the setting where publication bias and small-study effects inflate benefits. This overview is best read as the hypothesis the big trials then tested — and the confidence interval, wide in relative terms, rested on very few events.
cards.source: Teo KK et al. Effects of intravenous magnesium in suspected acute myocardial infarction: overview of randomised trials. BMJ. 1991. PMID: 1838289. cards.headline: Woods 1992 (LIMIT-2, n=2,316): 28-day mortality 7.8% on magnesium vs 10.3% on saline (24% relative reduction, p=0.04); left ventricular failure down 25% relative
cards.summary: Woods 1992 (LIMIT-2, n=2,316): 28-day mortality 7.8% on magnesium vs 10.3% on saline (24% relative reduction, p=0.04); left ventricular failure down 25% relative
cards.people: 2,316 patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction in a coronary care unit, assigned to intravenous magnesium sulphate (8 mmol over 5 minutes, then 65 mmol over 24 hours) or physiological saline; myocardial infarction was confirmed in 65% of each group.
cards.result: Mortality from all causes at 28 days was 7.8% in the magnesium group and 10.3% in the placebo group (p=0.04), a 24% relative reduction (95% CI 1–43%). Within the coronary care unit, the incidence of left ventricular failure was reduced by 25% relative (95% CI 7–39%; p=0.009). There was no significant difference in heart block or in use of antiarrhythmic drugs, cardioversion, or pacing. Side effects were transient flushing and an increased incidence of sinus bradycardia (p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: LIMIT-2 remains the one moderately sized positive trial, but its confidence interval reaches almost to zero (1% relative reduction), only 65% of entrants had a confirmed infarction, and it predates routine primary PCI. A single p=0.04 mortality result of this fragility is exactly what later mega-trials exist to check.
cards.source: Woods KL et al. Intravenous magnesium sulphate in suspected acute myocardial infarction: results of the second Leicester Intravenous Magnesium Intervention Trial (LIMIT-2). cards.headline: MAGIC Trial Investigators 2002 (MAGIC, n=6,213 high-risk STEMI): 30-day mortality 15.3% on magnesium vs 15.2% on placebo (OR 1.0; p=0.96) — no subgroup benefited
cards.summary: MAGIC Trial Investigators 2002 (MAGIC, n=6,213 high-risk STEMI): 30-day mortality 15.3% on magnesium vs 15.2% on placebo (OR 1.0; p=0.96) — no subgroup benefited
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MAGIC Trial Investigators 2002, MAGIC)
cards.people: 6,213 patients with acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction at high risk (aged 65 or older and eligible for reperfusion therapy, or of any age and not eligible for reperfusion), assigned to intravenous magnesium sulphate (2 g bolus, then 17 g over 24 hours; n=3,113) or matching placebo (n=3,100).
cards.result: At 30 days, 475 patients (15.3%) in the magnesium group and 472 (15.2%) in the placebo group had died (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.9–1.2; p=0.96). No benefit or harm was observed in eight prespecified subgroup analyses or in 15 additional exploratory analyses, and after multivariate adjustment the estimate was unchanged (1.0, 95% CI 0.8–1.1; p=0.53). The investigators concluded there is no indication for routine intravenous magnesium in STEMI in current coronary care practice.
cards.watchOut: MAGIC enrolled a deliberately high-risk population with 15% mortality, so its null does not directly retest LIMIT-2's lower-risk mix — but between them, the burden of proof sits on anyone claiming a benefit in a definable subgroup, and no subgroup in MAGIC showed one.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Three randomised evidence layers totalling about 9,800 patients: a 1991 overview of seven small trials (1,301 patients), LIMIT-2 (2,316 patients, 1992), and MAGIC (6,213 high-risk STEMI patients, 2002). The 58,050-patient ISIS-4 factorial trial also randomised intravenous magnesium; it is carded on shelf #3334 for its captopril question and is named here without figures.

shelves.title: Glucose–insulin–potassium in acute infarction: hospital mortality 16.1% vs 21% in the small old trials — 10.0% vs 9.7% in the 20,201-patient CREATE-ECLA trial that settled it
shelves.question: In acute myocardial infarction, does glucose–insulin–potassium infusion reduce death compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose · Cardioplegic Solutions/therapeutic use · Electrolytes/blood · Female · Glucose/therapeutic use · Heart Arrest/epidemiology · Humans · Insulin/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/mortality · Potassium/blood/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Shock, Cardiogenic/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by era. The early trials pointed to real benefit: an overview of nine randomised placebo-controlled trials (Fath-Ordoubadi F et al., PMID: 9286943; 1,932 patients) found hospital mortality of 16.1% on glucose–insulin–potassium versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.90; p=0.004) — a 28% proportional relative reduction, about 49 lives saved per 1,000 treated. The definitive modern trial reversed the picture: CREATE-ECLA (Mehta SR et al., PMID: 15671428) randomised 20,201 patients with ST-elevation infarction presenting within 12 hours to high-dose GIK for 24 hours plus usual care or usual care alone, and 30-day mortality was 10.0% on GIK versus 9.7% on control (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.95–1.13; p=0.45), with no differences in cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock, reinfarction, or heart failure, and consistency across subgroups including patients with and without diabetes and with and without reperfusion. PROPOSED SPLIT: a genuine signal in small pre-reperfusion trials, and no effect in the one trial large enough and modern enough to decide routine use.

cards.headline: Fath-Ordoubadi 1997 (overview of 9 trials, 1,932 patients): hospital mortality 16.1% on GIK vs 21% on placebo (OR 0.72; p=0.004)
cards.summary: Fath-Ordoubadi 1997 (overview of 9 trials, 1,932 patients): hospital mortality 16.1% on GIK vs 21% on placebo (OR 0.72; p=0.004)
cards.people: Nine randomised placebo-controlled trials (from 15 identified; five excluded for poor randomisation, one for recruiting only patients with diabetes) totalling 1,932 patients with acute myocardial infarction, treated largely before routine thrombolysis and primary angioplasty.
cards.result: Hospital mortality was reduced from 21% (205 of 972 patients) in the placebo group to 16.1% (154 of 956) in the GIK group (p=0.004; odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.90) — a 28% proportional relative mortality reduction (95% CI 10–43%), corresponding to 49 lives saved per 1,000 patients treated (95% CI 14–83).
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials were small, used differing GIK protocols, and belong to an era when one in five infarct patients died in hospital — a baseline risk modern reperfusion has cut by more than half. A relative benefit estimated at that baseline cannot be assumed to survive into contemporary care, which is what CREATE-ECLA then tested.
cards.source: Fath-Ordoubadi F et al. Glucose-insulin-potassium therapy for treatment of acute myocardial infarction: an overview of randomized placebo-controlled trials. Circulation. 1997. PMID: 9286943. cards.headline: Mehta 2005 (CREATE-ECLA, n=20,201): 30-day mortality 10.0% on GIK vs 9.7% on usual care (HR 1.03; p=0.45) — no subgroup benefited
cards.summary: Mehta 2005 (CREATE-ECLA, n=20,201): 30-day mortality 10.0% on GIK vs 9.7% on usual care (HR 1.03; p=0.45) — no subgroup benefited
cards.people: 20,201 patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset at 470 centres worldwide (mean age 58.6 years; evidence-based therapies commonly used), assigned to high-dose GIK intravenous infusion for 24 hours plus usual care (n=10,091) or usual care alone (n=10,110).
cards.result: At 30 days, 1,004 GIK patients (10.0%) and 976 control patients (9.7%) had died (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.95–1.13; p=0.45). There were no significant differences in cardiac arrest (1.4% vs 1.5%), cardiogenic shock (6.6% vs 6.3%), reinfarction (2.3% vs 2.4%), or heart failure at 7 days (17.1% vs 16.9%). The lack of benefit was consistent in prespecified subgroups, including diabetes status, heart failure at presentation, presentation timing, and reperfusion therapy.
cards.watchOut: The control group received no placebo infusion, so the trial was open — but its endpoint was all-cause mortality, which blinding cannot move. With 20,201 patients, this is the rare metabolic-therapy question that has actually been answered at scale; residual uncertainty is about exotic subgroups, not the main effect.
cards.source: Mehta SR et al. Effect of glucose-insulin-potassium infusion on mortality in patients with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: the CREATE-ECLA randomized controlled trial. randomised controlled trial (mehta 2005, create-ecla) 20,201 patients with st-elevation myocardial infarction presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset at 470 centres worldwide (mean age 58.6 years; evidence-based therapies commonly used), assigned to high-dose gik intravenous infusion for 24 hours plus usual care (n=10,091) or usual care alone (n=10,110). at 30 days, 1,004 gik patients (10.0%) and 976 control patients (9.7%) had died (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% ci 0.95–1.13; p=0.45). there were no significant differences in cardiac arrest (1.4% vs 1.5%), cardiogenic shock (6.6% vs 6.3%), reinfarction (2.3% vs 2.4%), or heart failure at 7 days (17.1% vs 16.9%). the lack of benefit was consistent in prespecified subgroups, including diabetes status, heart failure at presentation, presentation timing, and reperfusion therapy. the control group received no placebo infusion, so the trial was open — but its endpoint was all-cause mortality, which blinding cannot move. with 20,201 patients, this is the rare metabolic-therapy question that has actually been answered at scale; residual uncertainty is about exotic subgroups, not the main effect. mehta sr et al. effect of glucose-insulin-potassium infusion on mortality in patients with acute st-segment elevation myocardial infarction: the create-ecla randomized controlled trial. jama. 2005. pmid: 15671428. mesh: aged · blood glucose · cardioplegic solutions/therapeutic use · electrolytes/blood · female · glucose/therapeutic use · heart arrest/epidemiology · humans · insulin/therapeutic use · male · middle aged · myocardial infarction/drug therapy/mortality · potassium/blood/therapeutic use · recurrence · shock, cardiogenic/epidemiology

cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Two evidence layers: a 1997 meta-analysis of nine small randomised trials (1,932 patients, pre-reperfusion era) and CREATE-ECLA (20,201 patients, 2005, modern usual care).
cards.result: Hospital mortality in the old trials: 16.1% vs 21% (OR 0.72). Thirty-day mortality in CREATE-ECLA: 10.0% vs 9.7% (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95–1.13). PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit in the early small trials, none in the definitive modern trial.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: the shelf's operative conclusion rests on a 20,000-patient randomised trial. The split presentation matters because the old meta-analysis is still quoted; its absolute numbers (49 lives per 1,000) belong to a 21% baseline mortality that no longer exists.

shelves.title: Routine nitrates after myocardial infarction: intravenous nitrates cut mortality in the small early trials (136 vs 193 deaths), transdermal GTN in 19,394 GISSI-3 patients did not (OR 0.94)
shelves.question: After acute myocardial infarction, do routine nitrates reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Administration, Oral · Aged · Clinical Protocols · Creatinine/blood · Drug Therapy, Combination · Echocardiography · Electrocardiography · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Lisinopril/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Male · Myocardial Infarction/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Nitroglycerin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Odds Ratio · Risk Factors · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by formulation and era. The early evidence for intravenous nitrates was positive: an overview of ten randomised trials (Yusuf S et al., PMID: 2896919; about 2,000 patients) counted 136 deaths on intravenous nitroglycerin or nitroprusside versus 193 on control — a typical 35% relative reduction in the odds of death (p<0.001), concentrated in the first week. But when nitrates were given systematically to an unselected modern population, the effect vanished: in GISSI-3 (PMID: 7910229), 19,394 patients randomised within 24 hours of infarction to transdermal glyceryl trinitrate (intravenous for 24 hours, then transdermal 10 mg daily) or open control showed no independent effect of GTN on 6-week mortality (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05) or on mortality plus severe ventricular dysfunction (0.94, 0.87–1.02). The 58,050-patient ISIS-4 trial — carded on shelf #3334 for its captopril question — also randomised an oral mononitrate and is named here without figures. PROPOSED SPLIT: intravenous nitrates reduced mortality in small pre-reperfusion trials; routine scheduled nitrates for every infarct patient did not reduce mortality in the mega-trial era.

cards.headline: Yusuf 1988 (overview of 10 trials, ~2,000 patients): 136 deaths on intravenous nitrates vs 193 on control — a typical 35% relative reduction in the odds of death
cards.summary: Yusuf 1988 (overview of 10 trials, ~2,000 patients): 136 deaths on intravenous nitrates vs 193 on control — a typical 35% relative reduction in the odds of death
cards.people: About 2,000 patients randomised in ten trials of intravenous nitroglycerin or nitroprusside in acute myocardial infarction, in the era before routine reperfusion; each individual trial was too small to estimate effects on mortality reliably.
cards.result: In total there were 136 nitrate deaths and 193 control deaths; an overview of the separate trial results indicated a typical reduction of 35% (SD 10) in the odds of death (p<0.001, with 95% confidence limits of about one-sixth to one-half). Both nitroglycerin and nitroprusside reduced mortality, the reduction being non-significantly greater with nitroglycerin. The greatest reduction occurred during the first week or so of follow-up, with a non-significant further reduction thereafter.
cards.watchOut: Ten small trials and 329 deaths: the same small-study fragility as the magnesium and GIK overviews of the period, and 'intravenous nitrate for selected patients in a coronary care unit' is a different intervention from 'a nitrate for every comer'. The overview supports the physiology; it cannot carry a routine-use policy.
cards.source: Yusuf S et al. Effect of intravenous nitrates on mortality in acute myocardial infarction: an overview of the randomised trials. Lancet. 1988. PMID: 2896919. cards.headline: GISSI-3 1994 (n=19,394): transdermal glyceryl trinitrate had no independent effect on 6-week mortality (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05)
cards.summary: GISSI-3 1994 (n=19,394): transdermal glyceryl trinitrate had no independent effect on 6-week mortality (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05)
cards.people: 19,394 patients presenting within 24 hours of symptom onset at 200 Italian coronary care units (complete 6-week data in 18,895), randomised in a factorial design to 6 weeks of oral lisinopril or open control, and to nitrates (intravenous for 24 hours, then transdermal glyceryl trinitrate 10 mg daily) or open control; thrombolysis 72%, aspirin 84%, beta-blockade 31%.
cards.result: Overall 6-week mortality was 6.7%. The systematic administration of transdermal glyceryl trinitrate showed no independent effect on overall mortality (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05) or on the combined outcome of mortality and severe ventricular dysfunction (0.94, 0.87–1.02). (In the same trial, lisinopril reduced mortality, OR 0.88, 0.79–0.99 — that result belongs to the early-ACE-inhibitor shelf, #3334.)
cards.watchOut: The nitrate comparison was open-control rather than placebo-blinded, and non-protocol nitrates were allowed for clinical indications, which dilutes any effect toward the null. Even so, a trial of this size excludes the 35% relative reduction the early overview suggested for routine scheduled use.

shelves.title: Calcium-channel blockers after infarction: verapamil cut major events (18.0% vs 21.6%) in DAVIT II, diltiazem was neutral overall in MDPIT — and harmful when the chest film showed pulmonary congestion (HR 1.41)
shelves.question: After myocardial infarction, do calcium-channel blockers improve survival — and does the answer differ for diltiazem in patients with heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Clinical Trials as Topic · Diltiazem/therapeutic use · Electrocardiography · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology · Pulmonary Edema/complications · Recurrence · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by drug and, decisively, by left-ventricular function. In MDPIT (PMID: 2899840), 2,466 patients after infarction received diltiazem 240 mg daily or placebo for a mean of 25 months: total mortality was nearly identical (167 vs 166 deaths), and first recurrent cardiac events were 11% fewer on diltiazem without reaching significance (202 vs 226; hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.74–1.08) — but a significant bidirectional interaction (p=0.0042) split the result: in 1,909 patients without pulmonary congestion diltiazem reduced cardiac events (HR 0.77, 0.61–0.98), while in 490 patients with pulmonary congestion it increased them (HR 1.41, 1.01–1.96). In DAVIT II (PMID: 2147813), 1,775 patients received verapamil 360 mg daily or placebo for up to 18 months: 18-month mortality was 11.1% on verapamil versus 13.8% on placebo (HR 0.80, 0.63–1.05; p=0.108), and major events (death or reinfarction) were significantly fewer on verapamil (18.0% vs 21.6%; HR 0.80, 0.64–0.99; p=0.027). PROPOSED SPLIT: verapamil modestly reduced major events without a proven mortality benefit; diltiazem was neutral on average and harmful in patients with pulmonary congestion — left-ventricular dysfunction is the dividing line for this class after infarction.

cards.headline: MDPIT 1988 (n=2,466): diltiazem mortality identical (167 vs 166 deaths) — but cardiac events rose with pulmonary congestion (HR 1.41) and fell without it (HR 0.77)
cards.summary: MDPIT 1988 (n=2,466): diltiazem mortality identical (167 vs 166 deaths) — but cardiac events rose with pulmonary congestion (HR 1.41) and fell without it (HR 0.77)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Multicenter Diltiazem Postinfarction Trial Research Group 1988, MDPIT)
cards.people: 2,466 patients with previous infarction at 38 hospitals in the United States and Canada, assigned to diltiazem 240 mg per day (n=1,234) or placebo (n=1,232) and followed for 12–52 months (mean 25 months).
cards.result: Total mortality rates were nearly identical (167 deaths on diltiazem, 166 on placebo). There were 11% fewer first recurrent cardiac events (death from cardiac causes or nonfatal reinfarction) on diltiazem (202 vs 226; Cox hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.74–1.08). A significant (p=0.0042) bidirectional interaction with pulmonary congestion on chest radiography was observed: in 1,909 patients without pulmonary congestion, diltiazem was associated with fewer cardiac events (HR 0.77, 0.61–0.98); in 490 patients with pulmonary congestion, with more (HR 1.41, 1.01–1.96). A similar pattern held for ejection fraction dichotomised at 0.40.
cards.watchOut: The congestion split was a subgroup interaction — statistically significant and biologically coherent (a negative inotrope in a failing ventricle), but still a subgroup. It has nonetheless governed practice ever since: the trial's honest legacy is a warning label, not an indication.
cards.source: Multicenter Diltiazem Postinfarction Trial Research Group et al. The effect of diltiazem on mortality and reinfarction after myocardial infarction. New England Journal of Medicine. 1988. PMID: 2899840. cards.headline: DAVIT II 1990 (n=1,775): verapamil major events 18.0% vs 21.6% (HR 0.80; p=0.027); 18-month mortality 11.1% vs 13.8% (p=0.108, not significant)
cards.summary: DAVIT II 1990 (n=1,775): verapamil major events 18.0% vs 21.6% (HR 0.80; p=0.027); 18-month mortality 11.1% vs 13.8% (p=0.108, not significant)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Danish Study Group on Verapamil in Myocardial Infarction 1990, DAVIT II)
cards.people: 1,775 patients after acute myocardial infarction (878 assigned verapamil 360 mg/day, 897 placebo), treated for up to 18 months (mean 16 months) in a multicentre double-blind trial.
cards.result: Ninety-five deaths and 146 major events occurred in the verapamil group versus 119 deaths and 180 major events on placebo. Eighteen-month mortality rates were 11.1% and 13.8% (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.63–1.05; p=0.108), and major event rates 18.0% and 21.6% (HR 0.80, 0.64–0.99; p=0.027). Combining DAVIT II with the earlier DAVIT I in a meta-analysis, verapamil started from the second week after infarction reduced the pooled odds of death by 0.22 (95% CI 0.01–0.37; p=0.04) and of major events by 0.21 (0.05–0.35; p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: DAVIT II's own mortality endpoint missed significance; the pooled claim leans on the smaller earlier DAVIT I. Both trials predate modern reperfusion, statins, and routine beta-blockade, so the absolute event rates (and the room for a calcium blocker to help) belong to another era.

cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials totalling 4,241 patients after myocardial infarction: MDPIT (diltiazem, 2,466 patients) and DAVIT II (verapamil, 1,775 patients).
cards.result: Mortality: diltiazem 167 vs 166 deaths (identical); verapamil 11.1% vs 13.8% at 18 months (p=0.108). Major events: verapamil 18.0% vs 21.6% (p=0.027). Diltiazem by congestion: HR 0.77 without, HR 1.41 with pulmonary congestion. PROPOSED SPLIT — verapamil modestly favourable on events, diltiazem neutral-to-harmful depending on ventricular function.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the shelf carries a harm claim (diltiazem with pulmonary congestion, HR 1.41) — harm claims go to the developer personally. Neither trial supports starting these drugs after infarction in patients with heart failure.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real event reduction, bought with real bleeding, and the dose decides the trade. In ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 (Mega JL et al., PMID: 22077192), 15,526 patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome received rivaroxaban 2.5 mg or 5 mg twice daily or placebo, on top of antiplatelet therapy, for a mean of 13 months. The primary composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke) occurred in 8.9% on rivaroxaban versus 10.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.96; p=0.008). The 2.5 mg twice-daily dose reduced cardiovascular death (2.7% vs 4.1%; p=0.002) and death from any cause (2.9% vs 4.5%; p=0.002) — a survival benefit not seen with the 5 mg dose. The cost: major bleeding not related to bypass surgery in 2.1% versus 0.6% (p<0.001) and intracranial haemorrhage in 0.6% versus 0.2% (p=0.009), without a significant increase in fatal bleeding (0.3% vs 0.2%); fatal bleeding was less frequent on the 2.5 mg dose than the 5 mg dose (0.1% vs 0.4%; p=0.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): at 2.5 mg twice daily, rivaroxaban after acute coronary syndrome reduces events and cardiovascular death, at the price of roughly triple the major bleeding and triple the intracranial haemorrhage — a trade that has to be made patient by patient.

cards.headline: Mega 2012 (ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51, n=15,526): primary events 8.9% vs 10.7% (HR 0.84; p=0.008); 2.5 mg dose cut cardiovascular death to 2.7% vs 4.1% — major bleeding 2.1% vs 0.6%
cards.summary: Mega 2012 (ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51, n=15,526): primary events 8.9% vs 10.7% (HR 0.84; p=0.008); 2.5 mg dose cut cardiovascular death to 2.7% vs 4.1% — major bleeding 2.1% vs 0.6%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Mega 2012, ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51)
cards.people: 15,526 patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome, assigned to rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily, rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily, or placebo, in addition to standard antiplatelet therapy, for a mean of 13 months and up to 31 months.
cards.result: The primary efficacy end point (death from cardiovascular causes, myocardial infarction, or stroke) occurred in 8.9% on rivaroxaban versus 10.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.96; p=0.008), with significant improvement for both the 2.5 mg dose (9.1% vs 10.7%; p=0.02) and the 5 mg dose (8.8% vs 10.7%; p=0.03). The 2.5 mg dose reduced cardiovascular death (2.7% vs 4.1%; p=0.002) and all-cause death (2.9% vs 4.5%; p=0.002); the 5 mg dose did not. Rivaroxaban increased major bleeding not related to bypass grafting (2.1% vs 0.6%; p<0.001) and intracranial haemorrhage (0.6% vs 0.2%; p=0.009), without a significant increase in fatal bleeding (0.3% vs 0.2%; p=0.66); fatal bleeding was lower on 2.5 mg than 5 mg (0.1% vs 0.4%; p=0.04).
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), and its mortality finding lives in one dose arm of a two-dose trial — the 5 mg arm's failure to reduce death is part of the result, not a footnote. Background therapy was aspirin plus a thienopyridine of its era; how the trade looks on modern potent P2Y12 inhibition is extrapolation.
