shelves.title: An ACE inhibitor on day one of infarction: captopril saved about 5 lives per 1,000 in ISIS-4 (7.19% vs 7.69%) — intravenous enalapril in CONSENSUS II saved none and caused early hypotension in 12% vs 3%
shelves.question: In unselected patients with acute myocardial infarction, does starting an oral ACE inhibitor in the first day reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Captopril/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Isosorbide Dinitrate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Myocardial Infarction/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Thrombolytic Therapy · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, real, and route-dependent. ISIS-4 (PMID: 7661937) randomised 58,050 patients with suspected acute infarction to one month of oral captopril or placebo: 5-week mortality was 7.19% on captopril versus 7.69% on placebo — a 7% relative reduction (p=0.02), an absolute difference of about 4.9 fewer deaths per 1,000 patients treated for one month, maintained at 12 months (5.4 fewer per 1,000), at the cost of hypotension severe enough to stop treatment in 52 more patients per 1,000. The Chinese Cardiac Study (CCS-1, PMID: 7885123; 13,634 patients) pointed the same way without reaching significance: 4-week mortality 9.05% on captopril versus 9.59% on placebo (p=0.3). The strategy that failed was intravenous-first: CONSENSUS II (Swedberg K et al., PMID: 1495520) gave intravenous enalaprilat within 24 hours followed by oral enalapril to 6,090 patients and found 6-month mortality of 11.0% on enalapril versus 10.2% on placebo (relative risk 1.10, 95% CI 0.93–1.29), with early hypotension in 12% versus 3% (p<0.001). (GISSI-3's lisinopril result — mortality OR 0.88 — is carded on shelf #3331, where that trial's nitrate question lives.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): starting a modest oral ACE inhibitor within the first day of infarction saves roughly 5 lives per 1,000 treated for a month; the intravenous loading strategy does not share the benefit.

cards.headline: ISIS-4 1995 (n=58,050): captopril 5-week mortality 7.19% vs 7.69% (7% relative reduction; p=0.02) — about 5 fewer deaths per 1,000, with treatment-stopping hypotension in 52 more per 1,000
cards.summary: ISIS-4 1995 (n=58,050): captopril 5-week mortality 7.19% vs 7.69% (7% relative reduction; p=0.02) — about 5 fewer deaths per 1,000, with treatment-stopping hypotension in 52 more per 1,000
cards.type: Randomised factorial trial (ISIS-4 Collaborative Group 1995, ISIS-4)
cards.people: 58,050 patients entering 1,086 hospitals up to 24 hours (median 8 hours) after onset of suspected acute myocardial infarction, with no clear contraindications (in particular no cardiogenic shock or persistent severe hypotension), randomised in a 2×2×2 factorial design to one month of oral captopril (6.25 mg titrated to 50 mg twice daily) or placebo, oral mononitrate or placebo, and 24 hours of intravenous magnesium or open control; each comparison rests on about 29,000 versus 29,000 patients.
cards.result: For captopril: a significant 7% (SD 3) proportional relative reduction in 5-week mortality (2,088 deaths [7.19%] on captopril vs 2,231 [7.69%] on placebo; p=0.02), corresponding to an absolute difference of 4.9 (SD 2.2) fewer deaths per 1,000 patients treated for one month; the advantage appeared larger (perhaps about 10 fewer per 1,000) in higher-risk groups such as those with previous infarction or heart failure, and was maintained at 12 months (5.4 [SD 2.8] fewer per 1,000). Captopril increased hypotension severe enough to require termination of study treatment by 52 (SD 2) per 1,000, reported cardiogenic shock by 5 per 1,000, and some degree of renal dysfunction by 5 per 1,000, with no excess of deaths on days 0–1.
cards.watchOut: Five lives per 1,000 is a small absolute prize, honestly stated — worth having across millions of infarctions, easy to oversell to an individual patient. Patients with shock or severe hypotension were excluded, so the result does not license day-one ACE inhibition in the unstable.
cards.source: ISIS-4 Collaborative Group et al. ISIS-4: a randomised factorial trial assessing early oral captopril, oral mononitrate, and intravenous magnesium sulphate in 58,050 patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction. cards.headline: Chinese Cardiac Study (CCS-1) 1995 (n=13,634): captopril 4-week mortality 9.05% vs 9.59% (p=0.3) — same direction as ISIS-4, not significant alone
cards.summary: Chinese Cardiac Study (CCS-1) 1995 (n=13,634): captopril 4-week mortality 9.05% vs 9.59% (p=0.3) — same direction as ISIS-4, not significant alone
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Chinese Cardiac Study Collaborative Group 1995, CCS-1)
cards.people: 13,634 patients entering 650 Chinese hospitals up to 36 hours after onset of suspected acute myocardial infarction, randomised to one month of oral captopril (6.25 mg, then 12.5 mg three times daily) or matching placebo; this record is the trial's interim report.
cards.result: Captopril was associated with a non-significant reduction in 4-week mortality (617 deaths [9.05%] on captopril vs 654 [9.59%] on placebo; p=0.3). There was a significant excess of hypotension, mostly early, but no evidence of an adverse effect on early mortality, even among patients hypotensive at entry. Taken together with the other early ACE-inhibitor trials, the authors estimated such therapy typically prevents about 5 deaths per 1,000 patients treated for the first month.
cards.watchOut: An interim report of a trial stopped into a crowded field: on its own it proves nothing (p=0.3), and its value is directional concordance with ISIS-4 at a similar absolute scale. The hypotension excess recurs in every trial of this strategy and is the practical limit on day-one dosing.
cards.source: Chinese Cardiac Study Collaborative Group et al. Oral captopril versus placebo among 13,634 patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction: interim report from the Chinese Cardiac Study (CCS-1). Lancet. 1995. PMID: 7885123. cards.headline: Swedberg 1992 (CONSENSUS II, n=6,090): intravenous-then-oral enalapril — 6-month mortality 11.0% vs 10.2% (RR 1.10), early hypotension 12% vs 3%
cards.summary: Swedberg 1992 (CONSENSUS II, n=6,090): intravenous-then-oral enalapril — 6-month mortality 11.0% vs 10.2% (RR 1.10), early hypotension 12% vs 3%
cards.people: 6,090 patients with acute myocardial infarction and blood pressure above 100/60 mm Hg at 103 Scandinavian centres, assigned to enalapril (intravenous enalaprilat within 24 hours of chest-pain onset, then oral enalapril; n=3,044) or placebo (n=3,046), on top of conventional therapy.
cards.result: Life-table mortality at one and six months did not differ significantly (6.3% and 10.2% on placebo vs 7.2% and 11.0% on enalapril; p=0.26); the relative risk of death on enalapril was 1.10 (95% CI 0.93–1.29). Death from progressive heart failure occurred in 132 patients (4.3%) on enalapril versus 104 (3.4%) on placebo (p=0.06). Early hypotension (systolic <90 or diastolic <50 mm Hg) occurred in 12% of the enalapril group versus 3% on placebo (p<0.001). The investigators concluded that enalapril started within 24 hours does not improve survival over 180 days.
cards.watchOut: CONSENSUS II is the counterweight that keeps this shelf honest: 'ACE inhibitor early' is not one intervention. An intravenous load in freshly infarcted patients buys hypotension, and the point estimate for death leaned toward harm.
cards.source: Swedberg K et al. Effects of the early administration of enalapril on mortality in patients with acute myocardial infarction. Results of the Cooperative New Scandinavian Enalapril Survival Study II (CONSENSUS II). New England Journal of Medicine. 1992. PMID: 1495520. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 77,774 unselected infarct patients: ISIS-4 (oral captopril, 58,050), CCS-1 (oral captopril, 13,634), and CONSENSUS II (intravenous-then-oral enalapril, 6,090). GISSI-3's lisinopril arm (mortality OR 0.88) is carded on shelf #3331.
cards.result: Oral captopril: 5-week mortality 7.19% vs 7.69% (ISIS-4); 4-week mortality 9.05% vs 9.59% (CCS-1, not significant). Intravenous-first enalapril: 6-month mortality 11.0% vs 10.2% (RR 1.10), early hypotension 12% vs 3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for early oral treatment — about 5 deaths prevented per 1,000 treated for a month.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set: the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim, which the developer reviews personally. The absolute effect is small and the trials predate primary PCI as routine care; the modern question is narrower (who, at what blood pressure, on day one) than the one these trials answered.

shelves.title: Nicorandil in stable angina (IONA): the composite fell (13.1% vs 15.5%; HR 0.83) — driven by hospital admissions for chest pain, while coronary death or infarction did not reach significance (4.2% vs 5.2%; p=0.068)
shelves.question: In stable angina, does nicorandil reduce coronary events compared with placebo on top of standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina Pectoris/classification/drug therapy/mortality · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Nicorandil/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Risk Factors · Survival Analysis · United Kingdom · Vasodilator Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive composite whose hard core did not quite follow. In IONA (IONA Study Group, PMID: 11965271), 5,126 patients with stable angina and additional risk factors received nicorandil 20 mg twice daily or placebo on top of standard antianginal therapy for a mean of 1.6 years. The primary composite (coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned hospital admission for cardiac chest pain) occurred in 13.1% on nicorandil versus 15.5% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.97; p=0.014). But the secondary endpoint of coronary death or nonfatal infarction was not significantly different (4.2% vs 5.2%; HR 0.79, 0.61–1.02; p=0.068); acute coronary syndromes (6.1% vs 7.6%; p=0.028) and all cardiovascular events (14.7% vs 17.0%; p=0.027) did fall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nicorandil reduces coronary event composites in stable angina, with the reduction carried mainly by admissions and acute coronary syndrome presentations rather than by a proven fall in death or infarction.

cards.headline: IONA Study Group 2002 (IONA, n=5,126): primary composite 13.1% vs 15.5% (HR 0.83; p=0.014); coronary death or MI 4.2% vs 5.2% (p=0.068)
cards.summary: IONA Study Group 2002 (IONA, n=5,126): primary composite 13.1% vs 15.5% (HR 0.83; p=0.014); coronary death or MI 4.2% vs 5.2% (p=0.068)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (IONA Study Group 2002, IONA)
cards.people: 5,126 men and women with stable angina and additional risk factors, assigned to nicorandil 20 mg twice daily (n=2,565) or identical placebo (n=2,561) in addition to standard antianginal therapy; mean follow-up 1.6 years (SD 0.5); analysis by intention to treat.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned hospital admission for cardiac chest pain) occurred in 337 patients (13.1%) on nicorandil versus 398 (15.5%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.97; p=0.014). The secondary endpoint of coronary death or nonfatal MI did not differ significantly (107 events [4.2%] vs 134 [5.2%]; HR 0.79, 0.61–1.02; p=0.068). Acute coronary syndromes occurred in 156 (6.1%) versus 195 (7.6%) (HR 0.79, 0.64–0.98; p=0.028), and all cardiovascular events in 378 (14.7%) versus 436 (17.0%) (HR 0.86, 0.75–0.98; p=0.027).
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C). Its composite mixes a soft component — admission for chest pain, in patients taking an antianginal drug that relieves chest pain — with death and infarction, and the hard component missed significance. An antianginal that keeps people out of hospital is worth having; it is not yet a drug shown to prevent infarctions.
cards.source: IONA Study Group et al. Effect of nicorandil on coronary events in patients with stable angina: the Impact Of Nicorandil in Angina (IONA) randomised trial. Lancet. 2002. PMID: 11965271. shelves.title: Trimetazidine after successful PCI (ATPCI): primary events 23.3% vs 23.7% over four years in 6,007 patients — no reduction in angina recurrence or cardiac events
shelves.question: After successful PCI, does trimetazidine reduce angina recurrence and cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Africa, Northern/epidemiology · Aged · Angina, Stable/therapy · Angina, Unstable/therapy · Asia/epidemiology · Case-Control Studies · Coronary Angiography/methods/statistics & numerical data · Death · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Non-ST Elevated Myocardial Infarction/therapy · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods/trends · Placebos/administration & dosage · Recurrence · Safety · South America/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome · Trimetazidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large, long, clean null. In ATPCI (Ferrari R et al., PMID: 32877651), 6,007 patients who had undergone successful PCI — elective for stable angina, or urgent for unstable angina or non-ST-elevation infarction — received trimetazidine 35 mg modified-release twice daily or placebo on top of standard evidence-based therapy. After a median follow-up of 47.5 months, the primary composite (cardiac death; hospital admission for a cardiac event; recurrence or persistence of angina requiring a change in antianginal therapy; or recurrence or persistence of angina requiring coronary angiography) occurred in 23.3% on trimetazidine versus 23.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.88–1.09; p=0.73), with no significant differences in any individual component, and similar results in the elective and urgent PCI subgroups. Serious adverse events were also similar (40.9% vs 41.1% of patients). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine trimetazidine after successful PCI does not reduce angina recurrence or cardiac events over four years.

cards.headline: Ferrari 2020 (ATPCI, n=6,007): primary endpoint 23.3% on trimetazidine vs 23.7% on placebo (HR 0.98; p=0.73) — every component null
cards.summary: Ferrari 2020 (ATPCI, n=6,007): primary endpoint 23.3% on trimetazidine vs 23.7% on placebo (HR 0.98; p=0.73) — every component null
cards.people: 6,007 patients aged 21–85 years at 365 centres in 27 countries who had undergone successful PCI less than 30 days before randomisation (elective PCI for stable angina, or urgent PCI for unstable angina or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction), assigned to oral trimetazidine 35 mg modified-release twice daily (n=2,998) or matching placebo (n=3,009) added to standard background therapy; median follow-up 47.5 months.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint — a composite of cardiac death; hospital admission for a cardiac event; recurrence or persistence of angina requiring addition, switch, or dose increase of at least one antianginal drug; or recurrence or persistence of angina requiring coronary angiography — occurred in 700 patients (23.3%) on trimetazidine versus 714 (23.7%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.88–1.09; p=0.73). No individual component differed significantly, and results were similar for elective and urgent PCI. Serious adverse events occurred in 1,219 of 2,983 patients (40.9%) on trimetazidine and 1,230 of 2,990 (41.1%) on placebo. The trial is registered with the EU Clinical Trials Register (EudraCT 2010-022134-89).
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), but it is a big one with four years of follow-up and an angina-sensitive composite — if trimetazidine prevented recurrent angina after PCI, this design should have seen it. The result does not address trimetazidine as symptom treatment in patients who still have angina despite revascularisation attempts, a different and softer question.
cards.source: Ferrari R et al. Efficacy and safety of trimetazidine after percutaneous coronary intervention (ATPCI): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32877651. shelves.title: Allopurinol in chronic stable angina: 43 seconds longer to ST depression and 58 seconds longer total exercise than placebo — one 65-patient crossover trial, no events measured
shelves.question: In stable angina, does allopurinol improve exercise capacity and time to chest pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Allopurinol/administration & dosage · Angina Pectoris/drug therapy/physiopathology · Blood Pressure/drug effects · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Cardiovascular Agents/administration & dosage · Chronic Disease · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography/drug effects · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Rate/drug effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/analysis · Nitroglycerin/therapeutic use · Placebos · Time Factors · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Xanthine Oxidase/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clean physiological result in a very small trial. Noman A et al. (PMID: 20542554) randomised 65 patients with angiographically documented coronary disease, a positive exercise test, and stable angina to allopurinol 600 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks before crossover (60 analysed in the second period). Allopurinol lengthened the median time to ST depression to 298 seconds versus 249 seconds on placebo — an absolute difference of 43 seconds (95% CI 31–58; p=0.0002) — lengthened total exercise time by 58 seconds (95% CI 45–77; p=0.0003), and lengthened time to chest pain by 38 seconds (95% CI 17–55; p=0.001). No adverse effects of treatment were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose allopurinol improves exercise capacity in chronic stable angina by a modest margin; whether that translates into fewer events is untested, and this shelf rests on a single small crossover trial.

cards.headline: Noman 2010 (n=65, crossover): allopurinol beat placebo by 43 s to ST depression (p=0.0002), 58 s total exercise time (p=0.0003), 38 s to chest pain (p=0.001)
cards.summary: Noman 2010 (n=65, crossover): allopurinol beat placebo by 43 s to ST depression (p=0.0002), 58 s total exercise time (p=0.0003), 38 s to chest pain (p=0.001)
cards.people: 65 patients aged 18–85 years with angiographically documented coronary artery disease, a positive exercise tolerance test, and chronic stable angina for at least 2 months, at a hospital and two infirmaries in the United Kingdom; allopurinol 600 mg per day or placebo for 6 weeks before crossover (first period: 28 analysed on allopurinol, 32 on placebo; second period: all 60 analysed). Registered as ISRCTN 82040078.
cards.result: Allopurinol increased median time to ST depression to 298 s (IQR 211–408) from a baseline of 232 s (182–380), versus 249 s (200–375) on placebo (p=0.0002); the point estimate of the absolute difference was 43 s (95% CI 31–58). Median total exercise time rose to 393 s on allopurinol versus 307 s on placebo (difference 58 s, 95% CI 45–77; p=0.0003), and time to chest pain to 304 s versus 272 s (difference 38 s, 95% CI 17–55; p=0.001). No adverse effects of treatment were reported.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-five patients, six weeks per period, surrogate treadmill endpoints, and a completed-case analysis: this is a proof-of-mechanism trial, not a treatment trial. The dose (600 mg daily) is higher than typical gout dosing, and the much larger ALL-HEART trial of allopurinol in ischaemic heart disease — carded on its own live shelf — later found no cardiovascular outcome benefit, which bounds what these extra seconds can mean.
cards.source: Noman A et al. Effect of high-dose allopurinol on exercise in patients with chronic stable angina: a randomised, placebo controlled crossover trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20542554. Registry ID: ISRCTN 82040078. shelves.title: Vasospastic angina: in the only double-blind head-to-head, nifedipine and isosorbide mononitrate each cut spontaneous ischaemic attacks by about 90% with no difference between them — the whole randomised base is a few dozen patients
shelves.question: In vasospastic angina, how do calcium-channel blockers compare with nitrates and with placebo for preventing angina attacks?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Angina Pectoris, Variant/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Echocardiography · Electrocardiography/drug effects · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory/drug effects · Ergonovine · Exercise Test/drug effects · Female · Humans · Isosorbide Dinitrate/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Nifedipine/therapeutic use · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — calcium-channel blockers clearly suppress attacks in the clinic, but the randomised record behind that confidence is remarkably thin. In the only double-blind trial comparing the two classes head-to-head (Lombardi M et al., PMID: 8325315), 21 patients with angina at rest underwent Holter monitoring and ergonovine testing on placebo and on treatment: isosorbide-5-mononitrate reduced spontaneous ischaemic attacks by 87% and nifedipine by 95%, and induced attacks by 66% and 75% respectively, with no significant difference between the two drugs. A second small double-blind crossover (Ardissino D et al., PMID: 1746458) in 30 patients with Prinzmetal's angina found felodipine once daily and nifedipine four times daily similarly effective, with ischaemic episodes or attacks in 19% of patients on nifedipine and 11–26% on felodipine depending on dose. The larger literature is observational: a meta-analysis of four Japanese cohort studies (Nishigaki K et al., PMID: 20668353; 1,997 patients with positive spasm provocation tests, 143 major adverse cardiovascular events) compared calcium blockers against each other — benidipine's hazard ratio for major events was significantly lower than diltiazem's (adjusted HR 0.41; p=0.016) — but included no placebo or nitrate arm. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): calcium-channel blockers and long-acting nitrates each suppress vasospastic attacks in tiny short trials, with no proven difference between the classes and no randomised evidence on hard outcomes.

cards.headline: Lombardi 1993 (n=21, double-blind): spontaneous ischaemic attacks fell 87% on isosorbide-5-mononitrate and 95% on nifedipine vs placebo — no significant difference between the drugs
cards.summary: Lombardi 1993 (n=21, double-blind): spontaneous ischaemic attacks fell 87% on isosorbide-5-mononitrate and 95% on nifedipine vs placebo — no significant difference between the drugs
cards.people: 21 patients admitted to a coronary care unit with angina at rest, undergoing Holter monitoring and an echo-ergonovine test during placebo and during treatment with either oral isosorbide-5-mononitrate or oral nifedipine, allocated in a double-blind randomised design.
cards.result: Both drugs caused a statistically significant reduction in spontaneous ischaemic attacks (87% with isosorbide-5-mononitrate and 95% with nifedipine) and in ergonovine-induced ischaemic attacks (66% and 75% respectively) compared with placebo. No significant difference was found between the two drugs on either measure.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one patients and surrogate endpoints (Holter episodes and provoked spasm), with percentages computed on small attack counts — a single patient's attacks moving category would move these numbers. It answers 'do both classes work against placebo?' better than 'which class is better?', on which it is silent beyond 'no difference detected'.
cards.source: Lombardi M et al. Efficacy of isosorbide-5-mononitrate versus nifedipine in preventing spontaneous and ergonovine-induced myocardial ischaemia. A double-blind, placebo-controlled study. European Heart Journal. 1993. PMID: 8325315. cards.headline: Ardissino 1991 (n=30, double-blind crossover): felodipine once daily matched nifedipine four times daily — episodes in 19% on nifedipine vs 11–26% on felodipine (not significant)
cards.summary: Ardissino 1991 (n=30, double-blind crossover): felodipine once daily matched nifedipine four times daily — episodes in 19% on nifedipine vs 11–26% on felodipine (not significant)
cards.people: 30 consecutive patients with Prinzmetal's angina pectoris (27 completed), receiving felodipine 10 mg or 20 mg once daily and nifedipine 20 mg four times daily in randomised sequence over three consecutive 6-day periods, with 24-hour Holter monitoring and diary cards, after a 2-day placebo run-in.
cards.result: The regimens were similarly effective: primary endpoints (Holter-recorded ischaemic episodes and diary anginal attacks) occurred in 5 patients (19%) during nifedipine treatment, and in 7 (26%) on felodipine 10 mg and 3 (11%) on felodipine 20 mg (p=not significant). In follow-up, 26 patients continued felodipine 20 mg once daily for a mean of 6 months and 21 (81%) remained free of symptoms and Holter-recorded attacks.
cards.watchOut: Six days per treatment period is enough to count attacks, not to judge a chronic therapy; the follow-up phase was uncontrolled. This card supports 'one calcium blocker behaves much like another', not any claim about outcomes.
cards.source: Ardissino D et al. Felodipine (once daily) versus nifedipine (four times daily) for Prinzmetal's angina pectoris. American Journal of Cardiology. 1991. PMID: 1746458. cards.headline: Nishigaki 2010 (meta-analysis of 4 observational cohorts, 1,997 patients): benidipine's major-event hazard was lower than diltiazem's (adjusted HR 0.41; p=0.016) — no placebo or nitrate comparison exists at this scale
cards.summary: Nishigaki 2010 (meta-analysis of 4 observational cohorts, 1,997 patients): benidipine's major-event hazard was lower than diltiazem's (adjusted HR 0.41; p=0.016) — no placebo or nitrate comparison exists at this scale
cards.people: 1,997 Japanese patients with positive coronary spasm provocation tests in four previous studies, treated with benidipine (n=320), amlodipine (n=308), nifedipine (n=182), or diltiazem (n=960), alone or in combination; 143 major adverse cardiovascular events occurred (cardiac death 36, myocardial infarction 51, heart failure 26, stroke 65, aortic aneurysm 11).
cards.result: The hazard ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events was significantly lower in patients treated with benidipine than in those treated with diltiazem, and remained so after correction for patient characteristics that could have affected event occurrence (hazard ratio 0.41; p=0.016). There was no significant difference in the clinical characteristics affecting major events among the four calcium-blocker groups.
cards.watchOut: This is observational prescribing data pooled, not randomised evidence: who received benidipine rather than diltiazem was chosen by clinicians, and adjustment cannot remove that. It is carded to show the shape of the larger literature — comparisons among calcium blockers only — and it cannot carry a benefit claim on its own (Tier C).
cards.source: Nishigaki K et al. Prognostic effects of calcium channel blockers in patients with vasospastic angina--a meta-analysis. Circulation Journal. 2010. PMID: 20668353. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Two small double-blind trials (21 and 30 patients) and one meta-analysis of four observational cohorts (1,997 patients) in vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina.
cards.result: Against placebo: spontaneous attacks −87% (isosorbide-5-mononitrate) and −95% (nifedipine), no difference between classes. Between calcium blockers: felodipine ≈ nifedipine in the crossover; benidipine vs diltiazem major-event HR 0.41 in observational data. No randomised trial measures death or infarction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for attack suppression by either class.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set: the shelf rests on tiny trials plus observational evidence. The candidate question's premise — a randomised comparison of calcium blockers, nitrates, and placebo — exists only in the 21-patient Lombardi trial; the summary declares this swap of emphasis rather than pretending a larger randomised base exists.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lombardi M et al. European Heart Journal. 1993 (PMID: 8325315); Ardissino D et al. American Journal of Cardiology. 1991 (PMID: 1746458); Nishigaki K et al. Circulation Journal. 2010 (PMID: 20668353).

shelves.title: Drug-eluting stents beat bare-metal stents even when antiplatelet therapy must be short: safety composite 9.4% vs 12.9% in high-bleeding-risk patients, major events 12% vs 16% in the over-75s — bleeding no higher in either trial
shelves.question: In patients at high bleeding risk, do drug-eluting stents beat bare-metal stents on death, myocardial infarction, and revascularisation without excess bleeding on short dual antiplatelet therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Coronary Artery Disease/drug therapy/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Eluting Stents/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Polymers · Prosthesis Design · Sirolimus/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Stents/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two trials, two high-risk populations, the same answer. In LEADERS FREE (Urban P et al., PMID: 26466021), 2,466 patients at high bleeding risk received a polymer-free umirolimus-coated stent or a very similar bare-metal stent, all with just one month of dual antiplatelet therapy: at 390 days the primary safety composite (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or stent thrombosis) occurred in 9.4% on the drug-coated stent versus 12.9% on the bare-metal stent (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.91; p=0.005 for superiority), and clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation in 5.1% versus 9.8% (HR 0.50, 0.37–0.69; p<0.001). In SENIOR (Varenne O et al., PMID: 29102362), 1,200 patients aged 75 or older received a drug-eluting or bare-metal stent with short dual therapy (one month if stable, six months if unstable): the primary composite (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, or ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation) occurred in 12% versus 16% (relative risk 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.94; p=0.02), with bleeding complications no different (5% vs 5%; p=0.68) and stent thrombosis infrequent in both groups (1% vs 1%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): with short dual antiplatelet therapy, a drug-eluting (or drug-coated) stent is both safer and more effective than a bare-metal stent in patients at high bleeding risk or of advanced age — the historical reason for choosing bare metal no longer holds.

cards.headline: Urban 2015 (LEADERS FREE, n=2,466, high bleeding risk, 1 month of dual therapy): safety composite 9.4% vs 12.9% (HR 0.71; p=0.005 for superiority); target-lesion revascularisation 5.1% vs 9.8%
cards.summary: Urban 2015 (LEADERS FREE, n=2,466, high bleeding risk, 1 month of dual therapy): safety composite 9.4% vs 12.9% (HR 0.71; p=0.005 for superiority); target-lesion revascularisation 5.1% vs 9.8%
cards.people: 2,466 patients at high risk of bleeding undergoing PCI, assigned to a polymer-free, carrier-free umirolimus (biolimus A9) drug-coated stent or a very similar bare-metal stent; all patients received one month of dual antiplatelet therapy; follow-up to 390 days.
cards.result: The primary safety end point (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or stent thrombosis) occurred in 112 patients (9.4%) in the drug-coated-stent group and 154 (12.9%) in the bare-metal-stent group (risk difference −3.6 percentage points, 95% CI −6.1 to −1.0; hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.91; p<0.001 for noninferiority and p=0.005 for superiority). Clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation was needed in 59 patients (5.1%) versus 113 (9.8%) (risk difference −4.8 points, −6.9 to −2.6; HR 0.50, 0.37–0.69; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The winning device is a drug-coated stent without polymer — a specific technology, not every drug-eluting stent — and 'high bleeding risk' was defined by the trial's criteria. The result overturns the assumption that bare metal is the cautious choice when antiplatelet therapy must be short; it does not compare one month with longer dual therapy.
cards.source: Urban P et al. Polymer-free Drug-Coated Coronary Stents in Patients at High Bleeding Risk. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26466021. Registry ID: NCT01623180. cards.headline: Varenne 2018 (SENIOR, n=1,200 aged ≥75): major events 12% on DES vs 16% on BMS (RR 0.71; p=0.02); bleeding 5% vs 5%; stent thrombosis 1% vs 1%
cards.summary: Varenne 2018 (SENIOR, n=1,200 aged ≥75): major events 12% on DES vs 16% on BMS (RR 0.71; p=0.02); bleeding 5% vs 5%; stent thrombosis 1% vs 1%
cards.people: 1,200 patients aged 75 years or older at 44 centres in nine countries, with stable angina, silent ischaemia, or an acute coronary syndrome and at least one lesion of at least 70% stenosis eligible for PCI, assigned to a drug-eluting stent (n=596) or a similar bare-metal stent (n=604); intended dual antiplatelet therapy duration (1 month if stable, 6 months if unstable) was recorded before randomisation.
cards.result: The primary outcome (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, or ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation at one year) occurred in 68 patients (12%) in the DES group and 98 (16%) in the BMS group (relative risk 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.94; p=0.02). Bleeding complications were similar (26 [5%] vs 29 [5%]; RR 0.90, 0.51–1.54; p=0.68), and stent thrombosis was infrequent in both groups (3 [1%] vs 8 [1%]; RR 0.38; p=0.13).
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (patients and outcome assessors masked, operators not), and the composite is carried partly by revascularisation. But its population — everyone over 75, not a bleeding-risk subset — makes it the generalisability partner to LEADERS FREE's selected high-risk cohort.
cards.source: Varenne O et al. Drug-eluting stents in elderly patients with coronary artery disease (SENIOR): a randomised single-blind trial. Lancet. 2018. PMID: 29102362. Registry ID: NCT02099617. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 3,666 patients in whom dual antiplatelet therapy had to be short: LEADERS FREE (2,466 patients at high bleeding risk, one month of dual therapy) and SENIOR (1,200 patients aged 75 or older).
cards.result: Safety/major-event composites: 9.4% vs 12.9% (HR 0.71) and 12% vs 16% (RR 0.71). Revascularisation: 5.1% vs 9.8% in LEADERS FREE. Bleeding in SENIOR: 5% vs 5%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for drug-eluting/drug-coated stents over bare-metal stents in these populations.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: two large concordant randomised trials carry the shelf. The devices differ between trials (polymer-free drug-coated vs conventional drug-eluting), so the claim is about the strategy — an antiproliferative stent plus short dual therapy — rather than one named product.
cards.source: Synthesis of Urban P et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26466021); Varenne O et al. Lancet. 2018 (PMID: 29102362).

shelves.title: Bioresorbable scaffolds: within the noninferiority margin for target-lesion failure at one year in ABSORB III (7.8% vs 6.1%) — but device thrombosis ran at 3.5% vs 0.9% through two years in AIDA (HR 3.87)
shelves.question: In coronary disease, do bioresorbable scaffolds match metallic drug-eluting stents on target-lesion failure and stent thrombosis?
shelves.mesh: Absorbable Implants · Aged · Angina Pectoris/therapy · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease/mortality/therapy · Coronary Restenosis · Drug-Eluting Stents/adverse effects · Everolimus/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Metals · Middle Aged · Prosthesis Design
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by endpoint: the scaffold matched on the composite it was designed to match, and lost on the complication that ended it. In ABSORB III (Ellis SG et al., PMID: 26457558), 2,008 patients with stable or unstable angina received an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable (Absorb) scaffold or an everolimus-eluting cobalt-chromium stent: target-lesion failure at one year occurred in 7.8% versus 6.1% (difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −0.5 to 3.9; p=0.007 for noninferiority, p=0.16 for superiority), with device thrombosis in 1.5% versus 0.7% (p=0.13). In AIDA (Wykrzykowska JJ et al., PMID: 28402237), 1,845 patients undergoing routine PCI received the scaffold or a metallic stent: two-year target-vessel failure was 11.7% versus 10.7% (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.85–1.48; p=0.43), but definite or probable device thrombosis occurred in 3.5% versus 0.9% (HR 3.87, 1.78–8.42; p<0.001), and the data and safety monitoring board recommended early reporting because of safety concerns. PROPOSED SPLIT: bioresorbable scaffolds were noninferior for one-year target-lesion failure in selected lesions, but carried a roughly fourfold device-thrombosis rate in routine practice — a harm that led to the Absorb scaffold's withdrawal from the market.

cards.headline: Ellis 2015 (ABSORB III, n=2,008): target-lesion failure 7.8% scaffold vs 6.1% metallic stent at 1 year — noninferior (p=0.007), not superior (p=0.16); device thrombosis 1.5% vs 0.7%
cards.summary: Ellis 2015 (ABSORB III, n=2,008): target-lesion failure 7.8% scaffold vs 6.1% metallic stent at 1 year — noninferior (p=0.007), not superior (p=0.16); device thrombosis 1.5% vs 0.7%
cards.people: 2,008 patients with stable or unstable angina and noncomplex obstructive coronary disease, assigned 2:1 to an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable vascular (Absorb) scaffold (n=1,322) or an everolimus-eluting cobalt-chromium (Xience) metallic stent (n=686); primary endpoint target-lesion failure at one year, tested for noninferiority (margin 4.5 percentage points) and superiority.
cards.result: Target-lesion failure at one year occurred in 7.8% of the Absorb group and 6.1% of the Xience group (difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −0.5 to 3.9; p=0.007 for noninferiority, p=0.16 for superiority). Cardiac death (0.6% vs 0.1%; p=0.29), target-vessel myocardial infarction (6.0% vs 4.6%; p=0.18), and ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation (3.0% vs 2.5%; p=0.50) did not differ significantly. Device thrombosis within one year occurred in 1.5% versus 0.7% (p=0.13). The scaffold was funded by Abbott Vascular.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against a 4.5-point margin, in noncomplex lesions, at one year — before a bioresorbable device has finished resorbing — is the friendliest possible framing of this technology, and even here every component leaned toward the metal stent. The trial was not powered to judge thrombosis, which is where the technology failed.

cards.headline: Wykrzykowska 2017 (AIDA, n=1,845, routine practice): target-vessel failure 11.7% vs 10.7% (p=0.43) — but device thrombosis 3.5% vs 0.9% (HR 3.87; p<0.001); safety board forced early reporting
cards.summary: Wykrzykowska 2017 (AIDA, n=1,845, routine practice): target-vessel failure 11.7% vs 10.7% (p=0.43) — but device thrombosis 3.5% vs 0.9% (HR 3.87; p<0.001); safety board forced early reporting
cards.people: 1,845 patients undergoing PCI in routine clinical practice, assigned to an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold (n=924) or an everolimus-eluting metallic stent (n=921); primary endpoint target-vessel failure; median follow-up 707 days; the data and safety monitoring board recommended early reporting because of safety concerns.
cards.result: Target-vessel failure occurred in 105 scaffold patients and 94 stent patients (2-year cumulative rates 11.7% and 10.7%; hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.85–1.48; p=0.43). Cardiac death rates were 2.0% versus 2.7%, target-vessel myocardial infarction 5.5% versus 3.2%, and target-vessel revascularisation 8.7% versus 7.5%. Definite or probable device thrombosis occurred in 31 scaffold patients versus 8 stent patients (2-year rates 3.5% vs 0.9%; HR 3.87, 95% CI 1.78–8.42; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: AIDA's all-comers design is both its strength (this is what happened when ordinary operators used the device) and the scaffold's defence (implantation technique was still maturing). Either way, a fourfold thrombosis excess in a device whose selling point was long-term safety is disqualifying, and the commercial product was withdrawn.

shelves.title: Drug-coated balloon for small coronary vessels (BASKET-SMALL 2): major events 7.5% vs 7.3% at one year — noninferior to a drug-eluting stent, with nothing left behind
shelves.question: In small native coronary vessels, does a drug-coated balloon match a drug-eluting stent for late lumen loss and clinical events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary/methods · Coated Materials, Biocompatible/therapeutic use · Coronary Artery Disease/therapy · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one randomised test, the balloon matched the stent on events. In BASKET-SMALL 2 (Jeger RV et al., PMID: 30170854), 758 patients with de-novo lesions in coronary vessels under 3 mm in diameter were randomised after successful predilatation to a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon or a second-generation drug-eluting stent. At 12 months, major adverse cardiac events (cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 7.5% on the balloon versus 7.3% on the stent (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.58–1.64; p=0.9180), and noninferiority was formally shown in the per-protocol population (absolute difference 95% CI −3.83 to 3.93%, inside the 4% margin; p=0.0217). Cardiac deaths were 12 (3.1%) on the balloon versus 5 (1.3%) on the stent — a numerical imbalance the trial was not powered to resolve — while probable or definite stent thrombosis (0.8% vs 1.1%) and major bleeding (1.1% vs 2.4%) were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in small native vessels, a drug-coated balloon gives one-year clinical results statistically indistinguishable from a drug-eluting stent; the question the candidate asked about late lumen loss was not this trial's primary measure, and the shelf says so.

cards.headline: Jeger 2018 (BASKET-SMALL 2, n=758): major events 7.5% vs 7.3% at 12 months (HR 0.97) — noninferiority shown; cardiac death 3.1% vs 1.3% numerically favoured the stent
cards.summary: Jeger 2018 (BASKET-SMALL 2, n=758): major events 7.5% vs 7.3% at 12 months (HR 0.97) — noninferiority shown; cardiac death 3.1% vs 1.3% numerically favoured the stent
cards.people: 758 patients with de-novo lesions (<3 mm diameter) in coronary vessels and an indication for PCI, at multiple centres, randomly allocated after successful predilatation to angioplasty with a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon (n=382) or implantation of a second-generation drug-eluting stent (n=376); dual antiplatelet therapy per current guidelines; primary objective noninferiority for major adverse cardiac events at 12 months (margin: absolute difference of 4%).
cards.result: Noninferiority was shown: in the per-protocol population the 95% CI of the absolute difference in major adverse cardiac events was below the predefined margin (−3.83 to 3.93%; p=0.0217). At 12 months in the full-analysis population, major events (cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 7.5% on the balloon versus 7.3% on the stent (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.58–1.64; p=0.9180). Cardiac deaths numbered 5 (1.3%) on the stent and 12 (3.1%) on the balloon; probable or definite stent thrombosis occurred in 3 (0.8%) balloon versus 4 (1.1%) stent patients, and major bleeding in 4 (1.1%) versus 9 (2.4%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, one year of follow-up, and a noninferiority margin of 4 absolute points on a 7% event rate is generous — 'not proven worse by more than half again' is the precise claim. The cardiac-death imbalance (12 vs 5) is small-number noise until it isn't; longer follow-up of this cohort matters more than the headline.

shelves.title: Drug-coated balloon for in-stent restenosis: clearly better than a plain balloon (target-lesion failure 17.9% vs 28.6% in AGENT IDE) — clinically level with a repeat drug-eluting stent in RIBS V, though the stent left a wider lumen
shelves.question: For in-stent restenosis, does a drug-coated balloon match repeat drug-eluting stenting or balloon angioplasty for recurrence and events?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Aged · Paclitaxel · Coronary Restenosis/etiology/therapy · Stents · Treatment Outcome · Myocardial Infarction · Death
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by comparator. Against a plain balloon, the drug-coated balloon wins outright: in AGENT IDE (Yeh RW et al., PMID: 38460161), 600 patients with in-stent restenosis received a paclitaxel-coated or an uncoated balloon; one-year target-lesion failure occurred in 17.9% versus 28.6% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.42–0.84; p=0.003), with target-lesion revascularisation in 13.0% versus 24.7% and target-vessel myocardial infarction in 5.8% versus 11.1%, though cardiac death was numerically higher on the coated balloon (2.9% vs 1.6%; HR 1.75, 0.49–6.28; p=0.38). Against a repeat drug-eluting stent, it is a draw clinically and a loss angiographically: in RIBS V (Alfonso F et al., PMID: 24412457), 189 patients with bare-metal-stent restenosis received a drug-eluting balloon or an everolimus-eluting stent; the combined clinical outcome was 6% versus 8% (HR 0.76, 0.26–2.18; p=0.6) and target-vessel revascularisation 2% versus 6%, but minimal lumen diameter at follow-up was significantly larger with the stent (2.36 mm vs 2.01 mm; p<0.001). PROPOSED SPLIT: for in-stent restenosis, a drug-coated balloon beats plain angioplasty and matches repeat stenting on clinical events, while leaving a narrower lumen than a new stent.

cards.headline: Yeh 2024 (AGENT IDE, n=600): target-lesion failure 17.9% on paclitaxel-coated balloon vs 28.6% on uncoated balloon (HR 0.59; p=0.003) — superiority met
cards.summary: Yeh 2024 (AGENT IDE, n=600): target-lesion failure 17.9% on paclitaxel-coated balloon vs 28.6% on uncoated balloon (HR 0.59; p=0.003) — superiority met
cards.people: 600 patients with in-stent restenosis (lesion length <26 mm, reference vessel diameter >2.0 to ≤4.0 mm) at 40 United States centres, randomised 2:1 to a paclitaxel-coated balloon (n=406) or an uncoated balloon (n=194); mean age 68 years; 95.7% completed one-year follow-up.
cards.result: The primary endpoint of one-year target-lesion failure (ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or cardiac death) occurred in 17.9% on the paclitaxel-coated balloon versus 28.6% on the uncoated balloon (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.42–0.84; p=0.003), meeting superiority. Target-lesion revascularisation occurred in 13.0% versus 24.7% (HR 0.50, 0.34–0.74; p=0.001) and target-vessel MI in 5.8% versus 11.1% (HR 0.51, 0.28–0.92; p=0.02). Cardiac death was 2.9% versus 1.6% (HR 1.75, 0.49–6.28; p=0.38).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a plain balloon — the weakest available treatment — so superiority here establishes that the drug coating works, not that the balloon is the best option. The cardiac-death point estimate leans the wrong way on very few events; it does not overturn the composite, but it forbids calling the win costless.

cards.headline: Alfonso 2014 (RIBS V, n=189, bare-metal-stent restenosis): clinical outcome 6% (balloon) vs 8% (everolimus stent), p=0.6 — but minimal lumen diameter 2.01 vs 2.36 mm favoured the stent (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Alfonso 2014 (RIBS V, n=189, bare-metal-stent restenosis): clinical outcome 6% (balloon) vs 8% (everolimus stent), p=0.6 — but minimal lumen diameter 2.01 vs 2.36 mm favoured the stent (p<0.001)
cards.people: 189 patients with bare-metal-stent in-stent restenosis at 25 Spanish sites, allocated to a paclitaxel drug-eluting balloon (n=95) or an everolimus-eluting stent (n=94); primary endpoint minimal lumen diameter at 9 months; angiographic follow-up in 92% of eligible patients at a median of 249 days; clinical follow-up in all patients at a median of 365 days.
cards.result: At late angiography, the stent arm had a significantly larger minimal lumen diameter (2.36 ± 0.6 mm vs 2.01 ± 0.6 mm; p<0.001; absolute mean difference 0.35 mm, 95% CI 0.16–0.53) and a lower percent diameter stenosis (13 ± 17% vs 25 ± 20%; p<0.001), while late loss (0.04 ± 0.5 mm vs 0.14 ± 0.5 mm; p=0.14) and binary restenosis (4.7% vs 9.5%; p=0.22) were low and similar. The combined clinical outcome (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 6% versus 8% (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.26–2.18; p=0.6), and target-vessel revascularisation in 2% versus 6% (HR 0.32, 0.07–1.59; p=0.17).
cards.watchOut: A 189-patient trial cannot declare clinical equivalence — its confidence interval for the clinical composite runs from a 74% relative reduction to a doubling. What it does show is the recurring pattern of this comparison: the stent wins the angiogram, the balloon avoids another metal layer, and one year of events cannot tell them apart.

cards.people: Two randomised trials in in-stent restenosis: AGENT IDE (600 patients, drug-coated balloon vs uncoated balloon) and RIBS V (189 patients with bare-metal-stent restenosis, drug-eluting balloon vs everolimus-eluting stent).
cards.result: Versus plain balloon: target-lesion failure 17.9% vs 28.6% (HR 0.59). Versus repeat stent: clinical outcome 6% vs 8% (not significant), minimal lumen diameter 2.01 vs 2.36 mm favouring the stent. PROPOSED SPLIT — beats angioplasty alone; matches repeat stenting clinically at one year, not angiographically.

shelves.title: Rotational atherectomy in calcified lesions: it gets the stent in (strategy success 98% vs 81% in PREPARE-CALC) — but late lumen loss was worse, not better, in ROTAXUS (0.44 vs 0.31 mm), and clinical events never differed
shelves.question: In heavily calcified coronary lesions, does rotational atherectomy before stenting improve procedural success and outcomes compared with balloon preparation?
shelves.mesh: Absorbable Implants · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary/adverse effects/mortality · Atherectomy, Coronary/adverse effects/mortality · Cardiovascular Agents/administration & dosage · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease/diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy · Coronary Restenosis/etiology · Coronary Thrombosis/etiology · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Germany · Humans · Male · Neointima · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects/instrumentation/mortality · Prosthesis Design · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Sirolimus/administration & dosage · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Calcification/diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by what 'improve' means: delivery yes, vessel healing no, events unchanged. In PREPARE-CALC (Abdel-Wahab M et al., PMID: 30354632), 200 patients with severely calcified lesions were randomised to lesion preparation with rotational atherectomy or modified (scoring/cutting) balloons before a third-generation drug-eluting stent: strategy success was significantly more common with atherectomy (98% vs 81%; relative risk of failure with a balloon-first strategy 9.5, 95% CI 2.3–39.7; p=0.0001), at the cost of longer fluoroscopy (23.9 vs 19.6 minutes; p=0.03), while 9-month in-stent late lumen loss was similar (0.22 vs 0.16 mm; noninferiority met) and target-lesion revascularisation (2% vs 7%), stent thrombosis (0% vs 0%), and target-vessel failure (6% vs 8%) did not differ significantly. In ROTAXUS (Abdel-Wahab M et al., PMID: 23266232), 240 patients with complex calcified lesions received atherectomy or standard preparation before a paclitaxel-eluting stent: despite a higher acute lumen gain (1.56 vs 1.44 mm; p=0.01) and higher strategy success (92.5% vs 83.3%; p=0.03), in-stent late lumen loss at 9 months was higher with atherectomy (0.44 vs 0.31 mm; p=0.04), while binary restenosis (11.4% vs 10.6%), target-lesion revascularisation (11.7% vs 12.5%), definite stent thrombosis (0.8% vs 0%), and major adverse cardiac events (24.2% vs 28.3%) were similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: upfront rotational atherectomy reliably delivers and expands the stent in calcified lesions, but it does not improve late lumen loss or clinical outcomes over balloon preparation with bailout atherectomy.

cards.headline: Abdel-Wahab 2018 (PREPARE-CALC, n=200): strategy success 98% with rotational atherectomy vs 81% with modified balloons (p=0.0001); 9-month late lumen loss 0.22 vs 0.16 mm (noninferior)
cards.summary: Abdel-Wahab 2018 (PREPARE-CALC, n=200): strategy success 98% with rotational atherectomy vs 81% with modified balloons (p=0.0001); 9-month late lumen loss 0.22 vs 0.16 mm (noninferior)
cards.people: 200 patients with documented myocardial ischaemia and severely calcified native coronary lesions at two German centres (mean age 74.9 years; 76% men; 33.5% diabetes), randomised to lesion preparation with high-speed rotational atherectomy (n=100) or modified (scoring/cutting) balloons (n=100), followed by a third-generation sirolimus-eluting stent with bioabsorbable polymer.
cards.result: Strategy success (successful stent delivery and expansion with <20% residual stenosis, TIMI 3 flow, without crossover or stent failure) was significantly more common in the atherectomy group (98% vs 81%; relative risk of failure with a modified-balloon versus atherectomy strategy 9.5, 95% CI 2.3–39.7; p=0.0001), but fluoroscopy time was longer (23.9 ± 12.2 vs 19.6 ± 13.4 minutes; p=0.03). At 9 months, mean in-stent late lumen loss was 0.22 ± 0.40 mm with atherectomy versus 0.16 ± 0.39 mm with modified balloons (p=0.21; p=0.02 for noninferiority). Target-lesion revascularisation (2% vs 7%; p=0.17), definite or probable stent thrombosis (0% vs 0%), and target-vessel failure (6% vs 8%; p=0.78) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Two hundred patients at two expert German centres: strategy success is an operator-facing endpoint, and the balloon arm's 81% was achieved with bailout atherectomy available — the trial compares 'atherectomy first' with 'atherectomy if needed', not with 'atherectomy never'. Event counts are far too small to judge clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Abdel-Wahab M et al. High-Speed Rotational Atherectomy Versus Modified Balloons Prior to Drug-Eluting Stent Implantation in Severely Calcified Coronary Lesions. Circulation: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2018. PMID: 30354632. Registry ID: NCT02502851. cards.headline: Abdel-Wahab 2013 (ROTAXUS, n=240): atherectomy won acutely (gain 1.56 vs 1.44 mm) then lost late — in-stent late lumen loss 0.44 vs 0.31 mm (p=0.04); major events 24.2% vs 28.3% (NS)
cards.summary: Abdel-Wahab 2013 (ROTAXUS, n=240): atherectomy won acutely (gain 1.56 vs 1.44 mm) then lost late — in-stent late lumen loss 0.44 vs 0.31 mm (p=0.04); major events 24.2% vs 28.3% (NS)
cards.people: 240 patients with complex calcified native coronary lesions, randomised to rotational atherectomy followed by stenting (n=120) or stenting without atherectomy (standard therapy, n=120); stenting used a polymer-based slow-release paclitaxel-eluting stent; primary endpoint in-stent late lumen loss at 9 months.
cards.result: Strategy success was higher with atherectomy (92.5% vs 83.3%; p=0.03), with more crossovers in the standard group (12.5% vs 4.2%; p=0.02), and acute lumen gain was higher (1.56 ± 0.43 vs 1.44 ± 0.49 mm; p=0.01). But at 9 months in-stent late lumen loss was higher in the atherectomy group (0.44 ± 0.58 vs 0.31 ± 0.52 mm; p=0.04). In-stent binary restenosis (11.4% vs 10.6%; p=0.71), target-lesion revascularisation (11.7% vs 12.5%; p=0.84), definite stent thrombosis (0.8% vs 0%; p=1.0), and major adverse cardiac events (24.2% vs 28.3%; p=0.46) were similar.
cards.watchOut: The paclitaxel-eluting stent used here is a first-generation device no longer typical, and the trial's own interpretation — balloon dilation with only provisional atherectomy remains the default — is the opposite of a sales pitch for routine use. The late-loss penalty is the biological price of deeper vessel injury, and it appeared in the trial designed to find a benefit.
cards.source: Abdel-Wahab M et al. cards.people: Two randomised trials from the same German group totalling 440 patients with calcified coronary lesions: PREPARE-CALC (200 patients, vs modified balloons, modern stent) and ROTAXUS (240 patients, vs standard preparation, first-generation drug-eluting stent).
cards.result: Strategy success: 98% vs 81% and 92.5% vs 83.3%, both favouring upfront atherectomy. Late lumen loss: 0.22 vs 0.16 mm (similar) and 0.44 vs 0.31 mm (worse with atherectomy). Clinical events: no significant difference in either trial. PROPOSED SPLIT — a delivery tool, not an outcome tool.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the split. Neither trial was powered for death or infarction; the shelf's claim is confined to procedural success and angiographic outcomes, where the data actually live.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abdel-Wahab M et al. Circulation: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2018 (PMID: 30354632); Abdel-Wahab M et al. JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2013 (PMID: 23266232).

shelves.title: Upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition in non-ST-elevation ACS: no benefit in EARLY ACS (primary events 9.3% vs 10.0%) or in a 19,929-patient meta-analysis — and more bleeding both times
shelves.question: In non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, does routine upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition improve outcomes compared with provisional use during PCI?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Aged · Angina Pectoris/therapy · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Combined Modality Therapy · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Bypass · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electrocardiography · Eptifibatide · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology/therapy · Odds Ratio · Peptides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Platelet Glycoprotein GPIIb-IIIa Complex/antagonists & inhibitors · Thrombosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — starting the drug early, before the angiogram, bought nothing and cost blood. In EARLY ACS (Giugliano RP et al., PMID: 19332455), 9,492 patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes assigned to an invasive strategy received early routine eptifibatide (started at least 12 hours before angiography) or placebo with provisional eptifibatide after angiography: the primary composite at 96 hours occurred in 9.3% versus 10.0% (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06; p=0.23), death or myocardial infarction at 30 days in 11.2% versus 12.3% (OR 0.89, 0.79–1.01; p=0.08), and the early group had significantly higher rates of bleeding and red-cell transfusion. The wider randomised record agrees: a meta-analysis of seven trials (De Luca G et al., PMID: 21211597; 19,929 high-risk ACS patients undergoing an invasive strategy) found upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition did not decrease 30-day mortality (2.0% vs 2.0%; p=0.84) or myocardial infarction (7.0% vs 7.6%; p=0.11), but increased major bleeding (1.8% vs 1.3%; p=0.0002). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition does not improve outcomes over provisional use at PCI, and it increases bleeding.

cards.headline: Giugliano 2009 (EARLY ACS, n=9,492): early eptifibatide 9.3% vs delayed provisional 10.0% on the 96-hour composite (OR 0.92; p=0.23) — with significantly more bleeding and transfusion
cards.summary: Giugliano 2009 (EARLY ACS, n=9,492): early eptifibatide 9.3% vs delayed provisional 10.0% on the 96-hour composite (OR 0.92; p=0.23) — with significantly more bleeding and transfusion
cards.people: 9,492 patients with acute coronary syndromes without ST-segment elevation who were assigned to an invasive strategy, randomised to early routine eptifibatide (two 180 µg/kg boluses 10 minutes apart, then a standard infusion for at least 12 hours before angiography) or a matching placebo infusion with provisional eptifibatide after angiography (delayed group).
cards.result: The primary end point (death, myocardial infarction, recurrent ischaemia requiring urgent revascularisation, or thrombotic bailout during PCI at 96 hours) occurred in 9.3% of the early-eptifibatide group and 10.0% of the delayed group (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06; p=0.23). At 30 days, death or myocardial infarction occurred in 11.2% versus 12.3% (OR 0.89, 0.79–1.01; p=0.08). Patients in the early group had significantly higher rates of bleeding and red-cell transfusion; there was no significant difference in severe bleeding or non-haemorrhagic serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The trial's era matters: background therapy has since moved to more potent oral P2Y12 inhibition and radial access, both of which shrink any residual room for upstream intravenous platelet blockade. The null is nonetheless the direct answer to the timing question, tested at scale.
cards.source: Giugliano RP et al. Early versus delayed, provisional eptifibatide in acute coronary syndromes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19332455. Registry ID: NCT00089895. cards.headline: De Luca 2011 (meta-analysis of 7 trials, 19,929 patients): upstream vs downstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — mortality 2.0% vs 2.0%, MI 7.0% vs 7.6%, major bleeding 1.8% vs 1.3% (p=0.0002)
cards.summary: De Luca 2011 (meta-analysis of 7 trials, 19,929 patients): upstream vs downstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — mortality 2.0% vs 2.0%, MI 7.0% vs 7.6%, major bleeding 1.8% vs 1.3% (p=0.0002)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials involving 19,929 patients (9,981 upstream, 9,948 downstream) with high-risk acute coronary syndromes undergoing an early invasive strategy, comparing upstream administration of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, tirofiban, or eptifibatide) with selective downstream administration; trials from January 1990 to March 2010.
cards.result: Upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors did not decrease 30-day mortality (2.0% vs 2.0%; p=0.84) or recurrence of myocardial infarction (7.0% vs 7.6%; p=0.11), but were associated with a higher risk of major bleeding complications (1.8% vs 1.3%; p=0.0002). The authors concluded that an upstream strategy cannot be recommended in high-risk ACS patients undergoing an early invasive strategy.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools three different drugs and both ST-elevation and non-ST-elevation presentations within its 'high-risk ACS' frame, so it corroborates EARLY ACS rather than replacing it. Its bleeding estimate is the shelf's harm anchor: small in absolute terms, consistent, and paid for zero measured benefit.
cards.source: De Luca G et al. Meta-analysis of randomized trials of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in high-risk acute coronary syndromes patients undergoing invasive strategy. meta-analysis of randomised trials (de luca 2011) seven randomised trials involving 19,929 patients (9,981 upstream, 9,948 downstream) with high-risk acute coronary syndromes undergoing an early invasive strategy, comparing upstream administration of glycoprotein iib/iiia inhibitors (abciximab, tirofiban, or eptifibatide) with selective downstream administration; trials from january 1990 to march 2010. upstream glycoprotein iib/iiia inhibitors did not decrease 30-day mortality (2.0% vs 2.0%; p=0.84) or recurrence of myocardial infarction (7.0% vs 7.6%; p=0.11), but were associated with a higher risk of major bleeding complications (1.8% vs 1.3%; p=0.0002). the authors concluded that an upstream strategy cannot be recommended in high-risk acs patients undergoing an early invasive strategy. the meta-analysis pools three different drugs and both st-elevation and non-st-elevation presentations within its 'high-risk acs' frame, so it corroborates early acs rather than replacing it. its bleeding estimate is the shelf's harm anchor: small in absolute terms, consistent, and paid for zero measured benefit. de luca g et al. meta-analysis of randomized trials of glycoprotein iib/iiia inhibitors in high-risk acute coronary syndromes patients undergoing invasive strategy. american journal of cardiology. 2011. pmid: 21211597. mesh: acute coronary syndrome/drug therapy/surgery · humans · hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors/therapeutic use · myocardial revascularization · preoperative care/methods · randomized controlled trials as topic

shelves.title: Enoxaparin versus heparin in primary PCI: ATOLL missed its primary endpoint (28% vs 34%; p=0.06) but won its ischaemic secondary endpoints — and a 30,966-patient meta-analysis, partly non-randomised, favoured enoxaparin on death and bleeding
shelves.question: In primary PCI for STEMI, does enoxaparin match unfractionated heparin for death, myocardial infarction, and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage · Electrocardiography · Enoxaparin/administration & dosage · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Heparin/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Recurrence
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised trial and the pooled literature tell adjacent but different stories. In ATOLL (Montalescot G et al., PMID: 21856483), 910 STEMI patients received an intravenous bolus of enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg or unfractionated heparin before primary PCI: the primary endpoint (death, complication of myocardial infarction, procedure failure, or major bleeding at 30 days) occurred in 28% on enoxaparin versus 34% on heparin (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.68–1.01; p=0.06) — a miss — while the main secondary endpoint (death, recurrent acute coronary syndrome, or urgent revascularisation) fell significantly (7% vs 11%; RR 0.59, 0.38–0.91; p=0.015), as did death, complication of MI, or major bleeding (10% vs 15%; p=0.03), with major bleeding itself no different (5% vs 5%; p=0.79). The broader pooled evidence is more favourable: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies (Silvain J et al., PMID: 22306479; 30,966 PCI patients, of whom 10,243 were primary PCI) found enoxaparin associated with lower death (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.57–0.76), death or MI (0.68, 0.57–0.81), and major bleeding (0.80, 0.68–0.95), with the mortality reduction largest in primary PCI (relative risk 0.52, 0.42–0.64) — but that pool mixes randomised and non-randomised studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: in the head-to-head randomised trial enoxaparin matched heparin on its primary endpoint and bleeding while reducing ischaemic secondary endpoints; the stronger mortality claims come from a meta-analysis whose non-randomised components cannot carry them alone.

cards.headline: Montalescot 2011 (ATOLL, n=910): primary endpoint 28% enoxaparin vs 34% heparin (RR 0.83; p=0.06) — missed; main secondary endpoint 7% vs 11% (RR 0.59; p=0.015); major bleeding 5% vs 5%
cards.summary: Montalescot 2011 (ATOLL, n=910): primary endpoint 28% enoxaparin vs 34% heparin (RR 0.83; p=0.06) — missed; main secondary endpoint 7% vs 11% (RR 0.59; p=0.015); major bleeding 5% vs 5%
cards.people: 910 patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (450 enoxaparin, 460 unfractionated heparin), randomised — often by mobile intensive care teams before arrival — to an intravenous bolus of enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg or unfractionated heparin before primary PCI; patients who had received any prior anticoagulant were excluded; patients and caregivers were not masked.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (30-day death, complication of myocardial infarction, procedure failure, or major bleeding) occurred in 126 patients (28%) on enoxaparin versus 155 (34%) on heparin (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.68–1.01; p=0.06). Death (4% vs 6%; p=0.08), complication of MI (4% vs 6%; p=0.21), procedure failure (26% vs 28%; p=0.61), and major bleeding (5% vs 5%; p=0.79) did not differ individually. Enoxaparin significantly reduced the main secondary endpoint (30 [7%] vs 52 [11%]; RR 0.59, 0.38–0.91; p=0.015), the composite of death, complication of MI, or major bleeding (10% vs 15%; p=0.03), and death or complication of MI (8% vs 12%; p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 910 patients, and a primary endpoint diluted by 'procedure failure' (26–28% in both arms) — the trial was powered for a composite it then missed by p=0.06. Its secondary endpoints are hypothesis-supporting, not proof; the honest headline is 'matched on the primary, ahead on ischaemic secondaries'.

cards.headline: Silvain 2012 (meta-analysis, 23 studies, 30,966 PCI patients): enoxaparin vs heparin — death RR 0.66, death or MI RR 0.68, major bleeding RR 0.80; in primary PCI, death RR 0.52
cards.summary: Silvain 2012 (meta-analysis, 23 studies, 30,966 PCI patients): enoxaparin vs heparin — death RR 0.66, death or MI RR 0.68, major bleeding RR 0.80; in primary PCI, death RR 0.52
cards.people: 23 randomised and non-randomised studies representing 30,966 patients undergoing PCI (13,943 enoxaparin, 17,023 unfractionated heparin), including 10,243 patients (33.1%) undergoing primary PCI for STEMI, 8,750 undergoing secondary PCI after fibrinolysis, and 11,973 with non-ST-elevation ACS or stable disease; literature January 1996 to May 2011.
cards.result: Enoxaparin was associated with significant reductions in death (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.57–0.76; p<0.001), the composite of death or myocardial infarction (0.68, 0.57–0.81; p<0.001), complications of myocardial infarction (0.75, 0.60–0.85; p<0.001), and major bleeding (0.80, 0.68–0.95; p=0.009). In primary PCI, the reduction in death (0.52, 0.42–0.64; p<0.001) was particularly marked and was accompanied by less major bleeding (0.72, 0.56–0.93; p=0.01). All relative effects are labelled relative, as the record reports them.
cards.watchOut: The pool deliberately includes non-randomised comparisons, where who received enoxaparin was a clinical choice — confounding by indication can manufacture exactly this pattern of lower death and lower bleeding. ATOLL, the large randomised primary-PCI trial inside the same literature, found neither a mortality nor a bleeding difference, so the meta-analysis's stronger claims are flagged, not adopted (Tier C).
cards.source: Silvain J et al. Efficacy and safety of enoxaparin versus unfractionated heparin during percutaneous coronary intervention: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2012. PMID: 22306479. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: One randomised trial in primary PCI (ATOLL, 910 patients) and one systematic review of 23 randomised and non-randomised PCI studies (30,966 patients).
cards.result: ATOLL: primary endpoint 28% vs 34% (p=0.06); main secondary 7% vs 11% (p=0.015); major bleeding 5% vs 5%. Meta-analysis: death RR 0.66, major bleeding RR 0.80 overall; death RR 0.52 in primary PCI. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised evidence says 'matches, with better ischaemic secondaries'; the mortality claim rests on partly observational pooling.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set: the shelf's stronger reading depends on observational evidence inside the meta-analysis, and it carries a mortality benefit claim — both are developer-review triggers. The randomised-only reading is the conservative one and is stated first on the shelf.

shelves.title: Vascular closure devices after catheterisation: haemostasis is faster, major complications are no different — but groin infection is more frequent (0.6% vs 0.2%) in a meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials
shelves.question: After coronary stenting, do vascular closure devices reduce access-site complications and time to walking compared with manual compression?
shelves.mesh: Angiography · Angioplasty · Bandages · Blood Vessels · Humans · Pressure · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by endpoint: speed yes, safety neutral-to-worse. A meta-analysis of 31 prospective randomised studies (Biancari F et al., PMID: 20362708) including 7,528 patients randomised to a vascular closure device or manual/mechanical compression after diagnostic angiography and/or endovascular procedures found similar results for groin haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, and blood transfusion. Lower-limb ischaemia and other arterial ischaemic complications (0.3% vs 0%; p=0.07) and the need for surgery for vascular complications (0.7% vs 0.4%; p=0.10) were somewhat more frequent with closure devices, and groin infection was significantly more frequent (0.6% vs 0.2%; p=0.02). The one uniform advantage was a significantly shorter time to haemostasis with closure devices, more evident in patients undergoing PCI than in those undergoing diagnostic angiography, among whom adverse-event rates were similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: closure devices shorten time to haemostasis (and so may shorten recovery) without reducing access-site complications, and they add a small excess of groin infection and device-specific arterial complications.

cards.headline: Biancari 2010 (meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials, 7,528 patients): faster haemostasis with closure devices; infection 0.6% vs 0.2% (p=0.02); haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, transfusion all similar
cards.summary: Biancari 2010 (meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials, 7,528 patients): faster haemostasis with closure devices; infection 0.6% vs 0.2% (p=0.02); haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, transfusion all similar
cards.people: 31 prospective randomised studies including 7,528 patients randomised to vascular closure devices or manual/mechanical compression after diagnostic angiography and/or endovascular procedures; most studies excluded patients at high risk of puncture-site complications.
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed similar results in the two groups for groin haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, and blood transfusion. Lower-limb ischaemia and other arterial ischaemic complications (0.3% vs 0%; p=0.07) and need for surgery for vascular complications (0.7% vs 0.4%; p=0.10) were somewhat more frequent with closure devices, and groin infection was significantly more frequent with closure devices (0.6% vs 0.2%; p=0.02). Use of a closure device was uniformly associated with a significantly shorter time to haemostasis, a difference more evident in patients undergoing PCI; among patients undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography, the methods had similar adverse-event rates.
cards.watchOut: The trials pooled several device generations and mechanisms (clips, sutures, collagen plugs) as one intervention, and they mostly excluded the high-risk groins where a device might help or harm most. 'Time to haemostasis' is a process prize — the candidate question's 'time to walking' was not the meta-analysis's reported endpoint, and the shelf does not pretend otherwise.
