shelves.title: Pharmaco-invasive care for STEMI: STREAM matched primary PCI on death, shock, heart failure or reinfarction (12.4% vs 14.3%) with more intracranial bleeding — and TRANSFER-AMI showed routine early transfer beat delayed standard care (11.0% vs 17.2%)
shelves.question: In STEMI patients who cannot reach primary PCI quickly, does a pharmaco-invasive strategy — early fibrinolysis with routine transfer for angiography — match primary PCI for death and ischaemic events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Clopidogrel · Coronary Angiography · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electrocardiography · Enoxaparin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Heart Failure/prevention & control · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages/etiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Tenecteplase · Thrombolytic Therapy/methods · Ticlopidine/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Time-to-Treatment · Tissue Plasminogen Activator/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the strategy matches primary PCI in the trial that asked that question, and beats doing less in the trial that asked the other one. In STREAM (Armstrong PW et al., PMID: 23473396), 1,892 patients with STEMI presenting within 3 hours who could not undergo primary PCI within 1 hour received either prehospital fibrinolysis (tenecteplase, with angiography 6–24 hours later or urgently if lysis failed) or primary PCI: the primary composite (death, shock, congestive heart failure, or reinfarction at 30 days) occurred in 12.4% versus 14.3% (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.09; p=0.21), with emergency angiography required in 36.3% of the fibrinolysis group and more intracranial haemorrhages (1.0% vs 0.2%; p=0.04 — 0.5% vs 0.3% after the protocol amendment halving tenecteplase in patients 75 or older). In TRANSFER-AMI (Cantor WJ et al., PMID: 19553646), 1,059 high-risk STEMI patients lysed at non-PCI centres were randomised to routine transfer for PCI within 6 hours or standard treatment (rescue PCI if required, or delayed angiography): the primary composite at 30 days occurred in 11.0% versus 17.2% (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.87; p=0.004), with no significant difference in major bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT: when primary PCI cannot be delivered promptly, fibrinolysis with routine early transfer achieves outcomes statistically indistinguishable from primary PCI in STREAM — at the price of more intracranial bleeding — and is clearly better than lysis with delayed, selective transfer.

cards.headline: Armstrong 2013 (STREAM, n=1,892): primary composite 12.4% fibrinolysis-first vs 14.3% primary PCI (RR 0.86; p=0.21) — intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0.2% (p=0.04)
cards.summary: Armstrong 2013 (STREAM, n=1,892): primary composite 12.4% fibrinolysis-first vs 14.3% primary PCI (RR 0.86; p=0.21) — intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0.2% (p=0.04)
cards.people: 1,892 patients with STEMI who presented within 3 hours of symptom onset and could not undergo primary PCI within 1 hour, assigned to primary PCI or to fibrinolytic therapy (bolus tenecteplase — amended to half dose at age 75 or older — plus clopidogrel and enoxaparin) before transport to a PCI-capable hospital, with emergency angiography if fibrinolysis failed and otherwise angiography 6–24 hours after randomisation.
cards.result: The primary end point (death, shock, congestive heart failure, or reinfarction up to 30 days) occurred in 116 of 939 patients (12.4%) in the fibrinolysis group and 135 of 943 (14.3%) in the primary PCI group (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.09; p=0.21). Emergency angiography was required in 36.3% of the fibrinolysis group; the remainder underwent angiography at a median of 17 hours. More intracranial haemorrhages occurred with fibrinolysis (1.0% vs 0.2%; p=0.04; after the protocol amendment, 0.5% vs 0.3%; p=0.45); rates of non-intracranial bleeding were similar.
cards.watchOut: 'Not significantly different' in a trial not designed as a formal noninferiority test is weaker than 'proven equivalent' — the confidence interval (0.68–1.09) still admits a 9% relative disadvantage. And the population was early presenters (within 3 hours), the group in whom lysis works best; the result does not extend to late presenters.

cards.headline: Cantor 2009 (TRANSFER-AMI, n=1,059): routine transfer for PCI within 6 hours of lysis — primary composite 11.0% vs 17.2% with standard care (RR 0.64; p=0.004)
cards.summary: Cantor 2009 (TRANSFER-AMI, n=1,059): routine transfer for PCI within 6 hours of lysis — primary composite 11.0% vs 17.2% with standard care (RR 0.64; p=0.004)
cards.people: 1,059 high-risk STEMI patients receiving fibrinolytic therapy at centres without PCI capability, assigned to standard treatment (rescue PCI if required, or delayed angiography) or immediate transfer to another hospital for PCI within 6 hours of fibrinolysis; all received aspirin, tenecteplase, and heparin or enoxaparin, with clopidogrel recommended.
cards.result: Cardiac catheterisation was performed in 88.7% of the standard-treatment group at a median of 32.5 hours after randomisation and in 98.5% of the routine-early-PCI group at a median of 2.8 hours. At 30 days, the primary end point (death, reinfarction, recurrent ischaemia, new or worsening congestive heart failure, or cardiogenic shock) occurred in 11.0% of the routine-early-PCI group versus 17.2% of the standard group (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.87; p=0.004). There were no significant differences in major bleeding.
cards.watchOut: TRANSFER-AMI's comparator is not primary PCI but the older habit of lysing and waiting — so it proves the 'routine transfer' half of the pharmaco-invasive strategy, not equivalence with primary PCI. Its composite also includes recurrent ischaemia, the component most sensitive to simply doing angiography sooner.
cards.source: Cantor WJ et al. Routine early angioplasty after fibrinolysis for acute myocardial infarction. New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19553646. Registry ID: NCT00164190. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 2,951 STEMI patients: STREAM (1,892 patients, pharmaco-invasive vs primary PCI) and TRANSFER-AMI (1,059 patients, routine early transfer after lysis vs standard delayed care).
cards.result: Versus primary PCI: composite 12.4% vs 14.3% (RR 0.86, NS); intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0.2%. Versus standard post-lysis care: composite 11.0% vs 17.2% (RR 0.64; p=0.004). PROPOSED SPLIT — matches primary PCI within wide limits for early presenters, with an intracranial-bleeding cost; clearly beats lysis without routine transfer.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: two randomised trials carry the split. Both trials predate widespread radial primary PCI and current transfer networks; the shelf answers the strategy question for systems where PCI delay is real, which is the question as asked.
cards.source: Synthesis of Armstrong PW et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23473396); Cantor WJ et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19553646).

shelves.title: Opening a persistently occluded infarct artery days later (OAT): no reduction in death, reinfarction, or heart failure over four years (17.2% vs 15.6%) — and a trend toward more reinfarction with PCI (7.0% vs 5.3%)
shelves.question: In stable patients days to weeks after myocardial infarction with a persistently occluded infarct artery, does PCI improve death, reinfarction, or heart failure compared with medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Combined Modality Therapy · Coronary Stenosis/complications/drug therapy/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/epidemiology/etiology · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Myocardial Infarction/complications/therapy · Proportional Hazards Models · Secondary Prevention · Stents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the open-artery hypothesis, tested properly, failed. In the Occluded Artery Trial (Hochman JS et al., PMID: 17105759), 2,166 stable high-risk patients with a totally occluded infarct-related artery 3–28 days after myocardial infarction (ejection fraction under 50% or proximal occlusion) were randomised to routine PCI with stenting plus optimal medical therapy or optimal medical therapy alone. The four-year cumulative primary event rate (death, reinfarction, or NYHA class IV heart failure) was 17.2% with PCI versus 15.6% with medical therapy (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.92–1.45; p=0.20). Reinfarction occurred in 7.0% versus 5.3% (HR 1.36, 0.92–2.00; p=0.13) — nonfatal reinfarction 6.9% versus 5.0% (HR 1.44, 0.96–2.16; p=0.08), with only 0.6% of reinfarctions related to the assigned PCI procedures — while class IV heart failure (4.4% vs 4.5%) and death (9.1% vs 9.4%) were similar, and no subgroup interaction was found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routinely opening a persistently occluded infarct artery in stable patients days to weeks after infarction does not reduce death, reinfarction, or severe heart failure, and may increase reinfarction.

cards.headline: Hochman 2006 (OAT, n=2,166): 4-year primary events 17.2% with PCI vs 15.6% with medical therapy (HR 1.16; p=0.20); death 9.1% vs 9.4%; reinfarction trended higher with PCI (7.0% vs 5.3%)
cards.summary: Hochman 2006 (OAT, n=2,166): 4-year primary events 17.2% with PCI vs 15.6% with medical therapy (HR 1.16; p=0.20); death 9.1% vs 9.4%; reinfarction trended higher with PCI (7.0% vs 5.3%)
cards.people: 2,166 stable patients with total occlusion of the infarct-related artery 3–28 days after myocardial infarction who met a high-risk criterion (ejection fraction <50% or proximal occlusion), assigned to routine PCI and stenting with optimal medical therapy (n=1,082) or optimal medical therapy alone (n=1,084); follow-up four years.
cards.result: The four-year cumulative primary event rate (death, myocardial reinfarction, or NYHA class IV heart failure) was 17.2% in the PCI group and 15.6% in the medical therapy group (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.92–1.45; p=0.20). Reinfarction rates were 7.0% and 5.3% (HR 1.36, 0.92–2.00; p=0.13); nonfatal reinfarction 6.9% and 5.0% (HR 1.44, 0.96–2.16; p=0.08), with only six reinfarctions (0.6%) related to the assigned PCI procedures. NYHA class IV heart failure (4.4% vs 4.5%) and death (9.1% vs 9.4%) were similar, and there was no interaction between treatment effect and any subgroup variable (age, sex, race, infarct artery, ejection fraction, diabetes, Killip class, or time from infarction).
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), and its patients were stable — anyone with ongoing ischaemia, severe heart failure, or instability was outside the question, so the null licenses restraint only in patients who look like OAT's. The reinfarction trend is a trend, not a proven harm; the shelf states it as such.
cards.source: Hochman JS et al. Coronary intervention for persistent occlusion after myocardial infarction. New England Journal of Medicine. 2006. PMID: 17105759. Registry ID: NCT00004562. cards.people: One randomised trial of 2,166 stable patients with a persistently occluded infarct artery 3–28 days after myocardial infarction, routine PCI plus medical therapy versus medical therapy alone, four years.

shelves.title: Cyclosporine at reperfusion in STEMI: no better clinical outcomes in CIRCUS (59.0% vs 58.1%) and no better ST resolution or troponin in CYCLE — the reperfusion-injury idea failed both its tests
shelves.question: In STEMI treated with primary PCI, does intracoronary cyclosporine at reperfusion reduce infarct size or clinical events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Cyclophilins/antagonists & inhibitors · Cyclosporine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography · Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Heart Failure/epidemiology · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/therapy · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Ventricular Remodeling/drug effects · Peptidyl-Prolyl Isomerase D
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two trials, two designs, one answer; note the candidate asked about intracoronary cyclosporine, and both trials in fact gave it intravenously, which the shelf states plainly. In CIRCUS (Cung TT et al., PMID: 26321103), 970 patients with anterior STEMI and a completely occluded culprit artery received an intravenous bolus of cyclosporine 2.5 mg/kg or placebo before recanalisation in primary PCI: the one-year primary outcome (death, worsening heart failure during the initial hospitalisation, rehospitalisation for heart failure, or adverse left-ventricular remodelling) occurred in 59.0% on cyclosporine versus 58.1% on placebo (odds ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.78–1.39; p=0.77), with no reduction in any clinical component and no safety difference. In CYCLE (Ottani F et al., PMID: 26821623), 410 patients with large STEMI and TIMI flow 0–1 received intravenous cyclosporine 2.5 mg/kg or control before primary PCI: ST-segment resolution of at least 70% occurred in 52.0% versus 49.0% (p=0.55), day-4 high-sensitivity troponin T was similar (median 2,160 vs 2,068 ng/L; p=0.85), and ejection fraction, remodelling, and six-month clinical events did not differ, with six-month mortality numerically higher on cyclosporine (5.7% vs 3.2%; p=0.17). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): cyclosporine given at reperfusion does not reduce infarct size surrogates or improve clinical outcomes in STEMI.

cards.headline: Cung 2015 (CIRCUS, n=970): one-year primary outcome 59.0% on cyclosporine vs 58.1% on placebo (OR 1.04; p=0.77) — no component improved
cards.summary: Cung 2015 (CIRCUS, n=970): one-year primary outcome 59.0% on cyclosporine vs 58.1% on placebo (OR 1.04; p=0.77) — no component improved
cards.people: 970 patients with acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction undergoing PCI within 12 hours of symptom onset, with complete occlusion of the culprit artery, assigned to an intravenous bolus of cyclosporine 2.5 mg per kilogram or matching placebo before coronary recanalisation; 395 cyclosporine and 396 placebo patients had evaluable primary-outcome data at one year.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a composite of death from any cause, worsening of heart failure during the initial hospitalisation, rehospitalisation for heart failure, or adverse left-ventricular remodelling (an increase of at least 15% in left-ventricular end-diastolic volume) at one year — occurred in 59.0% of the cyclosporine group and 58.1% of the control group (odds ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.78–1.39; p=0.77). Cyclosporine did not reduce the incidence of the separate clinical components or of other events including recurrent infarction, unstable angina, and stroke, and the safety profile did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: The composite is dominated by the remodelling component, an imaging definition — but every clinical component was also null, so the softness of the composite is not hiding a benefit. About 18% of randomised patients lacked evaluable primary-outcome data, a real but symmetric weakness.
cards.source: Cung TT et al. Cyclosporine before PCI in Patients with Acute Myocardial Infarction. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26321103. Registry ID: NCT01502774. cards.headline: Ottani 2016 (CYCLE, n=410): ST resolution ≥70% in 52.0% on cyclosporine vs 49.0% on control (p=0.55); day-4 troponin 2,160 vs 2,068 ng/L (p=0.85); six-month mortality 5.7% vs 3.2% (p=0.17)
cards.summary: Ottani 2016 (CYCLE, n=410): ST resolution ≥70% in 52.0% on cyclosporine vs 49.0% on control (p=0.55); day-4 troponin 2,160 vs 2,068 ng/L (p=0.85); six-month mortality 5.7% vs 3.2% (p=0.17)
cards.people: 410 patients (mean age 63 years) with large STEMI within 6 hours of symptom onset, TIMI flow grade 0–1 in the infarct-related artery, committed to primary PCI at 31 cardiac care units, assigned to a single intravenous bolus of cyclosporine A 2.5 mg/kg (n=207) or control (n=203) just before primary PCI; primary endpoint ST-segment resolution of at least 70% at 60 minutes after TIMI flow grade 3.
cards.result: ST-segment resolution of at least 70% was found in 52.0% of cyclosporine patients and 49.0% of controls (p=0.55). Median high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T on day 4 was 2,160 ng/L on cyclosporine versus 2,068 ng/L on control (p=0.85). The groups did not differ in left-ventricular ejection fraction on day 4 or at 6 months, and infarct site did not influence efficacy. There were no acute allergic reactions; six-month mortality (5.7% vs 3.2%; p=0.17) and cardiogenic shock (2.4% vs 1.5%; p=0.33) showed non-significant excesses on cyclosporine.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and surrogate-led: CYCLE could have detected a reperfusion signal cheaply and found none, which is its value. Its mortality numbers are far too small to call harm — they are recorded here because a shelf that quotes only the null surrogates would be hiding the direction of the few deaths there were.

shelves.title: Erythropoietin at reperfusion in STEMI: infarct size unchanged in REVEAL (15.8% vs 15.0% of LV mass) and ejection fraction unchanged in HEBE III — with a safety signal in REVEAL's older patients and event composite
shelves.question: In STEMI, does erythropoietin at reperfusion reduce infarct size or improve outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary · Double-Blind Method · Epoetin Alfa · Erythropoietin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Hematinics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy/pathology · Myocardial Reperfusion · Myocardium/pathology · Placebos · Recombinant Proteins · Stents · Stroke · Thrombosis/chemically induced · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Left · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — no infarct-size benefit in either trial, and the safety leans are all in one direction. In REVEAL (Najjar SS et al., PMID: 21558517), 222 STEMI patients who had undergone successful PCI received a single intravenous bolus of epoetin alfa (60,000 units in the efficacy phase) or placebo within 4 hours of reperfusion: infarct size on cardiac MRI was 15.8% of left-ventricular mass on epoetin versus 15.0% on placebo at the first scan (p=0.67) and 10.6% versus 10.4% at 12 weeks (p=0.89); in a prespecified analysis of patients aged 70 or older, infarct size was larger on epoetin (19.9% vs 11.7% of LV mass; p=0.03), and in the safety cohort the composite of death, MI, stroke, or stent thrombosis occurred in 4.0% of epoetin patients versus 0% on placebo (p=0.04). In HEBE III (Voors AA et al., PMID: 20802250), 529 patients received a single 60,000 IU bolus of epoetin alfa after successful primary PCI or standard care alone: ejection fraction at six weeks was 0.53 versus 0.52 (p=0.41), enzymatic infarct size did not differ significantly, though major adverse cardiac events were fewer on epoetin (8 vs 19 events; p=0.032) on very small numbers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): erythropoietin at reperfusion does not reduce infarct size or improve ventricular function after STEMI, and REVEAL raises a specific concern in older patients.

cards.headline: Najjar 2011 (REVEAL, n=222): infarct size 15.8% vs 15.0% of LV mass (p=0.67) — and in patients ≥70, larger on epoetin (19.9% vs 11.7%; p=0.03); safety composite 4.0% vs 0% (p=0.04)
cards.summary: Najjar 2011 (REVEAL, n=222): infarct size 15.8% vs 15.0% of LV mass (p=0.67) — and in patients ≥70, larger on epoetin (19.9% vs 11.7%; p=0.03); safety composite 4.0% vs 0% (p=0.04)
cards.people: 222 patients with STEMI who underwent successful PCI (primary or rescue) at 28 United States sites, assigned to a single intravenous bolus of epoetin alfa or matching saline placebo within 4 hours of reperfusion; the trial had a dose-escalation safety phase and a single-dose (60,000 units) efficacy phase; infarct size was measured by cardiac magnetic resonance at 2–6 days and again at 12 ± 2 weeks.
cards.result: In the efficacy cohort, infarct size did not differ between groups on the first MRI (15.8% of LV mass [95% CI 13.3–18.2] on epoetin alfa vs 15.0% [12.6–17.3] on placebo; p=0.67; n=136) or the second (10.6% [8.4–12.8] vs 10.4% [8.5–12.3]; p=0.89; n=124). In a prespecified analysis of patients aged 70 years or older (n=21), mean infarct size in the first week was larger on epoetin (19.9% [14.0–25.7]) than on placebo (11.7% [7.2–16.1]; p=0.03). In the safety cohort, the composite of death, MI, stroke, or stent thrombosis occurred in 5 of 125 patients (4.0%) who received epoetin alfa and in none of 97 on placebo (p=0.04).
cards.watchOut: The harm signals rest on tiny numbers — 21 older patients in the subgroup, five events in the safety cohort — and would not convict on their own. But they point the same way as the null efficacy result, and erythropoietin has a plausible prothrombotic mechanism; the shelf reports them as concerns, not verdicts (Tier C).
cards.source: Najjar SS et al. Intravenous erythropoietin in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: REVEAL: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21558517. cards.headline: Voors 2010 (HEBE III, n=529): ejection fraction at 6 weeks 0.53 on epoetin vs 0.52 on control (p=0.41); enzymatic infarct size similar; major adverse cardiac events 8 vs 19 (p=0.032) on small numbers
cards.summary: Voors 2010 (HEBE III, n=529): ejection fraction at 6 weeks 0.53 on epoetin vs 0.52 on control (p=0.41); enzymatic infarct size similar; major adverse cardiac events 8 vs 19 (p=0.032) on small numbers
cards.people: 529 patients with a successful PCI for a first STEMI, randomised to standard medical care alone or with a single intravenous bolus of 60,000 IU epoetin alfa within 3 hours after PCI; primary endpoint left-ventricular ejection fraction after 6 weeks by planar radionuclide ventriculography; secondary endpoints included enzymatic infarct size and major adverse cardiovascular events.
cards.result: After a mean of 6.5 weeks, ejection fraction was 0.53 (± 0.10) in the epoetin group and 0.52 (± 0.11) in the control group (p=0.41). Median area under the curve for creatine kinase over 72 hours was 50,136 U/L per 72 h on epoetin versus 53,510 on control (p=0.058). More major adverse cardiac events occurred in the control group than in the epoetin group (19 vs 8 events; p=0.032). The investigators concluded that a single high dose of epoetin after successful PCI for STEMI did not improve ejection fraction at 6 weeks, while noting the favourable event count and safety profile.
cards.watchOut: HEBE III was open (no placebo bolus) and its one positive signal — 8 versus 19 events — is exactly the kind of small-count secondary finding that REVEAL's opposite safety signal cancels out. Two trials, two event leans in opposite directions, and identical nulls on the imaging endpoints: the imaging is what both trials were built to measure, and it is null in both.
cards.source: Voors AA et al. A single dose of erythropoietin in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. European Heart Journal. 2010. PMID: 20802250. Registry ID: NCT00449488. cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 751 STEMI patients receiving a single intravenous bolus of epoetin alfa (60,000 units) at or just after primary PCI: REVEAL (222 patients, MRI infarct size) and HEBE III (529 patients, ejection fraction).

Safety: REVEAL composite 4.0% vs 0% (p=0.04) and larger infarcts in patients ≥70 on epoetin; HEBE III events 8 vs 19 favouring epoetin on small counts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), with REVEAL's harm leans on the face of the shelf.

shelves.title: Bone-marrow cells after a heart attack: ejection fraction rose 2.5 points more than placebo in REPAIR-AMI, but the larger BAMI trial found no fewer deaths — 3.3% versus 3.8% at two years
shelves.question: After myocardial infarction, does intracoronary bone-marrow cell therapy improve ejection fraction, death, or reinfarction compared with control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bone Marrow Transplantation/methods · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Vessels · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intra-Arterial · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Recurrence · Stem Cell Transplantation/methods · Stroke Volume · Transplantation, Autologous · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a surrogate moved, survival did not. In REPAIR-AMI (Schächinger V et al., PMID: 16990384), 204 patients received intracoronary bone-marrow-derived progenitor cells or placebo 3–7 days after reperfused myocardial infarction: ejection fraction rose 5.5 points on cells versus 3.0 on placebo at 4 months (p=0.01), and the prespecified 1-year composite of death, recurrent infarction, or any revascularisation was significantly reduced (p=0.01). BAMI (Mathur A et al., PMID: 32860406), the larger mortality trial, recruited only 375 of its planned patients and found all-cause mortality at 2 years of 3.26% on cells versus 3.82% on control — no difference it could meaningfully test — with heart-failure hospitalisation in 2.7% versus 8.1% and stroke hospitalisations in 4 cell patients versus none. PROPOSED SPLIT: a modest ejection-fraction gain in one placebo-controlled trial, no demonstrated effect on death or reinfarction in the trial built to measure them.

cards.headline: Schächinger 2006 (REPAIR-AMI): ejection fraction +5.5 points on bone-marrow cells versus +3.0 on placebo at 4 months (p=0.01); 1-year composite of death, reinfarction, or revascularisation significantly reduced (p=0.01)
cards.summary: Schächinger 2006 (REPAIR-AMI): ejection fraction +5.5 points on bone-marrow cells versus +3.0 on placebo at 4 months (p=0.01); 1-year composite of death, reinfarction, or revascularisation significantly reduced (p=0.01)
cards.people: 204 patients with acute myocardial infarction after successful reperfusion therapy, randomised in a multicentre trial to intracoronary infusion of bone-marrow-derived progenitor cells or placebo medium into the infarct artery 3–7 days after reperfusion.
cards.result: Absolute improvement in global left ventricular ejection fraction at 4 months was 5.5±7.3% on cells versus 3.0±6.5% on placebo (p=0.01); patients with baseline ejection fraction at or below the median of 48.9% derived the most benefit (absolute improvement 5.0 percentage points; 95% CI 2.0 to 8.1). At 1 year, intracoronary cell infusion was associated with a reduction in the prespecified combined end point of death, recurrence of myocardial infarction, and any revascularisation procedure (p=0.01; the abstract reports the p-value without the event rates).
cards.watchOut: The powered endpoint is a 4-month ejection-fraction change — a surrogate — and the 1-year clinical composite is reported as a p-value without absolute rates in the record, in a trial of 204 patients not powered for death or reinfarction. The composite includes any revascularisation, the softest of its components.
cards.source: Schächinger V et al. Intracoronary bone marrow-derived progenitor cells in acute myocardial infarction. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2006. PMID: 16990384. cards.headline: Mathur 2020 (BAMI): mortality at 2 years 3.26% on cells versus 3.82% on control — but recruitment collapsed to 375 patients, so the trial itself says no definitive conclusion is possible
cards.summary: Mathur 2020 (BAMI): mortality at 2 years 3.26% on cells versus 3.82% on control — but recruitment collapsed to 375 patients, so the trial itself says no definitive conclusion is possible
cards.people: 375 patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction and ejection fraction ≤45% after primary angioplasty, randomised across Europe to intracoronary infusion of bone-marrow-derived mononuclear cells 2–8 days after primary PCI (185 patients) or optimal medical therapy alone (190 patients), followed for 2 years.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 2 years was 3.26% (6 deaths; 95% CI 1.48–7.12%) in the cell group and 3.82% (7 deaths; 95% CI 1.84–7.84%) in the control group. Hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 5 patients (2.7%) on cells versus 15 (8.1%) on control; no control patient and 4 cell patients (2.2%) were hospitalised for stroke. Neither adverse events nor serious adverse events differed between groups.
cards.watchOut: BAMI was designed as a hypothesis-testing mortality trial but, in the authors' own words, unexpectedly low recruitment means it 'no longer qualifies as a hypothesis-testing trial, but is instead an observational study with no definitive conclusions possible' — the heart-failure and stroke imbalances rest on 5–15 events each and cannot be read either way.
cards.source: Mathur A et al. The effect of intracoronary infusion of bone marrow-derived mononuclear cells on all-cause mortality in acute myocardial infarction: the BAMI trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: the ventricle squeezed a little harder in one trial; nobody has shown fewer deaths or reinfarctions
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ventricle squeezed a little harder in one trial; nobody has shown fewer deaths or reinfarctions
cards.people: Two randomised trials of intracoronary autologous bone-marrow cells after reperfused myocardial infarction: REPAIR-AMI (204 patients, placebo-controlled, ejection-fraction primary endpoint) and BAMI (375 patients, open control, mortality primary endpoint).
cards.result: Ejection fraction at 4 months: +5.5 versus +3.0 points (REPAIR-AMI, p=0.01). Death at 2 years: 3.26% versus 3.82% (BAMI, 13 deaths total). REPAIR-AMI's 1-year composite of death, reinfarction, or any revascularisation was significantly reduced (p=0.01) without rates in the record. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the mortality question rests on an under-recruited trial, so any survival claim either way is personally reviewable.
cards.watchOut: Cell preparations, timing (2–8 days), and control conditions differ between the trials, and BAMI's control arm received no placebo infusion — performance bias cannot be excluded for its soft endpoints. Neither trial was powered to detect a plausible effect on reinfarction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schächinger V et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16990384); Mathur A et al. European Heart Journal. 2020 (PMID: 32860406).

shelves.title: Adenosine in STEMI: no clinical benefit in 2,118 patients and no smaller infarcts in REFLO-STEMI — with a per-protocol harm signal in the smaller trial
shelves.question: In STEMI treated with primary PCI, does intracoronary or intravenous adenosine reduce infarct size or microvascular obstruction compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Prospective Studies · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction · Thrombectomy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoints both trials prespecified. AMISTAD II (Ross AM et al., PMID: 15936605) randomised 2,118 anterior-STEMI patients to intravenous adenosine or placebo: the primary composite of new heart failure, heart-failure rehospitalisation, or death at 6 months occurred in 17.9% on placebo versus 16.3% on pooled adenosine (16.5% and 16.1% by dose; p=0.43). REFLO-STEMI (Nazir SA et al., PMID: 27147610) gave high-dose intracoronary adenosine during primary PCI and found infarct size of 10.1% of left-ventricular mass versus 8.3% on control (p=0.062) and microvascular obstruction no different — with a per-protocol analysis showing more major adverse cardiac events on adenosine (hazard ratio 5.39 at 30 days). The one positive signal anywhere is a subset: infarct size 11% versus 27% (p=0.023) at the higher AMISTAD II dose in 243 imaged patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, two null primary endpoints, one hypothesis-generating dose subset.

cards.headline: Nazir 2016 (REFLO-STEMI): infarct size 10.1% versus 8.3% of left-ventricular mass (p=0.062) and microvascular obstruction unchanged — per-protocol major cardiac events higher on adenosine (HR 5.39)
cards.summary: Nazir 2016 (REFLO-STEMI): infarct size 10.1% versus 8.3% of left-ventricular mass (p=0.062) and microvascular obstruction unchanged — per-protocol major cardiac events higher on adenosine (HR 5.39)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded endpoints (Nazir 2016, REFLO-STEMI)
cards.people: 247 STEMI patients with single-vessel disease presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset, randomised 1:1:1 to intracoronary adenosine (2–3 mg total), sodium nitroprusside, or standard primary PCI, with drug given after thrombectomy and again after stenting; infarct size measured by cardiac MRI at 24–96 hours in 197 patients, clinical follow-up to 6 months.
cards.result: Infarct size (% left-ventricular mass, median) was 10.1 (IQR 4.7–16.2) on adenosine versus 8.3 (1.9–14.0) on control (p=0.062); microvascular obstruction was 1.0 versus 0.3 (% mass; p=0.205). On per-protocol analysis, infarct size was larger on adenosine (12.0 versus 8.3; p=0.031), major adverse cardiac events were increased at 30 days (HR 5.39; 95% CI 1.18–24.60; p=0.04) and 6 months (HR 6.53; 95% CI 1.46–29.2; p=0.01), and ejection fraction was lower (42.5±7.2% versus 45.7±8.0%; p=0.027).
cards.watchOut: The harm signal comes from a per-protocol analysis of a 247-patient trial with wide confidence intervals — it is a warning, not proof of harm — and the trial was open-label (endpoints blinded). Only 197 of 247 patients contributed the MRI primary endpoint.

cards.headline: Ross 2005 (AMISTAD II): primary endpoint 17.9% on placebo versus 16.3% on adenosine (p=0.43) — infarct size smaller only at the 70 µg/kg/min dose in a 243-patient imaging subset (11% versus 27%, p=0.023)
cards.summary: Ross 2005 (AMISTAD II): primary endpoint 17.9% on placebo versus 16.3% on adenosine (p=0.43) — infarct size smaller only at the 70 µg/kg/min dose in a 243-patient imaging subset (11% versus 27%, p=0.023)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Ross 2005, AMISTAD II)
cards.people: 2,118 patients with evolving anterior STEMI receiving thrombolysis or primary angioplasty, randomised to a 3-hour infusion of adenosine 50 µg/kg/min, adenosine 70 µg/kg/min, or placebo; infarct size measured by technetium-99m sestamibi tomography in a subset of 243 patients.
cards.result: The primary end point — new congestive heart failure beginning more than 24 hours after randomisation, first rehospitalisation for heart failure, or death within 6 months — occurred in 17.9% on placebo versus 16.3% on pooled adenosine (16.5% at 50 µg/kg/min and 16.1% at 70 µg/kg/min; p=0.43). Median infarct size in the imaging subset was 17% on pooled adenosine versus 27% on placebo (p=0.074), with a dose-response: 11% at the high dose (p=0.023 versus placebo) and 23% at the low dose (not significant).
cards.watchOut: The trial predates routine primary PCI (many patients received thrombolysis), used intravenous rather than intracoronary adenosine, and its only positive finding is a dose subgroup of a 243-patient imaging subset — exactly the kind of signal that needs its own trial, which the authors themselves called for.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two routes, two eras, the same answer on the primary endpoint — nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: two routes, two eras, the same answer on the primary endpoint — nothing
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 2,365 STEMI patients: AMISTAD II (2,118, intravenous adenosine with thrombolysis or angioplasty, clinical primary endpoint) and REFLO-STEMI (247, intracoronary adenosine at primary PCI, MRI primary endpoint).
cards.result: Clinical composite at 6 months: 17.9% placebo versus 16.3% adenosine (AMISTAD II). Infarct size: 10.1% versus 8.3% of left-ventricular mass (REFLO-STEMI, p=0.062). Subset signals point in opposite directions: smaller infarcts at the high intravenous dose in AMISTAD II's imaging subset, larger infarcts and more events per-protocol in REFLO-STEMI. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial tested the other's regimen, so 'adenosine' here is two different treatments; the honest summary is that neither regimen improved its primary endpoint, not that every adenosine strategy is disproven. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials carry the null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nazir SA et al. European Heart Journal. 2016 (PMID: 27147610); Ross AM et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2005 (PMID: 15936605).

shelves.title: Ischaemic postconditioning at primary PCI: death or heart-failure admission in 10.5% versus 11.2% over 38 months in DANAMI-3 — and reperfusion no better in POST
shelves.question: In STEMI, does ischaemic postconditioning at reperfusion reduce infarct size or clinical events compared with conventional primary PCI?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cause of Death · Coronary Vessels · Denmark · Female · Heart Failure/epidemiology · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Ischemic Postconditioning/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Myocardium · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods · Proportional Hazards Models · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction/therapy · Stents · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two multicentre randomised trials, concordantly null. In DANAMI-3 iPOST (Engstrøm T et al., PMID: 28249094), 1,234 STEMI patients were randomised to postconditioning or conventional primary PCI: the composite of all-cause death and heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 10.5% with postconditioning versus 11.2% without over a median 38 months (hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.66–1.30; p=0.66), with hazard ratios of 0.75 for death and 0.99 for heart failure, both non-significant. In POST (Hahn JY et al., PMID: 24068776), 700 patients showed complete ST-segment resolution in 40.5% versus 41.5% (p=0.79) and 30-day major adverse cardiac events in 4.3% versus 3.7% (p=0.70). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the balloon ritual added minutes and hope, and neither reperfusion quality nor clinical outcomes moved.

cards.headline: Engstrøm 2017 (DANAMI-3 iPOST): death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10.5% with postconditioning versus 11.2% with conventional PCI (HR 0.93; p=0.66) over a median 38 months
cards.summary: Engstrøm 2017 (DANAMI-3 iPOST): death or heart-failure hospitalisation 10.5% with postconditioning versus 11.2% with conventional PCI (HR 0.93; p=0.66) over a median 38 months
cards.people: 1,234 patients (79.0% men; mean age 62 years) with STEMI, symptom onset within 12 hours, and TIMI grade 0–1 flow in the infarct artery, randomised in Denmark to postconditioning — 4 repeated 30-second balloon occlusions each followed by 30 seconds of reperfusion after opening the artery, before stenting — or conventional primary PCI; median follow-up 38 months (IQR 24–58).
cards.result: The primary outcome (all-cause death or hospitalisation for heart failure) occurred in 65 patients (10.5%) with postconditioning and 69 (11.2%) with conventional PCI (hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.66–1.30; p=0.66). Component hazard ratios were 0.75 (95% CI 0.49–1.14; p=0.18) for all-cause death and 0.99 (95% CI 0.60–1.64; p=0.96) for heart failure.
cards.watchOut: The death hazard ratio of 0.75 has a confidence interval running from a halving to a 14% increase — the trial excludes a large benefit on the composite but not a modest one on death alone. Postconditioning was tested only in TIMI 0–1 flow at arrival, the subgroup where the mechanism should work best, which strengthens the null.
cards.source: Engstrøm T et al. Effect of Ischemic Postconditioning During Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiology. 2017. cards.headline: Hahn 2013 (POST): complete ST-segment resolution 40.5% versus 41.5% (p=0.79); 30-day major cardiac events 4.3% versus 3.7% (p=0.70)
cards.summary: Hahn 2013 (POST): complete ST-segment resolution 40.5% versus 41.5% (p=0.79); 30-day major cardiac events 4.3% versus 3.7% (p=0.70)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial with blinded endpoints (Hahn 2013, POST)
cards.people: 700 patients undergoing primary PCI for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset, randomised 1:1 in a multicentre Korean trial to postconditioning (4 cycles of 1-minute low-pressure balloon inflation separated by 1 minute of deflation, immediately after flow restoration) or conventional primary PCI.
cards.result: Complete ST-segment resolution (>70%) at 30 minutes occurred in 40.5% of the postconditioning group and 41.5% of the conventional group (absolute difference −1.0%; 95% CI −8.4 to 6.4; p=0.79). Myocardial blush grade 0 or 1 occurred in 17.2% versus 22.4% (p=0.20), and major adverse cardiac events at 30 days (death, myocardial infarction, severe heart failure, or stent thrombosis) in 4.3% versus 3.7% (p=0.70).
cards.watchOut: POST's primary endpoint is an electrocardiographic reperfusion measure at 30 minutes, not infarct size or survival, and the trial was open-label — but its null on the mechanism's own intermediate endpoint removes the usual excuse that the clinical trials were simply too small.
cards.source: Hahn JY et al. Ischemic postconditioning during primary percutaneous coronary intervention: the effects of postconditioning on myocardial reperfusion in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (POST) randomized trial. shelves.title: Metformin after STEMI in people without diabetes: ejection fraction 53.1% on metformin versus 54.8% on placebo at 4 months — numerically the wrong way (GIPS-III)
shelves.question: In non-diabetic patients with STEMI, does metformin after primary PCI improve ejection fraction compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/prevention & control · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one well-run trial, null on every measure. GIPS-III (Lexis CPH et al., PMID: 24687169) randomised 380 patients without diabetes presenting with STEMI to metformin 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 4 months after primary PCI. Ejection fraction by MRI at 4 months was 53.1% (95% CI 51.6–54.6%) on metformin versus 54.8% (95% CI 53.5–56.1%) on placebo (p=0.10) — the point estimate favours placebo. NT-proBNP was identical at 167 ng/L in both groups (p=0.66), major adverse cardiac events occurred in 6 patients (3.1%) on metformin versus 2 (1.1%) on placebo (p=0.16), and no lactic acidosis occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the animal-data promise of metformin as post-infarction cardioprotection did not survive contact with 380 randomised humans.

cards.headline: Lexis 2014 (GIPS-III): ejection fraction 53.1% versus 54.8% (p=0.10), NT-proBNP 167 versus 167 ng/L, major cardiac events 3.1% versus 1.1% — metformin did nothing measurable
cards.summary: Lexis 2014 (GIPS-III): ejection fraction 53.1% versus 54.8% (p=0.10), NT-proBNP 167 versus 167 ng/L, major cardiac events 3.1% versus 1.1% — metformin did nothing measurable
cards.people: 380 patients without diabetes presenting with STEMI and undergoing primary PCI at a single Dutch centre (2011–2013), randomised to metformin hydrochloride 500 mg twice daily (191 patients) or placebo (189 patients) for 4 months; ejection fraction assessed by MRI in 135 and 136 patients respectively, with no deaths and no losses to follow-up at 4 months.
cards.result: Left ventricular ejection fraction at 4 months was 53.1% (95% CI 51.6–54.6%) on metformin versus 54.8% (95% CI 53.5–56.1%) on placebo (p=0.10). NT-proBNP was 167 ng/L (IQR 65–393) versus 167 ng/L (IQR 74–383) (p=0.66). Major adverse cardiac events (death, reinfarction, or target-lesion revascularisation) occurred in 6 patients (3.1%) on metformin versus 2 (1.1%) on placebo (p=0.16). Creatinine and glycated haemoglobin did not differ, and there were no cases of lactic acidosis.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 380 patients with a 4-month MRI surrogate as its primary endpoint: it rules out the large ventricular-function benefit the animal data suggested, but it was never sized to detect an effect on death or reinfarction — events were so few (8 total) that the event comparison is decorative. Only 271 of 380 patients contributed the MRI endpoint.

shelves.question: In STEMI, does interleukin-6 blockade with tocilizumab improve myocardial salvage compared with placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for a scan measure, in one small trial. ASSAIL-MI (Broch K et al., PMID: 33858620) randomised 199 STEMI patients at three Norwegian PCI centres to a single 280 mg infusion of tocilizumab or placebo before PCI. The primary endpoint, myocardial salvage index on MRI at 3–7 days, was larger on tocilizumab by an adjusted 5.6 percentage points (95% CI 0.2 to 11.3; p=0.04), and microvascular obstruction was less extensive — but final infarct size, the measure patients would care about, was 7.2% versus 9.1% of myocardial volume (p=0.08), not significant, and adverse events were evenly distributed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single small trial moved the salvage index while its own final-infarct-size endpoint missed significance — promising physiology, unproven therapy. Tier C: single-trial benefit claim.

cards.people: 199 patients admitted with STEMI within 6 hours of symptom onset at 3 high-volume Norwegian PCI centres, randomised 1:1 to a single intravenous infusion of tocilizumab 280 mg (101 patients) or placebo (98 patients) promptly before PCI; primary endpoint the myocardial salvage index by MRI at 3–7 days.
cards.result: The myocardial salvage index was larger in the tocilizumab group (adjusted between-group difference 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI 0.2 to 11.3; p=0.04). Microvascular obstruction was less extensive on tocilizumab, but final infarct size did not differ significantly: 7.2% versus 9.1% of myocardial volume (p=0.08). Adverse events were evenly distributed across the treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval for the primary endpoint starts at 0.2 points — one or two patients' scans from null — and the trial's own final-infarct-size measure missed significance; the salvage index is a ratio that can improve while the absolute scar does not. A single 199-patient trial with no clinical-outcome power: Tier C.

shelves.title: Complete revascularisation in MI patients aged 75+: death, MI, stroke, or revascularisation in 15.7% versus 21.0% at one year (FIRE) — one trial, composite-driven
shelves.question: In older patients with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, does physiology-guided complete revascularisation beat culprit-only PCI for death and reinfarction?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Acute Kidney Injury/etiology · Myocardial Infarction/surgery/therapy · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects/methods · ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction/surgery/therapy · Stroke/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial in exactly the population the question asks about. FIRE (Biscaglia S et al., PMID: 37634150) randomised 1,445 patients aged 75 or older (median 80) with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease to physiology-guided complete revascularisation or culprit-only PCI. The primary composite — death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or any revascularisation at 1 year — occurred in 113 patients (15.7%) on complete revascularisation versus 152 (21.0%) on culprit-only (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57–0.93; p=0.01), and cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction in 8.9% versus 13.5% (hazard ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.47–0.88). The safety composite of contrast-associated kidney injury, stroke, or bleeding was 22.5% versus 20.4% (p=0.37). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real reduction in a composite that includes revascularisation, from a single trial — Tier C, because a cardiovascular-event benefit claim resting on one trial is the developer's to review.

cards.headline: Biscaglia 2023 (FIRE): primary composite 15.7% versus 21.0% (HR 0.73; p=0.01); cardiovascular death or MI 8.9% versus 13.5% (HR 0.64); safety composite 22.5% versus 20.4%
cards.summary: Biscaglia 2023 (FIRE): primary composite 15.7% versus 21.0% (HR 0.73; p=0.01); cardiovascular death or MI 8.9% versus 13.5% (HR 0.64); safety composite 22.5% versus 20.4%
cards.people: 1,445 patients aged 75 years or older (median age 80; 36.5% women; 35.2% admitted with STEMI) with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease undergoing PCI of the culprit lesion, randomised to physiology-guided complete revascularisation of functionally significant nonculprit lesions (720 patients; significance by pressure wire or angiography) or no further revascularisation (725 patients); outcomes at 1 year.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or any revascularisation) occurred in 113 patients (15.7%) in the complete-revascularisation group and 152 (21.0%) in the culprit-only group (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.93; p=0.01) — an absolute difference of 5.3 percentage points. Cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction occurred in 64 (8.9%) versus 98 (13.5%) (hazard ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.88). The safety composite (contrast-associated acute kidney injury, stroke, or bleeding) occurred in 22.5% versus 20.4% (p=0.37).
cards.watchOut: The record does not break out death alone, and the primary composite includes any revascularisation — the component most easily moved by the strategy itself, since culprit-only patients keep untreated lesions that later declare themselves. One trial, 1-year horizon, in patients already selected as fit for PCI: Tier C.
cards.source: Biscaglia S et al. Complete or Culprit-Only PCI in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37634150. Registry ID: NCT03772743. shelves.title: Routine invasive strategy in older NSTEMI patients: cardiovascular death or MI in 25.6% versus 26.3% over four years (SENIOR-RITA) — nonfatal MI lower, cardiovascular death numerically higher
shelves.question: In frail older patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, does a routine invasive strategy improve death or myocardial infarction compared with conservative management?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Combined Modality Therapy/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Conservative Treatment/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Coronary Angiography/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Frail Elderly · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Myocardial Revascularization/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Non-ST Elevated Myocardial Infarction/diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the composite the trial prespecified. SENIOR-RITA (Kunadian V et al., PMID: 39225274) randomised 1,518 patients aged 75 or older with NSTEMI (mean age 82; 32% frail) at 48 UK sites to an invasive strategy of angiography and revascularisation plus best medical therapy, or best medical therapy alone. Over a median 4.1 years, cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 193 patients (25.6%) on the invasive strategy versus 201 (26.3%) on conservative care (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.77–1.14; p=0.53). The components pointed in opposite directions: cardiovascular death 15.8% versus 14.2% (hazard ratio 1.11) and nonfatal MI 11.7% versus 15.0% (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57–0.99), with procedural complications in fewer than 1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the largest trial in this population found no net gain from routinely taking older NSTEMI patients to the catheter lab.

cards.headline: Kunadian 2024 (SENIOR-RITA): primary outcome 25.6% invasive versus 26.3% conservative (HR 0.94; p=0.53); cardiovascular death 15.8% versus 14.2%, nonfatal MI 11.7% versus 15.0%
cards.summary: Kunadian 2024 (SENIOR-RITA): primary outcome 25.6% invasive versus 26.3% conservative (HR 0.94; p=0.53); cardiovascular death 15.8% versus 14.2%, nonfatal MI 11.7% versus 15.0%
cards.people: 1,518 patients aged 75 years or older with NSTEMI at 48 UK sites (mean age 82 years; 45% women; 32% frail — frailty and high comorbidity burden were explicitly eligible), randomised 1:1 to an invasive strategy (coronary angiography and revascularisation plus best available medical therapy; 753 patients) or a conservative strategy (best available medical therapy alone; 765 patients); median follow-up 4.1 years.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction) occurred in 193 patients (25.6%) in the invasive-strategy group and 201 (26.3%) in the conservative group (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.14; p=0.53). Cardiovascular death occurred in 15.8% versus 14.2% (hazard ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.44); nonfatal myocardial infarction in 11.7% versus 15.0% (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.99). Procedural complications occurred in less than 1% of patients.
cards.watchOut: The nonfatal-MI reduction and the cardiovascular-death point estimate pull against each other, and neither alone was the primary endpoint — reading either component as the answer would misstate the trial. Crossover and the conservative group's later clinically driven angiography are part of a strategy trial's design, diluting contrasts over 4.1 years.
cards.source: Kunadian V et al. Invasive Treatment Strategy for Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39225274. Registry ID: ISRCTN11343602. shelves.question: In patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI or unstable angina, does an early invasive strategy improve death or myocardial infarction compared with a selective invasive strategy?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Angina, Unstable/mortality/therapy · Cardiovascular Agents/therapeutic use · Coronary Angiography/mortality/statistics & numerical data · Coronary Artery Bypass/methods/mortality · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Myocardial Infarction/mortality/therapy · Myocardial Revascularization/mortality/statistics & numerical data · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/methods/mortality · Postoperative Hemorrhage/etiology/mortality · Reoperation/mortality/statistics & numerical data · Stroke/etiology/mortality · Time-to-Treatment · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the composite, not for survival. The After Eighty study (Tegn N et al., PMID: 26794722) randomised 457 patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI or unstable angina in Norway to an early invasive strategy or conservative optimum medical treatment. Over a median 1.53 years, the primary composite of myocardial infarction, need for urgent revascularisation, stroke, and death occurred in 93 patients (40.6%) invasively managed versus 140 (61.4%) conservatively managed (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p=0.0001). But the components split: myocardial infarction hazard ratio 0.52 (p=0.0010) and urgent revascularisation 0.19 (p=0.0010), while stroke was 0.60 (p=0.2650) and death from any cause 0.89 (95% CI 0.62–1.28; p=0.5340) — no significant difference. Major bleeding was 1.7% versus 1.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer infarctions and far fewer urgent procedures, no shown survival gain, in a single 457-patient trial — Tier C.

cards.headline: Tegn 2016 (After Eighty): primary composite 40.6% versus 61.4% (HR 0.53; p=0.0001) — MI HR 0.52, urgent revascularisation HR 0.19, stroke HR 0.60, death HR 0.89
cards.summary: Tegn 2016 (After Eighty): primary composite 40.6% versus 61.4% (HR 0.53; p=0.0001) — MI HR 0.52, urgent revascularisation HR 0.19, stroke HR 0.60, death HR 0.89
cards.type: Randomised open-label multicentre trial (Tegn 2016, After Eighty study)
cards.people: 457 patients aged 80 years or older with NSTEMI or unstable angina admitted to 16 hospitals in south-east Norway, randomised to an invasive strategy (early coronary angiography with immediate assessment for PCI, bypass surgery, and optimum medical treatment; 229 patients) or a conservative strategy (optimum medical treatment alone; 228 patients); median follow-up 1.53 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome (myocardial infarction, need for urgent revascularisation, stroke, and death) occurred in 93 patients (40.6%) in the invasive group and 140 (61.4%) in the conservative group (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p=0.0001) — an absolute difference of 20.8 percentage points. Component hazard ratios: myocardial infarction 0.52 (95% CI 0.35–0.76; p=0.0010), need for urgent revascularisation 0.19 (0.07–0.52; p=0.0010), stroke 0.60 (0.25–1.46; p=0.2650), and death from any cause 0.89 (0.62–1.28; p=0.5340). Major bleeding complications occurred in 4 patients (1.7%) invasively versus 4 (1.8%) conservatively; minor bleeding in 23 (10.0%) versus 16 (7.0%). The authors note efficacy was diluted with increasing age after adjustment for creatinine and effect modification.
cards.watchOut: Almost half the composite's absolute gain is the urgent-revascularisation component — an endpoint the conservative strategy is structurally exposed to, since its patients keep untreated lesions. Death, the component patients ask about first, was not significantly reduced, and the trial predates SENIOR-RITA's larger null on cardiovascular death or MI (shelf #3357); the two must be read together.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a big composite win built from infarctions and procedures avoided, not from lives extended
cards.summary: Synthesis: a big composite win built from infarctions and procedures avoided, not from lives extended
cards.people: One randomised open-label trial (After Eighty, 457 patients aged ≥80 with NSTEMI or unstable angina, invasive versus conservative strategy, median 1.53-year follow-up).
cards.result: Composite 40.6% versus 61.4% (HR 0.53). Death HR 0.89 (not significant); stroke HR 0.60 (not significant); major bleeding 1.7% versus 1.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claim on a composite that includes death.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design with a procedure-counting composite invites ascertainment bias on the soft components; the hard components (death, stroke) are the honest counterweight and both are null here. Numbers needed: roughly 5 patients treated invasively to prevent one composite event, of uncertain composition.

shelves.title: OCT versus IVUS guidance for PCI: target-vessel failure 2.5% versus 3.1% in OCTIVUS and 5.2% versus 4.9% in OPINION — the light-based camera matched ultrasound in both trials
shelves.question: For guiding PCI, does optical coherence tomography match intravascular ultrasound for death, myocardial infarction, and revascularisation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention/adverse effects/methods · Coronary Angiography/methods · Tomography, Optical Coherence/methods · Prospective Studies · Drug-Eluting Stents/adverse effects · Ultrasonography, Interventional/adverse effects/methods · Treatment Outcome · Myocardial Infarction/etiology · Coronary Artery Disease/diagnostic imaging/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised head-to-head trials, both meeting noninferiority. OCTIVUS (Kang DY et al., PMID: 37634092) randomised 2,008 patients to OCT-guided or IVUS-guided PCI: the composite of cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-vessel revascularisation at 1 year occurred in 25 patients (2.5%) on OCT guidance versus 31 (3.1%) on IVUS guidance (absolute difference −0.6 percentage points; p<0.001 for noninferiority), with contrast-induced nephropathy in 1.4% versus 1.5% and major procedural complications in 2.2% versus 3.7% (p=0.047). OPINION (Kubo T et al., PMID: 29121226) found target-vessel failure in 5.2% on optical frequency-domain imaging versus 4.9% on IVUS at 12 months (noninferiority p=0.042), with identical in-stent restenosis rates of 1.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): OCT is not better than IVUS — it is, on two trials, its equal.

cards.headline: Kang 2023 (OCTIVUS): primary endpoint 2.5% on OCT guidance versus 3.1% on IVUS guidance (p<0.001 for noninferiority); major procedural complications 2.2% versus 3.7%
cards.summary: Kang 2023 (OCTIVUS): primary endpoint 2.5% on OCT guidance versus 3.1% on IVUS guidance (p<0.001 for noninferiority); major procedural complications 2.2% versus 3.7%
cards.people: 2,008 patients with significant coronary artery lesions undergoing PCI at South Korean centres, randomised 1:1 to OCT-guided (1,005 patients) or IVUS-guided (1,003 patients) PCI with drug-eluting stents; primary endpoint at 1 year.
cards.result: Primary end point events (cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 25 patients in the OCT group (Kaplan–Meier estimate 2.5%) and 31 in the IVUS group (3.1%) — absolute difference −0.6 percentage points (upper boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 0.97 points; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Contrast-induced nephropathy occurred in 14 patients (1.4%) versus 15 (1.5%) (p=0.85); major procedural complications in 22 (2.2%) versus 37 (3.7%) (p=0.047), with no imaging procedure-related complications observed.
cards.watchOut: Event rates were lower than expected, which widens the practical meaning of 'noninferior' — with 56 total events, the trial shows the strategies are close, not that they are identical, and the authors themselves flag the selected study population. Open-label design; operators knew which camera they were using.
cards.source: Kang DY et al. Optical Coherence Tomography-Guided or Intravascular Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: The OCTIVUS Randomized Clinical Trial. Circulation. 2023. PMID: 37634092. Registry ID: NCT03394079. cards.headline: Kubo 2017 (OPINION): target-vessel failure 5.2% on optical imaging versus 4.9% on IVUS (noninferiority p=0.042); in-stent restenosis 1.6% in both groups
cards.summary: Kubo 2017 (OPINION): target-vessel failure 5.2% on optical imaging versus 4.9% on IVUS (noninferiority p=0.042); in-stent restenosis 1.6% in both groups
cards.people: 829 patients undergoing PCI with a second-generation drug-eluting stent at Japanese centres, randomised 1:1 to optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI, the OCT variant used; 414 patients) or IVUS guidance (415 patients); primary endpoint target-vessel failure to 12 months, angiographic follow-up in 89.8%.
cards.result: Target-vessel failure (cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 21 of 401 patients (5.2%) with OFDI guidance and 19 of 390 (4.9%) with IVUS guidance (hazard ratio 1.07; upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI 1.80; p for noninferiority 0.042). Binary restenosis at 8 months was identical in-stent (1.6% versus 1.6%; p=1.00) and near-identical in-segment (6.2% versus 6.0%; p=1.00).
cards.watchOut: OPINION used one stent platform and one OFDI system in Japanese practice, and its noninferiority margin was generous relative to a 5% event rate — the upper confidence limit of 1.80 on the hazard ratio allows meaningful harm that the point estimate hides. Both trials answer 'is OCT as good', not 'is either better than angiography alone'.

cards.people: Two randomised non-inferiority trials of OCT-family guidance versus IVUS guidance for PCI: OCTIVUS (2,008 patients, 1-year clinical composite) and OPINION (829 patients, 12-month target-vessel failure plus 8-month angiography).
cards.result: Primary composites: 2.5% versus 3.1% (OCTIVUS) and 5.2% versus 4.9% (OPINION), both meeting noninferiority; restenosis identical where measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is a bounded claim: both trials permit small differences in either direction, and neither was powered for death alone. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the equivalence.

shelves.title: TAVR versus surgery in low/intermediate-risk aortic stenosis: death or stroke at one year in 5.4% versus 10.0% (DEDICATE) — noninferior, and numerically ahead, at one year only
shelves.question: In low- or intermediate-risk severe aortic stenosis, does transcatheter replacement match surgery for death or stroke at one year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Aortic Valve/surgery · Aortic Valve Stenosis/surgery/mortality · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/adverse effects/methods/mortality · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Stroke/epidemiology/etiology/mortality · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods/mortality · Risk Factors · Germany
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — at one year, in one trial. DEDICATE (Blankenberg S et al., PMID: 38588025) randomised 1,414 patients with severe aortic stenosis at low or intermediate surgical risk (median STS risk score 1.8%; mean age 74) at 38 German sites to transcatheter aortic-valve implantation or surgical replacement, with valve choice at operator discretion. The primary composite of death from any cause or fatal or nonfatal stroke at 1 year occurred in an estimated 5.4% on TAVI versus 10.0% on surgery (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.35–0.79; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Death from any cause was 2.6% versus 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.43; 95% CI 0.24–0.73) and stroke 2.9% versus 4.7% (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.35–1.06); procedural complications were 1.5% versus 1.0%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): TAVI more than matched surgery at one year — but one year is where TAVI's advantages are largest and its durability questions unasked, and a mortality claim from a single trial is Tier C.

cards.headline: Blankenberg 2024 (DEDICATE): death or stroke 5.4% versus 10.0% (HR 0.53); death alone 2.6% versus 6.2% (HR 0.43); stroke 2.9% versus 4.7%
cards.summary: Blankenberg 2024 (DEDICATE): death or stroke 5.4% versus 10.0% (HR 0.53); death alone 2.6% versus 6.2% (HR 0.43); stroke 2.9% versus 4.7%
cards.people: 1,414 patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis at low or intermediate surgical risk, eligible for both approaches, randomised at 38 German sites to TAVI (701 patients) or surgical aortic-valve replacement (713 patients); mean age 74±4 years, 57% men, median Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk score 1.8%; prosthesis type selected at operator discretion in both arms; primary outcome at 1 year.
cards.result: The Kaplan–Meier estimate of the primary outcome (death from any cause or fatal or nonfatal stroke) at 1 year was 5.4% in the TAVI group and 10.0% in the surgical group (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.79; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Death from any cause occurred in 2.6% versus 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.43; 95% CI 0.24 to 0.73); stroke in 2.9% versus 4.7% (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.06). Procedural complications occurred in 1.5% of TAVI patients and 1.0% of surgical patients.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority trial whose point estimates favour TAVI strongly at the single time point — 1 year — when surgery's upfront hazard is fully counted and transcatheter-valve durability is not yet tested; patients were mostly low-risk (median STS 1.8%), so 'intermediate' in the question is thinly populated, and operator-chosen prostheses make this a strategy comparison, not a device comparison. Mortality benefit from one trial: Tier C.

shelves.title: Small-annulus TAVR: clinical events matched (9.4% versus 10.6%), but valve dysfunction was 9.4% on the self-expanding valve versus 41.6% on the balloon-expandable (SMART)
shelves.question: In severe aortic stenosis with a small annulus, does a balloon-expandable valve match a self-expanding valve for valve function and clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Aortic Valve/surgery · Aortic Valve Stenosis/surgery/complications · Bioprosthesis/adverse effects · Heart Failure · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Prosthesis Design · Prosthesis Failure · Stroke/etiology · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement/adverse effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the patients fared the same; the valves did not. SMART (Herrmann HC et al., PMID: 38587261) randomised 716 patients with severe aortic stenosis and an annulus area of 430 mm² or less (mean age 80; 87% women) to a self-expanding supraannular valve or a balloon-expandable valve. The clinical coprimary endpoint — death, disabling stroke, or heart-failure rehospitalisation through 12 months — occurred in an estimated 9.4% with the self-expanding valve versus 10.6% with the balloon-expandable valve (difference −1.2 percentage points; p<0.001 for noninferiority). The valve-function coprimary endpoint split wide open: bioprosthetic-valve dysfunction in 9.4% versus 41.6% (difference −32.2 points; p<0.001 for superiority), mean gradient 7.7 versus 15.7 mmHg, effective orifice area 1.99 versus 1.50 cm², and moderate or severe prosthesis–patient mismatch at 30 days in 11.2% versus 35.3%. PROPOSED SPLIT: balloon-expandable matches on 12-month clinical outcomes and loses decisively on haemodynamics — whether that loss becomes clinical over time is the unanswered part. Tier C: single-trial, industry-funded.

cards.headline: Herrmann 2024 (SMART): death, disabling stroke, or heart-failure admission 9.4% versus 10.6% (noninferior) — valve dysfunction 9.4% versus 41.6%, gradient 7.7 versus 15.7 mmHg (superior) for the self-expanding valve
cards.summary: Herrmann 2024 (SMART): death, disabling stroke, or heart-failure admission 9.4% versus 10.6% (noninferior) — valve dysfunction 9.4% versus 41.6%, gradient 7.7 versus 15.7 mmHg (superior) for the self-expanding valve
cards.type: Randomised trial with coprimary non-inferiority and superiority endpoints (Herrmann 2024, SMART)
cards.people: 716 patients with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and aortic-valve annulus area ≤430 mm², treated at 83 sites in 13 countries (mean age 80 years; 87% women; mean STS Predicted Risk of Mortality 3.3%), randomised 1:1 to TAVR with a self-expanding supraannular valve or a balloon-expandable valve; endpoints through 12 months. The trial was funded by Medtronic, maker of the self-expanding valve tested.
cards.result: The Kaplan–Meier estimate of death, disabling stroke, or rehospitalisation for heart failure through 12 months was 9.4% with the self-expanding valve and 10.6% with the balloon-expandable valve (difference −1.2 percentage points; 90% CI −4.9 to 2.5; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Bioprosthetic-valve dysfunction occurred in an estimated 9.4% versus 41.6% (difference −32.2 points; 95% CI −38.7 to −25.6; p<0.001 for superiority). Mean gradient at 12 months was 7.7 versus 15.7 mmHg; effective orifice area 1.99 versus 1.50 cm²; haemodynamic structural valve dysfunction 3.5% versus 32.8%; moderate or severe prosthesis–patient mismatch at 30 days 11.2% versus 35.3% (all p<0.001). Major safety endpoints appeared similar.
cards.watchOut: The dysfunction composite is built largely from haemodynamic measures (gradient, mismatch) that favour a supraannular design by construction, in a trial funded by that design's manufacturer — the 32-point gap is real arithmetic on a partly definitional endpoint, while the clinical composite it should predict was identical at 12 months. Whether mismatch at this level shortens valve life or lives is exactly what 12 months cannot show. Tier C.

shelves.title: Valve-in-valve TAVR versus redo surgery for a failed surgical valve: early death 2.8% versus 5.0% in pooled observational data — but midterm mortality equal and the new valve leaks and pinches more
shelves.question: In failed surgical bioprosthetic aortic valves, does valve-in-valve TAVR match redo surgical replacement for death and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aortic Valve/diagnostic imaging/surgery · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement · Bioprosthesis · Reoperation · Heart Valve Prosthesis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/methods · Aortic Valve Stenosis · Aortic Valve Insufficiency/surgery/etiology · Myocardial Infarction/etiology · Stroke/etiology · Treatment Outcome · Risk Factors · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Multicenter Studies as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — valve-in-valve wins the first month and loses the echo. There are no randomised trials; two meta-analyses of observational studies agree on the shape. Raschpichler M et al. (PMID: 36533610) pooled 15 studies and 8,881 patients: short-term mortality was 2.8% after valve-in-valve TAVR versus 5.0% after redo surgery (risk ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.34–0.91; p=0.02) and acute kidney failure was less frequent (risk ratio 0.54), but midterm mortality did not differ (hazard ratio 1.27; 95% CI 0.72–2.25), while prosthetic regurgitation (risk ratio 4.18) and severe prosthesis–patient mismatch (risk ratio 3.12) were more frequent after valve-in-valve and gradients were higher. Nasir MM et al. (PMID: 38723857), pooling 24 studies and 25,216 patients, found 30-day mortality odds ratio 0.50, major bleeding odds ratio 0.28, and no difference in 1-year mortality — with more paravalvular leak and higher gradients after valve-in-valve. PROPOSED SPLIT: an early-survival advantage bought with worse valve haemodynamics, all of it confounded by who gets chosen for which procedure. Tier C: observational evidence throughout.

cards.headline: Raschpichler 2022: short-term mortality 2.8% versus 5.0% (RR 0.55) favouring valve-in-valve; midterm mortality HR 1.27 (not significant); regurgitation RR 4.18 and severe mismatch RR 3.12 against it
cards.summary: Raschpichler 2022: short-term mortality 2.8% versus 5.0% (RR 0.55) favouring valve-in-valve; midterm mortality HR 1.27 (not significant); regurgitation RR 4.18 and severe mismatch RR 3.12 against it
cards.people: 15 non-randomised studies totalling 8,881 patients with failed surgical aortic bioprostheses: 4,458 (50.2%) treated with valve-in-valve TAVR and 4,423 with redo surgical aortic valve replacement; literature searched to December 2021, protocol registered (PROSPERO CRD42021228752).
cards.result: Short-term mortality was 2.8% after valve-in-valve versus 5.0% after redo surgery (risk ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.34–0.91; p=0.02). Midterm mortality did not differ (hazard ratio 1.27; 95% CI 0.72–2.25). Acute kidney failure was less frequent after valve-in-valve (risk ratio 0.54; 95% CI 0.33–0.88; p=0.02), whereas prosthetic aortic valve regurgitation (risk ratio 4.18; 95% CI 1.88–9.3; p=0.003) and severe prosthesis–patient mismatch (risk ratio 3.12; 95% CI 2.35–4.1; p<0.001) occurred more frequently, and mean transvalvular gradient was higher (standardised mean difference 0.44; p=0.008). Stroke (p=0.26), myocardial infarction (p=0.93), and pacemaker implantation (p=0.21) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is observational: patients sent for redo surgery and patients offered a catheter procedure differ in age, frailty, and anatomy in ways adjustment cannot fully remove — the authors themselves call for a randomised trial. 'Short-term' and 'midterm' are pooled across studies with differing horizons.
cards.source: Raschpichler M et al. cards.headline: Nasir 2024: 30-day mortality OR 0.50 and major bleeding OR 0.28 favour valve-in-valve across 25,216 patients; 1-year mortality, stroke, and MI no different; device success lower (OR 0.25)
cards.summary: Nasir 2024: 30-day mortality OR 0.50 and major bleeding OR 0.28 favour valve-in-valve across 25,216 patients; 1-year mortality, stroke, and MI no different; device success lower (OR 0.25)
cards.people: 24 studies pooling 25,216 patients comparing valve-in-valve TAVR with redo surgical replacement for failed bioprosthetic aortic valves (stenosis population), literature to August 2023, mean follow-up 16.4 months.
cards.result: Valve-in-valve TAVR showed lower 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.58; p<0.00001), less new-onset atrial fibrillation (odds ratio 0.34; 95% CI 0.17 to 0.67; p=0.002), and fewer major bleeding events (odds ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.17 to 0.45; p<0.00001), but lower device success (odds ratio 0.25; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.53; p=0.0003). There were no significant differences in 1-year mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, post-procedure ejection fraction, or effective orifice area; paravalvular leaks, aortic regurgitation, and mean aortic-valve gradient were all increased with valve-in-valve.
cards.watchOut: This pool overlaps heavily with the earlier meta-analysis (the same registries re-pooled), so the two cards are not independent confirmations — and device success and paravalvular leak definitions vary by study. Confounding by indication is the whole ballgame here and no pooling removes it. Tier C.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two pools, one story — survive the month more often, live with a leakier, tighter valve
cards.summary: Synthesis: two pools, one story — survive the month more often, live with a leakier, tighter valve
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of exclusively observational comparisons (15 studies / 8,881 patients; 24 studies / 25,216 patients, with overlapping source studies) of valve-in-valve TAVR versus redo surgical replacement for failed surgical bioprostheses. No randomised trial exists in either record.
cards.result: Short-term mortality: 2.8% versus 5.0% (RR 0.55) and 30-day OR 0.50, favouring valve-in-valve. Midterm/1-year mortality: no difference (HR 1.27, NS; 1-year NS). Regurgitation, paravalvular leak, severe mismatch, and gradients: consistently worse after valve-in-valve. Stroke: no difference in either pool. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: observational evidence with strong selection effects.
cards.watchOut: Because the pools share primary studies, their agreement is weaker evidence than it looks. The honest clinical read is patient selection: high-risk patients gain most from avoiding redo surgery, and low-risk patients are precisely those in whom the haemodynamic penalty has longest to matter — the subgroup no observational pool can cleanly isolate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raschpichler M et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2022 (PMID: 36533610); Nasir MM et al. The American Journal of Cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 38723857).
