shelves.title: Prosthetic valve thrombosis: ultraslow low-dose thrombolysis freed 90% of valves in PROMETEE with 6.7% complications — but the older pooled comparison says surgery embolises and bleeds less
shelves.question: In prosthetic valve thrombosis, does slow-infusion low-dose thrombolysis match surgery for success, embolism, and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Echocardiography, Transesophageal · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Diseases/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Heart Valve Diseases/complications/surgery · Heart Valve Prosthesis/adverse effects · Heart Ventricles · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Prosthesis Failure · Retrospective Studies · Thrombolytic Therapy/methods · Thrombosis/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/etiology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the modern regimen looks gentle; the comparative evidence is old and points the other way. PROMETEE (Özkan M et al., PMID: 26299240) treated 114 patients (120 episodes of prosthetic valve thrombosis, 64.2% obstructive) at a single centre with transoesophageal-echo-guided ultraslow infusion of low-dose alteplase (25 mg over 25 hours, no bolus): overall thrombolytic success was 90% (95% CI 0.85–0.95) with an overall complication rate of 6.7% (3.3% nonfatal major, 2.5% minor, 0.8% death). The comparative record is a meta-analysis of observational studies (Karthikeyan G et al., PMID: 23329151) pooling 690 episodes: complete restoration of valve function in 86.5% with urgent surgery versus 69.7% with fibrinolysis (odds ratio 2.53; p=0.066, not significant), death in 13.5% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.95; not significant), but thromboembolism in 1.6% versus 16% (odds ratio 0.10; p<0.001), major bleeding in 1.4% versus 5% (odds ratio 0.27), and recurrent thrombosis in 7.1% versus 25.4% (odds ratio 0.25) — all favouring surgery. PROPOSED SPLIT: ultraslow thrombolysis succeeds often with few complications in expert hands, but it has never been randomised against surgery, and the regimens in the comparative pool predate it. Tier C.

cards.headline: Özkan 2015 (Ultra-slow PROMETEE): success 90% across 120 thrombosis episodes; complications 6.7% total, death 0.8% — with no surgical comparator
cards.summary: Özkan 2015 (Ultra-slow PROMETEE): success 90% across 120 thrombosis episodes; complications 6.7% total, death 0.8% — with no surgical comparator
cards.type: Single-centre prospective case series (Özkan 2015, Ultra-slow PROMETEE)
cards.people: 114 patients with prosthetic (mechanical) valve thrombosis in 120 episodes treated at one Turkish centre, 2009–2013 — obstructive thrombosis in 77 episodes (64.2%), nonobstructive in 43 (35.8%) — all receiving transoesophageal-echocardiography-guided ultraslow infusion of low-dose alteplase, 25 mg over 25 hours without bolus, repeated as needed.
cards.result: Overall thrombolytic success was 90% (95% CI 0.85–0.95). The overall complication rate was 6.7%: 3.3% nonfatal major, 2.5% minor, and 0.8% death. Predictors of unsuccessful thrombolysis included higher NYHA class (the only independent predictor on multivariable analysis), thrombus cross-sectional area, duration of suboptimal anticoagulation, lower baseline valve area, and atrial fibrillation; predictors of complications were atrial fibrillation, higher NYHA class, and thrombus area.
cards.watchOut: There is no comparison group at all: 90% success in a centre that pioneered the technique, in episodes two-thirds obstructive, cannot be set against surgical results from other eras and centres. NYHA class IV patients fared worst — exactly the patients for whom the surgery-versus-lysis decision is hardest.

complications 6.7% total, death 0.8% — with no surgical comparator in prosthetic valve thrombosis, does slow-infusion low-dose thrombolysis match surgery for success, embolism, and bleeding? single-centre prospective case series (özkan 2015, ultra-slow prometee) 114 patients with prosthetic (mechanical) valve thrombosis in 120 episodes treated at one turkish centre, 2009–2013 — obstructive thrombosis in 77 episodes (64.2%), nonobstructive in 43 (35.8%) — all receiving transoesophageal-echocardiography-guided ultraslow infusion of low-dose alteplase, 25 mg over 25 hours without bolus, repeated as needed. overall thrombolytic success was 90% (95% ci 0.85–0.95). the overall complication rate was 6.7%: 3.3% nonfatal major, 2.5% minor, and 0.8% death. predictors of unsuccessful thrombolysis included higher nyha class (the only independent predictor on multivariable analysis), thrombus cross-sectional area, duration of suboptimal anticoagulation, lower baseline valve area, and atrial fibrillation; predictors of complications were atrial fibrillation, higher nyha class, and thrombus area. there is no comparison group at all: 90% success in a centre that pioneered the technique, in episodes two-thirds obstructive, cannot be set against surgical results from other eras and centres. nyha class iv patients fared worst — exactly the patients for whom the surgery-versus-lysis decision is hardest. özkan m et al. ultraslow thrombolytic therapy: a novel strategy in the management of prosthetic mechanical valve thrombosis and the predictors of outcome: the ultra-slow prometee trial. american heart journal. 2015. pmid: 26299240. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · dose-response relationship, drug · echocardiography, transesophageal · female · fibrinolytic agents/administration & dosage · follow-up studies · heart diseases/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · heart valve diseases/complications/surgery · heart valve prosthesis/adverse effects · heart ventricles · humans · infusions, intravenous · male · middle aged · postoperative complications · practice guidelines as topic · prosthesis failure · retrospective studies · thrombolytic therapy/methods · thrombosis/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/etiology · time factors · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Karthikeyan 2013: valve function restored 86.5% (surgery) versus 69.7% (fibrinolysis), not significant — but thromboembolism 1.6% versus 16% (OR 0.10) and recurrence 7.1% versus 25.4% (OR 0.25) favoured surgery
cards.summary: Karthikeyan 2013: valve function restored 86.5% (surgery) versus 69.7% (fibrinolysis), not significant — but thromboembolism 1.6% versus 16% (OR 0.10) and recurrence 7.1% versus 25.4% (OR 0.25) favoured surgery
cards.people: 7 observational studies including 690 episodes of left-sided prosthetic valve thrombosis — 446 treated with urgent surgery and 244 with fibrinolytic therapy — each study contributing at least 5 patients per treatment.
cards.result: Complete restoration of valve function did not differ significantly: 86.5% with surgery versus 69.7% with fibrinolysis (odds ratio 2.53; 95% CI 0.94–6.78; p=0.066). In-hospital death was 13.5% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.95; 95% CI 0.63–5.98; p=0.244). Surgery was associated with significantly less thromboembolism (1.6% versus 16%; odds ratio 0.10; 95% CI 0.04–0.24; p<0.001), major bleeding (1.4% versus 5%; odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.08–0.98; p=0.046), and recurrent prosthetic valve thrombosis (7.1% versus 25.4%; odds ratio 0.25; 95% CI 0.08–0.74; p=0.013).
cards.watchOut: The fibrinolysis in these studies is largely older, faster, higher-dose practice — not the PROMETEE ultraslow regimen — so the embolism gap may describe a superseded technique; and sicker patients are channelled to lysis when surgery is refused or impossible, biasing death and success comparisons in unknowable directions. Heterogeneity for the primary outcome was high (I²=74%). Tier C.

cards.headline: Synthesis: success rates overlap; the safety comparison depends entirely on which decade's thrombolysis you mean
cards.summary: Synthesis: success rates overlap; the safety comparison depends entirely on which decade's thrombolysis you mean
cards.people: One single-arm series of the modern ultraslow regimen (PROMETEE, 120 episodes) and one meta-analysis of observational surgery-versus-fibrinolysis comparisons (690 episodes, largely older regimens). No randomised trial in either record.
cards.result: Ultraslow lysis success 90%, complications 6.7%, death 0.8% (single-arm). Pooled older comparison: success 86.5% versus 69.7% (NS), death 13.5% versus 9% (NS), thromboembolism 1.6% versus 16% favouring surgery. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: The two cards cannot be combined into a single verdict: PROMETEE's low complication rate is precisely the claim the older pool cannot test. A 2024 observational comparison restricted to patients without haemodynamic compromise exists in the literature but was not carded here; the coordinator may wish to note it as a reference-add candidate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Özkan M et al. American Heart Journal. 2015 (PMID: 26299240); Karthikeyan G et al. European Heart Journal. 2013 (PMID: 23329151).

shelves.title: Leadless versus transvenous pacemakers in Medicare: fewer chronic complications (adjusted HR 0.69) and reinterventions (HR 0.62) at two years — but pericardial effusion or perforation doubled at implant (0.8% versus 0.4%)
shelves.question: In patients who need permanent pacing but not defibrillation, does a leadless pacemaker reduce complications compared with a transvenous pacemaker?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Bradycardia/mortality/physiopathology/therapy · Cardiac Catheterization/methods · Cause of Death/trends · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Ventricles · Humans · Male · Pacemaker, Artificial · Retrospective Studies · Survival Rate/trends · Time Factors · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — safer by the year, riskier on the day. The Micra Coverage with Evidence Development study compared leadless with transvenous single-chamber ventricular pacemakers in US Medicare patients. At implant, adjusted acute complication rates were 7.7% versus 7.4% (Piccini JP et al., PMID: 34319383; risk difference 0.3 points; p=0.49), but pericardial effusion and/or perforation was significantly higher with the leadless device (0.8% versus 0.4%; p=0.004), while 6-month complications already favoured leadless (adjusted hazard ratio 0.77). At 2 years (El-Chami MF et al., PMID: 34788416), leadless patients had fewer reinterventions (adjusted hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.45–0.85) and fewer chronic complications (adjusted hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.81), with adjusted all-cause mortality no different (hazard ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.91–1.04). PROPOSED SPLIT: no leads means no lead problems — the trade is a doubled, still uncommon, risk of perforating the heart at implant. Tier C: all observational, in patients who were sicker at baseline (end-stage kidney disease in 12.0% versus 2.3%).

cards.headline: Piccini 2021 (Micra CED): adjusted acute complications 7.7% versus 7.4% (p=0.49) — pericardial effusion/perforation 0.8% versus 0.4% (p=0.004) against leadless; 6-month complications HR 0.77 for it
cards.summary: Piccini 2021 (Micra CED): adjusted acute complications 7.7% versus 7.4% (p=0.49) — pericardial effusion/perforation 0.8% versus 0.4% (p=0.004) against leadless; 6-month complications HR 0.77 for it
cards.type: Observational cohort study, Medicare claims (Piccini 2021, Micra CED)
cards.people: 15,408 US Medicare fee-for-service patients implanted in 2017–2018 with a leadless single-chamber ventricular pacemaker (5,746) or a transvenous single-chamber ventricular pacemaker (9,662), mean age 81.0 years; leadless patients were sicker (end-stage kidney disease 12.0% versus 2.3%; mean Charlson Comorbidity Index 5.1 versus 4.6).
cards.result: Unadjusted acute (30-day) complications were higher with leadless devices (8.4% versus 7.3%; p=0.02) but not after adjustment (7.7% versus 7.4%; risk difference 0.3; 95% CI −0.6 to 1.3; p=0.49). Pericardial effusion and/or perforation within 30 days was higher with leadless pacing in both unadjusted (0.8% versus 0.4%; p<0.001) and adjusted (0.8% versus 0.4%; risk difference 0.4; 95% CI 0.1 to 0.7; p=0.004) analyses. Six-month complications were lower with leadless pacing (adjusted hazard ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.62–0.96; p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Claims-based and non-randomised: the leadless group was deliberately chosen for patients at high infection or access risk (note the kidney-disease gap), so adjustment is doing heavy lifting in both directions. Only single-chamber ventricular systems are compared — nothing here speaks to dual-chamber pacing, which most patients receive.
cards.source: Piccini JP et al. Contemporaneous Comparison of Outcomes Among Patients Implanted With a Leadless vs Transvenous Single-Chamber Ventricular Pacemaker. JAMA Cardiology. 2021. PMID: 34319383. cards.headline: El-Chami 2022 (Micra CED 2-year): reinterventions HR 0.62 and chronic complications HR 0.69 favour leadless; all-cause mortality HR 0.97 — no difference
cards.summary: El-Chami 2022 (Micra CED 2-year): reinterventions HR 0.62 and chronic complications HR 0.69 favour leadless; all-cause mortality HR 0.97 — no difference
cards.type: Observational cohort study, 2-year follow-up (El-Chami 2022, Micra CED)
cards.people: US Medicare patients implanted March 2017–December 2018 with a leadless ventricular pacemaker (6,219, identified from claims linked to manufacturer device registration) or a transvenous ventricular pacemaker (10,212, from facilities that also implanted leadless devices); outcomes compared with Cox models over 2 years.
cards.result: Compared with transvenous pacing, leadless patients had significantly fewer reinterventions (adjusted hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.45–0.85; p=0.003) and fewer chronic complications (adjusted hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.81; p<0.0001). Adjusted all-cause mortality at 2 years did not differ (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.91–1.04; p=0.37). Baseline imbalance persisted: end-stage renal disease in 12.0% of leadless versus 2.3% of transvenous patients, Charlson index 5.1 versus 4.6.
cards.watchOut: Same cohort family as the 2021 report, extended — not an independent replication. 'Chronic complications' in claims data capture coded events (infection, dislodgement, pocket problems) that structurally cannot occur in the same way without a pocket or lead, so part of the advantage is definitional; the perforation disadvantage, by contrast, is a hard event. Tier C.
cards.source: El-Chami MF et al. Leadless vs. transvenous single-chamber ventricular pacing in the Micra CED study: 2-year follow-up. European Heart Journal. 2022. PMID: 34788416. cards.headline: Synthesis: the leadless bargain — pay a small upfront perforation risk, stop paying lead rent
cards.summary: Synthesis: the leadless bargain — pay a small upfront perforation risk, stop paying lead rent
cards.people: One continuously enrolling observational Medicare cohort (Micra CED) reported at 30 days/6 months (15,408 patients) and at 2 years (16,431 patients), comparing leadless with transvenous single-chamber ventricular pacing. No randomised comparison exists in these records.
cards.result: Acute complications: 7.7% versus 7.4% adjusted (NS). Pericardial effusion/perforation: 0.8% versus 0.4%. Chronic complications at 2 years: HR 0.69. Reinterventions: HR 0.62. Mortality: HR 0.97 (NS). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: observational evidence.
cards.watchOut: Both reports draw on the same study, so this shelf rests on one data source wearing two jackets; device retrieval at end of life, tricuspid injury over decades, and dual-chamber leadless systems are outside the record entirely.
cards.source: Synthesis of Piccini JP et al. JAMA Cardiology. 2021 (PMID: 34319383); El-Chami MF et al. European Heart Journal. 2022 (PMID: 34788416).

shelves.title: Extravascular ICD: defibrillation succeeded in 98.7% at implant and 92.6% were free of major complications at 6 months — against performance goals, not against a transvenous control
shelves.question: In patients who need a defibrillator without pacing, does a fully extravascular ICD defibrillate reliably with fewer lead complications than transvenous systems?
shelves.mesh: Arrhythmias, Cardiac/therapy · Defibrillators, Implantable/adverse effects · Electric Countershock/adverse effects · Humans · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for reliability; the 'fewer complications than transvenous' half of the question has no comparative data at all. The Extravascular ICD Pivotal Study (Friedman P et al., PMID: 36036522) was a prospective single-group premarket study: of 356 enrolled patients, 316 had an implantation attempt, and among 302 in whom ventricular arrhythmia was induced and testing completed, successful defibrillation at implantation was 98.7% (lower boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 96.6%, against a performance goal of 88%). Freedom from major system- or procedure-related complications at 6 months was 92.6% (lower boundary 89.0%, goal 79%); 25 major complications occurred in 23 of 316 patients (7.3%), with no major intraprocedural complications. Over a mean 10.6 months, 29 patients received 118 inappropriate shocks, antitachycardia pacing succeeded in an estimated 50.8% of episodes, and 8 systems were explanted without replacement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the device demonstrably shocks — whether it beats the transvenous systems it is meant to displace is untested. Tier C: single-arm evidence, sponsor-funded.

cards.headline: Friedman 2022 (Extravascular ICD Pivotal): defibrillation success 98.7% at implant; freedom from major complications 92.6% at 6 months; 29 patients received inappropriate shocks
cards.summary: Friedman 2022 (Extravascular ICD Pivotal): defibrillation success 98.7% at implant; freedom from major complications 92.6% at 6 months; 29 patients received inappropriate shocks
cards.type: Prospective single-group premarket study (Friedman 2022, Extravascular ICD Pivotal Study)
cards.people: 356 patients with a class I or IIa indication for an ICD enrolled globally, 316 with an implantation attempt of the extravascular ICD (single lead implanted substernally, capable of antitachycardia and pause-prevention pacing); defibrillation testing completed in 302 patients; mean follow-up 10.6 months. Funded by Medtronic.
cards.result: Successful defibrillation at implantation occurred in 98.7% of tested patients (lower boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 96.6%; p<0.001 against the 88% performance goal), and 299 of 316 patients (94.6%) were discharged with a working system. The Kaplan–Meier estimate of freedom from major system- or procedure-related complications at 6 months was 92.6% (lower boundary 89.0%; p<0.001 against the 79% goal); 25 major complications occurred in 23 of 316 patients (7.3%), with no major intraprocedural complications. Antitachycardia pacing success was estimated at 50.8% (95% CI 23.3 to 77.8); 29 patients received 118 inappropriate shocks for 81 arrhythmic episodes, and 8 systems were explanted without extravascular replacement.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm by design: every number is judged against a negotiated performance goal, not against a transvenous ICD — so the question's comparative half (fewer lead complications) is simply unanswered, and 6-month safety says nothing about substernal lead performance over the decades these devices stay implanted. Inappropriate shocks in 29 of ~316 patients within a year is the figure to watch as follow-up lengthens. Tier C.
cards.source: Friedman P et al. Efficacy and Safety of an Extravascular Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36036522. Registry ID: NCT04060680. cards.headline: Synthesis: a device that clears its own bar — the comparison that matters has not been run
cards.summary: Synthesis: a device that clears its own bar — the comparison that matters has not been run
cards.people: One prospective single-group pivotal study (356 enrolled, 316 implant attempts, mean follow-up 10.6 months) of a substernal-lead extravascular ICD in patients with a standard ICD indication.
cards.result: Defibrillation success 98.7%; discharged with a working system 94.6%; major complications in 7.3% by 6 months; inappropriate shocks in 29 patients; 8 explants. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-arm, sponsor-funded, no comparator.
cards.watchOut: Patients needing bradycardia pacing beyond pause-prevention, or resynchronisation, are outside this device's remit and outside this record. Long-term lead integrity in the substernal space is the open engineering question and cannot be answered at 10.6 months.
cards.source: Synthesis of Friedman P et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36036522).

shelves.title: Antibiotic envelope at device implant: major infection in 0.7% versus 1.2% at 12 months (WRAP-IT) — a 40% relative reduction on a 1-in-200 baseline, with no added complications
shelves.question: In patients receiving a cardiac implantable electronic device, does an absorbable antibiotic envelope reduce device infection compared with standard prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Bacterial Infections/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Defibrillators, Implantable/adverse effects · Female · Heart Diseases/therapy · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Minocycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pacemaker, Artificial/adverse effects · Prosthesis-Related Infections/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Rifampin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Single-Blind Method · Standard of Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real, relative, and small in absolute terms. WRAP-IT (Tarakji KG et al., PMID: 30883056) randomised 6,983 patients undergoing pocket revision, generator replacement, system upgrade, or initial CRT-defibrillator implantation to an absorbable antibiotic-eluting envelope (minocycline and rifampin) or standard prophylaxis alone. The primary infection endpoint — infection causing extraction or revision, long-term antibiotics with recurrence, or death — occurred in 25 envelope patients versus 42 controls (12-month Kaplan–Meier rates 0.7% versus 1.2%; hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.36–0.98; p=0.04), a 40% relative reduction worth 0.5 percentage points absolute: about 200 envelopes to prevent one major infection. Procedure- or system-related complications were 6.0% versus 6.9% (hazard ratio 0.87; noninferior), and major infections over the full follow-up (mean 20.7 months) remained lower (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.40–0.98). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): worth it where baseline infection risk is high; arithmetic, not enthusiasm, should decide where it is routine. Tier C: single trial, sponsor-funded.

cards.headline: Tarakji 2019 (WRAP-IT): primary infection endpoint 0.7% versus 1.2% (HR 0.60; p=0.04); complications 6.0% versus 6.9% — envelope noninferior for safety
cards.summary: Tarakji 2019 (WRAP-IT): primary infection endpoint 0.7% versus 1.2% (HR 0.60; p=0.04); complications 6.0% versus 6.9% — envelope noninferior for safety
cards.people: 6,983 patients undergoing a cardiac-device pocket revision, generator replacement, or system upgrade, or an initial cardiac resynchronisation therapy defibrillator implantation, randomised 1:1 to the absorbable antibiotic-eluting envelope (3,495) or no envelope (3,488), all receiving standard-of-care infection prevention; mean follow-up 20.7±8.5 months. Funded by Medtronic, the envelope's manufacturer.
cards.result: The primary end point (infection resulting in system extraction or revision, long-term antibiotic therapy with recurrence, or death within 12 months) occurred in 25 patients in the envelope group and 42 in the control group (12-month Kaplan–Meier estimates 0.7% and 1.2%; hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.98; p=0.04) — a 40% relative reduction and a 0.5-percentage-point absolute reduction. The safety end point (procedure- or system-related complications within 12 months) occurred in 201 versus 236 patients (6.0% versus 6.9%; hazard ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.06; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Major device-related infections through the entire follow-up occurred in 32 versus 51 patients (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.98).
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled higher-risk procedures (revisions, replacements, upgrades, CRT-D) — in low-risk first implants the baseline rate, and therefore the absolute gain, would be smaller still. The p-value of 0.04 on 67 total events is fragile, the trial is single and sponsor-funded, and the envelope's cost per infection prevented is a policy question the record does not price. Tier C.

shelves.title: Defibrillation testing at ICD implant: skipping it was noninferior in 3,577 randomised patients — first-shock efficacy and arrhythmic death unchanged (SIMPLE; NORDIC ICD)
shelves.question: In ICD recipients, does omitting defibrillation threshold testing at implant worsen shock efficacy or survival compared with routine testing?
shelves.mesh: Arrhythmias, Cardiac/mortality/therapy · Defibrillators, Implantable · Electric Countershock/methods/mortality · Female · Heart Failure/etiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Safety · Postoperative Complications/etiology/mortality · Prognosis · Prosthesis Implantation/methods/mortality · Risk Assessment · Single-Blind Method · Ventricular Fibrillation/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — where 'the treatment' is the test itself. SIMPLE (Healey JS et al., PMID: 25715991) randomised 2,500 first-ICD patients to implantation with or without defibrillation testing: the composite of arrhythmic death or failed appropriate shock occurred in 90 patients in the no-testing group versus 104 with testing (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65–1.14; p<0.0001 for noninferiority) over a mean 3.1 years, and 30-day safety composites were 5.6% versus 6.5% (p=0.33) and 3.2% versus 4.5% (p=0.08). NORDIC ICD (Bänsch D et al., PMID: 26112885) randomised 1,077 patients and found model-based first-shock efficacy noninferior without testing (difference 3.0% in favour of no testing; p for noninferiority <0.001), with procedure-related serious adverse events in 17.6% of tested patients versus 13.9% untested (p=0.095). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine testing at first implant can be omitted — it found nothing, fixed nothing, and its own risks were the only ones that showed up at all.

cards.headline: Healey 2015 (SIMPLE): arrhythmic death or failed shock in 90 patients without testing versus 104 with (HR 0.86; noninferiority p<0.0001); 30-day safety composites 5.6% versus 6.5%
cards.summary: Healey 2015 (SIMPLE): arrhythmic death or failed shock in 90 patients without testing versus 104 with (HR 0.86; noninferiority p<0.0001); 30-day safety composites 5.6% versus 6.5%
cards.people: 2,500 patients older than 18 receiving their first ICD for standard indications at 85 hospitals in 18 countries (2009–2011), randomised to implantation with defibrillation testing (1,253) or without (1,247); mean follow-up 3.1 years. Right-sided implants and patients awaiting transplantation were excluded.
cards.result: The primary outcome (arrhythmic death or failed appropriate shock) occurred in 90 patients in the no-testing group and 104 in the testing group (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65–1.14; p<0.0001 for noninferiority against a margin of 1.5). The first 30-day safety composite occurred in 69 patients (5.6%) without testing versus 81 (6.5%) with testing (p=0.33); the second composite, restricted to events most likely caused by testing itself, occurred in 3.2% versus 4.5% (p=0.08). Heart failure needing intravenous treatment was the most common adverse event in both groups (2% versus 2%).
cards.watchOut: SIMPLE used one manufacturer's devices and excluded right-sided implants and some complex cases — the populations in which testing might still earn its keep. Noninferiority was declared against a generous hazard-ratio margin of 1.5, though the observed point estimate (0.86) favours omitting the test, so the margin is not what carries the conclusion.
cards.source: Healey JS et al. Cardioverter defibrillator implantation without induction of ventricular fibrillation: a single-blind, non-inferiority, randomised controlled trial (SIMPLE). The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25715991. Registry ID: NCT00800384. cards.headline: Bänsch 2015 (NORDIC ICD): first-shock efficacy difference +3.0% in favour of no testing (noninferiority p<0.001); procedure-related serious adverse events in 17.6% of tested versus 13.9% of untested patients
cards.summary: Bänsch 2015 (NORDIC ICD): first-shock efficacy difference +3.0% in favour of no testing (noninferiority p<0.001); procedure-related serious adverse events in 17.6% of tested versus 13.9% of untested patients
cards.people: 1,077 patients randomised 1:1 (2011–2013) to first ICD implantation with (540) or without (537) standardised intra-operative defibrillation testing, all shocks programmed to 40 J regardless of test results; median follow-up 22.8 months.
cards.result: Model-based first-shock efficacy for true ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation episodes during follow-up was noninferior without testing, with a difference of 3.0% in favour of the no-test group (95% CI −3.0 to 9.0%; p for noninferiority <0.001 against a −10% margin). Within 30 days, 112 procedure-related serious adverse events occurred in 94 tested patients (17.6%) versus 89 events in 74 untested patients (13.9%) (p=0.095). The authors conclude defibrillation testing should no longer be recommended for routine left-sided ICD implantation.
cards.watchOut: The serious-adverse-event gap (17.6% versus 13.9%) is not significant and counts all procedure-related events, not only test-caused ones; first-shock efficacy is a model-based average over episodes, so patients with many episodes weigh more. Both trials predate widespread subcutaneous and extravascular systems, where testing practice differs.
cards.source: Bänsch D et al. Intra-operative defibrillation testing and clinical shock efficacy in patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators: the NORDIC ICD randomized clinical trial. European Heart Journal. 2015. PMID: 26112885. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, 3,577 patients — the ritual test can be retired for routine first implants
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, 3,577 patients — the ritual test can be retired for routine first implants
cards.people: Two randomised non-inferiority trials of omitting defibrillation testing at first ICD implant: SIMPLE (2,500 patients, clinical composite, 3.1-year mean follow-up) and NORDIC ICD (1,077 patients, first-shock efficacy, 22.8-month median follow-up).
cards.result: Arrhythmic death or failed shock: HR 0.86 favouring no testing (SIMPLE). First-shock efficacy: +3.0% favouring no testing (NORDIC ICD). Safety: no significant excess without testing in either trial; the only adverse-event gaps point against testing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: 'Routine' is the operative word — right-sided implants, congenital disease, and generator changes at high risk were excluded or scarce, and neither trial speaks to subcutaneous ICD testing, which follows a different logic. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Healey JS et al. The Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 25715991); Bänsch D et al. European Heart Journal. 2015 (PMID: 26112885).

shelves.title: His-bundle and physiologic pacing versus right-ventricular pacing: ejection fraction preserved (+5.3 points pooled) where RV pacing let it fall — mortality unchanged, heart-failure hospitalisation unmeasured in the pool
shelves.question: In patients who need ventricular pacing, does His-bundle pacing preserve ejection fraction and reduce heart-failure hospitalisation compared with right-ventricular pacing?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Pacing, Artificial/adverse effects/methods · Heart Block/therapy · Humans · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the ventricle's measurements, not yet for its events. The systematic review prepared for the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (Slotwiner DJ et al., PMID: 30412708) pooled 8 studies and 679 patients with ejection fraction above 35% needing pacing for heart block: physiologic pacing — biventricular or His-bundle — left ventricular volumes lower (end-diastolic −2.77 mL; end-systolic −7.09 mL) and ejection fraction preserved or increased by 5.328 percentage points (95% CI 2.86–7.8; p<0.0001) compared with right-ventricular pacing over a mean ~1.6 years; there was no effect on mortality, data on hospitalisations were unavailable, and functional benefit was clearest in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation after AV-node ablation. The randomised His-SYNC pilot (Upadhyay GA et al., PMID: 31096064) compared His-bundle resynchronisation with biventricular pacing — not RV pacing — in 41 CRT patients: QRS narrowed far more on His pacing (125 versus 164 ms on-treatment; p<0.001) with a trend to more echocardiographic response (80% versus 57%; p=0.14) and no difference in cardiovascular hospitalisation or mortality, amid 48% crossover from the His arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): physiologic pacing protects the ejection fraction that RV pacing spends; whether that converts into fewer heart-failure admissions is, on this record, unmeasured rather than shown. Tier C.

cards.headline: Slotwiner 2019 (guideline systematic review): ejection fraction +5.328 points and volumes lower with physiologic versus RV pacing across 679 patients; mortality unaffected; hospitalisation data unavailable
cards.summary: Slotwiner 2019 (guideline systematic review): ejection fraction +5.328 points and volumes lower with physiologic versus RV pacing across 679 patients; mortality unaffected; hospitalisation data unavailable
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis for the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline (Slotwiner 2019)
cards.people: 8 randomised and observational studies totalling 679 patients with left ventricular ejection fraction >35% requiring permanent pacing for heart block, comparing biventricular pacing or His-bundle pacing against right-ventricular pacing; mean follow-up ~1.6 years. Studies pooling patients above and below 35% ejection fraction could not be included because subset data were industry-held.
cards.result: With physiologic pacing (biventricular or His-bundle) versus right-ventricular pacing, left ventricular end-diastolic volume was lower by 2.77 mL (95% CI −4.37 to −1.1; p=0.001) and end-systolic volume by 7.09 mL (95% CI −11.27 to −2.91; p=0.0009), and ejection fraction remained preserved or increased by 5.328 percentage points (95% CI 2.86 to 7.8; p<0.0001). There was no effect on mortality; data on hospitalisations were unavailable; functional-status and quality-of-life data were not definitive. Benefit was more likely in patients with ejection fraction >35% but ≤52%, and patients with chronic atrial fibrillation who had AV-node ablation showed clear ejection-fraction improvement.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes His-bundle with biventricular pacing, mixes randomised with observational studies, and — remarkably — could not include larger mixed-EF studies because the subset data sit with industry; the hospitalisation half of this shelf's question is answered 'unavailable' by the review itself. An ejection-fraction difference of 5 points is a surrogate, however mechanistically satisfying. Tier C.

cards.summary: Upadhyay 2019 (His-SYNC pilot, on-treatment): QRS 125 versus 164 ms (p<0.001) for His versus biventricular pacing; echo response 80% versus 57% (p=0.14); no difference in hospitalisation or mortality — 48% crossed over from His
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial, secondary on-treatment analysis (Upadhyay 2019, His-SYNC)
cards.people: 41 patients meeting standard CRT indications (NYHA class II–IV, QRS >120 ms; mean age 64, 38% women, ejection fraction 28%, QRS 168 ms), randomised at multiple centres to His-bundle cardiac resynchronisation (21) or biventricular resynchronisation (20), with prespecified crossover — required in 48% of the His arm (most often failure to correct QRS in nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay) and 26% of the biventricular arm.
cards.result: On treatment-received analysis, His-bundle pacing narrowed QRS more than biventricular pacing (125±22 ms versus 164±25 ms; p<0.001; per-protocol 124±19 versus 162±24 ms; p<0.001). Echocardiographic response trended higher with His pacing (80% versus 57% treatment-received, p=0.14; 91% versus 54% per-protocol, p=0.078). No significant differences in cardiovascular hospitalisation or mortality were observed.
cards.watchOut: This card supports the mechanism, not the shelf's exact comparison: His-SYNC's comparator is biventricular pacing in a CRT (ejection fraction 28%) population, not right-ventricular pacing in bradycardia patients — and with 48% crossover, even its randomised contrast collapses into an on-treatment analysis of 41 patients. It is carded as supporting evidence and labelled as such.
cards.source: Upadhyay GA et al. On-treatment comparison between corrective His bundle pacing and biventricular pacing for cardiac resynchronization: A secondary analysis of the His-SYNC Pilot Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: the wiring-sparing strategies protect the ejection fraction; the event ledger is blank
cards.summary: Synthesis: the wiring-sparing strategies protect the ejection fraction; the event ledger is blank
cards.people: A guideline systematic review of physiologic versus right-ventricular pacing (8 studies, 679 patients, EF >35%) and one 41-patient randomised pilot of His-bundle versus biventricular resynchronisation (His-SYNC).
cards.result: Ejection fraction: +5.328 points pooled for physiologic versus RV pacing; LV volumes lower. Mortality: no effect. Heart-failure hospitalisation: unavailable in the pool; no difference in the pilot (against a biventricular comparator). QRS narrowing: markedly greater with His pacing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: surrogate-led evidence, hospitalisation unproven.
cards.watchOut: A dedicated His-bundle-versus-RV randomised trial with clinical endpoints does not appear in this record; left-bundle-branch-area pacing, the technique that largely succeeded His pacing, is a different shelf's question (see live shelf #2300 for the resynchronisation comparison).
cards.source: Synthesis of Slotwiner DJ et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 30412708); Upadhyay GA et al. Heart Rhythm. 2019 (PMID: 31096064).

shelves.title: Low-risk pulmonary embolism treated at home: recurrence 0.6% and death 0.6% in the randomised trial, 0.6% recurrence in HoT-PE — with 3.4 fewer days in hospital
shelves.question: In low-risk pulmonary embolism, can patients be treated safely at home from the start rather than admitted?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Ambulatory Care · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Enoxaparin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Health Resources/statistics & numerical data · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Hospitalization · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Readmission · Patient Satisfaction · Pulmonary Embolism/diagnosis/drug therapy · Recurrence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is the bed not occupied, at no measured cost in events. Aujesky D et al. (PMID: 21703676) randomised 344 patients with acute pulmonary embolism and low risk of death (PESI classes I–II) to discharge within 24 hours or inpatient care, both on enoxaparin then oral anticoagulation: recurrent venous thromboembolism within 90 days occurred in 1 outpatient (0.6%) versus no inpatients (noninferiority p=0.011), death within 90 days in 1 patient (0.6%) in each group, and major bleeding by 90 days in 3 outpatients (1.8%) versus no inpatients — while mean length of stay was 0.5 days versus 3.9 days. HoT-PE (Barco S et al., PMID: 31120118), a single-arm management trial of early discharge on rivaroxaban in 525 carefully selected low-risk patients (no instability, no right-ventricular dysfunction, no serious comorbidity), found symptomatic recurrence in 3 patients (0.6%), major bleeding in 6 (1.2%), and 2 cancer-related deaths (0.4%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in rigorously selected low-risk PE, home treatment is as safe as admission and returns three-plus days of hospital to the patient. Tier C: one randomised trial plus a single-arm study carry the safety claim.

cards.headline: Aujesky 2011: recurrent VTE 0.6% outpatient versus 0% inpatient (noninferior); death 0.6% in both; major bleeding by 90 days 1.8% versus 0%; stay 0.5 versus 3.9 days
cards.summary: Aujesky 2011: recurrent VTE 0.6% outpatient versus 0% inpatient (noninferior); death 0.6% in both; major bleeding by 90 days 1.8% versus 0%; stay 0.5 versus 3.9 days
cards.people: 344 patients with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism at low risk of death (pulmonary embolism severity index risk classes I or II) at 19 emergency departments in Switzerland, France, Belgium, and the USA (2007–2010), randomised to outpatient treatment (discharge ≤24 hours after randomisation; 171 in the primary analysis) or inpatient treatment (168), both with subcutaneous enoxaparin for at least 5 days followed by oral anticoagulation for at least 90 days.
cards.result: Symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism within 90 days occurred in 1 outpatient (0.6%) and no inpatients (95% upper confidence limit for the difference 2.7%; p=0.011 for noninferiority against a 4% margin). Death within 90 days occurred in 1 patient (0.6%) in each group. Major bleeding occurred in 2 outpatients (1.2%) versus no inpatients within 14 days, and in 3 outpatients (1.8%) versus no inpatients by 90 days (p=0.086 for noninferiority at 90 days). Mean length of stay was 0.5 days (SD 1.0) for outpatients and 3.9 days (SD 3.1) for inpatients.
cards.watchOut: Event counts are ones and threes: the trial proves recurrence is unlikely to be much worse at home, not that bleeding is identical — every major bleed in the trial happened in an outpatient. Selection was strict (PESI I–II, with the trial's other exclusions), and 'low-risk' here is a score plus a clinician's judgement, not a diagnosis. Tier C.
cards.source: Aujesky D et al. Outpatient versus inpatient treatment for patients with acute pulmonary embolism: an international, open-label, randomised, non-inferiority trial. The Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21703676. Registry ID: NCT00425542. cards.headline: Barco 2020 (HoT-PE): 525 selected low-risk patients sent home on rivaroxaban — recurrence 0.6%, major bleeding 1.2%, no PE-related deaths in the primary outcome
cards.summary: Barco 2020 (HoT-PE): 525 selected low-risk patients sent home on rivaroxaban — recurrence 0.6%, major bleeding 1.2%, no PE-related deaths in the primary outcome
cards.people: 525 patients with acute low-risk pulmonary embolism enrolled across seven countries (2014–2018), eligible only with no haemodynamic instability, no right-ventricular dysfunction or intracardiac thrombi, and no serious comorbidities; up to two nights of hospital stay permitted; all treated with rivaroxaban at the approved PE dose for at least 3 months (safety population 519). Registered as EudraCT 2013-001657-28.
cards.result: Symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism or PE-related death within 3 months — the primary outcome — occurred in 3 patients (0.6%; one-sided upper 99.6% CI 2.1%), all non-fatal recurrences, meeting the prespecified condition for early termination of the trial at its interim analysis. Major bleeding occurred in 6 patients (1.2%). Two patients (0.4%) died of cancer.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 0.6% is reassuring only against the backdrop of the randomised trial and historical inpatient rates, and the selection funnel (screened patients with RV dysfunction or comorbidity were excluded) is doing much of the work. The trial stopped early by design once the event count was low enough, so later-enrolled, less-selected patients are unrepresented.

cards.headline: Synthesis: home is a treatment setting, not a risk — provided the selection is the intervention
cards.summary: Synthesis: home is a treatment setting, not a risk — provided the selection is the intervention
cards.people: One randomised non-inferiority trial (344 PESI I–II patients, outpatient versus inpatient care) and one single-arm management trial (525 selected low-risk patients, early discharge on rivaroxaban).
cards.result: Recurrence: 0.6% at home in both studies. Death: 0.6% in each arm of the trial; no PE-related deaths in HoT-PE. Major bleeding: 1.8% versus 0% by 90 days in the trial; 1.2% in HoT-PE. Hospital days: 0.5 versus 3.9. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: safety rests on one randomised trial and one single-arm study.
cards.watchOut: Neither record supports sending home patients outside the selection criteria — right-ventricular dysfunction, instability, serious comorbidity, or an unsafe home situation all sat outside these trials. The bleeding imbalance in the randomised trial, though tiny in count, is the honest asterisk on 'safely'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aujesky D et al. The Lancet. 2011 (PMID: 21703676); Barco S et al. European Heart Journal. 2020 (PMID: 31120118).

shelves.title: High-intensity warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome: recurrence 10.7% on high intensity versus 3.4% on moderate in Crowther, 11.1% versus 5.5% in WAPS — more anticoagulation, numerically more clots, more minor bleeding
shelves.question: In antiphospholipid syndrome, does high-intensity warfarin prevent recurrent thrombosis better than standard-intensity warfarin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Antiphospholipid/blood · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antiphospholipid Syndrome/blood/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/prevention & control · Pulmonary Embolism/prevention & control · Secondary Prevention · Stroke · Venous Thrombosis/prevention & control · Warfarin/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — and the point estimates lean against the intensive strategy. Crowther MA et al. (PMID: 13679527) randomised 114 patients with antiphospholipid antibodies and previous thrombosis to warfarin targeted to INR 3.1–4.0 or 2.0–3.0: over a mean 2.7 years, recurrent thrombosis occurred in 6 of 56 patients (10.7%) on high intensity versus 2 of 58 (3.4%) on moderate intensity (hazard ratio 3.1; 95% CI 0.6–15.0), with major bleeding in 3 versus 4 patients (hazard ratio 1.0). WAPS (Finazzi G et al., PMID: 15869575) randomised 109 patients to high-intensity warfarin (INR 3.0–4.5) or conventional treatment (mostly warfarin INR 2.0–3.0): over a median 3.6 years, recurrent thrombosis occurred in 11.1% versus 5.5% (hazard ratio 1.97; 95% CI 0.49–7.89), while any bleeding occurred in 27.8% versus 14.6% (hazard ratio 2.18; 95% CI 0.92–5.15), major bleeding in 2 versus 3 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials agree that pushing the INR above 3 buys no protection — standard intensity is the evidence-based target, and the extra intensity is paid for in minor bleeding.

cards.headline: Crowther 2003: recurrent thrombosis 10.7% on high-intensity versus 3.4% on moderate-intensity warfarin (HR 3.1; 95% CI 0.6–15.0); major bleeding in 3 versus 4 patients
cards.summary: Crowther 2003: recurrent thrombosis 10.7% on high-intensity versus 3.4% on moderate-intensity warfarin (HR 3.1; 95% CI 0.6–15.0); major bleeding in 3 versus 4 patients
cards.people: 114 patients with antiphospholipid antibodies and previous thrombosis, randomised to warfarin adjusted to an INR of 3.1–4.0 (high intensity; 56 patients) or 2.0–3.0 (moderate intensity; 58 patients), followed for a mean of 2.7 years.
cards.result: Recurrent thrombosis occurred in 6 of 56 patients (10.7%) assigned to high-intensity warfarin and 2 of 58 (3.4%) assigned to moderate-intensity warfarin (hazard ratio for the high-intensity group 3.1; 95% CI 0.6 to 15.0). Major bleeding occurred in 3 patients on high intensity and 4 on moderate intensity (hazard ratio 1.0; 95% CI 0.2 to 4.8). The authors conclude high-intensity warfarin was not superior, and that the low recurrence rate at INR 2.0–3.0 suggests moderate intensity is appropriate.
cards.watchOut: Eight recurrences in total: the trial excludes the large protective effect retrospective studies had claimed for high intensity, but its confidence interval (0.6–15.0) cannot exclude moderate harm or small benefit in either direction. Achieved INR separation and time in range, the usual warfarin-trial caveats, bound how sharply the two strategies were actually contrasted.
cards.source: Crowther MA et al. A comparison of two intensities of warfarin for the prevention of recurrent thrombosis in patients with the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2003. PMID: 13679527. cards.headline: Finazzi 2005 (WAPS): recurrence 11.1% on high intensity versus 5.5% on conventional treatment (HR 1.97); any bleeding 27.8% versus 14.6% (HR 2.18), major bleeding 2 versus 3 patients
cards.summary: Finazzi 2005 (WAPS): recurrence 11.1% on high intensity versus 5.5% on conventional treatment (HR 1.97); any bleeding 27.8% versus 14.6% (HR 2.18), major bleeding 2 versus 3 patients
cards.people: 109 patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and previous thrombosis, randomised to high-intensity warfarin (INR 3.0–4.5; 54 patients) or conventional antithrombotic therapy (55 patients: warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 in 52, aspirin 100 mg alone in 3), followed for a median of 3.6 years; mean achieved INR 3.2 (SD 0.6) versus 2.5 (SD 0.3).
cards.result: Recurrent thrombosis was observed in 6 of 54 patients (11.1%) on high-intensity warfarin and 3 of 55 (5.5%) on conventional treatment (hazard ratio 1.97; 95% CI 0.49–7.89). Major and minor bleeding occurred in 15 patients (27.8%; two major) on high intensity and 8 (14.6%; three major) on conventional treatment (hazard ratio 2.18; 95% CI 0.92–5.15). The authors conclude high-intensity warfarin was not superior and was associated with more minor haemorrhagic complications.
cards.watchOut: The conventional arm is not purely moderate-intensity warfarin (3 patients took aspirin alone), and achieved INRs (3.2 versus 2.5) sit closer than the targets (3.0–4.5 versus 2.0–3.0) — the tested contrast is real but narrower than the labels. Nine recurrences total; like Crowther, this is a 'no large benefit' verdict, not proof of exact equivalence.

randomised trial (finazzi 2005, waps) 109 patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and previous thrombosis, randomised to high-intensity warfarin (inr 3.0–4.5; 54 patients) or conventional antithrombotic therapy (55 patients: warfarin inr 2.0–3.0 in 52, aspirin 100 mg alone in 3), followed for a median of 3.6 years; mean achieved inr 3.2 (sd 0.6) versus 2.5 (sd 0.3). recurrent thrombosis was observed in 6 of 54 patients (11.1%) on high-intensity warfarin and 3 of 55 (5.5%) on conventional treatment (hazard ratio 1.97; 95% ci 0.49–7.89). major and minor bleeding occurred in 15 patients (27.8%; two major) on high intensity and 8 (14.6%; three major) on conventional treatment (hazard ratio 2.18; 95% ci 0.92–5.15). the authors conclude high-intensity warfarin was not superior and was associated with more minor haemorrhagic complications. the conventional arm is not purely moderate-intensity warfarin (3 patients took aspirin alone), and achieved inrs (3.2 versus 2.5) sit closer than the targets (3.0–4.5 versus 2.0–3.0) — the tested contrast is real but narrower than the labels. nine recurrences total; like crowther, this is a 'no large benefit' verdict, not proof of exact equivalence. finazzi g et al. a randomized clinical trial of high-intensity warfarin vs. conventional antithrombotic therapy for the prevention of recurrent thrombosis in patients with the antiphospholipid syndrome (waps). journal of thrombosis and haemostasis. 2005. pmid: 15869575. mesh: administration, oral · adult · algorithms · antibodies, anticardiolipin/chemistry · anticoagulants/therapeutic use · antiphospholipid syndrome/drug therapy · aspirin/therapeutic use · clinical trials as topic · female · fibrinolytic agents/pharmacology · humans · international normalized ratio · male · middle aged · odds ratio · recurrence · risk · statistics as topic · thromboembolism/drug therapy · thrombosis/pathology/prevention & control · time factors · treatment outcome · warfarin/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Synthesis: 223 randomised patients, two trials, one direction — intensity above INR 3 does not protect
cards.summary: Synthesis: 223 randomised patients, two trials, one direction — intensity above INR 3 does not protect
cards.people: Two randomised trials in antiphospholipid syndrome with previous thrombosis: Crowther 2003 (114 patients, INR 3.1–4.0 versus 2.0–3.0, mean 2.7 years) and WAPS 2005 (109 patients, INR 3.0–4.5 versus conventional, median 3.6 years).
cards.result: Recurrence: 10.7% versus 3.4% (Crowther) and 11.1% versus 5.5% (WAPS) — numerically higher on high intensity in both. Major bleeding: 3 versus 4 patients and 2 versus 3 patients. Any bleeding (WAPS): 27.8% versus 14.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), with the minor-bleeding cost on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small and predate the direct-oral-anticoagulant era in APS (rivaroxaban in triple-positive APS is a separate live shelf, #1548); arterial versus venous index events are pooled in both records, and triple-positive patients are not isolated in either abstract. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Crowther MA et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2003 (PMID: 13679527); Finazzi G et al. Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2005 (PMID: 15869575).

shelves.title: Dalteparin in pregnancy for women with thrombophilia: the composite of pre-eclampsia, small babies, pregnancy loss and clots was 17.1% on dalteparin versus 18.9% without — no benefit, more minor bleeding
shelves.question: In pregnant women with thrombophilia and prior pregnancy complications, does antepartum dalteparin reduce placenta-mediated complications compared with no prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dalteparin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Cardiovascular/prevention & control · Pregnancy Outcome/epidemiology · Risk Factors · Thrombophilia/complications/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thromboembolism/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the large TIPPS trial and the individual-patient meta-analysis point the same way. In TIPPS, the composite of severe or early pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age infant, pregnancy loss or venous thromboembolism occurred in 17.1% on antepartum dalteparin versus 18.9% on no dalteparin (risk difference −1.8%, 95% CI −10.6 to 7.1). The individual-patient meta-analysis of eight trials (963 women) likewise found no significant reduction in recurrent placenta-mediated complications (14% versus 22%; relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.36–1.11, p=0.11), with a signal only in the subgroup whose previous complication was placental abruption in multicentre trials. The cost in TIPPS was minor bleeding: 19.6% versus 9.2% (p=0.01), with no difference in major bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic dalteparin does not prevent placenta-mediated complications in thrombophilic pregnancy and adds minor bleeding.

cards.headline: TIPPS (Rodger 2014): primary composite 17.1% on dalteparin versus 18.9% on no dalteparin — minor bleeding 19.6% versus 9.2%
cards.summary: TIPPS (Rodger 2014): primary composite 17.1% on dalteparin versus 18.9% on no dalteparin — minor bleeding 19.6% versus 9.2%
cards.people: 289 pregnant women with thrombophilia at increased risk of venous thromboembolism or with previous placenta-mediated complications, in 36 tertiary centres in five countries, randomised to prophylactic dalteparin 5000 IU once daily to 20 weeks then twice daily to at least 37 weeks, or no antepartum dalteparin; outcome adjudicators were masked.
cards.result: The primary composite (severe or early-onset pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age infant, pregnancy loss, or venous thromboembolism) occurred in 25/146 (17.1%) on dalteparin versus 27/143 (18.9%) on no dalteparin (risk difference −1.8%, 95% CI −10.6 to 7.1); the on-treatment analysis was 19.6% versus 17.0%. Major bleeding did not differ, but minor bleeding was more common on dalteparin (28/143, 19.6% versus 13/141, 9.2%; risk difference 10.4%, p=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (only adjudicators masked) and a 12-year recruitment period (2000–2012); the trial was powered for a composite that mixes clots with placental outcomes, and crossover occurred in both directions.
cards.source: Rodger MA et al. Antepartum dalteparin versus no antepartum dalteparin for the prevention of pregnancy complications in pregnant women with thrombophilia (TIPPS): a multinational open-label randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 25066248. Registry ID: NCT00967382, ISRCTN87441504. cards.headline: Rodger 2016 individual-patient meta-analysis of 8 trials (963 women): recurrent complications 14% on LMWH versus 22% without — relative risk 0.64 but confidence interval crossing 1
cards.summary: Rodger 2016 individual-patient meta-analysis of 8 trials (963 women): recurrent complications 14% on LMWH versus 22% without — relative risk 0.64 but confidence interval crossing 1
cards.people: 963 women from eight randomised trials (2000–2013) with a previous placenta-mediated complication (pre-eclampsia, abruption, small-for-gestational-age baby, or late pregnancy loss); 42% had thrombophilia; randomised to low-molecular-weight heparin or none.
cards.result: The composite of early or severe pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age (<5th percentile), late loss or abruption occurred in 62/444 (14%) on heparin versus 95/443 (22%) without (absolute difference −8%, 95% CI −17.3 to 1.4, p=0.09; relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.36–1.11, p=0.11) — not significant, with significant heterogeneity between single-centre and multicentre trials; in multicentre trials heparin helped only the previous-abruption subgroup (p=0.006).
cards.watchOut: Most component trials were small and single-centre; the pooled point estimate favours heparin but the interval is wide, so a modest benefit in a subgroup cannot be excluded — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, for the null.
cards.source: Rodger MA et al. Low-molecular-weight heparin and recurrent placenta-mediated pregnancy complications: a meta-analysis of individual patient data from randomised controlled trials. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27720497. shelves.title: Highlow: intermediate-dose heparin in pregnancy after a previous clot — recurrence 2% versus 3% on low dose, not significantly lower, bleeding identical at 4%
shelves.question: In pregnant women with a previous venous thromboembolism, does an intermediate dose of low-molecular-weight heparin prevent recurrence better than a fixed low dose?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Heparin, Low-Molecular-Weight/adverse effects · Venous Thromboembolism/drug therapy/epidemiology/prevention & control · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Postpartum Period · Pulmonary Embolism/prevention & control · Postpartum Hemorrhage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 1,110-woman Highlow trial, recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 11/555 (2%) on weight-adjusted intermediate-dose low-molecular-weight heparin versus 16/555 (3%) on fixed low-dose (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.32–1.47, p=0.33), with the antepartum split identical at 1% versus 1% and the small gap arising post partum (1% versus 2%). Major bleeding was the same in both groups (23/520, 4%, versus 20/525, 4%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.65–2.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the higher dose buys no proven protection, so the fixed low dose is the appropriate thromboprophylaxis dose in pregnancy after a previous clot.

cards.headline: Highlow (Bistervels 2022): recurrence 2% intermediate-dose versus 3% low-dose (p=0.33); major bleeding 4% in both groups
cards.summary: Highlow (Bistervels 2022): recurrence 2% intermediate-dose versus 3% low-dose (p=0.33); major bleeding 4% in both groups
cards.people: 1,110 pregnant women aged ≥18 with objectively confirmed previous venous thromboembolism, recruited before 14 weeks' gestation at 70 hospitals in nine countries, randomised to weight-adjusted intermediate-dose or fixed low-dose low-molecular-weight heparin once daily until 6 weeks post partum; outcomes centrally adjudicated.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism occurred in 11/555 (2%) on intermediate dose versus 16/555 (3%) on low dose (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.32–1.47; p=0.33) — antepartum 1% versus 1%, post partum 1% versus 2%. On-treatment major bleeding (safety population n=1,045): 23/520 (4%) versus 20/525 (4%) (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.65–2.09).
cards.watchOut: Open-label dosing and only 27 recurrence events in total, so the confidence interval cannot exclude a worthwhile benefit from the higher dose; event rates were low in both arms, which is itself the practical message.
cards.source: Bistervels IM et al. Intermediate-dose versus low-dose low-molecular-weight heparin in pregnant and post-partum women with a history of venous thromboembolism (Highlow study): an open-label, multicentre, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 36354038. Registry ID: NCT01828697. shelves.title: IDEAL DVT: stopping compression stockings early when symptoms settle was non-inferior to a fixed two years — post-thrombotic syndrome 29% versus 28%, and two-thirds could stop early
shelves.question: After a first deep-vein thrombosis, does individualising compression-stocking duration by symptoms match a fixed two years for preventing post-thrombotic syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postthrombotic Syndrome/prevention & control · Reference Standards · Safety · Single-Blind Method · Stockings, Compression/adverse effects · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two strategies, that is: in IDEAL DVT, post-thrombotic syndrome at 24 months occurred in 125/432 (29%) with symptom-guided individualised duration versus 118/424 (28%) with a fixed 24 months (absolute difference 1.1%, 95% CI −5.2 to 7.3), inside the 7.5% non-inferiority margin. Two-thirds of the individualised group (66%) were advised to stop before 24 months — 55% at 6 months — and the accompanying cost-effectiveness analysis found the individualised strategy cost-saving with a 99% probability of being cost-effective at €30,000 per QALY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tailoring stocking duration to Villalta scores matches fixed two-year wear for preventing post-thrombotic syndrome, with less burden and lower cost.

cards.headline: IDEAL DVT (ten Cate-Hoek 2018): post-thrombotic syndrome 29% individualised versus 28% fixed duration — non-inferior; 66% stopped stockings early
cards.summary: IDEAL DVT (ten Cate-Hoek 2018): post-thrombotic syndrome 29% individualised versus 28% fixed duration — non-inferior; 66% stopped stockings early
cards.type: Randomised single-blind non-inferiority trial (ten Cate-Hoek 2018, IDEAL DVT)
cards.people: 865 patients with acute proximal leg deep-vein thrombosis without pre-existing venous insufficiency, at 12 Dutch and 2 Italian hospitals; all wore 30–40 mm Hg stockings for 6 months, then either stopped when two consecutive Villalta scores were ≤4 (individualised) or continued to 24 months (standard); assessors were blinded to allocation.
cards.result: Post-thrombotic syndrome (Villalta ≥5 on two consecutive occasions) occurred in 125/432 (29%) individualised versus 118/424 (28%) standard (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.78–1.44; absolute difference 1.1%, 95% CI −5.2 to 7.3 — non-inferior). In the individualised group 283/432 (66%) stopped before 24 months (55% at 6 months, 11% at 12 months). Deaths were 17 (4%) versus 7 (2%), none treatment-related; no serious adverse events were attributed to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: This shelf compares durations, not stockings versus none — the separate question of whether stockings prevent post-thrombotic syndrome at all is answered elsewhere. The 7.5% non-inferiority margin is generous, and the death imbalance, though unrelated to treatment, is unexplained.
cards.source: Ten Cate-Hoek AJ et al. Individualised versus standard duration of elastic compression therapy for prevention of post-thrombotic syndrome (IDEAL DVT): a multicentre, randomised, single-blind, allocation-concealed, non-inferiority trial. cards.headline: Amin 2018 (IDEAL DVT cost-effectiveness): individualised duration saved costs with a 99% probability of cost-effectiveness at €30,000 per QALY
cards.summary: Amin 2018 (IDEAL DVT cost-effectiveness): individualised duration saved costs with a 99% probability of cost-effectiveness at €30,000 per QALY
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised trial (Amin 2018, IDEAL DVT)
cards.people: The same 865 IDEAL DVT patients (856 analysed after exclusions for early recurrence), with quality of life (EQ-5D and SF-36) and health-care and societal costs collected at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: From a societal perspective the individualised strategy was cost-saving: incremental net monetary benefit €3,205 (95% CI 502–5,741) per QALY by the Dutch EQ-5D tariff, €3,540 by SF-6D, and €4,071 by the UK EQ-5D tariff, where the strategy was both more effective and less costly; the probability of cost-effectiveness at a €30,000-per-QALY threshold was 99%.
cards.watchOut: Cost-effectiveness inherits the parent trial's non-inferiority assumption and Dutch cost structures; savings are real but modest per patient, and quality-of-life differences were small in both directions depending on the instrument.
cards.source: Amin EE et al. Individually shortened duration versus standard duration of elastic compression therapy for prevention of post-thrombotic syndrome: a cost-effectiveness analysis. The Lancet. Haematology. 2018. PMID: 30314712. Registry ID: NCT01429714. cards.summary: Synthesis: same syndrome rate, two-thirds freed from a second year of stockings, lower costs
cards.people: One randomised non-inferiority trial (n=865) with its pre-planned cost-effectiveness analysis.
cards.result: Post-thrombotic syndrome: 29% versus 28% (difference 1.1%, 95% CI −5.2 to 7.3). Early stopping: 66% of the individualised group. Cost-effectiveness probability: 99% at €30,000 per QALY. shelves.title: SURPRISE: a rivaroxaban tablet matched daily fondaparinux injections for superficial-vein thrombosis — events 3% versus 2% at 45 days, non-inferior, no major bleeding in either group
shelves.question: In acute superficial-vein thrombosis, does rivaroxaban match fondaparinux for preventing deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and extension?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Fondaparinux · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Polysaccharides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Embolism/etiology/prevention & control · Rivaroxaban/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Thrombosis/complications/drug therapy · Venous Thrombosis/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as an equally effective, less burdensome substitute: in the SURPRISE trial the composite of symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, progression or recurrence of superficial-vein thrombosis, and all-cause death at 45 days occurred in 7/211 (3%) on rivaroxaban 10 mg daily versus 4/224 (2%) on fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 0.6–6.4; p=0.0025 for non-inferiority against a 4.5% margin). There were no major bleeds in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rivaroxaban is a non-inferior oral alternative to 45 days of fondaparinux injections for superficial-vein thrombosis with additional risk factors — the benefit is convenience at equal protection, not greater protection.

cards.headline: SURPRISE (Beyer-Westendorf 2017): primary outcome 3% on rivaroxaban versus 2% on fondaparinux — non-inferior (p=0.0025); zero major bleeds
cards.summary: SURPRISE (Beyer-Westendorf 2017): primary outcome 3% on rivaroxaban versus 2% on fondaparinux — non-inferior (p=0.0025); zero major bleeds
cards.people: 472 adults with symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis at least 5 cm long in a supragenual segment plus at least one additional risk factor (age >65, male sex, previous venous thromboembolism, cancer, autoimmune disease, or non-varicose-vein thrombosis), at 27 German sites, randomised to rivaroxaban 10 mg orally or fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously once daily for 45 days; endpoint adjudication was masked.
cards.result: In the per-protocol set (n=435) the primary composite occurred in 7/211 (3%; 95% CI 1.6–6.7) on rivaroxaban versus 4/224 (2%; 0.7–4.5) on fondaparinux (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 0.6–6.4; p=0.0025 for non-inferiority). No major bleeding occurred in either group. The one death (rivaroxaban group, day 50) was from aortic dissection, unrelated to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, per-protocol primary analysis, and only 11 outcome events — the hazard ratio's interval (0.6–6.4) is wide, so non-inferiority rests on the pre-set absolute margin. Patients with thrombus within 3 cm of the sapheno-femoral junction or needing full-dose anticoagulation were excluded.
cards.source: Beyer-Westendorf J et al. Prevention of thromboembolic complications in patients with superficial-vein thrombosis given rivaroxaban or fondaparinux: the open-label, randomised, non-inferiority SURPRISE phase 3b trial. The Lancet. Haematology. 2017. PMID: 28219692. Registry ID: NCT01499953. shelves.title: API-CAT: after six months of treatment for cancer-associated clots, halving the apixaban dose kept recurrence at 2.1% versus 2.8% — non-inferior — and cut clinically relevant bleeding from 15.6% to 12.1%
shelves.question: In cancer-associated venous thromboembolism that has completed six months of anticoagulation, does continuing a reduced dose of apixaban match the full dose for recurrence and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Factor Xa Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/epidemiology · Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy · Pulmonary Embolism/drug therapy/etiology/prevention & control · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pyridones/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Recurrence · Venous Thrombosis/drug therapy/etiology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Incidence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the reduced dose as the better-balanced continuation: in API-CAT, recurrent venous thromboembolism over 12 further months occurred in 18 patients (cumulative incidence 2.1%) on apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily versus 24 (2.8%) on 5.0 mg twice daily (adjusted subhazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.41–1.41; p=0.001 for non-inferiority), while clinically relevant bleeding occurred in 102 (12.1%) versus 136 (15.6%) (adjusted subhazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.97; p=0.03). Mortality was 17.7% versus 19.6% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.86–1.06). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): after the first six months, reduced-dose apixaban protects as well as full dose with significantly less bleeding.

cards.headline: API-CAT (Mahé 2025): recurrence 2.1% reduced-dose versus 2.8% full-dose (non-inferior); bleeding 12.1% versus 15.6% (p=0.03); mortality 17.7% versus 19.6%
cards.summary: API-CAT (Mahé 2025): recurrence 2.1% reduced-dose versus 2.8% full-dose (non-inferior); bleeding 12.1% versus 15.6% (p=0.03); mortality 17.7% versus 19.6%
cards.people: 1,766 patients with active cancer and proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism who had completed at least 6 months of anticoagulation (median 8.0 months since the index event), randomised to apixaban 2.5 mg or 5.0 mg twice daily for 12 months, with blinded central adjudication; median treatment duration 11.8 months.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism: 18 patients (cumulative incidence 2.1%) on reduced dose versus 24 (2.8%) on full dose (adjusted subhazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.41–1.41; p=0.001 for non-inferiority against a margin of 2.00). Clinically relevant bleeding: 102 (12.1%) versus 136 (15.6%) (adjusted subhazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.97; p=0.03). Mortality: 17.7% versus 19.6% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.86–1.06).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its patients had already tolerated six months of anticoagulation — a selected, lower-risk remainder of the cancer-clot population. The recurrence interval (upper bound 1.41) excludes the pre-set non-inferiority margin but not a small true disadvantage.

shelves.title: PCI on top of modern medical therapy in severe ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction: no fewer deaths or heart-failure hospitalisations in REVIVED-BCIS2
shelves.question: In patients with severe ischaemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, extensive coronary artery disease and demonstrable myocardial viability, does adding percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to optimal medical therapy reduce death from any cause or hospitalisation for heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Heart Failure/etiology/therapy · *Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · *Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/drug therapy/etiology/mortality/surgery · Ventricular Function, Left · *Coronary Artery Disease/complications/drug therapy/mortality/surgery · Cardiovascular Agents/therapeutic use · Myocardial Ischemia/drug therapy/etiology/mortality/surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the one dedicated randomised trial, event rates were essentially identical: a primary-outcome event (death or heart-failure hospitalisation) occurred in 37.2% with PCI plus medical therapy and 38.0% with medical therapy alone over a median of 41 months (hazard ratio 0.99), and ejection fraction did not improve at 6 or 12 months. Pooled individual-patient data with the older surgical STICHES trial show that patients treated with medical therapy alone in the modern era fared better than medical-therapy patients in STICHES (adjusted hazard ratio 0.60), which is the most plausible explanation for why PCI added nothing: contemporary drug and device therapy has moved the baseline. Quality of life favoured PCI early but the difference had diminished by 24 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in severe ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction, PCI added to optimal medical therapy does not reduce death or heart-failure hospitalisation.

cards.headline: REVIVED-BCIS2 (Perera 2022): death or heart-failure hospitalisation in 37.2% with PCI plus medical therapy versus 38.0% with medical therapy alone (hazard ratio 0.99) over a median of 41 months
cards.summary: REVIVED-BCIS2 (Perera 2022): death or heart-failure hospitalisation in 37.2% with PCI plus medical therapy versus 38.0% with medical therapy alone (hazard ratio 0.99) over a median of 41 months
cards.people: 700 patients with left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less, extensive coronary artery disease amenable to PCI, and demonstrable myocardial viability, randomly assigned to PCI plus optimal medical therapy (347 patients) or optimal medical therapy alone (353 patients) — optimal therapy meaning individually adjusted drug and device therapy for heart failure.
cards.result: Over a median of 41 months, a primary-outcome event (death from any cause or hospitalisation for heart failure) occurred in 129 patients (37.2%) in the PCI group and 134 patients (38.0%) in the medical-therapy group (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.27; P = 0.96). Ejection fraction was similar at 6 months (mean difference -1.6 percentage points; 95% CI -3.7 to 0.5) and 12 months (0.9 percentage points; 95% CI -1.7 to 3.4). Quality-of-life scores favoured PCI at 6 and 12 months but the difference had diminished at 24 months.
cards.watchOut: Open-label strategy trial; results apply to patients with demonstrable viability and PCI-amenable disease, not to patients needing revascularisation for refractory angina or acute coronary syndromes.
cards.source: Perera et al. Percutaneous Revascularization for Ischemic Left Ventricular Dysfunction. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 36027563. Registry ID: NCT01920048. cards.headline: Pooled individual-patient analysis (Ryan 2025): medical therapy alone in REVIVED-BCIS2 beat medical therapy alone in STICHES (adjusted hazard ratio 0.60 for death or heart-failure hospitalisation)
cards.summary: Pooled individual-patient analysis (Ryan 2025): medical therapy alone in REVIVED-BCIS2 beat medical therapy alone in STICHES (adjusted hazard ratio 0.60 for death or heart-failure hospitalisation)
cards.type: Individual-patient-data pooled analysis of two randomised trials (REVIVED-BCIS2 and STICHES)
cards.people: 1,912 participants from REVIVED-BCIS2 and the surgical STICHES trial, all with ejection fraction of 35% or less and coronary artery disease receiving medical therapy, randomised to PCI (REVIVED-BCIS2) or bypass surgery (STICHES); median follow-up was 41 months in REVIVED-BCIS2 and 118 months in STICHES, with 98.3% completeness of follow-up for the primary outcome.
cards.result: Patients receiving medical therapy alone in REVIVED-BCIS2 had fewer primary-outcome events (death or heart-failure hospitalisation) than those receiving medical therapy alone in STICHES (adjusted hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.74; P < .001). Adjusted outcomes with bypass surgery in STICHES were worse than with medical therapy alone in REVIVED-BCIS2, underlining how much background therapy improved between the two trial eras.
cards.watchOut: A cross-trial, adjusted comparison — not a randomised head-to-head of PCI versus bypass surgery; era, follow-up length and case mix differ between the trials, so it explains rather than replaces the randomised REVIVED-BCIS2 result.
cards.source: Ryan et al. Medical therapy and outcomes in REVIVED-BCIS2 and STICHES: an individual patient data analysis. European heart journal. 2025. PMID: 40048661.
