cards.headline: Synthesis: PCI does not add prognostic benefit to modern medical therapy in severe ischaemic ventricular dysfunction
cards.summary: Synthesis: PCI does not add prognostic benefit to modern medical therapy in severe ischaemic ventricular dysfunction
cards.people: Patients with severe ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction considered for prognostic (not symptom-driven) PCI.
cards.result: The randomised comparison is unambiguous — 37.2% versus 38.0% for death or heart-failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 0.99) — and the pooled analysis shows the control arm itself has improved across eras. PCI in this setting should be justified by symptoms or acute presentations, not by an expectation of longer life or fewer heart-failure admissions.
cards.watchOut: These data do not address bypass surgery decided on contemporary therapy, nor PCI for limiting angina, which REVIVED-BCIS2 was not designed to test.
cards.source: Synthesis of REVIVED-BCIS2 (PMID: 36027563) and the REVIVED-BCIS2/STICHES individual-patient-data analysis (PMID: 40048661).

shelves.title: EDTA chelation after myocardial infarction: TACT reported fewer events, but TACT2 — the replication trial in patients with diabetes — found none
shelves.question: In patients with a previous myocardial infarction, does an edetate disodium (EDTA)-based chelation regimen reduce cardiovascular events — and does the effect hold in patients with diabetes, the population chosen for the replication trial?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angina Pectoris/*prevention & control · Atherosclerosis/complications/drug therapy · Chelating Agents/*therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Edetic Acid/*therapeutic use · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/mortality/*prevention & control · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Recurrence · Risk · Stroke/*prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two trials disagree. TACT (1,708 patients after myocardial infarction) reported its composite endpoint in 26% on chelation versus 30% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99), with no effect on total mortality (10% versus 11%; hazard ratio 0.93). TACT2 was built to replicate TACT in 959 patients who all had diabetes and a previous infarction — exactly where benefit was expected to be largest — and found the primary endpoint in 35.6% on chelation versus 35.7% on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16), despite chelation demonstrably lowering blood lead (median 9.03 to 3.46 µg/L by infusion 40). A treatment whose pivotal replication fails in the target population cannot be recommended on the first trial alone. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive trial with borderline significance and high consent withdrawal, one adequately designed null replication in diabetes — the chelation question stays open in name but the diabetes claim is refuted.

cards.headline: TACT (Lamas 2013): composite endpoint in 26% on EDTA chelation versus 30% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82; P = .035) — but 17% withdrew consent and mortality was unchanged
cards.summary: TACT (Lamas 2013): composite endpoint in 26% on EDTA chelation versus 30% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82; P = .035) — but 17% withdrew consent and mortality was unchanged
cards.people: 1,708 patients aged 50 years or older, at least 6 weeks after a myocardial infarction, with serum creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL or less, at 134 US and Canadian sites; 31% had diabetes. The regimen was 40 infusions of an EDTA-based chelation solution (839 patients) versus placebo infusions (869 patients), with a parallel oral vitamin comparison; median follow-up 55 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (death, recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for angina) occurred in 222 patients (26%) in the chelation group and 261 (30%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99; P = .035, against a prespecified final threshold of P = .036). Total mortality did not differ (87 deaths [10%] versus 93 [11%]; hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.25). Component effects were similar in size (myocardial infarction 6% versus 8%; revascularisation 15% versus 18%).
cards.watchOut: 289 patients (17%) withdrew consent during the trial — more in the placebo group — which can bias a borderline result; the trial was not powered for mortality, and the diabetes subgroup signal that motivated TACT2 was a subgroup finding.
cards.source: Lamas et al. Effect of disodium EDTA chelation regimen on cardiovascular events in patients with previous myocardial infarction: the TACT randomized trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23532240. Registry ID: NCT00044213. cards.headline: TACT2 (Lamas 2024): in patients with diabetes and previous infarction, primary endpoint in 35.6% on chelation versus 35.7% on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93) — the replication failed
cards.summary: TACT2 (Lamas 2024): in patients with diabetes and previous infarction, primary endpoint in 35.6% on chelation versus 35.7% on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93) — the replication failed
cards.people: 959 participants aged 50 years or older with diabetes and a myocardial infarction at least 6 weeks before recruitment, at 88 US and Canadian sites; 483 received at least one chelation infusion and 476 at least one placebo infusion, with twice-daily oral multivitamins or placebo in the factorial design; median follow-up 48 months.
cards.result: A primary endpoint event (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for unstable angina) occurred in 172 participants (35.6%) in the chelation group and 170 (35.7%) in the placebo group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16; P = .53); 5-year cumulative incidence was 45.8% versus 46.5%. Cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 18.4% versus 19.7% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.89), and death from any cause in 17.4% versus 17.6%. Chelation did lower blood lead — median from 9.03 µg/L at baseline to 3.46 µg/L at infusion 40, versus 9.3 to 8.7 µg/L on placebo (P < .001) — so the null result is not explained by failure to chelate.
cards.watchOut: TACT2 enrolled only patients with diabetes, so it refutes the diabetes claim directly; whether chelation helps any non-diabetic subgroup remains formally untested by a second trial.
cards.source: Lamas et al. Edetate Disodium-Based Chelation for Patients With a Previous Myocardial Infarction and Diabetes: TACT2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 39141382. Registry ID: NCT02733185. cards.headline: Synthesis: a borderline-positive first trial and a clean null replication in the very population expected to benefit most
cards.summary: Synthesis: a borderline-positive first trial and a clean null replication in the very population expected to benefit most
cards.people: Patients after myocardial infarction, with or without diabetes, offered EDTA chelation to reduce future events.
cards.result: TACT's hazard ratio of 0.82 came with 17% consent withdrawal and no mortality effect; TACT2, purpose-built for replication in diabetes, returned 35.6% versus 35.7%. Where a therapy is burdensome (40 infusions) and its best-case evidence is one contested trial, the balance of the randomised evidence does not support routine use, and in diabetes the question is answered: no benefit.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial tested chelation for angina symptoms or quality of life as a primary aim; the verdict here concerns event reduction only.
cards.source: Synthesis of TACT (PMID: 23532240) and TACT2 (PMID: 39141382).

shelves.title: Apabetalone after acute coronary syndrome in type 2 diabetes: the phase 3 BETonMACE trial missed its endpoint (10.3% versus 12.4%) despite a promising pooled phase 2 signal
shelves.question: In patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome, type 2 diabetes and low HDL cholesterol, does the BET protein inhibitor apabetalone, added to standard therapy, reduce cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/complications/*drug therapy · Blood Chemical Analysis · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/*drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/etiology · Proteins/*antagonists & inhibitors · Quinazolinones/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Stroke/etiology · Bromodomain Containing Proteins
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial did not confirm the early signal. A pooled analysis of three short phase 2 trials (798 patients) had found fewer major adverse cardiovascular events on apabetalone (5.9% versus 10.4%; P = 0.02), but those trials were lipid and imaging studies with events counted secondarily. In BETonMACE — 2,425 patients after an acute coronary syndrome, all with type 2 diabetes and low HDL cholesterol — the primary outcome occurred in 10.3% on apabetalone versus 12.4% on placebo over a median of 26.5 months (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.04; P = .11), and more patients stopped apabetalone for liver-enzyme elevations (2.9% versus 0.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): apabetalone does not significantly reduce major adverse cardiovascular events after acute coronary syndrome in type 2 diabetes; the phase 2 event signal was not reproduced at phase 3 scale.

cards.headline: Pooled phase 2 analysis (Nicholls 2018): major adverse cardiovascular events in 5.9% on apabetalone versus 10.4% on placebo (P = 0.02) across ASSERT, ASSURE and SUSTAIN
cards.summary: Pooled phase 2 analysis (Nicholls 2018): major adverse cardiovascular events in 5.9% on apabetalone versus 10.4% on placebo (P = 0.02) across ASSERT, ASSURE and SUSTAIN
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three phase 2 randomised trials
cards.people: 798 patients with established coronary artery disease in the ASSERT, ASSURE and SUSTAIN trials, treated with apabetalone or placebo for 3 to 6 months in studies designed around lipid parameters and coronary atherosclerosis imaging, not clinical events.
cards.result: Apabetalone raised apolipoprotein A-I by up to 6.7%, HDL cholesterol by up to 6.5% and large HDL particles by up to 23.3%, and lowered high-sensitivity C-reactive protein by 21.1%, without affecting atherogenic lipoproteins. Major adverse cardiovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for cardiovascular causes) occurred in 5.9% on apabetalone versus 10.4% on placebo (P = 0.02), with larger differences in patients with diabetes (5.4% versus 12.7%).
cards.watchOut: Events were few, follow-up was 3 to 6 months, and event reduction was not the trials' purpose — a classic hypothesis-generating pooled signal, with baseline imbalances between groups (the apabetalone group was less well treated with beta-blockers and antiplatelet agents).
cards.source: Nicholls et al. Selective BET Protein Inhibition with Apabetalone and Cardiovascular Events: A Pooled Analysis of Trials in Patients with Coronary Artery Disease. American journal of cardiovascular drugs : drugs, devices, and other interventions. 2018. PMID: 29027131. cards.people: 2,425 patients with an acute coronary syndrome in the preceding 7 to 90 days, type 2 diabetes and low HDL cholesterol, at 190 sites in 13 countries, randomised to apabetalone 100 mg twice daily (1,215) or placebo (1,210) on top of standard care; median follow-up 26.5 months, with full primary-outcome ascertainment in 95.7%.

cards.summary: Synthesis: an epigenetic therapy whose event signal shrank as the trials grew
cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes after an acute coronary syndrome, in whom apabetalone was proposed as add-on event prevention.

shelves.title: Carotid revascularisation on top of modern medical therapy: neither ECST-2 nor SPACE-2 showed added benefit for asymptomatic or low-risk stenosis
shelves.question: In patients with asymptomatic carotid stenosis, or symptomatic stenosis at low-to-intermediate predicted stroke risk, does adding carotid revascularisation (endarterectomy or stenting) to optimised modern medical therapy reduce stroke or death compared with medical therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Carotid Stenosis/therapy/surgery/complications/drug therapy · Male · Female · Aged · Middle Aged · *Endarterectomy, Carotid/methods · *Stroke/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Stents · Combined Modality Therapy · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — both modern trials point the same way, though neither is definitive alone. In SPACE-2 (513 patients with asymptomatic stenosis of at least 70%), the 5-year primary endpoint (any stroke or death within 30 days, or ipsilateral stroke within 5 years) occurred in 2.5% with endarterectomy plus medical therapy, 4.4% with stenting plus medical therapy and 3.1% with medical therapy alone; endarterectomy versus medical therapy alone gave a hazard ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.22 to 3.91), and five strokes occurred in the 30 days after each procedure type. In ECST-2 (429 patients, asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate-risk symptomatic stenosis), the 2-year hierarchical primary outcome produced a win ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.70) — no benefit either way — with non-fatal stroke in 11 patients on medical therapy alone versus 16 with added revascularisation. Event rates on modern medical therapy are now so low that the procedural risk consumes any plausible gain in these risk groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate-risk carotid stenosis, revascularisation added to optimised medical therapy has not been shown to reduce stroke or death.

cards.headline: SPACE-2 (Reiff 2022): 5-year primary endpoint in 2.5% (endarterectomy + medical therapy), 4.4% (stenting + medical therapy) and 3.1% (medical therapy alone); hazard ratio 0.93 for endarterectomy versus medical therapy alone
cards.summary: SPACE-2 (Reiff 2022): 5-year primary endpoint in 2.5% (endarterectomy + medical therapy), 4.4% (stenting + medical therapy) and 3.1% (medical therapy alone); hazard ratio 0.93 for endarterectomy versus medical therapy alone
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial (SPACE-2, with SPACE-2a and SPACE-2b substudies)
cards.people: 513 patients aged 50 to 85 years with asymptomatic carotid stenosis of at least 70%, at 36 centres in Austria, Germany and Switzerland: 203 allocated to carotid endarterectomy plus best medical treatment, 197 to carotid artery stenting plus best medical treatment, and 113 to best medical treatment alone; median follow-up 59.9 months.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint (any stroke or death within 30 days, or any ipsilateral ischaemic stroke within 5 years) occurred in 2.5% (95% CI 1.0 to 5.8) with endarterectomy plus medical therapy, 4.4% (2.2 to 8.6) with stenting plus medical therapy, and 3.1% (1.0 to 9.4) with medical therapy alone. Hazard ratios versus medical therapy alone were 0.93 (95% CI 0.22 to 3.91; P = 0.93) for endarterectomy and 1.55 (0.41 to 5.85; P = 0.52) for stenting. Five strokes and no deaths occurred within 30 days in each procedure group; over 5 years, three ipsilateral strokes occurred in both the stenting and medical-therapy groups and none in the endarterectomy group.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped far short of its planned 3,640 patients (513 recruited), so confidence intervals are wide and the result is 'no superiority shown' rather than proof of equivalence; patients and clinicians were unmasked.

cards.headline: ECST-2 (Donners 2025): 2-year win ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.70; P = 0.97) for optimised medical therapy alone versus medical therapy plus revascularisation — no benefit in either direction
cards.summary: ECST-2 (Donners 2025): 2-year win ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.70; P = 0.97) for optimised medical therapy alone versus medical therapy plus revascularisation — no benefit in either direction
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial with blinded outcome adjudication, 2-year interim analysis (ECST-2)
cards.people: 429 patients with asymptomatic or symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% or greater and a 5-year predicted ipsilateral stroke risk below 20% (Carotid Artery Risk score), at 30 centres in Europe and Canada: 215 assigned to optimised medical therapy alone and 214 to optimised medical therapy plus revascularisation (endarterectomy or stenting); median age 72 years.
cards.result: The hierarchical primary outcome (periprocedural death, fatal stroke or fatal myocardial infarction; non-fatal stroke; non-fatal myocardial infarction; new silent cerebral infarction on imaging) yielded 11.4% wins for medical therapy alone, 11.3% wins for added revascularisation and 77.3% ties (win ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.70; P = 0.97). Component counts for medical therapy alone versus added revascularisation: periprocedural death, fatal stroke or fatal myocardial infarction in 4 versus 3 patients; non-fatal stroke in 11 versus 16; non-fatal myocardial infarction in 7 versus 5; new silent cerebral infarction in 12 versus 7. One periprocedural death occurred in the revascularisation group.
cards.watchOut: These are 2-year interim results of an ongoing trial; the 5-year analysis may shift estimates, and the findings apply to patients selected as low-to-intermediate risk by the Carotid Artery Risk score — not to high-risk symptomatic stenosis, where older trials favoured surgery.

shelves.title: Iron reduction by phlebotomy in peripheral arterial disease (FeAST): mortality 20% versus 23% — no significant benefit from lowering iron stores
shelves.question: In patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease, does reducing body iron stores by regular phlebotomy reduce all-cause mortality, or death combined with nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/*epidemiology/*metabolism/prevention & control · Female · Ferritins/blood · Humans · Iron/*metabolism · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Peripheral Vascular Diseases/blood/*physiopathology · *Phlebotomy · Risk Factors · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the iron hypothesis failed its randomised test. In FeAST (1,277 patients with symptomatic but stable peripheral arterial disease), all-cause deaths occurred in 125 patients (20%) in the iron-reduction group and 148 (23%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = .17), and the secondary endpoint of death plus nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in 180 (28%) versus 205 (32%) (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.07; P = .20). A biomarker substudy of the same trial found that patients who died had had higher average ferritin (132.5 versus 83.6 ng/mL) and higher interleukin-6 — ferritin tracks inflammation and prognosis, but lowering iron stores did not convert that association into fewer events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): scheduled phlebotomy to reduce iron stores does not significantly reduce mortality or major cardiovascular events in peripheral arterial disease.

cards.headline: FeAST (Zacharski 2007): all-cause mortality 20% with iron reduction versus 23% in controls (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = .17) in 1,277 patients with peripheral arterial disease
cards.summary: FeAST (Zacharski 2007): all-cause mortality 20% with iron reduction versus 23% in controls (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = .17) in 1,277 patients with peripheral arterial disease
cards.type: Randomised controlled single-blinded multicentre trial (FeAST, VA Cooperative Study #410)
cards.people: 1,277 patients with symptomatic but stable peripheral arterial disease in the US Department of Veterans Affairs system, assigned to iron reduction by phlebotomy at 6-month intervals, titrated to avoid iron deficiency (636 patients), or to control care (641 patients), enrolled 1999 to 2005.
cards.result: All-cause deaths occurred in 125 patients (20%) in the iron-reduction group and 148 (23%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = .17). The secondary endpoint (death plus nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke) occurred in 180 patients (28%) versus 205 (32%) (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.07; P = .20). Neither endpoint approached significance despite successful separation of iron stores by design.
cards.watchOut: A single trial in a predominantly male veteran population; the confidence interval for mortality does not exclude a modest benefit, so the honest reading is 'no benefit shown', and subgroup claims (such as by age) from this trial are exploratory.
cards.source: Zacharski et al. Reduction of iron stores and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with peripheral arterial disease: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17299195. cards.headline: FeAST biomarker substudy (Depalma 2010): patients who died had higher follow-up ferritin (132.5 versus 83.6 ng/mL) and interleukin-6 — ferritin marks risk without proving iron causes it
cards.summary: FeAST biomarker substudy (Depalma 2010): patients who died had higher follow-up ferritin (132.5 versus 83.6 ng/mL) and interleukin-6 — ferritin marks risk without proving iron causes it
cards.type: Biomarker substudy of the FeAST randomised trial (observational within-trial analysis)
cards.people: 100 cancer-free FeAST participants at one health-care system (51 randomised to iron reduction, 49 to control), with ferritin, inflammatory biomarkers and lipids measured at entry and at 6-month intervals over 6 years; 23 participants died during the study.
cards.result: Mean follow-up ferritin was higher in the 23 participants who died (132.5 ng/mL; 95% CI 79.36 to 185.66) than in the 77 survivors (83.6 ng/mL; 95% CI 70.34 to 96.90; Wilcoxon P = .05), and follow-up interleukin-6 was likewise higher in those who died (21.68 versus 12.61 ng/mL; P = .018); ferritin correlated with interleukin-6 and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. The substudy also confirmed the main trial's null result: no difference between treatment groups in all-cause mortality or the secondary composite.
cards.watchOut: Observational biomarker analysis within one centre's substudy — it shows ferritin behaves as an inflammatory risk marker; it cannot show that lowering ferritin changes outcomes, and the randomised comparison in the parent trial says phlebotomy did not.
cards.source: Depalma et al. Ferritin levels, inflammatory biomarkers, and mortality in peripheral arterial disease: a substudy of the Iron (Fe) and Atherosclerosis Study (FeAST) Trial. cards.people: Patients with peripheral arterial disease in whom iron reduction has been proposed to lower cardiovascular risk.
cards.result: The randomised evidence (mortality hazard ratio 0.85, confidence interval crossing 1; composite hazard ratio 0.88) does not support phlebotomy as event prevention, and the substudy explains why the idea was attractive — ferritin is a marker of inflammatory burden — without rescuing the intervention.

shelves.title: Carvedilol after myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction (CAPRICORN): all-cause mortality 12% versus 15%, though the primary composite endpoint was neutral
shelves.question: In patients with left ventricular dysfunction after an acute myocardial infarction, treated with contemporary therapy including ACE inhibitors, does carvedilol reduce mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Carbazoles/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Carvedilol · Drug Administration Schedule · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/complications/*drug therapy/mortality · Propanolamines/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/*complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial, with its headline composite neutral and its mortality result favourable. In CAPRICORN (1,959 patients with ejection fraction of 40% or less after infarction), the primary endpoint of all-cause mortality or cardiovascular hospital admission occurred in 35% on carvedilol versus 37% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.07), but all-cause mortality alone was lower on carvedilol — 116 deaths (12%) versus 151 (15%), hazard ratio 0.77 (0.60 to 0.98; P = 0.03) — as were cardiovascular mortality and recurrent non-fatal infarction. A prespecified arrhythmia analysis of the same trial found substantially less atrial fibrillation or flutter (2.3% versus 5.4%; hazard ratio 0.41) and ventricular tachyarrhythmia (0.9% versus 3.9%; hazard ratio 0.24) on carvedilol. Because the mortality claim rests on a single trial whose primary composite was neutral, this shelf is flagged Tier C for the developer's eye. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): carvedilol after infarction with left ventricular dysfunction probably reduces mortality, on one trial whose primary composite endpoint did not reach significance.

cards.headline: CAPRICORN (Dargie 2001): all-cause mortality 12% on carvedilol versus 15% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.77; P = 0.03), but the primary composite was 35% versus 37% (hazard ratio 0.92) — not significant
cards.summary: CAPRICORN (Dargie 2001): all-cause mortality 12% on carvedilol versus 15% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.77; P = 0.03), but the primary composite was 35% versus 37% (hazard ratio 0.92) — not significant
cards.people: 1,959 patients with a proven acute myocardial infarction and left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less, randomised to carvedilol (975 patients; titrated from 6.25 mg to a maximum of 25 mg twice daily) or placebo (984), on top of contemporary evidence-based therapy including ACE inhibitors.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (all-cause mortality or hospital admission for cardiovascular problems) occurred in 340 patients (35%) on carvedilol and 367 (37%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.07). All-cause mortality alone was lower with carvedilol: 116 deaths (12%) versus 151 (15%) (hazard ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98; P = 0.03). Cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and the composite of all-cause mortality or non-fatal infarction were also lower on carvedilol.
cards.watchOut: Mortality was a component of — not the whole — primary endpoint, and the composite itself was neutral, so the mortality finding, while prespecified and significant, carries less weight than a clean positive primary outcome; this is one trial, conducted before primary PCI and modern antiplatelet therapy were universal.

shelves.title: Amlodipine in severe chronic heart failure: PRAISE was neutral overall, its striking non-ischaemic subgroup signal (46% relative mortality reduction) was tested in PRAISE-2 — and disappeared
shelves.question: In patients with severe chronic heart failure and ejection fraction below 30%, does amlodipine reduce death or major cardiovascular events — overall, and specifically in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, where the first trial suggested a large benefit?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amlodipine/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Calcium Channel Blockers/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Cardiomyopathy, Dilated/drug therapy/mortality · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Failure/*drug therapy/etiology/mortality · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/complications · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a textbook subgroup rise and fall. In PRAISE (1,153 patients with severe heart failure), the primary endpoint occurred in 39% on amlodipine versus 42% on placebo (a 9% relative reduction; P = 0.31) and death in 33% versus 38% (a 16% relative reduction; P = 0.07) — neutral overall — but in the non-ischaemic subgroup amlodipine appeared to cut death by 46% in relative terms (P < 0.001). PRAISE-2 then randomised 1,654 patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy specifically: 278 deaths on amlodipine versus 262 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29), and pooling both trials' non-ischaemic patients gave a mortality hazard ratio of 0.97 (0.83 to 1.13). Amlodipine caused more peripheral and pulmonary oedema. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): amlodipine neither prolongs nor shortens survival in severe heart failure of either cause; it appears safe when needed for angina or hypertension, but it is not a heart-failure treatment.

cards.headline: PRAISE (Packer 1996): primary endpoint 39% on amlodipine versus 42% on placebo (P = 0.31) and death 33% versus 38% (P = 0.07) — neutral overall, with a large apparent benefit confined to the non-ischaemic subgroup
cards.summary: PRAISE (Packer 1996): primary endpoint 39% on amlodipine versus 42% on placebo (P = 0.31) and death 33% versus 38% (P = 0.07) — neutral overall, with a large apparent benefit confined to the non-ischaemic subgroup
cards.people: 1,153 patients with severe chronic heart failure and ejection fraction below 30%, randomised to amlodipine (571 patients) or placebo (582) for 6 to 33 months on top of usual therapy, with randomisation stratified by ischaemic versus non-ischaemic cause.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (death from any cause or hospitalisation for major cardiovascular events) was reached in 39% of the amlodipine group and 42% of the placebo group — a 9% relative reduction (95% CI 24% relative reduction to 10% increase; P = 0.31). Death occurred in 33% on amlodipine versus 38% on placebo — a 16% relative reduction (95% CI 31% relative reduction to 2% increase; P = 0.07). In ischaemic disease there was no difference on either endpoint; in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, amlodipine was associated with a 31% relative reduction in the combined endpoint (P = 0.04) and a 46% relative reduction in death (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The non-ischaemic result was a subgroup of a neutral trial — precisely the setting where chance produces dramatic relative effects; the investigators themselves said it required further study, which PRAISE-2 then provided.
cards.source: Packer et al. Effect of amlodipine on morbidity and mortality in severe chronic heart failure. Prospective Randomized Amlodipine Survival Evaluation Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1996. PMID: 8813041. cards.headline: PRAISE-2 (Packer 2013): in 1,654 patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, 278 deaths on amlodipine versus 262 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.09) — the subgroup benefit did not replicate
cards.summary: PRAISE-2 (Packer 2013): in 1,654 patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, 278 deaths on amlodipine versus 262 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.09) — the subgroup benefit did not replicate
cards.people: 1,654 patients with severe heart failure due to a non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction below 30%), randomised to amlodipine (target 10 mg daily) or placebo added to conventional heart-failure therapy, followed for a median of 33 months.
cards.result: There were 278 deaths in the amlodipine group and 262 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29; P = 0.33), and risks of cardiovascular death and hospitalisation also did not differ. Combining the non-ischaemic patients from both PRAISE trials gave a mortality hazard ratio of 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; P = 0.66). Both trials saw more peripheral oedema and pulmonary oedema on amlodipine, and less uncontrolled hypertension and chest pain.
cards.watchOut: PRAISE-2 was published in full only in 2013, years after the trial was run; its result nonetheless stands as the direct, adequately sized test of the PRAISE subgroup hypothesis.
cards.source: Packer et al. JACC. Heart failure. 2013. PMID: 24621933. cards.headline: Synthesis: amlodipine is survival-neutral in severe heart failure — the PRAISE subgroup was a mirage
cards.summary: Synthesis: amlodipine is survival-neutral in severe heart failure — the PRAISE subgroup was a mirage
cards.people: Patients with severe chronic heart failure, including non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, in whom amlodipine is considered.
cards.result: Two large trials totalling over 2,800 patients agree that amlodipine does not change mortality in severe heart failure (PRAISE death 33% versus 38%, not significant; PRAISE-2 hazard ratio 1.09 in the very subgroup expected to benefit). Its role in heart failure is limited to treating coexisting angina or hypertension, accepting more oedema.
cards.watchOut: Neutrality for survival is not proof of safety for every calcium-channel blocker — this shelf grades amlodipine only; older agents in this class increased events in heart failure in other studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of PRAISE (PMID: 8813041) and PRAISE-2 (PMID: 24621933).

shelves.title: Tumour necrosis factor blockade in chronic heart failure: etanercept did not help (RENEWAL), and high-dose infliximab increased death or heart-failure hospitalisation (ATTACH)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, does blocking tumour necrosis factor-alpha — with etanercept or infliximab — improve clinical status, or reduce death and hospitalisation for heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Disease Susceptibility · Double-Blind Method · Etanercept · Female · Heart Failure/*drug therapy/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Immunoglobulin G/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Infections/epidemiology · Life Tables · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, Tumor Necrosis Factor/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/*antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the anti-cytokine idea in heart failure failed, with a dose-related harm signal. The pooled RENEWAL analysis of the RECOVER and RENAISSANCE trials found etanercept had no effect on the combined outcome of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (relative risk 1.1; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.33) and no effect on clinical status; both trials were stopped early for lack of benefit. In ATTACH (150 patients), infliximab did not improve clinical status at either dose, and the 10 mg/kg dose increased the combined risk of death or heart-failure hospitalisation through 28 weeks (hazard ratio 2.84; 95% CI 1.01 to 7.97). Because this is a harm claim, the shelf is flagged Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): TNF-alpha blockade does not help chronic heart failure and, at higher infliximab doses, probably harms — a caution whenever anti-TNF drugs are used in patients who also have heart failure.

cards.headline: RENEWAL (Mann 2004): etanercept versus placebo relative risk 1.1 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.33) for death or heart-failure hospitalisation — both component trials stopped early for lack of benefit
cards.summary: RENEWAL (Mann 2004): etanercept versus placebo relative risk 1.1 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.33) for death or heart-failure hospitalisation — both component trials stopped early for lack of benefit
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (RECOVER and RENAISSANCE, reported as RENEWAL)
cards.people: Patients with NYHA class II to IV chronic heart failure and ejection fraction of 0.30 or less: RECOVER randomised 1,123 patients to placebo or etanercept 25 mg once or twice weekly; RENAISSANCE randomised 925 to placebo or etanercept 25 mg two or three times weekly; the primary endpoint of each trial was clinical status at 24 weeks.
cards.result: Etanercept had no effect on clinical status in RENAISSANCE (P = 0.17) or RECOVER (P = 0.34), and no effect on the prespecified combined outcome of death or hospitalisation for chronic heart failure in the pooled RENEWAL analysis (etanercept-to-placebo relative risk 1.1; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.33; P = 0.33). Both trials were terminated prematurely under prespecified stopping rules for lack of benefit; the authors concluded the results rule out a clinically relevant benefit of etanercept on death or heart-failure hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Early termination limits precision for harm: the point estimate sits above 1 but the confidence interval includes meaningful benefit and harm — the firm conclusion is no benefit, with harm suggested rather than proven for etanercept.
cards.source: Mann et al. Targeted anticytokine therapy in patients with chronic heart failure: results of the Randomized Etanercept Worldwide Evaluation (RENEWAL). Circulation. 2004. PMID: 15023878. cards.headline: ATTACH (Chung 2003): infliximab 10 mg/kg increased death or heart-failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 2.84; 95% CI 1.01 to 7.97); neither dose improved clinical status
cards.summary: ATTACH (Chung 2003): infliximab 10 mg/kg increased death or heart-failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 2.84; 95% CI 1.01 to 7.97); neither dose improved clinical status
cards.people: 150 patients with stable NYHA class III or IV heart failure and ejection fraction of 35% or less, randomised to placebo (49 patients), infliximab 5 mg/kg (50) or infliximab 10 mg/kg (51), given at 0, 2 and 6 weeks, with follow-up to 28 weeks.
cards.result: Neither infliximab dose improved clinical status at 14 weeks (the primary endpoint), despite suppression of C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Through 28 weeks, hospitalisation for any reason occurred in 13 patients on placebo, 10 on infliximab 5 mg/kg and 20 on infliximab 10 mg/kg; the combined risk of death from any cause or hospitalisation for heart failure was increased at the 10 mg/kg dose (hazard ratio 2.84; 95% CI 1.01 to 7.97; nominal P = 0.043).
cards.watchOut: A small pilot trial — the harm estimate is imprecise and the P value nominal — but the dose ordering (harm only at the higher dose) and the absence of any efficacy signal make the safety message hard to dismiss.
cards.source: Chung et al. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, pilot trial of infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody to tumor necrosis factor-alpha, in patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure: results of the anti-TNF Therapy Against Congestive Heart Failure (ATTACH) trial. Circulation. 2003. PMID: 12796126. cards.headline: Synthesis: suppressing TNF-alpha in heart failure lowered inflammatory markers and helped no one
cards.summary: Synthesis: suppressing TNF-alpha in heart failure lowered inflammatory markers and helped no one
cards.people: Patients with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, including those receiving anti-TNF therapy for inflammatory disease.
cards.result: Across more than 2,100 randomised patients, TNF blockade produced no improvement in clinical status, death or heart-failure hospitalisation (etanercept relative risk 1.1), and high-dose infliximab increased the death-or-hospitalisation composite (hazard ratio 2.84). cards.watchOut: These trials tested short courses in advanced heart failure; they do not measure the long-term cardiac effects of anti-TNF drugs given for rheumatic or bowel disease in people without heart failure.
cards.source: Synthesis of RENEWAL (PMID: 15023878) and ATTACH (PMID: 12796126).

shelves.title: The SUPRIM cognitive behavioural stress-management programme after a coronary event: 41% relative fewer recurrent cardiovascular events over 8 years in one randomised trial
shelves.question: In patients recovering from a coronary heart disease event, does adding the SUPRIM programme — a structured, group cognitive behavioural therapy programme focused on stress management — to traditional care reduce recurrent cardiovascular events and myocardial infarction?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alcohol Drinking/epidemiology · *Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Coronary Disease/mortality/psychology/*therapy · Female · Humans · Life Style · Male · Myocardial Infarction/mortality/*prevention & control/psychology · Risk Factors · Smoking/epidemiology · Sweden
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-followed trial of a named programme, against a mixed wider literature. In SUPRIM (362 patients after a coronary event), the group offered 20 two-hour CBT sessions over 1 year had, over a mean of 94 months, a 41% relative lower rate of fatal and nonfatal first recurrent cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83), 45% relative fewer recurrent myocardial infarctions (hazard ratio 0.55; 0.36 to 0.85), and a non-significant 28% relative lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.72; 0.40 to 1.30), with a dose-response by attendance. The broader Cochrane review of psychological interventions in coronary disease (35 trials, 10,703 people) is cooler: no reduction in total mortality (risk ratio 0.90; 0.77 to 1.05) or non-fatal infarction (0.82; 0.64 to 1.05), with a possible reduction in cardiac mortality (0.79; 0.63 to 0.98) on low-quality evidence. Because the hard-outcome benefit rests substantially on one trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the SUPRIM stress-management CBT programme probably reduces recurrent events after a coronary event; psychological therapy in general has, at most, smaller and less certain effects.

cards.headline: SUPRIM (Gulliksson 2011): recurrent cardiovascular events hazard ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.83) and recurrent myocardial infarction 0.55 with CBT added to traditional care over a mean of 94 months
cards.summary: SUPRIM (Gulliksson 2011): recurrent cardiovascular events hazard ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.83) and recurrent myocardial infarction 0.55 with CBT added to traditional care over a mean of 94 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of a named programme (SUPRIM — Secondary Prevention in Uppsala Primary Health Care project)
cards.people: 362 women and men aged 75 years or younger, discharged after a coronary heart disease event within the previous 12 months in Uppsala, Sweden, randomised to traditional care alone (170 patients) or traditional care plus the SUPRIM cognitive behavioural therapy programme (192 patients): 20 two-hour group sessions over 1 year focused on stress management, with median attendance of 85% per session.
cards.result: During a mean follow-up of 94 months, the intervention group had a 41% relative lower rate of fatal and nonfatal first recurrent cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83; P = .002), a 45% relative lower rate of recurrent acute myocardial infarction (hazard ratio 0.55; 0.36 to 0.85; P = .007), and a non-significant 28% relative lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.72; 0.40 to 1.30; P = .28), after adjustment. There was a strong dose-response between session attendance and outcome, and no significant group differences in traditional risk factors during the first 2 years.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one centre, unblinded by necessity, with adjusted analyses; the event curves separated late, and the mechanism (no early risk-factor change) is unexplained — replication of this specific programme is lacking.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Richards 2017): across 35 trials and 10,703 people with coronary disease, psychological interventions did not reduce total mortality (risk ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Richards 2017): across 35 trials and 10,703 people with coronary disease, psychological interventions did not reduce total mortality (risk ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 35 randomised trials enrolling 10,703 adults with coronary heart disease (after myocardial infarction, revascularisation, or with angina or angiographic disease), comparing psychological interventions delivered by trained staff against usual care, with at least 6 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Moderate-quality evidence showed no reduction in total mortality (risk ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05; 7,776 participants) or revascularisation (risk ratio 0.94; 0.81 to 1.11). Low-quality evidence found no reduction in non-fatal myocardial infarction (risk ratio 0.82; 0.64 to 1.05) but a 21% relative reduction in cardiac mortality (risk ratio 0.79; 0.63 to 0.98), alongside small improvements in depression, anxiety and stress scores; the reviewers noted poor trial reporting and small-study bias for the cardiac-mortality outcome.
cards.watchOut: The review pools many different interventions, most multifactorial and few resembling SUPRIM's focused stress-management format — it tempers enthusiasm for psychological therapy in general without directly testing the SUPRIM programme.
cards.source: Richards et al. Psychological interventions for coronary heart disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28452408. cards.headline: Synthesis: one strong trial of one structured programme, inside a literature that is otherwise lukewarm
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial of one structured programme, inside a literature that is otherwise lukewarm
cards.people: Patients after a coronary event offered structured psychological or stress-management programmes.
cards.result: SUPRIM's hazard ratios (0.59 for recurrent events, 0.55 for recurrent infarction) are far larger than anything the pooled literature supports for psychological interventions generally (total mortality risk ratio 0.90). The fair reading: this specific, well-attended, year-long stress-management programme probably helps; generic psychological support should not be assumed to do the same.
cards.watchOut: SUPRIM predates contemporary secondary prevention; whether its effect adds to modern drug therapy at today's lower event rates is untested.
cards.source: Synthesis of SUPRIM (PMID: 21263103) and the Cochrane review of psychological interventions for coronary heart disease (PMID: 28452408).

shelves.title: Wait-and-see cardioversion in recent-onset atrial fibrillation (RACE 7 ACWAS): sinus rhythm at 4 weeks in 91% with delayed versus 94% with early cardioversion — noninferior, and 69% converted on their own
shelves.question: In haemodynamically stable patients presenting to the emergency department with recent-onset symptomatic atrial fibrillation, is a wait-and-see strategy (rate control first, cardioversion only if the arrhythmia persists beyond 48 hours) noninferior to early cardioversion for being in sinus rhythm at 4 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy/*therapy · Calcium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Digoxin/therapeutic use · *Electric Countershock/adverse effects · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Recurrence · *Time-to-Treatment · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — waiting did not cost rhythm outcomes, because most episodes stop by themselves. In RACE 7 ACWAS (437 patients with recent-onset, symptomatic atrial fibrillation in the emergency department), sinus rhythm at 4 weeks was present in 91% of the delayed-cardioversion group and 94% of the early-cardioversion group (difference -2.9 percentage points; 95% CI -8.2 to 2.2; P = 0.005 for noninferiority against a -10 margin). In the wait-and-see group, 69% converted spontaneously within 48 hours and only 28% needed the delayed cardioversion; atrial fibrillation recurred in 30% versus 29%, and cardiovascular complications occurred in 10 versus 8 patients within 4 weeks. A prespecified substudy found that when fibrillation recurred, heart rates were better controlled after the delayed strategy (median 100 versus 112 beats per minute). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for stable recent-onset atrial fibrillation, initial rate control with cardioversion in reserve achieves the same 4-week rhythm outcome as immediate cardioversion, while sparing most patients the procedure.

cards.headline: RACE 7 ACWAS (Pluymaekers 2019): sinus rhythm at 4 weeks in 193 of 212 (91%) with delayed versus 202 of 215 (94%) with early cardioversion — noninferior (P = 0.005 for noninferiority)
cards.summary: RACE 7 ACWAS (Pluymaekers 2019): sinus rhythm at 4 weeks in 193 of 212 (91%) with delayed versus 202 of 215 (94%) with early cardioversion — noninferior (P = 0.005 for noninferiority)
cards.people: 437 patients with haemodynamically stable, recent-onset (under 36 hours), symptomatic atrial fibrillation presenting to the emergency department, randomised to a wait-and-see approach (rate control only, with cardioversion delayed beyond 48 hours if fibrillation persisted; 218 patients) or early pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion (219 patients).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — sinus rhythm at 4 weeks — occurred in 193 of 212 patients (91%) in the delayed group and 202 of 215 (94%) in the early group (between-group difference -2.9 percentage points; 95% CI -8.2 to 2.2; P = 0.005 for noninferiority, margin -10). In the delayed group, conversion within 48 hours occurred spontaneously in 150 of 218 patients (69%) and after delayed cardioversion in 61 (28%); in the early group, 36 of 219 (16%) converted spontaneously before cardioversion and 171 (78%) after it. Recurrence of atrial fibrillation during monitoring occurred in 30% versus 29%, and cardiovascular complications within 4 weeks in 10 versus 8 patients.
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial in stable emergency-department patients with very recent onset; it does not apply to unstable patients, and the endpoint is rhythm status at 4 weeks — not stroke, mortality or symptoms over the long term.
cards.source: Pluymaekers et al. Early or Delayed Cardioversion in Recent-Onset Atrial Fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30883054. Registry ID: NCT02248753. cards.headline: RACE 7 substudy (van der Velden 2024): during recurrences, median heart rate was 100 beats per minute after the delayed strategy versus 112 after early cardioversion (P = .011)
cards.summary: RACE 7 substudy (van der Velden 2024): during recurrences, median heart rate was 100 beats per minute after the delayed strategy versus 112 after early cardioversion (P = .011)
cards.type: Prespecified subanalysis of the RACE 7 ACWAS randomised trial (same trial as the card above)
cards.people: 335 of the RACE 7 participants who used a handheld ECG device to record recurrences during the 4 weeks after the emergency visit; 99 patients (29.6%) recorded 314 episodes of recurrent atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: The average median resting heart rate during recurrences was 100 ± 21 beats per minute in the delayed-cardioversion group versus 112 ± 25 in the early-cardioversion group (P = .011), and optimal rate control (below 110 beats per minute) was seen in 68.4% of recordings after the delayed strategy versus 33.3% after early cardioversion (P = .01); on multivariable analysis, randomisation to the delayed strategy was independently associated with a lower recurrence heart rate (coefficient -12.09; P = .006).
cards.watchOut: A substudy of the same trial, in the subset who used the monitoring device — supportive colour on rate control, not independent evidence on the strategy itself.
cards.source: van der Velden et al. Cardioversion strategy impacts rate control during recurrences in patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: A subanalysis of the RACE 7 ACWAS trial. Clinical cardiology. 2024. PMID: 37872853. cards.headline: Synthesis: in stable recent-onset atrial fibrillation, patience performs as well as the paddles at 4 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: in stable recent-onset atrial fibrillation, patience performs as well as the paddles at 4 weeks
cards.people: Haemodynamically stable emergency-department patients with recent-onset symptomatic atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: One randomised trial shows the wait-and-see strategy matches early cardioversion for sinus rhythm at 4 weeks (91% versus 94%), mainly because 69% of episodes self-terminate within 48 hours; complications were similar (10 versus 8 patients). The gain is avoiding an immediate procedure in most patients, not better rhythm outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Anticoagulation decisions are governed by episode duration and stroke risk, not by which cardioversion strategy is chosen — this shelf does not grade thromboembolism prevention.

shelves.title: Angiotensin-receptor blockers to prevent atrial fibrillation recurrence: valsartan (GISSI-AF) and olmesartan (ANTIPAF) both failed against placebo
shelves.question: In patients with a history of atrial fibrillation who are in sinus rhythm, does an angiotensin II-receptor blocker — valsartan or olmesartan — reduce recurrence of atrial fibrillation or lower AF burden, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/*therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy/epidemiology/*prevention & control · Cardiomegaly/epidemiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Comorbidity · Diabetes Mellitus/epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Tetrazoles/*therapeutic use · Valine/*analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Valsartan
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials, in two different AF populations, both flat. In GISSI-AF (1,442 patients with prior atrial fibrillation plus cardiovascular disease, diabetes or atrial enlargement), recurrence occurred in 51.4% on valsartan versus 52.1% on placebo over 1 year (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; 96% CI 0.83 to 1.14), and more-than-one recurrence in 26.9% versus 27.9%. In ANTIPAF (430 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no structural heart disease, monitored with daily transtelephonic ECG — 87,818 recordings), the primary endpoint of AF burden did not differ between olmesartan and placebo (P = 0.770). Whatever ARBs do for blood pressure and ventricular remodelling, they do not keep atrial fibrillation away. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): ARBs should not be prescribed to prevent AF recurrence; their use in these patients stands or falls on their other indications.

cards.headline: GISSI-AF (Disertori 2009): atrial fibrillation recurred in 371 of 722 patients (51.4%) on valsartan versus 375 of 720 (52.1%) on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; P = 0.73)
cards.summary: GISSI-AF (Disertori 2009): atrial fibrillation recurred in 371 of 722 patients (51.4%) on valsartan versus 375 of 720 (52.1%) on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; P = 0.73)
cards.people: 1,442 patients in sinus rhythm who had had at least two documented episodes of atrial fibrillation in the previous 6 months or successful cardioversion in the previous 2 weeks, and who also had underlying cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or left atrial enlargement; followed for 1 year.
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation recurred in 371 of 722 patients (51.4%) in the valsartan group and 375 of 720 (52.1%) in the placebo group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; 96% CI 0.83 to 1.14; P = 0.73). More than one recurrence occurred in 194 patients (26.9%) on valsartan versus 201 (27.9%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.89; 99% CI 0.64 to 1.23; P = 0.34). Results were similar in all predefined subgroups, including patients not taking ACE inhibitors.
cards.watchOut: Recurrence was detected clinically rather than by continuous monitoring, so silent episodes were missed equally in both arms — a detection limitation that biases toward, not away from, the null actually observed.
cards.source: Disertori et al. Valsartan for prevention of recurrent atrial fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2009. PMID: 19369667. Registry ID: NCT00376272. cards.headline: ANTIPAF (Goette 2012): AF burden over 12 months did not differ between olmesartan and placebo (P = 0.770), despite 87,818 transtelephonic ECGs analysed
cards.summary: ANTIPAF (Goette 2012): AF burden over 12 months did not differ between olmesartan and placebo (P = 0.770), despite 87,818 transtelephonic ECGs analysed
cards.people: 430 patients with documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no structural heart disease, randomised to olmesartan 40 mg daily or placebo for 12 months (intention-to-treat population 425: 214 olmesartan, 211 placebo), with daily transtelephonic ECG recordings independent of symptoms; concomitant ARBs, ACE inhibitors and antiarrhythmic drugs were prohibited.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — AF burden, the percentage of days with documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation episodes during 12 months — was not different between the olmesartan and placebo groups (P = 0.770), in an analysis built on 87,818 tele-ECGs (a mean of 207 recordings per patient). Secondary outcome parameters likewise showed no advantage for olmesartan.
cards.watchOut: The PubMed record reports the burden comparison by P value without group percentages, so the card states the result exactly as the record gives it; the near-continuous rhythm monitoring makes a clinically important missed effect unlikely.
cards.source: Goette et al. Angiotensin II-antagonist in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (ANTIPAF) trial. Circulation. Arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2012. PMID: 22157519. Registry ID: NCT00098137. randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial (antipaf) 430 patients with documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no structural heart disease, randomised to olmesartan 40 mg daily or placebo for 12 months (intention-to-treat population 425: 214 olmesartan, 211 placebo), with daily transtelephonic ecg recordings independent of symptoms; concomitant arbs, ace inhibitors and antiarrhythmic drugs were prohibited. the primary endpoint — af burden, the percentage of days with documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation episodes during 12 months — was not different between the olmesartan and placebo groups (p = 0.770), in an analysis built on 87,818 tele-ecgs (a mean of 207 recordings per patient). secondary outcome parameters likewise showed no advantage for olmesartan. the pubmed record reports the burden comparison by p value without group percentages, so the card states the result exactly as the record gives it; the near-continuous rhythm monitoring makes a clinically important missed effect unlikely. goette et al. angiotensin ii-antagonist in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (antipaf) trial. circulation. arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2012. pmid: 22157519. registry id: nct00098137. mesh: angiotensin ii type 1 receptor blockers/*administration & dosage · atrial fibrillation/*drug therapy/epidemiology/physiopathology · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · electrocardiography/drug effects · female · follow-up studies · germany/epidemiology · humans · imidazoles/*administration & dosage · incidence · male · middle aged · prospective studies · tachycardia, paroxysmal/*drug therapy/epidemiology/physiopathology · tetrazoles/*administration & dosage · time factors · treatment outcome

shelves.title: Clopidogrel versus ticagrelor or prasugrel after NSTE-ACS at age 70 and older (POPular AGE): less bleeding on clopidogrel (18% versus 24%) with noninferior net clinical benefit
shelves.question: In patients aged 70 years or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, is clopidogrel — rather than the more potent ticagrelor or prasugrel — the better P2Y12 inhibitor when bleeding and net clinical benefit are weighed over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/*drug therapy/mortality · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Clopidogrel/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Myocardial Infarction/prevention & control · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Prasugrel Hydrochloride/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Stroke/prevention & control · Ticagrelor/adverse effects/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one trial dedicated to older patients, the gentler drug won on bleeding without losing on net benefit. In POPular AGE (1,002 patients aged 70 or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome), the primary bleeding outcome (PLATO major or minor bleeding) occurred in 88 patients (18%) on clopidogrel versus 118 (24%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.94; P = 0.02 for superiority), and the co-primary net clinical benefit outcome (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and major or minor bleeding) was noninferior on clopidogrel — 139 patients (28%) versus 161 (32%), an absolute difference of -4% (95% CI -10.0 to 1.4). Nearly half the ticagrelor group (47%) stopped their drug early, versus 22% on clopidogrel. Because the bleeding-benefit claim rests on a single trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in NSTE-ACS patients aged 70 and older, clopidogrel probably causes less bleeding than ticagrelor-based therapy without a net clinical penalty.

cards.headline: POPular AGE (Gimbel 2020): PLATO major or minor bleeding in 88 of 500 patients (18%) on clopidogrel versus 118 of 502 (24%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.71; P = 0.02 for superiority)
cards.summary: POPular AGE (Gimbel 2020): PLATO major or minor bleeding in 88 of 500 patients (18%) on clopidogrel versus 118 of 502 (24%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.71; P = 0.02 for superiority)
cards.type: Randomised open-label noninferiority trial with masked outcome assessment (POPular AGE)
cards.people: 1,002 patients aged 70 years or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome at 12 Dutch sites, randomised to clopidogrel (500 patients) or ticagrelor or prasugrel (502 patients; 95% received ticagrelor) for 12 months on top of standard care, with intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: The primary bleeding outcome occurred in 88 patients (18%) on clopidogrel versus 118 (24%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.94; P = 0.02 for superiority). The co-primary net clinical benefit outcome (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke, PLATO major and minor bleeding) occurred in 139 patients (28%) on clopidogrel versus 161 (32%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel — an absolute risk difference of -4% (95% CI -10.0 to 1.4; P = 0.03 for noninferiority against a 2% margin). Premature study-drug discontinuation occurred in 47% of the ticagrelor group versus 22% of the clopidogrel group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (though outcome assessors were masked) and a Dutch population aged 70+; the trial was powered for bleeding and net benefit, not for myocardial infarction or mortality separately, so a small ischaemic cost of clopidogrel cannot be excluded from this trial alone.
cards.source: Gimbel et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: in patients 70 and older, the trial built for them favours the less potent P2Y12 inhibitor on bleeding
cards.people: Patients aged 70 years or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome starting dual antiplatelet therapy.
cards.result: POPular AGE is the only randomised trial designed around this age group: clopidogrel gave 6 fewer bleeding events per 100 patients (18% versus 24%) and a net clinical benefit outcome that was noninferior and numerically better (28% versus 32%). shelves.title: Unguided DAPT de-escalation from ticagrelor to clopidogrel one month after myocardial infarction (TALOS-AMI): net events 4.6% versus 8.2%, with bleeding halved and no ischaemic penalty
shelves.question: In stabilised patients with acute myocardial infarction who have completed one month of aspirin plus ticagrelor after PCI without events, does switching the P2Y12 inhibitor to clopidogrel (unguided de-escalation) improve net clinical outcomes over months 1 to 12 compared with continuing ticagrelor?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Clopidogrel/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dual Anti-Platelet Therapy/*methods · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/*drug therapy/mortality/surgery · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Republic of Korea · Stroke · Ticagrelor/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large trial and a patient-level meta-analysis of four trials agree. In TALOS-AMI (2,697 stabilised post-infarction patients switched at 1 month), the primary net endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC type 2, 3 or 5 bleeding) occurred in 4.6% with de-escalation versus 8.2% continuing ticagrelor (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.76), driven by bleeding (3.0% versus 5.6%; hazard ratio 0.52), while the ischaemic composite was not significantly different (2.1% versus 3.1%; hazard ratio 0.69; 0.42 to 1.14). The individual-patient meta-analysis of four de-escalation trials (10,133 patients) found both fewer ischaemic events with de-escalation (2.3% versus 3.0%; hazard ratio 0.761) and less bleeding (6.5% versus 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.701), with no difference in all-cause death or major bleeding. Because the claim includes a cardiovascular-event composite benefit, this shelf is flagged Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): switching from ticagrelor to clopidogrel after the first event-free month following myocardial infarction reduces bleeding and net events without an ischaemic penalty.

cards.headline: TALOS-AMI (Kim 2021): primary net endpoint in 59 patients (4.6%) with de-escalation versus 104 (8.2%) continuing ticagrelor (hazard ratio 0.55; P for superiority = 0.0001)
cards.summary: TALOS-AMI (Kim 2021): primary net endpoint in 59 patients (4.6%) with de-escalation versus 104 (8.2%) continuing ticagrelor (hazard ratio 0.55; P for superiority = 0.0001)
cards.people: 2,697 patients with acute myocardial infarction treated with PCI at 32 South Korean institutes, who had received aspirin plus ticagrelor for the first month without major ischaemic or bleeding events, randomised to unguided de-escalation to clopidogrel plus aspirin (1,349 patients; switch without a loading dose) or continued ticagrelor plus aspirin (1,348), followed from month 1 to month 12.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC type 2, 3 or 5 bleeding) occurred in 59 patients (4.6%) in the de-escalation group and 104 (8.2%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.76; P < 0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.0001 for superiority). The ischaemic composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) occurred in 2.1% versus 3.1% (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.14; P = 0.15), and BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding in 3.0% versus 5.6% (hazard ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.77; P = 0.0012).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country (South Korea, where clopidogrel pharmacogenetics differ from European populations), and restricted to patients who had already completed an event-free first month — it does not support switching during the high-risk early phase.
cards.source: Kim et al. Unguided de-escalation from ticagrelor to clopidogrel in stabilised patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (TALOS-AMI): an investigator-initiated, open-label, multicentre, non-inferiority, randomised trial. cards.headline: Individual-patient meta-analysis (Kang 2023): across four trials and 10,133 patients, de-escalation lowered the ischaemic endpoint (2.3% versus 3.0%; hazard ratio 0.761) and bleeding (6.5% versus 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.701)
cards.summary: Individual-patient meta-analysis (Kang 2023): across four trials and 10,133 patients, de-escalation lowered the ischaemic endpoint (2.3% versus 3.0%; hazard ratio 0.761) and bleeding (6.5% versus 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.701)
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of four randomised trials (TROPICAL-ACS, POPular Genetics, HOST-REDUCE-POLYTECH-ACS, TALOS-AMI)
cards.people: 10,133 patients with acute coronary syndrome treated with PCI in four randomised trials comparing P2Y12 de-escalation strategies (guided by platelet-function or genetic testing, or unguided) against continued standard potent DAPT, with 1-year outcomes.
cards.result: The ischaemic composite endpoint (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular events) was lower with de-escalation (2.3% versus 3.0%; hazard ratio 0.761; 95% CI 0.597 to 0.972; P = 0.029), as was any bleeding (6.5% versus 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.701; 95% CI 0.606 to 0.811; P < 0.001). There were no significant differences in all-cause death or major bleeding events. Unguided de-escalation reduced bleeding more than guided de-escalation (P for interaction = 0.007), with no intergroup difference for ischaemic endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The pooled strategies are heterogeneous (dose reduction in one trial, switching in others, testing-guided in two) and TALOS-AMI contributes a large share of patients, so the meta-analysis corroborates rather than independently replicates the switch strategy.
cards.source: Kang et al. Dual antiplatelet therapy de-escalation in acute coronary syndrome: an individual patient meta-analysis. European heart journal. 2023. PMID: 36883613. cards.headline: Synthesis: after an event-free first month, stepping down platelet potency trades nothing ischaemic and buys less bleeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: after an event-free first month, stepping down platelet potency trades nothing ischaemic and buys less bleeding
cards.people: Stabilised post-PCI patients with myocardial infarction who have completed one month of potent DAPT without events.
cards.result: TALOS-AMI (net events 4.6% versus 8.2%) and the four-trial patient-level analysis (bleeding 6.5% versus 9.1%; ischaemic events 2.3% versus 3.0%) point the same way: de-escalation at one month is at worst ischaemically neutral and clearly reduces bleeding burden.
cards.watchOut: Neither source supports de-escalation before one month, in patients with early events, or as a response to high bleeding risk at presentation — those are different strategies with their own evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of TALOS-AMI (PMID: 34627490) and the DAPT de-escalation individual-patient meta-analysis (PMID: 36883613).

shelves.title: Gastric bypass for hypertension in obesity (GATEWAY): 84% cut their antihypertensive load by at least 30% at 1 year versus 13% on medical therapy — and the advantage held at 5 years
shelves.question: In patients with obesity and hypertension requiring at least two antihypertensive medications, does Roux-en-Y gastric bypass plus medical therapy reduce medication burden and produce hypertension remission more than medical therapy alone, at 1 year and at 5 years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · *Blood Pressure/drug effects · Body Mass Index · Brazil · Female · *Gastric Bypass/adverse effects · Humans · Hypertension/diagnosis/drug therapy/*physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/diagnosis/physiopathology/*surgery · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large, durable effect in one small, single-centre, unblinded trial. In GATEWAY (100 patients with obesity and hypertension on at least two drugs), the primary endpoint — cutting total antihypertensive medications by at least 30% while keeping blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg — was met at 12 months by 83.7% of the gastric bypass group versus 12.8% on medical therapy alone (rate ratio 6.6; 95% CI 3.1 to 14.0), and hypertension remission occurred in 51% (office measurement) versus 0%. At 5 years the pattern persisted: medication reduction in 80.7% versus 13.7% (relative risk 5.91), remission in 46.9% versus 2.4% (relative risk 19.66), and a mean medication count of 0.80 versus 2.97. Because this is a single small trial, the shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gastric bypass probably produces large, durable reductions in antihypertensive burden and frequent hypertension remission in obesity — an effect on medication load and blood pressure, with no randomised data on cardiovascular events from this trial.

cards.headline: GATEWAY at 12 months (Schiavon 2018): primary endpoint met by 41 of 49 patients (83.7%) after gastric bypass versus 6 of 47 (12.8%) on medical therapy (rate ratio 6.6); hypertension remission 51% versus 0%
cards.summary: GATEWAY at 12 months (Schiavon 2018): primary endpoint met by 41 of 49 patients (83.7%) after gastric bypass versus 6 of 47 (12.8%) on medical therapy (rate ratio 6.6); hypertension remission 51% versus 0%
cards.people: 100 patients with hypertension (on at least two medications at maximum doses, or more than two at moderate doses) and body mass index 30.0 to 39.9 kg/m², randomised to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone; 96% completed 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: Reduction of at least 30% in the total number of antihypertensive medications while maintaining blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg occurred in 41 of 49 patients (83.7%) in the bypass group versus 6 of 47 (12.8%) in the control group (rate ratio 6.6; 95% CI 3.1 to 14.0; P < 0.001). Hypertension remission was present in 25 of 49 patients (51%) by office measurement and 22 of 48 (45.8%) by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, whereas no medically treated patient was free of antihypertensive drugs at 12 months. Waist circumference, body mass index, fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and 10-year Framingham risk score were all lower in the bypass group.

shelves.title: Oral inotropic drugs in chronic heart failure killed: milrinone raised mortality by 28% relative (PROMISE), vesnarinone dose-dependently (VEST), ibopamine by a relative risk of 1.26 (PRIME II)
shelves.question: In patients with severe chronic heart failure, does long-term oral inotropic therapy — milrinone, vesnarinone or ibopamine — improve survival, or does it increase mortality despite better haemodynamics and symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiotonic Agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Evaluation · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/drug therapy/*mortality · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Milrinone · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Pyridones/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — three large randomised trials of three different oral inotropes, one direction. PROMISE (1,088 patients with severe heart failure): oral milrinone was associated with a 28% relative increase in all-cause mortality (95% CI 1 to 61; P = 0.038) and a 34% relative increase in cardiovascular mortality, with the worst effect in NYHA class IV (a 53% relative increase), plus more hospitalisations (44% versus 39%). VEST (3,833 patients): deaths were significantly fewer on placebo (242 deaths, 18.9%) than on vesnarinone 60 mg daily (292 deaths, 22.9%; P = 0.02), attributed to sudden arrhythmic death, even though quality of life improved more on vesnarinone. PRIME II (1,906 patients) was stopped early: 232 deaths (25%) on ibopamine versus 193 (20%) on placebo (relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.53). As a harm claim this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): chronic oral inotropic therapy increases mortality in severe heart failure — feeling better and pumping harder did not mean living longer.

cards.headline: PROMISE (Packer 1991): oral milrinone associated with a 28% relative increase in all-cause mortality (95% CI 1 to 61; P = 0.038) and 34% relative increase in cardiovascular mortality in severe heart failure
cards.summary: PROMISE (Packer 1991): oral milrinone associated with a 28% relative increase in all-cause mortality (95% CI 1 to 61; P = 0.038) and 34% relative increase in cardiovascular mortality in severe heart failure
cards.people: 1,088 patients with severe chronic heart failure (NYHA class III or IV) and advanced left ventricular dysfunction, randomised to oral milrinone 40 mg daily (561 patients) or placebo (527), all also receiving digoxin, diuretics and an ACE inhibitor; median follow-up 6.1 months.
cards.result: Milrinone was associated with a 28% relative increase in mortality from all causes (95% CI 1 to 61 percent; P = 0.038) and a 34% relative increase in cardiovascular mortality (95% CI 6 to 69 percent; P = 0.016); the adverse effect was greatest in NYHA class IV patients (a 53% relative increase; P = 0.006), and no subgroup benefited. Patients on milrinone had more hospitalisations (44% versus 39%; P = 0.041), more withdrawals from double-blind therapy (12.7% versus 8.7%), and more hypotension and syncope.
cards.watchOut: An older trial from the pre-beta-blocker era of heart-failure therapy; the class lesson (chronic inotropic stimulation is dangerous) has nonetheless been repeatedly confirmed, including by the two other trials on this shelf.
cards.source: Packer et al. Effect of oral milrinone on mortality in severe chronic heart failure. The PROMISE Study Research Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1991. PMID: 1944425. cards.headline: VEST (Cohn 1998): 242 deaths (18.9%) on placebo versus 292 (22.9%) on vesnarinone 60 mg daily (P = 0.02) — a dose-dependent increase in mortality driven by sudden death
cards.summary: VEST (Cohn 1998): 242 deaths (18.9%) on placebo versus 292 (22.9%) on vesnarinone 60 mg daily (P = 0.02) — a dose-dependent increase in mortality driven by sudden death
cards.people: 3,833 patients with NYHA class III or IV heart failure symptoms and ejection fraction of 30% or less despite optimal treatment, randomised to vesnarinone 30 mg daily, vesnarinone 60 mg daily, or placebo; mean follow-up 286 days.
cards.result: There were significantly fewer deaths in the placebo group (242 deaths, 18.9%) than in the 60-mg vesnarinone group (292 deaths, 22.9%), with longer survival on placebo (P = 0.02); the excess mortality on vesnarinone was attributed to sudden death, presumed arrhythmic. Quality of life had improved significantly more on 60-mg vesnarinone than placebo at 8 and 16 weeks (P < 0.001 and P = 0.003) — symptoms and survival moved in opposite directions. Trends in the 30-mg group resembled the 60-mg group.
cards.watchOut: The earlier short-term vesnarinone study had suggested a survival benefit at 60 mg — the definitive trial reversed it, a further warning against short-term inotrope data; absolute mortality counts for the 30-mg arm are not given in the record abstract.
cards.source: Cohn et al. A dose-dependent increase in mortality with vesnarinone among patients with severe heart failure. Vesnarinone Trial Investigators. The New England journal of medicine. 1998.
