cards.headline: PRIME II (Hampton 1997): trial stopped early after 232 deaths (25%) on ibopamine versus 193 (20%) on placebo (relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.53; P = 0.017)
cards.summary: PRIME II (Hampton 1997): trial stopped early after 232 deaths (25%) on ibopamine versus 193 (20%) on placebo (relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.53; P = 0.017)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, stopped early (PRIME II)
cards.people: 1,906 patients with advanced severe heart failure (NYHA class III and IV) and severe left ventricular disease, already on optimum heart-failure treatment, randomised to oral ibopamine 100 mg three times daily (953 patients) or placebo (953); the trial had been designed for 2,200 patients.
cards.result: The trial was stopped early because of excess deaths on ibopamine: 232 of 953 patients (25%) died in the ibopamine group versus 193 of 953 (20%) on placebo (relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.53; P = 0.017), over an average follow-up of about 350 days. In multivariate analysis, only baseline antiarrhythmic drug use independently predicted the excess fatality on ibopamine — an exploratory finding the authors flag for caution.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping can exaggerate effect sizes, but the direction matches PROMISE and VEST exactly; ibopamine's symptomatic benefits, shown in earlier studies, did not translate into survival.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three drugs, three trials, one verdict — chronic oral inotropy shortens life in severe heart failure
cards.summary: Synthesis: three drugs, three trials, one verdict — chronic oral inotropy shortens life in severe heart failure
cards.people: Patients with severe chronic heart failure offered long-term oral inotropic agents to improve symptoms or haemodynamics.
cards.result: Milrinone (+28% relative mortality), vesnarinone (22.9% versus 18.9% deaths at 60 mg) and ibopamine (relative risk 1.26) each increased mortality in trials totalling over 6,800 patients, despite better haemodynamics and, for vesnarinone, better quality-of-life scores. This is among the most consistent harm signals in heart-failure therapeutics.
cards.watchOut: The verdict covers chronic oral inotropic therapy in advanced heart failure; short-term intravenous inotropes for acute decompensation or palliation are separate questions not graded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of PROMISE (PMID: 1944425), the Vesnarinone Trial (PMID: 9854116) and PRIME II (PMID: 9100622).

shelves.title: Treating depression in heart failure with an SSRI: sertraline (SADHART-CHF) and escitalopram (MOOD-HF) improved neither mood more than placebo nor cardiovascular outcomes
shelves.question: In patients with chronic heart failure and major depression, does SSRI treatment — sertraline or escitalopram — reduce depression severity and improve cardiovascular outcomes, including death and hospitalisation, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Depression/epidemiology/*prevention & control · Female · Heart Failure/mortality/*psychology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Sertraline/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials, concordant on both mood and events. In SADHART-CHF (469 patients with heart failure and major depression), 12 weeks of sertraline changed the Hamilton depression score by -7.1 points versus -6.8 on placebo (between-group difference -0.4; 95% CI -1.7 to 0.92; P = 0.89 between groups) — both groups improved, the drug added nothing — and the composite cardiovascular status did not differ (P = 0.78). In MOOD-HF (372 patients, 24 months of escitalopram), the primary outcome of death or hospitalisation occurred in 63% on escitalopram versus 64% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.27), and depression scores again improved equally (between-group difference -0.9 points on the Montgomery-Åsberg scale; P = .26). Both drugs were safe in heart failure — that is the only positive finding. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): SSRIs do not treat depression better than placebo-plus-support in heart failure, and do not reduce death or hospitalisation; depression in heart failure still needs care, but not on the expectation these drugs change cardiac outcomes.

cards.headline: SADHART-CHF (O'Connor 2010): Hamilton depression score fell 7.1 points on sertraline versus 6.8 on placebo (P = 0.89 between groups); composite cardiovascular status also no different (P = 0.78)
cards.summary: SADHART-CHF (O'Connor 2010): Hamilton depression score fell 7.1 points on sertraline versus 6.8 on placebo (P = 0.89 between groups); composite cardiovascular status also no different (P = 0.78)
cards.people: 469 patients aged 45 years or older with heart failure (ejection fraction of 45% or less, NYHA class II to IV) and DSM-IV major depressive disorder, randomised to sertraline 50 to 200 mg daily (234 patients) or placebo (235) for 12 weeks; all participants also received nurse-facilitated support.
cards.result: The mean change in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale total score was -7.1 ± 0.5 on sertraline and -6.8 ± 0.5 on placebo (mean between-group change -0.4; 95% CI -1.7 to 0.92; P = 0.89 between groups, though both groups improved from baseline). The composite cardiovascular score worsened, improved or was unchanged in 29.9%, 40.6% and 29.5% on sertraline versus 31.1%, 43.8% and 25.1% on placebo (P = 0.78). Sertraline was safe in this population.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week trial — too short and too small to test mortality; the large placebo-group improvement (nurse support for everyone, plus spontaneous remission) is itself part of the lesson. MOOD-HF supplies the long-term outcome test.

randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (sadhart-chf) 469 patients aged 45 years or older with heart failure (ejection fraction of 45% or less, nyha class ii to iv) and dsm-iv major depressive disorder, randomised to sertraline 50 to 200 mg daily (234 patients) or placebo (235) for 12 weeks; all participants also received nurse-facilitated support. the mean change in hamilton depression rating scale total score was -7.1 ± 0.5 on sertraline and -6.8 ± 0.5 on placebo (mean between-group change -0.4; 95% ci -1.7 to 0.92; p = 0.89 between groups, though both groups improved from baseline). the composite cardiovascular score worsened, improved or was unchanged in 29.9%, 40.6% and 29.5% on sertraline versus 31.1%, 43.8% and 25.1% on placebo (p = 0.78). sertraline was safe in this population. a 12-week trial — too short and too small to test mortality; the large placebo-group improvement (nurse support for everyone, plus spontaneous remission) is itself part of the lesson. mood-hf supplies the long-term outcome test. o'connor et al. safety and efficacy of sertraline for depression in patients with heart failure: results of the sadhart-chf (sertraline against depression and heart disease in chronic heart failure) trial. journal of the american college of cardiology. 2010. pmid: 20723799. registry id: nct00078286. mesh: aged · antidepressive agents/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · chronic disease · depression/epidemiology/*prevention & control · female · heart failure/mortality/*psychology · humans · male · middle aged · sertraline/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use

cards.headline: MOOD-HF (Angermann 2016): death or hospitalisation in 116 patients (63%) on escitalopram versus 119 (64%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99; P = .92) over 24 months; depression scores improved equally
cards.summary: MOOD-HF (Angermann 2016): death or hospitalisation in 116 patients (63%) on escitalopram versus 119 (64%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99; P = .92) over 24 months; depression scores improved equally
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MOOD-HF), stopped early on data and safety monitoring advice
cards.people: 372 patients with NYHA class II to IV heart failure, ejection fraction below 45%, and depression confirmed by structured clinical interview, at 16 German tertiary centres, randomised to escitalopram 10 to 20 mg daily (185 patients) or placebo (187) in addition to optimal heart-failure therapy, for a planned 24 months.
cards.result: The composite primary outcome (all-cause death or hospitalisation) occurred in 116 patients (63%) in the escitalopram group and 119 (64%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.27; P = .92) over a median participation of about 18.5 months. The Montgomery-Åsberg depression score fell from 20.2 to 11.2 on escitalopram and from 21.4 to 12.5 on placebo by 12 weeks (between-group difference -0.9; 95% CI -2.6 to 0.7; P = .26). Safety parameters were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early on the monitoring committee's recommendation, limiting power for modest effects — but the point estimates sit exactly on the null for both mood and hard outcomes, matching SADHART-CHF.
cards.source: Angermann et al. Effect of Escitalopram on All-Cause Mortality and Hospitalization in Patients With Heart Failure and Depression: The MOOD-HF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27367876. cards.headline: Synthesis: in heart failure, depression improves with support and time — the SSRI adds nothing measurable
cards.summary: Synthesis: in heart failure, depression improves with support and time — the SSRI adds nothing measurable
cards.people: Patients with chronic heart failure and comorbid major depression.
cards.result: Across 841 randomised patients, SSRIs were safe but ineffective beyond placebo: depression scores moved identically (between-group differences of -0.4 and -0.9 points), and death or hospitalisation was 63% versus 64% in the long-term trial. The case for treating depression in heart failure rests on symptom care, not on these drugs improving mood scores or cardiac prognosis.
cards.watchOut: These trials do not test psychotherapy, collaborative care, or exercise for depression in heart failure, nor SSRIs for other indications in these patients; untreated depression remains a marker of poor prognosis even if the drug trials are null.
cards.source: Synthesis of SADHART-CHF (PMID: 20723799) and MOOD-HF (PMID: 27367876).

shelves.title: Adding mitral-valve repair to CABG in moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation: less residual regurgitation, but no better remodelling or survival at 2 years — and more early harm (CTSN)
shelves.question: In patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation undergoing coronary-artery bypass grafting, does adding mitral-valve repair to CABG improve left ventricular remodelling, survival and clinical outcomes compared with CABG alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology/mortality · *Coronary Artery Bypass · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mitral Valve Insufficiency/etiology/*surgery · Myocardial Ischemia/complications/*surgery · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Quality of Life · Ventricular Remodeling
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the valve leaks less, the patient does no better. In the CTSN trial (301 patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation), adding mitral repair to CABG did not improve the primary endpoint of ventricular remodelling at 1 year (left ventricular end-systolic volume index change -9.3 versus -9.4 mL/m²) and death was 6.7% with the combined procedure versus 7.3% with CABG alone (hazard ratio 0.90); at 2 years death was 10.0% versus 10.6% (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.83), again with no remodelling difference. Repair did durably reduce moderate-or-severe residual regurgitation (11.2% versus 32.3% at 2 years), but at the cost of longer bypass time, longer hospital stay, and more neurologic events and supraventricular arrhythmias. The small RIME trial (73 patients) found better peak oxygen consumption and remodelling measures with repair (+3.3 versus +0.8 mL/kg/min) with similar deaths (9% versus 5% at 1 year) — surrogate gains the larger trial's clinical outcomes do not confirm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine addition of mitral repair to CABG for moderate ischaemic regurgitation fixes the echocardiogram, not the prognosis.

cards.headline: CTSN at 1 year (Smith 2014): no remodelling advantage (volume-index change -9.3 versus -9.4 mL/m²); death 6.7% with repair versus 7.3% with CABG alone; more neurologic events with repair
cards.summary: CTSN at 1 year (Smith 2014): no remodelling advantage (volume-index change -9.3 versus -9.4 mL/m²); death 6.7% with repair versus 7.3% with CABG alone; more neurologic events with repair
cards.type: Randomised trial (Cardiothoracic Surgical Trials Network), 1-year report
cards.people: 301 patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation randomised to CABG alone or CABG plus mitral-valve repair; the primary endpoint was the left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVI) at 1 year, assessed by a rank-based test incorporating deaths.
cards.result: At 1 year, mean LVESVI among survivors was 49.6 ± 31.5 mL/m² in the combined-procedure group and 46.1 ± 22.4 mL/m² in the CABG-alone group (mean change from baseline -9.3 and -9.4 mL/m²), with no significant difference in the rank-based assessment (P = 0.61). Death occurred in 6.7% of the combined group and 7.3% of the CABG-alone group (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.38 to 2.12; P = 0.81). Moderate or severe mitral regurgitation was less common with repair (11.2% versus 31.0%; P < 0.001), but repair meant longer bypass time (P < 0.001), longer hospital stay (P = 0.002) and more neurologic events (P = 0.03), with no differences in major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events, readmissions, functional status or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was an imaging surrogate; the trial was not powered for mortality, which is why the 2-year report and the harm profile matter for the overall judgement.
cards.source: Smith et al. Surgical treatment of moderate ischemic mitral regurgitation. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 25405390. Registry ID: NCT00806988. cards.headline: CTSN at 2 years (Michler 2016): death 10.0% with repair versus 10.6% with CABG alone (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.83); residual moderate-or-severe regurgitation 11.2% versus 32.3%
cards.summary: CTSN at 2 years (Michler 2016): death 10.0% with repair versus 10.6% with CABG alone (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.83); residual moderate-or-severe regurgitation 11.2% versus 32.3%
cards.type: Randomised trial 2-year outcomes report (CTSN — same trial as the card above)
cards.people: The same 301 CTSN participants with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation, followed for 2 years for clinical and echocardiographic outcomes.
cards.result: At 2 years, mean LVESVI was 43.2 ± 20.6 mL/m² in the combined-procedure group and 41.2 ± 20.0 mL/m² in the CABG-alone group (improvements of -14.6 and -14.1 mL/m² from baseline), with no significant difference in the rank-based assessment including death (P = 0.71). Death occurred in 10.0% of the combined group and 10.6% of the CABG-alone group (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.83; P = 0.78). Moderate or severe residual regurgitation remained less frequent with repair (11.2% versus 32.3%; P < 0.001). Overall readmission and serious adverse event rates were similar, but neurologic events and supraventricular arrhythmias remained more frequent in the combined-procedure group.
cards.watchOut: Confidence intervals around mortality are wide (0.45 to 1.83); the trial excludes neither a modest benefit nor harm — but combined with more early adverse events, the burden of proof stays on adding the repair.
cards.source: Michler et al. Two-Year Outcomes of Surgical Treatment of Moderate Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 27040451. Registry ID: NCT00806988. cards.headline: RIME (Chan 2012): peak oxygen consumption improved more with repair (+3.3 versus +0.8 mL/kg/min; P < 0.001) in 73 patients, with similar deaths (9% versus 5% at 1 year)
cards.summary: RIME (Chan 2012): peak oxygen consumption improved more with repair (+3.3 versus +0.8 mL/kg/min; P < 0.001) in 73 patients, with similar deaths (9% versus 5% at 1 year)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (RIME — Randomized Ischemic Mitral Evaluation), stopped early
cards.people: 73 patients referred for CABG with moderate functional ischaemic mitral regurgitation and ejection fraction above 30%, randomised to CABG plus mitral annuloplasty (34 patients) or CABG alone (39); the study was stopped early after interim review.
cards.result: At 1 year, the primary endpoint of peak oxygen consumption improved more in the repair group (3.3 mL/kg/min versus 0.8 mL/kg/min; P < 0.001), as did left ventricular end-systolic volume index reduction (22.2 versus 4.4 mL/m²), regurgitant volume reduction (28.2 versus 9.2 mL/beat) and B-type natriuretic peptide reduction (557.4 versus 394.7 pg/mL). Operation duration, transfusion, intubation time and hospital stay were all greater with repair. Deaths were similar: 3% in both groups at 30 days, and 9% (repair) versus 5% (CABG alone) at 1 year (P = 0.66).
cards.watchOut: A small, single-centre, early-stopped trial reporting functional and imaging endpoints — hypothesis-supporting for physiology, but it cannot overturn the larger trial's neutral clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Chan et al. Coronary artery bypass surgery with or without mitral valve annuloplasty in moderate functional ischemic mitral regurgitation: final results of the Randomized Ischemic Mitral Evaluation (RIME) trial. Circulation. 2012. PMID: 23136163. Registry ID: NCT00413998. cards.summary: Synthesis: repair the valve and the regurgitation grade improves — remodelling, survival and readmissions do not
cards.people: Patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation already undergoing CABG, where the surgical team weighs adding mitral repair.
cards.result: The 301-patient CTSN trial found identical remodelling and mortality (2-year deaths 10.0% versus 10.6%) with fewer residual leaks but more neurologic events and arrhythmias from the added procedure; RIME's functional gains (peak oxygen consumption +3.3 versus +0.8 mL/kg/min) come from 73 patients and surrogate endpoints. shelves.title: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair versus mitral surgery for secondary mitral regurgitation (MATTERHORN): noninferior on efficacy at 1 year, with far fewer major adverse events (14.9% versus 54.8%)
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure and secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation who remain symptomatic on guideline-directed medical therapy, is transcatheter edge-to-edge repair noninferior to mitral-valve surgery for death, heart-failure hospitalisation, reintervention, assist-device implantation or stroke at 1 year — and how do early major adverse events compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Cardiac Catheterization/adverse effects · *Heart Failure/complications/mortality/surgery · *Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/adverse effects/methods · Hospitalization · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · *Mitral Valve/surgery · *Mitral Valve Insufficiency/etiology/mortality/surgery · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology/etiology · Stroke/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Heart-Assist Devices/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single, small noninferiority trial in which the catheter strategy matched surgery on outcomes and clearly beat it on early harm. In MATTERHORN (210 patients with heart failure and secondary mitral regurgitation, symptomatic despite guideline-directed therapy), the primary efficacy composite (death, heart-failure hospitalisation, mitral reintervention, assist-device implantation, or stroke within 1 year) occurred in 16.7% after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair versus 22.5% after surgery (estimated difference -6 percentage points; 95% CI -17 to 6; P < 0.001 for noninferiority). The primary safety endpoint — major adverse events within 30 days — occurred in 14.9% after repair versus 54.8% after surgery (difference -40 percentage points; 95% CI -51 to -27; P < 0.001). Because the claim rests on one trial of 210 patients with a composite that includes mortality, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for suitable patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, edge-to-edge repair probably achieves surgical-level 1-year outcomes with a much smaller early adverse-event burden.

cards.headline: MATTERHORN (Baldus 2024): efficacy composite in 16 of 96 patients (16.7%) after edge-to-edge repair versus 20 of 89 (22.5%) after surgery (P < 0.001 for noninferiority); 30-day major adverse events 14.9% versus 54.8%
cards.summary: MATTERHORN (Baldus 2024): efficacy composite in 16 of 96 patients (16.7%) after edge-to-edge repair versus 20 of 89 (22.5%) after surgery (P < 0.001 for noninferiority); 30-day major adverse events 14.9% versus 54.8%
cards.people: 210 patients with heart failure and secondary mitral regurgitation who remained symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy, at German centres, randomised 1:1 to transcatheter edge-to-edge repair or surgical mitral-valve repair or replacement; mean age 70.5 years, 39.9% women, mean ejection fraction 43.0%.
cards.result: Within 1 year, at least one component of the primary efficacy endpoint (death, hospitalisation for heart failure, mitral-valve reintervention, implantation of an assist device, or stroke) occurred in 16 of 96 patients with available data (16.7%) in the repair group and 20 of 89 (22.5%) in the surgery group (estimated mean difference -6 percentage points; 95% CI -17 to 6; P < 0.001 for noninferiority). A primary safety endpoint event (major adverse events within 30 days) occurred in 15 of 101 patients (14.9%) after repair versus 51 of 93 (54.8%) after surgery (estimated mean difference -40 percentage points; 95% CI -51 to -27; P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Small for a noninferiority claim on a mortality-containing composite, with incomplete outcome data (96 and 89 of about 105 per arm for the efficacy endpoint) and 1-year follow-up only; surgical candidacy and valve anatomy determine who these results apply to.

randomised noninferiority trial (matterhorn) 210 patients with heart failure and secondary mitral regurgitation who remained symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy, at german centres, randomised 1:1 to transcatheter edge-to-edge repair or surgical mitral-valve repair or replacement; mean age 70.5 years, 39.9% women, mean ejection fraction 43.0%. within 1 year, at least one component of the primary efficacy endpoint (death, hospitalisation for heart failure, mitral-valve reintervention, implantation of an assist device, or stroke) occurred in 16 of 96 patients with available data (16.7%) in the repair group and 20 of 89 (22.5%) in the surgery group (estimated mean difference -6 percentage points; 95% ci -17 to 6; p < 0.001 for noninferiority). a primary safety endpoint event (major adverse events within 30 days) occurred in 15 of 101 patients (14.9%) after repair versus 51 of 93 (54.8%) after surgery (estimated mean difference -40 percentage points; 95% ci -51 to -27; p < 0.001). small for a noninferiority claim on a mortality-containing composite, with incomplete outcome data (96 and 89 of about 105 per arm for the efficacy endpoint) and 1-year follow-up only; surgical candidacy and valve anatomy determine who these results apply to. baldus et al. transcatheter repair versus mitral-valve surgery for secondary mitral regurgitation. the new england journal of medicine. 2024. pmid: 39216093. registry id: nct02371512. mesh: aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · *cardiac catheterization/adverse effects · *heart failure/complications/mortality/surgery · *heart valve prosthesis implantation/adverse effects/methods · hospitalization · kaplan-meier estimate · *mitral valve/surgery · *mitral valve insufficiency/etiology/mortality/surgery · postoperative complications/epidemiology/etiology · stroke/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · heart-assist devices/statistics & numerical data

cards.headline: Synthesis: against surgery — the comparison that was missing — catheter repair holds its own at 1 year
cards.summary: Synthesis: against surgery — the comparison that was missing — catheter repair holds its own at 1 year
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic secondary mitral regurgitation on medical therapy who are candidates for either transcatheter repair or surgery.
cards.result: MATTERHORN is the first randomised head-to-head against surgery: efficacy was noninferior (16.7% versus 22.5% for the composite) and early major adverse events were roughly a quarter as frequent (14.9% versus 54.8%). Combined with the established trials of repair versus medical therapy alone (carded separately), the catheter approach now has randomised support on both flanks — but this shelf's grade stays POSSIBLE on a single 210-patient trial.
cards.watchOut: Long-term durability of edge-to-edge repair versus surgery beyond 1 year, and outcomes in patients at low surgical risk, remain untested by this trial.

shelves.title: Suppressing ventricular ectopy after myocardial infarction (CAST): encainide and flecainide tripled arrhythmic death (relative risk 3.6) and raised total mortality 2.5-fold; moricizine harmed too
shelves.question: In survivors of myocardial infarction with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic ventricular ectopy that can be suppressed by an antiarrhythmic drug, does long-term suppression with encainide, flecainide or moricizine reduce arrhythmic death and total mortality?
shelves.mesh: Actuarial Analysis · Anilides/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/drug therapy/*mortality · Electrocardiography · Encainide · Flecainide/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Arrest/mortality · Heart Failure/mortality · Humans · Morbidity · Myocardial Infarction/mortality · Patient Compliance
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the trial that taught medicine not to treat the surrogate. In CAST, patients whose ventricular ectopy was suppressed on encainide or flecainide were randomised to drug or placebo: death from arrhythmia or nonfatal cardiac arrest occurred in 33 of 730 patients (4.5%) on active drug versus 9 of 725 (1.2%) on placebo (relative risk 3.6; 95% CI 1.7 to 8.5), and total mortality was 7.7% versus 3.0% (relative risk 2.5; 1.6 to 4.5) over about 10 months, at which point the encainide/flecainide arms were stopped. The full report counted 43 arrhythmic deaths on drug versus 16 on placebo (P = 0.0004). CAST-II then tested moricizine: its 14-day initiation phase was stopped for excess deaths or cardiac arrests (17 of 665 versus 3 of 660), and the long-term phase showed no benefit (49 versus 42 arrhythmic deaths or arrests; adjusted P = 0.40). As a harm claim this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): suppressing asymptomatic ventricular ectopy after infarction with class I antiarrhythmic drugs increases mortality — the drugs did exactly what they were prescribed to do to the ECG, and patients died more.

cards.headline: CAST preliminary report (1989): death from arrhythmia or nonfatal cardiac arrest in 33 of 730 patients (4.5%) on encainide or flecainide versus 9 of 725 (1.2%) on placebo (relative risk 3.6); total mortality 7.7% versus 3.0% (relative risk 2.5)
cards.summary: CAST preliminary report (1989): death from arrhythmia or nonfatal cardiac arrest in 33 of 730 patients (4.5%) on encainide or flecainide versus 9 of 725 (1.2%) on placebo (relative risk 3.6); total mortality 7.7% versus 3.0% (relative risk 2.5)
cards.type: Randomised trial, preliminary report of early termination (CAST)
cards.people: Patients after myocardial infarction with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic ventricular arrhythmia (six or more ventricular premature beats per hour) whose ectopy was suppressed during a drug-titration phase; 1,727 of 2,309 recruited patients achieved suppression and were randomised to active drug or placebo, of whom 1,455 were in the encainide/flecainide comparison reported here; average follow-up 10 months.
cards.result: Patients on encainide or flecainide had a higher rate of death from arrhythmia or nonfatal cardiac arrest than placebo patients (33 of 730 [4.5%] versus 9 of 725 [1.2%]; relative risk 3.6; 95% CI 1.7 to 8.5), and higher total mortality (56 of 730 [7.7%] versus 22 of 725 [3.0%]; relative risk 2.5; 95% CI 1.6 to 4.5). Because of these results, the encainide and flecainide part of the trial was discontinued; the authors concluded neither drug should be used for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic ventricular arrhythmia after infarction, even though both suppressed the arrhythmia effectively.
cards.watchOut: A preliminary report published because the finding demanded immediate dissemination; the definitive mortality accounting is in the final report (next card). The result is specific to post-infarction ectopy suppression with these class IC agents — it does not grade flecainide's separate, selected uses in structurally normal hearts.
cards.source: The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial Investigators. Preliminary report: effect of encainide and flecainide on mortality in a randomized trial of arrhythmia suppression after myocardial infarction. The New England journal of medicine. 1989. cards.headline: CAST final report (Echt 1991): 43 deaths from arrhythmia on encainide or flecainide versus 16 on placebo (P = 0.0004); non-arrhythmic cardiac deaths also higher on drug (17 versus 5)
cards.summary: CAST final report (Echt 1991): 43 deaths from arrhythmia on encainide or flecainide versus 16 on placebo (P = 0.0004); non-arrhythmic cardiac deaths also higher on drug (17 versus 5)
cards.type: Randomised trial, final mortality and morbidity report (CAST)
cards.people: 1,498 randomised patients in the encainide (857 patients in drug/placebo comparison) and flecainide (641) components of CAST — survivors of myocardial infarction whose ventricular ectopy had been suppressed by the study drug — followed for a mean of 10 months before the arms were stopped.
cards.result: Of 89 deaths, 59 were from arrhythmia — 43 in patients receiving active drug versus 16 receiving placebo (P = 0.0004); 22 were from non-arrhythmic cardiac causes (17 on drug versus 5 on placebo; P = 0.01), almost all attributed to acute myocardial infarction with shock (11 versus 3) or chronic heart failure (4 versus 2); and 8 were non-cardiac (3 versus 5). Non-lethal events — disqualifying ventricular tachycardia, proarrhythmia, syncope, pacemaker need, heart failure, recurrent infarction, angina, or revascularisation — did not differ between drug and placebo groups.
cards.watchOut: Encainide was later withdrawn and flecainide's labelling restricted on the strength of this trial; the mechanism of the excess deaths remains formally unknown, which is why the lesson is taught as a surrogate-endpoint warning rather than a pharmacology verdict.
cards.source: Echt et al. Mortality and morbidity in patients receiving encainide, flecainide, or placebo. The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial. The New England journal of medicine. 1991. PMID: 1900101. cards.headline: CAST-II (1992): moricizine's 14-day initiation phase stopped for excess deaths or cardiac arrests (17 of 665 versus 3 of 660); long-term arrhythmic deaths or arrests 49 versus 42 (adjusted P = 0.40) — no benefit
cards.summary: CAST-II (1992): moricizine's 14-day initiation phase stopped for excess deaths or cardiac arrests (17 of 665 versus 3 of 660); long-term arrhythmic deaths or arrests 49 versus 42 (adjusted P = 0.40) — no benefit
cards.people: Survivors of myocardial infarction with ventricular premature depolarisations: 1,325 patients entered a 14-day blinded exposure phase of moricizine versus placebo, and 1,374 patients (1,155 with adequately suppressed ectopy, 219 partially suppressed) entered the long-term survival phase.
cards.result: CAST-II was stopped early: the first 14 days of moricizine after infarction were associated with excess mortality (17 of 665 patients died or had cardiac arrests, versus 3 of 660 on placebo), and conditional-power estimates gave less than an 8% chance that completing the trial would show a survival benefit. At completion of the long-term phase there were 49 deaths or cardiac arrests due to arrhythmias on moricizine and 42 on placebo (adjusted P = 0.40). The authors concluded moricizine, like the CAST-I drugs, was not only ineffective but harmful for this indication.
cards.watchOut: Early termination limits the long-term phase's precision; the initiation-phase harm (17 versus 3) is nonetheless a stark, randomised signal in the same direction as CAST-I.
cards.source: The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial II Investigators. Effect of the antiarrhythmic agent moricizine on survival after myocardial infarction. The New England journal of medicine. 1992. PMID: 1377359. cards.headline: Synthesis: suppressing the ectopy was achieved; suppressing death was not — mortality rose two- to three-fold
cards.summary: Synthesis: suppressing the ectopy was achieved; suppressing death was not — mortality rose two- to three-fold
cards.people: Survivors of myocardial infarction with frequent but asymptomatic ventricular ectopy.
cards.result: CAST and CAST-II randomised over 3,000 patients across three drugs of the same class and found the same thing: the surrogate (ectopy suppression) improved while arrhythmic death (relative risk 3.6) and total mortality (relative risk 2.5) worsened. It remains the canonical demonstration that a treatment can do exactly what it is designed to do and still kill.
cards.watchOut: The verdict binds the post-infarction ectopy-suppression indication; antiarrhythmic drugs retain legitimate, separately evidenced roles (symptomatic arrhythmias, selected structurally normal hearts, resuscitation) graded on other shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of the CAST preliminary report (PMID: 2473403), the CAST final report (PMID: 1900101) and CAST-II (PMID: 1377359).

shelves.title: Dofetilide in severe left ventricular dysfunction (DIAMOND): no effect on mortality after infarction or in heart failure (41% versus 42%; 31% versus 32%), but fewer heart-failure hospitalisations and effective rhythm control — at a 3.3% torsades price
shelves.question: In patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction — with chronic heart failure or after a recent myocardial infarction — does the class III antiarrhythmic dofetilide reduce all-cause mortality, and what does it do to heart-failure hospitalisation, atrial fibrillation and torsades de pointes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Atrial Fibrillation/*drug therapy/etiology/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography/drug effects · Female · Heart Failure/complications/*drug therapy/mortality · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phenethylamines/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Sulfonamides/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Survival Analysis · Torsades de Pointes/chemically induced · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for survival, the outcome these trials were built to test; the morbidity and rhythm effects are real but secondary. In DIAMOND-CHF (1,518 patients with symptomatic heart failure and severe ventricular dysfunction), 311 patients (41%) died on dofetilide versus 317 (42%) on placebo over a median of 18 months (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11), while hospitalisation for worsening heart failure fell (risk ratio 0.75; 0.63 to 0.89). In DIAMOND-MI (1,510 patients with severe dysfunction after infarction), all-cause mortality was 31% versus 32%, with cardiac and arrhythmic deaths also no different. Dofetilide converted atrial fibrillation (12% versus 1% at one month in DIAMOND-CHF) and maintained sinus rhythm (recurrence hazard ratio 0.35), but caused torsade de pointes in 25 patients (3.3%) versus none on placebo in DIAMOND-CHF, and in 7 patients (all on dofetilide) in DIAMOND-MI. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): dofetilide does not prolong life in severe ventricular dysfunction; it is a rhythm drug with a hospitalisation benefit and a proarrhythmic price that mandates in-hospital initiation.

cards.headline: DIAMOND-CHF (Torp-Pedersen 1999): deaths in 311 patients (41%) on dofetilide versus 317 (42%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11); heart-failure hospitalisation risk ratio 0.75; torsades in 25 patients (3.3%) versus none
cards.summary: DIAMOND-CHF (Torp-Pedersen 1999): deaths in 311 patients (41%) on dofetilide versus 317 (42%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11); heart-failure hospitalisation risk ratio 0.75; torsades in 25 patients (3.3%) versus none
cards.people: 1,518 patients with symptomatic congestive heart failure and severe left ventricular dysfunction at 34 Danish hospitals, randomised to dofetilide (762 patients) or placebo (756), with treatment initiated in hospital under 3 days of cardiac monitoring and dose adjustment; median follow-up 18 months; the primary endpoint was death from any cause.
cards.result: Deaths occurred in 311 patients (41%) in the dofetilide group and 317 (42%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11). Dofetilide significantly reduced hospitalisation for worsening congestive heart failure (risk ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.89). Among patients in atrial fibrillation at baseline, sinus rhythm was restored by one month in 22 of 190 (12%) on dofetilide versus 3 of 201 (1%) on placebo, and once restored, dofetilide maintained sinus rhythm better (hazard ratio for recurrence 0.35; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.57; P < 0.001). There were 25 cases of torsade de pointes on dofetilide (3.3%) versus none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Mortality neutrality was demonstrated in a monitored, dose-adjusted Danish trial population; the 3.3% torsades rate — despite in-hospital initiation — is the reason dofetilide initiation remains a monitored, specialist procedure.
cards.source: Torp-Pedersen et al. Dofetilide in patients with congestive heart failure and left ventricular dysfunction. Danish Investigations of Arrhythmia and Mortality on Dofetilide Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1999. PMID: 10486417. cards.headline: DIAMOND-MI (Kober 2000): all-cause mortality 230 patients (31%) on dofetilide versus 243 (32%) on placebo; cardiac and arrhythmic deaths also no different; 7 torsades cases, all on dofetilide
cards.summary: DIAMOND-MI (Kober 2000): all-cause mortality 230 patients (31%) on dofetilide versus 243 (32%) on placebo; cardiac and arrhythmic deaths also no different; 7 torsades cases, all on dofetilide
cards.people: 1,510 patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction (wall-motion index 1.2 or less, corresponding to ejection fraction of 35% or less) after a recent myocardial infarction, at 37 Danish coronary-care units, randomised to dofetilide (749 patients) or placebo (761); the primary endpoint was all-cause mortality.
cards.result: No significant differences were found in all-cause mortality (230 deaths [31%] on dofetilide versus 243 [32%] on placebo), cardiac mortality (191 [26%] versus 212 [28%]), or total arrhythmic deaths (129 [17%] versus 140 [18%]). In the 8% of patients with atrial fibrillation or flutter at entry, dofetilide restored sinus rhythm more often (25 of 59 versus 7 of 56; P = 0.002). Seven cases of torsade de pointes ventricular tachycardia occurred, all in the dofetilide group.
cards.watchOut: As in DIAMOND-CHF, the safety result depends on the trial's screening (QT and renal dosing) and monitored initiation; the trial cannot certify dofetilide as safe under looser conditions.
cards.source: Kober et al. Effect of dofetilide in patients with recent myocardial infarction and left-ventricular dysfunction: a randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2000. PMID: 11145491. cards.headline: Synthesis: the rare antiarrhythmic proven not to kill in ventricular dysfunction — but proven not to save life either
cards.summary: Synthesis: the rare antiarrhythmic proven not to kill in ventricular dysfunction — but proven not to save life either
cards.people: Patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction, with heart failure or after infarction, in whom an antiarrhythmic is needed for atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Across 3,028 randomised patients, dofetilide's mortality effect is null in both settings (41% versus 42%; 31% versus 32%), its heart-failure hospitalisation effect is favourable (risk ratio 0.75), its rhythm efficacy is clear, and its torsades risk (3.3% in DIAMOND-CHF) is the governing constraint. After CAST, 'does not increase mortality' was itself a valuable, hard-won result.
cards.watchOut: This shelf grades dofetilide in severe ventricular dysfunction; it does not compare dofetilide head-to-head with amiodarone or catheter ablation, which are separate questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of DIAMOND-CHF (PMID: 10486417) and DIAMOND-MI (PMID: 11145491).

shelves.title: Autologous cell therapy for 'no-option' critical limb ischaemia: amputations fell by about 60% across 16 small trials — deaths did not move at all
shelves.question: In adults with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and no revascularisation options, does autologous cell therapy improve amputation-free survival compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Bone Marrow Cells/cytology · Bone Marrow Transplantation/methods · Cell- and Tissue-Based Therapy · Humans · Ischemia/therapy · Peripheral Vascular Diseases/therapy · Transplantation, Autologous
shelves.balance: SPLIT — amputations down, mortality unchanged, and no trial pooled amputation-free survival directly. A meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials in 775 patients with no-option critical limb ischaemia (Wahid FSA et al., PMID: 29532760) found all-cause mortality rates similar between autologous cell-based therapy and non-cell-based care on high-quality evidence, while amputation rates fell by approximately 60% on moderate-quality evidence — a relative effect that clears the developer's floor for benefit — alongside improvements in ulcer healing, ankle–brachial index, transcutaneous oxygen, pain-free walking capacity and collateral vessel formation. Intramuscular bone marrow mononuclear cells and mobilised peripheral blood stem cells were the products that appeared to reduce amputation; bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells improved perfusion measures but not amputation. A Cochrane review of head-to-head trials (Abdul Wahid SF et al., PMID: 30155883) found only seven randomised trials (359 participants) comparing one cell source, dose or route against another, and identified no other comparisons — so no cell product or regimen is proven best. Because deaths did not fall, any gain in amputation-free survival would be carried entirely by the amputation reduction, and that composite was not the pooled endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT: fewer amputations (POSSIBLE benefit on moderate-quality pooled evidence), no mortality benefit, regimen unsettled.

cards.headline: Wahid 2018 meta-analysis (16 RCTs, 775 patients): amputation rate reduced by approximately 60% with cell therapy — all-cause mortality similar
cards.summary: Wahid 2018 meta-analysis (16 RCTs, 775 patients): amputation rate reduced by approximately 60% with cell therapy — all-cause mortality similar
cards.people: 775 patients with no-option critical limb ischaemia in 16 randomised clinical trials of autologous cell-based therapy — mobilised peripheral blood stem cells, bone marrow mononuclear cells, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, cultured bone marrow mononuclear cells (Ixmyelocel-T), cultured peripheral blood cells (VesCell) and CD34+ cells — versus non-cell-based therapy, searched to 2017.
cards.result: High-quality evidence showed similar all-cause mortality rates between cell-based therapy and non-cell-based therapy. Amputation rates were reduced by approximately 60% in patients receiving cell therapy compared with non-cell-based therapy (moderate-quality evidence) — a relative reduction, printed here without pooled absolute amputation rates because the record does not give them. Cell-therapy patients also improved in ulcer healing, ankle–brachial pressure index, transcutaneous oxygen pressure, pain-free walking capacity and collateral vessel formation (moderate-quality evidence). Intramuscular bone marrow mononuclear cells and mobilised peripheral blood stem cells may reduce amputation rate, rest pain and improve ulcer healing; intramuscular bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells improved rest pain, ulcer healing and pain-free walking distance but not amputation rate. Cell harvesting and implantation appeared safe, with similar adverse-event rates between groups.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen small trials of six different cell products are pooled into one number: the approximately 60% amputation reduction is an average across products that individually disagree (mesenchymal cells did not reduce amputation), the evidence for it is graded only moderate, and the review's own authors call for large randomised trials with long follow-up. Amputation-free survival — this shelf's question — was not itself a pooled endpoint; it is inferred from fewer amputations at unchanged mortality.
cards.source: Wahid FSA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Autologous Cell-based Therapy in Patients with No-option Critical Limb Ischaemia: A Meta-Analysis. Current Stem Cell Research & Therapy. 2018. PMID: 29532760. cards.headline: Cochrane 2018: only seven head-to-head trials (359 patients) compare cell sources, doses or routes against each other — no regimen is established
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018: only seven head-to-head trials (359 patients) compare cell sources, doses or routes against each other — no regimen is established
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Abdul Wahid 2018)
cards.people: 359 participants with 'no-option' critical lower limb ischaemia in seven randomised trials comparing autologous cell regimens against each other: bone marrow mononuclear cells versus mobilised peripheral blood stem cells, bone marrow mononuclear cells versus bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, high versus low cell dose, and intramuscular versus intra-arterial delivery.
cards.result: The review identified seven randomised trials (359 participants) covering those four head-to-head comparisons and no other comparisons. Most studies were at low risk of bias for random sequence generation, incomplete outcome data and selective outcome reporting, and at high risk of bias in blinding. The review therefore maps how thin the comparative evidence is: even accepting that cell therapy as a class reduces amputations, the published randomised record does not settle which cells, at what dose, or by which route.
cards.watchOut: This review deliberately does not compare cell therapy against standard care — it answers 'which regimen?' not 'does it work?' — so it cannot corroborate the amputation benefit; it only disciplines how the benefit may be claimed. Blinding was at high risk of bias across much of the underlying trial base, which matters for subjective endpoints such as pain and ulcer assessment.
cards.source: Abdul Wahid SF et al. Autologous cells derived from different sources and administered using different regimens for 'no-option' critical lower limb ischaemia patients. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 30155883. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real amputation signal pooled from small, unlike trials — with mortality flat and the best regimen unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real amputation signal pooled from small, unlike trials — with mortality flat and the best regimen unknown
cards.people: Sixteen randomised trials (775 patients) of autologous cell therapy versus non-cell-based care in no-option critical limb ischaemia, plus seven head-to-head regimen trials (359 participants) in the Cochrane review.
cards.result: Amputation: reduced by approximately 60% relative in the pooled analysis (moderate-quality evidence). Mortality: similar between cell therapy and control (high-quality evidence) — so amputation-free survival, if improved, improves through limb salvage alone. Safety: adverse-event rates similar; harvesting and implantation appeared well tolerated. Regimen: no source, dose or route proven superior in head-to-head trials. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: POSSIBLE (benefit) for amputation, POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for mortality.
cards.watchOut: The pooled amputation figure aggregates six different cell products, several of them commercial preparations (Ixmyelocel-T, VesCell) named here exactly as the review names them; a class average must not be read as a promise for any single product. Individual large or blinded trials in this field have disappointed before, and the band cap of POSSIBLE plus Tier C personal review applies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wahid FSA et al. Current Stem Cell Research & Therapy. 2018 (PMID: 29532760); Abdul Wahid SF et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30155883).

shelves.title: Platelet-test-guided de-escalation after PCI: TROPICAL-ACS stepped prasugrel down to clopidogrel with no net penalty (7% versus 9%) — and ANTARCTIC's monitoring-guided adjustment in the over-75s changed nothing at all (28% versus 28%)
shelves.question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome treated with PCI, does platelet-function-test-guided de-escalation or adjustment of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy improve net clinical outcomes compared with unguided standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/epidemiology/therapy · Clopidogrel · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Monitoring · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/epidemiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Platelet Function Tests · Prasugrel Hydrochloride/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Stroke/epidemiology · Ticlopidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — guidance by platelet testing has never significantly improved a net clinical outcome in a randomised trial; what it has shown is that stepping down is safe. TROPICAL-ACS (Sibbing D et al., PMID: 28855078) randomised 2,610 patients with biomarker-positive acute coronary syndrome after successful PCI to platelet-function-guided de-escalation (prasugrel for one week, clopidogrel for one week, then test-guided clopidogrel or prasugrel maintenance) or 12 months of prasugrel: the net clinical benefit endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC grade 2 or higher bleeding) at one year occurred in 7% versus 9% (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.06; P = 0.0004 for non-inferiority, P = 0.12 for superiority), the ischaemic composite in 3% versus 3%, and BARC 2 or higher bleeding in 5% versus 6% (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.13; P = 0.23). ANTARCTIC (Cayla G et al., PMID: 27581531), in 877 patients aged 75 or older stented for acute coronary syndrome, found platelet-function monitoring with prasugrel dose or drug adjustment produced the identical primary outcome rate as no monitoring — 28% versus 28% (hazard ratio 1.003; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.29; P = 0.98) — with no significant difference in bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): platelet-test guidance itself buys no proven outcome gain; TROPICAL-ACS supports guided de-escalation as a non-inferior way to use the cheaper, gentler drug, not as a superior strategy.

cards.headline: Sibbing 2017 (TROPICAL-ACS): guided de-escalation from prasugrel to clopidogrel non-inferior for net clinical benefit (7% versus 9%; HR 0.81) — superiority not shown (P = 0.12), ischaemic events 3% versus 3%, bleeding 5% versus 6%
cards.summary: Sibbing 2017 (TROPICAL-ACS): guided de-escalation from prasugrel to clopidogrel non-inferior for net clinical benefit (7% versus 9%; HR 0.81) — superiority not shown (P = 0.12), ischaemic events 3% versus 3%, bleeding 5% versus 6%
cards.people: 2,610 patients with biomarker-positive acute coronary syndrome and successful PCI at 33 European sites, planned for 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy, randomised to guided de-escalation (1 week prasugrel, 1 week clopidogrel, then platelet-function-test-guided maintenance with clopidogrel or prasugrel from day 14; n = 1,304) or prasugrel 10 mg for 12 months (n = 1,306).
cards.result: The primary endpoint of net clinical benefit (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC grade 2 or higher bleeding) at 1 year occurred in 95 patients (7%) in the guided de-escalation group versus 118 (9%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.06; P = 0.0004 for non-inferiority; P = 0.12 for superiority). The combined ischaemic risk (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke) was 3% versus 3% (32 versus 42 patients; P = 0.0115 for non-inferiority). BARC grade 2 or higher bleeding events numbered 64 (5%) versus 79 (6%) (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.13; P = 0.23).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a generous 30% margin is the proven claim — the trial does not show guided de-escalation is better, and most patients in the guided arm simply stayed on clopidogrel after testing, so the trial tests a step-down pathway more than it tests the assay. Open-label treatment with blinded assessment.
cards.source: Sibbing D et al. Guided de-escalation of antiplatelet treatment in patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (TROPICAL-ACS): a randomised, open-label, multicentre trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28855078. Registry ID: NCT01959451. cards.headline: Cayla 2016 (ANTARCTIC): platelet-function monitoring with treatment adjustment in patients 75 or older — primary outcome 28% versus 28% (HR 1.003; P = 0.98), bleeding no different
cards.summary: Cayla 2016 (ANTARCTIC): platelet-function monitoring with treatment adjustment in patients 75 or older — primary outcome 28% versus 28% (HR 1.003; P = 0.98), bleeding no different
cards.people: 877 patients aged 75 years or older who had undergone coronary stenting for acute coronary syndrome at 35 French centres, randomised to prasugrel 5 mg daily with platelet-function monitoring and dose or drug adjustment for inadequate response (n = 442) or prasugrel 5 mg daily with no monitoring or adjustment (n = 435), followed for 12 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, stent thrombosis, urgent revascularisation, and BARC bleeding types 2, 3 or 5) occurred in 120 patients (28%) in the monitoring group versus 123 (28%) in the conventional group (hazard ratio 1.003; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.29; P = 0.98). Rates of bleeding events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: ANTARCTIC tested monitoring with adjustment in both directions (mainly dose escalation within a low-dose prasugrel strategy in the elderly), not de-escalation to clopidogrel — it answers whether testing-guided tailoring helps at all, and its answer is no; the elderly, highest-risk population is exactly where a guidance benefit should have been easiest to find.
cards.source: Cayla G et al. Platelet function monitoring to adjust antiplatelet therapy in elderly patients stented for an acute coronary syndrome (ANTARCTIC): an open-label, blinded-endpoint, randomised controlled superiority trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27581531. Registry ID: NCT01538446. cards.summary: Synthesis: guidance never won — de-escalation proved safe, monitoring proved futile, and the assay is not the active ingredient
cards.people: Two randomised trials of platelet-function-test guidance after PCI for acute coronary syndrome: TROPICAL-ACS (2,610 patients, guided de-escalation from prasugrel) and ANTARCTIC (877 patients aged 75 or older, monitoring-guided adjustment).
cards.result: Net clinical benefit at 1 year: 7% versus 9% for guided de-escalation versus continued prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.81; non-inferior, not superior). Primary composite in the elderly monitoring trial: 28% versus 28% (hazard ratio 1.003). Bleeding: 5% versus 6% in TROPICAL-ACS (not significant) and no significant difference in ANTARCTIC. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the guidance strategy, with TROPICAL-ACS's non-inferiority of the step-down itself stated plainly.
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers platelet-function guidance only: genotype-guided selection is homed on Shelf #473 (POPular Genetics carded there) and unguided de-escalation on pack #4163 (TALOS-AMI) — neither is re-carded here. Both trials here were open-label with blinded endpoint assessment, the practical maximum blinding for a testing strategy.

shelves.title: Replacing saturated fat with linoleic-acid oils in the old diet-heart trials: cholesterol fell, deaths did not — Minnesota showed no mortality benefit and Sydney showed more deaths on the safflower-oil diet
shelves.question: In adults, does replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat reduce coronary events in the old diet-heart trials?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cause of Death · Cholesterol · Coronary Artery Disease · Coronary Disease · Diet, Fat-Restricted · Dietary Fats · Double-Blind Method · Female · History, 20th Century · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Linoleic Acid · Male · Middle Aged · Minnesota · Myocardial Infarction · Plant Oils · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the cholesterol hypothesis worked on the blood test and failed on deaths, in opposite directions in the two recovered trials. In the Minnesota Coronary Experiment (9,423 institutionalised participants; recovered-data analysis, Ramsden CE et al., PMID: 27071971), replacing saturated fat with corn oil lowered serum cholesterol by -13.8% versus -1.0% on the control diet, yet there was no mortality benefit in the full cohort or any prespecified subgroup, and each 30 mg/dL (0.78 mmol/L) fall in cholesterol was associated with a 22% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.22, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.32). In the Sydney Diet Heart Study (458 men after a coronary event; Ramsden CE et al., PMID: 23386268), the safflower-oil group had higher all-cause mortality (17.6% versus 11.8%; hazard ratio 1.62, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.64), cardiovascular mortality (17.2% versus 11.0%) and coronary mortality (16.3% versus 10.1%). The accompanying meta-analyses found no benefit on coronary death (Minnesota review: ratio 1.13, 0.83 to 1.54). PROPOSED SPLIT: for linoleic-acid-rich oils specifically, the recovered randomised record shows cholesterol lowering without coronary benefit, and a harm signal in secondary prevention — this does not test mixed polyunsaturated replacement as eaten in modern diets.

cards.headline: Minnesota Coronary Experiment (recovered data, Ramsden 2016): cholesterol -13.8% versus -1.0% on the corn-oil diet, no mortality benefit — and a 22% higher death risk per 30 mg/dL (0.78 mmol/L) cholesterol fall
cards.summary: Minnesota Coronary Experiment (recovered data, Ramsden 2016): cholesterol -13.8% versus -1.0% on the corn-oil diet, no mortality benefit — and a 22% higher death risk per 30 mg/dL (0.78 mmol/L) cholesterol fall
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial, recovered-data reanalysis (Minnesota Coronary Experiment, 1968–73)
cards.people: 9,423 women and men aged 20–97 in one nursing home and six state mental hospitals in Minnesota, randomised to a diet replacing saturated fat with linoleic acid from corn oil and corn-oil margarine, or a control diet high in saturated fat; longitudinal cholesterol data in 2,355 participants exposed for a year or more, 149 autopsy files.
cards.result: Serum cholesterol fell -13.8% on the intervention versus -1.0% on control (P<0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed no mortality benefit in the full randomised cohort or any prespecified subgroup, and no benefit for coronary atherosclerosis or myocardial infarction at autopsy. In covariate-adjusted models, each 30 mg/dL (0.78 mmol/L) reduction in serum cholesterol was associated with a 22% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.22, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.32, P<0.001). The systematic review of five such trials (n=10,808) found no benefit on coronary death (1.13, 0.83 to 1.54) or all-cause mortality (1.07, 0.90 to 1.27).
cards.watchOut: An institutional feeding trial from 1968–73 with short average exposure and high turnover; the cholesterol–death association is observational within the trial and may reflect illness lowering cholesterol. The intervention was specifically linoleic-acid-rich corn oil, not polyunsaturated fat in general.
cards.source: Ramsden CE et al. Re-evaluation of the traditional diet-heart hypothesis: analysis of recovered data from Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-73). BMJ. 2016. PMID: 27071971. cards.headline: Sydney Diet Heart Study (recovered data, Ramsden 2013): all-cause death 17.6% on safflower oil versus 11.8% on control (hazard ratio 1.62) after a coronary event
cards.summary: Sydney Diet Heart Study (recovered data, Ramsden 2013): all-cause death 17.6% on safflower oil versus 11.8% on control (hazard ratio 1.62) after a coronary event
cards.type: Single-blind randomised trial, recovered-data evaluation with updated meta-analysis (Sydney Diet Heart Study, 1966–73)
cards.people: 458 men aged 30–59 years with a recent coronary event attending a Sydney coronary care clinic, randomised to replace saturated fat with omega-6 linoleic acid from safflower oil and safflower-oil margarine (n=221) or to no specific dietary instruction (n=237).
cards.result: The intervention group had higher rates of death from all causes (17.6% versus 11.8%; hazard ratio 1.62, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.64, P=0.05), cardiovascular disease (17.2% versus 11.0%; 1.70, 1.03 to 2.80, P=0.04) and coronary heart disease (16.3% versus 10.1%; 1.74, 1.04 to 2.92, P=0.04). The updated meta-analysis of linoleic-acid intervention trials showed non-significant trends toward increased coronary death (1.33, 0.99 to 1.79) and cardiovascular death (1.27, 0.98 to 1.65).
cards.watchOut: A small, single-blind 1960s trial in men only, recovered decades later; the mortality differences rest on few events and borderline significance. It tests near-pure linoleic acid substitution, not the mixed-fat replacement in current guidelines.
cards.source: Ramsden CE et al. Use of dietary linoleic acid for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease and death: evaluation of recovered data from the Sydney Diet Heart Study and updated meta-analysis. BMJ. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: the two recovered diet-heart trials agree that linoleic substitution lowered cholesterol and did not lower deaths — and disagree only on whether it raised them
cards.summary: Synthesis: the two recovered diet-heart trials agree that linoleic substitution lowered cholesterol and did not lower deaths — and disagree only on whether it raised them
cards.people: Minnesota Coronary Experiment (9,423 institutionalised adults, primary prevention setting) and Sydney Diet Heart Study (458 men, secondary prevention), both 1966–73, both recovered and reanalysed in the 2010s.
cards.result: Cholesterol: -13.8% versus -1.0% (Minnesota). All-cause mortality: no benefit (Minnesota); 17.6% versus 11.8% against the intervention (Sydney). Pooled linoleic-acid trials: no coronary-death benefit (ratios 1.13–1.33, all confidence intervals crossing or approaching 1 from above). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: historical recovered-data evidence; the harm claim rests substantially on one small trial.
cards.watchOut: These trials isolate omega-6 linoleic acid. They do not answer what replacing saturated fat with mixed polyunsaturated and monounsaturated foods does in contemporary diets, and must not be read as a verdict on that broader question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ramsden CE et al. BMJ. 2016 (PMID: 27071971); Ramsden CE et al. BMJ. 2013 (PMID: 23386268).

shelves.title: Nurse-led transitional care in heart failure: the small 1990s trials cut readmissions by nearly half — the 2,494-patient modern trial found no effect on readmission, emergency visits or death (HR 0.99)
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure discharged from hospital, does a nurse-led transitional-care programme reduce readmission?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Female · Heart Failure/mortality/therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Ontario · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Patient-Centered Care · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Transitional Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by era and scale. The founding trials were strongly positive: in 282 high-risk patients aged 70+ discharged with heart failure (Rich MW et al., PMID: 7565975), a nurse-directed multidisciplinary intervention (education, diet, discharge planning, medication review, intensive follow-up) produced 53 readmissions versus 94 on conventional care (risk ratio 0.56; P=0.02), with heart-failure readmissions reduced by 56.2% in relative terms (24 vs 54 events) — while the primary outcome, survival for 90 days without readmission, was met by 91 of 142 versus 75 of 140 patients and did not reach significance (P=0.09), and deaths were not reported separately. A Scottish trial of specialist-nurse intervention begun before discharge (Blue L et al., PMID: 11576977; 165 patients) found death or heart-failure readmission in 37% versus 53% (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.96), with fewer readmissions for any reason (86 vs 114) and for heart failure (19 vs 45). But the definitive modern test was null: in the stepped-wedge PACT-HF trial (Van Spall HGC et al., PMID: 30806695; 2,494 patients across ten Ontario hospitals), a nurse-led transitional-care model (self-care education, structured discharge summary, family-physician follow-up within a week, nurse home visits and heart-function clinic for high-risk patients) did not improve the composite of all-cause readmission, emergency-department visit or death at three months (49.4% vs 50.2%; HR 0.99, 0.83 to 1.19) or readmission/ED visits at 30 days (HR 0.93, 0.73 to 1.18), though discharge-preparedness, transition-quality and quality-of-life scores improved. PROPOSED SPLIT: nurse-led transitional care worked against 1990s usual care; against contemporary usual care, the largest trial shows better-feeling discharges without fewer events — mortality included in the composites throughout, and nowhere reduced on its own.

cards.headline: Rich 1995: 53 vs 94 readmissions (risk ratio 0.56, P=0.02) with nurse-directed multidisciplinary care — primary outcome (survival without readmission) not significant (P=0.09)
cards.summary: Rich 1995: 53 vs 94 readmissions (risk ratio 0.56, P=0.02) with nurse-directed multidisciplinary care — primary outcome (survival without readmission) not significant (P=0.09)
cards.people: 282 high-risk patients aged 70 years or older hospitalised with congestive heart failure, randomised to a nurse-directed multidisciplinary intervention (n=142: comprehensive patient and family education, prescribed diet, social-service consultation and early-discharge planning, medication review, intensive follow-up) or conventional care (n=140), with 90-day follow-up.
cards.result: Survival for 90 days without readmission (the primary outcome) was achieved by 91 of 142 intervention patients versus 75 of 140 controls (P=0.09). Total readmissions numbered 53 versus 94 (risk ratio 0.56; P=0.02); heart-failure readmissions were reduced by 56.2% in relative terms (24 vs 54 events, P=0.04) and multiple readmissions occurred in 6.3% versus 16.4% (risk ratio 0.39; P=0.01). Quality-of-life scores improved more in the intervention group in a 126-patient subgroup (P=0.001), and overall cost of care was $460 less per patient. Deaths were not reported separately from the composite in the record.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1995 trial against the usual care of its day, with its own primary outcome formally negative — the readmission result is a secondary endpoint, and the mortality component cannot be separated from the record, which is why this shelf reports the composite exactly as published.
cards.source: Rich MW et al. A multidisciplinary intervention to prevent the readmission of elderly patients with congestive heart failure. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7565975. cards.headline: Blue 2001: death or heart-failure readmission 37% vs 53% (HR 0.61) with specialist nurses — heart-failure admissions 19 vs 45
cards.summary: Blue 2001: death or heart-failure readmission 37% vs 53% (HR 0.61) with specialist nurses — heart-failure admissions 19 vs 45
cards.people: 165 patients admitted with heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction to an acute medical admissions unit in a Scottish teaching hospital, randomised to specialist-nurse intervention (begun before discharge, with home visits for up to one year) or usual care.
cards.result: 31 patients (37%) in the intervention group died or were readmitted with heart failure versus 45 (53%) in the usual-care group (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% confidence interval 0.33 to 0.96). The intervention group had fewer readmissions for any reason (86 vs 114, P=0.018), fewer heart-failure admissions (19 vs 45, P<0.001) and fewer days in hospital for heart failure (mean 3.43 vs 7.46 days, P=0.0051).
cards.watchOut: 165 patients, one centre, and a composite driven by admissions rather than deaths — the confidence interval (0.33 to 0.96) only just excludes no effect, and the usual-care comparator predates modern heart-failure therapy and discharge practice.
cards.source: Blue L et al. Randomised controlled trial of specialist nurse intervention in heart failure. BMJ. 2001. PMID: 11576977. cards.headline: Van Spall 2019 (PACT-HF): 2,494 patients, ten hospitals — composite readmission/ED/death 49.4% vs 50.2% (HR 0.99); preparedness and quality of life better, events unchanged
cards.summary: Van Spall 2019 (PACT-HF): 2,494 patients, ten hospitals — composite readmission/ED/death 49.4% vs 50.2% (HR 0.99); preparedness and quality of life better, events unchanged
cards.type: Stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial (Van Spall 2019, PACT-HF)
cards.people: 2,494 adults hospitalised for heart failure across ten Ontario hospitals (mean age 77.7 years, 50.4% women); hospitals crossed over to a patient-centred transitional-care model (nurse-led self-care education, structured discharge summary, family-physician appointment within one week, and for high-risk patients structured nurse home visits and heart-function clinic care; n=1,104 patients) versus usual care at clinician discretion (n=1,390), with follow-up to six months.
cards.result: No significant difference in the first primary composite — all-cause readmission, emergency-department visit or death at three months: 545 events (49.4%) versus 698 (50.2%), hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.19) — or in the 30-day composite of readmission or ED visit (27.5% vs 29.3%; HR 0.93, 0.73 to 1.18). Secondary outcomes favoured the intervention: discharge-preparedness score (difference 2.65, P<.001), care-transition quality (6.16, P=.02) and EQ-5D quality of life at six weeks and six months (0.06, P=.02), with no difference in quality-adjusted life-years (0.00, −0.02 to 0.02; P=.98).
cards.watchOut: A stepped-wedge implementation trial tests a model as actually delivered across a whole health system, not an efficacy intervention in selected patients — its null may reflect dilution and already-decent usual care rather than the impossibility of transitional care working anywhere.
cards.source: Van Spall HGC et al. Effect of Patient-Centered Transitional Care Services on Clinical Outcomes in Patients Hospitalized for Heart Failure: The PACT-HF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 30806695. Registry ID: NCT02112227. cards.headline: Synthesis: the intervention did not change — usual care did. Events fell in 1995–2001 trials and not in 2019's, while patient-experience gains persisted
cards.summary: Synthesis: the intervention did not change — usual care did. Events fell in 1995–2001 trials and not in 2019's, while patient-experience gains persisted
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 2,941 patients discharged after heart-failure hospitalisation: two small single-centre trials (n=282, n=165) and one ten-hospital stepped-wedge trial (n=2,494).
cards.result: Readmissions: risk ratio 0.56 (Rich) and death-or-readmission HR 0.61 (Blue) in the early trials; composite event HR 0.99 (0.83 to 1.19) in PACT-HF. Mortality was reported only inside composites (37% vs 53% death-or-readmission in Blue; death inside the PACT-HF composite) and was not reduced as a stand-alone outcome in any trial. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Programmes sold to hospitals on the early trials' numbers should be re-underwritten against contemporary baselines; the honest modern claim is better-prepared patients, not fewer returns. Tier C: cardiovascular-event and mortality-adjacent claims are developer-reviewed in this band.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline for claudication: the largest trial found it indistinguishable from placebo (+64 m versus +65 m walked at 24 weeks) — and the Cochrane review could not pool the smaller, inconsistent trials that leaned its way
shelves.question: In adults with intermittent claudication from peripheral artery disease, does pentoxifylline improve pain-free and maximal walking distance compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Ankle Brachial Index · Humans · Intermittent Claudication/drug therapy · Pentoxifylline/therapeutic use · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Walking
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the honest summary is that pentoxifylline has never been shown, at any usable certainty, to make claudicants walk further. The Cochrane review (Broderick C et al., PMID: 33063850) gathered 24 studies with 3,377 participants, 17 of them against placebo, and could not pool them: the percentage improvement in pain-free walking distance over placebo ranged from −33.8% to 73.9% across trials, and in total walking distance from 1.2% to 155.9%, with the review rating any benefit low-certainty and finding no difference in ankle-brachial index or quality of life at moderate certainty. The largest single double-blind trial (Dawson DL et al., PMID: 11063952; 698 patients, 24 weeks) is blunter: maximal walking distance rose 64 m on pentoxifylline and 65 m on placebo (P=0.82 between them) — the drug and the dummy were indistinguishable, while cilostazol in the same trial gained 107 m. The drug is well tolerated (mainly gastrointestinal upset), so the question is not safety but whether there is any effect to buy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): on the record as it stands, pentoxifylline's walking benefit is unproven — the biggest trial is a flat null and the pooled record is too inconsistent to overturn it.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: 24 trials, 3,377 patients — results too inconsistent to pool; any walking benefit low-certainty, no gain in ankle-brachial index or quality of life
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: 24 trials, 3,377 patients — results too inconsistent to pool; any walking benefit low-certainty, no gain in ankle-brachial index or quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane, Broderick 2020; second update of a review first published 2012)
cards.people: 24 double-blind randomised trials with 3,377 participants with stable intermittent claudication (Fontaine stage II); 17 trials compared pentoxifylline with placebo and 7 with other drugs (flunarizine, aspirin, Ginkgo biloba extract, nylidrin, prostaglandin E1, buflomedil/nifedipine). Outcomes: pain-free walking distance, total (maximal) walking distance, ankle-brachial pressure index, quality of life, side effects; certainty assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Pooling was not possible: heterogeneity in dose, duration, baseline walking distance and participants was considerable, and risk of bias was generally unclear. Across the 17 placebo-controlled trials, the difference in percentage improvement for pentoxifylline over placebo ranged from −33.8% to 73.9% for pain-free walking distance (11 trials reporting) and from 1.2% to 155.9% for total walking distance (14 trials reporting) — some trials favoured placebo. Most individual studies suggested a possible improvement (low-certainty evidence). The five studies measuring pre-exercise ankle-brachial index found no evidence of a difference (moderate-certainty evidence), and the larger quality-of-life studies found no difference (moderate-certainty evidence). Pentoxifylline was generally well tolerated, with gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea the most common side effects (low-certainty evidence). The authors concluded the role of pentoxifylline in Fontaine stage II claudication remains uncertain.
cards.watchOut: A systematic review that cannot pool its trials is telling the reader the underlying trial record is incoherent — small, old, variably reported studies pointing in different directions. The low-certainty 'possible improvement' language should not be read as a measured effect size: no pooled estimate exists, and the range of trial results includes harm-side values.
cards.source: Broderick C et al. Pentoxifylline for intermittent claudication. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 33063850. Registry ID: none in the record.
