cards.headline: Dawson 2000: in the largest head-to-head trial, pentoxifylline gained 64 m and placebo 65 m (P=0.82) — while cilostazol gained 107 m in the same trial
cards.summary: Dawson 2000: in the largest head-to-head trial, pentoxifylline gained 64 m and placebo 65 m (P=0.82) — while cilostazol gained 107 m in the same trial
cards.people: 698 patients with moderate-to-severe intermittent claudication from 54 US outpatient vascular clinics, randomised to cilostazol 100 mg twice daily (n=227), pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily (n=232), or placebo (n=239) for 24 weeks; maximal walking distance measured by constant-speed, variable-grade treadmill testing at baseline and at 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 weeks.
cards.result: After 24 weeks, mean maximal walking distance increased by 107 m (a 54% mean increase) on cilostazol, by 64 m (30%) on pentoxifylline, and by 65 m (34%) on placebo. Cilostazol's gain was significantly greater than both pentoxifylline's and placebo's (P<0.001); pentoxifylline's improvement was similar to placebo's (P=0.82). Deaths and serious adverse event rates were similar in each group; side effects (headache, palpitations, diarrhoea) were more common on cilostazol, with similar withdrawal rates on cilostazol (16%) and pentoxifylline (19%). The authors' conclusion: pentoxifylline and placebo had similar effects.
cards.watchOut: This trial was designed and powered around cilostazol, and its pentoxifylline arm used the standard 400 mg three-times-daily dose — the null is a fair test of the drug as prescribed, not of an exotic regimen. A single trial, however large, sits beside a review of 24; the shelf's stamp rests on the two agreeing that no dependable benefit has been shown, not on this trial alone.
cards.source: Dawson DL et al. A comparison of cilostazol and pentoxifylline for treating intermittent claudication. The American Journal of Medicine. 2000. PMID: 11063952. cards.headline: Synthesis: a drug with a plausible mechanism, an incoherent trial record, and a flat null in its largest test — benefit unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: a drug with a plausible mechanism, an incoherent trial record, and a flat null in its largest test — benefit unproven
cards.people: The Cochrane systematic review of 24 double-blind randomised trials (3,377 participants; Broderick 2020) and the largest constituent head-to-head trial (698 patients; Dawson 2000).
cards.result: Pentoxifylline versus placebo on walking distance: unpoolable across trials (percentage-improvement ranges −33.8% to 73.9% pain-free, 1.2% to 155.9% total; low-certainty), and exactly null in the largest trial (+64 m versus +65 m, P=0.82). No demonstrated gain in ankle-brachial index or quality of life at moderate certainty. Tolerability is not the obstacle — gastrointestinal upset predominates. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the walking question only. Pentoxifylline has separate shelves in this library for venous leg ulcers, diabetic kidney disease and alcoholic hepatitis, where the evidence differs; nothing here should be read across to them. Tier C is set: the developer asked for this shelf personally, and its evidence base is a low-certainty review plus one large null trial.

shelves.title: Statins and walking distance in PAD: pain-free walking improved in trials of two different statins — atorvastatin 80 mg and simvastatin 40 mg — but maximal walking time did not move in the largest trial
shelves.question: In adults with peripheral artery disease and intermittent claudication, do statins improve walking distance — and do trials of two different statins agree?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Atorvastatin · Cholesterol/blood · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Female · Heptanoic Acids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intermittent Claudication/drug therapy/etiology · Male · Peripheral Vascular Diseases/complications/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Pyrroles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the distance walked before pain stops you, shown for two different statins. In the largest trial (Mohler ER 3rd et al., PMID: 12952839; 354 patients, 12 months), atorvastatin did not significantly change maximal walking time, but pain-free walking time improved on the 80 mg dose versus placebo (P=0.025), and a physical-activity questionnaire improved on both the 10 mg and 80 mg doses (P=0.011). Simvastatin carries the cleaner walking numbers: in 86 hypercholesterolaemic claudicants (Mondillo S et al., PMID: 12714124), six months of simvastatin 40 mg increased pain-free walking distance by 90 m more than placebo (95% CI 64 to 116) and total walking distance by 126 m more (95% CI 101 to 151), with ankle-brachial index gains alongside; and in older patients (Aronow WS et al., PMID: 12972114) simvastatin lengthened treadmill time to claudication onset by 24% at six months and 42% at one year while placebo did not significantly change. So the answer to 'two different statins?' is yes on the face of the trials — atorvastatin and simvastatin each improved pain-free walking — with the catch that the trials are small and old, and the biggest one's headline endpoint (maximal walking time) was null. None of this displaces the reason these patients take statins anyway: event prevention, for which the walking gain is a symptom bonus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins modestly improve pain-free walking distance in claudication, on concordant small trials of two different agents.

cards.headline: Mohler 2003 (atorvastatin): pain-free walking time improved on 80 mg (P=0.025) and daily activity improved on both doses — but maximal walking time, the headline endpoint, did not significantly change
cards.summary: Mohler 2003 (atorvastatin): pain-free walking time improved on 80 mg (P=0.025) and daily activity improved on both doses — but maximal walking time, the headline endpoint, did not significantly change
cards.people: 354 persons with intermittent claudication attributable to peripheral arterial disease, randomised to placebo, atorvastatin 10 mg daily, or atorvastatin 80 mg daily for 12 months. Outcomes: change in treadmill exercise time (maximal and pain-free walking time) and patient-reported physical activity and quality-of-life questionnaires.
cards.result: Maximal walking time after 12 months did not change significantly on atorvastatin. Pain-free walking time improved after 12 months in the 80 mg group compared with placebo (P=0.025). A physical-activity questionnaire showed improvement in ambulatory ability for both the 10 mg and 80 mg groups (P=0.011), whereas the Walking Impairment Questionnaire and the Short Form 36 did not show significant change. The authors concluded atorvastatin improves pain-free walking distance and community-based physical activity in intermittent claudication.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own hierarchy matters: the maximal-walking-time endpoint was null, and the positive findings sit in a secondary endpoint (pain-free walking time, high dose only) and one of three questionnaires. This is a real but modest and partly selective signal — which is why the shelf is POSSIBLE, and why the simvastatin trials beside it, with cleaner primary walking endpoints, do much of the carrying.
cards.source: Mohler ER 3rd et al. Cholesterol reduction with atorvastatin improves walking distance in patients with peripheral arterial disease. Circulation. 2003. PMID: 12952839. cards.headline: Mondillo 2003 (simvastatin): pain-free walking distance +90 m and total walking distance +126 m versus placebo at six months, with ankle-brachial index gains to match
cards.summary: Mondillo 2003 (simvastatin): pain-free walking distance +90 m and total walking distance +126 m versus placebo at six months, with ankle-brachial index gains to match
cards.people: 86 patients with peripheral arterial disease (Fontaine stage II), intermittent claudication and total cholesterol above 220 mg/dL, randomised to simvastatin 40 mg daily (43 patients) or placebo (43 patients); exercise testing, ankle-brachial indexes and a symptom questionnaire at 0, 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: At six months, mean pain-free walking distance had increased 90 m more in the simvastatin group than in the placebo group (95% CI 64 to 116 m; P<0.005), and total walking distance by 126 m more (95% CI 101 to 151 m; P<0.001). Ankle-brachial index rose by 0.09 more at rest (95% CI 0.06 to 0.12; P<0.01) and 0.19 more after exercise (95% CI 0.14 to 0.24; P<0.005), claudication symptoms improved more on simvastatin, and the walking effects were already significant at three months.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 86 patients selected for high cholesterol — the cleanest numbers on this shelf come from its smallest blinded trial, and the effect sizes (over 100 m on total walking distance) are larger than the bigger atorvastatin trial supports. Generalisation to claudicants with normal cholesterol is untested here.

randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (mondillo 2003) 86 patients with peripheral arterial disease (fontaine stage ii), intermittent claudication and total cholesterol above 220 mg/dl, randomised to simvastatin 40 mg daily (43 patients) or placebo (43 patients); exercise testing, ankle-brachial indexes and a symptom questionnaire at 0, 3 and 6 months. at six months, mean pain-free walking distance had increased 90 m more in the simvastatin group than in the placebo group (95% ci 64 to 116 m; p<0.005), and total walking distance by 126 m more (95% ci 101 to 151 m; p<0.001). ankle-brachial index rose by 0.09 more at rest (95% ci 0.06 to 0.12; p<0.01) and 0.19 more after exercise (95% ci 0.14 to 0.24; p<0.005), claudication symptoms improved more on simvastatin, and the walking effects were already significant at three months. a single-centre trial of 86 patients selected for high cholesterol — the cleanest numbers on this shelf come from its smallest blinded trial, and the effect sizes (over 100 m on total walking distance) are larger than the bigger atorvastatin trial supports. generalisation to claudicants with normal cholesterol is untested here. mondillo s et al. effects of simvastatin on walking performance and symptoms of intermittent claudication in hypercholesterolemic patients with peripheral vascular disease. the american journal of medicine. 2003. pmid: 12714124. registry id: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). mesh: aged · anticholesteremic agents/therapeutic use · blood pressure determination/methods · double-blind method · female · humans · hypercholesterolemia/complications/drug therapy · intermittent claudication/drug therapy/etiology · male · peripheral vascular diseases/complications · simvastatin/therapeutic use · walking/physiology

cards.headline: Aronow 2003 (simvastatin, older patients): treadmill time to claudication onset rose 24% at six months and 42% at one year on simvastatin; placebo did not significantly change
cards.summary: Aronow 2003 (simvastatin, older patients): treadmill time to claudication onset rose 24% at six months and 42% at one year on simvastatin; placebo did not significantly change
cards.people: Older patients with peripheral arterial disease treated with simvastatin or placebo, with treadmill exercise time until the onset of intermittent claudication measured at baseline, six months and one year. The published abstract does not state the sample size, and the record carries no randomisation or blinding terms — this card is corroboration, and the shelf's gate rests on the two double-blind trials above.
cards.result: Simvastatin significantly increased treadmill exercise time until the onset of intermittent claudication from baseline by 54 seconds (a 24% increase, p<0.0001) at six months and by 95 seconds (a 42% increase, p<0.0001) at one year after treatment. At six months and at one year, exercise time on placebo was not significantly different from baseline.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports within-group changes from baseline rather than a between-group contrast with confidence intervals, and states neither the sample size nor the design safeguards — the weakest card on the shelf, included because it is a second simvastatin dataset pointing the same way, and labelled accordingly.
cards.source: Aronow WS et al. Effect of simvastatin versus placebo on treadmill exercise time until the onset of intermittent claudication in older patients with peripheral arterial disease at six months and at one year after treatment. The American Journal of Cardiology. 2003. PMID: 12972114. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Synthesis: two statins, three small trials, one direction on pain-free walking — and a null on maximal walking time in the largest trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: two statins, three small trials, one direction on pain-free walking — and a null on maximal walking time in the largest trial
cards.people: Three placebo-controlled trials in intermittent claudication: atorvastatin (354 patients, 12 months; Mohler 2003) and simvastatin (86 patients, 6 months; Mondillo 2003; plus an older-patient cohort followed to one year, Aronow 2003).
cards.result: Pain-free walking: improved on atorvastatin 80 mg (P=0.025), by 90 m more than placebo on simvastatin 40 mg (95% CI 64 to 116), and time to claudication onset rose 24–42% on simvastatin in older patients. Maximal/total walking: +126 m total walking distance on simvastatin (95% CI 101 to 151) in the small trial, but no significant change in maximal walking time in the 354-patient atorvastatin trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a symptomatic gain on top of the event-prevention case for statins in PAD, not a substitute for it.
cards.watchOut: Every trial here predates modern background therapy and enrolment ran to hundreds, not thousands; no trial was powered for limb or cardiovascular events, and walking distance is a symptomatic endpoint. Tier C is not set — two concordant randomised double-blind trials of two different statins carry the shelf — but the developer should note the total randomised N is only about 440 in the blinded trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mohler ER 3rd et al. Circulation. 2003 (PMID: 12952839); Mondillo S et al. The American Journal of Medicine. 2003 (PMID: 12714124); Aronow WS et al. The American Journal of Cardiology. 2003 (PMID: 12972114).

shelves.title: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) in stage 3 kidney disease: trial-supported for atrial fibrillation at a creatinine-clearance dose — 15 mg at CrCl 30–49 matched warfarin in ROCKET-AF — with exposure up only ~1.5-fold and no trial data below CrCl 30
shelves.question: Can I take Xarelto (rivaroxaban) with stage 3 kidney disease? In a person with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–59) who needs anticoagulation — chiefly for atrial fibrillation — is rivaroxaban safe and effective, and at what dose?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Atrial Fibrillation/complications · Double-Blind Method · Embolism/prevention & control · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Morpholines/administration & dosage · Morpholines/adverse effects · Renal Insufficiency/complications · Rivaroxaban · Stroke/prevention & control · Thiophenes/administration & dosage · Thiophenes/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Warfarin/administration & dosage · Warfarin/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — yes-with-conditions for atrial fibrillation, and the condition is creatinine clearance (CrCl), not the CKD stage label alone. The pharmacokinetic foundation (Kubitza 2010, PMID: 21039764; 32 subjects given a single 10 mg dose) is that renal impairment raises rivaroxaban exposure only moderately: plasma AUC was 1.44-fold higher in mild impairment (CrCl 50–79 mL/min), 1.52-fold in moderate (30–49) and 1.64-fold in severe (<30) than in healthy controls, with factor Xa inhibition AUC up to 2.0-fold in severe impairment — the drug is only partly renally cleared, so exposure climbs but does not multiply. The outcome evidence is the ROCKET-AF renal subgroup (Fox 2011, PMID: 21873708): of 14,264 randomised patients, the 2,950 (20.7%) with CrCl 30–49 mL/min received the reduced 15 mg/day dose and had stroke or systemic embolism at 2.32 per 100 patient-years versus 2.77 on warfarin (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.57–1.23 — relative, printed beside the absolute rates), with the principal safety outcome (major plus clinically relevant non-major bleeding) at 17.82 versus 18.28 per 100 patient-years (P=0.76), intracranial bleeding 0.71 versus 0.88 (P=0.54), and fatal bleeding lower on rivaroxaban (0.28 versus 0.74 per 100 patient-years; P=0.047). Note what that means for 'stage 3': stage 3 spans CrCl/eGFR 30–59, and ROCKET-AF dosed by CrCl — 20 mg/day at CrCl ≥50, 15 mg/day at 30–49, and CrCl <30 was outside the trial. Real-world stage III data agree in direction: in a Quebec cohort of 8,899 patients with AF and stage III CKD (Perreault 2023, PMID: 38230301), rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg each presented a similar effectiveness and safety composite risk to warfarin. In the XARENO registry (Kreutz 2024, PMID: 38939389; 1,455 patients, eGFR 15–49, mean eGFR ≈37), rivaroxaban was associated with fewer adverse kidney outcomes than vitamin K antagonists (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.88 — relative, observational) and lower all-cause death (HR 0.76, 0.59–0.98), with no significant difference in net clinical benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the randomised support is a subgroup with confidence intervals that include harm, and everything beyond it is observational — so the honest answer is 'studied and usable in AF down to CrCl 30 at the reduced dose, with bleeding rates at least as high as the kidney disease itself makes them, and not trial-tested below CrCl 30'.

cards.headline: Kubitza 2010 (pharmacokinetics): a single 10 mg dose gave 1.52-fold higher rivaroxaban exposure at CrCl 30–49 mL/min and 1.64-fold below 30 — a moderate rise, not a multiplication
cards.summary: Kubitza 2010 (pharmacokinetics): a single 10 mg dose gave 1.52-fold higher rivaroxaban exposure at CrCl 30–49 mL/min and 1.64-fold below 30 — a moderate rise, not a multiplication
cards.type: Single-dose pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study across renal function strata (Kubitza 2010)
cards.people: 32 subjects stratified by measured creatinine clearance into four groups of 8: healthy controls (CrCl ≥80 mL/min), mild impairment (50–79), moderate impairment (30–49) and severe impairment (<30), each given a single 10 mg dose of rivaroxaban, with pharmacokinetics, factor Xa inhibition, prothrombin time prolongation and safety measured.
cards.result: Renal clearance of rivaroxaban decreased with increasing renal impairment, and plasma exposure rose correspondingly: AUC least-squares mean values were 1.44-fold (90% CI 1.1–1.9) higher in mild impairment, 1.52-fold (90% CI 1.2–2.0) in moderate impairment and 1.64-fold (90% CI 1.2–2.2) in severe impairment than in healthy controls. The pharmacodynamic effect rose more than the drug level: AUC for prothrombin time prolongation was 2.16-fold (90% CI 1.51–3.10) higher in moderate and 2.44-fold (1.70–3.49) in severe impairment, and AUC for factor Xa inhibition was 1.50-fold (1.07–2.10), 1.86-fold (1.34–2.59) and 2.0-fold (1.44–2.78) higher in mild, moderate and severe impairment respectively. The authors concluded that clearance falls and exposure and pharmacodynamic effects increase as expected for a partially renally excreted drug, but that the influence of renal function on rivaroxaban clearance was moderate, even in severe impairment.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two subjects, eight per stratum, one 10 mg dose, no clinical outcomes — this card explains WHY a dose reduction exists, not whether the reduced dose is safe or effective; that evidence is the ROCKET-AF card below. The gap between drug level (1.52-fold) and clotting effect (up to 2.16-fold on prothrombin time prolongation in moderate impairment) is the reason 'exposure rises only moderately' should not be read as 'effect rises only moderately'. Single-dose data also cannot show accumulation on daily dosing.
cards.source: Kubitza D, Becka M, Mueck W, Halabi A, Maatouk H, Klause N, Lufft V, Wand DD, Philipp T, Bruck H. Effects of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and safety of rivaroxaban, an oral, direct Factor Xa inhibitor. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2010. PMID: 21039764. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fox 2011 (ROCKET-AF renal subgroup): at CrCl 30–49 mL/min the reduced 15 mg dose matched warfarin — stroke/systemic embolism 2.32 versus 2.77 per 100 patient-years, major-plus-non-major bleeding 17.82 versus 18.28, fatal bleeding 0.28 versus 0.74
cards.summary: Fox 2011 (ROCKET-AF renal subgroup): at CrCl 30–49 mL/min the reduced 15 mg dose matched warfarin — stroke/systemic embolism 2.32 versus 2.77 per 100 patient-years, major-plus-non-major bleeding 17.82 versus 18.28, fatal bleeding 0.28 versus 0.74
cards.type: Prespecified renal subgroup analysis of a randomised double-blind trial (ROCKET-AF; Fox 2011)
cards.people: Prespecified renal analysis of ROCKET-AF: 14,264 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation randomised double-blind to rivaroxaban 20 mg/day (15 mg/day if creatinine clearance 30–49 mL/min) or dose-adjusted warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0). The 2,950 patients (20.7%) with CrCl 30–49 mL/min were older (mean 79 years) than those with CrCl >50 mL/min (73 years) and had higher event rates irrespective of treatment. Patients with CrCl below 30 mL/min were not enrolled.
cards.result: Among patients with CrCl 30–49 mL/min, the primary endpoint of stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 2.32 per 100 patient-years with rivaroxaban 15 mg/day versus 2.77 per 100 patient-years with warfarin (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.57–1.23 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates) in the per-protocol population; intention-to-treat gave HR 0.86 (0.63–1.17). Rates of the principal safety endpoint (major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding: 17.82 versus 18.28 per 100 patient-years; P=0.76) and intracranial bleeding (0.71 versus 0.88 per 100 patient-years; P=0.54) were similar with rivaroxaban or warfarin. Fatal bleeding occurred less often with rivaroxaban (0.28 versus 0.74 per 100 patient-years; P=0.047). The authors concluded that patients with moderate renal insufficiency have higher stroke and bleeding rates than those with normal renal function, that there was no evidence of heterogeneity in treatment effect across dosing groups, and that dose adjustment in ROCKET-AF yielded results consistent with the overall trial.
cards.watchOut: Map the trial onto the question carefully. 'Stage 3 kidney disease' (eGFR 30–59) is wider than the subgroup: ROCKET-AF gave the FULL 20 mg dose at CrCl 50–59 and the reduced 15 mg dose at 30–49, and it dosed by Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance, not by the eGFR a laboratory reports — the same patient can land in different bands by the two measures. The subgroup's confidence interval for stroke prevention (0.57–1.23) includes meaningful harm, so this is 'consistent with the overall trial', not independently proven. And the bleeding rates are high in absolute terms (about 18 per 100 patient-years for the composite safety outcome on either drug): kidney impairment itself, more than the choice between these two drugs, drives that.
cards.source: Fox KAA, Piccini JP, Wojdyla D, Becker RC, Halperin JL, Nessel CC, Paolini JF, Hankey GJ, Mahaffey KW, Patel MR, Singer DE, Califf RM. Prevention of stroke and systemic embolism with rivaroxaban compared with warfarin in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and moderate renal impairment. European Heart Journal. 2011. PMID: 21873708. Registry ID: none in the record (prespecified subgroup report; the abstract does not print a registration number). cards.headline: Perreault 2023 (Quebec stage III cohort): in 8,899 real-world patients with AF and stage III CKD, rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg each carried a similar effectiveness and safety composite risk to warfarin
cards.summary: Perreault 2023 (Quebec stage III cohort): in 8,899 real-world patients with AF and stage III CKD, rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg each carried a similar effectiveness and safety composite risk to warfarin
cards.type: Retrospective population cohort study in stage III CKD (Perreault 2023)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort from Quebec administrative databases, 2013–2017: 8,899 patients with atrial fibrillation and stage III chronic kidney disease newly starting oral anticoagulation — 3,335 on warfarin and 5,564 on a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban or rivaroxaban). Primary effectiveness outcome: composite of ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism and death within a year; primary safety outcome: composite of major bleeding within a year. Groups compared with inverse probability of treatment weighting and Cox models.
cards.result: Compared with warfarin, rivaroxaban 15 mg and rivaroxaban 20 mg each presented a similar effectiveness and safety composite risk (the abstract reports the rivaroxaban finding qualitatively, without printing dose-specific hazard ratios). For context within the same cohort, apixaban 5 mg was associated with a lower effectiveness composite risk (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.65–0.88 — relative), driven by lower mortality (HR 0.61, 0.43–0.88), and a similar safety risk (HR 0.94, 0.66–1.35); apixaban 2.5 mg had a similar effectiveness composite (HR 1.00, 0.79–1.26) and a lower safety risk (HR 0.65, 0.43–0.99). The authors concluded that rivaroxaban and apixaban appear effective and safe compared with warfarin in AF patients with stage III CKD, while noting appropriately sized randomised trials are still needed in this population.
cards.watchOut: Observational claims data: who received which dose was decided by clinicians, not chance, so confounding by indication (frailer patients channelled to lower doses or to warfarin) survives weighting. The abstract's rivaroxaban result is qualitative — no printed hazard ratios for the rivaroxaban doses — so this card supports 'no large real-world penalty detected', not a measured equivalence. Stage III here is an administrative code-based classification, not measured CrCl.
cards.source: Perreault S, Boivin Proulx LA, Lenglet A, Massy ZA, Dorais M. Effectiveness and safety of apixaban and rivaroxaban vs warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease. World Journal of Nephrology. 2023. PMID: 38230301. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective registry cohort). cards.headline: Kreutz 2024 (XARENO registry): at eGFR 15–49, rivaroxaban was associated with fewer adverse kidney outcomes than vitamin K antagonists (HR 0.62, relative) and lower all-cause death (HR 0.76) — with no significant difference in net clinical benefit
cards.summary: Kreutz 2024 (XARENO registry): at eGFR 15–49, rivaroxaban was associated with fewer adverse kidney outcomes than vitamin K antagonists (HR 0.62, relative) and lower all-cause death (HR 0.76) — with no significant difference in net clinical benefit
cards.type: Prospective observational registry with propensity weighting (XARENO; Kreutz 2024)
cards.people: XARENO, a prospective observational registry of patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and advanced chronic kidney disease (eGFR 15–49 mL/min/1.73 m²): 1,455 patients (764 rivaroxaban, 691 vitamin K antagonist), mean age 78 years, 44% women, mean eGFR 37.1 ± 9.0 on rivaroxaban and 36.4 ± 10.1 on VKA, followed for a median of 2.1 years with blinded adjudicated outcomes and propensity-score overlap weighting. The primary outcome was a composite of adverse kidney outcomes (eGFR decline to <15, need for chronic kidney replacement therapy, or acute kidney injury); a net clinical benefit composite (stroke or systemic embolism, major bleeding, myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, or cardiovascular death) was also analysed.
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 2.1 years, rivaroxaban was associated with less adverse kidney outcomes (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.88 — a relative measure) and lower all-cause death (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59–0.98) than VKA. No significant differences were observed in net clinical benefit. The authors concluded that patients receiving rivaroxaban had fewer adverse kidney events and lower all-cause mortality than those receiving VKA, supporting the use of rivaroxaban in this high-risk group.
cards.watchOut: A registry, not a trial: propensity weighting balances measured differences only, and a kidney-outcome advantage for rivaroxaban over VKA is exactly the kind of result channeling and residual confounding can manufacture — treat HR 0.62 as hypothesis-consistent, not causal proof. The population (eGFR 15–49, mean ≈37) is mostly stage 3b/4, sicker than a typical stage 3 patient, and the comparison that matters most to this shelf's question — bleeding — sits inside the net-benefit composite, which showed no significant difference and is not broken out in the abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: usable in stage 3 for atrial fibrillation at a creatinine-clearance-based dose — 20 mg at CrCl ≥50, 15 mg at 30–49 in the trial — with bleeding risk driven mainly by the kidney disease itself; untested below CrCl 30
cards.summary: Synthesis: usable in stage 3 for atrial fibrillation at a creatinine-clearance-based dose — 20 mg at CrCl ≥50, 15 mg at 30–49 in the trial — with bleeding risk driven mainly by the kidney disease itself; untested below CrCl 30
cards.people: One single-dose pharmacokinetic study (Kubitza 2010: 32 subjects), one prespecified randomised-trial renal subgroup (Fox 2011: 2,950 patients at CrCl 30–49 within ROCKET-AF's 14,264), one stage III administrative cohort (Perreault 2023: 8,899 patients), and one prospective registry at eGFR 15–49 (XARENO, Kreutz 2024: 1,455 patients, NCT02663076).
cards.result: Exposure: rivaroxaban AUC rises 1.44-fold (CrCl 50–79), 1.52-fold (30–49) and 1.64-fold (<30) versus healthy controls after a single dose, with clotting-effect measures rising more (Kubitza 2010). Outcomes at the reduced dose: stroke/systemic embolism 2.32 versus 2.77 per 100 patient-years and composite bleeding 17.82 versus 18.28 versus warfarin at CrCl 30–49, fatal bleeding 0.28 versus 0.74 (Fox 2011). Real-world stage III use showed no detected effectiveness or safety penalty for rivaroxaban 15 mg or 20 mg versus warfarin (Perreault 2023), and registry data at eGFR 15–49 associated rivaroxaban with fewer kidney outcomes (HR 0.62, relative) and no significant net-benefit difference versus VKA (Kreutz 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — GAP-E: one trial subgroup plus observational support, capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — GAP-E. Boundaries the cards cannot cross: (1) All outcome evidence here is for atrial fibrillation; rivaroxaban dosing for treating venous thromboembolism follows a different schedule and renal evidence base, not carded on this shelf. (2) ROCKET-AF excluded CrCl <30 mL/min, so stage 4–5 use rests on pharmacokinetics and registries only. (3) Trials dosed by Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance; a stage label or a laboratory eGFR alone does not pick the dose. (4) Nothing here weighs rivaroxaban against apixaban head-to-head in stage 3 — the Perreault cohort's apixaban signals are context, not a randomised comparison. Individual dosing decisions belong with the prescriber who can measure the patient's actual CrCl, weight, age and interacting medicines.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kubitza D et al. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2010 (PMID: 21039764); Fox KAA et al. European Heart Journal. 2011 (PMID: 21873708); Perreault S et al. World Journal of Nephrology. 2023 (PMID: 38230301); Kreutz R et al. JACC: Advances. 2024 (PMID: 38939389).

shelves.title: Ear-lobe creases (Frank's sign) and heart disease: a real observational association — pooled diagnostic odds ratio 3.27 with sensitivity 62% and specificity 67% across 37 studies — but association only, not causation, and too weak to diagnose or exclude coronary disease
shelves.question: 'Are ear-lobe creases a sign of heart disease?' — Is a diagonal earlobe crease (Frank's sign) associated with coronary artery disease, how strong and how diagnostically useful is the association, and is any of it causal?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials as Topic/methods · Coronary Artery Disease/diagnosis · Coronary Artery Disease/epidemiology · Ear Auricle/anatomy & histology · Ear Auricle/pathology · Humans
shelves.balance: The association is real, replicated, and weak — and it is association only. The 2014 meta-analysis of 37 studies and 31,188 participants pooled a sensitivity of 0.62 (95% CI 0.56–0.67) and specificity of 0.67 (0.61–0.73) for diagonal earlobe crease as a marker of coronary artery disease, with a diagnostic odds ratio of 3.27 (2.47–4.32, relative) (Lucenteforte 2014, PMID: 24866080) — performance far too poor to diagnose or exclude disease in an individual. The strongest design, the Copenhagen City Heart Study's 10,885 initially disease-free adults followed for 35 years, found earlobe crease among the visible ageing signs associated with ischaemic heart disease and myocardial infarction after adjustment for age and known risk factors, with risk rising stepwise by number of signs (hazard ratio up to 1.40 for ischaemic heart disease and 1.57 for infarction with 3–4 signs versus none — relative measures for the bundle of signs) (Christoffersen 2014, PMID: 24334176). The 2025 systematic review likewise found about a four-fold likelihood of coronary disease in people with the crease across 12 studies, independent of age and risk factors in all 10 studies that examined confounding (Curtis 2025, PMID: 34924071). No fetched study shows the crease causes coronary disease, that it adds usefully to standard risk factors for an individual patient, or that acting on it changes outcomes — it travels with age and with the same risk factors that cause the disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: an ear-lobe crease is a genuine statistical sign of higher coronary risk at group level, best read as a prompt to check the conventional risk factors — not as evidence that any individual has, or will get, heart disease.

cards.headline: Lucenteforte 2014: across 37 studies and 31,188 participants, earlobe crease had sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.67 for coronary artery disease — a weak test (diagnostic OR 3.27)
cards.summary: Lucenteforte 2014: across 37 studies and 31,188 participants, earlobe crease had sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.67 for coronary artery disease — a weak test (diagnostic OR 3.27)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of diagonal earlobe crease as a marker of coronary artery disease, 37 studies (Lucenteforte 2014)
cards.people: 31,188 participants in 37 studies (largely case-control and cross-sectional comparisons of people with and without coronary artery disease) pooled in a meta-analysis of diagonal earlobe crease as a marker of coronary artery disease.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI 0.56–0.67) and pooled specificity 0.67 (0.61–0.73): the crease was present in about 62% of people with coronary artery disease and absent in about 67% of people without it. The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 3.27 (95% CI 2.47–4.32) — a relative association measure. In plain terms, the crease misses roughly 4 in 10 people who have coronary disease and is also present in roughly 1 in 3 people who do not.
cards.watchOut: The PubMed record for this paper carries no abstract; the pooled figures carded here are as reported in the paper and verified this session against its full text and citing literature (including the KORA report, PMID: 34915852). Design caveat: most included studies compared people already known to have coronary disease with controls — a design that inflates diagnostic performance versus testing unselected people — and both the crease and coronary disease become commoner with age, the central confounder of this whole literature.
cards.source: Lucenteforte E, Romoli M, Zagli G, Gensini GF, Mugelli A, Vannacci A. Ear lobe crease as a marker of coronary artery disease: a meta-analysis. International Journal of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 24866080. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Christoffersen 2014: in 10,885 disease-free adults followed 35 years, earlobe crease was among the visible signs independently associated with ischaemic heart disease and heart attack
cards.summary: Christoffersen 2014: in 10,885 disease-free adults followed 35 years, earlobe crease was among the visible signs independently associated with ischaemic heart disease and heart attack
cards.type: Prospective general-population cohort study, Copenhagen City Heart Study (Christoffersen 2014)
cards.people: 10,885 men and women aged 20–93 years from the Copenhagen City Heart Study, all free of ischaemic heart disease at entry (1976–78), examined for visible age-related signs including earlobe crease, and followed to June 2011 (35 years, 100% follow-up) for ischaemic heart disease and myocardial infarction.
cards.result: During follow-up, 3,401 participants developed ischaemic heart disease and 1,708 had a myocardial infarction. Earlobe crease — together with frontoparietal baldness, crown baldness and xanthelasmata — was associated with increased risk of both outcomes after adjustment for age and other known cardiovascular risk factors. Risk rose stepwise with the number of signs present: compared with no signs, 3–4 signs carried a hazard ratio up to 1.40 (95% CI 1.20–1.62) for ischaemic heart disease and 1.57 (1.28–1.93) for myocardial infarction (P for trend <0.001) — relative measures, and for the bundle of signs rather than the crease alone.
cards.watchOut: This is the one design here that establishes the sign precedes the disease — but the headline hazard ratios belong to combinations of 3–4 ageing signs, not to an earlobe crease by itself, whose individual effect is smaller. Adjustment cannot remove all confounding: the crease may simply be a visible clock of the same ageing and risk-factor exposure that damages arteries. Association in a cohort, even adjusted and prospective, is not causation.
cards.source: Christoffersen M, Frikke-Schmidt R, Schnohr P, Jensen GB, Nordestgaard BG, Tybjærg-Hansen A. Visible age-related signs and risk of ischemic heart disease in the general population: a prospective cohort study. Circulation. 2014. PMID: 24334176. Registry ID: none in the record (prospective cohort). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Curtis 2025: 12 studies, 2,415 cases and 2,545 controls — people with a diagonal earlobe crease had about four times the likelihood of coronary artery disease
cards.summary: Curtis 2025: 12 studies, 2,415 cases and 2,545 controls — people with a diagonal earlobe crease had about four times the likelihood of coronary artery disease
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagonal earlobe crease and coronary artery disease (Curtis 2025)
cards.people: Patients in 12 studies pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagonal earlobe crease and coronary artery disease: 2,415 cases with coronary artery disease and 2,545 controls without it.
cards.result: Patients with a diagonal earlobe crease had an increased — approximately four times — likelihood of having coronary artery disease, as stated in the review's abstract (a relative association; the abstract does not report an exact pooled odds ratio, and none is quoted here). In all 10 included studies that examined confounding, the association was found to be independent of age and other known cardiovascular risk factors. The authors, writing for an ENT audience, argue the crease is worth looking for as a clinical sign.
cards.watchOut: Predominantly case-control data again — comparing people already diagnosed with coronary disease against controls overstates how the sign performs prospectively, and publication bias favours positive sign-association studies. 'Four times the likelihood' is the abstract's own summary phrasing; with no exact pooled estimate in the abstract, this shelf does not manufacture one. Independence from measured risk factors in observational data still leaves residual confounding (age above all) fully possible.
cards.source: Curtis J, Walford S. Why we should be looking for earlobe creases in ENT. A systematic review and meta-analysis of diagonal earlobe crease and coronary artery disease. cards.headline: Synthesis: Frank's sign is a real but weak association — sensitivity 62%, specificity 67% — observational only, with no evidence of causation or of benefit from acting on the crease itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: Frank's sign is a real but weak association — sensitivity 62%, specificity 67% — observational only, with no evidence of causation or of benefit from acting on the crease itself
cards.people: Three syntheses/cohorts: a 37-study diagnostic meta-analysis (Lucenteforte 2014 — 31,188 participants), a 10,885-person prospective cohort with 35-year follow-up (Christoffersen 2014), and a 12-study systematic review (Curtis 2025 — 2,415 cases, 2,545 controls). All are observational; no randomised or mechanistic study was carded.
cards.result: The association replicates across designs and decades: diagnostic odds ratio 3.27 (relative) with sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.67 (Lucenteforte 2014); prospective association after risk-factor adjustment, with stepwise hazard ratios up to 1.40–1.57 for bundles of ageing signs (Christoffersen 2014); approximately four-fold likelihood of coronary disease in case-control pooling (Curtis 2025). Against that: at 62% sensitivity and 67% specificity the crease cannot rule coronary disease in or out for an individual; the effect for the crease alone is smaller than the bundle figures; and no fetched evidence shows the crease causes arterial disease, adds predictive value beyond standard risk factors in a way that changes management, or that any intervention follows from the crease itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: ear-lobe creases are probably a genuine marker of higher coronary risk at population level — a reason to measure blood pressure, lipids and glucose, not a diagnosis and not a cause.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. The stamp is POSSIBLE because the evidence is observational-only, which caps the stamp by rule — and because the honest claim is narrow: association, not causation, not a screening test. A crease in a young person without risk factors and no crease in an older smoker are both common sights; conventional risk factors dominate any decision, and chest pain or other symptoms warrant assessment regardless of what anyone's earlobes look like.

cards.search: synthesis: frank's sign is a real but weak association — sensitivity 62%, specificity 67% — observational only, with no evidence of causation or of benefit from acting on the crease itself synthesis: frank's sign is a real but weak association — sensitivity 62%, specificity 67% — observational only, with no evidence of causation or of benefit from acting on the crease itself 'are ear-lobe creases a sign of heart disease?' — is a diagonal earlobe crease (frank's sign) associated with coronary artery disease, how strong and how diagnostically useful is the association, and is any of it causal? synthesis three syntheses/cohorts: a 37-study diagnostic meta-analysis (lucenteforte 2014 — 31,188 participants), a 10,885-person prospective cohort with 35-year follow-up (christoffersen 2014), and a 12-study systematic review (curtis 2025 — 2,415 cases, 2,545 controls). all are observational; no randomised or mechanistic study was carded. the association replicates across designs and decades: diagnostic odds ratio 3.27 (relative) with sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.67 (lucenteforte 2014); prospective association after risk-factor adjustment, with stepwise hazard ratios up to 1.40–1.57 for bundles of ageing signs (christoffersen 2014); approximately four-fold likelihood of coronary disease in case-control pooling (curtis 2025). against that: at 62% sensitivity and 67% specificity the crease cannot rule coronary disease in or out for an individual; shelves.title: HHT nosebleeds: nasal sprays of bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid all failed against saline; oral tranexamic acid shortens bleeds without reducing their number; pomalidomide improved severity scores in the one positive modern RCT
shelves.question: For hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), which drug treatments for nosebleeds have actually beaten placebo in trials?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Antifibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Bevacizumab/administration & dosage · Blood Transfusion · Double-Blind Method · Epistaxis/drug therapy · Epistaxis/etiology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Telangiectasia, Hereditary Hemorrhagic/complications · Tranexamic Acid/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the HHT epistaxis record divides cleanly by route and by rigour. Nasal sprays failed twice: in the NOSE trial (Whitehead 2016, PMID: 27599329; NCT01408030; 121 adults), bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid sprays were indistinguishable from saline placebo on bleed frequency (P = .97; medians 7.0–8.0 episodes/week in every arm), and Dupuis-Girod 2016 (PMID: 27599328; NCT02106520; 80 patients) found nasal bevacizumab at three doses numerically worse than placebo on monthly bleed duration (215–259 vs 200 minutes; P = .57), stopped for futility. Oral tranexamic acid does something narrower: in ATERO (Gaillard 2014, PMID: 25040799; NCT00355108; 118 patients, crossover) it shortened monthly bleeding duration by 17.3% relative (15.7 minutes absolute, 95% CI 5.5 to 27.6; P = 0.005) without changing frequency, and in Geisthoff 2014 (PMID: 25005464; NCT01031992; 22 patients) it missed its haemoglobin endpoint (P = 0.33) while cutting the epistaxis score by 54% relative (P = 0.0031). The one positive modern systemic RCT is pomalidomide: PATH-HHT (Al-Samkari 2024, PMID: 39292928; NCT03910244; 144 patients) improved epistaxis severity by −0.94 points versus placebo (95% CI −1.57 to −0.31; P = 0.004), past the 0.71-point clinical-significance threshold, and closed early at interim analysis. Systemic bevacizumab's dramatic numbers (severity score −3.33; haemoglobin +2.38 g/dL) come from 10 uncontrolled cohorts totalling 225 patients (Li 2025, PMID: 40095741). Across all 8 placebo-controlled RCTs pooled by Hsu 2019 (PMID: 30200816), tamoxifen was the only drug superior to placebo for frequency and severity, and no treatment changed haemoglobin or quality of life. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped. cards.headline: Whitehead 2016 (NOSE trial): no difference between bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid nasal sprays and saline placebo — median 7.0 to 8.0 bleeds a week in every arm
cards.summary: Whitehead 2016 (NOSE trial): no difference between bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid nasal sprays and saline placebo — median 7.0 to 8.0 bleeds a week in every arm
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 6 HHT centres (Whitehead 2016)
cards.people: 121 adults with HHT and an epistaxis severity score of at least 3.0, randomised at 6 HHT centres to twice-daily nasal sprays for 12 weeks: bevacizumab 1% (4 mg/day), estriol 0.1% (0.4 mg/day), tranexamic acid 10% (40 mg/day), or saline placebo; 106 completed the primary outcome.
cards.result: There was no difference in epistaxis frequency between any active spray and placebo (P = .97). Median weekly episodes at 12 weeks were: bevacizumab 7.0 (IQR 4.5–10.5), estriol 8.0 (4.0–12.0), tranexamic acid 7.5 (3.0–11.0), placebo 8.0 (3.0–14.0). There were also no differences in bleed duration, haemoglobin, ferritin, transfusion requirements or emergency-department visits.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's best-designed negative: three widely used topical therapies tested head-on against saline in the same trial, all indistinguishable from it. It does not test systemic (intravenous) bevacizumab or submucosal injection — different exposures, carded separately below.
cards.source: Whitehead et al. Effect of Topical Intranasal Therapy on Epistaxis Frequency in Patients With Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia: The NOSE Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27599329. Registry ID: NCT01408030. cards.headline: Dupuis-Girod 2016: nasal bevacizumab at three doses was no better than placebo (monthly bleed duration 215–259 minutes on drug versus 200 minutes on placebo; P = .57) — stopped for futility
cards.summary: Dupuis-Girod 2016: nasal bevacizumab at three doses was no better than placebo (monthly bleed duration 215–259 minutes on drug versus 200 minutes on placebo; P = .57) — stopped for futility
cards.people: 80 patients with HHT, randomised to bevacizumab nasal spray 25 mg, 50 mg or 75 mg (n=20, 20 and 19) or placebo (n=21); three doses given 14 days apart.
cards.result: Mean monthly epistaxis duration at 3 months was 259.2 minutes (25 mg), 244.0 minutes (50 mg), 215.0 minutes (75 mg) and 200.4 minutes (placebo) (P = .57) — numerically worse on drug at every dose. The trial was stopped before its phase 3 stage for futility.
cards.watchOut: Together with NOSE, this closes the question of bevacizumab as a nasal spray at these doses: two randomised trials, no signal, one stopped early for futility. It says nothing about intravenous bevacizumab, where systemic exposure is far higher.

cards.headline: Gaillard 2014 (ATERO): oral tranexamic acid shortened monthly nosebleed duration by 17.3% relative (15.7 minutes absolute) — but bleeds came just as often
cards.summary: Gaillard 2014 (ATERO): oral tranexamic acid shortened monthly nosebleed duration by 17.3% relative (15.7 minutes absolute) — but bleeds came just as often
cards.people: 118 patients with HHT in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial: oral tranexamic acid 3 g/day (1.5 g twice daily) and placebo, each for 3 months.
cards.result: Mean monthly epistaxis duration was shorter on tranexamic acid: a relative reduction of 17.3%, an absolute reduction of 15.7 minutes per month (95% CI 5.5 to 27.6; P = 0.005). Bleed frequency did not change (median 22.1 episodes per month on placebo versus 23.3 on tranexamic acid). No thrombophlebitis occurred during the trial.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen minutes a month is a modest prize for 3 g of drug a day in a population with arteriovenous malformations, where the long-term thrombotic safety of an antifibrinolytic is the standing worry; three months per period with no thrombophlebitis is reassurance of the weakest kind. The crossover design makes every patient their own control — good for precision on duration, silent on rare harms.
cards.source: Gaillard et al. [Tranexamic acid for epistaxis in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia — the ATERO trial; article title not captured verbatim this session]. cards.headline: Geisthoff 2014: oral tranexamic acid missed its haemoglobin endpoint (P = 0.33) but cut the epistaxis score by 54% relative (P = 0.0031) — in 22 patients
cards.summary: Geisthoff 2014: oral tranexamic acid missed its haemoglobin endpoint (P = 0.33) but cut the epistaxis score by 54% relative (P = 0.0031) — in 22 patients
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover phase IIIB trial (Geisthoff 2014)
cards.people: 22 patients with HHT (intention-to-treat) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover phase IIIB trial: oral tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily versus placebo, 3 months on each.
cards.result: The primary outcome, haemoglobin, did not change significantly (P = 0.33). The epistaxis score fell by 54% relative on tranexamic acid (P = 0.0031). No severe side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: A 22-patient crossover whose pre-set primary outcome was negative and whose positive outcome is a score, not a blood count or a transfusion avoided. Its direction agrees with ATERO (shorter, less severe bleeds on oral tranexamic acid), but it is far too small to add safety reassurance.

cards.headline: Al-Samkari 2024 (PATH-HHT): pomalidomide beat placebo on epistaxis severity by −0.94 points (P = 0.004) — past the 0.71-point threshold for clinical significance — and the trial closed early for efficacy
cards.summary: Al-Samkari 2024 (PATH-HHT): pomalidomide beat placebo on epistaxis severity by −0.94 points (P = 0.004) — past the 0.71-point threshold for clinical significance — and the trial closed early for efficacy
cards.people: 144 patients with HHT and a baseline mean epistaxis severity score of 5.0 (±1.5), randomised 2:1 to pomalidomide 4 mg daily (n=95) or placebo (n=49) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: The mean between-group difference in change in epistaxis severity score at 24 weeks was −0.94 points (95% CI −1.57 to −0.31; P = 0.004); a difference of at least 0.71 points is considered clinically significant. HHT-specific quality of life also favoured pomalidomide (difference −1.4 points, 95% CI −2.6 to −0.3). Adverse events were more common on pomalidomide, principally neutropenia, constipation and rash. The trial closed early after an interim analysis met its efficacy threshold.
cards.watchOut: One trial, stopped early — and early stopping for efficacy tends to inflate the estimated effect — for an immunomodulatory drug with neutropenia and its class's pregnancy-prevention controls, in a condition patients live with for decades. The result is genuinely positive and genuinely preliminary at the same time; replication and longer safety follow-up are the missing pieces.
cards.source: Al-Samkari et al. Pomalidomide for Epistaxis in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39292928. Registry ID: NCT03910244. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Li 2025 (systemic bevacizumab): severity scores fell by 3.33 points and haemoglobin rose by 2.38 g/dL after intravenous bevacizumab — across 10 studies and 225 patients, every one uncontrolled
cards.summary: Li 2025 (systemic bevacizumab): severity scores fell by 3.33 points and haemoglobin rose by 2.38 g/dL after intravenous bevacizumab — across 10 studies and 225 patients, every one uncontrolled
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of uncontrolled cohorts (Li 2025)
cards.people: 10 studies, 225 patients with HHT treated with systemic (intravenous) bevacizumab; all were uncontrolled before–after cohorts.
cards.result: Post-treatment versus pre-treatment, the epistaxis severity score fell by 3.33 points (mean difference −3.33, 95% CI −3.62 to −3.03) and haemoglobin rose by 2.38 g/dL (95% CI 1.45 to 3.30); all cohorts reported reduced red-cell and iron transfusion requirements. Hypertension was the most frequent adverse effect.
cards.watchOut: Before–after changes of this size, in patients started on treatment at their worst, are exactly what regression to the mean and publication bias produce. Both randomised trials of bevacizumab by the nasal route found nothing (cards above), and no randomised trial of the intravenous route was fetched this session. This card records why clinicians believe in systemic bevacizumab — and why that belief is not yet trial evidence.
cards.source: Li et al. [Systemic bevacizumab for epistaxis in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia — systematic review and meta-analysis; article title not captured verbatim this session]. cards.headline: Hsu 2019 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs): tamoxifen was the only drug superior to placebo for bleed frequency and severity; no treatment changed haemoglobin or quality of life
cards.summary: Hsu 2019 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs): tamoxifen was the only drug superior to placebo for bleed frequency and severity; no treatment changed haemoglobin or quality of life
cards.people: 8 randomised trials comparing medical treatment with placebo for HHT epistaxis, identified from PubMed, Embase, Scopus and the Cochrane Library to November 2017 (PROSPERO CRD42017081952).
cards.result: Bevacizumab, tranexamic acid and estrogen, regardless of route, had no significant influence on epistaxis frequency. Tamoxifen was superior to placebo in both frequency and severity of epistaxis. For duration, nasal bevacizumab, oral or nasal tranexamic acid and nasal estrogen did not differ from placebo, but submucosal bevacizumab injection showed lower duration (mean difference −219.00 minutes/month, 95% CI −271.90 to −166.10). No treatment significantly changed mean haemoglobin concentration (pooled mean difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.65 to 0.20) or quality of life (pooled standardised mean difference 0.07, 95% CI −0.16 to 0.30).
cards.watchOut: The tamoxifen signal rests on a small number of small, older trials (the pivotal double-blind trial, Yaniv 2009, NCT00375622, planned up to 60 patients on tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 6 months; its own outcome numbers were not captured this session) pooled across different outcome scales — enough for a hypothesis about a cheap, familiar drug, not enough for confidence. The submucosal-bevacizumab duration result likewise comes from a single small trial inside the pool.
cards.source: Hsu YP, Hsu CW, Bai CH, Cheng SW, Chen C. Medical Treatment for Epistaxis in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia: A Meta-analysis. Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: in HHT, the sprays failed, oral tranexamic acid shortens bleeds without preventing them, and the systemic claims rest on one early-stopped trial and uncontrolled series
cards.summary: Synthesis: in HHT, the sprays failed, oral tranexamic acid shortens bleeds without preventing them, and the systemic claims rest on one early-stopped trial and uncontrolled series
cards.people: Seven sources: two nasal-spray RCTs (Whitehead 2016, n=121, NCT01408030; Dupuis-Girod 2016, n=80, NCT02106520), two oral tranexamic acid crossover RCTs (Gaillard 2014, n=118, NCT00355108; Geisthoff 2014, n=22, NCT01031992), one systemic RCT (Al-Samkari 2024, n=144, NCT03910244), one meta-analysis of 8 placebo-controlled RCTs (Hsu 2019), and one meta-analysis of 10 uncontrolled systemic-bevacizumab cohorts (225 patients; Li 2025).
cards.result: No difference: nasal bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid versus saline (frequency P = .97); nasal bevacizumab dose-ranging versus placebo (duration P = .57, stopped for futility). Duration only: oral tranexamic acid −17.3% relative monthly duration (15.7 minutes absolute) with unchanged frequency; epistaxis score −54% relative in the smaller crossover, haemoglobin unchanged. Positive but early: pomalidomide −0.94 severity points versus placebo (P = 0.004), trial closed early. Uncontrolled only: systemic bevacizumab severity −3.33 points, haemoglobin +2.38 g/dL. Pooled RCT verdict: tamoxifen alone beat placebo on frequency and severity; nothing improved haemoglobin or quality of life. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: this shelf covers drug treatment of epistaxis in HHT. It does not cover gastrointestinal bleeding or visceral AVMs, iron and transfusion management, or procedural options (laser, embolisation, surgery); the doxycycline NOSTRIL trial (2022, PMID: 35108451 — negative on all three primary outcomes) was identified but not carded this session.

shelves.title: Swollen legs from venous disease: compression works, and adjustable beats tight — self-adjustable Velcro wraps cut leg volume 26% versus 19% for high-pressure bandages in a week, moderate stockings matched bandages, and adding physiotherapy changed nothing
shelves.question: In adults with swollen ankles, feet and legs from chronic venous insufficiency (peripheral oedema), which treatments — compression stockings, bandages, adjustable compression devices, or added physiotherapy — reduce leg volume, and how do they compare?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Scoped to chronic venous leg oedema — the form of swollen legs with randomised treatment trials; drug-induced, cardiac, renal and lymphatic oedema are different questions, and the library already homes venous-symptom drug treatments (horse chestnut, Shelf #2504; micronised flavonoid fraction, Shelf #3477). Compression is the base treatment in every carded trial. Moderate-pressure stockings (23–32 mmHg) matched high-pressure inelastic bandages at 7 days (leg volume −13.2% vs −15.6%, not significant; Mosti 2012, PMID: 22090466; 30 patients). Patient-adjustable Velcro devices beat bandages over the first week (median volume reduction 26% vs 19%, p < .001) because their pressure does not decay (Mosti 2015, PMID: 26160211; 36 patients). Adding a physiotherapy programme of exercise and self-drainage to compression made no difference to oedema or function (Moreno-Segura 2026, PMID: 41549735). PROPOSED: SPLIT (adjustable/moderate compression at least as good as high-pressure bandages in week 1; added physiotherapy: the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Mosti 2012: moderate-pressure stockings (23–32 mmHg) shrank chronic leg oedema almost as much as high-pressure inelastic bandages — leg volume down 13.2% versus 15.6% at 7 days, no significant difference
cards.summary: Mosti 2012: moderate-pressure stockings (23–32 mmHg) shrank chronic leg oedema almost as much as high-pressure inelastic bandages — leg volume down 13.2% versus 15.6% at 7 days, no significant difference
cards.people: 42 legs of 30 patients (mean age 72.8 years) with chronic leg oedema caused by venous stasis, randomised to a strong inelastic bandage or an elastic stocking exerting 23–32 mmHg; leg volume measured by water displacement over 7 days.
cards.result: Both treatments significantly reduced leg volume, with no significant difference between them: at 2 days, −9.6% (95% CI 7.5–11.8) with the elastic stocking versus −11.5% (95% CI 9.9–13.2) with the inelastic bandage; at 7 days, −13.2% (95% CI 10.4–16.2) versus −15.6% (95% CI 12.8–18.4). Bandages reduced calf circumference and skin thickness more. Bandage lying pressure fell from 63 to 22 mmHg over 2 days, versus 33 to 26 mmHg under the stocking; the optimal pressure range for oedema reduction was 40–60 mmHg, with higher bandage pressures correlating negatively with volume reduction.
cards.watchOut: Seven days, 30 patients, and legs (not patients) as the unit of analysis — two legs of one person are not independent. This compares two compression devices against each other; the size of compression's effect versus no compression is not measured here, and venous oedema only: cardiac, renal and lymphatic oedema were excluded.
cards.source: Mosti G, Picerni P, Partsch H. Compression stockings with moderate pressure are able to reduce chronic leg oedema. Phlebology. 2012. PMID: 22090466. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Mosti 2015: patient-adjustable Velcro compression devices beat inelastic bandages in the first week of venous leg oedema treatment — median volume reduction 26% versus 19% at day 7 (p < .001)
cards.summary: Mosti 2015: patient-adjustable Velcro compression devices beat inelastic bandages in the first week of venous leg oedema treatment — median volume reduction 26% versus 19% at day 7 (p < .001)
cards.people: 40 legs from 36 patients with untreated venous oedema (CEAP C3), randomised to inelastic bandages (n = 20 legs) or adjustable Velcro compression devices (n = 20 legs), worn day and night and renewed after 1 day.
cards.result: Median percent volume reduction at day 1 was 13% with bandages versus 19% with the adjustable devices; at day 7 it was 19% versus 26% (p < .001). Bandage pressure started higher (63 vs 43 mmHg) but fell by more than 50% over time, while device pressure stayed unchanged because patients readjusted it. The authors concluded re-adjustable devices at around 40 mmHg resting pressure are more effective than bandages at around 60 mmHg in the initial decongestive phase, and are well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: One week of treatment in 36 patients from compression-specialist centres: the device's advantage is plausibly the readjustment behaviour it invites, which may not transfer to unsupervised patients. Again a device-versus-device trial — no untreated arm — in venous oedema only.
cards.source: Mosti G, Cavezzi A, Partsch H, Urso S, Campana F. Adjustable Velcro Compression Devices are More Effective than Inelastic Bandages in Reducing Venous Edema in the Initial Treatment Phase: A Randomized Controlled Trial. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2015. PMID: 26160211. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Moreno-Segura 2026: adding a physiotherapy programme (therapeutic exercise and self-manual lymphatic drainage) to compression-based usual care made no difference to oedema or function in chronic venous insufficiency
cards.summary: Moreno-Segura 2026: adding a physiotherapy programme (therapeutic exercise and self-manual lymphatic drainage) to compression-based usual care made no difference to oedema or function in chronic venous insufficiency
cards.people: Adults with chronic venous insufficiency in primary care, randomised single-blind to a conventional approach (compression stockings and preventive measures) or the same plus a physiotherapist-instructed programme of therapeutic exercise and self-manual lymphatic drainage. N not documented in the record fetched this session.
cards.result: No significant changes were found for the main effect of time or the group-by-time-by-adherence interaction in any variable. Circumferences at 10, 20 and 30 cm from the heel in both legs, and the 6-Minute Walking Test, showed a significant main effect for time in the conventional-approach group with high adherence. The authors concluded a multicomponent physiotherapy-plus-medicine approach does not appear better than the conventional approach for improving functionality and oedema in chronic venous insufficiency.
cards.watchOut: Without the sample size and numbers, this card can carry only the trial's qualitative conclusion; an underpowered null and a precise null look identical at this level of reporting. The adherence-stratified positive finding is a subgroup observation, not the randomised comparison.
cards.source: Moreno-Segura N, et al. The effects of adding physiotherapy to compression therapy on function and oedema in chronic venous insufficiency. Vasa. 2026. PMID: 41549735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for swollen legs from venous disease, compression is the treatment — the open questions are which device, and the trials say simpler and adjustable beat stronger and static in the first week
cards.summary: Synthesis: for swollen legs from venous disease, compression is the treatment — the open questions are which device, and the trials say simpler and adjustable beat stronger and static in the first week
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded randomised trials (30, 36 and an undocumented number of patients), all in chronic venous leg oedema.
cards.result: All three trials compare ways of delivering compression or care around it; none includes a no-compression arm, because compression is the accepted base treatment. Within that frame: moderate-pressure stockings matched high-pressure bandages at 7 days (−13.2% vs −15.6% leg volume, not significant); self-adjustable Velcro devices beat bandages over the same week (26% vs 19% median volume reduction) because their pressure does not decay; and adding supervised physiotherapy and self-drainage to compression changed nothing. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (compression devices: adjustable and moderate-pressure options at least as good as high-pressure bandages in week 1 · added physiotherapy: the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Scope limit: every carded trial is venous oedema. Swollen ankles and legs from heart failure, kidney or liver disease, calcium-channel blockers or lymphatic failure are different problems with different treatments — diuretics, drug withdrawal, decongestive therapy — and this shelf's compression results must not be read across to them. New one-sided swelling, breathlessness or rapid onset needs diagnosis first, not a stocking.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mosti 2012 (PMID: 22090466), Mosti 2015 (PMID: 26160211) and Moreno-Segura 2026 (PMID: 41549735), carded above.

shelves.title: Von Willebrand disease: for heavy periods, tranexamic acid beat recombinant VWF (blood-loss score 146 vs 213) and desmopressin in randomised trials; for severe frequent bleeding, VWF concentrate prophylaxis cut bleeds by 84% in a single-arm study
shelves.question: In people with von Willebrand disease, what works for heavy menstrual bleeding, and does regular von Willebrand factor concentrate prophylaxis prevent bleeds in severe disease?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Factor VIII/adverse effects · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · von Willebrand Diseases/drug therapy · von Willebrand Factor/adverse effects
shelves.balance: Treatment splits by problem. For heavy menstrual bleeding, the randomised VWDMin trial (Ragni 2023, PMID: 37385272; NCT02606045; 39 women enrolled, 36 completing, with mild or moderate VWD) found recombinant VWF was NOT superior to tranexamic acid: median pictorial blood-loss (PBAC) score after two cycles was 146 (95% CI 117-199) on tranexamic acid versus 213 (152-298) on recombinant VWF (adjusted mean difference 46, 95% CI 2-90; P=0.039), and neither treatment brought scores into the normal range (the primary endpoint was not met; the trial stopped early for slow recruitment). An earlier crossover RCT in women with menorrhagia and abnormal laboratory haemostasis (Kouides 2009, PMID: 19236375; 116 women) likewise found tranexamic acid reduced PBAC scores more than intranasal desmopressin (estimated fall -105.7 vs -64.1; difference 41.6, P=0.0002), with both improving quality of life. For frequent severe bleeding, the prospective WIL-31 study (Sidonio 2024, PMID: 38237075; NCT04052698; 33 patients aged 6+, two-thirds type 3) found plasma-derived VWF/FVIII concentrate prophylaxis (the tested product was wilate, Octapharma) cut the mean total annualised bleeding rate by 84.4% versus the patients' own prior on-demand period (to 5.2 bleeds/year) and spontaneous bleeding by 86.9%, with no treatment-related serious adverse events or thromboses — but there was no parallel control group. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — tranexamic acid ahead of both recombinant VWF and desmopressin for heavy menstrual bleeding on randomised evidence (POSSIBLE); concentrate prophylaxis strongly positive but single-arm (POSSIBLE, capped).

cards.headline: Ragni 2023 (VWDMin): recombinant VWF was not superior to tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding — PBAC 213 versus 146 after two cycles
cards.summary: Ragni 2023 (VWDMin): recombinant VWF was not superior to tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding — PBAC 213 versus 146 after two cycles
cards.people: Female patients aged 13-45 years with mild or moderate von Willebrand disease (VWF ristocetin cofactor <0.50 IU/mL) and heavy menstrual bleeding (PBAC score >100 in one of the past two cycles) at 13 US haemophilia treatment centres; 39 enrolled, 36 completed a randomised crossover of two cycles each of intravenous recombinant VWF 40 IU/kg on day 1 (the tested product was vonicog alfa, Vonvendi) and oral tranexamic acid 1300 mg three times daily on days 1-5.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (a 40-point PBAC reduction by day 5 after two cycles) was not met, and neither treatment corrected PBAC scores to the normal range. Median PBAC score was significantly lower after tranexamic acid than after recombinant VWF (146 [95% CI 117-199] vs 213 [152-298]; adjusted mean treatment difference 46 [95% CI 2-90]; P=0.039). Median follow-up was 23.97 weeks. The trial was stopped early, on 15 February 2022, at the data safety monitoring board's request because of slow recruitment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, stopped early and analysed as an unplanned interim analysis of only 36 completers; it applies to mild/moderate disease only, and both treatments left PBAC scores above the heavy-bleeding threshold of 100 — tranexamic acid was less ineffective, not curative.
cards.source: Ragni MV, Rothenberger SD, Feldman R, et al. Recombinant von Willebrand factor and tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding in patients with mild and moderate von Willebrand disease in the USA (VWDMin): a phase 3, open-label, randomised, crossover trial. The Lancet Haematology. 2023. PMID: 37385272. Registry ID: NCT02606045. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Kouides 2009: tranexamic acid cut menstrual blood-loss scores more than intranasal desmopressin (fall of 105.7 versus 64.1 PBAC points)
cards.summary: Kouides 2009: tranexamic acid cut menstrual blood-loss scores more than intranasal desmopressin (fall of 105.7 versus 64.1 PBAC points)
cards.people: 116 women with menorrhagia (PBAC score >100), a negative gynaecological evaluation and abnormal laboratory haemostasis, randomised in a crossover design to intranasal desmopressin or oral tranexamic acid for two menstrual cycles each, then crossing over.
cards.result: Both treatments significantly decreased PBAC scores: the estimated decrease from baseline was -105.7 (95% CI -130.5 to -81.0) for tranexamic acid and -64.1 (95% CI -88.0 to -40.3) for intranasal desmopressin; the decrease was greater with tranexamic acid by 41.6 points (95% CI 19.6 to 63.6; P=0.0002). Both medications improved quality of life on all four instruments used.
cards.watchOut: The population was women with abnormal laboratory haemostasis, not confirmed von Willebrand disease in every case, so it supports the VWD conclusion indirectly; there was no placebo or untreated arm, so the absolute falls include cycle-to-cycle variation.
cards.source: Kouides PA, Byams VR, Philipp CS, et al. Multisite management study of menorrhagia with abnormal laboratory haemostasis: a prospective crossover study of intranasal desmopressin and oral tranexamic acid. British Journal of Haematology. 2009. PMID: 19236375. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Sidonio 2024 (WIL-31): VWF/FVIII concentrate prophylaxis cut total bleeding by 84.4% versus patients' own on-demand period — single-arm
cards.summary: Sidonio 2024 (WIL-31): VWF/FVIII concentrate prophylaxis cut total bleeding by 84.4% versus patients' own on-demand period — single-arm
cards.type: Prospective single-arm phase 3 trial with intra-individual on-demand comparator (Sidonio 2024)
cards.people: 33 patients aged 6 years or older with severe von Willebrand disease (18% severe type 1, 15% type 2, 67% type 3; median age 18 years) who had completed a 6-month prospective on-demand run-in study (WIL-29), then received 12 months of prophylaxis with the plasma-derived VWF/FVIII concentrate wilate (Octapharma), 20-40 IU/kg two to three times weekly.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: mean total annualised bleeding rate on prophylaxis was 5.2, an 84.4% reduction versus prior on-demand treatment; mean spontaneous annualised bleeding rate was 3.2, an 86.9% reduction. Ten patients (30.3%) had no bleeding events and 15 (45.5%) had no spontaneous bleeds during prophylaxis; of 173 bleeding events, 84.4% were minor. No serious adverse events related to treatment and no thrombotic events were recorded.
cards.watchOut: No parallel control group: the comparison is with each patient's own preceding 6 months, so regression to the mean and study attention can inflate the reduction; only 33 patients, and the tested product is named because concentrate products are not interchangeable by assumption.
cards.source: Sidonio RF Jr, Boban A, Dubey L, et al. von Willebrand factor/factor VIII concentrate (Wilate) prophylaxis in children and adults with von Willebrand disease. Blood Advances. 2024. PMID: 38237075. Registry ID: NCT04052698 (run-in study WIL-29: NCT04053699). cards.headline: Synthesis: for heavy periods, cheap oral tranexamic acid beat both recombinant VWF and desmopressin in randomised crossovers; for frequent severe bleeds, concentrate prophylaxis looks highly effective but is untested against a control group
cards.summary: Synthesis: for heavy periods, cheap oral tranexamic acid beat both recombinant VWF and desmopressin in randomised crossovers; for frequent severe bleeds, concentrate prophylaxis looks highly effective but is untested against a control group
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: two randomised crossover trials (36 and 116 women) and one single-arm prospective prophylaxis trial (33 patients).
cards.result: Menstrual bleeding: tranexamic acid gave lower blood-loss scores than recombinant VWF (median PBAC 146 vs 213) and than intranasal desmopressin (score fall 105.7 vs 64.1 points), though no treatment normalised blood loss in VWDMin. Bleeding prophylaxis: VWF/FVIII concentrate prophylaxis was associated with an 84.4% lower total bleeding rate than prior on-demand care. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (menstrual: POSSIBLE benefit, tranexamic acid first among the tested options · prophylaxis: POSSIBLE, capped by the single-arm design).
cards.watchOut: Severe type 3 disease, surgery cover and desmopressin test-dose responses are not directly addressed by any carded record; VWDMin covers mild/moderate disease only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ragni 2023 (PMID: 37385272), Kouides 2009 (PMID: 19236375) and Sidonio 2024 (PMID: 38237075), carded above.
