shelves.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White: in asymptomatic patients with high-risk pathways, prophylactic ablation cut arrhythmic events from 60% to 5% over 5 years (relative risk 0.08) in the randomised trial, and no ablated patient in a 2,169-patient registry developed ventricular fibrillation
shelves.question: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, does catheter ablation help — in particular, should asymptomatic patients at high risk of arrhythmia have prophylactic ablation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Catheter Ablation · Electrocardiography · Electrophysiologic Techniques, Cardiac · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Assessment · Survival Analysis · Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome/diagnosis · Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome/physiopathology · Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome/therapy
shelves.balance: For symptomatic WPW, catheter ablation is the established definitive treatment; the trial evidence addresses the harder question of prophylactic ablation in asymptomatic people found to be at high risk on electrophysiological testing. In Pappone 2003 (PMID: 14602878; 72 high-risk asymptomatic patients randomised from 224 eligible), arrhythmic events over 5 years occurred in 2 of 37 ablated patients (5%) versus 21 of 35 controls (60%); the 5-year Kaplan-Meier incidence was 7% versus 77% (relative risk 0.08, 95% CI 0.02-0.33; P<0.001), and one control patient presented with ventricular fibrillation. The paediatric trial (Pappone 2004, PMID: 15371577) found the same pattern in high-risk children aged 5-12: events in 1 of 20 ablated (5%) versus 12 of 27 controls (44%), with two control children suffering ventricular fibrillation and one sudden death; three ablation complications occurred, one needing hospitalisation. The group's 8-year registry (Pappone 2014, PMID: 25052405; 2,169 patients) found ablation successful in 98.5%, no malignant arrhythmia or ventricular fibrillation after ablation, and ventricular fibrillation in 1.5% of untreated patients — almost all children — predicted by a short accessory-pathway refractory period rather than by symptoms. All of this comes from one Milan group, the trials are small, and the endpoint is arrhythmic events, not mortality. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for prophylactic ablation in asymptomatic patients with high-risk electrophysiological features; no randomised evidence supports ablating low-risk asymptomatic patients.

cards.headline: Pappone 2003: prophylactic ablation cut 5-year arrhythmic events to 7% versus 77% without treatment (relative risk 0.08) in high-risk asymptomatic adults
cards.summary: Pappone 2003: prophylactic ablation cut 5-year arrhythmic events to 7% versus 77% without treatment (relative risk 0.08) in high-risk asymptomatic adults
cards.people: Asymptomatic patients with a Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern identified as high risk for arrhythmias (young age and inducible atrioventricular reciprocating tachycardia or atrial fibrillation at electrophysiological testing), randomised from 224 eligible patients in 1997-2002 to radiofrequency catheter ablation (n=37) or no treatment (n=35); endpoint was arrhythmic events over 5 years.
cards.result: Arrhythmic events occurred in 2 patients in the ablation group (5 percent) and 21 in the control group (60 percent); one control patient had ventricular fibrillation as the presenting arrhythmia. Five-year Kaplan-Meier estimates of arrhythmic-event incidence were 7 percent with ablation versus 77 percent in controls (P<0.001); the relative risk with ablation was 0.08 (95 percent confidence interval 0.02 to 0.33; P<0.001) — a 92% relative risk reduction, against absolute event rates of 5% versus 60% as counted in the record.
cards.watchOut: Only 72 randomised patients from a single centre, selected for high-risk features; the endpoint was any arrhythmic event, mostly tachycardias, not death — just one control patient had ventricular fibrillation, so the trial cannot show a mortality benefit.
cards.source: Pappone C, Santinelli V, Manguso F, et al. A randomized study of prophylactic catheter ablation in asymptomatic patients with the Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. New England Journal of Medicine. 2003. PMID: 14602878. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pappone 2004: in high-risk asymptomatic children, events occurred in 1 of 20 ablated (5%) versus 12 of 27 untreated (44%) — with two ventricular fibrillations and one sudden death among controls
cards.summary: Pappone 2004: in high-risk asymptomatic children, events occurred in 1 of 20 ablated (5%) versus 12 of 27 untreated (44%) — with two ventricular fibrillations and one sudden death among controls
cards.people: Asymptomatic children aged 5-12 years with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome at high risk for arrhythmias: of 165 eligible children, 60 were high risk; after 13 post-randomisation parental withdrawals, 20 underwent prophylactic radiofrequency ablation and 27 received no treatment.
cards.result: During follow-up, 1 child in the ablation group (5 percent) and 12 in the control group (44 percent) had arrhythmic events. Two control children had ventricular fibrillation and one died suddenly. The lower cumulative event rate with ablation remained significant after adjustment in a Cox regression analysis; independent predictors of events were absence of prophylactic ablation and multiple accessory pathways. Three ablation-related complications occurred, one of which led to hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Very small (47 analysed children) and 13 of 60 randomised children were withdrawn by parents before treatment, which can unbalance the groups; from the same single Milan centre as the adult trial.
cards.source: Pappone C, Manguso F, Santinelli R, et al. Radiofrequency ablation in children with asymptomatic Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15371577. cards.headline: Pappone 2014 (registry, 2,169 patients): ablation succeeded in 98.5% and no ablated patient developed ventricular fibrillation over 8 years, versus 1.5% of untreated patients
cards.summary: Pappone 2014 (registry, 2,169 patients): ablation succeeded in 98.5% and no ablated patient developed ventricular fibrillation over 8 years, versus 1.5% of untreated patients
cards.people: 2,169 symptomatic or asymptomatic Wolff-Parkinson-White patients referred for evaluation or ablation over 8 years, all with baseline electrophysiological testing: 1,168 underwent radiofrequency ablation (206 asymptomatic) and 1,001 did not (550 asymptomatic).
cards.result: Ablation was successful in 98.5% of the ablation group, and after ablation no patient developed malignant arrhythmias or ventricular fibrillation over the 8-year follow-up. In the untreated group, ventricular fibrillation occurred in 1.5% of patients, virtually exclusively (13 of 15) in children (median age 11 years), and was associated with a short accessory-pathway antegrade refractory period (P<0.001) and atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia initiating atrial fibrillation (P<0.001), but not with symptoms. Untreated patients were more likely to experience malignant arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation (log-rank P<0.001); the optimal refractory-period cutoff for predicting ventricular fibrillation was 240 milliseconds.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: patients who were ablated differed from those who were not (notably by symptoms), so the zero event rate after ablation is supportive, not proof; again a single-centre programme.
cards.source: Pappone C, Vicedomini G, Manguso F, et al. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome in the era of catheter ablation: insights from a registry study of 2169 patients. Circulation. 2014. PMID: 25052405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in asymptomatic WPW with high-risk electrical features, prophylactic ablation prevents most arrhythmic events in two small randomised trials; risk is set by the pathway's properties, not by symptoms
cards.summary: Synthesis: in asymptomatic WPW with high-risk electrical features, prophylactic ablation prevents most arrhythmic events in two small randomised trials; risk is set by the pathway's properties, not by symptoms
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: two small randomised trials (72 adults/young patients and 47 children) and one 2,169-patient prospective registry, all from one Milan programme.
cards.result: Ablation reduced arrhythmic events from 60% to 5% (adults, 5 years; relative risk 0.08) and from 44% to 5% (children); the registry found 98.5% ablation success, no post-ablation ventricular fibrillation, and a 1.5% ventricular fibrillation rate without ablation, concentrated in children with short pathway refractory periods. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for prophylactic ablation in high-risk asymptomatic patients — large effects, but small single-centre trials with arrhythmia, not mortality, as the endpoint.
cards.watchOut: No carded evidence covers drug treatment of acute pre-excited atrial fibrillation, ablation in symptomatic patients versus drugs, or ablation of low-risk asymptomatic patients; the shelf's claim is confined to prophylactic ablation in electrophysiologically high-risk asymptomatic patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pappone 2003 (PMID: 14602878), Pappone 2004 (PMID: 15371577) and Pappone 2014 (PMID: 25052405), carded above.

shelves.title: Loneliness and social isolation track with heart disease and stroke in the global longitudinal data — 29% relative higher risk of incident coronary heart disease (RR 1.29) and 32% relative higher risk of stroke (RR 1.32) — but an Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis found no association, and all evidence is observational
shelves.question: In adults, are loneliness and social isolation associated with incident coronary heart disease and stroke?
shelves.mesh: Bias; Coronary Disease/*etiology/psychology; Humans; Loneliness; Observational Studies as Topic; Risk Factors; Social Isolation; Stroke/*etiology/psychology
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. The disease-specific meta-analysis (Valtorta 2016; 16 longitudinal datasets, 4,628 coronary heart disease and 3,002 stroke events, follow-up 3–21 years) found poor social relationships associated with a pooled relative risk of 1.29 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) for incident coronary heart disease and 1.32 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68) for stroke (PMID: 27091846). The foundational 1988 Science review reached the same qualitative conclusion from prospective and experimental work (PMID: 3399889). Against that, a 2022 Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis of 3 longitudinal datasets (2,137 coronary and 590 stroke events) found no association in fully adjusted models and judged its own evidence inconclusive (PMID: 35263481). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, with a printed regional discordance.

cards.headline: Valtorta 2016: poor social relationships were associated with a 29% relative increase in incident coronary heart disease (pooled RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) and a 32% relative increase in stroke (pooled RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.68)
cards.summary: Valtorta 2016: poor social relationships were associated with a 29% relative increase in incident coronary heart disease (pooled RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) and a 32% relative increase in stroke (pooled RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.68)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies (Valtorta 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies in high-income countries published to May 2015: 23 papers from 16 longitudinal datasets, with 4,628 coronary heart disease events and 3,002 stroke events over follow-up of 3 to 21 years; 11 coronary and 8 stroke studies contributed to the meta-analysis.
cards.result: Poor social relationships (loneliness or social isolation) were associated with incident coronary heart disease at pooled relative risk 1.29 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) and incident stroke at pooled relative risk 1.32 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68) — both relative measures. Subgroup analyses found no differences by gender. The authors called for trials of whether targeting loneliness and isolation can prevent cardiovascular disease.
cards.watchOut: Observational only: both confidence intervals sit just above 1.0, definitions of loneliness/isolation varied across cohorts, and residual confounding (depression, socioeconomic position, smoking) is likely. No absolute event rates are pooled in the record.
cards.source: Valtorta NK, Kanaan M, Gilbody S, Ronzi S, Hanratty B. Heart. 2016. PMID: 27091846. Registry ID: CRD42014010225 (PROSPERO registration printed in the record). cards.headline: House 1988 (Science review): prospective studies consistently showed increased risk of death among people with few or low-quality social relationships, and experimental and quasi-experimental work pointed the same way
cards.summary: House 1988 (Science review): prospective studies consistently showed increased risk of death among people with few or low-quality social relationships, and experimental and quasi-experimental work pointed the same way
cards.people: Foundational narrative review of the theoretical and empirical literature on social relationships and health, including prospective studies controlling for baseline health status and experimental/quasi-experimental studies in humans and animals. N not documented as a single pooled sample in the record.
cards.result: The review concluded that prospective studies consistently show increased risk of death among persons with a low quantity, and sometimes low quality, of social relationships, and that experimental and quasi-experimental studies also suggest social isolation is a major risk factor for mortality from widely varying causes. It reported no single pooled effect size; mechanisms were stated to remain unexplored.
cards.watchOut: A 1988 narrative review with no meta-analytic numbers — carded as the field's founding synthesis, not as quantitative proof. Its mortality (not specifically coronary/stroke incidence) framing is broader than this shelf's question.

cards.headline: Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis 2022: in 3 longitudinal datasets (2,137 coronary and 590 stroke events) social isolation, lack of support and loneliness showed no association with cardiovascular incidence in fully adjusted models — the authors called their review inconclusive
cards.summary: Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis 2022: in 3 longitudinal datasets (2,137 coronary and 590 stroke events) social isolation, lack of support and loneliness showed no association with cardiovascular incidence in fully adjusted models — the authors called their review inconclusive
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies (Freak-Poli 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies from Australia and New Zealand published to June 2020: 5 papers from 3 longitudinal datasets, 2,137 coronary heart disease and 590 stroke events over 3 to 16 years of follow-up; only 2 coronary and 2 stroke outcomes were suitable for meta-analysis.
cards.result: The included papers reported no association between social health (social isolation, lack of social support, or loneliness) and incidence of cardiovascular disease in all fully adjusted models and most unadjusted models. The authors concluded the review was inconclusive — few studies, heavy reliance on self-reported cardiovascular disease — and called for studies using medical diagnoses.
cards.watchOut: A small regional evidence base (3 datasets) with self-reported outcomes — its null does not overturn the larger global pooling, but it is a genuine discordance and is printed on the face of this shelf rather than hidden.

shelves.title: Pet ownership and mortality (observational only): dog ownership was associated with a relative risk of death of 0.76 in a meta-analysis of 3.8 million people, but one meta-analysis found no significant dog-specific association — an association, not proof that getting a pet extends life
shelves.question: Is pet (especially dog) ownership associated with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Animals · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cats · Dogs · Health Status · Heart Disease Risk Factors · Human-Animal Bond · Humans · Ownership · Pets · Prognosis · Protective Factors · Quality of Life · Risk Assessment · Risk Reduction Behavior
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only; this face says so because no randomised evidence exists or could readily exist for pet ownership. A meta-analysis of dog ownership (PMID: 31592726; 10 studies, 3,837,005 participants) found dog ownership associated with a relative risk of 0.76 for all-cause mortality and 0.69 for cardiovascular death (relative measures; absolute rates were not reported in the fetched record). A nationwide Swedish cohort of 3,432,153 people (PMID: 29150678) found lower death and cardiovascular-death hazard ratios in dog owners, strongest in single-person households — but its twin subcohort could not replicate the reduced risk. A broader pet-ownership meta-analysis (PMID: 31815850; 26 studies) found lower cardiovascular mortality in pet owners overall (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81) yet no significant association for dog owners specifically on overall or cardiovascular mortality — a discordance printed here, not smoothed over. Healthy-owner and socioeconomic confounding remain plausible explanations for all of it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), association only.

cards.headline: El-Qushayri 2020: pet owners had lower cardiovascular mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81), but dog owners specifically showed no significant association with overall or cardiovascular mortality in this meta-analysis
cards.summary: El-Qushayri 2020: pet owners had lower cardiovascular mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81), but dog owners specifically showed no significant association with overall or cardiovascular mortality in this meta-analysis
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (El-Qushayri 2020)
cards.people: 26 studies of pet ownership and cardiovascular events and mortality, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis; hazard ratios are relative measures, and absolute mortality rates were not reported in the fetched record.
cards.result: Higher survival was observed in pet owners after pooling non-adjusted and adjusted hazard ratios for cardiovascular mortality: 0.73 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.86) and 0.81 (0.68 to 0.97) respectively (relative measures). For overall mortality the non-adjusted pooled hazard ratio was 0.73 (0.62 to 0.87) but the adjusted hazard ratio was 0.40 (0.04 to 3.78), not significant. Cat owners had a reduction in cardiovascular mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.79; 0.63 to 0.99) but not overall mortality (1.04; 0.90 to 1.21). No significant association between dog owners and survival was observed for overall or cardiovascular-specific mortality. Pet owners also had lower heart rate, mean arterial pressure and systolic blood pressure, with no difference in diastolic pressure or hypertension prevalence.
cards.watchOut: Observational pooling with discordant adjusted results — the all-cause adjusted estimate (0.40) has a confidence interval running from 0.04 to 3.78, and the dog-specific null in this analysis directly tempers the dog-focused card next to it.

cards.headline: Kramer 2019: dog ownership was associated with a 24% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.76) and a 31% relative reduction in cardiovascular death (relative risk 0.69) across 3.8 million participants
cards.summary: Kramer 2019: dog ownership was associated with a 24% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.76) and a 31% relative reduction in cardiovascular death (relative risk 0.69) across 3.8 million participants
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Kramer 2019)
cards.people: 10 observational studies published 1950 to May 2019, yielding data from 3,837,005 participants (530,515 events; mean follow-up 10.1 years); relative risks are relative measures, and absolute mortality rates were not reported in the fetched record. The review was registered on PROSPERO as CRD42018111048, as printed in the record.
cards.result: Dog ownership was associated with a relative risk of 0.76 for all-cause mortality versus non-ownership (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86) — a 24% relative risk reduction — with 6 studies showing a significant reduction. In individuals with prior coronary events, the relative risk for all-cause mortality was 0.35 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.69). For cardiovascular mortality, dog ownership conferred a relative risk of 0.69 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.71) — a 31% relative risk reduction. The authors note a possible limitation was that the analyses were not adjusted for confounders.
cards.watchOut: Unadjusted pooling of observational studies: people who own dogs differ from non-owners in health, income, housing and activity before any dog effect, and the striking 0.35 relative risk after coronary events comes from few studies with wide intervals.
cards.source: Kramer CK et al. Dog Ownership and Survival: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes. 2019. PMID: 31592726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mubanga 2017: in a Swedish nationwide cohort of 3.4 million, dog owners in single-person households had a death hazard ratio of 0.67 — but the twin subcohort could not replicate the reduced risk
cards.summary: Mubanga 2017: in a Swedish nationwide cohort of 3.4 million, dog owners in single-person households had a death hazard ratio of 0.67 — but the twin subcohort could not replicate the reduced risk
cards.people: A register-based prospective nationwide cohort of 3,432,153 people followed for up to 12 years (dog ownership 13.1%), with self-reported health and lifestyle data available for 34,202 participants in the Swedish Twin Register; hazard ratios are relative measures, and absolute rates were not reported in the fetched record.
cards.result: In single-person households, dog ownership was associated with lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.65 to 0.69) and cardiovascular death (0.64; 0.59 to 0.70); in multiple-person households the corresponding hazard ratios were 0.89 (0.87 to 0.91) and 0.85 (0.81 to 0.90). In single-person households dog ownership was also inversely associated with a composite cardiovascular outcome (0.92; 0.89 to 0.94), and hunting-breed ownership was associated with the lowest cardiovascular risk. Further analysis in the Twin Register could not replicate the reduced risk of cardiovascular disease or death, while also giving no indication of confounding by disability, comorbidities or lifestyle factors.
cards.watchOut: Register data cannot capture why people acquire dogs: healthier, more active people may both get dogs and live longer (reverse causation), and the non-replication in the twin subcohort — the part of the study best able to probe shared confounding — is printed on this card deliberately.
cards.source: Mubanga M et al. Dog ownership and the risk of cardiovascular disease and death - a nationwide cohort study. Scientific Reports. 2017. PMID: 29150678. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pet and dog ownership are associated with lower mortality in observational data, with relative risks around 0.7 to 0.8 — but confounding is uncontrolled, one meta-analysis is dog-null, and causation is not established
cards.summary: Synthesis: pet and dog ownership are associated with lower mortality in observational data, with relative risks around 0.7 to 0.8 — but confounding is uncontrolled, one meta-analysis is dog-null, and causation is not established
cards.people: The carded evidence: two observational meta-analyses (26 studies; and 10 studies with 3,837,005 participants) and one nationwide cohort of 3,432,153 people. No randomised evidence exists on this shelf.
cards.result: Dog ownership was associated with relative risks of 0.76 (all-cause) and 0.69 (cardiovascular death) in one meta-analysis (Kramer 2019), and with hazard ratios of 0.67 to 0.89 depending on household type in the Swedish cohort (Mubanga 2017). Against that, the broader pet meta-analysis found no significant dog-specific association (El-Qushayri 2020), and the Swedish twin subcohort did not replicate the cohort finding. All measures carded are relative; absolute mortality rates were not reported in the fetched records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational-only cap; an association to describe, never a reason to prescribe a pet.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here separates the dog from the life around the dog — walking, routine, companionship, income and baseline health all travel with ownership, and none of the carded studies randomised any of them.
cards.source: Synthesis of El-Qushayri AE et al. Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 31815850); Kramer CK et al. Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes. 2019 (PMID: 31592726); Mubanga M et al. Scientific Reports. 2017 (PMID: 29150678).

shelves.title: Dependent oedema and evening ankle swelling (visitor ask): calcium-channel blockers cause it in about 1 in 10 users (amlodipine 16.6% vs 6.2% on placebo), and reviewing the blocker — lower dose, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent — reduces it; compression evidence is homed at pack #5420
shelves.question: In adults whose ankles swell by the evening, what causes dependent oedema, and does anything help — leg elevation, compression stockings, or reviewing a calcium-channel blocker such as amlodipine?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Calcium Channel Blockers · Edema · Humans · Placebos · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the cause and the remedy point in different directions on this shelf. As a cause, calcium-channel blockers are established culprits: across 106 randomised trials (99,469 participants), peripheral oedema occurred in 10.7% on a calcium-channel blocker versus 3.2% on control/placebo, rising with dose and duration (Makani 2011, PMID: 21558959), and for amlodipine specifically the rate was 16.6% versus 6.2% on placebo (relative risk 2.9), although about 37% of oedema cases on amlodipine were estimated unrelated to the drug (Vukadinović 2019, PMID: 31107359). As a remedy, three randomised-trial meta-analyses agree that reviewing the blocker helps: adding a renin–angiotensin system blocker cut oedema incidence by 38% relative (RR 0.62; Makani 2011, PMID: 21295192), lower doses carried lower risk, and switching to a lipophilic dihydropyridine such as lercanidipine carried a relative risk of 0.44 versus first-generation agents (Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009, PMID: 19808126). Compression stockings for venous leg oedema are homed at pack #5420 and are NOT re-carded here; no trial evidence for leg elevation alone was carded on this shelf, and other causes of evening ankle swelling (venous insufficiency, heart failure, kidney or liver disease, other drugs) are separate questions. PROPOSED SPLIT (calcium-channel blockers a common, dose-dependent cause — harm; dose reduction, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent reduces it — benefit).

cards.headline: Makani 2011: across 106 randomised trials, peripheral oedema affected 10.7% on calcium-channel blockers versus 3.2% on control — dose- and duration-dependent, reaching 24% after 6 months
cards.summary: Makani 2011: across 106 randomised trials, peripheral oedema affected 10.7% on calcium-channel blockers versus 3.2% on control — dose- and duration-dependent, reaching 24% after 6 months
cards.people: 106 randomised trials with 99,469 participants (mean age 56 years), each enrolling at least 100 patients in the calcium-channel-blocker arm and lasting at least 4 weeks, in patients with hypertension.
cards.result: The weighted incidence of peripheral oedema was 10.7% with calcium-channel blockers versus 3.2% with controls/placebo (P < 0.0001), and withdrawal due to oedema was 2.1% versus 0.5%. Incidence and withdrawal rose with duration of therapy, reaching 24% and 5% respectively after 6 months. Oedema was more frequent with dihydropyridines (12.3%) than non-dihydropyridines (3.1%), with high-dose blockers (16.1%) than low-dose (5.7%, a 2.8-fold difference), and was 57% relatively lower with lipophilic dihydropyridines than traditional dihydropyridines (relative risk 0.43; 95% CI 0.34–0.53).
cards.watchOut: Pooled trial adverse-event reporting: oedema was a side-effect entry, not a primary outcome, in most included trials, and definitions varied — the percentages describe trial populations on these drugs, not an individual patient's personal risk.
cards.source: Makani H et al. Peripheral edema associated with calcium channel blockers: incidence and withdrawal rate--a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Journal of Hypertension. 2011. cards.headline: Vukadinović 2019: amlodipine tripled oedema versus placebo (16.6% vs 6.2%; RR 2.9) — but an estimated 37% of oedema on amlodipine was not caused by the drug, and lower doses carried lower risk
cards.summary: Vukadinović 2019: amlodipine tripled oedema versus placebo (16.6% vs 6.2%; RR 2.9) — but an estimated 37% of oedema on amlodipine was not caused by the drug, and lower doses carried lower risk
cards.people: 22 randomised, placebo-controlled trials with 7,226 patients with arterial hypertension or stable coronary artery disease treated with amlodipine.
cards.result: Oedema rate was 16.6% on amlodipine versus 6.2% on placebo (risk ratio 2.9; 95% CI 2.50–3.36; P < 0.0001). The placebo-adjusted rate was 63%, indicating 37% of oedema cases on amlodipine were unrelated to amlodipine. Low/medium doses (2.5–5 mg) carried a lower oedema risk ratio (2.01; 95% CI 1.41–2.88) than the high dose of 10 mg (3.08; 95% CI 2.62–3.60; P for interaction = 0.03). Headache was less frequent on amlodipine than placebo (7.9% vs 10.9%).
cards.watchOut: The 37%-unrelated estimate cuts both ways: stopping amlodipine will not cure every swollen ankle, and evening swelling that persists off the drug needs its own work-up rather than reassurance.

cards.headline: Makani 2011: adding a renin–angiotensin blocker to a calcium-channel blocker cut oedema incidence by 38% relative (RR 0.62) and withdrawal for oedema by 62% relative (RR 0.38) across 25 trials
cards.summary: Makani 2011: adding a renin–angiotensin blocker to a calcium-channel blocker cut oedema incidence by 38% relative (RR 0.62) and withdrawal for oedema by 62% relative (RR 0.38) across 25 trials
cards.people: 25 prospective randomised controlled trials with 17,206 patients with hypertension (mean age 56 years, 55% men; mean duration 9.2 weeks) comparing calcium-channel blocker monotherapy with blocker plus renin–angiotensin system blocker combination.
cards.result: Peripheral oedema incidence was 38% relatively lower with the combination than with blocker monotherapy (relative risk 0.62; 95% CI 0.53–0.74; P < .00001), and withdrawal due to oedema was 62% relatively lower (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.22–0.66; P = .002). On indirect comparison, ACE inhibitors appeared more efficacious than ARBs in reducing oedema (ratio of RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.64–0.84), but the authors state head-to-head studies are needed to prove this.
cards.watchOut: Short trials (mean 9.2 weeks) in hypertension populations, and the ACE-inhibitor-versus-ARB difference is an indirect comparison across trials, not a randomised head-to-head — treat it as a hint, not a verdict.
cards.source: Makani H et al. Effect of renin-angiotensin system blockade on calcium channel blocker-associated peripheral edema. The American Journal of Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21295192. cards.headline: Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009: switching to lercanidipine halved oedema versus first-generation dihydropyridines (RR 0.44; 52/742 vs 88/627) with no loss of blood-pressure effect
cards.summary: Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009: switching to lercanidipine halved oedema versus first-generation dihydropyridines (RR 0.44; 52/742 vs 88/627) with no loss of blood-pressure effect
cards.people: 8 randomised controlled trials of at least 4 weeks comparing lercanidipine with other dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers in mild-to-moderate hypertension (6 trials against first-generation agents — amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine; 4 against second-generation lipophilic agents).
cards.result: Blood-pressure lowering did not differ between lercanidipine and either generation. Versus first-generation agents, lercanidipine carried a lower risk of peripheral oedema (52/742 vs 88/627; RR 0.44; 95% CI 0.31–0.62) and of withdrawal because of oedema (RR 0.24; 95% CI 0.12–0.47), with no difference in flushing or headache. Versus second-generation lipophilic agents, oedema frequency did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Only 8 trials, searched to 2008, and the advantage is specifically against the older first-generation agents — it does not show lercanidipine beats other modern lipophilic blockers, and lercanidipine is not marketed in every country.
cards.source: Makarounas-Kirchmann K et al. Results of a meta-analysis comparing the tolerability of lercanidipine and other dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19808126. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: evening ankle swelling in a patient on a calcium-channel blocker is commonly the drug — dose-dependent and often fixable by dose reduction, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent; compression evidence lives at pack #5420
cards.summary: Synthesis: evening ankle swelling in a patient on a calcium-channel blocker is commonly the drug — dose-dependent and often fixable by dose reduction, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent; compression evidence lives at pack #5420
cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses of randomised trials (106 trials/99,469 participants; 22 placebo-controlled amlodipine trials/7,226 patients; 25 combination-therapy trials/17,206 patients) and one head-to-head tolerability meta-analysis (8 trials). No compression or leg-elevation trial is carded here.
cards.result: Calcium-channel blockers cause peripheral oedema in roughly 1 in 10 treated patients versus 3 in 100 on control, more at higher doses and with longer use (Makani 2011); for amlodipine the relative risk versus placebo was 2.9, with about a third of cases estimated unrelated to the drug (Vukadinović 2019). Adding a renin–angiotensin blocker reduced oedema by 38% relative (Makani 2011), and switching to a lipophilic agent such as lercanidipine reduced it versus first-generation agents (RR 0.44; Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009). Compression for chronic venous leg oedema is homed at pack #5420 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT (cause: harm; reviewing the blocker: benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the drug-cause and drug-review part of the visitor's question only: one-sided swelling, ulceration, breathlessness, or swelling that persists after the blocker is reviewed points to other causes that this evidence does not address.
cards.source: Synthesis of Makani H et al. Journal of Hypertension. 2011 (PMID: 21558959); Vukadinović D et al. Journal of Hypertension. 2019 (PMID: 31107359); Makani H et al. The American Journal of Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21295192); Makarounas-Kirchmann K et al. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009 (PMID: 19808126).

shelves.title: Cardiac sarcoidosis steroid-sparing treatment: no randomised trial results exist yet (CHASM CS-RCT pending) — observational evidence only shows similar inflammation suppression on methotrexate-based regimens and prednisone, with clinical-event differences not significant
shelves.question: In cardiac sarcoidosis, does methotrexate-based steroid-sparing treatment match prednisone for arrhythmia and cardiac outcomes with less steroid harm?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Humans · Prednisone · Fluorodeoxyglucose F18 · Methotrexate · Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography · Retrospective Studies · Stroke Volume · Cardiomyopathies · Radiopharmaceuticals · Ventricular Function, Left · Sarcoidosis · Positron-Emission Tomography · Myocarditis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no published randomised trial in cardiac sarcoidosis. The one randomised trial designed to answer this question, CHASM CS-RCT (NCT03593759; low-dose prednisone plus methotrexate versus standard-dose prednisone, 97 patients per group planned), has a published design paper (PMID: 31911261) but no published results in the records fetched this session, so it is described here and NOT carded as evidence. What exists is observational: a 61-patient retrospective cohort found FDG uptake fell similarly on prednisone, methotrexate, or both, with major adverse cardiovascular events in 33.3%, 20.0% and 10.0% respectively — a non-significant difference (P = 0.292; Vis 2023, PMID: 36640249); a 28-patient series found methotrexate-based maintenance reduced or eliminated FDG uptake in most patients after a short prednisone lead-in (Rosenthal 2019, PMID: 31538835); and a 2025 systematic review of 11 studies found all treatments reduced myocardial inflammation, with no statistically significant difference between subgroups (PMID: 40225494). Whether steroid harm is actually less has not been measured in a randomised comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only; the randomised answer is still pending.

cards.headline: Vis 2023: in 61 treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis patients, FDG uptake fell similarly on prednisone, methotrexate, or both — major cardiovascular events 33.3% vs 20.0% vs 10.0%, not significant (P = 0.292)
cards.summary: Vis 2023: in 61 treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis patients, FDG uptake fell similarly on prednisone, methotrexate, or both — major cardiovascular events 33.3% vs 20.0% vs 10.0%, not significant (P = 0.292)
cards.people: 61 newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis patients in a retrospective cohort (prednisone n = 21, methotrexate n = 30, combination n = 10), treated between January 2010 and December 2017, with FDG PET/CT response as the primary outcome and 24 months of clinical follow-up.
cards.result: At a median treatment duration of 6.2 months, 71.4% of patients were FDG PET/CT responders and overall myocardial maximum standardized uptake value fell from 6.9 to 3.4 (P < 0.001), with no significant differences between treatment groups. Over 24 months, at least one major adverse cardiovascular event occurred in 7 patients (33.3%) on prednisone, 6 (20.0%) on methotrexate and 1 (10.0%) on combination therapy (P = 0.292). Left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved in all groups. The authors conclude the results warrant further investigation of methotrexate.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and small: treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised, so the lower event count on methotrexate may reflect who was offered it; with 61 patients the study could not detect anything but very large differences in clinical events.
cards.source: Vis R et al. Prednisone vs methotrexate in treatment naïve cardiac sarcoidosis. Journal of Nuclear Cardiology. 2023. PMID: 36640249. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rosenthal 2019: in 28 patients (N printed on the face), methotrexate-based steroid-sparing maintenance after a short prednisone lead-in reduced FDG uptake in 88% and eliminated it in 60% — but 8 of 9 patients relapsed radiologically after stopping immunosuppression
cards.summary: Rosenthal 2019: in 28 patients (N printed on the face), methotrexate-based steroid-sparing maintenance after a short prednisone lead-in reduced FDG uptake in 88% and eliminated it in 60% — but 8 of 9 patients relapsed radiologically after stopping immunosuppression
cards.people: 28 treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis patients at a single academic centre followed for a mean 4.1 years; 25 received 4–8 weeks of high-dose prednisone (>30 mg/day) then taper to methotrexate with or without low-dose prednisone (<10 mg/day), and adalimumab was added in 19 with persistently active disease or methotrexate intolerance.
cards.result: Methotrexate with or without low-dose prednisone produced initial reduction (88%) or elimination (60%) of FDG uptake; adalimumab-containing regimens produced improved (84%) or resolved (63%) uptake. Radiologic relapse occurred in 8 of 9 patients after immunosuppression cessation, in 4 patients on methotrexate-containing regimens, and in no patients on adalimumab-containing regimens. The authors conclude steroid-sparing maintenance is effective after an initial response is confirmed, with ongoing radiologic surveillance needed.
cards.watchOut: N = 28, single centre, no untreated or prednisone-only comparison group, and most patients also received adalimumab — this shows a steroid-sparing regimen can hold remission, not that it matches prednisone.
cards.source: Rosenthal DG et al. Long-Term Corticosteroid-Sparing Immunosuppression for Cardiac Sarcoidosis. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2019. PMID: 31538835. cards.headline: Chaudhri 2025: across 11 studies, all cardiac sarcoidosis treatments reduced myocardial inflammation and between-treatment differences were not significant — methotrexate's effect size was largest (d = 1.65) on very heterogeneous evidence
cards.summary: Chaudhri 2025: across 11 studies, all cardiac sarcoidosis treatments reduced myocardial inflammation and between-treatment differences were not significant — methotrexate's effect size was largest (d = 1.65) on very heterogeneous evidence
cards.people: 11 pertinent studies (observational studies, case series, and randomised controlled trials as described by the review) of corticosteroids, methotrexate, infliximab, rituximab and combinations in cardiac sarcoidosis, searched to October 2024; total participant number not documented in the record.
cards.result: All treatments significantly reduced myocardial inflammation (SUVmax): methotrexate showed the highest effect size (d = 1.65, p < 0.001) and infliximab plus corticosteroids also reduced SUVmax (d = 1.61, p < 0.001). Left ventricular ejection fraction improved modestly across groups (largest d = 0.4, p = 0.05 for infliximab plus corticosteroids). Differences between subgroups were not statistically significant (p = 0.46 for SUVmax; p = 0.36 for LVEF). The authors keep corticosteroids as standard first-line treatment and support methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent, while calling for more research.
cards.watchOut: The review pools mostly observational studies and case series, and its headline effect sizes are within-treatment changes, not head-to-head comparisons — a large before–after change is not evidence one drug beats another.
cards.source: Chaudhri M et al. Steroids Versus Immunomodulators in Cardiac Sarcoidosis: A Systematic Review. Cureus. 2025. PMID: 40225494. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: methotrexate-based steroid-sparing treatment looks capable of suppressing cardiac sarcoidosis activity, but matching prednisone — and causing less harm — is unproven; the CHASM CS-RCT (NCT03593759) is the pending randomised test
cards.summary: Synthesis: methotrexate-based steroid-sparing treatment looks capable of suppressing cardiac sarcoidosis activity, but matching prednisone — and causing less harm — is unproven; the CHASM CS-RCT (NCT03593759) is the pending randomised test
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective head-to-head cohort (61 patients), one retrospective steroid-sparing maintenance series (28 patients), and one systematic review of 11 mostly observational studies. No randomised trial results are carded, because none are published in the records fetched this session.
cards.result: FDG uptake fell similarly whether patients started prednisone, methotrexate, or both, with no significant difference in major cardiovascular events over 24 months (Vis 2023). Methotrexate maintenance after a brief prednisone lead-in held remission in most of a small series, with relapse common after stopping (Rosenthal 2019). The 2025 review found no significant between-treatment differences (Chaudhri 2025). The CHASM CS-RCT design paper (PMID: 31911261; NCT03593759) states there are no published clinical trials in cardiac sarcoidosis and tests low-dose prednisone/methotrexate against standard-dose prednisone for non-inferiority — its results, not yet published in the fetched records, are what would settle this question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Steroid harm — the second half of the question — is asserted from pharmacology, not measured: none of the carded records randomised patients and counted steroid adverse effects, so 'less harm' remains an expectation, not a finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vis R et al. Journal of Nuclear Cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 36640249); Rosenthal DG et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2019 (PMID: 31538835); Chaudhri M et al. Cureus. 2025 (PMID: 40225494).

shelves.title: Beta-blockers in HFpEF — a genuine split: observational data link them to lower mortality, randomised and large matched-registry data show no difference in death or hospitalisation
shelves.question: Should beta-blockers be continued in HFpEF?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Heart Failure · Patient Readmission · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Function, Left
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence genuinely divides by study design, and the split is printed on the face. Two meta-analyses pooling mostly observational cohorts (Kaddoura 2024, PMID: 38184132, 27,188 patients; Bavishi 2015, PMID: 25034701, 27,099 patients) associate beta-blocker use with about a 19% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (OR/RR 0.81 in both), but neither shows a reduction in heart failure hospitalisation. Against that, the randomised trials inside Bavishi's pooling show no difference in mortality or hospitalisation, and the largest single dataset — the SwedeHF registry's propensity-matched analysis (Meyer 2021, PMID: 33971289; 4,412 matched users vs 2,206 non-users) — found beta-blocker use was not associated with HF admission (HR 0.95) or cardiovascular death (HR 0.94) (the treatment made no difference). No trial has randomised HFpEF patients already taking a beta-blocker to continuation versus withdrawal, so the 'continued' question is answered only indirectly. PROPOSED SPLIT — observational data link beta-blockers to lower mortality in HFpEF, but randomised and large matched-registry data show no difference in death or HF hospitalisation; there is no direct continuation-versus-withdrawal trial.

cards.headline: Kaddoura 2024 (B-HFpEF meta-analysis): beta-blocker use was associated with 19% lower relative odds of all-cause mortality in pooled cohort studies — but heart failure rehospitalisation and the mortality-plus-rehospitalisation composite showed no difference
cards.summary: Kaddoura 2024 (B-HFpEF meta-analysis): beta-blocker use was associated with 19% lower relative odds of all-cause mortality in pooled cohort studies — but heart failure rehospitalisation and the mortality-plus-rehospitalisation composite showed no difference
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised or observational cohort studies in HFpEF (left ventricular ejection fraction 50% or above); 16 studies and 27,188 patients were analysed, mean age range 62–84 years, predominantly female; 63.4% received a beta-blocker and 36.6% did not.
cards.result: In the pooled analysis of cohort studies, beta-blocker therapy was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality of 19% relative (odds ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.65–0.99, P = 0.044). Rehospitalisation for heart failure (OR 1.13; 95% CI 0.91–1.41, P = 0.27) and the composite of rehospitalisation with all-cause mortality (OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.78–1.32, P = 0.92) were similar between groups — the treatment made no difference to hospitalisation. The authors state the mortality finding rests on observational studies and that large randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: The mortality signal comes from cohort studies, where patients prescribed beta-blockers differ systematically (more atrial fibrillation and coronary disease, different frailty) in ways adjustment cannot fully remove; the same pooling shows no hospitalisation benefit.
cards.source: Kaddoura R et al. Beta-blocker therapy in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (B-HFpEF): A systematic review and meta-analysis. Current problems in cardiology. 2024. cards.headline: Bavishi 2015: the same split a decade earlier — observational studies showed lower mortality with beta-blockers (RR 0.81), while the two randomised trials showed no difference in mortality (RR 0.94) or HF hospitalisation
cards.summary: Bavishi 2015: the same split a decade earlier — observational studies showed lower mortality with beta-blockers (RR 0.81), while the two randomised trials showed no difference in mortality (RR 0.94) or HF hospitalisation
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 15 observational studies and two randomised controlled trials involving 27,099 patients with HFpEF, using a random-effects model for all-cause mortality and HF hospitalisation.
cards.result: In observational studies, beta-blocker therapy was associated with lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.72–0.90, P < 0.001) but not with HF hospitalisation (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.57–1.10 — the interval includes no effect). In the two randomised trials, beta-blocker use was not associated with all-cause mortality (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.67–1.32, P = 0.72) or HF hospitalisation (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.54–1.49, P = 0.68) — the treatment made no difference. The authors note both trials were underpowered with high loss to follow-up, and that the observational survival benefit was limited to studies with mean age under 75 years.
cards.watchOut: Two trials are too few to settle a mortality question, so the randomised null is itself fragile — but it is the only randomised evidence in the pooling, and it points the opposite way from the cohorts.
cards.source: Bavishi C et al. Beta-blockers in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a meta-analysis. Heart failure reviews. 2015. PMID: 25034701. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meyer 2021 (SwedeHF registry): in 4,412 propensity-matched beta-blocker users versus 2,206 non-users with HFpEF, HF admission ran 42% versus 44% and cardiovascular death 38% versus 40% at 5 years — no association with either outcome
cards.summary: Meyer 2021 (SwedeHF registry): in 4,412 propensity-matched beta-blocker users versus 2,206 non-users with HFpEF, HF admission ran 42% versus 44% and cardiovascular death 38% versus 40% at 5 years — no association with either outcome
cards.people: Patients with HFpEF (ejection fraction 50% or higher) in the Swedish Heart Failure Registry enrolled 2011–2018: 14,434 patients (median age 79 years, 51% women), 80% treated with a beta-blocker at baseline; the primary analysis is a 2:1 propensity-score matched cohort of 4,412 users and 2,206 non-users.
cards.result: At 5 years in the matched cohort, 42% (95% CI 40%–44%) of beta-blocker users versus 44% (95% CI 41%–47%) of non-users had an HF admission, and 38% versus 40% died from cardiovascular causes. In intention-to-treat analysis, beta-blocker use was not associated with HF admissions (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.87–1.05, P = .31) or cardiovascular death (HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.85–1.03, P = .19) — the treatment made no difference — and there were no associations with the secondary outcomes of all-cause hospitalisation or all-cause death.
cards.watchOut: Registry matching balances measured variables only, and 'use at baseline' is not the same as a randomised decision to continue or stop — but at 14,434 patients this is the largest HFpEF-specific dataset carded, and it finds nothing.
cards.source: Meyer M et al. Association Between β-Blockers and Outcomes in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: Current Insights From the SwedeHF Registry. Journal of cardiac failure. 2021. PMID: 33971289. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Heart Failure · Humans · Registries · Stroke Volume

cards.headline: Synthesis: beta-blockers in HFpEF are associated with lower mortality only in observational data; randomised trials and the largest matched registry show no difference in death or hospitalisation, and continuation versus withdrawal has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: beta-blockers in HFpEF are associated with lower mortality only in observational data; randomised trials and the largest matched registry show no difference in death or hospitalisation, and continuation versus withdrawal has never been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses (27,188 and 27,099 patients, overlapping study sets, mostly observational) and one national registry cohort (14,434 patients; 6,618 in the matched analysis). No carded study randomised patients to continue versus stop a beta-blocker.
cards.result: Observational pooling associates beta-blockers with a 19% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (OR/RR 0.81 in both meta-analyses) with no reduction in HF hospitalisation. The randomised subset shows no difference (mortality RR 0.94; hospitalisation RR 0.90), and SwedeHF's matched analysis shows no difference in HF admission (HR 0.95) or cardiovascular death (HR 0.94), with absolute 5-year rates of 42% versus 44% and 38% versus 40%. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit in observational data, no difference in randomised or large matched data.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses share many underlying cohorts, so they are not independent confirmations; and none of the carded evidence separates patients who need a beta-blocker for another reason (rate control, post-infarction, hypertension) from those taking it for HFpEF alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kaddoura R et al. Current problems in cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 38184132); Bavishi C et al. Heart failure reviews. 2015 (PMID: 25034701); Meyer M et al. Journal of cardiac failure. 2021 (PMID: 33971289).

shelves.title: LVAD versus medical therapy in advanced HFrEF: survival was 52% versus 25% at one year in the randomised REMATCH trial — a real survival benefit bought with far more serious adverse events
shelves.question: Does left ventricular assist device therapy improve survival in advanced HFrEF versus medical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Cause of Death · Equipment Design · Equipment Failure · Female · Heart Failure · Heart-Assist Devices · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one definitive randomised trial plus concordant prospective comparative data. In REMATCH (PMID: 11794191), the only randomised trial of a durable LVAD against medical therapy, transplant-ineligible patients with class IV symptoms had 1-year survival of 52% on the device versus 25% on optimal medical management, a 48% relative reduction in the risk of death (relative risk 0.52). The prospective ROADMAP comparison (PMID: 26483097) in less ill, non-inotrope-dependent ambulatory patients found 12-month survival of 80% with an LVAD versus 63% on medical management on as-treated analysis, with better function and quality of life — at the cost of far more adverse events, chiefly bleeding. MOMENTUM 3's intent analysis (PMID: 31939996) shows modern magnetically levitated devices sustain that benefit in destination-therapy patients, though it compares pumps, not device versus drugs. The harm side is real and printed on the cards: serious adverse events ran 2.35 times as often with the first-generation device. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — LVAD therapy improves survival over medical therapy in advanced HFrEF, with a heavy adverse-event burden.

cards.headline: Rose 2001 (REMATCH): in the only randomised LVAD-versus-medical-therapy trial, 1-year survival was 52% with the device versus 25% with optimal medical management — a 48% relative reduction in the risk of death
cards.summary: Rose 2001 (REMATCH): in the only randomised LVAD-versus-medical-therapy trial, 1-year survival was 52% with the device versus 25% with optimal medical management — a 48% relative reduction in the risk of death
cards.people: 129 patients with end-stage heart failure and New York Heart Association class IV symptoms who were ineligible for cardiac transplantation, randomly assigned to a left ventricular assist device (68 patients) or optimal medical management (61 patients).
cards.result: Kaplan-Meier analysis showed a reduction of 48% relative in the risk of death from any cause in the device group compared with the medical-therapy group (relative risk 0.52; 95% CI 0.34–0.78; P = 0.001). Survival at one year was 52% in the device group versus 25% in the medical-therapy group (P = 0.002), and at two years 23% versus 8% (P = 0.09). Quality of life was significantly improved at one year in the device group. The frequency of serious adverse events in the device group was 2.35 (95% CI 1.86–2.95) times that in the medical-therapy group, predominantly infection, bleeding and device malfunction.
cards.watchOut: REMATCH used a first-generation pulsatile device in transplant-ineligible class IV patients; its absolute survival figures understate what modern continuous-flow devices achieve, while its adverse-event profile overstates modern harm — the direction of the comparison is what carries forward.
cards.source: Rose EA et al. Long-term use of a left ventricular assist device for end-stage heart failure. The New England journal of medicine. 2001. PMID: 11794191. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Estep 2015 (ROADMAP): in ambulatory non-inotrope-dependent patients, 12-month survival was 80% with an LVAD versus 63% on optimal medical management (as-treated), and more LVAD patients survived with a ≥75 m walk improvement (39% vs 21%)
cards.summary: Estep 2015 (ROADMAP): in ambulatory non-inotrope-dependent patients, 12-month survival was 80% with an LVAD versus 63% on optimal medical management (as-treated), and more LVAD patients survived with a ≥75 m walk improvement (39% vs 21%)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre observational study of 200 ambulatory patients (97 LVAD, 103 optimal medical management) in New York Heart Association class IIIB/IV meeting destination-therapy indications but not dependent on intravenous inotropes; entry required at least one HF hospitalisation in the previous 12 months and a 6-minute walk distance under 300 m. LVAD patients were more severely ill at baseline (INTERMACS profile 4 in 65% vs 34%).
cards.result: More LVAD patients met the primary composite of survival on original therapy with improvement in 6-minute walk distance of at least 75 m at 12 months (39% LVAD vs 21% medical; odds ratio 2.4; 95% CI 1.2–4.8; P = 0.012). On as-treated analysis, 12-month survival was greater with LVAD than medical management (80% ± 4% vs 63% ± 5%; P = 0.022). Adverse events were higher with LVAD (1.89 events per patient-year, driven by bleeding at 1.22) than with medical management (0.83, driven by worsening HF at 0.68), and 80% of LVAD versus 62% of medical patients required hospitalisation. Quality of life and depression improved significantly more with LVAD.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: patients chose or were chosen for the device, and the LVAD group was sicker at baseline, so the survival gap could understate or overstate the device effect; the as-treated analysis further favours patients who stayed on their assigned strategy.
cards.source: Estep JD et al. Risk Assessment and Comparative Effectiveness of Left Ventricular Assist Device and Medical Management in Ambulatory Heart Failure Patients: Results From the ROADMAP Study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015. PMID: 26483097. Registry ID: NCT01452802. cards.headline: Goldstein 2020 (MOMENTUM 3 intent analysis): with modern devices, destination-therapy patients — the group REMATCH randomised against drugs — achieved 73.2% 2-year survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation with the magnetically levitated pump
cards.summary: Goldstein 2020 (MOMENTUM 3 intent analysis): with modern devices, destination-therapy patients — the group REMATCH randomised against drugs — achieved 73.2% 2-year survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation with the magnetically levitated pump
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised trial (MOMENTUM 3, Goldstein 2020)
cards.people: Prespecified secondary analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 randomised trial (1,020 patients with advanced heart failure receiving a HeartMate 3 magnetically levitated centrifugal-flow LVAD or a HeartMate II axial-flow LVAD), grouped by pre-implant intent: 396 bridge-to-transplant/candidacy patients and 624 destination-therapy patients (mean age 63 years) who were transplant-ineligible.
cards.result: The primary end point — survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation to remove or replace a malfunctioning device at 2 years — favoured the magnetically levitated pump in both intent groups: 76.8% versus 67.3% in bridge-to-transplant/candidacy (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.40–0.94) and 73.2% versus 58.7% in destination therapy (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.46–0.81). Improvements in quality of life and functional capacity occurred with either pump regardless of pre-implant strategy. This record reports no medical-therapy comparison and no effect size for device versus drugs — it is carded as the modern-device survival context for the destination-therapy population, not as comparative evidence.
cards.watchOut: MOMENTUM 3 randomised pump against pump, never device against medical therapy — the device-versus-drugs survival claim on this shelf rests on REMATCH and ROADMAP alone, and MOMENTUM's 2-year event-free survival cannot be set against REMATCH's medical arm across eras.
cards.source: Goldstein DJ et al. Association of Clinical Outcomes With Left Ventricular Assist Device Use by Bridge to Transplant or Destination Therapy Intent: The Multicenter Study of MagLev Technology in Patients Undergoing Mechanical Circulatory Support Therapy With HeartMate 3 (MOMENTUM 3) Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: LVAD therapy improves survival over medical therapy in advanced HFrEF — 52% versus 25% at 1 year in the one randomised trial, 80% versus 63% in the prospective ambulatory comparison — at a substantially higher adverse-event burden
cards.summary: Synthesis: LVAD therapy improves survival over medical therapy in advanced HFrEF — 52% versus 25% at 1 year in the one randomised trial, 80% versus 63% in the prospective ambulatory comparison — at a substantially higher adverse-event burden
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (129 transplant-ineligible class IV patients), one prospective observational comparison (200 ambulatory patients), and one modern-device trial analysis (1,020 patients, 624 destination therapy) carded for survival context. Total carded participants 1,349.
cards.result: REMATCH showed a 48% relative reduction in the risk of death with an LVAD versus medical therapy (relative risk 0.52; 1-year survival 52% vs 25%), with serious adverse events 2.35 times as frequent on the device. ROADMAP extended the comparison to less ill ambulatory patients: 12-month survival 80% versus 63% as-treated, better walk distance, quality of life and depression scores, and more bleeding-driven adverse events (1.89 vs 0.83 events per patient-year). MOMENTUM 3 shows destination-therapy patients on a modern magnetically levitated pump reach 73.2% survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation at 2 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — survival benefit over medical therapy, with heavy device-related harm.
cards.watchOut: Only REMATCH randomised device against drugs, with a device two generations old; every modern survival figure comes from pump-versus-pump trials or observational comparisons, so the size of the benefit against today's medical therapy is less certain than its direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rose EA et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11794191); Estep JD et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015 (PMID: 26483097); Goldstein DJ et al. JAMA cardiology. 2020 (PMID: 31939996).

shelves.title: Ablate and pace for refractory AF: symptoms and heart-failure events improved in one small randomised trial (HF composite 20% vs 38%) — survival did not differ
shelves.question: Does AV node ablation with pacing improve symptoms in refractory AF?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atrial Fibrillation · Atrioventricular Node · Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Catheter Ablation · Electrocardiography · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small randomised trial programme for the strategy itself, capped at POSSIBLE. In APAF-CRT (Brignole 2018, PMID: 30165479), AV junction ablation plus biventricular pacing beat pharmacological rate control on the composite of HF death, HF hospitalisation or worsening HF (20% vs 38%; HR 0.38) and produced a 36% decrease in AF symptoms and physical limitations at one year, in 102 elderly patients with severely symptomatic permanent AF and a prior HF hospitalisation. The AIRCRAFT long-term follow-up (Lim 2007, PMID: 17491103) agrees on symptoms — fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat, chest pain and breathlessness with ablate-and-pace — but found no survival difference and a similar decline in ejection fraction in both groups. PAVE (Doshi 2005, PMID: 16302897) answers the companion question of which pacing to use after ablation: biventricular pacing improved 6-minute walk and ejection fraction over right ventricular pacing alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — symptoms and HF outcomes improved in one small randomised trial, with concordant symptom findings at long-term follow-up; no survival benefit has been shown.

cards.headline: Brignole 2018 (APAF-CRT): AV junction ablation plus biventricular pacing cut the composite of HF death, HF hospitalisation or worsening HF to 20% versus 38% on drug rate control, and reduced AF symptoms and physical limitations by 36% at one year — in 102 patients
cards.summary: Brignole 2018 (APAF-CRT): AV junction ablation plus biventricular pacing cut the composite of HF death, HF hospitalisation or worsening HF to 20% versus 38% on drug rate control, and reduced AF symptoms and physical limitations by 36% at one year — in 102 patients
cards.people: 102 patients (mean age 72 ± 10 years) with severely symptomatic permanent atrial fibrillation of over 6 months, narrow QRS (110 ms or less) and at least one hospitalisation for heart failure in the previous year, randomly assigned to AV junction ablation and cardiac resynchronization (biventricular) pacing or to pharmacological rate-control therapy; a defibrillator was added in either arm according to guidelines. Median follow-up 16 months.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome of death due to HF, hospitalisation due to HF, or worsening HF occurred in 10 patients (20%) in the ablation-plus-CRT arm and 20 patients (38%) in the drug arm (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.18–0.81; P = 0.013). Fewer ablation-plus-CRT patients died from any cause or were hospitalised for HF (6 [12%] vs 17 [33%]; HR 0.28; 95% CI 0.11–0.72; P = 0.008) or were hospitalised for HF (5 [10%] vs 13 [25%]; HR 0.30; 95% CI 0.11–0.78; P = 0.024). Ablation-plus-CRT patients showed a 36% decrease in the specific symptoms and physical limitations of AF at one-year follow-up (P = 0.004).
cards.watchOut: Only 102 patients, all with a recent HF hospitalisation and narrow QRS, and the pacing was biventricular — the result does not automatically transfer to right-ventricular-only pacing or to symptomatic patients without heart failure.
cards.source: Brignole M et al. A randomized controlled trial of atrioventricular junction ablation and cardiac resynchronization therapy in patients with permanent atrial fibrillation and narrow QRS. European heart journal. 2018. PMID: 30165479. Registry ID: NCT02137187. cards.headline: Lim 2007 (AIRCRAFT long-term follow-up): ablate-and-pace patients reported fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat, chest pain and breathlessness 4–7 years on — but survival did not differ (P = 0.26) and ejection fraction declined similarly in both groups
cards.summary: Lim 2007 (AIRCRAFT long-term follow-up): ablate-and-pace patients reported fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat, chest pain and breathlessness 4–7 years on — but survival did not differ (P = 0.26) and ejection fraction declined similarly in both groups
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (AIRCRAFT, Lim 2007)
cards.people: Long-term follow-up of the AIRCRAFT randomised trial cohort: of 63 eligible patients randomised to AV junction ablation and pacing or to pharmacological rate control, 48 (23 ablation-and-pacing, 25 pharmacological therapy) were re-evaluated after 4–7 years (mean age 74 ± 7.5 years).
cards.result: The quality-of-life questionnaire showed ablation-and-pacing patients had fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat (P < 0.001), chest pain (P = 0.02) and difficulty breathing (P = 0.02); psychosocial scores and overall life satisfaction were similar. Death occurred in 10 pharmacological-therapy and 5 ablation-and-pacing patients, and survival analysis incorporating all 63 patients showed no statistical difference between the groups (P = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference to survival. Ejection fraction declined in both groups by 5 years (pharmacological 59% ± 12%; ablation-and-pacing 51% ± 17%), and NYHA class did not differ (1.4 vs 1.5, P = 0.48).
cards.watchOut: Only 48 of 63 randomised patients were re-evaluated, and baseline ejection fraction already differed between groups (54% ablation-and-pacing vs 62% pharmacological), so the symptom comparison rests on a small, incompletely followed cohort.
cards.source: Lim KT et al. Ablate and pace strategy for atrial fibrillation: long-term outcome of AIRCRAFT trial. Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology. 2007. cards.headline: Doshi 2005 (PAVE): once the AV node is ablated, biventricular pacing beat right ventricular pacing — 6-minute walk rose 31% versus 24% above baseline and ejection fraction was 0.46 versus 0.41 at 6 months
cards.summary: Doshi 2005 (PAVE): once the AV node is ablated, biventricular pacing beat right ventricular pacing — 6-minute walk rose 31% versus 24% above baseline and ejection fraction was 0.46 versus 0.41 at 6 months
cards.people: 184 patients requiring AV node ablation for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rates, randomised after ablation to a biventricular pacing system (n = 103) or a right ventricular pacing system (n = 81); 64% male, mean age 69 ± 10 years, mean ejection fraction 0.46 ± 0.16, 83% NYHA class II or III.
cards.result: At 6 months post-ablation, the biventricular group improved 6-minute walk distance by 31% above baseline (82.9 ± 94.7 m) versus 24% (61.2 ± 90.0 m) with right ventricular pacing (P = 0.04). Ejection fraction at 6 months was significantly greater with biventricular pacing (0.46 ± 0.13) than with right ventricular pacing (0.41 ± 0.13, P = 0.03). There were no significant differences in the quality-of-life parameters — the treatment made no difference on that measure. The walk-distance advantage appeared greater in patients with ejection fraction of 45% or below or NYHA class II/III symptoms.
cards.watchOut: PAVE randomised the pacing mode, not ablation versus drugs — it supports biventricular pacing as the companion to ablation (the mode APAF-CRT used), but it is not itself evidence that ablate-and-pace beats rate-control medication.
cards.source: Doshi RN et al. Left ventricular-based cardiac stimulation post AV nodal ablation evaluation (the PAVE study). Journal of cardiovascular electrophysiology. 2005. PMID: 16302897. cards.headline: Synthesis: ablate-and-pace improves symptoms in refractory permanent AF — a 36% symptom reduction and fewer HF events in one 102-patient trial, with concordant long-term symptom findings — but no survival benefit has been shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: ablate-and-pace improves symptoms in refractory permanent AF — a 36% symptom reduction and fewer HF events in one 102-patient trial, with concordant long-term symptom findings — but no survival benefit has been shown
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of ablation plus biventricular pacing versus drug rate control (102 patients), one randomised trial's long-term follow-up (63 randomised; 48 re-evaluated), and one randomised trial of pacing mode after ablation (184 patients). Total carded participants 349.
cards.result: APAF-CRT found the HF composite in 20% versus 38% (HR 0.38) and a 36% decrease in AF symptoms and physical limitations at one year with ablation plus biventricular pacing. AIRCRAFT's follow-up found fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat, chest pain and breathlessness with ablate-and-pace, no survival difference (P = 0.26), and similar ejection-fraction decline. PAVE shows the pacing half of the strategy works better biventricularly (walk distance +31% vs +24%; ejection fraction 0.46 vs 0.41). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — symptom benefit from a single small trial programme; survival unproven.
cards.watchOut: Ablation of the AV node is irreversible and commits the patient to lifelong pacing; the carded trials predate modern conduction-system pacing and enrolled narrow-QRS, HF-hospitalised or rapid-rate populations, so the symptom claim is narrower than the shelf question's wording.

shelves.title: Three months of DAPT after a drug-eluting stent: noninferior to 12 months for net events in two randomised trials of stable coronary disease (6.0% vs 5.8%; 4.7% vs 4.7%)
shelves.question: Is 3 months of DAPT as safe as 12 months after drug-eluting stent in stable coronary disease?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Aspirin · Clopidogrel · Coronary Artery Disease · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Drug-Eluting Stents · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Risk · Sirolimus · Stroke · Thrombosis · Ticlopidine
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised noninferiority trials in the target population agree, and a third trial of the same 3-month strategy in acute coronary syndrome points the same way. OPTIMIZE (Feres 2013, PMID: 24177257; 3,119 patients with stable coronary disease or low-risk ACS receiving zotarolimus-eluting stents) found net adverse clinical and cerebral events in 6.0% on 3 months of DAPT versus 5.8% on 12 months (P = .002 for noninferiority), with stent thrombosis between days 91–360 of 0.3% versus 0.1% (HR 3.97, interval very wide). RESET (Kim 2012, PMID: 22999717; 2,117 patients) likewise found its primary composite in 4.7% versus 4.7% (P < 0.001 for noninferiority), though its 3-month arm also received a specific stent, confounding duration with device. TICO (Kim 2020, PMID: 32543684) tested dropping aspirin at 3 months in ACS and found fewer net events (3.9% vs 5.9%; HR 0.66) driven by less major bleeding (1.7% vs 3.0%). The carded trials used zotarolimus- or sirolimus-eluting stents of their era. PROPOSED LIKELY — 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months for net events after drug-eluting stenting in stable coronary disease, with no demonstrated excess of stent thrombosis, and less bleeding when the second agent is dropped at 3 months.

cards.headline: Feres 2013 (OPTIMIZE): 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months after zotarolimus-eluting stents — net adverse events 6.0% versus 5.8% in 3,119 patients with stable coronary disease or low-risk ACS
cards.summary: Feres 2013 (OPTIMIZE): 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months after zotarolimus-eluting stents — net adverse events 6.0% versus 5.8% in 3,119 patients with stable coronary disease or low-risk ACS
cards.people: 3,119 patients at 33 sites in Brazil with stable coronary artery disease or a history of low-risk acute coronary syndrome undergoing PCI with zotarolimus-eluting stents, randomised to aspirin plus clopidogrel for 3 months (n = 1,563) or 12 months (n = 1,556); open-label noninferiority design with a 2.7% margin against an expected 9% event rate.
cards.result: The primary end point — net adverse clinical and cerebral events (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke or major bleeding) — occurred in 93 patients on short-term and 90 on long-term therapy (6.0% vs 5.8%; risk difference 0.17; 95% CI −1.52 to 1.86; P = .002 for noninferiority). Major adverse cardiac events at one year were 8.3% (128) versus 7.4% (114) (HR 1.12; 95% CI 0.87–1.45). Between days 91 and 360 there was no significant difference in net events (2.6% vs 2.6%; HR 1.03; 95% CI 0.66–1.60) or stent thrombosis (4 [0.3%] vs 1 [0.1%]; HR 3.97; 95% CI 0.44–35.49).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority within a 2.7% margin is not proof of equality, the stent-thrombosis comparison rests on 5 events with an interval running from 0.44 to 35.49, and the trial tested one stent platform in stable or low-risk patients — not high-risk ACS or complex lesions.
cards.source: Feres F et al. Three vs twelve months of dual antiplatelet therapy after zotarolimus-eluting stents: the OPTIMIZE randomized trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 24177257. Registry ID: NCT01113372.
