randomised noninferiority trial (optimize, feres 2013) 3,119 patients at 33 sites in brazil with stable coronary artery disease or a history of low-risk acute coronary syndrome undergoing pci with zotarolimus-eluting stents, randomised to aspirin plus clopidogrel for 3 months (n = 1,563) or 12 months (n = 1,556); open-label noninferiority design with a 2.7% margin against an expected 9% event rate. the primary end point — net adverse clinical and cerebral events (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke or major bleeding) — occurred in 93 patients on short-term and 90 on long-term therapy (6.0% vs 5.8%; risk difference 0.17; 95% ci −1.52 to 1.86; p = .002 for noninferiority). major adverse cardiac events at one year were 8.3% (128) versus 7.4% (114) (hr 1.12; 95% ci 0.87–1.45). between days 91 and 360 there was no significant difference in net events (2.6% vs 2.6%; hr 1.03; 95% ci 0.66–1.60) or stent thrombosis (4 [0.3%] vs 1 [0.1%]; hr 3.97; 95% ci 0.44–35.49). noninferiority within a 2.7% margin is not proof of equality, the stent-thrombosis comparison rests on 5 events with an interval running from 0.44 to 35.49, and the trial tested one stent platform in stable or low-risk patients — not high-risk acs or complex lesions. feres f et al. three vs twelve months of dual antiplatelet therapy after zotarolimus-eluting stents: the optimize randomized trial. jama. 2013. pmid: 24177257. registry id: nct01113372. mesh: acute coronary syndrome · aged · aspirin · clopidogrel · coronary artery disease · drug administration schedule · drug therapy, combination · drug-eluting stents · female · hemorrhage · humans · male · middle aged · myocardial infarction · platelet aggregation inhibitors · risk · sirolimus · stroke · thrombosis · ticlopidine

cards.headline: Kim 2012 (RESET): a 3-month DAPT strategy after a zotarolimus-eluting stent was noninferior to 12-month DAPT standard therapy — primary composite 4.7% versus 4.7%, stent thrombosis 0.2% versus 0.3%
cards.summary: Kim 2012 (RESET): a 3-month DAPT strategy after a zotarolimus-eluting stent was noninferior to 12-month DAPT standard therapy — primary composite 4.7% versus 4.7%, stent thrombosis 0.2% versus 0.3%
cards.people: 2,117 patients with coronary artery stenosis randomised to 3-month DAPT following Endeavor zotarolimus-eluting stent implantation (n = 1,059) or to 12-month DAPT following other drug-eluting stent implantation as standard therapy (n = 1,058).
cards.result: The primary composite end point (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, target-vessel revascularisation or bleeding) at one year occurred in 40 (4.7%) patients in the 3-month group versus 41 (4.7%) in the standard group (difference 0.0%; 95% CI −2.5 to 2.5; P = 0.84; P < 0.001 for noninferiority). The composite of any death, myocardial infarction or stent thrombosis was 0.8% versus 1.3% (difference −0.5%; 95% CI −1.5 to 0.5; P = 0.48), stent thrombosis 0.2% versus 0.3% (P = 0.65) with no further stent thrombosis after clopidogrel cessation in the 3-month group, and target-vessel revascularisation 3.9% versus 3.7% (P = 0.70).
cards.watchOut: RESET changed two things at once — the 3-month arm also received a specific zotarolimus-eluting stent while the 12-month arm received other stents — so its noninferiority is for the combined strategy, not for DAPT duration alone.
cards.source: Kim BK et al. A new strategy for discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy: the RESET Trial (REal Safety and Efficacy of 3-month dual antiplatelet Therapy following Endeavor zotarolimus-eluting stent implantation). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012. PMID: 22999717. Registry ID: NCT01145079. cards.headline: Kim 2020 (TICO): dropping aspirin at 3 months (ticagrelor monotherapy) after stenting for ACS produced fewer net events than 12 months of DAPT — 3.9% versus 5.9% (HR 0.66) — driven by major bleeding, 1.7% versus 3.0%
cards.summary: Kim 2020 (TICO): dropping aspirin at 3 months (ticagrelor monotherapy) after stenting for ACS produced fewer net events than 12 months of DAPT — 3.9% versus 5.9% (HR 0.66) — driven by major bleeding, 1.7% versus 3.0%
cards.people: 3,056 patients with acute coronary syndrome treated with drug-eluting (sirolimus-eluting) stents at 38 centres in South Korea (mean age 61 years, 20% women, 36% ST-elevation myocardial infarction), randomised to ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT (n = 1,527) or ticagrelor-based 12-month DAPT (n = 1,529); 97.4% completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary net adverse clinical event outcome (major bleeding plus death, myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, stroke or target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 59 patients (3.9%) on ticagrelor monotherapy after 3-month DAPT versus 89 (5.9%) on 12-month DAPT (absolute difference −1.98%; 95% CI −3.50% to −0.45%; HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.48–0.92; P = .01). Major bleeding occurred in 1.7% versus 3.0% (HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.34–0.91; P = .02). Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events did not differ significantly (2.3% vs 3.4%; HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.45–1.06; P = .09).
cards.watchOut: TICO enrolled ACS patients, not stable coronary disease, and its 3-month strategy continued ticagrelor alone rather than stopping the second agent outright — it supports the safety of shortening dual therapy at 3 months but in a higher-risk population with a different drug.
cards.source: Kim BK et al. Effect of Ticagrelor Monotherapy vs Ticagrelor With Aspirin on Major Bleeding and Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome: The TICO Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 32543684. Registry ID: NCT02494895. cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months in two randomised trials totalling 5,236 stented patients (net events 6.0% vs 5.8% and 4.7% vs 4.7%), and dropping aspirin at 3 months in ACS reduced net events through less bleeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months in two randomised trials totalling 5,236 stented patients (net events 6.0% vs 5.8% and 4.7% vs 4.7%), and dropping aspirin at 3 months in ACS reduced net events through less bleeding
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised noninferiority trials of 3 versus 12 months of DAPT after drug-eluting stenting (3,119 stable/low-risk and 2,117 mixed patients) and one randomised trial of aspirin discontinuation at 3 months in 3,056 ACS patients. Total carded participants 8,292.
cards.result: OPTIMIZE met noninferiority for net adverse clinical and cerebral events (6.0% vs 5.8%; P = .002 for noninferiority) with stent thrombosis of 0.3% versus 0.1% between days 91–360 on very few events. RESET met noninferiority for its primary composite (4.7% vs 4.7%; P < 0.001 for noninferiority) with stent thrombosis 0.2% versus 0.3%. TICO found the 3-month strategy superior on net events (3.9% vs 5.9%; HR 0.66), driven by major bleeding (1.7% vs 3.0%), with no significant difference in ischaemic events. PROPOSED LIKELY — 3 months is as safe as 12 months for net outcomes in the stable-disease populations randomised, with a bleeding advantage when dual therapy ends at 3 months.
cards.watchOut: Both noninferiority trials used zotarolimus-eluting stents of their era and excluded the highest-risk presentations; 'noninferior within the margin' leaves room for a small absolute excess of rare ischaemic events that trials of this size cannot exclude.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feres F et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 24177257); Kim BK et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012 (PMID: 22999717); Kim BK et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 32543684).

shelves.title: Evolocumab in peripheral arterial disease: in FOURIER's PAD subgroup it cut the primary composite by 21% relative (HR 0.79) with a 3.5% absolute reduction, and limb events fell 42% relative — from one trial programme
shelves.question: Does evolocumab reduce events in patients with peripheral arterial disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amputation, Surgical · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents · Biomarkers · Cholesterol, LDL · Down-Regulation · Dyslipidemias · Female · Humans · Limb Salvage · Male · Middle Aged · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Proprotein Convertase 9 · Risk Factors · Serine Proteinase Inhibitors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (FOURIER), capped at POSSIBLE. Within FOURIER's 27,564 statin-treated patients, the 3,642 with peripheral arterial disease had a 21% relative reduction in the primary composite with evolocumab (HR 0.79) and a 27% relative reduction in the key secondary composite (HR 0.73), with larger absolute risk reductions than in patients without PAD (3.5% for both composites) because their baseline risk was higher (Bonaca 2018, PMID: 29133605). The same trial showed evolocumab reduced major adverse limb events across all patients (HR 0.58) and, in a territory-wide analysis (Oyama 2021, PMID: 34537830), reduced first acute arterial events by 19% relative (HR 0.81), including peripheral vascular events (HR 0.58). A small dedicated randomised study in chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (Dhillon 2025, PMID: 39638643; N = 27, printed on the face) confirms large LDL-C lowering (82 to 34 mg/dL at 6 months) but reports no clinical events. The parent FOURIER trial's main record is homed on its own shelf and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — evolocumab reduced cardiovascular and limb events in the PAD subgroup of one large trial; no second outcomes trial in PAD exists.

cards.headline: Bonaca 2018 (FOURIER PAD analysis): among 3,642 patients with peripheral arterial disease, evolocumab reduced the primary composite by 21% relative (HR 0.79) and cardiovascular death, MI or stroke by 27% relative (HR 0.73) — an absolute reduction of 3.5% for each
cards.summary: Bonaca 2018 (FOURIER PAD analysis): among 3,642 patients with peripheral arterial disease, evolocumab reduced the primary composite by 21% relative (HR 0.79) and cardiovascular death, MI or stroke by 27% relative (HR 0.73) — an absolute reduction of 3.5% for each
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (FOURIER, Bonaca 2018)
cards.people: Prespecified analysis of the FOURIER randomised trial: 27,564 patients with atherosclerotic disease on statin therapy followed for a median of 2.2 years, of whom 3,642 (13.2%) had PAD at baseline (intermittent claudication with ankle brachial index under 0.85, or a prior peripheral vascular procedure); 1,505 of the PAD patients had no prior myocardial infarction or stroke.
cards.result: Evolocumab reduced the primary end point (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospital admission for unstable angina, or coronary revascularisation) consistently in patients with PAD (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66–0.94; P = 0.0098) and without PAD (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.80–0.93; P interaction = 0.40). For the key secondary end point (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) the HRs were 0.73 (95% CI 0.59–0.91; P = 0.0040) with PAD and 0.81 (95% CI 0.73–0.90) without. Because of their higher risk, PAD patients had larger absolute risk reductions: 3.5% for the primary end point (vs 1.6% without PAD) and 3.5% for the key secondary end point (vs 1.4%). Evolocumab reduced major adverse limb events (acute limb ischaemia, major amputation or urgent peripheral revascularisation) in all patients (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.38–0.88; P = 0.0093), with consistent effects in those with and without known PAD, and lower achieved LDL cholesterol tracked with lower limb-event risk down to under 10 mg/dL.
cards.watchOut: This is a subgroup of one trial, not a PAD trial: PAD patients were identified at baseline within a broader atherosclerosis trial, limb events were few enough that the limb analysis pools all 27,564 patients, and the record gives relative effects plus absolute reductions for the composites rather than the PAD group's raw event rates.
cards.source: Bonaca MP et al. Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Lowering With Evolocumab and Outcomes in Patients With Peripheral Artery Disease: Insights From the FOURIER Trial (Further Cardiovascular Outcomes Research With PCSK9 Inhibition in Subjects With Elevated Risk). Circulation. 2018. PMID: 29133605. Registry ID: NCT01764633. cards.headline: Oyama 2021 (FOURIER territory analysis): evolocumab reduced first acute arterial events by 19% relative across all vascular territories (HR 0.81), including peripheral vascular events by 42% relative (HR 0.58)
cards.summary: Oyama 2021 (FOURIER territory analysis): evolocumab reduced first acute arterial events by 19% relative across all vascular territories (HR 0.81), including peripheral vascular events by 42% relative (HR 0.58)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (FOURIER, Oyama 2021)
cards.people: Analysis of the FOURIER trial population: 27,564 patients with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease on statin therapy randomly assigned to evolocumab or placebo; acute arterial events were classified as coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular.
cards.result: Of 2,210 first acute arterial events, 74% were coronary, 22% cerebrovascular and 4% peripheral vascular. Evolocumab reduced first acute arterial events by 19% relative (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.74–0.88; P < 0.001), with reductions in acute coronary events (HR 0.83; 95% CI 0.75–0.91), cerebrovascular events (HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.65–0.92) and peripheral vascular events — acute limb ischaemia, major amputation or urgent peripheral revascularisation (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.38–0.88). Across 3,437 total (first plus recurrent) events, evolocumab reduced events by 24% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.76; 95% CI 0.69–0.85), with the reduction growing from 16% relative in the first year (HR 0.84) to 24% relative thereafter (HR 0.76).
cards.watchOut: Peripheral events were only 4% of first events, so the peripheral HR of 0.58 rests on a small event count within the same single trial — it corroborates the PAD analysis's limb finding but is not independent evidence.
cards.source: Oyama K et al. Effect of evolocumab on acute arterial events across all vascular territories : results from the FOURIER trial. European heart journal. 2021. PMID: 34537830. Registry ID: NCT01764633. MeSH: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Brain Ischemia · Humans · Proprotein Convertase 9 · Stroke

cards.headline: Dhillon 2025 (Evol-CLI): in a dedicated randomised study of just 27 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (small N on the face), evolocumab cut LDL cholesterol from 82 to 34 mg/dL at 6 months — no clinical event outcomes were reported
cards.summary: Dhillon 2025 (Evol-CLI): in a dedicated randomised study of just 27 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (small N on the face), evolocumab cut LDL cholesterol from 82 to 34 mg/dL at 6 months — no clinical event outcomes were reported
cards.people: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled single-centre study of monthly evolocumab for 6 months versus placebo in patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia after an index revascularisation for non-healing wounds, all on maximally tolerated statin therapy: 13 patients in the evolocumab arm and 14 in the placebo arm (total N = 27).
cards.result: The evolocumab arm had lower mean LDL cholesterol at 3 and 6 months than baseline (mean 82 mg/dL at baseline, 26 mg/dL at 3 months and 34 mg/dL at 6 months, P = 0.017); the placebo arm showed no significant difference from baseline. Evolocumab also increased brachial artery flow-mediated dilation and decreased carotid intima-media thickness at 6 months, with no deleterious effect on wound healing. The record reports no cardiovascular or limb event outcomes — the study was powered for LDL cholesterol change, so it cannot confirm or refute the event reductions seen in FOURIER.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-seven patients and surrogate end points only: this card shows the drug lowers LDL cholesterol even in the sickest PAD phenotype, and nothing about events — it must never be cited as outcome evidence.
cards.source: Dhillon GS et al. Effect of evolocumab in patients with chronic limb threatening ischemia (Evol-CLI study). small randomised controlled trial (evol-cli, dhillon 2025) double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled single-centre study of monthly evolocumab for 6 months versus placebo in patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia after an index revascularisation for non-healing wounds, all on maximally tolerated statin therapy: 13 patients in the evolocumab arm and 14 in the placebo arm (total n = 27). the evolocumab arm had lower mean ldl cholesterol at 3 and 6 months than baseline (mean 82 mg/dl at baseline, 26 mg/dl at 3 months and 34 mg/dl at 6 months, p = 0.017); the placebo arm showed no significant difference from baseline. evolocumab also increased brachial artery flow-mediated dilation and decreased carotid intima-media thickness at 6 months, with no deleterious effect on wound healing. the record reports no cardiovascular or limb event outcomes — the study was powered for ldl cholesterol change, so it cannot confirm or refute the event reductions seen in fourier. twenty-seven patients and surrogate end points only: this card shows the drug lowers ldl cholesterol even in the sickest pad phenotype, and nothing about events — it must never be cited as outcome evidence. dhillon gs et al. effect of evolocumab in patients with chronic limb threatening ischemia (evol-cli study). cardiovascular revascularization medicine : including molecular interventions. 2025. pmid: 39638643. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized · male · double-blind method · female · aged · treatment outcome · cholesterol, ldl · prospective studies · ischemia · time factors · middle aged · peripheral arterial disease · biomarkers · anticholesteremic agents · hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors · chronic disease · vasodilation · wound healing · carotid intima-media thickness · chronic limb-threatening ischemia · pcsk9 inhibitors · dyslipidemias · drug therapy, combination · proprotein convertase 9

cards.headline: Synthesis: in the one outcomes trial, evolocumab reduced cardiovascular events in PAD patients (HR 0.79 primary; HR 0.73 key secondary; 3.5% absolute reductions) and limb events across the trial (HR 0.58) — a single-programme result
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the one outcomes trial, evolocumab reduced cardiovascular events in PAD patients (HR 0.79 primary; HR 0.73 key secondary; 3.5% absolute reductions) and limb events across the trial (HR 0.58) — a single-programme result
cards.people: The carded evidence: two analyses of the FOURIER trial (27,564 patients, 3,642 with PAD) and one 27-patient randomised study in chronic limb-threatening ischaemia measuring LDL cholesterol and vascular surrogates. The parent FOURIER record itself is homed on its own shelf and is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: In PAD patients, evolocumab produced a 21% relative reduction in the primary composite (HR 0.79) and a 27% relative reduction in cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke (HR 0.73), each a 3.5% absolute reduction reflecting PAD patients' higher baseline risk. Major adverse limb events fell by 42% relative across the trial (HR 0.58), and total acute arterial events by 24% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.76). Evol-CLI confirms LDL cholesterol falls from 82 to 34 mg/dL on evolocumab in limb-threatening disease but reports no events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one definitive trial's subgroup, capped at POSSIBLE under the single-programme rule.
cards.watchOut: Every event number on this shelf comes from FOURIER; the PAD analysis is a baseline subgroup, limb events were uncommon, and no trial has randomised PAD patients specifically to evolocumab with event outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bonaca MP et al. Circulation. 2018 (PMID: 29133605); Oyama K et al. European heart journal. 2021 (PMID: 34537830); Dhillon GS et al. Cardiovascular revascularization medicine : including molecular interventions. 2025 (PMID: 39638643).

shelves.title: Inclisiran and cardiovascular events (unproven): LDL cholesterol falls by about half, and an exploratory pooled analysis found fewer composite events (OR 0.74) — but no dedicated outcomes trial has reported
shelves.question: Does inclisiran reduce cardiovascular events in high-risk patients?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Anticholesteremic Agents/therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control/drug therapy · Cholesterol, LDL · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Myocardial Infarction/epidemiology/prevention & control/drug therapy · RNA, Small Interfering · Stroke/prevention & control/drug therapy · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — event reduction is unproven; the completed evidence is LDL-lowering plus one exploratory events analysis, printed on the face. No dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial of inclisiran has reported in any record fetched this session. What exists: a prespecified exploratory, patient-level pooled analysis of the phase III LDL trials ORION-9, -10 and -11 (Ray 2023, PMID: 36331326; 3,655 patients, 18 months, events collected as non-adjudicated safety endpoints) found fewer composite major cardiovascular events with inclisiran (odds ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) but no significant difference in fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.50-1.27) or stroke (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.41-1.81) separately. The underlying trials were designed and powered for LDL cholesterol: the pooled phase III analysis (Wright 2021, PMID: 33663735) shows a placebo-corrected LDL reduction of 50.7% at day 510, and the phase II ORION-1 follow-up (Ray 2019, PMID: 31553410) shows the reduction is durable over a year with twice-yearly dosing. The LDL trials themselves (ORION-9/-10/-11 primary reports) are homed on live shelf #1103 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inclisiran halves LDL cholesterol and an exploratory pooled analysis is compatible with fewer cardiovascular events, but whether it reduces events awaits the larger, longer cardiovascular outcomes trials the analysis itself names.

cards.headline: Ray 2023: in a prespecified exploratory pooled analysis of ORION-9, -10 and -11 (3,655 patients, 18 months), inclisiran was associated with fewer composite major cardiovascular events (OR 0.74) — but not with significantly fewer heart attacks or strokes separately, and events were non-adjudicated safety endpoints
cards.summary: Ray 2023: in a prespecified exploratory pooled analysis of ORION-9, -10 and -11 (3,655 patients, 18 months), inclisiran was associated with fewer composite major cardiovascular events (OR 0.74) — but not with significantly fewer heart attacks or strokes separately, and events were non-adjudicated safety endpoints
cards.type: Pooled patient-level analysis of randomised trials, exploratory endpoint (Ray 2023)
cards.people: Patient-level pooled analysis of the phase III trials ORION-9, ORION-10 and ORION-11: patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, or an ASCVD risk equivalent, on maximally tolerated statin therapy, randomised 1:1 to inclisiran 284 mg or placebo on days 1 and 90 and 6-monthly thereafter for 18 months; 3,655 patients. Mean baseline LDL cholesterol was 2.88 mmol/L (approximately 111 mg/dL).
cards.result: At day 90 the placebo-corrected LDL reduction with inclisiran was 50.6%, an absolute reduction of 1.37 mmol/L (approximately 53 mg/dL) (both P < 0.0001). Over 18 months, 303 patients (8.3%) experienced a major cardiovascular event, including 74 (2.0%) fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarctions and 28 (0.8%) fatal and non-fatal strokes. Inclisiran significantly reduced the composite of major cardiovascular events [OR 0.74 (95% CI 0.58-0.94)] but not fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction [OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.50-1.27)] or fatal and non-fatal stroke [OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.41-1.81)] separately. The endpoint was a prespecified exploratory endpoint evaluated as part of safety assessments using a MedDRA basket, not an adjudicated trial outcome; the authors state the findings await confirmation in larger cardiovascular outcomes trials of longer duration.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and non-adjudicated: the composite was assembled from safety reporting in trials powered for LDL change, follow-up was only 18 months, and neither myocardial infarction nor stroke was significantly reduced on its own — this is a hypothesis-strengthening signal, not an outcomes result.
cards.source: Ray KK et al. Inclisiran and cardiovascular events: a patient-level analysis of phase III trials. European Heart Journal. 2023. PMID: 36331326. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wright 2021: pooled across the three phase III trials (3,660 participants), inclisiran lowered LDL cholesterol by 50.7% versus placebo at day 510 — the surrogate effect on which any event benefit would have to rest
cards.summary: Wright 2021: pooled across the three phase III trials (3,660 participants), inclisiran lowered LDL cholesterol by 50.7% versus placebo at day 510 — the surrogate effect on which any event benefit would have to rest
cards.type: Pooled patient-level analysis of randomised trials (Wright 2021)
cards.people: Patient-level pooled analysis of ORION-9 (heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, n = 482), ORION-10 (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, n = 1,561) and ORION-11 (ASCVD or ASCVD risk equivalents, n = 1,617): 3,660 participants on maximally tolerated statin therapy with or without other LDL-lowering agents, randomised 1:1 to inclisiran or placebo by subcutaneous injection on day 1, day 90 and every 6 months thereafter for 540 days.
cards.result: The placebo-corrected change in LDL cholesterol with inclisiran at day 510 was -50.7% (95% CI -52.9% to -48.4%; P < 0.0001); the time-adjusted change from baseline after day 90 to day 540 was -50.5% (95% CI -52.1% to -48.9%; P < 0.0001). Safety was similar in both groups; treatment-emergent adverse events at the injection site were more frequent with inclisiran than placebo (5.0% vs 0.7%) but were predominantly mild, and none were severe or persistent. Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase values and platelet counts did not differ between groups. No cardiovascular event outcome is reported as an endpoint in this record.
cards.watchOut: A pooled LDL analysis of the same three trials as the events card above — the participants overlap almost completely with Ray 2023, so the two cards are one trial programme seen twice, not independent confirmation; and LDL lowering, however large, is a surrogate for events.
cards.source: Wright RS et al. Pooled Patient-Level Analysis of Inclisiran Trials in Patients With Familial Hypercholesterolemia or Atherosclerosis. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2021. PMID: 33663735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ray 2019 (ORION-1 follow-up): one or two doses of inclisiran produced durable LDL reductions over a full year — time-averaged reductions of 29.5-38.7% after one dose and 29.9-46.4% after two doses in 501 patients
cards.summary: Ray 2019 (ORION-1 follow-up): one or two doses of inclisiran produced durable LDL reductions over a full year — time-averaged reductions of 29.5-38.7% after one dose and 29.9-46.4% after two doses in 501 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase II follow-up (Ray 2019)
cards.people: Prespecified analysis of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre phase II trial in patients with elevated LDL cholesterol despite maximally tolerated statin therapy: 501 randomised participants (65% men, mean age 63 years, 6% familial hypercholesterolaemia, 69% established ASCVD; baseline LDL cholesterol 128 mg/dL), given one dose (200, 300 or 500 mg on day 1) or two doses (100, 200 or 300 mg on days 1 and 90) of inclisiran or placebo, and followed until LDL returned to within 20% of its change from baseline (maximum 360 days).
cards.result: Time-averaged reduction in LDL cholesterol over 1 year ranged from 29.5% to 38.7% after a single dose and from 29.9% to 46.4% after two doses (P < .001 between groups), with similar effects on PCSK9; the two-dose 300-mg regimen produced the greatest mean reduction over 1 year. The proportion still followed at day 360 because LDL had not returned toward baseline ranged from 48.3% to 65.0% after a single dose and 55.9% to 83.1% after two doses. Incidence of adverse events was similar through 1 year. No cardiovascular event outcome is reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: A phase II dose-finding follow-up measuring LDL and PCSK9 only: it establishes durability of the surrogate effect with infrequent dosing and says nothing about heart attacks, strokes or deaths.
cards.source: Ray KK et al. Effect of 1 or 2 Doses of Inclisiran on Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Levels: One-Year Follow-up of the ORION-1 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 31553410. Registry ID: NCT02597127. cards.headline: Synthesis: inclisiran halves LDL cholesterol durably with twice-yearly dosing, and the only events evidence — an exploratory, non-adjudicated pooled analysis — points toward fewer major cardiovascular events without significantly reducing heart attack or stroke separately; no dedicated outcomes trial has reported
cards.summary: Synthesis: inclisiran halves LDL cholesterol durably with twice-yearly dosing, and the only events evidence — an exploratory, non-adjudicated pooled analysis — points toward fewer major cardiovascular events without significantly reducing heart attack or stroke separately; no dedicated outcomes trial has reported
cards.people: The carded evidence: one exploratory patient-level pooled events analysis of ORION-9/-10/-11 (3,655 patients, 18 months), the pooled phase III LDL analysis of the same programme (3,660 participants — the same patients, not additional evidence), and the phase II ORION-1 one-year follow-up (501 participants). Unique participants total roughly 4,200, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The primary ORION-9/-10/-11 LDL reports are homed on live shelf #1103 and are cross-pointed there, not re-carded here.
cards.result: Inclisiran reduced LDL cholesterol by 50.6-50.7% versus placebo in the phase III programme (Ray 2023; Wright 2021) and by 29.9-46.4% time-averaged over a year after two doses in phase II (Ray 2019). In the exploratory events analysis, 8.3% of patients had a major cardiovascular event over 18 months; the composite odds ratio favoured inclisiran [OR 0.74 (95% CI 0.58-0.94)] while myocardial infarction [OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.50-1.27)] and stroke [OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.41-1.81)] did not reach significance separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the LDL effect is certain and large; the event reduction is plausible and unproven, awaiting the dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trials.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the certain surrogate carry the uncertain outcome: on this shelf's face, inclisiran is an LDL-lowering drug with a promising exploratory events signal — nothing carded here is a completed cardiovascular outcomes trial.

shelves.title: Extended DAPT after myocardial infarction: fewer ischaemic events (7.8% vs 9.0% at 3 years in PEGASUS) and less cardiovascular death — bought with roughly double the major bleeding, but no more fatal bleeding
shelves.question: Should DAPT be extended beyond 12 months after MI in high ischemic risk patients?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Aged · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Intracranial Hemorrhages/chemically induced · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/drug therapy · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Purinergic P2Y Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Risk · Secondary Prevention · Ticagrelor
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit for ischaemic events, at the cost of more major bleeding) — one definitive large randomised trial in exactly this population plus a concordant collaborative meta-analysis. In PEGASUS-TIMI 54 (Bonaca 2015, PMID: 25773268), 21,162 patients 1 to 3 years after myocardial infarction were randomised to ticagrelor 90 mg or 60 mg twice daily or placebo, all on low-dose aspirin: at 3 years the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 7.85% (90 mg) and 7.77% (60 mg) versus 9.04% on placebo (hazard ratios 0.85 and 0.84 — relative reductions), while TIMI major bleeding rose from 1.06% to 2.60% and 2.30%, with intracranial or fatal bleeding essentially unchanged (0.63%, 0.71%, 0.60%). The collaborative meta-analysis restricted to patients with prior MI (Udell 2016, PMID: 26324537; 33,435 patients, six trials) found the same pattern: major adverse cardiovascular events 6.4% versus 7.5% (relative risk 0.78), cardiovascular death reduced (relative risk 0.85), major bleeding increased (1.85% versus 1.09%; relative risk 1.73) but not fatal bleeding. The broader post-stent meta-analysis (Cassese 2015, PMID: 25903112) adds a caution from a different population: prolonged DAPT after drug-eluting stenting reduced stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction but was associated with higher all-cause death (odds ratio 1.25) — a signal not seen in the post-MI-restricted analysis, and one reason the answer is framed for high-ischaemic-risk post-MI patients rather than all-comers. Post-stent DAPT duration itself is homed on live shelf #264 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): extending DAPT beyond 12 months after MI in high-ischaemic-risk patients reduces ischaemic events including cardiovascular death, and increases major (not fatal) bleeding — the trade-off, not the direction, is the clinical decision.

cards.headline: Bonaca 2015 (PEGASUS-TIMI 54): in 21,162 patients 1-3 years after myocardial infarction, ticagrelor plus aspirin cut the 3-year composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke from 9.04% to 7.85% (90 mg) and 7.77% (60 mg) — and roughly doubled TIMI major bleeding (2.60% and 2.30% vs 1.06%)
cards.summary: Bonaca 2015 (PEGASUS-TIMI 54): in 21,162 patients 1-3 years after myocardial infarction, ticagrelor plus aspirin cut the 3-year composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke from 9.04% to 7.85% (90 mg) and 7.77% (60 mg) — and roughly doubled TIMI major bleeding (2.60% and 2.30% vs 1.06%)
cards.people: 21,162 patients who had had a myocardial infarction 1 to 3 years earlier, randomised double-blind 1:1:1 to ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, ticagrelor 60 mg twice daily, or placebo; all patients were to receive low-dose aspirin and were followed for a median of 33 months.
cards.result: The two ticagrelor doses each reduced the primary efficacy end point (composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke) versus placebo, with Kaplan-Meier rates at 3 years of 7.85% (90 mg), 7.77% (60 mg) and 9.04% (placebo): hazard ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.96; P = 0.008) for 90 mg and 0.84 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.95; P = 0.004) for 60 mg — relative reductions of about 15-16% against absolute rates about 1.2-1.3 percentage points lower. Rates of TIMI major bleeding were higher with ticagrelor (2.60% with 90 mg and 2.30% with 60 mg) than with placebo (1.06%) (P < 0.001 for each dose versus placebo); rates of intracranial haemorrhage or fatal bleeding were 0.63%, 0.71% and 0.60% respectively.
cards.watchOut: PEGASUS enrolled patients who had already tolerated the first 1-3 years after infarction — a selected, lower-bleeding-risk group than unselected post-MI patients — and the absolute ischaemic gain (about 1.2 percentage points over 3 years) is the same order of size as the absolute major-bleeding cost (about 1.2-1.5 percentage points).
cards.source: Bonaca MP et al. Long-term use of ticagrelor in patients with prior myocardial infarction. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25773268. Registry ID: NCT01225562. cards.headline: Udell 2016: across six randomised trials in 33,435 patients with prior myocardial infarction, DAPT beyond 1 year reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (6.4% vs 7.5%; relative risk 0.78) and cardiovascular death (relative risk 0.85), and increased major bleeding (1.85% vs 1.09%; relative risk 1.73) but not fatal bleeding
cards.summary: Udell 2016: across six randomised trials in 33,435 patients with prior myocardial infarction, DAPT beyond 1 year reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (6.4% vs 7.5%; relative risk 0.78) and cardiovascular death (relative risk 0.85), and increased major bleeding (1.85% vs 1.09%; relative risk 1.73) but not fatal bleeding
cards.people: Collaborative meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing more than a year of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin alone in high-risk patients with a history of prior myocardial infarction: 33,435 patients followed over a mean of 31 months, from one trial of patients with prior MI (63.3% of the total) and five trials contributing subgroups of patients who presented with, or had a history of, prior MI (36.7%).
cards.result: Extended DAPT decreased major adverse cardiovascular events versus aspirin alone (6.4% vs 7.5%; relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.90; P = 0.001) and reduced cardiovascular death (2.3% vs 2.6%; relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.74-0.98; P = 0.03), with no increase in non-cardiovascular death (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.86-1.23; P = 0.76); the effect on all-cause mortality was relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.83-1.03; P = 0.13). Extended DAPT also reduced myocardial infarction (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.55-0.88), stroke (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.68-0.97) and stent thrombosis (relative risk 0.50, 95% CI 0.28-0.89). Major bleeding increased (1.85% vs 1.09%; relative risk 1.73, 95% CI 1.19-2.50; P = 0.004) but fatal bleeding did not (0.14% vs 0.17%; relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.53-1.58; P = 0.75). All relative risks are relative measures, printed with the absolute rates the record gives.
cards.watchOut: Most weight comes from the single prior-MI trial (PEGASUS-TIMI 54, carded above); the other five trials contribute prior-MI subgroups rather than dedicated post-MI randomisation, so this is strong corroboration of one large trial, not six independent ones.
cards.source: Udell JA et al. Long-term dual antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events in the subgroup of patients with previous myocardial infarction: a collaborative meta-analysis of randomized trials. European Heart Journal. 2016. PMID: 26324537. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cassese 2015: in the broader post-stent population (10 trials, 32,194 participants), prolonged DAPT reduced stent thrombosis (odds ratio 0.50) and myocardial infarction (odds ratio 0.55) but was associated with more major bleeding (odds ratio 1.67) and higher all-cause death (odds ratio 1.25)
cards.summary: Cassese 2015: in the broader post-stent population (10 trials, 32,194 participants), prolonged DAPT reduced stent thrombosis (odds ratio 0.50) and myocardial infarction (odds ratio 0.55) but was associated with more major bleeding (odds ratio 1.67) and higher all-cause death (odds ratio 1.25)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials of prolonged versus control dual antiplatelet therapy duration after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent implantation: 10 trials totalling 32,194 participants; median DAPT duration was 15 (12-24) months in the prolonged groups versus 6 (6-12) months in the control groups, with median follow-up of 19.5 months. This is a post-stent population, not restricted to patients after myocardial infarction.
cards.result: Prolonged versus control DAPT reduced stent thrombosis [odds ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.29-0.85), P = 0.01] and myocardial infarction [odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.45-0.67), P < 0.001], at the expense of higher major bleeding [odds ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.31-2.13), P < 0.001] and death [odds ratio 1.25 (95% CI 1.02-1.53), P = 0.03]. Prolonged DAPT did not influence cardiac death [odds ratio 1.08 (95% CI 0.82-1.44), P = 0.74] or cerebrovascular events [odds ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.57-1.24), P = 0.39]. The record reports odds ratios without absolute event rates for these outcomes, so no absolute rates are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Different question, neighbouring population: these are all-comer post-stent trials (the DAPT-duration question homed on live shelf #264), and their all-cause-death signal was not reproduced in the post-MI-restricted analysis above — it is carded here as the caution against extending this shelf's answer beyond high-ischaemic-risk post-MI patients.
cards.source: Cassese S et al. Prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy after drug-eluting stenting: meta-analysis of randomized trials. Clinical Research in Cardiology. 2015. PMID: 25903112. cards.headline: Synthesis: for high-ischaemic-risk patients more than a year after myocardial infarction, extended DAPT reduces ischaemic events — composite 7.8% vs 9.0% at 3 years in PEGASUS, cardiovascular death relative risk 0.85 in the post-MI meta-analysis — and increases major bleeding roughly 1.7-fold in relative terms, without increasing fatal bleeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: for high-ischaemic-risk patients more than a year after myocardial infarction, extended DAPT reduces ischaemic events — composite 7.8% vs 9.0% at 3 years in PEGASUS, cardiovascular death relative risk 0.85 in the post-MI meta-analysis — and increases major bleeding roughly 1.7-fold in relative terms, without increasing fatal bleeding
cards.people: The carded evidence: one definitive randomised trial in the exact population (PEGASUS-TIMI 54, 21,162 patients 1-3 years post-MI), one collaborative meta-analysis restricted to prior-MI patients (33,435 patients, six trials, dominated by PEGASUS), and one broader post-stent meta-analysis (32,194 participants, ten trials) carded as the caution. Totals far exceed any small-N threshold; the meta-analyses overlap the trial, so the unique-patient count is lower than the sum.
cards.result: Ticagrelor-based extended DAPT in PEGASUS: primary composite 7.85% (90 mg) and 7.77% (60 mg) versus 9.04% on aspirin alone at 3 years (hazard ratios 0.85 and 0.84, relative), with TIMI major bleeding 2.60% and 2.30% versus 1.06% and no material difference in intracranial or fatal bleeding. The post-MI meta-analysis concurs: major adverse cardiovascular events 6.4% versus 7.5% (relative risk 0.78), cardiovascular death relative risk 0.85, major bleeding 1.85% versus 1.09% (relative risk 1.73), fatal bleeding unchanged. The post-stent meta-analysis adds an all-cause-death signal (odds ratio 1.25) not seen post-MI. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, with increased major bleeding): extend DAPT beyond 12 months after MI where ischaemic risk is high and bleeding risk is acceptable.
cards.watchOut: The benefit and the harm are both real and similarly sized in absolute terms; the evidence supports extension in selected high-ischaemic-risk, low-bleeding-risk patients — it does not support indefinite DAPT for every post-MI patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bonaca MP et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25773268); Udell JA et al. European Heart Journal. 2016 (PMID: 26324537); Cassese S et al. Clinical Research in Cardiology. 2015 (PMID: 25903112).

shelves.title: Amlodipine oedema is dose-related and ARB combination reduces it: 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan versus 8.7% on amlodipine alone — and 0.9% at 5 mg versus 9.1% at 10 mg inside the same combination
shelves.question: Does amlodipine cause less edema at lower dose combined with ARB?
shelves.mesh: Amlodipine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Calcium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Edema/chemically induced · Female · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Nasopharyngitis/chemically induced · Tetrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Valine/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Valsartan
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised combination trials and a network meta-analysis point the same way: amlodipine oedema is dose-related, and pairing the amlodipine with a renin-angiotensin blocker lowers it. In the pivotal factorial trials (Philipp 2007, PMID: 17617280; 3,161 patients randomised across two studies), peripheral oedema occurred in 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine monotherapy (P = 0.014), while blood-pressure lowering was greater on the combination — so the lower oedema rate was not bought with weaker treatment. The dose gradient inside an ARB combination is direct in Sinkiewicz 2009 (PMID: 19192976; 947 patients uncontrolled on valsartan): peripheral oedema was reported in 9.1% on amlodipine 10 mg/valsartan 160 mg but only 0.9% on amlodipine 5 mg/valsartan 160 mg (valsartan alone 1.3%), with the 5-mg combination still lowering blood pressure significantly more than valsartan alone. The network meta-analysis of 71 trials (Liang 2022, PMID: 35234349; 56,283 patients) ranks dihydropyridine-plus-blocker combinations below dihydropyridine monotherapy for oedema as a class, while noting the mitigation is clearest for ACE-inhibitor combinations and was not shown for every ARB pairing (nifedipine plus ARB did not mitigate in its ranking). The earlier oedema meta-analyses carded in pack #5524 are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): yes — amlodipine causes less oedema at a lower dose combined with an ARB, and the combination lowers blood pressure more, not less.

cards.headline: Philipp 2007: across two factorial trials (3,161 patients), peripheral oedema occurred in 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine monotherapy (P = 0.014) — while the combination lowered blood pressure significantly more than either component
cards.summary: Philipp 2007: across two factorial trials (3,161 patients), peripheral oedema occurred in 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine monotherapy (P = 0.014) — while the combination lowered blood pressure significantly more than either component
cards.type: Randomised controlled trials, two factorial studies (Philipp 2007)
cards.people: Two multinational, multicentre, 8-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trials in adults with mild to moderate essential hypertension (mean sitting diastolic BP 95 to under 110 mm Hg). Study 1 randomised 1,911 patients (amlodipine 2.5 or 5 mg, valsartan 40-320 mg, their combinations, or placebo); study 2 randomised 1,250 patients (amlodipine 10 mg, valsartan 160 or 320 mg, their combinations, or placebo). Mean age 54.4 and 56.9 years; baseline BP 152.8/99.3 and 156.7/99.1 mm Hg.
cards.result: With few exceptions among the amlodipine 2.5-mg combinations, combination regimens produced significantly greater reductions in mean sitting diastolic and systolic BP than their individual components and placebo (P < 0.05), with a positive dose response; the highest response rate in study 1 was with amlodipine 5 mg + valsartan 320 mg (91.3%), versus 71.9% for amlodipine 5 mg and 40.9% for placebo. The incidence of peripheral oedema with combination therapy was significantly lower than with amlodipine monotherapy (5.4% vs 8.7%; P = 0.014), significantly higher than with valsartan monotherapy (2.1%; P < 0.001), and not significantly different from placebo (3.0%).
cards.watchOut: The pooled oedema comparison mixes amlodipine doses (2.5-10 mg across the two studies), and 8 weeks is short: oedema that emerges or forces discontinuation over years of treatment is not captured here.
cards.source: Philipp T et al. Two multicenter, 8-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group studies evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of amlodipine and valsartan in combination and as monotherapy in adult patients with mild to moderate essential hypertension. Clinical Therapeutics. 2007. PMID: 17617280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sinkiewicz 2009: the dose gradient inside an ARB combination is steep — peripheral oedema in 9.1% on amlodipine 10 mg/valsartan 160 mg versus 0.9% on amlodipine 5 mg/valsartan 160 mg (valsartan alone 1.3%), in 947 patients
cards.summary: Sinkiewicz 2009: the dose gradient inside an ARB combination is steep — peripheral oedema in 9.1% on amlodipine 10 mg/valsartan 160 mg versus 0.9% on amlodipine 5 mg/valsartan 160 mg (valsartan alone 1.3%), in 947 patients
cards.people: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled study in patients with essential hypertension not adequately controlled on valsartan: after washout and a single-blind valsartan 160 mg run-in, 947 patients (mean age 54.6 years) with mean sitting diastolic BP of 90 to under 110 mm Hg were randomised to amlodipine/valsartan 10/160 mg, amlodipine/valsartan 5/160 mg, or valsartan 160 mg once daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Both combinations lowered BP significantly more than valsartan alone (mean systolic/diastolic reductions 14.3/11.5 mm Hg for 10/160 mg and 12.2/9.6 mm Hg for 5/160 mg, versus 8.3/6.7 mm Hg; both P < 0.0001), and the 10/160 mg combination lowered BP significantly more than 5/160 mg. Responder rates were 81% (10/160 mg), 68% (5/160 mg) and 57% (valsartan alone). Peripheral oedema was the most frequent adverse event, reported with amlodipine/valsartan 10/160 mg in 9.1%, with 5/160 mg in 0.9%, and with valsartan 160 mg in 1.3% — a tenfold difference between the two amlodipine doses inside the same ARB combination.
cards.watchOut: Patients were selected for having tolerated a valsartan run-in, oedema was spontaneously reported rather than measured, and the trial ran 8 weeks — the 0.9% figure is a short-term, selected-population rate, though the within-trial dose contrast (0.9% vs 9.1%) is the point of the card.

cards.headline: Liang 2022: across 71 randomised trials (56,283 patients), dihydropyridines as a class raised oedema risk versus placebo, and second- or higher-generation dihydropyridine combinations with an ACE inhibitor, ARB or diuretic lowered oedema versus monotherapy — with amlodipine plus ACE inhibitor ranked the most mitigating combination
cards.summary: Liang 2022: across 71 randomised trials (56,283 patients), dihydropyridines as a class raised oedema risk versus placebo, and second- or higher-generation dihydropyridine combinations with an ACE inhibitor, ARB or diuretic lowered oedema versus monotherapy — with amlodipine plus ACE inhibitor ranked the most mitigating combination
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers for hypertension and chronic coronary artery disease: 71 studies with 56,283 patients included from 3,312 publications identified.
cards.result: Nifedipine ranked highest for inducing peripheral oedema (SUCRA 81.8%) and lacidipine least (SUCRA 12.8%); all dihydropyridines except lacidipine resulted in a higher relative risk of peripheral oedema compared with placebo (the record reports the class finding without a single pooled relative-risk figure). In the combination ranking, amlodipine plus an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor reduced peripheral oedema the most (SUCRA 16%), while nifedipine plus an angiotensin receptor blocker did not mitigate peripheral oedema (SUCRA 92.3%). The authors conclude that second- or higher-generation dihydropyridine combinations with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics lowered the chance of peripheral oedema compared with single dihydropyridine treatment.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings (SUCRA) are indirect and ranking-based, not head-to-head event rates — and this analysis is a partial counterweight to the shelf: the mitigation was clearest for ACE-inhibitor combinations, and at least one ARB pairing (with nifedipine) did not mitigate, so the claim rests mainly on the amlodipine/valsartan trials carded above.
cards.source: Liang L et al. Comparative peripheral edema for dihydropyridines calcium channel blockers treatment: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — amlodipine oedema is dose-related and is reduced by ARB combination: 5.4% on combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine alone in the factorial trials, and 0.9% at amlodipine 5 mg versus 9.1% at 10 mg inside the same valsartan combination, with better blood-pressure lowering on the combinations
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — amlodipine oedema is dose-related and is reduced by ARB combination: 5.4% on combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine alone in the factorial trials, and 0.9% at amlodipine 5 mg versus 9.1% at 10 mg inside the same valsartan combination, with better blood-pressure lowering on the combinations
cards.people: The carded evidence: two factorial randomised trials (3,161 patients), one randomised add-on trial with an internal amlodipine dose contrast (947 patients), and one network meta-analysis of 71 trials (56,283 patients). Totals far exceed any small-N threshold. The earlier calcium-channel-blocker oedema meta-analyses are homed in pack #5524 and are cross-pointed there, not re-carded here.
cards.result: Combination amlodipine/valsartan versus amlodipine monotherapy: peripheral oedema 5.4% versus 8.7% (P = 0.014), with significantly greater BP reductions on the combination (Philipp 2007). Within an ARB combination: oedema 0.9% at amlodipine 5 mg versus 9.1% at 10 mg, against 1.3% on valsartan alone (Sinkiewicz 2009). Across the class, combinations with renin-angiotensin blockers rank below monotherapy for oedema, most clearly for ACE-inhibitor pairings (Liang 2022). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): use the lower amlodipine dose inside an ARB combination when oedema is the concern — less oedema, more blood-pressure lowering.
cards.watchOut: All carded trials are short (8 weeks) industry-era combination studies with spontaneously reported oedema; the direction and the dose gradient are consistent, but long-term discontinuation-for-oedema rates at each dose are not what these trials measured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Philipp T et al. Clinical Therapeutics. 2007 (PMID: 17617280); Sinkiewicz W et al. Current Medical Research and Opinion. 2009 (PMID: 19192976); Liang L et al. Journal of Clinical Hypertension. 2022 (PMID: 35234349).

shelves.title: Exercise versus medication for blood pressure (indirect evidence only): no detectable difference from single drugs in hypertensive subgroups of a 391-trial network analysis — but no head-to-head trial has ever been run
shelves.question: Does exercise lower blood pressure as much as medication in hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Blood Pressure/drug effects/physiology · Calcium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage · Diuretics/administration & dosage · Exercise/physiology · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy/physiopathology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the comparison rests entirely on indirect (network) evidence, printed on the face: no randomised trial has ever compared exercise head-to-head with an antihypertensive drug. In the network meta-analysis of 391 randomised trials (Naci 2019, PMID: 30563873; 197 exercise trials with 10,461 participants and 194 medication trials with 29,281 participants), medications achieved greater systolic reductions than exercise across all populations combined (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg, 95% credible interval -5.02 to -2.91) — but among hypertensive participants specifically (only 56 exercise trials, 3,508 individuals), there were no detectable differences between endurance or dynamic resistance exercise and ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics. The exercise effect itself is real and dose-related: aerobic exercise at 150 minutes/week lowered systolic BP by 7.23 mm Hg in hypertensive adults (Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024, PMID: 37872373; 34 trials, 1,787 participants), and isometric training lowered systolic BP by 6.77 mm Hg across nine small trials (Carlson 2014, PMID: 24582191; 223 participants) — magnitudes in the range of a single drug. The larger network meta-analyses of exercise modalities (Edwards 2023; Cornelissen 2013) are already carded elsewhere in the library and were not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: in hypertensive patients, structured exercise lowers systolic blood pressure by amounts statistically indistinguishable from single-drug therapy in indirect comparisons — 'as much as medication' is plausible, not demonstrated, and exercise trials in hypertension remain few and small next to the drug trials.

cards.headline: Naci 2019: in a network meta-analysis of 391 randomised trials, medications beat exercise overall (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg systolic) — but among hypertensive participants there were no detectable differences between endurance or dynamic resistance exercise and ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics; no trial compared exercise with drugs directly
cards.summary: Naci 2019: in a network meta-analysis of 391 randomised trials, medications beat exercise overall (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg systolic) — but among hypertensive participants there were no detectable differences between endurance or dynamic resistance exercise and ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics; no trial compared exercise with drugs directly
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of exercise interventions (endurance, dynamic resistance, isometric resistance, and combined endurance and resistance) and of antihypertensive medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics): 391 trials in total — 197 exercise trials (10,461 participants) and 194 medication trials (29,281 participants). Only 56 exercise trials included hypertensive participants (systolic BP 140 mm Hg or above), corresponding to 3,508 individuals, while all medication trials included hypertensive populations.
cards.result: Compared with control, all types of exercise and all classes of antihypertensive medication lowered baseline systolic BP. In analyses combining all populations, antihypertensive medications achieved greater reductions than exercise interventions (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg, 95% credible interval -5.02 to -2.91). Among hypertensive populations, there were no detectable differences in systolic-lowering effects between ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics and endurance or dynamic resistance exercise. No randomised trial compared exercise against medication directly — every exercise-versus-drug contrast is indirect, through the network. In a 10% random sample, risk of bias was higher in exercise trials, mainly from lack of blinding and incomplete outcome data; small-study effects were present in both literatures.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison is indirect and population-mismatched: most exercise trials enrolled non-hypertensive people (whose BP has less room to fall), so the all-population result favours drugs by construction, and the hypertensive subgroup result — the one that answers this shelf — rests on just 56 trials and 3,508 people.
cards.source: Naci H et al. How does exercise treatment compare with antihypertensive medications? A network meta-analysis of 391 randomised controlled trials assessing exercise and medication effects on systolic blood pressure. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30563873. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024: aerobic exercise in hypertensive adults is dose-related — each 30 min/week lowered systolic BP by 1.78 mm Hg, with the greatest reduction at 150 min/week (systolic -7.23 mm Hg, diastolic -5.58 mm Hg) across 34 trials (1,787 participants)
cards.summary: Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024: aerobic exercise in hypertensive adults is dose-related — each 30 min/week lowered systolic BP by 1.78 mm Hg, with the greatest reduction at 150 min/week (systolic -7.23 mm Hg, diastolic -5.58 mm Hg) across 34 trials (1,787 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomised trials (Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomised trials of aerobic exercise in adults with hypertension, searched to April 2022: 34 trials with 1,787 participants; certainty rated with GRADE.
cards.result: Each 30 min/week of aerobic exercise reduced systolic BP by 1.78 mm Hg (95% CI -2.22 to -1.33; GRADE low), diastolic BP by 1.23 mm Hg (95% CI -1.53 to -0.93; GRADE moderate), resting heart rate by 1.08 beats/min and mean arterial pressure by 1.37 mm Hg. The dose-response was nonlinear, with the greatest decrement at 150 min/week: systolic -7.23 mm Hg (95% CI -9.08 to -5.39) and diastolic -5.58 mm Hg (95% CI -6.90 to -4.27). The authors conclude aerobic exercise produces a large, clinically important, dose-dependent BP reduction in hypertension, greatest at 150 min/week.
cards.watchOut: This card measures exercise against control, not against a drug — it sizes the exercise effect (about 7 mm Hg systolic at guideline-level volumes) so the reader can judge the network comparison on the anchor card; it does not itself compare exercise with medication.
cards.source: Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh B et al. Effects of aerobic exercise on blood pressure in patients with hypertension: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized trials. Hypertension Research. 2024. PMID: 37872373. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Carlson 2014: isometric resistance training lowered systolic BP by 6.77 mm Hg and diastolic by 3.96 mm Hg across 9 randomised trials — but the trials total only 223 participants and most enrolled normotensive people
cards.summary: Carlson 2014: isometric resistance training lowered systolic BP by 6.77 mm Hg and diastolic by 3.96 mm Hg across 9 randomised trials — but the trials total only 223 participants and most enrolled normotensive people
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Carlson 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of isometric exercise training lasting 4 or more weeks in adults, published 1966 to July 2013: 9 trials totalling 223 participants (127 exercise, 96 controls); 6 trials studied normotensive participants and 3 studied hypertensive patients.
cards.result: After isometric exercise training, systolic BP fell by a mean difference of 6.77 mm Hg (95% CI -7.93 to -5.62; P < .001), diastolic BP by 3.96 mm Hg (95% CI -4.80 to -3.12; P < .001), and mean arterial pressure by 3.94 mm Hg (95% CI -4.73 to -3.16; P < .001); resting heart rate fell slightly (mean difference -0.79 beats/min; P = .003). The authors note the magnitude was larger than previously reported for dynamic aerobic or resistance training, and suggest isometric training could serve as an adjunctive exercise modality.
cards.watchOut: Nine trials and 223 participants is a thin base, and two-thirds of the trials were in normotensive volunteers — the hypertensive-patient estimate is much less secure than the pooled figure suggests; small single-study Ns are printed on the face here as required.
cards.source: Carlson DJ et al. Isometric exercise training for blood pressure management: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2014. PMID: 24582191. cards.headline: Synthesis: exercise lowers systolic BP by roughly 6-7 mm Hg in hypertensive adults at achievable doses, and in the only exercise-versus-drug comparison — an indirect network analysis — that was statistically indistinguishable from single-drug therapy in hypertensive subgroups, though drugs won in the all-population analysis and no head-to-head trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: exercise lowers systolic BP by roughly 6-7 mm Hg in hypertensive adults at achievable doses, and in the only exercise-versus-drug comparison — an indirect network analysis — that was statistically indistinguishable from single-drug therapy in hypertensive subgroups, though drugs won in the all-population analysis and no head-to-head trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one network meta-analysis spanning 391 randomised trials (39,742 participants across exercise and drug literatures), one dose-response meta-analysis in hypertensive adults (34 trials, 1,787 participants), and one isometric-training meta-analysis (9 trials, 223 participants). Totals far exceed any small-N threshold, though the hypertensive exercise evidence inside the anchor analysis is only 56 trials and 3,508 people.
cards.result: Among hypertensive populations, endurance and dynamic resistance exercise showed no detectable difference from ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics on systolic BP; across all populations, medications achieved greater reductions (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg) (Naci 2019). Aerobic exercise at 150 min/week lowered systolic BP by 7.23 mm Hg in hypertensive adults (Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024); isometric training lowered it by 6.77 mm Hg in mostly normotensive samples (Carlson 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: 'as much as medication' is supported only by indirect comparison in hypertensive subgroups — exercise is a real antihypertensive intervention of single-drug magnitude, not a demonstrated substitute for drugs in a head-to-head trial.
cards.watchOut: Blood pressure is a surrogate: neither the exercise nor the drug trials in the network were powered for strokes or deaths, and adherence to structured exercise outside trials is the standing real-world caveat.
cards.source: Synthesis of Naci H et al. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30563873); Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh B et al. Hypertension Research. 2024 (PMID: 37872373); Carlson DJ et al. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2014 (PMID: 24582191).

shelves.title: Stopping NSAIDs to improve blood-pressure control (indirect evidence): starting an NSAID raises mean BP by about 5 mm Hg in hypertensive patients — the expected gain from stopping is that rise reversed, and it depends heavily on which NSAID it is
shelves.question: Should NSAIDs be stopped to improve blood pressure control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects/pharmacology · Antihypertensive Agents/antagonists & inhibitors · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selection Bias
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence, printed on the face: no randomised trial that randomises patients to stop versus continue an NSAID and measures blood pressure was found in the records fetched this session, so this shelf answers from the other direction — the size and drug-dependence of the pressor effect that stopping would remove. Two meta-analyses of randomised trials agree that starting an NSAID raises blood pressure in hypertensive patients: Johnson 1994 (PMID: 8037411; 38 placebo-controlled plus 12 comparative randomised trials) found a pooled rise in supine mean blood pressure of 5.0 mm Hg, with the largest antagonism against beta-blockers (6.2 mm Hg) and the largest pressor effect from piroxicam (6.2 mm Hg) and the least from sulindac and aspirin; Pope 1993 (PMID: 8435027; 54 studies, 1,324 participants, 92% hypertensive) found the effect confined to hypertensive subjects, with indomethacin raising mean arterial pressure by 3.59 mm Hg while sulindac, aspirin and ibuprofen had negligible average effects. A randomised ambulatory-BP trial in high-risk patients (Sowers 2005, PMID: 15668361; 404 patients with hypertension, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes) shows the effect is drug-specific in practice: rofecoxib raised 24-hour systolic BP by about 4 mm Hg and destabilised control in 30% of previously controlled patients, while celecoxib and naproxen did not significantly change 24-hour systolic BP. The PRECISION ambulatory-BP substudy is homed in pack #5289 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stopping an NSAID — particularly indomethacin, piroxicam or a strongly pressor agent in a patient whose control worsened on it — should be expected to improve blood pressure control by roughly the amount the drug raised it (a few mm Hg on average, more in susceptible patients), but that expectation is inferred from starting trials, not proven by a stopping trial.

cards.headline: Johnson 1994: across 38 placebo-controlled and 12 comparative randomised trials, NSAIDs raised supine mean blood pressure by 5.0 mm Hg and antagonised antihypertensive drugs — most against beta-blockers (6.2 mm Hg), with piroxicam the most pressor NSAID (6.2 mm Hg) and sulindac and aspirin the least
cards.summary: Johnson 1994: across 38 placebo-controlled and 12 comparative randomised trials, NSAIDs raised supine mean blood pressure by 5.0 mm Hg and antagonised antihypertensive drugs — most against beta-blockers (6.2 mm Hg), with piroxicam the most pressor NSAID (6.2 mm Hg) and sulindac and aspirin the least
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials of NSAID effects on blood pressure: 38 randomised placebo-controlled trials and 12 randomised trials comparing two or more NSAIDs (not placebo-controlled). The record does not state a single pooled participant total, so none is printed here.
cards.result: Pooled across trials, NSAIDs elevated supine mean blood pressure by 5.0 mm Hg (95% CI 1.2 to 8.7 mm Hg) and had no pooled effect on weight, creatinine clearance, plasma renin activity, or daily urinary sodium and prostaglandin excretion. NSAIDs antagonised the antihypertensive effect of beta-blockers (blood pressure elevation 6.2 mm Hg; 95% CI 1.1 to 11.4 mm Hg) more than vasodilators and diuretics. Among NSAIDs, piroxicam produced the most marked elevation (6.2 mm Hg; 95% CI 0.8 to 11.5 mm Hg), whereas sulindac and aspirin had the least hypertensive effect. The authors conclude NSAIDs may elevate blood pressure and antagonise antihypertensive medication enough to potentially increase hypertension-related morbidity.
cards.watchOut: These are trials of starting NSAIDs, mostly short-term: the inference that stopping reverses the rise is physiologically reasonable but is not itself randomised evidence, and the 5.0 mm Hg average conceals wide variation between drugs and patients.
cards.source: Johnson AG et al. Do nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs affect blood pressure? A meta-analysis. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1994. PMID: 8037411. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pope 1993: in 54 studies (1,324 participants, 92% hypertensive), the NSAID pressor effect appeared only in hypertensive subjects — indomethacin raised mean arterial pressure by 3.59 mm Hg, while sulindac, aspirin and ibuprofen had negligible average effects
cards.summary: Pope 1993: in 54 studies (1,324 participants, 92% hypertensive), the NSAID pressor effect appeared only in hypertensive subjects — indomethacin raised mean arterial pressure by 3.59 mm Hg, while sulindac, aspirin and ibuprofen had negligible average effects
cards.people: Meta-analysis of intervention studies of NSAIDs (or aspirin at 1.5 g/day or more) with documented blood pressure: 54 studies with 123 NSAID treatment arms; 1,324 participants, mean age 46 years, of whom 1,213 (92%) were hypertensive. Studies were at least 24 hours in duration; studies adjusting antihypertensive doses during NSAID treatment were excluded.
cards.result: The effects of NSAIDs on blood pressure were found solely in hypertensive subjects. Among these, after adjustment for dietary salt intake, mean arterial pressure rose by 3.59 mm Hg on indomethacin (57 treatment arms) and fell or barely changed on placebo (-2.59 mm Hg), ibuprofen (-0.83 mm Hg), aspirin (-1.76 mm Hg) and sulindac (-0.16 mm Hg); the effects of placebo, sulindac and aspirin differed statistically significantly from indomethacin. The authors conclude that in short-term use NSAIDs vary considerably in their effect on blood pressure, with indomethacin and naproxen associated with the largest increases and piroxicam, aspirin, ibuprofen and sulindac negligible on average. (The record's naproxen figure is typographically garbled in the fetched abstract and is therefore not printed numerically here.)
cards.watchOut: Short-term studies from the pre-COX-2 era with heterogeneous designs; the drug ranking (indomethacin worst, sulindac least) is the durable finding, and it means 'stop the NSAID' and 'switch the NSAID' are different interventions with different expected gains.
cards.source: Pope JE et al. A meta-analysis of the effects of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs on blood pressure. Archives of Internal Medicine. 1993. PMID: 8435027. cards.headline: Sowers 2005 (CRESCENT): in 404 patients with hypertension, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes, rofecoxib raised 24-hour systolic BP (130.3 to 134.5 mm Hg) and destabilised control in 30% of previously controlled patients — while celecoxib and naproxen did not significantly change 24-hour systolic BP
cards.summary: Sowers 2005 (CRESCENT): in 404 patients with hypertension, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes, rofecoxib raised 24-hour systolic BP (130.3 to 134.5 mm Hg) and destabilised control in 30% of previously controlled patients — while celecoxib and naproxen did not significantly change 24-hour systolic BP
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with ambulatory BP monitoring (Sowers 2005)
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial in patients with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and osteoarthritis: 404 patients randomised to celecoxib 200 mg once daily (n = 136), rofecoxib 25 mg once daily (n = 138), or naproxen 500 mg twice daily (n = 130) for 12 weeks, with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring at randomisation and at weeks 6 and 12. (Rofecoxib was later withdrawn from the market; it is carded here as the record's clearest demonstration that pressor effects differ by agent.)
cards.result: Osteoarthritis symptom relief was similar in all groups. Mean 24-hour systolic BP at week 6 rose significantly on rofecoxib (from 130.3 to 134.5 mm Hg; P < .001) but not on celecoxib (132.0 to 131.9 mm Hg; P = .54) or naproxen (133.7 to 133.0 mm Hg; P = .74); the between-drug differences were 3.78 mm Hg (rofecoxib versus celecoxib; 95% CI 1.18-6.38; P = .005) and 3.85 mm Hg (rofecoxib versus naproxen; 95% CI 1.15-6.55; P = .005). Among patients controlled at baseline, 30% on rofecoxib developed ambulatory hypertension by week 6 versus 16% on celecoxib (P = .05) and 19% on naproxen (not significant). The authors note destabilisation of hypertension control occurred to some extent in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: A drug-comparison trial, not a stopping trial — and one comparator (rofecoxib) is no longer marketed. Its lesson for this shelf is narrower: in a treated hypertensive patient, which NSAID it is matters as much as whether it is one, so uncontrolled BP on celecoxib or naproxen should not automatically be blamed on the NSAID.
cards.source: Sowers JR et al. The Effects of cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy on 24-hour blood pressure in patients with hypertension, osteoarthritis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. cards.headline: Synthesis: NSAIDs raise blood pressure in hypertensive patients by about 3.6-5.0 mm Hg on average (more with indomethacin or piroxicam, negligibly with sulindac or aspirin) — so stopping a pressor NSAID should improve control by roughly that amount, an inference from starting trials, since no randomised stopping trial was found
cards.summary: Synthesis: NSAIDs raise blood pressure in hypertensive patients by about 3.6-5.0 mm Hg on average (more with indomethacin or piroxicam, negligibly with sulindac or aspirin) — so stopping a pressor NSAID should improve control by roughly that amount, an inference from starting trials, since no randomised stopping trial was found
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of randomised starting-NSAID trials (50 randomised trials in Johnson 1994, participant total not stated in the record; 54 studies and 1,324 participants in Pope 1993) and one randomised ambulatory-BP drug-comparison trial (404 patients). The shelf total exceeds 1,700 documented participants, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled pressor effect of NSAIDs: +5.0 mm Hg supine mean BP (Johnson 1994); in hypertensive subjects only, indomethacin +3.59 mm Hg mean arterial pressure with sulindac, aspirin and ibuprofen negligible (Pope 1993). In treated hypertensive patients with diabetes, rofecoxib raised 24-hour systolic BP by about 4 mm Hg and destabilised control in 30%, while celecoxib and naproxen did not significantly change it (Sowers 2005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence: stop or switch the NSAID when control is poor, expecting a few mm Hg of improvement on average and more when the agent is a strongly pressor one; no carded trial has randomised the stopping itself.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is direction: every carded study starts or compares NSAIDs rather than withdrawing them, so the size of the fall on stopping in an individual patient — the actual clinical question — remains an extrapolation, and pain itself raises blood pressure when analgesia is withdrawn.
cards.source: Synthesis of Johnson AG et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1994 (PMID: 8037411); Pope JE et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 1993 (PMID: 8435027); Sowers JR et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005 (PMID: 15668361).
