shelves.title: Muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially: up to 85.8% versus placebo at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks (phase II, 233 participants) — a large surrogate effect with no cardiovascular outcomes evidence yet
shelves.question: Does muvalaplin lower Lp(a) levels?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Atherosclerosis/blood/drug therapy · Cardiovascular Diseases/blood/prevention & control · Diabetes Mellitus/blood/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/drug therapy/blood · Lipoprotein(a)/antagonists & inhibitors/blood · Hypolipidemic Agents · Apolipoproteins B/blood · C-Reactive Protein/analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, measuring a surrogate over 12 weeks. In the phase II KRAKEN trial (Nicholls 2025, PMID: 39556768), 233 participants with Lp(a) of 175 nmol/L or above and atherosclerotic disease, diabetes or familial hypercholesterolaemia were randomised to muvalaplin 10, 60 or 240 mg/day or placebo for 12 weeks: placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reductions were 47.6%, 81.7% and 85.8% respectively on the intact-Lp(a) assay (40.4%, 70.0% and 68.9% on the traditional apo(a)-based assay), with dose-dependent apolipoprotein B reductions and no safety or tolerability concerns. The phase I trial (Nicholls 2023, PMID: 37638695; 114 participants) had shown maximal placebo-adjusted reductions of 63-65% over 14 days with no clinically significant change in plasminogen. A 2024 landscape review (Anchouche 2024, PMID: 39576403) confirms the context: there are no approved Lp(a)-specific drugs and no completed outcomes trial for any of them, muvalaplin included. Muvalaplin is mentioned as fenced class context (explicitly 'not carded') on live shelf #1104, which homes the RNA-therapy Lp(a) trials; this shelf is its first evidence-card home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes, muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially and dose-dependently — by up to about 86% at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks — but whether that lowers cardiovascular events is entirely untested.

cards.headline: Nicholls 2025 (KRAKEN): in 233 participants with Lp(a) at or above 175 nmol/L, 12 weeks of muvalaplin lowered Lp(a) by 47.6% (10 mg), 81.7% (60 mg) and 85.8% (240 mg) versus placebo on the intact-Lp(a) assay — with no safety or tolerability concerns at any dose
cards.summary: Nicholls 2025 (KRAKEN): in 233 participants with Lp(a) at or above 175 nmol/L, 12 weeks of muvalaplin lowered Lp(a) by 47.6% (10 mg), 81.7% (60 mg) and 85.8% (240 mg) versus placebo on the intact-Lp(a) assay — with no safety or tolerability concerns at any dose
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase II (Nicholls 2025, KRAKEN)
cards.people: Phase II, placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind trial enrolling 233 participants with lipoprotein(a) concentrations of 175 nmol/L or greater, with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or familial hypercholesterolaemia, at 43 sites in Asia, Europe, Australia, Brazil and the United States (December 2022 to November 2023). Randomised to oral muvalaplin 10 mg/day (n = 34), 60 mg/day (n = 64) or 240 mg/day (n = 68), or placebo (n = 67), for 12 weeks. Median age 66 years; 33% female.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — placebo-adjusted percentage change in Lp(a) at week 12 — was -47.6% (95% CI 35.1%-57.7% reduction) at 10 mg/day, -81.7% (95% CI 78.1%-84.6%) at 60 mg/day and -85.8% (95% CI 83.1%-88.0%) at 240 mg/day using an intact Lp(a) assay, and -40.4%, -70.0% and -68.9% respectively using a traditional apolipoprotein(a)-based assay (percentages as printed in the record, stated here as reductions). Dose-dependent reductions in apolipoprotein B were 8.9% (95% CI -2.2% to 18.8%), 13.1% (95% CI 4.4%-20.9%) and 16.1% (95% CI 7.8%-23.7%). High-sensitivity C-reactive protein did not change. No safety or tolerability concerns were observed at any dosage. The authors state the effect of muvalaplin on cardiovascular events requires further investigation.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, 233 people, and a biomarker endpoint: the two assays disagree by up to 17 percentage points at the top dose because muvalaplin-bound apo(a) fragments register differently — so 'how much it lowers Lp(a)' partly depends on how Lp(a) is measured, and nothing here speaks to events.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. Oral Muvalaplin for Lowering of Lipoprotein(a): A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 39556768. Registry ID: NCT05563246. cards.headline: Nicholls 2023: in the phase I trial (114 participants), 14 days of muvalaplin lowered Lp(a) by up to 63-65% versus placebo, brought Lp(a) below 50 mg/dL in 93% of participants at doses of 100 mg or more, and did not significantly change plasminogen levels or activity
cards.summary: Nicholls 2023: in the phase I trial (114 participants), 14 days of muvalaplin lowered Lp(a) by up to 63-65% versus placebo, brought Lp(a) below 50 mg/dL in 93% of participants at doses of 100 mg or more, and did not significantly change plasminogen levels or activity
cards.people: Phase I randomised, double-blind, parallel-design study at one site in the Netherlands enrolling 114 participants: 55 in a single-ascending-dose group (healthy participants with any Lp(a) level; single doses of 1-800 mg or placebo) and 59 in a multiple-ascending-dose group (patients with Lp(a) of 30 mg/dL or higher; daily doses of 30-800 mg or placebo for 14 days). 105 completed the trial.
cards.result: Muvalaplin was not associated with tolerability concerns or clinically significant adverse effects. Lp(a) fell within 24 hours of the first dose and fell further with repeated dosing; the maximum placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reduction was 63% to 65%, resulting in Lp(a) levels below 50 mg/dL in 93% of participants, with similar effects at daily doses of 100 mg or more. Plasma half-life ranged from 70 to 414 hours across the 30-800 mg doses. No clinically significant changes in plasminogen levels or activity were observed — the selectivity check the drug was designed around, since it blocks the apo(a)-apoB100 interaction while avoiding the homologous plasminogen protein.
cards.watchOut: A 14-day, single-site, first-in-human study in mostly young, healthy volunteers: it establishes pharmacology and short-term tolerability only, and its participants are nothing like the high-risk patients in whom the drug would be used.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. Muvalaplin, an Oral Small Molecule Inhibitor of Lipoprotein(a) Formation: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37638695. Registry ID: NCT04472676. cards.headline: Anchouche 2024: as of this review, no Lp(a)-lowering drug is approved for routine use and no outcomes trial has completed for any candidate — muvalaplin is one of several early-stage agents whose event benefit is unproven
cards.summary: Anchouche 2024: as of this review, no Lp(a)-lowering drug is approved for routine use and no outcomes trial has completed for any candidate — muvalaplin is one of several early-stage agents whose event benefit is unproven
cards.people: Narrative review of the Lp(a)-lowering therapeutic pipeline (pelacarsen, olpasiran, lepodisiran, zerlasiran and muvalaplin), covering mechanism, trial stage and expected role; no participant population of its own.
cards.result: The review reports no outcome results for muvalaplin. Its stated position: elevated Lp(a) is a genetically determined, causal cardiovascular risk factor; several societies recommend Lp(a) screening at least once in all adults; there are currently no approved drugs aimed specifically at lowering Lp(a); the RNA-based candidates are in phase III outcomes trials (earliest conclusion 2025), while muvalaplin and the other small-molecule/newer candidates are in early-stage development. If the candidates prove effective in randomised trials, they would allow treatment of a presently unmitigated risk factor.
cards.watchOut: A review card is evidence about the state of the field, not about muvalaplin's effect size: it is carded so the shelf states plainly — from a fetched record — that no outcomes evidence exists, and it must never be cited as trial data.
cards.source: Anchouche K et al. Lp(a): A Rapidly Evolving Therapeutic Landscape. Current Atherosclerosis Reports. 2024. PMID: 39576403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially and dose-dependently (up to 85.8% versus placebo at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks in phase II; up to 65% over 14 days in phase I), with clean short-term tolerability and no plasminogen signal — and no evidence at all yet on cardiovascular events
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially and dose-dependently (up to 85.8% versus placebo at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks in phase II; up to 65% over 14 days in phase I), with clean short-term tolerability and no plasminogen signal — and no evidence at all yet on cardiovascular events
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase II randomised trial (233 participants with Lp(a) at or above 175 nmol/L), one phase I randomised trial (114 participants), and one narrative pipeline review with no participants. Total randomised participants 347, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reductions in KRAKEN were 47.6%, 81.7% and 85.8% at 10, 60 and 240 mg/day on the intact assay (40.4%, 70.0%, 68.9% on the apo(a)-based assay), with apolipoprotein B down up to 16.1% and no safety concerns (Nicholls 2025). Phase I showed 63-65% maximal reductions within 14 days and no significant plasminogen change (Nicholls 2023). No approved Lp(a)-specific drug and no completed outcomes trial exist for the class (Anchouche 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, surrogate endpoint: the Lp(a) lowering is large and real; the clinical benefit is unknown.
cards.watchOut: An oral drug that lowers a causal risk factor by 80%+ is exactly the profile that still requires an outcomes trial: Lp(a) lowering by other means has not yet been shown to reduce events in any completed trial carded in this library.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nicholls SJ et al. JAMA. 2025 (PMID: 39556768); Nicholls SJ et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37638695); Anchouche K et al. Current Atherosclerosis Reports. 2024 (PMID: 39576403).

shelves.title: Measure Lp(a) once in every adult? Consensus says yes (EAS 2022, NLA 2019) on cohort and genetic evidence — levels are stable for life and risk is continuous and causal — with no randomised screening trial behind the recommendation
shelves.question: Should Lp(a) be measured once in a lifetime in all adults?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aortic Valve Stenosis/complications · Atherosclerosis/etiology · Calcinosis/complications · Cardiovascular Diseases/complications · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans · Lipoprotein(a)/genetics · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/prognosis evidence and expert consensus only, printed on the face: no randomised trial of Lp(a) screening (measure everyone once versus do not) with clinical outcomes exists in the records fetched this session, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. The case for once-in-a-lifetime measurement rests on three legs, all carded. First, prognosis: in the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration's individual-participant analysis of 36 prospective studies (Erqou 2009, PMID: 19622820; 126,634 participants, 1.3 million person-years), Lp(a) was continuously and independently associated with coronary heart disease — adjusted relative risk 1.13 per 3.5-fold higher usual Lp(a) — and with ischaemic stroke (relative risk 1.10), but not with nonvascular mortality, and Lp(a) was highly consistent within individuals over several years, which is the property that makes a single lifetime measurement informative. Second, causality: Copenhagen genetic data (Kamstrup 2009, PMID: 19509380; about 40,000 participants across three studies) show genetically elevated Lp(a) tracks with myocardial infarction risk in a dose-dependent way consistent with a causal association. Third, consensus: the 2022 European Atherosclerosis Society statement (Kronenberg 2022, PMID: 36036785) recommends testing Lp(a) at least once in adults, and the National Lipid Association statement (Wilson 2019, PMID: 31147269) likewise supports testing to inform prevention — while both are explicit that, without a specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy of proven outcome benefit, what a high result changes today is the intensity of management of everything else. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: measuring Lp(a) once in every adult is recommended by both major consensus statements and is prognostically sound because levels are stable and causal — but it is a consensus recommendation resting on cohort and genetic evidence, not on a randomised screening trial.

cards.headline: Kronenberg 2022 (EAS consensus): the European Atherosclerosis Society panel recommends testing Lp(a) at least once in adults — on epidemiologic and genetic evidence in hundreds of thousands of people that Lp(a) is a causal, continuous risk factor, with cascade testing in familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature disease
cards.summary: Kronenberg 2022 (EAS consensus): the European Atherosclerosis Society panel recommends testing Lp(a) at least once in adults — on epidemiologic and genetic evidence in hundreds of thousands of people that Lp(a) is a causal, continuous risk factor, with cascade testing in familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature disease
cards.people: 2022 European Atherosclerosis Society consensus statement on lipoprotein(a) in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and aortic stenosis, updating the evidence and giving clinical guidance for testing and treating elevated Lp(a); it synthesises epidemiologic and genetic studies involving hundreds of thousands of individuals (no single study population of its own).
cards.result: The statement reports no new trial result. Its positions, as printed in the record: epidemiologic and genetic studies strongly support a causal and continuous association between Lp(a) concentration and cardiovascular outcomes in different ethnicities, and elevated Lp(a) is a risk factor even at very low LDL cholesterol levels; high Lp(a) is associated with aortic valve micro- and macrocalcification; current findings do not support Lp(a) as a risk factor for venous thrombotic events. The panel recommends testing Lp(a) concentration at least once in adults; cascade testing has potential value in familial hypercholesterolaemia or with a family or personal history of very high Lp(a) or premature ASCVD. Without specific Lp(a)-lowering therapies, early intensive risk-factor management is recommended, targeted by global risk and Lp(a) level; lipoprotein apheresis is an option for very high Lp(a) with progressive disease. Trials of specific Lp(a)-lowering treatments are stated to be critical to confirm clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: A consensus recommendation is guidance built on cohort and genetic evidence — it is not a screening trial, and the statement itself concedes there is as yet no specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy whose outcome benefit would complete the screening argument.
cards.source: Kronenberg F et al. Lipoprotein(a) in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and aortic stenosis: a European Atherosclerosis Society consensus statement. European Heart Journal. 2022. cards.headline: Erqou 2009 (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration): in 126,634 participants across 36 prospective studies, Lp(a) was continuously associated with coronary disease (adjusted relative risk 1.13 per 3.5-fold higher usual Lp(a); top-third rate 5.6 vs bottom-third 4.4 per 1,000 person-years) and ischaemic stroke (relative risk 1.10) — and was highly consistent within individuals over years
cards.summary: Erqou 2009 (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration): in 126,634 participants across 36 prospective studies, Lp(a) was continuously associated with coronary disease (adjusted relative risk 1.13 per 3.5-fold higher usual Lp(a); top-third rate 5.6 vs bottom-third 4.4 per 1,000 person-years) and ischaemic stroke (relative risk 1.10) — and was highly consistent within individuals over years
cards.people: Individual-participant meta-analysis of long-term prospective studies recording Lp(a) and subsequent vascular morbidity and mortality (January 1970 to March 2009): 126,634 participants in 36 studies, 1.3 million person-years of follow-up, 22,076 first-ever fatal or nonfatal vascular outcomes or nonvascular deaths, including 9,336 coronary heart disease outcomes and 1,903 ischaemic strokes; participants with known pre-existing coronary disease or stroke at baseline were excluded from the analyses.
cards.result: Lp(a) concentration was weakly correlated with several conventional risk factors and highly consistent within individuals over several years. Coronary rates in the top and bottom thirds of baseline Lp(a) were 5.6 (95% CI 5.4-5.9) and 4.4 (95% CI 4.2-4.6) per 1,000 person-years. The relative risk for coronary heart disease per 3.5-fold higher usual Lp(a) (1 SD) was 1.16 (95% CI 1.11-1.22) adjusted for age and sex, and 1.13 (95% CI 1.09-1.18) after further adjustment for lipids and other conventional factors — relative measures, printed with the absolute rates above. Corresponding adjusted relative risks were 1.10 (95% CI 1.02-1.18) for ischaemic stroke, 1.01 (95% CI 0.98-1.05) for nonvascular mortality, and 1.00 for cancer deaths — associations exclusive to vascular outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Prognostic association, however large and consistent, does not show that measuring Lp(a) changes management or outcomes — and the per-SD relative risk (1.13) is modest: Lp(a) refines risk at the extremes far more than it reclassifies the average adult.
cards.source: Erqou S et al. Lipoprotein(a) concentration and the risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, and nonvascular mortality. JAMA. 2009. PMID: 19622820. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kamstrup 2009: in Copenhagen studies totalling about 40,000 people, myocardial infarction risk rose stepwise with Lp(a) level — hazard ratio 2.6 above the 95th percentile versus below the 22nd — and genetic variants that raise Lp(a) raised risk in parallel, consistent with causation
cards.summary: Kamstrup 2009: in Copenhagen studies totalling about 40,000 people, myocardial infarction risk rose stepwise with Lp(a) level — hazard ratio 2.6 above the 95th percentile versus below the 22nd — and genetic variants that raise Lp(a) raised risk in parallel, consistent with causation
cards.type: Prospective cohort, cross-sectional and case-control genetic studies (Kamstrup 2009)
cards.people: Three studies of white individuals from Copenhagen, Denmark: the Copenhagen City Heart Study (prospective general-population study, 16 years of follow-up, n = 8,637, 599 myocardial infarctions), the Copenhagen General Population Study (cross-sectional, n = 29,388, 994 infarctions), and the Copenhagen Ischemic Heart Disease Study (case-control, n = 2,461, 1,231 infarctions). Plasma Lp(a), kringle IV type 2 (KIV-2) genotype and infarctions from 1976 to July 2007 were recorded.
cards.result: In the prospective study, multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios for myocardial infarction rose with Lp(a) percentile band: 1.2 (95% CI 0.9-1.6; 59 events/10,000 person-years) for the 22nd-66th percentile, 1.6 (95% CI 1.1-2.2; 75) for the 67th-89th, 1.9 (95% CI 1.2-3.0; 84) for the 90th-95th, and 2.6 (95% CI 1.6-4.1; 108) above the 95th percentile, versus 55 events/10,000 person-years below the 22nd percentile (trend P < .001). KIV-2 repeat number explained 21-27% of variation in Lp(a) levels, and genetically lower repeat number (higher Lp(a)) tracked with higher infarction risk across all three studies; on instrumental-variable analysis, genetically elevated Lp(a) carried a hazard ratio of 1.22 (95% CI 1.09-1.37) per doubling of Lp(a). Hazard ratios are relative measures, printed with the absolute event rates the record gives.
cards.watchOut: All participants were white Danes, and a causal risk factor is not automatically a useful screening test: the value of measuring everyone depends on how many high results change treatment — a question these data cannot answer.
cards.source: Kamstrup PR et al. Genetically elevated lipoprotein(a) and increased risk of myocardial infarction. JAMA. 2009. PMID: 19509380. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wilson 2019 (National Lipid Association): a US scientific statement likewise supports Lp(a) testing in clinical practice — elevated levels affect an estimated 20% of the population, with observational and genetic evidence for a causal role in myocardial infarction, stroke and aortic stenosis
cards.summary: Wilson 2019 (National Lipid Association): a US scientific statement likewise supports Lp(a) testing in clinical practice — elevated levels affect an estimated 20% of the population, with observational and genetic evidence for a causal role in myocardial infarction, stroke and aortic stenosis
cards.people: Scientific statement of the National Lipid Association reviewing evidence-based considerations for testing Lp(a) in clinical practice and using Lp(a) levels to inform treatment strategies in primary and secondary prevention; no study population of its own.
cards.result: The statement reports no new primary result. As printed in the record: Lp(a) is a well-recognised independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, with elevated levels estimated to be prevalent in 20% of the population; observational and genetic evidence strongly support a causal relationship between high Lp(a) and atherosclerotic events such as myocardial infarction and stroke, and valvular aortic stenosis. The statement reviews when to test and how levels should inform prevention strategies.
cards.watchOut: A second consensus voice agreeing with the first is not independent evidence — both statements rest on the same cohort and genetic literature carded above, and neither cites a trial showing that population measurement improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two major consensus statements recommend measuring Lp(a) at least once in adults, and the underlying evidence is strong for prognosis and causality — levels are stable within individuals (the property that makes 'once' enough), coronary risk rises continuously (relative risk 1.13 per SD) and reaches a hazard ratio of 2.6 at the top percentiles — but no randomised screening trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: two major consensus statements recommend measuring Lp(a) at least once in adults, and the underlying evidence is strong for prognosis and causality — levels are stable within individuals (the property that makes 'once' enough), coronary risk rises continuously (relative risk 1.13 per SD) and reaches a hazard ratio of 2.6 at the top percentiles — but no randomised screening trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one European consensus statement and one US scientific statement (no participants of their own), one individual-participant cohort meta-analysis (126,634 participants, 36 studies) and one three-study genetic programme (about 40,000 participants). Documented participants total over 165,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Lp(a) was highly consistent within individuals over several years and continuously associated with coronary disease and ischaemic stroke, but not nonvascular death (Erqou 2009). Genetic elevation tracked with infarction risk dose-dependently, consistent with causation (Kamstrup 2009). Both the EAS (Kronenberg 2022) and the NLA (Wilson 2019) recommend at-least-once testing in adults, with cascade testing in familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature disease, and — absent a proven Lp(a)-specific therapy — intensified management of other risk factors when the result is high. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: a reasonable, consensus-backed measurement whose outcome benefit has never been randomised.
cards.watchOut: Screening logic needs a treatment that changes outcomes: until an Lp(a)-lowering therapy proves event reduction, a high once-in-a-lifetime result mainly re-aims conventional prevention — valuable, but a weaker claim than the measurement's advocates sometimes make.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kronenberg F et al. European Heart Journal. 2022 (PMID: 36036785); Erqou S et al. JAMA. 2009 (PMID: 19622820); Kamstrup PR et al. JAMA. 2009 (PMID: 19509380); Wilson DP et al. Journal of Clinical Lipidology. 2019 (PMID: 31147269).

shelves.title: Lipoprotein apheresis in familial hypercholesterolemia (observational only): LDL falls by about two-thirds per course and on-treatment event rates are far below pre-treatment rates in every registry — with no randomised trial and progression still seen in homozygous children
shelves.question: Does lipoprotein apheresis improve outcomes in familial hypercholesterolemia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Component Removal/methods · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Disease Progression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Germany · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemias/blood/therapy · Hypolipidemic Agents/therapeutic use · Incidence · Lipoprotein(a)/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no randomised trial of lipoprotein apheresis, and every carded outcome study uses the same before-and-after design, comparing event rates in the years before apheresis started with the years on it — a design that flatters treatment, because patients start apheresis after events cluster. Within that limit the findings are consistent. In the prospective multicentre Pro(a)LiFe study (Leebmann 2013, PMID: 24056686; 170 patients with Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia and progressive disease on maximally tolerated therapy), mean annual major adverse coronary event rates fell from 0.41 in the two years before apheresis to 0.09 in the two years on it. The German registry (Schettler 2017, PMID: 28233268; 1,435 patients, 15,527 treatments) found the same pattern — a 78% lower MACE rate over two years on apheresis — with median per-session LDL reduction of 67.5% and side effects in 5.9% of treatments, mainly puncture problems. A small Polish FH series (Mickiewicz 2021, PMID: 33386762; 23 patients, N printed on the face) found event rates falling in parallel with 70% LDL reductions. In children with homozygous FH (Hudgins 2008, PMID: 18940291; 29 patients), biweekly apheresis lowered LDL by 75% acutely and 48% chronically and was well tolerated for years — yet atherosclerosis still progressed in 30%, and target LDL levels were not achieved. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: apheresis unquestionably removes LDL and Lp(a) at each session and event rates are much lower on treatment than before it in every registry, but the before-after design cannot separate the treatment effect from regression to the mean and the intensified care that surrounds it.

cards.headline: Leebmann 2013 (Pro(a)LiFe): in 170 patients with Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia and progressive cardiovascular disease, mean annual major adverse coronary events fell from 0.41 in the 2 years before apheresis to 0.09 in the 2 years on it (P < 0.0001) — a before-and-after comparison with no control group
cards.summary: Leebmann 2013 (Pro(a)LiFe): in 170 patients with Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia and progressive cardiovascular disease, mean annual major adverse coronary events fell from 0.41 in the 2 years before apheresis to 0.09 in the 2 years on it (P < 0.0001) — a before-and-after comparison with no control group
cards.people: Prospective observational multicentre study of 170 patients who commenced lipoprotein apheresis because of Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia and progressive cardiovascular disease despite maximally tolerated lipid-lowering treatment; mean age 51 years at the first cardiovascular event and 57 years at the first apheresis. Before apheresis, mean LDL cholesterol was 2.56 mmol/L (99.0 mg/dL, as printed in the record) and mean Lp(a) 104.9 mg/dL (as printed in the record). Event incidence in the two years before starting (y-2, y-1) was compared with the two years on treatment (y+1, y+2).
cards.result: Mean annual rates of major adverse coronary events declined from 0.41 for the 2 years before apheresis to 0.09 for the 2 years during apheresis (P < 0.0001); event rates including all vascular beds declined from 0.61 to 0.16 (P < 0.0001). Year by year, major adverse coronary event rates rose from 0.30 (y-2) to 0.54 (y-1) before apheresis, then fell to 0.14 (y+1) and 0.05 (y+2). The authors conclude that in patients with Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia, progressive disease and maximally tolerated medication, apheresis effectively lowered the incidence rate of cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is each patient against their own pre-treatment years — and event rates were rising steeply just before apheresis began (0.30 to 0.54), exactly the pattern that guarantees a fall afterwards even with an ineffective treatment (regression to the mean); the population is Lp(a)-driven disease, overlapping with but not identical to familial hypercholesterolaemia.
cards.source: Leebmann J et al. Lipoprotein apheresis in patients with maximally tolerated lipid-lowering therapy, lipoprotein(a)-hyperlipoproteinemia, and progressive cardiovascular disease: prospective observational multicenter study. Circulation. 2013. PMID: 24056686. Registry ID: DRKS00003119 (German Clinical Trials Register, from the record). cards.headline: Schettler 2017 (German Lipoprotein Apheresis Registry): in 1,435 patients and 15,527 treatments, median LDL fell 67.5% and Lp(a) 71.1% per treatment course, the MACE rate was 78% lower over 2 years on apheresis than in the 2 years before, and side effects occurred in 5.9% of treatments
cards.summary: Schettler 2017 (German Lipoprotein Apheresis Registry): in 1,435 patients and 15,527 treatments, median LDL fell 67.5% and Lp(a) 71.1% per treatment course, the MACE rate was 78% lower over 2 years on apheresis than in the 2 years before, and side effects occurred in 5.9% of treatments
cards.people: German Lipoprotein Apheresis Registry (GLAR), 2012-2016: retrospective and prospective observational data from 71 German apheresis centres on 1,435 patients undergoing lipoprotein apheresis for high LDL cholesterol and/or high Lp(a) with cardiovascular disease or progressive cardiovascular disease, on maximally tolerated lipid-lowering medication; 15,527 completely documented treatments. The registry population mixes familial hypercholesterolaemia and Lp(a)-driven indications, as German practice does.
cards.result: All treated patients showed a median LDL cholesterol reduction rate of 67.5% and a median Lp(a) reduction rate of 71.1%. Analysed in the Pro(a)LiFe pattern (event rates 1 and 2 years before versus 2 years on treatment), a MACE reduction of 78% was observed during two years of apheresis treatment. Side effects of apheresis treatment were low (5.9%) and mainly comprised puncture problems. The authors conclude the registry data show apheresis lowers the incidence rate of cardiovascular events in this population and is safe with a low rate of side effects.
cards.watchOut: Same before-and-after architecture as Pro(a)LiFe, at registry scale: the 78% figure is a relative reduction in event rates between two uncontrolled periods, not a treatment effect estimate, and indication mix means the FH-specific benefit cannot be separated out from this record.
cards.source: Schettler VJJ et al. The German Lipoprotein Apheresis Registry (GLAR) - almost 5 years on. Clinical Research in Cardiology Supplements. 2017. PMID: 28233268. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mickiewicz 2021: in 23 Polish patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia and hyper-Lp(a) (small N on the face), apheresis cut LDL by 70.0% and Lp(a) by 72.7% per session, and annual adverse event rates fell from 0.365 before treatment to 0.0 (median) on it
cards.summary: Mickiewicz 2021: in 23 Polish patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia and hyper-Lp(a) (small N on the face), apheresis cut LDL by 70.0% and Lp(a) by 72.7% per session, and annual adverse event rates fell from 0.365 before treatment to 0.0 (median) on it
cards.people: Longitudinal observational study in Poland of 23 patients with hyperlipoproteinaemia(a) and familial hypercholesterolaemia on maximally tolerated lipid-lowering therapy, undergoing 1,014 lipoprotein apheresis sessions between 2013 and 2020; pre-apheresis LDL cholesterol was 155 mg/dL (median; interquartile range 107-228) and Lp(a) 0.56 g/L (56 mg/dL). Annual event rates before and after starting apheresis were compared over matched periods within each patient. Study N = 23.
cards.result: Apheresis reduced LDL cholesterol to 50 mg/dL (median) and Lp(a) to 0.13 g/L (13 mg/dL) per session — percent reductions of 70.0% for LDL cholesterol and 72.7% for Lp(a). The annual rate of adverse cardiac and vascular events fell significantly (median 0.365 [0.0-0.585] before versus 0.0 [0.0-0.265] on treatment; P = .047), as did major adverse cardiac events (0.365 versus 0.0; P = .031). The authors conclude apheresis substantially reduces LDL cholesterol and Lp(a) and lowers cardiovascular event rates in these Polish patients.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-three patients, medians with wide interquartile ranges, and the same uncontrolled before-after design: this is the most FH-specific card on the shelf and also one of the smallest — directionally consistent with the registries, evidentially light.
cards.source: Mickiewicz A et al. Cardiovascular events in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia and hyperlipoproteinaemia (a): Indications for lipoprotein apheresis in Poland. Journal of Clinical Apheresis. 2021. PMID: 33386762. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Registry analysis of all 29 patients in the United States who began LDL apheresis before 18 years of age at 15 sites in the 11 years after FDA approval, plus a detailed chart review of 9 patients at one institute: 20 patients were currently treated, mean age at start 9 years (range 3-15), mean treatment duration 6 years (range 2-21); baseline LDL cholesterol 521 mg/dL (mean). Study N = 29.
cards.result: Baseline LDL cholesterol (521 ± 126 mg/dL) was acutely lowered by 75% and chronically lowered by 48% with biweekly sessions. Systemic adverse events were uncommon, and the authors conclude apheresis is well tolerated for decades even by very young children. However, atherosclerotic disease of the coronary arteries and/or aorta or aortic valve was evident in 12 patients (60%) at baseline and progressed to more severe, symptomatic disease in 6 (30%); target LDL levels were not achieved. This is the shelf's only homozygous-FH-specific long-term record, and it reports disease status rather than a controlled event comparison.
cards.watchOut: No comparator at all — in untreated homozygous FH, infarction and death by the teenage years are the expected course (as the record's own background states), so survival on treatment is suggestive; but the 30% progression rate is the necessary counterweight to any 'apheresis fixes FH' reading.
cards.source: Hudgins LC et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of low-density lipoprotein apheresis in childhood for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. American Journal of Cardiology. 2008. PMID: 18940291. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: apheresis removes about two-thirds of LDL cholesterol (and Lp(a)) per treatment course in every dataset, and event rates on treatment run far below the pre-treatment years (0.41 to 0.09 per year in Pro(a)LiFe; 78% lower MACE rate in the German registry) — all of it observational before-and-after evidence with no randomised trial, and with documented disease progression in homozygous children despite treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: apheresis removes about two-thirds of LDL cholesterol (and Lp(a)) per treatment course in every dataset, and event rates on treatment run far below the pre-treatment years (0.41 to 0.09 per year in Pro(a)LiFe; 78% lower MACE rate in the German registry) — all of it observational before-and-after evidence with no randomised trial, and with documented disease progression in homozygous children despite treatment
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective multicentre before-and-after study (170 patients), one national registry (1,435 patients, 15,527 treatments), one small FH series (23 patients), and one paediatric homozygous-FH registry (29 patients). Documented participants total over 1,600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the two small series carry their Ns on their faces.
cards.result: Per-session/course lipid removal is consistent: LDL -67.5% median and Lp(a) -71.1% median (GLAR); LDL -70.0% and Lp(a) -72.7% (Mickiewicz 2021); LDL -75% acute, -48% chronic in children (Hudgins 2008). Event rates on treatment were far lower than in the pre-treatment years in both adult datasets (Leebmann 2013; Schettler 2017) and in the small FH series (Mickiewicz 2021), with treatment side effects in 5.9% of sessions, mainly puncture problems. Against that, 30% of treated homozygous children progressed to more severe symptomatic disease (Hudgins 2008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: apheresis very probably improves outcomes in severe FH, on the strength of huge lipid removal and uniformly lower on-treatment event rates — but the effect size cannot be honestly quantified without a control group.
cards.watchOut: Every adult outcome number on this shelf compares patients with their own past: apheresis starts when disease is progressing fastest, so some of the apparent benefit is the calendar, not the machine — the shelf's stamp stays at POSSIBLE however large the before-after differences look.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leebmann J et al. Circulation. 2013 (PMID: 24056686); Schettler VJJ et al. Clinical Research in Cardiology Supplements. 2017 (PMID: 28233268); Mickiewicz A et al. shelves.title: Intensive blood-pressure control and thoracic aneurysm growth (untested as a strategy): beta-blockade slowed Marfan aortic dilatation versus no treatment in one small 1994 trial — no study has randomised a blood-pressure target, in Marfan or in degenerative aneurysm
shelves.question: Does intensive blood pressure control slow thoracic aortic aneurysm growth?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aortic Dissection/etiology · Aorta/pathology · Aortic Aneurysm/etiology/pathology · Aortic Valve Insufficiency/etiology · Dilatation, Pathologic · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure/etiology · Humans · Male · Marfan Syndrome/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Morbidity · Propranolol/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial has tested intensive versus standard blood-pressure targets for thoracic aortic aneurysm growth in any record fetched this session; the shelf is built from the nearest evidence, drug trials in Marfan aortopathy, and says so on its face. The one trial of a blood-pressure-lowering drug against no treatment (Shores 1994, PMID: 8152445; 70 patients with Marfan syndrome, open-label randomised propranolol, mean follow-up about 10 years) found the aortic-root dilatation rate was significantly slower on beta-blockade (slope 0.023 versus 0.084 per year, P < 0.001), with clinical endpoints reached in 5 treated versus 9 control patients. Adding an ARB on top of standard therapy splits: the COMPARE programme (van Andel 2020, PMID: 32548624; 233 randomised adults) found a small significant slowing of aortic-root dilatation over 3 years on losartan and, in self-selected long-term follow-up, fewer deaths (0 versus 5) and dissections (3 versus 11) among continuers — while a small double-blind add-on trial (Muiño-Mosquera 2017, PMID: 28657492; 22 patients, N on the face) found no additional effect of losartan on aortic growth (the treatment made no difference). The large losartan-versus-atenolol trial in young Marfan patients is homed on live shelf #1417 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Nothing carded here addresses degenerative (non-Marfan) thoracic aneurysm, and nothing compares BP targets or achieved BP levels. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): blood-pressure-lowering treatment probably slows aortic growth in heritable aortopathy — one small old open-label trial says yes for beta-blockade — but 'intensive control' as a strategy, and any benefit in ordinary degenerative thoracic aneurysm, are untested.

cards.headline: Shores 1994: in 70 patients with Marfan syndrome randomised open-label to propranolol or no treatment and followed about 10 years, the aortic-root dilatation rate was significantly slower on beta-blockade (slope 0.023 vs 0.084 per year, P < 0.001), with clinical endpoints in 5 treated versus 9 control patients
cards.summary: Shores 1994: in 70 patients with Marfan syndrome randomised open-label to propranolol or no treatment and followed about 10 years, the aortic-root dilatation rate was significantly slower on beta-blockade (slope 0.023 vs 0.084 per year, P < 0.001), with clinical endpoints in 5 treated versus 9 control patients
cards.people: Open-label randomised trial of propranolol in adolescent and adult patients with classic Marfan syndrome: 32 treated and 38 untreated (control) patients; propranolol dose individualised (mean 212 mg/day). Aortic-root dimensions and clinical endpoints (aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, cardiovascular surgery, congestive heart failure, death) were monitored for an average of 9.3 years in the control group and 10.7 years in the treatment group; all 70 patients were analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The mean slope of the regression line for aortic-root dimensions — the rate of dilatation — was significantly lower in the treatment group than in the control group (0.023 vs 0.084 per year, P < 0.001). Clinical endpoints were reached in 5 patients in the treatment group and 9 in the control group; the Kaplan-Meier survival curve for the treatment group differed significantly from the control group during the middle years and remained better throughout the study. The authors conclude prophylactic beta-adrenergic blockade is effective in slowing aortic dilatation and reducing aortic complications in some patients with Marfan syndrome. The record reports the dilatation slopes without units in the fetched abstract, and no blood-pressure values or targets, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The only carded trial of BP-lowering treatment versus none — and it is small (70 patients), open-label, from 1994, in Marfan syndrome specifically, testing a drug chosen to blunt ejection impulse and heart rate rather than to reach any blood-pressure target: it supports 'treat' much more than it supports 'treat intensively to a number'.
cards.source: Shores J et al. Progression of aortic dilatation and the benefit of long-term beta-adrenergic blockade in Marfan's syndrome. New England Journal of Medicine. 1994. PMID: 8152445. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van Andel 2020 (COMPARE long-term follow-up): in the 233-patient randomised Marfan trial, 3 years of losartan produced a small significant slowing of aortic-root dilatation; over a median 8 years, patients who continued losartan had fewer deaths (0 vs 5) and dissections (3 vs 11) than never-users — in a self-selected comparison
cards.summary: van Andel 2020 (COMPARE long-term follow-up): in the 233-patient randomised Marfan trial, 3 years of losartan produced a small significant slowing of aortic-root dilatation; over a median 8 years, patients who continued losartan had fewer deaths (0 vs 5) and dissections (3 vs 11) than never-users — in a self-selected comparison
cards.type: Randomised trial long-term follow-up, post-trial self-selected comparison (van Andel 2020)
cards.people: Long-term follow-up of the multicentre randomised COMPARE trial in adults with Marfan syndrome (inclusion 2008-2009): 233 patients randomised to losartan on top of regular treatment (beta-blockers in 71%) or no additional medication for 3 years. After the trial, patients chose whether to continue losartan; over a median follow-up of 8 years, 75 patients used losartan throughout and 78 control-group patients never used it. The continuer group was younger at inclusion (34 vs 41 years) and more often on beta-blockers (81% vs 64%).
cards.result: As summarised in this record, the original trial showed a small but significant beneficial effect of 3-year losartan treatment on aortic root dilatation rate, with no significant effect on clinical endpoints over 3 years. Over the full follow-up, 5 deaths, 14 aortic dissections, 23 aortic root replacements, 3 reoperations and 3 vascular graft implantations beyond the aortic root occurred. Patients who used losartan throughout had fewer events than controls: death 0 vs 5 (P = 0.014), aortic dissection 3 vs 11 (P = 0.013), elective aortic root replacement 10 vs 13 (P = 0.264), reoperation 1 vs 2 (P = 0.463), vascular graft implantation 0 vs 3 (P = 0.071), and composite endpoint 14 vs 26 (P = 0.019); results were similar after adjustment for age and beta-blocker use. The authors suggest a clinical benefit of combined losartan and beta-blocker treatment.
cards.watchOut: After year 3 the comparison is no longer randomised — patients chose to continue losartan, and continuers differed at baseline (younger, more beta-blocker use); the dilatation benefit over the randomised period is described in this record only as 'small but significant', without the rate figures, so none are printed.
cards.source: van Andel MM et al. Long-term clinical outcomes of losartan in patients with Marfan syndrome: follow-up of the multicentre randomized controlled COMPARE trial. European Heart Journal. 2020. PMID: 32548624. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Muiño-Mosquera 2017: in a double-blind trial of losartan added to beta-blocker therapy in 22 Marfan patients (small N on the face), aortic root growth over 3 years was identical in both groups (median 1 mm) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: Muiño-Mosquera 2017: in a double-blind trial of losartan added to beta-blocker therapy in 22 Marfan patients (small N on the face), aortic root growth over 3 years was identical in both groups (median 1 mm) — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: Prospective, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of losartan added to beta-blocker therapy in patients with Marfan syndrome, assessing aortic growth and ventricular function over 3 years, with aortic dissection, prophylactic aortic surgery and death as secondary outcomes: 22 patients enrolled. Study N = 22, printed on the face.
cards.result: There was a mild and similar increase in the aortic root during the 3 years of follow-up in both groups (median 1 mm, interquartile range -1 to 1.5, in the losartan group and 1 mm, interquartile range -0.25 to 1, in the placebo group; P = 1). Diastolic and systolic ventricular function was normal at baseline in both groups and remained stable. One patient in the placebo group had a subclavian artery dissection during follow-up. The authors conclude losartan on top of beta-blocker therapy has no additional effect on aortic growth or cardiac function in Marfan syndrome, while noting the results are underpowered.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two patients cannot exclude a worthwhile effect — the authors say so themselves — but as the only double-blind add-on trial carded, its null result is the counterweight to COMPARE's open-label-era findings, and the split between them is real.
cards.source: Muiño-Mosquera L et al. Efficacy of losartan as add-on therapy to prevent aortic growth and ventricular dysfunction in patients with Marfan syndrome: a randomized, double-blind clinical trial. Acta Cardiologica. 2017. PMID: 28657492. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial has tested intensive blood-pressure targets in thoracic aortic aneurysm; the nearest evidence — Marfan drug trials — shows beta-blockade slowed aortic-root dilatation versus no treatment in one small open-label trial, while ARB add-on evidence splits between a small dilatation benefit in COMPARE and a null result in the only double-blind add-on trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial has tested intensive blood-pressure targets in thoracic aortic aneurysm; the nearest evidence — Marfan drug trials — shows beta-blockade slowed aortic-root dilatation versus no treatment in one small open-label trial, while ARB add-on evidence splits between a small dilatation benefit in COMPARE and a null result in the only double-blind add-on trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open-label randomised trial of beta-blockade versus no treatment (70 patients with Marfan syndrome), one randomised ARB trial's long-term follow-up (233 patients with Marfan syndrome), and one small double-blind ARB add-on trial (22 patients with Marfan syndrome). Total randomised participants 325, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; every participant had Marfan syndrome, and none had ordinary degenerative thoracic aneurysm. The large losartan-versus-atenolol Marfan trial is homed on live shelf #1417 and cross-pointed there.
cards.result: Aortic-root dilatation slope was 0.023 versus 0.084 per year on propranolol versus control (P < 0.001), with clinical endpoints in 5 versus 9 patients (Shores 1994). Losartan slowed dilatation slightly over 3 randomised years in COMPARE, with fewer deaths and dissections in self-selected long-term continuers (van Andel 2020), but added nothing on top of beta-blockade in the double-blind trial (median growth 1 mm in both groups; Muiño-Mosquera 2017). No carded record compares blood-pressure targets, reports achieved BP against growth rate, or studies non-Marfan thoracic aneurysm. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): keep blood pressure treated in thoracic aneurysm — the growth-slowing claim for intensive control specifically is untested.
cards.watchOut: Extrapolation is this shelf's core weakness: Marfan aortopathy is a wall-biology disease in young patients, degenerative thoracic aneurysm is a different disease in older ones, and neither population has ever been randomised to a blood-pressure target — guideline BP advice for aneurysm rests on reasoning, not on a growth-rate trial.

synthesis the carded evidence: one open-label randomised trial of beta-blockade versus no treatment (70 patients with marfan syndrome), one randomised arb trial's long-term follow-up (233 patients with marfan syndrome), and one small double-blind arb add-on trial (22 patients with marfan syndrome). total randomised participants 325, so no small-n stamp labelling applies; every participant had marfan syndrome, and none had ordinary degenerative thoracic aneurysm. the large losartan-versus-atenolol marfan trial is homed on live shelf #1417 and cross-pointed there. aortic-root dilatation slope was 0.023 versus 0.084 per year on propranolol versus control (p < 0.001), with clinical endpoints in 5 versus 9 patients (shores 1994). losartan slowed dilatation slightly over 3 randomised years in compare, with fewer deaths and dissections in self-selected long-term continuers (van andel 2020), but added nothing on top of beta-blockade in the double-blind trial (median growth 1 mm in both groups; muiño-mosquera 2017). no carded record compares blood-pressure targets, reports achieved bp against growth rate, or studies non-marfan thoracic aneurysm. proposed maybe (weak evidence): keep blood pressure treated in thoracic aneurysm — the growth-slowing claim for intensive control specifically is untested. extrapolation is this shelf's core weakness: marfan aortopathy is a wall-biology disease in young patients, degenerative thoracic aneurysm is a different disease in older ones, and neither population has ever been randomised to a blood-pressure target — guideline bp advice for aneurysm rests on reasoning, not on a growth-rate trial. synthesis of shores j et al. new england journal of medicine. 1994 (pmid: 8152445); van andel mm et al. european heart journal. 2020 (pmid: 32548624); muiño-mosquera l et al. acta cardiologica. 2017 (pmid: 28657492).

shelves.title: Balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge to TAVI (observational only, split): symptoms and gradients improve and patients do reach TAVI — but the largest registry associates the bridge strategy with higher in-hospital mortality than direct TAVR
shelves.question: Does balloon aortic valvuloplasty help as a bridge to TAVI?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement mortality trends · Male · Female · Hospital Mortality trends · Aged, 80 and over · Aortic Valve Stenosis surgery mortality · Retrospective Studies · Balloon Valvuloplasty mortality trends · Registries · Aged · Japan epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) reliably opens the valve for a time: in a 112-patient prospective cohort where 51.8% of procedures were bridges to TAVI, valve area rose from 0.59 to 0.82 cm2 and mean gradient fell from 58.0 to 40.5 mm Hg (Daniec 2017, PMID: 27514931), and in a 224-patient contemporary cohort 61% of BAV was bridging, half of patients improved by at least one NYHA class at 30 days, and 40% of the bridge group reached TAVI/AVR within 12 months — though 12-month mortality was still 26% in the bridge group (Dawson 2020, PMID: 32341170). A systematic review of 27 studies and 4,123 patients found BAV safer in the TAVI era (in-hospital mortality 4.6% vs 8.5% in the earlier era), with 23.4% of contemporary BAV done as a bridge to TAVR (Kumar 2016, PMID: 27466275). Against this, the largest record — a 27,600-patient Japanese national registry — found patients bridged with BAV before TAVR died in hospital more often than patients taken straight to TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%), with bridging an independent correlate of death (Fujimoto 2024, PMID: 38977224); bridged patients are plausibly sicker and more often emergent, so confounding by indication likely explains part or all of that gap, but no randomised trial exists to settle it. PROPOSED SPLIT (symptom and haemodynamic benefit as a bridge in cohort data; a national-registry mortality signal against the bridge strategy versus direct TAVR) — observational only: BAV can carry selected unstable patients to TAVI, but the bridge strategy has never been shown to beat going straight to TAVI.

cards.headline: Fujimoto 2024: in a 27,600-patient national registry, patients bridged with balloon valvuloplasty before TAVR died in hospital more often than patients taken straight to TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%) — an observational association, not a randomised comparison
cards.summary: Fujimoto 2024: in a 27,600-patient national registry, patients bridged with balloon valvuloplasty before TAVR died in hospital more often than patients taken straight to TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%) — an observational association, not a randomised comparison
cards.people: 27,600 patients with aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR in Japan between October 2013 and March 2021, from a nationwide inpatient database: 27,387 direct TAVR and 213 who received balloon aortic valvuloplasty at least 1 day before TAVR as a bridge. Median age 85 years (interquartile range 82–88); 33.3% (9,188) were male.
cards.result: Overall in-hospital mortality was 1.3% and fell over time, but the BAV bridge-to-TAVR group had significantly higher in-hospital mortality than the direct TAVR group (5.6% vs 1.3%; P < .0001), in both unplanned/emergent and planned admission settings. Factors associated with in-hospital mortality included age, body mass index, chronic renal disease, percutaneous coronary intervention, and BAV bridge to TAVR. The authors conclude that practical criteria for BAV bridge to TAVR should be proposed to improve outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication is the central problem: patients are bridged precisely because they are unstable, emergent or temporarily unfit for TAVR, so a higher death rate in the bridged group is expected even if bridging itself helps them. Only 213 of 27,600 patients were bridged, and no adjustment in the record can fully remove that selection.
cards.source: Fujimoto T et al. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty bridge to transcatheter aortic valve replacement is associated with worse in-hospital mortality. International Journal of Cardiology. 2024. PMID: 38977224. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dawson 2020: in a 224-patient contemporary cohort, 61% of balloon valvuloplasty was bridging; half improved a NYHA class by 30 days, 40% of the bridge group reached TAVI/AVR within a year, and 12-month mortality was 26% in the bridge group versus 50% for destination BAV
cards.summary: Dawson 2020: in a 224-patient contemporary cohort, 61% of balloon valvuloplasty was bridging; half improved a NYHA class by 30 days, 40% of the bridge group reached TAVI/AVR within a year, and 12-month mortality was 26% in the bridge group versus 50% for destination BAV
cards.people: 224 patients (mean age 82.5 ± 8.3 years; 48% female) undergoing balloon aortic valvuloplasty at a single tertiary centre over 10 years. Indications were destination treatment in 39% and bridge to valve replacement in 61% — bridge to decision 29%, symptom relief while on the waitlist 27%, and temporary contraindications to TAVI/AVR 5%.
cards.result: Mean aortic pressure gradient fell by 38%. Procedural mortality was 0.5%, stroke 1.3% and major bleeding 0.9%. NYHA class improved by at least 1 in 50% of patients at 30 days. Twelve-month mortality was 36% overall — 26% in the bridging group and 50% in the destination group. Among the bridge-to-TAVI/AVR group, 40% proceeded to TAVI/AVR within 12 months of BAV. In multivariate analysis, active malignancy (OR 4.4, 95% CI 1.3 to 15.1), smoking history (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.3 to 7.9), LVEF 30% or below (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.3 to 7.6) and destination treatment (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.0 to 4.9) were associated with 12-month mortality.
cards.watchOut: There is no direct-TAVI or no-BAV comparator in this cohort: it shows bridging is feasible and symptoms improve, but the 60% of bridge patients who never reached valve replacement within a year — through death, refusal or new contraindications — is the sobering number.
cards.source: Dawson L et al. Utility of balloon aortic valvuloplasty in the transcatheter aortic valve implantation era. Open Heart. 2020. PMID: 32341170. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Daniec 2017: in a prospective 112-patient cohort, balloon valvuloplasty done mainly as a bridge to TAVI (51.8%) raised valve area from 0.59 to 0.82 cm2 and cut mean gradient from 58.0 to 40.5 mm Hg, with 12-month mortality of 22.3%
cards.summary: Daniec 2017: in a prospective 112-patient cohort, balloon valvuloplasty done mainly as a bridge to TAVI (51.8%) raised valve area from 0.59 to 0.82 cm2 and cut mean gradient from 58.0 to 40.5 mm Hg, with 12-month mortality of 22.3%
cards.people: 112 patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing 114 balloon aortic valvuloplasty procedures at two Polish interventional cardiology centres between October 2012 and July 2015, followed prospectively at 1, 6 and 12 months. Indications: bridge to TAVI 51.8%, bridge to surgical AVR 5.4%, before urgent noncardiac surgery 8.0%, symptom relief 33.0%, cardiogenic shock 1.8%.
cards.result: Periprocedural, in-hospital, 1-, 6- and 12-month mortality were 2.7%, 8.9%, 8.9%, 16.9% and 22.3% respectively; serious periprocedural adverse events occurred in 18.8% of patients. After the procedure, mean aortic valve area increased from 0.59 ± 0.18 to 0.82 ± 0.24 cm2, mean peak gradient fell from 94.0 ± 27.6 to 65.4 ± 20.0 mm Hg and mean gradient from 58.0 ± 17.8 to 40.5 ± 14.6 mm Hg (P < 0.05 for all). In patients with LVEF under 40%, ejection fraction improved significantly (median increase of 16%) at 1 and 6 months. The authors conclude the achieved effects can be sufficient in bridging patients for TAVI/AVR.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm cohort of 112 very-high-risk patients: the haemodynamic gains are real but temporary by design, nearly one in five had a serious periprocedural adverse event, and nothing here compares bridging against proceeding directly to TAVI.
cards.source: Daniec M et al. Acute and long-term outcomes of percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty for the treatment of severe aortic stenosis. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. 2017. PMID: 27514931. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kumar 2016: across 27 studies and 4,123 patients, balloon valvuloplasty in the TAVI era was safer than in the early era (in-hospital mortality 4.6% vs 8.5%), and 23.4% of contemporary procedures were bridges to TAVR
cards.summary: Kumar 2016: across 27 studies and 4,123 patients, balloon valvuloplasty in the TAVI era was safer than in the early era (in-hospital mortality 4.6% vs 8.5%), and 23.4% of contemporary procedures were bridges to TAVR
cards.people: Systematic review of all published balloon aortic valvuloplasty studies from 1986 to June 2013 reporting at least 50 procedures: 27 studies representing 4,123 patients, comparing the early/pre-TAVR era with the contemporary/TAVR era (before versus after 2005).
cards.result: Significant and comparable improvement in transaortic gradients, aortic valve area and cardiac output followed BAV in both eras. In the contemporary era, BAV was performed as a bridge to TAVR in 23.4% of patients. Procedural death (1.5% vs 2.9%; P < .01), in-hospital mortality (4.6% vs 8.5%; P < .001) and major vascular complications (4.0% vs 10.2%; P < .001) were all significantly lower for BAV procedures in the contemporary/TAVR era than in the early era.
cards.watchOut: Era comparisons mix better technique with different patient selection, and the review's outcomes are procedural — it cannot say whether patients bridged with BAV fare better than similar patients taken straight to TAVR, which is the comparison the registry card above attempts and the one no trial has made.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty in the Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Era. The Journal of Invasive Cardiology. 2016. PMID: 27466275. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: balloon valvuloplasty opens the valve, relieves symptoms and gets a substantial minority of unstable patients to TAVI — but the only large bridge-versus-direct comparison associates bridging with higher in-hospital mortality, and no randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: balloon valvuloplasty opens the valve, relieves symptoms and gets a substantial minority of unstable patients to TAVI — but the only large bridge-versus-direct comparison associates bridging with higher in-hospital mortality, and no randomised trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one national registry of 27,600 TAVR patients (213 bridged), one retrospective cohort of 224 BAV patients (61% bridging), one prospective cohort of 112 patients (51.8% bridged to TAVI) and one systematic review of 27 studies (4,123 patients). All observational; total carded participants exceed 30,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the limitation is design, not size.
cards.result: Haemodynamic benefit is consistent (valve area 0.59 to 0.82 cm2; mean gradient 58.0 to 40.5 mm Hg; Daniec 2017), symptom benefit is common (50% improved at least one NYHA class at 30 days; Dawson 2020), and procedural safety has improved in the TAVI era (in-hospital mortality 4.6% vs 8.5% in the early era; Kumar 2016). Yet only 40% of one bridge cohort reached TAVI/AVR within 12 months, and the 27,600-patient registry found higher in-hospital mortality with bridging than with direct TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%; Fujimoto 2024) — an association confounding by indication may explain but cannot be wished away. PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit in bridge cohorts; mortality signal against the bridge strategy in registry data) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Every card on this shelf is observational. The registry's harm signal and the cohorts' benefit signal can both be true — bridging rescues patients who cannot wait, while marking out the sickest patients in the system — and only a randomised comparison of bridge versus direct TAVI could separate the two.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fujimoto T et al. International Journal of Cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 38977224); Dawson L et al. Open Heart. 2020 (PMID: 32341170); Daniec M et al. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. 2017 (PMID: 27514931); Kumar A et al. The Journal of Invasive Cardiology. 2016 (PMID: 27466275).

shelves.title: Exercise restriction in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (unproven, observational only): never tested directly — but supervised exercise testing caused no serious events in 769 patients across three cohorts
shelves.question: Does exercise restriction prevent events in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aortic Valve physiopathology surgery · Aortic Valve Stenosis diagnosis mortality physiopathology surgery · Asymptomatic Diseases · Echocardiography · Electrocardiography · Exercise Test adverse effects · Female · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Predictive Value of Tests · Progression-Free Survival · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (restriction benefit unproven) — observational only, printed on the face. No study carded here, and none found this session, has ever randomised or compared asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis who were told to restrict exercise against patients who were not — so the preventive value of restriction itself is untested. What the evidence does test is the danger restriction is meant to avert: supervised exertion. Across three cohorts totalling 769 patients, symptom-limited exercise testing caused no serious adverse events: 797 treadmill tests in 316 patients with moderate or severe stenosis with no serious adverse events (Saeed 2018, PMID: 29654094); maximal exercise tests in 106 asymptomatic patients with no complications (Peidro 2007, PMID: 17114879); and cardiopulmonary exercise testing in 347 patients — 137 with severe stenosis — with no major events and minor events in 28% (Dhoble 2012, PMID: 22560172). These same records show exercise testing is prognostically useful (revealed symptoms in 29% at baseline in Saeed 2018, marking patients headed for valve replacement), which is an argument about testing, not about everyday exertion or its restriction. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit of exercise restriction unproven) — observational only: brief supervised exertion has repeatedly proved safe in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, but whether restricting ordinary exercise prevents events has never been tested.

cards.headline: Saeed 2018: 797 treadmill exercise tests in 316 patients with moderate or severe aortic stenosis produced no serious adverse events — testing also revealed hidden symptoms in 29%
cards.summary: Saeed 2018: 797 treadmill exercise tests in 316 patients with moderate or severe aortic stenosis produced no serious adverse events — testing also revealed hidden symptoms in 29%
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 316 patients (age 65 ± 12 years, 67% men) with moderate (210 patients, 66%) or severe (106 patients, 34%) aortic stenosis attending a specialist valve clinic, who underwent echocardiography and modified Bruce exercise treadmill tests; 797 tests in total (mean 2.5 ± 2.1 per patient).
cards.result: No serious adverse events were observed during exercise testing. Revealed symptoms were present in 29% (91 patients) at the baseline test — significantly more often in severe than moderate stenosis (38% vs 23%, P = 0.008) — and in 18%–59% during serial testing over 34.9 months of follow-up. Event-free survival at 24 months was 46% ± 4% in patients with revealed symptoms versus 70% ± 4% without. Over follow-up there were 264 events; 234 patients (74%) reached an indication for aortic valve replacement and 30 (9%) died, 20 of cardiovascular causes. The authors conclude exercise testing in moderate or severe aortic stenosis is safe and tolerable.
cards.watchOut: Safety of a supervised, stop-at-symptoms treadmill test is not the same question as safety of unrestricted everyday exertion, and this cohort mixes moderate with severe stenosis — the record supports 'testing is safe', not 'restriction is unnecessary'.
cards.source: Saeed S et al. Exercise testing in patients with asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic stenosis. Heart (British Cardiac Society). 2018. PMID: 29654094. Registry ID: none in the record. retrospective cohort (saeed 2018) retrospective cohort of 316 patients (age 65 ± 12 years, 67% men) with moderate (210 patients, 66%) or severe (106 patients, 34%) aortic stenosis attending a specialist valve clinic, who underwent echocardiography and modified bruce exercise treadmill tests; 797 tests in total (mean 2.5 ± 2.1 per patient). no serious adverse events were observed during exercise testing. revealed symptoms were present in 29% (91 patients) at the baseline test — significantly more often in severe than moderate stenosis (38% vs 23%, p = 0.008) — and in 18%–59% during serial testing over 34.9 months of follow-up. event-free survival at 24 months was 46% ± 4% in patients with revealed symptoms versus 70% ± 4% without. over follow-up there were 264 events; 234 patients (74%) reached an indication for aortic valve replacement and 30 (9%) died, 20 of cardiovascular causes. the authors conclude exercise testing in moderate or severe aortic stenosis is safe and tolerable. safety of a supervised, stop-at-symptoms treadmill test is not the same question as safety of unrestricted everyday exertion, and this cohort mixes moderate with severe stenosis — the record supports 'testing is safe', not 'restriction is unnecessary'. saeed s et al. exercise testing in patients with asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic stenosis. heart (british cardiac society). 2018. pmid: 29654094. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · aortic valve physiopathology surgery · aortic valve stenosis diagnosis mortality physiopathology surgery · asymptomatic diseases · echocardiography · electrocardiography · exercise test adverse effects · female · heart valve prosthesis implantation · humans · male · middle aged · predictive value of tests · progression-free survival · retrospective studies · risk factors · severity of illness index · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Peidro 2007: maximal exercise testing in 106 patients with asymptomatic aortic stenosis caused no complications; an abnormal test marked the patients who went on to surgery or death
cards.summary: Peidro 2007: maximal exercise testing in 106 patients with asymptomatic aortic stenosis caused no complications; an abnormal test marked the patients who went on to surgery or death
cards.people: 106 consecutive patients with asymptomatic moderate or severe aortic stenosis who performed a maximal exercise test; follow-up was completed in 102 patients (96.2%) over a median of 10.7 months. Mean age 63.9 years (± 15.1); 65 (61.3%) male; peak gradient 82.8 mm Hg (± 25.4), mean gradient 50.5 mm Hg (± 16.6), valve area 0.67 cm2 (± 0.16).
cards.result: There were no complications with exercise testing. The test was abnormal in 67 patients (65.7%). Among the 35 patients with a normal test there were no deaths and 10 aortic valve replacements (28.5%); among the 67 with an abnormal test, 37 (55.2%) had events (35 valve replacements and 2 deaths) (P < 0.0001). The authors conclude exercise testing may be performed safely in asymptomatic aortic stenosis and adds information to the decision for surgery.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre series of 106 selected patients referred for testing; zero complications in 106 tests rules out only very common harms, and the study says nothing about habitual exercise or about restricting it.
cards.source: Peidro R et al. Exercise testing in asymptomatic aortic stenosis. Cardiology. 2007. PMID: 17114879. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dhoble 2012: symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing in 347 patients with aortic stenosis — 137 of them severe — caused no major events; minor events occurred in 28%
cards.summary: Dhoble 2012: symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing in 347 patients with aortic stenosis — 137 of them severe — caused no major events; minor events occurred in 28%
cards.people: Retrospective descriptive study of 347 consecutive patients with aortic stenosis who underwent cardiopulmonary exercise testing at a tertiary referral centre: 65 (19%) mild, 145 (42%) moderate and 137 (40%) severe stenosis by echocardiographic criteria, all with preserved systolic function.
cards.result: No major events occurred during the tests — no death, cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular or supraventricular tachycardia, myocardial infarction or syncope. Minor events occurred in 97 patients (28%), including 10 who developed supraventricular arrhythmias without hypotension and one with asymptomatic nonsustained ventricular tachycardia; minor events also included hypotension, nonsustained arrhythmias, electrocardiographic changes and angina. The authors conclude symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing in referred patients with aortic stenosis appears associated with very low risk of major adverse cardiovascular events during testing.
cards.watchOut: Minor events in more than a quarter of patients — arrhythmias, hypotension, angina — are exactly the physiology that makes clinicians cautious about unsupervised maximal exertion; the record shows these were manageable under supervision, not that they are harmless without it.
cards.source: Dhoble A et al. Safety of symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing in patients with aortic stenosis. The American Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22560172. cards.headline: Synthesis: supervised exercise testing has caused no serious events in 769 carded patients with aortic stenosis, but exercise restriction itself has never been tested — the shelf answers the safety question, not the restriction question
cards.summary: Synthesis: supervised exercise testing has caused no serious events in 769 carded patients with aortic stenosis, but exercise restriction itself has never been tested — the shelf answers the safety question, not the restriction question
cards.people: The carded evidence: three observational cohorts of exercise testing in aortic stenosis — 316 patients and 797 tests (Saeed 2018), 106 patients (Peidro 2007) and 347 patients (Dhoble 2012) — totalling 769 patients, of whom at least 243 had severe stenosis by the records' own breakdowns. No carded study compares restricted versus unrestricted patients. Total N exceeds 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that the evidence is indirect for the question asked.
cards.result: Serious adverse events during supervised symptom-limited exercise testing: none in any of the three cohorts. Minor events occurred in 28% in the largest severe-stenosis series (Dhoble 2012). Exercise testing repeatedly unmasked symptoms and predicted valve replacement or death (Saeed 2018; Peidro 2007). Nothing in the carded records measures whether advising patients to restrict ordinary exercise prevents sudden death or any other event. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit of exercise restriction unproven) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf: guidelines restrict vigorous exertion in severe aortic stenosis on physiological reasoning and the known risk of sudden death in symptomatic disease, and the carded cohorts neither confirm nor refute that reasoning — they show supervised testing is safe, which is a different claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Saeed S et al. Heart. 2018 (PMID: 29654094); Peidro R et al. Cardiology. 2007 (PMID: 17114879); Dhoble A et al. The American Journal of Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22560172).
