shelves.title: Supervised exercise in peripheral arterial disease: improves walking distance and symptoms (about 210 m more than walking advice at three months) — no effect on the ankle brachial index or hard outcomes
shelves.question: Does supervised exercise improve symptoms in peripheral arterial disease?
shelves.mesh: Amputation, Surgical statistics & numerical data · Ankle Brachial Index · Exercise Therapy methods · Female · Humans · Intermittent Claudication therapy · Male · Pain Management methods · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors · Walking
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for walking distance and symptoms. Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials point the same way. Exercise programmes versus usual care or placebo improved pain-free walking distance by a mean of 82.11 m and maximum walking distance by 120.36 m, on high-quality evidence (Lane 2017, PMID: 29278423; 32 trials, 1,835 participants). Supervised exercise therapy specifically beat walking advice by a standardised mean difference of 0.80 — about 210 m more maximal walking distance at three months, high-quality evidence — and beat home-based exercise by about 120 m (Hageman 2018, PMID: 29627967; 21 studies, 1,400 participants). A third meta-analysis of 18 trials and 1,200 patients found intensive walking exercise improved maximal, pain-free and 6-minute walking distances over usual care with no excess of adverse events (relative risk 0.84; Lyu 2016, PMID: 25940390). The benefit is in walking capacity and some quality-of-life domains; exercise did not improve the ankle brachial index and no effect on mortality or amputation was shown. The head-to-head question against stenting is not re-asked here: CLEVER and ERASE are homed on live shelf #280 (supervised exercise vs stenting for claudication) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): supervised exercise improves walking distance and symptoms in peripheral arterial disease compared with usual care and walking advice.

cards.headline: Lane 2017 (Cochrane): exercise programmes improved pain-free walking distance by 82 m and maximum walking distance by 120 m over usual care or placebo in intermittent claudication — high-quality evidence across 32 trials
cards.summary: Lane 2017 (Cochrane): exercise programmes improved pain-free walking distance by 82 m and maximum walking distance by 120 m over usual care or placebo in intermittent claudication — high-quality evidence across 32 trials
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised controlled trials of an exercise regimen versus control or medical therapy in people with intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease: 32 studies, 1,835 participants with stable leg pain, follow-up from two weeks to two years. Supervised sessions were generally held at least twice a week; 27 trials compared exercise with usual care or placebo and 5 with medication or pneumatic compression.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of nine studies (391 participants) showed improvement in pain-free walking distance with exercise versus no exercise (mean difference 82.11 m, 95% CI 71.73 to 92.48, P < 0.00001, high-quality evidence), and pooling of 10 studies (500 participants) showed improved maximum walking distance (mean difference 120.36 m, 95% CI 50.79 to 189.92, P < 0.0007, high-quality evidence), with improvements seen for up to two years. Exercise did not improve the ankle brachial index (mean difference 0.04, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.08; 13 trials, 570 participants). There was no evidence of an effect on mortality (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.39 to 2.17; 5 trials, 540 participants) or amputation (relative risk 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.15; 1 trial, 177 participants). Quality of life improved in some domains at three and six months.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials were small (20–49 participants) and exercise regimens varied from walking to strength training and polestriding; the pooled walking gains are averages across programmes, and the review found no evidence that exercise changes the underlying arterial disease (ankle brachial index unchanged) or hard outcomes.
cards.source: Lane R et al. Exercise for intermittent claudication. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 29278423. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hageman 2018 (Cochrane): supervised exercise beat walking advice by about 210 m of maximal walking distance at three months and beat home-based exercise by about 120 m
cards.summary: Hageman 2018 (Cochrane): supervised exercise beat walking advice by about 210 m of maximal walking distance at three months and beat home-based exercise by about 120 m
cards.people: Cochrane review of parallel-group randomised trials comparing supervised exercise therapy (SET), structured home-based exercise therapy (HBET) and walking advice (WA) in intermittent claudication: 21 studies, 1,400 participants (635 SET, 320 HBET, 445 WA); programmes generally ran three sessions per week; follow-up six weeks to two years.
cards.result: SET improved maximal treadmill walking distance/time versus HBET (standardised mean difference 0.37, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.62, P = 0.004, moderate-quality evidence) and versus WA (standardised mean difference 0.80, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07, P < 0.00001, high-quality evidence) at three months — translating to about 120 m and 210 m more maximal walking distance respectively, with improvements shown for up to six and 12 months. HBET did not improve maximal walking distance versus WA (standardised mean difference 0.30, 95% CI −0.45 to 1.05, P = 0.43). SET was also more beneficial than WA for pain-free walking distance and self-reported functional impairment. Thirteen of the 1,400 participants died; no deaths were related to exercise therapy. Adherence to SET was approximately 80%.
cards.watchOut: The walking gains are treadmill-measured; the review is explicit that their clinical relevance, while likely positive, has not been definitively demonstrated, and quality-of-life differences between supervised and home-based programmes were supported only by low- or very-low-quality evidence.
cards.source: Hageman D et al. Supervised exercise therapy versus home-based exercise therapy versus walking advice for intermittent claudication. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29627967. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lyu 2016: across 18 trials and 1,200 patients, intensive walking exercise improved maximal, pain-free and 6-minute walking distances over usual care, with no significant difference in adverse events (relative risk 0.84)
cards.summary: Lyu 2016: across 18 trials and 1,200 patients, intensive walking exercise improved maximal, pain-free and 6-minute walking distances over usual care, with no significant difference in adverse events (relative risk 0.84)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing intensive walking exercise with usual care in peripheral arterial disease, including patients with and without intermittent claudication: 18 trials, 1,200 patients.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, intensive walking exercise significantly improved maximal walking distance, pain-free walking distance and 6-minute walking distance (P < 0.00001 for all). Subgroup analyses indicated less improvement in maximal walking distance in the subgroup with more patients with diabetes, and greater improvement in the subgroup with better baseline walking ability; similar improvements were seen for programmes of different durations and modalities. There was no significant difference in adverse events between the intensive walking and usual care groups (relative risk 0.84, 95% confidence interval 0.51 to 1.39, P = 0.50).
cards.watchOut: This review pools intensive walking programmes rather than supervision as such, and reports significance levels rather than pooled metre gains for its walking outcomes — the size of the benefit has to be taken from the Cochrane cards above.
cards.source: Lyu X et al. Intensive walking exercise for lower extremity peripheral arterial disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Diabetes. 2016. PMID: 25940390. cards.headline: Synthesis: supervised exercise improves walking distance and symptoms in peripheral arterial disease — about 210 m more maximal walking than walking advice at three months — without improving the ankle brachial index or any hard outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: supervised exercise improves walking distance and symptoms in peripheral arterial disease — about 210 m more maximal walking than walking advice at three months — without improving the ankle brachial index or any hard outcome
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Cochrane reviews (32 trials, 1,835 participants; 21 studies, 1,400 participants) and one further meta-analysis (18 trials, 1,200 patients) of randomised trials in peripheral arterial disease and intermittent claudication. Reviews overlap in their underlying trials, so participant totals are not additive; the unique randomised base comfortably exceeds 30 and no small-N labelling applies. The supervised-exercise-versus-stent trials (CLEVER, ERASE) are homed on live shelf #280 and are not carded here.
cards.result: Exercise improved pain-free walking distance by 82.11 m and maximum walking distance by 120.36 m over usual care or placebo (Lane 2017, high-quality evidence); supervised programmes beat walking advice by about 210 m and structured home-based programmes by about 120 m at three months (Hageman 2018). Intensive walking showed no excess of adverse events (relative risk 0.84; Lyu 2016). No carded record shows an effect on the ankle brachial index, mortality or amputation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for walking distance and symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Supervision is the active ingredient in the comparisons that matter most: unstructured advice to walk did not beat structured home programmes, and the benefit demonstrated is symptomatic — patients walk further and hurt later — not a change in the artery or in survival.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lane R et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 29278423); Hageman D et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 29627967); Lyu X et al. Journal of Diabetes. 2016 (PMID: 25940390).

shelves.title: Home-based walking in PAD (split by programme design): group-supported home walking prevented mobility loss — fully remote programmes did not improve walking distance
shelves.question: Does home-based walking exercise improve mobility in PAD?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy methods · Exercise physiology psychology · Exercise Therapy methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Motor Activity physiology · Peripheral Arterial Disease physiopathology psychology therapy · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Walking physiology psychology
shelves.balance: SPLIT (by programme design). Home-based walking helped when the programme brought patients together: in the GOALS trial, a group-mediated cognitive behavioural intervention promoting home walking — weekly on-site group meetings for six months, with 90% of exercise done at or near home — cut mobility loss at six months from 26.5% to 6.3% (odds ratio 0.19) and at 12 months from 18.5% to 5.2% (odds ratio 0.24) versus an attention control (McDermott 2015, PMID: 25994445; 194 randomised), and the same programme's 6-minute walk advantage persisted at 12 months (+34.1 m; McDermott 2014, PMID: 24850615). Home-based programmes without that on-site group structure did not improve walking: a wearable-monitor plus telephone-coaching intervention changed 6-minute walk by 5.5 m versus 14.4 m with usual care (difference −8.9 m, P = .31 — the treatment made no difference) in the HONOR trial (McDermott 2018, PMID: 29710165; 200 randomised), and a behavioural home-walking intervention in diabetes with PAD did not improve treadmill walking distance (24.5 m vs 39.2 m change, P = 0.60), though walking speed and mental-health quality of life improved (Collins 2011, PMID: 21873560; 145 randomised). PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit for group-supported home programmes; no walking benefit for fully remote programmes): whether home-based walking improves mobility in PAD depends on how the programme is built — periodic in-person group support appears to be the ingredient that makes home exercise work.

cards.headline: McDermott 2015 (GOALS): a group-supported home walking programme prevented mobility loss — 6.3% versus 26.5% at six months (odds ratio 0.19) and 5.2% versus 18.5% at 12 months
cards.summary: McDermott 2015 (GOALS): a group-supported home walking programme prevented mobility loss — 6.3% versus 26.5% at six months (odds ratio 0.19) and 5.2% versus 18.5% at 12 months
cards.people: 194 participants with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease randomised in the GOALS trial to a group-mediated cognitive behavioural intervention promoting home-based unsupervised exercise, or to a control group attending weekly health lectures. During months 1–6 the intervention group met weekly with other participants and a facilitator, using group support and self-regulatory skills to adhere to walking exercise; 90% of exercise was conducted at or near home. During months 6–12 each group received telephone contact only.
cards.result: Compared with controls, fewer intervention participants experienced mobility loss (inability to climb a flight of stairs or walk a quarter mile without assistance) at 6-month follow-up: 6.3% versus 26.5%, P = 0.002, odds ratio 0.19 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.58); and at 12-month follow-up: 5.2% versus 18.5%, P = 0.029, odds ratio 0.24 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.97). The intervention also improved fast-paced 4-metre walking velocity at 6 months (P = 0.005) and the Short Physical Performance Battery at 12 months (P = 0.027). Mobility loss was an exploratory outcome of the trial.
cards.watchOut: The exercise was unsupervised and home-based, but the adherence engine was weekly in-person group meetings — this trial does not show that simply telling patients to walk at home prevents mobility loss, and mobility loss was an exploratory, not the primary, outcome.
cards.source: McDermott MM et al. Unsupervised exercise and mobility loss in peripheral artery disease: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2015. PMID: 25994445. Registry ID: NCT00693940. cards.headline: McDermott 2014 (GOALS, 12-month follow-up): the home-walking programme's 6-minute walk advantage persisted six months after the group phase ended (+34.1 m versus control)
cards.summary: McDermott 2014 (GOALS, 12-month follow-up): the home-walking programme's 6-minute walk advantage persisted six months after the group phase ended (+34.1 m versus control)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 12-month follow-up report (GOALS; McDermott 2014)
cards.people: Participants in the GOALS randomised trial (194 randomised, per the trial's companion report) with peripheral artery disease, assigned to the group-mediated cognitive behavioural intervention promoting home-based walking exercise or to weekly on-site control lectures; phase I (months 1–6) used weekly on-site group meetings, and phase II (months 7–12) was telephone contact only. This report covers 12-month follow-up, six months after the intervention phase ended.
cards.result: Compared with controls, intervention participants increased their 6-minute walk distance from baseline to 12 months (355.4 to 381.9 m in the intervention group versus 353.1 to 345.6 m in controls; mean difference +34.1 m; 95% CI +14.6 to +53.5; P < 0.001) and improved their Walking Impairment Questionnaire speed score (mean difference +8.8; 95% CI +1.6 to +16.1; P = 0.018). Change in the Walking Impairment Questionnaire distance score did not differ between groups at 12 months (P = 0.139).
cards.watchOut: Same trial as the mobility-loss card above — the two reports are one programme's evidence, not two independent confirmations; and the durability shown is of a programme whose active phase included weekly on-site contact.
cards.source: McDermott MM et al. Home-based walking exercise in peripheral artery disease: 12-month follow-up of the GOALS randomized trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2014. PMID: 24850615. Registry ID: NCT00693940. cards.headline: McDermott 2018 (HONOR): a wearable-monitor and telephone-coaching home exercise programme did not improve walking performance at nine months (the treatment made no difference) — and worsened pain interference scores
cards.summary: McDermott 2018 (HONOR): a wearable-monitor and telephone-coaching home exercise programme did not improve walking performance at nine months (the treatment made no difference) — and worsened pain interference scores
cards.people: Randomised clinical trial at three US medical centres: 200 patients with peripheral artery disease randomised (June 2015 to April 2017) to home-based exercise (n = 99) — four weekly medical centre visits in the first month, then eight months of a wearable activity monitor and telephone coaching — or usual care (n = 101) with no onsite sessions, active exercise or coaching. Mean age 70.2 years (SD 10.4); 105 (52.5%) women; 182 (91%) completed nine-month follow-up.
cards.result: The mean change in 6-minute walk distance at nine months was 5.5 m in the intervention group versus 14.4 m in the usual care group (difference −8.9 m; 95% CI −26.0 to 8.2 m; P = .31) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome, whose minimal clinically important difference was 20 m. The intervention worsened the PROMIS pain interference score (difference 3.5; 95% CI 1.3 to 5.8; P = .002). There were no significant between-group differences in Walking Impairment Questionnaire scores, SF-36 physical functioning, or PROMIS mobility or satisfaction scores. The authors conclude the results do not support home-based exercise interventions of wearable devices and telephone counselling without periodic onsite visits.
cards.watchOut: A null result for this design of programme, not for home exercise in general: after the first month there were no onsite visits at all, which is exactly the ingredient the positive GOALS programme retained weekly.
cards.source: McDermott MM et al. Effect of a Home-Based Exercise Intervention of Wearable Technology and Telephone Coaching on Walking Performance in Peripheral Artery Disease: The HONOR Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29710165. Registry ID: NCT02462824. cards.headline: Collins 2011: a six-month behavioural home-walking intervention in diabetes with PAD did not improve maximal treadmill walking distance (P = 0.60), though walking speed scores and mental-health quality of life improved
cards.summary: Collins 2011: a six-month behavioural home-walking intervention in diabetes with PAD did not improve maximal treadmill walking distance (P = 0.60), though walking speed scores and mental-health quality of life improved
cards.people: Randomised, controlled, single-blind trial in university-affiliated community clinics: 145 participants (45 women) with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease, mean age 66.5 years (SD 10.1), randomised to a six-month behavioural intervention targeting readiness to engage in routine home walking for exercise, or to attention control.
cards.result: Intervention and control groups did not differ significantly in six-month change in maximal treadmill walking distance (average 24.5 m [SE 19.6] versus 39.2 m [SE 19.6]; P = 0.60) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome. Among secondary outcomes, average walking speed scores increased by 5.7 units in the intervention group and decreased by 1.9 units in controls (P = 0.03), and the mental-health quality-of-life subscale increased by 3.2 versus a decrease of 2.4 (P = 0.01). The authors suggest clinicians consider recommending home-based walking therapy for such patients on the strength of the speed and quality-of-life findings.
cards.watchOut: The positive secondary outcomes sit alongside a null primary outcome in a single 145-patient trial in the specific population of diabetes with PAD — hypothesis-raising for speed and quality of life, not evidence of improved walking distance.
cards.source: Collins TC et al. Effects of a home-based walking intervention on mobility and quality of life in people with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease: a randomized controlled trial. Diabetes Care. 2011. PMID: 21873560. Registry ID: NCT00611988. MeSH: Aged · Diabetes Mellitus therapy · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peripheral Arterial Disease therapy · Quality of Life · Walking physiology

cards.headline: Synthesis: home-based walking improves mobility in PAD when the programme includes periodic in-person group support (GOALS) — fully remote programmes (HONOR, Collins) did not improve walking distance
cards.summary: Synthesis: home-based walking improves mobility in PAD when the programme includes periodic in-person group support (GOALS) — fully remote programmes (HONOR, Collins) did not improve walking distance
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials totalling 539 unique participants — GOALS (194 randomised; two reports of one programme), HONOR (200 randomised) and Collins 2011 (145 randomised, diabetes with PAD). Total unique N exceeds 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: GOALS' group-supported home programme prevented mobility loss (6.3% vs 26.5% at six months; 5.2% vs 18.5% at 12 months) and added 34.1 m to the 6-minute walk at 12 months. HONOR's wearable-plus-telephone programme made no difference to 6-minute walk (−8.9 m difference, P = .31) and worsened pain interference. Collins' behavioural programme made no difference to treadmill walking distance (P = 0.60) with small gains in walking speed score and mental-health quality of life. PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit for group-supported home programmes; no walking benefit for fully remote programmes).
cards.watchOut: The split is by programme design across trials, not within one randomised comparison — adherence support is the plausible mechanism, but no trial has randomised the support itself, so the shelf states the pattern and labels it as such.
cards.source: Synthesis of McDermott MM et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2015 (PMID: 25994445) and 2014 (PMID: 24850615); McDermott MM et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29710165); Collins TC et al. Diabetes Care. 2011 (PMID: 21873560).

shelves.title: Early ambulation after DVT: does not worsen outcomes — no excess pulmonary embolism, progression or death versus bed rest across meta-analysis, registry and cohort evidence
shelves.question: Does early ambulation worsen outcomes after DVT?
shelves.mesh: Bed Rest methods · Disease Management · Early Ambulation methods · Humans · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism mortality therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic methods statistics & numerical data · Registries statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis mortality therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no worsening). The fear behind prescribing bed rest after deep vein thrombosis — that walking will shake a clot loose — is not borne out by any carded record. A meta-analysis of five randomised studies and prospective registries totalling 3,048 patients found early ambulation was not associated with a higher incidence of new pulmonary embolism than bed rest (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.63), with trends favouring ambulation for the composites of new embolism or thrombus progression and of embolism or death (Aissaoui 2009, PMID: 18691773). In the RIETE registry's 2,650 patients with acute DVT or pulmonary embolism, new symptomatic embolism over 15 days was uncommon (0.5% after DVT, 0.7% after PE) with no significant differences between bed-rest and ambulant patients in new embolism, fatal embolism or bleeding (Trujillo-Santos 2005, PMID: 15888839). And in 1,289 consecutive patients all treated with compression and walking exercises instead of bed rest, fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.23% (Partsch 2001, PMID: 11582950). The randomised base inside the meta-analysis is small, which caps the stamp: the answer rests on concordant meta-analytic, registry and cohort evidence rather than one large trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no worsening): early ambulation after DVT does not increase pulmonary embolism, thrombus progression or death in the available evidence.

cards.headline: Aissaoui 2009: in a meta-analysis of 3,048 patients, early ambulation after DVT or pulmonary embolism was not associated with more new pulmonary embolism than bed rest (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.63)
cards.summary: Aissaoui 2009: in a meta-analysis of 3,048 patients, early ambulation after DVT or pulmonary embolism was not associated with more new pulmonary embolism than bed rest (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.63)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of all randomised studies and prospective registries comparing bed rest versus early ambulation, each in addition to anticoagulation, in patients with deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or both: five studies retained, totalling 3,048 patients.
cards.result: Compared with bed rest, early ambulation was not associated with a higher incidence of a new pulmonary embolism (relative risk 1.03; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.63; P = 0.90). Early ambulation was associated with a trend toward a lower incidence of new pulmonary embolism combined with new or progressive deep vein thrombosis (relative risk 0.79; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.14; P = 0.21) and of new pulmonary embolism combined with overall mortality (relative risk 0.79; 95% CI 0.402 to 1.56; P = 0.50). The authors conclude the meta-analysis does not support the systematic recommendation of bed rest as part of the early management of DVT or pulmonary embolism.
cards.watchOut: Five studies mixing randomised trials with registries, and confidence intervals wide enough (0.65 to 1.63) to include a meaningful relative increase in embolism — the record excludes a large harm, not every harm; the point estimate and the trend on composites are reassuring, not definitive.
cards.source: Aissaoui N et al. A meta-analysis of bed rest versus early ambulation in the management of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, or both. International Journal of Cardiology. 2009. PMID: 18691773. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Trujillo-Santos 2005 (RIETE registry): among 2,650 patients with acute DVT or pulmonary embolism, bed rest made no significant difference to new embolism, fatal embolism or bleeding over 15 days
cards.summary: Trujillo-Santos 2005 (RIETE registry): among 2,650 patients with acute DVT or pulmonary embolism, bed rest made no significant difference to new embolism, fatal embolism or bleeding over 15 days
cards.people: 2,650 consecutively enrolled patients with objectively confirmed symptomatic acute DVT (2,038 patients) or pulmonary embolism (612 patients) in the Spanish RIETE registry, comparing patients prescribed strict bed rest during the first 15 days with those who ambulated; patients in whom ambulation was not possible were excluded. Strict bed rest was prescribed to 1,050 DVT patients (52%) and 385 PE patients (63%).
cards.result: New symptomatic, objectively confirmed pulmonary embolism developed during the 15-day period in 11 patients with DVT (0.5%) and 4 patients with PE (0.7%); five of these 15 patients (33%) died of their embolism. Age under 65 years (odds ratio 3.1; 95% CI 0.98 to 11) and cancer (odds ratio 3.0; 95% CI 0.98 to 9.1) were associated with new embolism. There were no significant differences between bedridden and ambulant patients in new pulmonary embolism events, fatal pulmonary embolism, or bleeding complications. The authors conclude bed rest has no influence on the risk of developing pulmonary embolism in acute lower-limb DVT — and, for the first time in their data, not even in acute submassive PE.
cards.watchOut: Registry treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised: patients kept in bed may have been sicker, which would bias against bed rest — yet bed rest still showed no advantage; conversely the comparison cannot prove ambulation is equally safe in the patients clinicians chose not to ambulate.
cards.source: Trujillo-Santos J et al. Bed rest or ambulation in the initial treatment of patients with acute deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism: findings from the RIETE registry. Chest. 2005. PMID: 15888839. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Bed Rest · Early Ambulation · Female · Humans · Male · Pulmonary Embolism prevention & control · Registries · Venous Thrombosis therapy

cards.headline: Partsch 2001: in 1,289 consecutive DVT patients all treated with compression and immediate walking instead of bed rest, fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.23% and major bleeding in 0.4%
cards.summary: Partsch 2001: in 1,289 consecutive DVT patients all treated with compression and immediate walking instead of bed rest, fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.23% and major bleeding in 0.4%
cards.people: 1,289 consecutive patients admitted with acute symptomatic deep vein thrombosis, all treated with leg compression and walking exercises instead of conventional bed rest and nearly all with low-molecular-weight heparin; endpoints were registered for the hospital stay, with ventilation/perfusion lung scans at admission and after 10 days.
cards.result: Pulmonary embolism was already present at admission in 53.4% of iliofemoral, 52.6% of femoral and 35.1% of lower-leg thromboses (two-thirds asymptomatic). New pulmonary embolism on the 10-day scan occurred in 7.4%, 6.4% and 3.4% respectively. Fatal events from pulmonary embolism occurred in 3 patients, all over 76 years (0.23%); 12 deaths (0.9%) were from malignant disease and 2 (0.15%) from other causes. Non-fatal bleeding complications occurred in 3.3%, including 5 patients (0.4%) with major bleeding; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia occurred in 3 patients (0.2%). The authors conclude the low incidence of recurrent and fatal embolism affirms the value of early ambulation with heavy leg compression in symptomatic acute leg DVT.
cards.watchOut: A single-strategy cohort with no bed-rest arm: it shows what happens when everyone walks (few fatal events), not a comparison — and new scan-detected embolism in 3.4%–7.4% by day 10, mostly silent, is the background rate any strategy must be judged against.

cards.headline: Synthesis: early ambulation after DVT does not worsen outcomes in any carded record — no excess of new embolism, progression or death across a meta-analysis, a 2,650-patient registry and a 1,289-patient walking cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: early ambulation after DVT does not worsen outcomes in any carded record — no excess of new embolism, progression or death across a meta-analysis, a 2,650-patient registry and a 1,289-patient walking cohort
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of five studies (3,048 patients), one prospective registry analysis (2,650 patients) and one consecutive cohort (1,289 patients) — total carded participants about 7,000 (the meta-analysis and the other records may share some underlying patients, so the total is not strictly additive). No small-N labelling applies; the limitation is the small randomised base within the meta-analysis.
cards.result: New pulmonary embolism with early ambulation versus bed rest: relative risk 1.03 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.63) in the meta-analysis (Aissaoui 2009). New symptomatic embolism over 15 days: 0.5% after DVT and 0.7% after PE, with no significant bed-rest-versus-ambulant differences (Trujillo-Santos 2005). Fatal embolism when all patients walked with compression: 0.23% (Partsch 2001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no worsening) — early ambulation after DVT does not increase pulmonary embolism, thrombus progression or death in the available evidence.
cards.watchOut: All carded patients were anticoagulated, and the walking cohorts used compression — the shelf's reassurance is about ambulation as part of anticoagulant treatment, not about walking instead of it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aissaoui N et al. International Journal of Cardiology. 2009 (PMID: 18691773); Trujillo-Santos J et al. Chest. 2005 (PMID: 15888839); Partsch H et al. VASA. 2001 (PMID: 11582950).

shelves.title: DOACs in antiphospholipid syndrome (harm signal): more recurrent thrombosis — arterial events especially — than warfarin, with no bleeding advantage; worst in triple-positive disease
shelves.question: Is DOAC therapy safe in antiphospholipid syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticoagulants therapeutic use · Antiphospholipid Syndrome drug therapy · Factor Xa Inhibitors therapeutic use · Female · Hemorrhage epidemiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Rivaroxaban therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Stroke epidemiology · Thrombosis epidemiology prevention & control · Vitamin K antagonists & inhibitors · Warfarin therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm). The safety problem with direct oral anticoagulants in antiphospholipid syndrome is not bleeding — it is recurrent thrombosis, especially arterial. In the carded randomised trial, rivaroxaban failed to show noninferiority to dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists over three years: recurrent thrombosis occurred in 11.6% on rivaroxaban versus 6.3% on a vitamin K antagonist (relative risk 1.83, 95% CI 0.71 to 4.76), stroke occurred in 9 patients on rivaroxaban versus 0 on the antagonist, and major bleeding was similar (6.3% vs 7.4%) (Ordi-Ros 2019, PMID: 31610549; 190 patients). A patient-level meta-analysis of 447 patients treated with a DOAC found 16% suffered a recurrent thrombosis while on treatment, with triple positivity carrying a four-fold risk (odds ratio 4.3) (Dufrost 2018, PMID: 30103045). Even in lower-risk single- or double-positive patients, a retrospective cohort found recurrent thromboembolism in 15.4% on a DOAC versus 5.3% on warfarin, not statistically significant in 96 patients, with no difference in major bleeding (Williams 2022, PMID: 34817786). The second randomised trial in this field — TRAPS, in triple-positive patients — is homed on live shelf #1548 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded; it points the same way. Because only one randomised trial is carded here, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): DOAC therapy in antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with more recurrent thrombosis — arterial events in particular — than vitamin K antagonist therapy, without a bleeding advantage.

cards.headline: Ordi-Ros 2019: rivaroxaban did not show noninferiority to vitamin K antagonists in thrombotic APS — recurrent thrombosis 11.6% versus 6.3%, stroke 9 versus 0, major bleeding similar
cards.summary: Ordi-Ros 2019: rivaroxaban did not show noninferiority to vitamin K antagonists in thrombotic APS — recurrent thrombosis 11.6% versus 6.3%, stroke 9 versus 0, major bleeding similar
cards.people: 190 adults (aged 18 to 75 years) with thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome at six Spanish university hospitals, randomised in a three-year, open-label noninferiority trial to rivaroxaban (20 mg/day, or 15 mg/day according to renal function) or dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists (target INR 2.0 to 3.0, or 3.1 to 4.0 with a history of recurrent thrombosis). The prespecified noninferiority margin for the risk ratio was 1.40.
cards.result: After three years, recurrent thrombosis occurred in 11 patients (11.6%) in the rivaroxaban group and 6 (6.3%) in the vitamin K antagonist group (relative risk 1.83 [95% CI, 0.71 to 4.76]) — noninferiority was not shown. Stroke occurred more commonly on rivaroxaban (9 events) than on vitamin K antagonists (0 events) (corrected relative risk 19.00 [CI, 1.12 to 321.9]). Major bleeding occurred in 6 patients (6.3%) on rivaroxaban and 7 (7.4%) on vitamin K antagonists (relative risk 0.86 [CI, 0.30 to 2.46]). A post hoc analysis suggested increased risk of recurrent thrombosis on rivaroxaban in patients with previous arterial thrombosis, livedo racemosa, or APS-related cardiac valvular disease. The authors conclude rivaroxaban showed a non-statistically significant near doubling of the risk of recurrent thrombosis.
cards.watchOut: The headline relative risk is not statistically significant (CI 0.71 to 4.76) and anticoagulation intensity was not measured in the rivaroxaban group; the stroke contrast (9 versus 0) rests on small numbers with a very wide corrected confidence interval — the trial shows failure of noninferiority and a consistent direction of harm, not a precise harm estimate.
cards.source: Ordi-Ros J et al. Rivaroxaban Versus Vitamin K Antagonist in Antiphospholipid Syndrome: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31610549. Registry ID: EudraCT 2010-019764-36 (named in the record). cards.headline: Dufrost 2018: in a patient-level meta-analysis of 447 APS patients treated with DOACs, 16% had a recurrent thrombosis on treatment — and triple positivity carried a four-fold risk (odds ratio 4.3)
cards.summary: Dufrost 2018: in a patient-level meta-analysis of 447 APS patients treated with DOACs, 16% had a recurrent thrombosis on treatment — and triple positivity carried a four-fold risk (odds ratio 4.3)
cards.people: Systematic review and patient-level data meta-analysis of studies from 2000 to March 2018 of antiphospholipid syndrome patients treated with direct oral anticoagulants: 47 studies, 447 patients — rivaroxaban n = 290, dabigatran n = 144, apixaban n = 13.
cards.result: Seventy-three of 447 patients (16%) experienced a recurrent thrombosis while on a DOAC, with a mean duration until thrombosis of 12.5 months; recurrence rates were 16.9% on anti-Xa inhibitors and 15% on dabigatran. Triple positivity (all three antiphospholipid antibodies) was associated with a four-fold increased risk of recurrent thrombosis (56% vs 23%; odds ratio 4.3 [95% CI 2.3 to 7.7], P < 0.0001), as was a higher number of clinical criteria for APS classification. In patients on anti-Xa inhibitors, a history of arterial thrombosis was associated with higher recurrence (32% vs 14%; odds ratio 2.8 [95% CI 1.4 to 5.7], P = 0.006). The authors conclude DOACs are not effective in all APS patients and should not be used routinely.
cards.watchOut: Mostly non-randomised reports, including case series, with no warfarin comparator arm: the 16% recurrence figure is a rate on treatment, not a comparison — its force comes from agreeing with the randomised card above about who fails (triple-positive and arterial disease).
cards.source: Dufrost V et al. Increased risk of thrombosis in antiphospholipid syndrome patients treated with direct oral anticoagulants. Results from an international patient-level data meta-analysis. Autoimmunity Reviews. 2018. PMID: 30103045. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Williams 2022: even in single- or double-positive APS, recurrent thromboembolism was 15.4% on a DOAC versus 5.3% on warfarin in a 96-patient retrospective cohort — not statistically significant, major bleeding not different
cards.summary: Williams 2022: even in single- or double-positive APS, recurrent thromboembolism was 15.4% on a DOAC versus 5.3% on warfarin in a 96-patient retrospective cohort — not statistically significant, major bleeding not different
cards.people: Single-centre retrospective cohort of 96 patients with single- or double-antibody-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and a history of venous thromboembolism, treated within one health system from 2015 to 2020: 57 prescribed warfarin and 39 prescribed a DOAC (90% rivaroxaban).
cards.result: The proportion with a recurrent thromboembolism was almost three times higher in the DOAC group (15.4%) than in the warfarin group (5.3%), although this was not statistically significant (P = 0.15). Major bleeding was not different between groups. The authors suggest rivaroxaban may pose an increased risk of recurrent thromboembolism even in lower-risk single- or double-positive APS, and caution that the findings should be applied carefully to DOACs other than rivaroxaban given their small representation.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-six patients, retrospectively assigned by what clinicians prescribed: the three-fold difference could be chance (P = 0.15) or confounding, and 90% of the DOAC exposure was one drug — this card extends the concern to lower-risk APS but cannot settle it.
cards.source: Williams B et al. Direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in patients with single or double antibody-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. Journal of Thrombosis and Thrombolysis. 2022. cards.headline: Synthesis: DOACs in APS fail on efficacy, not bleeding — more recurrent thrombosis (arterial events especially) than vitamin K antagonists in the carded trial, meta-analysis and cohort, with triple positivity the highest-risk marker
cards.summary: Synthesis: DOACs in APS fail on efficacy, not bleeding — more recurrent thrombosis (arterial events especially) than vitamin K antagonists in the carded trial, meta-analysis and cohort, with triple positivity the highest-risk marker
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (190 patients), one patient-level meta-analysis (447 patients on DOACs) and one retrospective cohort (96 patients) — total carded participants 733, so no small-N labelling applies. The TRAPS randomised trial in triple-positive APS is homed on live shelf #1548 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded.
cards.result: Recurrent thrombosis on rivaroxaban versus vitamin K antagonist: 11.6% vs 6.3% (relative risk 1.83), with stroke 9 versus 0 and similar major bleeding (Ordi-Ros 2019). Recurrence on DOACs across the literature: 16% of 447 patients, with triple positivity at odds ratio 4.3 (Dufrost 2018). In single- or double-positive disease: 15.4% versus 5.3% recurrence, not significant (Williams 2022). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — capped at POSSIBLE because only one randomised trial is carded on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: 'Safe' splits in two on this shelf: bleeding safety looks comparable to warfarin in every card, while thrombotic safety — the reason for anticoagulating APS at all — is worse. A reader who only asks about bleeding would take away exactly the wrong answer.

shelves.title: Acute pericarditis first-line therapy: NSAID plus colchicine — recurrence at 18 months cut from 32.3% to 10.7% (COPE) with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.40
shelves.question: Should NSAIDs plus colchicine be first line for acute pericarditis?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adrenal Cortex Hormones therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents adverse effects therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal therapeutic use · Aspirin therapeutic use · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Colchicine adverse effects therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericarditis drug therapy physiopathology · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). The randomised evidence for adding colchicine to conventional anti-inflammatory therapy (aspirin or another NSAID) in a first episode of acute pericarditis is concordant. In the COPE trial, colchicine plus aspirin cut recurrence at 18 months from 32.3% to 10.7% (P = 0.004; number needed to treat 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours from 36.7% to 11.7% (Imazio 2005, PMID: 16186437; 120 patients, open-label). The Cochrane review of the randomised trials found, for acute pericarditis, a hazard ratio of 0.40 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) for recurrence with colchicine added to an NSAID, and better symptom relief at 72 hours (risk ratio 1.4) (Alabed 2014, PMID: 25164988). A further meta-analysis of nine trials and 1,832 patients found recurrence odds ratio 0.42 and symptom persistence odds ratio 0.29, at the cost of more adverse events (relative risk 1.48), mainly gastrointestinal (Li 2016, PMID: 26979508). The second acute-pericarditis trial inside those reviews — ICAP, double-blind — is homed on live shelf #190 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. No carded trial tests an NSAID alone against placebo, so 'first line' rests on the combination's randomised evidence plus the universal use of NSAIDs as the trials' backbone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): NSAID plus colchicine should be first-line therapy for a first episode of acute pericarditis.

cards.headline: Imazio 2005 (COPE): adding colchicine to aspirin for a first episode of acute pericarditis cut recurrence at 18 months from 32.3% to 10.7% (number needed to treat 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours from 36.7% to 11.7%
cards.summary: Imazio 2005 (COPE): adding colchicine to aspirin for a first episode of acute pericarditis cut recurrence at 18 months from 32.3% to 10.7% (number needed to treat 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours from 36.7% to 11.7%
cards.people: 120 patients (mean age 56.9 ± 18.8 years; 54 men) with a first episode of acute pericarditis (idiopathic, viral, postpericardiotomy and connective-tissue-disease causes), randomised prospectively in an open-label design to conventional treatment with aspirin alone or conventional treatment plus colchicine (1.0 to 2.0 mg on the first day, then 0.5 to 1.0 mg/day for three months). Corticosteroids were restricted to patients with aspirin contraindications or intolerance. Follow-up totalled 2,873 patient-months.
cards.result: Colchicine significantly reduced the recurrence rate (recurrence at 18 months 10.7% versus 32.3%; P = 0.004; number needed to treat = 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours (11.7% versus 36.7%; P = 0.003). Colchicine was discontinued in 5 cases (8.3%) because of diarrhoea; no serious adverse effects were observed. The authors conclude colchicine plus conventional therapy led to a clinically important and statistically significant benefit over conventional treatment alone for a first episode of acute pericarditis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-programme: patients and clinicians knew who received colchicine, which can colour symptom reporting; the blinded confirmation (ICAP) is homed on live shelf #190 and cross-pointed in this pack's balance rather than re-carded.
cards.source: Imazio M et al. Colchicine in addition to conventional therapy for acute pericarditis: results of the COlchicine for acute PEricarditis (COPE) trial. Circulation. 2005. PMID: 16186437. Registry ID: none in the record. imazio 2005) 120 patients (mean age 56.9 ± 18.8 years; 54 men) with a first episode of acute pericarditis (idiopathic, viral, postpericardiotomy and connective-tissue-disease causes), randomised prospectively in an open-label design to conventional treatment with aspirin alone or conventional treatment plus colchicine (1.0 to 2.0 mg on the first day, then 0.5 to 1.0 mg/day for three months). corticosteroids were restricted to patients with aspirin contraindications or intolerance. follow-up totalled 2,873 patient-months. colchicine significantly reduced the recurrence rate (recurrence at 18 months 10.7% versus 32.3%; p = 0.004; number needed to treat = 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours (11.7% versus 36.7%; p = 0.003). colchicine was discontinued in 5 cases (8.3%) because of diarrhoea; no serious adverse effects were observed. the authors conclude colchicine plus conventional therapy led to a clinically important and statistically significant benefit over conventional treatment alone for a first episode of acute pericarditis. open-label and single-programme: patients and clinicians knew who received colchicine, which can colour symptom reporting; cards.headline: Alabed 2014 (Cochrane): in acute pericarditis, colchicine added to an NSAID reduced recurrence (hazard ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) and improved symptom relief at 72 hours (risk ratio 1.4)
cards.summary: Alabed 2014 (Cochrane): in acute pericarditis, colchicine added to an NSAID reduced recurrence (hazard ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) and improved symptom relief at 72 hours (risk ratio 1.4)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised controlled trials of colchicine to prevent pericarditis recurrence: four trials, 564 participants — two trials in recurrent pericarditis (204 participants) and two in acute pericarditis (360 participants) — comparing colchicine in addition to an NSAID (ibuprofen, aspirin or indomethacin) against the NSAID alone.
cards.result: In people with acute pericarditis there was moderate-quality evidence that colchicine reduces recurrence (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) at 18 months of follow-up; in recurrent pericarditis the hazard ratio was 0.37 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.58), with a number needed to treat of 4. Colchicine gave a greater chance of symptom relief at 72 hours (risk ratio 1.4; 95% CI 1.26 to 1.56; low-quality evidence). Adverse effects were mainly gastrointestinal (abdominal pain and diarrhoea): 9% on colchicine versus 7% on control (pooled relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 0.75 to 2.12; not statistically significant, P = 0.42), though more people stopped colchicine because of adverse events (relative risk 1.87; 95% CI 1.02 to 3.41). The authors note the evidence rests on a limited number of small trials.
cards.watchOut: The acute-pericarditis pooled estimate rests on two trials (COPE, carded here, and ICAP, homed on live shelf #190) from the same research programme — concordant and blinded in ICAP's case, but not independent replication by unrelated groups.
cards.source: Alabed S et al. Colchicine for pericarditis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25164988. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2016: across nine randomised trials and 1,832 patients, colchicine added to conventional therapy halved the odds of recurrence (odds ratio 0.42) and of symptom persistence (odds ratio 0.29), with more adverse events (relative risk 1.48)
cards.summary: Li 2016: across nine randomised trials and 1,832 patients, colchicine added to conventional therapy halved the odds of recurrence (odds ratio 0.42) and of symptom persistence (odds ratio 0.29), with more adverse events (relative risk 1.48)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of colchicine plus conventional therapy for pericarditis recurrence in acute pericarditis or postpericardiotomy syndrome: nine trials, 1,832 patients, mean follow-up 13.1 months.
cards.result: Colchicine therapy significantly decreased the risk of pericarditis recurrence (odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.52; P < 0.001; I2 = 17.0%), pericarditis-associated rehospitalisation (odds ratio 0.29; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.53; P < 0.0001) and persistence of symptoms at 72 hours (odds ratio 0.29; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.41; P = 0.000). Adverse events were higher in the colchicine group (relative risk 1.48; 95% CI 1.06 to 2.07; P = 0.02). In subgroup analysis, recurrence was significantly lower with colchicine irrespective of prednisone use and of the cause of pericarditis.
cards.watchOut: This pool mixes acute pericarditis with postpericardiotomy syndrome and recurrent disease, and overlaps the Cochrane card's trials — it widens the base but is not an independent body of evidence, and its adverse-event signal (relative risk 1.48) is the clearest quantified harm on the shelf.
cards.source: Li YL et al. Colchicine in addition to conventional therapy for pericarditis recurrence: An update meta-analysis. Herz. 2016. PMID: 26979508. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: NSAID plus colchicine halves recurrence after a first episode of acute pericarditis (18-month recurrence 10.7% vs 32.3% in COPE; pooled hazard ratio 0.40) — the randomised case for first-line combination therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: NSAID plus colchicine halves recurrence after a first episode of acute pericarditis (18-month recurrence 10.7% vs 32.3% in COPE; pooled hazard ratio 0.40) — the randomised case for first-line combination therapy
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open-label randomised trial (120 patients), one Cochrane review (four trials, 564 participants; 360 in acute pericarditis) and one meta-analysis (nine trials, 1,832 patients). The reviews' underlying trials overlap, so totals are not additive; the acute-pericarditis randomised base is two trials (COPE here; ICAP homed on live shelf #190). No small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Recurrence at 18 months: 10.7% with aspirin plus colchicine versus 32.3% with aspirin alone (COPE). Pooled acute-pericarditis recurrence hazard ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) and symptom relief at 72 hours risk ratio 1.4 (Cochrane). Across nine trials, recurrence odds ratio 0.42 with adverse events relative risk 1.48 (Li 2016). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): NSAID plus colchicine as first-line therapy for a first episode of acute pericarditis.
cards.watchOut: Every carded trial compares NSAID-plus-colchicine against NSAID alone — no trial isolates the NSAID's own contribution, and colchicine's adverse events, though mostly gastrointestinal and non-serious, are consistently more frequent on treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Imazio M et al. Circulation. 2005 (PMID: 16186437); Alabed S et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25164988); Li YL et al. Herz. 2016 (PMID: 26979508).

shelves.title: Corticosteroids and pericarditis recurrence (observational only): associated with two- to three-fold higher recurrence in adjusted analyses — confounding by indication unexcluded
shelves.question: Does corticosteroid use increase pericarditis recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents therapeutic use · Aspirin therapeutic use · Colchicine therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pericarditis drug therapy · Prednisone therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face, as the brief for this number anticipated: no trial has randomised patients to corticosteroids to test recurrence, so every card is an adjusted observational analysis. The signal is consistent. Within the CORE randomised trial's cohort, previous corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for further recurrences (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.10 to 8.26) (Imazio 2005, PMID: 16186468; 84 patients). In a 175-patient myopericarditis cohort, corticosteroid use independently predicted recurrence (hazard ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.47) (Collini 2024, PMID: 38238076). In a prospective 148-patient acute pericarditis cohort, recurrence risk was higher in patients switched to corticosteroids after NSAID failure (hazard ratio 3.22) and in those given corticosteroids first-line (hazard ratio 2.06) than in patients treated with NSAIDs only (Lazaros 2019, PMID: 29684577). A 2026 systematic review of 10 studies and 2,632 patients found the association inconsistent in acute pericarditis but present in most recurrent-pericarditis studies, with moderate risk of bias and limited adjustment for confounding (Razeghi 2026, PMID: 42552090). Confounding by indication — steroids go to the sickest, most refractory patients — runs through all of it and cannot be removed by these adjustments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: corticosteroid use in pericarditis is associated with roughly two- to three-fold higher recurrence in adjusted analyses.

cards.headline: Imazio 2005 (CORE cohort analysis): previous corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for further pericarditis recurrences (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.10 to 8.26) — an observational analysis inside a randomised trial (N = 84, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Imazio 2005 (CORE cohort analysis): previous corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for further pericarditis recurrences (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.10 to 8.26) — an observational analysis inside a randomised trial (N = 84, printed on the face)
cards.type: Multivariate observational analysis within a randomised trial (CORE; Imazio 2005)
cards.people: 84 consecutive patients with a first episode of recurrent pericarditis in the CORE trial, randomised to conventional treatment (aspirin alone, or prednisone 1.0–1.5 mg/kg daily for one month then tapered when aspirin was contraindicated) or conventional treatment plus colchicine, followed for a mean of 20 months (1,682 patient-months). The corticosteroid finding comes from the trial's multivariate analysis, not from a randomised corticosteroid comparison.
cards.result: In multivariate analysis, previous corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for further recurrences (odds ratio 2.89; 95% confidence interval 1.10 to 8.26; P = .04). For context, the trial's randomised comparison showed colchicine decreased the recurrence rate (actuarial rates at 18 months 24.0% vs 50.6%; P = .02; number needed to treat 4.0) — the corticosteroid association is the observational part of this record and is carded as such.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-four patients, and corticosteroids were given precisely when aspirin was contraindicated or had failed — the classic setup for confounding by indication, which a multivariate model on this number of patients can only partly correct.
cards.source: Imazio M et al. Colchicine as first-choice therapy for recurrent pericarditis: results of the CORE (COlchicine for REcurrent pericarditis) trial. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005. PMID: 16186468. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Collini 2024: in 175 patients with a first attack of myopericarditis, corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for recurrence (hazard ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.47)
cards.summary: Collini 2024: in 175 patients with a first attack of myopericarditis, corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for recurrence (hazard ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.47)
cards.people: Double-centre retrospective cohort of 175 consecutive patients admitted with a first attack of acute pericarditis with concomitant myocardial involvement (myopericarditis): mean age 46.2 ± 20.1 years, 25.1% female, 88.6% idiopathic/viral aetiology. Seventy-nine patients (45.1%) were treated with colchicine; median follow-up was 25.3 months (interquartile range 8.3–45.6); 58 patients (33.1%) had recurrences.
cards.result: In multivariable analysis, corticosteroid use (hazard ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.47; P = 0.018) and female sex (hazard ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.04 to 3.73; P = 0.037) were independent risk factors for recurrence. (The study's primary question was colchicine, which was associated with fewer recurrences — 19.2% vs 43.8% after propensity matching — with mild side effects in 3 patients, 1.7%.)
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and in myopericarditis rather than simple pericarditis: corticosteroids may have been chosen for patients with more myocardial involvement or worse early courses, and the record's adjustment cannot fully separate the drug from the reasons it was given.
cards.source: Collini V et al. Efficacy and safety of colchicine for the treatment of myopericarditis. Heart (British Cardiac Society). 2024. PMID: 38238076. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lazaros 2019: in a prospective cohort of 148 acute pericarditis patients, recurrence risk was about three-fold higher in patients switched to corticosteroids (hazard ratio 3.22) and two-fold higher with first-line corticosteroids (hazard ratio 2.06) than with NSAIDs only
cards.summary: Lazaros 2019: in a prospective cohort of 148 acute pericarditis patients, recurrence risk was about three-fold higher in patients switched to corticosteroids (hazard ratio 3.22) and two-fold higher with first-line corticosteroids (hazard ratio 2.06) than with NSAIDs only
cards.people: 148 patients with acute pericarditis followed prospectively for 18 months for recurrence: 110 received aspirin/NSAIDs and 38 corticosteroids as first-line treatment according to clinical indications; 37 patients with poor response to NSAIDs were switched to corticosteroid treatment.
cards.result: In Cox regression analysis, the risk of recurrence was higher in patients requiring a switch to corticosteroids (hazard ratio 3.22, 95% CI 1.70 to 6.13) and in those initially treated with corticosteroids (hazard ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 4.21) than in patients receiving NSAIDs only. Predictors of poor NSAID response and switching were female sex (odds ratio 3.57), younger age (odds ratio 0.75 per decade), PR-segment depression (odds ratio 4.43) and a secondary cause of pericarditis (odds ratio 13.52). The authors conclude that switching identifies the patients at highest risk of recurrence.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own framing cuts both ways: needing steroids marks refractory disease, so the hazard ratios measure a mixture of any drug effect and the prognosis of patients who fail first-line therapy — the switch group's 3.22 is the most confounded number on this shelf.
cards.source: Lazaros G et al. Predictors of switching from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to corticosteroids in patients with acute pericarditis and impact on clinical outcome. Hellenic Journal of Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 29684577. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Razeghi 2026: a systematic review of 10 studies and 2,632 patients found the corticosteroid–recurrence association inconsistent in acute pericarditis but present in most recurrent-pericarditis studies, with confounding throughout
cards.summary: Razeghi 2026: a systematic review of 10 studies and 2,632 patients found the corticosteroid–recurrence association inconsistent in acute pericarditis but present in most recurrent-pericarditis studies, with confounding throughout
cards.people: Systematic review of oral corticosteroids for acute or recurrent pericarditis, searching MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and Scopus to 26 November 2025: 10 studies (2 prospective, 8 retrospective) including 2,632 patients, of whom 800 were corticosteroid-treated. Prednisone was the most studied agent, with heterogeneous dosing (0.25–1.0 mg/kg/day) and non-standardised tapering; follow-up ranged from 1 to 6.7 years.
cards.result: Findings on recurrence were inconsistent in acute idiopathic and post-procedure pericarditis, while most studies in recurrent pericarditis reported higher recurrence with corticosteroid exposure. Overall risk of bias was moderate, with limited adjustment for confounding, and the authors conclude that observational data show variable associations with recurrence across clinical contexts and that high-quality randomised trials stratified by aetiology and acuity are needed. No pooled effect size is reported in the record — the synthesis is descriptive — and that absence is printed here rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: A descriptive synthesis without a pooled estimate: it disciplines the shelf's other cards — the association is real in the recurrent-disease literature and genuinely uncertain in first-episode acute pericarditis — rather than adding a fourth concordant number.
cards.source: Razeghi G et al. Prednisone in the Management of Pericarditis: A Systematic Review. Journal of Cardiovascular Pharmacology. 2026. PMID: 42552090. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: corticosteroid use is associated with roughly two- to three-fold higher pericarditis recurrence in every adjusted observational analysis carded — and confounding by indication is the standing alternative explanation (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: corticosteroid use is associated with roughly two- to three-fold higher pericarditis recurrence in every adjusted observational analysis carded — and confounding by indication is the standing alternative explanation (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: a multivariate analysis within a randomised trial cohort (84 patients), a retrospective myopericarditis cohort (175 patients), a prospective acute-pericarditis cohort (148 patients) and a systematic review (10 studies, 2,632 patients, overlapping the primary literature). Unique primary-cohort participants total over 400; no small-N labelling applies to the shelf as a whole, and the smallest study's N (84) is printed on its card face.
cards.result: Adjusted associations between corticosteroid use and recurrence: odds ratio 2.89 (CORE analysis), hazard ratio 2.27 (Collini 2024), hazard ratio 2.06 for first-line corticosteroids and 3.22 for switching to corticosteroids (Lazaros 2019). The systematic review found the pattern consistent in recurrent pericarditis and inconsistent in acute pericarditis (Razeghi 2026). No randomised evidence exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Steroids are given to patients who are failing, intolerant of, or contraindicated for first-line therapy — every card's adjustment fights that selection, none eliminates it. The shelf supports 'associated with more recurrence, plausibly causal, unproven' and nothing stronger.
cards.source: Synthesis of Imazio M et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005 (PMID: 16186468); Collini V et al. Heart. 2024 (PMID: 38238076); Lazaros G et al. Hellenic Journal of Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 29684577); Razeghi G et al. Journal of Cardiovascular Pharmacology. 2026 (PMID: 42552090).

shelves.title: Exercise restriction in myocarditis (untested, observational only): never compared with continued exercise — athlete cohorts managed with restriction showed resolved inflammation and very few events
shelves.question: Does exercise restriction improve recovery in myocarditis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Athletes · COVID-19 complications epidemiology · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Cine · Male · Mass Screening methods · Myocarditis diagnosis epidemiology etiology · Pandemics · Prevalence · Registries · SARS-CoV-2 · United States epidemiology
shelves.balance: MAYBE — observational only, printed on the face. Exercise restriction after myocarditis has never been compared with continued exercise in any carded study, randomised or otherwise: in every athlete cohort here, restriction was simply what was done with athletes found to have myocarditis, so the shelf can report outcomes under restriction, not the effect of restriction. Those outcomes were benign. In the Big Ten registry, 37 of 1,597 screened athletes (2.3%) were diagnosed with clinical or subclinical myocarditis after COVID-19, and on follow-up imaging the T2 signal of inflammation had resolved in all 27 re-imaged athletes, though late gadolinium enhancement persisted in 40.7% (Daniels 2021, PMID: 34042947). Among 789 professional athletes screened before return to play, five (0.6%) had inflammatory heart disease that resulted in restriction from play, and no adverse cardiac events occurred in athletes who resumed professional sport (Martinez 2021, PMID: 33662103). In the ORCCA cohort of 3,018 COVID-positive athletes, cardiac involvement was found in 0.7% and exactly one adverse cardiac event (0.03%) occurred over a median 113 days — judged likely unrelated to the infection (Moulson 2021, PMID: 33866822). None of this shows restriction improves recovery; it shows that a screen-restrict-return pathway was followed by very few events. PROPOSED MAYBE — observational only: whether exercise restriction improves recovery in myocarditis is untested; outcomes under restriction-based management in screened athletes were good.

cards.headline: Daniels 2021 (Big Ten registry): 37 of 1,597 screened athletes (2.3%) had COVID-19 myocarditis; on follow-up imaging inflammation (T2) had resolved in all re-imaged athletes, while scar signal persisted in 40.7%
cards.summary: Daniels 2021 (Big Ten registry): 37 of 1,597 screened athletes (2.3%) had COVID-19 myocarditis; on follow-up imaging inflammation (T2) had resolved in all re-imaged athletes, while scar signal persisted in 40.7%
cards.type: Registry cohort (Big Ten COVID-19 Cardiac Registry; Daniels 2021)
cards.people: Cohort study of competitive athletes with COVID-19 at 13 Big Ten universities, March to December 2020: cardiovascular testing in 1,597 athletes (964 men, 60.4%), with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging required for all athletes with COVID-19 under conference policy. Thirty-seven athletes (27 men) were diagnosed with COVID-19 myocarditis — 9 clinical and 28 subclinical.
cards.result: Myocarditis prevalence was 2.3% overall (range per programme 0%–7.6%). Had testing been based on cardiac symptoms alone, only 5 athletes would have been detected (0.31%); imaging all athletes increased detection 7.4-fold. Follow-up cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in 27 athletes (73.0%) demonstrated resolution of T2 elevation in all (100%) and persistent late gadolinium enhancement in 11 (40.7%). The authors note that variable ascertainment and the unknown implications of the imaging findings underscore the need for standardised testing; the record reports detection and imaging course, not a comparison of restricted versus unrestricted athletes.
cards.watchOut: This is a detection study: it shows imaging inflammation usually resolves over follow-up in athletes managed under conference return-to-play rules, but it never compares athletes who rested with athletes who did not — 'resolution happened' is not 'restriction caused resolution'.
cards.source: Daniels CJ et al. Prevalence of Clinical and Subclinical Myocarditis in Competitive Athletes With Recent SARS-CoV-2 Infection: Results From the Big Ten COVID-19 Cardiac Registry. JAMA Cardiology. 2021. PMID: 34042947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Martinez 2021: among 789 professional athletes screened after COVID-19, five (0.6%) had inflammatory heart disease that resulted in restriction from play — and no adverse cardiac events occurred in athletes who resumed sport
cards.summary: Martinez 2021: among 789 professional athletes screened after COVID-19, five (0.6%) had inflammatory heart disease that resulted in restriction from play — and no adverse cardiac events occurred in athletes who resumed sport
cards.people: Cross-sectional study of return-to-play cardiac testing (May to October 2020) in 789 professional athletes (mean age 25 years, SD 3; 777 men, 98.5%) from the major North American leagues who had tested positive for COVID-19: 460 (58.3%) with prior symptomatic illness and 329 (41.7%) asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic. Screening comprised troponin, electrocardiography and resting echocardiography a mean of 19 days (SD 17) after the positive test, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and/or stress echocardiography for abnormal results.
cards.result: Abnormal screening results were identified in 30 athletes (3.8%), prompting additional testing; five athletes (0.6%) ultimately had imaging findings suggesting inflammatory heart disease (myocarditis in 3, pericarditis in 2) that resulted in restriction from play. No adverse cardiac events occurred in athletes who underwent cardiac screening and resumed professional sport participation. The authors conclude that few cases of inflammatory heart disease were detected and a safe return to professional sports activity was achieved under the screening programme, with long-term follow-up ongoing.
cards.watchOut: Only three athletes had myocarditis; the reassurance is about the whole screen-and-restrict pathway in elite athletes with mostly mild COVID-19, and the absence of events in those cleared to play says nothing about what would have happened to the restricted athletes had they played.
cards.source: Martinez MW et al. Prevalence of Inflammatory Heart Disease Among Professional Athletes With Prior COVID-19 Infection Who Received Systematic Return-to-Play Cardiac Screening. JAMA Cardiology. 2021. PMID: 33662103. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moulson 2021 (ORCCA): cardiac involvement in 0.7% of 3,018 COVID-positive collegiate athletes, with one adverse cardiac event (0.03%) over a median 113 days — judged likely unrelated to the infection
cards.summary: Moulson 2021 (ORCCA): cardiac involvement in 0.7% of 3,018 COVID-positive collegiate athletes, with one adverse cardiac event (0.03%) over a median 113 days — judged likely unrelated to the infection
cards.people: Prospective multicentre observational cohort (ORCCA) at 42 US colleges and universities, September to December 2020: 19,378 athletes tested for SARS-CoV-2, of whom 3,018 tested positive and underwent cardiac evaluation (mean age 20 years, SD 1; 32% female). Cardiac involvement was defined by imaging criteria adapted from the Updated Lake Louise criteria.
cards.result: Definite, probable or possible cardiac involvement was identified in 21 of 3,018 athletes (0.7%). Predictors included cardiopulmonary symptoms (odds ratio 3.1 [95% CI 1.2 to 7.7]) and at least one abnormal triad test (odds ratio 37.4 [95% CI 13.3 to 105.3]). Five athletes (0.2%) required hospitalisation for noncardiac COVID-19 complications. During clinical surveillance (median follow-up 113 days, interquartile range 90–146), there was one (0.03%) adverse cardiac event, likely unrelated to SARS-CoV-2 infection. The authors conclude infection in young competitive athletes carries a low prevalence of cardiac involvement and a low short-term risk of clinical events.
cards.watchOut: Only 21 athletes had cardiac involvement, follow-up was a median of under four months, and management followed return-to-play protocols throughout — a low event rate under restriction cannot estimate the event rate without it.
cards.source: Moulson N et al. SARS-CoV-2 Cardiac Involvement in Young Competitive Athletes. Circulation. 2021. PMID: 33866822. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no study has tested exercise restriction against continued exercise in myocarditis — the carded cohorts show only that screen-restrict-return pathways in athletes were followed by resolved inflammation and very few events (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no study has tested exercise restriction against continued exercise in myocarditis — the carded cohorts show only that screen-restrict-return pathways in athletes were followed by resolved inflammation and very few events (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: three observational athlete cohorts from the COVID-19 era — 1,597 screened athletes with 37 myocarditis cases (Daniels 2021), 789 professional athletes with 5 restricted for inflammatory heart disease (Martinez 2021), and 3,018 evaluated athletes with 21 cardiac-involvement cases (Moulson 2021). Screened totals exceed 30, so no small-N labelling applies to the shelf; the myocarditis subgroups themselves are small (37, 3 and 21 athletes) and those numbers are printed on the card faces.
cards.result: Under restriction-based return-to-play management: imaging inflammation resolved in all 27 re-imaged Big Ten athletes (late gadolinium enhancement persisted in 40.7%); no adverse cardiac events occurred among professionals who resumed sport; and one adverse cardiac event (0.03%), judged unrelated, occurred across 3,018 ORCCA athletes. No carded record compares restricted with unrestricted patients, measures recovery as an outcome of restriction, or studies non-COVID myocarditis management. PROPOSED MAYBE — observational only: exercise restriction's effect on recovery in myocarditis is untested.
cards.watchOut: All three cohorts are COVID-19-era athlete screening studies: young, elite, mostly mild illness, and myocarditis largely subclinical and imaging-defined. Nothing here generalises cleanly to clinical myocarditis in non-athletes — and the restriction recommendation itself rests on sudden-death reasoning these studies were designed around, not on evidence they generated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Daniels CJ et al. JAMA Cardiology. 2021 (PMID: 34042947); Martinez MW et al. JAMA Cardiology. 2021 (PMID: 33662103); Moulson N et al. Circulation. 2021 (PMID: 33866822).

shelves.title: Yes — longer recording catches what one day misses: a 14-day patch found 96 arrhythmia events versus the Holter's 61 in the same patients, and randomised and Medicare evidence agree
shelves.question: Does a 14-day patch monitor diagnose palpitations better than 24-hour Holter?
shelves.mesh: Adhesives · Adult · Aged · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Atrial Fibrillation · Atrial Flutter · Atrioventricular Block · Electrocardiography · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Equipment Design · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Tachycardia, Supraventricular · Tachycardia, Ventricular · Time Factors · Ventricular Fibrillation
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — concordant evidence across four designs. Worn simultaneously in the same 146 patients, a 14-day adhesive patch detected 96 arrhythmia events against the 24-hour Holter's 61 (Barrett 2014, PMID: 24384108). Randomised evidence agrees in adjacent settings: after stroke/TIA a 14-day patch found paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in 16.3% versus 2.1% with short Holter (EPACS, PMID: 31349792), and in emergency-department palpitation patients prolonged symptom capture found a symptomatic rhythm in 55.6% versus 9.5% with standard care (IPED, PMID: 31193636). In 287,789 Medicare patients the long-term continuous/patch strategy had the highest adjusted odds of a new diagnosis and the lowest repeat testing (Reynolds 2024, PMID: 38072334). The mechanism is duration — intermittent rhythms are missed by a single day of recording — not superior sensing. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a 14-day patch monitor diagnoses palpitations better than 24-hour Holter.

cards.headline: Barrett 2014: wearing both devices at once, the 14-day adhesive patch detected 96 arrhythmia events versus 61 by the 24-hour Holter (P < .001) in 146 patients referred for arrhythmia evaluation
cards.summary: Barrett 2014: wearing both devices at once, the 14-day adhesive patch detected 96 arrhythmia events versus 61 by the 24-hour Holter (P < .001) in 146 patients referred for arrhythmia evaluation
cards.people: 146 patients referred for evaluation of cardiac arrhythmia who underwent simultaneous ambulatory ECG recording with a conventional 24-hour Holter monitor and a 14-day single-lead adhesive patch monitor (the Zio Patch, iRhythm Technologies — the specific tested device, named as the record names it). Arrhythmia events were any of 6 defined arrhythmias: supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation/flutter, pause over 3 seconds, atrioventricular block, ventricular tachycardia, or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation.
cards.result: Over the total wear time of both devices, the adhesive patch monitor detected 96 arrhythmia events compared with 61 events by the Holter monitor (P < .001, McNemar's test on the matched pairs). The authors conclude that prolonged monitoring with a single-lead, less-obtrusive adhesive patch could replace conventional Holter monitoring in patients referred for ambulatory ECG monitoring. The record does not report how many of the extra events occurred only after the first 24 hours, so no first-day comparison is carded.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is built into the design: 14 days of recording will almost inevitably catch more intermittent events than 24 hours, so this study measures the yield of longer monitoring more than any superiority of the patch hardware itself; it is a single-lead device, and patients were referred for arrhythmia evaluation generally, not palpitations alone.
cards.source: Barrett PM et al. Comparison of 24-hour Holter monitoring with 14-day novel adhesive patch electrocardiographic monitoring. The American Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24384108. Registry ID: NCT01559246.
