cards.headline: Reynolds 2024: in 287,789 Medicare patients, long-term continuous monitors — and one 14-day patch in particular — had the highest adjusted odds of a new arrhythmia diagnosis and the lowest odds of repeat testing versus Holter
cards.summary: Reynolds 2024: in 287,789 Medicare patients, long-term continuous monitors — and one 14-day patch in particular — had the highest adjusted odds of a new arrhythmia diagnosis and the lowest odds of repeat testing versus Holter
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of the full (100%) sample of Medicare claims: 287,789 diagnostic-naive patients who received first-time ambulatory cardiac monitoring in 2017–2018 (Holter 53.8%, mobile cardiac telemetry 22.5%, long-term continuous monitor [LTCM] 13.3%, event monitor 10.3%), with arrhythmia diagnosis at 3 months, repeat testing at 6 months, 90-day emergency/inpatient use and cost compared.
cards.result: As a category, LTCM was associated with the lowest 1-year incremental health care expenditures (mean Δ$10,159), followed by Holter ($10,755), event monitors ($11,462) and mobile cardiac telemetry ($12,532). In the device-specific analysis, one specific LTCM — the Zio XT 14-day patch (iRhythm Technologies, named in the record) — had the highest adjusted odds of diagnosis and the lowest adjusted odds of repeat testing compared with Holter, other event/telemetry strategies and other LTCM makers, consistently for ventricular tachycardia, atrioventricular block and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The record's abstract reports these adjusted odds in direction only and prints no odds-ratio values, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Claims data, not randomisation: clinicians chose the monitor, so patients given a patch may differ systematically from patients given a Holter, and a coded 'diagnosis' is not the same as a symptom-rhythm correlation in a patient with palpitations.

cards.headline: Kaura 2019 (EPACS randomised trial): after stroke or TIA, a 14-day patch detected paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in 16.3% versus 2.1% with short-duration Holter (odds ratio 8.9, relative)
cards.summary: Kaura 2019 (EPACS randomised trial): after stroke or TIA, a 14-day patch detected paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in 16.3% versus 2.1% with short-duration Holter (odds ratio 8.9, relative)
cards.people: Open-label randomised controlled trial of cardiac monitoring after a transient ischaemic attack or ischaemic stroke: 56 patients assigned to a 14-day ECG monitoring patch (Zio Patch, iRhythm Technologies) and 60 to short-duration Holter monitoring; 43 (76.8%) and 47 (78.3%) respectively had successful monitor placement with 90 days of follow-up. Primary outcome was detection of one or more episodes of ECG-documented paroxysmal atrial fibrillation lasting at least 30 seconds within 90 days.
cards.result: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was detected in 16.3% of the patch group (7 patients) versus 2.1% of the Holter group (1 patient), odds ratio 8.9 (95% CI 1.1–76.0; P = 0.026 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates 16.3% vs 2.1% beside it). Of 26 protocol failures, 23 (88.5%) were patient refusal of the outpatient short-duration monitor, versus 1 (3.8%) unsuccessful patch placement. A budget model estimated the patch service would avoid 10.8 more strokes per year than current Holter practice, with an associated saving of £113,630 in direct medical costs per year.
cards.watchOut: This is a stroke/TIA population being screened for silent atrial fibrillation, not patients with palpitations, and the randomised N is small (116) with a very wide confidence interval (1.1–76.0); it supports the duration principle, not a palpitations-specific yield figure.
cards.source: Kaura A et al. Early prolonged ambulatory cardiac monitoring in stroke (EPACS): an open-label randomised controlled trial. European Journal of Medical Research. 2019. PMID: 31349792. cards.headline: Reed 2019 (IPED randomised trial): in emergency-department patients with palpitations, adding a smartphone event recorder to standard care captured a symptomatic rhythm in 55.6% versus 9.5% at 90 days (relative risk 5.9)
cards.summary: Reed 2019 (IPED randomised trial): in emergency-department patients with palpitations, adding a smartphone event recorder to standard care captured a symptomatic rhythm in 55.6% versus 9.5% at 90 days (relative risk 5.9)
cards.people: Multi-centre open-label randomised trial in 10 UK hospital emergency departments: 243 participants aged 16 years or older presenting with palpitations or pre-syncope with no obvious cause at initial consultation were recruited; 124 were randomised to standard care plus a smartphone-based event recorder (AliveCor, the tested device named in the record) and 116 to standard care alone. Primary endpoint was the symptomatic rhythm detection rate at 90 days.
cards.result: A symptomatic rhythm was detected at 90 days in 69 of 124 intervention participants (55.6%) versus 11 of 116 controls (9.5%) (relative risk 5.9, 95% CI 3.3–10.5; P < 0.0001 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). Mean time to detection was 9.5 days versus 42.9 days (P < 0.0001). A symptomatic cardiac arrhythmia was detected in 8.9% versus 0.9% (relative risk 10.3, 95% CI 1.3–78.5; P = 0.006); the commonest symptomatic rhythms overall were sinus rhythm, sinus tachycardia and ectopic beats.
cards.watchOut: The recorder is patient-triggered and smartphone-based, not a continuous 14-day patch, and most captured rhythms were benign (sinus rhythm or ectopics) — the trial proves that giving palpitation patients a way to record during symptoms transforms diagnostic yield, which is the same duration/opportunity principle the patch exploits continuously.
cards.source: Reed MJ et al. Multi-centre Randomised Controlled Trial of a Smartphone-based Event Recorder Alongside Standard Care Versus Standard Care for Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department with Palpitations and Pre-syncope: The IPED (Investigation of Palpitations in the ED) study. cards.headline: Synthesis: longer recording wins on every design tested — paired head-to-head (96 vs 61 events), a randomised post-stroke trial (16.3% vs 2.1%), a randomised palpitations trial of prolonged capture (55.6% vs 9.5%), and 287,789 Medicare patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: longer recording wins on every design tested — paired head-to-head (96 vs 61 events), a randomised post-stroke trial (16.3% vs 2.1%), a randomised palpitations trial of prolonged capture (55.6% vs 9.5%), and 287,789 Medicare patients
cards.people: The carded evidence: one simultaneous paired comparison in 146 referred patients (Barrett 2014), one randomised trial in 116 post-stroke/TIA patients (Kaura 2019, EPACS), one randomised trial in 243 emergency-department palpitation patients (Reed 2019, IPED), and one retrospective Medicare claims cohort of 287,789 patients (Reynolds 2024). Total carded participants exceed 288,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Every comparison points the same way: the 14-day patch found more arrhythmia events than the 24-hour Holter worn at the same time (96 vs 61, P < .001); randomised patch monitoring found roughly eight times the paroxysmal atrial fibrillation of short Holter after stroke (16.3% vs 2.1%); prolonged symptom capture in palpitations found a symptomatic rhythm in over half of patients versus under a tenth with standard care; and in routine Medicare practice the long-term continuous/patch strategy carried the highest adjusted odds of diagnosis and the lowest repeat testing. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a 14-day patch monitor diagnoses more arrhythmias than a 24-hour Holter, because most palpitation-causing rhythms do not occur every day.
cards.watchOut: The yield advantage is a duration effect, not proof the patch is a better sensor: a single-lead patch can still miss or misclassify rhythms a multi-lead recording would clarify, and none of these studies shows that the extra diagnoses change hard outcomes such as stroke or death.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barrett PM et al. The American Journal of Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24384108); Reynolds MR et al. American Heart Journal. 2024 (PMID: 38072334); Kaura A et al. European Journal of Medical Research. 2019 (PMID: 31349792); Reed MJ et al. EClinicalMedicine. 2019 (PMID: 31193636).

shelves.title: Unproven in preserved LVEF (observational only): risk persists and MRI scar marks it, and ICDs fire appropriately in 39% of cardiac sarcoidosis recipients — but no ICD-versus-none comparison exists in this subgroup
shelves.question: Does an ICD prevent sudden death in cardiac sarcoidosis with preserved LVEF?
shelves.mesh: Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Defibrillators, Implantable · Humans · Incidence · Myocarditis · Risk Factors · Sarcoidosis · Tachycardia, Ventricular
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No trial has tested an ICD in cardiac sarcoidosis with preserved LVEF. What the observational record shows is: (1) risk is not confined to reduced ejection fraction — in 398 Finnish patients, 5-year sudden-death incidence was 4.8% even without a guideline ICD indication, and the indications themselves did not predict sudden death (Nordenswan 2022, PMID: 36000392); (2) in 51 patients with LVEF over 35%, MRI scar stratified that risk sharply (positive predictive value 22% for any scar, 100% for right-ventricular scar; Crawford 2014, PMID: 25266311); (3) ICDs in cardiac sarcoidosis deliver appropriate therapy in 39% of recipients but inappropriate therapy in 15%, in a meta-analysis whose pooled mean LVEF was only 38.4% (Halawa 2020, PMID: 32062788). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: an ICD plausibly prevents some sudden deaths in preserved-LVEF cardiac sarcoidosis, especially with MRI scar, but that prevention is unproven in this subgroup.

cards.headline: Nordenswan 2022: in 398 patients with clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis, 5-year sudden-death incidence was 4.8% even in patients WITHOUT a guideline ICD indication — the guidelines failed to find a truly low-risk group
cards.summary: Nordenswan 2022: in 398 patients with clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis, 5-year sudden-death incidence was 4.8% even in patients WITHOUT a guideline ICD indication — the guidelines failed to find a truly low-risk group
cards.people: 398 patients with clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis detected in Finland from 1988 through 2017 (histological diagnosis myocardial in 193, 'definite'; extracardiac in 205, 'probable'), classified by whether Class I or IIa ICD indications were present at presentation under the 2014 Heart Rhythm Society guideline, and followed for fatal or aborted sudden cardiac death (SCD) and sustained ventricular tachycardia over a median of 4.8 years.
cards.result: 41 patients (10.3%) had fatal (n = 8) or aborted (n = 33) SCD, and 98 (24.6%) experienced SCD or sustained ventricular tachycardia as the first event. Cumulative 5-year SCD incidence was 10.7% (95% CI 7.4%–15.4%) in patients with ICD indications versus 4.8% (95% CI 1.2%–19.1%) in those without (P = 0.176); in multivariable analysis SCD was predicted by definite histological diagnosis (P = 0.033) but not by Class I or IIa ICD indications (P = 0.210). In patients without ICD indications at presentation, the 5-year incidence of SCD, sustained ventricular tachycardia, and newly emerging ICD indications combined was 53% (95% CI 40%–71%). The authors conclude current guidelines fail to distinguish a truly low-risk group and that all patients with clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis should be considered for an ICD.
cards.watchOut: This cohort is clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis of all ejection fractions, not a preserved-LVEF-only population, and ICD receipt was itself unequal (78% of indicated vs 51% of non-indicated patients received one), so the comparison cannot isolate the ICD's effect on death.
cards.source: Nordenswan HK et al. Incidence of Sudden Cardiac Death and Life-Threatening Arrhythmias in Clinically Manifest Cardiac Sarcoidosis With and Without Current Indications for an Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator. cards.headline: Crawford 2014: in 51 cardiac sarcoidosis patients with LVEF over 35%, scar (delayed enhancement) on MRI separated risk — positive predictive value for death or VT/VF was 22% for any scar and 100% for right-ventricular scar at 48 months
cards.summary: Crawford 2014: in 51 cardiac sarcoidosis patients with LVEF over 35%, scar (delayed enhancement) on MRI separated risk — positive predictive value for death or VT/VF was 22% for any scar and 100% for right-ventricular scar at 48 months
cards.people: 51 patients with cardiac sarcoidosis and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) over 35% who underwent delayed-enhancement MRI, followed for 48.0 ± 20.2 months; 40 had no prior ventricular tachycardia (VT) (primary-prevention cohort) and 11 had a history of VT before the MRI.
cards.result: 22 of 51 patients had delayed enhancement (DE). DE was associated with risk of VT/ventricular fibrillation or death (P = 0.0032 for any DE; P < 0.0001 for right ventricular DE). The positive predictive values of any DE, multifocal DE, and right ventricular DE for death or VT/ventricular fibrillation at mean follow-up of 48 months were 22%, 48%, and 100% respectively. Among the 40 primary-prevention patients, 3 developed VT and 2 died; among the 11 with prior VT, 10 had subsequent VTs and 1 died. Patients without DE on MRI had a low risk of VT. (The record's printed percentage for DE prevalence is internally inconsistent with its own counts, so counts only are carded.)
cards.watchOut: 51 patients from one centre, and no comparison of ICD versus no ICD: this card shows risk exists and is scar-stratified in preserved/mildly reduced function — it does not show an ICD changes that risk, and a 100% positive predictive value rests on very few right-ventricular-DE patients.

cards.headline: Halawa 2020 (meta-analysis of ICDs in cardiac sarcoidosis): appropriate ICD therapy in 39% and inappropriate therapy in 15% over a mean 25 months — but the pooled mean LVEF was 38.4%, so this is mostly reduced-function evidence
cards.summary: Halawa 2020 (meta-analysis of ICDs in cardiac sarcoidosis): appropriate ICD therapy in 39% and inappropriate therapy in 15% over a mean 25 months — but the pooled mean LVEF was 38.4%, so this is mostly reduced-function evidence
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies with 585 patients with cardiac sarcoidosis who received an ICD (studies from 2000 to December 2018); 57% were male and the pooled mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 38.4%. Outcomes were appropriate and inappropriate ICD therapy and mortality over a mean follow-up of 25 months.
cards.result: Appropriate ICD treatments were reported in 39% of patients and inappropriate treatments in 15%, with a mortality rate of 8% over the mean 25-month follow-up. In a sub-analysis of four studies, patients receiving appropriate therapy did not differ from the rest of the cardiac sarcoidosis population in LVEF (mean difference −7.37%, 95% CI −16.89 to 2.15; P = 0.12), age, or primary versus secondary prevention indication; high-degree atrioventricular block was more common in patients with appropriate therapy (risk difference 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.14; P = 0.05). The authors conclude ICD placement in cardiac sarcoidosis is associated with a high incidence of both appropriate and inappropriate therapy.
cards.watchOut: An appropriate shock is a surrogate, not a death prevented — some treated arrhythmias would have stopped on their own — and with a pooled mean LVEF of 38.4% the meta-analysis cannot answer the preserved-LVEF question directly; there is no non-ICD control group in any pooled study.
cards.source: Halawa A et al. Outcome of implantable cardioverter defibrillator in cardiac sarcoidosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Interventional Cardiac Electrophysiology. 2020. PMID: 32062788. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: risk in preserved function is real and scar-stratified, and ICDs fire appropriately often in cardiac sarcoidosis — but no study has randomised, or even cleanly compared, ICD versus no ICD in preserved LVEF
cards.summary: Synthesis: risk in preserved function is real and scar-stratified, and ICDs fire appropriately often in cardiac sarcoidosis — but no study has randomised, or even cleanly compared, ICD versus no ICD in preserved LVEF
cards.people: The carded evidence: a nationwide cohort of 398 patients with clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis (Nordenswan 2022), a 51-patient MRI cohort restricted to LVEF over 35% (Crawford 2014), and a meta-analysis of 585 ICD recipients whose pooled mean LVEF was 38.4% (Halawa 2020). Total carded participants exceed 1,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design, not size.
cards.result: Sudden death occurred at a 5-year incidence of 4.8% even in patients without a guideline ICD indication, and guideline indications did not predict sudden death in multivariable analysis (Nordenswan 2022). In preserved/mildly reduced function, MRI scar identified the patients who went on to VT/VF or death, with positive predictive values rising from 22% (any scar) to 100% (right-ventricular scar), while patients without scar had low risk (Crawford 2014). ICDs in cardiac sarcoidosis deliver appropriate therapy in 39% of recipients — and inappropriate therapy in 15% (Halawa 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: an ICD plausibly prevents some sudden deaths in preserved-LVEF cardiac sarcoidosis, particularly with MRI scar, but prevention has never been tested in this subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Every favourable inference here is indirect: risk prediction (cohorts) plus device activity (appropriate shocks) does not equal mortality benefit, and device harms — inappropriate shocks in 15% — are measured in the same data that generate the optimism.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nordenswan HK et al. Circulation. 2022 (PMID: 36000392); Crawford T et al. Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology. 2014 (PMID: 25266311); Halawa A et al. Journal of Interventional Cardiac Electrophysiology. 2020 (PMID: 32062788).

shelves.title: For cardiac or unexplained syncope, the observational case is real (observational only): ~1.9% events/year and devices that fire — for clearly vasovagal syncope, the pooled evidence does not show added risk
shelves.question: Should patients with Brugada syndrome and syncope receive an ICD?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Brugada Syndrome · Death · Electrocardiography · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Registries · Ventricular Fibrillation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised trial. The registries consistently place syncope patients at intermediate, real risk: cardiac events at 1.9% per year with syncope versus 0.5% per year asymptomatic and 7.7% per year after aborted sudden death (FINGER, PMID: 20100972), with syncope plus a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicting events (hazard ratio 4.20, relative; PRELUDE, PMID: 22192666). Pooled data split syncope by type — cardiac (odds ratio 4.48) and unexplained (4.71) syncope were associated with major arrhythmic events, vasovagal syncope was not (PMID: 37021016) — and in ICD recipients syncope with type 1 ECG predicted appropriate shocks (hazard ratio 4.96, relative), while 20.2% had other device complications (PMID: 29025556). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: an ICD is most defensible for Brugada patients whose syncope is cardiac or unexplained, and least supported for clearly vasovagal syncope.

cards.headline: Probst 2010 (FINGER registry, 1,029 patients): cardiac events ran at 1.9% per year in Brugada patients with syncope — versus 0.5% per year in asymptomatic patients and 7.7% per year after aborted sudden death
cards.summary: Probst 2010 (FINGER registry, 1,029 patients): cardiac events ran at 1.9% per year in Brugada patients with syncope — versus 0.5% per year in asymptomatic patients and 7.7% per year after aborted sudden death
cards.people: 1,029 consecutive individuals (745 men, 72%; median age 45 years) with a type 1 Brugada ECG at baseline or after drug challenge, recruited at 11 tertiary centres in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Germany; presentation was aborted sudden cardiac death in 6%, otherwise unexplained syncope in 30%, and asymptomatic in 64%. Median follow-up was 31.9 months.
cards.result: 51 cardiac events (5%) occurred — 44 patients received appropriate ICD shocks and 7 died suddenly. The cardiac event rate per year was 7.7% in patients with aborted sudden death, 1.9% in patients with syncope, and 0.5% in asymptomatic patients. Symptoms and a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicted arrhythmic events; gender, family history of sudden death, inducibility at electrophysiological study, and SCN5A mutation status did not.
cards.watchOut: An appropriate ICD shock is counted as a cardiac event, so patients with devices generate 'events' that patients without devices cannot — the syncope group's rate is partly a measure of how often implanted devices fired, in a registry where implantation was itself driven by perceived risk.
cards.source: Probst V et al. Long-term prognosis of patients diagnosed with Brugada syndrome: Results from the FINGER Brugada Syndrome Registry. Circulation. 2010. PMID: 20100972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Priori 2012 (PRELUDE registry, 308 patients without prior arrest): syncope with a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicted arrhythmic events (hazard ratio 4.20, relative), while programmed stimulation inducibility did not — 9 of 14 events occurred in non-inducible patients
cards.summary: Priori 2012 (PRELUDE registry, 308 patients without prior arrest): syncope with a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicted arrhythmic events (hazard ratio 4.20, relative), while programmed stimulation inducibility did not — 9 of 14 events occurred in non-inducible patients
cards.people: 308 consecutive individuals (247 men, 80%; median age 44 years) with a spontaneous or drug-induced type 1 Brugada ECG and no history of cardiac arrest, enrolled prospectively, undergoing programmed electrical stimulation at enrolment and followed every 6 months for a median of 34 months.
cards.result: 14 arrhythmic events (4.5%) occurred (13 appropriate ICD shocks and 1 cardiac arrest). Programmed stimulation induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias in 40% of patients, but inducibility was not a predictor of events at follow-up — 9 of the 14 events occurred in non-inducible patients. History of syncope and spontaneous type I ECG (hazard ratio 4.20 — a relative measure), ventricular refractory period under 200 ms (hazard ratio 3.91), and QRS fragmentation (hazard ratio 4.94) were significant predictors of arrhythmias. The authors conclude inducibility cannot identify high-risk patients, whereas syncope and a spontaneous type I ECG help identify candidates for a prophylactic ICD.
cards.watchOut: Only 14 events drive every hazard ratio here, and the record presents syncope and spontaneous type 1 ECG together against a single hazard ratio of 4.20, so the independent contribution of syncope alone cannot be separated from this record.
cards.source: Priori SG et al. Risk stratification in Brugada syndrome: results of the PRELUDE (PRogrammed ELectrical stimUlation preDictive valuE) registry. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012. PMID: 22192666. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rattanawong 2023 (meta-analysis, 4,355 patients): cardiac syncope (odds ratio 4.48) and unexplained syncope (odds ratio 4.71) were associated with major arrhythmic events — vasovagal syncope was not (odds ratio 2.90, not significant, very wide interval)
cards.summary: Rattanawong 2023 (meta-analysis, 4,355 patients): cardiac syncope (odds ratio 4.48) and unexplained syncope (odds ratio 4.71) were associated with major arrhythmic events — vasovagal syncope was not (odds ratio 2.90, not significant, very wide interval)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies (2005–2019) involving 4,355 patients with Brugada syndrome, classifying syncope as cardiac, unexplained, vasovagal, or undifferentiated, and examining its association with major arrhythmic events (MAE).
cards.result: Overall, syncope was associated with an increased risk of MAE (odds ratio 3.90, 95% CI 2.22–6.85; P < .001; I² = 76.0% — a relative measure). By type: cardiac syncope odds ratio 4.48 (95% CI 2.87–7.01; P < .001), unexplained syncope odds ratio 4.71 (95% CI 1.34–16.57; P = .016), vasovagal syncope odds ratio 2.90 (95% CI 0.09–98.45; P = .554, not significant), and undifferentiated syncope odds ratio 2.01 (95% CI 1.00–4.03; P = .050). The authors conclude cardiac and unexplained syncope carry similar increased MAE risk, while vasovagal syncope does not.
cards.watchOut: Syncope classification was retrospective in the underlying cohorts and the vasovagal estimate is so imprecise (95% CI 0.09–98.45) that 'no association' means 'not demonstrated', not 'safe'; heterogeneity for the pooled syncope estimate was high (I² = 76%).
cards.source: Rattanawong P et al. Type of syncope and outcome in Brugada syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Arrhythmia. 2023. PMID: 37021016. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Hernandez-Ojeda 2017: among 104 Brugada patients with ICDs followed 9.3 years, 20.2% received appropriate shocks — type 1 ECG with syncope predicted them (hazard ratio 4.96, relative) — while 20.2% had other device complications and 8.7% inappropriate shocks
cards.summary: Hernandez-Ojeda 2017: among 104 Brugada patients with ICDs followed 9.3 years, 20.2% received appropriate shocks — type 1 ECG with syncope predicted them (hazard ratio 4.96, relative) — while 20.2% had other device complications and 8.7% inappropriate shocks
cards.people: 370 patients with Brugada syndrome in follow-up (age 43 ± 14 years; 74% male), of whom 104 (28.1%) received an ICD — 10 (9.6%) for secondary prevention and 94 (90.4%) for primary prevention — followed for 9.3 ± 5.1 years for shocks and complications.
cards.result: 21 patients (20.2%) experienced 81 appropriate shocks (incidence 2.2 per 100 person-years); the rate was higher in secondary prevention (P < .01), and 4 of 45 asymptomatic patients (8.9%) also received appropriate therapy. In multivariable analysis, type 1 electrocardiogram with syncope (hazard ratio 4.96, 95% CI 1.87 to 13.14; P < .01 — a relative measure) and secondary prevention indication (hazard ratio 6.85) predicted appropriate therapy. Nine patients (8.7%) experienced 37 inappropriate shocks, 21 patients (20.2%) had other ICD-related complications, and 3 patients (2.9%) died (1 electrical storm, 2 noncardiovascular). The authors conclude ICD therapy is effective in high-risk Brugada patients but carries a significant risk of device-related complications.
cards.watchOut: There is no non-ICD comparison group, so this cohort can show that devices fire in syncope patients and harm a fifth of recipients — it cannot show how many deaths the devices prevented, and appropriate shocks overcount fatal events because some treated arrhythmias would have self-terminated.
cards.source: Hernandez-Ojeda J et al. Patients With Brugada Syndrome and Implanted Cardioverter-Defibrillators: Long-Term Follow-Up. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 29025556. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: syncope in Brugada syndrome marks a roughly fourfold higher arrhythmic risk unless the syncope looks vasovagal — and ICDs in such patients fire appropriately in a fifth, at the cost of complications in a fifth (all observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: syncope in Brugada syndrome marks a roughly fourfold higher arrhythmic risk unless the syncope looks vasovagal — and ICDs in such patients fire appropriately in a fifth, at the cost of complications in a fifth (all observational)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective registries (FINGER, 1,029 patients; PRELUDE, 308 patients without prior arrest), a meta-analysis of 17 cohorts with 4,355 patients, and a 104-patient ICD cohort followed 9.3 years. Total carded participants exceed 5,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; every design is observational.
cards.result: Event rates rose stepwise by presentation — 0.5% per year asymptomatic, 1.9% per year with syncope, 7.7% per year after aborted sudden death (FINGER). Syncope with a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicted events (hazard ratio 4.20, relative), and pooled data separate syncope types: cardiac (odds ratio 4.48) and unexplained (4.71) syncope were associated with major arrhythmic events, vasovagal syncope was not. In ICD recipients, syncope with type 1 ECG predicted appropriate shocks (hazard ratio 4.96, relative), while 20.2% suffered other device complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: patients with Brugada syndrome and cardiac or unexplained syncope are the group in whom an ICD most plausibly prevents sudden death; the case is weakest for clearly vasovagal syncope.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of ICDs in Brugada syndrome exists or is likely: the entire recommendation rests on risk prediction plus device firing rates, and misclassifying a vasovagal faint as arrhythmic syncope commits a low-risk patient to decades of device risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of Probst V et al. Circulation. 2010 (PMID: 20100972); Priori SG et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2012 (PMID: 22192666); Rattanawong P et al. Journal of Arrhythmia. 2023 (PMID: 37021016); Hernandez-Ojeda J et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017 (PMID: 29025556).

shelves.title: Probably, in the series that report it (observational only): inducibility abolished in three-quarters or more and very low on-treatment event rates — uncontrolled evidence, with tolerability the main limit
shelves.question: Does quinidine reduce arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Cohort Studies · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quinidine · Treatment Outcome · Ventricular Fibrillation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised trial of quinidine in Brugada syndrome. In electrophysiology-guided cohorts, hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic inducible patients and abolished recurrences in all 4 patients with multiple ICD shocks (Hermida 2004, PMID: 15145111); over 33 years, 90% of retested patients responded to a class 1A drug (mostly quinidine) and no responder had an arrhythmic event on therapy, though 38% had side effects (Belhassen 2015, PMID: 26354972); and a long-term French cohort on hydroquinidine 600 mg/day recorded an arrhythmic event rate of 1.04% per year (Bouzeman 2014, PMID: 24068450). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: quinidine reduces arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome in every published series, with the strongest face-value case in patients with recurrent ICD shocks, but the evidence is uncontrolled and rests largely on a stimulation surrogate.

cards.headline: Hermida 2004: hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic Brugada patients with inducible arrhythmia, and prevented recurrence in all 4 patients who had been receiving multiple ICD shocks
cards.summary: Hermida 2004: hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic Brugada patients with inducible arrhythmia, and prevented recurrence in all 4 patients who had been receiving multiple ICD shocks
cards.people: 35 patients with Brugada syndrome drawn from a cohort of 106 (32 men; mean age 48 ± 11 years) who received hydroquinidine (the quinidine formulation used in this French programme): 31 asymptomatic patients with inducible arrhythmia managed by electrophysiology-guided therapy, and 4 patients with multiple appropriate ICD shocks. Patients who remained inducible on the drug, or could not tolerate it, received an ICD.
cards.result: Hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic patients who underwent electrophysiology-guided therapy. Syncope occurred in 2 of the 21 patients who received long-term therapy (17 ± 13 months) — 1 associated with QT prolongation and 1 unexplained, associated with probable noncompliance. In the asymptomatic patients who instead received an ICD (n = 10), one appropriate shock occurred over 13 ± 8 months. In patients with multiple ICD shocks, hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF recurrence in all cases during a mean follow-up of 14 ± 8 months. The authors suggest preventive hydroquinidine may be an alternative strategy to ICD placement in asymptomatic patients with inducible arrhythmia.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a laboratory surrogate — non-inducibility at repeat stimulation — in 35 selected patients with no untreated comparison group; preventing inducibility is not the same as preventing clinical arrhythmia or death, and 2 syncopes occurred on long-term therapy.
cards.source: Hermida JS et al. Hydroquinidine therapy in Brugada syndrome. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2004. PMID: 15145111. Registry ID: none in the record. electrophysiology-guided treatment cohort (hermida 2004) 35 patients with brugada syndrome drawn from a cohort of 106 (32 men; mean age 48 ± 11 years) who received hydroquinidine (the quinidine formulation used in this french programme): 31 asymptomatic patients with inducible arrhythmia managed by electrophysiology-guided therapy, and 4 patients with multiple appropriate icd shocks. patients who remained inducible on the drug, or could not tolerate it, received an icd. hydroquinidine prevented vt/vf inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic patients who underwent electrophysiology-guided therapy. syncope occurred in 2 of the 21 patients who received long-term therapy (17 ± 13 months) — 1 associated with qt prolongation and 1 unexplained, associated with probable noncompliance. in the asymptomatic patients who instead received an icd (n = 10), one appropriate shock occurred over 13 ± 8 months. in patients with multiple icd shocks, hydroquinidine prevented vt/vf recurrence in all cases during a mean follow-up of 14 ± 8 months. the authors suggest preventive hydroquinidine may be an alternative strategy to icd placement in asymptomatic patients with inducible arrhythmia. the primary endpoint is a laboratory surrogate — non-inducibility at repeat stimulation — in 35 selected patients with no untreated comparison group; preventing inducibility is not the same as preventing clinical arrhythmia or death, and 2 syncopes occurred on long-term therapy. hermida js et al. hydroquinidine therapy in brugada syndrome. journal of the american college of cardiology. 2004. pmid: 15145111. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · anti-arrhythmia agents · arrhythmias, cardiac · cohort studies · death, sudden, cardiac · female · humans · male · middle aged · quinidine · treatment outcome · ventricular fibrillation

cards.headline: Belhassen 2015 (33-year experience, 96 patients): no arrhythmic event occurred on class 1A therapy in any electrophysiological drug responder — but 38% had side effects that resolved on stopping the drug
cards.summary: Belhassen 2015 (33-year experience, 96 patients): no arrhythmic event occurred on class 1A therapy in any electrophysiological drug responder — but 38% had side effects that resolved on stopping the drug
cards.people: 96 patients with Brugada syndrome (88% male; mean age 39.8 ± 15.9 years) undergoing an aggressive programmed ventricular stimulation protocol: 10 cardiac arrest survivors, 27 with syncope, and 59 asymptomatic. Ventricular fibrillation was induced in 66 patients (100% of arrest survivors, 74% of syncope patients, 61% of asymptomatic patients); all but 6 of the 66 were retested on quinidine (n = 54), disopyramide (n = 2), or both (n = 4). Mean follow-up was 113.3 ± 71.5 months.
cards.result: 54 patients (90% of those retested) were electrophysiological responders to at least one class 1A drug, with similar efficacy (≈90%) in all patient groups. No arrhythmic event occurred during class 1A therapy in any drug responder, nor in patients with no baseline inducible ventricular fibrillation (who were left on no therapy); arrhythmic events occurred in only 2 cardiac arrest survivors treated with an ICD alone and did not recur on quinidine. 92 patients were alive at follow-up and 4 died of noncardiac causes; all 12 recurrent syncopes were attributed to vasovagal (n = 10) or nonarrhythmic (n = 2) mechanisms. Class 1A therapy caused side effects in 38% of patients, resolving after discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, uncontrolled 33-year series mixing quinidine with disopyramide, in which responders stayed on the drug and non-responders left the treatment group — a design that guarantees the on-treatment group looks good; event rates in untreated Brugada patients are also low, so zero events on therapy cannot be credited to the drug alone.
cards.source: Belhassen B et al. Management of Brugada Syndrome: Thirty-Three-Year Experience Using Electrophysiologically Guided Therapy With Class 1A Antiarrhythmic Drugs. Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology. 2015. PMID: 26354972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bouzeman 2014: in 44 asymptomatic Brugada patients with inducible VF treated with hydroquinidine 600 mg/day, 77% became non-inducible on the drug, and the overall arrhythmic event rate over ~6.6 years was 1.04% per year
cards.summary: Bouzeman 2014: in 44 asymptomatic Brugada patients with inducible VF treated with hydroquinidine 600 mg/day, 77% became non-inducible on the drug, and the overall arrhythmic event rate over ~6.6 years was 1.04% per year
cards.people: 44 consecutive asymptomatic type 1 Brugada patients with inducible ventricular fibrillation (VF) from two French reference centres (drawn from 397 Brugada patients; age 47 ± 10 years, 95% male), treated with hydroquinidine 600 mg/day targeting a therapeutic range of 3–6 µmol/L, with repeat programmed ventricular stimulation on the drug and mean follow-up of 6.6 ± 3 years; an ICD was implanted if inducibility persisted on the drug, the drug was not tolerated, or an arrhythmic event occurred.
cards.result: 34 patients (77%) were no longer inducible on hydroquinidine and were maintained on the drug alone over a mean 6.2 ± 3 years; in this group an ICD was eventually implanted in 4 patients (12%), with appropriate ICD therapy in 1. The 10 patients (22%) who remained inducible received an ICD and none received appropriate therapy over 7.7 ± 2 years. The overall annual rate of arrhythmic events was 1.04% (95% CI 0.00–2.21), with no significant difference by stimulation result on the drug; one-third of patients experienced device-related complications. The authors conclude event rates remain low over time and that residual inducibility on hydroquinidine is of limited value for predicting events.
cards.watchOut: This French hydroquinidine programme overlaps in era and strategy with Hermida 2004, so the cohorts should not be summed as independent evidence; and the event rate was low even in patients who remained inducible, undercutting the stimulation-guided logic the treatment rests on.
cards.source: Bouzeman A et al. Long-term follow-up of asymptomatic Brugada patients with inducible ventricular fibrillation under hydroquinidine. Europace. 2014. PMID: 24068450. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: quinidine abolishes inducibility in about three-quarters to 90% of tested Brugada patients and on-treatment event rates are very low — but every datum is observational, stimulation-guided, and without an untreated control (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: quinidine abolishes inducibility in about three-quarters to 90% of tested Brugada patients and on-treatment event rates are very low — but every datum is observational, stimulation-guided, and without an untreated control (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: three electrophysiology-guided treatment cohorts — 35 patients (Hermida 2004), 96 patients treated with class 1A drugs, mostly quinidine (Belhassen 2015), and 44 asymptomatic patients on hydroquinidine 600 mg/day (Bouzeman 2014). The French cohorts may overlap, so their Ns are not summed as independent; each individually exceeds the reference floor and the combined experience exceeds 30 patients, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Hydroquinidine prevented inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic inducible patients and stopped recurrences in all 4 multiple-shock patients (Hermida 2004); 90% of retested patients responded electrophysiologically to a class 1A drug and no responder had an arrhythmic event on therapy over a mean of ~9.4 years, at a 38% side-effect rate (Belhassen 2015); and in the long-term French cohort the annual arrhythmic event rate on the hydroquinidine strategy was 1.04% (Bouzeman 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: quinidine reduces arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome in every series that reports it, most convincingly for patients with recurrent ICD shocks, but the evidence is uncontrolled and built on a stimulation surrogate.
cards.watchOut: Availability and tolerability are the practical limits the efficacy data hide: side effects stopped the drug in over a third of one series, one syncope on therapy was linked to QT prolongation, and none of these cohorts compares quinidine against either placebo or an ICD for clinical events.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hermida JS et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2004 (PMID: 15145111); Belhassen B et al. Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology. 2015 (PMID: 26354972); Bouzeman A et al. Europace. 2014 (PMID: 24068450).

shelves.title: Yes, as corroboration (diagnostic evidence only): pooled discrimination is good (AUC 0.84), but sensitivity is ~41–61% and healthy controls faint too — a negative tilt does not exclude vasovagal syncope
shelves.question: Does tilt-table testing help diagnose vasovagal syncope?
shelves.mesh: Case-Control Studies · Humans · Syncope, Vasovagal · Tilt-Table Test
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-accuracy evidence only; no study carded here tests patient outcomes. Pooled across 55 case-control studies (4,361 patients, 1,791 controls), head-up tilt testing discriminated vasovagal patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (relative; Forleo 2013, PMID: 23041006). In primary protocols the yield is modest: 61% positive in recurrent unexplained syncope with 93% specificity (Morillo 1995, PMID: 7732979), and 41–49% positive against 10–13% false positives in healthy controls (Raviele 2000, PMID: 10802000). A structured history alone reached 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity (Sheldon 2006, PMID: 16223744), so tilt corroborates rather than replaces the story. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tilt-table testing helps diagnose vasovagal syncope as corroborating evidence — a positive test supports the diagnosis, a negative test does not exclude it.

cards.headline: Forleo 2013 (meta-analysis, 55 case-control studies): head-up tilt testing discriminated vasovagal patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (relative)
cards.summary: Forleo 2013 (meta-analysis, 55 case-control studies): head-up tilt testing discriminated vasovagal patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (relative)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 55 case-control studies published before March 2012 comparing head-up tilt test outcome in 4,361 patients with syncope of unknown origin against 1,791 control subjects without previous syncope, analysing the influence of age, test duration, tilt angle, and nitroglycerine or isoproterenol stimulation.
cards.result: Head-up tilt testing showed a good overall ability to discriminate between symptomatic patients and asymptomatic controls, with an area under the summary receiver-operating characteristics curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (P < 0.001 — a relative measure). A significant inverse relationship between sensitivity and specificity across studies was observed (P < 0.001). At multivariate analysis, advancing age and a 60° tilt angle reduced sensitivity and increased specificity; nitroglycerine significantly raised sensitivity while maintaining similar specificity compared with isoproterenol. The authors conclude tilt testing has high overall performance for diagnosing vasovagal syncope.
cards.watchOut: Case-control designs flatter diagnostic tests: comparing clearly affected patients with never-fainting controls is much easier than the real clinical task of sorting one unexplained faint from another, and the pooled record prints no single sensitivity/specificity pair — accuracy moves with protocol, age and angle.
cards.source: Forleo C et al. Head-up tilt testing for diagnosing vasovagal syncope: a meta-analysis. International Journal of Cardiology. 2013. PMID: 23041006. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Case-Control Studies · Humans · Syncope, Vasovagal · Tilt-Table Test

cards.headline: Morillo 1995: a low-dose isoproterenol tilt protocol was positive in 61% of 120 patients with recurrent unexplained syncope and falsely positive in 6.6% of controls — sensitivity 61%, specificity 93%, reproducibility 86% as the authors summarise it
cards.summary: Morillo 1995: a low-dose isoproterenol tilt protocol was positive in 61% of 120 patients with recurrent unexplained syncope and falsely positive in 6.6% of controls — sensitivity 61%, specificity 93%, reproducibility 86% as the authors summarise it
cards.people: 120 consecutive patients with recurrent unexplained syncope, 30 healthy controls, and 30 patients with documented syncope not related to a vasodepressor reaction, all undergoing head-up tilt at 60 degrees combined with a low-dose isoproterenol infusion (mean dose about 1.3–1.4 µg/min across groups); same-day reproducibility was assessed in 75 patients.
cards.result: Tilt was positive in 61% (73 of 120) of patients with unexplained syncope; the false-positive rate in both the control group and the documented-syncope group was 6.6%. Tilt was positive during the drug-free stage in 30 patients (25%) and isoproterenol was required in the remaining 43 (36%). The response was reproduced in 82% of patients with a baseline positive test and 93% with a baseline negative test. Overall, the authors report 'sensitivity' of 61%, specificity of 93%, and reproducibility of 86%; age 50 years or younger and two or more syncopal episodes in the preceding 6 months, without structural heart disease, increased the probability of a positive outcome.
cards.watchOut: 'Sensitivity' here means the positive rate in patients whose syncope was unexplained — there was no independent gold standard proving their syncope was vasovagal — and a 61% yield means roughly 4 in 10 such patients test negative on the day, so a negative tilt does not exclude vasovagal syncope.
cards.source: Morillo CA et al. Diagnostic accuracy of a low-dose isoproterenol head-up tilt protocol. American Heart Journal. 1995. PMID: 7732979. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Raviele 2000: sublingual nitroglycerin tilt and low-dose isoproterenol tilt were equivalent — positive in 49% versus 41% of 71 unexplained-syncope patients, and falsely positive in 10% versus 13% of 30 controls
cards.summary: Raviele 2000: sublingual nitroglycerin tilt and low-dose isoproterenol tilt were equivalent — positive in 49% versus 41% of 71 unexplained-syncope patients, and falsely positive in 10% versus 13% of 30 controls
cards.people: 71 patients with unexplained syncope (mean age 43 years) and 30 asymptomatic controls, each undergoing both a sublingual nitroglycerin tilt test (300 µg) and a low-dose isoproterenol tilt test (mean infusion 1.3 ± 0.5 µg/min) on separate days in randomised order; each protocol was 20 minutes at 60 degrees drug-free, then a further 20 minutes after the drug if syncope had not occurred.
cards.result: During the nitroglycerin test a positive response (syncope with sudden hypotension and bradycardia) occurred in 35 patients (49%), with drug intolerance in none; during the isoproterenol test the positive rate was 41%, with drug intolerance in 6%. A concordant response to both tests was observed in 53 cases (75%). Among controls, 3 subjects (10%) were positive on nitroglycerin and 4 (13%) on isoproterenol. The authors conclude the two tests are equivalent for evaluating unexplained syncope, with the nitroglycerin test simpler, better tolerated and safer.
cards.watchOut: One in ten healthy controls fainted 'positively' on the nitroglycerin protocol — a positive tilt is a susceptibility finding, not proof that the patient's real-life faint was vasovagal — and the patient positive rates (41–49%) are lower than in series using longer or more aggressive protocols.
cards.source: Raviele A et al. Comparison of diagnostic accuracy of sublingual nitroglycerin test and low-dose isoproterenol test in patients with unexplained syncope. The American Journal of Cardiology. 2000. PMID: 10802000. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sheldon 2006: a structured history alone distinguished vasovagal syncope with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity — the tilt test's main rival is the story, and tilt-negative patients were still mostly judged vasovagal
cards.summary: Sheldon 2006: a structured history alone distinguished vasovagal syncope with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity — the tilt test's main rival is the story, and tilt-negative patients were still mostly judged vasovagal
cards.people: 418 patients with syncope and no apparent structural heart disease who completed a 118-item historical questionnaire; causes were known in 323 patients — 235 with tilt-positive vasovagal syncope and 88 with other diagnoses such as complete heart block and supraventricular tachycardias — and a further 95 patients had syncope of unknown cause with a negative tilt test. A point score was derived by logistic regression and tested with receiver operator characteristic analysis and bootstrapping.
cards.result: The point score correctly classified 90% of patients, diagnosing vasovagal syncope with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity. The decision rule suggested that 68% of the 95 patients with syncope of unknown cause and a negative tilt test have vasovagal syncope. The authors conclude a simple point score of historical features distinguishes vasovagal syncope from syncope of other causes with very high sensitivity and specificity.
cards.watchOut: There is circularity here: tilt positivity partly defined the vasovagal group the history score was trained to identify, so the score's 89%/91% cannot be read as history beating tilt in a fair contest — what it does show is that tilt is not the reference standard for this diagnosis, and most tilt-negative unexplained faints were still judged vasovagal.
cards.source: Sheldon R et al. Diagnostic criteria for vasovagal syncope based on a quantitative history. European Heart Journal. 2006. PMID: 16223744. Registry ID: none in the record. diagnostic criteria study (sheldon 2006) 418 patients with syncope and no apparent structural heart disease who completed a 118-item historical questionnaire; causes were known in 323 patients — 235 with tilt-positive vasovagal syncope and 88 with other diagnoses such as complete heart block and supraventricular tachycardias — and a further 95 patients had syncope of unknown cause with a negative tilt test. a point score was derived by logistic regression and tested with receiver operator characteristic analysis and bootstrapping. the point score correctly classified 90% of patients, diagnosing vasovagal syncope with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity. the decision rule suggested that 68% of the 95 patients with syncope of unknown cause and a negative tilt test have vasovagal syncope. the authors conclude a simple point score of historical features distinguishes vasovagal syncope from syncope of other causes with very high sensitivity and specificity. there is circularity here: tilt positivity partly defined the vasovagal group the history score was trained to identify, so the score's 89%/91% cannot be read as history beating tilt in a fair contest — what it does show is that tilt is not the reference standard for this diagnosis, and most tilt-negative unexplained faints were still judged vasovagal. sheldon r et al. diagnostic criteria for vasovagal syncope based on a quantitative history. european heart journal. 2006. pmid: 16223744. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · female · humans · male · medical history taking · middle aged · prospective studies · sensitivity and specificity · surveys and questionnaires · syncope, vasovagal · tilt-table test

cards.headline: Synthesis: tilt testing genuinely discriminates — pooled AUC 0.84 across 55 studies — but with ~61% sensitivity in a primary protocol, ~7–13% false positives in controls, and a structured history performing at least as well, it supports a vasovagal diagnosis rather than settling it
cards.summary: Synthesis: tilt testing genuinely discriminates — pooled AUC 0.84 across 55 studies — but with ~61% sensitivity in a primary protocol, ~7–13% false positives in controls, and a structured history performing at least as well, it supports a vasovagal diagnosis rather than settling it
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of 55 case-control studies (4,361 patients, 1,791 controls; Forleo 2013), two primary diagnostic accuracy studies (Morillo 1995, 180 subjects; Raviele 2000, 101 subjects), and a 418-patient diagnostic criteria study (Sheldon 2006). Total carded participants exceed 6,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled, tilt testing discriminated symptomatic patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (relative). In primary protocols, positivity ran at 61% (isoproterenol, Morillo 1995) and 41–49% (isoproterenol vs nitroglycerin, Raviele 2000) in unexplained syncope, against false-positive rates of 6.6–13% in controls — so a positive test supports vasovagal syncope and a negative test barely dents it. A structured history classified patients with 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity (Sheldon 2006). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tilt-table testing helps diagnose vasovagal syncope as one corroborating piece of evidence — it is neither sensitive enough to rule the diagnosis out nor specific enough to rule it in alone.
cards.watchOut: No carded study tests whether tilt testing changes treatment or prevents recurrences — the entire evidence base is diagnostic accuracy against imperfect reference standards, so 'helps diagnose' should not be inflated into 'improves outcomes'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Forleo C et al. International Journal of Cardiology. 2013 (PMID: 23041006); Morillo CA et al. American Heart Journal. 1995 (PMID: 7732979); Raviele A et al. shelves.question: Does implantable loop recorder find the cause of unexplained syncope better than conventional testing?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials are concordant, which earns LIKELY for this diagnostic-yield question. Prolonged implantable monitoring diagnosed 52% versus 20% with conventional testing in the RAST trial (PMID: 11435336); early recorder use established a certain cause in 46.2% versus 5% in the FRESH randomised study (PMID: 25241220); and first-line recorder use reached an ECG diagnosis far faster (hazard ratio 35.5, relative), found a pacing indication in 22% versus 3%, and delayed the second syncope (EaSyAS II, PMID: 26462702). In the 570-patient PICTURE registry the recorder guided the diagnosis in 78% of recurrent events after a median of 13 prior inconclusive tests (PMID: 21097478). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): an implantable loop recorder finds the cause of unexplained syncope better than conventional testing.

cards.headline: Krahn 2001 (RAST randomised trial): a prolonged implantable-loop-recorder strategy diagnosed 52% of unexplained syncope versus 20% with conventional testing (P = 0.012) — and crossover to the recorder diagnosed 62% of the still-undiagnosed
cards.summary: Krahn 2001 (RAST randomised trial): a prolonged implantable-loop-recorder strategy diagnosed 52% of unexplained syncope versus 20% with conventional testing (P = 0.012) — and crossover to the recorder diagnosed 62% of the still-undiagnosed
cards.people: 60 patients (aged 66 ± 14 years, 33 male) with unexplained syncope randomised to 'conventional' testing (external loop recorder plus tilt and electrophysiological testing) or to prolonged monitoring with an implantable loop recorder for 1 year; patients who remained undiagnosed after their assigned strategy were offered crossover to the alternate strategy.
cards.result: A diagnosis was obtained in 14 of 27 patients randomised to prolonged monitoring compared with 6 of 30 undergoing conventional testing (52% versus 20%, P = 0.012). Crossover produced a diagnosis in 8 of 13 patients who completed monitoring versus 1 of 6 undergoing conventional testing (62% versus 17%, P = 0.069). Overall, prolonged monitoring was more likely to result in a diagnosis than conventional testing (55% versus 19%, P = 0.0014). Bradycardia was detected in 14 patients undergoing monitoring versus 3 undergoing conventional testing (40% versus 8%, P = 0.005). The authors conclude a prolonged monitoring strategy is more likely to provide a diagnosis and should be considered earlier.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-programme trial (60 randomised, with analysed denominators of 27 and 30 as printed in the record) from the first generation of loop recorders — the direction has been replicated since, but the absolute yields belong to that era's devices and referral patterns.
cards.source: Krahn AD et al. Randomized assessment of syncope trial: conventional diagnostic testing versus a prolonged monitoring strategy. Circulation. 2001. PMID: 11435336. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Podoleanu 2014 (FRESH randomised study): early implantable loop recorder established a certain cause of syncope in 46.2% versus 5% with conventional evaluation at 14 months (P < 0.001), with fewer advanced tests
cards.summary: Podoleanu 2014 (FRESH randomised study): early implantable loop recorder established a certain cause of syncope in 46.2% versus 5% with conventional evaluation at 14 months (P < 0.001), with fewer advanced tests
cards.people: National prospective randomised open-label multicentre study in France of 78 patients (32 men; mean age 66.2 ± 14.8 years; 4.3 ± 6.4 previous syncopes) with a single severe recent syncope or at least two syncopes in the past year, randomised to an early implantable loop recorder (ILR) strategy (n = 39) or a conventional evaluation strategy (n = 39), followed for 14 months for diagnostic yield, cost and quality of life.
cards.result: After 14 months, a certain cause of syncope was established in 18 patients (46.2%) in the ILR group and 2 patients (5%) in the conventional group (P < 0.001). Advanced cardiological tests were performed less frequently in the ILR group (0.03 ± 0.2 versus 0.2 ± 0.5 tests per patient; P = 0.05). Hospitalisation was non-significantly shorter in the ILR group (5.7 ± 3.2 versus 8.0 ± 1.4 days) and there was no difference in the quality-of-life main composite score. The authors conclude early ILR use has a superior diagnostic yield to conventional evaluation, with lower healthcare-related costs.
cards.watchOut: 78 low-risk patients in one country's health system, open-label, with a strict 'certain cause' endpoint that conventional testing rarely meets by design — the yield gap is real but its size depends on how diagnosis is defined and on the conventional pathway it is compared with.
cards.source: Podoleanu C et al. Early use of an implantable loop recorder in syncope evaluation: a randomized study in the context of the French healthcare system (FRESH study). Archives of Cardiovascular Diseases. 2014. PMID: 25241220. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sulke 2016 (EaSyAS II randomised trial): first-line implantable loop recorder reached an ECG diagnosis far faster than conventional management (hazard ratio 35.5, relative), found a pacing indication in 22% versus 3%, and was the only strategy that delayed the second syncope
cards.summary: Sulke 2016 (EaSyAS II randomised trial): first-line implantable loop recorder reached an ECG diagnosis far faster than conventional management (hazard ratio 35.5, relative), found a pacing indication in 22% versus 3%, and was the only strategy that delayed the second syncope
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled study of 246 patients (mean age 70.3 years) with unexplained syncope allocated to conventional management, a dedicated syncope clinic alone, an implantable loop recorder (ILR, remotely monitored) alone, or syncope clinic plus ILR; median follow-up was 20 months (interquartile range 15–25 months).
cards.result: Time to ECG diagnosis was significantly shorter with ILR alone versus conventional management (hazard ratio 35.5, P = 0.0004 — a relative measure) and with syncope clinic versus conventional (hazard ratio 25.6, P = 0.002); 74% of first syncopal events documented in the syncope-clinic groups occurred during provocative tilt testing. 22% of patients who received an ILR were found to have a bradycardia indication for permanent pacing, versus 3% of patients who did not. More investigative tests were undertaken in the conventional group than in any other, and only ILR patients had a significant increase in time to second syncope (P = 0.02), suggesting successful diagnosis and management of treatable causes.
cards.watchOut: A four-arm trial splits 246 patients thinly, and the headline hazard ratio of 35.5 measures speed of ECG diagnosis, not a 35-fold increase in diagnoses made; the syncope clinic achieved fast diagnoses too, mostly by provoking events on the tilt table rather than recording spontaneous ones.
cards.source: Sulke N et al. The benefit of a remotely monitored implantable loop recorder as a first line investigation in unexplained syncope: the EaSyAS II trial. Europace. 2016. PMID: 26462702. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Edvardsson 2011 (PICTURE registry, 570 patients): after a median of 13 prior tests without an answer, the loop recorder guided the diagnosis in 78% of recurrent events — 75% of them cardiac
cards.summary: Edvardsson 2011 (PICTURE registry, 570 patients): after a median of 13 prior tests without an answer, the loop recorder guided the diagnosis in 78% of recurrent events — 75% of them cardiac
cards.people: Prospective multicentre observational registry (2006–2009, 10 European countries and Israel) of patients with recurrent unexplained syncope or pre-syncope who received a Reveal implantable loop recorder (Plus, DX or XT — the tested devices named in the record), followed until the first recurrence leading to a diagnosis or for at least 1 year; follow-up visit data were available for 570 subjects, who had been evaluated by an average of three specialists and a median of 13 tests (range 9–20) before implantation, and 36% had experienced significant physical trauma with a syncopal episode.
cards.result: Syncope recurred in 19%, 26% and 36% of patients by 3, 6 and 12 months respectively (mean follow-up after implant 10 ± 6 months). Of 218 events within the study, an ILR-guided diagnosis was obtained in 170 cases (78%), of which 128 (75%) were cardiac. The authors conclude that, in contrast to the large number of inconclusive tests undertaken before implantation, the ILR revealed or contributed to establishing the mechanism of syncope in the vast majority of patients, supporting implantation early rather than late in the evaluation.
cards.watchOut: A registry with no comparison group, sponsored by the device pathway it evaluates: the 78% figure is the share of recurrences the recorder explained, not a comparison against conventional testing, and patients were selected precisely because conventional testing had already failed them.
cards.source: Edvardsson N et al. Use of an implantable loop recorder to increase the diagnostic yield in unexplained syncope: results from the PICTURE registry. Europace. 2011. PMID: 21097478. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials and a 570-patient registry all point the same way — the loop recorder finds the cause in roughly half of unexplained syncope, several-fold more than conventional testing, because it is recording when the next faint happens
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials and a 570-patient registry all point the same way — the loop recorder finds the cause in roughly half of unexplained syncope, several-fold more than conventional testing, because it is recording when the next faint happens
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials (Krahn 2001, 60 patients; Podoleanu 2014, 78 patients; Sulke 2016, 246 patients) and one prospective registry (Edvardsson 2011, 570 patients with follow-up data). Total carded participants exceed 900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Diagnosis rates with the recorder were 52% versus 20% for conventional testing (Krahn 2001), 46.2% versus 5% for a certain cause (Podoleanu 2014), and time to ECG diagnosis was dramatically shorter with the recorder (hazard ratio 35.5, relative; Sulke 2016), which also uncovered a pacing indication in 22% versus 3%. In everyday practice the recorder guided the diagnosis in 78% of recurrent events after a median of 13 prior inconclusive tests (Edvardsson 2011). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): an implantable loop recorder finds the cause of unexplained syncope better than conventional testing — the concordance of three randomised trials earns the LIKELY stamp for this diagnostic question.
cards.watchOut: Better diagnosis is not automatically better outcomes: the trials are powered for yield, not for mortality or injury, the recorder requires a minor surgical implant, and it only helps patients whose syncope recurs during the monitoring window — 64% of registry patients had not recurred by 12 months.
cards.source: Synthesis of Krahn AD et al. Circulation. 2001 (PMID: 11435336); Podoleanu C et al. Archives of Cardiovascular Diseases. 2014 (PMID: 25241220); Sulke N et al. Europace. 2016 (PMID: 26462702); Edvardsson N et al. Europace. 2011 (PMID: 21097478).

shelves.title: Associated with slower growth in all observational evidence (observational only): dose-dependent in a 998-man cohort and pooled at 0.82 mm/year slower — never tested in a randomised trial
shelves.question: Does statin therapy slow abdominal aortic aneurysm growth?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Aged · Prospective Studies · Middle Aged · Denmark · Risk Factors · Mass Screening · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; no randomised trial of statins for aneurysm growth was found in the records fetched. The observational evidence is concordant and dose-dependent: in 998 men with screening-detected small aneurysms, each extra defined daily dose of statin was associated with 0.22 mm/year slower growth, with relative hazards of 0.82 for repair and 0.83 for repair/rupture/death per doubling of dose (Skovbo 2025, PMID: 40631665). Meta-analyses of observational studies agree — 0.82 mm/year slower growth across 80,428 patients, though with I² = 86% heterogeneity (Salata 2018, PMID: 30371297), and a standardised mean difference of −0.42 across 4,647 patients (Takagi 2012, PMID: 22824348). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: statin therapy is associated with slower abdominal aortic aneurysm growth, but confounding by indication has never been excluded by randomisation.

cards.headline: Skovbo 2025: in 998 men with screening-detected small aneurysms, each extra defined daily dose of statin was associated with 0.22 mm/year slower growth, and each doubling of dose with a relative hazard of 0.82 for repair and 0.83 for repair/rupture/death
cards.summary: Skovbo 2025: in 998 men with screening-detected small aneurysms, each extra defined daily dose of statin was associated with 0.22 mm/year slower growth, and each doubling of dose with a relative hazard of 0.82 for repair and 0.83 for repair/rupture/death
cards.people: All men with screening-detected abdominal aortic aneurysms of 30–55 mm from two large Danish population-based randomised screening trials (Viborg Vascular Screening trial, inclusion 2008–2011, and the Danish Cardiovascular Screening trial, inclusion 2014–2018): 998 aneurysmal men (median age 69.5 years; median aneurysm diameter 35.4 mm), with statin exposure quantified from nationwide prescription registries in defined daily doses (DDD) and 5-year follow-up for growth rate, repair, rupture and death.
cards.result: Statin use was significantly associated with a reduced aneurysm growth rate: an increase of 1 DDD of statin per day was associated with an adjusted change in growth rate of −0.22 mm/year (95% CI −0.39 to −0.06; P = 0.009). The 5-year adjusted hazard ratio for undergoing repair per doubling of statin dose was 0.82 (95% CI 0.70–0.97; P = 0.023 — a relative measure), significant after 2.5 years, and the composite of surgery, rupture and all-cause death had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.83 per doubling of dose (95% CI 0.73–0.94; P = 0.003 — a relative measure). The authors note this is a nonrandomized study and conclude high-dose statin use was associated with decreased growth and lower risk of repair, rupture and death.
cards.watchOut: Men only, screening-detected aneurysms only, and statin dose was chosen by clinicians, not randomised: men prescribed higher doses differ from other men in cardiovascular risk, adherence and care intensity, any of which could produce a dose-response pattern without the statin slowing the aneurysm itself.

cards.headline: Salata 2018 (meta-analysis, 22 studies, 80,428 patients): statin use was associated with 0.82 mm/year slower aneurysm growth — with very high heterogeneity (I² = 86%) — plus lower rupture (odds ratio 0.63, relative) and perioperative mortality (odds ratio 0.55, relative)
cards.summary: Salata 2018 (meta-analysis, 22 studies, 80,428 patients): statin use was associated with 0.82 mm/year slower aneurysm growth — with very high heterogeneity (I² = 86%) — plus lower rupture (odds ratio 0.63, relative) and perioperative mortality (odds ratio 0.55, relative)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies of statins in abdominal aortic aneurysm (search to June 15, 2018): one case-control and 21 cohort studies involving 80,428 patients were included, with risk of bias rated low to moderate; outcomes were aneurysm growth, rupture, and 30-day mortality after repair, pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: Statin use was associated with a mean aneurysm growth rate reduction of 0.82 mm/year (95% CI 0.33 to 1.32; P = 0.001; I² = 86%). Statins were also associated with a lower rupture risk (odds ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.78; P < 0.0001; I² = 27% — a relative measure) and preoperative statin use with lower 30-day mortality following elective aneurysm repair (odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.83; P = 0.005; I² = 57% — a relative measure). The authors conclude statin therapy may be associated with a reduction in aneurysm progression, rupture, and perioperative mortality, and argue for widespread statin use in aneurysm patients.
cards.watchOut: Despite the search including randomised studies, the 22 included studies are one case-control and 21 cohort studies — the growth estimate is entirely observational, and I² = 86% means the underlying studies disagree with each other far more than the single pooled number suggests.

cards.headline: Takagi 2012 (meta-analysis of 11 observational comparative studies, 4,647 patients with small aneurysms): statin therapy was associated with slower growth (standardised mean difference −0.42), attenuated but still significant in the 7 adjusted high-quality studies (−0.37)
cards.summary: Takagi 2012 (meta-analysis of 11 observational comparative studies, 4,647 patients with small aneurysms): statin therapy was associated with slower growth (standardised mean difference −0.42), attenuated but still significant in the 7 adjusted high-quality studies (−0.37)
cards.people: Meta-analysis and meta-regression of comparative studies (randomised trials or observational comparative studies of statin therapy versus placebo or no statin) enrolling individuals with small abdominal aortic aneurysms (under 55 mm diameter) and reporting growth rate: 7 adjusted and 4 unadjusted observational comparative studies enrolling 4,647 patients were identified.
cards.result: Pooled analysis of all 11 studies suggested a significant reduction in aneurysm growth rate with statin therapy versus no statin (standardised mean difference −0.420, 95% CI −0.651 to −0.189). Combining only the 7 high-quality studies providing adjusted data attenuated the result but it remained statistically significant (standardised mean difference −0.367, 95% CI −0.566 to −0.168). The meta-regression coefficient for baseline diameter was statistically significant (−0.096, 95% CI −0.132 to −0.061), suggesting greater benefit at larger baseline diameter. The authors conclude statin therapy is likely effective in preventing growth of small aneurysms.
cards.watchOut: A standardised mean difference cannot be read as mm/year, the included studies overlap with the later Salata meta-analysis (so the two meta-analyses are not independent confirmations), and adjustment in the source cohorts cannot remove confounding by indication — statin users are patients already plugged into cardiovascular care.
cards.source: Takagi H et al. Effects of statin therapy on abdominal aortic aneurysm growth: a meta-analysis and meta-regression of observational comparative studies. cards.headline: Synthesis: every observational design agrees statin users' aneurysms grow more slowly — by about 0.2–0.8 mm/year, dose-dependently in the best cohort — but there is no randomised trial, and the pooled growth estimate carries I² = 86% heterogeneity (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: every observational design agrees statin users' aneurysms grow more slowly — by about 0.2–0.8 mm/year, dose-dependently in the best cohort — but there is no randomised trial, and the pooled growth estimate carries I² = 86% heterogeneity (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective screening cohort of 998 men with dose-response analysis (Skovbo 2025) and two meta-analyses of observational studies (Salata 2018, 80,428 patients in 22 studies; Takagi 2012, 4,647 patients in 11 studies — the meta-analyses overlap in their source studies and are not independent). Total carded participants exceed 80,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the absence of randomisation.
cards.result: Growth was slower in statin users in all three: −0.22 mm/year per defined daily dose with dose-dependent relative hazards of 0.82 for repair and 0.83 for repair/rupture/death per dose doubling (Skovbo 2025); a pooled 0.82 mm/year slower growth with lower rupture odds (Salata 2018); and a standardised mean difference of −0.42 favouring statins, −0.37 in adjusted studies (Takagi 2012). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: statin therapy is associated with slower abdominal aortic aneurysm growth, plausibly a real effect given the dose-response, but confounding by indication has never been excluded by a randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Patients with aneurysms usually have independent cardiovascular indications for a statin, so this shelf's open question is narrow — whether the statin also slows the aneurysm — and an affirmative observational answer should not be used to delay surveillance or repair thresholds, which none of these studies tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skovbo JS et al. Circulation. 2025 (PMID: 40631665); Salata K et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2018 (PMID: 30371297); Takagi H et al. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2012 (PMID: 22824348).
