shelves.title: Intermittent statin dosing in statin intolerance: LDL cholesterol falls by about a quarter to a third and most patients tolerate it in observational series — lipid effectiveness shown, cardiovascular outcomes untested
shelves.question: Is intermittent statin dosing effective for statin-intolerant patients?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alanine Transaminase · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol · Cholesterol, HDL · Cholesterol, LDL · Comorbidity · Creatine Kinase · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Fluorobenzenes · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines · Retrospective Studies · Rosuvastatin Calcium · Smoking · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · Triglycerides · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: For lowering LDL cholesterol and being tolerated, the observational and review evidence is consistently favourable; for cardiovascular outcomes there is no trial at all. In the largest series (Meek 2012, PMID: 22256801; 325 statin-intolerant patients), rosuvastatin 5 mg two to three times weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 32% and once-weekly dosing by 23%, and 89% of patients tolerated rosuvastatin over a median 14.9 months. A review of the intermittent-dosing literature (Keating 2013, PMID: 23482733; 10 publications) found at least 70% of previously intolerant patients tolerated an intermittent regimen without recurrence of treatment-limiting effects, with LDL cholesterol lowering of 12–38%. The one randomised comparison (Backes 2012, PMID: 22836073; N = 20, printed on the face) found rosuvastatin 80 mg once weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 29%, comparable to daily atorvastatin 10 mg — but in patients with dyslipidaemia, not documented statin intolerance. No study reports cardiovascular events, so effectiveness here means lipid lowering with tolerability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — intermittent dosing lowers LDL cholesterol substantially and is tolerated by most statin-intolerant patients in observational evidence; outcome benefit is untested.

cards.headline: Meek 2012: in 325 statin-intolerant patients, rosuvastatin 5 mg two to three times weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 32% and weekly dosing by 23%; 89% tolerated it (observational)
cards.summary: Meek 2012: in 325 statin-intolerant patients, rosuvastatin 5 mg two to three times weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 32% and weekly dosing by 23%; 89% tolerated it (observational)
cards.people: 325 patients at nine UK centres who had documented adverse effects on simvastatin (75%) or atorvastatin (63%), treated with rosuvastatin 5 mg daily or intermittently and followed for a median of 14.9 months; 59% were treated for primary prevention. Baseline LDL cholesterol 4.76 mmol/L (184 mg/dL) and total cholesterol 7.41 mmol/L (287 mg/dL) in the efficacy subset (n = 224).
cards.result: 289 patients (89%) tolerated rosuvastatin and remained adherent; 36 (11%) discontinued for adverse effects after a median of 5 months. Daily rosuvastatin (n = 134) reduced total cholesterol by 31% and LDL cholesterol by 43%; rosuvastatin 5 mg two to three times weekly (n = 79) reduced total cholesterol by 26% and LDL cholesterol by 32% (P < 0.001); weekly rosuvastatin (n = 11) reduced total cholesterol by 17% and LDL cholesterol by 23% (P < 0.001), with no effect on triglycerides. No myositis or rhabdomyolysis was observed. The authors conclude rosuvastatin 5 mg was safe and biochemically effective as daily or intermittent therapy in patients intolerant to other statins.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and uncontrolled: patients who could not tolerate intermittent dosing at all may never enter such a series, and there is no daily-dosing or placebo comparator, so the tolerability and lipid figures are descriptive, not comparative.
cards.source: Meek C et al. Daily and intermittent rosuvastatin 5 mg therapy in statin intolerant patients: an observational study. Current Medical Research and Opinion. 2012. PMID: 22256801. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Keating 2013: across 10 publications on intermittent dosing after statin-induced myopathy, at least 70% of patients tolerated the regimen and LDL cholesterol fell by 12–38%
cards.summary: Keating 2013: across 10 publications on intermittent dosing after statin-induced myopathy, at least 70% of patients tolerated the regimen and LDL cholesterol fell by 12–38%
cards.people: Patients with previous intolerance due to statin-induced myopathy, as reported in the 10 publications (excluding meeting abstracts) identified by a systematic literature search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science to December 2012, covering regimens from every-other-day to once-weekly atorvastatin and/or rosuvastatin.
cards.result: At least 70% of patients were able to tolerate an intermittent dosing strategy without recurrence of previous treatment-limiting adverse effects. The degree of LDL cholesterol lowering varied appreciably among studies (12–38%), and adding a nondaily statin regimen facilitated attainment of National Cholesterol Education Program goals for some patients. The authors conclude intermittent dosing (particularly with rosuvastatin and atorvastatin) is a useful strategy in previously intolerant patients, while noting that larger randomised trials are necessary to define its role and the optimal regimen. No cardiovascular-event outcomes are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A review of small, mostly uncontrolled series inherits their selection bias: the 70% tolerability figure describes patients offered and started on intermittent dosing in published reports, not all statin-intolerant patients.
cards.source: Keating AJ et al. Intermittent nondaily dosing strategies in patients with previous statin-induced myopathy. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2013. PMID: 23482733. cards.headline: Backes 2012 (HD-ROWS): rosuvastatin 80 mg once weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 29%, comparable to atorvastatin 10 mg daily — a randomised pilot in 20 patients with dyslipidaemia (N on the face), not a statin-intolerance trial
cards.summary: Backes 2012 (HD-ROWS): rosuvastatin 80 mg once weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 29%, comparable to atorvastatin 10 mg daily — a randomised pilot in 20 patients with dyslipidaemia (N on the face), not a statin-intolerance trial
cards.people: 20 adults aged 18–65 years with dyslipidaemia (LDL cholesterol over 100 mg/dL, triglycerides under 200 mg/dL), randomised double-blind to rosuvastatin 80 mg once weekly (n = 10) or atorvastatin 10 mg daily (n = 10) for 8 weeks. Randomised N = 20, printed here because it is small.
cards.result: Participants in each arm experienced significant and comparable reductions from baseline in total cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol and overall LDL cholesterol (−29%). Changes in HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were nonsignificant and similar between groups. Each regimen was well tolerated, with no major adverse events reported. The authors conclude once-weekly rosuvastatin produced comparable lipid changes to daily atorvastatin at the measured time points.
cards.watchOut: This pilot randomised 20 patients with dyslipidaemia — not documented statin-intolerant patients — so it supports the pharmacology of weekly dosing (a similar total weekly dose lowers LDL similarly) rather than tolerability in intolerance, and 8 weeks of lipids is not an outcome.
cards.source: Backes JM et al. The high-dose rosuvastatin once weekly study (the HD-ROWS). Journal of Clinical Lipidology. 2012. PMID: 22836073. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: intermittent statin dosing lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly a quarter to a third and is tolerated by most previously intolerant patients in observational evidence — with no cardiovascular-outcome trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: intermittent statin dosing lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly a quarter to a third and is tolerated by most previously intolerant patients in observational evidence — with no cardiovascular-outcome trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective series in statin-intolerant patients (N = 325), one systematic review of 10 intermittent-dosing publications in statin-induced myopathy, and one randomised pilot of weekly dosing (N = 20, dyslipidaemia rather than intolerance). Total documented participants exceed 340, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small pilot's N is printed on its card.
cards.result: Intermittent rosuvastatin lowered LDL cholesterol by 32% at two to three doses weekly and 23% once weekly, with 89% tolerating treatment (Meek 2012); the literature review found at least 70% tolerability and 12–38% LDL lowering (Keating 2013); weekly rosuvastatin matched daily atorvastatin for LDL lowering (−29% both) in the pilot (Backes 2012). No carded study reports cardiovascular events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for lipid lowering and tolerability.
cards.watchOut: Effectiveness on this shelf means LDL cholesterol and staying on therapy. Whether the smaller LDL reduction from intermittent dosing preserves the event reduction of daily dosing is biologically plausible but has never been tested in an outcomes trial.

shelves.title: Metformin for walking in PAD without diabetes: the PERMET randomised trial found no improvement in 6-minute walk distance (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: Does metformin improve walking in PAD patients without diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Hypoglycemic Agents · Lower Extremity · Metformin · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Walk Test · Walking · Treatment Outcome · Headache · Dyspepsia · Ankle Brachial Index
shelves.balance: No — the one completed randomised trial is a clean null. In PERMET (McDermott 2026, PMID: 41205146; 202 people with peripheral artery disease and without diabetes), 6-minute walk distance changed by −5.4 m on metformin and −5.3 m on placebo over 6 months (adjusted between-group difference 1.1 m, 95% CI −16.3 to 18.6; P = .90), and no secondary outcome improved (the treatment made no difference). The mechanistic rationale came from animal work in which metformin improved limb blood supply without improving physical performance (Krishna 2025, PMID: 40304545 — a mouse study, carded as preclinical rationale only, not human evidence). A second human trial, MOBILE IC (Reitz 2023, PMID: 36681798; NCT05132439), plans 200 non-diabetic veterans with claudication but had reported no results in its protocol record. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — metformin did not improve walking in PAD patients without diabetes in the completed randomised trial.

cards.headline: PERMET (McDermott 2026): metformin did not improve 6-minute walk distance in 202 people with PAD and without diabetes — change −5.4 m vs −5.3 m on placebo (difference 1.1 m, P = .90; the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: PERMET (McDermott 2026): metformin did not improve 6-minute walk distance in 202 people with PAD and without diabetes — change −5.4 m vs −5.3 m on placebo (difference 1.1 m, P = .90; the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 202 adults aged 50 years or older with lower-extremity peripheral artery disease and without diabetes, at 4 US centres, randomised to metformin (n = 97) or placebo (n = 105) for 6 months; 179 (89%) completed 6-month follow-up. Mean age 69.6 years; 28% female; 39% Black.
cards.result: 6-minute walk distance changed from 358.6 to 353.2 m on metformin (within-group change −5.4 m) and from 359.8 to 354.5 m on placebo (−5.3 m); the adjusted between-group difference was 1.1 m (95% CI, −16.3 to 18.6 m; P = .90), against a minimum clinically important difference of 8 to 20 m. Metformin did not significantly improve any secondary outcome (maximal or pain-free treadmill walking time, Walking Impairment Questionnaire scores, Short-Form 36 physical functioning, or brachial flow-mediated dilation). Serious adverse events were mainly cardiovascular (3.1% metformin vs 1.9% placebo); indigestion or stomach upset was more common on metformin (64.9% vs 40.6%). The authors conclude the results do not support metformin for improving walking performance in PAD.
cards.watchOut: PERMET enrolled 202 of a targeted 212 participants (95%), so it is close to its planned size and its confidence interval excludes the 20 m upper end of clinically important benefit but not a small benefit under about 18 m; the honest reading is no demonstrated improvement, not proof of exactly zero effect.
cards.source: McDermott MM et al. Metformin to Improve Walking Performance in Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease: The PERMET Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 41205146. cards.headline: Krishna 2025: in a mouse model of ongoing limb ischaemia, metformin improved hind-limb blood supply but not physical performance — preclinical rationale only, not human evidence
cards.summary: Krishna 2025: in a mouse model of ongoing limb ischaemia, metformin improved hind-limb blood supply but not physical performance — preclinical rationale only, not human evidence
cards.people: Animal study (not human evidence): apolipoprotein E-deficient mice with surgically induced stable hind-limb ischaemia, randomised 5 days after induction to metformin 300 mg/kg/day (n = 16) or vehicle (n = 15) by oral gavage for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Metformin improved hind-limb blood supply (P < 0.001) but did not improve treadmill physical performance, alongside increased phosphorylation of AMP-activated protein kinase and endothelial nitric oxide synthase and increased circulating nitric oxide (P < 0.05 for the measures as printed in the record). The authors note that laser-Doppler blood supply may not be an ideal outcome measure for gauging a drug's success in patients with PAD-related walking impairment. This card is the mechanistic background that motivated the human trials; it is not evidence about patients.
cards.watchOut: Mice are not patients: this card is included so the shelf shows why the hypothesis was plausible, and its own result — blood supply up, performance unchanged — foreshadows the human trial's null on walking. It must never be cited as clinical evidence.
cards.source: Krishna SM et al. Effect of metformin in a novel experimental model of peripheral artery disease. Clinical Science. 2025. PMID: 40304545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MOBILE IC (Reitz 2023): a second randomised trial in non-diabetic claudication (200 veterans planned, NCT05132439) exists as a protocol with no results reported in its record
cards.summary: MOBILE IC (Reitz 2023): a second randomised trial in non-diabetic claudication (200 veterans planned, NCT05132439) exists as a protocol with no results reported in its record
cards.people: Protocol for a randomised trial of 200 non-diabetic veterans with intermittent claudication, randomised 1:1 to metformin extended-release 1,000 mg/day or placebo for 180 days, with the primary outcome of 180-day maximum walking distance on the 6-minute walk test; participant results are not reported — this is a protocol record.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its stated hypothesis is that metformin will improve function, retard PAD progression, and improve systemic inflammation and mitochondrial function in non-diabetic patients with intermittent claudication. Until it reports, PERMET remains the only completed randomised test of the question on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about metformin: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the question has been tested twice in humans when only one completed trial exists.

shelves.title: Pulmonary valve replacement in repaired tetralogy of Fallot (observational only): associated with fewer deaths and ventricular tachycardia once the right ventricle is markedly dilated, with volumes normalising only if surgery precedes 160 mL/m2 — and no randomised evidence at all
shelves.question: Should adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot undergo pulmonary valve replacement for severe pulmonary regurgitation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adolescent · Young Adult · Adult · Pulmonary Valve · Tetralogy of Fallot · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Propensity Score · Registries · Tachycardia, Ventricular
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: no randomised trial exists, and the guideline meta-analysis found no eligible study that compared valve replacement with conservative therapy for mortality in adults. What exists is registry evidence that has strengthened with follow-up: the earlier INDICATOR analysis (977 patients, 5.3 years) found no significant association with death or sustained ventricular tachycardia (adjusted HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.36), while the later, larger analysis (1,143 patients, 8.3 years) found a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia in propensity-matched patients (adjusted HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21–0.81), concentrated in those with advanced right ventricular dilatation (end-systolic volume index over 80 mL/m2: HR 0.32) and absent at or below that threshold (HR 0.86). Volumes reliably fall after replacement and normalise only if preoperative end-diastolic volume is under 160 mL/m2 (Oosterhof 2007) — the anatomical argument for not waiting too long. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: replacement is associated with fewer deaths and sustained ventricular tachycardia, mainly once right ventricular dilatation is advanced, but every number here is non-randomised and confounding by indication runs in both directions.

cards.headline: Bokma 2023 (INDICATOR): propensity-matched patients who had pulmonary valve replacement had a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia (adjusted HR 0.41) — benefit concentrated in advanced right ventricular dilatation
cards.summary: Bokma 2023 (INDICATOR): propensity-matched patients who had pulmonary valve replacement had a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia (adjusted HR 0.41) — benefit concentrated in advanced right ventricular dilatation
cards.people: 1,143 patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot in the international INDICATOR registry (mean age 27 ± 14 years; 47% had pulmonary valve replacement), followed 8.3 ± 5.2 years; the primary outcome (earliest of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia) occurred in 82 patients, and replacement and non-replacement patients were matched 1:1 on a valve-replacement propensity score (matched cohort n = 524).
cards.result: In the matched cohort, the adjusted hazard ratio for the primary outcome with valve replacement versus no replacement was 0.41 (95% CI 0.21–0.81; multivariable model P = 0.010), with similar results in the full cohort. The benefit was concentrated in advanced right ventricular dilatation (interaction P = 0.046): with a right ventricular end-systolic volume index over 80 mL/m2, replacement was associated with a lower primary-outcome risk (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.16–0.62; P < 0.001), whereas at or below 80 mL/m2 there was no association (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.38–1.92; P = 0.70). All hazard ratios here are relative measures from an observational registry; the record does not print the absolute event rates by group.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching balances measured differences only: patients chosen for replacement differ in symptoms, anatomy and centre practice in ways no score fully captures, and the subgroup split at 80 mL/m2 — the most clinically quoted part — is an interaction analysis, not a randomised threshold.
cards.source: Bokma JP et al. Improved Outcomes After Pulmonary Valve Replacement in Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023. PMID: 37225360. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bokma 2018: the earlier analysis of the same registry (977 patients, 5.3 years) found NO significant association — adjusted HR 0.65 (0.31 to 1.36) for death or sustained ventricular tachycardia
cards.summary: Bokma 2018: the earlier analysis of the same registry (977 patients, 5.3 years) found NO significant association — adjusted HR 0.65 (0.31 to 1.36) for death or sustained ventricular tachycardia
cards.people: 977 subjects with repaired tetralogy of Fallot and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging from the same international registry (age 26 ± 15 years; 45% had pulmonary valve replacement), followed 5.3 ± 3.1 years; the primary outcome ((aborted) death and sustained ventricular tachycardia) occurred in 41 subjects and a secondary composite (heart failure, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, sustained supraventricular tachycardia) in 88.
cards.result: After propensity and other adjustment, the hazard ratio for valve replacement versus none (time-varying covariate) was 0.65 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.36; P = 0.25) for the primary outcome — the treatment made no statistically demonstrable difference — and 1.43 (95% CI 0.83 to 2.46; P = 0.19) for the secondary outcome. In the 426 subjects NOT meeting predefined consensus criteria for replacement, point estimates favoured no replacement (primary HR 2.53, 95% CI 0.79 to 8.06; secondary HR 2.31, 95% CI 1.07 to 4.97; P = 0.03). The authors concluded replacement was not associated with a reduced rate of death and sustained ventricular tachycardia at 5.3 years, with more events after replacement in patients outside consensus criteria.
cards.watchOut: This is not a contradiction of the 2023 paper so much as its earlier, shorter, smaller cut of the same registry — but it is the standing reminder that the apparent benefit emerged only with longer follow-up and remains one registry's observational signal.
cards.source: Bokma JP et al. A propensity score-adjusted analysis of clinical outcomes after pulmonary valve replacement in tetralogy of Fallot. Heart. 2018. PMID: 29092913. cards.headline: Oosterhof 2007: right ventricular volumes fell by a mean of 28% after replacement, but normalisation was achieved only when preoperative end-diastolic volume was under 160 mL/m2 (or end-systolic under 82 mL/m2)
cards.summary: Oosterhof 2007: right ventricular volumes fell by a mean of 28% after replacement, but normalisation was achieved only when preoperative end-diastolic volume was under 160 mL/m2 (or end-systolic under 82 mL/m2)
cards.type: Prospective surgical cohort with pre/post magnetic resonance imaging (Oosterhof 2007)
cards.people: 71 adult patients with corrected tetralogy of Fallot who underwent pulmonary valve replacement in a Dutch nationwide prospective follow-up study (1993–2006), each evaluated by cardiovascular magnetic resonance before and after surgery.
cards.result: Right ventricular volumes decreased by a mean of 28% after surgery, while right ventricular ejection fraction did not change significantly (42 ± 10% to 43 ± 10%; P = 0.34). Concomitant outflow-tract reduction produced a 25% larger decrease in volumes. Receiver-operating analysis gave cutoffs of 160 mL/m2 for normalisation of end-diastolic volume and 82 mL/m2 for end-systolic volume; the authors found no threshold above which volumes did not decrease at all — higher preoperative volumes still shrank, they just stopped normalising.
cards.watchOut: A remodelling study, not an outcomes study: it shows the ventricle recovers size best before 160/82 mL/m2, but shrinking volumes are a surrogate — this cohort cannot say earlier surgery prevents death or arrhythmia.
cards.source: Oosterhof T et al. Preoperative thresholds for pulmonary valve replacement in patients with corrected tetralogy of Fallot using cardiovascular magnetic resonance. Circulation. 2007. prospective surgical cohort with pre/post magnetic resonance imaging (oosterhof 2007) 71 adult patients with corrected tetralogy of fallot who underwent pulmonary valve replacement in a dutch nationwide prospective follow-up study (1993–2006), each evaluated by cardiovascular magnetic resonance before and after surgery. right ventricular volumes decreased by a mean of 28% after surgery, while right ventricular ejection fraction did not change significantly (42 ± 10% to 43 ± 10%; p = 0.34). concomitant outflow-tract reduction produced a 25% larger decrease in volumes. receiver-operating analysis gave cutoffs of 160 ml/m2 for normalisation of end-diastolic volume and 82 ml/m2 for end-systolic volume; the authors found no threshold above which volumes did not decrease at all — higher preoperative volumes still shrank, they just stopped normalising. a remodelling study, not an outcomes study: it shows the ventricle recovers size best before 160/82 ml/m2, but shrinking volumes are a surrogate — this cohort cannot say earlier surgery prevents death or arrhythmia. oosterhof t et al. preoperative thresholds for pulmonary valve replacement in patients with corrected tetralogy of fallot using cardiovascular magnetic resonance. circulation. 2007. pmid: 17620511. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · blood flow velocity · female · heart valve prosthesis implantation · heart ventricles · humans · magnetic resonance imaging · magnetic resonance imaging, cine · male · organ size · postoperative complications · preoperative care · prospective studies · pulmonary valve · pulmonary valve insufficiency · roc curve · recurrence · reoperation · stroke volume · tetralogy of fallot · time factors · ventricular outflow obstruction · ventricular remodeling

cards.headline: Mongeon 2019 (guideline meta-analysis): NO randomised trial or comparative cohort study has ever compared valve replacement with conservative therapy for mortality in adults — the comparative evidence base is empty
cards.summary: Mongeon 2019 (guideline meta-analysis): NO randomised trial or comparative cohort study has ever compared valve replacement with conservative therapy for mortality in adults — the comparative evidence base is empty
cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis for a guideline writing committee (Mongeon 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review conducted for the 2019 update of the Canadian Cardiovascular Society adult congenital heart disease guidelines; finding no eligible comparative study, the authors selected 10 cohort studies (total 657 patients) reporting outcomes after surgical pulmonary valve replacement in adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot and pulmonary regurgitation.
cards.result: After replacement, the pooled incidence rate of death was 1% per year (95% CI 0–1% per year) and of sustained ventricular arrhythmias 1% per year (95% CI 1%–2% per year). Symptoms improved (odds ratio for postoperative NYHA class over II 0.08, 95% CI 0.03–0.24 — a relative measure from uncontrolled before–after cohorts). Indexed right ventricular end-diastolic volume fell by 61.29 mL/m2 and end-systolic volume by 37.20 mL/m2, while ejection fraction did not change (0.19%, 95% CI −2.36% to 2.74%). The authors state plainly that studies comparing replacement with conservative therapy exclusively in adults are lacking.
cards.watchOut: Every favourable number in this review is a before–after change or an event rate with no untreated comparator — it describes what happens after surgery, not what surgery adds.
cards.source: Mongeon FP et al. Pulmonary Valve Replacement for Pulmonary Regurgitation in Adults With Tetralogy of Fallot: A Meta-analysis-A Report for the Writing Committee of the 2019 Update of the Canadian Cardiovascular Society Guidelines for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease. cards.headline: Synthesis: replacement reliably shrinks the right ventricle and is associated with fewer deaths and sustained ventricular tachycardia once dilatation is advanced — but all of it is observational, and the same registry was null at shorter follow-up
cards.summary: Synthesis: replacement reliably shrinks the right ventricle and is associated with fewer deaths and sustained ventricular tachycardia once dilatation is advanced — but all of it is observational, and the same registry was null at shorter follow-up
cards.people: The carded evidence: two analyses of one international registry (977 patients at 5.3 years; 1,143 at 8.3 years — overlapping populations, not additive), one 71-patient prospective imaging cohort, and a guideline meta-analysis of 10 uncontrolled cohorts (657 patients). The unique evidence base is well over 30 patients; the limitation is design, not size.
cards.result: Valve replacement was associated with a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia in the longer registry analysis (adjusted HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21–0.81), driven by patients with end-systolic volume index over 80 mL/m2 (HR 0.32), with no association below that threshold (HR 0.86) and a null result in the earlier analysis (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.36). Volumes fall about 28% after surgery and normalise only below preoperative thresholds of 160 mL/m2 (end-diastolic) and 82 mL/m2 (end-systolic). No randomised or comparative mortality evidence exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication cuts both ways here — sicker patients get referred (biasing against surgery) and survivors well enough for surgery get counted (biasing for it). The registry signal is the best evidence available, and it should be quoted with its design attached.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bokma JP et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 37225360); Bokma JP et al. Heart. 2018 (PMID: 29092913); Oosterhof T et al. Circulation. 2007 (PMID: 17620511); Mongeon FP et al. Canadian Journal of Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 31813508).

shelves.title: Apixaban versus rivaroxaban in atrial fibrillation (observational only): apixaban was associated with less gastrointestinal and major bleeding — gastrointestinal bleeding hazard ratio 0.72 in a 527,226-patient multinational cohort — with no substantial difference in stroke prevention
shelves.question: Is apixaban safer than rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in AF?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Administration, Oral · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Atrial Fibrillation/drug therapy · Cohort Studies · Dabigatran/adverse effects · Embolism/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Ischemic Stroke · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications · Rivaroxaban/adverse effects · United States · Clinical Trials as Topic · Pyrazoles · Pyridones · Pyridines · Thiazoles
shelves.balance: No randomised trial has ever compared apixaban with rivaroxaban head to head, so every card on this shelf is observational and the stamp is capped accordingly. The largest comparison (Lau 2022, PMID: 36315950; 527,226 new users across five databases in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States) found apixaban associated with a lower risk of gastrointestinal bleeding than rivaroxaban (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.79), consistently at standard dose, at reduced dose and in chronic kidney disease, and no substantial differences for ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism, intracranial haemorrhage or mortality. A meta-analysis of the ten real-world head-to-head studies (Mamas 2022, PMID: 34949473) points the same way and slightly further: stroke or systemic embolism HR 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95), major bleeding HR 0.62 (0.56 to 0.69) and gastrointestinal bleeding HR 0.57 (0.50 to 0.64), all relative measures favouring apixaban. In the highest-risk subgroup carded, US patients with atrial fibrillation and stage 4/5 chronic kidney disease (Fu 2024, PMID: 37839687), rivaroxaban was again associated with more major bleeding than apixaban (HR 1.69, 1.33 to 2.15) while the ischaemic-stroke comparison was imprecise (HR 0.71, 0.40 to 1.24). The direction is consistent everywhere it has been looked for — less bleeding on apixaban — but residual confounding in claims and registry data can manufacture exactly this pattern, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE and carries its observational-only label on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: apixaban appears safer than rivaroxaban on bleeding, with no consistent difference in stroke prevention.

cards.headline: Lau 2022: in 527,226 new DOAC users, apixaban carried a lower gastrointestinal bleeding risk than rivaroxaban (HR 0.72) — and no substantial difference in stroke, intracranial haemorrhage or death
cards.summary: Lau 2022: in 527,226 new DOAC users, apixaban carried a lower gastrointestinal bleeding risk than rivaroxaban (HR 0.72) — and no substantial difference in stroke, intracranial haemorrhage or death
cards.people: Patients newly diagnosed with atrial fibrillation from 2010 through 2019 who received a new direct oral anticoagulant prescription, in five standardised electronic health care databases covering 221 million people in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States: 527,226 new users in total (apixaban n = 281,320; dabigatran n = 61,008; edoxaban n = 12,722; rivaroxaban n = 172,176). Database-specific hazard ratios were estimated with Cox regression stratified by propensity score and pooled with a random-effects model.
cards.result: Apixaban use was associated with a lower risk of gastrointestinal bleeding than rivaroxaban (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.79), dabigatran (HR 0.81, 0.70 to 0.94) or edoxaban (HR 0.77, 0.66 to 0.91). No substantial differences were observed for the other outcomes (ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism, intracranial haemorrhage, all-cause mortality) or other comparisons. Results were consistent in patients aged 80 years or older, and the lower gastrointestinal bleeding risk with apixaban versus rivaroxaban was seen at standard dose (HR 0.72, 0.64 to 0.82), at reduced dose (HR 0.68, 0.61 to 0.77) and in chronic kidney disease (HR 0.68, 0.59 to 0.77). All hazard ratios are relative measures; the record does not print absolute event rates for the head-to-head comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Observational: doctors choose the drug, and patients channelled to apixaban may differ from those given rivaroxaban in ways propensity scores cannot fully remove — the record itself names residual confounding as its limitation.
cards.source: Lau WCY et al. Comparative Effectiveness and Safety Between Apixaban, Dabigatran, Edoxaban, and Rivaroxaban Among Patients With Atrial Fibrillation : A Multinational Population-Based Cohort Study. Annals of internal medicine. 2022. PMID: 36315950. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mamas 2022: pooling the ten real-world head-to-head studies, apixaban was associated with less stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.88), less major bleeding (HR 0.62) and less gastrointestinal bleeding (HR 0.57) than rivaroxaban
cards.summary: Mamas 2022: pooling the ten real-world head-to-head studies, apixaban was associated with less stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.88), less major bleeding (HR 0.62) and less gastrointestinal bleeding (HR 0.57) than rivaroxaban
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Mamas 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban or rivaroxaban and reporting stroke/systemic embolism and/or major bleeding: ten unique retrospective real-world evidence studies met inclusion (PROSPERO CRD42021251719, as printed in the record).
cards.result: The adjusted hazard ratio for stroke/systemic embolism was 0.88 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.95), indicating a significantly lower relative hazard with apixaban versus rivaroxaban. Major bleeding was significantly lower with apixaban (HR 0.62, 0.56 to 0.69), as was gastrointestinal bleeding (HR 0.57, 0.50 to 0.64). Meta-regression suggested the CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores of the included populations may modify which drug performs better. All measures are relative; the record does not print pooled absolute event rates.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of observational studies pools their biases as faithfully as their data: the concordance with Lau 2022 is reassuring about direction, but it cannot convert routine-practice comparisons into randomised evidence.
cards.source: Mamas MA et al. Meta-Analysis Comparing Apixaban Versus Rivaroxaban for Management of Patients With Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation. The American journal of cardiology. 2022. PMID: 34949473. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fu 2024: in atrial fibrillation with stage 4/5 chronic kidney disease, rivaroxaban was associated with more major bleeding than apixaban (HR 1.69), while the stroke comparison was too imprecise to read (HR 0.71, CI 0.40 to 1.24)
cards.summary: Fu 2024: in atrial fibrillation with stage 4/5 chronic kidney disease, rivaroxaban was associated with more major bleeding than apixaban (HR 1.69), while the stroke comparison was too imprecise to read (HR 0.71, CI 0.40 to 1.24)
cards.type: Propensity score-matched cohort study in advanced CKD (Fu 2024)
cards.people: Propensity score-matched cohorts from two nationwide US claims databases (Medicare and Optum Clinformatics, 2013 to 2022) of patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and non-dialysis-dependent CKD stage 4/5 starting an oral anticoagulant: warfarin versus apixaban matched cohort n = 12,488; rivaroxaban versus apixaban matched cohort n = 5,720; matching adjusted for 80 potential confounders.
cards.result: Compared with apixaban, rivaroxaban was associated with a higher rate of major bleeding (HR 1.69, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.15). No statistically significant difference in ischaemic stroke was observed for rivaroxaban versus apixaban (HR 0.71, 0.40 to 1.24), but the confidence interval was wide. All-cause mortality was similar (HR 0.94, 0.81 to 1.10). Warfarin, for context in the same study, also carried more major bleeding than apixaban (HR 1.85, 1.59 to 2.15). All hazard ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: This is the frailest, highest-bleeding-risk population in routine practice and the one the randomised DOAC trials largely excluded — the bleeding signal agrees with the general-population cohorts, but the stroke estimate is compatible with meaningful benefit or harm in either direction.
cards.source: Fu EL et al. Comparative Safety and Effectiveness of Warfarin or Rivaroxaban Versus Apixaban in Patients With Advanced CKD and Atrial Fibrillation: Nationwide US Cohort Study. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2024. PMID: 37839687. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: every large routine-practice comparison finds less bleeding on apixaban than rivaroxaban and no consistent difference in stroke prevention — but the comparison has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: every large routine-practice comparison finds less bleeding on apixaban than rivaroxaban and no consistent difference in stroke prevention — but the comparison has never been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multinational cohort of 527,226 new DOAC users (Lau 2022), one meta-analysis of ten real-world head-to-head studies (Mamas 2022), and one matched cohort of 5,720 rivaroxaban-versus-apixaban initiators with stage 4/5 CKD (Fu 2024). Total carded participants exceed 500,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation on this shelf is design, not size, and it is printed on the stamp.
cards.result: Gastrointestinal bleeding favoured apixaban over rivaroxaban in the multinational cohort (HR 0.72) and in the pooled real-world literature (HR 0.57); major bleeding favoured apixaban in the meta-analysis (HR 0.62) and in advanced CKD (rivaroxaban versus apixaban HR 1.69). Stroke or systemic embolism showed no substantial difference in the largest cohort, a small relative advantage to apixaban in the meta-analysis (HR 0.88), and an imprecise estimate in CKD (HR 0.71, CI 0.40 to 1.24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: If a head-to-head randomised trial is ever run it could shrink these differences: channelling of higher-bleeding-risk patients toward apixaban would bias against it, yet unmeasured frailty and dose-selection differences can bias in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lau WCY et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36315950); Mamas MA et al. The American journal of cardiology. 2022 (PMID: 34949473); Fu EL et al. American journal of kidney diseases. 2024 (PMID: 37839687).

shelves.title: Giant cell myocarditis (observational only): combination immunosuppression was associated with 12.3 versus 3.0 months average survival and suppresses the infiltrate — but relapse continues for years and fulminant disease still ends in transplantation
shelves.question: Does immunosuppression help giant cell myocarditis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Age of Onset · Aged · Autoimmune Diseases · Biopsy · Disease Progression · Female · Giant Cells · Heart Transplantation · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy · Inflammatory Bowel Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Myocarditis · Myocardium · Necrosis · Proportional Hazards Models · Recurrence · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: giant cell myocarditis is too rare and too lethal for randomised trials, and none is carded. The signal comes from the Multicenter Giant Cell Myocarditis Study: among 63 patients (death or transplantation in 89%, median survival 5.5 months), the 22 patients treated with corticosteroids plus cyclosporine and/or azathioprine survived an average of 12.3 months versus 3.0 months for the 30 untreated patients (p = 0.001; Cooper 1997, PMID: 9197214). A small prospective protocol study of combination immunosuppression (20 patients) found biopsy inflammation, necrosis and giant cells significantly reduced at 4 weeks, with 1 death and 2 transplantations in a year — and one fatal recurrence after immunosuppression was withdrawn (Cooper 2008, PMID: 19026310). Long-term registry follow-up shows the disease is suppressed, not cured: among 26 patients who survived the first year without transplantation, the combined rate of death, transplantation, assist-device placement or recurrence reached 47% at 5 years, with recurrences up to 8 years out (Maleszewski 2015, PMID: 25882774). In fulminant disease on mechanical circulatory support, immunosuppression rarely averted transplantation — 9 of 13 patients were transplanted and none survived long-term transplant-free (Montero 2018, PMID: 29306448). Immunosuppression for virus-negative lymphocytic myocarditis is a different question, homed on shelf #3062 and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: combination immunosuppression appears to prolong survival in giant cell myocarditis and should not be stopped casually, but most patients still die or need transplantation.

cards.headline: Cooper 1997: combination immunosuppression was associated with average survival of 12.3 months versus 3.0 months untreated — in a disease with 89% death or transplantation and 5.5-month median survival
cards.summary: Cooper 1997: combination immunosuppression was associated with average survival of 12.3 months versus 3.0 months untreated — in a disease with 89% death or transplantation and 5.5-month median survival
cards.people: Multicenter Giant Cell Myocarditis Study Group registry: 63 patients with idiopathic giant-cell myocarditis identified worldwide (33 men, 30 women; average age 42.6 years); 75% presented with congestive heart failure, 14% with ventricular arrhythmia and 5% with heart block; 19% had associated autoimmune disorders. Evidence type: retrospective multicentre case series with treatment comparison.
cards.result: Survival was worse than in lymphocytic myocarditis (P < 0.001); the rate of death or cardiac transplantation was 89% and median survival was 5.5 months from symptom onset. The 22 patients treated with corticosteroids and cyclosporine, azathioprine, or both survived for an average of 12.3 months, compared with an average of 3.0 months for the 30 patients who received no immunosuppressive therapy (P = 0.001). Of 34 transplanted patients, 9 (26%) had giant-cell infiltrate in the transplanted heart and 1 died of recurrent giant-cell myocarditis.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was not randomised: patients who lived long enough to be diagnosed and treated differ from those who died untreated within weeks, so some of the 12.3-versus-3.0-month gap is survivorship and selection, not drug effect — the comparison is the best this rare disease has produced, and it is still only an association.
cards.source: Cooper LT Jr et al. Idiopathic giant-cell myocarditis--natural history and treatment. Multicenter Giant Cell Myocarditis Study Group Investigators. The New England journal of medicine. 1997. PMID: 9197214. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cooper 2008: in a prospective protocol (N = 20 on the face), steroids plus cyclosporine shrank biopsy inflammation by 4 weeks — and stopping immunosuppression was followed by a fatal recurrence
cards.summary: Cooper 2008: in a prospective protocol (N = 20 on the face), steroids plus cyclosporine shrank biopsy inflammation by 4 weeks — and stopping immunosuppression was followed by a fatal recurrence
cards.people: Prospective multicentre study of immunosuppression for acute, biopsy-confirmed giant cell myocarditis (1999–2005): 11 subjects received high-dose steroids and cyclosporine and 9 received muromonab-CD3; mean age 60 years, mean 27 days from symptom onset to presentation. Study N = 20.
cards.result: During 1 year of treatment, 1 subject died (day 178, respiratory complications) and 2 received heart transplantations (days 2 and 27). Serial biopsies showed the degree of necrosis, cellular inflammation and giant cells decreased after 4 weeks of treatment (p = 0.001). One patient who completed the trial later died of a fatal recurrence after withdrawal of immunosuppression — the first demonstration, per the record, that recurrent, sometimes fatal, giant cell myocarditis can follow cessation of immunosuppression.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients and no control group: the biopsy improvement shows the drugs suppress the myocardial infiltrate, but survival benefit is inferred from the earlier retrospective series, and the two day-2 and day-27 transplantations show fulminant cases outrun the drugs.
cards.source: Cooper LT Jr et al. Usefulness of immunosuppression for giant cell myocarditis. The American journal of cardiology. 2008. PMID: 19026310. Registry ID: NCT00027443. cards.headline: Maleszewski 2015: even in 1-year survivors, giant cell myocarditis keeps coming back — combined death, transplant, device or recurrence rate 47% at 5 years, recurrences up to 8 years
cards.summary: Maleszewski 2015: even in 1-year survivors, giant cell myocarditis keeps coming back — combined death, transplant, device or recurrence rate 47% at 5 years, recurrences up to 8 years
cards.people: 26 patients with biopsy-proved giant cell myocarditis from a multicentre registry who had survived more than 1 year without heart transplantation (mean age 54.6 years, 65% women), followed retrospectively for a mean of 5.5 years from 1 year after diagnosis. Evidence type: registry long-term follow-up cohort.
cards.result: There were 3 deaths (12%), 5 heart transplantations (19%) and 1 ventricular assist device placement (4%); 3 histologically confirmed recurrences (12%) occurred between 1.5 and 8 years after diagnosis. Thirteen of 26 patients had 30 heart-failure episodes, 12 patients had 23 episodes of elevated creatinine, 13 patients had 41 infectious events, and 6 patients had 19 ventricular-arrhythmia episodes over 144 years of follow-up. Starting 1 year after diagnosis, the combined rate of death, transplantation, device placement and recurrence was 47% at 5 years.
cards.watchOut: By construction this cohort is the favourable tail — patients already alive at 1 year — and treatment was not standardised or compared, so it quantifies the disease's persistence under real-world care (including infection and renal costs of immunosuppression) rather than the drugs' efficacy.
cards.source: Maleszewski JJ et al. Long-term risk of recurrence, morbidity and mortality in giant cell myocarditis. The American journal of cardiology. 2015. PMID: 25882774. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Montero 2018: in fulminant giant cell myocarditis on mechanical support (N = 13 on the face), no patient survived long-term without transplantation — 9 of 13 were transplanted
cards.summary: Montero 2018: in fulminant giant cell myocarditis on mechanical support (N = 13 on the face), no patient survived long-term without transplantation — 9 of 13 were transplanted
cards.people: 13 patients with fulminant giant-cell myocarditis in refractory cardiogenic shock rescued by mechanical circulatory support at eight French intensive care units (2002–2016); median age 44 years, median left ventricular ejection fraction 15%, median blood lactate 4 mmol/L (≈36 mg/dL); venoarterial ECMO was the first support in 11 (85%). Cohort N = 13.
cards.result: Giant cell myocarditis was diagnosed before transplant or death in only 5 patients (38%) and treated with immunosuppressants; infections were the main complication (80%). Four patients died on support, 9 (69%) received heart transplantation, and no patient had long-term survival free from transplantation; all transplanted patients were alive 1 year later with no recurrence at a median follow-up of 42 months. The authors conclude that in fulminant disease, transplantation may be the only long-term survival option.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen fulminant cases, most diagnosed too late for immunosuppression to be the deciding treatment: this card bounds the claim — whatever immunosuppression does in diagnosed, non-fulminant disease, it did not rescue native hearts here.
cards.source: Montero S et al. Fulminant giant-cell myocarditis on mechanical circulatory support: Management and outcomes of a French multicentre cohort. International journal of cardiology. 2018. PMID: 29306448. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: immunosuppression is associated with longer survival (12.3 versus 3.0 months) and visibly suppresses the infiltrate — but giant cell myocarditis relapses for years, and fulminant cases still need transplantation
cards.summary: Synthesis: immunosuppression is associated with longer survival (12.3 versus 3.0 months) and visibly suppresses the infiltrate — but giant cell myocarditis relapses for years, and fulminant cases still need transplantation
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 63-patient multicentre series (Cooper 1997), a 20-patient prospective treatment protocol (Cooper 2008), a 26-patient long-term registry cohort (Maleszewski 2015) and a 13-patient fulminant cohort (Montero 2018) — 122 patients in total, with possible overlap between the registry cohorts, all observational. No randomised trial exists in the records fetched. Total exceeds 30 even allowing for overlap, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small single-study Ns (20, 13) are printed on their card faces.
cards.result: Combination immunosuppression was associated with average survival of 12.3 versus 3.0 months untreated (P = 0.001) in a disease with 89% death or transplantation. Biopsy inflammation, necrosis and giant cells fell significantly by 4 weeks on steroids plus cyclosporine, and a fatal recurrence followed drug withdrawal. Among 1-year survivors the 5-year combined event rate was 47% with recurrences to 8 years; in fulminant disease on mechanical support, 9 of 13 patients were transplanted and none survived transplant-free. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Every number here is observational and the treated-versus-untreated contrast is confounded by who survives to be treated; the stamp is POSSIBLE because the disease offers nothing better, not because the evidence is strong.

shelves.title: Bypass vs angioplasty below the knee — SPLIT: endovascular-first won on amputation-free survival in BASIL-2, vein bypass wins on patency in pooled series
shelves.question: Is bypass surgery better than angioplasty for infrapopliteal disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Aged · Endovascular Procedures · Amputation, Surgical · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia · Popliteal Artery · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · United Kingdom · Technology Assessment, Biomedical · Limb Salvage · Ischemia
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised trial and the patency literature point in opposite directions, and the split is named in the stamp. BASIL-2 (345 patients randomised to vein bypass-first or best endovascular-first for infrapopliteal chronic limb-threatening ischaemia) found amputation-free survival was WORSE with bypass-first: the primary outcome occurred in 63% versus 53% (adjusted HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.80), driven by more deaths (53% versus 45%). Against that, the pooled prospective literature finds vein grafts stay open longest: infrapopliteal great saphenous vein primary patency 87% at 1 year and 78% at 2 years, above all other interventions, while survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival at 2 years were broadly similar between endovascular treatment and vein bypass (Almasri 2019, 44 studies, 8,602 patients); and Romiti 2008 found crural angioplasty limb salvage (82.4% at 36 months) equivalent to bypass despite lower patency. So: bypass is not better on the trial's patient-centred outcome, and endovascular-first is not better on durability. PROPOSED SPLIT (trial outcome: endovascular-first; graft patency: vein bypass): for infrapopliteal disease, bypass-first did not improve amputation-free survival in BASIL-2, while vein grafts show the highest patency in pooled series.

cards.headline: BASIL-2 (2024 HTA report): amputation-free survival was worse with vein bypass-first than best endovascular-first — primary outcome 63% vs 53%, adjusted HR 1.35 — in 345 patients with infrapopliteal disease
cards.summary: BASIL-2 (2024 HTA report): amputation-free survival was worse with vein bypass-first than best endovascular-first — primary outcome 63% vs 53%, adjusted HR 1.35 — in 345 patients with infrapopliteal disease
cards.people: 345 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia due to atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease who required infrapopliteal revascularisation (with or without an additional more proximal procedure), randomised at 41 centres (39 UK, 1 Sweden, 1 Denmark) to vein bypass-first (n = 172) or best endovascular treatment-first (n = 173), followed for a minimum of 2 years. Pragmatic, open, phase III randomised trial.
cards.result: Non-amputation-free survival (major amputation or death) occurred in 108 of 172 (63%) bypass-first patients and 92 of 173 (53%) endovascular-first patients (adjusted hazard ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.80; P = 0.037). Deaths were 91 of 172 (53%) versus 77 of 173 (45%) (adjusted HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.87). Best endovascular-first was also £1,690 cheaper in hospital costs and dominated in the cost-utility analysis. The authors note recruitment was difficult and the target number of events was not achieved.
cards.watchOut: The bypass-first disadvantage was driven by deaths, not amputations, in an open pragmatic trial that under-recruited — a mortality gap of this kind can arise from case mix and perioperative burden and should not be read as proof bypass kills.
cards.source: Moakes CA et al. Vein bypass first vs. best endovascular treatment first revascularisation strategy for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia due to infra-popliteal disease: the BASIL-2 RCT. Health Technology Assessment. 2024. PMID: 39397484. Registry ID: ISRCTN27728689. cards.headline: Almasri 2019: across 44 prospective studies (8,602 patients), vein bypass had the highest infrapopliteal patency, but survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival at 2 years were broadly similar to endovascular treatment
cards.summary: Almasri 2019: across 44 prospective studies (8,602 patients), vein bypass had the highest infrapopliteal patency, but survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival at 2 years were broadly similar to endovascular treatment
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 prospective studies enrolling 8,602 patients with infrainguinal chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and at least 1 year of follow-up, searched to May 2017; infrapopliteal results reported within the review.
cards.result: Periprocedural mortality, amputation and major adverse cardiac events were similar across modalities. In infrapopliteal disease, great saphenous vein grafts had the highest patency (primary 87% at 1 year and 78% at 2 years; secondary 94% and 87%). Prosthetic bypass was notably inferior for amputation and patency, especially below the knee. Drug-eluting stents beat bare-metal stents on 1-year primary patency (73% vs 50%) and were at least comparable to balloon angioplasty (66%). Survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival at 2 years were broadly similar between endovascular interventions and vein bypass. The authors rate the included studies at moderate to high risk of bias and the quality of evidence low.
cards.watchOut: Pooled single-arm rates, not head-to-head randomisation: patients offered bypass differ from those offered angioplasty in anatomy and fitness, so patency gaps partly reflect who got which treatment.
cards.source: Almasri J et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of revascularization outcomes of infrainguinal chronic limb-threatening ischemia. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2019. PMID: 31221539. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Romiti 2008: crural angioplasty patency was limited versus bypass (primary patency 48.6% at 36 months) but limb salvage was equivalent (82.4% at 36 months)
cards.summary: Romiti 2008: crural angioplasty patency was limited versus bypass (primary patency 48.6% at 36 months) but limb salvage was equivalent (82.4% at 36 months)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 30 articles (1990–2006) reporting at least 15 infrapopliteal angioplasties for chronic critical limb ischaemia with 12-month patency or limb-salvage rates, compared against a meta-analysis of popliteal-to-distal vein bypass grafts. Participant total not stated as a single N in the record.
cards.result: Immediate technical success was 89.0% (±2.2%). cards.headline: Synthesis: bypass-first lost on amputation-free survival in the one infrapopliteal RCT, yet vein grafts stay open longest in pooled series — the answer splits by outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: bypass-first lost on amputation-free survival in the one infrapopliteal RCT, yet vein grafts stay open longest in pooled series — the answer splits by outcome
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (BASIL-2, N = 345), one systematic review of 44 prospective studies (N = 8,602), and one meta-analysis of 30 angioplasty series (total N not stated in the record). Total carded participants exceed 8,900, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: BASIL-2: amputation-free survival favoured endovascular-first (primary outcome 53% vs 63%; adjusted HR 1.35 for bypass-first), driven by deaths. Almasri 2019: 2-year survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival broadly similar, with the highest patency for vein grafts (87% primary at 1 year). Romiti 2008: angioplasty limb salvage 82.4% at 36 months, equivalent to bypass despite lower patency. PROPOSED SPLIT (trial outcome: endovascular-first; graft patency: vein bypass).
cards.watchOut: Only BASIL-2 compares the strategies head-to-head, and its result rests on a mortality difference in an under-recruited open trial; the patency advantage of vein bypass comes from non-randomised pooling.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moakes CA et al. Health Technology Assessment. 2024 (PMID: 39397484); Almasri J et al. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2019 (PMID: 31221539); Romiti M et al. Journal of Vascular Surgery. 2008 (PMID: 18372148).

shelves.title: Screening relatives for bicuspid aortic valve (observational only): echocardiography finds it in 6.6–14% of first-degree relatives — detection proven, outcome benefit modelled only
shelves.question: Does screening echocardiography detect bicuspid aortic valve disease in first-degree relatives?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease · Echocardiography · Family · Female · Humans · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Phenotype
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: detection yield is a cohort measurement, not a randomised comparison, and no trial shows screening changes outcomes. The yield is consistent and far above population background: bicuspid aortic valve was diagnosed in 14% of screened first-degree relatives in the Tessler 2022 family cohort, and in 6.6% of 482 screened first-degree relatives in the paediatric-cardiology programme of Massardier 2020 (which also found aortic valve dysfunction in 5.4% and ascending aorta dilatation in 2.9%). A cost-effectiveness model built on these yields (Tessler 2021) found screening dominant — more effective and less costly than no screening, saving €644 with a 0.3 quality-adjusted life-year gain — but that is a model, not an observed outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: yes, screening echocardiography detects bicuspid aortic valve in roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 15 first-degree relatives; whether detection improves their outcomes is untested in a trial.

cards.headline: Tessler 2022: bicuspid aortic valve was diagnosed in 14% of screened first-degree relatives in a family-based echocardiography cohort
cards.summary: Tessler 2022: bicuspid aortic valve was diagnosed in 14% of screened first-degree relatives in a family-based echocardiography cohort
cards.people: Patients with bicuspid aortic valve and their first-degree relatives evaluated by echocardiography: 70 cases from 31 families, plus 327 sporadic cases, at a single centre. Family-based screening cohort.
cards.result: Bicuspid aortic valve was diagnosed in 14% of the screened relatives — against a background the record describes as a 10-fold higher prevalence in first-degree relatives than in the general population. Morphologies among relatives: 12.3% type 0, 66.2% type 1 left–right fusion, 15.4% type 1 right–noncoronary, 4.6% type 1 noncoronary–left, 1.5% type 2. Morphology concordance within families (62% of 120 relative pairs, including literature pairs) was not significantly higher than expected by chance.
cards.watchOut: The 14% yield comes from families already engaged with a bicuspid clinic; yield in unselected relatives of every index case may be lower, and detection is not the same as benefit.
cards.source: Tessler I et al. Is Bicuspid Aortic Valve Morphology Genetically Determined? A Family-Based Study. American Journal of Cardiology. 2022. PMID: 34799086. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Massardier 2020: screening found bicuspid aortic valve in 6.6% of 482 screened first-degree relatives in paediatric cardiology practice — and only 67.6% of relatives were actually screened
cards.summary: Massardier 2020: screening found bicuspid aortic valve in 6.6% of 482 screened first-degree relatives in paediatric cardiology practice — and only 67.6% of relatives were actually screened
cards.people: 713 first-degree relatives of 213 consecutive paediatric bicuspid aortic valve index cases (median age 11 years) at a Quebec City centre, 2015–2018; screening echocardiography was completed in 482 relatives (67.6%), prescribed but not done in 19%, not prescribed in 13%, and declined in 1%. Retrospective analysis of a prospectively included cohort.
cards.result: Among screened relatives, 32 (6.6%) had a bicuspid aortic valve, 26 (5.4%) had aortic valve dysfunction, and 14 (2.9%) had ascending aorta dilatation by Z-score, including 6 (1.2%) with an ascending aorta of 45 mm or more. No significant prevalence differences were found between generations. The authors conclude the bicuspid prevalence in relatives matches prospective adult studies and supports guideline screening, while exhaustiveness of implementation remains a challenge.
cards.watchOut: A paediatric index-case programme: relatives screened are disproportionately parents and siblings of children, and a third of relatives never completed screening, so the 6.6% is a yield among attenders, not a population prevalence.
cards.source: Massardier C et al. First-Degree Relatives Screening of Patients with Bicuspid Aortic Valve: Effectiveness and Feasibility in Pediatric Cardiology Daily Practice. Pediatric Cardiology. 2020. PMID: 32851436. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tessler 2021: modelled cascade screening of first-degree relatives was dominant — €644 cheaper and +0.3 QALY versus no screening — a decision model, not observed outcomes
cards.summary: Tessler 2021: modelled cascade screening of first-degree relatives was dominant — €644 cheaper and +0.3 QALY versus no screening — a decision model, not observed outcomes
cards.people: Decision-analytic cost-effectiveness model of echocardiographic screening for first-degree relatives of a bicuspid aortic valve index case, using bicuspid probabilities and complications from the authors' familial cohort and published population cohorts; costs from list prices and literature. No patients were enrolled — printed plainly here.
cards.result: Screening first-degree relatives was the dominant strategy: more effective and less costly than no screening, with savings of €644 and a gain of 0.3 quality-adjusted life-years. Results held across one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses, including the full reported range of bicuspid rates among relatives; the incremental effect decreased gradually with increasing screening age. The authors conclude echocardiographic screening of relatives is clinically important, cost-effective and cost-saving within the model.
cards.watchOut: A model inherits its inputs: the QALY gain assumes detected relatives benefit from surveillance and timely intervention, which no carded trial has demonstrated.
cards.source: Tessler I et al. Cost-effectiveness analysis of screening for first-degree relatives of patients with bicuspid aortic valve. European Heart Journal - Quality of Care and Clinical Outcomes. 2021. PMID: 34227670. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: screening echocardiography detects bicuspid aortic valve in 6.6–14% of first-degree relatives across two independent programmes — detection is proven, outcome benefit is modelled only
cards.summary: Synthesis: screening echocardiography detects bicuspid aortic valve in 6.6–14% of first-degree relatives across two independent programmes — detection is proven, outcome benefit is modelled only
cards.people: The carded evidence: two screening cohorts (relatives screened: 482 in Massardier 2020; the Tessler 2022 family cohort of 31 families — relative denominator as reported in the record) and one decision model (no enrolled patients). cards.result: Detection yield: 14% of screened relatives (Tessler 2022); 6.6% bicuspid valve, 5.4% valve dysfunction, 2.9% aortic dilatation (Massardier 2020). Modelled value: screening dominant, €644 saved and +0.3 QALY (Tessler 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

shelves.title: Ambulatory monitoring in suspected white coat hypertension — MAYBE (weak evidence) for changing outcomes: it reclassifies patients and refines prognosis, but no trial tests monitoring-guided care
shelves.question: Does ambulatory blood pressure monitoring change outcomes in suspected white coat hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Humans · White Coat Hypertension
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the question as asked. No carded trial randomises patients with suspected white coat hypertension to ambulatory monitoring versus office-only care and measures events; what monitoring demonstrably changes is classification and predicted risk, not proven outcomes. Office measurement agrees poorly with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (accuracy 54.8%, specificity 31.9% in 569 primary-care patients; Grezzana 2017), so monitoring reclassifies a large share of suspected cases. The reclassified groups genuinely differ in prognosis: untreated white coat hypertension carried higher cardiovascular risk than normotension in two meta-analyses (hazard ratio 1.36 for cardiovascular events and 2.09 for cardiovascular mortality, Cohen 2019; 38% relative increase in cardiovascular disease in untreated cohorts, Huang 2017), while treated white coat effect showed no significant excess risk — meaning ambulatory confirmation separates people who need follow-up from people who may not need treatment escalation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ambulatory monitoring changes who is labelled hypertensive and refines prognosis on consistent observational evidence, but whether it changes hard outcomes has never been tested in a trial.

cards.headline: Cohen 2019: untreated white coat hypertension carried higher risk than normotension (cardiovascular events HR 1.36; cardiovascular mortality HR 2.09) — 27 studies, 64,273 participants
cards.summary: Cohen 2019: untreated white coat hypertension carried higher risk than normotension (cardiovascular events HR 1.36; cardiovascular mortality HR 2.09) — 27 studies, 64,273 participants
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Cohen 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 observational studies comprising 25,786 participants with untreated white coat hypertension or treated white coat effect and 38,487 with normal blood pressure, followed for a mean of 3 to 19 years. Diagnosis in the included studies rests on out-of-office (ambulatory/home) monitoring.
cards.result: Compared with normotension, untreated white coat hypertension was associated with increased cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.00), all-cause mortality (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.67) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.09, 95% CI 1.23 to 4.48); the event risk was attenuated in studies including stroke in the endpoint (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.54). Treated white coat effect showed no significant association with cardiovascular events (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.39), all-cause mortality (HR 1.11) or cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.04). The authors conclude out-of-office monitoring is critical in diagnosis and management.
cards.watchOut: Prognostic separation is not outcome change: these cohorts show the ambulatory label identifies higher-risk people, not that performing the test, or acting on it, prevents their events.
cards.source: Cohen JB et al. Cardiovascular Events and Mortality in White Coat Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31181575. cards.headline: Huang 2017: white coat hypertension raised cardiovascular risk only in untreated cohorts (38% relative increase) — in treated patients, neither cardiovascular risk nor mortality was increased
cards.summary: Huang 2017: white coat hypertension raised cardiovascular risk only in untreated cohorts (38% relative increase) — in treated patients, neither cardiovascular risk nor mortality was increased
cards.people: Meta-analysis of prospective cohorts: 23 cohorts (20,445 individuals) for cardiovascular risk in untreated patients, 11 cohorts (8,656) in treated patients, and 12 cohorts (21,336) in mixed populations.
cards.result: In untreated cohorts, white coat hypertension was associated with a 38% relative increase in cardiovascular disease risk and a 20% relative increase in total mortality versus normotension. In the mixed population the increases were 19% (cardiovascular disease) and 50% (total mortality). In treated patients, neither cardiovascular risk nor total mortality was increased. Meta-regression found neither clinic nor out-of-office blood pressure differences explained the cardiovascular risk. The authors conclude untreated white coat hypertension carries long-term risk and warrants close follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The treated/untreated split is observational — treated white coat patients differ from untreated ones in why they were treated — so 'treatment removes the risk' is a hypothesis this design cannot confirm.
cards.source: Huang Y et al. White-coat hypertension is a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases and total mortality. Journal of Hypertension. 2017. PMID: 28253216. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Grezzana 2017: office blood pressure agreed poorly with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in 569 primary-care patients (accuracy 54.8%, specificity 31.9%) — monitoring reclassifies a large share of suspected cases
cards.summary: Grezzana 2017: office blood pressure agreed poorly with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in 569 primary-care patients (accuracy 54.8%, specificity 31.9%) — monitoring reclassifies a large share of suspected cases
cards.people: Cross-sectional study of 569 hypertensive patients in primary health care whose blood pressure was measured conventionally by their physicians and then by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, independently; agreement assessed against European guideline thresholds (and, secondarily, stricter thresholds).
cards.result: Conventional measurement had 54.8% accuracy (95% CI 51–58%) against ambulatory monitoring, with 85% sensitivity and 31.9% specificity (kappa 0.155). With stricter ambulatory thresholds, accuracy fell to 45% (sensitivity 86.7%, specificity 29%, kappa 0.103). The authors note that reclassification by ambulatory monitoring can lead to different medical decisions in primary care. No patient outcomes were measured — printed plainly here.
cards.watchOut: Low specificity of office measurement is partly built into the comparison (ambulatory thresholds define the truth here): the study proves the two methods disagree and decisions change, not that ambulatory-led decisions are better.
cards.source: Grezzana GB et al. Impact of Different Normality Thresholds for 24-hour ABPM at the Primary Health Care Level. Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia. 2017. PMID: 28099585. cards.headline: Synthesis: ambulatory monitoring reclassifies suspected white coat hypertension and the reclassified groups differ in prognosis — but no trial shows monitoring itself changes outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: ambulatory monitoring reclassifies suspected white coat hypertension and the reclassified groups differ in prognosis — but no trial shows monitoring itself changes outcomes
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prognostic meta-analyses (27 studies / 64,273 participants; and 20,445 untreated-cohort individuals within 23 cohorts) and one diagnostic-agreement study (569 patients). All observational; no randomised trial of monitoring-guided management was found in the records fetched this session.
cards.result: Reclassification: office measurement accuracy 54.8% versus ambulatory monitoring (Grezzana 2017). Prognosis after classification: untreated white coat hypertension HR 1.36 for cardiovascular events and 2.09 for cardiovascular mortality versus normotension (Cohen 2019); 38% relative cardiovascular increase in untreated cohorts, no increase in treated patients (Huang 2017). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for outcome change.
cards.watchOut: The shelf answers a management question with prognostic evidence because that is all that exists: clinicians should not read 'reclassifies risk accurately' as 'monitoring saves lives' — that trial has not been done.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cohen JB et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31181575); Huang Y et al. Journal of Hypertension. 2017 (PMID: 28253216); Grezzana GB et al. Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia. 2017 (PMID: 28099585).
