shelves.title: Empagliflozin in chronic HFmrEF: the mildly-reduced subgroup benefits like the preserved group — pooled HFmrEF hazard ratio 0.77 for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation, driven by fewer hospitalisations
shelves.question: Does empagliflozin improve outcomes in heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Cause of Death · Prognosis · Risk Factors · Stroke Volume · Heart Failure · Diabetes Mellitus
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1574 covers empagliflozin started in hospital for acute heart failure (the EMPULSE question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — chronic heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF, ejection fraction 41–49%). The empagliflozin trial that enrolled this population, EMPEROR-Preserved, is homed on its own shelf and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports that separate the HFmrEF slice. A meta-analysis separating the ejection-fraction bands found the HFmrEF subgroup (n = 4,555) benefited at least as much as the preserved group (hazard ratio 0.77 for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation; Banerjee 2023). The prespecified five-trial Lancet meta-analysis found the composite benefit in the mildly-reduced/preserved trials (hazard ratio 0.80 among 12,251 participants) was consistent across ejection-fraction subgroups, with the effect carried mainly by fewer heart failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.74) rather than cardiovascular death (0.88, confidence interval touching 1.00) (Vaduganathan 2022). Within EMPEROR-Preserved itself, empagliflozin's outcome benefit was consistent across baseline health-status tertiles and health status improved modestly (Butler 2022). The honest limits: no trial has randomised HFmrEF patients alone, the mortality component is not separately significant, and the empagliflozin-specific evidence is one trial programme. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — empagliflozin improves the composite outcome in chronic HFmrEF, driven by fewer heart failure hospitalisations; capped at POSSIBLE because the empagliflozin evidence is a single trial programme read through its mildly-reduced subgroup.

cards.headline: Banerjee 2023: separating the ejection-fraction bands, SGLT2 inhibitors in HFmrEF (n = 4,555) cut cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.77 — the mildly-reduced slice benefits at least as much as the preserved slice
cards.summary: Banerjee 2023: separating the ejection-fraction bands, SGLT2 inhibitors in HFmrEF (n = 4,555) cut cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.77 — the mildly-reduced slice benefits at least as much as the preserved slice
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials or post-hoc trial analyses in heart failure with preserved (≥50%) or mildly reduced (41–49%) ejection fraction, regardless of diabetes; six trials pooling 15,769 patients with HFmrEF/HFpEF, of which the HFmrEF subgroup was 4,555 patients and the HFpEF subgroup 8,891.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with improved cardiovascular death/hospitalisation outcomes in HFmrEF/HFpEF combined (pooled hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.74–0.86, P < 0.001, I² = 0%). Analysed separately, the benefit remained significant in HFmrEF (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.67–0.89, P < 0.001) and in HFpEF (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.71–0.87), and in patients without baseline diabetes (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.70–0.91). A sensitivity analysis of the two large trials found only a trend toward fewer cardiovascular deaths (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.79–1.02, P = 0.08) — the benefit is carried by hospitalisations, not by a proven mortality reduction.
cards.watchOut: This is a class-level pooling (empagliflozin and dapagliflozin trials together) read at subgroup level: the HFmrEF hazard ratio is a subgroup estimate from trials that randomised the wider >40% ejection-fraction population, not a trial of HFmrEF patients alone.
cards.source: Banerjee M et al. SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes in heart failure with mildly reduced and preserved ejection fraction: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Indian Heart Journal. 2023. PMID: 36914068. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vaduganathan 2022: in the two mildly-reduced/preserved trials (12,251 participants) SGLT2 inhibitors reduced cardiovascular death or first heart failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 0.80), consistently across ejection-fraction subgroups
cards.summary: Vaduganathan 2022: in the two mildly-reduced/preserved trials (12,251 participants) SGLT2 inhibitors reduced cardiovascular death or first heart failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 0.80), consistently across ejection-fraction subgroups
cards.type: Prespecified meta-analysis of five randomised trials (Vaduganathan 2022)
cards.people: Prespecified fixed-effects meta-analysis with harmonised endpoint definitions: the two trials in heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, 12,251 participants), then all five heart failure trials including reduced-ejection-fraction and worsening-heart-failure trials (21,947 participants).
cards.result: In the mildly-reduced/preserved trials, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.73–0.87), with reductions in both components: cardiovascular death (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.00) and first heart failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.67–0.83). Across all five trials the composite hazard ratio was 0.77 (0.72–0.82) and all-cause mortality 0.92 (0.86–0.99). Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction — the mildly-reduced band was not an exception.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mildly-reduced/preserved estimate mixes HFmrEF with HFpEF and mixes two drugs; it establishes that benefit does not fade in the mildly-reduced band, but the empagliflozin-specific HFmrEF number comes from the subgroup pooling on the Banerjee card.
cards.source: Vaduganathan M et al. SGLT-2 inhibitors in patients with heart failure: a comprehensive meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 36041474. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Butler 2022: within EMPEROR-Preserved (ejection fraction >40%, including the HFmrEF band), empagliflozin's outcome benefit was consistent across baseline health-status tertiles and quality of life improved modestly by 12 weeks and sustained to 52 weeks
cards.summary: Butler 2022: within EMPEROR-Preserved (ejection fraction >40%, including the HFmrEF band), empagliflozin's outcome benefit was consistent across baseline health-status tertiles and quality of life improved modestly by 12 weeks and sustained to 52 weeks
cards.people: Patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (trial entry ejection fraction >40%, so including mildly reduced) in the EMPEROR-Preserved randomised trial of empagliflozin versus placebo; health status measured with the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) at baseline and 12, 32 and 52 weeks, analysed by baseline KCCQ Clinical Summary Score tertiles.
cards.result: The effect of empagliflozin on cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation was consistent across baseline KCCQ tertiles (hazard ratios 0.83 [95% CI 0.69–1.00], 0.70 [0.55–0.88] and 0.82 [0.62–1.08]; P for trend = 0.77), with similar results for total heart failure hospitalisations. Empagliflozin improved KCCQ Clinical Summary Score versus placebo by +1.03, +1.24 and +1.50 points at 12, 32 and 52 weeks (P < 0.01); at 12 weeks the odds of a ≥5-point improvement were higher with empagliflozin (odds ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.10–1.37) and the odds of ≥5-point deterioration lower (odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.75–0.97).
cards.watchOut: A secondary health-status analysis of the parent trial, not an HFmrEF-only report: it shows the programme's benefit and symptom gains extend across the enrolled >40% population that contains the HFmrEF band; the KCCQ gains (about 1–1.5 points on average) are modest.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in chronic HFmrEF, empagliflozin improves the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation — the separated HFmrEF pooling gives hazard ratio 0.77 — with the gain carried by fewer hospitalisations and a modest quality-of-life improvement
cards.summary: Synthesis: in chronic HFmrEF, empagliflozin improves the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation — the separated HFmrEF pooling gives hazard ratio 0.77 — with the gain carried by fewer hospitalisations and a modest quality-of-life improvement
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis separating HFmrEF (subgroup n = 4,555 within 15,769 pooled patients), one prespecified five-trial meta-analysis (12,251 participants in the mildly-reduced/preserved trials; 21,947 overall), and one health-status analysis of the EMPEROR-Preserved trial population (ejection fraction >40%). Total carded participants exceed 15,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is subgroup-level, single-programme empagliflozin evidence, printed here.
cards.result: HFmrEF-specific pooling: hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.67–0.89) for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation (Banerjee 2023). Mildly-reduced/preserved trials combined: hazard ratio 0.80 (0.73–0.87), hospitalisation component 0.74 (0.67–0.83), cardiovascular death 0.88 (0.77–1.00) (Vaduganathan 2022). Health status improved modestly and outcome benefit was consistent across health-status tertiles in EMPEROR-Preserved (Butler 2022). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme for empagliflozin, read through its mildly-reduced subgroup and concordant class pooling.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised HFmrEF patients alone, and no carded record shows a significant mortality reduction within the HFmrEF band itself; readers needing the parent trial's own numbers should follow the cross-point to the EMPEROR-Preserved home shelf, and readers with hospitalised acute heart failure to live shelf #1574.
cards.source: Synthesis of Banerjee M et al. Indian Heart Journal. 2023 (PMID: 36914068); Vaduganathan M et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 36041474); Butler J et al. Circulation. 2022 (PMID: 34779658).

shelves.title: CRT in HFrEF with LBBB: survival and hospitalisation benefit is concentrated in left bundle branch block — composite events cut by about a third (relative risk 0.64), and by 44% at QRS ≥150 ms — with no benefit in non-LBBB morphologies
shelves.question: Does cardiac resynchronization therapy improve survival in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left bundle branch block?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Electrocardiography · Heart Failure · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #274 covers cardiac resynchronization therapy in wide QRS generally; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the left bundle branch block (LBBB) population specifically, where the wide-QRS average conceals a morphology split. Trial-level meta-analysis found CRT reduced composite adverse clinical events in LBBB (relative risk 0.64) but made no difference in non-LBBB conduction abnormalities (relative risk 0.97, the treatment made no difference), with a highly significant difference between morphologies (Sipahi 2012). Patient-level pooling of eight pivotal trials (6,264 patients; 4,549 with LBBB) found the same pattern for heart failure hospitalisation or death — hazard ratio 0.56 in LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, no significant association at QRS <150 ms or in right bundle branch block — with similar relationships for all-cause death alone (Friedman 2023). Long-term MADIT-CRT follow-up in LBBB patients showed an approximately 60% relative reduction in heart failure events in both US and European cohorts and a significant 38% relative mortality reduction in the US cohort (Biton 2015), and a dedicated non-LBBB meta-analysis confirms the null on the other side of the split (Cunnington 2015). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — CRT improves survival-relevant outcomes in HFrEF with LBBB, most clearly at QRS ≥150 ms; the LBBB slice, not wide QRS alone, is where the benefit lives.

cards.headline: Sipahi 2012: across 4 randomised trials (5,356 patients), CRT cut composite adverse clinical events in LBBB (relative risk 0.64) but made no difference in non-LBBB wide QRS (relative risk 0.97) — the morphology difference was highly significant
cards.summary: Sipahi 2012: across 4 randomised trials (5,356 patients), CRT cut composite adverse clinical events in LBBB (relative risk 0.64) but made no difference in non-LBBB wide QRS (relative risk 0.97) — the morphology difference was highly significant
cards.people: Patients with systolic heart failure and a wide QRS in the four randomised CRT trials that reported adverse clinical events (all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalisations) by baseline QRS morphology; 5,356 patients in total, split into LBBB and non-LBBB (right bundle branch block and nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay) groups.
cards.result: In patients with LBBB at baseline, CRT produced a highly significant reduction in composite adverse clinical events (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.77, P = .00001). In non-LBBB patients there was no benefit (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.82–1.15, P = .75 — the treatment made no difference), examined separately for right bundle branch block (0.91, 0.69–1.20) and intraventricular conduction delay (1.19, 0.87–1.63). The difference in CRT effect between LBBB and non-LBBB patients was highly statistically significant (P = .0001). All relative risks are relative measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: A composite of mortality and heart failure hospitalisation events reported by morphology subgroup within trials — morphology was not itself randomised, so this is strong subgroup evidence rather than a dedicated LBBB trial.
cards.source: Sipahi I et al. Effect of QRS morphology on clinical event reduction with cardiac resynchronization therapy: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. American Heart Journal. 2012. PMID: 22305845. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy · Electrocardiography · Heart Failure · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Friedman 2023: pooling individual data from 8 pivotal CRT trials (6,264 patients; 4,549 with LBBB), CRT lowered heart failure hospitalisation or death in LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms (hazard ratio 0.56) — with similar relationships for all-cause death alone
cards.summary: Friedman 2023: pooling individual data from 8 pivotal CRT trials (6,264 patients; 4,549 with LBBB), CRT lowered heart failure hospitalisation or death in LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms (hazard ratio 0.56) — with similar relationships for all-cause death alone
cards.people: Individual patient data from eight pivotal CRT randomised trials (MIRACLE, MIRACLE-ICD, MIRACLE-ICD II, REVERSE, RAFT, BLOCK-HF, COMPANION and MADIT-CRT): 6,264 patients, median age 66 years, 25% women, 61% receiving CRT with or without a defibrillator; QRS morphology groups were LBBB (n = 4,549), right bundle branch block (n = 691) and intraventricular conduction delay (n = 1,024).
cards.result: CRT was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalisation or death overall (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% credible interval 0.65–0.84), concentrated in patients with QRS ≥150 ms and either LBBB (hazard ratio 0.56, 0.48–0.66) or intraventricular conduction delay (0.59, 0.39–0.89), but not right bundle branch block (0.97, 0.68–1.34; P for interaction < 0.001). No significant association was observed when QRS was <150 ms regardless of morphology. The record states that similar relationships were observed for the secondary endpoint of all-cause death.
cards.watchOut: Bayesian patient-level pooling across trials spanning two decades of background therapy; the survival relationship is reported qualitatively in the record ('similar relationships') without a separate LBBB mortality hazard ratio printed, so this shelf does not invent one.
cards.source: Friedman DJ et al. Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Improves Outcomes in Patients With Intraventricular Conduction Delay But Not Right Bundle Branch Block: A Patient-Level Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Circulation. 2023. PMID: 36700426. Registry ID: NCT00271154, NCT00251251, NCT00267098, NCT00180271 (as listed in the record). patient-level meta-analysis of randomised trials (friedman 2023) individual patient data from eight pivotal crt randomised trials (miracle, miracle-icd, miracle-icd ii, reverse, raft, block-hf, companion and madit-crt): 6,264 patients, median age 66 years, 25% women, 61% receiving crt with or without a defibrillator; qrs morphology groups were lbbb (n = 4,549), right bundle branch block (n = 691) and intraventricular conduction delay (n = 1,024). crt was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalisation or death overall (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% credible interval 0.65–0.84), concentrated in patients with qrs ≥150 ms and either lbbb (hazard ratio 0.56, 0.48–0.66) or intraventricular conduction delay (0.59, 0.39–0.89), but not right bundle branch block (0.97, 0.68–1.34; p for interaction < 0.001). no significant association was observed when qrs was <150 ms regardless of morphology. the record states that similar relationships were observed for the secondary endpoint of all-cause death. bayesian patient-level pooling across trials spanning two decades of background therapy; the survival relationship is reported qualitatively in the record ('similar relationships') without a separate lbbb mortality hazard ratio printed, so this shelf does not invent one. friedman dj et al. cardiac resynchronization therapy improves outcomes in patients with intraventricular conduction delay but not right bundle branch block: a patient-level meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. circulation. 2023. pmid: 36700426. registry id: nct00271154, nct00251251, nct00267098, nct00180271 (as listed in the record). mesh: humans · female · aged · male · bundle-branch block · cardiac resynchronization therapy · bayes theorem · randomized controlled trials as topic · defibrillators, implantable · heart failure · treatment outcome · electrocardiography

cards.headline: Biton 2015: in MADIT-CRT patients with LBBB, CRT-D cut heart failure events by about 60% in both US (n = 871) and European (n = 392) cohorts, with a significant 38% relative mortality reduction in the US cohort over long-term follow-up
cards.summary: Biton 2015: in MADIT-CRT patients with LBBB, CRT-D cut heart failure events by about 60% in both US (n = 871) and European (n = 392) cohorts, with a significant 38% relative mortality reduction in the US cohort over long-term follow-up
cards.type: Long-term randomised trial follow-up in LBBB (Biton 2015, MADIT-CRT)
cards.people: Patients with mild heart failure and an LBBB electrocardiogram pattern in the MADIT-CRT randomised trial of cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillator (CRT-D) versus defibrillator alone, enrolled in the United States (n = 871) and Europe (n = 392), followed long term for clinical and echocardiographic outcomes.
cards.result: CRT-D was associated with similar approximately 60% relative reductions in the risk of heart failure events in US and European LBBB patients after adjustment (P < 0.001 for both). US patients had a significant long-term mortality reduction of 38% (P = 0.02); in European patients the survival benefit was not statistically significant (hazard ratio 0.73, P = 0.18). Reverse remodelling at 1 year was associated with significantly better clinical outcomes in both groups. Reductions are relative measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: A geographic subgroup analysis of one trial in mild heart failure: the mortality reduction reached significance in the US cohort only, and European patients had more advanced disease at baseline — the consistent finding across cohorts is the heart-failure-event reduction.
cards.source: Biton Y et al. Long-term outcome with cardiac resynchronization therapy in mild heart failure patients with left bundle branch block from US and Europe MADIT-CRT. cards.people: Patients in five randomised CRT trials reporting outcomes by QRS morphology: 6,523 participants in total, of whom 1,766 had non-LBBB QRS morphology (right bundle branch block or intraventricular conduction delay).

cards.headline: Synthesis: CRT's survival-relevant benefit in HFrEF is an LBBB phenomenon — composite events relative risk 0.64 in LBBB versus 0.97–0.99 in non-LBBB, strongest at QRS ≥150 ms (hazard ratio 0.56), with long-term mortality reduction shown in the MADIT-CRT LBBB cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: CRT's survival-relevant benefit in HFrEF is an LBBB phenomenon — composite events relative risk 0.64 in LBBB versus 0.97–0.99 in non-LBBB, strongest at QRS ≥150 ms (hazard ratio 0.56), with long-term mortality reduction shown in the MADIT-CRT LBBB cohort
cards.people: The carded evidence: a trial-level morphology meta-analysis (4 trials, 5,356 patients), a patient-level meta-analysis (8 trials, 6,264 patients, 4,549 with LBBB), long-term MADIT-CRT follow-up restricted to LBBB (1,263 patients), and a non-LBBB contrast meta-analysis (5 trials, 6,523 patients). Participants overlap across the meta-analyses by design; the unique randomised base is the pivotal CRT trial programme, well over 30 patients, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: LBBB: composite events relative risk 0.64 (Sipahi 2012); heart failure hospitalisation or death hazard ratio 0.56 at QRS ≥150 ms with similar relationships for all-cause death (Friedman 2023); heart failure events reduced by about 60% relatively in both MADIT-CRT LBBB cohorts, mortality by 38% relatively in the US cohort (Biton 2015). Non-LBBB: hazard ratio 0.99, the treatment made no difference (Cunnington 2015). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised-trial evidence at trial level and patient level, specific to the LBBB slice.
cards.watchOut: Morphology subgroups were not randomised, and the cleanest mortality-specific LBBB number comes from one trial's geographic cohort; the claim is strongest for the composite of death or heart failure hospitalisation at QRS ≥150 ms.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sipahi I et al. American Heart Journal. 2012 (PMID: 22305845); Friedman DJ et al. Circulation. 2023 (PMID: 36700426); Biton Y et al. Heart Failure Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26216033); Cunnington C et al. Heart. 2015 (PMID: 25678498).

shelves.title: ICD in nonischemic cardiomyopathy — SPLIT over time: older trials and their meta-analysis show lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.75), but DANISH's 13-year follow-up shows no all-cause mortality reduction (0.96) while sudden-death protection persists (0.54)
shelves.question: Does an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator reduce mortality in nonischemic cardiomyopathy?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Arrhythmias, Cardiac · Cardiomyopathy, Dilated · Combined Modality Therapy · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Defibrillators, Implantable · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stroke Volume · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #90 is the broader prophylactic ICD shelf; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the nonischemic population specifically. The slice's largest trial, DANISH, is homed on the broader shelf and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports, including DANISH's own extended follow-up. The older randomised evidence favours the ICD: DEFINITE, in nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, cut sudden arrhythmic death sharply (hazard ratio 0.20) with a non-significant all-cause mortality trend (0.65) (Kadish 2004), and pooling the four pre-DANISH trials (1,874 patients) gave a significant all-cause mortality reduction (hazard ratio 0.75) (Al-Khatib 2017). Against that, DANISH's extended follow-up to a median 13.2 years found all-cause mortality essentially identical (52.9% versus 53.4%; hazard ratio 0.96 — the treatment made no difference to overall survival) while sudden cardiovascular death remained halved (hazard ratio 0.54), with the sudden-death benefit confined to patients aged 70 or younger (Butt 2025). The split is real and is named in the stamp: as background therapy improved and follow-up lengthened, preventing arrhythmic death stopped translating into longer overall survival in this population. PROPOSED SPLIT (older randomised evidence: benefit; DANISH long-term: no all-cause benefit, sudden-death benefit persists).

cards.headline: Kadish 2004 (DEFINITE): in 458 patients with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, an ICD cut sudden arrhythmic death (3 versus 14 deaths; hazard ratio 0.20) but the all-cause mortality reduction was not significant (28 versus 40 deaths; hazard ratio 0.65, P = 0.08)
cards.summary: Kadish 2004 (DEFINITE): in 458 patients with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, an ICD cut sudden arrhythmic death (3 versus 14 deaths; hazard ratio 0.20) but the all-cause mortality reduction was not significant (28 versus 40 deaths; hazard ratio 0.65, P = 0.08)
cards.people: 458 patients with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, left ventricular ejection fraction under 36%, and premature ventricular complexes or nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, randomised to standard medical therapy (n = 229) or standard therapy plus a single-chamber ICD (n = 229); mean ejection fraction 21%, with 86% on ACE inhibitors and 85% on beta-blockers; mean follow-up 29 months.
cards.result: There were 68 deaths: 28 in the ICD group versus 40 in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.40–1.06, P = 0.08 — not significant). Two-year mortality was 7.9% with an ICD versus 14.1% with standard therapy. Sudden deaths from arrhythmia were 3 with an ICD versus 14 without (hazard ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.06–0.71, P = 0.006). The trial establishes sudden-death prevention; its all-cause mortality result is a trend, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: A 2004 trial from before contemporary quadruple heart-failure therapy, stopped with fewer deaths than planned; its non-significant all-cause result should not be quoted as proof of a survival benefit.
cards.source: Kadish A et al. Prophylactic defibrillator implantation in patients with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15152060. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Al-Khatib 2017: pooling the four pre-DANISH randomised trials in nonischemic cardiomyopathy (1,874 patients), primary-prevention ICDs significantly reduced all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.75)
cards.summary: Al-Khatib 2017: pooling the four pre-DANISH randomised trials in nonischemic cardiomyopathy (1,874 patients), primary-prevention ICDs significantly reduced all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.75)
cards.people: Four randomised clinical trials meeting prespecified criteria (ICD versus medical therapy, at least 100 patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy, all-cause mortality reported over at least 12 months), totalling 1,874 unique patients — 937 ICD and 937 control.
cards.result: Pooling the four trials showed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality with an ICD (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.93, P = .008; P = .87 for heterogeneity). The authors conclude primary-prevention ICDs reduce all-cause mortality in nonischemic cardiomyopathy and support guideline recommendations — a conclusion drawn before DANISH's long-term data, which is the tension this shelf exists to display.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are the older, smaller trials (including DEFINITE on the card above); the meta-analysis predates DANISH's extended follow-up and its pooled estimate should not be read as the last word.
cards.source: Al-Khatib SM et al. Primary Prevention Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators in Patients With Nonischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Meta-analysis. JAMA Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28355432. cards.headline: Butt 2025 (DANISH extended follow-up, median 13.2 years): in 1,116 patients with nonischemic HFrEF, an ICD made no difference to all-cause death (52.9% versus 53.4%; hazard ratio 0.96) while sudden cardiovascular death stayed halved (hazard ratio 0.54), benefiting patients aged 70 or younger
cards.summary: Butt 2025 (DANISH extended follow-up, median 13.2 years): in 1,116 patients with nonischemic HFrEF, an ICD made no difference to all-cause death (52.9% versus 53.4%; hazard ratio 0.96) while sudden cardiovascular death stayed halved (hazard ratio 0.54), benefiting patients aged 70 or younger
cards.people: 1,116 patients with nonischemic systolic heart failure, ejection fraction ≤35%, NYHA class II–III (IV if resynchronization was planned) and elevated natriuretic peptides, randomised in the DANISH trial to primary-prevention ICD or usual care and followed until death or January 31, 2024 (median 13.2 years).
cards.result: 294 patients (52.9%) in the ICD group and 299 (53.4%) in the control group died: ICD implantation did not significantly reduce long-term all-cause death (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.82–1.13 — the treatment made no difference to overall survival). Sudden cardiovascular death was reduced (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.36–0.80), but age modified that effect: benefit at age ≤70 years (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.62) and none over 70 (1.27, 0.56–2.89; P for interaction = 0.01). Effects were generally consistent across other subgroups, including baseline resynchronization therapy.
cards.watchOut: Extended follow-up of a trial whose primary report is homed on live shelf #90 and is not re-carded here; over 13 years, competing non-arrhythmic deaths dominate, which is the proposed explanation for sudden-death protection without overall survival gain.
cards.source: Butt JH et al. Long-Term Effect of ICDs in Nonischemic Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction: Extended Follow-Up Analysis of DANISH. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2025. PMID: 41123523. Registry ID: NCT00542945 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis — SPLIT: sudden-death prevention is consistent (hazard ratios 0.20–0.54 across eras), but all-cause mortality benefit appears in the older pooled trials (0.75) and disappears in DANISH's 13-year follow-up (0.96)
cards.summary: Synthesis — SPLIT: sudden-death prevention is consistent (hazard ratios 0.20–0.54 across eras), but all-cause mortality benefit appears in the older pooled trials (0.75) and disappears in DANISH's 13-year follow-up (0.96)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial (DEFINITE, 458 patients), one meta-analysis of four randomised trials (1,874 patients, overlapping DEFINITE by design), and the extended follow-up of the DANISH randomised trial (1,116 patients). Total unique randomised patients across the carded reports exceed 3,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Sudden arrhythmic death: hazard ratio 0.20 (DEFINITE) and 0.54 for sudden cardiovascular death at 13.2 years (DANISH extended). All-cause mortality: hazard ratio 0.65 non-significant (DEFINITE), 0.75 significant in the pre-DANISH pooling, and 0.96 — no difference — in DANISH long-term follow-up, where deaths were 52.9% versus 53.4%. PROPOSED SPLIT (older randomised evidence: benefit on all-cause mortality; DANISH long-term follow-up: no all-cause mortality benefit, sudden-death benefit persists, concentrated at age ≤70).

shelves.title: Early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in acute heart failure: starting before or just after discharge is associated with fewer deaths (odds ratio 0.71) and fewer heart failure rehospitalisations (0.73) across 7 randomised trials — safety event rates were too low to judge
shelves.question: Does early initiation of an SGLT2 inhibitor during acute heart failure improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Heart Failure · Acute Disease · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome · Time Factors · Patient Readmission · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #70 covers SGLT2 inhibitors in established (chronic) heart failure, and live shelf #1574 covers empagliflozin started in hospitalised acute heart failure; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the timing question itself: starting an SGLT2 inhibitor early, during the acute admission or immediately after it, across agents. The two big acute-setting trials' primary reports are homed on those shelves and are not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of early initiation (before or within 3 days after discharge) across 7 randomised trials and 2,320 patients found lower all-cause death (odds ratio 0.71) and fewer heart failure rehospitalisations (odds ratio 0.73), with consistent results when initiation was before discharge — but safety outcomes could not be usefully determined because events were few (Cherbi 2025). The earliest pilot, EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF, found no difference on its primary symptom and diuretic outcomes (the treatment made no difference on dyspnoea score, diuretic response, NT-proBNP or length of stay) yet fewer combined worsening-heart-failure events at 60 days (Damman 2020). Programme secondary reports point the same way: empagliflozin improved symptoms and quality of life from day 15 in EMPULSE (Kosiborod 2022), and sotagliflozin increased days alive and out of hospital in SOLOIST-WHF, driven by fewer days dead (Szarek 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — early initiation improves outcomes; the stamp is capped because the pooled timing evidence leans on small trials and its safety side is unresolved.

cards.headline: Cherbi 2025: across 7 randomised trials (2,320 patients), early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in acute heart failure reduced all-cause death (odds ratio 0.71) and heart failure rehospitalisations (odds ratio 0.73) — but safety outcomes could not be usefully determined
cards.summary: Cherbi 2025: across 7 randomised trials (2,320 patients), early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in acute heart failure reduced all-cause death (odds ratio 0.71) and heart failure rehospitalisations (odds ratio 0.73) — but safety outcomes could not be usefully determined
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cherbi 2025)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in acute heart failure, where early meant initiation before or shortly after discharge (within 3 days); seven trials enrolling 2,320 patients in total, identified from PubMed, Embase and Cochrane to May 31, 2024.
cards.result: Early SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause death (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.92) and heart failure rehospitalisations (odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.94), persisting after adjustment for follow-up duration; initiation before discharge gave consistent efficacy results. Safety outcomes (acute kidney injury, ketoacidosis, urinary tract infection, hypotension, hypoglycaemia) could not be usefully determined because event rates were low and confidence intervals wide, and the effect of diabetes status remains basically unknown. Odds ratios are relative measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are mostly small (the largest acute-setting programmes are homed on shelves #70 and #1574 and contribute through their own reports), and a pooled odds ratio over short, varied follow-up is not the same as one large timing trial.
cards.source: Cherbi M et al. Early Initiation of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors in Acute Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2025. PMID: 40194974. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Damman 2020 (EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF, n = 80): empagliflozin started in acute decompensated heart failure made no difference to dyspnoea, diuretic response, NT-proBNP or length of stay — but the combined endpoint of worsening heart failure, rehospitalisation or death at 60 days was lower (10% versus 33%)
cards.summary: Damman 2020 (EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF, n = 80): empagliflozin started in acute decompensated heart failure made no difference to dyspnoea, diuretic response, NT-proBNP or length of stay — but the combined endpoint of worsening heart failure, rehospitalisation or death at 60 days was lower (10% versus 33%)
cards.people: 80 patients with acute decompensated heart failure, with and without diabetes (mean age 76 years, 33% women, 47% de novo heart failure, median NT-proBNP 5,236 pg/mL), randomised double-blind to empagliflozin 10 mg/day or placebo for 30 days. Small single-pilot N printed here on the face.
cards.result: No difference was observed in the primary outcomes — visual analogue scale dyspnoea score, diuretic response, change in NT-proBNP, or length of stay (the treatment made no difference on these measures). Empagliflozin reduced a combined endpoint of in-hospital worsening heart failure, rehospitalisation for heart failure or death at 60 days (4 patients [10%] versus 13 [33%]; P = 0.014), and urinary output to day 4 was greater (difference 3,449 mL, 95% CI 578–6,321; P < 0.01). Empagliflozin was safe and well tolerated, with no adverse effects on blood pressure or renal function.
cards.watchOut: An 80-patient pilot: the favourable combined endpoint is a secondary finding in a trial whose four primary outcomes were all null, and it should be read as hypothesis-supporting, not as proof.
cards.source: Damman K et al. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre pilot study on the effects of empagliflozin on clinical outcomes in patients with acute decompensated heart failure (EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF). European Journal of Heart Failure. 2020. PMID: 31912605. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kosiborod 2022 (EMPULSE): empagliflozin started once stabilised in hospital improved symptoms, physical limitations and quality of life by day 15 and through day 90 (KCCQ total symptom score +4.45 points versus placebo), with clinical benefit across all baseline symptom tertiles
cards.summary: Kosiborod 2022 (EMPULSE): empagliflozin started once stabilised in hospital improved symptoms, physical limitations and quality of life by day 15 and through day 90 (KCCQ total symptom score +4.45 points versus placebo), with clinical benefit across all baseline symptom tertiles
cards.people: 530 patients hospitalised for acute heart failure and stabilised, randomised to empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo for 90 days (265 per arm); baseline KCCQ total symptom score was low overall (mean 40.8 points), and effects were examined across baseline symptom tertiles.
cards.result: Empagliflozin-treated patients experienced greater clinical benefit (the hierarchical composite of death, heart failure events and KCCQ change) across the range of baseline symptoms, with win ratios of 1.49, 1.37 and 1.48 from lowest to highest tertile (P for interaction = 0.94). At 90 days, placebo-adjusted improvements favoured empagliflozin for KCCQ total symptom score (+4.45 points, 95% CI 0.32–8.59, P = 0.03), physical limitations (+4.80, P = 0.05), quality of life (+4.66, P = 0.04), clinical summary (+4.85, P = 0.02) and overall summary (+4.40, P = 0.03), with benefits seen as early as 15 days.
cards.watchOut: A health-status report of the EMPULSE programme whose primary report is homed on live shelf #1574; it answers how patients feel and function with early initiation, not the mortality question on its own.
cards.source: Kosiborod MN et al. Effects of Empagliflozin on Symptoms, Physical Limitations, and Quality of Life in Patients Hospitalized for Acute Heart Failure: Results From the EMPULSE Trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 35377706. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides · Heart Failure · Humans · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Szarek 2021 (SOLOIST-WHF): sotagliflozin started around discharge after worsening heart failure increased days alive and out of hospital (rate ratio 1.03), driven by fewer days dead (rate ratio 0.71) rather than fewer days in hospital
cards.summary: Szarek 2021 (SOLOIST-WHF): sotagliflozin started around discharge after worsening heart failure increased days alive and out of hospital (rate ratio 1.03), driven by fewer days dead (rate ratio 0.71) rather than fewer days in hospital
cards.people: 1,222 patients with type 2 diabetes and reduced or preserved ejection fraction recently hospitalised for worsening heart failure, randomised double-blind to sotagliflozin 200 mg daily (titratable to 400 mg) or placebo across 306 sites in 32 countries.
cards.result: Similar proportions were hospitalised at least once (38.5% sotagliflozin versus 41.4% placebo), but fewer sotagliflozin patients were hospitalised more than once (16.3% versus 22.1%), and deaths were 64 versus 76. Days alive and out of hospital were 3% higher with sotagliflozin (rate ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.00–1.06, P = 0.027) — 91.8 versus 88.9 such days per 100 days of follow-up — driven by a reduction in days dead (rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.99) rather than days hospitalised (1.9 versus 2.2 days).
cards.watchOut: A prespecified secondary analysis of a trial in patients with type 2 diabetes only, whose primary report is homed with the established-heart-failure evidence; the days-alive-out-of-hospital gain is real but small in absolute terms (2.9 days per 100).
cards.source: Szarek M et al. Effect of Sotagliflozin on Total Hospitalizations in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Worsening Heart Failure: A Randomized Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34152828. Registry ID: NCT03521934. cards.headline: Synthesis: early initiation — in hospital or within days of discharge — reduces death (odds ratio 0.71) and heart failure rehospitalisation (0.73) in pooled randomised data, with symptom gains visible by day 15; the pilot's primary outcomes were null and pooled safety remains undetermined
cards.summary: Synthesis: early initiation — in hospital or within days of discharge — reduces death (odds ratio 0.71) and heart failure rehospitalisation (0.73) in pooled randomised data, with symptom gains visible by day 15; the pilot's primary outcomes were null and pooled safety remains undetermined
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 7 early-initiation randomised trials (2,320 patients), one 80-patient pilot trial (N printed on its card), and secondary reports of the two large acute-setting programmes (530 and 1,222 patients; the programmes overlap the meta-analysis's trial set by design). Total carded participants exceed 2,300 unique patients, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Death odds ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.55–0.92) and rehospitalisation odds ratio 0.73 (0.57–0.94) for early initiation (Cherbi 2025). Pilot primary outcomes null, combined clinical endpoint 10% versus 33% at 60 days (Damman 2020). Symptoms and quality of life improved from day 15 (Kosiborod 2022); days alive and out of hospital increased, driven by fewer deaths (Szarek 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped because safety outcomes in the pooled timing evidence could not be determined and the largest trials' primary reports are homed on shelves #70 and #1574.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial randomised timing itself (early versus deferred start) as its primary question; 'early' is inferred from trials that started treatment in the acute window versus placebo, pooled after the fact.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cherbi M et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2025 (PMID: 40194974); Damman K et al. shelves.title: Edoxaban versus warfarin in elderly AF: in patients aged 75 or older, major bleeding was lower with edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.83) with a larger absolute gain than in younger patients (−82 events per 10,000 patient-years; intracranial haemorrhage −73)
shelves.question: Does edoxaban reduce bleeding compared with warfarin in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Double-Blind Method · Embolism · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridines · Stroke · Thiazoles · Treatment Outcome · Warfarin
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2447 covers edoxaban versus a vitamin K antagonist only after transcatheter aortic valve implantation; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — general elderly patients with atrial fibrillation. The ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 primary report is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on its prespecified elderly analysis and on the very-elderly ELDERCARE-AF programme. In ENGAGE, bleeding rates on warfarin climbed steeply with age (major bleeding 1.8%, 3.3% and 4.8% across the <65, 65–74 and ≥75 groups), and in the ≥75 group (n = 8,474) edoxaban significantly reduced major bleeding versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83) while stroke prevention was similar (hazard ratio 0.83, not significant), with absolute gains favouring edoxaban of 82 fewer major bleeds and 73 fewer intracranial haemorrhages per 10,000 patient-years (Kato 2016). The very-elderly evidence answers a neighbouring question — in patients aged 80 or older judged unsuitable for standard anticoagulation, 15 mg edoxaban prevented stroke versus placebo without a significant major-bleeding increase (Okumura 2020), consistently across the 80–84, 85–89 and ≥90 strata (Kuroda 2022) — which bounds the bleeding concern at the oldest ages but does not itself compare against warfarin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — edoxaban bleeds less than warfarin in elderly AF; capped at POSSIBLE because the warfarin comparison rests on one trial programme.

cards.headline: Kato 2016: in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 patients aged ≥75 (n = 8,474), edoxaban reduced major bleeding versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83) with stroke prevention similar (0.83) — and the absolute bleeding gain (−82 events per 10,000 patient-years; intracranial haemorrhage −73) was largest in the elderly
cards.summary: Kato 2016: in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 patients aged ≥75 (n = 8,474), edoxaban reduced major bleeding versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83) with stroke prevention similar (0.83) — and the absolute bleeding gain (−82 events per 10,000 patient-years; intracranial haemorrhage −73) was largest in the elderly
cards.type: Prespecified age-subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Kato 2016, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48)
cards.people: 21,105 patients with atrial fibrillation in the ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 randomised trial of edoxaban versus warfarin, in prespecified age groups <65 (n = 5,497), 65–74 (n = 7,134) and ≥75 years (n = 8,474); older patients had lower body weight and creatinine clearance and correspondingly higher edoxaban dose-reduction rates (10%, 18% and 41%).
cards.result: On warfarin, stroke/systemic embolism rates rose with age (1.1%, 1.8%, 2.3%) as did major bleeding (1.8%, 3.3%, 4.8%; P for trend < 0.001 for both), with no interaction between age group and treatment for the primary efficacy or safety outcomes. In the elderly (≥75 years), stroke/systemic embolism was similar with edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.66–1.04) while major bleeding was significantly reduced (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.70–0.99). The absolute risk differences in major bleeding (−82 events/10,000 patient-years) and intracranial haemorrhage (−73 events/10,000 patient-years) both favoured edoxaban in older patients.
cards.watchOut: A prespecified subgroup analysis of one trial: the elderly hazard ratios are subgroup estimates, and the parent trial's primary report is homed elsewhere in the library and not re-carded here.
cards.source: Kato ET et al. Efficacy and Safety of Edoxaban in Elderly Patients With Atrial Fibrillation in the ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 Trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2016. PMID: 27207971. Registry ID: NCT00781391. prespecified age-subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (kato 2016, engage af-timi 48) 21,105 patients with atrial fibrillation in the engage af-timi 48 randomised trial of edoxaban versus warfarin, in prespecified age groups <65 (n = 5,497), 65–74 (n = 7,134) and ≥75 years (n = 8,474); older patients had lower body weight and creatinine clearance and correspondingly higher edoxaban dose-reduction rates (10%, 18% and 41%). on warfarin, stroke/systemic embolism rates rose with age (1.1%, 1.8%, 2.3%) as did major bleeding (1.8%, 3.3%, 4.8%; p for trend < 0.001 for both), with no interaction between age group and treatment for the primary efficacy or safety outcomes. in the elderly (≥75 years), stroke/systemic embolism was similar with edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% ci 0.66–1.04) while major bleeding was significantly reduced (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% ci 0.70–0.99). the absolute risk differences in major bleeding (−82 events/10,000 patient-years) and intracranial haemorrhage (−73 events/10,000 patient-years) both favoured edoxaban in older patients. a prespecified subgroup analysis of one trial: the elderly hazard ratios are subgroup estimates, and the parent trial's primary report is homed elsewhere in the library and not re-carded here. kato et et al. efficacy and safety of edoxaban in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation in the engage af-timi 48 trial. journal of the american heart association. 2016. pmid: 27207971. registry id: nct00781391. mesh: age factors · aged · anticoagulants · atrial fibrillation · double-blind method · embolism · factor xa inhibitors · female · hemorrhage · humans · male · middle aged · pyridines · stroke · thiazoles · treatment outcome · warfarin

cards.headline: Okumura 2020 (ELDERCARE-AF): in 984 patients aged ≥80 unsuitable for standard anticoagulation, 15 mg edoxaban prevented stroke or systemic embolism versus placebo (2.3% versus 6.7% per year; hazard ratio 0.34) without a significant increase in major bleeding (3.3% versus 1.8%; hazard ratio 1.87, P = 0.09)
cards.summary: Okumura 2020 (ELDERCARE-AF): in 984 patients aged ≥80 unsuitable for standard anticoagulation, 15 mg edoxaban prevented stroke or systemic embolism versus placebo (2.3% versus 6.7% per year; hazard ratio 0.34) without a significant increase in major bleeding (3.3% versus 1.8%; hazard ratio 1.87, P = 0.09)
cards.people: 984 elderly Japanese patients (≥80 years) with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation who were not considered appropriate candidates for oral anticoagulant therapy at approved doses, randomised 1:1 to edoxaban 15 mg once daily (n = 492) or placebo (n = 492) in a phase 3 double-blind event-driven trial.
cards.result: The annualised rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% with edoxaban versus 6.7% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.19–0.61, P < 0.001), and major bleeding was 3.3% versus 1.8% (hazard ratio 1.87, 95% CI 0.90–3.89, P = 0.09 — not significant), with more gastrointestinal bleeding on edoxaban. Death from any cause did not differ substantially (9.9% versus 10.2%; hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.69–1.36). This card answers the very-elderly question against placebo — it does not compare edoxaban with warfarin, and it is carded to bound the bleeding question at the oldest ages, not as warfarin-comparison evidence.
cards.watchOut: Placebo comparator, a 15 mg dose below the standard AF dose, and a Japanese population selected for ineligibility for standard anticoagulation — none of that transfers directly to a warfarin comparison in general elderly patients.
cards.source: Okumura K et al. Low-Dose Edoxaban in Very Elderly Patients with Atrial Fibrillation. New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32865374. Registry ID: NCT02801669. cards.headline: Kuroda 2022: ELDERCARE-AF's stroke prevention with 15 mg edoxaban was consistent across the 80–84, 85–89 and ≥90 age strata (hazard ratios 0.41, 0.42 and 0.23; interaction P = 0.65), with bleeding numerically higher but not significantly so in every stratum
cards.summary: Kuroda 2022: ELDERCARE-AF's stroke prevention with 15 mg edoxaban was consistent across the 80–84, 85–89 and ≥90 age strata (hazard ratios 0.41, 0.42 and 0.23; interaction P = 0.65), with bleeding numerically higher but not significantly so in every stratum
cards.people: The 984 ELDERCARE-AF participants (mean ages 82.2, 86.8 and 92.3 years across the three strata; 57.4% women) in prespecified age strata 80–84 (placebo n = 181), 85–89 (n = 184) and ≥90 years (n = 127 in the placebo group), all ineligible for standard-dose anticoagulation for reasons including low creatinine clearance, low body weight, prior critical-organ bleeding, or NSAID/antiplatelet use.
cards.result: On placebo, stroke or systemic embolism rates rose with age: 3.9%, 7.3% and 10.1% per patient-year across the strata. Edoxaban consistently decreased those rates with no interaction with age (hazard ratios 0.41 [95% CI 0.13–1.31], 0.42 [0.17–0.99] and 0.23 [0.08–0.68]; interaction P = .65). Major bleeding and major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding were numerically higher with edoxaban but not statistically significant, with no interaction with age, and all-cause death did not differ in any stratum.
cards.watchOut: The same placebo-controlled very-elderly trial as the card above, cut by age: it shows the oldest old were not an exception for efficacy or a clear exception for bleeding, but it still does not compare edoxaban with warfarin.
cards.source: Kuroda M et al. cards.people: The carded evidence: the prespecified elderly analysis of ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (21,105 patients; ≥75 subgroup n = 8,474) for the warfarin comparison, and the ELDERCARE-AF trial and its age-strata subanalysis (984 patients ≥80, counted once) for the very-elderly boundary. Total unique patients exceed 20,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Versus warfarin at age ≥75: major bleeding hazard ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.70–0.99), absolute difference −82 major bleeds and −73 intracranial haemorrhages per 10,000 patient-years, stroke/systemic embolism hazard ratio 0.83 (0.66–1.04) (Kato 2016). Versus placebo at age ≥80 on 15 mg: stroke/systemic embolism hazard ratio 0.34, major bleeding hazard ratio 1.87 not significant (Okumura 2020), consistent across age strata to ≥90 (Kuroda 2022). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme for the warfarin comparison, capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Only the Kato card compares edoxaban with warfarin; the two ELDERCARE cards compare a 15 mg dose with placebo in patients judged unsuitable for standard anticoagulation, and must not be cited as warfarin-comparison evidence. The post-TAVI edoxaban question is homed on live shelf #2447.

shelves.title: Anticoagulation after successful AF ablation: in moderate-risk patients, stopping was not associated with more thromboembolism in pooled randomised data (3 trials, 2,324 patients) and continuing cost more major bleeding (risk difference +1.0%) — the randomised base is still small
shelves.question: Should anticoagulation be continued after successful atrial fibrillation ablation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anticoagulants · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hemorrhage · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Registries · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Stroke · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2248 covers one slice of this question — rivaroxaban versus aspirin in patients free of recurrence at least a year after ablation at moderate stroke risk (the OCEAN question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — continued anticoagulation generally, versus stopping, after successful ablation. That home trial's primary report is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports, including a meta-analysis that pools the randomised trials. Across three randomised trials and 2,324 patients at moderate baseline stroke risk (mean CHA2DS2-VASc about 2), discontinuation was not associated with a significant increase in stroke, systemic embolism, transient ischaemic attack or death, while continuation was associated with significantly more major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%), intracranial bleeding (0.6%), minor bleeding (2.2%) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (2.5%) (Kaisaier 2026). The one randomised trial of continuation itself, ODIn-AF, randomised 200 AF-free patients six months after pulmonary vein isolation to dabigatran or no anticoagulation and found no difference in new cerebral embolic lesions on MRI and no clinical strokes in either arm, with more serious adverse events on anticoagulation (Schrickel 2024). Registry practice shows the question is live: in a large US registry, 23% of higher-risk ablated patients had anticoagulation discontinued anyway, at a median 6.2 months (Freeman 2019). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit of discontinuation in moderate-risk patients) — the direction is consistent, but the randomised base is small, follow-up is short, and none of it licenses stopping in higher-risk patients.

cards.headline: Kaisaier 2026: pooling 3 randomised trials (2,324 patients) after successful ablation, stopping anticoagulation was not associated with more stroke, systemic embolism, TIA or death — while continuing was associated with significantly more major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%), intracranial bleeding (0.6%) and lesser bleeding
cards.summary: Kaisaier 2026: pooling 3 randomised trials (2,324 patients) after successful ablation, stopping anticoagulation was not associated with more stroke, systemic embolism, TIA or death — while continuing was associated with significantly more major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%), intracranial bleeding (0.6%) and lesser bleeding
cards.people: 2,324 patients with atrial fibrillation after successful catheter ablation in three randomised controlled trials (searched to November 2025); mean age 63–67 years, 71.4% men, average CHA2DS2-VASc score approximately 2 — a moderate-stroke-risk population.
cards.result: Oral anticoagulation discontinuation was not associated with a significant increase in the risks of stroke, ischemic stroke, stroke or systemic embolism, transient ischemic attack, and all-cause death. Continued anticoagulation was associated with significantly higher risks of major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%, 95% CI 0.2–1.7), intracranial bleeding (risk difference 0.6%, 95% CI 0.0–1.1), minor bleeding (risk difference 2.2%, 95% CI 0.2–4.1), and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (risk difference 2.5%, 95% CI 1.2–3.9); gastrointestinal bleeding did not differ. The authors state the findings apply primarily to moderate stroke risk and should not be extrapolated to higher-risk populations. Risk differences are absolute measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Only three trials and 2,324 patients, at moderate stroke risk, with the largest contributing trial homed on live shelf #2248; 'no significant increase' in thromboembolism over short follow-up is not proof of equivalence, especially for higher-risk patients.
cards.source: Kaisaier W et al. Discontinuation of Oral Anticoagulation After Successful Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation: Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. cards.headline: Schrickel 2024 (ODIn-AF): in 200 AF-free patients randomised 6 months after pulmonary vein isolation to dabigatran or no anticoagulation, new silent cerebral lesions did not differ (2% versus 0%, P = 0.15), no clinical strokes occurred in either arm, and serious adverse events were more frequent on anticoagulation (31.8% versus 19.4%)
cards.summary: Schrickel 2024 (ODIn-AF): in 200 AF-free patients randomised 6 months after pulmonary vein isolation to dabigatran or no anticoagulation, new silent cerebral lesions did not differ (2% versus 0%, P = 0.15), no clinical strokes occurred in either arm, and serious adverse events were more frequent on anticoagulation (31.8% versus 19.4%)
cards.people: 200 patients at intermediate-to-high embolic risk who were free of atrial fibrillation six months after pulmonary vein isolation, randomised to continued oral anticoagulation with dabigatran (n = 99) or no anticoagulation (n = 101) in a prospective multicentre open-label trial with blinded endpoint assessment; the primary endpoint was new silent cerebral embolic lesions on brain MRI at 12 months.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in new cerebral microlesions between the on-anticoagulation and off-anticoagulation arms (2 [2%] versus 0 [0%]; P = 0.1517), no new macro-embolic lesions on MRI, and no clinically apparent strokes in either group. Serious adverse events were more frequent in the anticoagulation arm (34 [31.8%] versus 18 [19.4%]; P = 0.0460); bleedings did not differ. The authors conclude discontinuation after successful isolation was not associated with an elevated risk of cerebral embolic events over 12 months.
cards.watchOut: A 200-patient trial powered for silent MRI lesions, not clinical stroke: zero clinical strokes in both arms over 12 months means the trial cannot exclude a clinically important difference in real embolic events.
cards.source: Schrickel JW et al. Prevention of cerebral thromboembolism by oral anticoagulation with dabigatran after pulmonary vein isolation for atrial fibrillation: the ODIn-AF trial. Clinical Research in Cardiology. 2024. PMID: 37921923. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Freeman 2019: in a large US registry, 23% of higher-risk patients who had ablation had their anticoagulation discontinued anyway (median 6.2 months after ablation), despite guideline recommendations to continue — real-world practice already runs ahead of the randomised evidence

cards.people: 21,595 patients in the ORBIT-AF registries, of whom 1,190 (6%) underwent de novo catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation; anticoagulation patterns were examined in ablated patients whose CHA2DS2-VASc score met the threshold for continued therapy (≥2 in men, ≥3 in women).
cards.result: Among ablated patients at higher stroke risk, 23% had oral anticoagulation discontinued after ablation, at a median time to discontinuation of 6.2 months. In the propensity-matched comparison within the same study (1,087 ablated patients matched to 1,087 treated with antiarrhythmic drugs only), there were no significant differences in all-cause or cardiovascular death or most major adverse events, while ablation was associated with more all-cause hospitalisation (hazard ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.05–1.46), particularly in the first 3 months. The record does not report outcomes split by whether anticoagulation was stopped, so this card is context about practice, not outcome evidence.
cards.watchOut: Observational registry data carded for practice context only: discontinuation was clinician- and patient-driven, and the record gives no outcome comparison between those who stopped and those who continued.
cards.source: Freeman JV et al. Outcomes and Anticoagulation Use After Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology. 2019. PMID: 31830822. cards.headline: Synthesis: for moderate-risk patients after successful ablation, the randomised evidence points one way — no significant thromboembolic penalty for stopping, and a consistent bleeding cost for continuing (major bleeding risk difference +1.0% with continuation) — but the base is 2,324 randomised patients and does not cover higher-risk patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: for moderate-risk patients after successful ablation, the randomised evidence points one way — no significant thromboembolic penalty for stopping, and a consistent bleeding cost for continuing (major bleeding risk difference +1.0% with continuation) — but the base is 2,324 randomised patients and does not cover higher-risk patients
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials (2,324 patients, overlapping the ODIn-AF trial and the home trial on shelf #2248 by design), one 200-patient randomised trial with an MRI endpoint, and one registry cohort of 21,595 patients (1,190 ablated) for practice context. Unique randomised patients total about 2,300, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, but the randomised base is small for a stroke-prevention question and that is printed here.
cards.result: Discontinuation versus continuation: no significant difference in stroke, systemic embolism, TIA or death; continuation associated with more major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%), intracranial bleeding (0.6%), minor bleeding (2.2%) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (2.5%) (Kaisaier 2026). ODIn-AF: no difference in silent cerebral lesions, no clinical strokes in either arm, more serious adverse events on anticoagulation (Schrickel 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit of discontinuation in moderate-risk patients) — direction consistent across the randomised reports, strength limited by sample size and follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Guidelines still recommend continuing anticoagulation by stroke-risk score regardless of ablation success; the carded trials enrolled moderate-risk patients with documented freedom from recurrence, and nothing here supports stopping in higher-risk patients or after recurrence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kaisaier W et al. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2026 (PMID: 42398953); Schrickel JW et al. Clinical Research in Cardiology. 2024 (PMID: 37921923); Freeman JV et al. Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology. 2019 (PMID: 31830822).

shelves.title: Digoxin safety in AF with heart failure — SPLIT by study design: randomised data are neutral on mortality (risk ratio 0.99), while observational data link digoxin to higher mortality (hazard ratios 1.14–1.23), including in the AF-with-HF subgroup of one large cohort
shelves.question: Is digoxin safe for rate control in atrial fibrillation with heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiotonic Agents · Digoxin · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1173 covers digoxin versus bisoprolol for quality of life in AF with heart failure symptoms (the RATE-AF question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — safety, specifically mortality, when digoxin is used for rate control in AF with heart failure. The evidence genuinely divides by design. Pooling by design, the BMJ systematic review found digoxin's mortality association shrank as methods improved — risk ratio 1.76 unadjusted, 1.61 adjusted, 1.18 in propensity-matched studies, and 0.99 (the treatment made no difference) in randomised trials — while hospital admissions fell slightly across all study types (Ziff 2015). An updated adjusted-data meta-analysis found the opposite headline: mortality hazard ratio 1.17 overall, 1.23 in AF and 1.11 in heart failure subgroups (Vamos 2019). Within AF specifically, one meta-analysis found digoxin associated with higher mortality overall (hazard ratio 1.23) but not in the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup (1.08, not significant) (Chamaria 2015), whereas a large propensity-matched Quebec cohort of patients ≥65 found higher mortality with digoxin in both the heart-failure (1.14) and no-heart-failure (1.17) groups (Shah 2014). No randomised trial of digoxin for rate control in AF with HF has been powered for mortality. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: neutral; observational: harm signal) — safety is not established in either direction.

cards.headline: Ziff 2015: digoxin's mortality association depended on study design — risk ratio 1.76 unadjusted, 1.61 adjusted, 1.18 propensity-matched, and 0.99 in randomised trials (no difference) — while hospital admissions were slightly lower with digoxin across all study types (0.92)
cards.summary: Ziff 2015: digoxin's mortality association depended on study design — risk ratio 1.76 unadjusted, 1.61 adjusted, 1.18 propensity-matched, and 0.99 in randomised trials (no difference) — while hospital admissions were slightly lower with digoxin across all study types (0.92)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis by study design (Ziff 2015)
cards.people: 52 studies comprising 621,845 patients treated with digoxin versus control (placebo or no treatment) across atrial fibrillation and heart failure, published 1960 to July 2014, with 4,006,210 patient-years of follow-up in 75 study analyses; digoxin users were on average 2.4 years older, with lower ejection fraction (33% versus 42%), more diabetes, and more diuretic and antiarrhythmic use.
cards.result: Compared with control, the pooled risk ratio for death with digoxin was 1.76 (95% CI 1.57–1.97) in unadjusted analyses, 1.61 (1.31–1.97) in adjusted analyses, 1.18 (1.09–1.26) in propensity-matched studies, and 0.99 (0.93–1.05) in randomised controlled trials — the treatment made no difference in the randomised data. Meta-regression confirmed baseline differences (including diuretic use as a marker of heart failure severity) significantly influenced the mortality association, and studies with better methods were more likely to report a neutral association (P < 0.001). Across all study types, digoxin reduced all-cause hospital admission (risk ratio 0.92, 0.89–0.95; n = 29,525). Risk ratios are relative measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The randomised stratum is dominated by trials in heart failure in sinus rhythm rather than AF rate control, so its neutrality does not directly acquit digoxin in the AF-with-HF population of this shelf's question.
cards.source: Ziff OJ et al. Safety and efficacy of digoxin: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational and controlled trial data. BMJ. 2015. PMID: 26321114. cards.headline: Vamos 2019: pooling adjusted survival data from 37 studies (825,061 patients), digoxin was associated with increased all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.17) — in AF (1.23) and in heart failure (1.11) subgroups alike, and more strongly in new users (1.47)
cards.summary: Vamos 2019: pooling adjusted survival data from 37 studies (825,061 patients), digoxin was associated with increased all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.17) — in AF (1.23) and in heart failure (1.11) subgroups alike, and more strongly in new users (1.47)
cards.people: 37 studies published to March 2018 reporting digoxin-associated mortality in atrial fibrillation or heart failure, totalling 825,061 patients — 627,620 in the AF subgroup and 197,441 in the heart failure subgroup; a new-user sensitivity analysis covered 41,687 patients.
cards.result: Based on adjusted survival data, digoxin use was associated with an increased relative risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.05–1.29, P < 0.01). The association held in the AF subgroup (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.17–1.30) and the heart failure subgroup (hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.06–1.16), and was stronger among new digoxin users (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.15–1.88). Hazard ratios are relative measures, as printed in the record; the underlying studies are observational, so these are associations, not randomised effects.
cards.watchOut: Almost entirely observational data: digoxin is prescribed to sicker patients, and adjustment cannot remove confounding by indication — the same limitation the Ziff card quantifies from the other direction.
cards.source: Vamos M et al. Meta-Analysis of Effects of Digoxin on Survival in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation or Heart Failure: An Update. American Journal of Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 30539748. cards.headline: Chamaria 2015: in AF overall, digoxin was associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.23) — but in the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup the association was not significant (1.08, 95% CI 0.99–1.18), while AF without heart failure showed the clearest harm association (1.38)
cards.summary: Chamaria 2015: in AF overall, digoxin was associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.23) — but in the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup the association was not significant (1.08, 95% CI 0.99–1.18), while AF without heart failure showed the clearest harm association (1.38)
cards.type: Meta-analysis in atrial fibrillation, by heart failure status (Chamaria 2015)
cards.people: 12 studies with 321,944 patients with atrial fibrillation comparing digoxin versus no digoxin, with adjusted hazard ratios, analysed overall and split by the presence or absence of heart failure.
cards.result: In all AF patients irrespective of heart failure status, digoxin was associated with increased all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.16–1.31). In patients with AF and heart failure, digoxin was not associated with increased mortality (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.99–1.18 — not significant). In AF patients without heart failure, digoxin was associated with increased all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.12–1.71). Hazard ratios are relative measures, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The AF-with-HF subgroup confidence interval (0.99–1.18) sits on the line: it excludes neither a small harm nor no effect, and the component studies are observational.
cards.source: Chamaria S et al. Digoxin Use to Control Ventricular Rate in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and Heart Failure Is Not Associated with Increased Mortality. cards.headline: Shah 2014: in a propensity-matched Quebec cohort of patients ≥65 hospitalised with AF, digoxin was associated with higher mortality both with heart failure (adjusted hazard ratio 1.14) and without it (1.17) — contradicting the AF-with-HF neutrality on the Chamaria card
cards.summary: Shah 2014: in a propensity-matched Quebec cohort of patients ≥65 hospitalised with AF, digoxin was associated with higher mortality both with heart failure (adjusted hazard ratio 1.14) and without it (1.17) — contradicting the AF-with-HF neutrality on the Chamaria card
cards.people: Population-based retrospective cohort of patients aged ≥65 admitted to hospital with a primary or secondary AF diagnosis in Quebec, Canada, 1998–2012, grouped by heart failure status and by whether a first digoxin prescription was filled within 30 days of discharge, with propensity score-matched digoxin and no-digoxin groups (matched cohort sizes are not documented in the record).
cards.result: In the propensity-matched heart failure group, digoxin use was associated with a 14% greater relative risk of all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.10–1.17); in the matched no-heart-failure group, the association was 17% greater (adjusted hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.14–1.19). The authors conclude digoxin was associated with greater mortality in older AF patients regardless of concomitant heart failure, and that large randomised trials or prospective cohorts are required to clarify the issue.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching balances measured variables only; digoxin dose, serum levels, renal function trajectories and the reasons clinicians chose digoxin (often frailty or hypotension limiting beta-blockade) are exactly the unmeasured factors that could produce this association.
cards.source: Shah M et al. Relation of digoxin use in atrial fibrillation and the risk of all-cause mortality in patients ≥65 years of age with versus without heart failure. American Journal of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 24950677. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis — SPLIT: randomised pooling is neutral on mortality (risk ratio 0.99) while observational pooling shows harm (hazard ratio 1.17–1.23); the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup itself splits — 1.08 (not significant) in one meta-analysis versus 1.14 in a large matched cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis — SPLIT: randomised pooling is neutral on mortality (risk ratio 0.99) while observational pooling shows harm (hazard ratio 1.17–1.23); the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup itself splits — 1.08 (not significant) in one meta-analysis versus 1.14 in a large matched cohort
cards.people: The carded evidence: two design-stratified meta-analyses (621,845 and 825,061 patients), one AF-specific meta-analysis split by heart failure status (321,944 patients), and one propensity-matched population cohort (size not documented in its record). Populations overlap across the meta-analyses by design; the total evidence base is far above 30 patients, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the limitation is confounding, not size.
cards.result: Randomised stratum: mortality risk ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.93–1.05), admissions risk ratio 0.92 (Ziff 2015). Observational pooling: mortality hazard ratio 1.17 overall, 1.23 in AF, 1.11 in HF (Vamos 2019). AF with HF specifically: hazard ratio 1.08 (0.99–1.18, not significant; Chamaria 2015) versus 1.14 (1.10–1.17; Shah 2014). PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised evidence: no mortality increase; observational evidence: higher mortality with digoxin) — the split is named in the stamp, and the quality-of-life comparison with bisoprolol remains homed on live shelf #1173.
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomised digoxin for rate control in AF with heart failure with mortality as its endpoint; until one does, both 'safe' and 'harmful' exceed what the evidence can carry, which is why the stamp is SPLIT rather than a verdict either way.
