shelves.title: Ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT: major bleeding roughly halved or better in two individual-patient meta-analyses (0.8% versus 2.1%, hazard ratio 0.37; 2.4% versus 4.5%, hazard ratio 0.54) with no significant increase in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
shelves.question: Is ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy safer than continued dual antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Ticagrelor · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Drug Therapy, Combination · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Aspirin · Myocardial Infarction · Hemorrhage · Stroke · Biomarkers · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #4163 covers a neighbouring de-escalation slice — switching from ticagrelor to clopidogrel at 1 month in stabilised myocardial infarction; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — dropping aspirin and continuing ticagrelor alone after 3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). The primary reports of the two anchor trials (TWILIGHT and TICO) are homed elsewhere in the library and are not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports. Pooling individual data from both trials in acute coronary syndrome (7,529 patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months reduced BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding between months 3 and 12 (0.8% versus 2.1%; hazard ratio 0.37) with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (2.4% versus 2.7%; hazard ratio 0.91) (Baber 2024). An independent individual-patient pooling of TICO with T-PASS (5,906 patients) found the same pattern: major bleeding 2.4% versus 4.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.54) and the ischaemic composite 1.9% versus 2.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.79, not significant) (Lee 2024). The benefit is largest where it matters most: in TWILIGHT's high-bleeding-risk patients, monotherapy cut BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding (6.3% versus 11.4%) with a larger absolute reduction in severe bleeding than in non-high-risk patients (Escaned 2021), and a risk-modelling analysis found the bleeding benefit consistent across bleeding- and ischaemic-risk strata with no offsetting ischaemic increase (Mendieta 2023). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — two independent individual-patient meta-analyses of randomised trials agree on a large relative bleeding reduction with no significant ischaemic cost.

cards.headline: Baber 2024: pooling individual data from TWILIGHT and TICO in ACS (7,529 patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT cut BARC 3 or 5 bleeding between months 3–12 (0.8% versus 2.1%; hazard ratio 0.37) with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (2.4% versus 2.7%)
cards.summary: Baber 2024: pooling individual data from TWILIGHT and TICO in ACS (7,529 patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT cut BARC 3 or 5 bleeding between months 3–12 (0.8% versus 2.1%; hazard ratio 0.37) with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (2.4% versus 2.7%)
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis (Baber 2024, TWILIGHT + TICO)
cards.people: Individual patient data from the randomised trials of patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing PCI who completed an initial 3-month course of DAPT (ticagrelor plus aspirin) and were then assigned to ticagrelor monotherapy or continued ticagrelor plus aspirin; pooled cohort 7,529 patients, mean age 62.8 years, 23.2% women, 55% with biomarker-positive ACS; patients with a major ischaemic or bleeding event in the first 3 months were excluded.
cards.result: Between 3 and 12 months, ticagrelor monotherapy significantly reduced BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding compared with ticagrelor plus aspirin (0.8% versus 2.1%; hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.24–0.56, P < 0.001) — a 63% relative reduction with a 1.3-percentage-point absolute reduction. Rates of all-cause death, myocardial infarction or stroke did not differ significantly (2.4% versus 2.7%; hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.68–1.21, P = 0.515 — the treatment made no difference on the ischaemic composite). Findings were unchanged in biomarker-positive ACS.
cards.watchOut: The analysis starts at 3 months in event-free survivors of the initial DAPT period: it says nothing about the first 3 months, and its ischaemic confidence interval (0.68–1.21) cannot exclude a modest ischaemic increase.
cards.source: Baber U et al. cards.headline: Lee 2024: pooling TICO and T-PASS individually (5,906 ACS patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after ≤3 months of DAPT halved major bleeding at 1 year (2.4% versus 4.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.54) with no significant difference in the ischaemic composite (1.9% versus 2.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.79)
cards.summary: Lee 2024: pooling TICO and T-PASS individually (5,906 ACS patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after ≤3 months of DAPT halved major bleeding at 1 year (2.4% versus 4.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.54) with no significant difference in the ischaemic composite (1.9% versus 2.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.79)
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis (Lee 2024, TICO + T-PASS)
cards.people: Individual patient data from two randomised trials (TICO and T-PASS) of 5,906 patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing drug-eluting stent implantation, comparing ticagrelor monotherapy after short-term (≤3 months) DAPT with ticagrelor-based 12-month DAPT; co-primary endpoints were the ischaemic composite (all-cause death, myocardial infarction or stroke) and BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding at 1 year.
cards.result: At 1 year, the ischaemic endpoint did not differ between ticagrelor monotherapy and ticagrelor-based DAPT (1.9% versus 2.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.56–1.13, P = .194 — not significant), while the bleeding endpoint was lower with monotherapy (2.4% versus 4.5%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.40–0.72, P < .001) — a 46% relative reduction with a 2.1-percentage-point absolute reduction. A secondary aggregate meta-analysis including the ACS subgroups of additional trials was consistent.
cards.watchOut: An independent pooling that shares the TICO trial with the Baber card — the two meta-analyses are corroborating analyses, not wholly independent evidence bases; T-PASS used an even shorter DAPT course in part, so 'after 3 months' is the upper bound of the pooled strategy.
cards.source: Lee YJ et al. Ticagrelor monotherapy for acute coronary syndrome: an individual patient data meta-analysis of TICO and T-PASS trials. European Heart Journal. 2024. PMID: 38750627. cards.headline: Escaned 2021 (TWILIGHT-HBR): in 1,064 high-bleeding-risk patients, ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months cut BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding (6.3% versus 11.4%; hazard ratio 0.53), with a larger absolute reduction in severe bleeding than in non-high-risk patients (−3.5% versus −0.5%) and no difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.summary: Escaned 2021 (TWILIGHT-HBR): in 1,064 high-bleeding-risk patients, ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months cut BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding (6.3% versus 11.4%; hazard ratio 0.53), with a larger absolute reduction in severe bleeding than in non-high-risk patients (−3.5% versus −0.5%) and no difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.people: Prespecified analysis of the TWILIGHT randomised trial in patients undergoing PCI with drug-eluting stents who completed 3 months of ticagrelor plus aspirin event-free and were randomised to ticagrelor plus aspirin or ticagrelor plus placebo for 12 months; 1,064 patients (17.2%) met the Academic Research Consortium definition of high bleeding risk.
cards.result: Ticagrelor monotherapy reduced the primary endpoint of BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding in high-bleeding-risk patients (6.3% versus 11.4%; hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.35–0.82) and in non-high-risk patients (3.5% versus 5.9%; hazard ratio 0.59, 0.46–0.77), with similar relative effects (P for interaction = 0.67) but a trend to greater absolute reduction in high-risk patients (−5.1% versus −2.3%). For BARC 3 or 5 bleeding the absolute reduction was significantly larger in high-risk patients (−3.5% versus −0.5%; P = 0.008). The key secondary endpoint of death, myocardial infarction or stroke did not differ significantly between arms irrespective of bleeding-risk status.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of one trial whose primary report is homed elsewhere; high-bleeding-risk patients were 17.2% of the trial, and subgroup absolute gains should not be generalised to unselected PCI patients.

cards.headline: Mendieta 2023: modelling TWILIGHT's 7,119 patients, the bleeding reduction with ticagrelor monotherapy was consistent across every bleeding-risk and ischaemic-risk stratum, and was not offset by more major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events at any risk level
cards.summary: Mendieta 2023: modelling TWILIGHT's 7,119 patients, the bleeding reduction with ticagrelor monotherapy was consistent across every bleeding-risk and ischaemic-risk stratum, and was not offset by more major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events at any risk level
cards.people: The total TWILIGHT study group (N = 7,119 high-risk PCI patients randomised after 3 months of DAPT), in whom BARC type 2, 3 or 5 bleeding occurred in 391 patients (5.5%) and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischaemic stroke) in 258 (3.6%); multivariable models generated individual bleeding and ischaemic risk scores.
cards.result: There was a consistent reduction in bleeding events with ticagrelor monotherapy compared with DAPT across both bleeding-risk and ischaemic-risk strata (P for interaction = 0.54 and 0.11 respectively), and the bleeding benefit was not offset by an increase in major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events at any level of bleeding or ischaemic risk. The authors conclude that 3 months after PCI, discontinuing aspirin and maintaining ticagrelor monotherapy reduces bleeding in both higher- and lower-bleeding-risk patients compared with continued DAPT.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc risk-modelling re-analysis of a single trial: it tests consistency of the trial's own result across risk strata and adds no new randomised patients.
cards.source: Mendieta G et al. Bleeding and Ischemic Risks of Ticagrelor Monotherapy After Coronary Interventions. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023. PMID: 37587580. Registry ID: NCT02270242. MeSH: Humans · Aspirin · Heart · Hemorrhage · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Ticagrelor

cards.headline: Synthesis: after 3 months of DAPT, dropping aspirin for ticagrelor alone cuts major bleeding by roughly half or more in relative terms (hazard ratios 0.37 and 0.54 in two individual-patient meta-analyses; absolute reductions 1.3–2.1 percentage points, larger at high bleeding risk) with no significant increase in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.summary: Synthesis: after 3 months of DAPT, dropping aspirin for ticagrelor alone cuts major bleeding by roughly half or more in relative terms (hazard ratios 0.37 and 0.54 in two individual-patient meta-analyses; absolute reductions 1.3–2.1 percentage points, larger at high bleeding risk) with no significant increase in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.people: The carded evidence: two individual-patient meta-analyses (7,529 and 5,906 patients, sharing the TICO trial), one prespecified high-bleeding-risk subgroup analysis (1,064 patients within TWILIGHT), and one risk-stratified re-analysis of TWILIGHT (7,119 patients). The underlying randomised base is the TWILIGHT, TICO and T-PASS trials — well over 30 patients in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; overlap between analyses is by design and is printed here.
cards.result: BARC 3 or 5 bleeding: 0.8% versus 2.1%, hazard ratio 0.37 (Baber 2024); 2.4% versus 4.5%, adjusted hazard ratio 0.54 (Lee 2024); BARC 2, 3 or 5 in high bleeding risk: 6.3% versus 11.4%, hazard ratio 0.53 (Escaned 2021). Ischaemic composites: hazard ratio 0.91 (0.68–1.21) and adjusted 0.79 (0.56–1.13), both non-significant. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — safer on bleeding, with no significant ischaemic penalty shown; the 1-month clopidogrel de-escalation slice remains homed on live shelf #4163.
cards.watchOut: All carded analyses concern patients who completed the initial DAPT period event-free and mostly had acute coronary syndrome; they do not address the first 3 months after PCI, chronic coronary syndrome populations, or patients who need oral anticoagulation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Baber U et al. Circulation. 2024 (PMID: 37870970); Lee YJ et al. European Heart Journal. 2024 (PMID: 38750627); Escaned J et al. European Heart Journal. 2021 (PMID: 34662382); Mendieta G et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 37587580).

shelves.title: FFR-guided PCI in multivessel disease generally (partial completion of the STEMI-only shelf #2280): fewer stents and fewer early events than angiography guidance, with the stable-disease advantage gone by 5 years
shelves.question: Does FFR-guided PCI improve outcomes compared with angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2280, which covers FFR versus angiography guidance only in STEMI with multivessel disease (the FLOWER-MI comparison); this shelf covers multivessel disease generally. The FAME primary 1-year report (PMID: 19144937) is already carded elsewhere in the library (pack #1537) and is not re-carded here; the free FAME 5-year report is carded instead. Across the general multivessel evidence the benefit is real but time-limited and setting-dependent: in FAME, FFR guidance cut major adverse cardiac events for up to 2 years and used far fewer stents (1.9 vs 2.7 per patient), but by 5 years events had converged (28% vs 31%; relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.75-1.10; p=0.31). In acute MI with multivessel disease (FRAME-AMI), FFR-guided selective PCI of non-infarct lesions beat angiography-guided PCI clearly (7.4% vs 19.7%; hazard ratio 0.43). A 2016 meta-analysis of 2,138 randomised patients found lower reinfarction with FFR guidance (odds ratio 0.67) but no significant mortality or overall MACE difference. Against that, routine pressure-wire assessment of all vessels at diagnostic angiography (RIPCORD 2) made no difference to cost, quality of life or events — FFR helps when it decides which identified multivessel lesions to stent, not as a blanket screening strategy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — FFR-guided PCI improves outcomes over angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease, principally by avoiding unnecessary stents and reducing early events and reinfarction; the advantage attenuates by 5 years in stable multivessel disease.

cards.headline: FAME 5-year: FFR guidance used far fewer stents (1.9 vs 2.7 per patient) and cut events for up to 2 years, but by 5 years major adverse cardiac events had converged — 28% vs 31% (relative risk 0.91; p=0.31)
cards.summary: FAME 5-year: FFR guidance used far fewer stents (1.9 vs 2.7 per patient) and cut events for up to 2 years, but by 5 years major adverse cardiac events had converged — 28% vs 31% (relative risk 0.91; p=0.31)
cards.people: Patients with multivessel coronary artery disease in the multicentre FAME trial (Belgium, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, the UK and the USA), randomly assigned to angiography-guided PCI (all identified stenoses stented; 496 patients in the 5-year analysis) or FFR-guided PCI (PCI only if FFR was 0.80 or less; 509 patients). The FAME 1-year primary report is carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded on this shelf.
cards.result: After 5 years, major adverse cardiac events occurred in 31% of patients (154 of 496) in the angiography-guided group versus 28% (143 of 509) in the FFR-guided group (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.75-1.10; p=0.31). The number of stents placed per patient was significantly higher with angiography guidance (mean 2.7 [SD 1.2] vs 1.9 [1.3], p<0.0001). The record states the FFR-guided strategy significantly decreased major adverse cardiac events for up to 2 years, with risks developing similarly from 2 to 5 years.
cards.watchOut: Open-label strategy trial: operators knew the assignment, and the early advantage is partly a stent-avoidance effect — by 5 years the event curves meet, so this card supports an early, not a permanent, outcome advantage in stable multivessel disease.
cards.source: van Nunen LX et al. Fractional flow reserve versus angiography for guidance of PCI in patients with multivessel coronary artery disease (FAME): 5-year follow-up of a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 26333474. Registry ID: NCT00267774. cards.headline: FRAME-AMI: in acute MI with multivessel disease, FFR-guided selective PCI of non-infarct lesions beat angiography-guided PCI — primary endpoint 7.4% vs 19.7% (hazard ratio 0.43)
cards.summary: FRAME-AMI: in acute MI with multivessel disease, FFR-guided selective PCI of non-infarct lesions beat angiography-guided PCI — primary endpoint 7.4% vs 19.7% (hazard ratio 0.43)
cards.people: 562 patients with acute myocardial infarction and multivessel coronary artery disease who had undergone successful PCI of the infarct-related artery, randomly assigned to FFR-guided PCI (FFR 0.80 or less; 284 patients) or angiography-guided PCI (diameter stenosis over 50%; 278 patients) for non-infarct-related artery lesions; 60.0% had immediate and 40.0% staged non-infarct PCI.
cards.result: PCI of the non-infarct artery was performed in 64.1% of the FFR-guided group and 97.1% of the angiography-guided group, with fewer stents with FFR guidance (2.2 vs 2.5, P<0.001). At a median follow-up of 3.5 years the primary endpoint (death, MI or repeat revascularisation) occurred in 18 of 284 patients in the FFR-guided group and 40 of 278 in the angiography-guided group (7.4% vs 19.7%; hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.25-0.75; P=0.003). Death occurred in 5 patients (2.1%) versus 16 (8.5%), MI in 7 (2.5%) versus 21 (8.9%), and unplanned revascularisation in 10 (4.3%) versus 16 (9.0%).
cards.watchOut: This is the acute-MI end of the multivessel spectrum, adjacent to — but a different trial and population from — the STEMI comparison homed on live shelf #2280; event counts are small (18 vs 40 primary events), so the large relative effect carries wide uncertainty.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 2,138 randomised patients: FFR guidance lowered reinfarction (odds ratio 0.67) but mortality, repeat revascularisation and overall MACE did not differ significantly
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 2,138 randomised patients: FFR guidance lowered reinfarction (odds ratio 0.67) but mortality, repeat revascularisation and overall MACE did not differ significantly
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing FFR-guided with angiography-guided PCI; 2,138 patients in total (1,080 FFR-guided versus 1,058 angiography-guided), searched in PubMed/Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane library.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ significantly between FFR-guided and angiography-guided PCI (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.39-1.25; P=0.22). Total repeated revascularisation (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.60-1.13; P=0.22), target lesion revascularisation (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.43-1.80; P=0.73) and major adverse cardiac events (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.64-1.06; P=0.13) were also not significantly different. FFR-guided PCI was associated with a significantly lower rate of reinfarction (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.47-0.96; P=0.03). The authors note the limited number of patients analysed means the reinfarction finding needs confirmation.
cards.watchOut: A 2016 synthesis of only 2,138 patients, dominated by FAME-era trials; it predates FRAME-AMI and cannot speak to modern practice, and its one significant endpoint (reinfarction) is the endpoint its own authors flag as needing confirmation.

cards.headline: RIPCORD 2: routine pressure-wire assessment of every vessel at diagnostic angiography made no difference — costs, quality of life and clinical events were the same as angiography alone (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: RIPCORD 2: routine pressure-wire assessment of every vessel at diagnostic angiography made no difference — costs, quality of life and clinical events were the same as angiography alone (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 1,100 patients undergoing invasive coronary angiography for stable angina or non-ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction at 17 UK centres, randomised to angiography alone (552 patients) or angiography with systematic pressure-wire (FFR) assessment of all epicardial vessels over 2.25 mm (548 patients).
cards.result: Median hospital costs at 1 year were similar (£4,136 with angiography alone vs £4,510 with angiography plus FFR; P=0.137), as was median quality of life (EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale 75 in both groups; P=0.88). Clinical events: deaths 5 versus 8, strokes 3 versus 4, myocardial infarctions 23 versus 22, unplanned revascularisations 26 versus 33; the composite hierarchical event rate was 8.7% (48 of 552) for angiography versus 9.5% (52 of 548) for angiography plus FFR (P=0.64) — the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: RIPCORD 2 tested FFR as a blanket diagnostic strategy in all-comers at angiography — a different use from FFR deciding treatment of already-identified multivessel stenoses — so its null result bounds, rather than contradicts, the FAME and FRAME-AMI findings.
cards.source: Stables RH et al. Routine Pressure Wire Assessment Versus Conventional Angiography in the Management of Patients With Coronary Artery Disease: The RIPCORD 2 Trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 35946404. Registry ID: NCT01070771. cards.headline: Synthesis: FFR guidance improves multivessel PCI outcomes mainly by stenting less — early event and reinfarction reductions are consistent, the stable-disease advantage fades by 5 years, and blanket pressure-wire screening adds nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: FFR guidance improves multivessel PCI outcomes mainly by stenting less — early event and reinfarction reductions are consistent, the stable-disease advantage fades by 5 years, and blanket pressure-wire screening adds nothing
cards.people: The carded evidence: the FAME 5-year report (1,005 patients analysed), FRAME-AMI in acute MI (562 patients), a 2016 meta-analysis of randomised trials (2,138 patients) and RIPCORD 2 (1,100 patients). Total carded participants exceed 4,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: FFR-guided PCI stented fewer lesions than angiography-guided PCI in both direct trials (FAME 1.9 vs 2.7 stents per patient; FRAME-AMI non-infarct PCI in 64.1% vs 97.1%). FRAME-AMI showed a large outcome advantage (7.4% vs 19.7%; HR 0.43); FAME's advantage was confined to the first 2 years (5-year MACE 28% vs 31%; RR 0.91, not significant); the meta-analysis found only reinfarction significantly reduced (OR 0.67); and systematic FFR at diagnostic angiography (RIPCORD 2) made no difference. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The STEMI-specific FFR-versus-angiography comparison is homed on live shelf #2280 and the FAME 1-year primary report is carded on pack #1537; neither is re-carded here — this shelf is the general multivessel completion of that partial coverage.

shelves.title: Left main disease with low complexity (partial completion of the general left-main shelf #551): CABG is not better on death — it wins on spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation, PCI wins on early stroke
shelves.question: Is CABG better than PCI for left main coronary disease with low complexity?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Artery Disease · Drug-Eluting Stents · Humans · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #551, the general left-main shelf (PCI as an alternative to CABG, built on the EXCEL and NOBLE primary reports, which are not re-carded here); this shelf isolates the low-complexity (low SYNTAX score) slice. In that slice the strategies divide by outcome rather than one winning outright. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the four left-main trials (4,394 patients, median SYNTAX score 25.0 — largely low or intermediate complexity) found no statistically significant difference in 5-year all-cause death (11.2% with PCI vs 10.2% with CABG; hazard ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.91-1.32), although a Bayesian analysis put an 85.7% probability on some excess mortality with PCI, most likely under 0.2% per year. A SYNTAX-stratified meta-analysis found clinical equipoise on major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events at low-to-intermediate SYNTAX scores (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70) with a CABG advantage only at high scores. What CABG does win, consistently and in this complexity band, is spontaneous myocardial infarction (6.2% vs 2.6%; HR 2.35 with PCI) and repeat revascularisation (18.3% vs 10.7%; HR 1.78); what PCI wins is early stroke (first-year HR 0.37). So for low-complexity left main disease CABG is not better on death or the main composite — it is better on infarction and durability, and worse on early stroke. PROPOSED SPLIT (death and the main composite at low complexity: the strategies made no significant difference; spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation: CABG better; early stroke: PCI better).

cards.headline: Individual-patient meta-analysis of all four left-main trials (median SYNTAX 25 — largely low/intermediate complexity): 5-year death 11.2% PCI vs 10.2% CABG (HR 1.10, not significant), but spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation clearly favoured CABG
cards.summary: Individual-patient meta-analysis of all four left-main trials (median SYNTAX 25 — largely low/intermediate complexity): 5-year death 11.2% PCI vs 10.2% CABG (HR 1.10, not significant), but spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation clearly favoured CABG
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials
cards.people: Individual patient data meta-analysis of the four randomised trials of PCI with drug-eluting stents versus CABG in left main coronary artery disease with at least 5 years of mortality follow-up (SYNTAX, PRECOMBAT, NOBLE and EXCEL): 4,394 patients, median SYNTAX score 25.0 (IQR 18.0-31.0), randomly assigned to PCI (n=2,197) or CABG (n=2,197). The EXCEL and NOBLE primary reports are carded on live shelf #551 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: The Kaplan-Meier estimate of 5-year all-cause death was 11.2% (95% CI 9.9-12.6) with PCI and 10.2% (9.0-11.6) with CABG (hazard ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.91-1.32; p=0.33) — a non-statistically significant absolute difference of 0.9% (95% CI -0.9 to 2.8); Bayesian analysis gave an 85.7% probability that 5-year death was greater with PCI, the difference more likely than not being under 1.0% (under 0.2% per year). Spontaneous myocardial infarction (6.2% vs 2.6%; HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.71-3.23; p<0.0001) and repeat revascularisation (18.3% vs 10.7%; HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.51-2.10; p<0.0001) were more common with PCI. Overall stroke did not differ (2.7% vs 3.1%; HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.59-1.21; p=0.36) but was lower with PCI in the first year (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.19-0.69). The authors describe the population as having, largely, low or intermediate coronary anatomical complexity.
cards.watchOut: 'Largely low or intermediate complexity' is the pooled population (median SYNTAX 25), not a low-SYNTAX-only subgroup analysis: the mortality estimate mixes low with intermediate scores, and the Bayesian signal means 'no significant difference' should not be read as proven equivalence.
cards.source: Sabatine MS et al. cards.headline: SYNTAX-stratified meta-analysis: at low-to-intermediate SYNTAX scores the strategies were in equipoise on MACCE (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70); the CABG advantage appeared only at high SYNTAX scores (HR 1.64)
cards.summary: SYNTAX-stratified meta-analysis: at low-to-intermediate SYNTAX scores the strategies were in equipoise on MACCE (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70); the CABG advantage appeared only at high SYNTAX scores (HR 1.64)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, SYNTAX-stratified
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the 4 randomised trials comparing 5-year outcomes of PCI with drug-eluting stents versus CABG in left main coronary artery disease: 4,394 patients (PCI n=2,197; CABG n=2,197), with outcomes stratified by SYNTAX (Synergy Between PCI with TAXUS and Cardiac Surgery) score.
cards.result: Compared with CABG, PCI showed non-inferiority on the composite of death, myocardial infarction and stroke (HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.84-1.75), death (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.81-1.40) and stroke (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.42-1.53). For major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events (MACCE), both strategies showed clinical equipoise in patients with a low-to-intermediate SYNTAX score (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70), while CABG had an advantage over PCI in those with a high SYNTAX score (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.20-2.24). PCI carried a higher risk of repeat revascularisation.
cards.watchOut: The low-complexity stratum here is 'low-to-intermediate' combined, and the same four trials underlie both meta-analyses on this shelf — they are two analyses of one evidence base, not independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Pooled analysis of the same four trials in predominantly low-to-intermediate complexity disease: 5-year mortality similar with PCI and CABG with and without ACS (11.3% vs 9.6% without ACS; HR 1.19, not significant)
cards.summary: Pooled analysis of the same four trials in predominantly low-to-intermediate complexity disease: 5-year mortality similar with PCI and CABG with and without ACS (11.3% vs 9.6% without ACS; HR 1.19, not significant)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of 4 randomised trials (ACS subgroup)
cards.people: Pooled individual patient data from SYNTAX, PRECOMBAT, NOBLE and EXCEL: 4,394 patients with left main disease (median age 66 years; 76.7% male), of whom 1,466 (33%) presented with an acute coronary syndrome; the record describes the population as largely stable patients with predominantly low to intermediate coronary anatomical complexity.
cards.result: Rates of all-cause mortality through 5 years with PCI versus CABG were 10.9% versus 11.5% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.68-1.27) in patients with ACS and 11.3% versus 9.6% (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.95-1.50) in patients without ACS (P=0.22 for interaction). Early stroke risk was lower with PCI versus CABG (no ACS: HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.75), whereas 5-year risks of spontaneous MI (no ACS: HR 3.03, 95% CI 1.94-4.72) and repeat revascularisation (no ACS: HR 1.90, 95% CI 1.54-2.33) were higher with PCI, regardless of ACS status.
cards.watchOut: This pooled analysis is stratified by ACS presentation, not by SYNTAX score; it is carded because its population is predominantly low-to-intermediate complexity, and its mortality figures should be read as the same four-trial evidence base seen from a second angle.

pooled analysis of 4 randomised trials (acs subgroup) pooled individual patient data from syntax, precombat, noble and excel: 4,394 patients with left main disease (median age 66 years; 76.7% male), of whom 1,466 (33%) presented with an acute coronary syndrome; the record describes the population as largely stable patients with predominantly low to intermediate coronary anatomical complexity. rates of all-cause mortality through 5 years with pci versus cabg were 10.9% versus 11.5% (hr 0.93, 95% ci 0.68-1.27) in patients with acs and 11.3% versus 9.6% (hr 1.19, 95% ci 0.95-1.50) in patients without acs (p=0.22 for interaction). early stroke risk was lower with pci versus cabg (no acs: hr 0.35, 95% ci 0.16-0.75), whereas 5-year risks of spontaneous mi (no acs: hr 3.03, 95% ci 1.94-4.72) and repeat revascularisation (no acs: hr 1.90, 95% ci 1.54-2.33) were higher with pci, regardless of acs status. this pooled analysis is stratified by acs presentation, not by syntax score; it is carded because its population is predominantly low-to-intermediate complexity, and its mortality figures should be read as the same four-trial evidence base seen from a second angle. gaba p et al. percutaneous coronary intervention vs coronary artery bypass graft surgery for left main disease in patients with and without acute coronary syndromes: a pooled analysis of 4 randomized clinical trials. jama cardiology. 2023. pmid: 37256598. registry id: nct01496651. mesh: humans · male · female · aged · randomized controlled trials as topic · percutaneous coronary intervention · coronary artery bypass · acute coronary syndrome · atherosclerosis · middle aged · stroke · coronary artery disease

cards.headline: Synthesis: in low-complexity left main disease CABG is not better on death or the main composite — its advantages are fewer spontaneous infarctions and fewer repeat procedures; PCI's advantage is fewer early strokes
cards.summary: Synthesis: in low-complexity left main disease CABG is not better on death or the main composite — its advantages are fewer spontaneous infarctions and fewer repeat procedures; PCI's advantage is fewer early strokes
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses and one pooled analysis, all of the same four randomised trials (SYNTAX, PRECOMBAT, NOBLE, EXCEL; 4,394 unique patients, median SYNTAX score 25.0). Total unique participants 4,394, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Five-year all-cause death did not differ significantly (11.2% PCI vs 10.2% CABG; HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.91-1.32), and at low-to-intermediate SYNTAX scores MACCE was in equipoise (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70). Spontaneous MI (6.2% vs 2.6%; HR 2.35) and repeat revascularisation (18.3% vs 10.7%; HR 1.78) favoured CABG; first-year stroke favoured PCI (HR 0.37). PROPOSED SPLIT (no significant difference on death/composite at low complexity; CABG better on MI and repeat revascularisation; PCI better on early stroke).
cards.watchOut: Every card on this shelf re-analyses the same four trials whose primary reports are homed on live shelf #551; there is no low-SYNTAX-only randomised trial, so the low-complexity answer is a subgroup reading of the general left-main evidence, printed as such.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sabatine MS et al. Lancet (London, England). 2021 (PMID: 34793745); Zhang J et al. Atherosclerosis. 2020 (PMID: 32713512); Gaba P et al. JAMA cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 37256598).

shelves.title: Aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban in stable coronary disease (partial completion of the post-ACS shelf #3333): the COMPASS combination cut events and mortality, with more major gastrointestinal bleeding
shelves.question: Does aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban reduce events in stable coronary disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Artery Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Morbidity · Myocardial Infarction · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Rivaroxaban · Stroke
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3333, which covers low-dose rivaroxaban added to antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome (the ATLAS ACS programme); this shelf covers the different population of stable coronary disease — the COMPASS population. The COMPASS primary report (PMID: 28844192) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on the trial's free stable-coronary-disease reports. In the dedicated coronary artery disease report (24,824 patients with stable CAD), rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily reduced the primary outcome of myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death versus aspirin alone (4% vs 6%; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.86) and reduced mortality (3% vs 4%; HR 0.77) — a 26% relative reduction in the primary outcome alongside a 2-percentage-point absolute difference — at the cost of more major bleeding (3% vs 2%; HR 1.66), mostly gastrointestinal, with no significant increase in intracranial or critical-organ bleeding. The benefit was consistent in women and men (MACE HR 0.72 and 0.76) and in patients with and without diabetes (primary-endpoint HR 0.74 and 0.77, with larger absolute reductions in diabetes), and stroke was roughly halved (HR 0.58). Rivaroxaban alone (5 mg twice daily) did not significantly improve the primary outcome in the CAD report (HR 0.89, p=0.094) — the benefit belongs to the combination. Because this is a single trial programme, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban reduces cardiovascular events and mortality in stable coronary disease, with more major (mainly gastrointestinal) bleeding.

cards.headline: COMPASS coronary-disease report (24,824 patients with stable CAD): rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin cut the primary outcome to 4% vs 6% (HR 0.74) and mortality to 3% vs 4% (HR 0.77), with major bleeding up to 3% vs 2% (HR 1.66)
cards.summary: COMPASS coronary-disease report (24,824 patients with stable CAD): rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin cut the primary outcome to 4% vs 6% (HR 0.74) and mortality to 3% vs 4% (HR 0.77), with major bleeding up to 3% vs 2% (HR 1.66)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial report, coronary artery disease population (COMPASS)
cards.people: 24,824 patients with stable coronary artery disease within the COMPASS trial (27,395 patients with stable coronary or peripheral artery disease enrolled at 602 centres in 33 countries), randomly assigned to rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily (8,313 patients), rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily alone (8,250) or aspirin alone (8,261). Eligible patients had prior myocardial infarction within 20 years, multivessel coronary disease, stable or unstable angina history, or prior multivessel PCI or bypass surgery. The COMPASS primary report is carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: The combination reduced the primary outcome (myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death) versus aspirin alone (347 [4%] of 8,313 vs 460 [6%] of 8,261; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.86, p<0.0001) — a 26% relative reduction with a 2-percentage-point absolute difference. Rivaroxaban alone did not significantly improve the primary outcome (411 [5%] of 8,250 vs 460 [6%]; HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.78-1.02, p=0.094). Major bleeding was more frequent with the combination (263 [3%] vs 158 [2%]; HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.37-2.03, p<0.0001), most commonly gastrointestinal (130 [2%] vs 61 [1%]), with no significant increase in intracranial or other critical-organ bleeding in the record. Mortality was lower with the combination (262 [3%] vs 339 [4%]; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.65-0.90, p=0.0012).
cards.watchOut: This is the coronary-disease report of one trial whose primary report is homed elsewhere in the library; the trial was stopped early for efficacy, which can exaggerate benefit, and the bleeding excess is the price printed on the same card.
cards.source: Connolly SJ et al. Rivaroxaban with or without aspirin in patients with stable coronary artery disease: an international, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 29132879. Registry ID: NCT01776424. cards.headline: COMPASS by sex: the combination's benefit was consistent in women and men (MACE HR 0.72 and 0.76), as was the bleeding increase (HR 2.22 and 1.60)
cards.summary: COMPASS by sex: the combination's benefit was consistent in women and men (MACE HR 0.72 and 0.76), as was the bleeding increase (HR 2.22 and 1.60)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (COMPASS)
cards.people: Sex-based analysis of the COMPASS comparison of rivaroxaban plus aspirin versus aspirin alone: 18,278 patients allocated to those two arms, of whom 22.1% were women; mean follow-up 23 months. The analysis covers patients with chronic coronary or peripheral artery disease.
cards.result: The combination's effect on major adverse cardiovascular events was consistent by sex (women: 3.8% vs 5.2%, HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.97; men: 4.2% vs 5.5%, HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.66-0.89; P interaction 0.75), as was the effect on major bleeding (women: 3.1% vs 1.4%, HR 2.22, 95% CI 1.42-3.46; men: 3.2% vs 2.0%, HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.29-1.97; P interaction 0.19). The trial overall reduced MACE by 24% relative during a mean follow-up of 23 months, as stated in the record. There was no significant interaction with baseline modified REACH risk score for MACE or major bleeding.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup consistency analysis of the same single trial — it shows the COMPASS result is not driven by one sex, but it is not independent evidence and mixes coronary with peripheral artery disease patients.
cards.source: Liang Y et al. Efficacy and safety of rivaroxaban plus aspirin in women and men with chronic coronary or peripheral artery disease. Cardiovascular research. 2021. PMID: 32289159. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: COMPASS in diabetes: similar relative benefit with and without diabetes (primary-endpoint HR 0.74 and 0.77), with larger absolute reductions in diabetes (2.3% vs 1.4% at 3 years)
cards.summary: COMPASS in diabetes: similar relative benefit with and without diabetes (primary-endpoint HR 0.74 and 0.77), with larger absolute reductions in diabetes (2.3% vs 1.4% at 3 years)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (COMPASS)
cards.people: Prespecified COMPASS analysis by diabetes status: 10,341 patients with diabetes mellitus and 17,054 without, among patients with established coronary or peripheral artery disease; the comparison is rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin (n=9,152) versus placebo plus aspirin (n=9,126).
cards.result: Relative risk reductions for the primary efficacy endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) were similar with diabetes (hazard ratio 0.74, P=0.002) and without (HR 0.77, P=0.005; P interaction 0.77), as for all-cause mortality (HR 0.81 and 0.84; P interaction 0.82). Absolute risk reductions appeared larger with diabetes: 2.3% versus 1.4% for the primary endpoint at 3 years, 1.9% versus 0.6% for all-cause mortality and 2.7% versus 1.7% for major vascular events. Bleeding hazards were similar by diabetes status, and the prespecified net benefit favoured the combination particularly in diabetes (2.7% versus 1.0%).
cards.watchOut: Absolute-benefit differences between subgroups reflect higher baseline risk in diabetes rather than a different drug effect — the record itself reports similar relative effects, and this remains one trial's data.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Role of Combination Antiplatelet and Anticoagulation Therapy in Diabetes Mellitus and Cardiovascular Disease: Insights From the COMPASS Trial. Circulation. 2020. PMID: 32223318. Registry ID: NCT01776424. cards.headline: COMPASS stroke analysis: the combination roughly halved stroke versus aspirin (0.9% vs 1.6% per year; HR 0.58), driven by ischaemic stroke (HR 0.51), including fewer fatal and disabling strokes
cards.summary: COMPASS stroke analysis: the combination roughly halved stroke versus aspirin (0.9% vs 1.6% per year; HR 0.58), driven by ischaemic stroke (HR 0.51), including fewer fatal and disabling strokes
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (COMPASS)
cards.people: Detailed stroke analysis of the full COMPASS population with stable coronary or peripheral artery disease: aspirin 100 mg daily (n=9,126), rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily (n=9,117), or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin (n=9,152); mean follow-up 23 months. Patients needing anticoagulation or with recent, lacunar or haemorrhagic stroke were excluded.
cards.result: Fewer patients had strokes on the combination than on aspirin (83 [0.9% per year] versus 142 [1.6% per year]; hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.44-0.76; P<0.0001). Ischaemic or uncertain strokes were reduced by nearly half (68 [0.7% per year] versus 132 [1.4% per year]; HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.38-0.68; P<0.0001). Fatal and disabling stroke (modified Rankin Scale 3-6) was also reduced (32 [0.3% per year] versus 55 [0.6% per year]; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37-0.89; P=0.01). Rivaroxaban alone showed no significant stroke difference versus aspirin (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.65-1.05). Prior stroke was the strongest predictor of incident stroke (HR 3.63).
cards.watchOut: Stroke was a component of the primary outcome, not the trial's sole question, and patients with prior lacunar or haemorrhagic stroke were excluded — the stroke benefit applies to the COMPASS-eligible stable population.
cards.source: Sharma M et al. Stroke Outcomes in the COMPASS Trial. Circulation. 2019. PMID: 30667279. Registry ID: NCT01776424. shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #4163, which covers DAPT de-escalation strategy in stabilised acute myocardial infarction; this shelf covers the different setting of complex PCI specifically, across presentations. The direct complex-PCI evidence points the same way on bleeding. In the TWILIGHT complex-PCI analysis (2,342 patients who had completed 3 months of ticagrelor plus aspirin), dropping aspirin and continuing ticagrelor alone halved clinically relevant bleeding (BARC type 2, 3 or 5: 4.2% vs 7.7%; hazard ratio 0.54) and major bleeding (BARC 3 or 5: 1.1% vs 2.6%; HR 0.41), with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (3.8% vs 4.9%; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15). A meta-analysis of 5 trials (8,328 complex-PCI patients) found major bleeding significantly reduced by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after 1-3 months of DAPT, consistently in complex and non-complex strata, with similar death, stent thrombosis and stroke — and, unexpectedly, less myocardial infarction in the complex stratum (HR 0.77). The SMART-CHOICE complex post-hoc analysis (498 patients, mostly clopidogrel monotherapy) likewise found no ischaemic penalty. The honest counterweight is STOPDAPT-3's complex subgroup, where clopidogrel monotherapy after 1 month did not beat aspirin monotherapy on bleeding (2.1% vs 2.7%, no significant interaction) — a comparison of two monotherapies, not of monotherapy versus continued DAPT. The evidence is subgroup and post-hoc analyses of trials not randomised on complexity, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — short DAPT followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy reduces bleeding after complex PCI without a detected ischaemic penalty, on subgroup-level evidence.

cards.headline: TWILIGHT complex PCI (2,342 patients): after 3 months of DAPT, ticagrelor monotherapy halved bleeding versus continued DAPT (BARC 2, 3 or 5: 4.2% vs 7.7%; HR 0.54; BARC 3 or 5: 1.1% vs 2.6%; HR 0.41), with no significant ischaemic difference
cards.summary: TWILIGHT complex PCI (2,342 patients): after 3 months of DAPT, ticagrelor monotherapy halved bleeding versus continued DAPT (BARC 2, 3 or 5: 4.2% vs 7.7%; HR 0.54; BARC 3 or 5: 1.1% vs 2.6%; HR 0.41), with no significant ischaemic difference
cards.type: Prespecified analysis of a randomised trial, complex-PCI subgroup (TWILIGHT)
cards.people: 2,342 patients undergoing complex PCI within the randomised, double-blind TWILIGHT trial (7,119 patients randomised overall): after 3 months of ticagrelor plus aspirin, event-free and adherent patients continued ticagrelor and were assigned to aspirin or placebo for 1 year. Complex PCI was defined as any of: 3 vessels treated, 3 or more lesions treated, total stent length over 60 mm, bifurcation with 2 stents, atherectomy use, left main PCI, bypass-graft or chronic total occlusion target lesions.
cards.result: Compared with ticagrelor plus aspirin, ticagrelor plus placebo (monotherapy) significantly lowered BARC type 2, 3 or 5 bleeding (4.2% vs 7.7%; hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.76) and BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding (1.1% vs 2.6%; HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80) at 1 year after randomisation. There were no significant between-group differences in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (3.8% vs 4.9%; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15), nor in stent thrombosis (no effect size printed in the record for stent thrombosis).
cards.watchOut: Only patients who completed the first 3 months of DAPT event-free and adherent were randomised, so the bleeding rates apply to that selected, lower-risk remainder — and the ischaemic confidence interval (0.52-1.15) cannot exclude a modest ischaemic increase.
cards.source: Dangas G et al. Ticagrelor With or Without Aspirin After Complex PCI. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2020. PMID: 32240761. Registry ID: NCT02270242. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 5 trials (8,328 complex-PCI patients): P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after 1-3 months of DAPT significantly reduced major bleeding, consistently across complexity strata, with similar death, stent thrombosis and stroke
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 5 trials (8,328 complex-PCI patients): P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after 1-3 months of DAPT significantly reduced major bleeding, consistently across complexity strata, with similar death, stent thrombosis and stroke
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials, complex-PCI strata
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised trials of P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after a short course of DAPT (1-3 months) versus standard DAPT (12 months or more): 5 trials, 31,627 patients, of whom 8,328 (26.3%) underwent complex PCI; protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021291027).
cards.result: P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy was associated with a similar risk of all-cause death, stent thrombosis and stroke to standard DAPT, with no evidence of interaction between complex and non-complex PCI strata. The risk of major bleeding was significantly reduced by monotherapy with a consistent treatment effect in both strata (P interaction 0.699; the record prints no pooled bleeding hazard ratio). For myocardial infarction there was heterogeneity (P interaction 0.027): monotherapy decreased MI risk in complex PCI (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60-0.99; P=0.042) but not in non-complex PCI (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.90-1.30). The authors conclude complex-PCI patients may derive more benefit and less harm from monotherapy after early aspirin withdrawal.
cards.watchOut: The pooled bleeding hazard ratio is not printed in the record, so the size of the pooled bleeding benefit cannot be quoted from this card — the quantified bleeding numbers on this shelf come from the TWILIGHT complex analysis; the complex-stratum MI finding is a subgroup interaction and should be read cautiously.
cards.source: Oliva A et al. P2Y12 Inhibitors Monotherapy in Patients Undergoing Complex vs Non-Complex Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials. cards.headline: SMART-CHOICE complex post-hoc (498 patients): P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy (78% clopidogrel) after 3 months of DAPT did not increase ischaemic events versus 12 months of DAPT (MACCE 3.8% vs 4.2%; HR 0.92)
cards.summary: SMART-CHOICE complex post-hoc (498 patients): P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy (78% clopidogrel) after 3 months of DAPT did not increase ischaemic events versus 12 months of DAPT (MACCE 3.8% vs 4.2%; HR 0.92)
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial, complex-PCI subgroup (SMART-CHOICE)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the SMART-CHOICE randomised trial (2,993 patients), including 498 complex PCIs defined by at least one of: 3 vessels treated, 3 or more stents implanted, 3 or more lesions treated, bifurcation with 2 or more stents, or total stent length 60 mm or more. Monotherapy was a P2Y12 inhibitor, mostly clopidogrel (78%).
cards.result: The complex-PCI group had a higher risk of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) than the non-complex group (4.0% vs 2.3%; HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.05-2.89; p=0.033) and a similar bleeding risk (BARC types 2-5: 2.6% vs 2.6%; HR 1.02). Within complex PCI, patients followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy versus 12 months of DAPT had similar MACCE rates (3.8% vs 4.2%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.38-2.21; p=0.853). The record reports no treatment-arm bleeding rates within the complex subgroup, so no bleeding effect size can be printed from this card.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and small (498 complex patients; MACCE confidence interval 0.38-2.21 is wide), and the monotherapy here is mostly clopidogrel rather than ticagrelor — it supports the absence of a large ischaemic penalty, not a bleeding claim.
cards.source: Roh JW et al. P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy in complex percutaneous coronary intervention: A post-hoc analysis of SMART-CHOICE randomized clinical trial. Cardiology journal. 2021. cards.headline: STOPDAPT-3 complex subgroup (1,415 patients): clopidogrel monotherapy beyond 1 month did not beat aspirin monotherapy on bleeding (2.1% vs 2.7%, no significant interaction) — the choice of monotherapy agent, not monotherapy itself, was what differed
cards.summary: STOPDAPT-3 complex subgroup (1,415 patients): clopidogrel monotherapy beyond 1 month did not beat aspirin monotherapy on bleeding (2.1% vs 2.7%, no significant interaction) — the choice of monotherapy agent, not monotherapy itself, was what differed
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (STOPDAPT-3)
cards.people: Prespecified complex-PCI subgroup of the STOPDAPT-3 trial's 30-day landmark analysis (N=5,833), including 1,415 patients (24.3%) who underwent complex PCI. The trial compared 1-month DAPT followed by aspirin monotherapy with 1-month prasugrel monotherapy followed by clopidogrel monotherapy.
cards.result: There was a significant interaction between complex PCI and the effect of the aspirin group relative to the clopidogrel group for cardiovascular events (complex PCI: 3.3% vs 5.2%; non-complex PCI: 4.3% vs 3.6%; interaction P=0.04) and net adverse clinical events (complex PCI: 4.8% vs 7.2%; non-complex: 5.3% vs 4.4%; interaction P=0.02), but not for bleeding events (complex PCI: 2.1% vs 2.7%; non-complex: 1.7% vs 1.4%; interaction P=0.35). The record attributes the cardiovascular-event interaction to a numerically lower risk with aspirin monotherapy in complex PCI.
cards.watchOut: Both arms stopped DAPT at 1 month — this card compares two monotherapies and cannot test monotherapy against continued DAPT; it is carded so the shelf does not imply every short-DAPT comparison after complex PCI favours the P2Y12 inhibitor.
cards.source: Domei T et al. Aspirin vs. clopidogrel monotherapy beyond 1 month after complex percutaneous coronary intervention: a pre-specified subgroup analysis of the STOPDAPT-3 trial. European heart journal. Cardiovascular pharmacotherapy. 2025. PMID: 39863419. Registry ID: NCT04609111. cards.headline: Synthesis: after complex PCI, dropping aspirin after 1-3 months of DAPT and continuing a P2Y12 inhibitor alone reduces bleeding (TWILIGHT major bleeding 1.1% vs 2.6%) with no detected ischaemic penalty — on subgroup-level, not complexity-randomised, evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: after complex PCI, dropping aspirin after 1-3 months of DAPT and continuing a P2Y12 inhibitor alone reduces bleeding (TWILIGHT major bleeding 1.1% vs 2.6%) with no detected ischaemic penalty — on subgroup-level, not complexity-randomised, evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: TWILIGHT complex analysis (2,342 patients), a 5-trial meta-analysis (8,328 complex-PCI patients among 31,627), SMART-CHOICE complex post-hoc (498 patients) and STOPDAPT-3 complex subgroup (1,415 patients). Unique participants exceed 10,000 across non-overlapping trial populations (the meta-analysis overlaps the trial analyses), so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Bleeding: BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding 4.2% versus 7.7% (HR 0.54) and BARC 3 or 5 bleeding 1.1% versus 2.6% (HR 0.41) with ticagrelor monotherapy in TWILIGHT; major bleeding significantly reduced in the meta-analysis with consistent effects by complexity. Ischaemic outcomes: no significant differences in death, MI or stroke in TWILIGHT (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15) or MACCE in SMART-CHOICE (HR 0.92). STOPDAPT-3 shows the agent chosen for monotherapy also matters. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No trial randomised patients on PCI complexity itself, and the de-escalation-in-AMI strategy homed on live shelf #4163 is a different question; this shelf's POSSIBLE stamp reflects subgroup evidence in the complex-PCI slice only.

shelves.title: Ranolazine in chronic coronary syndrome generally (partial completion of the post-PCI shelf #3087): consistent, modest symptom and exercise benefit across CARISA, TERISA and MERLIN — and no hard-event benefit
shelves.question: Does ranolazine improve angina symptoms in chronic coronary syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Acetanilides · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Aged · Amlodipine · Angina Pectoris · Atenolol · Calcium Channel Blockers · Cardiovascular Agents · Chronic Disease · Diltiazem · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Electrocardiography · Exercise Test · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia · Nitroglycerin · Piperazines · Ranolazine · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3087, which covers ranolazine only in angina with incomplete revascularisation after PCI (the RIVER-PCI population); this shelf covers chronic coronary syndrome generally — stable angina on background antianginal therapy, most of it never randomised around a PCI. The general stable-angina trials are concordant on symptoms. CARISA (823 patients with severe chronic angina on atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem) increased trough exercise duration more with ranolazine than placebo (115.6 vs 91.7 seconds gained; P=0.01) and cut angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week. TERISA (949 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic stable angina) reduced weekly angina episodes (3.8 vs 4.3; p=0.008) and nitroglycerin doses (1.7 vs 2.1; p=0.003). In the MERLIN-TIMI 36 chronic-angina subgroup (3,565 patients with prior angina), ranolazine reduced recurrent ischaemia (HR 0.78) and worsening angina (HR 0.77) but made no difference to cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction (HR 0.97). An updated meta-analysis of 18 trials (12,995 patients) found exercise duration up by 30 seconds and time to angina onset up by 40 seconds versus placebo. The benefit is symptomatic and functional — modest in absolute terms (about half an angina episode and 30 seconds of exercise) — with no mortality or infarction benefit shown. The RIVER-PCI report and the earlier stable-disease meta-analysis carded on #3087 are not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — ranolazine improves angina symptoms and exercise tolerance in chronic coronary syndrome, with no demonstrated reduction in death or myocardial infarction.

cards.headline: CARISA (823 patients with severe chronic angina): ranolazine on top of atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem increased trough exercise duration by 115.6 vs 91.7 seconds (P=0.01) and cut angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week
cards.summary: CARISA (823 patients with severe chronic angina): ranolazine on top of atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem increased trough exercise duration by 115.6 vs 91.7 seconds (P=0.01) and cut angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week
cards.people: 823 adults with symptomatic severe chronic angina at 118 outpatient settings, randomly assigned to twice-daily placebo or ranolazine 750 mg or 1000 mg, on standard doses of atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem; enrolled 1999-2001 in the Combination Assessment of Ranolazine In Stable Angina (CARISA) trial, with treadmill exercise testing at trough and peak after 2, 6 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: Trough exercise duration increased by 115.6 seconds from baseline in the pooled ranolazine groups versus 91.7 seconds in the placebo group (P=0.01); times to angina onset and to electrocardiographic ischaemia also increased, at peak more than at trough, independent of blood pressure, heart rate or background therapy, and persisted through 12 weeks. Ranolazine reduced angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week versus placebo (P<0.02). Survival among 750 patients taking ranolazine in the trial or its open-label extension was 98.4% at 1 year and 95.9% at 2 years (observational extension data, as reported in the record).
cards.watchOut: A 12-week symptom and exercise trial from the pre-contemporary-therapy era (1999-2001 enrolment): it proves short-term symptomatic benefit on top of one background agent, not long-term outcomes, and the survival figures come from an uncontrolled open-label extension.
cards.source: Chaitman BR et al. Effects of ranolazine with atenolol, amlodipine, or diltiazem on exercise tolerance and angina frequency in patients with severe chronic angina: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 14734593. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial (carisa) 823 adults with symptomatic severe chronic angina at 118 outpatient settings, randomly assigned to twice-daily placebo or ranolazine 750 mg or 1000 mg, on standard doses of atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem; enrolled 1999-2001 in the combination assessment of ranolazine in stable angina (carisa) trial, with treadmill exercise testing at trough and peak after 2, 6 and 12 weeks. trough exercise duration increased by 115.6 seconds from baseline in the pooled ranolazine groups versus 91.7 seconds in the placebo group (p=0.01); times to angina onset and to electrocardiographic ischaemia also increased, at peak more than at trough, independent of blood pressure, heart rate or background therapy, and persisted through 12 weeks. ranolazine reduced angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week versus placebo (p<0.02). survival among 750 patients taking ranolazine in the trial or its open-label extension was 98.4% at 1 year and 95.9% at 2 years (observational extension data, as reported in the record). a 12-week symptom and exercise trial from the pre-contemporary-therapy era (1999-2001 enrolment): it proves short-term symptomatic benefit on top of one background agent, not long-term outcomes, and the survival figures come from an uncontrolled open-label extension. chaitman br et al. effects of ranolazine with atenolol, amlodipine, or diltiazem on exercise tolerance and angina frequency in patients with severe chronic angina: a randomized controlled trial. jama. 2004. pmid: 14734593. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acetanilides · adrenergic beta-antagonists · aged · amlodipine · angina pectoris · atenolol · calcium channel blockers · cardiovascular agents · chronic disease · diltiazem · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · electrocardiography · exercise test · female · hemodynamics · humans · male · middle aged · myocardial ischemia · nitroglycerin · piperazines · ranolazine · survival analysis

cards.headline: TERISA (949 patients with diabetes and chronic stable angina): ranolazine reduced weekly angina episodes to 3.8 vs 4.3 (p=0.008) and nitroglycerin use to 1.7 vs 2.1 doses (p=0.003) over 8 weeks
cards.summary: TERISA (949 patients with diabetes and chronic stable angina): ranolazine reduced weekly angina episodes to 3.8 vs 4.3 (p=0.008) and nitroglycerin use to 1.7 vs 2.1 doses (p=0.003) over 8 weeks
cards.people: 949 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease and chronic stable angina despite 1 to 2 antianginal agents, at 104 centres in 14 countries; mean age 64 years, 61% men, mean diabetes duration 7.5 years, mean baseline HbA1c 7.3%. After a 4-week single-blind placebo run-in, patients were randomised to 8 weeks of ranolazine (target 1000 mg twice daily) or placebo, with angina and nitroglycerin use recorded in a daily electronic diary (98% data capture).
cards.result: Weekly angina frequency over the last 6 weeks was significantly lower with ranolazine than placebo (3.8 [95% CI 3.6-4.1] episodes vs 4.3 [95% CI 4.0-4.5]; p=0.008), as was weekly sublingual nitroglycerin use (1.7 [95% CI 1.6-1.9] doses vs 2.1 [95% CI 1.9-2.3]; p=0.003). There was no difference in the incidence of serious adverse events between groups.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain is about half an angina episode per week over 8 weeks in a diabetes-only population — statistically clear, clinically modest — and the placebo run-in design enriches for diary-adherent patients.
cards.source: Kosiborod M et al. Evaluation of ranolazine in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic stable angina: results from the TERISA randomized clinical trial (Type 2 Diabetes Evaluation of Ranolazine in Subjects With Chronic Stable Angina). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2013. PMID: 23500237. Registry ID: NCT01425359. cards.headline: MERLIN-TIMI 36 chronic-angina subgroup (3,565 patients): ranolazine reduced recurrent ischaemia (HR 0.78) and worsening angina (HR 0.77), but cardiovascular death or MI did not differ (HR 0.97 — the treatment made no difference to hard events)
cards.summary: MERLIN-TIMI 36 chronic-angina subgroup (3,565 patients): ranolazine reduced recurrent ischaemia (HR 0.78) and worsening angina (HR 0.77), but cardiovascular death or MI did not differ (HR 0.97 — the treatment made no difference to hard events)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (MERLIN-TIMI 36)
cards.people: Subgroup of 3,565 patients (54% of the trial) with prior chronic angina enrolled in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled MERLIN-TIMI 36 trial of patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome; median follow-up 350 days. Patients received evidence-based therapy (95% aspirin, 78% statins, 89% beta-blockers; average 2.9 antianginal agents).
cards.result: The primary endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or recurrent ischaemia) was less frequent with ranolazine (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.75-0.97; p=0.017), due entirely to a reduction in recurrent ischaemia (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.91; p=0.002). Ranolazine also reduced worsening angina (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59-1.00; p=0.048) and intensification of antianginal therapy (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64-0.92; p=0.005), and exercise duration at 8 months was greater (514 s vs 482 s; p=0.002). Cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction did not differ (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.80-1.16; p=0.71), nor did symptomatic arrhythmias (2.9% vs 2.9%) or total mortality (6.2% vs 6.4%).
cards.watchOut: These patients entered the trial with an acute coronary syndrome, so this is chronic angina observed through an ACS trial — the symptomatic findings align with the stable-angina trials, but the population is higher-risk than ordinary chronic coronary syndrome.
cards.source: Wilson SR et al. Efficacy of ranolazine in patients with chronic angina observations from the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled MERLIN-TIMI (Metabolic Efficiency With Ranolazine for Less Ischemia in Non-ST-Segment Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes) 36 Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2009. PMID: 19389561. Registry ID: NCT00099788. cards.headline: Updated meta-analysis (18 trials, 12,995 patients): ranolazine increased total exercise duration by 30 seconds and time to angina onset by 40 seconds versus placebo, without changing blood pressure or heart rate
cards.summary: Updated meta-analysis (18 trials, 12,995 patients): ranolazine increased total exercise duration by 30 seconds and time to angina onset by 40 seconds versus placebo, without changing blood pressure or heart rate
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of ranolazine versus placebo in patients with stable angina and macrovascular or microvascular coronary heart disease, searched in PubMed and the Cochrane library to September 2020: 18 trials, 12,995 patients. Trial quality was assessed with the RoB 2 tool. The earlier stable-disease meta-analysis carded on live shelf #3087 is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Ranolazine versus placebo increased total exercise duration by 30 seconds (95% CI 18-42), time to 1 mm ST-segment depression by 44 seconds (95% CI 30-54) and time to angina onset by 40 seconds (95% CI 30-54). Achieved blood pressure and resting heart rate did not differ between arms. The record also reports a 25% relative reduction in atrial fibrillation incidence and a mean HbA1c decrease of 0.4% (95% CI 0.3-0.5%) with ranolazine, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The pooled exercise gains (about 30-40 seconds) are averages across heterogeneous older trials including the CARISA-era studies on this shelf, so this card summarises rather than independently confirms them; the atrial-fibrillation and HbA1c findings are secondary observations, not the shelf's question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ranolazine consistently improves angina symptoms and exercise tolerance in chronic coronary syndrome — by about half an episode a week and about 30 seconds of exercise — with no demonstrated effect on death or myocardial infarction
cards.summary: Synthesis: ranolazine consistently improves angina symptoms and exercise tolerance in chronic coronary syndrome — by about half an episode a week and about 30 seconds of exercise — with no demonstrated effect on death or myocardial infarction
cards.people: The carded evidence: CARISA (823 patients), TERISA (949 patients), the MERLIN-TIMI 36 chronic-angina subgroup (3,565 patients) and an 18-trial meta-analysis (12,995 patients, overlapping the trial cards). Total unique participants exceed 5,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Weekly angina episodes 3.8 versus 4.3 (TERISA); trough exercise duration gain 115.6 versus 91.7 seconds (CARISA) and a pooled 30-second exercise advantage (meta-analysis); recurrent ischaemia HR 0.78 and worsening angina HR 0.77 (MERLIN subgroup); cardiovascular death or MI HR 0.97 — the treatment made no difference to hard events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for symptoms and exercise tolerance only.
cards.watchOut: The post-PCI incomplete-revascularisation population is homed on live shelf #3087 (RIVER-PCI, whose result was neutral on its primary outcome); this shelf's LIKELY applies to the general chronic-coronary-syndrome population and to symptoms, never to prognosis.

shelves.title: Pelacarsen and cardiovascular events (partial completion of the phase-2-lowering shelf #1104): Lp(a)HORIZON has now reported — large Lp(a) lowering, no event reduction (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: Does lowering Lp(a) with pelacarsen reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1104, which covers pelacarsen's phase 2 Lp(a) lowering only, with no outcome data; this shelf covers the cardiovascular-events slice, and the evidence status has changed since that shelf was built: the outcomes trial has now reported. Lp(a)HORIZON randomised 8,350 patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and Lp(a) of at least 70 mg/dL to monthly pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo. Pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) as expected (at 12 months, 64.4 nmol/L versus 233.4 nmol/L from a median baseline of 236 nmol/L), but over a median follow-up of 4.7 years the primary endpoint — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or urgent coronary revascularisation — occurred in 12.3% on pelacarsen and 12.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15; P=0.76): the treatment made no difference. The extended analyses found no benefit in any reframing — on-treatment (HR 0.98), uninterrupted treatment (HR 1.09), total events (rate ratio 1.00), or by achieved Lp(a) reduction — and the result held in the subgroup with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (HR 1.00). A separate phase 3b study confirms the surrogate effect is real and large (86% placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reduction in Black and Hispanic participants), so the null outcome result cannot be blamed on failure to lower Lp(a). One definitive large outcomes trial supports a LIKELY stamp for the null. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit — the treatment made no difference): pelacarsen lowers Lp(a) by roughly 70-86% but did not reduce cardiovascular events in Lp(a)HORIZON.

cards.headline: Lp(a)HORIZON (8,350 patients, median follow-up 4.7 years): pelacarsen cut Lp(a) to 64.4 vs 233.4 nmol/L at 12 months, but major adverse cardiovascular events were 12.3% vs 12.1% (HR 1.02; P=0.76) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: Lp(a)HORIZON (8,350 patients, median follow-up 4.7 years): pelacarsen cut Lp(a) to 64.4 vs 233.4 nmol/L at 12 months, but major adverse cardiovascular events were 12.3% vs 12.1% (HR 1.02; P=0.76) — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: 8,350 patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL, randomly assigned 1:1 to subcutaneous pelacarsen 80 mg monthly (4,157 in the efficacy analysis) or matching placebo (4,165); mean age 59.7 years, 27.0% women, median baseline Lp(a) 236 nmol/L. Median follow-up was 4.7 years. The trial is Lp(a)HORIZON (NCT04023552).
cards.result: At 12 months the Lp(a) level was 64.4 nmol/L in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol/L in the placebo group. A primary end-point event (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularisation) occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) on pelacarsen and 503 (12.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15; P=0.76) — the treatment made no difference. Among patients with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL, events occurred in 402 of 3,266 (12.3%) versus 403 of 3,274 (12.3%) (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.15; P=0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1,553 of 4,166 patients (37.3%) on pelacarsen and 1,709 of 4,154 (41.1%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A single — but large, long and definitive — outcomes trial: its confidence interval (0.90-1.15) excludes the event reduction the Lp(a) hypothesis predicted, yet pelacarsen was given monthly and started after established disease; the null is a result about this drug and regimen, not proof that Lp(a) is non-causal at every exposure window.
cards.source: Cho L et al. Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a). The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 43001734. Registry ID: NCT04023552. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: HORIZON extended analyses: no benefit in any reframing — on-treatment HR 0.98, uninterrupted treatment HR 1.09, total events rate ratio 1.00, and no association with achieved Lp(a) reduction
cards.summary: HORIZON extended analyses: no benefit in any reframing — on-treatment HR 0.98, uninterrupted treatment HR 1.09, total events rate ratio 1.00, and no association with achieved Lp(a) reduction
cards.type: Extended analyses of a randomised outcomes trial (Lp(a)HORIZON)
cards.people: Extended analyses of the Lp(a)HORIZON randomised population (8,322 patients in the efficacy analysis), covering on-treatment and uninterrupted-treatment populations, total (first and recurrent) primary events, 3-month landmark analyses by Lp(a) change and achieved level, and subgroups by baseline Lp(a), LDL cholesterol, high-sensitivity CRP and time from qualifying event.
cards.result: On treatment, a primary end point occurred in 380 participants (9.1%) assigned to pelacarsen and 434 (10.4%) assigned to placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.85-1.12). With uninterrupted treatment, events occurred in 167 participants (11.0%) on pelacarsen and 204 (10.1%) on placebo (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.89-1.34). Total primary events numbered 644 on pelacarsen and 646 on placebo (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.14). In landmark analyses there was no association between treatment and the primary end point in participants with an Lp(a) reduction at or above the median (170 nmol/L) (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.92-1.29) or an achieved Lp(a) at or below the median (69.5 nmol/L) (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.93-1.29), and no association in any key subgroup.
cards.watchOut: These are re-analyses of the same single trial, carded to show the null is robust to exposure and achieved-level framings — not independent confirmation; the on-treatment percentages use different denominators from the main intention-to-treat analysis and should not be compared across cards.

cards.headline: Lp(a)FRONTIERS EXPANSION (423 participants): pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) by 86% placebo-adjusted at 52 weeks in Black and Hispanic patients — confirming the surrogate effect behind the null outcomes result is real
cards.summary: Lp(a)FRONTIERS EXPANSION (423 participants): pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) by 86% placebo-adjusted at 52 weeks in Black and Hispanic patients — confirming the surrogate effect behind the null outcomes result is real
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, surrogate endpoint (Lp(a)FRONTIERS EXPANSION)
cards.people: 423 Black/African American and Hispanic participants in the USA with elevated Lp(a) (at least 125 nmol/L) and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, randomised 2:1 to monthly subcutaneous pelacarsen 80 mg (282 analysed) or placebo (140) for 12 months; median baseline Lp(a) 232.70 nmol/L (pelacarsen) and 219.25 nmol/L (placebo). This phase 3b trial's primary endpoint was Lp(a) change, not clinical events.
cards.result: The geometric mean ratio of Lp(a) to baseline at week 52 was 0.14 (95% CI 0.12-0.16) with pelacarsen and 0.98 (95% CI 0.80-1.20) with placebo; the between-group ratio was 0.14 (95% CI 0.11-0.18; P<0.0001), equivalent to an 86% placebo-adjusted reduction. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 66.0% (186) on pelacarsen and 61.4% (86) on placebo; serious events in 17.0% (48) and 15.0% (21); discontinuations for adverse events in 6.0% (17) and 3.6% (5).
cards.watchOut: A 423-person, 12-month surrogate-endpoint study: it is carded only to document that pelacarsen's Lp(a) lowering is large and consistent, so the HORIZON outcome null cannot be attributed to weak target engagement — it reports no cardiovascular-event comparison.
