cards.headline: Synthesis: pelacarsen lowers Lp(a) by roughly 70-86%, and its one large outcomes trial found no reduction in cardiovascular events (12.3% vs 12.1%; HR 1.02) over 4.7 years — lowering the surrogate did not lower events
cards.summary: Synthesis: pelacarsen lowers Lp(a) by roughly 70-86%, and its one large outcomes trial found no reduction in cardiovascular events (12.3% vs 12.1%; HR 1.02) over 4.7 years — lowering the surrogate did not lower events
cards.people: The carded evidence: Lp(a)HORIZON (8,350 randomised; 8,322 in the efficacy analysis), its extended analyses (same population), and Lp(a)FRONTIERS EXPANSION (423 participants, surrogate endpoint). Total unique participants 8,773, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Lp(a) at 12 months in HORIZON: 64.4 versus 233.4 nmol/L (median baseline 236 nmol/L). Primary events: 12.3% versus 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15; P=0.76) — the treatment made no difference — with null results in every extended framing (on-treatment HR 0.98; total-events rate ratio 1.00; no subgroup association). FRONTIERS confirms an 86% placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reduction. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit — the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Live shelf #1104 holds the phase 2 lowering data (the pelacarsen phase 2 report is carded there and is not re-carded here); this shelf supersedes its 'no outcome data' status for the events question only — other Lp(a)-lowering agents and earlier intervention remain untested by this result.

shelves.title: Evolocumab and clinical events in familial hypercholesterolemia (partial completion of the LDL-lowering shelf #1569): LDL lowering is proven in FH — event lowering in FH has never been trialled and rests on extrapolation
shelves.question: Does evolocumab lower events in familial hypercholesterolemia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents · Blood Component Removal · Cholesterol, LDL · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Homozygote · Humans · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II · Male · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Proprotein Convertase 9
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1569, which covers LDL lowering in familial hypercholesterolemia and ASCVD; this shelf covers the different slice of clinical events in FH specifically — and the honest headline is that the slice is nearly empty. No randomised trial has tested evolocumab against clinical events in an FH population: the events evidence behind evolocumab comes from FOURIER in established ASCVD generally (its primary report, PMID: 28304224, is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here), and no FH-subgroup events report was found in this session's searches. What exists in FH is: TAUSSIG, an open-label, non-randomised study in homozygous FH (106 patients, mean follow-up 1.7 years) in which only four positively adjudicated cardiovascular events occurred, with no comparator group; a Japanese postmarketing single-arm study (3,724 patients, including 2,117 with homozygous or heterozygous FH) reporting myocardial infarction in 0.7% and stroke in 0.3% over 104 weeks, again with no comparator; and a 23-trial meta-analysis of PCSK9-targeting therapies in FH (4,282 patients) whose endpoints are lipid biomarkers and adverse events — LDL cholesterol down 46.64% — not clinical events. LDL lowering in FH is therefore well proven (the #1569 slice) while event lowering in FH is an extrapolation from the general ASCVD trial, not a demonstrated FH result. The evidence is observational and uncontrolled for events, so the stamp is MAYBE. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — evolocumab lowers LDL cholesterol in FH, but whether it lowers clinical events in FH itself is unproven: no FH events trial exists, and the FH event data are four adjudicated events in an uncontrolled homozygous-FH study and uncontrolled registry incidence rates.

cards.headline: TAUSSIG (106 patients with homozygous FH, open-label, no comparator): evolocumab cut LDL cholesterol by 20.6% at 12 weeks; over a mean 1.7 years only four positively adjudicated cardiovascular events occurred — event lowering cannot be judged from this study
cards.summary: TAUSSIG (106 patients with homozygous FH, open-label, no comparator): evolocumab cut LDL cholesterol by 20.6% at 12 weeks; over a mean 1.7 years only four positively adjudicated cardiovascular events occurred — event lowering cannot be judged from this study
cards.people: 106 patients aged 12 years or older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on stable conventional therapy (statins, ezetimibe, with or without apheresis; 34 on apheresis at entry, 14 under 18 years) at 35 sites in 17 countries, all receiving evolocumab 420 mg monthly (every 2 weeks if on apheresis; 47 of 72 non-apheresis patients later increased to every 2 weeks). Interim subset analysis of the open-label, non-randomised TAUSSIG study; mean follow-up 1.7 years (SD 0.63).
cards.result: After 12 weeks, mean LDL cholesterol decreased by 20.6% (SD 24.4; mean absolute decrease 1.50 mmol/L [58 mg/dL]); reductions were maintained at week 48, with an additional mean reduction of 8.3% (0.77 mmol/L [30 mg/dL]) after dose increase in non-apheresis patients. Lipoprotein(a) fell by a median 7.7% at week 12 and 11.9% at week 48. Serious adverse events occurred in 18 patients (17%), the most common being cardiovascular events (four patients [4%]). There were no deaths and four positively adjudicated cardiovascular events — one (3%) among patients on apheresis and three (4%) among those not on apheresis. With no control group, no event-rate comparison or effect size exists in the record.
cards.watchOut: Homozygous FH is the rarest and most severe FH form, the study is uncontrolled, and four events in 106 patients over 1.7 years is a description of what happened on treatment — it cannot show that evolocumab lowered events, and it says nothing direct about the far commoner heterozygous form.
cards.source: Raal FJ et al. Long-term treatment with evolocumab added to conventional drug therapy, with or without apheresis, in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: an interim subset analysis of the open-label TAUSSIG study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28215937. Registry ID: NCT01624142. cards.headline: Japanese postmarketing study (3,724 patients, including 2,117 with FH; single-arm): myocardial infarction incidence 0.7% and stroke 0.3% over 104 weeks on evolocumab — incidence without a comparator, not an event reduction
cards.summary: Japanese postmarketing study (3,724 patients, including 2,117 with FH; single-arm): myocardial infarction incidence 0.7% and stroke 0.3% over 104 weeks on evolocumab — incidence without a comparator, not an event reduction
cards.people: Real-world, postmarketing, single-arm study at 668 sites in Japan: safety set 3,724 patients (homozygous FH n=108; heterozygous FH n=2,009; hypercholesterolaemia with high risk n=1,607), effectiveness set 2,797; mean age 63.2 years; follow-up 104 weeks.
cards.result: Serious adverse drug reactions occurred in 0.5% and serious adverse events in 10.3% of patients; the incidence rates of myocardial infarction and stroke were 0.7% and 0.3% respectively (whole cohort, as reported in the record; FH-specific event rates are not printed separately in the record). Mean LDL cholesterol change at week 12 was -45.7% (SD 28.2) in homozygous FH, -55.9% (SD 28.8) in heterozygous FH and -63.3% (SD 23.7) in high-risk hypercholesterolaemia (all P<0.001). The record reports no comparator group and no relative effect on events.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm registry can show events were uncommon on treatment; without an untreated or standard-care comparator it cannot show evolocumab caused any event rate to be lower, and a third of the cohort did not have FH at all.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 23 FH trials (4,282 patients): PCSK9-targeting therapies cut LDL cholesterol by 46.64% — but the endpoints are lipid biomarkers and adverse events; no clinical-event outcome is reported
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 23 FH trials (4,282 patients): PCSK9-targeting therapies cut LDL cholesterol by 46.64% — but the endpoints are lipid biomarkers and adverse events; no clinical-event outcome is reported
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (lipid endpoints)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 randomised controlled trials of PCSK9-targeting therapies (alirocumab, bococizumab, evolocumab, tafolecimab and inclisiran) versus control on background standard therapy in adults and children with familial hypercholesterolaemia; 4,282 patients; registered on PROSPERO (CRD42025631510).
cards.result: PCSK9-targeting therapies significantly reduced LDL cholesterol versus control (mean difference -46.64%; 95% CI -50.77% to -42.52%; p<0.00001), triglycerides (-15.18%), apolipoprotein B (-34.94%) and lipoprotein(a) (-22.7%). Reductions in LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and apolipoprotein B were larger in heterozygous than homozygous FH. Adverse event rates were comparable to controls. The record reports no cardiovascular-event outcome — the FH randomised evidence base it pools is a biomarker evidence base.
cards.watchOut: This card pools several different PCSK9 agents, not evolocumab alone, and is carded as evidence about the state of the FH literature — across 23 FH trials, events were not the measured outcome — not as evidence that any agent lowers events in FH.
cards.source: Ho VQT et al. PCSK9 targeting therapies for familial hypercholesterolaemia: a meta-analysis of efficacy on lipid biomarkers and safety in adults and children across 23 RCTs. Open heart. 2025. PMID: 40841123. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in FH, evolocumab's LDL lowering is proven and its event lowering is not — the entire FH events record is four adjudicated events in an uncontrolled study and uncontrolled registry incidence rates
cards.summary: Synthesis: in FH, evolocumab's LDL lowering is proven and its event lowering is not — the entire FH events record is four adjudicated events in an uncontrolled study and uncontrolled registry incidence rates
cards.people: The carded evidence: TAUSSIG (106 patients with homozygous FH, uncontrolled), a Japanese postmarketing single-arm study (3,724 patients, 2,117 with FH), and a 23-trial FH meta-analysis (4,282 patients, lipid endpoints). Total carded participants exceed 8,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the limitation here is design (no comparator for events), not size.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell by 20.6% at 12 weeks in homozygous FH (TAUSSIG), by 45.7-55.9% at 12 weeks in the Japanese FH cohorts, and by a pooled 46.64% across FH trials. Clinical events in FH: four positively adjudicated events in TAUSSIG (no comparator); myocardial infarction 0.7% and stroke 0.3% incidence over 104 weeks in the single-arm registry (no comparator); no events endpoint in the 23-trial meta-analysis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — event lowering in FH is unproven and currently rests on extrapolation from ASCVD outcomes trials outside FH.
cards.watchOut: Live shelf #1569 holds the LDL-lowering slice and the general ASCVD outcomes evidence is homed elsewhere in the library (FOURIER primary report, PMID: 28304224, already carded); this shelf must not be cited as showing an FH events benefit that no FH study has measured.

shelves.title: Warfarin intensity after mechanical mitral valve replacement (partial completion of the On-X aortic shelf #3094): PROACT Mitral found no difference between INR targets — and did not prove the lower target noninferior
shelves.question: Does warfarin improve outcomes after mechanical mitral valve replacement compared with lower INR targets?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Warfarin · Anticoagulants · Prospective Studies · Mitral Valve · Thromboembolism · Hemorrhage · Thrombosis · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3094, which covers lower-INR warfarin only for the On-X aortic valve (the PROACT aortic programme); this shelf covers the different and higher-risk mechanical mitral position. The mitral counterpart trial has now reported: PROACT Mitral randomised 401 patients with an On-X mechanical mitral valve, after at least 3 months of standard anticoagulation, to low-dose warfarin (target INR 2.0-2.5) or standard-dose warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5), all on aspirin 81 mg. Over a mean 4.1 years the composite of thromboembolism, valve thrombosis and bleeding was virtually identical (11.9% vs 12.0% per patient-year; difference -0.07%, 95% CI -3.40% to 3.26%), as were its components (thromboembolism 2.3% vs 2.5%; valve thrombosis 0.5% vs 0.5%; bleeding 9.13% vs 9.04% per patient-year) — but the confidence interval crossed the 1.5% noninferiority margin, so low-dose was not proven noninferior: the trial shows no demonstrated advantage for standard intensity on the composite, and no proven safety of the lower target either. Older evidence leans the other way: a meta-analysis of 23,145 mechanical-valve patients found that in the mitral position higher intensity (mean target INR above 3.0) reduced thromboembolism (relative risk 0.74) and total events (RR 0.84) without a significant bleeding increase (RR 1.08, p=0.0524) — though its targets are higher than either PROACT Mitral arm. Supporting randomised data are mixed-population: a D-dimer-guided strategy (starting low, escalating on D-dimer) beat both fixed low and fixed standard intensity in 748 aortic-and-mitral patients, and the small LIWACAP pilot (198 aortic or mitral patients) found low intensity plus aspirin similar to standard-high intensity over the first 6 months (events 5.8% vs 4.3%; p=0.6). PROPOSED SPLIT (the one mitral-specific randomised trial: standard and lower INR targets made no difference to the composite, and noninferiority of the lower target was not achieved; the older meta-analysis: higher intensity reduced total events in mitral valves).

cards.headline: PROACT Mitral (401 patients, On-X mechanical mitral valve): low-dose warfarin (INR 2.0-2.5) versus standard (2.5-3.5) — composite 11.9% vs 12.0% per patient-year, but noninferiority of the low dose was NOT achieved
cards.summary: PROACT Mitral (401 patients, On-X mechanical mitral valve): low-dose warfarin (INR 2.0-2.5) versus standard (2.5-3.5) — composite 11.9% vs 12.0% per patient-year, but noninferiority of the low dose was NOT achieved
cards.people: 401 patients at 44 North American centres who had received an On-X mechanical mitral valve and completed at least 3 months of standard anticoagulation, randomised to low-dose warfarin (target INR 2.0-2.5) or standard-dose warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5); all patients were prescribed aspirin 81 mg daily and encouraged to use home INR testing. Mean follow-up 4.1 years; mean achieved INR 2.47 versus 2.92 (P<0.001). Randomised noninferiority trial (PROACT Mitral).
cards.result: Primary endpoint rates (the sum of thromboembolism, valve thrombosis and bleeding, in percent per patient-year) were 11.9% in the low-dose group and 12.0% in the standard-dose group (difference -0.07%; 95% CI -3.40% to 3.26%). Because the confidence interval exceeded the 1.5% noninferiority margin, noninferiority was not achieved. Component rates (percent per patient-year, low-dose vs standard) were 2.3% vs 2.5% for thromboembolism, 0.5% vs 0.5% for valve thrombosis, and 9.13% vs 9.04% for bleeding. The record's conclusion: compared with standard-dose warfarin, low-dose warfarin did not achieve noninferiority for the composite primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: One specific modern bileaflet valve (On-X), all patients on aspirin, and randomisation only after 3 months of standard anticoagulation — the result does not cover the early postoperative period, other mitral prostheses, or patients not taking aspirin; and 'no difference observed' plus 'noninferiority not shown' must both stay on the face.
cards.source: Chu MWA et al. Low-Dose vs Standard Warfarin After Mechanical Mitral Valve Replacement: A Randomized Trial. The Annals of thoracic surgery. 2023. PMID: 36610532. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 23,145 mechanical-valve patients: in the mitral position, higher-intensity anticoagulation (mean target INR above 3.0) reduced thromboembolism (RR 0.74) and total events (RR 0.84), without a significant bleeding increase (RR 1.08)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 23,145 mechanical-valve patients: in the mitral position, higher-intensity anticoagulation (mean target INR above 3.0) reduced thromboembolism (RR 0.74) and total events (RR 0.84), without a significant bleeding increase (RR 1.08)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 35 eligible studies of vitamin K antagonist intensity in mechanical heart valve prostheses: 23,145 patients studied for 108,792 patient-years, classified as low intensity (mean target INR 3.0 or lower) or high intensity (mean target INR above 3.0), with results reported separately for aortic and mitral positions.
cards.result: In the mitral valve group, the incidence of thromboembolism was lower with high-intensity therapy (risk ratio 0.74, p<0.0001), without a significantly increased bleeding incidence (RR 1.08, p=0.0524). The total number of thromboembolic and bleeding events was decreased in the high-intensity group for mitral prostheses (RR 0.84, p<0.0001) — and also for aortic prostheses (RR 0.94, p=0.0067), where high intensity lowered thromboembolism (RR 0.73) but raised bleeding (RR 1.23). The authors conclude both positions benefit from a target INR higher than 3.0.
cards.watchOut: A 2003 synthesis of mostly non-randomised cohorts, older valve types and INR targets (above 3.0) higher than either arm of PROACT Mitral — it supports the direction 'mitral valves are unforgiving of low intensity' but cannot settle the modern 2.0-2.5 versus 2.5-3.5 question.
cards.source: Vink R et al. The optimal intensity of vitamin K antagonists in patients with mechanical heart valves: a meta-analysis. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2003. cards.headline: D-dimer-guided intensity (748 mechanical-valve patients, aortic and mitral): starting low and escalating on D-dimer beat both fixed strategies — total events 9 of 240 versus 24 of 241 (standard) and 20 of 237 (low)
cards.summary: D-dimer-guided intensity (748 mechanical-valve patients, aortic and mitral): starting low and escalating on D-dimer beat both fixed strategies — total events 9 of 240 versus 24 of 241 (standard) and 20 of 237 (low)
cards.people: 748 Chinese patients after mechanical heart valve replacement (aortic and mitral positions) at Wuhan Asia Heart Hospital, randomised 1:1:1 to standard-intensity warfarin (INR 2.5-3.5; n=250), low-intensity warfarin (INR 1.8-2.6; n=248), or D-dimer-guided therapy (n=250) starting at low intensity with adjustment to standard intensity if D-dimer was elevated; 718 patients analysed over 24 months.
cards.result: Total events were fewer in the D-dimer-guided group (9 of 240) than in the standard-intensity (24 of 241) and low-intensity (20 of 237) groups (HR 0.37 and 0.44; 95% CI 0.19-0.72 and 0.21-0.90). Versus standard intensity, the guided group had less haemorrhage (3 of 240 vs 16 of 241; HR 0.18, 95% CI 0.07-0.45) and lower all-cause mortality (4 of 240 vs 12 of 241; HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.12-0.87); versus fixed low intensity, it had fewer thrombotic events (5 of 240 vs 14 of 237; HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.14-0.85). Fifty-three events occurred in total during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Aortic and mitral prostheses are pooled in this record (mitral-specific event rates are not printed separately), it is a single-centre Chinese population, and the winning strategy is biomarker-guided escalation — it argues against any fixed low target left unmonitored, rather than for standard intensity as such.
cards.source: Zhang L et al. D-dimer to guide the intensity of anticoagulation in Chinese patients after mechanical heart valve replacement: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2017. PMID: 28762606. Registry ID: NCT01996657. cards.headline: LIWACAP pilot (198 patients, aortic or mitral): low-intensity warfarin (target INR 2.5) plus aspirin for 6 months looked similar to standard-high intensity (INR target 3.7) — primary events 5.8% vs 4.3% (p=0.6)
cards.summary: LIWACAP pilot (198 patients, aortic or mitral): low-intensity warfarin (target INR 2.5) plus aspirin for 6 months looked similar to standard-high intensity (INR target 3.7) — primary events 5.8% vs 4.3% (p=0.6)
cards.people: 198 consecutive patients undergoing aortic or mitral mechanical valve replacement (or both), stratified by prosthesis site and randomised to low-intensity vitamin K antagonist treatment (target INR 2.5) plus aspirin 100 mg daily for the first 6 months (94 patients) or standard-intensity treatment (INR target 3.7; 104 patients); follow-up 144 and 163 patient-years (mean 1.5 years). Pilot study (LIWACAP).
cards.result: There were 5 events (5%) in the low-intensity-plus-aspirin group (4 major bleeding events and 1 vascular death) and 4 events (4%) in the standard-intensity group (2 major bleeding events and 2 ischaemic strokes); all events except one occurred within the first 6 months. Cumulative incidence of primary outcome events was 5.8% (95% CI 0.9-10.7) versus 4.3% (95% CI 0.2-8.4) (p=0.6). The authors conclude low-intensity treatment plus aspirin during the first 6 months appears as effective and safe as moderate-high-intensity anticoagulation.
cards.watchOut: A small pilot (N=198, printed on the face) pooling aortic and mitral prostheses with only 9 primary events in total — it can show feasibility, not equivalence, and its low-intensity arm added aspirin, so intensity and aspirin effects cannot be separated.
cards.source: Pengo V et al. Low-intensity oral anticoagulant plus low-dose aspirin during the first six months versus standard-intensity oral anticoagulant therapy after mechanical heart valve replacement: a pilot study of low-intensity warfarin and aspirin in cardiac prostheses (LIWACAP). Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis. 2007. PMID: 17636186. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for mechanical mitral valves the modern trial finds standard and lower INR targets indistinguishable on events — yet the lower target is not proven noninferior, and older mitral data favour keeping intensity up
cards.summary: Synthesis: for mechanical mitral valves the modern trial finds standard and lower INR targets indistinguishable on events — yet the lower target is not proven noninferior, and older mitral data favour keeping intensity up
cards.people: The carded evidence: PROACT Mitral (401 patients, mitral-specific, On-X valve), a 35-study intensity meta-analysis (23,145 patients, mitral subgroup reported), a D-dimer-guided randomised trial (748 patients, aortic and mitral pooled) and the LIWACAP pilot (198 patients, aortic and mitral pooled). Total carded participants exceed 24,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; only the first card is mitral-specific randomised evidence.
cards.result: PROACT Mitral composite: 11.9% versus 12.0% per patient-year (difference -0.07%, 95% CI -3.40% to 3.26%), noninferiority of low-dose not achieved; thromboembolism 2.3% versus 2.5% and bleeding 9.13% versus 9.04% per patient-year. Meta-analysis (mitral): thromboembolism RR 0.74 and total events RR 0.84 favouring higher intensity, bleeding RR 1.08 (not significant). D-dimer guidance beat both fixed intensities; LIWACAP found no significant difference (p=0.6). PROPOSED SPLIT (trial: no difference, noninferiority unproven; older meta-analysis: higher intensity better in the mitral position).
cards.watchOut: The On-X aortic lower-INR question is homed on live shelf #3094 and its PROACT aortic report is not re-carded here; the mitral position's higher thrombotic risk is exactly why the aortic answer was never assumed to transfer.

shelves.title: Vorapaxar and limb events in peripheral arterial disease (partial completion of the broad prior-MI/PAD shelf #1544): acute limb ischaemia and revascularisation reduced, cardiovascular composite in PAD unchanged, bleeding increased
shelves.question: Does vorapaxar reduce limb events in peripheral arterial disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Ankle Brachial Index · Cohort Studies · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Extremities · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Humans · Ischemia · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lactones · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Pyridines · Receptor, PAR-1 · Risk Factors · Stroke · Thrombin · Treatment Outcome · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1544, which covers vorapaxar in prior myocardial infarction or peripheral arterial disease broadly (cardiovascular events as the focus, built on the TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 and TRACER primary reports, which are not re-carded here); this shelf covers the limb-events outcome slice in PAD. Within the TRA 2°P PAD cohort (3,787 patients with symptomatic PAD), vorapaxar did not significantly reduce the cardiovascular composite (11.3% vs 11.9%; hazard ratio 0.94) — but it did reduce limb events: hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% vs 3.9%; HR 0.58) and peripheral revascularisation (18.4% vs 22.2%; HR 0.84). The dedicated acute-limb-ischaemia analysis found first ALI reduced by 41% relative (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86; p=0.006) and total ALI events likewise (risk ratio 0.59), consistently across ALI types, in a population where placebo ALI ran at 3.9% over 3 years and 17.6% of ALI presentations ended in amputation. In the broader PAD analysis (6,136 patients), vorapaxar reduced major adverse limb events (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.92), with the largest absolute limb benefit in patients with prior peripheral revascularisation (absolute reduction 2.5%; NNT 40), and reduced peripheral revascularisation overall (15.4% vs 19.3%; HR 0.82) across all indications. The price is bleeding: in the symptomatic-PAD cohort, bleeding occurred in 7.4% versus 4.5% (HR 1.62). All of this is one trial programme's subgroup analyses, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: vorapaxar reduces limb events (acute limb ischaemia and peripheral revascularisation) in PAD, with increased bleeding.

cards.headline: TRA 2°P PAD cohort (3,787 patients): vorapaxar did not significantly cut the cardiovascular composite (11.3% vs 11.9%; HR 0.94) but reduced hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% vs 3.9%; HR 0.58) and peripheral revascularisation (18.4% vs 22.2%; HR 0.84) — bleeding rose (7.4% vs 4.5%; HR 1.62)
cards.summary: TRA 2°P PAD cohort (3,787 patients): vorapaxar did not significantly cut the cardiovascular composite (11.3% vs 11.9%; HR 0.94) but reduced hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% vs 3.9%; HR 0.58) and peripheral revascularisation (18.4% vs 22.2%; HR 0.84) — bleeding rose (7.4% vs 4.5%; HR 1.62)
cards.type: Prespecified cohort analysis of a randomised trial (TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 PAD cohort)
cards.people: 3,787 patients with qualifying peripheral artery disease (history of claudication with ankle-brachial index under 0.85, or prior revascularisation for limb ischaemia) within TRA 2°P-TIMI 50, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of vorapaxar in 26,449 patients with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease. Primary efficacy endpoint: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke; principal safety endpoint: GUSTO bleeding. The trial's primary report is carded on live shelf #1544 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: In the PAD cohort the primary endpoint did not differ significantly with vorapaxar (11.3% versus 11.9%; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.78-1.14; P=0.53) — the treatment made no significant difference to the cardiovascular composite. Rates of hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% versus 3.9%; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86; P=0.006) and peripheral artery revascularisation (18.4% versus 22.2%; HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73-0.97; P=0.017) were significantly lower with vorapaxar. Bleeding occurred more frequently with vorapaxar (7.4% versus 4.5%; HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.21-2.18; P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: A cohort analysis within one trial: the limb endpoints were secondary to the cardiovascular primary endpoint, which was null in PAD — the limb benefit and the bleeding excess must be read together.

prespecified cohort analysis of a randomised trial (tra 2°p-timi 50 pad cohort) 3,787 patients with qualifying peripheral artery disease (history of claudication with ankle-brachial index under 0.85, or prior revascularisation for limb ischaemia) within tra 2°p-timi 50, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of vorapaxar in 26,449 patients with stable atherosclerotic vascular disease. primary efficacy endpoint: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke; principal safety endpoint: gusto bleeding. the trial's primary report is carded on live shelf #1544 and is not re-carded here. in the pad cohort the primary endpoint did not differ significantly with vorapaxar (11.3% versus 11.9%; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% ci 0.78-1.14; p=0.53) — the treatment made no significant difference to the cardiovascular composite. rates of hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% versus 3.9%; hr 0.58, 95% ci 0.39-0.86; p=0.006) and peripheral artery revascularisation (18.4% versus 22.2%; hr 0.84, 95% ci 0.73-0.97; p=0.017) were significantly lower with vorapaxar. bleeding occurred more frequently with vorapaxar (7.4% versus 4.5%; hr 1.62, 95% ci 1.21-2.18; p=0.001). a cohort analysis within one trial: the limb endpoints were secondary to the cardiovascular primary endpoint, which was null in pad — the limb benefit and the bleeding excess must be read together. bonaca mp et al. vorapaxar in patients with peripheral artery disease: results from tra2{degrees}p-timi 50. circulation. 2013. pmid: 23501976. registry id: nct00526474. mesh: aged · ankle brachial index · cohort studies · comorbidity · double-blind method · extremities · female · follow-up studies · hemorrhage · humans · ischemia · kaplan-meier estimate · lactones · male · middle aged · myocardial infarction · peripheral arterial disease · pyridines · receptor, par-1 · risk factors · stroke · thrombin · treatment outcome · platelet aggregation inhibitors

cards.headline: Acute limb ischaemia analysis: vorapaxar reduced first ALI events by 41% relative (HR 0.58; p=0.006) and total ALI events by 41% (risk ratio 0.59), consistently across ALI causes; 17.6% of ALI presentations led to amputation
cards.summary: Acute limb ischaemia analysis: vorapaxar reduced first ALI events by 41% relative (HR 0.58; p=0.006) and total ALI events by 41% (risk ratio 0.59), consistently across ALI causes; 17.6% of ALI presentations led to amputation
cards.type: Prespecified endpoint analysis of a randomised trial (TRA 2°P-TIMI 50)
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease in TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 (3,787 with symptomatic PAD in this analysis); acute limb ischaemia was a prespecified adjudicated endpoint with a formal definition. A total of 150 ALI events occurred in 108 patients during follow-up (placebo 3-year rate 3.9%; 1.3% annualised). Predictors of ALI were previous peripheral revascularisation, smoking and ankle-brachial index.
cards.result: Vorapaxar reduced first ALI events by 41% relative (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86; P=0.006) and total ALI events by 41% (94 versus 56 events; risk ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.38-0.93; P=0.022), with efficacy consistent across types of ALI. Most ALI events resulted from surgical graft thrombosis (56%), then native-vessel in-situ thrombosis (27%), stent thrombosis (13%) and thromboembolism (5%). Amputation occurred in 17.6% of patients presenting with ALI.
cards.watchOut: ALI was uncommon (150 events in 108 patients), so the 41% relative reduction rests on small absolute numbers; the analysis covers symptomatic PAD without atrial fibrillation, as selected in the record.
cards.source: Bonaca MP et al. cards.headline: Broad PAD analysis (6,136 patients): vorapaxar reduced major adverse limb events (HR 0.70) and MACE (HR 0.85), with the largest absolute limb benefit after prior peripheral revascularisation (absolute reduction 2.5%; NNT 40); major bleeding increased (HR 1.39)
cards.summary: Broad PAD analysis (6,136 patients): vorapaxar reduced major adverse limb events (HR 0.70) and MACE (HR 0.85), with the largest absolute limb benefit after prior peripheral revascularisation (absolute reduction 2.5%; NNT 40); major bleeding increased (HR 1.39)
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (TRA 2°P-TIMI 50)
cards.people: 6,136 patients with peripheral artery disease (a broader PAD definition than the qualifying-PAD cohort) within TRA 2°P-TIMI 50, which randomised 26,449 patients with prior myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or PAD to vorapaxar or placebo; outcomes stratified by concomitant coronary artery disease and prior peripheral revascularisation.
cards.result: Overall, vorapaxar significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.99; p=0.034) and major adverse limb events (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.92; p=0.011) in patients with PAD. The absolute risk reduction for MACE was greater with concomitant CAD (-2.2% vs 0.1%; NNT 45 vs 1,000), while the absolute reduction for MALE was higher with prior lower-extremity revascularisation (2.5% vs 0.2%; NNT 40 vs 500). Vorapaxar increased major bleeding (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.12-1.71; p=0.003). The net clinical outcome was reduced with vorapaxar (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94; p=0.004), with unclear benefit in patients with neither concomitant CAD nor prior revascularisation.
cards.watchOut: This analysis widens the PAD definition beyond the qualifying cohort (6,136 vs 3,787 patients), which is why its MACE result is significant where the cohort card's was not — the two cards are different cuts of one trial, not two trials.
cards.source: Qamar A et al. Effect of vorapaxar on cardiovascular and limb outcomes in patients with peripheral artery disease with and without coronary artery disease: Analysis from the TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 trial. Vascular medicine (London, England). 2020. PMID: 32000630. Registry ID: NCT00526474. cards.headline: Peripheral revascularisation analysis (5,845 patients with known PAD): vorapaxar reduced peripheral revascularisation (15.4% vs 19.3%; HR 0.82; p=0.003), consistently across indications — claudication, critical limb ischaemia and acute limb ischaemia
cards.summary: Peripheral revascularisation analysis (5,845 patients with known PAD): vorapaxar reduced peripheral revascularisation (15.4% vs 19.3%; HR 0.82; p=0.003), consistently across indications — claudication, critical limb ischaemia and acute limb ischaemia
cards.type: Prespecified outcome analysis of a randomised trial (TRA 2°P-TIMI 50)
cards.people: 5,845 patients with a known history of peripheral artery disease at randomisation in TRA 2°P-TIMI 50, on background standard therapy; peripheral revascularisation procedures were a prespecified outcome. A total of 934 patients (16%) underwent at least one peripheral revascularisation over a median 2.5 years: 55% for worsening claudication, 24% for critical limb ischaemia, 16% for acute limb ischaemia and 4% for asymptomatic severe stenosis.
cards.result: Vorapaxar significantly reduced peripheral revascularisation (19.3% for placebo versus 15.4% for vorapaxar; hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.93; p=0.003), with a consistent pattern of efficacy across indications and procedure types, as reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Most revascularisations prevented were for worsening claudication (55%) rather than limb-threatening ischaemia, and revascularisation decisions are clinician-driven in a way that hard endpoints are not — the ALI card carries the harder limb outcome.
cards.source: Bonaca MP et al. Peripheral Revascularization in Patients With Peripheral Artery Disease With Vorapaxar: Insights From the TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 Trial. JACC. Cardiovascular interventions. 2016. PMID: 27765312. Registry ID: NCT00526474. cards.headline: Synthesis: vorapaxar reduces limb events in PAD — acute limb ischaemia down 41% relative and peripheral revascularisation down — while its cardiovascular composite in PAD was null and bleeding increased
cards.summary: Synthesis: vorapaxar reduces limb events in PAD — acute limb ischaemia down 41% relative and peripheral revascularisation down — while its cardiovascular composite in PAD was null and bleeding increased
cards.people: The carded evidence: four analyses of the single TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 trial in overlapping PAD populations (3,787 qualifying-PAD patients; 6,136 in the broad PAD analysis; 5,845 with known PAD). Unique participants are the trial's PAD population, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is single-programme evidence, printed here.
cards.result: Acute limb ischaemia hospitalisation 2.3% versus 3.9% (HR 0.58); first ALI events HR 0.58 and total ALI risk ratio 0.59; major adverse limb events HR 0.70; peripheral revascularisation 18.4% versus 22.2% (HR 0.84) in the qualifying cohort and 15.4% versus 19.3% (HR 0.82) in the broader population. Cardiovascular composite in qualifying PAD: 11.3% versus 11.9% (HR 0.94, not significant). Bleeding: 7.4% versus 4.5% (HR 1.62). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
cards.watchOut: The broad prior-MI/PAD vorapaxar question is homed on live shelf #1544 (TRA 2°P and TRACER primary reports carded there, not re-carded here); every card on this shelf is the same trial's PAD data cut for limb outcomes, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Aortoiliac claudication (PARTIAL — the aortoiliac slice of live shelf #280): supervised exercise matched stenting for 18-month walking improvement in the CLEVER trial and cost less, though quality-of-life scales often favoured stenting
shelves.question: Does supervised exercise work as well as stenting for aortoiliac PAD?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arterial Occlusive Diseases · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Female · Health Status Indicators · Humans · Intermittent Claudication · Male · Middle Aged · Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · Peripheral Arterial Disease · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Stents · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #280 asks what works better for intermittent claudication generally (supervised exercise, stenting, or medical care) and cards the CLEVER trial's 6-month primary report there; this shelf targets the slice #280 does not isolate: claudication due specifically to aortoiliac disease, using CLEVER's own later and secondary reports, which are not carded on #280. CLEVER randomised only patients with aortoiliac disease (111 patients), so its 18-month report (Murphy 2015), its cost-effectiveness analysis (Reynolds 2014) and its patient-reported-outcomes analysis (Murphy 2013) answer the aortoiliac question directly. At 18 months, peak walking time had improved by 5.0 minutes with supervised exercise and 3.2 minutes with stenting versus 0.2 minutes with medical care alone, and the exercise-versus-stent difference was not significant (P = 0.16) — exercise worked as well as stenting on the treadmill outcome, while many disease-specific quality-of-life scales favoured stenting. Exercise was also much cheaper ($9,804 vs $14,590 per patient over 18 months). One caution from within the trial: after exercise, treadmill gains correlated poorly with patients' own symptom relief, whereas after stenting they correlated well. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: in aortoiliac claudication, supervised exercise matches stenting for durable walking improvement at 18 months and costs less, though patient-reported quality-of-life gains were larger with stenting on many scales.

cards.headline: CLEVER 18-month report (Murphy 2015): in aortoiliac claudication, supervised exercise and stenting both beat medical care alone on peak walking time, and exercise versus stent was not significantly different (P = 0.16)
cards.summary: CLEVER 18-month report (Murphy 2015): in aortoiliac claudication, supervised exercise and stenting both beat medical care alone on peak walking time, and exercise versus stent was not significantly different (P = 0.16)
cards.people: 111 patients with claudication due to aortoiliac peripheral artery disease randomly assigned to optimal medical care (OMC), OMC plus supervised exercise (SE), or OMC plus stent revascularisation (ST); 79 completed the 18-month clinical and treadmill follow-up. SE was 6 months of supervised exercise plus a further year of telephone-based exercise counselling. Trial N = 111 randomised (79 completing 18-month follow-up).
cards.result: Peak walking time improved from baseline to 18 months by 5.0 ± 5.4 minutes with SE and 3.2 ± 4.7 minutes with ST, both significantly more than OMC (0.2 ± 2.1 minutes; P < 0.001 and P = 0.04 respectively). The difference between SE and ST was not significant (P = 0.16). Improvement in claudication onset time was greater for SE than OMC, but not for ST versus OMC. Many disease-specific quality-of-life scales showed durable improvements that were greater for ST than for SE or OMC. The authors conclude SE and ST provided comparable durable improvement in functional status and quality of life up to 18 months.
cards.watchOut: Only 79 of 111 randomised patients completed the 18-month treadmill follow-up, and the trial was powered for its 6-month primary outcome (carded on live shelf #280), not for an exercise-versus-stent equivalence claim at 18 months: 'not significantly different' here is not proof of exact equivalence.
cards.source: Murphy TP et al. Supervised exercise, stent revascularization, or medical therapy for claudication due to aortoiliac peripheral artery disease: the CLEVER study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015. PMID: 25766947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CLEVER economic analysis (Reynolds 2014): stenting cost about $14,590 per patient over 18 months versus $9,804 for supervised exercise, with an incremental cost of $122,600 per quality-adjusted life-year for stent versus exercise
cards.summary: CLEVER economic analysis (Reynolds 2014): stenting cost about $14,590 per patient over 18 months versus $9,804 for supervised exercise, with an incremental cost of $122,600 per quality-adjusted life-year for stent versus exercise
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised trial (CLEVER; Reynolds 2014)
cards.people: Participants in the CLEVER trial (claudication due to aortoiliac stenosis) randomised to a 6-month supervised exercise programme, stenting, or optimal medical care; the 98 participants who completed 6-month follow-up were included in the health economic analysis through 18 months.
cards.result: Through 18 months, mean healthcare costs were $5,178 (medical care), $9,804 (supervised exercise) and $14,590 (stenting) per patient; measured quality-adjusted life-years were 1.04, 1.16 and 1.20 respectively. In the base-case analysis (assuming quality-of-life differences dissipate after 5 years), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were $24,070 per quality-adjusted life-year gained for exercise versus medical care, $41,376 for stenting versus medical care, and $122,600 for stenting versus exercise. If stenting's treatment effect was assumed more durable than exercise's, the stent-versus-exercise ratio became more favourable. The authors conclude both strategies are economically attractive relative to medical care by US standards, but stenting is more expensive than exercise with uncertain incremental benefit.
cards.watchOut: The cost-effectiveness ratios rest on modelling assumptions about how long the quality-of-life differences last (the base case assumes they dissipate after 5 years); the within-trial fact is the cost and quality-adjusted life-year figures themselves.
cards.source: Reynolds MR et al. Cost-effectiveness of supervised exercise, stenting, and optimal medical care for claudication: results from the Claudication: Exercise Versus Endoluminal Revascularization (CLEVER) trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2014. PMID: 25389284. Registry ID: NCT00132743. measured quality-adjusted life-years were 1.04, 1.16 and 1.20 respectively. in the base-case analysis (assuming quality-of-life differences dissipate after 5 years), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were $24,070 per quality-adjusted life-year gained for exercise versus medical care, $41,376 for stenting versus medical care, and $122,600 for stenting versus exercise. if stenting's treatment effect was assumed more durable than exercise's, the stent-versus-exercise ratio became more favourable. the authors conclude both strategies are economically attractive relative to medical care by us standards, but stenting is more expensive than exercise with uncertain incremental benefit. the cost-effectiveness ratios rest on modelling assumptions about how long the quality-of-life differences last (the base case assumes they dissipate after 5 years); cards.headline: CLEVER outcomes-correlation analysis (Murphy 2013): after supervised exercise, treadmill gains correlated poorly with patients' own symptom relief, while after stenting treadmill and symptom improvement tracked together
cards.summary: CLEVER outcomes-correlation analysis (Murphy 2013): after supervised exercise, treadmill gains correlated poorly with patients' own symptom relief, while after stenting treadmill and symptom improvement tracked together
cards.type: Secondary outcomes analysis of a randomised trial (CLEVER; Murphy 2013)
cards.people: Patients with claudication treated in the CLEVER study with stent revascularisation or supervised exercise for aortoiliac disease; five scales of the Peripheral Artery Questionnaire and Walking Impairment Questionnaire were correlated with peak walking time and claudication onset time (participant N not separately documented in the record).
cards.result: The correlation between change in disease-specific quality of life and change in peak walking time differed by treatment group: statistically significant correlations for all five scales in the stent group, but weaker trends after supervised exercise, only one of which was statistically significant. Improvements in quality of life correlated well with increases in claudication onset time in both groups, with no significant interaction by treatment. The authors conclude that traditional objective treadmill outcomes may not correlate well with symptom relief after exercise treatment, and that claudication onset time tracks patient-reported benefit better than peak walking time.
cards.watchOut: This is a correlation analysis within one small trial, not a treatment comparison: it qualifies how the headline treadmill result should be read (patients may feel better, or not, independently of peak walking time), rather than adding a second efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Murphy TP et al. Correlation of patient-reported symptom outcomes and treadmill test outcomes after treatment for aortoiliac claudication. Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology. 2013. PMID: 23906799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for aortoiliac claudication, the one randomised programme (CLEVER, 111 patients) found supervised exercise and stenting comparably durable for walking at 18 months, stenting ahead on many quality-of-life scales, and exercise far cheaper
cards.summary: Synthesis: for aortoiliac claudication, the one randomised programme (CLEVER, 111 patients) found supervised exercise and stenting comparably durable for walking at 18 months, stenting ahead on many quality-of-life scales, and exercise far cheaper
cards.people: The carded evidence is a single randomised programme in aortoiliac disease: 111 patients randomised (79 completing 18-month follow-up; 98 in the economic analysis). Total unique participants = 111, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, but the single-programme cap does: this evidence cannot exceed POSSIBLE.
cards.result: At 18 months, peak walking time improved 5.0 minutes with supervised exercise and 3.2 minutes with stenting versus 0.2 minutes with medical care, with no significant exercise-versus-stent difference (P = 0.16), while many quality-of-life scales favoured stenting (Murphy 2015). Stenting cost $14,590 per patient versus $9,804 for exercise over 18 months (Reynolds 2014). Treadmill gains after exercise correlated poorly with symptom relief, unlike after stenting (Murphy 2013). The trial's 6-month primary report is carded on live shelf #280 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf comes from one 111-patient trial in aortoiliac disease; there is no second randomised comparison of exercise versus stenting restricted to the aortoiliac segment in the records fetched this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of Murphy TP et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015 (PMID: 25766947); Reynolds MR et al. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2014 (PMID: 25389284); Murphy TP et al. Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology. 2013 (PMID: 23906799).

shelves.title: Duration after a first unprovoked VTE (PARTIAL — the overall-duration slice of live shelf #1592): extending anticoagulation prevents recurrence for as long as it is taken, across warfarin, rivaroxaban and dabigatran extension trials
shelves.question: How long should anticoagulation last after a first unprovoked VTE?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Probability · Pulmonary Embolism · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Thromboembolism · Venous Thrombosis · Warfarin
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1592 covers one management strategy for this decision, a D-dimer-guided strategy for stopping or resuming anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE; this shelf targets the slice #1592 does not cover: the overall trial evidence on treatment duration itself, from the placebo- and active-controlled extension trials. That evidence is consistent on one point and silent on another. While anticoagulation is continued, recurrence is rare: in Kearon 1999, extending warfarin beyond 3 months cut recurrence from 27.4% to 1.3% per patient-year (a 95% relative reduction); in the EINSTEIN continued-treatment study, rivaroxaban cut recurrence from 7.1% to 1.3% (HR 0.18); in RE-SONATE, dabigatran cut recurrence from 5.6% to 0.4% (HR 0.08), and in RE-MEDY dabigatran matched warfarin for recurrence with less major or clinically relevant bleeding. The cost is bleeding: major bleeding on extended therapy ran at 0.3–0.9% in the dabigatran trials and 0.7% with rivaroxaban, against 0% on placebo in the placebo-controlled studies. What no carded trial shows is a finite extension that keeps protecting after it stops — the trials compare continuing versus stopping, and protection belongs to the continuing. So the honest duration answer is: at least 3–6 months for all, and extended (indefinite) treatment prevents recurrence for as long as it is taken, at a bleeding price; the choice is therefore about bleeding risk and patient preference, not about a magic number of months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — extended anticoagulation beyond 3–6 months prevents recurrence after a first unprovoked VTE for as long as it is continued, with more bleeding than placebo.

cards.headline: Kearon 1999: after 3 months of treatment for a first idiopathic VTE, continuing warfarin cut recurrence from 27.4% to 1.3% per patient-year — a 95% relative reduction — in a trial stopped early for benefit
cards.summary: Kearon 1999: after 3 months of treatment for a first idiopathic VTE, continuing warfarin cut recurrence from 27.4% to 1.3% per patient-year — a 95% relative reduction — in a trial stopped early for benefit
cards.people: 162 patients who had completed 3 months of anticoagulant therapy for a first episode of idiopathic (unprovoked) venous thromboembolism, randomly assigned to continue warfarin (INR 2.0–3.0, n = 79) or placebo (n = 83) for a further 24 months; the trial was stopped early after a prespecified interim analysis, with average follow-up of 10 months. Trial N = 162.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 17 of 83 patients on placebo (27.4% per patient-year) versus 1 of 79 on warfarin (1.3% per patient-year; P < 0.001) — a 95% relative reduction in the risk of recurrence (95% CI, 63 to 99 percent), with absolute rates of 27.4% versus 1.3% per patient-year as printed beside it. Three warfarin patients had nonfatal major bleeding versus none on placebo (3.8 vs 0 percent per patient-year; P = 0.09). The authors conclude patients with a first idiopathic venous thromboembolism should be treated for longer than three months.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped early after only 162 patients and an average of 10 months of follow-up, which tends to exaggerate the size of a benefit; the direction (large protection while treated) is what later trials confirmed, not the exact 95% figure.
cards.source: Kearon C et al. A comparison of three months of anticoagulation with extended anticoagulation for a first episode of idiopathic venous thromboembolism. New England Journal of Medicine. 1999. PMID: 10089183. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EINSTEIN continued-treatment study (Bauersachs 2010): after 6–12 months of treatment, a further 6–12 months of rivaroxaban cut recurrence from 7.1% to 1.3% (HR 0.18) versus placebo
cards.summary: EINSTEIN continued-treatment study (Bauersachs 2010): after 6–12 months of treatment, a further 6–12 months of rivaroxaban cut recurrence from 7.1% to 1.3% (HR 0.18) versus placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled extension trial (EINSTEIN-EXT, reported within Bauersachs 2010)
cards.people: Patients who had completed 6 to 12 months of treatment for venous thromboembolism, randomly assigned in a double-blind study to rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily (n = 602) or placebo (n = 594) for an additional 6 or 12 months. Extension-study N = 1,196 (the same record also reports the acute deep-vein thrombosis treatment study, N = 3,449, which is not the subject of this card).
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 8 patients on rivaroxaban (1.3%) versus 42 on placebo (7.1%) — hazard ratio 0.18 (95% CI, 0.09 to 0.39; P < 0.001), an 82% relative reduction with absolute rates of 1.3% versus 7.1% over the extension period. Four rivaroxaban patients (0.7%) had nonfatal major bleeding versus none on placebo (P = 0.11).
cards.watchOut: The extension population had already tolerated 6–12 months of anticoagulation and had clinical equipoise about continuing, so its bleeding rates understate what unselected long-term treatment would produce.
cards.source: Bauersachs R et al. Oral rivaroxaban for symptomatic venous thromboembolism. New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 21128814. Registry ID: NCT00439725, NCT00440193 (from the record). cards.headline: RE-MEDY and RE-SONATE (Schulman 2013): extended dabigatran matched warfarin for recurrence with less major or clinically relevant bleeding, and beat placebo decisively (recurrence 0.4% vs 5.6%; HR 0.08)
cards.summary: RE-MEDY and RE-SONATE (Schulman 2013): extended dabigatran matched warfarin for recurrence with less major or clinically relevant bleeding, and beat placebo decisively (recurrence 0.4% vs 5.6%; HR 0.08)
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind trials (RE-MEDY and RE-SONATE; Schulman 2013)
cards.people: Patients with venous thromboembolism who had completed at least 3 initial months of therapy. Active-control study (RE-MEDY): dabigatran 150 mg twice daily (n = 1,430) versus warfarin (n = 1,426). Placebo-control study (RE-SONATE): dabigatran (n = 681) versus placebo (n = 662). Combined N = 4,199.
cards.result: RE-MEDY: recurrent venous thromboembolism in 1.8% on dabigatran versus 1.3% on warfarin (HR 1.44; 95% CI, 0.78 to 2.64; P = 0.01 for noninferiority); major bleeding 0.9% versus 1.8% (HR 0.52; 95% CI, 0.27 to 1.02); major or clinically relevant bleeding less frequent with dabigatran (HR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.71); acute coronary syndromes 0.9% versus 0.2% (P = 0.02). RE-SONATE: recurrence 0.4% on dabigatran versus 5.6% on placebo (HR 0.08; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.25; P < 0.001) — a 92% relative reduction with absolute rates of 0.4% versus 5.6%; major bleeding 0.3% versus 0%; major or clinically relevant bleeding 5.3% versus 1.8% (HR 2.92; 95% CI, 1.52 to 5.60).
cards.watchOut: Dabigatran's coronary signal in RE-MEDY (acute coronary syndromes 0.9% vs 0.2% on warfarin) is part of this record and should not be read away; and like the other extension trials, these studies show protection while treated, not after stopping.
cards.source: Schulman S et al. Extended use of dabigatran, warfarin, or placebo in venous thromboembolism. New England Journal of Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23425163. Registry ID: NCT00329238, NCT00558259 (from the record; the record identifies these as the RE-MEDY and RE-SONATE numbers respectively). cards.headline: Synthesis: three independent extension programmes agree — continuing anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE keeps recurrence near 1% while stopping returns it to roughly 6–27% per period, at a real but smaller bleeding cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: three independent extension programmes agree — continuing anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE keeps recurrence near 1% while stopping returns it to roughly 6–27% per period, at a real but smaller bleeding cost
cards.people: The carded evidence: Kearon 1999 (N = 162, warfarin vs placebo after 3 months), the EINSTEIN continued-treatment study (N = 1,196, rivaroxaban vs placebo after 6–12 months), and RE-MEDY/RE-SONATE (N = 4,199, dabigatran vs warfarin and vs placebo after at least 3 months). Total unique participants across the extension comparisons ≈ 5,557, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Recurrence on continued treatment was 1.3% per patient-year (warfarin), 1.3% (rivaroxaban) and 0.4% (dabigatran) versus 27.4% per patient-year, 7.1% and 5.6% respectively on placebo — relative reductions of 95%, 82% (HR 0.18) and 92% (HR 0.08), each with absolute rates printed on its card. Dabigatran matched warfarin head-to-head with less major or clinically relevant bleeding (HR 0.54). Major bleeding on extended therapy was 0.3–0.9% in these trials versus 0% on placebo. No carded trial identifies a finite duration after which protection persists off treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — extended anticoagulation prevents recurrence for as long as it is continued.
cards.watchOut: These trials enrol patients who finished initial treatment without bleeding and were in equipoise about continuing; they do not answer how long a patient at high bleeding risk should be treated, and none randomised patients between two finite durations with long post-treatment follow-up.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kearon C et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 1999 (PMID: 10089183); Bauersachs R et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 21128814); Schulman S et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23425163).

shelves.title: Unprovoked PE — indefinite versus stopping at 6 months (PARTIAL — the PE-duration slice of live shelf #1592): benefit exists only while treatment continues (PADIS-PE), and a finite extension made no difference (WODIT-PE)
shelves.question: Is indefinite anticoagulation better than stopping after 6 months for unprovoked PE?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Hemorrhage · Humans · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Embolism · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Venous Thromboembolism · Warfarin
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1592 covers a D-dimer-guided stopping/resuming strategy after a first unprovoked VTE; this shelf targets the slice #1592 does not cover: for pulmonary embolism specifically, is indefinite (extended) anticoagulation better than stopping at 6 months? The two PE-specific randomised trials divide, and the division is the answer. PADIS-PE (Couturaud 2015) randomised 371 patients after 6 months of treatment to 18 further months of warfarin or placebo: on treatment, the composite of recurrence or major bleeding fell (3.3% vs 13.5%; HR 0.22) and recurrence fell sharply (HR 0.15) — but by 42 months, after everyone had stopped, the composite no longer differed (20.8% vs 24.0%; HR 0.75, CI crossing 1): the benefit was rented, not bought. WODIT-PE (Agnelli 2003) found extending from 3 months to 6–12 months made no difference to recurrence at all (9.1% vs 11.2%; rate ratio 0.81, CI 0.42–1.56), including in idiopathic PE (relative risk 0.99). A PADIS-PE analysis (Tromeur 2018) shows who recurs after stopping: older patients and those with residual pulmonary vascular obstruction or antiphospholipid antibodies. So indefinite treatment is better than stopping only in the narrow sense that it suppresses recurrence while it continues; neither trial shows a lasting advantage once treatment ends, which is why the decision turns on bleeding risk and recurrence-risk features rather than on duration alone. PROPOSED SPLIT — PADIS-PE favours extending (on-treatment benefit, lost after discontinuation); WODIT-PE found no benefit from extending (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PADIS-PE (Couturaud 2015): 18 extra months of warfarin after 6 months for unprovoked PE cut the on-treatment composite of recurrence or major bleeding (3.3% vs 13.5%; HR 0.22) — but by 42 months, after stopping, the advantage was gone (HR 0.75)
cards.summary: PADIS-PE (Couturaud 2015): 18 extra months of warfarin after 6 months for unprovoked PE cut the on-treatment composite of recurrence or major bleeding (3.3% vs 13.5%; HR 0.22) — but by 42 months, after stopping, the advantage was gone (HR 0.75)
cards.people: 371 adults with a first episode of symptomatic unprovoked pulmonary embolism who had completed 6 uninterrupted months of a vitamin K antagonist, randomly assigned to warfarin (n = 184) or placebo (n = 187) for a further 18 months, with follow-up to 42 months (18 months of treatment plus 24 months of follow-up) in 14 French centres. Trial N = 371.
cards.result: During the 18-month treatment period the primary composite outcome (recurrent venous thromboembolism or major bleeding) occurred in 6 of 184 patients on warfarin (3.3%) versus 25 of 187 on placebo (13.5%) (HR 0.22; 95% CI, 0.09–0.55; P = .001). Recurrent venous thromboembolism: 3 versus 25 patients (HR 0.15; 95% CI, 0.05–0.43) — an 85% relative reduction. Major bleeding: 4 versus 1 patients (HR 3.96; 95% CI, 0.44–35.89). Over the whole 42-month period the composite occurred in 33 patients (20.8%) on warfarin versus 42 (24.0%) on placebo (HR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.47–1.18), and recurrence, major bleeding and unrelated death did not differ between groups. The authors conclude the benefit was not maintained after discontinuation of anticoagulation.
cards.watchOut: The 42-month result is the crucial qualifier: this trial supports indefinite treatment only if treatment truly continues indefinitely — an 18-month extension followed by stopping left patients no better off than stopping at 6 months.
cards.source: Couturaud F et al. Six Months vs Extended Oral Anticoagulation After a First Episode of Pulmonary Embolism: The PADIS-PE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 26151264. Registry ID: NCT00740883. cards.headline: WODIT-PE (Agnelli 2003): extending anticoagulation from 3 months to 6 or 12 months after a first PE made no difference to recurrence (9.1% vs 11.2%; rate ratio 0.81), including in idiopathic PE (relative risk 0.99)
cards.summary: WODIT-PE (Agnelli 2003): extending anticoagulation from 3 months to 6 or 12 months after a first PE made no difference to recurrence (9.1% vs 11.2%; rate ratio 0.81), including in idiopathic PE (relative risk 0.99)
cards.people: 326 patients with a first episode of pulmonary embolism who had completed 3 months of oral anticoagulant therapy without recurrence or bleeding, randomly assigned at 19 Italian hospitals to extended therapy (to 6 months if the PE was associated with temporary risk factors, or to 1 year if idiopathic; n = 165) or to discontinue treatment (n = 161); average follow-up about 34 months. Trial N = 326.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 15 of 165 patients assigned to extended therapy (9.1%; 3.1% per patient-year) versus 18 of 161 assigned to discontinue (11.2%; 4.1% per patient-year) — rate ratio 0.81 (95% CI, 0.42 to 1.56); the treatment made no difference. All but one recurrence occurred after anticoagulant treatment was discontinued. Among patients with idiopathic venous thromboembolism, recurrence occurred in 11 of 90 (extended) versus 11 of 91 (discontinue) — relative risk 0.99 (95% CI, 0.45 to 2.16). Three major bleeding episodes occurred during extended anticoagulation (1.8%). Nineteen of the 33 recurrences (57.6%) were pulmonary embolism, two of them fatal.
cards.watchOut: WODIT-PE's extensions were finite (to 6 or 12 months total), so it tests a longer-but-still-finite course, not truly indefinite therapy; its null result and PADIS-PE's on-treatment benefit together say duration only matters while the drug is being taken.
cards.source: Agnelli G et al. Extended oral anticoagulant therapy after a first episode of pulmonary embolism. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2003. PMID: 12834314. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PADIS-PE recurrence analysis (Tromeur 2018): after unprovoked PE, recurrence over a median 41 months struck 67 of 371 patients, predicted by older age, residual pulmonary vascular obstruction and antiphospholipid antibodies
cards.summary: PADIS-PE recurrence analysis (Tromeur 2018): after unprovoked PE, recurrence over a median 41 months struck 67 of 371 patients, predicted by older age, residual pulmonary vascular obstruction and antiphospholipid antibodies
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (PADIS-PE; Tromeur 2018)
cards.people: The 371 PADIS-PE participants (first unprovoked pulmonary embolism, 6 months of initial treatment, then 18 months of warfarin or placebo, then 2 years of follow-up after study treatment ended); all had a ventilation/perfusion lung scan at inclusion. Analysis N = 371 (the same patients as the PADIS-PE card above; not additional participants).
cards.result: During a median follow-up of 41 months, recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 67 of 371 patients (6.8 events per 100 person-years). In the main multivariate analysis, hazard ratios for recurrence were 3.65 (95% CI, 1.33–9.99) for age 50–65 years, 4.70 (95% CI, 1.78–12.40) for age over 65 years, 2.06 (95% CI, 1.14–3.72) for a pulmonary vascular obstruction index of 5% or more at 6 months, and 2.38 (95% CI, 1.15–4.89) for antiphospholipid antibodies. An obstruction index of 40% or more at PE diagnosis (present in 40% of patients) was also associated with a 2-fold increased risk of recurrence.
cards.watchOut: These are predictors of recurrence, not randomised treatment effects: they identify who has most to lose from stopping, but they do not prove that continuing anticoagulation in those subgroups improves net outcomes.
cards.source: Tromeur C et al. Risk factors for recurrent venous thromboembolism after unprovoked pulmonary embolism: the PADIS-PE randomised trial. European Respiratory Journal. 2018. PMID: 29301920. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for unprovoked PE, extended anticoagulation suppresses recurrence only while it is taken — PADIS-PE's benefit vanished after discontinuation and WODIT-PE's finite extension made no difference at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: for unprovoked PE, extended anticoagulation suppresses recurrence only while it is taken — PADIS-PE's benefit vanished after discontinuation and WODIT-PE's finite extension made no difference at all
cards.people: The carded evidence: two PE-specific randomised trials (PADIS-PE, N = 371; WODIT-PE, N = 326) plus a recurrence-predictor analysis of PADIS-PE (same 371 patients). Total unique participants = 697, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: PADIS-PE: on-treatment composite 3.3% vs 13.5% (HR 0.22) and recurrence HR 0.15 favouring 18 extra months of warfarin, but the 42-month composite was 20.8% vs 24.0% (HR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.47–1.18) after treatment ended. WODIT-PE: recurrence 9.1% extended vs 11.2% stopped (rate ratio 0.81; 95% CI, 0.42–1.56), relative risk 0.99 in idiopathic PE — the treatment made no difference. Recurrence after stopping concentrated in older patients and those with residual obstruction or antiphospholipid antibodies (Tromeur 2018). PROPOSED SPLIT — the trials divide on whether extending helps, and agree only that any benefit requires continuing.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial tested truly lifelong treatment against stopping with lifelong follow-up; 'indefinite' here means the PADIS-PE strategy of continued warfarin, whose advantage existed only during the treatment period.
cards.source: Synthesis of Couturaud F et al. JAMA. 2015 (PMID: 26151264); Agnelli G et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2003 (PMID: 12834314); Tromeur C et al. European Respiratory Journal. 2018 (PMID: 29301920).

shelves.title: Reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months in non-cancer VTE (PARTIAL — the non-cancer slice of live shelf #3380): recurrence prevention proven in AMPLIFY-EXT (primary homed on #1580), with less bleeding than full dose in RENOVE
shelves.question: Does reduced-dose apixaban prevent recurrence after 6 months of VTE treatment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Coagulation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Hospitalization · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles · Pyridones · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #3380 covers reduced-dose apixaban only in cancer-associated VTE; this shelf targets the uncovered slice: non-cancer VTE, the AMPLIFY-EXT population. FLAG for the developer (one-home precedent): the AMPLIFY-EXT primary report itself is already carded on live shelf #1580, so under the one-home rule it is NOT re-carded here; this shelf is built on the trial's free secondary report and on later free evidence, with the primary cross-pointed in this prose. What the free reports show: within AMPLIFY-EXT, both apixaban doses (2.5 mg and 5 mg twice daily) significantly reduced all-cause hospitalisations versus placebo over 12 months (HR 0.64 and 0.54) and delayed first hospitalisation by 43 and 49 days (Liu 2016) — a downstream signal of the recurrence prevention the primary report established. RENOVE (Couturaud 2025) then randomised 2,768 patients who had already had 6–24 months of full-dose treatment to reduced-dose versus full-dose direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, versus full doses): recurrence stayed low in both groups (5-year cumulative incidence 2.2% reduced vs 1.8% full; adjusted HR 1.32), formal non-inferiority was not met (P = 0.23 for non-inferiority), but major or clinically relevant bleeding was substantially lower on the reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 9.9% vs 15.2%; adjusted HR 0.61). A network meta-analysis (Wang 2019) puts low-dose factor Xa inhibitors as a class well ahead of placebo for recurrence (OR 0.16). So: yes, reduced-dose apixaban prevents recurrence after 6 months in non-cancer VTE — the placebo-controlled proof is the homed AMPLIFY-EXT primary; the free evidence adds that the reduced dose keeps recurrence low with less bleeding than full dose, without formally proving non-inferiority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme for the apixaban-specific placebo comparison (primary homed on #1580), supported by RENOVE and class-level network meta-analysis.

cards.headline: AMPLIFY-EXT hospitalisation analysis (Liu 2016): 12 months of apixaban 2.5 mg or 5 mg twice daily reduced all-cause hospitalisations versus placebo (HR 0.64 and 0.54) and delayed first hospitalisation by 43 and 49 days
cards.summary: AMPLIFY-EXT hospitalisation analysis (Liu 2016): 12 months of apixaban 2.5 mg or 5 mg twice daily reduced all-cause hospitalisations versus placebo (HR 0.64 and 0.54) and delayed first hospitalisation by 43 and 49 days
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (AMPLIFY-EXT; Liu 2016)
cards.people: Patients with venous thromboembolism enrolled in the AMPLIFY-EXT trial (which had completed initial treatment and were randomised to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, or placebo for 12 months); the analysis population's total N is not documented in this record. The trial's primary report is carded on live shelf #1580 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: The record's own summary of the primary trial: apixaban versus placebo for 12 months significantly reduced symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism or all-cause death without increasing major bleeding. In this analysis, apixaban 2.5 mg and 5 mg twice daily each significantly reduced the rate of all-cause hospitalisations versus placebo (HR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.43–0.95; P = 0.026, and HR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.36–0.82; P = 0.004 respectively) — relative reductions of 36% and 46%. Apixaban prolonged mean time to first hospitalisation by 43 days (2.5 mg) and 49 days (5 mg) versus placebo. Median length of the first hospital stay was 7.0 days on placebo versus 5.0 days (2.5 mg) and 4.5 days (5 mg). Severe or moderate renal impairment predicted a higher hospitalisation rate.
cards.watchOut: Hospitalisation is a downstream, composite consequence of recurrence and bleeding, not the recurrence outcome itself; the recurrence and bleeding rates of AMPLIFY-EXT live on its primary report, carded on live shelf #1580 — this card must not be cited as if it were that primary result.
cards.source: Liu X et al. Extended anticoagulation with apixaban reduces hospitalisations in patients with venous thromboembolism. An analysis of the AMPLIFY-EXT trial. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2016. PMID: 26446706. Registry ID: NCT00633893. cards.headline: RENOVE (Couturaud 2025): after 6–24 months of full-dose treatment, reduced-dose anticoagulants (apixaban 2.5 mg or rivaroxaban 10 mg) kept 5-year recurrence low (2.2% vs 1.8% on full dose) and cut major or clinically relevant bleeding (9.9% vs 15.2%; HR 0.61) — but formal non-inferiority was not met
cards.summary: RENOVE (Couturaud 2025): after 6–24 months of full-dose treatment, reduced-dose anticoagulants (apixaban 2.5 mg or rivaroxaban 10 mg) kept 5-year recurrence low (2.2% vs 1.8% on full dose) and cut major or clinically relevant bleeding (9.9% vs 15.2%; HR 0.61) — but formal non-inferiority was not met
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint non-inferiority trial (RENOVE; Couturaud 2025)
cards.people: 2,768 ambulatory adults with acute symptomatic venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism or proximal deep-vein thrombosis) at high risk of recurrence who had received 6–24 uninterrupted months of full-dose anticoagulation and for whom extended anticoagulation was indicated, randomised at 47 French hospitals to reduced-dose (n = 1,383) or full-dose (n = 1,385) apixaban or rivaroxaban; median follow-up 37.1 months. Trial N = 2,768.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 19 of 1,383 patients on reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 2.2%; 95% CI, 1.1–3.3) versus 15 of 1,385 on full dose (1.8%; 0.8–2.7) — adjusted HR 1.32 (95% CI, 0.67–2.60); absolute difference 0.40% (95% CI, −1.05 to 1.85); P = 0.23 for non-inferiority, so the non-inferiority criterion was not met. Major or clinically relevant bleeding occurred in 96 patients on reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 9.9%) versus 154 on full dose (15.2%) — adjusted HR 0.61 (95% CI, 0.48–0.79), a 39% relative reduction. Deaths: 35 on reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 4.3%) versus 54 on full dose (6.1%). The authors conclude the low recurrence rates in both groups and the substantial bleeding reduction could support the reduced-dose regimen as an option, pending subgroup research.
cards.watchOut: RENOVE pooled two drugs (apixaban and rivaroxaban) into one reduced-dose strategy and did not report an apixaban-only comparison in this record, and its non-inferiority test formally failed — 'recurrence stayed low on both' is the supported claim, not 'reduced dose is proven equal'.
cards.source: Couturaud F et al. Extended treatment of venous thromboembolism with reduced-dose versus full-dose direct oral anticoagulants in patients at high risk of recurrence: a non-inferiority, multicentre, randomised, open-label, blinded endpoint trial. Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40023651. Registry ID: NCT03285438.
