0.8–2.7) — adjusted hr 1.32 (95% ci, 0.67–2.60); absolute difference 0.40% (95% ci, −1.05 to 1.85); p = 0.23 for non-inferiority, so the non-inferiority criterion was not met. major or clinically relevant bleeding occurred in 96 patients on reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 9.9%) versus 154 on full dose (15.2%) — adjusted hr 0.61 (95% ci, 0.48–0.79), a 39% relative reduction. deaths: 35 on reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 4.3%) versus 54 on full dose (6.1%). the authors conclude the low recurrence rates in both groups and the substantial bleeding reduction could support the reduced-dose regimen as an option, pending subgroup research. renove pooled two drugs (apixaban and rivaroxaban) into one reduced-dose strategy and did not report an apixaban-only comparison in this record, and its non-inferiority test formally failed — 'recurrence stayed low on both' is the supported claim, not 'reduced dose is proven equal'. couturaud f et al. extended treatment of venous thromboembolism with reduced-dose versus full-dose direct oral anticoagulants in patients at high risk of recurrence: a non-inferiority, multicentre, randomised, open-label, blinded endpoint trial. lancet. 2025. pmid: 40023651. registry id: nct03285438. mesh: humans · female · male · middle aged · venous thromboembolism · pyridones · administration, oral · aged · rivaroxaban · pyrazoles · anticoagulants · recurrence · factor xa inhibitors · pulmonary embolism · treatment outcome · adult · france · hemorrhage · secondary prevention · venous thrombosis · drug administration schedule

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis (Wang 2019): for extended VTE treatment, low-dose factor Xa inhibitors reduced recurrent VTE versus placebo (OR 0.16) and versus aspirin (OR 0.25) across 16 trials and more than 22,000 patients
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis (Wang 2019): for extended VTE treatment, low-dose factor Xa inhibitors reduced recurrent VTE versus placebo (OR 0.16) and versus aspirin (OR 0.25) across 16 trials and more than 22,000 patients
cards.people: Sixteen randomised trials totalling more than 22,000 patients studying vitamin K antagonists, direct oral anticoagulants or aspirin for secondary prevention of venous thromboembolism beyond 3 months; effects estimated with a random-effects Bayesian network meta-analysis. (The low-dose factor Xa inhibitor node comprises the reduced-dose apixaban and rivaroxaban regimens.)
cards.result: Compared with placebo or observation, the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism was lower with low-dose factor Xa inhibitors (OR 0.16; 95% credible interval, 0.06 to 0.38) — an 84% relative reduction in odds — as it was with standard-dose factor Xa inhibitors (OR 0.17) and standard-intensity vitamin K antagonists (OR 0.15). Versus aspirin, low-dose factor Xa inhibitors also reduced recurrence (OR 0.25; 0.09 to 0.66). All-cause mortality versus placebo was reduced with low-dose factor Xa inhibitors (OR 0.38; 0.12 to 0.995) and standard-intensity vitamin K antagonists (OR 0.44), while major bleeding was higher with standard-intensity vitamin K antagonists (OR 4.42 vs placebo) — the record reports no corresponding major-bleeding increase figure for the low-dose factor Xa inhibitor node. Effect estimates were consistent in patients with index pulmonary embolism and with unprovoked VTE.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates are indirect and class-level: the low-dose factor Xa inhibitor node combines apixaban 2.5 mg with rivaroxaban 10 mg trial data, so this card supports the reduced-dose strategy rather than isolating apixaban alone.
cards.source: Wang KL et al. Extended treatment of venous thromboembolism: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Heart. 2019. PMID: 30327391. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months prevents recurrence in non-cancer VTE — proven against placebo in AMPLIFY-EXT (primary report homed on live shelf #1580), corroborated here by fewer hospitalisations, RENOVE's low recurrence with less bleeding, and class-level network evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months prevents recurrence in non-cancer VTE — proven against placebo in AMPLIFY-EXT (primary report homed on live shelf #1580), corroborated here by fewer hospitalisations, RENOVE's low recurrence with less bleeding, and class-level network evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence on this shelf: a secondary analysis of AMPLIFY-EXT (analysis N not documented in its record; the primary report is carded on live shelf #1580), the RENOVE randomised trial (N = 2,768), and a network meta-analysis of 16 trials (more than 22,000 patients). Total carded participants exceed 24,000 counting the meta-analysis, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Apixaban (both doses) reduced hospitalisations versus placebo within AMPLIFY-EXT (HR 0.64 for 2.5 mg; Liu 2016). RENOVE found 5-year recurrence of 2.2% on reduced-dose versus 1.8% on full-dose anticoagulants (adjusted HR 1.32; non-inferiority not formally met) with major or clinically relevant bleeding of 9.9% versus 15.2% (adjusted HR 0.61) (Couturaud 2025). Low-dose factor Xa inhibitors as a class reduced recurrence versus placebo (OR 0.16) in network meta-analysis (Wang 2019). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the apixaban-specific placebo-controlled proof is a single trial programme whose primary report is homed on live shelf #1580.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite this shelf for the AMPLIFY-EXT recurrence and bleeding rates themselves — those numbers live on the primary report carded at live shelf #1580; this shelf answers the non-cancer reduced-dose question from the surrounding free evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Liu X et al. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2016 (PMID: 26446706); Couturaud F et al. Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40023651); Wang KL et al. Heart. 2019 (PMID: 30327391).

shelves.title: IVC filters when anticoagulation is impossible (PARTIAL — the cannot-anticoagulate slice of live shelf #1178): PE prevention plausible in established VTE, randomised trauma primary outcome neutral, thrombosis increased
shelves.question: Do IVC filters prevent PE in patients who cannot be anticoagulated?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Computed Tomography Angiography · Humans · Incidence · Injury Severity Score · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leg · Lung · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Embolism · Risk · Treatment Failure · Ultrasonography · Vena Cava Filters · Venous Thrombosis · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1178 covers a filter ADDED to anticoagulation (the PREPIC question); this shelf targets the uncovered slice: patients who cannot be anticoagulated at all, where the filter is the only mechanical option. The evidence divides by setting, and the stamp names the split. In severely injured patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation, the one randomised trial (Ho 2019, N = 240) found early filter placement made no difference to the composite of symptomatic PE or death at 90 days (13.9% vs 14.4%; HR 0.99) — the treatment made no difference on its primary outcome — although in the subgroup who received no prophylactic anticoagulation within 7 days, PE occurred in 0 of 46 filtered patients versus 5 of 34 unfiltered (14.7%). In established cancer-associated VTE with contraindications, a propensity-matched RIETE cohort (Quezada 2020) found filters associated with lower PE-related mortality (0.8% vs 4.0%) but higher recurrence (7.3% vs 3.2%) and no difference in all-cause death or major bleeding. The controlled-evidence synthesis (Bikdeli 2017) found filters reduce subsequent PE (OR 0.50) and increase deep-vein thrombosis (OR 1.70) with no change in all-cause mortality (OR 0.91) — but most of its included studies anticoagulated their patients, so it only partly speaks to this slice. Net: a filter probably prevents some PEs in patients who cannot be anticoagulated — most plausibly fatal PE in established VTE — at the price of more thrombosis, and the only randomised test in a contraindicated population was neutral on its primary outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised trauma evidence neutral on PE-or-death; observational VTE evidence shows less PE-related death but more recurrence; meta-analysis shows fewer PEs, more DVT, no mortality change.

cards.headline: Ho 2019 (NEJM trauma trial): in severely injured patients who could not receive anticoagulants, early IVC filter placement made no difference to symptomatic PE or death at 90 days (13.9% vs 14.4%; HR 0.99) — though no PE occurred in filtered patients who stayed unanticoagulated
cards.summary: Ho 2019 (NEJM trauma trial): in severely injured patients who could not receive anticoagulants, early IVC filter placement made no difference to symptomatic PE or death at 90 days (13.9% vs 14.4%; HR 0.99) — though no PE occurred in filtered patients who stayed unanticoagulated
cards.people: 240 severely injured patients (Injury Severity Score above 15; median score 27; median age 39 years) with a contraindication to anticoagulant agents, randomly assigned to a vena cava filter placed within 72 hours of admission or to no filter. Trial N = 240.
cards.result: The primary composite of symptomatic pulmonary embolism or death from any cause at 90 days occurred in 13.9% of the filter group and 14.4% of the control group (HR 0.99; 95% CI, 0.51 to 1.94; P = 0.98) — the treatment made no difference. Among the 46 filter-group and 34 control-group patients who did not receive prophylactic anticoagulation within 7 days after injury, pulmonary embolism developed in none of the filtered patients and in 5 control patients (14.7%), one of whom died (relative risk of pulmonary embolism, 0; 95% CI, 0.00 to 0.55). An entrapped thrombus was found in the filter in 6 patients.
cards.watchOut: This is prophylaxis after trauma, not treatment of established VTE: most participants could start anticoagulant prophylaxis within days, diluting any filter effect, and the favourable unanticoagulated subgroup is small (46 vs 34 patients) and defined after randomisation.
cards.source: Ho KM et al. A Multicenter Trial of Vena Cava Filters in Severely Injured Patients. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31259488. Registry ID: ACTRN12614000963628. cards.headline: RIETE cohort (Quezada 2020): in cancer-associated VTE with contraindications to anticoagulation, filter insertion was associated with lower PE-related mortality (0.8% vs 4.0%) but higher recurrence (7.3% vs 3.2%), and no significant difference in all-cause death
cards.summary: RIETE cohort (Quezada 2020): in cancer-associated VTE with contraindications to anticoagulation, filter insertion was associated with lower PE-related mortality (0.8% vs 4.0%) but higher recurrence (7.3% vs 3.2%), and no significant difference in all-cause death
cards.type: Prospective registry cohort with propensity matching (RIETE; Quezada 2020)
cards.people: Prospective RIETE registry cohort of 17,005 patients with cancer-associated thromboembolism, of whom 270 received an inferior vena cava filter because of a contraindication to anticoagulation; 247 filter patients were propensity-matched with 247 patients treated without a filter, with outcomes assessed through 30 days. Matched N = 494.
cards.result: In matched pairs, all-cause death was nonsignificantly lower with a filter (12.2% vs 17.0%; P = 0.13), PE-related mortality was significantly lower (0.8% vs 4.0%; P = 0.04), major bleeding did not differ (6.1% vs 5.7%; P = 0.85), and risk-adjusted recurrent thromboembolism was higher with a filter (7.3% vs 3.2%; P = 0.05). The authors conclude filter insertion in this population was associated with a lower risk of PE-related death and a higher risk of recurrences.
cards.watchOut: Observational and cancer-specific: despite propensity matching, patients chosen for filters differ from those not chosen in ways a registry cannot fully capture, and the 30-day window says nothing about long-term filter harms such as caval thrombosis or retrieval failure.
cards.source: Quezada A et al. Outcomes after Vena Cava Filter Use in Patients with Cancer-Associated Venous Thromboembolism and Contraindications to Anticoagulation. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2020. PMID: 32422681. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Bikdeli 2017): across 11 controlled studies, IVC filters reduced subsequent PE (OR 0.50) and increased DVT (OR 1.70), with no significant effect on PE-related or all-cause mortality
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Bikdeli 2017): across 11 controlled studies, IVC filters reduced subsequent PE (OR 0.50) and increased DVT (OR 1.70), with no significant effect on PE-related or all-cause mortality
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials and prospective controlled observational studies of inferior vena cava filters versus none in patients at risk of pulmonary embolism: 11 studies met inclusion criteria (6 randomised trials and 5 prospective observational studies) from 1,986 retrieved reports; total participant N is not documented in the record. Quality of evidence for the randomised trials was low to moderate.
cards.result: Patients receiving filters had a lower risk of subsequent pulmonary embolism (OR 0.50; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.75) — a 50% relative reduction in odds — an increased risk of deep-vein thrombosis (OR 1.70; 95% CI, 1.17 to 2.48), a nonsignificantly lower PE-related mortality (OR 0.51; 95% CI, 0.25 to 1.05), and no change in all-cause mortality (OR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.70 to 1.19) — the treatment made no difference to overall mortality. Results limited to randomised trials were similar, as were findings across sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies gave anticoagulation alongside (or compared against) filters, so this synthesis only partly answers the cannot-anticoagulate question; its PE reduction cannot simply be transferred to unanticoagulated patients, which is why this shelf's stamp rests on the two slice-specific cards.
cards.source: Bikdeli B et al. Inferior Vena Cava Filters to Prevent Pulmonary Embolism: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28935036. shelves.title: Aspirin after stopping anticoagulation (PARTIAL — the aspirin-versus-placebo slice of live shelf #1581): WARFASA, ASPIRE and their pooled analysis show about a one-third relative reduction in VTE recurrence
shelves.question: Does aspirin prevent VTE recurrence after stopping anticoagulation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Aspirin · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Pulmonary Embolism · Secondary Prevention · Venous Thromboembolism · Venous Thrombosis · Vitamin K
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1581 covers extended rivaroxaban therapy after VTE, where aspirin appears only as the comparator arm; this shelf targets the uncovered slice: aspirin versus placebo or no treatment after anticoagulation is stopped (the WARFASA and ASPIRE question). Two randomised trials and their pre-planned individual-patient pooled analysis answer it. WARFASA (Becattini 2012, N = 402) found aspirin 100 mg daily cut recurrence from 11.2% to 6.6% per year (HR 0.58) with one major bleed in each group. ASPIRE (Brighton 2012, N = 822) pointed the same way but its primary outcome narrowly missed significance (4.8% vs 6.5% per year; HR 0.74; P = 0.09), while its composite vascular outcomes fell significantly. The INSPIRE pooled analysis (Simes 2014, 1,224 patients) resolves the pair: aspirin reduced recurrent VTE from 7.5% to 5.1% per year (HR 0.68; P = 0.008) — a 32% relative reduction — and major vascular events from 8.7% to 5.7% per year (HR 0.66), with major bleeding of 0.5% versus 0.4% per year. Aspirin is much weaker than continued anticoagulation (see the duration evidence on pack #5829), but against nothing it works, cheaply and with little bleeding. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — aspirin after stopping anticoagulation reduces VTE recurrence by about a third relative to placebo, without a significant increase in major bleeding.

cards.headline: WARFASA (Becattini 2012): after 6–18 months of anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE, aspirin 100 mg daily cut recurrence from 11.2% to 6.6% per year (HR 0.58), with one major bleed in each group
cards.summary: WARFASA (Becattini 2012): after 6–18 months of anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE, aspirin 100 mg daily cut recurrence from 11.2% to 6.6% per year (HR 0.58), with one major bleed in each group
cards.people: 402 patients with first-ever unprovoked venous thromboembolism who had completed 6 to 18 months of oral anticoagulant treatment, randomly assigned to aspirin 100 mg daily (n = 205) or placebo (n = 197) for 2 years, with the option of extending treatment; median study period 24.6 months. Trial N = 402.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism recurred in 28 of 205 patients on aspirin versus 43 of 197 on placebo (6.6% vs 11.2% per year; HR 0.58; 95% CI, 0.36 to 0.93) — a 42% relative reduction, with absolute rates of 6.6% versus 11.2% per year. During the treatment period itself, recurrence was 5.9% versus 11.0% per year (HR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.92). One patient in each group had a major bleeding episode, and adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: WARFASA was a single investigator-initiated trial of 402 patients; its effect size (HR 0.58) is larger than the pooled estimate once ASPIRE is added, so the pooled HR 0.68 on the INSPIRE card is the safer number to quote.
cards.source: Becattini C et al. Aspirin for preventing the recurrence of venous thromboembolism. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22621626. Registry ID: NCT00222677. cards.headline: ASPIRE (Brighton 2012): aspirin missed significance on its primary recurrence outcome (4.8% vs 6.5% per year; HR 0.74; P = 0.09) but significantly reduced the composite of VTE, myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death (HR 0.66)
cards.summary: ASPIRE (Brighton 2012): aspirin missed significance on its primary recurrence outcome (4.8% vs 6.5% per year; HR 0.74; P = 0.09) but significantly reduced the composite of VTE, myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death (HR 0.66)
cards.people: 822 patients who had completed initial anticoagulant therapy after a first episode of unprovoked venous thromboembolism, randomly assigned to aspirin 100 mg daily (n = 411) or placebo (n = 411) for up to 4 years; median follow-up 37.2 months. Trial N = 822.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism recurred in 57 of 411 patients on aspirin versus 73 of 411 on placebo (4.8% vs 6.5% per year; HR 0.74; 95% CI, 0.52 to 1.05; P = 0.09) — a 26% relative reduction that did not reach significance on the primary outcome. Aspirin reduced the prespecified composite of venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death by 34% in relative terms (5.2% vs 8.0% per year; HR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.48 to 0.92; P = 0.01) and the net-benefit composite including major bleeding and death by 33% (HR 0.67; P = 0.01). Major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 1.1% per year on aspirin versus 0.6% on placebo (P = 0.22), not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: Read plainly: ASPIRE's own primary outcome was not significant (P = 0.09) — the shelf's LIKELY stamp rests on the two trials together and their pre-planned pooled analysis, not on ASPIRE alone.
cards.source: Brighton TA et al. Low-dose aspirin for preventing recurrent venous thromboembolism. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 23121403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: INSPIRE pooled analysis (Simes 2014): across WARFASA and ASPIRE (1,224 patients), aspirin reduced recurrent VTE from 7.5% to 5.1% per year (HR 0.68; P = 0.008) and major vascular events (HR 0.66), with major bleeding 0.5% vs 0.4% per year
cards.summary: INSPIRE pooled analysis (Simes 2014): across WARFASA and ASPIRE (1,224 patients), aspirin reduced recurrent VTE from 7.5% to 5.1% per year (HR 0.68; P = 0.008) and major vascular events (HR 0.66), with major bleeding 0.5% vs 0.4% per year
cards.type: Individual patient data pooled analysis of two randomised trials (INSPIRE; Simes 2014)
cards.people: Individual patient data from the WARFASA and ASPIRE trials: 1,224 patients with a first unprovoked venous thromboembolism who had completed anticoagulant treatment, followed for a median of 30.4 months; the pooled analysis was planned before either trial's results were known. Pooled N = 1,224 (the same patients as the two cards above; not additional participants).
cards.result: 193 patients had recurrent venous thromboembolism. Aspirin reduced recurrent VTE (5.1%/yr versus 7.5%/yr; HR 0.68; 95% CI, 0.51–0.90; P = 0.008) — a 32% relative reduction with absolute rates of 5.1% versus 7.5% per year — including deep-vein thrombosis (HR 0.66; P = 0.01) and, nonsignificantly, pulmonary embolism (HR 0.66; P = 0.08). Major vascular events fell from 8.7% to 5.7% per year (HR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.50–0.86; P = 0.002). Major bleeding was 0.5% per year on aspirin versus 0.4% on placebo. After adjustment for treatment adherence, recurrent VTE was reduced by 42% in relative terms (HR 0.58; P = 0.005). Subgroup analyses showed similar relative but larger absolute reductions in men and older patients.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of the same two trials is not a third independent trial; it sharpens the estimate (HR 0.68) but the evidence base remains WARFASA plus ASPIRE, and aspirin remains far weaker than continued anticoagulation for patients who can take it.
cards.source: Simes J et al. Aspirin for the prevention of recurrent venous thromboembolism: the INSPIRE collaboration. Circulation. 2014. PMID: 25156992. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: aspirin after stopping anticoagulation prevents about one recurrence in three relative to placebo (pooled HR 0.68), at a major-bleeding rate of about 0.5% per year
cards.summary: Synthesis: aspirin after stopping anticoagulation prevents about one recurrence in three relative to placebo (pooled HR 0.68), at a major-bleeding rate of about 0.5% per year
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised placebo-controlled trials (WARFASA, N = 402; ASPIRE, N = 822) and their pre-planned individual patient data pooled analysis (N = 1,224 unique patients). Total unique participants = 1,224, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: WARFASA: recurrence 6.6% vs 11.2% per year (HR 0.58). ASPIRE: 4.8% vs 6.5% per year (HR 0.74; P = 0.09, primary outcome not significant). INSPIRE pooled: 5.1% vs 7.5% per year (HR 0.68; P = 0.008), major vascular events HR 0.66, major bleeding 0.5% vs 0.4% per year. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials with a significant pre-planned pooled estimate.
cards.watchOut: The comparison here is aspirin versus nothing: for a patient who can continue anticoagulation, extended anticoagulation prevents far more recurrences (see pack #5829), so aspirin is the fallback for those stopping, not an equal alternative.
cards.source: Synthesis of Becattini C et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22621626); Brighton TA et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 23121403); Simes J et al. Circulation. 2014 (PMID: 25156992).

shelves.title: Beta-blockers versus no treatment in long QT syndrome (PARTIAL — the treated-versus-untreated slice of live shelf #3074): registry evidence associates therapy with far fewer cardiac events, observational only
shelves.question: Does beta-blocker therapy prevent events in long QT syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Atenolol · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Long QT Syndrome · Male · Metoprolol · Nadolol · Propranolol · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #3074 compares beta-blockers with each other in congenital long QT syndrome (which agent is best); this shelf targets the uncovered slice: beta-blocker therapy versus no treatment at all. No randomised trial exists — withholding standard therapy was never randomised — so the evidence is entirely observational, from the International LQTS Registry, and the stamp is capped accordingly and printed on the face. Moss 2000 compared matched periods before and after starting beta-blockers in 869 treated patients: cardiac event rates fell from 0.97 to 0.31 events per year in probands and from 0.26 to 0.15 in affected family members (P < 0.001) — but events continued on therapy, especially in patients symptomatic before treatment (32% had another event within 5 years) and after aborted cardiac arrest (14% had another arrest within 5 years). Goldenberg 2010 quantified the treated-versus-untreated contrast in high-risk LQT1/LQT2 patients: beta-blocker therapy was associated with a 67% relative risk reduction in LQT1 males and 71% in LQT2 females. Barsheshet 2012 adds the genotype nuance: in LQT1, the life-threatening-event benefit concentrated in cytoplasmic-loop KCNQ1 mutations (HR 0.12) and was not significant in other mutation groups (HR 0.82). The direction is consistent across three registry analyses spanning three decades of patients; the size of the benefit in any individual depends on genotype, mutation location, sex, age and prior symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: beta-blocker therapy is associated with substantially fewer cardiac events in congenital long QT syndrome, with residual risk concentrated in previously symptomatic patients.

cards.headline: Moss 2000 (International LQTS Registry): after starting beta-blockers, cardiac event rates fell from 0.97 to 0.31 per year in probands and 0.26 to 0.15 in family members (P < 0.001) — but a third of previously symptomatic patients had another event within 5 years on therapy
cards.summary: Moss 2000 (International LQTS Registry): after starting beta-blockers, cardiac event rates fell from 0.97 to 0.31 per year in probands and 0.26 to 0.15 in family members (P < 0.001) — but a third of previously symptomatic patients had another event within 5 years on therapy
cards.type: Observational registry cohort, before–after and on-therapy analysis (Moss 2000)
cards.people: 869 patients with congenital long QT syndrome treated with beta-blockers in the International LQTS Registry; effectiveness was analysed over matched 5-year periods before and after starting therapy, and by survivorship methods for events while on prescribed beta-blockers. Cohort N = 869.
cards.result: After initiation of beta-blockers, the rate of cardiac events fell significantly in probands (from 0.97 ± 1.42 to 0.31 ± 0.86 events per year) and in affected family members (from 0.26 ± 0.84 to 0.15 ± 0.69 events per year) (P < 0.001 for both). On therapy, patients symptomatic before beta-blockers (n = 598) had a hazard ratio of 5.8 (95% CI, 3.7 to 9.1) for recurrent cardiac events (syncope, aborted cardiac arrest or death) compared with asymptomatic patients, and 32% of them had another cardiac event within 5 years on prescribed beta-blockers. Patients with an aborted cardiac arrest before treatment (n = 113) had a hazard ratio of 12.9 (95% CI, 4.7 to 35.5) for aborted cardiac arrest or death on therapy, and 14% had another arrest (aborted or fatal) within 5 years.
cards.watchOut: The before–after comparison has no untreated parallel control group: event rates also fall with age and after a first-event workup, so the registry design can overstate the drug's share of the improvement; the on-therapy residual-risk figures are the record's most durable message.
cards.source: Moss AJ et al. Effectiveness and limitations of beta-blocker therapy in congenital long-QT syndrome. Circulation. 2000. PMID: 10673253. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Goldenberg 2010: in high-risk LQT1 and LQT2 patients, beta-blocker therapy was associated with a 67% relative reduction in cardiac events in LQT1 males and 71% in LQT2 females
cards.summary: Goldenberg 2010: in high-risk LQT1 and LQT2 patients, beta-blocker therapy was associated with a 67% relative reduction in cardiac events in LQT1 males and 71% in LQT2 females
cards.type: Observational registry cohort (International LQTS Registry; Goldenberg 2010)
cards.people: 971 patients with congenital long QT syndrome types 1 (n = 549) and 2 (n = 422) from the International LQTS Registry, followed from birth through age 40 years; cardiac events comprised syncope, aborted cardiac arrest or sudden cardiac death. Cohort N = 971 (registry population overlapping with the Moss 2000 card).
cards.result: Risk factors for cardiac events included the LQT1 genotype (HR 1.49; P = 0.003) and male sex (HR 1.31; P = 0.04) at ages 0–14 years, and the LQT2 genotype (HR 1.67; P < 0.001) and female sex (HR 2.58; P < 0.001) at ages 15–40 years, with the highest risk in LQT1 males (HR 1.93) and LQT2 females (HR 3.28) in their respective age groups. Beta-blocker therapy was associated with a significant risk reduction in these high-risk patients, including a 67% relative reduction (P = 0.02) in LQT1 males and a 71% relative reduction (P < 0.001) in LQT2 females. Life-threatening events rarely occurred as a presenting symptom among beta-blocker-treated patients; however, patients who had syncope during beta-blocker therapy had a subsequent aborted-arrest/sudden-death rate above 1 event per 100 patient-years.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was not randomised: patients prescribed beta-blockers differ from untreated patients (including by symptoms and genotype ascertainment), so the 67–71% figures are associations in high-risk subsets, not trial-grade effect sizes, and they do not extend to LQT3, which this study did not include.
cards.source: Goldenberg I et al. Beta-blocker efficacy in high-risk patients with the congenital long-QT syndrome types 1 and 2: implications for patient management. cards.headline: Barsheshet 2012: in LQT1, beta-blocker benefit against aborted cardiac arrest or sudden death was pronounced for cytoplasmic-loop KCNQ1 mutations (HR 0.12) but not significant for other mutation groups (HR 0.82)
cards.summary: Barsheshet 2012: in LQT1, beta-blocker benefit against aborted cardiac arrest or sudden death was pronounced for cytoplasmic-loop KCNQ1 mutations (HR 0.12) but not significant for other mutation groups (HR 0.82)
cards.type: Observational registry cohort with mechanistic substudy (Barsheshet 2012)
cards.people: 860 patients with genetically confirmed mutations in the KCNQ1 channel (LQT1), categorised by mutation location (cytoplasmic loops, membrane-spanning domain, C/N terminus, nonmissense); 27 aborted cardiac arrests and 78 sudden deaths occurred from birth through age 40 years. Cohort N = 860 (registry population overlapping with the other cards).
cards.result: After multivariable adjustment, cytoplasmic-loop missense mutations carried the highest risk of aborted cardiac arrest or sudden cardiac death (HR 2.75 versus nonmissense mutations; 95% CI, 1.29–5.86; P = 0.009). Beta-blocker therapy was associated with a significantly greater risk reduction in patients with cytoplasmic-loop mutations (HR 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02–0.73; P = 0.02) than in all other patients (HR 0.82; 95% CI, 0.31–2.13; P = 0.68), with a significant interaction (P = 0.04) — an 88% relative reduction in the cytoplasmic-loop group, and no significant reduction in the remainder. Expression studies showed cytoplasmic-loop mutations had a pronounced reduction in channel activation in response to beta-adrenergic stimulation, matching the clinical pattern.
cards.watchOut: The striking HR 0.12 rests on few life-threatening events (105 in the whole cohort) in a mutation subgroup; it identifies who benefits most, and its non-significant counterpart (HR 0.82) warns against quoting one average benefit for all LQT1 patients.

Mutations in cytoplasmic loops of the KCNQ1 channel and the risk of life-threatening events: implications for mutation-specific response to β-blocker therapy in type 1 long-QT syndrome. observational registry cohort with mechanistic substudy (barsheshet 2012) 860 patients with genetically confirmed mutations in the kcnq1 channel (lqt1), categorised by mutation location (cytoplasmic loops, membrane-spanning domain, c/n terminus, nonmissense); 27 aborted cardiac arrests and 78 sudden deaths occurred from birth through age 40 years. cohort n = 860 (registry population overlapping with the other cards). after multivariable adjustment, cytoplasmic-loop missense mutations carried the highest risk of aborted cardiac arrest or sudden cardiac death (hr 2.75 versus nonmissense mutations; 95% ci, 1.29–5.86; p = 0.009). beta-blocker therapy was associated with a significantly greater risk reduction in patients with cytoplasmic-loop mutations (hr 0.12; 95% ci, 0.02–0.73; p = 0.02) than in all other patients (hr 0.82; 95% ci, 0.31–2.13; p = 0.68), with a significant interaction (p = 0.04) — an 88% relative reduction in the cytoplasmic-loop group, and no significant reduction in the remainder. expression studies showed cytoplasmic-loop mutations had a pronounced reduction in channel activation in response to beta-adrenergic stimulation, matching the clinical pattern. the striking hr 0.12 rests on few life-threatening events (105 in the whole cohort) in a mutation subgroup; it identifies who benefits most, and its non-significant counterpart (hr 0.82) warns against quoting one average benefit for all lqt1 patients. barsheshet a et al. mutations in cytoplasmic loops of the kcnq1 channel and the risk of life-threatening events: implications for mutation-specific response to β-blocker therapy in type 1 long-qt syndrome. circulation. 2012. pmid: 22456477. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adrenergic beta-antagonists · adult · child · female · genetic predisposition to disease · heart arrest · humans · kcnq1 potassium channel · male · mutation · risk · romano-ward syndrome · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: with no randomised trial, three International LQTS Registry analyses agree that beta-blocker therapy is associated with far fewer cardiac events — with benefit varying by genotype, mutation location, sex and prior symptoms, and real residual risk in previously symptomatic patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: with no randomised trial, three International LQTS Registry analyses agree that beta-blocker therapy is associated with far fewer cardiac events — with benefit varying by genotype, mutation location, sex and prior symptoms, and real residual risk in previously symptomatic patients
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational: three analyses of the International LQTS Registry (N = 869 treated patients; N = 971 with LQT1/LQT2; N = 860 with KCNQ1 mutations). These cohorts overlap substantially, so unique participants are fewer than the summed 2,700 but well above any small-N threshold; the observational-only cap, not sample size, is what limits the stamp.
cards.result: Event rates fell after starting beta-blockers (probands 0.97 to 0.31 per year; Moss 2000); high-risk subsets showed 67–71% relative reductions on therapy (Goldenberg 2010); in LQT1 the life-threatening-event benefit concentrated in cytoplasmic-loop mutations (HR 0.12 vs 0.82 elsewhere; Barsheshet 2012). Residual risk on therapy: 32% of previously symptomatic patients had another event within 5 years, and 14% of post-arrest patients another arrest (Moss 2000). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: Which beta-blocker to choose is a different question, answered on live shelf #3074; this shelf's claim is only treated-versus-untreated, and it is associational throughout — confounding by indication cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moss AJ et al. Circulation. 2000 (PMID: 10673253); Goldenberg I et al. Journal of Cardiovascular Electrophysiology. 2010 (PMID: 20233272); Barsheshet A et al. Circulation. 2012 (PMID: 22456477).

shelves.title: Renal denervation off medications (SPLIT): it lowered pressure without drugs in non-resistant hypertension, but the resistant-hypertension effect is smaller and resistant patients off medication are untested — a partial completion of shelf #160
shelves.question: Does renal denervation lower blood pressure in resistant hypertension off medications?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Australia · Blood Pressure Determination · Catheter Ablation · Drug Resistance · Europe · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Safety · Prognosis · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Factors · Single-Blind Method · Sympathectomy · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #160, which covers renal denervation versus sham overall; this shelf homes the off-medication cut, and the large off-medication pivotal trial carded on #160 is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The precise population in the question — resistant hypertension studied while off all antihypertensive medication — has never been randomised in the records fetched: every resistant-hypertension denervation trial kept patients on medication, for the obvious safety reason. What exists is the two halves of the question in different trials. Off medication, in non-resistant uncontrolled hypertension, denervation beat sham in both carded trials: the SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED proof-of-concept (Townsend 2017; between-group difference −5.0 mm Hg in 24-hour systolic pressure at 3 months) and RADIANCE-HTN SOLO (Azizi 2018; baseline-adjusted difference −6.3 mm Hg in daytime ambulatory systolic pressure at 2 months). In resistant hypertension, the subgroup meta-analysis of all ten sham-controlled trials (Ahmed 2023) found the ambulatory effect smaller and not significant (24-hour systolic raw mean difference −1.86 mm Hg, confidence interval crossing zero), versus a significant −4.19 mm Hg in non-resistant trials, with a significant subgroup interaction for diastolic pressure (p = 0.02). PROPOSED SPLIT (off-medication efficacy shown in non-resistant hypertension; resistant-hypertension effect smaller and unproven off medication) — denervation does lower blood pressure without medication on board, but in resistant hypertension specifically the sham-controlled effect is weaker, and resistant patients off medication are an untested population, so the answer for them is inference, not evidence.

cards.headline: Townsend 2017 (SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED): off all antihypertensive medication, renal denervation lowered 24-hour systolic pressure by 5.5 mm Hg versus 0.5 mm Hg with sham at 3 months — a between-group difference of −5.0 mm Hg (p = 0.0414) — in uncontrolled, not resistant, hypertension
cards.summary: Townsend 2017 (SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED): off all antihypertensive medication, renal denervation lowered 24-hour systolic pressure by 5.5 mm Hg versus 0.5 mm Hg with sham at 3 months — a between-group difference of −5.0 mm Hg (p = 0.0414) — in uncontrolled, not resistant, hypertension
cards.type: Randomised sham-controlled trial (Townsend 2017, SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED proof-of-concept)
cards.people: 80 patients randomised (38 renal denervation, 42 sham) at 21 centres in the USA, Europe, Japan and Australia, in a multicentre, single-blind, randomised, sham-controlled proof-of-concept trial. Eligible patients were drug-naive or had discontinued their antihypertensive medications, with office systolic pressure 150 to under 180 mm Hg, office diastolic 90 mm Hg or above, and mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic 140 to under 170 mm Hg; drug surveillance verified the absence of antihypertensive medication. These were patients with uncontrolled hypertension off treatment — not resistant hypertension, which by definition is uncontrolled pressure despite three drugs.
cards.result: At 3 months, 24-hour systolic pressure fell by −5.5 mm Hg (95% confidence interval −9.1 to −2.0; p = 0.0031) with denervation and by −0.5 mm Hg (−3.9 to 2.9; p = 0.7644) with sham; the mean between-group difference favoured denervation (−5.0 mm Hg, 95% confidence interval −9.9 to −0.2; p = 0.0414), as did 24-hour diastolic (−4.4 mm Hg; p = 0.0024) and office pressures (−7.7 mm Hg systolic; p = 0.0155). No major adverse events occurred in either group. The authors describe the result as biological proof of principle for denervation's blood-pressure-lowering efficacy in the absence of medication.
cards.watchOut: Proof-of-concept size (80 patients, 3 months) and a milder population than the question asks about: entry pressures were capped (office systolic under 180, ambulatory under 170) and patients had taken at most a limited regimen before washout — nothing here shows what denervation does in a truly resistant patient withdrawn from a full regimen.

cards.headline: Azizi 2018 (RADIANCE-HTN SOLO): ultrasound renal denervation off medication lowered daytime ambulatory systolic pressure by 8.5 mm Hg versus 2.2 mm Hg with sham at 2 months — baseline-adjusted difference −6.3 mm Hg (p = 0.0001) — again in non-resistant hypertension
cards.summary: Azizi 2018 (RADIANCE-HTN SOLO): ultrasound renal denervation off medication lowered daytime ambulatory systolic pressure by 8.5 mm Hg versus 2.2 mm Hg with sham at 2 months — baseline-adjusted difference −6.3 mm Hg (p = 0.0001) — again in non-resistant hypertension
cards.people: 146 patients randomised (74 ultrasound renal denervation, 72 sham) at 39 centres in the USA and Europe, in a multicentre, single-blind, randomised, sham-controlled trial. Patients aged 18–75 with combined systolic-diastolic hypertension were eligible if ambulatory pressure was 135/85 to under 170/105 mm Hg after a 4-week discontinuation of up to two antihypertensive medications, and they remained off medication for the 2-month follow-up unless safety thresholds were exceeded. Discontinuation of at most two drugs defines a non-resistant population.
cards.result: The reduction in daytime ambulatory systolic pressure was greater with renal denervation (−8.5 mm Hg, standard deviation 9.3) than with the sham procedure (−2.2 mm Hg, standard deviation 10.0; baseline-adjusted difference between groups: −6.3 mm Hg, 95% confidence interval −9.4 to −3.1, p = 0.0001). No major adverse events were reported in either group. The authors conclude ultrasound denervation reduced ambulatory pressure at 2 months compared with sham in hypertension in the absence of medications.
cards.watchOut: Two months is the medication-free window only; the trial cannot speak to durability off medication, and like SPYRAL OFF MED it washed out at most two drugs — a resistant patient by definition fails three, including a diuretic, so this remains evidence about a different, less severe population.
cards.source: Azizi M et al. Endovascular ultrasound renal denervation to treat hypertension (RADIANCE-HTN SOLO): a multicentre, international, single-blind, randomised, sham-controlled trial. cards.headline: Ahmed 2023: across all ten sham-controlled trials, denervation's 24-hour systolic effect was significant in non-resistant hypertension (−4.19 mm Hg) but not in resistant hypertension (−1.86 mm Hg, confidence interval crossing zero) — and every resistant trial was conducted on medication
cards.summary: Ahmed 2023: across all ten sham-controlled trials, denervation's 24-hour systolic effect was significant in non-resistant hypertension (−4.19 mm Hg) but not in resistant hypertension (−1.86 mm Hg, confidence interval crossing zero) — and every resistant trial was conducted on medication
cards.people: Ten sham-controlled renal denervation trials including 1,544 participants (1,001 with resistant hypertension and 543 with essential, non-resistant hypertension; cumulative mean age 57 ± 3 years), in a prespecified trial-level subgroup meta-analysis. Resistant hypertension was defined as uncontrolled pressure despite three antihypertensive medications of different classes including a diuretic at maximum tolerated doses — a definition that requires patients to be taking medication, so no included resistant trial studied patients off medication.
cards.result: The raw mean difference in 24-hour systolic pressure between denervation and sham was statistically significant for non-resistant hypertension trials (−4.19 mm Hg; 95% confidence interval −6.07 to −2.30) but not for resistant hypertension trials (−1.86 mm Hg; 95% confidence interval −3.89 to 0.16 — the treatment made no significant difference); the subgroup interaction for systolic pressure did not reach significance (p = 0.10). For 24-hour diastolic pressure the pattern was the same (non-resistant −2.60 mm Hg, significant; resistant −0.67 mm Hg, not significant) and the subgroup interaction was significant (p = 0.02). The authors conclude denervation is a less effective intervention for patients with resistant hypertension.
cards.watchOut: Trial-level subgrouping: the resistant trials differ from the non-resistant ones in device generations, eras, medication adherence testing and sham design as well as in resistance itself, so the weaker resistant effect is a signal across trials, not a randomised comparison — and it still says nothing about resistant patients off medication, who appear in no trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: denervation lowers pressure off medication in non-resistant hypertension (−5.0 and −6.3 mm Hg versus sham), but the resistant-hypertension effect is smaller and non-significant in pooled sham-controlled data, and resistant patients off medication have never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: denervation lowers pressure off medication in non-resistant hypertension (−5.0 and −6.3 mm Hg versus sham), but the resistant-hypertension effect is smaller and non-significant in pooled sham-controlled data, and resistant patients off medication have never been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: two off-medication sham-controlled trials in non-resistant uncontrolled hypertension (80 and 146 randomised patients) and one subgroup meta-analysis of all ten sham-controlled trials (1,544 participants; 1,001 resistant, all studied on medication). The large off-medication pivotal trial carded on live shelf #160 is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Off medication: 24-hour systolic between-group difference −5.0 mm Hg at 3 months (Townsend 2017) and daytime ambulatory systolic difference −6.3 mm Hg at 2 months (Azizi 2018), both favouring denervation over sham. By resistance status: 24-hour systolic effect −4.19 mm Hg (significant) in non-resistant versus −1.86 mm Hg (not significant) in resistant trials (Ahmed 2023). No trial enrolled resistant patients while off medication. PROPOSED SPLIT (off-medication efficacy shown in non-resistant hypertension; resistant-hypertension effect smaller and unproven off medication).
cards.watchOut: The clinical temptation this shelf must resist is arithmetic — subtracting the off-medication effect and the resistant effect as if they were measured in the same patients. They were not: severity, adherence and background sympathetic drive differ, and withdrawing a full resistant regimen for a trial is unlikely ever to be done, so this gap is probably permanent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Townsend RR et al. Lancet. 2017 (PMID: 28859944); Azizi M et al. Lancet. 2018 (PMID: 29803590); Ahmed M et al. American Journal of Cardiology. 2023 (PMID: 36669381).

shelves.title: Renal denervation at 3 years: the blood-pressure fall is maintained — both sham-controlled programmes still favour denervation at 36 months and registry reductions persist, with no late safety signal reported
shelves.question: Does renal denervation maintain blood pressure lowering at 3 years?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Denervation · Humans · Hypertension · Kidney · Single-Blind Method · Sympathectomy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #160, which homes renal denervation versus sham at its primary (6-month) horizon; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, 3-year durability, and none of #160's carded records is re-carded here. Two sham-controlled programmes report 36-month outcomes and both still favour denervation: SPYRAL HTN-ON MED (Mahfoud 2022) found an adjusted ambulatory systolic difference of −10.0 mm Hg at 36 months on a similar medication burden, and the SYMPLICITY HTN-3 final report (Bhatt 2022) found adjusted differences of −22.1 mm Hg (office) and −16.5 mm Hg (ambulatory) — although HTN-3's 36-month contrast was built after unmasking, crossover and imputation, so it overstates the certainty of the gap. The uncontrolled evidence points the same way: Symplicity HTN-1 (Krum 2014) held −32.0/−14.4 mm Hg at 36 months, and the Global SYMPLICITY Registry (Mahfoud 2019) held −16.5 mm Hg office and −8.0 mm Hg ambulatory systolic reductions at 3 years in 1,742 patients, with eGFR declines of 7.1 (no CKD) and 3.7 (CKD) mL/min/1.73 m² and no long-term safety concerns reported. No carded record reports a late safety penalty. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): renal denervation's blood-pressure lowering is maintained at 3 years, with the caveat that the precise advantage over sham at 3 years is less certain than the trial reports' point estimates.

cards.headline: Mahfoud 2022 (SPYRAL HTN-ON MED): at 36 months ambulatory systolic pressure had fallen −18.7 mm Hg with renal denervation versus −8.6 mm Hg with sham — an adjusted treatment difference of −10.0 mm Hg — on a similar medication burden
cards.summary: Mahfoud 2022 (SPYRAL HTN-ON MED): at 36 months ambulatory systolic pressure had fallen −18.7 mm Hg with renal denervation versus −8.6 mm Hg with sham — an adjusted treatment difference of −10.0 mm Hg — on a similar medication burden
cards.people: 80 patients with uncontrolled hypertension (office systolic 150–180 mm Hg, diastolic ≥90 mm Hg, 24-hour ambulatory systolic 140 to <170 mm Hg) taking one to three antihypertensive drugs, randomised at 25 centres to radiofrequency renal denervation (n = 38) or a sham procedure (n = 42); patients and physicians were unmasked after 12 months and sham patients could cross over after 12 months.
cards.result: At 36 months the ambulatory systolic reduction was −18.7 mm Hg (SD 12.4) in the denervation group (n = 30) and −8.6 mm Hg (14.6) in the sham group (n = 32); adjusted treatment difference −10.0 mm Hg (95% CI −16.6 to −3.3; p = 0.0039). Differences at 36 months also favoured denervation for ambulatory diastolic (−5.9 mm Hg), morning systolic (−11.0 mm Hg) and night-time systolic (−11.8 mm Hg) pressure. Medication burden at 36 months was similar (2.13 vs 2.55 medications; p = 0.26). The record reports no short-term or long-term safety issues associated with renal denervation.
cards.watchOut: Only 80 patients were randomised and 62 contributed 36-month ambulatory data; after unmasking at 12 months, sham patients could cross over, so the 36-month comparison rests on the patients who remained and on a treatment programme whose early sham-controlled phase was small.
cards.source: Mahfoud F et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of renal denervation in the presence of antihypertensive drugs (SPYRAL HTN-ON MED): a randomised, sham-controlled trial. Lancet. 2022. randomised sham-controlled trial, 36-month pre-specified analysis (mahfoud 2022) 80 patients with uncontrolled hypertension (office systolic 150–180 mm hg, diastolic ≥90 mm hg, 24-hour ambulatory systolic 140 to <170 mm hg) taking one to three antihypertensive drugs, randomised at 25 centres to radiofrequency renal denervation (n = 38) or a sham procedure (n = 42); patients and physicians were unmasked after 12 months and sham patients could cross over after 12 months. at 36 months the ambulatory systolic reduction was −18.7 mm hg (sd 12.4) in the denervation group (n = 30) and −8.6 mm hg (14.6) in the sham group (n = 32); adjusted treatment difference −10.0 mm hg (95% ci −16.6 to −3.3; p = 0.0039). differences at 36 months also favoured denervation for ambulatory diastolic (−5.9 mm hg), morning systolic (−11.0 mm hg) and night-time systolic (−11.8 mm hg) pressure. medication burden at 36 months was similar (2.13 vs 2.55 medications; p = 0.26). the record reports no short-term or long-term safety issues associated with renal denervation. only 80 patients were randomised and 62 contributed 36-month ambulatory data; after unmasking at 12 months, sham patients could cross over, so the 36-month comparison rests on the patients who remained and on a treatment programme whose early sham-controlled phase was small. mahfoud f et al. long-term efficacy and safety of renal denervation in the presence of antihypertensive drugs (spyral htn-on med): a randomised, sham-controlled trial. lancet. 2022. pmid: 35390320. registry id: nct02439775. mesh: antihypertensive agents · blood pressure · blood pressure monitoring, ambulatory · denervation · humans · hypertension · kidney · single-blind method · sympathectomy · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Bhatt 2022 (SYMPLICITY HTN-3 final report): at 36 months office systolic pressure had fallen −26.4 mm Hg in the original denervation group versus −5.7 mm Hg in the sham group (adjusted difference −22.1 mm Hg), with similar adverse-event rates
cards.summary: Bhatt 2022 (SYMPLICITY HTN-3 final report): at 36 months office systolic pressure had fallen −26.4 mm Hg in the original denervation group versus −5.7 mm Hg in the sham group (adjusted difference −22.1 mm Hg), with similar adverse-event rates
cards.people: 535 adults aged 18–80 years with treatment-resistant hypertension (office systolic ≥160 mm Hg and 24-hour ambulatory systolic ≥135 mm Hg on three or more drugs including a diuretic) randomised 2:1 at 88 US centres to renal denervation with the single-electrode catheter (n = 364) or sham (n = 171); sham patients could cross over after the 6-month primary endpoint, and crossover patients' later values were imputed from their last pre-crossover masked measurement for group comparisons. 36-month data were available for 219 original denervation, 63 crossover and 33 non-crossover patients.
cards.result: At 36 months the change in office systolic pressure was −26.4 mm Hg (SD 25.9) with denervation versus −5.7 mm Hg (24.4) with sham (adjusted treatment difference −22.1 mm Hg, 95% CI −27.2 to −17.0; p ≤ 0.0001); the change in 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure was −15.6 mm Hg (20.8) versus −0.3 mm Hg (15.1) (adjusted difference −16.5 mm Hg, 95% CI −20.5 to −12.5). Time in therapeutic blood pressure range was 18% versus 9% despite a similar medication burden. The composite safety endpoint rate to 48 months was 15% (54 of 352) in the denervation group, 14% (13 of 96) in the crossover group and 14% (10 of 69) in the non-crossover group, with no evidence of late-emerging complications in the record.
cards.watchOut: This trial's 6-month primary endpoint was negative (the home shelf #160 covers that comparison); the large 36-month differences emerge after unmasking, crossover and imputation, and after differential follow-up (219 of 364 denervation patients had 36-month data) — so the 36-month gap is not a clean blinded comparison and is vulnerable to attrition and expectation effects.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Long-term outcomes after catheter-based renal artery denervation for resistant hypertension: final follow-up of the randomised SYMPLICITY HTN-3 Trial. Lancet. 2022. cards.headline: Krum 2014 (Symplicity HTN-1 final 3-year report): in the open-label first-generation cohort, office pressure remained −32.0/−14.4 mm Hg below baseline at 36 months, and 93% of patients had a systolic fall of at least 10 mm Hg
cards.summary: Krum 2014 (Symplicity HTN-1 final 3-year report): in the open-label first-generation cohort, office pressure remained −32.0/−14.4 mm Hg below baseline at 36 months, and 93% of patients had a systolic fall of at least 10 mm Hg
cards.people: Open-label study of 153 patients with treatment-resistant hypertension (systolic ≥160 mm Hg on at least three drugs including a diuretic at optimum doses), of whom 111 consented to 36-month follow-up and 88 had complete data at 36 months; mean age 57 years, mean baseline pressure 175/98 mm Hg, mean eGFR 85 mL/min/1.73 m². There was no control group.
cards.result: At 36 months systolic pressure had changed by −32.0 mm Hg (95% CI −35.7 to −28.2) and diastolic by −14.4 mm Hg (−16.9 to −11.9) from baseline. A systolic fall of 10 mm Hg or more was seen in 69% of patients at 1 month, 81% at 6 months, 85% at 12 months, 83% at 24 months and 93% at 36 months. One new renal artery stenosis requiring stenting and three deaths unrelated to denervation occurred during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: With no comparator, regression to the mean, medication changes and survivor effects (88 of 153 with complete 36-month data) can all inflate a before–after fall; this card supports durability of the observed reduction, not its size against sham.
cards.source: Krum H et al. Percutaneous renal denervation in patients with treatment-resistant hypertension: final 3-year report of the Symplicity HTN-1 study. Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24210779. Registry ID: NCT00483808. cards.headline: Mahfoud 2019 (Global SYMPLICITY Registry 3-year): in 1,742 real-world patients followed to 3 years, office systolic pressure was −16.5 mm Hg and 24-hour ambulatory systolic −8.0 mm Hg from baseline, with no long-term safety concerns reported
cards.summary: Mahfoud 2019 (Global SYMPLICITY Registry 3-year): in 1,742 real-world patients followed to 3 years, office systolic pressure was −16.5 mm Hg and 24-hour ambulatory systolic −8.0 mm Hg from baseline, with no long-term safety concerns reported
cards.people: Prospective open-label registry at 196 sites worldwide: 2,237 hypertensive patients treated with the first-generation catheter, of whom 1,742 were eligible for 3-year follow-up; baseline office systolic pressure 166 ± 25 mm Hg and 24-hour ambulatory systolic 154 ± 18 mm Hg; 21% had a baseline eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73 m². There was no control group.
cards.result: Reductions were sustained over 3 years: office systolic −16.5 ± 28.6 mm Hg (P < 0.001) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic −8.0 ± 20.0 mm Hg (P < 0.001). Between baseline and 3 years eGFR declined by 7.1 mL/min/1.73 m² in patients without CKD (baseline eGFR 87 ± 17) and by 3.7 mL/min/1.73 m² in patients with CKD (baseline eGFR 47 ± 11). The record reports no long-term safety concerns following the procedure.
cards.watchOut: Registry patients chose or were chosen for the procedure and were followed without a sham or drug-only comparator, so these falls cannot be separated from medication intensification and regression to the mean; the eGFR declines are described without a comparison group.
cards.source: Mahfoud F et al. Effects of renal denervation on kidney function and long-term outcomes: 3-year follow-up from the Global SYMPLICITY Registry. European Heart Journal. 2019. PMID: 30907413. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the blood-pressure fall after renal denervation does not wear off by 3 years — both sham-controlled trial programmes still show lower pressure at 36 months, and the open-label and registry cohorts show sustained reductions with no late safety signal in the records
cards.summary: Synthesis: the blood-pressure fall after renal denervation does not wear off by 3 years — both sham-controlled trial programmes still show lower pressure at 36 months, and the open-label and registry cohorts show sustained reductions with no late safety signal in the records
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised sham-controlled trial programmes reporting 36-month outcomes (SPYRAL HTN-ON MED, 80 randomised; SYMPLICITY HTN-3, 535 randomised), one open-label 3-year cohort (153 enrolled) and one prospective registry (2,237 treated, 1,742 with 3-year follow-up). Total carded participants exceed 2,900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Adjusted 36-month treatment differences favoured denervation in both trials: ambulatory systolic −10.0 mm Hg in SPYRAL HTN-ON MED and −16.5 mm Hg (ambulatory) / −22.1 mm Hg (office) in SYMPLICITY HTN-3, each on a similar medication burden. Uncontrolled cohorts showed sustained falls from baseline (office systolic −32.0 mm Hg in HTN-1; −16.5 mm Hg office and −8.0 mm Hg ambulatory in the registry). No late-emerging safety complications were reported in any carded record. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): blood-pressure lowering after renal denervation is maintained at 3 years.
cards.watchOut: The durability signal is consistent, but its magnitude at 3 years is softer than the numbers suggest: both trials unmasked patients well before 36 months, one imputed crossover values, and follow-up was incomplete — durability is likely, the exact extra fall versus sham at 3 years is not precisely known.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mahfoud F et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35390320); Bhatt DL et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 36130612); Krum H et al. Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24210779); Mahfoud F et al. European Heart Journal. 2019 (PMID: 30907413).

shelves.title: Low-risk PE at home on a DOAC (POSSIBLE): no PE-related deaths in the DOAC-specific studies and no clear difference from inpatient care — on a small, mixed literature whose own review calls itself inconclusive
shelves.question: Should adults with pulmonary embolism and low risk be treated at home with a direct oral anticoagulant?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Ambulatory Care · Anticoagulants · Confidence Intervals · Enoxaparin · Hemorrhage · Hospitalization · Humans · Pulmonary Embolism · Pyrazoles · Pyridones · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Rivaroxaban
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3373, which establishes home treatment of low-risk PE in general — the Aujesky randomised trial (enoxaparin-based) and the single-arm HoT-PE rivaroxaban study are carded there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers the slice #3373 leaves open: the specifically DOAC-based home strategy. The dedicated evidence is a 2025 systematic review of outpatient DOAC management (Khachatryan 2025, PMID: 41464832: 8 studies, 2 randomised and 6 non-randomised; no PE-related deaths in any included study, but heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis and the authors state no robust conclusions could be drawn). The randomised home-triage evidence behind it includes the HOME-PE trial — whose primary record is already carded elsewhere in the library and is therefore cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded — and its cancer post-hoc analysis (Chaibi 2024, PMID: 38308882), in which home-treated patients with active cancer had a 30-day composite rate of 4.3% (2/47) versus 1.0% (7/691) without cancer, while among patients with cancer home treatment itself was not associated with the outcome (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.15–9.47). The Cochrane comparison of outpatient versus inpatient care (Yoo 2019, PMID: 30839095; 2 trials, 451 participants, one of them a rivaroxaban-regimen trial) found no clear difference in mortality, bleeding or recurrence, on low-quality evidence with very wide intervals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a DOAC-based home pathway for rigorously selected low-risk PE looks as safe as admission in the available studies, but the DOAC-specific literature is small, mixed-design and explicitly inconclusive in its own systematic review. FLAG for the developer: this pack is built under one-home precedent (b) — the HOME-PE anchor is homed elsewhere, the slice is genuinely the DOAC strategy, and the three carded reports address that slice directly.

cards.headline: Khachatryan 2025: across 8 studies of outpatient PE treatment with DOACs there were no PE-related deaths — but designs were too heterogeneous to pool, and the authors state no robust conclusions could be drawn
cards.summary: Khachatryan 2025: across 8 studies of outpatient PE treatment with DOACs there were no PE-related deaths — but designs were too heterogeneous to pool, and the authors state no robust conclusions could be drawn
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials, non-randomised, retrospective, prospective studies, reviews and guidelines evaluating direct oral anticoagulants for outpatient treatment of pulmonary embolism: 833 publications identified, 8 studies finally included (2 randomised, 6 non-randomised — 2 retrospective, 4 prospective). Total participant N across the 8 studies is not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: No PE-related deaths were reported in any included study; bleeding events were reported in five studies and recurrent VTE rates in two. The review reports that apixaban and rivaroxaban were both safe with a low bleeding risk, that the sPESI score has disadvantages as the sole selection tool, and that Hestia, POMPE-C and RESI scores are preferable for selecting patients for home treatment. A meta-analysis could not be performed because of heterogeneity in designs, populations and outcome reporting, and the authors conclude that while results favoured outpatient management of selected patients, no robust conclusions could be drawn and large-scale prospective studies are required.
cards.watchOut: This is the only DOAC-specific synthesis and it disclaims its own conclusion: 'favoured outpatient management' rests on eight heterogeneous, mostly non-randomised studies.
cards.source: Khachatryan AS et al. Outpatient Management of Pulmonary Embolism Patients with Direct Oral Anticoagulants: A Systematic Review. Journal of clinical medicine. 2025. PMID: 41464832. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Chaibi 2024 (HOME-PE post-hoc): home-treated patients with active cancer had a 4.3% 30-day composite rate versus 1.0% without cancer — but among patients with cancer, home treatment itself was not associated with complications (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.15–9.47)
cards.summary: Chaibi 2024 (HOME-PE post-hoc): home-treated patients with active cancer had a 4.3% 30-day composite rate versus 1.0% without cancer — but among patients with cancer, home treatment itself was not associated with complications (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.15–9.47)
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial (Chaibi 2024, HOME-PE)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the HOME-PE randomised trial (haemodynamically stable symptomatic PE randomised to Hestia-criteria or sPESI triage for home treatment): 47 patients with active cancer treated at home, 691 without active cancer treated at home, and 33 with active cancer hospitalised only because cancer was their sole sPESI criterion. Main outcome: composite of recurrent VTE, major bleeding and all-cause death within 30 days.
cards.result: The composite outcome occurred in 4.3% (2/47) of home-treated patients with cancer versus 1.0% (7/691) without cancer (OR 4.98, 95% CI 1.15–21.49); in multivariable analysis active cancer was associated with complications among home-treated patients (OR 7.95, 95% CI 1.48–42.82). But patients with cancer treated at home (4.3%) fared no worse than patients with cancer who were hospitalised (3.0%, 1/33; OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.15–9.47) — relative measures with absolute rates as printed; the cancer subgroups are 47 and 33 patients, so every interval is wide.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, with 2 events in the key group of 47: it can reassure that home treatment was not the problem in cancer patients, but it cannot establish safety in that subgroup.
cards.source: Chaibi S et al. Outpatient management of cancer-associated pulmonary embolism: A post-hoc analysis from the HOME-PE trial. Thrombosis research. 2024. PMID: 38308882. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Outpatients · Pulmonary Embolism · Ambulatory Care · Risk Factors · Neoplasms

cards.headline: Yoo 2019 (Cochrane): outpatient versus inpatient treatment of low-risk PE — no clear difference in mortality, bleeding or recurrence across 2 trials and 451 participants, on low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Yoo 2019 (Cochrane): outpatient versus inpatient treatment of low-risk PE — no clear difference in mortality, bleeding or recurrence across 2 trials and 451 participants, on low-quality evidence
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Yoo 2019, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (2019 update) of randomised trials of outpatient versus inpatient treatment in adults with low-risk acute PE: 2 trials, 451 participants in total; both discharged the outpatient group within 36 hours of triage and followed participants for 90 days. One trial used the same regimen in both settings; the other used different regimens (its outpatient pathway was rivaroxaban-based, per the record's MeSH).
cards.result: No clear difference between outpatient and inpatient treatment for 30-day mortality (relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.01–7.98), 90-day mortality (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.06–15.58), major bleeding at 14 days (RR 4.91, 95% CI 0.24–101.57) or 90 days (RR 6.88, 95% CI 0.36–132.14), recurrent PE within 90 days (RR 2.95, 95% CI 0.12–71.85), or participant satisfaction (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90–1.04) — all relative measures; the review graded the outcome evidence low quality (moderate for satisfaction) because intervals were wide and events few.
cards.watchOut: Only 451 randomised participants underpin the whole outpatient question, and most were not on a DOAC-only pathway — this review supports the home strategy generally, not the DOAC version specifically.
cards.source: Yoo HH et al. Outpatient versus inpatient treatment for acute pulmonary embolism. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019. PMID: 30839095. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the DOAC home pathway inherits the general home-treatment evidence and adds a small, mixed, self-described inconclusive DOAC-specific literature
cards.summary: Synthesis: the DOAC home pathway inherits the general home-treatment evidence and adds a small, mixed, self-described inconclusive DOAC-specific literature
cards.people: The carded evidence: one DOAC-specific systematic review (8 studies, no pooling possible), one HOME-PE post-hoc analysis (738 home-treated patients in its comparison groups), and one Cochrane review of outpatient versus inpatient care (2 trials, 451 participants). The HOME-PE primary record and the HoT-PE rivaroxaban study are homed elsewhere in the library (shelf #3373 and the HOME-PE home) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: No PE-related deaths occurred in any study in the DOAC-specific review (Khachatryan 2025), home treatment was not associated with complications even in the cancer subgroup of HOME-PE (Chaibi 2024), and randomised outpatient-versus-inpatient comparisons show no clear difference in death, bleeding or recurrence (Yoo 2019). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): reasonable for rigorously selected low-risk patients, with the DOAC-specific certainty explicitly limited.
cards.watchOut: Selection is the treatment here: every reassuring number comes from patients first triaged as low risk by Hestia or sPESI-type rules, and the DOAC review warns against using sPESI alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khachatryan AS et al. Journal of clinical medicine. 2025 (PMID: 41464832); Chaibi S et al. Thrombosis research. 2024 (PMID: 38308882); Yoo HH et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019 (PMID: 30839095).

shelves.title: Mechanical thrombectomy in high-risk PE: treated cohorts show strikingly low mortality (1.9% in FLAME vs ~29% with other therapies) — but all the evidence is observational, and who gets the catheter may be the real treatment
shelves.question: Does mechanical thrombectomy improve outcomes in high-risk PE?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Observational Studies as Topic · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism · Thrombectomy · Thrombolytic Therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1585, which covers large-bore mechanical thrombectomy versus catheter-directed thrombolysis in intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (the randomised PEERLESS trial) — this pack covers the slice #1585 does not: high-risk (haemodynamically unstable, 'massive') PE, where no randomised trial exists and all evidence is observational, printed on the face. The dedicated study is FLAME (Silver 2023, PMID: 37847768): a prospective, nonrandomised comparison in which 53 high-risk patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy had an in-hospital primary composite rate of 17.0% (against a prespecified 32.0% performance goal) and in-hospital mortality of 1.9%, while 61 contemporaneous patients treated mostly with systemic thrombolysis or anticoagulation alone had a 63.9% composite rate and 29.5% mortality. Those context-arm figures match the background risk: a systematic review of 1,517 high-risk patients (Silver 2023, PMID: 39132523) puts in-hospital mortality at 28.3% and major bleeding at 13.8%. The FLASH registry (Toma 2023, PMID: 36349702) adds procedural safety in 800 mostly intermediate-risk patients — major adverse events 1.8%, 30-day mortality 0.8% — but only 7.9% of its patients were high-risk, printed plainly on its card. Selection decides who gets a thrombectomy catheter in every one of these datasets, so the mortality gap cannot be read as the device's effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: thrombectomy in high-risk PE is associated with strikingly low in-hospital mortality in selected patients, and a randomised answer does not exist.

cards.headline: FLAME 2023: in high-risk PE, thrombectomy patients had 17.0% on the in-hospital composite and 1.9% mortality, versus 63.9% and 29.5% in a non-randomised contemporary-therapy arm — an observational gap selection can explain
cards.summary: FLAME 2023: in high-risk PE, thrombectomy patients had 17.0% on the in-hospital composite and 1.9% mortality, versus 63.9% and 29.5% in a non-randomised contemporary-therapy arm — an observational gap selection can explain
cards.people: Patients with haemodynamically unstable high-risk ('massive') pulmonary embolism in a prospective, multicentre, nonrandomised, parallel-group observational study: 53 patients treated with FlowTriever mechanical thrombectomy (FlowTriever Arm) and 61 treated with other contemporary therapies (Context Arm — primarily systemic thrombolysis 68.9% or anticoagulation alone 23.0%). The primary endpoint was an in-hospital composite of all-cause mortality, bailout to an alternate thrombus-removal strategy, clinical deterioration, and major bleeding, compared in the FlowTriever Arm against a prespecified performance goal of 32.0%.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was reached in 9/53 (17.0%) FlowTriever Arm patients, significantly lower than the 32.0% performance goal (P < 0.01), and in 39/61 (63.9%) Context Arm patients. In-hospital mortality occurred in 1/53 (1.9%) patients in the FlowTriever Arm and in 18/61 (29.5%) patients in the Context Arm. The authors conclude that among patients selected for mechanical thrombectomy, a significantly lower associated rate of in-hospital adverse clinical outcomes was observed compared with the prespecified performance goal, primarily driven by the low all-cause mortality of 1.9%.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here was randomised: clinicians chose who received thrombectomy, and patients stable enough to reach a catheter laboratory differ from those given thrombolysis at the bedside — confounding by indication can manufacture most or all of a 1.9% vs 29.5% mortality gap, which is why this shelf's stamp is capped at POSSIBLE with 'observational only' printed.
cards.source: Silver MJ et al. Outcomes in High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism Patients Undergoing FlowTriever Mechanical Thrombectomy or Other Contemporary Therapies: Results From the FLAME Study. Circulation: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2023. PMID: 37847768. Registry ID: NCT04795167. cards.headline: Silver 2023 (meta-analysis): the untreated backdrop is grim — across 27 publications and 1,517 high-risk PE patients, in-hospital mortality averaged 28.3%, 30-day mortality 30.2%, major bleeding 13.8% and intracranial haemorrhage 3.6%
cards.summary: Silver 2023 (meta-analysis): the untreated backdrop is grim — across 27 publications and 1,517 high-risk PE patients, in-hospital mortality averaged 28.3%, 30-day mortality 30.2%, major bleeding 13.8% and intracranial haemorrhage 3.6%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of incidence (Silver 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies from 2010–2020 reporting patients with high-risk PE defined by American Heart Association and European Society of Cardiology criteria; 27 publications spanning 1,517 patients met the criteria. Incidences are weighted averages with 95% confidence intervals; the review itself informed the design and performance goal of the FLAME study carded above.
cards.result: In-hospital all-cause mortality averaged 28.3% (95% CI 20.9% to 37.0%), comparable to 30-day all-cause mortality of 30.2% (95% CI 22.3% to 39.6%). In-hospital major bleeding was 13.8% (95% CI 9.3% to 20.0%) and intracranial haemorrhage was reported in 3.6% (95% CI 2.2% to 5.9%). Risk of bias in the included publications was graded low-to-moderate, with substantial heterogeneity among studies, and the authors characterise the evidence as low-quality to moderate-quality. The record reports no treatment-comparison effect size — it is carded as the benchmark against which uncontrolled thrombectomy results are judged, and that role is printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: A benchmark built from heterogeneous published cohorts is not a control arm: FLAME's context arm (29.5% mortality) landing on this benchmark (28.3%) is reassuring about the context arm, but says nothing about whether FLAME's thrombectomy patients were comparable to either.
cards.source: Silver MJ et al. Incidence of Mortality and Complications in High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions. 2023. PMID: 39132523. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
