cards.headline: Toma 2023 (FLASH registry): mechanical thrombectomy in 800 real-world patients had 1.8% major adverse events and 0.8% 30-day mortality with immediate haemodynamic improvement — but only 7.9% were high-risk PE (printed on the face)
cards.summary: Toma 2023 (FLASH registry): mechanical thrombectomy in 800 real-world patients had 1.8% major adverse events and 0.8% 30-day mortality with immediate haemodynamic improvement — but only 7.9% were high-risk PE (printed on the face)
cards.people: The full US cohort of the FLASH prospective multicentre registry of patients treated with FlowTriever mechanical thrombectomy for pulmonary embolism: 800 patients, of whom 76.7% had intermediate-high-risk PE, 7.9% had high-risk PE (about 63 patients), and 32.1% had thrombolytic contraindications. The primary safety endpoint was a 48-hour major adverse event composite including device-related death, major bleeding and intraprocedural adverse events.
cards.result: Major adverse events occurred in 1.8% of patients. All-cause mortality was 0.3% at 48 hours and 0.8% at 30-day follow-up, with no device-related deaths. Immediate haemodynamic improvements included a 7.6 mmHg mean drop in mean pulmonary artery pressure (-23.0%; P < 0.0001) and a 0.3 L/min/m2 mean increase in cardiac index (18.9%; P < 0.0001) in patients with depressed baseline values; 62.6% of patients had no overnight intensive care unit stay. At 48 hours the echocardiographic right ventricle/left ventricle ratio fell from 1.23 to 0.98 (P < 0.0001) and severe dyspnoea fell from 66.5% to 15.6% (P < 0.0001) of patients.
cards.watchOut: Over 90% of this registry is not the shelf's population: its reassuring mortality (0.8% at 30 days) describes mostly intermediate-risk patients and must never be quoted as a high-risk PE result — the high-risk subgroup is about 63 patients and the record reports no separate outcomes for them.
cards.source: Toma C et al. Acute outcomes for the full US cohort of the FLASH mechanical thrombectomy registry in pulmonary embolism. EuroIntervention. 2023. PMID: 36349702. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Thrombectomy · Treatment Outcome · Pulmonary Embolism · Fibrinolytic Agents · Registries · Thrombolytic Therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: in high-risk PE, thrombectomy cohorts report mortality far below the ~28% background rate — but every dataset is observational and selection is the likeliest explanation for much of the gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: in high-risk PE, thrombectomy cohorts report mortality far below the ~28% background rate — but every dataset is observational and selection is the likeliest explanation for much of the gap
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective nonrandomised high-risk study (53 thrombectomy vs 61 contemporary-therapy patients), one incidence meta-analysis (27 publications, 1,517 high-risk patients), and one 800-patient device registry of whom about 63 (7.9%) were high-risk. Total patients in the directly comparative high-risk evidence: 114. No randomised trial of thrombectomy in high-risk PE appears in the records fetched this session.
cards.result: FLAME's thrombectomy arm reached its in-hospital composite in 17.0% versus a 32.0% performance goal, with mortality 1.9% versus 29.5% in the contemporary-therapy arm (Silver 2023, FLAME) — an arm whose mortality matches the pooled high-risk background of 28.3% in-hospital mortality and 13.8% major bleeding (Silver 2023, meta-analysis). FLASH shows the procedure can be delivered with 1.8% major adverse events and rapid haemodynamic improvement in a mostly intermediate-risk population (Toma 2023). Whether thrombectomy itself improves outcomes in high-risk PE — rather than marking the patients chosen to receive it — is untested by randomisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #1585 holds the randomised intermediate-risk comparison (PEERLESS); this shelf's high-risk evidence is two evidence classes weaker, and its stamp must not travel back onto the intermediate-risk question or forward onto any claim of proven mortality benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Silver MJ et al. Circulation: Cardiovascular Interventions. 2023 (PMID: 37847768); Silver MJ et al. Journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions. 2023 (PMID: 39132523); Toma C et al. EuroIntervention. 2023 (PMID: 36349702).

shelves.title: Iron when oral iron is not tolerated: intravenous iron works in prior oral failures (81.1% vs 5.5% response) and beats or matches oral iron head-to-head with far fewer intolerance dropouts
shelves.question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia, is intravenous iron more effective than oral iron when oral iron is not tolerated?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Female · Ferrosoferric Oxide · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Iron · Male · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #369 (and its parent #294), which cover intravenous versus oral iron in chronic kidney disease anaemia; this shelf covers the general oral-intolerant iron-deficiency anaemia population outside CKD, and does not re-card the CKD trials homed there. In the population this question names — patients whose oral iron had already failed or could not be used — the definitive trial could not ethically re-randomise patients to the oral iron they had failed, so it tested intravenous ferumoxytol against placebo (Vadhan-Raj 2014; 812 patients): a haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more by week 5 in 81.1% on ferumoxytol versus 5.5% on placebo, with mean haemoglobin up 2.7 versus 0.1 g/dL and fatigue scores also favouring iron. Where head-to-head testing against oral iron is possible, in inflammatory bowel disease anaemia, intravenous iron was more effective (odds ratio 1.57 for a haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more) and better tolerated, with discontinuation for adverse events or intolerance much lower on intravenous iron (odds ratio 0.27) (Bonovas 2016; 5 trials, 694 patients). In cancer chemotherapy anaemia, intravenous iron isomaltoside was noninferior to oral iron for haemoglobin rise, acted faster, and oral iron caused far more intolerance dropouts (8.0% versus 0.9%) (Birgegård 2016, PROFOUND; 350 patients). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): when oral iron is not tolerated or has failed, intravenous iron is more effective — it reliably raises haemoglobin in exactly that population, and head-to-head evidence where it exists shows equal or better efficacy with far fewer intolerance discontinuations.

cards.headline: Vadhan-Raj 2014: in 812 patients whose oral iron had failed or could not be used, intravenous ferumoxytol raised haemoglobin by 2.0 g/dL or more in 81.1% versus 5.5% on placebo
cards.summary: Vadhan-Raj 2014: in 812 patients whose oral iron had failed or could not be used, intravenous ferumoxytol raised haemoglobin by 2.0 g/dL or more in 81.1% versus 5.5% on placebo
cards.people: 812 adults with iron deficiency anaemia of any underlying cause and a history of unsatisfactory oral iron therapy, or in whom oral iron could not be used, randomised double-blind to intravenous ferumoxytol (n = 609) or placebo (n = 203); the primary endpoint was a haemoglobin increase of 2.0 g/dL or more at week 5.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was achieved by 81.1% on ferumoxytol versus 5.5% on placebo (P < 0.0001) — an absolute difference of 75.6 percentage points. Mean haemoglobin increase to week 5 was 2.7 versus 0.1 g/dL (P < 0.0001); achievement of haemoglobin 12 g/dL or above, time to response, and improvement in the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy fatigue score also significantly favoured ferumoxytol (all P < 0.0001, as printed in the record). Treatment-emergent adverse events were mainly mild to moderate, and the authors conclude ferumoxytol was effective and well tolerated in patients in whom oral iron was ineffective or could not be used.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is placebo, not oral iron — necessarily, since these patients had already failed or could not take oral iron; the card proves intravenous iron works in this population, and the head-to-head cards below supply the versus-oral comparison.
cards.source: Vadhan-Raj S et al. Efficacy and safety of IV ferumoxytol for adults with iron deficiency anemia previously unresponsive to or unable to tolerate oral iron. American Journal of Hematology. 2014. PMID: 23983177. Registry ID: NCT01114139. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (vadhan-raj 2014) 812 adults with iron deficiency anaemia of any underlying cause and a history of unsatisfactory oral iron therapy, or in whom oral iron could not be used, randomised double-blind to intravenous ferumoxytol (n = 609) or placebo (n = 203); the primary endpoint was a haemoglobin increase of 2.0 g/dl or more at week 5. the primary endpoint was achieved by 81.1% on ferumoxytol versus 5.5% on placebo (p < 0.0001) — an absolute difference of 75.6 percentage points. mean haemoglobin increase to week 5 was 2.7 versus 0.1 g/dl (p < 0.0001); achievement of haemoglobin 12 g/dl or above, time to response, and improvement in the functional assessment of chronic illness therapy fatigue score also significantly favoured ferumoxytol (all p < 0.0001, as printed in the record). treatment-emergent adverse events were mainly mild to moderate, and the authors conclude ferumoxytol was effective and well tolerated in patients in whom oral iron was ineffective or could not be used. the comparator is placebo, not oral iron — necessarily, since these patients had already failed or could not take oral iron; the card proves intravenous iron works in this population, and the head-to-head cards below supply the versus-oral comparison. vadhan-raj s et al. efficacy and safety of iv ferumoxytol for adults with iron deficiency anemia previously unresponsive to or unable to tolerate oral iron. american journal of hematology. 2014. pmid: 23983177. registry id: nct01114139. mesh: administration, oral · adult · anemia, iron-deficiency · female · ferrosoferric oxide · hematinics · hemoglobins · humans · infusions, intravenous · iron · male · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Bonovas 2016: head-to-head in inflammatory bowel disease anaemia, intravenous iron beat oral iron on haemoglobin response (odds ratio 1.57) and was stopped for intolerance far less often (odds ratio 0.27)
cards.summary: Bonovas 2016: head-to-head in inflammatory bowel disease anaemia, intravenous iron beat oral iron on haemoglobin response (odds ratio 1.57) and was stopped for intolerance far less often (odds ratio 0.27)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Bonovas 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials including 694 adults with inflammatory bowel disease, comparing intravenous versus oral iron head-to-head for correcting iron-deficiency anaemia (searches to July 2015). Risk of bias was high across the primary studies because patients and personnel were not blinded.
cards.result: Intravenous iron showed higher efficacy for achieving a haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more (odds ratio 1.57; 95% CI 1.13 to 2.18; relative measure). Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events or intolerance was lower in the intravenous groups (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.59), and gastrointestinal adverse events were consistently less frequent. Serious adverse events were more frequently reported on intravenous iron (odds ratio 4.57; 95% CI 1.11 to 18.8), though the majority were judged unrelated or unlikely to be related to the study medication. The authors conclude intravenous iron appears more effective and better tolerated than oral iron for IBD-associated anaemia.
cards.watchOut: IBD is the population where oral iron is most often genuinely not tolerated or not absorbed, so this is the closest head-to-head evidence for the question — but the serious-adverse-event signal, even if mostly judged unrelated, belongs on the face of the shelf.
cards.source: Bonovas S et al. Intravenous Versus Oral Iron for the Treatment of Anemia in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26765407. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Birgegård 2016 (PROFOUND): in cancer anaemia, intravenous iron isomaltoside was noninferior to oral iron for haemoglobin rise, acted faster — and oral iron drove 8.0% intolerance dropouts versus 0.9%
cards.summary: Birgegård 2016 (PROFOUND): in cancer anaemia, intravenous iron isomaltoside was noninferior to oral iron for haemoglobin rise, acted faster — and oral iron drove 8.0% intolerance dropouts versus 0.9%
cards.people: 350 patients with nonmyeloid malignancies and anaemia receiving chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 in a phase III open-label noninferiority trial to intravenous iron isomaltoside (single infusions up to 1,000 mg, or 500 mg bolus injections) or oral iron sulfate, at 47 hospitals or clinics in Asia, the United States and Europe; the primary outcome was change in haemoglobin from baseline to week 4.
cards.result: Iron isomaltoside was noninferior to oral iron on the primary outcome (difference estimate 0.016; 95% CI −0.26 to 0.29; P < 0.001 for noninferiority), with a faster onset of haemoglobin response in the infusion subgroup (superiority test P = 0.03 at week 1) and sustained effects in both groups to week 24. Fatigue score fell significantly by week 12 in the intravenous group (P < 0.001) but not the oral group (P = 0.057). Adverse drug reactions were more frequent on oral iron (18.8% versus 6.6%; P < 0.001), and discontinuation due to intolerance was 8.0% on oral iron versus 0.9% on intravenous iron (P = 0.001). Transient hypophosphatemia (phosphate under 2 mg/dL) occurred at similar low frequencies (7.1% infusion, 8.5% bolus, 5.4% oral).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority in patients who could still take oral iron is a weaker claim than superiority; its value to this shelf is the tolerability contrast — the intolerance that defines this shelf's population occurred almost entirely in the oral arm.
cards.source: Birgegård G et al. A Randomized Noninferiority Trial of Intravenous Iron Isomaltoside versus Oral Iron Sulfate in Patients with Nonmyeloid Malignancies and Anemia Receiving Chemotherapy: The PROFOUND Trial. Pharmacotherapy. 2016. PMID: 26927900. Registry ID: NCT01145638. cards.headline: Synthesis: in oral-intolerant iron-deficiency anaemia, intravenous iron reliably works (81.1% versus 5.5% response against placebo in prior oral failures) and, head-to-head, is at least as effective as oral iron with far fewer intolerance discontinuations
cards.summary: Synthesis: in oral-intolerant iron-deficiency anaemia, intravenous iron reliably works (81.1% versus 5.5% response against placebo in prior oral failures) and, head-to-head, is at least as effective as oral iron with far fewer intolerance discontinuations
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large double-blind trial in prior oral-iron failures or intolerant patients (812 participants), one head-to-head meta-analysis in inflammatory bowel disease (5 trials, 694 patients), and one head-to-head noninferiority trial in cancer chemotherapy anaemia (350 patients). Total carded participants 1,856, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Ferumoxytol versus placebo in oral-iron failures: haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more in 81.1% versus 5.5%, mean rise 2.7 versus 0.1 g/dL. Intravenous versus oral iron in IBD: response odds ratio 1.57, intolerance discontinuation odds ratio 0.27. Intravenous versus oral iron in cancer anaemia: noninferior haemoglobin rise, faster onset, intolerance discontinuation 0.9% versus 8.0%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The CKD version of this question is homed on live shelves #294 and #369 and is not re-carded here; intravenous iron also carries infusion-reaction and (for some preparations) hypophosphatemia risks that oral iron does not, weighed on the cards above.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vadhan-Raj S et al. American Journal of Hematology. 2014 (PMID: 23983177); Bonovas S et al. Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26765407); Birgegård G et al. Pharmacotherapy. 2016 (PMID: 26927900).

shelves.title: Catheter ablation and survival in AF with HFrEF (PARTIAL completion of live #271, precedent (b)): pooled benefit driven by the homed CASTLE-AF trial; free-standing trials split
shelves.question: Does catheter ablation improve survival in atrial fibrillation with HFrEF?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amiodarone · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Atrial Fibrillation · Catheter Ablation · Defibrillators, Implantable · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — with a prominent precedent-(b) flag. The trial that drives the survival claim, CASTLE-AF, is already homed on live shelf #271 and is therefore NOT carded here (its PMID is kept out of every card source line); this PARTIAL-completion shelf is built only on the free-standing HFrEF evidence around it. That surrounding evidence genuinely splits: meta-analyses pooling CASTLE-AF with smaller trials show lower mortality with ablation (9.0% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.52) but state their results are driven primarily by that one homed trial; AATAC found lower mortality with ablation versus amiodarone as a secondary endpoint (8% vs 18%); while the two free-standing trials least dependent on CASTLE-AF found no significant hard-outcome benefit — RAFT-AF's primary composite missed significance (hazard ratio 0.71, P = 0.066; stopped early for futility) and AMICA found no difference at all (the treatment made no difference). A second positive trial, CASTLE-HTx in end-stage heart failure, is already carded elsewhere in the library and is likewise not re-carded here. Net: a survival benefit in AF with HFrEF is POSSIBLE on the pooled record, but it has not been independently confirmed by a free-standing trial in this slice.

cards.headline: AATAC 2016: ablation beat amiodarone in persistent AF with heart failure (LVEF < 40%) — mortality 8% versus 18% (P = 0.037) as a secondary endpoint
cards.summary: AATAC 2016: ablation beat amiodarone in persistent AF with heart failure (LVEF < 40%) — mortality 8% versus 18% (P = 0.037) as a secondary endpoint
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised trial (AATAC, Di Biase 2016)
cards.people: 203 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, a dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D device, NYHA class II–III heart failure and LVEF < 40%, in an open-label multicentre randomised trial of catheter ablation (n = 102) versus amiodarone (n = 101), followed for a minimum of 24 months; the primary endpoint was AF recurrence.
cards.result: Freedom from AF recurrence at follow-up was 70% after ablation (after an average of 1.4 procedures) versus 34% on amiodarone (log-rank P < 0.001). Unplanned hospitalisation was 31% (32/102) versus 57% (58/101) (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.39–0.76 — a 45% relative risk reduction, with the absolute rates printed here), and all-cause mortality — a secondary endpoint — was significantly lower with ablation: 8% (8/102) versus 18% (18/101) (P = 0.037).
cards.watchOut: Mortality was a secondary endpoint in a trial powered on AF recurrence, the comparator is amiodarone alone (not contemporary rate control or guideline therapy), and single-procedure success varied widely by centre (29%–61%) — the survival signal is real in this trial but fragile.
cards.source: Di Biase L et al. Ablation Versus Amiodarone for Treatment of Persistent Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Congestive Heart Failure and an Implanted Device: Results From the AATAC Multicenter Randomized Trial. Circulation. 2016. PMID: 27029350. Registry ID: NCT00729911. cards.headline: RAFT-AF 2022: ablation-based rhythm control did not significantly reduce death or heart-failure events versus rate control (23.4% vs 32.5%; HR 0.71, P = 0.066) — stopped early for apparent futility
cards.summary: RAFT-AF 2022: ablation-based rhythm control did not significantly reduce death or heart-failure events versus rate control (23.4% vs 32.5%; HR 0.71, P = 0.066) — stopped early for apparent futility
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised trial with blinded adjudication (RAFT-AF, Parkash 2022)
cards.people: 411 patients with high-burden paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation, NYHA class II–III heart failure and elevated NT-proBNP, in a multicentre open-label trial with blinded outcome adjudication, randomised to ablation-based rhythm control (n = 214) or rate control (n = 197), with a minimum follow-up of 2 years; the primary outcome was the composite of all-cause mortality and all heart-failure events.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 50 patients (23.4%) on ablation-based rhythm control versus 64 (32.5%) on rate control (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.49–1.03; P = 0.066) — not statistically significant (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome by the trial's own test), and the trial was stopped early for apparent futility. Secondary measures favoured ablation: LVEF rose more (10.1% vs 3.8%; P = 0.017), 6-minute walk distance improved more, NT-proBNP fell more, and quality-of-life scores improved more; serious adverse events occurred in 50% of both groups.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for futility truncates the event count, and the confidence interval (0.49–1.03) cannot exclude a worthwhile benefit — RAFT-AF is 'not proven', not 'proven none'; its population also included some patients without severely reduced ejection fraction.
cards.source: Parkash R et al. Randomized Ablation-Based Rhythm-Control Versus Rate-Control Trial in Patients With Heart Failure and Atrial Fibrillation: Results from the RAFT-AF trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 35313733. Registry ID: NCT01420393. cards.headline: AMICA 2019: in advanced heart failure (LVEF ≤ 35%), ablation did not beat best medical therapy even on ejection fraction (+8.8% vs +7.3%, P = 0.36) — stopped early for futility
cards.summary: AMICA 2019: in advanced heart failure (LVEF ≤ 35%), ablation did not beat best medical therapy even on ejection fraction (+8.8% vs +7.3%, P = 0.36) — stopped early for futility
cards.people: Patients with persistent or longstanding persistent atrial fibrillation, LVEF ≤ 35% and an ICD/CRT-D indication, randomised to catheter ablation or best medical therapy (rate or rhythm control); 140 patients (68 ablation, 72 medical) were available for the 1-year endpoint analysis. The primary endpoint was the absolute increase in LVEF at 1 year.
cards.result: LVEF increased by 8.8% (95% CI 5.8%–11.9%) in the ablation group and by 7.3% (95% CI 4.3%–10.3%) in the medical-therapy group (P = 0.36) — the treatment made no difference — and there was no difference in secondary endpoints (6-minute walk, quality of life, NT-proBNP). Sinus rhythm at 1 year was recorded in 73.5% of the ablation group versus 50% of the medical group. The study was terminated early for futility; the authors suggest ablation benefit may shrink as heart failure becomes more advanced.
cards.watchOut: AMICA's primary endpoint was ejection fraction, not survival, and medical therapy itself produced a large LVEF rise (many tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathies recover with rate control) — it tempers the survival story in advanced disease rather than directly refuting a mortality effect.
cards.source: Kuck KH et al. Catheter Ablation Versus Best Medical Therapy in Patients With Persistent Atrial Fibrillation and Congestive Heart Failure: The Randomized AMICA Trial. Circulation. Arrhythmia and electrophysiology. 2019. PMID: 31760819. Registry ID: NCT00652522. cards.headline: Turagam 2019 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, 775 patients): ablation reduced all-cause mortality (9.0% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.52) — with the authors' own caveat that results were driven primarily by one trial
cards.summary: Turagam 2019 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, 775 patients): ablation reduced all-cause mortality (9.0% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.52) — with the authors' own caveat that results were driven primarily by one trial
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 6 randomised controlled trials (775 patients) comparing catheter ablation with drug therapy in adults with atrial fibrillation and heart failure, with at least 6 months of follow-up (search to 1 October 2018).
cards.result: Compared with drug therapy, ablation reduced all-cause mortality (9.0% versus 17.6%; relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.33–0.81) and heart-failure hospitalisations (16.4% versus 27.6%; relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.93), and improved LVEF (mean difference +6.95%), 6-minute walk distance (+20.93 m) and peak oxygen consumption; serious adverse events were numerically more common with ablation (7.2% versus 3.8%; relative risk 1.68, 95% CI 0.58–4.85, not significant). The authors list as limitations that results were driven primarily by 1 clinical trial — the CASTLE-AF trial homed on live shelf #271, which is not carded on this shelf — plus possible selection bias and open-label designs.
cards.watchOut: This pooled mortality figure inherits the homed CASTLE-AF trial's weight — it is evidence about the pooled literature, not independent confirmation; the pool also predates RAFT-AF (2022), the largest free-standing null trial on this shelf.

meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (turagam 2019) meta-analysis of 6 randomised controlled trials (775 patients) comparing catheter ablation with drug therapy in adults with atrial fibrillation and heart failure, with at least 6 months of follow-up (search to 1 october 2018). compared with drug therapy, ablation reduced all-cause mortality (9.0% versus 17.6%; relative risk 0.52, 95% ci 0.33–0.81) and heart-failure hospitalisations (16.4% versus 27.6%; relative risk 0.60, 95% ci 0.39–0.93), and improved lvef (mean difference +6.95%), 6-minute walk distance (+20.93 m) and peak oxygen consumption; serious adverse events were numerically more common with ablation (7.2% versus 3.8%; relative risk 1.68, 95% ci 0.58–4.85, not significant). the authors list as limitations that results were driven primarily by 1 clinical trial — the castle-af trial homed on live shelf #271, which is not carded on this shelf — plus possible selection bias and open-label designs. this pooled mortality figure inherits the homed castle-af trial's weight — it is evidence about the pooled literature, not independent confirmation; the pool also predates raft-af (2022), the largest free-standing null trial on this shelf. turagam mk et al. catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation in patients with heart failure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. annals of internal medicine. 2019. pmid: 30583296. registry id: none in the record. mesh: anti-arrhythmia agents · atrial fibrillation · catheter ablation · cause of death · exercise tolerance · heart failure · hospitalization · humans · oxygen consumption · postoperative complications · quality of life · randomized controlled trials as topic · risk assessment · stroke volume · walk test

cards.headline: Synthesis: the pooled record favours ablation for survival in AF with HFrEF, but the free-standing trials split — SPLIT, with the anchor trial homed on #271
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pooled record favours ablation for survival in AF with HFrEF, but the free-standing trials split — SPLIT, with the anchor trial homed on #271
cards.people: The carded evidence: two free-standing randomised trials with hard endpoints (AATAC 2016, n = 203; RAFT-AF 2022, n = 411), one randomised trial in advanced HFrEF (AMICA 2019, n = 140 analysed), and one meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (Turagam 2019, 775 patients). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: AATAC found lower mortality with ablation versus amiodarone (8% vs 18%, a secondary endpoint); Turagam's pooling found lower mortality (9.0% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.52) while conceding the result was driven primarily by one trial; RAFT-AF's primary composite of death or heart-failure events was not significant (hazard ratio 0.71, P = 0.066; stopped early for futility) and AMICA found no difference on any endpoint (the treatment made no difference). The driving trial (CASTLE-AF) and the end-stage CASTLE-HTx trial are carded elsewhere in the library — #271 for CASTLE-AF — and are deliberately not re-carded here under the one-home rule. PROPOSED SPLIT: survival benefit pooled-positive but single-trial-driven; independent free-standing confirmation is mixed.
cards.watchOut: Anyone quoting only the pooled relative risk 0.52, or only RAFT-AF's null, misstates this slice: the honest summary is that one homed trial carries the mortality claim and the surrounding trials divide around it.

shelves.title: Catheter ablation and mortality in ischaemic ventricular tachycardia (PARTIAL completion of live #713): ablation cuts shocks and ICD therapy, but no randomised report shows fewer deaths
shelves.question: Does catheter ablation reduce mortality in ventricular tachycardia with ischemic cardiomyopathy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Catheter Ablation · Death, Sudden, Cardiac · Defibrillators, Implantable · Electric Countershock · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Myocardial Infarction · Prospective Studies · Tachycardia, Ventricular · Ventricular Fibrillation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #713 already answers ablation versus escalating antiarrhythmic drugs in ICD patients with recurrent VT (VANISH, PMID 27149033, and PARTITA, PMID 35369700 — both homed there and not re-carded here), where death sat inside composite endpoints. This shelf asks the narrower question those composites leave open: does ablation itself reduce mortality? Five free randomised reports answer it, and none shows a mortality reduction. SMASH-VT (128 patients) found deaths of 9% with ablation versus 17% without (P=0.29 — the treatment made no difference) while ICD therapy fell sharply (hazard ratio 0.35). VTACH (110 patients) recorded five deaths against four. BERLIN VT, testing preventive against deferred ablation, found more deaths in the preventive arm (7.9% vs 2.4%, P=0.18) and was stopped early for futility. Pooling the three prophylactic-ablation trials (346 patients), the all-cause mortality odds ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.41–1.46) — no significant difference. The largest and newest trial, VANISH 2 (416 patients), lowered a composite that includes death (50.7% vs 60.6%; hazard ratio 0.75), but its record does not report mortality separately, so it cannot carry a survival claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: ablation's proven benefit is fewer shocks and less ICD therapy (homed on #713); a mortality benefit remains unproven, and every trial here was powered for arrhythmia endpoints, not death, so a modest survival effect is not excluded.

cards.headline: SMASH-VT 2007: prophylactic ablation cut ICD therapy (hazard ratio 0.35) but mortality was 9% vs 17% — the treatment made no difference to survival (P=0.29)
cards.summary: SMASH-VT 2007: prophylactic ablation cut ICD therapy (hazard ratio 0.35) but mortality was 9% vs 17% — the treatment made no difference to survival (P=0.29)
cards.people: 128 patients with previous myocardial infarction receiving an ICD for spontaneous ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, randomised to ICD implantation alone (n = 64) or ICD plus substrate-based catheter ablation (n = 64); no antiarrhythmic drugs were used.
cards.result: Over a mean follow-up of 22.5 months, appropriate ICD therapy occurred in 12% of the ablation group versus 33% of controls (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.15–0.78; P=0.007) and shocks in 9% versus 31% (P=0.003). Mortality, this shelf's outcome, was 9% in the ablation group versus 17% in the control group (P=0.29) — not significantly different; the treatment made no difference to survival. No patient died within 30 days of ablation.
cards.watchOut: With 128 patients and few deaths in total, SMASH-VT had almost no power for mortality, and its point estimate favours ablation — so this card shows 'not demonstrated', not 'disproven'; the same caution applies to every card on this shelf.
cards.source: Reddy VY et al. Prophylactic catheter ablation for the prevention of defibrillator therapy. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 18160685. Registry ID: ISRCTN62488166. cards.headline: VTACH 2010: ablation before ICD implantation delayed VT recurrence, but nine patients died — five in the ablation group, four in the control group
cards.summary: VTACH 2010: ablation before ICD implantation delayed VT recurrence, but nine patients died — five in the ablation group, four in the control group
cards.people: 110 patients aged 18–80 with stable ventricular tachycardia, previous myocardial infarction and left-ventricular ejection fraction ≤50%, randomised to catheter ablation plus ICD (n = 54) or ICD alone (n = 56) in 16 European centres; 107 were analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Time to recurrence of VT or ventricular fibrillation was longer with ablation (median 18.6 vs 5.9 months; hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.37–0.99; p=0.045). Nine patients died during the study — five in the ablation group and four in the control group — so the treatment made no difference to mortality. No death occurred within 30 days of ablation, and ablation-related complications occurred in two patients.
cards.watchOut: VTACH was open-label and powered for time to VT recurrence; its nine deaths cannot settle a survival question either way.
cards.source: Kuck KH et al. cards.headline: BERLIN VT 2020: ablating preventively rather than after three shocks did not reduce death or hospitalisation (hazard ratio 1.09) — deaths ran 7.9% vs 2.4% the other way, and the trial stopped early for futility
cards.summary: BERLIN VT 2020: ablating preventively rather than after three shocks did not reduce death or hospitalisation (hazard ratio 1.09) — deaths ran 7.9% vs 2.4% the other way, and the trial stopped early for futility
cards.people: 159 patients with stable ischaemic cardiomyopathy, left-ventricular ejection fraction 30–50% and documented VT, randomised at 26 centres to preventive VT ablation before ICD implantation (n = 76) or a deferred strategy of ablation after three ICD shocks (n = 83).
cards.result: Over a mean follow-up of 396 days, the primary composite of all-cause death or unplanned hospitalisation for symptomatic ventricular arrhythmia or worsening heart failure occurred in 32.9% of the preventive group and 27.7% of the deferred group (hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.62–1.92; P=0.77) — the treatment made no difference. Six patients died in the preventive group versus two in the deferred group (7.9% vs 2.4%; P=0.18), and heart-failure admissions also ran higher with preventive ablation (10.4% vs 2.3%; P=0.062), although sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia and appropriate ICD therapy were numerically less frequent. The trial was terminated early for futility on prespecified interim criteria.
cards.watchOut: BERLIN VT compares two ablation timings — everyone was meant to be ablated eventually — so it tests strategy, not ablation versus no ablation; its mortality numbers are small and early termination widens uncertainty in both directions.
cards.source: Willems S et al. Preventive or Deferred Ablation of Ventricular Tachycardia in Patients With Ischemic Cardiomyopathy and Implantable Defibrillator (BERLIN VT): A Multicenter Randomized Trial. Circulation. 2020. cards.headline: Atti 2018: pooling the three prophylactic-ablation trials (346 patients), ICD therapy fell (odds ratio 0.49) but all-cause mortality did not (odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.41–1.46)
cards.summary: Atti 2018: pooling the three prophylactic-ablation trials (346 patients), ICD therapy fell (odds ratio 0.49) but all-cause mortality did not (odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.41–1.46)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials (Atti 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the three randomised trials to November 2017 comparing prophylactic catheter ablation plus ICD against ICD alone in ischaemic cardiomyopathy (346 patients in total, including SMASH-VT and VTACH, carded above).
cards.result: Prophylactic ablation was associated with fewer ICD therapies (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.28–0.87) and fewer ICD shocks (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.22–0.64). There was no significant difference in all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.41–1.46; p=0.42), cardiovascular mortality (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.16–1.50) or major adverse events (odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.52–4.01) — on mortality, the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: The pooled confidence interval for mortality (0.41–1.46) is wide: these data exclude neither a worthwhile survival benefit nor harm, which is why this shelf's stamp stops at POSSIBLE rather than claiming a proven null.
cards.source: Atti V et al. Prophylactic catheter ablation of ventricular tachycardia in ischemic cardiomyopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing. 2018. PMID: 29680972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: VANISH 2 2025: first-line ablation beat antiarrhythmic drugs on a composite that includes death (50.7% vs 60.6%; hazard ratio 0.75) — but the record does not report mortality on its own
cards.summary: VANISH 2 2025: first-line ablation beat antiarrhythmic drugs on a composite that includes death (50.7% vs 60.6%; hazard ratio 0.75) — but the record does not report mortality on its own
cards.people: 416 patients with previous myocardial infarction, an ICD and clinically significant ventricular tachycardia (VT storm, appropriate ICD shock or antitachycardia pacing, or sustained VT terminated by emergency treatment), randomised internationally to catheter ablation within 14 days (n = 203) or antiarrhythmic drug therapy with sotalol or amiodarone (n = 213); median follow-up 4.3 years.
cards.result: A primary end-point event — death from any cause, or, more than 14 days after randomisation, VT storm, appropriate ICD shock, or sustained VT treated by medical intervention — occurred in 50.7% of the ablation group versus 60.6% of the drug group (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.58–0.97; P=0.03), a relative measure. Death is inside that composite, but the published record does not separate deaths by arm, so no mortality-specific claim can be taken from this trial. Within 30 days, death occurred in 2 ablation patients (1.0%) as a procedural-period adverse event, and 1 drug-group death (0.5%) was attributed to pulmonary toxicity of treatment.
cards.watchOut: A favourable composite that mixes death with shocks and VT episodes cannot be read as a survival benefit; VANISH (2016), the sister trial in drug-refractory VT, is homed on live shelf #713 and likewise found no significant mortality difference on its own.
cards.source: Sapp JL et al. Catheter Ablation or Antiarrhythmic Drugs for Ventricular Tachycardia. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39555820. Registry ID: NCT02830360. cards.headline: Synthesis: across five randomised reports, ablation reduces shocks and ICD therapy but no comparison shows fewer deaths
cards.summary: Synthesis: across five randomised reports, ablation reduces shocks and ICD therapy but no comparison shows fewer deaths
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials (SMASH-VT 128, VTACH 110, BERLIN VT 159, VANISH 2 416 patients) and one meta-analysis of the three prophylactic-ablation trials (346 patients). Total carded participants exceed 800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: On mortality itself, every randomised comparison is null: SMASH-VT 9% vs 17% (P=0.29), VTACH five deaths versus four, BERLIN VT 7.9% vs 2.4% (P=0.18, favouring deferral), pooled all-cause mortality odds ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.41–1.46), and VANISH 2 reporting no mortality-only figure. What ablation demonstrably reduces is arrhythmia burden — ICD therapy, shocks and VT recurrence — which is the benefit homed on live shelf #713. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: no mortality reduction has been shown for catheter ablation in ischaemic ventricular tachycardia; the trials were powered for arrhythmia outcomes, so a modest survival effect remains possible but unproven.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote VANISH 2's composite hazard ratio (0.75) as a mortality result — death is only one component, and the trial's record gives no deaths-by-arm count.

shelves.title: Spironolactone-centred medical treatment in primary aldosteronism not treated surgically (PARTIAL completion of live #3279): blood pressure falls substantially, but complete control is uncommon and renin suppression on treatment marks residual risk
shelves.question: Does spironolactone reduce blood pressure in primary aldosteronism unsuitable for surgery?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Delphi Technique · Hyperaldosteronism/drug therapy · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Spironolactone/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the slice live shelf #3279 leaves open: that shelf compares spironolactone WITH eplerenone head-to-head; this shelf asks what spironolactone-based medical treatment itself achieves in patients who are not treated surgically. The blood-pressure effect is large where it is measured directly: in 24 patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas managed medically for at least 5 years, blood pressure fell from 175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg (Ghose 1999). But complete control is uncommon at cohort scale: in the 1,258-patient international PAMO cohort on targeted medical treatment (spironolactone the dominant drug; median dose 40 mg daily in complete biochemical responders versus 25 mg), only 18.3% achieved a complete clinical response at 6–12 months and 18.2% had an absent response (Yang 2025). A 394-patient spironolactone series found doses above 50 mg bought no better blood-pressure control than 50 mg or less, at the cost of more adverse effects — 128 of 394 patients, mostly men (Sconfienza 2026). And blood-pressure control is not the whole story: medically treated patients whose renin stayed suppressed on treatment carried a higher cardiovascular event rate than essential-hypertension controls (adjusted HR 1.91 relative), while those titrated to unsuppressed renin did not (Hundemer 2018). No randomised trial has tested spironolactone against no treatment in non-surgical primary aldosteronism, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE and is labelled observational.

cards.headline: Ghose 1999: in 24 patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas treated medically for at least 5 years, blood pressure fell from 175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg on spironolactone-based treatment
cards.summary: Ghose 1999: in 24 patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas treated medically for at least 5 years, blood pressure fell from 175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg on spironolactone-based treatment
cards.people: 24 patients with documented aldosterone-producing adenomas at a large US tertiary referral centre who were treated medically (spironolactone-based) for at least 5 years rather than undergoing adrenalectomy — the surgery-unsuitable or surgery-declining end of the primary aldosteronism population; retrospective cohort with blood pressure and electrolytes at diagnosis and last follow-up.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure decreased from 175 mm Hg to 129 mm Hg (95% CI for the difference, 37.1 to 53.8 mm Hg) and diastolic from 106 mm Hg to 79 mm Hg (95% CI for the difference, 20.8 to 33.9 mm Hg). Serum potassium rose from 3.0 to 4.3 mmol/L (US laboratories report potassium in mEq/L, numerically identical). The authors concluded medical management of aldosterone-producing adenomas is a viable option for controlling blood pressure and potassium.
cards.watchOut: Only 24 patients, no untreated comparator, and additional antihypertensive drugs were part of 'medical management' — the 46/27 mm Hg fall is the effect of the whole medical regimen in a selected group who stayed on it for 5 years, not the isolated effect of spironolactone, and patients who failed medical therapy early are not in this cohort.
cards.source: Ghose RP et al. Medical management of aldosterone-producing adenomas. Annals of internal medicine. 1999. PMID: 10419425. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PAMO 2025: among 1,258 medically treated primary aldosteronism patients, 18.3% achieved a complete clinical response and 18.2% an absent response at 6–12 months; complete biochemical response in 52.9%
cards.summary: PAMO 2025: among 1,258 medically treated primary aldosteronism patients, 18.3% achieved a complete clinical response and 18.2% an absent response at 6–12 months; complete biochemical response in 52.9%
cards.type: International multicentre cohort study with consensus outcome criteria (PAMO, Yang 2025)
cards.people: 1,258 patients (mean age 52 years; 48.5% women) who started targeted medical treatment for primary aldosteronism between 2016 and 2021 at 28 centres internationally, assessed at 6–12 months against the new Primary Aldosteronism Medical Treatment Outcome (PAMO) consensus criteria for complete, partial or absent biochemical and clinical response; spironolactone was the dominant mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist used.
cards.result: Of 1,057 patients with biochemical outcome data, 559 (52.9%) had a complete biochemical response; the median daily spironolactone dose was significantly higher in complete biochemical responders than in others (40 mg [IQR 25–50] versus 25 mg [20–50]; P=0.011). Of 1,248 patients with clinical outcome data, 228 (18.3%) had a complete clinical response and 227 (18.2%) an absent response. Complete clinical response was more likely in women (odds ratio 2.099, 95% CI 1.485 to 2.968) and in patients needing fewer antihypertensive drugs at baseline, and less likely with microalbuminuria or left ventricular hypertrophy (OR 0.584, 95% CI 0.391 to 0.873).
cards.watchOut: 'Complete clinical response' under PAMO is a demanding endpoint (blood pressure normalised on no other antihypertensive drugs), so 18.3% understates how many patients improved; the cohort mixes spironolactone with other targeted drugs and doses, and there is no untreated or surgical comparator — this card measures what medical treatment achieves, not what it beats.
cards.source: Yang J et al. Outcomes after medical treatment for primary aldosteronism: an international consensus and analysis of treatment response in an international cohort. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2025. PMID: 39824204. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sconfienza 2026: in 394 patients on spironolactone for primary aldosteronism, doses above 50 mg gave no better blood-pressure control than 50 mg or less — and more adverse effects (39.1% vs 29.3%)
cards.summary: Sconfienza 2026: in 394 patients on spironolactone for primary aldosteronism, doses above 50 mg gave no better blood-pressure control than 50 mg or less — and more adverse effects (39.1% vs 29.3%)
cards.people: 394 patients with primary aldosteronism receiving spironolactone at a tertiary centre, divided at the population median dose into low-dose (50 mg daily or less) and higher-dose (over 50 mg daily) groups and followed for a median of 12 months after spironolactone was introduced; retrospective observational study.
cards.result: No significant differences were seen between the dose groups in blood pressure control, potassium or renin levels, or cardiovascular events at follow-up; the low-dose group achieved its control while taking more other antihypertensive drugs, especially diuretics. Adverse effects occurred in 128 patients overall, more often in men than women (44.7% versus 15.7%), with gynaecomastia the most frequent, followed by sexual dysfunction; adverse effects were more prevalent above 50 mg than at 50 mg or less (39.1% versus 29.3%), a difference significant in men (P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Dose was chosen by treating clinicians, not randomised — patients on higher doses may have had harder-to-control disease, which biases the comparison toward 'no difference'; the card supports a dose ceiling for tolerability, not proof that 50 mg is always enough.
cards.source: Sconfienza E et al. Efficacy and Safety of Treatment With Low Doses of Spironolactone in Patients With Primary Aldosteronism: A Retrospective Observational Study in a Tertiary Center. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2026. PMID: 41521906. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hundemer 2018: medically treated primary aldosteronism patients had blood pressure comparable to essential-hypertension controls yet higher cardiovascular event rates (adjusted HR 1.91 relative) — with the excess confined to patients whose renin stayed suppressed on treatment
cards.summary: Hundemer 2018: medically treated primary aldosteronism patients had blood pressure comparable to essential-hypertension controls yet higher cardiovascular event rates (adjusted HR 1.91 relative) — with the excess confined to patients whose renin stayed suppressed on treatment
cards.people: 602 patients with primary aldosteronism treated with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (surgical patients excluded) from a Boston hospital registry, 1991–2016, compared with 41,853 age-matched patients with essential hypertension from the same registry; retrospective cohort study of incident cardiovascular events, atrial fibrillation, diabetes and death.
cards.result: The two groups had comparable cardiovascular risk profiles and blood pressure throughout the study, yet incident cardiovascular events were higher in medically treated primary aldosteronism (56.3 [95% CI 48.8 to 64.7] versus 26.6 [26.1 to 27.2] events per 1000 person-years; adjusted hazard ratio 1.91 relative, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.25), as were death (adjusted HR 1.34 relative), diabetes (1.26 relative) and atrial fibrillation (1.93 relative). The excess cardiovascular and mortality risk was limited to patients whose renin activity remained suppressed (below 1 μg/L per h) on antagonist treatment (adjusted HR 2.83 relative for cardiovascular events); patients titrated to unsuppressed renin had no significant excess risk.
cards.watchOut: Registry data spanning 1991–2016 with treatment by the standards of the era; the renin-stratified analysis is observational within the cohort, so 'titrate to unsuppressed renin' is a hypothesis this study generates, not a strategy it randomised. Blood pressure itself was comparable between groups — the card's lesson is that pressure control alone did not erase the aldosterone-associated risk.
cards.source: Hundemer GL et al. Cardiometabolic outcomes and mortality in medically treated primary aldosteronism: a retrospective cohort study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 29129576. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: spironolactone-based treatment lowers blood pressure substantially in non-surgical primary aldosteronism, but complete control is the exception and under-titration leaves residual risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: spironolactone-based treatment lowers blood pressure substantially in non-surgical primary aldosteronism, but complete control is the exception and under-titration leaves residual risk
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small long-term adenoma cohort (Ghose 1999, 24 patients), one 1,258-patient international medical-treatment cohort (PAMO, Yang 2025), one 394-patient spironolactone dose series (Sconfienza 2026), and one 602-patient outcomes cohort (Hundemer 2018) — all observational; total carded participants exceed 2,200, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Blood pressure fell from 175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg over at least 5 years of medical management in the adenoma cohort; at cohort scale, 52.9% achieved complete biochemical response but only 18.3% complete clinical response (PAMO); doses above 50 mg added adverse effects without better control (Sconfienza); and cardiovascular risk on treatment remained elevated unless renin rose on treatment (Hundemer). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only: spironolactone reduces blood pressure in primary aldosteronism unsuitable for surgery, with dose adequacy — judged by renin as well as pressure — part of the effect. The spironolactone-versus-eplerenone comparison stays homed on live shelf #3279 and its trials are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Every card is observational: there is no placebo-controlled trial of spironolactone in this population, so the size of the drug's own effect (separate from companion drugs, regression to the mean, and survivor selection) cannot be read off these data — the stamp stays at POSSIBLE for that reason.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghose RP et al. Annals of internal medicine. 1999 (PMID: 10419425); Yang J et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2025 (PMID: 39824204); Sconfienza E et al. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2026 (PMID: 41521906); Hundemer GL et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018 (PMID: 29129576).

shelves.title: TAVI versus surgery at 10 years in intermediate-risk aortic stenosis (PARTIAL completion of live #3360): the answer splits by valve generation and access route
shelves.question: Is TAVI as durable as surgery at 10 years in intermediate-risk patients?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aortic Valve Stenosis/surgery,mortality,diagnostic imaging,diagnosis · Female · Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement/methods,mortality · Treatment Outcome · Male · Aged, 80 and over · Follow-Up Studies · Echocardiography · Aged · Time Factors · Heart Valve Prosthesis Implantation/methods · Aortic Valve/surgery,diagnostic imaging · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT (device generation and access route) — the 10-year answer live shelf #3360 could not give from its 1-year DEDICATE result. In the only fully randomised 10-year intermediate-risk comparison, PARTNER 2A (Thourani 2026; 1,910 patients who received a valve, mean STS score 5.8%), TAVI with the second-generation SAPIEN XT valve was associated with higher 10-year mortality than surgery (86.1% versus 82.8%; HR 1.13 relative; P=0.02) and four times the reintervention rate (6.3% versus 1.6%) — but the mortality gap was concentrated in the transthoracic (transapical/transaortic) access cohort (93.2% versus 85.1%), while transfemoral patients fared similarly (83.9% versus 82.1%). With the third-generation SAPIEN 3 valve, a propensity-matched comparison against the same surgical cohort found mortality (83.4% versus 82.3%; HR 1.01 relative) and reintervention (2.0% versus 1.9%) essentially identical at 10 years (Nazif 2026). On structural durability itself, the lower-risk NOTION trial found severe structural valve deterioration LESS often after TAVI than after surgical bioprostheses at 10 years (1.5% versus 10.0%; HR 0.2 relative), with bioprosthetic valve failure similar (9.7% versus 13.8%). PROPOSED SPLIT: durability at 10 years depends on which valve and which route — the early-generation transthoracic experience was worse than surgery; transfemoral and newer-generation results match it.

cards.headline: PARTNER 2A at 10 years (Thourani 2026): mortality 86.1% after SAPIEN XT TAVI versus 82.8% after surgery (HR 1.13, P=0.02), reintervention 6.3% versus 1.6% — with the mortality gap confined to transthoracic access
cards.summary: PARTNER 2A at 10 years (Thourani 2026): mortality 86.1% after SAPIEN XT TAVI versus 82.8% after surgery (HR 1.13, P=0.02), reintervention 6.3% versus 1.6% — with the mortality gap confined to transthoracic access
cards.people: 1,910 intermediate-risk patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis who received a valve in the PARTNER 2A randomised trial (57 centres, 2011–2013): 974 TAVI with the balloon-expandable SAPIEN XT system (Edwards Lifesciences; 76.9% transfemoral, the rest transapical/transaortic) and 936 surgical replacement; mean age 81.6 years, 45.4% women, mean STS score 5.8%; vital status at 10 years available for about 90% of each group after reconsent and vital-status sweeps.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 10 years was 86.1% after TAVI and 82.8% after surgery (hazard ratio 1.13 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.25; P=0.02). By access route, transfemoral mortality was similar (83.9% versus 82.1%; P=0.27), while transthoracic-access mortality was higher after TAVI (93.2% versus 85.1%; P<0.01; P for interaction=0.03). Cumulative aortic valve reintervention at 10 years was 6.3% after TAVI versus 1.6% after surgery (P<0.001). Among the few patients with 10-year echocardiograms (24 TAVI, 35 surgical), mean gradients were nearly identical (12.6 versus 12.7 mm Hg).
cards.watchOut: The valve is the second-generation SAPIEN XT, implanted in 2011–2013 with a substantial transthoracic-access minority — neither the device nor the access mix matches current transfemoral-first practice, and the authors' own stratification shows the mortality signal rides on the transthoracic cohort. Ten-year echocardiographic data survive for only a few dozen patients, so the gradient comparison is fragile.
cards.source: Thourani VH et al. 10-Year Randomized Outcomes of Transcatheter or Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement in Intermediate-Risk Aortic Stenosis. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2026. PMID: 42300821. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01314313. cards.headline: PARTNER 2 SAPIEN 3 at 10 years (Nazif 2026): propensity-matched mortality 83.4% versus 82.3% (HR 1.01) and reintervention 2.0% versus 1.9% — the third-generation valve matched surgery
cards.summary: PARTNER 2 SAPIEN 3 at 10 years (Nazif 2026): propensity-matched mortality 83.4% versus 82.3% (HR 1.01) and reintervention 2.0% versus 1.9% — the third-generation valve matched surgery
cards.type: Prospective registry with propensity-matched comparison to a randomised surgical cohort (PARTNER 2 SAPIEN 3i, Nazif 2026)
cards.people: Intermediate-risk patients treated with the third-generation balloon-expandable SAPIEN 3 valve in the PARTNER 2 SAPIEN 3 Intermediate-risk Registry (1,069 TAVI patients, enrolled 2014) compared with the 936 surgical patients of the PARTNER 2A randomised trial, using the same eligibility criteria; after 1:1 propensity matching, 783 patients per group (mean age about 82 years, 43% women, mean STS score 5.5%).
cards.result: At 10 years, all-cause mortality was 83.4% after SAPIEN 3 TAVI and 82.3% after surgery (hazard ratio 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.13; P=0.82) — the treatment made no difference. Aortic valve reintervention, adjusted for competing mortality, was 2.0% for TAVI and 1.9% for surgery (P=0.47). Among patients with 10-year echocardiograms (32 TAVI, 30 surgical), mean gradients were 11.0 versus 12.6 mm Hg.
cards.watchOut: This is not a randomised comparison: the SAPIEN 3 patients were enrolled a year or more later than the surgical cohort and matched statistically, so era effects and unmeasured differences remain possible despite matching — its 'no difference' carries less weight than a randomised null, and it shares the PARTNER 2A surgical arm with the preceding card rather than adding an independent surgical cohort.

cards.headline: NOTION at 10 years (Thyregod 2024): in lower-risk patients, the composite of death, stroke or MI was identical (65.5% both arms), and severe structural valve deterioration was less frequent after TAVI (1.5% vs 10.0%)
cards.summary: NOTION at 10 years (Thyregod 2024): in lower-risk patients, the composite of death, stroke or MI was identical (65.5% both arms), and severe structural valve deterioration was less frequent after TAVI (1.5% vs 10.0%)
cards.people: 280 patients with severe aortic stenosis at lower surgical risk (STS score under 4% in about 80%; mean age about 79 years) randomised to TAVI with the self-expanding CoreValve bioprosthesis (Medtronic; n=145) or surgical bioprosthetic replacement (n=135), followed for 10 years with Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 definitions of bioprosthetic valve dysfunction and failure.
cards.result: At 10 years the primary composite of all-cause mortality, stroke or myocardial infarction occurred in 65.5% after TAVI and 65.5% after surgery (hazard ratio 1.0 relative, 95% CI 0.7 to 1.3; P=0.9) — the treatment made no difference, with no difference in any component. Severe structural valve deterioration had occurred in 1.5% after TAVI versus 10.0% after surgery (HR 0.2 relative, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.7; P=0.02); severe non-structural dysfunction in 20.5% versus 43.0% (P<0.001); endocarditis in 7.2% versus 7.4%; and bioprosthetic valve failure in 9.7% versus 13.8% (HR 0.7 relative, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.5; P=0.4). No patient had clinical valve thrombosis.
cards.watchOut: NOTION's patients were mostly LOW surgical risk (STS under 4%), a step below this shelf's intermediate-risk population, and the trial is small (280 patients) with a first-generation self-expanding valve; its durability definitions also count surgical prosthesis–patient mismatch within non-structural dysfunction, which inflates the surgical arm's dysfunction rate relative to a pure deterioration comparison.
cards.source: Thyregod HGH et al. Transcatheter or surgical aortic valve implantation: 10-year outcomes of the NOTION trial. European heart journal. 2024. PMID: 38321820. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: at 10 years, TAVI durability in intermediate-risk patients splits by valve generation and access route — not by the catheter approach itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: at 10 years, TAVI durability in intermediate-risk patients splits by valve generation and access route — not by the catheter approach itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised 10-year follow-up in intermediate-risk patients (PARTNER 2A, 1,910 patients), one propensity-matched 10-year comparison of a newer-generation valve against the same surgical cohort (PARTNER 2 SAPIEN 3i, 783 matched pairs), and one randomised 10-year follow-up in lower-risk patients (NOTION, 280 patients). Total carded participants exceed 3,700, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Mortality at 10 years: 86.1% versus 82.8% favouring surgery with the second-generation SAPIEN XT (HR 1.13 relative), driven by transthoracic access; 83.4% versus 82.3% (HR 1.01 relative) with the third-generation SAPIEN 3; composite death/stroke/MI identical at 65.5% in NOTION. Reintervention: 6.3% versus 1.6% (XT), 2.0% versus 1.9% (SAPIEN 3). Severe structural deterioration in NOTION: 1.5% TAVI versus 10.0% surgery. PROPOSED SPLIT (device generation and access route): TAVI is as durable as surgery at 10 years in its modern transfemoral, newer-generation form; the early-generation transthoracic experience was not. The 1-year comparison stays homed on live shelf #3360 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Ten-year mortality above 80% in the intermediate-risk cohorts means most patients died with, not of, their valve — durability conclusions rest on the minority who survived, on small echocardiographic subsets, and on reintervention rates that competing mortality compresses; a 60-year-old choosing today still has no direct 10-year randomised data in their own age band.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thourani VH et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2026 (PMID: 42300821); Nazif TM et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2026 (PMID: 42300820); Thyregod HGH et al. European heart journal. 2024 (PMID: 38321820).

shelves.title: How long to anticoagulate after surgery-provoked VTE (PARTIAL completion of live #1581): recurrence after stopping is the lowest of any VTE type — about 0.7% per patient-year — so 3 months is the supported course unless enduring risk factors coexist
shelves.question: How long should anticoagulation last after provoked VTE from surgery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Incidence · Prognosis · Recurrence · Risk Assessment/methods · Risk Factors · Venous Thromboembolism/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT (enduring risk factors) — for the slice live shelf #1581 leaves open: that shelf covers extended rivaroxaban in equipoise VTE after 6–12 months of treatment; this shelf asks how long anticoagulation should run from the start after VTE provoked by surgery. Surgery-provoked VTE has the lowest recurrence risk of any VTE category once treatment stops: 0.7% per patient-year at 24 months, versus 4.2% for nonsurgical transient factors and 7.4% for unprovoked VTE (Iorio 2010). The 22-trial duration meta-analysis (Li 2025) found that for primary treatment — including VTE provoked by transient factors — longer courses (over 6 months) versus shorter (3–6 months) probably reduced recurrent PE only modestly (relative risk 0.66, CI crossing 1) while doubling major bleeding (relative risk 2.02); its authors conclude shorter courses are more beneficial for primary treatment of all VTE types, reserving indefinite treatment for unprovoked or chronic-risk VTE. The exception is the patient whose provoking surgery coexists with enduring risk factors: in HI-PRO (Piazza 2025), such patients randomised after at least 3 months of treatment to 12 further months of low-dose apixaban had recurrence in 1.3% versus 10.0% on placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT: 3 months for surgery-provoked VTE without enduring risk factors; extended low-dose treatment is trial-supported when enduring risk factors coexist.

cards.headline: Iorio 2010: after stopping anticoagulation, recurrence was 0.7% per patient-year for surgery-provoked VTE — versus 4.2% for nonsurgical transient factors and 7.4% for unprovoked VTE
cards.summary: Iorio 2010: after stopping anticoagulation, recurrence was 0.7% per patient-year for surgery-provoked VTE — versus 4.2% for nonsurgical transient factors and 7.4% for unprovoked VTE
cards.people: Systematic review of prospective cohort studies and randomised trials of patients with a first symptomatic VTE provoked by a transient risk factor, treated for at least 3 months and followed after treatment stopped: 11 studies and 2,268 patients for all transient factors at 24 months; the surgical-factor subgroup comprises 3 studies and 248 patients; the nonsurgical-factor subgroup, 3 studies and 509 patients.
cards.result: At 24 months after stopping therapy, the pooled recurrence rate was 3.3% per patient-year for all transient-factor VTE, 0.7% per patient-year for VTE provoked by a surgical factor, and 4.2% per patient-year for VTE provoked by a nonsurgical transient factor; in the same studies, recurrence after unprovoked VTE was 7.4% per patient-year. The rate ratio for a nonsurgical versus a surgical factor was 3.0, and for unprovoked versus nonsurgical factor 1.8. The authors conclude the recurrence risk is low if VTE is provoked by surgery — the finding on which a fixed short course rests.
cards.watchOut: The surgical subgroup is only 248 patients across 3 studies, so the 0.7% figure is imprecise even though the ordering (surgical lowest, by a wide margin) is consistent; these cohorts predate routine direct oral anticoagulant use, and recurrence was counted after a minimum of 3 months of treatment — the review does not test courses shorter than 3 months.
cards.source: Iorio A et al. Risk of recurrence after a first episode of symptomatic venous thromboembolism provoked by a transient risk factor: a systematic review. Archives of internal medicine. 2010. PMID: 20975016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2025: across 22 duration trials (11,617 participants), longer primary treatment (>6 months) versus shorter (3–6 months) doubled major bleeding (relative risk 2.02) with only a probable, imprecise reduction in recurrent PE (relative risk 0.66, CI 0.42 to 1.02)
cards.summary: Li 2025: across 22 duration trials (11,617 participants), longer primary treatment (>6 months) versus shorter (3–6 months) doubled major bleeding (relative risk 2.02) with only a probable, imprecise reduction in recurrent PE (relative risk 0.66, CI 0.42 to 1.02)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (Li 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (11,617 participants) comparing shorter (3–6 months) with longer (over 6 months) anticoagulation for primary VTE treatment, or discontinuation with indefinite therapy for secondary prevention; the primary-treatment analysis pools unprovoked VTE and VTE provoked by chronic or transient risk factors together.
cards.result: For primary treatment, longer versus shorter courses probably reduced recurrent PE (risk ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.02) and recurrent DVT (0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.14) — both confidence intervals crossing 1 — but were associated with higher mortality (risk ratio 1.43 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.41; moderate certainty) and a higher risk of major bleeding (risk ratio 2.02 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 3.98; high certainty). Indefinite therapy's clear benefits were confined to secondary prevention of unprovoked VTE and VTE provoked by chronic risk factors. The authors' summary: for the primary treatment of all types of VTE, a shorter (3–6 month) duration is more beneficial.
cards.watchOut: The primary-treatment pool mixes provoked and unprovoked VTE, so its bleeding-versus-recurrence trade is an average; applied to surgery-provoked VTE specifically — where the recurrence side of the scale is the lightest of any category (previous card) — the case against extending primary treatment is stronger than the pooled average suggests, not weaker.
cards.source: Li A et al. Duration of primary/secondary treatment to prevent recurrent venous thromboembolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Blood advances. 2025. PMID: 40198201. cards.headline: HI-PRO 2025: in provoked VTE with coexisting enduring risk factors, 12 months of low-dose apixaban after at least 3 months of treatment cut recurrence from 10.0% to 1.3% (HR 0.13) with one major bleed
cards.summary: HI-PRO 2025: in provoked VTE with coexisting enduring risk factors, 12 months of low-dose apixaban after at least 3 months of treatment cut recurrence from 10.0% to 1.3% (HR 0.13) with one major bleed
cards.people: 600 adults (mean age 59.5 years; 57.0% women) at a single centre with VTE after a transient provoking factor (surgery, trauma or immobility) PLUS at least one enduring risk factor, who had completed at least 3 months of anticoagulation, randomised double-blind to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months.
cards.result: Symptomatic recurrent VTE occurred in 4 of 300 patients (1.3%) on apixaban versus 30 of 300 (10.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.13 relative, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.36; P<0.001). Major bleeding occurred in 1 patient on apixaban and none on placebo; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding in 4.8% versus 1.7% (HR 2.68 relative, 95% CI 0.96 to 7.43; P=0.06). One apixaban patient and 3 placebo patients died, none from cardiovascular or haemorrhagic causes.
cards.watchOut: HI-PRO's placebo-arm recurrence of 10.0% is roughly fourteen times the surgical-provoked rate in the Iorio review — because entry required an enduring risk factor on top of the transient provoker. This trial must not be read as evidence for extending treatment after uncomplicated surgery-provoked VTE; it defines the exception (enduring risk factors present), not the rule.

randomised controlled trial (hi-pro, piazza 2025) 600 adults (mean age 59.5 years; 57.0% women) at a single centre with vte after a transient provoking factor (surgery, trauma or immobility) plus at least one enduring risk factor, who had completed at least 3 months of anticoagulation, randomised double-blind to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months. symptomatic recurrent vte occurred in 4 of 300 patients (1.3%) on apixaban versus 30 of 300 (10.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.13 relative, 95% ci 0.04 to 0.36; p<0.001). major bleeding occurred in 1 patient on apixaban and none on placebo; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding in 4.8% versus 1.7% (hr 2.68 relative, 95% ci 0.96 to 7.43; p=0.06). one apixaban patient and 3 placebo patients died, none from cardiovascular or haemorrhagic causes. hi-pro's placebo-arm recurrence of 10.0% is roughly fourteen times the surgical-provoked rate in the iorio review — because entry required an enduring risk factor on top of the transient provoker. this trial must not be read as evidence for extending treatment after uncomplicated surgery-provoked vte; it defines the exception (enduring risk factors present), not the rule. piazza g et al. apixaban for extended treatment of provoked venous thromboembolism. the new england journal of medicine. 2025. pmid: 40888734. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct04168203. mesh: adult · aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · administration, oral · anticoagulants/administration & dosage,adverse effects · double-blind method · factor xa inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · hemorrhage/chemically induced,epidemiology · kaplan-meier estimate · pyrazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · pyridones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · recurrence · risk factors · venous thromboembolism/drug therapy,epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · time factors · drug administration schedule · intention to treat analysis · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 months is the evidence-supported course after surgery-provoked VTE — extension is for the subgroup with enduring risk factors, not for the surgical provocation itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: 3 months is the evidence-supported course after surgery-provoked VTE — extension is for the subgroup with enduring risk factors, not for the surgical provocation itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of recurrence after stopping treatment, by provoking factor (Iorio 2010; surgical subgroup 248 patients within 2,268 transient-factor patients), one 22-trial duration meta-analysis (Li 2025; 11,617 participants), and one randomised trial of extended low-dose apixaban in provoked VTE with enduring risk factors (HI-PRO 2025; 600 patients). Total carded participants exceed 14,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Recurrence after stopping: 0.7% per patient-year (surgery-provoked) versus 7.4% (unprovoked). Longer primary treatment: major bleeding relative risk 2.02 against an imprecise PE benefit (relative risk 0.66, CI crossing 1). Extended low-dose apixaban where enduring risk factors coexist: recurrence 1.3% versus 10.0% (HR 0.13 relative). PROPOSED SPLIT (enduring risk factors): stop at 3 months after VTE provoked by surgery alone; consider extended low-intensity anticoagulation when enduring risk factors accompany the provocation. The extended-rivaroxaban equipoise question stays homed on live shelf #1581 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised surgery-provoked patients without enduring risk factors to 3 versus 6 or more months and reported the surgical subgroup separately — the 3-month answer is built from recurrence epidemiology plus the all-comers duration pool, which is why the stamp is a SPLIT at POSSIBLE strength rather than a LIKELY.
cards.source: Synthesis of Iorio A et al. Archives of internal medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20975016); Li A et al. Blood advances. 2025 (PMID: 40198201); Piazza G et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40888734).
