shelves.title: Continuing beta-blockers through major surgery in existing users (PARTIAL completion of live #352): withdrawal is associated with a three- to four-fold higher 30-day mortality in observational data; continuation is associated with lower mortality
shelves.question: In adults undergoing major surgery, should beta-blockers be continued perioperatively?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Aged · Cohort Studies · Databases, Factual · Female · Heart Arrest/mortality,prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morbidity · Myocardial Infarction/mortality,prevention & control · Perioperative Period · Retrospective Studies · Risk · Surgical Procedures, Operative · Treatment Outcome · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the continuation slice live shelf #352 leaves open: that shelf's evidence is about STARTING beta-blockers around surgery (POISE: harm) and it carries the guideline rule to continue chronic therapy as a recommendation, without primary evidence on continuation itself. The continuation evidence is entirely observational, and it points one way: withdrawal is dangerous. In 38,779 operations under a perioperative cardiac risk protocol, patients whose beta-blocker was withdrawn had a 30-day mortality odds ratio of 3.93 relative to the comparison pattern, while continuous use was associated with lower 30-day (OR 0.68 relative) and 1-year mortality (Wallace 2010). In 711 vascular surgery patients, continuous use was associated with a 1-year mortality hazard ratio of 0.4 relative to non-use, and withdrawal with a hazard ratio of 2.7 relative (Hoeks 2007). A 136,745-patient VA cohort found perioperative beta-blocker exposure associated with lower 30-day mortality in propensity-matched analysis (relative risk 0.73), with benefit concentrated in patients with two or more cardiac risk factors (London 2013). No trial has randomised existing users to continue versus stop, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE and is labelled observational — but the consistency of the withdrawal signal across cohorts is what the guideline rule rests on.

cards.headline: Wallace 2010: across 38,779 operations, perioperative beta-blocker withdrawal was associated with a 30-day mortality odds ratio of 3.93, while continuous use was associated with lower mortality (OR 0.68)
cards.summary: Wallace 2010: across 38,779 operations, perioperative beta-blocker withdrawal was associated with a 30-day mortality odds ratio of 3.93, while continuous use was associated with lower mortality (OR 0.68)
cards.people: 38,779 operations performed 1996–2008 at the San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center under its Perioperative Cardiac Risk Reduction protocol; in patients meeting protocol indications for perioperative beta-blockade, the pattern of use was classified as none, addition (started perioperatively), withdrawal (chronic therapy stopped), or continuous (chronic therapy maintained), with logistic regression, survival and propensity analyses of 30-day and 1-year mortality.
cards.result: Withdrawal was associated with increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio 3.93 relative, 95% CI 2.57 to 6.01; P<0.0001) and 1-year mortality (OR 1.96 relative, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.58; P<0.0001). Continuous use was associated with reduced 30-day mortality (OR 0.68 relative, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.98; P=0.04) and borderline-reduced 1-year mortality (OR 0.82 relative, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.0; P=0.05). Addition was also associated with lower mortality in this protocolised setting (30-day OR 0.52 relative; 1-year OR 0.64 relative). The authors conclude perioperative withdrawal of beta-blockers is associated with increased mortality.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre VA data in a protocolised programme: withdrawal was not randomised, and a beta-blocker may be stopped precisely because a patient is hypotensive, bleeding or deteriorating — confounding by indication that adjustment can only partly remove. The 'addition' finding also belongs to this centre's careful titration protocol and must not be read against POISE's day-of-surgery high-dose initiation harm, which is homed on live #352.
cards.source: Wallace AW et al. Association of the pattern of use of perioperative β-blockade and postoperative mortality. Anesthesiology. 2010. PMID: 20864832. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hoeks 2007: in 711 vascular surgery patients, continuous beta-blocker use was associated with a 1-year mortality hazard ratio of 0.4, and withdrawal with a hazard ratio of 2.7
cards.summary: Hoeks 2007: in 711 vascular surgery patients, continuous beta-blocker use was associated with a 1-year mortality hazard ratio of 0.4, and withdrawal with a hazard ratio of 2.7
cards.people: 711 consecutive peripheral vascular surgery patients at 11 hospitals in the Netherlands (May–December 2004), evaluated prospectively for cardiac risk factors, beta-blocker use pattern and 1-year mortality; 285 patients (40%) received beta-blockers continuously through the perioperative period, therapy was started in 29 and stopped in 21; propensity scores for beta-blocker use were calculated and regression models adjusted for confounders.
cards.result: One-year mortality was 11% overall. After adjustment for confounders and the propensity for use, continuous beta-blocker use remained significantly associated with lower 1-year mortality than non-use (hazard ratio 0.4 relative, 95% CI 0.2 to 0.7), whereas beta-blocker withdrawal was associated with higher 1-year mortality than non-use (hazard ratio 2.7 relative, 95% CI 1.2 to 5.9). Only 52% of the 281 high-risk patients received continuous therapy — the authors emphasise under-use in exactly the patients with most at stake.
cards.watchOut: The withdrawal group is only 21 patients, so the hazard ratio of 2.7 rests on few events and its confidence interval is wide (1.2 to 5.9); vascular surgery patients are also a high-cardiac-risk subset of 'major surgery', and the comparison is against non-users, mixing any harm of withdrawal with any benefit of simply being treated.
cards.source: Hoeks SE et al. Increase of 1-year mortality after perioperative beta-blocker withdrawal in endovascular and vascular surgery patients. European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery. 2007. PMID: 16935011. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: London 2013: in 136,745 veterans undergoing major noncardiac surgery, perioperative beta-blocker exposure was associated with lower 30-day mortality in propensity-matched analysis (relative risk 0.73), concentrated in higher-risk patients
cards.summary: London 2013: in 136,745 veterans undergoing major noncardiac surgery, perioperative beta-blocker exposure was associated with lower 30-day mortality in propensity-matched analysis (relative risk 0.73), concentrated in higher-risk patients
cards.people: 136,745 patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery at 104 Veterans Affairs medical centres, 2005–2010, in a retrospective cohort with 1:1 propensity matching (37,805 matched pairs); exposure was beta-blocker receipt on the day of or the day after surgery — in practice predominantly the continuation of chronic therapy in existing users, alongside some new exposure; outcomes were 30-day all-cause mortality and cardiac morbidity (cardiac arrest or Q-wave myocardial infarction).
cards.result: In the matched cohort, exposure was associated with lower 30-day mortality (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.83; P<0.001; number needed to treat 241). Stratified by Revised Cardiac Risk Index, the mortality association was significant only with two risk factors (relative risk 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.80; NNT 105), three factors (0.54, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.73; NNT 41) or four or more factors — patients at lowest risk showed no significant benefit. Cardiac morbidity was likewise lower with exposure in the higher-risk strata.
cards.watchOut: Exposure mixes continuation in chronic users with new perioperative starts, so this card supports the continuation conclusion only indirectly — the clean continuation-versus-withdrawal contrasts are the Wallace and Hoeks cards. As a database study it also cannot see why a drug was withheld on the day, the same confounding-by-indication caveat as the other cohorts.
cards.source: London MJ et al. Association of perioperative β-blockade with mortality and cardiovascular morbidity following major noncardiac surgery. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23613075. cards.headline: Synthesis: continue the chronic beta-blocker — every observational dataset agrees that withdrawal, not continuation, is the dangerous pattern
cards.summary: Synthesis: continue the chronic beta-blocker — every observational dataset agrees that withdrawal, not continuation, is the dangerous pattern
cards.people: The carded evidence: three observational cohorts — a 38,779-operation single-centre protocol cohort (Wallace 2010), a 711-patient prospective vascular surgery cohort (Hoeks 2007), and a 136,745-patient propensity-matched VA cohort (London 2013). Total carded participants exceed 175,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; there are no randomised trials of continuation versus withdrawal.
cards.result: Withdrawal: 30-day mortality odds ratio 3.93 relative (Wallace) and 1-year mortality hazard ratio 2.7 relative versus non-use (Hoeks). Continuation/continuous use: 30-day OR 0.68 relative (Wallace), 1-year HR 0.4 relative (Hoeks), and matched 30-day mortality relative risk 0.73 for perioperative exposure (London), with benefit concentrated in patients with two or more cardiac risk factors. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only: beta-blockers should be continued perioperatively in existing users undergoing major surgery. The initiation question — where the randomised evidence shows harm from starting on the day of surgery — stays homed on live shelf #352 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The whole shelf is observational: sicker, hypotensive or bleeding patients have their beta-blocker stopped, which manufactures part of the withdrawal signal, and no adjustment fully removes that. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, for exactly that reason — the direction is consistent, the causal size is not established.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wallace AW et al. Anesthesiology. 2010 (PMID: 20864832); Hoeks SE et al. European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery. 2007 (PMID: 16935011); London MJ et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 23613075).

shelves.title: Argatroban versus the other non-heparin anticoagulants in HIT (PARTIAL completion of pack #2817): similar clinical outcomes to bivalirudin in retrospective comparisons, no randomised head-to-head anywhere
shelves.question: In adults with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, is argatroban as effective as other non-heparin anticoagulants?
shelves.mesh: Antithrombins · Arginine · Female · Heparin · Hirudins · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Partial Thromboplastin Time · Peptide Fragments · Pipecolic Acids · Recombinant Proteins · Retrospective Studies · Sulfonamides · Thrombocytopenia · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of pack #2817, which homes argatroban against historical controls (Lewis 2001); the slice built here is the head-to-head question #2817 does not answer: argatroban versus the other non-heparin anticoagulants actually used — bivalirudin, lepirudin, danaparoid and fondaparinux. No randomised trial compares any of them. The direct evidence is three retrospective comparisons. Against bivalirudin (138 patients), argatroban matched it on time to therapeutic anticoagulation and on thromboembolic and bleeding events, with more supratherapeutic aPTT values (Skrupky 2010). A small three-way comparison (48 patients) found argatroban slower to reach target aPTT than bivalirudin and with more clinically significant bleeding than bivalirudin but less than lepirudin (Bain 2015). A national registry (195 patients) found no HIT-specific complications in fondaparinux-treated patients versus 11.7% with the approved agents pooled (argatroban, danaparoid, lepirudin) — a contrast the registry's own design cannot separate from confounding by indication, since the sickest patients are channelled to argatroban (Schindewolf 2017). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): nothing shows argatroban inferior on thrombotic outcomes, but 'as effective as' rests entirely on small, confounded retrospective comparisons.

cards.headline: Skrupky 2010: argatroban and bivalirudin were similar for HIT — therapeutic aPTT at a median 5.75 vs 5.50 hours, thromboembolism 4% vs 8%, bleeding 11% vs 9%
cards.summary: Skrupky 2010: argatroban and bivalirudin were similar for HIT — therapeutic aPTT at a median 5.75 vs 5.50 hours, thromboembolism 4% vs 8%, bleeding 11% vs 9%
cards.people: 138 adults at a large tertiary academic centre (2007–2008) who received bivalirudin (92 patients) or argatroban (46 patients) for at least 24 hours for known or suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; 78% were in an intensive care unit at initiation. Retrospective comparison.
cards.result: Median time to therapeutic anticoagulation goal was similar (argatroban 5.75 hours, interquartile range 3–17.7, vs bivalirudin 5.50 hours, 4–14.5; P = 0.499), as was the median percentage of aPTT values in range (70% vs 75%; P = 0.238), though more aPTT values were supratherapeutic on argatroban (18% vs 8%; P = 0.046). New thromboembolic events occurred in 2 argatroban patients (4%) and 7 bivalirudin patients (8%) (P = 0.718); bleeding events occurred in 11% on argatroban and 9% on bivalirudin (P > 0.999) — the treatment made no difference on clinical outcomes in this comparison.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre, with suspected as well as confirmed HIT included; argatroban is preferentially given to patients with liver dysfunction and bivalirudin to cardiac-surgery patients, so the groups differ before treatment starts.
cards.source: Skrupky LP et al. Comparison of bivalirudin and argatroban for the management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Pharmacotherapy. 2010. PMID: 21114390. cards.headline: Bain 2015: in 48 patients, bivalirudin reached therapeutic aPTT fastest (3.7 hours vs 14.2 argatroban vs 14.7 lepirudin) and bled least (7% vs 22% vs 56%)
cards.summary: Bain 2015: in 48 patients, bivalirudin reached therapeutic aPTT fastest (3.7 hours vs 14.2 argatroban vs 14.7 lepirudin) and bled least (7% vs 22% vs 56%)
cards.type: Retrospective comparative cohort (single centre, pharmacist-driven protocol)
cards.people: 48 patients treated with lepirudin, argatroban or bivalirudin for suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia between November 2010 and February 2012 under a pharmacist-driven protocol; retrospective cohort, patients treated for less than 24 hours excluded.
cards.result: Patients on bivalirudin reached a therapeutic aPTT more quickly than those on argatroban or lepirudin (3.7 hours vs 14.2 hours vs 14.7 hours; P < 0.001). Clinically significant bleeding was lower with bivalirudin than with argatroban or lepirudin (7% vs 22% vs 56%; P = 0.02). The INR rose more on argatroban than on lepirudin or bivalirudin (1.3 vs 0.3 vs 0.4; P = 0.4), and the average percentage of aPTTs in target range was 90% (bivalirudin), 66% (argatroban) and 67% (lepirudin) (P = 0.2).
cards.watchOut: Only 48 patients split three ways, so each arm is small and the bleeding contrast (56% on lepirudin) rests on very few events; the authors themselves call for a larger study. The endpoints are mostly process measures (aPTT control), not thrombosis prevented.
cards.source: Bain J et al. Comparison of bivalirudin to lepirudin and argatroban in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists. 2015. PMID: 26272889. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: German HIT registry 2017: no HIT-specific complications in 84 fondaparinux-treated patients versus 11.7% with approved agents (argatroban, danaparoid, lepirudin) — in a registry that cannot exclude confounding
cards.summary: German HIT registry 2017: no HIT-specific complications in 84 fondaparinux-treated patients versus 11.7% with approved agents (argatroban, danaparoid, lepirudin) — in a registry that cannot exclude confounding
cards.people: 195 hospitalised patients in a national multicentre registry with diagnosed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and at least intermediate clinical risk (4Ts score ≥ 4), treated first-line with argatroban (46 patients, 23.6%), lepirudin (4, 2.1%), danaparoid (61, 31.3%) or off-label fondaparinux (84, 43.1%). Retrospective registry study.
cards.result: The composite of HIT-specific complications (thromboembolic events, amputation, skin necrosis) occurred in 11.7% of patients treated with approved alternative anticoagulation and 0.0% of fondaparinux-treated patients; all-cause in-hospital mortality was 14.4% versus 0.0%, and bleeding complications 6.3% versus 4.8%. Post hoc analysis confirmed 'true' HIT in only 74 of 195 patients (38.0%), of whom 35 (47.3%) had been treated with fondaparinux. The authors conclude fondaparinux appears effective and safe in suspected acute HIT while calling randomised trials urgently needed.
cards.watchOut: The zero-event fondaparinux arm is the signature of confounding by indication: clinicians choose fondaparinux for stable patients and argatroban for the critically ill, and only 38% of the registry had confirmed HIT on post hoc review — this card cannot be read as fondaparinux beating argatroban, only as no signal that argatroban-treated patients did worse than their illness predicted.
cards.source: Schindewolf M et al. Use of Fondaparinux Off-Label or Approved Anticoagulants for Management of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 29169470. Registry ID: NCT01304238. cards.headline: Synthesis: no randomised head-to-head exists; retrospective comparisons show argatroban matching bivalirudin on clinical events, with weaker aPTT control signals and one confounded registry contrast — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no randomised head-to-head exists; retrospective comparisons show argatroban matching bivalirudin on clinical events, with weaker aPTT control signals and one confounded registry contrast — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two single-centre retrospective comparisons (138 and 48 patients) and one national registry (195 patients). Total carded participants: 381, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the weakness is design, not size.
cards.result: Argatroban and bivalirudin produced similar thromboembolic (4% vs 8%) and bleeding (11% vs 9%) rates in the largest direct comparison, with argatroban showing more supratherapeutic aPTT values (18% vs 8%); a smaller three-way study favoured bivalirudin on speed of anticoagulation and bleeding; and the registry's fondaparinux contrast is uninterpretable as a drug effect because of channelling. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): argatroban appears as effective as the other non-heparin anticoagulants on the outcomes measured, but the claim rests entirely on retrospective data. Argatroban versus historical controls stays homed on pack #2817 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Suspected-HIT contamination runs through all three reports (many patients treated for HIT do not have it), which dilutes any real drug difference toward no difference — 'no difference found' here is weaker than it looks.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skrupky LP et al. Pharmacotherapy. 2010 (PMID: 21114390); Bain J et al. American journal of health-system pharmacy. 2015 (PMID: 26272889); Schindewolf M et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017 (PMID: 29169470). Registry ID: NCT01304238 (registry card).

shelves.title: Implantable monitoring after cryptogenic stroke (PARTIAL completion of live #436): three randomised trials show several-fold more atrial fibrillation detected — a detection win, with stroke prevention untested
shelves.question: In adults with cryptogenic stroke, does prolonged monitoring with an implantable cardiac monitor detect atrial fibrillation more often than conventional follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atrial Fibrillation · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Physiologic · Stroke
shelves.balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #436 answers AF screening with wearable and implantable devices in people who feel well; this shelf asks the different, post-stroke question — after a cryptogenic or otherwise unexplained stroke, does prolonged implantable monitoring find atrial fibrillation that conventional follow-up misses? Three randomised trials agree, with large effects: CRYSTAL AF (cryptogenic stroke) found AF in 8.9% versus 1.4% by 6 months and 12.4% versus 2.0% by 12 months; STROKE AF (stroke attributed to large- or small-vessel disease) found 12.1% versus 1.8% at 12 months; PER DIEM (recent ischemic stroke, two-thirds of undetermined cause) found 15.3% with a 12-month implantable recorder versus 4.7% with a 30-day external recorder. Detection is therefore LIKELY proven. None of these trials was designed or powered to show that the extra detection prevents recurrent stroke — PER DIEM's recurrent-stroke numbers (3.3% versus 5.3%) were a non-significant secondary outcome — so this stamp covers detection yield only, not stroke prevention.

cards.headline: CRYSTAL AF 2014: after cryptogenic stroke, an insertable cardiac monitor detected atrial fibrillation in 8.9% versus 1.4% by 6 months and 12.4% versus 2.0% by 12 months
cards.summary: CRYSTAL AF 2014: after cryptogenic stroke, an insertable cardiac monitor detected atrial fibrillation in 8.9% versus 1.4% by 6 months and 12.4% versus 2.0% by 12 months
cards.people: 441 patients aged 40 years or older with cryptogenic stroke (no cause found after full evaluation, and no atrial fibrillation on at least 24 hours of ECG monitoring), randomised within 90 days of the stroke to long-term monitoring with an insertable cardiac monitor or conventional follow-up; primary end point was time to first detection of atrial fibrillation lasting more than 30 seconds within 6 months.
cards.result: By 6 months, atrial fibrillation had been detected in 8.9% of the monitor group (19 patients) versus 1.4% of the control group (3 patients) — hazard ratio 6.4 (95% CI 1.9–21.7, P<0.001), a relative effect with the absolute rates printed here. By 12 months, detection was 12.4% (29 patients) versus 2.0% (4 patients), hazard ratio 7.3 (95% CI 2.6–20.8, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: CRYSTAL AF enrolled strictly cryptogenic stroke; its control arm was conventional follow-up as practised at the time, not a modern prolonged external monitor — the comparison against a 30-day external recorder is PER DIEM's card, and the yield there is smaller.
cards.source: Sanna T et al. Cryptogenic stroke and underlying atrial fibrillation. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24963567. Registry ID: NCT00924638. cards.headline: STROKE AF 2021: even after stroke attributed to large- or small-vessel disease, implantable monitoring detected atrial fibrillation in 12.1% versus 1.8% at 12 months
cards.summary: STROKE AF 2021: even after stroke attributed to large- or small-vessel disease, implantable monitoring detected atrial fibrillation in 12.1% versus 1.8% at 12 months
cards.people: 496 patients (492 randomised) aged 60 years or older, or 50–59 with at least one additional stroke risk factor, whose index stroke was attributed to large-vessel atherosclerosis or small-vessel disease — a population not usually considered at high risk for atrial fibrillation — randomised to an insertable cardiac monitor within 10 days of the stroke (n = 242) or site-specific usual care such as ECGs, Holter monitoring, telemetry or event recorders (n = 250).
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation lasting more than 30 seconds was detected by 12 months in 27 patients (12.1%) in the monitor group versus 4 patients (1.8%) in the usual-care group — hazard ratio 7.4 (95% CI 2.6–21.3, P<0.001), a relative effect with the absolute rates printed here. Four of 221 patients who received a monitor (1.8%) had procedure-related adverse events (one site infection, two incision-site haemorrhages, one implant-site pain).
cards.watchOut: STROKE AF's strokes had a presumed non-cardioembolic cause, so its yield cannot be quoted as the cryptogenic-stroke yield; it widens, rather than replaces, the CRYSTAL AF finding. The trial tested detection, not whether treating the detected fibrillation prevents another stroke.
cards.source: Bernstein RA et al. Effect of Long-term Continuous Cardiac Monitoring vs Usual Care on Detection of Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Stroke Attributed to Large- or Small-Vessel Disease: The STROKE-AF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34061145. Registry ID: NCT02700945. cards.headline: PER DIEM 2021: 12 months of implantable monitoring detected atrial fibrillation in 15.3% versus 4.7% with a 30-day external loop recorder after ischemic stroke
cards.summary: PER DIEM 2021: 12 months of implantable monitoring detected atrial fibrillation in 15.3% versus 4.7% with a 30-day external loop recorder after ischemic stroke
cards.people: 300 patients within 6 months of an ischemic stroke and without known atrial fibrillation (66.3% with a stroke of undetermined etiology; median age 64.1 years; 40.3% women), randomised 1:1 at three Alberta hospitals to an implantable loop recorder for 12 months or an external loop recorder for 30 days; primary outcome was adjudicated definite or highly probable atrial fibrillation lasting at least 2 minutes within 12 months.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 15.3% (23/150) of the implantable group versus 4.7% (7/150) of the external group — an absolute difference of 10.7 percentage points (95% CI 4.0–17.3) and a risk ratio of 3.29 (95% CI 1.45–7.42, P = .003), a relative effect with the absolute rates printed here. Secondary outcomes mostly did not differ: recurrent ischemic stroke 3.3% versus 5.3%, intracerebral haemorrhage 0.7% versus 0.7%, death 2.0% versus 2.0%, and one device-related serious adverse event in the implantable group.
cards.watchOut: PER DIEM's comparator was itself prolonged external monitoring, so its smaller relative yield is the honest head-to-head against a good non-implant strategy; a third of its patients had strokes of known cause, and its atrial-fibrillation threshold (2 minutes) was longer than CRYSTAL AF's (30 seconds), so the three trials' percentages are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Buck BH et al. Effect of Implantable vs Prolonged External Electrocardiographic Monitoring on Atrial Fibrillation Detection in Patients With Ischemic Stroke: The PER DIEM Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34061146. Registry ID: NCT02428140. cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, three post-stroke populations, one direction — implantable monitoring finds several-fold more atrial fibrillation; stroke prevention by that route remains untested here
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, three post-stroke populations, one direction — implantable monitoring finds several-fold more atrial fibrillation; stroke prevention by that route remains untested here
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials totalling 1,233 randomised patients — CRYSTAL AF (441, cryptogenic stroke), STROKE AF (492, large- or small-vessel stroke) and PER DIEM (300, recent ischemic stroke) — each comparing implantable monitoring with conventional follow-up, usual care, or a 30-day external recorder. Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Detection at 12 months was 12.4% versus 2.0% (CRYSTAL AF, hazard ratio 7.3), 12.1% versus 1.8% (STROKE AF, hazard ratio 7.4) and 15.3% versus 4.7% (PER DIEM, risk ratio 3.29) — all relative effects, with the absolute rates printed on the cards. The screening-in-people-who-feel-well version of this question, including its weaker stroke-outcome evidence, is homed on live shelf #436 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY for the detection claim as asked; no card here shows fewer recurrent strokes.
cards.watchOut: A detection stamp is not a treatment stamp: these trials justify the monitor as a diagnostic strategy after unexplained stroke, and the decision to anticoagulate what it finds rests on evidence outside this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sanna T et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24963567); Bernstein RA et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 34061145); Buck BH et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 34061146).

shelves.title: Plozasiran specifically (PARTIAL completion of pack #5838): PALISADE's ~80% triglyceride fall and fewer pancreatitis episodes, with the SHASTA-2 trial left at its home
shelves.question: In adults with familial chylomicronemia syndrome or severe hypertriglyceridemia, does plozasiran reduce triglycerides and acute pancreatitis compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Apolipoprotein C-III · Double-Blind Method · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type I · Pancreatitis · RNA, Small Interfering · Triglycerides · Injections, Subcutaneous · Incidence
shelves.balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #5838 answers the class-level question (treating severe hypertriglyceridemia to prevent pancreatitis) and homes the SHASTA-2 trial of plozasiran in severe hypertriglyceridemia, which is therefore not re-carded here; live shelf #1105 covers the neighbouring drug olezarsen, a different agent. This shelf carries the plozasiran-specific evidence that is not homed elsewhere. In PALISADE — the phase 3 trial in persistent chylomicronemia (75 patients, median triglycerides 2,044 mg/dL at baseline) — plozasiran lowered triglycerides by about 80% against 17% on placebo at 10 months, and acute pancreatitis was less frequent (odds ratio 0.17, a relative effect from a secondary outcome with few events). A pooled phase 2 lipoprotein-particle analysis and a two-year open-label extension of the SHASTA-2 and MUIR programmes support a large, sustained triglyceride effect, but neither is a placebo-controlled pancreatitis test. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one pivotal trial for the pancreatitis claim, with concordant triglyceride data around it.

cards.headline: PALISADE 2025: in 75 patients with persistent chylomicronemia, plozasiran lowered triglycerides by about 80% versus 17% on placebo and pancreatitis was less frequent (odds ratio 0.17)
cards.summary: PALISADE 2025: in 75 patients with persistent chylomicronemia, plozasiran lowered triglycerides by about 80% versus 17% on placebo and pancreatitis was less frequent (odds ratio 0.17)
cards.people: 75 patients with persistent chylomicronemia (with or without a genetic diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome; median baseline fasting triglycerides 2,044 mg/dL), randomly assigned to subcutaneous plozasiran 25 mg or 50 mg or placebo every 3 months for 12 months; primary end point was the median percent change in fasting triglycerides at 10 months, with acute pancreatitis incidence a key secondary end point.
cards.result: At 10 months the median triglyceride change was −80% (25 mg) and −78% (50 mg) versus −17% on placebo (P<0.001). Acute pancreatitis occurred less often on plozasiran (odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.03–0.94, P = 0.03 — a relative effect; the record reports the odds ratio without arm-level event counts in its abstract). Adverse events were similar across groups (most commonly abdominal pain, nasopharyngitis, headache and nausea); severe and serious adverse events were less common with plozasiran, and hyperglycemia occurred in some patients with prediabetes or diabetes at baseline.
cards.watchOut: PALISADE is small (75 patients) and its pancreatitis result is a secondary outcome built on few events, so the odds ratio of 0.17 is fragile; the trial also enrolled persistent chylomicronemia with or without a genetic familial chylomicronemia diagnosis, so it does not isolate genetically proven familial chylomicronemia syndrome alone.
cards.source: Watts GF et al. Plozasiran for Managing Persistent Chylomicronemia and Pancreatitis Risk. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39225259. Registry ID: NCT05089084. cards.headline: Phase 2 particle analysis 2025: across SHASTA-2 (severe hypertriglyceridemia) and MUIR, plozasiran cut triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particles by about half, with no rise in total LDL particles or apolipoprotein B
cards.summary: Phase 2 particle analysis 2025: across SHASTA-2 (severe hypertriglyceridemia) and MUIR, plozasiran cut triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particles by about half, with no rise in total LDL particles or apolipoprotein B
cards.type: Randomised-trial lipoprotein substudy of two phase 2 trials (Ballantyne 2025)
cards.people: 403 patients from two phase 2 randomised trials — SHASTA-2 (severe hypertriglyceridemia, the trial homed on pack #5838) and MUIR (mixed hyperlipidemia) — who received two subcutaneous doses of plozasiran (10, 25 or 50 mg) or placebo at baseline and week 12, with nuclear magnetic resonance lipoprotein profiling; this report analyses particle numbers and sizes, not clinical events.
cards.result: Triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particles fell dose-dependently: placebo-adjusted total reductions of −46% in SHASTA-2 and −48% (pooled plozasiran) in MUIR, across all triglyceride-rich subclasses. Total LDL particle number was unchanged while large LDL particles rose (+53% in SHASTA-2, +88% in MUIR) and small LDL particles trended lower — a shift in particle size distribution with no increase in apolipoprotein B.
cards.watchOut: This is a biomarker report: particle shifts are mechanistically reassuring but are not triglyceride outcomes in a new population and say nothing about pancreatitis; half of its patients come from MUIR's mixed-hyperlipidemia population, which sits outside this shelf's question.
cards.source: Ballantyne CM et al. Effect of Targeting ApoC-III With Plozasiran on Lipoprotein Particle Size and Number in Hypertriglyceridemia. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2025. PMID: 40099777. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Open-label extension 2026: triglyceride reductions on plozasiran were sustained over two years in the SHASTA-2 and MUIR roll-over cohorts (−77% to −79% from baseline in severe hypertriglyceridemia)
cards.summary: Open-label extension 2026: triglyceride reductions on plozasiran were sustained over two years in the SHASTA-2 and MUIR roll-over cohorts (−77% to −79% from baseline in severe hypertriglyceridemia)
cards.type: Open-label extension of two randomised trials (Ballantyne 2026)
cards.people: Participants rolling over from the randomised SHASTA-2 trial (n = 229, severe hypertriglyceridemia with triglycerides >500 mg/dL) and MUIR trial (n = 353, mixed hyperlipidemia) into an open-label extension, transitioning to plozasiran 25 mg every 3 months, followed for two years for safety and fasting triglyceride change from baseline; there was no placebo group in the extension.
cards.result: In the SHASTA-2 cohort, mean triglyceride reductions from baseline were −77% at month 12 and −79% at month 24 (versus −71% at month 6 of the index randomised study); in MUIR, −62% and −63% (versus −56% at month 6). Common treatment-emergent adverse events included diabetes, COVID-19, upper respiratory tract infection and back pain, consistent with the earlier trials, and HbA1c remained stable.
cards.watchOut: An open-label extension has no comparator: sustained percentages are measured against each cohort's own baseline in patients who chose to continue, so this card supports durability and tolerability only — it cannot add causal weight to the triglyceride or pancreatitis claims.
cards.source: Ballantyne CM et al. Use of plozasiran across a spectrum of hypertriglyceridemia: Long-term efficacy and safety data from the open-label extension period of SHASTA-2 and MUIR Trials. American journal of preventive cardiology. 2026. PMID: 42291067. Registry ID: NCT05413135. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small pivotal trial carries the pancreatitis claim; the surrounding programme shows a large, durable triglyceride effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small pivotal trial carries the pancreatitis claim; the surrounding programme shows a large, durable triglyceride effect
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 randomised trial in persistent chylomicronemia (PALISADE, 75 patients), one pooled phase 2 particle substudy (403 patients) and one two-year open-label extension (582 roll-over patients). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, though the pivotal trial itself is small and is flagged on its card.
cards.result: PALISADE: triglycerides −80%/−78% versus −17% on placebo at 10 months, pancreatitis odds ratio 0.17 (95% CI 0.03–0.94) as a secondary outcome. The SHASTA-2 randomised trial in severe hypertriglyceridemia is homed on pack #5838 and the olezarsen trials on live shelf #1105; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single pivotal trial caps the stamp, and the pancreatitis finding rests on few events.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf's numbers with olezarsen's: the two drugs share a target (apolipoprotein C-III) but their trials, doses and pancreatitis event counts are separate, and the class-level pancreatitis pooling lives on pack #5838.

shelves.title: Coronary artery calcium for prediction and statin allocation (GAP-E, observational): MESA shows strong prediction and two-way reclassification — with no trial of the scanning strategy itself
shelves.question: In intermediate-risk adults, does coronary artery calcium scoring predict events and guide statin allocation better than risk scores alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calcinosis · Calcium · Coronary Angiography · Coronary Artery Disease · Coronary Disease · Coronary Vessels · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Racial Groups · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: This is a GAP-E prognosis and test-strategy shelf: the evidence is observational by design, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. In the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), a calcium score above 300 carried roughly ten times the adjusted coronary risk of a score of zero, and adding calcium to standard risk factors improved prediction in all four racial and ethnic groups studied. Head-to-head in intermediate-risk adults, calcium beat five rival markers on discrimination and reclassification (net reclassification improvement 0.659, against 0.160 for the next best, family history). For statin allocation the score cuts both ways: 41% of guideline-recommended statin candidates in MESA had a calcium score of zero with a low observed event rate (5.2 per 1,000 person-years), while among adults below the guideline's 7.5% risk threshold a high calcium score identified a small subgroup whose observed event rate exceeded that threshold. No randomised trial has tested a calcium-guided statin strategy against score-guided care, so 'guides allocation better' rests on reclassification and observed event rates, not on outcomes of the strategy itself.

cards.headline: MESA 2008: a coronary calcium score above 300 carried an adjusted coronary-event risk about ten times that of a zero score, in all four ethnic groups
cards.summary: MESA 2008: a coronary calcium score above 300 carried an adjusted coronary-event risk about ten times that of a zero score, in all four ethnic groups
cards.people: 6,722 men and women from the population-based Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (38.6% white, 27.6% black, 21.9% Hispanic, 11.9% Chinese) with no clinical cardiovascular disease at entry, scanned for coronary calcium and followed for a median of 3.8 years; 162 coronary events occurred, 89 of them major (myocardial infarction or coronary death).
cards.result: Compared with participants with no coronary calcium, the adjusted risk of a coronary event was increased by a factor of 7.73 with scores of 101–300 and 9.67 with scores above 300 (P<0.001 for both) — relative effects from an observational cohort. A doubling of the calcium score raised the risk of a major coronary event by 15–35% across the four groups, and prediction improved beyond standard risk factors in every group, with no major differences in predictive value between groups.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was short (median 3.8 years) and events few (162), and this is a cohort association: it shows calcium stratifies risk, not that acting on the scan changes outcomes.
cards.source: Detrano R et al. Coronary calcium as a predictor of coronary events in four racial or ethnic groups. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18367736. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MESA 2012: in intermediate-risk adults, calcium improved prediction more than five rival markers — net reclassification improvement 0.659 versus 0.160 for the next best
cards.summary: MESA 2012: in intermediate-risk adults, calcium improved prediction more than five rival markers — net reclassification improvement 0.659 versus 0.160 for the next best
cards.people: 1,330 intermediate-risk MESA participants (Framingham risk score above 5% and below 20%, without diabetes) with complete data on all six candidate markers — coronary artery calcium, carotid intima-media thickness, ankle-brachial index, brachial flow-mediated dilation, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and family history — followed for a median of 7.6 years, during which 94 coronary heart disease and 123 cardiovascular events occurred.
cards.result: Coronary calcium was independently associated with incident coronary disease (hazard ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.94–3.50, a relative effect), as were ankle-brachial index, C-reactive protein and family history, while carotid thickness and flow-mediated dilation were not. Added to the Framingham score plus race/ethnicity, calcium gave the largest discrimination gain (area under the curve 0.623 to 0.784) and by far the largest net reclassification improvement for coronary disease (0.659; family history 0.160, carotid thickness 0.102, C-reactive protein 0.079, ankle-brachial index 0.036, flow-mediated dilation 0.024).
cards.watchOut: Reclassification statistics describe how a marker reshuffles predicted risk in a cohort; they are not evidence that calcium-guided treatment prevents more events than score-guided treatment, which no trial here tests.
cards.source: Yeboah J et al. Comparison of novel risk markers for improvement in cardiovascular risk assessment in intermediate-risk individuals. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22910756. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MESA 2015: 41% of guideline-recommended statin candidates had a calcium score of zero — with a low observed event rate of 5.2 per 1,000 person-years
cards.summary: MESA 2015: 41% of guideline-recommended statin candidates had a calcium score of zero — with a low observed event rate of 5.2 per 1,000 person-years
cards.people: 4,758 MESA participants (mean age 59 years, 47% men) not on lipid-lowering therapy, classified by the 2013 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline; over a median 10.3 years there were 247 atherosclerotic cardiovascular events and 155 hard coronary events.
cards.result: The guideline recommended moderate- to high-intensity statins for 2,377 participants (50%), most because estimated 10-year risk was at least 7.5%. Of those recommended statins, 41% had a calcium score of zero, with an observed event rate of 5.2 atherosclerotic events per 1,000 person-years. Among the 589 participants merely considered for a statin, 57% had a zero score and an event rate of 1.5 per 1,000 person-years; across all eligible participants, 44% (1,316 of 2,966) had zero calcium and an observed 10-year event rate of 4.2 per 1,000 person-years.
cards.watchOut: A zero score's low event rate is an observed cohort rate over about ten years, not a guarantee — and this analysis applies the 2013 guideline's thresholds, so its percentages do not transfer unchanged to later guidelines or to populations unlike MESA's.
cards.source: Nasir K et al. Implications of Coronary Artery Calcium Testing Among Statin Candidates According to American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Cholesterol Management Guidelines: MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015. PMID: 26449135. Registry ID: none in the record. prospective cohort study (mesa, nasir 2015) 4,758 mesa participants (mean age 59 years, 47% men) not on lipid-lowering therapy, classified by the 2013 acc/aha cholesterol guideline; over a median 10.3 years there were 247 atherosclerotic cardiovascular events and 155 hard coronary events. the guideline recommended moderate- to high-intensity statins for 2,377 participants (50%), most because estimated 10-year risk was at least 7.5%. of those recommended statins, 41% had a calcium score of zero, with an observed event rate of 5.2 atherosclerotic events per 1,000 person-years. among the 589 participants merely considered for a statin, 57% had a zero score and an event rate of 1.5 per 1,000 person-years; across all eligible participants, 44% (1,316 of 2,966) had zero calcium and an observed 10-year event rate of 4.2 per 1,000 person-years. a zero score's low event rate is an observed cohort rate over about ten years, not a guarantee — and this analysis applies the 2013 guideline's thresholds, so its percentages do not transfer unchanged to later guidelines or to populations unlike mesa's. nasir k et al. implications of coronary artery calcium testing among statin candidates according to american college of cardiology/american heart association cholesterol management guidelines: mesa (multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis). journal of the american college of cardiology. 2015. pmid: 26449135. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · american heart association · atherosclerosis · calcium · coronary angiography · coronary artery disease · coronary vessels · ethnicity · female · follow-up studies · guideline adherence · humans · hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors · male · middle aged · prospective studies · risk assessment · risk factors · united states

cards.headline: MESA 2015: among adults below the 7.5% risk threshold, a high calcium score found a small subgroup whose observed event rate exceeded the statin threshold
cards.summary: MESA 2015: among adults below the 7.5% risk threshold, a high calcium score found a small subgroup whose observed event rate exceeded the statin threshold
cards.people: 5,185 MESA participants not taking statins (ages 45–84), of whom 4,185 had a calibrated pooled-cohort-equation 10-year risk below 7.5% — the group the 2013 guideline would not routinely treat — assessed for how often each additional risk marker reclassified them to statin eligibility and what their observed event rates were over 10 years.
cards.result: Most events occurred below the threshold: 57% of atherosclerotic events (183 of 320) arose in the under-7.5% group. Excluding diabetes, the calcium criterion (score at least 300, or at least the 75th percentile for age, sex and ethnicity) reclassified 6.8% upward, and that subgroup's observed event rate was 13.3% (relative risk 4.0, 95% CI 2.8–5.7, versus those not reclassified), with a number needed to screen of 14.7 to find one such person — the most efficient of the markers tested, ahead of family history (21.8), C-reactive protein (39.2), ankle-brachial index (176.5) and LDL cholesterol of at least 160 mg/dL (193.3).
cards.watchOut: The upward-reclassified subgroup is small (6.8%), so calcium scanning of everyone below the threshold mostly confirms low risk; the analysis is again observational and tied to the 2013 guideline's 7.5% line.
cards.source: Yeboah J et al. Utility of Nontraditional Risk Markers in Individuals Ineligible for Statin Therapy According to the 2013 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Cholesterol Guidelines. Circulation. 2015. PMID: 26224808. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: calcium predicts events beyond risk scores and reshuffles statin candidacy in both directions — all of it observational, with no trial of the strategy itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: calcium predicts events beyond risk scores and reshuffles statin candidacy in both directions — all of it observational, with no trial of the strategy itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: four prospective-cohort analyses, all from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (6,722 scanned at baseline; analysis sets of 1,330 to 5,185), with follow-up from 3.8 to about 10 years. Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Prediction: adjusted coronary risk rose to 9.67-fold for scores above 300 versus zero (Detrano 2008), and calcium's net reclassification improvement in intermediate-risk adults (0.659) dwarfed five rival markers (Yeboah 2012). Allocation: 41% of guideline-recommended candidates had zero calcium with low observed event rates (Nasir 2015), while a high score identified a treatable-risk subgroup below the score threshold (Yeboah 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational) — the evidence grades prediction and reclassification, not patient outcomes under a calcium-guided strategy.
cards.watchOut: All four cards come from one cohort (MESA): the consistency is within-cohort, and the library's calcium-progression shelf (live #2501, garlic extract) is a different question and is not evidence here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Detrano R et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18367736); Yeboah J et al. JAMA. 2012 (PMID: 22910756); Nasir K et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2015 (PMID: 26449135); Yeboah J et al. Circulation. 2015 (PMID: 26224808).

shelves.title: Clopidogrel plus aspirin after bypass surgery (PARTIAL completion of pack #3090): a SPLIT — blinded randomised null in CASCADE versus pooled, largely observational patency benefit off-pump
shelves.question: In adults after coronary artery bypass grafting, does dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel improve vein graft patency compared with aspirin alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aspirin · Clopidogrel · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Artery Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Hyperplasia · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Saphenous Vein · Ticlopidine · Treatment Outcome · Tunica Intima · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3090 answers the ticagrelor-plus-aspirin version of this question (DACAB) and homes that trial; this shelf asks the clopidogrel version. DACAB has no clopidogrel arm, so it contributes nothing here and is not carded. The evidence splits by design. The one double-blind randomised trial, CASCADE (113 patients), found no benefit from adding clopidogrel for a year: vein graft intimal area, overall patency (95.2% versus 95.5%) and vein graft patency (94.3% versus 93.2%) were all essentially identical (the treatment made no difference), and its 8-year follow-up still showed no patency or survival difference. Against that, a systematic review pooling 11 studies and 25,728 patients — six of them observational — found less early vein graft occlusion with dual therapy (relative risk 0.59), with the clearest benefit in off-pump surgery, alongside a trend to more major bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT (design): pooled and off-pump data favour dual therapy for early patency; the only blinded randomised test, in mostly on-pump surgery, found none.

cards.headline: CASCADE 2010: adding clopidogrel to aspirin for a year after bypass surgery made no difference to vein graft disease or patency (94.3% versus 93.2%)
cards.summary: CASCADE 2010: adding clopidogrel to aspirin for a year after bypass surgery made no difference to vein graft disease or patency (94.3% versus 93.2%)
cards.people: 113 patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting with saphenous vein grafts, randomised double-blind to aspirin 162 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily or aspirin 162 mg plus placebo for 1 year; primary outcome was vein graft intimal hyperplasia (mean intimal area) on intravascular ultrasound at 1 year, performed with angiography in 92 patients (81.4%).
cards.result: Vein graft intimal area did not differ (4.1 ± 2.0 versus 4.5 ± 2.1 mm², P = 0.44). Overall 1-year graft patency was 95.2% on aspirin–clopidogrel versus 95.5% on aspirin–placebo (P = 0.90), and vein graft patency was 94.3% versus 93.2% (P = 0.69) — the treatment made no difference. Freedom from major adverse cardiovascular events was 92.9% versus 91.1% (P = 0.76), and major bleeding was 1.8% versus 0% (P = 0.50).
cards.watchOut: CASCADE was a phase 2 trial of 113 patients powered for an ultrasound measure of graft wall thickening, not for occlusion or clinical events; its null is the best randomised evidence but cannot exclude a modest patency effect, particularly in off-pump surgery, which it did not isolate.
cards.source: Kulik A et al. Aspirin plus clopidogrel versus aspirin alone after coronary artery bypass grafting: the clopidogrel after surgery for coronary artery disease (CASCADE) Trial. Circulation. 2010. PMID: 21135365. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CASCADE 8-year follow-up 2018: still no difference in vein graft patency (89.1% versus 91.2%) or survival after a year of clopidogrel
cards.summary: CASCADE 8-year follow-up 2018: still no difference in vein graft patency (89.1% versus 91.2%) or survival after a year of clopidogrel
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, long-term follow-up (CASCADE, Hage 2018)
cards.people: The 113 CASCADE participants (56 clopidogrel, 57 placebo, each on aspirin for the first year after bypass surgery), re-evaluated at a median of 7.6 years for survival, major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events, functional status and — in surviving patients with adequate kidney function — vein graft patency on CT angiography.
cards.result: Survival was 85.5% overall with no difference between groups (P = .23). Long-term vein graft patency was 89.11% in the aspirin–clopidogrel group versus 91.23% in the aspirin–placebo group (P = .79) — the treatment made no difference. There was a non-significant trend toward freedom from death or major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events including revascularization (P = .11), no difference in angina or functional status, and less moderate-to-severe progression of native coronary disease in the clopidogrel group (odds ratio 0.3, 95% CI 0.1–0.8, P = .02), a secondary finding in a small sample.
cards.watchOut: Late patency was assessed only in survivors who could undergo CT angiography, and the native-disease-progression signal rests on small segment counts; neither converts the trial's null primary story into a benefit.
cards.source: Hage A et al. Eight-year follow-up of the Clopidogrel After Surgery for Coronary Artery Disease (CASCADE) trial. The Journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery. 2018. PMID: 28734623. Registry ID: NCT00228423. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2013: pooling 11 studies and 25,728 patients, dual therapy was associated with less early vein graft occlusion (relative risk 0.59) — with the benefit concentrated in off-pump surgery
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2013: pooling 11 studies and 25,728 patients, dual therapy was associated with less early vein graft occlusion (relative risk 0.59) — with the benefit concentrated in off-pump surgery
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (Deo 2013)
cards.people: Systematic review of 11 studies (5 randomised trials and 6 observational studies, 25,728 patients) comparing aspirin plus clopidogrel with aspirin with or without placebo after coronary artery bypass grafting, covering early vein graft occlusion, early mortality, perioperative myocardial infarction and major bleeding.
cards.result: Early saphenous vein graft occlusion was lower with dual therapy (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.43–0.82, P = 0.02 — a relative effect; the record does not print pooled absolute occlusion rates). In-hospital or 30-day mortality was 0.8% versus 1.9% (P<0.0001), angina or perioperative myocardial infarction did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.31–1.14), and major bleeding trended higher (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 1.00–1.37, P = 0.05). In off-pump surgery specifically, dual therapy was associated with 55% relative lower graft occlusion and 68% relative lower perioperative myocardial infarction than aspirin alone.
cards.watchOut: More than half the pooled weight is observational, where clopidogrel is preferentially given to patients clinicians judge at higher graft risk or after off-pump surgery — confounding by indication can manufacture exactly this pattern, which is why the blinded CASCADE result is kept on its own card rather than averaged away.
cards.source: Deo SV et al. Dual anti-platelet therapy after coronary artery bypass grafting: is there any benefit? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of cardiac surgery. 2013. PMID: 23488578. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the randomised answer is no difference; the pooled answer is fewer early occlusions, mostly off-pump — a split by study design
cards.summary: Synthesis: the randomised answer is no difference; the pooled answer is fewer early occlusions, mostly off-pump — a split by study design
cards.people: The carded evidence: one double-blind randomised trial and its 8-year follow-up (CASCADE, 113 patients) and one systematic review pooling 11 studies (25,728 patients, six observational). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: CASCADE found vein graft patency of 94.3% versus 93.2% at 1 year and 89.11% versus 91.23% at about 8 years (the treatment made no difference), while the pooled analysis found early occlusion relative risk 0.59 (95% CI 0.43–0.82) with a bleeding trend (relative risk 1.17) and benefit concentrated in off-pump surgery. The ticagrelor version of this question, including DACAB, is homed on pack #3090 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT (design): benefit in pooled, largely observational and off-pump data; no benefit in the blinded randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Quoting the pooled relative risk without its observational weight — or CASCADE's null without its small, on-pump-leaning sample — each misstates what this literature can actually support.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kulik A et al. Circulation. 2010 (PMID: 21135365); Hage A et al. The Journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery. 2018 (PMID: 28734623); Deo SV et al. Journal of cardiac surgery. 2013 (PMID: 23488578).

shelves.title: Oral semaglutide outcomes in depth (PARTIAL completion of live #356, precedent-(b) build): SOUL's total-events, heart-failure and risk-factor analyses — the primary SOUL and PIONEER 6 reports stay at their homes
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, does oral semaglutide reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Semaglutide · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Female · Heart Failure · Male · Double-Blind Method · Administration, Oral · Middle Aged · Aged · Hypoglycemic Agents
shelves.balance: PRECEDENT-(b) FLAG — read first. The primary SOUL report is homed on live shelf #72 and re-carded in the five-trial overview on live shelf #356, which also cards PIONEER 6; under the one-home rule neither primary report is carded here, and no figure from either appears in any card source line below. This shelf is built only from three distinct secondary reports of the SOUL programme that are not carded at either home, and it answers the dedicated oral-semaglutide question through them: a total-events analysis (first plus subsequent major cardiovascular events: mean ratio 0.86, a relative effect), a heart-failure analysis (composite heart-failure outcome hazard ratio 0.78 in participants with heart failure at baseline, 1.01 in those without) and a risk-factor analysis showing early, sustained improvements in HbA1c, weight, blood pressure and inflammation markers. All three reports describe one trial of 9,650 people, so the evidence base is a single programme and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PIONEER 6 (2019) established cardiovascular safety (non-inferiority) rather than superiority and is discussed at its home on #356, not carded here.

cards.headline: SOUL total-events analysis 2026: counting first and subsequent events, oral semaglutide produced 683 total major cardiovascular events versus 791 on placebo (mean ratio 0.86)
cards.summary: SOUL total-events analysis 2026: counting first and subsequent events, oral semaglutide produced 683 total major cardiovascular events versus 791 on placebo (mean ratio 0.86)
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised trial (SOUL, Marx 2026)
cards.people: All 9,650 SOUL participants (type 2 diabetes with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and/or chronic kidney disease, randomised 1:1 to once-daily oral semaglutide up to 14 mg or placebo on top of standard care at 444 centres in 33 countries; median follow-up 49.5 months), in a prespecified secondary analysis counting total — first and subsequent — 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke). The primary first-event report is homed on live shelf #72 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Total 3-point events numbered 683 on oral semaglutide (579 first and 104 subsequent) versus 791 on placebo (668 first and 123 subsequent) — mean ratio 0.86 (95% CI 0.76–0.97, P = .01), a relative effect. For 3-point events plus non-cardiovascular death there were 910 versus 1,048 total events (mean ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79–0.95, P = .004). Adverse events led to discontinuation in 15.5% on semaglutide versus 11.6% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A total-events analysis re-uses the same trial and the same first events as the primary report homed on #72; it deepens the estimate of event burden but is not independent confirmation, and its relative mean ratio should not be read as a second trial agreeing with the first.

cards.headline: SOUL heart-failure analysis 2026: the heart-failure composite fell with oral semaglutide only in participants who already had heart failure (hazard ratio 0.78 versus 1.01 without)
cards.summary: SOUL heart-failure analysis 2026: the heart-failure composite fell with oral semaglutide only in participants who already had heart failure (hazard ratio 0.78 versus 1.01 without)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (SOUL, Pop-Busui 2026)
cards.people: The 9,650 SOUL participants, of whom 2,229 (23.1%) had a history of heart failure at baseline (10.3% preserved ejection fraction, 6.1% reduced, 6.7% unknown subtype), in a secondary analysis of the prespecified composite heart-failure outcome (first heart-failure hospitalisation, urgent heart-failure visit, or cardiovascular death); mean follow-up 47.5 months.
cards.result: Among participants with heart failure at baseline, the composite heart-failure outcome hazard ratio was 0.78 (95% CI 0.63–0.96) — within that group, 0.59 (95% CI 0.39–0.86) with preserved ejection fraction and 0.98 (95% CI 0.70–1.38) with reduced ejection fraction — versus 1.01 (95% CI 0.84–1.20) in participants without baseline heart failure (interaction P = .06); all are relative effects, and the record does not print arm-level absolute rates for this composite in its abstract. Major cardiovascular events themselves fell similarly with or without baseline heart failure (hazard ratios 0.83 and 0.86; interaction P = .77), and serious adverse events in the heart-failure group were similar between arms (53.8% versus 57.1%).
cards.watchOut: The heart-failure split rests on a subgroup interaction that did not reach significance (P = .06) and on small ejection-fraction subgroups; it is a pattern to note, not proof that benefit is confined to patients with existing heart failure.
cards.source: Pop-Busui R et al. Oral Semaglutide and Heart Failure Outcomes in Persons With Type 2 Diabetes: A Secondary Analysis of the SOUL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2026. PMID: 41627802. Registry ID: NCT03914326. cards.headline: SOUL risk-factor analysis 2026: oral semaglutide improved HbA1c, weight, blood pressure and inflammatory markers early, and the gains persisted to week 156
cards.summary: SOUL risk-factor analysis 2026: oral semaglutide improved HbA1c, weight, blood pressure and inflammatory markers early, and the gains persisted to week 156
cards.type: Post hoc secondary analysis of a randomised trial (SOUL, Mulvagh 2026)
cards.people: 9,650 SOUL participants (mean age 66.1 years; 28.9% women) in a post hoc secondary analysis of the trial, comparing once-daily oral semaglutide (maximum 14 mg) with placebo, each on standard care, for change in glycated haemoglobin, body weight, blood pressure, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and lipids.
cards.result: Improvements appeared by week 13 (HbA1c −0.87 percentage points, body weight −2.54%, systolic blood pressure −3.84 mm Hg, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein −18.08% versus placebo) and were sustained: at week 156 the differences were HbA1c −0.47 percentage points (95% CI −0.52 to −0.42), body weight −3.26 percentage points (95% CI −3.55 to −2.98), systolic pressure −1.83 mm Hg (95% CI −2.47 to −1.18) and a C-reactive protein ratio of 0.77 (95% CI 0.74–0.81), with small favourable differences in total and non-HDL cholesterol and triglycerides and no significant difference in LDL cholesterol or diastolic pressure.
cards.watchOut: Risk-factor movement is a mechanism story, not an outcome: these changes are consistent with the trial's event reduction but, being post hoc and surrogate, they cannot substitute for the event data homed on live shelves #72 and #356. The author line and journal are taken from the record fetched this session; the analysis is a SOUL programme report distinct from the primary publication.

shelves.title: Metformin in heart failure (GAP-E, observational only): associated with lower mortality across cohorts — confounding by indication faced, no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: In adults with heart failure and type 2 diabetes, is metformin use associated with better survival than other glucose-lowering therapy?
shelves.mesh: Comorbidity · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Contraindications · Diabetic Angiopathies · Heart Failure · Hospitalization · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Metformin · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left
shelves.balance: GAP-E with care, as the slate directs: there is no randomised trial of metformin in heart failure — every carded source is observational, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The association is consistent: pooling nine cohort studies (about 34,000 patients), metformin users had lower mortality than controls, mostly sulfonylurea users (23% versus 37%; pooled adjusted estimate 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87), with no excess lactic acidosis signal (Eurich 2013). The founding cohort found the same direction against sulfonylurea monotherapy (Eurich 2005), and a later meta-regression found the association in preserved as well as reduced ejection fraction (Halabi 2020). Confounding by indication must be faced squarely, and it is, on every card: metformin was long withheld from the sickest heart-failure patients, so users were plausibly healthier at baseline in ways adjustment cannot fully remove — the observed 'benefit' may partly be the fingerprint of who was allowed to receive the drug. The defensible reading is narrower than a survival claim: metformin use in heart failure is associated with lower mortality in observational data and shows no safety signal, which is why guidelines permit it — not proof that it prolongs life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence only).

cards.headline: Eurich 2013 meta-analysis: across 9 cohort studies (about 34,000 patients), metformin was associated with lower mortality — 23% versus 37%, pooled adjusted estimate 0.80
cards.summary: Eurich 2013 meta-analysis: across 9 cohort studies (about 34,000 patients), metformin was associated with lower mortality — 23% versus 37%, pooled adjusted estimate 0.80
cards.people: Nine observational cohort studies comprising about 34,000 patients with diabetes mellitus and heart failure, comparing metformin with control glucose-lowering therapy (mostly sulfonylureas); no randomised controlled trials were identified by the reviewers. Most studies were published in 2010 and rated good quality.
cards.result: Metformin was associated with reduced all-cause mortality compared with controls (23% versus 37% crude mortality; pooled adjusted risk estimate 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87; I²=15%; P<0.001). In patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction the estimate was 0.91 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.14) — not significant — and in heart failure with chronic kidney disease 0.81 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.02). All-cause hospitalisation was slightly lower (pooled adjusted estimate 0.93, 95% CI 0.89 to 0.98), and metformin was not associated with increased lactic acidosis. The authors conclude metformin appears at least as safe as other glucose-lowering treatments in heart failure until trial data become available.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication is the central threat: for much of the study era metformin was contraindicated in heart failure, so clinicians gave it to patients they judged lower-risk — adjusted models cannot fully erase that selection, and the mortality gap (23% vs 37% crude) is larger than a glucose-lowering drug effect plausibly explains.
cards.source: Eurich DT et al. Comparative safety and effectiveness of metformin in patients with diabetes mellitus and heart failure: systematic review of observational studies involving 34,000 patients. Circulation. Heart failure. 2013. PMID: 23508758. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Eurich 2005 cohort: in 1,833 patients with incident heart failure and diabetes, death occurred in 33% on metformin versus 52% on sulfonylurea monotherapy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.70)
cards.summary: Eurich 2005 cohort: in 1,833 patients with incident heart failure and diabetes, death occurred in 33% on metformin versus 52% on sulfonylurea monotherapy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.70)
cards.people: 1,833 subjects with incident heart failure identified among 12,272 new users of oral antidiabetic agents in the Saskatchewan Health databases (1991–1996): metformin monotherapy (n=208), sulfonylurea monotherapy (n=773) or combination therapy (n=852); mean age 72 years, 57% men, average follow-up 2.5 years.
cards.result: Deaths occurred in 69 of 208 metformin-monotherapy patients (33%) versus 404 of 773 sulfonylurea-monotherapy patients (52%): adjusted hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.91). Combination therapy showed a similar association (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.72). The composite of death or hospitalisation was also lower with metformin (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.99), though time to first hospitalisation alone did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Administrative-data cohort from the era when metformin was formally contraindicated in heart failure: the 208 patients given metformin anyway were a selected group, and claims data capture neither ejection fraction nor heart-failure severity well — the hazard ratio measures an association in selected users, not a treatment effect.
cards.source: Eurich DT et al. Improved clinical outcomes associated with metformin in patients with diabetes and heart failure. Diabetes care. 2005. PMID: 16186261. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Halabi 2020 meta-regression: the metformin–mortality association appeared in preserved as well as reduced ejection fraction — still observational throughout
cards.summary: Halabi 2020 meta-regression: the metformin–mortality association appeared in preserved as well as reduced ejection fraction — still observational throughout
cards.people: Observational studies and any randomised trials reporting mortality in patients with heart failure treated with metformin, analysed by the proportion with preserved ejection fraction (EF above 50%); four studies reported the EF proportion and entered the EF analysis. Total N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Metformin treatment was associated with reduced mortality in both preserved and reduced ejection fraction groups after adjustment for heart-failure therapies such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers (β = −0.2, 95% CI −0.3 to −0.1; p=0.02), with a significantly greater protective association where EF was above 50% (p=0.003). The authors frame the finding as an association from observational series and call the preserved-EF benefit previously unexplored rather than established.
cards.watchOut: A study-level meta-regression on four EF-reporting studies cannot adjust for patient-level confounding; an association that strengthens in the subgroup (preserved EF) where metformin prescribing is least restricted is exactly the pattern confounding by indication would produce.
cards.source: Halabi A et al. Metformin treatment in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis. Cardiovascular diabetology. 2020. PMID: 32758236. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: metformin use in heart failure is consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data — association, not proven survival benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: metformin use in heart failure is consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data — association, not proven survival benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of nine cohort studies (about 34,000 patients), one large administrative cohort (1,833 patients with incident heart failure) and one meta-regression (total N not documented in the record). No randomised trials exist.
cards.result: Adjusted mortality estimates favour metformin over mostly sulfonylurea comparators (pooled estimate 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87; founding cohort hazard ratio 0.70), the association extends across ejection-fraction categories, and no lactic-acidosis or hospitalisation harm signal appears. Every source is observational and exposed to confounding by indication, because metformin was preferentially given to — or withheld from — patients by perceived risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence only): associated with better survival; causation unproven.
cards.watchOut: The clinical bottom line these data support is permissive — metformin need not be avoided in stable heart failure — not promotional: no patient should be started on metformin for a survival benefit that only randomised evidence could establish.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eurich DT et al. Circulation. Heart failure. 2013 (PMID: 23508758); Eurich DT et al. Diabetes care. 2005 (PMID: 16186261); Halabi A et al. Cardiovascular diabetology. 2020 (PMID: 32758236).

shelves.title: The exercise cardiac-output rise, apportioned: early stroke-volume doubling, linear heart-rate rise, and stroke-volume rescue when rate is blocked
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what determines the rise in cardiac output during exercise — the relative contributions of heart rate, stroke volume and peripheral vasodilation?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Cardiac Output · Heart · Heart Rate · Humans · Labetalol · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Exertion · Propranolol · Pulmonary Gas Exchange · Respiration · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe a roughly fourfold rise in cardiac output from rest to maximal exercise in untrained healthy adults, achieved by an early rise in stroke volume that plateaus at submaximal work, a heart-rate rise that continues linearly to maximum, and a large fall in total peripheral resistance from vasodilation in working muscle that lets output rise with only a modest rise in arterial pressure — venous return, driven by the muscle pump and sympathetic venoconstriction, keeping the heart filled so the Frank-Starling mechanism can operate. The carded human studies measure each leg. In 10 healthy men, output rose from 5.8 to 19.4 L/min while heart rate rose from 84 to 169 beats/min and stroke volume rose early (70 to 137 ml at 25% of VO2max) and then levelled off (116 ml at maximum) — and when beta-blockade capped heart rate near 90 beats/min, maximal output was fully maintained by a larger stroke volume (Bevilacqua 1989). At the top end, output and stroke volume plateau or fall beyond about 80% of peak power while heart rate keeps rising linearly (Mortensen 2005), and restoring heart rate by pacing under beta-blockade does not restore Doppler flow indices — stroke volume, not rate, is the adjustable reserve (Clifton 1990). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: heart rate carries the upper range of the output rise, stroke volume rises early then plateaus (and expands to compensate when rate is blocked), and peripheral vasodilation is what permits the rise without a proportional pressure rise.

cards.headline: Bevilacqua 1989: in 10 healthy men, exercise raised cardiac output 5.8 → 19.4 L/min — heart rate 84 → 169, stroke volume up early then level; under beta-blockade, stroke volume fully compensated for a capped heart rate
cards.summary: Bevilacqua 1989: in 10 healthy men, exercise raised cardiac output 5.8 → 19.4 L/min — heart rate 84 → 169, stroke volume up early then level; under beta-blockade, stroke volume fully compensated for a capped heart rate
cards.type: Human physiology study (graded treadmill exercise ± beta-blockade, Bevilacqua 1989)
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers studied after 1 week of placebo and after 1 week each of oral propranolol 80 mg twice daily or dilevalol 400 mg daily, in a randomised double-blind crossover; haemodynamics by CO2 rebreathing at rest and at 25, 50, 75 and 100% of VO2max on a treadmill.
cards.result: On placebo, cardiac output rose from 5.8 ± 2.1 L/min at rest to 19.4 ± 6.4 L/min at 100% of VO2max, mainly from heart rate rising 84 ± 6 to 169 ± 15 beats/min; stroke volume rose from 70 ± 27 ml at rest to 137 ± 65 ml at 25% of VO2max and then levelled off to 116 ± 41 ml at maximum. Under both beta-blockers, maximal-exercise cardiac output was maintained (20.1 ± 9.3 L/min on propranolol; 19.1 ± 8.6 on dilevalol) despite heart rates of only about 90–99 beats/min at maximum, because stroke volume increased significantly versus placebo; at 25% of VO2max, by contrast, output was significantly lower on blockade (9.4–9.6 vs 13.7 L/min) before the stroke-volume compensation caught up.
cards.watchOut: CO2-rebreathing output estimates carry wide standard deviations (note ± 6–9 L/min at maximum), and dilevalol has vasodilator activity propranolol lacks; the shared finding — stroke-volume compensation preserving maximal output — held for both drugs.
