cards.headline: Mortensen 2005: cardiac output rose linearly only to ~80% of peak power, then plateaued as stroke volume fell — while heart rate rose linearly to exhaustion (groups of 8 and 10)
cards.summary: Mortensen 2005: cardiac output rose linearly only to ~80% of peak power, then plateaued as stroke volume fell — while heart rate rose linearly to exhaustion (groups of 8 and 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (maximal cycling haemodynamics, Mortensen 2005) — N = 8 and 10
cards.people: Healthy male subjects studied during incremental and constant-load (372 ± 11 W, ~85% of peak power) cycling to exhaustion (n = 8) and during incremental cycling and knee-extensor exercise (n = 10), with systemic and leg haemodynamic measurements. N = 8 in the first protocol — printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: During incremental cycling, cardiac output and systemic oxygen delivery increased linearly to 80% of peak power (r² = 0.998, P < 0.001) and then plateaued in parallel with a decline in stroke volume and rising central venous and mean arterial pressures, while heart rate increased linearly until exhaustion (r² = 0.993, P < 0.001) and systemic oxygen extraction rose to 84 ± 2%. During constant-load cycling, output, stroke volume and oxygen delivery reached maximal values within about 5 minutes but fell before exhaustion. Leg blood flow and oxygen delivery levelled off at 73–88% of peak power.
cards.watchOut: Young trained-leaning male volunteers at maximal whole-body exercise; the late stroke-volume decline is a maximal-exercise phenomenon (rising pressures, falling filling time) and should not be read back onto submaximal exercise, where stroke volume plateaus rather than falls.
cards.source: Mortensen SP et al. Limitations to systemic and locomotor limb muscle oxygen delivery and uptake during maximal exercise in humans. The Journal of physiology. 2005. PMID: 15860533. cards.headline: Clifton 1990: pacing heart rate back up under propranolol did not restore exercise flow velocity or acceleration in 10 healthy men — stroke volume behaviour, not rate, was decisive
cards.summary: Clifton 1990: pacing heart rate back up under propranolol did not restore exercise flow velocity or acceleration in 10 healthy men — stroke volume behaviour, not rate, was decisive
cards.type: Human physiology study (Doppler exercise haemodynamics ± propranolol ± pacing, Clifton 1990)
cards.people: 10 healthy men studied during upright exercise under control conditions, after propranolol, and after propranolol plus transoesophageal atrial pacing to restore heart rate; Doppler echocardiographic aortic velocity, acceleration and flow velocity integral (a stroke-volume index).
cards.result: Propranolol significantly reduced aortic acceleration and velocity at all exercise stages versus control (P < 0.05). Raising heart rate by pacing during beta-blockade had no effect on acceleration or velocity compared with propranolol alone, showing those indices are independent of heart-rate change during upright exercise. The flow velocity integral was reduced by propranolol at low exercise (−1.14 cm, P < 0.05) but exceeded control at high exertion (+1.2 cm at stage 4); pacing during blockade reduced the integral at high levels — the authors conclude stroke volume at low exercise rises through increased contractility and augmented filling, with rate restoration unable to substitute.
cards.watchOut: Doppler velocity indices are surrogates, not volumetric cardiac output; the study's value is the pacing dissociation — it separates 'rate' from 'stroke volume/contractility' experimentally in a way output measurements alone cannot.
cards.source: Clifton GD et al. Influence of beta-adrenergic blockade upon hemodynamic response to exercise assessed by Doppler echocardiography. American heart journal. 1990. PMID: 1975152. cards.headline: Synthesis: heart rate carries the top of the range, stroke volume rises first and compensates when rate is capped, vasodilation permits the whole rise
cards.summary: Synthesis: heart rate carries the top of the range, stroke volume rises first and compensates when rate is capped, vasodilation permits the whole rise
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 10-man randomised crossover of graded treadmill exercise with and without beta-blockade (Bevilacqua 1989), maximal-cycling haemodynamics in groups of 8 and 10 men (Mortensen 2005), and a 10-man Doppler/pacing dissociation study (Clifton 1990).
cards.result: Output rose about 3.3-fold (5.8 to 19.4 L/min) with heart rate roughly doubling (84 to 169 beats/min) and stroke volume roughly doubling early (70 to 137 ml at 25% of VO2max) before levelling; beyond ~80% of peak power output plateaued as stroke volume declined while heart rate still rose linearly. When beta-blockade held maximal heart rate near 90–99 beats/min, maximal output was nonetheless fully maintained by increased stroke volume — the Frank-Starling reserve Guyton & Hall describe — and pacing rate back up added nothing. Peripheral vasodilation in working muscle is the permissive leg (textbook framing): it is what lets a 3–4-fold output rise occur against only a modest pressure rise, and leg blood flow itself levelled at 73–88% of peak power in the Mortensen protocols. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All carded groups were small samples of healthy (mostly young male) volunteers; trained athletes reach far higher outputs mainly through larger stroke volumes — a textbook point, not a carded result here.

American heart journal. 1990 (PMID: 1975152). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: The baroreflex as the fast pressure buffer: bidirectional human reflex testing, ganglion blockade, and the tilt-table division of labour
shelves.question: In humans, how does the arterial baroreflex determine short-term blood pressure variability and the response to standing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Pressure · Carotid Sinus · Digitalis Glycosides · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroglycerin · Phenylephrine · Pressoreceptors · Reflex
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbooks cast the arterial baroreflex as the fast buffer of blood pressure: carotid-sinus and aortic-arch stretch receptors fire in proportion to pressure, and the medullary response adjusts vagal outflow to the heart within a beat or two and sympathetic outflow to heart and vessels over seconds — which is why the reflex dominates short-term (seconds-to-minutes) pressure variability while contributing little to the long-term pressure level, and why standing, which pools blood and unloads the receptors, is answered by reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction. The carded human studies test each element with the classic tools. Neck-chamber suction/pressure and phenylephrine/nitroglycerin boluses move heart rate and pressure in the predicted reciprocal directions in man (Ferrari 1981). Ganglionic blockade shows how much resting pressure the autonomic (baroreflex-driven) system is holding up: trimethaphan dropped systolic pressure below 125 mmHg in every normotensive subject but left it at 164 mmHg in pure autonomic failure, where pressure is maintained without the reflex arc (Diedrich 2003). And during head-up tilt, abolishing the vagal cardiac limb left baroreflex control of pressure itself intact — standing pressure is defended mainly by sympathetic vasomotor control, with the cardiac limb chiefly vagal (Ogoh 2006). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Ferrari 1981: in 29 humans, baroreceptor stimulation (phenylephrine, neck suction) lowered heart rate and pressure, deactivation (nitroglycerin, neck pressure) raised both — the reflex demonstrated bidirectionally
cards.summary: Ferrari 1981: in 29 humans, baroreceptor stimulation (phenylephrine, neck suction) lowered heart rate and pressure, deactivation (nitroglycerin, neck pressure) raised both — the reflex demonstrated bidirectionally
cards.type: Human physiology study (pharmacological and neck-chamber baroreflex testing, Ferrari 1981)
cards.people: 29 normotensive or hypertensive subjects studied before and after intravenous lanatoside C (digitalis) 0.8 mg, with arterial baroreceptors stimulated and deactivated by phenylephrine and nitroglycerin injection, and carotid baroreceptors separately by neck suction and neck pressure, measuring heart rate and blood pressure responses.
cards.result: Baroreceptor stimulation reduced heart rate and blood pressure, while baroreceptor deactivation increased both variables — the bidirectional reflex pattern. Therapeutic-dose digitalis significantly increased the bradycardic and hypotensive effects of baroreceptor stimulation in both normotensive and hypertensive subjects, but did not affect the tachycardic and hypertensive responses to deactivation. The record reports the responses qualitatively without printing reflex-gain numbers, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: The study's own question was digitalis, and its abstract prints no numeric gains — it is carded for the bidirectional human demonstration with both classic methods (drug bolus and neck chamber) in the same subjects, not for any effect size. The 1969 Oxford-method paper (Smyth, Sleight & Pickering) that founded the phenylephrine technique carries no abstract in its PubMed record, so no figures from it are carded anywhere on this shelf.
cards.source: Ferrari A et al. Digitalis and baroreceptor reflexes in man. Circulation. 1981. PMID: 6778626. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diedrich 2003: ganglionic blockade dropped systolic pressure below 125 mmHg in all normotensive subjects but left it at 164 ± 7 mmHg in pure autonomic failure — how much pressure the reflex system holds
cards.summary: Diedrich 2003: ganglionic blockade dropped systolic pressure below 125 mmHg in all normotensive subjects but left it at 164 ± 7 mmHg in pure autonomic failure — how much pressure the reflex system holds
cards.type: Human physiology study (blood-pressure variability and ganglionic blockade across autonomic phenotypes, Diedrich 2003)
cards.people: Patients with multiple system atrophy (MSA, sympathetic-dependent supine hypertension), pure autonomic failure (PAF, sympathetic-independent), essential hypertension (HTN) and normotensive controls (NTN), studied supine with low-frequency systolic pressure variability (LF(SBP)) and trimethaphan 2–4 mg/min ganglionic blockade; the record does not print the group sizes (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Supine systolic pressure was 204 ± 8 (MSA), 185 ± 6 (PAF), 177 ± 9 (HTN) and 130 ± 4 mmHg (NTN). LF(SBP) was higher in MSA and HTN (5.7 ± 1.5 and 5.8 ± 1.4 mmHg²) than in NTN and PAF (3.3 ± 0.5 and 1.1 ± 0.5 mmHg²). Trimethaphan induced complete autonomic blockade and lowered systolic pressure below 125 mmHg in all NTN and all but one MSA patient (to 111 ± 3 and 97 ± 9 mmHg), while pressure remained elevated in PAF (164 ± 7 mmHg); hypertensive responses were variable (below 125 mmHg in three, still elevated in four). The fall in LF(SBP) correlated with the pressure fall.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, and three of the four groups are disease phenotypes chosen as mechanistic controls — the normotensive arm is the healthy-physiology anchor; the patient arms show what pressure and its variability look like when the reflex arc is interrupted at different points.
cards.source: Diedrich A et al. The sympathetic nervous system in hypertension: assessment by blood pressure variability and ganglionic blockade. Journal of hypertension. 2003. PMID: 12923400. cards.headline: Ogoh 2006: during 40° head-up tilt in 9 healthy subjects, vagal blockade cut carotid-cardiac baroreflex gain from −0.30 to −0.06 bpm/mmHg but left baroreflex control of pressure unchanged (N = 9, below 10)
cards.summary: Ogoh 2006: during 40° head-up tilt in 9 healthy subjects, vagal blockade cut carotid-cardiac baroreflex gain from −0.30 to −0.06 bpm/mmHg but left baroreflex control of pressure unchanged (N = 9, below 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (neck-chamber baroreflex gain during tilt ± vagal blockade, Ogoh 2006) — N = 9
cards.people: 9 healthy young subjects studied supine and during 40° head-up tilt, with carotid baroreflex responsiveness (maximal gain, G(MAX)) measured by variable neck pressure and suction (+40 to −80 Torr), with and without full cardiac vagal blockade by glycopyrrolate (12.0 ± 1.0 microgram/kg). N = 9 — printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Supine, glycopyrrolate raised heart rate from 54 ± 3 to 91 ± 3 bpm, mean arterial pressure from 76 ± 2 to 89 ± 2 mmHg and cardiac output from 4.9 ± 0.3 to 6.8 ± 0.3 L/min, and reduced the carotid-cardiac baroreflex gain from −0.30 ± 0.02 to −0.06 ± 0.01 bpm/mmHg (P < 0.05), with no significant effect on the gain of baroreflex control of mean arterial pressure. During tilt, baroreflex control of pressure was unchanged while cardiac gain increased; the authors conclude the cardiac limb is mediated primarily via parasympathetic activity, while maintenance of arterial pressure during postural stress is mediated primarily by reflex regulation of sympathetic activity and its effects on the systemic vasculature.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. Tilt to 40° is a mild orthostatic stress; the conclusion concerns the division of labour between the cardiac (vagal) and vasomotor (sympathetic) limbs, not the size of the whole standing response.
cards.source: Ogoh S et al. Carotid-cardiac baroreflex function does not influence blood pressure regulation during head-up tilt in humans. The journal of physiological sciences : JPS. 2006. cards.headline: Synthesis: the baroreflex buffers beat-to-beat pressure through a fast vagal cardiac limb and a sympathetic vasomotor limb — and standing is defended mainly by the vessels
cards.summary: Synthesis: the baroreflex buffers beat-to-beat pressure through a fast vagal cardiac limb and a sympathetic vasomotor limb — and standing is defended mainly by the vessels
cards.people: The carded evidence: bidirectional neck-chamber and drug-bolus testing in 29 subjects (Ferrari 1981), variability-plus-ganglion-blockade phenotyping including normotensive controls (Diedrich 2003, N not documented in the record), and neck-chamber gain measurement during tilt with vagal blockade in 9 healthy subjects (Ogoh 2006, N on the face).
cards.result: Stimulation and deactivation of the receptors moved heart rate and pressure reciprocally in man; removing autonomic outflow pharmacologically dropped normal supine systolic pressure from about 130 to 111 ± 3 mmHg but could not normalise pressure maintained without a functioning arc (164 ± 7 mmHg in pure autonomic failure); and during tilt the pressure-controlling gain survived complete vagal blockade (−0.30 to −0.06 bpm/mmHg for the cardiac gain) — the Ganong / Guyton & Hall division of labour, measured: short-term variability is what the reflex absorbs, and the response to standing is chiefly sympathetic vasoconstriction answering baroreceptor unloading. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The reflex resets within minutes to days, which is why none of this evidence bears on the long-term pressure level — a Ganong/Guyton point the cards support by omission: every carded effect is on the scale of seconds to a single posture change.

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). cards.headline: Buick 1980: raising haemoglobin alone raised VO2max — reinfusing about 900 mL of the runners' own stored blood lifted maximal oxygen uptake from 5.11 to 5.37 L/min and time to exhaustion from 7.20 to 9.65 minutes
cards.summary: Buick 1980: raising haemoglobin alone raised VO2max — reinfusing about 900 mL of the runners' own stored blood lifted maximal oxygen uptake from 5.11 to 5.37 L/min and time to exhaustion from 7.20 to 9.65 minutes
cards.people: 11 highly trained runners studied double-blind through five phases: before phlebotomy, after restoration of normal blood values, after a sham reinfusion of 50 mL saline, after autologous reinfusion of approximately 900 mL of freeze-preserved blood, and after control values were re-established.
cards.result: Reinfusion raised haemoglobin from 15.7 to 16.7 g/100 mL. Maximal oxygen consumption rose significantly 24 hours after reinfusion (5.11 to 5.37 L/min) and running time to exhaustion rose from 7.20 to 9.65 minutes, with the increase still present at 7 days; sham reinfusion changed nothing. The authors conclude there is a distinct increase in VO2max following induced erythrocythemia and that oxygen transport limits maximal aerobic capacity — a direct experimental isolation of the convective oxygen-delivery side of the VO2max limit, with muscle and extraction unchanged.
cards.watchOut: Elite runners (N=11) and an intervention (blood reinfusion) that is not a training model: it isolates oxygen content, so it speaks to the delivery term of the Fick relation, not to extraction changes with training.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (double-blind crossover experiment) | Buick FJ et al. Effect of induced erythrocythemia on aerobic work capacity. J Appl Physiol. 1980. PMID: 7380690. cards.headline: Synthesis: VO2max is set mainly by convective oxygen delivery — maximal cardiac output times arterial oxygen content — with peripheral extraction near its ceiling in trained humans
cards.summary: Synthesis: VO2max is set mainly by convective oxygen delivery — maximal cardiac output times arterial oxygen content — with peripheral extraction near its ceiling in trained humans
cards.people: Synthesis of Ekblom & Hermansen 1968, Saltin 1968 and Buick 1980, framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card).
cards.result: By the Fick relation (the textbook's framing), VO2max = maximal cardiac output × maximal arterial–venous oxygen difference. The carded human evidence assigns the larger share to the delivery side: VO2max moves with training state and blood volume in the same men (Saltin programme), and raising arterial oxygen content alone — haemoglobin 15.7 to 16.7 g/100 mL, muscle untouched — raised VO2max by about 5% and endurance time by about a third (Buick, N=11). The Ekblom & Hermansen athlete measurements anchor the central numbers in the textbook account (maximal cardiac output roughly 35–40 L/min in elite athletes, with arterial–venous difference widening to roughly 15–16 mL/100 mL — the textbook's account, since the fetched 1968 records print no abstracts). Peripheral extraction is therefore a real but secondary and less trainable term: in trained humans it is already near-maximal, and the inter-individual and training-related differences in VO2max are mostly differences in maximal cardiac output and oxygen-carrying capacity. Two of the three evidence records carry no abstract this session and print 'N not documented' on their faces, per the labelling rule.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: two of three evidence records lack abstracts this session, so the delivery-versus-extraction split rests on Buick's direct experiment plus textbook framing — the stamp reflects textbook-settled physiology, not three fully quantified carded trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ekblom B, Hermansen L. J Appl Physiol. 1968 (PMID: 4879852); Saltin B et al. Circulation. 1968 (PMID: 5696236); Buick FJ et al. J Appl Physiol. 1980 (PMID: 7380690). Registry IDs: none in the records (classic physiology).

shelves.title: Standing up: leg volume up 2.5% in 10 minutes, a brief 25% pressure dip, then a baroreflex resistance defence — the normal orthostatic response quantified
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much blood pools in the legs on standing, and how do baroreflex responses defend arterial pressure over the first minutes upright?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Pressure/physiology · Cardiac Output/physiology · Exercise/physiology · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic/physiopathology · Male · Posture · Vascular Resistance/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall (textbook framing, not evidence). Carded human measurements: healthy leg volume rises 2.48% over 10 minutes standing, bi-exponentially (Pannier 2010, N=16 healthy); the first seconds bring a transient 25% (23 mm Hg) pressure fall from a 36% fall in total peripheral resistance (Sprangers & Imholz 1991, N=8); the sustained defence is vasoconstrictor — systemic vascular resistance +33% at 7 minutes in non-fainters, with heart rate +20 beats/min at 2 minutes (ten Harkel & Wieling 1993, N=13) — against normal ranges defined in 92 healthy people with direct calf pooling demonstrated by radiotracer counting (Streeten 1988). The absolute pooled volume (roughly 500–700 mL) is given only as the textbook's account in the Synthesis, since no carded record prints it. The library's orthostatic shelves are drug-treatment shelves; the normal-response quantification was uncovered.

cards.headline: Pannier 2010: leg volume rose 2.48% over 10 minutes of quiet standing in 16 healthy people — a fast venous-pooling compartment plus a slow extravasation compartment
cards.summary: Pannier 2010: leg volume rose 2.48% over 10 minutes of quiet standing in 16 healthy people — a fast venous-pooling compartment plus a slow extravasation compartment
cards.people: 16 healthy individuals and 24 patients with varicose veins, studied prospectively with an optoelectric volume measurement system (Perometer) during 10 minutes standing. Only the healthy group's values are used for this shelf's question.
cards.result: During 10 minutes standing, leg volume increased significantly in the healthy group by 2.48% (varicose group 2.1%), in both upper and lower leg, with no significant right–left difference. The increase was rapid from the moment of standing and followed a bi-exponential course: a fast filling compartment (venous pooling) and a slow filling compartment reflecting extravasation, with further oedema forming over the course of a day. This is the carded direct quantification of pooling in healthy legs: the percentage is the record's number; the familiar absolute figure (roughly 500–700 mL shifted into the legs and splanchnic bed on standing) is the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall), given as such in the Synthesis.
cards.watchOut: Percentage of leg volume, not millilitres — the record prints no absolute pooled volume, so the textbook millilitre figure appears only as the textbook's account in the Synthesis; the healthy subgroup is 16 people.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Pannier F, Rabe E. Optoelectric volume measurements to demonstrate volume changes in the lower extremities during orthostasis. Int Angiol. 2010. PMID: 20924340. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Sprangers & Imholz 1991: the first seconds upright — mean pressure transiently falls 25% (23 mm Hg) because total peripheral resistance falls 36%, before the baroreflex defence engages
cards.summary: Sprangers & Imholz 1991: the first seconds upright — mean pressure transiently falls 25% (23 mm Hg) because total peripheral resistance falls 36%, before the baroreflex defence engages
cards.people: Eight healthy male subjects with beat-to-beat intra-arterial pressure measured on standing from supine, with stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance computed by a pulse-contour method; passive tilting and a brief 3-second bout of cycling used as comparison manoeuvres; right atrial and oesophageal pressures measured in two subjects.
cards.result: Standing elicited a transient 25% (23 mm Hg) fall in mean blood pressure, caused by a 36% fall in total peripheral resistance. Head-up tilt produced gradual changes reaching plateau levels in 20–30 seconds, and cycling produced a similar transient fall (17%, 18 mm Hg; resistance −41%). Right atrial pressure rose 10–15 mm Hg on standing without a matching oesophageal pressure change, pointing to the cardiopulmonary reflex as the primary effector of the initial peripheral vasodilation. That is, the very first event on standing is a brief vasodilator dip — the defence that follows has to overcome it, which is why the first-minutes response cannot be read off the initial seconds.
cards.watchOut: Very small study (N=8; atrial pressures in only 2 subjects) using a pulse-contour computation — the mechanism attribution (cardiopulmonary reflex) is the authors' inference, stated as such on the face.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Sprangers RL et al. Initial blood pressure fall on stand up and exercise explained by changes in total peripheral resistance. J Appl Physiol. 1991. cards.headline: ten Harkel & Wieling 1993: over the first minutes upright, non-fainters defend pressure by raising systemic vascular resistance (+33% at 7 minutes) while stroke volume and cardiac output responses match those of fainters
cards.summary: ten Harkel & Wieling 1993: over the first minutes upright, non-fainters defend pressure by raising systemic vascular resistance (+33% at 7 minutes) while stroke volume and cardiac output responses match those of fainters
cards.people: 13 healthy males without a history of syncope, studied during prolonged standing with Finapres blood pressure, pulse-contour stroke volume, cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance, and spectral analysis of pressure and heart-rate variability. Three fainted after 10–13 minutes; ten stayed upright for 20 minutes.
cards.result: The initial (first 30 seconds) adjustment was comparable for blood pressure, but the rebound bradycardia was smaller in fainters (heart rate at 22 seconds +13 ± 10 beats/min above control vs +1 ± 5 in non-fainters). Upright heart rate at 2 minutes was higher in fainters (+31 ± 2 vs +20 ± 5 beats/min), and blood pressure at 7 minutes was lower. Stroke volume and cardiac output responses were comparable between groups, but systemic vascular resistance gradually decreased in fainters from 5 minutes to fainting, versus +33 ± 19% at 7 minutes in non-fainters. The defence of pressure over the first minutes is therefore principally a vasoconstrictor (resistance) defence, and its failure — not a failure of cardiac output — is what precedes fainting.
cards.watchOut: Only 13 subjects and just 3 fainters — the fainter/non-fainter contrast is hypothesis-grade; the non-fainter defence values (+33% resistance, +20 beats/min) are the shelf's normative numbers.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | ten Harkel AD et al. Differences in circulatory control in normal subjects who faint and who do not faint during orthostatic stress. Clin Auton Res. 1993. PMID: 8324374. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Streeten 1988: the normal ranges for orthostatic pressure and heart-rate change were defined in 92 healthy people aged 18–64 — and gamma counting over the calf directly demonstrated gravitational pooling in the legs on standing
cards.summary: Streeten 1988: the normal ranges for orthostatic pressure and heart-rate change were defined in 92 healthy people aged 18–64 — and gamma counting over the calf directly demonstrated gravitational pooling in the legs on standing
cards.people: 92 individuals aged 18 to 64 years in whom the normal ranges of orthostatic blood-pressure and heart-rate changes were defined; plus 34 symptomatic individuals with intact sympathetic function (used here only for the pooling measurement method), in whom red-cell labelling with technetium-99m pertechnetate and external gamma counting over a fixed calf site compared recumbent and standing blood content.
cards.result: External gamma counting showed excessive gravitational pooling of blood in the legs of the symptomatic subgroups tested (five patients with orthostatic diastolic hypertension, four with pulse-pressure narrowing, ten with orthostatic tachycardia alone), against the normal ranges defined in the 92-person reference group; plasma norepinephrine was usually normal recumbent and rose above normal limits during 15–30 minutes standing in the 18 patients so observed. The card establishes two things for this shelf: a healthy reference distribution for the upright pressure/heart-rate response, and direct radiotracer demonstration that blood physically pools in the calf on standing — excessive in the patients, present as the normal phenomenon the baroreflex defence exists to counter.
cards.watchOut: The pooling demonstration was in symptomatic patients, not the 92-person healthy reference group — the card separates the two uses explicitly, and 'excessive' pooling in patients should not be read as the healthy volume.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (reference-range and pooling-measurement study) | Streeten DH et al. Abnormal orthostatic changes in blood pressure and heart rate in subjects with intact sympathetic nervous function: evidence for excessive venous pooling. J Lab Clin Med. 1988. PMID: 3343547. cards.headline: Synthesis: on standing, several hundred millilitres pool in the legs within seconds to minutes; pressure is defended first against a brief vasodilator dip, then by baroreflex vasoconstriction
cards.summary: Synthesis: on standing, several hundred millilitres pool in the legs within seconds to minutes; pressure is defended first against a brief vasodilator dip, then by baroreflex vasoconstriction
cards.people: Synthesis of Pannier 2010, Sprangers 1991, ten Harkel 1993 and Streeten 1988, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card). The library's orthostatic shelves are drug-treatment shelves; this shelf quantifies the normal response only.
cards.result: The sequence the carded human studies measure: (1) Pooling — leg volume rises rapidly on standing, +2.48% over 10 minutes in healthy legs (Pannier), bi-exponential (fast venous filling, slow extravasation); radiotracer counting confirms blood physically accumulating in the calf (Streeten). The textbook account (Guyton & Hall) puts the pooled volume at roughly 500–700 mL into the dependent veins — presented as the textbook's account, since no carded record prints an absolute millilitre figure. (2) The initial dip — mean pressure transiently falls 25% in the first seconds because total peripheral resistance falls 36%, a cardiopulmonary-reflex vasodilation (Sprangers). (3) The defence — over the following minutes the arterial baroreflex raises systemic vascular resistance (+33% at 7 minutes in those who stay upright, ten Harkel) with a moderate heart-rate rise (+20 beats/min at 2 minutes), holding pressure within the normal ranges Streeten defined in 92 healthy people; when the resistance response instead fades, fainting follows. Sjöstrand's classic blood-volume distribution work and Rowell's orthostasis programme are the historical anchors for this picture in the textbook framing; the carded numbers above are the fetched human measurements.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: no carded record prints an absolute pooled millilitre volume; that figure is Guyton & Hall's account and is labelled as such wherever it appears.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pannier F, Rabe E. Int Angiol. 2010 (PMID: 20924340); Sprangers RL et al. J Appl Physiol. 1991 (PMID: 2022542); ten Harkel AD et al. Clin Auton Res. 1993 (PMID: 8324374); Streeten DH et al. J Lab Clin Med. 1988 (PMID: 3343547). Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: Sweating and skin blood-flow thresholds (physiology): both switch on as core temperature climbs through its regulated zone, the two thresholds move together — about 0.6 °C lower at night, about 0.2 °C higher when hyperosmolar — and heat acclimation lowers the thresholds and the resting core temperature itself
shelves.question: In healthy humans, at what core temperatures do sweating and cutaneous vasodilation switch on, and how does heat acclimatisation shift those thresholds and sweat rates?
shelves.mesh: Adult · *Blood Circulation · *Body Temperature Regulation · *Circadian Rhythm · Female · Forearm/blood supply · Humans · Male · Physical Exertion · Regional Blood Flow · Skin Temperature · *Sweating · Time Factors · Vasomotor System/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): sweating and cutaneous vasodilation are threshold effectors — off below a core-temperature threshold in the regulated zone around 37 °C and rising steeply above it — the textbook's account of the set-point system. The carded primary studies (Nadel/Wenger programme) quantify how that threshold moves rather than printing one absolute onset temperature: thresholds for sweating and forearm vasodilation shifted together by about 0.57 °C and 0.63 °C between day and night (Wenger 1976), and were 0.57 °C (sweating) and 0.65 °C (vasodilation) higher at 16:00 than at 04:00 in a full circadian protocol (Stephenson 1984). Hyperosmolality raised both thresholds by 0.22 °C and cut the slope and maximum of the blood-flow response (Fortney 1984). Heat acclimation moves the system the other way: after a 9-day active acclimation protocol, baseline rectal and mean body temperature were significantly lower throughout heat stress and the mean-body-temperature thresholds for onset of both sweating and skin vasodilation were lower (Armstrong and Kenney 1993 — the Armstrong heat-acclimation programme's controlled-threshold study; the record's abstract is truncated at 250 words and gives the direction, not a numeric shift, so none is printed). Because no carded record prints a single absolute onset temperature, the absolute threshold is presented as the textbook's account (onset as core temperature rises through ~37 °C, varying with skin temperature, time of day and hydration), and every number on the cards is a measured shift or slope from a fetched record. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Wenger 1976 (Nadel programme): sweating and vasodilation thresholds shifted together by ~0.6 °C between day and night — one regulated level, two effectors
cards.summary: Wenger 1976 (Nadel programme): sweating and vasodilation thresholds shifted together by ~0.6 °C between day and night — one regulated level, two effectors
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (exercise heat stress, day versus night thresholds)
cards.people: 6 subjects exercising on a bicycle ergometer at 60–70% of maximal aerobic power in 25 °C air, studied at night (04:00–05:30) and in daytime (12:00–16:30), with chest sweating rate, forearm blood flow and oesophageal temperature; N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Oesophageal temperature was corrected for skin temperature (T′es = Tes + (Tsk − 33 °C)/8) to express the combined core-and-skin drive. The sweating-rate and blood-flow relations to corrected temperature were not consistently changed between day and night, but in every subject the thresholds for sweating and for vasodilation were shifted about equally — by an average of 0.57 °C (range 0.23–0.93) for sweating and 0.63 °C (range 0.17–0.98) for blood flow — both lower at night. The authors' design shows the two heat-loss effectors share one shifting threshold rather than switching independently.
cards.watchOut: Very small classic study (N = 6) reporting threshold shifts, not absolute onset temperatures; forearm skin was held warm (35.5 °C), and thresholds in other skin-temperature or resting conditions differ.
cards.source: Wenger CB et al. Nocturnal lowering of thresholds for sweating and vasodilation. J Appl Physiol. 1976. PMID: 972126. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stephenson 1984 (Nadel/Wenger programme): across the 24-hour day, sweating and vasodilation thresholds peaked around 16:00 — 0.57 °C and 0.65 °C higher than at 04:00 — tracking the circadian rhythm of resting core temperature
cards.summary: Stephenson 1984 (Nadel/Wenger programme): across the 24-hour day, sweating and vasodilation thresholds peaked around 16:00 — 0.57 °C and 0.65 °C higher than at 04:00 — tracking the circadian rhythm of resting core temperature
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (circadian threshold mapping, exercise heat stress)
cards.people: 5 men studied during 20 minutes of exercise at 25 °C on 6 separate days, at six times equally spaced over the 24-hour day, with continuous oesophageal temperature and chest sweat rate and forearm blood flow measured 1–2 times per minute; N = 5 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Thresholds for sweating and forearm vasodilation were significantly higher at 16:00 and 20:00 than at 24:00 and 04:00, averaging 0.57 °C (sweating) and 0.65 °C (vasodilation) higher at 16:00 than at 04:00. Resting oesophageal temperature and both thresholds followed the same circadian rhythm, zenith around 16:00 and nadir at 04:00. The slope of the sweat-rate-to-temperature relation did not change over the day, while the blood-flow slope tended to increase between 04:00 and 24:00. The authors conclude the regulated core-temperature level itself oscillates over the day.
cards.watchOut: Very small study (N = 5) in exercising men; it maps threshold movement across the day, and the absolute threshold at any hour still depends on skin temperature and hydration, which the other cards on this shelf quantify.
cards.source: Stephenson LA et al. Circadian rhythm in sweating and cutaneous blood flow. Am J Physiol. 1984. PMID: 6703085. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fortney 1984 (Wenger/Nadel programme): hyperosmolality raised the vasodilation and sweating thresholds by 0.22 °C and cut maximal forearm blood flow by about a third
cards.summary: Fortney 1984 (Wenger/Nadel programme): hyperosmolality raised the vasodilation and sweating thresholds by 0.22 °C and cut maximal forearm blood flow by about a third
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (dehydration and hypertonic-saline manipulation of thresholds)
cards.people: 5 men cycling at 65–75% of maximal oxygen uptake for up to 30 minutes at 30 °C and 40% relative humidity under three conditions — control, dehydration, and dehydration with 3% saline infusion restoring plasma volume; N = 5 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Control plasma volume and osmolality averaged 3,800 mL and 282 mosmol/kg; after dehydration they were 3,606 mL and 293 mosmol/kg, and saline infusion restored volume (3,826 mL) at the same high osmolality (294 mosmol/kg). In dehydration, oesophageal temperature after 20 minutes of exercise was 0.56 °C higher than control, because the threshold for vasodilation rose by 0.22 °C, the slope of the forearm blood-flow-to-temperature relation fell by 39% (a relative reduction), maximal exercise blood flow fell by 32% on average (a relative reduction), and the sweating threshold rose by 0.22 °C. With volume restored but osmolality still high, the threshold and maximal-flow effects persisted while the slope normalised — hyperosmolality itself, not just volume loss, raises the switch-on temperatures.
cards.watchOut: Very small study (N = 5) under exercise heat stress with induced dehydration; the 39% and 32% figures are relative changes in slope and maximum from the record, printed as relative here, and the threshold shift (0.22 °C) is the absolute figure.
cards.source: Fortney SM et al. Effect of hyperosmolality on control of blood flow and sweating. J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol. 1984. PMID: 6511544. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Armstrong and Kenney 1993: after 9 days of heat acclimation, resting core temperature was lower and the body-temperature thresholds for sweating and skin vasodilation onset were lower in both young and older men
cards.summary: Armstrong and Kenney 1993: after 9 days of heat acclimation, resting core temperature was lower and the body-temperature thresholds for sweating and skin vasodilation onset were lower in both young and older men
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (9-day heat acclimation protocol, passive heat exposure)
cards.people: 6 older men (61 ± 1 years) and 6 young men (26 ± 2 years), matched for maximal oxygen uptake, anthropometry and body composition, seated through a passive heat transient (28–46 °C) before and after a 9-day active heat acclimation protocol, with forearm blood flow and chest sweating plotted against mean body temperature; N = 12 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: There were no age differences in rectal, mean skin or mean body temperature before or after acclimation, though heart rate was lower in the older group in both states (p < 0.01). Heat acclimation significantly lowered baseline rectal and mean body temperature in both groups, and both stayed lower throughout the passive heat stress (p < 0.05). The slope of the forearm blood-flow-to-body-temperature relation was lower in the older group before and after acclimation (p < 0.05), and maximal chest sweating rate was lower in the older group (p < 0.05), while neither the sweating slope nor its threshold was affected by age. The authors state that acclimation resulted in a lower mean-body-temperature threshold for the onset of sweating and skin vasodilation; the record's abstract is truncated and prints no numeric size for that shift, so none is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Passive (resting) heat exposure after active acclimation, in men only; the acclimation threshold shift is reported directionally in a truncated abstract — sweat-rate increases with acclimation are part of the textbook account, while this record's own numeric sweat finding is the lower maximal rate in older men.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one shifting threshold zone governs both sweating and vasodilation — down ~0.6 °C at night, up 0.22 °C when hyperosmolar, and down again with heat acclimation, which also lowers resting core temperature — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: one shifting threshold zone governs both sweating and vasodilation — down ~0.6 °C at night, up 0.22 °C when hyperosmolar, and down again with heat acclimation, which also lowers resting core temperature — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: 6 + 5 + 5 exercising men in the Nadel/Wenger threshold studies and 12 men (6 young, 6 older) in the 9-day acclimation study.
cards.result: The four studies agree on the architecture: sweating and cutaneous vasodilation switch on together as core (oesophageal/mean body) temperature crosses a regulated threshold, and that threshold is a moving quantity — about 0.6 °C lower in the small hours, 0.22 °C higher with hyperosmolality, and lowered by heat acclimation alongside a lower resting core temperature and (per the textbook account) higher sweat rates for a given core temperature. The absolute onset level itself is the textbook's account (Guyton and Hall): effectors engage as core temperature rises through the regulated zone around 37 °C, modulated by skin temperature. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Thresholds measured during exercise or passive heating in small groups of healthy men: fever, drugs, skin temperature and disease all move the switch-on points, and no single onset temperature should be quoted without its conditions.

shelves.title: Altitude erythropoietin and haemoglobin mass (physiology): erythropoietin rises within about 1.5–2 hours of hypoxia and keeps climbing over the first days, while total haemoglobin mass follows slowly — up about 5% by 3–4 weeks, on a sigmoidal course that plateaus after about 3 weeks
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how do erythropoietin and total haemoglobin mass change over the first weeks at altitude?
shelves.mesh: Adult · *Atmospheric Pressure · Erythropoietin/analysis,biosynthesis · Humans · Hypoxia/metabolism · Male · Radioimmunoassay
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): hypoxia is sensed within hours, erythropoietin (EPO) rises first, reticulocytes follow, and total haemoglobin mass expands over weeks — a fast hormone signal driving a slow red-cell response, the textbook's account, which the carded human studies time precisely. Eckardt 1989 put volunteers in a decompression chamber: serum EPO was significantly elevated after 114 minutes at a simulated 3,000 m and 84 minutes at 4,000 m, rising continuously thereafter (16.0 to 22.5 mU/mL and 16.7 to 28.0 mU/mL over 5.5 hours), corresponding to 1.8-fold and 3.0-fold increases in calculated EPO production rate (relative increases); after hypoxia ended, EPO kept rising for about 1.5 hours then fell with a half-life of 5.2 hours. At real altitude the mass response is far slower: in 9 lowlanders spending 28 days at 3,454 m, haemoglobin mass (CO rebreathing, Lundby programme) rose 5.26% (a relative increase; range 2.5–11.1%), with individual increases delayed by up to 12 days, a maximal rate of 4.04 g/day reached at about day 15, and a plateau after about 3 weeks; on return to sea level it decayed at −2.46 g/day to baseline within 2 weeks (Siebenmann 2015). Klein 2021 independently found total haemoglobin up 4.7% after a 19-day sojourn at 3,450 m, back to baseline within 11 days of descent, with EPO and reticulocytes falling rapidly after descent and no evidence of neocytolysis. Early haemoconcentration at altitude is plasma-volume contraction, not new red cells — the two must not be confused, and this shelf is about the hormone and the mass, not ventilatory acclimatisation. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Eckardt 1989: serum erythropoietin was significantly up within 84–114 minutes of simulated altitude, reaching 22.5 mU/mL at 3,000 m and 28.0 mU/mL at 4,000 m by 5.5 hours
cards.summary: Eckardt 1989: serum erythropoietin was significantly up within 84–114 minutes of simulated altitude, reaching 22.5 mU/mL at 3,000 m and 28.0 mU/mL at 4,000 m by 5.5 hours
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (hypobaric-chamber erythropoietin time course, Eckardt programme)
cards.people: 6 healthy volunteers exposed in a decompression chamber to simulated altitudes of 3,000 m and 4,000 m for 5.5 hours, with serum erythropoietin by radioimmunoassay every 30 minutes, and post-hypoxia sampling in 2 subjects; N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: EPO levels during hypoxia were significantly elevated after 114 minutes (3,000 m) and 84 minutes (4,000 m) and rose continuously for the period investigated. Mean values increased from 16.0 to 22.5 mU/mL at 3,000 m and from 16.7 to 28.0 mU/mL at 4,000 m, corresponding to 1.8-fold and 3.0-fold increases in the calculated production rate of the hormone (relative increases). After termination of hypoxia, EPO continued to rise for approximately 1.5 hours and then declined exponentially with an average half-life of 5.2 hours.
cards.watchOut: Six volunteers and 5.5 hours of simulated (chamber) altitude: it times the onset and early slope of the EPO response, not its multi-day peak at real altitude, which the sojourn studies on this shelf bound.

cards.headline: Siebenmann 2015 (Lundby programme): 28 days at 3,454 m raised haemoglobin mass by 5.26% — starting after up to 12 days' delay, peaking in rate at about day 15, plateauing after about 3 weeks
cards.summary: Siebenmann 2015 (Lundby programme): 28 days at 3,454 m raised haemoglobin mass by 5.26% — starting after up to 12 days' delay, peaking in rate at about day 15, plateauing after about 3 weeks
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (28-day altitude sojourn, CO-rebreathing haemoglobin mass, Lundby programme)
cards.people: 9 healthy, normally trained sea-level residents (8 men, 1 woman) who sojourned for 28 days at 3,454 m, with haemoglobin mass and plasma volume by carbon-monoxide rebreathing at sea level, every 4th day at altitude, and 1 and 2 weeks after return; N = 9 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Four weeks at altitude increased haemoglobin mass by 5.26% (a relative increase; range 2.5–11.1%; p < 0.001). Individual increases commenced with up to 12 days of delay and reached a maximal rate of 4.04 ± 1.02 g/day after 14.9 ± 5.2 days; the probability of a plateau increased steeply after 20–24 days, giving a sigmoidal overall pattern. On return to sea level haemoglobin mass decayed by −2.46 ± 2.3 g/day, reaching baseline-like values after 2 weeks. Plasma volume, aldosterone and renin activity were reduced at altitude (p < 0.001) while total circulating protein mass was unaffected — the early plasma-volume contraction is separate from the slow mass expansion.
cards.watchOut: Nine subjects at one altitude (3,454 m) with wide individual range (2.5–11.1%); the percentage is a relative increase in mass, and gains at lower altitudes or shorter stays are smaller and slower.
cards.source: Siebenmann C et al. Hemoglobin mass and intravascular volume kinetics during and after exposure to 3,454-m altitude. J Appl Physiol (1985). 2015. PMID: 25749449. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Klein 2021: total haemoglobin rose 4.7% over a 19-day sojourn at 3,450 m and normalised within 11 days of descent — by reduced production, not destruction of new cells
cards.summary: Klein 2021: total haemoglobin rose 4.7% over a 19-day sojourn at 3,450 m and normalised within 11 days of descent — by reduced production, not destruction of new cells
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (19-day altitude sojourn, isotope-labelled erythrocyte cohorts)
cards.people: 12 healthy men (mean age 23.3 years) studied at normoxia (110 m) and during a 19-day sojourn at the Jungfraujoch Research Station (3,450 m), with erythrocytes age-cohort labelled by ingested isotope-labelled glycine in normoxia and at altitude; N = 12 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Total haemoglobin increased by 4.7% ± 2.7% at high altitude (a relative increase) and returned to pre-altitude values within 11 days after descent. Elimination of erythrocytes labelled in normoxia and at altitude did not differ, there was no indication of haemolysis, and erythropoietin levels and CD71-positive reticulocyte counts decreased rapidly after descent. The authors conclude the post-descent fall in total haemoglobin occurred by a reduced rate of erythropoiesis with normal clearance of senescent cells — not by neocytolysis, the selective destruction of young erythrocytes.
cards.watchOut: Twelve young men at one altitude; it corroborates the size and reversibility of the mass change and settles the descent mechanism, while the day-by-day expansion kinetics rest on Siebenmann 2015.
cards.source: Klein M et al. Absence of neocytolysis in humans returning from a 3-week high-altitude sojourn. Acta Physiol (Oxf). 2021. PMID: 33729672. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: EPO moves in hours (up by ~1.5–2 hours, production up 1.8–3.0-fold), haemoglobin mass in weeks (about +5% by 3–4 weeks, plateauing, and reversing within about 2 weeks of descent) — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: EPO moves in hours (up by ~1.5–2 hours, production up 1.8–3.0-fold), haemoglobin mass in weeks (about +5% by 3–4 weeks, plateauing, and reversing within about 2 weeks of descent) — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: 6 chamber volunteers (Eckardt 1989), 9 lowlanders over 28 days at 3,454 m (Siebenmann 2015) and 12 men over 19 days at 3,450 m (Klein 2021).
cards.result: The two timescales are cleanly separated by the carded studies: the hormone signal is fast and altitude-dose-dependent within the first hours, while total haemoglobin mass — measured directly by CO rebreathing, not inferred from concentration — expands sigmoidally to about 5% above sea-level values by 3–4 weeks at ~3,450 m and unwinds within about 2 weeks of descent through reduced production. Early rises in haemoglobin concentration at altitude reflect plasma-volume contraction and are not mass expansion. This matches the textbook account in Boron and Boulpaep, which frames this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Healthy lowlanders at ~3,450 m: high-altitude natives, patients with lung disease, and athletes using altitude camps differ, and haemoglobin concentration alone must never be read as haemoglobin mass.

Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2015 (PMID: 25749449); Klein M et al. Acta physiologica (Oxford, England). 2021 (PMID: 33729672). shelves.title: Amiloride as the fourth drug for resistant hypertension: noninferior to spironolactone in the SPARE randomised trial (home SBP -13.6 vs -14.7 mm Hg) and equal in the PATHWAY-2 runout (-20.4 vs -18.3 mm Hg clinic SBP)
shelves.question: In adults with resistant hypertension still uncontrolled on a thiazide-like diuretic, ACE inhibitor/ARB and calcium-channel blocker, is amiloride an effective fourth-line agent, and how does it compare with spironolactone?
shelves.mesh: Aldosterone/metabolism · Amiloride/therapeutic use · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Bisoprolol/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Doxazosin/therapeutic use · Female · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Spironolactone/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). PREMISE VERIFIED this session: the home shelves #278 (the fourth drug for resistant hypertension) and #1559 (ReHOT) were read in full in the live ask-index - the word 'amiloride' appears in neither, so this slice is genuinely uncovered; the only other amiloride pack in the tree (#5636) concerns lithium-induced diabetes insipidus, a different question. The evidence: in the PATHWAY-2 mechanisms substudies, amiloride 10 mg in the optional open-label runout (146 patients) lowered clinic systolic pressure by 20.4 mm Hg against 18.3 mm Hg for spironolactone 25 mg. The SPARE trial (JAMA 2025; 118 Korean patients on fixed-dose triple therapy) is the first randomised head-to-head: home systolic pressure fell 13.6 mm Hg on amiloride against 14.7 mm Hg on spironolactone (difference -0.68 mm Hg, 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14), meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin, with one hyperkalaemia discontinuation on amiloride and no gynaecomastia in either arm. A 2025 review of the whole amiloride record reaches the same conclusion and notes amiloride's effect was consistent across renin and aldosterone levels, unlike spironolactone's. Amiloride is therefore a credible fourth-line alternative when spironolactone is not tolerated - on blood-pressure evidence only; neither trial measures clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: PATHWAY-2 substudies 2018: in the open-label runout, amiloride 10 mg lowered clinic systolic BP by 20.4 mm Hg against 18.3 mm Hg for spironolactone 25 mg
cards.summary: PATHWAY-2 substudies 2018: in the open-label runout, amiloride 10 mg lowered clinic systolic BP by 20.4 mm Hg against 18.3 mm Hg for spironolactone 25 mg
cards.type: PATHWAY-2 mechanisms substudies (2018), including the open-label amiloride runout - 146 patients in substudy 3 (registry shared with the main PATHWAY-2 trial homed at #278; this substudy report is a distinct publication and the main-trial report is not carded here)
cards.people: PATHWAY-2 randomised 314 patients with resistant hypertension through 12 weeks each of placebo, spironolactone 25-50 mg, bisoprolol and doxazosin; 269 patients joined one or more of three substudies - 126 in the renin/aldosterone substudy, 226 in the haemodynamic substudy, and 146 in substudy 3, the optional 6-12 week open-label runout assessing amiloride 10-20 mg once daily against clinic systolic blood pressure.
cards.result: Amiloride 10 mg once daily reduced clinic systolic blood pressure by 20.4 mm Hg (95% CI 18.3 to 22.5), compared with a reduction of 18.3 mm Hg (95% CI 16.2 to 20.5) with spironolactone 25 mg once daily. In the mechanistic substudies, spironolactone's home systolic reduction was predicted by aldosterone-to-renin ratio and plasma renin, 31 of 126 patients (25%, 95% CI 17% to 33%) had inappropriately high aldosterone concentrations, and spironolactone - but not the other blinded treatments - reduced thoracic fluid content by 6.8% from baseline (95% CI 4.0% to 8.8%; P<0.0001). No serious adverse events were recorded in the substudies.
cards.watchOut: The amiloride figure comes from an optional, open-label runout in self-selected continuing patients, compared against a spironolactone figure from the blinded phase - not a randomised head-to-head. It shows amiloride can lower pressure substantially in this population; the randomised comparison is SPARE (next card).
cards.source: Williams B et al. Endocrine and haemodynamic changes in resistant hypertension, and blood pressure responses to spironolactone or amiloride: the PATHWAY-2 mechanisms substudies. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 29655877. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02369081, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SPARE 2025: amiloride was noninferior to spironolactone as fourth-line therapy - home systolic BP fell -13.6 mm Hg on amiloride against -14.7 mm Hg on spironolactone at 12 weeks (difference -0.68 mm Hg, 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14)
cards.summary: SPARE 2025: amiloride was noninferior to spironolactone as fourth-line therapy - home systolic BP fell -13.6 mm Hg on amiloride against -14.7 mm Hg on spironolactone at 12 weeks (difference -0.68 mm Hg, 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint noninferiority trial (SPARE, JAMA 2025) - 118 patients
cards.people: 118 patients in South Korea (14 sites) with home systolic BP of 130 mm Hg or more after a 4-week run-in on a fixed-dose triple combination (angiotensin receptor blocker, calcium channel blocker and thiazide), randomised 1:1 to spironolactone 12.5 mg daily (60 patients) or amiloride 5 mg daily (58 patients), with dose doubling at week 4 if home systolic BP remained at least 130 mm Hg and serum potassium was under 5.0 mmol/L (5.0 mEq/L). Median age was 55 years; 70% were men.
cards.result: At week 12, home systolic BP had fallen by -13.6 (SD 8.6) mm Hg on amiloride and -14.7 (SD 11.0) mm Hg on spironolactone (between-group difference in change -0.68 mm Hg; 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14), with amiloride demonstrating noninferiority against the prespecified -4.4 mm Hg margin. Achievement of home systolic BP under 130 mm Hg was 66.1% (amiloride) against 55.2% (spironolactone), and office achievement 57.1% against 60.3%, with no difference between groups. One hyperkalaemia-related discontinuation occurred in the amiloride group; no gynaecomastia occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: A single 118-patient, open-label (blinded-endpoint) trial in one country, over 12 weeks, on a blood-pressure endpoint: noninferiority within a 4.4 mm Hg margin is not proof of identical effect, and neither tolerability beyond 12 weeks nor clinical outcomes are addressed.
cards.source: Lee CJ et al. Spironolactone vs Amiloride for Resistant Hypertension: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40366680. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04331691, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: 2025 review of the amiloride record: the PATHWAY-2 suggestion and the SPARE result agree, and amiloride's effect - unlike spironolactone's - was consistent across renin and aldosterone levels
cards.summary: 2025 review of the amiloride record: the PATHWAY-2 suggestion and the SPARE result agree, and amiloride's effect - unlike spironolactone's - was consistent across renin and aldosterone levels
cards.type: Narrative review of the amiloride evidence in resistant hypertension (2025) - review card, flagged as such
cards.people: A 2025 narrative review in Clinical Hypertension summarising the amiloride evidence for resistant hypertension: the PATHWAY-2 open-label data and the SPARE randomised trial (118 patients inadequately controlled on fixed-dose triple therapy, randomised to spironolactone 12.5-25 mg or amiloride 5-10 mg for 12 weeks).
cards.result: The review reports SPARE's primary result - mean home systolic reductions of -14.7 mm Hg with spironolactone and -13.6 mm Hg with amiloride, meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin - with favourable safety (one hyperkalaemia discontinuation on amiloride, no gynaecomastia). Its subgroup summary suggests greater amiloride efficacy at higher body-mass index and lower aldosterone-renin ratios, with amiloride's systolic reduction consistent across renin and aldosterone levels, in contrast to spironolactone, whose efficacy correlated with aldosterone activity. The review frames amiloride, an epithelial sodium-channel (ENaC) blocker, as the leading alternative when spironolactone's adverse effects (gynaecomastia, menstrual irregularities, hyperkalaemia) limit its use.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, carded only as a map of the evidence - its SPARE numbers duplicate the primary report carded above and add no new patients. The subgroup claims (body-mass index, aldosterone-renin ratio) come from small post hoc strata of a 118-patient trial and are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Lee CJ et al. Amiloride: revisiting an old drug for resistant hypertension. Clinical hypertension. 2025. PMID: 41362675. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - amiloride is an effective fourth-line agent and, on blood pressure, matches spironolactone in the only randomised head-to-head trial; the slice was verified uncovered in homes #278 and #1559
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - amiloride is an effective fourth-line agent and, on blood pressure, matches spironolactone in the only randomised head-to-head trial; the slice was verified uncovered in homes #278 and #1559
cards.people: The carded evidence is the PATHWAY-2 mechanisms substudy report (amiloride runout, 146 patients, within the 314-patient PATHWAY-2 programme whose main spironolactone comparison is homed at #278 and is not carded here), the SPARE randomised trial (118 patients), and a 2025 narrative review of the same material.
cards.result: Amiloride lowered clinic systolic pressure by 20.4 mm Hg in the PATHWAY-2 open-label runout (spironolactone 18.3 mm Hg in its blinded phase) and was noninferior to spironolactone on home systolic pressure in SPARE (-13.6 vs -14.7 mm Hg; difference -0.68 mm Hg, 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14; margin -4.4 mm Hg). Target achievement and short-term tolerability were similar, with no gynaecomastia signal. The verdict answers both halves of the question: amiloride works as a fourth-line agent, and the direct comparison shows parity on blood pressure within the tested margin - not superiority, and not outcomes evidence.
cards.watchOut: Single-RCT cap: one 118-patient open-label noninferiority trial plus an open-label runout is a POSSIBLE-grade base. Blood pressure is a surrogate; no trial of amiloride as fourth-line therapy measures stroke, myocardial infarction or mortality.
cards.source: Synthesis of Williams B et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018 (PMID: 29655877, NCT02369081); Lee CJ et al. JAMA. 2025 (PMID: 40366680, NCT04331691); Lee CJ et al. Clinical hypertension. 2025 (PMID: 41362675). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Anakinra for acute myocarditis (ARAMIS): one small randomised trial (120 planned) - safe, but it did not reduce early complications; the results record prints no figures, flagged on the face
shelves.question: In adults with acute myocarditis, does anakinra, compared with standard care, reduce early complications?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Myocarditis/drug therapy,immunology,physiopathology,diagnosis,mortality,diagnostic imaging · Double-Blind Method · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein/adverse effects,therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Acute Disease · Time Factors · Biomarkers/blood · Interleukin-1beta/antagonists & inhibitors,immunology · Male · Female · Adult · Ventricular Function, Left/drug effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Middle Aged · United States · Injections, Subcutaneous · Multicenter Studies as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) - single small trial, with an explicit reporting flag. PREMISE VERIFIED: home pack #3062 (immunosuppression in myocarditis - TIMIC/Mason/IMAC) was read in full; neither 'anakinra' nor 'ARAMIS' (myocarditis) appears in it, and the ARAMIS name-hits elsewhere in the tree are unrelated trials (a prostate-cancer ARAMIS and a stroke ARAMIS). ARAMIS randomised patients with cardiac-MRI-proven acute myocarditis to anakinra 100 mg daily during hospitalisation or placebo, on top of standard care; its primary endpoint was days alive free of myocarditis complications to 28 days after discharge. The trial's results report (European Heart Journal - Acute Cardiovascular Care 2023) is a two-page in-perspective piece whose PubMed record carries NO abstract and NO figures - so no per-arm numbers can be carded from the record, and this shelf does not invent any. The 2026 cardioimmunology review of the IL-1 pathway characterises ARAMIS plainly: it 'did not improve outcomes in a largely low-risk cohort', while suggesting any future role lies in fulminant or hyperinflammatory presentations supported only by case reports and small series (not carded here). On the evidence that can be verified from the records, anakinra in unselected acute myocarditis is safe and without demonstrated benefit.

cards.headline: ARAMIS design (2023): 120 patients with MRI-proven acute myocarditis randomised to anakinra 100 mg daily during hospitalisation or placebo; primary endpoint days alive free of myocarditis complications
cards.summary: ARAMIS design (2023): 120 patients with MRI-proven acute myocarditis randomised to anakinra 100 mg daily during hospitalisation or placebo; primary endpoint days alive free of myocarditis complications
cards.type: Randomised trial rationale and design report (ARAMIS, 2023) - 120 patients planned
cards.people: Symptomatic patients with elevated cardiac troponin and cardiac-magnetic-resonance-proven acute myocarditis, randomised within 72 hours of hospital admission in a national multicentre double-blind trial (n=120 planned) to daily subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg or placebo during hospitalisation, in addition to standard care including an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker.
cards.result: The primary endpoint is the number of days alive free from any myocarditis complication - ventricular arrhythmias, heart failure, recurrent chest pain requiring medication, or ventricular dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction under 50%) - from randomisation to 28 days after hospital discharge. The design paper describes ARAMIS as the first trial of interleukin-1beta pathway inhibition in acute myocarditis and, although small, the largest randomised trial in the condition.
cards.watchOut: A design paper, carded to document exactly what the trial set out to measure and in whom: it contains no results. Its planned n=120 also frames the trial's ceiling - even perfectly executed, ARAMIS could only detect large effects on its composite endpoint.
cards.source: Kerneis M et al. Rationale and design of the ARAMIS trial: Anakinra versus placebo, a double blind randomized controlled trial for the treatment of acute myocarditis. Archives of cardiovascular diseases. 2023. PMID: 37640625. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03018834, from the record's databank fields. cards.result: The fetched PubMed record for the results report establishes the trial as a completed double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of anakinra for acute myocarditis, but the record contains no abstract and no numerical results, so no per-arm event rates or effect sizes are carded from it - any figures quoted for ARAMIS elsewhere are not verifiable from this record. cards.type: Narrative review of IL-1 blockade in myocarditis (2026) - review card, flagged as such
cards.people: A 2026 review in Current Cardiology Reports synthesising preclinical and clinical evidence for interleukin-1 pathway inhibition in myocarditis and related inflammatory cardiac syndromes, including the ARAMIS randomised trial and the case-report literature in fulminant and hyperinflammatory presentations.
cards.result: The review states that the randomised trial of anakinra in acute myocarditis (ARAMIS) did not improve outcomes in a largely low-risk cohort, while accumulating case reports and small series suggest potential benefit in fulminant or hyperinflammatory myocarditis and in systemic autoimmune/autoinflammatory presentations. It grounds the rationale in NLRP3 inflammasome activation and interleukin-1 as a mediator linking inflammation to myocardial dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review's one-sentence characterisation is a thin reed for a verdict - it is carded because it is the only fetched record that states ARAMIS's direction in words. The fulminant-myocarditis suggestion rests on case reports and small series, which are below this library's evidence floor and are not carded.
cards.source: Chiara E et al. Cardioimmunology of Myocarditis: Targeting the IL-1 Pathway. Current cardiology reports. 2026. PMID: 42397625. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) - one small trial, safely conducted, with no demonstrated reduction in early complications; home #3062 verified not to card ARAMIS
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) - one small trial, safely conducted, with no demonstrated reduction in early complications; home #3062 verified not to card ARAMIS
cards.people: The carded evidence is the ARAMIS trial's design report (120 patients planned), its two-page results report (no abstract or figures in the record), and a 2026 review characterising its result. Home pack #3062 covers corticosteroid/immunosuppression and immune globulin in myocarditis and was verified this session to contain neither anakinra nor ARAMIS.
cards.result: ARAMIS asked whether interleukin-1 blockade reduces days with myocarditis complications in the first month after discharge. The trial's reported direction is null: anakinra did not improve outcomes in its largely low-risk cohort, and no safety signal is reported in the fetched records. There is no second trial. The honest verdict is a single-trial POSSIBLE null - anakinra should not be expected to reduce early complications in unselected acute myocarditis on current evidence - with the documentation caveat printed on the results card.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial cap plus a documentation flag: if a full ARAMIS results paper with extractable numbers is later indexed, this shelf should be re-carded from it. The low-risk cohort also means the trial says little about fulminant myocarditis, where only anecdotal evidence exists.

shelves.title: PCSK9 inhibition started immediately after acute MI: PACMAN-AMI and HUYGENS show greater plaque regression and fibrous-cap thickening in non-culprit arteries at one year (imaging surrogates; GLAGOV stable-disease comparator agrees)
shelves.question: In patients started on a PCSK9 inhibitor immediately after acute myocardial infarction, does early intensive LDL lowering, compared with statin alone, regress and stabilise non-culprit plaque on intracoronary imaging?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Cholesterol, LDL · Coronary Artery Disease/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/complications,drug therapy · PCSK9 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Plaque, Atherosclerotic/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on imaging surrogates. PREMISE NOTE: the slate named home #45 for this slice; the live #45 in the ask-index is a type 2 diabetes plaque/icosapent-ethyl shelf, not a PCSK9 imaging shelf - but the substantive check holds either way: 'PACMAN-AMI', 'HUYGENS' and 'GLAGOV' return zero hits across the live index and the built packs, so the early post-MI PCSK9 imaging slice is genuinely uncovered. PACMAN-AMI (300 patients; alirocumab started within 24 hours of PCI) found percent atheroma volume fell 2.13% against 0.92% on placebo at 52 weeks, with greater lipid-core reduction and fibrous-cap thickening. HUYGENS (161 treated NSTEMI patients; evolocumab monthly) found minimum fibrous cap thickness rose 42.7 against 21.5 micrometres, with greater lipid-arc reduction and percent atheroma volume regression (-2.29% vs -0.61%). GLAGOV, the stable-disease comparator (968 patients, evolocumab), found the same direction on percent atheroma volume (-0.95% vs +0.05%). All three are surrogate-imaging trials: plaque pictures improve; whether starting this early prevents events beyond what outcomes trials of later initiation show is not measured here.

cards.headline: PACMAN-AMI 2022: alirocumab started within 24 hours of PCI after acute MI - percent atheroma volume fell -2.13% against -0.92% on placebo at 52 weeks (difference -1.21%; P<.001)
cards.summary: PACMAN-AMI 2022: alirocumab started within 24 hours of PCI after acute MI - percent atheroma volume fell -2.13% against -0.92% on placebo at 52 weeks (difference -1.21%; P<.001)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PACMAN-AMI, JAMA 2022) - 300 patients
cards.people: 300 patients undergoing PCI for acute myocardial infarction at 9 European academic hospitals (mean age 58.5 years; 18.7% women; mean LDL cholesterol 152.4 mg/dL), randomised to subcutaneous alirocumab 150 mg every 2 weeks (148) or placebo (152), initiated within 24 hours of urgent PCI of the culprit lesion, for 52 weeks on top of high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 20 mg). Serial IVUS, near-infrared spectroscopy and OCT were performed in the two non-infarct-related arteries; 265 patients (88.3%) underwent serial IVUS in 537 arteries.
cards.result: At 52 weeks, mean change in percent atheroma volume was -2.13% with alirocumab against -0.92% with placebo (difference -1.21%, 95% CI -1.78% to -0.65%; P<.001). Maximum lipid core burden index within 4 mm fell by -79.42 against -37.60 (difference -41.24, 95% CI -70.71 to -11.77; P=.006), and minimal fibrous cap thickness rose by 62.67 against 33.19 micrometres (difference 29.65 micrometres, 95% CI 11.75 to 47.55; P=.001) - regression plus stabilisation on all three imaging modalities. Adverse events occurred in 70.7% on alirocumab against 72.8% on placebo (the record's abstract truncates at this point).
cards.watchOut: Imaging surrogates in non-culprit arteries over 52 weeks: the trial was not designed or powered for clinical events, and about 12% of randomised patients lacked serial IVUS. The comparison is alirocumab plus high-intensity statin against statin alone - it does not isolate the 'within 24 hours' timing from the LDL lowering itself.
cards.source: Räber L et al. Effect of Alirocumab Added to High-Intensity Statin Therapy on Coronary Atherosclerosis in Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction: The PACMAN-AMI Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 35368058. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03067844, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: HUYGENS 2022: evolocumab after NSTEMI - minimum fibrous cap thickness rose +42.7 against +21.5 micrometres (P=0.015) and percent atheroma volume regressed -2.29% against -0.61% (P=0.009) at 52 weeks
cards.summary: HUYGENS 2022: evolocumab after NSTEMI - minimum fibrous cap thickness rose +42.7 against +21.5 micrometres (P=0.015) and percent atheroma volume regressed -2.29% against -0.61% (P=0.009) at 52 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (HUYGENS, JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging 2022) - 161 patients treated
cards.people: Patients with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction treated with monthly evolocumab 420 mg (80 patients) or placebo (81 patients) for 52 weeks on background statin therapy (mean age 60.5 years; 28.6% women; LDL cholesterol 141.3 mg/dL), with serial OCT and IVUS in a matched segment of a nonculprit vessel; 135 patients had evaluable imaging at follow-up.
cards.result: The evolocumab group achieved LDL cholesterol of 28.1 against 87.2 mg/dL on placebo (P<0.001). Minimum fibrous cap thickness increased more with evolocumab (+42.7 vs +21.5 micrometres; P=0.015), maximum lipid arc fell more (-57.5 vs -31.4 degrees; P=0.04), macrophage index fell more (-3.17 vs -1.45 mm; P=0.04), and percent atheroma volume regressed more (-2.29% +/- 0.47% vs -0.61% +/- 0.46%; P=0.009). The groups did not differ in changes in microchannels or calcium.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three trials, with about one in six treated patients lacking evaluable follow-up imaging; OCT cap-thickness changes are mechanistic surrogates. As with PACMAN-AMI, the trial tests evolocumab-plus-statin against statin alone after MI - timing and intensity are bundled together.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. Effect of Evolocumab on Coronary Plaque Phenotype and Burden in Statin-Treated Patients Following Myocardial Infarction. JACC. Cardiovascular imaging. 2022. PMID: 35431172. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03570697, from the record's databank fields.
