cards.headline: GLAGOV 2016 (stable-disease comparator): evolocumab in statin-treated patients with angiographic coronary disease - percent atheroma volume -0.95% against +0.05% on placebo (difference -1.0%; P<.001)
cards.summary: GLAGOV 2016 (stable-disease comparator): evolocumab in statin-treated patients with angiographic coronary disease - percent atheroma volume -0.95% against +0.05% on placebo (difference -1.0%; P<.001)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GLAGOV, JAMA 2016) - 968 patients with stable angiographic coronary disease (comparator trial, not post-MI)
cards.people: 968 patients with angiographic coronary disease at 197 hospitals worldwide (mean age 59.8 years; 27.8% women; mean LDL cholesterol 92.5 mg/dL), randomised to monthly evolocumab 420 mg (484) or placebo (484) for 76 weeks on top of statins, with serial IVUS; 846 patients had evaluable imaging. This trial enrolled stable patients, not patients after acute MI - it is carded as the stable-disease comparator, flagged as such.
cards.result: Time-weighted LDL cholesterol was 36.6 mg/dL on evolocumab against 93.0 mg/dL on placebo (difference -56.5 mg/dL; P<.001). Percent atheroma volume decreased 0.95% with evolocumab and increased 0.05% with placebo (difference -1.0%, 95% CI -1.8% to -0.64%; P<.001); normalised total atheroma volume fell 5.8 against 0.9 mm3 (difference -4.9 mm3; P<.001). Plaque regression occurred in 64.3% on evolocumab against 47.3% on placebo (difference 17.0%, 95% CI 10.4% to 23.6%; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: A comparator, not part of this shelf's post-MI question: GLAGOV's patients were stable, had much lower starting LDL (92.5 mg/dL), and were treated longer (76 weeks). Its role is to show the post-MI findings are the expected extension of the class's plaque effect, not a distinct early-treatment phenomenon.
cards.source: Nicholls SJ et al. Effect of Evolocumab on Progression of Coronary Disease in Statin-Treated Patients: The GLAGOV Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27846344. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01813422, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - starting a PCSK9 inhibitor immediately after acute MI regresses and stabilises non-culprit plaque more than statin alone at one year, on concordant imaging evidence from two trials; the slice was verified uncovered (no PACMAN-AMI, HUYGENS or GLAGOV home exists)
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - starting a PCSK9 inhibitor immediately after acute MI regresses and stabilises non-culprit plaque more than statin alone at one year, on concordant imaging evidence from two trials; the slice was verified uncovered (no PACMAN-AMI, HUYGENS or GLAGOV home exists)
cards.people: The carded evidence is PACMAN-AMI (300 post-MI patients, alirocumab started within 24 hours of PCI), HUYGENS (161 treated NSTEMI patients, evolocumab) and, as the flagged stable-disease comparator, GLAGOV (968 patients, evolocumab). The desk check found no existing home for any of the three trials in the live index or built packs; the slate's named home #45 is, in the live index, a diabetes plaque shelf that does not pose this question.
cards.result: Both post-MI trials agree across modalities: percent atheroma volume regressed about 1.2-1.7 percentage points more with the PCSK9 inhibitor than with statin alone, lipid content fell more, and fibrous caps thickened more (PACMAN-AMI minimal cap +62.67 vs +33.19 micrometres; HUYGENS minimum cap +42.7 vs +21.5 micrometres). Achieved LDL cholesterol was very low (28.1 mg/dL in HUYGENS). GLAGOV's stable-disease result (-0.95% vs +0.05%) is directionally identical. Nothing here measures myocardial infarction, death or revascularisation attributable to the early start.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate cap: intracoronary imaging improvement is a mechanism, not an outcome. The POSSIBLE stamp covers the imaging claim exactly as posed in the question - it must not be inflated into an events claim for immediate post-MI initiation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Räber L et al. JAMA. 2022 (PMID: 35368058, NCT03067844); Nicholls SJ et al. JACC. Cardiovascular imaging. 2022 (PMID: 35431172, NCT03570697); Nicholls SJ et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27846344, NCT01813422). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Mipomersen in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDL down by about a quarter, with injection-site reactions in 76% and a hepatic cost
shelves.question: In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on maximal lipid-lowering therapy, does mipomersen, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol, and at what hepatic/injection-site cost?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, one small HoFH trial. Raal 2010 randomised 51 HoFH patients on maximal therapy: LDL cholesterol −24.7% on mipomersen versus −3.3% on placebo at 26 weeks, with injection-site reactions in 76% versus 24% and ALT ≥3× the upper limit of normal in 12% versus none. The programme's severe-hypercholesterolaemia trial (McGowan 2012) and HeFH trial (Stein 2012, which measured a median +4.9% hepatic fat on MRI) are concordant on both efficacy and hepatic cost, and are flagged on their faces as neighbouring populations. No cardiovascular-outcome data exist. HoFH homes for lomitapide (#1568) and evinacumab (#1106) do not cover mipomersen — desk-checked this session.

cards.headline: Raal 2010 (HoFH, the anchor trial): mipomersen 200 mg weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 24.7% versus 3.3% on placebo at 26 weeks — but 76% had injection-site reactions and 12% had ALT rises of 3× the upper limit of normal or more
cards.summary: Raal 2010 (HoFH, the anchor trial): mipomersen 200 mg weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 24.7% versus 3.3% on placebo at 26 weeks — but 76% had injection-site reactions and 12% had ALT rises of 3× the upper limit of normal or more
cards.people: 51 patients aged 12 years and older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (clinical diagnosis or genetic confirmation), already on the maximum tolerated dose of a lipid-lowering drug, in nine lipid clinics in seven countries; 34 assigned to mipomersen 200 mg subcutaneously weekly and 17 to placebo for 26 weeks; 45 completed treatment.
cards.result: Mean baseline LDL cholesterol was 11.4 mmol/L (441 mg/dL) on mipomersen and 10.4 mmol/L (402 mg/dL) on placebo. The mean percentage change in LDL cholesterol was −24.7% (95% CI −31.6 to −17.7) with mipomersen versus −3.3% (−12.1 to 5.5) with placebo (P=0.0003) — percentage (relative) changes, printed as reported. The most common adverse events were injection-site reactions (26 of 34 [76%] on mipomersen versus 4 of 17 [24%] on placebo). Four patients (12%) on mipomersen, and none on placebo, had alanine aminotransferase increases to at least three times the upper limit of normal.
cards.watchOut: The only placebo-controlled trial in HoFH itself, and it is small (51 patients) with a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-outcome data. Percentages are relative changes from very high baselines, so absolute LDL remained far above target for most patients.
cards.source: Randomised controlled trial (phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled) | Raal FJ et al. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20227758. Registry ID: NCT00607373 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record). cards.headline: McGowan 2012 (severe hypercholesterolaemia): LDL fell 36% on mipomersen versus a 13% rise on placebo; ALT increase in 21%, AST increase in 13% and hepatic steatosis in 13% of treated patients, with 20.5% discontinuing for adverse events
cards.summary: McGowan 2012 (severe hypercholesterolaemia): LDL fell 36% on mipomersen versus a 13% rise on placebo; ALT increase in 21%, AST increase in 13% and hepatic steatosis in 13% of treated patients, with 20.5% discontinuing for adverse events
cards.people: 58 adults with severe hypercholesterolaemia — LDL cholesterol at least 7.8 mmol/L (302 mg/dL), or at least 5.1 mmol/L (197 mg/dL) plus coronary heart disease — on maximally tolerated lipid-lowering therapy (apheresis excluded); 39 randomised to mipomersen 200 mg weekly and 19 to placebo for 26 weeks. This is a neighbouring, more severe-hypercholesterolaemia population, not HoFH only — flagged as such.
cards.result: In the efficacy population (27 mipomersen, 18 placebo), mipomersen reduced LDL cholesterol by 36% from a baseline of 7.2 mmol/L (278 mg/dL) — a mean absolute reduction of 2.6 mmol/L (101 mg/dL) — while placebo LDL rose 13% from 6.5 mmol/L (251 mg/dL) (P<0.001). Apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) also fell significantly. Mild-to-moderate injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse events and flu-like symptoms were more common on mipomersen. Alanine transaminase increase occurred in 21%, aspartate transaminase increase in 13% and hepatic steatosis in 13% of mipomersen-treated patients; serious adverse events occurred in 6 of 39 (15.4%) versus 0 on placebo, and discontinuations for adverse events in 8 of 39 (20.5%) versus 1 of 19 (5.3%).
cards.watchOut: PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate attributed the severe-hypercholesterolaemia phase 3 trial to 'Stein 2012, Circulation'; the fetched record is McGowan et al., PLoS One 2012 — Stein's Circulation 2012 trial is the HeFH trial carded next. Efficacy numbers come from the 45-patient completer population, not all 58 randomised.
cards.source: Randomised controlled trial (phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled) | McGowan MP et al. PLoS One. 2012. PMID: 23152839. Registry ID: NCT00794664 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Stein 2012 (HeFH with coronary disease): LDL fell 28.0% versus a 5.2% rise on placebo, and MRI-measured hepatic fat rose a median 4.9% versus 0.4% — the programme's direct hepatic-fat measurement
cards.summary: Stein 2012 (HeFH with coronary disease): LDL fell 28.0% versus a 5.2% rise on placebo, and MRI-measured hepatic fat rose a median 4.9% versus 0.4% — the programme's direct hepatic-fat measurement
cards.people: 124 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia and coronary artery disease on maximally tolerated statin therapy with LDL cholesterol at least 2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL); 83 randomised to mipomersen 200 mg weekly and 41 to placebo for 26 weeks; 114 completed treatment. A neighbouring HeFH population, carded because it carries the programme's magnetic-resonance measurement of hepatic fat — flagged as not HoFH.
cards.result: Mean LDL cholesterol change was −28.0% (95% CI −34.0 to −22.1) on mipomersen versus +5.2% (−0.5 to +10.9) on placebo (P<0.001); apolipoprotein B fell 26.3%, total cholesterol 19.4% and lipoprotein(a) 21.1% relative to placebo (all P<0.001) — relative (percentage) measures as reported. Adverse events included injection-site reactions and influenza-like symptoms. Five mipomersen patients (6%) had two consecutive alanine aminotransferase values at least three times the upper limit of normal at least 7 days apart, none with significant bilirubin increases. Hepatic fat content increased a median of 4.9% with mipomersen versus 0.4% with placebo (P<0.001); the authors state the significance of the hepatic fat and transaminase increases was uncertain.
cards.watchOut: HeFH, not HoFH — carded for the hepatic-fat and transaminase safety quantification only; the efficacy figure should not be read as a second HoFH result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: mipomersen lowers LDL cholesterol by about a quarter in HoFH on top of maximal therapy — at the cost of injection-site reactions in most patients, flu-like symptoms, transaminase rises in about one in eight, and measurably increased hepatic fat
cards.summary: Synthesis: mipomersen lowers LDL cholesterol by about a quarter in HoFH on top of maximal therapy — at the cost of injection-site reactions in most patients, flu-like symptoms, transaminase rises in about one in eight, and measurably increased hepatic fat
cards.people: Synthesis of Raal 2010 (HoFH, n=51), McGowan 2012 (severe hypercholesterolaemia, n=58) and Stein 2012 (HeFH with coronary disease, n=124) — one development programme. HoFH homes elsewhere in the library cover lomitapide (live shelf #1568) and evinacumab (#1106); mipomersen had no home — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: In the HoFH trial itself, weekly mipomersen 200 mg lowered LDL cholesterol by 24.7% versus 3.3% on placebo over 26 weeks, from baselines around 10–11 mmol/L (about 400–440 mg/dL). The programme's other phase 3 trials point the same way (−36% in severe hypercholesterolaemia; −28.0% in HeFH). The cost is consistent across the programme: injection-site reactions in 76% of HoFH patients (versus 24% on placebo), more flu-like symptoms, alanine aminotransferase at least 3× the upper limit of normal in 12% of the HoFH trial (21% with any ALT increase in the severe-hypercholesterolaemia trial, where 13% developed hepatic steatosis and 20.5% stopped for adverse events), and a median 4.9% increase in MRI-measured hepatic fat in the HeFH trial. No carded trial measures cardiovascular events, so the benefit on the face is LDL lowering only.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: a single programme with one small HoFH trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The hepatic-fat signal's long-term significance was stated as uncertain by the trialists; nothing carded here follows patients beyond about 26 weeks of randomised treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raal FJ et al. Lancet. 2010 (PMID: 20227758; NCT00607373); McGowan MP et al. PLoS One. 2012 (PMID: 23152839; NCT00794664); Stein EA et al. Circulation. 2012 (PMID: 23060426; NCT00706849).

shelves.title: Natriuretic-peptide screening to prevent heart failure: STOP-HF cut LV dysfunction/HF to 5.3% vs 8.7%, and PONTIAC cut cardiac events in NT-proBNP-selected diabetes
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults at risk of heart failure (including diabetes), does natriuretic-peptide-guided screening with collaborative care/treatment intensification, compared with usual care, prevent LV dysfunction and incident HF?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Biomarkers/blood · Cardiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Diastole · Echocardiography · Emergency Medical Services/statistics & numerical data · Female · Heart Failure/diagnosis,prevention & control · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Patient Care Team · Prevalence · Primary Health Care · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a screening-strategy shelf, stamped as such. STOP-HF (n=1,374): BNP screening plus collaborative care reduced LV dysfunction with or without heart failure to 5.3% versus 8.7% (OR 0.55) and emergency cardiovascular hospitalisation rates (rate ratio 0.60), though heart failure alone (1.0% vs 2.1%) was not significant. PONTIAC (n=300, diabetes, NT-proBNP >125 pg/mL): intensified RAS-antagonist/beta-blocker up-titration reduced cardiac hospitalisation/death (HR 0.351). PARABLE is carded, flagged as a downstream-treatment trial rather than screening evidence. Each strategy has been tested once — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: STOP-HF 2013: BNP screening with collaborative care cut the combined endpoint of LV dysfunction or heart failure to 5.3% versus 8.7% (odds ratio 0.55) over a mean 4.2 years — but heart failure alone was 1.0% versus 2.1% and not significant (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.20)
cards.summary: STOP-HF 2013: BNP screening with collaborative care cut the combined endpoint of LV dysfunction or heart failure to 5.3% versus 8.7% (odds ratio 0.55) over a mean 4.2 years — but heart failure alone was 1.0% versus 2.1% and not significant (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.20)
cards.people: 1,374 asymptomatic adults with cardiovascular risk factors (mean age 64.8 years) from 39 Irish primary-care practices, randomised to usual primary care (n=677) or BNP screening (n=697); intervention patients with a BNP of 50 pg/mL or higher received echocardiography and collaborative care between primary care and a specialist cardiovascular service. Mean follow-up 4.2 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (asymptomatic LV dysfunction with or without newly diagnosed heart failure) occurred in 37 of 697 (5.3%) in the intervention group versus 59 of 677 (8.7%) in controls (odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.37–0.82, P=0.003 — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 3.4 percentage points). Asymptomatic LV dysfunction alone: 4.3% versus 6.6% (OR 0.57, 0.37–0.88). Heart failure alone: 7 (1.0%) versus 14 (2.1%) (OR 0.48, 0.20–1.20, P=0.12 — not significant). Emergency hospitalisation for major cardiovascular events was lower with screening (22.3 versus 40.4 per 1,000 patient-years; incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.45–0.81). The intervention group had more cardiovascular investigations (850 versus 496 per 1,000 patient-years) and more renin-angiotensin-aldosterone therapy at follow-up (56.5% versus 49.6%). 41.6% of the intervention group had at least one BNP reading of 50 pg/mL or higher.
cards.watchOut: The significant primary endpoint is dominated by echocardiographic LV dysfunction; the clinical heart-failure component alone (21 events total) was not significant. Screening also bought substantially more testing and treatment — the benefit cannot be separated from the collaborative-care package that followed a positive BNP.
cards.source: Randomised controlled trial (screening strategy) | Ledwidge M et al. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23821090. Registry ID: NCT00921960 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record). cards.headline: PONTIAC 2013: in 300 people with type 2 diabetes selected for NT-proBNP above 125 pg/mL, intensified up-titration of RAS antagonists and beta-blockers reduced cardiac hospitalisation/death (hazard ratio 0.351, 95% CI 0.127–0.975)
cards.summary: PONTIAC 2013: in 300 people with type 2 diabetes selected for NT-proBNP above 125 pg/mL, intensified up-titration of RAS antagonists and beta-blockers reduced cardiac hospitalisation/death (hazard ratio 0.351, 95% CI 0.127–0.975)
cards.people: 300 patients with type 2 diabetes, elevated NT-proBNP (above 125 pg/mL; median 265.5 pg/mL) and no history of cardiac disease, randomised to care at diabetes units alone (control) or additional cardiac-clinic care with accelerated up-titration of renin-angiotensin-system antagonists and beta-blockers to maximum tolerated doses (intensified). Primary endpoint: hospitalisation or death due to cardiac disease after 2 years. A biomarker-selected population — the trial tests treatment intensification in screen-positive patients, not screening of an unselected population.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was significantly reduced in the intensified group (hazard ratio 0.351, 95% CI 0.127–0.975, P=0.044 — a relative measure corresponding to a 65% relative risk reduction; the fetched record does not print the absolute event counts, so no absolute difference is quoted). All-cause hospitalisation and unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation/death were also lower (P<0.05 for all). Blood pressure fell in both groups; heart rate fell only in the intensified group (P=0.004), and significantly more intensified patients reached target drug doses (P<0.0001). The authors conclude NT-proBNP-selected intensification is an effective and safe primary-prevention intervention in diabetes.
cards.watchOut: One small single-programme trial (300 patients) with a just-significant P=0.044 and a wide confidence interval; the comparison bundles the biomarker selection with specialist-clinic intensification, so the NT-proBNP test's own contribution is not isolated.
cards.source: Randomised controlled trial (biomarker-selected prevention strategy) | Huelsmann M et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2013. PMID: 23810874. cards.headline: PARABLE 2023: after natriuretic-peptide selection, treating pre-HFpEF patients with sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan paradoxically increased left atrial volume index more, while a secondary events count favoured sacubitril/valsartan (adjusted HR 0.38) — a downstream-treatment trial, not a screening trial
cards.summary: PARABLE 2023: after natriuretic-peptide selection, treating pre-HFpEF patients with sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan paradoxically increased left atrial volume index more, while a secondary events count favoured sacubitril/valsartan (adjusted HR 0.38) — a downstream-treatment trial, not a screening trial
cards.people: 250 asymptomatic patients aged 40 and older with hypertension or diabetes, elevated BNP (above 20 pg/mL) or NT-proBNP (above 100 pg/mL), left atrial volume index above 28 mL/m² and preserved ejection fraction, recruited substantially through the STOP-HF programme in Dublin; randomised double-blind to sacubitril/valsartan titrated to 200 mg twice daily or valsartan 160 mg twice daily for 18 months. Carded as the strategy's downstream-treatment leg and flagged as a different comparison from screening versus usual care.
cards.result: Maximal left atrial volume index increased more on sacubitril/valsartan than on valsartan (change 6.9 versus 0.7 mL/m² as printed in the record; P<0.001) despite improvements in filling-pressure markers in both groups; pulse pressure and NT-proBNP fell more with sacubitril/valsartan. Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 6 patients (4.9%) on sacubitril/valsartan versus 17 (13.3%) on valsartan (adjusted hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.17–0.89 — a relative measure, from a secondary endpoint in a 250-patient trial). The authors state more work is needed to understand the increased cardiac volumes and long-term effects in pre-HFpEF.
cards.watchOut: PARABLE does not test screening: everyone was already biomarker-selected, its primary imaging endpoint moved in the unexpected direction, and the events result is a small secondary count. It is carded to show what the evidence looks like one step downstream of a positive screen — not as a third screening trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: natriuretic-peptide-guided screening plus intensified care reduced LV dysfunction/heart-failure endpoints in two randomised strategy trials (STOP-HF and PONTIAC) — each a single programme, with the clinical heart-failure endpoint in STOP-HF too small to be significant on its own
cards.summary: Synthesis: natriuretic-peptide-guided screening plus intensified care reduced LV dysfunction/heart-failure endpoints in two randomised strategy trials (STOP-HF and PONTIAC) — each a single programme, with the clinical heart-failure endpoint in STOP-HF too small to be significant on its own
cards.people: Synthesis of STOP-HF (Ledwidge 2013, n=1,374, BNP ≥50 pg/mL triggering echo plus collaborative care), PONTIAC (Huelsmann 2013, n=300, NT-proBNP-selected diabetes patients given intensified neurohumoral therapy) and PARABLE (Ledwidge 2023, n=250, treatment after selection). The library's natriuretic-peptide shelves cover diagnosis/prognosis in established or suspected heart failure; the screening-strategy question in asymptomatic at-risk adults had no home — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: Both strategy trials point the same way: STOP-HF reduced the combined LV-dysfunction/heart-failure endpoint from 8.7% to 5.3% (OR 0.55) and emergency cardiovascular hospitalisation rates by about 40% in relative terms, and PONTIAC reduced cardiac hospitalisation/death with a hazard ratio of 0.351 in biomarker-selected diabetes patients. The qualifications are structural: each strategy was tested once, the interventions bundle the test with echocardiography, specialist collaboration and drug up-titration, STOP-HF's heart-failure-only endpoint was not significant (1.0% versus 2.1%), and PARABLE shows that even after selection, which drug to intensify with remains unsettled. The stamp is therefore POSSIBLE for a screening strategy that probably prevents LV dysfunction and may prevent clinical heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: no carded trial randomises the test alone, and none reports a mortality endpoint — the claim supported is prevention of LV dysfunction and cardiac hospitalisation in at-risk adults, at the price of substantially more investigation and treatment in screen-positive patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ledwidge M et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 23821090; NCT00921960); Huelsmann M et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2013 (PMID: 23810874; NCT00562952); Ledwidge M et al. JAMA Cardiol. 2023 (PMID: 36884247; NCT04687111).

shelves.title: Hydrochlorothiazide and skin cancer: cumulative dose tracks squamous-cell carcinoma in Danish registries (OR 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg; 7.38 at ≥200,000 mg) — not seen in Taiwan
shelves.question: In people taking hydrochlorothiazide, is cumulative thiazide exposure associated with increased risk of cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma and other skin cancers?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects · Basal Cell Carcinoma/chemically induced,epidemiology · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/chemically induced,epidemiology · Case-Control Studies · Denmark/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Hydrochlorothiazide/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Assessment · Skin Neoplasms/chemically induced,epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational, capped and labelled. The Danish nationwide programme (Pedersen 2018; Pottegård 2017; Pedersen 2019) shows a specific, monotone cumulative-dose association: SCC odds ratio 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg and 7.38 at ≥200,000 mg, lip SCC 7.7 at ≥100,000 mg, with no signal for other antihypertensives. The counterweight is a nationwide Taiwanese study with no association for any skin cancer at high cumulative use — one evidence stream, one population, no sun-exposure adjustment anywhere. All measures are relative; absolute SCC risk remains low.

cards.headline: Pedersen 2018 (Denmark, nationwide): high cumulative hydrochlorothiazide use (≥50,000 mg) carried an odds ratio of 3.98 for squamous-cell carcinoma and 1.29 for basal-cell carcinoma, rising to 7.38 and 1.54 at ≥200,000 mg — a clear dose-response
cards.summary: Pedersen 2018 (Denmark, nationwide): high cumulative hydrochlorothiazide use (≥50,000 mg) carried an odds ratio of 3.98 for squamous-cell carcinoma and 1.29 for basal-cell carcinoma, rising to 7.38 and 1.54 at ≥200,000 mg — a clear dose-response
cards.people: Nationwide Danish case-control study: all nonmelanoma skin cancer cases from the Danish Cancer Registry, 2004–2012 (71,533 basal-cell and 8,629 squamous-cell cases, per the registry report of this study), matched 1:20 to population controls by age and sex; cumulative hydrochlorothiazide use was taken from the Danish Prescription Registry (1995–2012). Observational — no data on sun exposure were available, as the authors state.
cards.result: High use of hydrochlorothiazide (cumulative ≥50,000 mg) was associated with an odds ratio of 3.98 (95% CI 3.68–4.31) for squamous-cell carcinoma and 1.29 (1.23–1.35) for basal-cell carcinoma — relative measures. Dose-response was clear for both: at the highest cumulative category (≥200,000 mg), odds ratios were 7.38 (6.32–8.60) for squamous-cell and 1.54 (1.38–1.71) for basal-cell carcinoma. Use of other diuretics and antihypertensives was not associated with nonmelanoma skin cancer. The authors conclude hydrochlorothiazide use is associated with a substantially increased risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer, especially squamous-cell carcinoma.
cards.watchOut: Case-control odds ratios are not absolute risks: squamous-cell carcinoma is uncommon in absolute terms, so even a fourfold relative increase is a small absolute excess for most users. No sun-exposure data — the key confounder for a photosensitising drug — could be adjusted for.
cards.source: Nationwide case-control study (registry-based) | Pedersen SA et al. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2018. PMID: 29217346. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Pottegård 2017 (Denmark, lip cancer): ever-use of hydrochlorothiazide carried an odds ratio of 2.1 for squamous-cell carcinoma of the lip, 3.9 at high use (≥25,000 mg) and 7.7 at ≥100,000 mg; the authors estimate 11% of lip SCC cases attributable to the drug if causal
cards.summary: Pottegård 2017 (Denmark, lip cancer): ever-use of hydrochlorothiazide carried an odds ratio of 2.1 for squamous-cell carcinoma of the lip, 3.9 at high use (≥25,000 mg) and 7.7 at ≥100,000 mg; the authors estimate 11% of lip SCC cases attributable to the drug if causal
cards.people: Nationwide Danish case-control study of squamous-cell carcinoma of the lip: 633 case patients from the Cancer Registry (2004–2012) matched to 63,067 population controls by risk-set sampling; hydrochlorothiazide exposure from the Prescription Registry (1995–2012), with adjustment for predefined confounders from demographic, prescription and patient registries. Observational.
cards.result: Ever-use of hydrochlorothiazide was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.1 (95% CI 1.7–2.6) for lip squamous-cell carcinoma, rising to 3.9 (3.0–4.9) for high use (cumulative ≥25,000 mg) and 7.7 (5.7–10.5) at the highest cumulative dose (≥100,000 mg), with a clear dose-response (P<0.001) — all relative measures. No association was seen with other diuretics or non-diuretic antihypertensives. Assuming causality, the authors estimated 11% of lip squamous-cell carcinoma cases could be attributed to hydrochlorothiazide use.
cards.watchOut: Lip SCC is rare (633 cases in a whole country over 9 years), so the absolute excess is very small even at an odds ratio of 7.7; the attributable-fraction estimate explicitly assumes causality, which a case-control study cannot establish.
cards.source: Nationwide case-control study (registry-based) | Pottegård A et al. J Intern Med. 2017. PMID: 28480532. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Pedersen 2019 (Denmark, rarer skin tumours): high hydrochlorothiazide use was also associated with Merkel-cell carcinoma (OR 2.3 at ≥50,000 mg; 3.3 at ≥100,000 mg) and malignant adnexal skin tumours (OR 3.6; 5.6 at the highest dose)
cards.summary: Pedersen 2019 (Denmark, rarer skin tumours): high hydrochlorothiazide use was also associated with Merkel-cell carcinoma (OR 2.3 at ≥50,000 mg; 3.3 at ≥100,000 mg) and malignant adnexal skin tumours (OR 3.6; 5.6 at the highest dose)
cards.people: Nationwide Danish case-control study of all incident Merkel-cell carcinoma and malignant adnexal skin tumour cases, 2004–2015, matched individually to cancer-free population controls by risk-set sampling; cumulative hydrochlorothiazide exposure from nationwide registries. Observational; no sun-exposure data.
cards.result: Adjusted odds ratios for high use (≥50,000 mg) were 2.3 (95% CI 1.1–4.8) for Merkel-cell carcinoma and 3.6 (1.9–7.0) for malignant adnexal tumours, rising at the highest cumulative dose (≥100,000 mg) to 3.3 (1.3–8.3) and 5.6 (2.4–13.3) respectively — relative measures with wide intervals, reflecting how rare these tumours are. No increased risk was found for drugs with similar indications, apart from a tendency for Merkel-cell carcinoma with furosemide (OR 1.9, 0.9–4.0).
cards.watchOut: Same Danish registry system and overlapping investigators as the other two Danish cards — these are not three independent replications, and the rare-tumour estimates rest on small case numbers with wide confidence intervals.

cards.headline: Pottegård 2019 (Taiwan, nationwide): in an Asian population, hydrochlorothiazide showed NO overall association with lip cancer (OR 0.86), non-lip nonmelanoma skin cancer (OR 1.16) or melanoma (OR 1.07) even at high cumulative use (≥50,000 mg)
cards.summary: Pottegård 2019 (Taiwan, nationwide): in an Asian population, hydrochlorothiazide showed NO overall association with lip cancer (OR 0.86), non-lip nonmelanoma skin cancer (OR 1.16) or melanoma (OR 1.07) even at high cumulative use (≥50,000 mg)
cards.people: Nationwide Taiwanese case-control studies using the National Health Insurance Research Database: 29,082 patients with a first skin cancer diagnosis (2008–2015) — analysed separately as lip cancer, non-lip nonmelanoma skin cancer and melanoma — matched 1:10 to population controls. Observational; the population is predominantly Asian, unlike the Danish studies.
cards.result: Hydrochlorothiazide use showed no overall association with any of the three outcomes: odds ratios for high cumulative use (≥50,000 mg) were 0.86 (95% CI 0.09–7.81) for lip cancer, 1.16 (0.98–1.37) for non-lip nonmelanoma skin cancer and 1.07 (0.65–1.76) for melanoma. There was some evidence of a dose-response pattern for non-lip nonmelanoma skin cancer at very high doses (OR 1.66, 0.82–3.33 for 100,000–149,999 mg), and the null findings were robust across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. The authors conclude hydrochlorothiazide appears safe for skin cancer risk in an Asian population.
cards.watchOut: The lip-cancer interval (0.09–7.81) is so wide it excludes almost nothing — lip cancer is rare in Taiwan — and lower ultraviolet susceptibility in this population may genuinely mute a photosensitisation effect. This card bounds the Danish signal; it does not refute it in fair-skinned, high-UV populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: cumulative hydrochlorothiazide exposure is associated with squamous-cell skin cancer in a strong dose-response pattern in Danish nationwide data — an observational signal, largest in relative terms for SCC and lip SCC, not replicated in a Taiwanese population, and small in absolute terms
cards.summary: Synthesis: cumulative hydrochlorothiazide exposure is associated with squamous-cell skin cancer in a strong dose-response pattern in Danish nationwide data — an observational signal, largest in relative terms for SCC and lip SCC, not replicated in a Taiwanese population, and small in absolute terms
cards.people: Synthesis of Pedersen 2018 (nonmelanoma skin cancer, Denmark), Pottegård 2017 (lip SCC, Denmark), Pedersen 2019 (Merkel-cell and adnexal tumours, Denmark) and Pottegård 2019 (Taiwan, null). No thiazide–skin-cancer home exists in the library — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session; the hypertension shelves cover thiazide efficacy and metabolic effects only.
cards.result: The Danish programme is internally consistent: the association is specific to hydrochlorothiazide among antihypertensives, strongest for squamous-cell carcinoma (OR 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg cumulative), steepest at the lip (OR 7.7 at ≥100,000 mg), and monotone with cumulative dose — the pattern a photosensitising mechanism would predict. Three cautions keep the stamp at POSSIBLE: every card is observational with no sun-exposure adjustment; the three Danish cards share one registry system and investigator group, so they are one evidence stream, not three; and the one large non-European replication (Taiwan) found no association, plausibly because baseline susceptibility and ultraviolet exposure differ. In absolute terms, squamous-cell carcinoma is uncommon, so years of high-dose use translate into a small absolute excess for an individual patient — a reason for skin surveillance and sun protection in long-term users, weighed against a drug class with proven cardiovascular benefit.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: relative measures dominate this literature — no carded study prints a clean absolute excess per 1,000 users, so none is quoted. Regulatory reviews after these papers treated prolonged use (3+ years) as a potential risk; that context is noted in the summary, not carded, because it is not a primary study.

shelves.title: Liraglutide in advanced HFrEF: no improvement in clinical stability in FIGHT (n=300) and no LV-function benefit with more serious cardiac events in LIVE (n=241) — two concordant cautionary trials
shelves.question: In patients with advanced heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy (liraglutide), compared with placebo, improve clinical stability or cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1/agonists · Heart Failure/complications,mortality,physiopathology · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Liraglutide/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Treatment Outcome · United States · Ventricular Dysfunction, Left/complications,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) / no benefit, from the only two dedicated randomised trials of a GLP-1 receptor agonist in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure. FIGHT (Margulies 2016; n=300 recently hospitalised patients, median LVEF 25%) found no effect of liraglutide on its primary global-rank endpoint of clinical stability (mean rank 146 vs 156, P=0.31), with numerically more deaths (19 [12%] vs 16 [11%]; HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.14) and heart-failure rehospitalisations (63 [41%] vs 50 [34%]; HR 1.30, 0.89 to 1.88) — neither excess significant, both pointing the wrong way. LIVE (Jorsal 2017; n=241 stable patients, LVEF ≤45%) found no difference in LVEF change (mean difference −0.8%, P=0.24), a 7 b.p.m. heart-rate increase, and significantly more serious cardiac events on liraglutide (12 [10%] vs 3 [3%], P=0.04). Against these, one 32-patient three-arm pilot (Arturi 2017) reported an ejection-fraction rise on liraglutide; at that size it cannot outweigh 541 patients in the two placebo-controlled trials, and it is carded so the shelf shows the whole base. This shelf is distinct from the library's GLP-1 shelves in obesity-phenotype HFpEF, where the population and the results differ. Desk-check: home corpus mentions of liraglutide in heart failure are incidental outcome-trial subgroups; FIGHT and LIVE had no shelf.

cards.headline: FIGHT 2016: liraglutide did not improve post-hospitalisation clinical stability in 300 patients with advanced HFrEF — deaths 12% vs 11%, HF rehospitalisations 41% vs 34%
cards.summary: FIGHT 2016: liraglutide did not improve post-hospitalisation clinical stability in 300 patients with advanced HFrEF — deaths 12% vs 11%, HF rehospitalisations 41% vs 34%
cards.people: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 24 US sites: 300 patients with established heart failure and reduced LVEF recently hospitalised for acute heart failure (median age 61 years; 21% women; 59% with type 2 diabetes; median LVEF 25%; median NT-proBNP 2049 pg/mL), randomised to liraglutide (n=154, titrated to 1.8 mg/day) or placebo (n=146) for 180 days.
cards.result: The primary global-rank endpoint (time to death, time to HF rehospitalisation, and change in NT-proBNP) did not differ: mean rank 146 on liraglutide vs 156 on placebo (P=0.31) — the treatment made no difference to clinical stability. Deaths occurred in 19 (12%) vs 16 (11%) (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.14; P=0.78) and HF rehospitalisations in 63 (41%) vs 50 (34%) (HR 1.30, 0.89 to 1.88; P=0.17) — both numerically favouring placebo. No secondary endpoint (structure/function, 6-minute walk, quality of life) differed, and the diabetes subgroup showed no benefit either. The authors concluded the findings do not support liraglutide in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The death and rehospitalisation excesses are numerical, not statistically significant — this card supports 'no benefit, possible harm', not proven harm. Phase 2 size (n=300) limits precision on hard events.
cards.source: Margulies KB et al. Effects of Liraglutide on Clinical Stability Among Patients With Advanced Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27483064. Registry ID: NCT01800968. cards.headline: LIVE 2017: liraglutide did not improve ejection fraction in 241 stable HFrEF patients and serious cardiac events were more frequent (10% vs 3%)
cards.summary: LIVE 2017: liraglutide did not improve ejection fraction in 241 stable HFrEF patients and serious cardiac events were more frequent (10% vs 3%)
cards.people: Investigator-initiated multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial: 241 clinically stable patients with chronic heart failure and LVEF ≤45%, with and without type 2 diabetes, on optimal heart-failure treatment, randomised to liraglutide 1.8 mg once daily or matching placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Change in LVEF did not differ between groups (mean difference −0.8%, 95% CI −2.1 to 0.5; P=0.24) — the treatment made no difference to left ventricular function. Heart rate rose on liraglutide (mean difference 7 b.p.m., 95% CI 5 to 9; P<0.0001). Serious cardiac events occurred in 12 patients (10%) on liraglutide vs 3 (3%) on placebo (P=0.04). The authors stated the heart-rate rise and excess serious cardiac events raise concern about liraglutide in chronic heart failure with reduced LVEF.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no registry ID. Serious cardiac events were a safety count in a 241-patient trial — a signal concordant with FIGHT's direction, not a powered harm endpoint.
cards.source: Jorsal A et al. cards.headline: Arturi 2017: in a 32-patient three-arm pilot, liraglutide was associated with an ejection-fraction rise (41.5% to 46.3%) — far too small to outweigh FIGHT and LIVE
cards.summary: Arturi 2017: in a 32-patient three-arm pilot, liraglutide was associated with an ejection-fraction rise (41.5% to 46.3%) — far too small to outweigh FIGHT and LIVE
cards.people: Pilot randomised comparison in 32 Caucasian patients with type 2 diabetes and post-ischaemic chronic heart failure (NYHA II/III and/or LVEF ≤45%), all on standard heart-failure therapy plus metformin and/or sulfonylurea, allocated to add-on liraglutide, sitagliptin or insulin glargine for 52 weeks (about 10–11 patients per arm).
cards.result: LVEF rose only in the liraglutide arm (41.5 ± 2.2% to 46.3 ± 3%; P=0.001), with reductions in indexed end-systolic volume and increases in stroke volume, cardiac output, functional capacity and quality of life; sitagliptin and glargine arms showed no LVEF change. No hard clinical outcomes were tested.
cards.watchOut: Only 32 patients across three arms, open comparisons against active drugs rather than placebo, and surrogate echocardiographic endpoints — carded to show the full base honestly; it does not disturb the verdict carried by the 541 patients in FIGHT and LIVE.
cards.source: Arturi F et al. Liraglutide improves cardiac function in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic heart failure. Endocrine. 2017. PMID: 27830456. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant cautionary trials (541 patients) show no benefit and a possible harm signal; one 32-patient pilot disagrees on a surrogate
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant cautionary trials (541 patients) show no benefit and a possible harm signal; one 32-patient pilot disagrees on a surrogate
cards.people: Patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction: 300 in FIGHT, 241 in LIVE, and 32 in the three-arm pilot.
cards.result: Neither dedicated placebo-controlled trial found any benefit — not on clinical stability, ejection fraction, walk distance or quality of life — and both leaned the wrong way on cardiac events (numerical in FIGHT, statistically significant for serious cardiac events in LIVE). The single small positive pilot used echocardiographic surrogates. The balance is no demonstrated benefit with a possible harm signal in advanced/stable HFrEF; this does not speak to GLP-1 therapy for diabetes or obesity indications in other populations.
cards.watchOut: Liraglutide raised heart rate by about 7 b.p.m. in LIVE — a plausible mechanism for the caution in a population where resting tachycardia is adverse — but mechanism is not proof of the event excess.
cards.source: Synthesis of Margulies KB et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27483064); Jorsal A et al. Eur J Heart Fail. 2017 (PMID: 27790809); Arturi F et al. Endocrine. 2017 (PMID: 27830456).

shelves.title: Vericiguat in HFpEF: no improvement in quality of life or walking distance in VITALITY-HFpEF (n=789) — the treatment made no difference
shelves.question: In patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, does vericiguat, compared with placebo, improve quality of life or exercise capacity?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Tolerance/drug effects · Female · Guanylate Cyclase/metabolism · Heart Failure/drug therapy,physiopathology · Heterocyclic Compounds, 2-Ring/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hospitalization · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Stroke Volume · Treatment Failure · Walk Test
shelves.balance: No benefit demonstrated. VITALITY-HFpEF (Armstrong 2020; n=789 with recent decompensation) was built exactly on this shelf's question — its primary endpoint was the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire physical limitation score — and vericiguat at both 15 mg/day and 10 mg/day made no difference to that score or to 6-minute walking distance at 24 weeks (all differences near zero, numerically favouring placebo). The phase 2b SOCRATES-PRESERVED dose-finding trial (Pieske 2017; n=477) was also neutral on its primary endpoints (NT-proBNP and left atrial volume at 12 weeks); an exploratory quality-of-life signal in its 10 mg arm was the stated rationale for VITALITY's higher doses, and VITALITY did not confirm it. A VITALITY frailty analysis (Butler 2023) adds that vericiguat did not alter frailty status. Symptomatic hypotension was somewhat more frequent on vericiguat (6.4% at 15 mg vs 3.4% on placebo). Desk-check: home #970 covers vericiguat in HFrEF (VICTORIA and VICTOR) and was read — VITALITY-HFpEF is not carded there; the HFpEF slice was genuinely uncovered. Nothing here contradicts #970: the drug's modest post-worsening HFrEF signal does not extend to quality of life or exercise capacity in HFpEF.

cards.headline: VITALITY-HFpEF 2020: vericiguat did not improve KCCQ physical limitation score or 6-minute walk distance in 789 HFpEF patients — both doses neutral
cards.summary: VITALITY-HFpEF 2020: vericiguat did not improve KCCQ physical limitation score or 6-minute walk distance in 789 HFpEF patients — both doses neutral
cards.people: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 167 sites in 21 countries: 789 patients with chronic HFpEF (LVEF ≥45%, NYHA II–III) within 6 months of a decompensation (HF hospitalisation or IV diuretics) and with elevated natriuretic peptides (mean age 72.7 years; 49% women; mean EF 56%), randomised 1:1:1 to vericiguat titrated to 15 mg/day (n=264), 10 mg/day (n=263) or placebo (n=262) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Primary outcome (change in KCCQ physical limitation score, 0–100): least-squares mean changes were 5.5 (15 mg), 6.4 (10 mg) and 6.9 (placebo); differences vs placebo were −1.5 points (95% CI −5.5 to 2.5; P=0.47) and −0.5 (−4.6 to 3.5; P=0.80) — the treatment made no difference. Six-minute walking distance changes were 5.0 m, 8.7 m and 10.5 m respectively; differences vs placebo −5.5 m (P=0.45) and −1.8 m (P=0.81). Symptomatic hypotension occurred in 6.4% (15 mg), 4.2% (10 mg) and 3.4% (placebo); syncope in 1.5%, 0.8% and 0.4%.
cards.watchOut: Endpoints are quality-of-life and exercise measures over 24 weeks — the trial does not test mortality or hospitalisation in HFpEF, and this shelf's question is confined accordingly.

randomised controlled trial (vitality-hfpef) phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 167 sites in 21 countries: 789 patients with chronic hfpef (lvef ≥45%, nyha ii–iii) within 6 months of a decompensation (hf hospitalisation or iv diuretics) and with elevated natriuretic peptides (mean age 72.7 years; 49% women; mean ef 56%), randomised 1:1:1 to vericiguat titrated to 15 mg/day (n=264), 10 mg/day (n=263) or placebo (n=262) for 24 weeks. primary outcome (change in kccq physical limitation score, 0–100): least-squares mean changes were 5.5 (15 mg), 6.4 (10 mg) and 6.9 (placebo); differences vs placebo were −1.5 points (95% ci −5.5 to 2.5; p=0.47) and −0.5 (−4.6 to 3.5; p=0.80) — the treatment made no difference. six-minute walking distance changes were 5.0 m, 8.7 m and 10.5 m respectively; differences vs placebo −5.5 m (p=0.45) and −1.8 m (p=0.81). symptomatic hypotension occurred in 6.4% (15 mg), 4.2% (10 mg) and 3.4% (placebo); syncope in 1.5%, 0.8% and 0.4%. endpoints are quality-of-life and exercise measures over 24 weeks — the trial does not test mortality or hospitalisation in hfpef, and this shelf's question is confined accordingly. armstrong pw et al. effect of vericiguat vs placebo on quality of life in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction: the vitality-hfpef randomized clinical trial. jama. 2020. pmid: 33079152. registry id: nct03547583. mesh: administration, oral · aged · double-blind method · exercise tolerance/drug effects · female · guanylate cyclase/metabolism · heart failure/drug therapy,physiopathology · heterocyclic compounds, 2-ring/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · hospitalization · humans · least-squares analysis · male · middle aged · pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · quality of life · stroke volume · treatment failure · walk test

cards.headline: SOCRATES-PRESERVED 2017: vericiguat did not change NT-proBNP or left atrial volume at 12 weeks in 477 HFpEF patients; an exploratory KCCQ signal prompted the larger trial
cards.summary: SOCRATES-PRESERVED 2017: vericiguat did not change NT-proBNP or left atrial volume at 12 weeks in 477 HFpEF patients; an exploratory KCCQ signal prompted the larger trial
cards.people: Prospective randomised placebo-controlled double-blind phase 2b dose-finding study: 477 patients with HFpEF (EF ≥45%; 48% women; mean age 73 years) randomised within 4 weeks of HF hospitalisation (75%) or outpatient IV diuretic treatment (25%) to vericiguat 1.25 mg or 2.5 mg fixed, 5 mg or 10 mg titrated, or placebo (n=93) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Neither primary endpoint differed from placebo in the pooled three highest dose arms: change in log NT-proBNP (two-sided P=0.20) and change in left atrial volume (two-sided P=0.37) — the treatment made no difference. Vericiguat was well tolerated with low discontinuation and no blood-pressure change at 10 mg vs placebo. The prespecified exploratory KCCQ Clinical Summary Score improved by a mean 19.3 points in the 10 mg arm (mean difference from placebo 9.2 points), which the authors cited as warranting further study at higher doses — the study VITALITY-HFpEF then ran, with a neutral result (card 1).
cards.watchOut: The quality-of-life finding was exploratory, in one dose arm, at 12 weeks — hypothesis-generating only, and not confirmed when tested as a primary endpoint in VITALITY-HFpEF.

cards.headline: VITALITY-HFpEF frailty analysis 2023: vericiguat did not alter frailty status at 24 weeks; baseline frailty predicted later walking distance
cards.summary: VITALITY-HFpEF frailty analysis 2023: vericiguat did not alter frailty status at 24 weeks; baseline frailty predicted later walking distance
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised trial (VITALITY-HFpEF)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the VITALITY-HFpEF trial population: 739 patients categorised by patient-reported Fried frailty phenotype as not frail (27.3%), prefrail (37.6%) or frail (35.0%) at baseline, with frailty related to KCCQ physical limitation score, 6-minute walking distance (6MWD) and 24-week outcomes by treatment arm.
cards.result: Frail patients were older and more often women, with lower baseline KCCQ-PLS (48.4 vs 68.2 in the not frail) and 6MWD (250.7 m vs 328.5 m). Baseline frailty (unlike baseline KCCQ-PLS) predicted 24-week 6MWD after accounting for baseline 6MWD. By 24 weeks 45.5% had become less frail and 7.0% more frail — but treatment with vericiguat did not alter frailty status at 24 weeks, consistent with the parent trial's neutral primary result.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and observational within the trial — it corroborates the neutral treatment effect on a third patient-centred measure (frailty) but adds no independent randomised comparison.
cards.source: Kaul P et al. Patient-Reported Frailty and Functional Status in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: Insights From VITALITY-HFpEF. JACC Heart Fail. 2023. PMID: 36881394. shelves.title: AlloMap gene-expression profiling after heart transplant: IMAGE showed a non-inferior composite outcome with biopsies cut from 3.0 to 0.5 per person-year
shelves.question: In heart-transplant recipients, does gene-expression profiling (AlloMap) surveillance, compared with routine endomyocardial biopsy, safely reduce biopsies without increasing rejection or graft loss?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Biopsy/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data · Confidence Intervals · Endocardium/pathology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gene Expression Profiling · Graft Rejection/diagnosis,genetics,mortality · Heart Transplantation/mortality · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardium/pathology · Reoperation · Survival Rate · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY for the strategy as tested — in selected recipients more than 6 months post-transplant at low rejection risk. The named test, per the clarification exception, is the AlloMap peripheral-blood gene-expression profiling test as published in the IMAGE trial (Pham 2010, NEJM; n=602 randomised): the 2-year composite outcome was 14.5% on profiling-guided surveillance vs 15.3% on routine biopsy (HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.68; non-inferior), deaths were similar (6.3% vs 5.5%), and biopsies fell six-fold (0.5 vs 3.0 per person-year, P<0.001). The Outcomes AlloMap Registry (Khush 2019; n=1,504 prospective, multicentre) found the strategy performing concordantly outside the trial — moderate-to-severe cellular rejection prevalence ~2%, 5-year survival 94%, low composite event rates. An IMAGE cohort analysis (Kobashigawa 2014) adds prognostic texture: within-patient variability of profiling scores predicted future events (HR 1.76 per unit of variability) even though single scores did not. Limits printed on the face: IMAGE enrolled patients 6 months to 5 years post-transplant judged low-risk — the result does not cover the early high-risk period or antibody-mediated rejection surveillance.

cards.headline: IMAGE 2010: AlloMap profiling surveillance was non-inferior to routine biopsy (composite 14.5% vs 15.3% at 2 years) with six-fold fewer biopsies
cards.summary: IMAGE 2010: AlloMap profiling surveillance was non-inferior to routine biopsy (composite 14.5% vs 15.3% at 2 years) with six-fold fewer biopsies
cards.people: Randomised non-inferiority trial: 602 patients who had undergone cardiac transplantation 6 months to 5 years previously, assigned to rejection monitoring by gene-expression profiling (the AlloMap peripheral-blood test, as named in the publication) or by routine endomyocardial biopsies, in addition to clinical and echocardiographic assessment in both arms; median follow-up 19 months.
cards.result: The 2-year cumulative rate of the composite primary outcome (rejection with haemodynamic compromise, graft dysfunction from other causes, death, or retransplantation) was 14.5% with profiling vs 15.3% with biopsy (HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.68) — non-inferior. Death from any cause at 2 years: 6.3% vs 5.5% (P=0.82). Biopsies performed: 0.5 vs 3.0 per person-year of follow-up (P<0.001). The authors restricted the conclusion to selected patients more than 6 months post-transplant at low risk of rejection.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority in a selected, later post-transplant, low-risk population — not evidence for replacing biopsies in the first 6 months, in high-risk recipients, or for detecting antibody-mediated rejection.
cards.source: Pham MX et al. Gene-expression profiling for rejection surveillance after cardiac transplantation. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20413602. Registry ID: NCT00351559. cards.headline: Outcomes AlloMap Registry 2019: in 1,504 real-world recipients managed with profiling, rejection prevalence was ~2% and 5-year survival 94%
cards.summary: Outcomes AlloMap Registry 2019: in 1,504 real-world recipients managed with profiling, rejection prevalence was ~2% and 5-year survival 94%
cards.people: Prospective multicentre observational Outcomes AlloMap Registry (OAR): 1,504 patients aged ≥15 years and ≥55 days post-cardiac transplant managed with gene-expression profiling surveillance (69% Caucasian, 74% male, mean age 54.1 years). Primary outcome was death and a composite of haemodynamically significant rejection, graft dysfunction, retransplantation or death.
cards.result: Prevalence of moderate-to-severe acute cellular rejection (≥2R) was 2.0% from 2–6 months and 2.2% after 6 months. Survival at 1, 2 and 5 years post-transplant was 99%, 98% and 94%. The composite outcome occurred in 103 patients during follow-up. Higher profiling scores were not associated with coronary allograft vasculopathy (P=0.25), cancer (P=0.16) or non-CMV infection (P=0.10). The authors describe this as the largest contemporary GEP-surveillance cohort, with low rates of rejection, graft dysfunction, readmission and death among patients selected for the strategy.
cards.watchOut: Observational, with no biopsy-strategy comparator arm — it shows the strategy's real-world event rates are low in selected patients; the comparative safety claim rests on IMAGE (card 1).
cards.source: Moayedi Y et al. Risk evaluation using gene expression screening to monitor for acute cellular rejection in heart transplant recipients. J Heart Lung Transplant. 2019. PMID: 30352779. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: IMAGE cohort analysis 2014: variability of a patient's AlloMap scores over time predicted future events (HR 1.76 per unit), single scores did not
cards.summary: IMAGE cohort analysis 2014: variability of a patient's AlloMap scores over time predicted future events (HR 1.76 per unit), single scores did not
cards.type: Cohort analysis within a randomised trial (IMAGE)
cards.people: Cohort study within the IMAGE trial population: heart-transplant recipients whose rejection surveillance gene-expression profiling tests were performed at 1- to 6-month intervals; score variability was defined as the standard deviation of an individual's cumulative test scores (ordinal score range 0–39; threshold score binary at ≥34), modelled against future clinical events (allograft dysfunction or death).
cards.result: In multivariable Cox models, profiling score variability — but not the ordinal score (P=0.46) or being over threshold (P=0.77) — was independently associated with future clinical events (P<0.001; HR 1.76, 95% CI 1.4 to 2.3, per 1-unit increase in variability). Race, age at transplantation and time post-transplant were also associated with events univariately. The authors propose score variability as added prognostic information beyond a single test's rejection probability.
cards.watchOut: A prognostic refinement of the same trial's data, not a second randomised comparison — carded because it changes how the test is best used (trends, not single values), not as independent confirmation of IMAGE.
cards.source: Deng MC et al. Utility of gene expression profiling score variability to predict clinical events in heart transplant recipients. Transplantation. 2014. PMID: 24637869. Registry ID: NCT00351559. cards.headline: Synthesis: profiling-guided surveillance safely replaced most routine biopsies in selected recipients — one randomised trial plus concordant registry outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: profiling-guided surveillance safely replaced most routine biopsies in selected recipients — one randomised trial plus concordant registry outcomes
cards.people: Heart-transplant recipients: 602 randomised in IMAGE (with the score-variability cohort drawn from it) and 1,504 prospectively registered in the Outcomes AlloMap Registry.
cards.result: IMAGE met non-inferiority on a hard composite while cutting biopsies from 3.0 to 0.5 per person-year, with similar mortality; the registry shows equally low rejection and event rates when the strategy is used in practice; score variability adds prognostic information. The claim is bounded to the tested setting: recipients beyond 6 months post-transplant at low rejection risk.
cards.watchOut: The test evaluated is the AlloMap assay as published; other gene-expression or donor-derived cell-free DNA assays are different products and are not covered by this shelf.

shelves.title: Low ankle-brachial index in asymptomatic adults: about double the 10-year event rates within every Framingham category in 48,294 people — but later reviews judge the added reclassification small
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults, does a low ankle-brachial index predict cardiovascular events and mortality independently of traditional risk scores, and does adding it reclassify risk usefully?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ankle · Atherosclerosis/physiopathology · Blood Pressure · Brachial Artery · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality,physiopathology · Cohort Studies · Confidence Intervals · Female · Global Health · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Predictive Value of Tests · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: Two different claims, two different grades. The prognostic claim is strong: the Ankle Brachial Index Collaboration (Fowkes 2008) pooled individual data from 16 population cohorts (24,955 men, 23,339 women; 480,325 person-years) and found 10-year cardiovascular mortality of 18.7% in men with ABI ≤0.90 vs 4.4% with normal ABI (HR 4.2), and 12.6% vs 4.1% in women (HR 3.5), remaining ~2.9–3.0 after Framingham adjustment; a low ABI approximately doubled event rates within every Framingham risk category. The reclassification claim is weaker in later, bias-aware hands: the collaboration reported that adding ABI would change the risk category and treatment recommendations of ~19% of men and ~36% of women, but the USPSTF reviews (Lin 2013; Guirguis-Blake 2018) found the corrected net reclassification improvement was probably small, the largest discrimination gains were for ABI in women (C-statistic change 0.112, NRI 0.096 across 10 studies), and no adequately powered trial has tested whether ABI-guided management improves health outcomes — the one large treatment trial in screen-detected low ABI (aspirin, n=3,350) showed no event prevention and possible bleeding harm. This shelf is about ABI as a prognostic test in asymptomatic adults; it is distinct from coronary artery calcium scoring (pack #6049) and from the symptomatic peripheral-artery-disease treatment shelves.

cards.headline: ABI Collaboration 2008: low ABI (≈≤0.90) meant 10-year cardiovascular mortality of 18.7% vs 4.4% in men and 12.6% vs 4.1% in women, independent of Framingham score
cards.summary: ABI Collaboration 2008: low ABI (≈≤0.90) meant 10-year cardiovascular mortality of 18.7% vs 4.4% in men and 12.6% vs 4.1% in women, independent of Framingham score
cards.people: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 16 general-population cohort studies: 24,955 men and 23,339 women without previous coronary heart disease, ABI measured at baseline, followed for total and cardiovascular mortality over 480,325 person-years.
cards.result: Risk by ABI was reverse J-shaped, with ABI 1.11–1.40 the low-risk reference. Ten-year cardiovascular mortality with ABI ≤0.90 vs 1.11–1.40: men 18.7% (95% CI 13.3% to 24.1%) vs 4.4% (3.2% to 5.7%), HR 4.2 (3.3 to 5.4); women 12.6% (6.2% to 19.0%) vs 4.1% (2.2% to 6.1%), HR 3.5 (2.4 to 5.1). After Framingham adjustment the HRs remained 2.9 (2.3 to 3.7) in men and 3.0 (2.0 to 4.4) in women. A low ABI was associated with approximately twice the 10-year total mortality, cardiovascular mortality and major coronary event rate compared with the overall rate in each Framingham category, and including ABI in Framingham-based stratification would change the risk category and treatment recommendations of approximately 19% of men and 36% of women.
cards.watchOut: Prognostic association, not a treatment trial: the 19%/36% reclassification figures are the proportion whose category would change, not a bias-corrected measure of correct reclassification — later reviews (cards 2–3) discount them.

cards.headline: USPSTF review 2013: adding ABI to Framingham probably yields only a small net reclassification improvement, and treating screen-detected low ABI with aspirin did not prevent events
cards.summary: USPSTF review 2013: adding ABI to Framingham probably yields only a small net reclassification improvement, and treating screen-detected low ABI with aspirin did not prevent events
cards.people: Systematic evidence review for the US Preventive Services Task Force: population-based prognostic studies of ABI added to the Framingham Risk Score in asymptomatic adults, plus treatment trials and harms studies in screen-detected peripheral artery disease (MEDLINE and Cochrane Central, 1996–2012).
cards.result: One large meta-analysis (n=43,919 — the ABI Collaboration population) showed ABI could reclassify 10-year coronary risk but did not report net reclassification improvement (NRI); four heterogeneous risk-prediction studies indicated the NRI from adding ABI to Framingham was probably small for coronary or cardiovascular events. Of two treatment trials meeting criteria, the large one (n=3,350) found low-dose aspirin did not prevent cardiovascular events in people with a screen-detected low ABI and may have increased major bleeding. The authors concluded adding ABI to Framingham probably has limited value for predicting coronary or cardiovascular disease, and treatment benefits for asymptomatic screen-detected disease are not established.
cards.watchOut: Most prognostic studies did not allow a bias-corrected NRI to be calculated — 'probably small' is an inference from heterogeneous studies, and treatment evidence was limited to aspirin.
cards.source: Lin JS et al. cards.headline: USPSTF updated review 2018: ABI improved discrimination most in women (C-statistic change 0.112, NRI 0.096), less than coronary calcium overall; no outcome trials of ABI-guided care exist
cards.summary: USPSTF updated review 2018: ABI improved discrimination most in women (C-statistic change 0.112, NRI 0.096), less than coronary calcium overall; no outcome trials of ABI-guided care exist
cards.people: Updated systematic review for the USPSTF covering three nontraditional risk factors (ABI, high-sensitivity CRP, coronary artery calcium) in asymptomatic adults without known cardiovascular disease: 43 studies, N=267,244, including 10 ABI studies; outcomes were events, mortality, calibration/discrimination/reclassification and harms.
cards.result: Adding ABI, hsCRP or CAC each improved discrimination and reclassification to varying degrees; for ABI the improvements were greatest in women (C-statistic change 0.112; net reclassification index 0.096). The largest discrimination and reclassification gains overall were for CAC (C-statistic change 0.018 to 0.144; NRI 0.084 to 0.35), though CAC could inappropriately reclassify non-event patients upward. No adequately powered trial has evaluated whether risk assessment with any nontraditional factor improves patient health outcomes; harms evidence was largely limited to CAC radiation and downstream testing.
cards.watchOut: This review pools ABI with two other markers — ABI-specific estimates come from 10 studies of varying design; it supports 'modest, sex-dependent incremental value', not a screening recommendation.
cards.source: Lin JS et al. Nontraditional Risk Factors in Cardiovascular Disease Risk Assessment: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2018. cards.headline: Synthesis: low ABI is a powerful independent prognostic marker; its incremental value over standard scores is real but modest, and outcome benefit of acting on it is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: low ABI is a powerful independent prognostic marker; its incremental value over standard scores is real but modest, and outcome benefit of acting on it is unproven
cards.people: Asymptomatic adults: 48,294 in the ABI Collaboration cohorts and 267,244 across the 43 studies in the 2018 USPSTF review (10 ABI studies).
cards.result: A low ABI roughly doubles-to-quadruples cardiovascular mortality risk and stays predictive after Framingham adjustment — LIKELY as a prognostic association. Whether measuring it usefully reclassifies risk is POSSIBLE at best: category changes are frequent (19% of men, 36% of women) but corrected net reclassification is probably small, gains concentrate in women, and no trial shows ABI-guided treatment prevents events.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with coronary calcium scoring (#6049): the 2018 review suggests CAC reclassifies more strongly than ABI, which is a comparison between shelves, not a finding of this one.
cards.source: Synthesis of  et al. JAMA. 2008 (PMID: 18612117); Lin JS et al. Ann Intern Med. 2013 (PMID: 24026319); Lin JS et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29998301).

shelves.title: EBBINGHAUS: formal CANTAB testing in 1,204 FOURIER patients showed evolocumab was non-inferior to placebo on cognition — and 5 more years of follow-up stayed reassuring
shelves.question: In patients with cardiovascular disease treated with evolocumab, does profound LDL lowering impair cognition on formal neurocognitive testing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Atherosclerosis/drug therapy,psychology · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Cognition/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Male · Memory/drug effects · Middle Aged · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Prospective Studies · Psychological Tests · Self-Assessment · Proprotein Convertase 9
shelves.balance: LIKELY no impairment, on the strongest design available for this question: a prespecified, prospective, formally tested substudy rather than adverse-event counts. EBBINGHAUS (Giugliano 2017, NEJM) embedded the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) in FOURIER: 1,204 patients tested at baseline, week 24, yearly and end of trial (median 19 months) met non-inferiority on the spatial-working-memory strategy index and showed no between-group differences on any secondary domain, and exploratory analyses found no association between achieved LDL level and cognitive change. Two extensions widen the reassurance: patient-reported Everyday Cognition scores in the full FOURIER population (22,655 respondents; Gencer 2020) showed identical decline rates (3.7% evolocumab vs 3.6% placebo), including in the 2,338 patients who achieved LDL <20 mg/dL; and the EBBINGHAUS open-label extension (Zoungas 2025; 473 patients, median 5.1 additional years, median LDL 35 mg/dL) found no executive-function change in either original arm. Desk-check: home #191 mentions neurocognitive events only inside a FOURIER source line (adverse-event counts); no shelf posed the formal-testing question, which is this shelf's whole subject.

cards.headline: EBBINGHAUS 2017: evolocumab was non-inferior to placebo on formal CANTAB executive-function testing in 1,204 patients (median 19 months)
cards.summary: EBBINGHAUS 2017: evolocumab was non-inferior to placebo on formal CANTAB executive-function testing in 1,204 patients (median 19 months)
cards.people: Prespecified cognitive substudy of the FOURIER randomised trial: 1,204 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease on statin therapy, randomised to evolocumab or placebo, assessed prospectively with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) at baseline, week 24, yearly and at trial end. Primary endpoint: score on the spatial working memory strategy index of executive function (range 4–28; lower is better); non-inferiority margin 20% of the placebo-group standard deviation.
cards.result: Mean change in the primary endpoint was −0.21 ± 2.62 on evolocumab vs −0.29 ± 2.81 on placebo (P<0.001 for non-inferiority; P=0.85 for superiority) — the treatment made no difference to executive function. Secondary endpoints likewise did not differ: working memory (change −0.52 vs −0.93), episodic memory (−1.53 vs −1.53) and psychomotor speed (5.2 vs 0.9 msec). An exploratory analysis found no association between LDL cholesterol levels and cognitive change, including at the lowest achieved levels.
cards.watchOut: Median formal-testing follow-up was 19 months in a trial population screened to exclude dementia and major neurocognitive disorders — it answers the question for typical FOURIER-type patients, not for people at high baseline dementia risk (see card 3's caveat).
cards.source: Giugliano RP et al. Cognitive Function in a Randomized Trial of Evolocumab. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 28813214. Registry ID: NCT02207634. cards.headline: FOURIER patient-reported cognition 2020: decline reported by 3.7% on evolocumab vs 3.6% on placebo among 22,655 patients — including at LDL <20 mg/dL
cards.summary: FOURIER patient-reported cognition 2020: decline reported by 3.7% on evolocumab vs 3.6% on placebo among 22,655 patients — including at LDL <20 mg/dL
cards.type: Randomised trial — patient-reported outcomes analysis (FOURIER/EBBINGHAUS programme)
cards.people: Patient-reported cognition analysis of the full FOURIER randomised trial: 22,655 patients completed the 23-item Everyday Cognition (ECog) survey at the final visit (median treatment duration 2.2 years), rating memory and executive function against their own baseline (score ≥2 = reported decline), compared by randomised arm and by achieved LDL at week 4.
cards.result: Reported cognitive decline was essentially identical: total ECog ≥2 in 3.7% on evolocumab vs 3.6% on placebo (P=0.62); memory subdomain 6.0% vs 5.8%; executive 3.7% vs 3.6%. Among the 2,338 patients who achieved LDL <20 mg/dL, reported decline was 3.8% vs 4.5% in the 3,613 patients with LDL ≥100 mg/dL (P=0.57) — no gradient toward harm at the lowest LDL levels.
cards.watchOut: Self-report is a blunter instrument than the CANTAB battery (card 1) and is carded as breadth (whole-trial denominator), not as a substitute for formal testing.
cards.source: Gencer B et al. Cognition After Lowering LDL-Cholesterol With Evolocumab. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2020. PMID: 32381158. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EBBINGHAUS long-term extension 2025: no executive-function decline after a median 5.1 further years at median LDL 35 mg/dL (473 patients)
cards.summary: EBBINGHAUS long-term extension 2025: no executive-function decline after a median 5.1 further years at median LDL 35 mg/dL (473 patients)
cards.type: Open-label extension of a randomised substudy (EBBINGHAUS-OLE)
cards.people: Prospective open-label extension of the EBBINGHAUS substudy: 473 of the 1,974 parent-substudy patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (median age 62; 70% male; 91% White) enrolled after completing the randomised phase and followed for a median of 5.1 additional years (maximum 7.2 years from original randomisation), all receiving evolocumab, with annual cognitive testing; primary endpoint was change in the spatial working memory strategy index.
cards.result: Executive function did not change during the extension in either original arm: mean change +0.1 ± 2.8 in patients originally randomised to evolocumab (P=0.49) and −0.1 ± 2.5 in those originally on placebo who switched to evolocumab (P=0.64); final scores were similar (17.5 ± 3.7 vs 17.3 ± 3.7). Median LDL at 12 weeks into the extension was 35 mg/dL (IQR 21–55). The authors conclude sustained very low LDL via PCSK9 inhibition plus statin was not associated with cognitive impairment, while noting generalisability to adults at higher dementia risk needs further study.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (no concurrent placebo) and only 473 of 1,974 substudy patients continued — survivor and volunteer effects are possible; the randomised comparison itself is card 1.
cards.source: Zimerman A et al. Long-Term Cognitive Safety of Achieving Very Low LDL Cholesterol with Evolocumab. NEJM Evid. 2025. PMID: 39718423. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: formal testing, whole-trial self-report and 5-year extension all agree — profound LDL lowering with evolocumab did not impair cognition
cards.summary: Synthesis: formal testing, whole-trial self-report and 5-year extension all agree — profound LDL lowering with evolocumab did not impair cognition
cards.people: Patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease on statins: 1,204 formally tested in EBBINGHAUS, 22,655 self-reporting in FOURIER, and 473 followed long-term in the extension.
cards.result: The prespecified formal-testing substudy met non-inferiority with no domain differences and no LDL-level gradient; the whole-trial patient-reported data and the long-term extension at median LDL 35 mg/dL are concordant. For evolocumab-treated patients like those in FOURIER, cognitive impairment from profound LDL lowering is not supported — LIKELY no impairment over the horizons tested (up to ~7 years).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers evolocumab with formal testing; it does not by itself settle the same question for every PCSK9 agent or for patients with pre-existing cognitive impairment, who were largely excluded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Giugliano RP et al. N Engl J Med. 2017 (PMID: 28813214); Gencer B et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2020 (PMID: 32381158); Zimerman A et al. NEJM Evid. 2025 (PMID: 39718423).
