shelves.title: PCSK9 antibodies in confirmed statin intolerance: LDL fell 53–56% (GAUSS-2), 54.5% (GAUSS-3) and 45.0% (ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE) vs 15–17% on ezetimibe — with fewer muscle events than atorvastatin re-challenge
shelves.question: In patients with confirmed statin intolerance, do PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab), compared with placebo or ezetimibe, lower LDL cholesterol and improve statin re-challenge tolerance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Atorvastatin/adverse effects · Biomarkers/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Creatine Kinase/blood · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Ezetimibe/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects · Hypercholesterolemia/blood,drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Muscular Diseases/blood,chemically induced,prevention & control · Myalgia/blood,chemically induced,prevention & control · Myositis/blood,chemically induced,prevention & control · Rhabdomyolysis/blood,chemically induced,prevention & control · Time Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY for LDL lowering; the tolerance half of the question is answered more narrowly (see below). GAUSS-2 (Stroes 2014; n=307, intolerance by history) found evolocumab cut LDL by 53–56% vs ezetimibe's ~15–17% implied by the 37–39-point treatment differences, with muscle events in 12% on evolocumab vs 23% on ezetimibe. GAUSS-3 (Nissen 2016) is the design centrepiece: in phase A, 491 patients with reported intolerance to ≥2 statins underwent a blinded atorvastatin/placebo crossover and only 209 (42.6%) had symptoms on atorvastatin but not placebo — 'confirmed' intolerance is a minority of reported intolerance; in phase B (n=218), evolocumab lowered LDL by 54.5% (absolute −106.8 mg/dL) vs 16.7% (−31.0 mg/dL) on ezetimibe (P<0.001). ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE (Moriarty 2015; n=361) randomised alirocumab vs ezetimibe vs atorvastatin 20 mg re-challenge: LDL fell 45.0% vs 14.6% (difference 30.4 points; P<0.0001), and skeletal-muscle events were less frequent on alirocumab than on atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61, 0.38 to 0.99; P=0.042). On 'improved re-challenge tolerance' strictly: the trials show a PCSK9 antibody is better tolerated than re-challenged statin and lowers LDL far more than ezetimibe — they do not show PCSK9 therapy makes patients subsequently tolerate statins. Desk-check: homes #191 and #262 (PCSK9 outcomes) and #268/#5622 (statin-intolerance treatments: bempedoic acid, intermittent dosing) were checked — none cards the PCSK9-in-intolerance trials; the slice was unhomed. Cardiovascular outcomes in this population are untested by these LDL-endpoint trials.

cards.headline: GAUSS-3 2016: blinded re-challenge confirmed statin-only muscle symptoms in just 42.6% of 491 reported-intolerant patients; evolocumab then cut LDL 54.5% vs 16.7% on ezetimibe
cards.summary: GAUSS-3 2016: blinded re-challenge confirmed statin-only muscle symptoms in just 42.6% of 491 reported-intolerant patients; evolocumab then cut LDL 54.5% vs 16.7% on ezetimibe
cards.people: Two-stage randomised trial in 511 adults (phase A: 491; mean age 60.7 years; 50.1% women; entry LDL 212.3 mg/dL) with uncontrolled LDL and intolerance to ≥2 statins. Phase A: 24-week double-blind crossover of atorvastatin 20 mg vs placebo to identify symptoms occurring only on statin. Phase B: 218 patients (199 confirmed in phase A plus 19 with elevated creatine kinase) randomised 2:1 to evolocumab 420 mg monthly (n=145) or ezetimibe 10 mg daily (n=73) for 24 weeks; entry LDL 219.9 mg/dL.
cards.result: Phase A: muscle symptoms occurred in 209 of 491 (42.6%) on atorvastatin but not placebo — the remainder did not confirm. Phase B co-primary endpoints: LDL change at the mean of weeks 22–24 was −54.5% (95% CI −57.2% to −51.8%; absolute −106.8 mg/dL, to 103.6 mg/dL) on evolocumab vs −16.7% (−20.5% to −12.9%; −31.0 mg/dL, to 183.0 mg/dL) on ezetimibe (P<0.001); between-group difference −37.8 percentage points (−75.8 mg/dL). Week-24 results were near-identical (−52.8% vs −16.7%).
cards.watchOut: Phase B randomised only 218 patients and the endpoint is LDL, not cardiovascular events; the 42.6% confirmation rate also means most 'statin-intolerant' volunteers had symptoms on placebo too or on neither — a nocebo-era caution for applying the label.
cards.source: Nissen SE et al. Efficacy and Tolerability of Evolocumab vs Ezetimibe in Patients With Muscle-Related Statin Intolerance: The GAUSS-3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27039291. Registry ID: NCT01984424. cards.headline: ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE 2015: alirocumab cut LDL 45.0% vs 14.6% on ezetimibe in 361 statin-intolerant patients, with fewer muscle events than atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61)
cards.summary: ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE 2015: alirocumab cut LDL 45.0% vs 14.6% on ezetimibe in 361 statin-intolerant patients, with fewer muscle events than atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61)
cards.people: Randomised double-blind trial in 361 patients at moderate-to-high cardiovascular risk with statin intolerance (unable to tolerate ≥2 statins, including one at the lowest approved starting dose, due to muscle symptoms), after a 4-week single-blind placebo run-in (patients reporting muscle symptoms in run-in were withdrawn). Randomised 2:2:1 to alirocumab 75 mg every 2 weeks (increased to 150 mg at week 12 by week-8 LDL), ezetimibe 10 mg/day, or atorvastatin 20 mg/day re-challenge, for 24 weeks. Baseline mean LDL-C was 191.3 mg/dL.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (LDL change at week 24, intention-to-treat): alirocumab −45.0% (SE 2.2%) vs ezetimibe −14.6% (SE 2.2%); mean difference 30.4 percentage points (P<0.0001). Skeletal muscle-related events were less frequent with alirocumab than with atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.99; P=0.042). The authors conclude alirocumab gave greater LDL reductions than ezetimibe with fewer muscle events than re-challenged statin.
cards.watchOut: The atorvastatin re-challenge arm (~72 patients) is small, so the tolerance comparison (HR 0.61) is imprecise; and the placebo run-in removed placebo-symptomatic patients before randomisation, enriching for true intolerance.
cards.source: Moriarty PM et al. Efficacy and safety of alirocumab vs ezetimibe in statin-intolerant patients, with a statin rechallenge arm: The ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE randomized trial. J Clin Lipidol. 2015. PMID: 26687696. Registry ID: NCT01709513. cards.headline: GAUSS-2 2014: evolocumab cut LDL 53–56% vs ezetimibe in 307 statin-intolerant patients over 12 weeks; muscle events 12% vs 23%
cards.summary: GAUSS-2 2014: evolocumab cut LDL 53–56% vs ezetimibe in 307 statin-intolerant patients over 12 weeks; muscle events 12% vs 23%
cards.people: Phase 3 double-blind trial: 307 hypercholesterolaemic patients unable to tolerate effective statin doses (age 62 ± 10 years; baseline LDL 193 ± 59 mg/dL), randomised 2:2:1:1 to evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks or 420 mg monthly (with daily oral placebo) or subcutaneous placebo (with daily ezetimibe 10 mg) for 12 weeks. Co-primary endpoints: LDL change at the mean of weeks 10–12 and at week 12.
cards.result: Evolocumab reduced LDL by 53% to 56% from baseline, corresponding to treatment differences vs ezetimibe of 37% to 39% (P<0.001 for both regimens and both endpoints). Muscle adverse events occurred in 12% of evolocumab-treated patients vs 23% of ezetimibe-treated patients. Other treatment-emergent adverse events and laboratory abnormalities were comparable across groups.
cards.watchOut: Shortest of the three trials (12 weeks) and intolerance was by history without a blinded confirmation phase — GAUSS-3 (card 1) is the stricter test of the same question.
cards.source: Stroes E et al. Anti-PCSK9 antibody effectively lowers cholesterol in patients with statin intolerance: the GAUSS-2 randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 clinical trial of evolocumab. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2014. PMID: 24694531. Registry ID: NCT01763905. cards.headline: Synthesis: in confirmed or reported statin intolerance, PCSK9 antibodies lower LDL by ~45–56% — about 30–39 points more than ezetimibe — and are better tolerated than statin re-challenge
cards.summary: Synthesis: in confirmed or reported statin intolerance, PCSK9 antibodies lower LDL by ~45–56% — about 30–39 points more than ezetimibe — and are better tolerated than statin re-challenge
cards.people: Patients with statin intolerance: 491 entering GAUSS-3 (218 randomised in phase B), 361 in ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE, and 307 in GAUSS-2.
cards.result: Three randomised trials, two antibodies, one direction: LDL reductions of 53–56% (GAUSS-2), 54.5% (GAUSS-3) and 45.0% (ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE) against 14.6–16.7% on ezetimibe. Muscle events were fewer on antibody than on ezetimibe (GAUSS-2) or on atorvastatin re-challenge (ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE, HR 0.61). GAUSS-3 adds the discipline that blinded re-challenge confirms statin-specific symptoms in a minority (42.6%) of reported cases.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are LDL-endpoint trials of 12–24 weeks: none shows that PCSK9 therapy in this population prevents cardiovascular events, and none shows it restores statin tolerance — it substitutes for the statin rather than rehabilitating it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nissen SE et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27039291); Moriarty PM et al. J Clin Lipidol. 2015 (PMID: 26687696); Stroes E et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2014 (PMID: 24694531).

shelves.title: Ferric derisomaltose vs ferric carboxymaltose: hypophosphataemia in 7.9–8.1% vs 73.7–75.0% in the PHOSPHARE trials, and 8.3% vs 51.0% in IBD — an FGF23-mediated formulation effect
shelves.question: In patients with iron-deficiency anaemia needing intravenous iron, does ferric derisomaltose (iron isomaltoside), compared with ferric carboxymaltose, cause less hypophosphataemia and fewer downstream mineral/bone effects?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/complications,drug therapy · Biomarkers/blood,urine · Disaccharides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Ferric Compounds/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Headache/chemically induced · Hematinics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Hypophosphatemia/chemically induced,epidemiology · Incidence · Male · Maltose/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced · Phosphates/blood,urine
shelves.balance: LIKELY for the biochemical outcome; the long-term bone consequences are less completely mapped and are stated as such. Formulations are named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: ferric derisomaltose (published in the PHOSPHARE trials as iron isomaltoside, now known as ferric derisomaltose) vs ferric carboxymaltose. Wolf 2020 (JAMA) reports the two PHOSPHARE trials (NCT03238911, NCT03237065; 245 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia intolerant of or unresponsive to oral iron): hypophosphataemia by day 35 in 7.9%/8.1% on iron isomaltoside vs 75.0%/73.7% on ferric carboxymaltose, with parallel differences in FGF23, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D biomarkers. PHOSPHARE-IBD (Zoller 2023, Gut; n=97, double-blind, identical haemoglobin/weight-based dosing) replicated the direction in inflammatory bowel disease: 8.3% vs 51.0% (adjusted risk difference −42.8%), with fatigue improving more slowly on ferric carboxymaltose in proportion to the phosphate fall — a patient-felt downstream correlate. ExplorIRON-CKD (Kassianides 2024; n=26, non-dialysis CKD) supplies the mechanism in miniature: intact FGF23 rose 146.1% and 235.1% after successive ferric carboxymaltose doses vs 3.0% and 3.2% after ferric derisomaltose (P<0.001 and P=0.001), with greater falls in phosphate and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Desk-check: home #122 covers IV iron efficacy in heart failure (FAIR-HF lineage) and was read — it does not compare formulations on phosphate safety; pack #6115 mentions hypophosphataemia only as attenuating vitality gains in IBD. The formulation-safety comparison was unhomed.

cards.headline: PHOSPHARE 2020 (two trials, n=245): hypophosphataemia in 7.9%/8.1% on iron isomaltoside vs 75.0%/73.7% on ferric carboxymaltose by day 35
cards.summary: PHOSPHARE 2020 (two trials, n=245): hypophosphataemia in 7.9%/8.1% on iron isomaltoside vs 75.0%/73.7% on ferric carboxymaltose by day 35
cards.people: Two identically designed open-label randomised trials (30 US outpatient sites, 2017–2018): 245 adults with iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin ≤11 g/dL; ferritin ≤100 ng/mL) intolerant of or unresponsive to ≥1 month of oral iron, with reduced kidney function excluded. Trial A: 123 patients (mean age 45.1 years; 95.9% women). Trial B: 122 (mean age 42.6 years; 94.1% women). Intervention: iron isomaltoside (now known as ferric derisomaltose) 1,000 mg on day 0, or ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg on days 0 and 7 (formulations and doses as published). Primary endpoint: hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate <2.0 mg/dL) between baseline and day 35.
cards.result: Hypophosphataemia incidence was far lower on iron isomaltoside: trial A 7.9% vs 75.0% (adjusted rate difference −67.0%, 95% CI −77.4% to −51.5%; P<0.001); trial B 8.1% vs 73.7% (adjusted difference −65.8%, −76.6% to −49.8%; P<0.001). Biomarkers of mineral and bone homeostasis (including FGF23 and parathyroid hormone) moved adversely with ferric carboxymaltose. Common adverse drug reactions: nausea 1/125 (isomaltoside) vs 8/117 (carboxymaltose); headache 4/125 vs 5/117. The authors note further research is needed on the clinical importance of the difference.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 35-day horizon, and a biochemical primary endpoint in mostly younger women without kidney disease — fracture and osteomalacia outcomes over repeated dosing are not answered by these trials.

cards.headline: PHOSPHARE-IBD 2023: hypophosphataemia in 8.3% on ferric derisomaltose vs 51.0% on ferric carboxymaltose in 97 IBD patients — and fatigue recovered more slowly with the phosphate fall
cards.summary: PHOSPHARE-IBD 2023: hypophosphataemia in 8.3% on ferric derisomaltose vs 51.0% on ferric carboxymaltose in 97 IBD patients — and fatigue recovered more slowly with the phosphate fall
cards.people: Randomised double-blind trial at 20 outpatient hospital clinics in Europe: 97 adults with inflammatory bowel disease and iron-deficiency anaemia randomised 1:1 to ferric carboxymaltose (FCM, n=48 treated) or ferric derisomaltose (FDI, n=49 treated) at baseline and day 35 using identical haemoglobin- and weight-based dosing. Primary outcome: hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate <2.0 mg/dL) at any time to day 35 in the safety set. (Note: the abstract's arm sizes and event denominators are transposed between the two formulations in one sentence; the event rates 4/48 and 25/49 are as printed, with the adjusted difference favouring FDI.)
cards.result: Incident hypophosphataemia: 8.3% (4/48) on FDI vs 51.0% (25/49) on FCM (adjusted risk difference −42.8%, 95% CI −57.1% to −24.6%; P<0.0001). Both formulations corrected the anaemia. Patient-reported fatigue improved in both groups but more slowly and to a lesser extent with FCM, and slower fatigue improvement was associated with a greater fall in phosphate. The authors call for studies of the longer-term clinical consequences of the hypophosphataemia.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than the PHOSPHARE pair (n=97) and still a 35-day biochemical primary endpoint; the fatigue association is a secondary, correlational finding — suggestive of downstream effect, not proof of bone harm.

cards.headline: ExplorIRON-CKD 2024: intact FGF23 rose ~146% and ~235% after ferric carboxymaltose vs ~3% after ferric derisomaltose in 26 CKD patients — the mechanism, measured directly
cards.summary: ExplorIRON-CKD 2024: intact FGF23 rose ~146% and ~235% after ferric carboxymaltose vs ~3% after ferric derisomaltose in 26 CKD patients — the mechanism, measured directly
cards.people: Single-centre double-blind randomised exploratory trial: 26 patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD (stage 3a–5) and iron deficiency with/without anaemia, randomised 1:1 to ferric derisomaltose (FDI, n=14) or ferric carboxymaltose (FCM, n=12); 1,000 mg IV iron at baseline and 500–1,000 mg at 1 month, with intact FGF23, phosphate, vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, phosphaturia and bone-turnover markers followed to 3 months. Registered as EudraCT 2019-004370-26.
cards.result: Intact FGF23 increased significantly more with FCM than FDI after each dose (baseline to 1–2 days after dose 1: +146.1% [IQR 108.1 to 203.1] vs +3.0% [−15.1 to 13.8]; P<0.001; after dose 2: +235.1% [138.5 to 434.6] vs +3.2% [−3.5 to 25.4]; P=0.001). Phosphate fell significantly more with FCM by 2 weeks after the first dose, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D fell significantly more with FCM — the FGF23-mediated cascade the PHOSPHARE trials inferred, here measured head-to-head.
cards.watchOut: Only 26 patients and exploratory — carded for mechanism (why the formulation difference exists), not for the size of the clinical effect, which rests on cards 1–2. CKD patients were excluded from PHOSPHARE, so this also extends the finding to a population the main trials did not study.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised comparisons (368 patients) agree — ferric carboxymaltose causes far more FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia than ferric derisomaltose
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised comparisons (368 patients) agree — ferric carboxymaltose causes far more FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia than ferric derisomaltose
cards.people: Patients needing IV iron: 245 in the two PHOSPHARE trials, 97 in PHOSPHARE-IBD, and 26 in ExplorIRON-CKD.
cards.result: Hypophosphataemia rates on ferric derisomaltose were 7.9–8.3% across all three clinical trials vs 51.0–75.0% on ferric carboxymaltose; the mechanistic trial shows why (intact FGF23 surges only with carboxymaltose, driving phosphate and calcitriol down). Anaemia correction was comparable. LIKELY benefit for phosphate safety when choosing ferric derisomaltose; the frequency of fractures or osteomalacia after repeated carboxymaltose courses remains the open downstream question.
cards.watchOut: Dosing differed between programmes (single 1,000 mg isomaltoside vs split 750 mg ×2 carboxymaltose in PHOSPHARE; matched weight/haemoglobin dosing in PHOSPHARE-IBD) — the IBD trial's matched dosing is the cleaner formulation-only comparison, and it points the same way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wolf M et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 32016310); Zoller H et al. Gut. 2023 (PMID: 36343979); Kassianides X et al. BMC Nephrol. 2024 (PMID: 38347520).

shelves.title: Pulse pressure (physiology): stroke volume is ejected into an elastic reservoir — as the aorta stiffens, the forward wave grows, systolic pressure rises and diastolic falls, and isolated systolic hypertension is the haemodynamic signature of arterial ageing
shelves.question: What determines pulse pressure — stroke volume, arterial compliance (the Windkessel function) and wave reflection — and why does isolated systolic hypertension emerge with arterial stiffening?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · *Aorta · Blood Pressure/physiology · Female · Heart Rate/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pacemaker, Artificial
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, arterial-system chapters). In the textbook's Windkessel account, the elastic aorta and large arteries store roughly half the stroke volume during systole and discharge it during diastole, so pulse pressure is set by three things: the stroke volume ejected, the compliance of the arterial reservoir that receives it, and the reflected pressure wave returning from peripheral reflection sites — if it returns in diastole it supports diastolic pressure, but as pulse wave velocity rises with stiffening it returns ever earlier, augmenting systole instead. The carded human studies measure each limb of that account. Wave-reflection timing is real and movable: in paced patients the augmentation index fell by about 4% for every 10 beats/min rise in heart rate, purely because systole shortened and the reflected wave arrived relatively later (Wilkinson 2000). In healthy humans, worse endothelial function tracked higher aortic pulse wave velocity (r = −0.69), higher augmentation index (r = −0.59) and higher central pulse pressure (r = −0.34) — stiffness and reflection are biologically regulated, not fixed plumbing (McEniery 2006). And the longitudinal Framingham haemodynamic data settle the ageing question: pulse pressure widened markedly after midlife, faster in women, and the widening tracked the forward wave — proximal aortic stiffening raising characteristic impedance — far more strongly than it tracked wave reflection, whose coefficient actually fell as impedance rose (Mitchell 2023). That is why isolated systolic hypertension emerges: a stiff aorta converts the same stroke volume into a larger forward pressure wave, systolic pressure climbs, the diastolic cushion is lost, and diastolic pressure stagnates or falls. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Wilkinson 2000: in 22 paced patients, augmentation index fell by about 4% for every 10 beats/min rise in heart rate — wave reflection is a timing phenomenon
cards.summary: Wilkinson 2000: in 22 paced patients, augmentation index fell by about 4% for every 10 beats/min rise in heart rate — wave reflection is a timing phenomenon
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cardiac pacing with pulse wave analysis, Wilkinson programme)
cards.people: 22 subjects (13 male, mean age 63 years) with permanent cardiac pacemakers in situ, studied by non-invasive pulse wave analysis during incremental pacing from 60 to 110 beats/min, with central arterial waveforms, augmentation index (AIx) and central blood pressure derived, and brachial pressure recorded non-invasively.
cards.result: There was a significant inverse linear relationship between AIx and heart rate (r = −0.76; P < 0.001): for a 10 beats/min increment, AIx fell by around 4%. Ejection duration was also inversely related to heart rate (r = −0.51; P < 0.001). Peripheral systolic, diastolic and mean pressures rose with pacing, but central systolic pressure did not, and the peripheral-to-central pulse pressure ratio increased significantly (P < 0.001) — accounted for by the change in central augmentation. The authors attribute the effect to altered timing of the reflected pressure wave as the absolute duration of systole changes.
cards.watchOut: Pacemaker patients, not healthy volunteers, and pacing isolates timing only: the study shows the reflected wave's contribution to central pressure is timing-dependent — it does not by itself quantify how much of any individual's pulse pressure is reflection versus forward wave (the Framingham card on this shelf addresses that longitudinally).
cards.source: Wilkinson IB et al. The influence of heart rate on augmentation index and central arterial pressure in humans. The Journal of physiology. 2000. PMID: 10811742. cards.headline: McEniery 2006: in healthy humans, poorer endothelial function tracked stiffer arteries — aortic PWV r = −0.69, augmentation index r = −0.59, central pulse pressure r = −0.34
cards.summary: McEniery 2006: in healthy humans, poorer endothelial function tracked stiffer arteries — aortic PWV r = −0.69, augmentation index r = −0.59, central pulse pressure r = −0.34
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (pulse wave analysis and endothelial-function testing in healthy volunteers, Anglo-Cardiff programme)
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers in whom peripheral and central pulse pressure and augmentation index were measured at rest and global endothelial function assessed by pulse wave analysis responses to sublingual nitroglycerin and inhaled albuterol; aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) was measured in a subset of 89 subjects, and in a separate group of 89 subjects aortic PWV was measured alongside brachial flow-mediated dilatation. The record does not print the total number in the main cohort (N not documented in the record for the main group; subsets n = 89).
cards.result: Global endothelial function was significantly and inversely correlated with aortic PWV (r = −0.69; P < 0.001), augmentation index (r = −0.59; P < 0.001), and central (r = −0.34; P < 0.001) and peripheral pulse pressure (r = −0.15; P = 0.03), the central correlation being the stronger. After adjustment for confounders, endothelial function remained independently and inversely associated with aortic PWV and augmentation index; conduit-artery endothelial function (flow-mediated dilatation) was likewise inversely related to aortic PWV (r = 0.39 as printed in the record, P < 0.001) and remained independent after adjustment.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional correlations in healthy people: they establish that arterial stiffness and wave reflection vary with a biological regulator (endothelial function) in humans, not that improving endothelial function lowers pulse pressure — no intervention was tested.
cards.source: McEniery CM et al. Endothelial function is associated with pulse pressure, pulse wave velocity, and augmentation index in healthy humans. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2006. PMID: 16940223. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mitchell 2023 (Framingham): pulse pressure widened after midlife — fastest in women — and the widening tracked the forward wave (aortic stiffening), not wave reflection
cards.summary: Mitchell 2023 (Framingham): pulse pressure widened after midlife — fastest in women — and the widening tracked the forward wave (aortic stiffening), not wave reflection
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (longitudinal haemodynamic cohort, Framingham Heart Study)
cards.people: Participants in three Framingham cohorts — Generation 3 (N = 4,082), Omni-2 (N = 410) and New Offspring Spouse (N = 103); 53% women — with visit-specific pulse pressure, aortic characteristic impedance, forward and backward wave amplitude and global reflection coefficient at three sequential examinations, analysed in repeated-measures models adjusted for age, sex and risk-factor exposures.
cards.result: Pulse pressure increased markedly with age after midlife (age and age-squared terms, P < 0.0001), particularly in women, whose age slope was 3.1 ± 0.2 mm Hg/decade higher than men's (P < 0.0001). Change in pulse pressure was closely related to baseline forward wave amplitude (6.7 ± 0.2 mm Hg/SD in men, 7.3 ± 0.2 in women) and to change in forward wave amplitude (11.8 ± 0.1 and 11.7 ± 0.1 mm Hg/SD; all P < 0.0001), whereas relations with the global reflection coefficient were weaker (baseline 2.1 ± 0.15 and 2.0 ± 0.14; change 4.0 ± 0.13 and 3.4 ± 0.11 mm Hg/SD). The reflection coefficient fell as aortic characteristic impedance increased (P < 0.0001), consistent with impedance matching reducing relative wave reflection. The authors conclude proximal aortic stiffening is strongly associated with the longitudinal rise in pulse pressure, especially in women, with wave reflection playing a more modest part.
cards.watchOut: Observational haemodynamics: characteristic impedance and forward wave amplitude are derived from tonometry and flow modelling, so the forward-wave dominance is a model-based attribution — but it is longitudinal, within-person, and it directly contradicts the simpler story that earlier wave reflection alone explains systolic ageing.
cards.source: Mitchell GF et al. Longitudinal Hemodynamic Correlates of and Sex Differences in the Evolution of Blood Pressure Across the Adult Lifespan: The Framingham Heart Study. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2023. PMID: 37318016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pulse pressure = stroke volume into a reservoir whose compliance falls and whose forward wave grows with age
cards.summary: Synthesis: pulse pressure = stroke volume into a reservoir whose compliance falls and whose forward wave grows with age
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology (arterial-system chapters). No new data.
cards.result: The textbook Windkessel account and the human measurements agree. Pulse pressure is determined by (1) stroke volume, (2) large-artery compliance — the reservoir that buffers ejection — and (3) wave reflection, whose effect depends on when the reflected wave returns (Wilkinson 2000: a ~4% fall in augmentation index per 10 beats/min, a pure timing effect). Stiffness itself is biologically modulated in healthy humans (McEniery 2006). With ageing, the dominant event is proximal aortic stiffening: characteristic impedance rises, the forward wave enlarges, systolic pressure climbs while the diastolic reservoir function is lost — producing wide pulse pressure and isolated systolic hypertension, longitudinally documented in Framingham (Mitchell 2023), where reflection's relative contribution shrank rather than grew. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is physiology, not treatment: it explains why systolic pressure rises with arterial ageing, and deliberately does not address which drug class to use for isolated systolic hypertension — that question lives on the hypertension treatment shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 10811742, 16940223, 37318016), framed by Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Triglyceride clearance (physiology): lipoprotein lipase at the capillary wall hydrolyses chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride — switched on by apoC-II, braked by apoC-III and the ANGPTL proteins — and human loss-of-function genetics prove the brakes: APOC3 carriers run triglycerides ~40% lower, ANGPTL4 inactivation ~13% lower
shelves.question: How is triglyceride cleared from chylomicrons and VLDL by lipoprotein lipase, and how do apoC-II (activation), apoC-III and ANGPTL proteins (inhibition) regulate that clearance in humans?
shelves.mesh: Apolipoprotein C-III/blood,genetics · Black People/genetics · Coronary Disease/blood,genetics · Exome · Genotype · Heterozygote · Humans · Liver/pathology · *Mutation · Risk Factors · Sequence Analysis, DNA · Triglycerides/blood · White People/genetics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, lipid-transport sections). In the textbook account, lipoprotein lipase (LPL) sits on capillary endothelium in muscle and adipose tissue and hydrolyses the triglyceride core of chylomicrons and VLDL, releasing fatty acids for uptake; apoC-II, acquired from HDL, is the essential LPL activator — its inherited absence produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia because clearance fails — while apoC-III and the angiopoietin-like proteins ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit LPL and slow clearance. Human genetics supplies the proof in both directions, and it is the carded evidence here. Lifelong partial loss of the apoC-III brake lowers triglycerides by 39–44% (relative) in two independent 2014 NEJM datasets (Crosby; Jørgensen). Inactivating ANGPTL3 lowers triglycerides, LDL and HDL together, with coronary odds reduced (odds ratio 0.59; Dewey 2017), and pharmacologic inactivation in human volunteers reproduced the physiology, with fasting triglycerides falling up to 76% (a relative reduction). Inactivating ANGPTL4 (E40K) lowers triglycerides by 13% (relative) with higher HDL (Dewey 2016). No animal studies are carded; animal data appear only inside two records' supporting experiments and are flagged as such on the cards. Related drug shelves (evinacumab, apoC-III and ANGPTL3 antisense/antibody therapies) ask treatment questions; this shelf is the physiology those drugs exploit. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Crosby 2014: heterozygous APOC3 loss-of-function carriers (~1 in 150 people) had triglycerides 39% lower and circulating apoC-III 46% lower than non-carriers
cards.summary: Crosby 2014: heterozygous APOC3 loss-of-function carriers (~1 in 150 people) had triglycerides 39% lower and circulating apoC-III 46% lower than non-carriers
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (exome sequencing, Exome Sequencing Project / TG and HDL Working Group)
cards.people: Exome sequencing of 18,666 genes in 3,734 participants of European or African ancestry (Exome Sequencing Project), testing whether rare coding mutations were associated with plasma triglyceride levels, with coronary heart disease risk then evaluated in 110,970 persons. Four mutations drove the APOC3 signal: three loss-of-function (a nonsense mutation, R19X, and two splice-site mutations) and one missense mutation (A43T); approximately 1 in 150 persons was a heterozygous carrier of at least one.
cards.result: Triglyceride levels in carriers were 39% lower than in non-carriers (a relative difference; P < 1×10⁻²⁰), and circulating APOC3 levels were 46% lower (a relative difference; P = 8×10⁻¹⁰). The risk of coronary heart disease among 498 carriers of any rare APOC3 mutation was 40% lower than among 110,472 non-carriers (a relative reduction; odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.75; P = 4×10⁻⁶). Removing half of one LPL brake, lifelong, produces a large lifelong acceleration of triglyceride clearance — the human genetic demonstration that apoC-III restrains LPL-mediated clearance.
cards.watchOut: Heterozygous carriers — a partial, lifelong reduction of apoC-III, not its absence; and the coronary association, while consistent with the triglyceride physiology, is observational genetics, not a trial of apoC-III lowering.
cards.source: Crosby J et al. Loss-of-function mutations in APOC3, triglycerides, and coronary disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24941081. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jørgensen 2014: in 75,725 general-population participants, APOC3 loss-of-function heterozygosity meant 44% lower non-fasting triglycerides and 41% lower ischaemic vascular disease risk
cards.summary: Jørgensen 2014: in 75,725 general-population participants, APOC3 loss-of-function heterozygosity meant 44% lower non-fasting triglycerides and 41% lower ischaemic vascular disease risk
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (general-population cohorts, Copenhagen)
cards.people: 75,725 participants in two Copenhagen general-population studies, in whom non-fasting triglyceride levels were related to incident ischaemic vascular disease and ischaemic heart disease (10,797 and 7,557 events during follow-up), and APOC3 loss-of-function heterozygotes were compared with non-carriers.
cards.result: Participants with non-fasting triglycerides below 1.00 mmol/L (90 mg/dL, as converted in the record) had significantly lower cardiovascular incidence than those at 4.00 mmol/L (350 mg/dL) or more (hazard ratio for ischaemic vascular disease 0.43, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.54; for ischaemic heart disease 0.40, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.52). Heterozygosity for APOC3 loss-of-function mutations was associated with a mean reduction in non-fasting triglycerides of 44% (a relative reduction; P < 0.001), and with relative risk reductions of 41% for ischaemic vascular disease (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.86; P = 0.007) and 36% for ischaemic heart disease (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.99; P = 0.04) versus non-carriers.
cards.watchOut: An independent replication of the Crosby finding in a different population and design — the concordance of the triglyceride effect (~40% in both) is the physiological point; the disease-risk estimates remain genetic associations, not intervention effects.
cards.source: Jørgensen AB et al. Loss-of-function mutations in APOC3 and risk of ischemic vascular disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24941082. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dewey 2017: ANGPTL3 loss-of-function lowered all three lipid fractions and coronary odds (OR 0.59) — and antibody inactivation in human volunteers cut fasting triglycerides by up to 76%
cards.summary: Dewey 2017: ANGPTL3 loss-of-function lowered all three lipid fractions and coronary odds (OR 0.59) — and antibody inactivation in human volunteers cut fasting triglycerides by up to 76%
cards.type: Primary human genetic study with human pharmacologic inactivation (DiscovEHR programme)
cards.people: ANGPTL3 exons sequenced in 58,335 DiscovEHR participants, with loss-of-function association testing for lipids and for coronary artery disease in 13,102 case patients and 40,430 controls, plus follow-up in 23,317 cases and 107,166 controls from four population studies; the same programme tested the human monoclonal antibody evinacumab in healthy human volunteers with elevated triglycerides or LDL cholesterol (the record's registry ID, NCT01749878, belongs to that human volunteer study).
cards.result: Heterozygous ANGPTL3 loss-of-function carriers had significantly lower serum triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and LDL cholesterol than non-carriers. Loss-of-function variants were found in 0.33% of coronary cases and 0.45% of controls (adjusted odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.85; P = 0.004), confirmed in the follow-up studies. In humans, evinacumab caused a dose-dependent, placebo-adjusted reduction in fasting triglycerides of up to 76% and in LDL cholesterol of up to 23% (relative reductions). ANGPTL3 normally restrains both LPL and endothelial lipase, which is why its loss lowers triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and LDL/HDL together.
cards.watchOut: The record also contains mouse atherosclerosis experiments — animal work, not carded as evidence here; the card rests on the human genetics and the human volunteer antibody data. Evinacumab as a treatment is covered on its own drug shelf (#1106); this card uses the volunteer data only as physiological proof that the ANGPTL3 brake operates in humans.
cards.source: Dewey FE et al. Genetic and Pharmacologic Inactivation of ANGPTL3 and Cardiovascular Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28538136. Registry ID: NCT01749878 (copied from the record; the human evinacumab volunteer study). cards.headline: Dewey 2016: ANGPTL4 E40K inactivation — triglycerides 13% lower, HDL 7% higher, coronary odds ratio 0.81; homozygotes showed the largest lipid effects
cards.summary: Dewey 2016: ANGPTL4 E40K inactivation — triglycerides 13% lower, HDL 7% higher, coronary odds ratio 0.81; homozygotes showed the largest lipid effects
cards.people: ANGPTL4 exons sequenced in 42,930 DiscovEHR participants of predominantly European ancestry; the E40K missense variant and other inactivating mutations were tested against lipid levels, and against coronary artery disease in 10,552 case participants and 29,223 controls. The study identified 1,661 E40K heterozygotes, 17 E40K homozygotes, and 75 participants with 13 other monoallelic inactivating mutations.
cards.result: Triglyceride levels were 13% lower and HDL cholesterol 7% higher among E40K carriers than non-carriers (relative differences). E40K carriers were less likely to have coronary artery disease (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.92; P = 0.002). K40 homozygotes had markedly lower triglycerides and higher HDL cholesterol than heterozygotes — a gene-dose effect — and carriers of other inactivating mutations likewise had lower triglycerides, higher HDL and lower coronary likelihood. The record states the premise directly: activation of lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme inhibited by ANGPTL4, reduces circulating triglycerides.
cards.watchOut: ANGPTL4 acts mainly within adipose tissue and its inactivation effect (13%) is smaller than apoC-III's (~40%) — the two brakes are not interchangeable. The record's mouse/monkey antibody experiments are animal supporting data and are not part of this card's evidence.
cards.source: Dewey FE et al. Inactivating Variants in ANGPTL4 and Risk of Coronary Artery Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 26933753. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one enzyme, one activator, three brakes — and human genetics has tested each brake
cards.summary: Synthesis: one enzyme, one activator, three brakes — and human genetics has tested each brake
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human genetic studies, framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Ganong (lipid-transport sections). No new data.
cards.result: LPL hydrolyses chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride at the capillary endothelium. The textbook names apoC-II as its essential activator — human apoC-II deficiency, in which clearance fails and triglycerides accumulate severely, is the textbook's human proof of the 'on' switch (presented here as the textbook account; no deficiency cohort is carded). The 'off' switches are carded directly from human genetics: remove half of apoC-III and triglycerides fall ~39–44% (relative) in two independent populations (PMIDs 24941081, 24941082); inactivate ANGPTL3 and triglycerides, LDL and HDL all fall, with human antibody inactivation cutting fasting triglycerides up to 76% (relative) (PMID 28538136); inactivate ANGPTL4 and triglycerides fall 13% (relative) with a gene-dose gradient (PMID 26933753). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Genetic loss-of-function is lifelong and partial; it proves the regulatory physiology and the direction of each protein's effect, but the size of a drug's effect at a given dose is a separate, drug-shelf question.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 24941081, 24941082, 28538136, 26933753), framed by Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Myocardial substrate switching (physiology): the Randle cycle in the human heart — fatty acids and glucose compete, insulin and fatty-acid supply move the switch, and in human diabetes the heart is locked toward fat (94% of fatty acids taken up oxidised, glucose use halved) while human heart failure shows no single uniform shift
shelves.question: How does the heart switch between fatty-acid and glucose oxidation (the Randle glucose–fatty-acid cycle), and how is substrate selection altered in diabetes and heart failure in humans?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Coronary Circulation · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/diagnostic imaging,metabolism,physiopathology · Fatty Acids/metabolism · Female · Glucose/metabolism · Humans · Insulin/blood · Lactic Acid/blood · Male · Myocardium/metabolism · Oxygen Consumption · Positron-Emission Tomography
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, metabolic-integration chapters). The Randle glucose–fatty-acid cycle, as the textbooks present it, is reciprocal competition: fatty-acid oxidation raises acetyl-CoA and citrate, inhibiting pyruvate dehydrogenase and glycolysis, while insulin and glucose availability suppress fatty-acid use — so the heart burns whichever fuel the circulation delivers, minute by minute. Human PET studies confirm the switch operates in people and quantify its diabetic distortion. In type 1 diabetes, myocardial fatty-acid utilisation and oxidation were roughly four-fold higher than in controls, 94% of fatty acids taken up were oxidised, and glucose utilisation was halved (Herrero 2006); yet the switch was not broken — raising insulin and lowering free fatty acids still moved diabetic myocardium back toward glucose (Peterson 2008). In uncomplicated type 2 diabetes the same pattern held — glucose uptake down, fatty-acid uptake and oxidation up — alongside impaired diastolic function (Rijzewijk 2009). Heart failure is where the human data refuse the tidy animal story: in non-ischaemic human heart failure, women had higher fatty-acid uptake and metabolism than men and no uniform fall in fat oxidation was shown (Kadkhodayan 2017). The diabetes limb is concordant human physiology; the heart-failure limb is not settled in humans — hence EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Herrero 2006: in type 1 diabetes, human myocardial fatty-acid oxidation was 206 vs 50 nmol/g/min and glucose utilisation 207 vs 403 nmol/g/min versus controls — the switch thrown hard toward fat
cards.summary: Herrero 2006: in type 1 diabetes, human myocardial fatty-acid oxidation was 206 vs 50 nmol/g/min and glucose utilisation 207 vs 403 nmol/g/min versus controls — the switch thrown hard toward fat
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (PET myocardial substrate quantification, Peterson/Gropler programme)
cards.people: 11 otherwise healthy patients with type 1 diabetes (8 women; age 36 ± 10 years; HbA1c 8.4 ± 1.9%) and 11 healthy non-diabetic controls (5 women; age 25 ± 5 years), studied by positron emission tomography for myocardial blood flow, oxygen consumption, glucose utilisation, and fatty-acid utilisation, oxidation and the percentage of fatty acids oxidised.
cards.result: Plasma glucose (5.71 ± 0.98 vs 5.28 ± 0.65 µmol/ml, p = 0.04), free fatty acids (0.60 ± 0.24 vs 0.19 ± 0.07 µmol/ml, p < 0.0001) and myocardial oxygen consumption (6.64 ± 2.21 vs 4.51 ± 1.39 µmol/g/min, p = 0.007) were higher in the diabetic subjects. Myocardial fatty-acid utilisation was 213 ± 135 vs 57 ± 28 nmol/g/min (p = 0.0004), fatty-acid oxidation 206 ± 131 vs 50 ± 26 nmol/g/min (p = 0.0002), and the percentage of fatty acids oxidised 94 ± 6% vs 81 ± 19% (p = 0.04). Glucose utilisation moved the opposite way: 207 ± 108 vs 403 ± 191 nmol/g/min (p = 0.0008). Reciprocal substrate competition — the Randle pattern — measured directly in the human heart.
cards.watchOut: Small PET samples (11 per group) with wide standard deviations, and the diabetic group was older and more female than controls — the direction and reciprocity of the substrate shift are the finding; the exact fold-changes should not be over-read.
cards.source: Herrero P et al. Increased myocardial fatty acid metabolism in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2006. PMID: 16458143. cards.headline: Peterson 2008: the diabetic human heart still switches — glucose use rose with insulin and falling free fatty acids, fatty-acid use rose with fatty-acid supply
cards.summary: Peterson 2008: the diabetic human heart still switches — glucose use rose with insulin and falling free fatty acids, fatty-acid use rose with fatty-acid supply
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (PET substrate manipulation by insulin and lipid infusion/clamp)
cards.people: Non-diabetic control subjects and three groups of subjects with type 1 diabetes studied during euglycaemia, during hyperlipidaemia, and during a hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, with myocardial oxygen consumption and glucose and fatty-acid metabolism quantified by positron emission tomography. The record does not print the group sizes (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Type 1 diabetic subjects had higher myocardial oxygen consumption and lower myocardial glucose utilisation per unit insulin than controls — myocardial insulin resistance during euglycaemia. But metabolism remained manipulable: in type 1 diabetes, glucose utilisation increased with increasing plasma insulin and decreasing free fatty acid levels, while myocardial fatty-acid utilisation, oxidation and esterification rates increased with increasing plasma free fatty acids. Increasing insulin decreased fatty-acid esterification rates but increased the percentage of fatty acids going into esterification. The Randle switch in human diabetes is biased, not broken — substrate supply and insulin still set it.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, and the manipulations are acute infusions and clamps: they demonstrate the switch's responsiveness over hours, not how substrate selection behaves over years of diabetes.
cards.source: Peterson LR et al. Fatty acids and insulin modulate myocardial substrate metabolism in humans with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes. 2008. PMID: 17914030. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rijzewijk 2009: in 78 men with uncomplicated type 2 diabetes, myocardial glucose uptake was lower (260 vs 348) and fatty-acid oxidation higher (85 vs 63 nmol/ml/min), with worse diastolic function but unchanged high-energy phosphate metabolism
cards.summary: Rijzewijk 2009: in 78 men with uncomplicated type 2 diabetes, myocardial glucose uptake was lower (260 vs 348) and fatty-acid oxidation higher (85 vs 63 nmol/ml/min), with worse diastolic function but unchanged high-energy phosphate metabolism
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (PET/MRI substrate and function study in type 2 diabetes)
cards.people: 78 insulin-naive men with type 2 diabetes (age 56.5 ± 5.6 years; BMI 28.7 ± 3.5 kg/m²; HbA1c 7.1 ± 1.0%) with verified absence of cardiac ischaemia, and 24 normoglycaemic control subjects (age 54.5 ± 7.1 years; HbA1c 5.3 ± 0.2%), assessed by cardiac MRI for left ventricular function and by PET (H₂¹⁵O, ¹¹C-palmitate, ¹⁸FDG) for perfusion and substrate metabolism, with ³¹P-MRS for high-energy phosphate metabolism.
cards.result: Compared with controls, patients had impaired diastolic function (E/A ratio 1.04 ± 0.25 vs 1.26 ± 0.36, p = 0.003) and decreased myocardial glucose uptake (260 ± 128 vs 348 ± 154 nmol/ml/min, p = 0.015), while myocardial non-esterified fatty-acid uptake (88 ± 31 vs 68 ± 18 nmol/ml/min, p = 0.021) and oxidation (85 ± 30 vs 63 ± 19 nmol/ml/min, p = 0.007) were increased. There were no differences in myocardial high-energy phosphate metabolism or perfusion, and no association was found between diastolic function and cardiac substrate or high-energy phosphate metabolism — the substrate shift is real in human type 2 diabetes, but this study does not tie it directly to the functional impairment.
cards.watchOut: Men only, cross-sectional, and explicitly no association between the metabolic and functional measures: carded for the substrate-selection physiology, not as proof that fat oxidation causes diabetic cardiomyopathy.
cards.source: Rijzewijk LJ et al. Altered myocardial substrate metabolism and decreased diastolic function in nonischemic human diabetic cardiomyopathy: studies with cardiac positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2009. PMID: 19815124. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kadkhodayan 2017: in human non-ischaemic heart failure (EF ≤ 35%), women had higher fatty-acid uptake and metabolism than men — no uniform fat-to-glucose shift was demonstrated
cards.summary: Kadkhodayan 2017: in human non-ischaemic heart failure (EF ≤ 35%), women had higher fatty-acid uptake and metabolism than men — no uniform fat-to-glucose shift was demonstrated
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (PET substrate study in non-ischaemic heart failure) — N = 19
cards.people: 19 well-matched men and women with non-ischaemic heart failure (ejection fraction ≤ 35%), with myocardial blood flow and substrate metabolism quantified by positron emission tomography, and event-free survival followed prospectively.
cards.result: Women had higher myocardial blood flow, fatty-acid uptake and fatty-acid utilisation than men (P < 0.005, P < 0.005 and P < 0.05 respectively) and trended toward higher fatty-acid oxidation (P = 0.09), independent of age, obesity and insulin resistance. There were no sex-related differences in fasting myocardial glucose uptake or metabolism. Higher myocardial blood flow was related to improved event-free survival (hazard ratio 0.31, P = 0.02). The record's framing is the caution: animal models of heart failure shift from fatty-acid toward glucose metabolism, but these human data show sex-dependent fatty-acid metabolism persisting in the failing heart rather than a single uniform switch.
cards.watchOut: N = 19 and a sex-comparison design: it cannot settle what the average failing human heart does — which is precisely why this shelf's stamp is EMERGING for the heart-failure limb. Absolute flow and uptake values by sex are not printed in the record and are not invented here.
cards.source: Kadkhodayan A et al. Sex affects myocardial blood flow and fatty acid substrate metabolism in humans with nonischemic heart failure. Journal of nuclear cardiology : official publication of the American Society of Nuclear Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 27048307. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the switch is real in humans, locked toward fat in diabetes, and unsettled in heart failure
cards.summary: Synthesis: the switch is real in humans, locked toward fat in diabetes, and unsettled in heart failure
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human PET studies, framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (metabolic-integration chapters). No new data.
cards.result: The Randle cycle is measurable human physiology, not just biochemistry: fatty acids and glucose compete reciprocally in the living heart, and insulin plus fatty-acid supply move the switch even in diabetes (PMIDs 16458143, 17914030). In both type 1 and type 2 human diabetes the resting position of the switch is displaced — fatty-acid oxidation up several-fold, glucose use down by about a quarter to a half (PMIDs 16458143, 19815124). In heart failure, the animal-model prediction of a uniform shift to glucose is not confirmed by the human PET data carded here, which instead show persistent, sex-dependent fatty-acid metabolism (PMID 27048307). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (diabetes limb established in humans; heart-failure limb unresolved).
cards.watchOut: Metabolic-modulator drugs (partial fatty-acid oxidation inhibitors and similar) are treatment questions for their own shelves; this shelf establishes only how substrate selection works and how it is displaced.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 16458143, 17914030, 19815124, 27048307), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Coronary autoregulation (physiology): flow stays constant while pressure falls — until the plateau breaks — and in humans the break point shifts upward with hypertension and hypertrophy (flow fell 26% once pressure reached 90–80 mm Hg), with adenosine and K-ATP-channel metabolic coupling doing the day-to-day work
shelves.question: How does coronary autoregulation hold myocardial blood flow constant across perfusion pressures, which mediators (adenosine, metabolic coupling) dominate, and where does the autoregulatory range break in humans?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure/physiology · Cardiomegaly/physiopathology · Coronary Circulation/physiology · Coronary Vessels/physiopathology · Homeostasis/physiology · Humans · Hypertension/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroprusside · Thermodilution · Vascular Resistance/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, coronary-circulation chapter). In the textbook account, coronary flow is autoregulated: across a wide range of perfusion pressures, arteriolar resistance adjusts so flow matches myocardial oxygen demand — metabolic coupling — with adenosine, released as ATP is consumed, as the classic mediator, alongside other local signals including ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels. Below the lower limit of the range, vessels are maximally dilated and flow becomes pressure-dependent. The carded human studies measure the plateau, its break point, and its mediators in people. Lowering coronary perfusion pressure stepwise in patients with normal epicardial arteries left great-cardiac-vein flow unchanged down to the 60–70 mm Hg endpoints in controls and in hypertensives without hypertrophy — but in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy, flow began to fall at 90–80 mm Hg and was down 26% at the endpoint: the lower limit shifts upward when baseline flow is high and arteriolar dilation is impaired (Polese 1991). For mediators: blocking adenosine receptors with theophylline cut human coronary flow by 23% across rest, hypoxia and exercise (Edlund 1995), and blocking K-ATP channels with intracoronary glibenclamide blunted pacing-induced metabolic vasodilation (Farouque 2004); exogenous adenosine itself reproduces near-maximal human coronary vasodilation (Wilson 1990). SCOPE: this shelf covers the autoregulatory plateau and its mediators only — the magnitude of coronary flow reserve is a separate question, deliberately not built here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Polese 1991: human coronary flow held constant as perfusion pressure was lowered stepwise — except in hypertensive hypertrophy, where flow began falling at 90–80 mm Hg and was down 26% at the endpoint
cards.summary: Polese 1991: human coronary flow held constant as perfusion pressure was lowered stepwise — except in hypertensive hypertrophy, where flow began falling at 90–80 mm Hg and was down 26% at the endpoint
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (stepwise perfusion-pressure lowering with coronary sinus/great cardiac vein flow measurement)
cards.people: 24 men with effort-induced angina and angiographically normal left epicardial branches: 9 normotensive controls, 7 hypertensive patients with normal left ventricular mass (group I), and 8 hypertensive patients with augmented LV mass index from concentric hypertrophy (group II). Flow in the great cardiac vein was measured by thermodilution at baseline and during stepwise decreases in coronary perfusion pressure (5 mm Hg every 5 minutes) produced by titrated intravenous nitroprusside, to endpoints of 60 mm Hg in controls and 70 mm Hg in hypertensives.
cards.result: Baseline flow averaged 102 ml/min in normotensives, 104 ml/min in hypertensive group I and 148 ml/min in hypertensive group II. At the endpoints, flow was similar to baseline in the controls and in group I — the autoregulatory plateau, demonstrated directly in humans. In group II, coronary flow started to decline and myocardial oxygen extraction started to rise at perfusion pressures of 90–80 mm Hg, and at the endpoint flow was reduced by 26% (p < 0.01 from baseline). The patterns were not explained by changes in tension-time index or heart rate. The authors conclude that hypertension (reduced arteriolar dilator ability) plus hypertrophy (augmented baseline flow) shifts the point of exhaustion of coronary reserve to a higher perfusion pressure.
cards.watchOut: Great cardiac vein flow samples the anterior left ventricular territory, not whole-heart flow, and nitroprusside has its own vascular actions; within those limits this is the direct human demonstration of the plateau and of its upward-shifted lower limit in hypertrophy. The study's framing touches coronary reserve, but it is carded here only for the autoregulatory range — reserve magnitude is a separate shelf's question.
cards.source: Polese A et al. Upward shift of the lower range of coronary flow autoregulation in hypertensive patients with hypertrophy of the left ventricle. Circulation. 1991. PMID: 1825626. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wilson 1990: adenosine in humans reproduces maximal coronary vasodilation — a 16 µg intracoronary bolus raised flow velocity 4.6 ± 0.7-fold, matching papaverine
cards.summary: Wilson 1990: adenosine in humans reproduces maximal coronary vasodilation — a 16 µg intracoronary bolus raised flow velocity 4.6 ± 0.7-fold, matching papaverine
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (intracoronary/intravenous adenosine dose-response with Doppler flow velocity)
cards.people: Patients undergoing coronary studies with coronary blood flow velocity (CBFV) measured by a 3F coronary Doppler catheter: normal left coronary arteries (n = 20) and right coronary arteries (n = 5) for intracoronary boluses (2–16 µg), 6 patients for intracoronary infusions (10–240 µg/min), 25 normal patients for intravenous infusions (35–140 µg/kg/min), and 8 patients with microvascular vasodilator dysfunction; maximal CBFV was defined against intracoronary papaverine (4.5 ± 0.2 × resting CBFV).
cards.result: In normal left coronary arteries, 16 µg adenosine boluses caused hyperaemia similar to papaverine (4.6 ± 0.7 × resting CBFV); 12 µg boluses did the same in the right coronary artery (4.4 ± 1.0 × resting). Intracoronary infusions of 80 µg/min or more also caused maximal hyperaemia (4.4 ± 0.1 × resting), with only a minimal fall in arterial pressure (−6 ± 2 mm Hg) at up to 240 µg/min and no significant heart-rate or ECG change; hyperaemia was much briefer after adenosine than after papaverine. Intravenous adenosine at 140 µg/kg/min matched papaverine in 84% of patients. The endogenous mediator, given exogenously, can drive the human coronary bed to its vasodilator ceiling — the pharmacologic counterpart of the metabolic signal.
cards.watchOut: This card is carded for adenosine's mediator credentials — that the human coronary bed responds to it fully and briefly — not as a measurement of coronary flow reserve, whose magnitude is a separate question excluded from this shelf's scope. Exogenous responsiveness alone would not prove the endogenous role; the theophylline card supplies the blockade half of the argument.

cards.headline: Edlund 1995: blocking adenosine receptors with theophylline cut human coronary sinus flow by 23% at rest, in hypoxia and in exercise (N = 6)
cards.summary: Edlund 1995: blocking adenosine receptors with theophylline cut human coronary sinus flow by 23% at rest, in hypoxia and in exercise (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (adenosine-receptor blockade with coronary sinus flow measurement) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy subjects in whom coronary sinus blood flow (thermodilution) and cardiac oxygen extraction were measured breathing room air at rest and breathing 12% oxygen at rest and during light exercise, on two occasions — one during theophylline infusion at a dose lacking effects on myocardial work. N = 6, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Basal coronary sinus flow was 118 (67–168) ml/min; breathing 12% oxygen (arterial saturation 83% at rest, 77% in exercise) raised flow to 167 (93–214) ml/min at rest and 261 (179–343) ml/min in exercise, while oxygen extraction fell. Theophylline markedly attenuated the flow response to exogenous adenosine and decreased coronary sinus flow to 89 (58–119), 120 (79–161) and 190 (162–218) ml/min in the three states — an overall decrease of 23% (a relative reduction; P < 0.05), with calculated coronary vascular conductance also down 23% (P < 0.05) and oxygen extraction up 15% (P < 0.001). Endogenous adenosine therefore carries a measurable share of human coronary tone at rest and under metabolic stress — blockade evidence, the strongest kind for a mediator.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, and theophylline is not perfectly selective — but the dose was chosen to lack myocardial-work effects and it verifiably blocked exogenous adenosine responses in the same subjects, so the 23% flow fall is reasonably attributed to adenosine-receptor blockade. A 23% share also means adenosine is a contributor, not the whole of metabolic coupling — the K-ATP card shows another limb.

cards.headline: Farouque 2004: blocking K-ATP channels with intracoronary glibenclamide reduced resting coronary flow 9% and blunted pacing-induced metabolic vasodilation in 17 patients
cards.summary: Farouque 2004: blocking K-ATP channels with intracoronary glibenclamide reduced resting coronary flow 9% and blunted pacing-induced metabolic vasodilation in 17 patients
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (intracoronary K-ATP blockade during pacing-induced metabolic vasodilation)
cards.people: 17 patients (12 men; age 58 ± 10 years) studied in an angiographically smooth coronary artery after successful percutaneous intervention to another vessel, with coronary blood velocity by Doppler guidewire before and after subselective intracoronary glibenclamide (40 µg/min) versus vehicle; metabolic vasodilation was induced by 2 minutes of rapid right ventricular pacing and the hyperaemic time course recorded for 2 minutes.
cards.result: Compared with vehicle, glibenclamide reduced resting coronary blood flow by 9% (P = 0.04) and increased resting coronary vascular resistance by 15% (P = 0.03). It reduced pacing-induced peak flow (50.8 ± 6.8 vs 42.0 ± 5.4 ml/min, P = 0.001), peak flow corrected for baseline (25.1 ± 4.6 vs 17.6 ± 3.1 ml/min, P = 0.01), and total hyperaemic volume over 2 minutes (area under the flow–time curve 3,535 ± 397 vs 3,027 ± 326 ml, P = 0.001), while minimum coronary vascular resistance rose (2.6 ± 0.3 vs 3.1 ± 0.3 mm Hg/ml/min, P = 0.002). Vascular K-ATP channels — a downstream effector that several metabolic signals converge on — are part of how the human coronary bed matches flow to demand.
cards.watchOut: Patients with coronary disease (studied in a smooth artery after PCI elsewhere), and glibenclamide blockade is partial pharmacology, not a knockout: the finding is that K-ATP channels contribute measurably to human metabolic vasodilation, alongside — not instead of — adenosine.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a pressure-independent plateau, an upward-shifted break point in hypertrophy, and redundant metabolic mediators
cards.summary: Synthesis: a pressure-independent plateau, an upward-shifted break point in hypertrophy, and redundant metabolic mediators
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (coronary-circulation chapter). No new data.
cards.result: In humans, coronary flow is held constant as perfusion pressure falls — directly demonstrated to 60–70 mm Hg endpoints in non-hypertrophied hearts (PMID 1825626) — because arteriolar resistance tracks metabolic demand. The plateau's lower limit is not fixed: with hypertension plus hypertrophy it shifts up to roughly 90–80 mm Hg, below which flow fell 26% (PMID 1825626). The coupling is mediator-redundant: adenosine can drive the bed to maximum (PMID 2225364) and its blockade removes about a quarter of flow (PMID 8619329), while K-ATP channel blockade independently blunts metabolic vasodilation (PMID 15016638) — parallel pathways, which is why no single antagonist abolishes autoregulation. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope held as commissioned: this shelf covers the autoregulatory plateau and its mediators only. How large coronary flow reserve is, and what reduces it, is a separate question (slate-4 row 185) for a later wave and is not answered here.

shelves.title: Thermoregulation in ageing: cutaneous vasodilation is attenuated in older adults — a smaller nitric-oxide contribution, a blunted axon-reflex peak, reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, and less sweat output per gland
shelves.question: During heat stress, how much are reflex cutaneous vasodilation and sweating attenuated in healthy older adults compared with young adults, and what mechanisms (nitric oxide, axon reflex, active vasodilator sensitivity) account for the attenuation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging · Axons · Exercise · Humans · Nitric Oxide · Reflex · Skin · Sweating · Vasodilation
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: skin blood flow and sweating are the two heat-loss effectors driven by core temperature, and both are attenuated with healthy ageing. The fetched primary human studies agree on direction and mechanism. With local heating, the older plateau of cutaneous vascular conductance is lower and nitric oxide contributes less to it, and the axon-reflex initial peak is blunted (Minson 2002; N = 10 young vs 10 older, printed on the card). During exercise heat stress the conductance rise is shifted to a higher core temperature and forearm conductance runs 40–50% lower in older men, and blocking noradrenergic vasoconstriction does not explain the gap — the deficit is reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, not excess vasoconstriction (Kenney 1997; N = 15 vs 15). Sweat glands themselves respond less: methylcholine-stimulated sweat output per gland runs young > fit older > normally fit older men, with no difference in activated gland density — a per-gland, cholinergic-sensitivity deficit (Inoue 1999; N = 14 in total). These are classic small studies and their Ns are printed on each card's face. The neighbouring shelf #6263 asks when sweating and vasodilation switch on and how acclimation shifts those thresholds; this shelf asks the different, ageing-comparison question and cards none of #6263's references.

cards.headline: Local heating: older skin reaches a lower vasodilator plateau, nitric oxide contributes less, and the axon-reflex peak is blunted (N = 10 young vs 10 older)
cards.summary: Local heating: older skin reaches a lower vasodilator plateau, nitric oxide contributes less, and the axon-reflex peak is blunted (N = 10 young vs 10 older)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (local heating with microdialysis nitric-oxide blockade)
cards.people: 10 young (22 ± 2 years) and 10 older (77 ± 5 years) men and women; two forearm microdialysis sites heated to 42 °C for ~60 min, skin blood flow by laser-Doppler, expressed as % of maximal conductance (%CVCmax). Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Before nitric-oxide synthase blockade, the initial peak was 61 ± 2 %CVCmax in the young vs 46 ± 4 in the older, and the plateau was 93 ± 2 vs 82 ± 5 (both P < 0.05). When nitric oxide synthase was inhibited after 40 min of heating, conductance fell to the same value in both groups, so the overall contribution of nitric oxide to the plateau was less in the older subjects. The initial peak was also lower in the older subjects at both sites (52 ± 4 vs 38 ± 5 %CVCmax), implicating the axon reflex as well.
cards.watchOut: A local-heating, forearm-skin preparation: it isolates nitric-oxide and axon-reflex mechanisms cleanly but is not whole-body reflex heat stress, and with 10 per group it estimates mechanism, not population averages.
cards.source: Minson CT et al. Decreased nitric oxide- and axon reflex-mediated cutaneous vasodilation with age during local heating. J Appl Physiol. 2002. PMID: 12381749. cards.headline: Exercise heat stress: the conductance rise is shifted to higher core temperatures and forearm conductance runs 40–50% lower in older adults — reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, not excess vasoconstriction (N = 15 vs 15)
cards.summary: Exercise heat stress: the conductance rise is shifted to higher core temperatures and forearm conductance runs 40–50% lower in older adults — reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, not excess vasoconstriction (N = 15 vs 15)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (exercise heat stress with regional vasoconstrictor blockade)
cards.people: 15 young (22 ± 1 years) and 15 older (66 ± 1 years) men exercised at 50% of peak oxygen uptake in a 36 °C environment; one forearm site was pretreated with bretylium tosylate to block local noradrenergic vasoconstrictor release.
cards.result: The core-temperature rise associated with 50% of the conductance response was 0.22 ± 0.04 °C in the young vs 0.73 ± 0.04 °C in the older at the control site (0.39 ± 0.04 vs 0.85 ± 0.04 °C at the bretylium site) — bretylium did not remove the age difference, arguing against augmented vasoconstriction as the cause. After the initial ~0.2 °C rise in oesophageal temperature, total forearm vascular conductance was 40–50% lower in the older men (P < 0.01) for the remainder of exercise. Maximal conductance itself (75–86 %CVCmax) did not differ by age.
cards.watchOut: Men exercising in the heat — the reflex, whole-body counterpart to Reference 1's local test. The bretylium logic is only as strong as the verified blockade, which the authors checked with whole-body cooling.
cards.source: Kenney WL et al. Decreased active vasodilator sensitivity in aged skin. Am J Physiol. 1997. PMID: 9139942. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sweating: output per gland is lower in older men and falls with cholinergic stimulation — gland numbers activated do not differ (N = 14 in total)
cards.summary: Sweating: output per gland is lower in older men and falls with cholinergic stimulation — gland numbers activated do not differ (N = 14 in total)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (heat acclimation with pharmacological sweat-gland testing)
cards.people: 5 young men (23 ± 1 years), 4 highly fit older men (63 ± 3 years) and 5 normally fit older men (67 ± 3 years), heat-acclimated over 8 days of cycle exercise in the heat, with methylcholine injection tests before and after. Very small groups — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Methylcholine-stimulated sweat output per gland on chest, back and thigh ran young > highly fit older > normally fit older (forearm: young = highly fit older > normally fit older), while activated sweat gland density did not differ between groups at any site. Output per gland rose with acclimation in all groups, but the thigh increase was smaller in the older groups. The authors conclude that sweat-gland sensitivity to cholinergic stimulation decreases with ageing, over and above fitness.
cards.watchOut: Groups of 4–5 men: the per-gland ordering is consistent across four skin sites, which is what carries it, but no number here should be read as a precise population estimate.
cards.source: Inoue Y et al. Exercise- and methylcholine-induced sweating responses in older and younger men: effect of heat acclimation and aerobic fitness. Int J Biometeorol. 1999. PMID: 10232057. cards.headline: Synthesis: both heat-loss effectors are attenuated with ageing, at identified peripheral steps
cards.summary: Synthesis: both heat-loss effectors are attenuated with ageing, at identified peripheral steps
cards.people: 64 participants across the three primary studies carded (20 + 30 + 14), each study's N printed on its own card.
cards.result: Vasodilation: lower plateau with local heating, a smaller nitric-oxide contribution, a blunted axon-reflex peak, and a right-shifted, 40–50% smaller reflex conductance rise that vasoconstrictor blockade does not explain. Sweating: fewer activated glands is not the problem — each gland secretes less, with reduced cholinergic sensitivity. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) presents the same account; the quantitative values on this shelf come only from the fetched primary records. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: All three studies are small and two are in men only or mostly; the mechanism map is consistent, but effect sizes in women and in the very old rest on thinner data than the headline suggests.

shelves.title: Post-exercise hypotension: pressure falls for hours after one bout of dynamic exercise — roughly 8–10/3–5 mmHg in normotensive and 18–20/7–9 mmHg in hypertensive people — driven by sustained vasodilation, not by a fall in cardiac output
shelves.question: After a single bout of moderate-intensity dynamic exercise, how large and how prolonged is the fall in arterial pressure in normotensive versus hypertensive humans, and is it driven by a sustained fall in vascular resistance?
shelves.mesh: Baroreflex · Blood Pressure · Exercise · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypotension · Vascular Resistance · Vasodilator Agents
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: after dynamic exercise, arterial pressure settles below pre-exercise levels for hours because systemic vascular resistance stays reduced while cardiac output recovers. The fetched records support each element. In the primary laboratory study carded, 60 minutes of cycling at 60% of peak oxygen consumption left mean arterial pressure 5 mmHg lower and total peripheral resistance about 30% lower, while cardiac output was higher, not lower — and baroreflex heart-rate gain was augmented, restraining rather than causing the fall (Halliwill 1996, N = 12). The magnitude synthesis (Kenney & Seals 1993) puts maximal falls at 8–10 mmHg systolic and 3–5 diastolic in normotensive people versus 18–20 and 7–9 in hypertensive people, persisting 2–4 hours under laboratory conditions, with one free-living report of up to 13 hours. The mechanism review (Halliwill 2001) attributes the phenomenon to persistent reductions in vascular resistance mediated by the autonomic nervous system and vasodilator substances, more pronounced and longer in hypertension. Two of the three cards are expert syntheses rather than primary trials — labelled as such on their faces — because the primary literature is many small laboratory studies; the one primary study carded carries the haemodynamic mechanism directly.

cards.headline: The haemodynamics directly: after 60 minutes of cycling, pressure and resistance are down while cardiac output is up — vasodilation carries the fall (N = 12)
cards.summary: The haemodynamics directly: after 60 minutes of cycling, pressure and resistance are down while cardiac output is up — vasodilation carries the fall (N = 12)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (post-exercise haemodynamics and baroreflex testing)
cards.people: 12 healthy untrained men and women aged 21–28 years; 60 min of cycling at 60% of peak oxygen consumption, with systemic haemodynamics, carotid–cardiac baroreflex testing by neck pressure, and cardiac vagal tone measured after exercise. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Mean arterial pressure fell from 86 ± 2 to 81 ± 2 mmHg and total peripheral resistance from 23 ± 2 to 16 ± 1 units (both P < 0.05), while cardiac output rose from 3.9 ± 0.3 to 5.5 ± 0.5 L/min. Baroreflex slope increased from 4.7 ± 0.7 to 6.1 ± 0.9 ms/mmHg and its range from 186 ± 23 to 238 ± 30 ms, with no change in cardiac vagal tone — the authors conclude augmented baroreflex gain restrains, rather than contributes to, the hypotension, which appears mediated predominantly by vasodilation.
cards.watchOut: Twelve young normotensive volunteers and a laboratory recovery window: it establishes the resistance mechanism, but the size and duration figures for hypertensive people come from Reference 2's synthesis, not from this study.
