cards.headline: Size and duration: maximal falls average 18–20/7–9 mmHg in hypertensive versus 8–10/3–5 mmHg in normotensive people, lasting 2–4 hours in the laboratory (synthesis)
cards.summary: Size and duration: maximal falls average 18–20/7–9 mmHg in hypertensive versus 8–10/3–5 mmHg in normotensive people, lasting 2–4 hours in the laboratory (synthesis)
cards.type: Expert synthesis / review of the human and animal literature (labelled — not a primary trial)
cards.people: Synthesis of the post-exercise hypotension literature in normotensive and hypertensive humans (and spontaneously hypertensive rats) available to 1993; the phenomenon follows large-muscle dynamic exercise above 40% of peak aerobic capacity for 20–60 minutes.
cards.result: Maximal exercise-induced reductions averaged 18–20 mmHg systolic and 7–9 mmHg diastolic in hypertensive humans, versus 8–10 and 3–5 mmHg in normotensive humans. Post-exercise hypotension persisted 2–4 hours under laboratory conditions; whether it is sustained under free-living conditions was controversial, with one study indicating persistence for up to 13 hours. Candidate mechanisms listed include reduced limb and total peripheral resistance, reduced muscle sympathetic nerve discharge, altered baroreflex control, and reduced vascular responsiveness to alpha-adrenergic stimulation.
cards.watchOut: A 1993 synthesis: its averages pool heterogeneous small studies, and its animal-model material is context only — the human numbers on the face are the ones this shelf relies on. Duration beyond the laboratory remains the least settled figure on this shelf.

shelves.title: Longitudinal VO2max decline with ageing: not linear — it accelerates from 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s to over 20% per decade in the 70s, in active and sedentary people alike (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
shelves.question: How fast does peak oxygen consumption decline longitudinally with age in healthy adults — is the decline linear, or does it accelerate with each decade, and does habitual physical activity change the rate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging · Exercise · Female · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Fitness
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account of maximal oxygen consumption falling with age. The decisive fetched record is longitudinal: in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, 810 healthy adults measured serially over a median 7.9 years lost peak VO2 at a rate that accelerated with every decade — 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s rising to over 20% per decade in the 70s and beyond — and the same acceleration appeared in every quartile of self-reported leisure-time activity (Fleg 2005). The cross-sectional syntheses explain the apparent paradox that trained people lose more in absolute terms: endurance-trained women and men start higher and lose more millilitres per decade (−6.2 and −5.4 ml/kg/min per decade) than sedentary peers (−3.5 and −3.9), while the relative rate is essentially the same, about 10–11% per decade (Fitzgerald 1997, 4,884 women; Pimentel 2003, 153 men, in whom the trained decline steepened after ~50 alongside falling training volume). So habitual activity sets the level, not the relative slope — and cross-sectional estimates understate the true late-life loss. The neighbouring pack #6248 asks what limits VO2max; this shelf asks the different question of how fast it falls, and cards none of #6248's references.

cards.headline: BLSA longitudinal: the decline accelerates — 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s to over 20% per decade in the 70s, regardless of activity habits (N = 810)
cards.summary: BLSA longitudinal: the decline accelerates — 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s to over 20% per decade in the 70s, regardless of activity habits (N = 810)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (longitudinal cohort with serial exercise testing)
cards.people: 375 women and 435 men aged 21–87 years from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, free of clinical heart disease, with serial peak treadmill oxygen-consumption measurements over a median follow-up of 7.9 years; rates from a linear mixed-effects model adjusted for self-reported leisure-time physical activity.
cards.result: A longitudinal decline in peak VO2 occurred in each of the six age decades in both sexes, but the rate accelerated from 3% to 6% per 10 years in the 20s and 30s to >20% per 10 years in the 70s and beyond; the rate was larger in men than women from the 40s onward. Similar rates prevailed per kilogram of body weight or fat-free mass and in all quartiles of leisure-time physical activity. The oxygen pulse mirrored the peak VO2 decline, whereas maximal heart rate fell only 4–6% per 10 years with minimal acceleration.
cards.watchOut: A healthy, community-dwelling volunteer cohort with self-reported (not measured) activity; people who stay in longitudinal ageing studies are healthier than those who leave, so if anything the true population decline may be steeper.
cards.source: Fleg JL et al. Accelerated longitudinal decline of aerobic capacity in healthy older adults. Circulation. 2005. PMID: 16043637. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Women, cross-sectional meta-analysis: trained women lose more per decade in absolute terms, the same in relative terms — about 10–11% per decade at every activity level (4,884 women)
cards.summary: Women, cross-sectional meta-analysis: trained women lose more per decade in absolute terms, the same in relative terms — about 10–11% per decade at every activity level (4,884 women)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies (labelled — not longitudinal)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 239 subject groups from 109 studies involving 4,884 women aged 18–89 years, separated into sedentary (2,256), active (1,717) and endurance-trained (911) populations.
cards.result: Mean VO2max was 29.7 ± 7.8 (sedentary), 38.7 ± 9.2 (active) and 52.0 ± 10.5 ml/kg/min (endurance-trained). The absolute rate of decline was lowest in sedentary women (−3.5 ml/kg/min per decade), greater in active women (−4.4) and greatest in endurance-trained women (−6.2; all P < 0.001 versus each other) — but expressed as percent decrease from mean levels at ~25 years, the rates were similar across populations (−10.0 to −10.9% per decade). There was no obvious relationship between exercise status and the rate of decline in maximal heart rate.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional: each age point is a different group of women, so cohort and survivor effects are folded into the slope — which is exactly why Reference 1's longitudinal design is the shelf's anchor and this card is the activity-level comparison.
cards.source: Fitzgerald MD et al. Age-related declines in maximal aerobic capacity in regularly exercising vs. sedentary women: a meta-analysis. J Appl Physiol. 1997. PMID: 9216959. cards.headline: Men, cross-sectional: endurance-trained men decline faster in absolute terms (−5.4 vs −3.9 ml/kg/min per decade), hold their level until ~50, then steepen as training volume falls (N = 153)
cards.summary: Men, cross-sectional: endurance-trained men decline faster in absolute terms (−5.4 vs −3.9 ml/kg/min per decade), hold their level until ~50, then steepen as training volume falls (N = 153)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cross-sectional laboratory comparison)
cards.people: 153 healthy men aged 20–75 years — 64 sedentary and 89 endurance trained — with maximal treadmill VO2max measured in a controlled laboratory study.
cards.result: VO2max was higher in the endurance-trained men at any age, but its absolute rate of decline was greater in the trained than the sedentary men (−5.4 vs −3.9 ml/kg/min per decade; relative rates similar). VO2max declined linearly with age in the sedentary men but was maintained in the endurance-trained men until approximately 50 years, after which the accelerated decline was related to declining training volume (r = 0.46, P < 0.0001) and to rising 10-km running time, and was associated with a marked decline in oxygen pulse.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional and men only; the post-50 steepening in trained men tracks their reduced training volume, so part of the 'ageing' slope in athletes is a training-dose slope — the BLSA card shows the acceleration persists after activity adjustment in the general cohort.
cards.source: Pimentel AE et al. Greater rate of decline in maximal aerobic capacity with age in endurance-trained than in sedentary men. J Appl Physiol. 2003. PMID: 12533496. cards.summary: Synthesis: activity sets the level; ageing sets an accelerating relative slope

shelves.title: Efanesoctocog alfa weekly prophylaxis in severe haemophilia A without inhibitors (XTEND-1; XTEND-Kids — single-arm, intra-patient comparator): annualised bleeding rate 2.96 to 0.69 versus prestudy prophylaxis, factor VIII >40 IU/dL most of the week
shelves.question: In people with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors, does once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa prophylaxis maintain higher factor VIII levels and lower bleeding than standard prophylaxis? (XTEND-1 — single-arm, intra-patient comparator; label as such.)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence with an intra-patient comparator, labelled as such; there is no randomised parallel control in this programme. In XTEND-1 (von Drygalski 2023, PMID: 36720133), once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa 50 IU/kg in 133 patients aged 12 or older gave an estimated mean annualised bleeding rate of 0.71, and the intra-patient comparison showed the mean rate falling from 2.96 on prestudy factor VIII prophylaxis to 0.69 on efanesoctocog alfa (P<0.001), with factor VIII activity above 40 IU/dL for most of the week and 15 IU/dL at day 7; no inhibitors were detected. XTEND-Kids found the same pattern in 74 children, with no inhibitors (Malec 2024, PMID: 39018533). Matching-adjusted indirect comparisons against standard and extended half-life products also favour efanesoctocog alfa, but they are indirect and industry-modelled (Klamroth 2025, PMID: 39576433). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intra-patient design is stronger than a bare single-arm series, but without randomisation the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: von Drygalski 2023 (XTEND-1, single-arm phase 3, 159 patients): mean annualised bleeding rate 0.71 on weekly prophylaxis; intra-patient rate fell from 2.96 on prestudy prophylaxis to 0.69 (P<0.001); 97% of bleeds resolved with one injection
cards.summary: von Drygalski 2023 (XTEND-1, single-arm phase 3, 159 patients): mean annualised bleeding rate 0.71 on weekly prophylaxis; intra-patient rate fell from 2.96 on prestudy prophylaxis to 0.69 (P<0.001); 97% of bleeds resolved with one injection
cards.type: Single-arm phase 3 study with intra-patient prestudy comparator (XTEND-1, von Drygalski 2023) — no randomised control
cards.people: Previously treated patients aged 12 years or older with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors: group A (133 patients) received once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa prophylaxis (50 IU/kg) for 52 weeks; group B (26 patients) received on-demand efanesoctocog alfa for 26 weeks followed by weekly prophylaxis for 26 weeks.
cards.result: In group A the median annualised bleeding rate was 0 (interquartile range 0-1.04) and the estimated mean rate was 0.71 (95% CI 0.52-0.97). The key secondary intra-patient comparison showed the mean annualised bleeding rate falling from 2.96 (95% CI 2.00-4.37) during prestudy factor VIII prophylaxis to 0.69 (95% CI 0.43-1.11) on efanesoctocog alfa, superior to prestudy prophylaxis (P<0.001). In the overall population, 97% of bleeding episodes resolved with one injection. Weekly prophylaxis held mean factor VIII activity above 40 IU/dL for the majority of the week and at 15 IU/dL on day 7, and improved physical health (P<0.001), pain intensity (P=0.03) and joint health (P=0.01). No factor VIII inhibitors developed.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the headline comparison is against each patient's own prestudy period, which is vulnerable to regression to the mean, prestudy under-treatment and period effects. Patients were previously treated and inhibitor-free — the population least likely to develop inhibitors.
cards.source: von Drygalski A et al. Efanesoctocog Alfa Prophylaxis for Patients with Severe Hemophilia A. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36720133. Registry ID: NCT04161495. cards.headline: Malec 2024 (XTEND-Kids, single-arm phase 3, 74 children): no factor VIII inhibitors; median annualised bleeding rate 0.00 and mean 0.61; 64% had no treated bleeding episodes over 52 weeks
cards.summary: Malec 2024 (XTEND-Kids, single-arm phase 3, 74 children): no factor VIII inhibitors; median annualised bleeding rate 0.00 and mean 0.61; 64% had no treated bleeding episodes over 52 weeks
cards.type: Single-arm phase 3 study (XTEND-Kids, Malec 2024) — no comparator
cards.people: 74 previously treated boys younger than 12 years with severe haemophilia A (38 aged under 6 years, 36 aged 6 to under 12 years) receiving once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa prophylaxis (50 IU/kg) for 52 weeks; 73 were treated according to protocol.
cards.result: No factor VIII inhibitors developed (the primary endpoint). The median annualised rate of treated bleeding episodes was 0.00 (interquartile range 0.00-1.02) and the model-based mean was 0.61 (95% CI 0.42-0.90). Forty-seven patients (64%) had no treated bleeding episodes, 65 (88%) had no spontaneous bleeds and 61 (82%) had no joint bleeds; 41 of 43 bleeding episodes (95%) resolved with one injection. Mean factor VIII activity at steady state was above 40 IU/dL for 3 days and above 10 IU/dL for almost 7 days after a dose; the geometric mean terminal half-life was 40.0 hours. Most adverse events were nonserious and none assessed as related serious events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no prestudy intra-patient bleeding comparison reported in the record; 74 children over 52 weeks cannot exclude uncommon inhibitor development, and all were previously treated patients.
cards.source: Malec L et al. Efanesoctocog Alfa Prophylaxis for Children with Severe Hemophilia A. New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39018533. Registry ID: NCT04759131. cards.headline: Klamroth 2025 (matching-adjusted indirect comparisons from XTEND-1): efanesoctocog alfa associated with 2.24 fewer bleeds/year versus extended half-life and 3.61 fewer versus standard half-life prophylaxis
cards.summary: Klamroth 2025 (matching-adjusted indirect comparisons from XTEND-1): efanesoctocog alfa associated with 2.24 fewer bleeds/year versus extended half-life and 3.61 fewer versus standard half-life prophylaxis
cards.type: Matching-adjusted indirect comparison and meta-analysis (Klamroth 2025) — indirect, not a head-to-head trial
cards.people: Adolescent and adult patients with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors: efanesoctocog alfa data from XTEND-1 indirectly compared, after matching adjustment, with phase 3 trials of four extended half-life products (rurioctocog alfa pegol, efmoroctocog alfa, turoctocog alfa pegol, damoctocog alfa pegol) and two standard half-life octocog alfa products; comparison estimates were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: Efanesoctocog alfa was associated with significantly lower annualised bleeding rates than extended half-life therapies for any bleeds (mean difference -2.24, 95% CI -3.24 to -1.25), spontaneous bleeds (-1.52) and joint bleeds (-1.60), and than standard half-life therapies for any bleeds (-3.61, 95% CI -4.43 to -2.79), treated bleeds (-1.55), spontaneous bleeds (-2.52) and joint bleeds (-3.42) — on average 2.2 and 3.6 fewer bleeds per year respectively.
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons across trials with different populations, bleed definitions and eras; matching can only adjust for measured differences. This is supportive modelling, not randomised head-to-head evidence, and it reuses the same single-arm XTEND-1 data.
cards.source: Klamroth R et al. Efanesoctocog Alfa versus Standard and Extended Half-Life Factor VIII Prophylaxis in Adolescent and Adult Patients with Haemophilia A without Inhibitors. Advances in Therapy. 2025. PMID: 39576433. Registry ID: NCT04161495. MeSH: Adolescent; Adult; Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic; Drug Combinations; Factor VIII; Half-Life; Hemophilia A; Hemorrhage; Humans; Young Adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa holds near-normal factor VIII levels and very low bleeding rates in adults and children — POSSIBLE, on single-arm intra-patient evidence with no randomised comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa holds near-normal factor VIII levels and very low bleeding rates in adults and children — POSSIBLE, on single-arm intra-patient evidence with no randomised comparator
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: XTEND-1 (159 patients aged 12 or older), XTEND-Kids (74 children) and the indirect-comparison analysis built on XTEND-1.
cards.result: The pharmacology delivers what it promises — factor VIII activity above 40 IU/dL for most of the week on one injection — and bleeding rates are low in both age groups, with the adult intra-patient comparison (2.96 to 0.69 bleeds/year) the strongest single piece of evidence. No inhibitors were detected in 233 previously treated patients. What is missing is any randomised or parallel comparison, so benefit over modern extended half-life prophylaxis rests on intra-patient and indirect contrasts and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit), single-arm label on the face.
cards.watchOut: Previously treated, inhibitor-free patients only: nothing here addresses previously untreated patients, inhibitor patients, or head-to-head performance against emicizumab (homed at Shelves #671 and #1414).
cards.source: Synthesis of von Drygalski A et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36720133; Malec L et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39018533; Klamroth R et al. Advances in Therapy. 2025. PMID: 39576433. Registry IDs as on the cards above.

shelves.title: Concizumab prophylaxis in haemophilia A/B (with or without inhibitors): treated bleeding rates fell by about four-fifths or more versus no prophylaxis in the explorer7 and explorer8 phase 3 trials (annualised rate 1.7 versus 11.8 episodes with inhibitors)
shelves.question: In people with haemophilia A or B, with or without inhibitors, does concizumab prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes versus no prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Hemophilia A/drug therapy · *Hemophilia B/drug therapy · Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Injections, Subcutaneous
shelves.balance: Concizumab is a monoclonal antibody against tissue factor pathway inhibitor, given as a once-daily subcutaneous prophylaxis and designed to restore thrombin generation in all haemophilia types. Two randomised phase 3 trials from the single explorer programme ask the same question against no prophylaxis (on-demand factor treatment). In explorer7 (haemophilia A or B WITH inhibitors; Matsushita 2023), the estimated mean annualised bleeding rate for treated spontaneous and traumatic episodes was 1.7 episodes on concizumab versus 11.8 episodes with no prophylaxis — a rate ratio of 0.14, an 86% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed beside it. In explorer8 (haemophilia A or B WITHOUT inhibitors; Chowdary 2024), the annualised bleeding rate ratios were 0.14 for haemophilia A (an 86% relative reduction) and 0.21 for haemophilia B (a 79% relative reduction); the fetched record reports the ratios and does not print the two absolute annualised rates, so none are printed here. Both trials were paused after non-fatal thromboembolic events in three patients across the programme and restarted with a loading dose of 1.0 mg/kg followed by 0.2 mg/kg daily, adjustable by week-4 plasma concentration; no thromboembolic events were reported after restart in either trial, and explorer8 recorded one fatal intra-abdominal haemorrhage judged possibly treatment-related. The evidence is one sponsor programme with open-label designs and short randomised comparisons (at least 24 weeks without prophylaxis), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: explorer7 (Matsushita 2023): concizumab cut the treated bleeding rate from 11.8 to 1.7 episodes a year in haemophilia A/B with inhibitors (rate ratio 0.14)
cards.summary: explorer7 (Matsushita 2023): concizumab cut the treated bleeding rate from 11.8 to 1.7 episodes a year in haemophilia A/B with inhibitors (rate ratio 0.14)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (explorer7, haemophilia with inhibitors)
cards.people: 133 patients with haemophilia A or B with inhibitors enrolled; the primary randomised comparison was 19 patients assigned to no prophylaxis for at least 24 weeks (group 1) versus 33 assigned to concizumab prophylaxis for at least 32 weeks (group 2); a further 81 patients were non-randomly assigned to concizumab (groups 3 and 4).
cards.result: The estimated mean annualised bleeding rate for treated spontaneous and traumatic bleeding episodes was 11.8 episodes (95% CI 7.0 to 19.9) with no prophylaxis versus 1.7 episodes (95% CI 1.0 to 2.9) with concizumab — rate ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.29; P<0.001), an 86% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed here beside it. The overall median annualised bleeding rate across all concizumab groups (2, 3 and 4) was 0 episodes. After the restart with the revised dosing regimen, no thromboembolic events were reported, and concizumab plasma concentrations remained stable over time.
cards.watchOut: The randomised no-prophylaxis comparison is small (19 versus 33 patients) and most enrolled patients (81 of 133) received concizumab outside that comparison. The programme had been paused for non-fatal thromboembolic events in three patients receiving concizumab (one from this trial) before the dosing regimen was revised — the clean post-restart safety record covers a limited exposure period.
cards.source: Matsushita T et al. Phase 3 Trial of Concizumab in Hemophilia with Inhibitors. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37646676. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04083781. MeSH: Humans · *Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Body Weight · *Hemophilia A/complications/drug therapy · *Thromboembolism/prevention & control · Injections, Subcutaneous

cards.headline: explorer8 (Chowdary 2024): bleeding-rate ratios of 0.14 in haemophilia A and 0.21 in haemophilia B without inhibitors versus no prophylaxis
cards.summary: explorer8 (Chowdary 2024): bleeding-rate ratios of 0.14 in haemophilia A and 0.21 in haemophilia B without inhibitors versus no prophylaxis
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3a trial (explorer8, haemophilia without inhibitors)
cards.people: 148 male patients aged 12 years or older with severe haemophilia A or moderate/severe haemophilia B without inhibitors, randomly assigned or allocated after the trial restart: group 1 (no prophylaxis) 9 haemophilia A and 12 haemophilia B; group 2 (concizumab) 18 haemophilia A and 24 haemophilia B; groups 3 and 4 (non-randomised concizumab) 55 haemophilia A and 30 haemophilia B. 173 patients were screened at 69 sites in 31 countries.
cards.result: The estimated mean annualised bleeding rate ratio for treated spontaneous and traumatic bleeding episodes, concizumab versus no prophylaxis, was 0.14 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.29; p<0.0001) in haemophilia A — an 86% relative reduction — and 0.21 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.45; p<0.0001) in haemophilia B — a 79% relative reduction. These are relative measures: the fetched record does not print the two absolute annualised rates for this trial, so no absolute rates are claimed for explorer8. The most frequent adverse events on concizumab were SARS-CoV-2 infection (19 of 151 patients, 13%), raised fibrin D-dimers (12, 8%) and upper respiratory tract infection (10, 7%). There was one fatal adverse event possibly related to treatment (intra-abdominal haemorrhage in a group-4 patient with haemophilia A and long-standing hypertension). No thromboembolic events were reported between restart and the confirmatory cutoff.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with small randomised no-prophylaxis groups (21 versus 42 patients), and the trial shares the programme-wide pause for thromboembolic events (two of the three patients were from explorer8) before the concentration-guided dosing restart. The extension part was still ongoing at this report, so longer-term safety is not yet in this record.
cards.source: Chowdary P et al. Concizumab prophylaxis in people with haemophilia A or haemophilia B without inhibitors (explorer8): a prospective, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3a trial. The Lancet Haematology. 2024. PMID: 39521008. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04082429. cards.headline: explorer8 patient-reported outcomes (Angchaisuksiri 2025): bodily-pain and quality-of-life scores favoured concizumab over no prophylaxis at week 24
cards.summary: explorer8 patient-reported outcomes (Angchaisuksiri 2025): bodily-pain and quality-of-life scores favoured concizumab over no prophylaxis at week 24
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcome analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (explorer8)
cards.people: Male patients aged 12 years or older with haemophilia A or B without inhibitors in explorer8, randomised 1:2 to no prophylaxis/on-demand treatment (arm 1) or concizumab prophylaxis (arm 2), or allocated to concizumab (arms 3 and 4); outcomes from the SF-36v2, Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adults, Hemophilia Treatment Experience Measure and Haemophilia Patient Preference Questionnaire.
cards.result: The estimated treatment difference at week 24 (arm 2 minus arm 1) for change in SF-36v2 bodily pain was 9.5 points (95% CI 2.4 to 16.7) favouring concizumab, while physical functioning differed by 0.3 points (95% CI -5.1 to 5.6) — the treatment made no difference on that domain. Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adults total score differed by -18.0 points (95% CI -26.4 to -9.5) and its physical-health domain by -16.8 points (95% CI -32.2 to -1.4), both favouring concizumab, and the treatment-experience and preference questionnaires also favoured concizumab prophylaxis over no prophylaxis or previous treatment.
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported outcomes in an open-label trial are vulnerable to expectation effects — patients knew whether they were receiving daily prophylaxis or on-demand treatment — and this is a secondary analysis of the same single programme, not independent confirmation of the bleeding results.
cards.source: Angchaisuksiri P et al. Concizumab prophylaxis in people with hemophilia A or B without inhibitors: patient-reported outcome results from the phase 3 explorer8 study. cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, two randomised trials — a large relative reduction in treated bleeds with and without inhibitors, on a revised dose after a thrombosis pause
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, two randomised trials — a large relative reduction in treated bleeds with and without inhibitors, on a revised dose after a thrombosis pause
cards.people: Synthesis across explorer7 (133 enrolled, haemophilia with inhibitors) and explorer8 (148 assigned, haemophilia without inhibitors), the only randomised evidence for concizumab prophylaxis versus no prophylaxis.
cards.result: Both trials point the same way and by similar relative magnitudes: rate ratio 0.14 with inhibitors (absolute annualised rates 1.7 versus 11.8 episodes) and 0.14 (haemophilia A) / 0.21 (haemophilia B) without inhibitors. What the programme has not yet shown is long-term safety on the revised concentration-guided dose, any comparison against factor prophylaxis or other non-factor prophylaxis rather than no prophylaxis, and durability beyond the confirmatory cutoffs. The single-programme cap applies: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials are open-label and sponsor-run, the randomised no-prophylaxis arms are small, and the thromboembolic events that paused the programme mean the safety question is settled only for the post-restart regimen and follow-up so far.
cards.source: Synthesis of Matsushita T et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37646676); Chowdary P et al. The Lancet Haematology. 2024 (PMID: 39521008); Angchaisuksiri P et al. Research and Practice in Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2025 (PMID: 40166710)

shelves.title: Starling forces in humans (physiology): interstitial pressure is slightly negative, plasma colloid osmotic pressure ~24–26 mmHg and interstitial COP roughly 6–13 mmHg, so net filtration is small — and when filtration rises, falling interstitial COP (washdown) is the measured buffer; Guyton's ~17 mmHg total safety-factor budget is the textbook's account
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the Starling forces across capillaries — interstitial fluid pressure and colloid osmotic pressures — and how large are the safety factors against oedema?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Arteriosclerosis/physiopathology · Blood Pressure · Capillary Permeability · Catheterization · Extracellular Space · Female · Humans · Hydrostatic Pressure · Male · Middle Aged · Osmotic Pressure · Pregnancy · Regional Blood Flow
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): capillary exchange is set by four forces — capillary pressure pushing out, interstitial pressure (slightly negative, ~−3 mmHg in the textbook's account) pushing in, plasma colloid osmotic pressure (~28 mmHg in the textbook) pulling in, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure pulling out — leaving a small net filtration that lymph returns; against oedema the textbook budgets ~17 mmHg of safety factors (negative interstitial pressure ~3 mmHg, increased lymph flow ~7 mmHg, interstitial protein washdown ~7 mmHg). The carded human wick studies measure the same system at slightly lower absolute values: interstitial pressure −0.8 mmHg in healthy ankle tissue (Stranden & Myhre 1983), plasma COP 23.2 mmHg in early pregnancy and 25.6 mmHg in healthy children (Øian 1985; Guthe 2015), interstitial COP 9.2 mmHg at the ankle and up to 13.1 mmHg on the thorax. The washdown factor is not just textbook arithmetic — in pregnancy interstitial COP fell further than plasma COP as filtration rose (Øian), and when bypass dilution reversed the COP gradient, interstitial pressure rose measurably until the gradient recovered (Rein 1988). The lymph-flow limb of the safety budget and the ~17 mmHg total are presented as the textbook's account: no carded record here measures human lymph flow or prints that budget.

cards.headline: Stranden & Myhre 1983: in 20 healthy controls, ankle interstitial pressure was slightly negative (−0.8 mmHg) and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure 9.2 mmHg — the resting Starling balance measured by wicks
cards.summary: Stranden & Myhre 1983: in 20 healthy controls, ankle interstitial pressure was slightly negative (−0.8 mmHg) and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure 9.2 mmHg — the resting Starling balance measured by wicks
cards.type: Human physiological study (wick and wick-in-needle Starling-force measurements), Scand J Clin Lab Invest 1983
cards.people: 20 healthy controls and 27 patients with lower-limb atherosclerosis; subcutaneous tissue at the ankle; interstitial fluid collected by implanted nylon wicks and interstitial fluid pressure (Pif) measured by the wick-in-needle technique.
cards.result: Mean Pif in controls was −0.8 mmHg (patients −1.0 mmHg) — subatmospheric, as the Guyton account requires. Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure (COPif) was 9.2 mmHg in controls versus 5.9 mmHg in atherosclerosis. The calculated reabsorption pressure (the capillary pressure at which filtration balances) was 15.8 mmHg in controls and 18.3 mmHg in patients. In seven patients with arterial emboli Pif was much lower (mean −4.5 mmHg).
cards.watchOut: Healthy-control values come from one ankle site in one laboratory tradition (the Aukland school); interstitial pressure and COPif vary by tissue and site, and the atherosclerosis comparison group is a disease group, not part of the normal reference.
cards.source: Stranden E et al. Transcapillary forces in patients with lower limb ischemia. Scandinavian journal of clinical and laboratory investigation. 1983. PMID: 6622969. cards.headline: Øian 1985: in normal pregnancy the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure fell further than plasma COP (thorax 13.1→8.4 mmHg) — the washdown safety factor working in humans
cards.summary: Øian 1985: in normal pregnancy the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure fell further than plasma COP (thorax 13.1→8.4 mmHg) — the washdown safety factor working in humans
cards.type: Human physiological study (wick COP and wick-in-needle pressure in pregnancy), Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1985
cards.people: 10 normal pregnant women in the first trimester and 10 in the third trimester; interstitial fluid collected by implanted subcutaneous wicks (thorax and ankle), interstitial pressure by wick-in-needle, plasma colloid osmotic pressure (COPp) from blood.
cards.result: COPp fell from 23.2 mmHg (first trimester) to 21.1 mmHg (third trimester). COPi fell more: from 13.1 to 8.4 mmHg on the thorax and from 9.6 to 5.5 mmHg at the ankle, with only small changes in interstitial pressure. The authors' reading: the larger fall in COPi than in COPp opposes the increased filtration of pregnancy and prevents a rise in interstitial volume — the protein-washdown safety factor, measured — at the price of a reduced safety margin against oedema in late pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional (different women in each trimester), not longitudinal; pregnancy is a high-filtration state, so the absolute COP values are pregnancy values, while the direction of the COPi fall is the generalisable safety-factor finding.
cards.source: Øian P et al. Oedema-preventing mechanisms in subcutaneous tissue of normal pregnant women. British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1985. PMID: 4063227. cards.headline: Guthe 2015: in 99 healthy children, mean plasma colloid osmotic pressure was 25.6 mmHg — the modern reference value for the plasma side of the Starling balance
cards.summary: Guthe 2015: in 99 healthy children, mean plasma colloid osmotic pressure was 25.6 mmHg — the modern reference value for the plasma side of the Starling balance
cards.type: Human physiological study (plasma and wick interstitial COP reference values), PLoS One 2015
cards.people: 99 healthy children aged 2–10 years; nylon wicks implanted subcutaneously in arm and leg during sedation for minor surgery; COP of plasma and wick (interstitial) fluid measured in a colloid osmometer built for small samples.
cards.result: Mean plasma COP was 25.6 ± 3.3 mmHg. Plasma and interstitial COP did not differ by sex, arm versus leg site, or (under 8 years) by age; children aged 8–10 years had significantly higher COP in both plasma and interstitial fluid. Prolonged wick implantation did not change interstitial COP, and gravity had no significant effect on it. The authors note child values are comparable to adults.
cards.watchOut: Children, not adults, and wicks were placed during anaesthesia for minor surgery; the abstract prints the plasma mean but not a single interstitial mean value, so no interstitial number is claimed from this record.
cards.source: Guthe HJ et al. Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure in healthy children. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 25853713. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01044641. cards.headline: Rein 1988: during extracorporeal circulation the transcapillary COP gradient reversed (interstitial COP exceeded plasma COP) and interstitial pressure rose — the safety factors overwhelmed, in real time
cards.summary: Rein 1988: during extracorporeal circulation the transcapillary COP gradient reversed (interstitial COP exceeded plasma COP) and interstitial pressure rose — the safety factors overwhelmed, in real time
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial Starling forces around cardiac surgery), Cardiovasc Drugs Ther 1988
cards.people: 13 patients undergoing coronary surgery with extracorporeal circulation (ECC); COP of interstitial fluid by wick and by suction-blister, interstitial pressure by wick-in-needle, plasma COP from cubital venous blood, before, during and for 24 h after ECC.
cards.result: Plasma COP fell by about 50% during ECC and recovered within 6 h. Interstitial COP was higher than plasma COP during ECC and reached its minimum 4–5 h postoperatively; the normal gradient direction (plasma > interstitial) was restored after ECC but the pre-ECC interstitial level was not regained within 24 h. Interstitial pressure rose during ECC and for 2–3 h afterwards, returning to baseline within 24 h — a measured episode of net filtration predisposing to interstitial oedema until several hours after surgery.
cards.watchOut: A surgical/dilutional stress, not resting physiology — carded to show the forces moving and the safety margin being consumed, not as normal values; N = 13.
cards.source: Rein KA et al. Time-related changes in the Starling forces following extracorporeal circulation. Cardiovascular drugs and therapy. 1988. PMID: 3154633. cards.headline: Synthesis: the human wick measurements match the Guyton Starling picture — near-zero/negative interstitial pressure, plasma COP ~24–26 mmHg, interstitial COP roughly 6–13 mmHg — and the safety factors are the textbook's arithmetic on top of them
cards.summary: Synthesis: the human wick measurements match the Guyton Starling picture — near-zero/negative interstitial pressure, plasma COP ~24–26 mmHg, interstitial COP roughly 6–13 mmHg — and the safety factors are the textbook's arithmetic on top of them
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Stranden & Myhre 1983; Øian 1985; Guthe 2015; Rein 1988), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology as textbook framing.
cards.result: The measured forces agree across four decades of wick studies: interstitial pressure sits at or just below atmospheric (−0.8 mmHg in healthy ankle tissue), plasma COP is ~23–26 mmHg, and interstitial COP is substantial (about 9 mmHg at the ankle, 10–13 mmHg at the thorax in early pregnancy) — so the net filtration pressure at the capillary is small, not the large gradient a plasma-only view would suggest. The washdown safety factor is directly visible: when filtration rose in pregnancy, interstitial COP fell further than plasma COP, buffering volume (Øian); when the gradient was forcibly reversed by bypass dilution, interstitial pressure rose and oedema threatened until the gradient recovered (Rein). Guyton's quantitative safety-factor budget — roughly 3 mmHg from negative interstitial pressure, ~7 mmHg from increased lymph flow and ~7 mmHg from interstitial protein washdown, ~17 mmHg in total — is presented as the textbook's account: no carded human record prints that budget, and the lymph-flow limb in particular rests on the textbook synthesis of animal and human lymph work rather than on a carded human measurement here.
cards.watchOut: No carded record measures human lymph flow directly, so the lymph safety factor is carried as textbook framing only; capillary pressure itself is inferred (reabsorption pressure), never measured directly in these human studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 6622969, 4063227, 25853713, 3154633), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: EPO and haemoglobin recovery after blood loss (physiology): erythropoietin rises within 6 hours and peaks at days 7–14 after a 400 mL phlebotomy, haemoglobin nadirs at days 3–7 and haemoglobin mass is rebuilt in a mean of 36 days after a standard donation — while ferritin is still ~55% of baseline at day 56
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how quickly do erythropoietin and reticulocytes respond after acute blood loss or phlebotomy, and how long does haemoglobin take to recover?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Donors · Bloodletting · Erythropoiesis · Erythropoietin/blood · Female · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Male · Reticulocytes · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): erythropoietin, made mainly by the kidney in response to reduced oxygen delivery, drives reticulocyte production over days and red-cell mass over weeks. The phlebotomy/donation studies give that account a human clock — a different stimulus and time course from altitude hypoxia (pack #6266, cross-pointed; none of its studies re-carded). After 400 mL, erythropoietin is up within 6 hours (~20 mU/mL) but peaks only at days 7–14 (~26–29 mU/mL), haemoglobin nadirs at days 3–7, and haemoglobin concentration has not fully recovered by day 56 (Maeda 1992, N = 14). Measured properly as haemoglobin mass (CO rebreathing), a standard ~550 mL donation's 75 g loss is rebuilt in a mean of 36 ± 11 days, range 20–59 (Pottgiesser 2008, N = 29). The slowest limb is iron: ferritin is still ~55% of baseline at day 56 in repeat donors, with hepcidin shifting from day 1 (Lotfi 2015, N = 27). Reticulocyte values were sampled in these programmes but are not printed in the fetched abstracts, so the reticulocyte limb is carried as the textbook's account in the Synthesis, not as carded numbers.

cards.headline: Maeda 1992: after a single 400 mL phlebotomy, serum erythropoietin rose within 6 hours (to ~20 mU/mL), peaked at days 7–14 (~26–29 mU/mL), haemoglobin bottomed at days 3–7 — and haemoglobin had still not fully recovered by day 56
cards.summary: Maeda 1992: after a single 400 mL phlebotomy, serum erythropoietin rose within 6 hours (to ~20 mU/mL), peaked at days 7–14 (~26–29 mU/mL), haemoglobin bottomed at days 3–7 — and haemoglobin had still not fully recovered by day 56
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial EPO and haemoglobin after phlebotomy), Int J Hematol 1992
cards.people: 14 normal healthy subjects (8 men, 6 women) followed for 56 days after a single 400 mL phlebotomy, with serial haemoglobin, serum erythropoietin and iron measurements.
cards.result: Erythropoietin rose by 6 hours — from 14.6 ± 4.0 to 20.1 ± 5.4 mU/mL in men and 13.4 ± 4.1 to 20.7 ± 7.0 mU/mL in women — and kept rising to a peak at days 7–14 (25.5 ± 6.3 men; 28.7 ± 11.5 women) before declining toward baseline by day 56. Haemoglobin fell to a nadir at days 3–7, then rose gradually but did not completely recover to pre-phlebotomy levels by day 56. The authors judge the endogenous erythropoietin response to a 400 mL loss relatively small — the rationale for recombinant erythropoietin support in autologous donation programmes.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports erythropoietin and haemoglobin time courses; reticulocyte values, though in the record's MeSH, are not printed in the abstract, so no reticulocyte number is claimed from this record. A 400 mL loss is smaller than a standard ~500 mL donation.
cards.source: Maeda H et al. The effect of phlebotomy on serum erythropoietin levels in normal healthy subjects. International journal of hematology. 1992. PMID: 1511160. cards.headline: Pottgiesser 2008: after a standard ~550 mL donation, the lost haemoglobin mass (75 g, 8.8%) took a mean of 36 days to recover (range 20–59) by CO-rebreathing — inside the 56-day minimum donation interval
cards.summary: Pottgiesser 2008: after a standard ~550 mL donation, the lost haemoglobin mass (75 g, 8.8%) took a mean of 36 days to recover (range 20–59) by CO-rebreathing — inside the 56-day minimum donation interval
cards.type: Human physiological study (haemoglobin-mass recovery after donation, CO rebreathing), Transfusion 2008
cards.people: 29 male volunteers (30 ± 10 years) studied before and serially after 1-unit standard blood donation (~550 mL whole blood), with total haemoglobin mass measured by the optimised CO-rebreathing method until recovery criteria were met.
cards.result: Donation removed 75 ± 15 g of haemoglobin mass (8.8 ± 1.9%). Recovery took a mean of 36 ± 11 days, with a wide individual range of 20–59 days. Because haemoglobin concentration is confounded by plasma-volume shifts, haemoglobin mass is the direct recovery variable — and on that variable the authors confirm the minimal recommended donation interval (56 days for men) as adequate.
cards.watchOut: Men only, and haemoglobin mass — not erythropoietin or reticulocytes — is the measured variable; the slowest recoverer (59 days) exceeded the mean interval, a spread worth noticing alongside the reassuring mean.

cards.headline: Lotfi 2015: in 27 repeat donors followed for 56 days, ferritin was still only ~55% of baseline at day 56 and hepcidin shifted from day 1 — iron recovery lags haemoglobin recovery
cards.summary: Lotfi 2015: in 27 repeat donors followed for 56 days, ferritin was still only ~55% of baseline at day 56 and hepcidin shifted from day 1 — iron recovery lags haemoglobin recovery
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial iron/erythropoietic markers after donation), Transfus Med Hemother 2015
cards.people: 27 male repeat blood donors tested on the day of donation and at days 1, 3, 7, 10 and 56 afterwards: ferritin, hepcidin, transferrin, transferrin receptor, haemoglobin, erythropoietin, reticulocytes and reticulocyte haemoglobin, among other markers.
cards.result: At 56 days, average ferritin had fallen to 55% of the initial value (range 30–100%) — stores had not recovered even as haemoglobin recovered. Hepcidin showed the largest and most significant changes, beginning 1 day after donation and lasting the whole 56 days, with wide inter-individual variation; donors with a hepcidin/ferritin quotient below 0.3 regained 60% of initial ferritin by day 56, versus under 50% for those at or above 0.3. The serial design documents erythropoietin and reticulocyte sampling across the same window, though the abstract prints the iron-axis numbers rather than their values.
cards.watchOut: Repeat (iron-depleted-prone) male donors, not first-time donors; erythropoietin and reticulocyte values are not printed in the abstract and are not claimed here — the card carries the iron-recovery time course the record does print.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one unit of blood produces a small, slow erythropoietin signal (up within hours, peaking at 1–2 weeks), a haemoglobin nadir inside a week, haemoglobin-mass recovery in about 5 weeks, and iron stores still depleted at 8 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: one unit of blood produces a small, slow erythropoietin signal (up within hours, peaking at 1–2 weeks), a haemoglobin nadir inside a week, haemoglobin-mass recovery in about 5 weeks, and iron stores still depleted at 8 weeks
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Maeda 1992; Pottgiesser 2008; Lotfi 2015), framed by Guyton & Hall's red-cell regulation account as textbook framing. The altitude stimulus is a different shelf (pack #6266) and none of its studies is re-carded here.
cards.result: The time course is layered. Signal first: erythropoietin rises within 6 hours of a 400 mL loss but only modestly (to ~20 mU/mL, peaking ~26–29 mU/mL at days 7–14) — a blunted-looking response next to the altitude response on pack #6266, where hypoxia drives erythropoietin up within hours and far higher; blood loss works through the slower route of reduced red-cell mass at normal oxygen tension, which is the Guyton & Hall distinction between the two stimuli. Concentration next: haemoglobin bottoms at days 3–7 as plasma volume refills faster than red cells are replaced. Mass next: the ~75 g of haemoglobin in a standard donation is rebuilt in a mean of 36 days (range 20–59). Stores last: ferritin is still ~55% of baseline at day 56, with hepcidin suppressed from day 1 — the iron axis, not the erythropoietin axis, is the long pole of recovery, and it is why donation intervals and donor iron are governed by ferritin rather than by haemoglobin alone. Reticulocyte kinetics sit between signal and mass in the textbook account (a rise within days, peaking around 1–2 weeks); the carded abstracts sample reticulocytes serially but do not print their values, so that limb is presented as the textbook's account.
cards.watchOut: All three studies are in men or mixed small samples after a single loss; repeated donation, iron supplementation and female donor physiology shift the iron limb substantially and are separate questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 1511160, 18466177, 26733771), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. Altitude erythropoietin is homed on pack #6266 and deliberately not re-carded. No additional source.

shelves.title: Sweat electrolytes and acclimatisation (physiology) — PARTIAL slice: whole-body sweat sodium centres near 41 mmol/L (potassium ~3.6 mmol/L) with wide individual spread, and heat acclimation dilutes sweat — sodium/chloride fall to ~60% of day-1 values over 10 days — even as sweat volume rises
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the sodium concentration and total electrolyte loss in sweat, and how does heat acclimatisation change sweat composition?
shelves.mesh: *Acclimatization · Adult · Chlorides/metabolism · Eccrine Glands/metabolism · Exercise/physiology · Female · Hot Temperature · Humans · Male · Potassium/metabolism · Sodium/analysis,metabolism · Sweat/chemistry · Sweating/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — PARTIAL slice, flagged prominently. Home first: pack #6263 already homes sweating and vasodilation thresholds and sweat rates (and their acclimation shifts); none of its studies is re-carded here, and this shelf asks only the composition question #6263 does not: what is in the sweat, and how does acclimatisation change that? Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): the eccrine gland secretes a plasma-like fluid and the duct reabsorbs sodium, so composition depends on flow rate and on ductal reabsorptive capacity. The human data: by the reference whole-body washdown method, sweat sodium is 41 ± 19 mmol/L and potassium 3.6 ± 0.7 mmol/L during exercise in the heat, with regional patches overestimating sodium by ~44% (Baker 2009, N = 20). Acclimation dilutes sweat even as volume rises — sodium and chloride fall to ~60% of day-1 concentrations by day 10 of controlled hyperthermia, beginning by day 3, potassium unchanged (Klous 2020, N = 8); expressed against sweat rate, acclimation lowers sweat sodium by 15 mmol/L at any given rate, attributed to increased ductal reabsorption (Buono 2007, N = 8). One classic field study found no composition change with acclimatisation (Collins 1971, N = 6, at sea) and is carded as the counterweight.

cards.headline: Baker 2009: whole-body washdown put sweat sodium at 41 ± 19 mmol/L and potassium at 3.6 ± 0.7 mmol/L during exercise in the heat — regional patches overestimated sodium by ~44% (59 ± 27)
cards.summary: Baker 2009: whole-body washdown put sweat sodium at 41 ± 19 mmol/L and potassium at 3.6 ± 0.7 mmol/L during exercise in the heat — regional patches overestimated sodium by ~44% (59 ± 27)
cards.type: Human physiological study (whole-body washdown vs regional sweat collection), J Appl Physiol 2009
cards.people: 20 athletes (10 men, 10 women) cycling for 90 min in the heat inside a plastic chamber; whole-body washdown (the reference method, collecting all unevaporated sweat) compared simultaneously with regional absorbent patches at five sites.
cards.result: Whole-body sweat sodium concentration was 41 ± 19 meq/L (= mmol/L for sodium) and potassium 3.6 ± 0.7 meq/L; five-site regional collection significantly overestimated both (sodium 59 ± 27, potassium 4.4 ± 0.7 meq/L). The thigh was the best single predictor of whole-body sodium (within 1 ± 8 meq/L) and the chest for potassium. At typical sweat rates near 1 L/h, a whole-body sodium concentration of ~41 mmol/L implies on the order of 40 mmol (~0.9 g of sodium, ~2.3 g of salt) lost per litre of sweat — the arithmetic is this card's, from the record's concentration.
cards.watchOut: Inter-individual spread is enormous (SD 19 on a mean of 41 mmol/L) — there is no single 'normal' sweat sodium; these athletes were not a heat-acclimation protocol, and patch values must not be quoted as whole-body losses.
cards.source: Baker LB et al. Comparison of regional patch collection vs. whole body washdown for measuring sweat sodium and potassium loss during exercise. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2009. PMID: 19541738. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Klous 2020: over 10 days of controlled-hyperthermia acclimation, sweat sodium, chloride and lactate concentrations fell to ~60% of day-1 values while local sweat rate rose 36–58% — composition and rate adapt on different clocks
cards.summary: Klous 2020: over 10 days of controlled-hyperthermia acclimation, sweat sodium, chloride and lactate concentrations fell to ~60% of day-1 values while local sweat rate rose 36–58% — composition and rate adapt on different clocks
cards.type: Human physiological study (sweat composition across 10-day acclimation), J Therm Biol 2020
cards.people: 8 participants cycling in 33 °C / 65% relative humidity on 10 consecutive days, rectal temperature clamped at 38.5 °C (controlled hyperthermia); sweat collected from upper arm and upper back three times per session; a subgroup later underwent 28 days of decay and 5 days of re-acclimation.
cards.result: By day 10, local sweat rate was up 58% (arm) and 36% (back), while sodium, chloride and lactate concentrations had fallen significantly to ~60% of day-1 values at both sites; potassium did not change significantly (+11% arm, +8% back). The clocks differ: sodium/chloride conservation began by day 3, lactate fell from day 6, and sweat-rate increases arrived at days 7–8. Adaptations were partly conserved after 28 days of decay, and 5 days of re-acclimation appeared sufficient to restore them.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 and local (arm/back) collections, not whole-body washdown — concentrations are regional; the record reports the fall as a proportion (~60% of day 1) rather than absolute start/end mmol/L values, and none are invented here.
cards.source: Klous L et al. Sweat rate and sweat composition during heat acclimation. Journal of thermal biology. 2020. PMID: 33077118. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Buono 2007: after 10 days of exercise heat acclimation, the sweat sodium–sweat rate relationship shifted down by 15 mmol/L — at any given sweat rate, acclimated sweat is 15 mmol/L more dilute
cards.summary: Buono 2007: after 10 days of exercise heat acclimation, the sweat sodium–sweat rate relationship shifted down by 15 mmol/L — at any given sweat rate, acclimated sweat is 15 mmol/L more dilute
cards.type: Human physiological study (sweat sodium–rate relationship across acclimation), J Appl Physiol 2007
cards.people: 8 healthy male volunteers completing 10 days of exercise in the heat, with sweat osmolality and sodium concentration measured against sweat rate before and after acclimation; exercising heart rate fell 18 beats/min and core temperature 0.6 °C with acclimation.
cards.result: Acclimation did not change the slope of the sodium–rate relationship; it lowered its intercept by 15 mmol/L (and the osmolality intercept by 28 mosmol/kgH₂O), so sweat sodium was significantly lower at any given sweat rate after acclimation. The authors' mechanism: acclimation increases the sodium-reabsorption capacity of the eccrine sweat-gland duct — the gland makes more sweat and reclaims more of its sodium.
cards.watchOut: Forearm/regional sweat in 8 men; because sodium rises with sweat rate within a person, single-spot concentrations without a rate are not comparable between people or days.
cards.source: Buono MJ et al. Sodium ion concentration vs. sweat rate relationship in humans. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2007. PMID: 17600161. cards.headline: Collins 1971: the discordant classic — on a tanker voyage to the Persian Gulf, sweat losses reached 3–4 L/day in engine-room crew, and sweat sodium/potassium/nitrogen concentrations tracked the sweat rate but were NOT altered by acclimatisation
cards.summary: Collins 1971: the discordant classic — on a tanker voyage to the Persian Gulf, sweat losses reached 3–4 L/day in engine-room crew, and sweat sodium/potassium/nitrogen concentrations tracked the sweat rate but were NOT altered by acclimatisation
cards.type: Human physiological field study (metabolic balance and sweat losses at sea), Br J Ind Med 1971
cards.people: 3 medical students and 3 crew members studied in 3-day metabolic-balance experiments in Biscay, the South Atlantic and the Persian Gulf, with controlled-hyperthermia acclimatisation testing and full intake/output nutrient balances including sweat losses.
cards.result: Sweat losses reached 3–4 L/day in the two engine-room crew in the Persian Gulf, who trended toward more positive salt and water balance (intakes were adequate). Sweat concentrations of sodium, potassium and nitrogen were related to the rate of 24-hour sweat loss but were not altered by heat acclimatisation in this field study; the daily sweat losses of potassium, nitrogen and iron were too small to disturb their balances. Unacclimatised crew showed temporary cortisol rises with negative nitrogen and potassium balances at first heat exposure.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 in uncontrolled field conditions with salt supplements allowed — its null acclimatisation finding conflicts with the later controlled laboratory studies (Klous; Buono) and is carded as the honest counterweight: method and exposure control differ, and the balance is stated in the Synthesis.
cards.source: Collins KJ et al. Nutritional and environmental studies on an ocean-going oil tanker. 2. Heat acclimatization and nutrient balances. British journal of industrial medicine. 1971. cards.headline: Synthesis: whole-body sweat is roughly 40 mmol/L sodium and 3.6 mmol/L potassium with very wide individual spread; acclimation makes sweat more dilute (sodium down ~40%, or ~15 mmol/L at a given rate) even as volume rises — the composition slice pack #6263 does not cover
cards.summary: Synthesis: whole-body sweat is roughly 40 mmol/L sodium and 3.6 mmol/L potassium with very wide individual spread; acclimation makes sweat more dilute (sodium down ~40%, or ~15 mmol/L at a given rate) even as volume rises — the composition slice pack #6263 does not cover
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Baker 2009; Klous 2020; Buono 2007; Collins 1971), framed by Guyton & Hall's account of sweat-gland secretion and ductal reabsorption as textbook framing. Sweating thresholds and sweat rates are homed on pack #6263 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: The Guyton mechanism — a plasma-like primary secretion whose sodium is reabsorbed in the duct, so faster flow leaves less time for reabsorption and sweat gets saltier — is exactly what the human data show: sodium concentration rises with sweat rate within a person (Buono; Collins), and acclimation shifts the whole relationship down by increasing ductal reabsorption (Buono: −15 mmol/L intercept; Klous: sodium/chloride to ~60% of day-1 by day 10, beginning by day 3, while potassium is essentially unchanged). Whole-body composition by the reference washdown method centres near 41 mmol/L sodium and 3.6 mmol/L potassium, with a standard deviation near half the mean — individual losses at 1 L/h therefore range from well under 20 to over 60 mmol of sodium per hour, which is why replacement guidance is individualised. Collins 1971 stands as the field counterpoint (no composition change with acclimatisation at sea); the controlled laboratory protocols are the stronger design for the composition question, and the discrepancy is most plausibly methodological — uncontrolled exposure, salt supplementation and whole-day collections against clamped laboratory hyperthermia. Total daily losses scale with volume: 3–4 L/day in hot work (Collins) at ~40 mmol/L is on the order of 120–160 mmol of sodium a day before acclimation's dilution is counted.
cards.watchOut: Regional patches overestimate whole-body sodium by ~44% (Baker), so numbers from different collection methods are not interchangeable; chloride tracks sodium in the acclimation studies but absolute chloride values are not printed in the fetched abstracts.

shelves.title: Coronary flow reserve in healthy humans (physiology): flow can rise about fourfold above rest — 4.6 ± 0.9 by adenosine PET and 4.0–4.5 by transthoracic Doppler velocity reserve — measured non-invasively with PET tracers or bedside LAD Doppler during vasodilator infusion
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much can coronary blood flow rise above rest (coronary flow reserve), and how is it measured non-invasively?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Adenosine/pharmacology · Blood Flow Velocity · Coronary Circulation · Echocardiography, Doppler · Female · Humans · Male · Tomography, Emission-Computed · Vascular Resistance · Vasodilator Agents/pharmacology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): resting coronary flow is tightly autoregulated, and the circulation holds a large vasodilator reserve in hand. Adjacency, stated plainly: pack #6304 already homes coronary autoregulation — the pressure range over which flow is held constant and its adenosine/K-ATP mediators — and deliberately excluded reserve magnitude; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here, and this shelf asks only how large the reserve is in healthy humans and how it is measured without a catheter. The measurements converge across methods: by ¹³N-ammonia PET during adenosine, healthy young adults show a flow reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9 (hyperaemic flow 340 ± 57 mL/100 g/min; Muzik 1996, N = 10), and dipyridamole PET gives healthy hyperaemic flow of 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g (Parodi 1992, N = 13). By transthoracic Doppler of the LAD during ATP infusion — fully non-invasive — healthy velocity reserve is 4.02 ± 0.70 (Yamashita 2005, N = 11) and 4.5 ± 0.9 (Hirata 2004, N = 10). The honest summary is a range, ~4- to 4.6-fold, not a single canonical number.

cards.headline: Muzik 1996: by ¹³N-ammonia PET with adenosine, healthy young adults had a myocardial flow reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9 — hyperaemic flow 340 ± 57 vs rate-pressure-corrected rest flow 77 ± 16 mL/100 g/min
cards.summary: Muzik 1996: by ¹³N-ammonia PET with adenosine, healthy young adults had a myocardial flow reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9 — hyperaemic flow 340 ± 57 vs rate-pressure-corrected rest flow 77 ± 16 mL/100 g/min
cards.type: Human physiological study (quantitative PET myocardial flow reserve, healthy controls), J Am Coll Cardiol 1996
cards.people: 10 healthy young adult volunteers (the control arm of a Kawasaki-disease study) and 10 children with prior Kawasaki disease, studied with nitrogen-13 ammonia PET at rest and during adenosine stress; rest flows normalised to the rate-pressure product.
cards.result: In healthy volunteers, hyperaemic myocardial blood flow was 340 ± 57 mL/100 g/min against a corrected rest flow of 77 ± 16 mL/100 g/min, giving a myocardial flow reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9. (The Kawasaki children, by contrast, reached only 263 ± 64 with a reserve of 3.2 ± 0.7 — the disease comparison that makes the healthy value a reference.) Quantitative PET showed no regional perfusion abnormalities in either group.
cards.watchOut: The healthy arm is young adults serving as controls in a paediatric-disease study (N = 10); rest flow is rate-pressure-product-corrected, so the reserve ratio is a corrected ratio, as the record presents it.
cards.source: Muzik O et al. Quantification of myocardial blood flow and flow reserve in children with a history of Kawasaki disease and normal coronary arteries using positron emission tomography. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 1996. PMID: 8772768. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Parodi 1992: by dynamic PET, healthy subjects reached 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g after dipyridamole (and 2.15 ± 0.73 during atrial pacing) — against 2.35 in hypertensive patients on the same protocol
cards.summary: Parodi 1992: by dynamic PET, healthy subjects reached 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g after dipyridamole (and 2.15 ± 0.73 during atrial pacing) — against 2.35 in hypertensive patients on the same protocol
cards.type: Human physiological study (dynamic PET flow reserve, healthy controls), Drugs 1992
cards.people: 13 healthy subjects and 27 patients with essential hypertension and normal coronary arteries, studied by dynamic PET at rest, during atrial pacing and after dipyridamole infusion.
cards.result: Healthy myocardial blood flow rose to 2.15 ± 0.73 mL/min/g during atrial pacing and 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g after dipyridamole. Hypertensive patients started at 0.97 ± 0.25 mL/min/g at rest and reached only 1.60 ± 0.38 (pacing) and 2.35 ± 0.95 (dipyridamole) — both significantly below the healthy hyperaemic values. The record prints the healthy hyperaemic flows rather than a healthy rest flow or ratio, so this card claims the hyperaemic ceiling, not a reserve ratio.
cards.watchOut: A hypertension study's control arm (N = 13); dipyridamole and adenosine are related but not identical vasodilator stimuli, and pacing raises flow by demand rather than by vasodilation — three different routes to 'reserve' on one card, kept distinct in the text.
cards.source: Parodi O et al. Regional myocardial blood flow and coronary reserve in hypertensive patients. The effect of therapy. Drugs. 1992. PMID: 1283584. cards.headline: Yamashita 2005: by transthoracic Doppler echocardiography of the LAD with ATP infusion, coronary flow velocity reserve in 11 healthy young men was 4.02 ± 0.70 — a fully non-invasive bedside measurement
cards.summary: Yamashita 2005: by transthoracic Doppler echocardiography of the LAD with ATP infusion, coronary flow velocity reserve in 11 healthy young men was 4.02 ± 0.70 — a fully non-invasive bedside measurement
cards.type: Human physiological study (transthoracic Doppler coronary flow velocity reserve), Int J Cardiol 2005
cards.people: 11 healthy male volunteers (aged 23.3 ± 0.9 years) studied on three days (placebo, oral methionine, methionine + vitamin C) with coronary flow velocity reserve measured by transthoracic Doppler echocardiography of the left anterior descending artery during intravenous adenosine-triphosphate infusion; the placebo-day value is the normal reference. N = 11.
cards.result: On the control condition, hyperaemic average diastolic peak velocity and coronary flow velocity reserve were 87.2 ± 11.4 cm/s and 4.02 ± 0.70. Acute methionine loading (homocysteine 12.9 → 32.1 nmol/mL) cut reserve to 3.35 ± 0.52, and vitamin C co-administration prevented the fall — the study's oxidative-stress point. For this shelf the card carries the method and the healthy reserve: ~4.0 by bedside Doppler, concordant with PET.
cards.watchOut: Velocity reserve in one vessel (LAD), not absolute flow — velocity reserve equals flow reserve only if epicardial diameter is unchanged during hyperaemia; young men only.
cards.source: Yamashita K et al. Experimental hyperhomocysteinemia impairs coronary flow velocity reserve. International journal of cardiology. 2005. PMID: 16168809. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hirata 2004: in 10 healthy men, baseline coronary flow velocity reserve by transthoracic Doppler was 4.5 ± 0.9 — and black tea raised it to 5.2 ± 0.9 within hours
cards.summary: Hirata 2004: in 10 healthy men, baseline coronary flow velocity reserve by transthoracic Doppler was 4.5 ± 0.9 — and black tea raised it to 5.2 ± 0.9 within hours
cards.type: Human physiological study (Doppler flow velocity reserve, tea vs caffeine crossover), Am J Cardiol 2004
cards.people: 10 healthy male volunteers in a double-blind crossover comparison of black tea versus caffeine, with left-anterior-descending coronary flow velocity measured at baseline and during adenosine-triphosphate hyperaemia by transthoracic Doppler echocardiography, before and after each beverage. N = 10.
cards.result: Before beverage consumption, coronary flow velocity reserve was 4.5 ± 0.9. After black tea it rose to 5.2 ± 0.9 (p < 0.0001); the reserve ratio (after ÷ before) was 1.18 ± 0.07 for tea versus 1.04 ± 0.08 for caffeine. The card's physiology content is the second independent healthy Doppler reference (~4.5) and the demonstration that reserve is acutely modifiable by a dietary vasodilator exposure — reserve is a state, not a fixed anatomical constant.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 healthy men; the tea effect is an acute pharmacological observation from a small crossover, carded for its baseline reserve value and the modifiability point, not as a dietary recommendation.
cards.source: Hirata K et al. Black tea increases coronary flow velocity reserve in healthy male subjects. The American journal of cardiology. 2004. PMID: 15165919. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy coronary flow reserve is about 4- to 4.6-fold by PET and about 4.0–4.5 by bedside Doppler — measurable entirely non-invasively, and distinct from the autoregulation shelf (pack #6304)
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy coronary flow reserve is about 4- to 4.6-fold by PET and about 4.0–4.5 by bedside Doppler — measurable entirely non-invasively, and distinct from the autoregulation shelf (pack #6304)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Muzik 1996; Parodi 1992; Yamashita 2005; Hirata 2004), framed by Guyton & Hall's coronary-circulation account as textbook framing. Coronary autoregulation and its mediators are homed on pack #6304 and none of its studies is re-carded here.
cards.result: Two independent measurement families converge: quantitative PET gives a healthy reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9 (Muzik, adenosine, ¹³N-ammonia) with hyperaemic flow ~3.4 mL/min/g, and 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g after dipyridamole (Parodi); transthoracic Doppler velocity reserve gives 4.02 ± 0.70 (Yamashita) and 4.5 ± 0.9 (Hirata) in healthy young men. So the healthy coronary circulation can raise flow roughly fourfold-plus above rest — the reserve that autoregulation (pack #6304) spends to hold resting flow constant as pressure falls. Measurement is now routinely non-invasive: PET with ¹³N-ammonia or ¹⁵O-water gives absolute flow in mL/min/g; Doppler echocardiography gives a velocity ratio in the LAD at the bedside; cardiovascular MRI perfusion is the third route named in the textbooks, though no carded record on this shelf uses it, so it is named as a method, not evidenced here. Reserve is also a state variable — acutely lowered by a methionine load and raised by black tea in these small studies — not a fixed property of the vessel.
cards.watchOut: Healthy arms are small (N = 10–13) and mostly young men; vasodilator (adenosine/ATP/dipyridamole), tracer and correction methods differ between studies, so the honest claim is the convergent range (~4–4.6), not a single canonical number.

shelves.title: GLOBAL LEADERS strategy in all-comer PCI: 1 month of DAPT then ticagrelor alone was not superior to 12 months of conventional DAPT — the primary endpoint was not met (3.81% vs 4.37%; p=0.073) and major bleeding did not fall (2.04% vs 2.12%)
shelves.question: In adults undergoing PCI (all-comers, not only complex PCI), does a strategy of 1 month of dual antiplatelet therapy followed by ticagrelor monotherapy, compared with 12 months of conventional dual therapy, reduce bleeding without increasing ischaemic events?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL build: pack #5821 already covers short DAPT followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after complex PCI specifically; this pack builds only the uncovered all-comers slice — the GLOBAL LEADERS strategy trial itself — and cross-points to #5821 for the complex-PCI subgroup evidence. In GLOBAL LEADERS (15,968 all-comer PCI patients), 1 month of aspirin plus ticagrelor followed by 23 months of ticagrelor alone was not superior to 12 months of conventional DAPT followed by aspirin: the primary endpoint (death or new Q-wave myocardial infarction at 2 years) occurred in 3.81% versus 4.37% (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.75-1.01; p=0.073), and grade 3 or 5 bleeding was essentially identical (2.04% vs 2.12%; rate ratio 0.97). The prespecified GLASSY adjudication substudy (7,585 patients) found the strategy non-inferior for the ischaemic composite (7.14% vs 8.41%) but not superior, with BARC 3 or 5 bleeding unchanged (rate ratio 1.00). By presentation, bleeding fell in acute coronary syndrome patients (1.95% vs 2.68%) but not in stable disease (2.13% vs 1.62%; interaction p=0.007). So the honest answer to the question as posed is no: in all-comers this strategy did not reduce major bleeding, and its ischaemic safety rests on non-inferiority in an adjudicated substudy rather than on the parent trial's met primary endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the all-comer strategy as tested.

cards.headline: GLOBAL LEADERS (15,968 all-comers): the primary endpoint was not met — death or new Q-wave MI 3.81% on 1-month DAPT then ticagrelor alone vs 4.37% on conventional DAPT (rate ratio 0.87; p=0.073); grade 3 or 5 bleeding 2.04% vs 2.12%
cards.summary: GLOBAL LEADERS (15,968 all-comers): the primary endpoint was not met — death or new Q-wave MI 3.81% on 1-month DAPT then ticagrelor alone vs 4.37% on conventional DAPT (rate ratio 0.87; p=0.073); grade 3 or 5 bleeding 2.04% vs 2.12%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (GLOBAL LEADERS, primary report)
cards.people: 15,968 patients undergoing PCI with a biolimus A9-eluting stent for stable coronary artery disease or acute coronary syndromes at 130 sites in 18 countries, randomised to aspirin plus ticagrelor for 1 month then ticagrelor monotherapy for 23 months (n=7,980), or standard DAPT for 12 months (aspirin plus clopidogrel in stable disease, aspirin plus ticagrelor in acute coronary syndromes) then aspirin alone (n=7,988). Open-label, superiority design.
cards.result: At 2 years the primary endpoint (all-cause mortality or non-fatal centrally adjudicated new Q-wave myocardial infarction) occurred in 304 (3.81%) experimental versus 349 (4.37%) control patients (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.75-1.01; p=0.073) — superiority was not shown. Grade 3 or 5 Bleeding Academic Research Consortium bleeding occurred in 163 versus 169 patients (2.04% vs 2.12%; rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.78-1.20; p=0.77). No difference in treatment effect across stable versus acute presentation subgroups (p=0.93).
cards.watchOut: Open-label design with site-reported bleeding; the control arm mixed clopidogrel-based and ticagrelor-based DAPT by presentation, so this is a strategy comparison, not a pure drug comparison. The complex-PCI slice of this strategy question is homed separately in pack #5821 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Vranckx P et al. Ticagrelor plus aspirin for 1 month, followed by ticagrelor monotherapy for 23 months vs aspirin plus clopidogrel or ticagrelor for 12 months, followed by aspirin monotherapy for 12 months after implantation of a drug-eluting stent: a multicentre, open-label, randomised superiority trial. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 30166073. Registry ID: NCT01813435. cards.headline: GLASSY adjudication substudy (7,585 patients): ticagrelor monotherapy after 1 month was non-inferior but not superior for ischaemic events (7.14% vs 8.41%), and BARC 3 or 5 bleeding did not differ (rate ratio 1.00)
cards.summary: GLASSY adjudication substudy (7,585 patients): ticagrelor monotherapy after 1 month was non-inferior but not superior for ischaemic events (7.14% vs 8.41%), and BARC 3 or 5 bleeding did not differ (rate ratio 1.00)
cards.type: Prespecified adjudicated substudy of a randomised trial (GLASSY)
cards.people: 7,585 patients from the 20 top-enrolling GLOBAL LEADERS sites, with events adjudicated by an independent clinical event committee; same randomised strategies as the parent trial.
cards.result: The 2-year coprimary efficacy endpoint (all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent target vessel revascularisation) occurred in 271 (7.14%) experimental versus 319 (8.41%) conventional patients (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.72-0.99), fulfilling non-inferiority (p<0.001) but not superiority (p=0.0465 against a 0.025 threshold). BARC 3 or 5 bleeding rates did not differ (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.75-1.33; p=0.986). A time-dependent effect suggested lower myocardial infarction and definite stent thrombosis after year 1 on the experimental strategy.
cards.watchOut: A substudy of the parent trial, not an independent trial: it strengthens the ischaemic non-inferiority reading but cannot rescue the parent trial's unmet primary endpoint, and it confirms — with adjudicated events — that major bleeding was not reduced.
cards.source: Franzone A et al. Ticagrelor Alone Versus Dual Antiplatelet Therapy From 1 Month After Drug-Eluting Coronary Stenting. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2019. PMID: 31672177. Registry ID: NCT03231059 (GLASSY substudy of GLOBAL LEADERS, NCT01813435). cards.headline: By presentation (prespecified): no efficacy difference in ACS or stable disease; bleeding fell in ACS (1.95% vs 2.68%; rate ratio 0.73) but rose numerically in stable disease (2.13% vs 1.62%; interaction p=0.007)
cards.summary: By presentation (prespecified): no efficacy difference in ACS or stable disease; bleeding fell in ACS (1.95% vs 2.68%; rate ratio 0.73) but rose numerically in stable disease (2.13% vs 1.62%; interaction p=0.007)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial
cards.people: Prespecified subgroup analysis of GLOBAL LEADERS by clinical presentation: acute coronary syndromes (experimental n=3,750; reference n=3,737) versus stable coronary artery disease (experimental n=4,230; reference n=4,251).
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 3.92% versus 4.52% in ACS (rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.69-1.08) and 3.71% versus 4.23% in stable disease (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.08), with no interaction (p=0.926). Grade 3 or 5 bleeding, however, diverged: lower with the experimental strategy in ACS (73 [1.95%] vs 100 [2.68%]; rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.54-0.98) but higher numerically in stable disease (90 [2.13%] vs 69 [1.62%]; rate ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.97-1.81), interaction p=0.007.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup analysis of the same single trial: the ACS bleeding signal is hypothesis-generating and is offset by the opposite direction in stable disease; it does not change the all-comer answer.
cards.source: Vranckx P et al. Efficacy and Safety of Ticagrelor Monotherapy by Clinical Presentation: Pre-Specified Analysis of the GLOBAL LEADERS Trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2021. PMID: 34533034. Registry ID: NCT01813435.
