cards.headline: Synthesis: in all-comers, 1 month of DAPT then ticagrelor monotherapy did not reduce major bleeding and was not superior on ischaemic outcomes — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) as tested; complex-PCI evidence lives in pack #5821
cards.summary: Synthesis: in all-comers, 1 month of DAPT then ticagrelor monotherapy did not reduce major bleeding and was not superior on ischaemic outcomes — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) as tested; complex-PCI evidence lives in pack #5821
cards.people: Synthesis of the GLOBAL LEADERS programme carded above: the parent trial (15,968 patients), its adjudicated GLASSY substudy (7,585 patients) and its prespecified presentation subgroups.
cards.result: Across the programme, the strategy's primary endpoint was unmet, major (grade/BARC 3 or 5) bleeding was unchanged in both the parent trial and the adjudicated substudy, and ischaemic outcomes were non-inferior rather than superior. Any bleeding advantage is confined to the ACS subgroup and is contradicted in stable disease.
cards.watchOut: Do not import the complex-PCI bleeding benefit from pack #5821 into this all-comer question: the populations and comparators differ, and the all-comer trial itself showed no major-bleeding reduction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vranckx P et al. Lancet. 2018. PMID: 30166073; Franzone A et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2019. PMID: 31672177; Vranckx P et al. J Am Heart Assoc. 2021. PMID: 34533034.

shelves.title: Post-PCI FFR optimisation: optimisation raised final FFR modestly (median 0.81 to 0.86 in pooled patient data) but neither randomised trial showed fewer patients reaching FFR ≥0.90 as its primary result or a significant fall in target-vessel failure (FFR-REACT TVF 4.2% vs 4.8%)
shelves.question: In patients with a suboptimal fractional flow reserve (<0.90) after angiographically successful PCI, does physiology- or IVUS-guided post-PCI optimisation, compared with standard care, improve final FFR and reduce target-vessel failure?
shelves.mesh: Coronary Angiography; Coronary Artery Disease; Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial; Humans; Percutaneous Coronary Intervention; Stents; Time Factors; Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Both randomised trials of post-PCI optimisation missed their primary endpoints. TARGET-FFR (260 patients) found a physiology-guided incremental optimisation strategy did not significantly increase the proportion reaching a final FFR ≥0.90 (difference 10%, 95% CI -1.84 to 21.91; p=0.099), though it reduced the proportion left with FFR ≤0.80 (-11.2%, p=0.045); over two-thirds of patients had a suboptimal FFR after angiography-guided PCI. FFR-REACT (291 patients, all with post-PCI FFR <0.90) found IVUS-guided optimisation raised FFR in treated vessels (0.82 to 0.85) and got 20% of vessels to ≥0.90, but 1-year target-vessel failure was unchanged (4.2% vs 4.8%; p=0.79). An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 314 patients confirms optimisation raises FFR (median 0.81 to 0.86, p<0.001) — a surrogate gain. No outcomes-powered trial exists, so whether chasing the number prevents events is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: TARGET-FFR (260 patients): physiology-guided optimisation did NOT significantly increase final FFR ≥0.90 (difference 10%; p=0.099), but cut the proportion left with FFR ≤0.80 by 11.2% (p=0.045)
cards.summary: TARGET-FFR (260 patients): physiology-guided optimisation did NOT significantly increase final FFR ≥0.90 (difference 10%; p=0.099), but cut the proportion left with FFR ≤0.80 by 11.2% (p=0.045)
cards.people: 260 patients at a single centre randomised after angiographically guided PCI to a physiology-guided incremental optimisation strategy (PIOS, n=131) or blinded physiology assessment (control, n=129); 68.1% had an initial post-PCI FFR <0.90, and 30.5% of the PIOS group underwent further intervention (post-dilation and/or additional stenting).
cards.result: The primary outcome — proportion with final post-PCI FFR ≥0.90 — did not differ significantly (PIOS minus control 10%, 95% CI -1.84 to 21.91; p=0.099). The prioritised secondary outcome favoured optimisation: the proportion with a final FFR ≤0.80 was significantly reduced (-11.2%, 95% CI -21.87 to -0.35; p=0.045).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, feasibility-sized trial with a physiological (not clinical-outcome) primary endpoint; the significant result is on the secondary ≤0.80 threshold, not the primary ≥0.90 target.
cards.source: Collison D et al. Post-stenting fractional flow reserve vs coronary angiography for optimization of percutaneous coronary intervention (TARGET-FFR). European heart journal. 2021. PMID: 34279606. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Coronary Angiography; Coronary Artery Disease; Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial; Humans; Percutaneous Coronary Intervention; Stents; Time Factors; Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: FFR-REACT (291 patients, all post-PCI FFR <0.90): IVUS-guided optimisation raised FFR (0.82 to 0.85) and reached ≥0.90 in 20% of vessels, but 1-year target-vessel failure did not fall (4.2% vs 4.8%; p=0.79)
cards.summary: FFR-REACT (291 patients, all post-PCI FFR <0.90): IVUS-guided optimisation raised FFR (0.82 to 0.85) and reached ≥0.90 in 20% of vessels, but 1-year target-vessel failure did not fall (4.2% vs 4.8%; p=0.79)
cards.people: 291 patients (309 vessels) with post-PCI FFR <0.90 at angiographically successful PCI, randomised at a single centre to IVUS-guided optimisation (n=145 patients/152 vessels) or standard of care (n=146/157); mean post-PCI FFR was 0.84 ± 0.05, and 68.4% of intervention vessels underwent additional optimisation (additional stenting 34.9%, post-dilatation only 33.6%).
cards.result: Optimisation increased FFR in treated vessels from 0.82 ± 0.06 to 0.85 ± 0.05 (p<0.001), with a final FFR ≥0.90 in 20% of vessels. The primary endpoint, 1-year target-vessel failure (cardiac death, spontaneous target-vessel myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target-vessel revascularisation), was comparable: 4.2% versus 4.8% (p=0.79). Clinically driven target-vessel revascularisation trended lower (0.7% vs 4.2%; p=0.06). Event rates were lower than expected, limiting power.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and underpowered for clinical events because observed target-vessel failure was far below the assumed rate; four of five vessels could not be brought to FFR ≥0.90 despite IVUS guidance.
cards.source: Neleman T et al. FFR-Guided PCI Optimization Directed by High-Definition IVUS Versus Standard of Care: The FFR REACT Trial. JACC. Cardiovascular interventions. 2022. PMID: 35981832. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Coronary Angiography; Coronary Artery Disease; Fractional Flow Reserve, Myocardial; Humans; Percutaneous Coronary Intervention; Standard of Care; Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis (314 patients, 8 studies contributing data): optimisation raised median FFR from 0.81 to 0.86 (p<0.001) — a surrogate gain, with clinical benefit unestablished
cards.summary: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis (314 patients, 8 studies contributing data): optimisation raised median FFR from 0.81 to 0.86 (p<0.001) — a surrogate gain, with clinical benefit unestablished
cards.people: Systematic review and one-stage individual-patient-data meta-analysis of studies with paired FFR measurements before and after post-PCI optimisation after drug-eluting stent PCI; 11 studies met selection criteria and 8 provided patient data (314 patients undergoing optimisation).
cards.result: Median FFR improved from 0.81 (IQR 0.75-0.85) to 0.86 (IQR 0.81-0.89) after optimisation (p<0.001). Additional stenting produced a larger FFR increase than post-dilatation alone, while left-anterior-descending location and higher starting post-PCI FFR predicted smaller gains. The analysis addresses the FFR change, not a demonstrated reduction in clinical events.
cards.watchOut: Most contributing studies were not randomised comparisons of optimisation versus no optimisation, so the pooled FFR rise cannot be read as proof that optimisation improves prognosis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: optimisation improves the FFR number modestly but has not been shown to reduce target-vessel failure — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: optimisation improves the FFR number modestly but has not been shown to reduce target-vessel failure — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of TARGET-FFR (260 patients), FFR-REACT (291 patients) and the individual-patient-data meta-analysis (314 patients) carded above.
cards.result: Final FFR rises by roughly 0.03-0.05 with optimisation and the worst results (FFR ≤0.80) become less common, but only about one in five suboptimal vessels reaches ≥0.90, neither trial met its primary endpoint, and the one trial reporting target-vessel failure found no significant difference (the treatment made no difference to 1-year target-vessel failure in FFR-REACT).
cards.watchOut: A better final FFR is a surrogate: post-PCI FFR predicts events prognostically, but no trial has yet shown that acting to raise it changes those events.

shelves.title: PATHWAY-1: starting with losartan + hydrochlorothiazide lowered home systolic pressure faster than starting with monotherapy (4.9 mm Hg more fall over 32 weeks), but the monotherapy arm caught up once both groups were on combination therapy
shelves.question: In untreated adults with hypertension (systolic ≥150 or diastolic ≥95 mm Hg), does starting with a two-drug combination (losartan + hydrochlorothiazide), compared with starting with sequential monotherapy, achieve faster and better blood-pressure control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent; Adult; Aged; Amlodipine; Antihypertensive Agents; Blood Pressure; Dose-Response Relationship, Drug; Double-Blind Method; Doxazosin; Drug Therapy, Combination; Female; Follow-Up Studies; Humans; Hydrochlorothiazide; Hypertension; Losartan; Male; Middle Aged; Treatment Outcome; Young Adult
shelves.balance: PATHWAY-1 (605 untreated patients with BP ≥150/95 mm Hg) is the direct strategy trial: initial combination (losartan + hydrochlorothiazide) lowered home systolic BP 4.9 mm Hg more than initial monotherapy averaged over 32 weeks (p<0.001), with a uniform response across renin tertiles, whereas monotherapy response varied substantially by renin. But once the monotherapy group crossed to combination therapy, pressures converged (difference 1.2 mm Hg at 32 weeks, p=0.13) — the advantage is speed and early control, not a different final pressure. Wider evidence agrees on the surrogate: a meta-analysis of 33 trials (13,095 participants) found initial dual therapy lowered systolic pressure by 2.8-7.5 mm Hg more than standard-dose monotherapy depending on dose, with better control rates and no excess withdrawals. The Cochrane review, restricted to trials reporting clinical outcomes, found the event evidence very uncertain (only 568 participants in its main comparison). No difference in withdrawals for adverse events in PATHWAY-1. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster, more predictable control; event benefit unproven.

cards.headline: PATHWAY-1 (605 untreated patients): initial losartan + hydrochlorothiazide lowered home systolic BP 4.9 mm Hg more than initial monotherapy over 32 weeks (p<0.001), but the gap closed to 1.2 mm Hg once both arms were on combination therapy
cards.summary: PATHWAY-1 (605 untreated patients): initial losartan + hydrochlorothiazide lowered home systolic BP 4.9 mm Hg more than initial monotherapy over 32 weeks (p<0.001), but the gap closed to 1.2 mm Hg once both arms were on combination therapy
cards.people: 605 untreated patients aged 18-79 years with systolic BP ≥150 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥95 mm Hg, in a 1-year double-blind randomised trial: phase 1 (weeks 0-16) initial monotherapy (losartan 50-100 mg or hydrochlorothiazide 12.5-25 mg, crossing over at 8 weeks) versus initial combination (losartan 50-100 mg plus hydrochlorothiazide 12.5-25 mg); in phase 2 all received combination therapy, and in phase 3 amlodipine ± doxazosin could be added.
cards.result: Home systolic BP fell 4.9 mm Hg (range 3.7-6.0) less with initial monotherapy than with initial combination averaged over phases 1-2 (p<0.001), but caught up by 32 weeks (difference 1.2 mm Hg, 95% CI -0.4 to 2.8; p=0.13). In phase 1, response to each monotherapy differed substantially between renin tertiles, whereas response to combination therapy was uniform and at least 5 mm Hg greater than to monotherapy. Withdrawals due to adverse events did not differ between strategies.
cards.watchOut: A blood-pressure (surrogate) endpoint trial, not powered for cardiovascular events; by design everyone ended on combination therapy, so the trial measures the cost of starting sequentially — delayed control — rather than a permanent pressure difference.
cards.source: MacDonald TM et al. Combination Therapy Is Superior to Sequential Monotherapy for the Initial Treatment of Hypertension: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2017. PMID: 29151036. Registry ID: NCT00994617. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 33 trials (13,095 participants): initial dual therapy lowered systolic BP 2.8-7.5 mm Hg more than standard-dose monotherapy and improved control (relative risk up to 1.42), without more withdrawals
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 33 trials (13,095 participants): initial dual therapy lowered systolic BP 2.8-7.5 mm Hg more than standard-dose monotherapy and improved control (relative risk up to 1.42), without more withdrawals
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 randomised double-blind trials (13,095 participants, mean baseline BP 155/100 mm Hg) of dual combination therapy versus monotherapy as initial treatment in treatment-naïve or untreated adults, with regimens classified by dose relative to a standard dose.
cards.result: Compared with standard-dose monotherapy, dual combinations showed a dose-response in systolic BP reduction: mean differences 2.8 mm Hg (95% CI 1.6-4.0) for two sub-standard doses, 4.6 (3.4-5.7) for standard plus sub-standard, and 7.5 (5.4-9.5) for two standard doses; BP control relative risks were 1.11, 1.25 and 1.42 respectively (relative measures). Withdrawals due to adverse events did not differ significantly (2.9% vs 2.2%; relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 0.85-1.92).
cards.watchOut: Pooled across many different drug pairings, not the losartan + hydrochlorothiazide pairing specifically; endpoints are blood pressure and control rates, not clinical events.
cards.source: Salam A et al. Efficacy and safety of dual combination therapy of blood pressure-lowering drugs as initial treatment for hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of hypertension. 2019. PMID: 30986788. Registry ID: CRD42016032822 (PROSPERO, as in the record). MeSH: Antihypertensive Agents; Blood Pressure; Double-Blind Method; Drug Therapy, Combination; Humans; Hypertension; Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.headline: Cochrane review: for clinical outcomes (death, cardiovascular events) the initial-combination versus monotherapy evidence is very uncertain — only 568 participants in the main comparison, with extremely wide confidence intervals
cards.summary: Cochrane review: for clinical outcomes (death, cardiovascular events) the initial-combination versus monotherapy evidence is very uncertain — only 568 participants in the main comparison, with extremely wide confidence intervals
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (2020 update) of randomised double-blind trials of at least 12 months comparing two-drug combination with monotherapy as initial treatment for primary hypertension, requiring at least 50 participants per group and reporting mortality, cardiovascular events or serious adverse events; the main comparison pooled 3 trials (monotherapy 335, combination 233 participants).
cards.result: It is very uncertain whether combination versus monotherapy changes total mortality (relative risk 1.35, 95% CI 0.08-21.72), cardiovascular events (relative risk 0.98, 95% CI 0.22-4.41), serious adverse events (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.31-1.92) or withdrawals (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.53-1.35); all outcomes had 568 participants and very-low-certainty evidence, and the reviewers concluded the numbers were too small to draw any conclusion on clinical outcomes (relative measures throughout).
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane eligibility rules (hard outcomes, ≥12 months) exclude almost the entire initial-therapy trial literature, including PATHWAY-1's BP endpoints — so this card bounds what is known about events, not what is known about pressure control.
cards.source: Garjón J et al. First-line combination therapy versus first-line monotherapy for primary hypertension. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32026465. cards.headline: Synthesis: starting with two drugs controls pressure faster and more predictably; whether that speed prevents events is unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: starting with two drugs controls pressure faster and more predictably; whether that speed prevents events is unproven — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of PATHWAY-1 (605 patients), the 33-trial meta-analysis (13,095 participants) and the Cochrane outcomes review carded above.
cards.result: Initial combination therapy's demonstrated advantage is earlier, larger and more predictable blood-pressure lowering; once sequential starters reach combination therapy their pressures converge, and no adequately powered evidence shows fewer cardiovascular events from starting with two drugs.
cards.watchOut: Do not present the 4.9 mm Hg early advantage as a lasting difference: PATHWAY-1's own design shows convergence by 32 weeks.
cards.source: Synthesis of MacDonald TM et al. J Am Heart Assoc. 2017. PMID: 29151036; Salam A et al. J Hypertens. 2019. PMID: 30986788; Garjón J et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020. PMID: 32026465.

shelves.title: PATHWAY-3: amiloride + hydrochlorothiazide prevented the thiazide rise in 2-hour glucose (-0.42 mmol/L [about -7.6 mg/dL] vs hydrochlorothiazide alone) and lowered home systolic pressure more, at equipotent starting doses
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does amiloride combined with hydrochlorothiazide, compared with hydrochlorothiazide alone, lower blood pressure as well while preventing thiazide-induced glucose intolerance?
shelves.mesh: Aged; Amiloride; Diuretics; Double-Blind Method; Female; Glucose Intolerance; Humans; Hydrochlorothiazide; Hypertension; Male; Middle Aged
shelves.balance: PATHWAY-3 (441 patients with hypertension and at least one metabolic-syndrome component, diabetes excluded) randomised amiloride alone, hydrochlorothiazide alone, or the half-dose combination for 24 weeks. Two-hour oral-glucose-tolerance glucose, averaged over 12 and 24 weeks, was lower on the combination than on hydrochlorothiazide alone (mean difference -0.42 mmol/L [about -7.6 mg/dL], 95% CI -0.84 to -0.004; p=0.048) and lower still on amiloride alone (-0.55 mmol/L [about -9.9 mg/dL]; p=0.0093), while the combination lowered home systolic pressure significantly more than hydrochlorothiazide alone (p=0.0068) — so the pairing answers both halves of the question in one trial: as good or better on pressure, better on glucose. Older randomised evidence is consistent in direction: in the MRC elderly trial's metabolic analysis (4,396 patients), hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride produced no glucose difference versus placebo over 2 years. A 2026 factorial trial found amiloride 5 mg and 10 mg had similar, at-best-weak independent pressure effects alongside a thiazide-type diuretic, framing amiloride's role as metabolic protection rather than extra pressure lowering. Hyperkalaemia occurred in 4.8% on amiloride alone and 2.3% on the combination in PATHWAY-3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: PATHWAY-3 (441 patients): amiloride + hydrochlorothiazide kept 2-hour glucose 0.42 mmol/L (about 7.6 mg/dL) lower than hydrochlorothiazide alone (p=0.048) and lowered home systolic pressure significantly more (p=0.0068)
cards.summary: PATHWAY-3 (441 patients): amiloride + hydrochlorothiazide kept 2-hour glucose 0.42 mmol/L (about 7.6 mg/dL) lower than hydrochlorothiazide alone (p=0.048) and lowered home systolic pressure significantly more (p=0.0068)
cards.people: 441 patients aged 18-80 years with clinic systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg and home systolic BP ≥130 mm Hg on permitted background therapy (or untreated in defined circumstances), with at least one metabolic-syndrome component and no known diabetes, randomised 1:1:1 at 13 UK sites to 24 weeks of amiloride 10 mg (n=145), hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg (n=146), or amiloride 5 mg plus hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg (n=150), all doses doubled at 12 weeks; double-blind, phase 4.
cards.result: Two-hour glucose after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, averaged at 12 and 24 weeks, was significantly lower with amiloride than hydrochlorothiazide (mean difference -0.55 mmol/L [about -9.9 mg/dL], 95% CI -0.96 to -0.14; p=0.0093) and with the combination than hydrochlorothiazide (-0.42 mmol/L [about -7.6 mg/dL], 95% CI -0.84 to -0.004; p=0.048). Home systolic BP reduction did not differ between amiloride and hydrochlorothiazide alone, but the combination's fall was significantly greater than hydrochlorothiazide alone (p=0.0068). Hyperkalaemia was reported in 7 (4.8%) on amiloride and 3 (2.3%) on the combination; the highest recorded potassium was 5.8 mmol/L. Serious adverse events (13) did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial (glucose tolerance and home BP), not powered for incident diabetes or cardiovascular events; patients with known diabetes were excluded, so the glucose protection is shown in a non-diabetic metabolic-syndrome population.
cards.source: Brown MJ et al. Effect of amiloride, or amiloride plus hydrochlorothiazide, versus hydrochlorothiazide on glucose tolerance and blood pressure (PATHWAY-3): a parallel-group, double-blind randomised phase 4 trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2016. PMID: 26489809. Registry ID: NCT00797862. cards.headline: MRC elderly trial metabolic analysis (4,396 patients over 65): hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride produced no difference in glucose versus placebo over 2 years, though potassium fell and urate and cholesterol rose
cards.summary: MRC elderly trial metabolic analysis (4,396 patients over 65): hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride produced no difference in glucose versus placebo over 2 years, though potassium fell and urate and cholesterol rose
cards.type: Randomised trial metabolic substudy (MRC elderly trial)
cards.people: 4,396 patients over 65 in the Medical Research Council elderly hypertension trial, randomised to atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride, or placebo, with metabolic measurements at baseline and at years 1 and 2, analysed with linear mixed models.
cards.result: Versus placebo at year 1, the hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride arm showed greater mean reductions in potassium (-0.18 mmol/L [about -0.18 mEq/L], 95% CI -0.21 to -0.15), sodium (-1.45 mmol/L, 95% CI -1.62 to -1.29) and weight (-0.46 kg), and greater increases in cholesterol (0.16 mmol/L [about 6.2 mg/dL], 95% CI 0.10-0.22), urea (0.77 mmol/L, 95% CI 0.68-0.87) and urate (53.10 µmol/L, 95% CI 49.35-56.85). No group differences in glucose were found — the combination did not reproduce the glucose rise expected of thiazide alone.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is combination versus placebo (and atenolol), not versus hydrochlorothiazide alone, so it supports metabolic neutrality of the pairing rather than proving superiority over the thiazide on glucose; potassium still fell despite amiloride.
cards.source: Damian DJ et al. Changes in selected metabolic parameters in patients over 65 receiving hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride, atenolol or placebo in the MRC elderly trial. BMC cardiovascular disorders. 2016. PMID: 27716064. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised trial metabolic substudy (mrc elderly trial) 4,396 patients over 65 in the medical research council elderly hypertension trial, randomised to atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride, or placebo, with metabolic measurements at baseline and at years 1 and 2, analysed with linear mixed models. versus placebo at year 1, the hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride arm showed greater mean reductions in potassium (-0.18 mmol/l [about -0.18 meq/l], 95% ci -0.21 to -0.15), sodium (-1.45 mmol/l, 95% ci -1.62 to -1.29) and weight (-0.46 kg), and greater increases in cholesterol (0.16 mmol/l [about 6.2 mg/dl], 95% ci 0.10-0.22), urea (0.77 mmol/l, 95% ci 0.68-0.87) and urate (53.10 µmol/l, 95% ci 49.35-56.85). no group differences in glucose were found — the combination did not reproduce the glucose rise expected of thiazide alone. the comparison is combination versus placebo (and atenolol), not versus hydrochlorothiazide alone, so it supports metabolic neutrality of the pairing rather than proving superiority over the thiazide on glucose; potassium still fell despite amiloride. damian dj et al. changes in selected metabolic parameters in patients over 65 receiving hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride, atenolol or placebo in the mrc elderly trial. bmc cardiovascular disorders. 2016. pmid: 27716064. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adrenergic beta-1 receptor antagonists; age factors; aged; amiloride; antihypertensive agents; atenolol; biomarkers; blood glucose; body weight; cholesterol; diuretics; drug therapy, combination; female; humans; hydrochlorothiazide; hypertension; intention to treat analysis; linear models; male; potassium; single-blind method; sodium; sodium chloride symporter inhibitors; time factors; treatment outcome; united kingdom; urea; uric acid

cards.headline: Factorial RCT (2026): amiloride 5 mg versus 10 mg alongside a thiazide-type diuretic had similar blood-pressure and metabolic effects — no clear dose-response, suggesting amiloride's independent pressure effect is at best weak
cards.summary: Factorial RCT (2026): amiloride 5 mg versus 10 mg alongside a thiazide-type diuretic had similar blood-pressure and metabolic effects — no clear dose-response, suggesting amiloride's independent pressure effect is at best weak
cards.people: Patients with primary hypertension in a 12-week factorial, double-blind superiority trial comparing chlorthalidone 25 mg with hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg and, factorially, amiloride 5 mg with 10 mg, with office and ambulatory BP and laboratory follow-up. The record does not report the randomised N (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone had similar office and ambulatory effects (between-group difference for 24-hour systolic BP -1.1 mm Hg, 95% CI -8.0 to 5.9; p=0.8). Amiloride 5 mg and 10 mg had similar effects on BP and most laboratory parameters; serum sodium fell more with 10 mg. The authors conclude any independent BP-lowering effect of amiloride is at best weak — its value in the PATHWAY-3 pairing is potassium/glucose protection, not added pressure lowering.
cards.watchOut: This trial compares amiloride doses, not amiloride-plus-thiazide versus thiazide alone, and its record does not state the sample size; it is supporting context for how amiloride behaves beside a thiazide, not a second test of the PATHWAY-3 question.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the combination matches or beats hydrochlorothiazide on pressure and protects glucose tolerance — POSSIBLE (benefit), on one direct trial
cards.people: Synthesis of PATHWAY-3 (441 patients), the MRC elderly metabolic analysis (4,396 patients) and the 2026 factorial amiloride-dose trial carded above.
cards.result: The only direct randomised test shows amiloride + hydrochlorothiazide preventing the thiazide glucose rise while lowering pressure at least as well; older randomised metabolic data for the same pairing show no glucose penalty versus placebo. No trial shows fewer cases of diabetes or cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: Glucose tolerance over 24 weeks is a surrogate: PATHWAY-3 does not show that the combination prevents diabetes itself, and potassium monitoring remains necessary (hyperkalaemia 2.3% on the combination).

shelves.title: TRANSCEND: telmisartan did not significantly reduce the primary cardiovascular composite versus placebo in ACE-inhibitor-intolerant patients (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92; p=0.216), with a modest signal on the death/MI/stroke composite (13.0% vs 14.8%)
shelves.question: In high-risk vascular patients who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, does telmisartan, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged; Angioedema; Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors; Benzimidazoles; Benzoates; Cardiovascular Diseases; Cough; Female; Follow-Up Studies; Humans; Hypotension; Kaplan-Meier Estimate; Male; Risk Reduction Behavior; Single-Blind Method; Telmisartan; Therapeutic Equivalency
shelves.balance: PARTIAL build: live shelf #105 cards ONTARGET (telmisartan versus ramipril, and dual-blockade harm) inside a diabetic-kidney question; it does not card the placebo-controlled TRANSCEND trial, which is built here and cross-points back to #105. In TRANSCEND (5,926 ACE-inhibitor-intolerant patients with cardiovascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, median follow-up 56 months), telmisartan 80 mg did not significantly reduce the primary composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke or heart-failure hospitalisation (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.81-1.05; p=0.216), despite a 4.0/2.2 mm Hg lower mean pressure. The secondary composite without heart-failure hospitalisation was modestly lower (13.0% vs 14.8%; hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.76-1.00; p=0.048 unadjusted, p=0.068 after adjustment). The trial's own renal report found no benefit on the composite renal outcome (hazard ratio 1.29) — albuminuria rose less but estimated GFR fell more — and a prespecified analysis found no prevention of new diabetes (21.8% vs 22.4%). Telmisartan was well tolerated, with more hypotensive symptoms (0.98% vs 0.54% discontinuations). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a well-tolerated drug with, at most, a modest unconfirmed event signal in this population.

cards.headline: TRANSCEND (5,926 ACE-intolerant patients): telmisartan did not significantly cut the primary composite (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92; p=0.216); the death/MI/stroke composite was 13.0% vs 14.8% (hazard ratio 0.87; p=0.048 unadjusted, 0.068 adjusted)
cards.summary: TRANSCEND (5,926 ACE-intolerant patients): telmisartan did not significantly cut the primary composite (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92; p=0.216); the death/MI/stroke composite was 13.0% vs 14.8% (hazard ratio 0.87; p=0.048 unadjusted, 0.068 adjusted)
cards.people: 5,926 patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors, with cardiovascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, randomised after a 3-week run-in to telmisartan 80 mg/day (n=2,954) or placebo (n=2,972) on top of concomitant proven therapies; median follow-up 56 months; intention-to-treat.
cards.result: The primary outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalisation for heart failure) occurred in 465 (15.7%) on telmisartan versus 504 (17.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.81-1.05; p=0.216) — the treatment made no significant difference to the primary outcome. The secondary composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 384 (13.0%) versus 440 (14.8%) (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.76-1.00; p=0.048 unadjusted; p=0.068 after adjustment for multiplicity and overlap). Hospitalisation for a cardiovascular reason was lower (30.3% vs 33.0%; relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.85-0.99). Mean BP was 4.0/2.2 mm Hg lower on telmisartan. Fewer patients permanently discontinued telmisartan than placebo (21.6% vs 23.8%); hypotensive symptoms were the commonest reason (0.98% vs 0.54%). Hazard and relative risks are relative measures; absolute differences are printed beside them.
cards.watchOut: The headline secondary-composite p-value (0.048) does not survive the trial's own adjustment (0.068); many patients received other proven therapies, which may have diluted a modest effect. ONTARGET, the ramipril-comparison trial, is homed in live shelf #105 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Yusuf S et al (TRANSCEND Investigators). Effects of the angiotensin-receptor blocker telmisartan on cardiovascular events in high-risk patients intolerant to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2008. PMID: 18757085. Registry ID: NCT00153101. cards.headline: TRANSCEND renal report (5,927 patients): no benefit on the composite renal outcome (1.96% vs 1.55%; hazard ratio 1.29) — albuminuria rose less but estimated GFR fell more on telmisartan
cards.summary: TRANSCEND renal report (5,927 patients): no benefit on the composite renal outcome (1.96% vs 1.55%; hazard ratio 1.29) — albuminuria rose less but estimated GFR fell more on telmisartan
cards.people: The TRANSCEND population (adults with cardiovascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, without macroalbuminuria or heart failure, intolerant to ACE inhibitors), telmisartan 80 mg/day (n=2,954) versus placebo (n=2,972), mean follow-up 56 months; composite renal outcome of dialysis or doubling of serum creatinine, plus GFR and albuminuria changes.
cards.result: The composite renal outcome did not differ importantly (58 [1.96%] telmisartan vs 46 [1.55%] placebo; hazard ratio 1.29, 95% CI 0.87-1.89; p=0.20), and doubling of creatinine was more frequent on telmisartan (hazard ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.04-2.41), with only 7 versus 10 patients reaching dialysis. Albuminuria increased less with telmisartan (32% vs 63% rise; p<0.001), but estimated GFR fell more (mean change -3.2 vs -0.26 mL/min per 1.73 m²; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A secondary-outcomes report of the same single trial, in a population selected to exclude macroalbuminuria and heart failure — it cannot be read as evidence about telmisartan in established diabetic nephropathy, which is the population of live shelf #105.
cards.source: Mann JF et al. Effect of telmisartan on renal outcomes: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2009. PMID: 19451556. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: TRANSCEND diabetes analysis (3,488 patients without diabetes at entry): telmisartan did not prevent new diabetes (21.8% vs 22.4%; relative ratio 0.95) or increase regression to normoglycaemia
cards.summary: TRANSCEND diabetes analysis (3,488 patients without diabetes at entry): telmisartan did not prevent new diabetes (21.8% vs 22.4%; relative ratio 0.95) or increase regression to normoglycaemia
cards.type: Prespecified analysis of a randomised trial (TRANSCEND)
cards.people: 3,488 TRANSCEND participants free of diabetes at baseline (mean age 67 years, 61% male), randomised to telmisartan 80 mg (n=1,726) or placebo (n=1,762) plus usual care, median follow-up 56 months.
cards.result: Diabetes developed in 21.8% on telmisartan versus 22.4% on placebo (relative ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.83-1.10; p=0.51) — the treatment made no difference to incident diabetes. Among those with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, regression to normoglycaemia (26.9% vs 24.5%) and progression to diabetes (20.1% vs 21.1%) also did not differ (p=0.59).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup (non-diabetic at entry) of the same trial; it closes off a hoped-for metabolic benefit rather than adding an independent replication.
cards.source: Barzilay JI et al. Effects of telmisartan on glucose levels in people at high risk for cardiovascular disease but free from diabetes: the TRANSCEND study. Diabetes care. 2011. shelves.title: Zerlasiran lowers Lp(a) by more than 80% in phase 2 (time-averaged -81.3% to -85.6% vs placebo at 36 weeks) — PHASE 2 ONLY, surrogate endpoint, no cardiovascular outcomes trial has reported
shelves.question: In adults with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and elevated lipoprotein(a), does the siRNA zerlasiran, compared with placebo, lower lipoprotein(a) — and is any outcome benefit yet shown?
shelves.mesh: Aged; Female; Humans; Male; Middle Aged; Atherosclerosis; Double-Blind Method; Lipoprotein(a); Liver; RNA, Small Interfering; Injections, Subcutaneous
shelves.balance: ⚠ PHASE-2 ONLY, SURROGATE ENDPOINT — flagged on the face: every zerlasiran result is a lipoprotein(a) concentration change; no outcomes trial has reported, so no event benefit can be claimed. In the phase 2 ALPACAR-360 trial (178 patients with stable ASCVD and Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L), zerlasiran lowered time-averaged Lp(a) from baseline to week 36 by 81.3-85.6% more than placebo across the three dosing regimens, with median falls at week 36 of 90.0-96.4%; injection-site reactions were the commonest treatment-related effect and no serious adverse event was judged drug-related. The phase 1 single-ascending-dose study (32 participants without known cardiovascular disease) showed the same biology: maximal median Lp(a) falls of 46-98% by dose, persisting at least 150 days. A 2026 network meta-analysis of 25 Lp(a)-lowering trials (7,715 participants) placed zerlasiran's mean Lp(a) reduction at -80.6%, among the largest of the class. Whether an 80-90% Lp(a) fall converts into fewer events is exactly what this evidence cannot say. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, surrogate only), capped for phase-2-only evidence.

cards.headline: ALPACAR-360 phase 2 (178 patients with ASCVD): zerlasiran lowered time-averaged Lp(a) by 81.3-85.6% versus placebo to week 36; median falls 90.0-96.4% — surrogate endpoint only
cards.summary: ALPACAR-360 phase 2 (178 patients with ASCVD): zerlasiran lowered time-averaged Lp(a) by 81.3-85.6% versus placebo to week 36; median falls 90.0-96.4% — surrogate endpoint only
cards.people: 178 patients with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and serum Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L (median baseline 213 nmol/L) at 26 sites in Europe and South Africa, randomised to placebo or zerlasiran 450 mg every 24 weeks, 300 mg every 16 weeks, or 300 mg every 24 weeks (subcutaneous); primary outcome was time-averaged percent change in Lp(a) to 36 weeks, with follow-up to 60 weeks; 172 completed the trial.
cards.result: Least-squares mean time-averaged percent change in Lp(a) versus pooled placebo was -85.6% (95% CI -90.9 to -80.3) for 450 mg every 24 weeks, -82.8% (-88.2 to -77.4) for 300 mg every 16 weeks and -81.3% (-86.7 to -76.0) for 300 mg every 24 weeks. Median percent change at week 36 was -94.5%, -96.4% and -90.0% respectively. Mild injection-site pain occurred in 2.3-7.1% on the day after dosing; 20 serious adverse events occurred in 17 patients, none judged related to the study drug.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, 36-week primary endpoint, Lp(a) concentration only: the trial was not designed or powered to detect any difference in myocardial infarction, stroke or death, and none is reported.

cards.headline: APOLLO phase 1 (32 participants): a single dose of the siRNA (as SLN360) lowered Lp(a) dose-dependently — maximal median falls of 46% at 30 mg up to 98% at 600 mg, lasting at least 150 days
cards.summary: APOLLO phase 1 (32 participants): a single dose of the siRNA (as SLN360) lowered Lp(a) dose-dependently — maximal median falls of 46% at 30 mg up to 98% at 600 mg, lasting at least 150 days
cards.people: 32 adults with Lp(a) ≥150 nmol/L and no known clinically overt cardiovascular disease at 5 clinical research units (US, UK, Australia), randomised to a single subcutaneous dose of placebo (n=8) or the siRNA at 30, 100, 300 or 600 mg (n=6 each); primary outcome safety and tolerability, follow-up to 150 days.
cards.result: Maximal median percentage changes in Lp(a) were -10% on placebo and -46%, -86%, -96% and -98% at 30, 100, 300 and 600 mg respectively, with dose-dependent duration persisting at least 150 days after one dose. All 32 participants completed the trial; the two serious adverse event episodes (hospital admission for headache after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, and cholecystitis complications) were judged unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: Very small, single-dose, healthy-phenotype phase 1 study (6 participants per dose): it establishes dose-response and durability of the surrogate effect, nothing about repeated dosing outcomes or events. The agent was named SLN360 in this report and zerlasiran subsequently — the same siRNA.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis (25 trials, 7,715 participants): zerlasiran's mean Lp(a) reduction was -80.6% (95% CI -87.7 to -73.5), among the largest in the Lp(a)-lowering class — still all surrogate data
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis (25 trials, 7,715 participants): zerlasiran's mean Lp(a) reduction was -80.6% (95% CI -87.7 to -73.5), among the largest in the Lp(a)-lowering class — still all surrogate data
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 25 randomised trials (7,715 participants) of Lp(a)-targeted therapies — six siRNA agents, four antisense agents and one oral small-molecule inhibitor — with percentage change in Lp(a) as the primary outcome.
cards.result: SiRNA therapies achieved the greatest Lp(a) reductions: olpasiran mean difference -92.1% (95% CI -100.1 to -84.0) and zerlasiran -80.6% (95% CI -87.7 to -73.5), followed by muvalaplin (-76.8%) and pelacarsen (-54.2%) (all p<0.001). Injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse effect for injectables. No trial in the network reported a completed cardiovascular-outcomes result.
cards.watchOut: Indirect (network) comparisons across agents and doses, on the same surrogate endpoint; a class-wide surrogate ranking cannot substitute for an outcomes trial of zerlasiran itself.

shelves.title: MONITOR-HF: pulmonary-artery-pressure-guided care improved quality of life at 12 months (KCCQ difference 7.13 points; p=0.013) in 348 Dutch patients with NYHA class III heart failure, with consistent effects across ejection-fraction subgroups
shelves.question: In adults with heart failure across the ejection-fraction range in a European health system, does pulmonary-artery-pressure-guided management (CardioMEMS), compared with usual care, improve quality of life and reduce heart-failure hospitalisations?
shelves.mesh: Humans; Aged; Pulmonary Artery; Hemodynamic Monitoring; Quality of Life; Heart Failure; Chronic Disease
shelves.balance: PARTIAL build: live shelf #976 cards CHAMPION and GUIDE-HF (US trials framed on hospitalisation and death); the uncovered slice built here is MONITOR-HF — the European, quality-of-life-primary trial — cross-pointed to #976 for the rest of the CardioMEMS evidence. In MONITOR-HF (348 Dutch patients, NYHA class III with a previous heart-failure hospitalisation, median ejection fraction 30% but eligible irrespective of ejection fraction, on contemporary guideline therapy), CardioMEMS-guided management improved the primary endpoint: the mean change in KCCQ overall summary score at 12 months differed by 7.13 points in favour of monitoring (95% CI 1.51-12.75; p=0.013), with more responders (odds ratio 1.69 for ≥5-point improvement) and fewer deteriorations (odds ratio 0.45). The trial report states heart-failure hospitalisations were also reduced, though the fetched record does not print the event counts, so this pack does not quote a hospitalisation figure. A prespecified subgroup analysis (Eur Heart J 2024) found the quality-of-life, clinical and pressure effects consistent across age, sex, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, ejection fraction, aetiology and device subgroups after multiplicity adjustment. A Dutch cost-effectiveness analysis based on the trial estimated €20,753 per quality-adjusted life year gained, below the Dutch €50,000 threshold. The trial was open-label, which matters for a patient-reported primary endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: MONITOR-HF (348 patients): CardioMEMS-guided care improved KCCQ quality of life at 12 months by 7.13 points versus standard care (95% CI 1.51-12.75; p=0.013); device/system complications were uncommon (freedom 97.7%)
cards.summary: MONITOR-HF (348 patients): CardioMEMS-guided care improved KCCQ quality of life at 12 months by 7.13 points versus standard care (95% CI 1.51-12.75; p=0.013); device/system complications were uncommon (freedom 97.7%)
cards.people: 348 patients with chronic heart failure, NYHA class III and a previous heart-failure hospitalisation, irrespective of ejection fraction (median 30%, IQR 23-40; median age 69 years), randomised at 25 Dutch centres to haemodynamic monitoring with the CardioMEMS-HF system (n=176) or standard care (n=172), on contemporary guideline-directed therapy; open-label; primary endpoint the mean difference in KCCQ overall summary score at 12 months.
cards.result: KCCQ overall summary score changed by +7.05 points in the monitoring group versus -0.08 in standard care — a mean difference of 7.13 (95% CI 1.51-12.75; p=0.013). The odds of a ≥5-point improvement were higher with monitoring (odds ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.01-2.83; p=0.046) and the odds of a ≥5-point deterioration lower (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.26-0.77; p=0.0035). Freedom from device- or system-related complications was 97.7% and from sensor failure 98.8%. The report states heart-failure hospitalisations were reduced; the fetched record does not print those event counts, so none are quoted here. Odds ratios are relative measures; the absolute score changes are printed beside them.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial with a patient-reported primary endpoint — patients knew whether they were monitored, which can inflate quality-of-life differences; a single-country (Netherlands) health-system setting. CHAMPION and GUIDE-HF are homed in live shelf #976 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MONITOR-HF subgroup analysis: quality-of-life, clinical and pressure benefits were consistent across age, sex, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, ejection fraction, aetiology and device subgroups (all multiplicity-adjusted interaction p-values non-significant)
cards.summary: MONITOR-HF subgroup analysis: quality-of-life, clinical and pressure benefits were consistent across age, sex, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, ejection fraction, aetiology and device subgroups (all multiplicity-adjusted interaction p-values non-significant)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (MONITOR-HF)
cards.people: Prespecified subgroup analysis of the MONITOR-HF trial (348 patients), examining the primary quality-of-life endpoint and clinical and pulmonary-artery-pressure endpoints across eight predefined subgroupings, including left ventricular ejection fraction.
cards.result: Effects of pressure-guided therapy were consistent across subgroups, with no clinically relevant heterogeneity on any endpoint category after adjustment for multiple testing. Unadjusted trends toward smaller quality-of-life effects in older patients (interaction p=0.03) and in diabetes (p=0.01) did not persist after adjustment (adjusted p=0.33 and 0.06 respectively).
cards.watchOut: Subgroups of a 348-patient trial are small — consistency here means no detected heterogeneity, not proof of equal benefit in each subgroup, and ejection-fraction strata in particular are underpowered.

cards.headline: MONITOR-HF cost-effectiveness (Netherlands): pressure-guided therapy gained 0.58 quality-adjusted life years at €12,121 extra cost — €20,753 per QALY, below the Dutch €50,000 threshold
cards.summary: MONITOR-HF cost-effectiveness (Netherlands): pressure-guided therapy gained 0.58 quality-adjusted life years at €12,121 extra cost — €20,753 per QALY, below the Dutch €50,000 threshold
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis based on a randomised trial (MONITOR-HF)
cards.people: Markov-model cost-effectiveness analysis from the Dutch societal perspective over a lifetime horizon, built on patient-level data from MONITOR-HF (NYHA class III chronic heart failure with at least one previous hospitalisation), counting hospitalisation, monitoring, contact, laboratory and drug-change costs in both arms.
cards.result: Quality-adjusted life years per patient were 4.07 with pressure-guided therapy versus 3.481 with standard care (gain 0.58), at an increased cost of €12,121 per patient, giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €20,753 per quality-adjusted life year gained — below the Dutch willingness-to-pay threshold of €50,000 per QALY for heart failure.
cards.watchOut: A model, not a trial result: the estimate inherits the open-label trial's effect sizes and Dutch cost structures, and does not transfer directly to other health systems.
cards.source: Mokri H et al. shelves.title: apoB versus LDL-C: risk follows apoB when the two disagree — 7.3% versus 4.0% ten-year event rates at the same LDL-C of 130 mg/dL — while in the concordant majority the markers are interchangeable
shelves.question: In adults at cardiovascular risk, does apolipoprotein B (apoB) predict events better than LDL cholesterol — particularly when the two are discordant — and should it change treatment thresholds?
shelves.mesh: Apolipoproteins · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, HDL · Cholesterol, LDL · Cohort Studies · Humans · Predictive Value of Tests
shelves.balance: This is a prognosis question and the evidence is observational plus genetic. The consistent finding across designs is that when apoB and LDL-C disagree, risk follows apoB — because apoB counts atherogenic particles while LDL-C measures the cholesterol they happen to carry. INTERHEART (15,152 cases, 14,820 controls, 52 countries) found the apoB/apoA1 ratio was the strongest lipid marker of myocardial infarction (odds ratio 3.25 for the top versus lowest quintile; population attributable risk 49.2%). In UK Biobank discordance analysis (Sniderman 2024; 293,876 adults, 19,982 events over a median 11 years), apoB varied widely at any given LDL-C — at an LDL-C of 130 mg/dL the central 95% of apoB values spanned 85.8–108.8 mg/dL — 10-year event rates were 7.3% versus 4.0% for apoB one SD above versus below the mean at that LDL-C, and residual apoB stayed predictive after LDL-C, non-HDL-C and triglycerides were accounted for, while no cholesterol residual survived adjustment for apoB. Mendelian randomisation (Ference 2017) points the same causal way: genetic scores with naturally discordant LDL-C and apoB showed coronary risk tracking the change in apoB, not LDL-C. The counterweight is real and is carded: in a separate UK Biobank analysis (Welsh 2019; 346,686 participants), apoB, LDL-C and non-HDL-C had near-identical hazard ratios per SD (1.23, 1.20, 1.21) and adding apoB to a standard model did not improve discrimination — in unselected populations the markers are highly correlated (r over 0.90), so apoB's advantage is concentrated in the discordant minority, who are common enough (and include many people with diabetes, high triglycerides or metabolic syndrome) to matter clinically.

cards.headline: INTERHEART: the apoB/apoA1 ratio was the strongest lipid predictor of myocardial infarction — OR 3.25 top versus lowest quintile, population attributable risk 49.2% (15,152 cases, 14,820 controls)
cards.summary: INTERHEART: the apoB/apoA1 ratio was the strongest lipid predictor of myocardial infarction — OR 3.25 top versus lowest quintile, population attributable risk 49.2% (15,152 cases, 14,820 controls)
cards.people: Standardised case-control study of acute myocardial infarction in 52 countries: 15,152 cases and 14,820 controls, with nonfasting apolipoprotein measurements.
cards.result: A raised apoB/apoA1 ratio carried an odds ratio of 3.25 for the top versus lowest quintile and a population attributable risk of 49.2% for the top four quintiles versus the lowest — the largest population attributable risk of any single risk factor studied, ahead of smoking (35.7%). The association held in men and women, young and old, and in every region; the nine modifiable factors together accounted for 90% of the population attributable risk in men and 94% in women.
cards.watchOut: INTERHEART tested the apoB/apoA1 ratio, not apoB against LDL-C head-to-head, and it is a case-control study with a single post-infarction-era blood draw in cases; it establishes apoB's strength as a risk marker, not its superiority in discordance — that comes from cards 2 and 3.
cards.source: Yusuf S et al. Effect of potentially modifiable risk factors associated with myocardial infarction in 52 countries (the INTERHEART study): case-control study. Lancet. 2004. cards.headline: UK Biobank discordance analysis: at the same LDL-C of 130 mg/dL, 10-year event rates were 7.3% versus 4.0% for high versus low apoB (N = 293,876; 19,982 events)
cards.summary: UK Biobank discordance analysis: at the same LDL-C of 130 mg/dL, 10-year event rates were 7.3% versus 4.0% for high versus low apoB (N = 293,876; 19,982 events)
cards.type: Observational prospective cohort discordance analysis (prognosis evidence)
cards.people: 293,876 UK Biobank adults aged 40–73 years, free of cardiovascular disease at baseline, followed a median of 11 years for new-onset atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (19,982 events).
cards.result: Although apoB correlated strongly with LDL-C and non-HDL-C (r = 0.96 for both), the apoB range capturing 95% of observations at an LDL-C of 130 mg/dL was wide (85.8–108.8 mg/dL). At that LDL-C level, 10-year event rates were 7.3% for apoB more than 1 SD above the mean versus 4.0% for apoB more than 1 SD below it. In adjusted models, residual apoB remained a significant predictor after accounting for LDL-C (HR 1.06), non-HDL-C (HR 1.04) and triglycerides (HR 1.13), whereas the residuals of LDL-C, non-HDL-C and triglycerides were all non-significant once apoB was included.
cards.watchOut: Residual hazard ratios per unit are small (1.04–1.13) because they isolate the discordant component only; UK Biobank volunteers are healthier than the general population, and treatment during follow-up was not randomised.
cards.source: Sniderman AD et al. Discordance among apoB, non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides: implications for cardiovascular prevention. Eur Heart J. 2024. PMID: 38700053. cards.headline: Mendelian randomisation: when genetic variants move LDL-C and apoB discordantly, coronary risk tracks apoB, not LDL-C (102,837 participants; validated in 189,539)
cards.summary: Mendelian randomisation: when genetic variants move LDL-C and apoB discordantly, coronary risk tracks apoB, not LDL-C (102,837 participants; validated in 189,539)
cards.people: Mendelian randomisation analyses of CETP and HMGCR genetic scores in 102,837 participants from 14 studies (13,821 major cardiovascular events), externally validated in 189,539 participants from 48 studies (62,240 coronary heart disease cases).
cards.result: A CETP score alone lowered LDL-C and apoB concordantly and lowered event risk (OR 0.946) in proportion to either. But when the CETP score was combined with an HMGCR score so that LDL-C fell by the same amount while the apoB reduction was attenuated, the event benefit attenuated to non-significance (OR 0.985). In validation, a genetic score with naturally occurring LDL-C/apoB discordance showed similar coronary risk per unit change in apoB (OR 0.782 versus 0.793) but significantly attenuated risk per unit change in LDL-C (OR 0.916 versus 0.831; P<0.001 for difference).
cards.watchOut: Genetic instruments proxy lifelong, small exposure differences and the CETP score also raises HDL-C; the design supports apoB (particle number) as the causal quantity but cannot set a clinical apoB treatment threshold.
cards.source: Ference BA et al. Association of Genetic Variants Related to CETP Inhibitors and Statins With Lipoprotein Levels and Cardiovascular Risk. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28846118. cards.headline: Counterweight — UK Biobank prediction analysis: apoB added nothing to discrimination once standard lipids were in the model (N = 346,686; 6,216 events)
cards.summary: Counterweight — UK Biobank prediction analysis: apoB added nothing to discrimination once standard lipids were in the model (N = 346,686; 6,216 events)
cards.type: Observational prospective cohort prediction study (prognosis evidence)
cards.people: 346,686 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease and not taking statins, with 6,216 incident fatal or nonfatal cardiovascular events over a median 8.9 years; a further 68,649 statin-treated participants were analysed separately.
cards.result: Per 1 SD increase, adjusted hazard ratios were near-identical: apoB 1.23, direct LDL-C 1.20 and non-HDL-C 1.21, with the markers correlated at r over 0.90. Adding apoB and apoA1 to a risk model improved the C-index by 0.0089, essentially the same as adding total and HDL cholesterol (0.0084), and once total and HDL-C were in the model, adding apoB changed the C-index by only 0.0004. The authors concluded standard nonfasting total and HDL-C capture the lipid-associated risk for population prediction.
cards.watchOut: Population-average discrimination is exactly where a discordance advantage hides: with r over 0.90, most participants are concordant, so a null average result does not contradict the discordance findings in cards 2 and 3 — it bounds how much apoB adds for unselected screening.
cards.source: Welsh C et al. Comparison of Conventional Lipoprotein Tests and Apolipoproteins in the Prediction of Cardiovascular Disease. Circulation. 2019. PMID: 31216866. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in concordant patients the markers are interchangeable; in discordant patients, risk follows apoB
cards.summary: Synthesis: in concordant patients the markers are interchangeable; in discordant patients, risk follows apoB
cards.people: Over 750,000 participants across the carded case-control, cohort, discordance and genetic studies.
cards.result: ApoB is among the strongest single lipid risk markers worldwide (INTERHEART). Where apoB and LDL-C agree — most people — prediction is equivalent and apoB adds no discrimination (Welsh 2019). Where they disagree, event rates and genetic evidence both track apoB: a 7.3% versus 4.0% 10-year event-rate spread at identical LDL-C, and coronary risk per unit apoB preserved while risk per unit LDL-C attenuates under discordance. PROPOSED LIKELY (prognosis) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial has tested apoB-guided versus LDL-C-guided treatment thresholds, so the step from 'apoB predicts better in discordance' to 'treat to an apoB target' remains an inference endorsed by some guidelines, not a trial result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yusuf S et al. Lancet. 2004 (PMID: 15364185); Sniderman AD et al. Eur Heart J. 2024 (PMID: 38700053); Ference BA et al. JAMA. 2017 (PMID: 28846118); Welsh C et al. Circulation. 2019 (PMID: 31216866). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: The adiponectin paradox: in heart failure and CKD, higher adiponectin predicts higher mortality (HR 3.23 in chronic heart failure) — a wasting and natriuretic-peptide marker signal, not a toxic effect, and it adds little beyond natriuretic peptides
shelves.question: In adults with heart failure or CKD, why do higher adiponectin levels predict higher mortality (the adiponectin paradox), and does adiponectin add prognostic information beyond natriuretic peptides?
shelves.mesh: Adiponectin · Aged · Biomarkers · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Prognosis · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: The paradox is consistent across cohorts: adiponectin, an insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory adipokine whose low levels mark metabolic risk in healthy people, predicts higher mortality once heart failure or CKD is established. In Kistorp 2005's 195 chronic heart failure patients, the upper two adiponectin tertiles carried a hazard ratio for death of 3.23 versus the lowest tertile, independent of NT-proBNP and clinical severity — and adiponectin tracked NT-proBNP (beta 0.47) and low BMI, leading the authors to read it as a marker of wasting. In the Cardiovascular Health Study (Karas 2014; 3,228 older adults), adiponectin above the median predicted new-onset heart failure (HR 1.25 per SD). In CKD, the KNOW-CKD cohort (1,303 patients) ties high adiponectin to protein-energy wasting (top-quartile OR 10.54 for wasting), the likely mechanistic bridge: natriuretic peptides stimulate adiponectin release, failing kidneys clear less of it, and weight loss/wasting raises it — so high adiponectin flags advanced disease rather than causing it. The natriuretic-peptide entanglement is decisive in Lindberg 2015 (680 STEMI patients): adiponectin predicted death (HR 1.31 per SD) until proANP entered the model, when the association vanished. Mendelian randomisation analyses (for example in Liu 2016's diabetes cohort) have likewise found the causal direction, if anything, opposite to the observational one. Answer to the shelf question: higher adiponectin is a robust prognostic marker in HF/CKD, best explained as a compensatory, natriuretic-peptide-driven signal of wasting and disease severity — a marker, not a mediator — and it adds little once natriuretic peptides are known.

cards.headline: Chronic heart failure cohort: upper adiponectin tertiles carried a mortality hazard ratio of 3.23 versus the lowest tertile, independent of NT-proBNP (N = 195; 46 deaths)
cards.summary: Chronic heart failure cohort: upper adiponectin tertiles carried a mortality hazard ratio of 3.23 versus the lowest tertile, independent of NT-proBNP (N = 195; 46 deaths)
cards.people: Prospective study of 195 patients with chronic heart failure (mean age 69.3 years, mean ejection fraction 30%), with baseline plasma adiponectin and NT-proBNP and a median follow-up of 2.6 years, during which 46 patients (23.5%) died.
cards.result: Adiponectin correlated positively with NT-proBNP (beta = 0.47, P<0.001) and negatively with BMI (beta = −0.43, P<0.001). After adjustment for clinical severity variables (age, systolic blood pressure, ejection fraction under 25%, duration of heart failure, creatinine clearance) and for NT-proBNP, mortality hazard for the two upper adiponectin tertiles versus the lowest was 3.23 (P = 0.032). BMI itself predicted mortality (HR 0.63) until NT-proBNP was added (HR 0.74, P = 0.13). The authors interpreted high adiponectin as a marker for wasting.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-centre 2005 cohort (195 patients, 46 deaths) with wide uncertainty around the 3.23 hazard ratio; tertile grouping and residual confounding by disease severity and renal function cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Kistorp C et al. Plasma adiponectin, body mass index, and mortality in patients with chronic heart failure. Circulation. 2005. PMID: 16157772. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cardiovascular Health Study: adiponectin above the median predicted new-onset heart failure — HR 1.25 per SD (N = 3,228; 780 incident cases)
cards.summary: Cardiovascular Health Study: adiponectin above the median predicted new-onset heart failure — HR 1.25 per SD (N = 3,228; 780 incident cases)
cards.people: Community-based cohort of 3,228 adults aged 65 years or older without prevalent heart failure, atrial fibrillation or cardiovascular disease, with total and high-molecular-weight adiponectin measured at baseline.
cards.result: The adiponectin–heart failure relation was nonlinear: no association below the median (12.4 mg/L for total adiponectin), but above the median each SD increment carried a hazard ratio of 1.25 (95% CI 1.14–1.38) for incident heart failure after adjustment for potential confounders. The association appeared strongest in participants with lower BMI. Higher adiponectin also tended to accompany left ventricular systolic dysfunction and left atrial enlargement on echocardiography. High-molecular-weight adiponectin behaved the same way.
cards.watchOut: The threshold pattern (risk only above the median) and the stronger signal at low BMI fit the wasting-marker explanation better than a toxic effect of adiponectin; this is a general older population, not established heart failure or CKD.
cards.source: Karas MG et al. Relations of plasma total and high-molecular-weight adiponectin to new-onset heart failure in adults ≥65 years of age (from the Cardiovascular Health study). Am J Cardiol. 2014. PMID: 24169012. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CKD cohort: the highest adiponectin quartile carried an odds ratio of 10.54 for protein-energy wasting versus the lowest (N = 1,303 predialysis patients)
cards.summary: CKD cohort: the highest adiponectin quartile carried an odds ratio of 10.54 for protein-energy wasting versus the lowest (N = 1,303 predialysis patients)
cards.type: Observational cross-sectional analysis within a prospective CKD cohort (prognosis/mechanism evidence)
cards.people: 1,303 predialysis chronic kidney disease patients from the Korean KNOW-CKD multicentre cohort; protein-energy wasting was defined by at least three of: serum albumin under 3.8 g/dL, BMI under 23 kg/m², urine creatinine excretion in the lowest quartile, and dietary protein intake under 0.6 g/kg/day. Seventy-two patients (5.5%) met the wasting definition.
cards.result: Each 1 µg/mL higher adiponectin was associated with wasting at an odds ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 1.01–1.08) after multivariable adjustment, and the highest adiponectin quartile versus the lowest carried an odds ratio of 10.54 (95% CI 1.28–86.74). Among the wasting indicators, adiponectin was most closely tied to urine creatinine excretion, an indirect measure of muscle mass (beta = −2.21).
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional, so direction is unproven — wasting may raise adiponectin, adiponectin may mark the process, or reduced renal clearance may raise levels independently; the top-quartile confidence interval (1.28–86.74) is very wide because only 72 patients had wasting.
cards.source: Hyun YY et al. Serum adiponectin and protein-energy wasting in predialysis chronic kidney disease. Nutrition. 2017. PMID: 27692989. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: STEMI cohort: adiponectin predicted death (HR 1.31 per SD) — until proANP was added, when the association vanished (N = 680; 137 deaths over 5 years)
cards.summary: STEMI cohort: adiponectin predicted death (HR 1.31 per SD) — until proANP was added, when the association vanished (N = 680; 137 deaths over 5 years)
cards.people: Prospective cohort of 680 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (2006–2008), with admission adiponectin and pro-atrial natriuretic peptide (proANP) and 5-year follow-up (137 deaths; 170 major adverse cardiovascular events).
cards.result: Adiponectin and proANP were strongly associated at admission (r = 0.34, P<0.001), and in serially sampled patients adiponectin rose when proANP rose. Higher admission adiponectin predicted all-cause mortality and major adverse events (adjusted HR 1.31 per SD for each; 95% CI 1.07–1.60 and 1.09–1.57) — but the association vanished when proANP was included in the model. The authors concluded that concomitantly elevated natriuretic peptide levels confound the adiponectin–outcome association.
cards.watchOut: A post-infarction population rather than chronic HF/CKD, and proANP is a proxy for the natriuretic peptide axis rather than BNP/NT-proBNP themselves; still, it is the carded study that most directly answers whether adiponectin adds prognostic information beyond natriuretic peptides — here, it did not.
cards.source: Lindberg S et al. Interplay Between Adiponectin and Pro-Atrial Natriuretic Peptide and Prognosis in Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction. Am J Cardiol. 2015. PMID: 26361828. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the paradox resolves as a marker phenomenon — natriuretic peptides, wasting and reduced clearance raise adiponectin in advanced disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the paradox resolves as a marker phenomenon — natriuretic peptides, wasting and reduced clearance raise adiponectin in advanced disease
cards.people: Over 5,400 participants across the carded heart failure, older-adult, CKD and post-infarction cohorts; all evidence observational.
cards.result: Higher adiponectin predicted mortality in chronic heart failure (HR 3.23 for upper versus lowest tertiles, Kistorp 2005), incident heart failure in older adults (HR 1.25 per SD above the median), and tracked protein-energy wasting in CKD (top-quartile OR 10.54) — while its post-infarction prognostic association disappeared after adjustment for proANP. The coherent reading: adiponectin rises as a compensatory, natriuretic-peptide-driven signal of wasting and disease severity, so it marks risk rather than mediating it, and adds little prognostic information once natriuretic peptides are known. PROPOSED LIKELY (prognosis) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomises or intervenes on adiponectin, and Mendelian randomisation analyses elsewhere have not supported a causal harmful effect; 'marker not mediator' is the best-supported interpretation, not a proven mechanism in every subgroup (for example HFpEF, where obesity predominates, may behave differently).
cards.source: Synthesis of Kistorp C et al. Circulation. 2005 (PMID: 16157772); Karas MG et al. Am J Cardiol. 2014 (PMID: 24169012); Hyun YY et al. Nutrition. 2017 (PMID: 27692989); Lindberg S et al. Am J Cardiol. 2015 (PMID: 26361828). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Stunning and hibernation in humans: function fails after flow returns, and underperfused muscle stays alive by contracting less
shelves.question: In humans, what are myocardial stunning and hibernation — how long does contractile dysfunction persist after brief ischaemia and reperfusion, and how does chronically underperfused myocardium down-regulate function while staying viable?
shelves.mesh: Myocardial Stunning · Myocardial Contraction · Tomography, Emission-Computed · Coronary Circulation · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human evidence is thinner than the animal literature and this shelf says so on its face. Stunning in humans is demonstrated most cleanly after exercise-induced ischaemia: Ambrosio 1996 found regional function still impaired 30–60 minutes after exercise ended, with perfusion already normal — dysfunction outlasting ischaemia with restored flow is the definition. A careful radionuclide study of briefer episodes (rest angina, effort angina, balloon angioplasty inflations) found NO persistent dysfunction in recovery (Marzullo 1993, n = 52) — the honest null that bounds the claim: episode duration and depth decide whether stunning is detectable. Hibernation rests on PET: Tillisch 1986 showed preserved glucose uptake in akinetic segments predicted recovery after bypass with 85–92% predictive accuracy, far above Q-wave ECG (43%); Uren & Camici 1992 frame the flow–metabolism mismatch as the detection standard. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing is minimal here; the concepts are Rahimtoola's and Bolli's, presented through the carded human studies, with the animal stunning experiments (Heyndrickx; Bolli) named only as textbook/translational framing, never carded.

cards.headline: Ambrosio 1996: after exercise-induced angina, regional contraction stayed impaired for at least 30–60 minutes although perfusion and ECG had normalised — human stunning demonstrated
cards.summary: Ambrosio 1996: after exercise-induced angina, regional contraction stayed impaired for at least 30–60 minutes although perfusion and ECG had normalised — human stunning demonstrated
cards.type: Human physiological study (exercise testing with serial radionuclide function imaging), Circulation 1996
cards.people: Patients with coronary artery disease undergoing exercise testing with quantitative contractile-function measurement for up to 240 minutes after exercise: group A (n = 17) by regional ejection fraction on ⁹⁹ᵐTc radionuclide angiography; group B (n = 14) by computer-assisted systolic wall thickening, with ⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi perfusion imaging.
cards.result: Angina induced marked contractile dysfunction; haemodynamic and ECG changes normalised promptly, and in group B no perfusion defects were detectable 30 minutes after exercise — yet contractile function remained impaired well into recovery. At 30 minutes, regional ejection fraction of previously ischaemic areas was still 82.6 ± 4.6% of baseline in group A (P < 0.05); in group B, systolic thickening of previously ischaemic segments was still significantly impaired 60 minutes after exercise (33.8 ± 2.8% vs 40.5 ± 2.7% at baseline; P < 0.05). Dysfunction persisting after ischaemia resolves and flow is restored is myocardial stunning, shown here in patients.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was up to 240 minutes; the record's excerpt establishes impairment at 30–60 minutes, so this shelf does not print a precise full-recovery time the record does not state.
cards.source: Ambrosio G, Betocchi S, Pace L, Losi MA, et al. Prolonged impairment of regional contractile function after resolution of exercise-induced angina. Evidence of myocardial stunning in patients with coronary artery disease. Circulation. 1996. PMID: 8921788. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Marzullo 1993: after rest angina, effort angina or balloon angioplasty inflations, NO persistent dysfunction was seen in recovery in 52 patients — the null that bounds human stunning
cards.summary: Marzullo 1993: after rest angina, effort angina or balloon angioplasty inflations, NO persistent dysfunction was seen in recovery in 52 patients — the null that bounds human stunning
cards.type: Human physiological study (radionuclide angiography around spontaneous/provoked ischaemia), Am J Cardiol 1993
cards.people: Fifty-two patients in three groups: group 1, 15 patients studied before, during and after angina at rest; group 2, 17 patients before and after coronary angioplasty; group 3, 20 patients with stable angina before, during and after exercise-induced ischaemia. Global and regional function assessed by radionuclide angiography; medical therapy stopped 48 hours beforehand except diltiazem in the angioplasty group.
cards.result: Left ventricular dysfunction was evident during ischaemia in groups 1 and 3, and transient ischaemia was documented during balloon inflation in group 2 — but persistence of systolic or diastolic dysfunction was not observed in any of the three groups in the recovery phase after ischaemia (the treatment made no difference to recovery function because there was no residual deficit to measure). Read against Ambrosio, the pair of studies brackets the phenomenon: brief or milder human ischaemic episodes may recover too fast to catch, while the deeper exercise episodes of Ambrosio's protocol leave measurable stunning for at least an hour.
cards.watchOut: A null result with the imaging cadence of its era; it does not refute stunning after longer/deeper ischaemia (e.g. reperfused infarction) — it bounds the brief-episode claim, and the shelf presents it that way.
cards.source: Marzullo P, Parodi O, Sambuceti G, Marcassa C, et al. Does the myocardium become "stunned" after episodes of angina at rest, angina on effort, and coronary angioplasty? The American Journal of Cardiology. 1993. PMID: 8475867. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tillisch 1986: PET flow–metabolism pattern predicted which akinetic segments would recover after bypass — 85% (reversible) and 92% (irreversible) predictive accuracy in 17 patients
cards.summary: Tillisch 1986: PET flow–metabolism pattern predicted which akinetic segments would recover after bypass — 85% (reversible) and 92% (irreversible) predictive accuracy in 17 patients
cards.type: Human physiological/imaging study (preoperative PET vs post-bypass wall motion), N Engl J Med 1986
cards.people: Seventeen patients undergoing coronary-artery bypass surgery, with preoperative PET using nitrogen-13 ammonia (regional blood flow) and fluorine-18 deoxyglucose (exogenous glucose uptake); wall motion quantified by radionuclide or contrast angiography before and after grafting.
cards.result: Abnormal wall motion in regions with preserved glucose uptake on PET was predicted to be reversible, and in regions with depressed uptake irreversible. Abnormal contraction in 35 of 41 segments was correctly predicted to be reversible (85% predictive accuracy) and in 4 of 26 regions correctly predicted to be irreversible (92% predictive accuracy, as printed in the record); pathological Q waves predicted irreversibility in only 43% of regions. Preserved metabolism in underperfused, akinetic myocardium — the hibernation signature — identifies muscle that will contract again once flow is restored.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients; segment counts are the record's own (41 segments / 26 regions as printed). The study proves viability prediction; the down-regulation mechanism of hibernation is framing, not something this design measures.
cards.source: Tillisch J, Brunken R, Marshall R, Schwaiger M, et al. Reversibility of cardiac wall-motion abnormalities predicted by positron tomography. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1986. PMID: 3485252. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Uren & Camici 1992: hibernating myocardium defined for clinical detection — hypoperfused at rest, contractility reduced, glucose uptake preserved or increased (flow–metabolism mismatch) on PET
cards.summary: Uren & Camici 1992: hibernating myocardium defined for clinical detection — hypoperfused at rest, contractility reduced, glucose uptake preserved or increased (flow–metabolism mismatch) on PET
cards.type: Human-evidence review (PET detection of hibernating myocardium), Cardiovasc Drugs Ther 1992
cards.people: Review and synthesis of the human PET literature on chronically ischaemic, viable myocardium in patients with severe coronary artery disease, from the Hammersmith PET programme.
cards.result: Regions supplied by severely diseased arteries may develop chronic ischaemia at rest with reduced contractility, contributing to reduced global left ventricular function — yet after revascularisation contractility in these regions may return to normal: hibernating myocardium, defined as viable hypoperfused myocardium whose function can be restored. PET is presented as the best noninvasive method for quantifying regional blood flow and metabolism: with ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose, tissue that is hypoperfused at rest with preserved or increased glucose uptake (flow–metabolism mismatch) is identified with high predictive accuracy for recovery of contractile function. This card is the definitional/detection anchor for the hibernation limb; the primary predictive data are Tillisch's, carded above.
cards.watchOut: A review, carded explicitly as the definition/detection synthesis — not as a primary cohort. Whether resting flow in hibernating segments is truly reduced or near-normal with reduced flow reserve was debated in this era's literature; the shelf keeps the record's hypoperfusion wording and flags the debate here.
cards.source: Uren NG, Camici PG. Hibernation and myocardial ischemia: clinical detection by positron emission tomography. Cardiovascular Drugs and Therapy. 1992. PMID: 1637733.
