cards.headline: Synthesis: stunning is real but episode-dependent in humans; hibernation is a PET-proven viability state — dysfunction with metabolism intact
cards.summary: Synthesis: stunning is real but episode-dependent in humans; hibernation is a PET-proven viability state — dysfunction with metabolism intact
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (Ambrosio 1996; Marzullo 1993; Tillisch 1986; Uren & Camici 1992).
cards.result: Stunning — contractile dysfunction persisting after ischaemia ends and flow returns — is demonstrable in patients after exercise-induced ischaemia, with regional function still ~83% of baseline at 30 minutes and wall thickening still depressed at 60 minutes despite normal perfusion (Ambrosio). It is not an automatic sequel of every brief episode: after rest angina, effort angina or balloon inflations, one careful study found no residual dysfunction at all (Marzullo) — duration/depth of ischaemia and measurement timing decide detectability, and the post-infarction reperfusion literature (outside this shelf's carded set) is where the longest human stunning is seen. Hibernation is the chronic counterpart: akinetic, underperfused segments that keep glucose uptake recover after revascularisation with 85–92% PET predictive accuracy (Tillisch), the flow–metabolism mismatch being the clinical signature (Uren & Camici). The unifying physiology — function down-regulated while the myocyte stays alive — is Rahimtoola's hibernation concept and Bolli's stunning framework, developed substantially in animal models; those animal experiments are framing only here, and every number on this shelf is from the carded human studies.
cards.watchOut: Human primary data are thinner here than for most physiology shelves — two small imaging studies per limb, one of them a null and one a review. The stamp is ESTABLISHED for the existence and detection of both states, not for precise recovery timelines, which the fetched records do not pin down.

shelves.question: In humans, how does endothelium-dependent vasodilatation work — how is nitric-oxide-mediated tone demonstrated and quantified in vivo (intra-arterial acetylcholine/L-NMMA forearm studies; flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery)?
shelves.mesh: Endothelium, Vascular · Nitric Oxide · Vasodilation · Acetylcholine · Brachial Artery · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human demonstration chain is complete and quantitative. Vallance, Collier & Moncada (Lancet 1989) infused the nitric-oxide-synthesis inhibitor L-NMMA into the brachial artery of healthy volunteers: basal forearm flow fell ~50% and the acetylcholine response was blunted while glyceryl trinitrate's was not — basal and stimulated tone in man is partly NO-maintained. In coronary arteries, acetylcholine dilates normal vessels but paradoxically constricts atherosclerotic ones (Ludmer 1986: diameter 1.05 → 0.32 mm at the highest dose in advanced stenoses) — the in-vivo signature of a lost endothelial dilator mechanism. In essential hypertension the forearm acetylcholine response is selectively impaired (maximal flow 9.1 ± 5 vs 20.0 ± 8 mL/min/100 mL; Panza 1990) while direct smooth-muscle dilators still work. The non-invasive limb — the folded-in flow-mediated dilatation row — is Celermajer 1992: reactive-hyperaemia FMD of ~10 ± 2% in control arteries ≤6.0 mm, much reduced or absent in smokers, children with familial hypercholesterolaemia and adults with coronary disease, with GTN responses preserved in all groups. Guyton & Hall / Ganong framing (endothelium-derived relaxing factor identified as NO) is named as textbook framing; Furchgott's and Ignarro's animal/aortic-ring work is framing only, never carded.

cards.headline: Vallance, Collier & Moncada 1989: blocking NO synthesis with intra-arterial L-NMMA halved basal forearm blood flow in healthy volunteers — NO maintains resting tone in man
cards.summary: Vallance, Collier & Moncada 1989: blocking NO synthesis with intra-arterial L-NMMA halved basal forearm blood flow in healthy volunteers — NO maintains resting tone in man
cards.type: Human physiological study (intra-arterial inhibitor infusion with forearm plethysmography), Lancet 1989
cards.people: Healthy volunteers receiving infusions of NG-monomethyl-L-arginine (L-NMMA), a specific inhibitor of endothelium-derived nitric oxide synthesis, into the brachial artery, with forearm blood flow measured during basal conditions and during infused acetylcholine and glyceryl trinitrate. The record does not print the participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: L-NMMA caused a 50% fall in basal blood flow and attenuated the dilator response to infused acetylcholine but not that to glyceryl trinitrate. The dilator action of endothelium-derived NO therefore contributes to the control of basal and stimulated regional blood flow in man — the first direct human proof that resting arteriolar tone is actively held open by continuous NO release, and that acetylcholine's dilatation is NO-dependent while GTN's is not.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face. Forearm resistance vessels in healthy volunteers; extrapolation to other beds rests on the coronary and hypertension cards below.
cards.source: Vallance P, Collier J, Moncada S. Effects of endothelium-derived nitric oxide on peripheral arteriolar tone in man. Lancet. 1989. PMID: 2572793. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Ludmer 1986: acetylcholine dilated normal human coronary arteries but dose-dependently constricted atherosclerotic ones (1.05 → 0.32 mm) — endothelial dysfunction shown in vivo
cards.summary: Ludmer 1986: acetylcholine dilated normal human coronary arteries but dose-dependently constricted atherosclerotic ones (1.05 → 0.32 mm) — endothelial dysfunction shown in vivo
cards.type: Human physiological study (intracoronary acetylcholine challenge with quantitative angiography), N Engl J Med 1986
cards.people: Eight patients with advanced coronary stenoses (>50% narrowing), four subjects with angiographically normal coronary arteries, and six patients with mild atherosclerosis (<20% narrowing); graded acetylcholine and nitroglycerin infused into the left anterior descending artery with quantitative angiography. Small classic study — groups of 8, 4 and 6 printed on the face.
cards.result: In normal coronary arteries acetylcholine caused dose-dependent dilation, from 1.94 ± 0.16 mm to 2.16 ± 0.15 mm at the maximal dose (P < 0.01). All eight arteries with advanced stenoses instead constricted dose-dependently, from 1.05 ± 0.05 mm to 0.32 ± 0.16 mm at the highest concentration (P < 0.01), with temporary occlusion in five; five of six mildly diseased vessels also constricted. When endothelium fails, acetylcholine's direct smooth-muscle constrictor action is unmasked — the paradoxical response is the in-vivo test of coronary endothelial function.
cards.watchOut: Very small groups (8/4/6), printed on the face; an invasive research procedure in catheterisation patients. Diameters are the record's own segment measurements.
cards.source: Ludmer PL, Selwyn AP, Shook TL, Wayne RR, et al. Paradoxical vasoconstriction induced by acetylcholine in atherosclerotic coronary arteries. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1986. PMID: 3093861. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Panza 1990: in essential hypertension the forearm response to acetylcholine was selectively blunted (maximal flow 9.1 vs 20.0 mL/min/100 mL) while nitroprusside responses were preserved
cards.summary: Panza 1990: in essential hypertension the forearm response to acetylcholine was selectively blunted (maximal flow 9.1 vs 20.0 mL/min/100 mL) while nitroprusside responses were preserved
cards.type: Human physiological study (intra-arterial forearm dose–response), N Engl J Med 1990
cards.people: Eighteen patients with essential hypertension (mean age 50.7 ± 10 years; studied two weeks after withdrawal of antihypertensive medication) and 18 normal controls (mean age 49.9 ± 9 years); increasing concentrations of acetylcholine and sodium nitroprusside infused into the brachial artery, forearm blood flow by strain-gauge plethysmography.
cards.result: Basal forearm blood flow was similar in patients and controls (3.4 ± 1.3 vs 3.7 ± 0.8 mL/min/100 mL; not significant). Responses of flow and vascular resistance to acetylcholine were significantly reduced in the hypertensive patients (P < 0.0001): maximal forearm flow was 9.1 ± 5 mL/min/100 mL in patients vs 20.0 ± 8 in controls. Because nitroprusside — a direct smooth-muscle dilator — bypasses the endothelium, the selective acetylcholine defect localises the abnormality to endothelium-dependent relaxation rather than to the muscle itself.
cards.watchOut: Medication withdrawal for two weeks is part of the design; the record's excerpt prints the acetylcholine contrast in full and the shelf does not add a nitroprusside figure the excerpt does not state.
cards.source: Panza JA, Quyyumi AA, Brush JE Jr, Epstein SE. Abnormal endothelium-dependent vascular relaxation in patients with essential hypertension. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1990. PMID: 2355955. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Celermajer 1992: flow-mediated dilatation — the non-invasive FMD test — was ~10% in controls and much reduced or absent in smokers, FH children and coronary patients (n = 100)
cards.summary: Celermajer 1992: flow-mediated dilatation — the non-invasive FMD test — was ~10% in controls and much reduced or absent in smokers, FH children and coronary patients (n = 100)
cards.type: Human physiological study (non-invasive ultrasound FMD method and risk-group comparison), Lancet 1992
cards.people: One hundred subjects: 50 controls without vascular risk factors (aged 8–57 years), 20 cigarette smokers (17–62 years), 10 children with familial hypercholesterolaemia (8–16 years) and 20 patients with established coronary artery disease; high-resolution ultrasound of superficial femoral and brachial arteries at rest, during reactive hyperaemia (flow-mediated, endothelium-dependent dilatation) and after sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (endothelium-independent). Adequate scans in all but 6 cases.
cards.result: Flow-mediated dilatation was observed in arteries from all control subjects; it was inversely related to baseline vessel diameter (r = −0.81; P < 0.0001), and in arteries of 6.0 mm or less mean dilatation was 10 (SE 2)%. In smokers, children with familial hypercholesterolaemia and adults with coronary disease, flow-mediated dilatation was much reduced or absent (P < 0.001 vs each relevant control group), while dilatation to GTN was present in all groups. This is the founding human study of brachial FMD — the method limb folded into this shelf: a cuff, a hyperaemic flow surge, and an ultrasound percentage that reports endothelial NO function non-invasively.
cards.watchOut: FMD is diameter-dependent (hence the ≤6.0 mm reporting) and technique-sensitive; the 10% figure belongs to this protocol and era's ultrasound, and later standardised protocols report their own reference ranges.
cards.source: Celermajer DS, Sorensen KE, Gooch VM, Spiegelhalter DJ, et al. Non-invasive detection of endothelial dysfunction in children and adults at risk of atherosclerosis. Lancet. 1992. PMID: 1359209. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: one pathway, four human windows — L-NMMA removes basal tone, acetylcholine exposes diseased endothelium, hypertension blunts the forearm response, and FMD measures it without a catheter
cards.summary: Synthesis: one pathway, four human windows — L-NMMA removes basal tone, acetylcholine exposes diseased endothelium, hypertension blunts the forearm response, and FMD measures it without a catheter
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Vallance 1989; Ludmer 1986; Panza 1990; Celermajer 1992), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of endothelium-derived relaxing factor (nitric oxide) as textbook framing.
cards.result: Endothelium-dependent vasodilatation in humans is demonstrated, not inferred: (1) necessity — inhibiting NO synthesis halves resting forearm flow and blunts acetylcholine dilatation while sparing GTN (Vallance); (2) coronary expression — acetylcholine dilates normal arteries (+0.22 mm) and constricts atherosclerotic ones (down to 0.32 mm) (Ludmer); (3) disease quantification — hypertension halves the maximal forearm acetylcholine response (9.1 vs 20.0 mL/min/100 mL) with the muscle's own dilator machinery intact (Panza); (4) non-invasive measurement — reactive-hyperaemia FMD (~10% in healthy arteries ≤6 mm) is lost early in smokers, hypercholesterolaemic children and coronary patients while GTN responses persist (Celermajer). The animal ring experiments that identified EDRF as NO (Furchgott; Ignarro) are the textbook framing for the pathway; every measurement on this shelf is from living human vessels.
cards.watchOut: Each method interrogates a different bed and stimulus; concordance across all four — not any single test — is the established finding. No animal vessel data are carded.

shelves.title: Endothelial glycocalyx shedding in human sepsis: syndecan-1 and heparan sulfate are markedly raised and track organ failure and death (observational)
shelves.question: In human sepsis, what evidence shows endothelial glycocalyx shedding (circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate), and how do shedding markers relate to organ failure, fluid responsiveness and death?
shelves.mesh: Glycocalyx · Syndecan-1 · Heparan Sulfate · Sepsis · Shock, Septic · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the phenomenon, with the evidence graded honestly: every carded study is observational. In human sepsis the endothelial glycocalyx is shed — circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate and glycosaminoglycans are consistently and markedly elevated (Nelson 2008: syndecan-1 246 vs 26 ng/mL in controls, in only 18 patients; Steppan 2011: shedding in sepsis comparable to that after major abdominal surgery). Shedding markers track the cardiovascular SOFA score, respiratory failure, renal replacement, subsequent fluid volumes and death; the largest dataset, the 574-patient CLOVERS substudy, found 90-day mortality of 9.9%, 20.4% and 44.2% across baseline heparan sulfate tertiles (adjusted HR 3.12 per interquartile-range increase). Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): the glycocalyx is the endothelial surface layer that helps govern capillary permeability — these fragments are its debris in plasma. What is NOT established: that shedding causes organ failure rather than marking it, that it is sepsis-specific (surgery sheds it too), or that any glycocalyx-directed therapy improves outcomes — the randomised fluid comparison inside CLOVERS changed neither shedding nor outcome by shedding level.

cards.headline: Nelson 2008: in 18 patients with septic shock, circulating glycosaminoglycans and syndecan-1 were markedly raised — and highest in those who died (small N, printed)
cards.summary: Nelson 2008: in 18 patients with septic shock, circulating glycosaminoglycans and syndecan-1 were markedly raised — and highest in those who died (small N, printed)
cards.type: Human observational cohort (septic shock, with matched controls), Shock 2008
cards.people: 18 consecutive ICU patients with septic shock, with matched controls; arterial plasma glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) measured by Alcian blue assay and syndecan-1 by ELISA. Small classic cohort — N = 18 patients, printed on the face.
cards.result: Median plasma GAG was 2.7 µg/mL (IQR 1.9–4.8) in septic shock vs 1.8 µg/mL (1.7–2.0) in controls, and was higher in nonsurvivors (4.6 µg/mL [3.1–8.8], n = 8) than survivors (1.8 µg/mL [1.6–2.6], n = 10). Syndecan-1 was 246 ng/mL (180–496) in patients vs 26 ng/mL (23–31) in controls and correlated with the cardiovascular SOFA score. In vitro, GAGs at patient-range concentrations neutralised the antibacterial activity of plasma and of isolated antimicrobial peptides.
cards.watchOut: Only 18 patients — a first signal, not a prognostic tool. GAGs are not glycocalyx-specific (they also come from other extracellular matrix), and the antibacterial neutralisation was shown in vitro, not in patients.
cards.source: Nelson A, Berkestedt I, Schmidtchen A, Ljunggren L, Bodelsson M, et al. Increased levels of glycosaminoglycans during septic shock: relation to mortality and the antibacterial actions of plasma. Shock. 2008. PMID: 18497712. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Steppan 2011: syndecan-1 and heparan sulfate were high in sepsis — but almost as high after major abdominal surgery (150 people, three groups)
cards.summary: Steppan 2011: syndecan-1 and heparan sulfate were high in sepsis — but almost as high after major abdominal surgery (150 people, three groups)
cards.type: Human observational study (sepsis vs surgical vs healthy groups), J Surg Res 2011
cards.people: 150 individuals in three groups: patients with severe sepsis or septic shock, patients after major abdominal surgery without SIRS, and healthy volunteers; syndecan-1, heparan sulfate, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and IL-6 measured at diagnosis/surgery and 6, 24 and 48 hours later. Group sizes are not printed in the abstract record.
cards.result: Inflammatory markers were markedly higher in sepsis than after surgery or in volunteers. Glycocalyx markers (syndecan-1, heparan sulfate) were at sepsis-comparable levels after major abdominal surgery — significant shedding ('flaking') of the endothelial glycocalyx occurred in sepsis and, to a lesser extent, after major surgery. In sepsis, IL-6 correlated with syndecan-1, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and lactate.
cards.watchOut: Shedding is not sepsis-specific: major surgery alone shed the glycocalyx to a similar degree, so a high syndecan-1 cannot by itself diagnose sepsis or separate it from other major physiological insults.
cards.source: Steppan J, Hofer S, Funke B, Brenner T, Henrich M, Martin E, et al. Sepsis and major abdominal surgery lead to flaking of the endothelial glycocalix. The Journal of Surgical Research. 2011. PMID: 19560161. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smart 2018: in 44 ED patients with pneumonia sepsis, rising syndecan-1 predicted respiratory failure, ventilation and 30-day death
cards.summary: Smart 2018: in 44 ED patients with pneumonia sepsis, rising syndecan-1 predicted respiratory failure, ventilation and 30-day death
cards.type: Human prospective observational cohort (ED pneumonia sepsis), J Crit Care 2018
cards.people: 44 emergency department patients with sepsis due to pneumonia; endocan, syndecan-1 and hyaluronan measured on arrival and at 1, 3 and 12–24 hours. Small cohort — N = 44, printed on the face.
cards.result: Syndecan-1 rose significantly over the first 24 hours (endocan fell). Increased syndecan-1 was associated with higher odds of respiratory failure (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.05–1.33; P = 0.004), need for mechanical ventilation (OR 1.24, 1.04–1.48; P = 0.014) and 30-day mortality (OR 1.29, 1.07–1.55; P = 0.008), and correlated with neutrophil activation biomarkers; it was the best of the three glycocalyx biomarkers at predicting adverse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: 44 patients, one centre, pneumonia sepsis only; odds ratios are per-unit associations from a small sample and the abstract record does not print the unit increment — association, not a bedside prediction rule.
cards.source: Smart L, Bosio E, Macdonald SPJ, Dull R, Fatovich DM, Neil C, et al. Glycocalyx biomarker syndecan-1 is a stronger predictor of respiratory failure in patients with sepsis due to pneumonia, compared to endocan. Journal of Critical Care. 2018. PMID: 29936329. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Saoraya 2021: in 95 ED patients with sepsis, syndecan-1 tracked SOFA score, later fluid volumes, vasopressor dose and 90-day mortality
cards.summary: Saoraya 2021: in 95 ED patients with sepsis, syndecan-1 tracked SOFA score, later fluid volumes, vasopressor dose and 90-day mortality
cards.type: Human observational study (post hoc analysis within a fluid-resuscitation trial cohort), Am J Emerg Med 2021
cards.people: 95 adults with sepsis-induced hypoperfusion in a tertiary emergency department, in a post hoc analysis of a randomised fluid-resuscitation trial; syndecan-1 measured at baseline (T0) and hour 6 (T6).
cards.result: Median syndecan-1 was 207 ng/mL (IQR 135–438) at T0 and 207 (128–490) at T6. T0 levels correlated with baseline SOFA score (ρ = 0.35, P < 0.001). Levels at T0 and T6 correlated with subsequent fluid administration over 24 and 72 hours and were associated with septic shock diagnosis, maximum vasopressor dose and need for renal replacement therapy (P < 0.05); higher T6 levels were associated with higher 90-day mortality (P = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and observational: syndecan-1 predicted how much fluid clinicians went on to give, which may reflect severity driving both — it does not show that shedding causes the fluid requirement, or that syndecan-1 should guide fluid dosing.
cards.source: Saoraya J, Wongsamita L, Srisawat N, Musikatavorn K. Plasma syndecan-1 is associated with fluid requirements and clinical outcomes in emergency department patients with sepsis. The American Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33493833. Registry ID: none printed in the record. cards.headline: CLOVERS substudy 2025: in 574 patients with sepsis, baseline heparan sulfate split 90-day mortality 9.9% / 20.4% / 44.2% by tertile — and fluid strategy did not change shedding
cards.summary: CLOVERS substudy 2025: in 574 patients with sepsis, baseline heparan sulfate split 90-day mortality 9.9% / 20.4% / 44.2% by tertile — and fluid strategy did not change shedding
cards.type: Human biomarker substudy of a multicentre randomised trial (CLOVERS), Ann Am Thorac Soc 2025
cards.people: 574 patients from the CLOVERS randomised trial (liberal vs restrictive fluids in sepsis-induced hypotension), sampled by an enriched strategy; plasma heparan sulfate by mass spectrometry as the primary glycocalyx-degradation measure, syndecan-1 by immunoassay as the complementary index. Primary outcome: 90-day all-cause mortality.
cards.result: 90-day mortality rose steeply across baseline heparan sulfate tertiles: 9.9% (95% CI 7.0–12.7) in the lowest, 20.4% (15.6–25.0) in the middle and 44.2% (35.6–51.6) in the highest (P < 0.001); the adjusted hazard ratio per interquartile-range increase was 3.12 (2.18–4.46). Assigned fluid strategy had no effect on glycocalyx degradation at 24 hours, and there was no differential fluid-strategy effect on mortality by baseline heparan sulfate; syndecan-1 gave similar findings.
cards.watchOut: A strong prognostic gradient is not a treatment target: the randomised comparison inside this same study showed fluid strategy neither changed shedding nor worked differently at high shedding levels. No therapy aimed at the glycocalyx has an outcome trial behind it.
cards.source: Oshima K, Di Gravio C, Yan B, McMurtry SA, Burke R, Levoir LM, et al. Endothelial Glycocalyx Degradation in Sepsis: Analysis of the Crystalloid Liberal or Vasopressors Early Resuscitation in Sepsis (CLOVERS) Trial, a Multicenter, Phase 3, Randomized Trial. Annals of the American Thoracic Society. 2025. PMID: 40315385. Registry ID: NCT03434028. cards.headline: Synthesis: shedding is real, graded and prognostic — a marker of endothelial injury, not yet a target
cards.summary: Synthesis: shedding is real, graded and prognostic — a marker of endothelial injury, not yet a target
cards.people: Adults with sepsis and septic shock across five human studies carded above (cohorts of 18 to 574 patients), read with the textbook framing: in Guyton & Hall's account the glycocalyx is the carbohydrate-rich endothelial surface layer that helps govern capillary permeability and fluid exchange — the structure these plasma fragments come from.
cards.result: Every carded study found the same direction: circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate and total glycosaminoglycans are markedly elevated in human sepsis, rise early, and track organ failure (cardiovascular SOFA, respiratory failure, renal replacement), fluid administration and death — most strongly in the 574-patient CLOVERS substudy (adjusted HR 3.12 per interquartile-range rise in heparan sulfate). The honest limits: all prognostic evidence is observational; shedding also follows major surgery, so it is a general endothelial-injury signal, not a sepsis-specific one; and no intervention that protects or restores the glycocalyx has been shown to change outcomes. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the shedding phenomenon and its prognostic association; any therapeutic claim would be emerging at best.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the strength of the association smuggle in causation: sicker patients shed more, and shedding may be a readout of the same inflammatory injury that drives organ failure rather than its mechanism.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 18497712, 19560161, 29936329, 33493833, 40315385). Registry ID: NCT03434028 (CLOVERS substudy). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Fitusiran prophylaxis in haemophilia A or B: annualised bleeding rates cut from 18.1 to 1.7 (with inhibitors) and 31.0 to 3.1 (without) versus on-demand therapy — with thromboembolic events in 3–5% and a 2020 voluntary dosing pause that replaced fixed dosing with an antithrombin-target (15–35%) regimen
shelves.question: In people aged 12+ with haemophilia A or B, does monthly subcutaneous fitusiran (an antithrombin-lowering siRNA) prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes versus on-demand treatment or prior factor prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Male · Young Adult · Humans · Adult · Female · Hemophilia A/complications,drug therapy · Hemophilia B/complications,drug therapy · Alanine Transaminase · Hemorrhage/epidemiology · RNA, Small Interfering/therapeutic use · Acetylgalactosamine
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant open-label randomised phase 3 trials show large bleeding reductions, and the thrombotic safety history is stated here on the face, not in fine print. In ATLAS-INH (n=57, with inhibitors) mean annualised bleeding rate was 1.7 on monthly fitusiran versus 18.1 on on-demand bypassing agents (a 90.8% relative reduction); in ATLAS-A/B (n=120, without inhibitors) it was 3.1 versus 31.0 on on-demand factor concentrates (rate ratio 0.101). ATLAS-PPX showed further reductions after switching from prior prophylaxis. THE SAFETY HISTORY: suspected or confirmed thromboembolic events occurred in 2 participants (5%) in ATLAS-INH and 2 (3.0%) in ATLAS-PPX; alanine aminotransferase rose in 23–32% on fitusiran; the programme's original fixed-dose regimen was placed on a voluntary dosing pause in 2020 and replaced by an antithrombin-based regimen targeting antithrombin activity of 15–35%, after which the phase 2 extension (n=34, median 4.1 years) reported no thrombotic events and fewer transaminase and biliary events, with bleeding control maintained (median ABR 0.87). The carded trials used the superseded fixed 80 mg regimen — that caveat travels with every number above.

cards.headline: ATLAS-INH — Young 2023 (n=57, with inhibitors): mean annualised bleeding rate 1.7 on monthly fitusiran versus 18.1 on on-demand bypassing agents (a 90.8% relative reduction); 66% versus 5% had zero treated bleeds; suspected/confirmed thromboembolic events in 2 participants (5%)
cards.summary: ATLAS-INH — Young 2023 (n=57, with inhibitors): mean annualised bleeding rate 1.7 on monthly fitusiran versus 18.1 on on-demand bypassing agents (a 90.8% relative reduction); 66% versus 5% had zero treated bleeds; suspected/confirmed thromboembolic events in 2 participants (5%)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised phase 3 trial (Young 2023, ATLAS-INH)
cards.people: 57 men, boys and young adults aged ≥12 years with severe haemophilia A or B with inhibitors, previously treated with on-demand bypassing agents, at 26 sites in 12 countries, randomised 2:1 to once-monthly subcutaneous fitusiran 80 mg prophylaxis (n=38) or continued on-demand bypassing agents (n=19) for 9 months.
cards.result: Model-based mean annualised bleeding rate (ABR) was 1.7 (95% CI 1.0–2.7) on fitusiran versus 18.1 (10.6–30.8) on on-demand bypassing agents — a 90.8% relative reduction (95% CI 80.8–95.6; p<0.0001), an absolute difference of about 16 fewer bleeds per year. Twenty-five of 38 participants (66%) had zero treated bleeds on fitusiran versus 1 of 19 (5%) on demand. The commonest treatment-emergent adverse event on fitusiran was increased alanine aminotransferase (13 of 41 in the safety population, 32%; none on demand). Suspected or confirmed thromboembolic events were reported in 2 participants (5%) in the fitusiran group. No deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design, and the trial used the original fixed 80 mg regimen — the regimen the programme later replaced with antithrombin-targeted dosing after its thrombotic safety pause (see the long-term safety card). The 5% thromboembolic-event figure belongs on the face of any fitusiran claim, not in fine print.
cards.source: Young G et al. Efficacy and safety of fitusiran prophylaxis in people with haemophilia A or haemophilia B with inhibitors (ATLAS-INH): a multicentre, open-label, randomised phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2023. PMID: 37003287. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03417102, from the record. cards.headline: ATLAS-A/B — Srivastava 2023 (n=120, without inhibitors): estimated mean annualised bleeding rate 3.1 on fitusiran versus 31.0 on on-demand factor concentrates (rate ratio 0.101); 51% versus 5% had no treated bleeds; no treatment-related thrombosis in this trial
cards.summary: ATLAS-A/B — Srivastava 2023 (n=120, without inhibitors): estimated mean annualised bleeding rate 3.1 on fitusiran versus 31.0 on on-demand factor concentrates (rate ratio 0.101); 51% versus 5% had no treated bleeds; no treatment-related thrombosis in this trial
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised phase 3 trial (Srivastava 2023, ATLAS-A/B)
cards.people: 120 male participants aged ≥12 years with severe haemophilia A or B without inhibitors, previously treated on demand with clotting factor concentrates, at 45 sites in 17 countries, randomised 2:1 to once-monthly subcutaneous fitusiran 80 mg (n=80) or continued on-demand concentrates (n=40) for 9 months.
cards.result: Median ABR was 0.0 (IQR 0.0–3.4) on fitusiran versus 21.8 (8.4–41.0) on demand; estimated mean ABR was 3.1 (95% CI 2.3–4.3) versus 31.0 (21.1–45.5) — rate ratio 0.101 (0.064–0.159; p<0.0001), about a 90% relative reduction and roughly 28 fewer bleeds per year in absolute terms. Forty of 79 treated participants (51%) had no treated bleeds versus 2 of 40 (5%). Increased alanine aminotransferase was the commonest treatment-emergent adverse event on fitusiran (18 of 79, 23%). Serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 5 (6%) on fitusiran (including cholelithiasis in 2 and cholecystitis in 1) versus 5 (13%) on demand. No treatment-related thrombosis or deaths were reported in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Again open-label and on the original fixed-dose regimen. The absence of thrombosis here does not cancel the thromboembolic events in ATLAS-INH and ATLAS-PPX or the programme's earlier dosing pause — the safety history is programme-level, and this shelf presents it that way.
cards.source: Srivastava A et al. Fitusiran prophylaxis in people with severe haemophilia A or haemophilia B without inhibitors (ATLAS-A/B): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Haematology. 2023. PMID: 37003278. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03417245, from the record. cards.headline: ATLAS-PPX — Kenet 2024 (n=65 in the bleeding analysis, switched from prior prophylaxis): estimated mean annualised bleeding rate fell 79.7% relative in inhibitor patients and 46.4% relative in non-inhibitor patients versus their own prior prophylaxis period; thromboembolic events in 2 participants (3.0%)
cards.summary: ATLAS-PPX — Kenet 2024 (n=65 in the bleeding analysis, switched from prior prophylaxis): estimated mean annualised bleeding rate fell 79.7% relative in inhibitor patients and 46.4% relative in non-inhibitor patients versus their own prior prophylaxis period; thromboembolic events in 2 participants (3.0%)
cards.people: 80 males aged ≥12 years with haemophilia A or B, with or without inhibitors, who had been receiving bypassing-agent or factor-concentrate prophylaxis; 65 were eligible for the bleeding analysis (19 with inhibitors, 46 without). Participants continued prior prophylaxis for 6 months, then switched to once-monthly fitusiran 80 mg for 7 months, serving as their own controls.
cards.result: Observed median ABR was 0.0 in the fitusiran efficacy period in both subgroups, versus 6.5 (inhibitor) and 4.4 (non-inhibitor) during prior prophylaxis. Estimated mean ABR was reduced by 79.7% in relative terms in the inhibitor subgroup (P=.0021) and by 46.4% in relative terms in the non-inhibitor subgroup (P=.0598, not significant). Forty-one participants (63.1%) had zero treated bleeds on fitusiran versus 11 (16.9%) on prior prophylaxis. Two participants (3.0%) experienced suspected or confirmed thromboembolic events on fitusiran.
cards.watchOut: A before–after switch design with no parallel control group: period effects and regression to the mean can flatter the switch, and the non-inhibitor comparison did not reach significance. Its value is showing benefit persisted in people already on prophylaxis — the harder comparison — not in replacing the randomised trials.
cards.source: Kenet G et al. Fitusiran prophylaxis in people with hemophilia A or B who switched from prior BPA/CFC prophylaxis: the ATLAS-PPX trial. Blood. 2024. PMID: 38452197. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03549871, from the record. cards.headline: Long-term safety — Pipe 2025 (phase 2 extension, n=34, median exposure 4.1 years): the original fixed-dose regimen ran until a voluntary dosing pause in 2020, after which an antithrombin-based regimen targeting 15–35% activity was introduced; no thrombotic events occurred after the switch
cards.summary: Long-term safety — Pipe 2025 (phase 2 extension, n=34, median exposure 4.1 years): the original fixed-dose regimen ran until a voluntary dosing pause in 2020, after which an antithrombin-based regimen targeting 15–35% activity was introduced; no thrombotic events occurred after the switch
cards.people: 34 male participants (27 haemophilia A, 7 haemophilia B, with or without inhibitors) who had completed the phase 1 study, treated with monthly subcutaneous fitusiran 50 or 80 mg under the original dose regimen until a voluntary dosing pause in 2020, then under an antithrombin (AT)-based dose regimen targeting AT activity of 15–35%; median exposure 4.1 years.
cards.result: Adverse events on both regimens were consistent with fitusiran's identified risks. After implementation of the AT-based regimen there were no thrombotic events, and the incidence of elevated transaminases and biliary events was reduced compared with the original regimen. Observed median annualised bleed rate was 0.87 on the AT-based regimen versus 0.70 under the original regimen — bleeding control was maintained. Fitusiran provided haemostatic control during surgical and invasive procedures, and health-related quality of life improved versus baseline.
cards.watchOut: This is the card that carries the programme's safety history on the face: fixed dosing was paused voluntarily in 2020 and replaced by antithrombin-targeted dosing precisely because of the thrombotic risk of overshooting antithrombin suppression. The extension is small (n=34) and uncontrolled, so 'no thrombotic events after the switch' is reassuring, not proof the risk is gone.
cards.source: Pipe SW et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of fitusiran prophylaxis, and perioperative management, in people with hemophilia A or B. Blood advances. 2025. PMID: 39642315. cards.headline: Synthesis: bleeding rates cut by ~90% relative in two randomised trials — with a thrombotic safety history that changed the dosing regimen — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: bleeding rates cut by ~90% relative in two randomised trials — with a thrombotic safety history that changed the dosing regimen — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the ATLAS programme (ATLAS-INH, ATLAS-A/B, ATLAS-PPX) and the phase 2 long-term extension.
cards.result: Two open-label randomised phase 3 trials agree: monthly fitusiran prophylaxis reduced mean annualised bleeding rates from 18.1 to 1.7 (with inhibitors) and from 31.0 to 3.1 (without inhibitors) versus on-demand therapy — about a 90% relative reduction in both — and a switch study showed further reductions versus prior prophylaxis. The safety history is part of the result: thromboembolic events occurred in 5% (ATLAS-INH) and 3.0% (ATLAS-PPX) of participants, alanine aminotransferase rose in about a quarter to a third, the original fixed-dose regimen was voluntarily paused in 2020, and dosing was rebuilt around an antithrombin activity target of 15–35%, after which no thrombotic events were seen in the small extension cohort.
cards.watchOut: The carded randomised trials used the superseded fixed 80 mg regimen, so their exact bleeding and thrombosis rates may not transfer one-for-one to antithrombin-targeted dosing; long-term safety on the current regimen rests on a 34-person extension.
cards.source: Synthesis of Young G et al. Lancet (London, England). 2023 (PMID: 37003287); Srivastava A et al. The Lancet. Haematology. 2023 (PMID: 37003278); Kenet G et al. Blood. 2024 (PMID: 38452197); Pipe SW et al. Blood advances. 2025 (PMID: 39642315).

shelves.title: Osocimab for VTE prevention after knee arthroplasty (FOXTROT, phase 2): venographic VTE 15.7–17.9% on postoperative osocimab versus 26.3% on enoxaparin (non-inferior) — PHASE 2 trial with a venographic surrogate endpoint
shelves.question: In adults undergoing total knee arthroplasty, does a single pre- or post-operative dose of osocimab prevent venous thromboembolism versus enoxaparin, and versus apixaban, with what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Enoxaparin/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Factor Xa Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Preoperative Care · Pulmonary Embolism/prevention & control · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pyridones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Single-Blind Method · Venous Thromboembolism/prevention & control · Venous Thrombosis/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2, VENOGRAPHIC SURROGATE: both labels belong on the face. FOXTROT (813 randomised; 600 in the primary per-protocol analysis) is the only efficacy trial: a single postoperative intravenous osocimab dose of 0.6, 1.2 or 1.8 mg/kg met non-inferiority versus enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism at days 10–13 (15.7–17.9% versus 26.3%), and a preoperative 1.8 mg/kg dose (11.3%) met superiority criteria versus enoxaparin — but the endpoint was assessed by mandatory bilateral venography, so most events were asymptomatic clots found by screening, not symptomatic VTE. Apixaban's rate was 14.5% with no formal comparison. Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was up to 4.7% on osocimab versus 5.9% on enoxaparin and 2% on apixaban. Phase 1 studies confirm long dose-dependent aPTT prolongation from a single dose, and a 4-trial class meta-analysis favours factor XI inhibitors over low-molecular-weight heparin on the same surrogate (VTE odds ratio 0.50, a relative measure). Class pair: pack #6596 (milvexian) asks the same arthroplasty question for an oral factor XIa inhibitor.

cards.headline: FOXTROT — Weitz 2020 (phase 2, n=813 randomised; 600 in the primary per-protocol analysis): venographic VTE in 15.7–17.9% on postoperative osocimab 0.6–1.8 mg/kg versus 26.3% on enoxaparin (non-inferior); preoperative 1.8 mg/kg 11.3% (superior); apixaban 14.5% — PHASE 2 with a venographic surrogate endpoint
cards.summary: FOXTROT — Weitz 2020 (phase 2, n=813 randomised; 600 in the primary per-protocol analysis): venographic VTE in 15.7–17.9% on postoperative osocimab 0.6–1.8 mg/kg versus 26.3% on enoxaparin (non-inferior); preoperative 1.8 mg/kg 11.3% (superior); apixaban 14.5% — PHASE 2 with a venographic surrogate endpoint
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, adjudicator-blinded phase 2 non-inferiority trial (Weitz 2020, FOXTROT)
cards.people: 813 adults undergoing unilateral total knee arthroplasty at 54 hospitals in 13 countries (mean age 66.5 years, 74.2% women), randomised to a single intravenous osocimab dose — postoperatively 0.3, 0.6, 1.2 or 1.8 mg/kg, or preoperatively 0.3 or 1.8 mg/kg — or enoxaparin 40 mg daily (n=105) or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (n=105) for at least 10 days. The primary outcome was venous thromboembolism between days 10–13, assessed mainly by mandatory bilateral venography — a surrogate endpoint, since most venographic clots are asymptomatic.
cards.result: In the per-protocol population (n=600), VTE occurred in 23.7% (postoperative 0.3 mg/kg), 15.7% (0.6 mg/kg), 16.5% (1.2 mg/kg) and 17.9% (1.8 mg/kg) on osocimab; 29.9% (preoperative 0.3 mg/kg) and 11.3% (preoperative 1.8 mg/kg); 26.3% on enoxaparin; and 14.5% on apixaban. Postoperative doses of 0.6, 1.2 and 1.8 mg/kg met the 5% non-inferiority margin versus enoxaparin; the preoperative 1.8 mg/kg dose met criteria for superiority versus enoxaparin (risk difference 15.1 percentage points, 90% CI 4.9–25.2); both 0.3 mg/kg doses failed non-inferiority. Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in up to 4.7% on osocimab, 5.9% on enoxaparin and 2% on apixaban.
cards.watchOut: PHASE 2, SURROGATE ENDPOINT: the outcome is mostly silent venographic clots found because venography was mandatory, not symptomatic VTE or pulmonary embolism — the trial cannot show osocimab prevents clots patients would feel. There was no non-inferiority test against apixaban, whose rate (14.5%) was numerically the lowest of the standard arms. Class pair: pack #6596 (milvexian, AXIOMATIC-TKR) asks the same question for an oral factor XIa inhibitor.
cards.source: Weitz JI et al. Effect of Osocimab in Preventing Venous Thromboembolism Among Patients Undergoing Knee Arthroplasty: The FOXTROT Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 31935028. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03276143, from the record. cards.headline: Phase 1 — osocimab in healthy East Asian volunteers (two studies, n=77): single doses prolonged aPTT dose-dependently, exposure was not dose-proportional for AUC, and the antibody was generally well tolerated over 149 days
cards.summary: Phase 1 — osocimab in healthy East Asian volunteers (two studies, n=77): single doses prolonged aPTT dose-dependently, exposure was not dose-proportional for AUC, and the antibody was generally well tolerated over 149 days
cards.people: 27 healthy Japanese and 50 healthy Chinese male volunteers given single intravenous osocimab doses (0.3–5.0 mg/kg, varying by study) or subcutaneous doses (3.0–6.0 mg/kg), or placebo, and followed for 149 days for pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, immunogenicity and safety.
cards.result: Maximum plasma concentration was reached 1–3 hours after intravenous and 4–6 days after subcutaneous dosing. Exposure (AUC) deviated from dose proportionality — higher doses had higher apparent clearance and disproportionately lower total exposure — while Cmax was dose-proportional. Osocimab prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time dose-dependently, as its factor XIa mechanism predicts. Low-titre anti-drug antibodies were detected in 26 of 40 (65.0%) Chinese volunteers given osocimab. Adverse events were reported in 44.4% of Japanese and 70.0% of Chinese osocimab recipients (and in some placebo recipients); the authors conclude osocimab was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Healthy-volunteer pharmacology only: it establishes that a single dose engages factor XIa for a long period (the basis for FOXTROT's single-dose design), and says nothing about preventing clots. The 65% anti-drug-antibody figure in one study is a flag for a monoclonal antibody given once — its clinical meaning after a single perioperative dose is unknown.
cards.source: Dong Z et al. Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the factor XIa-inhibiting antibody osocimab in healthy male East Asian volunteers: Results from two phase 1 studies. cards.headline: Class meta-analysis — factor XI inhibitors versus low-molecular-weight heparin in major orthopaedic surgery (4 RCTs, 2,269 patients): VTE odds ratio 0.50 and major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding odds ratio 0.41, both relative measures
cards.summary: Class meta-analysis — factor XI inhibitors versus low-molecular-weight heparin in major orthopaedic surgery (4 RCTs, 2,269 patients): VTE odds ratio 0.50 and major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding odds ratio 0.41, both relative measures
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (2022)
cards.people: Four randomised trials (2,269 patients, 372 VTE events, 50 major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding events) of factor XI/XIa inhibitors — including FOXTROT (osocimab) and AXIOMATIC-TKR (milvexian) — versus low-molecular-weight heparin for thromboprophylaxis in major orthopaedic surgery, searched to May 2022.
cards.result: Across the class, factor XI inhibitors were associated with lower VTE incidence than low-molecular-weight heparin (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.36–0.69 — a relative measure) and fewer major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding events (odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.75). Transfusion need was lower but not significantly (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.32–1.48), and overall adverse-event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: This pools four different drugs and doses, and its VTE endpoint is the same venographic surrogate as the trials themselves — it strengthens the class signal for silent clots and bleeding, and cannot rescue the missing symptomatic-event evidence. It is carded once, here; pack #6596 (milvexian) cross-points to it rather than re-carding it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a single phase 2 trial on a venographic surrogate — postoperative osocimab was non-inferior to enoxaparin, no more — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single phase 2 trial on a venographic surrogate — postoperative osocimab was non-inferior to enoxaparin, no more — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of FOXTROT, the phase 1 pharmacology studies, and the orthopaedic factor XI class meta-analysis. Class pair: pack #6596 (milvexian).
cards.result: Osocimab's entire clinical efficacy record is one phase 2 trial (FOXTROT) whose endpoint was mainly mandatory-venography clots at days 10–13: postoperative single doses of 0.6–1.8 mg/kg were non-inferior to enoxaparin, a preoperative 1.8 mg/kg dose was superior to enoxaparin on that surrogate, and bleeding was no worse (up to 4.7% versus 5.9%). Phase 1 work confirms long, dose-dependent factor XIa engagement from a single dose, and a class meta-analysis favours factor XI inhibitors over low-molecular-weight heparin on the same surrogate. That is a proof of concept, stamped POSSIBLE, with PHASE 2 and VENOGRAPHIC SURROGATE on the face.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 trial (AXIOMATIC-TKR, n=1,242) with a venographic-predominant endpoint, labelled as such. Twice-daily milvexian showed a significant dose–response as reported: VTE in 21% at 25 mg, 11% at 50 mg, 9% at 100 mg and 8% at 200 mg twice daily, versus 21% on enoxaparin; once-daily dosing was mostly no better than enoxaparin (24–25% at 25–50 mg; 7% at 200 mg). The trial's formal comparison was against a prespecified 30% benchmark (pooled twice-daily incidence 12%, P<0.001), not a powered head-to-head. Bleeding of any severity was 4% in both groups; major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was 1% on milvexian versus 2% on enoxaparin. First-in-human and Japanese multiple-dose studies (n=104 and n=32) confirm the pharmacology behind twice-daily dosing — half-life ~8–14 hours and exposure-related aPTT prolongation — with no clinically significant bleeding in healthy volunteers. Class pair: pack #6595 (osocimab, FOXTROT); the orthopaedic factor XI class meta-analysis is carded there and cross-pointed from here.

cards.headline: AXIOMATIC-TKR — Weitz 2021 (phase 2, n=1,242): VTE fell dose-dependently on twice-daily milvexian — 21% at 25 mg, 11% at 50 mg, 9% at 100 mg, 8% at 200 mg — versus 21% on enoxaparin; major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding 1% versus 2% — phase 2, venographic endpoint
cards.summary: AXIOMATIC-TKR — Weitz 2021 (phase 2, n=1,242): VTE fell dose-dependently on twice-daily milvexian — 21% at 25 mg, 11% at 50 mg, 9% at 100 mg, 8% at 200 mg — versus 21% on enoxaparin; major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding 1% versus 2% — phase 2, venographic endpoint
cards.people: 1,242 patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty, randomised postoperatively to one of seven milvexian regimens (25, 50, 100 or 200 mg twice daily, or 25, 50 or 200 mg once daily) or enoxaparin 40 mg once daily. The primary efficacy outcome was venous thromboembolism — a composite of asymptomatic deep-vein thrombosis (found on screening venography), confirmed symptomatic VTE, or death from any cause; the principal safety outcome was bleeding.
cards.result: VTE occurred in 27/129 (21%) on milvexian 25 mg twice daily, 14/124 (11%) on 50 mg twice daily, 12/134 (9%) on 100 mg twice daily and 10/131 (8%) on 200 mg twice daily; on once-daily dosing, 7/28 (25%) at 25 mg, 30/127 (24%) at 50 mg and 8/123 (7%) at 200 mg; versus 54/252 (21%) on enoxaparin. The dose–response with twice-daily dosing was significant (one-sided P<0.001), and the pooled twice-daily incidence of 12% was significantly below the prespecified 30% benchmark (one-sided P<0.001). Bleeding of any severity occurred in 4% on milvexian and 4% on enoxaparin; major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 1% versus 2%; serious adverse events in 2% versus 4%.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 with a screening-venography composite: most events were asymptomatic clots, and the trial's formal test was against a prespecified 30% benchmark, not a powered head-to-head against enoxaparin — the dose–response is the real finding. Class pair: pack #6595 (osocimab, FOXTROT) asks the same question for an intravenous factor XIa antibody, and cards the class meta-analysis for both.

cards.headline: First-in-human — Perera 2022 (n=104 healthy adults): milvexian was safe and well tolerated with no clinically significant bleeding; aPTT prolongation tracked drug exposure; half-life 8.3–13.8 hours
cards.summary: First-in-human — Perera 2022 (n=104 healthy adults): milvexian was safe and well tolerated with no clinically significant bleeding; aPTT prolongation tracked drug exposure; half-life 8.3–13.8 hours
cards.people: Healthy adults in single-ascending-dose panels (6 panels of 8; n=48; milvexian 4–500 mg or placebo, with food-effect panels at 200 and 500 mg) and multiple-ascending-dose panels (7 panels of 8; n=56; once- or twice-daily milvexian or placebo for 14 days).
cards.result: All regimens were safe and well tolerated, with only mild treatment-emergent adverse events and no clinically significant bleeding events. Maximum concentration occurred 3 hours post-dose when fasted; terminal half-life ranged from 8.3 to 13.8 hours; absorption was dose-proportional from 20 to 200 mg and saturable above that; food increased bioavailability dose-dependently. Steady state was reached within 3 days (once daily) to 6 days (twice daily); renal excretion was under 20%. Activated partial thromboplastin time prolongation was directly related to drug exposure.
cards.watchOut: Supporting pharmacology only: the half-life and exposure–aPTT relation are why AXIOMATIC-TKR tested twice-daily dosing, but healthy-volunteer safety over 14 days cannot speak to bleeding after knee arthroplasty.
cards.source: Perera V et al. First-in-human study of milvexian, an oral, direct, small molecule factor XIa inhibitor. Clinical and translational science. 2022. PMID: 34558200. cards.headline: Multiple-dose study in healthy Japanese participants (n=32 in safety analyses): milvexian up to 500 mg daily for 14 days was generally well tolerated, with concentration-related aPTT prolongation and reduced factor XI clotting activity
cards.summary: Multiple-dose study in healthy Japanese participants (n=32 in safety analyses): milvexian up to 500 mg daily for 14 days was generally well tolerated, with concentration-related aPTT prolongation and reduced factor XI clotting activity
cards.people: Healthy Japanese participants receiving oral milvexian daily for 14 days under fasted conditions (50 mg, 200 mg) or fed conditions (500 mg), or placebo; 32 participants were included in safety and pharmacodynamic analyses (24 in pharmacokinetic analyses) after an unblinding event required one cohort to be discontinued and re-enrolled.
cards.result: Milvexian up to 500 mg daily for 14 days was generally well tolerated, with no deaths, serious adverse events or discontinuations for adverse events. Exposure increased between 50 mg and 200 mg; median time to maximum concentration was 2.5–3.0 hours fasted and 7.0–8.0 hours fed (500 mg); median half-life was 8.9–11.9 hours. Multiple dosing produced concentration-related prolongation of aPTT and decreased factor XI clotting activity.
cards.watchOut: A small supporting pharmacology study (N=32 printed plainly), included because it independently confirms the exposure–anticoagulation relation in a second population; it contributes no efficacy evidence, and the stamp rests on AXIOMATIC-TKR alone.
cards.source: Perera V et al. Safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of milvexian in healthy Japanese participants. Scientific reports. 2022. PMID: 35338177. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Mitapivat in sickle cell disease (RISE UP, n=207): haemoglobin response 41% versus 3% (co-primary met) but annualised pain crises 2.6 versus 3.1, p=0.12 (co-primary NOT met) — a split result
shelves.question: In people aged 16+ with sickle cell disease and recurrent pain crises, does mitapivat 100 mg twice daily raise haemoglobin and reduce annualised pain crises versus placebo over 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Anemia, Sickle Cell/drug therapy,complications · Double-Blind Method · Hemoglobins/analysis · Pyridines/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Pyruvate Kinase · Treatment Outcome · Vaso-Occlusive Crises · Benzaldehydes · Pyrazines · Pyrazoles
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the co-primary result is split, and this shelf presents it as a split. In RISE UP phase 3 (n=207, 52 weeks), mitapivat 100 mg twice daily produced a haemoglobin response in 41% versus 3% on placebo (adjusted difference 38 percentage points; p<0.0001) — that co-primary was met — but the annualised rate of sickle cell pain crises was 2.6 versus 3.1 (p=0.12), so the pain-crisis co-primary was NOT met: on that outcome the treatment made no significant difference. The phase 2 portion (n=79) showed the same haemoglobin effect (46–50% versus 4%), and a 10-patient open-label study (9 at 1 year) reported haemoglobin and crisis signals against historic baseline that randomised testing did not confirm. Serious adverse events were 20% on mitapivat versus 29% on placebo in phase 3. PARTIAL build: mitapivat's verified homes are live shelf #1803 (pyruvate kinase deficiency) and pack #4882 (thalassaemia) — their records are homed there, are not carded here, and are cross-pointed in the synthesis prose only; this pack builds only the sickle cell slice. The fetched RISE UP record reports no transfusion-burden result, so none is claimed.

cards.headline: RISE UP phase 3 — Andemariam 2026 (n=207): haemoglobin response 41% on mitapivat versus 3% on placebo (p<0.0001) — co-primary MET; annualised pain crises 2.6 versus 3.1 (p=0.12) — co-primary NOT met. A split result
cards.summary: RISE UP phase 3 — Andemariam 2026 (n=207): haemoglobin response 41% on mitapivat versus 3% on placebo (p<0.0001) — co-primary MET; annualised pain crises 2.6 versus 3.1 (p=0.12) — co-primary NOT met. A split result
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, global, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (Andemariam 2026, RISE UP)
cards.people: 207 patients older than 16 years with sickle cell disease, anaemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises, at 69 sites in 15 countries, randomised 2:1 to mitapivat 100 mg twice daily (n=138) or placebo (n=69) for 52 weeks. The co-primary endpoints were haemoglobin response (≥1.0 g/dL increase in average haemoglobin from week 24 to week 52 versus baseline) and the annualised rate of sickle cell pain crises.
cards.result: Haemoglobin response: 56 of 138 (41%) on mitapivat versus 2 of 69 (3%) on placebo (adjusted difference 38 percentage points, 95% CI 29–47; p<0.0001) — this co-primary endpoint was met. Annualised pain-crisis rate: 2.6 (95% CI 2.3–3.0) on mitapivat versus 3.1 (2.6–3.6) on placebo (p=0.1213) — this co-primary endpoint was NOT met; on the outcome patients feel most, the treatment made no significant difference. Serious adverse events were reported in 28 (20%) on mitapivat versus 20 (29%) on placebo, with one treatment-related serious event on mitapivat and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Present this trial as the split it is: a large, clear haemoglobin effect and a null pain-crisis effect in the same patients over the same year. The fetched record does not report a transfusion-burden result, so none is claimed on this shelf. Mitapivat's other homes are live shelf #1803 (pyruvate kinase deficiency) and pack #4882 (thalassaemia) — this pack builds only the sickle cell slice and does not re-card their records.

cards.headline: RISE UP phase 2 portion — Idowu 2025 (n=79, 12 weeks): haemoglobin response 46% on mitapivat 50 mg twice daily and 50% on 100 mg twice daily versus 4% on placebo
cards.summary: RISE UP phase 2 portion — Idowu 2025 (n=79, 12 weeks): haemoglobin response 46% on mitapivat 50 mg twice daily and 50% on 100 mg twice daily versus 4% on placebo
cards.type: Phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled portion of the RISE UP phase 2/3 trial (Idowu 2025)
cards.people: 79 patients aged ≥16 years with confirmed sickle cell disease (any genotype), baseline haemoglobin 5.5–10.5 g/dL and 2–10 pain crises in the prior 12 months, at 32 sites in 13 countries, randomised 1:1:1 to mitapivat 50 mg twice daily (n=26), mitapivat 100 mg twice daily (n=26) or placebo (n=27) for 12 weeks. Primary efficacy endpoint: haemoglobin response (≥1.0 g/dL increase in average haemoglobin from weeks 10–12 versus baseline).
cards.result: Haemoglobin response occurred in 12 of 26 (46%) on 50 mg and 13 of 26 (50%) on 100 mg versus 1 of 27 (4%) on placebo (two-sided p=0.0003 and p=0.0001). Serious adverse events occurred in 2 (8%), 4 (15%) and 3 (11%) respectively; grade ≥3 adverse events in 3 (12%), 5 (19%) and 2 (7%); none of the serious or grade ≥3 events was considered treatment-related and there were no treatment-related deaths. The commonest grade ≥3 events were infections and infestations.

cards.headline: Open-label phase 2 — van Dijk 2023 (N=10; 9 continued to 1 year): haemoglobin rose by a mean 1.1 g/dL and annualised vaso-occlusive events fell from a historic 1.33 to 0.64 — a very small, uncontrolled study, N printed plainly
cards.summary: Open-label phase 2 — van Dijk 2023 (N=10; 9 continued to 1 year): haemoglobin rose by a mean 1.1 g/dL and annualised vaso-occlusive events fell from a historic 1.33 to 0.64 — a very small, uncontrolled study, N printed plainly
cards.type: Phase 2, investigator-initiated, open-label study with 1-year fixed-dose extension (van Dijk 2023)
cards.people: 10 patients aged ≥16 years with sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbS/β0 or HbS/β+) in the dose-finding period, of whom 9 (90%) continued into the 1-year fixed-dose extension on mitapivat. N=10 printed on the face of this card per the small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Sustained haemoglobin improvement was seen at 1 year (mean increase 1.1 ± 0.7 g/dL; P=.0014), accompanied by decreases in haemolysis markers. The annualised rate of vaso-occlusive events fell from a historic baseline of 1.33 ± 1.32 to 0.64 ± 0.87 (P=.0489) across the combined dose-finding and extension periods. The ATP:2,3-DPG ratio and haemoglobin–oxygen affinity increased significantly; red-cell sickling (point of sickling) fell non-significantly. Treatment-emergent adverse events were mostly mild (transaminase increase and headache commonest); one non-treatment-related serious event (urinary tract infection) occurred in dose-finding, and in the extension one patient died of massive pulmonary embolism due to COVID-19, judged non-treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, no control group, and a historic-baseline comparison for the crisis rate — this study is hypothesis-generating only, and its crisis-rate signal was not confirmed by the randomised phase 3 trial carded above. It is carded because it is the programme's only long-duration sickle report before RISE UP, with its size printed plainly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: haemoglobin up, pain crises not significantly reduced — a SPLIT co-primary result — SPLIT stamp
cards.summary: Synthesis: haemoglobin up, pain crises not significantly reduced — a SPLIT co-primary result — SPLIT stamp
cards.people: Synthesis of the RISE UP phase 3 and phase 2 portions and the small open-label phase 2 study — the sickle cell slice only. Mitapivat's verified homes for its other diseases are live shelf #1803 (pyruvate kinase deficiency, ACTIVATE) and pack #4882 (thalassaemia, ENERGIZE/ENERGIZE-T); their records are homed there and are not carded or sourced here.
cards.result: The randomised evidence is consistent on blood and split on symptoms: mitapivat raises haemoglobin in sickle cell disease (response 41% versus 3% in phase 3; 46–50% versus 4% in the phase 2 portion), but in the only trial powered and run for a year to test it, annualised pain crises were 2.6 versus 3.1 with p=0.12 — not met. A 10-patient open-label study's crisis signal against historic baseline did not survive randomised testing. SPLIT is the honest stamp: benefit on the haemoglobin co-primary, no demonstrated benefit on the pain-crisis co-primary.
cards.watchOut: Haemoglobin response is a laboratory endpoint; whether a sustained ~1 g/dL rise without a demonstrated crisis reduction translates into organ protection or survival benefit is unanswered by every carded record, and the open-label extension of RISE UP is still ongoing.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andemariam B et al. Lancet (London, England). 2026 (PMID: 42913682); Idowu M et al. The Lancet. Haematology. 2025 (PMID: 39644907); van Dijk MJ et al. Blood advances. 2023 (PMID: 37934880).

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — the Frank–Starling relationship in intact humans: stroke volume tracks end-diastolic volume (not filling pressure) when preload is changed directly — curves built from wedge-pressure surrogates, steep in the young, flattened and shifted by a stiff, ageing ventricle
shelves.question: In intact humans, what does the Frank–Starling relationship look like when preload is changed directly (volume infusion, lower-body negative pressure, postural change) — how much does stroke volume rise per unit rise in filling pressure, and how do contractility and pericardial constraint shift or flatten the curve?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep): the Frank–Starling relationship — stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume along a curve whose slope and position are set by contractility and by pericardial/diastolic constraint — is presented in textbooks as settled physiology, and its direction in intact humans is not in doubt. What the primary human evidence actually consists of is thinner and older than the textbook confidence suggests, which is why this pack is graded EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. In healthy volunteers given 3 litres of saline over 3 hours (Kumar A et al., PMID: 15090949; 12 catheterised and 32 echocardiography volunteers), end-diastolic volume indexes and their changes tracked stroke volume index well, while pulmonary artery occlusion pressure and central venous pressure — the bedside 'preload' numbers — did not correlate with volumes or with the response to infusion at all: in intact humans the curve relates volume to output, and pressure is an unreliable stand-in for volume. Frank–Starling curves constructed from wedge pressure during lower-body negative pressure and saline infusion in 23 healthy young adults (Fu Q et al., PMID: 14527942) had maximal slopes of 12.5 ± 2.0 mL/mmHg in women versus 7.1 ± 1.5 mL/mmHg in men (stroke-index slopes 6.31 versus 4.29 mL·m⁻²·mmHg⁻¹) — a quantified human slope, from a pressure surrogate. When preload was manipulated by lower-body negative pressure and rapid saline infusion during right-heart catheterisation in 102 healthy seniors stratified by lifelong exercise dose (Bhella PS et al., PMID: 25236519), sedentary ageing was associated with a stiffer, less distensible ventricle (stiffness constant 0.062 ± 0.039) than lifelong competitive training (0.035 ± 0.033), with committed exercisers in between — the curve's diastolic substrate flattens with sedentary ageing and is preserved by training. There is no direct human pressure–volume-loop gold standard in healthy volunteers: every human 'curve' here is built from wedge-pressure or imaging surrogates across loading manoeuvres, and the classic catheterisation-era ventricular-function-curve programme (Ross & Braunwald era) survives in records whose abstracts could not be fetched and verified this session (one candidate, Mangano 1980, PMID: 7398014, carries no abstract in its PubMed record and was therefore refused as a card — see summary). Cross-point: pack #6076 (exercise cardiac output) invokes the Frank–Starling mechanism during exercise; this pack measures the preload–stroke-volume relation itself and does not re-card #6076's studies.

cards.headline: Kumar 2004 (healthy volunteers, N=12 catheterised + N=32 echo): after 3 L saline, changes in end-diastolic volume tracked changes in stroke volume — wedge and central venous pressures correlated with neither
cards.summary: Kumar 2004 (healthy volunteers, N=12 catheterised + N=32 echo): after 3 L saline, changes in end-diastolic volume tracked changes in stroke volume — wedge and central venous pressures correlated with neither
cards.type: Prospective interventional physiology study in healthy volunteers (Kumar 2004)
cards.people: Healthy volunteers in two groups: group 1 (n=12) with pulmonary artery catheterisation and radionuclide cineangiography, and group 2 (n=32) with volumetric echocardiography, each receiving 3 litres of normal saline over 3 hours.
cards.result: Initial pulmonary artery occlusion pressure and central venous pressure did not correlate significantly with initial end-diastolic volume indexes or cardiac performance. Changes in those pressures after saline also did not correlate with changes in volumes or performance. In contrast, end-diastolic volume indexes and their changes correlated well with stroke volume index and its changes, confirmed in group 2 with mathematically independent measurement techniques.
cards.watchOut: This is the pack's central caution, printed plainly: the human Frank–Starling relation is a volume–output relation. The filling pressures clinicians use as 'preload' failed as surrogates in healthy hearts here — a finding about measurement, in volunteers, not a patient-management trial.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure and central venous pressure fail to predict ventricular filling volume, cardiac performance, or the response to volume infusion in normal subjects. cards.headline: Fu 2004 (healthy young adults, N=23): Frank–Starling curves from wedge pressure during lower-body negative pressure and saline — maximal slope 12.5 ± 2.0 mL/mmHg in women versus 7.1 ± 1.5 in men
cards.summary: Fu 2004 (healthy young adults, N=23): Frank–Starling curves from wedge pressure during lower-body negative pressure and saline — maximal slope 12.5 ± 2.0 mL/mmHg in women versus 7.1 ± 1.5 in men
cards.people: 10 healthy young women and 13 healthy young men in whom Frank–Starling curves were constructed from pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, stroke volume and stroke index during lower-body negative pressure and saline infusion, with orthostatic tolerance tested by progressive lower-body negative pressure to presyncope.
cards.result: Women had steeper maximal Starling-curve slopes than men, whether expressed as stroke volume (12.5 ± 2.0 versus 7.1 ± 1.5 mL/mmHg, P<0.05) or stroke index (6.31 ± 0.8 versus 4.29 ± 0.6 mL·m⁻²·mmHg⁻¹, P<0.05). During progressive unloading, wedge pressure fell quickly then plateaued near presyncope; stroke volume at presyncope was 35% lower in women, with higher heart rates but similar arterial pressures and vascular resistance.
cards.watchOut: Classic small N (23 volunteers), printed on the face. The 'filling pressure' axis is wedge pressure — a surrogate for end-diastolic volume, and Kumar's card (above) shows how loose that coupling can be; the slope values are therefore the textbook-style account as measured by this method, not direct pressure–volume loops.
cards.source: Fu Q et al. Hemodynamics of orthostatic intolerance: implications for gender differences. American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology. 2004. PMID: 14527942. cards.headline: Bhella 2014 (healthy seniors, N=102): preload manipulated by lower-body negative pressure and rapid saline during catheterisation — sedentary ventricles were stiffer (stiffness constant 0.062) than lifelong competitive athletes' (0.035)
cards.summary: Bhella 2014 (healthy seniors, N=102): preload manipulated by lower-body negative pressure and rapid saline during catheterisation — sedentary ventricles were stiffer (stiffness constant 0.062) than lifelong competitive athletes' (0.035)
cards.type: Cross-sectional catheterisation physiology study across lifelong exercise doses (Bhella 2014)
cards.people: 102 healthy seniors stratified by lifelong exercise frequency — sedentary (<2 sessions/week), casual (2–3), committed (4–5) and competitive Masters athletes (6–7) — undergoing right-heart catheterisation and echocardiography while preload was manipulated with lower-body negative pressure and rapid saline infusion to define left ventricular pressure–volume relationships and Frank–Starling curves.
cards.result: Left ventricular distensibility at baseline was 21% greater in committed and 36% greater in competitive exercisers than in sedentary subjects. Group stiffness constants were: sedentary 0.062 ± 0.039, casual 0.079 ± 0.052, committed 0.055 ± 0.033, competitive 0.035 ± 0.033 — sedentary seniors stiffer than competitive athletes, casual exercise no better than sedentary, committed exercise largely preserving compliance. Systolic function changed little across groups.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional stratification by self-selected lifelong habits — the flatter curve of sedentary ageing is an association with a plausible mechanism, not a randomised training effect (the same laboratory's training trials are a separate question). Participants are older adults, so the curve described is the ageing heart's, not the young heart's.
cards.source: Bhella PS et al. Impact of lifelong exercise "dose" on left ventricular compliance and distensibility. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2014. PMID: 25236519. cards.headline: Synthesis: the relation is real and quantifiable in humans — EMERGING because every human curve is surrogate-built and the classic base is old
cards.summary: Synthesis: the relation is real and quantifiable in humans — EMERGING because every human curve is surrogate-built and the classic base is old
cards.people: Three primary human studies (44 saline-loaded volunteers; 23 young adults across unloading/loading; 102 catheterised seniors across preload manipulation), framed by Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook background only.
cards.result: Stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume when preload is changed directly; wedge-pressure slopes in young adults measure ~7–13 mL/mmHg; diastolic stiffness flattens the substrate with sedentary ageing. Filling pressures fail as volume surrogates (Kumar). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, Tier C: direction is certain, but no direct human pressure–volume gold standard in health exists, the quantified base is three studies, and the catheterisation-era classics could not be verified from fetched records this session.

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): venous return is driven by the gradient between mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf) — the equilibrated pressure in the systemic circulation at zero flow — and right atrial pressure, and the venous-return curve plots flow against right atrial pressure with its zero-flow intercept at Pmsf. In humans that intercept cannot be measured directly in an intact circulation; what the human literature measures is an ANALOGUE, and this pack says so plainly, as required. Parkin & Wright (PMID: 1919281) proposed deriving a mean systemic filling pressure analogue from cardiac output, right atrial pressure and arterial pressure by modelling a notional regional circulation at stop-flow — a model-derived estimate from the start, offered as a quantitative link between volume state and therapy. Maas JJ et al. (PMID: 22584797), in 11 mechanically ventilated postoperative cardiac-surgery patients, compared three estimates across supine, head-up tilt and 500 mL colloid loading: inspiratory-hold Pmsf averaged 20.9 ± 5.6 mmHg, arm equilibrium pressure 19.8 ± 5.7 mmHg, and the model analogue (Pmsa) 14.9 ± 4.0 mmHg — the analogue ran about 6 mmHg below the hold estimate (bias −6.0 ± 3.1 mmHg), while changes with tilt and loading were directionally concordant across methods. In a companion study (PMID: 22763909; 15 postoperative patients), systemic vascular compliance was linear at 64.3 ± 32.7 mL/mmHg and stressed volume was estimated at 1,265 ± 541 mL (28.5% of predicted blood volume) by extrapolating the Pmsf–volume curve to zero pressure. Guérin L, Teboul JL, Persichini R et al. (PMID: 26597901), in 30 patients with acute circulatory failure, built venous-return curves from cardiac index–central venous pressure pairs during ventilatory occlusions: in fluid responders, passive leg raising raised Psm from 25 ± 13 to 31 ± 13 mmHg and widened the Psm–CVP gradient by 20 ± 30%, while resistance to venous return did not change — volume recruitment moves the intercept, not the slope resistance, in that manoeuvre. Every measurement here is in postoperative or ICU PATIENTS, not healthy volunteers, and every 'Pmsf' value is method-dependent (hold, arm stop-flow, or model analogue disagree by several mmHg in the same patients). The honest statement is: the Guyton framework organises these bedside estimates coherently, but no study in this pack measured a Guyton venous-return curve directly in a healthy human.

cards.headline: Parkin & Wright 1991 (analogue programme, human circulation control studies; N not documented in the record): the Pmsf analogue is DERIVED from a notional stop-flow regional circulation — a model estimate, proposed as the quantitative link between volume state and therapy
cards.summary: Parkin & Wright 1991 (analogue programme, human circulation control studies; N not documented in the record): the Pmsf analogue is DERIVED from a notional stop-flow regional circulation — a model estimate, proposed as the quantitative link between volume state and therapy
cards.type: Physiology methods and closed-loop control study (Parkin & Wright 1991)
cards.people: Human circulatory-control studies reported by the Parkin programme, in which mean blood pressure, right atrial pressure and cardiac output were simultaneously controlled within desired tolerances using state-based control; the record does not document a participant N, and none is claimed.
cards.result: The authors propose mean systemic filling pressure as a parsimonious description of volume state and describe a method of deriving a mean systemic filling pressure analogue based on stopping the flow in a notional regional systemic circulation, with the ratio (PM − PRA)/PM offered as a global measure of cardioactive drug effect. The analogue is, by construction, computed from measured pressures and flow — not a pressure ever read off a stopped human circulation.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record — labelled plainly per the physiology rule. This is the conceptual source of the 'analogue' language the whole pack depends on; it is a methods paper, and its numbers are control tolerances, not population values.
cards.source: Parkin WG et al. Three dimensional closed loop control of the human circulation. International journal of clinical monitoring and computing. 1991. PMID: 1919281. cards.headline: Maas 2012a (postoperative cardiac-surgery patients, N=11): three Pmsf estimates in the same patients — inspiratory-hold 20.9 ± 5.6, arm equilibrium 19.8 ± 5.7, model analogue 14.9 ± 4.0 mmHg; analogue biased −6.0 mmHg below hold
cards.summary: Maas 2012a (postoperative cardiac-surgery patients, N=11): three Pmsf estimates in the same patients — inspiratory-hold 20.9 ± 5.6, arm equilibrium 19.8 ± 5.7, model analogue 14.9 ± 4.0 mmHg; analogue biased −6.0 mmHg below hold
cards.type: Bedside methods-comparison physiology study in ICU patients (Maas 2012)
cards.people: 11 mechanically ventilated postoperative cardiac surgery patients, studied supine, at 30° head-up tilt, and after 500 mL colloid loading, with inspiratory-hold manoeuvres, upper-arm stop-flow occlusion (30 seconds) and a Guytonian model analogue computed at each state.
cards.result: Mean values across states: Pmsf (hold) 20.9 ± 5.6 mmHg, arm equilibrium pressure 19.8 ± 5.7 mmHg, model analogue 14.9 ± 4.0 mmHg. Arm pressure and hold Pmsf were interchangeable (bias −1.0 ± 3.08 mmHg; limits of agreement −7.3 to 5.2); the model analogue differed significantly (bias −6.0 ± 3.1 mmHg; limits −12.4 to 0.3). Changes in all three tracked head-up tilt and volume loading in the same direction.
cards.watchOut: N=11 patients, printed plainly — postoperative, ventilated, vasoactively supported patients, not healthy volunteers. The ~6 mmHg method gap in the same patients at the same moment is the single most important number in this pack: 'the Pmsf' in humans is method-defined.
cards.source: Maas JJ et al. Estimation of mean systemic filling pressure in postoperative cardiac surgery patients with three methods. Intensive care medicine. 2012. PMID: 22584797.
