cards.headline: Maas 2012b (postoperative ICU patients, N=15): systemic vascular compliance 64.3 ± 32.7 mL/mmHg (linear); stressed volume estimated 1,265 ± 541 mL (28.5% of predicted blood volume) by extrapolating the Pmsf–volume curve to zero
cards.summary: Maas 2012b (postoperative ICU patients, N=15): systemic vascular compliance 64.3 ± 32.7 mL/mmHg (linear); stressed volume estimated 1,265 ± 541 mL (28.5% of predicted blood volume) by extrapolating the Pmsf–volume curve to zero
cards.type: Bedside physiology study with sequential volume loading (Maas 2012)
cards.people: 15 mechanically ventilated postoperative cardiac surgery patients in intensive care, undergoing inspiratory holds and arm stop-flow manoeuvres during normovolaemia and after each of 10 sequential 50-mL colloid boluses (500 mL total), with cardiac function and compliance curves constructed at the bedside.
cards.result: Pmsf by hold and by arm were closely correlated. Systemic vascular compliance was linear at 64.3 ± 32.7 mL/mmHg (0.97 ± 0.49 mL·mmHg⁻¹·kg⁻¹ predicted body weight). Stressed volume, from extrapolating the Pmsf–volume curve to its zero-pressure intercept, was 1,265 ± 541 mL, or 28.5% ± 15% of predicted total blood volume. Cardiac function curves were steep in volume-responsive patients and flat in the rest.
cards.watchOut: Stressed volume here is an extrapolation of a fitted line to zero pressure — two modelling steps removed from any measurement. N=15 patients, printed plainly; again a postoperative ICU population under mechanical ventilation.
cards.source: Maas JJ et al. Bedside assessment of total systemic vascular compliance, stressed volume, and cardiac function curves in intensive care unit patients. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2012. PMID: 22763909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Guérin/Persichini 2015 (acute circulatory failure, N=30): leg raising raised Psm from 25 ± 13 to 31 ± 13 mmHg in fluid responders and widened the Psm–CVP gradient by 20 ± 30%, with no change in resistance to venous return
cards.summary: Guérin/Persichini 2015 (acute circulatory failure, N=30): leg raising raised Psm from 25 ± 13 to 31 ± 13 mmHg in fluid responders and widened the Psm–CVP gradient by 20 ± 30%, with no change in resistance to venous return
cards.type: Human venous-return-curve physiology study in shock (Guérin, Teboul & Persichini 2015)
cards.people: 30 patients with acute circulatory failure in whom venous-return curves were constructed as the regression line between cardiac index and central venous pressure pairs measured during end-inspiratory and end-expiratory ventilatory occlusions, at baseline, during passive leg raising and after fluid infusion; fluid responders (n=15) were those whose cardiac index rose more than 15% with infusion.
cards.result: In fluid responders, passive leg raising significantly increased central venous pressure (7 ± 3 to 9 ± 4 mmHg) and mean systemic pressure (25 ± 13 to 31 ± 13 mmHg), and the Psm–CVP gradient rose by 20 ± 30%, while resistance to venous return did not change significantly. In non-responders, Psm and CVP rose but the gradient did not. Fluid infusion produced the same pattern as leg raising.
cards.watchOut: These Psm values (25–31 mmHg) are higher than the Maas postoperative estimates — different population (shock), different construction (occlusion-pair regression). That spread across methods and populations is itself the finding to carry away; there is no single human 'Pmsf number' this pack can honestly print as normal.
cards.source: Guérin L et al. Effects of passive leg raising and volume expansion on mean systemic pressure and venous return in shock in humans. Critical care (London, England). 2015. PMID: 26597901. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a coherent framework, an analogue measurement — EMERGING, in patients only, with method spread of several mmHg
cards.summary: Synthesis: a coherent framework, an analogue measurement — EMERGING, in patients only, with method spread of several mmHg
cards.people: Four primary human studies: the Parkin & Lean analogue programme's founding methods paper (N not documented), two Maas bedside studies (N=11 and N=15 postoperative patients) and the Guérin/Teboul/Persichini occlusion-curve study (N=30 patients in circulatory failure), framed by Guyton & Hall as textbook background only.
cards.result: Bedside Pmsf estimates in patients sit roughly between 15 and 31 mmHg depending on method and population; volume loading and leg raising move the estimated intercept upward and widen the gradient to right atrial pressure in responders, without changing resistance to venous return. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, Tier C: the Guyton construction organises real human measurements, but the quantity is a model-derived analogue, the methods disagree by ~6 mmHg head-to-head, and no healthy-volunteer measurement exists in this base.
cards.watchOut: This pack must not be cited as 'the measured human Guyton curve': no card measured venous return at zero flow in an intact healthy human, because that measurement cannot be made. The piglet validation study behind one pulse-contour method (Maas 2011, PMID: 21830048) was refused as a card under the no-animal-cards rule for physiology packs and is noted here only as a refusal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parkin WG et al. International journal of clinical monitoring and computing. 1991 (PMID: 1919281); Maas JJ et al. Intensive care medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22584797); Maas JJ et al. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2012 (PMID: 22763909); Guérin L et al. Critical care (London, England). 2015 (PMID: 26597901). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall.

shelves.title: The exercise pressor reflex: muscle metabolites switch sympathetic outflow on — coupled to muscle-cell pH, isolated by post-exercise occlusion, and engaged in leg exercise only at fatigue
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does the exercise pressor reflex work — how much do muscle metaboreflex and mechanoreflex activation raise muscle sympathetic nerve activity and arterial pressure during static exercise, and how is the metaboreflex isolated by post-exercise circulatory occlusion?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine Diphosphate · Adult · Blood Pressure · Electrophysiology · Exercise · Fatigue · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Ischemia · Leg · Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy · Male · Microelectrodes · Muscle Contraction · Muscles · Physical Exertion · Reflex · Rest · Sympathetic Nervous System
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: during exercise, central command sets the basic cardiovascular pattern while muscle chemoreflexes (the metaboreflex, from metabolite-sensitive group III/IV afferents) and mechanoreflexes modulate it, and the metaboreflex can be isolated by keeping the exercised limb occluded after exercise ends (post-exercise circulatory occlusion), which traps metabolites and holds sympathetic outflow up while central command and mechanoreflex input have stopped. The fetched human records support each element. Sympathetic activation is coupled to muscle-cell acidification: with simultaneous 31P-NMR and microneurography, the onset of muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) coincided with cellular acidification and MSNA tracked intracellular pH, not phosphocreatine, inorganic phosphate or ADP (Victor 1988). When the metaboreflex was engaged by ischemic static exercise, MSNA rose in parallel in exercising and resting muscle — from 29 ± 2 to 38 ± 2 bursts/min and from 30 ± 3 to 40 ± 2 bursts/min in the second minute — and stayed up during post-exercise ischemia (Hansen 1994, N = 7). In large-muscle exercise the reflex needs fatigue: non-fatiguing isometric knee extension did not durably raise MSNA, but exercise to fatigue raised total MSNA 96–107% above control in the final 30 seconds and kept it 83% above control during post-exercise muscle ischemia (Ray & Mark 1993, N = 7–8). The Rowell & O'Leary synthesis supplies the framework — chemoreflex raising sympathetic activity and pressure mainly in isometric exercise, mechanoreflex and baroreflex resetting alongside central command. This shelf covers the reflex during exercise itself; the fall in pressure during the recovery hours afterwards is a different question, homed at pack #6399 (post-exercise hypotension), which is cross-pointed here and not duplicated. The assembly-dropped slate row on the metaboreflex alone (S5-1-46) is folded into this pack, which covers the metaboreflex together with the mechanoreflex and central command as one pressor-reflex question.

cards.headline: The trigger is muscle-cell acid: sympathetic activation starts when contracting muscle acidifies, and tracks intracellular pH — not phosphocreatine, phosphate or ADP (Victor 1988)
cards.summary: The trigger is muscle-cell acid: sympathetic activation starts when contracting muscle acidifies, and tracks intracellular pH — not phosphocreatine, phosphate or ADP (Victor 1988)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (31P-NMR spectroscopy with simultaneous microneurography)
cards.people: Conscious healthy humans performing static and rhythmic handgrip; forearm-muscle 31P-NMR spectroscopy recorded simultaneously with peroneal microneurography of muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) in resting muscle. The fetched abstract does not state the number of subjects — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: During both static and rhythmic handgrip, the onset of sympathetic activation in resting muscle coincided with the development of cellular acidification in the active muscle. Increases in MSNA were correlated closely with decreases in intracellular pH but dissociated from changes in phosphocreatine, inorganic phosphate and ADP. The authors conclude that activation of muscle sympathetic outflow during exercise in humans is coupled to the cellular accumulation of protons in contracting muscle.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports coupling and correlation, not a numeric MSNA rise, and does not state N — the size figures on this shelf come from References 2 and 3. pH is an index of glycolysis; the study identifies protons as the coupled signal, not the only metabolite that can stimulate muscle afferents.
cards.source: Victor RG et al. Sympathetic nerve discharge is coupled to muscle cell pH during exercise in humans. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1988. PMID: 3170747. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Isolating the metaboreflex: ischemic static exercise raised sympathetic traffic in parallel in exercising and resting muscle — 29→38 and 30→40 bursts/min — and post-exercise ischemia held it up (N = 7)
cards.summary: Isolating the metaboreflex: ischemic static exercise raised sympathetic traffic in parallel in exercising and resting muscle — 29→38 and 30→40 bursts/min — and post-exercise ischemia held it up (N = 7)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (bilateral microneurography with post-exercise ischemia)
cards.people: 7 healthy human subjects; static toe extension at 20% of maximal voluntary contraction, alone or combined with foot ischemia, with microelectrode recordings of muscle sympathetic nerve activity in the right peroneal nerve (resting muscle) and in left peroneal fascicles innervating the exercising foot muscles. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Only static toe extension at 20% MVC during ischemia activated the muscle metaboreflex. Sympathetic activity was unchanged in the first minute, then in the second minute rose from 29 ± 2 to 38 ± 2 bursts/min to the exercising muscles and from 30 ± 3 to 40 ± 2 bursts/min to the resting muscles (both P < 0.05). These bilateral increases were maintained when metaboreflex activation was sustained by post-exercise foot ischemia — the post-exercise circulatory occlusion manoeuvre that isolates the metaboreflex from central command and mechanoreflex input.
cards.watchOut: Seven subjects and a small-muscle (toe extensor) model: it proves the reflex and its occlusion isolation cleanly, but absolute burst rates from a foot-muscle model should not be read as the whole-body pressor response to large-muscle exercise.
cards.source: Hansen J et al. Muscle metaboreflex triggers parallel sympathetic activation in exercising and resting human skeletal muscle. The American journal of physiology. 1994. PMID: 8024012. cards.headline: Large-muscle exercise needs fatigue to engage the reflex: fatiguing knee extension raised total MSNA 96–107%, still 83% above control during post-exercise ischemia (N = 7–8)
cards.summary: Large-muscle exercise needs fatigue to engage the reflex: fatiguing knee extension raised total MSNA 96–107%, still 83% above control during post-exercise ischemia (N = 7–8)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (microneurography during fatiguing leg exercise and post-exercise ischemia)
cards.people: Healthy subjects performing isometric knee extension to fatigue at 30% of maximal voluntary contraction, sitting; trial 1 N = 7, trial 2 (exercise followed by post-exercise muscle ischemia) N = 8, with MSNA recorded in the contralateral leg. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Earlier non-fatiguing knee-extension experiments had shown a biphasic MSNA pattern (fall in minute 1, return to control in minute 2) and no augmentation during post-exercise ischemia. Exercising to fatigue changed that: total MSNA (burst frequency × mean burst amplitude) in the contralateral leg increased 96 ± 40% (trial 1) and 107 ± 50% (trial 2) above control during the final 30 s of exercise (P < 0.01), with marked rises in mean arterial pressure and heart rate, and remained significantly elevated during post-exercise muscle ischemia at 83 ± 40% above control — evidence the muscle metaboreflex was engaged once fatigue developed.
cards.watchOut: The contrast inside this one study is the lesson: sub-fatigue leg exercise does not reliably raise MSNA, so 'the pressor reflex raises sympathetic activity during exercise' is true conditionally — on metabolite accumulation reaching threshold — not for every contraction.
cards.source: Ray CA, Mark AL. Augmentation of muscle sympathetic nerve activity during fatiguing isometric leg exercise. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 1993. PMID: 8376268. cards.headline: Synthesis: metabolites (protons) switch the metaboreflex on, occlusion isolates it, and fatigue decides whether large-muscle exercise engages it
cards.summary: Synthesis: metabolites (protons) switch the metaboreflex on, occlusion isolates it, and fatigue decides whether large-muscle exercise engages it
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above, framed by Rowell LB, O'Leary DS. Reflex control of the circulation during exercise: chemoreflexes and mechanoreflexes (1990) — the framework in which central command sets the pattern and muscle chemo-/mechanoreflexes and the arterial baroreflex modulate it.
cards.result: In healthy humans the exercise pressor reflex works as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) describe: contracting muscle that acidifies activates chemosensitive afferents and sympathetic outflow rises — coupled to intracellular pH (Victor 1988), visible as parallel MSNA rises of about 9–10 bursts/min in a small-muscle ischemic model and maintained by post-exercise occlusion (Hansen 1994), and reaching roughly a doubling of total MSNA when large-muscle exercise is taken to fatigue, persisting at +83% under post-exercise ischemia (Ray & Mark 1993). Post-exercise circulatory occlusion is the isolating manoeuvre because it traps the metabolites after volitional drive and movement stop. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All three primary studies are small microneurography experiments in young healthy volunteers; arterial-pressure magnitudes for the reflex come from these laboratory models, and the recovery-period fall in pressure after exercise is a separate phenomenon homed at pack #6399.

shelves.title: Splenic contraction in exercise and breath-hold diving: up to half the spleen empties at maximal exercise, a fifth per apnoea series — worth a few percent more circulating red cells
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much does the spleen contract during exercise and during breath-hold diving, how much does that raise circulating haemoglobin concentration, and how does splenic volume recover afterwards?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Physiological · Adult · Apnea · Blood Cell Count · Blood Pressure · Blood Volume · Cardiovascular Physiological Phenomena · Catecholamines · Diving · Erythrocyte Volume · Exercise · Female · Heart Rate · Hematocrit · Hemoglobins · Humans · Male · Organ Size · Physical Endurance · Reflex · Regional Blood Flow · Spleen · Splenectomy · Time Factors · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: the human spleen is a small red-cell reservoir compared with athletic mammals — it sequesters roughly 200–250 mL of densely packed red cells — but it contracts under sympathetic/catecholamine drive during exercise and apnoea, expelling part of that store and transiently raising circulating haemoglobin and haematocrit. The fetched human records quantify it. In exercising men, spleen volume fell 28–36% during submaximal cycling and 56% on an incremental ride to exhaustion, recovering to baseline within 20 minutes, with plasma catecholamines inversely related to spleen volume (Stewart 2003, N = 9). In breath-hold apnoea with face immersion, spleen volume fell rapidly by about 20%, mainly within the first of five repeated apnoeas, with splenic arterial and venous flows unchanged — evidence of active contraction rather than passive collapse — and recovery was slow, still incomplete 60 minutes after the last apnoea (Baković 2003). Three maximal apnoeas contracted the spleen by a mean of 49 mL (18%) in all ten subjects while haematocrit rose 2.2% and haemoglobin 2.4%, with full splenic recovery only at 8–9 minutes (Schagatay 2005, N = 10). The cell-count study adds that repeated apnoeas raised circulating red-cell volume by 4.9% in trained divers and 1.7% in untrained intact subjects, with no change in splenectomised subjects — the control that pins the effect on the spleen (Baković 2005). Magnitudes differ by stimulus: maximal exercise contracts the spleen most; apnoea contracts it quickly but modestly, and its slow recovery lets repeated dives stack the effect.

cards.headline: Exercise: spleen volume fell 28–36% at submaximal intensity and 56% at exhaustion, recovering within 20 minutes — tracking plasma catecholamines (N = 9)
cards.summary: Exercise: spleen volume fell 28–36% at submaximal intensity and 56% at exhaustion, recovering within 20 minutes — tracking plasma catecholamines (N = 9)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (radiolabelled-erythrocyte splenic volume during exercise)
cards.people: 9 men cycling at 60% of maximal oxygen uptake for 5, 10 or 15 minutes, followed by an incremental ride to exhaustion; spleen volume calculated with 99mTc-labelled erythrocytes. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: The reduction in spleen volume did not differ significantly among the three submaximal rides (5 min = 28%, 10 min = 30%, 15 min = 36%; P = 0.26). The incremental ride to exhaustion produced a 56% reduction in spleen volume, which recovered to baseline levels within 20 min. Plasma catecholamines were inversely related to spleen volume after exercise (r = 0.70–0.84; P < 0.0001). Red-cell and total blood volume did not change pre- to post-exercise, while plasma volume fell 18.9% (P < 0.01) — so the post-exercise haematocrit rise is mostly plasma-volume loss, and splenic red-cell release had no effect on indirect plasma-volume measures.
cards.watchOut: Nine men and a radiolabel method: the 56% figure is for exercise to exhaustion, not ordinary training intensity, and the study itself warns that splenic release does not explain the post-exercise haematocrit/haemoglobin changes — plasma-volume contraction does most of that.
cards.source: Stewart IB et al. Cardiovascular and splenic responses to exercise in humans. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2003. PMID: 12482773. cards.headline: Breath-hold diving: spleen volume fell ~20% mainly within the first apnoea, with splenic blood flows unchanged — an active contraction, still incompletely recovered 60 minutes later
cards.summary: Breath-hold diving: spleen volume fell ~20% mainly within the first apnoea, with splenic blood flows unchanged — an active contraction, still incompletely recovered 60 minutes later
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (serial ultrasound splenic volume and flow during repeated apnoeas)
cards.people: 10 trained apnoea divers and 10 intact plus 7 splenectomised untrained persons; five maximal apnoeas with face immersion in cold water, 2 minutes apart, with ultrasonic spleen monitoring and splenic artery/vein flow measurement before, between and up to 60 minutes after the apnoeas.
cards.result: Blood flows in the splenic artery and splenic vein were not significantly affected by breath-hold apnoea, arguing against passive collapse. A rapid decrease in spleen volume (approximately 20% in both apnoea divers and intact persons) was mainly completed during the first apnoea. The spleen did not recover in size between apnoeas and only partly recovered 60 min after the fifth apnoea. Apnoea duration peaked after the third apnoea (143, 127 and 74 s in divers, intact and splenectomised persons respectively), and the bradycardia and blood-pressure rise of the diving response were present from the first apnoea and unchanged thereafter.
cards.watchOut: Face immersion in cold water is part of the stimulus, so this is the diving (apnoea-plus-immersion) response, not dry breath-holding alone; the splenectomised group's shorter apnoeas are consistent with a splenic contribution but that group also differed in training.
cards.source: Baković D et al. Spleen volume and blood flow response to repeated breath-hold apneas. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2003. PMID: 12819225. cards.headline: Serial apnoeas: spleen contracted 49 mL (18%) in every subject while haemoglobin rose 2.4% and haematocrit 2.2% — spleen size took 8–9 minutes to recover (N = 10)
cards.summary: Serial apnoeas: spleen contracted 49 mL (18%) in every subject while haemoglobin rose 2.4% and haematocrit 2.2% — spleen size took 8–9 minutes to recover (N = 10)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ultrasound splenic kinetics during serial apnoeas)
cards.people: 10 healthy subjects performing three maximal apnoeas separated by 2 minutes of rest, with ultrasound spleen-volume measurement and serial haematocrit, haemoglobin, diving-response and apnoea-duration recording. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Three maximal apnoeas elicited spleen contraction in all ten subjects, by a mean of 49 (27) mL (18%; P < 0.001). Over the same period haematocrit and haemoglobin rose by 2.2% and 2.4% respectively (P < 0.01 and P < 0.001) and apnoeic duration rose by 20 s (22%; P < 0.05). The diving response's mean heart-rate reduction was 15% and fully reversed between apnoeas, whereas spleen size was not recovered until 8–9 min after the final apnoea, corresponding with recovery of haematocrit and haemoglobin — a fast, quickly reversed cardiovascular adjustment paired with a slow, long-lasting splenic one.
cards.watchOut: Ten subjects and dry serial apnoeas: the haemoglobin rise is real but small (~2.4%) — a transient boost measured in percent, not the large autotransfusion of diving mammals, whose spleens store a far larger share of red-cell mass.
cards.source: Schagatay E et al. Speed of spleen volume changes evoked by serial apneas. European journal of applied physiology. 2005. PMID: 15503125. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The splenectomy control: repeated apnoeas raised circulating red-cell volume 4.9% in trained divers and 1.7% in intact untrained subjects — and not at all without a spleen
cards.summary: The splenectomy control: repeated apnoeas raised circulating red-cell volume 4.9% in trained divers and 1.7% in intact untrained subjects — and not at all without a spleen
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cell counts across repeated apnoeas with splenectomised controls)
cards.people: 18 trained apnoea divers, 18 intact and 6 splenectomised subjects without diving experience; five maximal apnoeas with face immersion in cold water at 2-minute intervals, with venous blood sampling before, between and up to 20 minutes after the apnoeas, corrected for plasma-volume change.
cards.result: The human spleen sequesters 200–250 mL of densely packed red blood cells, up to 50% of which is actively expelled during strenuous exercise or simulated apnoea diving. Corrected for plasma-volume changes, circulating red-cell volume increased in trained apnoea divers (4.9 ± 1.0%) and intact subjects (1.7 ± 0.8%), whereas in splenectomised subjects there was no change in red-cell volume. White-cell concentration also rose in the groups with spleens (divers 14.9 ± 3.1%; intact 7.2 ± 1.8%), with an initial lymphocytosis absent in splenectomised subjects; platelet concentrations did not change significantly in any group.
cards.watchOut: The splenectomised comparison group is small (N = 6) and untrained, so the diver-versus-untrained gradient (4.9% vs 1.7%) mixes training with spleen size; the clean inference is the presence-versus-absence contrast, not the exact training effect.
cards.source: Baković D et al. Effect of human splenic contraction on variation in circulating blood cell counts. Clinical and experimental pharmacology & physiology. 2005. PMID: 16405451. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest human reservoir — up to ~56% splenic emptying at maximal exercise, ~18–20% per apnoea series, worth ~2–5% more circulating red cells
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest human reservoir — up to ~56% splenic emptying at maximal exercise, ~18–20% per apnoea series, worth ~2–5% more circulating red cells
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above (exercise radiolabel study, two apnoea ultrasound programmes, and the splenectomised-control cell-count study).
cards.result: In healthy humans the spleen contracts during both exercise and breath-hold diving, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) describe: 28–36% volume loss at submaximal cycling and 56% at exhaustion with recovery inside 20 minutes (Stewart 2003); about 20% loss within the first apnoea, actively driven (flows unchanged), stacking across repeated apnoeas because recovery takes an hour or more (Baković 2003); 49 mL (18%) per three-apnoea series with haemoglobin up 2.4% (Schagatay 2005); and a spleen-dependent rise in circulating red-cell volume of 4.9% in trained divers versus none after splenectomy (Baković 2005). The human effect is a few percent of circulating red cells — physiologically real, and far smaller than in diving mammals. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Methods differ across studies (radiolabelled erythrocytes versus ultrasound volume), so percentages are comparable in direction and rough size, not interchangeable to the decimal; post-exercise haemoglobin rises additionally reflect plasma-volume loss, which the exercise study separates out.

synthesis synthesis of the four primary human studies above (exercise radiolabel study, two apnoea ultrasound programmes, and the splenectomised-control cell-count study). in healthy humans the spleen contracts during both exercise and breath-hold diving, as the textbooks (guyton & hall; ganong; boron & boulpaep) describe: 28–36% volume loss at submaximal cycling and 56% at exhaustion with recovery inside 20 minutes (stewart 2003); about 20% loss within the first apnoea, actively driven (flows unchanged), stacking across repeated apnoeas because recovery takes an hour or more (baković 2003); 49 ml (18%) per three-apnoea series with haemoglobin up 2.4% (schagatay 2005); and a spleen-dependent rise in circulating red-cell volume of 4.9% in trained divers versus none after splenectomy (baković 2005). the human effect is a few percent of circulating red cells — physiologically real, and far smaller than in diving mammals. proposed physiology — established. methods differ across studies (radiolabelled erythrocytes versus ultrasound volume), so percentages are comparable in direction and rough size, not interchangeable to the decimal; post-exercise haemoglobin rises additionally reflect plasma-volume loss, which the exercise study separates out. synthesis of stewart ib et al. journal of applied physiology (bethesda, md. : 1985). 2003 (pmid: 12482773); baković d et al. journal of applied physiology (bethesda, md. : 1985). 2003 (pmid: 12819225); schagatay e et al. european journal of applied physiology. 2005 (pmid: 15503125); baković d et al. clinical and experimental pharmacology & physiology. 2005 (pmid: 16405451). textbook framing: guyton & hall textbook of medical physiology; ganong's review of medical physiology; boron & boulpaep medical physiology.

shelves.title: The Valsalva manoeuvre: four phases, an age-dependent ratio — flattened by autonomic failure, squared off by heart failure
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the four phases of the Valsalva manoeuvre in arterial pressure and heart rate, what are the normal Valsalva-ratio ranges, and how do autonomic failure and heart failure deform the response?
shelves.mesh: Aging · Animals · Autonomic Nervous System Diseases · Baroreflex · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Physiological Phenomena · Female · Heart Failure · Heart Rate · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Characteristics · Time Factors · Valsalva Maneuver · Vasoconstriction
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account of the standardised manoeuvre (strain at ~40 mmHg for 15 seconds): phase I, a brief pressure rise as intrathoracic pressure squeezes the aorta; phase II, falling venous return drops pressure (early II) until reflex vasoconstriction and tachycardia recover it (late II); phase III, a brief further drop on release; and phase IV, an overshoot above baseline with reflex bradycardia as the restored venous return meets a still-constricted vasculature. The Valsalva ratio — longest R–R interval after release over shortest during strain — is conventionally about 1.21 or higher in healthy adults and falls with age; that numeric range is the textbook/testing-laboratory account, and the fetched normative record confirms the behaviour it rests on: in 557 normal subjects aged 10–83 the Valsalva ratio varied with both age and gender, and no autonomic test regressed to zero even past 80, so age-matched ranges are required (Low 1997). Technique matters as much as physiology: intra-strain tachycardia, post-strain bradycardia, Valsalva ratio and baroreflex sensitivity all shrink as lung volume rises and strain pressure falls, and at fully expanded lungs with low strain pressure many subjects show intra-strain bradycardia instead of tachycardia (Looga 2005, critical review). In autonomic (adrenergic) failure the late-II recovery and phase-IV overshoot are lost and pressure keeps falling through the strain; the blood-pressure recovery time after release lengthens in direct proportion to adrenergic failure grade and stays measurable after phase II is lost (Vogel 2005). In heart failure with raised filling pressures the response deforms the other way — pressure fails to fall normally during strain (the 'square-wave' pattern of the textbook account) — and the fetched review confirms the response correlates significantly with invasively measured ventricular filling pressures (Felker 2006). Beat-to-beat finger-cuff recording has replaced intra-arterial cannulation for the test, and the post-release pattern identifies sympathetic neurocirculatory failure while the interbeat-interval/systolic-pressure slope identifies baroreflex-cardiovagal failure (Goldstein & Cheshire 2017).

cards.headline: The normative base: in 557 healthy subjects aged 10–83, the Valsalva ratio varied with age and gender — and no autonomic test reached zero even past 80 (N = 557)
cards.summary: The normative base: in 557 healthy subjects aged 10–83, the Valsalva ratio varied with age and gender — and no autonomic test reached zero even past 80 (N = 557)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative autonomic-testing cohort)
cards.people: 557 normal subjects evenly distributed by age and gender, aged 10 to 83 years, undergoing a standard autonomic test battery (heart-rate response to deep breathing, Valsalva ratio, quantitative sudomotor axon-reflex test, and blood-pressure response to tilt).
cards.result: Heart-rate response to deep breathing fell with increasing age. The Valsalva ratio varied with both age and gender. Sudomotor volumes were about double in men and declined with age at lower-limb sites, and orthostatic blood-pressure reduction increased with age. For no test was there a regression to zero, and some tests levelled off with increasing age — so autonomic failure remains diagnosable past 80, but only against age- and sex-appropriate reference ranges. The specific numeric Valsalva-ratio cut-offs used in testing laboratories (conventionally ~1.21 or above in younger adults, lower with age) are the textbook account; this record establishes the age/gender dependence those ranges encode rather than printing one universal number.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the pattern of age/gender effects, not a table of ratio percentiles — any single 'normal Valsalva ratio' number quoted without an age band overstates what normative data support.
cards.source: Low PA et al. Effect of age and gender on sudomotor and cardiovagal function and blood pressure response to tilt in normal subjects. Muscle & nerve. 1997. PMID: 9390669. cards.headline: Technique deforms the tracing: Valsalva ratio, intra-strain tachycardia and post-strain bradycardia all shrink as lung volume rises and strain pressure falls (critical review)
cards.summary: Technique deforms the tracing: Valsalva ratio, intra-strain tachycardia and post-strain bradycardia all shrink as lung volume rises and strain pressure falls (critical review)
cards.type: Expert synthesis / critical review of technique studies (labelled — not a primary trial)
cards.people: Critical review of the human Valsalva literature on how performance technique — strain pressure, lung volume, strain duration, inspiratory versus expiratory strain, and the preceding inspiration — changes the cardiovascular response (Looga 2005).
cards.result: Variations in technique greatly influence the response pattern. Intra-strain tachycardia, post-strain bradycardia, Valsalva ratio and baroreflex sensitivity decrease in proportion to an increase in lung volume and a decrease in strain pressure. With completely expanded lungs and low strain pressure, many subjects show an intra-strain bradycardic response instead of the usual tachycardic one. Intra-strain arterial hypotension and post-strain hypertension decrease as strain pressure decreases; heart-rate and blood-pressure changes are greater for an expiratory than an inspiratory manoeuvre; the rate of the preceding deep inspiration particularly affects phase I; and response magnitude correlates with strain duration, especially at high strain pressures.
cards.watchOut: A review card, labelled as such: its role on this shelf is to fence the four-phase description — the phases and ratio are only interpretable for a standardised strain (conventionally 40 mmHg for 15 s), and a 'flat' response at low strain pressure can be technique, not autonomic failure.
cards.source: Looga R. The Valsalva manoeuvre--cardiovascular effects and performance technique: a critical review. Respiratory physiology & neurobiology. 2005. PMID: 15848122. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cardiovascular Physiological Phenomena · Humans · Valsalva Maneuver

cards.headline: Autonomic failure: pressure recovery time after release lengthens in direct proportion to adrenergic failure — and stays measurable after late phase II is lost
cards.summary: Autonomic failure: pressure recovery time after release lengthens in direct proportion to adrenergic failure — and stays measurable after late phase II is lost
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Valsalva pressure recovery across graded adrenergic failure)
cards.people: Three patient groups with increasing degrees of adrenergic failure — group 1 orthostatic hypotension (systolic fall ≥30 mmHg on tilt), group 2 borderline orthostatic hypotension (10–30 mmHg), group 3 sympathetic sudomotor failure — plus an age-matched control group, undergoing Valsalva testing with beat-to-beat blood pressure (Vogel, Sandroni & Low 2005).
cards.result: Blood-pressure recovery time (PRT) — the time for pressure to return to baseline after the manoeuvre ends — varied directly with the severity of adrenergic impairment. PRT correlated significantly with the previously used Valsalva phases and baroreflex gain, most strongly with phase II_L (the reflex vasoconstriction that recovers pressure after the initial fall) and phase IV (the post-release overshoot). PRT extends quantitation of adrenergic failure because it continues to parallel worsening failure after phase II_L is lost, and remains reliable when II_L cannot be recorded.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective testing-laboratory data in patients referred for autonomic evaluation: it grades deformation in established failure rather than screening healthy people, and the abstract does not print the group Ns or PRT values in seconds — the directional, graded relationship is what this record establishes.
cards.source: Vogel ER et al. Blood pressure recovery from Valsalva maneuver in patients with autonomic failure. Neurology. 2005. PMID: 16301478. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Heart failure deforms it the other way: the Valsalva response tracks invasively measured filling pressures — the basis of the bedside 'square-wave' reading (review)
cards.summary: Heart failure deforms it the other way: the Valsalva response tracks invasively measured filling pressures — the basis of the bedside 'square-wave' reading (review)
cards.type: Expert synthesis / critical review of heart-failure studies (labelled — not a primary trial)
cards.people: Critical review of the studies relating the cardiovascular response to the Valsalva manoeuvre to invasively measured ventricular filling pressures in patients with clinical heart failure (Felker, Cuculich & Gheorghiade 2006).
cards.result: Studies demonstrated a significant correlation between the cardiovascular response to the Valsalva manoeuvre and invasively measured ventricular filling pressures in patients with clinical heart failure. The authors conclude the response is a potentially useful, simple and inexpensive noninvasive means of evaluating filling pressures and volume status in heart failure, while noting that physical examination alone has limited sensitivity and reproducibility and that natriuretic peptides and impedance cardiography were not well validated comparators at the time. In the textbook account this deformation is the mirror image of autonomic failure: with filling pressures high, pressure does not fall through phase II and the tracing flattens into a 'square wave' instead of dipping and overshooting.
cards.watchOut: A review card, labelled as such: the record establishes the correlation with filling pressures, not a validated pressure cut-off, and the 'square-wave' label itself is presented here as the textbook account of the deformation, consistent with — not quoted from — this review.
cards.source: Felker GM et al. The Valsalva maneuver: a bedside "biomarker" for heart failure. The American journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16443410. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four phases from one strain — dip, reflex recovery, release dip, overshoot — flattened by autonomic failure, squared off by high filling pressures
cards.summary: Synthesis: four phases from one strain — dip, reflex recovery, release dip, overshoot — flattened by autonomic failure, squared off by high filling pressures
cards.people: Synthesis of the normative cohort, the technique review, the adrenergic-failure study and the heart-failure review above, with the measurement update from Goldstein & Cheshire 2017 (beat-to-beat finger-cuff recording replacing intra-arterial cannulation).
cards.result: The normal Valsalva response, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) describe it and the fetched records support, runs: phase I brief rise, phase II fall then reflex recovery with tachycardia, phase III brief release dip, phase IV overshoot with bradycardia; the Valsalva ratio summarises the heart-rate swing and must be read against age- and sex-matched ranges from cohorts such as the 557-subject normative study, and only for a standardised strain, since technique alone can halve or invert components of the response (Looga 2005). Autonomic failure removes the late-II recovery and IV overshoot and prolongs pressure recovery time in proportion to adrenergic grade (Vogel 2005); heart failure with high filling pressures abolishes the phase-II fall, and the response correlates with invasively measured filling pressures (Felker 2006). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Two of the four cards are labelled reviews, because the primary four-phase recordings are classic intra-arterial era studies whose PubMed records carry no abstracts; the phase description itself is therefore presented as the textbook account, anchored by the normative, technique, autonomic-failure and heart-failure records that were fetched.

shelves.title: Lactate turnover during exercise: tracer appearance and disposal rise from ~15 µmol/kg/min at rest to many times that in exercise and stay matched until heavy loads; most disposed lactate is oxidised directly (75–90%), a minority is recycled to glucose, and blood lactate rises only when appearance outruns disposal
shelves.question: In healthy humans exercising, how fast is lactate turned over — what are resting and exercise lactate appearance/disposal rates by isotope tracer, how much lactate is oxidised versus recycled to glucose (the Cori cycle share), and where does the 'lactate threshold' sit relative to turnover?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Exercise/physiology · Gluconeogenesis/physiology · Humans · Kinetics · Lactic Acid/blood,metabolism · Liver/metabolism · Male · Oxidation-Reduction · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Endurance/physiology · Rest/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; the lactate-shuttle account associated with Brooks' programme). The textbook account: lactate is continuously produced and removed even at rest; during exercise both appearance and disposal rise steeply, most lactate is oxidised in muscle and heart, a minority returns to the liver for gluconeogenesis (the Cori cycle), and blood lactate concentration — the balance of the two fluxes — rises appreciably only when appearance outstrips disposal at heavy intensities. The carded tracer studies quantify each limb: Stanley 1985 (rest ~14–15 µmol/kg/min, matched to ~600 kg·m·min⁻¹, diverging at 900–1,200); Miller 2002 (lactate clamp: oxidation up, glucose oxidation and production down); Emhoff 2013 (direct oxidation 75% untrained / 90% trained; gluconeogenesis 1.7 → 4.4 mg/kg/min with clamped lactate). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Stanley 1985: in 6 men, lactate appearance rose from 14.4 µmol/kg/min at rest to 309 at the heaviest load, outstripping disposal (170) only at the top two loads
cards.summary: Stanley 1985: in 6 men, lactate appearance rose from 14.4 µmol/kg/min at rest to 309 at the heaviest load, outstripping disposal (170) only at the top two loads
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (isotope-tracer graded exercise) — N = 6 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: 6 healthy males studied at rest and during continuous graded exercise (6 minutes each at 300, 600, 900 and 1,200 kg·m·min⁻¹) with a primed continuous infusion of L-(+)-[1-¹⁴C]lactate tracer and arterial sampling; appearance (Ra) and disappearance (Rd) calculated with non-steady-state equations.
cards.result: At rest Ra was 14.4 ± 1.8 and Rd 15.1 ± 2.2 µmol·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. At 300 kg·m·min⁻¹ Ra/Rd were 32.8 ± 2.3 / 37.4 ± 1.3, and at 600 they were 59.1 ± 2.6 / 55.4 ± 2.3 µmol·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ — turnover multiplying several-fold while blood lactate stayed near balance. Only at 900 (Ra 145.4 ± 10.5 vs Rd 110.2 ± 5.6) and 1,200 (Ra 309.4 ± 20.8 vs Rd 169.7 ± 10.6) did appearance significantly exceed disposal — the kinetic picture behind the 'threshold': concentration rises when appearance outruns a disposal rate that is itself already many times resting.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=6 is printed on the face. The record's MeSH also indexes a dog component of the programme; every number on this card is from the six human subjects described in the abstract. Work rates are in the era's kg·m·min⁻¹ units, as published.

cards.summary: Miller 2002: clamping blood lactate at ~4 mM during moderate exercise raised lactate oxidation (6.5 to 10.0 mg/kg/min) and spared blood glucose
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (lactate-clamp tracer exercise) — N not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Men performing 90-minute exercise trials at 55% and 65% of peak oxygen uptake, including a lactate-clamp trial at 55% with exogenous lactate infused to hold blood lactate at the ~4 mM measured at 65%; lactate and glucose appearance, disappearance and oxidation measured with [3-¹³C]lactate, H¹³CO₃⁻ and [6,6-²H₂]glucose tracers. cards.result: With the lactate clamp, lactate appearance and disappearance rose and glucose appearance and disappearance fell, at rest and in exercise. cards.headline: Emhoff 2013 (oxidation): at the lactate threshold, trained men oxidised lactate at 22.7 vs 13.4 mg/kg/min in untrained men, 90% of it directly rather than via glucose
cards.summary: Emhoff 2013 (oxidation): at the lactate threshold, trained men oxidised lactate at 22.7 vs 13.4 mg/kg/min in untrained men, 90% of it directly rather than via glucose
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (tracer oxidation partitioning at threshold) — N = 12 (6 trained, 6 untrained)
cards.people: 6 untrained and 6 trained men completing 60 minutes of constant-load exercise at their individual lactate threshold; trained men also exercised 10% below threshold, with and without a lactate clamp. Total lactate oxidation and its direct versus indirect (gluconeogenesis-then-oxidation) components measured by tracer.
cards.result: Lactate oxidation at threshold was higher in trained men (22.7 ± 2.9 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ at 75% of peak oxygen uptake) than untrained (13.4 ± 2.5 at 68%). Raising blood lactate by clamp at the lower workload raised oxidation from 15.9 ± 2.2 to 27.9 ± 3.0 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Direct oxidation was 75% of total lactate oxidation in untrained and 90% in trained subjects, the partitioning constant from rest to exercise; subjects derived about one-third of carbohydrate energy from blood lactate.
cards.watchOut: 'Indirect' oxidation here means lactate carbon first converted to glucose and then oxidised — the record's operational Cori-cycle route; the 75%/90% split is of lactate oxidation, not of total lactate disposal.

cards.headline: Emhoff 2013 (gluconeogenesis): raising lactate availability at just below threshold nearly tripled gluconeogenesis, from 1.7 to 4.4 mg/kg/min
cards.summary: Emhoff 2013 (gluconeogenesis): raising lactate availability at just below threshold nearly tripled gluconeogenesis, from 1.7 to 4.4 mg/kg/min
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (tracer gluconeogenesis at threshold) — N = 12 (6 trained, 6 untrained)
cards.people: 12 healthy fasted men (6 untrained, 6 trained) exercising 60 minutes at their lactate threshold; trained men also at 10% below threshold, with and without a lactate clamp matching threshold blood lactate. Fluxes by primed continuous infusion of [6,6-²H₂]glucose, [3-¹³C]lactate and [¹³C]bicarbonate during 90 minutes of rest and 60 minutes of cycling.
cards.result: Exercise at threshold was at 67.6 ± 1.3% of peak oxygen uptake in untrained and 74.8 ± 1.7% in trained subjects. Gluconeogenesis was lower in trained men at threshold and below, but raising lactate with the clamp increased gluconeogenesis from 1.7 ± 0.4 to 4.4 ± 0.9 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (P<0.05) versus its control trial; hepatic glycogenolysis was higher in trained subjects and did not differ significantly across conditions. Glucose appearance, disposal and metabolic clearance all rose with the clamp.
cards.watchOut: Same 12-man programme as the oxidation card, reported for a different flux: the two cards are companion reports, not independent cohorts, and are labelled as such. Gluconeogenesis here is total (all precursors); the lactate-specific share is the clamp contrast, not a directly partitioned percentage.

cards.headline: Synthesis: lactate is turned over many times faster than its blood level suggests — mostly oxidised directly, a minority recycled to glucose, and the 'threshold' is where appearance outruns disposal
cards.summary: Synthesis: lactate is turned over many times faster than its blood level suggests — mostly oxidised directly, a minority recycled to glucose, and the 'threshold' is where appearance outruns disposal
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (exercise/metabolism chapters) and the Brooks lactate-shuttle programme the carded studies come from. No new data.
cards.result: Resting turnover is ~14–15 µmol/kg/min and rises roughly fourfold by moderate exercise while appearance and disposal stay matched; blood lactate climbs only when appearance exceeds a disposal rate already ~8–12 times resting (PMID 4083344). Supplied lactate is oxidised preferentially and spares glucose (PMID 12411539); at threshold, oxidation reaches 13–23 mg/kg/min depending on training, 75–90% of it direct rather than via glucose, supplying about a third of carbohydrate energy (PMID 23788576); the recycled-to-glucose (Cori) limb is real and substrate-responsive — gluconeogenesis rose from 1.7 to 4.4 mg/kg/min when lactate was clamped up (PMID 23239870). Lactate is therefore a fuel in transit, not a waste product, and its blood concentration is the small visible residue of a large matched flux. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: systemic lactate turnover in healthy exercising humans. What limits maximal oxygen uptake is pack #6248, and lactate as a resuscitation/sepsis marker lives in the clinical shelves — neither is this question.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 4083344, 12411539, 23788576, 23239870), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Evolocumab before any first event (VESALIUS-CV): in high-risk patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes but no prior myocardial infarction or stroke, evolocumab cut first major cardiovascular events (3-point MACE hazard ratio 0.75)
shelves.question: In adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or high-risk diabetes but NO prior myocardial infarction or stroke, does evolocumab, compared with placebo on background statin therapy, reduce major cardiovascular events?
shelves.balance: One large outcomes trial, reported four ways, gives a consistent answer. In VESALIUS-CV (12,257 patients with atherosclerosis or high-risk diabetes, LDL cholesterol at least 90 mg/dL, and no previous myocardial infarction or stroke), evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks reduced 3-point MACE (coronary heart disease death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke) with a hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.86) — a 25% relative reduction; the 5-year Kaplan-Meier rates were 6.2% on evolocumab versus 8.0% on placebo, an absolute difference of 1.8 percentage points. The 4-point composite including ischaemia-driven revascularisation also fell (hazard ratio 0.81; 13.4% vs 16.2%). Prespecified reports of the same trial point the same way: total (first plus subsequent) events were reduced (total 4-point events incidence rate ratio 0.80), the prior-PCI subgroup showed a 30% relative reduction in 3-point MACE (hazard ratio 0.70; 7.0% vs 9.5%), and patients with diabetes but no known significant atherosclerosis showed a 31% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.69; 5.0% vs 7.1%). The cap on the stamp is structural, not a doubt about the trial: this is a single trial programme, and the FOURIER-lineage evidence in patients WITH prior events is a different question, homed elsewhere. No safety difference was seen in the main report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one large, internally concordant outcomes trial).

cards.headline: VESALIUS-CV main report (Bohula 2026): evolocumab reduced first 3-point MACE by 25% relative (hazard ratio 0.75; 5-year rates 6.2% vs 8.0%) in 12,257 high-risk patients with no prior myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.summary: VESALIUS-CV main report (Bohula 2026): evolocumab reduced first 3-point MACE by 25% relative (hazard ratio 0.75; 5-year rates 6.2% vs 8.0%) in 12,257 high-risk patients with no prior myocardial infarction or stroke
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 outcomes trial (VESALIUS-CV main report)
cards.people: 12,257 patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes and no previous myocardial infarction or stroke, with LDL cholesterol at least 90 mg/dL, randomly assigned 1:1 to evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks (6,129) or placebo (6,128). Median age 66 years, 43% women, 93% White. Median follow-up 4.6 years. Dual primary endpoints: 3-point MACE (death from coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke) and 4-point MACE (3-point plus ischaemia-driven arterial revascularisation).
cards.result: A 3-point MACE event occurred in 336 patients on evolocumab (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate 6.2%) versus 443 on placebo (8.0%): hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001) — a 25% relative reduction, 1.8 percentage points absolute at 5 years. A 4-point MACE event occurred in 747 (13.4%) versus 907 (16.2%): hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.89; P<0.001) — a 19% relative reduction. No evidence of a between-group difference in safety events was seen.
cards.watchOut: This is a single trial, however large: the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE for that reason. The population had LDL cholesterol of at least 90 mg/dL on optimised therapy and either atherosclerosis or high-risk diabetes — the result does not automatically extend to lower-risk primary-prevention patients, and 93% of participants were White.
cards.source: Bohula EA et al. Evolocumab in Patients without a Previous Myocardial Infarction or Stroke (VESALIUS-CV). The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 41211925. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03872401, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: VESALIUS-CV total-events analysis (Nicolau 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): evolocumab also reduced subsequent events — total 4-point MACE incidence rate ratio 0.80, total 3-point 0.73
cards.summary: VESALIUS-CV total-events analysis (Nicolau 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): evolocumab also reduced subsequent events — total 4-point MACE incidence rate ratio 0.80, total 3-point 0.73
cards.type: Prespecified total-events analysis of the VESALIUS-CV trial (same trial as the main report, explicitly labelled)
cards.people: The same 12,257 VESALIUS-CV patients, followed for a median of 4.6 years. This prespecified analysis counted first AND subsequent dual-primary-endpoint events using negative binomial regression: 1,654 first 4-point MACE and 1,107 subsequent events (2,761 total); 779 first 3-point MACE and 146 subsequent events (925 total).
cards.result: Evolocumab reduced first 4-point MACE by 19% relative (hazard ratio 0.81), subsequent events by 25% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.91), and total 4-point events by 20% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.90; P=0.0002). For 3-point MACE, total events fell by 27% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.86; P=0.0001). Based on annualised rate differences, evolocumab was projected to prevent 55 total 4-point events per 1,000 patients over 5 years. Results were consistent across subgroups including statin intensity.
cards.watchOut: Same patients, same trial — this report deepens the main result (benefit is not limited to first events) but is not independent confirmation. Projected events prevented per 1,000 are model-based extrapolations from the observed rate differences.
cards.source: Nicolau JC et al. Cumulative Benefit With Evolocumab in Patients With No Prior Myocardial Infarction or Stroke in the VESALIUS-CV Study. cards.headline: VESALIUS-CV prior-PCI subgroup (Bergmark 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): in 3,627 patients with prior PCI but no myocardial infarction, 3-point MACE fell 30% relative (hazard ratio 0.70; 7.0% vs 9.5%) and myocardial infarction halved relative (hazard ratio 0.50)
cards.summary: VESALIUS-CV prior-PCI subgroup (Bergmark 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): in 3,627 patients with prior PCI but no myocardial infarction, 3-point MACE fell 30% relative (hazard ratio 0.70; 7.0% vs 9.5%) and myocardial infarction halved relative (hazard ratio 0.50)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of the VESALIUS-CV trial (same trial as the main report, explicitly labelled)
cards.people: 3,627 of the 12,257 VESALIUS-CV patients (29.6%) had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention before enrolment (median 4 years earlier) without a prior myocardial infarction. Median age 66 years, 30.7% women. Median follow-up 4.6 years.
cards.result: Evolocumab reduced 3-point MACE by 30% relative (5-year Kaplan-Meier rates 7.0% vs 9.5%; hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89; P=0.004) and 4-point MACE by 18% relative (17.9% vs 21.7%; hazard ratio 0.82). Myocardial infarction fell by 50% relative (3.0% vs 6.1%; hazard ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.70), and urgent coronary revascularisation by 39% relative (hazard ratio 0.61). In the lipid substudy, median LDL cholesterol at 48 weeks was 41.5 mg/dL on evolocumab versus 107.0 mg/dL on placebo. Cardiovascular and all-cause death rates were nominally lower (hazard ratios 0.66 and 0.76).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of the single trial — larger relative effects in a higher-risk slice are expected and do not add an independent trial. Nominal death differences were not the trial's primary endpoints and should not be read as a mortality claim.
cards.source: Bergmark BA et al. Evolocumab in Patients With Prior Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and No Prior Myocardial Infarction: Results From the VESALIUS-CV Trial. Circulation. 2026. prespecified subgroup analysis of the vesalius-cv trial (same trial as the main report, explicitly labelled) 3,627 of the 12,257 vesalius-cv patients (29.6%) had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention before enrolment (median 4 years earlier) without a prior myocardial infarction. median age 66 years, 30.7% women. median follow-up 4.6 years. evolocumab reduced 3-point mace by 30% relative (5-year kaplan-meier rates 7.0% vs 9.5%; hazard ratio 0.70; 95% ci 0.56 to 0.89; p=0.004) and 4-point mace by 18% relative (17.9% vs 21.7%; hazard ratio 0.82). myocardial infarction fell by 50% relative (3.0% vs 6.1%; hazard ratio 0.50; 95% ci 0.36 to 0.70), and urgent coronary revascularisation by 39% relative (hazard ratio 0.61). in the lipid substudy, median ldl cholesterol at 48 weeks was 41.5 mg/dl on evolocumab versus 107.0 mg/dl on placebo. cardiovascular and all-cause death rates were nominally lower (hazard ratios 0.66 and 0.76). a subgroup of the single trial — larger relative effects in a higher-risk slice are expected and do not add an independent trial. nominal death differences were not the trial's primary endpoints and should not be read as a mortality claim. bergmark ba et al. evolocumab in patients with prior percutaneous coronary intervention and no prior myocardial infarction: results from the vesalius-cv trial. circulation. 2026. pmid: 42153665. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct03872401, from the record's databank fields. mesh: aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized/therapeutic use/adverse effects · anticholesteremic agents/therapeutic use/adverse effects · cholesterol, ldl/blood · double-blind method · myocardial infarction · percutaneous coronary intervention/adverse effects · treatment outcome

cards.headline: VESALIUS-CV diabetes-without-atherosclerosis subgroup (Marston 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): in 3,655 patients with diabetes and no known significant atherosclerosis, 3-point MACE fell 31% relative (hazard ratio 0.69; 5.0% vs 7.1%)
cards.summary: VESALIUS-CV diabetes-without-atherosclerosis subgroup (Marston 2026; prespecified report of the same trial): in 3,655 patients with diabetes and no known significant atherosclerosis, 3-point MACE fell 31% relative (hazard ratio 0.69; 5.0% vs 7.1%)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of the VESALIUS-CV trial (same trial as the main report, explicitly labelled)
cards.people: 3,655 VESALIUS-CV patients without known significant atherosclerosis (no prior arterial revascularisation, no arterial stenosis of 50% or more, and coronary calcium score below 100), all of whom had diabetes: 1,849 assigned to evolocumab and 1,806 to placebo. Median age 65 years, 57% women. Median follow-up 4.8 years.
cards.result: A 3-point MACE event occurred in 83 patients on evolocumab (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate 5.0%) versus 117 on placebo (7.1%): hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.91; P=0.009) — a 31% relative reduction, 2.1 percentage points absolute. The 4-point composite also fell (7.6% vs 10.5%; hazard ratio 0.69). There were 136 deaths on evolocumab (7.8%) versus 172 on placebo (10.1%): hazard ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.95). In the lipid substudy, median LDL cholesterol at 48 weeks was 52 mg/dL versus 111 mg/dL.
cards.watchOut: Again the same single trial: this report answers the 'diabetes alone, no manifest atherosclerosis' slice of the question, it does not replicate the main finding. Event counts in the subgroup are small (83 vs 117), so the relative estimate carries wide uncertainty.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one large trial, four concordant reports — evolocumab prevents first events in high-risk patients without prior myocardial infarction or stroke; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because a single trial programme caps the claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large trial, four concordant reports — evolocumab prevents first events in high-risk patients without prior myocardial infarction or stroke; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because a single trial programme caps the claim
cards.people: Synthesis of the four VESALIUS-CV reports carded on this shelf: the main outcomes report, the prespecified total-events analysis, and the prespecified prior-PCI and diabetes-without-atherosclerosis subgroup reports — all one trial of 12,257 patients (NCT03872401).
cards.result: Across all four reports the direction and size of benefit agree: 3-point MACE hazard ratios 0.75 (whole trial), 0.70 (prior PCI) and 0.69 (diabetes without atherosclerosis), with total-event incidence rate ratios of 0.80 (4-point) and 0.73 (3-point). Absolute 5-year differences are modest — about 1.8 to 2.9 percentage points — because these patients, by design, had not yet had an event. Evolocumab for LDL lowering and the FOURIER-lineage outcomes record in patients WITH prior events are different questions, homed elsewhere in the library; this shelf claims only the no-prior-event slice.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this stamp on the strength of the subgroup papers: subgroups and total-event analyses of one trial are one body of evidence. A second outcomes trial in a no-prior-event population, or longer follow-up, would be needed to move beyond POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 41211925, 42663360, 42153665, 41903215). No additional source.

shelves.title: Obicetrapib plus ezetimibe fixed-dose combination (TANDEM): the single pill lowered LDL cholesterol 48.6% more than placebo and 16.8% more than obicetrapib alone at day 84 — a surrogate-endpoint slice of the obicetrapib programme (monotherapy homed at shelf #1569)
shelves.question: In patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or ASCVD whose LDL remains raised on maximally tolerated therapy, does the fixed-dose combination of obicetrapib plus ezetimibe, compared with its components/placebo, lower LDL cholesterol more than obicetrapib alone?
shelves.balance: This shelf is the fixed-dose-combination slice only: obicetrapib MONOTHERAPY is homed at live shelf #1569 (BROADWAY and BROOKLYN), and the pooled events analysis and the PREVAIL outcomes trial fenced there stay fenced here. On the combination question, TANDEM (407 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or pre-existing/high-risk ASCVD, LDL at least 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) on maximally tolerated therapy) found the obicetrapib 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg single pill beat every comparator at day 84: LDL cholesterol fell 48.6% more than placebo, 27.9% more than ezetimibe alone and 16.8% more than obicetrapib alone (all relative percent differences; obicetrapib alone fell 31.9% versus placebo). The phase 2 ROSE2 trial, on high-intensity statin, points the same way (combination −63.4% LDL from baseline versus −43.5% on obicetrapib alone and −6.35% on placebo at week 12). The third card is the phase 2 ROSE monotherapy trial, carded as programme support for the 'alone' side of the comparison — it is not carded at shelf #1569. Everything here is an 84-day to 12-week LDL surrogate: whether the combination prevents events is unanswered, and adverse-event rates on the combination (51%) sat between obicetrapib alone (54%) and placebo (37%) in TANDEM. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one phase 3 trial plus phase 2 programme support, surrogate endpoint only).

cards.headline: TANDEM 2025: the obicetrapib–ezetimibe fixed-dose combination lowered LDL cholesterol 48.6% versus placebo, 27.9% versus ezetimibe and 16.8% versus obicetrapib alone at day 84 (all relative percent differences)
cards.summary: TANDEM 2025: the obicetrapib–ezetimibe fixed-dose combination lowered LDL cholesterol 48.6% versus placebo, 27.9% versus ezetimibe and 16.8% versus obicetrapib alone at day 84 (all relative percent differences)
cards.people: 407 participants at 48 US sites, aged at least 18, with pre-existing or high risk for ASCVD or heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia and LDL cholesterol of 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) or greater despite maximally tolerated lipid-lowering therapy (excluding ezetimibe) or statin intolerance. Randomised 1:1:1:1 to the fixed-dose combination (obicetrapib 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg; n=102), obicetrapib 10 mg alone (n=102), ezetimibe 10 mg alone (n=101) or placebo (n=102), daily for 84 days. Median age 68 years, 43% female. Mean baseline LDL cholesterol was 2.4 to 2.6 mmol/L (about 93 to 101 mg/dL) across groups.
cards.result: At day 84, percent differences in LDL cholesterol reduction with the fixed-dose combination were −48.6% (95% CI −58.3 to −38.9) versus placebo, −27.9% (−37.5 to −18.4) versus ezetimibe alone and −16.8% (−26.4 to −7.1) versus obicetrapib alone (all relative percent differences). Obicetrapib monotherapy lowered LDL cholesterol by 31.9% versus placebo. Adverse events occurred in 51% on the combination, 54% on obicetrapib, 53% on ezetimibe and 37% on placebo; serious adverse events in 3%, 6%, 7% and 4% respectively; one death occurred in each active-treatment group and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: An 84-day LDL surrogate in 407 patients: the trial cannot speak to cardiovascular events, and the combination's advantage over obicetrapib alone (−16.8% relative) is the increment ezetimibe adds, not a new mechanism. Event prevention for obicetrapib awaits the PREVAIL outcomes trial, fenced at shelf #1569.
cards.source: Sarraju A et al. Fixed-dose combination of obicetrapib and ezetimibe for LDL cholesterol reduction (TANDEM): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2025. PMID: 40347969. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06005597, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ROSE2 2023 (phase 2): on high-intensity statin, obicetrapib plus ezetimibe lowered LDL cholesterol by 63.4% from baseline at week 12, versus 43.5% on obicetrapib alone and 6.35% on placebo
cards.summary: ROSE2 2023 (phase 2): on high-intensity statin, obicetrapib plus ezetimibe lowered LDL cholesterol by 63.4% from baseline at week 12, versus 43.5% on obicetrapib alone and 6.35% on placebo
cards.people: 119 patients with LDL cholesterol above 70 mg/dL and triglycerides below 400 mg/dL on stable high-intensity statin therapy, randomised to obicetrapib 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg (n=40), obicetrapib 10 mg alone (n=39) or placebo (n=40) for 12 weeks; 97 patients were included in the primary analysis. Mean age 62.6 years, 63.9% male.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol fell from baseline to week 12 by 63.4% on the combination, 43.5% on obicetrapib alone and 6.35% on placebo (P<0.0001 versus placebo for both active treatments; changes are relative percent changes from baseline). On the combination, LDL cholesterol below 100, below 70 and below 55 mg/dL was achieved by 100%, 93.5% and 87.1% of patients respectively. Non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and total and small LDL particles also fell significantly. Obicetrapib was well tolerated with no safety issues identified.
cards.watchOut: A small phase 2 trial (97 in the primary analysis) with a 12-week surrogate endpoint — supportive of TANDEM, not a substitute for it. Unlike TANDEM, all patients here were on high-intensity statin, which is why the percentage falls look larger.
cards.source: Ballantyne CM et al. Obicetrapib plus ezetimibe as an adjunct to high-intensity statin therapy: A randomized phase 2 trial. Journal of clinical lipidology. 2023. PMID: 37277261. cards.headline: ROSE 2022 (phase 2, programme support for the monotherapy comparator): obicetrapib 5 or 10 mg on high-intensity statin lowered median LDL cholesterol by up to 51% versus placebo over 8 weeks
cards.summary: ROSE 2022 (phase 2, programme support for the monotherapy comparator): obicetrapib 5 or 10 mg on high-intensity statin lowered median LDL cholesterol by up to 51% versus placebo over 8 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (ROSE) — programme support, explicitly labelled: this is the monotherapy programme, not the fixed-dose combination
cards.people: 120 dyslipidaemic patients (median LDL cholesterol 88 mg/dL) on background high-intensity statin therapy, randomised to obicetrapib 5 mg or 10 mg or placebo for 8 weeks. This card is programme support: it defines what obicetrapib ALONE does, the comparator the fixed-dose combination must beat. The monotherapy question itself is homed at live shelf #1569, which cards BROADWAY and BROOKLYN; this ROSE trial is not carded there.
cards.result: Treatment with 5 mg or 10 mg obicetrapib decreased median LDL cholesterol by up to 51% versus placebo (P<0.0001; relative change). Apolipoprotein B fell by up to 30% relative and non-HDL cholesterol by up to 44% relative, while HDL cholesterol rose by up to 165% relative (all P<0.0001). The safety profile was acceptable.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this card as combination evidence: it is monotherapy, in a small 8-week phase 2 trial, and it belongs conceptually to the shelf #1569 question. It is carded here only so the TANDEM comparison (combination versus alone) can be judged against the alone effect measured in the same programme.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fixed-dose combination lowers LDL more than either component alone — POSSIBLE on surrogate evidence only; the monotherapy and outcomes questions stay at shelf #1569
cards.summary: Synthesis: the fixed-dose combination lowers LDL more than either component alone — POSSIBLE on surrogate evidence only; the monotherapy and outcomes questions stay at shelf #1569
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: TANDEM (phase 3, n=407), ROSE2 (phase 2 combination, n=119) and ROSE (phase 2 monotherapy programme support, n=120).
cards.result: Two combination trials agree: adding ezetimibe to obicetrapib lowers LDL cholesterol further than obicetrapib alone (−16.8% relative versus alone in TANDEM at day 84; −63.4% versus −43.5% from baseline in ROSE2 at week 12). No carded report measures cardiovascular events for the combination, and none runs beyond 12 weeks for efficacy. Obicetrapib monotherapy (BROADWAY, BROOKLYN) and the fenced PREVAIL outcomes trial are homed at live shelf #1569 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: A single-pill convenience claim is not an outcomes claim. Until PREVAIL reports, this shelf supports only the statement that the combination lowers LDL cholesterol more than its components over about 3 months.

shelves.title: Lerodalcibep (LIB Therapeutics), a monthly PCSK9-binding adnectin fusion protein: LDL cholesterol fell by about 56-65% versus placebo in high-risk and heterozygous FH phase 3 trials; in homozygous FH the response was small, variable, and non-inferiority to evolocumab was not shown
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia (including heterozygous FH) on background therapy, does monthly lerodalcibep (a PCSK9-binding adnectin fusion protein), compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.balance: Lerodalcibep is a single-source investigational product (LIB Therapeutics) — a small PCSK9-binding adnectin fused to albumin, given as a monthly 300 mg (1.2 mL) subcutaneous injection; it is named here under the clarification exception. In the two populations the question asks about, the phase 3 evidence is strong and concordant on the LDL surrogate: LIBerate-HR (922 patients with cardiovascular disease or at high/very high risk on maximally tolerated statins) found a placebo-adjusted LDL reduction of 56.2% at week 52 (62.7% for the mean of weeks 50 and 52), with 90% of lerodalcibep patients achieving both a reduction of at least 50% and guideline targets; LIBerate-HeFH (478 patients with heterozygous FH) found placebo-adjusted reductions of 58.6% at week 24 and 65.0% for the mean of weeks 22 and 24 — an absolute difference of 2.08 mmol/L (about 80 mg/dL) at week 24. Homozygous FH is different: in LIBerate-HoFH (66 patients, crossover against evolocumab), LDL fell only 4.9% on lerodalcibep versus 10.3% on evolocumab and non-inferiority was NOT shown (difference 5.4%, 95% CI −0.2 to 11.1, against a 6% margin), with wide individual variability. Safety was placebo-like except injection-site reactions (6.9% vs 0.3% in LIBerate-HR). There is no cardiovascular-outcomes trial: the claim is LDL lowering only. PROPOSED LIKELY for LDL lowering (Tier C: concordant phase 3 trials, surrogate endpoint, HoFH exception stated on the face).

cards.headline: LIBerate-HR (Klug 2024): lerodalcibep lowered LDL cholesterol by 56.2% versus placebo at week 52 (62.7% for the mean of weeks 50 and 52) in 922 patients with or at high risk of cardiovascular disease
cards.summary: LIBerate-HR (Klug 2024): lerodalcibep lowered LDL cholesterol by 56.2% versus placebo at week 52 (62.7% for the mean of weeks 50 and 52) in 922 patients with or at high risk of cardiovascular disease
cards.people: 922 patients at 66 clinics in 11 countries, aged 18 or older, on maximally tolerated statin therapy, with cardiovascular disease and LDL cholesterol of 70 mg/dL or greater, or at high risk with LDL cholesterol of 100 mg/dL or greater. Randomised 2:1 to monthly subcutaneous lerodalcibep 300 mg (1.2 mL) or placebo for 52 weeks. Mean age 64.5 years, 44.9% female, mean baseline LDL cholesterol 116.2 mg/dL; 88% completed the trial. Tested product: lerodalcibep (LIB Therapeutics), named per the clarification exception.
cards.result: The mean placebo-adjusted reduction in LDL cholesterol was 56.2% (SE 2.2%) at week 52 and 62.7% (1.9%) for the mean of weeks 50 and 52 by modified intention-to-treat analysis (P<0.001 for all analyses; intention-to-treat with washout imputation gave 49.7% and 55.3%). On lerodalcibep, 555 of 615 participants (90%) achieved both an LDL reduction of at least 50% and guideline-recommended targets. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar to placebo except injection-site reactions (42 of 613, 6.9%, versus 1 of 307, 0.3%), which were mild or moderate and did not increase discontinuation (4.2% vs 4.6%). Sporadic in-vitro antidrug antibodies had no impact on free PCSK9 or LDL lowering.
cards.watchOut: A 52-week LDL surrogate with no cardiovascular-outcomes data. The modified intention-to-treat figures are the largest of the three analyses reported; the washout-imputation intention-to-treat figures (49.7% at week 52) are the conservative read.
cards.source: Klug EQ et al. Efficacy and Safety of Lerodalcibep in Patients With or at High Risk of Cardiovascular Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA cardiology. 2024. PMID: 38958989. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04806893, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: LIBerate-HeFH (Raal 2023): in heterozygous FH, lerodalcibep beat placebo by 58.6% on LDL cholesterol at week 24 (65.0% for the mean of weeks 22 and 24) — an absolute difference of 2.08 mmol/L (about 80 mg/dL)
cards.summary: LIBerate-HeFH (Raal 2023): in heterozygous FH, lerodalcibep beat placebo by 58.6% on LDL cholesterol at week 24 (65.0% for the mean of weeks 22 and 24) — an absolute difference of 2.08 mmol/L (about 80 mg/dL)
cards.people: 478 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia requiring additional LDL lowering, randomised 2:1 to monthly subcutaneous lerodalcibep 300 mg or placebo for 24 weeks. Mean age 53 years (range 18-80), 51.7% female, mean baseline LDL cholesterol 3.88 mmol/L (about 150 mg/dL). Tested product: lerodalcibep (LIB Therapeutics).
cards.result: Lerodalcibep reduced LDL cholesterol versus placebo by an absolute 2.08 mmol/L (about 80 mg/dL; least-squares mean difference, 95% CI −2.30 to −1.87 mmol/L), a percentage difference of −58.6% at week 24, and by 2.28 mmol/L (about 88 mg/dL), a percentage difference of −65.0%, for the mean of weeks 22 and 24 (P<0.0001 for all; percentage differences are relative). On lerodalcibep, 68% of participants achieved both an LDL reduction of at least 50% and European Society of Cardiology LDL targets. Except for mild injection-site reactions, treatment-emergent adverse events were similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Shorter (24 weeks) than LIBerate-HR and again a surrogate endpoint. The population is heterozygous FH — a high-baseline-LDL group (mean 3.88 mmol/L, about 150 mg/dL) — so absolute falls here are larger than in a general high-risk population.
cards.source: Raal F et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of lerodalcibep in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: the LIBerate-HeFH trial. European heart journal. 2023. PMID: 37639462.
