cards.headline: LIBerate-HoFH (Raal 2025): in homozygous FH, LDL fell only 4.9% on lerodalcibep versus 10.3% on evolocumab in a crossover trial — non-inferiority was NOT shown (difference 5.4%, 95% CI −0.2 to 11.1; margin 6%)
cards.summary: LIBerate-HoFH (Raal 2025): in homozygous FH, LDL fell only 4.9% on lerodalcibep versus 10.3% on evolocumab in a crossover trial — non-inferiority was NOT shown (difference 5.4%, 95% CI −0.2 to 11.1; margin 6%)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, crossover, non-inferiority phase 3 trial (LIBerate-HoFH)
cards.people: 66 patients aged 10 years or older with genetically confirmed homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia at 12 lipid clinics in six countries, randomised to monthly lerodalcibep 300 mg or monthly evolocumab 420 mg for 24 weeks, an 8-week washout, then crossover to the other treatment for 24 weeks. Mean age 28.7 years, 30% paediatric, 55% female; mean baseline LDL cholesterol 10.59 mmol/L (about 410 mg/dL). Tested products: lerodalcibep (LIB Therapeutics) and evolocumab, as named in the publication.
cards.result: Mean LDL cholesterol reduction at week 24 was −4.9% (SE 3.5) on lerodalcibep versus −10.3% (3.5) on evolocumab; the mean difference was 5.4% (95% CI −0.2 to 11.1), which did not show non-inferiority at the prespecified 6% margin. Averaged across all monthly visits, responses were −9.1% and −10.8% respectively. Individual response varied considerably but was generally similar within the same patient on both drugs; neither genotyping nor free-PCSK9 suppression predicted response. Both drugs were well tolerated with no treatment-related serious adverse events; injection-site reactions occurred in 1 of 65 patients on lerodalcibep versus 15 of 62 on evolocumab.
cards.watchOut: This is the split in the programme: in homozygous FH — where little functional LDL-receptor activity remains — PCSK9 binding lowers LDL only modestly with either agent, and lerodalcibep did not meet its non-inferiority margin. Do not carry the heterozygous-FH effect size into homozygous FH. The trial included children from age 10, unlike the adult trials on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: monthly lerodalcibep lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly 56-65% versus placebo in high-risk and heterozygous FH patients — LIKELY for LDL lowering only; homozygous FH is a stated exception and events are untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: monthly lerodalcibep lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly 56-65% versus placebo in high-risk and heterozygous FH patients — LIKELY for LDL lowering only; homozygous FH is a stated exception and events are untested
cards.people: Synthesis of the three LIBerate phase 3 trials carded on this shelf: LIBerate-HR (n=922), LIBerate-HeFH (n=478) and LIBerate-HoFH (n=66) — a total carded evidence base of 1,466 randomised patients.
cards.result: Two placebo-controlled trials in the question's populations are concordant and large in effect (placebo-adjusted LDL reductions of 49.7-62.7% in LIBerate-HR depending on analysis, and 58.6-65.0% in LIBerate-HeFH), with a placebo-like safety profile apart from injection-site reactions. The homozygous FH crossover trial qualifies the claim: responses there were small and variable on both PCSK9 agents, and non-inferiority to evolocumab was not shown. No trial measures cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: LIKELY applies to the LDL claim in adults with hypercholesterolaemia or heterozygous FH on background therapy — not to event reduction, and not to homozygous FH, where the honest statement is that lerodalcibep performed similarly to evolocumab within wide variability but missed its non-inferiority margin.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 38958989, 37639462, 39870096). No additional source.

shelves.title: Solbinsiran (Eli Lilly), an ANGPTL3 siRNA, in mixed dyslipidaemia: phase 2 only — the 400 mg dose lowered apolipoprotein B by 14.3% versus placebo at day 180, but the 100 mg and 800 mg doses did not (a non-monotonic dose response on surrogate endpoints)
shelves.question: In adults with mixed dyslipidaemia, does the ANGPTL3 siRNA solbinsiran, compared with placebo, lower apolipoprotein B and triglycerides?
shelves.balance: Solbinsiran is a single-source investigational product (Eli Lilly) — a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against hepatic ANGPTL3 (development code LY3561774), named under the clarification exception. The whole human record is early-phase. In the phase 2 PROLONG-ANG3 trial (205 adults with mixed dyslipidaemia on moderate- or high-intensity statins, given two injections 90 days apart), the placebo-adjusted change in apolipoprotein B at day 180 was −14.3% (relative) for the 400 mg dose (P=0.0085) but −2.8% (P=0.69) for 100 mg and −8.3% (P=0.14) for 800 mg — the middle dose worked and the highest dose did not reach significance, a non-monotonic pattern that weakens causal confidence. The phase 1 study (third and fourth cards — the single-ascending-dose and repeat-dose parts of one publication, NCT04644809) showed dose-dependent ANGPTL3 suppression of up to 86-89% with triglyceride falls of up to about 70-73%, so the pharmacology is real; what is unproven is a reliable dose, a durable lipid effect at phase 3 scale, and any effect on cardiovascular events. Treatment-emergent adverse events in PROLONG-ANG3 were no more frequent on solbinsiran (44-60% across doses) than placebo (65%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: phase 2 only, surrogate endpoints, non-monotonic dose response).

cards.headline: PROLONG-ANG3 (Ray 2025, phase 2): solbinsiran 400 mg lowered apolipoprotein B by 14.3% versus placebo at day 180 (P=0.0085), but 100 mg (−2.8%; P=0.69) and 800 mg (−8.3%; P=0.14) did not — only the middle dose met the primary endpoint
cards.summary: PROLONG-ANG3 (Ray 2025, phase 2): solbinsiran 400 mg lowered apolipoprotein B by 14.3% versus placebo at day 180 (P=0.0085), but 100 mg (−2.8%; P=0.69) and 800 mg (−8.3%; P=0.14) did not — only the middle dose met the primary endpoint
cards.people: 205 adults with mixed dyslipidaemia at 41 sites in seven countries, on moderate- or high-intensity statins, with fasting triglycerides 1.69 to 5.64 mmol/L (about 150 to 500 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol at least 1.81 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) and non-HDL cholesterol at least 3.36 mmol/L (130 mg/dL). Randomised 1:2:2:2 to solbinsiran 100 mg (n=30), 400 mg (n=58) or 800 mg (n=59) or placebo (n=58), by subcutaneous injection on days 0 and 90, followed for at least 270 days. Median age 57 years, 54% female. Median baseline apolipoprotein B 111 mg/dL, triglycerides 2.64 mmol/L (about 234 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol 3.16 mmol/L (about 122 mg/dL). Tested product: solbinsiran (Eli Lilly).
cards.result: The placebo-adjusted percent change in apolipoprotein B at day 180 (primary outcome; relative changes) was −2.8% (95% CI −15.5 to 11.9; P=0.69) for 100 mg, −14.3% (−23.6 to −3.9; P=0.0085) for 400 mg and −8.3% (−18.3 to 2.9; P=0.14) for 800 mg. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 60% (100 mg), 52% (400 mg), 44% (800 mg) and 65% (placebo) of patients; the drug was reported as generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, with a surrogate primary endpoint and a non-monotonic dose response — the highest dose missing significance is the single most important fact on this card. Two injections and 180 days say nothing about long-term dosing or events.
cards.source: Ray KK et al. Durability and efficacy of solbinsiran, a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA targeting ANGPTL3, in adults with mixed dyslipidaemia (PROLONG-ANG3): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2025. PMID: 40179932. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05256654, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Solbinsiran phase 1, single-ascending-dose part (Ray 2025; one part of the phase 1 publication, NCT04644809): single doses of 24-960 mg reduced ANGPTL3 by up to 86% and triglycerides by up to 73% in participants with mixed dyslipidaemia
cards.summary: Solbinsiran phase 1, single-ascending-dose part (Ray 2025; one part of the phase 1 publication, NCT04644809): single doses of 24-960 mg reduced ANGPTL3 by up to 86% and triglycerides by up to 73% in participants with mixed dyslipidaemia
cards.type: Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study — part 1 of 2 of one publication (explicitly labelled: the same PMID also carries the repeat-dose card below; both parts belong to the one phase 1 study, NCT04644809)
cards.people: Participants with mixed dyslipidaemia in the single-ascending-dose part of the phase 1 study of solbinsiran (LY3561774, Eli Lilly): single subcutaneous doses of 24 to 960 mg or matching placebo, with safety, pharmacokinetics, ANGPTL3 and lipid parameters followed over 169 days. N not documented in the fetched record for this part. The same publication's preclinical (mouse and monkey) experiments are not carded — this shelf rests on human data only.
cards.result: A single dose produced dose-dependent mean percentage reductions from baseline in ANGPTL3 of up to 86% (SE 4%), triglycerides up to 73% (7%), LDL cholesterol up to 30% (16%), non-HDL cholesterol up to 41% (12%) and apolipoprotein B up to 30% (11%), with sustained effects at higher doses (P<0.0001 for all; relative changes). Adverse events were mostly mild, with similar incidence on solbinsiran and placebo.
cards.watchOut: First-in-human pharmacology, not an efficacy trial: small dose cohorts (exact N not documented in the fetched record), healthy-volunteer-style follow-up of 169 days, and percent falls from baseline rather than a powered placebo comparison. It establishes that the drug engages its target in humans — nothing more.

cards.headline: Solbinsiran phase 1, repeat-dose part (Ray 2025; part 2 of 2 of the same publication, NCT04644809): two doses (days 1 and 29) of 208 or 480 mg reduced ANGPTL3 by 89% and triglycerides by up to 70%
cards.summary: Solbinsiran phase 1, repeat-dose part (Ray 2025; part 2 of 2 of the same publication, NCT04644809): two doses (days 1 and 29) of 208 or 480 mg reduced ANGPTL3 by 89% and triglycerides by up to 70%
cards.type: Phase 1 repeat-dose study — part 2 of 2 of one publication (explicitly labelled: same PMID and same phase 1 study as the single-dose card above)
cards.people: Participants with mixed dyslipidaemia in the repeat-dose part of the same phase 1 study: subcutaneous solbinsiran 208 mg or 480 mg, or matching placebo, on days 1 and 29, followed over 169 days. N not documented in the fetched record for this part. Tested product: solbinsiran (LY3561774, Eli Lilly).
cards.result: Repeat dosing reduced ANGPTL3 by 89% (SE 6%), triglycerides by up to 70% (13%), LDL cholesterol by up to 42% (14%), non-HDL cholesterol by up to 46% (14%) and apolipoprotein B by up to 36% (13%) (P<0.0001 for all; relative changes from baseline). Nuclear magnetic resonance analysis showed reductions in total triglyceride-rich lipoprotein and LDL particle numbers. Adverse events were mostly mild and similar in incidence to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Same limits as the single-dose part, and the two phase 1 cards are one publication — together they count as programme support for PROLONG-ANG3, not as two independent trials. The larger lipid falls here than in phase 2 (at higher, more frequent doses) underline that the therapeutic dose is not yet settled.

cards.headline: Synthesis: solbinsiran engages ANGPTL3 in humans and lowered apolipoprotein B at one phase 2 dose — MAYBE (weak evidence): phase 2 only, surrogate endpoints, and a non-monotonic dose response
cards.summary: Synthesis: solbinsiran engages ANGPTL3 in humans and lowered apolipoprotein B at one phase 2 dose — MAYBE (weak evidence): phase 2 only, surrogate endpoints, and a non-monotonic dose response
cards.people: Synthesis of the solbinsiran human reports carded on this shelf: PROLONG-ANG3 (phase 2, n=205) and the phase 1 publication's single-dose and repeat-dose parts (N not documented in the fetched record). Total documented randomised evidence base: 205 patients.
cards.result: The pharmacodynamic chain is consistent — ANGPTL3 suppression of up to 86-89% across the programme with falls in triglycerides, LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B — but the one randomised efficacy trial met its apolipoprotein B endpoint at the middle dose only. The ANGPTL3 family neighbours are different agents with their own shelves: evinacumab (live shelf #1106) and zodasiran (pack #3105); neither answers the solbinsiran question.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here supports a clinical claim yet. A phase 3 trial with a settled dose — and ultimately an outcomes trial — would be needed to move this stamp; if the 800 mg failure reflects a real inverted-U response rather than chance, the programme may not clear that bar.

shelves.title: GMRx2 (Widaplik, George Medicines) — a low-dose triple single pill of telmisartan/amlodipine/indapamide: it beat each of its dual combinations and beat placebo, lowering home systolic pressure by a further 2.5-5.4 mm Hg over duals at 12 weeks
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does the low-dose triple single-pill combination GMRx2 (telmisartan/amlodipine/indapamide), compared with dual combinations or placebo, lower blood pressure?
shelves.balance: The tested product must be named: GMRx2 (marketed as Widaplik), developed by George Medicines — a single pill combining low doses of telmisartan, amlodipine and indapamide (quarter dose 10/1.25/0.625 mg; half dose 20/2.5/1.25 mg; standard dose 40/5/2.5 mg). Two phase 3 trials answer the two halves of the question. Against its own dual components (1,385 patients), continued GMRx2 half dose, doubled at week 6, left home systolic pressure at week 12 lower than every dual pairing: by 2.5 mm Hg versus telmisartan-indapamide, 5.4 mm Hg versus telmisartan-amlodipine and 4.4 mm Hg versus amlodipine-indapamide, with clinic control below 140/90 mm Hg in 74% versus 53-61%. Against placebo (295 patients with mild-to-moderate elevation, initial treatment), home systolic pressure fell by a placebo-corrected 7.3 mm Hg (quarter dose) and 8.2 mm Hg (half dose) at week 4, with clinic control of 65-70% versus 37%. Withdrawal for adverse events did not differ significantly in either trial, and a 50-patient open-label extension of the placebo trial (third card) kept home control at 60% at one year. All endpoints are blood pressure — a validated surrogate for this drug class, but no trial here measures strokes or events. PROPOSED LIKELY for blood-pressure lowering (Tier C: two concordant phase 3 trials of one programme, surrogate endpoint).

cards.headline: GMRx2 versus dual combinations (Rodgers 2024, Lancet): the triple pill lowered home systolic pressure more than every dual pairing at week 12 — by 2.5, 5.4 and 4.4 mm Hg — with clinic control 74% versus 53-61%
cards.summary: GMRx2 versus dual combinations (Rodgers 2024, Lancet): the triple pill lowered home systolic pressure more than every dual pairing at week 12 — by 2.5, 5.4 and 4.4 mm Hg — with clinic control 74% versus 53-61%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-controlled international phase 3 trial
cards.people: 1,385 adults with hypertension taking zero to three antihypertensive drugs, recruited in Australia, the Czech Republic, New Zealand, Poland, Sri Lanka, the UK and the USA. After a 4-week run-in on GMRx2 half dose (telmisartan 20 mg/amlodipine 2.5 mg/indapamide 1.25 mg), participants were randomised 2:1:1:1 to continued GMRx2 (n=551) or to telmisartan-indapamide (n=276), telmisartan-amlodipine (n=282) or amlodipine-indapamide (n=276), with doses doubled at week 6 unless contraindicated. Mean age 59 years, 51% female; mean clinic pressure at randomisation 133/81 mm Hg. Tested product: GMRx2 (Widaplik), George Medicines.
cards.result: At week 12, mean home systolic pressure was 126 mm Hg on GMRx2 — lower than each dual combination by −2.5 mm Hg (95% CI −3.7 to −1.3) versus telmisartan-indapamide, −5.4 (−6.8 to −4.1) versus telmisartan-amlodipine and −4.4 (−5.8 to −3.1) versus amlodipine-indapamide (all P<0.0001). Clinic pressure differences at week 12 were 4.3/3.5, 5.6/3.7 and 6.3/4.5 mm Hg respectively (all P<0.001). Clinic control below 140/90 mm Hg was 74% on GMRx2 versus 53-61% on the duals. Withdrawal for adverse events: 2% on GMRx2 versus 1% in each dual group, with no statistically significant differences.
cards.watchOut: Every participant had already tolerated GMRx2 half dose during the 4-week run-in before randomisation, which flatters tolerability and means the comparison is 'stay on triple versus step down to a dual', not a from-scratch start. The increments over the best dual (2.5 mm Hg) are real but modest.
cards.source: Rodgers A et al. Efficacy and safety of a novel low-dose triple single-pill combination of telmisartan, amlodipine and indapamide, compared with dual combinations for treatment of hypertension: a randomised, double-blind, active-controlled, international clinical trial. Lancet (London, England). 2024. PMID: 39426836. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04518293, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: GMRx2 versus placebo for initial treatment (Rodgers 2024, JACC): placebo-corrected home systolic reductions of 7.3 mm Hg (quarter dose) and 8.2 mm Hg (half dose) at week 4; clinic control 65-70% versus 37%
cards.summary: GMRx2 versus placebo for initial treatment (Rodgers 2024, JACC): placebo-corrected home systolic reductions of 7.3 mm Hg (quarter dose) and 8.2 mm Hg (half dose) at week 4; clinic control 65-70% versus 37%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (initial treatment)
cards.people: 295 adults with hypertension taking zero or one blood-pressure drug, whose home systolic pressure was 130-154 mm Hg after a 2-week placebo run-in (mean home pressure 139/86 mm Hg). Randomised 2:2:1 to GMRx2 quarter dose (telmisartan 10 mg/amlodipine 1.25 mg/indapamide 0.625 mg), GMRx2 half dose (20/2.5/1.25 mg) or placebo. Mean age 51 years, 56% female; 96% completed. Tested product: GMRx2 (Widaplik), George Medicines.
cards.result: Placebo-corrected least-squares mean differences in home systolic pressure at week 4 were −7.3 mm Hg (95% CI −10.2 to −4.5) for quarter dose and −8.2 mm Hg (−11.3 to −5.2) for half dose; clinic reductions were 8.0/4.0 and 9.5/4.9 mm Hg. Clinic control below 140/90 mm Hg at week 4 was 37% on placebo, 65% on quarter dose and 70% on half dose (both P<0.001 versus placebo). Discontinuation for an adverse event occurred in 1.6% on placebo, 0% on quarter dose and 5.1% on half dose; out-of-range sodium or potassium occurred in 6.3%, 10.6% and 10.1% respectively, with no participant reaching sodium below 130 or above 150 mmol/L or potassium below 3.0 or above 6.0 mmol/L.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week, mild-to-moderate hypertension trial (home systolic 130-154 mm Hg after run-in): it establishes initial-treatment efficacy and short-term tolerability, not durability or safety in more severe hypertension. The half-dose discontinuation rate (5.1%) was numerically above placebo.
cards.source: Rodgers A et al. Efficacy and Safety of a Novel Low-Dose Triple Single-Pill Combination Compared With Placebo for Initial Treatment of Hypertension. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2024. PMID: 39217570. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04518306, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: GMRx2 open-label extension (Salam 2025; follow-up report of the placebo trial's participants): with GMRx2-based treatment titrated in ordinary care, home blood-pressure control was 60% and clinic control 88% at one year, with no discontinuations for adverse events
cards.summary: GMRx2 open-label extension (Salam 2025; follow-up report of the placebo trial's participants): with GMRx2-based treatment titrated in ordinary care, home blood-pressure control was 60% and clinic control 88% at one year, with no discontinuations for adverse events
cards.type: Open-label extension study (follow-up report of the NCT04518306 trial, explicitly labelled — not a separate randomised trial)
cards.people: 50 participants from Sri Lanka and Nigeria who had completed the 4-week double-blind phase of the placebo-controlled trial (NCT04518306) entered the open-label extension, with GMRx2 quarter, half or standard doses (10/1.25/0.625, 20/2.5/1.25, 40/5/2.5 mg) plus add-on drugs as needed toward a home target below 130/80 mm Hg; 48 (96%) completed one year. Mean age 49 years, 60% female. Mean home pressure at extension entry was 126/79 mm Hg.
cards.result: At one year, home blood-pressure control (below 130/80 mm Hg) was 60% and clinic control (below 140/90 mm Hg) was 88%. Mean home pressure was 120/78 mm Hg and clinic pressure 122/77 mm Hg at one year. No participant discontinued trial treatment because of an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, small (n=50) and drawn from two countries' completers of the parent trial, with add-on drugs allowed — this card speaks to durability and tolerability in practice, not to efficacy, and must not be counted as a third randomised trial.

cards.summary: Synthesis: GMRx2 lowers blood pressure more than placebo and more than any of its dual pairings — LIKELY for blood-pressure lowering; long-term and event outcomes are untested in randomised trials
cards.people: Synthesis of the GMRx2 reports carded on this shelf: the dual-comparison phase 3 trial (n=1,385), the placebo-controlled initial-treatment phase 3 trial (n=295) and its 50-patient open-label extension — a total randomised evidence base of 1,680 patients.
cards.result: The two randomised trials are concordant: the triple pill beats placebo by about 7-8 mm Hg home systolic at 4 weeks and beats each dual combination by 2.5-5.4 mm Hg at 12 weeks, with control rates of 65-74% and no significant excess of withdrawals for adverse events. The extension suggests the effect persists to one year in ordinary care. The initial-therapy quarter-dose quadpill question (QUARTET) is a different product and question, homed at live shelf #1551.
cards.watchOut: Blood pressure is the endpoint throughout. Patients with resistant hypertension on three drugs are not the population of these trials — that is the separate QUADRO question (shelf #6654, stopped at build: single report).

shelves.title: Intravenous vernakalant for acute atrial fibrillation in the emergency department (RAFF4): conversion 62.4% versus 48.3% on procainamide, in about half the time (21.8 vs 44.7 minutes) — concordant with the older ACT placebo trials and AVRO versus amiodarone; available in Europe and Canada, not the US
shelves.question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with acute atrial fibrillation suitable for pharmacological cardioversion, does intravenous vernakalant, compared with procainamide (or amiodarone/placebo), convert to sinus rhythm faster and more often?
shelves.balance: Four randomised reports, three comparators, one direction. In the emergency-department head-to-head that matches this question (RAFF4, 350 patients in 12 Canadian EDs, open-label), vernakalant converted 62.4% of patients within 30 minutes of infusion versus 48.3% on procainamide (adjusted absolute difference 15.0 percentage points), roughly twice as fast (21.8 vs 44.7 minutes), with fewer patients needing electrical cardioversion (33.7% vs 44.2%) and similar, mostly mild adverse events. The older programme agrees: against amiodarone (AVRO, 254 patients, double-blind), conversion within 90 minutes was 51.7% versus 5.2%; against placebo in the ACT trials (Roy 2008, 336 patients; Pratt 2010 pooled ACT report, 265 treated), short-duration atrial fibrillation converted in about 51% versus about 4%. The honest limits: vernakalant works on recent-onset atrial fibrillation (hours to a few days) and much less well on longer-duration episodes or atrial flutter; serious events were uncommon but real (hypotension, and one death in a patient with severe aortic stenosis in the pooled ACT report); and the drug is marketed in Europe and Canada but is NOT available in the United States. PROPOSED LIKELY for rapid conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation (Tier C: concordant randomised trials; RAFF4 open-label).

cards.headline: RAFF4 (Stiell 2025): in the emergency department, vernakalant converted acute atrial fibrillation in 62.4% versus 48.3% on procainamide, in 21.8 versus 44.7 minutes, with fewer electrical cardioversions (33.7% vs 44.2%)
cards.summary: RAFF4 (Stiell 2025): in the emergency department, vernakalant converted acute atrial fibrillation in 62.4% versus 48.3% on procainamide, in 21.8 versus 44.7 minutes, with fewer electrical cardioversions (33.7% vs 44.2%)
cards.people: 350 patients with acute atrial fibrillation for whom acute rhythm control was a safe option, at 12 tertiary-care emergency departments in Canada, randomised 1:1 to intravenous vernakalant (n=178) or intravenous procainamide (n=172); patients who did not convert rapidly were offered electrical cardioversion. Primary outcome: conversion to sinus rhythm within 30 minutes of completion of the drug infusion.
cards.result: Conversion was 62.4% on vernakalant versus 48.3% on procainamide (adjusted absolute difference 15.0%, 95% CI 4.6% to 25.0%; P=0.005; adjusted odds ratio 1.87). Time to conversion was faster (21.8 vs 44.7 minutes; mean difference −22.9 minutes; P<0.001), and fewer vernakalant patients underwent attempted electrical cardioversion (33.7% vs 44.2%; odds ratio 0.62; P=0.033). Adverse events were similar in both groups, generally mild and brief, and most patients were discharged home. In patients younger than 70, the advantage was larger (73.3% vs 47.2%; adjusted odds ratio 3.1; interaction P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: Open-label: treating teams knew the drug, which can colour decisions about electrical cardioversion and discharge, though the primary endpoint (electrocardiographic conversion within 30 minutes) is objective. Canadian tertiary EDs and a selected 'safe for rhythm control' population — not all-comers with acute atrial fibrillation.
cards.source: Stiell IG et al. Vernakalant versus procainamide for rapid cardioversion of patients with acute atrial fibrillation (RAFF4): randomised clinical trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2025. PMID: 41218981. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04485195, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: AVRO (Camm 2011): vernakalant converted recent-onset atrial fibrillation within 90 minutes in 51.7% versus 5.2% on amiodarone (median 11 minutes in responders)
cards.summary: AVRO (Camm 2011): vernakalant converted recent-onset atrial fibrillation within 90 minutes in 51.7% versus 5.2% on amiodarone (median 11 minutes in responders)
cards.people: 254 adults with atrial fibrillation of 3 to 48 hours' duration eligible for cardioversion (232 in the primary efficacy comparison: 116 per group), randomised to vernakalant (3 mg/kg over 10 minutes, then a second 2 mg/kg infusion if still in atrial fibrillation) plus sham amiodarone, or amiodarone (5 mg/kg over 60 minutes plus a 50 mg maintenance infusion) plus sham vernakalant. Primary endpoint: conversion to sinus rhythm within 90 minutes.
cards.result: Conversion within 90 minutes was achieved in 60 of 116 vernakalant patients (51.7%) versus 6 of 116 amiodarone patients (5.2%) (P<0.0001; absolute difference 46.5 percentage points). Median time to conversion in responders was 11 minutes. More vernakalant patients reported no atrial fibrillation symptoms at 90 minutes (53.4% vs 32.8%; P=0.0012). Serious adverse events or events leading to discontinuation were uncommon, and there were no cases of torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, or polymorphic or sustained ventricular tachycardia.
cards.watchOut: The 90-minute window is structurally unfair to amiodarone, which converts slowly over hours — AVRO proves speed, not ultimate conversion. Patients with atrial fibrillation beyond 48 hours were excluded, as in the whole vernakalant programme.
cards.source: Camm AJ et al. A randomized active-controlled study comparing the efficacy and safety of vernakalant to amiodarone in recent-onset atrial fibrillation. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2011. PMID: 21232669. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00668759, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ACT phase 3 (Roy 2008): against placebo, vernakalant converted short-duration atrial fibrillation in 51.7% versus 4.0% (median 11 minutes); longer-duration episodes responded far less
cards.summary: ACT phase 3 (Roy 2008): against placebo, vernakalant converted short-duration atrial fibrillation in 51.7% versus 4.0% (median 11 minutes); longer-duration episodes responded far less
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ACT programme)
cards.people: 336 patients randomised and treated, stratified by atrial fibrillation duration: short duration (3 hours to 7 days; n=220) and long duration (8 to 45 days; n=116). Vernakalant (3 mg/kg over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg 15 minutes later if atrial fibrillation persisted) versus placebo, randomised 2:1. Primary endpoint: conversion to sinus rhythm for at least 1 minute within 90 minutes, in the short-duration group.
cards.result: In short-duration atrial fibrillation, 75 of 145 vernakalant patients (51.7%) converted versus 3 of 75 placebo patients (4.0%) (P<0.001), with a median time to conversion of 11 minutes. Across both duration strata, 83 of 221 vernakalant patients (37.6%) converted versus 3 of 115 on placebo (2.6%) (P<0.001) — the lower overall rate reflects weak efficacy in 8-45-day episodes. Transient dysgeusia and sneezing were the most common side effects. Four vernakalant-related serious adverse events (hypotension in two, complete atrioventricular block, and cardiogenic shock) occurred in three patients.
cards.watchOut: The placebo comparison is from the registration era and the drug's benefit is concentrated in episodes under 7 days — the long-duration stratum is where the claim thins. Serious hypotension-type events, though rare, are the reason vernakalant is avoided in severe aortic stenosis and advanced heart failure.
cards.source: Roy D et al. Vernakalant hydrochloride for rapid conversion of atrial fibrillation: a phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Circulation. 2008. PMID: 18332267. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00468767, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pooled ACT report (Pratt 2010): across the ACT population, vernakalant converted atrial fibrillation in 39.8% versus 3.3% on placebo; one patient with severe aortic stenosis had hypotension and ventricular fibrillation and died
cards.summary: Pooled ACT report (Pratt 2010): across the ACT population, vernakalant converted atrial fibrillation in 39.8% versus 3.3% on placebo; one patient with severe aortic stenosis had hypotension and ventricular fibrillation and died
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial report (pooled ACT programme analysis, Pratt 2010)
cards.people: Patients with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter in the ACT programme, randomised 1:1 to vernakalant (n=138) or placebo (n=138), stratified by arrhythmia duration of 3 hours to 7 days versus 8 to 45 days; 265 patients received treatment, receiving the two-infusion vernakalant regimen (3 mg/kg, then 2 mg/kg) or placebo. Primary endpoint: conversion of short-duration atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm for at least 1 minute within 90 minutes.
cards.result: In short-duration atrial fibrillation, 44 of 86 vernakalant patients (51.2%) converted versus 3 of 84 on placebo (3.6%) (P<0.0001), with a median time to conversion of 8 minutes in responders. Across the whole atrial fibrillation population, conversion was 47 of 118 (39.8%) versus 4 of 121 (3.3%) (P<0.0001). Transient dysgeusia and sneezing were the most common adverse events. One vernakalant patient with severe aortic stenosis experienced hypotension and ventricular fibrillation and died.
cards.watchOut: This report overlaps the ACT programme of the Roy 2008 card — it is programme corroboration, not a wholly independent trial population, and it is carded for its safety signal as much as its efficacy: the aortic-stenosis death is the clearest harm marker in the vernakalant record and is reflected in the drug's contraindications.

cards.headline: Synthesis: vernakalant converts recent-onset atrial fibrillation faster and more often than procainamide, amiodarone (at 90 minutes) or placebo — LIKELY, within its licensed niche (Europe and Canada, not the US) and its duration limits
cards.summary: Synthesis: vernakalant converts recent-onset atrial fibrillation faster and more often than procainamide, amiodarone (at 90 minutes) or placebo — LIKELY, within its licensed niche (Europe and Canada, not the US) and its duration limits
cards.people: Synthesis of the four randomised reports carded on this shelf: RAFF4 (n=350), AVRO (n=254), the ACT phase 3 trial (n=336) and the pooled ACT report (n=265 treated) — noting the two ACT reports share a programme and partly a population.
cards.result: Every comparison points the same way: conversion of about 51-62% on vernakalant versus 48.3% on procainamide (RAFF4, with a speed advantage), 5.2% on amiodarone at 90 minutes (AVRO), and about 4% on placebo in short-duration episodes (ACT). Median conversion times of 8-22 minutes compare with 44.7 minutes for procainamide. Harms are usually transient (dysgeusia, sneezing, hypotension), with rare serious events concentrated in structurally vulnerable patients.
cards.watchOut: LIKELY covers rapid pharmacological conversion of recent-onset (under 7 days, best under 48 hours) atrial fibrillation in suitable ED patients. It does not cover atrial flutter, long-duration episodes, or settings where vernakalant is not marketed — including the United States.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 41218981, 21232669, 18332267, 21029824). No additional source.

shelves.title: Marstacimab (Hympavzi, Pfizer) prophylaxis in haemophilia A/B: treated bleeding fell sharply versus prior on-demand or prophylaxis care in the phase 3 BASIS trial — with and without inhibitors
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with severe haemophilia A or moderate-to-severe haemophilia B, with or without inhibitors, does once-weekly subcutaneous marstacimab (anti-TFPI), versus on-demand or prior routine prophylaxis, reduce treated bleeding?
shelves.balance: Marstacimab (Hympavzi, Pfizer) is a monoclonal antibody against tissue factor pathway inhibitor, given as a 300 mg loading dose then 150 mg subcutaneously once weekly. In BASIS, participants were observed for 6 months on their prior on-demand or routine prophylaxis care, then treated for 12 months; the headline comparisons are therefore within-patient (run-in vs on-treatment), a design labelled observational in structure on the face of each card — regression to the mean and period effects cannot be excluded the way a randomised parallel arm would exclude them. The effects are nonetheless large: in the non-inhibitor cohort, mean annualised bleeding rate (ABR) for treated bleeds fell from 39.86 to 3.20 against prior on-demand care, and from 7.90 to 5.09 against prior routine prophylaxis; in the inhibitor cohort (n=51 treated), from 19.78 to 1.39 against prior on-demand bypassing-agent care. No deaths or thromboembolic events occurred in either cohort — the class harm that matters most for rebalancing agents — but a single programme with 167 treated phase 3 participants cannot exclude uncommon thrombosis. One home per agent is this library's rule for the rebalancing class: concizumab (pack #6431), fitusiran (pack #6594) and efanesoctocog alfa (pack #6430) each have their own shelf; marstacimab's is this one, and there is no head-to-head trial between these agents.

cards.headline: BASIS non-inhibitor cohort (Matino 2025): ABR 39.86 → 3.20 vs prior on-demand care; 7.90 → 5.09 vs prior routine prophylaxis
cards.summary: BASIS non-inhibitor cohort (Matino 2025): ABR 39.86 → 3.20 vs prior on-demand care; 7.90 → 5.09 vs prior routine prophylaxis
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label, single-arm trial with observational run-in comparator (BASIS), Blood 2025
cards.people: Males aged 12–74 with severe haemophilia A (FVIII <1%) or moderately severe to severe haemophilia B (FIX ≤2%) without inhibitors. Of 128 enrolled in the 6-month observational phase, 116 received once-weekly subcutaneous marstacimab 150 mg in the 12-month active treatment phase (on-demand group n=33; routine-prophylaxis group n=83). Primary endpoints: ABR for treated bleeds vs the observational phase, and safety.
cards.result: On-demand group: mean ABR fell from 39.86 (95% CI 33.05–48.07) to 3.20 (2.10–4.88); estimated ABR ratio 0.080 (0.057–0.113), P<.0001. Routine-prophylaxis group: mean ABR fell from 7.90 (5.14–10.66) to 5.09 (3.40–6.78); estimated difference −2.81 (−5.42 to −0.20), P=.0349, meeting noninferiority and superiority. No deaths or thromboembolic events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with no randomised parallel control: the comparator is each patient's own preceding 6 months. Bleeding ascertainment and behaviour can change on entering a treatment phase, so the ABR ratios are within-patient estimates, not randomised effects.
cards.source: Matino D et al. Marstacimab prophylaxis in hemophilia A/B without inhibitors: results from the phase 3 BASIS trial. Blood. 2025. PMID 40608864 · NCT03938792. cards.headline: BASIS inhibitor cohort (Matino 2026): ABR 19.78 → 1.39 vs prior on-demand bypassing-agent care (ratio 0.07)
cards.summary: BASIS inhibitor cohort (Matino 2026): ABR 19.78 → 1.39 vs prior on-demand bypassing-agent care (ratio 0.07)
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label, single-arm trial with observational run-in comparator (BASIS inhibitor cohort), Blood 2026
cards.people: Males aged 12 to <75 with severe haemophilia A or moderately severe to severe haemophilia B WITH inhibitors, receiving bypassing agents (on-demand or routine prophylaxis) during a 6-month observational phase. Of 60 in the observational phase, 51 entered the active treatment phase on once-weekly subcutaneous marstacimab. On-demand subgroup n=48.
cards.result: On-demand group: mean estimated ABR fell from 19.78 (95% CI 16.12–24.27) to 1.39 (0.85–2.29); ABR ratio 0.07 (0.042–0.118), P<.0001 — consistent by haemophilia type (ratio 0.05 in haemophilia A, n=40; 0.13 in haemophilia B, n=8). Health-related quality of life improved. Adverse events were common but mostly mild; one treatment-related grade 3 skin rash led to discontinuation; antidrug antibodies in 19.6% with no apparent effect on efficacy or safety; no thromboembolic events.
cards.watchOut: A second cohort report of the same single trial, explicitly labelled as such — not an independent replication. The haemophilia B inhibitor subgroup is 8 patients; cohort-level N (51 treated) is small, as the balance states.
cards.source: Matino D et al. Efficacy and safety of marstacimab prophylaxis in hemophilia A/B with inhibitors: results from the phase 3 BASIS trial. Blood. 2026. PMID 41351884 · NCT03938792 (same BASIS trial as PMID 40608864, inhibitor cohort report). cards.headline: Phase 1b/2 (Mahlangu 2023): 26 participants, 3 months — ABR significantly reduced vs pretreatment and an external on-demand control
cards.summary: Phase 1b/2 (Mahlangu 2023): 26 participants, 3 months — ABR significantly reduced vs pretreatment and an external on-demand control
cards.type: Phase 1b/2 dose-escalation study, British Journal of Haematology 2023
cards.people: 26 treated participants with haemophilia A or B, with or without inhibitors (haemophilia A without inhibitor 16; haemophilia A with inhibitor 7; haemophilia B 3), in four escalating weekly-dose cohorts (300 mg; 300 mg loading then 150 mg; 450 mg; 300 mg for the inhibitor cohort), treated for 3 months.
cards.result: 24 of 26 completed. Treatment-emergent adverse events in 80.8%. ABR during treatment was significantly reduced versus an external on-demand control group and versus pretreatment ABR (both p<0.0001), with reductions across all dose cohorts; pharmacodynamic biomarker changes indicated TFPI targeting.
cards.watchOut: Small, short, and compared partly against an external control — a dose-finding and proof-of-mechanism study that supports, and cannot substitute for, the phase 3 programme.
cards.source: Mahlangu JN et al. A phase 1b/2 clinical study of marstacimab, targeting human tissue factor pathway inhibitor, in haemophilia. Br J Haematol. 2023. PMID 35999026 · NCT02974855. cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme, large within-patient ABR falls, no thrombosis seen — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme, large within-patient ABR falls, no thrombosis seen — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BASIS non-inhibitor (116 treated) and inhibitor (51 treated) cohort reports of one trial, plus a 26-participant phase 1b/2 study.
cards.result: Treated bleeding fell by roughly 90% or more against prior on-demand care and modestly against prior routine prophylaxis, in both inhibitor and non-inhibitor populations, with no thromboembolic events reported. cards.watchOut: No randomised parallel-group comparison and no head-to-head trial against concizumab, fitusiran or emicizumab exists in the carded record; cross-agent ABR comparisons across programmes are not valid.

shelves.title: Denecimig (Mim8; Frehemgo, Novo Nordisk) prophylaxis in haemophilia A: treated bleeding cut by 96–99% relative versus on-demand care in FRONTIER2 — no head-to-head trial against emicizumab
shelves.question: In adults and adolescents ≥12 years with haemophilia A, with or without inhibitors, does denecimig (FVIIIa-mimetic bispecific antibody) once weekly or once monthly, versus on-demand treatment or prior factor prophylaxis, reduce treated bleeding?
shelves.balance: Denecimig (Mim8; Frehemgo, Novo Nordisk) is a bispecific antibody that mimics activated factor VIII, given subcutaneously once weekly or once monthly at weight-tiered doses. In FRONTIER2, against on-demand treatment the annualised treated-bleed rate fell by 96.4% relative (weekly) and 98.7% relative (monthly) — absolute rates 0.57 and 0.20 bleeds/year against 15.76 on on-demand care. Against patients' own prior factor prophylaxis (within-patient run-in comparison), the relative decreases were 54.0% and 42.8% (absolute 2.25 vs 4.90 and 1.78 vs 3.12 bleeds/year). Injection-site reactions occurred in 2.6% of injections; no thromboembolic events and no neutralising antibodies were reported in the carded reports. The neighbouring home is emicizumab (live shelf #1414, the HAVEN programme) — cross-pointed here in prose; its PMIDs are not carded on this shelf, and there is NO head-to-head trial of denecimig against emicizumab, so no comparative claim between the two mimetics can be made. FRONTIER2 was open-label. Paediatric (FRONTIER3) and every-2-week extension (FRONTIER4) reports support the programme's safety picture but are single-arm.

cards.headline: FRONTIER2 (Mancuso 2026): treated-bleed rate 0.57 (weekly) and 0.20 (monthly) vs 15.76 bleeds/year on on-demand care — 96.4% and 98.7% relative reductions
cards.summary: FRONTIER2 (Mancuso 2026): treated-bleed rate 0.57 (weekly) and 0.20 (monthly) vs 15.76 bleeds/year on on-demand care — 96.4% and 98.7% relative reductions
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (FRONTIER2), New England Journal of Medicine 2026
cards.people: 254 patients aged ≥12 years with haemophilia A with or without FVIII inhibitors, randomised in a phase 3 trial. Pretrial on-demand cohort (58): 17 continued on-demand (group 1), 21 denecimig weekly (2a), 20 monthly (2b). Pretrial prophylaxis cohort (196): 98 weekly (group 3), 98 monthly (group 4), compared within-patient against clotting-factor prophylaxis during run-in. Denecimig dose tiered by body weight, fixed 0.8 mL injection volume.
cards.result: Vs on-demand: estimated mean annualised treated-bleed rate 0.57 (95% CI 0.25–1.30) weekly and 0.20 (0.06–0.71) monthly vs 15.76 (10.70–23.20) — relative decreases 96.4% and 98.7%, P<0.001 for both (relative measures; absolute rates beside them). Vs prior prophylaxis (within-patient): 2.25 vs 4.90 (54.0% relative decrease; P=0.006) weekly and 1.78 vs 3.12 (42.8% relative decrease; P=0.006) monthly. Injection-site reactions in 103 of 4005 injections (2.6%); no thromboembolic events and no clinical evidence of neutralising anti-denecimig antibodies.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design. The on-demand comparison is randomised; the prophylaxis comparison is within-patient against a run-in period, not a randomised parallel arm. Relative reductions are labelled relative, with absolute rates on the face.
cards.source: Mancuso ME et al. Mim8 Bispecific Antibody Prophylaxis in Hemophilia A with or without Inhibitors. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID 42054679 · NCT05053139. cards.headline: FRONTIER3 (Kenet 2026): 70 children aged 1–11 — mean treated-bleed ABR 0.25–0.53 across dosing periods; 74–88% had zero treated bleeds
cards.summary: FRONTIER3 (Kenet 2026): 70 children aged 1–11 — mean treated-bleed ABR 0.25–0.53 across dosing periods; 74–88% had zero treated bleeds
cards.type: Phase 3 single-arm study (FRONTIER3), Research and Practice in Thrombosis and Haemostasis 2026
cards.people: 70 children aged 1–11 years with haemophilia A with or without FVIII inhibitors, in the phase 3 FRONTIER3 study: subcutaneous denecimig once weekly for 26 weeks (Part 1), then caregivers chose weekly (38) or monthly (32) dosing for a further 26 weeks (Part 2). Primary endpoint: treatment-emergent adverse events.
cards.result: All 70 completed both parts. All treatment-emergent adverse events were mild/moderate and none led to discontinuation; no thromboembolic events or clinical evidence of neutralising antibodies; injection-site reactions ~1% of injections. Estimated mean ABR for treated bleeds: 0.53 (Part 1 weekly), 0.42 (Part 2 weekly), 0.25 (Part 2 monthly); no bleeds in inhibitor-positive children; all 10 baseline target joints resolved; 98% of caregivers preferred denecimig to prior therapy.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: the low bleed rates are descriptive, and caregiver preference (98%) is an unblinded, single-arm measure. It extends the programme to children; it does not add comparative efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Kenet G et al. Denecimig (Mim8) prophylaxis in children with hemophilia A with or without factor VIII inhibitors. Res Pract Thromb Haemost. 2026. PMID 42835127 · NCT05306418. cards.headline: FRONTIER4 (Matsushita 2026): every-2-week dosing in 37 patients — mean ABR 0.38; 83.8% had zero treated bleeds over 26 weeks
cards.summary: FRONTIER4 (Matsushita 2026): every-2-week dosing in 37 patients — mean ABR 0.38; 83.8% had zero treated bleeds over 26 weeks
cards.type: Open-label extension interim analysis (FRONTIER4), Blood Advances 2026
cards.people: 37 patients aged ≥12 years with haemophilia A with or without inhibitors who had completed the denecimig phase 2 study and at least 12 weeks of its extension, entering arm 1 of the FRONTIER4 open-label extension on denecimig once every 2 weeks (weight-tiered) for 26 weeks; mean prior denecimig exposure 1.73 years.
cards.result: 60 treatment-emergent adverse events in 20 patients, 98.3% mild/moderate, none fatal and none leading to permanent discontinuation; 2 patients reported 14 injection-site reactions. Estimated mean annualised bleeding rate 0.38 bleeds per patient-year; 83.8% experienced zero treated bleeds. Denecimig plasma concentrations were stable through week 26.
cards.watchOut: An extension population of prior trial participants who had already tolerated denecimig for a mean 1.73 years — survivor-selected, single-arm, and interim. It informs dosing-interval feasibility, not comparative efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, a randomised win against on-demand care, within-patient win against prior prophylaxis — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, a randomised win against on-demand care, within-patient win against prior prophylaxis — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FRONTIER2 (254 randomised, ≥12 years), FRONTIER3 (70 children, single-arm), FRONTIER4 Q2W arm (37, extension).
cards.result: Denecimig reduced treated bleeding versus on-demand care (randomised) and versus prior factor prophylaxis (within-patient), with a 2.6%-of-injections injection-site reaction rate and no thromboembolic events in the carded reports. A single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit). No head-to-head trial against emicizumab (live #1414) exists.

shelves.title: Efgartigimod in primary immune thrombocytopenia: the intravenous form worked in ADVANCE IV (22% vs 5% sustained response); the subcutaneous form failed in ADVANCE SC (13.7% vs 16.2%) — a split record by formulation
shelves.question: In adults with chronic primary immune thrombocytopenia, does efgartigimod, versus placebo, produce a sustained platelet response?
shelves.balance: The record splits by formulation, and this shelf keeps the two apart. Intravenous efgartigimod (10 mg/kg) in ADVANCE IV produced a sustained platelet response in 22% of chronic-ITP patients vs 5% on placebo (adjusted difference 16 percentage points) — a real but modest absolute yield in a heavily pretreated population (mean 10.6 years since diagnosis; 67% had received at least three prior ITP therapies). The subcutaneous PH20 formulation in ADVANCE SC did not beat placebo at all (13.7% vs 16.2%, p=0.51), with the report noting platelet rises higher than expected on placebo and lower than expected on efgartigimod. Regulatory status therefore differs by formulation, and the IV result must not be used to carry the SC product. An earlier phase 2 trial of the IV form (n=38) pointed the same way as ADVANCE IV. Efgartigimod's other homes in this library are different diseases and questions — generalised myasthenia gravis (live #1116, ADAPT) and CIDP (pack #6560, ADHERE); their PMIDs are not carded here and lend this shelf no support. Other ITP homes: fostamatinib (pack #1800) and rilzabrutinib (pack #4873).

cards.headline: ADVANCE IV (Broome 2023): intravenous efgartigimod — sustained platelet response 22% vs 5% on placebo in chronic ITP
cards.summary: ADVANCE IV (Broome 2023): intravenous efgartigimod — sustained platelet response 22% vs 5% on placebo in chronic ITP
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ADVANCE IV), Lancet Haematology 2023
cards.people: 131 adults (≥18 years) with chronic or persistent primary ITP, average platelet count <30 × 10⁹/L, who had responded to at least one previous ITP therapy, at 71 sites in Asia, Europe and North America; randomised 2:1 to intravenous efgartigimod 10 mg/kg (86) or placebo (45) over 24 weeks, with dosing frequency adjustable after week 4. Primary endpoint (in the chronic population, 78 efgartigimod / 40 placebo): sustained platelet response — platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L for at least 4 of the last 6 weeks.
cards.result: Sustained response in 22% (17/78) on efgartigimod vs 5% (2/40) on placebo (p=0.032; adjusted difference 16% [95% CI 2.6–26.4]). Median weeks of disease control 2.0 vs 0.0 (p=0.0009). Most adverse events were mild to moderate; headache 16% vs 13%, haematuria 16% vs 16%, petechiae 15% vs 27%.
cards.watchOut: The absolute yield is modest — about 1 in 5 chronic patients achieved the sustained response — in a population with long-standing, multiply pretreated disease. This result is for the intravenous formulation only.
cards.source: Broome CM et al. Lancet Haematol. 2023. PMID 37778358 · NCT04188379. cards.headline: ADVANCE SC (Cooper 2026): subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 — primary endpoint NOT met, 13.7% vs 16.2% on placebo (p=0.51)
cards.summary: ADVANCE SC (Cooper 2026): subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 — primary endpoint NOT met, 13.7% vs 16.2% on placebo (p=0.51)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ADVANCE SC), American Journal of Hematology 2026
cards.people: 207 adults with primary ITP and platelet counts <30 × 10⁹/L who had received more than one prior ITP therapy, randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg (137) or placebo (70) over 24 weeks; 92.8% had chronic ITP and 74.9% had received at least three previous therapies; median time since diagnosis 7.0 years. Primary endpoint: platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L for at least four of the six visits during weeks 19–24 (124 efgartigimod / 68 placebo in the primary analysis).
cards.result: Primary endpoint achieved by 13.7% (17/124) on efgartigimod PH20 SC vs 16.2% (11/68) on placebo (p=0.51; adjusted difference −3.5% [95% CI −14.7 to 7.0]). Superiority was not demonstrated for the primary or secondary endpoints. The formulation was well tolerated, with most adverse events mild to moderate and comparable between groups; the authors note platelet increases were higher than expected with placebo and lower than expected with efgartigimod.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial of a different formulation and dose route — it does not erase ADVANCE IV, and ADVANCE IV does not rescue it. Any statement about 'efgartigimod in ITP' that does not name the formulation is incomplete.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Newland 2020): intravenous efgartigimod — 46% vs 25% reached platelet counts ≥50 × 10⁹/L on at least two occasions
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Newland 2020): intravenous efgartigimod — 46% vs 25% reached platelet counts ≥50 × 10⁹/L on at least two occasions
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, American Journal of Hematology 2020
cards.people: 38 adults with primary ITP, predominantly refractory to previous lines of therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to four weekly intravenous infusions of placebo (12), efgartigimod 5 mg/kg (13) or efgartigimod 10 mg/kg (13).
cards.result: Efgartigimod reduced total IgG by up to 63.7% (mean change from baseline). Platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L on at least two occasions in 46% on efgartigimod vs 25% on placebo, and ≥50 × 10⁹/L for at least 10 cumulative days in 38% vs 0%; a reduced proportion of efgartigimod patients had bleeding. Treatment was well tolerated with a favourable safety profile.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=38), short (four infusions) proof-of-concept trial of the IV form — it supports the intravenous programme only and says nothing about the subcutaneous formulation that later failed at phase 3.

shelves.title: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, Takeda) in congenital TTP: no acute events on prophylaxis in the phase 3 crossover trial (n=48 — the recruitable population of an ultra-rare disease), with activity restored to ~101% of normal
shelves.question: In patients with congenital thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, does recombinant ADAMTS13 prophylaxis, versus standard (plasma-based) therapy, prevent acute TTP events and maintain ADAMTS13 activity?
shelves.balance: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, Takeda) replaces the missing enzyme in congenital TTP. The phase 3 trial was an open-label crossover — every patient received both recombinant ADAMTS13 (40 IU/kg IV) and standard plasma-based therapy in randomised order — because a placebo arm was not ethical in this disease; that design is stated, not apologised for. No acute TTP event occurred during recombinant prophylaxis, versus one event (annualised rate 0.05) on standard therapy, and mean maximum ADAMTS13 activity was 101% of normal vs 19%. Thrombocytopenia manifestations were less frequent on recombinant therapy (annualised rate 0.74 vs 1.73), drug-related adverse events were less frequent (9% vs 48%), and no patient interrupted recombinant treatment for adverse events (vs 8 on standard therapy); no neutralising antibodies developed. The N of 48 is small because congenital TTP is ultra-rare — it is close to the recruitable trial population, and the stamp line carries it for that reason. Supporting evidence is a 15-patient first-in-human pharmacokinetic study and a 14-patient Japanese real-world switch series (observational, labelled as such), which included 5 patients with end-stage renal disease whom the phase 3 trial excluded. This shelf is about congenital TTP only; caplacizumab in acquired (immune) TTP is a different disease and question, homed at live #846.

cards.headline: Phase 3 crossover (Scully 2024): zero acute TTP events on recombinant ADAMTS13 prophylaxis vs one on standard therapy; maximum activity 101% vs 19% of normal
cards.summary: Phase 3 crossover (Scully 2024): zero acute TTP events on recombinant ADAMTS13 prophylaxis vs one on standard therapy; maximum activity 101% vs 19% of normal
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label, randomised crossover trial, New England Journal of Medicine 2024
cards.people: 48 patients with congenital TTP randomised 1:1 to two 6-month prophylaxis periods — recombinant ADAMTS13 40 IU/kg intravenously or standard therapy (plasma-derived products) — followed by the alternate treatment, then recombinant ADAMTS13 for all for a further 6 months; 32 completed the trial. Primary outcome: acute TTP events. This was an interim analysis triggered by at least 30 patients completing.
cards.result: No acute TTP event during recombinant prophylaxis; one patient had an acute event during standard-therapy prophylaxis (mean annualised event rate 0.05). Thrombocytopenia, the most frequent TTP manifestation, had an annualised rate of 0.74 on recombinant vs 1.73 on standard therapy. Adverse events in 71% vs 84%; drug-related adverse events in 9% vs 48%; interruption/discontinuation for adverse events in 0 vs 8 patients. Mean maximum ADAMTS13 activity 101% vs 19%. No neutralising antibodies.
cards.watchOut: Event counts are tiny by necessity — zero vs one acute event cannot carry a precise effect estimate; the persuasive findings are the activity restoration (101% vs 19%) and the manifestation and tolerability pattern. Open-label, interim analysis, ultra-rare disease.
cards.source: Scully M et al. Recombinant ADAMTS13 in Congenital Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID 38692292 · NCT03393975. cards.headline: Phase 1 first-in-human (Scully 2017): single-dose recombinant ADAMTS13 in 15 patients — well tolerated, no anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies, dose-related activity
cards.summary: Phase 1 first-in-human (Scully 2017): single-dose recombinant ADAMTS13 in 15 patients — well tolerated, no anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies, dose-related activity
cards.people: 15 adolescents and adults with severe congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (plasma activity <6%), in a prospective multicentre dose-escalation study of single-dose recombinant ADAMTS13 (BAX 930) at 5, 20 or 40 U/kg.
cards.result: Well tolerated; no serious adverse events and no anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies. Approximate dose proportionality for maximum concentration and exposure; ADAMTS13 antigen and activity rose dose-dependently, reaching maximum within 1 hour, with dose-dependent von Willebrand factor cleavage and reduced multimer size — pharmacodynamic activity in patients.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic/safety study (N = 15, printed on the face) with single doses — it establishes that the enzyme can be delivered and is active, not that prophylaxis prevents events.

cards.headline: Japanese real-world switch (Sakai 2025, observational): 14 patients switched from plasma to recombinant ADAMTS13 — peak activity 68.4% vs 15.9% with plasma, no allergic reactions
cards.summary: Japanese real-world switch (Sakai 2025, observational): 14 patients switched from plasma to recombinant ADAMTS13 — peak activity 68.4% vs 15.9% with plasma, no allergic reactions
cards.people: 14 Japanese patients with congenital TTP who switched from fresh frozen plasma to recombinant ADAMTS13 in routine care, including 5 patients with end-stage renal disease who had been excluded from the phase 3 trial. Observational real-world comparison of the two products within these patients.
cards.result: Median peak ADAMTS13 activity 15 minutes after administration was 68.4% with recombinant ADAMTS13 vs 15.9% with plasma (P<.001); activity at 1 week was 11.6% vs 5.1% (P<.001). No allergic reactions after recombinant administration were reported, and patients valued the convenience of a single infusion.
cards.watchOut: Observational, 14 patients, no randomised comparison and no clinical-event endpoint — it corroborates the pharmacology and tolerability in a broader population (including dialysis patients), nothing more. Labelled observational; observational evidence caps at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Lusutrombopag for thrombocytopenia of chronic liver disease before procedures: two phase 3 trials — 79.2% vs 12.5% (L-PLUS 1) and 64.8% vs 29.0% (L-PLUS 2) avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion
shelves.question: In adults with chronic liver disease and severe thrombocytopenia scheduled for an invasive procedure, does lusutrombopag, versus placebo, avoid the need for platelet transfusion?
shelves.balance: Lusutrombopag is an oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonist given as 3 mg daily for up to 7 days before a planned invasive procedure. Both phase 3 trials met their primary endpoints: in L-PLUS 1 (Japan), 79.2% vs 12.5% avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion; in L-PLUS 2 (global), 64.8% vs 29.0% met the composite of avoiding pre-procedure transfusion and rescue therapy for bleeding (difference 36.7 percentage points [95% CI 24.9–48.5]). An integrated analysis of the two trials (a labelled pooled report of the same trials, not independent evidence) found the same pattern in patients with and without hepatocellular carcinoma (68.0% vs 8.9% and 77.0% vs 21.6%). Platelet counts stayed ≥50 × 10⁹/L for a median 19.2 days in L-PLUS 2. Thrombotic events were uncommon and similar to placebo in the carded reports (one per group in L-PLUS 1), but portal-vein thrombosis is the class harm to watch with thrombopoietin agonists in liver disease. The neighbouring home is avatrombopag in the same indication (packs #2819/#6129) — a distinct drug and programme, cross-pointed here; the two are not merged and there is no carded head-to-head comparison. Per-trial results are printed from the primary papers, not from the pooled NICE figure (transfusion-avoidance relative risk 3.42, a relative measure) cited in the slate.

cards.headline: L-PLUS 1 (Hidaka 2019): 79.2% vs 12.5% avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion
cards.summary: L-PLUS 1 (Hidaka 2019): 79.2% vs 12.5% avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (L-PLUS 1), Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2019
cards.people: 96 patients with chronic liver disease and thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50,000/µL) undergoing invasive procedures at 81 centres in Japan, randomised 1:1 to lusutrombopag 3 mg once daily or placebo for up to 7 days. Primary endpoint: proportion not requiring platelet transfusion before the invasive procedure.
cards.result: No pre-procedure transfusion required in 79.2% (38/48) on lusutrombopag vs 12.5% (6/48) on placebo (P<.0001). Protocol-defined response (platelet count ≥50,000/µL with a rise ≥20,000/µL) in 77.1% vs 6.3% (P<.0001). In the lusutrombopag group without transfusion, counts reached ≥50,000/µL by a median of 5 days and stayed at or above that level for an adjusted mean of 21.09 days. Adverse drug reactions 8.3% vs 2.1%; one thrombotic event in each group, neither with an excessive platelet rise.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (Japan) trial with a transfusion-avoidance endpoint — it shows procedures could proceed without transfusion, not that bleeding or survival improved.

cards.headline: L-PLUS 2 (Peck-Radosavljevic 2019): 64.8% vs 29.0% avoided transfusion and rescue therapy (difference 36.7 percentage points)
cards.summary: L-PLUS 2 (Peck-Radosavljevic 2019): 64.8% vs 29.0% avoided transfusion and rescue therapy (difference 36.7 percentage points)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (L-PLUS 2), Hepatology 2019
cards.people: 215 adults with chronic liver disease and baseline platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L undergoing invasive procedures, in a global phase 3 trial, randomised to lusutrombopag 3 mg once daily or placebo for ≤7 days, with the procedure scheduled 2–7 days after the last dose. Primary endpoint: avoidance of preprocedure platelet transfusion and of rescue therapy for bleeding.
cards.result: Primary endpoint met by 64.8% (70/108) on lusutrombopag vs 29.0% (31/107) on placebo (P<0.0001; difference 36.7 percentage points [95% CI 24.9–48.5]). Median duration of platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L was 19.2 days with lusutrombopag (without transfusion) vs 0.0 days with placebo (with transfusion) (P=0.0001). Adverse events were mostly mild or moderate and similar between groups (47.7% vs 48.6%).
cards.watchOut: The registry ID for L-PLUS 2 (NCT02389621) appears in companion reports of this programme rather than in this record, so it is not printed in this card's source line. Endpoint remains transfusion avoidance; Child-Pugh C patients were scarcely represented in the pivotal trials.

cards.headline: Integrated analysis of L-PLUS 1 & 2 (Alkhouri 2020) — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials: benefit held with and without hepatocellular carcinoma
cards.summary: Integrated analysis of L-PLUS 1 & 2 (Alkhouri 2020) — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials: benefit held with and without hepatocellular carcinoma
cards.type: Integrated (pooled) analysis of the L-PLUS 1 and L-PLUS 2 phase 3 trials, Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2020
cards.people: Per-protocol population of 270 patients pooled from L-PLUS 1 (Japan) and L-PLUS 2 (global), including 95 with hepatocellular carcinoma; all had Child-Pugh class A or B disease, platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L, and a procedure scheduled in 9–14 days; lusutrombopag 3 mg or placebo daily for ≤7 days.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (no transfusion before the procedure and no rescue therapy for bleeding within 7 days after) achieved by 68.0% vs 8.9% (P<.0001) in patients with HCC and 77.0% vs 21.6% (P<.0001) in patients without HCC. Lusutrombopag reduced transfusions, raised platelet counts for about 3 weeks, and reduced bleeding events, with thrombosis risk similar to placebo in this analysis.
cards.watchOut: This is a pooled re-analysis of the two trials carded above — explicitly labelled, and it adds subgroup reassurance (HCC vs no HCC), not independent replication. The LIKELY stamp rests on the two trials themselves.

shelves.title: Danazol in telomere diseases: one small single-arm trial showed telomere elongation and blood-count responses — but an independent cohort found no difference in attrition, and a second trial found it poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis
shelves.question: In patients with telomere maintenance/repair defects (telomere biology disorders), does danazol 800 mg/day slow telomere attrition and improve blood counts?
shelves.balance: Danazol 800 mg/day is a high, prolonged androgen dose, and the evidence tier here is the best available for an ultra-rare disease — which is not the same as proof. The anchor is Townsley 2016: a prospective single-arm phase 1–2 study, halted early because the primary endpoint was met in every evaluable patient; but only 12 of 27 enrolled patients were evaluable for that endpoint (intention-to-treat 44%), and there was no control group, so natural history and selection are unmeasured. Its long-term follow-up report (a second, explicitly labelled report of the same trial) found responses were usually lost a median 1.6 years after stopping, that lower-dose re-treatment re-induced responses in 6 of 7 evaluable patients, and no signal that danazol expanded premalignant clones. Against this, an independent NIH-cohort observational study found telomere attrition rates statistically indistinguishable between androgen-treated and untreated dyskeratosis congenita patients (−62 vs −76 base pairs/year, p=.71; adjusted p=.24) — a direct tension the stamp names as SPLIT. ANDROTELO, a second single-arm phase 2 trial at the same daily dose in telomere-related-gene carriers, found danazol poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis (only 10 of 24 completed 12 months; 9 stopped for side effects), though all 5 marrow-failure patients completed treatment with at least a partial response. Androgen class effects at this dose need full weight: grade ≤2 liver-enzyme elevation in 41% and muscle cramps in 33% in Townsley, plus the class's virilising, hepatic and lipid effects with prolonged use.

cards.headline: Townsley 2016 (phase 1–2, single-arm): primary attrition endpoint met by all 12 evaluable patients; haematologic response in 19 of 24 (79%) at 3 months
cards.summary: Townsley 2016 (phase 1–2, single-arm): primary attrition endpoint met by all 12 evaluable patients; haematologic response in 19 of 24 (79%) at 3 months
cards.type: Phase 1–2 prospective single-arm study, New England Journal of Medicine 2016
cards.people: 27 patients enrolled with telomere diseases (defects in telomere maintenance/repair causing marrow failure, liver cirrhosis and pulmonary fibrosis), treated with oral danazol 800 mg/day for 24 months. Primary efficacy endpoint: a 20% reduction in the annual rate of telomere attrition at 24 months. The trial was halted early after 27 enrolments because the endpoint was met in every evaluable patient.
cards.result: 12 of 12 evaluable patients met the primary endpoint (intention-to-treat 12/27, 44% [95% CI 26–64]). Unexpectedly, 11 of 12 evaluable patients (92%) gained telomere length at 24 months (mean increase 386 bp [95% CI 178–593]); similar increases at 6 months (16/21; mean 175 bp) and 12 months (16/18; mean 360 bp). Haematologic responses in 19/24 (79%) evaluable at 3 months and 10/12 (83%) at 24 months. Grade ≤2 liver-enzyme elevation in 41% and muscle cramps in 33%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, no comparator, and the headline 'all evaluable patients' rests on 12 of 27 enrolled — the intention-to-treat figure (44%) is on this card's face for that reason. Early stopping for efficacy in a small single-arm study inflates apparent effects.
cards.source: Townsley DM et al. Danazol Treatment for Telomere Diseases. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID 27192671 · NCT01441037. cards.headline: Long-term follow-up (Lee 2026) — second, explicitly labelled report of the same Townsley trial: responses lost a median 1.6 years after stopping; median overall survival 7.7 years
cards.summary: Long-term follow-up (Lee 2026) — second, explicitly labelled report of the same Townsley trial: responses lost a median 1.6 years after stopping; median overall survival 7.7 years
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the phase 1–2 trial, Blood Advances 2026
cards.people: Long-term follow-up of the same NCT01441037 cohort (26 evaluable patients; phenotypes included marrow failure 24, pulmonary fibrosis 13, liver fibrosis 6), treated with danazol 800 mg daily for 2 years or until study closure; median follow-up 3.3 years (range 0.3–12.6).
cards.result: After danazol discontinuation, median time to loss of haematologic response was 1.6 years in 12 evaluable patients. Median event-free survival 5.7 years; median overall survival 7.7 years, with 62% (16 patients) known to have died at last follow-up (infection the most common known cause). Eight patients restarted danazol post-trial at a median dose of 200 mg, with a second haematologic response in 86% (6/7 evaluable). No marked expansion of pre-existing clones or acquisition of new ones after therapy; telomere length by flow-FISH was stable over time, with no significant elongation in the limited serial samples.
cards.watchOut: A second report of one trial, not independent evidence. Its flow-FISH telomere measurements (stable, no significant elongation) sit in tension with the original qPCR-based elongation claim — a measurement-method caveat that belongs with any quotation of the 2016 result.
cards.source: Lee NC et al. Danazol treatment for telomere biology disorders: long-term results of a phase 1/2 study. Blood Adv. 2026. PMID 41115243 · NCT01441037 (same trial as PMID 27192671). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: ANDROTELO (Sicre de Fontbrune 2026): danazol 400 mg twice daily in telomere-related-gene carriers — poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis; all 5 marrow-failure patients responded at least partially
cards.summary: ANDROTELO (Sicre de Fontbrune 2026): danazol 400 mg twice daily in telomere-related-gene carriers — poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis; all 5 marrow-failure patients responded at least partially
cards.type: Phase 2 prospective open-label single-arm trial (ANDROTELO), ERJ Open Research 2026
cards.people: 30 carriers of pathogenic/likely pathogenic telomere-related-gene variants: 25 with pulmonary fibrosis (PF) and 5 with bone-marrow failure (BMF), in a multicentre prospective open-label single-arm phase 2 trial of danazol 400 mg twice daily for 12 months. One PF patient withdrew consent.
cards.result: Only 10 of 24 PF patients (42%) completed the 12-month treatment; discontinuations were for side effects (9), death (3), lung transplantation (1) and disease progression (1). Of 14 PF patients evaluated at month 12, 8 showed a relative FVC decline of <5%; median relative decrease in FVC was −10% and in DLCO −10.3%. All 5 BMF patients completed treatment and exhibited at least a partial response. The authors conclude danazol was poorly tolerated in TRG-related PF, precluding efficacy assessment in that group.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, and the pulmonary-fibrosis majority could not stay on the drug — tolerability at 800 mg/day is itself a finding. The marrow-failure subgroup is 5 patients, below the evidence floor on its own; it is reported here only as part of the whole trial.
cards.source: Sicre de Fontbrune F et al. Efficacy and safety of danazol for pulmonary fibrosis or bone-marrow failure associated with telomere-related gene mutation (ANDROTELO). ERJ Open Res. 2026. cards.headline: Khincha 2018 (observational): telomere attrition did NOT differ between androgen-treated and untreated dyskeratosis congenita patients (−62 vs −76 bp/year; p=.71)
cards.summary: Khincha 2018 (observational): telomere attrition did NOT differ between androgen-treated and untreated dyskeratosis congenita patients (−62 vs −76 bp/year; p=.71)
cards.type: Observational longitudinal cohort comparison, Blood Advances 2018
cards.people: 26 patients with dyskeratosis congenita in longitudinal inherited-marrow-failure cohort studies: 10 androgen-treated (danazol among the androgens used) and 16 untreated. Telomere length in six leukocyte subsets measured by flow-FISH over time; generalised estimating equations compared attrition rates, adjusted for age at sample collection.
cards.result: Annual median total-lymphocyte telomere attrition was −62 base pairs/year in androgen-treated patients vs −76 bp/year in untreated patients (unadjusted P=.71); the adjusted longitudinal model likewise found no statistically significant difference (P=.24), with similar results in each leukocyte subset. The authors counsel caution in recommending androgen therapy for non-marrow-failure manifestations until mechanisms are better understood.
cards.watchOut: Observational and small (10 treated), with treatment not randomised and androgens pooled — it cannot refute the trial, but it is the only comparative attrition data carded, and it points the other way. Labelled observational; observational evidence caps at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Khincha PP et al. Similar telomere attrition rates in androgen-treated and untreated patients with dyskeratosis congenita. Blood Adv. 2018. PMID 29853525. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — a positive single-arm trial, a null observational comparison, and a tolerability failure in lung disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — a positive single-arm trial, a null observational comparison, and a tolerability failure in lung disease
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Townsley phase 1–2 (27 enrolled) and its long-term report, ANDROTELO (30), Khincha observational cohort (26).
cards.result: Haematologic responses to danazol in telomere diseases are consistent across the single-arm trials (79% at 3 months in Townsley; at least partial responses in all 5 ANDROTELO marrow-failure patients), but the telomere-attrition claim — the trials' mechanistic headline — is contradicted by the only comparative study, and tolerability at 800 mg/day failed in pulmonary fibrosis. The stamp is SPLIT, naming the split; no randomised trial exists or is likely in this ultra-rare population.

shelves.title: The diving response: face immersion plus apnoea cuts heart rate by a third in trained divers and slows oxygen use — the integrated cardiovascular picture
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the integrated diving response — how much do heart rate and cardiac output fall and peripheral vascular resistance rise with face immersion in cold water plus apnoea, how is blood redistributed to heart and brain, and how do trained divers differ from untrained people?
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, nervous regulation of the circulation; Boron & Boulpaep): the diving response is a trigeminally triggered, vagally mediated bradycardia with sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction that redistributes the reduced cardiac output toward heart and brain — that redistribution account is the textbook's, and the cards below measure its human signatures (heart rate, blood pressure, pulmonary oxygen uptake), not cardiac output or regional flow directly. This shelf builds only the slice pack #6633 does not home: #6633 cards the spleen-contraction and haemoglobin side of apnoea (its PMIDs are not reused here), and pack #6644 homes the breath-hold breaking point. What the primary human studies add: face immersion augments the apnoea response at rest and in exercise, trained divers show the deepest bradycardia, and the response measurably conserves the lung oxygen store. Classic studies are small; every N is printed on its card.

cards.headline: Trained divers exercising: face immersion deepened the heart-rate fall from 21% to 33% and slowed arterial desaturation (N = 8)
cards.summary: Trained divers exercising: face immersion deepened the heart-rate fall from 21% to 33% and slowed arterial desaturation (N = 8)
cards.people: 8 trained breath-hold divers performing steady-state cycle exercise at 100 W, with 30-second apnoeas in air and 30-second apnoeas with face immersion in cold water (10 °C).
cards.result: Heart rate fell and blood pressure rose during apnoeas; compared with apnoea in air, face immersion augmented the heart-rate reduction from 21% to 33% (P < 0.001) and the blood-pressure increase from 34% to 42% (P < 0.05). Arterial oxygen saturation fell less with face immersion (5.2% versus 6.8% from eupnoeic control, P < 0.05) — the augmented response slows depletion of the lung oxygen store.
cards.watchOut: Eight trained divers — the trained end of the spectrum, not a population average; 30-second apnoeas at a fixed workload.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (apnoea and exercise in breath-hold divers). Andersson JP et al.. Diving response and arterial oxygen saturation during apnea and exercise in breath-hold divers. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2002. PMID: 12183481. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Apnea · Arteries · Blood Pressure · Diving · Exercise · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Oxygen
