cards.headline: Exercising apnoea: oxygen uptake from the lungs fell 22% in air and 25% with face immersion; lactate rose 20% (N = 15)
cards.summary: Exercising apnoea: oxygen uptake from the lungs fell 22% in air and 25% with face immersion; lactate rose 20% (N = 15)
cards.people: 15 subjects performing steady-state cycle exercise at 80 W, with 40-second apnoeas in air and 40-second apnoeas with face immersion in cold (10 °C) water.
cards.result: Heart rate decreased and blood pressure increased during apnoeas, both augmented by face immersion. Oxygen uptake from the lungs fell 22% versus eupnoeic control during apnoea in air and 25% with face immersion. Plasma lactate rose 11% after apnoea in air and 20% after face-immersion apnoea, indicating increased anaerobic metabolism while the oxygen store is conserved.
cards.watchOut: Pulmonary oxygen uptake is an indirect window on cardiac output and redistribution — the study infers, and the card does not overstate, a fall in cardiac output rather than measuring it.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (cardiovascular and respiratory responses to apnoeas in exercising humans). Andersson JP et al.. Cardiovascular and respiratory responses to apneas with and without face immersion in exercising humans. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2004. PMID: 14578373. cards.headline: At rest: face immersion cut pulmonary oxygen uptake to 3.4 from 4.6 ml/min/kg in eupnoea (N = 16)
cards.summary: At rest: face immersion cut pulmonary oxygen uptake to 3.4 from 4.6 ml/min/kg in eupnoea (N = 16)
cards.people: 16 resting subjects performing apnoea in air and apnoea with face immersion in cold water (10 °C), with apnoea durations predetermined and identical between conditions (average 145 s; individual maximum average 184 s).
cards.result: Oxygen uptake from the lungs was 4.6 ml min⁻¹ kg⁻¹ in resting eupnoeic control, 3.6 during apnoea in air and 3.4 during apnoea with face immersion — the augmented diving response reduces pulmonary gas exchange at rest, preserving the lung oxygen store for vital organs and allowing longer apnoeas.
cards.watchOut: Resting, near-maximal-duration apnoeas in volunteers — the resting response is smaller in absolute terms than the exercising one and should not be extrapolated to active diving.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (pulmonary gas exchange and the diving response at rest). Andersson JP et al.. Pulmonary gas exchange is reduced by the cardiovascular diving response in resting humans. Respiratory physiology & neurobiology. 2008. PMID: 18088568. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Face versus forearm immersion: face immersion alone lowered heart rate 9% during breathing; either site produced maximal vasoconstriction (N = 19 and N = 23)
cards.summary: Face versus forearm immersion: face immersion alone lowered heart rate 9% during breathing; either site produced maximal vasoconstriction (N = 19 and N = 23)
cards.people: 19 subjects (part I) and 23 subjects (part II) undergoing cold-water (9–11 °C) immersion of the forearm, the face, or both, during eupnoea and during apnoea, in a two-part protocol of eight tests.
cards.result: Cold-water immersion of either the forearm or the face was enough to elicit the most pronounced thermoregulatory vasoconstriction during both eupnoea and apnoea. During eupnoea, heart-rate responses to forearm immersion (3% increase) and face immersion (9% decrease) were additive when combined (3% decrease) — identifying the face, via the trigeminal field, as the specific trigger of the bradycardic component.
cards.watchOut: Two overlapping volunteer panels in one report, carded once; skin capillary flow and heart rate are the readouts — central haemodynamics were not measured.

Cardiovascular responses to cold-water immersions of the forearm and face, and their relationship to apnoea. European journal of applied physiology. 2000. PMID: 11192066. cards.headline: Synthesis: an established, oxygen-conserving reflex — measured in heart rate, pressure and gas exchange, framed by the textbook for flow redistribution
cards.summary: Synthesis: an established, oxygen-conserving reflex — measured in heart rate, pressure and gas exchange, framed by the textbook for flow redistribution
cards.people: Four primary human studies (N = 8, 15, 16 and 19/23) from the Andersson/Schagatay programme, spanning trained divers, exercising volunteers and resting subjects.
cards.result: The pattern is concordant: apnoea slows the heart and raises pressure; cold-water face immersion augments both; pulmonary oxygen uptake falls by roughly a quarter in exercise, delaying desaturation — the oxygen-conserving function the textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) assigns to redistribution toward heart and brain. Cardiac output and regional flows were not directly measured in the carded studies, so those quantities are presented as the textbook's account, not as carded measurements. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Cross-points: pack #6633 (splenic contraction in apnoea — its PMIDs are not reused here) and pack #6644 (breath-hold breaking point).
cards.watchOut: Small volunteer panels throughout, several from a single research programme; trained-diver figures (33% bradycardia) describe trained divers, not untrained people, in whom responses are present but smaller.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andersson JP et al. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2002 (PMID: 12183481); Andersson JP et al. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2004 (PMID: 14578373); Andersson JP et al. Respiratory physiology & neurobiology. 2008 (PMID: 18088568); Andersson J et al. shelves.title: Functional sympatholysis: contracting muscle blunts sympathetic vasoconstriction by more than half — a protection that ageing and oestrogen loss erode
shelves.question: In healthy humans exercising, how is muscle blood flow protected from sympathetic vasoconstriction — how large is functional sympatholysis (the blunting of sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction in exercising versus resting muscle), and how is it demonstrated with intra-arterial agonist infusions, tyramine and lower-body negative pressure during exercise?
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, local control of blood flow and sympathetic control during exercise): metabolites in contracting muscle override sympathetic vasoconstrictor signals locally, so the sympathetic outflow that constricts resting muscle and viscera during exercise spares the working muscle. The human demonstration is pharmacological and elegant: infuse tyramine (which releases endogenous noradrenaline) or α-agonists into the brachial artery and compare the vasoconstriction they produce in a resting forearm against the same forearm doing rhythmic handgrip — conductance falls by roughly half or less in the contracting muscle. The carded studies add the time course (blunting within 10–20 seconds of onset), the mechanism probe (nitric-oxide blockade does not restore the constriction, so NO alone is not the obligatory mediator), and the human limits (the protection is impaired in older men and in postmenopausal women, and restored by oestrogen in the latter). Adjacent shelves: pack #6632 (the exercise pressor reflex that raises pressure) and pack #6076 (what sets cardiac output in exercise) — different questions, cross-pointed only.

cards.headline: Dinenno & Joyner 2003: tyramine vasoconstriction blunted in contracting muscle — and nitric-oxide blockade did not restore it
cards.summary: Dinenno & Joyner 2003: tyramine vasoconstriction blunted in contracting muscle — and nitric-oxide blockade did not restore it
cards.people: Healthy men in sequential intra-arterial protocols (n = 6 and n = 8 for the two nitric-oxide-synthase inhibitors, n = 4 heavy-exercise and n = 5 agonist sub-protocols); forearm blood flow by Doppler ultrasound during rhythmic handgrip versus an adenosine vasodilator control condition, with intra-arterial tyramine and α-agonists before and after local NOS inhibition.
cards.result: Vasoconstrictor responses to endogenous noradrenaline release (tyramine) were significantly blunted during moderate exercise compared with the adenosine condition, and NOS inhibition with L-NMMA or L-NAME did not restore them — in contracting human muscle, nitric oxide is not the obligatory mediator of functional sympatholysis. Responses were repeatable in time-control subjects.
cards.watchOut: Sub-protocol Ns of 4–8, printed here as the record gives them; forearm handgrip at moderate intensity is the model — whole-body exercise adds reflex layers this preparation deliberately removes.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (blunted sympathetic vasoconstriction in contracting skeletal muscle; nitric oxide probe). Dinenno FA et al.. Blunted sympathetic vasoconstriction in contracting skeletal muscle of healthy humans: is nitric oxide obligatory? The Journal of physiology. 2003. PMID: 12949223. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dinenno 2005: in young men exercise cut the tyramine response from −56% to −25% of conductance — in older men the blunting was lost (−36% to −30%)
cards.summary: Dinenno 2005: in young men exercise cut the tyramine response from −56% to −25% of conductance — in older men the blunting was lost (−36% to −30%)
cards.people: 7 young (25 ± 2 years) and 8 older (65 ± 2 years) healthy men; forearm vascular conductance responses to intra-arterial tyramine, phenylephrine (α1) and clonidine (α2) during rhythmic handgrip at 15% maximum voluntary contraction versus intra-arterial adenosine.
cards.result: In young men, vasoconstrictor responses during exercise were blunted versus adenosine for all three agents: tyramine −25 ± 1% versus −56 ± 6%, phenylephrine −11 ± 4% versus −39 ± 4%, clonidine −12 ± 4% versus −38 ± 5% (all P < 0.005). In older men, exercise did not significantly blunt the tyramine response (−30 ± 2% versus −36 ± 7%; P = 0.4) — functional sympatholysis is impaired with age.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen men total; the ageing contrast is cross-sectional, and 'impaired' describes these agonist responses in forearm muscle — not a whole-body exercise capacity claim.

cards.headline: Tschakovsky & Hughson 2003: sympatholysis switches on within seconds — the lower-body-negative-pressure deficit in conductance was abolished after the first 10–20 seconds of exercise (N = 9)
cards.summary: Tschakovsky & Hughson 2003: sympatholysis switches on within seconds — the lower-body-negative-pressure deficit in conductance was abolished after the first 10–20 seconds of exercise (N = 9)
cards.people: 9 healthy subjects performing 5 minutes of moderate dynamic forearm handgrip with and without −60 mmHg lower-body negative pressure (LBNP) to raise sympathetic outflow; beat-by-beat forearm blood flow, arterial pressure and heart rate.
cards.result: At rest, LBNP reduced forearm vascular conductance by 30% (P = 0.004). At exercise onset the initial conductance plateau (10–20 s) was lower under LBNP (101.6 ± 4.1 versus 126.6 ± 4.1 ml min⁻¹ 100 mmHg⁻¹, P = 0.003), but the difference was quickly abolished during the slower second phase — local substances released with the first contractions rapidly blunt sympathetic vasoconstriction.
cards.watchOut: N = 9; LBNP is a reflex sympathetic stimulus, complementary to the direct agonist-infusion cards — the two designs converging is the strength of the shelf.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (rapid blunting of sympathetic vasoconstriction at exercise onset). Tschakovsky ME et al.. Rapid blunting of sympathetic vasoconstriction in the human forearm at the onset of exercise. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2003. PMID: 12524374. cards.headline: Fadel 2004: postmenopausal women lost sympatholysis (muscle oxygenation fell 12% exercising versus 3% in premenopausal women) — oestrogen restored it (N = 8 + 8)
cards.summary: Fadel 2004: postmenopausal women lost sympatholysis (muscle oxygenation fell 12% exercising versus 3% in premenopausal women) — oestrogen restored it (N = 8 + 8)
cards.people: 8 premenopausal and 8 postmenopausal women; muscle oxygenation by near-infrared spectroscopy in resting and exercising forearm during lower-body negative pressure, with the postmenopausal group re-studied after 1 month of transdermal oestradiol.
cards.result: In premenopausal women, LBNP decreased muscle oxygenation by 20 ± 1% in the resting forearm but only 3 ± 2% in the exercising forearm (P < 0.05) — intact sympatholysis. In postmenopausal women the falls were 15 ± 3% at rest and 12 ± 4% exercising (not significantly different) — sympatholysis impaired — and the impairment was reversed by oestrogen therapy, per the study's design and title finding.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen women and an indirect oxygenation readout rather than measured flow; the oestrogen-reversal limb is a within-study intervention in 8 women — characterisation, not a treatment recommendation.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (sympatholysis in pre- and postmenopausal women; oestrogen reversal). Fadel PJ et al.. Augmented sympathetic vasoconstriction in exercising forearms of postmenopausal women is reversed by oestrogen therapy. The Journal of physiology. 2004. PMID: 15498809. cards.headline: Synthesis: a fast, large, locally mediated protection — with defined human limits
cards.summary: Synthesis: a fast, large, locally mediated protection — with defined human limits
cards.people: Four primary human studies (forearm models; Ns 4–8 per sub-protocol, 15, 9, and 16), using intra-arterial tyramine/agonist infusions and lower-body negative pressure as the sympathetic stimuli.
cards.result: Contracting muscle blunts sympathetic vasoconstriction by roughly half or more (tyramine −56% → −25% of conductance in young men), the blunting is present within 10–20 seconds of contraction onset, it is not abolished by nitric-oxide blockade, and it is impaired in older men and postmenopausal women and restored by oestrogen in the latter — the Guyton & Hall local-control account, demonstrated quantity by quantity in humans. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Every card is a forearm/handgrip preparation in small volunteer panels; leg exercise and whole-body haemodynamics are extrapolations the textbook makes and the cards do not.

shelves.title: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: the heart speeds with each breath in and slows out — a vagally gated rhythm set mainly by breathing rate
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is respiratory sinus arrhythmia — how much does heart rate speed in inspiration and slow in expiration, how much of it is vagal efferent traffic versus central irradiation and the Bainbridge/baroreflex loops, and how do breathing rate and tidal volume scale it in the classic blockade and pacing studies?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall and Ganong frame respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) as the visible signature of phasic vagal efferent traffic to the sinus node: vagal motoneuron firing is gated by the respiratory cycle (suppressed in inspiration, released in expiration), so heart period shortens as a breath begins and lengthens as it ends. The fetched human records support that framing quantitatively. In 17 seated volunteers breathing at controlled rates and volumes, RSA was large and stable below 6 breaths/min — a low-frequency intercept of 20 ± 5 beats/min of peak-to-trough heart-rate swing — and rolled off above a corner frequency of 7.2 ± 1.5 cycles/min, with RSA scaling linearly with tidal volume (Hirsch & Bishop 1981). Eckberg's controlled-breathing study in 6 healthy young adults showed the complementary asymmetry: a 50% increase in tidal volume raised the peak-valley P-P interval by only about 15%, while lengthening the breathing interval widened RSA asymptotically — breathing rate matters more than depth (Eckberg 1983). The mechanism is central gating of vagal outflow interacting with the baroreflex, not a purely reflex loop: in 6 volunteers, carotid baroreceptor stimuli (neck suction) delivered in inspiration produced blunted sinus-node responses at moderate intensity, while intense stimuli broke through the gate (Eckberg & Orshan 1977); and in 22 healthy young adults, low-dose atropine paradoxically increased RSA and baroreflex responses while high-dose atropine abolished them exponentially, with resting RSA correlating with baroreflex responsiveness at r = 0.78 (Raczkowska, Eckberg & Ebert 1983). The Bainbridge reflex and central irradiation from the respiratory centre are named in the textbooks as contributing loops; no carded record here isolates the Bainbridge contribution, so that part stands as the textbook's account rather than a measured share. Net: RSA in health is a vagally mediated, respiration-gated rhythm whose size is set mainly by breathing interval, modestly by tidal volume, and which fades as breathing quickens past roughly 7 breaths/min.

cards.headline: The scaling law: RSA is large and stable below 6 breaths/min (swing 20 ± 5 beats/min), then rolls off above a corner frequency of ~7.2 cycles/min — and scales linearly with tidal volume (N = 17)
cards.summary: The scaling law: RSA is large and stable below 6 breaths/min (swing 20 ± 5 beats/min), then rolls off above a corner frequency of ~7.2 cycles/min — and scales linearly with tidal volume (N = 17)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled breathing-pattern RSA quantification) — N = 17
cards.people: 17 seated healthy subjects breathing through a mouthpiece and nose-clip at voluntarily controlled tidal volumes and breathing frequencies, plus spontaneous quiet breathing; inspiratory breath-hold served as the zero-frequency condition.
cards.result: Log RSA plotted against log breathing frequency at each tidal volume gave a consistent individual curve: a large, stable RSA at frequencies below 6 cycles/min (the low-frequency intercept, 20 ± 5 beats/min), inversely proportional to age only up to 35 years; above a characteristic corner frequency (fC, 7.2 ± 1.5 cycles/min) RSA fell with a constant roll-off slope of 21 ± 3.4 dB/decade. The RSA–tidal-volume relationship was linear, so RSA–frequency curves at different volumes normalised onto a single curve, and spontaneous-breathing data points fell on that same curve.
cards.watchOut: Breathing was voluntarily controlled through a mouthpiece, which itself can alter autonomic state; the durable claims are the shape of the relationship (plateau, corner frequency, roll-off, linear volume scaling), not any one subject's intercept.
cards.source: Hirsch JA, Bishop B. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in humans: how breathing pattern modulates heart rate. The American journal of physiology. 1981. PMID: 7315987. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Lung Volume Measurements · Male · Middle Aged · Respiration · Tidal Volume

cards.headline: Breathing interval beats tidal volume: lengthening the breath widens RSA asymptotically, but a 50% larger tidal volume adds only ~15% to the peak-valley interval (N = 6)
cards.summary: Breathing interval beats tidal volume: lengthening the breath widens RSA asymptotically, but a 50% larger tidal volume adds only ~15% to the peak-valley interval (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled breathing, vagal-outflow inference) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy young men and women breathing at controlled intervals of 2.5–10 s with nominal tidal volumes of 1,000 and 1,500 ml while heartbeat intervals were recorded.
cards.result: As breathing interval increased, the longest heart periods became longer, the shortest became shorter, and peak-valley P-P intervals increased asymptotically. Peak-valley intervals also rose with tidal volume, but the influence was small: a 50% increase of tidal volume increased the average peak-valley P-P interval by only about 15%. Timing was phase-locked: heart-period shortening began in inspiration at short breathing intervals and in expiration at long ones, whereas heart-period lengthening began in early expiration at every interval studied — evidence that respiration-related vagal motoneuron activity begins in expiration and is incompletely expressed at fast breathing rates.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, printed plainly: this is a classic mechanistic study whose value is the phase timing and the rate-versus-depth asymmetry, and its inference that sinus arrhythmia tracks vagal outflow rests on the near-fixed latency between vagal activity changes and heart-period changes stated by the author.
cards.source: Eckberg DL. Human sinus arrhythmia as an index of vagal cardiac outflow. Journal of applied physiology: respiratory, environmental and exercise physiology. 1983. PMID: 6853303. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The respiratory gate in action: moderate baroreflex stimuli are inhibited during inspiration, but intense stimuli break through (N = 6)
cards.summary: The respiratory gate in action: moderate baroreflex stimuli are inhibited during inspiration, but intense stimuli break through (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (neck-suction baroreflex stimulation across the respiratory cycle) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy young adults whose carotid baroreceptors were stimulated with two intensities of neck suction delivered in early inspiration or expiration, at 100% or 150% of each subject's normal tidal volume.
cards.result: Sinus-node responses to moderate baroreflex stimuli were inhibited by inspiration, but responses to intense stimuli were not influenced by the phase of respiration. Supranormal tidal volume did not diminish responses to inspiratory baroreflex stimuli, but significantly reduced responses to expiratory stimuli. The authors read this as evidence for a central respiratory–baroreceptor reflex interaction in man whose strength depends on the level of afferent baroreceptor activity and the depth of inspiration — the gate is leaky for strong inputs.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, printed plainly, and neck suction stimulates carotid baroreceptors non-physiologically; the card supports the existence and stimulus-dependence of central gating, not a numerical share of RSA attributable to the baroreflex in spontaneous breathing.
cards.source: Eckberg DL, Orshan CR. Respiratory and baroreceptor reflex interactions in man. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1977. PMID: 853124. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Carotid Sinus · Female · Heart · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Pressoreceptors · Reflex · Respiration · Tidal Volume

cards.headline: Blockade proof of the vagal mechanism: low-dose atropine enlarges RSA, high-dose atropine abolishes it — and resting RSA tracks baroreflex responsiveness (r = 0.78) (N = 22)
cards.summary: Blockade proof of the vagal mechanism: low-dose atropine enlarges RSA, high-dose atropine abolishes it — and resting RSA tracks baroreflex responsiveness (r = 0.78) (N = 22)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (graded muscarinic blockade of RSA and baroreflex responses) — N = 22
cards.people: 22 healthy young adults studied before and after low-dose (0.725 microgram/kg) or high-dose (0.043 mg/kg) atropine sulfate infusions, with RSA measured as peak-valley P-P changes during controlled breathing and baroreflex responses provoked by neck suction.
cards.result: Resting RSA correlated highly significantly with baroreflex responses (r = 0.78, P = 0.002). Low-dose atropine increased the magnitude of both sinus arrhythmia and baroreflex responses; large-dose atropine reduced both in an exponential fashion. The authors link RSA to baroreflex responsiveness and infer that vagal cardiac efferent activity is modulated by inhibitory muscarinic receptors — partial blockade amplifies vagal motoneuron responses to baroreceptor input, full blockade silences the efferent limb that produces RSA.
cards.watchOut: The low-dose atropine amplification is a receptor-level inference from a pharmacological probe, not a direct recording of vagal traffic; what the record directly shows is the dose-dependent rise-then-abolition of RSA and its correlation with baroreflex gain.
cards.source: Raczkowska M, Eckberg DL, Ebert TJ. Muscarinic cholinergic receptors modulate vagal cardiac responses in man. Journal of the autonomic nervous system. 1983. PMID: 6875192. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: RSA is a vagally gated rhythm — set mainly by breathing interval, modestly by depth, open to strong baroreflex input, and erased by full muscarinic blockade
cards.summary: Synthesis: RSA is a vagally gated rhythm — set mainly by breathing interval, modestly by depth, open to strong baroreflex input, and erased by full muscarinic blockade
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in healthy humans, as the fetched records show it: heart rate speeds in inspiration and slows in expiration because vagal motoneuron firing is centrally gated by the respiratory cycle. The swing is large and stable at slow breathing rates (low-frequency intercept 20 ± 5 beats/min below 6 breaths/min), rolls off above a corner frequency of about 7.2 cycles/min, scales linearly with tidal volume but far more steeply with breathing interval (a 50% deeper breath adds only ~15%), is phase-locked so that heart-period lengthening begins in early expiration, is blunted for moderate baroreflex inputs during inspiration while strong inputs break through, and is abolished exponentially by high-dose atropine after paradoxical amplification at low dose. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the vagal-gating mechanism and its breathing-pattern scaling are concordant across blockade, baroreflex-probe and controlled-breathing records; the Bainbridge contribution named in textbooks is not separately quantified by any carded record and is carried as the textbook's account.
cards.watchOut: All four studies are small (N = 6–22) laboratory studies in young healthy adults with controlled breathing; absolute RSA amplitudes in free-living, older or sleeping humans will differ, so the shelf's durable claims are the mechanism and the scaling relationships.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hirsch JA, Bishop B. The American journal of physiology. 1981 (PMID: 7315987); Eckberg DL. Journal of applied physiology: respiratory, environmental and exercise physiology. 1983 (PMID: 6853303); Eckberg DL, Orshan CR. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1977 (PMID: 853124); Raczkowska M, Eckberg DL, Ebert TJ. Journal of the autonomic nervous system. 1983 (PMID: 6875192). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Heart-rate recovery after exercise: a vagal first half-minute, then a sympathetic tail that tracks noradrenaline washout
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast does heart rate fall in the first 1–2 minutes after stopping maximal exercise (heart-rate recovery), what autonomic sequence produces the fast and slow phases on blockade studies, and how do fitness and age change the time constant?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall frames post-exercise recovery as the mirror of the exercise response: the fast early fall in heart rate is vagal reactivation, and the slower tail is sympathetic withdrawal as muscle metaboreflex input and circulating catecholamines clear. The fetched blockade and time-course records support that two-phase account with numbers. In 6 men recovering from peak treadmill exercise, heart rate fell exponentially under every condition — no drugs, atropine, propranolol, or both — with the exponential coefficients differing most between parasympathetic and sympathetic blockade (Savin 1982). Imai's protocol separated the phases directly: in 8 normal volunteers, the time constants of heart-rate decay over the first 30 s (T30) and first 120 s (T120) after exercise were both markedly prolonged by atropine, but T30 was almost independent of exercise intensity and of sympathetic blockade, marking it as primarily vagal reactivation, while T120 also tracked sympathetic activity and workload; recovery was accelerated in trained cross-country skiers and blunted in heart-failure patients (Imai 1994). Perini's catecholamine study in 6 sedentary young men put times on the slow phase: heart rate fell mono-exponentially with tau values of 13.6, 32.7 and 55.8 s after exercise at 21%, 43% and 65% of VO2max, dropped about 35 beats/min in the first minute regardless of intensity (prompt vagal restoration), and thereafter tracked the exponential decay of venous noradrenaline (tau ~87–101 s) (Perini 1989). Pierpont's modelling study adds the measurement caution: a single-exponential time constant is a reasonable index after submaximal exercise but fits maximal-exercise recovery poorly (Pierpont 2000). So in health the first half-minute is a vagal event, the next minutes are sympathetic washout, and both fitness and intensity move the constants in predictable directions.

cards.headline: Recovery is exponential under every blockade condition — and the exponential's coefficients move most between parasympathetic and sympathetic blockade (N = 6)
cards.summary: Recovery is exponential under every blockade condition — and the exponential's coefficients move most between parasympathetic and sympathetic blockade (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (autonomic blockade of post-exercise heart-rate recovery) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 men whose heart rate was followed after peak treadmill exercise under four conditions: parasympathetic blockade with atropine sulfate (0.03 mg/kg), sympathetic blockade with propranolol hydrochloride (0.20 mg/kg), double blockade with both drugs, and no drugs.
cards.result: Heart rate recovered in an exponential manner after dynamic exercise in every subject under every treatment mode (P less than 0.01 for each fit; mean correlation across treatments r = 0.94). The fitted coefficients a and b differed most between parasympathetic blockade and sympathetic blockade. The authors conclude that the exponential character of cardiodeceleration after peak exercise is an intrinsic property of the circulation, present under each experimental condition, with the autonomic limbs shaping its rate.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, printed plainly, and the exponential fit is a description, not a mechanism split by itself: the vagal-versus-sympathetic attribution comes from comparing the blockade conditions here and is quantified by References 2 and 3.
cards.source: Savin WM, Davidson DM, Haskell WL. Autonomic contribution to heart rate recovery from exercise in humans. Journal of applied physiology: respiratory, environmental and exercise physiology. 1982. PMID: 7153152. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The first 30 seconds are vagal: T30 is prolonged by atropine but almost independent of exercise intensity and sympathetic blockade — and recovery is faster in athletes (blockade protocol N = 8)
cards.summary: The first 30 seconds are vagal: T30 is prolonged by atropine but almost independent of exercise intensity and sympathetic blockade — and recovery is faster in athletes (blockade protocol N = 8)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (autonomic blockade, post-exercise decay time constants) — N = 8 healthy volunteers (plus athlete and heart-failure contrast groups)
cards.people: 8 normal volunteers who exercised at six levels (maximal, anaerobic threshold, threshold with propranolol, threshold with atropine, threshold with both drugs, and 50% of threshold) for the blockade protocol; T30 and T120 at anaerobic threshold were also measured in 9 cross-country skiers and 20 patients with chronic heart failure as contrast groups.
cards.result: The time constants of beat-by-beat heart-rate decay for the first 30 s (T30) and first 120 s (T120) after exercise were both markedly prolonged by atropine administration, indicating both are mediated by vagal reactivation. T30 was almost independent of exercise intensity and sympathetic blockade, whereas T120 was affected by sympathetic nerve activity and exercise workload — so T30 indexes vagal reactivation specifically. As the paper's title states, vagally mediated recovery was accelerated in the athletes and blunted in the heart-failure patients; the healthy-volunteer blockade data are what this shelf cards.
cards.watchOut: The athlete and heart-failure arms are contrast groups showing the index moves with training and disease; the physiology claim for health rests on the 8 volunteers' blockade protocol, and the abstract's healthy-volunteer results are reported without the absolute T30/T120 values, which are therefore not printed here.

cards.headline: The slow phase tracks noradrenaline washout: heart-rate tau lengthens with exercise intensity (13.6 s at 21% of VO2max to 55.8 s at 65%), while the first minute's ~35 beats/min fall does not (N = 6)
cards.summary: The slow phase tracks noradrenaline washout: heart-rate tau lengthens with exercise intensity (13.6 s at 21% of VO2max to 55.8 s at 65%), while the first minute's ~35 beats/min fall does not (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (heart-rate and catecholamine recovery time courses) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 sedentary young men recovering from three cycle-ergometer exercise bouts at 21% ± 2.8%, 43% ± 2.1% and 65% ± 2.3% of VO2max, with serial venous noradrenaline concentrations measured alongside heart rate.
cards.result: Heart rate decreased mono-exponentially with tau values of 13.6 ± 1.6 s, 32.7 ± 5.6 s and 55.8 ± 8.1 s after the three intensities. Noradrenaline did not change after the low-intensity bout; after medium and high intensity it rose during exercise, then, after a 1-minute lag, decreased exponentially (tau 87 s and 101 s). In the 1st minute of recovery heart rate fell about 35 beats/min regardless of intensity — attributed to prompt restoration of vagal tone — while from the 2nd to 5th minute heart rate and noradrenaline were linearly related (100 pg/ml change in noradrenaline corresponding to about 5 beats/min), attributing the later fall to sympathetic activity returning to pre-exercise levels.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 sedentary young men, printed plainly, and venous noradrenaline is an indirect index of sympathetic activity; the card's durable claims are the intensity scaling of tau and the dissociation between the intensity-independent first minute and the catecholamine-tracking tail.
cards.source: Perini R et al. Plasma norepinephrine and heart rate dynamics during recovery from submaximal exercise in man. European journal of applied physiology and occupational physiology. 1989. PMID: 2767070. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Measurement caution: a single-exponential time constant is a fair parasympathetic index after submaximal exercise but fits maximal-exercise recovery poorly (N = 9)
cards.summary: Measurement caution: a single-exponential time constant is a fair parasympathetic index after submaximal exercise but fits maximal-exercise recovery poorly (N = 9)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (model-fitting validation of recovery time constants) — N = 9
cards.people: 9 healthy volunteers (age 24–46) who performed treadmill exercise at maximal effort and at two submaximal Bruce-protocol stages, with post-exercise heart-rate recovery fitted to a first-order exponential decay.
cards.result: The fitted time constant (T) stabilised only after 3 minutes of post-exercise monitoring. After maximal exercise, T varied unacceptably with small changes in the onset of monitoring (e.g. −16.7 ± 16.6, −13.2%, within the first 5 s) and residuals of the fitted curve were non-random. After submaximal exercise, T values were consistent (e.g. −1.9 ± 3.2, −4.2%, in the first 5 s) with more nearly random residuals. The authors conclude first-order decay is an inadequate model for recovery after maximal exercise but may be reasonable for submaximal levels.
cards.watchOut: This card grades the measurement, not the mechanism: quoted recovery time constants from maximal-exercise protocols (including References 1–3 where maximal or near-maximal) should be read as approximations whose value depends on the monitoring window and exercise level.
cards.source: Pierpont GL, Stolpman DR, Gornick CC. Heart rate recovery post-exercise as an index of parasympathetic activity. Journal of the autonomic nervous system. 2000. PMID: 10785283. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phases — a vagal first half-minute that fitness speeds and intensity barely moves, then a sympathetic tail that tracks catecholamine washout and lengthens with workload
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phases — a vagal first half-minute that fitness speeds and intensity barely moves, then a sympathetic tail that tracks catecholamine washout and lengthens with workload
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Heart-rate recovery in healthy humans, as the fetched records show it: the fall is exponential in form under all autonomic conditions. The fast phase (first ~30 s, Imai's T30) is vagal reactivation — markedly prolonged by atropine, almost independent of exercise intensity and sympathetic blockade, accelerated by endurance training. The first minute drops heart rate by about 35 beats/min even after light exercise; thereafter the decline tracks venous noradrenaline decay (tau ~87–101 s) as sympathetic activity returns to baseline, and the overall heart-rate tau lengthens with prior intensity (13.6 s after 21% of VO2max versus 55.8 s after 65%). Single-exponential constants are trustworthy chiefly for submaximal exercise. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the vagal-fast / sympathetic-slow sequence is demonstrated independently by blockade, catecholamine-tracking and model-fitting studies. The prognostic use of 1-minute recovery in patients is a clinical question and is not this shelf's claim.
cards.watchOut: Every carded study is small (N = 6–9 healthy volunteers in the mechanistic protocols); the constants quoted are laboratory values in young adults, and age effects on the time constant are asserted by the textbook framing rather than quantified by a carded age-comparison record on this shelf.

European journal of applied physiology and occupational physiology. 1989 (PMID: 2767070); Pierpont GL, Stolpman DR, Gornick CC. Journal of the autonomic nervous system. 2000 (PMID: 10785283). shelves.title: Oxygen-uptake kinetics at exercise onset: a 15-second cardiodynamic phase, then an exponential rise with a ~30-second time constant
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast do oxygen-uptake kinetics respond at exercise onset — what is the phase II time constant for pulmonary VO2 in moderate exercise, how much does it slow in heavy/severe domains and with ageing or deconditioning, and what does the oxygen deficit represent?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame the exercise on-transient in phases: an immediate cardiodynamic phase (phase I, the first ~10–15 s, driven by the rise in pulmonary blood flow before venous blood from the exercising muscle reaches the lungs), then phase II, in which pulmonary VO2 rises mono-exponentially toward the steady state with a time constant (tau) that mirrors muscle VO2 consumption, leaving an oxygen deficit that is repaid by the aerobic system catching up. The fetched human records measure each piece. Grassi's group measured leg VO2 directly by thermodilution leg blood flow plus arteriovenous O2 difference in 6 trained subjects and found phase I confined to the first 10–15 s, then mono-exponential phase II responses whose half-times were statistically indistinguishable between alveolar VO2 (25.5 ± 2.6 s) and leg VO2 (27.9 ± 5.7 s) — pulmonary kinetics faithfully track muscle kinetics after phase I (Grassi 1996). DeLorey's near-infrared programme timed the muscle side: in 11 young adults the phase II pulmonary tau was 30 ± 8 s while muscle deoxygenation, after a 13 ± 2 s delay, rose faster (tau 10 ± 3 s) (DeLorey 2003). Ageing slows phase II substantially — tau 26 ± 7 s in young adults versus 42 ± 9 s in older adults at the same relative moderate intensity (DeLorey 2004) — and a heavy-intensity warm-up ('priming') speeds the older tau from 38 ± 5 s to 30 ± 7 s while leaving young adults unchanged (DeLorey 2004). In heavy and severe domains the textbooks describe an additional delayed slow component that prolongs or prevents the steady state; that feature is carried here as the textbook's account (Whipp's slow-component synthesis is a review, not a primary record, and is not carded — see the Synthesis card).

cards.headline: Muscle VO2 measured directly: after a 10–15 s cardiodynamic phase I, leg and alveolar VO2 rise mono-exponentially with indistinguishable half-times (~26–28 s) (N = 6)
cards.summary: Muscle VO2 measured directly: after a 10–15 s cardiodynamic phase I, leg and alveolar VO2 rise mono-exponentially with indistinguishable half-times (~26–28 s) (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (direct leg VO2 kinetics by thermodilution and arteriovenous difference) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 trained subjects (age 22.8 ± 4.4 years; maximal O2 uptake 59.1 ± 5.3 ml/kg/min) studied during the transition from unloaded pedalling to 183 ± 20 W (below ventilatory threshold), with leg blood flow by constant-infusion thermodilution and frequent arteriovenous O2 content differences across the leg, giving leg VO2 every 3–4 s.
cards.result: Two phases were recognised in every variable. During the first 10–15 s of loaded pedalling (phase I), alveolar VO2, leg blood flow and leg O2 delivery rose rapidly while leg VO2 rose only slightly and the arteriovenous O2 difference actually decreased. Thereafter (phase II) all variables rose mono-exponentially with similar time courses, and half-times were not significantly different: 25.5 ± 2.6 s for alveolar VO2, 26.6 ± 7.6 s for leg blood flow, 23.5 ± 1.3 s for the arteriovenous difference and 27.9 ± 5.7 s for leg VO2. The authors conclude that, measured this way, alveolar and leg VO2 kinetics at the on-transition are similar — breath-by-breath pulmonary kinetics are a valid window on muscle kinetics after phase I.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 highly trained young men, printed plainly, at one moderate workload; the phase I duration and phase II half-times are for below-threshold cycling and should not be extrapolated to heavy or severe domains.
cards.source: Grassi B et al. Muscle O2 uptake kinetics in humans: implications for metabolic control. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 1996. PMID: 8964765. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Blood Flow Velocity · Exercise · Humans · Kinetics · Male · Muscles · Oxygen · Time Factors

cards.headline: Muscle deoxygenation starts after a ~13 s delay, then rises faster (tau ~10 s) than pulmonary phase II VO2 (tau 30 ± 8 s) (N = 11)
cards.summary: Muscle deoxygenation starts after a ~13 s delay, then rises faster (tau ~10 s) than pulmonary phase II VO2 (tau 30 ± 8 s) (N = 11)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (breath-by-breath VO2 with near-infrared muscle deoxygenation) — N = 11
cards.people: 11 young adults (5 men, 6 women; 23 ± 3 years) performing repeated transitions on 3 separate days from 20 W to a constant work rate at 80% of lactate threshold, with breath-by-breath pulmonary VO2 and vastus lateralis near-infrared spectroscopy (deoxy-, oxy- and total haemoglobin/myoglobin).
cards.result: The phase II time constant for pulmonary VO2 was 30 ± 8 s, significantly slower (P < 0.01) than the time constant for muscle deoxygenation (10 ± 3 s), which itself began only after a time delay of 13 ± 2 s from exercise onset. After that delay, local muscle deoxygenation kinetics were faster than phase II pulmonary VO2 (and presumably muscle O2 consumption), reflecting increased O2 extraction and a transient mismatch between local muscle O2 consumption and perfusion.
cards.watchOut: Near-infrared deoxyhaemoglobin is an index of the local delivery-to-utilisation balance, not a direct VO2 measurement; the direct leg-VO2 anchor is Reference 1, and this card's contribution is the timing relationship (delay, then faster deoxygenation).
cards.source: DeLorey DS, Kowalchuk JM, Paterson DH. Relationship between pulmonary O2 uptake kinetics and muscle deoxygenation during moderate-intensity exercise. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2003. PMID: 12679363. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ageing slows phase II: tau 26 ± 7 s in young adults versus 42 ± 9 s in older adults at the same relative moderate intensity (N = 12)
cards.summary: Ageing slows phase II: tau 26 ± 7 s in young adults versus 42 ± 9 s in older adults at the same relative moderate intensity (N = 12)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (young-versus-older phase II kinetics comparison) — N = 12 (6 young, 6 older)
cards.people: 6 young adults (25 ± 3 years) and 6 older adults (68 ± 3 years) performing repeated transitions from 20 W to moderate-intensity cycling at 80% of estimated lactate threshold, with breath-by-breath pulmonary VO2 and vastus lateralis near-infrared spectroscopy.
cards.result: The phase II time constant for pulmonary VO2 was slower (P < 0.01) in older adults (42 ± 9 s) than in young adults (26 ± 7 s). The delay before muscle deoxygenation began was similar (young 12 ± 2 s; older 11 ± 1 s), as was the deoxygenation time constant after the delay, but the increase in deoxygenation per unit increase in VO2 was greater in older adults (13 ± 4 versus 7 ± 2 microM per l per min; P < 0.01). The authors interpret the slower older VO2 kinetics as accompanied by slower adaptation of local muscle blood flow and O2 delivery.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (6 per age band) at one relative intensity; the comparison is young-versus-older cross-sectional, so cohort and habitual-activity differences are folded into the 'ageing' label the authors use.
cards.source: DeLorey DS, Kowalchuk JM, Paterson DH. Effect of age on O(2) uptake kinetics and the adaptation of muscle deoxygenation at the onset of moderate-intensity cycling exercise. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2004. PMID: 15003999. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Priming works in older muscle: a heavy-intensity warm-up speeds the older phase II tau from 38 ± 5 s to 30 ± 7 s, while young adults are unchanged (N = 11)
cards.summary: Priming works in older muscle: a heavy-intensity warm-up speeds the older phase II tau from 38 ± 5 s to 30 ± 7 s, while young adults are unchanged (N = 11)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (priming-exercise effect on VO2 kinetics, young versus older) — N = 11 (6 young, 5 older)
cards.people: 6 young adults (25 ± 3 years) and 5 older adults (68 ± 3 years) performing step transitions from 20 W to moderate-intensity cycling (80% of lactate threshold), preceded either by no warm-up or by 6 minutes of heavy-intensity warm-up exercise, with breath-by-breath VO2 and vastus lateralis near-infrared spectroscopy.
cards.result: After heavy warm-up, muscle oxyhaemoglobin and total haemoglobin were elevated above the no-warm-up baseline in both age groups. In older adults the phase II VO2 time constant was faster (P < 0.05) after heavy warm-up (30 ± 7 s) than with no warm-up (38 ± 5 s); in young adults it was similar (26 ± 7 s versus 25 ± 5 s). The authors suggest that in older adults VO2 kinetics may be limited by slow adaptation of muscle blood flow and O2 delivery, which priming partially relieves.
cards.watchOut: The older group here is 5 subjects, printed plainly, and its no-warm-up tau (38 ± 5 s) differs slightly from Reference 3's older cohort (42 ± 9 s) — different subjects and days; the durable claim is the direction and selectivity of the priming effect, not a single older tau value.
cards.source: DeLorey DS, Kowalchuk JM, Paterson DH. Effects of prior heavy-intensity exercise on pulmonary O2 uptake and muscle deoxygenation kinetics in young and older adult humans. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 2004. PMID: 15133009. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a ~15-second cardiodynamic phase, then a mono-exponential phase II with tau ~26–30 s in young adults, ~40 s in older adults, partially re-speeded by priming
cards.summary: Synthesis: a ~15-second cardiodynamic phase, then a mono-exponential phase II with tau ~26–30 s in young adults, ~40 s in older adults, partially re-speeded by priming
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Oxygen-uptake kinetics at exercise onset in healthy humans, as the fetched records show them: phase I occupies the first 10–15 s (cardiodynamic — pulmonary blood flow rises before muscle venous effluent arrives, and directly measured leg VO2 barely moves); phase II then rises mono-exponentially with a half-time of ~26–28 s (tau ~30 ± 8 s) in young adults during moderate exercise, with muscle deoxygenation beginning after a ~13 s delay and then proceeding faster than pulmonary VO2. Ageing slows phase II to a tau of about 42 s, and heavy-intensity priming restores part of that loss in older adults (38 → 30 s) while doing nothing in the young. The oxygen deficit is the area between the steady-state requirement and this exponential rise — the energetic shortfall the phosphocreatine and anaerobic systems bridge, as the textbooks frame it. REFUSAL NOTED: the heavy/severe-domain slow component (Whipp's synthesis, Medicine and science in sports and exercise 1994, PMID: 7741865) is a review/model paper rather than a primary human record, so it is not carded; heavy-domain slowing is presented in this pack's balance as the textbook's account only. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the moderate-domain on-transient and its ageing/priming behaviour, which rest on concordant direct and breath-by-breath measurements.
cards.watchOut: All carded data are moderate-domain cycling in small laboratory cohorts (N = 5–11 per group); running, arm exercise and heavy/severe domains have different kinetics, and the slow component above the lactate threshold is deliberately not quantified here because its anchor record is a synthesis, not a primary study.

shelves.title: Red-cell lifespan in health: ~106–120 days by every labelling method — once each label's own leak is corrected
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how long do red cells live — what did the classic chromium-51, DF32P and biotin-labelling studies measure as mean red-cell lifespan (~120 days), how is senescent-cell removal signalled, and how much do lifespan estimates differ between labelling methods?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). Methods disagree until their label artefacts are handled, then converge: biotin enumeration matches 51Cr once the early loss of ~half the biotin label is recognised (Mock, PMID 10037125) and works in healthy volunteers (Cordle & Mock, PMID 10532599, N = 20); corrected 51Cr and DF32P agree fairly well, with 51Cr elution ≤2.3%/day (Uchida, PMID 996847); and an independent stable-isotope cohort label measures lifespan 106 ± 21 days (2 SD) in 9 normal people (Khera, PMID 25293624). Refusals: Ashby's differential-agglutination studies — the original human lifespan measurements — predate PubMed indexing and no verifiable record could be fetched, so they are not carded; the ICSH 51Cr panel document (PMID 7426443) has an empty abstract in its record and likewise could not be verified, so it is not carded either. Both refusals are stated on the Synthesis card.

cards.headline: Mock 1999: biotin-labelled red cells reproduce 51Cr survival — with a catch: about half the biotin label leaves the cells in the first weeks, then disappearance turns linear at a near-normal lifespan
cards.summary: Mock 1999: biotin-labelled red cells reproduce 51Cr survival — with a catch: about half the biotin label leaves the cells in the first weeks, then disappearance turns linear at a near-normal lifespan
cards.people: Humans in whom red-cell survival was measured simultaneously by enumeration of biotin-labelled red cells (flow cytometry with fluorescein-avidin), by total biotin-label disappearance (125I-streptavidin), and by the standard 51Cr method. N not documented in the fetched record's abstract.
cards.result: Biotinylated cells persisted in the circulation with life spans approaching normal. About one-half of the biotin label left the circulation over the first few weeks, producing early curvilinear disappearance — consistent with about half the label leaving the red cells themselves rather than the cells dying. The permanently attached half produced linear disappearance and approximately normal life-span estimates from the later linear curve. Red-cell survival can therefore be measured accurately in humans without radiation, provided the early label-loss phase is not mistaken for cell loss.
cards.watchOut: Validation study whose abstract prints no N and no single lifespan number: it establishes that the biotin method agrees with 51Cr after the early label-loss phase — the quantitative lifespan estimate in this pack comes from the Khera card.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Mock DM et al. Measurement of red cell survival using biotin-labeled red cells: validation against 51Cr-labeled red cells. Transfusion. 1999. PMID: 10037125. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Cordle & Mock 1999: in 20 healthy subjects given autologous biotin-labelled red cells, survival was measurable in all — and 3 of 20 transiently made antibodies to the labelled cells
cards.summary: Cordle & Mock 1999: in 20 healthy subjects given autologous biotin-labelled red cells, survival was measurable in all — and 3 of 20 transiently made antibodies to the labelled cells
cards.people: 20 healthy subjects transfused with autologous biotin-labelled red cells, with plasma screened before transfusion and serially for up to 6 months (and to 12 months in one subject), plus 20 non-transfused normal controls. Ns printed on the face.
cards.result: No control plasma and no pre-transfusion sample reacted with biotin-labelled cells, and post-transfusion recovery and survival of the labelled cells were determined in the transfused subjects — the method works in healthy volunteers. However, 3 of the 20 subjects transiently produced IgG antibodies to biotin-labelled red cells after transfusion (disappearing within 6 months in two and 12 months in the third), without altered circulating kinetics in those three. The record recommends antibody testing when multiple biotin-labelled transfusions are used to study red-cell volume or kinetics.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its healthy-volunteer survival measurements and its safety caveat; the abstract does not print the numerical survival values, so no lifespan figure is taken from this card.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Cordle DG et al. Antibodies provoked by the transfusion of biotin-labeled red cells. Transfusion. 1999. PMID: 10532599. cards.headline: Uchida 1976: corrected 51Cr and DF32P mean red-cell lifespan estimates agreed fairly well — the disagreement lives in the 51Cr elution correction (≤2.3%/day)
cards.summary: Uchida 1976: corrected 51Cr and DF32P mean red-cell lifespan estimates agreed fairly well — the disagreement lives in the 51Cr elution correction (≤2.3%/day)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (method comparison, normals and patients)
cards.people: Normal subjects and patients with various haematological disorders in whom mean red-cell life-span was measured with both 51Cr and DF32P, with 51Cr results corrected for chromium elution using correction factors. Subgroup Ns not documented in the fetched record's abstract.
cards.result: Mean red-cell life-span by the two methods agreed fairly well once 51Cr results were corrected for elution. The elution rate was 2.3% per day or less in the disorders studied, except where extracorpuscular haemolytic agents operated (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, congestive splenomegaly). The authors concluded that corrected 51Cr estimates are more useful and sufficient than uncorrected 51Cr or DF32P. Method-dependence is explicit: an uncorrected 51Cr curve understates lifespan because the label leaks from living cells — the same label-loss problem the biotin method shows in its first weeks.
cards.watchOut: Mixed normals-and-patients series with no subgroup Ns in the abstract; carded for the head-to-head method comparison and elution rates, not for a normals-only lifespan value.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Uchida T et al. Evaluation of recommended methods for radioisotopes red cell survival studies. Tohoku J Exp Med. 1976. PMID: 996847. cards.headline: Khera 2015: oral 15N-glycine labelling in 9 haematologically normal people measured a red-cell lifespan of 106 ± 21 days, with wide true variation between individuals
cards.summary: Khera 2015: oral 15N-glycine labelling in 9 haematologically normal people measured a red-cell lifespan of 106 ± 21 days, with wide true variation between individuals
cards.people: Nine haematologically normal diabetic and non-diabetic subjects whose red cells were labelled as an age cohort by oral 15N-glycine incorporation into heme; in seven, mean red-cell age by the biotin method from ~5 years earlier was available for comparison.
cards.result: Mean red-cell age was 58.7 ± 9.1 days and red-cell lifespan was 106 ± 21 days (values ± 2 SD as printed in the record) — a ±15–20% spread between haematologically normal individuals, consistent with previous techniques. Mean red-cell age by stable isotope correlated strongly with the same individuals' earlier biotin measurements (R² = 0.79): the variation is a stable personal trait, not measurement noise. The textbook ~120 days is thus the top of a genuinely variable normal range centred nearer ~106–120 days depending on method.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, printed on the face, mixing diabetic and non-diabetic (all haematologically normal) subjects; the ±21 days is printed as 2 SD, so the SD is ~10 days — do not quote 21 as the SD.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Khera PK et al. Use of an oral stable isotope label to confirm variation in red blood cell mean age that influences HbA1c interpretation. Am J Hematol. 2015. PMID: 25293624. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.people: Synthesis of Mock 1999, Cordle & Mock 1999, Uchida 1976 and Khera 2015, framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: A healthy red cell lives roughly four months. The modern isotope-cohort measurement puts lifespan at 106 ± 21 days (2 SD) with mean cell age 58.7 days, and shows the between-person spread is real and stable over years. The classic labels converge on the same answer only after correction: 51Cr leaks from living cells at up to ~2.3%/day, so uncorrected 51Cr curves understate lifespan, while corrected 51Cr agrees with DF32P; biotin enumeration agrees with 51Cr after its own early phase, in which about half the label (not half the cells) is lost. Senescent removal itself — splenic culling of stiffened, surface-changed old cells — is the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall); the carded records measure the lifespan, not the removal signal. Two named classics are deliberately not carded: Ashby's differential-agglutination survival studies (the original measurements) have no fetchable PubMed record, and the International Committee's 51Cr method document (PMID 7426443) returns an empty abstract, so its content could not be verified this session.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: every method measures a labelled cohort's disappearance, not individual cell ages; label elution (51Cr, biotin) is the standing artefact, and the ~120-day textbook figure and the 106-day isotope figure differ by method and cohort, not by error alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID: 10037125; PMID: 10532599; PMID: 996847; PMID: 25293624. Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: Platelet survival and production in health: ~8.4–9.3 days, near-linear disappearance, and a third of the pool resting in the spleen
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how long do platelets circulate and how fast are they produced — what did radiolabelled-platelet survival studies measure (~9–10 days, linear versus exponential disappearance), and what fraction of production replaces the circulating pool daily, including splenic pooling of the labelled cohort?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). Two independent 111In programmes in healthy volunteers put mean survival at 8.4 ± 0.8 days (Hill-Zobel, PMID 3766525, N = 12) and 224 ± 23 hours ≈ 9.3 days with near-linear disappearance (Wessels & Heyns, PMID 3928383, N = 28); only ~60% of labelled platelets are recovered in blood because roughly a third pools exchangeably in the spleen. The label matters at the second digit: 51Cr reads slightly longer than 111In and needs no free-label correction (Dewanjee, PMID 3084883). Harker & Finch's programme founded this field; its fetched records were patient cohorts, so its normal-control values are not carded here — the healthy-volunteer numbers above carry the pack.

cards.headline: Hill-Zobel 1986: in 12 normal volunteers, 111In platelet mean survival was 8.4 ± 0.8 days, only 59% was recovered in blood — the spleen held ~43% within 30 minutes
cards.summary: Hill-Zobel 1986: in 12 normal volunteers, 111In platelet mean survival was 8.4 ± 0.8 days, only 59% was recovered in blood — the spleen held ~43% within 30 minutes
cards.people: 12 normal volunteers (plus 4 asplenic subjects and 4 patients with splenomegaly) given autologous 111In-oxine-labelled platelets, with serial blood sampling and organ imaging; normal-volunteer figures are the ones quoted here.
cards.result: In normal controls, initial recovery of infused labelled platelets was 59.2 ± 9.3% — the missing ~40% is the exchangeable splenic pool: at 30 minutes 42.7 ± 12.2% of the infused platelets had pooled in the spleen (liver 12.6 ± 3.7%). Mean platelet survival by the multiple-hit model was 8.4 ± 0.8 days in normals (9.2 ± 1.0 asplenic; 6.2 ± 0.6 splenomegaly). At 10 days, 37% of the label was sequestered in spleen and 24% in liver of normal subjects — together 61% of destruction accounted for by those two organs.
cards.watchOut: Survival depends on the model fitted (multiple-hit here); the asplenic and splenomegaly arms are comparators that prove the splenic pooling interpretation, not healthy physiology themselves.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Hill-Zobel RL et al. Organ distribution and fate of human platelets: studies of asplenic and splenomegalic patients. Am J Hematol. 1986. PMID: 3766525. cards.headline: Wessels & Heyns 1985: with a representative platelet harvest in 28 normal volunteers, disappearance was almost linear and mean survival was 224 ± 23 hours (~9.3 days)
cards.summary: Wessels & Heyns 1985: with a representative platelet harvest in 28 normal volunteers, disappearance was almost linear and mean survival was 224 ± 23 hours (~9.3 days)
cards.people: 28 normal human volunteers whose platelets were harvested by repeated washing from the red-cell layer (harvesting efficiency 98.3 ± 2.8%, labelling efficiency 86.4 ± 6.8% with 111In-oxine), reinjected autologously and followed, with whole-body quantification in 6 volunteers.
cards.result: The disappearance of labelled platelets was almost linear — consistent with predominantly age-dependent (senescent) removal rather than random destruction. Mean platelet survival was 224 ± 23 hours (≈ 9.3 days). At equilibrium 61 ± 12% of labelled platelets were recovered in the circulation, with 31.1 ± 6.1% in the spleen and 9.6 ± 1.2% in the liver; by the end of the lifespan, sequestration had risen to 35.6 ± 9.7% (spleen) and 28.7 ± 8.3% (liver). A ~9-day lifespan implies roughly one-ninth of the circulating-plus-pooled platelet mass — about 11% — is replaced daily (arithmetic derived from the carded lifespan).
cards.watchOut: The method was designed to fix a real bias — standard harvests lose a functionally active subpopulation — so its slightly longer survival (9.3 versus 8.4 days) may be the more representative figure; the daily-replacement percentage is arithmetic from the lifespan, not a directly measured production rate in this record.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Wessels P et al. An improved method for the quantification of the in vivo kinetics of a representative population of 111In-labelled human platelets. Eur J Nucl Med. 1985. PMID: 3928383. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Dewanjee 1986: the label changes the answer — in healthy volunteers 51Cr gave slightly longer platelet survival than either 111In label, with a sex difference seen only with 51Cr
cards.summary: Dewanjee 1986: the label changes the answer — in healthy volunteers 51Cr gave slightly longer platelet survival than either 111In label, with a sex difference seen only with 51Cr
cards.people: Healthy volunteers whose platelet survival was measured with three markers: 51Cr (disodium chromate), 111In-oxine in ACD-saline, and 111In-tropolone in ACD-plasma. N not documented in the fetched record's abstract.
cards.result: Mean platelet survival with 51Cr was slightly longer than with both indium labels and showed a sex difference not seen with 111In-oxine; the two indium labels gave similar survival results to each other. The differences were attributed to where the label sits on the cell and how the kidney handles free label after release: protein-bound plasma 51Cr stayed low and constant, while plasma 111In rose with time — so 111In survival calculations require routine correction for free label, and 51Cr calculations do not. Method-dependence is therefore printed on the face of this pack: 'platelet survival' is ~8–10 days by any label, but the second digit belongs to the method.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints no N and no numerical survival times — carded for the head-to-head label comparison and the free-label correction rule, with the numerical values in this pack taken from the Hill-Zobel and Wessels cards.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Dewanjee MK et al. Comparison of three platelet markers for measurement of platelet survival time in healthy volunteers. Mayo Clin Proc. 1986. PMID: 3084883. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Synthesis: Platelet survival and production in health: ~8.4–9.3 days, near-linear disappearance, and a third of the pool resting in the spleen
cards.summary: Synthesis: Platelet survival and production in health: ~8.4–9.3 days, near-linear disappearance, and a third of the pool resting in the spleen
cards.people: Synthesis of Hill-Zobel 1986, Wessels & Heyns 1985 and Dewanjee 1986, framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: A healthy platelet circulates for about 9 days (8.4 ± 0.8 days by multiple-hit modelling of 111In survival; 224 ± 23 hours ≈ 9.3 days with a representative harvest), so about one-ninth of the total platelet mass — roughly 11% — must be produced daily to hold the count steady (arithmetic from the carded lifespans). Disappearance is almost linear, the signature of senescence-limited removal with only a small random component, and the spleen is both reservoir and graveyard: ~31–43% of labelled platelets pool there exchangeably at equilibrium (which is why only ~59–61% are ever recovered in blood), and spleen plus liver account for most terminal sequestration. Estimates are method-dependent at the margins — 51Cr reads slightly longer than 111In labels and handles free label differently — so the honest statement is a range, ~8–10 days, with the method named.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: survival values are model-dependent (multiple-hit versus linear fits differ), and production rates here are derived from lifespan plus pool sizes rather than measured by a direct production assay in healthy volunteers.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID: 3766525; PMID: 3928383; PMID: 3084883. Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: Neutrophil turnover: marrow transit is settled (~6.6 days, ~0.9 × 10⁹/kg/day) — blood lifespan is not (hours by DF32P versus 5.4 days by deuterium)
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast do neutrophils turn over — what is the circulating half-life measured by in-vivo labelling (DF32P and modern deuterium studies), how large is the marginated pool relative to the circulating pool on epinephrine/exercise mobilisation, and how long is marrow transit from mitosis to release?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). The stamp is EMERGING because the central number is genuinely unsettled: the classic DF32P programme implied a blood half-life of hours, but Dancey (PMID 956397, N = 13 normals) showed inside one study that DF32P elutes and overstates turnover (1.62 versus 0.87 × 10⁹/kg/day by thymidine), while Pillay's in-vivo deuterium labelling (PMID 20410504) measured a 5.4-day circulatory lifespan. What is settled: marrow postmitotic transit ~6.6 days and production ~0.85–0.87 × 10⁹/kg/day (Dancey), and a marginated pool comparable to the circulating pool within a total blood pool of 79 × 10⁷/kg (Bishop & Athens, PMID 5638121, N = 5). Both lifespan traditions are presented; neither is smoothed over.

cards.headline: Dancey 1976: in 13 normal subjects the postmitotic marrow pool was 5.59 × 10⁹/kg with a 6.6-day transit — and DF32P gave nearly double the turnover of 3H-thymidine in the same people
cards.summary: Dancey 1976: in 13 normal subjects the postmitotic marrow pool was 5.59 × 10⁹/kg with a 6.6-day transit — and DF32P gave nearly double the turnover of 3H-thymidine in the same people
cards.people: 13 normal human subjects in whom marrow neutrophil cellularity was measured from marrow sections and erythron iron turnover, maturational categories were checked by 3H-thymidine autoradiography, and circulating turnover was measured with both 3H-thymidine and DF32P labelling, including doubly labelled isologous cells.
cards.result: Total marrow neutrophils were 7.70 ± 1.20 × 10⁹ cells/kg: mitotic pool 2.11 ± 0.36, postmitotic pool (metamyelocytes, bands, segmented) 5.59 ± 0.90 × 10⁹/kg. Postmitotic transit time was 6.60 ± 0.03 days, giving marrow production of 0.85 × 10⁹ cells/kg/day; effective production from 3H-thymidine-labelled circulating cells was 0.87 ± 0.13 — in agreement. But DF32P labelling of circulating neutrophils gave a turnover of 1.62 ± 0.46 × 10⁹ cells/kg/day, and doubly labelled cells showed lower recovery and a shorter half-life for the 32P label — the classic label elutes, so DF32P overstates turnover and understates blood half-life. Method-dependence is demonstrated inside one study, in normal man.
cards.watchOut: The famous short blood half-life of the Athens DF32P programme is not printed as a number in this record's abstract — only that DF32P gave a shorter half-life and lower recovery than thymidine; the hours-scale half-life quoted in teaching is the textbook's account of that programme, labelled as such in this pack.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Dancey JT et al. Neutrophil kinetics in man. J Clin Invest. 1976. PMID: 956397. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Bishop & Athens 1968: in 5 normal subjects the total blood granulocyte pool was 79 × 10⁷/kg — and cortisol expanded both the circulating and the marginated pools (to 138) while cutting egress to tissue by ~75%
cards.summary: Bishop & Athens 1968: in 5 normal subjects the total blood granulocyte pool was 79 × 10⁷/kg — and cortisol expanded both the circulating and the marginated pools (to 138) while cutting egress to tissue by ~75%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Athens DF32P programme)
cards.people: Five normal subjects whose granulocytes were labelled with radioactive diisopropylfluorophosphate (DF32P) before and after an intravenous injection of 200 mg cortisol, with egress measured by the skin-window technique.
cards.result: At baseline the mean total blood granulocyte pool was 79 × 10⁷ cells/kg, comprising circulating and marginal pools of comparable scale. After cortisol the pool rose to 138 × 10⁷ cells/kg, reflecting an increase in both the circulating and the marginal granulocyte pools; labelling showed the blood pool was simultaneously diluted at an accelerated rate by unlabelled cells entering from marrow, while egress of granulocytes to an inflammatory exudate fell by a mean of 75% (range 45–98%). Steroid granulocytosis is thus demargination plus marrow release plus reduced egress — and the marginated pool it reveals is roughly as large as the circulating pool it is usually hidden from.
cards.watchOut: N = 5, printed on the face, and a perturbation study: pool sizes are baseline measurements in normals, but the mobilisation figures describe the cortisol response, not resting physiology alone.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Bishop CR et al. Leukokinetic studies. 13. A non-steady-state kinetic evaluation of the mechanism of cortisone-induced granulocytosis. J Clin Invest. 1968. PMID: 5638121. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Pillay 2010: in-vivo 2H2O labelling measured a human circulatory neutrophil lifespan of 5.4 days — at least ten times the classic DF32P-based estimate
cards.summary: Pillay 2010: in-vivo 2H2O labelling measured a human circulatory neutrophil lifespan of 5.4 days — at least ten times the classic DF32P-based estimate
cards.people: Healthy humans labelled in vivo with heavy water (2H2O) under homeostatic conditions, with neutrophil lifespan estimated from label incorporation into and loss from circulating neutrophils (companion mouse experiments in the same report are not carded here). N not documented in the fetched record's abstract.
cards.result: In-vivo deuterium labelling gave an average circulatory neutrophil lifespan of 5.4 days — at least 10 times longer than the previously reported lifespans acquired by ex vivo labelling or manipulation (the DF32P lineage, which labels cells outside their normal state and whose label elutes, per the Dancey card). The authors argue the short classic lifespan is an artefact of the labelling method and that a 5.4-day lifespan forces reappraisal of neutrophil functions in health. The dispute is unresolved in the carded literature: marrow transit (~6.6 days, Dancey) is agreed; what is contested is how long the cell then spends in blood.
cards.watchOut: A model-dependent estimate from label kinetics, not a direct observation of single cells; subsequent modelling debate (deuterium availability and model assumptions) is real — which is why this pack's stamp is EMERGING, and why the classic and modern numbers are both kept on the face.

cards.headline: Synthesis: Neutrophil turnover: marrow transit is settled (~6.6 days, ~0.9 × 10⁹/kg/day) — blood lifespan is not (hours by DF32P versus 5.4 days by deuterium)
cards.summary: Synthesis: Neutrophil turnover: marrow transit is settled (~6.6 days, ~0.9 × 10⁹/kg/day) — blood lifespan is not (hours by DF32P versus 5.4 days by deuterium)
cards.people: Synthesis of Dancey 1976, Bishop & Athens 1968 and Pillay 2010, framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: Neutrophil production is well measured: a postmitotic marrow pool of ~5.6 × 10⁹/kg transiting in ~6.6 days delivers ~0.85–0.87 × 10⁹ cells/kg/day (thymidine-based, internally consistent by two routes in Dancey). In blood, roughly half the granulocytes are marginated at any moment — the total blood pool (79 × 10⁷/kg) is about double the circulating pool sampled by venepuncture, and cortisol can expand both pools while throttling egress. The lifespan dispute is methodological at root: DF32P labels cells ex vivo and elutes, yielding shorter half-lives and higher apparent turnover even in doubly labelled cells; in-vivo deuterium labelling, which labels DNA at division and follows the cohort, yields 5.4 days. Until a method without either artefact settles it, the honest face of this shelf carries both numbers with their methods attached — hence PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: epinephrine/exercise mobilisation is the classic clinical demonstration of the marginated pool, but no verifiable primary record of those specific experiments was fetched this session; the pool-size evidence carded here is the Athens programme's DF32P pool measurement under cortisol perturbation.
