shelves.title: Recaticimab (long-acting PCSK9 antibody, dosing up to every 12 weeks) for hypercholesterolaemia
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does recaticimab — a long-acting PCSK9 monoclonal antibody engineered for dosing intervals up to 12 weeks — compared with placebo on background therapy, lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.balance: Three phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from one programme in China agree: recaticimab lowered LDL cholesterol by roughly 45–62% relative to placebo across regimens given every 4, 8 or 12 weeks — as monotherapy in nonfamilial hypercholesterolaemia (REMAIN-1, n=703), as add-on to statins (REMAIN-2, n=689, effect maintained to week 48), and in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (REMAIN-3, n=143). An earlier phase 1b/2 study (n=110) showed the same pattern. SINGLE-REGION flag: every trial was conducted in China, where recaticimab (Jiangsu Hengrui) is approved; generalisability beyond that population is untested in print. SURROGATE flag: LDL cholesterol is the only efficacy outcome — there is no cardiovascular-event trial, so no event claim is made. Safety was comparable to placebo apart from more injection-site reactions. The extended dosing interval (up to every 12 weeks, versus every 2–4 weeks for the established PCSK9 antibodies) is the intervention's distinguishing feature and held up at the 450 mg every-12-weeks regimen in all three trials.

cards.headline: REMAIN-1 phase 3 (2024): recaticimab monotherapy lowered LDL cholesterol 45.0–52.8% relative to placebo, including at every-12-weeks dosing, n = 703
cards.summary: REMAIN-1 phase 3 (2024): recaticimab monotherapy lowered LDL cholesterol 45.0–52.8% relative to placebo, including at every-12-weeks dosing, n = 703
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, JACC 2024
cards.people: 703 patients in China with nonfamilial hypercholesterolaemia and mixed hyperlipidaemia at low-to-moderate ASCVD risk (fasting LDL cholesterol 2.6 to <4.9 mmol/L [≈101 to <190 mg/dL], fasting triglycerides ≤5.6 mmol/L [≈496 mg/dL], 10-year ASCVD risk <10%), randomised to subcutaneous recaticimab 150 mg every 4 weeks, 300 mg every 8 weeks or 450 mg every 12 weeks, or matching placebo, on background lipid-lowering diet, at 59 sites in China.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, recaticimab further reduced LDL cholesterol by 49.6% (95% CI 44.2% to 54.9%) at 150 mg every 4 weeks, 52.8% (48.3% to 57.2%) at 300 mg every 8 weeks and 45.0% (41.0% to 49.0%) at 450 mg every 12 weeks (P < 0.0001 for all) — relative reductions. Safety was comparable to placebo; with 24 weeks of treatment the most common treatment-related adverse event was injection-site reaction (23 patients, 4.9%).
cards.watchOut: Monotherapy on a background diet, in a low-to-moderate-risk Chinese population; LDL cholesterol is a surrogate — no cardiovascular outcomes. Primary endpoints were read at week 12 or 16 by regimen, with treatment continued to week 24.
cards.source: Xu M, Wang Z, Zhang Y, et al. Recaticimab Monotherapy for Nonfamilial Hypercholesterolemia and Mixed Hyperlipemia: The Phase 3 REMAIN-1 Randomized Trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;84(20):2026-2036. PMID: 39387764. No registry ID appears in the fetched record. cards.headline: REMAIN-2 phase 3 (2024): recaticimab added to statins lowered LDL cholesterol 53.4–62.2% relative to placebo at week 24, sustained to week 48, n = 689
cards.summary: REMAIN-2 phase 3 (2024): recaticimab added to statins lowered LDL cholesterol 53.4–62.2% relative to placebo at week 24, sustained to week 48, n = 689
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, JACC 2024
cards.people: 689 patients with nonfamilial hypercholesterolaemia on stable moderate- or high-intensity statin (with or without ezetimibe or fenofibrate) for at least 4 weeks, with LDL cholesterol ≥1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) if they had ASCVD or ≥2.6 mmol/L (≈101 mg/dL) if not (mean age 55.8 years; 64.4% male; ASCVD history 69.5%; mean baseline LDL cholesterol 2.8 mmol/L [≈108 mg/dL]), randomised to recaticimab 150 mg every 4 weeks, 300 mg every 8 weeks or 450 mg every 12 weeks, or matching placebo, for 48 weeks.
cards.result: Percentage change in LDL cholesterol from baseline to week 24 differed from placebo by −62.2% (95% CI −67.0% to −57.4%), −59.7% (−65.0% to −54.4%) and −53.4% (−58.7% to −48.2%) for the three regimens respectively (P < 0.0001) — relative reductions, maintained through week 48. Non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) also favoured recaticimab. Treatment-related adverse events (28.5% vs 26.6%) and serious treatment-related adverse events (0.4% vs 0.4%) were similarly low in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Add-on design: the comparison is recaticimab plus statin versus placebo plus statin, so the figures are the antibody's added effect on top of statins. Single-country (China) evidence; surrogate endpoint only.
cards.source: Sun Y, Lv Q, Guo Y, et al. Recaticimab as Add-On Therapy to Statins for Nonfamilial Hypercholesterolemia: The Randomized, Phase 3 REMAIN-2 Trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;84(20):2037-2047. PMID: 39505412. No registry ID appears in the fetched record. cards.headline: REMAIN-3 phase 3 in HeFH (2025): LDL cholesterol fell 54.4% on recaticimab 150 mg every 4 weeks versus 4.5% on placebo at week 12, n = 143
cards.summary: REMAIN-3 phase 3 in HeFH (2025): LDL cholesterol fell 54.4% on recaticimab 150 mg every 4 weeks versus 4.5% on placebo at week 12, n = 143
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Cardiovascular Research 2025
cards.people: 143 patients at 25 sites in China with a genetic or clinical diagnosis of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, on stable lipid-lowering therapy for at least 28 days, with fasting LDL cholesterol ≥2.6 mmol/L (≈101 mg/dL), or ≥1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) with a history of ASCVD, and fasting triglycerides ≤5.6 mmol/L (≈496 mg/dL), randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous recaticimab 150 mg (n=95) or placebo (n=48) every 4 weeks for 12 weeks.
cards.result: At week 12 the mean percentage change in LDL cholesterol was −54.4% (95% CI −57.9 to −50.8%) on recaticimab versus −4.5% (−9.4 to 0.3%) on placebo, a treatment difference of −49.8 percentage points (95% CI −55.8 to −43.9; P < 0.0001) — a relative reduction. Non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) also improved. Treatment-related adverse events were comparable (27.4% vs 25.0%); injection-site reaction (8.4% vs 0%) and increased blood creatine phosphokinase (5.3% vs 2.1%) were more frequent on recaticimab.
cards.watchOut: REMAIN-3 tested only the every-4-weeks regimen, so the extended-interval claim in HeFH rests on REMAIN-1 and REMAIN-2. Twelve weeks is short, the trial is single-country, and LDL cholesterol is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: Phase 1b/2 (2022): recaticimab on atorvastatin lowered LDL cholesterol 48.4–59.5% relative to placebo across schedules up to every 12 weeks, n = 110
cards.summary: Phase 1b/2 (2022): recaticimab on atorvastatin lowered LDL cholesterol 48.4–59.5% relative to placebo across schedules up to every 12 weeks, n = 110
cards.type: Phase 1b/2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, BMC Medicine 2022
cards.people: 110 patients with hypercholesterolaemia on a stable dose of atorvastatin 10 or 20 mg/day with LDL cholesterol ≥2.6 mmol/L (≈101 mg/dL) (main baseline range 3.360–3.759 mmol/L [≈130–145 mg/dL]), randomised 5:1 to subcutaneous recaticimab (91 patients) or placebo (19) at schedules from 75 mg every 4 weeks to 450 mg every 12 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean percentage reductions in LDL cholesterol from baseline to end of treatment, relative to placebo, ranged from −48.37% to −59.51% across the recaticimab dose and schedule groups — relative reductions. No serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred; the most common events were upper respiratory tract infection and increases in alanine aminotransferase, blood glucose and gamma-glutamyltransferase.
cards.watchOut: Early-phase, small per-schedule cohorts recruited sequentially rather than in parallel; hypothesis-confirming support for the phase 3 programme, not independent proof. Background statin was moderate-intensity atorvastatin only.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials agree on large LDL reductions at intervals up to 12 weeks — in China, on a surrogate endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials agree on large LDL reductions at intervals up to 12 weeks — in China, on a surrogate endpoint
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: REMAIN-1 (703), REMAIN-2 (689), REMAIN-3 (143) and the phase 1b/2 study (110) — 1,645 randomised patients in total, all in China.
cards.result: Every randomised comparison points the same way: recaticimab lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly half relative to placebo, whether given alone, added to a statin, or in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, and the 450 mg every-12-weeks regimen retains most of the effect of monthly dosing. That concordance across three phase 3 trials earns LIKELY for the LDL question asked. What the evidence does not show: any cardiovascular-event benefit, any data outside China, or safety beyond about a year.
cards.watchOut: Do not extrapolate the LDL reduction to event reduction: no outcomes trial of recaticimab has been published. Approval and availability are currently China-specific.
cards.source: Synthesis of the four cards above (PMIDs 39387764, 39505412, 40911402, 35039035). No additional source.

shelves.title: Sovleplenib for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ESLIM-01)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic immune thrombocytopenia who have failed prior therapy, does the SYK inhibitor sovleplenib, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic/drug therapy · Platelet Count · Syk Kinase/antagonists & inhibitors · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Chronic Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-country (China), single-programme record. The phase 3 ESLIM-01 trial (188 patients, all Asian, median 4 previous lines of therapy) found a durable platelet response in 48% on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo, and the earlier phase 1b/2 trial pointed the same way at the 300 mg dose; a 2026 network meta-analysis of the kinase-inhibitor trials in ITP is consistent. That caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no trial outside China, no head-to-head against another SYK inhibitor, and no bleeding or mortality endpoint. The same-target drug fostamatinib is homed on its own shelf (#1800) and the thrombopoietin receptor agonists for ITP are homed separately (live shelf #672) — those records are not carded here. Harms in ESLIM-01 were mostly mild or moderate; grade 3 or higher neutrophil-count decrease and hypertension each occurred in 3% on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo, and serious treatment-emergent events were 21% versus 18%.

cards.headline: Phase 1b/2 trial (Liu 2023): at the recommended 300 mg dose, 63% met the early platelet endpoint versus 9% on placebo, and the overall response rate was 80% on continuous 300 mg treatment
cards.summary: Phase 1b/2 trial (Liu 2023): at the recommended 300 mg dose, 63% met the early platelet endpoint versus 9% on placebo, and the overall response rate was 80% on continuous 300 mg treatment
cards.people: 45 adults aged 18–75 in China with primary immune thrombocytopenia for more than 6 months who had not responded to, or had relapsed after, first-line treatment (or had relapsed after splenectomy), randomised 3:1 across sovleplenib dose groups (100, 200, 300 or 400 mg once daily) or placebo for an 8-week double-blind period, followed by a 16-week open-label period on sovleplenib. All participants were Asian; median age 40 years.
cards.result: The main endpoint (platelet count at least 30 × 10⁹/L and double baseline at two consecutive visits in weeks 0–8 without rescue therapy) was met by 3 of 6 (50%) at 100 mg, 3 of 6 (50%) at 200 mg, 10 of 16 (63%) at 300 mg and 2 of 6 (33%) at 400 mg, versus 1 of 11 (9%) on placebo. In the 300 mg group the overall response rate over 0–24 weeks was 80% (16 of 20, counting continuous treatment plus placebo crossovers). The recommended phase 2 dose was set at 300 mg once daily. No fatal treatment-emergent adverse events were recorded.
cards.watchOut: Very small dose groups (6–16 patients each) with wide confidence intervals — this report dose-finds and signals activity; it cannot estimate the response rate precisely. The 80% overall response figure mixes randomised and crossover/open-label treatment.
cards.source: Liu X et al. Sovleplenib (HMPL-523), a novel Syk inhibitor, for patients with primary immune thrombocytopenia in China: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 1b/2 study. The Lancet. Haematology. 2023. PMID: 37028433. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03951623. cards.headline: ESLIM-01 phase 3 (Hu 2024): durable platelet response in 48% (61/126) on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo (difference 48%, p<0.0001)
cards.summary: ESLIM-01 phase 3 (Hu 2024): durable platelet response in 48% (61/126) on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo (difference 48%, p<0.0001)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Hu 2024, ESLIM-01)
cards.people: 188 adults aged 18–75 with chronic primary immune thrombocytopenia and ECOG performance status 0–1 who had received one or more previous treatments, at 34 centres in China, randomised 2:1 to oral sovleplenib 300 mg once daily (126) or placebo (62) for 24 weeks. 66% were female, all were of Asian ethnicity, the median number of previous ITP therapy lines was 4, and 71% had previously received thrombopoietin or a thrombopoietin receptor agonist.
cards.result: Durable response (platelet count at least 50 × 10⁹/L on at least four of six scheduled visits between weeks 14 and 24, unaffected by rescue treatment) occurred in 61 of 126 (48%) on sovleplenib versus 0 of 62 on placebo (difference 48%, 95% CI 40–57; p<0.0001). Median time to response was 8 days versus 30 days. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 99% versus 85%, mostly mild or moderate; grade 3 or higher events included decreased platelet count (7% vs 10%), decreased neutrophil count (3% vs 0%) and hypertension (3% vs 0%). Serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 21% versus 18%; there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Single-country trial in an all-Asian population with heavily pretreated disease — generalisability beyond that setting is untested. The endpoint is a platelet-count response, not bleeding or survival, and follow-up in the blinded phase was 24 weeks.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis (Abulehia 2026): across five kinase-inhibitor trials in ITP (660 patients), sovleplenib 300 mg had the largest platelet-response ratio versus placebo — an indirect comparison only
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis (Abulehia 2026): across five kinase-inhibitor trials in ITP (660 patients), sovleplenib 300 mg had the largest platelet-response ratio versus placebo — an indirect comparison only
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of five clinical trials (660 patients in total) of Bruton tyrosine kinase and spleen tyrosine kinase inhibitors (rilzabrutinib, sovleplenib and fostamatinib) versus placebo in primary immune thrombocytopenia, analysed with a frequentist random-effects model.
cards.result: All three drugs significantly improved platelet response (at least 50 × 10⁹/L) versus placebo. Sovleplenib 300 mg showed the largest relative effect (risk ratio 30.51, 95% CI 4.33–214.90 — a relative measure with a very wide interval, reflecting the 0% placebo response in its trial), followed by rilzabrutinib and fostamatinib. No significant differences in overall adverse events were found, and no clear class-level superiority was established; the authors call for large head-to-head trials.
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons across trials with different populations and response definitions; the extreme risk ratio for sovleplenib is driven by a zero-event placebo arm and its confidence interval spans 4 to 215. This card corroborates direction, not ranking.
cards.source: Abulehia A et al. Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Bruton Tyrosine Kinase and Spleen Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors in Immune Thrombocytopenia: A Network Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials. EJHaem. 2026. PMID: 42894830. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: sovleplenib produces durable platelet responses in heavily pretreated chronic ITP in the Chinese trial programme — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: sovleplenib produces durable platelet responses in heavily pretreated chronic ITP in the Chinese trial programme — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports: one phase 1b/2 trial (45 patients), one phase 3 trial (188 patients) and one network meta-analysis (five trials, 660 patients).
cards.result: Both randomised trials of sovleplenib itself were positive on platelet response, with the phase 3 durable-response difference of 48 percentage points against a 0% placebo rate. The evidence is one programme in one country, with a surrogate (platelet-count) endpoint and 24 weeks of blinded follow-up, so the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit), not higher. Nothing here compares sovleplenib directly with fostamatinib (homed at shelf #1800) or with the thrombopoietin receptor agonists (homed at live shelf #672).
cards.watchOut: An open-label extension of ESLIM-01 was described as ongoing in the phase 3 report; no journal report of it was found this session, so long-term durability beyond the carded follow-up is unproven.
cards.source: Synthesis of Liu X et al. The Lancet. Haematology. 2023 (PMID: 37028433); Hu Y et al. The Lancet. Haematology. 2024 (PMID: 38885672); Abulehia A et al. EJHaem. 2026 (PMID: 42894830), all carded above.

shelves.title: Rituximab for immune thrombocytopenia (RITP)
shelves.question: In adults with primary immune thrombocytopenia unresponsive to corticosteroids, does rituximab, versus placebo, reduce long-term treatment failure (splenectomy or meeting splenectomy criteria) and produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic/drug therapy · Rituximab/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Recurrence · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the record splits by time horizon. Short-term platelet responses are common on rituximab (81% overall response in RITP versus 73% on placebo, not significant; about 65% at 3 months in the low-dose randomised comparison), and responders who do respond stay in response longer on rituximab (median 8.2 versus 1.8 months in the RITP extended follow-up). But the only placebo-controlled trial powered on the outcome that matters — long-term treatment failure (splenectomy or meeting splenectomy criteria) — was negative: 58% versus 69% failure, hazard ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.55–1.45, p=0.65), and by 5 years only about one in five patients in the low-dose trial remained in sustained response on either regimen. Harms to weigh: in RITP, infections occurred in 40% on rituximab versus 24% on placebo (p=0.09), and rituximab carries the class risks of infusion reactions, prolonged B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinaemia with repeated courses. Rituximab's records in vasculitis, Sjögren syndrome, myositis and lupus nephritis are homed on their own shelves and are not carded here — this shelf is the ITP question only.

cards.headline: RITP trial (Ghanima 2015): treatment failure 58% on rituximab versus 69% on placebo (HR 0.89, p=0.65) — the primary endpoint was NEGATIVE, despite an 81% overall response rate
cards.summary: RITP trial (Ghanima 2015): treatment failure 58% on rituximab versus 69% on placebo (HR 0.89, p=0.65) — the primary endpoint was NEGATIVE, despite an 81% overall response rate
cards.people: 112 adults (109 treated and analysed: 55 rituximab, 54 placebo) with primary immune thrombocytopenia unresponsive to corticosteroids and platelet counts below 30 × 10⁹/L, in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial; treatment was four weekly infusions of rituximab 375 mg/m² or placebo, with corticosteroids the only permitted concurrent therapy, followed for 78 weeks.
cards.result: Treatment failure (splenectomy, or meeting splenectomy criteria after week 12) occurred in 32 of 55 (58%) on rituximab versus 37 of 54 (69%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.55–1.45; p=0.65). Overall response was 81% versus 73% (p=0.15) and complete response 58% versus 50% (p=0.12). Among responders, time to relapse was longer on rituximab for overall response (36 vs 7 weeks; p=0.01). Bleeding occurred in 38% versus 50% (p=0.08) and infection in 40% versus 24% (p=0.09).
cards.watchOut: The trial was not powered to exclude a small benefit — the confidence interval (0.55–1.45) is wide — so the honest reading is 'no demonstrated reduction in long-term treatment failure', not proof of no effect. Response rates on placebo were strikingly high (73%), reflecting concurrent corticosteroids and the natural history of ITP.
cards.source: Ghanima W et al. Rituximab as second-line treatment for adult immune thrombocytopenia (the RITP trial): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 25662413. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00344149. cards.headline: RITP extended follow-up (Tjønnfjord 2020): responses lasted longer on rituximab (median 8.2 vs 1.8 months), most patients still relapsed, and splenectomy was 13 versus 22 (p=0.12)
cards.summary: RITP extended follow-up (Tjønnfjord 2020): responses lasted longer on rituximab (median 8.2 vs 1.8 months), most patients still relapsed, and splenectomy was 13 versus 22 (p=0.12)
cards.type: Extended follow-up report of the RITP randomised trial (Tjønnfjord 2020)
cards.people: Extended retrospective follow-up of the RITP trial population: data were collected for 72 (83%) of the 84 patients who had not been splenectomised during the original 78-week trial, with a median follow-up after randomisation of 72 months (interquartile range 62–82).
cards.result: Median duration of response among initial responders was 8.2 months (interquartile range 5.5–16.7) on rituximab versus 1.8 months (1.3–3.6) on placebo (p=0.036). In total 35 patients underwent splenectomy (13 rituximab, 22 placebo; p=0.12). Eleven patients (10%) died during the study — five on rituximab and six on placebo — including four deaths from severe bleeding. The authors conclude that most rituximab-treated patients eventually relapsed.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same trial, not an independent trial — it extends the RITP record rather than adding a new one. Follow-up data were retrospective and missing for 17% of the non-splenectomised patients, and the splenectomy difference did not reach significance.
cards.source: Tjønnfjord E et al. Long-term outcomes of patients treated with rituximab as second-line treatment for adult immune thrombocytopenia - Follow-up of the RITP study. British journal of haematology. 2020. PMID: 32342497. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Low-dose rituximab dose-comparison RCT (Chen 2026): two low-dose regimens performed the same — about 65% response at 3 months, falling to about 18–20% sustained at 5 years
cards.summary: Low-dose rituximab dose-comparison RCT (Chen 2026): two low-dose regimens performed the same — about 65% response at 3 months, falling to about 18–20% sustained at 5 years
cards.type: Randomised open-label dose-comparison trial with 5-year follow-up (Chen 2026)
cards.people: 104 Chinese adults with glucocorticoid-resistant/dependent or relapsed immune thrombocytopenia in a multicentre prospective open-label randomised trial, assigned 1:1 to rituximab 100 mg weekly for 4 weeks (49 completed) or a single rituximab 375 mg/m² dose (51 completed), with response followed until relapse or for 5 years and safety assessed at 1 year.
cards.result: Overall response at 3 months was 65.3% (32/49) with weekly low-dose versus 64.7% (33/51) with the single dose; complete response 42.9% versus 39.2%. Sustained response rates fell steadily in both groups — at 5 years, 20.4% versus 17.6% — with no statistically significant differences between regimens at any time point. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract and pulmonary infections.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or standard-dose arm: this trial compares two ways of giving rituximab, so it cannot show whether rituximab beats no rituximab — that question belongs to RITP. Its value here is the 5-year attrition curve: roughly four of five initial responders had relapsed by 5 years on either regimen.
cards.source: Chen Y et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of low-dose rituximab in immune thrombocytopenia: a multicentre, prospective, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Annals of hematology. 2026. PMID: 41741872. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01719692. cards.headline: Synthesis: rituximab raises platelets in most patients for a time, but has not been shown to change the long-term course of ITP — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: rituximab raises platelets in most patients for a time, but has not been shown to change the long-term course of ITP — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports: the RITP placebo-controlled trial (112 patients) and its extended follow-up, plus an independent low-dose dose-comparison randomised trial (104 patients) with 5-year follow-up.
cards.result: The split is consistent across reports: response rates of roughly 65–81% early on, longer response duration than placebo among responders, but no demonstrated reduction in long-term treatment failure or splenectomy in the one placebo-controlled trial, and sustained response in only about one in five patients at 5 years. A clinician choosing rituximab is buying months of response for many patients, not a proven change in the disease's long-term course.
cards.watchOut: Observational series report higher long-term remission rates than these randomised reports; the randomised record is the one carded here, and it is the more conservative — and more trustworthy — estimate.

shelves.title: Avatrombopag for immune thrombocytopenia
shelves.question: In adults and in children with chronic immune thrombocytopenia and an insufficient response to prior therapy, does avatrombopag, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic/drug therapy,blood · Receptors, Thrombopoietin/agonists · Platelet Count · Thiazoles/therapeutic use · Thiophenes/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant trials, but the adult pivotal trial randomised only 49 patients, which keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Avatrombopag beat placebo on platelet response in adults (median 12.4 versus 0.0 cumulative weeks of response; day-8 response 65.6% versus 0%) and in children and adolescents (durable response 28% versus 0%), and a small open-label Japanese phase 3 study (19 patients, labelled as such) was consistent. This shelf is the avatrombopag slice only: the thrombopoietin receptor agonist class question for ITP is homed at live shelf #672, which cards romiplostim and eltrombopag — those studies are not carded here — and avatrombopag's other indications are homed separately (chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia at pack #2819; pre-procedure use in chronic liver disease at pack #6129). The endpoint throughout is platelet response, a surrogate; no carded trial was powered for bleeding or mortality. Class cautions for thrombopoietin receptor agonists (thrombosis at high platelet counts, dose holds above 250 × 10⁹/L in the paediatric programme) belong in counselling.

cards.headline: Adult phase 3 trial (Jurczak 2018): median cumulative weeks of platelet response 12.4 on avatrombopag versus 0.0 on placebo (p<0.0001); day-8 response 65.6% versus 0%
cards.summary: Adult phase 3 trial (Jurczak 2018): median cumulative weeks of platelet response 12.4 on avatrombopag versus 0.0 on placebo (p<0.0001); day-8 response 65.6% versus 0%
cards.people: 49 adults with chronic immune thrombocytopenia and platelet counts below 30 × 10⁹/L, in a 6-month multicentre randomised double-blind parallel-group phase 3 study (32 avatrombopag 20 mg/day, 17 placebo), with an open-label extension phase.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — cumulative number of weeks of platelet response (at least 50 × 10⁹/L) without rescue therapy — was a median of 12.4 weeks on avatrombopag versus 0.0 weeks on placebo (p<0.0001). At day 8, platelet response was 65.63% versus 0.0% (p<0.0001), and use of concomitant ITP medications was reduced on avatrombopag. The most common adverse events were headache and contusion, and the safety profile was consistent with the earlier phase 2 studies.
cards.watchOut: Only 49 patients — a very small pivotal trial, with a 0% placebo response that flatters the contrast. Results are a platelet-count surrogate over 6 months, not bleeding outcomes.

cards.headline: Paediatric phase 3b trial AVA-PED-301 (Grace 2025): durable platelet response 28% (15/54) on avatrombopag versus 0% on placebo (p=0.0077) in children and adolescents
cards.summary: Paediatric phase 3b trial AVA-PED-301 (Grace 2025): durable platelet response 28% (15/54) on avatrombopag versus 0% on placebo (p=0.0077) in children and adolescents
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3b trial (Grace 2025, AVA-PED-301)
cards.people: 75 children and adolescents aged 1 to under 18 years with primary immune thrombocytopenia for at least 6 months and an insufficient response to previous treatment, in a global multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3b study, assigned 3:1 to avatrombopag (54; 20 mg tablet daily if aged 6 or over, 10 mg oral suspension daily if aged 1 to under 6, titrated to platelets 50–150 × 10⁹/L) or placebo (21), over a 12-week core phase.
cards.result: Durable platelet response (at least six of eight weekly counts at least 50 × 10⁹/L in the last 8 weeks, without rescue therapy) was achieved by 15 of 54 (28%) on avatrombopag versus 0 of 21 on placebo (difference 28%, 95% CI 16–40; p=0.0077); the alternative primary endpoint of platelet response was met by 44 of 54 (81%) versus 0% (p<0.0001). The most common adverse events were petechiae, epistaxis and headache; serious adverse events occurred in 9% versus 5%. No deaths, thromboembolic events or grade 3 or higher bleeding events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week core phase in 75 children — durability beyond 12 weeks and long-term safety in growing children rest on extension data, not on this blinded comparison. The durable-response rate (28%) is much lower than the any-response rate (81%); do not quote the larger figure as durability.
cards.source: Grace RF et al. Avatrombopag for the treatment of children and adolescents with immune thrombocytopenia (AVA-PED-301): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3b study. The Lancet. cards.headline: Japanese adult phase 3 study (Yamaguchi 2025) — open-label, no comparator, n=19: mean 13.5 cumulative weeks of platelet response; day-8 response 63.2%
cards.summary: Japanese adult phase 3 study (Yamaguchi 2025) — open-label, no comparator, n=19: mean 13.5 cumulative weeks of platelet response; day-8 response 63.2%
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 3 study — observational-style evidence, labelled as such (Yamaguchi 2025)
cards.people: 19 Japanese adults aged 18 or over with chronic immune thrombocytopenia (at least 12 months), an insufficient response to prior treatment and average platelet counts below 30 × 10⁹/L, in a confirmatory open-label phase 3 study of avatrombopag starting at 20 mg/day over a 26-week core phase. Mean age 56 years; 78.9% were female.
cards.result: The mean cumulative number of weeks of platelet response (at least 50 × 10⁹/L, without rescue therapy) was 13.5 weeks (95% CI 9.1–17.8). Platelet response at day 8 was achieved by 63.2% of patients. Adverse events occurred in 94.7% and serious adverse events in 15.8% during the core phase; there were no thromboembolic events or deaths.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients, no placebo arm: this study can show consistency with the randomised trials in a Japanese population, nothing more. It is carded as supporting evidence only and does not raise the stamp.

cards.headline: Synthesis: avatrombopag produces platelet responses in adults and in children with chronic ITP — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: avatrombopag produces platelet responses in adults and in children with chronic ITP — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports: the adult placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (49 patients), the paediatric placebo-controlled phase 3b trial (75 patients) and the open-label Japanese phase 3 study (19 patients) — 143 patients in total across the carded reports.
cards.result: Both placebo-controlled trials were clearly positive on platelet response, in adults and in children, and the small open-label study was consistent. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE (benefit) because the adult pivotal trial is small, the follow-up is short, and every endpoint is a platelet-count surrogate rather than bleeding. The class context — romiplostim and eltrombopag — is homed at live shelf #672 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc analysis of the paediatric trial exists; it re-analyses the same trial carded above and adds no new patients, so it is not carded separately (one home per study).

shelves.title: Afamelanotide for erythropoietic protoporphyria
shelves.question: In adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, does the afamelanotide 16 mg implant every 60 days, versus placebo, increase pain-free sunlight exposure and reduce phototoxic reactions?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Protoporphyria, Erythropoietic/drug therapy · alpha-MSH/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Sunlight/adverse effects · Pain/prevention & control · Drug Implants · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (combined 168 patients) both found more pain-free sunlight exposure and fewer phototoxic reactions on afamelanotide (Scenesse, Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals — the specific tested product, named under the clarification exception), and large observational cohorts since approval point the same way. Two cautions belong on the face. First, partial unblinding is intrinsic: the drug visibly darkens skin, so patients could often tell their allocation, and the endpoints are patient-reported exposure and pain — the randomised differences (median pain-free sunlight 69.4 vs 40.8 hours in the US trial; 6.0 vs 0.8 hours in the EU trial) should be read with that bias in mind; the far lower EU figures reflect different exposure recording and climate, not a different drug effect. Second, afamelanotide does not lower protoporphyrin: the US cohort found no improvement in protoporphyrin levels or liver biochemistries, so it treats light tolerance, not the underlying disease or its liver risk. The oral challenger for the same disease, bitopertin, is a separate question (see the bitopertin shelf).

cards.headline: Two phase 3 RCTs (Langendonk 2015): pain-free sunlight exposure was longer on afamelanotide in both trials — median 69.4 vs 40.8 hours (US, p=0.04) and 6.0 vs 0.8 hours (EU, p=0.005) — with fewer phototoxic reactions (77 vs 146 in the EU trial)
cards.summary: Two phase 3 RCTs (Langendonk 2015): pain-free sunlight exposure was longer on afamelanotide in both trials — median 69.4 vs 40.8 hours (US, p=0.04) and 6.0 vs 0.8 hours (EU, p=0.005) — with fewer phototoxic reactions (77 vs 146 in the EU trial)
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported together (Langendonk 2015)
cards.people: 168 adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria in two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials — 74 patients in the European Union and 94 in the United States — assigned 1:1 to a subcutaneous implant of afamelanotide 16 mg or placebo every 60 days (five implants over 270 days in the EU study; three over 180 days in the US study).
cards.result: In the US study, median duration of pain-free direct sunlight exposure after 6 months was 69.4 hours on afamelanotide versus 40.8 hours on placebo (p=0.04). In the EU study, median pain-free time after 9 months was 6.0 versus 0.8 hours (p=0.005), and phototoxic reactions numbered 77 on afamelanotide versus 146 on placebo (p=0.04). Quality of life improved with afamelanotide in both trials. Adverse events were mostly mild, and serious adverse events were not thought to be related to the study drug.
cards.watchOut: Partial unblinding is unavoidable — afamelanotide visibly darkens the skin — and both primary measures (hours of sunlight without pain, reaction counts) are patient-recorded, so expectation effects can inflate the differences. The tenfold difference in absolute hours between the US and EU trials shows how setting-dependent the endpoint is.
cards.source: Langendonk JG et al. Afamelanotide for Erythropoietic Protoporphyria. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26132941. cards.headline: German post-authorisation cohort (Homey 2025) — observational: 200 treated patients reported significantly improved quality of life, and 91% who started treatment were still on it
cards.summary: German post-authorisation cohort (Homey 2025) — observational: 200 treated patients reported significantly improved quality of life, and 91% who started treatment were still on it
cards.type: Observational post-authorisation registry cohort — no comparator (Homey 2025)
cards.people: 200 patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria enrolled in the German arm of the European post-authorisation safety study and disease registry (EUPAS13004), all of whom received afamelanotide 16 mg according to the product information; there was no untreated comparison group in this report. Observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Quality of life (EPP-QoL) increased significantly compared with baseline (p<0.0001), and 91.0% of patients who started treatment continued being treated. The short- and long-term safety profile under real-world conditions was consistent with the clinical trials, including in patients over 70 years of age.
cards.watchOut: No untreated controls and no blinded outcomes: continuation on treatment (91%) is a satisfaction signal, not proof of effect, and quality-of-life change from baseline in an unblinded registry is exactly the design most prone to expectation bias. Carded as real-world corroboration of the randomised trials, not as independent proof.
cards.source: Homey B et al. cards.headline: US single-centre cohort (Leaf 2024) — observational: median time to phototoxic symptoms after sunlight rose from 12.5 minutes before treatment to 120 minutes on afamelanotide (p<0.001), with no change in protoporphyrin levels
cards.summary: US single-centre cohort (Leaf 2024) — observational: median time to phototoxic symptoms after sunlight rose from 12.5 minutes before treatment to 120 minutes on afamelanotide (p<0.001), with no change in protoporphyrin levels
cards.people: 29 adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria or X-linked protoporphyria who received at least one afamelanotide dose at a single US porphyria centre in 2021–2022; 26 received at least two implants. Observational before-and-after evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Among patients receiving at least two implants, the median time to symptom onset after sunlight exposure was 12.5 minutes (interquartile range 5–20) before afamelanotide and 120 minutes (60–240) during treatment (p<0.001). Quality of life improved on two instruments. There were no improvements in median metal-free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, plasma protoporphyrin or liver biochemistries during versus before treatment.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine patients, no control group, and a self-reported time-to-symptoms endpoint in patients who knew they were treated — the tenfold rise is best read as consistent with the trials, not as a precise effect size. The null protoporphyrin and liver results are the important discipline: symptom benefit without disease modification.

cards.headline: Synthesis: afamelanotide increases pain-free light exposure in erythropoietic protoporphyria — LIKELY (benefit) for light tolerance, with no evidence of disease modification
cards.summary: Synthesis: afamelanotide increases pain-free light exposure in erythropoietic protoporphyria — LIKELY (benefit) for light tolerance, with no evidence of disease modification
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports: two randomised phase 3 trials (168 patients), a 200-patient observational registry cohort and a 29-patient observational US cohort.
cards.result: The randomised trials agree on direction for pain-free sunlight exposure and phototoxic reactions, and the observational record since approval is concordant, supporting LIKELY (benefit) for light tolerance and quality of life — discounted for the intrinsic partial unblinding of a skin-darkening drug with patient-reported endpoints. No carded report shows any effect on protoporphyrin levels or liver disease, so the benefit is symptomatic protection, not treatment of the underlying porphyria.
cards.watchOut: All carded evidence is in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (the small US cohort also included X-linked protoporphyria); paediatric use is not addressed by these reports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langendonk JG et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26132941); Homey B et al. Photodermatology, photoimmunology & photomedicine. 2025 (PMID: 40082741); Leaf RK et al. Life. 2024 (PMID: 38929673), all carded above.

shelves.title: Revumenib in relapsed or refractory acute leukaemia: about one in four patients reached complete remission in single-arm trials
shelves.question: In patients with relapsed/refractory acute leukaemia with KMT2A rearrangement (or NPM1-mutated AML), does the menin inhibitor revumenib produce complete remissions?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Histone-Lysine N-Methyltransferase/genetics* · Middle Aged · Adult · Myeloid-Lymphoid Leukemia Protein/genetics* · Male · Female · Aged · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy,genetics* · Young Adult · Nucleophosmin* · Adolescent · Proto-Oncogene Proteins/genetics* · Gene Rearrangement · Benzamides · Spiro Compounds
shelves.balance: Single-arm evidence throughout — there is no randomised comparator, so remission rates cannot be turned into a survival claim. In AUGMENT-101 phase 2, revumenib (Revuforj, Syndax Pharmaceuticals) produced complete remission or remission with partial haematological recovery (CR+CRh) in 22.8% of efficacy-evaluable patients with KMT2A-rearranged leukaemia (57 patients) and 23.4% in NPM1-mutated AML (64 efficacy-evaluable adults), with overall response rates of 63.2% and 46.9% respectively; the earlier phase 1 study reported a 30% CR/CRh rate. Class harms are defining: differentiation syndrome occurred in 16.0% (grade ≥3 events listed) and QTc prolongation in 13.8% in the KMT2A cohort, alongside febrile neutropenia in 37.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): roughly one in four heavily pretreated patients reaches CR/CRh, and some responders proceed to transplant — promising targeted activity, unproven against any alternative.

cards.headline: AUGMENT-101 phase 2 (KMT2A-rearranged): CR+CRh 22.8% and overall response 63.2% in 57 efficacy-evaluable patients — with no control arm
cards.summary: AUGMENT-101 phase 2 (KMT2A-rearranged): CR+CRh 22.8% and overall response 63.2% in 57 efficacy-evaluable patients — with no control arm
cards.people: 94 patients (median age 37 years, range 1.3–75) with relapsed/refractory KMT2A-rearranged acute leukaemia treated with revumenib every 12 hours in 28-day cycles across 22 sites in five countries; efficacy was assessed in the 57 patients with centrally confirmed KMT2A rearrangement.
cards.result: CR+CRh rate 22.8% (95% CI 12.7 to 35.8), exceeding the prespecified null hypothesis of 10% (P=.0036). Overall response rate 63.2% (95% CI 49.3 to 75.6); 15 of 22 responders (68.2%) had no detectable residual disease. Grade ≥3 adverse events included febrile neutropenia 37.2%, differentiation syndrome 16.0% and QTc prolongation 13.8%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 10% null is a historical benchmark, not a randomised comparison, and the efficacy denominator (57) is much smaller than the treated population (94) — always quote the evaluable denominator. Differentiation syndrome and QTc prolongation are class harms that need active monitoring.
cards.source: Issa GC et al. Menin Inhibition With Revumenib for KMT2A-Rearranged Relapsed or Refractory Acute Leukemia (AUGMENT-101). cards.headline: AUGMENT-101 phase 2 (NPM1-mutated AML): CR+CRh 23.4% and overall response 46.9% in 64 efficacy-evaluable adults; median remission duration 4.7 months
cards.summary: AUGMENT-101 phase 2 (NPM1-mutated AML): CR+CRh 23.4% and overall response 46.9% in 64 efficacy-evaluable adults; median remission duration 4.7 months
cards.people: 84 patients with relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML received at least one dose of revumenib (median age 63 years; 35.9% of the efficacy population had received ≥3 previous lines and 75.0% previous venetoclax); the protocol-defined efficacy-evaluable population was 64 adults.
cards.result: CR+CRh rate 23.4% (1-sided P=.0014); overall response rate 46.9%. Median duration of CR+CRh was 4.7 months. Of 30 responders, 5 (16.7%) proceeded to haematopoietic stem-cell transplant and 3 resumed revumenib after transplant. Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation in 4 patients (4.8%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and heavily pretreated: remissions are real but their median duration (4.7 months) is short, and there is no comparator to show whether revumenib beats salvage chemotherapy or a venetoclax-based approach in this population.

cards.summary: Phase 1 first-in-human study: 30% CR/CRh in the efficacy population, with QT prolongation the only dose-limiting toxicity
cards.people: Patients with relapsed or refractory acute leukaemia with KMT2A rearrangement or NPM1 mutation in the first-in-human phase 1 portion of AUGMENT-101 (the record does not state the total enrolled N in its abstract).
cards.result: Therapy was associated with a low frequency of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events and a 30% rate of complete remission or complete remission with partial haematological recovery in the efficacy analysis population. Asymptomatic QT-interval prolongation was the only dose-limiting toxicity. Remissions occurred in leukaemias refractory to multiple previous lines, with clearance of residual disease and differentiation of blasts, including differentiation syndrome.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study: its job was safety and dose, not efficacy estimation, and the abstract does not give the efficacy-population denominator — the phase 2 cohorts above are the efficacy record to quote.

shelves.title: Noradrenaline spillover in humans: ~0.33 µg/m²/min reaches plasma at rest — a clearance-filtered, organ-specific index of sympathetic firing, not the plasma level itself
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much noradrenaline spills over into plasma — total-body and regional (cardiac, renal) noradrenaline spillover rates by isotope-dilution, how do they rise with exercise, standing and age, and how little of synaptic release does plasma clearance-based spillover capture?
shelves.mesh: Norepinephrine · Sympathetic Nervous System · Kinetics · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for isotope-dilution noradrenaline kinetics in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong (sympathetic transmitter kinetics). The method-defining record (Esler, 34 normal subjects) gives resting total spillover of 0.33 µg/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61) with clearance 1.32 ± 0.28 L/m²/min, and shows plasma concentration alone misleads wherever clearance changes. The carded limbs are concordant: ageing raises plasma noradrenaline chiefly by reducing clearance (total spillover unchanged; hepatomesenteric spillover 50% higher in old men at rest — a relative difference); exercise raises limb spillover with active muscle mass, steeply above ~70% VO₂max, without matching vasoconstriction (N = 6); cardiac spillover is higher in older than younger healthy subjects (20.1 vs 14.3 ng/min) and roughly tripled in cardiac failure (59 vs 18 ng/min); and regional regulation is organ-specific (renal spillover +49%/+26% relative after enalaprilat in healthy subjects, cardiac and total unchanged). How little of synaptic release spillover captures is presented as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card — no carded record measures total synaptic release. Cross-point: pack #6632 (exercise pressor reflex) measures nerve traffic, not transmitter kinetics.

cards.headline: Esler 1982: the method-defining measurement — resting total noradrenaline spillover in 34 normal subjects was 0.33 µg/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61), with plasma clearance 1.32 ± 0.28 L/m²/min, and plasma noradrenaline concentration alone proved an unreliable guide
cards.summary: Esler 1982: the method-defining measurement — resting total noradrenaline spillover in 34 normal subjects was 0.33 µg/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61), with plasma clearance 1.32 ± 0.28 L/m²/min, and plasma noradrenaline concentration alone proved an unreliable guide
cards.type: Human radiotracer methods study (noradrenaline isotope-dilution kinetics), J Cardiovasc Pharmacol 1982
cards.people: 34 normal subjects given a steady intravenous infusion of tritiated l-noradrenaline (0.35 µCi/m²/min) to plateau; noradrenaline plasma clearance calculated from steady-state tracer concentration and spillover from plasma noradrenaline specific radioactivity (isotope dilution). Contrast groups in the same record: 8 patients with idiopathic peripheral autonomic insufficiency and 6 clonidine-treated hypertensive patients.
cards.result: Mean noradrenaline spillover at rest in normal subjects was 0.33 micrograms/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61), and noradrenaline plasma clearance was 1.32 ± 0.28 L/m²/min. As the method predicts, spillover was reduced where sympathetic activity is subnormal (0.16 ± 0.09 in autonomic insufficiency; 0.11 ± 0.07 µg/m²/min on clonidine). Clearance fell with age — which, the record shows, is what produces the previously described rise in plasma noradrenaline concentration with ageing — and chronic beta-blockade unexpectedly reduced clearance. Plasma noradrenaline concentration was not in agreement with release-rate values where clearance was abnormal: concentration is spillover divided by clearance, and only the tracer method separates the two.
cards.watchOut: Spillover is the fraction of neurally released noradrenaline that escapes reuptake and local metabolism and reaches plasma — an index of sympathetic firing, not a census of synaptic release itself (see the balance).
cards.source: Esler M, Leonard P, O'Dea K, Jackman G, Jennings G, Korner P. Biochemical quantification of sympathetic nervous activity in humans using radiotracer methodology: fallibility of plasma noradrenaline measurements. Journal of Cardiovascular Pharmacology. 1982. PMID: 6175831. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Humans · Hypertension · Kinetics · Norepinephrine · Sympathetic Nervous System · Tritium

cards.headline: Mazzeo 1997: ageing raises plasma noradrenaline by cutting clearance, not by raising total spillover — hepatomesenteric spillover was 50% higher in old men at rest, and total spillover rose with exercise in both groups (8 young, 7 old)
cards.summary: Mazzeo 1997: ageing raises plasma noradrenaline by cutting clearance, not by raising total spillover — hepatomesenteric spillover was 50% higher in old men at rest, and total spillover rose with exercise in both groups (8 young, 7 old)
cards.type: Human radiotracer study (total and regional spillover, ageing and exercise), J Appl Physiol 1997
cards.people: Eight young (26 ± 3 years) and seven old (69 ± 5 years) men studied at rest and during 20 minutes of submaximal cycling at 50% of peak work capacity, with continuous intravenous [³H]norepinephrine infusion for total-body and regional (hepatomesenteric) spillover. Small groups — 8 and 7 printed on the face.
cards.result: Arterial noradrenaline was higher in old subjects at rest (280 ± 36 vs 196 ± 27 in the record's printed units), but total norepinephrine spillover did not differ between groups at rest; hepatomesenteric spillover was 50% greater in the old (51 ± 7 vs 34 ± 5 ng/min), and norepinephrine clearance was significantly lower in the old (−23% relative at rest, and still depressed during exercise). During exercise, plasma noradrenaline rose in both groups, hepatomesenteric spillover remained 36% higher in the old (a relative difference), and whole-body spillover again did not differ by age. The ageing plasma-noradrenaline rise is therefore a clearance-and-regional story, not a whole-body release story — a distinction invisible without the tracer.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 + 7 men, one exercise intensity (50% peak) — the age pattern is the finding; absolute spillover at other intensities and in women is not in this record.
cards.source: Mazzeo RS, Rajkumar C, Jennings G, Esler M. Norepinephrine spillover at rest and during submaximal exercise in young and old subjects. Journal of Applied Physiology. 1997. PMID: 9173952. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Savard 1989: noradrenaline spillover from skeletal muscle rises with active muscle mass, steeply above ~70% of VO₂max — in resting as well as exercising legs, without neurogenic vasoconstriction (6 men)
cards.summary: Savard 1989: noradrenaline spillover from skeletal muscle rises with active muscle mass, steeply above ~70% of VO₂max — in resting as well as exercising legs, without neurogenic vasoconstriction (6 men)
cards.type: Human radiotracer study (skeletal-muscle spillover during exercise), Am J Physiol 1989
cards.people: Six healthy men performing 15-minute bouts of one-legged knee extension alone and combined with the other leg and/or the arms, at work intensities averaging 24–71% of maximal aerobic capacity; femoral-vein thermodilution leg blood flow and arterial/venous noradrenaline, with limb noradrenaline spillover calculated as the index of sympathetic activity to the limb. Small study: N = 6 printed on the face.
cards.result: Noradrenaline spillover increased gradually in the resting leg and, to a larger extent, in the exercising legs as total active muscle mass increased, with a steeper rise at approximately 70% of VO₂max. These increases were not accompanied by significant changes in leg blood flow or leg vascular conductance at the intensities examined — rising sympathetic activity to muscle during whole-body exercise up to ~71% of VO₂max was not matched by neurogenic vasoconstriction of the muscle vascular bed in this preparation.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, knee-extension model rather than whole-body locomotion; the spillover–flow dissociation is shown up to ~71% VO₂max and should not be extrapolated to maximal exercise.
cards.source: Savard GK, Richter EA, Strange S, Kiens B, Christensen NJ, Saltin B. Norepinephrine spillover from skeletal muscle during exercise in humans: role of muscle mass. The American Journal of Physiology. 1989. PMID: 2603969. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Kingwell 1994: cardiac noradrenaline spillover was 20.1 ± 3.0 ng/min in older versus 14.3 ± 2.5 in younger healthy subjects, and 59 ± 4 in cardiac failure versus 18 ± 3 in healthy volunteers — while 0.1 Hz heart-rate variability moved the opposite way
cards.summary: Kingwell 1994: cardiac noradrenaline spillover was 20.1 ± 3.0 ng/min in older versus 14.3 ± 2.5 in younger healthy subjects, and 59 ± 4 in cardiac failure versus 18 ± 3 in healthy volunteers — while 0.1 Hz heart-rate variability moved the opposite way
cards.type: Human radiotracer study (cardiac spillover versus MSNA and heart-rate variability), Circulation 1994
cards.people: Healthy volunteers drawn from a pool of 52, compared across conditions of cardiac sympathetic denervation (pure autonomic failure n = 4, dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency n = 1, cardiac transplantation n = 9), sympathetic activation in cardiac failure (n = 15) and ageing (n = 10), with cardiac noradrenaline spillover (coronary-sinus sampling), muscle sympathetic nerve activity and heart-rate spectral analysis measured head to head.
cards.result: In autonomic failure and early after transplantation, cardiac noradrenaline spillover was negligible; late after transplantation it returned to normal. Older individuals (60–75 years) had higher muscle sympathetic nerve activity (31.3 ± 5.8 vs 22.9 ± 1.9 bursts/min) and higher cardiac noradrenaline spillover (20.1 ± 3.0 vs 14.3 ± 2.5 ng/min, P < 0.05) than younger subjects (18–35), yet total and 0.1 Hz heart-rate variability were reduced by 89% and 93% (relative reductions). Cardiac failure showed the same dissociation: cardiac spillover 59 ± 4 vs 18 ± 3 ng/min in healthy volunteers (P < 0.01) with reduced 0.1 Hz variability. The record's conclusion: 0.1 Hz heart-rate variability is not directly related to cardiac spillover, which is the more direct measure of cardiac sympathetic firing.
cards.watchOut: Several limbs are small patient groups (autonomic failure 4, DBH deficiency 1) printed on the face; the healthy ageing and cardiac-failure contrasts carry the normative weight.
cards.source: Kingwell BA, Thompson JM, Kaye DM, McPherson GA, Jennings GL, Esler MD. Heart rate spectral analysis, cardiac norepinephrine spillover, and muscle sympathetic nerve activity during human sympathetic nervous activation and failure. Circulation. 1994. PMID: 8026003. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Johansson 2003: regional spillover is separately regulated — intravenous enalaprilat raised renal noradrenaline spillover by 49% and 26% (relative) at two doses in 30 healthy subjects while cardiac and total-body spillover did not change
cards.summary: Johansson 2003: regional spillover is separately regulated — intravenous enalaprilat raised renal noradrenaline spillover by 49% and 26% (relative) at two doses in 30 healthy subjects while cardiac and total-body spillover did not change
cards.type: Human radiotracer study (regional spillover under ACE inhibition in health), J Hypertens 2003
cards.people: 30 healthy normotensive subjects catheterised (radial artery, right renal vein and coronary sinus) with isotope-dilution spillover measured at baseline and 30–40 minutes after intravenous enalaprilat 1.25 mg or 2.5 mg, in subjects without an activated renin–angiotensin system.
cards.result: Mean arterial pressure fell by 5% (a relative change) after the higher dose and was unchanged after the lower dose, while renal noradrenaline spillover increased after both doses — by 49% and by 26% respectively (relative increases, P < 0.05 for both). Cardiac and total-body noradrenaline spillover remained unchanged after both doses, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (measured in 8 subjects after 2.5 mg) fell by 43% (relative). A sympathetic index can therefore move in one organ bed and nowhere else: total-body spillover would have reported 'no change' while renal sympathetic outflow rose by half.
cards.watchOut: An acute pharmacological probe in healthy subjects — it demonstrates organ-specific regulation of spillover, not a chronic effect of ACE inhibition.
cards.source: Johansson M, Rundqvist B, Petersson M, Lambert G, Friberg P. Regional norepinephrine spillover in response to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition in healthy subjects. Journal of Hypertension. 2003. PMID: 12817186. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: spillover is sympathetic firing seen through a clearance filter — about 0.33 µg/m²/min at rest in health, organ-specific, and only a spillover fraction of what synapses release
cards.summary: Synthesis: spillover is sympathetic firing seen through a clearance filter — about 0.33 µg/m²/min at rest in health, organ-specific, and only a spillover fraction of what synapses release
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human radiotracer records above (the Esler method programme, the ageing/exercise study, the skeletal-muscle exercise study, the cardiac spillover comparison and the regional-regulation study), framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on sympathetic transmitter kinetics.
cards.result: The method is the message: isotope dilution separates the rate at which noradrenaline enters plasma (spillover) from the rate at which plasma clears it, and the carded records show why the separation matters — ageing raises plasma noradrenaline mainly by reducing clearance while total spillover stays flat (regional hepatomesenteric spillover rises); exercise raises limb spillover with active muscle mass, steeply above ~70% of VO₂max, without matching vasoconstriction; cardiac spillover roughly triples in cardiac failure while a popular non-invasive proxy (0.1 Hz heart-rate variability) falls; and a drug probe can raise renal spillover by about half (relative) while total-body spillover reports no change. Resting total-body spillover in health is about 0.33 µg/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61). On the question of how much of synaptic release spillover captures: the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall / Ganong framing) is that most neurally released noradrenaline is recaptured by the nerve ending or metabolised locally and only a minority fraction escapes into plasma — spillover is therefore a faithful index of firing-rate changes, not a quantitative census of transmitter release, and this shelf presents that fraction qualitatively as the textbook's account because no carded record measures total synaptic release directly. Cross-point: the exercise pressor-reflex shelf in this library (pack #6632) measures sympathetic nerve traffic by microneurography — a different quantity from transmitter kinetics, and not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: All carded values are tracer-method values: they assume steady state and tracer–tracee indistinguishability, and regional values depend on organ plasma flow and extraction in the sampled bed.

shelves.title: Albumin transcapillary escape rate: ~5% of the intravascular mass leaves per hour in health — roughly doubled by arterial or portal pressure, acute inflammation and major surgery
shelves.question: In humans, how fast does albumin escape the circulation — what is the transcapillary escape rate of labelled albumin in health (per cent of intravascular mass per hour), and how does it rise in inflammation, burns and sepsis?
shelves.mesh: Serum Albumin · Capillary Permeability · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the transcapillary escape rate (TER) of labelled albumin in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall (capillary exchange; albumin distribution). PARTIAL slice, built after reading its home pack #6499 in full: that pack asks only how the albumin synthesis rate is regulated — 'escape' and 'transcapillary' appear nowhere in it — so distribution kinetics are the genuinely unasked half, cross-pointed in prose here and not duplicated. The healthy reference is concordant across laboratories: ~5.2–5.4%/h (Parving normals, N = 28 in the cirrhosis record) and 4.3 ± 2.6%/h (Ballmer normals). Rises, each beside its own record's normals: severe hypertension 7.8 ± 0.9%/h (N = 7), cirrhosis with portal hypertension 10.2%/h (N = 9, elevated in every patient), acute infectious inflammation 8.6 ± 3.4%/h (N = 8), and major surgery (escape elevated intra-operatively; 24 ± 17 g shifted by mass balance). Two qualifications are carried on the face: chronic malignancy barely raised TER (6.6%/h), and one modern acute-inflammation cohort had a normal TER despite marked hypoalbuminemia while synthesis rose ~50% (relative) — a low plasma albumin proves neither leak nor failed synthesis. The classic burns/sepsis permeability report already has a home elsewhere in the library and is cross-pointed in prose only, per the one-home rule; ≥3 free primary reports verified this session, so the slice is built as a full pack, not synthesis-only.

cards.headline: Parving 1977 (hypertension): transcapillary escape rate of albumin was 7.8 ± 0.9%/h in untreated essential hypertension versus a normal mean of 5.2 ± 1.0%/h — and it tracked mean arterial pressure (7 patients)
cards.summary: Parving 1977 (hypertension): transcapillary escape rate of albumin was 7.8 ± 0.9%/h in untreated essential hypertension versus a normal mean of 5.2 ± 1.0%/h — and it tracked mean arterial pressure (7 patients)
cards.type: Human tracer study (labelled-albumin transcapillary escape in hypertension), Scand J Clin Lab Invest 1977
cards.people: Seven untreated men with essential hypertension (average blood pressure 193/119 mmHg; four with grade I–III funduscopic changes), with simultaneous transcapillary escape rates of albumin and IgG measured from the initial disappearance of intravenously injected ¹³¹I-albumin and ¹²⁵I-IgG; normal comparison values are the record's own laboratory normals. Small patient group: N = 7 printed on the face.
cards.result: Transcapillary escape rate of albumin (TERalb) was 7.8 ± 0.9 (SD) %/h in the hypertensive subjects versus a normal mean of 5.2 ± 1.0 %/h, and TER of IgG was 4.7 ± 1.0 versus 3.0 ± 0.7 %/h (both P < 0.01); both escape rates correlated positively with mean arterial pressure (P < 0.001), with the IgG/albumin escape ratio unchanged. Daily urinary albumin excretion rose from a normal average of 9.1 mg/24 h to 96 mg/24 h. The record's interpretation: increased filtration through normal pores between microvascular endothelial cells, driven by the high arterial pressure — pressure alone, without structural leak, raises the escape rate by about half (a relative rise from ~5.2 to ~7.8%/h).
cards.watchOut: N = 7 hypertensive men against laboratory normal values; severe hypertension (193/119) — the pressure–escape slope should not be extrapolated to mild hypertension from this record alone.
cards.source: Parving HH, Jensen HA, Westrup M. Increased transcapillary escape rate of albumin and IgG in essential hypertension. Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation. 1977. PMID: 616047. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Parving 1977 (cirrhosis): escape rate was elevated in every cirrhotic patient — mean 10.2%/h, range 8.8–12.3 — against 5.4%/h (range 3.5–7.2) in 28 normal subjects (9 patients)
cards.summary: Parving 1977 (cirrhosis): escape rate was elevated in every cirrhotic patient — mean 10.2%/h, range 8.8–12.3 — against 5.4%/h (range 3.5–7.2) in 28 normal subjects (9 patients)
cards.type: Human tracer study (labelled-albumin transcapillary escape in cirrhosis), Scand J Clin Lab Invest 1977
cards.people: Nine patients with cirrhosis of the liver (six with ascites; wedged hepatic venous or splenic pulp pressure 20–30 mmHg, mean 26), with TERalb determined from the disappearance of intravenously injected ¹²⁵I-labelled human serum albumin over the first 60 minutes; the record's comparison group is 28 normal subjects. Small patient group: N = 9 printed on the face.
cards.result: Plasma albumin was low but plasma volume slightly enlarged, so intravascular albumin mass was only moderately reduced — yet TERalb was significantly elevated in all nine patients, mean 10.2%/h (range 8.8–12.3), roughly double the normal mean of 5.4%/h (range 3.5–7.2). The record's interpretation: increased filtration out of the portal-system vessels under raised portal venous pressure, with the doubled escape rate probably contributing to oedema and ascites formation. Together with the hypertension card, this fixes the healthy reference: about 5–5.5% of the intravascular albumin mass escapes per hour in health.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, all with portal hypertension — the doubling is shown for the portal-hypertensive state, and the record attributes it to filtration pressure rather than to a generalised endothelial leak.
cards.source: Parving HH, Ranek L, Lassen NA. Increased transcapillary escape rate of albumin in patients with cirrhosis of the liver. Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation. 1977. PMID: 594644. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Ballmer 1994: in acute infectious inflammation, escape rate rose to 8.6 ± 3.4%/h versus normal 4.3 ± 2.6%/h — and, unexpectedly, the higher the plasma albumin, the higher the escape rate (8 acute, 9 chronic patients)
cards.summary: Ballmer 1994: in acute infectious inflammation, escape rate rose to 8.6 ± 3.4%/h versus normal 4.3 ± 2.6%/h — and, unexpectedly, the higher the plasma albumin, the higher the escape rate (8 acute, 9 chronic patients)
cards.type: Human tracer study (albumin escape in acute versus chronic inflammation), Metabolism 1994
cards.people: Patients with acute infectious disease (n = 8) and chronic malignant disease (n = 9), with transcapillary escape rate (TER) and outflux of albumin measured after intravenous injection of 2 µCi ¹²⁵I-albumin, alongside positive and negative acute-phase proteins and interleukin-6. Small groups — 8 and 9 printed on the face.
cards.result: In acute infectious disease, TER was increased to 8.6 ± 3.4%/h and albumin outflux to 114 ± 60 mg/kg/h, against the record's normal values of 4.3 ± 2.6%/h and 108 ± 7 mg/kg/h. Unexpectedly, plasma albumin correlated positively with TER (r = 0.83, P = 0.011) and with outflux (r = 0.87, P = 0.005) in the acute group — escape was fastest while albumin was still relatively preserved, not after it had fallen. In chronic malignant disease, TER was only slightly elevated (6.6 ± 2.4%/h), outflux was within normal limits (92 ± 35 mg/kg/h), and no albumin–escape correlation appeared. Acute inflammation roughly doubles the escape rate; chronic malignancy barely moves it.
cards.watchOut: The record's normal TER (4.3 ± 2.6%/h) sits below the Parving laboratory's (~5.2–5.4%/h) — laboratory and protocol differences of about 1%/h are part of this literature, and the shelf keeps each record's own normals beside its patients.
cards.source: Ballmer PE, Ochsenbein AF, Schütz-Hofmann S. Transcapillary escape rate of albumin positively correlates with plasma albumin concentration in acute but not in chronic inflammatory disease. Metabolism: Clinical and Experimental. 1994. PMID: 7515458. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Komáromi 2016: measured simultaneously, synthesis and escape dissociate — acute inflammation raised synthesis by ~50% (relative) with a normal escape rate, while escape rose intra-operatively during pancreatic surgery (10 healthy, 10 inflamed, 10 surgical)
cards.summary: Komáromi 2016: measured simultaneously, synthesis and escape dissociate — acute inflammation raised synthesis by ~50% (relative) with a normal escape rate, while escape rose intra-operatively during pancreatic surgery (10 healthy, 10 inflamed, 10 surgical)
cards.type: Human tracer study (simultaneous albumin synthesis and escape, inflammation and surgery), Crit Care 2016
cards.people: Healthy volunteers (n = 10), patients with acute inflammatory abdominal disease (n = 10) and patients undergoing elective pancreatic resection (n = 10); albumin synthesis measured by deuterium-labelled phenylalanine incorporation, and plasma volume and transcapillary escape rate with ¹²³I- and ¹²⁵I-labelled albumin, the two tracers compared head to head. Registered NCT01686776.
cards.result: A ~50% elevated (relative) de-novo albumin synthesis rate was seen in acute inflammation with marked hypoalbuminemia, while patients with marginal hypoalbuminemia before surgery had a normal synthesis rate. The transcapillary escape rate was elevated intra-operatively during the reconstructive phase of pancreatic surgery, when plasma albumin was decreased but stable — but in acute inflammation with marked hypoalbuminemia, the escape rate was no different from normal, directly qualifying the assumption that inflammatory hypoalbuminemia is a leak phenomenon in every setting. The two iodine tracers were exchangeable for plasma volume but usable only at group level for escape rate. The record's conclusion: a plasma albumin concentration, on its own, reflects neither synthesis nor escape.
cards.watchOut: Groups of 10; the escape-rate tracer comparison was group-level only, and the inflammation limb's normal escape rate is a finding about this acute-abdominal-inflammation cohort — it does not erase the Ballmer card's doubled escape in acute infection, and the tension between the two is carried on this shelf's face.
cards.source: Komáromi A, Estenberg U, Hammarqvist F, Rooyackers O, Wernerman J, Norberg Å. Simultaneous assessment of the synthesis rate and transcapillary escape rate of albumin in inflammation and surgery. Critical Care. 2016. PMID: 27846908. Registry ID: NCT01686776 (from the record). cards.headline: Norberg 2016: in major abdominal surgery, plasma albumin fell by more than 40% (relative) during the first part of the operation and 24 ± 17 g of albumin had left the circulation by 1 hour after the end of surgery (10 patients)
cards.summary: Norberg 2016: in major abdominal surgery, plasma albumin fell by more than 40% (relative) during the first part of the operation and 24 ± 17 g of albumin had left the circulation by 1 hour after the end of surgery (10 patients)
cards.type: Human mass-balance study (perioperative albumin extravasation), Crit Care 2016
cards.people: Ten patients studied during oesophageal or pancreatic surgery, with plasma albumin measured repeatedly over 72 hours and albumin and haemoglobin mass balance derived from plasma albumin, blood haemoglobin and haematocrit — a mass-balance measure of albumin extravasation rather than a labelled-albumin escape rate. Small cohort: N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: Plasma albumin fell rapidly from baseline (32.8 ± 4.8 g/L, i.e. about 3.3 g/dL) to 18.7 ± 4.8 g/L (about 1.9 g/dL) by the start of surgical reconstruction (P < 0.001) and was thereafter stable to postoperative day 3. Cumulative perioperative albumin shift rose until 1 hour after the end of surgery, by which time 24 ± 17 g had been lost from the circulation (P < 0.001). The surgical limb of the escape story is therefore fast and early: most of the albumin leaves during the dissection phase, not as a slow postoperative leak — and the plasma level then stays flat for days despite that loss having stopped.
cards.watchOut: Mass-balance shift over hours is not the same quantity as a tracer TER in %/h — carded as the surgical time-course limb, not converted into an escape rate.
cards.source: Norberg Å, Rooyackers O, Segersvärd R, Wernerman J. Leakage of albumin in major abdominal surgery. Critical Care. 2016. PMID: 27117323. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Abdomen · Aged · Capillary Permeability · Female · Fluid Shifts · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Serum Albumin

cards.headline: Synthesis: about 5% of intravascular albumin escapes per hour in health; pressure and acute inflammation roughly double it — but a low plasma albumin, by itself, proves neither leak nor failed synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 5% of intravascular albumin escapes per hour in health; pressure and acute inflammation roughly double it — but a low plasma albumin, by itself, proves neither leak nor failed synthesis
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human records above (the two Parving 1977 escape-rate studies, the Ballmer acute-versus-chronic inflammation study, and the two 2016 Stockholm kinetic studies), framed by Guyton & Hall on capillary exchange and albumin distribution. This pack is the distribution half of albumin physiology: its home companion, pack #6499 in this library, asks how the albumin synthesis rate is regulated — synthesis is cross-pointed there and not duplicated here; the Starling-forces pack (#6445) covers the forces, not these measured escape rates.
cards.result: The healthy reference is consistent across laboratories and decades: transcapillary escape rate of albumin ≈ 5.2–5.4%/h in the Parving records' normal subjects and 4.3 ± 2.6%/h in the Ballmer record's normals — call it about 5% of the intravascular mass per hour, with ~1%/h of inter-laboratory spread. What raises it, from the carded records: arterial pressure (7.8%/h in severe untreated hypertension, tracking mean arterial pressure), portal pressure (10.2%/h in cirrhosis, elevated in every patient), acute infectious inflammation (8.6%/h) and major surgery (escape elevated intra-operatively; 24 ± 17 g shifted out of the circulation by 1 hour post-operation, with plasma albumin down >40% in relative terms during the first operative phase). The qualifications are as much the content as the rises: chronic malignancy barely raised escape (6.6%/h), one modern acute-inflammation cohort had a normal escape rate despite marked hypoalbuminemia while its synthesis rate rose ~50% (relative), and in acute infection escape was highest while albumin was still preserved. So the plasma level is a balance of synthesis, escape, dilution and loss — never a leak meter on its own. The burns and sepsis limbs named in this row's question are not carded here: the classic increased-vascular-permeability report in burns/sepsis already has its home elsewhere in this library under the one-home rule, so it is cross-pointed in this prose only and no value from it is reprinted on this shelf. Guyton & Hall's framing — albumin's escape and lymphatic return as the circulation's protein circulation — is the textbook account within which these measured rates sit.
cards.watchOut: Escape-rate normals differ by ~1%/h between laboratories and tracer protocols; every patient value on this shelf is printed beside its own record's normal value, and none should be detached from it.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 616047, 594644, 7515458, 27846908, 27117323), with Guyton & Hall textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
