shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine rests on a single small randomised phase 2 programme (BRIGHT AML 1003, n=132 with AML or high-risk MDS): median survival 8.8 vs 4.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51, relative) and complete remission 17.0% vs 2.3%, with the advantage maintained on long-term analysis (hazard ratio 0.495) and strongest in secondary AML. All four cards here are that one trial and its analyses — the single-programme precedent caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the small N is printed on the face. Fenced, not carded: the phase 3 BRIGHT AML 1019 trials of glasdegib with intensive chemotherapy in fitter patients did not confirm benefit — a different slice that warns against extrapolation. The shelf also cannot answer the modern comparison against venetoclax-based regimens, which were not the control here.

cards.headline: BRIGHT AML 1003 phase 2 randomised trial (132 patients): glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine doubled median survival (8.8 vs 4.9 months; hazard ratio 0.51) and raised complete remission from 2.3% to 17.0%
cards.summary: BRIGHT AML 1003 phase 2 randomised trial (132 patients): glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine doubled median survival (8.8 vs 4.9 months; hazard ratio 0.51) and raised complete remission from 2.3% to 17.0%
cards.people: 132 patients with newly diagnosed AML or high-risk MDS unsuitable for intensive chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 to glasdegib 100 mg daily plus low-dose cytarabine (88 patients) or low-dose cytarabine alone (44 patients).
cards.result: Median overall survival was 8.8 months with the combination vs 4.9 months with low-dose cytarabine alone (hazard ratio 0.51, 80% CI 0.39 to 0.67 — a relative measure; the absolute median gain was about 3.9 months). Complete remission was achieved by 17.0% vs 2.3%. Commonest grade 3/4 non-haematologic events on the combination were pneumonia (16.7%) and fatigue (14.3%). Efficacy was seen across mutational profiles.
cards.watchOut: A small randomised phase 2 (n=132) with 80% confidence intervals in the primary report — a promising signal, not phase 3 confirmation; the trial also enrolled high-risk MDS patients.
cards.source: Randomized comparison of low dose cytarabine with or without glasdegib in patients with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia or high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Leukemia. 2019. cards.headline: Long-term analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003: the survival advantage held (hazard ratio 0.495; median 8.3 vs 4.3 months), driven most strongly by secondary AML
cards.summary: Long-term analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003: the survival advantage held (hazard ratio 0.495; median 8.3 vs 4.3 months), driven most strongly by secondary AML
cards.type: Long-term analysis of the randomised phase 2 trial
cards.people: The AML patients of BRIGHT AML 1003 followed long-term (90% had died at analysis; longest follow-up 36 months): glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine in 78 patients (38 de novo, 40 secondary AML) vs low-dose cytarabine alone in 38 (18 de novo, 20 secondary).
cards.result: Overall survival favoured the combination (hazard ratio 0.495, 95% CI 0.325 to 0.752, relative; median 8.3 vs 4.3 months). In post hoc subgroups the benefit was large in secondary AML (hazard ratio 0.287; median 9.1 vs 4.1 months) and only a trend in de novo AML (hazard ratio 0.720, 95% CI 0.395 to 1.312; median 6.6 vs 4.3 months). Adverse-event incidence fell after the first 90 days of therapy (83.7% vs 98.7%).
cards.watchOut: Same trial, same patients — a durability report, not independent evidence; the de novo/secondary split is post hoc.

cards.summary: Exposure–survival modelling of BRIGHT AML 1003: the survival benefit did not depend on glasdegib exposure level
cards.type: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling analysis of the randomised trial
cards.people: Population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003 AML patients (treatment-response analysis: 78 combination vs 38 control; exposure-response analysis: 75 combination patients).
cards.result: Modelled survival favoured glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine at any time point (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.66, relative), corresponding to roughly 5 months' prolongation of median survival. Variability in glasdegib exposure at the 100 mg daily dose did not significantly affect survival, and no demographic, laboratory or disease covariate altered the survival probability — supporting the fixed dose and implying dose reductions need not forfeit benefit.
cards.watchOut: A model fitted to the same small trial's data; it refines the dose question but adds no new patients or independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Response-based analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003: benefit extended to patients who never reached complete remission
cards.summary: Response-based analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003: benefit extended to patients who never reached complete remission
cards.type: Post hoc response-based analysis of the randomised phase 2 trial
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of BRIGHT AML 1003 AML patients by response (combination n=78; control n=38); complete remission rates were 19.2% vs 2.6% in this analysis set.
cards.result: Among patients who did NOT achieve complete remission, glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine still improved survival versus low-dose cytarabine alone (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.98, relative; median 5.0 vs 4.1 months). Count recovery was more frequent on the combination (neutrophils at least 1000/µL: 45.6% vs 35.5%; haemoglobin at least 9 g/dL: 54.4% vs 38.7%; platelets at least 100,000/µL: 29.8% vs 9.7%), and transfusion independence was achieved by 15.0% vs 2.9%.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc responder analyses are vulnerable to guarantee-time bias; treat the non-responder survival signal as supportive, not decisive.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a single small randomised phase 2 programme shows a consistent survival benefit for glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine — POSSIBLE, with the phase 3 intensive-chemotherapy failure fenced outside this question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single small randomised phase 2 programme shows a consistent survival benefit for glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine — POSSIBLE, with the phase 3 intensive-chemotherapy failure fenced outside this question
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BRIGHT AML 1003 (132 randomised patients with AML or high-risk MDS) and three analyses of the same trial.
cards.result: Every analysis of the one randomised comparison points the same way (hazard ratios 0.42–0.51, relative), but it remains one small phase 2 trial (n=132) multiply analysed — the single-programme precedent caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Fence: the phase 3 BRIGHT AML 1019 programme, which added glasdegib to intensive chemotherapy in fitter patients — a different question — did not confirm a benefit, and is not carded here; it warns against extrapolating this result beyond the unfit, low-dose-cytarabine setting.
cards.watchOut: Low-dose cytarabine alone is itself a weak control by current standards; this shelf does not compare glasdegib combinations against venetoclax-based therapy, which is the comparison clinicians now face.

shelves.title: Fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin improves survival in favourable- and intermediate-risk AML across five randomised trials — with no benefit in adverse cytogenetics and veno-occlusive disease as the price to watch
shelves.question: In patients with de novo CD33-positive AML, does adding fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin to standard induction chemotherapy, versus chemotherapy alone, improve event-free and overall survival?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — adding fractionated-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin (3 mg/m² on days 1, 4, 7) to standard induction improves outcomes in de novo CD33-positive AML: ALFA-0701 showed 2-year event-free survival of 40.8% vs 17.1% (hazard ratio 0.58, relative), and the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (3,325 patients) found improved 5-year survival driven by fewer relapses, not more remissions. The benefit is cytogenetically graded and that gradient is the shelf: absolute survival benefit 20.7% in favourable-risk, 5.7% in intermediate-risk, and none (odds ratio 0.99) in adverse-risk disease. History on the face: the drug was withdrawn in 2010 after single-bolus dosing failed (SWOG S0106) and returned on fractionated dosing; 3 mg/m² caused fewer early deaths than 6 mg/m² at equal efficacy. Defining harms: veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and prolonged thrombocytopenia; a transplant-subset analysis found no excess post-transplant veno-occlusive disease or mortality. LIKELY is earned by multiple independent randomised trials with a concordant individual-patient synthesis.

cards.headline: ALFA-0701 phase 3 primary report (280 patients): fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin raised 2-year event-free survival from 17.1% to 40.8% and overall survival from 41.9% to 53.2%
cards.summary: ALFA-0701 phase 3 primary report (280 patients): fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin raised 2-year event-free survival from 17.1% to 40.8% and overall survival from 41.9% to 53.2%
cards.people: 280 adults aged 50–70 with previously untreated de novo AML at 26 French centres, randomised to standard daunorubicin–cytarabine induction and consolidation with or without fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin 3 mg/m² on days 1, 4 and 7 of induction and day 1 of each consolidation course (139 analysed per arm).
cards.result: At 2 years, event-free survival was 40.8% with gemtuzumab ozogamicin vs 17.1% without (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.78, relative); overall survival was 53.2% vs 41.9% (hazard ratio 0.69, 0.49 to 0.98); relapse-free survival was 50.3% vs 22.7% (hazard ratio 0.52). Complete response rates did not differ significantly (81% vs 75%). Persistent thrombocytopenia was more common with gemtuzumab ozogamicin (16% vs 3%), without more deaths from toxicity.
cards.watchOut: The trial predates routine CD33/cytogenetic-guided selection used today; benefit in this report is an average across cytogenetic groups, which the meta-analysis card below unpacks.
cards.source: Effect of gemtuzumab ozogamicin on survival of adult patients with de-novo acute myeloid leukaemia (ALFA-0701): a randomised, open-label, phase 3 study. Lancet (London, England). 2012. cards.headline: ALFA-0701 final report: blinded independent review confirmed the event-free-survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.66); final overall survival favoured gemtuzumab ozogamicin but was not significant
cards.summary: ALFA-0701 final report: blinded independent review confirmed the event-free-survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.66); final overall survival favoured gemtuzumab ozogamicin but was not significant
cards.people: The ALFA-0701 randomised population (271 patients in this report) with follow-up to April 2013 for final overall survival and independent review of event-free survival.
cards.result: Independent review confirmed event-free survival (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.89 — a 34% relative reduction in the risk of events). Final overall survival favoured the gemtuzumab ozogamicin arm but did not reach significance. Early death rates did not differ. The main added toxicity was prolonged thrombocytopenia; veno-occlusive disease (including after transplant) occurred in 6 patients on gemtuzumab ozogamicin vs 2 on control.
cards.watchOut: The survival endpoint of the single positive fractionated-dose trial is formally negative at final analysis — the shelf's survival claim leans on the five-trial meta-analysis, not on ALFA-0701 alone.
cards.source: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin for de novo acute myeloid leukemia: final efficacy and safety updates from the open-label, phase III ALFA-0701 trial. Haematologica. 2019. PMID: 30076173. cards.headline: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (3,325 patients): gemtuzumab ozogamicin improved 5-year survival, with the absolute benefit concentrated in favourable (20.7%) and intermediate (5.7%) cytogenetics and none in adverse cytogenetics
cards.summary: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (3,325 patients): gemtuzumab ozogamicin improved 5-year survival, with the absolute benefit concentrated in favourable (20.7%) and intermediate (5.7%) cytogenetics and none in adverse cytogenetics
cards.type: Meta-analysis of individual patient data from five randomised trials
cards.people: Individual patient data from five centrally randomised trials (3,325 adults aged 15 or older with AML other than acute promyelocytic leukaemia) of gemtuzumab ozogamicin added to first-course intensive induction chemotherapy vs chemotherapy alone.
cards.result: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin did not raise complete remission rates (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.07 — the treatment made no difference to remission), but reduced relapse (odds ratio 0.81, 0.73 to 0.90, relative) and improved overall survival at 5 years (odds ratio 0.90, 0.82 to 0.98, relative). Absolute 6-year survival benefit: 20.7% in favourable cytogenetics (odds ratio 0.47), 5.7% in intermediate (odds ratio 0.84), and 2.2% — no benefit — in adverse cytogenetics (odds ratio 0.99, 0.83 to 1.18). Doses of 3 mg/m² caused fewer early deaths than 6 mg/m² with equal efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The five trials used differing doses and schedules, including the older single-bolus dosing that led to the drug's 2010 withdrawal after SWOG S0106; the cytogenetic gradient, not the pooled average, is the clinically usable result.
cards.source: Addition of gemtuzumab ozogamicin to induction chemotherapy in adult patients with acute myeloid leukaemia: a meta-analysis of individual patient data from randomised controlled trials. cards.headline: ALFA-0701 transplant analysis (85 transplanted patients): fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin did not increase post-transplant veno-occlusive disease or mortality
cards.summary: ALFA-0701 transplant analysis (85 transplanted patients): fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin did not increase post-transplant veno-occlusive disease or mortality
cards.type: Transplant-outcomes analysis of the randomised phase 3 trial
cards.people: 85 ALFA-0701 patients who received allogeneic stem-cell transplant in first complete remission or after relapse/induction failure (32 after gemtuzumab ozogamicin, 53 control).
cards.result: Post-transplant survival, non-relapse mortality and relapse did not differ between arms (the treatment made no difference to post-transplant outcomes in this subset). Veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome after transplant or conditioning occurred in 3 patients (2 gemtuzumab ozogamicin, 1 control who later received gemtuzumab ozogamicin as follow-up therapy). The authors concluded fractionated-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin does not preclude transplant as consolidation.
cards.watchOut: Only 85 patients and few veno-occlusive events — reassuring but underpowered to exclude a modest transplant-related harm; veno-occlusive disease remains the drug's defining toxicity.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fractionated-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin improves survival in favourable- and intermediate-risk AML across five randomised trials — LIKELY, with no benefit in adverse cytogenetics
cards.summary: Synthesis: fractionated-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin improves survival in favourable- and intermediate-risk AML across five randomised trials — LIKELY, with no benefit in adverse cytogenetics
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the ALFA-0701 randomised trial (280 patients, primary and final reports plus its transplant analysis) and the five-trial individual-patient-data meta-analysis (3,325 patients).
cards.result: The story has three acts and all belong on the face: single-bolus dosing failed and the drug was withdrawn in 2010; fractionated 3 mg/m² dosing in ALFA-0701 produced a large event-free-survival benefit; and the pooled individual-patient data show a real but cytogenetically graded survival benefit (absolute 20.7% favourable, 5.7% intermediate, none adverse). LIKELY rests on multiple independent randomised trials plus a concordant individual-patient synthesis. Defining harm: veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and prolonged thrombocytopenia.
cards.watchOut: Patients with adverse cytogenetics should not be promised benefit — the pooled odds ratio there is 0.99. CD33 expression testing and cytogenetic risk, not the pooled average, should drive the decision.

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides cleanly by endpoint. On responses, enasidenib works: 40.3% overall response and 19.3% complete remission in the single-arm pivotal study, and in the randomised IDHENTIFY trial (319 older patients with late-stage IDH2-mutated relapsed/refractory AML) a 40.5% vs 9.9% response rate, better event-free survival, haematologic improvement (42.4% vs 11.2%) and red-cell transfusion independence (31.7% vs 9.3%). On survival, the only randomised test was null: median overall survival 6.5 vs 6.2 months (hazard ratio 0.86, P=0.23; the treatment made no difference to the primary endpoint), with the caveat that 12% of the control arm never received randomised treatment and many patients in both arms received later AML therapies. An observational real-world comparison favouring enasidenib on survival is carded but labelled and discounted — it does not outrank the randomised null. Class harms: differentiation syndrome and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia. The MDS subgroup (17 patients, 53% response) is programme context only.

cards.headline: AG221-C-001 phase 1/2 pivotal cohort: enasidenib produced a 40.3% overall response rate and 19.3% complete remissions in relapsed/refractory IDH2-mutated AML — single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: AG221-C-001 phase 1/2 pivotal cohort: enasidenib produced a 40.3% overall response rate and 19.3% complete remissions in relapsed/refractory IDH2-mutated AML — single-arm, no comparator
cards.people: Patients with IDH2-mutated relapsed or refractory AML in the phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study of enasidenib (100 mg daily selected for expansion); 176 patients in the relapsed/refractory AML efficacy group implied by the report (34 complete remissions = 19.3%). No concurrent control group.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 40.3%, with complete remission in 19.3% and a median response duration of 5.8 months. Median overall survival was 9.3 months in relapsed/refractory patients and 19.7 months in those who reached complete remission. Grade 3–4 enasidenib-related events included indirect hyperbilirubinaemia (12%) and IDH-inhibitor-associated differentiation syndrome (7%). Responses came with cellular differentiation and maturation, typically without aplasia.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm response rates without a comparator cannot separate drug effect from patient selection; survival figures by responder status are not evidence the drug extends life.

cards.headline: IDHENTIFY phase 3 (319 patients): enasidenib did NOT improve overall survival versus conventional care (6.5 vs 6.2 months; hazard ratio 0.86, P=0.23) — the primary endpoint was missed — but response, event-free survival and transfusion independence all favoured enasidenib
cards.summary: IDHENTIFY phase 3 (319 patients): enasidenib did NOT improve overall survival versus conventional care (6.5 vs 6.2 months; hazard ratio 0.86, P=0.23) — the primary endpoint was missed — but response, event-free survival and transfusion independence all favoured enasidenib
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (primary endpoint not met)
cards.people: 319 patients aged 60 or older with IDH2-mutated AML relapsed or refractory to two or three prior regimens, randomised to enasidenib 100 mg daily (158) or a preselected conventional care regimen (161: azacitidine, intermediate- or low-dose cytarabine, or supportive care).
cards.result: Median overall survival was 6.5 vs 6.2 months (hazard ratio 0.86; P=0.23) — the treatment made no difference to the primary endpoint, overall survival. Secondary endpoints favoured enasidenib: overall response 40.5% vs 9.9%, event-free survival median 4.9 vs 2.6 months (hazard ratio 0.68, relative), time to treatment failure 4.9 vs 1.9 months, haematologic improvement 42.4% vs 11.2%, and red-cell transfusion independence 31.7% vs 9.3%. One-year survival was 37.5% vs 26.1%. The authors note survival was confounded by early dropout (12% of the control arm received no randomised treatment) and subsequent therapies (30–43%).
cards.watchOut: This is the only randomised test of enasidenib in this population and it is null on survival — any shelf claim must be built around that, with the response/transfusion benefits stated as secondary-endpoint findings.

cards.headline: Real-world chart review (200 patients, observational): enasidenib-treated patients responded more (77% vs 52%) and lived longer than patients given other first salvage therapy, after adjustment
cards.summary: Real-world chart review (200 patients, observational): enasidenib-treated patients responded more (77% vs 52%) and lived longer than patients given other first salvage therapy, after adjustment
cards.people: Chart abstraction of patients with relapsed/refractory IDH2-mutated AML treated with enasidenib in US practice (124 patients, 2018–2019) or other first-line relapsed/refractory therapy (76 patients, 2016–2017). Observational, non-randomised, different treatment eras.
cards.result: Overall response was 77% with enasidenib vs 52% with other therapy. Median progression-free survival was 8 vs 5 months (adjusted hazard ratio 0.36, relative) and median overall survival 11 vs 6 months (adjusted hazard ratio 0.37, relative). Fewer enasidenib patients were hospitalised during salvage therapy (14% vs 46%).
cards.watchOut: Era and selection effects are built in (enasidenib patients treated later, chosen for the drug); the adjusted hazard ratios are far larger than the randomised IDHENTIFY result and should be discounted accordingly — the randomised trial outranks this card.

cards.result: The split is the answer: response endpoints consistently favour enasidenib (40% single-arm; 40.5% vs 9.9% randomised), while the only randomised survival test was null (hazard ratio 0.86, P=0.23), albeit confounded by control-arm dropout and crossover to later therapies. The frontline enasidenib-plus-intensive-chemotherapy phase 1 study asks a different (newly diagnosed, combination) question and is not carded here.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — olutasidenib (Rezlidhia, Rigel Pharmaceuticals) rests entirely on single-arm evidence from one phase 1/2 programme: in the pivotal cohort of 153 heavily pretreated patients with relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML, complete remission/CRh was 35% and overall response 48%, with a median CR/CRh duration of about 25 months and median survival of 11.5 months, confirmed at the final 5-year analysis. There is no randomised or controlled comparison, so single-arm framing applies throughout and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. Response varied by mutation subtype (R132C 42% vs R132H 17%) and fell with more prior regimens. Defining harms: differentiation syndrome (14% in the pivotal cohort, including one fatal case) and cytopenias; hepatotoxicity is a labelled class concern. The programme's MDS cohort (22 patients, mostly combination therapy) and its maintenance-after-response report — whose record carries no extractable results and so was not carded — are context, not support.

cards.headline: Phase 2 pivotal cohort, interim report (153 patients): olutasidenib monotherapy gave a 35% complete-remission/CRh rate and 48% overall response in relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML — single-arm
cards.summary: Phase 2 pivotal cohort, interim report (153 patients): olutasidenib monotherapy gave a 35% complete-remission/CRh rate and 48% overall response in relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML — single-arm
cards.people: 153 IDH1-inhibitor-naïve patients with IDH1-R132-mutated relapsed or refractory AML (median age 71; median 2 prior regimens, range 1–7) receiving olutasidenib 150 mg twice daily in the pivotal cohort of the phase 1/2 trial. No concurrent control.
cards.result: Complete remission plus CR with partial haematologic recovery (CR/CRh) was 35% and overall response 48%, similar in patients with and without prior venetoclax. Median duration of CR/CRh was 25.9 months (with 55% censored at data cut), median overall response duration 11.7 months and median overall survival 11.6 months. Of 86 transfusion-dependent patients, 34% achieved 56-day transfusion independence. Grade 3–4 events in at least 10%: febrile neutropenia 20%, anaemia 20%, thrombocytopenia 16%, neutropenia 13%. Differentiation syndrome occurred in 14% (9% grade 3 or worse, one fatal case).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: response rates have no comparator, and the long median CR/CRh duration is computed among responders only, with heavy censoring.

cards.people: The same pivotal cohort at study completion (153 treated; median age 71; 66% had received at least 2 prior regimens, 39% a hypomethylating agent), with 2 further years of follow-up beyond the interim report.
cards.result: CR/CRh was 35% (95% CI 27 to 43), with full complete remission in 32% of responders' outcomes as reported; overall response was 48%. Median time to CR/CRh was 1.9 months, median duration of CR/CRh 25.3 months, and median overall survival 11.5 months (95% CI 8.3 to 15.5). Patients with 1–2 prior regimens did better (CR/CRh 41%, median survival 13 months) than those with at least 3 (24%, 8.9 months). Response varied by mutation: R132C 42%, R132L/G/S 33%, R132H 17%. Few new adverse events and no discontinuations for adverse events occurred beyond year 3.
cards.watchOut: Interim and final reports describe the same patients — together they establish durability, not independent replication. The authors' suggestion to sustain therapy at least 6 months reflects slow responses in a minority (12% of responders needed at least 4 months).

cards.summary: Phase 1 dose-finding (78 patients): olutasidenib 150 mg twice daily was selected as the recommended dose; relapsed/refractory AML response was 41% on monotherapy
cards.people: 78 patients with IDH1-mutated AML or MDS in the phase 1 part of the phase 1/2 trial, receiving olutasidenib monotherapy (32 patients) or olutasidenib plus azacitidine (46 patients) at doses from 150 mg daily to 300 mg daily.
cards.result: No dose-limiting toxicities were reported and 150 mg twice daily was declared the recommended phase 2 dose. In relapsed/refractory AML, overall response was 41% (9 of 22) on monotherapy and 46% (12 of 26) on the combination. Commonest grade 3–4 events on monotherapy: thrombocytopenia 28%, febrile neutropenia 22%, anaemia 22%. No deaths were considered drug-related.
cards.watchOut: Small dose-finding cohorts mixing AML and MDS and two regimens; its role here is dose provenance for the pivotal cohort, not efficacy proof.

cards.headline: MDS cohort of the same programme (22 patients): olutasidenib with or without azacitidine gave a 59% overall response in higher-risk IDH1-mutated MDS; monotherapy alone responded in 2 of 6

cards.people: 22 patients with intermediate- to very-high-risk IDH1-mutated MDS (median age 74), treated with olutasidenib monotherapy (6 patients, 4 relapsed/refractory and 2 treatment-naïve) or olutasidenib plus azacitidine (16 patients) within the phase 1/2 trial.
cards.result: Overall response was 59% in the intention-to-treat set (complete remission 27%, marrow complete remission 32%) and 68% in response-evaluable patients. Monotherapy response was 33% (2 of 6 — and half the monotherapy patients received half the recommended dose or less) vs 69% (11 of 16) for the combination. Median response duration was 14.6 months and median overall survival 27.2 months. Differentiation syndrome occurred in 3 patients (14%, one grade 3); QT prolongation in 1 combination patient. Of transfusion-dependent patients, 62% (red-cell) and 67% (platelet) achieved 56-day transfusion independence.
cards.watchOut: A different disease slice (MDS) and mostly combination therapy — programme context showing where the monotherapy data are thinnest; do not carry its response rate into the AML question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — olutasidenib produces durable complete remissions in about a third of relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML patients — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — olutasidenib produces durable complete remissions in about a third of relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML patients — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 1 dose-finding study (78 patients), the phase 2 pivotal cohort interim and final reports (153 patients) and the MDS cohort (22 patients), all from one phase 1/2 programme (NCT02719574).
cards.result: The pivotal result is consistent across interim and final cuts: CR/CRh 35%, overall response 48%, median CR/CRh duration about 25 months, median survival 11.5 months — in a heavily pretreated population with no randomised comparator, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and every rate must be read as single-arm. Harms that define the drug: differentiation syndrome (14%, one fatal case in the interim report) and the hepatotoxicity/cytopenia profile of the class; the maintenance-after-response report in this programme could not be carded because its record carries no extractable results. Product naming (clarification exception): olutasidenib (Rezlidhia, Rigel Pharmaceuticals).
cards.watchOut: Cross-trial comparisons with ivosidenib are not evidence; no head-to-head or randomised trial of olutasidenib exists in this population.

shelves.title: Ziftomenib alone induces complete remissions in about a fifth of relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML patients — a three-report single-arm base (one of them a pharmacokinetic analysis), with differentiation syndrome the key harm
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory NPM1-mutated AML, does ziftomenib monotherapy, versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Nucleophosmin · Aged · Middle Aged · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy,genetics,pathology · Male · Female · Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Mutation · Nuclear Proteins/genetics · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy,genetics · Humans · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy,genetics,pathology · Middle Aged · Male · Female · Nucleophosmin · Aged · Adult · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Aged, 80 and over · Humans · Nucleophosmin · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy,genetics · Female · Male · Mutation · Middle Aged · Nuclear Proteins/genetics · Adult · Aged · Models, Biological · Antineoplastic Agents/pharmacokinetics,administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — ziftomenib (Komzifti, Kura Oncology) monotherapy in relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML rests on exactly three on-question monotherapy reports, all from the single KOMET-001 programme: the phase 2 pivotal cohort (92 patients; CR/CRh 22%, overall response 33%, 61% of responders MRD-negative), the phase 1 study (83 patients; 35% complete remission in the 20-patient NPM1 subgroup at the 600 mg recommended dose), and a population-pharmacokinetic/exposure–response analysis in the same monotherapy population showing flat exposure–response and supporting the fixed 600 mg dose. That third report is a modelling analysis, not an independent efficacy trial — the floor is met, but the base is thin, single-programme and entirely single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Median response duration was 4.6 months and median survival 6.6 months in phase 2. Differentiation syndrome is the defining harm (25% any grade in phase 2; one treatment-related death in phase 1). The combination report (ziftomenib with venetoclax and azacitidine, same population) is a different question and is cross-pointed in prose only, never carded here.

cards.headline: KOMET-001 phase 2 (92 patients): ziftomenib monotherapy met its primary endpoint — CR/CRh 22% in relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML, with 61% of responders MRD-negative
cards.summary: KOMET-001 phase 2 (92 patients): ziftomenib monotherapy met its primary endpoint — CR/CRh 22% in relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML, with 61% of responders MRD-negative
cards.people: 92 adults with relapsed or refractory NPM1-mutated AML (median age 69) treated with ziftomenib 600 mg once daily in the registration-enabling phase 2 part of KOMET-001. Single-arm, no concurrent control.
cards.result: The complete remission/CR with partial haematologic recovery rate was 22% (95% CI 14 to 32), meeting the primary endpoint; 61% of responders were negative for measurable residual disease. Overall response rate was 33% with a median duration of 4.6 months. Median overall survival was 6.6 months. Responses were comparable regardless of prior therapy (including venetoclax) or co-mutations. Grade 3-or-worse events: febrile neutropenia 26%, anaemia 20%, thrombocytopenia 20%. Differentiation syndrome occurred in 25% (15% grade 3, none grade 4–5) and was manageable with protocol mitigation; 3% discontinued for ziftomenib-related events.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: a 22% CR/CRh rate in a population with no good options is meaningful, but there is no randomised evidence that ziftomenib extends survival, and median response duration was under 5 months.
cards.source: Ziftomenib in Relapsed or Refractory NPM1-Mutated AML. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2025. PMID: 40997296. Registry ID: NCT04067336 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: KOMET-001 phase 1 (83 patients): dose-finding across molecular subtypes — at the 600 mg recommended dose, 35% of NPM1-mutated patients reached complete remission
cards.summary: KOMET-001 phase 1 (83 patients): dose-finding across molecular subtypes — at the 600 mg recommended dose, 35% of NPM1-mutated patients reached complete remission
cards.people: 83 adults with relapsed or refractory AML of any molecular subtype in phase 1a dose escalation (ziftomenib 50–1000 mg daily), and NPM1-mutated or KMT2A-rearranged patients in phase 1b randomised between 200 mg and 600 mg cohorts.
cards.result: At the recommended phase 2 dose of 600 mg, 9 of 36 patients with KMT2A rearrangement or NPM1 mutation (25%) achieved CR/CRh, and 7 of 20 NPM1-mutated patients (35%) achieved complete remission; no responses occurred at 200 mg. Commonest grade 3-or-worse events: anaemia 24%, febrile neutropenia 22%, pneumonia 19%, differentiation syndrome 15%, thrombocytopenia 13%, sepsis 12%. Two treatment-related deaths occurred (one differentiation syndrome, one cardiac arrest). Differentiation syndrome severity in KMT2A-rearranged patients led to halting their enrolment.
cards.watchOut: Phase 1 mixes doses, subtypes and intents; the NPM1-specific numbers come from a 20-patient subgroup at the recommended dose — supportive of the phase 2 result, not independent confirmation of it.

cards.headline: Population pharmacokinetic and exposure–response analysis: no exposure measure predicted efficacy or safety in NPM1-mutated patients — a flat exposure–response supporting the fixed 600 mg dose
cards.summary: Population pharmacokinetic and exposure–response analysis: no exposure measure predicted efficacy or safety in NPM1-mutated patients — a flat exposure–response supporting the fixed 600 mg dose
cards.people: Pharmacokinetic modelling in healthy volunteers and relapsed/refractory AML patients, with exposure–response analyses in the relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML patients treated with ziftomenib monotherapy in the programme (the record does not state the analysis population's N — N not documented).
cards.result: A two-compartment model described ziftomenib pharmacokinetics; mutation status (NPM1-mutated vs KMT2A-rearranged), weight, sex, race, age, mild-to-moderate renal or hepatic impairment and P-gp inhibition did not affect exposure. Across six efficacy-endpoint combinations and twelve safety endpoints, no steady-state exposure measure was statistically related to efficacy or safety — flat exposure–response profiles over a wide exposure range, supporting a wide therapeutic margin at 600 mg once daily. Co-administered azole antifungals had no clinically meaningful effect on efficacy or safety profiles.
cards.watchOut: This is a modelling analysis of patients from the same KOMET-001 programme, not a third efficacy trial — it is carded as the third on-question monotherapy report because it verifies in the NPM1-mutated monotherapy population, but it adds dose justification, not independent efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Population Pharmacokinetics and Exposure-Response Analysis of Ziftomenib in Relapsed or Refractory Acute Myeloid Leukemia Patients With NPM1 Mutation. cards.headline: Synthesis: ziftomenib monotherapy produces complete remissions in about a fifth to a third of relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML patients — POSSIBLE on a three-report, single-programme, single-arm base
cards.summary: Synthesis: ziftomenib monotherapy produces complete remissions in about a fifth to a third of relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML patients — POSSIBLE on a three-report, single-programme, single-arm base
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: KOMET-001 phase 2 (92 patients), KOMET-001 phase 1 (83 patients) and the programme's population-pharmacokinetic/exposure–response analysis.
cards.result: The efficacy story is two single-arm reports from one programme (CR/CRh 22% in phase 2; 35% complete remission in the small phase 1 NPM1 subgroup at the same dose), plus a modelling report confirming flat exposure–response at 600 mg. That meets the three-report floor for this shelf, but only just, and nothing here is randomised — POSSIBLE is the ceiling. Differentiation syndrome is the defining harm (25% in phase 2, one treatment-related death in phase 1). The ziftomenib-plus-venetoclax-plus-azacitidine combination report in this population asks a different (combination) question and is cross-pointed here in prose only — it is not carded into this monotherapy shelf. Product naming (clarification exception): ziftomenib (Komzifti, Kura Oncology).

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — for the shelf's combined question, with the two limbs stated separately. Second line: the randomised TRANSFORM trial (184 transplant-eligible patients with primary refractory or early-relapsed large B-cell lymphoma) showed large, durable event-free and progression-free survival advantages for lisocabtagene maraleucel over salvage chemotherapy plus autologous transplant (event-free survival hazard ratio 0.375, progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.422 — relative measures; 36-month progression-free survival 51% vs 26.5%), while overall survival was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.757) in a trial where 66% of controls crossed over to liso-cel. Third line or later: the evidence is the single-arm TRANSCEND study (73% objective response, 53% complete response; 5-year survival 38% in efficacy-evaluable patients, 33% of everyone leukapheresed) plus a concordant real-world analysis in older, comorbid patients — single-arm evidence caps that limb, and so the shelf, at POSSIBLE. Liso-cel is a defined-composition product (separate CD4 and CD8 CAR T components at equal target doses) and is named exactly for that reason. Grade 3-or-worse cytokine release syndrome was 2–3% and neurotoxicity about 10% across reports; there is no head-to-head trial against any other CAR T product, and cross-product comparisons are not made here.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM phase 3, 3-year follow-up (184 patients): second-line liso-cel beat standard salvage chemotherapy/transplant on event-free survival (median 29.5 vs 2.4 months; hazard ratio 0.375) and progression-free survival, with overall survival not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.757) after 66% crossover
cards.summary: TRANSFORM phase 3, 3-year follow-up (184 patients): second-line liso-cel beat standard salvage chemotherapy/transplant on event-free survival (median 29.5 vs 2.4 months; hazard ratio 0.375) and progression-free survival, with overall survival not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.757) after 66% crossover
cards.people: 184 transplant-eligible adults with primary refractory or early-relapsed (within 12 months) large B-cell lymphoma, randomised 1:1 to lisocabtagene maraleucel (100 × 10⁶ CAR T cells) or standard care (salvage immunochemotherapy, then high-dose chemotherapy and autologous transplant in responders).
cards.result: At median follow-up of 33.9 months, median event-free survival was 29.5 months with liso-cel vs 2.4 months with standard care (hazard ratio 0.375, 95% CI 0.259 to 0.542, relative); median progression-free survival was not reached vs 6.2 months (hazard ratio 0.422), with 36-month progression-free survival 51% vs 26.5%. Median overall survival was not reached in either arm (hazard ratio 0.757, 95% CI 0.481 to 1.191 — not significant); 36-month survival was 63% vs 52%, and a crossover-adjusted analysis favoured liso-cel (hazard ratio 0.566). Two-thirds (66%) of the standard-care arm crossed over to receive liso-cel.
cards.watchOut: The null overall-survival result is entangled with the 66% crossover — read it as 'no proven survival difference in a trial where most controls later got the drug', not as proof of no survival effect in either direction.
cards.source: Lisocabtagene Maraleucel Versus Standard of Care for Second-Line Relapsed/Refractory Large B-Cell Lymphoma: 3-Year Follow-Up From the Randomized, Phase III TRANSFORM Study. cards.headline: TRANSCEND NHL 001 (269 treated; 256 efficacy-evaluable): third-line-or-later liso-cel gave a 73% objective response and 53% complete response — single-arm
cards.summary: TRANSCEND NHL 001 (269 treated; 256 efficacy-evaluable): third-line-or-later liso-cel gave a 73% objective response and 53% complete response — single-arm
cards.people: Adults with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (median 3 prior lines; 67% chemotherapy-refractory; including double/triple-hit, transformed and primary mediastinal histologies) treated with liso-cel — a defined-composition CD19 CAR T product given as separate CD4 and CD8 components at equal target doses — at 14 US centres. No concurrent control.
cards.result: Objective response was 73% and complete response 53% in the efficacy-evaluable set. Grade 3-or-worse events: neutropenia 60%, anaemia 37%, thrombocytopenia 27%. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 42% and neurological events in 30%, but grade 3-or-worse rates were low: cytokine release syndrome 2%, neurological events 10%. One patient died of diffuse alveolar damage after a 50 × 10⁶-cell dose.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm response rates in third line have no randomised anchor in this study; the comparative claim for liso-cel comes from TRANSFORM (second line), a fitter, transplant-eligible population.

cards.headline: TRANSCEND 5-year follow-up: median survival 27.5 months and 5-year survival 38% in efficacy-evaluable patients (33% counting everyone leukapheresed)
cards.summary: TRANSCEND 5-year follow-up: median survival 27.5 months and 5-year survival 38% in efficacy-evaluable patients (33% counting everyone leukapheresed)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the single-arm study
cards.people: Patients from TRANSCEND NHL 001 (345 leukapheresed, 270 treated) followed into a separate long-term follow-up study, including 84 patients alive at study completion who enrolled in long-term follow-up.
cards.result: Among 257 efficacy-evaluable patients, median overall survival was 27.5 months and estimated 5-year overall survival 38%; in the full leukapheresed set, median survival was 15.2 months and 5-year survival 33% — the gap between the two sets is the cost of manufacturing time and patients never infused. Median disease-specific survival was 67.8 months (5-year rate 52%). Most deaths occurred within 2 years of infusion; no new safety signals emerged, with low rates of late severe infection and second primary malignancies.
cards.watchOut: The 78% 5-year survival in the long-term-follow-up subset describes patients already alive at study completion — a survivor subset, not a treatment effect; use the 38%/33% figures.
cards.source: Five-year survival outcomes of lisocabtagene maraleucel in R/R LBCL from the TRANSCEND NHL 001 study. Blood. 2026. PMID: 42237652. cards.headline: Real-world consortium analysis (101 infused patients, observational): commercial liso-cel matched trial results in older, comorbid patients — day-90 response 66%, complete response 60%
cards.summary: Real-world consortium analysis (101 infused patients, observational): commercial liso-cel matched trial results in older, comorbid patients — day-90 response 66%, complete response 60%
cards.people: 101 patients receiving commercial liso-cel at 7 US centres (median age 71; 35% aged 75 or older; 68% with Charlson comorbidity index at least 3; 33% would have been ineligible for TRANSCEND). Retrospective, no comparator.
cards.result: Any-grade cytokine release syndrome occurred in 49% (3% grade 3 or worse) and immune-effector-cell neurotoxicity in 26% (10% grade 3 or worse). Day-90 overall response was 66% with 60% complete responses; at median follow-up of 15.5 months, 12-month progression-free survival was 55% and overall survival 68%. Bridging therapy was used in 60% (43% polatuzumab-based). A normal LDH before lymphodepletion predicted better outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Observational and centre-selected; its value is transportability (trial-like results in trial-ineligible patients), not comparative efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: liso-cel is randomised-proven in second line and durably active in later lines — POSSIBLE for the combined question, because the later-line limb is single-arm
cards.summary: Synthesis: liso-cel is randomised-proven in second line and durably active in later lines — POSSIBLE for the combined question, because the later-line limb is single-arm
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the TRANSFORM randomised phase 3 trial (184 patients, second line), the TRANSCEND single-arm study (269 treated, third line or later) with its 5-year follow-up, and a real-world consortium analysis (101 patients).
cards.result: In second line, liso-cel's event-free and progression-free survival advantages over salvage chemotherapy/transplant pathways are large and randomised (hazard ratios 0.375 and 0.422, relative), with overall survival unproven under heavy crossover. In third line or later, the evidence is single-arm (73% response, 53% complete response; 5-year survival 38%) with concordant real-world results — hence POSSIBLE for the shelf's combined question rather than a stronger stamp. Severe cytokine release syndrome (2–3% grade 3 or worse) and neurotoxicity (10%) run lower than historical CD19 CAR T experience, but no head-to-head trial against another CAR T product exists, so any cross-product comparison is fenced off as unproven.
cards.watchOut: Defined-composition product: liso-cel is manufactured as separate CD4 and CD8 CAR T components dosed in equal target amounts — results should not be assumed to transfer to other CD19 CAR T products, or theirs to it.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — brexucabtagene autoleucel in relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma rests entirely on the single-arm ZUMA-2 programme: in the licensed post-BTK-inhibitor population, objective response was 93% and complete response 67% at primary analysis, holding at 91%/68% at 3 years, with median duration of response 36.5 months and median overall survival 46.5 months at 5 years. Cohort 3 extends similar responses (91% objective, 73% complete) to BTK-inhibitor-naïve patients — a different slice, labelled as such and not merged into the licensed-population claim. Single-arm evidence throughout caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no randomised comparison against any alternative. The harm burden is heavy and belongs on the face: grade 3-or-worse cytopenias 94%, infections 32%, grade 3-or-worse neurological events 31%, and 22% non-relapse mortality among responders by 5 years. ZUMA-3 in B-cell ALL is a different disease — cross-pointed in prose only.

cards.headline: ZUMA-2 primary analysis (68 treated; 60 in the primary efficacy set): brexu-cel gave a 93% objective response and 67% complete response in mantle cell lymphoma after a BTK inhibitor — single-arm
cards.summary: ZUMA-2 primary analysis (68 treated; 60 in the primary efficacy set): brexu-cel gave a 93% objective response and 67% complete response in mantle cell lymphoma after a BTK inhibitor — single-arm
cards.people: 74 enrolled patients with relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma after up to five prior therapies, all previously treated with a BTK inhibitor; brexucabtagene autoleucel (KTE-X19) was manufactured for 71 and infused in 68 at 2 × 10⁶ CAR T cells/kg after leukapheresis, optional bridging and conditioning chemotherapy. No concurrent control.
cards.result: In the primary efficacy analysis (60 patients followed at least 7 months), objective response was 93% (95% CI 84 to 98) and complete response 67% (53 to 78); in all 74 enrolled patients, response was 85% and complete response 59%. At median follow-up of 12.3 months, 57% of the primary set remained in remission; estimated 12-month progression-free survival was 61% and overall survival 83%. Grade 3-or-worse events: cytopenias 94%, infections 32%, cytokine release syndrome 15%, neurological events 31% (none fatal); two grade 5 infectious events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the response rates are striking but uncontrolled, and the licensed population is specifically post-BTK-inhibitor — cohort 3 (below) is a different, BTK-inhibitor-naïve slice and must not be merged into this claim.
cards.source: KTE-X19 CAR T-Cell Therapy in Relapsed or Refractory Mantle-Cell Lymphoma. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32242358. single-arm phase 2 trial 74 enrolled patients with relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma after up to five prior therapies, all previously treated with a btk inhibitor; brexucabtagene autoleucel (kte-x19) was manufactured for 71 and infused in 68 at 2 × 10⁶ car t cells/kg after leukapheresis, optional bridging and conditioning chemotherapy. no concurrent control. in the primary efficacy analysis (60 patients followed at least 7 months), objective response was 93% (95% ci 84 to 98) and complete response 67% (53 to 78); in all 74 enrolled patients, response was 85% and complete response 59%. at median follow-up of 12.3 months, 57% of the primary set remained in remission; estimated 12-month progression-free survival was 61% and overall survival 83%. grade 3-or-worse events: cytopenias 94%, infections 32%, cytokine release syndrome 15%, neurological events 31% (none fatal); two grade 5 infectious events occurred. single-arm: the response rates are striking but uncontrolled, and the licensed population is specifically post-btk-inhibitor — cohort 3 (below) is a different, btk-inhibitor-naïve slice and must not be merged into this claim. kte-x19 car t-cell therapy in relapsed or refractory mantle-cell lymphoma. the new england journal of medicine. 2020. pmid: 32242358. registry id: nct02601313 (clinicaltrials.gov, from the record). mesh: adult · aged · antigens, cd19/therapeutic use · antineoplastic agents/therapeutic use · combined modality therapy · humans · immunotherapy, adoptive/adverse effects · infusions, intravenous · leukapheresis · lymphoma, mantle-cell/drug therapy,mortality,therapy · middle aged · receptors, chimeric antigen/antagonists & inhibitors · recurrence · survival analysis · t-lymphocytes/transplantation · vidarabine/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use

cards.headline: ZUMA-2 three-year follow-up (68 treated): response held at 91% with 68% complete responses; median duration of response 28.2 months and median survival 46.6 months
cards.summary: ZUMA-2 three-year follow-up (68 treated): response held at 91% with 68% complete responses; median duration of response 28.2 months and median survival 46.6 months
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the single-arm phase 2 trial
cards.people: All 68 ZUMA-2 treated patients (post-BTK-inhibitor relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma) at a median follow-up of 35.6 months, including subgroups by prior therapy and high-risk features.
cards.result: Objective response was 91% (95% CI 81.8 to 96.7) with 68% complete responses. Median duration of response was 28.2 months, median progression-free survival 25.8 months and median overall survival 46.6 months. Responses were consistent across prior-BTK-inhibitor type and high-risk subgroups. Only 3% of treatment-emergent adverse events of interest occurred during this longer follow-up window. Prior bendamustine was associated with attenuated T-cell functionality, more so when given within 6 months of leukapheresis.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up of the same single-arm cohort — durability evidence, not independent confirmation; subgroup consistency is descriptive.
cards.source: Three-Year Follow-Up of KTE-X19 in Patients With Relapsed/Refractory Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Including High-Risk Subgroups, in the ZUMA-2 Study. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2023. PMID: 35658525. Registry ID: NCT02601313 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: ZUMA-2 five-year follow-up (cohort 1, 68 treated): median duration of response 36.5 months and median survival 46.5 months; in complete responders, median survival was 60.2 months
cards.summary: ZUMA-2 five-year follow-up (cohort 1, 68 treated): median duration of response 36.5 months and median survival 46.5 months; in complete responders, median survival was 60.2 months
cards.type: Five-year follow-up report of the single-arm phase 2 trial
cards.people: The pivotal ZUMA-2 cohort 1 at a median follow-up of 67.8 months; the report also describes two small previously unpublished sets (10 patients who received axicabtagene ciloleucel in cohort 1 and 14 patients given a lower brexu-cel dose in cohort 2), which are not carded as evidence here.
cards.result: Median duration of response was 36.5 months (among the 60 responders assessed) and median overall survival 46.5 months (95% CI 24.5 to 60.2); among the 46 patients with complete response, median survival was 60.2 months. Among responders, the 5-year cumulative incidence of relapse-related mortality was 40% and of non-relapse mortality 22%. No grade 5 cytokine release syndrome or neurological events, no subsequent T-cell malignancies and no new safety signals were reported.
cards.watchOut: Responder-based survival (60.2 months in complete responders) is guaranteed-time-biased; the whole-cohort median (46.5 months) is the honest figure. The 22% non-relapse mortality among responders is a real long-term cost of the therapy and its sequelae.
cards.source: Five-year follow-up of patients with relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma treated with anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in ZUMA-2, Cohorts 1 and 2. Journal of hematology & oncology. 2026. PMID: 42036693. Registry ID: NCT02601313 and NCT05041309 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: ZUMA-2 cohort 3 primary analysis (86 treated) — a different slice, BTK-inhibitor-naïve patients: objective response 91%, complete response 73%
cards.summary: ZUMA-2 cohort 3 primary analysis (86 treated) — a different slice, BTK-inhibitor-naïve patients: objective response 91%, complete response 73%
cards.people: 95 enrolled adults with relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma who had NOT previously received a BTK inhibitor; 86 received brexu-cel at 2 × 10⁶ CAR T cells/kg. Median follow-up 15.5 months. Single-arm.
cards.result: Objective response was 91% (95% CI 82.5 to 95.9) and complete response 73% (62.6 to 82.2) in treated patients; among all 95 enrolled, response was 82% and complete response 66%. Estimated 12-month progression-free survival was 75%, duration-of-response rate 80% and overall survival 90%. Most patients (88%) had treatment-related grade 3-or-worse events, including 4 treatment-related grade 5 events.
cards.watchOut: This cohort answers a neighbouring question (patients not yet exposed to a BTK inhibitor) — it widens the population in whom responses are seen but is not evidence about the licensed post-BTK-inhibitor population, and its follow-up is much shorter.

cards.headline: Synthesis: brexu-cel produces high, durable complete-response rates in post-BTK-inhibitor mantle cell lymphoma — POSSIBLE, because every report is single-arm
cards.summary: Synthesis: brexu-cel produces high, durable complete-response rates in post-BTK-inhibitor mantle cell lymphoma — POSSIBLE, because every report is single-arm
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the ZUMA-2 programme — primary analysis (68 treated), 3-year and 5-year follow-ups of the same cohort, and cohort 3 in BTK-inhibitor-naïve patients (86 treated).
cards.result: Response depth and durability are consistent across five years of follow-up (complete response 67–68%; median duration of response up to 36.5 months; median survival 46.5 months in the whole treated cohort), and a separate cohort shows similar responses before BTK-inhibitor exposure. But there is no randomised or concurrent control anywhere in this programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and all rates are single-arm. Harms are substantial: grade 3-or-worse cytopenias in 94%, infections in 32%, neurological events grade 3 or worse in 31% at primary analysis, and a 22% 5-year non-relapse mortality among responders. ZUMA-3 (B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia) is a different disease and is cross-pointed here in prose only — none of its data are carded into this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Patients who never reach infusion (74 enrolled, 68 treated) and the bridging period are part of the real-world cost; intention-to-treat response was 85%, not 93%.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 32242358, 35658525, 42036693, 41160777). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Obecabtagene autoleucel in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (FELIX): 77% remission, low severe immunotoxicity — single-arm evidence
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does obecabtagene autoleucel, versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions with lower severe immunotoxicity than earlier CD19 CAR T products?
shelves.mesh: Precursor B-Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma · Immunotherapy, Adoptive · Receptors, Chimeric Antigen · Antigens, CD19 · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: Single-programme, single-arm evidence: every card comes from the one FELIX phase 1b/2 study (no randomised or concurrent control exists). In the morphologic-disease cohort, overall remission was 77% and median overall survival in infused patients was 15.6 months, with grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome in only 2.4% and grade ≥3 neurotoxicity in 7.1% — the low severe-immunotoxicity claim rests on the product's intermediate-affinity CAR and its tumour-burden-guided split dosing, and the burden analysis (grade ≥3 CRS 2% vs 3%, ICANS 4% vs 9% in low- vs high-burden groups) is consistent with that design rather than proof of it. The external-control comparison favours obe-cel over historical non-CAR therapy but is a propensity-matched, non-randomised comparison and is labelled as such. Cross-product claims of lower toxicity than earlier CD19 CAR T products are cross-trial impressions only; no head-to-head trial exists. Product naming (clarification exception): obecabtagene autoleucel (Aucatzyl, Autolus) — the tested product as published.

cards.headline: FELIX primary: in adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL and morphologic disease, obecabtagene autoleucel produced overall remission in 77% — with grade ≥3 CRS in only 2.4%
cards.summary: FELIX primary: in adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL and morphologic disease, obecabtagene autoleucel produced overall remission in 77% — with grade ≥3 CRS in only 2.4%
cards.type: Phase 1b/2 single-arm multicentre trial (FELIX), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 153 adults (≥18 years) with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia enrolled in the phase 1b/2 FELIX study; 127 (83.0%) received at least one infusion and were evaluable. Cohort 2A (morphologic disease, n=94) carried the primary endpoint; cohort 2B had measurable residual disease. Obe-cel is an autologous 4-1BB anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy using an intermediate-affinity CAR, given as tumour-burden-guided split-dose infusions. No concurrent control group.
cards.result: In cohort 2A (median follow-up 20.3 months), overall remission occurred in 77% (95% CI 67–85): complete remission 55% and complete remission with incomplete haematologic recovery 21%; the prespecified null hypotheses (remission ≤40%, complete remission ≤20%) were rejected (P<0.001). In all 127 infused patients, median event-free survival was 11.9 months and median overall survival 15.6 months (12-month overall survival 61.1%). Grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome developed in 2.4% and grade ≥3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome in 7.1%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 77% remission rate has no concurrent comparator, and the low severe-toxicity rates are a within-trial observation — any claim of lower toxicity than other CD19 CAR T products is a cross-trial impression, not a tested comparison.
cards.source: Roddie C, Sandhu KS, Tholouli E, et al. Obecabtagene Autoleucel in Adults with B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39602653. Registry ID: NCT04404660. cards.headline: FELIX tumour-burden analysis: split dosing by marrow blast burden kept grade ≥3 CRS at 2–3% and grade ≥3 ICANS at 4–9%, with remission 85% (low burden) vs 73% (high burden)
cards.summary: FELIX tumour-burden analysis: split dosing by marrow blast burden kept grade ≥3 CRS at 2–3% and grade ≥3 ICANS at 4–9%, with remission 85% (low burden) vs 73% (high burden)
cards.people: Patients in the FELIX phase 1b/2 study analysed by pre-lymphodepletion tumour burden: low-burden group ≤20% bone marrow blasts, high-burden group >20%, receiving burden-guided split-dose obe-cel infusions.
cards.result: Tumour burden drove CAR T-cell expansion (a 50% increase in burden, e.g. 70% vs 20% blasts, was associated with a 1.9-fold increase in maximal expansion, 95% CI 1.4–2.6). Grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome occurred in 2% (low burden) vs 3% (high burden) and grade ≥3 neurotoxicity in 4% vs 9%. Overall remission was 85% in the low-burden group and 73% in the high-burden group. The authors conclude the burden-guided split-dose strategy may mitigate immunotoxicity while maintaining efficacy, while noting further study is needed.
cards.watchOut: A within-trial subgroup analysis of the same single-arm study — it shows toxicity stayed low in both burden groups, but with no non-split-dose arm it cannot prove the split dosing caused the low rates.
cards.source: Jabbour E, Sandhu KS, Shaughnessy P, et al. Tumor burden-guided dosing contributes to mitigation of immunotoxicities following treatment with obecabtagene autoleucel in adult patients with relapsed/refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Haematologica. 2026. PMID: 41504229. Registry ID: NCT04404660. cards.headline: FELIX external-control comparison: remission 67.3% with obe-cel vs 51.4% with matched historical non-CAR therapy (odds ratio 1.9) — a non-randomised comparison
cards.summary: FELIX external-control comparison: remission 67.3% with obe-cel vs 51.4% with matched historical non-CAR therapy (odds ratio 1.9) — a non-randomised comparison
cards.people: Intent-to-treat FELIX population (n=107) compared by propensity-score matching with external control arms derived from historical trials of standard non-CAR T-cell therapies: blinatumomab, inotuzumab ozogamicin, and conventional chemotherapy, in adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL.
cards.result: Overall remission was 67.3% with obe-cel vs 51.4% with external controls (odds ratio 1.9; P=0.0257). Median overall survival favoured obe-cel both censoring for transplant (15.1 vs 7.0 months; P=0.0015) and without censoring (13.9 vs 7.8 months; P=0.0430), and median event-free survival was 9.8 vs 2.5 months (P<0.0001). Grade ≥3 adverse event rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Observational comparison against historical trial controls, labelled as such: matching cannot remove confounding by era, eligibility and supportive care, so this supports — but cannot substitute for — a randomised comparison, which does not exist.
cards.source: Topp MS, Shah BD, Jabbour E, et al. Comparison of obecabtagene autoleucel versus an external control arm in adult patients with relapsed/refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Leukemia. 2026. PMID: 42469475. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FELIX kinetics analysis: loss of CAR T-cell persistence was associated with poorer event-free survival (hazard ratio 2.7)
cards.summary: FELIX kinetics analysis: loss of CAR T-cell persistence was associated with poorer event-free survival (hazard ratio 2.7)
cards.type: Phase 1b/2 correlative analysis (FELIX), Cancer Res Commun 2026
cards.people: Peripheral blood samples from the 127 obe-cel-infused FELIX patients, comparing CAR T-cell measurement by flow cytometry and droplet digital PCR, and relating persistence and B-cell aplasia to event-free survival.
cards.result: Droplet digital PCR was more sensitive than flow cytometry (58.8% of surface-flow-negative samples were PCR-positive) and correlated with both flow assays. Loss of CAR T-cell persistence was associated with poorer event-free survival (hazard ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.4–5.4, as a time-dependent variable and at month 3); B-cell recovery showed a weaker association (hazard ratio 1.7, 95% CI 0.7–3.8).
cards.watchOut: A biomarker correlation within the same single-arm trial: persistence may mark, rather than cause, durable control, and the analysis does not change the efficacy estimate from the primary report.
cards.source: Roddie C, Day W, Raymond M, et al. CAR T-cell Kinetics, Persistence, and Clinical Outcomes in Adult Patients with Relapsed/Refractory B-cell ALL Treated with Obecabtagene Autoleucel in the FELIX Study. cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm FELIX evidence — 77% remission with unusually low severe immunotoxicity; no randomised comparison exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm FELIX evidence — 77% remission with unusually low severe immunotoxicity; no randomised comparison exists
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded FELIX reports above (primary report, n=127 infused; tumour-burden analysis; external-control comparison, n=107; kinetics analysis, n=127) — all one programme, one trial.
cards.result: Obecabtagene autoleucel produced overall remission in 77% of adults with morphologic relapsed/refractory B-ALL, median overall survival of 15.6 months in infused patients, and grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome in 2.4% and grade ≥3 neurotoxicity in 7.1% — rates the programme attributes to its intermediate-affinity CAR and tumour-burden-guided split dosing, with the burden analysis (remission 85% low-burden vs 73% high-burden; severe toxicity low in both) consistent with that account. A propensity-matched external-control comparison favoured obe-cel over historical blinatumomab, inotuzumab ozogamicin or chemotherapy (remission 67.3% vs 51.4%), but it is observational and labelled as such. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the entire base is single-arm: remission and toxicity are described, not compared, and cross-product toxicity claims have no head-to-head test.
cards.watchOut: One trial, four reports: the reports corroborate each other but are not independent evidence — a second programme or a randomised trial would be needed to move this stamp.

shelves.title: Mosunetuzumab in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma: complete responses ~60%, fixed duration — single-arm evidence
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after ≥2 prior lines, does fixed-duration mosunetuzumab (CD20×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce durable complete responses?
shelves.mesh: Lymphoma, Follicular · Antibodies, Bispecific · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Single-arm evidence throughout: no randomised or concurrent control exists for mosunetuzumab in follicular lymphoma. The intravenous pivotal phase 2 (n=90, ≥2 prior lines) found a complete response rate of 60.0% against a 14% historical-control benchmark, with cytokine release syndrome in 44% — predominantly grade 1–2 and confined to cycle 1 under step-up dosing. The subcutaneous pivotal analysis (n=94) showed non-inferior exposure to the intravenous form with complete responses in 61.7%, median progression-free survival 23.7 months, and a numerically lower cytokine release syndrome rate (29.8% vs 44.4% in the within-study intravenous cohort) — a formulation comparison, not a randomised one. An older-patient subgroup found responses at least as high at age ≥65 (complete response 70.0% in the pivotal follicular cohort) with no excess serious adverse events. Fixed duration (complete responders stop after cycle 8) is part of the tested intervention. Cross-point: the library's DLBCL bispecific shelf asks a different question in a different disease with different molecules and is not duplicated here.

cards.headline: Pivotal phase 2 (intravenous): complete response in 60.0% of 90 patients with follicular lymphoma after ≥2 prior lines — against a 14% historical benchmark
cards.summary: Pivotal phase 2 (intravenous): complete response in 60.0% of 90 patients with follicular lymphoma after ≥2 prior lines — against a 14% historical benchmark
cards.people: 90 adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma (grade 1–3a), relapsed or refractory to ≥2 previous lines including an anti-CD20 therapy and an alkylating agent, ECOG performance status 0–1, at 49 centres in seven countries. Intravenous mosunetuzumab in 21-day cycles with cycle-1 step-up dosing (1 mg, 2 mg, then 60 mg); complete responders completed treatment after cycle 8, others continued up to 17 cycles. Single-arm.
cards.result: Independent-review complete response was recorded in 54 of 90 patients (60.0%, 95% CI 49.1–70.2), significantly higher than the 14% historical-control complete response rate with copanlisib (P<0.0001), meeting the primary endpoint; median follow-up was 18.3 months. Cytokine release syndrome was the most common adverse event (44%), predominantly grade 1 (26%) or grade 2 (17%) and primarily confined to cycle 1. The most common grade 3–4 events were neutropenia (27%), hypophosphataemia (17%), hyperglycaemia (8%) and anaemia (8%); serious adverse events occurred in 47% and no treatment-related fatal adverse event occurred.
cards.watchOut: The 14% comparator is a historical benchmark from a different drug's population, not a concurrent control — the trial demonstrates activity, not superiority over any current alternative.
cards.source: Budde LE, Sehn LH, Matasar M, et al. Safety and efficacy of mosunetuzumab, a bispecific antibody, in patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma: a single-arm, multicentre, phase 2 study. The Lancet Oncology. 2022. PMID: 35803286. Registry ID: NCT02500407. cards.headline: Subcutaneous pivotal analysis: complete response 61.7% in 94 patients, median progression-free survival 23.7 months, cytokine release syndrome 29.8% vs 44.4% for intravenous
cards.summary: Subcutaneous pivotal analysis: complete response 61.7% in 94 patients, median progression-free survival 23.7 months, cytokine release syndrome 29.8% vs 44.4% for intravenous
cards.type: Phase 2 pivotal primary analysis (subcutaneous), Am J Hematol 2026
cards.people: 94 patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma after ≥2 prior therapies receiving subcutaneous mosunetuzumab at the recommended phase 2 dose (5 mg cycle 1 day 1, then 45 mg), median follow-up 26.1 months, reported alongside a within-study intravenous comparator cohort (n=90, follow-up 22.5 months) from the same programme.
cards.result: Co-primary pharmacokinetic endpoints were met, showing non-inferior exposure of subcutaneous vs intravenous dosing. Overall response was 76.6% (95% CI 66.7–84.7) and complete response 61.7% (95% CI 51.1–71.5); median duration of complete response was 34.6 months and median progression-free survival 23.7 months. Cytokine release syndrome was numerically less frequent and less severe with subcutaneous dosing (29.8% vs 44.4% any grade; grade ≥2 in 9.6% vs 18.9%).
cards.watchOut: The intravenous cohort is a within-study comparator, not a randomised arm — the lower cytokine release syndrome rate with subcutaneous dosing is a numerical, cross-cohort difference.
cards.source: Bartlett NL, Sehn LH, Assouline S, et al. Fixed-Duration Subcutaneous Mosunetuzumab in Relapsed/Refractory Follicular Lymphoma: Pivotal Phase 2 Primary Analysis. American Journal of Hematology. 2026. PMID: 41862428. Registry ID: NCT02500407. cards.headline: Older-patient subgroup: in the pivotal follicular cohort, complete response was 70.0% at age ≥65 vs 55.0% younger, with no excess serious adverse events
cards.summary: Older-patient subgroup: in the pivotal follicular cohort, complete response was 70.0% at age ≥65 vs 55.0% younger, with no excess serious adverse events
cards.type: Phase 1/2 subgroup analysis, Br J Haematol 2026
cards.people: Subgroup analysis of a phase 1/2 study (NCT02500407): 218 patients with relapsed/refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma from the phase 1 expansion cohort (102 aged ≥65, 116 younger) and 90 patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma from the pivotal cohort (30 aged ≥65, 60 younger), all treated with mosunetuzumab.
cards.result: In B-cell lymphoma, cytokine release syndrome was less frequent in older than younger patients (33.3% vs 44.8%) and serious adverse events were similar (45.1% vs 46.6%). In follicular lymphoma, overall response was 86.7% and complete response 70.0% in older patients vs 76.7% and 55.0% in younger patients; median progression-free survival was 17.9 months in older patients vs 12.0 months in younger, and time to next treatment was not reached vs 18.1 months.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of the same programme (30 older follicular patients): reassuring on tolerability in older patients, but far too small to establish an age advantage — the higher older-patient response rates are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Thiruvengadam SK, Popplewell LL, Herrera AF, et al. Mosunetuzumab is effective and well tolerated in older patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma: Subgroup analysis of a phase I/II study. British Journal of Haematology. 2026. shelves.title: Loncastuximab tesirine in relapsed/refractory DLBCL (LOTIS-2): ~48% responses in trials, less in real-world use — single-arm evidence
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines, does loncastuximab tesirine (CD19 antibody–drug conjugate), versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse · Immunoconjugates · Antigens, CD19 · Benzodiazepines · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Single-arm pivotal evidence with a sobering real-world limb. LOTIS-2 (n=145, ≥2 prior lines) found an overall response rate of 48.3% with complete responses in 24.1%, and the long-term report shows the complete responders drive the benefit (24-month survival 68.2% in complete responders; median overall survival 9.5 months overall). A Chinese phase 2 (n=64) reproduced the response rate (51.6%). But the largest real-world series (n=187, 21 US centres, more heavily pretreated and higher-risk than LOTIS-2) found responses of only 32% and median overall survival of 4.6 months — labelled observational. The pyrrolobenzodiazepine-dimer payload's signature harms belong on the face: oedema and effusions, photosensitivity, and gamma-glutamyltransferase elevation (grade ≥3 in 17% in LOTIS-2), alongside neutropenia (26%) and thrombocytopenia (18%). Responses cannot be separated into antibody vs payload effects. Product naming (clarification exception): loncastuximab tesirine (Zynlonta, ADC Therapeutics) — the tested product as published.

cards.headline: LOTIS-2 primary: overall response 48.3% and complete response 24.1% in 145 patients with DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines
cards.summary: LOTIS-2 primary: overall response 48.3% and complete response 24.1% in 145 patients with DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines
cards.people: 145 adults with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after ≥2 multiagent systemic treatments (including double-hit, triple-hit, transformed and primary refractory disease), ECOG 0–2, at 28 sites in the USA, UK, Italy and Switzerland. Loncastuximab tesirine 150 µg/kg for two cycles, then 75 µg/kg, every 21 days for up to 1 year. Single-arm, open-label.
cards.result: 70 of 145 patients responded (overall response rate 48.3%, 95% CI 39.9–56.7): 35 complete and 35 partial responses. The most common grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events were neutropenia (26%), thrombocytopenia (18%) and increased gamma-glutamyltransferase (17%). Serious adverse events occurred in 39%; treatment-emergent events with a fatal outcome occurred in 6%, none considered related to loncastuximab tesirine.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: a 48.3% response rate in a population with no good options is meaningful activity, but there is no concurrent control and median survival in the full cohort (see long-term card) remained under 10 months.
cards.source: Caimi PF, Ai W, Alderuccio JP, et al. Loncastuximab tesirine in relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (LOTIS-2): a multicentre, open-label, single-arm, phase 2 trial. The Lancet Oncology. 2021. PMID: 33989558. Registry ID: NCT03589469. cards.headline: LOTIS-2 long-term: complete responders did durably well (24-month survival 68.2%), but median overall survival for all 145 patients was 9.5 months
cards.summary: LOTIS-2 long-term: complete responders did durably well (24-month survival 68.2%), but median overall survival for all 145 patients was 9.5 months
cards.people: All 145 LOTIS-2 patients at the final data cutoff (September 15, 2022), with subsets of complete responders who remained event-free for ≥1 and ≥2 years from treatment start.
cards.result: Overall response remained 48.3% (70 of 145); 36 patients (24.8%) achieved complete response, of whom 44% were event-free at ≥1 year and 31% at ≥2 years. Median overall survival was 9.5 months and median progression-free survival 4.9 months in the all-treated population; among complete responders neither median was reached, with 24-month overall survival 68.2% (95% CI 50.0–81.0) and progression-free survival 72.5%. No new safety concerns were detected.
cards.watchOut: The durable-benefit story is concentrated in the one patient in four who reaches complete response; quoting the complete-responder survival without the 9.5-month all-patient median would misstate the drug's average effect.
cards.source: Caimi PF, Ai WZ, Alderuccio JP, et al. Loncastuximab tesirine in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: long-term efficacy and safety from the phase II LOTIS-2 study.
