cards.headline: Chinese phase 2: overall response 51.6% and complete response 23.4% in 64 heavily pretreated patients — consistent with LOTIS-2
cards.summary: Chinese phase 2: overall response 51.6% and complete response 23.4% in 64 heavily pretreated patients — consistent with LOTIS-2
cards.people: 64 Chinese adults with relapsed/refractory DLBCL who had failed ≥2 lines of systemic therapy (median 3 prior lines, range 2–12), treated with loncastuximab tesirine 150 µg/kg for two cycles then 75 µg/kg every 3 weeks for up to 1 year, in the OL-ADCT-402-001 bridging study. Single-arm.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 51.6% (95% CI 38.7–64.2) and complete response rate 23.4%. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent events were mostly haematological; increased gamma-glutamyltransferase occurred in 25.0% and hypokalaemia in 18.8%. Serious treatment-emergent events were reported in 35 of 64 patients, with four fatal events.
cards.watchOut: A bridging replication, not independent comparative evidence: it confirms the response rate transports across populations, but it is the same single-arm design with the same absence of a control.
cards.source: Lin N, Sun X, Zhou H, et al. Loncastuximab tesirine in Chinese patients with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a multicenter, open-label, single-arm, phase II trial. cards.headline: US real-world series (observational): in 187 higher-risk patients, response was 32% and median overall survival 4.6 months — below the LOTIS-2 figures
cards.summary: US real-world series (observational): in 187 higher-risk patients, response was 32% and median overall survival 4.6 months — below the LOTIS-2 figures
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 187 patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL treated with loncastuximab tesirine at 21 US centres — higher-risk than LOTIS-2, with more bulky disease (17% vs 0%), high-grade B-cell histology (22% vs 8%) and more prior lines (median 4 vs 3). Observational, no control group.
cards.result: Complete response rate was 14% and overall response rate 32%; median event-free survival was 2.1 months and median overall survival 4.6 months. Bulky disease and high-grade histology were associated with significantly worse outcomes; non-germinal-centre origin and complete response to the most recent prior line were associated with better outcomes. The authors attribute the gap versus LOTIS-2 to the higher-risk, more heavily pretreated real-world population.
cards.watchOut: Observational and labelled as such: the lower real-world figures reflect who actually receives the drug (later lines, bulkier, higher-grade disease) as much as the drug itself — but they are the best estimate of expected outcomes in unselected practice.
cards.source: Zelikson V, Gurumurthi A, Sawalha Y, et al. Loncastuximab in high-risk and heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a realworld analysis from 21 US centers. Haematologica. 2025. PMID: 39540227. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ~48–52% responses in trials, 32% in real-world use; benefit concentrated in complete responders — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: ~48–52% responses in trials, 32% in real-world use; benefit concentrated in complete responders — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above (LOTIS-2 primary and long-term, n=145; Chinese phase 2, n=64; US real-world cohort, n=187).
cards.result: Loncastuximab tesirine reproducibly produces responses in about half of trial patients with DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines (48.3% LOTIS-2; 51.6% Chinese phase 2), and the quarter who reach complete response can do durably well (24-month survival 68.2%) — while the all-patient median overall survival in LOTIS-2 was 9.5 months and a higher-risk real-world cohort (observational) saw 32% responses and 4.6 months median survival. Signature harms are the pyrrolobenzodiazepine payload's: gamma-glutamyltransferase elevation, oedema/effusions and photosensitivity, plus cytopenias. With no randomised comparison anywhere in the base, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Trial and real-world numbers describe different populations; neither should be quoted alone as 'the' response rate for this drug.

shelves.title: Tafasitamab plus lenalidomide in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL (L-MIND): durable responses, single-arm base
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL ineligible for autologous transplant, does tafasitamab plus lenalidomide, versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Lenalidomide · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Single-arm pivotal evidence, tempered by real-world data. L-MIND (n=80, transplant-ineligible, 1–3 prior lines) found objective responses in 60% at the primary analysis and 57.5% at the final 5-year analysis, with complete responses in ~41–43% and median overall survival of 33.5 months — durable for the responders. But there is no randomised comparison: the matched Re-MIND analysis sometimes cited alongside is observational, and the two real-world limbs carded here are explicitly observational — a US multicentre retrospective study whose record reports substantially lower progression-free and overall survival than L-MIND (its abstract reports no patient number, printed as N not documented), and the Spanish GELTAMO series (n=99; response 51% in the intention-to-treat cohort, median overall survival 12.2 months). Responses also cannot be attributed to tafasitamab alone: lenalidomide is an active partner drug, and GELTAMO found lenalidomide dose intensity itself predicted response and survival. The honest face: a well-tolerated, chemotherapy-free option with durable complete responses in a minority-to-half of trial patients, unproven against any comparator.

cards.headline: L-MIND primary: objective response 60% and complete response 43% in 80 transplant-ineligible patients — single-arm
cards.summary: L-MIND primary: objective response 60% and complete response 43% in 80 transplant-ineligible patients — single-arm
cards.people: 80 adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL after 1–3 prior systemic regimens (including an anti-CD20 therapy), ineligible for high-dose chemotherapy and autologous transplant, ECOG 0–2, at 35 hospitals in ten countries. Tafasitamab 12 mg/kg plus lenalidomide 25 mg/day for up to 12 cycles, then tafasitamab monotherapy until progression. Single-arm, open-label.
cards.result: 48 of 80 patients had an objective response (60%, 95% CI 48–71): 34 complete responses (43%) and 14 partial responses (18%), at median follow-up 13.2 months. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent events were dominated by neutropenia (48% of 81 safety patients), thrombocytopenia (17%) and febrile neutropenia (12%); serious adverse events occurred in 51%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with an active partner drug: the 60% response rate belongs to the combination in a selected, transplant-ineligible population and cannot be credited to tafasitamab alone or compared directly with other regimens.
cards.source: Salles G, Duell J, González Barca E, et al. Tafasitamab plus lenalidomide in relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (L-MIND): a multicentre, prospective, single-arm, phase 2 study. The Lancet Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32511983. Registry ID: NCT02399085. cards.headline: L-MIND final 5-year analysis: response 57.5%, complete response 41.3%, median overall survival 33.5 months; duration of response not reached
cards.summary: L-MIND final 5-year analysis: response 57.5%, complete response 41.3%, median overall survival 33.5 months; duration of response not reached
cards.people: The same 80 L-MIND patients at the final analysis (data cutoff November 14, 2022), including exploratory splits by one vs ≥2 prior lines of therapy.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 57.5% with complete responses in 41.3% (n=33). Median duration of response was not reached; median progression-free survival was 11.6 months (95% CI 5.7–45.7) and median overall survival 33.5 months (95% CI 18.3–not reached) at 65.6 months median follow-up for survival. Patients with one prior line responded more often (67.5%; 52.5% complete) than those with ≥2 prior lines (47.5%; 30% complete). Adverse events were consistent with earlier reports, decreased during tafasitamab monotherapy, and raised no new safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: Long follow-up of the same single-arm cohort: the 33.5-month median survival describes a trial-selected population with no comparator, and the earlier-line subgroup advantage is exploratory.
cards.source: Duell J, Abrisqueta P, Andre M, et al. Tafasitamab for patients with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: final 5-year efficacy and safety findings in the phase II L-MIND study. Haematologica. 2024. PMID: 37646664. Registry ID: NCT02399085. cards.summary: US real-world study (observational): tafasitamab–lenalidomide outcomes substantially below L-MIND, in sicker patients — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Multicentre retrospective real-world cohort of patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma treated with tafasitamab–lenalidomide in US practice; the record's abstract reports no patient number (N not documented). cards.result: Patients receiving tafasitamab–lenalidomide in this real-world evaluation had substantially lower progression-free survival and overall survival than patients in the L-MIND registration trial — the record's abstract states the direction and the population explanation (more comorbidity and high-risk disease) without printing comparative figures.
cards.watchOut: Observational, labelled as such, and abstract-only in the record: it establishes that trial results did not transport intact to sicker real-world patients, but it cannot quantify the gap — no numbers or N are printed in the record.

cards.headline: GELTAMO real-world series (observational): response 51% and median overall survival 12.2 months in 99 Spanish patients
cards.summary: GELTAMO real-world series (observational): response 51% and median overall survival 12.2 months in 99 Spanish patients
cards.type: Retrospective real-world series (observational, GELTAMO), Blood Adv 2025
cards.people: 99 patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL in Spain who received at least one dose of tafasitamab plus lenalidomide (intention-to-treat cohort); 83 completed at least one full cycle (efficacy cohort). Retrospective, observational.
cards.result: Overall response was 51% in the intention-to-treat cohort and 61% in the efficacy cohort (complete response 35% and 42%). Median progression-free survival was 4.9 and 10.9 months and median overall survival 12.2 and 21.8 months in the two cohorts respectively; median duration of response was not reached and complete responders did excellently. Poor performance status (ECOG 2–4), double-hit lymphoma and refractory/progressing disease after the previous therapy independently predicted worse progression-free survival. Lenalidomide relative dose intensity significantly affected response, progression-free survival and overall survival. Treatment was generally well tolerated.

cards.headline: Synthesis: durable complete responses in L-MIND, weaker real-world transport, no randomised comparison — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: durable complete responses in L-MIND, weaker real-world transport, no randomised comparison — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above (L-MIND primary and final analysis, n=80; US real-world study, N not documented; GELTAMO series, n=99).
cards.result: Tafasitamab plus lenalidomide produced objective responses in 57.5–60% and complete responses in ~41–43% of transplant-ineligible trial patients, with median overall survival of 33.5 months at 5 years and duration of response not reached — a genuinely durable limb for responders. There is no randomised trial of the combination against anything, and the contribution of tafasitamab beyond lenalidomide is unisolated. Stamp capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: The absence of a randomised comparison is the shelf's central fact: matched observational analyses cited elsewhere do not close that gap and are not carded as if they did.

shelves.title: Belantamab mafodotin combinations in relapsed/refractory myeloma (DREAMM-7/8): two positive phase 3 trials after the DREAMM-3 monotherapy failure
shelves.question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥1 prior line, does belantamab mafodotin plus bortezomib–dexamethasone (vs daratumumab–bortezomib–dexamethasone) or plus pomalidomide–dexamethasone (vs bortezomib–pomalidomide–dexamethasone) improve progression-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Myeloma · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bortezomib · Pomalidomide · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: A three-act story, and all three acts are on the face. Act one: belantamab mafodotin won accelerated approval as monotherapy, then the phase 3 DREAMM-3 trial of the single agent vs pomalidomide–dexamethasone missed its primary endpoint (progression-free survival hazard ratio 1.03; the treatment made no difference) and the drug was withdrawn in the US. Act two: two randomised phase 3 combination trials were clearly positive — DREAMM-7 (BVd vs DVd, n=494): median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months (hazard ratio 0.41, a relative measure), with an overall-survival benefit at the updated analysis (hazard ratio 0.58); DREAMM-8 (BPd vs PVd, n=302, lenalidomide-exposed): hazard ratio 0.52 for progression or death, 12-month progression-free survival 71% vs 51%. Act three: re-approval as combination therapy. The defining harm is ocular: ocular events in 79% on BVd vs 29% on DVd in DREAMM-7 (mostly managed with dose modification, visual-acuity events mostly resolving), and blurred vision reported as severe or very severe by 43% of BPd patients in the DREAMM-8 patient-reported outcomes — the reason for the monitoring burden that accompanies this drug. The LIKELY stamp applies to the combinations only; the monotherapy limb is null and carded as such.

cards.headline: DREAMM-7 primary: belantamab–bortezomib–dexamethasone beat daratumumab–bortezomib–dexamethasone — median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months (hazard ratio 0.41)
cards.summary: DREAMM-7 primary: belantamab–bortezomib–dexamethasone beat daratumumab–bortezomib–dexamethasone — median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months (hazard ratio 0.41)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (DREAMM-7), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 494 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥1 prior line, randomised open-label to belantamab mafodotin + bortezomib + dexamethasone (BVd, n=243) or daratumumab + bortezomib + dexamethasone (DVd, n=251); median follow-up 28.2 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 36.6 months (95% CI 28.4–not reached) with BVd vs 13.4 months (95% CI 11.1–17.5) with DVd (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.41, 95% CI 0.31–0.53; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians printed beside it). Overall survival at 18 months was 84% vs 73%. Complete response or better with MRD-negative status occurred in 25% vs 10%. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 95% vs 78%; ocular events were more common with BVd (79% vs 29%), were managed with dose modifications, and worsening visual acuity mostly resolved.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a 95% grade ≥3 adverse-event rate on BVd: the progression-free benefit is large and blinded-review supported, but tolerability — ocular events above all — is the price, and nearly every patient had a serious-grade event.
cards.source: Hungria V, Robak P, Hus M, et al. Belantamab Mafodotin, Bortezomib, and Dexamethasone for Multiple Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38828933. cards.headline: DREAMM-7 updated survival analysis: overall survival hazard ratio 0.58 favouring BVd, median duration of response 40.8 vs 17.8 months
cards.summary: DREAMM-7 updated survival analysis: overall survival hazard ratio 0.58 favouring BVd, median duration of response 40.8 vs 17.8 months
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial updated analysis (DREAMM-7), Lancet Oncol 2025
cards.people: The same 494 DREAMM-7 patients (BVd n=243, DVd n=251) at the second interim analysis, data cutoff October 7, 2024, median follow-up 39.4 months, at 142 centres in 20 countries.
cards.result: Median overall survival was not reached in either group; the hazard ratio for death was 0.58 (95% CI 0.43–0.79; P=0.0002 — a relative measure) favouring BVd. MRD-negativity in patients with complete response or better was 25% vs 10%, median duration of response 40.8 vs 17.8 months, and progression-free survival on next-line therapy also favoured BVd (hazard ratio 0.59). The most common grade 3–4 event was thrombocytopenia (56% vs 35%); serious adverse events occurred in 53% vs 38%, and treatment-related serious events led to death in 3% vs 1%.
cards.watchOut: Median survival was not reached in either arm, so the survival claim rests on the hazard ratio and event pattern rather than a median difference — and the trial remains open-label.

cards.headline: DREAMM-8 primary: belantamab–pomalidomide–dexamethasone beat bortezomib–pomalidomide–dexamethasone in lenalidomide-exposed myeloma (hazard ratio 0.52)
cards.summary: DREAMM-8 primary: belantamab–pomalidomide–dexamethasone beat bortezomib–pomalidomide–dexamethasone in lenalidomide-exposed myeloma (hazard ratio 0.52)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (DREAMM-8), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 302 lenalidomide-exposed patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥1 prior line, randomised open-label to belantamab mafodotin + pomalidomide + dexamethasone (BPd, n=155) or pomalidomide + bortezomib + dexamethasone (PVd, n=147); median follow-up 21.8 months.
cards.result: Estimated 12-month progression-free survival was 71% (95% CI 63–78) with BPd vs 51% (95% CI 42–60) with PVd (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.52, 95% CI 0.37–0.73; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute 12-month rates printed beside it). Overall survival data were immature. Response (partial response or better) occurred in 77% vs 72%, but complete response or better was 40% vs 16% — the benefit is in depth and durability of response more than in the headline response rate.
cards.watchOut: Overall survival was immature at the primary report, and the near-identical overall response rates (77% vs 72%) mean the case for BPd rests on complete-response depth and progression-free survival — with the class ocular toxicity (see Synthesis) fully present.

cards.headline: DREAMM-3 (the null act): single-agent belantamab mafodotin did NOT improve progression-free survival vs pomalidomide–dexamethasone (hazard ratio 1.03) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: DREAMM-3 (the null act): single-agent belantamab mafodotin did NOT improve progression-free survival vs pomalidomide–dexamethasone (hazard ratio 1.03) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (DREAMM-3), Lancet Haematol 2023
cards.people: 325 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥2 prior lines (including lenalidomide and a proteasome inhibitor), randomised 2:1 open-label at 108 sites to single-agent belantamab mafodotin 2.5 mg/kg every 21 days (n=218) or pomalidomide + low-dose dexamethasone (n=107); median follow-up ~11 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 11.2 months (95% CI 6.4–14.5) with belantamab mafodotin vs 7.0 months (95% CI 4.6–10.6) with pomalidomide–dexamethasone, but the hazard ratio was 1.03 (95% CI 0.72–1.47; P=0.56) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint. Most common grade 3–4 events were thrombocytopenia (23%) and anaemia (16%) on belantamab; serious adverse events occurred in 43% vs 39%. This missed primary endpoint is the trial that led to the drug's US withdrawal as monotherapy, before the positive combination trials.
cards.watchOut: A different question slice — monotherapy in later-line disease — carded because the shelf's story is unintelligible without it: the same drug that failed alone succeeded in combinations, and the medians-vs-hazard-ratio contrast (11.2 vs 7.0 months, HR 1.03) is a standing warning against reading medians without the hazard ratio.
cards.source: Dimopoulos MA, Hungria VTM, Radinoff A, et al. Efficacy and safety of single-agent belantamab mafodotin versus pomalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (DREAMM-3): a phase 3, open-label, randomised study. The Lancet Haematology. 2023. PMID: 37793771. Registry ID: NCT04162210. cards.headline: Synthesis: combinations LIKELY — two concordant positive phase 3 trials after a null monotherapy trial; ocular toxicity is the defining cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: combinations LIKELY — two concordant positive phase 3 trials after a null monotherapy trial; ocular toxicity is the defining cost
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded randomised trials above (DREAMM-7 primary and survival update, n=494; DREAMM-8, n=302; DREAMM-3 monotherapy, n=325).
cards.result: For belantamab mafodotin combinations in myeloma after ≥1 prior line, two independent phase 3 randomised trials agree: DREAMM-7 (BVd vs DVd) — median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months, hazard ratio 0.41, overall-survival hazard ratio 0.58 at update; DREAMM-8 (BPd vs PVd) — hazard ratio 0.52, 12-month progression-free survival 71% vs 51%, complete responses 40% vs 16%. That concordance supports LIKELY for the combinations. The counterweight is carded, not buried: single-agent belantamab failed in DREAMM-3 (hazard ratio 1.03; the treatment made no difference) and the drug was withdrawn before its combination re-approval. Ocular toxicity defines the harm line — ocular events in 79% vs 29% in DREAMM-7 and severe blurred vision commonly reported by patients in DREAMM-8's patient-reported outcomes — managed by dose modification and structured eye monitoring rather than avoided.
cards.watchOut: The LIKELY stamp covers the two tested combinations at their tested line of therapy — it does not rehabilitate monotherapy, which has a carded null phase 3 result, and it does not extend to untested partners or earlier lines.

synthesis synthesis of the four carded randomised trials above (dreamm-7 primary and survival update, n=494; dreamm-8, n=302; dreamm-3 monotherapy, n=325). for belantamab mafodotin combinations in myeloma after ≥1 prior line, two independent phase 3 randomised trials agree: dreamm-7 (bvd vs dvd) — median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months, hazard ratio 0.41, overall-survival hazard ratio 0.58 at update; dreamm-8 (bpd vs pvd) — hazard ratio 0.52, 12-month progression-free survival 71% vs 51%, complete responses 40% vs 16%. that concordance supports likely for the combinations. the counterweight is carded, not buried: single-agent belantamab failed in dreamm-3 (hazard ratio 1.03; the treatment made no difference) and the drug was withdrawn before its combination re-approval. ocular toxicity defines the harm line — ocular events in 79% vs 29% in dreamm-7 and severe blurred vision commonly reported by patients in dreamm-8's patient-reported outcomes — managed by dose modification and structured eye monitoring rather than avoided. the likely stamp covers the two tested combinations at their tested line of therapy — it does not rehabilitate monotherapy, which has a carded null phase 3 result, and it does not extend to untested partners or earlier lines. synthesis of the carded records above (pmids 38828933, 40680754, 38828951, 37793771). registry id: nct04246047 (dreamm-7); nct04484623 (dreamm-8); nct04162210 (dreamm-3). mesh: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Elranatamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (MagnetisMM-3): 61% responses, single-arm — infection burden is the defining harm
shelves.question: In patients with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does elranatamab (BCMA×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Myeloma · B-Cell Maturation Antigen · Antibodies, Bispecific · Remission Induction · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: Single-arm evidence: MagnetisMM-3 cohort A (n=123, no prior BCMA-directed therapy) is the whole trial base — objective responses in 61.0%, with 35.0% complete response or better, and medians for duration of response, progression-free and overall survival not yet reached at 14.7 months. The US subgroup (n=47 of the same cohort, longer follow-up) is consistent (response 66.0%; median overall survival 43.6 months) but is a subset of the same patients, not independent evidence. The real-world ALTITUDE claims cohorts (n=183 and n=391, observational) show the drug is dosed less intensively in practice than on label, with 60.7–70.0% of patients estimated alive at 18 months. The mandatory harm line for the BCMA-bispecific class is infection: infections in 69.9% (grade 3–4 in 39.8%) in the trial, alongside cytokine release syndrome in 57.7% (no grade 3–4 events) and neutropenia (grade 3–4 in 48.8%). Cross-point: the library's teclistamab shelf asks the same class question for a different molecule and is not duplicated here.

cards.headline: MagnetisMM-3 cohort A: objective response 61.0% in 123 BCMA-naïve patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma — single-arm
cards.summary: MagnetisMM-3 cohort A: objective response 61.0% in 123 BCMA-naïve patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma — single-arm
cards.people: 123 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma and no prior BCMA-directed therapy (cohort A), receiving subcutaneous elranatamab weekly after two step-up priming doses, with persistent responders switching to biweekly dosing after six cycles. Single-arm phase 2; responses by blinded independent central review.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 61.0% (75 of 123), with 35.0% achieving complete response or better, meeting the primary endpoint. Fifty responders switched to biweekly dosing and 80.0% of them improved or maintained their response for ≥6 months. At median follow-up 14.7 months, median duration of response, progression-free survival and overall survival were not reached (15-month rates 71.5%, 50.9% and 56.7%). Infections occurred in 69.9% (grade 3–4 in 39.8%), cytokine release syndrome in 57.7% (grade 3–4 in 0%), anaemia in 48.8% and neutropenia in 48.8% (grade 3–4 in 48.8%); grade 3–4 events fell from 58.6% to 46.6% after the switch to biweekly dosing.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: response depth is well documented, but with no comparator the survival figures (medians not reached) cannot be read as a survival benefit — and the infection burden, including grade 3–4 infections in two of five patients, is part of the treatment's real cost.
cards.source: Lesokhin AM, Tomasson MH, Arnulf B, et al. Elranatamab in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma: phase 2 MagnetisMM-3 trial results. Nature Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37582952. Registry ID: NCT04649359. MeSH: Humans · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy · B-Cell Maturation Antigen · Progression-Free Survival · Remission Induction

cards.headline: MagnetisMM-3 US subgroup: response 66.0% and median overall survival 43.6 months in 47 US patients at 39.6 months follow-up
cards.summary: MagnetisMM-3 US subgroup: response 66.0% and median overall survival 43.6 months in 47 US patients at 39.6 months follow-up
cards.people: Post hoc subgroup of the 47 US-enrolled BCMA-naïve patients within MagnetisMM-3 cohort A (of 123 evaluable), receiving elranatamab 76 mg weekly after step-up dosing, with protocol response-adapted de-escalation to every-2-week and then every-4-week dosing.
cards.result: At median follow-up 39.6 months, objective response was 66.0% (95% CI 50.7–79.1) and complete response or better 42.6%; median duration of response was 40.8 months, median progression-free survival 27.3 months and median overall survival 43.6 months. Infections occurred in 70.2% (grade 3/4 in 42.6%), fatigue in 61.7% and cytokine release syndrome in 61.7% (grade 3/4 in 0%). Of responders who de-escalated dosing, 77.8% (weekly→every 2 weeks) and 87.5% (→every 4 weeks) maintained or improved their response for ≥6 months.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc subgroup of the same 123-patient cohort — its longer follow-up matures the parent trial's estimates but adds no independent patients, and subgroup medians in 47 patients carry wide uncertainty (progression-free survival 95% CI 4.3–not estimable).
cards.source: Nooka AK, Strouse C, Larson SM, et al. Efficacy and safety of elranatamab in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma: A US subgroup analysis from MagnetisMM-3. Cancer. 2026. PMID: 42159085. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ALTITUDE real-world cohorts (observational): 183 and 391 US patients, dosed less often than label, 60.7–70.0% estimated alive at 18 months
cards.summary: ALTITUDE real-world cohorts (observational): 183 and 391 US patients, dosed less often than label, 60.7–70.0% estimated alive at 18 months
cards.people: Two US retrospective real-world cohorts of patients with multiple myeloma who initiated elranatamab after August 2023: ALTITUDE-1 (administrative claims, n=183) and ALTITUDE-2 (fee-for-service data, n=391). Median ages 73 and 75 years; 43.2% and 33.0% were penta-drug exposed and 17.5% and 21.0% had prior BCMA exposure. Observational, no control group.
cards.result: Real-world dosing was less intensive than the label (27.9 and 27.1 vials per year vs 39 expected). Neither median time-to-next-treatment-or-death nor median overall survival was reached; landmark estimates put 70.0% (ALTITUDE-1) and 60.7% (ALTITUDE-2) of patients alive at 18 months. The authors judge effectiveness consistent with MagnetisMM-3 despite the older, heavily pretreated population and sparser dosing.
cards.watchOut: Observational claims data, labelled as such: no response assessment, no comparator, and survival landmarks without a control arm cannot confirm the trial's effect — they show the drug is used, and dosed more sparingly, in older real-world patients.
cards.source: Banerjee R, Mohan M, Shah B, et al. Real-world treatment patterns and outcomes of patients with multiple myeloma initiating elranatamab: results from the ALTITUDE-1 and ALTITUDE-2 retrospective cohort studies. Future Oncology. 2026. PMID: 42021581. Registry ID: NCT04649359 (as listed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: elranatamab gives deep responses in ~61% of BCMA-naïve relapsed myeloma — single-arm base, infection is the defining harm — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: elranatamab gives deep responses in ~61% of BCMA-naïve relapsed myeloma — single-arm base, infection is the defining harm — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above (MagnetisMM-3 cohort A, n=123, and its US subgroup, n=47; ALTITUDE real-world cohorts, n=183 and n=391).
cards.result: Elranatamab produced objective responses in 61.0% of BCMA-naïve, triple-class-exposed relapsed/refractory myeloma patients (35.0% complete response or better), with responses durable enough that medians were unreached at 14.7 months and de-escalation to biweekly, then monthly, dosing held responses in most switchers. The US subgroup's longer follow-up (median overall survival 43.6 months) is consistent but not independent. Real-world cohorts confirm use in older, heavily pretreated patients at lower dose intensity. Infection is the class-defining harm (69.9% any grade, 39.8% grade 3–4 in the trial). With no randomised or controlled evidence, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Count the evidence once: the US subgroup is inside the pivotal cohort, so the trial base is 123 patients, however many reports describe them.

shelves.title: Talquetamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (MonumenTAL-1): responses ~67–74% at 3 years — GPRC5D taste/skin/nail toxicity defines the harm line
shelves.question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥3 prior lines, does talquetamab (GPRC5D×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce responses, including after prior T-cell-redirection therapy?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Myeloma · Antibodies, Bispecific · Receptors, G-Protein-Coupled · Cytokine Release Syndrome · Dysgeusia
shelves.balance: Single-arm evidence throughout, from the one MonumenTAL-1 programme. The phase 1 primary report established the two recommended subcutaneous doses (0.4 mg/kg weekly, 0.8 mg/kg every other week) with responses in 70% and 64% of heavily pretreated patients (median six prior lines). The 3-year follow-up (n=143 weekly, n=154 every-other-week, plus a 78-patient prior-T-cell-redirection cohort) shows overall responses of 67–74% across cohorts — including after prior T-cell-redirection therapy — with median overall survival of 34.0 months (weekly) and not reached (every-other-week). The defining harm line is unique to the GPRC5D target: on-target off-tumour effects on taste, skin, nails and weight — taste changes in 72–76% and dysgeusia in ~57–63% at the recommended doses in the primary report, skin events in ~67–70% — characterised in detail by the China cohort card (n=41), where they were predominantly grade 1–2, mostly resolved, and rarely forced dose change. Cytokine release syndrome was common (73–79%) but almost entirely low-grade, and the programme reports lower high-grade infection rates than BCMA bispecifics — a cross-trial impression, fenced as such.

cards.headline: MonumenTAL-1 phase 1 primary: responses in 70% (weekly) and 64% (every-other-week) at the recommended subcutaneous doses in heavily pretreated myeloma
cards.summary: MonumenTAL-1 phase 1 primary: responses in 70% (weekly) and 64% (every-other-week) at the recommended subcutaneous doses in heavily pretreated myeloma
cards.type: Phase 1 dose-finding trial (MonumenTAL-1), N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 232 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (median six prior lines, or unable to receive established therapies) receiving talquetamab intravenously (n=102) or subcutaneously (n=130) across dose levels in phase 1; the recommended phase 2 subcutaneous doses were 405 µg/kg weekly (n=30) and 800 µg/kg every other week (n=44). No concurrent control.
cards.result: At the weekly dose, responses occurred in 70% (95% CI 51–85) with median duration of response 10.2 months (median follow-up 11.7 months); at the every-other-week dose, 64% (95% CI 48–78) with median duration 7.8 months (follow-up 4.2 months). Common adverse events at the recommended doses were cytokine release syndrome (77% and 80%, all but one event grade 1–2), skin-related events (67% and 70%) and dysgeusia (63% and 57%); one dose-limiting grade 3 rash occurred at the 800-µg dose level.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study: the recommended-dose cohorts are 30 and 44 patients, follow-up at the every-other-week dose was only 4.2 months, and the response percentages carry wide confidence intervals — the 3-year follow-up card is the mature read of the same programme.
cards.source: Chari A, Minnema MC, Berdeja JG, et al. Talquetamab, a T-Cell-Redirecting GPRC5D Bispecific Antibody for Multiple Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36507686. Registry ID: NCT03399799. cards.headline: MonumenTAL-1 3-year follow-up: responses 67–74% across cohorts, including 78 patients previously treated with T-cell redirection; median survival 34.0 months to not reached
cards.summary: MonumenTAL-1 3-year follow-up: responses 67–74% across cohorts, including 78 patients previously treated with T-cell redirection; median survival 34.0 months to not reached
cards.people: Patients naïve to T-cell redirection therapy receiving talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg weekly (n=143) or 0.8 mg/kg every other week (n=154), and a separate cohort with prior T-cell redirection therapy (n=78, either dose); median follow-up 38, 31 and 30 months respectively, as of September 2024.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 67–74% across the three cohorts and complete response or better 33–42%. Median progression-free survival was 7.5, 11.2 and 7.7 months and median overall survival 34.0 months, not reached, and 28.3 months (36-month survival 49.3%, 60.8% and 44.6%). The most common adverse events were cytokine release syndrome (73–79%; grade 3/4 in 0.6–2.1%), taste changes (72–76%) and infections (61–78%; grade 3/4 in 21–26%). Ataxia/balance disorders occurred in 5.3% with no grade 4/5 events; dose reductions and discontinuations for adverse events remained low and no patient died from a talquetamab-related event.
cards.watchOut: Still single-arm: the prior-redirection cohort's responses show activity after BCMA-directed therapy, but sequencing claims (which bispecific first) have no comparative test anywhere in this programme.
cards.source: Rasche L, Schinke C, Touzeau C, et al. Talquetamab in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma: 3-year follow-up of the phase 1/2 MonumenTAL-1 study. Blood. 2026. PMID: 42561120. Registry ID: NCT03399799; NCT04634552. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: MonumenTAL-1 China cohort: GPRC5D on-target effects (taste, skin, nails) were predominantly grade 1–2, mostly resolved, and rarely required dose change in 41 patients
cards.summary: MonumenTAL-1 China cohort: GPRC5D on-target effects (taste, skin, nails) were predominantly grade 1–2, mostly resolved, and rarely required dose change in 41 patients
cards.type: Phase 1/2 cohort safety report (MonumenTAL-1 China), Hematology 2026
cards.people: 41 adult Chinese patients with heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory myeloma in MonumenTAL-1 receiving subcutaneous talquetamab 0.4 mg/kg weekly (n=29) or 0.8 mg/kg every other week (n=12); median treatment duration 7.7 and 7.1 months. A safety-focused cohort report.
cards.result: GPRC5D-associated on-target/off-tumour adverse events — oral events (dysgeusia, dry mouth), skin events (rash, non-rash skin toxicity) and nail disorders — were predominantly grade 1–2 (one grade 3 non-rash skin toxicity), and 50–100% had resolved by data cutoff. Events were managed with supportive therapies; talquetamab dose modification was needed in one case (grade 2 weight decrease). The authors conclude the GPRC5D effects were generally mild, consistent with the known profile, and manageable without dose modification in most patients.
cards.watchOut: A 41-patient safety cohort of the same programme: it characterises the unique GPRC5D harm profile and its manageability, but 'mostly resolved' spans a wide 50–100% range by event type, and taste/weight effects can persist while treatment continues.

cards.headline: Synthesis: talquetamab responds in roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of heavily pretreated myeloma, including after prior T-cell redirection — single-arm, POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: talquetamab responds in roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of heavily pretreated myeloma, including after prior T-cell redirection — single-arm, POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded MonumenTAL-1 reports above (phase 1 primary, n=232 across doses; 3-year follow-up cohorts, n=143 + 154 + 78; China safety cohort, n=41).
cards.result: Talquetamab, the only GPRC5D×CD3 bispecific in this library, produced responses in 70% and 64% at its recommended doses in phase 1 and 67–74% across cohorts at 3 years, with complete responses or better in 33–42% and median overall survival of 34.0 months (weekly dosing) to not reached (every-other-week) — including responses in patients already treated with T-cell redirection. Its harm signature is target-specific and unlike the BCMA class: taste changes in ~72–76%, skin and nail toxicity, and weight loss, predominantly low-grade and manageable, alongside common but almost always low-grade cytokine release syndrome (73–79%; grade 3/4 ≤2.1%). Every report is single-arm from one programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Comparisons with BCMA bispecifics (infection rates, sequencing) are cross-trial impressions in the source reports, not findings — no head-to-head or randomised evidence exists for this molecule.

shelves.title: Linvoseltamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (LINKER-MM1): 71% responses on a response-adapted schedule — single-programme evidence
shelves.question: In patients with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does linvoseltamab (BCMA×CD3 bispecific, response-adapted dosing), versus no concurrent control or real-world standard care, produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Myeloma · Antibodies, Bispecific · B-Cell Maturation Antigen · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Single-programme, single-arm evidence (the standing single-programme precedent applies — it is stated on the face): LINKER-MM1's 200 mg cohort (n=117, triple-class exposed) produced an objective response rate of 71% with 50–52% complete response or better and a median duration of response of 29.4 months, under the programme's defining response-adapted schedule — weekly to week 14, then every 2 weeks, then every 4 weeks in patients reaching at least a very good partial response by week 24. That de-escalating schedule is part of the tested intervention's identity and is named as such. The comparative limb is an external-control analysis (LINKER-MM1 phase 2 cohort n=105 vs 149 real-world standard-care patients, inverse-probability weighted; response odds ratio 3.8, survival hazard ratio 0.41) — observational, labelled as such, and supportive only. Patient-reported outcomes improved in responders and worsened numerically in non-responders, tracking response rather than adding an independent benefit claim. Harms mirror the BCMA class: infections in ~74–75% (grade ≥3 in ~48% in the follow-up report), cytokine release syndrome 46% (grade 3 in 1% in follow-up), neutropenia 44%.

cards.headline: LINKER-MM1 primary: response 71% and complete response or better 50% in 117 patients at the 200 mg dose, median duration of response 29.4 months
cards.summary: LINKER-MM1 primary: response 71% and complete response or better 50% in 117 patients at the 200 mg dose, median duration of response 29.4 months
cards.type: Phase 1/2 trial primary report (LINKER-MM1), J Clin Oncol 2024
cards.people: 117 patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma treated with linvoseltamab 200 mg (median age 70 years; 39% high-risk cytogenetics; 28% penta-refractory), eligible after ≥3 lines including a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory drug and an anti-CD38 antibody, or triple-class refractory. Phase 2 schedule: weekly through week 14, then every 2 weeks; patients with at least a very good partial response by week 24 moved to every-4-week dosing (response-adapted schedule). A 50 mg cohort (n=104) is reported alongside. Single-arm.
cards.result: At median follow-up 14.3 months, objective response at 200 mg was 71% with 50% achieving complete response or better; median duration of response was 29.4 months (95% CI 19.2–not evaluable). At 50 mg, response was 48% with 21% complete response or better. Among 200 mg patients, cytokine release syndrome occurred in 46.2% in total (35.0% grade 1, 10.3% grade 2, 0.9% grade 3), neutropenia in 42.7% (grade 3 in 18.8%, grade 4 in 23.1%), anaemia grade 3 in 30.8%, neurotoxicity in 7.7%, and infections in 74.4% (grade 3 in 33.3%, grade 4 in 2.6%), with infection frequency and severity declining over time.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 200 mg vs 50 mg contrast (71% vs 48%) is a dose comparison within one study, not evidence against any other therapy — and the response-adapted every-4-week schedule means the tested intervention is the schedule, not a fixed dose.
cards.source: Bumma N, Richter J, Jagannath S, et al. Linvoseltamab for Treatment of Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2024. PMID: 38879802. Registry ID: NCT03761108. cards.headline: LINKER-MM1 longer follow-up: response 71% with complete response or better 52%, median overall survival 31.4 months at 21.3 months follow-up
cards.summary: LINKER-MM1 longer follow-up: response 71% with complete response or better 52%, median overall survival 31.4 months at 21.3 months follow-up
cards.type: Phase 1/2 longer follow-up (LINKER-MM1), Clin Lymphoma Myeloma Leuk 2026
cards.people: The same 117 patients treated with linvoseltamab 200 mg in LINKER-MM1, at a data cutoff of July 23, 2024 (median follow-up 21.3 months), including high-risk subgroup analyses.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 71% (complete response or better 52%); median duration of response was 29.4 months, median progression-free survival was not reached, and median overall survival was 31.4 months. MRD negativity (10⁻⁵ threshold) was achieved in 94% of evaluable patients with complete response or better, and response rates were ≥50% in every subgroup assessed, including extramedullary disease, stage 3 and high-risk cytogenetics. The most common events were cytokine release syndrome (46%; grade 3 in 1%, mostly during step-up dosing), neutropenia (44%; grade ≥3 in 43%) and infections (75%; grade ≥3 in 48%), with infection rates decreasing after 6 months. No new safety signals emerged.
cards.watchOut: The same 117 patients as the primary report with longer follow-up — maturation, not replication; the 94% MRD-negativity figure applies only to the evaluable complete-responder subset, not to all treated patients.

cards.headline: External-control comparison (observational): linvoseltamab response odds ratio 3.8 and survival hazard ratio 0.41 vs real-world standard care, weighted
cards.summary: External-control comparison (observational): linvoseltamab response odds ratio 3.8 and survival hazard ratio 0.41 vs real-world standard care, weighted
cards.type: External-control comparative study (observational), Blood Cancer J 2026
cards.people: LINKER-MM1 phase 2 linvoseltamab 200 mg cohort (n=105) compared with an external control of 149 patients from two US electronic health record databases (COTA and Guardian Research Network) treated with real-world standard care, with LINKER-MM1 eligibility criteria applied and inverse probability of treatment weighting used to balance baseline characteristics. No control patient received CAR T-cell therapy or a bispecific antibody. Observational comparison.
cards.result: Linvoseltamab had a higher objective response rate than real-world standard care (weighted odds ratio 3.8, 95% CI 2.5–6.6) and longer median progression-free survival (weighted hazard ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.23–0.39), time to next treatment (weighted hazard ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.15–0.26) and overall survival (weighted hazard ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.32–0.52) — all relative measures from a weighted, non-randomised comparison.
cards.watchOut: Observational and labelled as such: weighting balances measured characteristics only, the control regimens were heterogeneous (no bispecific or CAR T exposure), and these hazard ratios must not be read with randomised-trial weight.
cards.source: Kumar S, Weisel KC, Spin P, et al. Effectiveness of linvoseltamab versus real-world standard-of-care in triple-class-exposed relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma in the United States. Blood Cancer Journal. 2026. PMID: 41922313. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LINKER-MM1 quality of life: pain, fatigue and global health improved by week 16–20 and were maintained — in responders; non-responders worsened numerically
cards.summary: LINKER-MM1 quality of life: pain, fatigue and global health improved by week 16–20 and were maintained — in responders; non-responders worsened numerically
cards.type: Phase 1/2 patient-reported outcomes analysis (LINKER-MM1), Blood Neoplasia 2026
cards.people: The 117 LINKER-MM1 patients treated with linvoseltamab 200 mg (83 responders with at least a partial response; 34 non-responders), assessed with EORTC QLQ-C30, the myeloma module QLQ-MY20 and EQ-5D-3L at baseline, week 4 and every 4 weeks, through week 104.
cards.result: Nominal statistically significant improvements from baseline were observed on all QLQ-C30/QLQ-MY20 scales and the EQ-5D-3L visual analogue scale overall; improvements in global health status/quality of life, fatigue and pain seen by week 16 were maintained at most subsequent assessments, with pain reaching the clinically meaningful threshold at week 20 and generally maintained through week 104. Among responders, improvements were significant on all scales; non-responders reported numerical worsening on most scales.
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported benefit tracks tumour response almost exactly (responders improve, non-responders worsen) in an unblinded single-arm study — it corroborates the response data rather than evidencing an independent quality-of-life effect.

shelves.title: First-line steroids in newly diagnosed ITP: SPLIT — dexamethasone faster early, no proven durability advantage over prednisone
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed primary ITP, does high-dose dexamethasone (40 mg × 4 days, one or more cycles), versus standard-dose prednisone tapered over weeks, produce faster and more durable platelet responses?
shelves.mesh: Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic · Dexamethasone · Prednisone · Platelet Count · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and the split is the answer to the commonest first-line ITP question. On speed and early response, high-dose dexamethasone wins: Wei 2016 (n=192 randomised; 95 dexamethasone, 97 prednisone) found initial overall response 82.1% vs 67.4% and complete response 50.5% vs 26.8%, with shorter time to response; the meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (n=1,138) likewise found higher response at 14 days (79% vs 59%; relative risk 1.22). On durability, the advantage disappears: Wei's sustained response was 40.0% vs 41.2% (the treatment made no difference), the meta-analysis found no difference in overall response at 6 months (54% vs 43%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.79–1.71), and the second randomised trial (n=113) found persistent responses at 12 months actually favouring prednisone (80.65% vs 55.56%). Regimens differ between trials (one or two 4-day dexamethasone courses in Wei; three courses every 14 days in Mazzucconi), which is part of why the durability limb is inconsistent. Harm burden differs by shape rather than clearly by total: short intense dexamethasone pulses (generally tolerated better in Wei; fewer reported toxicities in the meta-analysis) vs weeks of tapered prednisone exposure. Practical read: choose dexamethasone when a rapid rise matters (severe bleeding risk), without expecting more durable remission.

cards.headline: Wei 2016 RCT: initial response 82.1% with high-dose dexamethasone vs 67.4% with prednisone — but sustained response 40.0% vs 41.2% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Wei 2016 RCT: initial response 82.1% with high-dose dexamethasone vs 67.4% with prednisone — but sustained response 40.0% vs 41.2% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 192 adults with newly diagnosed primary immune thrombocytopenia randomised to high-dose dexamethasone 40 mg/day for 4 days (n=95; non-responders received one additional 4-day course) or prednisone 1.0 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks then tapered (n=97), in a prospective multicentre randomised trial.
cards.result: One or two dexamethasone courses produced higher overall initial response (82.1% vs 67.4%; P=.044) and complete response (50.5% vs 26.8%; P=.001), with shorter time to response (P<.001); a baseline bleeding score ≥8 predicted lower initial response. Sustained response was 40.0% on dexamethasone vs 41.2% on prednisone (P=.884) — the treatment made no difference to durability. Initial complete response predicted sustained response; antiplatelet autoantibodies predicted against it. High-dose dexamethasone was generally tolerated better.
cards.watchOut: The largest single trial, and its two halves point in opposite directions — early response for dexamethasone, durability a tie; quoting either half alone misstates the trial.
cards.source: Wei Y, Ji XB, Wang YW, et al. High-dose dexamethasone vs prednisone for treatment of adult immune thrombocytopenia: a prospective multicenter randomized trial. Blood. 2016. PMID: 26480931. Registry ID: NCT01356511. cards.headline: Mazzucconi 2024 RCT: initial responses favoured dexamethasone (93.88% vs 78.57%), but 12-month persistent responses favoured prednisone (80.65% vs 55.56%)
cards.summary: Mazzucconi 2024 RCT: initial responses favoured dexamethasone (93.88% vs 78.57%), but 12-month persistent responses favoured prednisone (80.65% vs 55.56%)
cards.people: 113 adults (18–80 years) with newly diagnosed untreated primary ITP (platelet count ≤20, or >20 but <50 ×10⁹/L, with bleeding score ≥8) randomised to prednisone 1 mg/kg/day days 0–28 (arm A, n=59) or high-dose dexamethasone 40 mg/day for 4 days every 14 days for three courses (arm B, n=54); median follow-up 44.4 months.
cards.result: Total initial responses in evaluable patients were 78.57% (44 of 56) on prednisone vs 93.88% (46 of 49) on dexamethasone (P=0.0284). Total final responses at day 180 were 60.47% vs 58.97% (P=0.8907) — no difference. Total persistent responses at 12 months from initial response were 80.65% (25 of 31) on prednisone vs 55.56% (20 of 36) on dexamethasone (P=0.0292), favouring prednisone. Seven relapses occurred; overall survival was 100% at 48 months. Both regimens were well tolerated; the authors conclude dexamethasone gives effective but less long-lasting initial responses than prednisone.
cards.watchOut: The 12-month persistence comparison is made among initial responders only (31 and 36 patients), and this trial's dexamethasone schedule (three courses) is more intensive than Wei's — regimen differences, not just drug differences, may drive the divergent durability result.
cards.source: Mazzucconi MG, Rodeghiero F, Avvisati G, et al. Prednisone vs high-dose dexamethasone in newly diagnosed adult primary immune thrombocytopenia: a randomized trial. Blood Advances. 2024. PMID: 38231017. Registry ID: NCT00657410. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (n=1,138): response at 14 days favoured dexamethasone (relative risk 1.22); response at 6 months did not (relative risk 1.16, CI crosses 1)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (n=1,138): response at 14 days favoured dexamethasone (relative risk 1.22); response at 6 months did not (relative risk 1.16, CI crosses 1)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Lancet Haematol 2016
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (n=1,138) in previously untreated immune thrombocytopenia, of which five adult trials (n=533) compared one to three cycles of dexamethasone 40 mg/day for 4 days with prednisone 1 mg/kg for 14–28 days then tapered; adults and children analysed separately.
cards.result: In adults, there was no difference in overall platelet response at 6 months (pooled proportions 54% vs 43%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.79–1.71; P=0.44 — a relative measure, with the absolute proportions printed beside it). At 14 days, overall response was higher with dexamethasone (79% vs 59%; relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 1.00–1.49; P=0.048). The dexamethasone group had fewer reported toxicities, and long-term response was similar when analysed by cumulative corticosteroid dose. No difference in initial response was seen between high-dose regimens in children.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis card: the 6-month relative risk's confidence interval (0.79–1.71) is wide enough to include a meaningful benefit either way — 'no proven difference' is the accurate claim, not 'proven equivalent' — and the pooled trials used differing dexamethasone cycle counts.
cards.source: Mithoowani S, Gregory-Miller K, Goy J, et al. High-dose dexamethasone compared with prednisone for previously untreated primary immune thrombocytopenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Haematology. 2016. PMID: 27658982. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — dexamethasone is faster and stronger early; neither drug is proven more durable, and one trial favours prednisone for persistence
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — dexamethasone is faster and stronger early; neither drug is proven more durable, and one trial favours prednisone for persistence
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above (Wei 2016 RCT, n=192; Mazzucconi 2024 RCT, n=113; meta-analysis of 9 RCTs, n=1,138).
cards.result: The randomised record divides cleanly by time horizon. Early: high-dose dexamethasone produces more and faster responses (Wei: initial response 82.1% vs 67.4%, complete response 50.5% vs 26.8%; meta-analysis at 14 days: 79% vs 59%, relative risk 1.22). Late: sustained response in Wei was 40.0% vs 41.2% (the treatment made no difference), the meta-analysis found no 6-month difference (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.79–1.71), and Mazzucconi's 12-month persistent responses favoured prednisone (80.65% vs 55.56%). The split is named in the stamp: pick dexamethasone for speed in severe presentations, not for durability; steroid-harm burden differs by regimen shape (short intense pulses vs a weeks-long taper) rather than by a proven total-toxicity winner.
cards.watchOut: Dexamethasone schedules differ across the trials (one–two courses vs three courses), so 'high-dose dexamethasone' is a family of regimens; the durability disagreement between Wei and Mazzucconi may be a schedule effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 26480931, 38231017, 27658982). Registry ID: NCT01356511; NCT00657410. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Thymic involution: the epithelial space shrinks from the first year of life, TREC output falls with age, and the adult naive T-cell pool is kept up mainly by peripheral division
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast does thymic epithelial volume and thymic output (signal-joint T-cell receptor excision circles, recent thymic emigrants) fall from childhood to old age, how much of the naive T-cell pool in older adults is maintained by peripheral division rather than new thymic production, and what happens to repertoire diversity?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue/anatomy & histology · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aging · Child · Child, Preschool · Connective Tissue/anatomy & histology · Female · Humans · Infant · Lymphoid Tissue/anatomy & histology · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Size · Puberty · Thymus Gland/anatomy & histology,blood supply,growth & development
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the involution and output decline, framed by the standard textbook account (Guyton & Hall / Ganong tradition): the thymus is largest relative to body size in childhood and its T-cell-producing epithelial tissue is progressively replaced by fat and connective tissue with age. The primary human record fetched agrees and quantifies it: morphometry of 204 thymuses (ages 1 month to 107 years) shows total organ size roughly constant (median 19.5 cm3) while the epithelial space involutes continuously from the first year of life on a negative-logarithmic course, independent of puberty (Steinmann 1985). Function follows structure: T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) measurements show thymic output declining with age yet remaining substantial into late adulthood (Douek 1998). Two cautions are EMERGING-grade within this shelf: TREC content is diluted by peripheral division, so it is only an indirect gauge of output (Hazenberg 2000), and deuterium-labelling work concludes the adult human naive pool is maintained almost exclusively by peripheral division rather than new thymic production (den Braber 2012) — the exact quantitative split between production and peripheral maintenance in the elderly is model-dependent. Repertoire diversity figures that no fetched record measured are not stated here.

cards.headline: Steinmann 1985: in 204 human thymuses the total organ stayed ~19.5 cm3 while the epithelial space involuted continuously from the first year of life
cards.summary: Steinmann 1985: in 204 human thymuses the total organ stayed ~19.5 cm3 while the epithelial space involuted continuously from the first year of life
cards.type: Primary human morphometric study (autopsy and biopsy series)
cards.people: 204 persons aged 1 month to 107 years: 136 thymuses removed completely at autopsy after sudden death, plus biopsy material from immunologically healthy cardiac patients, measured by stereological and morphometric methods.
cards.result: Total thymic size remained unchanged with ageing under normal conditions (median 19.5 cm3; individual maximum 5-70 cm3, reached in the first year of life). Perivascular space, Hassall's bodies and connective tissue enlarged from the first year, peaking at 10-25 years; adipose tissue replaced the perivascular space and connective tissue extensively after age 15. The volumes of the thymic epithelium (cortex and medulla) showed continuous involution from the first year to the end of life, approximated by simple negative logarithmic functions, and the velocity and nature of that involution did not change with puberty.
cards.watchOut: Morphometry of autopsy/biopsy material, not living volunteers: sudden-death and cardiac-surgery sources may not perfectly represent healthy ageing, and epithelial volume is a structural proxy for output, not a direct measure of T-cell production.
cards.source: Steinmann GG et al. The involution of the ageing human thymic epithelium is independent of puberty. A morphometric study. Scandinavian journal of immunology. 1985. PMID: 4081647. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Douek 1998: TREC-measured thymic function declines with age but substantial output is maintained into late adulthood
cards.summary: Douek 1998: TREC-measured thymic function declines with age but substantial output is maintained into late adulthood
cards.type: Primary human TREC quantification study (healthy ageing and HIV cohorts)
cards.people: Healthy children and adults across the age span, with HIV-infected adults before and during highly active antiretroviral therapy as the perturbation limb; thymic output was quantified in blood and lymphoid tissue by measuring the excisional DNA products of T-cell receptor gene rearrangement (TRECs). The record's abstract does not state a single pooled N for the healthy cohort.
cards.result: Thymic function declined with age, but substantial output was maintained into late adulthood. HIV infection decreased measurable thymic function, and in adults treated with HAART there was a rapid and sustained increase in thymic output in most subjects — evidence that the adult thymus can still contribute new naive T cells to immune reconstitution.
cards.watchOut: N not documented as a single figure in the record for the healthy ageing limb. TRECs do not replicate when a T cell divides, so peripheral division dilutes the signal — the next card quantifies why TREC counts alone overstate or understate true output.
cards.source: Douek DC et al. Changes in thymic function with age and during the treatment of HIV infection. Nature. 1998. PMID: 9872319. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hazenberg 2000: in healthy people, falling thymic output lowers TREC content only when naive T cells also divide — TREC is an indirect gauge
cards.summary: Hazenberg 2000: in healthy people, falling thymic output lowers TREC content only when naive T cells also divide — TREC is an indirect gauge
cards.type: Primary human mechanistic study of TREC dynamics
cards.people: Healthy individuals and HIV-1-infected patients, in whom TREC content of the naive T-cell population was tracked against cell-division rates; the record's abstract does not state cohort Ns.
cards.result: In healthy individuals, declining thymic output affected TREC content only when accompanied by naive T-cell division. The rapid TREC decline in HIV-1 infection and its rise after HAART were better explained by changes in peripheral T-cell division rates than by thymic impairment or recovery. The authors conclude TREC content in healthy people is only indirectly related to thymic output.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record's abstract. This card disciplines the Douek card rather than contradicting it: age-related TREC decline is real, but converting it into a precise thymic-output number requires a division model.
cards.source: Hazenberg MD et al. Increased cell division but not thymic dysfunction rapidly affects the T-cell receptor excision circle content of the naive T cell population in HIV-1 infection. cards.headline: den Braber 2012: deuterium labelling shows the adult human naive T-cell pool is maintained almost exclusively by peripheral division, unlike the mouse
cards.summary: den Braber 2012: deuterium labelling shows the adult human naive T-cell pool is maintained almost exclusively by peripheral division, unlike the mouse
cards.type: Primary human in-vivo deuterium-labelling and modelling study (with mouse comparison)
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers across adult ages studied with in-vivo deuterated-water labelling, TREC analysis and CD31 expression, with parallel mouse experiments and mathematical modelling; the record's abstract does not state the human N.
cards.result: Ageing affected naive T-cell maintenance fundamentally differently in mice and humans: the mouse naive pool was sustained almost exclusively by thymus output throughout life, whereas maintenance of the adult human naive T-cell pool occurred almost exclusively through peripheral T-cell division. The authors warn this constrains extrapolating T-cell dynamics from mouse to human.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record's abstract, and the human conclusion is model-based (labelling kinetics plus TREC/CD31 data fitted to a model) — this is the EMERGING-grade quantitative limb of the shelf, not a direct count. Animal data appear here only as the paper's labelled comparison, not as a human evidence card.
cards.source: den Braber I et al. Maintenance of peripheral naive T cells is sustained by thymus output in mice but not humans. Immunity. 2012. PMID: 22365666. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: involution and falling output are ESTABLISHED; the production-versus-division split in old age is model-dependent
cards.summary: Synthesis: involution and falling output are ESTABLISHED; the production-versus-division split in old age is model-dependent
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Steinmann 1985 (204 human thymuses), Douek 1998 (healthy ageing TREC cohorts), Hazenberg 2000 (healthy and HIV cohorts) and den Braber 2012 (deuterium-labelled healthy adults).
cards.result: Structure and function agree: the T-cell-producing epithelial space involutes continuously from infancy (independent of puberty) while total organ size barely changes, and TREC-measured output falls with age but persists into late adulthood. The adult naive pool's numbers are nonetheless largely preserved, because — on the labelling evidence — peripheral division, not new thymic production, does most of the maintenance work in adult humans. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall / Ganong) matches this account; the precise percentage split in the very old, and direct repertoire-diversity counts, remain model-dependent and are not asserted as settled numbers here.
cards.watchOut: No classic anchor was refused on this shelf. Do not quote a single 'percent per year' output figure as measured fact: the ~3%/year epithelial decline often cited for this literature is a textbook-style summary of the morphometric curve, and the fetched Steinmann record itself reports the logarithmic course, not that single rate.

shelves.title: Normal carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity by age and blood pressure
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is normal carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity by age and blood-pressure category — the Reference Values for Arterial Stiffness Collaboration distributions — and how much of the age rise is pressure-dependent versus intrinsic wall stiffening?
shelves.mesh: Pulse Wave Analysis/methods · Vascular Stiffness/physiology · Blood Pressure/physiology · Reference Values · Carotid Arteries/physiology · Femoral Arteries/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's account of arterial distensibility — a stiffer aorta transmits the pulse wave faster — the human reference data are consistent across three large primary studies. The Reference Values for Arterial Stiffness Collaboration (11,092 reference individuals; 1455 with optimal/normal pressure as the 'normal' subset) established cfPWV reference tables by age decade and blood-pressure category, finding the age rise steepens at higher pressures and the pressure effect grows with age. In strictly healthy ELSA-Brasil adults (2158), cfPWV was higher in men (8.74 ± 1.15 vs 8.31 ± 1.13 m/s) and higher whenever mean arterial pressure reached 85 mmHg; major risk factors doubled the age-related slope of rise (about 0.09 vs 0.05 m/s per year in men), so much of the population age rise is pressure/risk-factor-dependent, with a residual rise in healthy normotensive people that reflects intrinsic wall stiffening. The Spanish EVA study (501 randomly sampled adults) found a mean cfPWV of 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s at ages 35–75, with age, sex and mean pressure explaining 49% of variance. Cross-points: endothelial vasodilatation/flow-mediated dilatation is a different quantity, covered elsewhere in the library.

cards.headline: Reference Values Collaboration 2010: in 11,092 reference individuals, carotid–femoral PWV rose with age and with blood-pressure category — each amplifying the other
cards.summary: Reference Values Collaboration 2010: in 11,092 reference individuals, carotid–femoral PWV rose with age and with blood-pressure category — each amplifying the other
cards.people: Data from 16,867 subjects and patients at 13 centres in 8 European countries, with PWV converted to a common standard; the reference population was 11,092 people free of overt cardiovascular disease, non-diabetic and untreated with antihypertensive or lipid-lowering drugs, of whom 1455 with optimal/normal blood pressure formed the 'normal value' population.
cards.result: Pulse wave velocity increased with age and with blood-pressure category; the increase with age was more pronounced at higher blood-pressure categories, and the increase with blood pressure was more important in older subjects. The study established reference values by age decade and blood-pressure category, and proposed normal values from the non-hypertensive, no-added-risk-factor subset. The record presents the distributions in its tables rather than printing decade values in the abstract, so this card claims the pattern and the population, not unrecorded numbers.
cards.watchOut: Pooled across centres and devices with conversion formulae — the standardisation is a strength for size and a caveat for any single device's readings; the 'normal' subset (1455) is far smaller than the reference population (11,092), so normal-range tails are less precise.
cards.source: Reference Values for Arterial Stiffness' Collaboration. Determinants of pulse wave velocity in healthy people and in the presence of cardiovascular risk factors: 'establishing normal and reference values'. Eur Heart J. 2010. PMID: 20530030. cards.headline: ELSA-Brasil 2018: in 2158 strictly healthy adults, cfPWV was higher in men (8.74 versus 8.31 m/s) and rose faster with age when risk factors were present
cards.summary: ELSA-Brasil 2018: in 2158 strictly healthy adults, cfPWV was higher in men (8.74 versus 8.31 m/s) and rose faster with age when risk factors were present
cards.people: 2158 healthy adults (1412 women) aged 35–74 from the ELSA-Brasil cohort of 15,105, after excluding diabetes, blood pressure above optimal/normal, body mass index ≤18.5 or ≥25 kg/m², current/former smoking and prior cardiovascular disease.
cards.result: cfPWV predictors were similar in both sexes (age, mean arterial pressure, heart rate), but cfPWV was higher in men than women (8.74 ± 1.15 vs 8.31 ± 1.13 m/s; adjusted for age and mean arterial pressure, P<0.001) at every age interval, and higher whenever mean arterial pressure was ≥85 mmHg. In the full cohort, major risk factors doubled the age-related slope of cfPWV rise (men 0.0919 vs 0.0504 m/s per year; women 0.0960 vs 0.0606 m/s per year) — direct evidence that much of the population age rise is risk-factor/pressure-driven rather than intrinsic ageing alone.
cards.watchOut: A Brazilian occupational cohort with a strict health filter — values describe unusually healthy 35–74-year-olds and should not be applied to unfiltered clinic populations.
cards.source: Baldo MP et al. Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity in a healthy adult sample: The ELSA-Brasil study. Int J Cardiol. 2018. PMID: 29111104. cards.headline: EVA Study 2020: in 501 randomly sampled Spanish adults without cardiovascular disease, mean cfPWV was 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s, rising with age and blood pressure
cards.summary: EVA Study 2020: in 501 randomly sampled Spanish adults without cardiovascular disease, mean cfPWV was 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s, rising with age and blood pressure
cards.people: 501 participants aged 35–75 without cardiovascular disease, recruited by random sampling stratified by age and sex in Spain (mean age 55.9 years, 50.3% women); measurements with SphigmoCor and Vasera VS-1500 devices. Registry: NCT02623894.
cards.result: Mean values: carotid–femoral PWV 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s (with cardio-ankle vascular index 8.01 ± 1.44 and brachial-ankle PWV 12.93 ± 2.68 m/s). All stiffness measures except the augmentation index were higher in men and increased with age and blood pressure. Age, sex and mean blood pressure explained 49% of cfPWV variance; hypertension was associated with higher cfPWV (odds ratio 3.38 in the logistic model).
cards.watchOut: A single-country sample of 501 — its mean is a population average across ages 35–75, not an age-specific norm; device and path-length conventions differ between laboratories, so absolute values travel imperfectly.
cards.source: Gómez-Sánchez M et al. Reference values of arterial stiffness parameters and their association with cardiovascular risk factors in the Spanish population. The EVA Study. cards.headline: Synthesis: cfPWV norms are age-and-pressure tables, not a single number — and about half the population age rise tracks pressure and risk factors
cards.summary: Synthesis: cfPWV norms are age-and-pressure tables, not a single number — and about half the population age rise tracks pressure and risk factors
cards.people: Three primary human reference studies totalling 13,751 reference individuals (11,092 European reference population; 2158 strictly healthy Brazilians; 501 randomly sampled Spaniards). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's account of arterial compliance and pulse-wave transmission: a stiffer, less distensible aorta transmits the pressure wave faster, which is the physical basis of the measurement — the textbook framing is context, not an evidence card.
cards.result: Every study found cfPWV rising with age and with blood-pressure category, the two effects amplifying each other; men run higher than women at the same age (8.74 vs 8.31 m/s in the healthy ELSA-Brasil sample). The Spanish population mean was 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s across ages 35–75. ELSA-Brasil quantifies the pressure/risk-factor share: major risk factors doubled the age-related slope of rise, so a large part of 'normal ageing' values in unfiltered populations is pressure-dependent stiffening, with an intrinsic wall component remaining in strictly healthy, normotensive samples. Where decade-by-decade table values are not printed in the fetched records, they are presented here as the collaborations' published tables, not as numbers this shelf re-derives.
cards.watchOut: cfPWV is method-sensitive (device, transit-path measurement, conversion formulae). Compare a patient's value only against reference tables built with a compatible method, and always against their own age-and-pressure stratum.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.
