shelves.title: Normative heart rate variability values by age and sex
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal short-term heart rate variability values (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF power) by age and sex, and how steeply do time- and frequency-domain indices fall across adult life?
shelves.mesh: Heart Rate/physiology · Autonomic Nervous System/physiology · Reference Values · Electrocardiography · Age Factors · Sex Characteristics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of autonomic control of the heart — beat-to-beat variation as the visible signature of vagal and sympathetic modulation of the sinoatrial node — four primary human datasets agree on the shape of normality. A 44-study collation (21,438 healthy participants) found published short-term HRV values lower than the 1996 Task Force norms, with enormous inter-individual variation in spectral measures (up to 260,000%). The Danish DanFunD population study (6891 adults) provides age- and sex-stratified time- and frequency-domain reference values, with parasympathetic predominance commoner in women and younger adults. A Korean cohort (1828) shows conventional time- and frequency-domain indices falling more steeply with age than entropy measures, and Framingham (2722) shows age and heart rate are the dominant determinants of every measure (partial R² 0.125–0.389), ahead of blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, caffeine and common drugs. Exact percentile values live in these studies' tables, matched by age, sex and recording method; where a fetched record does not print a number, this shelf presents it as that study's published table rather than re-deriving it. Cross-point: respiratory sinus arrhythmia — the underlying vagal mechanism — is shelved separately.

cards.headline: Nunan 2010: across 44 studies (21,438 healthy participants), short-term HRV values in the literature ran lower than the 1996 Task Force norms, with huge inter-individual variation in spectral measures
cards.summary: Nunan 2010: across 44 studies (21,438 healthy participants), short-term HRV values in the literature ran lower than the 1996 Task Force norms, with huge inter-individual variation in spectral measures
cards.type: Quantitative systematic review of primary normative studies
cards.people: 44 studies published January 1997–September 2008 reporting short-term heart rate variability in normally healthy individuals, collating 21,438 participants.
cards.result: Values for short-term HRV measures from the literature were lower than the 1996 Task Force norms, with a degree of homogeneity for common measures across studies — but large inter-individual variation (up to 260,000%), particularly for spectral (frequency-domain) measures. The authors identify methodological discrepancies behind disparate values, including failure to recognise RR-data editing procedures, and call for large population studies across the full age spectrum and updated measurement recommendations. The record does not print a single pooled SDNN/RMSSD table in its abstract, so this card claims the direction and the variability, not unrecorded point values.
cards.watchOut: A review of heterogeneous small studies is a map of the literature, not a norm: recording length, posture, breathing and editing choices move HRV values as much as physiology does.
cards.source: Nunan D et al. A quantitative systematic review of normal values for short-term heart rate variability in healthy adults. Pacing Clin Electrophysiol. 2010. PMID: 20663071. cards.headline: DanFunD 2024: in 6891 Danish adults aged 18–72, time- and frequency-domain HRV varied hugely by age and sex — parasympathetic predominance commoner in women and the young
cards.summary: DanFunD 2024: in 6891 Danish adults aged 18–72, time- and frequency-domain HRV varied hugely by age and sex — parasympathetic predominance commoner in women and the young
cards.people: 6891 men and women aged 18–72 recruited from 10 municipalities in the greater Copenhagen area (participation rate 29.5%), with short-term HRV measures related to age and sex.
cards.result: Both time- and frequency-domain measures showed huge variation across sex and age groups. Women had a higher median heart rate than men, and the heart-rate association with age was U-shaped. Measures indicating parasympathetic predominance over sympathetic activity were more frequent in women and in younger age groups. The authors provide age- and sex-specific reference values in the time and frequency domains for epidemiological and clinical use; the abstract reports the patterns rather than the full percentile tables.
cards.watchOut: A 29.5% participation rate invites healthy-volunteer bias, and a single short recording per person cannot capture day-to-day within-person variability — reference percentiles describe populations, not a patient's fixed trait.
cards.source: Brinth LS et al. Normative values of short-term heart rate variability in a cross-sectional study of a Danish population. The DanFunD study. Scand J Public Health. 2024. PMID: 36250428. cards.headline: Lee 2018: in 1828 Koreans, most HRV indices fell steeply with age — conventional time/frequency measures more than entropy measures — and low LF/HF predicted mortality
cards.summary: Lee 2018: in 1828 Koreans, most HRV indices fell steeply with age — conventional time/frequency measures more than entropy measures — and low LF/HF predicted mortality
cards.people: 1828 consecutive people aged 20–84 (64.8% men) with no serious comorbid conditions; RR intervals from 10-minute electrocardiograms were used to compute time-domain, frequency-domain and nonlinear HRV measures; 54 died during 10 years of follow-up (14 cardiac deaths).
cards.result: Greater age-dependence was seen for most conventional parameters, including low-frequency and high-frequency power, than for Shannon entropy, approximate entropy and sample entropy. In multivariate analysis the LF/HF ratio (odds ratio 0.876; P=0.025), Shannon entropy (odds ratio 0.372; P=0.028) and approximate entropy (odds ratio 0.093; P=0.030) predicted all-cause mortality, alongside age itself (odds ratio 1.141; P<0.001). Normative values by age are presented in the paper's tables.
cards.watchOut: Participants were clinic-recruited people without serious comorbidity rather than a random population sample, and the mortality analysis rests on 54 deaths — the normative tables are the card's main contribution, the prediction its secondary signal.
cards.source: Lee CH et al. Normative Values of Short-Term Heart Rate Variability Parameters in Koreans and Their Clinical Value for the Prediction of Mortality. Heart Lung Circ. 2018. PMID: 28592377. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Tsuji 1996 (Framingham): in 2722 adults, age and heart rate were the major determinants of every HRV measure (partial R² 0.125–0.389)
cards.summary: Tsuji 1996 (Framingham): in 2722 adults, age and heart rate were the major determinants of every HRV measure (partial R² 0.125–0.389)
cards.type: Community cohort determinants and normative-values study
cards.people: 2722 Framingham Heart Study subjects (mean age 55 ± 14 years) whose first 2 hours of ambulatory electrocardiography were reprocessed for HRV, after excluding non-sinus rhythm, >10% premature beats, short recordings and antiarrhythmic use; five frequency-domain and three time-domain measures were obtained, with normative values from a healthy subset adjusted for age and heart rate.
cards.result: Higher heart rate, older age, beta-blocker use, prior myocardial infarction or heart failure, diuretic use, diastolic pressure ≥90 mmHg, diabetes, ≥3 cups of coffee daily and smoking were each associated with lower values of one or more HRV measures; female sex and systolic pressure ≥160 mmHg were associated with higher values of some measures. Age and heart rate dominated (partial R² 0.125 to 0.389 for the three principal measures: low-frequency power, high-frequency power and the standard deviation of normal RR intervals).
cards.watchOut: Two-hour ambulatory recordings are not interchangeable with the 5-minute resting recordings of the other cards — duration is a method variable, and 1996 recording/editing practice predates current standards, as the Nunan review warns.
cards.source: Tsuji H et al. Determinants of heart rate variability. J Am Coll Cardiol. 1996. PMID: 8917269. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: HRV falls steeply with age in every dataset; any 'normal value' is meaningless without age, sex, heart rate and recording method attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: HRV falls steeply with age in every dataset; any 'normal value' is meaningless without age, sex, heart rate and recording method attached
cards.people: Four primary human datasets totalling over 32,000 participants (44-study collation 21,438; DanFunD 6891; Korean cohort 1828; Framingham 2722). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of autonomic control of the sinoatrial node — vagal activity dominating beat-to-beat (high-frequency) variation and mixed sympathetic–vagal influences at low frequencies — as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-point: respiratory sinus arrhythmia, the breath-by-breath vagal mechanism, is covered elsewhere in the library.
cards.result: Time-domain (SDNN, RMSSD) and frequency-domain (LF, HF power) indices decline across adult life in every population studied, more steeply for conventional measures than for entropy measures; women show more parasympathetic-predominant patterns and higher heart rates; and in Framingham, age and heart rate together explained more of HRV than any clinical factor. Literature values run below the older Task Force norms, and inter-individual scatter — especially for spectral measures — is enormous, so reference use requires the age/sex/method-matched tables from these studies rather than any single cut-off.
cards.watchOut: Recording length (2-hour ambulatory vs 5–10-minute resting), posture, breathing, time of day, caffeine, smoking and common drugs (beta-blockers, diuretics) all move HRV. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: True maximal heart rate: 208 − 0.7×age beats 220 − age on average, and no equation predicts an individual
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is true maximal heart rate by age — how accurate are the 220−age (Fox) and 208−0.7×age (Tanaka) equations against measured maxima, and what is the between-person scatter around any age prediction?
shelves.mesh: Heart Rate/physiology · Aging/physiology · Age Factors · Exercise Test · Predictive Value of Tests · Reference Values · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of sinoatrial-node ageing and maximal sympathetic drive — maximal heart rate falls roughly linearly with age whatever the training state — the measurement literature is concordant on both the better equation and its limits. The Tanaka meta-analysis (351 studies, 492 groups, 18,712 subjects) derived HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age (r = −0.90), cross-validated almost identically (209 − 0.7×age) in 514 laboratory-tested healthy adults, independent of sex and habitual activity; 220 − age systematically underestimates true maxima in older adults. But group accuracy is not individual accuracy: in 99 graded treadmill tests every one of nine equations showed poor Bland–Altman agreement with measured maxima, and in 320 soccer players the fitted equation still carried a standard error of the estimate of 8.6 beats/min, with Fox overestimating by a mean of 2.8 beats/min and Tanaka underestimating by 3.3 beats/min in that sample. The settled teaching: use 208 − 0.7×age for group-level prescription, and expect any individual's true maximum to sit roughly ±10 beats/min or more from any prediction — measure it when the number matters. Cross-point: VO2peak reference standards are shelved separately.

cards.headline: Tanaka 2001: across 18,712 subjects, HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age (r = −0.90) — and 220 − age underestimates maxima in older adults
cards.summary: Tanaka 2001: across 18,712 subjects, HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age (r = −0.90) — and 220 − age underestimates maxima in older adults
cards.type: Meta-analysis of measured maxima with laboratory cross-validation
cards.people: Meta-analysis of group mean maximal heart rates from 351 studies (492 groups, 18,712 subjects), cross-validated in a laboratory study measuring HRmax in 514 healthy subjects; men and women across the adult age range and across habitual activity levels.
cards.result: Maximal heart rate was strongly related to age (r = −0.90), giving the prediction equation HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × age; the laboratory cross-validation produced a virtually identical equation, 209 − 0.7 × age. The regression line did not differ between men and women and was not influenced by wide variations in habitual physical activity. The authors conclude the then-standard 220 − age equation underestimates HRmax in older adults, which underestimates both the true stress of exercise testing and appropriate prescribed exercise intensity in that group.
cards.watchOut: A group-mean meta-analysis plus a healthy-volunteer validation sample: the equation describes the average line through the data, and the paper's own framing is population prescription — the between-person scatter around the line is quantified by the other cards, not this one.
cards.source: Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2001. PMID: 11153730. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shookster 2020: in 99 graded treadmill tests, all nine prediction equations agreed poorly with measured HRmax
cards.summary: Shookster 2020: in 99 graded treadmill tests, all nine prediction equations agreed poorly with measured HRmax
cards.people: 99 graded treadmill exercise tests ending at volitional fatigue, included only if the respiratory exchange ratio exceeded 1.10 (an effort criterion for a true maximum); measured HRmax was compared with nine age-predicted equations (Fox, Gellish, Gulati, Tanaka, Arena, Astrand, Nes, Fairbarn and others as published).
cards.result: Significant differences between measured and predicted HRmax were found for the Gulati, Astrand, Nes and Fairbarn (male) equations (P < 0.05). Bland–Altman plots showed wide limits of agreement for all nine equations, indicating poor agreement between measured and predicted maxima; most equations showed proportional bias, under- and over-estimating at the low and high ends of measured HRmax, with the Fox equation the exception and, in the authors' judgement, the best option for a general population on that criterion. The authors recommend using measured HRmax from an exercise test whenever accuracy matters.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre test series (N = 99, printed plainly) in people referred for or volunteering for treadmill testing: it ranks equations against each other but its 'best equation' verdict (Fox) conflicts with the larger meta-analytic verdict (Tanaka) — the robust common finding is the wide individual scatter, not the ranking.
cards.source: Shookster D et al. Accuracy of Commonly Used Age-Predicted Maximal Heart Rate Equations. Int J Exerc Sci. 2020. PMID: 33042384. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Nikolaidis 2015: in 320 soccer players, measured HRmax was 197.6 ± 9.4 beats/min; Fox overestimated by 2.8 and Tanaka underestimated by 3.3 beats/min, with an 8.6 beats/min standard error
cards.summary: Nikolaidis 2015: in 320 soccer players, measured HRmax was 197.6 ± 9.4 beats/min; Fox overestimated by 2.8 and Tanaka underestimated by 3.3 beats/min, with an 8.6 beats/min standard error
cards.type: Measured-versus-predicted comparison in a large athletic sample
cards.people: 320 competitive soccer players — 162 adolescents (15.8 ± 1.5 years) and 158 adults (23.4 ± 4.6 years) — performing a graded exercise field test (Conconi protocol) to measure maximal heart rate, compared against the Fox (220 − age) and Tanaka (208 − 0.7 × age) equations.
cards.result: Measured HRmax was 197.6 ± 9.4 beats/min overall (200.2 ± 7.9 in adolescents; 195.0 ± 10.0 in adults), and the sample's own fitted equation was HRmax = 212.3 − 0.75 × age (r = −0.41) with a standard error of the estimate of 8.6 beats/min. In the total sample, Fox overestimated measured HRmax by a mean difference of 2.8 beats/min (95% CI 1.6 to 3.9) while Tanaka underestimated it by 3.3 beats/min (95% CI −4.5 to −2.2); in adolescents Fox overestimated by 4.0 and Tanaka underestimated by 3.2 beats/min, while in adults Tanaka underestimated by 5.0 beats/min and Fox did not differ significantly (1.6 beats/min). The authors conclude neither equation validated in this population.
cards.watchOut: Young trained athletes on a field test: the equation biases here describe that population and protocol, and the weak age correlation (r = −0.41) reflects the narrow age range — the transferable numbers are the ±9–10 beats/min standard deviations of measured maxima within an age band.
cards.source: Nikolaidis PT. Maximal heart rate in soccer players: measured versus age-predicted. Biomedical journal (Biomed J). 2015. PMID: 25179696. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 208 − 0.7×age is the better average; ±10 beats/min is the honest individual uncertainty
cards.summary: Synthesis: 208 − 0.7×age is the better average; ±10 beats/min is the honest individual uncertainty
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 18,712 subjects with a 514-person laboratory validation, a 99-test equation-accuracy study, and a 320-athlete measured-versus-predicted comparison. Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of sinoatrial ageing and maximal chronotropic drive, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-point: VO2peak reference percentile standards (the FRIEND registry) are shelved separately.
cards.result: Age predicts maximal heart rate strongly at group level (r = −0.90 across nearly nineteen thousand subjects), the Tanaka equation 208 − 0.7×age sits closer to the measured line than 220 − age — which underestimates true maxima in older adults — and neither sex nor habitual activity moves the line materially. At individual level every equation fails precision: measured maxima scatter with standard deviations of about 9–10 beats/min within narrow age bands, a fitted equation's standard error was 8.6 beats/min, and Bland–Altman limits were wide for all nine equations tested. Prescribe intensity from equations for groups; test for the individual.
cards.watchOut: Equation rankings conflict between the smaller accuracy studies (Fox favoured in one) and the meta-analysis (Tanaka favoured); this shelf reports both and rests its stamp on the concordant findings — the age slope, the older-age Fox bias, and the large individual scatter. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session; one record (PMID 33042384) carried no MeSH in the fetched record, and its source line says so.

shelves.title: FRIEND reference standards for peak oxygen uptake: treadmill medians fall from 48.0 (men) and 37.6 (women) mL/kg/min in the twenties to 24.4 and 18.3 in the seventies, with cycle values systematically lower
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are reference percentile values for peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) by age, sex and exercise mode — the FRIEND registry standards for treadmill and cycle ergometry — and how fast does VO2peak fall per decade in each sex?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Cohort Studies · Exercise Test · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Fitness · Reference Values · Registries · Research · Sex Factors · United States
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence). This shelf answers the measurement question — population percentile standards for peak oxygen uptake — which is a different question from the determinants question homed on the existing VO2max-limits shelf (what limits maximal oxygen uptake: cardiac output versus peripheral extraction); that shelf is cross-pointed here in prose only, and none of its studies is re-carded. The carded base is one registry programme (FRIEND) in three reports: treadmill standards (N=7,783), cycle-ergometry standards (N=4,494) and the updated combined standards (N=22,379). The pattern is concordant across all three: values are higher in men than women at every age, higher on the treadmill than the cycle, and fall with age at roughly 10% per decade in relative terms in the original reports (13.5–16.4% per decade in the updated report, printed beside the absolute falls of 4.0–4.3 mL/kg/min per decade). Registry volunteers are self-selected people referred for or volunteering for maximal exercise testing, not a random population sample — the standards describe tested, apparently healthy adults without cardiovascular disease, and the updated treadmill standards came in 1.5–4.6 mL/kg/min lower than the 2015 standards as the sample broadened.

cards.headline: FRIEND treadmill standards 2015: median VO2max fell from 48.0 mL/kg/min in men and 37.6 in women aged 20–29 to 24.4 and 18.3 at ages 70–79 — about a 10% relative fall per decade
cards.summary: FRIEND treadmill standards 2015: median VO2max fell from 48.0 mL/kg/min in men and 37.6 in women aged 20–29 to 24.4 and 18.3 at ages 70–79 — about a 10% relative fall per decade
cards.people: 7,783 maximal treadmill cardiopulmonary exercise tests (respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.0) from men and women aged 20–79 years without cardiovascular disease, contributed by 8 US laboratories to the FRIEND registry (tests from January 2014 to February 2015).
cards.result: Percentiles of maximal oxygen consumption were determined for each decade from age 20 through 79, separately by sex. The 50th percentile fell from 48.0 (men) and 37.6 (women) mLO2·kg-1·min-1 at ages 20–29 to 24.4 (men) and 18.3 (women) at ages 70–79 — an absolute fall of 23.6 mL/kg/min in men and 19.3 in women across five decades, described by the authors as a rate of decline of approximately 10% per decade (a relative rate; the absolute decade medians are printed here beside it). FRIEND values differed from Norwegian CPX reference data and from older US standards derived from workload estimation rather than measured gas exchange.
cards.watchOut: Registry volunteers tested in experienced laboratories — self-selected, apparently healthy adults, not a random population sample; values apply to maximal treadmill tests meeting the effort criterion, not to submaximal or estimated fitness.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (registry reference-standards report) | Kaminsky LA, Arena R, Myers J. cards.headline: FRIEND cycle-ergometry standards 2017: median VO2max fell from 41.9 mL/kg/min in men and 31.0 in women aged 20–29 to 19.5 and 14.8 at ages 70–79 — cycle values run below treadmill values at every age
cards.summary: FRIEND cycle-ergometry standards 2017: median VO2max fell from 41.9 mL/kg/min in men and 31.0 in women aged 20–29 to 19.5 and 14.8 at ages 70–79 — cycle values run below treadmill values at every age
cards.people: 4,494 maximal cycle-ergometer cardiopulmonary exercise tests (respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.1) from men and women aged 20–79 years from 27 states, without cardiovascular disease, contributed by 10 US laboratories to the FRIEND registry (April 2014 to May 2016).
cards.result: Percentiles of maximum oxygen consumption were determined per decade and sex for cycle ergometry. The 50th percentile fell from 41.9 (men) and 31.0 (women) mLO2/kg/min at ages 20–29 to 19.5 (men) and 14.8 (women) at ages 70–79 — absolute falls of 22.4 and 16.2 mL/kg/min, a rate of decline of approximately 10% per decade (relative rate, with the absolute medians printed beside it). At the youngest decade the cycle medians sit about 6 mL/kg/min below the treadmill medians from the same registry, confirming that mode-specific standards are required: a cycle value must not be read against treadmill percentiles.
cards.watchOut: A stricter effort criterion (respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.1) than the treadmill report (≥1.0) — cross-mode comparisons carry that protocol difference as well as the true mode difference.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (registry reference-standards report) | Kaminsky LA, Imboden MT, Arena R, Myers J. cards.headline: Updated FRIEND standards 2022 (N=22,379): average decline 13.5% per decade on the treadmill (4.0 mL/kg/min) and 16.4% per decade on the cycle (4.3 mL/kg/min); updated treadmill standards sit 1.5–4.6 mL/kg/min below the 2015 standards
cards.summary: Updated FRIEND standards 2022 (N=22,379): average decline 13.5% per decade on the treadmill (4.0 mL/kg/min) and 16.4% per decade on the cycle (4.3 mL/kg/min); updated treadmill standards sit 1.5–4.6 mL/kg/min below the 2015 standards
cards.people: 22,379 cardiopulmonary exercise tests (16,278 treadmill and 6,101 cycle ergometer) from apparently healthy adults aged 20–89 years, contributed by 34 US laboratories to the FRIEND registry (tests conducted 1968–2021).
cards.result: Percentiles of peak oxygen consumption were determined per decade (20 through 89 years), sex and exercise mode, under both respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.0 and ≥1.1 effort criteria; mean peak values were observationally similar under either criterion. For both sexes the 50th percentile fell with age, was higher in men at every age, and was higher for treadmill than cycle testing. The average rate of decline per decade over six decades was 13.5% (relative), 4.0 mLO2·kg-1·min-1 (absolute), for treadmill testing and 16.4% (relative), 4.3 mLO2·kg-1·min-1 (absolute), for cycle testing. The updated treadmill standards were 1.5–4.6 mLO2·kg-1·min-1 lower than the 2015 standards, while the updated cycling standards were generally comparable to the 2017 standards — a reminder that reference values move as the reference sample broadens.
cards.watchOut: Tests span 1968–2021 and 34 laboratories — equipment and protocol generations differ across the pooled sample; the standards are for apparently healthy tested adults, and percentile position is not by itself a diagnosis or a prognosis.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (registry reference-standards update) | Kaminsky LA, Arena R, Myers J, Peterman JE. cards.headline: Synthesis: peak oxygen uptake has usable age-, sex- and mode-specific percentile standards — men above women, treadmill above cycle, and a fall of roughly a tenth to a sixth of the value per decade
cards.summary: Synthesis: peak oxygen uptake has usable age-, sex- and mode-specific percentile standards — men above women, treadmill above cycle, and a fall of roughly a tenth to a sixth of the value per decade
cards.people: Synthesis of Kaminsky 2015 (treadmill, N=7,783), Kaminsky 2017 (cycle, N=4,494) and Kaminsky 2022 (updated combined, N=22,379), framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card).
cards.result: The three FRIEND reports agree on the shape of normal cardiorespiratory fitness. At the median, a healthy man in his twenties reaches about 48 mL/kg/min on a treadmill and about 42 on a cycle; a healthy woman reaches about 38 and 31 respectively. By the seventies those medians have roughly halved (treadmill 24.4 and 18.3; cycle 19.5 and 14.8). The relative rate of decline is approximately 10% per decade in the original reports and 13.5% (treadmill) to 16.4% (cycle) per decade in the updated report, corresponding to absolute falls of about 4.0–4.3 mL/kg/min per decade — relative and absolute figures are printed together throughout this shelf, per the standing wording rule. Three practical consequences: read a result only against the standard for its own exercise mode; expect the percentile, not the raw value, to carry the age comparison; and treat the standards as describing self-selected tested volunteers, so a low percentile is a prompt for clinical context, not a stand-alone verdict. This shelf is the population-standards companion to the existing shelf on what limits maximal oxygen uptake (cardiac output versus peripheral extraction), which asks the mechanism question and is not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: all three reports come from one registry programme (FRIEND) — the standards are internally concordant but rest on a single, self-selected US testing population, not on independent population samples.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kaminsky LA et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2015 (PMID: 26455884); Kaminsky LA et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2017 (PMID: 27938891); Kaminsky LA et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2022 (PMID: 34809986). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Siltuximab in idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease: the one randomised trial found durable responses in 34% versus 0% on placebo, with real-world cohorts concordant
shelves.question: In patients with HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, does the anti-IL-6 antibody siltuximab, versus placebo (both with best supportive care), produce durable tumour and symptomatic responses and prolong progression-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Castleman Disease/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Progression-Free Survival · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial anchors this shelf and everything else is its supporting limb, labelled as such. The pivotal double-blind trial (van Rhee 2014, n=79, HIV-negative/HHV-8-negative symptomatic disease) found durable tumour and symptomatic responses in 34% on siltuximab plus best supportive care versus 0% on placebo plus best supportive care, with similar grade ≥3 adverse-event rates despite much longer exposure on the drug. A post-hoc analysis of the same trial (same programme, labelled) shows progression-free survival significantly prolonged (median not reached versus 14.5 months). The independent real-world limbs — a 48-patient Greek/Romanian retrospective cohort with a 71.1% overall response rate among the 38 assessed, and a 9-patient Italian named-patient series (N = 9, sub-floor, printed on its face and not counted toward this shelf's evidence floor) — are observational and graded accordingly. A single randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE even with concordant cohorts.

cards.headline: van Rhee 2014: the pivotal randomised trial (n=79) — durable tumour and symptomatic response 34% (18/53) on siltuximab versus 0% (0/26) on placebo, p=0.0012
cards.summary: van Rhee 2014: the pivotal randomised trial (n=79) — durable tumour and symptomatic response 34% (18/53) on siltuximab versus 0% (0/26) on placebo, p=0.0012
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, Lancet Oncol 2014
cards.people: Seventy-nine HIV-negative, HHV-8-seronegative patients with symptomatic multicentric Castleman disease at 38 hospitals in 19 countries, randomised 2:1 to siltuximab 11 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks (n=53) or placebo (n=26), all with best supportive care, treated until treatment failure; primary endpoint durable tumour and symptomatic response lasting at least 18 weeks (intention-to-treat).
cards.result: Durable tumour and symptomatic responses occurred in 18 of 53 patients (34%) on siltuximab versus none of 26 on placebo (difference 34.0%, 95% CI 11.1–54.8; p=0.0012). Grade ≥3 adverse events (47% vs 54%) and serious adverse events (23% vs 19%) were similar between groups despite longer median treatment on siltuximab (375 vs 152 days). The commonest grade ≥3 events on siltuximab were fatigue and night sweats; three patients (6%) had serious events judged related to the drug (lower respiratory tract infection, anaphylactic reaction, sepsis).
cards.watchOut: The trial predates the modern idiopathic-MCD diagnostic criteria and response definitions, and two-thirds of siltuximab patients did not achieve the durable composite response — the 34% figure, not a majority benefit, is the claim.
cards.source: van Rhee F, Wong RS, Munshi N et al. Siltuximab for multicentric Castleman's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2014. PMID: 25042199. Registry ID: NCT01024036. cards.headline: van Rhee 2022: progression-free-survival analysis of the SAME randomised programme — median PFS not reached on siltuximab versus 14.5 months on placebo (p=.0001); responses normalise labs and symptoms months before lymph nodes
cards.summary: van Rhee 2022: progression-free-survival analysis of the SAME randomised programme — median PFS not reached on siltuximab versus 14.5 months on placebo (p=.0001); responses normalise labs and symptoms months before lymph nodes
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the pivotal randomised trial (one programme), Blood Adv 2022
cards.people: Post-hoc analyses of the same phase 2 randomised trial population (79 patients: siltuximab n=53, placebo plus best supportive care n=26), examining progression-free survival and the sequence in which laboratory, clinical and lymph-node abnormalities normalised among the 18 siltuximab responders. Same programme as the card above — labelled, not an independent trial.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly improved with siltuximab (p=.0001): median PFS was 14.5 months (95% CI 13.6 to upper bound not reached) on placebo and was not reached on siltuximab. Among responders, abnormalities normalised in sequence — thrombocytosis first, then symptomatic response, C-reactive protein, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, lymph-node response, hyperfibrinogenaemia and immunoglobulin G — with some laboratory tests and nodes taking months to normalise. The authors support continued frontline use, as international guidelines recommend.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and within the same 79 patients — the PFS read strengthens the trial's own story but adds no new population; crossover and subsequent therapy after treatment failure are not controlled in this analysis.
cards.source: van Rhee F, Rosenthal A, Kanhai K et al. Siltuximab is associated with improved progression-free survival in idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease. Blood advances. 2022. PMID: 35793409. Registry ID: NCT01024036. MeSH: Antibodies, Monoclonal · Castleman Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Progression-Free Survival

cards.headline: Jitaru 2024: real-world Greek/Romanian cohort (n=48, observational) — overall response 71.1% among 38 assessed, 3-year survival 74%
cards.summary: Jitaru 2024: real-world Greek/Romanian cohort (n=48, observational) — overall response 71.1% among 38 assessed, 3-year survival 74%
cards.people: Forty-eight adults with idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease treated with siltuximab in routine practice in Greece and Romania (2017–2022), retrospectively analysed; mean age 65 years, 68.8% male, 75% had received one prior line of therapy, median nine cycles given; responses assessed by Castleman Disease Collaborative Network guidelines in the 38 patients with response data. Observational cohort — no comparator.
cards.result: The overall response rate was 71.1% (complete response 55.3%, partial response 15.8%) among the 38 assessed patients. Estimated 3-year overall survival was 74% and median survival 123 months as reported. The commonest adverse events were elevated liver enzymes, anxiety, allergic reactions and nausea/diarrhoea; serious adverse events occurred in 16.7% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, comparator-free, and 10 of 48 patients lacked response data — responder denominators flatter the drug; the very long reported median survival reflects a prevalent, treatment-selected cohort, not a trial estimate.
cards.source: Jitaru C, Symeonidis A, Badelita S et al. Siltuximab in Idiopathic Multicentric Castleman Disease: Real-World Experience. Journal of hematology. 2024. PMID: 39493599. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Tonialini 2018: Italian named-patient programme in relapsed/refractory disease — N = 9 (sub-floor, printed on the face): 3 of 9 responded, with durable control in all three responders
cards.summary: Tonialini 2018: Italian named-patient programme in relapsed/refractory disease — N = 9 (sub-floor, printed on the face): 3 of 9 responded, with durable control in all three responders
cards.type: Retrospective named-patient-programme series (observational, N = 9), Hematol Oncol 2018
cards.people: All nine patients (N = 9) who received siltuximab in Italy under a named-patient programme for relapsed or refractory multicentric Castleman disease, in a multicentre retrospective observational analysis; median treatment duration 285 days (range 104–1113). This report is below the ≥10-patient floor and is carded for completeness with its N printed — it does not count toward the shelf's evidence floor.
cards.result: The overall response rate was 33.3% (3 of 9); none of the three responders had relapsed at analysis, with response durations of 20, 23 and 37 months. Toxicity was mild: grade 1–2 fatigue and pruritus in two patients, grade 1 weight gain in one, grade 2 local oedema in two, and grade 1–2 upper respiratory tract infection in three (33.3%); no infusion-related reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: N = 9 — the smallest card on this shelf, in the hardest (relapsed/refractory) population; its lower response rate (33.3%) versus the real-world cohort's 71.1% is a population difference, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Tonialini L, Bonfichi M, Ferrero S et al. Siltuximab in relapsed/refractory multicentric Castleman disease: Experience of the Italian NPP program. Hematological oncology. 2018. PMID: 30074630. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, placebo-beating response effect from one randomised trial, supported by concordant real-world cohorts — POSSIBLE by the single-trial cap
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, placebo-beating response effect from one randomised trial, supported by concordant real-world cohorts — POSSIBLE by the single-trial cap
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: the pivotal randomised trial (n=79) and its post-hoc progression-free-survival analysis (same programme), a 48-patient real-world cohort, and a 9-patient sub-floor named-patient series (not counted toward the floor).
cards.result: Siltuximab produces durable tumour and symptomatic responses in about a third of patients where placebo produced none, prolongs progression-free survival within the same trial, and shows higher response rates in less pretreated real-world practice. Harms are dominated by fatigue, night sweats and infection risk, with rare serious drug-related events including anaphylaxis and sepsis. Because the controlled evidence is a single trial of 79 patients, the stamp is POSSIBLE; the observational limbs agree with the trial but cannot raise it.
cards.watchOut: HHV-8-positive and HIV-associated multicentric disease are different questions (driven by viral IL-6 and rituximab-based care) — nothing on this shelf transfers to them.

shelves.title: Emapalumab in primary HLH: single-arm pivotal response 63% in previously treated children, about 70% bridged to transplant — real-world and pre-transplant cohorts concordant
shelves.question: In children with primary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that is refractory, recurrent, progressive or intolerant of conventional therapy, does the anti-interferon-γ antibody emapalumab, versus no concurrent control, produce responses and bridge patients to transplantation?
shelves.mesh: Lymphohistiocytosis, Hemophagocytic/complications/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Interferon-gamma/antagonists & inhibitors · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Chimerism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: the pivotal evidence is a single-arm phase 2/3 study (GAP-E), so response and transplant-bridging rates are framed without any comparator claim. In that study (Locatelli 2020, n=34), 63% of previously treated children responded — significantly above the prespecified 40% null — about 70% proceeded to transplantation, and about three-quarters were alive at last observation. Two observational limbs, labelled as such, point the same way: the 46-patient US real-world primary-HLH cohort (REAL-HLH) reproduced the pivotal trial's pattern, and a 50-patient single-centre retrospective comparison found children who received emapalumab shortly before reduced-intensity transplant had markedly less mixed chimerism (48% vs 77%) and better intervention-free survival (73% vs 43%), though overall survival did not differ significantly. Product naming, clarification exception: emapalumab (Gamifant, Sobi). Cross-point in prose only: the malignancy-associated (secondary) HLH real-world population is a different question and is not carded here. The defining harm is infection: severe infections developed in 10 of 34 pivotal-trial patients during treatment, in a disease whose immune suppression is itself profound.

cards.headline: Locatelli 2020: pivotal single-arm phase 2/3 (n=34) — response 63% in previously treated children (versus a 40% prespecified null, p=0.02), 70% proceeded to transplant, 74% alive at last observation
cards.summary: Locatelli 2020: pivotal single-arm phase 2/3 (n=34) — response 63% in previously treated children (versus a 40% prespecified null, p=0.02), 70% proceeded to transplant, 74% alive at last observation
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2–3 pivotal study, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: Thirty-four patients aged 18 years or younger with primary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis — 27 previously treated with conventional therapy and 7 previously untreated — in an open-label, single-group phase 2–3 study of emapalumab (anti-interferon-γ antibody) with dexamethasone, with treatment timed around allogeneic transplantation and long-term follow-up to 1 year after transplant or last dose; 26 patients completed the study. Single-arm — no concurrent control.
cards.result: Overall response was 63% in the previously treated group and 65% among all patients who received an infusion — both significantly above the prespecified null hypothesis of 40% (p=0.02 and p=0.005). Seventy percent of previously treated patients (65% of all infused) proceeded to transplantation, and at last observation 74% of previously treated patients (71% of all infused) were alive. Emapalumab was not associated with organ toxicity; severe infections developed in 10 patients during treatment, and one patient discontinued because of disseminated histoplasmosis.
cards.watchOut: The 40% null benchmark is a historical judgement, not a randomised control — response in HLH is partly a function of how sick patients are at entry, and the previously untreated subgroup is only 7 patients. Infection, not organ toxicity, is the harm that matters.
cards.source: Locatelli F, Jordan MB, Allen C et al. Emapalumab in Children with Primary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32374962. Registry ID: NCT01818492, NCT02069899. cards.headline: Verkamp 2024: retrospective pre-transplant comparison (50 children, observational) — emapalumab before reduced-intensity transplant halves mixed chimerism (48% vs 77%) and improves intervention-free survival (73% vs 43%); overall survival not significantly different
cards.summary: Verkamp 2024: retrospective pre-transplant comparison (50 children, observational) — emapalumab before reduced-intensity transplant halves mixed chimerism (48% vs 77%) and improves intervention-free survival (73% vs 43%); overall survival not significantly different
cards.people: Fifty children with haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis undergoing a first reduced-intensity-conditioning transplant at one institution (2014–2022): 22 received emapalumab within 21 days before conditioning and 28 did not. Retrospective comparative cohort — observational evidence, labelled; the cohort is HLH broadly, not restricted to genetically confirmed primary HLH.
cards.result: Mixed chimerism (<95% donor) occurred in 48% of the emapalumab group versus 77% of the comparison group (p=.03), and severe mixed chimerism (<25% donor) in 5% versus 38% (p<.01). Intervention-free survival (no donor lymphocyte infusion, CD34-selected boost, second transplant or death within 5 years) was 73% versus 43% (p=.03), with the largest gap in infants under 12 months (75% vs 20%, p<.01). Overall survival was higher with emapalumab but not significantly (82% vs 71%, p=.39).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and era-confounded (emapalumab patients are necessarily from later years, when transplant practice also evolved); the survival comparison is null, so the claim is about graft stability, not proven longer life.
cards.source: Verkamp B, Jodele S, Sabulski A et al. Emapalumab therapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis before reduced-intensity transplantation improves chimerism. Blood. 2024. PMID: 39190435. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: REAL-HLH 2024: US real-world primary-HLH cohort (n=46, observational) — 90.5% pre-transplant survival among the transplant-eligible, 12-month survival probability 73.1%, no discontinuations for adverse events
cards.summary: REAL-HLH 2024: US real-world primary-HLH cohort (n=46, observational) — 90.5% pre-transplant survival among the transplant-eligible, 12-month survival probability 73.1%, no discontinuations for adverse events
cards.type: Multicentre retrospective real-world cohort (observational), Blood Adv 2024
cards.people: Forty-six patients meeting primary-HLH classification criteria, treated with at least one dose of emapalumab across 33 US hospitals (November 2018 to October 2021) in the retrospective REAL-HLH study; median age at diagnosis 1.0 year, 15 of 46 in intensive care at initiation, 35 of 46 previously treated; emapalumab was started for refractory (19), recurrent (14) or progressive (7) disease. Observational — no comparator.
cards.result: Key laboratory parameters normalised in most assessed patients — fibrinogen 97.4% (37/38), absolute neutrophil count 88.9% (40/45), platelets 84.8% (39/46), chemokine ligand 9 72.7% (24/33) and ferritin 44.4% (20/45). Forty-two patients (91.3%) were transplant-eligible; pre-transplant survival was 90.5% (38/42), 31 proceeded to transplant and 74.2% of those transplanted were alive at the end of follow-up. The 12-month survival probability from emapalumab initiation for the whole cohort was 73.1%. There were no discontinuations because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A treated-cohort description without a control arm: survival figures reflect the whole modern package of care (including transplant), and ferritin — the marker families watch — normalised in under half of patients.
cards.source: Chandrakasan S, Jordan MB, Baker A et al. Real-world treatment patterns and outcomes in patients with primary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis treated with emapalumab. Blood advances. 2024. PMID: 38429096. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: emapalumab controls primary HLH and bridges most children to transplant on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with infection the standing harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: emapalumab controls primary HLH and bridges most children to transplant on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with infection the standing harm
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above: the single-arm pivotal study (n=34), a retrospective pre-transplant comparative cohort (n=50), and the US real-world primary-HLH cohort (n=46).
cards.result: Across trial and real-world settings, roughly two-thirds of refractory/recurrent primary-HLH patients respond to emapalumab plus dexamethasone, most responders reach transplant, and pre-transplant chimerism outcomes look better when the drug is used before reduced-intensity conditioning. None of this is randomised, so the stamp is POSSIBLE and every rate on this shelf is a proportion without a concurrent denominator. The secondary/malignancy-associated HLH population studied elsewhere is a different question, cross-pointed in the balance and not carded.
cards.watchOut: Primary HLH still requires transplantation for cure — emapalumab's role on this evidence is disease control and bridging, and severe infection during interferon-γ blockade (including disseminated fungal infection) is the risk that bounds its use.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 32374962, 39190435, 38429096). Registry ID: NCT01818492, NCT02069899 as carded. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Tagraxofusp in BPDCN: single-arm complete-response rate 72% in untreated patients at the 12 µg/kg dose, about half bridged to transplant — capillary leak syndrome is the defining harm
shelves.question: In patients with blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm, does the CD123-directed cytotoxin tagraxofusp, versus no concurrent control, produce complete responses, and can responders be bridged to stem-cell transplantation?
shelves.mesh: Recombinant Fusion Proteins/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Capillary Leak Syndrome/chemically induced · Leukemia, Myeloid/drug therapy/mortality · Dendritic Cells · Interleukin-3 Receptor alpha Subunit/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: all carded evidence is single-arm (GAP-E), so response rates are framed without a comparator. In the pivotal multicohort trial (Pemmaraju 2019), untreated patients at the 12 µg/kg dose achieved the primary outcome (complete response plus clinical complete response) in 72%, with an overall response rate of 90% and 45% bridged to stem-cell transplantation; the long-term report of the same programme (labelled one programme) puts the treatment-naive complete-response rate at 57% in the larger 12 µg/kg population with a median response duration of 24.9 months. The 2026 real-world frontline cohort (n=32, Letter-format, observational) found similar response rates (overall 82.1%, complete 60.7%) — but its propensity-matched comparison against a pre-tagraxofusp historical cohort showed no survival advantage (2-year survival 59.4% vs 60.8%), an honesty anchor this shelf keeps on its face. Capillary leak syndrome is the defining, potentially fatal harm: 19–21% in the trial reports and 53.1% in the real-world cohort, managed per the product label with albumin monitoring, weight/fluid checks and dose holds. Product naming, clarification exception: tagraxofusp (Elzonris, Stemline/Menarini). Cross-point in prose only: the tagraxofusp-plus-azacitidine-plus-venetoclax combination programme is a different question and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Pemmaraju 2019: pivotal multicohort trial (47 patients) — complete/clinical-complete response 72% and overall response 90% in untreated patients at 12 µg/kg, 45% bridged to transplant; capillary leak syndrome in 19%
cards.summary: Pemmaraju 2019: pivotal multicohort trial (47 patients) — complete/clinical-complete response 72% and overall response 90% in untreated patients at 12 µg/kg, 45% bridged to transplant; capillary leak syndrome in 19%
cards.type: Open-label multicohort single-arm pivotal trial, N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: Forty-seven adults with untreated (n=32) or relapsed (n=15) blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (median age 70, range 22–84) in an open-label multicohort study of tagraxofusp (CD123-directed cytotoxin: interleukin-3 fused to truncated diphtheria toxin) at 7 or 12 µg per kilogram intravenously on days 1–5 of each 21-day cycle, continued until progression or unacceptable toxicity. Single-arm — no concurrent control.
cards.result: Among the 29 previously untreated patients who received 12 µg/kg, the primary outcome (complete response plus clinical complete response) occurred in 21 (72%) and the overall response rate was 90%; 45% of these patients went on to stem-cell transplantation, and survival at 18 and 24 months was 59% and 52%. Among the 15 previously treated patients the response rate was 67% and median overall survival 8.5 months. The commonest adverse events were raised alanine aminotransferase (64%), aspartate aminotransferase (60%), hypoalbuminaemia (55%), peripheral oedema (51%) and thrombocytopenia (49%). Capillary leak syndrome was reported in 19% and was associated with one death in each dose subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Capillary leak syndrome killed patients in both dose subgroups — the response headline must never be quoted without it. The 72% figure is the 29-patient 12 µg/kg untreated subgroup, not the whole 47.
cards.source: Pemmaraju N, Lane AA, Sweet KL et al. Tagraxofusp in Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic-Cell Neoplasm. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 31018069. Registry ID: NCT02113982. cards.headline: Pemmaraju 2022: long-term report of the SAME programme (84 patients at 12 µg/kg) — treatment-naive complete response 57%, median duration 24.9 months, 51% of complete responders bridged to transplant
cards.summary: Pemmaraju 2022: long-term report of the SAME programme (84 patients at 12 µg/kg) — treatment-naive complete response 57%, median duration 24.9 months, 51% of complete responders bridged to transplant
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the pivotal trial (one programme), J Clin Oncol 2022
cards.people: Long-term results, including the continued-access phase, of the same prospective trial (NCT02113982): 84 of 89 enrolled patients received tagraxofusp 12 µg/kg daily (65 treatment-naive, 19 relapsed/refractory), median follow-up 34.0 months. Same programme as the card above — labelled, not an independent population.
cards.result: In treatment-naive patients the overall response rate was 75% and 57% achieved complete response plus clinical complete response; median time to remission was 39 days (range 14–131) and median complete-response duration 24.9 months (95% CI 3.8 to not reached). Nineteen patients (51%) of those achieving complete response were bridged to stem-cell transplant. The commonest adverse events were again transaminase elevations and hypoalbuminaemia, mostly in cycle 1 and transient. Capillary leak syndrome occurred in 21% (grade ≥3 in 7%).

cards.headline: Schroeder 2026: real-world frontline cohort (32 patients, Letter, observational) — response 82.1% and complete response 60.7%, capillary leak in 53.1%, but matched historical comparison shows NO survival advantage (2-year survival 59.4% vs 60.8%)
cards.summary: Schroeder 2026: real-world frontline cohort (32 patients, Letter, observational) — response 82.1% and complete response 60.7%, capillary leak in 53.1%, but matched historical comparison shows NO survival advantage (2-year survival 59.4% vs 60.8%)
cards.type: Multicentre real-world cohort, Letter format (observational), J Hematol Oncol 2026
cards.people: Thirty-two patients with blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm treated with frontline tagraxofusp across 13 tertiary centres (2019–2024), retrospectively analysed and contextualised against a historical pre-tagraxofusp cohort of 40 patients; median age 71.5 years, with skin (93.8%), bone-marrow (84.4%) and peripheral-blood (53.1%) involvement. Letter-format multicentre observational report.
cards.result: The overall response rate was 82.1% with complete responses in 60.7%. Capillary leak syndrome occurred in 53.1% (grade ≥3 in 47.1% as reported), with no unexpected safety signals. Two-year overall and progression-free survival were 40.5% and 30.4% at a median follow-up of 18.4 months. Nearly half proceeded to allogeneic transplant, but the propensity-matched comparison with the non-tagraxofusp cohort showed comparable 2-year survival (59.4% vs 60.8%, p=0.9), and frontline tagraxofusp was not associated with survival in pooled multivariable analysis (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.37–2.15, a relative measure; p=0.803).
cards.watchOut: The survival null against historical controls is the most important number on this card: high response rates plus more transplants did not translate into demonstrably longer life in this comparison, and the much higher real-world capillary-leak rate (53.1% vs ~20% in trials) suggests trial reporting understated it or real-world patients are frailer.
cards.source: Schroeder JC, Faustmann P, Janjetovic S et al. Outcomes of front-line tagraxofusp in patients with blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) in a real-world scenario. Journal of hematology & oncology. 2026. PMID: 42844632. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: tagraxofusp induces deep, often transplant-enabling remissions in BPDCN on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with capillary leak syndrome and an unproven survival benefit bounding the claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: tagraxofusp induces deep, often transplant-enabling remissions in BPDCN on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with capillary leak syndrome and an unproven survival benefit bounding the claim
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above: the pivotal single-arm programme (47 patients in the primary report; 84 at the licensed dose in the long-term report — one programme) and a 32-patient real-world frontline cohort with a 40-patient historical comparison.
cards.result: The drug clearly does something chemotherapy-era BPDCN care struggled to do: complete responses in roughly 57–72% of untreated patients, median complete-response duration about 25 months, and about half of complete responders bridged to transplant. What is not shown — anywhere — is a controlled survival benefit, and the one matched real-world comparison found none. The stamp is therefore POSSIBLE: a response-and-bridging claim, not a survival claim, with capillary leak syndrome (albumin monitoring, dose holds per the label) as the price of admission.
cards.watchOut: Patients with low albumin or cardiac comorbidity are at highest capillary-leak risk; the trial populations were selected accordingly, which is part of why real-world harm rates run higher.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 31018069, 35820082, 42844632). Registry ID: NCT02113982 as carded. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Moxetumomab pasudotox in relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukaemia: single-arm durable complete response 36% at long-term follow-up, with most complete responders MRD-negative — a withdrawn product whose remissions outlast it
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory hairy cell leukaemia after purine-analogue therapy, does the CD22 immunotoxin moxetumomab pasudotox, versus no concurrent control, produce durable complete remissions with minimal-residual-disease clearance?
shelves.mesh: Leukemia, Hairy Cell/drug therapy/pathology · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Bacterial Toxins/therapeutic use · Exotoxins/therapeutic use · Neoplasm, Residual/drug therapy · Remission Induction · Sialic Acid Binding Ig-like Lectin 2/immunology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: all carded evidence is single-arm (GAP-E), framed without a comparator throughout. The pivotal trial (n=80, at least two prior systemic therapies including a purine analogue) produced complete responses in 41% and — at long-term follow-up of the same programme, labelled as such — a durable complete-response rate of 36%, with 82% of complete responders MRD-negative and a median progression-free survival without loss of haematologic remission of 71.7 months. The earlier phase 1 programme (two overlapping reports of the same dose-escalation study and its extension cohort, labelled as one programme) found the same pattern: complete remissions in about half to two-thirds, lasting longer when MRD-negative (median 42.1 vs 13.5 months). The defining harms are capillary leak syndrome and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, each in up to about 10% and generally reversible. Market history belongs on the face: the product was withdrawn from the US market in 2023 for commercial reasons and later from the EU — this shelf's value is the durable MRD-negative remissions it demonstrated in a no-option population, and the frontline purine-analogue question lives in its own home (pack #5300) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Kreitman 2018: pivotal single-arm trial (n=80) — durable complete response 30%, complete response 41%, overall response 75%, and 85% of complete responders MRD-negative
cards.summary: Kreitman 2018: pivotal single-arm trial (n=80) — durable complete response 30%, complete response 41%, overall response 75%, and 85% of complete responders MRD-negative
cards.type: Multicentre open-label single-arm pivotal trial, Leukemia 2018
cards.people: Eighty adults with relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukaemia after at least two prior systemic therapies including at least one purine nucleoside analogue (79% male, median age 60), treated in a multicentre open-label pivotal study with moxetumomab pasudotox (recombinant CD22-targeting immunotoxin) 40 µg/kg intravenously on days 1, 3 and 5 every 28 days for up to 6 cycles; response and minimal residual disease assessed by blinded independent central review. Single-arm — no concurrent control.
cards.result: The durable complete-response rate was 30%, the complete-response rate 41% and the objective response rate 75%; 64 patients (80%) achieved haematologic remission. Among complete responders, 27 (85%) achieved MRD negativity by immunohistochemistry. The most frequent adverse events were peripheral oedema (39%), nausea (35%), fatigue (34%) and headache (33%). Treatment-related serious haemolytic uraemic syndrome (7.5%) and capillary leak syndrome (5%) were reversible and generally manageable with supportive care and discontinuation (6 patients, 7.5%).
cards.watchOut: Heavily pretreated, purine-analogue-experienced patients only — these response rates say nothing about earlier lines, where cladribine's record (a different shelf) is far larger.
cards.source: Kreitman RJ, Dearden C, Zinzani PL et al. Moxetumomab pasudotox in relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukemia. Leukemia. 2018. PMID: 30030507. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kreitman 2021: long-term follow-up of the SAME pivotal trial — durable complete response 36%, median PFS without loss of haematologic remission 71.7 months, no treatment-related deaths
cards.summary: Kreitman 2021: long-term follow-up of the SAME pivotal trial — durable complete response 36%, median PFS without loss of haematologic remission 71.7 months, no treatment-related deaths
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of the pivotal trial (one programme), J Hematol Oncol 2021
cards.people: Long-term follow-up (median 24.6 months) of the same 80-patient pivotal trial (NCT01829711): patients had received a median of three prior lines, 49% were purine-analogue-refractory and 38% unfit for purine-analogue retreatment; 63% completed six cycles. Same programme as the card above — labelled, not an independent population.
cards.result: The durable complete-response rate (complete response with haematologic remission lasting over 180 days) was 36% (29 patients, 95% CI 26–48%); complete response with remission ≥360 days was 33% and overall complete response 41%. Twenty-seven complete responders (82%) were MRD-negative — 34% of all treated patients — and complete responses lasting ≥60 months occurred in 61% as reported; median progression-free survival without loss of haematologic remission was 71.7 months. Haemolytic uraemic and capillary leak syndromes were each reported in ≤10% (grade 3–4 in ≤5%), were generally reversible, and there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: The durable complete-response rate rose from 30% to 36% between reports as follow-up matured and definitions were applied to the full dataset — quote the later figure with its definition (remission >180 days), not the two interchangeably.
cards.source: Kreitman RJ, Dearden C, Zinzani PL et al. Moxetumomab pasudotox in heavily pre-treated patients with relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukemia (HCL): long-term follow-up from the pivotal trial. Journal of hematology & oncology. 2021. cards.headline: Kreitman 2012: phase 1 dose-escalation (n=28) — overall response 86% and complete remission 46% across dose levels, no dose-limiting toxicity; the programme's first human evidence
cards.summary: Kreitman 2012: phase 1 dose-escalation (n=28) — overall response 86% and complete remission 46% across dose levels, no dose-limiting toxicity; the programme's first human evidence
cards.type: Phase 1 dose-escalation trial, J Clin Oncol 2012
cards.people: Twenty-eight patients with relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukaemia after at least two prior therapies and abnormal blood counts, in a phase 1 dose-escalation trial of moxetumomab pasudotox (CAT-8015/HA22) at 5–50 µg/kg every other day for three doses per cycle, up to 16 cycles (median four); three to four patients at each dose below 50 µg/kg and 12 at 50 µg/kg.
cards.result: Dose-limiting toxicity was not observed. The overall response rate was 86% across all dose levels and 13 patients (46%) achieved complete remission; only one complete remission lasted less than 1 year, with median disease-free survival not reached at 26 months. Two patients had transient grade 2 haemolytic-uraemic-syndrome laboratory abnormalities (peak creatinine 1.53–1.66 mg/dL). Common drug-related toxicities (25–64%) were grade 1–2 hypoalbuminaemia, transaminase elevations, oedema, headache, hypotension, nausea and fatigue. Neutralising antibodies developed in 38% of the 26 immunogenicity-evaluable patients overall but in only 5% after cycle 1.
cards.watchOut: Dose-escalation samples cannot support a response-rate estimate (the 86% pools five dose levels in 28 patients); its durable contribution is the safety profile and the proof that remissions occur at tolerable doses.
cards.source: Kreitman RJ, Tallman MS, Robak T et al. Phase I trial of anti-CD22 recombinant immunotoxin moxetumomab pasudotox (CAT-8015 or HA22) in patients with hairy cell leukemia. Journal of clinical oncology. 2012. PMID: 22355053. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kreitman 2018 (Blood): phase 1 MRD extension — 33 patients at 50 µg/kg (overlapping the phase 1 card, one programme): complete remission 64%, and MRD-negative remissions last far longer (median 42.1 vs 13.5 months)
cards.summary: Kreitman 2018 (Blood): phase 1 MRD extension — 33 patients at 50 µg/kg (overlapping the phase 1 card, one programme): complete remission 64%, and MRD-negative remissions last far longer (median 42.1 vs 13.5 months)
cards.type: Phase 1 extension and MRD analysis (one programme), Blood 2018
cards.people: A 21-patient extension cohort at 50 µg/kg every other day for three doses in 4-week cycles, combined with the 12 previously reported patients at that dose level from the phase 1 trial above — a combined 33-patient cohort of the same programme (NCT00586924), with 32 patients evaluable for minimal residual disease by bone-marrow aspirate flow cytometry. Labelled as overlapping the previous card.
cards.result: The combined cohort achieved a 64% complete-remission rate and 88% overall response rate, with median complete-remission duration of 42.4 months and no dose-limiting toxicity across 143 cycles. Among evaluable complete responders, median remission duration was 42.1 months (range 24.0–69.2) in 11 MRD-negative patients versus 13.5 months (4.9–42.4) in 9 MRD-positive patients (p<0.001); 10 MRD-negative complete responders remained in ongoing remission at study end, 9 of them MRD-free. The authors note this was, to their knowledge, the only non-chemotherapy regimen shown to eliminate MRD in a substantial fraction of hairy-cell patients.
cards.watchOut: The MRD comparison is within-cohort and non-randomised — MRD-negative patients may have had more favourable disease to begin with; it establishes association with remission duration, not proof that chasing MRD negativity itself prolongs remission.
cards.source: Kreitman RJ, Tallman MS, Robak T et al. Minimal residual hairy cell leukemia eradication with moxetumomab pasudotox: phase 1 results and long-term follow-up. Blood. 2018. PMID: 29487070. Registry ID: NCT00586924. cards.headline: Synthesis: durable, often MRD-negative complete remissions in about a third of multiply relapsed patients — POSSIBLE on single-arm evidence, for a product the market withdrew
cards.summary: Synthesis: durable, often MRD-negative complete remissions in about a third of multiply relapsed patients — POSSIBLE on single-arm evidence, for a product the market withdrew
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: the pivotal programme (80 patients, primary and long-term reports — one programme) and the phase 1 programme (28 patients plus its 33-patient high-dose extension — one programme).
cards.result: Two independent single-arm programmes converge: moxetumomab pasudotox produces complete remissions in roughly 36–46% of heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory patients, most complete responders clear MRD, and MRD-negative remissions are long (median beyond 3.5 years in the phase 1 cohort; median progression-free survival without loss of remission 71.7 months in the pivotal follow-up). Capillary leak syndrome and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, each up to ~10% and generally reversible, are the defining harms. The stamp is POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence throughout — and the shelf records that the product was withdrawn from the US market in 2023 (commercial decision) and later the EU, so its present role is as evidence for the CD22-immunotoxin approach in a population with few options.
cards.watchOut: Availability, not efficacy, is now the binding constraint on this drug; any successor CD22 immunotoxin would need its own shelf rather than inheriting this one's numbers.

shelves.title: Nelarabine added to frontline therapy in newly diagnosed T-ALL: disease-free survival 88.2% vs 82.1% in the one large randomised trial, with neurotoxicity the defining harm
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and young adults with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does adding nelarabine to intensive multi-agent chemotherapy, versus the same chemotherapy without nelarabine, improve disease-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols / therapeutic use · Arabinonucleosides / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Asparaginase / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Child · Cohort Studies · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Leucovorin / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Male · Methotrexate / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Polyethylene Glycols / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Precursor T-Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma / drug therapy · Prednisone / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Child · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Adolescent · Adult · Female · Asparaginase / therapeutic use · Precursor Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma / drug therapy · Neoplasm, Residual · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols / adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Disease-Free Survival · Precursor B-Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma / drug therapy · Dexamethasone / adverse effects · Prednisolone / therapeutic use · T-Lymphocytes · Arabinonucleosides · Humans · Adult · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Precursor T-Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma / drug therapy, mortality · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols / adverse effects, therapeutic use, administration & dosage · Arabinonucleosides / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Neurotoxicity Syndromes / etiology · Treatment Outcome · Disease-Free Survival · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial carries the claim, supported by two non-randomised programme reports. In COG AALL0434 (1,562 evaluable patients; 323 randomised to nelarabine vs 336 to no nelarabine in the relevant comparison), 5-year disease-free survival was 88.2% with nelarabine vs 82.1% without (P = .029), and isolated/combined CNS relapse was much less frequent (1.3% vs 6.9%, P = .0001); there was no interaction with the methotrexate randomisation (P = .41), and the best arm was escalating-dose methotrexate plus nelarabine (5-year disease-free survival 91%, n = 147). The Japanese ALL-T11 programme (349 patients) gave nelarabine to high- and very-high-risk patients without randomising it and reported 3-year event-free survival of 86.4% overall. The adult JALSG T-ALL213-O study was small (24 analysed, only 14 actually received nelarabine) and found grade 3 peripheral neuropathy and/or gait disturbance in 7 of 14 treated patients (50%) — far above the 3% grade 3 peripheral motor neuropathy rate in ALL-T11 and the acceptable, arm-similar toxicity in AALL0434. Neurotoxicity (central and peripheral) is the defining harm and the reason for the boxed warning. The relapsed-disease nelarabine combination experience (NECTAR) is a different, relapsed slice and is cross-pointed here only, not carded.

cards.headline: AALL0434 2020: adding nelarabine improved 5-year disease-free survival, 88.2% vs 82.1%, and cut CNS relapse from 6.9% to 1.3% (1,562 evaluable patients)
cards.summary: AALL0434 2020: adding nelarabine improved 5-year disease-free survival, 88.2% vs 82.1%, and cut CNS relapse from 6.9% to 1.3% (1,562 evaluable patients)
cards.people: 1,562 evaluable patients aged 1-31 years with newly diagnosed T-ALL receiving augmented Berlin-Frankfurt-Muenster therapy; intermediate- and high-risk patients (and those with overt CNS disease) were randomised after induction to six 5-day courses of nelarabine or none (323 vs 336 in the disease-free-survival comparison), within a 2 x 2 pseudo-factorial design that also randomised methotrexate strategy.
cards.result: Five-year disease-free survival was 88.2% with nelarabine vs 82.1% without (P = .029); the four-arm comparison was significant (P = .01) with no interaction between the methotrexate and nelarabine randomisations (P = .41), and the best arm (escalating-dose methotrexate plus nelarabine, n = 147) reached 91%. Isolated and combined CNS relapses were 1.3% with nelarabine vs 6.9% without (P = .0001). Overall 5-year event-free survival for the whole cohort was 83.7% and overall survival 89.5%. Toxicities, including neurotoxicity, were acceptable and similar between arms.
cards.watchOut: The randomised nelarabine comparison covers 659 of the 1,562 patients (intermediate/high-risk and CNS-positive); low-risk patients and induction failures were not part of it, and the abstract does not report overall survival split by nelarabine arm.
cards.source: Children's Oncology Group AALL0434: A Phase III Randomized Clinical Trial Testing Nelarabine in Newly Diagnosed T-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. J Clin Oncol. 2020. PMID: 32813610. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00408005. cards.headline: ALL-T11 2023: a nelarabine-containing programme in 349 children and young adults reached 3-year event-free survival of 86.4%, but nelarabine itself was not randomised
cards.summary: ALL-T11 2023: a nelarabine-containing programme in 349 children and young adults reached 3-year event-free survival of 86.4%, but nelarabine itself was not randomised
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre trial (nelarabine given by risk group, not randomised)
cards.people: 349 eligible patients aged under 25 years with newly diagnosed T-ALL in a nationwide Japanese phase 2 trial; nelarabine (650 mg/m2/day for 5 days) was given to high-risk and very-high-risk patients as part of a BFM-type backbone with intensified L-asparaginase and protracted intrathecal therapy (the trial's randomisation compared block therapies in the very-high-risk group, not nelarabine).
cards.result: Three-year event-free survival was 86.4% (95% CI 82.3 to 89.7) and 3-year overall survival 91.3% for the whole cohort, with composite complete remission after induction in 89% and transplantation in only 10%. Grade 3 peripheral motor neuropathy occurred in 11 of 349 patients (3%) and sensory neuropathy in 6 (2%); febrile neutropenia affected 84%, and three patients died of treatment-related causes during induction.
cards.watchOut: Because nelarabine was assigned by risk stratum rather than randomised, this programme cannot separate nelarabine's contribution from the asparaginase intensification and intrathecal changes made at the same time.
cards.source: Nelarabine, intensive L-asparaginase, and protracted intrathecal therapy for newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children and young adults (ALL-T11). Lancet Haematol. 2023. PMID: 37167992. Registry ID: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials jRCTs041180145, as named in the record. cards.headline: T-ALL213-O 2025: in adults, nelarabine combinations looked active in a very small study, but half of treated patients had severe neuropathy
cards.summary: T-ALL213-O 2025: in adults, nelarabine combinations looked active in a very small study, but half of treated patients had severe neuropathy
cards.people: 24 analysed adults aged 25-64 years with newly diagnosed T-ALL in a Japanese phase 2 trial of nelarabine-combined chemotherapy; 10 patients never received nelarabine because therapy ended before the relevant consolidation, leaving 14 nelarabine-treated patients for the neurotoxicity reading.
cards.result: Three-year event-free survival was 70% (lower 90% confidence limit 52%, above the study's 25% threshold); 5-year event-free survival was 66% and overall survival 70%. Complete remission rates were 75% after first induction, 100% after the nelarabine-containing second induction, and 88% overall. Severe neuropathy after nelarabine was frequent: 7 of 14 treated patients (50%) had grade 3 peripheral neuropathy and/or gait disturbance, which the authors judged stronger than previously reported.
cards.watchOut: Only 24 patients, historical comparison for the survival claim, and just 14 patients behind the 50% severe-neuropathy figure — the harm signal is real but imprecise, and the dose/schedule differed from AALL0434.
cards.source: Nelarabine-combined chemotherapy improves outcome of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia but shows more severe neurotoxicity: JALSG T-ALL213-O. Cancer Sci. 2025. PMID: 39572007. Registry ID: UMIN000010642, as named in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: nelarabine added up front improves disease-free survival in young patients with T-ALL — POSSIBLE, resting on one large randomised trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: nelarabine added up front improves disease-free survival in young patients with T-ALL — POSSIBLE, resting on one large randomised trial
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 3 randomised trial (1,562 evaluable; 659 in the nelarabine comparison), one 349-patient phase 2 programme in which nelarabine was not randomised, and one 24-patient adult phase 2 study.
cards.result: The randomised evidence shows a 6.1-percentage-point absolute disease-free-survival gain and a large reduction in CNS relapse from adding nelarabine, without a demonstrated overall-survival split by arm in the record carded. Supporting programmes are consistent but cannot isolate the drug. The price is neurotoxicity: acceptable and arm-similar in the large trial, but severe in half of the small adult cohort — dose, schedule and patient selection matter.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is the frontline question only; nelarabine in relapsed/refractory T-ALL (including the NECTAR combination) is a separate slice and is not evidence for this question.
