shelves.title: Pelabresib plus ruxolitinib in JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis (MANIFEST-2): spleen response 65.9% vs 35.2%, but the symptom advantage was not significant
shelves.question: In adults with JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis, does adding the BET inhibitor pelabresib to ruxolitinib, versus ruxolitinib alone, improve spleen-volume response, symptoms and anaemia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Janus Kinase Inhibitors / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Primary Myelofibrosis / drug therapy, pathology · Spleen / pathology, drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Benzazepines · Isoxazoles · Nitriles · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Humans · Aged · Janus Kinase Inhibitors / adverse effects · Primary Myelofibrosis / drug therapy · Protein Kinase Inhibitors / adverse effects · Nitriles / therapeutic use · Hemoglobins / therapeutic use · Janus Kinase 2 / genetics · Treatment Outcome · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Humans · Myelodysplastic Syndromes / diagnosis, drug therapy, genetics · Myeloproliferative Disorders / drug therapy · Leukemia, Myelomonocytic, Chronic / drug therapy · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute / diagnosis, drug therapy, genetics · Antineoplastic Agents / therapeutic use · Tablets / therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 randomised trial (MANIFEST-2, 430 patients) anchors the shelf, which caps the stamp, supported by the earlier single-arm MANIFEST programme. The spleen claim is strong: spleen-volume reduction of at least 35% at week 24 in 65.9% on pelabresib plus ruxolitinib vs 35.2% on ruxolitinib alone (absolute difference 30.4 percentage points). The symptom claim is weaker and must stay subordinate: absolute total-symptom-score change differed by -1.94 points (P = 0.0545, not significant) and the symptom-response rates were 52.3% vs 46.3% (confidence interval crossing zero) — on symptoms, the combination made no proven difference. The anaemia claim is secondary and mixed: anaemia as an adverse event was actually less frequent on the combination (44.8% vs 55.1%), and the phase 2 programme reported haemoglobin improvement in 36%, but no randomised anaemia endpoint is carded. Added harms of the combination are thrombocytopenia (52.8% vs 37.4%; grade 3 or worse 13.2% vs 6.1%) and gastrointestinal effects from the wider programme. Nearby homes ask different questions: ruxolitinib alone, momelotinib, pacritinib and fedratinib each have their own shelves.

cards.headline: MANIFEST-2 2025: pelabresib plus ruxolitinib doubled the spleen response, 65.9% vs 35.2% at week 24, in 430 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients
cards.summary: MANIFEST-2 2025: pelabresib plus ruxolitinib doubled the spleen response, 65.9% vs 35.2% at week 24, in 430 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients
cards.people: 430 adults with JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis randomised 1:1 to pelabresib 125 mg once daily (14 days on, 7 off) plus ruxolitinib (214 patients) or placebo plus ruxolitinib (216 patients); primary endpoint was spleen-volume reduction of at least 35% at week 24.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 65.9% on the combination vs 35.2% on ruxolitinib alone (difference 30.4 percentage points, 95% CI 21.6 to 39.3; P < 0.001). Symptoms did not separate significantly: absolute total-symptom-score change was -15.99 vs -14.05 (difference -1.94, 95% CI -3.92 to 0.04; P = 0.0545) and symptom response (at least 50% reduction) was 52.3% vs 46.3% (difference 6.0 points, 95% CI -3.5 to 15.5). Thrombocytopenia occurred in 52.8% (grade 3 or worse 13.2%) vs 37.4% (6.1%), and anaemia in 44.8% (23.1%) vs 55.1% (36.5%).
cards.watchOut: The proven benefit is spleen volume (with exploratory cytokine and marrow findings); the key symptom endpoints did not reach significance, so this trial does not show patients feel better on the combination than on ruxolitinib alone.
cards.source: Pelabresib plus ruxolitinib for JAK inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis: a randomized phase 3 trial. Nat Med. 2025. PMID: 40065169. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04603495. cards.headline: MANIFEST phase 2 2023: the single-arm combination cohort found a 68% spleen response at week 24 in 84 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients
cards.summary: MANIFEST phase 2 2023: the single-arm combination cohort found a 68% spleen response at week 24 in 84 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients
cards.people: 84 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients with myelofibrosis (median age 68; 66% with haemoglobin under 10 g/dL at baseline) treated open-label with pelabresib plus ruxolitinib in the MANIFEST phase 2 programme; no control arm.
cards.result: At week 24, 68% (57 of 84) achieved at least 35% spleen-volume reduction and 56% (46 of 82) achieved at least a 50% symptom-score reduction; 36% had improved haemoglobin (mean rise 1.3 g/dL), 28% of evaluable patients had at least one grade of fibrosis improvement, and responses persisted at week 48 (60% spleen response). Grade 3 or 4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 12% and anaemia in 35%; three patients discontinued for toxicity, and 95% continued the combination beyond 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 68% spleen response cannot be compared directly with MANIFEST-2's randomised 65.9% vs 35.2%, and the haemoglobin/fibrosis findings are uncontrolled observations within the same development programme.

cards.headline: MANIFEST phase 1 2024: pelabresib alone in 44 patients with acute leukaemia or high-risk MDS set the dose and the gastrointestinal tolerability profile
cards.summary: MANIFEST phase 1 2024: pelabresib alone in 44 patients with acute leukaemia or high-risk MDS set the dose and the gastrointestinal tolerability profile
cards.type: Phase 1 dose-finding study (pelabresib monotherapy, other myeloid diseases)
cards.people: 44 patients with acute leukaemia, high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome or MDS/myeloproliferative neoplasms (not myelofibrosis, and not the combination) receiving pelabresib monotherapy at doses from 24 to 400 mg in the MANIFEST phase 1 study.
cards.result: The maximum tolerated dose was 225 mg (tablet) once daily on a 14-days-on, 7-days-off cycle; the most frequent drug-related adverse events were nausea, decreased appetite and fatigue. One patient with chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia had a partial remission; stable disease occurred in 25.8% of acute myeloid leukaemia patients and 38.5% of high-risk MDS patients. The recommended phase 2 dose carried into the myelofibrosis programme was 125 mg once daily.
cards.watchOut: This card is dose and safety background only: a different population and monotherapy, so it contributes nothing to the estimate of the combination's benefit in myelofibrosis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: adding pelabresib to ruxolitinib clearly shrinks spleens, with symptoms unproven — POSSIBLE, one randomised trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: adding pelabresib to ruxolitinib clearly shrinks spleens, with symptoms unproven — POSSIBLE, one randomised trial
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 3 randomised trial (430 patients), one single-arm phase 2 combination cohort (84 patients) and one phase 1 monotherapy study (44 patients, other diseases).
cards.result: The randomised spleen benefit is large (65.9% vs 35.2%, an absolute gain of about 31 percentage points), but the symptom endpoints in the same trial made no significant difference, and anaemia claims rest on secondary and uncontrolled data. One randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The combination's added price is more thrombocytopenia; anaemia adverse events were, unusually, less frequent than with ruxolitinib alone.
cards.watchOut: No card here shows a survival, fibrosis-reversal or leukaemia-transformation benefit; marrow and cytokine findings are exploratory and should not be presented as disease modification proven in patients.

shelves.title: Mogamulizumab in previously treated cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (MAVORIC): progression-free survival 7.7 vs 3.1 months, with responses concentrated in blood and Sezary disease
shelves.question: In patients with previously treated mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome, does the anti-CCR4 antibody mogamulizumab, versus vorinostat, improve progression-free survival and produce responses, particularly in blood-involved disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Australia · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Europe · Female · Histone Deacetylase Inhibitors / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Humans · Japan · Lymphoma, T-Cell, Cutaneous / drug therapy, mortality, pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Mycosis Fungoides / drug therapy, mortality, pathology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasm Staging · Progression-Free Survival · Sezary Syndrome / drug therapy, mortality, pathology · Time Factors · United States · Vorinostat / administration & dosage, adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized / adverse effects · Humans · Lymphoma, T-Cell, Cutaneous / pathology · Mycosis Fungoides / diagnosis, drug therapy · Sezary Syndrome / drug therapy, pathology · Skin Neoplasms / drug therapy, pathology · Vorinostat · Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized / therapeutic use, pharmacology · Lymphoma, T-Cell, Cutaneous / drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Skin Neoplasms / drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 randomised trial (MAVORIC, 372 patients) anchors the shelf, with a post hoc analysis, a small French real-world cohort and a 2026 systematic review as support. MAVORIC found median progression-free survival of 7.7 months on mogamulizumab vs 3.1 months on vorinostat (hazard ratio 0.53, a relative measure; the absolute medians are printed on the card). The compartment split is the shelf's clinical point: in the pooled systematic review, response rates were 52.5% in Sezary syndrome vs 31.1% in mycosis fungoides, and 82.6% in the blood compartment vs 43.7% in skin. Benefit did not depend on how many or which prior therapies patients had received (post hoc MAVORIC analysis). Two harms are mandatory on the face: mogamulizumab-associated rash, which can mimic progression and lead to wrong treatment decisions, and the warning that giving mogamulizumab before allogeneic transplantation increases the risk of severe graft-versus-host disease. Grade 3-4 adverse events in MAVORIC were 41% in both arms; in the French cohort (21 patients), 10 of 21 had grade III-IV events.

cards.headline: MAVORIC 2018: mogamulizumab prolonged progression-free survival vs vorinostat, median 7.7 vs 3.1 months, in 372 previously treated patients
cards.summary: MAVORIC 2018: mogamulizumab prolonged progression-free survival vs vorinostat, median 7.7 vs 3.1 months, in 372 previously treated patients
cards.people: 372 adults with relapsed or refractory mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome who had failed at least one previous systemic therapy, randomised 1:1 at 61 centres to mogamulizumab 1.0 mg/kg intravenously (186 patients) or vorinostat 400 mg daily (186 patients); open-label, stratified by subtype and stage.
cards.result: Investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 7.7 months (95% CI 5.7 to 10.3) with mogamulizumab vs 3.1 months (2.9 to 4.1) with vorinostat (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.69; P < 0.0001). Grade 3-4 adverse events occurred in 41% of patients in both groups. The commonest serious adverse events with mogamulizumab were pyrexia (4%) and cellulitis (3%); two of three on-treatment deaths with mogamulizumab (sepsis, polymyositis) were considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with investigator-assessed progression, and vorinostat is a modest comparator; the record carded does not report the overall response rate, which is carried instead by the systematic-review card below.

cards.headline: MAVORIC prior-therapy analysis 2021: mogamulizumab's benefit did not vary with the number or type of prior systemic therapies
cards.summary: MAVORIC prior-therapy analysis 2021: mogamulizumab's benefit did not vary with the number or type of prior systemic therapies
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial
cards.people: Patients from the MAVORIC trial (mogamulizumab vs vorinostat), grouped post hoc by the number of prior systemic therapies, the immunomodulatory activity of the immediately preceding therapy, and the time elapsed since it.
cards.result: Overall response rate, progression-free survival and duration of response did not vary with the number of prior therapies; response and duration of response were consistent regardless of the type of immediately prior therapy, and neither its immunomodulatory activity nor the interval since treatment generally affected response or progression-free survival on mogamulizumab.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and reported without subgroup numbers in the record's abstract: 'did not vary' in underpowered subgroups is absence of a detected interaction, not proof that prior therapy never matters.
cards.source: Lack of impact of type and extent of prior therapy on outcomes of mogamulizumab therapy in patients with cutaneous T cell lymphoma in the MAVORIC trial. Leuk Lymphoma. 2021. PMID: 34304674. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01728805 (the parent MAVORIC trial, as named in the record). cards.headline: French real-world cohort 2022: estimated progression-free survival of 22 months in 21 advanced patients, with grade III-IV events in 10
cards.summary: French real-world cohort 2022: estimated progression-free survival of 22 months in 21 advanced patients, with grade III-IV events in 10
cards.people: 21 patients with advanced mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome treated with mogamulizumab in six French university hospitals after national authorisation (three further patients excluded as already in MAVORIC); median follow-up 11.6 months. Observational, retrospective.
cards.result: Four patients had a complete response, eight a partial response, one stable disease, three progression, and five had died; estimated progression-free survival was 22 months. Twenty of 21 patients had adverse events, 10 of them grade III-IV, with a median of 21 days from starting mogamulizumab to the first event.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one patients, no comparator, and an estimated 22-month progression-free survival that sits far above MAVORIC's randomised 7.7 months — selection and follow-up differences, not a better drug effect, are the likely explanation.

cards.headline: Systematic review 2026: pooled response 41.2% overall, but 82.6% in blood vs 43.7% in skin and 52.5% in Sezary syndrome vs 31.1% in mycosis fungoides
cards.summary: Systematic review 2026: pooled response 41.2% overall, but 82.6% in blood vs 43.7% in skin and 52.5% in Sezary syndrome vs 31.1% in mycosis fungoides
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (7 studies, 453 patients)
cards.people: Seven studies comprising 453 patients with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma treated with mogamulizumab monotherapy (trials and cohorts), in a prospectively registered systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: Pooled overall response rate was 41.2% (95% CI 30.2 to 53.2), with a significant subgroup difference between Sezary syndrome (52.5%) and mycosis fungoides (31.1%). The pooled blood-compartment response rate was 82.6%, superior to the skin-compartment rate of 43.7%. Pooled incidence of serious adverse events was 18.8%. Heterogeneity was high for the response estimates (I-squared up to about 81%).
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies overlap with MAVORIC and the real-world cohorts carded above, so this is a summary of the same evidence, not independent confirmation; heterogeneity is high.
cards.source: Efficacy and Safety of Mogamulizumab for Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clin Lymphoma Myeloma Leuk. 2026. PMID: 42236443. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD420251171992, as named in the record. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E): every card is an uncontrolled phase 2 report from one development programme, so response rates have no comparator and the stamp is capped. In chronic phase, major cytogenetic response occurred in 23% of 62 T315I patients (complete haematologic response 77%) and in 22% of 46 patients resistant/intolerant to at least two TKIs; the programme's final pooled analysis put chronic-phase major cytogenetic response at 18% with a median duration of 12.5 months and median overall survival of 40.3 months. Accelerated-phase results are weaker: major haematologic response 37% in one report but only 14% achieved or maintained in the pooled final analysis, with no major cytogenetic response and median survival of 14.3 months. Myelosuppression is the dominant harm — grade 3 or worse haematologic toxicity in 79% (chronic phase) and 73% (accelerated phase) in the pooled analysis, with grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia in 54-76% across reports; about 10% of chronic-phase patients stopped for toxicity. Product naming (clarification): omacetaxine mepesuccinate is marketed as Synribo; the carded records do not name a company. The higher-risk MDS phase 2 experience is a different disease and is cross-pointed only.

cards.headline: T315I chronic-phase phase 2 2012: complete haematologic response in 77% and major cytogenetic response in 23% of 62 patients, with no control arm
cards.summary: T315I chronic-phase phase 2 2012: complete haematologic response in 77% and major cytogenetic response in 23% of 62 patients, with no control arm
cards.people: 62 patients with chronic-phase CML carrying the BCR-ABL T315I mutation after tyrosine kinase inhibitor failure, treated with subcutaneous omacetaxine 1.25 mg/m2 twice daily (14 days per 28-day cycle until haematologic response, then 7 days as maintenance); median 7 cycles received. Single-arm.
cards.result: Complete haematologic response was achieved in 48 patients (77%) with a median duration of 9.1 months; 14 patients (23%) achieved a major cytogenetic response, including complete cytogenetic response in 10 (16%). Median progression-free survival was 7.7 months. Grade 3/4 haematologic toxicity included thrombocytopenia (76%), neutropenia (44%) and anaemia (39%); non-haematologic events were mostly grade 1/2 (infection 42%, diarrhoea 40%, nausea 34%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm in a selected T315I population: a 77% haematologic response rate in chronic-phase CML partly reflects the disease phase, and only the 23% cytogenetic figure speaks to deeper benefit.
cards.source: Phase 2 study of subcutaneous omacetaxine mepesuccinate after TKI failure in patients with chronic-phase CML with T315I mutation. Blood. 2012. PMID: 22896000. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00375219. cards.headline: Chronic-phase phase 2 2013: haematologic response in 67% and major cytogenetic response in 22% of 46 patients resistant or intolerant to at least two TKIs
cards.summary: Chronic-phase phase 2 2013: haematologic response in 67% and major cytogenetic response in 22% of 46 patients resistant or intolerant to at least two TKIs
cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm trial (chronic phase, multi-TKI failure)
cards.people: 46 patients with chronic-phase CML resistant or intolerant to two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors (all had received imatinib, 83% dasatinib, 57% nilotinib), treated with subcutaneous omacetaxine on the same induction/maintenance schedule; median 4.5 cycles. Single-arm, multicentre.
cards.result: Haematologic response was achieved or maintained in 31 patients (67%), median duration 7.0 months; 10 patients (22%) achieved a major cytogenetic response, including 2 (4%) complete cytogenetic responses. Median progression-free survival was 7.0 months and overall survival 30.1 months. Grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 54%, neutropenia in 48% and anaemia in 33%; non-haematologic events were predominantly grade 1/2.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, and this trial is part of the same phase 2 programme pooled in the final-analysis card below — the reports overlap and must not be counted as independent trials.
cards.source: Phase 2 study of subcutaneous omacetaxine mepesuccinate for chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia patients resistant to or intolerant of tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Am J Hematol. 2013. cards.headline: Advanced-CML phase 2 report 2015: major haematologic response in 37% of accelerated-phase and 9% of blast-phase patients
cards.summary: Advanced-CML phase 2 report 2015: major haematologic response in 37% of accelerated-phase and 9% of blast-phase patients
cards.type: Phase 2 report of two single-arm trials (accelerated and blast phase)
cards.people: 51 patients in accelerated phase and 44 in myeloid blast phase with CML previously treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, from the two phase 2 trials CML-202 and CML-203, treated with subcutaneous omacetaxine until response, then maintenance until progression. Single-arm.
cards.result: Major haematologic response was 37% in accelerated phase and 9% in blast phase (22% and 5% respectively in patients with a history of T315I). Cytogenetic responses were also evaluated. Most grade 3/4 adverse events were related to myelosuppression and were generally manageable.
cards.watchOut: The blast-phase slice sits at the edge of this shelf's chronic/accelerated-phase question and is carded only because the publication reports both phases together; its 9% response rate should not be read as part of the accelerated-phase estimate.

cards.headline: Final pooled analysis 2015: chronic-phase major cytogenetic response 18% lasting a median 12.5 months; accelerated phase weaker, with grade 3+ blood toxicity in about three quarters
cards.summary: Final pooled analysis 2015: chronic-phase major cytogenetic response 18% lasting a median 12.5 months; accelerated phase weaker, with grade 3+ blood toxicity in about three quarters
cards.type: Pooled final analysis of the programme's two phase 2 trials (single-arm)
cards.people: Patients with chronic-phase or accelerated-phase CML resistant and/or intolerant to two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors in the programme's two phase 2 trials, in a final pooled analysis with 24 months of follow-up, focusing on patients receiving more than 3 cycles (50 chronic-phase, 14 accelerated-phase for the long-term survival figures). Single-arm programme.
cards.result: In chronic phase, 18% achieved a major cytogenetic response (median duration 12.5 months), responses lasted at least 12 months in 3 of 14 responders, and median overall survival was 40.3 months. In accelerated phase, 14% achieved or maintained a major haematologic response (median 4.7 months), no major cytogenetic response was achieved, and median overall survival was 14.3 months. Grade 3 or higher haematologic toxicities occurred in 79% (chronic) and 73% (accelerated); discontinuation for toxicity was 10% and 5% respectively.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-analysis of the same programme carded above — it adds follow-up and the most conservative response figures, not independent confirmation; survival figures have no comparator and reflect phase and prior therapy as much as drug.

cards.headline: Synthesis: omacetaxine produces real but modest responses in multi-TKI-failure CML — POSSIBLE, single-arm throughout, labelled as such
cards.summary: Synthesis: omacetaxine produces real but modest responses in multi-TKI-failure CML — POSSIBLE, single-arm throughout, labelled as such
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: four single-arm phase 2 reports from one programme (62 T315I chronic-phase, 46 chronic-phase, 51 accelerated-phase and 44 blast-phase patients, plus the pooled final analysis of the same trials).
cards.result: About one in five chronic-phase patients reaches a major cytogenetic response that can last about a year, including patients with T315I whom TKIs cannot treat; accelerated-phase benefit is smaller and shorter. There is no randomised or controlled evidence at all, so POSSIBLE is the ceiling. The treatment burden is myelosuppression: grade 3/4 cytopenias in most patients, managed by dose adjustment.
cards.watchOut: Response rates from uncontrolled salvage trials cannot be compared numerically with TKI response rates from other shelves; the populations and phases differ.

shelves.question: In adults with chronic- or accelerated-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia resistant to prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including BCR::ABL1 T315I-mutated disease, does olverembatinib, versus no concurrent control, produce cytogenetic and molecular responses?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E), generated almost entirely in China, where olverembatinib was first approved (2021); no randomised trial exists in the carded record. The phase 1/2 programme (165 patients, over 80% after at least two TKIs) reported 3-year cumulative major cytogenetic response of 79.0% in chronic phase (complete cytogenetic response 69.0%, major molecular response 56.0%) and 47.4% in accelerated phase, with the highest rates in single-T315I disease. A retrospective dose comparison (216 patients starting at 40 mg every other day vs 66 at 30 mg) found no significant difference in responses or outcomes between doses — on efficacy the lower dose made no difference — but significantly fewer dose reductions or discontinuations for adverse events (21% vs 41%). A 130-patient accelerated-phase cohort reported 6-year cumulative major cytogenetic response of 59% and survival of 71%. Common treatment-related events in the programme were skin hyperpigmentation, hypertriglyceridaemia, proteinuria and severe thrombocytopenia. Arterial occlusive events are a class concern with third-generation BCR::ABL1 inhibitors, but no rates from this drug's carded records are printed here and ponatinib's rates must not be imported into this shelf.

cards.headline: Phase 1/2 programme 2022: 3-year cumulative major cytogenetic response 79.0% in chronic phase and 47.4% in accelerated phase among 165 TKI-resistant patients
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 programme 2022: 3-year cumulative major cytogenetic response 79.0% in chronic phase and 47.4% in accelerated phase among 165 TKI-resistant patients
cards.type: Phase 1/2 single-arm programme (chronic and accelerated phase)
cards.people: 165 Chinese adults with TKI-resistant CML (127 chronic phase, 38 accelerated phase; over 80% had received at least two prior TKIs) in an open-label multicentre phase 1/2 programme of olverembatinib every other day; the phase 2 dose was 40 mg every other day. Single-arm; the population was selected for T315I-mutated disease in the phase 2 studies.
cards.result: Among chronic-phase patients, 3-year cumulative incidences were: major cytogenetic response 79.0%, complete cytogenetic response 69.0%, major molecular response 56.0%, MR4.0 44.0% and MR4.5 39.0%; the highest response rates were in patients with a single T315I mutation. Among accelerated-phase patients the corresponding figures were 47.4%, 47.4%, 44.7%, 39.3% and 32.1%. Common treatment-related adverse events included skin hyperpigmentation, hypertriglyceridaemia, proteinuria and severe thrombocytopenia.
cards.watchOut: Cumulative-incidence response figures from a single-arm, T315I-enriched programme are not comparable with response rates from unselected or randomised cohorts, and there is no control arm against which to judge survival.
cards.source: Olverembatinib (HQP1351), a well-tolerated and effective tyrosine kinase inhibitor for patients with T315I-mutated chronic myeloid leukemia: results of an open-label, multicenter phase 1/2 trial. J Hematol Oncol. 2022. PMID: 35982483. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03883087 and NCT03883100 (phase 2 studies, as named in the record). cards.headline: Dose comparison 2025: starting at 30 mg every other day matched 40 mg on responses, with far fewer dose reductions or stops for adverse events (21% vs 41%)
cards.summary: Dose comparison 2025: starting at 30 mg every other day matched 40 mg on responses, with far fewer dose reductions or stops for adverse events (21% vs 41%)
cards.people: 282 patients with chronic-phase CML in whom other TKIs had failed, in a multicentre retrospective study comparing the recommended starting dose of olverembatinib 40 mg every other day (216 patients) with a reduced starting dose of 30 mg (66 patients), with propensity-score matching. Observational.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in cytogenetic and molecular responses, or in outcomes, between the two dose cohorts — on efficacy the doses made no difference. The proportion still receiving the original dose at last follow-up was higher in the 30 mg cohort (64% vs 44%, P = 0.004), and the proportion who had a dose reduction or permanently discontinued because of adverse events was lower (21% vs 41%, P = 0.003).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: doctors chose who started at 30 mg, so residual confounding could hide a real efficacy difference in either direction despite propensity matching.
cards.source: Optimizing olverembatinib dose in chronic phase chronic myeloid leukemia. Haematologica. 2025. PMID: 40304058. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Accelerated-phase cohort 2026: 6-year cumulative major cytogenetic response 59% and survival 71% in 130 consecutive patients
cards.summary: Accelerated-phase cohort 2026: 6-year cumulative major cytogenetic response 59% and survival 71% in 130 consecutive patients
cards.people: 130 consecutive patients who presented in, or transformed to, accelerated-phase CML and received olverembatinib after failing at least one TKI; 91 carried BCR::ABL1 T315I and 62 were in second chronic phase; median follow-up 28 months. Cohort study, no comparator.
cards.result: Six-year cumulative incidences were: major cytogenetic response 59% (95% CI 49 to 69), complete cytogenetic response 53%, major molecular response 52% and MR4.0 42%. Six-year transformation-free survival was 81%, CML-related survival 76% and overall survival 71%. Treatment-related adverse events were described as acceptable; worse outcomes tracked with longer diagnosis-to-treatment interval, prior failure to reach complete haematologic response, anaemia, higher blast percentages and high-risk additional chromosomal abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-style consecutive cohort with no comparator and a median follow-up (28 months) far shorter than the 6-year horizon of its cumulative estimates — the tail of those curves rests on few patients.
cards.source: Olverembatinib in accelerated-phase chronic myeloid leukemia: efficacy and safety evaluation. Haematologica. 2026. PMID: 41098110. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: olverembatinib produces deep responses in TKI-resistant and T315I CML — POSSIBLE, single-arm and single-country evidence, labelled as such
cards.summary: Synthesis: olverembatinib produces deep responses in TKI-resistant and T315I CML — POSSIBLE, single-arm and single-country evidence, labelled as such
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 1/2 single-arm programme (165 patients), one retrospective dose comparison (282 patients) and one accelerated-phase cohort (130 patients), all in China.
cards.result: Response depth (complete cytogenetic and major molecular responses in roughly half or more of chronic-phase patients) is well beyond what earlier salvage options achieved in similar uncontrolled settings, and 30 mg every other day appears as effective as 40 mg with better tolerability. But with no randomised trial and no non-Chinese cohort carded, POSSIBLE is the ceiling, and cross-trial numerical comparisons with other third-generation inhibitors are not licensed by this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Regulatory status outside China is not established by the carded records; the shelf's claims are bounded to the Chinese trial and cohort populations in which the drug was studied.

shelves.title: Hetrombopag in immune thrombocytopenia: platelet response 58.9-64.3% vs 5.9% on placebo in adults and 61.4% vs 9.7% in children — China-generated evidence, not FDA/EMA-approved
shelves.question: In adults, and in children and adolescents, with persistent or chronic primary immune thrombocytopenia, does the thrombopoietin-receptor agonist hetrombopag, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses and reduce bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydrazones / adverse effects, therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy · Pyrazolones / adverse effects, therapeutic use · Receptors, Thrombopoietin / agonists · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Adolescent · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Benzoates / therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Hydrazines / therapeutic use · Platelet Count · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy, blood · Pyrazolones / therapeutic use · Receptors, Thrombopoietin / agonists · Treatment Outcome · Hydrazones · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Drug Tapering · Humans · Hydrazones · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / diagnosis, drug therapy · Pyrazolones / therapeutic use · Thrombocytopenia / chemically induced, diagnosis, drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Male · Female · Retrospective Studies · Middle Aged · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy · Adult · Receptors, Thrombopoietin / agonists · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Platelet Count · Young Adult · Hydrazines / therapeutic use, adverse effects, administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (adults; children and adolescents) from one Chinese development programme agree on a large platelet-response benefit, which is strong, but a single programme in a single country caps the stamp; the drug is approved in China and is not FDA/EMA-approved, and that is stated plainly. Adults: response at week 8 in 58.9% (2.5 mg) and 64.3% (5 mg) vs 5.9% on placebo (odds ratios 25.97 and 32.81 — relative measures; the absolute rates are printed on the card). Children aged 6-17: response at week 10 in 61.4% vs 9.7% (absolute difference 52.7 percentage points), with sustained response 43.9% vs 0%. The extension study supplies the durability warning: when hetrombopag was tapered to withdrawal, 88.1% relapsed, at a median of just 15 days — this is a maintenance treatment, not a cure. Harms are mainly infections (upper respiratory tract infection in 42-58% across reports) and liver-enzyme elevations (treatment-related hepatotoxicity events in 17.5% over 24 weeks in the paediatric trial, all grade 1-2). The chemotherapy-induced-thrombocytopenia reports are a different question — cross-point only.

cards.headline: Adult phase 3 2021: platelet response at week 8 in 58.9% (2.5 mg) and 64.3% (5 mg) on hetrombopag vs 5.9% on placebo
cards.summary: Adult phase 3 2021: platelet response at week 8 in 58.9% (2.5 mg) and 64.3% (5 mg) on hetrombopag vs 5.9% on placebo
cards.people: Adults with ITP who had not responded to, or had relapsed after, previous treatment, randomised double-blind to hetrombopag 2.5 mg, hetrombopag 5 mg or placebo for 10 weeks, followed by a 14-week open-label period (the record's abstract does not state the total randomised N — printed as such). Response meant a platelet count of at least 50 x 10^9/L.
cards.result: The primary endpoint at week 8 was achieved by 58.9% on hetrombopag 2.5 mg (odds ratio 25.97, 95% CI 9.83 to 68.63 — a relative measure) and 64.3% on 5 mg (odds ratio 32.81) vs 5.9% on placebo (P < 0.0001 for both). Hetrombopag also reduced bleeding risk and rescue-therapy use across the 8 weeks, and the durable response was maintained through 24 weeks. With 24-week treatment the commonest adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (42.2%), urinary tract infection (17.1%), immune thrombocytopenic purpura (17.1%) and haematuria (15%).
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled window is only 10 weeks and the trial was retrospectively registered; the abstract does not state the total N, so the shelf does not invent one.
cards.source: A multicenter, randomized phase III trial of hetrombopag: a novel thrombopoietin receptor agonist for the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia. J Hematol Oncol. 2021. PMID: 33632264. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03222843. cards.headline: Paediatric phase 3 2026: response at week 10 in 61.4% on hetrombopag vs 9.7% on placebo in 88 children and adolescents, sustained response 43.9% vs 0%
cards.summary: Paediatric phase 3 2026: response at week 10 in 61.4% on hetrombopag vs 9.7% on placebo in 88 children and adolescents, sustained response 43.9% vs 0%
cards.people: 88 children and adolescents aged 6-17 years with ITP and an inadequate response or relapse after prior treatment, randomised 2:1 to once-daily hetrombopag (starting dose 2.5 mg; 57 patients) or placebo (31 patients) for 12 weeks, then a 12-week open-label extension.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (platelet count at least 50 x 10^9/L at week 10) was met by 61.4% vs 9.7% (absolute difference 52.7 percentage points, 95% CI 35.9 to 69.5; P < 0.0001); sustained response was 43.9% vs 0%. Rescue therapy was needed by 21.1% vs 45.2%. Upper respiratory tract infection was the commonest adverse event (57.9% vs 45.2%); alanine aminotransferase elevations occurred in 7.0% on hetrombopag vs 0%, and over 24 weeks treatment-related hepatotoxicity events occurred in 17.5% (10 of 57), all grade 1-2 and none causing discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (China) trial of 88 patients with a 12-week blinded window; the liver-enzyme signal (17.5% over 24 weeks) needs the monitoring it implies, even though every event was grade 1-2.
cards.source: Efficacy and safety of hetrombopag, a novel thrombopoietin receptor agonist, in children and adolescents with immune thrombocytopenia: results from a randomized, multicenter, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. J Hematol Oncol. 2026. PMID: 41952212. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04737850. cards.headline: Extension study 2022: tapering hetrombopag to withdrawal relapsed 88.1% of patients at a median of 15 days — benefit requires continued treatment
cards.summary: Extension study 2022: tapering hetrombopag to withdrawal relapsed 88.1% of patients at a median of 15 days — benefit requires continued treatment
cards.type: Open-label extension of the adult phase 3 trial (same programme)
cards.people: Patients from the adult phase 3 trial (same programme, NCT03222843) entering a dose-tapering-to-withdrawal stage (194 patients) or a further 24-week long-term extension (339 patients in the hetrombopag group). Open-label.
cards.result: Among 194 patients who tapered to withdrawal, 171 (88.1%) relapsed, at a median of 15.0 days from the start of tapering. In the long-term extension, 42.5% of patients responded at at least 75% of their assessments and 74.9% reached a platelet count of at least 30 x 10^9/L (and at least twice baseline) at least once. Commonest adverse events over the whole programme were upper respiratory tract infection (53.1%), thrombocytopenia (27.1%) and urinary tract infection (21.2%).
cards.watchOut: An extension of the adult trial carded above, not an independent study: its unique contribution is the withdrawal lesson — counts fall within about two weeks of stopping in nearly nine of ten patients.
cards.source: Dose tapering to withdrawal stage and long-term efficacy and safety of hetrombopag for the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia: Results from an open-label extension study. J Thromb Haemost. 2022. PMID: 34821020. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03222843. cards.headline: Real-world cohort 2025: response in 71% at week 12 among 50 patients, with no serious adverse events — observational
cards.summary: Real-world cohort 2025: response in 71% at week 12 among 50 patients, with no serious adverse events — observational
cards.people: 50 patients with ITP treated with hetrombopag monotherapy (starting dose 2.5 mg or 5.0 mg daily) in routine practice, in a retrospective cohort study. Observational, no comparator.
cards.result: The response rate (platelet count at least 50 x 10^9/L) was 71% at week 12, with a median time to response of 7 days and mean platelet count rising from 16 x 10^9/L at baseline to 104 x 10^9/L at week 12. The 5 mg group responded better as early as week 2; 6 of 11 patients switched from 2.5 mg to 5 mg then responded, and 7 of 8 patients switching from eltrombopag responded. No serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, uncontrolled and small: the 71% figure includes dose-switching and prior-TPO-RA switchers, so it describes a clinic's experience, not a treatment effect.
cards.source: Real-world experience of hetrombopag in immune thrombocytopenia treatment: a retrospective cohort study. Eur J Med Res. 2025. PMID: 40615922. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: hetrombopag raises platelets in adults and children with ITP — POSSIBLE, one Chinese programme, and stopping it usually ends the response
cards.summary: Synthesis: hetrombopag raises platelets in adults and children with ITP — POSSIBLE, one Chinese programme, and stopping it usually ends the response
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (adults; 88 children/adolescents), the adult trial's extension, and a 50-patient retrospective cohort — all from China.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted response gains of roughly 53 percentage points in both age groups are large and concordant, with less rescue therapy and bleeding risk. One development programme in one country caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the drug is not FDA/EMA-approved. The withdrawal data are part of the answer: 88.1% relapse a median 15 days after tapering off, so hetrombopag controls ITP while taken rather than curing it.
cards.watchOut: Platelet response is the proven endpoint; the carded trials were not powered to show reductions in major bleeding or mortality, and none should be implied.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 33632264, 41952212, 34821020, 40615922). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Dapsone in primary ITP: SPLIT — older series and a pooled analysis suggest about half respond, but the one randomised trial found no significant benefit and most patients stopped the drug
shelves.question: In adults with primary immune thrombocytopenia needing a low-cost second-line option, does dapsone, versus no concurrent control or standard care, produce platelet responses, and at what haemolytic cost?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dapsone / therapeutic use, adverse effects, administration & dosage · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Adult · Humans · Dapsone / therapeutic use, adverse effects · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Male · Female · Humans · Child · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy · Platelet Count · Dapsone / therapeutic use · Retrospective Studies · Thrombocytopenia / drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is between designs. On one side, the observational record: a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (4 studies, over 270 patients) pooled an overall response rate of 47% and a complete response rate of 28%, and two paediatric series report responses in about two thirds of children. On the other side, the only randomised trial (93 adults, prednisone plus dapsone vs prednisone alone, reported together with a 46-patient real-world cohort in the same 2025 publication) found a week-52 response of 21.7% vs 8.5% (P = .17) — on its primary endpoint the added dapsone made no significant difference — while 78.3% of the dapsone arm discontinued the drug after a median of 4.6 weeks, mostly for adverse events; the trial authors concluded the risk-benefit ratio is unfavourable and preferred standard second-line options where available. The haemolytic cost is real: the meta-analysis found a mean haemoglobin fall of 1.74 g/dL and adverse effects in 18% (haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia commonest). Haemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency — G6PD testing belongs before use), methaemoglobinaemia and dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome are the defining harms. The dapsone gel shelf for acne is a different formulation and question.

cards.headline: Randomised trial plus cohort 2025: dapsone added to prednisone made no significant difference at week 52 (21.7% vs 8.5%, P = .17), and 78.3% stopped dapsone
cards.summary: Randomised trial plus cohort 2025: dapsone added to prednisone made no significant difference at week 52 (21.7% vs 8.5%, P = .17), and 78.3% stopped dapsone
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (N = 93) plus real-world cohort (N = 46), reported in one publication
cards.people: One publication reporting two studies, labelled separately. (1) A multicentre randomised controlled trial in 93 adults with primary ITP, transient corticosteroid response and platelet count at most 30 x 10^9/L (or at most 50 with bleeding), randomised to prednisone for 3 weeks plus dapsone for 12 months vs prednisone alone. (2) A subsequent real-world observational cohort of 46 adults starting dapsone 100 mg/day.
cards.result: In the trial, the week-52 response rate (platelet count over 30 x 10^9/L and at least twice baseline) was 21.7% (95% CI 10.9 to 36.4) with dapsone vs 8.5% (2.7 to 18.6) without (P = .17) — the treatment made no significant difference on the primary endpoint. In the dapsone arm, 78.3% discontinued after a median of 4.6 weeks, because of adverse events (66.7% of discontinuations) or lack of efficacy (33.3%). In the cohort, adverse events occurred in 30.4%, led to discontinuation in 23.9%, and 13.6% met the primary efficacy endpoint. The authors concluded the risk-benefit ratio is unfavourable and standard second-line options should be used where available.
cards.watchOut: This is the only randomised evidence on the shelf and it is negative on significance with very high discontinuation — the trial was small, so a modest benefit is not excluded, but tolerability, not power, is its loudest message.
cards.source: Efficacy and safety of dapsone in adult primary immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2025. PMID: 39874521. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02627417 and NCT02877706. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis 2025: pooled overall response 47% and complete response 28% across 4 studies and over 270 patients, with a mean haemoglobin fall of 1.74 g/dL
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis 2025: pooled overall response 47% and complete response 28% across 4 studies and over 270 patients, with a mean haemoglobin fall of 1.74 g/dL
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (4 studies, over 270 patients)
cards.people: Four eligible studies (observational studies and interventional trials) encompassing over 270 adults with ITP treated with dapsone, pooled in a PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: The pooled complete response rate was 28% and the overall response rate 47%. Dapsone was associated with a mean haemoglobin decrease of 1.74 g/dL; relapse occurred in approximately 21% of patients; adverse effects — most commonly haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia — were reported in 18% and were generally not severe.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 47% comes predominantly from uncontrolled series in which spontaneous and concomitant-treatment responses count toward the drug; it cannot be reconciled with the randomised trial's result except by design — which is exactly this shelf's split.

cards.headline: Paediatric series 2024: at least a partial response in 64.4% of 45 children with chronic ITP over a median 50 months of follow-up — retrospective
cards.summary: Paediatric series 2024: at least a partial response in 64.4% of 45 children with chronic ITP over a median 50 months of follow-up — retrospective
cards.people: 45 children with chronic ITP at a tertiary centre in South India who received dapsone as a single second-line agent (of 103 children with chronic ITP seen 2012-2016); 37.8% boys. Retrospective, no comparator.
cards.result: An early response to dapsone was seen in 37.8% of patients; over a median long-term follow-up of 50 months, at least a partial response was seen in 64.4%. The authors judged dapsone's initial response and sustained remission comparable to other available second-line agents in children.
cards.watchOut: Childhood chronic ITP remits spontaneously in a substantial minority over 50 months, so a long-follow-up uncontrolled series will credit some natural remissions to the drug.

cards.headline: Paediatric refractory series 2020: overall response in 21 of 29 children (72%) refractory to rituximab, splenectomy or eltrombopag — retrospective
cards.summary: Paediatric refractory series 2020: overall response in 21 of 29 children (72%) refractory to rituximab, splenectomy or eltrombopag — retrospective
cards.type: Retrospective paediatric case series (observational, N = 29 analysed)
cards.people: 29 analysed children (of 44 enrolled) under 14 years with chronic ITP refractory to rituximab (19), splenectomy (8) or eltrombopag (6), treated with dapsone 1-2 mg/kg/day after excluding dapsone intolerance and G6PD deficiency; median age 9.8 years. Retrospective, no comparator.
cards.result: Overall response occurred in 21 of 29 children (72%): complete response in 7 (24%) and partial response in 14 (48%), all sustained for at least 3 months, at a median of 2.9 months to response; relapse rate was 21% over a median 28 months. Major side effects were methaemoglobinaemia (1 case) and skin ulceration (2 cases); in three children dapsone was tapered and stopped without relapse.
cards.watchOut: Only 29 of 44 enrolled children were analysed, G6PD-deficient and dapsone-intolerant children were excluded up front, and there is no control group — the 72% is a best-case reading in a selected refractory population.
cards.source: Dapsone: An Old but Effective Therapy in Pediatric Refractory Immune Thrombocytopenia. Indian J Hematol Blood Transfus. 2020. PMID: 33100711. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: dapsone in ITP is SPLIT — uncontrolled series say about half respond; the one randomised trial says no proven benefit and poor tolerability
cards.summary: Synthesis: dapsone in ITP is SPLIT — uncontrolled series say about half respond; the one randomised trial says no proven benefit and poor tolerability
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one publication containing a 93-patient randomised trial and a 46-patient cohort, a 4-study meta-analysis (over 270 patients), and two retrospective paediatric series (45 and 29 patients).
cards.result: Where dapsone is the only affordable second-line option, the observational record (pooled overall response 47%; paediatric series 64-72%) explains its continued use. But the randomised comparison — the only design that can separate drug effect from natural history — found no significant benefit (the treatment made no difference on its primary endpoint, P = .17) and a 78.3% discontinuation rate, at a haemolytic cost averaging a 1.74 g/dL haemoglobin fall. The stamp is SPLIT, naming that design split, and G6PD testing precedes any use.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here supports dapsone ahead of thrombopoietin-receptor agonists, rituximab or splenectomy where those are available — the randomised trial's own authors say so; its remaining case is cost and access.

shelves.title: Helicobacter pylori eradication in H. pylori-positive ITP: SPLIT by biogeography — about half respond in Japanese, Italian and Korean cohorts, far fewer in US and northern-European and paediatric data
shelves.question: In adults with immune thrombocytopenia who test positive for Helicobacter pylori, does eradication therapy, versus no eradication, raise platelet counts and produce durable responses?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antibodies, Bacterial / immunology · Antigens, Bacterial / blood, immunology · Bacterial Proteins / blood, immunology · Biopsy · Blood Platelets / drug effects, physiology · Chronic Disease · DNA, Bacterial / genetics · Drug Therapy, Combination / therapeutic use · Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastric Mucosa / microbiology, pathology · Gastroscopy · Helicobacter Infections / blood, complications, drug therapy · Helicobacter pylori / genetics, immunology, pathogenicity · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Count · Polymerase Chain Reaction · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / blood, complications · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Virulence / drug effects · Anemia / drug therapy · Anti-Bacterial Agents / therapeutic use · Helicobacter Infections / complications, drug therapy · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Prospective Studies · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / complications · Thrombocytopenia / complications · Helicobacter Infections / blood, microbiology · Helicobacter pylori / drug effects · Humans · Platelet Count · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / blood, microbiology · Treatment Outcome · Adult · Aged · Amoxicillin / therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents / therapeutic use · Blood Platelets / drug effects, pathology · Clarithromycin / therapeutic use · Female · Helicobacter Infections / drug therapy, immunology · Helicobacter pylori / physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Count · Purpura, Thrombocytopenic, Idiopathic / drug therapy, immunology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is biogeography and age, and it is the shelf. In the large systematic review (25 studies, 1,555 patients), overall response after eradication was 50.3% and complete response 42.7%, with response rates tending to be higher in countries with high background H. pylori prevalence (the Japanese and Italian cohorts) and lower in US and northern-European data; patients starting below 30 x 10^9/L responded less (overall response 35.2%). The randomised evidence is small but real: the first RCT found a platelet response in 46.2% of the eradication group vs 0% without eradication, and a Korean phase 3 trial in moderate thrombocytopenia found a significant response difference (P = 0.017) after sequential eradication. Against that, the meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (6 trials, 241 patients) found only a borderline overall-response advantage (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.71 — a relative measure) and, in children, the eradication group made no significant difference (odds ratio 1.80, confidence interval crossing 1). The underlying randomised trials are small — the largest carded enrolled 28 H. pylori-positive patients — so testing for and eradicating H. pylori is a reasonable, cheap step in H. pylori-positive ITP, with response expectations set by region: roughly one in two in high-prevalence settings, substantially fewer elsewhere. Eradication regimens varied by era and region (standard triple therapy in the early trials; 10-day sequential therapy in the Korean phase 3).

cards.headline: First randomised trial 2005: platelet response in 46.2% of the eradication group vs 0% without eradication, in H. pylori-positive chronic ITP
cards.summary: First randomised trial 2005: platelet response in 46.2% of the eradication group vs 0% without eradication, in H. pylori-positive chronic ITP
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (primary trial; 25 H. pylori-positive patients randomised)
cards.people: Adults with chronic ITP who underwent gastroscopy with culture-confirmed H. pylori infection: of 36 ITP patients, 25 (69.4%) were H. pylori-positive and were randomly assigned to standard eradication therapy or no eradication; eradication succeeded in 84.6% of those treated. Response meant complete (platelet count over 150 x 10^3/microL) or partial (rise over 50 x 10^3/microL).
cards.result: The platelet response rate was 46.2% in the eradication group vs 0% in the non-eradication group, a significant difference. No clinical factor distinguished responders from non-responders, and H. pylori virulence factors and urease activity were not associated with response; anti-CagA antibody titres were significantly higher in responders (P = 0.04).
cards.watchOut: A primary trial, but a tiny one — 25 infected patients behind the headline percentages, from a single high-prevalence setting; it establishes that the effect exists somewhere, not its size everywhere.
cards.source: Effect of Helicobacter pylori eradication in patients with chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura-a randomized controlled trial. Am J Gastroenterol. 2005. PMID: 15929755. cards.headline: Korean phase 3 trial 2022: sequential eradication produced a significant platelet-response difference (P = 0.017) in moderate ITP, but enrolment stopped early at 28 patients
cards.summary: Korean phase 3 trial 2022: sequential eradication produced a significant platelet-response difference (P = 0.017) in moderate ITP, but enrolment stopped early at 28 patients
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised trial (primary trial; terminated early, N = 28)
cards.people: Patients with persistent or chronic ITP and moderate thrombocytopenia (platelet count 30-80 x 10^3/microL) and confirmed active H. pylori infection, randomised to 10-day sequential eradication therapy or control; 28 H. pylori-positive patients were enrolled before early termination, 17 of them to the treatment group. Primary endpoint was overall platelet response at 3 months.
cards.result: Eradication was achieved in 15 of 17 treated patients (88.2%) at 3 months, and the platelet response rate differed significantly between the successfully eradicated treatment group and the control group (P = 0.017). Enrolment terminated early because national insurance and treatment guidelines for H. pylori-positive patients changed in Korea during the study.
cards.watchOut: Terminated early at 28 patients and restricted to moderate, asymptomatic-range thrombocytopenia — it does not address severe or bleeding ITP, and the record's abstract does not print the two response percentages, only the P value.

cards.headline: Systematic review 2009: overall response 50.3% and complete response 42.7% after eradication across 25 studies and 1,555 patients, higher in high-prevalence countries
cards.summary: Systematic review 2009: overall response 50.3% and complete response 42.7% after eradication across 25 studies and 1,555 patients, higher in high-prevalence countries
cards.type: Systematic review (25 studies, 1,555 patients; mostly uncontrolled)
cards.people: 25 published studies including 1,555 patients with ITP, of whom 696 were evaluable for the effect of H. pylori eradication on platelet count; studies reporting at least 15 patients were selected. Predominantly uncontrolled cohorts.
cards.result: The weighted mean complete response (platelet count at least 100 x 10^9/L) was 42.7% (95% CI 31.8 to 53.9) and overall response (at least 30 x 10^9/L and at least doubling) was 50.3% (41.6 to 59.0). In 222 patients with baseline platelet count under 30 x 10^9/L, complete response was 20.1% and overall response 35.2%. Response rates tended to be higher in countries with a high background prevalence of H. pylori infection and in patients with milder thrombocytopenia.
cards.watchOut: Almost entirely uncontrolled series: in cohorts assembled because they were H. pylori-positive and treated, spontaneous fluctuation and publication bias inflate the response rate relative to what a randomised comparison would show.
cards.source: Effects of eradication of Helicobacter pylori infection in patients with immune thrombocytopenic purpura: a systematic review. Blood. 2009. PMID: 18945961. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of randomised trials 2018: overall platelet response odds ratio 1.93 across 6 trials and 241 patients, but no significant difference in children
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of randomised trials 2018: overall platelet response odds ratio 1.93 across 6 trials and 241 patients, but no significant difference in children
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials (6 trials, 241 patients)
cards.people: Six randomised studies totalling 241 patients (125 in eradication groups, 116 in control groups) with ITP, in the first meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials of H. pylori eradication.
cards.result: Patients in the eradication group had a significantly higher overall platelet response rate than controls (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.71; P = 0.05 — a relative measure, on the border of significance). In the subgroup analysis of children, the eradication group made no significant difference (odds ratio 1.80, 95% CI 0.88 to 3.65; P = 0.11). The authors called for large randomised trials in adults and children.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials and a confidence interval that only just excludes 1: the randomised-trial estimate is far more modest than the 50% response of the uncontrolled literature, and the paediatric subgroup is null.

cards.headline: Korean cohort 2020: one year after eradication, platelet counts had risen 2.78-fold in the eradicated group vs 1.36-fold with sustained infection
cards.summary: Korean cohort 2020: one year after eradication, platelet counts had risen 2.78-fold in the eradicated group vs 1.36-fold with sustained infection
cards.type: Cohort study of eradication outcomes (observational, N = 61 analysed)
cards.people: 61 patients with ITP in whom H. pylori eradication was analysed (within a cohort in which H. pylori prevalence was 54.3%, 75 of 138); first-line eradication therapy (the record's indexing names amoxicillin and clarithromycin among the agents used) succeeded in 71.4% (35 of 49). Observational, no randomisation.
cards.result: Patients who achieved a complete response at 2 months maintained higher platelet counts thereafter. At 1 year, platelet counts had increased 2.78 times baseline in the eradicated group, 1.36 times in the sustained-infection group and 1.33 times in the no-infection group (P = 0.016), supporting a durable effect confined to patients in whom eradication actually succeeded.
cards.watchOut: Comparing successful vs failed eradication is not a randomised comparison: patients whose infection clears may differ from those whose does not, so the 2.78-fold figure overstates the effect of prescribing eradication.
cards.source: Helicobacter pylori eradication affects platelet count recovery in immune thrombocytopenia. Sci Rep. 2020. PMID: 32523043. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: eradicating H. pylori helps a substantial minority of H. pylori-positive ITP patients — SPLIT by region and age, with small randomised trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: eradicating H. pylori helps a substantial minority of H. pylori-positive ITP patients — SPLIT by region and age, with small randomised trials
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two primary randomised trials (25 and 28 H. pylori-positive patients), a 25-study systematic review (1,555 patients), a 6-trial randomised meta-analysis (241 patients) and a 61-patient cohort.
cards.result: Successful eradication is followed by a platelet response in roughly half of adults in high-prevalence (Japanese, Italian, Korean) cohorts, less in severe thrombocytopenia, and the randomised-trial-only estimate is a modest, borderline relative advantage with a null paediatric subgroup. The honest summary is SPLIT: worth testing for and treating in H. pylori-positive ITP — cheap, finite and occasionally durable — but the expected yield depends on where the patient lives and how low the count is.
cards.watchOut: No card shows a bleeding or survival benefit, and eradication is an adjunct step in the work-up — not a substitute for standard ITP therapy in patients who are bleeding or severely thrombocytopenic.

shelves.title: Ruxolitinib in steroid-refractory or dependent chronic GVHD (REACH3): overall response 49.7% vs 25.6% and median failure-free survival 38.4 vs 5.7 months at 3 years
shelves.question: In patients aged 12 years and older with glucocorticoid-refractory or glucocorticoid-dependent chronic graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic transplantation, does ruxolitinib, versus investigator's-choice best available therapy, improve overall response and failure-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Cytomegalovirus Infections / etiology · Female · Glucocorticoids / therapeutic use · Graft vs Host Disease / drug therapy · Humans · Immunologic Factors / adverse effects, therapeutic use · Janus Kinases / antagonists & inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Photopheresis · Pyrazoles / adverse effects, therapeutic use · Pyrimidines · Survival Analysis · Thrombocytopenia / chemically induced · Treatment Failure · Young Adult · Humans · Nitriles · Graft vs Host Disease / drug therapy, mortality · Pyrimidines · Pyrazoles / therapeutic use, adverse effects · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Adult · Chronic Disease · Adrenal Cortex Hormones / therapeutic use · Aged · Young Adult · Cross-Over Studies · Graft vs Host Disease / drug therapy, etiology · Nitriles · Humans · Pyrazoles / therapeutic use, adverse effects · Pyrimidines / therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Male · Female · Adult · Chronic Disease · Aged · Japan · Treatment Outcome · Steroids / therapeutic use · Young Adult · Adolescent · East Asian People
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised programme (REACH3) carries the shelf, which caps the stamp, however large its effects. In 329 patients aged 12 years and older, overall response at week 24 was 49.7% on ruxolitinib vs 25.6% on investigator's-choice best available therapy (odds ratio 2.99, a relative measure; absolute rates printed on the card), symptom response was 24.2% vs 11.0%, and at the 3-year final analysis median failure-free survival was 38.4 vs 5.7 months (hazard ratio 0.36, a relative measure). The Japanese subgroup (37 patients) pointed the same way. Two structural cautions: the trial was open-label against a heterogeneous comparator list, and best-available-therapy patients could cross over to ruxolitinib (70 did, responding at rates consistent with the main trial), which limits any survival reading — median overall survival was not reached and no survival advantage is claimed here. Added harms against best available therapy are cytopenias (grade 3 or worse thrombocytopenia 15.2% vs 10.1% and anaemia 12.7% vs 7.6% to week 24) and infection vigilance; cytomegalovirus infection/reactivation rates were similar. Ruxolitinib was FDA-approved for this indication in September 2021. The acute-GVHD ruxolitinib shelf is a different question and its evidence is not used here; belumosudil and axatilimab shelves cover later-line chronic GVHD.

cards.headline: REACH3 2021: overall response at week 24 in 49.7% on ruxolitinib vs 25.6% on best available therapy, in 329 patients with steroid-refractory or dependent chronic GVHD
cards.summary: REACH3 2021: overall response at week 24 in 49.7% on ruxolitinib vs 25.6% on best available therapy, in 329 patients with steroid-refractory or dependent chronic GVHD
cards.people: 329 patients aged 12 years or older with moderate or severe glucocorticoid-refractory or glucocorticoid-dependent chronic GVHD after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, randomised to ruxolitinib 10 mg twice daily (165 patients) or the investigator's choice from 10 commonly used options considered best available therapy (164 patients); open-label.
cards.result: Overall response (complete or partial) at week 24 was 49.7% vs 25.6% (odds ratio 2.99; P < 0.001). Median failure-free survival was over 18.6 months vs 5.7 months (hazard ratio 0.37; P < 0.001), and symptom response on the modified Lee Symptom Scale was 24.2% vs 11.0% (odds ratio 2.62; P = 0.001). Grade 3 or higher adverse events to week 24 included thrombocytopenia (15.2% vs 10.1%) and anaemia (12.7% vs 7.6%); cytomegalovirus infection and reactivation rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against a menu of comparators of varying strength, so the size of the response gap partly reflects the softness of 'best available therapy' in a population defined by having already failed steroids.
cards.source: Ruxolitinib for Glucocorticoid-Refractory Chronic Graft-versus-Host Disease. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 34260836. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03112603. cards.headline: REACH3 3-year final analysis 2025: median failure-free survival 38.4 vs 5.7 months, with responses maintained in 59.6% vs 26.7% at 36 months
cards.summary: REACH3 3-year final analysis 2025: median failure-free survival 38.4 vs 5.7 months, with responses maintained in 59.6% vs 26.7% at 36 months
cards.type: Three-year final analysis of the REACH3 phase 3 trial (same programme)
cards.people: The same 329 REACH3 patients (165 ruxolitinib, 164 best available therapy), followed for 3 years; after week 24 patients continued randomised treatment, entered long-term follow-up, or crossed over from best available therapy to ruxolitinib (70 patients). Same trial as the card above — one programme.
cards.result: Median failure-free survival was 38.4 months on ruxolitinib vs 5.7 months on best available therapy (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.49); median duration of response was not reached vs 6.4 months. At 36 months, the probability of failure-free survival was 56.5% vs 18.2% and of maintaining a response 59.6% vs 26.7%. Median overall survival was not reached; non-relapse mortality and malignancy relapse/recurrence events were low. Crossover patients had a week-24 overall response of 50.0% and a best overall response of 81.4% during crossover. No new safety signals were observed.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same trial, not a second trial: it adds durability, and the crossover design means the long-term comparison is no longer ruxolitinib vs no ruxolitinib — no overall-survival claim can be drawn.

cards.summary: REACH3 Japanese subgroup 2024: response 50% vs 20% and failure-free survival 18.6 vs 3.7 months in 37 patients — consistent, but small
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of the REACH3 phase 3 trial (same programme, N = 37)
cards.people: 37 Japanese patients from REACH3 with steroid-refractory or dependent chronic GVHD, comparing ruxolitinib 10 mg twice daily with best available therapy; at data cut-off 17 patients remained on treatment and 20 had discontinued. Subgroup of the carded trial.
cards.result: Overall response at week 24 was 50% on ruxolitinib vs 20% on best available therapy (odds ratio 4.13, 95% CI 0.90 to 18.9); best overall response was 68.2% vs 46.7%. Median failure-free survival was 18.6 vs 3.7 months (hazard ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.85). The commonest grade 3 or worse adverse events to week 24 were anaemia (22.7% vs 6.7%) and pneumonia (22.7% vs 20.0%).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven patients with wide confidence intervals (the response odds ratio's interval crosses 1): consistency with the main trial is reassuring, but this subgroup adds precision to nothing.

shelves.title: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide prophylaxis (BMT CTN 1703): GVHD-free, relapse-free survival 52.7% vs 34.9% at 1 year in reduced-intensity matched-donor transplantation
shelves.question: In adults undergoing reduced-intensity or non-myeloablative matched-donor allogeneic transplantation, does post-transplant cyclophosphamide plus tacrolimus plus mycophenolate prophylaxis, versus tacrolimus plus methotrexate, improve GVHD-free, relapse-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome / etiology, prevention & control · Cyclophosphamide / administration & dosage · Graft vs Host Disease / prevention & control, etiology · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation / adverse effects, methods · Methotrexate / administration & dosage · Mycophenolic Acid / administration & dosage · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local / drug therapy · Tacrolimus / administration & dosage · Unrelated Donors · Hematologic Neoplasms / surgery · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols / therapeutic use · Humans · Cyclophosphamide / therapeutic use, administration & dosage, adverse effects · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Graft vs Host Disease / prevention & control · Quality of Life · Bone Marrow Transplantation / adverse effects · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Adult · Immunosuppressive Agents / therapeutic use · Methotrexate / administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Tacrolimus / administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Mycophenolic Acid / administration & dosage, therapeutic use, analogs & derivatives · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Cyclophosphamide / therapeutic use, administration & dosage · Graft vs Host Disease / prevention & control, etiology, mortality · Hematologic Neoplasms / therapy · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation / adverse effects · Immunosuppressive Agents / therapeutic use · Methotrexate / therapeutic use · Transplantation Conditioning / methods · Transplantation, Homologous · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single trial programme (BMT CTN 1703) carries the shelf, which caps the stamp, with three reports of that one trial carded and labelled as one programme. In 431 adults receiving reduced-intensity conditioning and HLA-matched related or matched/7-of-8-mismatched unrelated donor grafts, GVHD-free, relapse-free survival at 1 year was 52.7% with post-transplant cyclophosphamide plus tacrolimus plus mycophenolate vs 34.9% with tacrolimus plus methotrexate (hazard ratio 0.64 for the composite event — a relative measure; absolute rates printed on the card), and the advantage held at 2 years (42.4% vs 28.8%). Patients on the cyclophosphamide regimen also reported lower chronic-GVHD symptom burden in the first year. Overall survival, disease-free survival, relapse, transplant-related death and engraftment did not differ substantially between the groups — on those endpoints the regimens made no clear difference; the gain is in GVHD control and time free of immunosuppression. The population fence is part of the tested intervention's identity: reduced-intensity conditioning, matched donors, peripheral-blood grafts predominating. Nothing here generalises to myeloablative conditioning or haploidentical transplantation, which have their own literatures and shelves.

cards.headline: BMT CTN 1703 2023: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival at 1 year 52.7% with post-transplant cyclophosphamide prophylaxis vs 34.9% with tacrolimus/methotrexate (431 patients)
cards.summary: BMT CTN 1703 2023: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival at 1 year 52.7% with post-transplant cyclophosphamide prophylaxis vs 34.9% with tacrolimus/methotrexate (431 patients)
cards.people: 431 adults with haematologic cancers undergoing allogeneic transplantation from an HLA-matched related donor or a matched or 7/8-mismatched unrelated donor after reduced-intensity conditioning, randomised 1:1 to cyclophosphamide-tacrolimus-mycophenolate prophylaxis (214 patients) or tacrolimus-methotrexate (217 patients). Primary endpoint: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival at 1 year (events: grade III-IV acute GVHD, chronic GVHD needing systemic immunosuppression, relapse/progression, or death).
cards.result: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival was significantly more common with the cyclophosphamide regimen (hazard ratio for the composite event 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P = 0.001); adjusted 1-year GVHD-free, relapse-free survival was 52.7% (95% CI 45.8 to 59.2) vs 34.9% (28.6 to 41.3). Patients on the cyclophosphamide regimen appeared to have less severe acute and chronic GVHD and higher immunosuppression-free survival at 1 year. Overall and disease-free survival, relapse, transplantation-related death and engraftment did not differ substantially between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven by GVHD events: on survival and relapse taken separately the regimens made no substantial difference, so the claim is better GVHD-free life after transplant, not longer life.
cards.source: Post-Transplantation Cyclophosphamide-Based Graft-versus-Host Disease Prophylaxis. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37342922. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03959241. cards.headline: BMT CTN 1703 companion 2025: the GVHD-free advantage held at 2 years (42.4% vs 28.8%), and patients reported lower GVHD symptom burden
cards.summary: BMT CTN 1703 companion 2025: the GVHD-free advantage held at 2 years (42.4% vs 28.8%), and patients reported lower GVHD symptom burden
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes companion and 2-year update of the BMT CTN 1703 trial (same programme)
cards.people: Patients from BMT CTN 1703 (same trial as the card above) completing patient-reported outcomes (Lee Chronic GVHD Symptom Score and PROMIS subscales, in English and Spanish speakers) at baseline and days 100, 180 and 365, with updated 2-year clinical endpoints for the parent trial. One programme.
cards.result: Updated 2-year GVHD-free, relapse-free survival remained significantly higher with post-transplant cyclophosphamide prophylaxis (42.4% vs 28.8%, P = .001). The cyclophosphamide arm had significantly lower Lee Chronic GVHD Symptom Scale scores (P = .01), indicating lower symptom burden, with nutrition and mouth subscores also better (P < .01 for both). No significant differences were identified in haemorrhagic cystitis symptoms or in the PROMIS subscales — on those measures the regimens made no difference.
cards.watchOut: A companion report of the same patients: it adds the patient's experience and a second year of follow-up, not independent confirmation, and symptom scores come from the subset who completed the questionnaires.

cards.headline: BMT CTN 1703 subgroup aged 70 and over 2025: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival 67.1% vs 29.5% and adjusted 1-year survival 94.3% vs 60.2% in 96 patients
cards.summary: BMT CTN 1703 subgroup aged 70 and over 2025: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival 67.1% vs 29.5% and adjusted 1-year survival 94.3% vs 60.2% in 96 patients
cards.type: Age subgroup analysis of the BMT CTN 1703 phase 3 trial (same programme, N = 96)
cards.people: 96 patients aged 70 years or older enrolled in BMT CTN 1703 (same trial as the cards above), analysed as a subgroup comparing post-transplant cyclophosphamide-based prophylaxis with tacrolimus/methotrexate after reduced-intensity conditioning.
cards.result: The cyclophosphamide regimen maintained superiority for the primary endpoint (GVHD-free, relapse-free survival 67.1% vs 29.5%, P = .001), contributed to lower 1-year non-relapse mortality through GVHD control and improved immunosuppression-free survival, and was associated with lower relapse/progression rates and significantly improved adjusted 1-year survival (94.3% vs 60.2%, P = .001). The authors argued the regimen should be considered standard prophylaxis for older adults.
cards.watchOut: A 96-patient subgroup of a trial whose overall survival comparison was null: the striking 94.3% vs 60.2% adjusted survival split is hypothesis-generating, not a proven survival benefit in older patients.
cards.source: Impact of posttransplant cyclophosphamide-based GVHD prophylaxis in patients 70 years and older: an update from BMT CTN 1703. Blood Adv. 2025. PMID: 40305657.
