shelves.title: Abatacept added to standard prophylaxis for acute GVHD prevention (ABA2)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing unrelated-donor allogeneic transplantation, does adding abatacept to calcineurin-inhibitor-based prophylaxis, versus prophylaxis alone, reduce severe acute GVHD without increasing relapse or infection?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept/therapeutic use · Graft vs Host Disease/prevention & control · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Unrelated Donors · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme (the ABA2 trial, reported three ways, plus one small single-arm paediatric cohort) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In ABA2's randomised 8/8-matched stratum, grade 3–4 acute GVHD by day +100 was 6.8% on abatacept versus 14.8% on placebo (P = .13 — not conventionally significant on the primary endpoint, in a phase 2 trial designed with a higher type-1 error), while severe-GVHD-free survival favoured abatacept (93.2% vs 82%, P = .05). The 7/8-mismatched stratum was single-arm: grade 3–4 acute GVHD of 2.3% against 30.2% in a non-randomised registry comparator — a comparison that cannot carry the same weight. The exposure–response report adds a dose lesson, not new patients: patients whose first-dose trough reached at least 39 µg/mL had a lower grade 2–4 GVHD risk (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure), while those below that trough looked indistinguishable from placebo. The paediatric bone-marrow-failure cohort (10 children) showed tolerability and no severe acute or chronic GVHD, but it is a single-arm phase 1 experience. EBV reactivation and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease are the monitoring burden that comes with co-stimulation blockade: one probable PTLD case occurred in the small paediatric cohort, and the exposure analysis found no association between higher exposure and CMV or EBV viraemia. The licensed slice (FDA approval December 2021, with a calcineurin inhibitor and methotrexate, for patients aged 2 years and over receiving matched or 1-allele-mismatched unrelated-donor grafts) is the population this shelf covers.

cards.headline: ABA2 randomised stratum (Watkins 2021): grade 3–4 acute GVHD 6.8% on abatacept versus 14.8% on placebo (P = .13); severe-GVHD-free survival 93.2% versus 82% (P = .05) — the 7/8-mismatched stratum was single-arm (2.3% versus 30.2% in registry controls)
cards.summary: ABA2 randomised stratum (Watkins 2021): grade 3–4 acute GVHD 6.8% on abatacept versus 14.8% on placebo (P = .13); severe-GVHD-free survival 93.2% versus 82% (P = .05) — the 7/8-mismatched stratum was single-arm (2.3% versus 30.2% in registry controls)
cards.type: Phase 2 trial — randomised double-blind stratum (8/8 matched) plus single-arm stratum (7/8 mismatched) (Watkins 2021, ABA2)
cards.people: 185 unrelated-donor haematopoietic cell transplant recipients with haematological malignancies in two strata: 142 in the randomised, double-blind 8/8-HLA-matched stratum (calcineurin inhibitor/methotrexate plus abatacept versus plus placebo; median follow-up 716 days) and 43 in the single-arm 7/8-HLA-mismatched stratum (abatacept added, compared with CIBMTR registry controls; median follow-up 708 days). Adults and children were enrolled.
cards.result: In the 8/8 stratum, day +100 grade 3–4 acute GVHD was 6.8% with abatacept versus 14.8% with placebo (P = .13; hazard ratio 0.45, with the absolute rates printed here). Severe acute-GVHD-free survival was 93.2% versus 82% (P = .05). In the 7/8 stratum, grade 3–4 acute GVHD was 2.3% on abatacept versus 30.2% in the non-randomised matched CIBMTR cohort (P < .001), and severe-GVHD-free survival was 97.7% versus 58.7% (P < .001). Immunological analysis showed control of T-cell activation in abatacept-treated patients, and adding abatacept was reported as safe.
cards.watchOut: The design split is the whole story: only the 8/8 stratum was randomised, and its primary endpoint did not reach conventional significance (P = .13, in a phase 2 design using a higher type-1 error of 0.2). The dramatic 7/8 figures come from a registry comparison, which is vulnerable to selection and era effects — do not quote 2.3% versus 30.2% as if it were a randomised contrast.
cards.source: Watkins B et al. Phase II Trial of Costimulation Blockade With Abatacept for Prevention of Acute GVHD. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2021. PMID: 33449816. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ABA2 exposure–response (Takahashi 2023) — second report of the same trial: a first-dose abatacept trough of at least 39 µg/mL was associated with lower grade 2–4 GVHD risk (hazard ratio 0.35, relative); below that trough, risk was indistinguishable from placebo
cards.summary: ABA2 exposure–response (Takahashi 2023) — second report of the same trial: a first-dose abatacept trough of at least 39 µg/mL was associated with lower grade 2–4 GVHD risk (hazard ratio 0.35, relative); below that trough, risk was indistinguishable from placebo
cards.type: Exposure–response / pharmacokinetic analysis of the ABA2 trial — same programme, labelled (Takahashi 2023)
cards.people: Patients from the ABA2 trial (the trial carded above — this is a pharmacokinetic/exposure analysis of the same programme, not a new cohort), with population pharmacokinetics modelled and the trough concentration after dose 1 tested against grade 2–4 acute GVHD through day +100. About 60% of ABA2 patients attained a trough of at least 39 µg/mL on the standard regimen.
cards.result: A first-dose trough of at least 39 µg/mL was associated with a favourable grade 2–4 acute GVHD risk (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.19–0.65; P < .001 — a relative measure, with no absolute rates in this record), whereas a trough below 39 µg/mL was associated with risk indistinguishable from placebo (P = .37). No significant association was found between trough level and relapse, or cytomegalovirus or Epstein-Barr virus viraemia.
cards.watchOut: The 39 µg/mL threshold was derived from the same data that test it (recursive partitioning), so it is a hypothesis about dosing, not a validated target — and exposure was not randomised, so higher troughs may track with other patient features.
cards.source: Takahashi T et al. Higher abatacept exposure after transplant decreases acute GVHD risk without increasing adverse events. Blood. 2023. PMID: 37319437. cards.headline: Paediatric bone-marrow-failure cohort (2023): 4 doses of abatacept added to cyclosporine/mycophenolate were tolerable in 10 children undergoing unrelated-donor transplant — no severe acute or chronic GVHD, 1 probable PTLD; N = 10
cards.summary: Paediatric bone-marrow-failure cohort (2023): 4 doses of abatacept added to cyclosporine/mycophenolate were tolerable in 10 children undergoing unrelated-donor transplant — no severe acute or chronic GVHD, 1 probable PTLD; N = 10
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1 trial in paediatric non-malignant disease — no comparator (Blood Advances 2023)
cards.people: 10 children with non-malignant bone marrow failure disorders undergoing unrelated-donor haematopoietic cell transplantation with reduced-intensity or non-myeloablative conditioning at a single centre, receiving abatacept added to cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil prophylaxis. Single-arm phase 1 trial. N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: Nine patients engrafted (1 primary graft rejection with inadequate cell dose; 1 secondary rejection with concurrent CMV viraemia). No patient developed severe acute or chronic GVHD, and 8 patients were off systemic immunosuppression at 1 year. Two deaths occurred, both unrelated to abatacept. One patient developed probable post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease, responsive to rituximab and immunosuppression withdrawal. Immune reconstitution did not appear impacted. Four doses of abatacept were deemed tolerable.
cards.watchOut: Ten children, no comparator, a different (non-malignant) population from ABA2: this card supports tolerability in children only. It cannot confirm GVHD prevention, and its one probable PTLD case in 10 patients is exactly the harm that needs monitoring at scale.
cards.source: Stenger EO et al. Abatacept GVHD prophylaxis in unrelated hematopoietic cell transplantation for pediatric bone marrow failure. Blood advances. 2023. PMID: 36724508. cards.headline: Synthesis: adding abatacept to calcineurin-inhibitor prophylaxis probably reduces severe acute GVHD in unrelated-donor transplant — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: adding abatacept to calcineurin-inhibitor prophylaxis probably reduces severe acute GVHD in unrelated-donor transplant — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the ABA2 phase 2 trial (142 randomised 8/8-matched and 43 single-arm 7/8-mismatched recipients), its exposure–response analysis (same patients), and a 10-child single-arm paediatric bone-marrow-failure cohort.
cards.result: The randomised evidence shows a halving of severe acute GVHD that missed conventional significance on the primary endpoint (6.8% vs 14.8%, P = .13) with a significant severe-GVHD-free-survival advantage (93.2% vs 82%); the single-arm mismatched stratum and the exposure–response analysis point the same way, and the paediatric cohort adds tolerability. Because everything rests on one trial programme and the randomised primary endpoint was not conventionally significant, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit). EBV reactivation/PTLD monitoring belongs with any use.
cards.watchOut: No second randomised trial exists in this record: relapse, infection and survival effects at scale, and the proposed exposure target, remain unconfirmed outside the ABA2 programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Watkins B et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2021 (PMID: 33449816); Takahashi T et al. Blood. 2023 (PMID: 37319437); Blood advances. 2023 (PMID: 36724508), all carded above.

shelves.title: Romiplostim for refractory aplastic anaemia
shelves.question: In patients with aplastic anaemia refractory to immunosuppressive therapy, does romiplostim, versus no concurrent control, produce haematologic responses, including trilineage responses?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Aplastic/drug therapy · Anemia, Refractory/drug therapy · Thrombopoietin/therapeutic use · Receptors, Thrombopoietin/agonists · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — all of the evidence is single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no randomised or concurrent-control comparison anywhere on this shelf, so response rates have no counterfactual. In the phase 2/3 study, 84% of 31 patients refractory to immunosuppressive therapy achieved some haematological response by week 27, with trilineage response in 39% at week 53 — striking in a refractory population, but a proportion, not a treatment effect. The nationwide Japanese post-marketing surveillance (470 patients) found similar response proportions in routine practice (78.6% at 27 weeks among those assessed) and gives the best harm picture: adverse drug reactions in 18.1%, with thromboembolism in 1.49% and haematopoietic tumour in 1.28% recorded as reactions of special interest. The eltrombopag-refractory series is small (10 patients, 7 responding) and supports switching within the class, no more. Clonal evolution is the standing worry with thrombopoietin-receptor agonists in aplastic anaemia: 2 of 31 patients in the phase 2/3 study developed cytogenetic abnormalities (one later returned to a normal karyotype), and marrow and cytogenetic monitoring is part of the treatment's follow-up burden, not an optional extra. Romiplostim for immune thrombocytopenia and for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia are different questions, homed elsewhere, and none of that record is carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 2/3 study (2021): 84% of 31 patients with refractory aplastic anaemia achieved a haematological response at week 27 on high-dose romiplostim; trilineage response 39% at week 53 — single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: Phase 2/3 study (2021): 84% of 31 patients with refractory aplastic anaemia achieved a haematological response at week 27 on high-dose romiplostim; trilineage response 39% at week 53 — single-arm, no comparator
cards.type: Single-arm open-label phase 2/3 study — no comparator (Br J Haematol 2021)
cards.people: 31 patients with aplastic anaemia refractory to immunosuppressive therapy, with platelet counts of 30 × 10⁹/L or less, in a multicentre open-label phase 2/3 study. Romiplostim was given subcutaneously at 10 µg/kg once weekly for 4 weeks, then titrated weekly (5–20 µg/kg) by platelet response for up to 52 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — any haematological (platelet, neutrophil or erythrocyte) response at week 27 — was achieved by 84% of patients (95% CI 66–95%). Trilineage response was 39% (95% CI 22–58%) at week 53. The most common treatment-related adverse events were headache and muscle spasms (each 13%); all were mild or moderate except three patients with grade 3 hepatic events, and none necessitated discontinuation. Two patients developed cytogenetic abnormalities, of whom one returned to a normal karyotype at last follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: an 84% response rate in patients selected for refractory thrombocytopenia cannot separate drug effect from natural fluctuation and transfusion practice, and the wide confidence interval (66–95%) reflects the 31-patient base. The cytogenetic abnormalities in 2 patients are the clonal-evolution signal that long-term monitoring must track.
cards.source: Jang JH et al. Efficacy and safety of romiplostim in refractory aplastic anaemia: a Phase II/III, multicentre, open-label study. British journal of haematology. 2021. PMID: 33152120. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nationwide Japanese post-marketing surveillance (2026): 470 patients — haematological response 78.6% at 27 weeks among those assessed; adverse drug reactions 18.1%, thromboembolism 1.49%, haematopoietic tumour 1.28%
cards.summary: Nationwide Japanese post-marketing surveillance (2026): 470 patients — haematological response 78.6% at 27 weeks among those assessed; adverse drug reactions 18.1%, thromboembolism 1.49%, haematopoietic tumour 1.28%
cards.type: Nationwide post-marketing surveillance — observational, no comparator (Ann Hematol 2026)
cards.people: 470 patients with refractory aplastic anaemia at 220 institutions in Japan who started romiplostim between June 2019 and September 2021, in an all-case post-marketing surveillance study (mean age 66.3 years; 43.4% male). Romiplostim was given subcutaneously once weekly for 52 weeks, with bone-marrow fibrosis and haematopoietic tumours monitored for up to 2 years. Observational, no comparator — labelled as such.
cards.result: Romiplostim was discontinued in 219 of 470 patients (46.6%). Adverse events occurred in 57.0% and adverse drug reactions in 18.1%. Reactions of special interest included thromboembolism (1.49%), haematopoietic tumour (1.28%) and haemorrhage (0.46%); during follow-up, haematopoietic tumours as drug reactions were observed in 2 of 310 patients (0.65%). Haematological response was achieved in 257 of 327 assessed patients (78.6%) at 27 weeks and 205 of 244 (84.0%) at 52 weeks; platelet and red-cell transfusion independence or reduced requirement was achieved in roughly four-fifths of those assessed.
cards.watchOut: Response denominators shrink over time (327 assessed at 27 weeks, 244 at 52 weeks of 470 registered), so the percentages describe patients still assessed, not all starters — and nearly half discontinued. Surveillance attribution of tumours and thrombosis as 'drug reactions' is a reporting classification, not proof of causation.
cards.source: Itagaki M et al. Long-term safety and effectiveness of romiplostim in patients with refractory aplastic anemia: a nationwide, all-case, post-marketing surveillance study in Japan. Annals of hematology. 2026. PMID: 42223664. Registry ID: UMIN000056465 (as stated in the record). cards.headline: Eltrombopag-refractory series (Ise 2020): 7 of 10 patients who had failed maximum-dose eltrombopag responded after switching to romiplostim 20 µg/kg/week; N = 10
cards.summary: Eltrombopag-refractory series (Ise 2020): 7 of 10 patients who had failed maximum-dose eltrombopag responded after switching to romiplostim 20 µg/kg/week; N = 10
cards.type: Retrospective case series — eltrombopag-refractory switch population (Int J Hematol 2020)
cards.people: 10 patients with aplastic anaemia who had failed to respond to the maximum dose of eltrombopag and were switched to romiplostim at its maximum dose (20 µg/kg/week), in a retrospective study with a median follow-up of 12 months. N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: Seven of 10 patients (70%) achieved a neutrophil, erythroid or platelet response, including one complete response. No patient showed the platelet-count fluctuations reported with romiplostim in immune thrombocytopenia, and no patient stopped romiplostim because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, retrospective, no comparator: 7 responses could reflect switching, time, or selection. It supports trying the switch after eltrombopag failure; it does not estimate how often the switch works in general.

cards.headline: Synthesis: romiplostim produces haematological responses in refractory aplastic anaemia — POSSIBLE (benefit), entirely single-arm evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: romiplostim produces haematological responses in refractory aplastic anaemia — POSSIBLE (benefit), entirely single-arm evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the phase 2/3 study (31 patients) and its long-term follow-up (same programme), the nationwide Japanese surveillance cohort (470 patients), and the eltrombopag-refractory switch series (10 patients).
cards.result: Response proportions are consistently high across a small trial, a large real-world cohort and a switch series (84% at week 27 in the trial; 78.6% at 27 weeks in surveillance; 7 of 10 after eltrombopag failure), with trilineage responses in a substantial minority. But every report is single-arm, so none of these numbers is a measured treatment effect, and the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit). The harms that travel with the drug — thromboembolism, marrow fibrosis and clonal evolution/haematopoietic tumours — require the monitoring the surveillance study was built around.
cards.watchOut: Whether romiplostim changes survival, transfusion burden over years, or clonal-evolution risk versus other salvage options cannot be answered from single-arm data — no comparative claim is made on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of British journal of haematology. 2021 (PMID: 33152120); Mitani K et al. Blood advances. 2024 (PMID: 38134300); Annals of hematology. 2026 (PMID: 42223664); Ise M et al. International journal of hematology. 2020 (PMID: 32876852), all carded above.

shelves.title: Avapritinib for advanced systemic mastocytosis (EXPLORER / PATHFINDER)
shelves.question: In adults with advanced systemic mastocytosis (aggressive systemic mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis with an associated haematological neoplasm, or mast cell leukaemia), does avapritinib, versus no concurrent control or best available therapy, produce overall responses and improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Mastocytosis, Systemic/drug therapy · Avapritinib · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-kit/genetics · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Pyrroles/therapeutic use · Triazines/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal evidence is single-arm (EXPLORER phase 1 and PATHFINDER phase 2, one programme), which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the only comparative report is a retrospective external comparison against best available therapy, which is observational and labelled as such. Response rates were consistent: overall response 75% in both the phase 1 response-evaluable set (53 patients) and the PATHFINDER interim set (32 response-evaluable of 62 enrolled), and 71% in the pooled previously-treated analysis (31 response-evaluable patients). Mast-cell burden fell deeply (at least 50% reductions in tryptase in 89–99% and in marrow mast cells in 88–92% across reports). The external comparison found better survival on avapritinib than on best available therapy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.48 — a relative measure, from a non-randomised comparison, so confounding by era and selection is expected). The defining harms are intracranial haemorrhage — 13% overall in EXPLORER but only 1% in patients without severe thrombocytopenia, which is why platelet-count gating is part of the tested intervention — and cognitive effects, alongside periorbital oedema and cytopenias (grade 3 or worse neutropenia 24%, thrombocytopenia 16%, anaemia 16% in PATHFINDER). This shelf is the advanced-disease question only: avapritinib in indolent systemic mastocytosis is homed at pack #6906 and in PDGFRA D842V gastrointestinal stromal tumour at pack #6709, and none of that record is carded here.

cards.headline: EXPLORER phase 1 (DeAngelo 2021): overall response rate 75% and complete remission 36% in 53 response-evaluable patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis; intracranial bleeding in 13% overall but 1% without severe thrombocytopenia
cards.summary: EXPLORER phase 1 (DeAngelo 2021): overall response rate 75% and complete remission 36% in 53 response-evaluable patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis; intracranial bleeding in 13% overall but 1% without severe thrombocytopenia
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1 trial — no comparator (DeAngelo 2021, EXPLORER)
cards.people: 86 patients treated with avapritinib 30–400 mg once daily in a phase 1 dose-escalation/expansion study, 69 with centrally confirmed advanced systemic mastocytosis (aggressive systemic mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis with an associated haematological neoplasm, or mast cell leukaemia); 53 were response-evaluable. Single-arm, no comparator. The recommended phase 2 dose was 200 mg daily.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 75% and complete remission rate 36% in the 53 response-evaluable patients. At least 50% reductions in marrow mast cells and serum tryptase occurred in 92% and 99% of patients respectively, and molecular remission of KIT D816V was reported. The most frequent adverse events were periorbital oedema (69%), anaemia (55%), diarrhoea (45%), thrombocytopenia (44%) and nausea (44%). Intracranial bleeding occurred in 13% overall, but in only 1% of patients without severe thrombocytopenia (platelets below 50 × 10⁹/L).
cards.watchOut: A phase 1 dose-finding study across 30–400 mg: response figures come from the 53 response-evaluable patients, not all 86 treated, and doses above the later 200 mg standard are in the mix. The 13% intracranial-bleeding figure is inseparable from the thrombocytopenic population treated before platelet gating was applied.

cards.headline: PATHFINDER phase 2 interim (Gotlib 2021): overall response rate 75% (95% CI 57–89) in 32 response-evaluable patients at a 200 mg starting dose; grade 3 or worse neutropenia 24%, thrombocytopenia 16%, anaemia 16%
cards.summary: PATHFINDER phase 2 interim (Gotlib 2021): overall response rate 75% (95% CI 57–89) in 32 response-evaluable patients at a 200 mg starting dose; grade 3 or worse neutropenia 24%, thrombocytopenia 16%, anaemia 16%
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial, prespecified interim analysis — no comparator (Gotlib 2021, PATHFINDER)
cards.people: 62 patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis in a single-arm pivotal phase 2 trial, treated primarily at a once-daily starting dose of avapritinib 200 mg; the prespecified interim analysis reports 32 response-evaluable patients with sufficient follow-up for response assessment. Single-arm, no comparator.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met (P = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ against the prespecified null), with an overall response rate of 75% (95% CI 57–89), including 19% complete remission with full or partial haematological recovery. Reductions of at least 50% from baseline occurred in serum tryptase (93%), bone marrow mast cells (88%) and KIT D816V variant allele fraction (60%). The most frequent grade 3 or worse adverse events were neutropenia (24%), thrombocytopenia (16%) and anaemia (16%).
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis: the 75% response rate rests on 32 of 62 enrolled patients — those with enough follow-up to be assessed — so the denominator flatters the estimate relative to all starters. The statistical test is against a prespecified historical null, not against a concurrent control.

cards.headline: Pooled previously-treated analysis (Reiter 2022) — EXPLORER/PATHFINDER combined, labelled one programme: response rate 71% (22 of 31 response-evaluable) after at least one prior systemic therapy; median overall survival not reached at 17.7 months
cards.summary: Pooled previously-treated analysis (Reiter 2022) — EXPLORER/PATHFINDER combined, labelled one programme: response rate 71% (22 of 31 response-evaluable) after at least one prior systemic therapy; median overall survival not reached at 17.7 months
cards.type: Pooled analysis of EXPLORER and PATHFINDER — same programme, labelled (Blood Advances 2022)
cards.people: Patients from EXPLORER and PATHFINDER (the two trials carded above — this pooled analysis is a further report of the same programme, not a new cohort) who had received at least one prior systemic therapy before avapritinib; 31 were response-evaluable. Median follow-up 17.7 months.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 71% (95% CI 52–86%; 22 of 31), including 19% (6 of 31) complete remission or complete remission with partial count recovery. Median time to response was 2.3 months; median duration of response and median overall survival were not reached. Reductions of at least 50% in marrow mast cells (89%), KIT D816V variant allele fraction (66%) and serum tryptase (89%), and of at least 35% in spleen size (70%), occurred in most patients. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 94% of patients (57% grade 3 or worse); 81% remained on treatment at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Pooled re-reporting of the same two trials: it answers the previously-treated question but adds no independent patients, and 'median survival not reached' at 17.7 months in a selected trial population is not a survival estimate.

cards.headline: Comparison versus best available therapy (Reiter 2022): avapritinib cohort had better survival than a retrospective best-available-therapy cohort (adjusted hazard ratio 0.48, relative) — observational comparison, not a randomised trial
cards.summary: Comparison versus best available therapy (Reiter 2022): avapritinib cohort had better survival than a retrospective best-available-therapy cohort (adjusted hazard ratio 0.48, relative) — observational comparison, not a randomised trial
cards.people: 176 patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis treated with avapritinib in EXPLORER/PATHFINDER, compared with 141 patients treated with best available therapy in a multicentre retrospective chart review at six sites (four European, two American), with adjustment for key covariates. Observational comparison — labelled as such.
cards.result: The avapritinib cohort had significantly better overall survival (adjusted hazard ratio 0.48; 95% CI 0.29–0.79; P = .004 — a relative measure) and significantly longer duration of treatment (hazard ratio 0.36; 95% CI 0.26–0.51; P < .001) than the best-available-therapy cohort. The mean maximum reduction in serum tryptase was 60.3 percentage points greater in the avapritinib cohort (95% CI −72.8 to −47.9; P < .001).
cards.watchOut: Trial patients versus chart-review patients from a different era and referral pattern: covariate adjustment cannot remove confounding by eligibility, era or centre. The hazard ratio is the only comparative survival evidence for this drug in this disease, and it should be read as supportive, not definitive.
cards.source: Reiter A et al. Efficacy of avapritinib versus best available therapy in the treatment of advanced systemic mastocytosis. Leukemia. 2022. PMID: 35790816. cards.headline: Synthesis: avapritinib produces deep responses in advanced systemic mastocytosis — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-arm pivotal evidence with an observational comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: avapritinib produces deep responses in advanced systemic mastocytosis — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-arm pivotal evidence with an observational comparison
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: EXPLORER phase 1 (86 treated, 53 response-evaluable), PATHFINDER phase 2 (62 enrolled, 32 response-evaluable at interim), their pooled previously-treated analysis (same programme), and the retrospective comparison against best available therapy (176 versus 141).
cards.result: Response rates of 71–75% with deep reductions in mast-cell burden are consistent across the programme, and the one comparative analysis favours avapritinib for survival. Because the pivotal trials are single-arm and the comparison is retrospective, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit). Intracranial haemorrhage risk — concentrated in patients with platelets below 50 × 10⁹/L — and cognitive effects are the defining harms, and platelet gating is part of safe use. The indolent systemic mastocytosis question is homed at pack #6906 and is not evidence here.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of avapritinib in advanced systemic mastocytosis exists in this record; long-term survival benefit and the size of the intracranial-bleeding risk under modern platelet gating remain estimates from non-randomised data.
cards.source: Synthesis of DeAngelo DJ et al. Nature medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34873347); Gotlib J et al. Nature medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34873345); Reiter A et al. Blood advances. 2022 (PMID: 35640224); Reiter A et al. Leukemia. 2022 (PMID: 35790816), all carded above.

shelves.title: Anselamimab (CAEL-101) added to anti-plasma-cell therapy in AL amyloidosis (CARES)
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed Mayo stage IIIa/IIIb AL amyloidosis, does adding anselamimab to standard anti-plasma-cell therapy (CyBorD, with or without daratumumab), versus standard therapy alone, improve the hierarchical composite of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations?
shelves.mesh: Immunoglobulin Light-chain Amyloidosis/drug therapy,mortality · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Immunoglobulin Light Chains · Immunoglobulin kappa-Chains · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and the headline is the null: in the CARES phase 3 programme (two randomised trials, stage IIIa and IIIb, 406 patients), adding the antifibril antibody anselamimab (CAEL-101; Caelum/AstraZeneca) to standard anti-plasma-cell therapy made no difference on the primary endpoint in the overall population (the treatment made no difference: hierarchical composite win ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.83–1.50, P = .332; all-cause mortality hazard ratio 0.80, P = .290). A published erratum to the CARES report (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(26):2563) is linked to the paper in the record and is incorporated on the CARES card; the figures carded here are those of the record as fetched this session. The split is by light-chain isotype: in the small kappa subgroup (n = 72) the composite favoured anselamimab, with a 62% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.38; nominal P = .012) and a 71% relative reduction in cardiovascular hospitalisations (incidence rate ratio 0.29; nominal P = .028) — nominal, subgroup, small-N findings that are a hypothesis for a kappa-restricted trial, NOT population benefit, and the lambda population showed no clinical benefit. The earlier record explains why the drug was plausible: in the phase 1a/b study 15 of 24 patients (63%) with organ involvement had a therapeutic response, and a phase 2 study (25 patients) found the antibody tolerable alongside CyBorD with or without daratumumab — but tolerability and early organ responses did not translate into a positive phase 3 primary endpoint. The anti-plasma-cell question in AL amyloidosis (daratumumab plus CyBorD) is a different question, homed at pack #2648; this shelf is only about amyloid removal by an antifibril antibody.

cards.headline: CARES phase 3 programme (Wechalekar 2026): primary endpoint NOT met in the overall population — win ratio 1.11 (P = .332) in 406 patients (the treatment made no difference); the kappa subgroup (n = 72) showed a signal at nominal significance only
cards.summary: CARES phase 3 programme (Wechalekar 2026): primary endpoint NOT met in the overall population — win ratio 1.11 (P = .332) in 406 patients (the treatment made no difference); the kappa subgroup (n = 72) showed a signal at nominal significance only
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 programme — two trials (stage IIIa and IIIb) reported together (Wechalekar 2026, CARES)
cards.people: 406 newly diagnosed patients with European-modification Mayo 2004 stage IIIa or IIIb AL amyloidosis, randomised across the two CARES trials (stage IIIa, NCT04512235; stage IIIb, NCT04504825) to anselamimab or placebo, each with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone (CyBorD), with or without daratumumab. The primary endpoint was a hierarchical composite of time to all-cause mortality and frequency of cardiovascular hospitalisations.
cards.result: In the overall population the primary endpoint was not met: win ratio 1.11 (95% CI 0.83–1.50; P = .332); hazard ratio for all-cause mortality 0.80 (95% CI 0.57–1.13; P = .290); cardiovascular hospitalisation rates 0.59 versus 0.89 (P = .145) — the treatment made no difference on the primary composite. In the kappa-isotype subgroup (n = 72), the win ratio was 2.06 (95% CI 0.98–4.31; P = .100), with a 62% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.38; 95% CI 0.17–0.86; nominal P = .012) and a 71% relative reduction in cardiovascular hospitalisations (incidence rate ratio 0.29; 95% CI 0.10–0.87; nominal P = .028), plus improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall score. No clinical benefit was observed in the lambda population. Anselamimab was generally well tolerated, with comparable safety between arms.
cards.watchOut: The kappa findings carry nominal P values in a 72-patient subgroup of a trial whose primary endpoint failed, and the subgroup win ratio itself was not significant (P = .100): subgroup signals after a negative primary are hypothesis-generating, and the paper's own conclusion framing ('significantly improved in kappa') rests on those nominal component P values. A published erratum to this report exists (cited in the source line); the numbers carded are those of the record as fetched this session.

cards.headline: Phase 2 safety study (Valent 2026): anselamimab with CyBorD, with or without daratumumab, was tolerable in 25 patients — no dose-limiting toxicities; serious and fatal events were adjudicated unrelated to the study drug
cards.summary: Phase 2 safety study (Valent 2026): anselamimab with CyBorD, with or without daratumumab, was tolerable in 25 patients — no dose-limiting toxicities; serious and fatal events were adjudicated unrelated to the study drug
cards.type: Open-label phase 2 safety/tolerability study — no comparator (Eur J Cancer 2026)
cards.people: 25 adults with AL amyloidosis (European-modification Mayo stages I–IIIa) and measurable haematological disease in an open-label, sequential-cohort phase 2 dose-selection study: 13 received anselamimab plus CyBorD and 12 received anselamimab plus CyBorD plus daratumumab. Anselamimab was given as 4 weekly infusions, then every 2 weeks to week 50.
cards.result: All 25 participants had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, most mild to moderate. Sixteen (64.0%) had serious events, 4 (16.0%) discontinued study drug because of events, and 3 (12.0%) had fatal events — all serious and fatal events were adjudicated as unrelated to the study drug. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred. Best cardiac responses occurred at week 50 (47.4% of evaluable participants) and best renal responses at weeks 62 and 98 (85.7% of evaluable participants).
cards.watchOut: A 25-patient safety study in stages I–IIIa — a less advanced population than CARES (IIIa/IIIb) — with no comparator: it can support tolerability only, and its week-50/98 organ-response percentages rest on small evaluable subsets.
cards.source: Valent J et al. Safety and tolerability of anselamimab in participants with light chain amyloidosis: Results from a phase 2 study. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 2026. PMID: 42784867. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04304144 (as stated in the record). cards.headline: Phase 1a/b study (Edwards 2021): CAEL-101 was tolerated with no drug-related serious events in 27 patients, and 15 of 24 patients with organ involvement (63%) had a therapeutic response — the early signal the phase 3 programme then tested
cards.summary: Phase 1a/b study (Edwards 2021): CAEL-101 was tolerated with no drug-related serious events in 27 patients, and 15 of 24 patients with organ involvement (63%) had a therapeutic response — the early signal the phase 3 programme then tested
cards.type: Open-label phase 1a/b dose-escalation study — no comparator (Edwards 2021)
cards.people: 27 patients with AL amyloidosis, most with organ involvement, in an open-label phase 1a/b study: phase 1a received a single escalating-dose infusion of CAEL-101 (0.5–500 mg/m²) and phase 1b received 4 weekly infusions. Most patients had deep haematological responses but persistent organ disease before treatment. Single-arm, no comparator.
cards.result: There were no drug-related serious adverse events or dose-limiting toxicities, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Of 24 patients with cardiac, renal, hepatic, gastrointestinal or soft-tissue involvement, 15 (63%) had a therapeutic response by serum biomarkers or objective imaging, with a median time to response of 3 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Organ 'responses' in 24 patients without a control arm, in a disease where biomarkers fluctuate and concurrent anti-plasma-cell therapy was also working: this is precisely the kind of early signal that a phase 3 trial exists to test — and CARES then returned a null primary endpoint.
cards.source: Edwards CV et al. Phase 1a/b study of monoclonal antibody CAEL-101 (11-1F4) in patients with AL amyloidosis. Blood. 2021. PMID: 34521113. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02245867. cards.headline: Phase 1 long-term follow-up (Hughes 2025) — same phase 1 programme, labelled: 22 patients followed for 6 years; median organ and haematological progression-free survival over 5 years and median overall survival over 9 years in this selected cohort
cards.summary: Phase 1 long-term follow-up (Hughes 2025) — same phase 1 programme, labelled: 22 patients followed for 6 years; median organ and haematological progression-free survival over 5 years and median overall survival over 9 years in this selected cohort
cards.type: Long-term follow-up (Research Letter) of the phase 1a/b trial — same programme, labelled (Blood Advances 2025)
cards.people: 22 unique patients from the phase 1a/b CAEL-101 trial carded above (8 in phase 1a and 19 in phase 1b, 5 participating in both), with previously treated systemic AL amyloidosis and persistent organ dysfunction; biomarker data were obtained retrospectively for 6 years after enrolment. This is a follow-up report of the same programme, not a new cohort. Cardiac involvement was present in 12 of 22 (54.6%) and renal involvement in 10 of 22 (45.5%).
cards.result: Through the first 12 months, over 80% of patients with cardiac involvement had at least stable disease, over 40% ultimately achieved a response, and 75% were alive at 5 years; in renal disease, 50% had at least stable disease through 12 months and 40% achieved a renal response. Median organ and haematological progression-free survival was over 5 years and median overall survival over 9 years, in patients enrolled a median of about 1.5 years from diagnosis. The authors report the drug as safe and tolerated over 10 years of observation.
cards.watchOut: Survivor-selected follow-up of 22 phase 1 patients who had already survived a median 1.6 years from diagnosis before enrolment: long median survival in such a cohort reflects who could enrol as much as any drug effect, and there is no comparator. It does not soften the CARES null.
cards.source: Hughes MS et al. Long-term follow-up of patients with AL amyloidosis treated on a phase 1 trial of CAEL-101. Blood advances. 2025. PMID: 40674707. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02245867 (the phase 1 trial, as stated in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: anselamimab added to standard therapy made no difference on the CARES primary endpoint overall — SPLIT, with a kappa-subgroup signal that is a hypothesis, not a population benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: anselamimab added to standard therapy made no difference on the CARES primary endpoint overall — SPLIT, with a kappa-subgroup signal that is a hypothesis, not a population benefit
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the CARES phase 3 programme (406 randomised patients, stages IIIa/IIIb), the phase 2 safety study (25 patients), and the phase 1a/b study (27 patients) with its 22-patient long-term follow-up (same programme).
cards.result: The only randomised efficacy evidence is CARES, and it is negative in the overall population (win ratio 1.11, P = .332 — the treatment made no difference on the primary composite of mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations). Within it, the kappa-isotype subgroup (n = 72) showed nominally significant relative reductions in mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations while the lambda population showed no benefit — that isotype split, not an overall benefit, is what the evidence supports, hence SPLIT. Early-phase organ responses and long-term follow-up describe a tolerable, biologically active antibody; they do not override a negative phase 3 primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: A kappa-restricted confirmatory trial is the only honest next step for the subgroup claim; until one reports, anselamimab should not be described as improving outcomes in AL amyloidosis overall.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wechalekar AD et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2026 (PMID: 42212672; erratum PMID: 42546230 incorporated on the card); Valent J et al. shelves.title: Motixafortide plus G-CSF for stem-cell mobilisation in multiple myeloma (GENESIS)
shelves.question: In patients with multiple myeloma undergoing autologous transplantation, does one dose of motixafortide plus G-CSF, versus placebo plus G-CSF (with plerixafor rescue available), mobilise enough CD34+ cells for collection in ≤2 apheresis days?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Mobilization/methods · Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor/therapeutic use · Antigens, CD34 · Transplantation, Autologous · Heterocyclic Compounds/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one clean phase 3 randomised trial (GENESIS) anchors the shelf, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Against placebo plus G-CSF, one dose of motixafortide (Aphexda, BioLineRx) plus G-CSF was dramatically better at the collection goal: 92.5% versus 26.2% collected at least 6 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg within two apheresis procedures, and 88.8% versus 9.5% did so in a single apheresis. The honest complication is the comparator that matters in many centres: in the single-centre real-world comparison (30 patients per group), motixafortide plus G-CSF was feasible but NOT superior to plerixafor plus G-CSF — yields and procedure times were similar, 27 patients per group reached targets in one day, and motixafortide caused substantially more injection-site and systemic reactions requiring intervention, with extra premedication and monitoring workload; that centre kept plerixafor as its default. The third carded report is a companion, not myeloma evidence: in allogeneic donors, one motixafortide injection (without the GENESIS regimen) collected the target in most donors within two leukaphereses (25 donor–recipient pairs enrolled, 24 evaluable), which supports the drug's mobilisation pharmacology in a different setting. Harms on the GENESIS regimen were mainly transient grade 1/2 injection-site reactions (pain 50%, erythema 27.5%, pruritus 21.3%).

cards.headline: GENESIS phase 3 (Crees 2023): motixafortide plus G-CSF met the collection goal in ≤2 aphereses in 92.5% versus 26.2% on placebo plus G-CSF, and in a single apheresis in 88.8% versus 9.5%
cards.summary: GENESIS phase 3 (Crees 2023): motixafortide plus G-CSF met the collection goal in ≤2 aphereses in 92.5% versus 26.2% on placebo plus G-CSF, and in a single apheresis in 88.8% versus 9.5%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Crees 2023, GENESIS)
cards.people: 122 adults with multiple myeloma undergoing autologous transplantation at 18 sites in five countries, randomised 2:1 to one dose of motixafortide plus G-CSF or placebo plus G-CSF for stem-cell mobilisation (plerixafor rescue available under the protocol). The primary endpoint was collecting at least 6 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg within two apheresis procedures; the secondary endpoint was achieving that goal in one apheresis.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 92.5% on motixafortide plus G-CSF versus 26.2% on placebo plus G-CSF (odds ratio 53.3; 95% CI 14.12–201.33; P < .0001 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates printed here). The single-apheresis goal was met by 88.8% versus 9.5% (odds ratio 118.0; 95% CI 25.36–549.35; P < .0001). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were transient grade 1/2 injection-site reactions (pain 50%, erythema 27.5%, pruritus 21.3%), and the regimen was reported as safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is placebo plus G-CSF, not plerixafor: GENESIS proves motixafortide mobilises far better than G-CSF alone, and says nothing directly about the plerixafor comparison clinicians actually face — that comparison is the next card, and it is not favourable. The enormous odds ratios reflect the very low placebo-arm success rate, not a 50-fold clinical difference.
cards.source: Crees ZD et al. Motixafortide and G-CSF to mobilize hematopoietic stem cells for autologous transplantation in multiple myeloma: a randomized phase 3 trial. Nature medicine. 2023. PMID: 37069359. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03246529. cards.headline: Allogeneic-donor companion (Crees 2023, Blood Advances): one motixafortide injection collected at least 2 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg in ≤2 leukaphereses in 11 of 13 evaluable donors at the 1.0 mg/kg dose — 25 donor–recipient pairs enrolled; a different setting from the myeloma question
cards.summary: Allogeneic-donor companion (Crees 2023, Blood Advances): one motixafortide injection collected at least 2 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg in ≤2 leukaphereses in 11 of 13 evaluable donors at the 1.0 mg/kg dose — 25 donor–recipient pairs enrolled; a different setting from the myeloma question
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 study in allogeneic donors — Research Letter, companion setting (Blood Advances 2023)
cards.people: 25 donor–recipient pairs enrolled in a multicentre, open-label, single-arm, 2-part phase 2 study of motixafortide mobilisation for allogeneic transplantation (24 donors evaluable for the primary endpoint; 22 recipients completed allogeneic transplant; median donor age 55 years). Donors received a single motixafortide injection (1.0 mg/kg in part 1; 1.25 mg/kg in part 2) without the GENESIS G-CSF combination regimen. Companion evidence — a healthy-donor, allogeneic setting, not myeloma autologous mobilisation.
cards.result: In part 1, 11 of 13 evaluable donors (85%) receiving motixafortide 1.0 mg/kg collected at least 2 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg within 2 leukaphereses (median 5.18 × 10⁶), and 8 of those 11 (73%) did so in a single leukapheresis. No serious adverse events, long-term treatment-related adverse events or treatment-related deaths were observed in this report.
cards.watchOut: Different population (healthy allogeneic donors), different regimen (single-agent motixafortide, lower collection target of 2 × 10⁶/kg versus the GENESIS 6 × 10⁶/kg) and no comparator: this card supports that the drug mobilises stem cells, and must not be read as added evidence about myeloma collection success.

cards.headline: Single-centre real-world comparison (Close 2026): motixafortide plus G-CSF was NOT superior to plerixafor plus G-CSF in myeloma — similar yields, 27 of 30 per group reaching targets in 1 day, but substantially more reactions requiring intervention on motixafortide
cards.summary: Single-centre real-world comparison (Close 2026): motixafortide plus G-CSF was NOT superior to plerixafor plus G-CSF in myeloma — similar yields, 27 of 30 per group reaching targets in 1 day, but substantially more reactions requiring intervention on motixafortide
cards.type: Single-centre real-world comparison — prospective cohort versus matched retrospective cohort (Transfusion 2026)
cards.people: 60 patients with multiple myeloma at a single centre: a prospective cohort of 30 receiving motixafortide plus G-CSF compared with a contemporary, covariate-matched retrospective cohort of 30 receiving plerixafor plus G-CSF, under institutional apheresis practice. Observational comparison — labelled as such.
cards.result: Twenty-nine of 30 motixafortide patients completed mobilisation. CD34+ yields and apheresis procedure times were similar between groups, and 27 patients per group reached collection targets in 1 day — motixafortide was feasible but not superior to plerixafor (the treatment made no difference on collection outcomes in this comparison). Motixafortide recipients had substantially higher rates of injection-site and systemic adverse reactions requiring intervention, plus additional workflow demands for premedication and post-injection monitoring; the centre kept plerixafor as its default and reserved motixafortide for selected patients.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 30 patients per group, non-randomised: the 'not superior' finding is a feasibility signal, not an equivalence trial — but it is the only direct plerixafor comparison on this shelf, and its tolerability and workflow findings run against motixafortide.

cards.headline: Synthesis: motixafortide plus G-CSF mobilises far better than G-CSF alone — POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single phase 3 trial; superiority over plerixafor is not shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: motixafortide plus G-CSF mobilises far better than G-CSF alone — POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single phase 3 trial; superiority over plerixafor is not shown
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: GENESIS (122 randomised myeloma patients), the allogeneic-donor phase 2 companion (25 donor–recipient pairs), and the single-centre real-world plerixafor comparison (60 myeloma patients). Each of the three reports has its N confirmed from its record or full text this session, meeting this shelf's floor condition.
cards.result: Against placebo plus G-CSF the effect is large and unambiguous (92.5% vs 26.2% meeting the ≤2-apheresis goal). Against plerixafor plus G-CSF — the active alternative — the only direct comparison found similar collection outcomes with more reactions on motixafortide. A single randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit), and the benefit is specifically 'versus G-CSF alone'.
cards.watchOut: No randomised head-to-head trial against plerixafor, and no carded evidence here on engraftment or transplant outcomes after motixafortide-mobilised grafts in myeloma — collection success is a surrogate for the transplant result.

shelves.title: Tazemetostat for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after at least two prior lines, does tazemetostat, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses in EZH2-mutant and wild-type disease?
shelves.mesh: Lymphoma, Follicular/drug therapy,genetics · Enhancer of Zeste Homolog 2 Protein/antagonists & inhibitors,genetics · Benzamides/therapeutic use · Morpholines · Pyridones · Mutation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — every cohort is single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: response rates have no comparator, and follicular lymphoma can behave indolently, so duration figures need particular care. The pattern across three independent cohorts is consistent and graded by EZH2 status: objective response in about two-thirds of EZH2-mutant disease (69% in the pivotal phase 2, 63.6% in the Chinese bridging study, 76.5% in the small Japanese phase 2) versus about one-third in wild-type disease (35% in both the pivotal and Chinese studies, the latter investigator-assessed). The propensity-matched re-analysis of the pivotal trial is a companion, not a cohort: after matching, wild-type response rose to 50% and progression-free survival looked similar between groups, which warns that part of the mutant-versus-wild-type gap may be baseline differences rather than biology. Harms were modest in the pivotal trial (treatment-related grade 3 or worse events in single digits per type; no treatment-related deaths), though all patients in the Chinese study had treatment-related events and 13.6% had grade 3 or worse. Product naming (clarification exception): tazemetostat (Tazverik, Epizyme/Ipsen). The epithelioid-sarcoma programme is a different, solid-tumour question and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Pivotal phase 2 (Morschhauser 2020): objective response 69% in EZH2-mutant (31 of 45) versus 35% in wild-type (19 of 54) relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma — single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: Pivotal phase 2 (Morschhauser 2020): objective response 69% in EZH2-mutant (31 of 45) versus 35% in wild-type (19 of 54) relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma — single-arm, no comparator
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2 trial — no comparator (Morschhauser 2020)
cards.people: 99 adults with follicular lymphoma (grades 1, 2, 3a or 3b) relapsed or refractory after at least two systemic therapies, at 38 sites, categorised by central EZH2 testing: 45 mutant and 54 wild-type. All received tazemetostat 800 mg orally twice daily in continuous 28-day cycles. Median follow-up was 22.0 months (mutant) and 35.9 months (wild-type).
cards.result: Objective response rate was 69% (95% CI 53–82; 31 of 45) in the mutant cohort and 35% (95% CI 23–49; 19 of 54) in the wild-type cohort. Median duration of response was 10.9 months (mutant) and 13.0 months (wild-type); median progression-free survival was 13.8 and 11.1 months respectively. Treatment-related grade 3 or worse events among all 99 patients included thrombocytopenia (3%), neutropenia (3%) and anaemia (2%); serious treatment-related events occurred in 4% and there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: The mutant and wild-type cohorts were not randomised against each other or against anything else: the 69% versus 35% contrast mixes drug biology with differing prognosis and follow-up (22.0 versus 35.9 months). Response rate in an indolent lymphoma without a control arm cannot show that patients live longer or feel better.
cards.source: Morschhauser F et al. Tazemetostat for patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma: an open-label, single-arm, multicentre, phase 2 trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2020. PMID: 33035457. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01897571. cards.headline: Chinese bridging phase 2 (Cao 2025): response 63.6% in 22 EZH2-mutant patients and 35.0% (investigator-assessed) in 20 wild-type patients — an independent single-arm cohort replicating the pivotal pattern
cards.summary: Chinese bridging phase 2 (Cao 2025): response 63.6% in 22 EZH2-mutant patients and 35.0% (investigator-assessed) in 20 wild-type patients — an independent single-arm cohort replicating the pivotal pattern
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 bridging study — no comparator (EClinicalMedicine 2025)
cards.people: 42 adults with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (grades 1–3a) at 19 sites in China: 22 with EZH2-mutant disease (the registration-intent bridging cohort; 31.8% had three prior lines and 27.3% four or more) and 20 with wild-type disease. All received tazemetostat 800 mg twice daily. Median follow-up 14.4 months in the mutant cohort.
cards.result: In the mutant cohort, independent-review objective response rate was 63.6% (95% CI 40.7–82.8%), clinical benefit rate 90.9%, median duration of response not reached (18-month duration-of-response rate 51.6%), and median progression-free survival 15.4 months. In the wild-type cohort, investigator-assessed response was 35.0% (95% CI 15.4–59.2%), clinical benefit rate 85.0%, and median duration of response 8.4 months. All patients had treatment-related adverse events and 13.6% (mutant cohort) had grade 3 or worse treatment-related events, most commonly haematological.
cards.watchOut: Small cohorts (22 and 20) with wide confidence intervals, and the wild-type response was investigator-assessed rather than independently reviewed — a softer read than the mutant cohort's primary endpoint. It replicates the pivotal trial's pattern; it does not add a comparison.
cards.source: Cao J et al. Efficacy and safety of tazemetostat, an EZH2 inhibitor, in Chinese patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma: a multicentre, single-arm, phase 2 study. EClinicalMedicine. 2025. PMID: 40896460. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05467943. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Japanese phase 2 (Izutsu 2021): response 76.5% in the 17-patient EZH2-mutant follicular lymphoma cohort, with median progression-free survival not reached at 12.9 months — a third independent cohort; its 3-year follow-up kept the response at 70.6%
cards.summary: Japanese phase 2 (Izutsu 2021): response 76.5% in the 17-patient EZH2-mutant follicular lymphoma cohort, with median progression-free survival not reached at 12.9 months — a third independent cohort; its 3-year follow-up kept the response at 70.6%
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2 study — EZH2-mutant disease only (Cancer Science 2021; 3-year follow-up 2024)
cards.people: 20 eligible Japanese patients with relapsed/refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma harbouring an EZH2 mutation: 17 in the follicular lymphoma cohort and 3 in a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma cohort (not this shelf's question). All received tazemetostat 800 mg twice daily until progression or unacceptable toxicity.
cards.result: In the follicular lymphoma cohort the objective response rate was 76.5%, including 35.3% complete and 41.2% partial responses; median progression-free survival was not reached at a median follow-up of 12.9 months (estimated progression-free rates 94.1% at 12 months and 73.2% at 15 months). The most common grade 3 treatment-emergent event was lymphopenia (2 patients); treatment-emergent events led to discontinuation in 4 of the 20 patients overall. In the study's 3-year follow-up report (median follow-up 35.0 months), the follicular cohort's response rate was 70.6% and median progression-free survival remained not reached, with no unexpected grade 3 or worse treatment-related events.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen follicular patients, mutant-only, at an early data cut: 'median progression-free survival not reached' with 12.9 months of follow-up in an indolent lymphoma is a weak durability claim, and the 3 diffuse large B-cell patients in the study are a different disease and are not counted here.
cards.source: Izutsu K et al. Phase II study of tazemetostat for relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with EZH2 mutation in Japan. Cancer science. 2021. PMID: 34159682. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03456726 (as stated in the study's follow-up record). Follow-up report: Izutsu K et al. International journal of hematology. 2024. PMID: 39179948. cards.headline: Propensity-matched re-analysis (Proudman 2022) — a companion analysis of the pivotal trial's own data, not an independent cohort: after matching, wild-type response was 50% versus 71% in mutant, and progression-free survival converged
cards.summary: Propensity-matched re-analysis (Proudman 2022) — a companion analysis of the pivotal trial's own data, not an independent cohort: after matching, wild-type response was 50% versus 71% in mutant, and progression-free survival converged
cards.type: Propensity-matched secondary analysis of the pivotal trial — companion, not independent evidence (Oncotarget 2022)
cards.people: The pivotal phase 2 trial's 99 patients (45 mutant, 54 wild-type), re-analysed with 1:1 propensity matching on baseline characteristics, yielding 56 matched participants (28 per group). Same trial, labelled as a companion.
cards.result: Before matching, response rates were 35% (wild-type) and 69% (mutant) and median progression-free survival 11.1 versus 13.8 months. After matching, response rates were 50% (95% CI 31–69) in wild-type and 71% (95% CI 54–88) in mutant, and median progression-free survival was 14.3 versus 14.8 months — suggesting part of the apparent mutant advantage reflected baseline disparities between the cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Matching discarded 43 of 99 patients and can only adjust for measured characteristics; the narrowed gap is a caution about the cohort contrast, not proof that mutation status is irrelevant.
cards.source: Proudman DG et al. Tazemetostat in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma: a propensity score-matched analysis of E7438-G000-101 trial outcomes. Oncotarget. 2022. PMID: 35574216. Registry ID: none in the record (analysis of the trial registered as NCT01897571). cards.headline: Synthesis: tazemetostat produces responses in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, more often in EZH2-mutant disease — POSSIBLE (benefit), entirely single-arm evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: tazemetostat produces responses in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, more often in EZH2-mutant disease — POSSIBLE (benefit), entirely single-arm evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: three independent single-arm cohorts (pivotal phase 2, 99 patients; Chinese bridging study, 42 patients; Japanese phase 2, 17 follicular patients) plus a propensity-matched re-analysis of the pivotal trial (companion). The third independent on-question cohort (Japanese phase 2) was verified at build, meeting this shelf's floor condition.
cards.result: Mutant-disease response rates of 63.6–76.5% and wild-type rates of about 35% are consistent across three cohorts from three regions, with generally manageable toxicity. But no cohort has a comparator, response is a surrogate, and the matched re-analysis shrinks the mutant-versus-wild-type contrast — so the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit), with the EZH2 gradient stated as observed, not proven causal.
cards.watchOut: Whether tazemetostat improves survival or quality of life against chemoimmunotherapy, lenalidomide-based therapy or bispecific antibodies is untested in this record; an ongoing randomised combination trial may change the picture but reports no results here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Morschhauser F et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2020 (PMID: 33035457); Cao J et al. EClinicalMedicine. 2025 (PMID: 40896460); Izutsu K et al. Cancer science. 2021 (PMID: 34159682); Proudman DG et al. Oncotarget. 2022 (PMID: 35574216), all carded above.

shelves.title: Heart-rate recovery after exercise: normal distribution, the ≤12-beat threshold and reproducibility
shelves.question: In healthy adults, how fast does heart rate fall after maximal exercise — the normal heart-rate-recovery distribution at 1 and 2 minutes by age, sex and fitness, its within-person reproducibility, and where the abnormal threshold (≤12 beats at 1 minute) came from?
shelves.mesh: Heart Rate/physiology · Exercise Test · Reference Values · Recovery of Function · Reproducibility of Results · Vagus Nerve/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, exercise and autonomic chapters; Boron & Boulpaep, cardiovascular control — recovery of heart rate after exercise is a function of vagal reactivation, as the Cole record itself states). Three different questions are often confused, and the carded record separates them. (1) Where the abnormal line came from: Cole's 1999 referred-patient cohort (2,428 adults having diagnostic exercise testing — NOT healthy volunteers, and labelled so on its card) defined an abnormal 1-minute recovery as a fall of 12 beats/min or less and showed it predicted death (relative risk 4.0 unadjusted, 2.0 adjusted). (2) The normal distribution: a 2025 cycle-ergometry study of 9,917 tested subjects derived normal values from its 2,242 apparently healthy members, defining blunted recovery as below the 5th percentile for age — all indices were age-dependent — and blunted HRR1/HRR2 remained the strongest mortality predictors (hazard ratios 1.70 and 1.57). (3) Reproducibility: in UK Biobank repeat testing about 3 years apart, heart-rate dynamics during exercise and 1-minute recovery were highly reproducible within a person (intra-individual correlations 0.70–0.81 for the dynamics indices), with abnormal values consistent about 60–70% of the time. The mechanism of the fall itself — a vagal first phase and a sympathetic tail — is a separate shelf (pack #6800) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Recovery protocol matters: Cole used a symptom-limited treadmill protocol and the 2025 study cycle ergometry, and active versus passive recovery changes the numbers, so values are carded per-protocol.

cards.headline: Cole 1999 (threshold-deriving cohort, referred patients): a 1-minute heart-rate recovery of ≤12 beats/min was abnormal — present in 26% — and predicted death (relative risk 4.0 unadjusted, 2.0 adjusted)
cards.summary: Cole 1999 (threshold-deriving cohort, referred patients): a 1-minute heart-rate recovery of ≤12 beats/min was abnormal — present in 26% — and predicted death (relative risk 4.0 unadjusted, 2.0 adjusted)
cards.people: 2,428 consecutive adults (mean age 57 ± 12 years; 63% men) without heart failure, coronary revascularisation or pacemakers, undergoing symptom-limited exercise testing with thallium single-photon-emission computed tomography for diagnostic purposes, followed for six years. This is a referred patient cohort, not healthy volunteers — its role is threshold derivation.
cards.result: Heart-rate recovery was the fall from peak exercise to one minute after cessation; ≤12 beats/min was defined as abnormal and occurred in 639 patients (26%). There were 213 deaths. A low recovery value was strongly predictive of death in univariate analysis (relative risk, 4.0; 95% confidence interval, 3.0 to 5.2; P < 0.001) and remained predictive after adjustment for age, sex, medications, perfusion defects, risk factors, resting heart rate, exercise heart-rate change and workload (adjusted relative risk, 2.0; 95% confidence interval, 1.5 to 2.7; P < 0.001). Both relative risks are relative measures, printed beside the cohort's absolute mortality experience (213 deaths among 2,428 patients over six years).
cards.watchOut: The ≤12 beats/min line was derived in symptomatic referred patients (mean age 57) on a treadmill protocol, not in healthy volunteers — applying it as a 'normal value' for healthy people is an extrapolation; its authority is prognostic, in the population it came from.

threshold-deriving referred-patient cohort (cole 1999) 2,428 consecutive adults (mean age 57 ± 12 years; 63% men) without heart failure, coronary revascularisation or pacemakers, undergoing symptom-limited exercise testing with thallium single-photon-emission computed tomography for diagnostic purposes, followed for six years. this is a referred patient cohort, not healthy volunteers — its role is threshold derivation. heart-rate recovery was the fall from peak exercise to one minute after cessation; ≤12 beats/min was defined as abnormal and occurred in 639 patients (26%). there were 213 deaths. a low recovery value was strongly predictive of death in univariate analysis (relative risk, 4.0; 95% confidence interval, 3.0 to 5.2; p < 0.001) and remained predictive after adjustment for age, sex, medications, perfusion defects, risk factors, resting heart rate, exercise heart-rate change and workload (adjusted relative risk, 2.0; 95% confidence interval, 1.5 to 2.7; p < 0.001). both relative risks are relative measures, printed beside the cohort's absolute mortality experience (213 deaths among 2,428 patients over six years). the ≤12 beats/min line was derived in symptomatic referred patients (mean age 57) on a treadmill protocol, not in healthy volunteers — applying it as a 'normal value' for healthy people is an extrapolation; its authority is prognostic, in the population it came from. cole cr et al. heart-rate recovery immediately after exercise as a predictor of mortality. the new england journal of medicine. 1999. pmid: 10536127. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · analysis of variance · cohort studies · exercise/physiology · exercise test · female · heart rate/physiology · humans · male · middle aged · mortality · prognosis · proportional hazards models · thallium radioisotopes · tomography, emission-computed, single-photon · vagus nerve/physiology

cards.headline: Jou 2025: normal heart-rate recovery values from 2,242 apparently healthy members of 9,917 cycle-test subjects — recovery is age-dependent, and blunted HRR1/HRR2 (below the 5th percentile) carried hazard ratios of 1.70 and 1.57 for death
cards.summary: Jou 2025: normal heart-rate recovery values from 2,242 apparently healthy members of 9,917 cycle-test subjects — recovery is age-dependent, and blunted HRR1/HRR2 (below the 5th percentile) carried hazard ratios of 1.70 and 1.57 for death
cards.type: Normative-values and prognosis study, cycle ergometry (Jou 2025)
cards.people: 9,917 subjects (45% females) aged 18–85 years who performed a cycle exercise test; normal values for peak heart rate, heart-rate reserve and heart-rate recovery at 1 and 2 minutes (HRR1, HRR2) were defined from the 2,242 individuals who were apparently healthy; mortality was followed for a median of 8.6 years.
cards.result: All heart-rate indices were age-dependent and independent predictors of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Blunted HRR1 and HRR2 (below the 5th percentile) were the strongest predictors of all-cause mortality in the overall population (HRR1 hazard ratio 1.70, 95% confidence interval 1.49–1.94; HRR2 hazard ratio 1.57, 1.37–1.79 — relative measures) and in subjects with normal exercise capacity (HRR1 hazard ratio 1.96, 1.61–2.39; HRR2 hazard ratio 1.76, 1.46–2.12). Combining blunted indices added prognostic value (HRR1 + HRR2 hazard ratio 1.96, 1.68–2.29). The record's abstract defines the 5th-percentile approach but does not print the beats/min values of those percentiles by age, so no percentile table is quoted here.
cards.watchOut: Cycle ergometry values are not interchangeable with treadmill values (peak heart rate and recovery differ by modality), and the 'apparently healthy' reference subset was drawn from people referred for exercise testing — a cleaner base than Cole's symptomatic cohort, but not a random population sample.

cards.headline: Orini 2017 UK Biobank: heart-rate dynamics in exercise and 1-minute recovery are reproducible within a person over about 3 years (intra-individual correlations 0.70–0.81; abnormal values consistent 60–70% of the time)
cards.summary: Orini 2017 UK Biobank: heart-rate dynamics in exercise and 1-minute recovery are reproducible within a person over about 3 years (intra-individual correlations 0.70–0.81; abnormal values consistent 60–70% of the time)
cards.people: 1,187 individuals from the UK Biobank cardio physical-fitness assessment who repeated a standard (submaximal) exercise stress test twice, a mean of 34.2 ± 2.8 months apart; 821 met inclusion criteria for the reproducibility analysis (peak workload difference between tests ≤10 W).
cards.result: Intra-individual correlation between the two tests' heart-rate profiles was very high and higher than inter-individual correlation (0.92 ± 0.08 vs 0.87 ± 0.11, P < 0.01). Index correlations: ρ = 0.81 for maximum heart rate during exercise, ρ = 0.71 for minimum heart rate during recovery, ρ = 0.70 for heart-rate changes during exercise and recovery, and ρ = 0.64 for resting heart rate. Bland–Altman plots showed good agreement with a small consistent bias, and the intra-individual consistency of abnormal values was about 60–70%.
cards.watchOut: The UK Biobank test was submaximal, so this card speaks to reproducibility of the dynamics and of the 1-minute recovery window as measured there — not to maximal-test HRR values; and 60–70% consistency of 'abnormal' labels means a single borderline test mislabels a substantial minority on retest.
cards.source: Orini M et al. Long-term intra-individual reproducibility of heart rate dynamics during exercise and recovery in the UK Biobank cohort. PloS one. 2017. PMID: 28873397. cards.headline: Synthesis: heart rate normally falls briskly in the first 1–2 minutes after maximal exercise; ≤12 beats at 1 minute is the (patient-derived) abnormal line, age-specific 5th percentiles are the modern normal-value approach, and the measurement is reproducible over years
cards.summary: Synthesis: heart rate normally falls briskly in the first 1–2 minutes after maximal exercise; ≤12 beats at 1 minute is the (patient-derived) abnormal line, age-specific 5th percentiles are the modern normal-value approach, and the measurement is reproducible over years
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: Cole's 2,428 referred patients (threshold derivation), Jou's 9,917 cycle-test subjects with 2,242 apparently healthy (normal values), and Orini's 821 UK Biobank repeat testers (reproducibility).
cards.result: The distribution question, the threshold question and the reproducibility question have three different homes in the record. Normal values are age-dependent and best expressed as age-specific percentiles (below the 5th percentile = blunted, Jou 2025); the widely used ≤12 beats/min at 1 minute comes from Cole's referred cohort, where it carried an adjusted relative risk of death of 2.0; and within a person the recovery dynamics repeat well over ~3 years (ρ ≈ 0.70–0.81). The autonomic mechanism of the fall — vagal reactivation first, sympathetic withdrawal after — is homed at pack #6800 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: vagal-reactivation physiology is textbook-settled and the distribution, threshold and reproducibility limbs are each supported by a large fetched record.
cards.watchOut: No carded record prints a full beats/min percentile table by age and sex in its abstract — the 2025 normal values exist as 5th-percentile definitions in the full text. Treadmill (Cole) and cycle (Jou) protocols, and active versus passive recovery, give different numbers; a value is only interpretable beside its protocol.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cole CR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1999 (PMID: 10536127); Jou J et al. European journal of preventive cardiology. 2025 (PMID: 39325720); Orini M et al. shelves.title: Left-ventricular global longitudinal strain: normal values by speckle-tracking echocardiography
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are normal left-ventricular global longitudinal strain values by speckle-tracking echocardiography — the meta-analytic normal range, the EACVI NORRE reference ranges, and how much do vendor, sex and age shift them?
shelves.mesh: Reference Values · Echocardiography/methods · Ventricular Function, Left/physiology · Healthy Volunteers · Sex Factors · Age Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the central range, with vendor dependence as a core caveat (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cardiac muscle / ventricular function; strain imaging itself is textbook-thin, as the slate row directs, and the shelf rests on the primary measurement literature). Two meta-analyses and one large multicentre reference study converge on the same centre: mean left-ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS) in healthy adults is about −19% to −20% (2D meta-analysis: −19.7%, with study means spanning −15.9% to −22.1%; 3D meta-analysis: −19.05%, study means −15.8% to −23.4%). The EACVI NORRE study (549 healthy volunteers, vendor-independent analysis software) puts the lowest expected value at −16.7% in men and −17.8% in women — that is, a healthy GLS is generally more negative than about −17%. What is NOT settled is a single universal cut-off: between-study heterogeneity is very high (I² ≈ 99% in the 3D analysis), analysis software was consistently associated with the reported values, and systolic blood pressure — not age, sex, frame rate or equipment — tracked GLS variation in the 2D meta-regression. So the honest summary is a centre (about −19.5%), a lower reference boundary (about −17% by NORRE), and a standing instruction to interpret a value beside its vendor/software and the patient's blood pressure, never against one universal number.

cards.headline: Yingchoncharoen 2013 meta-analysis (2,597 subjects, 24 studies): normal 2D GLS mean −19.7% (95% CI −20.4 to −18.9), study means spanning −15.9% to −22.1%
cards.summary: Yingchoncharoen 2013 meta-analysis (2,597 subjects, 24 studies): normal 2D GLS mean −19.7% (95% CI −20.4 to −18.9), study means spanning −15.9% to −22.1%
cards.people: 2,597 healthy normal subjects pooled from 24 studies reporting left-ventricular strain by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography (searched through August 2011); effects of demographic, haemodynamic and equipment variables were sought by meta-regression.
cards.result: Reported normal GLS values varied from −15.9% to −22.1% (mean, −19.7%; 95% CI, −20.4% to −18.9%). Normal global circumferential strain varied from −20.9% to −27.8% (mean, −23.3%; 95% CI, −24.6% to −22.1%) and global radial strain from 35.1% to 59.0% (mean, 47.3%; 95% CI, 43.6% to 51.0%). There was significant between-study heterogeneity; in meta-regression, blood pressure — but not age, gender, frame rate or equipment — was associated with variation in normal GLS values.
cards.watchOut: A mean of −19.7% with study means spread over six percentage points is a centre, not a cut-off: an individual laboratory's healthy range can sit well inside or outside another's, and the blood-pressure association means a GLS read without the day's systolic pressure is only half-interpreted.
cards.source: Yingchoncharoen T et al. Normal ranges of left ventricular strain: a meta-analysis. Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography. 2013. PMID: 23218891.
