cards.headline: Truong 2019 3D meta-analysis (2,346 subjects, 33 datasets): normal 3D GLS mean −19.05%, but heterogeneity I² = 99% and analysis software significantly shifted every strain value
cards.summary: Truong 2019 3D meta-analysis (2,346 subjects, 33 datasets): normal 3D GLS mean −19.05%, but heterogeneity I² = 99% and analysis software significantly shifted every strain value
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of normal 3D strain ranges (Truong 2019)
cards.people: 2,346 healthy subjects pooled from 33 datasets reporting left-ventricular strain by three-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography (searches through January 2019); demographic, clinical and vendor variables assessed by meta-regression.
cards.result: Normal mean GLS across studies varied from −15.80% to −23.40% (mean, −19.05%; 95% CI, −18.18% to −19.93%; I² = 99.0%). Global circumferential strain mean was −22.42%, global radial strain 47.48% and global area strain −35.03%, all with I² above 99%. Software for strain analysis was consistently associated with variations in normal strain values (GLS: P = .016; GCS: P < .001; GRS: P < .001; GAS: P < .001).
cards.watchOut: Three-dimensional and two-dimensional strain are different measurements and their ranges must not be interchanged; with I² at 99%, the pooled mean describes the literature's centre, while any single patient's classification still depends on the local platform and software version.

cards.headline: Sugimoto 2017 EACVI NORRE study (549 healthy volunteers, 22 centres): lowest expected longitudinal strain −16.7% in men and −17.8% in women with vendor-independent software
cards.summary: Sugimoto 2017 EACVI NORRE study (549 healthy volunteers, 22 centres): lowest expected longitudinal strain −16.7% in men and −17.8% in women with vendor-independent software
cards.people: 549 healthy subjects (mean age 45.6 ± 13.3 years) enrolled at 22 collaborating institutions of the Normal Reference Ranges for Echocardiography (NORRE) study; all 2D datasets were analysed with one vendor-independent software package to allow homogeneous measurement across equipment.
cards.result: The lowest expected values of LV strain (mean ± 1.96 SD) were −16.7% in men and −17.8% in women for longitudinal strain, −22.3% and −23.6% for circumferential strain, 20.6% and 21.5% for radial strain, and 2.2 and 1.9 degrees for twist. In multivariable analysis, longitudinal strain decreased with age while circumferential and radial strain moved oppositely, and male gender was associated with lower strain values. Inter-vendor differences persisted for circumferential and radial strain despite the vendor-independent software, but importantly no inter-vendor differences were noted in longitudinal strain.
cards.watchOut: NORRE's harmonised analysis is the best-case scenario — one software package for all comers — and real-world laboratories using vendor-native software should expect wider scatter than NORRE's limits imply, particularly for circumferential and radial strain, where vendor differences survived even here.
cards.source: Sugimoto T et al. Echocardiographic reference ranges for normal left ventricular 2D strain: results from the EACVI NORRE study. European heart journal. Cardiovascular Imaging. 2017. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy GLS centres on about −19% to −20%, with a NORRE lower reference boundary near −17%; software/vendor and blood pressure move the value, so no single universal cut-off exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy GLS centres on about −19% to −20%, with a NORRE lower reference boundary near −17%; software/vendor and blood pressure move the value, so no single universal cut-off exists
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the 2D meta-analysis (2,597 subjects, 24 studies), the 3D meta-analysis (2,346 subjects, 33 datasets) and the EACVI NORRE reference study (549 healthy volunteers, 22 centres).
cards.result: The three records agree on the centre (mean GLS −19.7% by 2D, −19.05% by 3D) and NORRE supplies sex-specific lower limits (−16.7% men, −17.8% women) obtained under harmonised analysis. They also agree on the caveats: heterogeneity is extreme, analysis software significantly shifts values, and systolic blood pressure tracks GLS. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the central range and its lower boundary under stated platform conditions; a platform-free universal threshold is explicitly not claimed.
cards.watchOut: A further strain synthesis located during building had an empty abstract in PubMed and was not used, in line with the rule that unverifiable records are not carded. Serial measurements in one patient should stay on one platform and software version; a change of vendor can manufacture an apparent change in GLS.

shelves.title: QT interval distribution: QTc by age, sex and correction formula
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the distribution of the QT interval — how QTc varies by age, sex and heart-rate correction formula (Bazett vs Fridericia vs Framingham linear), and what fraction of a general population exceeds the conventional 450/470 ms thresholds under each formula?
shelves.mesh: Electrocardiography · Heart Rate/physiology · Long QT Syndrome/epidemiology · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ECG chapters — the QT interval lengthens as heart rate falls, so every quoted QT is a corrected QT and the correction formula is part of the measurement). The carded record makes one point four ways: the formula reclassifies the same ECG. Bazett's square-root formula (1920) was derived from only 39 young subjects; in the Framingham baseline ECGs (5,018 adults) it overcorrected at fast heart rates and undercorrected at slow ones, while a simple linear correction (QTLC = QT + 0.154 × (1 − RR)) fitted better. In 31,558 young active people, Bazett again performed least favourably at removing the heart-rate effect and Fridericia best, and Bazett-based cut points captured less than half of those in the top percentiles of uncorrected QT — the authors propose Fridericia thresholds of 460 ms (men) and 470 ms (women), with 485 ms marking prolongation. In a general population of 20,261 adults, corrected QT averaged about 413–419 ms in men and 419–422 ms in women across iron-store strata — women run longer than men, as every record here agrees. The multiparameter healthy-subject study adds that QT dispersion and related indices correlate with age and that simultaneous ECG parameters are reproducible. Practical reading: always print the formula beside the value; a QTc of 460 ms by Bazett at a fast heart rate and 460 ms by Fridericia are not the same finding.

cards.headline: Sagie 1992 Framingham (5,018 adults): Bazett's formula overcorrects at fast heart rates and undercorrects at slow ones; a linear correction (QTLC = QT + 0.154 × (1 − RR)) fitted better
cards.summary: Sagie 1992 Framingham (5,018 adults): Bazett's formula overcorrects at fast heart rates and undercorrects at slow ones; a linear correction (QTLC = QT + 0.154 × (1 − RR)) fitted better
cards.people: 5,018 subjects (2,239 men, 2,779 women; mean age 44 years, range 28–62) from the Framingham Heart Study, persons with coronary artery disease excluded; QT measured on the initial baseline electrocardiogram and compared across sex-specific deciles of RR interval.
cards.result: Mean RR interval was 0.81 s (range 0.5–1.47), heart rate 74 beats/min (range 41–120), and mean QT 0.35 s (range 0.24–0.49) in men and 0.36 s (range 0.26–0.48) in women. The linear regression model yielded the correction QTLC = QT + 0.154 (1 − RR) for a reference RR of 1 s, applying to men and women. Bazett's formula — derived in 1920 from observations in only 39 young subjects — overcorrects QT at fast heart rates and undercorrects it at low heart rates; lower and upper limits of normal QT in relation to RR were generated from these data.
cards.watchOut: Framingham's age range (28–62) and exclusion of coronary disease bound the claim: the linear formula was fitted in middle-aged adults at resting rates of 41–120 beats/min and should not be extrapolated to children, athletes at very low rates, or tachycardias beyond the fitted range.
cards.source: Sagie A et al. An improved method for adjusting the QT interval for heart rate (the Framingham Heart Study). The American journal of cardiology. 1992. PMID: 1519533. cards.headline: Henriksen 2016 (20,261 general-population adults): corrected QT averaged about 413–419 ms in men and 419–422 ms in women across iron-store strata — women longer than men throughout
cards.summary: Henriksen 2016 (20,261 general-population adults): corrected QT averaged about 413–419 ms in men and 419–422 ms in women across iron-store strata — women longer than men throughout
cards.people: 20,261 individuals from the Danish General Suburban Population Study; QT interval examined by ferritin concentration, transferrin saturation, iron and transferrin concentrations and haemochromatosis genotype (C282Y/C282Y), with a meta-analysis of thalassaemia major case–control studies.
cards.result: Age- and C-reactive-protein-adjusted mean corrected QT for ferritin ≥99th percentile versus the 25th–<50th percentile was 418.9 ms vs 412.7 ms in men (P < 0.001) and 422.4 ms vs 419.1 ms in women (P = 0.78); for transferrin saturation the corresponding values were 417.6 vs 412.6 ms in men (P = 0.02) and 421.5 vs 419.4 ms in women (P = 0.86). Haemochromatosis genotype was not associated with QT length. The record's abstract does not name the correction formula used, so the values are printed here as 'corrected QT as reported' and must not be attributed to a specific formula.
cards.watchOut: The study's question was iron stores, not normative distribution — its QTc means are printed here as population-distribution evidence (the largest fetched sample), and its sex gap (women ~3–6 ms longer across strata) is the distribution finding; the unnamed correction formula is a real limitation for cross-study comparison.

cards.headline: Michelucci 2002 (105 healthy subjects, 21–80 years): simultaneously measured ECG parameters — including Bazett and Fridericia QTc — were reproducible, with QT dispersion and related indices correlating with age
cards.summary: Michelucci 2002 (105 healthy subjects, 21–80 years): simultaneously measured ECG parameters — including Bazett and Fridericia QTc — were reproducible, with QT dispersion and related indices correlating with age
cards.people: 105 healthy subjects (age range 21–80 years), equally distributed for age decades and sex, recorded with extended-length ECG (5-minute recordings at 5 MHz sampling); 30 subjects repeated three additional recordings 30 minutes apart on a second day for reproducibility.
cards.result: The panel recorded RR interval, QRS duration, QT corrected by the Bazett and Fridericia formulae, QT dispersion, T-wave complexity, activation-recovery interval dispersion, RR variability and filtered-QRS measures simultaneously. QRS duration, activation-recovery interval dispersion and filtered QRS differed between the sexes; the standard deviation of RR intervals, T-wave complexity and QT dispersion were significantly correlated with age; and reproducibility was good for each parameter. The record's abstract reports agreement with published values but does not print the QTc numbers themselves, so none are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: N = 105 spread across six decades and two sexes leaves about nine subjects per cell — adequate for reproducibility and correlation claims, far too thin for percentile limits; this card supports the measurement's stability and age correlations, not threshold values.
cards.source: Michelucci A et al. Simultaneous assessment of electrocardiographic parameters for risk stratification: validation in healthy subjects. Italian heart journal. 2002. PMID: 12066563. cards.headline: Hadley 2019 (31,558 young active people): Bazett performed least favourably and Fridericia best at removing the heart-rate effect; proposed Fridericia thresholds 460 ms (men), 470 ms (women), 485 ms for marked prolongation
cards.summary: Hadley 2019 (31,558 young active people): Bazett performed least favourably and Fridericia best at removing the heart-rate effect; proposed Fridericia thresholds 460 ms (men), 470 ms (women), 485 ms for marked prolongation
cards.type: Population formula-comparison study, young active cohort (Hadley 2019)
cards.people: 31,558 young active individuals undergoing ECGs for preparticipation sports or community screening (2,174 grade school, 18,547 high school, 10,822 college; mean age 17 years, range 12–35; 45% female; 67% white, 11% of African descent).
cards.result: Bazett performed least favourably for removing the effect of heart rate, whereas Fridericia performed best and fit the raw data most closely (R of 0.65), including at screening-relevant percentiles. Recommended risk cut points using Bazett's correction identified less than half of the athletes in the 99th or 99.5th percentiles of the uncorrected QT by heart-rate range; use of Fridericia correction increased capture rates by over 50% (relative increase, as reported). The authors support Fridericia-corrected thresholds of 460 ms for men and 470 ms for women (and 485 ms for marked prolongation) for the preparticipation examination, rather than Bazett correction.
cards.watchOut: A young athletic screening population (mean age 17): its thresholds answer the screening question in the young, and its formula ranking (Fridericia over Bazett) agrees with Framingham's middle-aged data — but percentile positions in older or unwell populations will differ, and 'capture' here is percentile capture, not proven sudden-death prevention.
cards.source: Hadley D et al. QT Corrections for Long QT Risk Assessment: Implications for the Preparticipation Examination. Clinical journal of sport medicine. 2019. PMID: 31241530. cards.headline: Synthesis: QTc is a formula-dependent number — Bazett (from 39 young subjects in 1920) distorts at rate extremes, linear and Fridericia corrections fit populations better, and women run about 3–6 ms longer than men
cards.summary: Synthesis: QTc is a formula-dependent number — Bazett (from 39 young subjects in 1920) distorts at rate extremes, linear and Fridericia corrections fit populations better, and women run about 3–6 ms longer than men
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: Framingham's 5,018 adults (formula derivation), the Danish general population of 20,261 (distribution), Michelucci's 105 healthy subjects (reproducibility and age correlations), and Hadley's 31,558 young active people (formula comparison and thresholds).
cards.result: Across 57,000 people in four records, the same conclusions recur: corrected QT is longer in women; the correction formula changes who crosses any threshold, with Bazett worst at heart-rate extremes in both a middle-aged cohort and a young athletic one; and simultaneous ECG parameters are reproducible enough that a discordant QTc usually reflects the formula or the rate, not measurement noise. Conventional 450/470 ms thresholds are Bazett-era conventions; the Fridericia-based proposal (460 men / 470 women, 485 marked) is the record's modern alternative. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: rate-dependence of QT and the formulae's behaviour are textbook-settled and concordant across the fetched population records.
cards.watchOut: One carded record (Henriksen 2016) does not name its correction formula in the abstract, and one (Michelucci 2002) prints no QTc values there — both are used only for what their records confirm. Any QTc quoted without its formula and the heart rate at measurement is, on this evidence, an incomplete measurement.

shelves.title: Resting pulmonary artery pressures in healthy humans: catheter and echocardiographic reference values
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are resting pulmonary artery pressures — mean pulmonary artery pressure and systolic pressure by invasive catheterisation and by echocardiographic tricuspid-regurgitant velocity — and how much do they rise with age, body-mass index and exercise?
shelves.mesh: Reference Values · Pulmonary Artery/physiology · Echocardiography, Doppler · Cardiac Catheterization/standards · Tricuspid Valve Insufficiency/diagnostic imaging · Age Factors · Body Mass Index
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, pulmonary circulation; Boron & Boulpaep, pulmonary haemodynamics). The invasive and echocardiographic records tell one consistent story. By right-heart catheterisation (systematic review: 1,187 healthy individuals, 47 studies), resting mean pulmonary artery pressure is 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, essentially independent of sex and ethnicity, slightly higher after age 50 (14.7 ± 4.0) than under 30 (12.8 ± 3.1), and it rarely exceeds 20 mmHg at rest — while exercise values are a different matter, frequently exceeding 30 mmHg in people over 50 even at mild exercise (29.4 ± 8.4 mmHg). By echocardiography, pulmonary artery systolic pressure in 3,790 echocardiographically normal subjects averaged 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg, with an upper 95% limit of 37.2 mmHg in lower-risk subjects and values over 40 mmHg in 6% of those over 50 and 5% of those with BMI over 30 — age and BMI move the echo number. The tricuspid-regurgitant velocity that feeds the echo estimate averages about 2.0 m/s in healthy adults (prospective cohort 2.01 ± 0.29 m/s; pooled 1.96 m/s), with a 95% quantile of 2.55 m/s. Reading: a resting mean pressure near 14 mmHg and a TR velocity under about 2.5 m/s are the healthy centre and edge; echo systolic estimates up to about 40 mmHg occur in healthy older or heavier people and are not, alone, pulmonary hypertension.

cards.headline: Kovacs 2009 systematic review of invasive data (1,187 healthy individuals, 47 studies): resting mean pulmonary artery pressure 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, rarely exceeding 20 mmHg
cards.summary: Kovacs 2009 systematic review of invasive data (1,187 healthy individuals, 47 studies): resting mean pulmonary artery pressure 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, rarely exceeding 20 mmHg
cards.type: Systematic review of invasive catheterisation data (Kovacs 2009)
cards.people: 1,187 healthy individuals from 47 right-heart-catheterisation studies in 13 countries, stratified by sex, age, geographical origin, body position and exercise level.
cards.result: Mean pulmonary artery pressure (Ppa) at rest was 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, independent of sex and ethnicity; posture mattered slightly (supine 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, upright 13.6 ± 3.1 mmHg) and age modestly (<30 years: 12.8 ± 3.1 mmHg; 30–50 years: 12.9 ± 3.0 mmHg; ≥50 years: 14.7 ± 4.0 mmHg). Resting Ppa rarely exceeds 20 mmHg. During mild exercise Ppa was 19.4 ± 4.8 mmHg under age 50 versus 29.4 ± 8.4 mmHg at ≥50 years (P < 0.001), so exercise values frequently exceed 30 mmHg in older healthy people. (The review notes the then-current guideline diagnostic lines of 25 mmHg at rest and 30 mmHg on exercise as the context its data test.)
cards.watchOut: A review of many small catheter studies rather than one cohort — its strength is the pooled N of 1,187 with consistent technique (direct pressure measurement); its exercise limb warns against importing the resting 'rarely above 20' rule into exercise, where healthy older people routinely exceed the old 30 mmHg line.
cards.source: Kovacs G et al. Pulmonary arterial pressure during rest and exercise in healthy subjects: a systematic review. The European respiratory journal. 2009. PMID: 19324955. (the review notes the then-current guideline diagnostic lines of 25 mmhg at rest and 30 mmhg on exercise as the context its data test.) a review of many small catheter studies rather than one cohort — its strength is the pooled n of 1,187 with consistent technique (direct pressure measurement); its exercise limb warns against importing the resting 'rarely above 20' rule into exercise, where healthy older people routinely exceed the old 30 mmhg line. kovacs g et al. pulmonary arterial pressure during rest and exercise in healthy subjects: a systematic review. the european respiratory journal. 2009. pmid: 19324955. registry id: none in the record. mesh: blood pressure · cardiac catheterization/standards · exercise · heart ventricles · humans · hypertension, pulmonary/diagnosis,physiopathology · reference values · rest

cards.headline: McQuillan 2001 (3,790 echocardiographically normal subjects): mean pulmonary artery systolic pressure 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg, upper 95% limit 37.2 mmHg, with >40 mmHg in 6% of those over 50
cards.summary: McQuillan 2001 (3,790 echocardiographically normal subjects): mean pulmonary artery systolic pressure 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg, upper 95% limit 37.2 mmHg, with >40 mmHg in 6% of those over 50
cards.people: 3,790 subjects (2,432 women, 1,358 men; ages 1–89 years) with a measured pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) drawn from 15,596 normal Doppler transthoracic echocardiograms in a clinical database of 102,818 patients; PASP calculated by the modified Bernoulli equation with right atrial pressure assumed to be 10 mmHg.
cards.result: Mean PASP was 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg (range 15–57 mmHg). PASP was independently associated with age, body mass index, male sex, left-ventricular posterior wall thickness and ejection fraction (all P < 0.001). The estimated upper 95% limit among lower-risk subjects was 37.2 mmHg; a PASP over 40 mmHg was found in 6% of those over 50 years old and 5% of those with BMI over 30 kg/m², and 28% of all normal subjects had a PASP over 30 mmHg. The authors support age- and BMI-corrected expected ranges.
cards.watchOut: The assumed right atrial pressure of 10 mmHg is baked into every value — a laboratory assuming 5 or 15 mmHg will shift its whole distribution; and 'echocardiographically normal' patients in a clinical database are not screened healthy volunteers, so the upper tail (to 57 mmHg) partly reflects that referral filter.
cards.source: McQuillan BM et al. Clinical correlates and reference intervals for pulmonary artery systolic pressure among echocardiographically normal subjects. Circulation. 2001. PMID: 11733397. cards.headline: Marra 2018 (614 prospectively assessed healthy adults plus pooled 981): mean tricuspid regurgitation velocity 2.01 ± 0.29 m/s, pooled mean 1.96 m/s, 95% quantile 2.55 m/s
cards.summary: Marra 2018 (614 prospectively assessed healthy adults plus pooled 981): mean tricuspid regurgitation velocity 2.01 ± 0.29 m/s, pooled mean 1.96 m/s, 95% quantile 2.55 m/s
cards.type: Prospective healthy-cohort study with pooled meta-analysis (Marra 2018)
cards.people: 614 healthy individuals (mean age 45.7 ± 14.7 years; 60.26% women) prospectively assessed by transthoracic echocardiography, plus a pooled meta-analysis of 16 published studies with tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRV) values in healthy subjects (n = 981).
cards.result: In the prospective cohort, mean TRV was 2.01 ± 0.29 m/s; it correlated significantly but weakly and positively with age, body mass index, systolic and diastolic blood pressure and left atrial volume, and negatively with mitral inflow E/A ratio, with no significant difference between males and females. Combining the prospective data with the literature datasets gave a mean TRV of 1.96 m/s (95% CI 1.91–2.02 m/s) and a 95% quantile of 2.55 m/s, which the authors propose as a cut-off to be confirmed in at-risk populations.
cards.watchOut: TRV is measurable only when a tricuspid regurgitant jet exists and is well aligned, so healthy-cohort TRV distributions describe the measurable subset; the 2.55 m/s 95% quantile is a distributional edge in health, not a validated disease threshold — the authors say it must be confirmed in at-risk populations.
cards.source: Marra AM et al. Reference Ranges and Determinants of Tricuspid Regurgitation Velocity in Healthy Adults Assessed by Two-Dimensional Doppler-Echocardiography. Respiration. 2018. PMID: 30021211. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: resting mean pulmonary pressure is about 14 mmHg by catheter (rarely over 20), echo systolic pressure averages about 28 mmHg with an upper edge near 37–40 in older or heavier healthy people, and TR velocity centres near 2.0 m/s (95% quantile 2.55)
cards.summary: Synthesis: resting mean pulmonary pressure is about 14 mmHg by catheter (rarely over 20), echo systolic pressure averages about 28 mmHg with an upper edge near 37–40 in older or heavier healthy people, and TR velocity centres near 2.0 m/s (95% quantile 2.55)
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the invasive systematic review (1,187 healthy individuals), the echocardiographic reference study (3,790 normal subjects) and the TR-velocity cohort with pooled analysis (614 prospective + 981 pooled).
cards.result: The three measurement routes agree once their quantities are kept separate: catheter mean pressure ~14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg at rest with a small age rise; echo systolic pressure ~28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg, rising with age and BMI so that values over 40 mmHg occur in about 1 in 17 healthy people over 50; and the underlying TR velocity ~2.0 m/s with a healthy 95% quantile of 2.55 m/s. Exercise is the exception that proves the resting rule — healthy older people frequently exceed 30 mmHg mean pressure at mild exercise. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the resting values are concordant across invasive and non-invasive records spanning five decades of technique.
cards.watchOut: Mean (catheter), systolic (echo estimate) and velocity (TR jet) are three different numbers for one circulation — the commonest reading error is comparing an echo systolic estimate against the catheter mean-pressure reference. Echo estimates also embed an assumed right atrial pressure (10 mmHg in the largest study).
cards.source: Synthesis of Kovacs G et al. The European respiratory journal. 2009 (PMID: 19324955); McQuillan BM et al. Circulation. 2001 (PMID: 11733397); Marra AM et al. Respiration. 2018 (PMID: 30021211), all carded above. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (pulmonary circulation); Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (pulmonary haemodynamics). Cross-point: pack #6911 (pregnancy haemodynamics — a different physiological state).

shelves.title: Total blood volume, haemoglobin mass and plasma volume in healthy humans
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large are total blood volume, red-cell (haemoglobin) mass and plasma volume — measured by carbon-monoxide rebreathing and by indicator dilution — per kilogram and by sex, training state and body composition, and how well do the classic prediction formulas (Nadler) match measured values?
shelves.mesh: Blood Volume/physiology · Hemoglobins/analysis · Plasma Volume · Carbon Monoxide · Reproducibility of Results · Physical Endurance/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, body-fluid compartments; Boron & Boulpaep, blood-volume regulation — the haemoglobin concentration that laboratories report is the ratio of total haemoglobin mass to plasma volume, so concentration alone cannot say whether the mass, the volume or both have changed). The carded record gives the measured quantities three ways. First, method precision: the optimised CO-rebreathing method repeats to a typical error of about 2% (and to within 0.8% for a repeated 1.0 mL/kg bolus), can be repeated within 3 hours if oxygen is used to clear carbon monoxide, and a 30-second single-breath variant matches the established method in healthy volunteers. Second, absolute values: in small healthy samples total haemoglobin mass was about 776–849 g (Plumb 808 ± 190 g in 24 subjects; Turner 785–791 g in 12; Krehl 843 ± 293 g in 11), so the healthy absolute range in these samples is broad and tracks body size. Third, the per-kilogram and training comparison: elite runners carry about 14.0–14.2 g/kg of haemoglobin mass and about 100–102 mL/kg of blood volume, and endurance-trained people carry roughly 30% more haemoglobin mass than untrained controls. The classic Nadler prediction formulas are named here only as the textbook-era prediction approach: none of the fetched records tests them head-to-head against measured volumes, so no accuracy figure is printed for them. Cross-points: haemoglobin mass after altitude exposure is homed at pack #6266 and after blood loss at pack #6448 — this shelf is the at-rest baseline, not a change-over-time question.

cards.headline: Plumb 2018 (24 subjects): total haemoglobin mass 807.9 ± 189.7 g by optimised CO rebreathing, typical error 2.0%, and repeatable within 3 hours when oxygen clears the carbon monoxide
cards.summary: Plumb 2018 (24 subjects): total haemoglobin mass 807.9 ± 189.7 g by optimised CO rebreathing, typical error 2.0%, and repeatable within 3 hours when oxygen clears the carbon monoxide
cards.people: 24 subjects undergoing 3 days of testing, two optimised carbon-monoxide rebreathing (oCOR) tests per day, 3 hours apart, with different CO-clearance methods between tests (supplemental oxygen alone, moderate exercise, or both) to keep carboxyhaemoglobin below 10%.
cards.result: Mean (SD) total haemoglobin mass was 807.9 ± 189.7 g (first test, day 1). Oxygen breathing alone lowered carboxyhaemoglobin from 6.64% at the end of the first test to 2.95% at the start of the second (a mean absolute fall of 3.69%); the falls were 4.00% for exercise and 4.31% for the combination. The test–retest reliability for total haemoglobin mass was good, with a mean typical error of 2.0%. The authors conclude the oCOR method is safe and can be repeated within 3 hours when carbon monoxide is suitably cleared, with oxygen alone sufficient.
cards.watchOut: N = 24 and a method study, not a population survey — the 808 g mean is the value in these subjects (a broad SD of ±190 g signals a size-mixed sample), and the 2.0% typical error is the precision of the method, not the spread between people.
cards.source: Plumb JOM et al. Replicating measurements of total hemoglobin mass (tHb-mass) within a single day: precision of measurement; feasibility and safety of using oxygen to expedite carbon monoxide clearance. Physiological reports. 2018. PMID: 30203465. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Turner 2014 (12 participants): total haemoglobin mass 776–791 g across CO boluses of 0.6–1.4 mL/kg — repeatable to within 0.8%, but a high bolus read 1.4–1.9% lower
cards.summary: Turner 2014 (12 participants): total haemoglobin mass 776–791 g across CO boluses of 0.6–1.4 mL/kg — repeatable to within 0.8%, but a high bolus read 1.4–1.9% lower
cards.people: 12 participants (10 males, 2 females; age 27 ± 6 years, height 177 ± 11 cm, mass 73.9 ± 12.1 kg) who each completed the optimised CO-rebreathing method on four occasions at different CO boluses (LOW 0.6 mL/kg; MED1 1.0 mL/kg, repeated as MED2; HIGH 1.4 mL/kg).
cards.result: Total haemoglobin mass was significantly less with the HIGH CO bolus (776 ± 148 g) than with LOW (791 ± 149 g) or MED1 (788 ± 149 g); MED2 was 785 ± 150 g. Measurement was repeatable to within 0.8%, but a small and notable difference (1.4–1.9% less) appeared with the HIGH bolus, attributed by the authors to differences in CO uptake kinetics. The authors conclude a bolus of 1.0 mL/kg gives adequate precision with acceptable safety using the newer haemoxymeter.
cards.watchOut: A 12-person precision study: the 1.4–1.9% high-bolus bias is small against the ~30% training difference carded elsewhere, but it is the same order as the method's own typical error, so bolus dose must be stated beside any reported mass.
cards.source: Turner G et al. The influence of carbon monoxide bolus on the measurement of total haemoglobin mass using the optimized CO-rebreathing method. Physiological measurement. 2014. PMID: 24451475. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Krehl 2021 (11 healthy volunteers): a single breath of CO with a 30-second breath hold gave total haemoglobin mass 849 ± 311 g — essentially the same as optimised rebreathing (843 ± 293 g)
cards.summary: Krehl 2021 (11 healthy volunteers): a single breath of CO with a 30-second breath hold gave total haemoglobin mass 849 ± 311 g — essentially the same as optimised rebreathing (843 ± 293 g)
cards.type: Method feasibility study, single-breath CO method (Krehl 2021)
cards.people: 11 healthy volunteers who each performed four CO-rebreathing tests in randomised order: two with the established optimised method (2 minutes of rebreathing) and two with a single inhalation of the same CO volume followed by a breath hold of 15 or 30 seconds, with exhaled CO tracked for 20 minutes.
cards.result: Total haemoglobin mass was 843 ± 293 g by optimised CO rebreathing, 821 ± 288 g by the single-breath 15-second hold (difference P < 0.05) and 849 ± 311 g by the 30-second hold. Bland–Altman analysis showed the 15-second variant read slightly lower than the established method (−21.8 ± 15.3 g) and the 30-second variant read similarly. The authors conclude a single CO inhalation with a 30-second breath hold can determine haemoglobin mass in healthy subjects, and that validation in ventilated patients is still required.
cards.watchOut: N = 11 healthy volunteers and a feasibility design — the point is that the single-breath method is not materially biased in health (30-second hold), not that it is validated for the ventilated patients it was designed for; the record explicitly defers that validation.
cards.source: Krehl LM et al. A carbon monoxide 'single breath' method to measure total haemoglobin mass: a feasibility study. Experimental physiology. 2021. PMID: 33369791. cards.headline: Prommer 2007 (36 people): endurance-trained non-divers carried about 30% more total haemoglobin mass than untrained controls and trained apnoea divers
cards.summary: Prommer 2007 (36 people): endurance-trained non-divers carried about 30% more total haemoglobin mass than untrained controls and trained apnoea divers
cards.people: Trained apnoea divers (n = 10), SCUBA divers performing apnoeas without long-term apnoea training (n = 7), endurance-trained non-divers (n = 9) and untrained non-divers (n = 10); spleen volume by ultrasound before and after five dives to 4 m, with total haemoglobin mass and plasma volume by CO rebreathing.
cards.result: Repeated apnoea dives shrank the spleen by 25% in trained apnoea divers (P < 0.001) with no significant effect in controls. Total haemoglobin mass did not differ between trained apnoea divers, untrained SCUBA divers and untrained non-divers, but it was 30% lower than in endurance-trained non-divers — that is, endurance training, not apnoea training, was associated with the larger haemoglobin mass in this sample.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (7–10 per group) and a cross-sectional design: the 30% figure is a group difference, not a training-effect estimate — genetics and self-selection into endurance sport are inside it, and the record does not test whether training a sedentary person closes the gap.
cards.source: Prommer N et al. Total haemoglobin mass and spleen contraction: a study on competitive apnea divers, non-diving athletes and untrained control subjects. cross-sectional comparative study (prommer 2007) trained apnoea divers (n = 10), scuba divers performing apnoeas without long-term apnoea training (n = 7), endurance-trained non-divers (n = 9) and untrained non-divers (n = 10); spleen volume by ultrasound before and after five dives to 4 m, with total haemoglobin mass and plasma volume by co rebreathing. repeated apnoea dives shrank the spleen by 25% in trained apnoea divers (p < 0.001) with no significant effect in controls. total haemoglobin mass did not differ between trained apnoea divers, untrained scuba divers and untrained non-divers, but it was 30% lower than in endurance-trained non-divers — that is, endurance training, not apnoea training, was associated with the larger haemoglobin mass in this sample. small groups (7–10 per group) and a cross-sectional design: the 30% figure is a group difference, not a training-effect estimate — genetics and self-selection into endurance sport are inside it, and the record does not test whether training a sedentary person closes the gap. prommer n et al. total haemoglobin mass and spleen contraction: a study on competitive apnea divers, non-diving athletes and untrained control subjects. european journal of applied physiology. 2007. pmid: 17874121. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · apnea/diagnostic imaging,physiopathology · blood volume/physiology · body weight/physiology · carbon monoxide · diving/physiology · erythrocyte volume · female · hematocrit · hemoglobins/physiology · humans · male · middle aged · oxygen consumption/physiology · physical fitness/physiology · plasma volume/physiology · spleen/diagnostic imaging,physiology · total lung capacity/physiology · ultrasonography

cards.headline: Prommer 2010 Kenyan elite runners: relative haemoglobin mass 14.2 ± 1.0 g/kg and blood volume 101.9 ± 4.5 mL/kg — the same, per kilogram, as elite German runners (14.0 ± 0.7 g/kg; 99.6 ± 5.8 mL/kg)
cards.summary: Prommer 2010 Kenyan elite runners: relative haemoglobin mass 14.2 ± 1.0 g/kg and blood volume 101.9 ± 4.5 mL/kg — the same, per kilogram, as elite German runners (14.0 ± 0.7 g/kg; 99.6 ± 5.8 mL/kg)
cards.people: 10 male Kenyan runners (10-km best time 28:29 ± 00:27 min) living at 2,090 m, studied during a 6-week training camp at near sea level, compared with elite German runners (10-km best 30:39 ± 00:24 min). Total haemoglobin mass, blood volume and maximal oxygen uptake were measured.
cards.result: Relative total haemoglobin mass was 14.2 ± 1.0 g/kg in the Kenyans and 14.0 ± 0.7 g/kg in the Germans; blood volume was 101.9 ± 4.5 mL/kg and 99.6 ± 5.8 mL/kg respectively. The Kenyans were lighter (57.2 ± 7.0 kg vs 66.5 ± 6.3 kg), and their absolute haemoglobin mass fell during the stay at near sea level (813 ± 90 g to 767 ± 90 g, P < 0.001) and blood volume fell (5,828 ± 703 mL to 5,513 ± 708 mL, P < 0.01). Relative maximal oxygen uptake was similar in both groups (71.5 ± 5.0 vs 70.7 ± 3.7 mL/kg/min).
cards.watchOut: Ten Kenyans against a German comparison group whose N is not printed in the record's abstract — the per-kilogram equivalence is the finding, and absolute values in these athletes (~810 g, ~5.8 L) sit far above the small general samples carded above, which is why blood volume must be read per kilogram and per population, never as one number for all humans.
cards.source: Prommer N et al. Total hemoglobin mass and blood volume of elite Kenyan runners. Medicine and science in sports and exercise. 2010. PMID: 19952848. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: total haemoglobin mass in healthy adults runs about 780–850 g in small general samples (≈14 g/kg in elite endurance athletes, with blood volume ≈100 mL/kg), is about 30% higher with endurance training, and is measured by CO rebreathing to about 2% precision
cards.summary: Synthesis: total haemoglobin mass in healthy adults runs about 780–850 g in small general samples (≈14 g/kg in elite endurance athletes, with blood volume ≈100 mL/kg), is about 30% higher with endurance training, and is measured by CO rebreathing to about 2% precision
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: three CO-rebreathing method studies (Plumb 2018, N = 24; Turner 2014, N = 12; Krehl 2021, N = 11) and two population-value studies (Prommer 2007, N = 36 across four groups; Prommer 2010, elite Kenyan and German runners).
cards.result: Haemoglobin concentration is a ratio — total haemoglobin mass divided by plasma volume — and the method record shows the mass half of that ratio can now be measured repeatedly to about 2% by CO rebreathing, by a 1.0 mL/kg bolus or a 30-second single breath. The population record shows the mass is large in absolute terms (about 780–850 g in the small general samples) and strikingly training-dependent (about 30% higher in endurance-trained people; about 14 g/kg and ~100 mL/kg blood volume in elite runners). No fetched record validates the classic Nadler prediction formulas against measured values, so no accuracy claim for them is made; they are named here only as the textbook-era prediction approach. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the CO-rebreathing measurement and its training gradient are concordant across the fetched human records.
cards.watchOut: The population values rest on small samples (11–36 people) and on athletes; a large healthy-population survey of blood volume by sex, training state and body composition does not exist in the carded record, so the ~100 mL/kg and ~14 g/kg figures are elite-runner values, not population norms.
cards.source: Synthesis of Plumb JOM et al. Physiological reports. 2018 (PMID: 30203465); Turner G et al. Physiological measurement. 2014 (PMID: 24451475); Krehl LM et al. Experimental physiology. 2021 (PMID: 33369791); Prommer N et al. European journal of applied physiology. 2007 (PMID: 17874121); Prommer N et al. Medicine and science in sports and exercise. 2010 (PMID: 19952848), all carded above. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (body-fluid compartments); Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (blood-volume regulation). Cross-points: pack #6266 (haemoglobin mass at altitude) and pack #6448 (recovery after blood loss) — change-over-time questions, not this shelf's at-rest baseline.

shelves.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate by age and sex: the healthy population distribution
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the erythrocyte sedimentation rate by age and sex — the population distribution in subjectively healthy adults and the empirical upper-limit rules (age/2 for men, (age+10)/2 for women) — and how do haemoglobin, fibrinogen and the test method (Westergren vs automated) shift it?
shelves.mesh: Blood Sedimentation · Reference Values · Age Factors · Sex Characteristics · Norway · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing is brief: Guyton & Hall, blood cells, inflammation and ESR — as the slate row directs, the shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). Three healthy-population datasets, spanning 1990 to 2025 and totalling more than 9,000 people, agree on the shape: ESR rises with age, is higher in women than in men at every age, and most healthy people have low values — in the 1996 Norwegian population study about 76% of all recordings were under 9 mm/h. The Norwegian 95% upper reference limits were, at ages 20, 55 and 90: men 12, 14 and 19 mm/h; women 18, 21 and 23 mm/h. A 2025 Italian study using the Westergren method and two automated analysers found almost identical reference intervals (women ≥18 years: 1–22 mm/h; men under 70: 1–14 mm/h; men 70+: 1–22 mm/h), with the automated analysers averaging within 1 mm/h of the gold standard. The classic age/2 (men) and (age+10)/2 (women) rules are the textbook account of the upper limit — and the fetched population limits sit well below them (at age 55 the rules would allow about 28 mm/h for men and 33 mm/h for women, against measured 95% limits of 14 and 21 mm/h), so the rules are generous, not tight. Method matters: Westergren and automated values are close but not identical — the CUBE 30 Touch read up to 29 mm/h in the upper limit for men over 70 against 22 mm/h by Westergren — so a value should be read beside its method. One classic was refused: Böttiger & Svedberg 1967 (a paper titled 'Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and age') has an EMPTY abstract in PubMed, so its numbers could not be verified from the record and it is not carded; the refusal is recorded on the Synthesis card.

cards.headline: Wetteland 1996 (3,910 healthy Norwegian adults): ESR means about 3 mm/h (men) and 6 mm/h (women) at age 20, rising to 10 and 11 at age 90; 95% upper limits 12–19 mm/h (men), 18–23 mm/h (women)
cards.summary: Wetteland 1996 (3,910 healthy Norwegian adults): ESR means about 3 mm/h (men) and 6 mm/h (women) at age 20, rising to 10 and 11 at age 90; 95% upper limits 12–19 mm/h (men), 18–23 mm/h (women)
cards.people: 2,145 men and 1,765 women aged 20–90 years (93% blood donors) from the Oslo area, with single ESR recordings by the classical or a modified Westergren method, analysed statistically.
cards.result: ESR rose significantly with age — parabolically in men, linearly in women. Predicted mean values for men were about 3 mm/h at 20 years, 6 mm/h at 55 years and 10 mm/h at 90 years; for women about 6, 9 and 11 mm/h respectively, significantly higher in women up to age 75. The upper reference levels expected to be exceeded by chance in only 5% of single recordings, at ages 20, 55 and 90, were 12, 14 and 19 mm/h for men and 18, 21 and 23 mm/h for women. About 76% of all values were lower than 9 mm/h.
cards.watchOut: A 93% blood-donor sample — healthier and younger-skewed than the general population — so these limits describe subjectively healthy adults; the authors themselves warn that a person's own baseline and its rise over years matters more than any single population limit.
cards.source: Wetteland P et al. Population-based erythrocyte sedimentation rates in 3910 subjectively healthy Norwegian adults. A statistical study based on men and women from the Oslo area. Journal of internal medicine. 1996. PMID: 8862121. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dalhøj 1990 (4,202 blood donors, 18–65 years): ESR is log-normally distributed, higher in women at every age, and false-positive rates climb sharply with age at fixed cut-offs
cards.summary: Dalhøj 1990 (4,202 blood donors, 18–65 years): ESR is log-normally distributed, higher in women at every age, and false-positive rates climb sharply with age at fixed cut-offs
cards.people: 4,202 consecutive blood donors aged 18–65 years, erythrocyte sedimentation rate determined by the Westergren method.
cards.result: The distribution of values was log-normal for both females and males. The median value was highest in females for all age classes, and although both the median and the range rose with age in both sexes, the increase was most pronounced in females. Used as a screening test, the fraction of false positives rose markedly after age 45 years using cut-offs of 15 and 20 mm/h, and after age 55 years using 25 mm/h. The authors suggest raising the most frequently used cut-off values, with one cut-off for premenopausal women and another, higher one for postmenopausal women, while a single cut-off seems adequate for men.
cards.watchOut: The record is a short abstract from a Danish journal and prints no median values by age class — its contribution is the distributional shape (log-normal), the sex gap at every age, and the demonstration that a single fixed cut-off is a false-positive machine after age 45.
cards.source: Dalhøj J et al. Blood sedimentation rate in healthy persons. Ugeskrift for laeger. 1990. PMID: 2309346. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Blood Sedimentation · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Factors

cards.headline: Lorubbio 2025 (989 presumably healthy people): Westergren and automated analysers agree within about 1 mm/h — reference intervals 1–22 mm/h (women) and 1–14 mm/h (men under 70), 1–22 mm/h (men 70+)
cards.summary: Lorubbio 2025 (989 presumably healthy people): Westergren and automated analysers agree within about 1 mm/h — reference intervals 1–22 mm/h (women) and 1–14 mm/h (men under 70), 1–22 mm/h (men 70+)
cards.type: Reference-interval study, Westergren versus automated methods (Lorubbio 2025)
cards.people: 989 (presumably healthy) participants from Arezzo Hospital, Italy; erythrocyte sedimentation rate reference intervals established according to CLSI for the Westergren gold standard and the automated VES-MATIC 5 (VM5) and CUBE 30 Touch (C30T) analysers.
cards.result: There were significant differences between women and men and age-related increases in ESR by all three analytical methods. The average and median values from VM5 and C30T were respectively 1 mm/h smaller and higher than the gold standard. A single range was identified for females aged ≥18 years (Westergren: 1–22 mm/h; VM5: 1–22 mm/h; C30T: 1–25 mm/h). For men, two ranges: 18 to under 69 years (Westergren: 1–14 mm/h; VM5: 1–14 mm/h; C30T: 1–18 mm/h) and 70 years or above (Westergren: 1–22 mm/h; VM5: 1–23 mm/h; C30T: 1–29 mm/h).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, hospital-recruited 'presumably healthy' participants — the health filter is looser than the blood-donor studies — and the analysers' upper limits diverge at the top end (C30T 1–29 mm/h in older men versus Westergren 1–22), so an automated value near its upper limit is not the same reading as a Westergren value there.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ESR in health is low (about three-quarters under 9 mm/h), rises with age, and runs higher in women; the age/2-style rules are generous, and Westergren and automated methods are close but not identical
cards.summary: Synthesis: ESR in health is low (about three-quarters under 9 mm/h), rises with age, and runs higher in women; the age/2-style rules are generous, and Westergren and automated methods are close but not identical
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: Wetteland's 3,910 Norwegian adults (1996), Dalhøj's 4,202 Danish blood donors (1990) and Lorubbio's 989 Italian participants (2025) — three Westergren-anchored datasets totalling more than 9,000 healthy people.
cards.result: The distribution is settled in shape: log-normal, higher in women, rising with age, with 95% upper limits of roughly 12–19 mm/h in men and 18–23 mm/h in women (Wetteland, age-dependent), corroborated by the 2025 automated-era intervals (women 1–22 mm/h; men 1–14 mm/h under 70, 1–22 mm/h at 70+). The classic upper-limit rules (age/2 for men, (age+10)/2 for women) would allow far higher values than these population limits, so they are a permissive screen, not a tight normal. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the age/sex distribution is concordant across three decades of method generations. REFUSAL, recorded as required: Böttiger & Svedberg 1967 ('Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and age', British medical journal, PMID: 6020854) was NOT carded — its PubMed record has an empty abstract and its numbers could not be verified from the record this session.
cards.watchOut: ESR is a non-specific inflammatory measure, not a diagnosis: fibrinogen and haemoglobin shift it, and a rising personal baseline over years should be taken seriously even while each reading stays inside the population limits. A value is only interpretable beside its method (Westergren vs automated analyser) and the person's age and sex.

synthesis synthesis of the carded reports: wetteland's 3,910 norwegian adults (1996), dalhøj's 4,202 danish blood donors (1990) and lorubbio's 989 italian participants (2025) — three westergren-anchored datasets totalling more than 9,000 healthy people. the distribution is settled in shape: log-normal, higher in women, rising with age, with 95% upper limits of roughly 12–19 mm/h in men and 18–23 mm/h in women (wetteland, age-dependent), corroborated by the 2025 automated-era intervals (women 1–22 mm/h; men 1–14 mm/h under 70, 1–22 mm/h at 70+). the classic upper-limit rules (age/2 for men, (age+10)/2 for women) would allow far higher values than these population limits, so they are a permissive screen, not a tight normal. proposed physiology — established: the age/sex distribution is concordant across three decades of method generations. refusal, recorded as required: böttiger & svedberg 1967 ('normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and age', british medical journal, pmid: 6020854) was not carded — its pubmed record has an empty abstract and its numbers could not be verified from the record this session. esr is a non-specific inflammatory measure, not a diagnosis: fibrinogen and haemoglobin shift it, and a rising personal baseline over years should be taken seriously even while each reading stays inside the population limits. a value is only interpretable beside its method (westergren vs automated analyser) and the person's age and sex. synthesis of wetteland p et al. journal of internal medicine. 1996 (pmid: 8862121); dalhøj j et al. ugeskrift for laeger. 1990 (pmid: 2309346); lorubbio m et al. diagnostics. 2025 (pmid: 40361919), all carded above. textbook framing: guyton & hall textbook of medical physiology (blood cells, inflammation and esr) — brief; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature. refused record: böttiger le & svedberg ca. british medical journal. 1967 (pmid: 6020854) — empty abstract, not carded.

shelves.title: Benralizumab in hypereosinophilic syndrome: NATRON phase 3 (n=133) cut first-flare hazard (HR 0.35, relative); phase 2 programme (n=20) with follow-up to 10.1 years — two programmes
shelves.question: In patients with FIP1L1::PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome, does benralizumab (anti-IL-5 receptor α, 30 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo, added to background therapy, reduce disease flares and allow background-therapy tapering?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Hypereosinophilic Syndrome · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Aged · Adolescent · Male · Aged, 80 and over · Young Adult · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a base of TWO programmes, labelled as such (per the assembly adjudication): Programme 1 — NATRON, the phase 3 randomised trial (n=133), in which benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks added to background therapy reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.69 — a relative effect) over 24 weeks, with similar adverse-event rates (64.2% vs 66.7%). Programme 2 — the small phase 2 randomised trial (n=20) in which 90% versus 30% achieved at least a 50% eosinophil-count reduction at week 12, plus its long-term report: 14 of the 20 followed on open-label extension, with eosinophil suppression sustained and 10 participants treated for at least 8 years (maximum exposure 10.1 years). Mepolizumab in HES is a different drug with its own home (pack #6982) — cross-pointed, not re-carded. The NATRON erratum is not carded.

cards.headline: NATRON phase 3 RCT (Ogbogu 2026) — Programme 1: benralizumab reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.69, relative) in 133 randomised patients
cards.summary: NATRON phase 3 RCT (Ogbogu 2026) — Programme 1: benralizumab reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.69, relative) in 133 randomised patients
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (NATRON) — Programme 1 of two on this shelf
cards.people: 133 patients with FIP1L1::PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome (median age 51 years, range 14–87; 62% female) were randomised 1:1 to benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks or placebo for 24 weeks, in addition to background therapy. The primary endpoint was time to first HES flare.
cards.result: Benralizumab significantly reduced the risk of a first flare versus placebo: hazard ratio 0.35 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.69; P=0.0024) — a relative hazard reduction of about 65%. Adverse events occurred in 64.2% of benralizumab-treated and 66.7% of placebo-treated patients, and the safety profile was consistent with benralizumab's known profile.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week trial with a time-to-first-flare endpoint: the hazard ratio is a relative measure and the abstract reports no absolute flare rates, so the absolute benefit cannot be stated from this record. The accompanying erratum to this report is not carded.
cards.source: Ogbogu PU et al. Benralizumab versus placebo for hypereosinophilic syndrome: a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Nature Medicine. 2026. PMID: 41917160. cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Kuang 2019) — Programme 2: at least a 50% eosinophil-count reduction at week 12 in 9 of 10 patients on benralizumab vs 3 of 10 on placebo, in a trial of only 20 patients
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Kuang 2019) — Programme 2: at least a 50% eosinophil-count reduction at week 12 in 9 of 10 patients on benralizumab vs 3 of 10 on placebo, in a trial of only 20 patients
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with open-label and extension phases — Programme 2 of two on this shelf (n=20)
cards.people: 20 symptomatic patients with PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome and an absolute eosinophil count of at least 1000 cells per cubic millimeter, all on stable background therapy, received three monthly subcutaneous injections of benralizumab 30 mg or placebo, followed by an open-label phase in which background therapy could be tapered, and an extension phase.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥50% reduction in absolute eosinophil count at week 12) occurred in 9 of 10 patients (90%) on benralizumab versus 3 of 10 (30%) on placebo (P=0.02). In the open-label phase, clinical and haematologic responses occurred in 17 of 19 patients (89%) and were sustained for 48 weeks in 14 of 19 (74%); in 9 of those 14 (64%) background therapies could be tapered. Bone marrow and tissue eosinophilia were also suppressed. The most common drug-related adverse events, headache and elevated lactate dehydrogenase, occurred in 32% of patients after the first dose and resolved within 48 hours in all; other adverse events were similarly frequent in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 20 patients and a laboratory primary endpoint (eosinophil-count reduction) in the randomised phase; the 48-week response and tapering figures come from the uncontrolled open-label phase.
cards.source: Kuang FL et al. Benralizumab for PDGFRA-Negative Hypereosinophilic Syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30943337. Registry ID: NCT00001406; NCT02130882. cards.headline: Long-term report of Programme 2 (Kuang 2025): 14 of the 20 phase 2 patients followed on open-label extension — 10 treated for at least 8 years (maximum 10.1 years) with eosinophils still suppressed and no adverse event attributed to benralizumab
cards.summary: Long-term report of Programme 2 (Kuang 2025): 14 of the 20 phase 2 patients followed on open-label extension — 10 treated for at least 8 years (maximum 10.1 years) with eosinophils still suppressed and no adverse event attributed to benralizumab
cards.type: Long-term open-label extension report of the phase 2 programme carded above (Programme 2 — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 14 of the 20 patients from the phase 2 trial carded above were followed on an open-label extension of benralizumab treatment for PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome — a report OF Programme 2, not a third trial.
cards.result: Of the 14 long-term participants, 3 withdrew for loss of efficacy and 1 died of a cause unrelated to the drug after 2 to 6 years; the remaining 10 received benralizumab for at least 8 years (maximum exposure 10.1 years), with peripheral eosinophil counts suppressed throughout. Eight participants attempted tapering from monthly to every-2-month dosing and 5 resumed monthly dosing because of increased symptoms and/or eosinophil counts. There were 11 serious adverse events (10 hospitalisations and 1 death from antibiotic-associated toxic epidermal necrolysis), none attributed to benralizumab; 8 participants reported mild, self-limited injection-site reactions (23 in total); 3 malignancies and no parasitic infections were reported, and immunoglobulin levels and T-, B- and natural killer-cell counts remained stable.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled extension of a 20-patient trial, with only 14 entering long-term follow-up: it informs durability and long-term tolerability in survivors on treatment, not efficacy against any comparator.
cards.source: Kuang FL et al. Long-Term Efficacy and Safety of Benralizumab Treatment for PDGFRA-Negative Hypereosinophilic Syndrome. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. cards.headline: Synthesis: two programmes — NATRON phase 3 (n=133) showed fewer first flares on benralizumab (hazard ratio 0.35, relative), and the phase 2 programme (n=20, with follow-up to 10.1 years) showed deep, durable eosinophil suppression
cards.summary: Synthesis: two programmes — NATRON phase 3 (n=133) showed fewer first flares on benralizumab (hazard ratio 0.35, relative), and the phase 2 programme (n=20, with follow-up to 10.1 years) showed deep, durable eosinophil suppression
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf — two programmes, three reports.
cards.result: Benralizumab reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo in the phase 3 NATRON trial (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.69, relative) with adverse-event rates similar to placebo over 24 weeks. The earlier phase 2 programme is consistent in mechanism and direction (90% vs 30% achieving ≥50% eosinophil reduction at week 12) and its extension suggests the effect can be maintained for years in patients who stay on treatment, with background therapy tapered in some. The two programmes must not be counted as three trials: the 2025 report is the phase 2 trial's own long-term follow-up.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Beraprost in pulmonary arterial hypertension: SPLIT — walk benefit at 12 weeks in one trial (n=130), but the 12-month trial's (n=116) benefit attenuated and was gone by 9–12 months
shelves.question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO/NYHA functional class II–III), does oral beraprost sodium versus placebo improve exercise capacity and delay disease progression?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea · Epoprostenol · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Heart Failure · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypertension, Pulmonary · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vasodilator Agents
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The two randomised trials disagree in time-frame and durability. The European 12-week trial (n=130) found beraprost improved exercise capacity versus placebo (difference in mean change in 6-minute walk distance 25.1 m, 95% CI 1.8 to 48.3). The US 12-month trial (n=116) found less disease progression at 6 months and better walk distance at 3 and 6 months, but the effect attenuated and was not evident at 9 or 12 months. The third card is a network meta-analysis of the prostacyclin-analogue class (epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost and beraprost pooled) — it is a class synthesis, NOT a third beraprost trial, and within it beraprost's own signal was a higher withdrawal probability versus iloprost. A second prostacyclin network meta-analysis that has been withdrawn is deliberately NOT carded (fenced). Beraprost is licensed for PAH in Japan and parts of Asia, not in the US/EU — printed on the face. Other prostacyclin-pathway drugs (selexipag, treprostinil, ralinepag) have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: European RCT (Galiè 2002): beraprost improved 12-week exercise capacity versus placebo — difference in mean change in 6-minute walk distance 25.1 m (95% CI 1.8 to 48.3)
cards.summary: European RCT (Galiè 2002): beraprost improved 12-week exercise capacity versus placebo — difference in mean change in 6-minute walk distance 25.1 m (95% CI 1.8 to 48.3)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (European), 12 weeks, maximal tolerated beraprost vs placebo
cards.people: 130 patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension in NYHA functional class II–III were randomised to the maximal tolerated dose of beraprost sodium (median dose 80 μg four times daily) or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in exercise capacity on the 6-minute walk test.
cards.result: Beraprost improved exercise capacity and symptoms: the between-group difference in mean change in 6-minute walk distance at week 12 was 25.1 m (95% CI 1.8 to 48.3; P=0.036), and the difference in Borg dyspnea index was −0.94 (95% CI −1.63 to −0.24; P=0.009). In the subgroup with primary pulmonary hypertension the walk-distance difference was 46.1 m (95% CI 3.0 to 89.3; P=0.035). Cardiopulmonary haemodynamics and NYHA functional class showed no statistically significant changes. Drug-related adverse events were common during titration and decreased during maintenance.
cards.watchOut: A short 12-week trial with a walk-distance endpoint: it cannot speak to disease progression or survival, and the haemodynamic and functional-class secondaries did not change significantly.
cards.source: Galiè N et al. Effects of beraprost sodium, an oral prostacyclin analogue, in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2002. PMID: 11985913. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: US RCT (Barst 2003): beraprost showed less disease progression at 6 months, but the benefit attenuated and was NOT evident at 9 or 12 months over a 12-month trial
cards.summary: US RCT (Barst 2003): beraprost showed less disease progression at 6 months, but the benefit attenuated and was NOT evident at 9 or 12 months over a 12-month trial
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (US), 12 months, maximal tolerated beraprost vs placebo
cards.people: 116 patients with WHO functional class II–III primary pulmonary hypertension or PAH related to collagen vascular disease or congenital systemic-to-pulmonary shunts were randomised to the maximal tolerated dose of beraprost sodium (median dose 120 μg four times daily) or placebo for 12 months. The primary endpoint was disease progression (death, transplantation, epoprostenol rescue, or >25% decrease in peak oxygen consumption).
cards.result: Beraprost-treated patients showed less evidence of disease progression at six months (P=0.002), but this effect was not evident at either shorter or longer follow-up. Walk distance likewise improved versus placebo at 3 months (by 22 m from baseline) and 6 months (by 31 m; P=0.010 and P=0.016), but not at 9 or 12 months. Drug-related adverse events were common and were those of the disease and/or expected prostacyclin effects. The authors concluded that benefit may occur early in treatment but attenuates with time.
cards.watchOut: The longer of the only two beraprost trials — and the one that tempers the shelf: every benefit signal in it was confined to the first 6 months. It enrolled an older PAH population mix (primary, connective-tissue and congenital-shunt disease) from the pre-combination-therapy era.
cards.source: Barst RJ et al. Beraprost therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2003. PMID: 12821234. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Network meta-analysis of the prostacyclin class (Zhang 2016) — a class synthesis card, NOT a third beraprost trial: beraprost's own signal was a higher withdrawal probability versus iloprost (odds ratio 10.07, relative)
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis of the prostacyclin class (Zhang 2016) — a class synthesis card, NOT a third beraprost trial: beraprost's own signal was a higher withdrawal probability versus iloprost (odds ratio 10.07, relative)
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of the prostacyclin-analogue class (beraprost is one pooled limb — a synthesis card, not a beraprost trial)
cards.people: Randomised trials of four prostacyclin analogues — epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost and beraprost — in pulmonary arterial hypertension, retrieved to 1 August 2015; beraprost is one limb of the pool, contributing the two trials carded above.
cards.result: In the network analysis, epoprostenol showed the most favourable profile (the authors recommended it as an alternative for moderate/advanced PAH); direct and indirect comparisons differed for several outcomes. For beraprost specifically, participants taking beraprost were more probable to withdraw than those given iloprost (odds ratio 10.07, 95% CI 1.47 to 160.65 — a relative odds measure with a very wide interval). No beraprost-specific walk-distance advantage over placebo was established by this analysis beyond the pooled class results.
cards.watchOut: A class pool, not beraprost evidence in its own right: it must not be counted as a third beraprost trial. A different prostacyclin network meta-analysis that has been withdrawn is fenced and is deliberately not carded on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: beraprost improved walk distance over 12 weeks in one trial, but in the 12-month trial every benefit was confined to the first 6 months — an early, non-sustained effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: beraprost improved walk distance over 12 weeks in one trial, but in the 12-month trial every benefit was confined to the first 6 months — an early, non-sustained effect
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Two randomised trials (n=130 and n=116) and one class network meta-analysis make up the base. The short trial was positive on exercise capacity (25.1 m walk-distance difference at 12 weeks); the long trial found progression and walk benefits at 3–6 months that were no longer evident at 9–12 months. Read together, beraprost has a real but early and attenuating effect in functional class II–III PAH, with common prostacyclin-type adverse events during titration; it is licensed for PAH in Japan and parts of Asia, not in the US or EU.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Ferritin reference intervals are unsettled: laboratory lower limits (median 8 µg/L women, 25 µg/L men) sit below the 30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold, and primary intervals span 11 to 88 µg/L at the lower limit
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for serum ferritin — and why do laboratory lower limits sit below the ~30 µg/L threshold that best detects iron deficiency — by sex, age and menopausal status, and how much do inflammation and assay choice move the limits?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / iron metabolism; Boron & Boulpaep, haematology sections — brief framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. The row's core teaching is a gap, carded head-on: a systematic review of 61 studies (21,882 women, 23,650 men) finds laboratory lower limits a median 8 µg/L (women) and 25 µg/L (men) — below the ~30 µg/L threshold that best detects iron deficiency — on source data at high risk of bias. Four primary datasets show the spread that produces it: geriatric Shanghai intervals (24.44-627.09 µg/L men; 48.18-554.88 women, Roche), a Kenyan IFCC cohort with CRP measured (only the 15 µg/L cut-off anchored to anaemia), 1,223 Chinese Han men (88.2-771.7 µg/L), and a two-assay study with iron deficiency and inflammation explicitly excluded (men 12-399 / 14-415 µg/L; menopausal split in women). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: every interval is printed beside its cohort's inflammation handling. Units µg/L (= ng/mL) throughout. The ESR shelf is the prose cross-point. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Systematic review of how ferritin reference intervals were made (61 studies; 21,882 women and 23,650 men): laboratory lower limits are a median 8 µg/L in women and 25 µg/L in men — below the 30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold — and half the source studies never screened for iron-deficiency risk (Truong 2024)
cards.summary: Systematic review of how ferritin reference intervals were made (61 studies; 21,882 women and 23,650 men): laboratory lower limits are a median 8 µg/L in women and 25 µg/L in men — below the 30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold — and half the source studies never screened for iron-deficiency risk (Truong 2024)
cards.type: Synthesis — systematic review of ferritin reference-interval studies (labelled review, not primary data)
cards.people: Systematic review (labelled synthesis, not a primary dataset) of studies determining ferritin reference intervals in healthy adults, plus grey-literature reference intervals for the five most common ferritin assays; 2,306 records screened, 61 full texts included, 37 studies eligible for the lower-limit (LLN) analysis in the general population (21,882 female and 23,650 male participants). Review registration CRD42022268844 as stated in the record.
cards.result: Across the literature, ferritin LLNs sat consistently below 30 µg/L — the concentration the review notes has high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing iron deficiency in adults: LLN median 8 µg/L (IQR 5-15), mean 9 µg/L (SD 11) in females; median 25 µg/L (IQR 16-44), mean 25 µg/L (SD 29) in males. The five commonest commercial assays reported LLNs of median 11 µg/L (IQR 9-12) for females and 22 µg/L (IQR 22-24) for males. Methodological quality was poor: 30 of 61 studies (49%) did not explicitly screen for iron-deficiency risk in their 'normal' samples, and 32 (52%) followed no reference-interval establishment guideline. The authors conclude the data driving ferritin intervals are at high risk of bias and propose evidence-based clinical decision limits instead. Values in µg/L (= ng/mL) throughout this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A review of intervals, not an interval: its medians summarise how laboratories' limits were historically derived — the primary intervals are the cards below, and they disagree with each other far more than the review's medians suggest.
cards.source: Truong J et al. The origin of ferritin reference intervals: a systematic review. The Lancet. Haematology. 2024. PMID: 38937026. cards.headline: Geriatric Shanghai reference intervals (469 healthy Han Chinese, ages 61-95; Roche Cobas e602): ferritin 24.44-627.09 µg/L in men and 48.18-554.88 µg/L in women (Wang 2023)
cards.summary: Geriatric Shanghai reference intervals (469 healthy Han Chinese, ages 61-95; Roche Cobas e602): ferritin 24.44-627.09 µg/L in men and 48.18-554.88 µg/L in women (Wang 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (serum ferritin reference intervals, geriatric population, named assay)
cards.people: 469 healthy Chinese Han subjects aged 61-95 years (median 71) recruited from a Shanghai health examination centre in 2021; serum ferritin measured on a Roche Cobas 8000 e602 analyser, with 14 biochemical parameters measured for correlation analysis. Intervals printed in the record as ng/mL, numerically identical to µg/L.
cards.result: Established reference intervals for serum ferritin were 24.44-627.09 in males and 48.18-554.88 in females — notably, the female lower limit here is HIGHER than the male, the reverse of younger-adult intervals. The record reports a sex difference with P = 0.06 as printed. Ferritin correlated with seven parameters: BMI (P = 0.02), gamma-glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase, triglycerides, HDL, total protein and prealbumin (each P < 0.01); further correlations (AST, globulin) appeared only within BMI strata. The authors link ferritin in the elderly to nutrition and metabolism.
cards.watchOut: An over-60s interval only: geriatric lower limits (24-48 µg/L) sit far above the young-adult laboratory LLNs in the review card, and the record does not describe CRP-based exclusion of inflammation — ferritin's acute-phase behaviour is the standing caveat for every card on this shelf.

cards.headline: Kenyan IFCC reference-interval programme cohort (528 healthy adults, ages 18-65, CRP measured): only the 15 µg/L ferritin cut-off was associated with anaemia — ruling it out, not in (Omuse 2022)
cards.summary: Kenyan IFCC reference-interval programme cohort (528 healthy adults, ages 18-65, CRP measured): only the 15 µg/L ferritin cut-off was associated with anaemia — ruling it out, not in (Omuse 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ferritin distribution and cut-off behaviour in a healthy adult population, inflammation marker measured)
cards.people: 528 healthy adults aged 18-65 years (254 men, 274 women) recruited in four Kenyan counties at 1,683-2,099 m altitude, as part of the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry global reference-interval study; complete blood count, C-reactive protein, iron, transferrin, transferrin saturation and ferritin analysed against anaemia at several ferritin cut-offs.
cards.result: At a ferritin cut-off of 15 µg/L (with haemoglobin cut-offs 14.5 g/dL in men and 12 g/dL in women), iron-deficiency anaemia prevalence was 0.8% in males and 7.3% in females. The odds of anaemia were highest below 15 µg/L; that cut-off's performance for anaemia was sensitivity 28.6% / specificity 98.4% in males and sensitivity 83.3% / specificity 78.0% in females. Only the 15 µg/L cut-off was associated with anaemia, usable for ruling OUT iron deficiency as its cause. The authors call for sex-specific cut-offs derived against bone-marrow stainable iron in sub-Saharan Africa. The fetched record reports the cohort's ferritin-anaemia behaviour within the IFCC programme; it does not print a Kenyan percentile reference interval itself, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A population with chronic low-grade inflammation and altitude exposure: ferritin's acute-phase rise is exactly what this cohort was designed around (CRP measured alongside), so its cut-off behaviour must not be exported to low-inflammation populations.
cards.source: Omuse G et al. Ferritin and its association with anaemia in a healthy adult population in Kenya. PloS one. 2022. PMID: 36240192. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chinese Han male population survey (1,223 men, ages 20-69; electrochemiluminescence): central-95% ferritin interval 88.2-771.7 µg/L (nonparametric) — far higher than previously reported levels (Li 2011)
cards.summary: Chinese Han male population survey (1,223 men, ages 20-69; electrochemiluminescence): central-95% ferritin interval 88.2-771.7 µg/L (nonparametric) — far higher than previously reported levels (Li 2011)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (serum ferritin reference values, male population survey, named assay)
cards.people: 1,223 screened Chinese Han men aged 20-69 years from the Fangchenggang Area Male Health and Examination Survey (FAMHES); serum ferritin by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay; two-sided central-95-percentile reference values calculated by both parametric and nonparametric methods.
cards.result: Ferritin values were log-normally distributed. The central-95-percentile reference interval was 88.2-771.7 µg/L by the nonparametric method and 104.0-832.2 µg/L by the parametric method — both far above the male intervals in the other cards on this shelf. Ferritin did not differ between non-smoking and smoking groups (P = 0.921) or non-drinking and drinking groups (P = 0.584), and did not rise with age (P = 0.808), but higher ferritin was associated with higher BMI (r = 0.266, P < 10^-5 as printed). The authors note their reference values are higher than previously reported reference levels.
cards.watchOut: Men only, one region, one assay — and a lower limit (88 µg/L) above many laboratories' entire young-adult range: this card is the shelf's standing proof that a 'reference interval' is a population-plus-method artefact, not a biological constant.
