cards.headline: Two-assay reference values with inflammation and iron deficiency excluded (77 men, 182 women): N-Latex men 12-399 µg/L, women <50 years 11-102, women ≥50 years 17-219 — Ferritin Flex near-identical (Hamwi 2002)
cards.summary: Two-assay reference values with inflammation and iron deficiency excluded (77 men, 182 women): N-Latex men 12-399 µg/L, women <50 years 11-102, women ≥50 years 17-219 — Ferritin Flex near-identical (Hamwi 2002)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (per-assay ferritin reference values, exclusions stated)
cards.people: 77 men and 182 women establishing reference values for two Dade Behring ferritin assays — Ferritin Flex on the Dimension RxL (calibrated against the 3rd International Standard, recombinant) and N-Latex Ferritin on the BNA II nephelometer (2nd International Standard, spleen). Exclusion criteria: iron deficiency or iron-deficiency anaemia, inflammation, liver disease, malignancy, and other haematological or chronic disorders — the explicit inflammation handling this shelf requires on the face.
cards.result: Reference values (5th-95th percentiles — a 90% interval, not the conventional 95%): N-Latex — men 12-399 µg/L; women <50 years 11-102 µg/L; women ≥50 years 17-219 µg/L. Ferritin Flex — men 14-415 µg/L; women <50 years 11-111 µg/L; women ≥50 years 22-224 µg/L. The two assays correlated very closely (r = 0.993); linearity was acceptable down to 2 µg/L for Ferritin Flex but only 15 µg/L for N-Latex; mean recovery of the 3rd International Standard was ~80% for both. The menopausal-age split in women (lower limits 11 vs 17-22 µg/L) is visible in both assays.
cards.watchOut: A 5th-95th percentile interval is narrower than the 2.5th-97.5th intervals elsewhere on this shelf — comparing its limits directly with central-95% intervals overstates agreement; and ~80% recovery of the international standard is itself an assay-accuracy caveat.
cards.source: Hamwi A et al. Reference values for a heterogeneous ferritin assay and traceability to the 3rd International Recombinant Standard for Ferritin (NIBSC code 94/572). Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2002. PMID: 12059077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ferritin's laboratory lower limits (median 8 µg/L in women, 25 µg/L in men across 61 studies) sit below the ~30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold, and primary intervals disagree by population, age, menopausal status and assay — from 11 µg/L (women <50, Hamwi) to a male lower limit of 88 µg/L (Li)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ferritin's laboratory lower limits (median 8 µg/L in women, 25 µg/L in men across 61 studies) sit below the ~30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold, and primary intervals disagree by population, age, menopausal status and assay — from 11 µg/L (women <50, Hamwi) to a male lower limit of 88 µg/L (Li)
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (blood / iron metabolism) and Boron & Boulpaep (haematology sections) — brief framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature. The core teaching is the gap: the systematic review of 61 studies finds laboratory lower limits consistently below the 30 µg/L concentration with high sensitivity and specificity for iron deficiency, on source data at high risk of bias — 49% of studies never screened their 'healthy' samples for iron-deficiency risk (Truong 2024). The primary intervals show why no single repair exists: geriatric Shanghai limits run 24.44-627.09 µg/L (men) and 48.18-554.88 µg/L (women) on a Roche platform (Wang 2023); a Kenyan IFCC cohort with CRP measured finds only the 15 µg/L cut-off behaviourally anchored to anaemia (Omuse 2022); 1,223 Chinese Han men give a central-95% interval of 88.2-771.7 µg/L (Li 2011); and a rigorously excluded two-assay study gives male limits of 12-399 / 14-415 µg/L with a menopausal split in women (Hamwi 2002). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant — every interval above is printed beside its cohort's inflammation handling, as the cards state. Units: µg/L throughout (= ng/mL). Cross-point in prose only: the built ESR reference shelf, a fellow inflammation-sensitive analyte. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the normative base is unsettled — intervals diverge severalfold between populations and methods and the historical lower limits are, on the review's own quality assessment, not rigorously derived.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a ferritin reference interval without its population, its assay and its inflammation/iron-deficiency exclusions — and never treat 'within the reference interval' as 'iron-replete' when the interval's lower limit sits below the 30 µg/L decision threshold.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #6292: #6292 asks whether a low ABI PREDICTS events and reclassifies risk — a prognostic question; the population DISTRIBUTION itself, including the high-ABI / incompressible limb a low-ABI-centred prognostic shelf does not present, is this shelf's question alone. The stop-condition set for this row is met on fetched records: beyond the Scottish anchor (28,980 adults over 50 free of clinical cardiovascular disease; mean 1.06 in men, 1.01 in women; Price 2008), three further primary population datasets reporting the distribution itself were verified — NHANES 1999–2000 (ABI <0.90 in 4.3% of adults 40+; Selvin 2004), MESA normal-value modelling (1,775 healthy adults with ABI 1.00–1.30; Aboyans 2007) and the Strong Heart Study (low ABI 4.9%, high ABI >1.40 in 9.2% of 4,393 adults; Resnick 2004). cards.headline: Central Scotland survey (28,980 adults over 50, free of clinical cardiovascular disease): ABI approximately normal — mean 1.06 (SD 0.13) in men, 1.01 (SD 0.11) in women; ABI ≤0.90 in 10.9% (Price 2008)
cards.summary: Central Scotland survey (28,980 adults over 50, free of clinical cardiovascular disease): ABI approximately normal — mean 1.06 (SD 0.13) in men, 1.01 (SD 0.11) in women; ABI ≤0.90 in 10.9% (Price 2008)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population ABI distribution by age, sex and deprivation)
cards.people: Cross-sectional survey of 28,980 men and women aged over 50 years living in central Scotland and free of clinical cardiovascular disease; ABI distribution described by age, sex and deprivation.
cards.result: The ABI was approximately normally distributed in both sexes: mean 1.06 (SD 0.13) in men and 1.01 (SD 0.11) in women. Overall 10.9% of participants had an ABI ≤0.90 — more women (13.6%) than men (7.3%) — and the fraction rose with increasing age and with deprivation, from 6.7% in the most affluent to 14.4% in the most deprived participants. The authors show the classified fraction is highly cutpoint-sensitive (≤0.85, ≤0.95 and ≤1.0 give very different 'at-risk' shares) and caution that any cutpoint, and possibly sex- and age-specific cutpoints, must be chosen with the resulting population share in mind. The fetched record does not name the measurement device, and none is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Adults over 50 only, and 'free of clinical cardiovascular disease' by the survey's definition: the 10.9% ≤0.90 share is an older-population share — the younger NHANES card's 4.3% (<0.90, age 40+) is the contrast, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Price JF et al. Frequency of a low ankle brachial index in the general population by age, sex and deprivation: cross-sectional survey of 28,980 men and women. European journal of cardiovascular prevention and rehabilitation : official journal of the European Society of Cardiology, Working Groups on Epidemiology & Prevention and Cardiac Rehabilitation and Exercise Physiology. 2008. PMID: 18525397. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: NHANES 1999–2000 (2,174 adults aged 40+): ABI <0.90 in either leg in 4.3% of US adults — 14.5% at age 70+ (Selvin 2004)
cards.summary: NHANES 1999–2000 (2,174 adults aged 40+): ABI <0.90 in either leg in 4.3% of US adults — 14.5% at age 70+ (Selvin 2004)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (nationally representative low-ABI prevalence, NHANES)
cards.people: 2,174 participants aged 40 years and older from the nationally representative 1999–2000 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey; peripheral arterial disease defined as an ankle–brachial index <0.90 in either leg — the either-leg convention is this study's, carded as published.
cards.result: The prevalence of ABI <0.90 was 4.3% (95% CI 3.1–5.5) among adults aged 40+, corresponding to roughly 5 million US individuals, and 14.5% (CI 10.8–18.2) among those aged 70+. In age- and sex-adjusted analyses, prevalent low ABI was positively associated with black race/ethnicity, current smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and low kidney function (odds ratios, a relative measure, from 1.68 to 4.46 as reported), and over 95% of persons with a low ABI had one or more cardiovascular risk factors. This dataset reports the low limb of the distribution nationally; it does not report a high-ABI fraction.
cards.watchOut: A 1999–2000 survey with an either-leg <0.90 definition: prevalence figures move with the leg convention and the cutpoint (≤0.90 vs <0.90), as the Scottish card's cutpoint analysis shows — compare like with like.
cards.source: Selvin E et al. Prevalence of and risk factors for peripheral arterial disease in the United States: results from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1999-2000. Circulation. 2004. PMID: 15262830. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MESA normal-value analysis (1,775 healthy adults with ABI 1.00–1.30 and no major risk factors): women run ~0.02 lower than men and black participants ~0.02 lower than non-Hispanic whites, after full adjustment (Aboyans 2007)
cards.summary: MESA normal-value analysis (1,775 healthy adults with ABI 1.00–1.30 and no major risk factors): women run ~0.02 lower than men and black participants ~0.02 lower than non-Hispanic whites, after full adjustment (Aboyans 2007)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (determinants of the normal ABI value, MESA)
cards.people: Cross-sectional analysis within the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (US population study): a selected subgroup of 1,775 participants with unequivocally normal ABIs (1.00 to 1.30), additionally excluding anyone with a major PAD risk factor (smoking, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension); ABI modelled against demographic, clinical, biological and social variables.
cards.result: Within this deliberately normal subgroup there was no association between ABI level and subclinical cardiovascular disease (coronary calcium or carotid plaque). Male sex, weight and higher education were positively correlated with ABI; black race, triglycerides, past-smoker pack-years and pulse pressure were negatively correlated. In the fully adjusted model, women had ABI values about 0.02 lower than men and black participants about 0.02 lower than non-Hispanic whites. The authors' point is distributional: a single 0.90 threshold disregards small, highly significant intrinsic sex and ethnicity differences in the normal value, which can distort population estimates of disease burden.
cards.watchOut: A selected normal subgroup (ABI 1.00–1.30, risk factors excluded) by design: it estimates how the NORMAL value shifts with sex and ethnicity, not the population's low/high fractions — those are the Scottish, NHANES and Strong Heart cards.
cards.source: Aboyans V et al. Intrinsic contribution of gender and ethnicity to normal ankle-brachial index values: the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). Journal of vascular surgery. 2007. PMID: 17264011. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Strong Heart Study (4,393 American Indian adults, bilateral ABI): low ABI (<0.90) in 4.9% and high ABI (>1.40, incompressible range) in 9.2% (Resnick 2004)
cards.summary: Strong Heart Study (4,393 American Indian adults, bilateral ABI): low ABI (<0.90) in 4.9% and high ABI (>1.40, incompressible range) in 9.2% (Resnick 2004)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population distribution of low and high ABI, Strong Heart Study)
cards.people: 4,393 American Indian participants in the population-based Strong Heart Study, with bilateral ankle–brachial index measurements at baseline. This card reports only the baseline distribution fractions the study itself publishes; the study's mortality follow-up is prognostic and belongs to home pack #6292's territory, not this slice.
cards.result: A low ABI (<0.90) was present in 216 participants (4.9%) and a high ABI (>1.40) in 404 participants (9.2%) — the high, incompressible-artery limb roughly twice as common as the low limb in this population. Diabetes, albuminuria and hypertension were all more frequent in both the low and the high groups than in the normal-ABI group (diabetes 60.2% low, 67.8% high, 44.4% normal; P < 0.0001). The authors conclude the upper limit of normal ABI should not exceed 1.40. This is the shelf's high-limb anchor: a prognostic shelf centred on low ABI does not present this fraction, which is why the distribution needed its own shelf.
cards.watchOut: A population with a high diabetes burden: the 9.2% high-ABI share reflects that case mix (medial calcification tracks diabetes) and should not be transplanted to a low-diabetes population — the fraction is population-specific, the existence and size order of the high limb is the general finding.
cards.source: Resnick HE et al. Relationship of high and low ankle brachial index to all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality: the Strong Heart Study. Circulation. 2004. PMID: 14970108. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ABI centres just above 1.0 (men 1.06, women 1.01 at age 50+), the ≤0.90 share runs 4–11% depending on age and leg convention, and the high ≥1.40 limb is real and population-dependent (9.2% in Strong Heart)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ABI centres just above 1.0 (men 1.06, women 1.01 at age 50+), the ≤0.90 share runs 4–11% depending on age and leg convention, and the high ≥1.40 limb is real and population-dependent (9.2% in Strong Heart)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four population datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (peripheral circulation) generally; the shelf rests on the primary population literature. PARTIAL slice of home pack #6292 (low-ABI prognosis and reclassification): prognosis is #6292's question, the distribution is this shelf's, and no study is shared. The distribution: approximately normal, centred at 1.06 (SD 0.13) in older men and 1.01 (SD 0.11) in older women (Price 2008, N = 28,980), with an intrinsic ~0.02 downward shift for women and for black participants inside the normal range itself (Aboyans 2007, MESA). The low limb: ≤0.90 in 10.9% of CVD-free Scots over 50 (13.6% of women, 7.3% of men; rising with age and deprivation), against <0.90 in either leg in 4.3% of US adults 40+ and 14.5% at 70+ (Selvin 2004) — the spread is age, cutpoint (≤ vs <) and leg convention, carded per study, not disagreement about shape. shelves.title: Standing norms are method-split: beat-to-beat initial hypotension in 32.9% at 50+ but cuff OH in 6.9% — while young lean-test adults rise ~10 beats/min and nobody meets criteria (PARTIAL slice of #6251)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, how much do blood pressure and heart rate change on standing — the beat-to-beat time course over the first 3 minutes, the size and frequency of the initial fall, and 1- and 3-minute values on a bedside active-stand / 10-minute lean test — by age, and what fraction of healthy people meet the consensus orthostatic-hypotension thresholds?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, autonomic / circulatory control chapters; Boron & Boulpaep, cardiovascular control. PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #6251: #6251 asks how much blood POOLS in the legs on standing and how baroreflexes defend pressure — a mechanism question; it does not give bedside normative change values, normograms or threshold-meeting frequencies, which are this shelf's question alone. The stop-condition set for this row is met on fetched records: beyond the two mining anchors — TILDA beat-to-beat normograms in 4,475 adults aged 50+ (Finucane 2014) and 10-minute lean-test norms in 112 younger adults without orthostatic intolerance (Iftekhar 2025) — two further primary datasets reporting supine-to-standing change values were verified, including the younger coverage TILDA lacks: the Malmö Offspring Study (5,259 general-population adults, mean age 41.9, 3-minute standing change; Johansson 2023) and a healthy-volunteer Finapres study spanning ages 18–74 with active standing (Ndayisaba 2015, N = 81). Beat-to-beat and cuff/lean measurements give different 'normals' and are carded per-method, never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: TILDA active stand, beat-to-beat (4,475 adults aged 50+): responses stabilise within 30 s at 50–59 but take longer when older — initial orthostatic hypotension in 32.9%, orthostatic hypotension in 6.9%, impaired stabilisation in 15.6% (Finucane 2014)
cards.summary: TILDA active stand, beat-to-beat (4,475 adults aged 50+): responses stabilise within 30 s at 50–59 but take longer when older — initial orthostatic hypotension in 32.9%, orthostatic hypotension in 6.9%, impaired stabilisation in 15.6% (Finucane 2014)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population beat-to-beat orthostatic normograms, TILDA)
cards.people: Nationally representative Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing participants aged 50 years or older who underwent an active stand test with beat-to-beat systolic and diastolic blood pressure and heart-rate recording (n = 4,475); normograms estimated with generalized additive models, and prevalence of impaired stabilisation, initial orthostatic hypotension and orthostatic hypotension reported.
cards.result: Orthostatic responses in adults aged 50–59 stabilised within 30 seconds of standing; older groups took 30 seconds or longer. Impaired blood-pressure stabilisation affected 15.6% (95% CI 14.1–17.1) overall, rising with age to 41.2% (CI 30.0–52.4) at age 80+. Initial orthostatic hypotension occurred in 32.9% (CI 31.2–34.6) of the population aged 50+, with no age gradient. Orthostatic hypotension prevalence was 6.9% (CI 5.9–7.8) overall, rising to 18.5% (CI 9.0–28.0) at 80+. These are beat-to-beat (continuous) normals: the one-in-three initial-hypotension figure is a transient first-seconds phenomenon that cuff measurements at 1 and 3 minutes cannot see, and the two methods' frequencies must not be merged.
cards.watchOut: Age 50+ only — the younger-adult gap this shelf's other cards exist to fill. Beat-to-beat initial orthostatic hypotension (32.9%) is not comparable with cuff-defined orthostatic hypotension at 1/3 minutes (6.9% in the same cohort): method first, number second.
cards.source: Finucane C et al. Age-related normative changes in phasic orthostatic blood pressure in a large population study: findings from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA). Circulation. 2014. PMID: 25278101. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 10-minute lean test norms (112 adults without orthostatic intolerance, mean age 35.3): heart rate rises on average 9.89 ± 8.15 beats/min, systolic pressure initially rises 7.55 ± 10.88 mm Hg — and nobody met OH or PoTS criteria (Iftekhar 2025)
cards.summary: 10-minute lean test norms (112 adults without orthostatic intolerance, mean age 35.3): heart rate rises on average 9.89 ± 8.15 beats/min, systolic pressure initially rises 7.55 ± 10.88 mm Hg — and nobody met OH or PoTS criteria (Iftekhar 2025)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative 10-minute lean-test data in adults without orthostatic intolerance)
cards.people: 112 individuals with complete datasets (60.7% female; mean age 35.3 ± 15.1 years; BMI 24.8 ± 4.0), recruited from the general population of a metropolitan city, with no history or symptoms of orthostatic intolerance, autonomic dysfunction, post-infection conditions or neurological conditions with haemodynamic instability. Standardised 10-minute lean test: supine blood pressure and heart rate after 2 minutes lying, then measurements every minute while leaning against a wall for 10 minutes, with symptoms recorded each minute.
cards.result: On standing, the average heart-rate change was an increase of 9.89 ± 8.15 beats/min; the sustained increase (present at two consecutive readings) averaged 6.23 ± 6.94 beats/min. The predominant blood-pressure response was a systolic rise, the average initial increase being 7.55 ± 10.88 mm Hg. None of the 112 participants met the diagnostic criteria for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome during the test. The authors present this as the first normative lean-test dataset in a relatively younger population. These are cuff, once-a-minute, lean-test values — a different measurement from TILDA's beat-to-beat active stand, carded separately by design.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, N = 112, and 30.6% had some background medical condition (none an exclusion condition): the cleanest young-adult bedside norms available, but one centre's norms. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Iftekhar N et al. Normative data for the 10-min lean test in adults without orthostatic intolerance. Frontiers in neurology. 2025. PMID: 41111962. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Malmö Offspring Study (5,259 general-population adults, mean age 41.9): orthostatic systolic change after 3 minutes standing distributes in both directions — the lowest and highest quartiles both carry the stiffest arteries (Johansson 2023)
cards.summary: Malmö Offspring Study (5,259 general-population adults, mean age 41.9): orthostatic systolic change after 3 minutes standing distributes in both directions — the lowest and highest quartiles both carry the stiffest arteries (Johansson 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population orthostatic blood-pressure adaptation at 3 minutes, Malmö Offspring Study)
cards.people: Observational population-based study of 5,259 individuals living in Malmö, Sweden (mean age 41.9 ± 14.5 years; 52.1% women) — a predominantly younger and middle-aged general-population sample. Orthostatic blood-pressure adaptation assessed after 3 minutes standing, related to carotid-femoral pulse-wave velocity and radial pulse-wave analysis.
cards.result: Orthostatic systolic blood-pressure difference at 3 minutes spread across quartiles in both directions (falls and rises): the highest aortic stiffness and central pressures were found in both the lowest and the highest quartiles of orthostatic systolic difference (P < 0.001) — a U-shaped pattern in a young-to-middle-aged population. Aortic stiffness and central pressure decreased gradually across increasing quartiles of orthostatic diastolic difference (P < 0.001). After full adjustment, orthostatic diastolic difference remained associated with aortic stiffness (P = 0.001) and central pressure (P < 0.001), and systolic difference with central systolic pressure (P = 0.009); subclinical orthostatic hypotension showed no significant association with stiffness or central haemodynamics. The record reports the change distribution in quartiles, not a mean change value, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A 3-minute cuff-protocol population measurement, not a beat-to-beat time course: it fills the younger-age and population-distribution gap for the 3-minute value, and says nothing about the first 30 seconds, where TILDA's initial-hypotension phenomenon lives.
cards.source: Johansson M et al. Orthostatic blood pressure adaptations, aortic stiffness, and central hemodynamics in the general population: insights from the Malmö Offspring Study (MOS). Clinical autonomic research : official journal of the Clinical Autonomic Research Society. 2023. PMID: 36473959. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy-volunteer Finapres study (81 adults, ages 18–74): no sex effect on orthostatic heart-rate or blood-pressure change; the heart-rate and diastolic responses attenuate with age (Ndayisaba 2015)
cards.summary: Healthy-volunteer Finapres study (81 adults, ages 18–74): no sex effect on orthostatic heart-rate or blood-pressure change; the heart-rate and diastolic responses attenuate with age (Ndayisaba 2015)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (sex and age effects on orthostatic change in healthy adults, Finapres)
cards.people: 81 healthy volunteers (41 women, 40 men; ages 18–74 years) undergoing extensive cardiovascular autonomic testing with Finapres finger arterial pressure, ECG and impedance cardiography: rest, 60-degree head-up tilt for 45 minutes, active standing for 5 minutes, Valsalva manoeuvre and deep breathing. Mean values and orthostatic changes (differences from baseline) of heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure, stroke volume and total peripheral resistance were calculated and modelled by sex and age. N = 81 printed on the face.
cards.result: Resting heart rate was higher in women (P = 0.035) and resting and tilt blood pressure, resting total peripheral resistance and tilt stroke volume were higher in men — but there was no significant impact of sex on the orthostatic CHANGES in heart rate or blood pressure. Mean total peripheral resistance during tilt increased with age (P = 0.001), particularly in older women. Orthostatic changes in heart rate and diastolic blood pressure became attenuated with age (P = 0.018 and P = 0.006), as did the deep-breathing and Valsalva ratios. The fetched record reports directions and significance for the change values, not numeric deltas, and this card claims no mm Hg or beats/min figures from it.
cards.watchOut: N = 81 healthy volunteers across a 56-year age span: it establishes the age-attenuation direction in genuinely healthy people including young adults, at small N — the population-scale quantification is TILDA (50+) and Malmö (3-minute), and the three must not be averaged.
cards.source: Ndayisaba JP et al. Sex and age effects on cardiovascular autonomic function in healthy adults. Clinical autonomic research : official journal of the Clinical Autonomic Research Society. 2015. PMID: 26285905. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: on standing, healthy pressure is defended within ~30 s in the young and slower with age — initial beat-to-beat hypotension is common (32.9% at 50+), cuff orthostatic hypotension uncommon (6.9%), and young lean-test hearts rise ~10 beats/min with systolic pressure rising, not falling
cards.summary: Synthesis: on standing, healthy pressure is defended within ~30 s in the young and slower with age — initial beat-to-beat hypotension is common (32.9% at 50+), cuff orthostatic hypotension uncommon (6.9%), and young lean-test hearts rise ~10 beats/min with systolic pressure rising, not falling
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (autonomic / circulatory control) and Boron & Boulpaep (cardiovascular control). PARTIAL slice of home pack #6251 (leg pooling and baroreflex defence mechanisms): mechanism is #6251's question, bedside normative change values are this shelf's, and no study is shared. The time course, per method: beat-to-beat, stabilisation takes under 30 seconds at 50–59 and 30 seconds or more at older ages, with initial orthostatic hypotension in 32.9% and sustained orthostatic hypotension in 6.9% of a population 50+ sample, the latter rising to 18.5% at 80+ (Finucane 2014, TILDA, N = 4,475). At the bedside in younger adults, the 10-minute lean test gives a mean heart-rate rise of 9.89 ± 8.15 beats/min and an initial systolic RISE of 7.55 ± 10.88 mm Hg, with zero of 112 healthy people meeting OH or PoTS criteria (Iftekhar 2025). At population scale in younger adults, the 3-minute systolic change spreads in both directions across quartiles (Johansson 2023, N = 5,259, mean age 41.9), and in healthy volunteers the heart-rate and diastolic change responses attenuate with age with no sex effect on the changes themselves (Ndayisaba 2015, N = 81). So a meaningful fraction of healthy older people meet consensus orthostatic-hypotension thresholds on beat-to-beat testing, while healthy younger people on a lean test essentially do not — the threshold-meeting frequency is a function of age AND method, and the orthostatic-treatment shelves presuppose thresholds this shelf interrogates. Stop-condition note: this row required a third primary dataset beyond TILDA and the lean test; Malmö Offspring and the healthy-volunteer Finapres study were verified from fetched records, giving four datasets in total. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Never merge beat-to-beat and cuff/lean 'normals': the initial fall exists only in the continuous record, and a 1- or 3-minute cuff value in the same person can be normal while the beat-to-beat trace meets initial-hypotension criteria.

shelves.title: Ongericimab in hypercholesterolaemia: LDL cholesterol down by about two-thirds versus placebo in three Chinese phase 3 trials — surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia (primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, and statin-intolerant patients), does the PCSK9 monoclonal antibody ongericimab, compared with placebo on background therapy, lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents · Biomarkers · China · Cholesterol, LDL · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Dyslipidemias · East Asian People · Hypercholesterolemia · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Proprotein Convertase 9 · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the surrogate only. Three Chinese phase 3 trials consistently show ongericimab lowering LDL cholesterol by about two-thirds versus placebo on background therapy: least-squares mean differences of −67.7% (150 mg every 2 weeks) in primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia, −66.2% in statin-intolerant patients, and −69.4% to −80.6% in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo; a device study (programme support) shows syringe and autoinjector delivery perform alike. These percentages are changes in LDL cholesterol, a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of ongericimab exists (class outcomes evidence is cross-pointed to the evolocumab/alirocumab shelves). The evidence is single-region (China; ongericimab is a single-source Junshi Biosciences product approved there).

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT in primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia (Wang 2024): ongericimab lowered LDL cholesterol by a least-squares mean difference of −67.7% (150 mg every 2 weeks) and −61.2% (300 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo at week 24
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT in primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia (Wang 2024): ongericimab lowered LDL cholesterol by a least-squares mean difference of −67.7% (150 mg every 2 weeks) and −61.2% (300 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo at week 24
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ongericimab add-on to optimised lipid-lowering therapy
cards.people: 806 Chinese patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia on stable optimised lipid-lowering therapy who had not reached LDL targets, randomised 2:1:2:1 to ongericimab 150 mg or placebo every 2 weeks, or ongericimab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks, for 52 weeks; 802 received at least one dose.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in percentage change in LDL cholesterol from baseline to week 24 was −67.7% (95% CI −72.5% to −63.0%; P<0.0001) for ongericimab 150 mg every 2 weeks versus its placebo, and −61.2% (95% CI −67.1% to −55.2%; P<0.0001) for 300 mg every 4 weeks versus its placebo; reductions were sustained to week 52 and other lipid parameters moved favourably. Adverse-event incidence was similar in the ongericimab and placebo groups. These are percentage changes in LDL cholesterol, a surrogate endpoint — not reductions in cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: Single-region evidence (China) on a surrogate endpoint; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of ongericimab exists — outcomes evidence for the PCSK9 class sits on the evolocumab/alirocumab shelves and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Wang X et al. Efficacy and Safety of Ongericimab in Chinese Patients With Primary Hypercholesterolemia and Mixed Dyslipidemia. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2024. cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT in statin-intolerant patients (Shao 2025): ongericimab 150 mg every 2 weeks lowered LDL cholesterol by a least-squares mean difference of −66.2% versus placebo at week 12
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT in statin-intolerant patients (Shao 2025): ongericimab 150 mg every 2 weeks lowered LDL cholesterol by a least-squares mean difference of −66.2% versus placebo at week 12
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, statin-intolerant patients
cards.people: 139 Chinese statin-intolerant adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia or mixed dyslipidaemia randomised 2:1 to ongericimab 150 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 2 weeks for a 12-week double-blind period, followed by 40 weeks of open-label ongericimab.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in percentage change in LDL cholesterol from baseline to week 12 was −66.2% (P<0.0001) for ongericimab versus placebo, sustained to week 52; non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, total cholesterol and lipoprotein(a) also fell significantly. Treatment-emergent adverse-event incidence was comparable between groups. The percentage figures are changes in LDL cholesterol (a surrogate), not event reductions.
cards.watchOut: The randomised comparison lasts only 12 weeks (the remaining 40 weeks are open-label, all on ongericimab), and the population is Chinese statin-intolerant patients — the result does not by itself establish long-term or outcomes benefit.

cards.result: Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in China — primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia (806 patients; LDL difference −67.7% at 150 mg every 2 weeks and −61.2% at 300 mg every 4 weeks at week 24), statin-intolerant patients (139 patients; −66.2% at week 12) and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (135 patients; −69.4% and −80.6% at week 24) — consistently show large percentage reductions in LDL cholesterol with adverse-event rates similar to placebo, and a fourth, device-comparison study (programme support) shows prefilled-syringe and autoinjector delivery perform alike. Ongericimab is a single-source product (Junshi Biosciences), approved in China; the evidence base is single-region.

shelves.title: Susoctocog alfa in acquired haemophilia A (REBUILD): bleeds resolved in most patients in three single-arm reports (n=28 trial; n=53 and n=50 cohorts) — inhibitors to porcine factor VIII are the defining harm
shelves.question: In adults with acquired haemophilia A and a serious bleeding episode, does susoctocog alfa (recombinant porcine-sequence factor VIII, dosed and titrated against measured factor VIII activity), versus no concurrent control, control bleeding at 24 hours, and with what immunogenicity and thrombotic cost?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Animals · Antibodies, Neutralizing · Autoantibodies · Cross Reactions · Factor VIII · Female · Hemophilia A · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recombinant Proteins · Swine · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence throughout, with no concurrent control in any report, so response proportions cannot be read as comparative efficacy. The pivotal prospective phase 2/3 trial (n=28) found a positive response at 24 hours in all 28 subjects and ultimate bleed control in 24 of 28, with no related serious adverse events or thrombotic events. Two post-authorisation cohorts (US n=53; EU n=50) found 80.3% of treated bleeds and 37 of 50 initial bleeding events resolved, respectively. The defining harm is immunogenicity against the porcine sequence: treatment-related serious adverse events in 12.0% in the US study, most commonly inhibitors to porcine factor VIII (8.0%), and 4 of 5 probably-related serious events in the EU study were anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitor events. A Japanese phase II/III report enrolled only 5 patients — below the library floor — and is excluded from this shelf, as the commissioning row directs; it is not carded and carries no weight here. Product naming under the clarification exception: susoctocog alfa (Obizur, Takeda), a recombinant porcine-sequence factor VIII whose dose can be titrated against measured factor VIII activity, unlike bypassing agents — that monitoring contrast is context, not comparative evidence.

cards.headline: Pivotal phase 2/3 trial OBI-1 (Kruse-Jarres 2015): all 28 subjects with acquired haemophilia A had a positive response at 24 hours and bleeding was ultimately controlled in 24 of 28 — single-arm, no control group
cards.summary: Pivotal phase 2/3 trial OBI-1 (Kruse-Jarres 2015): all 28 subjects with acquired haemophilia A had a positive response at 24 hours and bleeding was ultimately controlled in 24 of 28 — single-arm, no control group
cards.type: Prospective open-label single-arm phase 2/3 trial (OBI-1), susoctocog alfa titrated to factor VIII activity
cards.people: 28 subjects with acquired haemophilia A and a serious bleeding episode, treated prospectively with OBI-1 (susoctocog alfa): an initial dose of 200 U/kg, then titrated to maintain target factor VIII activity levels alongside clinical assessment.
cards.result: All 28 subjects had a positive response to treatment 24 hours after initiation, despite inhibition of factor VIII activity immediately after infusion in 10 subjects with baseline anti-porcine factor VIII inhibitors. Control of the qualifying bleed was ultimately achieved in 24 of 28 subjects. No related serious adverse events, thrombotic events, allergic reactions or thrombocytopenia occurred.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with 28 subjects: a 100% 24-hour response proportion has no comparator, and some bleeds in acquired haemophilia A stop with concurrent care — this proportion cannot be read as proof of comparative efficacy.

cards.headline: US post-authorisation safety study (Tarantino 2023): 80.3% of 71 treated bleeds resolved; treatment-related serious adverse events in 12.0%, most commonly inhibitors to porcine factor VIII (8.0%)
cards.summary: US post-authorisation safety study (Tarantino 2023): 80.3% of 71 treated bleeds resolved; treatment-related serious adverse events in 12.0%, most commonly inhibitors to porcine factor VIII (8.0%)
cards.type: Non-interventional post-authorisation safety study (US PASS), uncontrolled real-world cohort
cards.people: 53 adults with acquired haemophilia A enrolled in the US post-authorisation safety study (30 prospective, 23 retrospective), with data collected for 180 days after susoctocog alfa treatment.
cards.result: Six patients experienced seven treatment-related serious adverse events (incidence 12.0%); the most common was factor VIII inhibition — inhibiting antibodies to recombinant porcine factor VIII (incidence 8.0%, 95% CI 2.2 to 19.2). Five patients reported seven thromboembolic events, one of them a serious event possibly related to treatment. Of bleeding events treated, 80.3% (57 of 71) resolved; the median dose per infusion was 50 (range 10–300) units/kg, a median of 6.0 infusions were given, and median time from bleed onset to resolution was 14.0 days. No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled real-world data mixing retrospective and prospective collection: resolution proportions reflect the whole package of care, and inhibitor rates depend on how hard investigators looked for them.
cards.source: Tarantino MD et al. Real-world safety and effectiveness of recombinant porcine sequence factor VIII in acquired haemophilia A: A non-interventional, post-authorization safety study. cards.summary: EU PASS (Miesbach 2024): 37 of 50 initial bleeding events resolved (median 8.0 days); 5 probably-related serious adverse events, 4 of them anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitor events; no thromboembolic events
cards.type: Non-interventional post-authorisation safety study (EU PASS), uncontrolled real-world cohort
cards.people: 50 adults with acquired haemophilia A enrolled in the EU post-authorisation safety study, with data collected retrospectively or prospectively for up to 180 days after the last susoctocog alfa dose; 31 completed the study. Median first dose was 54.0 (range 11–200) U/kg.
cards.result: Thirty patients reported 46 serious adverse events; 5 serious events were considered probably related to susoctocog alfa — 1 lack of efficacy and 4 immunogenicity events (drug resistance due to factor VIII inhibition in one patient, a positive anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitor test in one, and de novo anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitors in two). No hypersensitivity reactions or thromboembolic events were reported. Of the 50 initial bleeding events, 37 resolved, in a median of 8.0 (interquartile range 4.0–16.0) days.
cards.watchOut: Only 31 of 50 patients completed the study, and effectiveness is again uncontrolled; the consistent finding across both PASS cohorts is the immunogenicity cost, not a comparative benefit.

cards.result: Every report on this shelf is single-arm: the pivotal OBI-1 trial (all 28 subjects responding at 24 hours; bleed control in 24 of 28; no related serious events in that small trial), the US PASS cohort (80.3% of 71 bleeds resolved; treatment-related serious events 12.0%, inhibitors 8.0%) and the EU PASS cohort (37 of 50 initial bleeds resolved; 4 of 5 probably-related serious events were inhibitor events). There is no randomised or concurrent-control evidence, so the shelf supports 'bleeds commonly resolve and factor VIII activity can be monitored and titrated' — not superiority over bypassing agents. A further Japanese report enrolled only 5 patients, below the library floor; it is excluded and not carded, as the commissioning row directs.

shelves.title: Bomedemstat in myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 single-arm reports): spleen reduction in 66% with data (MF) and platelet response in 77% evaluable (ET)
shelves.question: In patients with myelofibrosis refractory/resistant to, inadequately controlled by, or intolerant of approved therapy, or with essential thrombocythemia requiring cytoreduction after inadequate response/intolerance to at least 1 standard therapy, does the irreversible LSD1 inhibitor bomedemstat (dose-titrated to a target platelet count), versus no concurrent control, reduce spleen volume (myelofibrosis) or durably control platelet count (essential thrombocythemia), and does it reduce driver-mutation variant allele frequency?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Primary Myelofibrosis · Female · Male · Aged · Middle Aged · Histone Demethylases · Treatment Outcome · Aged, 80 and over · Adult · Enzyme Inhibitors · Benzamides · Piperazines · Triazoles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports, one in myelofibrosis (phase 1/2, n=89) and one in essential thrombocythemia (phase 2, n=73), both single-arm with no concurrent control, and the two disease slices are labelled separately and never pooled. In myelofibrosis, 23 of 35 patients with week-24 spleen-volume data (66%) had a spleen-volume reduction and 9 (26%) a reduction of 20% or more, against thrombocytopenia in 48% and grade 3–5 adverse events in 69%. In essential thrombocythemia, response (platelets 400 ×10⁹/L or below without new thromboembolism) occurred in 49 of 64 evaluable patients (77%) at week 24, with haemorrhagic events in 15 of 73 (21%). There is no polycythaemia-vera report and no third report at floor. The dose is titrated to a target platelet count, so the titration is part of the tested intervention.

cards.headline: Phase 1/2 in myelofibrosis (Gill 2026): of 35 patients with week-24 spleen data, 66% had a spleen-volume reduction and 26% a reduction of ≥20% — single-arm; thrombocytopenia 48%, grade 3–5 events 69%
cards.summary: Phase 1/2 in myelofibrosis (Gill 2026): of 35 patients with week-24 spleen data, 66% had a spleen-volume reduction and 26% a reduction of ≥20% — single-arm; thrombocytopenia 48%, grade 3–5 events 69%
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 1/2 study in myelofibrosis, bomedemstat titrated to platelet count
cards.people: 89 participants with myelofibrosis refractory or resistant to, inadequately controlled by, or intolerant of approved therapies, treated open-label with bomedemstat 0.25, 0.5 or 0.6 mg/kg once daily, titrated to a target platelet count of 50 ×10⁹/L to 75 ×10⁹/L.
cards.result: Of 35 participants with spleen-volume data at week 24, 23 (66%) had a reduction in spleen volume and 9 (26%) a reduction of 20% or more. Mean platelet and white-cell counts normalised over 24 weeks and haemoglobin remained stable; most symptoms, including fatigue, improved. Of 35 with paired bone-marrow data, 8 (23%) improved fibrosis by at least 1 grade and 21 (60%) were stable; of 36 with driver mutations and week-24 data, 56% had a reduction in variant allele frequency. Adverse events occurred in 97%: most commonly thrombocytopenia (48%) and dysgeusia (36%); 62 participants (69%) had a grade 3 to 5 event, and 3 (3%) died of adverse events judged unrelated to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and heavily pretreated: only 35 of 89 participants had week-24 spleen-volume data, so the 66% figure describes a completer subset, not all treated patients; there is no comparator for symptoms or survival.
cards.source: Gill H et al. The lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) inhibitor bomedemstat in myelofibrosis: results from a phase 1/2 study. Blood advances. 2026. PMID: 42054549. cards.headline: Phase 2 in essential thrombocythemia (Gill 2026): response in 49 of 64 evaluable patients (77%) at week 24 — single-arm; haemorrhagic events in 21%, grade 3–4 events in 47%
cards.summary: Phase 2 in essential thrombocythemia (Gill 2026): response in 49 of 64 evaluable patients (77%) at week 24 — single-arm; haemorrhagic events in 21%, grade 3–4 events in 47%
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2 study in essential thrombocythemia, bomedemstat titrated to platelet count
cards.people: 73 participants with essential thrombocythemia requiring cytoreduction after inadequate response to, or intolerance of, at least 1 standard therapy, treated with bomedemstat starting at 0.6 mg/kg per day, titrated to a target platelet count of 200 ×10⁹/L to 400 ×10⁹/L.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, 49 of 64 evaluable participants (77%) achieved the response definition (platelet count 400 ×10⁹/L or below without new thromboembolic events). Durable platelet control (400 ×10⁹/L or below for at least 12 weeks) occurred in 52 of 72 (72%), and durable white-cell control in 61 of 72 (85%); haemoglobin remained stable. Variant allele frequency of CALR, JAK2 or MPL fell in 39 of 46 evaluable participants (85%). By week 24, 2 of 73 (3%) had a thrombotic event and 15 of 73 (21%) a haemorrhagic event. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 34 of 73 (47%) over the treatment period; treatment was interrupted in 40% and permanently stopped in 15%; no participant died from an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: platelet control is the drug's titration target, so response partly reflects the dosing design; the 21% haemorrhage rate in a disease treated to prevent thrombosis is the counterweight and has no control rate to compare against.
cards.source: Gill H et al. Phase 2 study of the lysine-specific demethylase 1 inhibitor bomedemstat for essential thrombocythemia. Blood advances. 2026. PMID: 41758981. Registry ID: NCT04254978. cards.people: The two reports carded above only: myelofibrosis (n=89 treated) and essential thrombocythemia (n=73 treated), both with bomedemstat dose-titrated to platelet count.
cards.result: Across both single-arm reports, the recurring harms were thrombocytopenia (48% in myelofibrosis) and dysgeusia (36% in myelofibrosis), with grade 3–5 events in 69% of myelofibrosis patients and grade 3–4 events in 47% of essential-thrombocythemia patients, haemorrhagic events in 21% of the thrombocythemia cohort, and permanent discontinuation in 15% of that cohort. Driver-mutation variant allele frequency fell in 56% of evaluable myelofibrosis patients (20 of 36 with data) and 85% of evaluable thrombocythemia patients (39 of 46) — exploratory, uncontrolled measures that do not by themselves establish disease modification.
cards.watchOut: This card re-reads the same two reports for harms and allele frequency; it adds no patients and must not be counted as a third report — the shelf's base remains exactly 2 reports.

shelves.title: hs-troponin 99th-percentile limits are assay- and rule-bound: NHANES URLs 19 (T) / 13 / 5 / 37 ng/L (I assays) vs manufacturers up to 46.5; outlier removal alone moved Siemens URLs from ~60 to ~13.5 ng/L
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the 99th-percentile upper reference limit for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (and T) — by assay, sex and age — how large is the male–female gap, and how much do reference-population selection rules (imaging / biomarker screening vs questionnaire only) and outlier handling move the limit that defines myocardial injury?
shelves.mesh: Male · Female · Adult · Humans · Troponin T · Troponin I · Nutrition Surveys · Reference Values · Ethnicity · Biomarkers · Age Factors · Asian People · Biomarkers/blood · China · Middle Aged · Sensitivity and Specificity · Sex Factors · Troponin I/blood · Troponin I/analysis · Sex Factors · Troponin T/blood · Myocardial Infarction/blood,diagnosis
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, cardiac muscle / excitation — the framing is brief for a measurement row, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-limit literature, and says so. This is a measurement row only: it carries no ACS diagnostic-pathway recommendations, which live on the chest-pain shelves. The evidence's central fact is that the 99th-percentile upper reference limit (URL) is a property of assay × sex × age × selection rules, not a universal troponin number: in strictly healthy NHANES adults (n=2,746) the hs-cTnT URL matched the manufacturer (19 ng/L) while the three hs-cTnI URLs came out well below manufacturers' (Abbott 13 vs 28 ng/L; Ortho 5 vs 11 ng/L; Siemens 37 vs 46.5 ng/L); in 2,183 healthy Chinese adults the VITROS hs-cTnI URL was 11.1 ng/L overall (men 12.5, women 9.6), higher at age ≥55; in a strictly selected Korean population the two Siemens hs-cTnI URLs were about 60 ng/L BEFORE outlier elimination and about 13.5 ng/L AFTER removing ~8% of samples as outliers — a more than fourfold swing from a statistical rule alone; and the 2024 systematic review (19 studies, 11 hs-cTnI and 9 hs-cTnT assays) found female 99th percentiles below male and overall values in over 90% of hs-cTnI studies and 8 of 9 hs-cTnT studies. URLs were significantly lower under age 40 than at 60+ for all four NHANES assays, and did not differ by race/ethnicity there. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the sex gap and assay dependence are consistent, but the limit itself moves severalfold with reference-population selection and outlier handling, so no settled single threshold exists to state.

cards.headline: NHANES four-assay URLs (McEvoy 2023): in 2,746 strictly healthy US adults, hs-cTnT URL 19 ng/L matched the manufacturer, but hs-cTnI URLs were far below manufacturers' — Abbott 13 (vs 28), Ortho 5 (vs 11), Siemens 37 (vs 46.5) ng/L; URLs differed by sex and age, not race/ethnicity

cards.type: Primary human physiology study (99th-percentile URLs for four hs-troponin assays, NHANES healthy subgroup)
cards.people: Stored samples from 12,545 US adults in NHANES 1999–2004, of whom 2,746 met criteria for the strictly defined healthy reference subgroup (mean age 37 years, 50% men); hs-troponin T measured on one Roche assay and hs-troponin I on three assays (Abbott, Siemens, Ortho); 99th percentile URLs estimated by the recommended nonparametric method, overall and by sex, race/ethnicity and age group.
cards.result: The hs-cTnT URL was 19 ng/L, matching the manufacturer-reported 19 ng/L. The hs-cTnI URLs were 13 ng/L (95% CI 10 to 15) for Abbott against a manufacturer URL of 28 ng/L; 5 ng/L (95% CI 4 to 7) for Ortho against 11 ng/L; and 37 ng/L (95% CI 27 to 66) for Siemens against 46.5 ng/L. URLs differed significantly by sex for all assays, did not differ by race/ethnicity, and were significantly lower in healthy adults under 40 years than in those aged 60 years or over for all four assays (all P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Stored 1999–2004 samples assayed later, and a 'strictly healthy' subgroup that is only 22% of participants and young (mean 37): both features pull URLs down relative to the older, questionnaire-screened populations behind some manufacturer values — that dependence is the lesson, not a defect to hide.

cards.headline: Chinese VITROS hs-cTnI URLs (He 2022): 2,183 healthy adults — overall 99th percentile 11.1 ng/L (men 12.5, women 9.6), significantly higher at age 55 and over in both sexes; 78.8% of men and 70.1% of women had detectable values (limit of detection 0.43 ng/L)
cards.summary: Chinese VITROS hs-cTnI URLs (He 2022): 2,183 healthy adults — overall 99th percentile 11.1 ng/L (men 12.5, women 9.6), significantly higher at age 55 and over in both sexes; 78.8% of men and 70.1% of women had detectable values (limit of detection 0.43 ng/L)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age- and sex-specific hs-cTnI 99th-percentile URLs, VITROS assay, healthy Chinese adults)
cards.people: 2,183 apparently healthy Chinese individuals (1,051 men and 1,132 women aged 20–95 years), screened by questionnaire and then selected to International Federation of Clinical Chemistry criteria using surrogate biomarkers for diabetes, myocardial dysfunction and renal dysfunction; hs-cTnI measured on the VITROS 5600 system (Ortho Clinical Diagnostics).
cards.result: The overall 99th percentile URL was 11.1 ng/L — 12.5 ng/L in men and 9.6 ng/L in women, a male–female gap of about 3 ng/L on this assay. In both sexes the URL was significantly higher in those aged 55 years or over than in those under 55, especially in women. The assay met the IFCC high-sensitivity performance standard, with hs-cTnI above the 0.43 ng/L limit of detection in 78.8% of men and 70.1% of women. The authors note their URLs differ from the manufacturer's declared values.
cards.watchOut: Same manufacturer's platform family as the NHANES Ortho assay yet a different URL (11.1 here vs 5 ng/L there): population, age structure and selection rules — not the analyser alone — set the number. Never quote 11.1 ng/L as 'the' troponin I limit.

cards.headline: Outlier-elimination experiment (Ahn 2022): in 767 strictly selected healthy adults, two Siemens hs-cTnI URLs were ~60 ng/L before outlier removal and ~13.5 ng/L after removing 8% of samples — the statistical rule alone moved the limit more than fourfold
cards.summary: Outlier-elimination experiment (Ahn 2022): in 767 strictly selected healthy adults, two Siemens hs-cTnI URLs were ~60 ng/L before outlier removal and ~13.5 ng/L after removing 8% of samples — the statistical rule alone moved the limit more than fourfold
cards.type: Primary human physiology / methods study (effect of outlier elimination on hs-cTnI 99th-percentile URLs, two Siemens assays)
cards.people: Strictly selected healthy reference population of 380 men and 387 women, verified with an NT-proBNP assay; 99th percentile URLs calculated for the Centaur XPT and Atellica IM high-sensitivity troponin I assays (both Siemens) before and after outlier elimination.
cards.result: Before outlier elimination the URLs were 60.4 ng/L for Centaur hsTnI (men 74.7; women 57.5) and 59.6 ng/L for Atellica hsTnI (men 75.2; women 55.1). After eliminating 61 samples (8.0%) for Centaur and 58 (7.6%) for Atellica, the URLs fell to 13.5 ng/L (men 15.3; women 11.9) and 13.4 ng/L (men 15.5; women 12.9) respectively — significantly lower. Measurable fractions in the reference population were 91.5% and 93.4%, and coefficients of variation at the URLs were 5.2% and 3.5%.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's starkest caution: a URL near 60 ng/L and a URL near 13 ng/L were computed from the SAME samples on the SAME assays — anyone citing a troponin threshold without its derivation rules is citing half a fact.

cards.headline: Sex-specific synthesis (Cao 2024): across 19 studies (11 hs-cTnI and 9 hs-cTnT assays), female 99th percentiles were lower than male and overall in over 90% of hs-cTnI studies and 8 of 9 hs-cTnT studies — yet sex-specific cut-offs remain little adopted
cards.summary: Sex-specific synthesis (Cao 2024): across 19 studies (11 hs-cTnI and 9 hs-cTnT assays), female 99th percentiles were lower than male and overall in over 90% of hs-cTnI studies and 8 of 9 hs-cTnT studies — yet sex-specific cut-offs remain little adopted
cards.type: Systematic review (sex-specific hs-cTnI and hs-cTnT 99th-percentile thresholds)
cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA) of original studies published November 2017 to November 2021 deriving sex-specific 99th percentiles from healthy reference populations of more than 300 adults using high-sensitivity assays: 19 studies met criteria, covering 11 different hs-cTnI assays and 9 different hs-cTnT assays.
cards.result: More than 90% of hs-cTnI studies (13 of 14) found lower female than male and overall 99th percentiles; one multi-assay study found a higher female percentile on only one of nine hs-cTnI assays. For hs-cTnT, 8 of 9 studies (88.9%) found lower female percentiles. The authors argue that adopting sex-specific cut-offs could increase myocardial infarction diagnosis in females, while noting they are not widely adopted in practice — a practice observation, carded as such, not a diagnostic recommendation from this measurement shelf.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis of direction, not a pooled number: it establishes that the sex gap is near-universal across assays while leaving each assay's own gap to its primary study — the cards above carry those numbers.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the 99th percentile is assay-, sex-, age- and rule-bound — hs-cTnI URLs carded here run from 5 ng/L (Ortho, NHANES) to ~60 ng/L (Siemens before outlier removal) in healthy adults, women sit consistently below men, and there is no universal troponin threshold to print
cards.summary: Synthesis: the 99th percentile is assay-, sex-, age- and rule-bound — hs-cTnI URLs carded here run from 5 ng/L (Ortho, NHANES) to ~60 ng/L (Siemens before outlier removal) in healthy adults, women sit consistently below men, and there is no universal troponin threshold to print
cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded above (2,746 NHANES healthy adults; 2,183 healthy Chinese adults; 767 strictly selected Korean adults; 19-study systematic review).
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (cardiac muscle / excitation) — framing brief; the reference-limit literature carries the shelf. Four concordant lessons: (1) assay identity dominates (four assays, four URLs in the same NHANES samples); (2) women have lower URLs than men on essentially every assay studied; (3) URLs rise with age (significantly lower under 40 than at 60+ on all NHANES assays; higher at 55+ on VITROS); (4) derivation rules — how 'healthy' was screened and whether outliers were eliminated — can move a URL more than fourfold (Ahn 2022). The companion natriuretic-peptide reference shelf (NT-proBNP) is the cross-point; ACS pathways are not this shelf's content. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the pattern (sex gap, age rise, assay dependence) is consistent across every dataset, but the limit that defines myocardial injury remains a derived, assay-specific quantity rather than settled physiology.
cards.watchOut: Clinical use must take the URL from the local assay's own validated reference study — importing another assay's or another population's 99th percentile is the exact error these four reports document.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: NT-proBNP reference intervals (pg/mL = ng/L): 97.5th percentile 225 (men) / 292 (women) at 50–59 years, women up to +150% in their 20s, and 37.4% of healthy over-65s above the 125 cut-off
shelves.question: In healthy people, what are the reference intervals for NT-proBNP — the median and 97.5th percentile by age decade and sex — how steeply do values rise with age and differ by sex and ethnicity, and what fraction of healthy people fall below the proposed "natriuretic peptide deficiency" range?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cardiac failure / natriuretic peptide chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, cardiovascular control — framing only; the row rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Values are in pg/mL, which is the same number as ng/L (1 pg/mL = 1 ng/L) — the equivalence is stated on every card. Age dominates this analyte: a single adult interval is misleading, so values are carded per age band. In healthy NHANES adults (1,949 with values in the interval study) the 97.5th percentile at 50–59 years was 225 ng/L in men and 292 ng/L in women; women run higher than men from late adolescence to middle age (in the companion NHANES normative analysis the female–male difference peaked at 150.5% at age 20–30 years), and non-Hispanic Black participants ran lower than White participants (up to 40.2% lower at 30–40 years). In strictly screened community-dwelling older adults (reference sample 441 of 2,459), 37.4% of healthy people over 65 had NT-proBNP above the 125 ng/L heart-failure cut-off, with 97.5th percentiles from 264 to 2,641 ng/L across age/sex strata — the fixed cut-off and the healthy distribution collide in old age. The 'natriuretic peptide deficiency' limb is a distribution fact, not a treatment claim: deficiency was defined as below the cohort's 2.5th percentile and an estimated 9.1 million US individuals fell in that range. A US–Vietnam comparison (1,157 healthy people) found medians of 28 vs 16 ng/L — real but small beside the age effect. The troponin reference shelf is the companion cross-point. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (the age/sex pattern and its size are concordant across four independent populations; the exact 97.5th percentile in the oldest strata remains imprecise, as the older-adult card states).

cards.headline: NHANES reference intervals (Mu 2023): healthy US adults — 97.5th percentile at 50–59 years 225 ng/L (pg/mL) in men and 292 ng/L in women; values higher in women from late adolescence to middle age and rising again through older age
cards.summary: NHANES reference intervals (Mu 2023): healthy US adults — 97.5th percentile at 50–59 years 225 ng/L (pg/mL) in men and 292 ng/L in women; values higher in women from late adolescence to middle age and rising again through older age
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (NT-proBNP reference intervals, NHANES healthy population, Elecsys assay)
cards.people: Healthy individuals from NHANES 1999–2004 with NT-proBNP measured on the Elecsys assay (Roche e601): values available for 1,949 healthy adults (and 5,250 healthy children and adolescents, outside this shelf's adult focus); reference intervals calculated by four methods, with final intervals from the robust method partitioned by age and sex.
cards.result: NT-proBNP varied by age in a U-shaped lifespan pattern — higher in early childhood, lower in late adolescence, and highest through middle and older age. Females tended to have higher concentrations than males from late adolescence until middle age. The upper reference limit (97.5th percentile) for 50- to 59-year-old men was 225 ng/L (90% CI 158 to 236) and for 50- to 59-year-old women 292 ng/L (90% CI 242 to 348) — ng/L and pg/mL are the same number for this analyte. The authors conclude age- and sex-specific intervals may be necessary to characterise risk precisely.
cards.watchOut: One assay (Elecsys) and survey stored samples: the decade-specific 97.5th percentiles are the product, and pooling them into a single 'adult normal range' would erase the age gradient that is this analyte's main feature.
cards.source: Mu S et al. NT-proBNP Reference Intervals in Healthy U.S. Children, Adolescents, and Adults. The journal of applied laboratory medicine. 2023. PMID: 37279581. cards.headline: NHANES normative levels and 'deficiency' (Shetty 2024): 18,145 healthy US individuals — women up to 150.5% higher than men at 20–30 years, non-Hispanic Black participants up to 40.2% lower than White at 30–40 years; an estimated 9.1 million US individuals fall below the 2.5th-percentile 'deficiency' line
cards.summary: NHANES normative levels and 'deficiency' (Shetty 2024): 18,145 healthy US individuals — women up to 150.5% higher than men at 20–30 years, non-Hispanic Black participants up to 40.2% lower than White at 30–40 years; an estimated 9.1 million US individuals fall below the 2.5th-percentile 'deficiency' line
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (NT-proBNP normative levels and deficiency prevalence, NHANES)
cards.people: Healthy NHANES 1999–2004 participants with NT-proBNP measurements: 18,145 individuals (median age 33.9 years, 49.8% male, 68.5% non-Hispanic White); weighted multivariable-adjusted models compared concentrations by sex and by race and ethnicity within age groups; natriuretic peptide deficiency was defined as a concentration below the study cohort's 2.5th percentile.
cards.result: Female–male differences were small at 1–10 years (4.2%, 95% CI −3.3 to 12.2) and largest at 20–30 years (women 150.5% higher, 95% CI 123.5 to 180.8). Compared with non-Hispanic White individuals, non-Hispanic Black individuals had lower concentrations from childhood (19.6% lower at 1–10 years) with the largest gap at 30–40 years (40.2% lower, 95% CI 33.7 to 46.0). An estimated 9.1 million US individuals met the study's deficiency definition, and deficiency was associated with more hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity and insulin resistance — an association reported by the authors, carded here as a distribution fact, not a treatment claim.
cards.watchOut: 'Deficiency' here is a statistical line (below the 2.5th percentile of this cohort) with a cardiometabolic association — it is not a diagnosed hormone-deficiency state and this shelf makes no supplementation or treatment claim from it.

cards.headline: Older-adult reference values (Braisch 2022): in a strictly screened reference sample of 441 healthy people aged 65+, 37.4% had NT-proBNP above the 125 ng/L cut-off; 97.5th percentiles ranged 592–824 ng/L in men and 264–2,641 ng/L in women by age band
cards.summary: Older-adult reference values (Braisch 2022): in a strictly screened reference sample of 441 healthy people aged 65+, 37.4% had NT-proBNP above the 125 ng/L cut-off; 97.5th percentiles ranged 592–824 ng/L in men and 264–2,641 ng/L in women by age band
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (NT-proBNP reference values, community-dwelling older adults, two population cohorts)
cards.people: Two German population cohorts (ActiFE n=1,450 and SHIP-TREND-0 n=1,009; 2,459 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and over), from which a reference sample of 441 participants (227 and 214) was built by excluding diabetes, cardiovascular and pulmonary disease and requiring blood pressure, haemoglobin, kidney function, CRP, BMI and hs-cTnI within set ranges; median and 97.5th percentiles reported by sex and age band.
cards.result: NT-proBNP rose with age and was higher in women than men. Despite the strict screening, 165 of 441 reference participants (37.4%) had values above 125 ng/L — the European Society of Cardiology ambulatory heart-failure cut-off. The 97.5th percentiles (upper reference limits) in men were 663, 824, 592 and 697 ng/L for ages 65–69, 70–74, 75–79 and 80+ years; in women they were 343, 463, 2,641 and 1,276 ng/L for the same bands. In a secondary subgroup with ejection fraction at least 50% and no diastolic dysfunction (n=97), 39.2% still exceeded 125 ng/L. The authors call for age-specific cut-offs in older adults.
cards.watchOut: The oldest female stratum's 2,641 ng/L limit rests on few observations and breaks the otherwise smooth age pattern (the 75–79 band exceeds the 80+ band in both sexes) — treat single-stratum limits over 75 as imprecise; the robust finding is that healthy older adults commonly exceed 125 ng/L.

cards.headline: US–Vietnam comparison (Gaggin 2014): 1,157 healthy age- and sex-matched adults — median NT-proBNP 28 ng/L (US) vs 16 ng/L (Vietnam), a difference that persisted after adjustment, while hs-cTnT differences vanished after adjustment
cards.summary: US–Vietnam comparison (Gaggin 2014): 1,157 healthy age- and sex-matched adults — median NT-proBNP 28 ng/L (US) vs 16 ng/L (Vietnam), a difference that persisted after adjustment, while hs-cTnT differences vanished after adjustment
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (NT-proBNP and hs-cTnT reference-interval evaluation, US and Vietnam — NT-proBNP limb)
cards.people: 1,157 healthy individuals (mean age 41.2 years, 48.0% male) prospectively enrolled in the US (n=565) and Vietnam (n=592), age- and sex-matched; hs-cTnT and NT-proBNP measured in all; medians compared unadjusted and adjusted for age, sex, BMI, study site, race and vital signs. Carded here for its NT-proBNP limb; its troponin limb is cross-pointed to the companion troponin shelf, not re-carded.
cards.result: Median NT-proBNP was 28 ng/L in US participants versus 16 ng/L in Vietnamese participants (P<0.001), and the difference remained significant after adjustment. (For context within the same study, median hs-cTnT was 3.7 vs 3.0 ng/L and its between-country difference was no longer significant after adjustment.) The authors concluded previously derived reference intervals for both analytes may be applied in Asian populations, the NT-proBNP difference being small beside the age and sex effects on the other cards.
cards.watchOut: Medians, not upper limits: this card compares centres of distribution between populations and cannot be used to set a 97.5th percentile for either country.

cards.headline: Synthesis: NT-proBNP in health is an age curve, not a number — 97.5th percentiles of 225 (men) and 292 (women) ng/L at 50–59 years, women higher through midlife, Black adults lower, and over a third of strictly healthy over-65s above the 125 ng/L heart-failure cut-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: NT-proBNP in health is an age curve, not a number — 97.5th percentiles of 225 (men) and 292 (women) ng/L at 50–59 years, women higher through midlife, Black adults lower, and over a third of strictly healthy over-65s above the 125 ng/L heart-failure cut-off
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above (1,949 healthy NHANES adults with interval values; 18,145 NHANES normative participants; 441 strictly screened older adults from 2,459; 1,157 US and Vietnamese adults).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (natriuretic peptides / cardiac failure) and Boron & Boulpaep (cardiovascular control); the primary interval literature carries the shelf. All values are pg/mL = ng/L. The pattern is concordant everywhere: concentrations rise steeply with age, run higher in women through midlife (peak sex gap +150.5% at 20–30 years), run lower in non-Hispanic Black than White adults (up to −40.2%), and sit modestly lower in Vietnamese than US adults at the median (16 vs 28 ng/L). The clinical consequence is distributional: a fixed 125 ng/L cut-off labels 37.4% of strictly healthy over-65s as above range, so in older adults the healthy 97.5th percentile (roughly 600–800 ng/L in men; unstable, up to 2,641 ng/L, in the oldest female stratum) is the honest comparator. 'Deficiency' below the 2.5th percentile captures an estimated 9.1 million US individuals and is a distribution fact with cardiometabolic associations, not a treatment indication. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age/sex pattern; the oldest-stratum limits remain imprecise, as printed on that card.
cards.watchOut: Never interpret an older adult's NT-proBNP against a young adult interval or a single all-age cut-off without the age band: the same 300 ng/L value is above the 97.5th percentile at 50–59 years in men and unremarkable at 75 years.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Full blood count intervals must be partitioned: red cells by sex, neutrophils by ancestry — Duffy-null ANC 820–6,370/µL (Namibia) to 1,210–5,390/µL (US), with 21.7–50.9% misclassified as neutropenic by standard ranges
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the full blood count — haemoglobin, white cell count and differential (including absolute neutrophil count), and platelet count — by sex, age and ancestry, and how much lower are neutrophil counts in healthy Duffy-null individuals?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / white-cell chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, haematology sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Ancestry-specific intervals are the content of this shelf, not a caveat. Three multicentre interval studies (4,642 healthy Han Chinese adults; 750 healthy Japanese adults at seven centres, white-cell parameters; a healthy urban South African population reported by ancestry group under the international C-RIDL protocol) establish sex-specific red-cell intervals and confirm lower white-cell and neutrophil counts in African-ancestry participants — the fetched records of these three report their intervals in full tables and describe their structure and comparisons rather than printing every limit in the abstract, so this shelf cards their design, their comparisons and the numbers their records DO print, and invents none. The numeric centre of the shelf is the Duffy-null study (8,018 healthy Duffy-null adults across four continents): absolute neutrophil count reference intervals of 820–6,370/µL (Namibia), 1,140–5,290/µL (Saudi Arabia), 1,185–5,462/µL (UK) and 1,210–5,390/µL (US), against which institutional intervals misclassified 21.7–50.9% of healthy Duffy-null people as neutropenic. The haemoglobin limb (absorbed into this row under the one-home rule) is the multinational anaemia cut-off evaluation: pooled healthy fifth percentiles of 10.81 g/dL in women (and 9.65 g/dL in children) sat BELOW current WHO cut-offs, with sTfR inflection points at 11.01 g/dL in women. Haemoglobin is in g/dL throughout (g/L = g/dL × 10). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the structure (sex-split red cells; ancestry-split neutrophils; Duffy-null limits), with the per-analyte numeric tables of the three regional studies residing in their full reports, as each card states.

cards.headline: Han Chinese CBC intervals (Wu 2015): 4,642 healthy adults at six centres — red-cell count, haemoglobin and haematocrit intervals are sex-specific; platelet intervals needed a separate Chengdu range; thalassaemia carriers shifted red-cell profile limits
cards.summary: Han Chinese CBC intervals (Wu 2015): 4,642 healthy adults at six centres — red-cell count, haemoglobin and haematocrit intervals are sex-specific; platelet intervals needed a separate Chengdu range; thalassaemia carriers shifted red-cell profile limits
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (complete blood count reference intervals, healthy Han Chinese adults, multicentre)
cards.people: Multicentre collaborative study: 4,642 healthy Han Chinese adults (2,136 men, 2,506 women) recruited at six clinical centres (Shenyang, Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an); blood collected in K2EDTA and analysed for the full complete blood count; consensus intervals tested for instrument, region, age and sex dependence.
cards.result: Red blood cell count, haemoglobin and haematocrit were higher in males than females at all ages, and their reference intervals were established separately for each sex. Other CBC parameters showed no significant instrument-, region-, age- or sex-dependent difference — with one exception: median and mean platelet counts at the Chengdu centre were significantly lower than at the other centres, so a separate platelet interval was required for Chengdu. Thalassaemia carriers in the sample affected the lower or upper limits of several red-cell profiles. The fetched record describes the interval structure and these comparisons; the full numeric tables are in the report itself, and this card prints no invented limits.
cards.watchOut: Population-bound by design: intervals derived because American and European ranges from older instruments did not fit Chinese samples — importing them back the other way repeats the original error, and the Chengdu platelet exception shows even within-country pooling can fail.
cards.source: Wu X et al. Complete blood count reference intervals for healthy Han Chinese adults. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 25769040. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Japanese white-cell intervals (Takami 2021): 750 healthy adults at seven centres — white-cell and differential intervals by sex, with age-related falls in total white-cell count in both sexes and in neutrophils in women; analyser and microscopy agreed for neutrophils, lymphocytes and eosinophils but not monocytes or basophils
cards.summary: Japanese white-cell intervals (Takami 2021): 750 healthy adults at seven centres — white-cell and differential intervals by sex, with age-related falls in total white-cell count in both sexes and in neutrophils in women; analyser and microscopy agreed for neutrophils, lymphocytes and eosinophils but not monocytes or basophils
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (white blood cell parameter reference intervals, healthy Japanese adults, multicentre)
cards.people: 750 healthy adults (447 women, 303 men; aged 18–67 years, median 40) attending regular medical checkups at seven Japanese centres; white-blood-cell parameters measured by automated haematocytometers and by manual microscopic blood-film review; reference intervals determined by sex.
cards.result: The study established sex-specific reference intervals for white-cell parameters in healthy Japanese adults. Age-specific decreases were noted in white-cell counts in both sexes and in neutrophil counts in women. Automated and microscopic methods correlated favourably for neutrophils, lymphocytes and eosinophils, but not for monocytes or basophils — so the differential's rarer cells are method-bound. The fetched record reports the interval structure and these patterns rather than printing each limit, and this card claims no numeric limits from it.
cards.watchOut: White-cell intervals only (the red-cell and platelet limbs are on the companion cards), and the monocyte/basophil method disagreement means a differential from a film review and one from an analyser are not interchangeable for those cells.
cards.source: Takami A et al. Reference intervals of white blood cell parameters for healthy adults in japan. International journal of laboratory hematology. 2021. PMID: 33586915.
