cards.headline: South African FBC intervals (Smit 2019): healthy urban Western Cape population under the C-RIDL protocol — white cell (P=0.016), monocyte (P<0.001) and neutrophil (P=0.034) counts differed significantly by ancestry group, with African-ancestry participants lower; Mixed Ancestry intervals resembled European-ancestry intervals
cards.summary: South African FBC intervals (Smit 2019): healthy urban Western Cape population under the C-RIDL protocol — white cell (P=0.016), monocyte (P<0.001) and neutrophil (P=0.034) counts differed significantly by ancestry group, with African-ancestry participants lower; Mixed Ancestry intervals resembled European-ancestry intervals
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (full blood count and differential reference ranges by ancestry group, healthy South African population)
cards.people: Healthy urban South African population in the Western Cape from the three major ancestry groups of the region (African descent, Mixed Ancestry, Caucasian), studied under the strict Committee on Reference Intervals and Decision Limits (C-RIDL) protocol as part of its international project; full blood count and differential performed on a Beckman Coulter ACT 5 diff AL analyser within 2–4 hours of collection, reported as mean (SD) with 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
cards.result: Reference ranges for Caucasian and Mixed Ancestry individuals were similar. White cell count (P=0.016), monocyte count (P<0.001), neutrophil count (P=0.034) and red cell indices differed significantly among the three groups, confirming lower white cell and neutrophil counts in participants of African descent; eosinophil, lymphocyte, red cell counts and platelet counts showed no statistically or clinically significant differences across groups. cards.headline: Duffy-null neutrophil intervals (Hibbs 2026): 8,018 healthy Duffy-null adults on four continents — ANC reference intervals 820–6,370/µL (Namibia) to 1,210–5,390/µL (US); institutional intervals misclassified 21.7–50.9% of these healthy people as neutropenic
cards.summary: Duffy-null neutrophil intervals (Hibbs 2026): 8,018 healthy Duffy-null adults on four continents — ANC reference intervals 820–6,370/µL (Namibia) to 1,210–5,390/µL (US); institutional intervals misclassified 21.7–50.9% of these healthy people as neutropenic
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ANC and WBC reference intervals in healthy Duffy-null adults, multinational)
cards.people: Cross-sectional multinational study of healthy Duffy-null individuals: 8,018 participants — 880 from dedicated cohorts (blood donors in Namibia, Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom; primary care patients in the United States) and 7,138 from UK and US biobanks; absolute neutrophil counts (ANC) and white blood cell counts (WBC) compared across regions and against institutional reference intervals.
cards.result: Duffy-null reference intervals were: Namibia ANC 820–6,370/µL, WBC 2.51–9.85 ×10⁹/L; Saudi Arabia ANC 1,140–5,290/µL, WBC 3.72–10.71 ×10⁹/L; United Kingdom ANC 1,185–5,462/µL, WBC 3.1–8.8 ×10⁹/L; United States ANC 1,210–5,390/µL, WBC 3.00–9.66 ×10⁹/L — with no significant differences between cohorts, and biobank analyses showing no significant ANC difference between Black and non-Black Duffy-null participants. Institutional reference intervals misclassified 27.9% (Namibia), 50.9% (Saudi Arabia), 26.0% (UK) and 21.7% (US) of these healthy people as neutropenic. The authors conclude Duffy-specific reference intervals are essential for equitable, accurate decisions.
cards.watchOut: The lower ANC is a genotype-associated distribution, present across ethnic groups among Duffy-null people — the clinical error this card exists to prevent is labelling a healthy Duffy-null adult neutropenic (and triggering work-up or drug withholding) against a non-Duffy interval.
cards.source: Hibbs SP et al. Multinational assessment of absolute neutrophil counts and white blood cell counts among healthy Duffy-null adults. Blood. 2026. PMID: 41191521. cards.headline: Haemoglobin cut-off limb (Addo 2021): across 25 countries, the pooled healthy fifth percentile was 10.81 g/dL in nonpregnant women (sTfR inflection 11.01 g/dL) — BELOW current WHO anaemia cut-offs; this row's haemoglobin limb, carded here under the one-home rule
cards.summary: Haemoglobin cut-off limb (Addo 2021): across 25 countries, the pooled healthy fifth percentile was 10.81 g/dL in nonpregnant women (sTfR inflection 11.01 g/dL) — BELOW current WHO anaemia cut-offs; this row's haemoglobin limb, carded here under the one-home rule
cards.type: Primary human physiology / evaluation study (haemoglobin anaemia cut-offs in healthy individuals, multinational surveys) — haemoglobin limb of this row
cards.people: Cross-sectional evaluation of WHO haemoglobin cut-offs using 30 household population-based nutrition surveys (2005–2016, 25 countries): after excluding iron deficiency, vitamin A deficiency, inflammation and malaria, the healthy sample was 25,880 nonpregnant women aged 15–49 years (and 13,445 preschool children, outside this shelf's adult focus except as printed); survey-specific and pooled fifth percentiles estimated, with haemoglobin-for-soluble-transferrin-receptor curves used to find inflection points reflecting tissue iron deficiency.
cards.result: Among women, survey-specific healthy fifth percentiles ranged from 8.83 g/dL (Gujarat, India) to 12.09 g/dL (US), with a pooled fifth percentile of 10.81 g/dL (95% CI 10.35 to 11.27) — in g/L, 108.1 g/L. The haemoglobin-for-sTfR curve's inflection point in women was 11.01 g/dL (95% CI 10.95 to 11.09). Current WHO cut-offs sit higher than the pooled fifth percentile and nearly all survey-specific estimates; the authors note the lower proposed cut-offs are statistically significant but also reflect compensatory increased erythropoiesis, and that outcome-based studies could confirm them. (In children the pooled fifth percentile was 9.65 g/dL with an inflection at 9.61 g/dL.)
cards.watchOut: A fifth-percentile statistical cut-off in screened-healthy survey populations is not the same object as a clinical anaemia threshold tied to outcomes: the authors themselves flag that the lower values coincide with compensatory erythropoiesis, so this card informs the interval question without re-writing anaemia practice.
cards.source: Addo OY et al. Evaluation of Hemoglobin Cutoff Levels to Define Anemia Among Healthy Individuals. JAMA network open. 2021. PMID: 34357395. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the full blood count needs partitioning — red-cell intervals by sex, white-cell and neutrophil intervals by ancestry, and Duffy-null adults (ANC lower limit 820–1,210/µL by region) must not be read against non-Duffy ranges that misclassify up to half of them as neutropenic
cards.summary: Synthesis: the full blood count needs partitioning — red-cell intervals by sex, white-cell and neutrophil intervals by ancestry, and Duffy-null adults (ANC lower limit 820–1,210/µL by region) must not be read against non-Duffy ranges that misclassify up to half of them as neutropenic
cards.people: Synthesis of the five primary reports carded above (4,642 Han Chinese adults; 750 Japanese adults; a three-ancestry-group South African population; 8,018 Duffy-null adults; 25,880 healthy women in the haemoglobin limb).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (blood and white cells) and Boron & Boulpaep (haematology) — framing brief; the interval literature carries the shelf. The structure is consistent across continents: haemoglobin, red-cell count and haematocrit run higher in men and take sex-specific intervals (Wu 2015); white-cell counts fall with age and neutrophils are lower in African-ancestry groups (Takami 2021; Smit 2019); the Duffy-null genotype explains much of that neutrophil difference, with multinational lower limits of 820–1,210/µL and misclassification rates of 21.7–50.9% under institutional intervals (Hibbs 2026); and the haemoglobin threshold itself is unsettled at the margin, the healthy female fifth percentile (10.81 g/dL) sitting below WHO cut-offs (Addo 2021). Analyser generation is named per study, as the row requires. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for this partitioned structure; the regional studies' full numeric tables live in their reports, as their cards state.
cards.watchOut: Applying a single-population interval to a differently partitioned patient is the recurring error on every card: check sex for red cells, ancestry/Duffy status for neutrophils, and centre for platelets before calling any count abnormal.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Normal temperature is not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C): oral mean 98.2 °F (36.8 °C) in 148 volunteers, upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), diurnal swing 0.9 °F (0.5 °C); review ranges by site put axillary at 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is normal body temperature — the mean and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by measurement site (oral, axillary, tympanic, core), time of day, age and sex — and how far below 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) does the modern population mean sit?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Temperature · Female · Humans · Male · Reference Values · Thermometers · Aged · Axilla · Middle Aged · Mouth · Pakistan · Population · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, chapter on body temperature and its regulation, and Boron & Boulpaep, thermoregulation — the classic Wunderlich axioms this shelf re-examines are textbook content. The modern record agrees that 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) is not the population mean: Mackowiak's 148 volunteers gave a mean oral temperature of 98.2 °F (36.8 °C) with an overall upper limit of 99.9 °F (37.7 °C) and a diurnal swing of 0.9 °F (0.5 °C); a systematic review of 7,636 subjects gives site-specific ranges that never merge — oral 96.3–99.3 °F (35.73–37.41 °C), axillary distinctly lower at 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C) — and older adults run about 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower. Site and time of day are part of the measurement. Cross-point pack #6263 (sweating / vasodilation thresholds — thermoregulatory responses, not resting values). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Mackowiak 1992: in 148 healthy volunteers aged 18–40 the mean oral temperature was 98.2 °F (36.8 °C), not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) — upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), 98.9 °F (37.2 °C) in the early morning, with a 0.9 °F (0.5 °C) diurnal swing
cards.summary: Mackowiak 1992: in 148 healthy volunteers aged 18–40 the mean oral temperature was 98.2 °F (36.8 °C), not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) — upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), 98.9 °F (37.2 °C) in the early morning, with a 0.9 °F (0.5 °C) diurnal swing
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oral temperature distribution, healthy volunteers)
cards.people: 148 healthy men and women aged 18–40 years, volunteers in Shigella vaccine trials at the University of Maryland Center for Vaccine Development; oral temperatures measured one to four times daily for 3 consecutive days with an electronic digital thermometer.
cards.result: Mean oral temperature was 36.8 °C (98.2 °F) rather than Wunderlich's 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), and the upper limit of the normal range was 37.7 °C (99.9 °F) rather than 38.0 °C (100.4 °F). Mean temperature varied diurnally with a 6 AM nadir and a 4–6 PM zenith and a mean amplitude of variability of 0.5 °C (0.9 °F); women had slightly higher temperatures than men. The authors conclude 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) should be abandoned as a concept in clinical thermometry, with 37.2 °C (98.9 °F) in the early morning and 37.7 °C (99.9 °F) overall as the upper limit of the normal oral range in healthy adults aged 40 or younger.
cards.watchOut: A young, healthy inpatient volunteer sample (18–40 years) with oral electronic readings only: its limits describe that site and age band, not axillary or older-adult values — those are the other cards' slices.
cards.source: Mackowiak PA et al. A critical appraisal of 98.6 degrees F, the upper limit of the normal body temperature, and other legacies of Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich. JAMA. 1992. cards.headline: Systematic review (Geneva 2019): 36 prospective studies, 7,636 subjects, 9,227 measurement sites — site-specific ranges (mean ± 2 SD): rectal 97.4–100.0 °F (36.32–37.76 °C), oral 96.3–99.3 °F (35.73–37.41 °C), axillary 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C); older adults 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower
cards.summary: Systematic review (Geneva 2019): 36 prospective studies, 7,636 subjects, 9,227 measurement sites — site-specific ranges (mean ± 2 SD): rectal 97.4–100.0 °F (36.32–37.76 °C), oral 96.3–99.3 °F (35.73–37.41 °C), axillary 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C); older adults 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower
cards.type: Systematic review of primary physiology studies (normal body temperature by site)
cards.people: 36 prospective articles (1935 to December 2017) presenting measured normal body temperature in healthy human subjects aged 18 or older, comprising 9,227 measurement sites from 7,636 subjects, analysed by measurement site.
cards.result: Calculated ranges (mean ± 2 standard deviations) were: rectal 36.32–37.76 °C (97.4–100.0 °F), tympanic 35.76–37.52 °C (96.4–99.5 °F), urine 35.61–37.61 °C (96.1–99.7 °F), oral 35.73–37.41 °C (96.3–99.3 °F), and axillary 35.01–36.93 °C (95.0–98.5 °F). Older adults (age ≥60) had lower temperature than younger adults (age <60) by 0.23 °C (0.4 °F) on average; gender difference was insignificant. The authors conclude the most important patient factors are site of measurement and age.
cards.watchOut: Pooled ranges span decades of devices and populations: they are the best site-specific summary available, but a single study's thermometer and protocol will sit narrower than these review-wide bands.

cards.summary: Pakistan population range (Adhi 2008): 200 healthy people — oral range 97.0–99.8 °F (36.1–37.7 °C), mean 98.4 °F (36.9 °C); axillary readings averaged 0.85 °F lower than oral but ranged from 2.6 °F lower to 1.1 °F higher, so no uniform oral equivalent exists
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oral and bilateral axillary temperature range, general population)
cards.people: 200 healthy individuals accompanying patients at clinics at the Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation, Pakistan (May–June 2006); oral and left and right axillary temperatures recorded with an ordinary mercury-in-glass thermometer.
cards.result: The range for normal oral temperatures was 97 °F to 99.8 °F (36.1–37.7 °C), mean 98.4 °F (36.9 °C). There were no significant age-related (P = 0.68) or ambient-temperature-related (P = 0.51) variations, but women had slightly higher temperatures than men (mean 98.5 °F vs 98.3 °F; 36.9 °C vs 36.8 °C; P = 0.01). The difference between oral and axillary temperatures varied widely — axillary up to 2.6 °F lower or up to 1.1 °F higher than oral, mean difference 0.85 °F — and the authors conclude axillary temperature should be interpreted with caution because there is no uniform oral equivalent.
cards.watchOut: Mercury-in-glass readings in clinic attendants in one hot season: the oral–axillary gap it measures is a property of that technique and setting, and its wide scatter — not just its mean — is the finding.
cards.source: Adhi M et al. Range for normal body temperature in the general population of Pakistan. JPMA. The Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association. 2008. PMID: 18998317. cards.headline: Synthesis: normal temperature is a site- and time-specific range, not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) — oral mean about 98.2–98.4 °F (36.8–36.9 °C), overall oral upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), axillary lower and unreliable as an oral substitute, older adults about 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal temperature is a site- and time-specific range, not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) — oral mean about 98.2–98.4 °F (36.8–36.9 °C), overall oral upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), axillary lower and unreliable as an oral substitute, older adults about 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (body temperature and its regulation) and Boron & Boulpaep (thermoregulation). Mackowiak 1992 (148 young volunteers, oral) sets the mean at 98.2 °F (36.8 °C), the early-morning upper limit at 98.9 °F (37.2 °C) and the overall upper limit at 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), with a 0.9 °F (0.5 °C) diurnal swing from a 6 AM nadir to a 4–6 PM zenith. The Geneva 2019 systematic review (7,636 subjects) gives the site ladder — rectal highest, then tympanic, oral and axillary lowest at 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C) — and a 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower mean at age ≥60. Adhi 2008 (200 people, oral plus bilateral axillary) confirms an oral mean of 98.4 °F (36.9 °C) and shows the axillary–oral difference scattering from −2.6 °F to +1.1 °F around a −0.85 °F mean. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three concordant sources across three decades agree that 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) overstates the modern mean and that site, time of day and age move the value. Fever-mechanism and therapeutic-cooling shelves are different questions; pack #6263 (thermoregulatory response thresholds) is the cross-point.
cards.watchOut: Never merge sites: an axillary 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) and an oral 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) are different measurements, and a single reading without its time of day discards the 0.9 °F (0.5 °C) diurnal swing printed on the Mackowiak card.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Echo reference ranges are population-bound: NORRE limits higher in men and age-dependent, septal e′ <8 cm/s in 55% of healthy ≥60s, INDEA indexed volumes much smaller than Western guidelines, MESA guidelines labelling 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are echocardiographic chamber-size and Doppler reference ranges — left and right ventricular dimensions and volumes, atrial volumes, wall thickness and the standard diastolic Doppler indices — by age, sex, body size and ethnicity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Cohort Studies · Echocardiography · Female · Heart Atria · Heart Ventricles · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Stroke Volume · Young Adult · Echocardiography, Doppler · Diastole · India · Healthy Aging
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, cardiac mechanics (framing general — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative imaging literature, and says so). Four normative programmes: the EACVI NORRE chamber study (734 healthy volunteers; limits higher in men, age-dependent, mostly persisting after body-surface-area normalisation), the NORRE Doppler study (449 volunteers; septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 55% of healthy people aged ≥60 — a 'disease' cut-off sitting inside normality), INDEA (880 healthy Indians; indexed LV volumes much smaller than the ASE/EACVI 2015 guideline values — ethnicity-specific ranges are content, not caveat) and MESA (608 healthy older adults; current guidelines labelled 81.6% of them abnormal). Indexing changes who counts as dilated, and each card states indexed and unindexed findings as published. The INDEA paper's strain limb is NOT carded here — strain is homed at Slate 9's S9-4-22 shelf; only its chamber data are used. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: NORRE chamber size (Kou 2014): 734 healthy volunteers at 22 centres — upper and lower reference limits higher in men than women, varying with age, and most age changes persisting after body-surface-area normalisation
cards.summary: NORRE chamber size (Kou 2014): 734 healthy volunteers at 22 centres — upper and lower reference limits higher in men than women, varying with age, and most age changes persisting after body-surface-area normalisation
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (echocardiographic chamber-size reference ranges, NORRE)
cards.people: 734 healthy volunteers (320 men, 414 women; mean age 45.8 ± 13.3 years) enrolled at 22 collaborating institutions of the Normal Reference Ranges for Echocardiography (NORRE) study; comprehensive two-dimensional echocardiography to EACVI chamber-quantitation protocols. The fetched abstract reports the pattern of the reference ranges; it does not print the numeric limits, and this card claims none.
cards.result: There were no sex differences in age or cholesterol; women had significantly smaller body surface areas and lower blood pressure. Upper and lower reference limits for cardiac chamber size were higher in men than in women, and the reference values varied with age; these age-related changes persisted for most parameters after normalisation for body surface area. The authors conclude the NORRE ranges require body-size normalisation together with age- and sex-specific assessment for most echocardiographic parameters.
cards.watchOut: The reference product is the published limit tables, not the abstract: anyone applying a NORRE limit must take the number from the paper's tables for the exact parameter, sex and age band — no limit is quoted from this card.
cards.source: Kou S et al. Echocardiographic reference ranges for normal cardiac chamber size: results from the NORRE study. European heart journal. Cardiovascular Imaging. 2014. PMID: 24451180. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: NORRE Doppler (Caballero 2015): 449 healthy volunteers — E and e′ fall with age and E/e′ rises; septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 19.7% of healthy 40–60-year-olds and 55% of those aged ≥60, while average E/e′ stayed below 15 in the majority
cards.summary: NORRE Doppler (Caballero 2015): 449 healthy volunteers — E and e′ fall with age and E/e′ rises; septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 19.7% of healthy 40–60-year-olds and 55% of those aged ≥60, while average E/e′ stayed below 15 in the majority
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (echocardiographic Doppler reference ranges, NORRE)
cards.people: 449 healthy volunteers (198 men, 251 women; mean age 45.8 ± 13.7 years) at the NORRE collaborating institutions; comprehensive Doppler echocardiography to EACVI acquisition and measurement protocols.
cards.result: Most Doppler diastolic parameters (e′, E/e′) and right ventricular systolic s′ velocity were similar in men and women; left ventricular s′ velocity was higher in men. E wave and e′ were higher in younger subjects and decreased progressively in older ones, while the E/e′ ratio increased with ageing. Septal e′ below 8 cm/s was present in 19.7% of subjects in the 40–60 year group and in 55% of those aged ≥60; however, the cut-off of average E/e′ below 15 (or lateral E/e′ below 13) held in the majority of patients. The authors conclude age-specific reference values are needed, especially for diagnosing LV systolic and diastolic dysfunction and estimating filling pressures.
cards.watchOut: The e′ finding cuts both ways: a septal e′ below 8 cm/s is the majority finding in healthy people over 60, so applying a single young-adult cut-off manufactures diastolic dysfunction — age-specific ranges are the card's lesson.
cards.source: Caballero L et al. Echocardiographic reference ranges for normal cardiac Doppler data: results from the NORRE Study. European heart journal. Cardiovascular Imaging. 2015. PMID: 25896355. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: INDEA, India (Sengupta 2021): 880 healthy volunteers at six centres — men larger unindexed but not indexed; indexed LV volumes much smaller than the ASE/EACVI 2015 guideline values (chamber data only — this paper's strain limb is not carded here)
cards.summary: INDEA, India (Sengupta 2021): 880 healthy volunteers at six centres — men larger unindexed but not indexed; indexed LV volumes much smaller than the ASE/EACVI 2015 guideline values (chamber data only — this paper's strain limb is not carded here)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (echocardiographic chamber-dimension normative values, INDEA, India) — chamber limb only
cards.people: 880 healthy volunteers (mean age 39.7 ± 12.3 years, 63.8% men) from six centres across India in the Indian Normative Data of Echocardiography Analyzed (INDEA) study; comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography to guideline recommendations, with chamber dimensions (LV end-diastolic diameter and volume, RV basal diameter, left atrial volume) indexed to body surface area, analysed in three age groups (≤35, 36–55, ≥56 years). Only the chamber-dimension data are carded; the study's global longitudinal strain limb belongs to the strain shelf's territory and is not used here.
cards.result: Compared with women, men had larger cardiac chamber dimensions and volumes, but not when indexed. Women had higher LV systolic function; RV systolic function did not differ. The indexed LV volumes in INDEA were much smaller than those recommended in the ASE/EACVI 2015 chamber quantification guidelines, but similar to those reported for Indian patients in the World Alliance Societies of Echocardiography (WASE) Normal Values Study. The authors conclude India-specific reference values should be followed instead of the largely Western guideline values.
cards.watchOut: Ethnicity-specific ranges are the finding, not a caveat: applying Western indexed-volume limits to Indian adults misclassifies in the direction this card prints. Do not import this paper's strain values onto this shelf.
cards.source: Sengupta SP et al. Normative values of cardiac chamber dimensions and global longitudinal strain in Indians: the Indian Normative Data of Echocardiography Analyzed (INDEA) study. The international journal of cardiovascular imaging. 2021. PMID: 33047178. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MESA older adults (Mukherjee 2024): 608 healthy adults aged ≥65 selected from 3,032 scanned — women smaller with better function, White participants largest and Chinese smallest even after body-size adjustment, and current guidelines labelled 81.6% of these healthy people abnormal
cards.summary: MESA older adults (Mukherjee 2024): 608 healthy adults aged ≥65 selected from 3,032 scanned — women smaller with better function, White participants largest and Chinese smallest even after body-size adjustment, and current guidelines labelled 81.6% of these healthy people abnormal
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (echocardiographic normative values in healthy older adults, MESA)
cards.people: 608 participants (mean age 69.5 ± 7.0 years, 46.2% male, 47.5% White) fulfilling healthy-ageing inclusion criteria (no cardiopulmonary or cardiometabolic conditions) among 3,032 individuals who underwent two-dimensional echocardiography at exam 6 of the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis; normative values defined as mean ± 1.96 SD, compared across sex and race/ethnicity.
cards.result: The healthy cohort had lower NT-proBNP, higher 6-minute walk distance and better Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores than the wider scanned group. Women had significantly smaller chamber sizes and better biventricular systolic function. White participants had the largest chamber dimensions and Chinese participants the smallest, even after adjustment for body size. Current guidelines identified 81.6% of these healthy older adults as having cardiac abnormalities. The authors conclude guideline thresholds built on younger individuals may not address the changes of normal ageing.
cards.watchOut: A highly selected healthy subset (608 of 3,032): its ranges describe healthy ageing, not the average 70-year-old — and its 81.6% figure indicts the guideline cut-offs, not the participants.
cards.source: Mukherjee M et al. Normative Values of Echocardiographic Chamber Size and Function in Older Healthy Adults: The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis. Circulation. Cardiovascular imaging. 2024. PMID: 38716661. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: chamber and Doppler normality is age-, sex-, body-size- and ethnicity-specific — NORRE's limits, INDEA's smaller indexed volumes, and MESA's finding that guidelines call 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal all say the reference population is part of the measurement
cards.summary: Synthesis: chamber and Doppler normality is age-, sex-, body-size- and ethnicity-specific — NORRE's limits, INDEA's smaller indexed volumes, and MESA's finding that guidelines call 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal all say the reference population is part of the measurement
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (cardiac mechanics; general framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative imaging literature). NORRE chamber (Kou 2014; 734 volunteers) and NORRE Doppler (Caballero 2015; 449 volunteers) set the European reference pattern: limits higher in men, age-dependent, mostly BSA-resistant, with septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 55% of healthy people ≥60. INDEA (Sengupta 2021; 880 Indians, chamber data only — its strain limb is not carded here) shows indexed LV volumes much smaller than ASE/EACVI 2015 values, and MESA (Mukherjee 2024; 608 healthy older adults) shows sex and race/ethnicity differences persisting after body-size adjustment, with current guidelines labelling 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: four large, protocol-standardised normative programmes converge on the same structure — there is no single normal echo number, only a number for an age, a sex, a body size and a population.
cards.watchOut: Quote a limit only with its source population and indexing: an unindexed dimension, an indexed volume and a Doppler index from three different reference populations cannot be combined into one 'normal range'.

synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. framed by boron & boulpaep (cardiac mechanics; general framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative imaging literature). norre chamber (kou 2014; 734 volunteers) and norre doppler (caballero 2015; 449 volunteers) set the european reference pattern: limits higher in men, age-dependent, mostly bsa-resistant, with septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 55% of healthy people ≥60. indea (sengupta 2021; 880 indians, chamber data only — its strain limb is not carded here) shows indexed lv volumes much smaller than ase/eacvi 2015 values, and mesa (mukherjee 2024; 608 healthy older adults) shows sex and race/ethnicity differences persisting after body-size adjustment, with current guidelines labelling 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal. physiology — established: four large, protocol-standardised normative programmes converge on the same structure — there is no single normal echo number, only a number for an age, a sex, a body size and a population. quote a limit only with its source population and indexing: an unindexed dimension, an indexed volume and a doppler index from three different reference populations cannot be combined into one 'normal range'. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, endothelial physiology / vascular control; Guyton & Hall, local control of blood flow. PARTIAL logic, stated on the face: pack #6497, read at question level, asks how NO-mediated endothelium-dependent dilatation is DEMONSTRATED and quantified (forearm acetylcholine / L-NMMA studies and FMD as a method) — a mechanism question giving no normative distribution; this shelf is the distribution slice only and does not re-card #6497's studies. The dedicated reference study (Königstein 2021; 457 healthy non-smokers aged 20–91, sex-specific percentiles) shows FMD falling steeply with age — relative declines of 63.6% in women and 47.1% in men across 20–91 years — and its 6.4% FMD value is a cardiovascular-risk discrimination cut-off in that cohort, NOT a universal normal limit, and is never presented as one here. Supporting limbs are small and print their Ns (four age/sex groups of 16–19; a 30-person fibrinogen study with a short abstract, supporting only). FMD is notoriously protocol-sensitive: values are carded per protocol population and never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: First FMD reference values (Königstein 2021): 457 healthy non-smoking adults aged 20–91 — from age 20 to 91, FMD fell by a relative 63.6% in women and 47.1% in men, low-flow-mediated constriction rose, and sex-specific percentiles are provided; the 6.4% FMD cut-off discriminated elevated cardiovascular risk in this cohort only
cards.summary: First FMD reference values (Königstein 2021): 457 healthy non-smoking adults aged 20–91 — from age 20 to 91, FMD fell by a relative 63.6% in women and 47.1% in men, low-flow-mediated constriction rose, and sex-specific percentiles are provided; the 6.4% FMD cut-off discriminated elevated cardiovascular risk in this cohort only
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (FMD / L-FMC / vasoactive-range reference values, healthy adults 20–91)
cards.people: 457 non-smoking adults aged 20–91 years without chronic diseases or medication, with normal heart function and very low cardiovascular risk; brachial low-flow-mediated constriction (L-FMC), flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) and their composite vasoactive range (VAR) measured by ultrasound, with sex-specific percentiles calculated.
cards.result: From 20 to 91 years of age, L-FMC increased by a relative 86.1% (women) and 105.3% (men), FMD decreased by a relative 63.6% (women) and 47.1% (men), and VAR decreased by a relative 58.3% and 55.2% respectively — relative (percentage) changes across the age span, as printed, not percentage-point changes. Discriminatory cut-offs for elevated cardiovascular risk were 0.24% for L-FMC (sensitivity 0.42, specificity 0.67), 6.4% for FMD (sensitivity 0.71, specificity 0.60) and 6.3% for VAR (sensitivity 0.62, specificity 0.73); VAR had the highest discrimination (area under the ROC curve 0.72, vs 0.67 for FMD and 0.54 for L-FMC). Percentiles crossed the risk cut-offs between 50 and 55 years in men and 70 and 75 years in women.
cards.watchOut: The 6.4% FMD figure is a risk-discrimination cut-off fitted in this very-low-risk cohort (sensitivity 0.71, specificity 0.60) — presenting it as a universal lower limit of normal would invert the study; the percentiles, by sex and age, are the reference product.
cards.source: Königstein K et al. Endothelial function of healthy adults from 20 to 91 years of age: prediction of cardiovascular risk by vasoactive range. Journal of hypertension. 2021. PMID: 33470736. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Middle-aged healthy men (Yan 2005): 1,578 men without known cardiovascular disease — brachial FMD and carotid intima-media thickness were entirely uncorrelated (r = −0.006, P = 0.82), so the FMD distribution and the structural distribution describe different things
cards.summary: Middle-aged healthy men (Yan 2005): 1,578 men without known cardiovascular disease — brachial FMD and carotid intima-media thickness were entirely uncorrelated (r = −0.006, P = 0.82), so the FMD distribution and the structural distribution describe different things
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (brachial FMD distribution and its dissociation from carotid IMT, healthy middle-aged men)
cards.people: 1,578 middle-aged men without known cardiovascular disease, in whom traditional risk factors, carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) and brachial artery flow-mediated dilatation were all measured and analysed against each other. The fetched abstract reports the FMD–IMT relationship and FMD's risk-factor correlates; it does not print a mean FMD value, and this card claims none.
cards.result: Carotid IMT correlated with age, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, fasting glucose, total and LDL cholesterol and the overall Framingham risk score (P < 0.001 for all), whereas impaired brachial FMD correlated with systolic and diastolic blood pressure (P < 0.01). No relationship was observed between carotid IMT and brachial FMD for the entire cohort (r = −0.006, P = 0.82) or in subgroups defined by traditional risk factors or by quintiles of IMT and FMD. The authors conclude the two are unique, independent surrogates measuring different aspects and stages of early atherosclerosis.
cards.watchOut: Men only, and carded for the dissociation, not for a normative mean (none is printed in the record): a normal FMD in this cohort said nothing about carotid structure, and vice versa.
cards.source: Yan RT et al. Relationship between carotid artery intima-media thickness and brachial artery flow-mediated dilation in middle-aged healthy men. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2005. PMID: 15963396. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brachial vs popliteal FMD in four small age/sex groups (Nakamura 2019): group Ns 16–19 printed — brachial FMD was preserved in middle-aged men (11.4 ± 1.5% vs 10.6 ± 1.5% in young men) while popliteal FMD fell (6.4 ± 1.0% vs 8.7 ± 1.6%); no significant brachial–popliteal difference in women
cards.summary: Brachial vs popliteal FMD in four small age/sex groups (Nakamura 2019): group Ns 16–19 printed — brachial FMD was preserved in middle-aged men (11.4 ± 1.5% vs 10.6 ± 1.5% in young men) while popliteal FMD fell (6.4 ± 1.0% vs 8.7 ± 1.6%); no significant brachial–popliteal difference in women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (brachial and popliteal FMD in four small healthy age/sex groups)
cards.people: Four healthy non-smoking groups: young men (mean 26 ± 2 years, n = 17), middle-aged men (mean 50 ± 3 years, n = 19), young women (mean 27 ± 2 years, n = 16) and middle-aged women (mean 51 ± 2 years, n = 18) — total 70; brachial and popliteal flow-mediated vasodilation measured, with nitrate/nitrite (NOx) and asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) levels. Small groups, printed here and on the face, never load-bearing alone.
cards.result: In young men, brachial and popliteal FMD did not differ significantly (10.6 ± 1.5% vs 8.7 ± 1.6%, P = 0.06); in middle-aged men popliteal FMD was significantly lower than brachial (11.4 ± 1.5% vs 6.4 ± 1.0%, P < 0.001) — note brachial FMD itself did not fall between the young and middle-aged male groups. In women there were no significant brachial–popliteal differences in either age group. Popliteal FMD correlated with plasma NOx and ADMA and their ratio in men but not in women. The authors conclude lower-limb flow-mediated function declines by middle age in healthy men but not women, possibly via competitive inhibition of L-arginine.
cards.watchOut: Groups of 16–19 cannot set reference limits: this card's value is the within-person brachial–popliteal contrast and the sex difference in the ageing pattern, both hypothesis-grade at these Ns.
cards.source: Nakamura A et al. Decline of popliteal artery flow-mediated dilation with aging and possible involvement of asymmetric dimethylarginine in healthy men. Journal of medical ultrasonics (2001). 2019. PMID: 31011935. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Supporting limb only (Allen 2000): 30 healthy non-smokers — normal plasma fibrinogen was inversely associated with brachial FMD (r = −0.56, P = 0.001); short abstract (409 characters), no FMD values printed, supporting only
cards.summary: Supporting limb only (Allen 2000): 30 healthy non-smokers — normal plasma fibrinogen was inversely associated with brachial FMD (r = −0.56, P = 0.001); short abstract (409 characters), no FMD values printed, supporting only
cards.type: Supporting primary physiology report (fibrinogen and FMD in healthy adults) — supporting only, not a normative dataset
cards.people: 30 healthy non-smoking adults in a study of age-associated increases in fibrinogen and brachial artery flow-mediated dilatation. Supporting limb only, as commissioned: the fetched abstract is short and prints no group FMD values, and none are claimed.
cards.result: The findings demonstrate an inverse association between normal plasma fibrinogen levels and vascular function (r = −0.56, P = 0.001), suggesting elevated plasma fibrinogen within the normal range may decrease the artery's responsiveness to vasodilatory signals such as shear stress. Carded, labelled supporting only, because it identifies a within-normal-range correlate that shifts an individual's FMD away from the age/sex percentile — it is not a normative dataset.
cards.watchOut: n = 30 and a 409-character abstract: this limb can suggest a correlate, never a limit — if it stood alone this row would stop; it does not stand alone.
cards.source: Allen JD et al. Influence of age and normal plasma fibrinogen levels on flow-mediated dilation in healthy adults. The American journal of cardiology. 2000. PMID: 10980232. cards.result: Distribution slice only: the mechanism of endothelium-dependent dilatation is homed at pack #6497, cross-pointed and not re-carded. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (endothelial physiology / vascular control) and Guyton & Hall (local control of blood flow). Königstein 2021 (457 healthy adults) supplies the sex-specific percentiles and the age gradients, with its 6.4% FMD risk cut-off explicitly not a normal limit. Yan 2005 (1,578 healthy men) shows FMD uncorrelated with carotid IMT (r = −0.006). Nakamura 2019 (four groups of 16–19) shows the popliteal artery ageing before the brachial in men, with brachial values preserved (11.4 ± 1.5% at mean age 50). Allen 2000 (n = 30, supporting only) adds fibrinogen as a within-normal correlate (r = −0.56). PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: one dedicated reference study, one large dissociation cohort and two small limbs, all protocol-sensitive — the distribution is documented, but no cross-protocol reference standard yet exists.
cards.watchOut: Cuff position, occlusion duration, baseline diameter and edge-detection method all move FMD: never compare a value against these percentiles without the protocol that produced it.

shelves.title: Lorundrostat phase 3 programme in uncontrolled hypertension (PARTIAL vs live #743): Launch-HTN — office systolic pressure fell a placebo-adjusted 9.1 mm Hg; Advance-HTN — 24-hour systolic pressure fell 7.9 mm Hg at the stable 50 mg dose; a two-trial, surrogate-endpoint base
shelves.question: In adults with uncontrolled or treatment-resistant hypertension, does the aldosterone synthase inhibitor lorundrostat, compared with placebo on background therapy, lower blood pressure in its phase 3 programme (Launch-HTN; Advance-HTN)? (PARTIAL — the phase 3 slice of live shelf #743, which cards lorundrostat's phase 2 Target-HTN trial and the class question.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Aldosterone · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Cytochrome P-450 CYP11B2 · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hypertension · Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme Inhibitors · Coronary Vasospasm · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL shelf — LIKELY (benefit) for blood-pressure lowering, on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 reports from 2 distinct trials, stated here on the face. This shelf cards ONLY lorundrostat's phase 3 programme; lorundrostat's phase 2 Target-HTN trial is carded at live shelf #743 (the aldosterone-synthase class question, with baxdrostat) and is NOT re-carded here (one-home rule) — #743 is cross-pointed, and this shelf is the phase 3 slice #743 fenced rather than carded. Launch-HTN (phase 3, 1,083 randomised): pooled lorundrostat 50 mg lowered automated office systolic pressure by a least-squares mean difference of −9.1 mm Hg versus placebo at week 6. Advance-HTN (285 randomised; its PubMed record types it Clinical Trial, Phase II — that designation is printed on its card, not silently upgraded): placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic reductions of −7.9 mm Hg (stable 50 mg dose) and −6.5 mm Hg (dose-adjustment group) at week 12. Harms were the class harms: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and reduced kidney function occurred more often on lorundrostat, with small numbers of discontinuations for each. Blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for lorundrostat or its class — printed here, as at #743.

cards.headline: Launch-HTN phase 3 RCT (Saxena 2025): lorundrostat 50 mg lowered automated office systolic pressure by a placebo-adjusted 9.1 mm Hg at week 6 in uncontrolled and treatment-resistant hypertension
cards.summary: Launch-HTN phase 3 RCT (Saxena 2025): lorundrostat 50 mg lowered automated office systolic pressure by a placebo-adjusted 9.1 mm Hg at week 6 in uncontrolled and treatment-resistant hypertension
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Launch-HTN), lorundrostat added to 2–5 background antihypertensive medications vs placebo
cards.people: 1,083 adults with uncontrolled hypertension, including treatment-resistant hypertension, on 2 to 5 prescribed antihypertensive medications (mean age 61.6 years; 46.9% female; 63.3% with body-mass index ≥30), enrolled at 159 clinic sites in 13 countries (November 2023–September 2024). Randomised 1:2:1 to lorundrostat 50 mg with possible escalation to 100 mg (n=270), lorundrostat 50 mg for 12 weeks (n=541), or placebo (n=272).
cards.result: For the pooled 50 mg lorundrostat group (n=808), the least-squares mean change in automated office systolic blood pressure at week 6 was −16.9 mm Hg (95% CI −19.0 to −14.9) versus −7.9 mm Hg (95% CI −11.5 to −4.2) on placebo — a least-squares mean difference of −9.1 mm Hg (95% CI −13.3 to −4.9; P<.001). Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and reduction in kidney function were reported more often with lorundrostat than placebo; discontinuations for these events were uncommon (in the 50 mg group: 2 participants [0.37%] for hyperkalaemia, 2 [0.37%] for hyponatraemia, 3 [0.56%] for reduced kidney function). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 49.9% of participants (538/1078) and were mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was at week 6 — a short, surrogate (blood-pressure) endpoint; dose escalation to 100 mg was conditional on prespecified criteria including potassium ≤4.8 mmol/L (≈18.8 mg/dL), so the escalated-dose experience is a selected subgroup.

cards.headline: Advance-HTN RCT (Laffin 2025): lorundrostat lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by a placebo-adjusted 7.9 mm Hg at the stable 50 mg dose and 6.5 mm Hg in the dose-adjustment group at week 12 — its PubMed record types this trial as Phase II
cards.summary: Advance-HTN RCT (Laffin 2025): lorundrostat lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure by a placebo-adjusted 7.9 mm Hg at the stable 50 mg dose and 6.5 mm Hg in the dose-adjustment group at week 12 — its PubMed record types this trial as Phase II
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Advance-HTN) — typed Clinical Trial, Phase II in its PubMed record (printed as recorded; the phase 3 programme framing of this shelf rests on Launch-HTN)
cards.people: 285 participants receiving 2 to 5 antihypertensive medications with office blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg, who after a 3-week standardised regimen still had average 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure ≥130/80 mm Hg; randomised to placebo (n=95), lorundrostat stable dose 50 mg daily (n=94), or lorundrostat 50 mg rising to 100 mg if systolic pressure remained ≥130 mm Hg after 4 weeks (n=96). Mean age 60 years; 53% were Black.
cards.result: At week 12 the least-squares mean change in 24-hour average systolic blood pressure was −15.4 mm Hg (stable-dose group), −13.9 mm Hg (dose-adjustment group) and −7.4 mm Hg (placebo): placebo-adjusted changes of −7.9 mm Hg (97.5% CI −13.3 to −2.6) and −6.5 mm Hg (97.5% CI −11.8 to −1.2) respectively. The placebo-adjusted change at week 4 in the combined lorundrostat groups was −5.3 mm Hg (95% CI −8.4 to −2.3). A potassium level above 6.0 mmol/L (≈23.5 mg/dL) occurred in 5 participants (5%) in the stable-dose group, 7 (7%) in the dose-adjustment group and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Much smaller than Launch-HTN (285 randomised) and typed phase II in the record, so it is supportive rather than co-definitive; the endpoint is 24-hour ambulatory pressure, a surrogate, and hyperkalaemia above 6.0 mmol/L (≈23.5 mg/dL) occurred only on lorundrostat.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two distinct randomised trials, one direction — lorundrostat lowers systolic pressure by roughly 7–9 mm Hg beyond placebo on background therapy, with electrolyte and kidney harms to monitor; no outcomes trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: two distinct randomised trials, one direction — lorundrostat lowers systolic pressure by roughly 7–9 mm Hg beyond placebo on background therapy, with electrolyte and kidney harms to monitor; no outcomes trial exists
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (Launch-HTN, n=1,083; Advance-HTN, n=285).
cards.result: Launch-HTN (phase 3) found a placebo-adjusted office systolic reduction of −9.1 mm Hg at week 6; Advance-HTN (typed phase II in its record) found placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic reductions of −7.9 mm Hg (stable 50 mg) and −6.5 mm Hg (dose-adjustment) at week 12. The consistent cost was more hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and reduced kidney function on lorundrostat than placebo. This is a two-trial, surrogate-endpoint base (FLOOR-RISK, printed on the face): it supports LIKELY (benefit) for blood-pressure lowering in uncontrolled and treatment-resistant hypertension, and says nothing about stroke, myocardial infarction or mortality, for which no trial exists. The phase 2 limb and the class comparison stay at live shelf #743.

shelves.title: Momelotinib vs ruxolitinib / best available therapy in myelofibrosis (SIMPLIFY-1/-2): a split result — spleen noninferiority, symptom noninferiority missed, no post-ruxolitinib superiority, transfusion benefit throughout (MOMENTUM homed at #4865)
shelves.question: In patients with myelofibrosis — Janus kinase inhibitor-naive (SIMPLIFY-1) or previously treated with ruxolitinib with suboptimal response or haematologic toxicity (SIMPLIFY-2) — does momelotinib 200 mg once daily, versus ruxolitinib or best available therapy, achieve spleen-volume and symptom responses, and does it improve transfusion outcomes and survival? (PARTIAL shelf: momelotinib versus danazol, MOMENTUM, is homed at pack #4865 and is not re-carded here.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Benzamides · Disease-Free Survival · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Janus Kinase Inhibitors · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Patient Safety · Primary Myelofibrosis · Prognosis · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Retreatment · Risk Assessment · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a PARTIAL shelf: momelotinib versus danazol in anaemic myelofibrosis (the MOMENTUM trial) is homed at pack #4865 and is cross-pointed here in prose only, never re-carded; this shelf cards only the unasked SIMPLIFY head-to-head slice, and fedratinib is homed separately at pack #7014. The result is genuinely split. In JAK-inhibitor-naive patients (SIMPLIFY-1, n=432), momelotinib was noninferior to ruxolitinib for spleen-volume response (26.5% vs 29%; noninferior, P=.011) but noninferiority was NOT met for symptom response (28.4% vs 42.2%; P=.98), while transfusion rate, independence and dependence all favoured momelotinib (nominal P at most .019). In ruxolitinib-pretreated patients (SIMPLIFY-2, n=156), momelotinib was NOT superior to best available therapy for spleen response (7% vs 6%; P=.90) — and the control was effectively continued ruxolitinib in 89% of patients. Survival was similar in both trials (overall-survival hazard ratios 1.02 and 0.98, both relative measures, both non-significant). Peripheral neuropathy is momelotinib's recurring harm (10–11% versus 0–5%).

cards.headline: SIMPLIFY-1 phase 3 RCT (Mesa 2017): spleen response noninferior to ruxolitinib (26.5% vs 29%; P=.011) but symptom-response noninferiority NOT met (28.4% vs 42.2%; P=.98); transfusion outcomes favoured momelotinib
cards.summary: SIMPLIFY-1 phase 3 RCT (Mesa 2017): spleen response noninferior to ruxolitinib (26.5% vs 29%; P=.011) but symptom-response noninferiority NOT met (28.4% vs 42.2%; P=.98); transfusion outcomes favoured momelotinib
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (SIMPLIFY-1), momelotinib vs ruxolitinib, JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis
cards.people: 432 patients with high-risk, intermediate-2 risk, or symptomatic intermediate-1 risk myelofibrosis who were Janus kinase inhibitor-naive, randomised to momelotinib 200 mg once daily or ruxolitinib 20 mg twice daily (or per label) for 24 weeks, after which all patients could receive open-label momelotinib.
cards.result: A reduction in spleen volume of at least 35% at week 24 (the primary endpoint) was achieved by 26.5% on momelotinib and 29% on ruxolitinib (noninferior; P=.011). A reduction of at least 50% in total symptom score was seen in 28.4% versus 42.2% — noninferiority was not met (P=.98). Transfusion rate, transfusion independence and transfusion dependence were all improved with momelotinib (all nominal P at most .019). The most common grade 3-or-worse haematologic abnormalities in either group were thrombocytopenia and anaemia; grade 3-or-worse infections occurred in 7% on momelotinib versus 3% on ruxolitinib, and treatment-emergent peripheral neuropathy in 10% (all grade 2 or less) versus 5% (all grade 3 or less).
cards.watchOut: The two co-headline reads point opposite ways — spleen noninferiority met, symptom noninferiority missed by a wide margin (28.4% vs 42.2%) — and the transfusion advantages carry nominal P values. This trial must not be summarised as a general win over ruxolitinib.

cards.headline: SIMPLIFY-2 phase 3 RCT (Harrison 2018): momelotinib NOT superior to best available therapy for spleen response after ruxolitinib (7% vs 6%; P=.90) — and 89% of the control arm was continued ruxolitinib
cards.summary: SIMPLIFY-2 phase 3 RCT (Harrison 2018): momelotinib NOT superior to best available therapy for spleen response after ruxolitinib (7% vs 6%; P=.90) — and 89% of the control arm was continued ruxolitinib
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (SIMPLIFY-2), momelotinib vs best available therapy, ruxolitinib-pretreated myelofibrosis
cards.people: 156 patients with myelofibrosis previously treated with ruxolitinib for at least 28 days who required red-cell transfusions on ruxolitinib or had a ruxolitinib dose reduction below 20 mg twice daily with grade 3 thrombocytopenia, anaemia or bleeding, randomised 2:1 (104 momelotinib 200 mg once daily, 52 best available therapy) for 24 weeks at 52 centres; best available therapy was ruxolitinib in 46 of 52 control patients (89%).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — spleen-volume reduction of at least 35% at week 24 — occurred in 7 of 104 (7%) on momelotinib and 3 of 52 (6%) on best available therapy (proportion difference 0.01; 95% CI −0.09 to 0.10; P=.90): momelotinib was not superior. Treatment completion of the 24-week phase was 70% versus 77%. The most common grade 3-or-worse adverse events were anaemia (14% vs 14%) and thrombocytopenia (7% vs 6%); peripheral neuropathy occurred in 11 of 104 (11%, one grade 3) on momelotinib versus none on best available therapy. Serious events were reported in 35% versus 23%; deaths due to adverse events in 6 patients (6%) on momelotinib and 4 (8%) on best available therapy.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 'best available therapy' control was continued ruxolitinib in 89% — so the trial effectively asks whether switching to momelotinib beats staying on ruxolitinib in patients already failing it, and the answer for spleen response was no. A different population from SIMPLIFY-1; the two trials are never pooled on this shelf.

cards.headline: Joint survival analysis of SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 (Mesa 2022): overall survival similar in both trials (hazard ratios 1.02 and 0.98 — relative measures, both non-significant); transfusion independence tracked with better survival
cards.summary: Joint survival analysis of SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 (Mesa 2022): overall survival similar in both trials (hazard ratios 1.02 and 0.98 — relative measures, both non-significant); transfusion independence tracked with better survival
cards.type: Joint overall-survival / leukaemia-free-survival analysis of the SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 trials (same two trials as the cards above — not independent trials)
cards.people: The randomised populations of SIMPLIFY-1 (JAK-inhibitor-naive; momelotinib versus ruxolitinib then momelotinib) and SIMPLIFY-2 (ruxolitinib-exposed; momelotinib versus best available therapy then momelotinib), in a joint report of mature overall survival and leukaemia-free survival with retrospective analyses of transfusion independence and survival.
cards.result: Survival distributions were similar between arms in both studies: SIMPLIFY-1 overall-survival hazard ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.43) and leukaemia-free-survival hazard ratio 1.08 (0.78 to 1.50), with 2-year overall survival 81.6% (momelotinib) versus 80.6% (ruxolitinib then momelotinib); SIMPLIFY-2 overall-survival hazard ratio 0.98 (0.59 to 1.62) and leukaemia-free-survival hazard ratio 0.97 (0.59 to 1.60), with 2-year overall survival 65.8% versus 61.2% (all hazard ratios are relative measures). Baseline transfusion independence was associated with improved survival in both studies (hazard ratios 0.474, P=.0001, and 0.226, P=.0005), and week-24 transfusion-independence response in JAK-inhibitor-naive momelotinib patients was associated with improved overall survival in univariate (hazard ratio 0.323; P<.0001) and multivariate (hazard ratio 0.311; P<.0001) analyses.
cards.watchOut: After the randomised phases, control patients crossed to momelotinib, so these are strategy comparisons (immediate versus deferred momelotinib), not pure drug-versus-drug survival tests; the transfusion-independence survival associations are retrospective and associational, not randomised effects.
cards.source: Mesa R et al. Overall survival in the SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 phase 3 trials of momelotinib in patients with myelofibrosis. Leukemia. 2022. PMID: 35869266. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Longitudinal symptom analysis of the SIMPLIFY trials (Mesa 2023): overall symptom improvement similar between momelotinib and ruxolitinib in SIMPLIFY-1 (total symptom score difference under 1.5 points at every visit); control-arm symptoms deteriorated in SIMPLIFY-2 while momelotinib's improved
cards.summary: Longitudinal symptom analysis of the SIMPLIFY trials (Mesa 2023): overall symptom improvement similar between momelotinib and ruxolitinib in SIMPLIFY-1 (total symptom score difference under 1.5 points at every visit); control-arm symptoms deteriorated in SIMPLIFY-2 while momelotinib's improved
cards.type: Longitudinal symptom-benefit companion analysis of SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 (same trials as above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: Patients from the SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 phase 3 trials, in a longitudinal analysis of change from baseline in total symptom score over 24 weeks using mixed-effect repeated-measures models, with item-level analyses — a companion analysis of the two trials carded above, not a new trial.
cards.result: In SIMPLIFY-1, momelotinib and ruxolitinib groups reported similar overall symptom improvements, with a total symptom score difference of under 1.5 points between groups at each post-baseline visit, and item-level odds ratios for symptom improvement ranging from 0.75 to 1.21 (odds ratios are relative measures). In SIMPLIFY-2, symptom improvement on momelotinib was consistent with SIMPLIFY-1 while the control arm progressively deteriorated, and the likelihood of improvement on each symptom item was higher in the momelotinib arm. Similar or greater proportions of momelotinib patients were categorised as improved or stable compared with control in SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 respectively.
cards.watchOut: A continuous longitudinal read, which is kinder to momelotinib than SIMPLIFY-1's landmark responder endpoint (28.4% vs 42.2%, noninferiority missed) — both reads are printed on this shelf and neither replaces the other; this is a re-analysis of the same patients, not confirmation in new patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the SIMPLIFY slice is split — spleen noninferiority without symptom noninferiority against ruxolitinib in JAK-inhibitor-naive disease, no spleen superiority against (mostly continued) ruxolitinib after ruxolitinib failure, similar survival in both trials, and a consistent transfusion advantage as momelotinib's distinguishing claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: the SIMPLIFY slice is split — spleen noninferiority without symptom noninferiority against ruxolitinib in JAK-inhibitor-naive disease, no spleen superiority against (mostly continued) ruxolitinib after ruxolitinib failure, similar survival in both trials, and a consistent transfusion advantage as momelotinib's distinguishing claim
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf. The separate MOMENTUM question (momelotinib versus danazol in myelofibrosis with anaemia) is homed at pack #4865 and is not carded here.
cards.result: SIMPLIFY-1 (n=432, JAK-inhibitor-naive): spleen response 26.5% versus 29% (noninferior), symptom response 28.4% versus 42.2% (noninferiority not met), transfusion outcomes favouring momelotinib. SIMPLIFY-2 (n=156, post-ruxolitinib): spleen response 7% versus 6% against best available therapy that was ruxolitinib in 89% (not superior). Joint survival analysis: overall-survival hazard ratios 1.02 and 0.98 (relative measures), i.e. no survival difference in either setting. Peripheral neuropathy (10–11% on momelotinib) is the consistent added harm. Two trials, two populations — reported separately throughout, never pooled.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Ponatinib vs imatinib in frontline Ph+ ALL (PhALLCON, one trial): MRD-negative remission doubled (34.4% vs 16.7%) — a remission-depth benefit; survival not yet established
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does frontline ponatinib (30 mg/day, reduced to 15 mg on MRD-negative complete remission), versus imatinib (600 mg/day), each with reduced-intensity chemotherapy, increase MRD-negative complete remission and event-free survival, and with what arterial-occlusive cost? (Single programme: the PhALLCON trial.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antineoplastic Agents · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Fusion Proteins, bcr-abl · Imatinib Mesylate · Imidazoles · Philadelphia Chromosome · Precursor Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Pyridazines · Remission Induction · Adolescent
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (PhALLCON), three reports. Ponatinib (30 mg/day, reduced to 15 mg on achieving MRD-negative complete remission) with reduced-intensity chemotherapy doubled the primary endpoint versus imatinib (600 mg/day): MRD-negative complete remission at the end of cycle 3 in 34.4% (53/154) versus 16.7% (13/78) (risk difference 0.18; P=.002). The primary endpoint is a molecular-depth endpoint, not a survival endpoint: event-free survival was immature at the interim cutoff (median not reached versus 29 months; the prespecified event count had not been met), and in the quality-adjusted analysis restricted mean overall survival was itself similar between arms (1082.2 versus 1024.8 days; P=.373). The two companion reports (patient-reported outcomes; Q-TWiST, with mean time without symptoms or toxicity 214.5 days longer on ponatinib) are supportive analyses of the same patients and must not upgrade this into a survival claim. Arterial occlusive events — the reason for ponatinib's dose-reduction-on-response design — were infrequent and comparable (2.5% versus 1.2%) at this cutoff.

cards.headline: PhALLCON phase 3 primary report (Jabbour 2024): MRD-negative complete remission at end of cycle 3 in 34.4% on ponatinib versus 16.7% on imatinib (risk difference 0.18; P=.002); event-free survival immature
cards.summary: PhALLCON phase 3 primary report (Jabbour 2024): MRD-negative complete remission at end of cycle 3 in 34.4% on ponatinib versus 16.7% on imatinib (risk difference 0.18; P=.002); event-free survival immature
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label randomised trial (PhALLCON), ponatinib vs imatinib with reduced-intensity chemotherapy, frontline Ph+ ALL — interim primary analysis
cards.people: 245 adults aged 18 or older with newly diagnosed Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia at 77 sites (2019–2022), randomised 2:1 to ponatinib 30 mg/day or imatinib 600 mg/day, each with reduced-intensity chemotherapy, followed by single-agent tyrosine kinase inhibitor after cycle 20; the ponatinib dose was reduced to 15 mg on achievement of MRD-negative complete remission. The primary-endpoint analysis covered 232 patients with centrally verified p190 or p210 isoforms (154 ponatinib, 78 imatinib); median age was 54 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — MRD-negative complete remission (BCR::ABL1 at most 0.01%, MR4, centrally assessed) maintained for at least 4 weeks at the end of cycle 3 — was significantly higher with ponatinib: 34.4% (53/154) versus 16.7% (13/78) (risk difference 0.18; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.29; P=.002). At the data cutoff, event-free survival (the key secondary endpoint) had not met the prespecified number of events; median event-free survival was not reached on ponatinib and was 29 months on imatinib. The most common adverse events were similar between groups, and arterial occlusive events were infrequent and comparable (ponatinib 2.5%; imatinib 1.2%).
cards.watchOut: Single-programme evidence and an interim analysis: the proven benefit is depth of remission (MRD-negative complete remission), a molecular endpoint — event-free survival had not reached its prespecified event count, so no survival benefit is established by this report.
cards.source: Jabbour E et al. Ponatinib vs Imatinib in Frontline Philadelphia Chromosome-Positive Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38722621. Registry ID: NCT03589326. cards.headline: PhALLCON patient-reported outcomes (Ashaye 2025): least-squares mean changes favoured ponatinib, with significant differences in FACT-Leu subscale, Trial Outcome Index and FACT-Leu total at end of induction (exploratory endpoints, same trial)
cards.summary: PhALLCON patient-reported outcomes (Ashaye 2025): least-squares mean changes favoured ponatinib, with significant differences in FACT-Leu subscale, Trial Outcome Index and FACT-Leu total at end of induction (exploratory endpoints, same trial)
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes companion report of the PhALLCON trial (same trial as the primary card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 238 PhALLCON patients (159 ponatinib, 79 imatinib) with at least one patient-reported outcome assessment, using the FACT-Leu questionnaire and EQ-5D-5L; differences in least-squares mean changes from baseline to end of induction and end of consolidation, and time to confirmed improvement or deterioration, were analysed.
cards.result: Least-squares mean changes from baseline favoured ponatinib, with significant and meaningful differences in the FACT-Leu subscale, Trial Outcome Index and FACT-Leu total score at end of induction, and across the primary domains except the FACT-Leu subscale at end of consolidation. Median time to confirmed improvement was shorter with ponatinib than imatinib for key measures, and ponatinib-treated patients tended to report being less bothered by treatment side effects (FACT-GP5).
cards.watchOut: Exploratory endpoints in an open-label trial — patients knew which tyrosine kinase inhibitor they were taking, which can colour symptom reporting; a companion analysis of the same 245-patient trial, not a second trial.

Leukemia. 2025. PMID: 40240572. Registry ID: NCT03589326. cards.headline: PhALLCON Q-TWiST analysis (Ashaye 2025): mean time without symptoms or toxicity 214.5 days longer with ponatinib (P=.004) and relative Q-TWiST gain 10.98% — while restricted mean overall survival itself was similar (1082.2 vs 1024.8 days; P=.373)
cards.summary: PhALLCON Q-TWiST analysis (Ashaye 2025): mean time without symptoms or toxicity 214.5 days longer with ponatinib (P=.004) and relative Q-TWiST gain 10.98% — while restricted mean overall survival itself was similar (1082.2 vs 1024.8 days; P=.373)
cards.type: Post hoc Q-TWiST (model-based quality-adjusted) companion analysis of the PhALLCON trial (same trial as above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: All randomised PhALLCON patients (ponatinib n=164, imatinib n=81) in a post hoc quality-adjusted time-without-symptoms-or-toxicity analysis partitioning overall survival into time with grade 3-or-worse toxicity (TOX), time without symptoms or toxicity (TWiST), and time after progression (REL), with utility-weighted restricted means.
cards.result: Restricted mean overall survival was similar between arms (1082.2 vs 1024.8 days; P=.373). Mean TWiST was 214.5 days longer with ponatinib (95% CI 70.3 to 358.7; P=.004), time after progression was shorter by 175.9 days (P=.021), and time with toxicity did not differ significantly (P=.228). The relative Q-TWiST gain was 10.98%, above the 10% threshold the authors prespecified as clinically important, and sensitivity analyses varying utilities, follow-up and the toxicity definition supported the base case.
cards.watchOut: A model-based, post hoc quality-adjusted analysis: the Q-TWiST gain is driven by longer time before progression, while overall survival itself did not differ — it must not be read as a survival benefit. Third report of one trial, not a third trial.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (a single programme: the PhALLCON trial and two companion analyses of the same patients).
cards.result: Primary endpoint (molecular depth): MRD-negative complete remission 34.4% versus 16.7% (risk difference 0.18; P=.002). Survival: event-free survival immature at the primary cutoff (median not reached versus 29 months, prespecified event count not met); restricted mean overall survival similar in the Q-TWiST analysis (1082.2 vs 1024.8 days; P=.373). Companions: patient-reported outcomes favoured ponatinib on several FACT-Leu domains (exploratory, open-label), and quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity was 214.5 days longer (model-based). shelves.title: Blinatumomab vs chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (TOWER, one trial): survival 7.7 vs 4.0 months, deeper remissions, better quality of life
shelves.question: In adults with heavily pretreated, Philadelphia chromosome-negative relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does the CD19xCD3 bispecific T-cell engager blinatumomab, versus standard-of-care chemotherapy, prolong overall survival and deepen remission, and with what quality-of-life effect? (Single programme: the TOWER trial.)

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (TOWER), three reports. In heavily pretreated, Philadelphia chromosome-negative relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL, blinatumomab prolonged overall survival versus standard chemotherapy: median 7.7 versus 4.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.71 — a relative measure; the absolute frame, a 3.7-month median gain in a population with very short expected survival, is the honest headline). Remission was deeper (complete remission with full haematologic recovery 34% vs 16%; with full, partial or incomplete recovery 44% vs 25%) and 6-month event-free survival was 31% versus 12%. Grade 3-or-worse adverse events were similarly frequent (87% vs 92%), and the exposure-adjusted analysis found lower event rates per patient-year on blinatumomab for most categories except cytokine-release syndrome. Health-related quality of life favoured blinatumomab across subscales. This is strictly the relapsed/refractory setting: blinatumomab consolidation in MRD-negative frontline disease is a separate question (pack #7369, E1910), and blinatumomab in children is homed at pack #5008 — both cross-pointed in prose only.

cards.headline: TOWER phase 3 primary report (Kantarjian 2017): median overall survival 7.7 versus 4.0 months with blinatumomab versus chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.71, relative); complete remission with full recovery 34% versus 16%
cards.summary: TOWER phase 3 primary report (Kantarjian 2017): median overall survival 7.7 versus 4.0 months with blinatumomab versus chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.71, relative); complete remission with full recovery 34% versus 16%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (TOWER), blinatumomab vs standard-of-care chemotherapy, relapsed/refractory B-cell precursor ALL
cards.people: 405 adults with heavily pretreated, Philadelphia chromosome-negative, relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, randomised 2:1 (271 blinatumomab, 134 standard-of-care chemotherapy); 376 received at least one dose. The primary endpoint was overall survival.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 7.7 months on blinatumomab versus 4.0 months on chemotherapy (hazard ratio for death 0.71; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.93; P=0.01 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute medians). Remission within 12 weeks was higher with blinatumomab: complete remission with full haematologic recovery 34% versus 16% (P<0.001) and complete remission with full, partial or incomplete recovery 44% versus 25% (P<0.001). Six-month event-free survival estimates were 31% versus 12% (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.71; P<0.001 — relative), and median duration of remission was 7.3 versus 4.6 months. Allogeneic stem-cell transplantation followed in 24% of each group. Grade 3-or-worse adverse events were reported in 87% (blinatumomab) versus 92% (chemotherapy).
cards.watchOut: Single-programme evidence (one trial). The relative hazard ratio of 0.71 sits on short absolute survival — median 7.7 months in the better arm — in a heavily pretreated population; both frames are printed and neither should be quoted alone.
cards.source: Kantarjian H et al. Blinatumomab versus Chemotherapy for Advanced Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28249141. Registry ID: NCT02013167. cards.headline: TOWER quality-of-life report (Topp 2018): post-treatment health-related quality of life favoured blinatumomab across QLQ-C30 subscales; time-to-deterioration hazard ratios 0.42 to 0.81 (relative measures)
cards.summary: TOWER quality-of-life report (Topp 2018): post-treatment health-related quality of life favoured blinatumomab across QLQ-C30 subscales; time-to-deterioration hazard ratios 0.42 to 0.81 (relative measures)
cards.type: Health-related quality-of-life companion report of the TOWER trial (same trial as the primary card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 342 of the 405 TOWER randomised patients (247 blinatumomab, 95 chemotherapy) with a baseline and at least one postbaseline EORTC QLQ-C30 assessment — a companion analysis of the TOWER trial carded above, not a new trial.
cards.result: Patients receiving blinatumomab reported better post-treatment health-related quality of life across all QLQ-C30 subscales on descriptive mean change from baseline. Hazard ratios for time to deterioration of 10 or more points in quality of life or death ranged from 0.42 to 0.81 in favour of blinatumomab (relative measures), with the upper bounds of the 95% confidence intervals below 1.0 across all measures except insomnia, social functioning and financial difficulties; sensitivity analyses excluding death as an event were consistent. In mixed-model analyses, P<.05 was reached for blinatumomab versus chemotherapy for all subscale measures except financial difficulties.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with differential survival and assessment completion (247 versus 95 patients analysed) can bias quality-of-life comparisons in favour of the better-performing arm; a supportive companion, not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Topp MS et al. Health-related quality of life in adults with relapsed/refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with blinatumomab. Blood. 2018. PMID: 29739753. cards.headline: TOWER exposure-adjusted safety analysis (Stein 2018): after adjusting for longer time on treatment, grade 3-or-worse event rates per patient-year were lower with blinatumomab (10.73 vs 45.27) except cytokine-release syndrome, which was higher (0.16 vs 0)
cards.summary: TOWER exposure-adjusted safety analysis (Stein 2018): after adjusting for longer time on treatment, grade 3-or-worse event rates per patient-year were lower with blinatumomab (10.73 vs 45.27) except cytokine-release syndrome, which was higher (0.16 vs 0)
cards.type: Exposure-adjusted adverse-event companion analysis of the TOWER trial (same trial as above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The TOWER safety population (267 patients received blinatumomab, median 2 cycles, range 1–9; 109 received chemotherapy, median 1 cycle, range 1–4) in an exploratory exposure-adjusted adverse-event analysis of the trial carded above.
cards.result: Nearly all patients in both arms experienced an adverse event, and crude serious adverse-event incidence was higher for blinatumomab; grade 3-or-worse rates were higher in blinatumomab cycle 1 than cycle 2 (76% vs 37%). After adjusting for time on treatment, exposure-adjusted rates of grade 3-or-worse events were significantly lower for blinatumomab than chemotherapy overall (10.73 vs 45.27 events per patient-year; P<.001), and for infections (1.63 vs 6.49; P<.001), cytopenias (3.64 vs 20.07; P<.001) and neurologic events (0.38 vs 0.95; P=.008). The exposure-adjusted rate of grade 3-or-worse cytokine-release syndrome was higher for blinatumomab (0.16 vs 0 events per patient-year; P=.038) — the class harm of a T-cell engager, alongside neurotoxicity, that any use must plan for.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and adjustment-dependent: the crude rates (grade 3-or-worse events in 87% versus 92%; higher crude serious-event incidence on blinatumomab) and the exposure-adjusted rates tell different stories because blinatumomab patients stayed on treatment longer — both are printed; the adjustment does not erase the cytokine-release and neurologic risks.
cards.source: Stein AS et al. Exposure-adjusted adverse events comparing blinatumomab with chemotherapy in advanced acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Blood advances. 2018. PMID: 29954814.
