cards.people: Synthesis of the three cohorts carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (cardiac muscle / circulation; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary CMR reference literature). Hudsmith's 108 volunteers set the absolute scale (LV end-diastolic volume 160 ± 29 mL men, 135 ± 26 mL women; RV end-diastolic 190 ± 33 vs 148 ± 35 mL). Maceira's modelling establishes that ranges must be normalised to sex, body surface area and age jointly. UK Biobank's 804-person healthy reference cohort extends the ranges to all four chambers at ages 45-74 (LV ejection fraction 61 ± 5% women, 58 ± 5% men; indexed LV mass 42 ± 7 vs 53 ± 9 g/m2). Echocardiographic deformation (global longitudinal strain) is homed at pack #7163 and resting pulmonary artery pressures at pack #7165 — neither is re-carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: contouring conventions move volumes and mass materially, one carded record prints no numeric ranges in its abstract, and the largest cohort is single-ethnicity and aged 45-74.
cards.watchOut: Never apply a CMR range across contouring conventions or to echocardiographic volumes; age and sex strata are part of the range, not adjustments after the fact.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In adults with essential hypertension, does the non-steroidal mineralocorticoid-receptor blocker esaxerenone, compared with placebo, eplerenone or trichlormethiazide, lower blood pressure?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for blood-pressure lowering only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. ESAX-HTN (phase 3, 1,001 patients): esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day was non-inferior to eplerenone 50 mg/day for sitting and 24-hour blood-pressure reduction, the 5 mg/day dose reduced blood pressure significantly more than 2.5 mg/day, and target sitting blood pressure was reached by 31.5%, 41.2% and 27.5% respectively. The phase 2 placebo-controlled study showed a dose-response (sitting change −20.6/−10.4 mm Hg at 5 mg vs −7.0/−3.8 mm Hg on placebo and −17.4/−8.5 mm Hg on eplerenone). EXCITE-HT: esaxerenone was non-inferior to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy for morning home blood pressure. PARTIAL: pack #3204 already homes esaxerenone for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease (the ESAX-DN programme) — this shelf cards only the essential-hypertension slice and cross-points #3204; none of #3204's studies is re-carded. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Japanese; esaxerenone is approved in Japan for hypertension and is not FDA/EMA-approved. Blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists for this agent. Hyperkalaemia is the class harm and leads the harm side: serum potassium elevations were more frequent on esaxerenone in EXCITE-HT and rose dose-proportionally in phase 2.

cards.headline: ESAX-HTN phase 3 RCT (Ito 2020): esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day non-inferior to eplerenone 50 mg/day for sitting and 24-hour blood-pressure reduction; 5 mg/day beat 2.5 mg/day; target sitting BP reached by 31.5%, 41.2% and 27.5%
cards.summary: ESAX-HTN phase 3 RCT (Ito 2020): esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day non-inferior to eplerenone 50 mg/day for sitting and 24-hour blood-pressure reduction; 5 mg/day beat 2.5 mg/day; target sitting BP reached by 31.5%, 41.2% and 27.5%
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind trial (ESAX-HTN), esaxerenone vs eplerenone in essential hypertension
cards.people: 1,001 Japanese adults with essential hypertension, randomised evenly after a 4-week washout to esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day, esaxerenone 5 mg/day or eplerenone 50 mg/day once daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day was non-inferior to eplerenone for reductions in sitting and 24-hour blood pressure; reductions with esaxerenone 5 mg/day were significantly greater than with 2.5 mg/day, and diurnal measurements showed persistent 24-hour antihypertensive effects in all groups. The proportions achieving target sitting blood pressure (<140/90 mm Hg) were 31.5% (esaxerenone 2.5 mg), 41.2% (esaxerenone 5 mg) and 27.5% (eplerenone). Adverse-event incidences were similar across groups and all events were mild or moderate. (The fetched abstract does not print the groups' exact mm Hg changes, and none are claimed here.)
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against an active mineralocorticoid-receptor blocker, not a placebo-controlled win; single-region (Japan) evidence; blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Ito S et al. Double-Blind Randomized Phase 3 Study Comparing Esaxerenone (CS-3150) and Eplerenone in Patients With Essential Hypertension (ESAX-HTN Study). Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2020. PMID: 31786983. Registry ID: NCT02890173. cards.headline: Phase 2 placebo-controlled dose-ranging RCT (Ito 2019): sitting BP changes of −20.6/−10.4 mm Hg on esaxerenone 5 mg vs −7.0/−3.8 mm Hg on placebo and −17.4/−8.5 mm Hg on eplerenone over 12 weeks, with a dose-response

cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study with an open-label eplerenone comparator arm
cards.people: 426 Japanese patients with essential hypertension, randomised to esaxerenone 1.25, 2.5 or 5 mg/day, placebo, or eplerenone 50–100 mg/day (open-label comparator arm) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Sitting systolic/diastolic changes were −7.0/−3.8 mm Hg on placebo, −10.7/−5.0 mm Hg (1.25 mg), −14.3/−7.6 mm Hg (2.5 mg) and −20.6/−10.4 mm Hg (5 mg) on esaxerenone, and −17.4/−8.5 mm Hg on eplerenone; the 2.5 and 5 mg doses differed significantly from placebo for sitting (both P<0.001) and 24-hour (both P<0.0001) blood pressure. Adverse-event incidence was similar across groups. Serum potassium initially increased in proportion to esaxerenone dose and was stable from week 2 to week 12.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's placebo-controlled anchor; the eplerenone arm was open-label. Serum potassium rising with dose is the harm to watch. Single-region (Japan) evidence.

cards.headline: EXCITE-HT RCT (Kario 2024): esaxerenone non-inferior to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy for morning home blood pressure (least-squares mean difference −2.2/−0.6 mm Hg); serum potassium elevations more frequent on esaxerenone
cards.summary: EXCITE-HT RCT (Kario 2024): esaxerenone non-inferior to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy for morning home blood pressure (least-squares mean difference −2.2/−0.6 mm Hg); serum potassium elevations more frequent on esaxerenone
cards.type: Multicentre randomised open-label equivalence/non-inferiority trial (EXCITE-HT), esaxerenone vs trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy
cards.people: 585 Japanese patients with uncontrolled essential hypertension on an angiotensin-receptor blocker or calcium-channel blocker (295 esaxerenone, 290 trichlormethiazide), randomised open-label to esaxerenone or trichlormethiazide as second-line treatment for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of esaxerenone to trichlormethiazide was demonstrated for morning home blood pressure: least-squares mean change differences at end of treatment were −2.2 mm Hg systolic (95% CI −3.6 to −0.8) and −0.6 mm Hg diastolic (95% CI −1.4 to 0.2), against non-inferiority margins of 3.9/2.1 mm Hg. Morning home, bedtime home and office blood pressure all fell significantly in both groups (all P<0.001). Serum potassium elevations occurred more frequently with esaxerenone and reductions more frequently with trichlormethiazide; uric acid elevations were more frequent with trichlormethiazide; no gout cases occurred; estimated GFR reductions were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design and an active-comparator non-inferiority question; the potassium signal (elevations more frequent on esaxerenone) is the class harm appearing again. Single-region (Japan) evidence.
cards.source: Kario K et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the hypertension slice of esaxerenone — placebo-controlled dose-response in phase 2, non-inferiority to eplerenone in phase 3, non-inferiority to trichlormethiazide second-line — with hyperkalaemia as the standing harm; the diabetic-albuminuria slice is homed at pack #3204 and is not re-carded here
cards.summary: Synthesis: the hypertension slice of esaxerenone — placebo-controlled dose-response in phase 2, non-inferiority to eplerenone in phase 3, non-inferiority to trichlormethiazide second-line — with hyperkalaemia as the standing harm; the diabetic-albuminuria slice is homed at pack #3204 and is not re-carded here
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (1,001 + 426 + 585 patients, all in Japan).
cards.result: Esaxerenone lowered blood pressure dose-dependently versus placebo in phase 2 (up to −20.6/−10.4 mm Hg sitting at 5 mg vs −7.0/−3.8 mm Hg on placebo), was non-inferior to eplerenone 50 mg/day in the phase 3 ESAX-HTN study (with 5 mg/day superior to 2.5 mg/day and the highest target-achievement rate, 41.2%), and was non-inferior to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy in EXCITE-HT. Serum potassium elevation is the consistent harm. A long-term single-arm phase 3 mono/combination study from this programme is programme support only and is not carded (no comparator). This shelf is a PARTIAL slice: esaxerenone's albuminuria question in diabetic kidney disease is already homed at pack #3204 (ESAX-DN programme) — see that pack for the kidney slice; no study from #3204 is carded here (one-home rule). No cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists for esaxerenone in hypertension, and blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; all evidence is Japanese, esaxerenone is not FDA/EMA-approved, and potassium monitoring is integral to the intervention as trialled.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Serum free light chain reference intervals: kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L and ratio 0.46–1.23 (Freelite verification) vs kappa 7.20–20.0 and ratio 0.5–2.11 on Optilite; Saudi intervals run higher; renal impairment breaks the manufacturer's ratio interval
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum free light chains — kappa, lambda and the kappa/lambda ratio — by assay platform, age and renal function, and how far do locally derived intervals sit from the manufacturer's original interval?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/immunology · Creatinine/blood · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin kappa-Chains/blood · Immunoglobulin lambda-Chains/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Paraproteinemias/blood · Reference Values · Serum/immunology · South Africa · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, plasma-protein and renal-handling sections — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four independent populations, carded PER ASSAY PLATFORM because the intervals are assay-specific and must never be printed platform-free. The locally derived intervals cluster near — but not on — the manufacturer's original interval: in 120 healthy South African adults (113 analysed after exclusions; Freelite) the 95% intervals were kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L, lambda 8.7–25.9 mg/L and ratio 0.46–1.23, most values falling within the manufacturer's limits; in 246 healthy Spanish blood donors (Optilite analyser) kappa was 7.20–20.0 mg/L and lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L, with a kappa/lambda diagnostic interval of 0.5–2.11 as published — and using the local versus manufacturer intervals reclassified 14.5% of MGUS and 16.3% of myeloma results in their collected data. In 180 healthy Saudi adults (Freelite reagents, IFCC harmonised protocol) the new intervals for free kappa and the ratio were shifted HIGHER than the manufacturer-adapted intervals (the record does not print the numeric limits, and this shelf claims none for that dataset). The renal-function limb is core content: renal impairment elevates the ratio and produces a high false-positive rate against the manufacturer's interval, and the 2023 Clinical Chemistry study (Freelite on a Roche Cobas c501) derived renally robust single intervals — ratio-based and principal-component-based — with significantly lower false-positive rates and equivalent sensitivity for monoclonal gammopathy. The immunoglobulin limb of the Saudi dataset is NOT carded here (one dataset, one home). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Renal-function limb (Azimi 2023): a single renally robust reference interval for serum free light chains is achievable — new ratio-based and PCA-based intervals (Freelite on Roche Cobas c501) had significantly lower false-positive rates across renal function than the manufacturer's interval, with equivalent sensitivity for monoclonal gammopathy
cards.summary: Renal-function limb (Azimi 2023): a single renally robust reference interval for serum free light chains is achievable — new ratio-based and PCA-based intervals (Freelite on Roche Cobas c501) had significantly lower false-positive rates across renal function than the manufacturer's interval, with equivalent sensitivity for monoclonal gammopathy
cards.type: Primary reference-interval study (serum free light chains across varying renal function; FREELITE assay on Roche Cobas c501)
cards.people: Retrospective data-mining cohorts assembled to reflect the spectrum of renal function seen in clinical practice (the record does not print a single reference-population N, and none is claimed here). Two new reference intervals — one based on the serum free light chain ratio and one on a novel principal-component-analysis metric — were developed for the FREELITE assay (Binding Site) on the Roche Cobas c501 instrument (Roche), against the manufacturer's interval, which was defined in a healthy cohort.
cards.result: Renal impairment elevates the free-light-chain ratio, leading to a high false-positive rate when the manufacturer's (healthy-cohort) interval is used. Compared with that interval, both new methods exhibited significantly lower false-positive rates and greater robustness to renal function while maintaining equivalent sensitivity for monoclonal gammopathy diagnosis; the point estimate for sensitivity was highest for the PCA-based approach, though not significantly different. The authors conclude that renally robust interpretation using a single reference interval is possible when the reference cohort reflects the variation in renal function observed in practice, and that further studies are needed to determine whether the PCA metric offers superior sensitivity. The fetched record does not print the numeric limits of the new intervals, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Platform-bound by construction (Freelite reagents on one named analyser) and method-bound in a second way: the PCA-based metric is a new derived quantity, not the familiar ratio, so its interval cannot be applied to a laboratory reporting the plain kappa/lambda ratio.
cards.source: Azimi V et al. A Single Reference Interval for Interpreting Serum Free Light Chains across Patients with Varying Renal Function. Clinical chemistry. 2023. PMID: 37147848. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Saudi population intervals (Borai 2024, 180 healthy adults, Freelite): locally derived intervals for free kappa and the kappa/lambda ratio were shifted HIGHER than the manufacturer-adapted intervals; no sex partition was required except for IgM (the immunoglobulin limb is not carded on this shelf)
cards.summary: Saudi population intervals (Borai 2024, 180 healthy adults, Freelite): locally derived intervals for free kappa and the kappa/lambda ratio were shifted HIGHER than the manufacturer-adapted intervals; no sex partition was required except for IgM (the immunoglobulin limb is not carded on this shelf)
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (serum free light chains, Freelite, healthy Saudi adults, IFCC harmonised protocol)
cards.people: 180 healthy Saudi adults recruited under the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine's global protocol for harmonised reference-interval studies; all sera were assayed with Freelite reagents (Binding Site). Variation attributable to sex, age, BMI and region was calculated as a standard-deviation ratio (SDR); the ratio interval was derived parametrically and validated in patients with hypo- and hypergammaglobulinaemia.
cards.result: The new reference intervals for free kappa and for the free-light-chain ratio were shifted to a higher side from the manufacturer-adapted intervals. Based on the SDR cut-off (>0.4), between-sex partition intervals were not required for any analyte except IgM. Validation samples from patients with hypo- or hypergammaglobulinaemia and without multiple myeloma all fell within the new interval. BMI, smoking and exercise were not relevant sources of variation for any analyte. The authors conclude the locally derived intervals are more reliable for Saudi patients than the manufacturer's or other countries' intervals. The fetched record does not print the numeric limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: One dataset, one home: this study's immunoglobulin (IgG/IgA/IgM) intervals belong to a different question and are deliberately not carded here. The direction of the shift (higher than the manufacturer) is the carded finding; any laboratory needing the actual Saudi limits must take them from the full text, not from this shelf.

primary reference-interval dataset (serum free light chains, freelite, healthy saudi adults, ifcc harmonised protocol) 180 healthy saudi adults recruited under the international federation of clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine's global protocol for harmonised reference-interval studies; all sera were assayed with freelite reagents (binding site). variation attributable to sex, age, bmi and region was calculated as a standard-deviation ratio (sdr); the ratio interval was derived parametrically and validated in patients with hypo- and hypergammaglobulinaemia. the new reference intervals for free kappa and for the free-light-chain ratio were shifted to a higher side from the manufacturer-adapted intervals. based on the sdr cut-off (>0.4), between-sex partition intervals were not required for any analyte except igm. validation samples from patients with hypo- or hypergammaglobulinaemia and without multiple myeloma all fell within the new interval. bmi, smoking and exercise were not relevant sources of variation for any analyte. the authors conclude the locally derived intervals are more reliable for saudi patients than the manufacturer's or other countries' intervals. the fetched record does not print the numeric limits, and this card claims none. one dataset, one home: this study's immunoglobulin (igg/iga/igm) intervals belong to a different question and are deliberately not carded here. the direction of the shift (higher than the manufacturer) is the carded finding; any laboratory needing the actual saudi limits must take them from the full text, not from this shelf. borai a et al. establishment of reference intervals for free light chains and immunoglobulins in saudi population. clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2024. pmid: 37787915. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · humans · hypergammaglobulinemia · saudi arabia · immunoglobulin light chains · paraproteinemias · reference values · middle eastern people

cards.headline: South African verification (Zemlin 2013, 120 healthy adults, 113 analysed): 95% reference intervals — kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L, lambda 8.7–25.9 mg/L, ratio 0.46–1.23 — mostly within the manufacturer's recommended limits
cards.summary: South African verification (Zemlin 2013, 120 healthy adults, 113 analysed): 95% reference intervals — kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L, lambda 8.7–25.9 mg/L, ratio 0.46–1.23 — mostly within the manufacturer's recommended limits
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (verification of serum free-light-chain intervals in healthy South African adults)
cards.people: 120 healthy South African adults in whom reference intervals for kappa and lambda free light chains were established; creatinine was measured to exclude renal dysfunction and serum protein electrophoresis performed, and after exclusion of subjects with abnormal electrophoreses 113 subjects were available for analysis.
cards.result: The 95% reference interval was 6.3–20.6 mg/L for kappa free light chains, 8.7–25.9 mg/L for lambda free light chains and 0.46–1.23 for the free-light-chain ratio. All creatinine values were within normal limits. Most values fell within the manufacturer's recommended limits, and the authors concluded those limits could be used for their population.
cards.watchOut: A verification study in 113 analysed subjects with normal creatinine: it verifies the manufacturer's interval in people with normal renal function and says nothing about the renal-impairment range, where the ratio interval is known to fail (see the Azimi card).
cards.source: Zemlin AE et al. Verification of serum reference intervals for free light chains in a local South African population. Journal of clinical pathology. 2013. PMID: 23801498. cards.headline: Spanish donor intervals on the Optilite analyser (Rocamonde 2023, 246 healthy blood donors): kappa 7.20–20.0 mg/L, lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L, kappa/lambda diagnostic interval 0.5–2.11 as published — local vs manufacturer intervals reclassified 14.5% of MGUS and 16.3% of myeloma results
cards.summary: Spanish donor intervals on the Optilite analyser (Rocamonde 2023, 246 healthy blood donors): kappa 7.20–20.0 mg/L, lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L, kappa/lambda diagnostic interval 0.5–2.11 as published — local vs manufacturer intervals reclassified 14.5% of MGUS and 16.3% of myeloma results
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (serum free light chains on the Optilite analyser, healthy Spanish blood donors, CLSI EP28-A3C)
cards.people: 246 healthy blood donors in Spain whose fresh sera were analysed to establish local reference intervals for kappa and lambda free light chains on the Optilite analyser, following the CLSI EP28-A3C protocol; the diagnostic-interval comparison used 1,025 collected results including patients with MGUS and multiple myeloma.
cards.result: The 95% reference interval for free kappa was 7.20–20.0 mg/L and for free lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L; the diagnostic interval for the kappa/lambda ratio was 0.5–2.11 (printed with mg/L units in the record, although a ratio is dimensionless — reproduced here as published). Comparing the manufacturer's diagnostic intervals with the locally established ones across the 1,025 collected results, discordant results were reported in 14.5% of patients with MGUS and 16.3% of patients with multiple myeloma. The authors conclude the findings underline the importance of establishing reference intervals by instrument platform and for the target population.
cards.watchOut: Platform is the variable: these are Optilite-analyser intervals in blood donors, and the reclassification figures (14.5% and 16.3% discordance) are the practical proof that a Freelite interval and an Optilite interval are not interchangeable paperwork — they change who is called abnormal.
cards.source: Rocamonde L et al. Serum Free Light Chain Reference Intervals in a Local Population in Spain using the Optilite Analyser. Clinical laboratory. 2023. PMID: 36649521. cards.headline: Synthesis: free-light-chain intervals are real but platform- and population-bound — local intervals sit near the manufacturer's (kappa ≈6.3–7.2 to 20.0–20.6 mg/L; ratio upper limits 1.23 to 2.11 by platform), run higher in the Saudi population, and widen in effect as renal function falls
cards.summary: Synthesis: free-light-chain intervals are real but platform- and population-bound — local intervals sit near the manufacturer's (kappa ≈6.3–7.2 to 20.0–20.6 mg/L; ratio upper limits 1.23 to 2.11 by platform), run higher in the Saudi population, and widen in effect as renal function falls
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep (plasma proteins and renal handling; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature). Two datasets print full numeric intervals that broadly corroborate each other while differing by platform: South African verification (Freelite; kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L, lambda 8.7–25.9 mg/L, ratio 0.46–1.23; Zemlin 2013) and Spanish donors (Optilite; kappa 7.20–20.0 mg/L, lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L, ratio interval 0.5–2.11 as published; Rocamonde 2023). The Saudi dataset (Freelite, n=180) found its local kappa and ratio intervals shifted higher than the manufacturer's (Borai 2024), and the renal-function study shows why any single healthy-cohort interval misleads in kidney disease — renal impairment raises the ratio and inflates false positives, which a renally robust single interval can correct without losing sensitivity (Azimi 2023). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the intervals and their platform, population and renal-function dependencies are consistently demonstrated across four independent populations.
cards.watchOut: Never print a free-light-chain interval without its assay platform, and never apply a healthy-cohort ratio interval to a patient with renal impairment without the renal caveat on the Azimi card.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Flow-cytometry subset reference intervals: CD3+ ~71–77%, CD4+ ~41–45%, CD8+ ~30%, CD19+ ~13–14% across four populations — panel- and population-bound, distinct from FBC pack #7321
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for peripheral-blood lymphocyte and leukocyte subsets measured by flow cytometry — CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19/CD20 B cells, CD16/CD56 natural-killer cells and regulatory T cells, as percentages and absolute counts — by age, sex and population, and how much do panel, platform and population move them? (The flow-cytometric slice presupposed by, and distinct from, the full-blood-count reference intervals at pack #7321.)

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / white-cell chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary immunophenotyping reference literature, and says so. PARTIAL-adjacent distinction, stated on the face: pack #7321 cards full-blood-count reference intervals (haemoglobin, total white-cell count, the automated differential and platelets) and reports no flow-cytometric subset percentages; this shelf is the immunophenotyping slice #7321 presupposes, and NONE of #7321's datasets is re-carded here. Four independent flow-cytometry populations: harmonised Human Immunophenotyping Consortium panels across six European centres (more than 300 healthy volunteers, absolute and relative frequencies of T, regulatory-T, B, NK and myeloid subpopulations); a population-based 10-colour study of 608 German adults aged 40–79 (men higher for monocytes and NK cells, women higher for B, helper-T and regulatory-T cells; cytotoxic-T counts falling about 8% per 5 years of age); 221 Iranian adults aged 20–40 with full numeric subset means (CD3+ 70.90%, CD4+ 41.04%, CD8+ 31.11%, CD19+ 12.77%, CD56+ 15.53%, CD4/CD8 ratio 1.39); and 50 Omani adults with median-based intervals (CD3+ 76.5%, CD4+ 45%, CD8+ 29.5%, CD19+ 14%, NK 7%) — the Omani N (50 total) is printed on its card. Intervals are panel- and platform-specific (harmonised HIPC vs 10-colour vs 4-colour) and percentages and absolute counts are carded as published, never converted silently. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the direction of the sex and age effects and the broad subset proportions agree, but every interval is bound to its panel, platform and population, and one anchor's record reports its programme and scope rather than numeric limits.

cards.headline: Harmonised HIPC panels, six European centres (Oras 2020): absolute and relative frequencies of T, regulatory-T, B, NK and myeloid subpopulations in more than 300 healthy volunteers, analysed in a harmonised manner across platforms
cards.summary: Harmonised HIPC panels, six European centres (Oras 2020): absolute and relative frequencies of T, regulatory-T, B, NK and myeloid subpopulations in more than 300 healthy volunteers, analysed in a harmonised manner across platforms
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (harmonised HIPC flow-cytometry reference intervals, six European centres)
cards.people: More than 300 healthy volunteers across six European FOCIS Centers of Excellence; whole blood analysed with four adapted Human Immunophenotyping Consortium (HIPC) core panels (T / regulatory-T / B / natural-killer and myeloid cells) in a clinical-diagnostic setting, harmonised across different platforms.
cards.result: The consortium's product is the harmonised reference dataset itself: absolute and relative frequencies of the main leukocyte subpopulations in peripheral blood, generated with common panels across six centres and multiple platforms. The fetched record states the programme's design, panels and scope; it does not print the numeric interval tables, and this card claims none — the numeric centre of this shelf is the Iranian and Omani datasets below.
cards.watchOut: Harmonisation is this dataset's point and its limit: intervals generated on HIPC panels across platforms are the multi-centre reference, but the fetched record prints no numeric limits — do not attach another dataset's numbers to this card.

cards.headline: Population-based 10-colour flow cytometry, Germany (Melzer 2015): sex- and age-band-specific intervals in 608 adults aged 40–79 — men higher for monocytes and NK cells, women higher for B, helper-T and regulatory-T cells; cytotoxic-T counts fell about 8% per 5 years of age
cards.summary: Population-based 10-colour flow cytometry, Germany (Melzer 2015): sex- and age-band-specific intervals in 608 adults aged 40–79 — men higher for monocytes and NK cells, women higher for B, helper-T and regulatory-T cells; cytotoxic-T counts fell about 8% per 5 years of age
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (10-colour flow-cytometry reference intervals, population-based, Germany)
cards.people: 608 healthy German adults from the Leipzig region, aged 40 to 79 years; in-depth immunophenotyping by 10-colour flow cytometry covering granulocyte, monocyte and lymphocyte subsets; reference intervals derived by sex and by age band (40–59 and 60–79 years).
cards.result: Men had significantly higher cell counts for monocytes (P < 0.001) and NK cells (P < 0.001), whereas women had higher counts for B cells (P < 0.001), helper-T cells (P < 0.001) and regulatory T cells (P = 0.008). With increasing age, cytotoxic-T cell counts decreased (about 8% within 5 years) and NK cell counts increased (under 4% within 5 years). The authors note these cross-sectional age patterns need longitudinal confirmation. The fetched record reports these comparisons and the interval structure; the full numeric tables are in the report itself.
cards.watchOut: An older cohort by design (40–79 years): its intervals are not young-adult intervals, and its age gradients are cross-sectional, not longitudinal — the authors say so themselves.
cards.source: Melzer S et al. Reference intervals for leukocyte subsets in adults: Results from a population-based study using 10-color flow cytometry. Cytometry. Part B, Clinical cytometry. 2015. PMID: 25704947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Iranian adults aged 20–40 (Kamallou 2014): CD3+ 70.90 ± 7.54% (1,800.87 cells/µL), CD4+ 41.04%, CD8+ 31.11%, CD19+ 12.77%, CD56+ 15.53%, CD4/CD8 ratio 1.39 ± 0.48 in 221 healthy HIV-negative adults
cards.summary: Iranian adults aged 20–40 (Kamallou 2014): CD3+ 70.90 ± 7.54% (1,800.87 cells/µL), CD4+ 41.04%, CD8+ 31.11%, CD19+ 12.77%, CD56+ 15.53%, CD4/CD8 ratio 1.39 ± 0.48 in 221 healthy HIV-negative adults
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (flow-cytometry lymphocyte subset reference values, Iran)
cards.people: 221 healthy HIV-negative Iranian adults (112 women, 109 men), aged 20 to 40 years; lymphocyte subsets expressing CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 and CD56 measured by flow cytometry, reported as percentages and absolute counts.
cards.result: Total mean percentage and absolute count were: CD3+ 70.90 ± 7.54% (1,800.87 ± 471.09 cells/µL); CD4+ 41.04 ± 7.86% (1,039.99 ± 338.02 cells/µL); CD8+ 31.11 ± 6.60% (783.95 ± 234.87 cells/µL); CD19+ 12.77 ± 4.56% (328.37 ± 153.17 cells/µL); CD56+ 15.53 ± 6.34% (388.62 ± 176.17 cells/µL). The CD4+/CD8+ ratio was 1.39 ± 0.48. The average percentages of CD3+ (P = 0.017) and CD4+ (P = 0.003) cells were higher in women, while CD19+ percentage tended to be higher in men (P = 0.02); CD8+ and CD56+ subsets did not differ by sex.
cards.watchOut: A young-adult (20–40) single-population dataset reporting means ± SD rather than percentile intervals: its values anchor the young-adult end of this shelf and differ in form from the German cohort's age-banded intervals — the forms are not interchangeable.

cards.people: 50 healthy Omani adults (men and women, aged 18 to 57 years), age- and sex-balanced; total, age- and sex-specific reference ranges established by four-colour flow cytometry with an extensive monoclonal-antibody panel; values expressed as medians with 95% confidence intervals.
cards.result: Median subset values (95% CI) were: T cells CD3+ 76.5% (57 to 89), CD4+ 45% (31 to 58), CD8+ 29.5% (19 to 43); B cells CD19+ 14% (6 to 23) and CD20+ 14% (6 to 23); NK cells CD16+ 9% (3 to 22), CD56+ 13% (5 to 24) and CD3−/(CD16+/CD56+) 7% (3 to 20). The authors found these ranges similar to those reported in the rest of the world.
cards.watchOut: N = 50 total — the smallest dataset on this shelf, printed here on the face: its wide confidence intervals (e.g. CD3+ 57 to 89%) reflect that size, and its medians should be read beside the larger Iranian (n=221) and German (n=608) datasets, not alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: four flow-cytometry populations agree on the broad subset architecture (CD3+ ~71–77%, CD4+ ~41–45%, CD8+ ~30%, CD19+ ~13–14%) and on sex effects, but every interval is panel-, platform- and population-bound — and none of this duplicates the full-blood-count shelf #7321
cards.summary: Synthesis: four flow-cytometry populations agree on the broad subset architecture (CD3+ ~71–77%, CD4+ ~41–45%, CD8+ ~30%, CD19+ ~13–14%) and on sex effects, but every interval is panel-, platform- and population-bound — and none of this duplicates the full-blood-count shelf #7321
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (immunity / white-cell chapters; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary immunophenotyping reference literature). The numeric datasets converge on the broad proportions — CD3+ 70.90% (Iran, mean) and 76.5% (Oman, median); CD4+ 41.04% and 45%; CD8+ 31.11% and 29.5%; CD19+ 12.77% and 14% — while the German 10-colour cohort adds the sex and age structure (men higher monocytes and NK cells; women higher B, helper-T and regulatory-T cells; cytotoxic-T counts falling ~8% per 5 years) and the six-centre HIPC programme supplies the harmonised multi-platform reference framework. The distinction from pack #7321 stands as printed in the balance: #7321 is the full blood count (haemoglobin, total white count, differential, platelets); this shelf is flow-cytometric subset immunophenotyping, and no #7321 dataset is carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: convergence on proportions and effects, with intervals that remain specific to panel (HIPC vs 10-colour vs 4-colour), platform and population, and one anchor reporting programme scope rather than numeric limits in its record.
cards.watchOut: Percentages and absolute counts are carded as published and never converted silently; if pack #7321 is ever widened from the full blood count to all haematology reference intervals, this shelf collapses into it (one-home rule).
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Bococizumab (SPIRE): LDL −56% relative, but antidrug antibodies eroded the effect and the outcomes trials split (HR 0.99 vs 0.79; combined 0.88, NS) — programme discontinued
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia at high cardiovascular risk, does the humanised PCSK9 antibody bococizumab, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular events — and why did antidrug antibodies end the programme (the SPIRE programme)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, LDL · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypercholesterolemia · Injections, Subcutaneous · Lipids · Male · Middle Aged · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Proprotein Convertase 9 · Risk Factors · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Cohort Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Proprotein Convertases · Serine Endopeptidases
shelves.balance: Discontinued agent — the flag leads: bococizumab was NEVER marketed. It is the only humanised (not fully human) PCSK9 antibody in its class, and the immunogenicity that attenuated its LDL effect is the central fact of the programme, printed in its own NEJM companion paper. The outcomes headline is DISCORDANT BY TRIAL and must not be presented as an outcomes win: in SPIRE-1 and SPIRE-2 (27,438 randomised, 93% on statins), LDL change at week 14 was −56.0% relative on bococizumab vs +2.9% on placebo, but the primary composite hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.22; P = 0.94) in the lower-risk, shorter trial and 0.79 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.97; P = 0.02) in the higher-risk, longer trial, combining to HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.02; P = 0.08) — not significant. Both trials were STOPPED EARLY when the sponsor discontinued development, in part over high antidrug-antibody rates, so follow-up was truncated (median 10 months). In the six pooled lipid trials (4,300 randomised), LDL fell 54.2% relative at week 12 vs a 1.0% rise on placebo, but high-titre antidrug antibodies in a substantial proportion markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of that lowering, and wide variability persisted even without antibodies. Injection-site reactions ran 10.4% vs 1.3% in the outcomes trials.

cards.headline: SPIRE-1 and SPIRE-2 (Ridker 2017): bococizumab cut LDL by −56.0% relative at week 14, but cardiovascular results were discordant — HR 0.99 (P = 0.94) in the lower-risk trial vs HR 0.79 (P = 0.02) in the higher-risk trial; combined HR 0.88 (P = 0.08); both trials stopped early (27,438 randomised)
cards.summary: SPIRE-1 and SPIRE-2 (Ridker 2017): bococizumab cut LDL by −56.0% relative at week 14, but cardiovascular results were discordant — HR 0.99 (P = 0.94) in the lower-risk trial vs HR 0.79 (P = 0.02) in the higher-risk trial; combined HR 0.88 (P = 0.08); both trials stopped early (27,438 randomised)
cards.type: Two parallel phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled cardiovascular-outcomes randomised trials (SPIRE-1 and SPIRE-2), bococizumab vs placebo — stopped early
cards.people: 27,438 patients at high cardiovascular risk across two parallel multinational trials with different LDL entry criteria (SPIRE-1: baseline LDL at least 70 mg/dL [1.8 mmol/L]; SPIRE-2: at least 100 mg/dL [2.6 mmol/L]), randomised to bococizumab 150 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks or placebo; 93% were on statin therapy at baseline. Median follow-up was 10 months overall (7 months in the lower-risk trial, 12 months in the higher-risk trial) because both trials were stopped early.
cards.result: At 14 weeks, mean LDL change was −56.0% on bococizumab vs +2.9% on placebo (between-group difference −59.0 percentage points; median reduction 64.2%; P < 0.001) — relative changes, as published. The primary endpoint (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, hospitalisation for unstable angina requiring urgent revascularisation, or cardiovascular death) gave: lower-risk trial — 173 events in each group, HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.22; P = 0.94); higher-risk trial — 179 vs 224 events, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.97; P = 0.02); combined — HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.02; P = 0.08), hazard ratios being relative measures. Injection-site reactions were more common on bococizumab (10.4% vs 1.3%; P < 0.001). The trials were stopped early after the sponsor elected to discontinue bococizumab development, owing in part to high rates of antidrug antibodies seen elsewhere in the programme.
cards.watchOut: Truncated follow-up (median 10 months) after an early stop for programme discontinuation: the combined estimate is not significant, the two trials disagree, and the higher-risk trial's positive result rests on 12 months of median follow-up — SPIRE is not an outcomes win and must not be summarised as one.
cards.source: Ridker PM et al. Cardiovascular Efficacy and Safety of Bococizumab in High-Risk Patients. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28304242. Registry ID: NCT01975376; NCT01975389. cards.headline: Antidrug-antibody analysis of six pooled lipid trials (Ridker 2017): LDL fell 54.2% relative at week 12 vs +1.0% on placebo in 4,300 patients — but high-titre antidrug antibodies in a substantial proportion markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of the lowering
cards.summary: Antidrug-antibody analysis of six pooled lipid trials (Ridker 2017): LDL fell 54.2% relative at week 12 vs +1.0% on placebo in 4,300 patients — but high-titre antidrug antibodies in a substantial proportion markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of the lowering
cards.type: Pooled analysis of six parallel randomised lipid-lowering trials (SPIRE lipid programme) — antidrug-antibody and durability analysis
cards.people: 4,300 patients with hyperlipidaemia across six parallel multinational lipid-lowering trials, randomised to bococizumab 150 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 2 weeks and followed for up to 12 months; 96% were on statin therapy at enrolment. Lipid changes were stratified by the presence or absence of antidrug antibodies detected during treatment.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, LDL fell by 54.2% on bococizumab vs a 1.0% rise on placebo (absolute between-group difference −55.2 percentage points; relative changes as published), with significant between-group differences also in total cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) (all P < 0.001). However, high-titre antidrug antibodies developed in a substantial proportion of bococizumab patients and markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of the LDL reduction; and even among patients with no antidrug antibodies, the relative LDL reduction varied widely at both 12 and 52 weeks. Major cardiovascular events occurred in 57 (2.5%) on bococizumab vs 55 (2.7%) on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.39; P = 0.83). The most common adverse event was injection-site reaction (12.7 per 100 person-years).
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's central fact, not a side note: a humanised antibody provoked antidrug antibodies that eroded its own effect over time — the reason the sponsor stopped the entire programme, including the outcomes trials on the card above.
cards.source: Ridker PM et al. Lipid-Reduction Variability and Antidrug-Antibody Formation with Bococizumab. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28304227. cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging (Ballantyne 2015): bococizumab lowered LDL by 53.4 mg/dL (150 mg every 2 weeks) and 44.9 mg/dL (300 mg every 4 weeks) vs placebo at week 12 in 354 statin-treated patients — despite protocol dose reductions in about a third of participants
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging (Ballantyne 2015): bococizumab lowered LDL by 53.4 mg/dL (150 mg every 2 weeks) and 44.9 mg/dL (300 mg every 4 weeks) vs placebo at week 12 in 354 statin-treated patients — despite protocol dose reductions in about a third of participants
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging randomised trial, bococizumab vs placebo on statins
cards.people: 354 subjects with LDL cholesterol at least 80 mg/dL on stable statin therapy, randomised to subcutaneous placebo or bococizumab 50, 100 or 150 mg every 14 days, or placebo or bococizumab 200 or 300 mg every 28 days, for 24 weeks (multicentre, double-blind); 351 received treatment (100 placebo, 251 bococizumab). Doses were reduced if LDL persistently fell to 25 mg/dL or below.
cards.result: The most efficacious doses were 150 mg every 2 weeks and 300 mg every 4 weeks: versus placebo, they reduced LDL at week 12 by 53.4 mg/dL and 44.9 mg/dL respectively (absolute changes, as published) — despite dose reductions in 32.5% and 34.2% of subjects by week 10 or 8. Model-based simulation assuming no dose reductions predicted larger falls (72.2 and 55.4 mg/dL). Adverse events were similar across placebo and bococizumab groups, and few subjects (7; 2%) discontinued for treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week LDL (surrogate) endpoint from the programme's optimistic phase — before the antidrug-antibody problem was characterised; its clean short-term tolerability did not predict the immunogenicity that ended the programme.
cards.source: Ballantyne CM et al. Results of bococizumab, a monoclonal antibody against proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9, from a randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging study in statin-treated subjects with hypercholesterolemia. The American journal of cardiology. 2015. PMID: 25784512. Registry ID: NCT01592240. cards.result: The SPIRE programme is a complete rise-and-fall record. The phase 2 dose-ranging trial established potent LDL lowering on statins (Ballantyne 2015: −53.4 mg/dL at the top every-2-week dose). The six pooled lipid trials then showed why the effect could not be trusted to last: antidrug antibodies in a substantial proportion of patients markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of LDL lowering, with wide variability even in antibody-negative patients (Ridker 2017, PMID 28304227). The outcomes trials, stopped early when the sponsor discontinued development, split by risk stratum — null in the lower-risk trial (HR 0.99), positive in the higher-risk trial (HR 0.79), combined HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.02; P = 0.08) on a median 10 months of follow-up (Ridker 2017, PMID 28304242). Bococizumab, the class's only humanised antibody, was never marketed; the approved fully human PCSK9 antibodies are homed on their own shelves and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Percent LDL changes on this shelf are relative measures and are labelled as such; the phase 2 card's mg/dL figures are the absolute changes its report publishes. See the individual cards for each report's limits.

shelves.title: Tafolecimab (CREDIT programme, China only): LDL down 57–65% relative versus placebo in three phase 3 trials — a surrogate benefit with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial
shelves.question: In Chinese adults with hypercholesterolaemia (non-familial, heterozygous familial, or at high/very high cardiovascular risk), does the fully human PCSK9 antibody tafolecimab, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol (the CREDIT-1, CREDIT-2 and CREDIT-4 programme)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Apolipoproteins · Cholesterol, LDL · East Asian People · Hypercholesterolemia · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/drug therapy · Lipoprotein(a) · PCSK9 Inhibitors/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for LDL lowering, on a single-region (China) surrogate base. Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of the fully human PCSK9 antibody tafolecimab in Chinese patients all showed large LDL-cholesterol reductions: CREDIT-1 (non-familial hypercholesterolaemia, 618 randomised, 48 weeks) treatment differences versus placebo of −65.0% relative on 450 mg every 4 weeks and −57.3% relative on 600 mg every 6 weeks; CREDIT-2 (heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 149 randomised, 12-week double-blind period) −57.4% and −61.9% relative; CREDIT-4 (high/very high cardiovascular risk, 303 dosed) a least-squares mean LDL change of −68.9% versus −5.8% on placebo (difference −63.0% relative). All percent changes are relative measures. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: every trial was conducted in China, where tafolecimab is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. LDL cholesterol is a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of tafolecimab exists, and no outcomes claim is made on this shelf. Its single-region class sibling recaticimab is homed separately (pack #6821) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: CREDIT-1 (Huo 2023): tafolecimab lowered LDL by −65.0% relative (450 mg every 4 weeks) and −57.3% relative (600 mg every 6 weeks) versus placebo at 48 weeks in non-familial hypercholesterolaemia
cards.summary: CREDIT-1 (Huo 2023): tafolecimab lowered LDL by −65.0% relative (450 mg every 4 weeks) and −57.3% relative (600 mg every 6 weeks) versus placebo at 48 weeks in non-familial hypercholesterolaemia
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CREDIT-1), tafolecimab 450 mg Q4W or 600 mg Q6W vs placebo, 48 weeks
cards.people: 618 Chinese patients with non-familial hypercholesterolaemia — at high or very high cardiovascular risk with screening LDL-C ≥1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL), or with screening LDL-C ≥3.4 mmol/L (≈131 mg/dL) — on stable lipid-lowering therapy, randomised 2:2:1:1 to subcutaneous tafolecimab 450 mg every 4 weeks, tafolecimab 600 mg every 6 weeks, or matching placebo regimens for a 48-week double-blind period; 614 received at least one dose (411 tafolecimab, 203 placebo). Sponsored by Innovent Biologics, Inc.
cards.result: At week 48 the treatment differences versus placebo in LDL-C percent change (on-treatment estimand) were −65.0% relative (97.5% CI −70.2 to −59.9) for 450 mg every 4 weeks and −57.3% relative (97.5% CI −64.0 to −50.7) for 600 mg every 6 weeks, both P < 0.0001. Significantly more tafolecimab patients achieved ≥50% LDL-C reductions and LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) and <1.4 mmol/L (≈54 mg/dL) than placebo patients at both regimens (all P < 0.0001). Non-HDL-C, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) also fell significantly. The commonest treatment-emergent adverse events on tafolecimab were upper respiratory infection, urinary tract infection and hyperuricemia.
cards.watchOut: The longest of the three CREDIT trials, but still an LDL (surrogate) trial in a single country: it shows cholesterol lowering in Chinese patients, not fewer heart attacks or strokes, and says nothing about performance in other populations.
cards.source: Huo Y et al. Tafolecimab in Chinese patients with non-familial hypercholesterolemia (CREDIT-1): a 48-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. The Lancet regional health. Western Pacific. 2023. PMID: 37808342. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: CREDIT-2 (Chai 2023): in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, LDL treatment differences of −57.4% relative (150 mg every 2 weeks) and −61.9% relative (450 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo at 12 weeks
cards.summary: CREDIT-2 (Chai 2023): in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, LDL treatment differences of −57.4% relative (150 mg every 2 weeks) and −61.9% relative (450 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo at 12 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CREDIT-2) in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 12-week double-blind period
cards.people: 149 Chinese patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia diagnosed by Simon Broome criteria, on stable lipid-lowering therapy for at least 4 weeks, randomised 2:2:1:1 to subcutaneous tafolecimab 150 mg every 2 weeks, tafolecimab 450 mg every 4 weeks, or matching placebo, for a 12-week double-blind period followed by 12 weeks of open-label tafolecimab; 148 received at least one dose.
cards.result: At week 12 the treatment differences versus placebo in LDL-C percent change (on-treatment estimand) were −57.4% relative (97.5% CI −69.2 to −45.5) for 150 mg every 2 weeks and −61.9% relative (97.5% CI −73.4 to −50.4) for 450 mg every 4 weeks, both P < 0.0001. Significantly more tafolecimab patients achieved ≥50% LDL-C reductions or LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) at week 12 (all P < 0.0001), and non-HDL-C, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) fell significantly; effects were maintained to week 24 on open-label treatment. Commonest adverse events on tafolecimab in the double-blind period were upper respiratory tract infection, increased blood creatine phosphokinase, increased alanine and aspartate aminotransferase, and hypertension.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week primary endpoint in 149 patients: the double-blind comparison is short, and the week-24 persistence figures come from the open-label phase in which everyone received tafolecimab.
cards.source: Chai M et al. cards.headline: CREDIT-4 (Qi 2023): in high/very high cardiovascular risk patients, LDL fell −68.9% on tafolecimab versus −5.8% on placebo at 12 weeks (difference −63.0% relative)
cards.summary: CREDIT-4 (Qi 2023): in high/very high cardiovascular risk patients, LDL fell −68.9% on tafolecimab versus −5.8% on placebo at 12 weeks (difference −63.0% relative)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CREDIT-4) at high/very high cardiovascular risk, 12 weeks
cards.people: 303 Chinese patients — with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia by Simon Broome criteria, or non-familial hypercholesterolaemia at high or very high cardiovascular risk — with screening LDL-C ≥1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL), randomised 2:1 to tafolecimab 450 mg every 4 weeks (205 dosed) or placebo (98 dosed) for a 12-week double-blind period.
cards.result: The least-squares mean percent change in LDL-C at week 12 was −68.9% (SE 1.4%) on tafolecimab versus −5.8% (SE 1.8%) on placebo — a difference of −63.0% relative (95% CI −66.5 to −59.6; P < 0.0001). More tafolecimab patients achieved ≥50% LDL-C reductions and LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) and <1.4 mmol/L (≈54 mg/dL) at week 12 (all P < 0.0001), and non-HDL-C, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) were markedly reduced. Urinary tract infection occurred in 5.9% on tafolecimab versus 4.1% on placebo, and hyperuricemia in 3.4% versus 4.1%.
cards.watchOut: The population is defined by cardiovascular risk, but the trial measures only 12 weeks of cholesterol change: high risk of events is the entry criterion, not an outcome this trial tested.
cards.source: Qi L et al. Tafolecimab in Chinese Patients With Hypercholesterolemia (CREDIT-4): A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Trial. JACC. Asia. 2023. PMID: 37614541. Registry ID: NCT04709536. MeSH: none in the record

cards.result: Three concordant Chinese phase 3 trials (618, 149 and 303 patients) show tafolecimab lowers LDL cholesterol by roughly 57–65% relative versus placebo across non-familial hypercholesterolaemia, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia and high/very-high-risk patients, with a tolerability profile dominated by infections and hyperuricemia in these reports. The limits are structural and are printed on the face: the evidence is single-region (China; approved there, not FDA/EMA-approved), the primary endpoints are 12 weeks in CREDIT-2 and CREDIT-4 and 48 weeks in CREDIT-1, and LDL cholesterol is a surrogate — no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of tafolecimab exists, so this shelf supports an LDL-lowering claim only.

shelves.title: ANA in healthy people: 'positive' is threshold-made — 26.0% at 1:40 and 9.5% at 1:160 in Japan, 54.3% any fluorescence in Mexico, 13.8% overall in US NHANES
shelves.question: In healthy general populations, what proportion of people carry antinuclear antibodies (ANA) by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells — prevalence by titre threshold (1:40, 1:80, 1:160), staining pattern, age and sex — which disease-specific autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-centromere, anti-U1RNP and others) are found in people with no rheumatic disease, and how much do assay and threshold move the 'positive' fraction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Antinuclear/blood · Autoimmune Diseases/blood,epidemiology · Centromere/immunology · Female · Humans · Japan/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Examination · Ribonucleoprotein, U1 Small Nuclear/immunology · Ribonucleoproteins/immunology · Rural Health · Seroepidemiologic Studies · Surveys and Questionnaires · SS-A Antigen · Adolescent · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/blood,ethnology · Autoimmune Diseases/blood,ethnology · Blood Donors · Child · Family · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic/blood,ethnology · Mexico · Personnel, Hospital · Prevalence · Young Adult · Antibodies, Antinuclear/blood,immunology · Black People · Cross-Sectional Studies · Nutrition Surveys · Sex Factors · United States/epidemiology · White People · Black or African American
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / autoimmunity sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so. Threshold-dependence is the answer: three independent general-population datasets (2,181 Japanese town residents; 304 healthy Mexican individuals; 4,754 US NHANES participants aged 12 years and over) give 'positive' fractions of 26.0% at a 1:40 threshold and 9.5% at 1:160 (Japan), 54.3% for any fluorescence across titres 1:40–1:320 (Mexico), and 13.8% overall (NHANES) — different kinds of 'positive' that are never merged into one number on this shelf. Every prevalence prints with its titre threshold and assay. Disease-specific autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-centromere, anti-U1RNP) are found in people with no rheumatic disease, and in the Japanese cohort 57% of examined disease-specific-positive individuals were clinically healthy. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the base is three large independent population datasets concordant on the core claim (ANA is common in healthy people and the fraction is set by the threshold), not a single small series.

cards.headline: Japanese small-town cohort (Hayashi 2008): IF-ANA positivity 26.0% at 1:40 and 9.5% at 1:160 in 2,181 residents — and 57% of examined disease-specific-positive individuals were clinically healthy
cards.summary: Japanese small-town cohort (Hayashi 2008): IF-ANA positivity 26.0% at 1:40 and 9.5% at 1:160 in 2,181 residents — and 57% of examined disease-specific-positive individuals were clinically healthy
cards.type: Primary human physiology / population dataset (ANA prevalence and disease-specific autoantibodies, Japanese general population)
cards.people: 2,181 residents of a small Japanese town undergoing annual physical examinations over a 5-year period; immunofluorescence (IF) screening of serum, with IF-positive individuals further tested for disease-specific ANAs using eight enzyme immunoassays, and physical status determined by questionnaires and medical examinations.
cards.result: IF-ANA positivity was 26.0% at a 1:40 dilution and 9.5% at 1:160, with females significantly more often positive than males (P < 0.0001). Among 566 IF-ANA-positive individuals, 100 individuals carried 114 disease-specific ANAs: anti-SSA/Ro in 58, anti-centromere in 30 and anti-U1RNP in 11 individuals; anti-Sm, anti-Scl-70 and anti-Jo-1 were undetectable. Of 60 disease-specific ANA-positive individuals available for examination, 6 had Sjögren's syndrome, 5 were suspected of Sjögren's syndrome and 5 had rheumatoid arthritis — while 34 (57%) were clinically healthy; 30% (18/60) manifested systemic rheumatic diseases and 50% showed no detectable signs or symptoms, as published.
cards.watchOut: A single small-town Japanese cohort: the 1:40 and 1:160 figures are two thresholds on the same sera, not two populations — the gap between them (26.0% vs 9.5%) is the threshold lesson itself.
cards.source: Hayashi N et al. Prevalence of disease-specific antinuclear antibodies in general population: estimates from annual physical examinations of residents of a small town over a 5-year period. Modern rheumatology. 2008. PMID: 18283522. Registry ID: none in the record. primary human physiology / population dataset (ana prevalence and disease-specific autoantibodies, japanese general population) 2,181 residents of a small japanese town undergoing annual physical examinations over a 5-year period; immunofluorescence (if) screening of serum, with if-positive individuals further tested for disease-specific anas using eight enzyme immunoassays, and physical status determined by questionnaires and medical examinations. if-ana positivity was 26.0% at a 1:40 dilution and 9.5% at 1:160, with females significantly more often positive than males (p < 0.0001). among 566 if-ana-positive individuals, 100 individuals carried 114 disease-specific anas: anti-ssa/ro in 58, anti-centromere in 30 and anti-u1rnp in 11 individuals; anti-sm, anti-scl-70 and anti-jo-1 were undetectable. of 60 disease-specific ana-positive individuals available for examination, 6 had sjögren's syndrome, 5 were suspected of sjögren's syndrome and 5 had rheumatoid arthritis — while 34 (57%) were clinically healthy; 30% (18/60) manifested systemic rheumatic diseases and 50% showed no detectable signs or symptoms, as published. a single small-town japanese cohort: the 1:40 and 1:160 figures are two thresholds on the same sera, not two populations — the gap between them (26.0% vs 9.5%) is the threshold lesson itself. hayashi n et al. prevalence of disease-specific antinuclear antibodies in general population: estimates from annual physical examinations of residents of a small town over a 5-year period. modern rheumatology. 2008. pmid: 18283522. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antibodies, antinuclear/blood · autoimmune diseases/blood,epidemiology · centromere/immunology · female · humans · japan/epidemiology · male · middle aged · physical examination · ribonucleoprotein, u1 small nuclear/immunology · ribonucleoproteins/immunology · rural health · seroepidemiologic studies · surveys and questionnaires · ss-a antigen

cards.headline: Mexican healthy-individuals study (Marin 2009): fluorescence detected in 54.3% of 304 healthy people — speckled pattern commonest, titres mostly 1:40 (35.4%)
cards.summary: Mexican healthy-individuals study (Marin 2009): fluorescence detected in 54.3% of 304 healthy people — speckled pattern commonest, titres mostly 1:40 (35.4%)
cards.type: Primary human physiology / population dataset (ANA prevalence, pattern and titre in three healthy Mexican groups)
cards.people: 304 apparently healthy Mexican individuals in three groups: 104 blood donors, 100 hospital personnel (doctors, laboratory technicians, nurses) and 100 relatives of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis; ANA determined by immunofluorescence microscopy on HEp-2 cells.
cards.result: Fluorescence was detected in 165 of 304 serum samples (54.3%). The most frequent pattern was speckled (50.3% of positives). Titres were 1:40 in 35.4%, 1:80 in 13.4%, 1:160 in 3.2% and 1:320 in 1.3%. There was a trend toward higher ANA levels in hospital personnel, and medical doctors showed the speckled pattern more often and at higher titres. The authors suggest a speckled pattern should be considered positive only at a titre of 1:160 or higher, and that ANA should generally not be tested without clinical indication.
cards.watchOut: The 54.3% figure counts any fluorescence at any titre in a mixed sample that includes relatives of autoimmune patients and hospital staff — it is not comparable with a 1:160-threshold prevalence, and this shelf never merges it with one.
cards.source: Marin GG et al. Prevalence of antinuclear antibodies in 3 groups of healthy individuals: blood donors, hospital personnel, and relatives of patients with autoimmune diseases. Journal of clinical rheumatology : practical reports on rheumatic & musculoskeletal diseases. 2009. PMID: 20009966. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: US NHANES dataset (Satoh 2012): ANA prevalence 13.8% (95% CI 12.2–15.5) in 4,754 individuals aged 12 years and over — 17.8% in females vs 9.6% in males, rising with age
cards.summary: US NHANES dataset (Satoh 2012): ANA prevalence 13.8% (95% CI 12.2–15.5) in 4,754 individuals aged 12 years and over — 17.8% in females vs 9.6% in males, rising with age
cards.type: Primary human physiology / population dataset (ANA prevalence and correlates, US NHANES 1999–2004)
cards.people: 4,754 individuals aged 12 years and older from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999–2004 (cross-sectional analysis); ANAs assessed by indirect immunofluorescence, with staining patterns and specific autoantibody reactivities (immunoprecipitation) determined in ANA-positive individuals. The dataset includes adolescents from age 12 — that age range is printed here on the face.
cards.result: ANA prevalence was 13.8% (95% CI 12.2 to 15.5), increasing with age (P = 0.01) and higher in females than males (17.8% versus 9.6%; P < 0.001), the female-to-male ratio peaking at 40–49 years. Prevalence was modestly higher in African Americans than whites (age-adjusted prevalence odds ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.70) and lower in overweight and obese individuals (age-adjusted POR 0.74) than in persons of normal weight. Among ANA-positive individuals, nuclear patterns were seen in 84.6%, cytoplasmic in 21.8% and nucleolar in 6.1%; the most common specific autoantibodies were anti-Ro (3.9%) and anti-Su (2.4%). The authors estimate more than 32 million persons in the US have ANAs.
cards.watchOut: Ages 12 and over, not adults only: adolescent values are inside the 13.8% headline, and the record's own threshold and method (indirect immunofluorescence) define the number — it sits between the Japanese 1:40 and 1:160 figures because it is a different threshold-and-population product, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Satoh M et al. Prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of antinuclear antibodies in the United States. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2012. PMID: 22237992. cards.headline: Synthesis: ANA 'positivity' in healthy people is a threshold artefact before it is a finding — 9.5% to 54.3% across three populations depending on titre cut-off, pattern and who was sampled
cards.summary: Synthesis: ANA 'positivity' in healthy people is a threshold artefact before it is a finding — 9.5% to 54.3% across three populations depending on titre cut-off, pattern and who was sampled
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary population datasets carded above (2,181 + 304 + 4,754 = 7,239 people).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (immunity / autoimmunity; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature). The three datasets agree on the physiology: antinuclear antibodies are common in people with no rheumatic disease, commoner in women and with age, and the fraction called 'positive' is set by the titre threshold — 26.0% at 1:40 falling to 9.5% at 1:160 in the same Japanese sera; 54.3% for any fluorescence in the Mexican sample, where only 3.2% reached 1:160; 13.8% overall in NHANES. Disease-specific autoantibodies also occur in health (anti-Ro/SSA commonest in both datasets that measured them), and most disease-specific-positive Japanese individuals examined were clinically healthy. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three independent general-population datasets, 7,239 people in total, concordant on threshold-dependence — the numbers must always travel with their threshold, assay and population.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a single ANA prevalence without its titre threshold: a 1:40 'positive' and a 1:160 'positive' are different claims, and no pooled prevalence is offered on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Avasimibe (ACAT inhibitor, never marketed): A-PLUS IVUS trial null on plaque progression and LDL cholesterol ROSE 7.8–10.9% relative — development ended
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia or coronary atherosclerosis, does the ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase) inhibitor avasimibe (CI-1011), compared with placebo or atorvastatin alone, improve lipid levels or slow coronary atherosclerosis progression (the A-PLUS programme)?

shelves.balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Avasimibe was never marketed; development ended after A-PLUS. The balance is a null imaging trial in which the drug RAISED LDL cholesterol, one 8-week lipid trial whose only wins were triglyceride and VLDL cholesterol (surrogate measures, with no significant change in total, LDL or HDL cholesterol or apolipoprotein B), and a 27-patient crossover in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia where avasimibe alone changed nothing. IVUS plaque volume and lipid levels are surrogate endpoints; no clinical-outcomes trial exists, and the programme must not be presented as lipid efficacy. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (no benefit).

cards.headline: A-PLUS IVUS trial (Tardif 2004): avasimibe did NOT slow coronary plaque progression (change in total plaque volume +0.7 mm³ placebo vs +7.7, +4.1, +4.8 mm³ on drug) — and LDL cholesterol increased 7.8%, 9.1% and 10.9% relative on avasimibe vs 1.7% on placebo
cards.summary: A-PLUS IVUS trial (Tardif 2004): avasimibe did NOT slow coronary plaque progression (change in total plaque volume +0.7 mm³ placebo vs +7.7, +4.1, +4.8 mm³ on drug) — and LDL cholesterol increased 7.8%, 9.1% and 10.9% relative on avasimibe vs 1.7% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled IVUS progression trial (A-PLUS), avasimibe vs placebo on background lipid-lowering therapy
cards.people: Patients with coronary atherosclerosis in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of avasimibe 50, 250 or 750 mg daily for up to 24 months, on background lipid-lowering therapy as needed to reach a target baseline LDL cholesterol below 125 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L); 87–89% received concurrent statin therapy, and mean total plaque volume at baseline was approximately 200 mm³. The fetched record prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in total plaque volume was +0.7 mm³ on placebo versus +7.7, +4.1 and +4.8 mm³ on avasimibe 50, 250 and 750 mg (adjusted P = 0.17, 0.37 and 0.37). Percent atheroma volume increased in all groups (+0.4% placebo; +0.7%, +0.8%, +1.0% on avasimibe; P = NS). LDL cholesterol increased during the study by 1.7% on placebo but by 7.8%, 9.1% and 10.9% on the three avasimibe doses (P < 0.05 in all groups) — relative changes as published. The authors concluded avasimibe did not favourably alter coronary atherosclerosis as assessed by IVUS and caused a mild increase in LDL cholesterol.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate imaging endpoint (IVUS plaque volume), not clinical events — and the direction on LDL cholesterol was adverse. The A-PLUS design paper is not a report and is not carded; no randomised N is printed in the fetched record, so none is stated.
cards.source: Tardif JC et al. Effects of the acyl coenzyme A:cholesterol acyltransferase inhibitor avasimibe on human atherosclerotic lesions. Circulation. 2004. PMID: 15533865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Combined-hyperlipidaemia lipid trial (Insull 2001): triglycerides fell up to 23% relative and VLDL cholesterol up to 30% relative — with NO significant change in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol or apolipoprotein B
cards.summary: Combined-hyperlipidaemia lipid trial (Insull 2001): triglycerides fell up to 23% relative and VLDL cholesterol up to 30% relative — with NO significant change in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol or apolipoprotein B
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled lipid trial, avasimibe in combined hyperlipidaemia
cards.people: 130 men and women with combined hyperlipidaemia and low HDL cholesterol; after an 8-week placebo and dietary-controlled baseline period, randomised double-blind to placebo or avasimibe 50, 125, 250 or 500 mg once daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: At all evaluated doses, avasimibe produced prompt and significant reductions (P < 0.05) in plasma triglycerides and VLDL cholesterol, with mean reductions of up to 23% and 30% respectively (relative changes as published), apparently independent of dose. No statistically significant changes were detected in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol or apolipoprotein B; apolipoprotein A-I fell significantly only at the 500 mg dose, a finding whose relevance the authors state is not known. All doses were well tolerated over 8 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks, surrogate lipid endpoints only: the triglyceride/VLDL signal never came with an LDL or apolipoprotein B reduction, and the larger A-PLUS trial (card above) later showed LDL rising on the drug.
cards.source: Insull W et al. Efficacy and short-term safety of a new ACAT inhibitor, avasimibe, on lipids, lipoproteins, and apolipoproteins, in patients with combined hyperlipidemia. Atherosclerosis. 2001. PMID: 11427213. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Homozygous FH crossover (Raal 2003): avasimibe alone produced NO significant lipid change in 27 subjects; added to atorvastatin it deepened the total-cholesterol fall (−22% vs −18% relative, P < 0.05) but not significantly the LDL fall (−23% vs −19%)
cards.summary: Homozygous FH crossover (Raal 2003): avasimibe alone produced NO significant lipid change in 27 subjects; added to atorvastatin it deepened the total-cholesterol fall (−22% vs −18% relative, P < 0.05) but not significantly the LDL fall (−23% vs −19%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind 3-sequence crossover trial, avasimibe ± atorvastatin in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia
cards.people: 27 subjects with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia in a double-blind, randomised, 3-sequence crossover trial of atorvastatin 80 mg daily, avasimibe 750 mg daily and the combination, each for 6 weeks (18 weeks total) after a 4-week washout.
cards.result: Avasimibe monotherapy produced no significant lipid changes. The combination lowered total cholesterol significantly more than atorvastatin alone (−22% versus −18% relative; P < 0.05). All other combination-versus-atorvastatin differences were not statistically significant, including triglycerides (−24% versus −13%), LDL cholesterol (−23% versus −19%), VLDL cholesterol (−24% versus −13%) and HDL cholesterol (−11% versus −6%) — relative changes as published.
cards.watchOut: A 27-patient crossover in a rare homozygous population over 6-week periods: the one significant difference (total cholesterol) is a surrogate in a tiny sample and does not rescue a programme whose large imaging trial was null with LDL rising.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three reports, no efficacy story — a null IVUS trial with LDL rising, a triglyceride-only lipid signal, and a 27-patient crossover; avasimibe was never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: three reports, no efficacy story — a null IVUS trial with LDL rising, a triglyceride-only lipid signal, and a 27-patient crossover; avasimibe was never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (A-PLUS IVUS trial, randomised N not printed in its record; 130-patient lipid trial; 27-patient homozygous-FH crossover).
cards.result: Avasimibe, an ACAT inhibitor, did not favourably alter coronary atherosclerosis in A-PLUS (plaque volume rose numerically more on drug than placebo at every dose) and raised LDL cholesterol by 7.8–10.9% relative versus 1.7% on placebo. Its earlier lipid trial lowered only triglycerides and VLDL cholesterol, with no significant LDL, total-cholesterol, HDL or apolipoprotein B change, and in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia the drug alone changed nothing. No clinical-outcomes trial exists. Development ended after A-PLUS and no product was marketed — the stamp is LIKELY (no benefit), with the LDL increase printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: Do not present the triglyceride/VLDL reductions or the single significant total-cholesterol difference in the crossover as lipid efficacy: on the endpoints that matter for this class (LDL cholesterol, plaque progression) the programme was null to adverse.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Eprotirome was never marketed: its phase 3 (AKKA) was prematurely terminated when another study found cartilage damage in dogs, leaving an analysable remnant of 69 patients at 6 weeks, and AKKA must not be presented as a completed phase 3. On the surrogate endpoint the signal is consistent: LDL cholesterol fell 22% relative at 100 µg in the AKKA remnant, 28–32% relative at 50–100 µg added to statins over 12 weeks, and 23–31% relative in primary hypercholesterolaemia — but liver enzymes rose in every trial, free thyroxine fell, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) on LDL lowering alone, with the termination and the dog-cartilage signal on the face.

cards.headline: AKKA phase 3 (Sjouke 2014): TERMINATED over cartilage damage in dogs — in the 69 patients reaching 6 weeks, LDL changed +9% on placebo, −12% on eprotirome 50 µg (P = 0.0677) and −22% on 100 µg (P = 0.0045), relative changes
cards.summary: AKKA phase 3 (Sjouke 2014): TERMINATED over cartilage damage in dogs — in the 69 patients reaching 6 weeks, LDL changed +9% on placebo, −12% on eprotirome 50 µg (P = 0.0677) and −22% on 100 µg (P = 0.0045), relative changes
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (AKKA), eprotirome in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia — prematurely terminated
cards.people: 236 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia who had not reached LDL targets on at least 8 weeks of statin therapy with or without ezetimibe, randomised to placebo (80), eprotirome 50 µg (79) or eprotirome 100 µg (77) at 53 sites in 11 countries; the trial was planned for 52–76 weeks but was prematurely terminated when another study found that eprotirome causes cartilage damage in dogs, so only the 69 patients who reached 6 weeks (23 placebo, 24 on 50 µg, 22 on 100 µg) were analysed.
cards.result: Mean LDL cholesterol changed by +9% (95% CI −2 to 20) on placebo, −12% (P = 0.0677 vs placebo) on 50 µg and −22% (P = 0.0045) on 100 µg — relative changes as published. Aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, conjugated bilirubin and gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase all rose significantly versus placebo (P ≤ 0.0006); four patients discontinued or interrupted treatment for transaminase rises (AST up to six times the upper limit of normal, ALT three to seven times). Free thyroxine fell 19% and 27% on the two doses; thyroid-stimulating hormone and free tri-iodothyronine did not change. The authors state the findings, with the dog cartilage damage, raise serious doubts about selective thyroid hormone mimetics for LDL lowering.
cards.watchOut: Not a completed phase 3: 236 randomised but only 69 analysable at 6 weeks because the programme was stopped over an animal cartilage signal. The LDL numbers come from that remnant and must never be quoted without the termination beside them.
cards.source: Sjouke B et al. Eprotirome in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia (the AKKA trial): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2014. PMID: 24731671. Registry ID: NCT01410383.
