shelves.title: Tezosentan in acute heart failure (VERITAS/RITZ): haemodynamics improved, dyspnoea and outcomes did not — 26% vs 26% death or worsening heart failure at 7 days
shelves.question: In adults hospitalised with acute decompensated heart failure, does the intravenous dual endothelin-receptor antagonist tezosentan, compared with placebo, improve dyspnoea, haemodynamics or clinical outcomes (the RITZ / VERITAS programme)?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Cardiac Output · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea · Endothelin Receptor Antagonists · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Pulmonary Wedge Pressure · Pyridines · Tetrazoles · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Resistance · Vasodilator Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — the null headline leads. Tezosentan, an intravenous dual endothelin-receptor antagonist, genuinely improved haemodynamics in a 292-patient invasive trial (cardiac index up, wedge pressure down 3.9 mm Hg more than placebo), but that physiology converted into nothing clinically: in VERITAS-1 and VERITAS-2 (1,448 randomised) dyspnoea did not improve more than placebo in either trial and death or worsening heart failure at 7 days was 26% in each group (odds ratio 0.99); in RITZ-4 (acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome) the composite endpoint was numerically worse on tezosentan (28.9% vs 24.2%, not significant) with more symptomatic hypotension. Tezosentan was never marketed. Haemodynamics and dyspnoea scores are surrogate / soft endpoints.

cards.headline: VERITAS-1 and VERITAS-2 (McMurray 2007): tezosentan did NOT improve dyspnoea in either trial, and death or worsening heart failure at 7 days was 26% in each group (OR 0.99)
cards.summary: VERITAS-1 and VERITAS-2 (McMurray 2007): tezosentan did NOT improve dyspnoea in either trial, and death or worsening heart failure at 7 days was 26% in each group (OR 0.99)
cards.type: Two identical concurrent double-blind randomised trials (VERITAS-1 and VERITAS-2) reported in one paper, IV tezosentan vs placebo in acute heart failure
cards.people: 1,448 patients randomised (730 tezosentan vs 718 placebo) across two identical concurrent trials; 1,435 received treatment as assigned. Patients were admitted within the previous 24 hours with persisting dyspnoea and a respiratory rate ≥24/min plus natriuretic-peptide, clinical or radiologic congestion criteria or left ventricular systolic dysfunction; mean age 70 years, mean ejection fraction 29% where measured.
cards.result: Tezosentan (5 mg/h for 30 minutes, then 1 mg/h for 24–72 hours) did not improve dyspnoea more than placebo in either trial: mean treatment differences in dyspnoea area under the curve over 24 hours were −12 mm·h (95% CI −105 to 81; P = .80) in VERITAS-1 and −25 mm·h (95% CI −119 to 69; P = .60) in VERITAS-2. The combined incidence of death or worsening heart failure at 7 days was 26% in each treatment group (odds ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21; P = .95). The authors concluded tezosentan did not improve symptoms or clinical outcomes in acute heart failure.
cards.watchOut: Two large, well-powered trials with flatly null results on both coprimary endpoints — this is the programme's definitive evidence and outweighs the haemodynamic trial carded below.
cards.source: McMurray JJ et al. Effects of tezosentan on symptoms and clinical outcomes in patients with acute heart failure: the VERITAS randomized controlled trials. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17986694. Registry ID: NCT00525707; NCT00524433. cards.headline: RITZ-4 (O'Connor 2003): in acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome, the composite endpoint was numerically worse on tezosentan (28.9% vs 24.2%, P = 0.52), with more symptomatic hypotension
cards.summary: RITZ-4 (O'Connor 2003): in acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome, the composite endpoint was numerically worse on tezosentan (28.9% vs 24.2%, P = 0.52), with more symptomatic hypotension
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial (RITZ-4), IV tezosentan vs placebo in acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome
cards.people: 193 patients with acute decompensated heart failure associated with acute coronary syndrome, randomised to tezosentan (25 mg/h for 1 hour, then 50 mg/h for 23–47 hours) or placebo.
cards.result: The primary composite — death, worsening heart failure, recurrent ischaemia, or recurrent or new myocardial infarction within 72 hours — occurred in 28.9% on tezosentan (95% CI 20.1% to 39.0%) vs 24.2% on placebo (95% CI 16.0% to 34.1%), P = 0.5152, not significant. Tezosentan showed no pro-ischaemic effect, but symptomatic hypotension was more frequent in the treatment group.
cards.watchOut: A 193-patient trial: the numerical excess on the composite is not significant, but there is no hint of benefit, and the hypotension signal matches the dose-related adverse events of the haemodynamic trial.
cards.source: O'Connor CM et al. Tezosentan in patients with acute heart failure and acute coronary syndromes: results of the Randomized Intravenous TeZosentan Study (RITZ-4). Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2003. PMID: 12742280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Haemodynamic trial (Torre-Amione 2003): tezosentan raised cardiac index and lowered wedge pressure by 3.9 mm Hg more than placebo (P < 0.0001) — a real physiological effect that did not become clinical benefit
cards.summary: Haemodynamic trial (Torre-Amione 2003): tezosentan raised cardiac index and lowered wedge pressure by 3.9 mm Hg more than placebo (P < 0.0001) — a real physiological effect that did not become clinical benefit
cards.type: Double-blind randomised invasive haemodynamic trial, IV tezosentan 50 or 100 mg/h vs placebo in acute decompensated heart failure
cards.people: 292 patients hospitalised for acute decompensated heart failure needing intravenous treatment and central haemodynamic monitoring, with cardiac index ≤2.5 L/min/m² and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≥15 mm Hg, randomised double-blind to 24-hour tezosentan 50 or 100 mg/h or placebo.
cards.result: After 6 hours, cardiac index had risen and wedge pressure fallen significantly more on both tezosentan doses than on placebo (mean treatment effects 0.38 and 0.37 L/min/m² for cardiac index and −3.9 mm Hg for wedge pressure at each dose; P < 0.0001), maintained during the infusion and for at least 6 hours after it stopped. There was a tendency to better dyspnoea scores and less clinical worsening at 24 hours. Adverse events were more frequent on tezosentan and dose-related: headache, asymptomatic hypotension, early worsening of renal function, nausea and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: Haemodynamics are surrogate endpoints: this trial proves the drug moves cardiac index and wedge pressure, and VERITAS proves that moving them did not improve dyspnoea or outcomes. The wedge-pressure result must not be presented as clinical benefit.
cards.source: Torre-Amione G et al. Hemodynamic and clinical effects of tezosentan, an intravenous dual endothelin receptor antagonist, in patients hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2003. PMID: 12849674. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Xamoterol in chronic heart failure: symptom benefit in mild disease — but 9.1% vs 3.7% mortality in severe heart failure; the harm leads
shelves.question: In adults with chronic heart failure, does the beta-1 partial agonist xamoterol, compared with placebo or digoxin, improve symptoms and exercise capacity — and what did it do to mortality in severe heart failure?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adrenergic beta-Agonists · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Blood Pressure · Cardiac Complexes, Premature · Discriminant Analysis · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Evaluation · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Exercise Test · Female · Heart Failure · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Propanolamines · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Research Design · Tachycardia · Xamoterol
shelves.balance: SPLIT, severity-dependent — and the mortality harm leads. In the programme's largest trial, 516 patients with severe (NYHA class III–IV) heart failure, xamoterol improved breathlessness scores but not exercise duration, and significantly MORE patients died on xamoterol within 100 days: 32 (9.1%) vs 6 (3.7%) on placebo (P = 0.02) — an absolute excess of 5.4 percentage points. The mirror image comes from milder disease: a sponsor programme summary of randomised monotherapy studies in 425 patients with mild-to-moderate heart failure (labelled a programme report) found improved exercise capacity, signs, symptoms and quality of life, and a 19-patient crossover found xamoterol comparable to digoxin on exercise duration. The mild-disease symptom reports must not be pooled against the severe-disease mortality result. Xamoterol was withdrawn / never marketed for heart failure in the US. Exercise capacity and symptom scores are surrogate / soft endpoints.

cards.headline: Severe heart failure trial (Xamoterol in Severe Heart Failure Study Group 1990): breathlessness improved but exercise did not — and 9.1% on xamoterol vs 3.7% on placebo died within 100 days (P = 0.02)
cards.summary: Severe heart failure trial (Xamoterol in Severe Heart Failure Study Group 1990): breathlessness improved but exercise did not — and 9.1% on xamoterol vs 3.7% on placebo died within 100 days (P = 0.02)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised trial, xamoterol vs placebo in severe (NYHA III–IV) heart failure
cards.people: 516 patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure despite diuretics and ACE inhibitors, randomised double-blind to xamoterol 200 mg twice daily (n = 352) or placebo (n = 164) for 13 weeks.
cards.result: There was no difference between treatments in loss of clinical signs. Visual analogue and Likert scores indicated breathlessness was less severe on xamoterol, but exercise duration and total work done did not differ. Xamoterol reduced maximum exercise heart rate and systolic blood pressure and showed no arrhythmogenic activity. On intention-to-treat analysis, 32 patients (9.1%) in the xamoterol group and 6 (3.7%) in the placebo group died within 100 days of randomisation (P = 0.02) — an absolute mortality excess of 5.4 percentage points on xamoterol.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's largest trial and its only mortality evidence — it carries the greatest weight on this shelf. A partial beta-1 agonist that stimulates a failing heart at rest plausibly explains harm in severe disease even while easing breathlessness.
cards.source: Xamoterol in Severe Heart Failure Study Group et al. Xamoterol in severe heart failure. Lancet. 1990. PMID: 1694945. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: 425 patients with mild-to-moderate heart failure enrolled across the sponsor's randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled monotherapy studies, summarised in this published programme report by the European 'Corwin' Group.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, xamoterol produced improvements in exercise capacity, clinical signs, symptoms and quality of life, with a low incidence of adverse experiences. cards.headline: Digoxin crossover (Sorensen 1989): in 19 patients with NYHA class II–III heart failure, exercise duration rose 17% relative on xamoterol vs 27% relative on digoxin — no significant difference between the drugs
cards.summary: Digoxin crossover (Sorensen 1989): in 19 patients with NYHA class II–III heart failure, exercise duration rose 17% relative on xamoterol vs 27% relative on digoxin — no significant difference between the drugs
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial, xamoterol vs digoxin in moderate chronic heart failure (n = 19)
cards.people: 19 patients with cardiac failure (NYHA class II–III) in a randomised double-blind crossover with 6-week treatment periods; 15 patients completed the crossover phase, and 13 were followed for 3–6 months on whichever drug they had responded to best.
cards.result: In the 15 completers there was no significant difference in exercise duration between digoxin and xamoterol; exercise duration increased by 27% relative to baseline on digoxin and by 17% relative on xamoterol. Maximum exercise heart rate, blood pressure and rate-pressure product were significantly lower on xamoterol; systolic time interval was shorter on digoxin; echocardiographic parameters did not change. The short-term results were maintained in the 3–6-month follow-up of responders.
cards.watchOut: A 19-patient crossover (15 completers) — small, short, and never load-bearing; it is carded only to complete the programme record. Percent exercise gains are relative to baseline in a handful of patients.
cards.source: Sorensen EV et al. Digoxin and xamoterol in patients with moderate chronic heart failure. A double-blind, randomized, controlled study. Cardiovascular Drugs and Therapy. 1989. PMID: 2577283. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Flosequinan in chronic heart failure: PROFILE — mortality increased (HR 1.39), trial stopped for harm; REFLECT/FACET exercise wins do not offset it
shelves.question: In adults with chronic heart failure, does the oral vasodilator / inotrope flosequinan, compared with placebo (added to digoxin, diuretics and an ACE inhibitor), improve exercise capacity and symptoms — and what did its mortality trial show (the PROFILE programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cause of Death · Chronic Disease · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Female · Heart Failure · Heart Rate · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Long-Term Care · Male · Neurotransmitter Agents · Prospective Studies · Quinolines · Risk Factors · Vasodilator Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the mortality harm leads, printed first and heaviest. Flosequinan, an oral vasodilator with inotropic effects, won consistently on exercise and symptoms in two smaller trials (REFLECT: maximal exercise time +96 s vs +47 s on placebo; FACET: median exercise time +64 s vs +5 s at the once-daily dose, with a better quality-of-life score). But in PROFILE, the one trial large enough to measure survival (2,354 patients with NYHA class III–IV disease and ejection fraction ≤35%), flosequinan increased mortality: 255 deaths vs 192 on placebo over an average of 10 months, hazard ratio 1.39 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.67; P = 0.0006) — a 39% relative increase — and the trial was terminated early on the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation because of that harm. The exercise results must not be presented as benefit without the mortality record attached. Flosequinan was withdrawn and is not marketed. PROFILE's primary results were published only in 2017, 24 years after the trial.

cards.headline: PROFILE (Packer 2017): flosequinan INCREASED mortality in severe chronic heart failure — 255 vs 192 deaths, HR 1.39 (P = 0.0006) — and the trial was stopped early for that harm
cards.summary: PROFILE (Packer 2017): flosequinan INCREASED mortality in severe chronic heart failure — 255 vs 192 deaths, HR 1.39 (P = 0.0006) — and the trial was stopped early for that harm
cards.type: Randomised mortality trial (PROFILE), flosequinan vs placebo in severe chronic heart failure — terminated early for harm
cards.people: 2,354 patients with NYHA functional class III–IV heart failure and ejection fraction ≤35%, randomised after a run-in period to long-term flosequinan 75 or 100 mg/day or placebo, in addition to usual therapy (digitalis, diuretics and ACE inhibitors).
cards.result: The trial was terminated on the recommendation of the Data and Safety Monitoring Board: during an average of 10 months of follow-up, 255 patients died in the flosequinan group vs 192 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.67; P = 0.0006 — a hazard ratio is a relative measure, here a 39% relative increase in mortality). Flosequinan also increased disease progression, heart rate and neurohormonal activation. During the first month, flosequinan patients were more likely to report improved well-being — the symptomatic benefit and the mortality harm coexist in the same trial.
cards.watchOut: The primary report appeared only in 2017, 24 years after the trial — a programme read from its 1990s exercise trials alone looks like a benefit story. PROFILE is the definitive evidence on this shelf and is carded first.
cards.source: Packer M et al. Long-Term Effects of Flosequinan on the Morbidity and Mortality of Patients With Severe Chronic Heart Failure: Primary Results of the PROFILE Trial After 24 Years. JACC: Heart Failure. 2017. PMID: 28501522. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: REFLECT (Packer 1993): flosequinan improved exercise time (+96 s vs +47 s on placebo, P = 0.022) and symptoms (55% vs 36% benefited) over 3 months
cards.summary: REFLECT (Packer 1993): flosequinan improved exercise time (+96 s vs +47 s on placebo, P = 0.022) and symptoms (55% vs 36% benefited) over 3 months
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial (REFLECT), flosequinan vs placebo added to digoxin and diuretics in chronic heart failure
cards.people: 193 patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–III, ejection fraction <40%) receiving digoxin and diuretics, randomised double-blind to flosequinan 100 mg once daily (n = 93) or placebo (n = 100) for 3 months.
cards.result: After 12 weeks, maximal treadmill exercise time increased by 96 s on flosequinan vs 47 s on placebo (P = 0.022 for the difference). Maximal oxygen consumption rose 1.7 vs 0.6 mL/kg per min (P = 0.05). Symptomatically, 55% of flosequinan patients vs 36% on placebo benefited (P = 0.018), and fewer flosequinan patients worsened enough to need a medication change or withdrawal (P = 0.07). By intention to treat, 7 patients on flosequinan and 2 on placebo died — a small numerical imbalance the trial could not resolve, later answered by PROFILE.
cards.watchOut: A 3-month, 193-patient exercise trial: its endpoints are surrogates, and its own deaths (7 vs 2) already leaned the way PROFILE later proved. Never present this card's exercise win without the PROFILE card.
cards.source: Packer M et al. Double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the efficacy of flosequinan in patients with chronic heart failure. Principal Investigators of the REFLECT Study. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 1993. PMID: 8509565. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FACET (Massie 1993): added to diuretic, digoxin and an ACE inhibitor, flosequinan 100 mg once daily increased median exercise time by 64 s vs 5 s on placebo and improved quality of life — the twice-daily dose did not
cards.summary: FACET (Massie 1993): added to diuretic, digoxin and an ACE inhibitor, flosequinan 100 mg once daily increased median exercise time by 64 s vs 5 s on placebo and improved quality of life — the twice-daily dose did not
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial (FACET), flosequinan (two dose regimens) vs placebo added to diuretic, digoxin and ACE inhibitor
cards.people: 322 patients with predominantly NYHA class II–III congestive heart failure and ejection fraction ≤35%, stabilised on a diuretic, digoxin and an ACE inhibitor, randomised double-blind to flosequinan 100 mg once daily, flosequinan 75 mg twice daily, or placebo for 16 weeks.
cards.result: After 16 weeks, flosequinan 100 mg once daily produced a significant increment in median exercise time (64 s) compared with placebo (5 s), whereas the 75 mg twice-daily group did not show a statistically significant increase. The once-daily dose also improved the overall Minnesota Living With Heart Failure score significantly versus placebo; both active doses improved the physical component, but the twice-daily dose trended toward worsening the emotional component. The authors themselves noted that evidence the studied dose adversely affected survival meant the benefit-to-risk ratio needed individual assessment.
cards.watchOut: Exercise time and quality-of-life scores are surrogate / soft endpoints, and the benefit was dose-regimen-specific. This trial ran on triple background therapy — and PROFILE still found excess mortality on the same class of regimen.
cards.source: Massie BM et al. Can further benefit be achieved by adding flosequinan to patients with congestive heart failure who remain symptomatic on diuretic, digoxin, and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor? Results of the flosequinan-ACE inhibitor trial (FACET). Circulation. 1993. PMID: 8339411. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Fimasartan in hypertension (Korea-only programme): non-inferior to losartan, superior to valsartan on ambulatory pressure in FAST — 6–12-week blood-pressure trials, no outcomes data
shelves.question: In Korean adults with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension, does the angiotensin-receptor blocker fimasartan, compared with losartan, valsartan, placebo or its own monotherapy (when combined with amlodipine), lower blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Antihypertensive Agents · Biphenyl Compounds · Blood Pressure · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Losartan · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pyrimidines · Republic of Korea · Severity of Illness Index · Tetrazoles · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-region (Korea) programme, and that flag leads: every anchor is a Korean trial of 6–12 weeks with blood pressure, a surrogate endpoint, as the outcome; there is no outcomes trial and fimasartan is not marketed in the US or Europe. Within that fence the results are consistent across four phase 3/4 reports: fimasartan was non-inferior to losartan on sitting diastolic pressure at 12 weeks (−11.26 mm Hg from baseline; between-group difference 2.70 mm Hg favouring fimasartan in a post-hoc comparison), low-dose fimasartan 30 mg beat placebo (−9.93 vs −2.08 mm Hg diastolic) and valsartan 80 mg, adding amlodipine to fimasartan lowered sitting systolic pressure far more than continuing fimasartan alone (−20.5 vs −7.8 mm Hg), and in the FAST forced-titration trial fimasartan 120 mg beat valsartan 160 mg on office systolic (−16.26 vs −12.81 mm Hg) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure (−15.22 vs −9.45 mm Hg) at 6 weeks. Tolerability was comparable to the comparators throughout. Within-class comparisons are against first-generation ARBs at standard doses; the FAST result must not be generalised beyond its 6-week forced-titration design.

cards.headline: Phase 3 vs losartan (Lee 2012): fimasartan 60/120 mg was non-inferior to losartan 50/100 mg on sitting diastolic pressure at 12 weeks (−11.26 vs −8.56 mm Hg from baseline)
cards.summary: Phase 3 vs losartan (Lee 2012): fimasartan 60/120 mg was non-inferior to losartan 50/100 mg on sitting diastolic pressure at 12 weeks (−11.26 vs −8.56 mm Hg from baseline)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind non-inferiority randomised trial, fimasartan vs losartan in Korean patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension
cards.people: 506 Korean adults aged 18–70 with mild-to-moderate hypertension, randomised double-blind to fimasartan 60/120 mg (n = 256) or losartan 50/100 mg (n = 250) with optional titration for 12 weeks, with an optional 12-week extension.
cards.result: At week 12, sitting diastolic pressure had fallen −11.26 mm Hg on fimasartan and −8.56 mm Hg on losartan (each P < 0.0001 vs baseline); the between-group difference was 2.70 mm Hg (P = 0.0002) and the lower limit of the 95% CI (1.27 mm Hg) exceeded the prespecified non-inferiority margin (−2.5 mm Hg), meeting the non-inferiority primary endpoint — with a post-hoc comparison suggesting superiority. Adverse drug reactions: 7.84% on fimasartan vs 10.40% on losartan (P = 0.3181, not significant). Efficacy and tolerability were maintained over the 24-week extension.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Korea) trial with a blood-pressure surrogate endpoint; the superiority reading is a post-hoc comparison on top of a met non-inferiority endpoint, and the comparator is a first-generation ARB at standard doses.
cards.source: Lee SE et al. Efficacy and tolerability of fimasartan, a new angiotensin receptor blocker, compared with losartan (50/100 mg): a 12-week, phase III, multicenter, prospective, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, dose escalation clinical trial with an optional 12-week extension phase in adult Korean patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension. Clinical Therapeutics. 2012. PMID: 22381711. Registry ID: NCT00922480. cards.headline: Low-dose phase 3 (Youn 2014): fimasartan 30 mg lowered sitting diastolic pressure −9.93 mm Hg vs −2.08 on placebo at 8 weeks (P < 0.0001), and beat valsartan 80 mg
cards.summary: Low-dose phase 3 (Youn 2014): fimasartan 30 mg lowered sitting diastolic pressure −9.93 mm Hg vs −2.08 on placebo at 8 weeks (P < 0.0001), and beat valsartan 80 mg
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised trial, low-dose fimasartan vs placebo and valsartan in mild-to-moderate hypertension
cards.people: 293 patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension randomised double-blind to fimasartan 30 mg (n = 115), placebo (n = 117) or valsartan 80 mg (n = 61) at fixed doses for 8 weeks; mean age 54.24 years, 219 men.
cards.result: At week 8, sitting diastolic pressure changed −9.93 mm Hg on fimasartan vs −2.08 mm Hg on placebo (P < 0.0001), and sitting systolic pressure −15.35 vs −2.30 mm Hg (P < 0.0001). Fimasartan also beat valsartan 80 mg at weeks 4 and 8 (week-8 diastolic −9.93 vs −5.47 mm Hg, P = 0.0021; systolic −15.35 vs −7.49 mm Hg, P = 0.0021). Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild, there were no serious treatment-emergent events, and incidences did not differ significantly between groups (19.1% fimasartan, 22.6% placebo, 13.6% valsartan).
cards.watchOut: An 8-week, fixed low-dose comparison in a Korean population; the valsartan arm (n = 61) is half the size of the other arms, and blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: Amlodipine combination phase 3 (Kim 2016): in fimasartan non-responders, fimasartan/amlodipine 60/10 mg lowered sitting systolic pressure −20.5 mm Hg vs −7.8 on continued fimasartan (P < 0.0001)
cards.summary: Amlodipine combination phase 3 (Kim 2016): in fimasartan non-responders, fimasartan/amlodipine 60/10 mg lowered sitting systolic pressure −20.5 mm Hg vs −7.8 on continued fimasartan (P < 0.0001)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised trial, fimasartan/amlodipine vs fimasartan monotherapy in fimasartan non-responders
cards.people: 143 patients whose hypertension had not responded to 4 weeks of fimasartan 60 mg (sitting systolic pressure ≥140 mm Hg), randomised double-blind to continued fimasartan 60 mg or fimasartan/amlodipine 60/10 mg for 8 weeks; 137 had efficacy data, mean age 59.1 years.
cards.result: At week 8, sitting systolic pressure had fallen −20.5 mm Hg on the combination vs −7.8 mm Hg on continued fimasartan (P < 0.0001), with the separation already present at week 4 (−20.1 vs −8.1 mm Hg). Response rate at week 8: 82.1% vs 32.9% (P < 0.0001); control rate 79.1% vs 31.4% (P < 0.0001). Adverse drug reactions occurred in 9 patients (6.3%) with no significant difference between groups and no serious drug-related events.
cards.watchOut: An enriched non-responder population: the large combination effect is what adding a calcium-channel blocker is expected to do, and the comparison is against staying on the drug that had already failed — not against another combination.
cards.source: Kim KI et al. A Randomized, Double-blind, Multicenter, Phase III Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Fimasartan/Amlodipine Combined Therapy Versus Fimasartan Monotherapy in Patients With Essential Hypertension Unresponsive to Fimasartan Monotherapy. cards.headline: FAST phase 4 (Chung 2020): fimasartan 120 mg beat valsartan 160 mg on office systolic (−16.26 vs −12.81 mm Hg, P = 0.0298) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure (−15.22 vs −9.45, P = 0.0009) at 6 weeks
cards.summary: FAST phase 4 (Chung 2020): fimasartan 120 mg beat valsartan 160 mg on office systolic (−16.26 vs −12.81 mm Hg, P = 0.0298) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure (−15.22 vs −9.45, P = 0.0009) at 6 weeks
cards.type: Phase 4 double-blind forced-titration randomised trial (FAST), fimasartan vs valsartan with an olmesartan reference arm, office and ambulatory blood pressure
cards.people: 369 Korean patients with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension randomised (365 in the full analysis set: fimasartan 155, valsartan 157, olmesartan 53 as a reference arm) to forced titration — standard doses for 2 weeks, then fimasartan 120 mg, valsartan 160 mg or olmesartan 20 mg for 4 weeks — with ambulatory monitoring before and after the 6-week treatment.
cards.result: After 6 weeks, sitting systolic pressure fell −16.26 mm Hg on fimasartan vs −12.81 mm Hg on valsartan (P = 0.0298), and sitting diastolic −7.63 vs −5.14 mm Hg (P = 0.0211). Mean 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure fell −15.22 vs −9.45 mm Hg (P = 0.0009) and ambulatory diastolic −8.74 vs −5.98 mm Hg (P = 0.0140); night-time ambulatory reductions were also larger on fimasartan. The olmesartan reference arm did not differ significantly from fimasartan on any endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks of forced titration to maximum doses in Korean patients — the ambulatory advantage must not be generalised beyond that design, population and duration, and the olmesartan reference arm was small (n = 53).
cards.source: Chung WB et al. Effect of Fimasartan versus Valsartan and Olmesartan on Office and Ambulatory Blood Pressure in Korean Patients with Mild-to-Moderate Essential Hypertension: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Active Control, Three-Parallel Group, Forced Titration, Multicenter, Phase IV Study (Fimasartan Achieving Systolic Blood Pressure Target (FAST) Study). Drug Design, Development and Therapy. 2020. PMID: 32158190. Registry ID: NCT02495324. cards.headline: Synthesis: four Korean phase 3/4 reports agree fimasartan lowers blood pressure at least as well as first-generation ARBs — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region programme with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: four Korean phase 3/4 reports agree fimasartan lowers blood pressure at least as well as first-generation ARBs — a surrogate-endpoint, single-region programme with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: phase 3 vs losartan (506 randomised), low-dose phase 3 vs placebo/valsartan (293), amlodipine-combination phase 3 (143) and FAST phase 4 (369) — all in Korean patients.
cards.result: Non-inferior to losartan on diastolic pressure at 12 weeks with a post-hoc difference favouring fimasartan; superior to placebo and to valsartan 80 mg at the 30 mg dose; a large added effect when amlodipine is combined in non-responders (−20.5 vs −7.8 mm Hg systolic); and superior to valsartan 160 mg on office and 24-hour ambulatory pressure in FAST. Tolerability matched comparators in every report. POSSIBLE (benefit) on blood pressure only, under the single-region flag.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Manidipine in hypertension with type 2 diabetes: DEMAND's kidney primary outcome was null (GFR slope P = 0.87/0.53) — blood pressure matched enalapril; albuminuria beat amlodipine in one small trial
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (with or without microalbuminuria), does the dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker manidipine, compared with enalapril, delapril-based therapy or amlodipine, lower blood pressure and albuminuria (the DEMAND programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · Calcium Channel Blockers · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Dihydropyridines · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Indans · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrobenzenes · Piperazines · Prognosis · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and DEMAND's null primary outcome leads. The programme's only long-term trial, DEMAND (380 hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes, 3 years), found NO difference in its primary outcome: median monthly GFR decline was 0.32 mL/min/1.73 m² on manidipine/delapril, 0.36 on delapril and 0.30 on placebo (P = 0.87 and P = 0.53), with albuminuria stable in all three groups. DEMAND's striking hazard ratio for major cardiovascular events on the combination vs placebo (0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.78) rests on a secondary endpoint with a wide confidence interval in a 380-patient trial and is printed as such, never as an outcomes win. Around that null: manidipine lowered blood pressure as effectively as enalapril over 24 weeks in 111 patients (responders 66.7% vs 60.0%, not significant), and in one small 91-patient trial with 2:1 randomisation, adding manidipine to full-dose renin-angiotensin blockade reduced urinary albumin excretion far more than adding amlodipine at equal blood-pressure reduction (65.5% relative vs 20% relative at 6 months). Albuminuria and blood pressure are surrogate endpoints. Manidipine is marketed in parts of Europe and Asia, not the US.

cards.headline: DEMAND (Ruggenenti 2011): 3-year manidipine/delapril did NOT slow GFR decline vs delapril or placebo (primary outcome null, P = 0.87 / 0.53); albuminuria was stable in all groups
cards.summary: DEMAND (Ruggenenti 2011): 3-year manidipine/delapril did NOT slow GFR decline vs delapril or placebo (primary outcome null, P = 0.87 / 0.53); albuminuria was stable in all groups
cards.type: 3-year double-blind randomised trial (DEMAND), manidipine/delapril vs delapril vs placebo in hypertensive type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 380 hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria <200 mg/min, randomised double-blind to manidipine/delapril 10/30 mg (n = 126), delapril 30 mg (n = 127) or placebo (n = 127) for 3 years; GFR was centrally measured by iohexol plasma clearance.
cards.result: The primary outcome was null: median monthly GFR decline was 0.32 mL/min/1.73 m² on combined therapy, 0.36 on delapril and 0.30 on placebo (P = 0.87 and P = 0.53 vs combined therapy and delapril respectively), and albuminuria was stable in all three groups. On secondary endpoints, the hazard ratio for major cardiovascular events for combined therapy vs placebo was 0.17 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.78; P = 0.023 — a relative measure), the hazard ratio for developing retinopathy was 0.27 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.99; P = 0.048) among 192 patients without retinopathy at entry, and odds ratios for peripheral neuropathy favoured both active arms vs placebo. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The nephroprotection claim this trial was built to test failed on its primary outcome. The cardiovascular hazard ratio of 0.17 comes from a secondary endpoint with a very wide confidence interval (0.04 to 0.78) in 380 patients — few events; it is hypothesis-generating, not an outcomes win.
cards.source: Ruggenenti P et al. Effects of manidipine and delapril in hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: the delapril and manidipine for nephroprotection in diabetes (DEMAND) randomized clinical trial. Hypertension. 2011. PMID: 21931073. Registry ID: NCT00157586. cards.headline: Vs enalapril (Luque Otero 2005): manidipine lowered blood pressure as effectively as enalapril over 24 weeks (164/97.5 → 141/84.5 vs 159/98 → 139/86 mm Hg; responders 66.7% vs 60.0%, NS)
cards.summary: Vs enalapril (Luque Otero 2005): manidipine lowered blood pressure as effectively as enalapril over 24 weeks (164/97.5 → 141/84.5 vs 159/98 → 139/86 mm Hg; responders 66.7% vs 60.0%, NS)
cards.type: 24-week double-blind randomised trial, manidipine vs enalapril monotherapy in hypertension with type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 111 patients with type 2 diabetes and mild-to-moderate hypertension randomised double-blind to manidipine 10 mg (n = 53) or enalapril 10 mg (n = 58), doubled in non-responders, for 24 weeks; mean age 62 years.
cards.result: Blood pressure fell from 164/97.5 to 141/84.5 mm Hg on manidipine and from 159/98 to 139/86 mm Hg on enalapril (each P < 0.01 vs baseline); responder rates were 66.7% vs 60.0%, not significantly different, and 24-hour ambulatory reductions were similar in both groups. HbA1c fell from 6.7% to 6.2% in the manidipine group only (P < 0.05), and blood glucose from 152 to 143 mg/dL in that group; neither drug affected heart rate, and adverse-event incidence was similar.
cards.watchOut: A 111-patient, 24-week blood-pressure trial powered only to detect a >3 mm Hg diastolic difference; the HbA1c fall in the manidipine arm is a within-group secondary finding in a trial not designed as a diabetes-treatment comparison.
cards.source: Luque Otero M et al. Manidipine versus enalapril monotherapy in patients with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, 24-week study. Clinical Therapeutics. 2005. PMID: 15811479. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: AMANDHA (Martinez-Martin 2008): added to full-dose renin-angiotensin blockade, manidipine cut urinary albumin excretion 65.5% relative vs 20% relative on amlodipine at 6 months (P < 0.01), at equal blood-pressure reduction
cards.summary: AMANDHA (Martinez-Martin 2008): added to full-dose renin-angiotensin blockade, manidipine cut urinary albumin excretion 65.5% relative vs 20% relative on amlodipine at 6 months (P < 0.01), at equal blood-pressure reduction
cards.type: Randomised add-on trial (AMANDHA), manidipine vs amlodipine in diabetic hypertension with microalbuminuria on renin-angiotensin blockade
cards.people: 91 diabetic patients with uncontrolled hypertension and microalbuminuria despite at least 6 months of full-dose renin-angiotensin system blockade, randomised 2:1 to add-on manidipine 20 mg (n = 61) or amlodipine 10 mg (n = 30) for 6 months, with an 18-month extension phase monitoring microalbuminuria.
cards.result: Manidipine and amlodipine decreased blood pressure to a similar extent. Urinary albumin excretion fell 65.5% relative on manidipine vs 20% relative on amlodipine at 6 months (P < 0.01), and 62.7% vs 16.6% relative at the end of the extension phase (P < 0.01). Manidipine was better tolerated than amlodipine.
cards.watchOut: One 91-patient trial with a 2:1 randomisation and a surrogate endpoint (albumin excretion) — and DEMAND, the programme's larger and longer trial, found albuminuria stable with no separation between its groups. The AMANDHA result is a signal, not a settled advantage.
cards.source: Martinez-Martin FJ et al. Add-on manidipine versus amlodipine in diabetic patients with hypertension and microalbuminuria: the AMANDHA study. Expert Review of Cardiovascular Therapy. 2008. PMID: 19018688. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Azilsartan medoxomil in hypertension: 80 mg beat valsartan 320 mg and olmesartan 40 mg on 24-hour pressure (−14.3 mm Hg placebo-adjusted); chlorthalidone combination strongly additive
shelves.question: In adults with essential hypertension, does the angiotensin-receptor blocker azilsartan medoxomil, compared with olmesartan, valsartan, telmisartan or (combined with chlorthalidone) its own components, lower clinic and ambulatory blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers · Antihypertensive Agents · Benzimidazoles · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Imidazoles · Male · Middle Aged · Oxadiazoles · Tetrazoles · Treatment Outcome · Valine · Valsartan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — azilsartan medoxomil is a marketed agent (US/EU) whose absence from the library is a coverage gap, not a discontinued-programme story; it is presented plainly as the last unrowed ARB. Three reports, all 6–8-week blood-pressure (surrogate) trials, with no outcomes trial: in the 1,291-patient ambulatory head-to-head, azilsartan 80 mg lowered placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic pressure −14.3 mm Hg, more than valsartan 320 mg (−10.0, P < 0.001) and olmesartan 40 mg (−11.7, P = 0.009), with azilsartan 40 mg non-inferior to olmesartan 40 mg; in the 1,714-patient factorial trial, azilsartan/chlorthalidone 40/25 and 80/25 mg combinations lowered trough ambulatory systolic pressure 28.9 mm Hg, exceeding either component alone by about 13–14 mm Hg, with dose-dependent discontinuations and creatinine elevations; and in a 303-patient Indian phase 3 trial (single-region, flagged), azilsartan 40 and 80 mg were non-inferior to telmisartan 40 mg on trough sitting systolic pressure (−27.2 and −28.2 vs −26.7 mm Hg). The within-class superiority claims rest on maximum-dose comparisons in a single sponsor programme.

cards.headline: Ambulatory head-to-head (White 2011): azilsartan 80 mg lowered 24-hour systolic pressure −14.3 mm Hg (placebo-adjusted), more than valsartan 320 mg (−10.0, P < 0.001) and olmesartan 40 mg (−11.7, P = 0.009)
cards.summary: Ambulatory head-to-head (White 2011): azilsartan 80 mg lowered 24-hour systolic pressure −14.3 mm Hg (placebo-adjusted), more than valsartan 320 mg (−10.0, P < 0.001) and olmesartan 40 mg (−11.7, P = 0.009)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised ambulatory blood-pressure trial, azilsartan medoxomil vs valsartan, olmesartan and placebo in stage 1–2 hypertension
cards.people: 1,291 patients with stage 1–2 hypertension randomised double-blind to azilsartan medoxomil 40 or 80 mg, valsartan 320 mg, olmesartan 40 mg or placebo, with ambulatory and clinic blood-pressure measurement; mean age 56 years, baseline 24-hour mean systolic pressure 145 mm Hg.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was change in 24-hour mean systolic pressure. Azilsartan 80 mg was superior to both comparators at their maximal approved doses: placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic reduction −14.3 mm Hg vs −10.0 mm Hg on valsartan 320 mg (P < 0.001) and −11.7 mm Hg on olmesartan 40 mg (P = 0.009). Azilsartan 40 mg was non-inferior to olmesartan 40 mg (difference −1.4 mm Hg, 95% CI −3.3 to 0.5). For clinic systolic pressure both azilsartan doses were superior to the comparators. Safety and tolerability were similar across placebo and all four active treatments.
cards.watchOut: Maximum-dose versus maximum-dose comparisons within one sponsor programme, over weeks, on a surrogate endpoint: a 2.6–4.3 mm Hg ambulatory edge over other ARBs is a pharmacological ranking, not evidence of fewer cardiovascular events.
cards.source: White WB et al. Effects of the angiotensin receptor blocker azilsartan medoxomil versus olmesartan and valsartan on ambulatory and clinic blood pressure in patients with stages 1 and 2 hypertension. Hypertension. 2011. PMID: 21282560. Registry ID: NCT00696436. cards.headline: Factorial combination trial (Sica 2012): azilsartan/chlorthalidone 40/25 and 80/25 mg lowered trough ambulatory systolic pressure 28.9 mm Hg — 13.8 mm Hg more than azilsartan 80 mg alone and 13 mm Hg more than chlorthalidone 25 mg alone

cards.type: Double-blind factorial randomised trial, azilsartan medoxomil / chlorthalidone fixed-dose combinations vs components in stage 2 hypertension
cards.people: 1,714 patients with clinic systolic pressure 160–190 mm Hg randomised double-blind in a factorial design to azilsartan medoxomil 0/20/40/80 mg and/or chlorthalidone 0/12.5/25 mg for 8 weeks; mean age 57 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was change to 8 weeks in trough (hour 22–24) ambulatory systolic pressure. For the pooled azilsartan/chlorthalidone 40/25 mg and 80/25 mg groups, trough systolic pressure fell 28.9 mm Hg, exceeding azilsartan 80 mg monotherapy by 13.8 mm Hg and chlorthalidone 25 mg monotherapy by 13 mm Hg (both P < .001). Discontinuation rates and elevations in serum creatinine were dose-dependent and occurred more often in the combination groups.
cards.watchOut: An 8-week factorial pharmacology trial in severe-range clinic hypertension: the combination's extra ~13 mm Hg is expected additivity, bought with dose-dependent discontinuations and creatinine rises, both printed on the card.

cards.headline: Indian phase 3 (Sinha 2021) — single-region trial, flagged: azilsartan 40 and 80 mg were non-inferior to telmisartan 40 mg on trough sitting systolic pressure (−27.2 and −28.2 vs −26.7 mm Hg at 6 weeks)
cards.summary: Indian phase 3 (Sinha 2021) — single-region trial, flagged: azilsartan 40 and 80 mg were non-inferior to telmisartan 40 mg on trough sitting systolic pressure (−27.2 and −28.2 vs −26.7 mm Hg at 6 weeks)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (India — single-region, flagged), azilsartan vs telmisartan in essential hypertension
cards.people: 303 Indian adults with essential hypertension randomised to azilsartan 40 mg, azilsartan 80 mg or telmisartan 40 mg for 6 weeks; primary endpoint change in mean trough sitting clinic systolic pressure at week 6.
cards.result: Trough sitting systolic pressure fell −27.2 mm Hg on azilsartan 40 mg, −28.2 mm Hg on azilsartan 80 mg and −26.7 mm Hg on telmisartan 40 mg (per-protocol; intention-to-treat values near-identical), meeting the trial's non-inferiority criterion against telmisartan. Trough sitting diastolic falls were −13.1, −12.9 and −13.0 mm Hg respectively, not significantly different between groups, and ambulatory pressure differences were likewise similar (P > 0.05). Headache and dizziness were the commonest treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (India) 6-week trial against a mid-dose comparator (telmisartan 40 mg): it supports non-inferiority in that population and design, and adds nothing about outcomes or other populations.
cards.source: Sinha S et al. Evaluation of the Efficacy and Safety of Azilsartan in Adult Patients with Essential Hypertension: A Randomized, Phase-III Clinical Study in India. shelves.title: Velaglucerase alfa in type 1 Gaucher disease: small-N base on the face (N = 25 + N = 34 treated; extension N = 57) — haemoglobin +2.4 g/dL, non-inferior to imiglucerase
shelves.question: In children and adults with type 1 Gaucher disease, does enzyme replacement with velaglucerase alfa, compared with imiglucerase or between its own two doses, improve haemoglobin, platelet counts and spleen volume?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Female · Gaucher Disease · Glucosylceramidase · Hemoglobins · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Count · Recombinant Proteins · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-N rare-disease base, and the counts lead: the entire randomised base for velaglucerase alfa (VPRIV, the tested product as published) in type 1 Gaucher disease is 59 patients across two trials (N = 25 and N = 34 treated), with no placebo-controlled trial. In the 25-patient dose-comparison trial (no untreated arm, so its within-group gains are uncontrolled), haemoglobin rose +2.43 and +2.44 g/dL on the 60 and 45 U/kg doses over 12 months, platelet counts rose about 66% relative, and spleen volume fell 50.4% and 39.9% relative. In the 34-treated-patient head-to-head, velaglucerase 60 U/kg was non-inferior to imiglucerase 60 U/kg on haemoglobin change at 9 months (difference +0.14 g/dL, non-inferiority margin −1.0 g/dL met), with antibodies in 0 of 17 velaglucerase patients vs 4 of 17 (23.5%) on imiglucerase. The third report is a long-term extension of the SAME patients (57 enrolled, 1.2–4.8 years), carded and labelled as a programme report: gains were maintained, with no drug-related serious adverse event. Percent changes are relative measures. Endpoints are haematological / organ-volume surrogates; no fracture, bone-crisis or mortality outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: Dose-comparison phase 3 (Gonzalez 2013) — N = 25: velaglucerase 60 and 45 U/kg both raised haemoglobin ≈ +2.4 g/dL over 12 months; spleen volume fell 50.4% and 39.9% relative; no placebo arm
cards.summary: Dose-comparison phase 3 (Gonzalez 2013) — N = 25: velaglucerase 60 and 45 U/kg both raised haemoglobin ≈ +2.4 g/dL over 12 months; spleen volume fell 50.4% and 39.9% relative; no placebo arm
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind dose-comparison randomised trial (N = 25), velaglucerase alfa 60 vs 45 U/kg in treatment-naïve type 1 Gaucher disease
cards.people: 25 treatment-naïve, anaemic patients with type 1 Gaucher disease aged 4–62 years, randomised double-blind to intravenous velaglucerase alfa 60 U/kg (n = 12) or 45 U/kg (n = 13) every other week for 12 months; primary endpoint change in haemoglobin in the 60 U/kg arm.
cards.result: At 12 months, mean haemoglobin rose +2.43 g/dL on 60 U/kg (+23.3% relative) and +2.44 g/dL on 45 U/kg (+23.8% relative), both P < 0.001 vs baseline. Mean platelet counts rose +65.9% relative (+50.9 × 10⁹/L, P = 0.002) and +66.4% relative (+40.9 × 10⁹/L, P = 0.01). Mean spleen volume fell −50.4% relative (14.0 to 5.8 multiples of normal, P = 0.003) on 60 U/kg and −39.9% relative (14.5 to 9.5 multiples of normal, P = 0.009) on 45 U/kg. No drug-related serious adverse events or withdrawals; one patient developed antibodies.
cards.watchOut: N = 25 and NO untreated or placebo arm: both doses improved, so the trial shows the drug's effects are dose-similar, but the within-group gains themselves are uncontrolled. Small-N rare-disease evidence — the N is printed on the face, as the commissioning row directs.
cards.source: Gonzalez DE et al. Enzyme replacement therapy with velaglucerase alfa in Gaucher disease: Results from a randomized, double-blind, multinational, Phase 3 study. American Journal of Hematology. 2013. PMID: 23386328. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Head-to-head vs imiglucerase (Ben Turkia 2013) — N = 34 treated: velaglucerase was non-inferior on haemoglobin (difference +0.14 g/dL; margin −1.0 g/dL met); antibodies 0/17 vs 4/17 (23.5%) on imiglucerase
cards.summary: Head-to-head vs imiglucerase (Ben Turkia 2013) — N = 34 treated: velaglucerase was non-inferior on haemoglobin (difference +0.14 g/dL; margin −1.0 g/dL met); antibodies 0/17 vs 4/17 (23.5%) on imiglucerase
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind non-inferiority randomised trial (N = 34 treated), velaglucerase alfa vs imiglucerase in treatment-naïve Gaucher disease
cards.people: 35 treatment-naïve patients aged 3–73 years with anaemia and thrombocytopenia or organomegaly, randomised double-blind to velaglucerase alfa or imiglucerase, each 60 U/kg every other week for 9 months; 34 received study drug (17 per arm, intent-to-treat), 20 had been splenectomised.
cards.result: The mean change in haemoglobin from baseline to 9 months differed by +0.14 g/dL (intent-to-treat) and +0.16 g/dL (per-protocol, 15 per arm) between velaglucerase and imiglucerase; the lower bound of the one-sided 97.5% confidence interval lay within the predefined −1.0 g/dL non-inferiority margin in both populations, confirming non-inferiority. Secondary endpoints did not differ significantly. Most adverse events were mild to moderate. No velaglucerase patient developed antibodies to either drug, whereas 4 of 17 imiglucerase patients (23.5%) developed IgG antibodies to imiglucerase, cross-reactive with velaglucerase in one patient.
cards.watchOut: N = 34 treated: non-inferiority on a haemoglobin surrogate against the previous standard of care, with a wide-ish −1.0 g/dL margin for a disease this rare. The immunogenicity contrast (0/17 vs 4/17) rests on very small denominators.
cards.source: Ben Turkia H et al. Velaglucerase alfa enzyme replacement therapy compared with imiglucerase in patients with Gaucher disease. American Journal of Hematology. 2013. PMID: 23400823. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme report — long-term extension (Hughes 2015) — N = 57 (the same patients as the two trials above): gains in haemoglobin, platelets, organ volumes and biomarkers were maintained over 1.2–4.8 years, with no drug-related serious adverse event
cards.summary: Programme report — long-term extension (Hughes 2015) — N = 57 (the same patients as the two trials above): gains in haemoglobin, platelets, organ volumes and biomarkers were maintained over 1.2–4.8 years, with no drug-related serious adverse event
cards.type: Programme report: single long-term extension study of the two phase 3 trials carded above (same patients — not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: 57 patients aged 3–62 years at the baseline of the two phase 3 trials carded above, enrolled into a single extension study on velaglucerase alfa 60 U/kg every other week for 1.2–4.8 years (10 patients had a dose reduction). Labelled programme report: the same trial population followed longer, not independent evidence.
cards.result: Combining the initial trials and the extension, significant improvements in haematology variables, organ volumes, plasma biomarkers and (in adults) lumbar spine bone mineral density Z-score were seen in the first 24 months from baseline and were maintained over longer-term treatment. No patient had a drug-related serious adverse event or withdrew for an adverse event; one patient died after a convulsion reported as unrelated to the study drug, and only one patient tested positive for anti-velaglucerase alfa antibodies.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled extension of the same 59-patient randomised base: maintenance of gains in patients who stayed on treatment cannot exclude survivor and selection effects, and it adds follow-up time, not new patients.
cards.source: Hughes DA et al. Velaglucerase alfa (VPRIV) enzyme replacement therapy in patients with Gaucher disease: Long-term data from phase III clinical trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: three reports, two trials, 59 randomised patients — velaglucerase improves haemoglobin, platelets and spleen volume and matches imiglucerase, on surrogate endpoints with no placebo-controlled trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: three reports, two trials, 59 randomised patients — velaglucerase improves haemoglobin, platelets and spleen volume and matches imiglucerase, on surrogate endpoints with no placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the dose-comparison trial (N = 25), the imiglucerase head-to-head (N = 34 treated) and the extension programme report (N = 57, the same patients).
cards.result: Haemoglobin: +2.43/+2.44 g/dL within-group on the two doses (uncontrolled, no placebo arm); +0.14 g/dL difference vs imiglucerase with non-inferiority met. Platelets: ≈ +66% relative on both doses. Spleen volume: −50.4% and −39.9% relative. Antibodies: 1 of 25 in the dose trial; 0/17 vs 4/17 against imiglucerase. Long-term: gains maintained 1.2–4.8 years, no drug-related serious adverse event. POSSIBLE (benefit) — the standard of evidence the rare-disease shelves in this library rest on, with every N on the face.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Enlicitide in non-HeFH hypercholesterolaemia: LDL −57.1% relative vs +3.0% on placebo (CORALreef Lipids, n = 2,909); beat ezetimibe and bempedoic acid — outcomes pending (HeFH homed at #3106)
shelves.question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk (not restricted to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia), does the oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide (MK-0616), compared with placebo or oral non-statin therapies, lower LDL cholesterol (the non-HeFH slice of the CORALreef programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Apolipoproteins B · Atherosclerosis · Aza Compounds · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, LDL · Double-Blind Method · Hypercholesterolemia · Lipoprotein(a) · PCSK9 Inhibitors · Pyrrolidines · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the non-HeFH slice only (the heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia question is homed at pack #3106, cross-pointed and not re-carded). Enlicitide, the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, lowers LDL cholesterol by injectable-class magnitudes in general hypercholesterolaemia: in the phase 2b trial (published under the development code MK-0616 only) placebo-adjusted LDL changes at 8 weeks were −41.2% to −60.9% relative across the 6–30 mg doses; in CORALreef Lipids (2,909 patients with a prior major atherosclerotic event or at risk of a first event, mean baseline LDL 96.1 mg/dL) mean LDL change at week 24 was −57.1% relative on enlicitide 20 mg vs +3.0% on placebo (adjusted difference −55.8 percentage points), sustained in direction at week 52; and in a 56-day active-comparator trial enlicitide (−64.6% relative) beat bempedoic acid (−6.3%), ezetimibe (−27.8%) and their combination (−36.5%). Adverse-event rates resembled placebo or comparators throughout. All endpoints are LDL cholesterol, a surrogate; the active-comparator trial ran only 56 days, and NO cardiovascular-outcomes trial of enlicitide exists — the injectable PCSK9 class's outcomes record must not be borrowed. Percent LDL changes are relative measures.

cards.headline: Phase 2b (Ballantyne 2023; published as MK-0616): placebo-adjusted LDL changes at 8 weeks were −41.2%, −55.7%, −59.1% and −60.9% relative at 6, 12, 18 and 30 mg (all P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Phase 2b (Ballantyne 2023; published as MK-0616): placebo-adjusted LDL changes at 8 weeks were −41.2%, −55.7%, −59.1% and −60.9% relative at 6, 12, 18 and 30 mg (all P < 0.001)
cards.type: Phase 2b double-blind dose-ranging randomised trial, oral PCSK9 inhibitor MK-0616 (enlicitide) vs placebo in hypercholesterolaemia
cards.people: 381 participants with hypercholesterolaemia across a wide range of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk, randomised (1:1:1:1:1) to MK-0616 (enlicitide) 6, 12, 18 or 30 mg once daily or placebo for 8 weeks, with 8 further weeks of safety follow-up; 380 treated, median age 62 years, 49% women.
cards.result: All doses significantly reduced LDL cholesterol vs placebo at week 8: least-squares mean differences of −41.2% (6 mg), −55.7% (12 mg), −59.1% (18 mg) and −60.9% (30 mg) relative, all P < 0.001 — a clear dose response flattening above 12 mg. Adverse events occurred in 39.5–43.4% on MK-0616 vs 44.0% on placebo, and discontinuations for adverse events were 2 or fewer participants in any group.
cards.watchOut: Published under the development code MK-0616 only — a generic-name search misses this report entirely. Eight weeks on a surrogate endpoint in 381 participants: it establishes dose and pharmacology, not durability or outcomes.
cards.source: Ballantyne CM et al. Phase 2b Randomized Trial of the Oral PCSK9 Inhibitor MK-0616. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023. PMID: 36889610. Registry ID: NCT05261126. cards.headline: CORALreef Lipids (Navar 2026): enlicitide 20 mg lowered LDL −57.1% relative vs +3.0% on placebo at week 24 (adjusted difference −55.8 points, P < 0.001) in 2,909 patients
cards.summary: CORALreef Lipids (Navar 2026): enlicitide 20 mg lowered LDL −57.1% relative vs +3.0% on placebo at week 24 (adjusted difference −55.8 points, P < 0.001) in 2,909 patients
cards.type: Phase 3 multinational double-blind randomised trial (CORALreef Lipids), enlicitide vs placebo in hypercholesterolaemia with ASCVD or ASCVD risk (non-HeFH population)
cards.people: 2,909 participants in the intention-to-treat population (1,935 enlicitide 20 mg daily vs 969 placebo; 5 received neither) — adults with a prior major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease event and LDL ≥55 mg/dL, or at risk of a first event with LDL ≥70 mg/dL; mean age 63 years, 39.3% women, mean baseline LDL 96.1 mg/dL; treatment for 52 weeks, primary endpoint mean percent LDL change at week 24.
cards.result: Mean LDL change at week 24 was −57.1% relative (95% CI −61.8 to −52.5) on enlicitide vs +3.0% (95% CI 0.9 to 5.1) on placebo — an adjusted between-group difference of −55.8 percentage points (95% CI −60.9 to −50.7; P < 0.001). Week-52 LDL change and week-24 non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) changes were also significantly greater with enlicitide (P < 0.001 for all). The incidence of adverse events did not appear to differ between the groups.
cards.watchOut: An LDL surrogate endpoint, however large the effect: this trial does not show enlicitide prevents the events its population is at risk of, and a mean baseline LDL of 96.1 mg/dL means absolute LDL falls vary widely by starting level. The HeFH population is a different question, homed at pack #3106.
cards.source: Navar AM et al. A Placebo-Controlled Trial of the Oral PCSK9 Inhibitor Enlicitide. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026. PMID: 41879224. Registry ID: NCT05952856. cards.headline: Active-comparator phase 3 (Catapano 2026): enlicitide lowered LDL −64.6% relative at 56 days, superior to bempedoic acid (−6.3%), ezetimibe (−27.8%) and the combination (−36.5%)
cards.summary: Active-comparator phase 3 (Catapano 2026): enlicitide lowered LDL −64.6% relative at 56 days, superior to bempedoic acid (−6.3%), ezetimibe (−27.8%) and the combination (−36.5%)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind active-comparator randomised trial (CORALreef AddOn), enlicitide vs bempedoic acid, ezetimibe and their combination on background statins
cards.people: 301 statin-treated adults (98% on moderate- to high-intensity statins) with LDL ≥55 mg/dL and a previous major atherosclerotic event, or LDL ≥70 mg/dL at intermediate-to-high risk of a first event, randomised 2:1:1:2 to enlicitide 20 mg (n = 101), bempedoic acid 180 mg (n = 50), ezetimibe 10 mg (n = 50) or bempedoic acid plus ezetimibe (n = 100) once daily for 56 days; 298 completed.
cards.result: Mean LDL change at day 56 was −64.6% relative (95% CI −68.3 to −60.9) on enlicitide vs −6.3% (−13.5 to 0.8) on bempedoic acid, −27.8% (−32.3 to −23.4) on ezetimibe and −36.5% (−40.8 to −32.2) on the combination — enlicitide superior to each comparator (all P < 0.001). Reductions in apolipoprotein B and non-HDL cholesterol were also greater on enlicitide (all P < 0.001). Proportions with adverse events and discontinuations for adverse events were similar across arms.
cards.watchOut: Only 56 days, with no placebo arm and small comparator groups (n = 50 each for bempedoic acid and ezetimibe alone): a short-term LDL ranking among oral add-ons, not a durability or outcomes comparison.
cards.source: Catapano AL et al. Oral PCSK9 Inhibitor Enlicitide Versus Oral Nonstatin Therapies: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2026. PMID: 42017875. Registry ID: NCT06450366. shelves.title: Chromogranin A reference intervals are assay- and sample-type-bound: serum 21.0–108.0 vs plasma 31.0–153.0 ng/mL; second serum interval 30.3–94.4 ng/mL; 44% decay at 48 hours
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for chromogranin A — the central 95% range in serum and in EDTA plasma — how far apart are the intervals given by different assays measuring nominally the same protein, how large are within-person and between-person biological variation, and how fast does the measured value decay in a stored sample?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, on three independent datasets. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep have no chromogranin A reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing neuroendocrine secretion biology only. The intervals are assay- and sample-type-specific to an unusual degree, and that specificity is the content: in paired samples from 145 healthy male donors, EDTA plasma ran a median 26% higher than serum (reference ranges 31.0–153.0 vs 21.0–108.0 ng/mL, immunoradiometric assay); a second serum dataset (120 healthy individuals) gave 30.3–94.4 ng/mL, with within-person variation 11.9% vs between-person 50.2% and measured values decaying 44% by 48 hours at 4 °C; and an ELISA evaluation found a cross-assay slope of 9.05 against the reference-laboratory method. No interval is printed without its assay and sample type.

cards.headline: Serum vs EDTA plasma in 145 healthy male blood donors (Glinicki 2015): plasma chromogranin A runs 15–75% higher (median 26%) — separate reference ranges 21.0–108.0 ng/mL (serum) and 31.0–153.0 ng/mL (plasma) by immunoradiometric assay
cards.summary: Serum vs EDTA plasma in 145 healthy male blood donors (Glinicki 2015): plasma chromogranin A runs 15–75% higher (median 26%) — separate reference ranges 21.0–108.0 ng/mL (serum) and 31.0–153.0 ng/mL (plasma) by immunoradiometric assay
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (paired serum / plasma reference ranges, immunoradiometric assay)
cards.people: 145 healthy male blood donors aged 19–61 years (mean 35.7); paired blood collected into EDTA2K (plasma) and clot-activator (serum) tubes; chromogranin A measured by immunoradiometric kit (CIS bio, France). Men only — printed as such.
cards.result: Median chromogranin A was 42.0 ng/mL in serum (range 16–108) vs 58.0 ng/mL in EDTA plasma (range 23–153); plasma values were 15–75% higher than paired serum values (median difference 26%; P < 0.0001), with a serum–plasma correlation of r = 0.8493. The 2.5th–97.5th percentile reference ranges were 21.0–108.0 ng/mL for serum and 31.0–153.0 ng/mL for plasma. The authors conclude the serum–plasma difference demands separate reference ranges by sample type, and that each laboratory should recommend only one sample material.
cards.watchOut: Men only, one assay: the serum and plasma intervals are not interchangeable, and neither interval transfers to a different assay — see the cross-assay bias card below.
cards.source: Glinicki P et al. Comparison of chromogranin A (CgA) levels in serum and plasma (EDTA2K) and the respective reference ranges in healthy males. Endokrynologia Polska. 2015. PMID: 25754282. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reference interval and stability in 120 healthy individuals (Pedersen 2014): median 41.2 ng/mL, interval 30.3–94.4 ng/mL — but measured values decayed 15.6% at 24 hours and 44% at 48 hours at 4 °C
cards.summary: Reference interval and stability in 120 healthy individuals (Pedersen 2014): median 41.2 ng/mL, interval 30.3–94.4 ng/mL — but measured values decayed 15.6% at 24 hours and 44% at 48 hours at 4 °C
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (reference interval, biological variation and sample stability)
cards.people: Serum samples from 120 healthy individuals for the reference interval; a separate preanalytical study in 10 healthy subjects sampled at three time points over three days, fasting and non-fasting, with re-measurement after storage at 4 °C.
cards.result: The median chromogranin A concentration was 41.2 ng/mL with a reference interval of 30.3–94.4 ng/mL (2.5–97.5 percentile). Within-subject biological variation was 11.9% vs between-subject variation of 50.2%; analytical imprecision was 4.3%. Concentrations did not vary with fasting (P = 0.74), sex (P = 0.66) or time of day (P = 0.30). On re-analysis at 4 °C, measured concentrations decayed significantly — a mean decrease of 15.6% after 24 hours and 44% after 48 hours — making sample stability a major preanalytical issue for the assay tested.
cards.watchOut: The storage-decay finding prints beside any interval claim from this shelf: a sample re-measured at 48 hours can read 44% lower, so the interval applies to promptly handled samples on this assay, not to stored ones.
cards.source: Pedersen L et al. Preanalytical factors of importance for measurement of Chromogranin A. Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry. 2014. PMID: 24804936. cards.headline: Assay-evaluation dataset (Lim 2019): the CisBio ELISA showed acceptable precision but a large systematic bias against the reference-laboratory assay (slope 9.05) — chromogranin A results are method-specific; preliminary reference study in 60 healthy volunteers in serum and 60 in plasma
cards.summary: Assay-evaluation dataset (Lim 2019): the CisBio ELISA showed acceptable precision but a large systematic bias against the reference-laboratory assay (slope 9.05) — chromogranin A results are method-specific; preliminary reference study in 60 healthy volunteers in serum and 60 in plasma
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (assay evaluation with preliminary reference-range study, ELISA)
cards.people: Analytical evaluation of the CisBio chromogranin A ELISA, including 70 waste serum samples from a clinical laboratory compared with a reference laboratory's proprietary ELISA, paired serum/plasma samples from 24 patients, and a preliminary reference-range study in healthy volunteers (60 in serum, 60 in plasma). The fetched abstract prints no numeric reference-range values from that preliminary study, and this card claims none.
cards.result: Within-run precision ranged from 3.0% to 5.1% and between-run precision from 4.8% to 12.9%; the limit of blank was 2.4 ng/mL and recovery ranged from 88% to 102%. Against the reference-laboratory assay there was a statistically significant bias: comparison slope 9.05, intercept −18.0, correlation coefficient 0.955. Serum and plasma values correlated well within the CisBio method. The authors conclude analytical performance was acceptable but chromogranin A results are method-specific owing to lack of standardisation and differing antibodies.
cards.watchOut: A slope of 9.05 against another assay is the shelf's central warning: a numeric chromogranin A result — and any interval applied to it — is meaningless without its assay named alongside.
cards.source: Lim M et al. Evaluation of CisBio ELISA for Chromogranin A Measurement. The journal of applied laboratory medicine. 2019. PMID: 31639703. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: IV clevidipine in cardiac surgery: target BP in ~5–6 minutes (failure ~8% vs ~80% on placebo); ECLIPSE outcomes null except mortality vs nitroprusside
shelves.question: In adults undergoing cardiac surgery who develop acute perioperative hypertension, does intravenous clevidipine, compared with placebo, nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside or nicardipine, control blood pressure — and how did the comparators differ on 30-day death, myocardial infarction, stroke and renal dysfunction (the ESCAPE / ECLIPSE programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Calcium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Preoperative Care · Pyridines/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Acute Disease · Adult · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Pyridines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Calcium Channel Blockers/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hypertension/drug therapy,physiopathology · Intraoperative Complications/drug therapy · Nicardipine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Nitroglycerin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Nitroprusside/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Perioperative Care
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for rapid perioperative blood-pressure control, a surrogate endpoint. In ESCAPE-1 and ESCAPE-2, intravenous clevidipine failed to reach target in only 7.5% (4/53) and 8.2% (5/61) of treated patients vs 82.7% (43/52) and 79.6% (39/49) on placebo infusion, with median times to target of 6.0 and 5.3 minutes — contrasts against placebo in pre-selected hypertensive patients, printed with their treated denominators. The clinically informative report is ECLIPSE (three open-label trials in one paper, 1,512 treated): 30-day myocardial infarction, stroke and renal dysfunction did not differ against nitroglycerin, nitroprusside or nicardipine, and mortality did not differ vs nitroglycerin or nicardipine but was higher on nitroprusside than on clevidipine (P = 0.04). No patient-important outcome benefit over modern comparators is shown.

cards.headline: ESCAPE-1, preoperative (Levy 2007): treatment failure 7.5% (4/53) on clevidipine vs 82.7% (43/52) on placebo (P < 0.0001); median time to target systolic reduction 6.0 minutes
cards.summary: ESCAPE-1, preoperative (Levy 2007): treatment failure 7.5% (4/53) on clevidipine vs 82.7% (43/52) on placebo (P < 0.0001); median time to target systolic reduction 6.0 minutes
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ESCAPE-1), preoperative cardiac surgery
cards.people: 152 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery with current or recent hypertension were randomised to clevidipine or placebo (20% lipid emulsion) preoperatively; 105 met post-randomisation entry criteria (systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg after arterial catheter insertion) and received infusion (0.4–8.0 µg/kg/min) for at least 30 minutes. The failure rates below use the treated denominators (53 vs 52), printed as such.
cards.result: Treatment failure (failure to reduce systolic BP by ≥15% from baseline, or discontinuation for any reason) occurred in 7.5% (4/53) on clevidipine vs 82.7% (43/52) on placebo (P < 0.0001); treatment success was 92.5% on clevidipine. Median time to target (≥15% systolic reduction) was 6.0 minutes (95% CI 6 to 8). A modest increase in heart rate occurred during clevidipine administration, and adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The huge contrast is against a placebo lipid infusion in patients pre-selected for systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg — it shows the drug lowers blood pressure, which was never in doubt; only 105 of 152 randomised patients entered the treated analysis, and blood-pressure control is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Levy JH et al. Clevidipine effectively and rapidly controls blood pressure preoperatively in cardiac surgery patients: the results of the randomized, placebo-controlled efficacy study of clevidipine assessing its preoperative antihypertensive effect in cardiac surgery-1. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2007. PMID: 17898366. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (escape-1), preoperative cardiac surgery 152 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery with current or recent hypertension were randomised to clevidipine or placebo (20% lipid emulsion) preoperatively; 105 met post-randomisation entry criteria (systolic bp ≥160 mm hg after arterial catheter insertion) and received infusion (0.4–8.0 µg/kg/min) for at least 30 minutes. the failure rates below use the treated denominators (53 vs 52), printed as such. treatment failure (failure to reduce systolic bp by ≥15% from baseline, or discontinuation for any reason) occurred in 7.5% (4/53) on clevidipine vs 82.7% (43/52) on placebo (p < 0.0001); treatment success was 92.5% on clevidipine. median time to target (≥15% systolic reduction) was 6.0 minutes (95% ci 6 to 8). a modest increase in heart rate occurred during clevidipine administration, and adverse events were similar between groups. the huge contrast is against a placebo lipid infusion in patients pre-selected for systolic bp ≥160 mm hg — it shows the drug lowers blood pressure, which was never in doubt; only 105 of 152 randomised patients entered the treated analysis, and blood-pressure control is a surrogate endpoint. levy jh et al. clevidipine effectively and rapidly controls blood pressure preoperatively in cardiac surgery patients: the results of the randomized, placebo-controlled efficacy study of clevidipine assessing its preoperative antihypertensive effect in cardiac surgery-1. anesthesia and analgesia. 2007. pmid: 17898366. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · antihypertensive agents/therapeutic use · blood pressure/drug effects · calcium channel blockers/therapeutic use · cardiac surgical procedures · double-blind method · female · humans · hypertension/drug therapy · male · middle aged · preoperative care · pyridines/therapeutic use · treatment outcome · vasodilator agents/therapeutic use

cards.headline: ESCAPE-2, postoperative (Singla 2008): treatment failure 8.2% (5/61) on clevidipine vs 79.6% (39/49) on placebo (P < 0.0001); median time to target 5.3 minutes
cards.summary: ESCAPE-2, postoperative (Singla 2008): treatment failure 8.2% (5/61) on clevidipine vs 79.6% (39/49) on placebo (P < 0.0001); median time to target 5.3 minutes
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ESCAPE-2), postoperative cardiac surgery
cards.people: 206 patients undergoing cardiac surgery were randomised preoperatively; 110 met post-randomisation entry criteria (systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg within 4 hours postoperatively, needing ≥15% reduction) and received clevidipine (0.4–8.0 µg/kg/min) or placebo lipid emulsion for 30 minutes to a maximum of 1 hour. Failure rates use the treated denominators (61 vs 49), printed as such.
cards.result: Treatment failure (inability to decrease systolic BP by ≥15% within 30 minutes, or discontinuation for any reason) occurred in 8.2% (5/61) on clevidipine vs 79.6% (39/49) on placebo (P < 0.0001); treatment success was 91.8% on clevidipine. Median time to target systolic pressure was 5.3 minutes (95% CI 4 to 7). No clinically significant increase in heart rate was observed, and adverse event rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Same caveat as ESCAPE-1: a placebo-infusion comparator in pre-selected hypertensive patients, 110 of 206 randomised patients in the treated analysis, and a blood-pressure (surrogate) endpoint — the patient-important outcome evidence is the ECLIPSE card below.
cards.source: Singla N et al. Treatment of acute postoperative hypertension in cardiac surgery patients: an efficacy study of clevidipine assessing its postoperative antihypertensive effect in cardiac surgery-2 (ESCAPE-2), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2008. PMID: 18635468. Registry ID: none in the record.
