cards.headline: ECLIPSE programme (Aronson 2008) — three prospective randomised open-label comparison trials reported in one paper, labelled as such: no difference in 30-day death / MI / stroke / renal dysfunction for MI, stroke or renal dysfunction; mortality higher on nitroprusside than clevidipine (P = 0.04), not different vs nitroglycerin or nicardipine
cards.summary: ECLIPSE programme (Aronson 2008) — three prospective randomised open-label comparison trials reported in one paper, labelled as such: no difference in 30-day death / MI / stroke / renal dysfunction for MI, stroke or renal dysfunction; mortality higher on nitroprusside than clevidipine (P = 0.04), not different vs nitroglycerin or nicardipine
cards.type: Three prospective randomised open-label comparison trials in one report (ECLIPSE programme), clevidipine vs nitroglycerin / nitroprusside / nicardipine
cards.people: 1,964 patients undergoing cardiac surgery at 61 centres were enrolled across three parallel randomised open-label trials; 1,512 met post-randomisation criteria requiring acute hypertension treatment and were randomised 1:1 to clevidipine vs nitroglycerin or nitroprusside perioperatively, or vs nicardipine postoperatively.
cards.result: The primary safety outcome (30-day incidence of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or renal dysfunction) did not differ for myocardial infarction, stroke or renal dysfunction between clevidipine and any comparator. Mortality did not differ between clevidipine and nitroglycerin or nicardipine, but was significantly higher on sodium nitroprusside than on clevidipine (P = 0.04). Clevidipine kept blood pressure within the prespecified range more effectively than nitroglycerin (P = 0.0006) or nitroprusside (P = 0.003), and was equivalent to nicardipine on the prespecified range, with fewer excursions beyond narrowed limits.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trials, and the nitroprusside mortality contrast is a secondary reading of a safety composite — it is the programme's only patient-important outcome difference and must not be upgraded into a proven mortality benefit of clevidipine.
cards.source: Aronson S et al. The ECLIPSE trials: comparative studies of clevidipine to nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside, and nicardipine for acute hypertension treatment in cardiac surgery patients. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2008. PMID: 18806012. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: clevidipine controls perioperative blood pressure within minutes (ESCAPE failure ~8% vs ~80% on placebo infusion), while ECLIPSE — the clinically informative report — found patient-important outcomes null except for higher mortality on nitroprusside than clevidipine
cards.summary: Synthesis: clevidipine controls perioperative blood pressure within minutes (ESCAPE failure ~8% vs ~80% on placebo infusion), while ECLIPSE — the clinically informative report — found patient-important outcomes null except for higher mortality on nitroprusside than clevidipine
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The ESCAPE trials (105 and 110 treated patients from 152 and 206 randomised) show rapid, titratable blood-pressure lowering against placebo infusion — a pharmacological effect on a surrogate endpoint, in patients pre-selected for hypertension. ECLIPSE (1,512 treated of 1,964 enrolled, three open-label trials in one report) is the comparative evidence: no difference in myocardial infarction, stroke or renal dysfunction against nitroglycerin, nitroprusside or nicardipine; mortality no different vs nitroglycerin or nicardipine and higher on nitroprusside than clevidipine (P = 0.04). Blood-pressure control within prespecified ranges favoured clevidipine over nitroglycerin and nitroprusside and matched nicardipine. The single-arm ACCELERATE intracerebral-haemorrhage pilot and the VELOCITY subgroup analysis are programme support only and are not carded, as the commissioning row directs.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: ESCAPE denominators are the treated subsets, and ECLIPSE's nitroprusside mortality contrast is a secondary reading of open-label safety data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Rilmenidine: old small base — BP normalised 61% vs 23% on placebo at 4 weeks (N = 126); LVH regression no different from nifedipine (per-protocol N = 56)
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension, does the centrally acting imidazoline-receptor agonist rilmenidine, compared with placebo, nifedipine or lisinopril, lower blood pressure and regress left ventricular hypertrophy?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Agonists/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy,physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Oxazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Random Allocation · Rilmenidine · Xerostomia/diagnosis · Adult · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Calcium Channel Blockers/therapeutic use · Diastole · Echocardiography · Electrocardiography, Ambulatory · Hypertension/complications · Hypertrophy, Left Ventricular/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Nifedipine/therapeutic use · Oxazoles/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Heart Rate/drug effects · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Lisinopril/therapeutic use · Metabolic Syndrome/complications · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — old, small, surrogate-only, and those flags lead. Rilmenidine's randomised base is a 1988 programme paper (two 4-week double-blind placebo-controlled trials in one report, 126 patients; blood-pressure normalisation 61% vs 23%), a 1-year double-blind LVH trial vs nifedipine whose result is a per-protocol analysis of 56 patients with no between-group difference (LV mass index −22.1 vs −26.9 g/m², P = 0.5), and a 12-week open-label ambulatory trial vs lisinopril in 51 women with no significant between-group blood-pressure difference. There is no outcomes trial, the agent was never marketed in the US, and blood pressure and LV mass are surrogates. The three reports' effects are never pooled — different comparators answer different questions.

cards.headline: Placebo-controlled programme paper (Ostermann 1988) — two double-blind multicentre trials reported in one paper, labelled as such: blood pressure normalised in 61% on rilmenidine vs 23% on placebo (P < 0.001) over 4 weeks
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled programme paper (Ostermann 1988) — two double-blind multicentre trials reported in one paper, labelled as such: blood pressure normalised in 61% on rilmenidine vs 23% on placebo (P < 0.001) over 4 weeks
cards.type: Two double-blind multicentre placebo-controlled trials in one report (programme paper), 4 weeks each
cards.people: 126 patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension after a 4-week placebo run-in: study 1 (mild hypertension) rilmenidine 1 mg/day (n = 31) vs placebo (n = 35) for 4 weeks; study 2 (moderate hypertension) rilmenidine 1 mg twice daily (n = 30) vs placebo (n = 30) for 4 weeks. Two component trials in one paper — counted as one report.
cards.result: Rilmenidine significantly reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure vs placebo in both studies. Blood pressure was normalised (systolic <160 and diastolic ≤90 mm Hg) in 61% of rilmenidine patients vs 23% on placebo (P < 0.001); at 1 mg/day, 84% of mild hypertensive patients were normalised. All 61 rilmenidine patients completed the studies; 8 of 65 placebo patients were withdrawn for rising blood pressure. Dry mouth did not differ significantly from placebo at 1 mg/day; at 2 mg/day dry mouth was significantly more frequent but transient, no longer significant at study end; daytime drowsiness did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks per component trial, 126 patients total, and a normalisation threshold (diastolic ≤90 mm Hg) from 1988 practice — this is short-term surrogate evidence, and the two component trials are never counted as two independent reports.
cards.source: Ostermann G et al. Efficacy and acceptability of rilmenidine for mild to moderate systemic hypertension. The American journal of cardiology. 1988. PMID: 2894164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LVH trial vs nifedipine (Sadowski 1998): left ventricular mass index fell 22.1 ± 23.3 g/m² on rilmenidine vs 26.9 ± 29.5 g/m² on slow-release nifedipine over 1 year — both P < 0.001 within group, between-group difference NOT significant (P = 0.5), in a per-protocol analysis of 56
cards.summary: LVH trial vs nifedipine (Sadowski 1998): left ventricular mass index fell 22.1 ± 23.3 g/m² on rilmenidine vs 26.9 ± 29.5 g/m² on slow-release nifedipine over 1 year — both P < 0.001 within group, between-group difference NOT significant (P = 0.5), in a per-protocol analysis of 56
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial vs slow-release nifedipine, 1 year (per-protocol primary analysis)
cards.people: 73 patients with essential mild-to-moderate hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy were included (35 rilmenidine 1–2 mg/day, 38 slow-release nifedipine 40 mg/day), double-blind for 1 year after a 1-month placebo run-in; 56 patients (24 vs 32) completed without major protocol deviation and form the per-protocol primary analysis.
cards.result: Left ventricular mass index fell from 176.9 ± 41.3 to 154.8 ± 40.2 g/m² on rilmenidine (a decrease of 22.1 ± 23.3 g/m²; P < 0.001) and from 172.6 ± 35.1 to 145.6 ± 36.4 g/m² on nifedipine (a decrease of 26.9 ± 29.5 g/m²; P < 0.001); the between-group difference was not significant (P = 0.5). Diastolic pressure was controlled to ≈88.5 mm Hg on rilmenidine vs ≈85.6 mm Hg on nifedipine in the per-protocol population. Fifteen patients withdrew and two completed with a major protocol deviation.
cards.watchOut: A per-protocol analysis of 56 of 73 included patients, on a surrogate (LV mass index): within-group falls in both arms with no between-group difference show blood-pressure lowering regresses LVH — they do not show any rilmenidine-specific effect.
cards.source: Sadowski Z et al. Regression of left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertensive patients after 1 year of treatment with rilmenidine: a double-blind, randomized, controlled (versus nifedipine) study. Journal of hypertension. Supplement : official journal of the International Society of Hypertension. 1998. PMID: 9747912. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ambulatory trial vs lisinopril (Anichkov 2005): 24-hour ambulatory pressure fell −11.9/−7.7 mm Hg on rilmenidine vs −11.0/−6.7 mm Hg on lisinopril over 12 weeks (no significant between-group difference); 24-hour heart rate fell −3.6 vs +0.3 bpm (P = 0.002)
cards.summary: Ambulatory trial vs lisinopril (Anichkov 2005): 24-hour ambulatory pressure fell −11.9/−7.7 mm Hg on rilmenidine vs −11.0/−6.7 mm Hg on lisinopril over 12 weeks (no significant between-group difference); 24-hour heart rate fell −3.6 vs +0.3 bpm (P = 0.002)
cards.type: Randomised open-label blinded-endpoint ambulatory-BP trial vs lisinopril, 12 weeks (women with metabolic syndrome)
cards.people: 51 hypertensive women with metabolic syndrome randomised in an open-label, blinded-endpoint study to rilmenidine 1 mg (n = 24) or lisinopril 10 mg (n = 27) once or twice daily for 12 weeks, with ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring before and after treatment.
cards.result: Ambulatory 24-hour systolic / diastolic pressure fell −11.9 ± 1.9 / −7.7 ± 0.8 mm Hg on rilmenidine and −11.0 ± 1.8 / −6.7 ± 0.7 mm Hg on lisinopril (both P < 0.001 within group), with no significant between-group difference. Rilmenidine reduced 24-hour heart rate (−3.6 ± 0.8 vs +0.3 ± 0.8 bpm; P = 0.002) and produced a greater fall in night-time diastolic pressure (P = 0.046). Rilmenidine significantly increased HDL cholesterol and decreased fasting glucose within group (P = 0.009 and P = 0.012), but between-group differences in lipids and glucose were not significant.
cards.watchOut: 51 women, open-label, 12 weeks, surrogate endpoints throughout — and the three reports on this shelf use three different comparators (placebo, nifedipine, lisinopril) answering three different questions; their blood-pressure effects are never pooled.

cards.result: Three reports, three comparators, no pooling: the 1988 programme paper (two 4-week double-blind trials in one report, 126 patients) shows short-term blood-pressure lowering vs placebo; the 1998 LVH trial (73 included, 56 per-protocol) shows LV mass regression indistinguishable from slow-release nifedipine over 1 year; and the 2005 ambulatory trial (51 women with metabolic syndrome) shows 24-hour lowering indistinguishable from lisinopril over 12 weeks, with a heart-rate difference (−3.6 vs +0.3 bpm). Blood pressure and LV mass index are surrogate endpoints; there is no cardiovascular-outcomes trial, and the 1-year open acceptability study in the programme is uncontrolled for efficacy and is not carded, as the commissioning row directs. Sizes are printed on the face of every card, as the row requires.

shelves.title: IV fenoldopam vs nitroprusside in acute severe hypertension (PARTIAL vs pack #2911): equivalent blood-pressure control in three pre-modern trials — a surrogate only, no clinical outcomes
shelves.question: In adults with acute severe hypertension, does intravenous fenoldopam (a dopamine-1 agonist), compared with sodium nitroprusside, control blood pressure as effectively and safely? PARTIAL beside pack #2911, which homes fenoldopam in cardiac-surgery acute kidney injury — that question is not re-asked here.
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Pressure · Female · Fenoldopam · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroprusside · Prospective Studies · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference), on a PARTIAL slice beside pack #2911. This shelf cards only the acute-severe-hypertension comparison; fenoldopam in cardiac-surgery acute kidney injury is homed at pack #2911 and is not re-carded here. Three randomised comparisons from 1990–1995 — all open-label or single-blind, all against sodium nitroprusside, all with blood pressure (a surrogate) as the outcome — found the two agents equivalent in controlling and maintaining diastolic pressure: the Fenoldopam Study Group trial (183 enrolled; 15 patients per arm excluded from the efficacy analysis for protocol violations), a 33-patient single-blind trial, and an open-label crisis study whose abstract prints no N (none is claimed here). Equivalence here means equivalent pressure lowering over hours, in trials far too small to compare harms and from the pre-modern era; neither agent was compared with any modern alternative, and this slice's tidy equivalence is not a reason to prefer fenoldopam over modern agents. A renal-effects substudy (n = 11) is sub-floor — support only, never load-bearing, not counted and not carded.

cards.headline: Fenoldopam Study Group RCT (Panacek 1995): fenoldopam and nitroprusside were equivalent in controlling and maintaining diastolic pressure in 183 enrolled patients with acute severe hypertension
cards.summary: Fenoldopam Study Group RCT (Panacek 1995): fenoldopam and nitroprusside were equivalent in controlling and maintaining diastolic pressure in 183 enrolled patients with acute severe hypertension
cards.type: Prospective randomised open-label multicentre trial (Fenoldopam Study Group), IV fenoldopam vs sodium nitroprusside
cards.people: 183 adults (90 fenoldopam, 93 nitroprusside) aged 21–80 years with supine diastolic blood pressure at least 120 mm Hg, enrolled at 24 academic centres, randomised open-label to intravenous fenoldopam or sodium nitroprusside titrated to a diastolic pressure of 95–110 mm Hg (or a maximum 40 mm Hg reduction) for at least 6 hours; 15 patients per arm were excluded from the efficacy analysis for protocol violations.
cards.result: The two agents were equivalent in controlling and maintaining diastolic blood pressure. Nitroprusside reduced systolic pressure slightly more during the first 0.5–1 hour, and both systolic and diastolic pressure were reduced more on fenoldopam in the subset receiving infusions during the 12–24-hour period. Adverse-effect profiles and times to achieve target pressure were similar, with no clinically relevant difference.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with 30 of 183 enrolled patients (15 per arm) excluded from the efficacy analysis for protocol violations; the outcome is blood pressure over hours — a surrogate — with no clinical-outcome measurement.

cards.headline: Single-blind RCT (Pilmer 1993): 33 patients — fenoldopam lowered pressure from 217/145 to 187/112 mm Hg and nitroprusside from 210/136 to 172/103 mm Hg, with no significant difference in effect or adverse events
cards.summary: Single-blind RCT (Pilmer 1993): 33 patients — fenoldopam lowered pressure from 217/145 to 187/112 mm Hg and nitroprusside from 210/136 to 172/103 mm Hg, with no significant difference in effect or adverse events
cards.type: Randomised single-blind trial, IV fenoldopam mesylate vs sodium nitroprusside
cards.people: 33 patients with severe systemic hypertension (diastolic blood pressure at least 120 mm Hg), randomised single-blind to intravenous fenoldopam mesylate (n = 15) or sodium nitroprusside (n = 18), each titrated to a goal diastolic pressure of 95–110 mm Hg (or a reduction of at least 40 mm Hg).
cards.result: Fenoldopam reduced blood pressure from 217/145 to 187/112 mm Hg at a mean infusion rate of 0.5 µg/kg/min, with a mean time to goal of 1.5 (SD 1.4) hours; nitroprusside reduced pressure from 210/136 to 172/103 mm Hg at 1.2 µg/kg/min, with a mean response time of 2 (SD 2.5) hours. There was no significant difference in the magnitude of effect or in adverse-event rates between the two agents.
cards.watchOut: Only 33 patients, single-blind, from 1993: it can speak to short-term pressure lowering only, and is far too small to compare uncommon harms.
cards.source: Pilmer BL et al. Fenoldopam mesylate versus sodium nitroprusside in the acute management of severe systemic hypertension. Journal of clinical pharmacology. 1993. PMID: 8103527. cards.type: Randomised open-label comparison, IV fenoldopam mesylate vs sodium nitroprusside in severe hypertension / hypertensive crisis (N not documented in the fetched abstract)
cards.people: Patients with severe hypertension or hypertensive crisis randomised in an open-label comparison of intravenous fenoldopam mesylate versus sodium nitroprusside, titrated to a diastolic pressure below 110 mm Hg (or a reduction of at least 40 mm Hg for the highest pressures), maintained for at least 1 hour and then weaned over 2 hours. The fetched abstract prints no participant number, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: Both agents successfully controlled blood pressure in all patients by the end of the maintenance periods, and analysis of variance showed the changes induced by fenoldopam did not differ significantly from those induced by nitroprusside for any measured variable. The incidence of listed side effects was similar in both groups. Toxic levels of thiocyanate were detected in 2 patients treated with nitroprusside, which the authors note might favour fenoldopam where renal function is decreased.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched abstract — printed as such, per the standing labelling rule; a 1990 open-label study with a blood-pressure endpoint and a 2-patient thiocyanate observation that is a safety signal, not a comparative harm finding.

shelves.title: Serum ceruloplasmin reference values: upper limit ~25 mg/dL in men vs ~45 mg/dL in young women (1,706 donors); oral contraceptives raise the mean ~65% (181 vs 110 IU/ml, 1987)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for serum ceruloplasmin — the central range by sex and age — how large is the sex difference, how strongly do oestrogen exposure (oral contraceptives, pregnancy, lactation) and population move the values, and why do the published datasets report in different units (mg/dL vs IU/ml) that cannot be merged?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Ceruloplasmin/analysis,metabolism · Male · Female · Adult · Reference Values · Middle Aged · Italy · Adolescent · Young Adult · Aged · Healthy Volunteers · Biomarkers/blood · Age Factors · Iron/blood · Sex Factors · Ceruloplasmin/analysis · Contraceptive Agents, Female/pharmacology · Copper/blood · Parity · Zinc/blood · Breast Feeding · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Confidence Intervals · Democratic Republic of the Congo · Evaluation Studies as Topic · Haptoglobins/analysis · Immunodiffusion · Inflammation/blood · Orosomucoid/analysis · Pregnancy/blood · Albumins · Ceruloplasmin · Cholesterol/blood · Oman · Prevalence · Smoking · Vitamin A/blood · alpha-Tocopherol/blood
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no ceruloplasmin reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing copper transport and acute-phase biology only, and says so. Four independent datasets, never pooled: the modern anchor (1,706 healthy Italian blood donors, 2024) derives quantile-regression reference curves in mg/dL — the upper reference value plateauing at about 25 mg/dL around age 25 in men, while in women it rose to about 45 mg/dL in young adults before falling below 30 mg/dL after the fifties. The oestrogen effect is large: in 200 healthy young women (1987), oral-contraceptive users averaged 181 ± 43.9 IU/ml against 110 ± 22.7 IU/ml in non-users — a ~65% higher mean, a relative comparison labelled as such. Units are assay-era property (IU/ml in 1987 vs mg/dL in 2024) and are never converted or merged. Three of the four datasets are women-only or women-predominant, so sex and hormonal status print on every card and no mixed 'adult range' is offered. The Zairean dataset's non-pregnant / non-lactating subgroup is small (N = 27) and prints as such; the Omani dataset's N is not documented in its record and prints as such. This shelf gives reference values only — Wilson-disease diagnostic accuracy is a different question and is not asked here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Italian blood-donor reference curves (Pelucchi 2024): 1,706 healthy donors — upper reference value plateaus at ~25 mg/dL in men, but reaches ~45 mg/dL in young women before falling below 30 mg/dL after the fifties
cards.summary: Italian blood-donor reference curves (Pelucchi 2024): 1,706 healthy donors — upper reference value plateaus at ~25 mg/dL in men, but reaches ~45 mg/dL in young women before falling below 30 mg/dL after the fifties
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (quantile-regression reference curves, healthy blood donors)
cards.people: 1,706 consecutive healthy Italian blood donors (1,285 men and 421 women) aged 18 to 65 years, enrolled May 2019 to July 2022; serum ceruloplasmin reference intervals identified through quantile regression, with relationships to age, sex, iron and metabolic status examined by linear regression.
cards.result: Mean serum ceruloplasmin was influenced by sex and slightly by age. The lower reference value rose slightly with increasing age in both men and women and did not appear to be influenced by sex. The upper reference value differed by sex and age: in men it increased to a plateau of about 25 mg/dL around 25 years of age, while in women it initially increased to around 45 mg/dL in young adults and then fell sharply to below 30 mg/dL for adults after their fifties — a pattern the authors suggest possibly reflects differing hormonal status. The study's product is sex- and age-specific reference curves, not a single adult interval.
cards.watchOut: Blood donors are a screened-healthy population and the female curve's high young-adult upper value (~45 mg/dL) is precisely why a single mixed-sex interval would mislead; the record reports the curves' shape and plateau values, and this card claims no single 2.5th–97.5th percentile pair from it.
cards.source: Pelucchi S et al. Reference Values of Ceruloplasmin across the Adult Age Range in a Large Italian Healthy Population. The journal of applied laboratory medicine. 2024. PMID: 39239918. cards.headline: Oestrogen effect in young women (Heese 1987): ceruloplasmin 181 ± 43.9 IU/ml in oral-contraceptive users vs 110 ± 22.7 IU/ml in non-users — a ~65% higher mean (relative comparison)
cards.summary: Oestrogen effect in young women (Heese 1987): ceruloplasmin 181 ± 43.9 IU/ml in oral-contraceptive users vs 110 ± 22.7 IU/ml in non-users — a ~65% higher mean (relative comparison)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (reference values partitioned by oral-contraceptive use, women only)
cards.people: 200 healthy nulliparous female students aged 18–23 years resident in Cape Town: 100 who had been taking low-dosage triphasic oral contraceptives for a minimum of 3 months, and 100 not taking contraceptives; reference values established for serum copper, ceruloplasmin, zinc and haematological indices.
cards.result: Mean ceruloplasmin was 181 ± 43.9 IU/ml in contraceptive users versus 110 ± 22.7 IU/ml in non-users — users' mean about 65% higher, a relative comparison labelled as such; both differences from non-users were statistically significant. Mean serum copper showed the same pattern (26.5 ± 4.2 µmol/L in users versus 16.9 ± 2.7 µmol/L in non-users), while serum zinc did not differ (14.1 ± 2.1 vs 14.7 ± 2.0 µmol/L). There were no differences in haematological parameters except a significantly higher mean corpuscular volume in contraceptive users.
cards.watchOut: Units are IU/ml (1987 assay era) and are never converted to or merged with the mg/dL values of the 2024 dataset; the population is women aged 18–23 only, and the contraceptive formulations of 1987 are not today's — the card establishes the size and direction of the oestrogen effect, not a current pill-specific value.

cards.headline: Zairean women's reference levels (Kuvibidila 1994): ceruloplasmin and CRP means higher in pregnancy; non-pregnant women's ceruloplasmin sat within published Western ranges (non-pregnant subgroup N = 27)
cards.summary: Zairean women's reference levels (Kuvibidila 1994): ceruloplasmin and CRP means higher in pregnancy; non-pregnant women's ceruloplasmin sat within published Western ranges (non-pregnant subgroup N = 27)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (reference levels by pregnancy / lactation status, women only)
cards.people: 419 healthy Zairean women of reproductive age (15–45 years): 180 lactating (Group I), 212 pregnant (Group II) and 27 neither pregnant nor lactating (Group III); acute-phase proteins including ceruloplasmin measured by radial immunodiffusion. The non-pregnant / non-lactating subgroup — the group comparable to a general reference population — is small (N = 27) and prints as such.
cards.result: The ranges for the acute-phase proteins were wider than for Western adults. The means and medians of alpha 1-acid glycoprotein were lower in pregnant than non-pregnant women, and those of C-reactive protein and ceruloplasmin were higher in pregnancy. In non-pregnant women, the mean levels and 95% confidence limits of CRP, ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin were within published ranges for healthy Western adults, while those of alpha 1-acid glycoprotein were higher; in pregnant women only alpha 1-acid glycoprotein and haptoglobin were within published ranges. The fetched record prints no numeric ceruloplasmin values, and this card claims none — its content is the pregnancy elevation and the Western-range concordance in non-pregnant women.
cards.watchOut: Women only, an acute-phase-reactant panel measured by radial immunodiffusion in 1994, and the key comparison subgroup has N = 27: the dataset supports 'pregnancy raises ceruloplasmin; non-pregnant values concord with Western ranges' and nothing more precise.

cards.headline: Omani reference ranges (Abiaka 2008): ceruloplasmin by immunonephelometry significantly higher in women than men; N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Omani reference ranges (Abiaka 2008): ceruloplasmin by immunonephelometry significantly higher in women than men; N not documented in the record
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (reference ranges in healthy adults, both sexes; N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Healthy Omani men and women — N not documented in the record (the fetched record does not print the sample size, and none is claimed). Ceruloplasmin ('caeruloplasmin' in the record) was measured by immunonephelometry, alongside copper and zinc by atomic absorption spectrophotometry and albumin and cholesterol by spectrophotometry.
cards.result: Reference ranges of serum micronutrient concentrations and micromineral ratios were established for Omani subjects. Significantly higher (P < 0.0001) copper and ceruloplasmin concentrations, copper:zinc and copper:ceruloplasmin ratios, and lower zinc, retinol, alpha-tocopherol and cholesterol concentrations were present in women compared with men. The copper:caeruloplasmin ratio was 6.99 ± 0.84 µmol/g overall (mean ± SD). Age was associated with ceruloplasmin concentrations in men, and smokers had lower copper:caeruloplasmin ratios than non-smokers (P = 0.002). Deficiency incidence was ≤5% for all investigated parameters. The fetched record prints no numeric ceruloplasmin concentration or interval, and this card claims none — its content is the established ranges' existence and the significant female-higher sex difference.
cards.watchOut: With N not documented in the record and no numeric ceruloplasmin values printed there, this dataset corroborates the sex difference and the practice of population-specific ranges; it cannot be weighted against the 1,706-donor dataset or quoted for a number.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ceruloplasmin reference values are sex-, age- and hormone-dependent — upper reference ~25 mg/dL in men vs ~45 mg/dL in young women (2024, mg/dL), with oral contraceptives raising the mean by ~65% (1987, IU/ml, never merged)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ceruloplasmin reference values are sex-, age- and hormone-dependent — upper reference ~25 mg/dL in men vs ~45 mg/dL in young women (2024, mg/dL), with oral contraceptives raising the mean by ~65% (1987, IU/ml, never merged)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by the primary reference literature alone — Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep carry no ceruloplasmin reference chapter, and the textbooks frame only copper transport and acute-phase biology. Pelucchi 2024 (1,706 Italian donors) gives the modern curves in mg/dL: upper reference plateau ~25 mg/dL in men from about age 25, ~45 mg/dL in young women falling below 30 mg/dL after the fifties, with the lower reference value rising slightly with age in both sexes. Heese 1987 (200 young women) quantifies the oestrogen effect in IU/ml: 181 ± 43.9 on oral contraceptives versus 110 ± 22.7 off them, a ~65% higher mean (relative comparison). Kuvibidila 1994 (419 Zairean women; non-pregnant subgroup N = 27) found ceruloplasmin higher in pregnancy and non-pregnant values within published Western ranges, printing no numeric values in its record. Abiaka 2008 (Omani adults, N not documented in the record) established ranges with ceruloplasmin significantly higher in women. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the direction of every modifier (female sex, oestrogen, pregnancy) is consistent across four datasets spanning 1987–2024, but the units and assays are era-bound and unmergeable, three datasets are women-only or women-predominant, and only one dataset is large and modern.
cards.watchOut: Never convert IU/ml (1987) into mg/dL (2024) or pool the datasets into one adult range: sex and hormonal status are part of every value. This shelf is reference values only — it says nothing about ceruloplasmin's diagnostic accuracy for Wilson disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Complement C3 / C4 reference intervals: C3 0.656–1.52 g/L (65.6–152 mg/dL) and C4 0.181–0.561 g/L (18.1–56.1 mg/dL) in 1,234 Chinese Han men, BMI-dependent; 1980s nephelometry datasets as comparators
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum complement C3 and C4 — the central 95% ranges by immunoturbidimetric / nephelometric assay — how strongly do body-mass index and age move them, and how far do the modern population-derived intervals sit from the rate-nephelometry intervals of the early 1980s?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Asian People/ethnology · Body Mass Index · China/ethnology · Complement C3/analysis,biosynthesis · Complement C4/analysis,biosynthesis · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nephelometry and Turbidimetry/methods,standards · Reference Values · Young Adult · Age Factors · Child · Child, Preschool · Complement C3/analysis · Complement C4/analysis · Decision Making · Fetal Blood · Immunoglobulin A/analysis · Immunoglobulin G/analysis · Immunoglobulin M/analysis · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Nephelometry and Turbidimetry · Adolescent · Female · Haptoglobins/analysis · Immunoglobulins/analysis · Nephelometry and Turbidimetry/methods · Statistics as Topic
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / complement sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per assay era and never pooled: the modern anchor (Qin 2014; 1,234 healthy Chinese Han men aged 20–69, FAMHES, immunoturbidimetry) gives two-sided 95% reference intervals of 0.656–1.52 g/L for C3 (65.6–152 mg/dL) and 0.181–0.561 g/L for C4 (18.1–56.1 mg/dL), with BMI positively associated with both (r = 0.342 and 0.258) and BMI-specific intervals calculated — a men-only dataset, printed as such and never presented as adult-universal. The 1982 rate-nephelometry dataset (Jolliff; 750 well children and 120 healthy adults — the adult slice is the cardable one and prints with its N) established intervals by the then-new method, but its fetched record prints no numeric C3 / C4 intervals, and none is claimed. The 1981 dataset (Hapke; two geographically separate healthy populations; N not documented in the record and printed as such) is carded for its methods finding: mean ± 2 SD intervals are unsafe for these analytes and non-parametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals should be used. The 1981–82 intervals are historical comparators for the 2014 immunoturbidimetric intervals, never pooled with them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: FAMHES reference intervals (Qin 2014): 1,234 healthy Chinese Han men — C3 0.656–1.52 g/L (65.6–152 mg/dL), C4 0.181–0.561 g/L (18.1–56.1 mg/dL) by immunoturbidimetry, BMI positively associated with both
cards.summary: FAMHES reference intervals (Qin 2014): 1,234 healthy Chinese Han men — C3 0.656–1.52 g/L (65.6–152 mg/dL), C4 0.181–0.561 g/L (18.1–56.1 mg/dL) by immunoturbidimetry, BMI positively associated with both
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (population reference-interval derivation, men only, immunoturbidimetry)
cards.people: 1,234 healthy male subjects aged 20–69 years from the Fangchenggang Area Male Health and Examination Survey (FAMHES), China; serum complement C3 and C4 measured by immunoturbidimetry; two-sided 95% reference intervals calculated using parametric statistical methods. A men-only dataset — it prints as such on every use.
cards.result: Serum C3 values were normally distributed and C4 values log-normally distributed. The two-sided 95% reference intervals (mean ± 2 SD, as published) were 0.656–1.52 g/L for C3 — 65.6–152 mg/dL — and 0.181–0.561 g/L for C4 — 18.1–56.1 mg/dL. Body-mass index had a significant positive association with C3 (r = 0.342) and C4 (r = 0.258), age a significant positive association with C4 (r = 0.117), and both C3 and C4 increased significantly with BMI (P < 0.001); BMI-specific reference intervals were also calculated. No significant differences were found between smoking or drinking groups. The authors note the intervals show a slight deviation compared with previously reported reference levels and recommend BMI-specific reference values in clinical laboratories.
cards.watchOut: Men only, one ethnicity and one region, one assay: these intervals must not be presented as adult-universal, and the BMI association means a single interval already misfits at the BMI extremes of the very population it was derived in — the BMI-specific intervals are part of the result.
cards.source: Qin X et al. Determination of reference intervals for serum complement C3 and C4 levels in Chinese Han ethnic males. Clinical laboratory. 2014. PMID: 24839820. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rate-nephelometry intervals (Jolliff 1982): intervals for C3 and C4 established in 750 well children and 120 healthy adults by the then-new method — the adult slice (N = 120) is the cardable one; the record prints no numeric intervals
cards.summary: Rate-nephelometry intervals (Jolliff 1982): intervals for C3 and C4 established in 750 well children and 120 healthy adults by the then-new method — the adult slice (N = 120) is the cardable one; the record prints no numeric intervals
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (rate-nephelometry reference intervals; adult slice N = 120)
cards.people: A population of 750 well children and 120 healthy adults; reference intervals for serum IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C4 established by rate nephelometry, previous studies having been based on immunodiffusion. Only the 120-adult slice answers this shelf's question, and it prints with its N.
cards.result: The study's product is the set of rate-nephelometry reference intervals themselves: the authors report that their results generally agree with previously established immunoglobulin ranges, except for some disagreement as to the ages at which adult values are attained. The fetched record prints no numeric C3 or C4 interval values, and this card claims none — the dataset is carded as the historical rate-nephelometry comparator establishing that method-specific intervals for these analytes were derived in healthy adults in the early 1980s, four decades before the immunoturbidimetric intervals carded above, and it is never pooled with them.
cards.watchOut: Mostly a paediatric dataset (750 children) with a modest adult slice (N = 120), from the rate-nephelometry era: usable as a historical comparator and a methods landmark, not as a source of current adult limits — and no numbers may be quoted from it, since its record prints none.
cards.source: Jolliff CR et al. Reference intervals for serum IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C4 as determined by rate nephelometry. Clinical chemistry. 1982. PMID: 7055895. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (distribution / interval-method study, two healthy populations; N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Two geographically separate healthy populations in which nephelometrically determined IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C4 and haptoglobin distributions were studied. N not documented in the record — the fetched record does not print the populations' sizes, and per the standing reference-floor labelling rule this card prints 'N not documented' rather than any number.
cards.result: Evaluation of the distributions by several tests of statistical normality showed the tests vary considerably in power — data one test rejects as Gaussian may be accepted by another — and no rules exist to decide which test best applies. The authors conclude that the uncritical application of mean ± 2 SD for the reference range of clinical laboratory tests may be fraught with error that is not obvious and may not provide clinically useful information, and they recommend determination of reference ranges by a non-parametric percentile estimate (2.5 to 97.5 per cent), which makes no a priori assumptions about the population distribution, pending a large-scale empirical investigation of limits at desired specificity and sensitivity for disease states.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its method finding, not for any interval value — it prints none in its record. Its warning applies directly to the shelf's modern anchor: the 2014 intervals were calculated parametrically (mean ± 2 SD, with C4 log-normal), which is exactly the practice this 1981 study questions for these analytes.
cards.source: Hapke M et al. The establishment of normal limits for serum proteins measured by the rate nephelometer. Concepts of normality revisited. Human pathology. 1981. PMID: 7319488. cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (immunity / complement sections; the framing is brief and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature). Qin 2014 (1,234 Chinese Han men, immunoturbidimetry) gives C3 0.656–1.52 g/L (65.6–152 mg/dL) and C4 0.181–0.561 g/L (18.1–56.1 mg/dL), with BMI positively associated with both (r = 0.342 / 0.258) and BMI-specific intervals calculated. Jolliff 1982 established rate-nephelometry intervals including a 120-adult slice, printing no numeric values in its record. Hapke 1981 (two healthy populations, N not documented in the record) showed normality tests disagree on these analytes' distributions and recommended non-parametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals over mean ± 2 SD. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: only one dataset is large, modern and numeric, and it is men-only and single-population; the two older datasets are assay-era comparators that print no intervals in their records, so no cross-population or female interval can honestly be stated from this base.
cards.watchOut: Never pool the 1981–82 rate-nephelometry material with the 2014 immunoturbidimetric intervals, and never present the FAMHES men-only intervals as adult-universal: sex, population, BMI and assay all move these values, and two of the three datasets cannot supply a number at all.

shelves.title: Haptoglobin reference interval: 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women in 2,923 healthy subjects — and the interval should be partitioned by the rs2000999 polymorphism
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for plasma / serum haptoglobin — the central range by sex — how much of its variation is genetic (the HP phenotype and the rs2000999 polymorphism), and how far do pregnancy and population move the levels of this acute-phase protein in people without inflammation?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / haemolysis sections (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so). Three datasets: the STANISLAS Family Study derivation in 2,923 selected healthy subjects is the only dataset that prints a full sex-specific interval — plasma haptoglobin 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women — and its distinctive finding is genetic partitioning: sex, age, smoking, haemoglobin and the rs2000999 polymorphism were the strongest predictors, with levels falling with each minor allele, so an unpartitioned interval mixes genotypes with systematically different levels. The other two datasets are SHARED CROSS-ANALYTE anchors, stated on the face: the 1994 Zairean women's dataset (419 women by pregnancy / lactation status; haptoglobin means did not differ between groups) is shared with the ceruloplasmin shelf, and the 1981 nephelometry distributions paper (N not documented in its record) is shared with the complement C3/C4 shelf — the same papers measured several serum proteins, which is not double-counting one population for one analyte. Haptoglobin is an acute-phase protein, so every dataset's health screen is part of the interval's meaning. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — only one of the three datasets prints a full numeric interval, and the other two print no haptoglobin range in their records, so the interval is established for the STANISLAS population rather than as a universal range.

cards.headline: STANISLAS reference derivation (Shahabi 2012): plasma haptoglobin 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women in 2,923 selected healthy subjects — with rs2000999 the strongest genetic predictor, levels falling with each minor allele
cards.summary: STANISLAS reference derivation (Shahabi 2012): plasma haptoglobin 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women in 2,923 selected healthy subjects — with rs2000999 the strongest genetic predictor, levels falling with each minor allele
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (reference-interval derivation, STANISLAS Family Study)
cards.people: 3,129 'apparently' disease-free individuals of the French STANISLAS Family Study were analysed for biological predictors; reference ranges were then established in a subgroup of 2,923 selected healthy subjects.
cards.result: Plasma haptoglobin reference values ranged 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in males and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in females. On stepwise regression, sex (gender as published), age, smoking, plasma haemoglobin and the newly discovered HP polymorphism rs2000999 were the strongest biological predictors of haptoglobin concentration, and levels in both sexes and all age groups were negatively associated with the presence and number of rs2000999 minor alleles. The authors conclude rs2000999 should be considered for partitioning the reference values and may help set decision limits.
cards.watchOut: Haptoglobin is an acute-phase protein: the interval describes screened healthy people without inflammation and does not apply during inflammatory states; the population is of French origin, and the partitioning finding means a single unpartitioned range mixes genotypes with systematically different levels.
cards.source: Shahabi P et al. Clinical necessity of partitioning of human plasma haptoglobin reference intervals by recently-discovered rs2000999. Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry. 2012. PMID: 22579477. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zairean women's reference levels (Kuvibidila 1994): haptoglobin means did NOT differ between lactating, pregnant and non-pregnant/non-lactating women, and non-pregnant women's levels sat within published Western ranges — SHARED CROSS-ANALYTE anchor (also anchors the ceruloplasmin shelf, where the same paper's ceruloplasmin limb is carded)
cards.summary: Zairean women's reference levels (Kuvibidila 1994): haptoglobin means did NOT differ between lactating, pregnant and non-pregnant/non-lactating women, and non-pregnant women's levels sat within published Western ranges — SHARED CROSS-ANALYTE anchor (also anchors the ceruloplasmin shelf, where the same paper's ceruloplasmin limb is carded)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (reference levels in healthy women by pregnancy / lactation status) — shared cross-analyte anchor, stated on the face
cards.people: 419 healthy Zairean women aged 15–45 years in the reproductive age group: 180 lactating (Group I), 212 pregnant (Group II) and 27 neither pregnant nor lactating (Group III); acute-phase proteins measured by radial immunodiffusion.
cards.result: Ranges for the acute-phase proteins were wider than for Western adults. Means and medians of alpha 1-acid glycoprotein were lower in pregnant than non-pregnant women, and C-reactive protein and ceruloplasmin were higher in pregnancy — but there were NO differences in mean haptoglobin levels between the three groups. In non-pregnant women, the mean levels and 95% confidence limits of haptoglobin (with CRP and ceruloplasmin) were within published ranges for healthy Western adults. The authors conclude the same cut-off points used for Western adults may be used in non-pregnant Zairean women.
cards.watchOut: Women only, and the non-pregnant / non-lactating subgroup is small (N = 27) and prints as such; the record prints no numeric haptoglobin range, so this card supports the pregnancy / population claim only — it is not a second interval derivation. This paper is shared with the ceruloplasmin shelf because it measured several acute-phase proteins; that sharing is cross-analyte, not a second haptoglobin population count.
cards.source: Kuvibidila S et al. Reference levels of acute phase reactant proteins in healthy Zairean women in the reproductive age group. The Journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 1994. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (blood / haemolysis; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature). One dataset prints the interval: in 2,923 selected healthy STANISLAS subjects, plasma haptoglobin ranged 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women, with sex, age, smoking, haemoglobin and rs2000999 the strongest predictors and levels falling with each minor allele — the case for genotype-partitioned intervals (Shahabi 2012). Pregnancy and lactation did not move mean haptoglobin in 419 healthy Zairean women, whose non-pregnant levels sat within published Western ranges (Kuvibidila 1994; shared cross-analyte with the ceruloplasmin shelf). The 1981 two-population study supplies the construction rule — non-parametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals, not mean ± 2 SD (Hapke 1981; shared cross-analyte with the complement C3/C4 shelf; N not documented in its record). PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the numeric interval rests on one large derivation, and no card on this shelf prints an interval as universal.
cards.watchOut: Every value is assay- and population-bound and describes people screened free of inflammation; haptoglobin rises with inflammation, so these ranges must never be applied to an acutely ill patient as if they were a disease cut-off.

cards.search: synthesis synthesis in healthy adults, what is the reference interval for plasma / serum haptoglobin — the central range by sex — how much of its variation is genetic (the hp phenotype and the rs2000999 polymorphism), and how far do pregnancy and population move the levels of this acute-phase protein in people without inflammation? synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. framed by guyton & hall (blood / haemolysis; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature). one dataset prints the interval: in 2,923 selected healthy stanislas subjects, plasma haptoglobin ranged 0.08–1.97 g/l (8–197 mg/dl) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/l (8–219 mg/dl) in women, with sex, age, smoking, haemoglobin and rs2000999 the strongest predictors and levels falling with each minor allele — the case for genotype-partitioned intervals (shahabi 2012). pregnancy and lactation did not move mean haptoglobin in 419 healthy zairean women, whose non-pregnant levels sat within published western ranges (kuvibidila 1994; shared cross-analyte with the ceruloplasmin shelf). the 1981 two-population study supplies the construction rule — non-parametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals, not mean ± 2 sd (hapke 1981; shared cross-analyte with the complement c3/c4 shelf; n not documented in its record). physiology — emerging: the numeric interval rests on one large derivation, and no card on this shelf prints an interval as universal. every value is assay- and population-bound and describes people screened free of inflammation; haptoglobin rises with inflammation, so these ranges must never be applied to an acutely ill patient as if they were a disease cut-off. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, vascular sections (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so). Three datasets, three modalities, carded per modality and never merged: echocardiography (Hamburg City Health Study, 1,687 healthy subjects, aortic root at four levels in systole and diastole), contrast CT (Copenhagen General Population Study, 902 rigorously screened healthy subjects, maximal diameters at seven landmarks from the sinuses of Valsalva to the infrarenal abdominal aorta) and MRI (MESA, 3,573 participants, ascending-aorta diameter with upper limits defined in a healthy subgroup). All three agree on the structure: men are larger absolutely at every level, diameters rise with age and body surface area — and in the Hamburg echo data the sex order REVERSES once diameters are indexed to body surface area (women larger at all levels), so indexed and absolute diameters answer different questions and no card gives one without naming which it is. The MESA dataset is a general population cohort with a defined healthy subgroup for its upper limits, not a screened-healthy sample like Copenhagen's, and that distinction prints. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population datasets across three modalities agree on the age, sex and indexing structure of normal aortic size, with numeric limits printed per modality.

cards.headline: Echocardiography — Hamburg City Health Study (Wenzel 2021): aortic-root reference values at four levels in 1,687 healthy subjects; women smaller absolutely but LARGER at all levels after body-surface-area indexing, with strong age dependence and reference formulas from age, sex, weight and height
cards.summary: Echocardiography — Hamburg City Health Study (Wenzel 2021): aortic-root reference values at four levels in 1,687 healthy subjects; women smaller absolutely but LARGER at all levels after body-surface-area indexing, with strong age dependence and reference formulas from age, sex, weight and height
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (echocardiographic aortic-root reference values, population-based cohort)
cards.people: 1,687 healthy subjects (mean age 57.1 ± 7.7 years; 681 male and 1,006 female) derived from the first prospectively recruited 10,000 Hamburg City Health Study participants; aortic-root dimensions measured in systole and diastole by standardised 2-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography at four levels: aortic annulus, sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction and ascending aorta.
cards.result: Female sex was associated with significantly smaller absolute aortic-root dimensions, while indexing for body surface area resulted in a reverse effect at all levels — women larger once indexed. There was a strong age dependency of all aortic-root diameters and of the annulus / sinotubular junction ratio in both sexes. Multivariate analysis found age, sex, weight, height and body surface area to be significant determinants of aortic-root size, and formulas were generated to calculate individual reference values from age, sex, weight and height. The fetched record prints the structure and determinants rather than a table of numeric limits, and this card claims no numeric echo limit beyond what is stated.
cards.watchOut: Echocardiographic root diameters only, measured at four root levels in systole and diastole — not interchangeable with CT or MRI diameters, and the indexing reversal means an absolute and an indexed value for the same aorta can point in opposite sex directions; every use must name which it is.
cards.source: Wenzel JP et al. Transthoracic echocardiographic reference values of the aortic root: results from the Hamburg City Health Study. The international journal of cardiovascular imaging. 2021. PMID: 34324091. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CT — Copenhagen General Population Study (Pham 2019): normal maximal diameters at seven aortic landmarks in 902 rigorously screened healthy subjects; men larger at all levels (P < 0.001), with sex, age and body surface area determinants throughout
cards.summary: CT — Copenhagen General Population Study (Pham 2019): normal maximal diameters at seven aortic landmarks in 902 rigorously screened healthy subjects; men larger at all levels (P < 0.001), with sex, age and body surface area determinants throughout
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (contrast-CT aortic reference values, rigorously screened healthy subjects)
cards.people: 902 healthy subjects selected from 3,000 adults undergoing cardiovascular thoracic and abdominal CT angiography, after exclusion of self-reported angina, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, cardiovascular medication (including diuretics, statins or aspirin), body mass index ≥30 kg/m2, diabetes (self-reported or blood glucose >8 mmol/L (144 mg/dL)), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Median age 52 years; 396 were men. Maximal diameters were measured retrospectively at seven regions: sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending aorta, mid-descending aorta, abdominal aorta at the diaphragm, abdominal aorta at the coeliac trunk, and infrarenal abdominal aorta.
cards.result: Men had significantly larger aortic diameters at all levels than women (P < 0.001). Multivariable analysis found sex, age and body surface area associated with increasing aortic dimensions, and aortic dimensions followed an almost identical pattern throughout the vessel regardless of sex. The study's product is the set of normal maximal-diameter values by landmark from contrast-enhanced CT; the fetched record states the determinants and pattern rather than printing each landmark's numeric limit, and this card claims none beyond what is stated.
cards.watchOut: This is the screened-healthy dataset of the three — its exclusions (no hypertension, no statins, BMI under 30, no diabetes) are part of what its 'normal' means. CT maximal diameters are not interchangeable with echo or MRI measurements, and measurement level (sinus vs ascending vs infrarenal) prints on every use.
cards.source: Pham MHC et al. Normal values of aortic dimensions assessed by multidetector computed tomography in the Copenhagen General Population Study. European heart journal. Cardiovascular Imaging. 2019. PMID: 30809640. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MRI — MESA (Turkbey 2014): ascending-aorta upper limits (95th percentile, healthy subgroup) of 20, 21, 22 and 23 mm/m² in men and 21, 22, 22 and 28 mm/m² in women across the 45–54 to 75–84 age bands; diameter rises about 1 mm per decade and is about 1.9 mm larger in men and 0.9 mm larger in hypertensive participants
cards.summary: MRI — MESA (Turkbey 2014): ascending-aorta upper limits (95th percentile, healthy subgroup) of 20, 21, 22 and 23 mm/m² in men and 21, 22, 22 and 28 mm/m² in women across the 45–54 to 75–84 age bands; diameter rises about 1 mm per decade and is about 1.9 mm larger in men and 0.9 mm larger in hypertensive participants
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (MRI ascending-aortic reference values, general population cohort with a healthy subgroup)
cards.people: 3,573 Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis participants aged 45–84 years; mean ascending thoracic aortic luminal diameter measured by gradient-echo phase-contrast cine MRI. The median and upper normal limit (95th percentile) were defined in a 'healthy' subgroup of this general population cohort, as were wall-thickness values.
cards.result: The upper limits of body-surface-area-indexed ascending-aortic diameter for age categories 45–54, 55–64, 65–74 and 75–84 years are 21, 22, 22 and 28 mm/m² in women and 20, 21, 22 and 23 mm/m² in men. Mean ascending-aortic wall thickness was 2.8 mm. Age, sex and body surface area were major determinants (about +1 mm per 10 years; about +1.9 mm in men than women; about +1 mm per 0.23 m²; all P < 0.001), and diameter in hypertensive participants was +0.9 mm larger than in normotensive participants (P < 0.001). Diameter rose gradually with ageing in both sexes among all race/ethnic groups.
cards.watchOut: MESA is a general population cohort, not a screened-healthy sample like the Copenhagen dataset — its upper limits come from a defined healthy subgroup, and the distinction prints. These are indexed (mm/m²) MRI limits for the ascending aorta only; they do not transfer to echo or CT or to other aortic levels.

cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (vascular sections; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). Three datasets, three modalities, never merged: echocardiographic aortic-root values at four levels in 1,687 healthy Hamburg subjects, with women smaller absolutely but larger after body-surface-area indexing at all levels (Wenzel 2021); contrast-CT maximal diameters at seven landmarks in 902 rigorously screened healthy Copenhagen subjects, men larger at all levels (Pham 2019); and MRI ascending-aorta limits in 3,573 MESA participants — indexed upper limits rising by age band to 23 mm/m² in men and 28 mm/m² in women at 75–84 years, with diameter rising about 1 mm per decade (Turkbey 2014). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the age, sex and indexing structure of normal aortic size is consistent across all three, provided each value keeps its modality and measurement level.
cards.watchOut: Never merge diameters across modalities or levels, and never quote an indexed limit as an absolute diameter (or the reverse): the Hamburg indexing reversal shows the two answer different questions.

shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal spleen dimensions on imaging — sonographic length and volume, and CT volume — by sex and body height, how badly does the conventional 12 cm upper limit of sonographic length misclassify healthy men, and how stable is a spleen measurement on repeat scanning?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, per modality. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, reticuloendothelial / spleen sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The row's distinctive finding: in 1,230 healthy stem-cell-donor volunteers (Chow 2016), spleen length and volume were independently associated with sex, height and weight, and the previously reported 12 cm upper limit was exceeded by 26% of men (234 of 906) and 6% of women (20 of 324) — a fixed limit labels a quarter of healthy men enlarged; repeat measurement in 75 volunteers was stable (median length difference 0.10 cm). The Turkish cohort (Tiryaki 2024; 1,918 adults; shared with shelf #7720 for its kidney limb) found splenic length did not differ across BMI groups while splenic thickness did. On CT, in 4,732 healthy Japanese adults (Tamura 2025), the final reference model predicted spleen volume from weight alone (3.08 + 1.96 × weight in kg; mean absolute error 38.5 mL). The founding 1983 derivation (Niederau; 915 healthy subjects) set 95th-percentile upper limits prospectively for liver, spleen, pancreas and portal vein; its abstract reports the method and cohort, and spleen-specific figures are not printed in the fetched record — none are claimed from it here. Sonographic length, sonographic volume and CT volume are different quantities and are never merged. The donor cohort is a screened-healthy population, not a general-population sample, and prints as such. Cross-point: spleen contraction during exercise and diving (pack #6633) is a mechanism question, not a size norm.

cards.headline: Donor cohort (Chow 2016): 1,230 healthy volunteers — spleen length and volume independently associated with sex, height and weight; the 12 cm upper limit was exceeded by 26% of men (234 of 906) and 6% of women (20 of 324); repeat length differed by a median 0.10 cm
cards.summary: Donor cohort (Chow 2016): 1,230 healthy volunteers — spleen length and volume independently associated with sex, height and weight; the 12 cm upper limit was exceeded by 26% of men (234 of 906) and 6% of women (20 of 324); repeat length differed by a median 0.10 cm
cards.type: Sonographic reference-value derivation in healthy stem-cell-donor volunteers (1,230 volunteers; 75 with repeat measurement)
cards.people: Retrospective review of 1,230 healthy stem-cell-donor volunteers who consented to donation and research use of anonymised data; sonographic spleen length and volume correlated with anthropometric data by multiple linear regression, with upper limits of normal derived by linear regression through the 95th percentile within height cohorts (women 155–179 cm; men 165–199 cm) and validated against observed values; 75 volunteers were measured twice for stability. A screened-healthy donor population, not a general-population sample — stated here on the face.
cards.result: Spleen length and volume were significantly and independently associated with sex (length: P < .001; volume: P = .012), body height (P < .001 for both) and weight (P < .001 for both), with men and taller, heavier individuals having longer and larger spleens. The spleen length of 20 of 324 women (6%) and 234 of 906 men (26%) exceeded the previously reported upper limit of normal of 12 cm. Repeat measurements were quite stable: spleen length median difference 0.10 cm (range, −1.8 to 1.7 cm) and volume median difference 3 cm3 (range, −106 to 142 cm3). The authors propose height- and sex-corrected percentile algorithms (with a mobile application) in place of the fixed limit.
cards.watchOut: The height-corrected formulae apply within the studied height bands (women 155–179 cm; men 165–199 cm) — outside them the percentiles are extrapolations. The 26% figure is the argument against any fixed cut-off, including a corrected one applied without its band.
cards.source: Chow KU et al. Spleen Size Is Significantly Influenced by Body Height and Sex: Establishment of Normal Values for Spleen Size at US with a Cohort of 1200 Healthy Individuals. Radiology. 2016. PMID: 26509293. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Turkish community cohort (Tiryaki 2024) — spleen limb of a cohort shared with shelf #7720: 1,918 healthy adults — splenic length did NOT differ significantly across BMI groups (P = 0.583) while splenic thickness did (P = 0.016)
cards.summary: Turkish community cohort (Tiryaki 2024) — spleen limb of a cohort shared with shelf #7720: 1,918 healthy adults — splenic length did NOT differ significantly across BMI groups (P = 0.583) while splenic thickness did (P = 0.016)
cards.type: Population ultrasonographic reference study in healthy Turkish adults (1,918 adults) — spleen limb; cohort shared with shelf #7720 (kidney limb)
cards.people: 1,918 healthy Turkish adults older than 18 years (987 women, 931 men; mean age 40.74 ± 15.95 years) with ultrasonographic liver, spleen and kidney dimensions and BMI recorded. Shared cohort: the same study is carded on shelf #7720 for its kidney limb — the cohort is counted once per measurement, as stated on both shelves.
cards.result: The difference between BMI groups in splenic length was not statistically significant (P = 0.583), while the difference in splenic thickness was significant (P = 0.016). The study obtained mean normal standard values for liver, spleen and kidney dimensions in this population; liver length and depth differed significantly by sex (P = 0.000 and P = 0.004). cards.headline: Japanese CT volumetry (Tamura 2025): 4,732 healthy adults with automated segmentation — the final spleen-volume reference model used weight alone (predicted volume = 3.08 + 1.96 × weight in kg), mean absolute error 38.5 mL

cards.type: CT volumetric reference derivation in healthy Japanese adults (4,732 adults; automated segmentation)
cards.people: 4,732 healthy Japanese adults (Data Set 1) undergoing unenhanced abdominal CT, with spleen volumes measured by a deep-learning automated segmentation tool (mean Dice coefficient 0.95; median processing time 26.6 s); a multivariable model using sex, age, weight and height was developed and validated, and an external cohort of 136 patients with histologically confirmed liver disease (Data Set 2) tested volume-defined splenomegaly for fibrosis staging.
cards.result: The final predictive model used weight alone (predicted spleen volume = 3.08 + 1.96 × weight [kg]), with a mean absolute error of 38.5 mL. In the liver-disease cohort, splenomegaly prevalence by Z-score rose with fibrosis stage (for Z ≥ +1: 0.0% at F1, 32.7% F2, 54.3% F3, 74.4% F4; for Z ≥ +2: 0.0%, 16.3%, 34.3%, 48.8%), and the area under the curve for detecting cirrhosis (F4) was 0.73. The authors conclude the model enables objective identification of splenomegaly from routine clinical parameters.
cards.watchOut: A CT volume in mL is not convertible into a sonographic length in cm — the modalities are carded separately and never merged. The weight-only equation is a Japanese-population model with a 38.5 mL mean absolute error; the fibrosis-staging limb is a clinical use of the norm, not part of the norm itself.

cards.headline: Founding sonographic derivation (Niederau 1983): 915 healthy subjects — prospective normal values and 95th-percentile upper limits for liver, spleen, pancreas and portal vein; diameter–body-size correlations were poor (r ≤ 0.3); spleen-specific figures are not printed in the fetched record and none are claimed here
cards.summary: Founding sonographic derivation (Niederau 1983): 915 healthy subjects — prospective normal values and 95th-percentile upper limits for liver, spleen, pancreas and portal vein; diameter–body-size correlations were poor (r ≤ 0.3); spleen-specific figures are not printed in the fetched record and none are claimed here
cards.type: Prospective sonographic normal-values derivation (915 healthy subjects) — founding multi-organ study, spleen upper-limit limb
cards.people: 915 healthy subjects examined prospectively with ultrasound, with sex, age, weight, height and body surface area recorded in each case; normal values and upper limits (95th percentile) determined for liver, spleen, pancreas and portal vein size. Carded for the upper-limit derivation: the fetched abstract reports the method and cohort, and spleen-specific figures are taken from the full text at any future re-verification, not from the abstract.
cards.result: Correlations of longitudinal and transverse organ diameters with physical data were poor (r less than or equal to 0.3), so the authors did not consider it necessary to correct the measurements accordingly. The liver is oriented longitudinally in slender subjects and transversely in heavy subjects, so both longitudinal and anteroposterior diameters need measuring — the longitudinal diameter alone gives too high or too low a value respectively.
cards.watchOut: A 1983 derivation on period equipment, and the historical source of fixed upper limits of the kind the 2016 donor cohort shows misclassifying healthy men. Its poor diameter–habitus correlations (r ≤ 0.3) sit in tension with the modern height/weight associations — technique and population differ, and the tension prints rather than being resolved here.

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: sonographic donor cohort (1,230 volunteers), Turkish community cohort (1,918 adults; shared with shelf #7720, counted once per measurement), Japanese CT cohort (4,732 adults) and the founding prospective sonographic derivation (915 subjects). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall frame spleen function briefly; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so.
cards.result: Never print a spleen value without its modality and population: a length (cm, ultrasound), a sonographic volume and a CT volume (mL) are three quantities. The one stand-alone prohibition this shelf establishes: 12 cm is not a definition of splenomegaly — at that line, a quarter of healthy men are 'enlarged'. Measurement itself is stable (median repeat length difference 0.10 cm), so the error is in the limit, not the ruler.

shelves.title: Brentuximab vedotin plus CHP versus CHOP in untreated CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma (ECHELON-2 — one trial, 4 reports): median PFS 48.2 vs 20.8 months, and at 5 years PFS 51.4% vs 43.0% and overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% — with peripheral neuropathy in 52% vs 55%
shelves.question: In adults with previously untreated CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma, does replacing vincristine with brentuximab vedotin (A+CHP) versus CHOP improve progression-free and overall survival — and does the benefit hold at 5 years, and does interim PET or consolidative stem-cell transplant modify it?

shelves.balance: One trial — ECHELON-2 (452 patients randomised 1:1) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such and never pooled with any other trial. The primary report found median progression-free survival 48.2 vs 20.8 months (hazard ratio 0.71 [95% CI 0.54–0.93], P = 0.0110 — a relative measure). At 5 years (median follow-up 47.6 months), PFS was 51.4% vs 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% CI 0.53–0.91] — relative) and overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% (hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.99] — relative; the interval just inside significance, printed with its interval, not as a bare win). The pricing harm is on the face: peripheral neuropathy occurred in 52% on A+CHP vs 55% on CHOP — it did not fall when vincristine was removed — with febrile neutropenia 18% vs 15% and fatal adverse events 3% vs 4%; neuropathy had resolved or improved in 72% (A+CHP) and 78% (CHOP) of affected patients at 5 years. The two ancillary reports are exploratory and labelled: interim PET4-negative status was prognostic in BOTH arms (not a reason to choose one arm), and the stem-cell-transplant analysis is a non-randomised subgroup analysis in complete responders, never a randomised transplant comparison.

cards.headline: ECHELON-2 primary report (Horwitz 2019): median progression-free survival 48.2 months on A+CHP vs 20.8 months on CHOP (hazard ratio 0.71 [95% CI 0.54–0.93], P = 0.0110 — a relative measure); peripheral neuropathy 52% vs 55%, febrile neutropenia 18% vs 15%, fatal adverse events 3% vs 4%
cards.summary: ECHELON-2 primary report (Horwitz 2019): median progression-free survival 48.2 months on A+CHP vs 20.8 months on CHOP (hazard ratio 0.71 [95% CI 0.54–0.93], P = 0.0110 — a relative measure); peripheral neuropathy 52% vs 55%, febrile neutropenia 18% vs 15%, fatal adverse events 3% vs 4%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (ECHELON-2 primary report), A+CHP vs CHOP in untreated CD30-positive PTCL
cards.people: 452 adults with previously untreated CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma at 132 sites in 17 countries, randomised 1:1 (226 per arm) to brentuximab vedotin plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin and prednisone (A+CHP) or CHOP, for six or eight 21-day cycles, in a double-blind double-dummy trial. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by blinded independent central review, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 48.2 months (95% CI 35.2–not evaluable) in the A+CHP group and 20.8 months (12.7–47.6) in the CHOP group (hazard ratio 0.71 [95% CI 0.54–0.93], p = 0.0110 — a relative measure). Adverse events were similar between groups, including febrile neutropenia (41 [18%] on A+CHP vs 33 [15%] on CHOP) and peripheral neuropathy (117 [52%] vs 124 [55%]). Fatal adverse events occurred in 7 (3%) patients on A+CHP and 9 (4%) on CHOP. The authors conclude front-line A+CHP is superior to CHOP, with significant improvement in progression-free and overall survival.
cards.watchOut: The counter-intuitive harm fact: removing vincristine did not reduce peripheral neuropathy (52% vs 55%) — brentuximab vedotin carries its own neuropathy. The trial targeted 75% systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, so read the result as strongest in that subtype.
cards.source: Horwitz S et al. Brentuximab vedotin with chemotherapy for CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma (ECHELON-2): a global, double-blind, randomised, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 30522922. Registry ID: NCT01777152. cards.headline: ECHELON-2 5-year results (Horwitz 2022): 5-year PFS 51.4% vs 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% CI 0.53–0.91] — relative) and 5-year overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% (hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.99] — relative); neuropathy resolved or improved in 72% on A+CHP and 78% on CHOP
cards.summary: ECHELON-2 5-year results (Horwitz 2022): 5-year PFS 51.4% vs 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% CI 0.53–0.91] — relative) and 5-year overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% (hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.99] — relative); neuropathy resolved or improved in 72% on A+CHP and 78% on CHOP
cards.type: 5-year update report of the ECHELON-2 randomised phase 3 trial — same trial, later follow-up
cards.people: The same 452 ECHELON-2 patients (226 per arm), in an exploratory 5-year update with progression-free survival per investigator; median follow-up 47.6 months. This is a later report of the one trial on this shelf, not a second trial.
cards.result: 5-year progression-free survival rates were 51.4% (95% CI 42.8–59.4%) with A+CHP vs 43.0% (35.8–50.0%) with CHOP (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.53–0.91 — a relative measure), and 5-year overall survival rates were 70.1% (63.3–75.9%) vs 61.0% (54.0–67.3%) (hazard ratio 0.72; 95% CI 0.53–0.99 — a relative measure). Peripheral neuropathy was resolved or improved in 72% (84 of 117) of patients in the A+CHP arm and 78% (97 of 124) in the CHOP arm. Among patients who relapsed and subsequently received brentuximab vedotin, objective response was 59% after A+CHP and 50% after CHOP.
cards.watchOut: The overall-survival hazard ratio's confidence interval (0.53–0.99) just reaches significance — print it with its interval. This record carries no registry ID, and its source line says so, even though it reports the same NCT01777152 trial.

cards.type: Post hoc exploratory interim-PET (PET4) analysis of the ECHELON-2 trial — ancillary report, same trial
cards.people: Post hoc exploratory analysis of the 452 ECHELON-2 patients; interim PET after cycle 4 (PET4) was determined by Deauville score (1–3 negative, 4–5 positive) by independent review. 32 patients in the BV-CHP arm and 41 in the CHOP arm were not evaluable for PET4. Same trial, ancillary report.
cards.result: In both arms, PET4-negative status was associated with improved progression-free survival (BV-CHP: hazard ratio 0.36 [95% CI 0.19–0.66]; CHOP: 0.26 [0.17–0.41] — relative measures) and overall survival (BV-CHP: 0.38 [0.18–0.78]; CHOP: 0.24 [0.14–0.41] — relative) compared with PET4-positive status. The same pattern held in the systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma subgroup.
cards.watchOut: A prognostic marker that works identically in both arms cannot guide the choice between the arms — never present PET4 as a treatment-selection test on this base. Post hoc and exploratory, with 73 of 452 patients not evaluable.
cards.source: Iyer S et al. Association of PET4 response with outcomes of BV-CHP vs CHOP in the ECHELON-2 trial in CD30+ peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Blood advances. 2025. PMID: 40829107. Registry ID: NCT01777152.
