cards.headline: Stem-cell-transplant analysis (Savage 2022): in complete responders, consolidative transplant was associated with a PFS hazard ratio of 0.36 (a relative 64% lower risk of a PFS event), median PFS not reached vs 55.66 months — an exploratory, NON-randomised subgroup analysis, never a randomised transplant comparison
cards.summary: Stem-cell-transplant analysis (Savage 2022): in complete responders, consolidative transplant was associated with a PFS hazard ratio of 0.36 (a relative 64% lower risk of a PFS event), median PFS not reached vs 55.66 months — an exploratory, NON-randomised subgroup analysis, never a randomised transplant comparison
cards.type: Exploratory subgroup analysis of consolidative stem-cell transplant within ECHELON-2 — ancillary report, same trial, non-randomised comparison
cards.people: Exploratory subgroup analysis of ECHELON-2 patients with previously untreated CD30-positive PTCL (ALK-negative anaplastic large-cell lymphoma and non-ALCL) who were in complete response after frontline A+CHP or CHOP; median PFS follow-up 47.57 months. Same trial, ancillary report. Transplant was chosen clinically, not randomised.
cards.result: The progression-free survival hazard ratio was 0.36, equating to a 64% relative reduction in the risk of a PFS event in patients who underwent consolidative stem-cell transplant; median PFS was not reached in patients who underwent transplant vs 55.66 months in those who did not. Results favoured transplant in both the ALK-negative ALCL and non-ALCL subgroups. The authors state the data support consideration of consolidative transplant in patients who achieve complete response after A+CHP.
cards.watchOut: Patients who reach complete response and proceed to transplant differ from those who do not (fitness, response depth, survival to transplant) — this association is confounded by selection and immortal-time effects and must never be quoted as the effect of transplant.
cards.source: Savage KJ et al. Role of stem cell transplant in CD30+ PTCL following frontline brentuximab vedotin plus CHP or CHOP in ECHELON-2. Blood advances. 2022. PMID: 35470385. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial (ECHELON-2, 452 patients), 4 reports — A+CHP improved median progression-free survival (48.2 vs 20.8 months; relative HR 0.71) and at 5 years overall survival was 70.1% vs 61.0% (relative HR 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.99]), while peripheral neuropathy was as common as on CHOP (52% vs 55%) despite vincristine's removal; PET4 is prognostic in both arms and the transplant analysis is exploratory and non-randomised

cards.result: This is the T-cell-lymphoma trial in this library with an overall-survival advantage over CHOP, and its stamp rests on that one programme alone — the programme basis is stated here and on the face.
cards.watchOut: Never pool these 4 reports as if they were 4 trials, and never present the ancillary PET or transplant analyses as randomised evidence.

shelves.title: Brentuximab vedotin versus physician's choice in previously treated CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (ALCANZA — one trial, 4 reports): durable response (ORR4) 56.3% vs 12.5%, median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months at final data, and a large skin-symptom gain — priced in peripheral neuropathy (67% any grade)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma), does brentuximab vedotin improve durable objective response and progression-free survival versus physician's choice (methotrexate or bexarotene) — and at what symptom and neuropathy cost?

shelves.balance: One trial — ALCANZA (131 patients randomised; 128 in the intention-to-treat population) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such. The primary endpoint is a durable-response endpoint, not survival: objective global response lasting ≥4 months (ORR4) was 56.3% vs 12.5% at the primary analysis and 54.7% vs 12.5% in the final data, with median progression-free survival 16.7 vs 3.5 months — no overall-survival advantage is printed in these reports, and the shelf does not present PFS as a survival claim. The comparator (methotrexate or bexarotene) is weak by design, and the trial is open-label — the honest frame is a large durable-response and symptom gain in a rare, incurable disease: the Skindex-29 symptom score fell by a mean maximum of −27.96 vs −8.62 (difference −18.9 [95% CI −26.6 to −11.2]), exceeding the study-defined minimally important difference, while general quality-of-life measures (FACT-G, EQ-5D) were comparable between arms. The price is peripheral neuropathy: 67% any grade on brentuximab vedotin in the primary report (44 patients in the final data, of whom 86% had complete resolution or improvement to grade 1–2). Response was seen across CD30-expression levels and regardless of large-cell transformation in the exploratory sub-analysis.

cards.headline: ALCANZA primary report (Prince 2017): objective global response lasting ≥4 months (ORR4) in 56.3% (36 of 64) on brentuximab vedotin vs 12.5% (8 of 64) on physician's choice (difference 43.8% [95% CI 29.1–58.4], P < .0001); peripheral neuropathy in 67% vs 6%
cards.summary: ALCANZA primary report (Prince 2017): objective global response lasting ≥4 months (ORR4) in 56.3% (36 of 64) on brentuximab vedotin vs 12.5% (8 of 64) on physician's choice (difference 43.8% [95% CI 29.1–58.4], P < .0001); peripheral neuropathy in 67% vs 6%
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial (ALCANZA primary report), brentuximab vedotin vs physician's choice in CD30-positive CTCL
cards.people: 131 adults with previously treated CD30-positive mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma across 52 centres in 13 countries, randomised (66 to brentuximab vedotin 1.8 mg/kg every 3 weeks for up to 16 cycles; 65 to physician's choice of methotrexate or bexarotene for up to 48 weeks); 128 analysed in the intention-to-treat population (64 per arm). Open-label trial; median follow-up 22.9 months.
cards.result: ORR4 was 56.3% (36 of 64) with brentuximab vedotin vs 12.5% (8 of 64) with physician's choice (between-group difference 43.8% [95% CI 29.1–58.4]; p < 0.0001). Grade 3–4 adverse events were reported in 27 of 66 (41%) on brentuximab vedotin and 29 of 62 (47%) on physician's choice. Peripheral neuropathy was seen in 44 of 66 (67%) on brentuximab vedotin (21 grade 2, 6 grade 3) and 4 of 62 (6%) on physician's choice. One of four on-treatment deaths was deemed treatment-related in the brentuximab vedotin group; no on-treatment deaths were reported in the physician's choice group.
cards.watchOut: ORR4 is a durable-response endpoint, not survival. The comparator is methotrexate or bexarotene — a weak control by design — and the trial is open-label, so the size of the response gap must be read in that frame.
cards.source: Prince HM et al. Brentuximab vedotin or physician's choice in CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (ALCANZA): an international, open-label, randomised, phase 3, multicentre trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28600132. Registry ID: NCT01578499. cards.headline: ALCANZA final data (Horwitz 2021): ORR4 54.7% vs 12.5% (P < .001), complete response 17.2% vs 1.6% (P = .002), median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months (P < .001), time to next treatment hazard ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.17–0.42 — relative); of 44 patients with neuropathy, 86% resolved completely or improved to grade 1–2
cards.summary: ALCANZA final data (Horwitz 2021): ORR4 54.7% vs 12.5% (P < .001), complete response 17.2% vs 1.6% (P = .002), median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months (P < .001), time to next treatment hazard ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.17–0.42 — relative); of 44 patients with neuropathy, 86% resolved completely or improved to grade 1–2
cards.type: Final-data report of the ALCANZA randomised phase 3 trial — same trial, longer follow-up
cards.people: The same ALCANZA trial at median follow-up 45.9 months; adults with previously treated CD30-expressing mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, randomised to brentuximab vedotin (n = 64) or physician's choice (n = 64) as reported in this final analysis. Later report of the one trial on this shelf, not a second trial.
cards.result: Final data: ORR4 54.7% vs 12.5% (P < .001); complete response 17.2% vs 1.6% (P = .002); median progression-free survival 16.7 vs 3.5 months (P < .001); median time to next treatment 14.2 vs 5.6 months (hazard ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.17–0.42 — a relative measure; P < .001). Of 44 brentuximab-treated patients with any-grade peripheral neuropathy (grade 3 in 6, grade 4 in none), 86% (38 of 44) had complete resolution (26 of 44) or improvement to grades 1–2 (12 of 44); neuropathy was ongoing in 18 patients, all grade 1–2.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival of 16.7 vs 3.5 months is not an overall-survival claim — no survival advantage is printed in these reports. The arm sizes here (64 per arm) are the intention-to-treat population of the 131 randomised.
cards.source: Horwitz SM et al. Randomized phase 3 ALCANZA study of brentuximab vedotin vs physician's choice in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: final data. Blood advances. 2021. PMID: 34507350. cards.headline: Quality-of-life report (Dummer 2020): Skindex-29 symptom score fell by a mean maximum of −27.96 on brentuximab vedotin vs −8.62 on physician's choice (difference −18.9 [95% CI −26.6 to −11.2], adjusted P < .001), exceeding the minimally important difference (9.0–12.3); FACT-G and EQ-5D changes were comparable between arms
cards.summary: Quality-of-life report (Dummer 2020): Skindex-29 symptom score fell by a mean maximum of −27.96 on brentuximab vedotin vs −8.62 on physician's choice (difference −18.9 [95% CI −26.6 to −11.2], adjusted P < .001), exceeding the minimally important difference (9.0–12.3); FACT-G and EQ-5D changes were comparable between arms
cards.type: Patient-reported quality-of-life report of the ALCANZA trial — same trial, ancillary report
cards.people: Patients in the ALCANZA trial (same trial, patient-reported-outcome report), assessed with the Skindex-29 skin-specific questionnaire, the FACT-G general cancer questionnaire and the EQ-5D. The symptom-domain score was the key secondary endpoint.
cards.result: Mean maximum reduction from baseline in the Skindex-29 symptom domain was greater with brentuximab vedotin than physician's choice (−27.96 vs −8.62); the difference of −18.9 (95% CI −26.6 to −11.2; adjusted p < 0.001) exceeded the study-defined minimally important difference of 9.0–12.3. Mean changes in total FACT-G scores were similar between arms (0.15 vs −2.29), and EQ-5D changes were also comparable. Among brentuximab-treated patients with peripheral neuropathy, the mean maximum Skindex-29 symptom reduction was −35.54 vs −11.11 in patients without neuropathy, and neuropathy had no meaningful effect on FACT-G or EQ-5D scores.
cards.watchOut: The symptom gain is skin-specific (Skindex-29): general quality of life did not separate between arms, in an open-label trial where patients knew their treatment — both facts belong beside the headline symptom number.
cards.source: Dummer R et al. Patient-reported quality of life in patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: Results from the randomised phase III ALCANZA study. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 2020. PMID: 32502876. Registry ID: NCT01578499. cards.headline: CD30-expression sub-analysis (Kim 2021): brentuximab vedotin's ORR4 advantage held across CD30-expression levels (40.9% vs 9.5% where the minimum biopsy was <10%; 57.1% vs 10.3% where all biopsies were ≥10%) and regardless of large-cell transformation (64.7% vs 17.6% with LCT; 38.7% vs 6.5% without)
cards.summary: CD30-expression sub-analysis (Kim 2021): brentuximab vedotin's ORR4 advantage held across CD30-expression levels (40.9% vs 9.5% where the minimum biopsy was <10%; 57.1% vs 10.3% where all biopsies were ≥10%) and regardless of large-cell transformation (64.7% vs 17.6% with LCT; 38.7% vs 6.5% without)
cards.type: Exploratory sub-analysis of the ALCANZA trial by CD30 expression and large-cell transformation in mycosis fungoides — same trial, ancillary report
cards.people: Exploratory sub-analysis of ALCANZA patients with mycosis fungoides only (same trial), categorised by centrally reviewed baseline CD30 expression (CD30min <10%: at least one biopsy below 10%; CD30min ≥10%: all biopsies at least 10%; eligibility required at least one biopsy with ≥10% CD30 expression) and by large-cell transformation (LCT) status.
cards.result: Superior ORR4 with brentuximab vedotin vs physician's choice was observed in patients with CD30min <10% (40.9% vs 9.5%), CD30min ≥10% (57.1% vs 10.3%), LCT (64.7% vs 17.6%) and no LCT (38.7% vs 6.5%). Brentuximab vedotin also improved median progression-free survival vs physician's choice in every subgroup (16.7 vs 2.3 months; 15.5 vs 3.9 months; 15.5 vs 2.8 months; 16.1 vs 3.5 months, respectively). Safety profiles were generally comparable across subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory subgroup percentages from one trial's mycosis fungoides subset — small cells, no multiplicity control, and eligibility already required at least one biopsy with ≥10% CD30 expression, so this does not establish benefit in truly CD30-low disease.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial (ALCANZA, 131 randomised), 4 reports — brentuximab vedotin gave durable responses (ORR4 54.7% vs 12.5% at final data), longer progression-free survival (16.7 vs 3.5 months) and a skin-symptom gain exceeding the minimally important difference versus methotrexate or bexarotene, priced in peripheral neuropathy in two-thirds of treated patients; no overall-survival advantage is printed
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial (ALCANZA, 131 randomised), 4 reports — brentuximab vedotin gave durable responses (ORR4 54.7% vs 12.5% at final data), longer progression-free survival (16.7 vs 3.5 months) and a skin-symptom gain exceeding the minimally important difference versus methotrexate or bexarotene, priced in peripheral neuropathy in two-thirds of treated patients; no overall-survival advantage is printed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The programme basis is one trial, stated here and on the face. The honest frame is a large durable-response and symptom gain in a rare, incurable disease against a weak comparator — not a survival therapy.
cards.watchOut: Never present the PFS figures as survival, never pool the 4 reports as separate trials, and keep the open-label design and weak comparator beside the response gap.

shelves.title: Lenalidomide plus rituximab (R²) versus rituximab–chemotherapy in untreated advanced follicular lymphoma (RELEVANCE — one trial, 4 reports): similar efficacy at 3, 6 and 10 years (10-year PFS 46.4% vs 46.6%; overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1%) — an equivalence result, with less neutropenia but more grade 3/4 skin reactions on R²
shelves.question: In adults with previously untreated advanced follicular lymphoma, is chemotherapy-free lenalidomide plus rituximab (R²) as effective as rituximab plus chemotherapy — and does the toxicity trade (less neutropenia, more skin reactions) change the choice?

shelves.balance: One trial — RELEVANCE (1,030 patients randomised: R² n = 513, R-chemotherapy n = 517, both followed by rituximab maintenance) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such. The verdict is equivalence, not superiority: both co-primary endpoints were similar at every maturity. Complete response at 120 weeks was 48% vs 53% (P = 0.13, not significant) with interim 3-year progression-free survival 77% vs 78%; at 6 years, PFS was 60% vs 59% (hazard ratio 1.03 [95% CI 0.84–1.27] — a relative measure centred on no difference) and overall survival 89% in both groups; at 10 years, median PFS was 110.6 vs 102.8 months but the 10-year PFS rates were 46.4% vs 46.6% and overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1% — the median-PFS difference must not be read as a win. The toxicity trade belongs whole on the face: grade 3/4 neutropenia 32% on R² vs 50% on R-chemotherapy and febrile neutropenia 2% vs 7% favoured R², while grade 3/4 cutaneous reactions 7% vs 1% favoured R-chemotherapy — a different toxicity bill, not a smaller one. Secondary primary malignancies were 11% vs 13% at 6 years (P = .34). The molecular-response ancillary study is a labelled ancillary report of the same trial, in a French subset.

cards.headline: RELEVANCE primary report (Morschhauser 2018): complete response at 120 weeks 48% on R² vs 53% on R-chemotherapy (P = 0.13 — not significant) and interim 3-year PFS 77% vs 78% — similar efficacy, not superiority; grade 3/4 neutropenia 32% vs 50% and febrile neutropenia 2% vs 7% favoured R², grade 3/4 cutaneous reactions 7% vs 1% favoured R-chemotherapy
cards.summary: RELEVANCE primary report (Morschhauser 2018): complete response at 120 weeks 48% on R² vs 53% on R-chemotherapy (P = 0.13 — not significant) and interim 3-year PFS 77% vs 78% — similar efficacy, not superiority; grade 3/4 neutropenia 32% vs 50% and febrile neutropenia 2% vs 7% favoured R², grade 3/4 cutaneous reactions 7% vs 1% favoured R-chemotherapy
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 superiority trial (RELEVANCE primary report), R² vs rituximab–chemotherapy in untreated follicular lymphoma
cards.people: 1,030 patients with previously untreated advanced follicular lymphoma randomised to rituximab plus lenalidomide (n = 513; 18 cycles of the two drugs) or rituximab plus the investigator's choice of one of three rituximab-based chemotherapy regimens (n = 517), each followed by rituximab maintenance every 8 weeks for 12 cycles. Co-primary endpoints: complete response (confirmed or unconfirmed) at 120 weeks and progression-free survival. This was designed as a superiority trial.
cards.result: The rate of confirmed or unconfirmed complete response at 120 weeks was similar: 48% (95% CI 44–53) in the rituximab–lenalidomide group and 53% (95% CI 49–57) in the rituximab–chemotherapy group (P = 0.13). Interim 3-year progression-free survival was 77% (95% CI 72–80) and 78% (95% CI 74–82), respectively. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 32% on R² vs 50% on R-chemotherapy, and febrile neutropenia of any grade in 2% vs 7%; grade 3 or 4 cutaneous reactions occurred in 7% on R² vs 1% on R-chemotherapy. The authors conclude efficacy was similar and the safety profile differed.
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial that did not show superiority: 'similar' here is the observed result, not a formally tested non-inferiority claim — read the confidence intervals on the later reports before calling the regimens equivalent for an individual patient.
cards.source: Morschhauser F et al. Rituximab plus Lenalidomide in Advanced Untreated Follicular Lymphoma. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 30184451. Registry ID: NCT01476787 and NCT01650701. cards.headline: RELEVANCE 6-year results (Morschhauser 2022): 6-year PFS 60% on R² vs 59% on R-chemotherapy (hazard ratio 1.03 [95% CI 0.84–1.27] — a relative measure centred on no difference) and 6-year overall survival 89% in both groups; secondary primary malignancies 11% vs 13% (P = .34); no new safety signals
cards.summary: RELEVANCE 6-year results (Morschhauser 2022): 6-year PFS 60% on R² vs 59% on R-chemotherapy (hazard ratio 1.03 [95% CI 0.84–1.27] — a relative measure centred on no difference) and 6-year overall survival 89% in both groups; secondary primary malignancies 11% vs 13% (P = .34); no new safety signals
cards.type: 6-year update report of the RELEVANCE randomised phase 3 trial — same trial, longer follow-up
cards.people: The same 1,030 RELEVANCE patients, second interim analysis at median follow-up 72 months. Later report of the one trial on this shelf, not a second trial.
cards.result: 6-year progression-free survival was 60% for R² and 59% for R-chemotherapy (hazard ratio 1.03 [95% CI 0.84–1.27] — a relative measure), and 6-year overall survival was estimated at 89% in both groups; median PFS and overall survival were not reached in either group. Overall response after progression was 61% and 59%, and 5-year estimated survival after progression was 69% and 74%, respectively. Transformation rates per year were 0.68% and 0.45%, and secondary primary malignancies occurred in 11% and 13% (P = .34). No new safety signals were observed. The authors conclude R² provides an acceptable chemotherapy-free alternative.
cards.watchOut: This record lists only one of the trial's two ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, and its source line reflects its own record. The hazard ratio of 1.03 with an interval spanning 0.84–1.27 is compatible with modest benefit or modest harm — equivalence is a clinical reading of the whole follow-up, not a single statistic.

cards.headline: RELEVANCE 10-year analysis (Gower 2026): median PFS 110.6 months on R² vs 102.8 months on R-chemotherapy, but 10-year PFS rates 46.4% vs 46.6%, overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1% and time to next treatment 62.2% vs 66.3%; 87 deaths in each group
cards.summary: RELEVANCE 10-year analysis (Gower 2026): median PFS 110.6 months on R² vs 102.8 months on R-chemotherapy, but 10-year PFS rates 46.4% vs 46.6%, overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1% and time to next treatment 62.2% vs 66.3%; 87 deaths in each group
cards.type: 10-year final analysis of the RELEVANCE randomised phase 3 trial — same trial, final follow-up
cards.people: The same 1,030 RELEVANCE patients (R² n = 513; R-chemotherapy n = 517) in the final analysis at 120 months of follow-up. Later report of the one trial on this shelf, not a second trial.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival by independent review was 110.6 months with R² vs 102.8 months with R-chemotherapy, while the 10-year PFS rates were 46.4% for R² and 46.6% for R-chemotherapy. Median overall survival and time to next lymphoma treatment were not reached in either arm; 10-year overall survival rates were 82.4% vs 81.1%, and 10-year time-to-next-treatment rates 62.2% vs 66.3%. Patients with progression within 24 months had a poorer prognosis (hazard ratio 6.215 for death; P < .0001 — a relative measure), with no difference between groups. Second primary malignancies occurred at 2.11 cases per 100 patient-years (95% CI 1.80–2.46). In each group, 87 patients died, mainly from lymphoma progression and second primary malignancies. Only 9 transformations occurred after 24 months (3 with R² vs 6 with R-chemotherapy).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the 110.6 vs 102.8-month median-PFS difference read as a win: the 10-year PFS rates are 46.4% vs 46.6% and time to next treatment numerically favours R-chemotherapy (66.3% vs 62.2%). Medians and landmark rates answer different questions in curves this flat.
cards.source: Gower N et al. Lenalidomide plus rituximab for previously untreated advanced follicular lymphoma: the 10-year RELEVANCE trial analysis. Blood. 2026. PMID: 41915772. cards.headline: Molecular-response ancillary study (Delfau-Larue 2020): complete molecular response at week 24 in 90% (105 of 117) on R² vs 77% (70 of 90) on R-chemotherapy (P = .022) in the French BCL2-JH-positive subset; patients achieving complete molecular response had 3-year PFS 84% vs 55% with detectable disease (P = .015), irrespective of arm
cards.summary: Molecular-response ancillary study (Delfau-Larue 2020): complete molecular response at week 24 in 90% (105 of 117) on R² vs 77% (70 of 90) on R-chemotherapy (P = .022) in the French BCL2-JH-positive subset; patients achieving complete molecular response had 3-year PFS 84% vs 55% with detectable disease (P = .015), irrespective of arm
cards.type: Ancillary molecular-response (MRD) study of the RELEVANCE trial, French LYSA subset — same trial, ancillary report
cards.people: LYSA ancillary study of RELEVANCE (same trial): of 440 French RELEVANCE participants, the 222 patients with a BIOMED-2-detectable BCL2-JH translocation at diagnosis were analysed; minimal residual disease was quantified by droplet digital PCR (sensitivity ≤10⁻⁴) at week 24 (end of induction).
cards.result: At week 24, 98% and 78% of patients achieved complete molecular response in peripheral blood and bone marrow, respectively (both arms combined as reported). Complete molecular response (in blood and/or marrow) had a significant impact on progression-free survival, with 3-year PFS of 84% for patients with complete molecular response and 55% for those with detectable minimal residual disease (P = .015). Complete molecular response at week 24 was reached more frequently in the R² arm (105 of 117; 90%) than in the R-chemotherapy arm (70 of 90; 77%) (P = .022). The poor prognostic value of persistent molecular disease was observed irrespective of treatment arm (interaction test P = .31).
cards.watchOut: A biomarker ancillary study in less than a quarter of the trial's patients (222 of 1,030, French subset, translocation-positive only): the higher molecular-response rate on R² did not translate into a clinical PFS advantage in the parent trial, and molecular response must not be quoted as a substitute for it.

shelves.title: Viscoelastic test reference ranges (TEG / ROTEM) in healthy adults: population-derived ranges sit far from manufacturers' ranges (up to 74% of healthy volunteers outside on at least one parameter), with sex, age and native-vs-citrated differences throughout
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference ranges for whole-blood viscoelastic clotting tests — thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) — how far do population-derived ranges sit from the manufacturers' ranges, how do the ranges differ by sex, age and population, and how much do native vs citrated-recalcified samples move the ROTEM values? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep haemostasis sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Coagulation · Blood Group Antigens · Female · Humans · Male · Racial Groups · Reference Values · Thrombelastography
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — reference ranges for whole-blood viscoelastic tests rest on 6 independent populations (4 TEG, 2 ROTEM), counted per modality and never merged. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep, haemostasis sections — framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Population-derived TEG ranges sit materially apart from the manufacturers' ranges: the manufacturer's ranges would have labelled 8.5% of 118 healthy Brazilian volunteers coagulopathic (specificity 81%), 74% of 200 North Indian volunteers had at least one value outside the manufacturer's range, and about 40% of a second Indian sample (120 volunteers, including 33 children) fell outside at least one manufacturer range — three different comparisons (diagnosis-level vs any-parameter), each printed with its own definition. Sex differences recur (women more hypercoagulable in the Brazilian and Beijing datasets). For ROTEM, native-blood (NATEM) clotting time, α-angle and maximum clot firmness correlated with age in 132 healthy adults; and recalcification itself moves the values — TRUE-NATEM clotting time 872–1595 s vs NATEM 757–1327 s in a dataset whose volunteer N is not documented in its abstract, labelled as such. Activator and sample handling (citrated kaolin vs native) print on every card.

cards.headline: TEG dataset 1 of 4 (Scarpelini 2009, Brazil, N = 118 healthy volunteers, citrated kaolin TEG on a Haemoscope 5000): 95% ranges R 3.8–9.8 min, K 0.7–3.4 min, α-angle 47.8–77.7°, MA 49.7–72.7 mm, LY30 −2.3 to 5.77%, coagulation index −5.1 to 3.6 — and the manufacturer's ranges would have diagnosed coagulopathy in 10 of these healthy volunteers (8.5%; specificity 81%), with no disease found on extensive investigation
cards.summary: TEG dataset 1 of 4 (Scarpelini 2009, Brazil, N = 118 healthy volunteers, citrated kaolin TEG on a Haemoscope 5000): 95% ranges R 3.8–9.8 min, K 0.7–3.4 min, α-angle 47.8–77.7°, MA 49.7–72.7 mm, LY30 −2.3 to 5.77%, coagulation index −5.1 to 3.6 — and the manufacturer's ranges would have diagnosed coagulopathy in 10 of these healthy volunteers (8.5%; specificity 81%), with no disease found on extensive investigation
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — TEG reference ranges, healthy volunteers (citrated kaolin, Haemoscope 5000)
cards.people: 118 healthy adult volunteers (pregnant people, those on anticoagulants and those with a bleeding disorder excluded), tested with a standardised citrated-blood kaolin technique; volunteers outside the manufacturer's normal range underwent extensive coagulation investigations. Women were significantly more hypercoagulable than men; ageing was not associated with hypercoagulability.
cards.result: Reference ranges for 95% of volunteers: R 3.8–9.8 min, K 0.7–3.4 min, α-angle 47.8–77.7 degrees, MA 49.7–72.7 mm, LY30 −2.3 to 5.77%, coagulation index −5.1 to 3.6. Most values differed significantly from the manufacturer's, whose ranges had 81% specificity in this population and would incorrectly identify 8.5% of healthy volunteers as coagulopathic. The authors supported the manufacturer's own recommendation that each institution determine its own normal values.
cards.watchOut: The 8.5% figure is a diagnosis-level misclassification (labelled coagulopathic, then cleared by investigation) — a different comparison from the any-parameter out-of-range rates in the Indian datasets, and never averaged with them. Method is citrated kaolin on one device; native-blood values would differ.

cards.headline: TEG dataset 2 of 4 (Subramanian 2014, North India, N = 200 healthy volunteers — 100 men, 100 women, aged 20–50): 95% ranges r-time 1.8–14.2 min, k-time 0.7–7.3 min, α-angle 27.3–72.3°, MA 32.1–87.9 mm — and 74% (149/200) had at least one value outside the manufacturer's reference range, against 14.5% (29/200) outside this population's own derived range
cards.summary: TEG dataset 2 of 4 (Subramanian 2014, North India, N = 200 healthy volunteers — 100 men, 100 women, aged 20–50): 95% ranges r-time 1.8–14.2 min, k-time 0.7–7.3 min, α-angle 27.3–72.3°, MA 32.1–87.9 mm — and 74% (149/200) had at least one value outside the manufacturer's reference range, against 14.5% (29/200) outside this population's own derived range
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — TEG reference ranges, healthy North Indian volunteers (TEM-A, non-additive whole blood)
cards.people: 200 healthy North Indian volunteers (100 males, 100 females, aged 20–50 years) enrolled over 2011–2012; thromboelastometry on a TEM-A automated thromboelastometer (Framar Biomedica) using whole blood non-additive (360 µL), with prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time and platelet count for all volunteers.
cards.result: The 95% reference ranges (mean ± 1.96 SD) were r-time 1.8–14.2 min, k-time 0.7–7.3 min, α-angle 27.3–72.3° and MA 32.1–87.9 mm. Maximum clot strength was higher in women than men, not statistically significantly. Overall 14.5% (29/200) had at least one abnormal parameter on the population's own range while 74% (149/200) had deranged values on the manufacturer's range, with statistically significant variation between the ranges on every parameter (P<0.001). The authors recommended each laboratory determine normal values for its target population and cautioned that TEG cannot replace conventional coagulation tests.
cards.watchOut: 74% is an any-parameter out-of-range rate, not a coagulopathy diagnosis rate — the comparison differs from the Brazilian dataset's 8.5% and the two are never merged. The device and sample handling (TEM-A, non-additive whole blood) also differ from the citrated-kaolin datasets; ranges print per method.
cards.source: Subramanian et al. Establishing a normal reference range for thromboelastography in North Indian healthy volunteers. Indian journal of pathology & microbiology. 2014. PMID: 24739830. cards.headline: TEG dataset 3 of 4 (Ji 2011, Beijing, N = 137 healthy volunteers, citrated kaolin, Haemoscope 5000): 95% ranges R 3.8–8.4 min, K 0.8–3.3 min, α-angle 46.2–76.2°, MA 50.0–70.8 mm, LY30 −3.3 to 4.0%, CI −3.8 to 2.9 — 24.1% (33/137) had at least one abnormal parameter on the population range and 7.3% (10/137) would have been considered coagulopathic on the manufacturer's values (specificity 76.0%), with significant sex differences on all parameters and lower fibrinogen function than the manufacturer's Western reference population
cards.summary: TEG dataset 3 of 4 (Ji 2011, Beijing, N = 137 healthy volunteers, citrated kaolin, Haemoscope 5000): 95% ranges R 3.8–8.4 min, K 0.8–3.3 min, α-angle 46.2–76.2°, MA 50.0–70.8 mm, LY30 −3.3 to 4.0%, CI −3.8 to 2.9 — 24.1% (33/137) had at least one abnormal parameter on the population range and 7.3% (10/137) would have been considered coagulopathic on the manufacturer's values (specificity 76.0%), with significant sex differences on all parameters and lower fibrinogen function than the manufacturer's Western reference population
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — TEG reference ranges, healthy Beijing volunteers (citrated kaolin, Haemoscope 5000)
cards.people: 137 healthy adult volunteers resident in Beijing for over three years (enrolled June–August 2010), tested with citrated blood and kaolin activator on a Haemoscope 5000, with prothrombin time, APTT, thrombin time and plasma fibrinogen measured on the same sample.
cards.result: Reference ranges for 95% of volunteers: R 3.8–8.4 min, K 0.8–3.3 min, α-Angle 46.2–76.2°, MA 50.0–70.8 mm, LY30 −3.3% to 4.0% and CI −3.8 to 2.9. Overall 24.1% (33/137) had at least one abnormal parameter while 7.3% (10/137) would have been considered coagulopathy on the manufacturer's values (test specificity 76.0%). Chinese healthy volunteers had lower fibrinogen function than the manufacturer's Western reference population, and R, K, α-Angle, MA and CI differed significantly between men and women (all P<0.01). The authors supported each institute determining its own normal reference values.
cards.watchOut: Two different out-of-range rates appear in this one report — 24.1% any-parameter on the population range and 7.3% diagnosis-level on the manufacturer's — and each prints with its definition. Same device family and activator as the Brazilian dataset, yet the ranges and sex pattern are population-specific.

cards.headline: TEG dataset 4 of 4 (Ahammad 2020, India, N = 120 healthy volunteers — 87 adults and 33 children, composition printed on the face): kaolin-activated TEG ranges R-time 3.8–10.6, K-time 1.2–3.1, angle 44.9–72.0, MA 41.2–64.5, LY30 0–9.9, CI −3.7 to 3.4 — about 40% had at least one abnormal parameter on the manufacturer's range, falling to 12.5% on the derived ranges, with significant age- and sex-group differences in R-time, K-time and angle
cards.summary: TEG dataset 4 of 4 (Ahammad 2020, India, N = 120 healthy volunteers — 87 adults and 33 children, composition printed on the face): kaolin-activated TEG ranges R-time 3.8–10.6, K-time 1.2–3.1, angle 44.9–72.0, MA 41.2–64.5, LY30 0–9.9, CI −3.7 to 3.4 — about 40% had at least one abnormal parameter on the manufacturer's range, falling to 12.5% on the derived ranges, with significant age- and sex-group differences in R-time, K-time and angle
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — TEG reference ranges, healthy Indian population including children (kaolin-activated, citrated whole blood)
cards.people: 120 healthy volunteers (55 adult males, 32 adult females and 33 children) screened for bleeding history and drugs affecting coagulation; kaolin-activated TEG on citrated whole blood, analysing R-time, K-time, angle, MA, LY30 and CI. The adult subset is 87; the 33 children are part of the printed composition and are not silently counted as adults.
cards.result: Derived reference ranges for all volunteers irrespective of age and sex: R-time 3.8–10.6, K-time 1.2–3.1, angle 44.9–72.0, MA 41.2–64.5, LY30 0–9.9 and CI −3.7 to 3.4. Statistically significant differences were observed between age and sex groups for R-time, K-time and angle. The authors concluded population-specific ranges should be derived before TEG is used clinically.

cards.result: For ROTEM, age correlated positively with maximum clot firmness and α-angle (P = 0.001) and negatively with clotting time (P = 0.039). Thrombin peak and endogenous thrombin potential at 5 pmol/L tissue factor correlated significantly with α-angle and maximum clot firmness. Age-related changes in both assays were not linear. This report publishes correlations and age patterns for NATEM rather than a full reference-interval table — carded as such, with no interval invented for it.
cards.watchOut: No reference intervals are printed from this dataset because its abstract reports correlations, not intervals — the interval-bearing ROTEM dataset is the next card. Its thrombin-generation results are cross-pointed, not carded, to avoid double-homing one report's two limbs.

cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — ROTEM Delta reference values, native vs recalcified citrated blood (volunteer N not documented)
cards.people: Healthy adult volunteers aged 18–65 years (any medical condition or medication affecting coagulation excluded), tested on a ROTEM Delta with fresh native whole blood (TRUE-NATEM) and with recalcified citrated blood (NATEM). N not documented — the abstract does not state the number of volunteers, and no number is claimed here.
cards.result: TRUE-NATEM reference values: CT 872–1595 s, A10 14–34 mm, A20 26–48 mm, CFT 314–839 s, MCF 34–55 mm, α-angle 17–40°. NATEM reference values: CT 757–1327 s, A10 19–43 mm, A20 33–55 mm, CFT 219–615 s, MCF 37–61 mm, α-angle 24–51°, ML 0–3%. Comparing NATEM with TRUE-NATEM, CT and CFT decreased and MCF and α-angle increased — the recalcification process itself shows significant activation of coagulation. Female volunteers had enhanced coagulation when activators were used; ethnicity showed no difference. The authors underlined native whole blood as the gold-standard reference.
cards.watchOut: 'N not documented' applies to this dataset per the standing labelling rule — it is carded for its paired native-vs-citrated comparison, not for any sample-size weight. The native/citrated gap is the content: a NATEM interval must never be applied to a native-blood result, or vice versa.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 6 independent populations — 4 TEG and 2 ROTEM, counted per modality and never merged — establish that viscoelastic reference ranges are population-, sex-, device- and sample-handling-specific: population-derived TEG ranges repeatedly sit apart from manufacturers' ranges (8.5% diagnosis-level misclassification in Brazil; 74% any-parameter out-of-range in North India; ~40% in the second Indian dataset), and ROTEM values move materially with recalcification alone (TRUE-NATEM CT 872–1595 s vs NATEM 757–1327 s)
cards.summary: Synthesis: 6 independent populations — 4 TEG and 2 ROTEM, counted per modality and never merged — establish that viscoelastic reference ranges are population-, sex-, device- and sample-handling-specific: population-derived TEG ranges repeatedly sit apart from manufacturers' ranges (8.5% diagnosis-level misclassification in Brazil; 74% any-parameter out-of-range in North India; ~40% in the second Indian dataset), and ROTEM values move materially with recalcification alone (TRUE-NATEM CT 872–1595 s vs NATEM 757–1327 s)
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: TEG — Brazil (N = 118), North India (N = 200), Beijing (N = 137), India (N = 120, including 33 children); ROTEM — healthy adults (N = 132) and native-vs-citrated volunteers (N not documented). Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep haemostasis sections) is framing only; the shelf rests on these primary datasets.
cards.result: The consistent finding across datasets is that a laboratory's own population range classifies healthy people very differently from the manufacturer's range, and that sex, age, activator and citrate handling move the values. Pregnancy-specific viscoelastic ranges are a different population and are not carded here. Cross-points: plasma coagulation screening tests (pack #7393) and calibrated thrombin generation (pack #6965) are different measurement families.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each dataset's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Reticulocyte-profile reference intervals in healthy adults: intervals are platform-specific — reticulocyte haemoglobin content 22.84–29.70 pg on the Mindray BC-6200 vs 29.95–35.12 pg in Chengdu and 30.9–35.7 pg on the BC-6800, across 4 independent populations
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the reticulocyte profile — absolute reticulocyte count, reticulocyte percentage, immature reticulocyte fraction, reticulocyte haemoglobin content / equivalent (CHr / Ret-He / RHE) and mean reticulocyte volume — how far apart do the intervals sit between analyser platforms (Beckman Coulter DxH, Sysmex, Mindray) and populations, and which parameters need sex partitioning? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, red-cell / erythropoiesis sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · Reticulocyte Count · Male · Female · Reference Values · Reticulocytes · Middle Aged · Adolescent · Young Adult · Cohort Studies
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — reticulocyte-profile reference intervals rest on 4 independent populations, and platform is the content: no haemoglobin-content figure prints without its analyser. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, red-cell / erythropoiesis sections — framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. The Madrid dataset (175 healthy adults, Beckman Coulter DxH 900) established intervals for 14 reticulocyte-profile parameters per CLSI EP28-A3c, with sex partitioning required for two derived parameters (low haemoglobin density, microcytic anaemia factor) but not the core reticulocyte measures; its abstract does not print the numeric intervals, and none are invented here. The Chengdu dataset (691 healthy Han adults) gives reticulocyte haemoglobin content 29.95–35.12 pg (men) and 29.77–34.52 pg (women), mean reticulocyte volume 99.76–115.97 fL (men) and 98.72–113.83 fL (women), and reticulocyte percentage 0.485–1.504%. The Mindray BC-6800 dataset (184 healthy adults) gives reticulocytes 23.2–93.2 ×10⁹/L and haemoglobin equivalent 30.9–35.7 pg, with the Sysmex XE-5000 comparison showing a different upper count limit (101.3 vs 93.2 ×10⁹/L). The Thai BC-6200 dataset — the smallest, N = 60, printed on the face — gives a haemoglobin-content interval of 22.84–29.70 pg, well below the Chengdu and BC-6800 intervals on other platforms. Counts print in ×10⁹/L as in the records.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 4 (Posada-Franco 2024, Madrid, N = 175 healthy adults aged 18–62, Beckman Coulter DxH 900): reference intervals established for 14 reticulocyte-profile parameters per CLSI EP28-A3c, with sex partitioning required for two derived parameters (low haemoglobin density and microcytic anaemia factor) but not for the core reticulocyte measures — the abstract does not print the numeric intervals, and none are claimed here

cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — reticulocyte-profile reference intervals, Beckman Coulter DxH 900 (CLSI EP28-A3c)
cards.people: 175 healthy adults (18 to 62 years) recruited from the blood donation centre of Hospital Clínico San Carlos, Madrid, Spain, with whole blood assayed for 14 haematological parameters of the reticulocyte profile on the Beckman Coulter DxH 900 analyser; intervals estimated by non-parametric, Harrell-Davis bootstrap and robust methods, with partitioning judged by Lahti's method.
cards.result: Intervals estimated by the non-parametric and Harrell-Davis bootstrap methods were very similar; robust-method intervals were narrower. Gender partitioning was required for two parameters — low haemoglobin density (LHD) and microcytic anaemia factor (MAF) — while the rest of the parameters did not need partitioning. The authors' stated rationale is that, absent standardisation, each laboratory should establish reference ranges for its own methodology and instrumentation.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the partitioning finding and the platform, not numeric intervals — its abstract reports that 14 intervals were established without printing them, and no interval is reconstructed here. Do not borrow another platform's numbers to fill it in.

cards.people: 184 healthy adults of both sexes for the reference intervals (with a further 368 subjects with various pathological conditions used for the analyser's diagnostic-efficiency evaluation, not for the intervals); reticulocytes and extended parameters quantified on the Mindray BC-6800 and compared with the Sysmex XE-5000.
cards.result: Reference intervals on the BC-6800: reticulocytes 23.2–93.2 ×10⁹/L; immature reticulocyte fraction 0.015–0.14; mean reticulocyte haemoglobin equivalent (RHE) 30.9–35.7 pg; mean reticulocyte volume 97.8–118 fL. Imprecision was close to the analytic goal, carryover (2.3%) was negligible and time-stability excellent up to 8 hours. Against the XE-5000, overall correlation on counting was good despite the difference in the upper reference limit (93.2 vs 101.3 ×10⁹/L), and total agreement of RHE was 91.6%.
cards.watchOut: The immature reticulocyte fraction here is a fraction (0.015–0.14), while the Thai dataset reports IRF as a percentage (2.71–15.28%) — same quantity, different expression, never mixed. The 368 pathological subjects belong to the efficiency limb only and are not part of the healthy denominator.

cards.headline: Dataset 4 of 4 (Aphaiwiwat 2025, Thailand, N = 60 healthy adults — the smallest dataset, printed on the face — Mindray BC-6200): reticulocytes 34.88–118.50 ×10⁹/L, immature reticulocyte fraction 2.71–15.28%, and reticulocyte haemoglobin content 22.84–29.70 pg — well below the Chengdu (29.95–35.12 pg) and BC-6800 (30.9–35.7 pg) intervals — with counts correlating r > 0.9785 against flow cytometry and manual microscopy
cards.summary: Dataset 4 of 4 (Aphaiwiwat 2025, Thailand, N = 60 healthy adults — the smallest dataset, printed on the face — Mindray BC-6200): reticulocytes 34.88–118.50 ×10⁹/L, immature reticulocyte fraction 2.71–15.28%, and reticulocyte haemoglobin content 22.84–29.70 pg — well below the Chengdu (29.95–35.12 pg) and BC-6800 (30.9–35.7 pg) intervals — with counts correlating r > 0.9785 against flow cytometry and manual microscopy
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — reticulocyte reference intervals, Mindray BC-6200, Thai adults (small N = 60)
cards.people: 60 healthy Thai adults of both sexes for the reference intervals (with 182 leftover samples from individuals with pathological conditions used for method comparison), with reticulocyte counts on the Mindray BC-6200 compared against manual microscopy and flow cytometry as the reference method.
cards.result: Reference intervals on the BC-6200: reticulocytes 34.88–118.50 ×10⁹/L; immature reticulocyte fraction 2.71–15.28%; reticulocyte haemoglobin content (RHE) 22.84–29.70 pg. Imprecision was below the manufacturer's claim, carryover was <0.001% and time-stability excellent up to 24 hours. Reticulocyte counts correlated strongly between the analyser, manual microscopy and flow cytometry (r > 0.9785). The authors concluded the BC-6200 is a reliable alternative for reticulocyte counting while noting further studies are needed on clinical utility in diagnosing haematological conditions.
cards.watchOut: N = 60 exceeds the ~10-human reference floor but is small for an interval study, and its N prints here rather than being rounded up by the larger datasets. Its haemoglobin-content interval (22.84–29.70 pg) barely overlaps the other platforms' — the clearest single demonstration on this shelf that the interval belongs to the analyser, not to the analyte alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 4 independent populations establish reticulocyte-profile reference intervals per platform — DxH 900 intervals for 14 parameters with sex partitioning needed only for two derived measures (numeric intervals not printed in that abstract), Chengdu RHE 29.95–35.12 pg (men) with reticulocyte percentage 0.485–1.504%, BC-6800 reticulocytes 23.2–93.2 ×10⁹/L with RHE 30.9–35.7 pg, and BC-6200 reticulocytes 34.88–118.50 ×10⁹/L with RHE 22.84–29.70 pg — so no reticulocyte haemoglobin figure is meaningful without its analyser named
cards.summary: Synthesis: 4 independent populations establish reticulocyte-profile reference intervals per platform — DxH 900 intervals for 14 parameters with sex partitioning needed only for two derived measures (numeric intervals not printed in that abstract), Chengdu RHE 29.95–35.12 pg (men) with reticulocyte percentage 0.485–1.504%, BC-6800 reticulocytes 23.2–93.2 ×10⁹/L with RHE 30.9–35.7 pg, and BC-6200 reticulocytes 34.88–118.50 ×10⁹/L with RHE 22.84–29.70 pg — so no reticulocyte haemoglobin figure is meaningful without its analyser named
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: Madrid (N = 175, Beckman Coulter DxH 900), Chengdu (N = 691, healthy Han adults), BC-6800 series (N = 184 healthy adults) and Thai BC-6200 series (N = 60 healthy adults) — four independent populations, intervals kept per platform and per population. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, red-cell / erythropoiesis sections) is framing only; the shelf rests on these datasets. A fifth candidate dataset was excluded at verification as veterinary (dogs) and is not counted.
cards.result: Sex partitioning is parameter-specific (required for low haemoglobin density and microcytic anaemia factor in Madrid; published as sex-specific intervals in Chengdu), and count intervals differ by platform at both ends (upper limit 93.2 vs 118.50 ×10⁹/L across the Mindray datasets, with the Sysmex XE-5000 at 101.3). Cross-point: full-blood-count reference intervals (pack #7321) cover haemoglobin, white cells and platelets, not reticulocyte parameters.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each dataset's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Peripheral thermometry vs core temperature in adults: 3 overlapping syntheses (labelled as syntheses, never independent cohorts) — limits of agreement beyond the acceptable ±0.5 °C, fever-detection sensitivity only 64%, and only oesophageal measurement clinically acceptable in ICU
shelves.question: At the bedside, how accurately do peripheral thermometers (tympanic membrane, temporal artery, axillary and oral) estimate core body temperature in adults — what are their pooled limits of agreement against central thermometry (pulmonary artery, bladder, oesophageal, rectal), how poor is fever detection, and does any non-invasive method reach clinically acceptable accuracy in intensive care? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Axilla · Child · Fever/diagnosis · Humans · Hypothermia/diagnosis · Mouth · Temporal Arteries · Thermometers/standards · Tympanic Membrane
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts, everywhere. The largest (75 studies, 8,682 patients) found pooled 95% limits of agreement outside the pre-defined clinically acceptable ±0.5 °C range — −1.44 °C to 1.46 °C in febrile adults and −2.07 °C to 1.90 °C in hypothermia — with fever-detection sensitivity of only 64% beside specificity of 96%. The adult-ICU synthesis (13 studies, 632 patients, 105,375 measurements) found axillary, tympanic infrared and zero-heat-flux thermometers all underestimated intravascular temperature, only oesophageal measurement was clinically acceptable, and heterogeneity was 99–100%. The oldest, smallest synthesis (3 febrile-ICU studies) is the most favourable — mean differences within ±0.2 °C for most tympanic combinations and the one oral study — and that disagreement between syntheses is content, not noise to be averaged away. No single 'peripheral thermometers are accurate / inaccurate' verdict prints without method, population and the limits-of-agreement framing; no card implies a thermometer-guided pathway improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 1 of 3 (Niven 2015, Annals of Internal Medicine — 75 studies, 8,682 patients, adults and children): pooled 95% limits of agreement against central thermometry fell outside the pre-defined clinically acceptable ±0.5 °C range, especially in fever (−1.44 °C to 1.46 °C in adults) and hypothermia (−2.07 °C to 1.90 °C in adults); fever-detection sensitivity was low at 64% (95% CI 55–72%) with specificity 96% (93–97%)
cards.summary: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 1 of 3 (Niven 2015, Annals of Internal Medicine — 75 studies, 8,682 patients, adults and children): pooled 95% limits of agreement against central thermometry fell outside the pre-defined clinically acceptable ±0.5 °C range, especially in fever (−1.44 °C to 1.46 °C in adults) and hypothermia (−2.07 °C to 1.90 °C in adults); fever-detection sensitivity was low at 64% (95% CI 55–72%) with specificity 96% (93–97%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (synthesis 1 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Prospective studies comparing peripheral thermometers (tympanic membrane, temporal artery, axillary or oral) with central thermometers (pulmonary artery catheter, urinary bladder, oesophageal or rectal) in adults and children; 75 studies, 8,682 patients. Most studies were at high or unclear risk of patient-selection bias (74%) or index-test bias (67%). One of 3 overlapping syntheses on this shelf — labelled as such, never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Compared with central thermometers, peripheral thermometers had pooled 95% limits of agreement outside the pre-defined clinically acceptable range (±0.5 °C), especially among patients with fever (−1.44 °C to 1.46 °C for adults; −1.49 °C to 0.43 °C for children) and hypothermia (−2.07 °C to 1.90 °C for adults; no data for children). For detection of fever, sensitivity was low (64%, 95% CI 55–72%) but specificity was high (96%, 93–97%). Only 1 study reported sensitivity and specificity for detection of hypothermia. The authors conclude peripheral thermometers do not have clinically acceptable accuracy and should not be used when accurate measurement will influence clinical decisions.
cards.watchOut: The largest synthesis and the least favourable: limits of agreement — not mean bias — are the accuracy measure here, and they are roughly three times the acceptable width in febrile adults. Fever sensitivity of 64% means about a third of fevers are missed at the bedside by a peripheral reading.
cards.source: Niven DJ et al. Accuracy of peripheral thermometers for estimating temperature: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of internal medicine. 2015. PMID: 26571241. cards.headline: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 2 of 3 (Cutuli 2021, adult ICU — 13 cohort studies, 632 patients, 105,375 measurements): axillary, tympanic infrared and zero-heat-flux thermometers all underestimated intravascular temperature, only oesophageal measurement showed clinically acceptable accuracy, and heterogeneity was 99–100%
cards.summary: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 2 of 3 (Cutuli 2021, adult ICU — 13 cohort studies, 632 patients, 105,375 measurements): axillary, tympanic infrared and zero-heat-flux thermometers all underestimated intravascular temperature, only oesophageal measurement showed clinically acceptable accuracy, and heterogeneity was 99–100%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis in adult ICU patients (synthesis 2 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Published studies reporting accuracy and precision of non-invasive peripheral thermometers (index test) in adult ICU patients against intravascular temperature measurement (reference test), searched 1966–2017; 13 cohort studies, 632 patients and 105,375 measurements; study quality assessed with QUADAS-2. One of 3 overlapping syntheses on this shelf — labelled as such, never an independent cohort. This record carries no MeSH terms (source line reads 'MeSH: none in the record').
cards.result: Axillary, tympanic infrared and zero-heat-flux thermometers all underestimated intravascular temperature. Only oesophageal measurements showed clinically acceptable accuracy. There were too few studies to assess precision for any technique. Study heterogeneity was high (99–100%), and risk of bias for the index test was unclear, mostly because of no device calibration or control for confounders. The authors conclude non-invasive peripheral thermometers have low accuracy in ICU patients and their clinical and trial-related use is unreliable and potentially misleading.
cards.watchOut: 105,375 measurements in only 632 patients — measurement count is not patient count, and the two must never be interchanged in a summary of this shelf. Heterogeneity of 99–100% means the pooled bias figures describe an average across unlike studies, not a property of any one device.

cards.headline: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 3 of 3 (Jefferies 2011, febrile critically ill adults — 3 studies against pulmonary-artery core temperature): studies were too heterogeneous and too poorly reported for meta-analysis; mean differences were within ±0.2 °C in five of seven tympanic combinations and in the one oral study, but outside that range for all three rectal combinations
cards.summary: Peripheral thermometry synthesis 3 of 3 (Jefferies 2011, febrile critically ill adults — 3 studies against pulmonary-artery core temperature): studies were too heterogeneous and too poorly reported for meta-analysis; mean differences were within ±0.2 °C in five of seven tympanic combinations and in the one oral study, but outside that range for all three rectal combinations
cards.type: Systematic review in febrile critically ill adults (synthesis 3 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Clinical trials comparing peripheral thermometry in critically ill adult patients with core temperatures >37.5 °C against pulmonary-artery catheter core temperature; 3 studies identified. The oldest synthesis on this shelf, and the most favourable to tympanic/oral measurement — the disagreement between syntheses is content. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — labelled as such, never an independent cohort.
cards.result: The studies were heterogeneous and all failed to report appropriate measurements of variation, which prevented meta-analysis and limited interpretation. Mean differences were within ±0.2 °C in five of seven tympanic thermometer/mode/temperature combinations and in the one oral thermometer studied; all three rectal thermometer/temperature combinations reported mean differences outside this range. The authors suggest tympanic and oral thermometry provide, on average, accurate measures of core temperature within the febrile range, while calling for further studies with appropriate statistical methods.
cards.watchOut: Near-zero mean bias in 3 small febrile-range studies is not accuracy: a thermometer can average correctly while individual readings stray widely — which is exactly what the largest synthesis's limits of agreement show. This card must never be quoted without the limits-of-agreement card beside it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 overlapping syntheses — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts — agree that peripheral thermometers underestimate or stray widely from core temperature (limits of agreement beyond ±0.5 °C; fever sensitivity 64% in the largest synthesis; only oesophageal measurement clinically acceptable in ICU), against near-zero mean bias in the small, oldest febrile-range review
cards.summary: Synthesis: 3 overlapping syntheses — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts — agree that peripheral thermometers underestimate or stray widely from core temperature (limits of agreement beyond ±0.5 °C; fever sensitivity 64% in the largest synthesis; only oesophageal measurement clinically acceptable in ICU), against near-zero mean bias in the small, oldest febrile-range review
cards.people: All syntheses carded on this shelf: Niven 2015 (75 studies, 8,682 patients), Cutuli 2021 (13 ICU cohort studies, 632 patients, 105,375 measurements) and Jefferies 2011 (3 febrile-ICU studies). Their primary-study sets overlap; the count on this shelf is 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts.
cards.result: The headline is disagreement-plus-weakness, and it must be printed by method and population: tympanic, temporal, axillary and oral readings do not reach clinically acceptable agreement with central temperature where agreement has been pooled properly, and fever detection misses about a third of fevers in the largest synthesis. No card on this shelf implies any thermometer-guided fever-management pathway improves outcomes — this is a measurement shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each synthesis's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Wells score for suspected deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (two related rules, figures never merged): derivation strata of 3% / 17% / 75% in DVT, high-stratum likelihood ratio 5.2 and low-stratum 0.25, and a 1.2% residual DVT probability for 'unlikely' plus negative D-dimer
shelves.question: In adults with suspected deep-vein thrombosis or suspected pulmonary embolism, how well does the Wells score (the two related clinical prediction rules — for DVT: prior VTE, active cancer, immobilisation/paralysis, localised tenderness, whole-leg and calf swelling, pitting oedema, collateral veins, and an alternative diagnosis at least as likely; for PE: the DVT items plus prior PE, tachycardia, haemoptysis and clinical signs of DVT, with PE judged the top diagnosis) stratify the probability of disease — what prevalence did the derivation cohort find in each stratum, what likelihood ratios do the meta-analyses give for the high and low strata in DVT, what happens to the residual probability when an 'unlikely' Wells score is combined with a negative D-dimer in the individual-patient-data meta-analyses of each condition, and how does the score's accuracy compare with the revised Geneva score in PE — including where the two-tier version underperforms the three-tier version?

shelves.balance: The two limbs are different rules sharing a name and an originator; every figure prints with its limb (DVT vs PE) and its version (two-tier vs three-tier) attached, and the limbs are never merged. DVT limb: the 1997 derivation/management cohort (593 outpatients; programme-labelled — the originators' own report) found DVT in 3% of low, 17% of moderate and 75% of high pretest-probability patients — 1997 Canadian outpatient figures, printed with their setting. The 2005 meta-analysis found individual features weak (best rule-in features malignancy, likelihood ratio 2.71, and previous DVT, 2.25 — labelled as likelihood ratios) while the Wells score stratified into high (LR 5.2) and low (LR 0.25) probability groups. The 2014 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (13 studies, 10,002 outpatients) found an unlikely Wells score (≤1) plus a negative D-dimer carried a DVT probability of 1.2% (95% CI 0.7–1.8), a combination occurring in 29% of patients — with the cancer penalty printed beside the headline: in patients with cancer the combination occurred in only 9% and carried a 2.2% probability, and the authors judge it neither safe nor efficient in cancer. The one randomised anchor (1,096 outpatients) tests a D-dimer STRATEGY built on the score, not the score itself: among patients ruled out initially, 3-month confirmed VTE was 0.4% (D-dimer strategy) vs 1.4% (ultrasound-alone control), and D-dimer testing cut ultrasound use from 1.34 to 0.78 tests per patient. PE limb: the 2016 meta-analysis gave Wells a weighted AUC of 0.778 vs revised Geneva 0.693; the 2016 IPD meta-analysis (7,268 patients) found imaging could be withheld in 28% (fixed D-dimer threshold) rising to 33% (age-adjusted), with failure rates below 3% in every subgroup; the 2025 comparative network meta-analysis (40 studies, 37,027 patients) found three-tier Wells and three-tier revised Geneva similar for ruling out PE (negative likelihood ratios 0.34 vs 0.39, labelled as such) while the two-tier Wells underperformed in every aspect (negative LR 0.56). No card on this shelf implies Wells-guided pathways improve outcomes — no anchor tests that.

cards.headline: DVT limb — derivation/management cohort (1997, programme-labelled — the originators' own report): DVT prevalence was 3% in the low, 17% in the moderate and 75% in the high pretest-probability stratum
cards.summary: DVT limb — derivation/management cohort (1997, programme-labelled — the originators' own report): DVT prevalence was 3% in the low, 17% in the moderate and 75% in the high pretest-probability stratum
cards.type: Derivation / management cohort — DVT limb (originators' own report, programme-labelled)
cards.people: 593 consecutive outpatients with suspected deep-vein thrombosis whose pretest probability was calculated with the clinical model (the Wells score), then managed by stratum-specific ultrasound/venography pathways with 3-month follow-up; 95 patients (16.0%) had DVT overall. 1997 Canadian outpatient setting — printed with the figures.
cards.result: DVT was present in 3% of the low stratum (10 of 329), 17% of the moderate stratum (32 of 193) and 75% of the high stratum (53 of 71). Only 3 (0.6%) of the 501 patients diagnosed as not having DVT had thromboembolic events during 3-month follow-up, and only 33 (5.6%) of 593 required venography, with serial testing limited to 166 (28%). The authors concluded management based on clinical probability plus proximal ultrasound is safe and feasible.
cards.watchOut: Derivation-cohort prevalences are 1997 Canadian outpatient figures and print with their setting; they are not transportable probabilities for other settings. This report derives and manages with the same model — it is not an independent validation.
cards.source: Wells PS et al. Value of assessment of pretest probability of deep-vein thrombosis in clinical management. Lancet (London, England). 1997. PMID: 9428249. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DVT limb — meta-analysis (2005): individual clinical features were weak (best rule-in features malignancy, likelihood ratio 2.71, and previous DVT, 2.25), while the Wells score stratified patients into high (likelihood ratio 5.2) and low (likelihood ratio 0.25) probability groups — all figures are likelihood ratios, labelled as such
cards.summary: DVT limb — meta-analysis (2005): individual clinical features were weak (best rule-in features malignancy, likelihood ratio 2.71, and previous DVT, 2.25), while the Wells score stratified patients into high (likelihood ratio 5.2) and low (likelihood ratio 0.25) probability groups — all figures are likelihood ratios, labelled as such
cards.type: Meta-analysis of clinical assessment — DVT limb
cards.people: Meta-analysis of cohort studies (1966 to January 2005, four languages) comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard in suspected DVT; random-effects pooling with meta-regression.
cards.result: Only malignancy (LR 2.71), previous DVT (LR 2.25), recent immobilisation (LR 1.98), calf-diameter difference (LR 1.80) and recent surgery (LR 1.76) were useful for ruling in DVT, and only absence of calf swelling (LR 0.67) or of a calf-diameter difference (LR 0.57) for ruling out. The Wells score was more valuable than any individual characteristic, stratifying into high (LR 5.2), intermediate and low (LR 0.25) probability. The score seemed able to stratify only for proximal DVT and performed better in younger cohorts and cohorts excluding previous thromboembolism. Pooled estimates were subject to substantial heterogeneity, and only published studies were included.
cards.watchOut: Likelihood ratios, not risks — labelled as such wherever printed. Heterogeneity was substantial; the score's performance varied by cohort composition.
cards.source: Goodacre S et al. Meta-analysis: The value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Annals of internal medicine. 2005. PMID: 16027455. cards.headline: DVT limb — individual-patient-data meta-analysis (2014): an unlikely Wells score (≤1) combined with a negative D-dimer was associated with a DVT probability of 1.2% (95% CI 0.7–1.8) — but in patients with cancer the probability was 2.2% and the combination occurred in only 9%, and the authors judge it neither safe nor efficient in cancer
cards.summary: DVT limb — individual-patient-data meta-analysis (2014): an unlikely Wells score (≤1) combined with a negative D-dimer was associated with a DVT probability of 1.2% (95% CI 0.7–1.8) — but in patients with cancer the probability was 2.2% and the combination occurred in only 9%, and the authors judge it neither safe nor efficient in cancer
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis — DVT limb (Wells plus D-dimer exclusion)
cards.people: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis merging 13 study datasets, 10,002 consecutive outpatients with suspected DVT in whom all Wells variables were scored and a reference standard performed; subgroups included cancer, suspected recurrent events, sex, D-dimer assay type and care setting.
cards.result: Increasing Wells scores tracked increasing DVT probability, with estimated probabilities almost twofold higher in patients with cancer, in suspected recurrent events, and (less so) in males. The unlikely-score (≤1) plus negative-D-dimer combination was associated with a 1.2% probability of DVT (95% CI 0.7–1.8) and occurred in 29% (95% CI 20–40) of patients, consistently across assay type, sex and care setting. In cancer patients the same combination occurred in only 9% and carried a 2.2% probability; for suspected recurrent events, only the modified Wells rule (one extra point for the previous event) was safe.
cards.watchOut: The cancer penalty prints beside the headline 1.2% wherever that figure appears. 'Unlikely' here is the ≤1 cut-off of the dichotomised rule — a version label that travels with the figure.
cards.source: Geersing GJ et al. Exclusion of deep vein thrombosis using the Wells rule in clinically important subgroups: individual patient data meta-analysis. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2014. PMID: 24615063. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DVT limb — randomised management trial (2003): tests a D-dimer STRATEGY built on the score, not the score itself — among patients ruled out by the initial strategy, confirmed VTE during 3 months occurred in 0.4% of the D-dimer group vs 1.4% of controls, and D-dimer testing reduced ultrasound use from 1.34 to 0.78 tests per patient
cards.summary: DVT limb — randomised management trial (2003): tests a D-dimer STRATEGY built on the score, not the score itself — among patients ruled out by the initial strategy, confirmed VTE during 3 months occurred in 0.4% of the D-dimer group vs 1.4% of controls, and D-dimer testing reduced ultrasound use from 1.34 to 0.78 tests per patient
cards.type: Randomised management trial — DVT limb (D-dimer strategy built on the Wells categorisation)
cards.people: 1,096 outpatients with suspected lower-extremity DVT, first categorised by the clinical model as likely or unlikely, then randomised to ultrasound imaging alone (530, control) or D-dimer testing (566) with ultrasound omitted when the D-dimer was negative and the patient was clinically unlikely. Overall prevalence of DVT or PE was 15.7%.
cards.result: Among patients in whom DVT was ruled out by the initial strategy, confirmed venous thromboembolic events during 3 months occurred in 2 patients (0.4%, 95% CI 0.05–1.5) in the D-dimer group vs 6 (1.4%, 0.5–2.9) in controls (P = 0.16 — not significant). D-dimer testing significantly reduced ultrasound use (mean 1.34 to 0.78 tests per patient, P = 0.008), and 218 patients (39%) in the D-dimer group required no ultrasound at all.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: this anchor tests a testing strategy, not the score's accuracy, and prints as such. The 0.4% vs 1.4% difference was not statistically significant — never print it as a proven outcome benefit.
cards.source: Wells PS et al. Evaluation of D-dimer in the diagnosis of suspected deep-vein thrombosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 14507948. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PE limb — meta-analysis (2016): for the Wells score, sensitivity ranged 63.8–79.3% and specificity 48.8–90.0% across studies, with weighted AUC 0.778 (95% CI 0.740–0.818), against the revised Geneva score's AUC 0.693 (0.653–0.736)
cards.summary: PE limb — meta-analysis (2016): for the Wells score, sensitivity ranged 63.8–79.3% and specificity 48.8–90.0% across studies, with weighted AUC 0.778 (95% CI 0.740–0.818), against the revised Geneva score's AUC 0.693 (0.653–0.736)
cards.type: Meta-analysis — PE limb (Wells vs revised Geneva accuracy)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies assessing the Wells score and the revised Geneva score for diagnosing suspected pulmonary embolism (searches to April 2015).
cards.result: For the Wells score, sensitivity ranged from 63.8% to 79.3% and specificity from 48.8% to 90.0% across studies; the overall weighted AUC was 0.778 (95% CI 0.740–0.818). For the revised Geneva score, sensitivity ranged 55.3–73.6% and the weighted AUC was 0.693 (0.653–0.736). The confidence intervals did not overlap, and the authors concluded the Wells score was more accurate; meta-regression showed accuracy was not related to PE prevalence, and restricting to prospective studies left the results robust.
cards.watchOut: PE-limb figures only — never merged with the DVT limb. The wide study-level sensitivity/specificity ranges print with the pooled AUC; a single pooled sensitivity/specificity pair for Wells in PE does not exist in this report.

cards.headline: PE limb — IPD meta-analysis (2016): the proportion in whom imaging could be withheld on a PE-unlikely Wells score plus negative D-dimer (efficiency) rose from 28% with a fixed D-dimer threshold to 33% with the age-adjusted threshold, and the 3-month failure rate stayed below 3% in every subgroup examined
cards.summary: PE limb — IPD meta-analysis (2016): the proportion in whom imaging could be withheld on a PE-unlikely Wells score plus negative D-dimer (efficiency) rose from 28% with a fixed D-dimer threshold to 33% with the age-adjusted threshold, and the 3-month failure rate stayed below 3% in every subgroup examined
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis — PE limb (Wells rule plus fixed vs age-adjusted D-dimer)
cards.people: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 6 prospective studies (7,268 patients) in which PE management was guided by the dichotomised Wells rule and quantitative D-dimer testing; subgroups included inpatients, cancer, COPD, previous VTE, delayed presentation and age ≥75.
cards.result: Efficiency (imaging withheld) increased from 28% with the fixed D-dimer threshold (≤500 µg/L) to 33% with the age-adjusted threshold — a 5% absolute increase, more prominent in elderly patients (12%) and less in inpatients (2.6%). The 3-month symptomatic VTE failure rate of the age-adjusted strategy was below 3% in all subgroups examined. Limitations (the authors'): post hoc analysis, between-study differences, various D-dimer assays, and limited power for the failure rate.
cards.watchOut: This is the dichotomised (two-tier) Wells rule used as an exclusion strategy with D-dimer — a different use from the three-tier stratification figures elsewhere on this shelf; the version travels with the figure.

cards.headline: PE limb — comparative network meta-analysis (2025): three-tier Wells and three-tier revised Geneva performed similarly for ruling out PE (negative likelihood ratios 0.34 vs 0.39, labelled as such), while the TWO-tier Wells score underperformed in every aspect (negative likelihood ratio 0.56)
cards.summary: PE limb — comparative network meta-analysis (2025): three-tier Wells and three-tier revised Geneva performed similarly for ruling out PE (negative likelihood ratios 0.34 vs 0.39, labelled as such), while the TWO-tier Wells score underperformed in every aspect (negative likelihood ratio 0.56)
cards.type: Bayesian network meta-analysis — PE limb (comparative accuracy of pre-test probability scores)
cards.people: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 40 studies, 37,027 patients with suspected PE, comparing pre-test clinical probability scores (protocol registered, PROSPERO CRD42023464118; risk of bias by QUADAS-2).
cards.result: Three-tier revised Geneva and three-tier Wells performed similarly for ruling out PE (negative likelihood ratio 0.39, 95% credible interval 0.27–0.58, vs 0.34, 0.25–0.45 — labelled as likelihood ratios). Revised Geneva performed better on imaging utilisation (positive LR 6.65 vs 5.59) and on differentiating D-dimer from imaging pathways (diagnostic odds ratio 8.03 vs 7.40, labelled as such). The two-tier Wells score underperformed in all aspects (negative LR 0.56, 0.45–0.68; positive LR 2.43; DOR 4.41). The authors note revised Geneva's independence from subjective items supports it over three-tier Wells despite the small differences.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the two-tier Wells underperformance prints on this shelf's face — the 2016 IPD exclusion strategy (card 6) uses the two-tier rule WITH D-dimer, which is the context in which it was tested; never cite the two-tier score alone as equivalent to the three-tier.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Wells rules stratify probability in both limbs — DVT exclusion with D-dimer is quantitatively settled except in cancer; in PE the three-tier versions of Wells and Geneva are near-equal and the two-tier Wells is the weak version
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Wells rules stratify probability in both limbs — DVT exclusion with D-dimer is quantitatively settled except in cancer; in PE the three-tier versions of Wells and Geneva are near-equal and the two-tier Wells is the weak version
cards.people: Seven reports: DVT limb — derivation cohort (593), meta-analysis, IPD meta-analysis (10,002) and one randomised D-dimer-strategy trial (1,096); PE limb — two meta-analyses (11 studies; 6 studies / 7,268 patients IPD) and one network meta-analysis (40 studies, 37,027 patients). The limbs share a name and an originator, not a rule.
cards.result: DVT: strata 3% / 17% / 75% at derivation; high-stratum LR 5.2, low-stratum LR 0.25; unlikely-plus-negative-D-dimer residual probability 1.2% overall but 2.2% in cancer, where the strategy is neither safe nor efficient. PE: Wells AUC 0.778 vs Geneva 0.693 (2016 pooling) but three-tier parity for rule-out in 2025 (negative LRs 0.34 vs 0.39), age-adjusted D-dimer raising withholding efficiency from 28% to 33% with failure <3%, and two-tier Wells underperforming throughout (negative LR 0.56). No anchor shows Wells-guided care improving patient outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Prediction accuracy only: no card on this shelf licenses a claim that using the score improves outcomes. Every figure keeps its limb and version label.
