shelves.title: Ankle-brachial index accuracy for peripheral arterial disease: 3 overlapping syntheses — pooled sensitivity 65–75%, specificity 86–89%, and only one eligible primary study in exertional leg pain
shelves.question: In adults with suspected lower-limb peripheral arterial disease, how accurately does the ankle-brachial index (ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure, abnormal at ≤0.90) detect angiographically or duplex-confirmed arterial stenosis — what pooled sensitivity, specificity and AUC do the meta-analyses deliver, and how thin is the eligible primary evidence in exertional leg pain, where the Cochrane review found only one study? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiography · Ankle Brachial Index · Comorbidity · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Peripheral Arterial Disease/diagnosis,physiopathology · Predictive Value of Tests · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. Pooled sensitivity fell from 75% (2013 meta-analysis, 4 studies, 569 patients) to 65% (2025 meta-analysis, 15 studies, 3,460 participants) while specificity held at 86–89% and AUC stayed around 0.86–0.87. In the population with exertional leg pain, the Cochrane review scrutinised 49 studies and found only one eligible study (85 participants, 158 legs). Accuracy differs by method — oscillometric vs hand-held Doppler and operator training — and no figure prints without its method. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf: no card implies ABI screening programmes improve outcomes (the asymptomatic prognostic question is pack #6292, a different question).

cards.headline: ABI synthesis 1 of 3 (Xu 2013, meta-analysis against angiography — 4 studies, 569 patients, 922 limbs): at ABI ≤0.90, pooled sensitivity was 75% and specificity 86%, summary AUC 0.87 and diagnostic odds ratio 15.33 (labelled as such)
cards.summary: ABI synthesis 1 of 3 (Xu 2013, meta-analysis against angiography — 4 studies, 569 patients, 922 limbs): at ABI ≤0.90, pooled sensitivity was 75% and specificity 86%, summary AUC 0.87 and diagnostic odds ratio 15.33 (labelled as such)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (synthesis 1 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Studies of ABI ≤0.90 for peripheral artery disease diagnosis compared with angiography; 4 studies, 569 patients (922 limbs). One of 3 overlapping syntheses on this shelf — labelled as such, never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity 75% and specificity 86% for ABI ≤0.90; area under the summary receiver operating curve 0.87, diagnostic accuracy (Q*) 0.80, diagnostic odds ratio 15.33 (95% CI 9.39 to 25.02), positive likelihood ratio 4.18 and negative likelihood ratio 0.29 (both labelled as such). Significant heterogeneity was evident in pooled sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios, though not in the diagnostic odds ratio.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery; the PubMed record fetched this session gives The Canadian journal of cardiology — the record governs the source line. The oldest and smallest synthesis gives the most favourable sensitivity (75%); the larger 2025 synthesis pools sensitivity at only 65% — do not quote 75% as the settled figure.

cards.headline: ABI synthesis 3 of 3 — Cochrane review in exertional leg pain (Crawford 2016): of 49 studies scrutinised, only one (85 participants, 158 legs) met eligibility; in that study oscillometric ABI gave sensitivity 97% and specificity 89% for significant femoropopliteal disease, against Doppler ABI at 95% / 56% in untrained hands
cards.summary: ABI synthesis 3 of 3 — Cochrane review in exertional leg pain (Crawford 2016): of 49 studies scrutinised, only one (85 participants, 158 legs) met eligibility; in that study oscillometric ABI gave sensitivity 97% and specificity 89% for significant femoropopliteal disease, against Doppler ABI at 95% / 56% in untrained hands
cards.type: Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy review (synthesis 3 of 3; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: Adults presenting with leg pain on walking relieved by rest, in primary care or hospital outpatients, without critical limb ischaemia; reference standard duplex ultrasonography or angiography. 49 studies scrutinised, 48 excluded; one eligible study, 85 participants (158 legs), limb-level data. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort. This record carries no MeSH terms (source line reads 'MeSH: none in the record').
cards.result: Only one study met eligibility and provided limb-level accuracy data. For femoropopliteal stenosis, oscillometric ABI sensitivity was 97% (95% CI 93% to 99%) and specificity 89% (67% to 95%); manual Doppler ABI sensitivity was 95% (89% to 97%) and specificity 56% (33% to 70%), performed by untrained personnel — the lower Doppler specificity was attributed to undetectable pulses in 12 of 27 legs with normal or non-significant vessels. The ABI threshold was not reported in that study. The reviewers conclude the evidence in exertional leg pain is sparse.
cards.watchOut: The near-perfect oscillometric figures come from a single 85-participant study — never present them as pooled ABI performance. Method and operator training move specificity from 56% to 89% in the same study.

shelves.title: Respiratory-rate measurement accuracy — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports (a 49-study systematic review + one 130-patient GP study): five structural sources of inaccuracy, and tachypnoea sensitivity 86% when the rate is counted vs 43% when it is estimated
shelves.question: At the bedside, how accurate is the manually counted respiratory rate — the vital sign that feeds every early-warning score — what five sources of inaccuracy does the quantitative systematic review of 49 studies identify, and how accurate are general practitioners' respiratory-rate assessments in acutely ill patients when the rate is actually counted for a full period versus estimated? (FLOOR-RISK: basis is exactly 2 reports — 1 systematic review of 49 studies + 1 primary study, N = 130 — printed on the face and carried in the stamp line. A results-free device-agreement protocol, PMID 32706740, is excluded from the base.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Hospitalization · Humans · Respiratory Rate
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, per the coordinator's ruling: this shelf's basis is exactly 2 reports — one quantitative systematic review of 49 studies and one primary study — printed here, in the title and in the stamp line; the primary study is carded in two labelled slices, never counted twice. The review (Kallioinen 2021) identifies five sources of inaccuracy in manually measured adult respiratory rate: an awareness effect (being observed artefactually lowers the rate), systematic underscoring with shorter counting periods, substantial inter- and intra-observer variability in either direction, value bias (particular values over-represented, suggesting estimation rather than counting) and widespread recording omission, worse in inpatient than in triage contexts; no single pooled error figure is printed from it. The primary study (Loots 2022, 130 acutely ill adults, 14 Dutch out-of-hours GPs, reference measurement) found GPs counted the rate in only 33 patients (25%); when counted, mean difference 0.27 breaths/min (95% CI −5.7 to 6.3) with tachypnoea (≥22/min) sensitivity 86% (57% to 98%), but when estimated, sensitivity fell to 43% (22% to 66%). One apparent third report (PMID 32706740) is a protocol with recruitment not yet started and no results, and is excluded — the exclusion is stated on the face. This is a measurement shelf: no card implies any counting protocol improves patient outcomes.

cards.headline: Systematic review (Kallioinen 2021, Journal of Advanced Nursing — quantitative systematic review of 49 studies of manually measured adult respiratory rate): five sources of inaccuracy identified — an awareness effect (being observed artefactually lowers the rate), systematic underscoring with shorter counting periods, substantial inter- and intra-observer variability in either direction, value bias (particular values over-represented, suggesting estimation rather than counting) and widespread recording omission, worse in inpatient than in triage/admission contexts
cards.summary: Systematic review (Kallioinen 2021, Journal of Advanced Nursing — quantitative systematic review of 49 studies of manually measured adult respiratory rate): five sources of inaccuracy identified — an awareness effect (being observed artefactually lowers the rate), systematic underscoring with shorter counting periods, substantial inter- and intra-observer variability in either direction, value bias (particular values over-represented, suggesting estimation rather than counting) and widespread recording omission, worse in inpatient than in triage/admission contexts
cards.type: Quantitative systematic review of 49 studies (report 1 of exactly 2 on this FLOOR-RISK shelf)
cards.people: Adults whose respiratory rate was manually measured in the 49 primary studies included in this quantitative systematic review (searched Medline, CINAHL and Cochrane Library to 31 July 2019). One of exactly 2 reports on this FLOOR-RISK shelf — a synthesis of 49 studies, not 49 independent reports carded here.
cards.result: Included studies (N = 49) identified five sources of inaccuracy. The awareness effect creates an artefactual reduction in actual respiratory rate, and observation methods involving shorter counts cause systematic underscoring. Individual measurements can differ substantially in either direction between observations due to inter- or intra-observer variability. Value bias, where particular respiratory rates are over-represented (suggesting estimation), is a widespread problem. Recording omission is also widespread, with higher average rates in inpatient versus triage/admission contexts. The authors advise counting rather than estimating, 60-second counts whenever possible, measuring without the patient's awareness, and documenting the value. No single pooled error figure is printed from this review — the row's flag binds: its sources are qualitative-quantitative syntheses of heterogeneous primary studies.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports (this systematic review of 49 studies + 1 primary study) — printed here, in the title, the balance and the stamp. The five sources are a synthesis of heterogeneous primary studies; no card prints a single pooled error from them, and no card implies any counting protocol improves patient outcomes — this is a measurement shelf.

cards.summary: Primary study, labelled slice 1 of 2 of the SAME report (Loots 2022, BJGP Open — 130 acutely ill adults on out-of-hours home visits by 14 GPs in the Netherlands, against a reference measurement): GPs actually counted the respiratory rate in only 33 patients (25%); when counted, the mean difference from the reference was just 0.27 breaths per minute (95% CI −5.7 to 6.3) and sensitivity for tachypnoea at ≥22/min was 86% (95% CI 57% to 98%)
cards.type: Observational mixed-methods primary study — labelled slice 1 of 2 (counted-measurement limb) of 1 report; NOT an independent second primary study
cards.people: 130 acutely ill adult patients seen on out-of-hours home visits at three GP cooperatives in the Netherlands, observed across 14 GPs, with the GP-assessed rate compared against a reference measurement; semi-structured interviews accompanied the observations. Labelled slice 1 of 2 of this one report — the counted-measurement limb. This record carries no MeSH in PubMed; its source line says so, and the shelf's top-level MeSH is taken from the review card.
cards.result: Observations of 130 acutely ill patients were included. In 33 patients (25%) the GP counted the respiratory rate. A mean difference of 0.27 breaths per minute (95% CI −5.7 to 6.3) with the reference measurement was found. At a cut-off of ≥22 breaths per minute, sensitivity was 86% (95% CI 57% to 98%) when the GP counted the rate. The near-zero mean difference sits inside wide limits (the interval spans −5.7 to +6.3 breaths per minute), so average accuracy coexists with substantial individual-measurement spread — the review card's variability source made concrete.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports on this shelf. This is one labelled slice of the single primary study (N = 130), never a second primary study. The setting is Dutch out-of-hours GP home visits — the counted-accuracy figure does not transport automatically to ward or emergency-department counting.

cards.headline: Primary study, labelled slice 2 of 2 of the SAME report (Loots 2022, BJGP Open — same 130 patients, same 14 GPs): when the rate was NOT counted but estimated, sensitivity for tachypnoea at ≥22/min fell to 43% (95% CI 22% to 66%) — the counted-vs-estimated contrast (86% vs 43%) is this shelf's headline, and GPs gave both medical and practical reasons for not routinely measuring the rate

cards.type: Observational mixed-methods primary study — labelled slice 2 of 2 (estimated-measurement limb) of 1 report; NOT an independent report
cards.people: The same 130 acutely ill adults and 14 GPs as slice 1: in the 75% of patients whose rate was not counted, GPs were asked to estimate the rate, dichotomised as ≥22 or <22 breaths per minute, against the same reference measurement. Labelled slice 2 of 2 of this one report — the estimation/feasibility limb.
cards.result: When GPs estimated respiratory rates, sensitivity at the ≥22 breaths-per-minute cut-off was 43% (95% CI 22% to 66%) — against 86% (57% to 98%) when counted, in the same study. GPs reported both medical and practical reasons for not routinely measuring the respiratory rate, while remaining aware of its importance in acutely ill adults; the authors conclude counted measurements are accurate, but in most patients the rate was not counted and was often underestimated when estimated.
cards.watchOut: The 86% vs 43% contrast is within one study of 130 patients and its confidence intervals are wide and overlapping at their edges (57–98% vs 22–66%) — printed with those intervals wherever the contrast appears. Excluded from this shelf's base, as the row directs: PMID 32706740, a device-agreement study whose PubMed record is a protocol with recruitment not yet started and no results — excluded, and the exclusion is stated here on the face.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports (1 quantitative systematic review of 49 studies + 1 primary study of 130 patients, carded in two labelled slices): manually counted respiratory rate is accurate on average when it is actually counted for a full period (mean difference 0.27 breaths/min; tachypnoea sensitivity 86%), but in ordinary practice it is usually not counted at all, and estimation halves tachypnoea sensitivity (43%) — while the review documents five structural sources of inaccuracy (awareness effect, short-count underscoring, observer variability, value bias, recording omission)

The results-free protocol PMID 32706740 is excluded from the base, as stated on slice 2.
cards.result: The measurement, not any treatment, is the subject: respiratory rate feeds every early-warning score, so its inaccuracy propagates into MEWS/NEWS-type scores (cross-point: the MEWS shelf #7824 and the built NEWS territory use this same vital sign as an input). No card on this shelf claims any counting protocol improves patient outcomes.

shelves.title: Total serum IgE distribution in healthy non-atopic adults (PHYS, 4 datasets, 1984–2001 PRIST/CAP era): geometric means 12.1–43.7 across populations, 95% range up to 3.2–602.5 kU/L — population- and assay-dependent, no single normal figure
shelves.question: What is the distribution of total serum IgE in healthy non-atopic adults — what geometric mean and upper reference limit do the population datasets report, and how wide is the spread between populations and between men and women? (PHYSIOLOGY: 1984–2001 PRIST/CAP assay era prints on the face; values are log-normally distributed, so geometric means print.)

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four population datasets, 1984–2001, spanning PRIST- and CAP-era methods — the assay era prints on the face, because absolute values are not interchangeable across assay generations and each dataset's value prints with its method era and population. The distribution is wide and log-normal (geometric means print, never arithmetic): a 1984 Canadian reference group (from 1,814 rural white adults; reference-group N not documented in the abstract) had mean IgE 12.1 U/mL with an upper normal limit of 87.3 U/mL; non-atopic Greek adults (1,187) had geometric means of 38 IU/mL (men) and 29.3 IU/mL (women); Italian 'normals' (558 of 1,905, a mixed-age dataset whose adult stratum is the limb used here) had adult geometric means of 29 kU/L (men) and 19 kU/L (women); and 542 non-atopic young Kuwaiti adults (CAP assay) had a geometric mean of 43.7 kU/L with a 95% range of 3.2–602.5 kU/L. The width of the distribution is the content: no single 'normal IgE' figure is printed. Atopy definitions differ across datasets (questionnaire/history, prick, skin-test based) and print. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (population- and assay-dependence of the distribution).

cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 4 (Holford-Strevens 1984, Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology — 1,814 rural white Canadian adults aged 20–65, PRIST assay): in the non-allergic reference group (positive skin reactions, allergic history and smoking excluded — its own N is not separately documented in the abstract), the mean total IgE was 12.1 U/mL and the upper limit of the normal range was estimated at 87.3 U/mL
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — total serum IgE reference values, PRIST era (dataset 1 of 4)
cards.people: 1,814 white, rural Canadian adults aged 20–65 who had allergy skin testing and total IgE measured by the PRIST method; the reference group was derived by excluding subjects with positive allergic skin reactions, a history of allergic disorders, and smoking — the reference group's own size is not documented in the abstract and prints as such. A 1984 PRIST-era dataset — the assay era prints on the face.
cards.result: The mean level of total IgE in the reference group was 12.1 U/ml. The upper limit of the normal range was estimated at 87.3 U/ml. IgE levels did not differ between the sexes or with age in this adult population.
cards.watchOut: 1984 PRIST-era values are not interchangeable with later assay generations. The reference-group N is not documented in the abstract — no N is imported for it; the documented denominator is the 1,814 studied.

cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 4 (Grigoreas 1993, Allergy — 1,187 Greek adults aged 20–60, Phadebas PRIST): geometric mean IgE in non-atopic subjects was 38 IU/mL in men and 29.3 IU/mL in women (atopic: 120.5 IU/mL in men and 99.8 IU/mL in women, as fetched from the record)
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 4 (Grigoreas 1993, Allergy — 1,187 Greek adults aged 20–60, Phadebas PRIST): geometric mean IgE in non-atopic subjects was 38 IU/mL in men and 29.3 IU/mL in women (atopic: 120.5 IU/mL in men and 99.8 IU/mL in women, as fetched from the record)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — total serum IgE by atopy and sex, PRIST era (dataset 2 of 4)
cards.people: 1,187 randomly stratified Greek subjects (793 men, 394 women) aged 20–60, classified atopic (257 men, 118 women) or non-atopic (536 men, 276 women) by skin prick testing with aeroallergens; total IgE by Phadebas PRIST, presented as geometric means. A 1993 PRIST-era dataset — the era prints on the face.
cards.result: At any age, atopic males (120.5 vs 38 IU/ml) and females (99.8 vs 29.3 IU/ml) had higher mean IgE than non-atopic subjects (P < 0.0001). In the non-atopic sample, IgE did not differ with age (P > 0.05), and non-atopic males (38 IU/ml) had higher levels than non-atopic females (29.3 IU/ml) (P < 0.05). The authors note Greek adults had higher IgE than populations from other nations in the comparisons available to them.
cards.watchOut: Atopy here is skin-prick-defined; definitions differ across the four datasets (history/skin test, prick testing, symptom-plus-skin-test, CAP screening) and print with each value. Geometric means only — IgE is log-normally distributed and no arithmetic mean is printed as a distribution centre.

cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 4 (Simoni 2001, European Journal of Epidemiology — 1,905 residents of the Po River Delta, Italy, aged 8–73, PRIST assay): among 558 'normals' (no respiratory symptoms, negative skin tests, non-current smokers), adult geometric mean IgE was 29 kU/L in men and 19 kU/L in women
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 4 (Simoni 2001, European Journal of Epidemiology — 1,905 residents of the Po River Delta, Italy, aged 8–73, PRIST assay): among 558 'normals' (no respiratory symptoms, negative skin tests, non-current smokers), adult geometric mean IgE was 29 kU/L in men and 19 kU/L in women
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — total serum IgE reference values, PRIST era (dataset 3 of 4)
cards.people: 1,905 residents of the Po Delta area (near Venice) aged 8–78 as titled (8–73 as abstracted), with total serum IgE by PRIST; 'normals' (N = 558) had no asthma or asthmatic/rhinitic symptoms, were non-current smokers and skin prick-test negative. The adult values are this shelf's limb; the dataset's child-adolescent geometric mean (45 kU/L) is context, not an adult figure.
cards.result: In normal adults the geometric mean was 29 kU/L (SD 3.3; 95% CI 25–40) in males and 19 kU/L (SD 3.8; 95% CI 16–22) in females; in normal children-adolescents it was 45 kU/L (95% CI 38–63). The diagnostic sensitivity of the IgE test was low while specificity was very high. The authors conclude separate total serum IgE reference values are necessary by age (children-adolescents vs adults) and, in adults, by sex.
cards.watchOut: A mixed-age dataset (8–73): only its adult stratum anchors this shelf's adult question, flagged here as in the balance. PRIST-era values; not interchangeable across assay generations.

cards.headline: Dataset 4 of 4 (Ezeamuzie 1999, Clinical and Experimental Allergy — 542 non-atopic healthy young adults in Kuwait, CAP assay): geometric mean total IgE was 43.7 kU/L with a 95% reference range of 3.2–602.5 kU/L — the width of the distribution is this dataset's content
cards.summary: Dataset 4 of 4 (Ezeamuzie 1999, Clinical and Experimental Allergy — 542 non-atopic healthy young adults in Kuwait, CAP assay): geometric mean total IgE was 43.7 kU/L with a 95% reference range of 3.2–602.5 kU/L — the width of the distribution is this dataset's content
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — total serum IgE reference values, CAP era (dataset 4 of 4)
cards.people: 542 randomly selected Phadiatop-negative (non-atopic) young adults aged 18–50 (mean 28.9 years; male:female ratio 1.3), drawn from 1,057 screened young adults in Kuwait (atopy detected in 423, 40.0%); total IgE by the Pharmacia CAP method. A 1999 CAP-era dataset — the assay generation differs from the three PRIST datasets and prints on the face.
cards.result: Total serum IgE in non-atopics covered a very wide range (<2–1993 kU/L) with a geometric mean of 43.7 kU/L. The reference range (95% CI of log IgE) was 3.2–602.5 kU/L; the 90% CI was 11.7–162 kU/L. The geometric mean was significantly higher in males than females (53.7 vs 35.5 kU/L, P < 0.001) and in smokers than non-smokers (64.6 vs 40.7 kU/L, P < 0.01), and was independent of age. Despite significantly lower geometric means in non-atopics than in asymptomatic atopics (213.8 kU/L) and allergic asthmatics (626.6 kU/L), the 95% ranges of the three groups overlapped considerably.
cards.watchOut: No single 'normal IgE' figure may be printed from this shelf: this dataset's own 95% range spans two orders of magnitude (3.2–602.5 kU/L), and its group ranges overlap the atopic groups' — a distribution statement, not a diagnostic cut-off.

shelves.title: Platelet indices reference intervals in healthy adults (PHYS, 4 datasets): MPV intervals are analyser-bound — 7.2–11.7 fL (CELL-DYN) vs 9.6–13.1 and 9.20–13.30 fL (Sysmex) — never a single merged range
shelves.question: What are the reference intervals for the platelet indices — mean platelet volume (MPV), platelet distribution width and the immature platelet fraction — in healthy adults, and how much do the intervals move with the analyser used to derive them? (PHYSIOLOGY: each interval prints with its named analyser and population; no merged interval.)

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Analyser dependence is the headline, not a caveat: the MPV lower reference limit moves from 7.2 fL (CELL-DYN 3700 SL, Turkish cohort — final healthy N = 326 after screening 2,298, printed as the final N) to 9.6 fL (Sysmex XE-5000, Danish GESUS, N = 1,674) and 9.20 fL (Sysmex XE-2100, Chinese Han, N = 4,642, with significant regional differences and the published interval excluding Chengdu), with ELSA-Brasil (N = 580; analyser not named in the abstract) at 8.9–11.8 fL. Each interval prints with its named analyser (specific tested platforms named per the standing product rule) and population, and no merged MPV interval is printed. The immature platelet fraction interval (1.3–9.0%) rests on the Danish dataset alone. EDTA dwell time artefactually raises MPV and is uncontrolled in several datasets, which prints. The platelet-count values inside these datasets are background to the built platelet-count physiology and are not re-presented as new. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the existence and analyser-dependence of the intervals; values never transport across platforms.

cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 4 (Demirin 2011, Thrombosis Research — Turkish healthy volunteers; of 2,298 screened subjects, 326 met the final healthy-cohort criteria): on the CELL-DYN 3700 SL analyser MPV was 8.9 ± 1.4 fL with 95% of individuals between 7.2 and 11.7 fL
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — MPV reference range, CELL-DYN 3700 SL (dataset 1 of 4)
cards.people: 2,298 Turkish adults (mean age 50, range 18–92) screened with stepwise exclusions (smoking, diabetes, hypertension, coronary disease, dyslipidemia, COPD, cancer, chronic drug use including antiplatelets, heavy drinking, metabolic syndrome, low ejection fraction, raised creatinine, abnormal liver tests or TSH); 326 participants (204 women, 122 men; mean age 41 ± 16) constituted the final healthy cohort — the final N prints, not the screened N. Complete blood counts on a CELL-DYN 3700 SL analyser (Abbott Diagnostics) within 6 hours — the named analyser prints with the interval.
cards.result: Mean MPV of the final healthy cohort was 8.9 ± 1.4 fL, with no significant difference among age groups. Ninety-five percent of individuals had an MPV between 7.2 and 11.7 fL. The authors advise that a patient with an MPV beyond this range be evaluated carefully, especially for occlusive arterial diseases — an authors' interpretive remark, printed as such, not a validated action threshold.
cards.watchOut: The documented interval belongs to the CELL-DYN platform and this heavily screened cohort (326 of 2,298 screened): it does not transport to Sysmex platforms, whose lower limits on this shelf are 9.2–9.6 fL. EDTA dwell time artefactually raises MPV and is uncontrolled across datasets — the fetched record here specifies counting within 6 hours.
cards.source: Demirin H et al. Normal range of mean platelet volume in healthy subjects: Insight from a large epidemiologic study. Thrombosis research. 2011. PMID: 21620440. cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 4 (Joergensen 2016, Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation — Danish general-population cohort (GESUS), 1,674 healthy individuals, Sysmex XE-5000): MPV reference interval 9.6–13.1 fL and immature platelet fraction 1.3–9.0% — with no significant age, sex or smoking-status difference
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 4 (Joergensen 2016, Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation — Danish general-population cohort (GESUS), 1,674 healthy individuals, Sysmex XE-5000): MPV reference interval 9.6–13.1 fL and immature platelet fraction 1.3–9.0% — with no significant age, sex or smoking-status difference
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — MPV and IPF reference intervals, Sysmex XE-5000 (dataset 2 of 4)
cards.people: 1,674 apparently healthy individuals (910 women, 764 men) from the Danish General Suburban Population Study, with MPV and immature platelet fraction (IPF) measured on a Sysmex XE-5000 hematology analyser and reference intervals established non-parametrically — the named analyser prints with the interval.
cards.result: The reference interval was 9.6–13.1 fL for MPV and 1.3–9.0% for IPF. No significant age, sex or smoking-status difference was observed; the authors describe both parameters as remarkably stable across age, sex and smoking status in this population.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's only IPF interval — a single-platform, single-population figure, printed as such. Its MPV lower limit (9.6 fL) sits above the CELL-DYN dataset's entire mean: platform, not biology, is the first explanation for interval differences on this shelf.

cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 4 (Hong 2015, Journal of Clinical Laboratory Analysis — 4,642 healthy Chinese Han adults, Sysmex XE-2100): MPV reference interval 9.20–13.30 fL and platelet count 127–341 ×10⁹/L, with significant regional differences across China for all platelet indices
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 4 (Hong 2015, Journal of Clinical Laboratory Analysis — 4,642 healthy Chinese Han adults, Sysmex XE-2100): MPV reference interval 9.20–13.30 fL and platelet count 127–341 ×10⁹/L, with significant regional differences across China for all platelet indices
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — platelet-index reference intervals, Sysmex XE-2100 (dataset 3 of 4)
cards.people: 4,642 healthy Chinese Han volunteers (mean age 43) recruited from six regions of China, with platelet indices measured on Sysmex XE-2100 hematology analysers whose traceability was verified — the named analyser prints with the interval. The published intervals exclude the Chengdu reference people, whose values differed (lowest counts, highest MPV/PDW/P-LCR), as the abstract states.
cards.result: There were significant region-based differences for all platelet indices. Excluding Chengdu, the derived reference intervals were: platelet count 127–341 ×10⁹/L; MPV 9.20–13.30 fL; PDW 9.90–19.00%; platelet-large cell ratio 18.10–52.00%; plateletcrit 16.00–41.00% (all as published). The authors conclude region-specific reference intervals are essential.
cards.watchOut: The headline interval is a five-region interval with Chengdu excluded by the authors — printing it as 'the Chinese interval' without that exclusion misstates the dataset. This shelf's only PDW interval set, printed as published (in % in this record).
cards.source: Hong J et al. Investigation on reference intervals and regional differences of platelet indices in healthy Chinese Han adults. Journal of clinical laboratory analysis. 2015. PMID: 24390860. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dataset 4 of 4 (Maluf 2015, Platelets — ELSA-Brasil, 580 healthy participants free of the cohort's major diseases; the cohort's analyser is not named in the abstract): MPV reference interval 8.9–11.8 fL, PDW 9.6–15.3 fL and platelet-large cell ratio 15.6–39.5% as published
cards.summary: Dataset 4 of 4 (Maluf 2015, Platelets — ELSA-Brasil, 580 healthy participants free of the cohort's major diseases; the cohort's analyser is not named in the abstract): MPV reference interval 8.9–11.8 fL, PDW 9.6–15.3 fL and platelet-large cell ratio 15.6–39.5% as published
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — platelet volume index reference intervals, ELSA-Brasil (dataset 4 of 4)
cards.people: 580 individuals (of an initial 3,115) constituting the ELSA-Brasil healthy reference sample: blood count within 2 hours of collection, no continuous medication, self-rated good/very good health, no diabetes or hypertension diagnosis, non-smoking, no metabolic syndrome, BMI <30 kg/m² and platelet/haemoglobin/creatinine within reference values. The 2-hour counting window prints — EDTA dwell time raises MPV artefactually.
cards.result: The reference intervals were: MPV 8.9–11.8 fL; PDW 9.6–15.3 fL; platelet-large cell ratio 15.6–39.5% (units as published). The parameters were not significantly affected by age, gender, smoking, obesity or alcohol abuse in this sample, but significant differences were found among self-rated race/color groups.
cards.watchOut: The analyser is not named in this record's abstract — no platform is imported for this dataset, and its interval therefore cannot be assigned to a platform family. PDW prints here in fL as published, against % in the Chinese dataset: the two PDW expressions are not merged.

cards.headline: Synthesis: platelet-index reference intervals are analyser- and population-bound — MPV 7.2–11.7 fL on CELL-DYN (screened Turkish cohort, final N = 326), 9.6–13.1 fL on Sysmex XE-5000 (Danish, N = 1,674, with the shelf's only IPF interval, 1.3–9.0%), 9.20–13.30 fL on Sysmex XE-2100 (Chinese Han, N = 4,642, Chengdu excluded, with PDW 9.90–19.00%), and 8.9–11.8 fL in ELSA-Brasil (N = 580, analyser not named in the abstract) — the MPV lower limit moves from 7.2 fL to 9.2–9.6 fL across platforms, and no merged MPV interval is printed
cards.summary: Synthesis: platelet-index reference intervals are analyser- and population-bound — MPV 7.2–11.7 fL on CELL-DYN (screened Turkish cohort, final N = 326), 9.6–13.1 fL on Sysmex XE-5000 (Danish, N = 1,674, with the shelf's only IPF interval, 1.3–9.0%), 9.20–13.30 fL on Sysmex XE-2100 (Chinese Han, N = 4,642, Chengdu excluded, with PDW 9.90–19.00%), and 8.9–11.8 fL in ELSA-Brasil (N = 580, analyser not named in the abstract) — the MPV lower limit moves from 7.2 fL to 9.2–9.6 fL across platforms, and no merged MPV interval is printed
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: Demirin 2011, Joergensen 2016, Hong 2015 and Maluf 2015. The platelet-count values inside these datasets are background only — the built platelet-count physiology territory is not re-presented here; the indices (MPV / PDW / IPF) are this shelf's question.
cards.result: PHYSIOLOGY framing only — no intervention stamp applies. EDTA dwell time artefactually raises MPV and is uncontrolled in several datasets; intervals transport only with their named analyser and population.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
